hi.inOneMinute: A standard form contract is a contract whose terms are printed or written in advance by one party (usually a big company, the State or a service provider) and offered to everyone on a "take it or leave it" basis. The other party cannot bargain; he can only sign, click or take the ticket. Railway and bus tickets, insurance policies, bank forms, courier consignment notes, dry-cleaning bills, builder-buyer agreements and website "I agree" terms are all standard forms. In the USA they are called "contracts of adhesion" ( LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre ). Such contracts save time, but they are often used to slip in exemption clauses that cut down the stronger party's liability. The law protects the weaker party in five ways: Notice. A printed term binds only if reasonable notice of it was given before or at the time of the contract ( Parker ; Olley ; Thornton ). A mere receipt is not a contract document ( Chapelton ). Signature. A person who signs a document is normally bound by it, read or not ( L'Estrange v. Graucob ; Bharathi Knitting v. DHL ). Strict reading. An unclear term is read against the party who drafted it ( contra proferentem ). Unfair terms. Courts will not enforce an unfair and unreasonable clause imposed by a party with superior bargaining power; such a clause can be void under Section 23 as opposed to public policy ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ; Lilly White ). A clause barring the usual legal proceedings is void under Section 28 . Consumer law. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the State and National Commissions can declare an unfair contract term null and void (Sections 2(46), 49(2), 59(2)); Pioneer v. Govindan Raghavan applied this to a builder's one-sided agreement. Online terms accepted by clicking "I agree" are standard forms too; such contracts are valid under Section 10A of the IT Act, and the same protections apply. In the exam, define, give examples, then explain each protection with a case. In real life, this tells you when the "terms and conditions" on a bill, ticket or website really bind you.
legalProvision: There is no single section on standard form contracts . The rules come from case law and these provisions.

Section 23, Indian Contract Act, 1872. What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not. The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless— it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent ; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy. In each of these cases, the consideration or object of an agreement is said to be unlawful. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.

Section 28, Indian Contract Act, 1872 (main part). Agreements in restraint of legal proceedings, void. Every agreement,— (a) by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights; or (b) which extinguishes the rights of any party thereto, or discharges any party thereto, from any liability, under or in respect of any contract on the expiry of a specified period so as to restrict any party from enforcing his rights, is void to the extent.

Section 10A, Information Technology Act, 2000. Validity of contracts formed through electronic means. Where in a contract formation, the communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, the revocation of proposals and acceptances, as the case may be, are expressed in electronic form or by means of an electronic records, such contract shall not be deemed to be unenforceable solely on the ground that such electronic form or means was used for that purpose.

Section 2(46), Consumer Protection Act, 2019. "unfair contract" means a contract between a manufacturer or trader or service provider on one hand, and a consumer on the other, having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer, including the following, namely:— (i) requiring manifestly excessive security deposits to be given by a consumer for the performance of contractual obligations; or (ii) imposing any penalty on the consumer, for the breach of contract thereof which is wholly disproportionate to the loss occurred due to such breach to the other party to the contract; or (iii) refusing to accept early repayment of debts on payment of applicable penalty; or (iv) entitling a party to the contract to terminate such contract unilaterally, without reasonable cause; or (v) permitting or has the effect of permitting one party to assign the contract to the detriment of the other party who is a consumer, without his consent; or (vi) imposing on the consumer any unreasonable charge, obligation or condition which puts such consumer to disadvantage;

Section 49(2), Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1), the State Commission may also declare any terms of contract, which is unfair to any consumer, to be null and void.

Section 59(2), Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Without prejudice to sub-section (1), the National Commission may also declare any terms of contract, which is unfair to any consumer to be null and void.
In simple words

Section 23: an agreement (or a clause) whose object is opposed to public policy is void . The Supreme Court used this to strike down an unfair clause in a standard form ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ). Section 28: a clause that stops a party from going to court at all, or cuts down the time for suing, is void to that extent . Arbitration clauses are saved by the exceptions to the section. Section 10A, IT Act: a contract is not invalid merely because the offer and acceptance were made electronically , for example by clicking "I agree". Section 2(46), CPA 2019: an unfair contract is a contract between a trader or service provider and a consumer with terms that significantly change the consumer's rights , such as excessive deposits, disproportionate penalties or one-sided termination. Sections 49(2) and 59(2), CPA 2019: the State Commission and the National Commission can declare an unfair term null and void . A complaint that an unfair contract has been adopted is a "complaint" under Section 2(6)(i); such complaints go to the State Commission (consideration up to ₹10 crore, Section 47(1)(a)(ii)) or the National Commission (above ₹10 crore, Section 58(1)(a)(ii)).
hi.meaning: What a standard form contract is A standard form contract is a contract in which: the terms are drafted in advance by one party , usually in print or on a screen; the same terms are offered to every customer ; the other party has no real chance to bargain ; he must accept the whole form or go without the goods or service. The Supreme Court described the position in LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995): "In dotted line contracts there would be no occasion for a weaker party to bargain or to assume to have equal bargaining power. He has either to accept or leave the services or goods in terms of the dotted line contract." Other names Contract of adhesion: "In USA, the standard forms of contracts are called 'Contracts of Adhesion'" ( LIC ). The weaker party merely "adheres" to terms set by the other. Dotted line contract: the customer only signs "on the dotted line" ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ; Pioneer ). E-contracts: online standard forms. In a click-wrap contract the user clicks "I agree" after the terms are shown; in a browse-wrap contract the terms are only on a link and the site says that using it means accepting them; in a shrink-wrap contract the terms come inside the package of a product such as software. Why they are used, and the danger Advantages Dangers Saves time when thousands of similar contracts are made (railways, insurance, banks) The customer usually does not read the small print Same terms for everyone; easy to administer The drafter can insert exemption clauses limiting his liability Lower cost of each transaction Unequal bargaining power: "take it or leave it" Running example Priya gives a silk saree worth ₹12,000 to Sparkle Dry Cleaners for cleaning. She pays ₹300 and gets a printed bill. On the back, in small print: "Liability for loss or damage is limited to 10 times the cleaning charge." The saree is lost. Under the clause, Sparkle would pay only ₹3,000 (10 × ₹300), and Priya would lose ₹9,000 (₹12,000 − ₹3,000). Below we test whether the clause binds her.
keyPoints: Standard form: terms drafted by one party; "take it or leave it"; "contracts of adhesion" ( LIC ). Unsigned terms bind only with reasonable notice ( Parker ). Notice must be before or at the time of contract ( Olley ; Thornton ). A mere receipt is not a contract document ( Chapelton ). Signed terms bind, read or not ( L'Estrange ; Bharathi Knitting ). Contra proferentem : unclear terms read against the drafter. Unfair clause between unequal parties is void under Section 23 ( Brojo Nath Ganguly ). Clause barring courts is void under Section 28 ; arbitration saved. CPA 2019: State and National Commissions may declare unfair terms null and void (Sections 49(2), 59(2)); Pioneer . Click-wrap contracts are valid (IT Act, Section 10A).

caseLaws.name: Parker v
caseLaws.facts: South Eastern Railway Co. (1877) Facts. Parker left a bag in a railway cloakroom, paid 2d and received a ticket whose back limited the company's liability to £10. The bag was lost. Principle. An unsigned ticket's conditions bind if the company gave reasonable notice of them, even if the customer did not read them. (1877) 2 CPD 416 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on the reasonable notice test. L'Estrange v. F. Graucob Ltd. (1934) Facts. A café owner signed an order form for a slot machine; small print excluded all warranties. The machine did not work. Principle. A person who signs a contractual document is bound by it, whether or not he has read it. [1934] 2 KB 394. Why it matters. It is the leading case on signed standard forms . Lilly White v. R. Munuswami (1964) Facts. A customer's new saree (Rs. 220) was lost by a dry cleaner whose bill limited liability to 50% of the market price. Principle. Such a term "cannot be enforced by a court, merely, because it is printed on the reverse of a bill." AIR 1966 Mad 13 (Madras High Court). Why it matters. It is the Indian authority against unreasonable printed exemption clauses . Bharathi Knitting Co. v. DHL Worldwide Express Courier (1996) Facts. The sender signed a courier consignment note limiting the courier's liability to US$100. Principle. "When there is a specific term in the contract, the parties are bound by the terms in the contract." (1996) 4 SCC 704. Why it matters. It applies the signature rule in India. Central Inland Water Transport Corporation v. Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986) Facts. A Government company's service rule let it terminate permanent employees on three months' notice or pay, without reasons. Ganguly's services were terminated under it on 26 February 1983. Principle. The Courts will "strike down an unfair and unreasonable contract, or an unfair and unreasonable clause in a contract, entered into between parties who are not equal in bargaining power"; such a clause is void under Section 23. AIR 1986 SC 1571 : (1986) 3 SCC 156. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian case on unconscionable terms in standard forms . LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) Facts. LIC's term insurance policy under Table 58 was offered only to persons in Government, quasi-Government or reputed commercial firms. The condition was challenged as discriminatory. Principle. "In dotted line contracts there would be no occasion for a weaker party to bargain"; the restricting clause was unconstitutional and severable, and LIC's terms must be reasonable, just and fair. AIR 1995 SC 1811 : (1995) 5 SCC 482. Why it matters. It explains standard form ("adhesion") contracts and the weaker party's lack of choice. Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan (2019) Facts. A builder's agreement charged the buyer 18% interest a year for delayed payments but gave the buyer only 9% a year for the builder's delay in possession. Principle. "A term of a contract will not be final and binding if it is shown that the flat purchasers had no option but to sign on the dotted line, on a contract framed by the builder." [2019] 5 SCR 1169. Why it matters. It applies the protection against one-sided standard forms to consumer contracts .

selfTest.q: 1. What is a "contract of adhesion"?
selfTest.a: The American name for a standard form contract, where the weaker party only adheres to terms set by the other ( LIC ).

selfTest.q: 2. Why was the hotel not protected in Olley?
selfTest.a: The notice was in the bedroom, seen after the contract was made at the reception desk.

selfTest.q: 3. Why was the sender bound in Bharathi Knitting?
selfTest.a: He signed the consignment note containing the US$100 limit.

selfTest.q: 4. Under which section did the Supreme Court strike down Rule 9(i) in Brojo Nath Ganguly?
selfTest.a: Section 23, as opposed to public policy.

selfTest.q: 5. Which Commissions can declare an unfair contract term null and void under the CPA 2019?
selfTest.a: The State Commission (Section 49(2)) and the National Commission (Section 59(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. Which section of the IT Act makes click-wrap contracts valid?
selfTest.a: Section 10A.

law-of-contract-i-u1-t3.subtitle: Sections 2(b), 7, 8 and 9 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Acceptance is the "yes" that turns an offer into a promise. Under Section 2(b), when the person to whom a proposal is made signifies his assent to it, the proposal is accepted, and a proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise . To be valid, the acceptance must be absolute and unqualified , expressed in a usual and reasonable manner or in the manner the offer prescribes (Section 7), communicated to the offeror, and given by the offeree while the offer is still open . Acceptance may be by words or by conduct , including by performing the conditions of the offer (Sections 8, 9). Silence is not acceptance. In exams, marks come from the definition, Section 7 quoted, each essential with a case ( Hyde v. Wrench , Felthouse v. Bindley , Carlill , Powell v. Lee , Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar ), and the counter-offer rule. In real life, it tells you whether your reply closed the deal or only opened a new round of bargaining.
legalProvision: Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;

Section 7. Acceptance must be absolute. In order to convert a proposal into a promise, the acceptance must— (1) be absolute and unqualified; (2) be expressed in some usual and reasonable manner, unless the proposal prescribes the manner in which it is to be accepted. If the proposal prescribes a manner in which it is to be accepted, and the acceptance is not made in such manner, the proposer may, within a reasonable time after the acceptance is communicated to him, insist that his proposal shall be accepted in the prescribed manner, and not otherwise; but if he fails to do so, he accepts the acceptance.

Section 8. Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration. Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance of the proposal.

Section 9. Promises, express and implied. In so far as the proposal or acceptance of any promise is made in words, the promise is said to be express. In so far as such proposal or acceptance is made otherwise than in words, the promise is said to be implied.

Section 3 (relevant part). The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

Section 6 (relevant part). A proposal is revoked— … (2) by the lapse of the time prescribed in such proposal for its acceptance, or, if no time is so prescribed, by the lapse of a reasonable time, without communication of the acceptance; (3) by the failure of the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent to acceptance; …
In simple words

Section 2(b): acceptance is the offeree showing his assent . Once he does, the offer becomes a promise . Section 7(1): the "yes" must be complete . A "yes, but …" is not acceptance. Section 7(2): accept in a normal, reasonable way , or in the way the offer asks . If the offeree uses another way, the offeror must object within a reasonable time ; if he keeps quiet, the acceptance stands. Section 8: doing what the offer asks (or taking the consideration offered) is acceptance. Section 9: acceptance can be express (in words) or implied (by conduct). Section 3: acceptance is made by an act or omission meant to communicate it. Section 6(2), (3): acceptance must come before the offer lapses , and after any condition precedent is fulfilled.
en.meaning:
What acceptance does

Acceptance is the second half of an agreement. Offer + acceptance = promise (Section 2(b)) = agreement (Section 2(e)). At the moment of acceptance the offeror loses the freedom to walk away, so the law insists that the acceptance be clear and complete.

Section 2(b) broken into parts

Words of Section 2(b) What it means "the person to whom the proposal is made" Only the offeree can accept (for a general offer , any member of the public who knows of it) "signifies" The assent must be shown outwardly, by words or conduct; a decision kept in one's mind is not enough "his assent thereto " Agreement to that proposal , on its terms "A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise" The moment of acceptance is the moment of agreement

Why the law insists on these rules

If a changed reply counted as acceptance, the offeror would be bound to terms he never offered. If a secret decision counted, the offeror would never know whether he was bound. If silence counted, anyone could force a contract on another by a letter.

Running example

Meena writes to Ravi : "I will sell you my sewing machine, model XL-200, for ₹8,000 . Delivery at my house on Sunday. Reply by letter by Friday. " The letter reaches Ravi on Tuesday.

We will look at several replies Ravi might give and test each against the rules.
keyPoints: Acceptance = signifying assent to a proposal; the proposal then becomes a promise (Section 2(b)). It must be absolute and unqualified (Section 7(1)); a changed reply is a counter-offer that kills the original offer ( Hyde v. Wrench ). It must follow the prescribed manner , or a usual and reasonable one; an offeror who does not object in reasonable time accepts the acceptance (Section 7(2)). It must be communicated ; a mental decision is not enough ( Felthouse v. Bindley ), and it must come from the offeree or his authorised agent ( Powell v. Lee ). It can be by conduct or performance (Sections 8, 9; Carlill ; Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar ). It must be given while the offer is open (Section 6). Silence is not acceptance. In auctions subject to confirmation, the contract is complete only on confirmation ( Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram ).

caseLaws.name: Hyde v
caseLaws.facts: Wrench (1840) Facts. Wrench offered to sell his farm for £1,000. Hyde's agent offered £950, which Wrench later refused. Hyde then tried to accept the £1,000 offer. Principle. A counter-offer rejects the original offer, which cannot afterwards be revived by an acceptance. (1840) 49 ER 132. Why it matters. It is the leading case on absolute acceptance and counter-offers (Section 7(1)). Felthouse v. Bindley (1862) Facts. An uncle offered to buy his nephew's horse for £30 15s, saying he would treat it as his if he heard no more. The nephew decided to sell but never told him; the horse was sold at auction by mistake. Principle. Acceptance must be communicated to the offeror; silence is not acceptance. 142 ER 1037 : (1862) 11 CB (NS) 869. Why it matters. It shows that a mental decision to accept is not enough. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893) Facts. The company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball as directed. Mrs Carlill used it and caught influenza. Principle. A general offer can be accepted by performing its conditions; the offeror may dispense with notice of acceptance. [1893] 1 QB 256 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It illustrates acceptance by performance (Section 8). Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar v. Union of India (2006) Facts. The Railways sent cheques for Rs. 9,111 and Rs. 9,032 against larger claims, stating that encashment would be full and final settlement. The claimant encashed them without prior protest and then sued for the balance. Principle. Encashing the cheques was acceptance by conduct of the offer of full and final settlement; the offeree cannot change his mind afterwards. (2006) 5 SCC 311 : AIR 2006 SC 2331. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian Supreme Court case on acceptance by conduct . Powell v. Lee (1908) Facts. School managers resolved to appoint Powell as headmaster. One manager, without authority, told him of the decision; the managers later appointed someone else. Principle. Acceptance must be communicated by the offeree or his authorised agent; unauthorised information is not acceptance. (1908) 99 LT 284. Why it matters. It shows who must communicate the acceptance. Union of India v. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram (1969) Facts. The highest bid of Rs. 4,01,000 at an auction of a liquor licence needed the Chief Commissioner's confirmation, which was never given. Principle. Where a bid is subject to confirmation, the contract is complete only on confirmation, not on the fall of the hammer. AIR 1971 SC 2295 : (1970) 2 SCR 594. Why it matters. It shows when acceptance happens in auctions subject to approval.

selfTest.q: 1. What is acceptance under the Act?
selfTest.a: When the person to whom a proposal is made signifies his assent to it (Section 2(b)).

selfTest.q: 2. Meena offers delivery at her house. Ravi replies, "I accept at ₹8,000, delivery at my house." Is this acceptance?
selfTest.a: No. Changing the place of delivery is a new term, so the reply is a counter-offer (Section 7(1)); it rejects Meena's offer ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 3. The offer says "reply by letter". The offeree replies by email, and the offeror does nothing. Is there a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. Under Section 7(2), the offeror who fails to insist on the prescribed manner within a reasonable time accepts the acceptance.

selfTest.q: 4. After making a counter-offer, can the offeree accept the original offer?
selfTest.a: No. The counter-offer rejected it ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is encashing a cheque sent "in full and final settlement" an acceptance?
selfTest.a: Yes, acceptance by conduct, if done without protest ( Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar v. Union of India ).

selfTest.q: 6. Is the highest bid at an auction subject to confirmation a concluded contract?
selfTest.a: No, not until it is confirmed ( Union of India v. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram ).

te.meaning:
అంగీకారం ఏం చేస్తుంది

ఒప్పందంలో అంగీకారం రెండో సగం. ఆఫర్ + అంగీకారం = వాగ్దానం (సెక్షన్ 2(b)) = ఒప్పందం (సెక్షన్ 2(e)). అంగీకారం జరిగిన క్షణం నుంచి ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు వెనక్కు తగ్గే స్వేచ్ఛ కోల్పోతారు. అందుకే అంగీకారం స్పష్టంగా, పూర్తిగా ఉండాలని చట్టం పట్టుబడుతుంది.

సెక్షన్ 2(b) ను భాగాలుగా

సెక్షన్ 2(b) లోని మాటలు అర్థం "the person to whom the proposal is made" offeree మాత్రమే అంగీకరించగలరు (ప్రజలందరికీ చేసే ఆఫర్ అయితే, దాని గురించి తెలిసిన ఎవరైనా) "signifies" సమ్మతిని మాటలతో గానీ ప్రవర్తనతో గానీ బయటకు చూపాలి ; మనసులో అనుకుంటే చాలదు "his assent thereto " ఆ ప్రతిపాదనకే , దాని షరతులతోనే సమ్మతి "A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise" అంగీకారం జరిగిన క్షణమే ఒప్పందం జరిగిన క్షణం

చట్టం ఈ నియమాలపై ఎందుకు పట్టుబడుతుంది

మార్చిన జవాబును అంగీకారంగా లెక్కిస్తే, ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు తాము ఎప్పుడూ ఇవ్వని షరతులకు కట్టుబడాల్సి వస్తుంది. రహస్యంగా తీసుకున్న నిర్ణయాన్ని లెక్కిస్తే, తాను కట్టుబడ్డానో లేదో ఆఫర్ చేసినవారికి ఎప్పటికీ తెలియదు. మౌనాన్ని లెక్కిస్తే, ఒక ఉత్తరం రాసి ఎవరైనా ఇంకొకరిపై కాంట్రాక్టును రుద్దవచ్చు.

మన ఉదాహరణ

మీనా , రవి కి ఇలా ఉత్తరం రాసింది: "నా కుట్టు మిషన్, మోడల్ XL-200, ను ₹8,000 కి నీకు అమ్ముతాను. ఆదివారం నా ఇంటి దగ్గర డెలివరీ. శుక్రవారం లోగా ఉత్తరం ద్వారా జవాబు ఇవ్వు. " ఉత్తరం మంగళవారం రవికి అందింది.

రవి ఇవ్వగల కొన్ని జవాబులను తీసుకుని, ఒక్కొక్కదాన్నీ నియమాలతో పరీక్షిద్దాం.

selfTest.q: 1. చట్టం ప్రకారం అంగీకారం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఎవరికి ప్రతిపాదన చేశారో ఆ వ్యక్తి దానికి తన సమ్మతిని తెలియజేయడం (సెక్షన్ 2(b)).

selfTest.q: 2. మీనా తన ఇంటి దగ్గర డెలివరీ అని ఆఫర్ చేసింది. రవి "₹8,000 కి అంగీకరిస్తున్నాను, మా ఇంటికి డెలివరీ" అని జవాబిచ్చాడు. ఇది అంగీకారమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. డెలివరీ స్థలాన్ని మార్చడం కొత్త షరతు, కాబట్టి జవాబు counter-offer (సెక్షన్ 7(1)); అది మీనా ఆఫర్‌ను తిరస్కరిస్తుంది ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 3. ఆఫర్ "ఉత్తరం ద్వారా జవాబు ఇవ్వు" అంది. offeree ఈమెయిల్ ద్వారా జవాబిచ్చాడు; ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు ఏమీ చేయలేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు ఉందా?
selfTest.a: ఉంది. సెక్షన్ 7(2) ప్రకారం, సహేతుకమైన సమయంలో నిర్దేశించిన పద్ధతిపై పట్టుబట్టని ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు ఆ అంగీకారాన్ని అంగీకరించినట్టే.

selfTest.q: 4. Counter-offer చేసిన తర్వాత offeree అసలు ఆఫర్‌ను అంగీకరించగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. Counter-offer దాన్ని తిరస్కరించింది ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 5. "పూర్తి, తుది పరిష్కారం"గా పంపిన చెక్కును నగదు చేసుకోవడం అంగీకారమా?
selfTest.a: అవును, అభ్యంతరం లేకుండా చేస్తే ప్రవర్తన ద్వారా అంగీకారం ( Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar v. Union of India ).

selfTest.q: 6. ఆమోదానికి లోబడిన వేలంలో అత్యధిక బిడ్ పూర్తయిన కాంట్రాక్టా?
selfTest.a: కాదు, ఆమోదం వచ్చే వరకు కాదు ( Union of India v. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram ).

hi.inOneMinute: Acceptance is the "yes" that turns an offer into a promise. Under Section 2(b), when the person to whom a proposal is made signifies his assent to it, the proposal is accepted, and a proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise . To be valid, the acceptance must be absolute and unqualified , expressed in a usual and reasonable manner or in the manner the offer prescribes (Section 7), communicated to the offeror, and given by the offeree while the offer is still open . Acceptance may be by words or by conduct , including by performing the conditions of the offer (Sections 8, 9). Silence is not acceptance. In exams, marks come from the definition, Section 7 quoted, each essential with a case ( Hyde v. Wrench , Felthouse v. Bindley , Carlill , Powell v. Lee , Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar ), and the counter-offer rule. In real life, it tells you whether your reply closed the deal or only opened a new round of bargaining.
legalProvision: Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;

Section 7. Acceptance must be absolute. In order to convert a proposal into a promise, the acceptance must— (1) be absolute and unqualified; (2) be expressed in some usual and reasonable manner, unless the proposal prescribes the manner in which it is to be accepted. If the proposal prescribes a manner in which it is to be accepted, and the acceptance is not made in such manner, the proposer may, within a reasonable time after the acceptance is communicated to him, insist that his proposal shall be accepted in the prescribed manner, and not otherwise; but if he fails to do so, he accepts the acceptance.

Section 8. Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration. Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance of the proposal.

Section 9. Promises, express and implied. In so far as the proposal or acceptance of any promise is made in words, the promise is said to be express. In so far as such proposal or acceptance is made otherwise than in words, the promise is said to be implied.

Section 3 (relevant part). The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

Section 6 (relevant part). A proposal is revoked— … (2) by the lapse of the time prescribed in such proposal for its acceptance, or, if no time is so prescribed, by the lapse of a reasonable time, without communication of the acceptance; (3) by the failure of the acceptor to fulfil a condition precedent to acceptance; …
In simple words

Section 2(b): acceptance is the offeree showing his assent . Once he does, the offer becomes a promise . Section 7(1): the "yes" must be complete . A "yes, but …" is not acceptance. Section 7(2): accept in a normal, reasonable way , or in the way the offer asks . If the offeree uses another way, the offeror must object within a reasonable time ; if he keeps quiet, the acceptance stands. Section 8: doing what the offer asks (or taking the consideration offered) is acceptance. Section 9: acceptance can be express (in words) or implied (by conduct). Section 3: acceptance is made by an act or omission meant to communicate it. Section 6(2), (3): acceptance must come before the offer lapses , and after any condition precedent is fulfilled.
hi.meaning: What acceptance does Acceptance is the second half of an agreement. Offer + acceptance = promise (Section 2(b)) = agreement (Section 2(e)). At the moment of acceptance the offeror loses the freedom to walk away, so the law insists that the acceptance be clear and complete. Section 2(b) broken into parts Words of Section 2(b) What it means "the person to whom the proposal is made" Only the offeree can accept (for a general offer , any member of the public who knows of it) "signifies" The assent must be shown outwardly, by words or conduct; a decision kept in one's mind is not enough "his assent thereto " Agreement to that proposal , on its terms "A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise" The moment of acceptance is the moment of agreement Why the law insists on these rules If a changed reply counted as acceptance, the offeror would be bound to terms he never offered. If a secret decision counted, the offeror would never know whether he was bound. If silence counted, anyone could force a contract on another by a letter. Running example Meena writes to Ravi : "I will sell you my sewing machine, model XL-200, for ₹8,000 . Delivery at my house on Sunday. Reply by letter by Friday. " The letter reaches Ravi on Tuesday. We will look at several replies Ravi might give and test each against the rules.
keyPoints: Acceptance = signifying assent to a proposal; the proposal then becomes a promise (Section 2(b)). It must be absolute and unqualified (Section 7(1)); a changed reply is a counter-offer that kills the original offer ( Hyde v. Wrench ). It must follow the prescribed manner , or a usual and reasonable one; an offeror who does not object in reasonable time accepts the acceptance (Section 7(2)). It must be communicated ; a mental decision is not enough ( Felthouse v. Bindley ), and it must come from the offeree or his authorised agent ( Powell v. Lee ). It can be by conduct or performance (Sections 8, 9; Carlill ; Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar ). It must be given while the offer is open (Section 6). Silence is not acceptance. In auctions subject to confirmation, the contract is complete only on confirmation ( Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram ).

caseLaws.name: Hyde v
caseLaws.facts: Wrench (1840) Facts. Wrench offered to sell his farm for £1,000. Hyde's agent offered £950, which Wrench later refused. Hyde then tried to accept the £1,000 offer. Principle. A counter-offer rejects the original offer, which cannot afterwards be revived by an acceptance. (1840) 49 ER 132. Why it matters. It is the leading case on absolute acceptance and counter-offers (Section 7(1)). Felthouse v. Bindley (1862) Facts. An uncle offered to buy his nephew's horse for £30 15s, saying he would treat it as his if he heard no more. The nephew decided to sell but never told him; the horse was sold at auction by mistake. Principle. Acceptance must be communicated to the offeror; silence is not acceptance. 142 ER 1037 : (1862) 11 CB (NS) 869. Why it matters. It shows that a mental decision to accept is not enough. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893) Facts. The company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball as directed. Mrs Carlill used it and caught influenza. Principle. A general offer can be accepted by performing its conditions; the offeror may dispense with notice of acceptance. [1893] 1 QB 256 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It illustrates acceptance by performance (Section 8). Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar v. Union of India (2006) Facts. The Railways sent cheques for Rs. 9,111 and Rs. 9,032 against larger claims, stating that encashment would be full and final settlement. The claimant encashed them without prior protest and then sued for the balance. Principle. Encashing the cheques was acceptance by conduct of the offer of full and final settlement; the offeree cannot change his mind afterwards. (2006) 5 SCC 311 : AIR 2006 SC 2331. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian Supreme Court case on acceptance by conduct . Powell v. Lee (1908) Facts. School managers resolved to appoint Powell as headmaster. One manager, without authority, told him of the decision; the managers later appointed someone else. Principle. Acceptance must be communicated by the offeree or his authorised agent; unauthorised information is not acceptance. (1908) 99 LT 284. Why it matters. It shows who must communicate the acceptance. Union of India v. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram (1969) Facts. The highest bid of Rs. 4,01,000 at an auction of a liquor licence needed the Chief Commissioner's confirmation, which was never given. Principle. Where a bid is subject to confirmation, the contract is complete only on confirmation, not on the fall of the hammer. AIR 1971 SC 2295 : (1970) 2 SCR 594. Why it matters. It shows when acceptance happens in auctions subject to approval.

selfTest.q: 1. What is acceptance under the Act?
selfTest.a: When the person to whom a proposal is made signifies his assent to it (Section 2(b)).

selfTest.q: 2. Meena offers delivery at her house. Ravi replies, "I accept at ₹8,000, delivery at my house." Is this acceptance?
selfTest.a: No. Changing the place of delivery is a new term, so the reply is a counter-offer (Section 7(1)); it rejects Meena's offer ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 3. The offer says "reply by letter". The offeree replies by email, and the offeror does nothing. Is there a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. Under Section 7(2), the offeror who fails to insist on the prescribed manner within a reasonable time accepts the acceptance.

selfTest.q: 4. After making a counter-offer, can the offeree accept the original offer?
selfTest.a: No. The counter-offer rejected it ( Hyde v. Wrench ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is encashing a cheque sent "in full and final settlement" an acceptance?
selfTest.a: Yes, acceptance by conduct, if done without protest ( Bhagwati Prasad Pawan Kumar v. Union of India ).

selfTest.q: 6. Is the highest bid at an auction subject to confirmation a concluded contract?
selfTest.a: No, not until it is confirmed ( Union of India v. Bhim Sen Walaiti Ram ).

en.meaning:
Under Section 2(d), consideration must move at:

Explanation. Consideration must be given at the desire of the promisor — an act done voluntarily or at someone else's request is not valid consideration.

In Durga Prasad v. Baldeo, the plaintiff's claim failed because:

Explanation. His original effort was done at the Collector's request, not the shopkeepers' — so it wasn't valid consideration for their later promise to pay commission.

Which of these is required for consideration to be valid?

Explanation. Consideration must be real and lawful, but need not be adequate — courts don't assess fairness of the exchange, only that something of value was genuinely given.

Under Section 25, which of these is NOT a listed exception to 'no consideration, no contract'?

en.meaning:
The doctrine of privity of contract means:

Explanation. Privity of contract means only the actual parties to an agreement have standing to sue or be sued on it — a stranger generally cannot enforce it.

In Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co. v. Selfridge & Co., Dunlop could not sue Selfridge because:

Explanation. Only a party can sue on a contract, and no consideration moved from Dunlop to Selfridge. All the Lords relied on the lack of consideration, and Lord Haldane also relied on privity.

Which of these is NOT a recognised exception to privity of contract in India?

Explanation. Inadequate consideration is unrelated to privity exceptions. The recognised exceptions include trusts/beneficiaries, family arrangements, agency, assignment, and acknowledgment/estoppel.

Chinnaya v. Ramayya established that in India:

law-of-contract-i-u1-t2.subtitle: Sections 2(a), 2(c), 4 and 29 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Every contract starts with an offer . The Act calls it a proposal . Under Section 2(a), a person makes a proposal when he signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other . A valid offer must be definite , must be made with the intention of being bound on acceptance , and must be communicated to the person who is to accept it. It must be different from an invitation to offer , such as a price list, a shop display, an advertisement for an auction, or a call for tenders. In exams, marks come from the definition, the list of essentials with a case for each, and the offer versus invitation-to-offer distinction ( Harvey v. Facey , MacPherson v. Appanna ). In real life, this decides whether you can say "I accept" and hold the other person to a bargain.
legalProvision: Section 2(a). When one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence, he is said to make a proposal;
Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;
Section 2(c). The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee";

Section 3. Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals. The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

Section 4 (first paragraph). The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Illustration (a): A proposes, by letter, to sell a house to B at a certain price. The communication of the proposal is complete when B receives the letter.

Section 8. Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration. Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance of the proposal.

Section 9. Promises, express and implied. In so far as the proposal or acceptance of any promise is made in words, the promise is said to be express. In so far as such proposal or acceptance is made otherwise than in words, the promise is said to be implied.
Section 29. Agreements void for uncertainty. Agreements, the meaning of which is not certain, or capable of being made certain, are void.
In simple words

Section 2(a): an offer is a willingness to do or not do something, shown to another person, in order to get his "yes" . Section 2(b), (c): when that "yes" comes, the offer becomes a promise . The offeror is the promisor ; the acceptor is the promisee . Section 3: an offer can be made by words or conduct (any act or omission meant to communicate it). Section 4: an offer is communicated only when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree. Section 8: some offers are accepted by doing what they ask (useful for offers to the public). Section 9: an offer in words is express ; one made by conduct is implied . Section 29: an offer so vague that no certain agreement can come out of it produces a void agreement.
en.meaning:
Offer and proposal mean the same thing

The Act uses the word proposal . English law and most textbooks use offer . They mean the same thing. The person who makes it is the offeror (proposer, promisor). The person to whom it is made is the offeree (promisee once he accepts).

Section 2(a) broken into parts

Words of Section 2(a) What it means Example "When one person signifies to another" The offer must be shown (communicated) to another person Meena writes to Ravi "his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything" It can be an offer to do or not to do something To sell a sewing machine; or not to open a rival shop "with a view to obtaining the assent of that other" It is made to get the other's acceptance , with an intention to be bound if he accepts "Will you buy it for ₹8,000?"

Why the law needs a clear offer

A contract is formed the moment an offer is accepted. So the law must be able to point to one definite offer whose acceptance closes the deal. If every price list, advertisement or enquiry were an offer, a shopkeeper could be bound to sell to a thousand people the same item. That is why the law separates a true offer from a mere invitation to offer .

Running example

Meena writes a letter to Ravi : "I will sell you my sewing machine, model XL-200, for ₹8,000 . Delivery at my house on Sunday. Please reply by Friday."

We will test this letter against every essential below.
keyPoints: Offer = proposal (Section 2(a)): willingness to do or abstain, shown to another, to obtain his assent . It must be made with an intention to be bound on acceptance. It must be definite (Section 29). It must be communicated ; communication is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree (Section 4). An invitation to offer (display, price list, auction notice, tender notice, quotation) is not an offer. A general offer can be accepted by anyone who knows of it and performs its conditions (Section 8; Carlill ). Offers may be express or implied (Section 9). Silence cannot be made acceptance ( Felthouse v. Bindley ).

caseLaws.name: Harvey v
caseLaws.facts: Facey (1893) Facts. Harvey telegraphed asking whether Facey would sell Bumper Hall Pen and his lowest cash price. Facey replied "Lowest price for Bumper Hall Pen £900." Harvey telegraphed that he agreed to buy at £900; Facey did not reply. Principle. A statement of the lowest price in reply to an enquiry is not an offer to sell. Harvey's last telegram was only an offer, never accepted. [1893] AC 552 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It is the leading case separating an offer from a mere quotation of price. MacPherson v. M.N. Appanna (1951) Facts. The owner of a bungalow in Mercara, told of an offer of Rs. 6,000, cabled "Won't accept less than rupees ten thousand." Appanna wrote to confirm his offer of ten thousand; the owner sold to another for Rs. 11,000. Principle. A statement of the lowest price at which one would sell is not an offer; there was no concluded contract. AIR 1951 SC 184 : 1951 SCR 161. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's adoption of Harvey v. Facey in India. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893) Facts. The company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball three times daily for two weeks, and deposited £1,000 with a bank. Mrs Carlill used it as directed and caught influenza. Principle. An offer can be made to the world at large; it is accepted by anyone who performs the conditions, and notice of acceptance can be dispensed with. [1893] 1 QB 256 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on general offers . Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (1913) Facts. A servant was sent to search for his master's missing nephew. While he was away, the master announced a reward. The servant found the boy and later claimed the reward. Principle. A person who does the act without knowing of the offer cannot claim to have accepted it. Allahabad High Court, 1913. Why it matters. It shows that an offer must be communicated (known) before it can be accepted. Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v. Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd. (1953) Facts. Boots let customers pick certain medicines from open shelves and pay at a cash desk, where a pharmacist supervised. The Society said the sale took place at the shelf, without supervision. Principle. Display of goods is an invitation to offer. The customer offers to buy at the cash desk, and the seller accepts there. [1953] 1 QB 401 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on display of goods . Felthouse v. Bindley (1862) Facts. An uncle offered to buy his nephew's horse for £30 15s, writing that if he heard no more he would consider the horse his. The nephew did not reply; the horse was sold at auction by mistake. Principle. An offeror cannot make the offeree's silence an acceptance. 142 ER 1037 : (1862) 11 CB (NS) 869. Why it matters. It limits what conditions an offeror can put in an offer.

selfTest.q: 1. What does the Act call an offer?
selfTest.a: A proposal (Section 2(a)).

selfTest.q: 2. Is a reply stating "lowest price ₹9 lakh" an offer?
selfTest.a: No. It is a statement of price ( Harvey v. Facey ; MacPherson v. Appanna ).

selfTest.q: 3. When is the communication of an offer complete?
selfTest.a: When it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made (Section 4).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a person who returns a lost article without knowing of the reward claim it?
selfTest.a: No. He did not know of the offer ( Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt ).

selfTest.q: 5. Are goods on a supermarket shelf an offer?
selfTest.a: No. They are an invitation to offer; the customer offers at the counter ( Boots ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can an offeror say "your silence will mean acceptance"?
selfTest.a: He can say it, but it does not bind the offeree ( Felthouse v. Bindley ).

సులభమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 2(a): ఆఫర్ అంటే ఏదైనా చేయడానికి లేదా చేయకుండా ఉండడానికి ఉన్న సుముఖత , అవతలి వ్యక్తి "సరే" అనిపించుకోవడానికి అతనికి తెలియజేసినది. సెక్షన్ 2(b), (c): ఆ "సరే" వచ్చినప్పుడు ఆఫర్ వాగ్దానం అవుతుంది. ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు promisor ; అంగీకరించినవారు promisee . సెక్షన్ 3: ఆఫర్‌ను మాటలతో గానీ ప్రవర్తనతో గానీ చేయవచ్చు (తెలియజేయాలనే ఉద్దేశంతో చేసే ఏ చర్య లేదా విస్మరణ అయినా). సెక్షన్ 4: ఆఫర్ అందుకున్న వ్యక్తికి తెలిసినప్పుడే ఆఫర్ తెలియజేయడం పూర్తవుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 8: కొన్ని ఆఫర్లను అవి అడిగిన పని చేయడం ద్వారా అంగీకరించవచ్చు (ప్రజలకు చేసే ఆఫర్లలో ఇది ఉపయోగం). సెక్షన్ 9: మాటల్లో చేసిన ఆఫర్ express (స్పష్టమైనది); ప్రవర్తనతో చేసినది implied (సూచితమైనది). సెక్షన్ 29: నిశ్చితమైన ఒప్పందం ఏర్పడలేనంత అస్పష్టమైన ఆఫర్ వల్ల వచ్చే ఒప్పందం void .
te.meaning:
ఆఫర్, ప్రతిపాదన ఒకటే

చట్టం proposal (ప్రతిపాదన) అనే పదాన్ని వాడుతుంది. ఇంగ్లీష్ చట్టం, చాలా పుస్తకాలు offer అంటాయి. రెండింటి అర్థం ఒకటే. ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు offeror (ప్రతిపాదకుడు, promisor). ఎవరికి చేశారో వారు offeree (అంగీకరించాక promisee).

సెక్షన్ 2(a) భాగాలుగా

సెక్షన్ 2(a) మాటలు అర్థం ఉదాహరణ "When one person signifies to another" ఆఫర్‌ను మరొకరికి తెలియజేయాలి మీనా రవికి ఉత్తరం రాస్తుంది "his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything" ఏదైనా చేయడానికి లేదా చేయకుండా ఉండడానికి ఆఫర్ చేయవచ్చు కుట్టు మిషన్ అమ్మడం; లేదా పోటీ దుకాణం తెరవకపోవడం "with a view to obtaining the assent of that other" అవతలి వ్యక్తి అంగీకారం పొందడానికి చేయాలి; అంగీకరిస్తే కట్టుబడాలనే ఉద్దేశం ఉండాలి "₹8,000 కు కొంటారా?"

స్పష్టమైన ఆఫర్ చట్టానికి ఎందుకు అవసరం?

ఆఫర్‌ను అంగీకరించిన క్షణమే కాంట్రాక్టు ఏర్పడుతుంది. కాబట్టి ఏ ఒక్క నిశ్చితమైన ఆఫర్ అంగీకారంతో బేరం ముగిసిందో చట్టం చూపించగలగాలి. ప్రతి ధరల జాబితా, ప్రకటన, విచారణ ఆఫర్ అయితే, ఒక దుకాణదారు ఒకే వస్తువును వెయ్యి మందికి అమ్మడానికి కట్టుబడిపోతాడు. అందుకే చట్టం నిజమైన ఆఫర్ ను కేవలం ఆఫర్ చేయమనే ఆహ్వానం నుంచి వేరు చేస్తుంది.

మన ఉదాహరణ

మీనా రవి కి ఉత్తరం రాస్తుంది: "నా కుట్టు మిషన్, మోడల్ XL-200 ను నీకు ₹8,000 కు అమ్ముతాను. ఆదివారం మా ఇంట్లో అప్పగిస్తాను. శుక్రవారంలోగా జవాబు ఇవ్వు."

ఈ ఉత్తరాన్ని కింద ప్రతి ముఖ్య అంశంతో పరీక్షిద్దాం.

selfTest.q: 1. చట్టం ఆఫర్‌ను ఏమని పిలుస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: Proposal (ప్రతిపాదన) (సెక్షన్ 2(a)).

selfTest.q: 2. "అతి తక్కువ ధర ₹9 లక్షలు" అనే జవాబు ఆఫరా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అది ధర చెప్పడం మాత్రమే ( Harvey v. Facey ; MacPherson v. Appanna ).

selfTest.q: 3. ఆఫర్ తెలియజేయడం ఎప్పుడు పూర్తవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: ఎవరికి చేశారో వారికి తెలిసినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 4).

selfTest.q: 4. బహుమతి గురించి తెలియకుండా పోయిన వస్తువును తిరిగి ఇచ్చిన వ్యక్తి బహుమతి అడగవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అడగలేడు. అతనికి ఆఫర్ గురించి తెలియదు ( Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt ).

selfTest.q: 5. సూపర్ మార్కెట్ అల్మారాల్లోని వస్తువులు ఆఫరా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అవి ఆఫర్ చేయమనే ఆహ్వానం; కస్టమర్ కౌంటర్ దగ్గర ఆఫర్ చేస్తాడు ( Boots ).

selfTest.q: 6. "నీ మౌనమే అంగీకారం" అని ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు అనవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అనవచ్చు, కానీ అది offeree ని బంధించదు ( Felthouse v. Bindley ).

hi.inOneMinute: Every contract starts with an offer . The Act calls it a proposal . Under Section 2(a), a person makes a proposal when he signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other . A valid offer must be definite , must be made with the intention of being bound on acceptance , and must be communicated to the person who is to accept it. It must be different from an invitation to offer , such as a price list, a shop display, an advertisement for an auction, or a call for tenders. In exams, marks come from the definition, the list of essentials with a case for each, and the offer versus invitation-to-offer distinction ( Harvey v. Facey , MacPherson v. Appanna ). In real life, this decides whether you can say "I accept" and hold the other person to a bargain.
legalProvision: Section 2(a). When one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other to such act or abstinence, he is said to make a proposal;
Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;
Section 2(c). The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee";

Section 3. Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals. The communication of proposals, the acceptance of proposals, and the revocation of proposals and acceptances, respectively, are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate such proposal, acceptance or revocation, or which has the effect of communicating it.

Section 4 (first paragraph). The communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Illustration (a): A proposes, by letter, to sell a house to B at a certain price. The communication of the proposal is complete when B receives the letter.

Section 8. Acceptance by performing conditions, or receiving consideration. Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance of the proposal.

Section 9. Promises, express and implied. In so far as the proposal or acceptance of any promise is made in words, the promise is said to be express. In so far as such proposal or acceptance is made otherwise than in words, the promise is said to be implied.
Section 29. Agreements void for uncertainty. Agreements, the meaning of which is not certain, or capable of being made certain, are void.
In simple words

Section 2(a): an offer is a willingness to do or not do something, shown to another person, in order to get his "yes" . Section 2(b), (c): when that "yes" comes, the offer becomes a promise . The offeror is the promisor ; the acceptor is the promisee . Section 3: an offer can be made by words or conduct (any act or omission meant to communicate it). Section 4: an offer is communicated only when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree. Section 8: some offers are accepted by doing what they ask (useful for offers to the public). Section 9: an offer in words is express ; one made by conduct is implied . Section 29: an offer so vague that no certain agreement can come out of it produces a void agreement.
hi.meaning: Offer and proposal mean the same thing The Act uses the word proposal . English law and most textbooks use offer . They mean the same thing. The person who makes it is the offeror (proposer, promisor). The person to whom it is made is the offeree (promisee once he accepts). Section 2(a) broken into parts Words of Section 2(a) What it means Example "When one person signifies to another" The offer must be shown (communicated) to another person Meena writes to Ravi "his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything" It can be an offer to do or not to do something To sell a sewing machine; or not to open a rival shop "with a view to obtaining the assent of that other" It is made to get the other's acceptance , with an intention to be bound if he accepts "Will you buy it for ₹8,000?" Why the law needs a clear offer A contract is formed the moment an offer is accepted. So the law must be able to point to one definite offer whose acceptance closes the deal. If every price list, advertisement or enquiry were an offer, a shopkeeper could be bound to sell to a thousand people the same item. That is why the law separates a true offer from a mere invitation to offer . Running example Meena writes a letter to Ravi : "I will sell you my sewing machine, model XL-200, for ₹8,000 . Delivery at my house on Sunday. Please reply by Friday." We will test this letter against every essential below.
keyPoints: Offer = proposal (Section 2(a)): willingness to do or abstain, shown to another, to obtain his assent . It must be made with an intention to be bound on acceptance. It must be definite (Section 29). It must be communicated ; communication is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the offeree (Section 4). An invitation to offer (display, price list, auction notice, tender notice, quotation) is not an offer. A general offer can be accepted by anyone who knows of it and performs its conditions (Section 8; Carlill ). Offers may be express or implied (Section 9). Silence cannot be made acceptance ( Felthouse v. Bindley ).

caseLaws.name: Harvey v
caseLaws.facts: Facey (1893) Facts. Harvey telegraphed asking whether Facey would sell Bumper Hall Pen and his lowest cash price. Facey replied "Lowest price for Bumper Hall Pen £900." Harvey telegraphed that he agreed to buy at £900; Facey did not reply. Principle. A statement of the lowest price in reply to an enquiry is not an offer to sell. Harvey's last telegram was only an offer, never accepted. [1893] AC 552 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It is the leading case separating an offer from a mere quotation of price. MacPherson v. M.N. Appanna (1951) Facts. The owner of a bungalow in Mercara, told of an offer of Rs. 6,000, cabled "Won't accept less than rupees ten thousand." Appanna wrote to confirm his offer of ten thousand; the owner sold to another for Rs. 11,000. Principle. A statement of the lowest price at which one would sell is not an offer; there was no concluded contract. AIR 1951 SC 184 : 1951 SCR 161. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's adoption of Harvey v. Facey in India. Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. (1893) Facts. The company advertised a £100 reward to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball three times daily for two weeks, and deposited £1,000 with a bank. Mrs Carlill used it as directed and caught influenza. Principle. An offer can be made to the world at large; it is accepted by anyone who performs the conditions, and notice of acceptance can be dispensed with. [1893] 1 QB 256 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on general offers . Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (1913) Facts. A servant was sent to search for his master's missing nephew. While he was away, the master announced a reward. The servant found the boy and later claimed the reward. Principle. A person who does the act without knowing of the offer cannot claim to have accepted it. Allahabad High Court, 1913. Why it matters. It shows that an offer must be communicated (known) before it can be accepted. Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v. Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd. (1953) Facts. Boots let customers pick certain medicines from open shelves and pay at a cash desk, where a pharmacist supervised. The Society said the sale took place at the shelf, without supervision. Principle. Display of goods is an invitation to offer. The customer offers to buy at the cash desk, and the seller accepts there. [1953] 1 QB 401 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It is the leading case on display of goods . Felthouse v. Bindley (1862) Facts. An uncle offered to buy his nephew's horse for £30 15s, writing that if he heard no more he would consider the horse his. The nephew did not reply; the horse was sold at auction by mistake. Principle. An offeror cannot make the offeree's silence an acceptance. 142 ER 1037 : (1862) 11 CB (NS) 869. Why it matters. It limits what conditions an offeror can put in an offer.

selfTest.q: 1. What does the Act call an offer?
selfTest.a: A proposal (Section 2(a)).

selfTest.q: 2. Is a reply stating "lowest price ₹9 lakh" an offer?
selfTest.a: No. It is a statement of price ( Harvey v. Facey ; MacPherson v. Appanna ).

selfTest.q: 3. When is the communication of an offer complete?
selfTest.a: When it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made (Section 4).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a person who returns a lost article without knowing of the reward claim it?
selfTest.a: No. He did not know of the offer ( Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt ).

selfTest.q: 5. Are goods on a supermarket shelf an offer?
selfTest.a: No. They are an invitation to offer; the customer offers at the counter ( Boots ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can an offeror say "your silence will mean acceptance"?
selfTest.a: He can say it, but it does not bind the offeree ( Felthouse v. Bindley ).

law-of-contract-i-u2-t1.subtitle: Sections 10, 11 and 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Capacity means the legal power to bind yourself by a contract. Section 10 says an agreement is a contract only if it is made by "parties competent to contract". Section 11 says who is competent. A person must pass three tests : He is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject. He is of sound mind (tested under Section 12). He is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject. Capacity is about legal status , not intelligence or a fair price. A clever 17-year-old lacks it. An ordinary adult has it. If a party lacks capacity, there is no contract at all. The Privy Council held in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903) that a minor 's agreement is void , not merely voidable . In exams, the three tests, the Section 12 test of sound mind with its two rules and illustrations, and the reasons given in Mohori Bibee earn the marks. In real life, capacity decides whether a shop can sue a teenager for the price of a phone, or a buyer can keep land bought from a seriously ill seller.
legalProvision: Section 10. What agreements are contracts. All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void. Nothing herein contained shall affect any law in force in India and not hereby expressly repealed by which any contract is required to be made in writing or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.

Section 11. Who are competent to contract. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 12. What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting. A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract, if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests. A person who is usually of unsound mind, but occasionally of sound mind, may make a contract when he is of sound mind. A person who is usually of sound mind, but occasionally of unsound mind, may not make a contract when he is of unsound mind. Illustration (a): A patient in a lunatic asylum, who is at intervals of sound mind, may contract during those intervals. Illustration (b): A sane man, who is delirious from fever or who is so drunk that he cannot understand the terms of a contract, or form a rational judgment as to its effect on his interests, cannot contract whilst such delirium or drunkenness lasts.
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 4(a). "minor" means a person who has not completed the age of eighteen years;

Indian Majority Act, 1875, Section 3 (as the bare Act note to Section 11 points to it): every person domiciled in India attains majority on completing the age of eighteen years . Older versions of Section 3 fixed twenty-one years for a minor for whom a court had appointed a guardian, or whose property was under a Court of Wards, before he turned eighteen. Mohori Bibee (1895 facts) was decided under that 21-year rule. See the verification report on whether the 21-year rule is still in force.
In simple words

Section 10: capacity is one of the conditions of every contract . No capacity, no contract. Section 11: three tests. Old enough, sound mind, and no legal bar. Section 12: "sound mind" is tested at the time of the contract . Can the person (1) understand the contract, and (2) judge how it affects his interests? A person who is usually unsound may contract in a clear interval. A person who is usually sound may not contract while he is delirious or very drunk. Majority: the general age is 18 .
en.meaning:
Capacity to contract (also called competence) is the legal ability of a person to make a contract that binds him. A person who has it is "competent to contract".

The law asks about the person, not the bargain. A very fair price does not cure a missing capacity. And a foolish bargain made by a competent adult is still a contract.

Who is not competent. Section 11 gives three groups:

Minors – persons below the age of majority. Persons of unsound mind – at the time of contracting (Section 12). Persons disqualified by law – adults of sound mind who are barred by a particular law (for example, an alien enemy in some situations).

"According to the law to which he is subject." Section 11 does not fix an age itself. It takes the age from the law that governs the person. For persons domiciled in India, the Indian Majority Act, 1875 fixes it. The bare Act places a note under Section 11: "See the Indian Majority Act, 1875 (9 of 1875)."

Why the law has this rule.

To protect the weak. A child or a person who cannot understand a deal could easily be exploited. To give certainty. A fixed age and a clear test let the other side know where it stands before it deals. Because a contract rests on consent. Only a person who can understand and judge can truly agree.

Capacity and free consent are different. Capacity asks who the person is. Free consent asks how his agreement was obtained ( coercion , fraud and so on). A competent adult who is cheated has capacity, but his consent is not free.
keyPoints: Section 10 makes "parties competent to contract" a condition of every contract. Section 11 has three tests: age of majority, sound mind, no disqualification by law. The general age of majority in India is 18. Section 12: sound mind = ability to understand the contract and judge its effect on one's interests, at the time of making it. Usually unsound but sometimes sound: may contract in a lucid interval. Usually sound but sometimes unsound: may not contract while unsound. Capacity is a legal status; a fair price does not cure its absence. A minor's agreement is void ( Mohori Bibee ), and coming of age does not cure it ( Suraj Narain Dube ). Necessaries: the supplier is reimbursed from the incapable person's property only (Section 68). A Hindu natural guardian cannot bind the minor by a personal covenant and needs court permission to sell the minor's immovable property (HMGA Section 8).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. On 20 July 1895 Dharmodas Ghose, still an infant, mortgaged his houses to a money lender, Brahmo Dutt, to secure Rs. 20,000. The lender's attorney had received a written notice from the infant's mother, his court-appointed guardian, that he was under 21. The infant sued to have the mortgage declared void. Principle. "The Act makes it essential that all contracting parties should be 'competent to contract,'" and a person incompetent by reason of infancy "cannot make a contract within the meaning of the Act". The mortgage was void; Sections 64 and 65 did not apply. Privy Council, 4 March 1903, (1903) LR 30 IA 114 : ILR 30 Cal 539. Why it matters. It is the leading authority that capacity is an essential of a contract and that a minor's agreement is void, not voidable. Suraj Narain Dube v. Sukhu Aheer (1928) Facts. Sukhu, a minor, executed a bond for Rs. 40 on 24 June 1919. After attaining majority, on 17 June 1923, he and his mother executed a fresh bond for Rs. 76 (Rs. 40 plus Rs. 36 interest) for the old loan. Principle. Following Mohori Bibee , the majority of the Full Bench said: "it is now settled law that a contract by a minor is not only voidable, but is altogether void." The new promise had no fresh consideration and was not enforceable. Allahabad High Court (Full Bench), AIR 1928 All 440. Why it matters. It shows that capacity is tested on the date of the original agreement; coming of age later does not cure it.

selfTest.q: 2. What is the test of sound mind in Section 12?
selfTest.a: Whether, at the time of making the contract, the person can understand it and form a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.

selfTest.q: 3. A patient in a mental hospital signs a sale deed during a clear interval and fully understands it. Is it valid?
selfTest.a: Yes. A person usually of unsound mind may contract when of sound mind (Section 12, Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 4. A buyer aged 17 promises to pay ₹70,000 in instalments. Can the seller sue him for the balance?
selfTest.a: No. He is a minor, so the agreement is void ( Mohori Bibee ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a person of unsound mind personally liable for necessaries supplied to him?
selfTest.a: No. The supplier is reimbursed from his property (Section 68).

selfTest.q: 6. Does a Hindu natural guardian need court permission to sell the minor's land?
selfTest.a: Yes, previous permission of the court is needed (HMGA Section 8(2)(a)); a sale without it is voidable at the minor's instance (Section 8(3)).

legalProvision: Section 10. What agreements are contracts. All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void. Nothing herein contained shall affect any law in force in India and not hereby expressly repealed by which any contract is required to be made in writing or in the presence of witnesses, or any law relating to the registration of documents.

Section 11. Who are competent to contract. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 12. What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting. A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract, if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests. A person who is usually of unsound mind, but occasionally of sound mind, may make a contract when he is of sound mind. A person who is usually of sound mind, but occasionally of unsound mind, may not make a contract when he is of unsound mind. Illustration (a): A patient in a lunatic asylum, who is at intervals of sound mind, may contract during those intervals. Illustration (b): A sane man, who is delirious from fever or who is so drunk that he cannot understand the terms of a contract, or form a rational judgment as to its effect on his interests, cannot contract whilst such delirium or drunkenness lasts.
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, Section 4(a). "minor" means a person who has not completed the age of eighteen years;

Indian Majority Act, 1875, సెక్షన్ 3 (సెక్షన్ 11 కింద బేర్ యాక్ట్ నోట్ దీన్నే సూచిస్తుంది): భారతదేశంలో నివాసం (domicile) ఉన్న ప్రతి వ్యక్తి 18 సంవత్సరాలు పూర్తి చేసినప్పుడు మేజర్ అవుతాడు. పాత సెక్షన్ 3 ప్రకారం, 18 ఏళ్లు నిండకముందే కోర్టు గార్డియన్‌ను నియమించిన మైనర్‌కు, లేదా ఆస్తి Court of Wards చేతిలో ఉన్న మైనర్‌కు మేజర్ వయస్సు 21 సంవత్సరాలు . సెక్షన్ 10: ప్రతి కాంట్రాక్టుకు capacity ఒక షరతు. Capacity లేకపోతే కాంట్రాక్టు లేదు. సెక్షన్ 11: మూడు పరీక్షలు. తగిన వయస్సు, స్థిరమైన మనస్సు, చట్టపరమైన అడ్డంకి లేకపోవడం. సెక్షన్ 12: "sound mind" ను కాంట్రాక్టు చేసే సమయంలోనే పరీక్షిస్తారు. ఆ వ్యక్తి (1) కాంట్రాక్టును అర్థం చేసుకోగలడా, (2) అది తన ప్రయోజనాలపై ఎలా ప్రభావం చూపుతుందో తీర్మానించగలడా? సాధారణంగా మనస్సు స్థిరంగా లేని వ్యక్తి స్పష్టమైన విరామంలో కాంట్రాక్టు చేయవచ్చు. సాధారణంగా స్థిరంగా ఉన్న వ్యక్తి జ్వర భ్రాంతిలో గానీ బాగా తాగిన స్థితిలో గానీ ఉన్నప్పుడు కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేడు. మేజర్ వయస్సు: సాధారణ వయస్సు 18 .
te.meaning:
కాంట్రాక్టు సామర్థ్యం (competence అని కూడా అంటారు) అంటే తనను బంధించే కాంట్రాక్టు చేసే చట్టపరమైన శక్తి. అది ఉన్న వ్యక్తి "competent to contract ".

చట్టం వ్యక్తి గురించి అడుగుతుంది, బేరం గురించి కాదు. చాలా న్యాయమైన ధర ఉన్నా, లేని capacity రాదు. సమర్థుడైన పెద్దవాడు చేసిన తెలివి తక్కువ బేరం కూడా కాంట్రాక్టే.

ఎవరు సమర్థులు కారు. సెక్షన్ 11 మూడు వర్గాలను చూపుతుంది:

మైనర్లు – మేజర్ వయస్సు రానివారు. మనస్సు స్థిరంగా లేనివారు – కాంట్రాక్టు చేసే సమయంలో (సెక్షన్ 12). చట్టం అనర్హులుగా చేసినవారు – మనస్సు స్థిరంగా ఉన్న పెద్దవారే, కానీ ఒక ప్రత్యేక చట్టం అడ్డుకుంటుంది (ఉదా: కొన్ని పరిస్థితుల్లో శత్రు దేశ పౌరుడు).

"According to the law to which he is subject." సెక్షన్ 11 స్వయంగా వయస్సును నిర్ణయించదు. ఆ వ్యక్తికి వర్తించే చట్టం నుంచి తీసుకుంటుంది. భారతదేశంలో నివాసం ఉన్నవారికి Indian Majority Act, 1875 దాన్ని నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. బేర్ యాక్ట్ సెక్షన్ 11 కింద ఈ నోట్ ఉంది: "See the Indian Majority Act, 1875 (9 of 1875)."

చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది.

బలహీనులను రక్షించడానికి. పిల్లవాడిని గానీ, బేరాన్ని అర్థం చేసుకోలేని వ్యక్తిని గానీ సులభంగా మోసం చేయవచ్చు. నిశ్చితత కోసం. స్థిరమైన వయస్సు, స్పష్టమైన పరీక్ష ఉంటే, బేరం చేసే ముందే అవతలి పక్షానికి తన స్థానం తెలుస్తుంది. కాంట్రాక్టు సమ్మతిపై ఆధారపడుతుంది కాబట్టి. అర్థం చేసుకుని, తీర్మానించగలిగిన వ్యక్తి మాత్రమే నిజంగా అంగీకరించగలడు.

Capacity, free consent వేర్వేరు. Capacity ఆ వ్యక్తి ఎవరు అని అడుగుతుంది. Free consent అతని అంగీకారం ఎలా పొందారని అడుగుతుంది (బలవంతం, మోసం మొదలైనవి). మోసపోయిన సమర్థుడైన పెద్దవాడికి capacity ఉంటుంది, కానీ అతని సమ్మతి స్వేచ్ఛాయుతం కాదు.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 12 లో స్థిరమైన మనస్సుకు పరీక్ష ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు చేసే సమయంలో ఆ వ్యక్తి దాన్ని అర్థం చేసుకుని, తన ప్రయోజనాలపై దాని ప్రభావం గురించి హేతుబద్ధమైన తీర్మానం చేయగలడా అనేది.

selfTest.q: 3. మానసిక ఆసుపత్రిలోని రోగి స్పష్టమైన విరామంలో, పూర్తిగా అర్థం చేసుకుని అమ్మకం దస్తావేజుపై సంతకం చేస్తాడు. అది చెల్లుతుందా?
selfTest.a: చెల్లుతుంది. సాధారణంగా మనస్సు స్థిరంగా లేని వ్యక్తి స్థిరంగా ఉన్నప్పుడు కాంట్రాక్టు చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 12, దృష్టాంతం (a)).

selfTest.q: 4. 17 ఏళ్ల కొనుగోలుదారు ₹70,000 వాయిదాల్లో చెల్లిస్తానని వాగ్దానం చేస్తాడు. బకాయి కోసం అమ్మినవాడు దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అతను మైనర్, కాబట్టి ఒప్పందం void ( Mohori Bibee ).

selfTest.q: 5. మనస్సు స్థిరంగా లేని వ్యక్తికి సరఫరా చేసిన necessaries కోసం అతను వ్యక్తిగతంగా బాధ్యుడా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సరఫరాదారుకు అతని ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 68).

selfTest.q: 6. మైనర్ భూమి అమ్మడానికి హిందూ సహజ గార్డియన్‌కు కోర్టు అనుమతి కావాలా?
selfTest.a: కావాలి, కోర్టు ముందస్తు అనుమతి అవసరం (HMGA సెక్షన్ 8(2)(a)); అది లేకుండా చేసిన అమ్మకం మైనర్ కోరితే voidable (సెక్షన్ 8(3)).
