Inside it two boxes: free consent, Section 14, not caused by any of the five factors, gives a valid contract if the other essentials are met; and consent not free, caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake, which is voidable under Sections 19 and 19A, or void for a mutual mistake of fact under Section 20.
keyPoints: Consent is agreeing on the same thing in the same sense (Section 13). Consent is free if not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake (Section 14). "Caused" means it would not have been given "but for" the factor. Coercion, undue influence, fraud and misrepresentation make a contract voidable; a mutual mistake of essential fact makes it void. A mistake of Indian law, or a one-sided mistake of fact, does not make a contract voidable. No avoidance for misrepresentation or fraudulent silence if the truth could be discovered with ordinary diligence. A party who rescinds must restore benefits (Section 64) and may claim compensation (Section 75). Suit to rescind: three years from knowledge of the facts (Article 59).

caseLaws.name: Raffles v
caseLaws.facts: Wichelhaus (1864) Facts. 125 bales of Surat cotton were sold "to arrive ex Peerless from Bombay". Two ships named Peerless sailed from Bombay, one in October and one in December; the buyer meant the October ship and the seller tendered cotton from the December ship. Principle. The buyer's plea that he meant a different ship was held a good answer; the court gave judgment for the buyer without stating reasons, after counsel argued there was no consensus ad idem . (1864) 2 H & C 906 (Court of Exchequer). Why it matters. It is the standard example of parties not agreeing on the same thing in the same sense, which is the consent required by Section 13. Ningawwa v. Byrappa (1968) Facts. In 1938 a young, illiterate woman executed a gift deed in favour of her husband, believing it covered only two plots in one village. The husband had fraudulently included two valuable plots she had inherited in another village. Principle. Fraud as to the character of a document makes the transaction void; fraud as to its contents makes it only voidable. Here the fraud was as to the contents, so the gift was voidable, and her suit within three years of discovering the fraud succeeded. AIR 1968 SC 956 : (1968) 2 SCR 797. Why it matters. It marks the line between absence of consent (void) and consent caused by fraud (voidable). Central Inland Water Transport Corporation v. Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986) Facts. A Government company's service rules let it end a permanent employee's service by giving three months' notice in writing, or three months' basic pay and dearness allowance instead. Employees removed under that rule challenged it. Principle. Unfair terms imposed through inequality of bargaining power rarely fall within undue influence under Section 16(1); such an unconscionable term is void under Section 23 as opposed to public policy. (1986) 2 SCR 278. Why it matters. It shows the limits of the five factors and how the law deals with unfair bargains that are not caused by them.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 14 say about free consent?
selfTest.a: Consent is free when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.

selfTest.q: 2. What is the effect of consent caused by fraud?
selfTest.a: The contract is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused; he may instead insist on performance (Section 19).

selfTest.q: 3. When does a mistake make an agreement void?
selfTest.a: When both parties are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement (Section 20).

selfTest.q: 4. A seller lies about a house, but the buyer never believed him and bought after his own survey. Can the buyer avoid the contract?
selfTest.a: No. The lie did not cause his consent (Section 19, Explanation).

selfTest.q: 5. Within what time must a suit to rescind a contract be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to rescind first became known to him (Article 59, Limitation Act).

selfTest.q: 6. Is a gift deed obtained by lying about which plots it covers void or voidable?
selfTest.a: Voidable, because the fraud was as to its contents, not its character ( Ningawwa v. Byrappa ).

law-of-contract-i-u2-t7.subtitle: Sections 18 and 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Misrepresentation is a false statement, or a similar wrong, that misleads the other party without any intent to deceive (Section 18). The person who makes it may honestly believe it. The other party relies on it and enters into the contract. Section 18 has three kinds: a positive assertion of something untrue, made without proper grounds, though the maker believes it (Section 18(1)); a breach of duty that, without intent to deceive, gains an advantage by misleading the other (Section 18(2)); causing, however innocently , a party to make a mistake about the substance of the thing (Section 18(3)). Effect. The contract is voidable at the misled party's option. He may instead insist on performance and be put in the position he would have been in if the statement had been true (Section 19). He has no right to avoid it if he could have found the truth "with ordinary diligence " (Exception), or if the statement did not cause his consent (Explanation). In exams, the line between misrepresentation and fraud earns the marks. In real life this covers the honest but careless seller, broker or agent.
legalProvision: Section 18. "Misrepresentation" defined. "Misrepresentation" means and includes— (1) the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true; (2) any breach of duty which, without an intent to deceive, gains an advantage to the person committing it, or any one claiming under him; by misleading another to his prejudice, or to the prejudice of any one claiming under him; (3) causing, however innocently, a party to an agreement, to make a mistake as to the substance of the thing which is the subject of the agreement.

Section 19 (relevant parts). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. A party to a contract whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation, may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true. Exception. —If such consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence, fraudulent within the meaning of section 17, the contract, nevertheless, is not voidable, if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. Explanation. —A fraud or misrepresentation which did not cause the consent to a contract of the party on whom such fraud was practised, or to whom such misrepresentation was made, does not render a contract voidable. Illustration (b). A, by a misrepresentation, leads B erroneously to believe that, five hundred maunds of indigo are made annually at A's factory. B examines the accounts of the factory, which show that only four hundred maunds of indigo have been made. After this B buys the factory. The contract is not voidable on account of A's misrepresentation.
In simple words

Section 18(1): saying something untrue as a fact, when your information does not justify saying it, even though you believe it. Section 18(2): failing in a duty you owe, without meaning to deceive, in a way that misleads the other to his loss and brings you (or someone claiming under you) a gain. Section 18(3): innocently making the other party mistaken about what the thing really is. Section 19: the misled party may avoid the contract , or keep it and insist on being put where he would be if the statement were true. He loses the right to avoid if he could easily have found the truth, or if the statement did not make him agree.
en.meaning:
Misrepresentation is an untrue statement of fact (or a breach of duty, or an innocent cause of mistake) that induces the other party to contract, made without intent to deceive .

Elements.

Element What it means Source 1. A representation of fact A statement about a past or present fact. Not a mere opinion, sales talk ("best shop in town") or a statement of future intention Section 18(1) "positive assertion … of that which is not true" 2. It is untrue The fact stated is false Section 18(1) 3. No intent to deceive The maker believes it, or has no dishonest purpose Section 18(1) "though he believes it to be true"; 18(2) "without an intent to deceive" 4. Made without proper grounds (for 18(1)) His information does not warrant the statement Section 18(1) "in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it" 5. It caused the consent He would not have agreed but for it Section 14; Section 19 Explanation 6. Truth not discoverable with ordinary diligence If he could easily have checked, he cannot avoid Section 19 Exception

Why the law allows avoidance. The misled party's consent was not free (Section 14). The law does not treat the maker as a cheat; it simply lets the misled party undo a bargain that rested on a false basis.

Misrepresentation and fraud . Both are false statements; the difference is the mind of the maker. Fraud (Section 17) needs an intent to deceive (or to induce the contract by deceit ). In Derry v. Peek (1889), the House of Lords held that "fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made (1) knowingly, or (2) without belief in its truth, or (3) recklessly, careless whether it be true or false". A statement made in an honest belief is not fraud, even if there were no reasonable grounds for it. Under the Indian Act, such an honest but unwarranted statement falls within Section 18(1).
keyPoints: Misrepresentation is an untrue statement, breach of duty or innocent cause of mistake, made without intent to deceive (Section 18). It must be a statement of fact, and it must have caused the consent. It makes the contract voidable at the misled party's option; he may instead insist on performance (Section 19). No avoidance if the truth could be discovered with ordinary diligence (Exception; Illustration (b)). On rescission: restore benefits (Section 64), compensation for damage (Section 75). Honest belief, even careless, is not fraud ( Derry v. Peek ). Right to rescind may be lost by affirmation, delay, third-party rights or impossibility of restitution.

caseLaws.name: Derry v
caseLaws.facts: Peek (1889) Facts. A tramway company's special Act allowed steam power only with the Board of Trade's consent. The directors' prospectus said the company had the right to use steam power. The Board of Trade refused consent, and the company was wound up. Principle. Fraud is proved only when a false statement is made "knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly"; a statement made in honest belief is not fraud, even without reasonable grounds. (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (House of Lords). Why it matters. It draws the line between fraud and an honest but careless statement, which is misrepresentation under Section 18(1). Dick Bentley Productions v. Harold Smith (Motors) (1965) Facts. A car dealer told a buyer that a Bentley had done only 20,000 miles since a replacement engine and gearbox. It had in fact done about 100,000 miles. The dealer was in a position to know the true history; the buyer was not. Principle. A representation made to induce a contract, and which does induce it, is prima facie a warranty (a term), so the buyer could claim damages. [1965] 1 WLR 623 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It shows the contrast between a statement that only induces a contract (misrepresentation) and one that becomes a term (breach and damages).

selfTest.q: 1. How does misrepresentation differ from fraud?
selfTest.a: In misrepresentation the maker has no intent to deceive and may believe the statement. Fraud needs an intent to deceive (Section 17; Derry v. Peek ).

selfTest.q: 2. When is a contract not voidable despite a misrepresentation?
selfTest.a: When the misled party had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, or when the misrepresentation did not cause his consent (Section 19).

selfTest.q: 3. What may the misled party do besides avoiding the contract?
selfTest.a: Insist that the contract be performed and that he be put in the position he would have been in if the statement had been true (Section 19).

selfTest.q: 4. A seller honestly but wrongly leads a buyer to think a ring is gold when it is brass. Which clause of Section 18 applies?
selfTest.a: Section 18(3): innocently causing a mistake as to the substance of the thing.

selfTest.q: 5. Is "this flat will double in value in five years" a misrepresentation?
selfTest.a: Usually not. It is a forecast or opinion, not a statement of existing fact.

selfTest.q: 6. Within what time must a suit to rescind for misrepresentation be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to rescind first became known to him (Article 59).

legalProvision: Section 18. "Misrepresentation" defined. "Misrepresentation" means and includes— (1) the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true; (2) any breach of duty which, without an intent to deceive, gains an advantage to the person committing it, or any one claiming under him; by misleading another to his prejudice, or to the prejudice of any one claiming under him; (3) causing, however innocently, a party to an agreement, to make a mistake as to the substance of the thing which is the subject of the agreement.

Section 19 (relevant parts). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. A party to a contract whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation, may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true. Exception. —If such consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence, fraudulent within the meaning of section 17, the contract, nevertheless, is not voidable, if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. Explanation. —A fraud or misrepresentation which did not cause the consent to a contract of the party on whom such fraud was practised, or to whom such misrepresentation was made, does not render a contract voidable. Illustration (b). A, by a misrepresentation, leads B erroneously to believe that, five hundred maunds of indigo are made annually at A's factory. B examines the accounts of the factory, which show that only four hundred maunds of indigo have been made. After this B buys the factory. The contract is not voidable on account of A's misrepresentation.
సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే

సెక్షన్ 18(1): తనకున్న సమాచారం ఆధారంగా చెప్పలేని విషయాన్ని వాస్తవంగా చెప్పడం; అది నిజం కాదు; కానీ చెప్పినవాడు నమ్మాడు. సెక్షన్ 18(2): మోసగించే ఉద్దేశం లేకుండా, తాను నిర్వర్తించాల్సిన విధిని ఉల్లంఘించడం; దాని వల్ల ఎదుటివాడు తప్పుదారి పట్టి నష్టపోతాడు, తనకు (లేదా తన తరఫున హక్కు కోరేవాడికి) లాభం వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 18(3): ఆ వస్తువు అసలు ఏమిటో అనే విషయంలో ఎదుటి పక్షం పొరపాటు పడేలా అమాయకంగా చేయడం. సెక్షన్ 19: తప్పుదారి పట్టినవాడు కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయవచ్చు; లేదా ఉంచుకుని, ప్రకటన నిజమైతే ఉండే స్థితిలో ఉంచమని పట్టుబట్టవచ్చు. సులభంగా నిజం తెలుసుకోగలిగి ఉంటే, లేదా ఆ ప్రకటన వల్ల ఒప్పుకోకపోతే, రద్దు చేసే హక్కు పోతుంది.
te.meaning:
తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం అంటే ఎదుటి పక్షాన్ని కాంట్రాక్టులోకి దించే, నిజం కాని వాస్తవ ప్రకటన (లేదా విధి ఉల్లంఘన, లేదా అమాయకంగా కలిగించిన పొరపాటు); ఇది మోసగించే ఉద్దేశం లేకుండా జరుగుతుంది.

అంశాలు.

అంశం అర్థం ఆధారం 1. వాస్తవం గురించి ప్రకటన గతం లేదా ప్రస్తుతం ఉన్న వాస్తవం గురించి ప్రకటన. కేవలం అభిప్రాయం, అమ్మకపు పొగడ్త ("ఊళ్లో ఇదే బెస్ట్ షాపు"), భవిష్యత్తు ఉద్దేశం కాదు సెక్షన్ 18(1) "positive assertion … of that which is not true" 2. అది నిజం కాదు చెప్పిన వాస్తవం తప్పు సెక్షన్ 18(1) 3. మోసగించే ఉద్దేశం లేదు చెప్పినవాడు నమ్ముతాడు, లేదా అతనికి నిజాయితీ లేని ఉద్దేశం లేదు సెక్షన్ 18(1) "though he believes it to be true"; 18(2) "without an intent to deceive" 4. తగిన ఆధారం లేకుండా చెప్పడం (18(1) కోసం) అతని సమాచారం ఆ ప్రకటనను సమర్థించదు సెక్షన్ 18(1) "in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it" 5. అది సమ్మతికి కారణమైంది ఆ ప్రకటన లేకపోతే అతను ఒప్పుకునేవాడు కాదు సెక్షన్ 14; సెక్షన్ 19 Explanation 6. సాధారణ జాగ్రత్తతో నిజం తెలుసుకోలేకపోవడం సులభంగా తనిఖీ చేయగలిగి ఉంటే రద్దు చేయలేడు సెక్షన్ 19 Exception

చట్టం రద్దుకు ఎందుకు అనుమతిస్తుంది. తప్పుదారి పట్టినవాడి సమ్మతి స్వేచ్ఛాయుతమైనది కాదు (సెక్షన్ 14). చట్టం చెప్పినవాణ్ని మోసగాడిగా చూడదు; తప్పుడు పునాదిపై నిలిచిన బేరాన్ని తప్పుదారి పట్టినవాడు రద్దు చేసుకునే అవకాశం మాత్రమే ఇస్తుంది.

తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం, మోసం. రెండూ తప్పుడు ప్రకటనలే; తేడా చెప్పినవాడి మనసులో ఉంటుంది. మోసానికి (సెక్షన్ 17) మోసగించే ఉద్దేశం (లేదా మోసంతో కాంట్రాక్టులోకి దించే ఉద్దేశం) కావాలి. Derry v. Peek (1889) కేసులో హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్ ఇలా చెప్పింది: " fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made (1) knowingly, or (2) without belief in its truth, or (3) recklessly, careless whether it be true or false". నిజాయితీగా నమ్మి చేసిన ప్రకటన, దానికి సహేతుకమైన ఆధారాలు లేకపోయినా, మోసం కాదు. భారత చట్టం ప్రకారం అలాంటి నిజాయితీతో కూడిన, కానీ ఆధారం లేని ప్రకటన సెక్షన్ 18(1) కిందకు వస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం మోసం నుంచి ఎలా భిన్నం?
selfTest.a: తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యంలో చెప్పినవాడికి మోసగించే ఉద్దేశం ఉండదు, అతను ఆ ప్రకటనను నమ్మవచ్చు. మోసానికి మోసగించే ఉద్దేశం కావాలి (సెక్షన్ 17; Derry v. Peek ).

selfTest.q: 2. తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం ఉన్నా కాంట్రాక్టు ఎప్పుడు రద్దు చేయదగినది కాదు?
selfTest.a: తప్పుదారి పట్టినవాడికి సాధారణ జాగ్రత్తతో నిజం తెలుసుకునే మార్గం ఉన్నప్పుడు, లేదా ఆ ప్రకటన అతని సమ్మతికి కారణం కానప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 19).

selfTest.q: 3. కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయడం కాకుండా తప్పుదారి పట్టినవాడు ఏం చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు అమలు కావాలని, ప్రకటన నిజమైతే ఉండే స్థితిలో తనను ఉంచాలని పట్టుబట్టవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 19).

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక అమ్మకందారు నిజాయితీగానే కానీ తప్పుగా, ఇత్తడి ఉంగరం బంగారమని కొనుగోలుదారు అనుకునేలా చేస్తాడు. సెక్షన్ 18 లో ఏ క్లాజు వర్తిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 18(3): వస్తువు స్వరూపం గురించి అమాయకంగా పొరపాటు కలిగించడం.

selfTest.q: 5. "ఈ ఫ్లాట్ విలువ ఐదేళ్లలో రెట్టింపు అవుతుంది" అనేది తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యమా?
selfTest.a: సాధారణంగా కాదు. అది అంచనా లేదా అభిప్రాయం; ఇప్పుడు ఉన్న వాస్తవ ప్రకటన కాదు.

selfTest.q: 6. తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం కారణంగా రద్దు కోసం దావా ఎంత కాలంలో వేయాలి?
selfTest.a: రద్దు చేసే హక్కు ఇచ్చే వాస్తవాలు వాదికి మొదట తెలిసినప్పటి నుంచి మూడు సంవత్సరాలలో (Article 59).

hi.inOneMinute: Misrepresentation is a false statement, or a similar wrong, that misleads the other party without any intent to deceive (Section 18). The person who makes it may honestly believe it. The other party relies on it and enters into the contract. Section 18 has three kinds: a positive assertion of something untrue, made without proper grounds, though the maker believes it (Section 18(1)); a breach of duty that, without intent to deceive, gains an advantage by misleading the other (Section 18(2)); causing, however innocently , a party to make a mistake about the substance of the thing (Section 18(3)). Effect. The contract is voidable at the misled party's option. He may instead insist on performance and be put in the position he would have been in if the statement had been true (Section 19). He has no right to avoid it if he could have found the truth "with ordinary diligence " (Exception), or if the statement did not cause his consent (Explanation). In exams, the line between misrepresentation and fraud earns the marks. In real life this covers the honest but careless seller, broker or agent.
legalProvision: Section 18. "Misrepresentation" defined. "Misrepresentation" means and includes— (1) the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true; (2) any breach of duty which, without an intent to deceive, gains an advantage to the person committing it, or any one claiming under him; by misleading another to his prejudice, or to the prejudice of any one claiming under him; (3) causing, however innocently, a party to an agreement, to make a mistake as to the substance of the thing which is the subject of the agreement.

Section 19 (relevant parts). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. A party to a contract whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation, may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true. Exception. —If such consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence, fraudulent within the meaning of section 17, the contract, nevertheless, is not voidable, if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. Explanation. —A fraud or misrepresentation which did not cause the consent to a contract of the party on whom such fraud was practised, or to whom such misrepresentation was made, does not render a contract voidable. Illustration (b). A, by a misrepresentation, leads B erroneously to believe that, five hundred maunds of indigo are made annually at A's factory. B examines the accounts of the factory, which show that only four hundred maunds of indigo have been made. After this B buys the factory. The contract is not voidable on account of A's misrepresentation.
In simple words

Section 18(1): saying something untrue as a fact, when your information does not justify saying it, even though you believe it. Section 18(2): failing in a duty you owe, without meaning to deceive, in a way that misleads the other to his loss and brings you (or someone claiming under you) a gain. Section 18(3): innocently making the other party mistaken about what the thing really is. Section 19: the misled party may avoid the contract , or keep it and insist on being put where he would be if the statement were true. He loses the right to avoid if he could easily have found the truth, or if the statement did not make him agree.
hi.meaning: Misrepresentation is an untrue statement of fact (or a breach of duty, or an innocent cause of mistake) that induces the other party to contract, made without intent to deceive . Elements. Element What it means Source 1. A representation of fact A statement about a past or present fact. Not a mere opinion, sales talk ("best shop in town") or a statement of future intention Section 18(1) "positive assertion … of that which is not true" 2. It is untrue The fact stated is false Section 18(1) 3. No intent to deceive The maker believes it, or has no dishonest purpose Section 18(1) "though he believes it to be true"; 18(2) "without an intent to deceive" 4. Made without proper grounds (for 18(1)) His information does not warrant the statement Section 18(1) "in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it" 5. It caused the consent He would not have agreed but for it Section 14; Section 19 Explanation 6. Truth not discoverable with ordinary diligence If he could easily have checked, he cannot avoid Section 19 Exception Why the law allows avoidance. The misled party's consent was not free (Section 14). The law does not treat the maker as a cheat; it simply lets the misled party undo a bargain that rested on a false basis. Misrepresentation and fraud . Both are false statements; the difference is the mind of the maker. Fraud (Section 17) needs an intent to deceive (or to induce the contract by deceit ). In Derry v. Peek (1889), the House of Lords held that "fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made (1) knowingly, or (2) without belief in its truth, or (3) recklessly, careless whether it be true or false". A statement made in an honest belief is not fraud, even if there were no reasonable grounds for it. Under the Indian Act, such an honest but unwarranted statement falls within Section 18(1).
keyPoints: Misrepresentation is an untrue statement, breach of duty or innocent cause of mistake, made without intent to deceive (Section 18). It must be a statement of fact, and it must have caused the consent. It makes the contract voidable at the misled party's option; he may instead insist on performance (Section 19). No avoidance if the truth could be discovered with ordinary diligence (Exception; Illustration (b)). On rescission: restore benefits (Section 64), compensation for damage (Section 75). Honest belief, even careless, is not fraud ( Derry v. Peek ). Right to rescind may be lost by affirmation, delay, third-party rights or impossibility of restitution.

caseLaws.name: Derry v
caseLaws.facts: Peek (1889) Facts. A tramway company's special Act allowed steam power only with the Board of Trade's consent. The directors' prospectus said the company had the right to use steam power. The Board of Trade refused consent, and the company was wound up. Principle. Fraud is proved only when a false statement is made "knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly"; a statement made in honest belief is not fraud, even without reasonable grounds. (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (House of Lords). Why it matters. It draws the line between fraud and an honest but careless statement, which is misrepresentation under Section 18(1). Dick Bentley Productions v. Harold Smith (Motors) (1965) Facts. A car dealer told a buyer that a Bentley had done only 20,000 miles since a replacement engine and gearbox. It had in fact done about 100,000 miles. The dealer was in a position to know the true history; the buyer was not. Principle. A representation made to induce a contract, and which does induce it, is prima facie a warranty (a term), so the buyer could claim damages. [1965] 1 WLR 623 (Court of Appeal). Why it matters. It shows the contrast between a statement that only induces a contract (misrepresentation) and one that becomes a term (breach and damages).

selfTest.q: 1. How does misrepresentation differ from fraud?
selfTest.a: In misrepresentation the maker has no intent to deceive and may believe the statement. Fraud needs an intent to deceive (Section 17; Derry v. Peek ).

selfTest.q: 2. When is a contract not voidable despite a misrepresentation?
selfTest.a: When the misled party had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, or when the misrepresentation did not cause his consent (Section 19).

selfTest.q: 3. What may the misled party do besides avoiding the contract?
selfTest.a: Insist that the contract be performed and that he be put in the position he would have been in if the statement had been true (Section 19).

selfTest.q: 4. A seller honestly but wrongly leads a buyer to think a ring is gold when it is brass. Which clause of Section 18 applies?
selfTest.a: Section 18(3): innocently causing a mistake as to the substance of the thing.

selfTest.q: 5. Is "this flat will double in value in five years" a misrepresentation?
selfTest.a: Usually not. It is a forecast or opinion, not a statement of existing fact.

selfTest.q: 6. Within what time must a suit to rescind for misrepresentation be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from when the facts entitling the plaintiff to rescind first became known to him (Article 59).

law-of-contract-i-u2-t2.subtitle: Sections 10, 11, 68 and 183 to 184 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872; section 33 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: A minor 's agreement is void from the very beginning ( void ab initio ). It is not merely voidable . The minor cannot be sued on it, cannot be made to pay damages for breaking it, and cannot make it valid later by ratification . The Privy Council settled this in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903). The law still softens the rule in a few places: A supplier of necessaries is paid from the minor's property (Section 68). A minor may receive a benefit , for example as a mortgagee who has paid the money. A court may ask a minor to give back a benefit he still holds (Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 33(2)(b)). A guardian may, within his powers and for the minor's benefit, make a contract that binds the minor. In exams, this is a favourite problem question. Marks come from Mohori Bibee , the "no ratification, no estoppel" points, restitution, necessaries, and the minor as beneficiary , partner and agent. In real life, it tells a lender or a shop what it can and cannot recover after dealing with someone under 18.
legalProvision: Section 2(g). An agreement not enforceable by law is said to be void;

Section 10 (first paragraph). All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 11. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person.

Section 184. Who may be an agent. As between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent, but no person who is not of the age of majority and of sound mind can become an agent, so as to be responsible to his principal according to the provisions in that behalf herein contained.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 33(2). Where a defendant successfully resists any suit on the ground— … (b) that the agreement sought to be enforced against him in the suit is void by reason of his not having been competent to contract under section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), the court may, if the defendant has received any benefit under the agreement from the other party, require him to restore, so far as may be, such benefit to that party, to the extent to which he or his estate has benefited thereby.

Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Section 30(1). A person who is a minor according to the law to which he is subject may not be a partner in a firm, but, with the consent of all the partners for the time being, he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership.
In simple words

Sections 2(g), 10, 11: a minor is not "competent to contract ", so his agreement is not a contract. It is an agreement not enforceable by law, that is, void. Section 68: a person who supplies necessaries to a minor is repaid out of the minor's property , not by the minor personally. Section 184: a minor can act as an agent for others, but he cannot be made answerable to his principal. Specific Relief Act, Section 33(2)(b): if a minor wins a suit because his agreement is void, the court may make him give back the benefit he received, but only to the extent he or his estate is still better off. Partnership Act, Section 30: a minor cannot be a partner, but can be admitted to the benefits of a partnership.
en.meaning:
A minor's agreement is an agreement in which one of the parties had not completed the age of majority (generally 18) on the date it was made. The Act does not say "void" in so many words. The Privy Council reached that result in Mohori Bibee by reading Sections 2, 10 and 11 together, and by looking at Sections 68, 183, 184, 64 and 65 (see Diagram 1 ). Diagram 1. The Privy Council read the Act's sections together and concluded that a minor's agreement is void, not voidable. flowchart TD A["Section 11
A minor is not competent to contract"] B["Section 10
Only agreements of parties competent
to contract are contracts"] C["Section 2(g)
An agreement not enforceable by law is void"] D["Sections 68, 183, 184
The Act treats a minor as unable to bind himself"] E["Sections 64, 65
Assume a contract between competent parties
so they do not apply"] R["RESULT: minor's agreement is VOID AB INITIO
(Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, 1903)"] F["No estoppel where the truth is known
No order to repay the money"] A --> B B --> C C --> R D --> R E --> R R --> F Text description Section 11: a minor is not competent to contract. Section 10: only agreements by competent parties are contracts. Section 2(g): an agreement not enforceable by law is void. Sections 68, 183 and 184 show the Act treats minors as unable to bind themselves. Sections 64 and 65 assume a contract between competent parties, so they do not apply. Result: a minor's agreement is void ab initio; no estoppel where the truth is known; no order to repay. Void ab initio means void from the start. The agreement never was a contract. Nobody needs to cancel it, and nobody can make it good later. Why the law takes this strict view. To protect minors. A young person may not understand a bargain and may be easily exploited. Making every agreement void is the strongest protection. Because it follows from the Act. Section 10 requires "parties competent to contract". If one party is not competent, there is no contract to call voidable. To keep the rule simple. Lenders and sellers are told plainly: deal with a minor at your own risk. What is "the effect"? The topic asks what follows from this voidness. The answer has many parts: no suit on the agreement, no ratification, no estoppel , limited restitution , necessaries, benefits to the minor, guardian's contracts, sureties, and the minor as partner, agent and shareholder. Each is explained below.
keyPoints: A minor's agreement is void ab initio ( Mohori Bibee , 1903). It cannot be ratified on attaining majority; a fresh agreement with fresh consideration is needed ( Suraj Narain Dube ). A false statement of age does not estop the minor ( Mohori Bibee ; Ajudhia Prasad ). Sections 64 and 65 do not apply; restitution only under Specific Relief Act Section 33, and only to the extent of benefit. Necessaries: reimbursed from the minor's property, never a personal liability (Section 68). A minor can take a benefit, for example as a mortgagee who has paid in full ( Raghava Chariar ). A minor can be an agent but is not responsible to his principal (Section 184). A minor can only be admitted to the benefits of a partnership (Partnership Act Section 30). A guardian's contract binds the minor if within the guardian's competence and for the minor's benefit ( Srikakulam ). On a surety for a minor's debt, give both views ( Edavan ; Kashiba ).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. An infant mortgaged his houses on 20 July 1895 to a money lender for Rs. 20,000. The lender's attorney had received written notice of the minority from the infant's court-appointed guardian. The infant sued to cancel the mortgage; the lender asked that at least the money advanced be repaid. Principle. An infant is not competent to contract, so his agreement is void. There was no estoppel because the lender knew the truth, and Sections 64 and 65 did not apply; no repayment was ordered. (1903) LR 30 IA 114 : ILR 30 Cal 539 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It decided that a minor's agreement is void, not voidable, and is the starting point of every answer on this topic. Suraj Narain Dube v. Sukhu Aheer (1928) Facts. Sukhu borrowed Rs. 40 on a bond while a minor (1919). After majority (1923), he and his mother executed a new bond for Rs. 76, being the old Rs. 40 with interest. Principle. A minor's agreement "is altogether void", and the earlier advance in minority is not consideration for a fresh promise after majority. AIR 1928 All 440 (Full Bench, majority). Why it matters. It shows that a minor's agreement cannot be ratified on attaining majority. Ajudhia Prasad v. Chandan Lal (1937) Facts. Two persons over 18 but under 21, who had a certificated guardian, executed a mortgage in 1925. Their minority was concealed. The lower court found fraud and decreed the money. Principle. "neither Section 64 nor Section 65 deals with a case where a party is incompetent to enter into a contract at all"; no personal money decree can be passed against a minor, and estoppel cannot be pleaded against the statute. AIR 1937 All 610 (Full Bench). Why it matters. Even a minor who deceives the other side cannot be made to pay under the void agreement. Srikakulam Subrahmanyam v. Kurra Subba Rao (1948) Facts. A Hindu widow, as guardian of her minor son, agreed in writing in 1935 to sell family land for Rs. 17,200 to pay off the dead father's debts. The buyers paid off a Rs. 1,200 mortgage debt and were put in possession, but no sale deed was executed or registered. The minor later sued for possession. Principle. A contract by a guardian binds the minor if it is within the guardian's competence and for the minor's benefit; here the minor was the "transferor" and was barred by Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. (1948) 50 Bom LR 646 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It marks the line between a minor's own void agreement and a valid contract made on his behalf by his guardian. Edavan Kavingal Kelappan Nambiar v. Moolakal Kunhi Raman (1956) Facts. A minor took money in a kuri (chit) transaction, and a surety guaranteed the instalments. The suit failed against the minor, but the trial court decreed against the surety. Principle. "the liability of the surety is only ancillary and can rest only on a valid obligation on the part of the party"; the surety was not liable. AIR 1957 Mad 164. Why it matters. It answers whether a surety for a minor's void debt can be sued, and explains Kashiba as a case of indemnity.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a minor's agreement void or voidable?
selfTest.a: Void ab initio ( Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose , 1903).

selfTest.q: 2. A minor borrows ₹50,000 and on turning 18 writes "I confirm this loan". Is he now liable?
selfTest.a: No. A void agreement cannot be ratified. A fresh agreement with fresh consideration is needed ( Suraj Narain Dube ).

selfTest.q: 3. A minor lies that he is 21 and gets a loan. Can the lender use estoppel to stop him pleading minority?
selfTest.a: No. Estoppel does not take away the protection of minority ( Mohori Bibee ; Ajudhia Prasad ).

selfTest.q: 4. What can a court order a minor to give back?
selfTest.a: Under Specific Relief Act Section 33(2)(b), the benefit he received, only to the extent he or his estate has benefited.

selfTest.q: 5. Is a minor personally liable for necessaries?
selfTest.a: No. The supplier is reimbursed from the minor's property (Section 68).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a minor enforce a mortgage in his favour after he has paid the whole mortgage money?
selfTest.a: Yes ( Raghava Chariar v. Srinivasa Raghava Chariar , 1916).

Is a minor's agreement void or voidable? Void ab initio Mohori Bibee (1903)
Can he ratify it at 18? No; a fresh agreement with fresh consideration is needed Suraj Narain Dube (1928)
Is he estopped by a false statement of age? No Mohori Bibee; Ajudhia Prasad (1937); BSA Section 121
Must he repay under Sections 64 or 65? No Mohori Bibee; Ajudhia Prasad
Can the court order him to restore a benefit? Yes, in its discretion, to the extent he is still benefited Specific Relief Act Section 33
Necessaries? Supplier paid from his property, not by him personally Section 68
Can he take a benefit? Yes, where he has performed fully Raghava Chariar (1916)
Can he be an agent? Yes, but not responsible to his principal Section 184
Guardian's contract? Binds him if within the guardian's competence and for his benefit Srikakulam (1948); Mir Sarwarjan (1911); HMGA Section 8
Surety for his debt? Views differ; indemnity is enforceable Edavan (1956); Kashiba (1894)
Partner? Only admitted to the benefits Partnership Act Section 30

legalProvision: Section 2(g). An agreement not enforceable by law is said to be void;

Section 10 (first paragraph). All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 11. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person.

Section 184. Who may be an agent. As between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent, but no person who is not of the age of majority and of sound mind can become an agent, so as to be responsible to his principal according to the provisions in that behalf herein contained.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 33(2). Where a defendant successfully resists any suit on the ground— … (b) that the agreement sought to be enforced against him in the suit is void by reason of his not having been competent to contract under section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), the court may, if the defendant has received any benefit under the agreement from the other party, require him to restore, so far as may be, such benefit to that party, to the extent to which he or his estate has benefited thereby.

Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Section 30(1). A person who is a minor according to the law to which he is subject may not be a partner in a firm, but, with the consent of all the partners for the time being, he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership.
సులభమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్లు 2(g), 10, 11: మైనర్ "competent to contract " కాదు, కాబట్టి అతని ఒప్పందం కాంట్రాక్టు కాదు. అది చట్టం అమలు చేయించని ఒప్పందం, అంటే void. సెక్షన్ 68: మైనర్‌కు necessaries సరఫరా చేసినవారికి మైనర్ ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లిస్తారు, మైనర్ వ్యక్తిగతంగా కాదు. సెక్షన్ 184: మైనర్ ఇతరుల తరఫున ఏజెంటుగా పని చేయవచ్చు, కానీ తన ప్రిన్సిపల్‌కు అతన్ని బాధ్యుడిని చేయలేం. Specific Relief Act, సెక్షన్ 33(2)(b): ఒప్పందం void కాబట్టి మైనర్ దావాలో గెలిస్తే, తాను పొందిన ప్రయోజనాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వమని కోర్టు ఆదేశించవచ్చు , కానీ అతను లేదా అతని ఆస్తి ఇంకా ఎంత లాభపడి ఉందో ఆ మేరకు మాత్రమే. Partnership Act, సెక్షన్ 30: మైనర్ భాగస్వామి కాలేడు, కానీ భాగస్వామ్యపు ప్రయోజనాలకు చేర్చుకోవచ్చు .

మైనర్ ఒప్పందం అంటే ఒప్పందం చేసిన తేదీకి ఒక పక్షం మేజర్ వయస్సు (సాధారణంగా 18) పూర్తి చేయని ఒప్పందం. చట్టం "void" అని నేరుగా చెప్పదు. సెక్షన్లు 2, 10, 11 కలిపి చదివి, సెక్షన్లు 68, 183, 184, 64, 65 ను పరిశీలించి Mohori Bibee లో ప్రివీ కౌన్సిల్ ఆ ఫలితానికి వచ్చింది ( Diagram 1 చూడండి). Diagram 1. చట్టంలోని సెక్షన్లను కలిపి చదివి, మైనర్ ఒప్పందం voidable కాదు, void అని ప్రివీ కౌన్సిల్ తేల్చింది. flowchart TD A["సెక్షన్ 11
మైనర్ కాంట్రాక్టు చేయడానికి సమర్థుడు కాదు"] B["సెక్షన్ 10
సమర్థులైన పక్షాల ఒప్పందాలే కాంట్రాక్టులు"] C["సెక్షన్ 2(g)
చట్టం అమలు చేయించని ఒప్పందం void"] D["సెక్షన్లు 68, 183, 184
మైనర్ తనను తాను బంధించుకోలేడని చట్టం చూపుతుంది"] E["సెక్షన్లు 64, 65
సమర్థుల మధ్య కాంట్రాక్టును ఊహిస్తాయి
కాబట్టి వర్తించవు"] R["ఫలితం: మైనర్ ఒప్పందం మొదటి నుంచే VOID
(Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, 1903)"] F["నిజం తెలిసినప్పుడు estoppel లేదు
డబ్బు తిరిగి ఇవ్వమని ఆదేశం లేదు"] A --> B B --> C C --> R D --> R E --> R R --> F వచన వివరణ సెక్షన్ 11: మైనర్ సమర్థుడు కాదు. సెక్షన్ 10: సమర్థుల ఒప్పందాలే కాంట్రాక్టులు. సెక్షన్ 2(g): చట్టం అమలు చేయించని ఒప్పందం void. సెక్షన్లు 68, 183, 184 మైనర్ తనను బంధించుకోలేడని చూపుతాయి. సెక్షన్లు 64, 65 వర్తించవు. ఫలితం: మైనర్ ఒప్పందం మొదటి నుంచే void. Void ab initio అంటే మొదటి నుంచే చెల్లనిది. ఆ ఒప్పందం ఎప్పుడూ కాంట్రాక్టు కాదు. దాన్ని ఎవరూ రద్దు చేయాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు, తర్వాత ఎవరూ దాన్ని సరిచేయలేరు. చట్టం ఇంత కఠినంగా ఎందుకు ఉంది. మైనర్లను రక్షించడానికి. చిన్న వయస్సు వ్యక్తి బేరాన్ని అర్థం చేసుకోలేకపోవచ్చు, సులభంగా మోసపోవచ్చు. ప్రతి ఒప్పందాన్ని void చేయడమే బలమైన రక్షణ. చట్టం నుంచే ఇది వస్తుంది కాబట్టి. సెక్షన్ 10 "parties competent to contract" ను కోరుతుంది. ఒక పక్షం సమర్థుడు కాకపోతే, voidable అని పిలవడానికి కాంట్రాక్టే లేదు. నియమం సరళంగా ఉండటానికి. అప్పిచ్చేవారికి, అమ్మేవారికి స్పష్టంగా చెబుతుంది: మైనర్‌తో వ్యవహరిస్తే రిస్కు మీదే. "ప్రభావం" అంటే ఏమిటి? ఈ void స్వభావం నుంచి ఏం జరుగుతుందని ఈ అంశం అడుగుతుంది. సమాధానంలో చాలా భాగాలు ఉన్నాయి: ఒప్పందంపై దావా లేదు, ratification లేదు, estoppel లేదు, పరిమిత restitution , necessaries, మైనర్‌కు ప్రయోజనాలు, గార్డియన్ కాంట్రాక్టులు, జామీనుదారులు, భాగస్వామిగా, ఏజెంటుగా, షేర్‌హోల్డర్‌గా మైనర్. ప్రతి దాన్నీ కింద వివరిస్తాం.

selfTest.q: 1. మైనర్ ఒప్పందం void యా voidable యా?
selfTest.a: Void ab initio ( Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose , 1903).

selfTest.q: 2. ఒక మైనర్ ₹50,000 అప్పు తీసుకుని, 18 నిండాక "ఈ అప్పును ధృవీకరిస్తున్నాను" అని రాస్తాడు. ఇప్పుడు బాధ్యుడా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. Void ఒప్పందాన్ని ratify చేయలేం. కొత్త ప్రతిఫలంతో కొత్త ఒప్పందం కావాలి ( Suraj Narain Dube ).

selfTest.q: 3. తనకు 21 ఏళ్లని అబద్ధం చెప్పి మైనర్ అప్పు తీసుకుంటాడు. మైనారిటీ వాదించకుండా అప్పిచ్చినవాడు estoppel ఉపయోగించగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. Estoppel మైనారిటీ రక్షణను తీసివేయదు ( Mohori Bibee ; Ajudhia Prasad ).

selfTest.q: 4. మైనర్‌ను కోర్టు ఏం తిరిగి ఇవ్వమని ఆదేశించగలదు?
selfTest.a: Specific Relief Act సెక్షన్ 33(2)(b) కింద, అతను పొందిన ప్రయోజనాన్ని, అతను లేదా అతని ఆస్తి లాభపడిన మేరకు మాత్రమే.

selfTest.q: 5. Necessaries కోసం మైనర్ వ్యక్తిగతంగా బాధ్యుడా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సరఫరాదారుకు మైనర్ ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 68).

selfTest.q: 6. తనఖా డబ్బు మొత్తం ఇచ్చిన తర్వాత, తన పేరున ఉన్న తనఖాను మైనర్ అమలు చేయించగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును ( Raghava Chariar v. Srinivasa Raghava Chariar , 1916).

hi.inOneMinute: A minor 's agreement is void from the very beginning ( void ab initio ). It is not merely voidable . The minor cannot be sued on it, cannot be made to pay damages for breaking it, and cannot make it valid later by ratification . The Privy Council settled this in Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903). The law still softens the rule in a few places: A supplier of necessaries is paid from the minor's property (Section 68). A minor may receive a benefit , for example as a mortgagee who has paid the money. A court may ask a minor to give back a benefit he still holds (Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 33(2)(b)). A guardian may, within his powers and for the minor's benefit, make a contract that binds the minor. In exams, this is a favourite problem question. Marks come from Mohori Bibee , the "no ratification, no estoppel" points, restitution, necessaries, and the minor as beneficiary , partner and agent. In real life, it tells a lender or a shop what it can and cannot recover after dealing with someone under 18.
legalProvision: Section 2(g). An agreement not enforceable by law is said to be void;

Section 10 (first paragraph). All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 11. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person.

Section 184. Who may be an agent. As between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent, but no person who is not of the age of majority and of sound mind can become an agent, so as to be responsible to his principal according to the provisions in that behalf herein contained.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 33(2). Where a defendant successfully resists any suit on the ground— … (b) that the agreement sought to be enforced against him in the suit is void by reason of his not having been competent to contract under section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), the court may, if the defendant has received any benefit under the agreement from the other party, require him to restore, so far as may be, such benefit to that party, to the extent to which he or his estate has benefited thereby.

Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Section 30(1). A person who is a minor according to the law to which he is subject may not be a partner in a firm, but, with the consent of all the partners for the time being, he may be admitted to the benefits of partnership.
In simple words

Sections 2(g), 10, 11: a minor is not "competent to contract ", so his agreement is not a contract. It is an agreement not enforceable by law, that is, void. Section 68: a person who supplies necessaries to a minor is repaid out of the minor's property , not by the minor personally. Section 184: a minor can act as an agent for others, but he cannot be made answerable to his principal. Specific Relief Act, Section 33(2)(b): if a minor wins a suit because his agreement is void, the court may make him give back the benefit he received, but only to the extent he or his estate is still better off. Partnership Act, Section 30: a minor cannot be a partner, but can be admitted to the benefits of a partnership.
hi.meaning:
A minor's agreement is an agreement in which one of the parties had not completed the age of majority (generally 18) on the date it was made. The Act does not say "void" in so many words. The Privy Council reached that result in Mohori Bibee by reading Sections 2, 10 and 11 together, and by looking at Sections 68, 183, 184, 64 and 65 (see Diagram 1 ). Diagram 1. The Privy Council read the Act's sections together and concluded that a minor's agreement is void, not voidable. flowchart TD A["Section 11
A minor is not competent to contract"] B["Section 10
Only agreements of parties competent
to contract are contracts"] C["Section 2(g)
An agreement not enforceable by law is void"] D["Sections 68, 183, 184
The Act treats a minor as unable to bind himself"] E["Sections 64, 65
Assume a contract between competent parties
so they do not apply"] R["RESULT: minor's agreement is VOID AB INITIO
(Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, 1903)"] F["No estoppel where the truth is known
No order to repay the money"] A --> B B --> C C --> R D --> R E --> R R --> F Text description Section 11: a minor is not competent to contract. Section 10: only agreements by competent parties are contracts. Section 2(g): an agreement not enforceable by law is void. Sections 68, 183 and 184 show the Act treats minors as unable to bind themselves. Sections 64 and 65 assume a contract between competent parties, so they do not apply. Result: a minor's agreement is void ab initio; no estoppel where the truth is known; no order to repay. Void ab initio means void from the start. The agreement never was a contract. Nobody needs to cancel it, and nobody can make it good later. Why the law takes this strict view. To protect minors. A young person may not understand a bargain and may be easily exploited. Making every agreement void is the strongest protection. Because it follows from the Act. Section 10 requires "parties competent to contract". If one party is not competent, there is no contract to call voidable. To keep the rule simple. Lenders and sellers are told plainly: deal with a minor at your own risk. What is "the effect"? The topic asks what follows from this voidness. The answer has many parts: no suit on the agreement, no ratification, no estoppel , limited restitution , necessaries, benefits to the minor, guardian's contracts, sureties, and the minor as partner, agent and shareholder. Each is explained below.
keyPoints: A minor's agreement is void ab initio ( Mohori Bibee , 1903). It cannot be ratified on attaining majority; a fresh agreement with fresh consideration is needed ( Suraj Narain Dube ). A false statement of age does not estop the minor ( Mohori Bibee ; Ajudhia Prasad ). Sections 64 and 65 do not apply; restitution only under Specific Relief Act Section 33, and only to the extent of benefit. Necessaries: reimbursed from the minor's property, never a personal liability (Section 68). A minor can take a benefit, for example as a mortgagee who has paid in full ( Raghava Chariar ). A minor can be an agent but is not responsible to his principal (Section 184). A minor can only be admitted to the benefits of a partnership (Partnership Act Section 30). A guardian's contract binds the minor if within the guardian's competence and for the minor's benefit ( Srikakulam ). On a surety for a minor's debt, give both views ( Edavan ; Kashiba ).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. An infant mortgaged his houses on 20 July 1895 to a money lender for Rs. 20,000. The lender's attorney had received written notice of the minority from the infant's court-appointed guardian. The infant sued to cancel the mortgage; the lender asked that at least the money advanced be repaid. Principle. An infant is not competent to contract, so his agreement is void. There was no estoppel because the lender knew the truth, and Sections 64 and 65 did not apply; no repayment was ordered. (1903) LR 30 IA 114 : ILR 30 Cal 539 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It decided that a minor's agreement is void, not voidable, and is the starting point of every answer on this topic. Suraj Narain Dube v. Sukhu Aheer (1928) Facts. Sukhu borrowed Rs. 40 on a bond while a minor (1919). After majority (1923), he and his mother executed a new bond for Rs. 76, being the old Rs. 40 with interest. Principle. A minor's agreement "is altogether void", and the earlier advance in minority is not consideration for a fresh promise after majority. AIR 1928 All 440 (Full Bench, majority). Why it matters. It shows that a minor's agreement cannot be ratified on attaining majority. Ajudhia Prasad v. Chandan Lal (1937) Facts. Two persons over 18 but under 21, who had a certificated guardian, executed a mortgage in 1925. Their minority was concealed. The lower court found fraud and decreed the money. Principle. "neither Section 64 nor Section 65 deals with a case where a party is incompetent to enter into a contract at all"; no personal money decree can be passed against a minor, and estoppel cannot be pleaded against the statute. AIR 1937 All 610 (Full Bench). Why it matters. Even a minor who deceives the other side cannot be made to pay under the void agreement. Srikakulam Subrahmanyam v. Kurra Subba Rao (1948) Facts. A Hindu widow, as guardian of her minor son, agreed in writing in 1935 to sell family land for Rs. 17,200 to pay off the dead father's debts. The buyers paid off a Rs. 1,200 mortgage debt and were put in possession, but no sale deed was executed or registered. The minor later sued for possession. Principle. A contract by a guardian binds the minor if it is within the guardian's competence and for the minor's benefit; here the minor was the "transferor" and was barred by Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act. (1948) 50 Bom LR 646 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It marks the line between a minor's own void agreement and a valid contract made on his behalf by his guardian. Edavan Kavingal Kelappan Nambiar v. Moolakal Kunhi Raman (1956) Facts. A minor took money in a kuri (chit) transaction, and a surety guaranteed the instalments. The suit failed against the minor, but the trial court decreed against the surety. Principle. "the liability of the surety is only ancillary and can rest only on a valid obligation on the part of the party"; the surety was not liable. AIR 1957 Mad 164. Why it matters. It answers whether a surety for a minor's void debt can be sued, and explains Kashiba as a case of indemnity.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a minor's agreement void or voidable?
selfTest.a: Void ab initio ( Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose , 1903).

selfTest.q: 2. A minor borrows ₹50,000 and on turning 18 writes "I confirm this loan". Is he now liable?
selfTest.a: No. A void agreement cannot be ratified. A fresh agreement with fresh consideration is needed ( Suraj Narain Dube ).

selfTest.q: 3. A minor lies that he is 21 and gets a loan. Can the lender use estoppel to stop him pleading minority?
selfTest.a: No. Estoppel does not take away the protection of minority ( Mohori Bibee ; Ajudhia Prasad ).

selfTest.q: 4. What can a court order a minor to give back?
selfTest.a: Under Specific Relief Act Section 33(2)(b), the benefit he received, only to the extent he or his estate has benefited.

selfTest.q: 5. Is a minor personally liable for necessaries?
selfTest.a: No. The supplier is reimbursed from the minor's property (Section 68).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a minor enforce a mortgage in his favour after he has paid the whole mortgage money?
selfTest.a: Yes ( Raghava Chariar v. Srinivasa Raghava Chariar , 1916).

law-of-contract-i-u2-t8.subtitle: Sections 17 and 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Fraud is a deliberate act meant to deceive a party into a contract (Section 17). The Act lists five acts: stating as a fact what you do not believe to be true; actively hiding a fact you know; making a promise with no intention of keeping it; any other act fitted to deceive; any act or omission the law specially declares fraudulent. The act must be done by a party , with his connivance (secret approval), or by his agent , with intent to deceive the other party or to induce him to contract. Silence. Mere silence is not fraud, unless there is a duty to speak , or the silence is itself equivalent to speech (Explanation). Effect. The contract is voidable at the deceived party's option. He may instead insist on performance and be put in the position he would have been in if the statements had been true (Section 19). The diligence exception protects fraudulent silence only, never an active lie. In exams, the five acts, the silence rule and Derry v. Peek earn the marks. In real life this is the law behind false sales claims, fake documents and loan scams.
legalProvision: Section 17. "Fraud" defined. "Fraud" means and includes any of the following acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with intent to deceive another party thereto or his agent, or to induce him to enter into the contract:— (1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; (2) the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact; (3) a promise made without any intention of performing it; (4) any other act fitted to deceive; (5) any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent. Explanation. —Mere silence as to facts likely to affect the willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud, unless the circumstances of the case are such that, regard being had to them, it is the duty of the person keeping silence to speak, or unless his silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech. Illustrations. (a) A sells, by auction, to B, a horse which A knows to be unsound. A says nothing to B about the horse's unsoundness. This is not fraud in A. (b) B is A's daughter and has just come of age. Here, the relation between the parties would make it A's duty to tell B if the horse is unsound. (c) B says to A—"If you do not deny it, I shall assume that the horse is sound." A says nothing. Here, A's silence is equivalent to speech. (d) A and B, being traders, enter upon a contract. A has private information of a change in prices which would affect B's willingness to proceed with the contract. A is not bound to inform B.

Section 19 (relevant parts). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. A party to a contract whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation, may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true. Exception. —If such consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence, fraudulent within the meaning of section 17, the contract, nevertheless, is not voidable, if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. Explanation. —A fraud or misrepresentation which did not cause the consent to a contract of the party on whom such fraud was practised, or to whom such misrepresentation was made, does not render a contract voidable. Illustrations. (a) A, intending to deceive B, falsely represents that five hundred maunds of indigo are made annually at A's factory, and thereby induces B to buy the factory. The contract is voidable at the option of B. (c) A fraudulently informs B that A's estate is free from incumbrance. B thereupon buys the estate. The estate is subject to a mortgage. B may either avoid the contract, or may insist on its being carried out and the mortgage debt redeemed. (d) B, having discovered a vein of ore on the estate of A, adopts means to conceal, and does conceal, the existence of the ore from A. Through A's ignorance B is enabled to buy the estate at an under-value. The contract is voidable at the option of A. (e) A is entitled to succeed to an estate at the death of B; B dies: C, having received intelligence of B's death, prevents the intelligence reaching A, and thus induces A to sell him his interest in the estate. The sale is voidable at the option of A.
In simple words

Who: a party, someone acting with his secret approval, or his agent. What: one of the five acts. Why: to deceive the other party (or his agent), or to make him enter the contract . Silence: keeping quiet is not fraud , unless you had a duty to speak or your silence itself "said" something. Result: the deceived party may cancel, or keep the contract and insist on being put where he would be if the statements were true.
en.meaning:
Fraud is one of the five acts in Section 17, done by a party (or with his connivance, or by his agent) with intent to deceive the other party or to induce him to enter the contract.

Elements.

Element What it means Source 1. One of the five acts False suggestion, active concealment, promise without intention, act fitted to deceive, act declared fraudulent Section 17(1)–(5) 2. By the right person A party, with his connivance, or his agent Section 17 opening words 3. Intent to deceive or induce The dishonest mind Section 17 opening words 4. It caused the consent The deceived party would not have agreed but for it Section 14; Section 19 Explanation 5. The deceived party suffered by it In the tort of deceit , loss must be shown; for avoiding the contract under Section 19, it is enough that consent was caused by the fraud Section 19

The mental element. In Derry v. Peek (1889), Lord Herschell stated three propositions: "First, in order to sustain an action of deceit, there must be proof of fraud, and nothing short of that will suffice. Secondly, fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made (1) knowingly, or (2) without belief in its truth, or (3) recklessly, careless whether it be true or false … Thirdly, if fraud be proved, the motive of the person guilty of it is immaterial. It matters not that there was no intention to cheat or injure the person to whom the statement was made." He added: "To prevent a false statement being fraudulent, there must, I think, always be an honest belief in its truth."

Fraud and misrepresentation . An honest but careless statement is not fraud; it may be misrepresentation (Section 18). The difference lies in the mind of the maker.

The policy. Fraus omnia vitiat : fraud spoils everything. The law will not let a person keep the gain of his own deceit.
keyPoints: Fraud is one of five acts done by a party, with his connivance or by his agent, with intent to deceive or induce the contract (Section 17). Mere silence is not fraud, unless there is a duty to speak or silence equals speech. A promise is fraudulent only if there was no intention to perform it when it was made. The contract is voidable at the deceived party's option, or he may insist on performance (Section 19). The diligence exception does not protect active fraud. Honest belief defeats fraud; motive is immaterial ( Derry v. Peek ). Time runs from discovery of the fraud (Limitation Act Section 17).

caseLaws.name: Derry v
caseLaws.facts: Peek (1889) Facts. A tramway company's special Act allowed steam power only with the Board of Trade's consent. The directors' prospectus said the company had the right to use steam power. The Board of Trade refused consent, and the company was wound up. Principle. Fraud is a false representation made "knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly"; motive is immaterial; an honest belief in the truth defeats a claim in deceit. (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (House of Lords). Why it matters. It fixes the mental element of fraud and separates it from honest but careless statements. Shri Krishan v. Kurukshetra University (1975) Facts. A teacher took evening LL.B. classes and was allowed to sit the Part II examination. The University later cancelled his candidature for short attendance and alleged fraud and suppression. Principle. "Where a person on whom fraud is committed is in a position to discover the truth by due diligence, fraud is not proved." AIR 1976 SC 376 : (1976) 1 SCC 311. Why it matters. It shows that a party who had the facts in its own hands cannot easily claim it was deceived.

selfTest.q: 2. When is silence fraud?
selfTest.a: When the circumstances make it the person's duty to speak, or when the silence is in itself equivalent to speech.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the effect of fraud on a contract?
selfTest.a: The contract is voidable at the option of the deceived party; he may instead insist on performance (Section 19).

selfTest.q: 4. A promises to supply goods next month and honestly means to, but later fails. Is this fraud?
selfTest.a: No. It is a breach of contract. Fraud under Section 17(3) needs no intention to perform at the time of the promise.

selfTest.q: 5. Can a party guilty of an active lie say the other could have checked?
selfTest.a: No. The Exception to Section 19 covers only misrepresentation and fraudulent silence.

selfTest.q: 6. When does time begin to run for a suit based on fraud?
selfTest.a: When the plaintiff discovers the fraud or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it (Limitation Act, Section 17).

legalProvision: Section 17. "Fraud" defined. "Fraud" means and includes any of the following acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with intent to deceive another party thereto or his agent, or to induce him to enter into the contract:— (1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; (2) the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact; (3) a promise made without any intention of performing it; (4) any other act fitted to deceive; (5) any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent. Explanation. —Mere silence as to facts likely to affect the willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud, unless the circumstances of the case are such that, regard being had to them, it is the duty of the person keeping silence to speak, or unless his silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech. Illustrations. (a) A sells, by auction, to B, a horse which A knows to be unsound. A says nothing to B about the horse's unsoundness. This is not fraud in A. (b) B is A's daughter and has just come of age. Here, the relation between the parties would make it A's duty to tell B if the horse is unsound. (c) B says to A—"If you do not deny it, I shall assume that the horse is sound." A says nothing. Here, A's silence is equivalent to speech. (d) A and B, being traders, enter upon a contract. A has private information of a change in prices which would affect B's willingness to proceed with the contract. A is not bound to inform B.

Section 19 (relevant parts). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. A party to a contract whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation, may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true. Exception. —If such consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence, fraudulent within the meaning of section 17, the contract, nevertheless, is not voidable, if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. Explanation. —A fraud or misrepresentation which did not cause the consent to a contract of the party on whom such fraud was practised, or to whom such misrepresentation was made, does not render a contract voidable. Illustrations. (a) A, intending to deceive B, falsely represents that five hundred maunds of indigo are made annually at A's factory, and thereby induces B to buy the factory. The contract is voidable at the option of B. (c) A fraudulently informs B that A's estate is free from incumbrance. B thereupon buys the estate. The estate is subject to a mortgage. B may either avoid the contract, or may insist on its being carried out and the mortgage debt redeemed. (d) B, having discovered a vein of ore on the estate of A, adopts means to conceal, and does conceal, the existence of the ore from A. Through A's ignorance B is enabled to buy the estate at an under-value. The contract is voidable at the option of A. (e) A is entitled to succeed to an estate at the death of B; B dies: C, having received intelligence of B's death, prevents the intelligence reaching A, and thus induces A to sell him his interest in the estate. The sale is voidable at the option of A.
సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే

ఎవరు: ఒక పక్షం, అతని రహస్య ఆమోదంతో పనిచేసేవాడు, లేదా అతని ఏజెంట్. ఏమిటి: ఐదు చర్యల్లో ఒకటి. ఎందుకు: ఎదుటి పక్షాన్ని (లేదా అతని ఏజెంట్ ను) మోసగించడానికి, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టులోకి దించడానికి. మౌనం: మౌనంగా ఉండటం మోసం కాదు; మాట్లాడాల్సిన విధి ఉంటే, లేదా మౌనమే ఏదో "చెబితే" తప్ప. ఫలితం: మోసపోయినవాడు రద్దు చేయవచ్చు; లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు ఉంచుకుని, ప్రకటనలు నిజమైతే ఉండే స్థితిలో ఉంచమని పట్టుబట్టవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
మోసం అంటే సెక్షన్ 17 లోని ఐదు చర్యల్లో ఒకటి; దాన్ని ఒక పక్షం (లేదా అతని రహస్య ఆమోదంతో, లేదా అతని ఏజెంట్) ఎదుటి పక్షాన్ని మోసగించే ఉద్దేశంతో , లేదా కాంట్రాక్టులోకి దించే ఉద్దేశంతో చేయాలి.

అంశాలు.

అంశం అర్థం ఆధారం 1. ఐదు చర్యల్లో ఒకటి తప్పుడు సూచన, చురుకైన దాచివేత, ఉద్దేశం లేని వాగ్దానం, మోసగించే చర్య, మోసపూరితమని ప్రకటించిన చర్య సెక్షన్ 17(1)–(5) 2. సరైన వ్యక్తి చేయాలి పక్షం, అతని రహస్య ఆమోదంతో, లేదా అతని ఏజెంట్ సెక్షన్ 17 ప్రారంభ పదాలు 3. మోసగించే లేదా దించే ఉద్దేశం నిజాయితీ లేని మనసు సెక్షన్ 17 ప్రారంభ పదాలు 4. సమ్మతికి కారణమైంది అది లేకపోతే మోసపోయినవాడు ఒప్పుకునేవాడు కాదు సెక్షన్ 14; సెక్షన్ 19 Explanation 5. మోసపోయినవాడు దాని వల్ల నష్టపోయాడు deceit టార్ట్ లో నష్టం చూపాలి; సెక్షన్ 19 కింద రద్దుకు, సమ్మతి మోసం వల్ల కలిగిందని చూపితే చాలు సెక్షన్ 19

మానసిక అంశం. Derry v. Peek (1889) కేసులో లార్డ్ హెర్షెల్ మూడు సూత్రాలు చెప్పారు: "First, in order to sustain an action of deceit, there must be proof of fraud , and nothing short of that will suffice. Secondly, fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made (1) knowingly, or (2) without belief in its truth, or (3) recklessly, careless whether it be true or false … Thirdly, if fraud be proved, the motive of the person guilty of it is immaterial. It matters not that there was no intention to cheat or injure the person to whom the statement was made." ఇంకా ఇలా అన్నారు: "To prevent a false statement being fraudulent, there must, I think, always be an honest belief in its truth."

మోసం, తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం. నిజాయితీతో కూడిన, కానీ అజాగ్రత్త ప్రకటన మోసం కాదు; అది తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం (misrepresentation) కావచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 18). తేడా చెప్పినవాడి మనసులో ఉంటుంది.

విధానం. Fraus omnia vitiat : మోసం అన్నింటినీ పాడు చేస్తుంది. తన సొంత మోసం వల్ల వచ్చిన లాభాన్ని ఎవరూ ఉంచుకోవడానికి చట్టం అనుమతించదు.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 17 కింద మోసమయ్యే ఐదు చర్యలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: నమ్మనివాడు చేసే తప్పుడు వాస్తవ సూచన; చురుకైన దాచివేత; నెరవేర్చే ఉద్దేశం లేని వాగ్దానం; మోసగించడానికి తగిన ఇతర ఏ చర్య అయినా; చట్టం ప్రత్యేకంగా మోసపూరితమని ప్రకటించిన ఏ చర్య లేదా విస్మరణ అయినా.

selfTest.q: 2. మౌనం ఎప్పుడు మోసం అవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: పరిస్థితుల వల్ల ఆ వ్యక్తికి మాట్లాడాల్సిన విధి ఉన్నప్పుడు, లేదా మౌనమే మాటతో సమానమైనప్పుడు.

selfTest.q: 3. మోసం కాంట్రాక్టుపై ఏ ప్రభావం చూపుతుంది?
selfTest.a: మోసపోయిన పక్షం ఇష్టం మేరకు కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయదగినది; లేదా అతను అమలుకు పట్టుబట్టవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 19).

selfTest.q: 4. వచ్చే నెల సరుకు సరఫరా చేస్తానని A వాగ్దానం చేస్తాడు, నిజాయితీగా అలాగే చేయాలనుకుంటాడు, కానీ తర్వాత విఫలమవుతాడు. ఇది మోసమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. ఇది కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘన. సెక్షన్ 17(3) కింద మోసానికి, వాగ్దానం చేసిన సమయంలోనే నెరవేర్చే ఉద్దేశం లేకపోవాలి.

selfTest.q: 5. చురుకైన అబద్ధం చెప్పినవాడు, ఎదుటివాడు తనిఖీ చేసుకోవచ్చు కదా అనగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. సెక్షన్ 19 Exception తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యానికి, మోసపూరిత మౌనానికి మాత్రమే వర్తిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 6. మోసం ఆధారంగా దావాకు కాలం ఎప్పుడు మొదలవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: వాది మోసాన్ని కనుగొన్నప్పుడు, లేదా సహేతుకమైన జాగ్రత్తతో కనుగొనగలిగినప్పుడు (పరిమితి చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 17).
