hi.inOneMinute: Fraud is a deliberate act meant to deceive a party into a contract (Section 17). The Act lists five acts: stating as a fact what you do not believe to be true; actively hiding a fact you know; making a promise with no intention of keeping it; any other act fitted to deceive; any act or omission the law specially declares fraudulent. The act must be done by a party , with his connivance (secret approval), or by his agent , with intent to deceive the other party or to induce him to contract. Silence. Mere silence is not fraud, unless there is a duty to speak , or the silence is itself equivalent to speech (Explanation). Effect. The contract is voidable at the deceived party's option. He may instead insist on performance and be put in the position he would have been in if the statements had been true (Section 19). The diligence exception protects fraudulent silence only, never an active lie. In exams, the five acts, the silence rule and Derry v. Peek earn the marks. In real life this is the law behind false sales claims, fake documents and loan scams.
legalProvision: Section 17. "Fraud" defined. "Fraud" means and includes any of the following acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, or by his agent, with intent to deceive another party thereto or his agent, or to induce him to enter into the contract:— (1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; (2) the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge or belief of the fact; (3) a promise made without any intention of performing it; (4) any other act fitted to deceive; (5) any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent. Explanation. —Mere silence as to facts likely to affect the willingness of a person to enter into a contract is not fraud, unless the circumstances of the case are such that, regard being had to them, it is the duty of the person keeping silence to speak, or unless his silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech. Illustrations. (a) A sells, by auction, to B, a horse which A knows to be unsound. A says nothing to B about the horse's unsoundness. This is not fraud in A. (b) B is A's daughter and has just come of age. Here, the relation between the parties would make it A's duty to tell B if the horse is unsound. (c) B says to A—"If you do not deny it, I shall assume that the horse is sound." A says nothing. Here, A's silence is equivalent to speech. (d) A and B, being traders, enter upon a contract. A has private information of a change in prices which would affect B's willingness to proceed with the contract. A is not bound to inform B.

Section 19 (relevant parts). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. A party to a contract whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation, may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true. Exception. —If such consent was caused by misrepresentation or by silence, fraudulent within the meaning of section 17, the contract, nevertheless, is not voidable, if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. Explanation. —A fraud or misrepresentation which did not cause the consent to a contract of the party on whom such fraud was practised, or to whom such misrepresentation was made, does not render a contract voidable. Illustrations. (a) A, intending to deceive B, falsely represents that five hundred maunds of indigo are made annually at A's factory, and thereby induces B to buy the factory. The contract is voidable at the option of B. (c) A fraudulently informs B that A's estate is free from incumbrance. B thereupon buys the estate. The estate is subject to a mortgage. B may either avoid the contract, or may insist on its being carried out and the mortgage debt redeemed. (d) B, having discovered a vein of ore on the estate of A, adopts means to conceal, and does conceal, the existence of the ore from A. Through A's ignorance B is enabled to buy the estate at an under-value. The contract is voidable at the option of A. (e) A is entitled to succeed to an estate at the death of B; B dies: C, having received intelligence of B's death, prevents the intelligence reaching A, and thus induces A to sell him his interest in the estate. The sale is voidable at the option of A.
In simple words

Who: a party, someone acting with his secret approval, or his agent. What: one of the five acts. Why: to deceive the other party (or his agent), or to make him enter the contract . Silence: keeping quiet is not fraud , unless you had a duty to speak or your silence itself "said" something. Result: the deceived party may cancel, or keep the contract and insist on being put where he would be if the statements were true.
hi.meaning: Fraud is one of the five acts in Section 17, done by a party (or with his connivance, or by his agent) with intent to deceive the other party or to induce him to enter the contract. Elements. Element What it means Source 1. One of the five acts False suggestion, active concealment, promise without intention, act fitted to deceive, act declared fraudulent Section 17(1)–(5) 2. By the right person A party, with his connivance, or his agent Section 17 opening words 3. Intent to deceive or induce The dishonest mind Section 17 opening words 4. It caused the consent The deceived party would not have agreed but for it Section 14; Section 19 Explanation 5. The deceived party suffered by it In the tort of deceit , loss must be shown; for avoiding the contract under Section 19, it is enough that consent was caused by the fraud Section 19 The mental element. In Derry v. Peek (1889), Lord Herschell stated three propositions: "First, in order to sustain an action of deceit, there must be proof of fraud, and nothing short of that will suffice. Secondly, fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made (1) knowingly, or (2) without belief in its truth, or (3) recklessly, careless whether it be true or false … Thirdly, if fraud be proved, the motive of the person guilty of it is immaterial. It matters not that there was no intention to cheat or injure the person to whom the statement was made." He added: "To prevent a false statement being fraudulent, there must, I think, always be an honest belief in its truth." Fraud and misrepresentation . An honest but careless statement is not fraud; it may be misrepresentation (Section 18). The difference lies in the mind of the maker. The policy. Fraus omnia vitiat : fraud spoils everything. The law will not let a person keep the gain of his own deceit.
keyPoints: Fraud is one of five acts done by a party, with his connivance or by his agent, with intent to deceive or induce the contract (Section 17). Mere silence is not fraud, unless there is a duty to speak or silence equals speech. A promise is fraudulent only if there was no intention to perform it when it was made. The contract is voidable at the deceived party's option, or he may insist on performance (Section 19). The diligence exception does not protect active fraud. Honest belief defeats fraud; motive is immaterial ( Derry v. Peek ). Time runs from discovery of the fraud (Limitation Act Section 17).

caseLaws.name: Derry v
caseLaws.facts: Peek (1889) Facts. A tramway company's special Act allowed steam power only with the Board of Trade's consent. The directors' prospectus said the company had the right to use steam power. The Board of Trade refused consent, and the company was wound up. Principle. Fraud is a false representation made "knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly"; motive is immaterial; an honest belief in the truth defeats a claim in deceit. (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (House of Lords). Why it matters. It fixes the mental element of fraud and separates it from honest but careless statements. Shri Krishan v. Kurukshetra University (1975) Facts. A teacher took evening LL.B. classes and was allowed to sit the Part II examination. The University later cancelled his candidature for short attendance and alleged fraud and suppression. Principle. "Where a person on whom fraud is committed is in a position to discover the truth by due diligence, fraud is not proved." AIR 1976 SC 376 : (1976) 1 SCC 311. Why it matters. It shows that a party who had the facts in its own hands cannot easily claim it was deceived.

selfTest.q: 2. When is silence fraud?
selfTest.a: When the circumstances make it the person's duty to speak, or when the silence is in itself equivalent to speech.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the effect of fraud on a contract?
selfTest.a: The contract is voidable at the option of the deceived party; he may instead insist on performance (Section 19).

selfTest.q: 4. A promises to supply goods next month and honestly means to, but later fails. Is this fraud?
selfTest.a: No. It is a breach of contract. Fraud under Section 17(3) needs no intention to perform at the time of the promise.

selfTest.q: 5. Can a party guilty of an active lie say the other could have checked?
selfTest.a: No. The Exception to Section 19 covers only misrepresentation and fraudulent silence.

selfTest.q: 6. When does time begin to run for a suit based on fraud?
selfTest.a: When the plaintiff discovers the fraud or could with reasonable diligence have discovered it (Limitation Act, Section 17).

law-of-contract-i-u2-t6.subtitle: Sections 16 and 19A of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Undue influence exists where the relations between the parties are such that one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other , and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other (Section 16(1)). There is no threat and no lie. The pressure comes quietly from a relationship of trust, authority or dependence. Section 16 has three parts: Section 16(1): the two elements: a position to dominate, and its use for an unfair advantage. Section 16(2): situations where a person is deemed to be in a position to dominate: real or apparent authority, a fiduciary relation , or a contract with a person whose mental capacity is affected by age, illness, or mental or bodily distress. Section 16(3): if the dominant person's transaction appears unconscionable , the burden of proof shifts to him to show there was no undue influence. Effect. The contract is voidable at the option of the party influenced. The court may set it aside absolutely , or, if he received a benefit, on just terms (Section 19A). In exams, the Section 16 test, the burden of proof and the order of inquiry in Raghunath Prasad v. Sarju Prasad earn the marks. In real life this rule protects patients, elderly parents, disciples, borrowers and others who depend on someone.
legalProvision: Section 16. "Undue influence" defined. (1) A contract is said to be induced by "undue influence" where the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one of the parties is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other. (2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing principle, a person is deemed to be in a position to dominate the will of another— (a) where he holds a real or apparent authority over the other, or where he stands in a fiduciary relation to the other; or (b) where he makes a contract with a person whose mental capacity is temporarily or permanently affected by reason of age, illness, or mental or bodily distress. (3) Where a person who is in a position to dominate the will of another, enters into a contract with him, and the transaction appears, on the face of it or on the evidence adduced, to be unconscionable, the burden of proving that such contract was not induced by undue influence shall lie upon the person in a position to dominate the will of the other. Nothing in this sub-section shall affect the provisions of section 111 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872). Illustrations (a) A having advanced money to his son, B, during his minority, upon B's coming of age obtains, by misuse of parental influence, a bond from B for a greater amount than the sum due in respect of the advance. A employs undue influence. (b) A, a man enfeebled by disease or age, is induced, by B's influence over him as his medical attendant, to agree to pay B an unreasonable sum for his professional services. B employs undue influence. (c) A, being in debt to B, the money-lender of his village, contracts a fresh loan on terms which appear to be unconscionable. It lies on B to prove that the contract was not induced by undue influence. (d) A applies to a banker for a loan at a time when there is stringency in the money market. The banker declines to make the loan except at an unusually high rate of interest. A accepts the loan on these terms. This is a transaction in the ordinary course of business, and the contract is not induced by undue influence.

Section 19A. Power to set aside contract induced by undue influence. When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. Any such contract may be set aside either absolutely or, if the party who was entitled to avoid it has received any benefit thereunder, upon such terms and conditions as to the Court may seem just. Illustrations (a) A's son has forged B's name to a promissory note. B under threat of prosecuting A's son, obtains a bond from A for the amount of the forged note. If B sues on this bond, the Court may set the bond aside. (b) A, a money-lender, advances Rs. 100 to B, an agriculturist, and, by undue influence, induces B to execute a bond for Rs. 200 with interest at 6 per cent. per month. The Court may set the bond aside, ordering B to repay the Rs. 100 with such interest as may seem just.

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 114. Where there is a question as to the good faith of a transaction between parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence, the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the party who is in a position of active confidence. Illustrations. (a) The good faith of a sale by a client to an advocate is in question in a suit brought by the client. The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the advocate. (b) The good faith of a sale by a son just come of age to a father is in question in a suit brought by the son. The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the father.
In simple words

Section 16(1): two things are needed: (i) a relationship that lets one side dominate the other's will, and (ii) use of that position to get an unfair advantage. Section 16(2): the law assumes the first element in three situations: authority (real or apparent), a relation of trust ( fiduciary ), and dealing with a person whose mind is weakened by age, illness or distress. Section 16(3): if the bargain looks unconscionable, the stronger side must prove it did not use undue influence . Section 16(3) does not cut down the Evidence Act rule (old Section 111, now BSA Section 114): a person in "active confidence" must prove the good faith of the transaction. Section 19A: the weaker party may avoid the contract; the court may set it aside fully, or on fair terms if he got something under it.
en.meaning:
Undue influence is the misuse of a position of dominance over another person's will to get an unfair advantage from him.

The two elements (Section 16(1)).

Element Question Example 1. Position to dominate the will Do the relations between the parties let one control the other's decisions? Guru and devoted disciple; doctor and very sick patient 2. Use of that position for an unfair advantage Did he actually use it, and was the result unfair to the other? Disciple gives her house to the guru; patient promises an unreasonable fee

Both must be present. A fair deal between a doctor and a patient is not undue influence. An unfair deal between strangers on equal footing is not undue influence either (it may be something else, or just a bad bargain).

"Between the parties". Section 16(1) speaks of "the relations subsisting between the parties". The dominant person must be a party to the contract (or act through one). This is different from coercion , which can come from anyone.

Why the law does this. A person who signs because someone he trusts or depends on has taken over his judgment has not really chosen. But the bargain may still suit him, so the law makes the contract voidable and lets him decide.

Unconscionable means so unfair that it shocks the conscience, for example a sale of a house at one-sixth of its value, or interest so high that a small loan grows to many times its size.
keyPoints: Two elements: a position to dominate, and its use for an unfair advantage (Section 16(1)). Deemed dominance: authority, fiduciary relation, weakened mental capacity (Section 16(2)); the list is not closed. Burden shifts to the dominant person if the transaction appears unconscionable (Section 16(3)); BSA Section 114 for active confidence. Dominance first, then undue influence, then burden ( Raghunath Prasad ). Urgent need of money or high interest alone does not prove dominance. A hard bargain in the ordinary course of business is not undue influence (Illustration (d)). Effect: voidable; set aside absolutely or on just terms (Section 19A).

caseLaws.name: Raghunath Prasad v
caseLaws.facts: Sarju Prasad (1923) Facts. A member of a wealthy joint family mortgaged property in 1910 for Rs. 9,999 at 2 per cent per month, with unpaid interest added to principal yearly. He later pleaded undue influence, relying only on the harsh terms and his urgent need of money. Principle. The court must first find a position to dominate; only then does the question of undue influence, and then the burden of proof, arise. Urgent need of money does not itself give the lender that position. (1924) 26 Bom LR 595 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It gives the three-stage order of inquiry under Section 16 that courts still follow. Subhas Chandra Das Mushib v. Ganga Prosad Das Mushib (1966) Facts. In 1944 a very old man (about 90 when he died in 1948) and his daughter executed a deed of settlement of village properties in favour of his grandson. One of his sons sued to set it aside, and the High Court presumed undue influence from the close relationship and the donor's old age. Principle. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's decree , applying the three stages from Raghunath Prasad : "merely because the parties were nearly related to each other no presumption of undue influence can arise"; a position to dominate must be found first. AIR 1967 SC 878 : (1967) 1 SCR 331. Why it matters. It confirms in Indian law that dominance must be proved before the burden shifts. Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v. Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd. (1962) Facts. In a dispute inside a family company, some members alleged that company resolutions of 1945 had been procured by coercion and undue influence by the eldest member, Ladli Prasad, who they said was in a dominant position over them. Principle. "the party pleading must therefore be required to plead the precise nature of the influence exercised, the manner of use of the influence, and the unfair advantage obtained by the other." AIR 1963 SC 1279 : (1964) 1 SCR 270. Why it matters. A vague plea of undue influence fails at the start. LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) Facts. The Life Insurance Corporation offered a cheap term policy only to persons employed in Government, semi-Government or reputed commercial firms. Principle. The restriction was arbitrary and violated Article 14; courts may strike down an unfair term in a contract offered by a State body to the public. (1995) Supp 1 SCR 349. Why it matters. It is a related case on unequal bargaining power. It does not apply Section 16.

selfTest.q: 1. What two things must be shown for undue influence?
selfTest.a: That one party was in a position to dominate the other's will, and that he used that position to obtain an unfair advantage (Section 16(1)).

selfTest.q: 2. When does the burden of proof move to the dominant party?
selfTest.a: When he is in a position to dominate, enters into a contract with the other, and the transaction appears unconscionable on its face or on the evidence (Section 16(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. Is a contract induced by undue influence void or voidable?
selfTest.a: Voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused (Section 19A).

selfTest.q: 4. Does a very high rate of interest by itself raise a presumption of undue influence?
selfTest.a: No. Dominance must be shown first ( Raghunath Prasad ; Illustration (d)).

selfTest.q: 5. What can the court do if the influenced party received a benefit?
selfTest.a: Set the contract aside on such terms and conditions as seem just, for example repayment of the actual loan with fair interest (Section 19A, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 6. Who must prove good faith in a sale by a client to his advocate?
selfTest.a: The advocate (BSA Section 114, Illustration (a)).

legalProvision: Section 16. "Undue influence" defined. (1) A contract is said to be induced by "undue influence" where the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one of the parties is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other. (2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing principle, a person is deemed to be in a position to dominate the will of another— (a) where he holds a real or apparent authority over the other, or where he stands in a fiduciary relation to the other; or (b) where he makes a contract with a person whose mental capacity is temporarily or permanently affected by reason of age, illness, or mental or bodily distress. (3) Where a person who is in a position to dominate the will of another, enters into a contract with him, and the transaction appears, on the face of it or on the evidence adduced, to be unconscionable, the burden of proving that such contract was not induced by undue influence shall lie upon the person in a position to dominate the will of the other. Nothing in this sub-section shall affect the provisions of section 111 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872). Illustrations (a) A having advanced money to his son, B, during his minority, upon B's coming of age obtains, by misuse of parental influence, a bond from B for a greater amount than the sum due in respect of the advance. A employs undue influence. (b) A, a man enfeebled by disease or age, is induced, by B's influence over him as his medical attendant, to agree to pay B an unreasonable sum for his professional services. B employs undue influence. (c) A, being in debt to B, the money-lender of his village, contracts a fresh loan on terms which appear to be unconscionable. It lies on B to prove that the contract was not induced by undue influence. (d) A applies to a banker for a loan at a time when there is stringency in the money market. The banker declines to make the loan except at an unusually high rate of interest. A accepts the loan on these terms. This is a transaction in the ordinary course of business, and the contract is not induced by undue influence.

Section 19A. Power to set aside contract induced by undue influence. When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. Any such contract may be set aside either absolutely or, if the party who was entitled to avoid it has received any benefit thereunder, upon such terms and conditions as to the Court may seem just. Illustrations (a) A's son has forged B's name to a promissory note. B under threat of prosecuting A's son, obtains a bond from A for the amount of the forged note. If B sues on this bond, the Court may set the bond aside. (b) A, a money-lender, advances Rs. 100 to B, an agriculturist, and, by undue influence, induces B to execute a bond for Rs. 200 with interest at 6 per cent. per month. The Court may set the bond aside, ordering B to repay the Rs. 100 with such interest as may seem just.

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 114. Where there is a question as to the good faith of a transaction between parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence, the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the party who is in a position of active confidence. Illustrations. (a) The good faith of a sale by a client to an advocate is in question in a suit brought by the client. The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the advocate. (b) The good faith of a sale by a son just come of age to a father is in question in a suit brought by the son. The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the father.

సెక్షన్ 16(1): రెండు విషయాలు కావాలి: (i) ఒక వైపు అవతలి వైపు ఇష్టాన్ని ఆధిపత్యంలో పెట్టుకోగల సంబంధం, (ii) అన్యాయమైన లాభం కోసం ఆ స్థానాన్ని వాడడం. సెక్షన్ 16(2): మూడు సందర్భాల్లో మొదటి అంశం ఉన్నట్టు చట్టం భావిస్తుంది: అధికారం (వాస్తవ లేదా కనిపించే), విశ్వాస సంబంధం (fiduciary), వయస్సు, అనారోగ్యం లేదా బాధ వల్ల మనస్సు బలహీనపడిన వ్యక్తితో వ్యవహారం. సెక్షన్ 16(3): బేరం అన్యాయంగా కనిపిస్తే, తాను అనుచిత ప్రభావం వాడలేదని బలమైన వైపే రుజువు చేయాలి. సాక్ష్య చట్టం నియమాన్ని (పాత సెక్షన్ 111, ఇప్పుడు BSA సెక్షన్ 114) సెక్షన్ 16(3) తగ్గించదు: "active confidence" స్థానంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి వ్యవహారపు మంచి విశ్వాసాన్ని ( good faith ) రుజువు చేయాలి. సెక్షన్ 19A: బలహీనమైన పక్షం కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయవచ్చు; దాని కింద ఏమైనా పొంది ఉంటే కోర్టు పూర్తిగా గానీ, న్యాయమైన షరతులతో గానీ రద్దు చేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
అనుచిత ప్రభావం అంటే అన్యాయమైన లాభం పొందడానికి మరో వ్యక్తి ఇష్టంపై ఉన్న ఆధిపత్య స్థానాన్ని దుర్వినియోగం చేయడం .

రెండు అంశాలు (సెక్షన్ 16(1)).

అంశం ప్రశ్న ఉదాహరణ 1. ఇష్టంపై ఆధిపత్య స్థానం పక్షాల మధ్య సంబంధం ఒకరు మరొకరి నిర్ణయాలను నియంత్రించేలా ఉందా? గురువు, భక్తురాలైన శిష్యురాలు; డాక్టర్, చాలా అనారోగ్యంతో ఉన్న రోగి 2. అన్యాయమైన లాభం కోసం ఆ స్థానాన్ని వాడడం అతను నిజంగా దాన్ని వాడాడా, ఫలితం అవతలి వ్యక్తికి అన్యాయమా? శిష్యురాలు తన ఇంటిని గురువుకు ఇస్తుంది; రోగి అన్యాయమైన ఫీజు ఇస్తానంటాడు

రెండూ ఉండాలి. డాక్టర్, రోగి మధ్య న్యాయమైన వ్యవహారం అనుచిత ప్రభావం కాదు. సమాన స్థాయిలో ఉన్న అపరిచితుల మధ్య అన్యాయమైన వ్యవహారం కూడా అనుచిత ప్రభావం కాదు (అది వేరే ఏదైనా కావచ్చు, లేదా కేవలం చెడ్డ బేరం).

"పక్షాల మధ్య". సెక్షన్ 16(1) "the relations subsisting between the parties" గురించి మాట్లాడుతుంది. ఆధిపత్య వ్యక్తి కాంట్రాక్టుకు పక్షం అయి ఉండాలి (లేదా పక్షం ద్వారా వ్యవహరించాలి). ఎవరైనా వాడగలిగే బలవంతానికి ఇది భిన్నం.

చట్టం ఇలా ఎందుకు చేస్తుంది. తాను నమ్మే లేదా ఆధారపడే వ్యక్తి తన తీర్మానాన్ని తన చేతిలోకి తీసుకోవడం వల్ల సంతకం చేసిన వ్యక్తి నిజంగా ఎంచుకోలేదు. కానీ బేరం ఇంకా అతనికి నచ్చవచ్చు; కాబట్టి చట్టం కాంట్రాక్టును voidable చేసి, అతన్నే నిర్ణయించుకోనిస్తుంది.

Unconscionable అంటే మనస్సాక్షిని కుదిపేంత అన్యాయం – ఉదాహరణకు విలువలో ఆరో వంతుకు ఇంటి అమ్మకం, లేదా చిన్న అప్పు ఎన్నో రెట్లు పెరిగేంత అధిక వడ్డీ.

selfTest.q: 1. అనుచిత ప్రభావానికి ఏ రెండు విషయాలు చూపాలి?
selfTest.a: ఒక పక్షం అవతలి వ్యక్తి ఇష్టంపై ఆధిపత్య స్థానంలో ఉన్నాడని, అన్యాయమైన లాభం పొందడానికి ఆ స్థానాన్ని వాడాడని (సెక్షన్ 16(1)).

selfTest.q: 2. రుజువు భారం ఆధిపత్య పక్షంపైకి ఎప్పుడు మారుతుంది?
selfTest.a: అతను ఆధిపత్య స్థానంలో ఉండి, అవతలి వ్యక్తితో కాంట్రాక్టు చేసి, ఆ వ్యవహారం చూడగానే లేదా సాక్ష్యంపై అన్యాయంగా కనిపించినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 16(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. అనుచిత ప్రభావం వల్ల కలిగిన కాంట్రాక్టు void యా voidable యా?
selfTest.a: ఎవరి సమ్మతి అలా కలిగిందో ఆ పక్షం ఇష్టం మేరకు voidable (సెక్షన్ 19A).

selfTest.q: 4. చాలా ఎక్కువ వడ్డీ రేటు ఒక్కటే అనుచిత ప్రభావం ఊహను కలిగిస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మొదట ఆధిపత్యం చూపాలి ( Raghunath Prasad ; దృష్టాంతం (d)).

selfTest.q: 5. ప్రభావానికి గురైన పక్షం ప్రయోజనం పొంది ఉంటే కోర్టు ఏం చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: న్యాయమైన షరతులతో కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయవచ్చు; ఉదాహరణకు నిజంగా తీసుకున్న అప్పును న్యాయమైన వడ్డీతో తిరిగి చెల్లించమనవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 19A, దృష్టాంతం (b)).

selfTest.q: 6. క్లయింట్ తన అడ్వకేట్‌కు చేసిన అమ్మకంలో మంచి విశ్వాసాన్ని ఎవరు రుజువు చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: అడ్వకేట్ (BSA సెక్షన్ 114, దృష్టాంతం (a)).

hi.inOneMinute: Undue influence exists where the relations between the parties are such that one party is in a position to dominate the will of the other , and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other (Section 16(1)). There is no threat and no lie. The pressure comes quietly from a relationship of trust, authority or dependence. Section 16 has three parts: Section 16(1): the two elements: a position to dominate, and its use for an unfair advantage. Section 16(2): situations where a person is deemed to be in a position to dominate: real or apparent authority, a fiduciary relation , or a contract with a person whose mental capacity is affected by age, illness, or mental or bodily distress. Section 16(3): if the dominant person's transaction appears unconscionable , the burden of proof shifts to him to show there was no undue influence. Effect. The contract is voidable at the option of the party influenced. The court may set it aside absolutely , or, if he received a benefit, on just terms (Section 19A). In exams, the Section 16 test, the burden of proof and the order of inquiry in Raghunath Prasad v. Sarju Prasad earn the marks. In real life this rule protects patients, elderly parents, disciples, borrowers and others who depend on someone.
legalProvision: Section 16. "Undue influence" defined. (1) A contract is said to be induced by "undue influence" where the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one of the parties is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other. (2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing principle, a person is deemed to be in a position to dominate the will of another— (a) where he holds a real or apparent authority over the other, or where he stands in a fiduciary relation to the other; or (b) where he makes a contract with a person whose mental capacity is temporarily or permanently affected by reason of age, illness, or mental or bodily distress. (3) Where a person who is in a position to dominate the will of another, enters into a contract with him, and the transaction appears, on the face of it or on the evidence adduced, to be unconscionable, the burden of proving that such contract was not induced by undue influence shall lie upon the person in a position to dominate the will of the other. Nothing in this sub-section shall affect the provisions of section 111 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872). Illustrations (a) A having advanced money to his son, B, during his minority, upon B's coming of age obtains, by misuse of parental influence, a bond from B for a greater amount than the sum due in respect of the advance. A employs undue influence. (b) A, a man enfeebled by disease or age, is induced, by B's influence over him as his medical attendant, to agree to pay B an unreasonable sum for his professional services. B employs undue influence. (c) A, being in debt to B, the money-lender of his village, contracts a fresh loan on terms which appear to be unconscionable. It lies on B to prove that the contract was not induced by undue influence. (d) A applies to a banker for a loan at a time when there is stringency in the money market. The banker declines to make the loan except at an unusually high rate of interest. A accepts the loan on these terms. This is a transaction in the ordinary course of business, and the contract is not induced by undue influence.

Section 19A. Power to set aside contract induced by undue influence. When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. Any such contract may be set aside either absolutely or, if the party who was entitled to avoid it has received any benefit thereunder, upon such terms and conditions as to the Court may seem just. Illustrations (a) A's son has forged B's name to a promissory note. B under threat of prosecuting A's son, obtains a bond from A for the amount of the forged note. If B sues on this bond, the Court may set the bond aside. (b) A, a money-lender, advances Rs. 100 to B, an agriculturist, and, by undue influence, induces B to execute a bond for Rs. 200 with interest at 6 per cent. per month. The Court may set the bond aside, ordering B to repay the Rs. 100 with such interest as may seem just.

Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 114. Where there is a question as to the good faith of a transaction between parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence, the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the party who is in a position of active confidence. Illustrations. (a) The good faith of a sale by a client to an advocate is in question in a suit brought by the client. The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the advocate. (b) The good faith of a sale by a son just come of age to a father is in question in a suit brought by the son. The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the father.
In simple words

Section 16(1): two things are needed: (i) a relationship that lets one side dominate the other's will, and (ii) use of that position to get an unfair advantage. Section 16(2): the law assumes the first element in three situations: authority (real or apparent), a relation of trust ( fiduciary ), and dealing with a person whose mind is weakened by age, illness or distress. Section 16(3): if the bargain looks unconscionable, the stronger side must prove it did not use undue influence . Section 16(3) does not cut down the Evidence Act rule (old Section 111, now BSA Section 114): a person in "active confidence" must prove the good faith of the transaction. Section 19A: the weaker party may avoid the contract; the court may set it aside fully, or on fair terms if he got something under it.
hi.meaning: Undue influence is the misuse of a position of dominance over another person's will to get an unfair advantage from him. The two elements (Section 16(1)). Element Question Example 1. Position to dominate the will Do the relations between the parties let one control the other's decisions? Guru and devoted disciple; doctor and very sick patient 2. Use of that position for an unfair advantage Did he actually use it, and was the result unfair to the other? Disciple gives her house to the guru; patient promises an unreasonable fee Both must be present. A fair deal between a doctor and a patient is not undue influence. An unfair deal between strangers on equal footing is not undue influence either (it may be something else, or just a bad bargain). "Between the parties". Section 16(1) speaks of "the relations subsisting between the parties". The dominant person must be a party to the contract (or act through one). This is different from coercion , which can come from anyone. Why the law does this. A person who signs because someone he trusts or depends on has taken over his judgment has not really chosen. But the bargain may still suit him, so the law makes the contract voidable and lets him decide. Unconscionable means so unfair that it shocks the conscience, for example a sale of a house at one-sixth of its value, or interest so high that a small loan grows to many times its size.
keyPoints: Two elements: a position to dominate, and its use for an unfair advantage (Section 16(1)). Deemed dominance: authority, fiduciary relation, weakened mental capacity (Section 16(2)); the list is not closed. Burden shifts to the dominant person if the transaction appears unconscionable (Section 16(3)); BSA Section 114 for active confidence. Dominance first, then undue influence, then burden ( Raghunath Prasad ). Urgent need of money or high interest alone does not prove dominance. A hard bargain in the ordinary course of business is not undue influence (Illustration (d)). Effect: voidable; set aside absolutely or on just terms (Section 19A).

caseLaws.name: Raghunath Prasad v
caseLaws.facts: Sarju Prasad (1923) Facts. A member of a wealthy joint family mortgaged property in 1910 for Rs. 9,999 at 2 per cent per month, with unpaid interest added to principal yearly. He later pleaded undue influence, relying only on the harsh terms and his urgent need of money. Principle. The court must first find a position to dominate; only then does the question of undue influence, and then the burden of proof, arise. Urgent need of money does not itself give the lender that position. (1924) 26 Bom LR 595 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It gives the three-stage order of inquiry under Section 16 that courts still follow. Subhas Chandra Das Mushib v. Ganga Prosad Das Mushib (1966) Facts. In 1944 a very old man (about 90 when he died in 1948) and his daughter executed a deed of settlement of village properties in favour of his grandson. One of his sons sued to set it aside, and the High Court presumed undue influence from the close relationship and the donor's old age. Principle. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's decree , applying the three stages from Raghunath Prasad : "merely because the parties were nearly related to each other no presumption of undue influence can arise"; a position to dominate must be found first. AIR 1967 SC 878 : (1967) 1 SCR 331. Why it matters. It confirms in Indian law that dominance must be proved before the burden shifts. Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v. Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd. (1962) Facts. In a dispute inside a family company, some members alleged that company resolutions of 1945 had been procured by coercion and undue influence by the eldest member, Ladli Prasad, who they said was in a dominant position over them. Principle. "the party pleading must therefore be required to plead the precise nature of the influence exercised, the manner of use of the influence, and the unfair advantage obtained by the other." AIR 1963 SC 1279 : (1964) 1 SCR 270. Why it matters. A vague plea of undue influence fails at the start. LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) Facts. The Life Insurance Corporation offered a cheap term policy only to persons employed in Government, semi-Government or reputed commercial firms. Principle. The restriction was arbitrary and violated Article 14; courts may strike down an unfair term in a contract offered by a State body to the public. (1995) Supp 1 SCR 349. Why it matters. It is a related case on unequal bargaining power. It does not apply Section 16.

selfTest.q: 1. What two things must be shown for undue influence?
selfTest.a: That one party was in a position to dominate the other's will, and that he used that position to obtain an unfair advantage (Section 16(1)).

selfTest.q: 2. When does the burden of proof move to the dominant party?
selfTest.a: When he is in a position to dominate, enters into a contract with the other, and the transaction appears unconscionable on its face or on the evidence (Section 16(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. Is a contract induced by undue influence void or voidable?
selfTest.a: Voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused (Section 19A).

selfTest.q: 4. Does a very high rate of interest by itself raise a presumption of undue influence?
selfTest.a: No. Dominance must be shown first ( Raghunath Prasad ; Illustration (d)).

selfTest.q: 5. What can the court do if the influenced party received a benefit?
selfTest.a: Set the contract aside on such terms and conditions as seem just, for example repayment of the actual loan with fair interest (Section 19A, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 6. Who must prove good faith in a sale by a client to his advocate?
selfTest.a: The advocate (BSA Section 114, Illustration (a)).

law-of-contract-i-u2-t9.subtitle: Sections 20, 21 and 22 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A mistake is a wrong belief about a fact or about the law, held when the agreement is made. The Act does not define it; it states its effect : Kind Effect Section Both parties mistaken about a fact essential to the agreement Agreement void 20 Wrong opinion about value Not a mistake of fact; no relief 20, Explanation Mistake about Indian law Contract not voidable 21 Mistake about foreign law Treated as a mistake of fact 21 One party mistaken about a fact Contract not voidable merely for that 22 So only one kind spoils the agreement completely: a shared mistake about an essential fact . A mistake by one party alone gives relief only where the other side caused it (fraud or misrepresentation ), or where a person signed a document radically different from what he thought ( non est factum ). In exams, the three sections and their illustrations are the core. In real life the rule tells you that you carry the risk of your own error.
legalProvision: Section 20. Agreement void where both parties are under mistake as to matter of fact. Where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. Explanation. —An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement, is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact. Illustrations. (a) A agrees to sell to B a specific cargo of goods supposed to be on its way from England to Bombay. It turns out that, before the day of the bargain, the ship conveying the cargo had been cast away and the goods lost. Neither party was aware of the facts. The agreement is void. (b) A agrees to buy from B a certain horse. It turns out that the horse was dead at the time of the bargain, though neither party was aware of the fact. The agreement is void. (c) A, being entitled to an estate for the life of B, agrees to sell it to C. B was dead at the time of the agreement, but both parties were ignorant of the fact. The agreement is void.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact. Illustration. A and B make a contract grounded on the erroneous belief that a particular debt is barred by the Indian Law of Limitation: the contract is not voidable.

Section 22. Contract caused by mistake of one party as to matter of fact. A contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one of the parties to it being under a mistake as to a matter of fact.
Section 14 (relevant part). Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by— … (5) mistake, subject to the provisions of sections 20, 21 and 22.
In simple words

Section 20: if both sides are wrong about a basic fact that the deal rests on, there is no deal at all. Being wrong about the price or worth of the thing does not count. Section 21: you cannot escape a contract by saying you did not know Indian law. Foreign law is treated as a fact. Section 22: if only you were wrong, that alone does not let you escape the contract.
en.meaning:
Mistake means an erroneous belief, held at the time of the agreement , about a fact or about the law. The effect depends on three questions:

Whose mistake? Both parties, or only one? About what? A fact, Indian law, or foreign law? How important? Is the fact essential to the agreement, or only about value?

Section 20: three conditions.

Condition What it means 1. Both parties are mistaken A shared (mutual or common) mistake 2. About a matter of fact Not law, not opinion about value 3. The fact is essential to the agreement It goes to the root: existence of the thing, its identity, or a basic quality the deal rests on

Why the law treats mistakes differently. A shared mistake on an essential fact means there was nothing real to agree about; the agreement fails. But where only one side is wrong, the law protects the other side, who did nothing wrong and relied on the deal. Every person must look after his own interests.

Mistake and consent. Where the parties do not agree on the same thing in the same sense (Section 13), there is no consent at all. Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864) is the standard example: two ships named Peerless .
keyPoints: A mistake of both parties on an essential fact makes the agreement void (Section 20). A wrong opinion about value is not a mistake of fact. A mistake of one party does not make the contract voidable merely for that reason (Section 22). A mistake of Indian law has no effect. A mistake of foreign law is a mistake of fact (Section 21). A mistake caused by the other side's fraud or misrepresentation gives relief under Section 19. A signature on a radically different document may be disowned by non est factum, if the signer was not careless. Money paid under a void agreement or by mistake must be returned (Sections 65, 72).

caseLaws.name: Raffles v
caseLaws.facts: Wichelhaus (1864) Facts. 125 bales of Surat cotton were sold "to arrive ex Peerless from Bombay". Two ships named Peerless sailed from Bombay, one in October and one in December; the buyer meant the October ship and the seller tendered cotton from the December ship. Principle. The buyer's plea that he meant a different ship was held a good answer on demurrer, and judgment was given for the buyer. (1864) 2 H & C 906 (Court of Exchequer). Why it matters. The standard example of parties not agreeing on the same thing, so there is no contract. Ningawwa v. Byrappa (1968) Facts. A young, illiterate woman executed a gift deed in favour of her husband, believing it covered only two plots in one village. The husband had fraudulently included two valuable plots she had inherited in another village. Principle. Fraud as to the character of a document makes the transaction void; fraud as to its contents makes it only voidable. Here it was as to contents, so the gift was voidable. AIR 1968 SC 956 : (1968) 2 SCR 797. Why it matters. It marks when a mistake about a signed document destroys consent altogether (non est factum) and when it only makes the deal voidable. Tarsem Singh v. Sukhminder Singh (1998) Facts. An agreement of 1988 to sell agricultural land in Village Panjetha, Patiala, was made at a rate per unit of area, and ₹77,000 was paid as earnest money. Both parties were mistaken about the area (kanals or bighas) and so about the price. Principle. A mutual mistake about the area, an essential fact, made the agreement void under Section 20; the seller was bound under Section 65 to refund the earnest money. "Unilateral mistake is outside the scope of this Section." (1998) 3 SCC 471 : AIR 1998 SC 1400. Why it matters. It is a Supreme Court application of Sections 20 and 65 together: void agreement, money returned.

selfTest.q: 1. What makes an agreement void for mistake under Section 20?
selfTest.a: Both parties being under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement.

selfTest.q: 2. Does a mistake of Indian law make a contract voidable?
selfTest.a: No (Section 21). A mistake as to a law not in force in India is treated like a mistake of fact.

selfTest.q: 3. Does a wrong opinion about the value of the thing count as a mistake of fact?
selfTest.a: No. The Explanation to Section 20 says it does not.

selfTest.q: 4. A sells B a horse. Unknown to both, it died an hour earlier. B has paid ₹40,000. What can B do?
selfTest.a: The agreement is void (Section 20, Illustration (b)). B can recover ₹40,000 (Section 65).

selfTest.q: 5. When does a one-sided mistake give relief?
selfTest.a: When the other side caused it by fraud or misrepresentation (Sections 17, 18(3), 19), or when the signer was misled about the nature of the document (non est factum).

selfTest.q: 6. What is the difference between fraud as to the character and as to the contents of a document?
selfTest.a: Fraud as to character makes the transaction void; fraud as to contents makes it voidable ( Ningawwa v. Byrappa ).

సెక్షన్ 20: బేరం ఆధారపడిన ప్రాథమిక వాస్తవం గురించి ఇద్దరూ తప్పుగా అనుకుంటే, బేరమే ఉండదు. వస్తువు ధర లేదా విలువ గురించి తప్పుగా అనుకోవడం దీని కిందకు రాదు. సెక్షన్ 21: భారత చట్టం తెలియదని చెప్పి కాంట్రాక్టు నుంచి తప్పించుకోలేరు. విదేశీ చట్టాన్ని వాస్తవంగా చూస్తారు. సెక్షన్ 22: మీరు ఒక్కరే తప్పుగా అనుకుంటే, దాని వల్ల మాత్రమే కాంట్రాక్టు నుంచి బయటపడలేరు.
te.meaning:
పొరపాటు అంటే ఒప్పందం సమయంలో ఒక వాస్తవం గురించి గానీ, చట్టం గురించి గానీ ఉన్న తప్పు నమ్మకం. దాని ప్రభావం మూడు ప్రశ్నలపై ఆధారపడుతుంది:

ఎవరి పొరపాటు? ఇద్దరిదా, ఒక్కరిదా? దేని గురించి? వాస్తవమా, భారత చట్టమా, విదేశీ చట్టమా? ఎంత ముఖ్యం? ఆ వాస్తవం ఒప్పందానికి అత్యవసరమైనదా , లేక కేవలం విలువ గురించా?

సెక్షన్ 20: మూడు షరతులు.

షరతు అర్థం 1. ఇద్దరు పక్షాలూ పొరపడాలి ఉమ్మడి (mutual లేదా common) పొరపాటు 2. వాస్తవం గురించి చట్టం గురించి కాదు, విలువపై అభిప్రాయం కాదు 3. ఆ వాస్తవం ఒప్పందానికి అత్యవసరం మూలాన్ని తాకేది: వస్తువు ఉనికి, దాని గుర్తింపు, లేదా బేరం ఆధారపడిన ప్రాథమిక గుణం

చట్టం పొరపాట్లను వేర్వేరుగా ఎందుకు చూస్తుంది. అత్యవసర వాస్తవం గురించి ఉమ్మడి పొరపాటు అంటే, ఒప్పుకోవడానికి నిజంగా ఏమీ లేదు; ఒప్పందం విఫలమవుతుంది. కానీ ఒక్క పక్షమే పొరపడితే, ఏ తప్పూ చేయకుండా ఆ బేరాన్ని నమ్ముకున్న ఎదుటి పక్షాన్ని చట్టం కాపాడుతుంది. ప్రతి వ్యక్తీ తన ప్రయోజనాలను తానే చూసుకోవాలి.

పొరపాటు, సమ్మతి. పక్షాలు ఒకే విషయాన్ని ఒకే అర్థంలో ఒప్పుకోకపోతే (సెక్షన్ 13), అసలు సమ్మతే లేదు. Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864) దీనికి ప్రామాణిక ఉదాహరణ: Peerless అనే పేరుతో రెండు ఓడలు.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 20 కింద ఒప్పందాన్ని పొరపాటు వల్ల చెల్లనిదిగా చేసేది ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఒప్పందానికి అత్యవసరమైన వాస్తవం గురించి ఇద్దరు పక్షాలూ పొరపడటం.

selfTest.q: 2. భారత చట్టం గురించిన పొరపాటు కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయదగినదిగా చేస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు (సెక్షన్ 21). భారతదేశంలో అమలులో లేని చట్టం గురించిన పొరపాటును వాస్తవ పొరపాటు లాగే చూస్తారు.

selfTest.q: 3. వస్తువు విలువ గురించిన తప్పు అభిప్రాయం వాస్తవ పొరపాటా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సెక్షన్ 20 Explanation అలా చెబుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. A, B కి ఒక గుర్రాన్ని అమ్ముతాడు. ఇద్దరికీ తెలియకుండా, అది గంట ముందే చనిపోయింది. B ₹40,000 చెల్లించాడు. B ఏం చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు (సెక్షన్ 20, Illustration (b)). B ₹40,000 తిరిగి పొందవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 65).

selfTest.q: 5. ఒక్క పక్షం పొరపాటుకు ఉపశమనం ఎప్పుడు దొరుకుతుంది?
selfTest.a: ఎదుటి పక్షం మోసం లేదా తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యంతో దాన్ని కలిగించినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్లు 17, 18(3), 19), లేదా పత్రం స్వభావం గురించి సంతకం చేసినవాణ్ని తప్పుదారి పట్టించినప్పుడు (non est factum).

selfTest.q: 6. పత్రం స్వభావం గురించి మోసానికి, దాని విషయం గురించి మోసానికి తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: స్వభావం గురించి మోసం లావాదేవీని చెల్లనిదిగా చేస్తుంది; విషయం గురించి మోసం రద్దు చేయదగినదిగా చేస్తుంది ( Ningawwa v. Byrappa ).

hi.inOneMinute: A mistake is a wrong belief about a fact or about the law, held when the agreement is made. The Act does not define it; it states its effect : Kind Effect Section Both parties mistaken about a fact essential to the agreement Agreement void 20 Wrong opinion about value Not a mistake of fact; no relief 20, Explanation Mistake about Indian law Contract not voidable 21 Mistake about foreign law Treated as a mistake of fact 21 One party mistaken about a fact Contract not voidable merely for that 22 So only one kind spoils the agreement completely: a shared mistake about an essential fact . A mistake by one party alone gives relief only where the other side caused it (fraud or misrepresentation ), or where a person signed a document radically different from what he thought ( non est factum ). In exams, the three sections and their illustrations are the core. In real life the rule tells you that you carry the risk of your own error.
legalProvision: Section 20. Agreement void where both parties are under mistake as to matter of fact. Where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. Explanation. —An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement, is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact. Illustrations. (a) A agrees to sell to B a specific cargo of goods supposed to be on its way from England to Bombay. It turns out that, before the day of the bargain, the ship conveying the cargo had been cast away and the goods lost. Neither party was aware of the facts. The agreement is void. (b) A agrees to buy from B a certain horse. It turns out that the horse was dead at the time of the bargain, though neither party was aware of the fact. The agreement is void. (c) A, being entitled to an estate for the life of B, agrees to sell it to C. B was dead at the time of the agreement, but both parties were ignorant of the fact. The agreement is void.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact. Illustration. A and B make a contract grounded on the erroneous belief that a particular debt is barred by the Indian Law of Limitation: the contract is not voidable.

Section 22. Contract caused by mistake of one party as to matter of fact. A contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one of the parties to it being under a mistake as to a matter of fact.
Section 14 (relevant part). Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by— … (5) mistake, subject to the provisions of sections 20, 21 and 22.
In simple words

Section 20: if both sides are wrong about a basic fact that the deal rests on, there is no deal at all. Being wrong about the price or worth of the thing does not count. Section 21: you cannot escape a contract by saying you did not know Indian law. Foreign law is treated as a fact. Section 22: if only you were wrong, that alone does not let you escape the contract.
hi.meaning: Mistake means an erroneous belief, held at the time of the agreement , about a fact or about the law. The effect depends on three questions: Whose mistake? Both parties, or only one? About what? A fact, Indian law, or foreign law? How important? Is the fact essential to the agreement, or only about value? Section 20: three conditions. Condition What it means 1. Both parties are mistaken A shared (mutual or common) mistake 2. About a matter of fact Not law, not opinion about value 3. The fact is essential to the agreement It goes to the root: existence of the thing, its identity, or a basic quality the deal rests on Why the law treats mistakes differently. A shared mistake on an essential fact means there was nothing real to agree about; the agreement fails. But where only one side is wrong, the law protects the other side, who did nothing wrong and relied on the deal. Every person must look after his own interests. Mistake and consent. Where the parties do not agree on the same thing in the same sense (Section 13), there is no consent at all. Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864) is the standard example: two ships named Peerless .
keyPoints: A mistake of both parties on an essential fact makes the agreement void (Section 20). A wrong opinion about value is not a mistake of fact. A mistake of one party does not make the contract voidable merely for that reason (Section 22). A mistake of Indian law has no effect. A mistake of foreign law is a mistake of fact (Section 21). A mistake caused by the other side's fraud or misrepresentation gives relief under Section 19. A signature on a radically different document may be disowned by non est factum, if the signer was not careless. Money paid under a void agreement or by mistake must be returned (Sections 65, 72).

caseLaws.name: Raffles v
caseLaws.facts: Wichelhaus (1864) Facts. 125 bales of Surat cotton were sold "to arrive ex Peerless from Bombay". Two ships named Peerless sailed from Bombay, one in October and one in December; the buyer meant the October ship and the seller tendered cotton from the December ship. Principle. The buyer's plea that he meant a different ship was held a good answer on demurrer, and judgment was given for the buyer. (1864) 2 H & C 906 (Court of Exchequer). Why it matters. The standard example of parties not agreeing on the same thing, so there is no contract. Ningawwa v. Byrappa (1968) Facts. A young, illiterate woman executed a gift deed in favour of her husband, believing it covered only two plots in one village. The husband had fraudulently included two valuable plots she had inherited in another village. Principle. Fraud as to the character of a document makes the transaction void; fraud as to its contents makes it only voidable. Here it was as to contents, so the gift was voidable. AIR 1968 SC 956 : (1968) 2 SCR 797. Why it matters. It marks when a mistake about a signed document destroys consent altogether (non est factum) and when it only makes the deal voidable. Tarsem Singh v. Sukhminder Singh (1998) Facts. An agreement of 1988 to sell agricultural land in Village Panjetha, Patiala, was made at a rate per unit of area, and ₹77,000 was paid as earnest money. Both parties were mistaken about the area (kanals or bighas) and so about the price. Principle. A mutual mistake about the area, an essential fact, made the agreement void under Section 20; the seller was bound under Section 65 to refund the earnest money. "Unilateral mistake is outside the scope of this Section." (1998) 3 SCC 471 : AIR 1998 SC 1400. Why it matters. It is a Supreme Court application of Sections 20 and 65 together: void agreement, money returned.

selfTest.q: 1. What makes an agreement void for mistake under Section 20?
selfTest.a: Both parties being under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement.

selfTest.q: 2. Does a mistake of Indian law make a contract voidable?
selfTest.a: No (Section 21). A mistake as to a law not in force in India is treated like a mistake of fact.

selfTest.q: 3. Does a wrong opinion about the value of the thing count as a mistake of fact?
selfTest.a: No. The Explanation to Section 20 says it does not.

selfTest.q: 4. A sells B a horse. Unknown to both, it died an hour earlier. B has paid ₹40,000. What can B do?
selfTest.a: The agreement is void (Section 20, Illustration (b)). B can recover ₹40,000 (Section 65).

selfTest.q: 5. When does a one-sided mistake give relief?
selfTest.a: When the other side caused it by fraud or misrepresentation (Sections 17, 18(3), 19), or when the signer was misled about the nature of the document (non est factum).

selfTest.q: 6. What is the difference between fraud as to the character and as to the contents of a document?
selfTest.a: Fraud as to character makes the transaction void; fraud as to contents makes it voidable ( Ningawwa v. Byrappa ).

law-of-contract-i-u2-t10.subtitle: Sections 10, 23 and 24 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An agreement is a contract only if its consideration and its object are lawful (Section 10). Section 23 says both are lawful unless one of five grounds applies: it is forbidden by law ; if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law ; it is fraudulent ; it involves or implies injury to the person or property of another ; the Court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy . If any ground applies, the consideration or object is unlawful , and the agreement is void . If even part of a single consideration or object is unlawful, the whole agreement is void (Section 24). Void is wider than unlawful. A wager is void (Section 30) but not forbidden by law ( Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya ). In exams, the five grounds and the Act's illustrations earn the marks. In real life, no court will enforce a deal to break the law.
legalProvision: Section 10. What agreements are contracts. All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 23. What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not. The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless— it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy. In each of these cases, the consideration or object of an agreement is said to be unlawful. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.

Section 24. Agreements void, if considerations and objects unlawful in part. If any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any one or any part of any one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void. Illustration. A promises to superintend, on behalf of B, a legal manufacture of indigo, and an illegal traffic in other articles. B promises to pay to A a salary of 10,000 rupees a year. The agreement is void, the object of A's promise, and the consideration for B's promise, being in part unlawful.

Related sections. Section 2(g): "An agreement not enforceable by law is said to be void." Sections 57 and 58 save the legal part of reciprocal and alternative promises (see Illegal agreements ). Section 65: a person who has received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void must restore it or make compensation.
In simple words

Section 10: a lawful consideration and a lawful object are two of the essentials of every contract. Section 23: what you promise, and what you aim at, must not break the law, get round the law, cheat, harm someone, or offend morality or public policy . If they do, the agreement is void. Section 24: if even a part of a single bargain is unlawful, the whole bargain fails.
en.meaning:
Object is the purpose the parties set out to achieve by the agreement. Consideration is what each party gives or promises in return . Under Section 2(d) it is an act, an abstinence or a promise, done or made at the promisor's desire by the promisee or any other person. Section 23 treats both alike: if either is unlawful, the agreement is void. How Section 23 is worded. It starts from lawfulness: the consideration or object "is lawful, unless" a listed ground applies. So the party who says an agreement is unlawful must bring it within one of the grounds. The five grounds at a glance. Ground Meaning in short Act's illustration Forbidden by law Punishable or prohibited by a statute or rule made under it (h): dropping a robbery prosecution for money Defeats a law Allowed on its face, but would get round a law (i): defaulter buying back his own estate through a benamidar Fraudulent Aims at or involves a fraud (e): dividing gains made by fraud; (g): agent secretly getting a lease of his principal's land Injury to person or property of another Involves or implies harm to someone (no illustration; see example below) Immoral or opposed to public policy As regarded by the Court (f): paying for a government job; (j): mukhtar selling his influence; (k): letting a daughter for concubinage See Diagram 1 . Would permitting it leave every law intact? Is it free from fraud? Does it avoid injury to the person or property of another? Does the Court regard it as neither immoral nor opposed to public policy? A "No" to any question makes the object or consideration unlawful and the agreement void (Section 23); restore any advantage (Section 65). If all are "Yes", it is lawful; but if any part of a single consideration or object is unlawful, the whole agreement is void (Section 24), subject to Sections 57 and 58.
keyPoints: Section 23 makes the consideration or object lawful unless a listed ground applies. The grounds: forbidden by law, defeating a law, fraud, injury to another, and immorality or public policy. An agreement with an unlawful object or consideration is void. Section 24: an unlawful part of a single bargain makes the whole agreement void. "Forbidden by law" means acts punishable under the penal law or prohibited by special laws. Void is wider than unlawful: a wager is void but not unlawful. Section 65: an advantage received under an agreement discovered to be void must be restored.

caseLaws.name: Gherulal Parakh v
caseLaws.facts: Mahadeodas Maiya (1959) Facts. Two parties formed a partnership to enter into forward contracts for wheat with other firms and share profit and loss equally. The transactions made a loss; one partner paid it and sued the other for half. Principle. A wagering contract is void under Section 30 but not forbidden by law, so an agreement collateral to it (the partnership) is not unlawful under Section 23; "immoral" is confined to settled heads, and public policy is invoked only in clear cases of harm to the public. AIR 1959 SC 781 : [1959] Supp 2 SCR 406. Why it matters. It explains "forbidden by law", "immoral" and "public policy" in Section 23, and shows that void and unlawful are different.

selfTest.q: 1. When is the object or consideration of an agreement unlawful?
selfTest.a: When it is forbidden by law, would defeat a law, or is fraudulent; when it involves or implies injury to another's person or property; or when the Court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy (Section 23).

selfTest.q: 2. What is the effect of an unlawful object?
selfTest.a: The agreement is void (Section 23).

selfTest.q: 3. What does Section 24 say about an agreement partly unlawful?
selfTest.a: If any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any part of one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void.

selfTest.q: 4. Is a wagering agreement "forbidden by law" under Section 23?
selfTest.a: No. It is void under Section 30 but not forbidden by law ( Gherulal Parakh ).

selfTest.q: 5. A promises B ₹5,000 to withdraw a robbery prosecution that B has started against A's son. Is this lawful?
selfTest.a: No. Like Illustration (h), the object is unlawful and the agreement is void.

selfTest.q: 6. How does a "fraudulent object" differ from fraud under Section 17?
selfTest.a: Under Section 17, fraud is used to obtain consent and the contract is voidable. A fraudulent object means the agreement's purpose is to defraud, and the agreement is void.

సెక్షన్ 10: చట్టబద్ధమైన ప్రతిఫలం, చట్టబద్ధమైన లక్ష్యం ప్రతి కాంట్రాక్టుకూ అవసరమైన రెండు అంశాలు. సెక్షన్ 23: మీరు ఇచ్చే వాగ్దానం, మీరు ఆశించే లక్ష్యం చట్టాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించకూడదు, చట్టాన్ని తప్పించుకోకూడదు, మోసం చేయకూడదు, ఎవరికీ హాని చేయకూడదు, నైతికతను లేదా ప్రజా విధానాన్ని దెబ్బతీయకూడదు. అలా చేస్తే ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు. సెక్షన్ 24: ఒకే బేరంలో ఒక భాగం చట్టవిరుద్ధమైనా, మొత్తం బేరం విఫలమవుతుంది.

లక్ష్యం (object) అంటే ఒప్పందం ద్వారా పక్షాలు సాధించాలనుకునే ఉద్దేశం . ప్రతిఫలం ( consideration ) అంటే ప్రతి పక్షం బదులుగా ఇచ్చేది లేదా వాగ్దానం చేసేది . సెక్షన్ 2(d) ప్రకారం అది వాగ్దానం చేసినవాడి కోరిక మేరకు, వాగ్దానం పొందినవాడు లేదా ఇంకెవరైనా చేసిన చర్య, మానుకోవడం, లేదా వాగ్దానం. సెక్షన్ 23 రెండింటినీ ఒకేలా చూస్తుంది: ఏది చట్టవిరుద్ధమైనా, ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు. సెక్షన్ 23 పదజాలం. అది చట్టబద్ధత నుంచి మొదలవుతుంది: ప్రతిఫలం లేదా లక్ష్యం "is lawful, unless" జాబితాలోని కారణం వర్తిస్తే తప్ప. కాబట్టి ఒప్పందం చట్టవిరుద్ధమని చెప్పే పక్షమే దాన్ని ఏదో ఒక కారణం కిందకు తీసుకురావాలి. ఐదు కారణాలు ఒక్క చూపులో. కారణం క్లుప్తంగా అర్థం చట్టంలోని illustration చట్టం నిషేధించినది చట్టం లేదా దాని కింది నియమం శిక్షించేది లేదా నిషేధించేది (h): డబ్బు కోసం దోపిడీ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ ఉపసంహరించడం చట్టాన్ని నిష్ఫలం చేసేది పైకి అనుమతించినట్టే ఉన్నా, చట్టాన్ని తప్పించుకునేది (i): బకాయిదారు బినామీ ద్వారా తన ఎస్టేట్ ను తిరిగి కొనడం మోసపూరితమైనది మోసాన్ని లక్ష్యంగా పెట్టుకున్నది లేదా అందులో మోసం ఉన్నది (e): మోసంతో వచ్చిన లాభాలు పంచుకోవడం; (g): ఏజెంట్ రహస్యంగా యజమాని భూమిని లీజుకు ఇప్పించడం ఇంకొకరి శరీరానికి లేదా ఆస్తికి హాని ఎవరికైనా హాని కలిగించేది లేదా సూచించేది (illustration లేదు; కింది ఉదాహరణ చూడండి) అనైతికం లేదా ప్రజా విధానానికి వ్యతిరేకం కోర్టు అలా భావిస్తే (f): ప్రభుత్వ ఉద్యోగం కోసం డబ్బు; (j): ముఖ్తార్ తన ప్రభావాన్ని అమ్ముకోవడం; (k): కూతురిని ఉంపుడుగత్తెగా అద్దెకు ఇవ్వడం Diagram 1 చూడండి. selfTest.q: 1. ఒప్పందం లక్ష్యం లేదా ప్రతిఫలం ఎప్పుడు చట్టవిరుద్ధం?
selfTest.a: చట్టం నిషేధించినప్పుడు, చట్టాన్ని నిష్ఫలం చేసేటప్పుడు, మోసపూరితమైనప్పుడు; ఇంకొకరి శరీరానికి లేదా ఆస్తికి హాని కలిగించినప్పుడు లేదా సూచించినప్పుడు; లేదా కోర్టు దాన్ని అనైతికంగా, ప్రజా విధానానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా భావించినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 23).

selfTest.q: 2. చట్టవిరుద్ధమైన లక్ష్యం ప్రభావం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు (సెక్షన్ 23).

selfTest.q: 3. పాక్షికంగా చట్టవిరుద్ధమైన ఒప్పందం గురించి సెక్షన్ 24 ఏం చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: ఒకటి లేదా అంతకంటే ఎక్కువ లక్ష్యాలకు ఒకే ప్రతిఫలంలో ఏ భాగమైనా, లేదా ఒకే లక్ష్యానికి అనేక ప్రతిఫలాల్లో ఏదైనా లేదా దాని భాగమైనా చట్టవిరుద్ధమైతే, ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు.

selfTest.q: 4. పందెం ఒప్పందం సెక్షన్ 23 కింద "forbidden by law" అవుతుందా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అది సెక్షన్ 30 కింద చెల్లదు, కానీ చట్టం నిషేధించినది కాదు ( Gherulal Parakh ).

selfTest.q: 5. A కొడుకుపై B వేసిన దోపిడీ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ ను ఉపసంహరించడానికి A, B కి ₹5,000 ఇస్తానని వాగ్దానం చేస్తాడు. ఇది చట్టబద్ధమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. Illustration (h) లాగే, లక్ష్యం చట్టవిరుద్ధం; ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు.

selfTest.q: 6. "మోసపూరిత లక్ష్యం", సెక్షన్ 17 కింద మోసం ఎలా భిన్నం?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 17 కింద సమ్మతి పొందడానికి మోసం వాడతారు; కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయదగినది. మోసపూరిత లక్ష్యం అంటే ఒప్పందం ఉద్దేశమే మోసగించడం; ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు.

చట్టం నిషేధించినది చట్టం లేదా దాని కింది నియమం శిక్షించేది లేదా నిషేధించేది (h): డబ్బు కోసం దోపిడీ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ ఉపసంహరించడం
చట్టాన్ని నిష్ఫలం చేసేది పైకి అనుమతించినట్టే ఉన్నా, చట్టాన్ని తప్పించుకునేది (i): బకాయిదారు బినామీ ద్వారా తన ఎస్టేట్ ను తిరిగి కొనడం
మోసపూరితమైనది మోసాన్ని లక్ష్యంగా పెట్టుకున్నది లేదా అందులో మోసం ఉన్నది (e): మోసంతో వచ్చిన లాభాలు పంచుకోవడం; (g): ఏజెంట్ రహస్యంగా యజమాని భూమిని లీజుకు ఇప్పించడం
ఇంకొకరి శరీరానికి లేదా ఆస్తికి హాని ఎవరికైనా హాని కలిగించేది లేదా సూచించేది (illustration లేదు; కింది ఉదాహరణ చూడండి)
అనైతికం లేదా ప్రజా విధానానికి వ్యతిరేకం కోర్టు అలా భావిస్తే (f): ప్రభుత్వ ఉద్యోగం కోసం డబ్బు; (j): ముఖ్తార్ తన ప్రభావాన్ని అమ్ముకోవడం; (k): కూతురిని ఉంపుడుగత్తెగా అద్దెకు ఇవ్వడం

hi.inOneMinute: An agreement is a contract only if its consideration and its object are lawful (Section 10). Section 23 says both are lawful unless one of five grounds applies: it is forbidden by law ; if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law ; it is fraudulent ; it involves or implies injury to the person or property of another ; the Court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy . If any ground applies, the consideration or object is unlawful , and the agreement is void . If even part of a single consideration or object is unlawful, the whole agreement is void (Section 24). Void is wider than unlawful. A wager is void (Section 30) but not forbidden by law ( Gherulal Parakh v. Mahadeodas Maiya ). In exams, the five grounds and the Act's illustrations earn the marks. In real life, no court will enforce a deal to break the law.
legalProvision: Section 10. What agreements are contracts. All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 23. What considerations and objects are lawful, and what not. The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless— it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy. In each of these cases, the consideration or object of an agreement is said to be unlawful. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void.

Section 24. Agreements void, if considerations and objects unlawful in part. If any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any one or any part of any one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void. Illustration. A promises to superintend, on behalf of B, a legal manufacture of indigo, and an illegal traffic in other articles. B promises to pay to A a salary of 10,000 rupees a year. The agreement is void, the object of A's promise, and the consideration for B's promise, being in part unlawful.

Related sections. Section 2(g): "An agreement not enforceable by law is said to be void." Sections 57 and 58 save the legal part of reciprocal and alternative promises (see Illegal agreements ). Section 65: a person who has received an advantage under an agreement discovered to be void must restore it or make compensation.
In simple words

Section 10: a lawful consideration and a lawful object are two of the essentials of every contract. Section 23: what you promise, and what you aim at, must not break the law, get round the law, cheat, harm someone, or offend morality or public policy . If they do, the agreement is void. Section 24: if even a part of a single bargain is unlawful, the whole bargain fails.
hi.meaning:
Object is the purpose the parties set out to achieve by the agreement. Consideration is what each party gives or promises in return . Under Section 2(d) it is an act, an abstinence or a promise, done or made at the promisor's desire by the promisee or any other person. Section 23 treats both alike: if either is unlawful, the agreement is void. How Section 23 is worded. It starts from lawfulness: the consideration or object "is lawful, unless" a listed ground applies. So the party who says an agreement is unlawful must bring it within one of the grounds. The five grounds at a glance. If all are "Yes", it is lawful; but if any part of a single consideration or object is unlawful, the whole agreement is void (Section 24), subject to Sections 57 and 58.
keyPoints: Section 23 makes the consideration or object lawful unless a listed ground applies. The grounds: forbidden by law, defeating a law, fraud, injury to another, and immorality or public policy. An agreement with an unlawful object or consideration is void. Section 24: an unlawful part of a single bargain makes the whole agreement void. "Forbidden by law" means acts punishable under the penal law or prohibited by special laws. Void is wider than unlawful: a wager is void but not unlawful. Section 65: an advantage received under an agreement discovered to be void must be restored.

caseLaws.name: Gherulal Parakh v
caseLaws.facts: Mahadeodas Maiya (1959) Facts. Two parties formed a partnership to enter into forward contracts for wheat with other firms and share profit and loss equally. The transactions made a loss; one partner paid it and sued the other for half. Principle. A wagering contract is void under Section 30 but not forbidden by law, so an agreement collateral to it (the partnership) is not unlawful under Section 23; "immoral" is confined to settled heads, and public policy is invoked only in clear cases of harm to the public. AIR 1959 SC 781 : [1959] Supp 2 SCR 406. Why it matters. It explains "forbidden by law", "immoral" and "public policy" in Section 23, and shows that void and unlawful are different.

selfTest.q: 1. When is the object or consideration of an agreement unlawful?
selfTest.a: When it is forbidden by law, would defeat a law, or is fraudulent; when it involves or implies injury to another's person or property; or when the Court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy (Section 23).

selfTest.q: 2. What is the effect of an unlawful object?
selfTest.a: The agreement is void (Section 23).

selfTest.q: 3. What does Section 24 say about an agreement partly unlawful?
selfTest.a: If any part of a single consideration for one or more objects, or any part of one of several considerations for a single object, is unlawful, the agreement is void.

selfTest.q: 4. Is a wagering agreement "forbidden by law" under Section 23?
selfTest.a: No. It is void under Section 30 but not forbidden by law ( Gherulal Parakh ).

selfTest.q: 5. A promises B ₹5,000 to withdraw a robbery prosecution that B has started against A's son. Is this lawful?
selfTest.a: No. Like Illustration (h), the object is unlawful and the agreement is void.

selfTest.q: 6. How does a "fraudulent object" differ from fraud under Section 17?
selfTest.a: Under Section 17, fraud is used to obtain consent and the contract is voidable. A fraudulent object means the agreement's purpose is to defraud, and the agreement is void.
