en.inOneMinute: Accord and satisfaction is a way to end a claim by taking something different from what was promised. The accord is the agreement to accept the substitute. The satisfaction is the giving and accepting of that substitute. When both are complete, the original claim is discharged. The idea sits inside Section 63, which lets a promisee accept "any satisfaction which he thinks fit". In exams it is a short-note topic. In real life it is what a settlement "in full and final satisfaction" of a claim does.
legalProvision: Section 63. Promisee may dispense with or remit performance of promisee. Every promisee may dispense with or remit, wholly or in part, the performance of the promisee made to him, or may extend the time for such performance, or may accept instead of it any satisfaction which he thinks fit. Illustrations. (b) A owes B 5,000 rupees. A pays to B, and B accepts, in satisfaction of the whole debt, 2,000 rupees paid at the time and place at which the 5,000 rupees were payable. The whole debt is discharged. (c) A owes B 5,000 rupees. C pays to B 1,000 rupees, and B accepts them, in satisfaction of his claim on A. This payment is a discharge of the whole claim. (d) A owes B, under a contract, a sum of money, the amount of which has not been ascertained. A, without ascertaining the amount, gives to B, and B, in satisfaction thereof, accepts, the sum of 2,000 rupees. This is a discharge of the whole debt, whatever may be its amount.
Related provisions
Section 41. Effect of accepting performance from third person. When a promisee accepts performance of the promise from a third person, he cannot afterwards enforce it against the promisor.

Section 19. Voidability of agreements without free consent. When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

Section 19A. Power to set aside contract induced by undue influence. When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. Any such contract may be set aside either absolutely or, if the party who was entitled to avoid it has received any benefit thereunder, upon such terms and conditions as to the Court may seem just.
In simple words

The Act does not use the words " accord and satisfaction ". The idea comes from the words "any satisfaction which he thinks fit" in Section 63. Illustrations (b), (c) and (d) show a claim discharged by a substitute that the promisee accepted.
en.meaning:
Accord and satisfaction means the discharge of a claim by the performance of a substituted obligation that the claimant agreed to accept. Part What it is Accord The agreement to accept a substitute Satisfaction The giving and accepting of that substitute Why the law allows it. A promisee owns his claim and may settle it on any terms he chooses. It also gives people a reason to settle disputes. See Diagram 1 for the stages. Diagram 1. Read the boxes from top to bottom. The original claim ends only at the last box. flowchart TD C["1. The original claim
A owes B a promised performance
(e.g. a carved table worth ₹80,000)"] A["2. The accord
B agrees to accept something different
(e.g. a ready-made table)
Original claim still stands"] S["3. The satisfaction
A gives the substitute
and B accepts it"] D["4. Discharge
The original claim ends (s.63)"] X["Substitute never given:
the original claim remains"] C --> A A --> S S --> D A -. "No satisfaction" .-> X Text description Stage 1, the original claim: A owes B a promised performance, for example a carved table worth ₹80,000. Stage 2, the accord: B agrees to accept something different instead, for example a ready-made table; the original claim still stands. Stage 3, the satisfaction: A gives the substitute and B accepts it. Stage 4, discharge: the original claim ends (Section 63). If the substitute is never given, the original claim remains.
keyPoints: The accord is the agreement to accept a substitute. The satisfaction is its performance. The original claim is discharged when the substitute is given and accepted (Section 63). The promisee may accept any satisfaction he thinks fit. A voluntary full and final settlement ends the claim and the right to arbitrate it. A disputed voucher does not by itself bar arbitration; the claimant must prove fraud, coercion, undue influence or economic duress ( Boghara Polyfab ). Consent to a settlement must be free (Sections 14 to 19A). A settlement caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation is voidable (Section 19). Novation replaces the contract at once. Accord and satisfaction ends the claim when the substitute is given.

caseLaws.name: National Insurance Co
caseLaws.facts: Ltd. v. Boghara Polyfab Pvt. Ltd. (2008) Facts. The insured's goods were damaged in the Surat floods of August 2004. The surveyor assessed the loss at Rs 3,18,26,025, but the insurer paid Rs 2,33,94,964 against a discharge voucher in full and final settlement. The insured then claimed the balance in arbitration, saying the voucher was signed under coercion. Principle. A claim cannot be rejected "merely or solely" because a discharge voucher was signed, if its validity is disputed. Withholding an admitted amount until a voucher is signed "is unfair, irregular and illegal". The Court held, prima facie , that "there is no accord and satisfaction in this case and the dispute is arbitrable", and dismissed the insurer's appeal. (2009) 1 SCC 267 : AIR 2009 SC 170 (Supreme Court, 18 September 2008). Why it matters. It is the main Indian authority on discharge vouchers and full and final settlements. Union of India v. Kishorilal Gupta & Bros. (1959) Facts. The firm had three contracts of 1943 and 1944 with the Government to make and supply military stores, each with an arbitration clause. After disputes, the parties made a settlement in place of the contracts, and the question was whether the arbitration clause survived. Principle. The majority held that the settlement was a substituted agreement, so the arbitration clause " perished with the original contract". Sarkar J. dissented: in accord and satisfaction "The contract is not annihilated but the obligations under it cease to be enforceable", so it "does not destroy the arbitration clause". AIR 1959 SC 1362 : 1960 (1) SCR 493 (Supreme Court, 21 May 1959). Why it matters. It shows how a substituted contract and accord and satisfaction differ in effect. Pinnel's Case (1602) Facts. On a bond for £8 10s, the debtor pleaded that the creditor had accepted a smaller sum in full satisfaction. (1602) 5 Co Rep 117a. Principle. At common law, a smaller sum paid on the due day cannot satisfy a larger debt. A different thing accepted in its place can. Why it matters. It is the origin of the idea. Section 63 goes further on part payment.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two parts of accord and satisfaction?
selfTest.a: The accord is the agreement to accept a substitute. The satisfaction is the giving and acceptance of that substitute.

selfTest.q: 2. When is the original claim discharged?
selfTest.a: When the substitute is given and accepted (Section 63).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a claimant undo a full and final settlement only because he needed cash?
selfTest.a: No. Financial need alone, without pressure from the other side, leaves the settlement his free choice ( Boghara Polyfab ). He must prove fraud, coercion, undue influence or a similar defect.

selfTest.q: 4. A company releases admitted dues only if the claimant signs a full and final voucher. Does the voucher bar arbitration?
selfTest.a: No. Boghara Polyfab says such a voucher will not be a bar to arbitration.

selfTest.q: 5. B agrees to take a refrigerator instead of rent, but it is never delivered. Is the rent claim discharged?
selfTest.a: No. Without the satisfaction, the original claim remains.

selfTest.q: 1. అకార్డ్ అండ్ శాటిస్ఫాక్షన్‌లో రెండు భాగాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: ప్రత్యామ్నాయాన్ని అంగీకరిస్తానన్న ఒప్పందం అకార్డ్. ఆ ప్రత్యామ్నాయాన్ని ఇవ్వడం, అంగీకరించడం శాటిస్ఫాక్షన్.

selfTest.q: 2. అసలు క్లెయిమ్ ఎప్పుడు తీరుతుంది?
selfTest.a: ప్రత్యామ్నాయం ఇవ్వబడి అంగీకరించబడినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 63).

selfTest.q: 3. తనకు నగదు అవసరం ఉందనే కారణంతో మాత్రమే క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవ్యక్తి పూర్తి, తుది సెటిల్‌మెంట్‌ను రద్దు చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అవతలి పక్షం నుంచి ఒత్తిడి లేకుండా కేవలం ఆర్థిక అవసరం ఉంటే సెటిల్‌మెంట్ అతని స్వేచ్ఛా నిర్ణయమే ( Boghara Polyfab ). అతను మోసం, బలవంతం, అనుచిత ప్రభావం లేదా అలాంటి లోపాన్ని నిరూపించాలి.

selfTest.q: 4. క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవ్యక్తి పూర్తి, తుది వోచర్‌పై సంతకం చేస్తేనే ఒక కంపెనీ ఒప్పుకున్న బాకీలను విడుదల చేస్తుంది. ఆ వోచర్ ఆర్బిట్రేషన్‌ను అడ్డుకుంటుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అలాంటి వోచర్ ఆర్బిట్రేషన్‌కు అడ్డు కాదని Boghara Polyfab చెబుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 5. అద్దెకు బదులు ఫ్రిజ్ తీసుకోవడానికి B ఒప్పుకుంటాడు, కానీ అది ఎప్పుడూ డెలివరీ కాలేదు. అద్దె క్లెయిమ్ తీరిందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. శాటిస్ఫాక్షన్ లేకుండా అసలు క్లెయిమ్ అలాగే ఉంటుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: Accord and satisfaction is a way to end a claim by taking something different from what was promised. The accord is the agreement to accept the substitute. The satisfaction is the giving and accepting of that substitute. When both are complete, the original claim is discharged. The idea sits inside Section 63, which lets a promisee accept "any satisfaction which he thinks fit". In exams it is a short-note topic. In real life it is what a settlement "in full and final satisfaction" of a claim does.
legalProvision: Section 63. Promisee may dispense with or remit performance of promisee. Every promisee may dispense with or remit, wholly or in part, the performance of the promisee made to him, or may extend the time for such performance, or may accept instead of it any satisfaction which he thinks fit. Illustrations. (b) A owes B 5,000 rupees. A pays to B, and B accepts, in satisfaction of the whole debt, 2,000 rupees paid at the time and place at which the 5,000 rupees were payable. The whole debt is discharged. (c) A owes B 5,000 rupees. C pays to B 1,000 rupees, and B accepts them, in satisfaction of his claim on A. This payment is a discharge of the whole claim. (d) A owes B, under a contract, a sum of money, the amount of which has not been ascertained. A, without ascertaining the amount, gives to B, and B, in satisfaction thereof, accepts, the sum of 2,000 rupees. This is a discharge of the whole debt, whatever may be its amount.
Related provisions
Section 41. Effect of accepting performance from third person. When a promisee accepts performance of the promise from a third person, he cannot afterwards enforce it against the promisor.

Section 19. Voidability of agreements without free consent. When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

Section 19A. Power to set aside contract induced by undue influence. When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused. Any such contract may be set aside either absolutely or, if the party who was entitled to avoid it has received any benefit thereunder, upon such terms and conditions as to the Court may seem just.
In simple words

The Act does not use the words " accord and satisfaction ". The idea comes from the words "any satisfaction which he thinks fit" in Section 63. Illustrations (b), (c) and (d) show a claim discharged by a substitute that the promisee accepted.
hi.meaning:
Accord and satisfaction means the discharge of a claim by the performance of a substituted obligation that the claimant agreed to accept. Part What it is Accord The agreement to accept a substitute Satisfaction The giving and accepting of that substitute Why the law allows it. A promisee owns his claim and may settle it on any terms he chooses. It also gives people a reason to settle disputes. See Diagram 1 for the stages. Diagram 1. Read the boxes from top to bottom. The original claim ends only at the last box. flowchart TD C["1. The original claim
A owes B a promised performance
(e.g. a carved table worth ₹80,000)"] A["2. The accord
B agrees to accept something different
(e.g. a ready-made table)
Original claim still stands"] S["3. The satisfaction
A gives the substitute
and B accepts it"] D["4. Discharge
The original claim ends (s.63)"] X["Substitute never given:
the original claim remains"] C --> A A --> S S --> D A -. "No satisfaction" .-> X Text description Stage 1, the original claim: A owes B a promised performance, for example a carved table worth ₹80,000. Stage 2, the accord: B agrees to accept something different instead, for example a ready-made table; the original claim still stands. Stage 3, the satisfaction: A gives the substitute and B accepts it. Stage 4, discharge: the original claim ends (Section 63). If the substitute is never given, the original claim remains.
keyPoints: The accord is the agreement to accept a substitute. The satisfaction is its performance. The original claim is discharged when the substitute is given and accepted (Section 63). The promisee may accept any satisfaction he thinks fit. A voluntary full and final settlement ends the claim and the right to arbitrate it. A disputed voucher does not by itself bar arbitration; the claimant must prove fraud, coercion, undue influence or economic duress ( Boghara Polyfab ). Consent to a settlement must be free (Sections 14 to 19A). A settlement caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation is voidable (Section 19). Novation replaces the contract at once. Accord and satisfaction ends the claim when the substitute is given.

caseLaws.name: National Insurance Co
caseLaws.facts: Ltd. v. Boghara Polyfab Pvt. Ltd. (2008) Facts. The insured's goods were damaged in the Surat floods of August 2004. The surveyor assessed the loss at Rs 3,18,26,025, but the insurer paid Rs 2,33,94,964 against a discharge voucher in full and final settlement. The insured then claimed the balance in arbitration, saying the voucher was signed under coercion. Principle. A claim cannot be rejected "merely or solely" because a discharge voucher was signed, if its validity is disputed. Withholding an admitted amount until a voucher is signed "is unfair, irregular and illegal". The Court held, prima facie , that "there is no accord and satisfaction in this case and the dispute is arbitrable", and dismissed the insurer's appeal. (2009) 1 SCC 267 : AIR 2009 SC 170 (Supreme Court, 18 September 2008). Why it matters. It is the main Indian authority on discharge vouchers and full and final settlements. Union of India v. Kishorilal Gupta & Bros. (1959) Facts. The firm had three contracts of 1943 and 1944 with the Government to make and supply military stores, each with an arbitration clause. After disputes, the parties made a settlement in place of the contracts, and the question was whether the arbitration clause survived. Principle. The majority held that the settlement was a substituted agreement, so the arbitration clause " perished with the original contract". Sarkar J. dissented: in accord and satisfaction "The contract is not annihilated but the obligations under it cease to be enforceable", so it "does not destroy the arbitration clause". AIR 1959 SC 1362 : 1960 (1) SCR 493 (Supreme Court, 21 May 1959). Why it matters. It shows how a substituted contract and accord and satisfaction differ in effect. Pinnel's Case (1602) Facts. On a bond for £8 10s, the debtor pleaded that the creditor had accepted a smaller sum in full satisfaction. (1602) 5 Co Rep 117a. Principle. At common law, a smaller sum paid on the due day cannot satisfy a larger debt. A different thing accepted in its place can. Why it matters. It is the origin of the idea. Section 63 goes further on part payment.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two parts of accord and satisfaction?
selfTest.a: The accord is the agreement to accept a substitute. The satisfaction is the giving and acceptance of that substitute.

selfTest.q: 2. When is the original claim discharged?
selfTest.a: When the substitute is given and accepted (Section 63).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a claimant undo a full and final settlement only because he needed cash?
selfTest.a: No. Financial need alone, without pressure from the other side, leaves the settlement his free choice ( Boghara Polyfab ). He must prove fraud, coercion, undue influence or a similar defect.

selfTest.q: 4. A company releases admitted dues only if the claimant signs a full and final voucher. Does the voucher bar arbitration?
selfTest.a: No. Boghara Polyfab says such a voucher will not be a bar to arbitration.

selfTest.q: 5. B agrees to take a refrigerator instead of rent, but it is never delivered. Is the rent claim discharged?
selfTest.a: No. Without the satisfaction, the original claim remains.

en.meaning:
What does Section 37 of the Indian Contract Act require of the parties to a contract?

Explanation. Section 37 states that the parties to a contract must perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the Act or any other law.

Which of the following is NOT one of the six recognised modes of discharge of a contract?

Explanation. The six modes are performance, agreement, impossibility, lapse of time, operation of law, and breach. Registration is not a recognised mode of discharge.

Novation, rescission, and alteration are all examples of discharge by:

Explanation. Section 62 covers novation, rescission, and alteration together as discharge by mutual agreement between the parties.

The Doctrine of Frustration is dealt with under which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?

en.inOneMinute: Remission means the promisee gives up, wholly or in part, his right to have a promise performed. Under Section 63 he may also extend the time for performance, or accept some other satisfaction instead. The promisor is then freed to that extent. The right belongs to the promisee, so he may give it up. In exams, the four powers in Section 63 and the five illustrations earn the marks. In real life, it is the law behind a creditor settling a debt for less.
legalProvision: Section 63. Promisee may dispense with or remit performance of promisee. Every promisee may dispense with or remit, wholly or in part, the performance of the promisee made to him, or may extend the time for such performance, or may accept instead of it any satisfaction which he thinks fit. Illustrations. (a) A promises to paint a picture for B. B afterwards forbids him to do so. A is no longer bound to perform the promise. (b) A owes B 5,000 rupees. A pays to B, and B accepts, in satisfaction of the whole debt, 2,000 rupees paid at the time and place at which the 5,000 rupees were payable. The whole debt is discharged. (c) A owes B 5,000 rupees. C pays to B 1,000 rupees, and B accepts them, in satisfaction of his claim on A. This payment is a discharge of the whole claim. (d) A owes B, under a contract, a sum of money, the amount of which has not been ascertained. A, without ascertaining the amount, gives to B, and B, in satisfaction thereof, accepts, the sum of 2,000 rupees. This is a discharge of the whole debt, whatever may be its amount. (e) A owes B 2,000 rupees, and is also indebted to other creditors. A makes an arrangement with his creditors, including B, to pay them a [composition] of eight annas in the rupee upon their respective demands. Payment to B of 1,000 rupees is a discharge of B's demand.
Related provisions
Section 41. Effect of accepting performance from third person. When a promisee accepts performance of the promise from a third person, he cannot afterwards enforce it against the promisor.

Section 44. Effect of release of one joint promisor. Where two or more persons have made a joint promise, a release of one of such joint promisors by the promisee does not discharge the other joint promisor or joint promisors; neither does it free the joint promisors so released from responsibility to the other joint promisor or joint promisors.

Section 55 (third paragraph). If, in case of a contract voidable on account of the promisor's failure to perform his promise at the time agreed, the promisee accepts performance of such promise at any time other than that agreed, the promisee cannot claim compensation for any loss occasioned by the non-performance of the promise at the time agreed, unless, at the time of such acceptance, he gives notice to the promisor of his intention to do so.

Section 135. A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety, unless the surety assents to such contract.
In simple words
A promisee may do four things under Section 63:

Dispense with performance: tell the promisor not to perform at all. Remit performance, wholly or in part: give up all or part of what is owed. Extend the time for performance. Accept any satisfaction he thinks fit in place of the performance.
en.meaning:
Remission is the promisee's act of giving up, wholly or in part, the performance of a promise made to him. The Act uses the verbs "dispense with" and "remit". It does not define remission as a separate term. Why the law allows it. The right to performance is the promisee's, so he may give it up. It also removes a harsh English rule. In English law, a promise to accept a smaller sum for a larger debt was not binding without fresh consideration ( Foakes v. Beer ). Section 63 does not follow that rule. See Diagram 1 for the four powers and the Act's illustrations. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. (Illustration (e))"] P --> D P --> R P --> T P --> S D --> Da R --> Ra T --> Ta S --> Sc S --> Sd S --> Se Text description The promisee's powers under Section 63 branch into four. One: dispense with performance; the promisee forbids the work, and the promisor is no longer bound (Illustration (a)). Two: remit performance, wholly or in part; accepting 2,000 rupees for a debt of 5,000 rupees discharges the whole debt (Illustration (b)). Three: extend the time for performance; this rests on agreement with the promisor, and the promisee cannot extend time alone (Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel). Four: accept any satisfaction he thinks fit; a third person pays part and the whole claim is discharged (Illustration (c)); an unascertained sum is paid and the whole debt is discharged (Illustration (d)); a composition with all creditors, and payment discharges the demand (Illustration (e)).
keyPoints: Remission is the promisee's giving up of performance, wholly or in part (Section 63). The promisee may also extend time or accept any satisfaction he thinks fit. Acceptance of a lesser sum in satisfaction discharges the whole debt. Section 63 does not follow the English rule in Foakes v. Beer . An extension of time rests on agreement. The promisee cannot extend time alone. Remission creates no new contract. Novation does. Accepting late performance without notice bars compensation for the delay (Section 55). Accepting performance from a third person bars enforcement against the promisor (Section 41). Release of one joint promisor does not free the others (Section 44).

caseLaws.name: Kapur Chand Godha v
caseLaws.facts: Mir Nawab Himayat Ali Khan Azamjah (1962) Facts. On 31 January 1937 the appellant's firm sold jewellery worth Rs 13,20,750 to the Prince of Berar, and its claim later stood at about Rs 27,79,078. The Hyderabad authorities paid the firm Rs 20 lakh in full satisfaction of the claim (Rs 11,25,000 on 27 September 1949 and Rs 8,75,000 on 14 February 1950), and the firm accepted it. On 5 February 1951 it sued the Prince for Rs 9,99,940. Principle. The case was "completely covered by s. 63 and illustration (c)". Payment by a third person, accepted in satisfaction, discharged the whole claim; Section 41 also applied. [1963] 2 SCR 168 : AIR 1963 SC 250 (Supreme Court, 12 April 1962). Why it matters. It applies Section 63, Illustration (c) to a real debt: a creditor who accepts less in full satisfaction cannot sue for the rest. Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel v. Lalbhai Trikumlal Mills Ltd. (1958) Facts. A contract for the sale of goods fixed a time for delivery. A letter of 15 August 1942 said that the time for delivery was "automatically understood as extended". The question was whether time had been validly extended. Principle. "Both the buyer and the seller must agree to extend time." One party cannot extend it alone, and the claimed extension was in any case void for vagueness under Section 29. AIR 1958 SC 512 : 1959 SCR 213 (Supreme Court, 21 March 1958). Why it matters. It limits the power to extend time under Section 63: an extension rests on agreement. Foakes v. Beer (1884) Facts. On a judgment debt of £2,090 19s, the creditor agreed not to take proceedings if the debtor paid £500 at once and £150 every half year until the whole was paid. The debtor paid the whole sum, and the creditor then claimed interest. (1884) 9 App Cas 605. Principle. A promise to accept part payment lacks consideration, because the debtor already owes the whole. Why it matters. Section 63 does not follow this English rule.

selfTest.q: 1. What four things may a promisee do under Section 63?
selfTest.a: Dispense with or remit performance wholly or in part, extend the time, and accept any satisfaction he thinks fit.

selfTest.q: 2. A owes B 5,000 rupees. B accepts 2,000 rupees in full satisfaction at the time and place payable. Is the debt discharged?
selfTest.a: Yes. The whole debt is discharged (Section 63, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a promisee extend the time for performance alone?
selfTest.a: No. Both parties must agree ( Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel ).

selfTest.q: 4. A's friend pays B part of A's debt, and B accepts it in satisfaction of his whole claim. Can B sue A for the rest?
selfTest.a: No. The whole claim is discharged (Section 63, Illustration (c); Kapur Chand Godha ).

selfTest.q: 5. Does Section 63 require fresh consideration for a remission?
selfTest.a: No. Section 63 does not mention consideration, unlike the English rule in Foakes v. Beer .

సెక్షన్ 63 కింద వాగ్దానగ్రహీత నాలుగు పనులు చేయవచ్చు:

నెరవేర్పును వద్దనడం (dispense with) : అసలు నెరవేర్చవద్దని వాగ్దానకర్తకు చెప్పడం. నెరవేర్పును పూర్తిగా గానీ పాక్షికంగా గానీ మాఫీ చేయడం (remit) : రావాల్సినదాంట్లో అంతా గానీ కొంత గానీ వదులుకోవడం. నెరవేర్చే సమయాన్ని పొడిగించడం . నెరవేర్పుకు బదులు తనకు సరైనదనిపించే ఏ సంతృప్తినైనా అంగీకరించడం .
te.meaning:
మాఫీ అంటే తనకు చేసిన వాగ్దానం నెరవేర్పును వాగ్దానగ్రహీత పూర్తిగా గానీ పాక్షికంగా గానీ వదులుకోవడం. చట్టం "dispense with", "remit" అనే క్రియలను వాడుతుంది. మాఫీని వేరే పదంగా నిర్వచించలేదు. చట్టం దీన్ని ఎందుకు అనుమతిస్తుంది? నెరవేర్పు హక్కు వాగ్దానగ్రహీతది, కాబట్టి అతను దాన్ని వదులుకోవచ్చు. ఇది ఒక కఠినమైన ఇంగ్లిష్ నియమాన్ని కూడా తొలగిస్తుంది. ఇంగ్లిష్ చట్టంలో, పెద్ద అప్పుకు బదులు చిన్న మొత్తం తీసుకుంటానన్న వాగ్దానం కొత్త ప్రతిఫలం (consideration) లేకుండా బంధించదు ( Foakes v. Beer ). సెక్షన్ 63 ఆ నియమాన్ని అనుసరించదు. నాలుగు అధికారాలను, చట్టంలోని Illustrations ను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 63 కింద వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఏ నాలుగు పనులు చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: నెరవేర్పును వద్దనడం లేదా పూర్తిగా గానీ పాక్షికంగా గానీ మాఫీ చేయడం, సమయాన్ని పొడిగించడం, తనకు సరైనదనిపించే ఏ సంతృప్తినైనా అంగీకరించడం.

selfTest.q: 2. A, B కి 5,000 రూపాయలు బాకీ. చెల్లించాల్సిన సమయం, స్థలంలో B, 2,000 రూపాయలను పూర్తి సంతృప్తిగా అంగీకరిస్తాడు. అప్పు తీరిందా?
selfTest.a: అవును. మొత్తం అప్పు తీరింది (సెక్షన్ 63, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఒక్కడే నెరవేర్చే సమయాన్ని పొడిగించవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. రెండు పక్షాలూ అంగీకరించాలి ( Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel ).

selfTest.q: 4. A అప్పులో కొంత భాగాన్ని A స్నేహితుడు B కి చెల్లిస్తాడు; B దాన్ని తన మొత్తం క్లెయిమ్‌కు సంతృప్తిగా అంగీకరిస్తాడు. మిగతాదాని కోసం B, A పై దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మొత్తం క్లెయిమ్ తీరిపోయింది (సెక్షన్ 63, Illustration (c); Kapur Chand Godha ).

selfTest.q: 5. మాఫీకి సెక్షన్ 63 కొత్త ప్రతిఫలాన్ని కోరుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. Foakes v. Beer లోని ఇంగ్లిష్ నియమంలా కాకుండా, సెక్షన్ 63 ప్రతిఫలం గురించి ఏమీ చెప్పదు.

సెక్షన్ 63 62 63 ("any satisfaction which he thinks fit")

hi.inOneMinute: Remission means the promisee gives up, wholly or in part, his right to have a promise performed. Under Section 63 he may also extend the time for performance, or accept some other satisfaction instead. The promisor is then freed to that extent. The right belongs to the promisee, so he may give it up. In exams, the four powers in Section 63 and the five illustrations earn the marks. In real life, it is the law behind a creditor settling a debt for less.
legalProvision: Section 63. Promisee may dispense with or remit performance of promisee. Every promisee may dispense with or remit, wholly or in part, the performance of the promisee made to him, or may extend the time for such performance, or may accept instead of it any satisfaction which he thinks fit. Illustrations. (a) A promises to paint a picture for B. B afterwards forbids him to do so. A is no longer bound to perform the promise. (b) A owes B 5,000 rupees. A pays to B, and B accepts, in satisfaction of the whole debt, 2,000 rupees paid at the time and place at which the 5,000 rupees were payable. The whole debt is discharged. (c) A owes B 5,000 rupees. C pays to B 1,000 rupees, and B accepts them, in satisfaction of his claim on A. This payment is a discharge of the whole claim. (d) A owes B, under a contract, a sum of money, the amount of which has not been ascertained. A, without ascertaining the amount, gives to B, and B, in satisfaction thereof, accepts, the sum of 2,000 rupees. This is a discharge of the whole debt, whatever may be its amount. (e) A owes B 2,000 rupees, and is also indebted to other creditors. A makes an arrangement with his creditors, including B, to pay them a [composition] of eight annas in the rupee upon their respective demands. Payment to B of 1,000 rupees is a discharge of B's demand.
Related provisions
Section 41. Effect of accepting performance from third person. When a promisee accepts performance of the promise from a third person, he cannot afterwards enforce it against the promisor.

Section 44. Effect of release of one joint promisor. Where two or more persons have made a joint promise, a release of one of such joint promisors by the promisee does not discharge the other joint promisor or joint promisors; neither does it free the joint promisors so released from responsibility to the other joint promisor or joint promisors.

Section 55 (third paragraph). If, in case of a contract voidable on account of the promisor's failure to perform his promise at the time agreed, the promisee accepts performance of such promise at any time other than that agreed, the promisee cannot claim compensation for any loss occasioned by the non-performance of the promise at the time agreed, unless, at the time of such acceptance, he gives notice to the promisor of his intention to do so.

Section 135. A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety, unless the surety assents to such contract.
In simple words
A promisee may do four things under Section 63:

Dispense with performance: tell the promisor not to perform at all. Remit performance, wholly or in part: give up all or part of what is owed. Extend the time for performance. Accept any satisfaction he thinks fit in place of the performance.
hi.meaning:
Remission is the promisee's act of giving up, wholly or in part, the performance of a promise made to him. The Act uses the verbs "dispense with" and "remit". It does not define remission as a separate term. Why the law allows it. The right to performance is the promisee's, so he may give it up. It also removes a harsh English rule. In English law, a promise to accept a smaller sum for a larger debt was not binding without fresh consideration ( Foakes v. Beer ). Section 63 does not follow that rule. See Diagram 1 for the four powers and the Act's illustrations. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. The bottom boxes are the Act's illustrations. flowchart TD P["Promisee's powers

One: dispense with performance; the promisee forbids the work, and the promisor is no longer bound (Illustration (a)). Two: remit performance, wholly or in part; accepting 2,000 rupees for a debt of 5,000 rupees discharges the whole debt (Illustration (b)). Three: extend the time for performance; this rests on agreement with the promisor, and the promisee cannot extend time alone (Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel). Four: accept any satisfaction he thinks fit; a third person pays part and the whole claim is discharged (Illustration (c)); an unascertained sum is paid and the whole debt is discharged (Illustration (d)); a composition with all creditors, and payment discharges the demand (Illustration (e)).
keyPoints: Remission is the promisee's giving up of performance, wholly or in part (Section 63). The promisee may also extend time or accept any satisfaction he thinks fit. Acceptance of a lesser sum in satisfaction discharges the whole debt. Section 63 does not follow the English rule in Foakes v. Beer . An extension of time rests on agreement. The promisee cannot extend time alone. Remission creates no new contract. Novation does. Accepting late performance without notice bars compensation for the delay (Section 55). Accepting performance from a third person bars enforcement against the promisor (Section 41). Release of one joint promisor does not free the others (Section 44).

caseLaws.name: Kapur Chand Godha v
caseLaws.facts: Mir Nawab Himayat Ali Khan Azamjah (1962) Facts. On 31 January 1937 the appellant's firm sold jewellery worth Rs 13,20,750 to the Prince of Berar, and its claim later stood at about Rs 27,79,078. The Hyderabad authorities paid the firm Rs 20 lakh in full satisfaction of the claim (Rs 11,25,000 on 27 September 1949 and Rs 8,75,000 on 14 February 1950), and the firm accepted it. On 5 February 1951 it sued the Prince for Rs 9,99,940. Principle. The case was "completely covered by s. 63 and illustration (c)". Payment by a third person, accepted in satisfaction, discharged the whole claim; Section 41 also applied. [1963] 2 SCR 168 : AIR 1963 SC 250 (Supreme Court, 12 April 1962). Why it matters. It applies Section 63, Illustration (c) to a real debt: a creditor who accepts less in full satisfaction cannot sue for the rest. Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel v. Lalbhai Trikumlal Mills Ltd. (1958) Facts. A contract for the sale of goods fixed a time for delivery. A letter of 15 August 1942 said that the time for delivery was "automatically understood as extended". The question was whether time had been validly extended. Principle. "Both the buyer and the seller must agree to extend time." One party cannot extend it alone, and the claimed extension was in any case void for vagueness under Section 29. AIR 1958 SC 512 : 1959 SCR 213 (Supreme Court, 21 March 1958). Why it matters. It limits the power to extend time under Section 63: an extension rests on agreement. Foakes v. Beer (1884) Facts. On a judgment debt of £2,090 19s, the creditor agreed not to take proceedings if the debtor paid £500 at once and £150 every half year until the whole was paid. The debtor paid the whole sum, and the creditor then claimed interest. (1884) 9 App Cas 605. Principle. A promise to accept part payment lacks consideration, because the debtor already owes the whole. Why it matters. Section 63 does not follow this English rule.

selfTest.q: 1. What four things may a promisee do under Section 63?
selfTest.a: Dispense with or remit performance wholly or in part, extend the time, and accept any satisfaction he thinks fit.

selfTest.q: 2. A owes B 5,000 rupees. B accepts 2,000 rupees in full satisfaction at the time and place payable. Is the debt discharged?
selfTest.a: Yes. The whole debt is discharged (Section 63, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a promisee extend the time for performance alone?
selfTest.a: No. Both parties must agree ( Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel ).

selfTest.q: 4. A's friend pays B part of A's debt, and B accepts it in satisfaction of his whole claim. Can B sue A for the rest?
selfTest.a: No. The whole claim is discharged (Section 63, Illustration (c); Kapur Chand Godha ).

selfTest.q: 5. Does Section 63 require fresh consideration for a remission?
selfTest.a: No. Section 63 does not mention consideration, unlike the English rule in Foakes v. Beer .

en.inOneMinute: Novation means the parties replace an existing contract with a new one. The old contract ends at once, and only the new one can be enforced. The new contract may be between the same parties on new terms, or it may bring in a new party in place of an old one. Every party must agree. Without that, the old contract stands. In exams, novation is a short-note topic: give the section, the two forms, the need for consent and the effect. In real life it explains how a debt or a contract is moved from one person to another.
legalProvision: Section 62. Effect of novation, rescission, and alteration of contract. If the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it, or to rescind or alter it, the original contract, need not be performed. Illustrations. (a) A owes money to B under a contract. It is agreed between A, B and C that B shall thenceforth accept C as his debtor, instead of A. The old debt of A to B is at an end, and a new debt from C to B has been contracted. (b) A owes B 10,000 rupees. A enters into an arrangement with B and gives B a mortgage of his (A's) estate for 5,000 rupees in place of the debt of 10,000 rupees. This is a new contract and extinguishes the old. (c) A owes B 1,000 rupees under a contract. B owes C 1,000 rupees B orders A to credit C with 1,000 rupees in his books, but C does not assent to the arrangement. B still owes C 1,000 rupees, and no new contract has been entered into.
Related provisions

Section 135. Discharge of surety when creditor compounds with, gives time to, or agrees not to sue, principal debtor. A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety, unless the surety assents to such contract.

Section 137. Creditor's forbearance to sue does not discharge surety. Mere forbearance on the part of the creditor to sue the principal debtor or to enforce any other remedy against him does not, in the absence of any provision in the guarantee to the contrary, discharge the surety.

Section 139. Discharge of surety by creditor's act or omission impairing surety's eventual remedy. If the creditor does any act which is inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and the eventual remedy of the surety himself against the principal debtor is thereby impaired, the surety is discharged.

Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 16(1). The arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, and for that purpose,— (a) an arbitration clause which forms part of a contract shall be treated as an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract; and (b) a decision by the arbitral tribunal that the contract is null and void shall not entail ipso jure the invalidity of the arbitration clause.
In simple words

If the parties agree to put a new contract in place of the old one, the old one need not be performed. The new contract may be between the same parties (Illustration (b)) or with a new party (Illustration (a)). If anyone whose consent is needed does not agree, there is no new contract (Illustration (c)). The same section also covers rescission (cancelling) and alteration (changing terms).
en.meaning:
Novation is the substitution of a new contract for an existing one, by agreement of all the parties. The word comes from the Latin novare , "to make new". Section 62 does not use the word "novation" in its text, though its heading does. The text describes the idea in the words "substitute a new contract". The two forms of novation Form What changes Illustration to Section 62 Same parties, new terms A new contract between the same parties replaces the old (b): a mortgage for 5,000 rupees in place of a debt of 10,000 rupees New party A new person replaces an old party, with everyone's consent (a): C replaces A as B's debtor Why the law allows novation. The parties made the first contract, so they may replace it. Novation gives the old contract a clean end, so no one can later enforce both. See Diagram 1 for the tests. Diagram 1. Start at the top. No: there is nothing to replace. Question 2: was a new contract made in its place, between the same parties on new terms or with a new party (Section 62)? No: this is not novation; it may be an alteration or a remission. Question 3: did every party, including any new party, agree (Section 62, Illustration (c))? No: there is no novation and the old contract stands. Question 4: did the parties intend the new contract to replace the old one completely? No: the old contract survives, for example where the new arrangement is only conditional (Lata Construction). Yes to all: the old contract is discharged and only the new contract can be enforced.
keyPoints: Novation is the replacement of a contract by a new contract (Section 62). It may be between the same parties on new terms, or it may substitute a party. Every party must consent, including the new party. The old contract is discharged and cannot be enforced. A conditional or partial substitute is not a novation ( Lata Construction ). Rescission cancels. Alteration changes terms. Novation replaces. A creditor's composition with, or time given to, the principal debtor discharges the surety unless he assents (Section 135). Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 16(1): an arbitration clause is independent of the other terms of the contract.

caseLaws.name: Lata Construction v
caseLaws.facts: Dr. Rameshchandra Ramniklal Shah (1999) Facts. In 1987 the developers agreed to give the buyers flat AG-2 in a building at Vile Parle, Mumbai, and took payments for it. On 23 February 1991 they signed a new agreement to pay ₹9,51,000 in lieu of the flat, in three instalments , stating that the buyers' 1987 rights would end only on full payment. The sum was not paid as agreed, and the buyers' complaint succeeded before the National Consumer Commission. Principle. "There should be complete substitution of a new contract in place of the old." Since the old rights were to end only on payment, "there was no substitution of the earlier agreement in its entirety by the new agreement". The appeal was dismissed. AIR 2000 SC 380 : (2000) 1 SCC 586 (Supreme Court, 12 August 1999). Why it matters. A conditional or partial arrangement is not novation, and the old contract survives. Union of India v. Kishorilal Gupta & Bros. (1959) Facts. Contracts for the supply of goods to the Government contained arbitration clauses. After disputes arose, the parties made a settlement agreement in place of the earlier contracts. The question was whether the arbitration clauses in the old contracts still applied. Principle. The majority held that the settlement was a substituted agreement, so the arbitration clause "perished with the original contract". AIR 1959 SC 1362 : 1960 (1) SCR 493 (Supreme Court, 21 May 1959; Subba Rao J. for the majority, Sarkar J. dissenting). Why it matters. A replaced contract takes its collateral terms, such as an arbitration clause, with it. Scarf v. Jardine (1882) Facts. The House of Lords considered a change in the members of a trading firm and the liability of a retiring partner to a creditor. (1882) 7 App Cas 345. Principle. Novation is a new contract replacing an existing one, between the same or different parties. A creditor who accepts the new debtor in place of the old cannot also hold the old. Why it matters. It is the English source of the idea in Section 62.

selfTest.q: 1. What does novation do to the old contract?
selfTest.a: It discharges it. Only the new contract can be enforced (Section 62).

selfTest.q: 2. Can a debtor transfer his debt to another person without the creditor's consent?
selfTest.a: No. A new debtor takes his place only if the creditor and all others agree (Section 62, Illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 3. How is novation different from alteration?
selfTest.a: Novation puts a new contract in place of the old one. Alteration changes terms of the same contract among the same parties.

selfTest.q: 4. A new agreement says the old rights end only when the new price is fully paid. The price is never paid. Is there a novation?
selfTest.a: No. The substitution was not complete, so the old contract survives ( Lata Construction ).

selfTest.q: 5. Does mere delay by the creditor in suing the principal debtor discharge the surety?
selfTest.a: No. Mere forbearance to sue does not discharge the surety (Section 137).

నోవేషన్ అంటే అన్ని పక్షాల అంగీకారంతో ఉన్న కాంట్రాక్టు స్థానంలో కొత్త కాంట్రాక్టును పెట్టడం. ఈ పదం లాటిన్ novare ("కొత్తగా చేయడం") నుంచి వచ్చింది. సెక్షన్ 62 శీర్షికలో "novation" అనే పదం ఉంది, కానీ సెక్షన్ పాఠంలో లేదు. పాఠం ఈ ఆలోచనను "substitute a new contract " అనే మాటలతో చెబుతుంది. నోవేషన్ రెండు రూపాలు రూపం ఏం మారుతుంది సెక్షన్ 62 Illustration అవే పక్షాలు, కొత్త షరతులు అవే పక్షాల మధ్య కొత్త కాంట్రాక్టు పాతదాని స్థానంలో వస్తుంది (b): 10,000 రూపాయల అప్పు స్థానంలో 5,000 రూపాయలకు తనఖా కొత్త పక్షం అందరి అంగీకారంతో పాత పక్షం స్థానంలో కొత్త వ్యక్తి (a): B కి రుణగ్రహీతగా A స్థానంలో C చట్టం నోవేషన్‌ను ఎందుకు అనుమతిస్తుంది? మొదటి కాంట్రాక్టు పక్షాలే చేసుకున్నారు, కాబట్టి దాన్ని మార్చుకోవచ్చు. నోవేషన్ పాత కాంట్రాక్టుకు స్పష్టమైన ముగింపు ఇస్తుంది; తర్వాత ఎవరూ రెండింటినీ అమలు చేయించలేరు. పరీక్షలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. selfTest.q: 1. నోవేషన్ పాత కాంట్రాక్టుకు ఏం చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: దాన్ని ముగిస్తుంది. కొత్త కాంట్రాక్టును మాత్రమే అమలు చేయించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 62).

selfTest.q: 2. రుణదాత అంగీకారం లేకుండా రుణగ్రహీత తన అప్పును వేరొకరికి బదిలీ చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. రుణదాత, మిగతా అందరూ అంగీకరిస్తేనే కొత్త రుణగ్రహీత అతని స్థానంలోకి వస్తాడు (సెక్షన్ 62, Illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 3. నోవేషన్ మార్పుకు ఎలా భిన్నం?
selfTest.a: నోవేషన్ పాతదాని స్థానంలో కొత్త కాంట్రాక్టును పెడుతుంది. మార్పు అవే పక్షాల మధ్య అదే కాంట్రాక్టు షరతులను మారుస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. కొత్త ధర పూర్తిగా చెల్లించినప్పుడే పాత హక్కులు ముగుస్తాయని కొత్త ఒప్పందం చెబుతుంది. ధర ఎప్పుడూ చెల్లించలేదు. నోవేషన్ జరిగిందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మార్పు పూర్తి కాలేదు, కాబట్టి పాత కాంట్రాక్టు నిలుస్తుంది ( Lata Construction ).

selfTest.q: 5. ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై దావా వేయడంలో రుణదాత కేవలం ఆలస్యం చేస్తే జామీనుదారు విముక్తుడవుతాడా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. కేవలం దావా వేయకుండా ఆగడం జామీనుదారును విముక్తుడిని చేయదు (సెక్షన్ 137).

hi.inOneMinute: Novation means the parties replace an existing contract with a new one. The old contract ends at once, and only the new one can be enforced. The new contract may be between the same parties on new terms, or it may bring in a new party in place of an old one. Every party must agree. Without that, the old contract stands. In exams, novation is a short-note topic: give the section, the two forms, the need for consent and the effect. In real life it explains how a debt or a contract is moved from one person to another.
legalProvision: Section 62. Effect of novation, rescission, and alteration of contract. If the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it, or to rescind or alter it, the original contract, need not be performed. Illustrations. (a) A owes money to B under a contract. It is agreed between A, B and C that B shall thenceforth accept C as his debtor, instead of A. The old debt of A to B is at an end, and a new debt from C to B has been contracted. (b) A owes B 10,000 rupees. A enters into an arrangement with B and gives B a mortgage of his (A's) estate for 5,000 rupees in place of the debt of 10,000 rupees. This is a new contract and extinguishes the old. (c) A owes B 1,000 rupees under a contract. B owes C 1,000 rupees B orders A to credit C with 1,000 rupees in his books, but C does not assent to the arrangement. B still owes C 1,000 rupees, and no new contract has been entered into.
Related provisions

Section 135. Discharge of surety when creditor compounds with, gives time to, or agrees not to sue, principal debtor. A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety, unless the surety assents to such contract.

Section 137. Creditor's forbearance to sue does not discharge surety. Mere forbearance on the part of the creditor to sue the principal debtor or to enforce any other remedy against him does not, in the absence of any provision in the guarantee to the contrary, discharge the surety.

Section 139. Discharge of surety by creditor's act or omission impairing surety's eventual remedy. If the creditor does any act which is inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and the eventual remedy of the surety himself against the principal debtor is thereby impaired, the surety is discharged.

Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 16(1). The arbitral tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, and for that purpose,— (a) an arbitration clause which forms part of a contract shall be treated as an agreement independent of the other terms of the contract; and (b) a decision by the arbitral tribunal that the contract is null and void shall not entail ipso jure the invalidity of the arbitration clause.
In simple words

If the parties agree to put a new contract in place of the old one, the old one need not be performed. The new contract may be between the same parties (Illustration (b)) or with a new party (Illustration (a)). If anyone whose consent is needed does not agree, there is no new contract (Illustration (c)). The same section also covers rescission (cancelling) and alteration (changing terms).
hi.meaning:
Novation is the substitution of a new contract for an existing one, by agreement of all the parties. The word comes from the Latin novare , "to make new". Section 62 does not use the word "novation" in its text, though its heading does. The text describes the idea in the words "substitute a new contract". The two forms of novation Form What changes Illustration to Section 62 Same parties, new terms A new contract between the same parties replaces the old (b): a mortgage for 5,000 rupees in place of a debt of 10,000 rupees New party A new person replaces an old party, with everyone's consent (a): C replaces A as B's debtor Why the law allows novation. The parties made the first contract, so they may replace it. Novation gives the old contract a clean end, so no one can later enforce both. See Diagram 1 for the tests. Diagram 1. Start at the top. Each question must be answered "Yes" to move down. Any "No" shows where the claim of novation fails. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Was there a valid
existing contract?"} Q2{"2. Was a new contract made in its place,
same parties on new terms
or with a new party? (s.62)"} Q3{"3. Did every party, including
any new party, agree?
(s.62, Illustration (c))"} Q4{"4. Did they intend the new contract
to replace the old one completely?"} N1["No novation: nothing to replace"] N2["Not novation: may be an
alteration or a remission"] N3["No novation: the old contract stands"] N4["No novation: the old contract survives
(e.g. conditional arrangement,
Lata Construction)"] R["NOVATION
Old contract discharged;
only the new one can be enforced"] Q1 -- "No" --> N1 Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2 Q2 -- "No" --> N2 Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3 Q3 -- "No" --> N3 Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4 Q4 -- "No" --> N4 Q4 -- "Yes" --> R Text description Question 1: was there a valid existing contract? No: there is nothing to replace. Question 2: was a new contract made in its place, between the same parties on new terms or with a new party (Section 62)? No: this is not novation; it may be an alteration or a remission. Question 3: did every party, including any new party, agree (Section 62, Illustration (c))? No: there is no novation and the old contract stands. Question 4: did the parties intend the new contract to replace the old one completely? No: the old contract survives, for example where the new arrangement is only conditional (Lata Construction). Yes to all: the old contract is discharged and only the new contract can be enforced.
keyPoints: Novation is the replacement of a contract by a new contract (Section 62). It may be between the same parties on new terms, or it may substitute a party. Every party must consent, including the new party. The old contract is discharged and cannot be enforced. A conditional or partial substitute is not a novation ( Lata Construction ). Rescission cancels. Alteration changes terms. Novation replaces. A creditor's composition with, or time given to, the principal debtor discharges the surety unless he assents (Section 135). Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, Section 16(1): an arbitration clause is independent of the other terms of the contract.

caseLaws.name: Lata Construction v
caseLaws.facts: Dr. Rameshchandra Ramniklal Shah (1999) Facts. In 1987 the developers agreed to give the buyers flat AG-2 in a building at Vile Parle, Mumbai, and took payments for it. On 23 February 1991 they signed a new agreement to pay ₹9,51,000 in lieu of the flat, in three instalments , stating that the buyers' 1987 rights would end only on full payment. The sum was not paid as agreed, and the buyers' complaint succeeded before the National Consumer Commission. Principle. "There should be complete substitution of a new contract in place of the old." Since the old rights were to end only on payment, "there was no substitution of the earlier agreement in its entirety by the new agreement". The appeal was dismissed. AIR 2000 SC 380 : (2000) 1 SCC 586 (Supreme Court, 12 August 1999). Why it matters. A conditional or partial arrangement is not novation, and the old contract survives. Union of India v. Kishorilal Gupta & Bros. (1959) Facts. Contracts for the supply of goods to the Government contained arbitration clauses. After disputes arose, the parties made a settlement agreement in place of the earlier contracts. The question was whether the arbitration clauses in the old contracts still applied. Principle. The majority held that the settlement was a substituted agreement, so the arbitration clause "perished with the original contract". AIR 1959 SC 1362 : 1960 (1) SCR 493 (Supreme Court, 21 May 1959; Subba Rao J. for the majority, Sarkar J. dissenting). Why it matters. A replaced contract takes its collateral terms, such as an arbitration clause, with it. Scarf v. Jardine (1882) Facts. The House of Lords considered a change in the members of a trading firm and the liability of a retiring partner to a creditor. (1882) 7 App Cas 345. Principle. Novation is a new contract replacing an existing one, between the same or different parties. A creditor who accepts the new debtor in place of the old cannot also hold the old. Why it matters. It is the English source of the idea in Section 62.

selfTest.q: 1. What does novation do to the old contract?
selfTest.a: It discharges it. Only the new contract can be enforced (Section 62).

selfTest.q: 2. Can a debtor transfer his debt to another person without the creditor's consent?
selfTest.a: No. A new debtor takes his place only if the creditor and all others agree (Section 62, Illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 3. How is novation different from alteration?
selfTest.a: Novation puts a new contract in place of the old one. Alteration changes terms of the same contract among the same parties.

selfTest.q: 4. A new agreement says the old rights end only when the new price is fully paid. The price is never paid. Is there a novation?
selfTest.a: No. The substitution was not complete, so the old contract survives ( Lata Construction ).

selfTest.q: 5. Does mere delay by the creditor in suing the principal debtor discharge the surety?
selfTest.a: No. Mere forbearance to sue does not discharge the surety (Section 137).

law-of-contract-i-u3-t9.subtitle: Sections 39, 53 to 55 and 73 to 75 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A breach happens when a party fails or refuses to perform his promise without lawful excuse. A breach does not end the contract by itself. It gives the innocent party a choice. He may treat the contract as ended and claim compensation, or he may keep it alive. A breach may come before the due date ( anticipatory ) or on or after it ( actual ). In exams, the choice, the sections and the difference from frustration earn the marks. In real life, it tells a wronged party what he can do the day the other side lets him down.
legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Illustrations. (a) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her 100 rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night A wilfully absents herself from the theatre. B is at liberty to put an end to the contract. (b) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two night's in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her at the rate of 100 rupees for each night. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself. With the assent of B, A sings on the seventh night. B has signified his acquiescence in the continuance of the contract, and cannot now put an end to it, but is entitled to compensation for the damage sustained by him through A's failure to sing on the sixth night.

Section 53. Liability of party preventing event on which the contract is to take effect. When a contract contains reciprocal promises, and one party to the contract prevents the other from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented; and he is entitled to compensation from the other party for any loss which he may sustain in consequence of the non-performance of the contract.

Section 54. Effect of default as to that promise which should be first performed, in contract consisting of reciprocal promises. When a contract consists of reciprocal promises, such that one of them cannot be performed, or that its performance cannot be claimed till the other has been performed, and the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss which such other party may sustain by the non-performance of the contract.

Section 55. Effect of failure to perform at fixed time, in contract in which time is essential. When a party to a contract promises to do a certain thing at or before a specified time, or certain things at or before specified times, and fails to do any such thing at or before the specified time, the contract, or so much of it as has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee, if the intention of the parties was that time should be of the essence of the contract. Effect of such failure when time is not essential. —If it was not the intention of the parties that time should be of the essence of the contract, the contract does not become voidable by the failure to do such thing at or before the specified time; but the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure. Effect of acceptance of performance at time other than that agreed upon. —If, in case of a contract voidable on account of the promisor's failure to perform his promise at the time agreed, the promisee accepts performance of such promise at any time other than that agreed, the promisee cannot claim compensation for any loss occasioned by the non-performance of the promise at the time agreed, unless, at the time of such acceptance, he gives notice to the promisor of his intention to do so.

Section 73 (first two paragraphs and Explanation). When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Explanation. —In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74 (first paragraph). When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Section 65, Illustration (c). A, a singer, contracts with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre for two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her a hundred rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself from the theatre, and B, in consequence, rescinds the contract. B must pay A for the five nights on which she had sung.
In simple words

Section 39. If a party refuses, or disables himself from performing, the whole of his promise, the promisee may end the contract , unless he has shown by words or conduct that he accepts its continuance. Sections 53 and 54. Preventing the other party, or failing in the promise that had to come first, is a breach with its own results. Section 55. Late performance: voidable if time is of the essence; otherwise compensation only. Sections 73 to 75. The innocent party gets compensation for loss that is not remote; a named sum is cut down to reasonable compensation; a party who rightfully rescinds also gets compensation. Section 65, Illustration (c). If he rescinds, he must pay for what he received.
en.meaning:
Breach of contract is the failure or refusal of a party to perform his promise without lawful excuse. The Act does not define it. It deals with its effects in Sections 39, 53 to 55 and 73 to 75. Why the law gives the innocent party a choice. He did nothing wrong. He should not be forced to stay bound to a party who has let him down. He should also be free to keep the contract if he wants performance. See Diagram 1 for the kinds of breach and what follows. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. The bottom boxes show the right each kind of breach gives. flowchart TD B["Breach of contract
(ss.39, 53 to 55)"] A["Anticipatory breach"] C["Actual breach"] A1["Refusal or disabling act
before the due date (s.39):
end the contract and sue at once,
or wait for the due date"] C1["Failure at the due time (s.55):
time of the essence: voidable;
otherwise compensation only"] C2["Refusal during performance (s.39):
the promisee may end the contract"] C3["Prevention by a party (s.53):
avoid the contract and
claim compensation"] B --> A B --> C A --> A1 C --> C1 C --> C2 C --> C3 Text description Breach of contract (Sections 39, 53 to 55) has two kinds. Anticipatory breach: a refusal or disabling act before the due date (Section 39); the promisee may end the contract and sue at once, or wait for the due date. Actual breach has three forms: failure to perform at the due time (Section 55), where the contract is voidable at the promisee's option if time is of the essence, and otherwise compensation only; refusal during performance (Section 39), where the promisee may end the contract; and prevention by a party (Section 53), where the prevented party may avoid the contract and claim compensation.
keyPoints: A breach is a failure or refusal to perform without lawful excuse. It may be anticipatory (before the due date) or actual (on or after it). A breach gives the innocent party a choice. It does not end the contract automatically. He may end the contract and claim compensation, unless he has accepted its continuance (Section 39). If he ends the contract, he must pay for the part performance he received (Section 65). Prevention (Section 53), default in order (Section 54) and delay with time of the essence (Section 55) are special cases. Limitation: three years for compensation and for specific performance (Limitation Act, Articles 55 and 54). Compensation may be claimed with specific performance (Specific Relief Act, Section 21). Dismissal of a specific performance suit bars a later suit for compensation for that breach (Section 24).

caseLaws.name: Hochster v
caseLaws.facts: De La Tour (1853) Facts. In April 1852 De La Tour engaged Hochster as a courier for a three-month tour of Europe from 1 June 1852, at £10 a month. On 11 May 1852 he wrote that he had changed his mind and declined Hochster's services. Hochster sued on 22 May, before 1 June. Principle. A party who renounces the contract before the day for performance commits a breach, and the other party may sue at once without waiting for that day. Judgment for the plaintiff. (1853) 2 E & B 678 : 118 ER 922 (Queen's Bench, Lord Campbell C.J., 25 June 1853). Why it matters. It is the origin of anticipatory breach. Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das (1963) Facts. By an agreement of 21 March 1949 the seller agreed to sell leasehold rights in land and a building in Delhi. He received Rs 25,000: Rs 1,000 as earnest money and Rs 24,000 towards the price. The sale was not completed, and the seller sued to forfeit the whole Rs 25,000 under the contract. Principle. Section 74 applies to a stipulation for forfeiture of money already paid, so the court may award only reasonable compensation, not exceeding the sum named. With no proof of loss, the seller could keep only the Rs 1,000 earnest money, whose forfeiture was not challenged. [1964] 1 SCR 515 : AIR 1963 SC 1405 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench, 15 January 1963). Why it matters. It limits what the wronged party may keep. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) Facts. Millers at Gloucester had their mill stopped by a broken crank shaft. They gave the shaft to carriers to take to engineers as a pattern for a new one. The carriers delayed delivery, and the mill stayed idle longer. The Court of Exchequer ordered a new trial. Principle. Damages for breach are those "arising naturally, i.e., according to the usual course of things, from such breach of contract itself", or "such as may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of the breach of it". (1854) 9 Ex 341 : 156 ER 145 (Alderson B., 23 February 1854). Why it matters. It is the source of the rule on remote loss in Section 73.

selfTest.q: 1. Does a breach end a contract automatically?
selfTest.a: No. The innocent party may choose to end it or keep it alive (Section 39).

selfTest.q: 2. When does the promisee lose the right to end the contract under Section 39?
selfTest.a: When he signifies by words or conduct that he accepts its continuance.

selfTest.q: 3. How is breach different from frustration?
selfTest.a: Breach comes from a party's own default and gives the innocent party a choice and damages. Frustration comes from an outside event and makes the contract void automatically.

selfTest.q: 4. The manager ends the contract after the singer stays away on the sixth night. Must he pay her anything?
selfTest.a: Yes. He must pay her for the five nights on which she sang (Section 65, Illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 5. Within what time must a suit for compensation for breach be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from when the contract is broken (Limitation Act, Article 55).

సెక్షన్ 39. ఒక పక్షం తన వాగ్దానం మొత్తాన్ని నెరవేర్చడానికి నిరాకరిస్తే, లేదా నెరవేర్చలేని స్థితికి తనను తాను తెచ్చుకుంటే, వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించవచ్చు; కాంట్రాక్టు కొనసాగడానికి మాటలతో గానీ ప్రవర్తనతో గానీ అంగీకారం చూపితే తప్ప. సెక్షన్లు 53, 54. అవతలి పక్షాన్ని అడ్డుకోవడం, లేదా ముందు నెరవేర్చాల్సిన వాగ్దానంలో విఫలమవడం, వాటి సొంత ఫలితాలతో కూడిన ఉల్లంఘన. సెక్షన్ 55. ఆలస్యమైన నెరవేర్పు: సమయం ప్రధానమైతే రద్దు చేయదగినది; లేకపోతే పరిహారం మాత్రమే. సెక్షన్లు 73 నుంచి 75. అమాయక పక్షానికి దూరపు నష్టం కాని నష్టానికి పరిహారం వస్తుంది; కాంట్రాక్టులో పేర్కొన్న మొత్తాన్ని సహేతుక పరిహారానికి తగ్గిస్తారు; సక్రమంగా రద్దు చేసిన పక్షానికీ పరిహారం వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 65, Illustration (c). అతను రద్దు చేస్తే, తాను పొందినదానికి చెల్లించాలి.

hi.inOneMinute: A breach happens when a party fails or refuses to perform his promise without lawful excuse. A breach does not end the contract by itself. It gives the innocent party a choice. He may treat the contract as ended and claim compensation, or he may keep it alive. A breach may come before the due date ( anticipatory ) or on or after it ( actual ). In exams, the choice, the sections and the difference from frustration earn the marks. In real life, it tells a wronged party what he can do the day the other side lets him down.
legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Illustrations. (a) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her 100 rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night A wilfully absents herself from the theatre. B is at liberty to put an end to the contract. (b) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two night's in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her at the rate of 100 rupees for each night. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself. With the assent of B, A sings on the seventh night. B has signified his acquiescence in the continuance of the contract, and cannot now put an end to it, but is entitled to compensation for the damage sustained by him through A's failure to sing on the sixth night.

Section 53. Liability of party preventing event on which the contract is to take effect. When a contract contains reciprocal promises, and one party to the contract prevents the other from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented; and he is entitled to compensation from the other party for any loss which he may sustain in consequence of the non-performance of the contract.

Section 54. Effect of default as to that promise which should be first performed, in contract consisting of reciprocal promises. When a contract consists of reciprocal promises, such that one of them cannot be performed, or that its performance cannot be claimed till the other has been performed, and the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss which such other party may sustain by the non-performance of the contract.

Section 55. Effect of failure to perform at fixed time, in contract in which time is essential. When a party to a contract promises to do a certain thing at or before a specified time, or certain things at or before specified times, and fails to do any such thing at or before the specified time, the contract, or so much of it as has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee, if the intention of the parties was that time should be of the essence of the contract. Effect of such failure when time is not essential. —If it was not the intention of the parties that time should be of the essence of the contract, the contract does not become voidable by the failure to do such thing at or before the specified time; but the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure. Effect of acceptance of performance at time other than that agreed upon. —If, in case of a contract voidable on account of the promisor's failure to perform his promise at the time agreed, the promisee accepts performance of such promise at any time other than that agreed, the promisee cannot claim compensation for any loss occasioned by the non-performance of the promise at the time agreed, unless, at the time of such acceptance, he gives notice to the promisor of his intention to do so.

Section 73 (first two paragraphs and Explanation). When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Explanation. —In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74 (first paragraph). When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Section 65, Illustration (c). A, a singer, contracts with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre for two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her a hundred rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself from the theatre, and B, in consequence, rescinds the contract. B must pay A for the five nights on which she had sung.
In simple words

Section 39. If a party refuses, or disables himself from performing, the whole of his promise, the promisee may end the contract , unless he has shown by words or conduct that he accepts its continuance. Sections 53 and 54. Preventing the other party, or failing in the promise that had to come first, is a breach with its own results. Section 55. Late performance: voidable if time is of the essence; otherwise compensation only. Sections 73 to 75. The innocent party gets compensation for loss that is not remote; a named sum is cut down to reasonable compensation; a party who rightfully rescinds also gets compensation. Section 65, Illustration (c). If he rescinds, he must pay for what he received.
hi.meaning:
Breach of contract is the failure or refusal of a party to perform his promise without lawful excuse. The Act does not define it. It deals with its effects in Sections 39, 53 to 55 and 73 to 75. Why the law gives the innocent party a choice. He did nothing wrong. He should not be forced to stay bound to a party who has let him down. He should also be free to keep the contract if he wants performance. See Diagram 1 for the kinds of breach and what follows. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. The bottom boxes show the right each kind of breach gives. flowchart TD B["Breach of contract
(ss.39, 53 to 55)"] A["Anticipatory breach"] C["Actual breach"] A1["Refusal or disabling act

or wait for the due date"] C1["Failure at the due time (s.55):
