claim compensation"] B --> A B --> C A --> A1 C --> C1 C --> C2 C --> C3 Text description Breach of contract (Sections 39, 53 to 55) has two kinds. Anticipatory breach: a refusal or disabling act before the due date (Section 39); the promisee may end the contract and sue at once, or wait for the due date. Actual breach has three forms: failure to perform at the due time (Section 55), where the contract is voidable at the promisee's option if time is of the essence, and otherwise compensation only; refusal during performance (Section 39), where the promisee may end the contract; and prevention by a party (Section 53), where the prevented party may avoid the contract and claim compensation.
keyPoints: A breach is a failure or refusal to perform without lawful excuse. It may be anticipatory (before the due date) or actual (on or after it). A breach gives the innocent party a choice. It does not end the contract automatically. He may end the contract and claim compensation, unless he has accepted its continuance (Section 39). If he ends the contract, he must pay for the part performance he received (Section 65). Prevention (Section 53), default in order (Section 54) and delay with time of the essence (Section 55) are special cases. Limitation: three years for compensation and for specific performance (Limitation Act, Articles 55 and 54). Compensation may be claimed with specific performance (Specific Relief Act, Section 21). Dismissal of a specific performance suit bars a later suit for compensation for that breach (Section 24).

caseLaws.name: Hochster v
caseLaws.facts: De La Tour (1853) Facts. In April 1852 De La Tour engaged Hochster as a courier for a three-month tour of Europe from 1 June 1852, at £10 a month. On 11 May 1852 he wrote that he had changed his mind and declined Hochster's services. Hochster sued on 22 May, before 1 June. Principle. A party who renounces the contract before the day for performance commits a breach, and the other party may sue at once without waiting for that day. Judgment for the plaintiff. (1853) 2 E & B 678 : 118 ER 922 (Queen's Bench, Lord Campbell C.J., 25 June 1853). Why it matters. It is the origin of anticipatory breach. Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das (1963) Facts. By an agreement of 21 March 1949 the seller agreed to sell leasehold rights in land and a building in Delhi. He received Rs 25,000: Rs 1,000 as earnest money and Rs 24,000 towards the price. The sale was not completed, and the seller sued to forfeit the whole Rs 25,000 under the contract. Principle. Section 74 applies to a stipulation for forfeiture of money already paid, so the court may award only reasonable compensation, not exceeding the sum named. With no proof of loss, the seller could keep only the Rs 1,000 earnest money, whose forfeiture was not challenged. [1964] 1 SCR 515 : AIR 1963 SC 1405 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench, 15 January 1963). Why it matters. It limits what the wronged party may keep. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) Facts. Millers at Gloucester had their mill stopped by a broken crank shaft. They gave the shaft to carriers to take to engineers as a pattern for a new one. The carriers delayed delivery, and the mill stayed idle longer. The Court of Exchequer ordered a new trial. Principle. Damages for breach are those "arising naturally, i.e., according to the usual course of things, from such breach of contract itself", or "such as may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties, at the time they made the contract, as the probable result of the breach of it". (1854) 9 Ex 341 : 156 ER 145 (Alderson B., 23 February 1854). Why it matters. It is the source of the rule on remote loss in Section 73.

selfTest.q: 1. Does a breach end a contract automatically?
selfTest.a: No. The innocent party may choose to end it or keep it alive (Section 39).

selfTest.q: 2. When does the promisee lose the right to end the contract under Section 39?
selfTest.a: When he signifies by words or conduct that he accepts its continuance.

selfTest.q: 3. How is breach different from frustration?
selfTest.a: Breach comes from a party's own default and gives the innocent party a choice and damages. Frustration comes from an outside event and makes the contract void automatically.

selfTest.q: 4. The manager ends the contract after the singer stays away on the sixth night. Must he pay her anything?
selfTest.a: Yes. He must pay her for the five nights on which she sang (Section 65, Illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 5. Within what time must a suit for compensation for breach be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from when the contract is broken (Limitation Act, Article 55).

en.inOneMinute: An actual breach happens when a party fails to perform at the time performance is due, or performs badly or only in part, or refuses during performance. The other party can always claim compensation. He can end the contract only if the breach goes to the whole promise or time was of the essence. Compensation follows Sections 73 to 75. In exams, the line between a breach that ends the contract and one that gives damages only earns the marks. In real life, it tells a buyer or owner whether to cancel or to claim the cost of putting things right.

Section 53. Liability of party preventing event on which the contract is to take effect. When a contract contains reciprocal promises, and one party to the contract prevents the other from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented; and he is entitled to compensation from the other party for any loss which he may sustain in consequence of the non-performance of the contract.

Section 54. Effect of default as to that promise which should be first performed, in contract consisting of reciprocal promises. When a contract consists of reciprocal promises, such that one of them cannot be performed, or that its performance cannot be claimed till the other has been performed, and the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss which such other party may sustain by the non-performance of the contract.

Section 55. Effect of failure to perform at fixed time, in contract in which time is essential. When a party to a contract promises to do a certain thing at or before a specified time, or certain things at or before specified times, and fails to do any such thing at or before the specified time, the contract, or so much of it as has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee, if the intention of the parties was that time should be of the essence of the contract. Effect of such failure when time is not essential. —If it was not the intention of the parties that time should be of the essence of the contract, the contract does not become voidable by the failure to do such thing at or before the specified time; but the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure.

Section 65, Illustration (b). A contracts with B to deliver to him 250 maunds of rice before the first of May. A delivers 130 maunds only before that day, and none after. B retains the 130 maunds after the first of May. He is bound to pay A for them.

Section 73. Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract. When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Explanation. —In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74. Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.
Related provisions

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 11. Stipulations as to time. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale. Whether any other stipulation as to time is of the essence of the contract or not depends on the terms of the contract.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 12. Condition and warranty. (1) A stipulation in a contract of sale with reference to goods which are the subject thereof may be a condition or a warranty. (2) A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated. (3) A warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a claim for damages but not to a right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. (4) Whether a stipulation in a contract of sale is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition, though called a warranty in the contract.
In simple words

Section 39. Where a party refuses to perform, or disables himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract unless he has accepted its continuance. Section 53. If one party prevents the other from performing, the contract becomes voidable at the prevented party's option. He may claim compensation. Section 54. A party who fails in the promise that had to be performed first cannot claim the other party's performance and must compensate him. Section 55. Where time is of the essence and performance is late, the contract is voidable at the promisee's option. Otherwise the promisee may claim compensation for the delay. Section 65, Illustration (b). A delivers 130 maunds of the 250 maunds of rice he promised before the date. B keeps the 130 maunds after that date. He must pay A for them. Section 73. Compensation for loss that naturally arose from the breach, or that the parties knew was likely. No compensation for remote and indirect loss. The means of remedying the inconvenience must be taken into account. Section 74. Where a sum is named for breach, or a penalty is stipulated , the court awards reasonable compensation not exceeding that amount. Section 75. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for the damage he has sustained.
en.meaning:
Actual breach is a breach committed at the time performance is due or during performance. It differs from an anticipatory breach, which comes before the due date. The Act does not give it a separate name. It deals with it in the sections above. An actual breach may take four forms: Failure to perform at the time fixed. Defective or incomplete performance. Refusal in the course of performance. Prevention of the other party's performance. The law gives the innocent party a remedy for each. Diagram 1 shows the questions to ask. Diagram 1. Start at the top. Each box must be answered "yes" to move down. A "no" shows where the claim to end the contract fails. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Did a party fail to perform when due,
perform defectively, or refuse
during performance?"} N1["No actual breach"] Q2{"2. Was the failure without lawful excuse?
(not frustration, not a refused tender,
not the promisee's own prevention)"} N2["The promisor is excused:
no breach"] Q3{"3. Does the breach go to the whole promise,
or was time of the essence? (ss.39, 55)"} N3["Compensation only (ss.55, 73);
he must still perform his own part"] R["Result (ss.39, 55, 65, 73, 75):
end the contract and claim compensation;
pay for any benefit received;
if he accepts continuance,
he can still claim compensation"] Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| R Text description Question 1: did a party fail to perform when due, perform defectively, or refuse during performance? If no, there is no actual breach. Question 2: was the failure without lawful excuse (not frustration, not a refused tender, not the promisee's own prevention)? If no, the promisor is excused and there is no breach. Question 3: does the breach go to the whole promise, or was time of the essence (Sections 39, 55)? If no, the promisee may claim compensation only (Sections 55, 73) and must still perform his own part. If yes, the result (Sections 39, 55, 65, 73, 75): the promisee may end the contract and claim compensation; he must pay for any benefit received; if he accepts the contract's continuance, he can still claim compensation.
keyPoints: Actual breach is a breach at the due time or during performance. Every actual breach gives a right to compensation (Section 73). The right to end the contract needs a breach of the whole promise or time of the essence (Sections 39, 55). Remote and indirect loss is not compensated. The innocent party must reduce his loss. Where a sum is named for breach, the court awards reasonable compensation not above it (Section 74). A party who rescinds must pay for benefits received and may claim compensation (Sections 65, 75). Condition v warranty in sale of goods: Sale of Goods Act, Section 12. Compensation suit: three years from the breach (Limitation Act, Article 55). Compensation may be claimed with specific performance (Specific Relief Act, Section 21).

caseLaws.name: Fateh Chand v
caseLaws.facts: Balkishan Das (1963) Facts. By an agreement of 21 March 1949 the seller agreed to sell leasehold rights in land and a building in Delhi. He received Rs 25,000 (Rs 1,000 as earnest money and Rs 24,000 towards the price). The sale was not completed, and the contract said the whole sum would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 covers forfeiture of money already paid. Proof of actual loss is not needed, but a breach causing no legal injury gives no compensation. The seller kept only the Rs 1,000 earnest money. [1964] 1 SCR 515 : AIR 1963 SC 1405 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench, 15 January 1963). Why it matters. It limits what a wronged party may keep. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) Facts. Millers in Gloucester sent a broken crank shaft by carrier to Greenwich to be copied for a new one. The carrier delayed delivery and the mill stayed idle. Principle. Damages are those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably contemplated by both parties. Special circumstances count only if "communicated by the plaintiffs to the defendants, and thus known to both parties". (1854) 9 Ex 341 : 156 ER 145 (Court of Exchequer, Alderson B., 23 February 1854). Why it matters. It is the source of the rule on remote loss in Section 73. Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi (2011) Facts. Under an agreement of 17 January 1981 a buyer agreed to buy 24 acres 95 cents at Rs 15,000 an acre. The balance was payable in three instalments , and clause 6 said "payments on due dates is the essence of this contract". She paid part and missed the last payment dates. The sellers cancelled the agreement by notice of 2 August 1981. Principle. The clauses made time for payment the essence, so her default justified the cancellation (paras 17, 19 and 20). The money she paid was ordered to be refunded with interest. [2011] 8 SCR 874 (Supreme Court, 4 July 2011). Why it matters. A breach of a time-essential term lets the seller end the contract.

selfTest.q: 1. When can a promisee end the contract after an actual breach?
selfTest.a: When the breach goes to the whole promise (Section 39) or time was of the essence (Section 55).

selfTest.q: 2. What loss does Section 73 compensate?
selfTest.a: Loss that arose naturally from the breach, or that the parties knew to be likely when they made the contract. Remote and indirect loss is excluded.

selfTest.q: 3. A debtor does not pay on the day, and the creditor is ruined. What does the debtor owe?
selfTest.a: Only the principal and interest up to the day of payment (Section 73, Illustration (n)).

selfTest.q: 4. A builder finishes the house but uses cheaper paint on one wall. Can the owner cancel the contract?
selfTest.a: No. He may claim the cost of repainting, but the breach does not go to the whole promise.

selfTest.q: 5. Under the Sale of Goods Act, what is the difference between a condition and a warranty?
selfTest.a: Breach of a condition gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated. Breach of a warranty gives a claim for damages only (Section 12).

సెక్షన్ 39. ఒక పక్షం తన వాగ్దానం మొత్తాన్ని నెరవేర్చడానికి నిరాకరిస్తే, లేదా నెరవేర్చలేని స్థితికి తనను తాను తెచ్చుకుంటే, కాంట్రాక్టు కొనసాగడాన్ని వాగ్దానగ్రహీత అంగీకరించి ఉండకపోతే, అతను కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 53. ఒక పక్షం అవతలి పక్షాన్ని నెరవేర్చకుండా అడ్డుకుంటే, అడ్డుకోబడిన పక్షం ఇష్టం మేరకు కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయదగినది అవుతుంది. అతను పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 54. ముందు నెరవేర్చాల్సిన వాగ్దానంలో విఫలమైన పక్షం అవతలి పక్షం నెరవేర్పును కోరలేడు, అతనికి పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి. సెక్షన్ 55. సమయమే ప్రధానమై నెరవేర్పు ఆలస్యమైతే, వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఇష్టం మేరకు కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయదగినది. లేకపోతే ఆలస్యానికి వాగ్దానగ్రహీత పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 65, Illustration (b). తేదీకి ముందు ఇస్తానన్న 250 మణుగుల బియ్యంలో A 130 మణుగులు మాత్రమే ఇస్తాడు. ఆ తేదీ తర్వాత కూడా B ఆ 130 మణుగులను ఉంచుకుంటాడు. వాటికి B, A కు చెల్లించాలి. సెక్షన్ 73. ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చిన నష్టానికి, లేదా వచ్చే అవకాశం ఉందని పక్షాలకు తెలిసిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం. దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టానికి పరిహారం లేదు. అసౌకర్యాన్ని సరిదిద్దడానికి ఉన్న మార్గాలను లెక్కలోకి తీసుకోవాలి. సెక్షన్ 74. ఉల్లంఘనకు ఒక మొత్తాన్ని పేర్కొన్నా, జరిమానా షరతు పెట్టినా, ఆ మొత్తాన్ని మించకుండా సహేతుక పరిహారాన్ని కోర్టు ఇస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 75. కాంట్రాక్టును సక్రమంగా రద్దు చేసిన వ్యక్తికి తనకు కలిగిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం వస్తుంది.

అప్పటికీ పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు"] Q1 -->|"కాదు"| N1 Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2 Q2 -->|"కాదు"| N2 Q2 -->|"అవును"| Q3 Q3 -->|"కాదు"| N3 Q3 -->|"అవును"| R వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: ఒక పక్షం గడువు సమయానికి నెరవేర్చలేదా, లోపభూయిష్టంగా నెరవేర్చాడా, లేదా మధ్యలో నిరాకరించాడా? కాదు అయితే వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘన లేదు. ప్రశ్న 2: ఆ వైఫల్యానికి చట్టబద్ధమైన కారణం లేదా (ఫ్రస్ట్రేషన్ కాదు, తిరస్కరించిన టెండర్ కాదు, వాగ్దానగ్రహీత సొంత అడ్డంకి కాదు)? కాదు అయితే వాగ్దానకర్తకు మినహాయింపు, ఉల్లంఘన లేదు. ప్రశ్న 3: ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి వర్తిస్తుందా, లేదా సమయమే ప్రధానమా (సెక్షన్లు 39, 55)? కాదు అయితే వాగ్దానగ్రహీత పరిహారం మాత్రమే కోరవచ్చు (సెక్షన్లు 55, 73), తన భాగాన్ని ఇంకా నెరవేర్చాలి. అవును అయితే ఫలితం (సెక్షన్లు 39, 55, 65, 73, 75): వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించి పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు; పొందిన లాభానికి చెల్లించాలి; కాంట్రాక్టు కొనసాగడాన్ని అంగీకరిస్తే, అప్పటికీ పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘన తర్వాత వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ఎప్పుడు ముగించవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి వర్తించినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 39), లేదా సమయమే ప్రధానమైనప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 55).

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 73 ఏ నష్టానికి పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చిన నష్టానికి, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు చేసేటప్పుడు వచ్చే అవకాశం ఉందని పక్షాలకు తెలిసిన నష్టానికి. దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టం మినహాయింపు.

selfTest.q: 3. రుణగ్రహీత నిర్ణీత రోజున చెల్లించడు, రుణదాత నాశనమవుతాడు. రుణగ్రహీత ఎంత చెల్లించాలి?
selfTest.a: అసలు మొత్తం, చెల్లించిన రోజు వరకు వడ్డీ మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 73, Illustration (n)).

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక బిల్డర్ ఇల్లు పూర్తి చేస్తాడు, కానీ ఒక గోడకు చౌక రంగు వేస్తాడు. యజమాని కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మళ్లీ రంగు వేయించే ఖర్చు కోరవచ్చు, కానీ ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి వర్తించదు.

selfTest.q: 5. సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం కింద షరతుకూ హామీకీ తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: షరతు ఉల్లంఘన కాంట్రాక్టును తిరస్కరించినట్టు భావించే హక్కు ఇస్తుంది. హామీ ఉల్లంఘన నష్టపరిహారం దావా మాత్రమే ఇస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 12).

hi.inOneMinute: An actual breach happens when a party fails to perform at the time performance is due, or performs badly or only in part, or refuses during performance. The other party can always claim compensation. He can end the contract only if the breach goes to the whole promise or time was of the essence. Compensation follows Sections 73 to 75. In exams, the line between a breach that ends the contract and one that gives damages only earns the marks. In real life, it tells a buyer or owner whether to cancel or to claim the cost of putting things right.
legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance.

Section 53. Liability of party preventing event on which the contract is to take effect. When a contract contains reciprocal promises, and one party to the contract prevents the other from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented; and he is entitled to compensation from the other party for any loss which he may sustain in consequence of the non-performance of the contract.

Section 54. Effect of default as to that promise which should be first performed, in contract consisting of reciprocal promises. When a contract consists of reciprocal promises, such that one of them cannot be performed, or that its performance cannot be claimed till the other has been performed, and the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss which such other party may sustain by the non-performance of the contract.

Section 55. Effect of failure to perform at fixed time, in contract in which time is essential. When a party to a contract promises to do a certain thing at or before a specified time, or certain things at or before specified times, and fails to do any such thing at or before the specified time, the contract, or so much of it as has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee, if the intention of the parties was that time should be of the essence of the contract. Effect of such failure when time is not essential. —If it was not the intention of the parties that time should be of the essence of the contract, the contract does not become voidable by the failure to do such thing at or before the specified time; but the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure.

Section 65, Illustration (b). A contracts with B to deliver to him 250 maunds of rice before the first of May. A delivers 130 maunds only before that day, and none after. B retains the 130 maunds after the first of May. He is bound to pay A for them.

Section 73. Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract. When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Explanation. —In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74. Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.
Related provisions

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 11. Stipulations as to time. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale. Whether any other stipulation as to time is of the essence of the contract or not depends on the terms of the contract.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 12. Condition and warranty. (1) A stipulation in a contract of sale with reference to goods which are the subject thereof may be a condition or a warranty. (2) A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated. (3) A warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a claim for damages but not to a right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. (4) Whether a stipulation in a contract of sale is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition, though called a warranty in the contract.
In simple words

Section 39. Where a party refuses to perform, or disables himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract unless he has accepted its continuance. Section 53. If one party prevents the other from performing, the contract becomes voidable at the prevented party's option. He may claim compensation. Section 54. A party who fails in the promise that had to be performed first cannot claim the other party's performance and must compensate him. Section 55. Where time is of the essence and performance is late, the contract is voidable at the promisee's option. Otherwise the promisee may claim compensation for the delay. Section 65, Illustration (b). A delivers 130 maunds of the 250 maunds of rice he promised before the date. B keeps the 130 maunds after that date. He must pay A for them. Section 73. Compensation for loss that naturally arose from the breach, or that the parties knew was likely. No compensation for remote and indirect loss. The means of remedying the inconvenience must be taken into account. Section 74. Where a sum is named for breach, or a penalty is stipulated , the court awards reasonable compensation not exceeding that amount. Section 75. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for the damage he has sustained.
hi.meaning:
Actual breach is a breach committed at the time performance is due or during performance. It differs from an anticipatory breach, which comes before the due date. The Act does not give it a separate name. It deals with it in the sections above. An actual breach may take four forms: Failure to perform at the time fixed. Defective or incomplete performance. Refusal in the course of performance. Prevention of the other party's performance. The law gives the innocent party a remedy for each. Diagram 1 shows the questions to ask. Diagram 1. Start at the top. Each box must be answered "yes" to move down. A "no" shows where the claim to end the contract fails. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Did a party fail to perform when due,
perform defectively, or refuse
during performance?"} N1["No actual breach"] Q2{"2. Was the failure without lawful excuse?
(not frustration, not a refused tender,
not the promisee's own prevention)"} N2["The promisor is excused:
no breach"] Q3{"3. Does the breach go to the whole promise,
or was time of the essence? (ss.39, 55)"} N3["Compensation only (ss.55, 73);
he must still perform his own part"] R["Result (ss.39, 55, 65, 73, 75):
end the contract and claim compensation;
pay for any benefit received;
if he accepts continuance,
he can still claim compensation"] Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| R Text description Question 1: did a party fail to perform when due, perform defectively, or refuse during performance? If no, there is no actual breach. Question 2: was the failure without lawful excuse (not frustration, not a refused tender, not the promisee's own prevention)? If no, the promisor is excused and there is no breach. Question 3: does the breach go to the whole promise, or was time of the essence (Sections 39, 55)? If no, the promisee may claim compensation only (Sections 55, 73) and must still perform his own part. If yes, the result (Sections 39, 55, 65, 73, 75): the promisee may end the contract and claim compensation; he must pay for any benefit received; if he accepts the contract's continuance, he can still claim compensation.
keyPoints: Actual breach is a breach at the due time or during performance. Every actual breach gives a right to compensation (Section 73). The right to end the contract needs a breach of the whole promise or time of the essence (Sections 39, 55). Remote and indirect loss is not compensated. The innocent party must reduce his loss. Where a sum is named for breach, the court awards reasonable compensation not above it (Section 74). A party who rescinds must pay for benefits received and may claim compensation (Sections 65, 75). Condition v warranty in sale of goods: Sale of Goods Act, Section 12. Compensation suit: three years from the breach (Limitation Act, Article 55). Compensation may be claimed with specific performance (Specific Relief Act, Section 21).

caseLaws.name: Fateh Chand v
caseLaws.facts: Balkishan Das (1963) Facts. By an agreement of 21 March 1949 the seller agreed to sell leasehold rights in land and a building in Delhi. He received Rs 25,000 (Rs 1,000 as earnest money and Rs 24,000 towards the price). The sale was not completed, and the contract said the whole sum would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 covers forfeiture of money already paid. Proof of actual loss is not needed, but a breach causing no legal injury gives no compensation. The seller kept only the Rs 1,000 earnest money. [1964] 1 SCR 515 : AIR 1963 SC 1405 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench, 15 January 1963). Why it matters. It limits what a wronged party may keep. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) Facts. Millers in Gloucester sent a broken crank shaft by carrier to Greenwich to be copied for a new one. The carrier delayed delivery and the mill stayed idle. Principle. Damages are those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably contemplated by both parties. Special circumstances count only if "communicated by the plaintiffs to the defendants, and thus known to both parties". (1854) 9 Ex 341 : 156 ER 145 (Court of Exchequer, Alderson B., 23 February 1854). Why it matters. It is the source of the rule on remote loss in Section 73. Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi (2011) Facts. Under an agreement of 17 January 1981 a buyer agreed to buy 24 acres 95 cents at Rs 15,000 an acre. The balance was payable in three instalments , and clause 6 said "payments on due dates is the essence of this contract". She paid part and missed the last payment dates. The sellers cancelled the agreement by notice of 2 August 1981. Principle. The clauses made time for payment the essence, so her default justified the cancellation (paras 17, 19 and 20). The money she paid was ordered to be refunded with interest. [2011] 8 SCR 874 (Supreme Court, 4 July 2011). Why it matters. A breach of a time-essential term lets the seller end the contract.

selfTest.q: 1. When can a promisee end the contract after an actual breach?
selfTest.a: When the breach goes to the whole promise (Section 39) or time was of the essence (Section 55).

selfTest.q: 2. What loss does Section 73 compensate?
selfTest.a: Loss that arose naturally from the breach, or that the parties knew to be likely when they made the contract. Remote and indirect loss is excluded.

selfTest.q: 3. A debtor does not pay on the day, and the creditor is ruined. What does the debtor owe?
selfTest.a: Only the principal and interest up to the day of payment (Section 73, Illustration (n)).

selfTest.q: 4. A builder finishes the house but uses cheaper paint on one wall. Can the owner cancel the contract?
selfTest.a: No. He may claim the cost of repainting, but the breach does not go to the whole promise.

selfTest.q: 5. Under the Sale of Goods Act, what is the difference between a condition and a warranty?
selfTest.a: Breach of a condition gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated. Breach of a warranty gives a claim for damages only (Section 12).

en.inOneMinute: An anticipatory breach happens when a party refuses to perform, or makes himself unable to perform, before the time for performance arrives. The other party need not wait for the due date. He has two choices: He may accept the refusal, end the contract and sue at once. Or he may keep the contract alive and wait. The choice has risks. In exams, the meaning, the two choices and the cases earn the marks. In real life, it decides whether you can act the day a supplier says he will not deliver.
legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Illustrations. (a) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her 100 rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night A wilfully absents herself from the theatre. B is at liberty to put an end to the contract. (b) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two night's in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her at the rate of 100 rupees for each night. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself. With the assent of B, A sings on the seventh night. B has signified his acquiescence in the continuance of the contract, and cannot now put an end to it, but is entitled to compensation for the damage sustained by him through A's failure to sing on the sixth night.
Related provisions

Section 73, Illustration (c). A contracts to buy of B, at a stated price, 50 maunds of rice, no time being fixed for delivery. A afterwards informs B that he will not accept the rice if tendered to him. B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the amount, if any, by which the contract price exceeds that which B can obtain for the rice at the time when A informs B that he will not accept it.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(c). Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— ... (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— ... (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
In simple words

Section 39 covers both a refusal and a disabling act, if it goes to the whole promise. The promisee "may" end the contract. He loses that right if he shows, by words or conduct, that he accepts the contract's continuance. Section 73, Illustration (c) measures the loss at the time the defaulter announces his refusal.
en.meaning:
Anticipatory breach is a breach committed before the time fixed for performance. It takes two forms: Form What happens Example Express repudiation The party says he will not perform A seller writes, "I will not deliver" Implied repudiation His conduct makes performance impossible He sells to another buyer the very goods he promised The words of the Act. The Act does not use the words "anticipatory breach". Section 39 covers it in the words "refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing". The English case Hochster v. De La Tour gave the doctrine its shape. Why the law lets the innocent party act early. Waiting helps no one. He can look for another supplier at once and so reduce his loss. See Diagram 1 for the moments in order. Diagram 1. Read from top to bottom. After the refusal, follow the branch the promisee chooses. flowchart TD M["Contract made"] R["Before the due date:
refusal or disabling act
covering the whole promise (s.39)"] Q{"What does the
promisee choose?"} A["Accept the repudiation:
contract ends; sue at once
for damages (s.73); mitigate"] A2["Cannot later ask for
specific performance"] W["Affirm and wait:
contract binds both sides;
the other party may withdraw"] W2["At the due date: must be
ready and willing; an event in
between may defeat the claim"] M --> R R --> Q Q -->|"Accept"| A A --> A2 Q -->|"Affirm"| W W --> W2 Text description The contract is made. Before the due date, one party refuses to perform, or disables himself from performing, his whole promise (Section 39). The promisee then chooses. If he accepts the repudiation, the contract ends, he may sue at once for damages under Section 73 and must mitigate his loss, but he cannot later ask for specific performance. If he affirms and waits, the contract stays binding on both sides and the other party may withdraw his refusal; at the due date the promisee must be ready and willing to perform, and an event in between may defeat his claim (Avery v. Bowden).
keyPoints: Anticipatory breach is a refusal or disabling act before the due date (Section 39). The refusal must be clear and cover the whole promise. The promisee may accept it, end the contract and sue at once ( Hochster ). Or he may affirm the contract and wait, staying ready and willing. If he waits, an intervening event may defeat his claim ( Avery v. Bowden ). After accepting the repudiation he can claim damages but not specific performance ( Jawahar Lal Wadhwa ). Section 39 covers refusal and also disabling oneself from performing. Specific performance needs proof of readiness and willingness (Specific Relief Act, Section 16(c)).

caseLaws.name: Hochster v
caseLaws.facts: De La Tour (1853) Facts. In April 1852 De La Tour engaged Hochster as a courier for a three-month tour from 1 June 1852. On 11 May 1852 he wrote that he had changed his mind and declined Hochster's services. Hochster sued on 22 May. Principle. The injured party has "an option ... either to sue immediately, or to wait till the time when the act was to be done, still holding it as prospectively binding". Judgment for the plaintiff. (1853) 2 E & B 678 : 118 ER 922 (Queen's Bench, 25 June 1853). Why it matters. It is the origin of the doctrine. Frost v. Knight (1872) Facts. Knight promised to marry Miss Frost on his father's death. While the father was still alive, he told her he would not marry her. LR 7 Ex 111. Principle. She could sue once he made clear he would not perform, without waiting for the father's death. Why it matters. It confirms Hochster for a promise with an uncertain date. Avery v. Bowden (1855) Facts. A charterer's agent told the ship's master at Odessa that no cargo would be supplied. The master stayed on. War made performance illegal before the time for loading ended. (1855) 5 E & B 714. Principle. A promisee who does not accept the repudiation keeps the contract alive and takes the risk. The shipowner lost. Why it matters. It shows the risk of waiting. Jawahar Lal Wadhwa v. Haripada Chakroberty (1988) Facts. Under an agreement of 6 September 1973, an advance of Rs 5,000 was paid and monthly payments of Rs 105 followed. On 16 January 1976 notice was given repudiating the agreement. The dispute went to arbitration, and an award of 18 March 1988 granted Rs 58,498.60. Principle. A party who accepts an anticipatory breach and treats the contract as ended may claim damages, not specific performance. A party who keeps the contract alive must show that he was ready and willing to perform. AIR 1989 SC 606 : (1989) 1 SCC 76 (Supreme Court, 14 October 1988). Why it matters. It states the two courses in Indian law.

selfTest.q: 1. What is anticipatory breach?
selfTest.a: A refusal to perform, or an act disabling performance, made before the time for performance arrives (Section 39).

selfTest.q: 2. What two choices does the promisee have?
selfTest.a: He may accept the repudiation, end the contract and sue at once, or keep the contract alive and wait for the due date.

selfTest.q: 3. Why is waiting risky?
selfTest.a: An event before the due date may discharge the contract, as war did in Avery v. Bowden , and then the promisee loses his claim.

selfTest.q: 4. A builder says he may be a week late because labour is short. Is this an anticipatory breach?
selfTest.a: No. It is not a clear refusal of the whole promise.

selfTest.q: 5. After accepting the repudiation, can the promisee sue for specific performance?
selfTest.a: No. He may claim damages only ( Jawahar Lal Wadhwa ).

ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘన అంటే నెరవేర్చడానికి నిర్ణయించిన సమయానికి ముందే జరిగే ఉల్లంఘన. దీనికి రెండు రూపాలు: రూపం ఏం జరుగుతుంది ఉదాహరణ స్పష్టమైన నిరాకరణ (repudiation) తాను నెరవేర్చనని పక్షం చెబుతాడు "నేను సరుకు ఇవ్వను" అని అమ్మకందారు రాస్తాడు సూచిత నిరాకరణ అతని ప్రవర్తనే నెరవేర్పును అసాధ్యం చేస్తుంది వాగ్దానం చేసిన అవే సరుకులను వేరే కొనుగోలుదారుకు అమ్మేస్తాడు చట్టంలోని మాటలు. చట్టం "ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘన" అనే మాటను వాడదు. సెక్షన్ 39 దీన్ని "refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing" అనే మాటలతో కవర్ చేస్తుంది. ఈ సిద్ధాంతానికి రూపం ఇచ్చింది ఇంగ్లీష్ కేసు Hochster v. De La Tour . అమాయక పక్షానికి ముందుగానే చర్య తీసుకోవడానికి చట్టం ఎందుకు అనుమతిస్తుంది? ఆగడం వల్ల ఎవరికీ లాభం లేదు. అతను వెంటనే వేరే సరఫరాదారు కోసం చూసి తన నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించుకోవచ్చు. ఈ దశలు ఏ క్రమంలో వస్తాయో చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. selfTest.q: 1. ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘన అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: నెరవేర్చాల్సిన సమయం రాకముందే నెరవేర్చడానికి నిరాకరించడం, లేదా నెరవేర్పును అసాధ్యం చేసే చర్య (సెక్షన్ 39).

selfTest.q: 2. వాగ్దానగ్రహీతకు ఏ రెండు ఎంపికలు ఉన్నాయి?
selfTest.a: నిరాకరణను అంగీకరించి, కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించి, వెంటనే దావా వేయవచ్చు. లేదా కాంట్రాక్టును కొనసాగించి గడువు తేదీ వరకు ఆగవచ్చు.

hi.inOneMinute: An anticipatory breach happens when a party refuses to perform, or makes himself unable to perform, before the time for performance arrives. The other party need not wait for the due date. He has two choices: He may accept the refusal, end the contract and sue at once. Or he may keep the contract alive and wait. The choice has risks. In exams, the meaning, the two choices and the cases earn the marks. In real life, it decides whether you can act the day a supplier says he will not deliver.
legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Illustrations. (a) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her 100 rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night A wilfully absents herself from the theatre. B is at liberty to put an end to the contract. (b) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two night's in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her at the rate of 100 rupees for each night. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself. With the assent of B, A sings on the seventh night. B has signified his acquiescence in the continuance of the contract, and cannot now put an end to it, but is entitled to compensation for the damage sustained by him through A's failure to sing on the sixth night.
Related provisions

Section 73, Illustration (c). A contracts to buy of B, at a stated price, 50 maunds of rice, no time being fixed for delivery. A afterwards informs B that he will not accept the rice if tendered to him. B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the amount, if any, by which the contract price exceeds that which B can obtain for the rice at the time when A informs B that he will not accept it.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(c). Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— ... (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— ... (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
In simple words

Section 39 covers both a refusal and a disabling act, if it goes to the whole promise. The promisee "may" end the contract. He loses that right if he shows, by words or conduct, that he accepts the contract's continuance. Section 73, Illustration (c) measures the loss at the time the defaulter announces his refusal.
hi.meaning:
Anticipatory breach is a breach committed before the time fixed for performance. It takes two forms: Form What happens Example Express repudiation The party says he will not perform A seller writes, "I will not deliver" Implied repudiation His conduct makes performance impossible He sells to another buyer the very goods he promised The words of the Act. The Act does not use the words "anticipatory breach". Section 39 covers it in the words "refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing". The English case Hochster v. De La Tour gave the doctrine its shape. Why the law lets the innocent party act early. Waiting helps no one. He can look for another supplier at once and so reduce his loss. See Diagram 1 for the moments in order. Diagram 1. Read from top to bottom. After the refusal, follow the branch the promisee chooses. flowchart TD M["Contract made"] R["Before the due date:
refusal or disabling act
covering the whole promise (s.39)"] Q{"What does the
promisee choose?"} A["Accept the repudiation:
contract ends; sue at once
for damages (s.73); mitigate"] A2["Cannot later ask for
specific performance"] W["Affirm and wait:
contract binds both sides;
the other party may withdraw"] W2["At the due date: must be
ready and willing; an event in
between may defeat the claim"] M --> R R --> Q Q -->|"Accept"| A A --> A2 Q -->|"Affirm"| W W --> W2 Text description The contract is made. Before the due date, one party refuses to perform, or disables himself from performing, his whole promise (Section 39). The promisee then chooses. If he accepts the repudiation, the contract ends, he may sue at once for damages under Section 73 and must mitigate his loss, but he cannot later ask for specific performance. If he affirms and waits, the contract stays binding on both sides and the other party may withdraw his refusal; at the due date the promisee must be ready and willing to perform, and an event in between may defeat his claim (Avery v. Bowden).
keyPoints: Anticipatory breach is a refusal or disabling act before the due date (Section 39). The refusal must be clear and cover the whole promise. The promisee may accept it, end the contract and sue at once ( Hochster ). Or he may affirm the contract and wait, staying ready and willing. If he waits, an intervening event may defeat his claim ( Avery v. Bowden ). After accepting the repudiation he can claim damages but not specific performance ( Jawahar Lal Wadhwa ). Section 39 covers refusal and also disabling oneself from performing. Specific performance needs proof of readiness and willingness (Specific Relief Act, Section 16(c)).

caseLaws.name: Hochster v
caseLaws.facts: De La Tour (1853) Facts. In April 1852 De La Tour engaged Hochster as a courier for a three-month tour from 1 June 1852. On 11 May 1852 he wrote that he had changed his mind and declined Hochster's services. Hochster sued on 22 May. Principle. The injured party has "an option ... either to sue immediately, or to wait till the time when the act was to be done, still holding it as prospectively binding". Judgment for the plaintiff. (1853) 2 E & B 678 : 118 ER 922 (Queen's Bench, 25 June 1853). Why it matters. It is the origin of the doctrine. Frost v. Knight (1872) Facts. Knight promised to marry Miss Frost on his father's death. While the father was still alive, he told her he would not marry her. LR 7 Ex 111. Principle. She could sue once he made clear he would not perform, without waiting for the father's death. Why it matters. It confirms Hochster for a promise with an uncertain date. Avery v. Bowden (1855) Facts. A charterer's agent told the ship's master at Odessa that no cargo would be supplied. The master stayed on. War made performance illegal before the time for loading ended. (1855) 5 E & B 714. Principle. A promisee who does not accept the repudiation keeps the contract alive and takes the risk. The shipowner lost. Why it matters. It shows the risk of waiting. Jawahar Lal Wadhwa v. Haripada Chakroberty (1988) Facts. Under an agreement of 6 September 1973, an advance of Rs 5,000 was paid and monthly payments of Rs 105 followed. On 16 January 1976 notice was given repudiating the agreement. The dispute went to arbitration, and an award of 18 March 1988 granted Rs 58,498.60. Principle. A party who accepts an anticipatory breach and treats the contract as ended may claim damages, not specific performance. A party who keeps the contract alive must show that he was ready and willing to perform. AIR 1989 SC 606 : (1989) 1 SCC 76 (Supreme Court, 14 October 1988). Why it matters. It states the two courses in Indian law.

selfTest.q: 1. What is anticipatory breach?
selfTest.a: A refusal to perform, or an act disabling performance, made before the time for performance arrives (Section 39).

selfTest.q: 2. What two choices does the promisee have?
selfTest.a: He may accept the repudiation, end the contract and sue at once, or keep the contract alive and wait for the due date.

selfTest.q: 3. Why is waiting risky?
selfTest.a: An event before the due date may discharge the contract, as war did in Avery v. Bowden , and then the promisee loses his claim.

selfTest.q: 4. A builder says he may be a week late because labour is short. Is this an anticipatory breach?
selfTest.a: No. It is not a clear refusal of the whole promise.

selfTest.q: 5. After accepting the repudiation, can the promisee sue for specific performance?
selfTest.a: No. He may claim damages only ( Jawahar Lal Wadhwa ).

law-of-contract-i-u3-t4.subtitle: Sections 42 to 45 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: When two or more persons make a promise together, they are joint promisors . Sections 42 to 45 answer four questions: who must perform, whom the promisee may sue, how the promisors share the burden among themselves, and what happens if one of them is released or dies. The core rule is Section 43. The promisee may compel any one or more of the joint promisors to perform the whole promise. The one who pays may then make the others contribute equally . If one cannot contribute, the rest bear that loss equally . In exams, the illustrations to Section 43 earn the marks, because they test the arithmetic of contribution. In real life, these rules govern joint loans, partnership debts and co-signed notes.
legalProvision: Section 42. Devolution of joint liabilities. When two or more persons have made a joint promise, then, unless a contrary intention appears by the contract, all such persons, during their joint lives, and, after the death of any of them, his representative jointly with the survivor or survivors, and, after the death of the last survivor, the representatives of all jointly, must fulfil the promise.

Section 43. Any one of joint promisors may be compelled to perform. When two or more persons make a joint promise, the promisee may, in the absence of express agreement to the contrary, compel any [one or more] of such joint promisors to perform the whole of the promise. Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares. Explanation. —Nothing in this section shall prevent a surety from recovering from his principal, payments made by the surety on behalf of the principal, or entitle the principal to recover anything from the surety on account of payments made by the principal. Illustrations. (a) A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. D may compel either A or B or C to pay him 3,000 rupees. (b) A, B and C jointly promise to pay D the sum of 3,000 rupees. C is compelled to pay the whole. A is insolvent, but his assets are sufficient to pay one-half of his debts. C is entitled to receive 500 rupees from A's estate, and 1,250 rupees from B. (c) A, B and C are under a joint promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. C is unable to pay anything, and A is compelled to pay the whole. A is entitled to receive 1,500 rupees from B. (d) A, B and C are under a joint promise to pay D 3,000 rupees, A and B being only sureties for C. C fails to pay. A and B are compelled to pay the whole sum. They are entitled to recover it from C.

Section 44. Effect of release of one joint promisor. Where two or more persons have made a joint promise, a release of one of such joint promisors by the promisee does not discharge the other joint promisor or joint promisors; neither does it free the joint promisors so released from responsibility to the other joint promisor or joint promisors.

Section 45. Devolution of joint rights. When a person has made a promise to two or more persons jointly, then, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract, the right to claim performance rests, as between him and them, with them during their joint lives, and, after the death of any of them, with the representative of such deceased person jointly with the survivor or survivors, and, after the death of the last survivor, with the representatives of all jointly. Illustration. A, in consideration of 5,000 rupees, lent to him by B and C, promises B and C jointly to repay them that sum with interest on a day specified. B dies. The right to claim performance rests with B's representative jointly with C during C's life, and after the death of C with the representatives of B and C jointly.
Related provisions
Section 38 (last paragraph). An offer to one of several joint promisees has the same legal consequences as an offer to all of them.

Section 132. Where two persons contract with a third person to undertake a certain liability, and also contract with each other that one of them shall be liable only on the default of the other, the third person not being a party to such contract, the liability of each of such two persons to the third person under the first contract is not affected by the existence of the second contract, although such third person may have been aware of its existence.

Section 138. Release of one co-surety does not discharge others. Where there are co-sureties, a release by the creditor of one of them does not discharge the others; neither does it free the surety so released from his responsibility to the other sureties.

Limitation Act, 1963, Section 20(2). Nothing in the said sections renders one of several joint contractors, partners, executors or mortgagees chargeable by reason only of a written acknowledgment signed by, or of a payment made by, or by the agent of, any other or others of them.
In simple words

All joint promisors must perform; on a death, the dead one's representative steps in beside the survivors (Section 42). The promisee may pick any one of them and ask him for the whole (Section 43). Between themselves, they share equally; a defaulter 's share is split equally among the rest (Section 43). Releasing one does not free the others, and the released one still owes his share to the others (Section 44). A promise made to several persons jointly is enforced by them jointly (Section 45).
en.meaning:
A joint promise is one promise made by two or more persons together, so that each is answerable for the whole. "A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees" is the Act's example. Two relationships run side by side: Relationship Rule Section Promisors and promisee The promisee may compel any one or more to perform the whole 43, first paragraph Promisors among themselves Each must contribute equally; a defaulter's loss is shared equally 43, second and third paragraphs Why the law has these rules. The promisee contracted with the whole group, so he should not lose because one member is poor, absent or dead. The promisors chose to bind themselves together, so it is fair that they settle the burden equally among themselves. The Indian rule differs from the old English common law rule. Under the English rule, joint debtors had to be sued together, and a release of one released all. Sections 43 and 44 reject both points. See Diagram 1 for how the burden passes from the promisee to the promisors and between them. Diagram 1. First the promisee collects the whole from any one promisor. Then the promisors settle equally among themselves. flowchart TD J["A, B and C jointly promise
to pay D 3,000 rupees"] S1["Step 1: D may compel any one or more
to pay the whole 3,000 rupees
(s.43, para 1)"] S2["Step 2: the one who paid may compel
the others to contribute equally
(1,000 rupees each) (s.43, para 2)"] S3["Step 3: if one defaults in contribution,
the rest bear that loss equally
(s.43, para 3)"] R["If D releases one promisor:
the others are not discharged;
the released one still owes
contribution to the others (s.44)"] J --> S1 S1 --> S2 S2 --> S3 J -. "Release" .-> R Text description A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. Step 1: D may compel any one or more of them to pay the whole 3,000 rupees (Section 43, first paragraph). Step 2: the one who paid may compel each of the others to contribute equally, 1,000 rupees each (Section 43, second paragraph). Step 3: if one of them defaults in contribution, the remaining promisors bear that loss in equal shares (Section 43, third paragraph). Side note: if D releases one promisor, the others are not discharged, and the released one is still responsible to the others (Section 44).
keyPoints: All joint promisors must perform; on death, the representative joins the survivors (Section 42). The promisee may compel any one or more to perform the whole, unless expressly agreed otherwise (Section 43). Contribution among promisors is equal, unless the contract shows otherwise (Section 43). A defaulter's share is borne equally by the others (Section 43; Illustration (b)). The duty to contribute is separate from the duty to the creditor ( S.P. Abraham Servai ). A release of one does not discharge the others or free the released one from contribution (Section 44). Joint rights rest with the joint promisees jointly (Section 45); an offer to one is an offer to all (Section 38). An acknowledgment by one joint contractor does not bind the others (Limitation Act, Section 20(2)).

caseLaws.name: S
caseLaws.facts: P. Abraham Servai v. Raphial Muthirian (1914) Facts. The plaintiff and the defendant were jointly liable on a promissory note of 25 June 1903. The creditor's decree of 5 August 1911 was against the plaintiff alone for the whole balance, because the claim on the note was barred against the defendant. The plaintiff paid the decree on 9 March 1912 and sued the defendant for contribution. Principle. "The duty to contribute is clearly distinct from the duty to pay to the promisee." The bar of limitation that protected the defendant against the creditor did not protect him against his co-promisor, and the plaintiff succeeded. (1914) 27 MLJ 746 : ILR 39 Mad 288 (Madras High Court, 13 November 1914). Why it matters. Contribution under Section 43 survives even when the creditor could no longer sue the co-promisor. Mannava Annapurnamma v. Uppala Akkayya (1913) Facts. A promissory note was made in favour of three payees. The question referred to a Full Bench was "whether one of three payees of a negotiable instrument can give a valid discharge of the entire debt without the concurrence of the other two payees". Principle. Later Madras judgments ( Appavu Chettiar , 1913; Peri Ramasami v. Chandra Kottaya , 1924) state the Full Bench rule as: an actual payment to one of the joint promisees discharges the debt as against the others, but a mere promise to pay at a future date is not a discharge. ILR 36 Mad 544 : (1913) 24 MLJ 333 (Full Bench, Madras High Court). Why it matters. It applies the joint-promisee rule (Sections 38 and 45) to payment of a joint debt.

selfTest.q: 1. A, B and C jointly owe D 3,000 rupees. Must D sue all three?
selfTest.a: No. He may compel any one or more of them to pay the whole (Section 43).

selfTest.q: 2. In Illustration (c), why does B pay A 1,500 rupees?
selfTest.a: B's own share is 1,000 rupees, and C's unpaid share of 1,000 rupees is shared equally by A and B, adding 500 rupees.

selfTest.q: 3. D releases B. Is A still liable?
selfTest.a: Yes. A release of one joint promisor does not discharge the others (Section 44).

selfTest.q: 4. After the release, can A claim contribution from B?
selfTest.a: Yes. The release does not free B from responsibility to the other promisors (Section 44).

selfTest.q: 5. B and C jointly lend money to A, and B dies. Who may claim repayment?
selfTest.a: B's representative jointly with C (Section 45, Illustration).

Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares. Explanation. —Nothing in this section shall prevent a surety from recovering from his principal, payments made by the surety on behalf of the principal, or entitle the principal to recover anything from the surety on account of payments made by the principal. Illustrations. (a) A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. D may compel either A or B or C to pay him 3,000 rupees. (b) A, B and C jointly promise to pay D the sum of 3,000 rupees. C is compelled to pay the whole. A is insolvent, but his assets are sufficient to pay one-half of his debts. C is entitled to receive 500 rupees from A's estate, and 1,250 rupees from B. (c) A, B and C are under a joint promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. C is unable to pay anything, and A is compelled to pay the whole. A is entitled to receive 1,500 rupees from B. (d) A, B and C are under a joint promise to pay D 3,000 rupees, A and B being only sureties for C. C fails to pay. A and B are compelled to pay the whole sum. They are entitled to recover it from C.

Section 44. Effect of release of one joint promisor. Where two or more persons have made a joint promise, a release of one of such joint promisors by the promisee does not discharge the other joint promisor or joint promisors; neither does it free the joint promisors so released from responsibility to the other joint promisor or joint promisors.

Section 45. Devolution of joint rights. When a person has made a promise to two or more persons jointly, then, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract, the right to claim performance rests, as between him and them, with them during their joint lives, and, after the death of any of them, with the representative of such deceased person jointly with the survivor or survivors, and, after the death of the last survivor, with the representatives of all jointly. Illustration. A, in consideration of 5,000 rupees, lent to him by B and C, promises B and C jointly to repay them that sum with interest on a day specified. B dies. The right to claim performance rests with B's representative jointly with C during C's life, and after the death of C with the representatives of B and C jointly.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు
Section 38 (last paragraph). An offer to one of several joint promisees has the same legal consequences as an offer to all of them.

Section 132. Where two persons contract with a third person to undertake a certain liability, and also contract with each other that one of them shall be liable only on the default of the other, the third person not being a party to such contract, the liability of each of such two persons to the third person under the first contract is not affected by the existence of the second contract, although such third person may have been aware of its existence.

Section 138. Release of one co-surety does not discharge others. Where there are co-sureties, a release by the creditor of one of them does not discharge the others; neither does it free the surety so released from his responsibility to the other sureties.

Limitation Act, 1963, Section 20(2). Nothing in the said sections renders one of several joint contractors, partners, executors or mortgagees chargeable by reason only of a written acknowledgment signed by, or of a payment made by, or by the agent of, any other or others of them.

ఉమ్మడి వాగ్దానకర్తలందరూ నెరవేర్చాలి; ఒకరు చనిపోతే, అతని ప్రతినిధి బతికి ఉన్నవారితో కలిసి బాధ్యత వహిస్తాడు (సెక్షన్ 42). వాగ్దానగ్రహీత వారిలో ఎవరినైనా ఎంచుకుని మొత్తం అడగవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 43). తమలో తాము వారు సమానంగా పంచుకుంటారు; ఎగవేసినవాడి వాటాను మిగతావారు సమానంగా పంచుకుంటారు (సెక్షన్ 43). ఒకరిని విడుదల చేసినా మిగతావారు విముక్తులు కారు; విడుదలైనవాడు మిగతావారికి తన వాటా ఇంకా ఇవ్వాలి (సెక్షన్ 44). చాలా మందికి ఉమ్మడిగా చేసిన వాగ్దానాన్ని వారే ఉమ్మడిగా అమలు చేయించాలి (సెక్షన్ 45).

ఉమ్మడి వాగ్దానం అంటే ఇద్దరు లేదా అంతకంటే ఎక్కువ మంది కలిసి చేసిన ఒకే వాగ్దానం; ప్రతి ఒక్కరూ మొత్తానికి జవాబుదారు. "A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees" అనేది చట్టం ఇచ్చిన ఉదాహరణ. రెండు సంబంధాలు పక్కపక్కనే నడుస్తాయి: సంబంధం నియమం సెక్షన్ వాగ్దానకర్తలు, వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఎవరో ఒకరిని లేదా కొందరిని మొత్తం నెరవేర్చమని వాగ్దానగ్రహీత బలవంతం చేయవచ్చు 43, మొదటి పేరా వాగ్దానకర్తలు తమలో తాము ప్రతి ఒక్కరూ సమానంగా వాటా ఇవ్వాలి; ఎగవేసినవాడి నష్టం సమానంగా పంచుకోవాలి 43, రెండో, మూడో పేరాలు చట్టం ఈ నియమాలు ఎందుకు పెట్టింది? వాగ్దానగ్రహీత మొత్తం బృందంతో కాంట్రాక్టు చేశాడు; బృందంలో ఒకరు పేదవాడైనా, కనిపించకపోయినా, చనిపోయినా అతను నష్టపోకూడదు. వాగ్దానకర్తలు కలిసి కట్టుబడాలని తామే ఎంచుకున్నారు; కాబట్టి భారాన్ని తమలో తాము సమానంగా తీర్చుకోవడం న్యాయం. భారత నియమం పాత ఇంగ్లిష్ కామన్ లా నియమానికి భిన్నం. ఇంగ్లిష్ నియమం ప్రకారం ఉమ్మడి రుణగ్రహీతలపై అందరిపై కలిపే దావా వేయాలి, ఒకరిని విడుదల చేస్తే అందరూ విడుదలవుతారు. సెక్షన్లు 43, 44 ఈ రెండు అంశాలనూ తిరస్కరిస్తాయి. భారం వాగ్దానగ్రహీత నుంచి వాగ్దానకర్తలకు, తర్వాత వారి మధ్య ఎలా వెళ్తుందో చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. ముందు వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఏ ఒక్క వాగ్దానకర్త నుంచైనా మొత్తం వసూలు చేస్తాడు. తర్వాత వాగ్దానకర్తలు తమలో తాము సమానంగా తీర్చుకుంటారు. flowchart TD J["A, B, C కలిసి D కి 3,000 రూపాయలు

"విడుదల" .-> R వచన వివరణ A, B, C కలిసి D కి 3,000 రూపాయలు చెల్లిస్తామని ఉమ్మడిగా వాగ్దానం చేస్తారు. దశ 1: D వారిలో ఎవరో ఒకరిని లేదా కొందరిని మొత్తం 3,000 రూపాయలు చెల్లించమని బలవంతం చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 43, మొదటి పేరా). దశ 2: చెల్లించినవాడు మిగతా ప్రతి ఒక్కరినీ సమానంగా, చెరి 1,000 రూపాయలు వాటా ఇవ్వమని బలవంతం చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 43, రెండో పేరా). దశ 3: ఒకరు వాటా ఇవ్వడంలో ఎగవేస్తే, ఆ నష్టాన్ని మిగతావారు సమాన వాటాల్లో భరిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 43, మూడో పేరా). పక్క గమనిక: D ఒక వాగ్దానకర్తను విడుదల చేస్తే మిగతావారు విముక్తులు కారు, విడుదలైనవాడు మిగతావారికి ఇంకా బాధ్యుడు (సెక్షన్ 44).

selfTest.q: 1. A, B, C కలిసి D కి 3,000 రూపాయలు ఉమ్మడిగా బాకీ. D ముగ్గురిపైనా దావా వేయాలా?
selfTest.a: అక్కర్లేదు. వారిలో ఎవరో ఒకరిని లేదా కొందరిని మొత్తం చెల్లించమని బలవంతం చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 43).

selfTest.q: 2. Illustration (c) లో B, A కి 1,500 రూపాయలు ఎందుకు ఇవ్వాలి?
selfTest.a: B సొంత వాటా 1,000 రూపాయలు; C చెల్లించని 1,000 రూపాయల వాటాను A, B సమానంగా పంచుకుంటారు, దానితో 500 రూపాయలు కలుస్తాయి.

selfTest.q: 3. D, B ని విడుదల చేస్తాడు. A ఇంకా బాధ్యుడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ఒక ఉమ్మడి వాగ్దానకర్త విడుదల మిగతావారిని విముక్తులను చేయదు (సెక్షన్ 44).

selfTest.q: 4. విడుదల తర్వాత A, B నుంచి వాటా కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. విడుదల B ని మిగతా వాగ్దానకర్తలకు ఉన్న బాధ్యత నుంచి విముక్తుడిని చేయదు (సెక్షన్ 44).

selfTest.q: 5. B, C కలిసి A కి ఉమ్మడిగా అప్పు ఇచ్చారు, B చనిపోయాడు. తిరిగి చెల్లించమని ఎవరు కోరవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: B ప్రతినిధి, C తో కలిసి (సెక్షన్ 45, Illustration).

hi.inOneMinute: When two or more persons make a promise together, they are joint promisors . Sections 42 to 45 answer four questions: who must perform, whom the promisee may sue, how the promisors share the burden among themselves, and what happens if one of them is released or dies. The core rule is Section 43. The promisee may compel any one or more of the joint promisors to perform the whole promise. The one who pays may then make the others contribute equally . If one cannot contribute, the rest bear that loss equally . In exams, the illustrations to Section 43 earn the marks, because they test the arithmetic of contribution. In real life, these rules govern joint loans, partnership debts and co-signed notes.
legalProvision: Section 42. Devolution of joint liabilities. When two or more persons have made a joint promise, then, unless a contrary intention appears by the contract, all such persons, during their joint lives, and, after the death of any of them, his representative jointly with the survivor or survivors, and, after the death of the last survivor, the representatives of all jointly, must fulfil the promise.

Section 43. Any one of joint promisors may be compelled to perform. When two or more persons make a joint promise, the promisee may, in the absence of express agreement to the contrary, compel any [one or more] of such joint promisors to perform the whole of the promise. Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares. Explanation. —Nothing in this section shall prevent a surety from recovering from his principal, payments made by the surety on behalf of the principal, or entitle the principal to recover anything from the surety on account of payments made by the principal. Illustrations. (a) A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. D may compel either A or B or C to pay him 3,000 rupees. (b) A, B and C jointly promise to pay D the sum of 3,000 rupees. C is compelled to pay the whole. A is insolvent, but his assets are sufficient to pay one-half of his debts. C is entitled to receive 500 rupees from A's estate, and 1,250 rupees from B. (c) A, B and C are under a joint promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. C is unable to pay anything, and A is compelled to pay the whole. A is entitled to receive 1,500 rupees from B. (d) A, B and C are under a joint promise to pay D 3,000 rupees, A and B being only sureties for C. C fails to pay. A and B are compelled to pay the whole sum. They are entitled to recover it from C.

Section 44. Effect of release of one joint promisor. Where two or more persons have made a joint promise, a release of one of such joint promisors by the promisee does not discharge the other joint promisor or joint promisors; neither does it free the joint promisors so released from responsibility to the other joint promisor or joint promisors.

Section 45. Devolution of joint rights. When a person has made a promise to two or more persons jointly, then, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract, the right to claim performance rests, as between him and them, with them during their joint lives, and, after the death of any of them, with the representative of such deceased person jointly with the survivor or survivors, and, after the death of the last survivor, with the representatives of all jointly. Illustration. A, in consideration of 5,000 rupees, lent to him by B and C, promises B and C jointly to repay them that sum with interest on a day specified. B dies. The right to claim performance rests with B's representative jointly with C during C's life, and after the death of C with the representatives of B and C jointly.
Related provisions
Section 38 (last paragraph). An offer to one of several joint promisees has the same legal consequences as an offer to all of them.

Section 132. Where two persons contract with a third person to undertake a certain liability, and also contract with each other that one of them shall be liable only on the default of the other, the third person not being a party to such contract, the liability of each of such two persons to the third person under the first contract is not affected by the existence of the second contract, although such third person may have been aware of its existence.

Section 138. Release of one co-surety does not discharge others. Where there are co-sureties, a release by the creditor of one of them does not discharge the others; neither does it free the surety so released from his responsibility to the other sureties.

Limitation Act, 1963, Section 20(2). Nothing in the said sections renders one of several joint contractors, partners, executors or mortgagees chargeable by reason only of a written acknowledgment signed by, or of a payment made by, or by the agent of, any other or others of them.
In simple words

All joint promisors must perform; on a death, the dead one's representative steps in beside the survivors (Section 42). The promisee may pick any one of them and ask him for the whole (Section 43). Between themselves, they share equally; a defaulter 's share is split equally among the rest (Section 43). Releasing one does not free the others, and the released one still owes his share to the others (Section 44). A promise made to several persons jointly is enforced by them jointly (Section 45).
hi.meaning:
A joint promise is one promise made by two or more persons together, so that each is answerable for the whole. "A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees" is the Act's example. Two relationships run side by side: Relationship Rule Section Promisors and promisee The promisee may compel any one or more to perform the whole 43, first paragraph Promisors among themselves Each must contribute equally; a defaulter's loss is shared equally 43, second and third paragraphs Why the law has these rules. The promisee contracted with the whole group, so he should not lose because one member is poor, absent or dead. The promisors chose to bind themselves together, so it is fair that they settle the burden equally among themselves. The Indian rule differs from the old English common law rule. Under the English rule, joint debtors had to be sued together, and a release of one released all. Sections 43 and 44 reject both points. See Diagram 1 for how the burden passes from the promisee to the promisors and between them. Diagram 1. First the promisee collects the whole from any one promisor. Then the promisors settle equally among themselves. flowchart TD J["A, B and C jointly promise
to pay D 3,000 rupees"] S1["Step 1: D may compel any one or more
to pay the whole 3,000 rupees
(s.43, para 1)"] S2["Step 2: the one who paid may compel
the others to contribute equally
(1,000 rupees each) (s.43, para 2)"] S3["Step 3: if one defaults in contribution,
the rest bear that loss equally
(s.43, para 3)"] R["If D releases one promisor:
