contribution to the others (s.44)"] J --> S1 S1 --> S2 S2 --> S3 J -. "Release" .-> R Text description A, B and C jointly promise to pay D 3,000 rupees. Step 1: D may compel any one or more of them to pay the whole 3,000 rupees (Section 43, first paragraph). Step 2: the one who paid may compel each of the others to contribute equally, 1,000 rupees each (Section 43, second paragraph). Step 3: if one of them defaults in contribution, the remaining promisors bear that loss in equal shares (Section 43, third paragraph). Side note: if D releases one promisor, the others are not discharged, and the released one is still responsible to the others (Section 44).
keyPoints: All joint promisors must perform; on death, the representative joins the survivors (Section 42). The promisee may compel any one or more to perform the whole, unless expressly agreed otherwise (Section 43). Contribution among promisors is equal, unless the contract shows otherwise (Section 43). A defaulter's share is borne equally by the others (Section 43; Illustration (b)). The duty to contribute is separate from the duty to the creditor ( S.P. Abraham Servai ). A release of one does not discharge the others or free the released one from contribution (Section 44). Joint rights rest with the joint promisees jointly (Section 45); an offer to one is an offer to all (Section 38). An acknowledgment by one joint contractor does not bind the others (Limitation Act, Section 20(2)).

caseLaws.name: S
caseLaws.facts: P. Abraham Servai v. Raphial Muthirian (1914) Facts. The plaintiff and the defendant were jointly liable on a promissory note of 25 June 1903. The creditor's decree of 5 August 1911 was against the plaintiff alone for the whole balance, because the claim on the note was barred against the defendant. The plaintiff paid the decree on 9 March 1912 and sued the defendant for contribution. Principle. "The duty to contribute is clearly distinct from the duty to pay to the promisee." The bar of limitation that protected the defendant against the creditor did not protect him against his co-promisor, and the plaintiff succeeded. (1914) 27 MLJ 746 : ILR 39 Mad 288 (Madras High Court, 13 November 1914). Why it matters. Contribution under Section 43 survives even when the creditor could no longer sue the co-promisor. Mannava Annapurnamma v. Uppala Akkayya (1913) Facts. A promissory note was made in favour of three payees. The question referred to a Full Bench was "whether one of three payees of a negotiable instrument can give a valid discharge of the entire debt without the concurrence of the other two payees". Principle. Later Madras judgments ( Appavu Chettiar , 1913; Peri Ramasami v. Chandra Kottaya , 1924) state the Full Bench rule as: an actual payment to one of the joint promisees discharges the debt as against the others, but a mere promise to pay at a future date is not a discharge. ILR 36 Mad 544 : (1913) 24 MLJ 333 (Full Bench, Madras High Court). Why it matters. It applies the joint-promisee rule (Sections 38 and 45) to payment of a joint debt.

selfTest.q: 1. A, B and C jointly owe D 3,000 rupees. Must D sue all three?
selfTest.a: No. He may compel any one or more of them to pay the whole (Section 43).

selfTest.q: 2. In Illustration (c), why does B pay A 1,500 rupees?
selfTest.a: B's own share is 1,000 rupees, and C's unpaid share of 1,000 rupees is shared equally by A and B, adding 500 rupees.

selfTest.q: 3. D releases B. Is A still liable?
selfTest.a: Yes. A release of one joint promisor does not discharge the others (Section 44).

selfTest.q: 4. After the release, can A claim contribution from B?
selfTest.a: Yes. The release does not free B from responsibility to the other promisors (Section 44).

selfTest.q: 5. B and C jointly lend money to A, and B dies. Who may claim repayment?
selfTest.a: B's representative jointly with C (Section 45, Illustration).

en.meaning:
Under Section 38, which of the following is NOT a requirement for a valid tender?

Explanation. A tender is valid even if refused — Section 38 discharges the promisor from liability once a valid tender is proved, regardless of whether the promisee accepts it.

What is the legal effect of a valid tender that the promisee wrongfully refuses to accept?

Explanation. Section 38 provides that a promisor who has made a valid tender is not responsible for non-performance and does not lose any rights under the contract.

Under Section 40, who must perform a contract requiring personal skill, such as painting a portrait?

Explanation. Section 40 requires personal performance where the contract shows the parties intended it, or where the nature of the contract requires personal skill or credit.

Under Section 41, what happens if a promisee accepts performance from a third person?

law-of-contract-i-u3-t8.subtitle: Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: If an act is impossible from the start, the agreement is void . If it becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made, through no fault of the promisor, the contract becomes void at that moment. This is the doctrine of frustration , found in Section 56. The doctrine is narrow. A rise in cost, a delay or a bad bargain is not enough. In exams, the grounds, the limits and the cases decide the marks. In real life, it decides who bears the loss when a fire, a war, a new law or a pandemic upsets a contract.
legalProvision: Section 56. Agreement to do impossible act. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. Contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful. —A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Compensation for loss through non-performance of act known to be impossible or unlawful. —Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or, with reasonable diligence, might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must make compensation to such promisee for any loss which such promisee sustains through the non-performance of the promise. Illustrations. (a) A agrees with B to discover treasure by magic. The agreement is void. (b) A and B contract to marry each other. Before the time fixed for the marriage, A goes mad. The contract becomes void. (c) A contracts to marry B, being already married to C, and being forbidden by the law to which he is subject to practise polygamy, A must make compensation to B for the loss caused to her by the non-performance of his promise. (d) A contracts to take in cargo for B at a foreign port. A's Government afterwards declares war against the country in which the port is situated. The contract becomes void when war is declared. (e) A contracts to act at a theatre for six months in consideration of a sum paid in advance by B. On several occasions A is too ill to act. The contract to act on those occasions becomes void.
Related provisions

Section 32. Enforcement of contracts contingent on an event happening. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced by law unless and until that event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.

Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it. Illustration (d). A contracts to sing for B at a concert for 1,000 rupees, which are paid in advance. A is too ill to sing. A is not bound to make compensation to B for the loss of the profits which B would have made if A had been able to sing, but must refund to B the 1,000 rupees paid in advance.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 7. Goods perishing before making of contract. Where there is a contract for the sale of specific goods, the contract is void if the goods without the knowledge of the seller have, at the time when the contract was made, perished or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the contract.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 8. Goods perishing before sale but after agreement to sell. Where there is an agreement to sell specific goods, and subsequently the goods without any fault on the part of the seller or buyer perish or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the agreement before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is thereby avoided.
In simple words

First paragraph. An agreement to do something impossible in itself is void from the start. Second paragraph. If the act later becomes impossible, or unlawful by an event the promisor could not prevent, the contract becomes void at that moment. Third paragraph. A promisor who knew, or should have known, of the impossibility must compensate a promisee who did not know. Section 65. Whoever received an advantage must give it back or pay for it.
en.meaning:
Frustration is the discharge of a contract because a later event makes performance impossible or unlawful, or destroys the purpose the parties had in view. Section 56 does not use the word "frustration". It speaks of impossibility. In India the two words describe the same doctrine. Why the law excuses the parties. The law does not compel what is impossible. The maxim lex non cogit ad impossibilia says the law does not require the impossible. It would be unjust to make a promisor pay damages for failing to do what no one could do. See Diagram 1 for the tests under the second paragraph. Diagram 1. Go down the questions in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the question. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Did an event after the contract make
performance impossible or unlawful,
or destroy its basis? (s.56, para 2)"} Q2{"2. Could the promisor not prevent it,
and was it not caused by his own
act or default?"} Q3{"3. Is performance impossible or radically
different, not merely costlier, slower
or harder? (Satyabrata Ghose; Energy Watchdog)"} Q4{"4. Is the event outside any contract clause
dealing with it, and outside any risk
a party took on?"} N1["No frustration"] N2["Self-induced impossibility:
not frustration"] N3["Hardship: not frustration"] N4["The clause governs (e.g. force majeure, s.32),
or the party bears the risk he took on
(Naihati Jute Mills)"] R["FRUSTRATED: the contract becomes void
when performance becomes impossible
or unlawful; advantages restored (s.65)"] Q1 -- "No" --> N1 Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2 Q2 -- "No" --> N2 Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3 Q3 -- "No" --> N3 Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4 Q4 -- "No" --> N4 Q4 -- "Yes" --> R Text description Question 1: did an event after the contract was made make performance impossible or unlawful, or destroy its basis (Section 56, second paragraph)? No: there is no frustration. Question 2: was the event one the promisor could not prevent, and not caused by his own act or default? No: self-induced impossibility is not frustration. Question 3: is performance impossible or radically different, and not merely costlier, slower or harder (Satyabrata Ghose; Energy Watchdog)? No: hardship is not frustration. Question 4: is the event outside any clause in the contract that deals with it, and outside any risk a party took on? No: the clause governs, for example a force majeure clause (Section 32), or the party bears the risk he took on (Naihati Jute Mills). Yes to all: the contract becomes void when performance becomes impossible or unlawful, and each party must restore any advantage received (Section 65).
keyPoints: Section 56: an act impossible in itself makes the agreement void. A later impossibility or illegality makes the contract void when it happens. Frustration is automatic. No one chooses. Satyabrata Ghose : Section 56 is exhaustive in India, and "impossible" includes impracticable and useless performance. Grounds: destruction of the subject matter, failure of the foundation event, death or incapacity, change of law, war. Not frustration: higher cost, delay, a temporary hindrance, self-induced impossibility, a risk taken on by a party, risk allocated by the contract. Effect: both parties are discharged and advantages are restored (Section 65). The third paragraph gives compensation to a promisee who did not know of the impossibility. Sale of Goods Act: Section 7 (goods perished before the contract) and Section 8 (goods perish after the agreement, before risk passes). A term of the contract that discharges performance falls under Section 32, not Section 56 ( Satyabrata Ghose ). Covid-19 is not an automatic ground. Courts look at the contract and the real cause.

caseLaws.name: Taylor v
caseLaws.facts: Caldwell (1863) Facts. By an agreement of 27 May 1861, Caldwell agreed to let the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall to Taylor for concerts on four days in June to August 1861, at £100 a day. The hall was destroyed by fire before the first day. Principle. A contract that depends on the continued existence of a thing carries an implied condition that the parties are excused if it is destroyed without their fault. (1863) 3 B & S 826 : 122 ER 309 (Queen's Bench, Blackburn J., 6 May 1863). Why it matters. It is the origin of the doctrine in English law. Krell v. Henry (1903) Facts. Henry hired a flat in Pall Mall for 26 and 27 June 1902, the days of the planned coronation processions. The contract did not mention the coronation. The processions were cancelled. Principle. The Court of Appeal held the contract frustrated, because the processions were its foundation. [1903] 2 KB 740. Why it matters. It applies frustration where the purpose fails but the thing still exists. Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. (1953) Facts. A land company sold building plots and undertook to build roads and drains. During the Second World War part of the land was requisitioned for military purposes. The company said the contract was frustrated. Principle. Section 56 is exhaustive of the law in India. "Impossible" is wider than physical impossibility. The requisition was temporary in nature and no time was fixed for performance, so the contract was not frustrated. [1954] SCR 310 : AIR 1954 SC 44 (Supreme Court, 16 November 1953). Why it matters. It is the leading Indian authority on Section 56. Alopi Parshad & Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) Facts. The appellants were agents for buying and supplying ghee for the Army under a 1937 agreement, revised in 1942 at lower rates. When wartime conditions became abnormal, they claimed payment at higher rates than those agreed. Principle. "A contract is not frustrated merely because the circumstances in which it was made are altered." The Act does not let a party claim rates different from the stipulated rates "on some vague plea of equity". The appeal was dismissed. [1960] 2 SCR 793 : AIR 1960 SC 588 (Supreme Court, 20 January 1960). Why it matters. It is the standard case that hardship is not impossibility. Naihati Jute Mills Ltd. v. Khyaliram Jagannath (1967) Facts. On 7 July 1958 the mills agreed to buy 2,000 bales of jute to be imported from Pakistan, and undertook to obtain the import licence. The Jute Commissioner refused the licence. The mills pleaded frustration. Principle. The mills had taken upon themselves "the absolute burden of furnishing the licence", so impossibility was no defence. "A contract is not frustrated merely because the circumstances in which it was made are altered", and courts cannot absolve a party "merely because its performance has become onerous". Even after frustration, the contract survives for deciding disputes under its arbitration clause. The appeal was dismissed. [1968] 1 SCR 821 (Supreme Court, 19 October 1967). Why it matters. Courts cannot excuse a party from an onerous bargain or from a risk he took on. Davis Contractors Ltd. v. Fareham Urban District Council (1956) Facts. Builders agreed to build 78 houses in eight months for £92,425. Shortages of labour and materials made the job take 22 months and cost £115,223. They argued frustration and claimed a reasonable sum. Principle. The House of Lords held that the contract was not frustrated. An unexpected turn of events that makes a contract more onerous is not a ground to relieve the contractor. [1956] AC 696. Why it matters. It supplies the "radically different" test. Energy Watchdog v. CERC (2017) Facts. Power generators won bids to supply electricity at fixed tariffs, using coal imported from Indonesia. A change in Indonesian law raised the price of that coal, and they sought relief for force majeure and change in law . Principle. "An unexpected rise in the price of coal will not absolve the generating companies from performing their part of the contract", because "this was a risk they knowingly took" (para 40). Frustration applies "within narrow limits" (para 37). A change in Indian law, though not in Indonesian law, could be a change in law under the contract. [2017] 3 SCR 153 : (2017) 14 SCC 80 (Supreme Court, 11 April 2017). Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court statement of the limits of Section 56. Halliburton Offshore Services Inc. v. Vedanta Ltd. (2020) Facts. A contractor relied on the Covid-19 lockdown as force majeure to stop encashment of bank guarantees under a contract of 25 April 2018 whose completion dates fell in 2019. The Delhi High Court made an ad interim order on 20 April 2020 and vacated it on 29 May 2020. Principle. "The past non-performance of the Contractor cannot be condoned due to the COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020 in India." The decision was at the interim stage; the force majeure question was left for the arbitration. O.M.P. (I) (COMM.) 88/2020 (Delhi High Court, Prathiba M. Singh J., 29 May 2020). Why it matters. Covid-19 is not an automatic ground of frustration or force majeure.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three paragraphs of Section 56?
selfTest.a: An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. A contract to do an act that later becomes impossible or unlawful becomes void when it happens. A promisor who knew of the impossibility must compensate a promisee who did not.

selfTest.q: 2. Does a sharp rise in cost frustrate a contract?
selfTest.a: No. Hardship or a bad bargain is not impossibility ( Alopi Parshad ; Energy Watchdog ).

selfTest.q: 3. What follows when a contract is frustrated?
selfTest.a: It becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Each party must restore any advantage received under Section 65.

selfTest.q: 4. A buyer promises to obtain an import licence, and the licence is refused. Is the contract frustrated?
selfTest.a: No, if the buyer took on an absolute obligation to obtain it ( Naihati Jute Mills ).

selfTest.q: 5. Under which section does a force majeure clause in the contract operate?
selfTest.a: Section 32, not Section 56 ( Satyabrata Ghose ; Energy Watchdog ).

legalProvision: Section 56. Agreement to do impossible act. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. Contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful. —A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Compensation for loss through non-performance of act known to be impossible or unlawful. —Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or, with reasonable diligence, might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must make compensation to such promisee for any loss which such promisee sustains through the non-performance of the promise. Illustrations. (a) A agrees with B to discover treasure by magic. The agreement is void. (b) A and B contract to marry each other. Before the time fixed for the marriage, A goes mad. The contract becomes void. (c) A contracts to marry B, being already married to C, and being forbidden by the law to which he is subject to practise polygamy, A must make compensation to B for the loss caused to her by the non-performance of his promise. (d) A contracts to take in cargo for B at a foreign port. A's Government afterwards declares war against the country in which the port is situated. The contract becomes void when war is declared. (e) A contracts to act at a theatre for six months in consideration of a sum paid in advance by B. On several occasions A is too ill to act. The contract to act on those occasions becomes void.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు

Section 32. Enforcement of contracts contingent on an event happening. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced by law unless and until that event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.

Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it. Illustration (d). A contracts to sing for B at a concert for 1,000 rupees, which are paid in advance. A is too ill to sing. A is not bound to make compensation to B for the loss of the profits which B would have made if A had been able to sing, but must refund to B the 1,000 rupees paid in advance.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 7. Goods perishing before making of contract. Where there is a contract for the sale of specific goods, the contract is void if the goods without the knowledge of the seller have, at the time when the contract was made, perished or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the contract.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 8. Goods perishing before sale but after agreement to sell. Where there is an agreement to sell specific goods, and subsequently the goods without any fault on the part of the seller or buyer perish or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the agreement before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is thereby avoided.
సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే

మొదటి పేరా. దానికదే అసాధ్యమైన పని చేయడానికి చేసుకున్న ఒప్పందం మొదటి నుంచే శూన్యం. రెండో పేరా. పని తర్వాత అసాధ్యమైతే, లేదా వాగ్దానకర్త ఆపలేని సంఘటన వల్ల చట్టవిరుద్ధమైతే, ఆ క్షణంలోనే కాంట్రాక్టు శూన్యమవుతుంది. మూడో పేరా. అసాధ్యమని తెలిసిన లేదా తెలుసుకోవాల్సిన వాగ్దానకర్త, తెలియని వాగ్దానగ్రహీతకు పరిహారం ఇవ్వాలి. సెక్షన్ 65. ఎవరు లాభం పొందారో వారు దాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి, లేదా దానికి పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 56 లోని మూడు పేరాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: దానికదే అసాధ్యమైన పని చేయడానికి చేసుకున్న ఒప్పందం శూన్యం. తర్వాత అసాధ్యం లేదా చట్టవిరుద్ధం అయిన పని చేయడానికి చేసుకున్న కాంట్రాక్టు, అది జరిగినప్పుడు శూన్యమవుతుంది. అసాధ్యత తెలిసిన వాగ్దానకర్త, తెలియని వాగ్దానగ్రహీతకు పరిహారం ఇవ్వాలి.

selfTest.q: 2. ఖర్చు బాగా పెరిగితే కాంట్రాక్టు ఫ్రస్ట్రేట్ అవుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కష్టం లేదా నష్టపు బేరం అసాధ్యత కాదు ( Alopi Parshad ; Energy Watchdog ).

selfTest.q: 3. కాంట్రాక్టు ఫ్రస్ట్రేట్ అయితే ఏమవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: పని అసాధ్యం లేదా చట్టవిరుద్ధం అయినప్పుడు అది శూన్యమవుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 65 కింద ప్రతి పక్షం పొందిన లాభాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి.

selfTest.q: 4. దిగుమతి లైసెన్స్ తెస్తానని ఒక కొనుగోలుదారు వాగ్దానం చేస్తాడు; లైసెన్స్ నిరాకరించబడుతుంది. కాంట్రాక్టు ఫ్రస్ట్రేట్ అయిందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు, దాన్ని తెచ్చే సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యతను కొనుగోలుదారు తీసుకుంటే ( Naihati Jute Mills ).

selfTest.q: 5. కాంట్రాక్టులోని ఫోర్స్ మెజ్యూర్ క్లాజు ఏ సెక్షన్ కింద పనిచేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 32, సెక్షన్ 56 కాదు ( Satyabrata Ghose ; Energy Watchdog ).

hi.inOneMinute: If an act is impossible from the start, the agreement is void . If it becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made, through no fault of the promisor, the contract becomes void at that moment. This is the doctrine of frustration , found in Section 56. The doctrine is narrow. A rise in cost, a delay or a bad bargain is not enough. In exams, the grounds, the limits and the cases decide the marks. In real life, it decides who bears the loss when a fire, a war, a new law or a pandemic upsets a contract.
legalProvision: Section 56. Agreement to do impossible act. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. Contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful. —A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Compensation for loss through non-performance of act known to be impossible or unlawful. —Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or, with reasonable diligence, might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must make compensation to such promisee for any loss which such promisee sustains through the non-performance of the promise. Illustrations. (a) A agrees with B to discover treasure by magic. The agreement is void. (b) A and B contract to marry each other. Before the time fixed for the marriage, A goes mad. The contract becomes void. (c) A contracts to marry B, being already married to C, and being forbidden by the law to which he is subject to practise polygamy, A must make compensation to B for the loss caused to her by the non-performance of his promise. (d) A contracts to take in cargo for B at a foreign port. A's Government afterwards declares war against the country in which the port is situated. The contract becomes void when war is declared. (e) A contracts to act at a theatre for six months in consideration of a sum paid in advance by B. On several occasions A is too ill to act. The contract to act on those occasions becomes void.
Related provisions

Section 32. Enforcement of contracts contingent on an event happening. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced by law unless and until that event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.

Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it. Illustration (d). A contracts to sing for B at a concert for 1,000 rupees, which are paid in advance. A is too ill to sing. A is not bound to make compensation to B for the loss of the profits which B would have made if A had been able to sing, but must refund to B the 1,000 rupees paid in advance.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 7. Goods perishing before making of contract. Where there is a contract for the sale of specific goods, the contract is void if the goods without the knowledge of the seller have, at the time when the contract was made, perished or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the contract.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 8. Goods perishing before sale but after agreement to sell. Where there is an agreement to sell specific goods, and subsequently the goods without any fault on the part of the seller or buyer perish or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the agreement before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is thereby avoided.
In simple words

First paragraph. An agreement to do something impossible in itself is void from the start. Second paragraph. If the act later becomes impossible, or unlawful by an event the promisor could not prevent, the contract becomes void at that moment. Third paragraph. A promisor who knew, or should have known, of the impossibility must compensate a promisee who did not know. Section 65. Whoever received an advantage must give it back or pay for it.
hi.meaning:
Frustration is the discharge of a contract because a later event makes performance impossible or unlawful, or destroys the purpose the parties had in view. Section 56 does not use the word "frustration". It speaks of impossibility. In India the two words describe the same doctrine. Why the law excuses the parties. The law does not compel what is impossible. The maxim lex non cogit ad impossibilia says the law does not require the impossible. It would be unjust to make a promisor pay damages for failing to do what no one could do. See Diagram 1 for the tests under the second paragraph. Diagram 1. Go down the questions in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the question. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Did an event after the contract make
performance impossible or unlawful,
or destroy its basis? (s.56, para 2)"} Q2{"2. Could the promisor not prevent it,
and was it not caused by his own
act or default?"} Q3{"3. Is performance impossible or radically
different, not merely costlier, slower
or harder? (Satyabrata Ghose; Energy Watchdog)"} Q4{"4. Is the event outside any contract clause
dealing with it, and outside any risk
a party took on?"} N1["No frustration"] N2["Self-induced impossibility:
not frustration"] N3["Hardship: not frustration"] N4["The clause governs (e.g. force majeure, s.32),
or the party bears the risk he took on
(Naihati Jute Mills)"] R["FRUSTRATED: the contract becomes void
when performance becomes impossible
or unlawful; advantages restored (s.65)"] Q1 -- "No" --> N1 Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2 Q2 -- "No" --> N2 Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3 Q3 -- "No" --> N3 Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4 Q4 -- "No" --> N4 Q4 -- "Yes" --> R Text description Question 1: did an event after the contract was made make performance impossible or unlawful, or destroy its basis (Section 56, second paragraph)? No: there is no frustration. Question 2: was the event one the promisor could not prevent, and not caused by his own act or default? No: self-induced impossibility is not frustration. Question 3: is performance impossible or radically different, and not merely costlier, slower or harder (Satyabrata Ghose; Energy Watchdog)? No: hardship is not frustration. Question 4: is the event outside any clause in the contract that deals with it, and outside any risk a party took on? No: the clause governs, for example a force majeure clause (Section 32), or the party bears the risk he took on (Naihati Jute Mills). Yes to all: the contract becomes void when performance becomes impossible or unlawful, and each party must restore any advantage received (Section 65).
keyPoints: Section 56: an act impossible in itself makes the agreement void. A later impossibility or illegality makes the contract void when it happens. Frustration is automatic. No one chooses. Satyabrata Ghose : Section 56 is exhaustive in India, and "impossible" includes impracticable and useless performance. Grounds: destruction of the subject matter, failure of the foundation event, death or incapacity, change of law, war. Not frustration: higher cost, delay, a temporary hindrance, self-induced impossibility, a risk taken on by a party, risk allocated by the contract. Effect: both parties are discharged and advantages are restored (Section 65). The third paragraph gives compensation to a promisee who did not know of the impossibility. Sale of Goods Act: Section 7 (goods perished before the contract) and Section 8 (goods perish after the agreement, before risk passes). A term of the contract that discharges performance falls under Section 32, not Section 56 ( Satyabrata Ghose ). Covid-19 is not an automatic ground. Courts look at the contract and the real cause.

caseLaws.name: Taylor v
caseLaws.facts: Caldwell (1863) Facts. By an agreement of 27 May 1861, Caldwell agreed to let the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall to Taylor for concerts on four days in June to August 1861, at £100 a day. The hall was destroyed by fire before the first day. Principle. A contract that depends on the continued existence of a thing carries an implied condition that the parties are excused if it is destroyed without their fault. (1863) 3 B & S 826 : 122 ER 309 (Queen's Bench, Blackburn J., 6 May 1863). Why it matters. It is the origin of the doctrine in English law. Krell v. Henry (1903) Facts. Henry hired a flat in Pall Mall for 26 and 27 June 1902, the days of the planned coronation processions. The contract did not mention the coronation. The processions were cancelled. Principle. The Court of Appeal held the contract frustrated, because the processions were its foundation. [1903] 2 KB 740. Why it matters. It applies frustration where the purpose fails but the thing still exists. Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. (1953) Facts. A land company sold building plots and undertook to build roads and drains. During the Second World War part of the land was requisitioned for military purposes. The company said the contract was frustrated. Principle. Section 56 is exhaustive of the law in India. "Impossible" is wider than physical impossibility. The requisition was temporary in nature and no time was fixed for performance, so the contract was not frustrated. [1954] SCR 310 : AIR 1954 SC 44 (Supreme Court, 16 November 1953). Why it matters. It is the leading Indian authority on Section 56. Alopi Parshad & Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) Facts. The appellants were agents for buying and supplying ghee for the Army under a 1937 agreement, revised in 1942 at lower rates. When wartime conditions became abnormal, they claimed payment at higher rates than those agreed. Principle. "A contract is not frustrated merely because the circumstances in which it was made are altered." The Act does not let a party claim rates different from the stipulated rates "on some vague plea of equity". The appeal was dismissed. [1960] 2 SCR 793 : AIR 1960 SC 588 (Supreme Court, 20 January 1960). Why it matters. It is the standard case that hardship is not impossibility. Naihati Jute Mills Ltd. v. Khyaliram Jagannath (1967) Facts. On 7 July 1958 the mills agreed to buy 2,000 bales of jute to be imported from Pakistan, and undertook to obtain the import licence. The Jute Commissioner refused the licence. The mills pleaded frustration. Principle. The mills had taken upon themselves "the absolute burden of furnishing the licence", so impossibility was no defence. "A contract is not frustrated merely because the circumstances in which it was made are altered", and courts cannot absolve a party "merely because its performance has become onerous". Even after frustration, the contract survives for deciding disputes under its arbitration clause. The appeal was dismissed. [1968] 1 SCR 821 (Supreme Court, 19 October 1967). Why it matters. Courts cannot excuse a party from an onerous bargain or from a risk he took on. Davis Contractors Ltd. v. Fareham Urban District Council (1956) Facts. Builders agreed to build 78 houses in eight months for £92,425. Shortages of labour and materials made the job take 22 months and cost £115,223. They argued frustration and claimed a reasonable sum. Principle. The House of Lords held that the contract was not frustrated. An unexpected turn of events that makes a contract more onerous is not a ground to relieve the contractor. [1956] AC 696. Why it matters. It supplies the "radically different" test. Energy Watchdog v. CERC (2017) Facts. Power generators won bids to supply electricity at fixed tariffs, using coal imported from Indonesia. A change in Indonesian law raised the price of that coal, and they sought relief for force majeure and change in law . Principle. "An unexpected rise in the price of coal will not absolve the generating companies from performing their part of the contract", because "this was a risk they knowingly took" (para 40). Frustration applies "within narrow limits" (para 37). A change in Indian law, though not in Indonesian law, could be a change in law under the contract. [2017] 3 SCR 153 : (2017) 14 SCC 80 (Supreme Court, 11 April 2017). Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court statement of the limits of Section 56. Halliburton Offshore Services Inc. v. Vedanta Ltd. (2020) Facts. A contractor relied on the Covid-19 lockdown as force majeure to stop encashment of bank guarantees under a contract of 25 April 2018 whose completion dates fell in 2019. The Delhi High Court made an ad interim order on 20 April 2020 and vacated it on 29 May 2020. Principle. "The past non-performance of the Contractor cannot be condoned due to the COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020 in India." The decision was at the interim stage; the force majeure question was left for the arbitration. O.M.P. (I) (COMM.) 88/2020 (Delhi High Court, Prathiba M. Singh J., 29 May 2020). Why it matters. Covid-19 is not an automatic ground of frustration or force majeure.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three paragraphs of Section 56?
selfTest.a: An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. A contract to do an act that later becomes impossible or unlawful becomes void when it happens. A promisor who knew of the impossibility must compensate a promisee who did not.

selfTest.q: 2. Does a sharp rise in cost frustrate a contract?
selfTest.a: No. Hardship or a bad bargain is not impossibility ( Alopi Parshad ; Energy Watchdog ).

selfTest.q: 3. What follows when a contract is frustrated?
selfTest.a: It becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Each party must restore any advantage received under Section 65.

selfTest.q: 4. A buyer promises to obtain an import licence, and the licence is refused. Is the contract frustrated?
selfTest.a: No, if the buyer took on an absolute obligation to obtain it ( Naihati Jute Mills ).

selfTest.q: 5. Under which section does a force majeure clause in the contract operate?
selfTest.a: Section 32, not Section 56 ( Satyabrata Ghose ; Energy Watchdog ).

en.meaning:
Under Section 59, who has the first right to appropriate a payment to a specific debt?

Explanation. Section 59 gives the debtor the first right to direct which debt a payment should be applied to, either expressly or by clear implication.

If the debtor does not specify which debt a payment is for, Section 60 allows the creditor to apply it to:

Explanation. Section 60 gives the creditor discretion to apply an unspecified payment to any lawful debt, including one barred by the Limitation Act.

If neither the debtor nor the creditor appropriates a payment, Section 61 applies it:

Explanation. Section 61 applies unappropriated payments to debts in chronological order — the earliest debt is treated as discharged first.

Which English case established the "first in, first out" logic that Section 61 mirrors?

en.meaning:
Explanation. Actual breach happens at the time performance is due, or during performance itself, when a party fails to perform or performs defectively.

Anticipatory breach occurs when:

Explanation. Anticipatory breach happens when a party, before the time fixed for performance, clearly renounces the contract or makes performance impossible through their own conduct.

In Hochster v. De La Tour (1853), the injured party sued for breach:

Explanation. Hochster sued on 22 May 1852, well before the 1 June start date, immediately after De La Tour's clear renunciation on 11 May.

According to Hochster v. De La Tour, once a party clearly renounces a contract before performance is due, the injured party:

Explanation. The injured party need not wait for the due date — they may treat the contract as discharged at once and sue for damages immediately.

en.meaning:
Section 62 covers all of the following EXCEPT:

Explanation. Section 62 covers novation, rescission, and alteration as forms of discharge by agreement. Frustration is covered separately under Section 56.

Explanation. Novation requires the consent of all parties involved, including any new party being brought into the substituted contract.

What distinguishes rescission from novation?

Explanation. Rescission is a plain cancellation with no replacement, whereas novation substitutes an entirely new contract for the old one.

Under Section 63, a promisee can do all of the following WITHOUT needing fresh consideration EXCEPT:

Explanation. Section 63 allows a promisee to remit, extend time, or accept different satisfaction without fresh consideration — it does not allow demanding more than originally promised.

law-of-contract-i-u4-t1.subtitle: Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872: relations resembling those created by contract

en.inOneMinute: A quasi contract is not a contract. It is a duty that the law puts on one person to pay or to return something, although the parties never made an agreement. The law does this so that nobody keeps a benefit at another person's cost. Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 list the cases, in a chapter headed "Of Certain Relations Resembling Those Created by Contract". The idea behind all five sections is unjust enrichment . In exams, the meaning, the idea of unjust enrichment, the five sections and Moses v. Macferlan earn the marks. In real life, it decides who pays when work, goods or money change hands and there is no valid contract.
legalProvision: Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person.

Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other.

Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.
Section 71. Responsibility of finder of goods. A person who finds goods belonging to another, and takes them into his custody, is subject to the same responsibility as a bailee.

Section 72. Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion. A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it.
Related provision

Section 73 (third paragraph). Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract.
In simple words

Section 68: a person who supplies necessaries suited to the condition in life of a person unable in law to contract , or of anyone that person must support, is paid back from the property of the incapable person. Section 69: a person who is interested in the payment of money that another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is paid back by the other. Section 70: where a person lawfully does anything for another, or delivers anything to him, not meaning to do it free of charge, and the other enjoys the benefit, the other must pay compensation or restore the thing. Section 71: a person who finds goods belonging to another and takes them into his keeping has the same responsibility as a bailee . Section 72: a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion must repay or return it. Section 73, third paragraph: when such an obligation is not discharged, the injured person gets the same compensation as if he had contracted for it and the contract had been broken.
en.meaning:
The Act does not define quasi contract. It speaks only of "relations resembling those created by contract". The word "quasi" means "as if". The law treats the parties as if they had made a contract, but only to enforce a duty to pay or to restore. Where the duty comes from. The Supreme Court explained the source of the duty in Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968). It is "not founded upon any contract or tort but upon a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution". In plain words, the duty comes from the law, not from the parties' promise. The same idea is called restitution : giving back a benefit received. Why the law has it. The idea behind the chapter is unjust enrichment . The Latin maxim nemo debet locupletari ex aliena jactura means that no one should be made richer at another's loss. Contract law cannot help here, because there is no promise to enforce. The law therefore creates the duty itself. In State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons the Supreme Court said: "What s. 70 prevents is unjust enrichment and it applies as much to individuals as to corporations and Government." See Diagram 1 for the five situations. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. Each bottom box is one situation in which the law makes a person pay or return something. flowchart TD Q["Quasi contract

Claims by a supplier or payer: necessaries for an incapable person, Section 68, paid from that person's property; payment by an interested person, Section 69, reimbursed by the person bound by law to pay. Claims for a benefit received: non-gratuitous act with benefit enjoyed, Section 70, compensation or restoration; goods found and taken into custody, Section 71, the finder is treated as a bailee; money paid or thing delivered by mistake or under coercion, Section 72, must be repaid or returned.
keyPoints: A quasi contract is a duty imposed by law, with no agreement between the parties. It rests on unjust enrichment: no one should be enriched at another's loss. Sections 68 to 72 cover necessaries, an interested payer, a non-gratuitous act, a finder and a payment by mistake or coercion. The claim is for reimbursement, compensation or restoration, not damages for breach. Section 73, third paragraph, gives the same compensation as on a breach when such an obligation is not discharged. Section 70 applies even where a Government contract is invalid for want of form ( B.K. Mondal ). The duty rests on "a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution" ( Mulamchand ). It does not apply where a valid contract governs the dispute ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

caseLaws.name: Moses v
caseLaws.facts: Macferlan (1760) Facts. Moses endorsed promissory notes to Macferlan on his promise not to sue Moses on them. Macferlan sued him on them in the Court of Conscience, and Moses had to pay. Moses then sued to get the money back. Principle. Where a defendant is obliged by the ties of natural justice and equity to refund money, the law implies a debt and gives an action to recover it. (1760) 2 Burr 1005 : 97 ER 676 (Court of King's Bench, Lord Mansfield CJ). Why it matters. It is the foundation of the law on unjust enrichment, which Sections 68 to 72 apply. State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. In 1944 a firm of contractors built a road, offices and storage sheds at Arambagh and Khanakul for the Civil Supplies Department, on its officers' requests. No contract was made in the form required by Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The State refused to pay Rs. 19,325. Principle. Section 70 "deals with cases where there is no valid contract". The State must pay when it voluntarily accepts and enjoys the work. AIR 1962 SC 779 : 1962 Supp (1) SCR 876 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It is the leading authority that a quasi-contractual claim does not depend on any contract, and that the State is bound like a citizen. Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968) Facts. A Section 70 claim was made against a State on a contract that did not comply with Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The Court held Section 175(3) mandatory and based on public policy. Principle. If the three conditions of Section 70 are met, the claim lies. It rests on "a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution", and not on any contract. (1968) 3 SCR 214 (Supreme Court). Why it matters. It states the legal basis of every quasi-contractual claim. Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v. Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf (1958) Facts. A Banaras firm dealing in bullion and in forward contracts in silver paid sales tax for 1948-49 to 1950-51, in all Rs. 1,365-12-0 as stated in the judgment. The Allahabad High Court later held the tax on forward transactions beyond the State's power. The firm asked for a refund. Principle. "Mistake" in Section 72 covers a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact. AIR 1959 SC 135 : 1959 SCR Supp (1) 1350 (Supreme Court, 23 September 1958). Why it matters. It applies unjust enrichment to a refund from the State. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. MTNL deducted money from Tata Communications' bills. Clause 16.2(c) of the purchase order limited liquidated damages to a maximum of 12 per cent. The Supreme Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1766 of 2019 on 27 February 2019. Principle. Each section of this chapter assumes there is no contractual relationship. The dispute was governed by Section 74, so only the contract figure could be claimed and the excess had to be refunded. Why it matters. It shows the limit of quasi contract: a claim under the chapter cannot override a valid contract.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a quasi contract a contract?
selfTest.a: No. It is a duty imposed by law, resembling a contract. No offer, acceptance or consent is needed.

selfTest.q: 2. Which principle lies behind Sections 68 to 72?
selfTest.a: Unjust enrichment: no one should be enriched at another's loss.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a person claiming under Section 70 sue for damages for breach?
selfTest.a: No. He can claim only compensation for the benefit, or restoration of the thing, because there is no contract ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a State escape a Section 70 claim because its officers did not make the contract in the required form?
selfTest.a: No. If it voluntarily accepted and enjoyed the work, it must pay ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. A valid purchase order fixes liquidated damages. Can a party add a quantum meruit claim under Section 70?
selfTest.a: No. Where a valid contract governs the dispute, the claim lies under the contract ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

సెక్షన్ 68: చట్టప్రకారం కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేని వ్యక్తికి, లేదా అతను పోషించాల్సిన వారికి, వారి జీవన స్థితికి తగిన అవసరమైన వస్తువులు (necessaries) సరఫరా చేసిన వ్యక్తికి, ఆ అసమర్థుడి ఆస్తి నుంచి డబ్బు తిరిగి వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 69: మరొకరు చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సిన డబ్బు చెల్లింపులో ఆసక్తి ఉండి, అందుకే దాన్ని చెల్లించిన వ్యక్తికి ఆ మరొకరు తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి. సెక్షన్ 70: ఒకరు మరొకరి కోసం చట్టబద్ధంగా ఏదైనా పని చేసినా, ఏదైనా అందజేసినా, అది ఉచితంగా చేయాలనే ఉద్దేశం లేకపోయి, ఆ మరొకరు దాని ప్రయోజనాన్ని అనుభవిస్తే, అతను పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి లేదా ఆ వస్తువును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. సెక్షన్ 71: మరొకరికి చెందిన వస్తువులను కనుగొని తన అధీనంలోకి తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తికి బెయిలీ (bailee) కి ఉన్న బాధ్యతే ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 72: పొరపాటు (mistake) వల్ల గానీ, బలవంతం (coercion) వల్ల గానీ ఎవరికైనా డబ్బు చెల్లించినా, ఏదైనా అందజేసినా, అతను దాన్ని తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. సెక్షన్ 73, మూడో పేరా: అలాంటి బాధ్యత నెరవేరకపోతే, నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తికి, అతను కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకుని ఆ కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనకు గురైనట్లే అదే పరిహారం వస్తుంది.

చట్టం క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు ను నిర్వచించలేదు. "relations resembling those created by contract " (కాంట్రాక్టు సృష్టించే సంబంధాలను పోలిన సంబంధాలు) అని మాత్రమే చెబుతుంది. "quasi" అంటే "ఉన్నట్లుగా". పక్షాలు కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నట్లుగా చట్టం భావిస్తుంది, కానీ చెల్లించే లేదా తిరిగి ఇచ్చే బాధ్యతను అమలు చేయడానికి మాత్రమే. బాధ్యత ఎక్కడి నుంచి వస్తుంది. Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968) లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఈ బాధ్యత మూలాన్ని వివరించింది. ఇది "not founded upon any contract or tort but upon a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution". సరళంగా, ఈ బాధ్యత పక్షాల వాగ్దానం నుంచి కాదు, చట్టం నుంచి వస్తుంది. దీన్నే రెస్టిట్యూషన్ (restitution) అని కూడా అంటారు: పొందిన ప్రయోజనాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం. చట్టం దీన్ని ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. ఈ అధ్యాయం వెనుక ఉన్న ఆలోచన అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత . nemo debet locupletari ex aliena jactura అనే లాటిన్ సూత్రం అర్థం: మరొకరి నష్టంతో ఎవరూ ధనవంతులు కాకూడదు. ఇక్కడ అమలు చేయడానికి వాగ్దానమే లేదు కాబట్టి కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం సహాయం చేయలేదు. అందుకే చట్టమే ఆ బాధ్యతను సృష్టిస్తుంది. Mondal & Sons లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఇలా చెప్పింది: "What s. 70 prevents is unjust enrichment and it applies as much to individuals as to corporations and Government." ఐదు సందర్భాలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. అందజేసిన వస్తువు (సె. 72): తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి"] Q --> A Q --> B A --> S68 A --> S69 B --> S70 B --> S71 B --> S72 వచన వివరణ క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు, సెక్షన్లు 68 నుంచి 72, రెండు గుంపులుగా చీలుతుంది. సరఫరాదారు లేదా చెల్లింపుదారు క్లెయిమ్‌లు: అసమర్థుడికి అవసరమైన వస్తువులు, సెక్షన్ 68, అతని ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లింపు; ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యక్తి చెల్లింపు, సెక్షన్ 69, చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సినవారు తిరిగి చెల్లిస్తారు. పొందిన ప్రయోజనానికి క్లెయిమ్‌లు: ఉచితం కాని పని, ప్రయోజనం అనుభవించడం, సెక్షన్ 70, పరిహారం లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం; కనుగొని అధీనంలోకి తీసుకున్న వస్తువులు, సెక్షన్ 71, కనుగొన్నవారు బెయిలీ; పొరపాటు లేదా బలవంతంతో చెల్లించిన డబ్బు లేదా అందజేసిన వస్తువు, సెక్షన్ 72, తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి.

selfTest.a: కాదు. ఇది కాంట్రాక్టును పోలిన, చట్టం విధించే బాధ్యత. ప్రతిపాదన, అంగీకారం, సమ్మతి అవసరం లేదు.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్లు 68 నుంచి 72 వెనుక ఏ సూత్రం ఉంది?
selfTest.a: అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత: మరొకరి నష్టంతో ఎవరూ సంపన్నులు కాకూడదు.

selfTest.q: 3. సెక్షన్ 70 కింద క్లెయిమ్ చేసే వ్యక్తి ఉల్లంఘనకు నష్టపరిహారం కోసం దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు లేదు కాబట్టి ప్రయోజనానికి పరిహారం, లేదా వస్తువు తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం మాత్రమే కోరగలడు ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. అధికారులు కోరిన రూపంలో కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేదని రాష్ట్రం సెక్షన్ 70 క్లెయిమ్ నుంచి తప్పించుకోగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పనిని స్వచ్ఛందంగా అంగీకరించి అనుభవిస్తే చెల్లించాలి ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. చెల్లుబాటయ్యే purchase order ముందే నష్టపరిహారాన్ని నిర్ణయించింది. ఒక పక్షం సెక్షన్ 70 కింద క్వాంటమ్ మెరిట్ క్లెయిమ్ జోడించగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు వివాదాన్ని నియంత్రిస్తే క్లెయిమ్ ఆ కాంట్రాక్టు కిందే ఉంటుంది ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

hi.inOneMinute: A quasi contract is not a contract. It is a duty that the law puts on one person to pay or to return something, although the parties never made an agreement. The law does this so that nobody keeps a benefit at another person's cost. Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 list the cases, in a chapter headed "Of Certain Relations Resembling Those Created by Contract". The idea behind all five sections is unjust enrichment . In exams, the meaning, the idea of unjust enrichment, the five sections and Moses v. Macferlan earn the marks. In real life, it decides who pays when work, goods or money change hands and there is no valid contract.
legalProvision: Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person.

Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other.

Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.
Section 71. Responsibility of finder of goods. A person who finds goods belonging to another, and takes them into his custody, is subject to the same responsibility as a bailee.

Section 72. Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion. A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it.
Related provision

Section 73 (third paragraph). Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract.
In simple words

Section 68: a person who supplies necessaries suited to the condition in life of a person unable in law to contract , or of anyone that person must support, is paid back from the property of the incapable person. Section 69: a person who is interested in the payment of money that another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is paid back by the other. Section 70: where a person lawfully does anything for another, or delivers anything to him, not meaning to do it free of charge, and the other enjoys the benefit, the other must pay compensation or restore the thing. Section 71: a person who finds goods belonging to another and takes them into his keeping has the same responsibility as a bailee . Section 72: a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion must repay or return it. Section 73, third paragraph: when such an obligation is not discharged, the injured person gets the same compensation as if he had contracted for it and the contract had been broken.
hi.meaning:
The Act does not define quasi contract. It speaks only of "relations resembling those created by contract". The word "quasi" means "as if". The law treats the parties as if they had made a contract, but only to enforce a duty to pay or to restore. Where the duty comes from. The Supreme Court explained the source of the duty in Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968). It is "not founded upon any contract or tort but upon a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution". In plain words, the duty comes from the law, not from the parties' promise. The same idea is called restitution : giving back a benefit received. Why the law has it. The idea behind the chapter is unjust enrichment . The Latin maxim nemo debet locupletari ex aliena jactura means that no one should be made richer at another's loss. Contract law cannot help here, because there is no promise to enforce. The law therefore creates the duty itself. In State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons the Supreme Court said: "What s. 70 prevents is unjust enrichment and it applies as much to individuals as to corporations and Government." See Diagram 1 for the five situations. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. Each bottom box is one situation in which the law makes a person pay or return something. flowchart TD Q["Quasi contract

compensation, or restoration of the thing"] S71["Goods found and taken into custody (s. 71):

or under coercion (s. 72): repay or return"] Q --> A Q --> B A --> S68 A --> S69 B --> S70 B --> S71 B --> S72 Text description Quasi contract, Sections 68 to 72, branches into two groups. Claims by a supplier or payer: necessaries for an incapable person, Section 68, paid from that person's property; payment by an interested person, Section 69, reimbursed by the person bound by law to pay. Claims for a benefit received: non-gratuitous act with benefit enjoyed, Section 70, compensation or restoration; goods found and taken into custody, Section 71, the finder is treated as a bailee; money paid or thing delivered by mistake or under coercion, Section 72, must be repaid or returned.
keyPoints: A quasi contract is a duty imposed by law, with no agreement between the parties. It rests on unjust enrichment: no one should be enriched at another's loss. Sections 68 to 72 cover necessaries, an interested payer, a non-gratuitous act, a finder and a payment by mistake or coercion. The claim is for reimbursement, compensation or restoration, not damages for breach. Section 73, third paragraph, gives the same compensation as on a breach when such an obligation is not discharged. Section 70 applies even where a Government contract is invalid for want of form ( B.K. Mondal ). The duty rests on "a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution" ( Mulamchand ). It does not apply where a valid contract governs the dispute ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

caseLaws.name: Moses v
caseLaws.facts: Macferlan (1760) Facts. Moses endorsed promissory notes to Macferlan on his promise not to sue Moses on them. Macferlan sued him on them in the Court of Conscience, and Moses had to pay. Moses then sued to get the money back. Principle. Where a defendant is obliged by the ties of natural justice and equity to refund money, the law implies a debt and gives an action to recover it. (1760) 2 Burr 1005 : 97 ER 676 (Court of King's Bench, Lord Mansfield CJ). Why it matters. It is the foundation of the law on unjust enrichment, which Sections 68 to 72 apply. State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. In 1944 a firm of contractors built a road, offices and storage sheds at Arambagh and Khanakul for the Civil Supplies Department, on its officers' requests. No contract was made in the form required by Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The State refused to pay Rs. 19,325. Principle. Section 70 "deals with cases where there is no valid contract". The State must pay when it voluntarily accepts and enjoys the work. AIR 1962 SC 779 : 1962 Supp (1) SCR 876 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It is the leading authority that a quasi-contractual claim does not depend on any contract, and that the State is bound like a citizen. Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968) Facts. A Section 70 claim was made against a State on a contract that did not comply with Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The Court held Section 175(3) mandatory and based on public policy. Principle. If the three conditions of Section 70 are met, the claim lies. It rests on "a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution", and not on any contract. (1968) 3 SCR 214 (Supreme Court). Why it matters. It states the legal basis of every quasi-contractual claim. Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v. Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf (1958) Facts. A Banaras firm dealing in bullion and in forward contracts in silver paid sales tax for 1948-49 to 1950-51, in all Rs. 1,365-12-0 as stated in the judgment. The Allahabad High Court later held the tax on forward transactions beyond the State's power. The firm asked for a refund. Principle. "Mistake" in Section 72 covers a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact. AIR 1959 SC 135 : 1959 SCR Supp (1) 1350 (Supreme Court, 23 September 1958). Why it matters. It applies unjust enrichment to a refund from the State. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. MTNL deducted money from Tata Communications' bills. Clause 16.2(c) of the purchase order limited liquidated damages to a maximum of 12 per cent. The Supreme Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1766 of 2019 on 27 February 2019. Principle. Each section of this chapter assumes there is no contractual relationship. The dispute was governed by Section 74, so only the contract figure could be claimed and the excess had to be refunded. Why it matters. It shows the limit of quasi contract: a claim under the chapter cannot override a valid contract.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a quasi contract a contract?
selfTest.a: No. It is a duty imposed by law, resembling a contract. No offer, acceptance or consent is needed.

selfTest.q: 2. Which principle lies behind Sections 68 to 72?
selfTest.a: Unjust enrichment: no one should be enriched at another's loss.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a person claiming under Section 70 sue for damages for breach?
selfTest.a: No. He can claim only compensation for the benefit, or restoration of the thing, because there is no contract ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a State escape a Section 70 claim because its officers did not make the contract in the required form?
selfTest.a: No. If it voluntarily accepted and enjoyed the work, it must pay ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. A valid purchase order fixes liquidated damages. Can a party add a quantum meruit claim under Section 70?
selfTest.a: No. Where a valid contract governs the dispute, the claim lies under the contract ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t2.subtitle: Section 68 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A minor or a person of unsound mind cannot make a binding contract. Yet he must eat, dress and stay healthy. Section 68 lets a person who supplies him with necessaries be paid back from his property. The supplier cannot sue the incapable person on a promise, because there is none. He claims under the law, and only against the property. In exams, the two tests for necessaries and the property-only rule earn the marks. In real life, it protects the grocer, the doctor and the school that serve a minor.
legalProvision: Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person. Illustrations. (a) A supplies B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to his condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property. (b) A supplies the wife and children of B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to their condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property.
Related provisions

Section 11. Who are competent to contract. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 12 (first sentence). What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting. A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract, if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 26 (second paragraph). Minor. —A minor may draw, indorse, deliver and negotiate such instrument so as to bind all parties except himself.
In simple words

If a person who cannot contract , or anyone he must support by law, is supplied with necessaries that suit his condition in life, the supplier is paid back from that person's property. "Lunatic" is the Act's old word for a person of unsound mind. A person can contract only if he is a major, of sound mind , and not disqualified by law (Section 11). A minor may sign a promissory note , but the note binds everyone except the minor (Section 26, Negotiable Instruments Act).
en.meaning:
Section 68 is one of the five situations in which the law imposes a duty without agreement (a quasi contract ). It applies to a person who is "incapable of entering into a contract". That means a person who fails the test of Section 11: a minor, a person of unsound mind, or a person disqualified by law. What are necessaries. The Act does not define necessaries. It gives the test in the section itself: they must be "suited to his condition in life". The courts add a second test, which is the person's actual need at the time of supply. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness to both sides. The law protects a minor from bad bargains by making his agreements void . It does not want him to starve for that reason. So it lets the supplier recover, but only from the minor's own property. This prevents unjust enrichment . See Diagram 1 for the questions a court asks. Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the box. flowchart TD Q1["1. Is the person supplied incapable of contracting,
or someone such a person must support? (s. 68)"] Q2["2. Are the goods or services necessaries,
suited to his condition in life? (s. 68)"] Q3["3. Did he actually need them when supplied,
and was he not already enough supplied?"] Q4["4. Does the incapable person own property?"] Y["Supplier is reimbursed from the
incapable person's property.
The person himself is not liable."] N1["s. 68 does not apply.
Ordinary contract law decides."] N2["No claim."] N3["No claim."] N4["Nothing from which
to be reimbursed."] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4 Q4 -->|"Yes"| Y Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q4 -->|"No"| N4 Text description Question 1: is the person supplied incapable of entering into a contract, or someone whom such a person must support? If no, Section 68 does not apply and ordinary contract law decides. Question 2: are the goods or services necessaries, suited to his condition in life? If no, there is no claim. Question 3: did he actually need them when they were supplied, and was he not already enough supplied? If no, there is no claim. Question 4: does the incapable person own property? If no, there is nothing from which to be reimbursed. If every answer is yes, the supplier is reimbursed from the incapable person's property; the person himself is not liable.
keyPoints: Section 68 repays a person who supplies necessaries to someone incapable of contracting. Persons incapable of contracting are those who fail Section 11: a minor, a person of unsound mind, a disqualified person. Necessaries must suit the person's condition in life and his actual need. The supplier is repaid from the incapable person's property only. The incapable person is not personally liable ( Mohori Bibee ). Dependants of the incapable person are covered (Illustration (b)). A promissory note signed by a minor does not bind him, so the supplier claims under Section 68. A minor is outside Section 70, because Section 68 provides for his case ( B.K. Mondal ).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. On 20 July 1895 Dharmodas Ghose, a minor, mortgaged his houses to Brahmo Dutt, a moneylender, to secure Rs. 20,000. The lender's attorney knew he was a minor. The Privy Council decided the appeal on 4 March 1903. Principle. A minor is not competent to contract, and his agreement is void. Sections 64 and 65 do not apply, because they assume a contract between competent parties. Under Section 68 the infant is not liable even for necessaries, "though a statutory claim is created against his property". [1903] UKPC 12 (Privy Council, 4 March 1903). Why it matters. It is the reason a supplier of necessaries has no contract claim and must use Section 68. State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. The State argued that it was like a minor, and so could not be made to pay under Section 70 where its contract was invalid. Principle. The Court said a minor is outside Section 70 because "his case has been specifically provided for by s. 68", and because he cannot voluntarily accept a benefit. The State was not in that position. AIR 1962 SC 779 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It confirms that Section 68 is the special rule for incapable persons. Nash v. Inman (1908) Facts. A Savile Row tailor sued Inman, a Cambridge undergraduate who was a minor, for clothes that included eleven fancy waistcoats. The trial judge found that Inman was already amply supplied with clothes. [1908] 2 KB 1 (Court of Appeal). Principle. The supplier must prove that the goods suited the minor's condition in life and that he was not already sufficiently supplied with them. Why it matters. It supplies the second test for necessaries. Kanhayalal Bisandayal Bhiwapurkar v. Indarchandji Hamirmalji Sisodia (1947) Facts. An eye specialist sued a husband for Rs. 188 for removing his wife's cataract, under an agreement with her and her son-in-law. Principle. Section 68 covers "the dependent of a person incompetent to contract". The husband "was not incompetent to contract", so it did not apply. AIR 1947 Nag 84 (Nagpur High Court). Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 68.

selfTest.q: 1. From whom is a supplier of necessaries reimbursed under Section 68?
selfTest.a: From the property of the incapable person. The person himself is not liable.

selfTest.q: 2. What two tests decide whether goods are necessaries?
selfTest.a: They must suit his condition in life, and they must meet his actual requirements at the time of supply.

selfTest.q: 3. A grocer holds a minor's promissory note for necessaries. Can he sue on the note?
selfTest.a: No. The note does not bind the minor. The grocer claims the price of the necessaries under Section 68 from the minor's property.

selfTest.q: 4. A supplies food to the wife and children of B, a person of unsound mind. Can A recover?
selfTest.a: Yes. A is reimbursed from B's property (Section 68, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 5. A doctor treats a woman under an agreement with her and sues her husband, who is a competent adult, under Section 68. Will he succeed?
selfTest.a: No. Section 68 applies only where the person bound to support is incapable of contracting ( Kanhayalal ).

legalProvision: Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person. Illustrations. (a) A supplies B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to his condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property. (b) A supplies the wife and children of B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to their condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు

Section 11. Who are competent to contract. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 12 (first sentence). What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting. A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract, if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 26 (second paragraph). Minor. —A minor may draw, indorse, deliver and negotiate such instrument so as to bind all parties except himself.
సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే

కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేని వ్యక్తికి, లేదా అతను చట్టప్రకారం పోషించాల్సిన ఎవరికైనా, అతని జీవన స్థితికి తగిన అవసరమైన వస్తువులు సరఫరా అయితే, సరఫరాదారుకు ఆ వ్యక్తి ఆస్తి నుంచి డబ్బు తిరిగి వస్తుంది. "Lunatic" అనేది మతిస్థిమితం లేని వ్యక్తికి చట్టంలోని పాత పదం. మేజర్ అయి, స్థిరమైన మనస్సు (sound mind) ఉండి, ఏ చట్టం ద్వారానూ అనర్హుడు కాని వ్యక్తి మాత్రమే కాంట్రాక్టు చేయగలడు (సెక్షన్ 11). మైనర్ ప్రామిసరీ నోటుపై సంతకం చేయవచ్చు, కానీ ఆ నోటు మైనర్‌ను తప్ప మిగతా అందరినీ బంధిస్తుంది (Negotiable Instruments Act, సెక్షన్ 26).
te.meaning:
ఒప్పందం లేకుండా చట్టం బాధ్యత విధించే ఐదు సందర్భాల్లో ( క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు ) సెక్షన్ 68 ఒకటి. ఇది "incapable of entering into a contract " (కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేని) వ్యక్తికి వర్తిస్తుంది. అంటే సెక్షన్ 11 పరీక్షలో నెగ్గని వ్యక్తి: మైనర్, మతిస్థిమితం లేని వ్యక్తి, లేదా చట్టం ద్వారా అనర్హుడైన వ్యక్తి. అవసరమైన వస్తువులు అంటే ఏమిటి. చట్టం necessaries ని నిర్వచించలేదు. సెక్షన్‌లోనే పరీక్ష ఇచ్చింది: అవి "suited to his condition in life" (అతని జీవన స్థితికి తగినవి) అయి ఉండాలి. కోర్టులు రెండో పరీక్షను జోడిస్తాయి: సరఫరా సమయంలో ఆ వ్యక్తికి నిజంగా ఉన్న అవసరం. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం రెండు పక్షాలకూ న్యాయం. మైనర్ ఒప్పందాలను చెల్లనివి (void) గా చేసి, చట్టం అతన్ని చెడ్డ బేరాల నుంచి కాపాడుతుంది. ఆ కారణంగా అతను ఆకలితో ఉండాలని చట్టం కోరుకోదు. కాబట్టి సరఫరాదారు డబ్బు వసూలు చేసుకోవచ్చు, కానీ మైనర్ సొంత ఆస్తి నుంచి మాత్రమే. ఇది అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత ను నివారిస్తుంది. కోర్టు అడిగే ప్రశ్నలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పెట్టెలను వరుసగా కిందికి చదవండి. "కాదు" అనే జవాబు మిమ్మల్ని పక్కన ఉన్న ఫలితానికి పంపుతుంది. flowchart TD Q1["1. సరఫరా పొందినవారు కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేనివారా,
లేదా అలాంటి వ్యక్తి పోషించాల్సినవారా? (సె. 68)"] Q2["2. సరుకులు లేదా సేవలు అతని జీవన స్థితికి
తగిన అవసరమైన వస్తువులా? (సె. 68)"] Q3["3. సరఫరా సమయంలో నిజంగా అవసరమా,
ఇప్పటికే తగినంత లేదా?"] Q4["4. అసమర్థుడికి ఆస్తి ఉందా?"] Y["సరఫరాదారుకు అసమర్థుడి ఆస్తి
నుంచి చెల్లింపు. ఆ వ్యక్తి
స్వయంగా బాధ్యుడు కాడు."] N1["సె. 68 వర్తించదు.
సాధారణ కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం నిర్ణయిస్తుంది."] N2["క్లెయిమ్ లేదు."] N3["క్లెయిమ్ లేదు."] N4["చెల్లించడానికి
ఏమీ లేదు."] Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2 Q2 -->|"అవును"| Q3 Q3 -->|"అవును"| Q4 Q4 -->|"అవును"| Y Q1 -->|"కాదు"| N1 Q2 -->|"కాదు"| N2 Q3 -->|"కాదు"| N3 Q4 -->|"కాదు"| N4 వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: సరఫరా పొందినవారు కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేనివారా, లేదా అలాంటి వ్యక్తి పోషించాల్సినవారా? కాకపోతే సెక్షన్ 68 వర్తించదు, సాధారణ కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. ప్రశ్న 2: సరుకులు లేదా సేవలు అతని జీవన స్థితికి తగిన అవసరమైన వస్తువులా? కాకపోతే క్లెయిమ్ లేదు. ప్రశ్న 3: సరఫరా సమయంలో అతనికి నిజంగా అవసరమా, ఇప్పటికే తగినంత లేదా? కాకపోతే క్లెయిమ్ లేదు. ప్రశ్న 4: అసమర్థుడికి ఆస్తి ఉందా? లేకపోతే చెల్లించడానికి ఏమీ లేదు. అన్నీ అవును అయితే సరఫరాదారుకు అసమర్థుడి ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లింపు; ఆ వ్యక్తి స్వయంగా బాధ్యుడు కాడు.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 68 కింద అవసరమైన వస్తువులు సరఫరా చేసినవారికి ఎవరి నుంచి తిరిగి చెల్లింపు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: అసమర్థుడి ఆస్తి నుంచి. ఆ వ్యక్తి స్వయంగా బాధ్యుడు కాడు.

selfTest.q: 2. సరుకులు అవసరమైన వస్తువులా కాదా అని ఏ రెండు పరీక్షలు నిర్ణయిస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: అవి అతని జీవన స్థితికి తగినవి కావాలి, సరఫరా సమయంలో అతని నిజమైన అవసరాలను తీర్చాలి.

selfTest.q: 3. అవసరమైన వస్తువుల కోసం ఒక కిరాణా వ్యాపారి దగ్గర మైనర్ ప్రామిసరీ నోటు ఉంది. ఆ నోటుపై దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. నోటు మైనర్‌ను బంధించదు. వ్యాపారి సెక్షన్ 68 కింద మైనర్ ఆస్తి నుంచి అవసరమైన వస్తువుల ధరను క్లెయిమ్ చేస్తాడు.

selfTest.q: 4. మతిస్థిమితం లేని B భార్యాపిల్లలకు A ఆహారం సరఫరా చేస్తాడు. A కు డబ్బు వస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: వస్తుంది. B ఆస్తి నుంచి A కు తిరిగి చెల్లింపు వస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 68, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 5. ఒక డాక్టరు ఒక స్త్రీతో ఒప్పందం ప్రకారం ఆమెకు చికిత్స చేసి, సమర్థుడైన పెద్దవాడైన ఆమె భర్తపై సెక్షన్ 68 కింద దావా వేస్తాడు. గెలుస్తాడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పోషించాల్సిన వ్యక్తి కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేనివాడు అయినప్పుడే సెక్షన్ 68 వర్తిస్తుంది ( Kanhayalal ).
