hi.inOneMinute: A minor or a person of unsound mind cannot make a binding contract. Yet he must eat, dress and stay healthy. Section 68 lets a person who supplies him with necessaries be paid back from his property. The supplier cannot sue the incapable person on a promise, because there is none. He claims under the law, and only against the property. In exams, the two tests for necessaries and the property-only rule earn the marks. In real life, it protects the grocer, the doctor and the school that serve a minor.
legalProvision: Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person. Illustrations. (a) A supplies B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to his condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property. (b) A supplies the wife and children of B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to their condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property.
Related provisions

Section 11. Who are competent to contract. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 12 (first sentence). What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting. A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract, if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 26 (second paragraph). Minor. —A minor may draw, indorse, deliver and negotiate such instrument so as to bind all parties except himself.
In simple words

If a person who cannot contract , or anyone he must support by law, is supplied with necessaries that suit his condition in life, the supplier is paid back from that person's property. "Lunatic" is the Act's old word for a person of unsound mind. A person can contract only if he is a major, of sound mind , and not disqualified by law (Section 11). A minor may sign a promissory note , but the note binds everyone except the minor (Section 26, Negotiable Instruments Act).
hi.meaning:
Section 68 is one of the five situations in which the law imposes a duty without agreement (a quasi contract ). It applies to a person who is "incapable of entering into a contract". That means a person who fails the test of Section 11: a minor, a person of unsound mind, or a person disqualified by law. What are necessaries. The Act does not define necessaries. It gives the test in the section itself: they must be "suited to his condition in life". The courts add a second test, which is the person's actual need at the time of supply. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness to both sides. The law protects a minor from bad bargains by making his agreements void . It does not want him to starve for that reason. So it lets the supplier recover, but only from the minor's own property. This prevents unjust enrichment . See Diagram 1 for the questions a court asks. Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. incapable person's property.
The person himself is not liable."] N1["s. 68 does not apply.

to be reimbursed."] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4 Q4 -->|"Yes"| Y Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q4 -->|"No"| N4 Text description Question 1: is the person supplied incapable of entering into a contract, or someone whom such a person must support? If no, Section 68 does not apply and ordinary contract law decides. Question 2: are the goods or services necessaries, suited to his condition in life? If no, there is no claim. Question 3: did he actually need them when they were supplied, and was he not already enough supplied? If no, there is no claim. Question 4: does the incapable person own property? If no, there is nothing from which to be reimbursed. If every answer is yes, the supplier is reimbursed from the incapable person's property; the person himself is not liable.
keyPoints: Section 68 repays a person who supplies necessaries to someone incapable of contracting. Persons incapable of contracting are those who fail Section 11: a minor, a person of unsound mind, a disqualified person. Necessaries must suit the person's condition in life and his actual need. The supplier is repaid from the incapable person's property only. The incapable person is not personally liable ( Mohori Bibee ). Dependants of the incapable person are covered (Illustration (b)). A promissory note signed by a minor does not bind him, so the supplier claims under Section 68. A minor is outside Section 70, because Section 68 provides for his case ( B.K. Mondal ).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. On 20 July 1895 Dharmodas Ghose, a minor, mortgaged his houses to Brahmo Dutt, a moneylender, to secure Rs. 20,000. The lender's attorney knew he was a minor. The Privy Council decided the appeal on 4 March 1903. Principle. A minor is not competent to contract, and his agreement is void. Sections 64 and 65 do not apply, because they assume a contract between competent parties. Under Section 68 the infant is not liable even for necessaries, "though a statutory claim is created against his property". [1903] UKPC 12 (Privy Council, 4 March 1903). Why it matters. It is the reason a supplier of necessaries has no contract claim and must use Section 68. State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. The State argued that it was like a minor, and so could not be made to pay under Section 70 where its contract was invalid. Principle. The Court said a minor is outside Section 70 because "his case has been specifically provided for by s. 68", and because he cannot voluntarily accept a benefit. The State was not in that position. AIR 1962 SC 779 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It confirms that Section 68 is the special rule for incapable persons. Nash v. Inman (1908) Facts. A Savile Row tailor sued Inman, a Cambridge undergraduate who was a minor, for clothes that included eleven fancy waistcoats. The trial judge found that Inman was already amply supplied with clothes. [1908] 2 KB 1 (Court of Appeal). Principle. The supplier must prove that the goods suited the minor's condition in life and that he was not already sufficiently supplied with them. Why it matters. It supplies the second test for necessaries. Kanhayalal Bisandayal Bhiwapurkar v. Indarchandji Hamirmalji Sisodia (1947) Facts. An eye specialist sued a husband for Rs. 188 for removing his wife's cataract, under an agreement with her and her son-in-law. Principle. Section 68 covers "the dependent of a person incompetent to contract". The husband "was not incompetent to contract", so it did not apply. AIR 1947 Nag 84 (Nagpur High Court). Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 68.

selfTest.q: 1. From whom is a supplier of necessaries reimbursed under Section 68?
selfTest.a: From the property of the incapable person. The person himself is not liable.

selfTest.q: 2. What two tests decide whether goods are necessaries?
selfTest.a: They must suit his condition in life, and they must meet his actual requirements at the time of supply.

selfTest.q: 3. A grocer holds a minor's promissory note for necessaries. Can he sue on the note?
selfTest.a: No. The note does not bind the minor. The grocer claims the price of the necessaries under Section 68 from the minor's property.

selfTest.q: 4. A supplies food to the wife and children of B, a person of unsound mind. Can A recover?
selfTest.a: Yes. A is reimbursed from B's property (Section 68, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 5. A doctor treats a woman under an agreement with her and sues her husband, who is a competent adult, under Section 68. Will he succeed?
selfTest.a: No. Section 68 applies only where the person bound to support is incapable of contracting ( Kanhayalal ).

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes a person must pay another's debt to save his own interest. Section 69 gives him a right to be paid back by the person who should have paid. Two things must be present. The payer has a real interest in the payment, and the other person is bound by law to pay. The payer must pay "therefore", that is, because of that interest. In exams, the two conditions and the Act's illustration of the Bengal lease earn the marks. In real life, it protects a tenant, buyer or co-owner who pays a landlord's or seller's dues to stop a forced sale.
legalProvision: Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other. Illustration. B holds land in Bengal, on a lease granted by A, the zamindar. The revenue payable by A to the Government being in arrear, his land is advertised for sale by the Government. Under the revenue law, the consequence of such sale will be the annulment of B's lease. B, to prevent the sale and the consequent annulment of his own lease, pays to the Government the sum due from A. A is bound to make good to B the amount so paid.
Related provisions

Section 43 (second and third paragraphs). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares.

Section 145. Implied promise to indemnify surety. In every contract of guarantee there is an implied promise by the principal debtor to indemnify the surety, and the surety is entitled to recover from the principal debtor whatever sum he has rightfully paid under the guarantee, but, no sums which he has paid wrongfully.
Section 72, Illustration (a). A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B.
In simple words

A person who is interested in the payment of money that another is bound by law to pay, and who pays it for that reason, gets the money back from the other. In the illustration, B, the lessee , pays the revenue that A, the zamindar, owed, to stop a sale that would end B's lease. A must make good to B what B paid. "In arrear" means unpaid after it fell due.
en.meaning:
Section 69 is one of the five situations of quasi contract . The Act does not define "interested". It does not need to, because the section describes the whole claim: an interested person pays what another must pay by law, and the other reimburses him. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness. The payer saved the debtor from the result of his own default. If the law let the debtor keep that saving for free, the debtor would be made richer at the payer's cost. This is unjust enrichment , and the law prevents it. Not a promise. The claim does not come from any promise by the debtor. It comes from the law. English source. The English earlier form of the rule is Exall v. Partridge (1799). See Diagram 1 for the parties in the Act's own illustration. Diagram 1. The boxes are the parties. The arrows say what each one does. The dotted arrow shows what the law gives B. flowchart LR A["A, the zamindar
owes land revenue, unpaid"] G["The Government
advertises A's land for sale"] B["B, the lessee
a sale would annul his lease"] A -->|"owes revenue"| G B -->|"pays the revenue due from A,
to save his lease"| G B -.->|"s. 69: A must make good
the amount paid"| A N["If B had no interest and paid out of kindness:
no right to be reimbursed"] B --- N Text description A, the zamindar, owes land revenue to the Government and has not paid. The Government advertises A's land for sale; the sale would annul the lease of B, the lessee. B pays the Government the revenue due from A, to save his lease. The Government's claim for that revenue ends. Under Section 69, A must make good to B the amount paid. If B had no interest and paid only out of kindness, he would have no right to be reimbursed.
keyPoints: Section 69 reimburses a person who pays money that another was bound by law to pay. The payer must be interested in the payment; a legal proprietary interest is not needed ( Seksaria ). The payment must be made "therefore", to protect that interest. The other person's duty may come from a statute, a contract or a decree. The right is to the sum paid and nothing more. A volunteer with no interest has no claim. The debtor's promise is not needed; the right comes from the law.

caseLaws.name: Govindram Gordhandas Seksaria v
caseLaws.facts: State of Gondal (1949) Facts. The State of Gondal sold two Bombay mills (the Currimbhoy and Mahomedbhoy Mills) to Seksaria, who sub-sold them to a company. Municipal taxes of Rs. 1,24,092-1-0 were outstanding on the mills. Neither the seller nor the debenture trustees in possession paid. On 23 February 1939 the company paid Rs. 78,466-12-0 to the Municipality to avoid a forced sale, and claimed reimbursement. Principle. "Interested" does not require a legal proprietary interest. "Bound by law to pay" extends "to any obligation which is an effective bond in law", including one arising by contract. The company recovered under Section 69. Privy Council, 19 December 1949 : (1950) 52 Bom LR 450. Why it matters. It gives the widest reading of the two conditions of Section 69. Radha Madhub Samonta v. Sasti Ram Sen (1899) Facts. The plaintiff bought a putni (a kind of tenure) at a sale in May 1892. On 12 May 1894 the sale was set aside, and the zamindar's appeal against that order was pending. During the appeal the zamindar demanded the rent that had fallen due, and on 16 May 1895 the plaintiff paid about Rs. 2,000. He then sued the defaulting putnidars (the tenure holders) for reimbursement under Section 69. Principle. Maclean CJ said: "It is difficult to say that, at the time the plaintiff made the payment, he was not interested." He was not "a mere volunteer". The putnidars' liability for the rent "cannot be disputed", so they were bound by law to pay. (1899) ILR 26 Cal 826 (Calcutta High Court, 22 February 1899). Why it matters. A doubtful title does not defeat the payer's interest. Exall v. Partridge (1799) Facts. Exall left his carriage at the premises of Partridge, a coachbuilder, for repair. The landlord seized the carriage as distress for rent that Partridge and his co-tenants owed. Exall paid the rent to recover the carriage and sued Partridge and the others. (1799) 8 TR 308 (Court of King's Bench). Principle. The payment was compulsory and not voluntary, so Exall could recover the money. Why it matters. It is the English forerunner of Section 69.

selfTest.q: 1. What two conditions does Section 69 require?
selfTest.a: The payer must be interested in the payment, and the other person must be bound by law to pay the money.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a stranger who pays a debt out of kindness recover under Section 69?
selfTest.a: No. He has no interest in the payment, so the section does not apply.

selfTest.q: 3. In the Act's illustration, why is B entitled to be reimbursed?
selfTest.a: B paid the Government the revenue that A owed, to prevent a sale that would end B's lease. B was interested and A was bound by law to pay.

selfTest.q: 4. Does "bound by law to pay" cover a duty that arises from a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. It extends to any obligation which is an effective bond in law, including one under a contract ( Seksaria ).

selfTest.q: 5. Mohan pays ₹1,20,000 of Lata's property tax to save his lease. How much can he recover?
selfTest.a: ₹1,20,000, the sum he paid. Section 69 gives reimbursement, not profit or damages.

Illustration లో, కౌలుదారు B, తన కౌలును రద్దు చేసే అమ్మకాన్ని ఆపడానికి, జమీందారు A బాకీ పడిన శిస్తును చెల్లిస్తాడు. B చెల్లించినదాన్ని A తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. "In arrear" అంటే గడువు తీరినా చెల్లించనిది.
te.meaning:
క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు లోని ఐదు సందర్భాల్లో సెక్షన్ 69 ఒకటి. చట్టం "interested" (ఆసక్తి ఉన్న) ను నిర్వచించలేదు. నిర్వచించాల్సిన అవసరం కూడా లేదు, ఎందుకంటే సెక్షన్ మొత్తం క్లెయిమ్‌ను వివరిస్తుంది: మరొకరు చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సినదాన్ని ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యక్తి చెల్లిస్తాడు, ఆ మరొకరు అతనికి తిరిగి చెల్లిస్తాడు. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం న్యాయం. అప్పుదారు (debtor) తన సొంత పొరపాటు ఫలితం నుంచి చెల్లింపుదారు అతన్ని కాపాడాడు. ఆ మేలును అప్పుదారు ఉచితంగా ఉంచుకోనిస్తే, చెల్లింపుదారు ఖర్చుతో అప్పుదారు ధనవంతుడవుతాడు. ఇదే అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత , చట్టం దాన్ని నివారిస్తుంది. వాగ్దానం కాదు. క్లెయిమ్ అప్పుదారు చేసిన ఏ వాగ్దానం నుంచీ రాదు. చట్టం నుంచి వస్తుంది. ఇంగ్లిష్ మూలం. ఈ నియమానికి ముందున్న ఇంగ్లిష్ రూపం Exall v. Partridge (1799). చట్టంలోని Illustration లోని పక్షాలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 69 ఏ రెండు షరతులను కోరుతుంది?
selfTest.a: చెల్లింపుదారుకు ఆ చెల్లింపులో ఆసక్తి ఉండాలి, మరొక వ్యక్తి ఆ డబ్బును చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సి ఉండాలి.

selfTest.q: 2. దయతో ఒక బాకీని చెల్లించిన అపరిచితుడు సెక్షన్ 69 కింద డబ్బు తిరిగి పొందగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అతనికి చెల్లింపులో ఆసక్తి లేదు, కాబట్టి సెక్షన్ వర్తించదు.

selfTest.q: 3. చట్టంలోని Illustration లో B కి తిరిగి చెల్లింపు ఎందుకు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: B కౌలును ముగించే అమ్మకాన్ని ఆపడానికి, A బాకీ ఉన్న శిస్తును B ప్రభుత్వానికి చెల్లించాడు. B కి ఆసక్తి ఉంది, A చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సి ఉంది.

selfTest.q: 4. కాంట్రాక్టు నుంచి వచ్చే బాధ్యతను "bound by law to pay" కవర్ చేస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: చేస్తుంది. కాంట్రాక్టు కింద వచ్చేదానితో సహా, చట్టప్రకారం అమలు చేయగల ఏ బాధ్యతకైనా అది విస్తరిస్తుంది ( Seksaria ).

selfTest.q: 5. తన కౌలును కాపాడుకోవడానికి మోహన్ లత ఆస్తి పన్ను ₹1,20,000 చెల్లిస్తాడు. అతను ఎంత తిరిగి పొందగలడు?
selfTest.a: ₹1,20,000, తాను చెల్లించిన మొత్తం. సెక్షన్ 69 తిరిగి చెల్లింపు ఇస్తుంది, లాభం లేదా నష్టపరిహారం కాదు.

hi.inOneMinute: Sometimes a person must pay another's debt to save his own interest. Section 69 gives him a right to be paid back by the person who should have paid. Two things must be present. The payer has a real interest in the payment, and the other person is bound by law to pay. The payer must pay "therefore", that is, because of that interest. In exams, the two conditions and the Act's illustration of the Bengal lease earn the marks. In real life, it protects a tenant, buyer or co-owner who pays a landlord's or seller's dues to stop a forced sale.
legalProvision: Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other. Illustration. B holds land in Bengal, on a lease granted by A, the zamindar. The revenue payable by A to the Government being in arrear, his land is advertised for sale by the Government. Under the revenue law, the consequence of such sale will be the annulment of B's lease. B, to prevent the sale and the consequent annulment of his own lease, pays to the Government the sum due from A. A is bound to make good to B the amount so paid.
Related provisions

Section 43 (second and third paragraphs). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares.

Section 145. Implied promise to indemnify surety. In every contract of guarantee there is an implied promise by the principal debtor to indemnify the surety, and the surety is entitled to recover from the principal debtor whatever sum he has rightfully paid under the guarantee, but, no sums which he has paid wrongfully.
Section 72, Illustration (a). A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B.
In simple words

A person who is interested in the payment of money that another is bound by law to pay, and who pays it for that reason, gets the money back from the other. In the illustration, B, the lessee , pays the revenue that A, the zamindar, owed, to stop a sale that would end B's lease. A must make good to B what B paid. "In arrear" means unpaid after it fell due.
hi.meaning:
Section 69 is one of the five situations of quasi contract . The Act does not define "interested". It does not need to, because the section describes the whole claim: an interested person pays what another must pay by law, and the other reimburses him. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness. The payer saved the debtor from the result of his own default. If the law let the debtor keep that saving for free, the debtor would be made richer at the payer's cost. This is unjust enrichment , and the law prevents it. Not a promise. The claim does not come from any promise by the debtor. It comes from the law. English source. The English earlier form of the rule is Exall v. Partridge (1799). See Diagram 1 for the parties in the Act's own illustration. Diagram 1. The boxes are the parties. The arrows say what each one does. The dotted arrow shows what the law gives B. flowchart LR A["A, the zamindar
owes land revenue, unpaid"] G["The Government
advertises A's land for sale"] B["B, the lessee
a sale would annul his lease"] A -->|"owes revenue"| G B -->|"pays the revenue due from A,
to save his lease"| G B -.->|"s. 69: A must make good
the amount paid"| A N["If B had no interest and paid out of kindness:
no right to be reimbursed"] B --- N Text description A, the zamindar, owes land revenue to the Government and has not paid. The Government advertises A's land for sale; the sale would annul the lease of B, the lessee. B pays the Government the revenue due from A, to save his lease. The Government's claim for that revenue ends. Under Section 69, A must make good to B the amount paid. If B had no interest and paid only out of kindness, he would have no right to be reimbursed.
keyPoints: Section 69 reimburses a person who pays money that another was bound by law to pay. The payer must be interested in the payment; a legal proprietary interest is not needed ( Seksaria ). The payment must be made "therefore", to protect that interest. The other person's duty may come from a statute, a contract or a decree. The right is to the sum paid and nothing more. A volunteer with no interest has no claim. The debtor's promise is not needed; the right comes from the law.

caseLaws.name: Govindram Gordhandas Seksaria v
caseLaws.facts: State of Gondal (1949) Facts. The State of Gondal sold two Bombay mills (the Currimbhoy and Mahomedbhoy Mills) to Seksaria, who sub-sold them to a company. Municipal taxes of Rs. 1,24,092-1-0 were outstanding on the mills. Neither the seller nor the debenture trustees in possession paid. On 23 February 1939 the company paid Rs. 78,466-12-0 to the Municipality to avoid a forced sale, and claimed reimbursement. Principle. "Interested" does not require a legal proprietary interest. "Bound by law to pay" extends "to any obligation which is an effective bond in law", including one arising by contract. The company recovered under Section 69. Privy Council, 19 December 1949 : (1950) 52 Bom LR 450. Why it matters. It gives the widest reading of the two conditions of Section 69. Radha Madhub Samonta v. Sasti Ram Sen (1899) Facts. The plaintiff bought a putni (a kind of tenure) at a sale in May 1892. On 12 May 1894 the sale was set aside, and the zamindar's appeal against that order was pending. During the appeal the zamindar demanded the rent that had fallen due, and on 16 May 1895 the plaintiff paid about Rs. 2,000. He then sued the defaulting putnidars (the tenure holders) for reimbursement under Section 69. Principle. Maclean CJ said: "It is difficult to say that, at the time the plaintiff made the payment, he was not interested." He was not "a mere volunteer". The putnidars' liability for the rent "cannot be disputed", so they were bound by law to pay. (1899) ILR 26 Cal 826 (Calcutta High Court, 22 February 1899). Why it matters. A doubtful title does not defeat the payer's interest. Exall v. Partridge (1799) Facts. Exall left his carriage at the premises of Partridge, a coachbuilder, for repair. The landlord seized the carriage as distress for rent that Partridge and his co-tenants owed. Exall paid the rent to recover the carriage and sued Partridge and the others. (1799) 8 TR 308 (Court of King's Bench). Principle. The payment was compulsory and not voluntary, so Exall could recover the money. Why it matters. It is the English forerunner of Section 69.

selfTest.q: 1. What two conditions does Section 69 require?
selfTest.a: The payer must be interested in the payment, and the other person must be bound by law to pay the money.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a stranger who pays a debt out of kindness recover under Section 69?
selfTest.a: No. He has no interest in the payment, so the section does not apply.

selfTest.q: 3. In the Act's illustration, why is B entitled to be reimbursed?
selfTest.a: B paid the Government the revenue that A owed, to prevent a sale that would end B's lease. B was interested and A was bound by law to pay.

selfTest.q: 4. Does "bound by law to pay" cover a duty that arises from a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. It extends to any obligation which is an effective bond in law, including one under a contract ( Seksaria ).

selfTest.q: 5. Mohan pays ₹1,20,000 of Lata's property tax to save his lease. How much can he recover?
selfTest.a: ₹1,20,000, the sum he paid. Section 69 gives reimbursement, not profit or damages.

law-of-contract-i-u4-t4.subtitle: Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A person does work for you, or hands you goods, expecting to be paid. There is no valid contract . You accept the work or goods and use them. Section 70 says you must pay for them, or give them back. Three conditions must be met: a lawful act, no intention to give it free, and a benefit that you enjoyed. The person asked to pay must have been free to refuse. In exams, the three conditions and State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons earn the marks. In real life, it protects contractors and suppliers whose contract fails for a technical reason.
legalProvision: Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered. Illustrations. (a) A, a tradesman, leaves goods at B's house by mistake. B treats the goods as his own. He is bound to pay A for them. (b) A saves B's property from fire. A is not entitled to compensation from B, if the circumstances show that he intended to act gratuitously.
Related provisions

Constitution of India, Article 299(1). All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.

Government of India Act, 1935, Section 175(3) (as summarised in the headnote to B.K. Mondal ): all contracts made in the exercise of the executive authority of a province shall be expressed to be made by the Governor of the province and shall be executed on behalf of the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.
In simple words

Where a person lawfully does something for another, or delivers something to him, not meaning it to be free of charge, and the other receives and uses the benefit, the other must pay compensation for it or give it back. Illustration (a): goods left at the wrong house by mistake, and used as one's own, must be paid for. Illustration (b): a person who saves another's property from fire, meaning it as a favour, cannot claim payment. Contracts of the Government must be made in the form Article 299(1) lays down (earlier, Section 175(3) of the 1935 Act).
en.meaning:
Section 70 is the widest of the five quasi-contractual claims. It covers any lawful act or delivery that was not meant as a gift . Gratuitous and non-gratuitous. A "gratuitous" act is one done free of charge, as a favour or gift. A "non-gratuitous" act is one done in the expectation of payment. Why the law has this rule. The reason is unjust enrichment . The person who accepted the benefit should not keep it for nothing. In B.K. Mondal the Supreme Court said that Section 70 "deals with cases where there is no valid contract". The claim is for compensation or restoration. It is not for damages for breach of contract . See Diagram 1 for the questions a court asks. Diagram 1. Start at the top. If an answer ends the claim, stop at the box beside it. Otherwise follow the arrow down. flowchart TD Q1["1. Did the claimant lawfully do something for
the other person, or deliver something to him?"] Q2["2. Did he act without
intending it as a gift?"] Q3["3. Could the other person refuse or return it,
and did he instead accept and enjoy the benefit?"] Q4["4. Is there a valid contract that fixes
the payment for the same work?"] Y["All tests met: compensation for the thing
done or delivered, or restoration (s. 70)"] N1["No claim"] N2["Meant as a gift: no claim
(Illustration (b))"] N3["No choice, or not accepted:
no claim"] C["The claim lies under the contract,
not s. 70"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4 Q4 -->|"No"| Y Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q4 -->|"Yes"| C Text description Question 1: did the claimant lawfully do something for the other person, or deliver something to him? If no, there is no claim. Question 2: did he act without intending it as a gift? If it was meant as a gift, there is no claim (Illustration (b)). Question 3: could the other person have refused or returned the thing, and did he instead accept and enjoy the benefit? If he had no choice or did not accept, there is no claim. Question 4: is there a valid contract that fixes the payment for the same work? If yes, the claim lies under the contract, not Section 70. If no, all tests are met: the other person must pay compensation for the thing done or delivered, or restore it.
keyPoints: Section 70 has three conditions: a lawful act, no intention to give it free, and a benefit enjoyed. "Lawfully" is an essential part of the section; the act must not be fraudulent, dishonest or gratuitous. The receiver must be free to refuse or return, and must voluntarily accept. The claim is for compensation or restoration, not damages for breach. It applies where there is no valid contract, including a Government contract made without the prescribed form. A request is not an element of Section 70. It does not apply where a valid contract fixes the payment. A minor is outside Section 70 because Section 68 provides for his case.

caseLaws.name: State of West Bengal v
caseLaws.facts: B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. In 1944 a firm of contractors built a kutcha road, guard room, office, kitchen and rooms for clerks at Arambagh, and storage sheds at Khanakul, for the State's Civil Supplies Department, on its officers' requests. It claimed Rs. 19,325. The contracts did not meet Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. Principle. Section 70 has three conditions and applies where there is no valid contract. The State had voluntarily accepted and used the work, so it had to pay. AIR 1962 SC 779 : 1962 Supp (1) SCR 876 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It is the leading case on Section 70. Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968) Facts. A Section 70 claim was made against a State on a contract that did not comply with Section 175(3). The Court held Section 175(3) mandatory and based on public policy. Principle. If the three conditions are met, the claimant can invoke Section 70. He cannot sue for specific performance or damages, because there is no contract. His claim rests on "quasi-contract or restitution". (1968) 3 SCR 214 (Supreme Court). Why it matters. It states the nature of the Section 70 claim. Alopi Parshad and Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) Facts. Under a written agreement of 3 May 1937, the agents bought ghee for the Government at fixed rates. An arbitration award gave them further sums. The Supreme Court held the award liable to be set aside and dismissed the agents' appeal. Principle. "For work done or services rendered pursuant to the terms of a contract, compensation quantum meruit cannot be awarded where the contract provides for the consideration payable". AIR 1960 SC 588 : (1960) 2 SCR 793 (Supreme Court, 20 January 1960). Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 70 and of quantum meruit. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. MTNL retained money from Tata Communications' bills under a purchase order that capped liquidated damages at 12 per cent. The Supreme Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1766 of 2019 on 27 February 2019. Principle. Each section in this chapter assumes no contractual relationship. Section 74 governed, so only the contract figure could be claimed and the excess was refunded. Why it matters. It supports the rule that a party governed by a contract must claim under the contract.

selfTest.q: 1. What three conditions does Section 70 require?
selfTest.a: The claimant lawfully did something for, or delivered something to, another. He did not mean it as a gift. The other person enjoyed the benefit.

selfTest.q: 2. A neighbour saves your goods from a fire out of goodwill. Can he claim payment?
selfTest.a: No. He acted gratuitously (Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. Can the State escape Section 70 because its officers did not follow the form for Government contracts?
selfTest.a: No. It must pay if it voluntarily accepted and enjoyed the work ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 4. A tradesman leaves goods at your house by mistake and you return them at once. Must you pay?
selfTest.a: No. You did not accept or enjoy them. Liability arises only on voluntary acceptance ( B.K. Mondal ; Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a supplier claim quantum meruit under Section 70 when a valid contract fixes his rates?
selfTest.a: No. The contract rate governs ( Alopi Parshad ; MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

legalProvision: Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered. Illustrations. (a) A, a tradesman, leaves goods at B's house by mistake. B treats the goods as his own. He is bound to pay A for them. (b) A saves B's property from fire. A is not entitled to compensation from B, if the circumstances show that he intended to act gratuitously.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు

Constitution of India, Article 299(1). All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.

Government of India Act, 1935, Section 175(3) (as summarised in the headnote to B.K. Mondal ): all contracts made in the exercise of the executive authority of a province shall be expressed to be made by the Governor of the province and shall be executed on behalf of the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.
సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే

ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరి కోసం చట్టబద్ధంగా ఏదైనా చేసినా, ఏదైనా అందజేసినా, అది ఉచితంగా కాదని ఉద్దేశించి, ఆ మరొకరు దాని ప్రయోజనాన్ని పొంది వాడుకుంటే, అతను దానికి పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. Illustration (a): పొరపాటున వేరే ఇంట్లో వదిలిన సరుకులను సొంతవిగా వాడుకుంటే వాటికి డబ్బు చెల్లించాలి. Illustration (b): సహాయంగా ఉద్దేశించి మరొకరి ఆస్తిని అగ్ని నుంచి కాపాడిన వ్యక్తి డబ్బు అడగలేడు. ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టులు Article 299(1) చెప్పిన రూపంలో చేయాలి (ఇంతకుముందు 1935 చట్టం సెక్షన్ 175(3)).
te.meaning:
ఐదు క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు క్లెయిమ్‌లలో సెక్షన్ 70 అత్యంత విస్తృతమైనది. దానం (gift) గా ఉద్దేశించని ఏ చట్టబద్ధమైన పనినైనా, అందజేతనైనా ఇది కవర్ చేస్తుంది. ఉచితం, ఉచితం కానిది. "gratuitous" (ఉచిత) పని అంటే సహాయంగా లేదా దానంగా ఉచితంగా చేసినది. "non-gratuitous" (ఉచితం కాని) పని అంటే చెల్లింపు ఆశించి చేసినది. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత . ప్రయోజనాన్ని అంగీకరించినవాడు దాన్ని ఏమీ ఇవ్వకుండా ఉంచుకోకూడదు. సెక్షన్ 70 "deals with cases where there is no valid contract " అని B.K. Mondal లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. క్లెయిమ్ పరిహారం లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం కోసం. కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనకు నష్టపరిహారం (damages) కోసం కాదు. కోర్టు అడిగే ప్రశ్నలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పై నుంచి మొదలుపెట్టండి. ఒక జవాబు క్లెయిమ్‌ను ముగిస్తే పక్కన ఉన్న పెట్టె దగ్గర ఆగండి. లేకపోతే బాణం వెంట కిందికి వెళ్లండి. flowchart TD Q1["1. క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవాడు మరొకరి కోసం చట్టబద్ధంగా
ఏదైనా చేశాడా, లేదా అందజేశాడా?"] Q2["2. దానంగా ఉద్దేశించకుండా
చేశాడా?"] Q3["3. మరొకరు నిరాకరించగలిగినా, తిరిగి ఇవ్వగలిగినా,
ప్రయోజనాన్ని అంగీకరించి అనుభవించారా?"] Q4["4. అదే పనికి చెల్లింపును నిర్ణయించే
చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు ఉందా?"] Y["అన్ని పరీక్షలూ నెరవేరాయి: చేసినదానికి లేదా
అందజేసినదానికి పరిహారం, లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం (సె. 70)"] N1["క్లెయిమ్ లేదు"] N2["దానంగా ఉద్దేశించారు: క్లెయిమ్ లేదు
(Illustration (b))"] N3["ఎంపిక లేదు, లేదా అంగీకరించలేదు:
క్లెయిమ్ లేదు"] C["క్లెయిమ్ కాంట్రాక్టు కింద ఉంటుంది,
సె. 70 కింద కాదు"] Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2 Q2 -->|"అవును"| Q3 Q3 -->|"అవును"| Q4 Q4 -->|"లేదు"| Y Q1 -->|"కాదు"| N1 Q2 -->|"కాదు"| N2 Q3 -->|"కాదు"| N3 Q4 -->|"ఉంది"| C వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవాడు మరొకరి కోసం చట్టబద్ధంగా ఏదైనా చేశాడా, లేదా అందజేశాడా? లేకపోతే క్లెయిమ్ లేదు. ప్రశ్న 2: దానంగా ఉద్దేశించకుండా చేశాడా? దానంగా ఉద్దేశిస్తే క్లెయిమ్ లేదు (Illustration (b)). ప్రశ్న 3: మరొకరు నిరాకరించగలిగి లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వగలిగి, అలా చేయకుండా ప్రయోజనాన్ని అంగీకరించి అనుభవించారా? ఎంపిక లేకపోయినా, అంగీకరించకపోయినా క్లెయిమ్ లేదు. ప్రశ్న 4: అదే పనికి చెల్లింపును నిర్ణయించే చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు ఉందా? ఉంటే క్లెయిమ్ కాంట్రాక్టు కింద, సెక్షన్ 70 కింద కాదు. లేకపోతే అన్ని పరీక్షలూ నెరవేరాయి: మరొకరు పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి, లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 70 ఏ మూడు షరతులను కోరుతుంది?
selfTest.a: క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవాడు మరొకరి కోసం చట్టబద్ధంగా ఏదైనా చేశాడు లేదా అందజేశాడు. దాన్ని దానంగా ఉద్దేశించలేదు. మరొకరు ప్రయోజనాన్ని అనుభవించారు.

selfTest.q: 2. ఒక పొరుగువాడు సద్భావనతో మీ సరుకులను అగ్ని నుంచి కాపాడుతాడు. అతను డబ్బు అడగగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అతను ఉచితంగా చేశాడు (Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. అధికారులు ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టుల రూపాన్ని పాటించలేదని రాష్ట్రం సెక్షన్ 70 నుంచి తప్పించుకోగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పనిని స్వచ్ఛందంగా అంగీకరించి అనుభవిస్తే చెల్లించాలి ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక వ్యాపారి పొరపాటున మీ ఇంట్లో సరుకులు వదిలితే, మీరు వెంటనే తిరిగి ఇచ్చేస్తారు. మీరు చెల్లించాలా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మీరు వాటిని అంగీకరించలేదు, అనుభవించలేదు. స్వచ్ఛంద అంగీకారంపైనే బాధ్యత పుడుతుంది ( B.K. Mondal ; Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 5. చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు రేట్లను నిర్ణయించినప్పుడు సరఫరాదారు సెక్షన్ 70 కింద క్వాంటమ్ మెరిట్ క్లెయిమ్ చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు రేటే వర్తిస్తుంది ( Alopi Parshad ; MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

hi.inOneMinute: A person does work for you, or hands you goods, expecting to be paid. There is no valid contract . You accept the work or goods and use them. Section 70 says you must pay for them, or give them back. Three conditions must be met: a lawful act, no intention to give it free, and a benefit that you enjoyed. The person asked to pay must have been free to refuse. In exams, the three conditions and State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons earn the marks. In real life, it protects contractors and suppliers whose contract fails for a technical reason.
legalProvision: Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered. Illustrations. (a) A, a tradesman, leaves goods at B's house by mistake. B treats the goods as his own. He is bound to pay A for them. (b) A saves B's property from fire. A is not entitled to compensation from B, if the circumstances show that he intended to act gratuitously.
Related provisions

Constitution of India, Article 299(1). All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.

Government of India Act, 1935, Section 175(3) (as summarised in the headnote to B.K. Mondal ): all contracts made in the exercise of the executive authority of a province shall be expressed to be made by the Governor of the province and shall be executed on behalf of the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise.
In simple words

Where a person lawfully does something for another, or delivers something to him, not meaning it to be free of charge, and the other receives and uses the benefit, the other must pay compensation for it or give it back. Illustration (a): goods left at the wrong house by mistake, and used as one's own, must be paid for. Illustration (b): a person who saves another's property from fire, meaning it as a favour, cannot claim payment. Contracts of the Government must be made in the form Article 299(1) lays down (earlier, Section 175(3) of the 1935 Act).
hi.meaning:
Section 70 is the widest of the five quasi-contractual claims. It covers any lawful act or delivery that was not meant as a gift . Gratuitous and non-gratuitous. A "gratuitous" act is one done free of charge, as a favour or gift. A "non-gratuitous" act is one done in the expectation of payment. Why the law has this rule. The reason is unjust enrichment . The person who accepted the benefit should not keep it for nothing. In B.K. Mondal the Supreme Court said that Section 70 "deals with cases where there is no valid contract". The claim is for compensation or restoration. It is not for damages for breach of contract . See Diagram 1 for the questions a court asks. Diagram 1. Start at the top. If an answer ends the claim, stop at the box beside it. Otherwise follow the arrow down. flowchart TD Q1["1. Did the claimant lawfully do something for
the other person, or deliver something to him?"] Q2["2. Did he act without
intending it as a gift?"] Q3["3. Could the other person refuse or return it,
and did he instead accept and enjoy the benefit?"] Q4["4. Is there a valid contract that fixes
the payment for the same work?"] Y["All tests met: compensation for the thing
done or delivered, or restoration (s. 70)"] N1["No claim"] N2["Meant as a gift: no claim
(Illustration (b))"] N3["No choice, or not accepted:
no claim"] C["The claim lies under the contract,
not s. 70"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4 Q4 -->|"No"| Y Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q4 -->|"Yes"| C Text description Question 1: did the claimant lawfully do something for the other person, or deliver something to him? If no, there is no claim. Question 2: did he act without intending it as a gift? If it was meant as a gift, there is no claim (Illustration (b)). Question 3: could the other person have refused or returned the thing, and did he instead accept and enjoy the benefit? If he had no choice or did not accept, there is no claim. Question 4: is there a valid contract that fixes the payment for the same work? If yes, the claim lies under the contract, not Section 70. If no, all tests are met: the other person must pay compensation for the thing done or delivered, or restore it.
keyPoints: Section 70 has three conditions: a lawful act, no intention to give it free, and a benefit enjoyed. "Lawfully" is an essential part of the section; the act must not be fraudulent, dishonest or gratuitous. The receiver must be free to refuse or return, and must voluntarily accept. The claim is for compensation or restoration, not damages for breach. It applies where there is no valid contract, including a Government contract made without the prescribed form. A request is not an element of Section 70. It does not apply where a valid contract fixes the payment. A minor is outside Section 70 because Section 68 provides for his case.

caseLaws.name: State of West Bengal v
caseLaws.facts: B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. In 1944 a firm of contractors built a kutcha road, guard room, office, kitchen and rooms for clerks at Arambagh, and storage sheds at Khanakul, for the State's Civil Supplies Department, on its officers' requests. It claimed Rs. 19,325. The contracts did not meet Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. Principle. Section 70 has three conditions and applies where there is no valid contract. The State had voluntarily accepted and used the work, so it had to pay. AIR 1962 SC 779 : 1962 Supp (1) SCR 876 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It is the leading case on Section 70. Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968) Facts. A Section 70 claim was made against a State on a contract that did not comply with Section 175(3). The Court held Section 175(3) mandatory and based on public policy. Principle. If the three conditions are met, the claimant can invoke Section 70. He cannot sue for specific performance or damages, because there is no contract. His claim rests on "quasi-contract or restitution". (1968) 3 SCR 214 (Supreme Court). Why it matters. It states the nature of the Section 70 claim. Alopi Parshad and Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) Facts. Under a written agreement of 3 May 1937, the agents bought ghee for the Government at fixed rates. An arbitration award gave them further sums. The Supreme Court held the award liable to be set aside and dismissed the agents' appeal. Principle. "For work done or services rendered pursuant to the terms of a contract, compensation quantum meruit cannot be awarded where the contract provides for the consideration payable". AIR 1960 SC 588 : (1960) 2 SCR 793 (Supreme Court, 20 January 1960). Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 70 and of quantum meruit. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. MTNL retained money from Tata Communications' bills under a purchase order that capped liquidated damages at 12 per cent. The Supreme Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1766 of 2019 on 27 February 2019. Principle. Each section in this chapter assumes no contractual relationship. Section 74 governed, so only the contract figure could be claimed and the excess was refunded. Why it matters. It supports the rule that a party governed by a contract must claim under the contract.

selfTest.q: 1. What three conditions does Section 70 require?
selfTest.a: The claimant lawfully did something for, or delivered something to, another. He did not mean it as a gift. The other person enjoyed the benefit.

selfTest.q: 2. A neighbour saves your goods from a fire out of goodwill. Can he claim payment?
selfTest.a: No. He acted gratuitously (Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 3. Can the State escape Section 70 because its officers did not follow the form for Government contracts?
selfTest.a: No. It must pay if it voluntarily accepted and enjoyed the work ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 4. A tradesman leaves goods at your house by mistake and you return them at once. Must you pay?
selfTest.a: No. You did not accept or enjoy them. Liability arises only on voluntary acceptance ( B.K. Mondal ; Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a supplier claim quantum meruit under Section 70 when a valid contract fixes his rates?
selfTest.a: No. The contract rate governs ( Alopi Parshad ; MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t6.subtitle: Section 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: If you pay money by mistake, or hand over goods because you are forced to, the person who received them must give them back. Section 72 says so in one sentence. You do not have to prove that the receiver did anything wrong. In exams, the double payment by joint debtors, the illegal railway charge, and the rule that "mistake" covers both fact and law earn the marks. In real life, it is the basis of refunds of excess payments and of taxes collected without authority.
legalProvision: Section 72. Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion. A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it. Illustrations (a) A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B. (b) A railway company refuses to deliver up certain goods to the consignee, except upon the payment of an illegal charge for carriage. The consignee pays the sum charged in order to obtain the goods. He is entitled to recover so much of the charge as was illegally excessive.
Related provisions

Section 43 (second paragraph). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract.

Section 15. "Coercion" defined. "Coercion" is the committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) or the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.

Section 65. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it. Illustration (a). A pays B 1,000 rupees in consideration of B's promising to marry C, A's daughter. C is dead at the time of the promise. The agreement is void, but B must repay A the 1,000 rupees.
In simple words

Section 72: whoever receives money, or any thing, that was paid or delivered by mistake or under coercion must repay the money or return the thing. Illustration (a): a joint debt paid twice by mistake. The creditor must repay the second payment. Illustration (b): goods held back until an illegal charge is paid. The consignee (the person to whom goods are sent) recovers the part of the charge that was more than the law allowed. Section 43: each joint promisor may make the others contribute equally.
en.meaning:
Section 72 is the last of the five quasi-contractual situations. It has two grounds. The first is a payment or delivery made by mistake . The second is a payment or delivery made under coercion . In both, the receiver has something that the giver never meant to give freely. Why the law has this rule. The reason is unjust enrichment . The receiver should not keep what he had no right to take. The section does not ask whether the receiver was honest. It asks only whether the payment came from a mistake or from compulsion. See Diagram 1 for the questions that a court asks. Diagram 1. Start at the top. If the answer to a box ends the claim, stop at the result beside it. Otherwise follow the arrow down to the next box. flowchart TD Q1["1. Was money paid, or a thing delivered,
to the person who now holds it?"] Q1 -->|"No"| X1["Section 72 does not apply"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2["2. By mistake, of fact or of law,
or under coercion in the wide sense?"] Q2 -->|"No"| X2["A free and informed payment:
the receiver need not return it"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3["3. Was the sum legally due
from the giver anyway?"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| X3["Not recoverable:
he paid only what he owed"] Q3 -->|"No"| R["The receiver must repay the money
or return the thing"] Text description Question 1: was money paid, or a thing delivered, to the person who now holds it? If no, Section 72 does not apply. Question 2: was it paid or delivered by mistake, whether of fact or of law, or under coercion in the wide sense of compulsion? If no, it was a free and informed payment, and the receiver need not return it. Question 3: was the sum legally due from the giver anyway, for example under a contract? If yes, it cannot be recovered, because the giver paid only what he owed. If all the tests are met, the receiver must repay the money or return the thing.
keyPoints: Money paid or goods delivered by mistake or under coercion must be repaid or returned (Section 72). Mistake covers both fact and law ( Shiba Prasad Singh ; Kanhaiya Lal ). Coercion in Section 72 means any compulsion, not just the technical meaning in Section 15. The receiver's good faith is not the test. A sum that was legally due cannot be recovered. Joint debtors who pay twice: the receiver repays the second payer (Illustration (a)), and contribution follows under Section 43.

caseLaws.name: Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v
caseLaws.facts: Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf (1958) Facts. A Banaras firm dealing in bullion and in forward contracts in silver paid sales tax for 1948-49, 1949-50 and 1950-51. The Allahabad High Court later held the tax on forward transactions ultra vires (beyond the power of the State). The firm sought a refund of Rs. 1,365-12-0. Principle. "Mistake" in Section 72 "comprises within its scope a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact". It made no difference that the State had spent the money. AIR 1959 SC 135 (Supreme Court, Bhagwati J, 23 September 1958). Why it matters. It is the leading Supreme Court case on refunds under Section 72. Sri Sri Shiba Prasad Singh v. Maharaja Srish Chandra Nandi (1949) Facts. A coal mining lease in the Jharia estate was granted on 22 October 1898. Under the lease, the higher royalty rates (5 annas and 2 annas 6 pies a ton) were payable only while railway freight stayed low. Freight rose on 1 April 1921, so only the lower rates (3 annas and 1 anna 6 pies) were due from then. The lessee went on paying the higher rates until 30 September 1923, Rs. 63,680 more than was due. When the lessor sued for royalties in 1936, the lessee claimed to set off the excess. Principle. Section 72 "makes no distinction between mistakes of fact and mistakes of law". A payment by mistake is one "not legally due and which could not have been enforced". The Privy Council dismissed the lessor's suit with costs. (1949) LR 76 IA 244 : (1950) 52 Bom LR 17 (Privy Council, 18 July 1949). Why it matters. It settled that mistake of law is within Section 72. Moses v. Macferlan (1760) Facts. Moses endorsed notes to Macferlan on a promise that Macferlan would not sue him on them. Macferlan sued him in the Court of Conscience, and Moses had to pay. Moses then sued to recover the money. Principle. The action for money had and received lies wherever the defendant is obliged by natural justice and equity to refund the money. Why it matters. It is the English root of the principle that Section 72 applies.

selfTest.q: 1. Does Section 72 cover a mistake of law?
selfTest.a: Yes. The Privy Council in Shiba Prasad Singh and the Supreme Court in Kanhaiya Lal held that mistake covers both fact and law.

selfTest.q: 2. Is the meaning of coercion in Section 72 the same as in Section 15?
selfTest.a: No. Section 72 uses the word in its wide, ordinary sense of compulsion.

selfTest.q: 3. A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C. A pays, and B pays again by mistake. What must C do?
selfTest.a: C must repay the second payment to B (Section 72, Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 4. The State spent tax money that it had collected under a law later struck down. Can it refuse a refund on that ground?
selfTest.a: No. In Kanhaiya Lal the Supreme Court held that spending the money made no difference.

selfTest.q: 5. A tenant pays the full rent that his lease requires and later regrets it. Can he recover under Section 72?
selfTest.a: No. The rent was legally due, so it was not paid "by mistake".

సెక్షన్ 72: పొరపాటున లేదా బలవంతం కింద చెల్లించిన డబ్బును, లేదా అప్పగించిన ఏ వస్తువునైనా పొందిన వ్యక్తి, ఆ డబ్బును తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి లేదా ఆ వస్తువును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. Illustration (a): ఒక ఉమ్మడి అప్పు పొరపాటున రెండుసార్లు చెల్లించబడింది. అప్పిచ్చినవాడు రెండో చెల్లింపును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. Illustration (b): చట్టవిరుద్ధమైన ఛార్జీ చెల్లించే వరకు వస్తువులను ఆపి ఉంచారు. Consignee (వస్తువులు ఎవరికి పంపబడ్డాయో ఆ వ్యక్తి) చట్టం అనుమతించిన దాని కంటే ఎక్కువగా ఉన్న ఛార్జీ భాగాన్ని తిరిగి పొందుతాడు. సెక్షన్ 43: ప్రతి ఉమ్మడి వాగ్దానకర్త మిగతావారిని సమానంగా వాటా ఇచ్చేలా చేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
ఐదు క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు సందర్భాల్లో సెక్షన్ 72 చివరిది. దీనికి రెండు ఆధారాలు ఉన్నాయి. మొదటిది పొరపాటు వల్ల చేసిన చెల్లింపు లేదా అప్పగింత. రెండోది బలవంతం (coercion) కింద చేసిన చెల్లింపు లేదా అప్పగింత. రెండింటిలోనూ, ఇచ్చినవారు స్వేచ్ఛగా ఇవ్వాలని ఎప్పుడూ అనుకోనిది పొందినవారి దగ్గర ఉంటుంది. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత . తీసుకునే హక్కు లేనిదాన్ని పొందినవారు ఉంచుకోకూడదు. పొందినవారు నిజాయితీపరుడా కాదా అని సెక్షన్ అడగదు. చెల్లింపు పొరపాటు వల్ల జరిగిందా, బలవంతం వల్ల జరిగిందా అని మాత్రమే అడుగుతుంది. కోర్టు అడిగే ప్రశ్నలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పై నుంచి మొదలుపెట్టండి. ఒక పెట్టె జవాబు క్లెయిమ్‌ను ముగిస్తే, పక్కన ఉన్న ఫలితం దగ్గర ఆగండి. లేకపోతే బాణాన్ని అనుసరించి కింది పెట్టెకు వెళ్లండి. flowchart TD Q1["1. ఇప్పుడు దాన్ని కలిగి ఉన్న వ్యక్తికి
డబ్బు చెల్లించబడిందా, లేదా వస్తువు అప్పగించబడిందా?"] Q1 -->|"కాదు"| X1["సెక్షన్ 72 వర్తించదు"] Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2["2. వాస్తవానికి లేదా చట్టానికి సంబంధించిన పొరపాటు వల్ల,
లేదా విస్తృత అర్థంలో బలవంతం కింద?"] Q2 -->|"కాదు"| X2["స్వేచ్ఛగా, తెలిసి చేసిన చెల్లింపు:
పొందినవారు తిరిగి ఇవ్వనవసరం లేదు"] Q2 -->|"అవును"| Q3["3. ఆ మొత్తం ఇచ్చినవారి నుంచి
ఎలాగూ చట్టప్రకారం బాకీ ఉందా?"] Q3 -->|"అవును"| X3["తిరిగి రాదు:
బాకీ ఉన్నదే చెల్లించారు"] Q3 -->|"కాదు"| R["పొందినవారు డబ్బును తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి
లేదా వస్తువును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి"] వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: ఇప్పుడు దాన్ని కలిగి ఉన్న వ్యక్తికి డబ్బు చెల్లించబడిందా, లేదా వస్తువు అప్పగించబడిందా? లేకపోతే సెక్షన్ 72 వర్తించదు. ప్రశ్న 2: వాస్తవానికి లేదా చట్టానికి సంబంధించిన పొరపాటు వల్ల, లేదా విస్తృత అర్థంలో బలవంతం కింద చెల్లించబడిందా లేదా అప్పగించబడిందా? లేకపోతే అది స్వేచ్ఛగా, తెలిసి చేసిన చెల్లింపు, పొందినవారు తిరిగి ఇవ్వనవసరం లేదు. ప్రశ్న 3: ఉదాహరణకు కాంట్రాక్టు కింద, ఆ మొత్తం ఇచ్చినవారి నుంచి ఎలాగూ చట్టప్రకారం బాకీ ఉందా? అవును అయితే తిరిగి రాదు, ఎందుకంటే ఇచ్చినవారు తాను బాకీ ఉన్నదే చెల్లించారు. అన్ని పరీక్షలూ నెరవేరితే, పొందినవారు డబ్బును తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి లేదా వస్తువును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 72 చట్టానికి సంబంధించిన పొరపాటును కవర్ చేస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: అవును. పొరపాటు వాస్తవాన్ని, చట్టాన్ని రెండింటినీ కవర్ చేస్తుందని Shiba Prasad Singh లో ప్రివీ కౌన్సిల్, Kanhaiya Lal లో సుప్రీం కోర్టు చెప్పాయి.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 72 లో coercion అర్థం, సెక్షన్ 15 లోని అర్థం ఒకటేనా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సెక్షన్ 72 ఆ పదాన్ని బలవంతం అనే విస్తృతమైన, సాధారణ అర్థంలో వాడుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 3. A, B కలిసి C కి 100 rupees బాకీ. A చెల్లిస్తాడు, B పొరపాటున మళ్లీ చెల్లిస్తాడు. C ఏం చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: C రెండో చెల్లింపును B కి తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి (సెక్షన్ 72, Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 4. తర్వాత కొట్టివేయబడిన చట్టం కింద వసూలు చేసిన పన్ను డబ్బును రాష్ట్రం ఖర్చు చేసేసింది. ఆ కారణంతో రీఫండ్‌ను నిరాకరించగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. డబ్బు ఖర్చు చేసేయడం తేడా చేయదని Kanhaiya Lal లో సుప్రీం కోర్టు చెప్పింది.

selfTest.q: 5. లీజు కోరిన పూర్తి అద్దెను ఒక అద్దెదారు చెల్లించి తర్వాత బాధపడతాడు. సెక్షన్ 72 కింద తిరిగి పొందగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అద్దె చట్టప్రకారం బాకీ ఉంది, కాబట్టి అది "by mistake" చెల్లించినది కాదు.

hi.inOneMinute: If you pay money by mistake, or hand over goods because you are forced to, the person who received them must give them back. Section 72 says so in one sentence. You do not have to prove that the receiver did anything wrong. In exams, the double payment by joint debtors, the illegal railway charge, and the rule that "mistake" covers both fact and law earn the marks. In real life, it is the basis of refunds of excess payments and of taxes collected without authority.
legalProvision: Section 72. Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion. A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it. Illustrations (a) A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B. (b) A railway company refuses to deliver up certain goods to the consignee, except upon the payment of an illegal charge for carriage. The consignee pays the sum charged in order to obtain the goods. He is entitled to recover so much of the charge as was illegally excessive.
Related provisions

Section 43 (second paragraph). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract.

Section 15. "Coercion" defined. "Coercion" is the committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860) or the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.

Section 65. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it. Illustration (a). A pays B 1,000 rupees in consideration of B's promising to marry C, A's daughter. C is dead at the time of the promise. The agreement is void, but B must repay A the 1,000 rupees.
In simple words

Section 72: whoever receives money, or any thing, that was paid or delivered by mistake or under coercion must repay the money or return the thing. Illustration (a): a joint debt paid twice by mistake. The creditor must repay the second payment. Illustration (b): goods held back until an illegal charge is paid. The consignee (the person to whom goods are sent) recovers the part of the charge that was more than the law allowed. Section 43: each joint promisor may make the others contribute equally.
hi.meaning:
Section 72 is the last of the five quasi-contractual situations. It has two grounds. The first is a payment or delivery made by mistake . The second is a payment or delivery made under coercion . In both, the receiver has something that the giver never meant to give freely. Why the law has this rule. The reason is unjust enrichment . The receiver should not keep what he had no right to take. The section does not ask whether the receiver was honest. It asks only whether the payment came from a mistake or from compulsion. See Diagram 1 for the questions that a court asks. Diagram 1. Start at the top. If the answer to a box ends the claim, stop at the result beside it. Otherwise follow the arrow down to the next box. flowchart TD Q1["1. Was money paid, or a thing delivered,
to the person who now holds it?"] Q1 -->|"No"| X1["Section 72 does not apply"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2["2. By mistake, of fact or of law,
or under coercion in the wide sense?"] Q2 -->|"No"| X2["A free and informed payment:
the receiver need not return it"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3["3. Was the sum legally due
from the giver anyway?"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| X3["Not recoverable:
he paid only what he owed"] Q3 -->|"No"| R["The receiver must repay the money
or return the thing"] Text description Question 1: was money paid, or a thing delivered, to the person who now holds it? If no, Section 72 does not apply. Question 2: was it paid or delivered by mistake, whether of fact or of law, or under coercion in the wide sense of compulsion? If no, it was a free and informed payment, and the receiver need not return it. Question 3: was the sum legally due from the giver anyway, for example under a contract? If yes, it cannot be recovered, because the giver paid only what he owed. If all the tests are met, the receiver must repay the money or return the thing.
keyPoints: Money paid or goods delivered by mistake or under coercion must be repaid or returned (Section 72). Mistake covers both fact and law ( Shiba Prasad Singh ; Kanhaiya Lal ). Coercion in Section 72 means any compulsion, not just the technical meaning in Section 15. The receiver's good faith is not the test. A sum that was legally due cannot be recovered. Joint debtors who pay twice: the receiver repays the second payer (Illustration (a)), and contribution follows under Section 43.

caseLaws.name: Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v
caseLaws.facts: Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf (1958) Facts. A Banaras firm dealing in bullion and in forward contracts in silver paid sales tax for 1948-49, 1949-50 and 1950-51. The Allahabad High Court later held the tax on forward transactions ultra vires (beyond the power of the State). The firm sought a refund of Rs. 1,365-12-0. Principle. "Mistake" in Section 72 "comprises within its scope a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact". It made no difference that the State had spent the money. AIR 1959 SC 135 (Supreme Court, Bhagwati J, 23 September 1958). Why it matters. It is the leading Supreme Court case on refunds under Section 72. Sri Sri Shiba Prasad Singh v. Maharaja Srish Chandra Nandi (1949) Facts. A coal mining lease in the Jharia estate was granted on 22 October 1898. Under the lease, the higher royalty rates (5 annas and 2 annas 6 pies a ton) were payable only while railway freight stayed low. Freight rose on 1 April 1921, so only the lower rates (3 annas and 1 anna 6 pies) were due from then. The lessee went on paying the higher rates until 30 September 1923, Rs. 63,680 more than was due. When the lessor sued for royalties in 1936, the lessee claimed to set off the excess. Principle. Section 72 "makes no distinction between mistakes of fact and mistakes of law". A payment by mistake is one "not legally due and which could not have been enforced". The Privy Council dismissed the lessor's suit with costs. (1949) LR 76 IA 244 : (1950) 52 Bom LR 17 (Privy Council, 18 July 1949). Why it matters. It settled that mistake of law is within Section 72. Moses v. Macferlan (1760) Facts. Moses endorsed notes to Macferlan on a promise that Macferlan would not sue him on them. Macferlan sued him in the Court of Conscience, and Moses had to pay. Moses then sued to recover the money. Principle. The action for money had and received lies wherever the defendant is obliged by natural justice and equity to refund the money. Why it matters. It is the English root of the principle that Section 72 applies.

selfTest.q: 1. Does Section 72 cover a mistake of law?
selfTest.a: Yes. The Privy Council in Shiba Prasad Singh and the Supreme Court in Kanhaiya Lal held that mistake covers both fact and law.

selfTest.q: 2. Is the meaning of coercion in Section 72 the same as in Section 15?
selfTest.a: No. Section 72 uses the word in its wide, ordinary sense of compulsion.

selfTest.q: 3. A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C. A pays, and B pays again by mistake. What must C do?
selfTest.a: C must repay the second payment to B (Section 72, Illustration (a)).

selfTest.q: 4. The State spent tax money that it had collected under a law later struck down. Can it refuse a refund on that ground?
selfTest.a: No. In Kanhaiya Lal the Supreme Court held that spending the money made no difference.

selfTest.q: 5. A tenant pays the full rent that his lease requires and later regrets it. Can he recover under Section 72?
selfTest.a: No. The rent was legally due, so it was not paid "by mistake".
