hi.inOneMinute: When a contract is broken, the injured party must act sensibly. He must take reasonable steps to keep his loss small . He cannot sit still, let the loss grow, and then bill the wrongdoer for all of it. Loss that reasonable steps would have avoided is not paid . The rule comes from the Explanation to Section 73 : in estimating the loss, "the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience" must be taken into account. It is a limit on what he can claim , not a duty anyone can sue him for. Reasonable costs of mitigating are recoverable, and gains made by mitigating are deducted. In exams, the meaning, the rules (reasonable steps, nothing extraordinary, costs, gains, burden of proof) and the cases ( Murlidhar Chiranjilal , Jamal , British Westinghouse , Payzu ) earn the marks. In real life, the rule decides how much of a large loss a court will actually award.
legalProvision: Section 73 (first two paragraphs). When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.

Explanation. In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustration (a). A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery. A breaks his promise. B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Illustration (b). A hires B's ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned. B's ship does not go to Bombay, but A has opportunities of procuring suitable conveyance for the cargo upon terms as advantageous as those on which he had chartered the ship. A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.
In simple words

Section 73 pays for loss that arises naturally from the breach, and for loss both sides knew was likely. It does not pay for remote loss. The Explanation says: count what the injured party could have done to reduce the loss. Illustration (a) measures the loss by the price at which the buyer might have bought elsewhere, so he is expected to buy elsewhere. Illustration (b) shows the other side: the reasonable trouble and expense of mitigating is paid by the wrongdoer. Illustrations (c), (d), (g) and (h) also measure loss by the market price, which shows what the injured party could have got elsewhere.
hi.meaning:
Mitigation means taking reasonable steps to reduce the loss caused by a breach. The Supreme Court stated the rule in Murlidhar Chiranjilal v. Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1961). It said there are two settled principles under Section 73 read with its Explanation: the injured party is to be placed, as far as money can do it, in as good a situation as if the contract had been performed; but he has a duty to take all reasonable steps to mitigate the loss, and he cannot claim any part of the damage that is due to his neglect to take such steps. The Privy Council said the same earlier in Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915). Why the law has this rule. Fairness. The wrongdoer should pay for the loss his breach caused, not for the part the injured party could easily have avoided. It is not a true "duty". The injured party is not liable to anyone for failing to mitigate. The wrongdoer cannot sue him. He only loses the right to recover the avoidable part of the loss. See Diagram 1 (from breach to the claim: where mitigation fits). Diagram 1. Damages are fixed at the date of breach. Sita waits to 1 July and pays ₹2,600; extra ₹30,000 is avoidable and not paid. Reasonable cost of mitigation, ₹2,000 lorry, is added. Any gain from mitigation is set off. Claim allowed ₹32,000. Burden of proving failure to mitigate is on the wrongdoer.
keyPoints: The injured party must take reasonable steps to reduce his loss (Explanation to Section 73). Avoidable loss cannot be recovered. He need not take extraordinary or risky steps, or accept a lower-status job. The reasonable cost of mitigation is recoverable (illustration (b)). A gain made by mitigating is set off against the damages. The wrongdoer must prove the failure to mitigate. For goods, the loss is fixed at the date of breach . Delay is at the injured party's risk. Failure to mitigate only reduces the damages. No one can sue for it.

caseLaws.name: Murlidhar Chiranjilal v
caseLaws.facts: Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1961) Facts. A seller failed to supply canvas under a contract for delivery at Kanpur, to be sent to Calcutta. The buyer claimed damages at the Calcutta price. Principle. Under Section 73 and its Explanation, the buyer must take all reasonable steps to mitigate. Damages are the Kanpur market price on the date of breach minus the contract price. The buyer did not prove the Kanpur price and got nothing. AIR 1962 SC 366. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court authority on the duty to mitigate. Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915) Facts. Buyers failed to take 23,500 shares on 30 December 1911. The seller sold them later, mostly at higher prices. Principle. The loss is the difference between the contract price and the market price on the date of breach. Later market movements are the seller's own risk. (1915) LR 43 IA 6; ILR 43 Cal 493 (PC). Why it matters. It fixes the date of assessment and states the duty to mitigate. British Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Co. v. Underground Electric Railways Co. of London (1912) Facts. Turbines supplied for a power station were less efficient than promised. The buyers replaced them with better turbines from another maker. Principle. The injured party must take all reasonable steps to reduce his loss, but need not take steps a prudent person would not ordinarily take. A gain from reasonable mitigation is set off. [1912] AC 673. Why it matters. It states the main rules of mitigation and was relied on by the Supreme Court in Murlidhar Chiranjilal . Payzu Ltd. v. Saunders (1919) Facts. A seller refused to continue supplying on credit but offered the same goods at the same price for cash. The buyer refused and bought elsewhere at a higher price. Principle. The buyer should have accepted the reasonable offer. His damages were limited to what he would have lost by accepting it. [1919] 2 KB 581. Why it matters. Mitigation may include accepting an offer from the wrongdoer. Harichand & Co. v. Gosho Kabushiki Kaisha (1924) Facts. The buyer refused goods on 5 April 1921. The sellers resold only on 25 May 1921, while the market kept falling. Principle. Undue delay in reselling in a falling market is a failure to mitigate. The sellers got only the market difference on the day after the breach. (1924) 26 Bom LR 921; AIR 1925 Bom 28. Why it matters. It applies the rule to an Indian sale of goods. Prafulla Ranjan Sarkar v. Hindusthan Building Society Ltd. (1959) Facts. A society's Secretary was dismissed with only one month's salary. The court found he was entitled to nine months' notice. Principle. Failure to mitigate is a question of fact, and the burden of proving it is on the defendant. With no evidence from the defendant, he got nine months' salary in full. AIR 1960 Cal 214. Why it matters. It places the burden of proof on the wrongdoer.

selfTest.q: 1. Where is the duty to mitigate found in the Act?
selfTest.a: In the Explanation to Section 73.

selfTest.q: 2. Sita could buy rice on the due date at ₹2,300 a bag, but waited and paid ₹2,600. The contract price was ₹2,000 for 100 bags. How much does Ravi pay?
selfTest.a: ₹30,000, that is (₹2,300 − ₹2,000) × 100. The extra ₹30,000 was avoidable.

selfTest.q: 3. Can the wrongdoer sue the injured party for failing to mitigate?
selfTest.a: No. Failure to mitigate only reduces the damages by the avoidable part.

selfTest.q: 4. What happens to a gain made while mitigating?
selfTest.a: It is set off against the damages ( British Westinghouse ).

selfTest.q: 5. Who must prove that the injured party failed to mitigate?
selfTest.a: The wrongdoer (defendant) ( Prafulla Ranjan Sarkar ).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t10.subtitle: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, read with section 73

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes a contract fixes in advance what a party must pay if he breaks it. That is a liquidated sum, or, if it is meant to frighten, a penalty . Sometimes the contract says nothing, and the court works out the loss after the breach. Those are unliquidated damages, under Section 73. Section 74 governs every sum named for breach. The injured party gets reasonable compensation, never more than the sum named . Indian law does not split the named sum into a valid "liquidated damages" clause and a void "penalty" clause. Both are treated alike ( Fateh Chand , 1963). Loss is still essential, and where loss can be proved it must be proved ( Kailash Nath , 2015). In exams, Section 74, Fateh Chand , Kailash Nath , the upper limit and proof of loss earn the marks. In real life, the rule decides how much a seller can keep of an advance, or how much a buyer can deduct for late delivery.
legalProvision: Section 74. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for. Explanation. A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty. Exception. When any person enters into any bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of the same nature, or, under the provisions of any law, or under the orders of the Central Government or of any State Government, gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay the whole sum mentioned therein. Explanation. A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested.

Section 73 (summary). Compensation is given for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or that the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from it. It is not given for remote and indirect loss.
In simple words

Section 74: if the contract names a sum for breach, or contains any other penalty (such as forfeiting money already paid), the court gives reasonable compensation , and the sum named is the ceiling . Explanation: a jump in interest on default may be a penalty. Exception: bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty are payable in full . A contract with the Government is not, by itself, a public duty. Section 73: where nothing is named, the court assesses the loss itself.
en.meaning:
Liquidated damages are a sum the contract fixes in advance as payable on breach, as a genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss. Unliquidated damages are not fixed in advance. The court assesses them after the breach, under Section 73 . A penalty is a sum fixed mainly to frighten a party into performing ( in terrorem ). It is out of proportion to any likely loss. Earnest money is a deposit paid when the contract is made, as a sign that the payer means to perform. It usually goes towards the price. The English background. Under English common law, a genuine pre-estimate was enforced in full as liquidated damages , and a penalty was not enforced at all. In Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963), the Supreme Court said Section 74 is "an attempt to eliminate the somewhat elaborate refinements" of that English distinction. India has one rule for both : reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named. Why the law has this rule. Damages compensate and do not punish. A party should not get a windfall just because the contract named a large figure. But a fair pre-estimate saves the trouble of proving a loss that is hard to measure. See Diagram 1 (how a court applies Section 74). Diagram 1. Yes: is it a bail-bond or public duty bond? Yes: whole sum payable (Exception). No: was there any loss? No: nothing (Kailash Nath). Yes: can the loss be proved? Yes: actual proved loss, capped at the sum named. No, hard to prove, and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate: the sum may be awarded (ONGC v. Saw Pipes). Never above the sum named (MTNL).
keyPoints: Section 74 applies to a named sum and to any penalty , including forfeiture. The court awards reasonable compensation . The sum named is the upper limit . India does not distinguish liquidated damages from a penalty ( Fateh Chand ). Loss is a sine qua non. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved ( Kailash Nath ). Proof is excused where loss is hard to prove and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate ( ONGC v. Saw Pipes ). Forfeiture of reasonable earnest money: two lines of authority. Increased interest on default may be a penalty. An acceleration clause for a real debt is not. Bail-bonds and public duty bonds are payable in full . Unliquidated damages are assessed by the court under Section 73 .

caseLaws.name: Fateh Chand v
caseLaws.facts: Balkishan Dass (1963) Facts. A buyer agreed to buy a Delhi property for Rs. 1,12,500, paid Rs. 1,000 earnest money and Rs. 24,000 towards the price, and failed to complete. The contract said Rs. 25,000 would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 applies to every stipulation by way of penalty, including forfeiture of money paid. Only reasonable compensation up to the sum named is given. AIR 1963 SC 1405. Why it matters. It removed the English distinction in India. The seller kept only the Rs. 1,000. Maula Bux v. Union of India (1969) Facts. A supplier of potatoes, and of poultry, eggs and fish, to the Government gave deposits of Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 8,500 as security. On his default, the Government forfeited them without proving loss. Principle. Reasonable earnest money may be forfeited. But a security deposit is not earnest money. Where loss can be measured in money, it must be proved. AIR 1970 SC 1955. Why it matters. It limits forfeiture of deposits to real, proved loss. ONGC Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003) Facts. Saw Pipes supplied casing pipes late. The contract fixed liquidated damages at 1% per week of delay, up to 10%, and ONGC deducted them. Principle. A genuine pre-estimate is payable without proof of actual loss, unless the other side shows it is unreasonable. (2003) 5 SCC 705. Why it matters. It explains when proof of loss is not required. Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA (2015) Facts. DDA forfeited ₹78 lakh earnest money (25% of a ₹3.12 crore bid). It later re-auctioned the plot for ₹11.78 crore. Principle. Loss is a sine qua non under Section 74. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved. Section 74 applies to forfeiture of earnest money. (2015) 4 SCC 136. Why it matters. It is the leading summary of Section 74. DDA, with no loss, had to refund. Construction and Design Services v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) Facts. A contractor was late in building a sewage pumping station. DDA claimed the agreed compensation for delay. Principle. Loss may be presumed for a delayed public utility project. Where only a maximum is fixed, the court may award part as reasonable compensation. Half the claim was awarded. Supreme Court, decided 4 February 2015. Why it matters. It shows how the burden of proof works. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. A purchase order capped liquidated damages at 12%. MTNL deducted more from the bills. Principle. A higher amount than the contract fixes cannot be awarded. The excess had to be refunded. Why it matters. It applies the upper limit under Section 74. K.R. Suresh v. R. Poornima (2025) Facts. Under a 2007 agreement to sell property for ₹55,50,000, the buyer paid ₹20,00,000 and failed to pay the balance. The vendors forfeited the advance. Principle. The earnest money clause was not penal, so Section 74 did not apply. Even if it did, the vendors' proved losses exceeded the sum forfeited. 2025 INSC 617. Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court word on earnest money.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the upper limit of compensation under Section 74?
selfTest.a: The sum named in the contract, or the penalty stipulated .

selfTest.q: 2. Does Indian law treat liquidated damages and a penalty differently?
selfTest.a: No. Section 74 gives reasonable compensation up to the sum named in both ( Fateh Chand ).

selfTest.q: 3. A contract fixes ₹500 for each month of delay. The seller is six months late and the buyer's loss is ₹6,500. What can the buyer recover?
selfTest.a: At most ₹3,000, because the sum named is the upper limit.

selfTest.q: 4. Is any compensation payable under Section 74 if there is no loss at all?
selfTest.a: No. Loss is a sine qua non ( Kailash Nath ).

selfTest.q: 5. Which instruments are enforced for the whole sum?
selfTest.a: Bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty (the Exception to Section 74).

Section 73 (సారాంశం). ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సాధారణ పరిస్థితుల్లో సహజంగా వచ్చిన నష్టానికి, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు జరగవచ్చని పక్షాలకు తెలిసిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం ఇస్తారు. దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టానికి ఇవ్వరు.
సులభమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 74: ఉల్లంఘనకు కాంట్రాక్టు ఒక మొత్తం పేర్కొంటే, లేదా వేరే ఏదైనా జరిమానా (ఇప్పటికే చెల్లించిన డబ్బును జప్తు చేయడం వంటిది) ఉంటే, కోర్టు సహేతుక పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది. పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం గరిష్ట పరిమితి . Explanation: ఉల్లంఘన జరిగినప్పటి నుంచి వడ్డీ పెంచడం జరిమానా కావచ్చు . Exception: బెయిల్ బాండ్లు, recognizances, ప్రజా విధికి ఇచ్చే బాండ్ల మొత్తాన్ని పూర్తిగా చెల్లించాలి. ప్రభుత్వంతో కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నంత మాత్రాన అది ప్రజా విధి కాదు. సెక్షన్ 73: ఏ మొత్తమూ పేర్కొనని చోట, కోర్టే నష్టాన్ని అంచనా వేస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
Liquidated damages (ముందే నిర్ణయించిన నష్టపరిహారం ) అంటే జరగబోయే నష్టానికి నిజాయితీగా ముందుగా వేసిన అంచనాగా (genuine pre-estimate), ఉల్లంఘనపై చెల్లించాల్సినదిగా కాంట్రాక్టు ముందుగానే నిర్ణయించిన మొత్తం. Unliquidated damages (నిర్ణయించని నష్టపరిహారం) ముందుగా నిర్ణయించినవి కావు . ఉల్లంఘన తర్వాత సెక్షన్ 73 కింద కోర్టు వాటిని అంచనా వేస్తుంది. జరిమానా (penalty) అంటే ఒక పక్షాన్ని భయపెట్టి కాంట్రాక్టు అమలు చేయించడానికే ( in terrorem ) ప్రధానంగా నిర్ణయించిన మొత్తం. జరగవచ్చిన ఏ నష్టానికీ ఇది సరితూగదు. బయానా (earnest money) అంటే కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకునేటప్పుడు, చెల్లించేవాడు కాంట్రాక్టు అమలు చేయాలనుకుంటున్నాడని చూపడానికి చెల్లించే డిపాజిట్. సాధారణంగా ఇది ధరలో భాగంగా లెక్కకు వస్తుంది. ఇంగ్లీష్ నేపథ్యం. ఇంగ్లీష్ common law కింద, నిజాయితీ అంచనాను liquidated damages గా పూర్తిగా అమలు చేసేవారు, జరిమానాను అసలు అమలు చేసేవారు కాదు. Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963) లో, సెక్షన్ 74 ఆ ఇంగ్లీష్ తేడాలోని "somewhat elaborate refinements" ను తొలగించే ప్రయత్నమని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. భారతదేశంలో రెండింటికీ ఒకే నియమం : పేర్కొన్న మొత్తానికి మించని సహేతుక పరిహారం. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. నష్టపరిహారం నష్టాన్ని పూడుస్తుంది, శిక్షించదు. కాంట్రాక్టులో పెద్ద సంఖ్య రాసినంత మాత్రాన ఒక పక్షానికి అనుకోని లాభం రాకూడదు. కానీ కొలవడం కష్టమైన నష్టాన్ని నిరూపించే శ్రమను న్యాయమైన ముందస్తు అంచనా తప్పిస్తుంది. selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 74 కింద పరిహారానికి గరిష్ట పరిమితి ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టులో పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం, లేదా నిర్ణయించిన జరిమానా.

selfTest.q: 2. భారత చట్టం liquidated damages ను, జరిమానాను వేర్వేరుగా చూస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. రెండింటిలోనూ సెక్షన్ 74 పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం వరకు సహేతుక పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది ( Fateh Chand ).

selfTest.q: 3. ఆలస్యమైన ప్రతి నెలకు ₹500 అని కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్ణయించింది. అమ్మకందారు ఆరు నెలలు ఆలస్యం చేశాడు, కొనుగోలుదారు నష్టం ₹6,500. కొనుగోలుదారుకు ఎంత వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: గరిష్టంగా ₹3,000, ఎందుకంటే పేర్కొన్న మొత్తమే గరిష్ట పరిమితి.

selfTest.q: 4. ఏ నష్టమూ లేకపోతే సెక్షన్ 74 కింద ఏదైనా పరిహారం వస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. నష్టం sine qua non ( Kailash Nath ).

selfTest.q: 5. ఏ పత్రాలకు మొత్తం సొమ్ము చెల్లించాలి?
selfTest.a: బెయిల్ బాండ్లు, recognizances, ప్రజా విధికి ఇచ్చే బాండ్లు (సెక్షన్ 74 కి Exception).

hi.inOneMinute: Sometimes a contract fixes in advance what a party must pay if he breaks it. That is a liquidated sum, or, if it is meant to frighten, a penalty . Sometimes the contract says nothing, and the court works out the loss after the breach. Those are unliquidated damages, under Section 73. Section 74 governs every sum named for breach. The injured party gets reasonable compensation, never more than the sum named . Indian law does not split the named sum into a valid "liquidated damages" clause and a void "penalty" clause. Both are treated alike ( Fateh Chand , 1963). Loss is still essential, and where loss can be proved it must be proved ( Kailash Nath , 2015). In exams, Section 74, Fateh Chand , Kailash Nath , the upper limit and proof of loss earn the marks. In real life, the rule decides how much a seller can keep of an advance, or how much a buyer can deduct for late delivery.
legalProvision: Section 74. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for. Explanation. A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty. Exception. When any person enters into any bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of the same nature, or, under the provisions of any law, or under the orders of the Central Government or of any State Government, gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay the whole sum mentioned therein. Explanation. A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested.

Section 73 (summary). Compensation is given for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or that the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from it. It is not given for remote and indirect loss.
In simple words

Section 74: if the contract names a sum for breach, or contains any other penalty (such as forfeiting money already paid), the court gives reasonable compensation , and the sum named is the ceiling . Explanation: a jump in interest on default may be a penalty. Exception: bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty are payable in full . A contract with the Government is not, by itself, a public duty. Section 73: where nothing is named, the court assesses the loss itself.
hi.meaning:
Liquidated damages are a sum the contract fixes in advance as payable on breach, as a genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss. Unliquidated damages are not fixed in advance. The court assesses them after the breach, under Section 73 . A penalty is a sum fixed mainly to frighten a party into performing ( in terrorem ). It is out of proportion to any likely loss. Earnest money is a deposit paid when the contract is made, as a sign that the payer means to perform. It usually goes towards the price. The English background. Under English common law, a genuine pre-estimate was enforced in full as liquidated damages , and a penalty was not enforced at all. In Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963), the Supreme Court said Section 74 is "an attempt to eliminate the somewhat elaborate refinements" of that English distinction. India has one rule for both : reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named. Why the law has this rule. Damages compensate and do not punish. A party should not get a windfall just because the contract named a large figure. But a fair pre-estimate saves the trouble of proving a loss that is hard to measure. See Diagram 1 (how a court applies Section 74). Diagram 1. Yes: is it a bail-bond or public duty bond? Yes: whole sum payable (Exception). No: was there any loss? No: nothing (Kailash Nath). Yes: can the loss be proved? Yes: actual proved loss, capped at the sum named. No, hard to prove, and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate: the sum may be awarded (ONGC v. Saw Pipes). Never above the sum named (MTNL).
keyPoints: Section 74 applies to a named sum and to any penalty , including forfeiture. The court awards reasonable compensation . The sum named is the upper limit . India does not distinguish liquidated damages from a penalty ( Fateh Chand ). Loss is a sine qua non. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved ( Kailash Nath ). Proof is excused where loss is hard to prove and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate ( ONGC v. Saw Pipes ). Forfeiture of reasonable earnest money: two lines of authority. Increased interest on default may be a penalty. An acceleration clause for a real debt is not. Bail-bonds and public duty bonds are payable in full . Unliquidated damages are assessed by the court under Section 73 .

caseLaws.name: Fateh Chand v
caseLaws.facts: Balkishan Dass (1963) Facts. A buyer agreed to buy a Delhi property for Rs. 1,12,500, paid Rs. 1,000 earnest money and Rs. 24,000 towards the price, and failed to complete. The contract said Rs. 25,000 would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 applies to every stipulation by way of penalty, including forfeiture of money paid. Only reasonable compensation up to the sum named is given. AIR 1963 SC 1405. Why it matters. It removed the English distinction in India. The seller kept only the Rs. 1,000. Maula Bux v. Union of India (1969) Facts. A supplier of potatoes, and of poultry, eggs and fish, to the Government gave deposits of Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 8,500 as security. On his default, the Government forfeited them without proving loss. Principle. Reasonable earnest money may be forfeited. But a security deposit is not earnest money. Where loss can be measured in money, it must be proved. AIR 1970 SC 1955. Why it matters. It limits forfeiture of deposits to real, proved loss. ONGC Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003) Facts. Saw Pipes supplied casing pipes late. The contract fixed liquidated damages at 1% per week of delay, up to 10%, and ONGC deducted them. Principle. A genuine pre-estimate is payable without proof of actual loss, unless the other side shows it is unreasonable. (2003) 5 SCC 705. Why it matters. It explains when proof of loss is not required. Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA (2015) Facts. DDA forfeited ₹78 lakh earnest money (25% of a ₹3.12 crore bid). It later re-auctioned the plot for ₹11.78 crore. Principle. Loss is a sine qua non under Section 74. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved. Section 74 applies to forfeiture of earnest money. (2015) 4 SCC 136. Why it matters. It is the leading summary of Section 74. DDA, with no loss, had to refund. Construction and Design Services v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) Facts. A contractor was late in building a sewage pumping station. DDA claimed the agreed compensation for delay. Principle. Loss may be presumed for a delayed public utility project. Where only a maximum is fixed, the court may award part as reasonable compensation. Half the claim was awarded. Supreme Court, decided 4 February 2015. Why it matters. It shows how the burden of proof works. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. A purchase order capped liquidated damages at 12%. MTNL deducted more from the bills. Principle. A higher amount than the contract fixes cannot be awarded. The excess had to be refunded. Why it matters. It applies the upper limit under Section 74. K.R. Suresh v. R. Poornima (2025) Facts. Under a 2007 agreement to sell property for ₹55,50,000, the buyer paid ₹20,00,000 and failed to pay the balance. The vendors forfeited the advance. Principle. The earnest money clause was not penal, so Section 74 did not apply. Even if it did, the vendors' proved losses exceeded the sum forfeited. 2025 INSC 617. Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court word on earnest money.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the upper limit of compensation under Section 74?
selfTest.a: The sum named in the contract, or the penalty stipulated .

selfTest.q: 2. Does Indian law treat liquidated damages and a penalty differently?
selfTest.a: No. Section 74 gives reasonable compensation up to the sum named in both ( Fateh Chand ).

selfTest.q: 3. A contract fixes ₹500 for each month of delay. The seller is six months late and the buyer's loss is ₹6,500. What can the buyer recover?
selfTest.a: At most ₹3,000, because the sum named is the upper limit.

selfTest.q: 4. Is any compensation payable under Section 74 if there is no loss at all?
selfTest.a: No. Loss is a sine qua non ( Kailash Nath ).

selfTest.q: 5. Which instruments are enforced for the whole sum?
selfTest.a: Bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty (the Exception to Section 74).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t9.subtitle: Sections 73 and 75 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Damages are money paid to a party who has suffered by a breach of contract. The aim is to put him, as far as money can, where he would have been if the contract had been performed. Damages compensate . They do not punish . Section 73 sets the limits. The loss must arise naturally from the breach, or be one the parties knew was likely when they made the contract. Remote and indirect loss is not paid. The kinds of damages are general (ordinary), special, nominal, exemplary, liquidated and unliquidated . Damages for mental distress are not given in an ordinary commercial contract. In exams, the kinds of damages with an example each, the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale , the market-price measure and the Act's illustrations earn the marks. In real life, they decide how much a wronged party can actually recover.
legalProvision: Section 73. When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract. Explanation. In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74 (first part). When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
In simple words

Section 73, first paragraph: pay for loss that arises naturally from the breach (first limb), and for loss both parties knew was likely when they contracted (second limb). Section 73, second paragraph: do not pay for remote and indirect loss. Section 73, third paragraph: the same rule applies to quasi-contractual obligations. Explanation: count what the injured party could have done to reduce the loss. Section 74: if the contract names a sum for breach, the court gives reasonable compensation up to that sum.
The Act gives eighteen illustrations, (a) to (r), to Section 73. The table in section 9 below groups them by the rule each one shows.
en.meaning:
Damages are the compensation, in money, that the law awards to a person for loss caused to him by a breach of contract. The Act uses the word "compensation". "Damages" is the word used in courts and exam questions. The aim is compensation, not punishment. The injured party should be no worse off and no better off than if the contract had been performed. That is why: he gets his actual, proved loss, not a reward; he cannot claim remote loss; he cannot claim loss he could have avoided (mitigation); a penalty clause is cut down to reasonable compensation (Section 74). Four questions decide whether a loss is recoverable (see Diagram 1 ): Diagram 1. Ask the four questions in order. flowchart TD L["A loss after a breach"] --> Q1{"1. Caused by the breach?"} Q1 -- "No" --> X1["Not recoverable"] Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"2. Arose naturally, OR both parties
knew it was likely when contracting?"} Q2 -- "No" --> X2["Remote and indirect · not paid
Section 73, para 2"] Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3{"3. Loss and amount proved?"} Q3 -- "No" --> X3["Nominal damages only"] Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4{"4. Could reasonable steps
have reduced it?"} Q4 -- "Yes" --> X4["Avoidable part cut
Explanation to Section 73"] Q4 -- "No" --> OK["Compensation for the loss
Section 73"] X4 --> OK Text description 1 Was the loss caused by the breach? No: nothing. 2 Did it arise naturally, or did both parties know it was likely when contracting? No: remote, not paid. 3 Is the loss and its amount proved? No: nominal damages only. 4 Could reasonable steps have reduced it? Yes: avoidable part cut. Result: compensation for the proved, natural or foreseen, unavoidable loss. Was the loss caused by the breach? Did it arise naturally , or did both parties know it was likely when they contracted? If not, it is remote. Has the claimant proved the loss and its amount? If not, only nominal damages . Could he have reduced it by reasonable steps? If yes, the avoidable part is cut.
keyPoints: Damages compensate for loss caused by the breach. They do not punish. Section 73 pays for natural loss and for loss both parties knew was likely, but not for remote and indirect loss. The kinds are general, special, nominal, exemplary, liquidated and unliquidated . Special damages need knowledge of the special circumstances when the contract was made . Nominal damages are given when breach is proved but no loss. Exemplary damages are generally not given in contract. No damages for mental agony in an ordinary commercial contract. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) is the source of the two limbs of Section 73. For goods, the measure is the market price against the contract price at the date of breach .

caseLaws.name: Hadley v
caseLaws.facts: Baxendale (1854) Facts. A Gloucester mill's crank shaft broke. The owners sent it by carrier to Greenwich as a pattern for a new one. The carrier delayed delivery, and the mill lost profits. Principle. Damages are those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably in the contemplation of both parties when they contracted. Special circumstances count only if communicated. (1854) 9 Exch 341; 156 ER 145. Why it matters. Its two limbs are written into Section 73. Karsandas H. Thacker v. Saran Engineering Co. (1965) Facts. A seller agreed to supply 200 tons of scrap iron at Rs. 100 a ton, then said he could not deliver. The buyer had agreed to resell to a third party. Principle. The seller was not liable for the buyer's payment to the third party, because that contract was not communicated. The buyer proved no market-price loss. AIR 1965 SC 1981. Why it matters. It applies Section 73 to remote loss and to the measure of damages. Victoria Laundry (Windsor) Ltd. v. Newman Industries Ltd. (1949) Facts. A boiler for a laundry was delivered late. The laundry claimed ordinary lost profits and the profits of special Government dyeing contracts. Principle. Ordinary profits were recoverable. The special profits were not, because the supplier did not know of those contracts. [1949] 2 KB 528. Why it matters. It applies the two limbs to a business loss. C. Czarnikow Ltd. v. Koufos (The Heron II) (1967) Facts. A ship carrying sugar to Basra arrived late, after the sugar price had fallen. Principle. The test of remoteness in contract is whether the loss was "not unlikely" to result. [1969] 1 AC 350. Why it matters. It states how likely a loss must be under the second limb. Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915) Facts. Buyers failed to take 23,500 shares on 30 December 1911. The seller sold them later. Principle. The measure is the contract price minus the market price on the date of breach. (1915) LR 43 IA 6 (PC). Why it matters. It fixes the date at which the loss is measured. Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Union of India (2000) Facts. A housing authority failed to allot plots as promised. ₹50,000 was awarded for "mental agony". Principle. Damages for mental agony are not given for breach of an ordinary commercial contract. The award was set aside. (2000) 6 SCC 113. Why it matters. It limits damages for mental distress in contract.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two limbs of the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale?
selfTest.a: Loss arising naturally from the breach, and loss both parties reasonably contemplated, when contracting, as the probable result of breach.

selfTest.q: 2. Ravi fails to deliver 100 bags of rice at ₹2,000. The market price on the due date is ₹2,300. What are the general damages?
3. When can special damages be recovered?
selfTest.a: Only if the special circumstances were known to both parties when the contract was made.

selfTest.q: 4. Are exemplary damages normally awarded for breach of contract?
selfTest.a: No. Contract damages compensate. Textbooks list breach of promise to marry and wrongful dishonour of a cheque as exceptions.

selfTest.q: 5. What are nominal damages?
selfTest.a: A small sum given when a breach is proved but no real loss is shown.

సెక్షన్ 73 కి చట్టం (a) నుంచి (r) వరకు పద్దెనిమిది illustrations ఇచ్చింది. కింది 9వ భాగంలోని పట్టిక, ఒక్కొక్కటి ఏ నియమాన్ని చూపిస్తుందో దాని ప్రకారం వాటిని వర్గీకరిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. Hadley v. Baxendale నియమంలోని రెండు భాగాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చే నష్టం; కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలూ సహేతుకంగా ఊహించిన నష్టం.

selfTest.q: 2. ₹2,000 చొప్పున 100 బస్తాల బియ్యాన్ని రవి డెలివరీ చేయలేదు. గడువు తేదీ నాటి మార్కెట్ ధర ₹2,300. సాధారణ నష్టపరిహారం ఎంత?
3. ప్రత్యేక నష్టపరిహారం ఎప్పుడు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడే ప్రత్యేక పరిస్థితులు ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలిసి ఉంటేనే.

selfTest.q: 4. కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనకు సాధారణంగా శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారం ఇస్తారా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు నష్టపరిహారం నష్టాన్ని పూడుస్తుంది. పెళ్లి వాగ్దానం ఉల్లంఘన, చెక్కును తప్పుగా తిరస్కరించడం మినహాయింపులుగా పాఠ్యపుస్తకాలు చెబుతాయి.

selfTest.q: 5. నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నిరూపితమై, నిజమైన నష్టం చూపించనప్పుడు ఇచ్చే చిన్న మొత్తం.

hi.inOneMinute: Damages are money paid to a party who has suffered by a breach of contract. The aim is to put him, as far as money can, where he would have been if the contract had been performed. Damages compensate . They do not punish . Section 73 sets the limits. The loss must arise naturally from the breach, or be one the parties knew was likely when they made the contract. Remote and indirect loss is not paid. The kinds of damages are general (ordinary), special, nominal, exemplary, liquidated and unliquidated . Damages for mental distress are not given in an ordinary commercial contract. In exams, the kinds of damages with an example each, the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale , the market-price measure and the Act's illustrations earn the marks. In real life, they decide how much a wronged party can actually recover.
legalProvision: Section 73. When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract. Explanation. In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74 (first part). When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
In simple words

Section 73, first paragraph: pay for loss that arises naturally from the breach (first limb), and for loss both parties knew was likely when they contracted (second limb). Section 73, second paragraph: do not pay for remote and indirect loss. Section 73, third paragraph: the same rule applies to quasi-contractual obligations. Explanation: count what the injured party could have done to reduce the loss. Section 74: if the contract names a sum for breach, the court gives reasonable compensation up to that sum.
The Act gives eighteen illustrations, (a) to (r), to Section 73. The table in section 9 below groups them by the rule each one shows.
hi.meaning:
Damages are the compensation, in money, that the law awards to a person for loss caused to him by a breach of contract. The Act uses the word "compensation". "Damages" is the word used in courts and exam questions. The aim is compensation, not punishment. The injured party should be no worse off and no better off than if the contract had been performed. That is why: he gets his actual, proved loss, not a reward; he cannot claim remote loss; he cannot claim loss he could have avoided (mitigation); a penalty clause is cut down to reasonable compensation (Section 74). Four questions decide whether a loss is recoverable (see Diagram 1 ): Diagram 1. Ask the four questions in order. flowchart TD L["A loss after a breach"] --> Q1{"1. Caused by the breach?"} Q1 -- "No" --> X1["Not recoverable"] Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"2. Arose naturally, OR both parties
knew it was likely when contracting?"} Q2 -- "No" --> X2["Remote and indirect · not paid
Section 73, para 2"] Q2 -- "Yes" --> Q3{"3. Loss and amount proved?"} Q3 -- "No" --> X3["Nominal damages only"] Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4{"4. Could reasonable steps
have reduced it?"} Q4 -- "Yes" --> X4["Avoidable part cut
Explanation to Section 73"] Q4 -- "No" --> OK["Compensation for the loss
Section 73"] X4 --> OK Text description 1 Was the loss caused by the breach? No: nothing. 2 Did it arise naturally, or did both parties know it was likely when contracting? No: remote, not paid. 3 Is the loss and its amount proved? No: nominal damages only. 4 Could reasonable steps have reduced it? Yes: avoidable part cut. Result: compensation for the proved, natural or foreseen, unavoidable loss. Was the loss caused by the breach? Did it arise naturally , or did both parties know it was likely when they contracted? If not, it is remote. Has the claimant proved the loss and its amount? If not, only nominal damages . Could he have reduced it by reasonable steps? If yes, the avoidable part is cut.
keyPoints: Damages compensate for loss caused by the breach. They do not punish. Section 73 pays for natural loss and for loss both parties knew was likely, but not for remote and indirect loss. The kinds are general, special, nominal, exemplary, liquidated and unliquidated . Special damages need knowledge of the special circumstances when the contract was made . Nominal damages are given when breach is proved but no loss. Exemplary damages are generally not given in contract. No damages for mental agony in an ordinary commercial contract. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) is the source of the two limbs of Section 73. For goods, the measure is the market price against the contract price at the date of breach .

caseLaws.name: Hadley v
caseLaws.facts: Baxendale (1854) Facts. A Gloucester mill's crank shaft broke. The owners sent it by carrier to Greenwich as a pattern for a new one. The carrier delayed delivery, and the mill lost profits. Principle. Damages are those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably in the contemplation of both parties when they contracted. Special circumstances count only if communicated. (1854) 9 Exch 341; 156 ER 145. Why it matters. Its two limbs are written into Section 73. Karsandas H. Thacker v. Saran Engineering Co. (1965) Facts. A seller agreed to supply 200 tons of scrap iron at Rs. 100 a ton, then said he could not deliver. The buyer had agreed to resell to a third party. Principle. The seller was not liable for the buyer's payment to the third party, because that contract was not communicated. The buyer proved no market-price loss. AIR 1965 SC 1981. Why it matters. It applies Section 73 to remote loss and to the measure of damages. Victoria Laundry (Windsor) Ltd. v. Newman Industries Ltd. (1949) Facts. A boiler for a laundry was delivered late. The laundry claimed ordinary lost profits and the profits of special Government dyeing contracts. Principle. Ordinary profits were recoverable. The special profits were not, because the supplier did not know of those contracts. [1949] 2 KB 528. Why it matters. It applies the two limbs to a business loss. C. Czarnikow Ltd. v. Koufos (The Heron II) (1967) Facts. A ship carrying sugar to Basra arrived late, after the sugar price had fallen. Principle. The test of remoteness in contract is whether the loss was "not unlikely" to result. [1969] 1 AC 350. Why it matters. It states how likely a loss must be under the second limb. Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915) Facts. Buyers failed to take 23,500 shares on 30 December 1911. The seller sold them later. Principle. The measure is the contract price minus the market price on the date of breach. (1915) LR 43 IA 6 (PC). Why it matters. It fixes the date at which the loss is measured. Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Union of India (2000) Facts. A housing authority failed to allot plots as promised. ₹50,000 was awarded for "mental agony". Principle. Damages for mental agony are not given for breach of an ordinary commercial contract. The award was set aside. (2000) 6 SCC 113. Why it matters. It limits damages for mental distress in contract.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two limbs of the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale?
selfTest.a: Loss arising naturally from the breach, and loss both parties reasonably contemplated, when contracting, as the probable result of breach.

selfTest.q: 2. Ravi fails to deliver 100 bags of rice at ₹2,000. The market price on the due date is ₹2,300. What are the general damages?
3. When can special damages be recovered?
selfTest.a: Only if the special circumstances were known to both parties when the contract was made.

selfTest.q: 4. Are exemplary damages normally awarded for breach of contract?
selfTest.a: No. Contract damages compensate. Textbooks list breach of promise to marry and wrongful dishonour of a cheque as exceptions.

selfTest.q: 5. What are nominal damages?
selfTest.a: A small sum given when a breach is proved but no real loss is shown.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t4.subtitle: Section 26 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes two people truly agree on a deal, but the paper they sign says something else: a wrong figure, a missing clause, a misdescribed boundary. Rectification fixes the paper, not the deal. Section 26 allows it where fraud or a mutual mistake made the document fail to state the parties' real intention. The remedy is narrow and the court may refuse it. In exams, the grounds, the three routes and the contrast with rescission earn the marks. In real life, it saves a good bargain from a clerk's error.
legalProvision: Section 26. When instrument may be rectified. (1) When, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing [not being the articles of association of a company to which the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), applies] does not express their real intention, then— (a) either party or his representative in interest may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified; or (b) the plaintiff may, in any suit in which any right arising under the instrument is in issue, claim in his pleading that the instrument be rectified; or (c) a defendant in any such suit as is referred to in clause (b), may, in addition to any other defence open to him, ask for rectification of the instrument. (2) If, in any suit in which a contract or other instrument is sought to be rectified under sub-section (1), the court finds that the instrument, through fraud or mistake, does not express the real intention of the parties, the court may, in its discretion, direct rectification of the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value. (3) A contract in writing may first be rectified, and then if the party claiming rectification has so prayed in his pleading and the court thinks fit, may be specifically enforced. (4) No relief for the rectification of an instrument shall be granted to any party under this section unless it has been specifically claimed: Provided that where a party has not claimed any such relief in his pleading, the court shall, at any stage of the proceeding, allow him to amend the pleading on such terms as may be just for including such claim.
Related provisions (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 20. Agreement void where both parties are under mistake as to matter of fact. Where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. Explanation. —An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement, is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.

Section 22. Contract caused by mistake of one party as to matter of fact. A contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one of the parties to it being under a mistake as to a matter of fact.
In simple words

Section 26(1): when fraud or a mutual mistake makes a written contract or other instrument fail to state the parties' real intention, either party or his representative in interest may sue to have it corrected. The same relief may be claimed in a pending suit, or asked for by a defendant. A company's articles of association are left out. Section 26(2): the court may, in its discretion , correct the instrument to state the real intention, so far as this does not harm rights that third persons acquired in good faith and for value. Section 26(3): a written contract may first be corrected and then, if this was prayed for and the court thinks fit, specifically enforced. Section 26(4): no relief unless it is specifically claimed, but the court shall allow an amendment of the pleading at any stage on just terms. Contract Act Sections 20 to 22: these deal with mistake in the agreement itself, not in the writing.
en.meaning:
Rectification means the court corrects the wording of a written instrument. An instrument is any document that records rights or duties, such as a sale agreement, a deed or a lease. The court does not make a new bargain. It records the bargain that was truly made. The question this section answers. When may a court correct a signed document so that it says what the parties really agreed? Why the law has this rule. The law normally treats a signed document as the final record of the deal. But if both sides agreed on one thing and the paper says another, holding them to the paper would enforce a bargain neither of them made. Rectification is a narrow exception that brings the paper back in line with the real agreement. The court asks four questions in order. Did the parties reach a concluded agreement with a real, shared intention (Section 26(1))? If not, there is nothing to rectify; the question is one of mistake or no contract. Does the writing fail to express that intention (Section 26(1))? If not, the document stands as written. Is the cause fraud or a mutual mistake, and not a one-sided mistake (Section 26(1))? If not, Section 26 does not apply. Can the correction be made without harming a third person who acquired rights in good faith and for value (Section 26(2))? If not, the court cannot rectify against that person. If all the answers are yes, the court may, in its discretion, rectify the instrument. A contract so rectified can then be specifically enforced (Section 26(3)). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the box. flowchart TD Q1{"1. A concluded agreement with a
real, shared intention? s. 26(1)"} Q1 -->|"No"| N1["Nothing to rectify:
a question of mistake or no contract"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"2. Does the writing fail to
express that intention? s. 26(1)"} Q2 -->|"No"| N2["The document stands as written"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"3. Caused by fraud or a mutual mistake,
not a one-sided mistake? s. 26(1)"} Q3 -->|"No"| N3["Section 26 does not apply"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4{"4. No harm to a third person who acquired
rights in good faith and for value? s. 26(2)"} Q4 -->|"No"| N4["The court cannot rectify
against that person"] Q4 -->|"Yes"| Y["The court may, in its discretion, rectify;
then specific performance (s. 26(3))"] Text description Question 1: did the parties reach a concluded agreement with a real, shared intention? If no, there is nothing to rectify; it is a question of mistake or no contract. Question 2: does the writing fail to express that intention? If no, the document stands as written. Question 3: is the cause fraud or a mutual mistake, not a one-sided mistake? If no, Section 26 does not apply. Question 4: can it be rectified without harming a third person who acquired rights in good faith and for value? If no, the court cannot rectify against that person. If all answers are yes, the court may, in its discretion, rectify, and a contract so rectified can then be specifically enforced under Section 26(3).
keyPoints: Section 26 corrects the document, not the deal. Grounds: fraud or a mutual mistake. A one-sided mistake is not enough. Three routes: separate suit, claim in a suit, defendant's request. The court has a discretion. It cannot prejudice third persons who acted in good faith and for value. A contract can be rectified and then specifically enforced in the same suit (Section 26(3)). Rectification must be specifically claimed, but the court shall allow an amendment (Section 26(4)). Rectification records the bargain made. It does not substitute a different bargain ( Venkatesha , 2026).

caseLaws.name: Venkatesha v
caseLaws.facts: K.M. Venkatamuniyappa (2026) Facts. A 1971 sale deed conveyed land in Sy. No. 1/4. A rectification deed of 1997, made only between a later buyer and his own vendor, tried to change the survey number to Sy. No. 162. The original owner was not a party. Principle. Section 26 is "a limited equitable jurisdiction ". "Rectification, therefore, rectifies the expression of a concluded bargain; it does not substitute one bargain for another." The appeal was allowed and the dismissal of the suit restored. 2026 INSC 705, decided 14 July 2026 (Dipankar Datta and Vipul M. Pancholi JJ). Why it matters. It is a recent Supreme Court statement of what Section 26 can and cannot do. Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864) Facts. A contract for 125 bales of Surat cotton "to arrive ex Peerless" from Bombay. Two ships called Peerless sailed, one in October and one in December. Principle. Each side meant a different ship. On demurrer, the plea was held a good answer. Where the parties never agreed on the same thing, the problem is mistake, not wrong wording. (1864) 2 H & C 906. Why it matters. It marks the line between a mistake in recording an agreement (Section 26) and no agreement at all.

selfTest.q: 1. On what two grounds may an instrument be rectified?
selfTest.a: Fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties.

selfTest.q: 2. Whose rights does Section 26(2) protect?
selfTest.a: Third persons who acquired rights in good faith and for value.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a rectified contract be specifically enforced?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 26(3) allows a contract to be rectified and then enforced, if the party prayed for it and the court thinks fit.

selfTest.q: 4. A defendant finds a typing error in the agreement he is sued on. Must he file a separate suit?
selfTest.a: No. As a defendant he may ask for rectification in addition to any other defence (Section 26(1)(c)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a company's articles of association be rectified under Section 26?
selfTest.a: No. Section 26(1) leaves them out.

legalProvision: Section 26. When instrument may be rectified. (1) When, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing [not being the articles of association of a company to which the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), applies] does not express their real intention, then— (a) either party or his representative in interest may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified; or (b) the plaintiff may, in any suit in which any right arising under the instrument is in issue, claim in his pleading that the instrument be rectified; or (c) a defendant in any such suit as is referred to in clause (b), may, in addition to any other defence open to him, ask for rectification of the instrument. (2) If, in any suit in which a contract or other instrument is sought to be rectified under sub-section (1), the court finds that the instrument, through fraud or mistake, does not express the real intention of the parties, the court may, in its discretion, direct rectification of the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value. (3) A contract in writing may first be rectified, and then if the party claiming rectification has so prayed in his pleading and the court thinks fit, may be specifically enforced. (4) No relief for the rectification of an instrument shall be granted to any party under this section unless it has been specifically claimed: Provided that where a party has not claimed any such relief in his pleading, the court shall, at any stage of the proceeding, allow him to amend the pleading on such terms as may be just for including such claim.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 20. Agreement void where both parties are under mistake as to matter of fact. Where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. Explanation. —An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement, is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.

Section 22. Contract caused by mistake of one party as to matter of fact. A contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one of the parties to it being under a mistake as to a matter of fact.
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 26(1): మోసం లేదా పరస్పర పొరపాటు వల్ల ఒక రాతపూర్వక కాంట్రాక్టు లేదా ఇతర పత్రం పక్షాల నిజమైన ఉద్దేశాన్ని చెప్పకపోతే, ఏ పక్షమైనా లేదా అతని ప్రతినిధి దాన్ని సరిచేయించడానికి దావా వేయవచ్చు. నడుస్తున్న దావాలో కూడా ఇదే ఉపశమనం కోరవచ్చు, లేదా ప్రతివాది అడగవచ్చు. కంపెనీ articles of association కు ఇది వర్తించదు. సెక్షన్ 26(2): మూడో వ్యక్తులు సద్భావంతో, విలువ చెల్లించి పొందిన హక్కులకు హాని కలగనంత వరకు, నిజమైన ఉద్దేశాన్ని చెప్పేలా కోర్టు తన విచక్షణతో పత్రాన్ని సరిచేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 26(3): రాతపూర్వక కాంట్రాక్టును ముందు సరిచేసి, తర్వాత, అలా కోరి ఉండి కోర్టు సరైనదని భావిస్తే, నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 26(4): ప్రత్యేకంగా కోరకపోతే ఉపశమనం లేదు; కానీ ఏ దశలోనైనా న్యాయమైన షరతులపై pleading సవరణకు కోర్టు అనుమతించాలి. Contract Act సెక్షన్లు 20 నుంచి 22: ఇవి రాతలోని పొరపాటుతో కాదు, ఒప్పందంలోని పొరపాటుతో వ్యవహరిస్తాయి.
te.meaning:
పత్రం సవరణ అంటే ఒక రాతపూర్వక పత్రంలోని పదాలను కోర్టు సరిచేయడం. పత్రం (instrument) అంటే హక్కులు లేదా బాధ్యతలను నమోదు చేసే ఏ దస్తావేజైనా, ఉదాహరణకు అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం, డీడ్ లేదా లీజు. కోర్టు కొత్త ఒప్పందం చేయదు. నిజంగా జరిగిన ఒప్పందాన్నే నమోదు చేస్తుంది. ఈ సెక్షన్ జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. పక్షాలు నిజంగా ఒప్పుకున్నదే చెప్పేలా, సంతకం చేసిన పత్రాన్ని కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు సరిచేయవచ్చు? చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు. సాధారణంగా సంతకం చేసిన పత్రాన్నే ఒప్పందానికి చివరి రికార్డుగా చట్టం చూస్తుంది. కానీ ఇద్దరూ ఒకటి ఒప్పుకుని కాగితం మరొకటి చెబితే, కాగితానికే కట్టుబడమంటే ఇద్దరిలో ఎవరూ చేసుకోని ఒప్పందాన్ని అమలు చేసినట్లవుతుంది. కాగితాన్ని నిజమైన ఒప్పందానికి అనుగుణంగా తెచ్చే పరిమిత మినహాయింపే పత్రం సవరణ. కోర్టు క్రమంగా నాలుగు ప్రశ్నలు అడుగుతుంది. పక్షాలు నిజమైన, ఉమ్మడి ఉద్దేశంతో పూర్తి ఒప్పందానికి వచ్చారా (సెక్షన్ 26(1))? రాకపోతే సరిచేయడానికి ఏమీ లేదు; ఇది పొరపాటు లేదా కాంట్రాక్టే లేని ప్రశ్న. రాత ఆ ఉద్దేశాన్ని చెప్పలేకపోయిందా (సెక్షన్ 26(1))? చెబితే పత్రం రాసినట్లే నిలుస్తుంది. కారణం మోసమా లేదా పరస్పర పొరపాటా, ఒక్కరి పొరపాటు కాదా (సెక్షన్ 26(1))? కాకపోతే సెక్షన్ 26 వర్తించదు. సద్భావంతో, విలువ చెల్లించి హక్కులు పొందిన మూడో వ్యక్తికి హాని లేకుండా సవరణ చేయగలమా (సెక్షన్ 26(2))? చేయలేకపోతే ఆ వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కోర్టు సరిచేయలేదు. అన్నీ అవును అయితే, కోర్టు తన విచక్షణతో పత్రాన్ని సరిచేయవచ్చు. అలా సరిచేసిన కాంట్రాక్టును తర్వాత నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 26(3)). మూడో వ్యక్తికి హాని లేదా? సె. 26(2)"} Q4 -->|"కాదు"| N4["ఆ వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా
కోర్టు సరిచేయలేదు"] Q4 -->|"అవును"| Y["కోర్టు విచక్షణతో సరిచేయవచ్చు;
తర్వాత నిర్దిష్ట అమలు (సె. 26(3))"] వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: పక్షాలు నిజమైన, ఉమ్మడి ఉద్దేశంతో పూర్తి ఒప్పందానికి వచ్చారా? రాకపోతే సరిచేయడానికి ఏమీ లేదు; ఇది పొరపాటు లేదా కాంట్రాక్టే లేని ప్రశ్న. ప్రశ్న 2: రాత ఆ ఉద్దేశాన్ని చెప్పలేకపోయిందా? చెబితే పత్రం రాసినట్లే నిలుస్తుంది. ప్రశ్న 3: కారణం మోసమా లేదా పరస్పర పొరపాటా, ఒక్కరి పొరపాటు కాదా? కాకపోతే సెక్షన్ 26 వర్తించదు. ప్రశ్న 4: సద్భావంతో, విలువ చెల్లించి హక్కులు పొందిన మూడో వ్యక్తికి హాని లేకుండా సరిచేయగలమా? లేకపోతే ఆ వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కోర్టు సరిచేయలేదు. అన్నీ అవును అయితే, కోర్టు విచక్షణతో సరిచేయవచ్చు; అలా సరిచేసిన కాంట్రాక్టును సెక్షన్ 26(3) కింద నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. ఏ రెండు కారణాలపై పత్రాన్ని సరిచేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: మోసం, లేదా పక్షాల పరస్పర పొరపాటు.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 26(2) ఎవరి హక్కులను కాపాడుతుంది?
selfTest.a: సద్భావంతో, విలువ చెల్లించి హక్కులు పొందిన మూడో వ్యక్తుల హక్కులను.

selfTest.q: 3. సరిచేసిన కాంట్రాక్టును నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. పక్షం కోరి ఉండి, కోర్టు సరైనదని భావిస్తే, కాంట్రాక్టును సరిచేసి తర్వాత అమలు చేయడానికి సెక్షన్ 26(3) అనుమతిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. తనపై వేసిన దావాలోని ఒప్పందంలో ప్రతివాదికి టైపింగ్ పొరపాటు కనిపిస్తుంది. అతను విడిగా దావా వేయాలా?
selfTest.a: అవసరం లేదు. ప్రతివాదిగా, ఇతర రక్షణలతో పాటు సవరణ కోరవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 26(1)(c)).

selfTest.q: 5. కంపెనీ articles of association ను సెక్షన్ 26 కింద సరిచేయవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సెక్షన్ 26(1) వాటిని మినహాయిస్తుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: Sometimes two people truly agree on a deal, but the paper they sign says something else: a wrong figure, a missing clause, a misdescribed boundary. Rectification fixes the paper, not the deal. Section 26 allows it where fraud or a mutual mistake made the document fail to state the parties' real intention. The remedy is narrow and the court may refuse it. In exams, the grounds, the three routes and the contrast with rescission earn the marks. In real life, it saves a good bargain from a clerk's error.
legalProvision: Section 26. When instrument may be rectified. (1) When, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing [not being the articles of association of a company to which the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956), applies] does not express their real intention, then— (a) either party or his representative in interest may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified; or (b) the plaintiff may, in any suit in which any right arising under the instrument is in issue, claim in his pleading that the instrument be rectified; or (c) a defendant in any such suit as is referred to in clause (b), may, in addition to any other defence open to him, ask for rectification of the instrument. (2) If, in any suit in which a contract or other instrument is sought to be rectified under sub-section (1), the court finds that the instrument, through fraud or mistake, does not express the real intention of the parties, the court may, in its discretion, direct rectification of the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value. (3) A contract in writing may first be rectified, and then if the party claiming rectification has so prayed in his pleading and the court thinks fit, may be specifically enforced. (4) No relief for the rectification of an instrument shall be granted to any party under this section unless it has been specifically claimed: Provided that where a party has not claimed any such relief in his pleading, the court shall, at any stage of the proceeding, allow him to amend the pleading on such terms as may be just for including such claim.
Related provisions (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 20. Agreement void where both parties are under mistake as to matter of fact. Where both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void. Explanation. —An erroneous opinion as to the value of the thing which forms the subject-matter of the agreement, is not to be deemed a mistake as to a matter of fact.

Section 21. Effect of mistakes as to law. A contract is not voidable because it was caused by a mistake as to any law in force in India; but a mistake as to a law not in force in India has the same effect as a mistake of fact.

Section 22. Contract caused by mistake of one party as to matter of fact. A contract is not voidable merely because it was caused by one of the parties to it being under a mistake as to a matter of fact.
In simple words

Section 26(1): when fraud or a mutual mistake makes a written contract or other instrument fail to state the parties' real intention, either party or his representative in interest may sue to have it corrected. The same relief may be claimed in a pending suit, or asked for by a defendant. A company's articles of association are left out. Section 26(2): the court may, in its discretion , correct the instrument to state the real intention, so far as this does not harm rights that third persons acquired in good faith and for value. Section 26(3): a written contract may first be corrected and then, if this was prayed for and the court thinks fit, specifically enforced. Section 26(4): no relief unless it is specifically claimed, but the court shall allow an amendment of the pleading at any stage on just terms. Contract Act Sections 20 to 22: these deal with mistake in the agreement itself, not in the writing.
hi.meaning:
Rectification means the court corrects the wording of a written instrument. An instrument is any document that records rights or duties, such as a sale agreement, a deed or a lease. The court does not make a new bargain. It records the bargain that was truly made. The question this section answers. When may a court correct a signed document so that it says what the parties really agreed? Why the law has this rule. The law normally treats a signed document as the final record of the deal. But if both sides agreed on one thing and the paper says another, holding them to the paper would enforce a bargain neither of them made. Rectification is a narrow exception that brings the paper back in line with the real agreement. The court asks four questions in order. Did the parties reach a concluded agreement with a real, shared intention (Section 26(1))? If not, there is nothing to rectify; the question is one of mistake or no contract. Does the writing fail to express that intention (Section 26(1))? If not, the document stands as written. Is the cause fraud or a mutual mistake, and not a one-sided mistake (Section 26(1))? If not, Section 26 does not apply. Can the correction be made without harming a third person who acquired rights in good faith and for value (Section 26(2))? If not, the court cannot rectify against that person. If all the answers are yes, the court may, in its discretion, rectify the instrument. A contract so rectified can then be specifically enforced (Section 26(3)). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. real, shared intention? s. 26(1)"} Q1 -->|"No"| N1["Nothing to rectify:

express that intention? s. 26(1)"} Q2 -->|"No"| N2["The document stands as written"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"3. Caused by fraud or a mutual mistake,
not a one-sided mistake? s. 26(1)"} Q3 -->|"No"| N3["Section 26 does not apply"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4{"4. No harm to a third person who acquired
rights in good faith and for value? s. 26(2)"} Q4 -->|"No"| N4["The court cannot rectify
against that person"] Q4 -->|"Yes"| Y["The court may, in its discretion, rectify;
then specific performance (s. 26(3))"] Text description Question 1: did the parties reach a concluded agreement with a real, shared intention? If no, there is nothing to rectify; it is a question of mistake or no contract. Question 2: does the writing fail to express that intention? If no, the document stands as written. Question 3: is the cause fraud or a mutual mistake, not a one-sided mistake? If no, Section 26 does not apply. Question 4: can it be rectified without harming a third person who acquired rights in good faith and for value? If no, the court cannot rectify against that person. If all answers are yes, the court may, in its discretion, rectify, and a contract so rectified can then be specifically enforced under Section 26(3).
keyPoints: Section 26 corrects the document, not the deal. Grounds: fraud or a mutual mistake. A one-sided mistake is not enough. Three routes: separate suit, claim in a suit, defendant's request. The court has a discretion. It cannot prejudice third persons who acted in good faith and for value. A contract can be rectified and then specifically enforced in the same suit (Section 26(3)). Rectification must be specifically claimed, but the court shall allow an amendment (Section 26(4)). Rectification records the bargain made. It does not substitute a different bargain ( Venkatesha , 2026).

caseLaws.name: Venkatesha v
caseLaws.facts: K.M. Venkatamuniyappa (2026) Facts. A 1971 sale deed conveyed land in Sy. No. 1/4. A rectification deed of 1997, made only between a later buyer and his own vendor, tried to change the survey number to Sy. No. 162. The original owner was not a party. Principle. Section 26 is "a limited equitable jurisdiction ". "Rectification, therefore, rectifies the expression of a concluded bargain; it does not substitute one bargain for another." The appeal was allowed and the dismissal of the suit restored. 2026 INSC 705, decided 14 July 2026 (Dipankar Datta and Vipul M. Pancholi JJ). Why it matters. It is a recent Supreme Court statement of what Section 26 can and cannot do. Raffles v. Wichelhaus (1864) Facts. A contract for 125 bales of Surat cotton "to arrive ex Peerless" from Bombay. Two ships called Peerless sailed, one in October and one in December. Principle. Each side meant a different ship. On demurrer, the plea was held a good answer. Where the parties never agreed on the same thing, the problem is mistake, not wrong wording. (1864) 2 H & C 906. Why it matters. It marks the line between a mistake in recording an agreement (Section 26) and no agreement at all.

selfTest.q: 1. On what two grounds may an instrument be rectified?
selfTest.a: Fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties.

selfTest.q: 2. Whose rights does Section 26(2) protect?
selfTest.a: Third persons who acquired rights in good faith and for value.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a rectified contract be specifically enforced?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 26(3) allows a contract to be rectified and then enforced, if the party prayed for it and the court thinks fit.

selfTest.q: 4. A defendant finds a typing error in the agreement he is sued on. Must he file a separate suit?
selfTest.a: No. As a defendant he may ask for rectification in addition to any other defence (Section 26(1)(c)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a company's articles of association be rectified under Section 26?
selfTest.a: No. Section 26(1) leaves them out.
