law-of-contract-i-u5-t1.subtitle: Specific Relief Act, 1963 and the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018

en.inOneMinute: Damages give money for a broken promise. Sometimes the injured person needs the thing itself: the plot of land, the document set right, the wrong stopped. The Specific Relief Act, 1963 gives these remedies. They are called specific relief . The Act has seven kinds of relief: recovery of possession, specific performance , rectification, rescission, cancellation, declaration and injunction . The Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018 changed the Act by a large amount from 1 October 2018. Above all, specific performance of a contract is now the rule ("shall be enforced"), and no longer a matter of the court's choice. In exams, the scheme of the Act, Sections 3 and 4, and the 2018 changes earn the marks. Add the Supreme Court's answer on whether the 2018 changes apply to contracts made before 1 October 2018.
legalProvision: Section 1. Short title, extent and commencement. (1) This Act may be called the Specific Relief Act, 1963. (2) It extends to the whole of India [***]. (3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint.
(The date appointed was 1 March 1964. The words "except the State of Jammu and Kashmir" were omitted from sub-section (2) with effect from 31 October 2019.)

Section 2. Definitions. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "obligation" includes every duty enforceable by law; (b) "settlement" means an instrument (other than a will or codicil as defined by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925)), whereby the destination or devolution of successive interests in movable or immovable property is disposed of or is agreed to be disposed of; (c) "trust" has the same meaning as in section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 (2 of 1882), and includes an obligation in the nature of a trust within the meaning of Chapter IX of that Act; (d) "trustee" includes every person holding property in trust; (e) all other words and expressions used herein but not defined, and defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), have the meanings respectively assigned to them in that Act.

Section 3. Savings. Except as otherwise provided herein, nothing in this Act shall be deemed— (a) to deprive any person of any right to relief, other than specific performance, which he may have under any contract; or (b) to affect the operation of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908), on documents.

Section 4. Specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing penal laws. Specific relief can be granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights and not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

Section 10 (as substituted in 2018). Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.
Sections 5 to 42 contain the seven kinds of relief (see Diagram 1 ). Sections 43 and 44 were repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1974, with effect from 20 December 1974.
In simple words

Section 1: the Act applies to the whole of India. It came into force on 1 March 1964. Section 2: defines obligation, settlement, trust and trustee . Words the Act does not define, but the Indian Contract Act does, carry their Contract Act meaning. Section 3: the Act does not take away any right to relief, other than specific performance , that a person has under a contract. It does not affect the Indian Registration Act, 1908. Section 4: specific relief is given only to enforce a person's own civil rights. It is never given merely to enforce a penal (criminal) law. Section 10 (new): the court shall enforce specific performance of a contract. The only exceptions are those in Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16.
en.meaning:
Specific relief means relief in the exact form the person is entitled to. The court orders the actual thing: the land handed over, the contract performed, the document corrected, the right declared, the wrong stopped. Damages are only the money value of the loss. The Act does not define "specific relief", but its title and Section 4 show its scope. The Act's own description. The preamble calls it "An Act to define and amend the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief." It is the second law on the subject. It replaced the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and was made after the Law Commission's Ninth Report. Why the law has it. At common law in England, courts at first gave only damages. Courts of Equity began to order specific performance where damages would be inadequate. That is why these remedies come from equity (a branch of law based on fairness, as against strict rules) and why, before 2018, the court had a wide discretion (freedom to decide) whether to grant them. The 2018 Amendment made specific performance the rule. Many other reliefs in the Act, such as injunctions (Section 36) and declarations (Section 34), are still discretionary . The structure. The Act has three Parts and eight Chapters. Part I, Preliminary: Sections 1 to 4. Part II, Specific Relief: Chapters I to VI, Sections 5 to 35. Part III, Preventive Relief : Chapters VII and VIII, Sections 36 to 44 (Sections 43 and 44 repealed). The Schedule: the list of infrastructure projects, added in 2018. See Diagram 1 for the scheme of the Act. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. (ss. 43-44 repealed)"] Text description The Specific Relief Act, 1963 has three Parts and a Schedule. Part I, Preliminary, is Sections 1 to 4. Part II, Specific Relief, has six kinds of relief: recovery of possession (Sections 5 to 8), specific performance (Sections 9 to 25), rectification (Section 26), rescission (Sections 27 to 30), cancellation (Sections 31 to 33) and declaratory decrees (Sections 34 and 35). Part III, Preventive Relief, is injunctions (Sections 36 to 42; Sections 43 and 44 repealed). The Schedule, added in 2018, lists infrastructure projects.
keyPoints: Specific relief gives the thing itself. Damages give its money value. Act 47 of 1963, in force from 1 March 1964. It replaced the 1877 Act. It has three Parts, eight Chapters and a Schedule. Sections 43 and 44 are repealed. Seven kinds of relief: possession, specific performance, rectification, rescission, cancellation, declaration and injunction (Sections 5 to 42). Section 2(e) borrows Contract Act meanings. Section 3 saves other remedies. Section 4 limits the Act to individual civil rights. The 2018 Amendment came into force on 1 October 2018. Section 10 now says "shall be enforced", subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16. The old discretion in Section 20 was replaced by substituted performance. Katta Sujatha Reddy (2022) held the amendment prospective. The 2024 review recalled that judgment without deciding the point again.

caseLaws.name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v
caseLaws.facts: Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (2022) Facts. A purchaser under two agreements of 26 and 27 March 1997 for about 40 acres in Budvel Village, Ranga Reddy District, paid ₹34,80,850 of ₹40,20,000. The balance was due within three months. The purchaser sued in 2002. The High Court held the amended Section 10 retrospective and decreed the suit in part. Principle. The 2018 Amendment is prospective and "cannot apply to those transactions that took place prior to its coming into force". The Court also held the suit barred by limitation and the purchaser not ready and willing. Civil Appeal No. 5822 of 2022, decided 25 August 2022 (Ramana CJI, Krishna Murari and Hima Kohli JJ). On 8 November 2024 the Court recalled this judgment in review and restored the High Court's decree, without deciding the prospective point again (2024 INSC 861). Why it matters. It is the leading authority on whether the amended Section 10 applies to older contracts. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan (1997) Facts. An agreement of 15 December 1978 to sell a house in Madurai for ₹60,000 required the sale within six months. The buyer paid ₹5,000 and did nothing for about two and a half years. He sent notice on 11 July 1981 and sued on 23 August 1981, after prices had risen sharply. Principle. Not every suit for specific performance must be decreed merely because it is filed within limitation. Total inaction for 2½ years together with a steep rise in prices made the relief inequitable . (1997) 3 SCC 1 : AIR 1997 SC 1751. Why it matters. It shows how the old discretion under Sections 10 and 20 worked before 2018, and why delay and readiness still matter. Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh (1967) Facts. Tenant-cultivators of agricultural land in Gwalior district said the landlord forcibly stopped them from cultivating and had the land cultivated by others. They sued for restoration of possession under a Gwalior law similar to Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. Principle. The Court approved the Privy Council's words: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession". In such a suit the question of title is irrelevant. AIR 1968 SC 620 : (1968) 2 SCR 203, decided 29 November 1967. Why it matters. It supports the rule now in Section 6 of the 1963 Act. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two house sites in Matwada, Warangal were sold to the plaintiffs by Rukminibai in 1968 and the same land was sold to the defendant by her brother in 1977. The plaintiffs sued only for a permanent injunction. Principle. A suit for injunction alone lies where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and his title is not under a cloud. Where the title is in dispute, he must sue for declaration and consequential injunction. (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It shows how declaration and injunction under the Act work together.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 4 of the Act say?
selfTest.a: Specific relief can be granted only to enforce individual civil rights. It cannot be granted for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

selfTest.q: 2. On what date did the 2018 Amendment come into force?
selfTest.a: On 1 October 2018.

selfTest.q: 3. What does the amended Section 10 say?
selfTest.a: The specific performance of a contract "shall be enforced" by the court, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16.

selfTest.q: 4. What did the old Section 20 say, and what does the new Section 20 deal with?
selfTest.a: The old Section 20 made the jurisdiction to decree specific performance discretionary. The new Section 20 deals with substituted performance after at least 30 days' written notice.

selfTest.q: 5. Does the Act take away the right to claim damages under the Contract Act?
selfTest.a: No. Section 3 saves every right to relief under a contract other than specific performance.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "obligation" includes every duty enforceable by law; (b) "settlement" means an instrument (other than a will or codicil as defined by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925)), whereby the destination or devolution of successive interests in movable or immovable property is disposed of or is agreed to be disposed of; (c) "trust" has the same meaning as in section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 (2 of 1882), and includes an obligation in the nature of a trust within the meaning of Chapter IX of that Act; (d) "trustee" includes every person holding property in trust; (e) all other words and expressions used herein but not defined, and defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), have the meanings respectively assigned to them in that Act.

Section 3. Savings. Except as otherwise provided herein, nothing in this Act shall be deemed— (a) to deprive any person of any right to relief, other than specific performance, which he may have under any contract; or (b) to affect the operation of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908), on documents.

Section 4. Specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing penal laws. Specific relief can be granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights and not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

Section 10 (as substituted in 2018). Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.

సెక్షన్ 1: చట్టం భారతదేశం అంతటికీ వర్తిస్తుంది. ఇది 1 మార్చి 1964 నుంచి అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది. సెక్షన్ 2: obligation, settlement, trust, trustee అనే పదాలను నిర్వచిస్తుంది. ఈ చట్టం నిర్వచించని, కానీ కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం నిర్వచించిన పదాలకు కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం అర్థమే వర్తిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 3: కాంట్రాక్టు కింద ఒక వ్యక్తికి ఉన్న, నిర్దిష్ట అమలు తప్ప, మరే ఉపశమన హక్కునూ ఈ చట్టం తీసివేయదు. Indian Registration Act, 1908 ను ఇది ప్రభావితం చేయదు. సెక్షన్ 4: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమనం ఒక వ్యక్తి సొంత పౌర హక్కులను అమలు చేయడానికి మాత్రమే. కేవలం శిక్షా (క్రిమినల్) చట్టాన్ని అమలు చేయడానికి దీన్ని ఎప్పుడూ ఇవ్వరు. సెక్షన్ 10 (కొత్తది): కోర్టు కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్దిష్ట అమలును తప్పనిసరిగా అమలు చేయాలి. మినహాయింపులు సెక్షన్ 11(2), సెక్షన్ 14, సెక్షన్ 16 లోనివి మాత్రమే.
te.meaning:
నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమనం అంటే వ్యక్తికి హక్కు ఉన్న అదే రూపంలో ఇచ్చే ఉపశమనం. కోర్టు అసలు వస్తువునే ఆదేశిస్తుంది: భూమిని అప్పగించడం, కాంట్రాక్టును నెరవేర్చడం, పత్రాన్ని సరిదిద్దడం, హక్కును ప్రకటించడం, తప్పును ఆపడం. నష్టపరిహారం నష్టానికి డబ్బు విలువ మాత్రమే. చట్టం "specific relief" ను నిర్వచించదు, కానీ దాని పేరు, సెక్షన్ 4 దాని పరిధిని చూపుతాయి. చట్టం తన గురించి చెప్పేది. ప్రవేశిక (preamble) దీన్ని "An Act to define and amend the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief." అంటుంది. ఈ విషయంపై ఇది రెండో చట్టం. ఇది Specific Relief Act, 1877 స్థానంలో వచ్చింది, లా కమిషన్ తొమ్మిదో నివేదిక తర్వాత రూపొందింది. చట్టంలో ఇది ఎందుకు ఉంది. ఇంగ్లండ్‌లో కామన్ లా కోర్టులు మొదట నష్టపరిహారం మాత్రమే ఇచ్చేవి. నష్టపరిహారం సరిపోని చోట Courts of Equity నిర్దిష్ట అమలును ఆదేశించడం మొదలుపెట్టాయి. అందుకే ఈ పరిష్కారాలు equity (కఠిన నియమాలకు బదులు న్యాయబద్ధతపై ఆధారపడిన చట్ట శాఖ) నుంచి వచ్చాయి. అందుకే 2018 కి ముందు వాటిని ఇవ్వాలా వద్దా అనే దానిపై కోర్టుకు విస్తృత విచక్షణ (నిర్ణయించే స్వేచ్ఛ) ఉండేది. 2018 సవరణ నిర్దిష్ట అమలును నియమంగా మార్చింది. చట్టంలోని ఇతర అనేక ఉపశమనాలు, ఉదాహరణకు injunctions (సెక్షన్ 36), declarations (సెక్షన్ 34), ఇప్పటికీ కోర్టు విచక్షణపైనే ఆధారపడతాయి. నిర్మాణం. చట్టంలో మూడు భాగాలు (Parts), ఎనిమిది అధ్యాయాలు (Chapters) ఉన్నాయి. Part I, Preliminary: సెక్షన్లు 1 నుంచి 4. Part II, Specific Relief: అధ్యాయాలు I నుంచి VI, సెక్షన్లు 5 నుంచి 35. Part III, Preventive Relief : అధ్యాయాలు VII, VIII, సెక్షన్లు 36 నుంచి 44 (సెక్షన్లు 43, 44 రద్దయ్యాయి). The Schedule: మౌలిక సదుపాయ (infrastructure) ప్రాజెక్టుల జాబితా, 2018 లో చేర్చబడింది. చట్టం నిర్మాణం కోసం Diagram 1 చూడండి. Part II, Specific Relief, లో ఆరు రకాల ఉపశమనాలు: స్వాధీనం తిరిగి పొందడం (సెక్షన్లు 5 నుంచి 8), నిర్దిష్ట అమలు (సెక్షన్లు 9 నుంచి 25), పత్రం సవరణ (సెక్షన్ 26), కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు (సెక్షన్లు 27 నుంచి 30), పత్రం రద్దు (సెక్షన్లు 31 నుంచి 33), ప్రకటన డిక్రీలు (సెక్షన్లు 34, 35). Part III, Preventive Relief, injunctions (సెక్షన్లు 36 నుంచి 42; సెక్షన్లు 43, 44 రద్దు). 2018 లో చేర్చిన Schedule infrastructure ప్రాజెక్టుల జాబితా ఇస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. చట్టంలోని సెక్షన్ 4 ఏమి చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమనాన్ని వ్యక్తిగత పౌర హక్కులను అమలు చేయడానికి మాత్రమే ఇవ్వవచ్చు. కేవలం శిక్షా చట్టాన్ని అమలు చేసే ఉద్దేశంతో ఇవ్వలేం.

selfTest.q: 2. 2018 సవరణ ఏ తేదీన అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: 1 అక్టోబర్ 2018 న.

selfTest.q: 3. సవరించిన సెక్షన్ 10 ఏమి చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్దిష్ట అమలును కోర్టు "shall be enforced", సెక్షన్ 11(2), సెక్షన్ 14, సెక్షన్ 16 కు లోబడి.

selfTest.q: 4. పాత సెక్షన్ 20 ఏమి చెప్పింది, కొత్త సెక్షన్ 20 దేని గురించి?
selfTest.a: పాత సెక్షన్ 20 నిర్దిష్ట అమలు డిక్రీ ఇచ్చే అధికారాన్ని విచక్షణాధికారంగా చేసింది. కొత్త సెక్షన్ 20 కనీసం 30 రోజుల లిఖిత నోటీసు తర్వాత ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు గురించి.

selfTest.q: 5. కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం కింద నష్టపరిహారం కోరే హక్కును ఈ చట్టం తీసివేస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. నిర్దిష్ట అమలు తప్ప, కాంట్రాక్టు కింద ఉన్న ప్రతి ఉపశమన హక్కును సెక్షన్ 3 కాపాడుతుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: Damages give money for a broken promise. Sometimes the injured person needs the thing itself: the plot of land, the document set right, the wrong stopped. The Specific Relief Act, 1963 gives these remedies. They are called specific relief . The Act has seven kinds of relief: recovery of possession, specific performance , rectification, rescission, cancellation, declaration and injunction . The Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018 changed the Act by a large amount from 1 October 2018. Above all, specific performance of a contract is now the rule ("shall be enforced"), and no longer a matter of the court's choice. In exams, the scheme of the Act, Sections 3 and 4, and the 2018 changes earn the marks. Add the Supreme Court's answer on whether the 2018 changes apply to contracts made before 1 October 2018.
legalProvision: Section 1. Short title, extent and commencement. (1) This Act may be called the Specific Relief Act, 1963. (2) It extends to the whole of India [***]. (3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint.
(The date appointed was 1 March 1964. The words "except the State of Jammu and Kashmir" were omitted from sub-section (2) with effect from 31 October 2019.)

Section 2. Definitions. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "obligation" includes every duty enforceable by law; (b) "settlement" means an instrument (other than a will or codicil as defined by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925)), whereby the destination or devolution of successive interests in movable or immovable property is disposed of or is agreed to be disposed of; (c) "trust" has the same meaning as in section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 (2 of 1882), and includes an obligation in the nature of a trust within the meaning of Chapter IX of that Act; (d) "trustee" includes every person holding property in trust; (e) all other words and expressions used herein but not defined, and defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), have the meanings respectively assigned to them in that Act.

Section 3. Savings. Except as otherwise provided herein, nothing in this Act shall be deemed— (a) to deprive any person of any right to relief, other than specific performance, which he may have under any contract; or (b) to affect the operation of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908), on documents.

Section 4. Specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing penal laws. Specific relief can be granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights and not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

Section 10 (as substituted in 2018). Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.
Sections 5 to 42 contain the seven kinds of relief (see Diagram 1 ). Sections 43 and 44 were repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1974, with effect from 20 December 1974.
In simple words

Section 1: the Act applies to the whole of India. It came into force on 1 March 1964. Section 2: defines obligation, settlement, trust and trustee . Words the Act does not define, but the Indian Contract Act does, carry their Contract Act meaning. Section 3: the Act does not take away any right to relief, other than specific performance , that a person has under a contract. It does not affect the Indian Registration Act, 1908. Section 4: specific relief is given only to enforce a person's own civil rights. It is never given merely to enforce a penal (criminal) law. Section 10 (new): the court shall enforce specific performance of a contract. The only exceptions are those in Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16.
hi.meaning:
Specific relief means relief in the exact form the person is entitled to. The court orders the actual thing: the land handed over, the contract performed, the document corrected, the right declared, the wrong stopped. Damages are only the money value of the loss. The Act does not define "specific relief", but its title and Section 4 show its scope. The Act's own description. The preamble calls it "An Act to define and amend the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief." It is the second law on the subject. It replaced the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and was made after the Law Commission's Ninth Report. Why the law has it. At common law in England, courts at first gave only damages. Courts of Equity began to order specific performance where damages would be inadequate. That is why these remedies come from equity (a branch of law based on fairness, as against strict rules) and why, before 2018, the court had a wide discretion (freedom to decide) whether to grant them. The 2018 Amendment made specific performance the rule. Many other reliefs in the Act, such as injunctions (Section 36) and declarations (Section 34), are still discretionary . The structure. The Act has three Parts and eight Chapters. Part I, Preliminary: Sections 1 to 4. Part II, Specific Relief: Chapters I to VI, Sections 5 to 35. Part III, Preventive Relief : Chapters VII and VIII, Sections 36 to 44 (Sections 43 and 44 repealed). The Schedule: the list of infrastructure projects, added in 2018. See Diagram 1 for the scheme of the Act. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. The bottom boxes are the seven kinds of relief, with their sections. flowchart TD A["Specific Relief Act, 1963"] A --> P1["Part I: Preliminary

infrastructure projects"] P2 --> R1["Recovery of possession

(ss. 43-44 repealed)"] Text description The Specific Relief Act, 1963 has three Parts and a Schedule. Part I, Preliminary, is Sections 1 to 4. Part II, Specific Relief, has six kinds of relief: recovery of possession (Sections 5 to 8), specific performance (Sections 9 to 25), rectification (Section 26), rescission (Sections 27 to 30), cancellation (Sections 31 to 33) and declaratory decrees (Sections 34 and 35). Part III, Preventive Relief, is injunctions (Sections 36 to 42; Sections 43 and 44 repealed). The Schedule, added in 2018, lists infrastructure projects.
keyPoints: Specific relief gives the thing itself. Damages give its money value. Act 47 of 1963, in force from 1 March 1964. It replaced the 1877 Act. It has three Parts, eight Chapters and a Schedule. Sections 43 and 44 are repealed. Seven kinds of relief: possession, specific performance, rectification, rescission, cancellation, declaration and injunction (Sections 5 to 42). Section 2(e) borrows Contract Act meanings. Section 3 saves other remedies. Section 4 limits the Act to individual civil rights. The 2018 Amendment came into force on 1 October 2018. Section 10 now says "shall be enforced", subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16. The old discretion in Section 20 was replaced by substituted performance. Katta Sujatha Reddy (2022) held the amendment prospective. The 2024 review recalled that judgment without deciding the point again.

caseLaws.name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v
caseLaws.facts: Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (2022) Facts. A purchaser under two agreements of 26 and 27 March 1997 for about 40 acres in Budvel Village, Ranga Reddy District, paid ₹34,80,850 of ₹40,20,000. The balance was due within three months. The purchaser sued in 2002. The High Court held the amended Section 10 retrospective and decreed the suit in part. Principle. The 2018 Amendment is prospective and "cannot apply to those transactions that took place prior to its coming into force". The Court also held the suit barred by limitation and the purchaser not ready and willing. Civil Appeal No. 5822 of 2022, decided 25 August 2022 (Ramana CJI, Krishna Murari and Hima Kohli JJ). On 8 November 2024 the Court recalled this judgment in review and restored the High Court's decree, without deciding the prospective point again (2024 INSC 861). Why it matters. It is the leading authority on whether the amended Section 10 applies to older contracts. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan (1997) Facts. An agreement of 15 December 1978 to sell a house in Madurai for ₹60,000 required the sale within six months. The buyer paid ₹5,000 and did nothing for about two and a half years. He sent notice on 11 July 1981 and sued on 23 August 1981, after prices had risen sharply. Principle. Not every suit for specific performance must be decreed merely because it is filed within limitation. Total inaction for 2½ years together with a steep rise in prices made the relief inequitable . (1997) 3 SCC 1 : AIR 1997 SC 1751. Why it matters. It shows how the old discretion under Sections 10 and 20 worked before 2018, and why delay and readiness still matter. Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh (1967) Facts. Tenant-cultivators of agricultural land in Gwalior district said the landlord forcibly stopped them from cultivating and had the land cultivated by others. They sued for restoration of possession under a Gwalior law similar to Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. Principle. The Court approved the Privy Council's words: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession". In such a suit the question of title is irrelevant. AIR 1968 SC 620 : (1968) 2 SCR 203, decided 29 November 1967. Why it matters. It supports the rule now in Section 6 of the 1963 Act. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two house sites in Matwada, Warangal were sold to the plaintiffs by Rukminibai in 1968 and the same land was sold to the defendant by her brother in 1977. The plaintiffs sued only for a permanent injunction. Principle. A suit for injunction alone lies where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and his title is not under a cloud. Where the title is in dispute, he must sue for declaration and consequential injunction. (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It shows how declaration and injunction under the Act work together.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 4 of the Act say?
selfTest.a: Specific relief can be granted only to enforce individual civil rights. It cannot be granted for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

selfTest.q: 2. On what date did the 2018 Amendment come into force?
selfTest.a: On 1 October 2018.

selfTest.q: 3. What does the amended Section 10 say?
selfTest.a: The specific performance of a contract "shall be enforced" by the court, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16.

selfTest.q: 4. What did the old Section 20 say, and what does the new Section 20 deal with?
selfTest.a: The old Section 20 made the jurisdiction to decree specific performance discretionary. The new Section 20 deals with substituted performance after at least 30 days' written notice.

selfTest.q: 5. Does the Act take away the right to claim damages under the Contract Act?
selfTest.a: No. Section 3 saves every right to relief under a contract other than specific performance.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t2.subtitle: Sections 5 to 8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: If someone throws you out of your land, the law gives you two doors. One asks you to prove that you own it (Section 5). The other asks only whether you were in possession and were removed without due process of law (Section 6). Sections 7 and 8 do the same work for goods. No one may force a person out of his property by self-help, not even the true owner. A person in settled possession can be removed only through a court. In exams, the six-month possessory suit under Section 6 is asked most often. In real life, it protects tenants, shopkeepers and farmers from being put on the street overnight.
legalProvision: Section 5. Recovery of specific immovable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

Section 6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property. (1) If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. (2) No suit under this section shall be brought— (a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government. (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed. (4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.
(The words "through whom he has been in possession or any person" were inserted in sub-section (1) by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 7. Recovery of specific movable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific movable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). Explanation 1. —A trustee may sue under this section for the possession of movable property to the beneficial interest in which the person for whom he is trustee is entitled. Explanation 2. —A special or temporary right to the present possession of movable property is sufficient to support a suit under this section.

Section 8. Liability of person in possession, not as owner, to deliver to persons entitled to immediate possession. Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of movable property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession, in any of the following cases:— (a) when the thing claimed is held by the defendant as the agent or trustee of the plaintiff; (b) when compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed; (c) when it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss; (d) when the possession of the thing claimed has been wrongfully transferred from the plaintiff. Explanation. —Unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall, in respect of any article of movable property claimed under clause (b) or clause (c) of this section, presume— (a) that compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed, or, as the case may be; (b) that it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss.
Related provisions (Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule)

Article 64. For possession of immovable property based on previous possession and not on title, when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed. – Twelve years. – The date of dispossession.
Article 65. For possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title. – Twelve years. – When the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.
In simple words

Section 5: a person entitled to possess particular land or a building may sue for it in the ordinary way under the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 6: a person put out of land or a building without his consent and without due process of law may sue to get it back. The defendant cannot defend by saying he owns it. The suit must be filed within six months and cannot be against the Government. There is no appeal or review. Anyone may still file a separate suit on title. Section 7: the same as Section 5, for particular goods. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to present possession is enough. Section 8: a person who holds a particular article but does not own it can be made to hand over that very article, in four cases. In two of them the court presumes that money is not enough. Articles 64 and 65: an ordinary suit on earlier possession, or on title, may be filed within 12 years.
en.meaning:
Possession here means actual control of the property. Settled possession means possession that has continued for some time with the owner's knowledge. The law protects it even against the owner. In Krishna Ram Mahale (1989) the Supreme Court held that such a person "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he has no right to remain. The question this part of the Act answers. Who is entitled to possession, and how may he get it back? The answer for land is a choice between two suits. A title suit under Section 5 proves ownership and decides it for good. A possessory suit under Section 6 is quick, but it proves only earlier possession and unlawful removal. It does not decide who owns the land. Why the law has this rule. If every owner could retake property by force whenever he believed he was right, disputes would end in violence. The Privy Council's words, approved by the Supreme Court, are: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court." See Diagram 1 for how to choose the suit. Diagram 1. Answer each question from the top. A "No" sends you to the box on the side. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Is the property immovable
(land or a building)?"} Q1 -->|"No"| M["Movable property:
ss. 7 and 8"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"2. Was the plaintiff in possession and removed
without consent and without due process?
s. 6(1)"} Q2 -->|"No"| T["Title suit, s. 5
12 years (Art. 65)"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"3. Within six months of dispossession,
and not against the Government?
s. 6(2)"} Q3 -->|"No"| L["Title suit, s. 5, or suit on earlier
possession within 12 years (Art. 64);
defendant may plead title"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| S["s. 6 suit lies: title no defence;
no appeal or review (s. 6(3));
title suit still open (s. 6(4))"] Text description Question 1: is the property immovable? If no, use Sections 7 and 8 for movable property. Question 2: was the plaintiff in possession and removed without his consent and without due process of law? If no, file a title suit under Section 5 (12 years, Article 65). Question 3: is the suit within six months of dispossession and not against the Government? If no, file a title suit under Section 5, or a suit on earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64), where the defendant may plead title. If all answers are yes, a Section 6 suit lies: title is no defence, there is no appeal or review, and a title suit remains open under Section 6(4).
keyPoints: Section 5 is a title suit under the Code of Civil Procedure (12 years, Article 65). Section 6 is a quick suit on possession. Section 6: six months, not against the Government, no appeal or review, title no defence. Since 2018, a person through whom the dispossessed person was in possession can also sue. Section 6(4) always saves a separate suit on title. After six months, a suit on earlier possession lies within 12 years (Article 64), but the defendant may plead title. Settled possession is protected even against the true owner ( Lallu Yeshwant Singh ; Krishna Ram Mahale ). Section 7: recovery of movables. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to possession is enough. Section 8: four cases where a non-owner must deliver the article, with a presumption for the plaintiff in clauses (b) and (c).

caseLaws.name: Lallu Yeshwant Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Rao Jagdish Singh (1967) Facts. Gairdakhilkar (tenant) cultivators in Gwalior district said the landlord forcibly stopped them from cultivating and had the land cultivated by others. The landlord said their rights had ended because land revenue was not paid. They sued under Section 326 of the Gwalior Qanoon Mal, which is similar to Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. Principle. The tenants' rights did not end automatically. Under Section 9 the question of title is irrelevant, and a landlord cannot use force to throw out his tenant. AIR 1968 SC 620 : (1968) 2 SCR 203, decided 29 November 1967 (Sikri and Shah JJ). Why it matters. It is the foundation of the "no self-help" rule now in Section 6. Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao (1989) Facts. The owner of a restaurant in Parel, Bombay had let the plaintiff conduct it under a 1956 agreement. On 15 February 1959 he took possession behind her back, in collusion with others, relying on notices she said she never received. She sued within a few weeks. Principle. A person in settled possession "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he had no right to remain. The appeal was dismissed with costs, and the Court Receiver was appointed to take possession. (1989) 4 SCC 131 : AIR 1989 SC 2097, decided 9 August 1989. Why it matters. It states the "no self-help" rule in the clearest terms. Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander (1968) Facts. The plaintiff sued in 1942 for possession of about 131 acres of Government poramboke land in former Travancore, from which he said the Society's men had removed him in October 1939. The suit was filed long after six months and was based on his earlier possession. Principle. In a suit under Section 9 of the 1877 Act the plaintiff need not prove title. After six months the defendant may raise title; the plaintiff may still sue on earlier possession within 12 years. AIR 1968 SC 1165 : (1968) 3 SCR 163 (Hidayatullah, Sikri, Hegde JJ). Why it matters. It explains how Section 6 relates to ordinary suits for possession. Sanjay Kumar Pandey v. Gulbahar Sheikh (2004) Facts. A trial court decreed a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The defendants filed a revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the High Court dismissed the suit. Principle. The unsuccessful party's remedy "is to file a suit based on title". A revision is available "only by way of an exception". The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and sent the revision back for a fresh hearing. (2004) 4 SCC 664 : AIR 2004 SC 3354, decided 2 April 2004. Why it matters. It shows how Section 6(3) and Section 6(4) work in practice.

selfTest.q: 1. Within what time must a Section 6 suit be filed?
selfTest.a: Within six months from the date of dispossession.

selfTest.q: 2. Can the defendant in a Section 6 suit plead that he is the owner?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(1) says the suit lies notwithstanding any other title that may be set up.

selfTest.q: 3. Does an appeal lie from a decree in a Section 6 suit?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(3) bars appeal and review. A suit on title remains open under Section 6(4).

selfTest.q: 4. A person dispossessed eight months ago has no title deed. Can he still sue?
selfTest.a: Yes. He may sue on his earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64). If the defendant proves a better title, he fails.

selfTest.q: 5. A hirer of a tractor loses it to a stranger. Can he sue under Section 7?
selfTest.a: Yes. Explanation 2 says a special or temporary right to present possession is enough.

legalProvision: Section 5. Recovery of specific immovable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

Section 6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property. (1) If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. (2) No suit under this section shall be brought— (a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government. (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed. (4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.
("through whom he has been in possession or any person" అనే పదాలు 2018 చట్టం నం. 18 ద్వారా, 1 అక్టోబర్ 2018 నుంచి సబ్-సెక్షన్ (1) లో చేర్చబడ్డాయి.)

Section 7. Recovery of specific movable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific movable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). Explanation 1. —A trustee may sue under this section for the possession of movable property to the beneficial interest in which the person for whom he is trustee is entitled. Explanation 2. —A special or temporary right to the present possession of movable property is sufficient to support a suit under this section.

Section 8. Liability of person in possession, not as owner, to deliver to persons entitled to immediate possession. Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of movable property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession, in any of the following cases:— (a) when the thing claimed is held by the defendant as the agent or trustee of the plaintiff; (b) when compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed; (c) when it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss; (d) when the possession of the thing claimed has been wrongfully transferred from the plaintiff. Explanation. —Unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall, in respect of any article of movable property claimed under clause (b) or clause (c) of this section, presume— (a) that compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed, or, as the case may be; (b) that it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు (Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule)

Article 64. For possession of immovable property based on previous possession and not on title, when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed. – Twelve years. – The date of dispossession.
Article 65. For possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title. – Twelve years. – When the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.

సెక్షన్ 5: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట భూమిని లేదా భవనాన్ని స్వాధీనం చేసుకునే హక్కు ఉన్న వ్యక్తి, సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్ కింద సాధారణ పద్ధతిలో దాని కోసం దావా వేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 6: తన సమ్మతి లేకుండా, చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా భూమి లేదా భవనం నుంచి బయటకు గెంటబడిన వ్యక్తి దాన్ని తిరిగి పొందడానికి దావా వేయవచ్చు. తానే యజమాని అని చెప్పి ప్రతివాది తప్పించుకోలేడు. దావా ఆరు నెలల్లో వేయాలి, ప్రభుత్వంపై వేయలేం. అప్పీల్ గానీ, రివ్యూ గానీ ఉండదు. ఎవరైనా టైటిల్‌పై వేరే దావా వేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 7: నిర్దిష్ట వస్తువుల కోసం సెక్షన్ 5 లాంటిదే. ట్రస్టీ దావా వేయవచ్చు; ప్రస్తుత స్వాధీనానికి ప్రత్యేక లేదా తాత్కాలిక హక్కు ఉన్నా చాలు. సెక్షన్ 8: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట వస్తువును యజమాని కాకుండా తన దగ్గర ఉంచుకున్న వ్యక్తిని, నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో, అదే వస్తువును అప్పగించేలా చేయవచ్చు. వాటిలో రెండింటిలో డబ్బు సరిపోదని కోర్టు ఊహిస్తుంది. ఆర్టికల్స్ 64, 65: పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై లేదా టైటిల్‌పై సాధారణ దావాను 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో వేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
ఇక్కడ స్వాధీనం (possession) అంటే ఆస్తిపై వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ. స్థిరపడిన స్వాధీనం అంటే యజమానికి తెలిసి కొంతకాలం కొనసాగిన స్వాధీనం. యజమానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కూడా చట్టం దాన్ని కాపాడుతుంది. Krishna Ram Mahale (1989) లో, అలాంటి వ్యక్తి "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law" అని, అతనికి అక్కడ ఉండే హక్కు లేకపోయినా ఇదే నియమమని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. చట్టంలోని ఈ భాగం సమాధానం చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. స్వాధీనానికి ఎవరు అర్హులు, దాన్ని ఎలా తిరిగి పొందవచ్చు? భూమికి సమాధానం రెండు దావాల మధ్య ఎంపిక. సెక్షన్ 5 కింది టైటిల్ దావా యాజమాన్యాన్ని రుజువు చేసి శాశ్వతంగా తేలుస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6 కింది స్వాధీన దావా త్వరితమైనది, కానీ అది పూర్వ స్వాధీనం, చట్టవిరుద్ధ తొలగింపులను మాత్రమే రుజువు చేస్తుంది. భూమి ఎవరిదో అది తేల్చదు. చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు ఉంది. తాను సరైనవాడినని నమ్మిన ప్రతిసారీ ప్రతి యజమాని బలవంతంగా ఆస్తిని తిరిగి తీసుకోగలిగితే, వివాదాలు హింసలో ముగుస్తాయి. సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఆమోదించిన Privy Council మాటలు: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court." ఏ దావా ఎంచుకోవాలో Diagram 1 లో చూడండి. అప్పీల్, రివ్యూ లేవు (సె. 6(3));
టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంది (సె. 6(4))"] వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: ఆస్తి స్థిరాస్తా? కాకపోతే, చరాస్తికి సెక్షన్లు 7, 8 వాడండి. ప్రశ్న 2: వాది స్వాధీనంలో ఉండి, తన సమ్మతి లేకుండా, చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా తొలగించబడ్డాడా? కాకపోతే, సెక్షన్ 5 కింద టైటిల్ దావా (12 సంవత్సరాలు, ఆర్టికల్ 65). ప్రశ్న 3: స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన ఆరు నెలల్లో, ప్రభుత్వంపై కాకుండా దావా వేస్తున్నారా? కాకపోతే, సెక్షన్ 5 కింద టైటిల్ దావా, లేదా 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా (ఆర్టికల్ 64); అందులో ప్రతివాది టైటిల్ వాదించవచ్చు. అన్నీ అవును అయితే, సెక్షన్ 6 దావా నిలుస్తుంది: టైటిల్ రక్షణ కాదు, అప్పీల్ లేదా రివ్యూ లేదు, సెక్షన్ 6(4) కింద టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాను ఎంత కాలంలో వేయాలి?
selfTest.a: స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన తేదీ నుంచి ఆరు నెలల్లో.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాలో ప్రతివాది తానే యజమానినని వాదించవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మరే టైటిల్ వాదించినా దావా నిలుస్తుందని సెక్షన్ 6(1) చెబుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 3. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాలోని డిక్రీపై అప్పీల్ ఉంటుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. సెక్షన్ 6(3) అప్పీల్, రివ్యూలను నిషేధిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(4) కింద టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. ఎనిమిది నెలల క్రితం స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన వ్యక్తికి టైటిల్ పత్రం లేదు. అతను ఇంకా దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో తన పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా వేయవచ్చు (ఆర్టికల్ 64). ప్రతివాది మెరుగైన టైటిల్ రుజువు చేస్తే, అతను ఓడిపోతాడు.

selfTest.q: 5. ట్రాక్టర్ అద్దెకు తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తి దాన్ని ఒక అపరిచితుడి వల్ల కోల్పోతాడు. అతను సెక్షన్ 7 కింద దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ప్రస్తుత స్వాధీనానికి ప్రత్యేక లేదా తాత్కాలిక హక్కు చాలని Explanation 2 చెబుతుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: If someone throws you out of your land, the law gives you two doors. One asks you to prove that you own it (Section 5). The other asks only whether you were in possession and were removed without due process of law (Section 6). Sections 7 and 8 do the same work for goods. No one may force a person out of his property by self-help, not even the true owner. A person in settled possession can be removed only through a court. In exams, the six-month possessory suit under Section 6 is asked most often. In real life, it protects tenants, shopkeepers and farmers from being put on the street overnight.
legalProvision: Section 5. Recovery of specific immovable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

Section 6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property. (1) If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. (2) No suit under this section shall be brought— (a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government. (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed. (4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.
(The words "through whom he has been in possession or any person" were inserted in sub-section (1) by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 7. Recovery of specific movable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific movable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). Explanation 1. —A trustee may sue under this section for the possession of movable property to the beneficial interest in which the person for whom he is trustee is entitled. Explanation 2. —A special or temporary right to the present possession of movable property is sufficient to support a suit under this section.

Section 8. Liability of person in possession, not as owner, to deliver to persons entitled to immediate possession. Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of movable property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession, in any of the following cases:— (a) when the thing claimed is held by the defendant as the agent or trustee of the plaintiff; (b) when compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed; (c) when it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss; (d) when the possession of the thing claimed has been wrongfully transferred from the plaintiff. Explanation. —Unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall, in respect of any article of movable property claimed under clause (b) or clause (c) of this section, presume— (a) that compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed, or, as the case may be; (b) that it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss.
Related provisions (Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule)

Article 64. For possession of immovable property based on previous possession and not on title, when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed. – Twelve years. – The date of dispossession.
Article 65. For possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title. – Twelve years. – When the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.
In simple words

Section 5: a person entitled to possess particular land or a building may sue for it in the ordinary way under the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 6: a person put out of land or a building without his consent and without due process of law may sue to get it back. The defendant cannot defend by saying he owns it. The suit must be filed within six months and cannot be against the Government. There is no appeal or review. Anyone may still file a separate suit on title. Section 7: the same as Section 5, for particular goods. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to present possession is enough. Section 8: a person who holds a particular article but does not own it can be made to hand over that very article, in four cases. In two of them the court presumes that money is not enough. Articles 64 and 65: an ordinary suit on earlier possession, or on title, may be filed within 12 years.
hi.meaning:
Possession here means actual control of the property. Settled possession means possession that has continued for some time with the owner's knowledge. The law protects it even against the owner. In Krishna Ram Mahale (1989) the Supreme Court held that such a person "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he has no right to remain. The question this part of the Act answers. Who is entitled to possession, and how may he get it back? The answer for land is a choice between two suits. A title suit under Section 5 proves ownership and decides it for good. A possessory suit under Section 6 is quick, but it proves only earlier possession and unlawful removal. It does not decide who owns the land. Why the law has this rule. If every owner could retake property by force whenever he believed he was right, disputes would end in violence. The Privy Council's words, approved by the Supreme Court, are: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court." Question 2: was the plaintiff in possession and removed without his consent and without due process of law? If no, file a title suit under Section 5 (12 years, Article 65). Question 3: is the suit within six months of dispossession and not against the Government? If no, file a title suit under Section 5, or a suit on earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64), where the defendant may plead title. If all answers are yes, a Section 6 suit lies: title is no defence, there is no appeal or review, and a title suit remains open under Section 6(4).
keyPoints: Section 5 is a title suit under the Code of Civil Procedure (12 years, Article 65). Section 6 is a quick suit on possession. Section 6: six months, not against the Government, no appeal or review, title no defence. Since 2018, a person through whom the dispossessed person was in possession can also sue. Section 6(4) always saves a separate suit on title. After six months, a suit on earlier possession lies within 12 years (Article 64), but the defendant may plead title. Settled possession is protected even against the true owner ( Lallu Yeshwant Singh ; Krishna Ram Mahale ). Section 7: recovery of movables. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to possession is enough. Section 8: four cases where a non-owner must deliver the article, with a presumption for the plaintiff in clauses (b) and (c).

caseLaws.name: Lallu Yeshwant Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Rao Jagdish Singh (1967) Facts. Gairdakhilkar (tenant) cultivators in Gwalior district said the landlord forcibly stopped them from cultivating and had the land cultivated by others. The landlord said their rights had ended because land revenue was not paid. They sued under Section 326 of the Gwalior Qanoon Mal, which is similar to Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. Principle. The tenants' rights did not end automatically. Under Section 9 the question of title is irrelevant, and a landlord cannot use force to throw out his tenant. AIR 1968 SC 620 : (1968) 2 SCR 203, decided 29 November 1967 (Sikri and Shah JJ). Why it matters. It is the foundation of the "no self-help" rule now in Section 6. Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao (1989) Facts. The owner of a restaurant in Parel, Bombay had let the plaintiff conduct it under a 1956 agreement. On 15 February 1959 he took possession behind her back, in collusion with others, relying on notices she said she never received. She sued within a few weeks. Principle. A person in settled possession "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he had no right to remain. The appeal was dismissed with costs, and the Court Receiver was appointed to take possession. (1989) 4 SCC 131 : AIR 1989 SC 2097, decided 9 August 1989. Why it matters. It states the "no self-help" rule in the clearest terms. Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander (1968) Facts. The plaintiff sued in 1942 for possession of about 131 acres of Government poramboke land in former Travancore, from which he said the Society's men had removed him in October 1939. The suit was filed long after six months and was based on his earlier possession. Principle. In a suit under Section 9 of the 1877 Act the plaintiff need not prove title. After six months the defendant may raise title; the plaintiff may still sue on earlier possession within 12 years. AIR 1968 SC 1165 : (1968) 3 SCR 163 (Hidayatullah, Sikri, Hegde JJ). Why it matters. It explains how Section 6 relates to ordinary suits for possession. Sanjay Kumar Pandey v. Gulbahar Sheikh (2004) Facts. A trial court decreed a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The defendants filed a revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the High Court dismissed the suit. Principle. The unsuccessful party's remedy "is to file a suit based on title". A revision is available "only by way of an exception". The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and sent the revision back for a fresh hearing. (2004) 4 SCC 664 : AIR 2004 SC 3354, decided 2 April 2004. Why it matters. It shows how Section 6(3) and Section 6(4) work in practice.

selfTest.q: 1. Within what time must a Section 6 suit be filed?
selfTest.a: Within six months from the date of dispossession.

selfTest.q: 2. Can the defendant in a Section 6 suit plead that he is the owner?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(1) says the suit lies notwithstanding any other title that may be set up.

selfTest.q: 3. Does an appeal lie from a decree in a Section 6 suit?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(3) bars appeal and review. A suit on title remains open under Section 6(4).

selfTest.q: 4. A person dispossessed eight months ago has no title deed. Can he still sue?
selfTest.a: Yes. He may sue on his earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64). If the defendant proves a better title, he fails.

selfTest.q: 5. A hirer of a tractor loses it to a stranger. Can he sue under Section 7?
selfTest.a: Yes. Explanation 2 says a special or temporary right to present possession is enough.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t5.subtitle: Sections 27 to 30 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: Rescission means undoing a contract. A person who signed a voidable contract, or a contract that is unlawful for a hidden reason, can ask the court to set it aside. The parties are then put back, as far as possible, to where they stood before the contract. Chapter IV of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 (Sections 27 to 30) deals with this. The court "may" rescind and "may" refuse, so the four bars in Section 27(2), Sections 28 and 29 and the duty to do equity matter as much as the grounds. In exams, the grounds in Section 27(1), the bars, the effect on benefits received, and the difference from cancellation and rectification are the main points. In real life, this is how a buyer cheated into a bad deal gets his money back through the court.
legalProvision: Section 27. When rescission may be adjudged or refused. (1) Any person interested in a contract may sue to have it rescinded, and such rescission may be adjudged by the court in any of the following cases, namely:— (a) where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; (b) where the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the court may refuse to rescind the contract— (a) where the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract; or (b) where, owing to the change of circumstances which has taken place since the making of the contract (not being due to any act of the defendant himself), the parties cannot be substantially restored to the position in which they stood when the contract was made; or (c) where third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice and for value; or (d) where only a part of the contract is sought to be rescinded and such part is not severable from the rest of the contract. Explanation. —In this section "contract" in relation to the territories to which the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (4 of 1882), does not extend, means a contract in writing.

Section 28. Rescission in certain circumstances of contracts for the sale or lease of immovable property, the specific performance of which has been decreed. (1) Where in any suit a decree for specific performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property has been made and the purchaser or lessee does not, within the period allowed by the decree or such further period as the court may allow, pay the purchase money or other sum which the court has ordered him to pay, the vendor or lessor may apply in the same suit in which the decree is made, to have the contract rescinded and on such application the court may, by order, rescind the contract either so far as regards the party in default or altogether, as the justice of the case may require. (2) Where a contract is rescinded under sub-section (1), the court— (a) shall direct the purchaser or the lessee, if he has obtained possession of the property under the contract, to restore such possession to the vendor or lessor, and (b) may direct payment to the vendor or lessor of all the rents and profits which have accrued in respect of the property from the date on which possession was so obtained by the purchaser or lessee until restoration of possession to the vendor or lessor, and, if the justice of the case so requires, the refund of any sum paid by the vendee or the lessee as earnest money or deposit in connection with the contract. (3) If the purchase or lessee pays the purchase money or other sum which he is ordered to pay under the decree within the period referred to in sub-section (1), the court may, on application made in the same suit, award the purchaser or lessee such further relief as he may be entitled to, including in appropriate cases all or any of the following reliefs, namely:— (a) the execution of a proper conveyance or lease by the vendor or lessor; (b) the delivery of possession, or partition and separate possession, of the property on the execution of such conveyance or lease. (4) No separate suit in respect of any relief which may be claimed under this section shall lie at the instance of a vendor, purchaser, lessor or lessee, as the case may be. (5) The costs of any proceedings under this section shall be in the discretion of the court.

Section 29. Alternative prayer for rescission in suit for specific performance. A plaintiff instituting a suit for the specific performance of a contract in writing may pray in the alternative that, if the contract cannot be specifically enforced, it may be rescinded and delivered up to be cancelled; and the court, if it refuses to enforce the contract specifically, may direct it to be rescinded and delivered up accordingly.

Section 30. Court may require parties rescinding to do equity. On adjudging the rescission of a contract, the court may require the party to whom such relief is granted to restore, so far as may be, any benefit which he may have received from the other party and to make any compensation to him which justice may require.
Related provisions (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 19 (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
Section 19A (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

Section 64. When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party thereto need not perform any promise therein contained in which he is promisor. The party rescinding a voidable contract shall, if he have received any benefit thereunder from another party to such contract, restore such benefit, so far as may be, to the person from whom it was received.
Section 66. The rescission of a voidable contract may be communicated or revoked in the same manner, and subject to the same rules, as apply to the communication or revocation of a proposal.
In simple words

Section 27(1): any person interested in a contract may sue to have it set aside. The court may order rescission where the contract is voidable or terminable (capable of being ended) by the plaintiff, or where it is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. Section 27(2): the court may refuse rescission in four cases: later approval (ratification), no restoration possible, third-party rights, and a part that cannot be separated. Explanation to Section 27: where the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 does not extend, "contract" means a contract in writing. Section 28: rescission after a decree for specific performance of a sale or lease of immovable property, where the buyer or lessee does not pay. Section 29: a plaintiff in a suit for specific performance of a written contract may pray in the alternative for rescission. Section 30: the court may require the party granted rescission to restore benefits and make compensation as justice requires.
en.meaning:
Rescission is the setting aside of a contract by the court. The Act uses the word for a contract. Its word for undoing a written instrument is cancellation (Sections 31 to 33). When is a contract voidable? A contract is valid until the injured party chooses to cancel it where consent was caused by coercion , fraud or misrepresentation (Section 19, Indian Contract Act, 1872) or by undue influence (Section 19A). The question this part of the Act answers. When will the court set a contract aside, and on what terms? Two ways to rescind. The injured party can tell the other side that he rescinds, communicating it like a proposal (Section 66 of the Contract Act). Or he can ask the court under Section 27. The grounds for rescission by the court (Section 27(1)). The contract is voidable by the plaintiff (Section 27(1)(a)): coercion, fraud or misrepresentation (Contract Act, Section 19), or undue influence (Section 19A). The contract is terminable by the plaintiff (Section 27(1)(a)): he has a right to end it. The contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face (Section 27(1)(b)), but only if the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff. See Diagram 1 for the grounds. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. The green boxes are the final grounds. flowchart TD A["Suit to rescind a contract
s. 27(1)"] A --> V["Contract voidable by the plaintiff
s. 27(1)(a)"] A --> T["Contract terminable by the plaintiff
s. 27(1)(a): he has a right to end it"] A --> U["Unlawful for causes not apparent on its face
s. 27(1)(b): only if the defendant
is more to blame"] V --> V1["Coercion, fraud or misrepresentation
Contract Act, s. 19"] V --> V2["Undue influence
Contract Act, s. 19A"] style T fill:#d9f2d9,stroke:#2e7d32 style U fill:#d9f2d9,stroke:#2e7d32 style V1 fill:#d9f2d9,stroke:#2e7d32 style V2 fill:#d9f2d9,stroke:#2e7d32 Text description A suit to rescind a contract under Section 27(1) has three grounds. First, the contract is voidable by the plaintiff (Section 27(1)(a)): because of coercion, fraud or misrepresentation (Contract Act, Section 19), or undue influence (Section 19A). Second, the contract is terminable by the plaintiff (Section 27(1)(a)): he has a right to end it. Third, the contract is unlawful for causes not apparent on its face (Section 27(1)(b)), only if the defendant is more to blame than the plaintiff.
keyPoints: Rescission (Sections 27 to 30) undoes a contract. Cancellation (Sections 31 to 33) undoes an instrument. Grounds: voidable or terminable by the plaintiff; unlawful for causes not apparent on its face if the defendant is more to blame. Any person interested in the contract may sue. The court "may" rescind and "may" refuse (Section 27). Four bars: ratification, no restoration, third-party rights, part not severable. Section 28: rescission in the same suit after a decree for sale or lease if the buyer does not pay. Section 29: rescission as an alternative prayer. The injured party may rescind by communicating it (Contract Act, Sections 64 and 66) or sue under Section 27. The court may require restoration of benefits and compensation (Section 30).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. Dharmodas Ghose, a minor, mortgaged his houses to a money-lender, Brahmo Dutt, to secure ₹20,000. The lender's agent knew he was under age. The minor sued to have the mortgage declared void. Principle. A minor's agreement is void, not voidable. Sections 64 and 65 of the Contract Act assume a contract between competent parties and did not apply. Repayment was not ordered, because the lender knew of the minority. Privy Council, (1903) LR 30 IA 114. Why it matters. Rescission needs a contract. The case also shows how a court weighs restoration.

selfTest.q: 1. In which cases may the court adjudge rescission under Section 27(1)?
selfTest.a: Where the contract is voidable or terminable by the plaintiff, or unlawful for causes not apparent on its face and the defendant is more to blame.

selfTest.q: 2. Which sections of the Contract Act let a party rescind a voidable contract without going to court?
selfTest.a: Section 66 (how rescission is communicated) and Section 64 (its consequences).

selfTest.q: 4. In which suit does a seller apply for rescission under Section 28?
selfTest.a: In the same suit in which the decree for specific performance was made.

selfTest.q: 5. What may the court require of a party granted rescission?
selfTest.a: To restore any benefit received from the other party and to make any compensation that justice requires (Section 30).

(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the court may refuse to rescind the contract— (a) where the plaintiff has expressly or impliedly ratified the contract; or (b) where, owing to the change of circumstances which has taken place since the making of the contract (not being due to any act of the defendant himself), the parties cannot be substantially restored to the position in which they stood when the contract was made; or (c) where third parties have, during the subsistence of the contract, acquired rights in good faith without notice and for value; or (d) where only a part of the contract is sought to be rescinded and such part is not severable from the rest of the contract. Explanation. —In this section "contract" in relation to the territories to which the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (4 of 1882), does not extend, means a contract in writing.

Section 28. Rescission in certain circumstances of contracts for the sale or lease of immovable property, the specific performance of which has been decreed. (1) Where in any suit a decree for specific performance of a contract for the sale or lease of immovable property has been made and the purchaser or lessee does not, within the period allowed by the decree or such further period as the court may allow, pay the purchase money or other sum which the court has ordered him to pay, the vendor or lessor may apply in the same suit in which the decree is made, to have the contract rescinded and on such application the court may, by order, rescind the contract either so far as regards the party in default or altogether, as the justice of the case may require. (2) Where a contract is rescinded under sub-section (1), the court— (a) shall direct the purchaser or the lessee, if he has obtained possession of the property under the contract, to restore such possession to the vendor or lessor, and (b) may direct payment to the vendor or lessor of all the rents and profits which have accrued in respect of the property from the date on which possession was so obtained by the purchaser or lessee until restoration of possession to the vendor or lessor, and, if the justice of the case so requires, the refund of any sum paid by the vendee or the lessee as earnest money or deposit in connection with the contract. (3) If the purchase or lessee pays the purchase money or other sum which he is ordered to pay under the decree within the period referred to in sub-section (1), the court may, on application made in the same suit, award the purchaser or lessee such further relief as he may be entitled to, including in appropriate cases all or any of the following reliefs, namely:— (a) the execution of a proper conveyance or lease by the vendor or lessor; (b) the delivery of possession, or partition and separate possession, of the property on the execution of such conveyance or lease. (4) No separate suit in respect of any relief which may be claimed under this section shall lie at the instance of a vendor, purchaser, lessor or lessee, as the case may be. (5) The costs of any proceedings under this section shall be in the discretion of the court.

Section 29. Alternative prayer for rescission in suit for specific performance. A plaintiff instituting a suit for the specific performance of a contract in writing may pray in the alternative that, if the contract cannot be specifically enforced, it may be rescinded and delivered up to be cancelled; and the court, if it refuses to enforce the contract specifically, may direct it to be rescinded and delivered up accordingly.

Section 30. Court may require parties rescinding to do equity. On adjudging the rescission of a contract, the court may require the party to whom such relief is granted to restore, so far as may be, any benefit which he may have received from the other party and to make any compensation to him which justice may require.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు (Indian Contract Act, 1872)

Section 19 (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
Section 19A (first paragraph). When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

Section 64. When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party thereto need not perform any promise therein contained in which he is promisor. The party rescinding a voidable contract shall, if he have received any benefit thereunder from another party to such contract, restore such benefit, so far as may be, to the person from whom it was received.
Section 66. The rescission of a voidable contract may be communicated or revoked in the same manner, and subject to the same rules, as apply to the communication or revocation of a proposal.
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 27(1): కాంట్రాక్టుపై ఆసక్తి ఉన్న ఏ వ్యక్తైనా దాన్ని పక్కన పెట్టమని దావా వేయవచ్చు. కాంట్రాక్టు వాది ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది లేదా ముగించదగినది (terminable) అయితే, లేదా బయటకు కనిపించని కారణాలతో చట్టవిరుద్ధమై, వాది కంటే ప్రతివాది ఎక్కువ తప్పు చేసి ఉంటే, కోర్టు రద్దుకు ఆదేశించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 27(2): నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో కోర్టు రద్దు నిరాకరించవచ్చు: తర్వాత ఆమోదం (ratification), పూర్వ స్థితికి తీసుకురాలేకపోవడం, మూడో వ్యక్తుల హక్కులు, వేరు చేయలేని భాగం. సెక్షన్ 27 Explanation: Transfer of Property Act, 1882 వర్తించని చోట "contract" అంటే రాతపూర్వక కాంట్రాక్టు. సెక్షన్ 28: స్థిరాస్తి అమ్మకం లేదా లీజుకు నిర్దిష్ట అమలు డిక్రీ తర్వాత, కొనుగోలుదారు లేదా కౌలుదారు చెల్లించకపోతే రద్దు. సెక్షన్ 29: రాతపూర్వక కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్దిష్ట అమలు దావాలో వాది ప్రత్యామ్నాయంగా రద్దు కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 30: రద్దు పొందిన పక్షం ప్రయోజనాలను తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలని, న్యాయం కోరినంత పరిహారం చెల్లించాలని కోర్టు కోరవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
రద్దు అంటే కోర్టు ఒక కాంట్రాక్టును పక్కన పెట్టడం. చట్టం ఈ పదాన్ని కాంట్రాక్టుకు వాడుతుంది. రాతపూర్వక పత్రాన్ని తొలగించడానికి దాని పదం cancellation (సెక్షన్లు 31 నుంచి 33). కాంట్రాక్టు ఎప్పుడు రద్దు చేయదగినది? సమ్మతి బలవంతం (coercion), మోసం (fraud) లేదా తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం (misrepresentation) వల్ల (Indian Contract Act, 1872 సెక్షన్ 19), లేదా అనుచిత ప్రభావం (undue influence) వల్ల (సెక్షన్ 19A) కలిగితే, నష్టపోయిన పక్షం రద్దు చేసుకునే వరకు కాంట్రాక్టు చెల్లుతుంది. ఈ భాగం జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు కాంట్రాక్టును పక్కన పెడుతుంది, ఏ షరతులపై? రద్దు చేయడానికి రెండు మార్గాలు. నష్టపోయిన పక్షం, ప్రతిపాదనను తెలియజేసినట్లే, తాను రద్దు చేస్తున్నానని అవతలి పక్షానికి తెలియజేయవచ్చు (Contract Act సెక్షన్ 66). లేదా సెక్షన్ 27 కింద కోర్టును అడగవచ్చు. కోర్టు రద్దు చేసే కారణాలు (సెక్షన్ 27(1)). కాంట్రాక్టు వాది ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది (సెక్షన్ 27(1)(a)): బలవంతం, మోసం లేదా తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం (Contract Act, సెక్షన్ 19), లేదా అనుచిత ప్రభావం (సెక్షన్ 19A). కాంట్రాక్టు వాది ముగించదగినది (సెక్షన్ 27(1)(a)): దాన్ని ముగించే హక్కు అతనికి ఉంది. కాంట్రాక్టు బయటకు కనిపించని కారణాలతో చట్టవిరుద్ధం (సెక్షన్ 27(1)(b)), కానీ ప్రతివాది వాది కంటే ఎక్కువ తప్పు చేసి ఉంటేనే. కారణాల కోసం Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. పై పెట్టె నుంచి మొదలుపెట్టి గీతల వెంట కిందికి చదవండి. ఆకుపచ్చ పెట్టెలు చివరి కారణాలు. flowchart TD A["కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు దావా

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 27(1) కింద కోర్టు ఏ సందర్భాల్లో రద్దుకు ఆదేశించవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు వాది రద్దు చేయదగినది లేదా ముగించదగినది అయినప్పుడు, లేదా బయటకు కనిపించని కారణాలతో చట్టవిరుద్ధమై ప్రతివాది ఎక్కువ తప్పు చేసినప్పుడు.

selfTest.q: 2. కోర్టుకు వెళ్లకుండా రద్దు చేయదగిన కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయడానికి Contract Act లోని ఏ సెక్షన్లు అనుమతిస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 66 (రద్దును ఎలా తెలియజేయాలి), సెక్షన్ 64 (దాని పరిణామాలు).

selfTest.q: 4. సెక్షన్ 28 కింద అమ్మకందారు ఏ దావాలో రద్దుకు దరఖాస్తు చేస్తాడు?
selfTest.a: నిర్దిష్ట అమలు డిక్రీ ఇచ్చిన అదే దావాలో.

selfTest.q: 5. రద్దు పొందిన పక్షాన్ని కోర్టు ఏం కోరవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: అవతలి పక్షం నుంచి పొందిన ప్రయోజనాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలని, న్యాయం కోరిన పరిహారం చెల్లించాలని (సెక్షన్ 30).
