en.inOneMinute: An injunction can come early in a suit or at its end. A temporary injunction protects the plaintiff while the case is going on. A perpetual injunction is the final order that ends the case in the plaintiff's favour. Section 37 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 draws the line. Temporary injunctions are governed by the Code of Civil Procedure. Perpetual injunctions are granted only by a decree on the merits. In exams, the six-point comparison and the three tests are the core. In real life, the temporary order is what stops a wall or a sale today; the perpetual order is what the plaintiff takes home after the trial.
legalProvision: Section 36. Preventive relief how granted. Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual.

Section 37. Temporary and perpetual injunctions. (1) Temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specific time, or until the further order of the court, and they may be granted at any stage of a suit, and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). (2) A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit; the defendant is thereby perpetually enjoined from the assertion of a right, or from the commission of an act, which would be contrary to the rights of the plaintiff.

Section 38. Perpetual injunction when granted. (1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred to by this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. (2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in Chapter II. (3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX (" Temporary Injunctions and Interlocutory Orders") – stated closely, not quoted

Rule 1: where it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that (a) any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit; (b) the defendant threatens, or intends, to remove or dispose of his property with a view to defrauding his creditors; or (c) the defendant threatens to dispossess the plaintiff or otherwise cause injury to him in relation to any property in dispute, the court may grant a temporary injunction , until the disposal of the suit or until further orders. Rule 2: in a suit to restrain a breach of contract or other injury, the plaintiff may, at any time after the suit begins and before or after judgment, apply for a temporary injunction to restrain the breach or injury complained of, on such terms as the court thinks fit. Rule 2A: on disobedience or breach of an injunction, the court may order the property of the person guilty to be attached, and may order him to be detained in civil prison for a term not exceeding three months. An attachment cannot remain in force for more than one year; after that, the property may be sold and compensation paid to the injured party. Rule 3: before granting an injunction, the court shall direct notice to the opposite party, except where the object of granting the injunction would be defeated by the delay. If it grants one without notice, it must record its reasons, and the applicant must at once send the other side copies of the application, the affidavit, the plaint and the documents relied on, and file an affidavit that he has done so. Rule 3A: where an injunction is granted without notice, the court shall make an endeavour to finally dispose of the application within thirty days; if it cannot, it must record its reasons. Rule 4: any order for an injunction may be discharged, varied or set aside by the court on the application of a party dissatisfied with it.
In simple words

Section 36: preventive relief is given by injunction, temporary or perpetual, at the court's discretion . Section 37(1): a temporary injunction lasts until a specific time, or until the court's further order. It may be granted at any stage of a suit. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 regulates it. Section 37(2): a perpetual injunction can be granted only by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits. The defendant is perpetually enjoined (ordered to refrain) from asserting a right, or committing an act, contrary to the plaintiff's rights. Section 38: a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation in the plaintiff's favour, and in four cases of invasion of property rights. Order XXXIX: Rules 1 and 2 give the grounds for a temporary injunction. Rule 2A deals with disobedience. Rule 3 requires notice. Rule 4 allows the order to be discharged, varied or set aside.
en.meaning:
A temporary injunction is an order that holds the position until a set time or further order. It does not decide who is right. A perpetual injunction is the final order granted by the decree. It decides the dispute on the merits and binds the defendant for good. The word "perpetual" refers to the permanence of the decree, not to a different kind of act. The question this topic answers. At what stage of a suit can each kind of injunction be granted, on what basis, and what is its effect? Why the law has two kinds. A trial takes time. If nothing could be done until the decree, the property in dispute might be sold, a wall might be built, or a secret might be leaked. The temporary injunction keeps things as they are until the court can decide. The perpetual injunction then gives the final answer. The two in one suit. The timeline shows how the two fit into the life of one suit. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Read the boxes from top to bottom. Green marks the final order. flowchart TD S1["1. Plaint

Step 2, application: he applies in the suit for a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2. Step 3, notice and order: the court hears the other side under Rule 3; in urgent cases it may pass an ad interim order without notice, recording reasons. Step 4, temporary injunction: the order lasts until a stated time or further order under Section 37(1). Step 5, decree: after the hearing on the merits, the court may grant a perpetual injunction under Section 37(2).
keyPoints: Temporary: any stage, until a time or further order, Order XXXIX. Perpetual: decree on the merits only. Three tests for a temporary injunction: prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury. A temporary order does not decide the suit. Section 38(3): four cases of invasion of property rights for a perpetual injunction. A bare suit for a perpetual injunction needs possession and no real cloud on title. Disobedience: Order XXXIX, Rule 2A for a temporary injunction; Order XXI, Rule 32 for a decree.

caseLaws.name: Dalpat Kumar v
caseLaws.facts: Prahlad Singh (1992) Facts. In the fourth round of litigation over a Jaipur house that the first appellant claimed to have agreed to buy on 14 June 1979 for ₹51,000, the Supreme Court considered a temporary injunction against dispossession, which the trial court had refused and the High Court had granted. Decided 16 December 1991; (1992) 1 SCC 719 : AIR 1993 SC 276. Principle. A prima facie case alone is not enough. The court must also find that refusal would cause irreparable injury and that the balance of convenience favours the plaintiff (para 5). The High Court's order was set aside (para 7). Why it matters. It is the standard Indian authority for the three tests. Wander Ltd. v. Antox India (1990) Facts. Wander owned the trade mark "Cal-De-Ce" for calcium tablets that Antox had made for it. In Antox's passing off suit, the single judge of the Madras High Court refused an interim injunction; the Division Bench granted it on appeal. Decided 26 April 1990; 1990 Supp SCC 727. Principle. An appellate court should not interfere with a trial court's discretionary order "except where the discretion has been shown to have been exercised arbitrarily, or capriciously or perversely", or where settled principles were ignored (para 9). The single judge's order was restored. Why it matters. It limits appeals against temporary orders. American Cyanamid v. Ethicon (1975) Facts. A patent holder for absorbable surgical sutures sought an interim injunction to stop a rival from launching a suture in the United Kingdom before trial. Principle. The court asks whether there is a serious question to be tried, then weighs damages and the balance of convenience. [1975] AC 396 (HL). Why it matters. It is the English approach, a contrast with the Indian three tests. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two sites in Matwada, Warangal, were claimed under two lines of sale from one family: the plaintiffs bought from Rukminibai by deeds of 9 December 1968, and the defendants claimed through her brother. The plaintiffs sued only for a perpetual injunction. Principle. A bare injunction suit lies only where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and there is no real cloud on title. Otherwise a declaration is also needed (paras 11 and 12). (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It marks when a perpetual injunction alone is the right suit.

selfTest.q: 1. When can a perpetual injunction be granted?
selfTest.a: Only by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit (Section 37(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. What law regulates temporary injunctions?
selfTest.a: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, mainly Order XXXIX (Section 37(1)).

selfTest.q: 4. What must a court do if it grants a temporary injunction without notice?
selfTest.a: Record its reasons (Order XXXIX, Rule 3), and try to decide the application within 30 days (Rule 3A).

selfTest.q: 5. When will an appellate court interfere with a trial court's temporary order?
selfTest.a: Only where the discretion was exercised arbitrarily, capriciously or perversely, or settled principles were ignored ( Wander v. Antox ).

Rule 1: అఫిడవిట్ ద్వారా గానీ మరో విధంగా గానీ ఇది రుజువైతే: (a) దావాలో వివాదంలో ఉన్న ఏదైనా ఆస్తి దావాలోని ఏ పక్షం వల్లనైనా వృథా, నష్టం లేదా అన్యాక్రాంతం (alienation) అయ్యే ప్రమాదంలో ఉంది; (b) ప్రతివాది తన రుణదాతలను మోసగించే ఉద్దేశంతో తన ఆస్తిని తొలగిస్తానని లేదా అమ్మేస్తానని బెదిరిస్తున్నాడు, లేదా ఉద్దేశిస్తున్నాడు; లేదా (c) ప్రతివాది వాదిని స్వాధీనం నుంచి తొలగిస్తానని, లేదా వివాదంలోని ఆస్తికి సంబంధించి అతనికి హాని చేస్తానని బెదిరిస్తున్నాడు – అప్పుడు కోర్టు, దావా పరిష్కారం అయ్యే వరకు లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వుల వరకు తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వవచ్చు. Rule 2: కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనను లేదా ఇతర హానిని ఆపే దావాలో, దావా మొదలైన తర్వాత ఏ సమయంలోనైనా, తీర్పుకు ముందు లేదా తర్వాత, ఫిర్యాదు చేసిన ఉల్లంఘన లేదా హానిని ఆపడానికి వాది తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ కోసం దరఖాస్తు చేయవచ్చు; కోర్టు తగిన షరతులపై ఇవ్వవచ్చు. Rule 2A: నిషేధాజ్ఞను ఉల్లంఘిస్తే, తప్పు చేసిన వ్యక్తి ఆస్తిని జప్తు చేయమని కోర్టు ఆదేశించవచ్చు, మూడు నెలలకు మించని కాలం సివిల్ జైలులో నిర్బంధించమని ఆదేశించవచ్చు. జప్తు ఒక సంవత్సరానికి మించి అమలులో ఉండదు; ఆ తర్వాత ఆస్తిని అమ్మి, నష్టపోయిన పక్షానికి పరిహారం చెల్లించవచ్చు. Rule 3: నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇచ్చే ముందు, ఆలస్యం వల్ల నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఉద్దేశం దెబ్బతినే సందర్భంలో తప్ప, కోర్టు ఎదుటి పక్షానికి నోటీసు ఇవ్వాలి. నోటీసు లేకుండా ఇస్తే, కారణాలు నమోదు చేయాలి; దరఖాస్తుదారు వెంటనే దరఖాస్తు, అఫిడవిట్, plaint , ఆధారపడిన పత్రాల ప్రతులను ఎదుటి పక్షానికి పంపి, పంపినట్లు అఫిడవిట్ దాఖలు చేయాలి. Rule 3A: నోటీసు లేకుండా నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇస్తే, ముప్పై రోజుల్లో దరఖాస్తును తుదిగా పరిష్కరించడానికి కోర్టు ప్రయత్నించాలి; చేయలేకపోతే కారణాలు నమోదు చేయాలి. Order XXXIX: Rules 1, 2 తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞకు కారణాలు ఇస్తాయి. Rule 2A ఉల్లంఘన గురించి. Rule 3 నోటీసును కోరుతుంది. Rule 4 ఉత్తర్వును రద్దు చేయడానికి, మార్చడానికి లేదా పక్కన పెట్టడానికి అనుమతిస్తుంది.

తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ (temporary injunction ) అంటే నిర్ణీత సమయం లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వు వరకు పరిస్థితిని యథాతథంగా ఉంచే ఉత్తర్వు. ఎవరు సరైనవారో అది నిర్ణయించదు. శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ( perpetual injunction) అంటే డిక్రీ ద్వారా ఇచ్చే తుది ఉత్తర్వు. అది merits పై వివాదాన్ని నిర్ణయించి, ప్రతివాదిని శాశ్వతంగా కట్టుబడి ఉంచుతుంది. "శాశ్వతం" అనే పదం డిక్రీ శాశ్వతత్వాన్ని సూచిస్తుంది, వేరే రకం పనిని కాదు. ఈ అంశం జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. దావాలో ఏ దశలో ఏ రకం నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వవచ్చు, ఏ ఆధారంపై, దాని ప్రభావం ఏమిటి? రెండు రకాలు ఎందుకు. విచారణకు సమయం పడుతుంది. డిక్రీ వరకు ఏమీ చేయలేకపోతే, వివాదంలోని ఆస్తి అమ్ముడుపోవచ్చు, గోడ కట్టేయవచ్చు, రహస్యం బయటపడవచ్చు. కోర్టు నిర్ణయించే వరకు తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ పరిస్థితిని అలాగే ఉంచుతుంది. తర్వాత శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ తుది జవాబు ఇస్తుంది. ఒకే దావాలో రెండూ. ఒకే దావా జీవితంలో రెండూ ఎక్కడ వస్తాయో కాలరేఖ చూపుతుంది. selfTest.q: 1. శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఎప్పుడు ఇవ్వవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: దావా విచారణలో, merits పై ఇచ్చే డిక్రీ ద్వారా మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 37(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞలను ఏ చట్టం నియంత్రిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1908, ముఖ్యంగా Order XXXIX (సెక్షన్ 37(1)).

selfTest.q: 4. నోటీసు లేకుండా తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇస్తే కోర్టు ఏమి చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: కారణాలు నమోదు చేయాలి (Order XXXIX, Rule 3), 30 రోజుల్లో దరఖాస్తును నిర్ణయించడానికి ప్రయత్నించాలి (Rule 3A).

selfTest.q: 5. ట్రయల్ కోర్టు తాత్కాలిక ఉత్తర్వులో అప్పీలు కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు జోక్యం చేసుకుంటుంది?
selfTest.a: విచక్షణను ఏకపక్షంగా, ఇష్టానుసారంగా లేదా వక్రంగా వాడినప్పుడు, లేదా స్థిరపడిన సూత్రాలను పట్టించుకోనప్పుడు మాత్రమే ( Wander v. Antox ).

hi.inOneMinute: An injunction can come early in a suit or at its end. A temporary injunction protects the plaintiff while the case is going on. A perpetual injunction is the final order that ends the case in the plaintiff's favour. Section 37 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 draws the line. Temporary injunctions are governed by the Code of Civil Procedure. Perpetual injunctions are granted only by a decree on the merits. In exams, the six-point comparison and the three tests are the core. In real life, the temporary order is what stops a wall or a sale today; the perpetual order is what the plaintiff takes home after the trial.
legalProvision: Section 36. Preventive relief how granted. Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual.

Section 37. Temporary and perpetual injunctions. (1) Temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specific time, or until the further order of the court, and they may be granted at any stage of a suit, and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). (2) A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit; the defendant is thereby perpetually enjoined from the assertion of a right, or from the commission of an act, which would be contrary to the rights of the plaintiff.

Section 38. Perpetual injunction when granted. (1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred to by this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. (2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in Chapter II. (3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX (" Temporary Injunctions and Interlocutory Orders") – stated closely, not quoted

Rule 1: where it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that (a) any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit; (b) the defendant threatens, or intends, to remove or dispose of his property with a view to defrauding his creditors; or (c) the defendant threatens to dispossess the plaintiff or otherwise cause injury to him in relation to any property in dispute, the court may grant a temporary injunction , until the disposal of the suit or until further orders. Rule 2: in a suit to restrain a breach of contract or other injury, the plaintiff may, at any time after the suit begins and before or after judgment, apply for a temporary injunction to restrain the breach or injury complained of, on such terms as the court thinks fit. Rule 2A: on disobedience or breach of an injunction, the court may order the property of the person guilty to be attached, and may order him to be detained in civil prison for a term not exceeding three months. An attachment cannot remain in force for more than one year; after that, the property may be sold and compensation paid to the injured party. Rule 3: before granting an injunction, the court shall direct notice to the opposite party, except where the object of granting the injunction would be defeated by the delay. If it grants one without notice, it must record its reasons, and the applicant must at once send the other side copies of the application, the affidavit, the plaint and the documents relied on, and file an affidavit that he has done so. Rule 3A: where an injunction is granted without notice, the court shall make an endeavour to finally dispose of the application within thirty days; if it cannot, it must record its reasons. Rule 4: any order for an injunction may be discharged, varied or set aside by the court on the application of a party dissatisfied with it.
In simple words

Section 36: preventive relief is given by injunction, temporary or perpetual, at the court's discretion . Section 37(1): a temporary injunction lasts until a specific time, or until the court's further order. It may be granted at any stage of a suit. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 regulates it. Section 37(2): a perpetual injunction can be granted only by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits. The defendant is perpetually enjoined (ordered to refrain) from asserting a right, or committing an act, contrary to the plaintiff's rights. Section 38: a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation in the plaintiff's favour, and in four cases of invasion of property rights. Order XXXIX: Rules 1 and 2 give the grounds for a temporary injunction. Rule 2A deals with disobedience. Rule 3 requires notice. Rule 4 allows the order to be discharged, varied or set aside.
hi.meaning:
A temporary injunction is an order that holds the position until a set time or further order. It does not decide who is right. A perpetual injunction is the final order granted by the decree. It decides the dispute on the merits and binds the defendant for good. The word "perpetual" refers to the permanence of the decree, not to a different kind of act. The question this topic answers. At what stage of a suit can each kind of injunction be granted, on what basis, and what is its effect? Why the law has two kinds. A trial takes time. If nothing could be done until the decree, the property in dispute might be sold, a wall might be built, or a secret might be leaked. The temporary injunction keeps things as they are until the court can decide. The perpetual injunction then gives the final answer. The two in one suit. The timeline shows how the two fit into the life of one suit. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Read the boxes from top to bottom. Green marks the final order. flowchart TD S1["1. Plaint

Step 2, application: he applies in the suit for a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2. Step 3, notice and order: the court hears the other side under Rule 3; in urgent cases it may pass an ad interim order without notice, recording reasons. Step 4, temporary injunction: the order lasts until a stated time or further order under Section 37(1). Step 5, decree: after the hearing on the merits, the court may grant a perpetual injunction under Section 37(2).
keyPoints: Temporary: any stage, until a time or further order, Order XXXIX. Perpetual: decree on the merits only. Three tests for a temporary injunction: prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury. A temporary order does not decide the suit. Section 38(3): four cases of invasion of property rights for a perpetual injunction. A bare suit for a perpetual injunction needs possession and no real cloud on title. Disobedience: Order XXXIX, Rule 2A for a temporary injunction; Order XXI, Rule 32 for a decree.

caseLaws.name: Dalpat Kumar v
caseLaws.facts: Prahlad Singh (1992) Facts. In the fourth round of litigation over a Jaipur house that the first appellant claimed to have agreed to buy on 14 June 1979 for ₹51,000, the Supreme Court considered a temporary injunction against dispossession, which the trial court had refused and the High Court had granted. Decided 16 December 1991; (1992) 1 SCC 719 : AIR 1993 SC 276. Principle. A prima facie case alone is not enough. The court must also find that refusal would cause irreparable injury and that the balance of convenience favours the plaintiff (para 5). The High Court's order was set aside (para 7). Why it matters. It is the standard Indian authority for the three tests. Wander Ltd. v. Antox India (1990) Facts. Wander owned the trade mark "Cal-De-Ce" for calcium tablets that Antox had made for it. In Antox's passing off suit, the single judge of the Madras High Court refused an interim injunction; the Division Bench granted it on appeal. Decided 26 April 1990; 1990 Supp SCC 727. Principle. An appellate court should not interfere with a trial court's discretionary order "except where the discretion has been shown to have been exercised arbitrarily, or capriciously or perversely", or where settled principles were ignored (para 9). The single judge's order was restored. Why it matters. It limits appeals against temporary orders. American Cyanamid v. Ethicon (1975) Facts. A patent holder for absorbable surgical sutures sought an interim injunction to stop a rival from launching a suture in the United Kingdom before trial. Principle. The court asks whether there is a serious question to be tried, then weighs damages and the balance of convenience. [1975] AC 396 (HL). Why it matters. It is the English approach, a contrast with the Indian three tests. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two sites in Matwada, Warangal, were claimed under two lines of sale from one family: the plaintiffs bought from Rukminibai by deeds of 9 December 1968, and the defendants claimed through her brother. The plaintiffs sued only for a perpetual injunction. Principle. A bare injunction suit lies only where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and there is no real cloud on title. Otherwise a declaration is also needed (paras 11 and 12). (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It marks when a perpetual injunction alone is the right suit.

selfTest.q: 1. When can a perpetual injunction be granted?
selfTest.a: Only by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit (Section 37(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. What law regulates temporary injunctions?
selfTest.a: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, mainly Order XXXIX (Section 37(1)).

selfTest.q: 4. What must a court do if it grants a temporary injunction without notice?
selfTest.a: Record its reasons (Order XXXIX, Rule 3), and try to decide the application within 30 days (Rule 3A).

selfTest.q: 5. When will an appellate court interfere with a trial court's temporary order?
selfTest.a: Only where the discretion was exercised arbitrarily, capriciously or perversely, or settled principles were ignored ( Wander v. Antox ).

law-of-contract-i-u5-t3.subtitle: Sections 9 to 25 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as amended in 2018

en.inOneMinute: When a party breaks a contract, the injured party can ask the court to make the other side keep its promise. That order is called specific performance . It is the most important remedy in the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Since 1 October 2018, the court shall enforce a contract as a rule, unless a section bars it. Three provisions can bar it: the kind of contract (Sections 11(2) and 14) and the plaintiff's own conduct (Section 16). Substituted performance under Section 20 works through Sections 14(a) and 16(a). In exams, you must know all of these, with the main cases. In real life, this is the remedy a buyer uses when a seller backs out of a land or flat sale because prices have gone up.
legalProvision: Section 9. Defences respecting suits for relief based on contract. Except as otherwise provided herein where any relief is claimed under this Chapter in respect of a contract, the person against whom the relief is claimed may plead by way of defence any ground which is available to him under any law relating to contracts.

Section 10. Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.
(Section 10 was substituted by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 11. Cases in which specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforceable. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, specific performance of a contract shall, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust. (2) A contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.
(In Section 11(1), " contract shall" replaced "contract may, in the discretion of the court" from 1 October 2018.)

Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— (a) where a party to the contract has obtained substituted performance of contract in accordance with the provisions of section 20; (b) a contract, the performance of which involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.
(Section 14 was substituted by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 16. Personal bars to relief. Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— (a) who has obtained substituted performance of contract under section 20; or (b) who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that on his part remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with, or in subversion of, the relation intended to be established by the contract; or (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— (i) where a contract involves the payment of money, it is not essential for the plaintiff to actually tender to the defendant or to deposit in court any money except when so directed by the court; (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
(In 2018, clause (a) was substituted, "who fails to aver and prove" became "who fails to prove", and "must aver" in Explanation (ii) became "must prove".)

Section 20. Substituted performance of contract. (1) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), and, except as otherwise agreed upon by the parties, where the contract is broken due to non-performance of promise by any party, the party who suffers by such breach shall have the option of substituted performance through a third party or by his own agency, and, recover the expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent or suffered by him, from the party committing such breach. (2) No substituted performance of contract under sub-section (1) shall be undertaken unless the party who suffers such breach has given a notice in writing, of not less than thirty days, to the party in breach calling upon him to perform the contract within such time as specified in the notice, and on his refusal or failure to do so, he may get the same performed by a third party or by his own agency: Provided that the party who suffers such breach shall not be entitled to recover the expenses and costs under sub-section (1) unless he has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency. (3) Where the party suffering breach of contract has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency after giving notice under sub-section (1), he shall not be entitled to claim relief of specific performance against the party in breach. (4) Nothing in this section shall prevent the party who has suffered breach of contract from claiming compensation from the party in breach.
Related provision ( Limitation Act, 1963 , Schedule)
Article 54. For specific performance of a contract. – Three years. – The date fixed for the performance, or, if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.
In simple words

Section 9: the defendant may raise any defence that the law of contract allows. Section 10: specific performance shall be enforced, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16. Sections 11 to 13: contracts connected with trusts, part of a contract, and rights against a vendor with a defective title. Section 14: four kinds of contract that cannot be specifically enforced. Section 14A: the court may engage experts. Sections 15 to 19: who may sue and against whom, personal bars, no title, enforcement only with a variation. Section 20: substituted performance. Sections 20A to 20C: infrastructure projects, Special Courts, and a 12-month time limit for suits. Sections 21 to 25: compensation, possession and refund of earnest money , a sum named for breach, bar of a later suit, and awards. Article 54: the suit must be filed within three years.
en.meaning:
Specific performance is a court order that a party must actually do what he promised in the contract. It differs from damages , which give money. It is the natural remedy where the subject matter is one of a kind, such as land, because no sum of money buys exactly the same plot. The question this part of the Act answers. When will the court make a party actually perform his contract, instead of paying money? The answer since 2018. The Act does not say that the court has no freedom left. It says the court shall enforce the contract unless a named bar applies. A plaintiff must clear a series of tests. Is there a valid, subsisting contract, with no defence under the law of contract? If not, there is nothing to enforce (Section 9). Is the suit filed in time, within three years of the date fixed for performance or of refusal? If not, the suit is barred by Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Is the contract one that the Act allows to be enforced? If it is barred by Section 11(2) or Section 14, damages are the remedy. Is the plaintiff free of the personal bars? If he took substituted performance, cannot perform, or cannot prove readiness and willingness , he fails (Section 16). If all the tests are met, the court shall enforce the contract (Section 10). It may add compensation and possession (Sections 21 and 22). See Diagram 1 for the order of the tests. Diagram 1. no contract-law defence?"} Q1 -->|"No"| N1["Nothing to enforce
(s. 9)"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"2. Suit within three years of the
date fixed, or of refusal?"} Q2 -->|"No"| N2["Barred by Article 54,
Limitation Act, 1963"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"3. Contract outside
s. 11(2) and s. 14?"} Q3 -->|"No"| N3["Not enforceable:
damages are the remedy"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4{"4. Plaintiff free of the
personal bars in s. 16?"} Q4 -->|"No"| N4["Relief refused: substituted performance,
misconduct, or no readiness and willingness"] Q4 -->|"Yes"| Y["The court shall enforce the contract (s. 10);
may add compensation and possession (ss. 21, 22)"] Text description Question 1: is there a valid, subsisting contract with no defence under the law of contract? If no, there is nothing to enforce (Section 9). Question 2: is the suit within three years of the date fixed for performance or of refusal? If no, it is barred by Article 54 of the Limitation Act. Question 3: is the contract outside Section 11(2) and Section 14? If no, damages are the remedy. Question 4: is the plaintiff free of the personal bars in Section 16 (substituted performance, incapacity or misconduct, readiness and willingness)? If no, relief is refused. If all answers are yes, the court shall enforce the contract under Section 10 and may add compensation and possession under Sections 21 and 22.
keyPoints: Section 10 (after 2018): specific performance shall be enforced as a rule, subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16. Before 1 October 2018 it was "may", in the court's discretion. Katta Sujatha Reddy (2022): the amendment is prospective. The 2024 review recalled that judgment without deciding the point again. Section 14 has four classes: substituted performance obtained, continuous duty, personal qualifications, determinable contracts. Section 16(c): the plaintiff must prove continuous readiness and willingness. Readiness is financial capacity and willingness is conduct. Filing within limitation (three years, Article 54) is not enough. Delay and price rise can defeat relief. Section 20: substituted performance after 30 days' written notice. It bars a later claim for specific performance but not compensation. Sections 21 and 22: compensation, possession and refund of earnest money must be claimed in the plaint, but the court shall allow amendment. Sections 20A to 20C: no injunction that delays a listed infrastructure project; Special Courts; suits disposed of within 12 months (plus six).

caseLaws.name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v
caseLaws.facts: Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (2022) Facts. A purchaser under two agreements of March 1997 for Acs. 40.08 in Budvel village, for a total of ₹40,20,000, paid ₹34,80,850 but did not pay the balance within the three months fixed. It sued in 2002 (O.S. No. 88 of 2002). Principle. The 2018 amendment to Section 10 is substantive and prospective; it does not apply to transactions made before it came into force. On the old law, the Court held the suit barred under Article 54 and the purchaser not ready and willing. Civil Appeal No. 5822 of 2022, decided 25 August 2022. The judgment was recalled in review on 8 November 2024 (2024 INSC 861), and the High Court's decree was restored. Why it matters. It is the leading statement on the date of effect of the amended Section 10, read with its 2024 review. Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi (2011) Facts. Under an agreement of 17 January 1981 for 24.95 acres at ₹3,75,000, the buyer paid ₹1,00,000 as advance and was to pay the balance of ₹2,75,000 in three instalments . The agreement said payment on the due dates was of the essence. He paid ₹1,25,000 of the balance and missed the rest. The sellers cancelled on 2 August 1981. Principle. Time for payment was of the essence, and the buyer was not ready and willing. Older cases holding time not of the essence in land sales "may no longer apply" because of steep rises in prices. The buyer got a refund with interest. (2011) 12 SCC 18 : AIR 2011 SC 3234. Why it matters. It links delay, price rise and Section 16(c). K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan (1997) Facts. On 15 December 1978 a buyer agreed to buy a house in Madurai for ₹60,000, to be completed in six months, and paid ₹5,000. He gave notice only on 11 July 1981 and sued on 23 August 1981, after prices had risen. Principle. A suit need not be decreed merely because it is within limitation. "Total inaction" for two and a half years, with a steep rise in prices, made relief inequitable . (1997) 3 SCC 1 : AIR 1997 SC 1751. Why it matters. It shows that a court looks at all circumstances, not only the limitation period. J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao (2010) Facts. The owners of 30 acres 86 cents agreed on 3 February 2006 to sell for ₹5,55,48,000 and received ₹75,00,000. The land was mortgaged to a bank for a sister concern's loan. The buyers deposited ₹2,45,00,000 in a bank and sued. Principle. The buyers proved readiness and willingness. Readiness refers to financial capacity; willingness refers to the conduct of the plaintiff wanting performance. The plaintiff need not tender the money unless the court directs. Civil Appeal Nos. 9821-9822 of 2010, decided 22 November 2010. Why it matters. It explains the two limbs of Section 16(c). N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao (1995) Facts. On 9 April 1979 a buyer agreed to buy a house in Madras for ₹2,30,000, paid ₹10,000 and was in possession as a tenant. He did not deposit ₹2,00,000 when the court directed it, and the lender he relied on had no cash. Principle. "Continuous readiness and willingness" is a condition precedent. The amount "must of necessity be proved to be available", judged by the plaintiff's conduct before and after the suit. The courts below rightly found him not ready and willing. (1995) 5 SCC 115 : AIR 1996 SC 116. Why it matters. It is a standard authority for readiness and willingness. K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd. (1999) Facts. In 1972 the owner of a bungalow at 6 Tolstoy Marg, New Delhi agreed to sell it to builders, who paid part of the price. The land was later caught by the urban land ceiling law and partly acquired. The builders sued in 1979. Principle. Performance would cause the seller hardship he did not foresee, so specific performance was refused. The buyers got the price paid back with 12% interest, and ₹3,25,000 as compensation under Section 21. Section 18 did not allow enforcement with a variation. (1999) 5 SCC 77 : AIR 1999 SC 2309. Why it matters. It shows compensation under Section 21 where performance is refused. Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Zaheer Khan (2006) Facts. A sports agency had a promotion agreement with the cricketer for 30 October 2000 to 29 October 2003. Clause 31(b) gave it a right to match third-party offers, which it said applied after the term. The cricketer signed with another agent, and the agency sought an injunction. Principle. At the interim stage, the Court held that a covenant restricting the cricketer after the term was a restraint of trade , hit by Section 27 of the Contract Act and void. The injunction would in substance be specific performance of a contract of personal service. The agency could be compensated in money. (2006) 4 SCC 227 : AIR 2006 SC 3426. Why it matters. It explains the bar on enforcing personal service contracts, now Section 14(c). Indian Oil Corporation v. Amritsar Gas Service (1991) Facts. Indian Oil terminated an LPG distributorship. The arbitrator ordered the distributorship to be restored. The agreement could be ended by either party on 30 days' notice. Principle. The agreement was revocable and for personal service, so it was determinable in nature and could not be specifically enforced. Restoration was contrary to Section 14(1). The only relief was compensation for the 30-day notice period. (1991) 1 SCC 533. Why it matters. It is the standard authority for determinable contracts, now Section 14(d).

selfTest.q: 2. What must the plaintiff prove under Section 16(c)?
selfTest.a: That he has performed, or has always been ready and willing to perform, the essential terms that are to be performed by him.

selfTest.q: 3. How much notice does Section 20 require before substituted performance?
selfTest.a: Written notice of not less than 30 days.

selfTest.q: 4. A seller owns 9.8 of the 10 acres he agreed to sell. Can the buyer get the 9.8 acres?
selfTest.a: Yes. The shortfall is small and can be compensated in money, so the court may order the sale of 9.8 acres with compensation for the rest (Section 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a court grant possession if the plaintiff asked only for specific performance?
selfTest.a: No. Section 22(2) requires possession to be specifically claimed, but the court shall allow the plaint to be amended at any stage.

selfTest.q: 6. Within what time must a suit for specific performance be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from the date fixed for performance, or, if none is fixed, from notice of refusal (Article 54).

సెక్షన్ 9: కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం అనుమతించే ఏ రక్షణనైనా ప్రతివాది వాదించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 10: సెక్షన్ 11(2), సెక్షన్ 14, సెక్షన్ 16 కు లోబడి నిర్దిష్ట అమలు తప్పనిసరిగా అమలు చేయాలి. సెక్షన్లు 11 నుంచి 13: ట్రస్టులకు సంబంధించిన కాంట్రాక్టులు, కాంట్రాక్టులో ఒక భాగం, లోపమున్న టైటిల్ గల అమ్మకందారుపై హక్కులు. సెక్షన్ 14: నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయలేని నాలుగు రకాల కాంట్రాక్టులు. సెక్షన్ 14A: కోర్టు నిపుణులను నియమించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్లు 15 నుంచి 19: ఎవరు దావా వేయవచ్చు, ఎవరిపై; వ్యక్తిగత అడ్డంకులు; టైటిల్ లేకపోవడం; మార్పుతో మాత్రమే అమలు. సెక్షన్ 20: ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు. సెక్షన్లు 20A నుంచి 20C: infrastructure ప్రాజెక్టులు, ప్రత్యేక కోర్టులు, దావాలకు 12 నెలల గడువు. సెక్షన్లు 21 నుంచి 25: పరిహారం, స్వాధీనం, బయానా (earnest money) వాపసు, ఉల్లంఘనకు పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం, తర్వాతి దావాకు అడ్డు, అవార్డులు. ఆర్టికల్ 54: దావాను మూడు సంవత్సరాల్లో వేయాలి.

నిర్దిష్ట అమలు అంటే, కాంట్రాక్టులో వాగ్దానం చేసినదే ఆ పక్షం నిజంగా చేయాలని కోర్టు ఇచ్చే ఆదేశం. ఇది డబ్బు ఇచ్చే నష్టపరిహారం (damages) కంటే భిన్నమైనది. విషయం భూమి లాగా ఒక్కటే ఉండేదైతే ఇదే సహజమైన పరిష్కారం, ఎందుకంటే ఎంత డబ్బు ఇచ్చినా అదే స్థలం దొరకదు. ఈ భాగం జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. డబ్బు చెల్లించడానికి బదులు, ఒక పక్షం తన కాంట్రాక్టును నిజంగా నెరవేర్చేలా కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు చేస్తుంది? 2018 నుంచి జవాబు. కోర్టుకు ఏ స్వేచ్ఛా మిగలలేదని చట్టం చెప్పదు. పేర్కొన్న అడ్డంకి వర్తిస్తే తప్ప కోర్టు కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయాలి అని చెబుతుంది. వాది వరుసగా కొన్ని పరీక్షలు దాటాలి. చెల్లుబాటు అయ్యే, ఇంకా అమలులో ఉన్న కాంట్రాక్టు ఉందా, కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం కింద రక్షణ ఏదీ లేకుండా? లేకపోతే అమలు చేయడానికి ఏమీ లేదు (సెక్షన్ 9). నెరవేర్పుకు నిర్ణయించిన తేదీ నుంచి లేదా నిరాకరణ నుంచి మూడు సంవత్సరాల్లో దావా వేశారా? లేకపోతే Limitation Act, 1963 ఆర్టికల్ 54 దావాను అడ్డుకుంటుంది. ఈ కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయడానికి చట్టం అనుమతిస్తుందా? సెక్షన్ 11(2) లేదా సెక్షన్ 14 అడ్డుకుంటే, నష్టపరిహారమే పరిష్కారం. వాదికి వ్యక్తిగత అడ్డంకులు లేవా? అతను ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు తీసుకుంటే, నెరవేర్చలేకపోతే, లేదా సిద్ధత, సుముఖత రుజువు చేయలేకపోతే, ఓడిపోతాడు (సెక్షన్ 16). అన్ని పరీక్షలు దాటితే, కోర్టు కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయాలి (సెక్షన్ 10). పరిహారం, స్వాధీనం కూడా ఇవ్వవచ్చు (సెక్షన్లు 21, 22). పరీక్షల క్రమం కోసం Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. పై నుంచి మొదలుపెట్టండి. ఒక పెట్టెకు సమాధానం దావాను ముగిస్తే, పక్కన ఉన్న పెట్టె దగ్గర ఆగండి. లేకపోతే బాణం వెంట కింది పెట్టెకు వెళ్లండి. flowchart TD Q1{"1. చెల్లుబాటు అయ్యే, అమలులో ఉన్న కాంట్రాక్టు,
కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం రక్షణ లేదా?"} Q1 -->|"కాదు"| N1["అమలు చేయడానికి ఏమీ లేదు
(సె. 9)"] Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2{"2. నిర్ణయించిన తేదీ లేదా నిరాకరణ నుంచి
మూడు సంవత్సరాల్లో దావా?"} Q2 -->|"కాదు"| N2["ఆర్టికల్ 54 అడ్డు,
Limitation Act, 1963"] Q2 -->|"అవును"| Q3{"3. కాంట్రాక్టు సె. 11(2),
సె. 14 బయట ఉందా?"} Q3 -->|"కాదు"| N3["అమలు చేయలేరు:
నష్టపరిహారమే పరిష్కారం"] Q3 -->|"అవును"| Q4{"4. సె. 16 వ్యక్తిగత అడ్డంకులు
వాదికి లేవా?"} Q4 -->|"కాదు"| N4["ఉపశమనం నిరాకరణ: ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు,
దుష్ప్రవర్తన, లేదా సిద్ధత, సుముఖత లేకపోవడం"] Q4 -->|"అవును"| Y["కోర్టు కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయాలి (సె. 10);
పరిహారం, స్వాధీనం కూడా ఇవ్వవచ్చు (సె. 21, 22)"] వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం కింద రక్షణ లేని, చెల్లుబాటు అయ్యే, అమలులో ఉన్న కాంట్రాక్టు ఉందా? లేకపోతే అమలు చేయడానికి ఏమీ లేదు (సెక్షన్ 9). ప్రశ్న 2: నెరవేర్పుకు నిర్ణయించిన తేదీ లేదా నిరాకరణ నుంచి మూడు సంవత్సరాల్లో దావా వేశారా? లేకపోతే Limitation Act ఆర్టికల్ 54 అడ్డుకుంటుంది. ప్రశ్న 3: కాంట్రాక్టు సెక్షన్ 11(2), సెక్షన్ 14 బయట ఉందా? లేకపోతే నష్టపరిహారమే పరిష్కారం. ప్రశ్న 4: సెక్షన్ 16 లోని వ్యక్తిగత అడ్డంకులు (ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు, అసమర్థత లేదా దుష్ప్రవర్తన, సిద్ధత, సుముఖత) వాదికి లేవా? ఉంటే ఉపశమనం నిరాకరించబడుతుంది. అన్నీ అవును అయితే, సెక్షన్ 10 కింద కోర్టు కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయాలి; సెక్షన్లు 21, 22 కింద పరిహారం, స్వాధీనం కూడా ఇవ్వవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 10 కింద నిర్దిష్ట అమలును అడ్డుకునే మూడు నిబంధనలు ఏవి?
2. సెక్షన్ 16(c) కింద వాది ఏం రుజువు చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: తాను నెరవేర్చాల్సిన ముఖ్యమైన షరతులను నెరవేర్చానని, లేదా వాటిని నెరవేర్చడానికి ఎల్లప్పుడూ సిద్ధంగా, సుముఖంగా ఉన్నానని.

selfTest.q: 3. ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పుకు ముందు సెక్షన్ 20 ఎంత నోటీసు కోరుతుంది?
selfTest.a: కనీసం 30 రోజుల రాతపూర్వక నోటీసు.

selfTest.q: 4. అమ్ముతానన్న 10 ఎకరాల్లో అమ్మకందారుకు 9.8 ఎకరాలే ఉన్నాయి. కొనుగోలుదారు 9.8 ఎకరాలు పొందగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. లోటు చిన్నది, డబ్బుతో పూడ్చవచ్చు; కాబట్టి కోర్టు 9.8 ఎకరాల అమ్మకానికి ఆదేశించి, మిగతాదానికి పరిహారం ఇవ్వవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 5. వాది నిర్దిష్ట అమలు మాత్రమే కోరితే కోర్టు స్వాధీనం ఇవ్వగలదా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. సెక్షన్ 22(2) ప్రకారం స్వాధీనం ప్రత్యేకంగా కోరాలి; కానీ ఏ దశలోనైనా plaint సవరణకు కోర్టు అనుమతించాలి.

selfTest.q: 6. నిర్దిష్ట అమలు దావాను ఎంత కాలంలో వేయాలి?
selfTest.a: నెరవేర్పుకు నిర్ణయించిన తేదీ నుంచి, తేదీ లేకపోతే నిరాకరణ తెలిసిన తేదీ నుంచి మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (ఆర్టికల్ 54).

visuals.html:
నిబంధన కాంట్రాక్టు రకం చట్టం ఎందుకు అడ్డుకుంటుంది ఉదాహరణ
సెక్షన్ 11(2) అధికారాలకు మించి లేదా ట్రస్టు ఉల్లంఘనలో ట్రస్టీ చేసిన కాంట్రాక్టు తప్పుతో ట్రస్టు ఆస్తి కట్టుబడకూడదు అమ్మే అధికారం లేకుండా ట్రస్టీ ట్రస్టు భూమి అమ్మడం
సెక్షన్ 14(a) ఇప్పటికే ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు పొందడం వాది మరో పరిష్కారాన్ని ఎంచుకున్నాడు యజమాని కొత్త కాంట్రాక్టర్‌తో గోడ కట్టించుకున్నాడు

hi.inOneMinute: When a party breaks a contract, the injured party can ask the court to make the other side keep its promise. That order is called specific performance . It is the most important remedy in the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Since 1 October 2018, the court shall enforce a contract as a rule, unless a section bars it. Three provisions can bar it: the kind of contract (Sections 11(2) and 14) and the plaintiff's own conduct (Section 16). Substituted performance under Section 20 works through Sections 14(a) and 16(a). In exams, you must know all of these, with the main cases. In real life, this is the remedy a buyer uses when a seller backs out of a land or flat sale because prices have gone up.
legalProvision: Section 9. Defences respecting suits for relief based on contract. Except as otherwise provided herein where any relief is claimed under this Chapter in respect of a contract, the person against whom the relief is claimed may plead by way of defence any ground which is available to him under any law relating to contracts.

Section 10. Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.
(Section 10 was substituted by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 11. Cases in which specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforceable. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, specific performance of a contract shall, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust. (2) A contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.
(In Section 11(1), " contract shall" replaced "contract may, in the discretion of the court" from 1 October 2018.)

Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— (a) where a party to the contract has obtained substituted performance of contract in accordance with the provisions of section 20; (b) a contract, the performance of which involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.
(Section 14 was substituted by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 16. Personal bars to relief. Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— (a) who has obtained substituted performance of contract under section 20; or (b) who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that on his part remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with, or in subversion of, the relation intended to be established by the contract; or (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— (i) where a contract involves the payment of money, it is not essential for the plaintiff to actually tender to the defendant or to deposit in court any money except when so directed by the court; (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
(In 2018, clause (a) was substituted, "who fails to aver and prove" became "who fails to prove", and "must aver" in Explanation (ii) became "must prove".)

Section 20. Substituted performance of contract. (1) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), and, except as otherwise agreed upon by the parties, where the contract is broken due to non-performance of promise by any party, the party who suffers by such breach shall have the option of substituted performance through a third party or by his own agency, and, recover the expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent or suffered by him, from the party committing such breach. (2) No substituted performance of contract under sub-section (1) shall be undertaken unless the party who suffers such breach has given a notice in writing, of not less than thirty days, to the party in breach calling upon him to perform the contract within such time as specified in the notice, and on his refusal or failure to do so, he may get the same performed by a third party or by his own agency: Provided that the party who suffers such breach shall not be entitled to recover the expenses and costs under sub-section (1) unless he has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency. (3) Where the party suffering breach of contract has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency after giving notice under sub-section (1), he shall not be entitled to claim relief of specific performance against the party in breach. (4) Nothing in this section shall prevent the party who has suffered breach of contract from claiming compensation from the party in breach.
Related provision ( Limitation Act, 1963 , Schedule)
Article 54. For specific performance of a contract. – Three years. – The date fixed for the performance, or, if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.
In simple words

Section 9: the defendant may raise any defence that the law of contract allows. Section 10: specific performance shall be enforced, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16. Sections 11 to 13: contracts connected with trusts, part of a contract, and rights against a vendor with a defective title. Section 14: four kinds of contract that cannot be specifically enforced. Section 14A: the court may engage experts. Sections 15 to 19: who may sue and against whom, personal bars, no title, enforcement only with a variation. Section 20: substituted performance. Sections 20A to 20C: infrastructure projects, Special Courts, and a 12-month time limit for suits. Sections 21 to 25: compensation, possession and refund of earnest money , a sum named for breach, bar of a later suit, and awards. Article 54: the suit must be filed within three years.
hi.meaning:
Specific performance is a court order that a party must actually do what he promised in the contract. It differs from damages , which give money. It is the natural remedy where the subject matter is one of a kind, such as land, because no sum of money buys exactly the same plot. The question this part of the Act answers. When will the court make a party actually perform his contract, instead of paying money? The answer since 2018. The Act does not say that the court has no freedom left. It says the court shall enforce the contract unless a named bar applies. A plaintiff must clear a series of tests. Is there a valid, subsisting contract, with no defence under the law of contract? If not, there is nothing to enforce (Section 9). Is the suit filed in time, within three years of the date fixed for performance or of refusal? If not, the suit is barred by Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Is the contract one that the Act allows to be enforced? If it is barred by Section 11(2) or Section 14, damages are the remedy. Is the plaintiff free of the personal bars? If he took substituted performance, cannot perform, or cannot prove readiness and willingness , he fails (Section 16). If all the tests are met, the court shall enforce the contract (Section 10). It may add compensation and possession (Sections 21 and 22). See Diagram 1 for the order of the tests. Diagram 1. If no, there is nothing to enforce (Section 9). Question 2: is the suit within three years of the date fixed for performance or of refusal? If no, it is barred by Article 54 of the Limitation Act. Question 3: is the contract outside Section 11(2) and Section 14? If no, damages are the remedy. Question 4: is the plaintiff free of the personal bars in Section 16 (substituted performance, incapacity or misconduct, readiness and willingness)? If no, relief is refused. If all answers are yes, the court shall enforce the contract under Section 10 and may add compensation and possession under Sections 21 and 22.
keyPoints: Section 10 (after 2018): specific performance shall be enforced as a rule, subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16. Before 1 October 2018 it was "may", in the court's discretion. Katta Sujatha Reddy (2022): the amendment is prospective. The 2024 review recalled that judgment without deciding the point again. Section 14 has four classes: substituted performance obtained, continuous duty, personal qualifications, determinable contracts. Section 16(c): the plaintiff must prove continuous readiness and willingness. Readiness is financial capacity and willingness is conduct. Filing within limitation (three years, Article 54) is not enough. Delay and price rise can defeat relief. Section 20: substituted performance after 30 days' written notice. It bars a later claim for specific performance but not compensation. Sections 21 and 22: compensation, possession and refund of earnest money must be claimed in the plaint, but the court shall allow amendment. Sections 20A to 20C: no injunction that delays a listed infrastructure project; Special Courts; suits disposed of within 12 months (plus six).

caseLaws.name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v
caseLaws.facts: Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (2022) Facts. A purchaser under two agreements of March 1997 for Acs. 40.08 in Budvel village, for a total of ₹40,20,000, paid ₹34,80,850 but did not pay the balance within the three months fixed. It sued in 2002 (O.S. No. 88 of 2002). Principle. The 2018 amendment to Section 10 is substantive and prospective; it does not apply to transactions made before it came into force. On the old law, the Court held the suit barred under Article 54 and the purchaser not ready and willing. Civil Appeal No. 5822 of 2022, decided 25 August 2022. The judgment was recalled in review on 8 November 2024 (2024 INSC 861), and the High Court's decree was restored. Why it matters. It is the leading statement on the date of effect of the amended Section 10, read with its 2024 review. Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi (2011) Facts. Under an agreement of 17 January 1981 for 24.95 acres at ₹3,75,000, the buyer paid ₹1,00,000 as advance and was to pay the balance of ₹2,75,000 in three instalments . The agreement said payment on the due dates was of the essence. He paid ₹1,25,000 of the balance and missed the rest. The sellers cancelled on 2 August 1981. Principle. Time for payment was of the essence, and the buyer was not ready and willing. Older cases holding time not of the essence in land sales "may no longer apply" because of steep rises in prices. The buyer got a refund with interest. (2011) 12 SCC 18 : AIR 2011 SC 3234. Why it matters. It links delay, price rise and Section 16(c). K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan (1997) Facts. On 15 December 1978 a buyer agreed to buy a house in Madurai for ₹60,000, to be completed in six months, and paid ₹5,000. He gave notice only on 11 July 1981 and sued on 23 August 1981, after prices had risen. Principle. A suit need not be decreed merely because it is within limitation. "Total inaction" for two and a half years, with a steep rise in prices, made relief inequitable . (1997) 3 SCC 1 : AIR 1997 SC 1751. Why it matters. It shows that a court looks at all circumstances, not only the limitation period. J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao (2010) Facts. The owners of 30 acres 86 cents agreed on 3 February 2006 to sell for ₹5,55,48,000 and received ₹75,00,000. The land was mortgaged to a bank for a sister concern's loan. The buyers deposited ₹2,45,00,000 in a bank and sued. Principle. The buyers proved readiness and willingness. Readiness refers to financial capacity; willingness refers to the conduct of the plaintiff wanting performance. The plaintiff need not tender the money unless the court directs. Civil Appeal Nos. 9821-9822 of 2010, decided 22 November 2010. Why it matters. It explains the two limbs of Section 16(c). N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao (1995) Facts. On 9 April 1979 a buyer agreed to buy a house in Madras for ₹2,30,000, paid ₹10,000 and was in possession as a tenant. He did not deposit ₹2,00,000 when the court directed it, and the lender he relied on had no cash. Principle. "Continuous readiness and willingness" is a condition precedent. The amount "must of necessity be proved to be available", judged by the plaintiff's conduct before and after the suit. The courts below rightly found him not ready and willing. (1995) 5 SCC 115 : AIR 1996 SC 116. Why it matters. It is a standard authority for readiness and willingness. K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd. (1999) Facts. In 1972 the owner of a bungalow at 6 Tolstoy Marg, New Delhi agreed to sell it to builders, who paid part of the price. The land was later caught by the urban land ceiling law and partly acquired. The builders sued in 1979. Principle. Performance would cause the seller hardship he did not foresee, so specific performance was refused. The buyers got the price paid back with 12% interest, and ₹3,25,000 as compensation under Section 21. Section 18 did not allow enforcement with a variation. (1999) 5 SCC 77 : AIR 1999 SC 2309. Why it matters. It shows compensation under Section 21 where performance is refused. Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Zaheer Khan (2006) Facts. A sports agency had a promotion agreement with the cricketer for 30 October 2000 to 29 October 2003. Clause 31(b) gave it a right to match third-party offers, which it said applied after the term. The cricketer signed with another agent, and the agency sought an injunction. Principle. At the interim stage, the Court held that a covenant restricting the cricketer after the term was a restraint of trade , hit by Section 27 of the Contract Act and void. The injunction would in substance be specific performance of a contract of personal service. The agency could be compensated in money. (2006) 4 SCC 227 : AIR 2006 SC 3426. Why it matters. It explains the bar on enforcing personal service contracts, now Section 14(c). Indian Oil Corporation v. Amritsar Gas Service (1991) Facts. Indian Oil terminated an LPG distributorship. The arbitrator ordered the distributorship to be restored. The agreement could be ended by either party on 30 days' notice. Principle. The agreement was revocable and for personal service, so it was determinable in nature and could not be specifically enforced. Restoration was contrary to Section 14(1). The only relief was compensation for the 30-day notice period. (1991) 1 SCC 533. Why it matters. It is the standard authority for determinable contracts, now Section 14(d).

selfTest.q: 2. What must the plaintiff prove under Section 16(c)?
selfTest.a: That he has performed, or has always been ready and willing to perform, the essential terms that are to be performed by him.

selfTest.q: 3. How much notice does Section 20 require before substituted performance?
selfTest.a: Written notice of not less than 30 days.

selfTest.q: 4. A seller owns 9.8 of the 10 acres he agreed to sell. Can the buyer get the 9.8 acres?
selfTest.a: Yes. The shortfall is small and can be compensated in money, so the court may order the sale of 9.8 acres with compensation for the rest (Section 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a court grant possession if the plaintiff asked only for specific performance?
selfTest.a: No. Section 22(2) requires possession to be specifically claimed, but the court shall allow the plaint to be amended at any stage.

selfTest.q: 6. Within what time must a suit for specific performance be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from the date fixed for performance, or, if none is fixed, from notice of refusal (Article 54).

law-of-contract-i-u5-t11.subtitle: Sections 38 and 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: A prohibitory injunction tells a person to stop doing something. A mandatory injunction tells him to do something, usually to undo what he has done. The first is the ordinary kind. The second is stronger, and the court grants it with more care. Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 covers the ordinary perpetual injunction. Section 39 covers the mandatory one. In exams, "Mandatory Injunction" is a short-note question. You must give Section 39, the difference from the prohibitory kind, and the test for interim relief. In real life, a prohibitory order stops a wall going up; a mandatory order makes the builder pull it down.
legalProvision: Section 38. Perpetual injunction when granted. (1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred to by this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. (2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in Chapter II. (3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.

Section 39. Mandatory injunctions. When, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts.

Section 40. Damages in lieu of, or in addition to, injunction. (1) The plaintiff in a suit for perpetual injunction under section 38, or mandatory injunction under section 39, may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction and the court may, if it thinks fit, award such damages. (2) No relief for damages shall be granted under this section unless the plaintiff has claimed such relief in his plaint: Provided that where no such damages have been claimed in the plaint, the court shall, at any stage of the proceedings, allow the plaintiff to amend the plaint on such terms as may be just for including such claim. (3) The dismissal of a suit to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff shall bar his right to sue for damages for such breach.
In simple words

Section 38: a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in the plaintiff's favour, and where the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to property, in the four cases listed. The Act does not use the word "prohibitory". Section 39: where, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts. Section 40: damages may be claimed in addition to, or in place of, an injunction under Section 38 or 39.
en.meaning:
A prohibitory injunction forbids an act. A mandatory injunction compels (forces) an act. Section 39 says the court may both "prevent the breach complained of" and "compel performance of the requisite acts". So a mandatory injunction has two parts: a restraint and a positive order. The question this topic answers. When will the court only say "do not", and when will it go further and say "do" or "undo"? Why the law has both. Stopping a wrong is not enough once the wrong is already in place. A wall already built across a passage keeps blocking it, even if the builder is forbidden to build more. Only an order to remove it gives real relief. But such an order can cost the defendant heavily, so the law asks for more before granting it. How the court decides. The decision tree shows how a court approaches a request for a mandatory injunction. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. If no, a prohibitory injunction under Section 38 is enough. Question 2: is the act one that the court is capable of enforcing (Section 39)? If no, the court cannot grant a mandatory injunction. Question 3: is the plaintiff asking for it only until the end of the suit, that is interim relief (Order XXXIX)? If no, the court decides at the hearing and may order it by decree. Question 4: does the plaintiff show a strong case, serious or irreparable injury, and a balance of convenience in his favour (Dorab Cawasji Warden)? If no, the interim mandatory injunction is refused. If all answers are yes, the court may grant an interim mandatory injunction to restore the last non-contested status or to undo an act illegally done.
keyPoints: Prohibitory: "do not" (Section 38). Mandatory: "do" or "undo" (Section 39). Section 39 needs a necessary act that the court is capable of enforcing. Interim mandatory injunction: strong case, serious or irreparable injury, balance of convenience ( Dorab Cawasji Warden ). It is granted to restore the last non-contested status or to undo an illegal act. Damages may be claimed with or instead of the injunction (Section 40).

caseLaws.name: Dorab Cawasji Warden v
caseLaws.facts: Coomi Sorab Warden (1990) Facts. The widow and sons of one brother sold their undivided half of "Dorab Villa", Bandra, to an outsider by a sale deed of 16 April 1987, and he was let into possession. The trial court granted an interim mandatory injunction against his remaining in possession, but a High Court single judge set it aside. Principle. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's order and told the respondents "to undo what they have done". Such an injunction needs a strong case, serious or irreparable injury and balance of convenience. It restores the last non-contested status or undoes an illegal act. Decided 13 February 1990; (1990) 2 SCC 117 : AIR 1990 SC 867. Why it matters. It is the Indian standard for interim mandatory relief. Redland Bricks Ltd. v. Morris (1970) Facts. A brick company's excavation on its own land caused the neighbours' land to slip, and a mandatory injunction was granted below requiring the company to restore support. Principle. A mandatory injunction is discretionary and is granted only on "a very strong probability" that grave danger will accrue to the plaintiff in the future. The order must tell the defendant "exactly in fact what he has to do". The House of Lords discharged the order, which did not do so. [1970] AC 652 (HL). Why it matters. It shows the caution courts use with mandatory orders. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two sites in Matwada, Warangal, were claimed under two lines of sale from one family: the plaintiffs bought from Rukminibai by deeds of 9 December 1968, and the defendants claimed through her brother. The plaintiffs sued only for a perpetual injunction. Principle. A bare injunction suit lies only where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and there is no real cloud on title (paras 11 and 12). (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It shows when a prohibitory injunction is the right remedy in a title dispute.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section deals with mandatory injunctions?
selfTest.a: Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

selfTest.q: 2. What two conditions does Section 39 set?
selfTest.a: The performance of the acts must be necessary to prevent the breach, and the acts must be ones the court is capable of enforcing.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the standard for an interim mandatory injunction?
selfTest.a: A strong case of a higher standard than prima facie, necessity to prevent serious or irreparable injury, and balance of convenience in the plaintiff's favour.

selfTest.q: 4. Why must a mandatory order be precise?
selfTest.a: So that the defendant knows exactly in fact what he has to do ( Redland Bricks ).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a mandatory injunction be temporary?
selfTest.a: Yes. It may be granted before trial (interim) or by the decree (perpetual, Section 37(2)).

legalProvision: Section 38. Perpetual injunction when granted. (1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred to by this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. (2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in Chapter II. (3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.

Section 39. Mandatory injunctions. When, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts.

Section 40. Damages in lieu of, or in addition to, injunction. (1) The plaintiff in a suit for perpetual injunction under section 38, or mandatory injunction under section 39, may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction and the court may, if it thinks fit, award such damages. (2) No relief for damages shall be granted under this section unless the plaintiff has claimed such relief in his plaint: Provided that where no such damages have been claimed in the plaint, the court shall, at any stage of the proceedings, allow the plaintiff to amend the plaint on such terms as may be just for including such claim. (3) The dismissal of a suit to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff shall bar his right to sue for damages for such breach.
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 38: వాదికి అనుకూలంగా ఉన్న బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపడానికి, ప్రతివాది వాది ఆస్తి హక్కును ఆక్రమిస్తే లేదా ఆక్రమిస్తానని బెదిరిస్తే చెప్పిన నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో, శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వవచ్చు. చట్టం "prohibitory" అనే పదం వాడదు. సెక్షన్ 39: బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపడానికి, కోర్టు అమలు చేయగల కొన్ని పనులను చేయమని బలవంతం చేయడం అవసరమైతే, కోర్టు తన విచక్షణతో ఫిర్యాదు చేసిన ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపే నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వవచ్చు, అవసరమైన పనులను చేయమని కూడా బలవంతం చేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 40: సెక్షన్ 38 లేదా 39 కింది నిషేధాజ్ఞతో పాటు, లేదా దానికి బదులుగా నష్టపరిహారం కోరవచ్చు.

నిషేధాత్మక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఒక పనిని నిషేధిస్తుంది. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఒక పనిని బలవంతంగా చేయిస్తుంది. కోర్టు "prevent the breach complained of", "compel performance of the requisite acts" రెండూ చేయవచ్చని సెక్షన్ 39 చెబుతుంది. కాబట్టి తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞకు రెండు భాగాలు: ఒక నిరోధం, ఒక సానుకూల ఆదేశం. ఈ అంశం జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు "చేయవద్దు" అని మాత్రమే చెబుతుంది, ఎప్పుడు ఇంకా ముందుకు వెళ్లి "చేయి" లేదా "రద్దు చేయి" అంటుంది? రెండూ ఎందుకు. తప్పు ఇప్పటికే జరిగి ఉంటే, దాన్ని ఆపితే సరిపోదు. దారికి అడ్డంగా ఇప్పటికే కట్టిన గోడ, బిల్డర్‌ను ఇంకా కట్టవద్దని నిషేధించినా, దారిని అడ్డుకుంటూనే ఉంటుంది. దాన్ని తొలగించమనే ఉత్తర్వే నిజమైన ఉపశమనం ఇస్తుంది. కానీ అలాంటి ఉత్తర్వు ప్రతివాదికి భారీ ఖర్చు కలిగించవచ్చు, కాబట్టి ఇచ్చే ముందు చట్టం ఎక్కువ అడుగుతుంది. కోర్టు ఎలా నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞ అభ్యర్థనను కోర్టు ఎలా పరిశీలిస్తుందో decision tree చూపుతుంది. selfTest.q: 1. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞల గురించి ఏ సెక్షన్ చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 39.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 39 ఏ రెండు షరతులు పెడుతుంది?
selfTest.a: పనులు చేయడం ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపడానికి అవసరం కావాలి, ఆ పనులను కోర్టు అమలు చేయగలగాలి.

selfTest.q: 3. మధ్యంతర తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞకు ప్రమాణం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: prima facie కంటే ఉన్నత ప్రమాణం గల బలమైన కేసు, తీవ్రమైన లేదా సరిచేయలేని హానిని నివారించాల్సిన అవసరం, వాదికి అనుకూలమైన సౌలభ్యం సమతుల్యత.

selfTest.q: 4. తప్పనిసరి ఉత్తర్వు ఎందుకు ఖచ్చితంగా ఉండాలి?
selfTest.a: ప్రతివాది తాను ఏమి చేయాలో ఖచ్చితంగా తెలుసుకోవడానికి ( Redland Bricks ).

selfTest.q: 5. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞ తాత్కాలికం కావచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. విచారణకు ముందు (మధ్యంతరం) గానీ, డిక్రీ ద్వారా (శాశ్వతం, సెక్షన్ 37(2)) గానీ ఇవ్వవచ్చు.
