law-of-contract-i-u5-t17.subtitle: Sections 10 to 14 and 17 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963; sections 32 and 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Two linked questions are asked together. First, which kinds of contract can the court enforce? Since 1 October 2018 the answer is almost all of them. Only the contracts listed in Sections 11(2), 14 and 17 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 are barred. Second, what if an event beyond a party's control stops it from performing? Floods, wars, strikes, government bans and pandemics can do this. A force majeure clause (Section 32 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) or Section 56 of the Contract Act then decides the result, and higher cost alone never counts. In exams, go through the kinds of contract one by one, with the section and an example. Then separate the clause route from the no-clause route, list what must be shown, and add the Covid-19 cases.
legalProvision: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 10. Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 11. Cases in which specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforceable. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, specific performance of a contract shall, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust. (2) A contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 12. Specific performance of part of contract. (1) Except as otherwise hereinafter provided in this section, the court shall not direct the specific performance of a part of a contract. (2) Where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, but the part which must be left unperformed be a only a small proportion to the whole in value and admits of compensation in money, the court may, at the suit of either party, direct the specific performance of so much of the contract as can be performed, and award compensation in money for the deficiency. (3) Where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, and the part which must be left unperformed either— (a) forms a considerable part of the whole, though admitting of compensation in money; or (b) does not admit of compensation in money; he is not entitled to obtain a decree for specific performance; but the court may, at the suit of the other party, direct the party in default to perform specifically so much of his part of the contract as he can perform, if the other party— (i) in a case falling under clause (a), pays or has paid the agreed consideration for the whole of the contract reduced by the consideration for the part which must be left unperformed and in a case falling under clause (b) pays or has paid the consideration for the whole of the contract without any abatement; and (ii) in either case, relinquishes all claims to the performance of the remaining part of the contract and all right to compensation, either for the deficiency or for the loss or damage sustained by him through the default of the defendant. (4) When a part of a contract which, taken by itself, can and ought to be specifically performed, stands on a separate and independent footing from another part of the same contract which cannot or ought not to be specifically performed, the court may direct specific performance of the former part. Explanation. —For the purposes of this section, a party to a contract shall be deemed to be unable to perform the whole of his part of it if a portion of its subject-matter existing at the date of the contract has ceased to exist at the time of its performance.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— (a) where a party to the contract has obtained substituted performance of contract in accordance with the provisions of section 20; (b) a contract, the performance of which involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 17. Contract to sell or let property by one who has no title, not specifically enforceable. (1) A contract to sell or let any immovable property cannot be specifically enforced in favour of a vendor or lessor— (a) who, knowing himself not to have any title to the property, has contracted to sell or let the property; (b) who, though he entered into the contract believing that he had a good title to the property, cannot at the time fixed by the parties or by the court for the completion of the sale or letting, give the purchaser or lessee a title free from reasonable doubt. (2) The provisions of sub-section (1) shall also apply, as far as may be, to contracts for the sale or hire of movable property. Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 32. Enforcement of contracts contingent on an event happening. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced by law unless and until that event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.

Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 56. Agreement to do impossible act. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. Contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful.—A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Compensation for loss through non-performance of act known to be impossible or unlawful.— Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or, with reasonable diligence, might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must make compensation to such promisee for any loss which such promisee sustains through the non- performance of the promise.

Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it.
In short:

Section 10: specific performance shall be enforced, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16. Section 11: a contract connected with a trust is enforced (Section 11(1)). A trustee 's contract in excess of his powers or in breach of trust is not (Section 11(2)). Section 12: part of a contract is enforced only in the cases the section lists. Section 14: not enforceable: (a) substituted performance obtained; (b) a continuous duty the court cannot supervise (watch over and direct); (c) so dependent on personal qualifications that the court cannot enforce its material terms; (d) a contract determinable (capable of being ended at will) in its nature. Section 17: a vendor (seller of property) or lessor with no title cannot enforce a contract to sell or let. Contract Act, Section 32: a contingent contract (one depending on an uncertain event) cannot be enforced until the event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contract Act, Section 56, second paragraph: a contract to do an act which later becomes impossible, or unlawful by an event the promisor could not prevent, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Contract Act, Section 65: a person who has received an advantage under a contract that becomes void must restore it or make compensation for it.
en.meaning:
A contract is specifically enforceable if no provision bars it and the plaintiff is not barred personally. The court therefore asks first about the kind of contract. The decision tree puts the questions in the order of the sections. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. A "No" answer sends you to the red result beside the box. If every answer is "Yes", you reach the green box. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Not a trustee's contract beyond
his powers or in breach of trust? (s. 11(2))"} Q1 -->|"No"| X1["Cannot be enforced"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"2. Plaintiff has not obtained
substituted performance? (s. 14(a))"} Q2 -->|"No"| X2["Cannot be enforced"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"3. No continuous duty the
court cannot supervise? (s. 14(b))"} Q3 -->|"No"| X3["Cannot be enforced"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4{"4. Not dependent on personal
qualifications? (s. 14(c))"} Q4 -->|"No"| X4["Cannot be enforced"] Q4 -->|"Yes"| Q5{"5. Not determinable
in its nature? (s. 14(d))"} Q5 -->|"No"| X5["Cannot be enforced"] Q5 -->|"Yes"| OK["The court shall enforce it (s. 10),
if the plaintiff clears s. 16"] style OK fill:#d9f2d9,stroke:#2e7d32 style X1 fill:#fde0e0,stroke:#c62828 style X2 fill:#fde0e0,stroke:#c62828 style X3 fill:#fde0e0,stroke:#c62828 style X4 fill:#fde0e0,stroke:#c62828 style X5 fill:#fde0e0,stroke:#c62828 Text description Step 1: is the contract free of Section 11(2), that is, not a trustee's contract in excess of his powers or in breach of trust? If no, it cannot be enforced. Step 2: has the plaintiff not already obtained substituted performance (Section 14(a))? If he has, it cannot be enforced. Step 3: does the contract avoid a continuous duty the court cannot supervise (Section 14(b))? If not, it cannot be enforced. Step 4: does it avoid dependence on the personal qualifications of a party (Section 14(c))? If not, it cannot be enforced. Step 5: is it free of being determinable in its nature (Section 14(d))? If not, it cannot be enforced. If every answer is yes, the contract is of a kind the court shall enforce (Section 10), provided the plaintiff clears the personal bars in Section 16. Is the contract free of Section 11(2), that is, it is not a trustee's contract in excess of his powers or in breach of trust? If no, it cannot be enforced. Has the plaintiff not already obtained substituted performance (Section 14(a))? If he has, it cannot be enforced. Does the contract avoid a continuous duty that the court cannot supervise (Section 14(b))? If not, it cannot be enforced. Does it avoid dependence on the personal qualifications of a party (Section 14(c))? If not, it cannot be enforced. Is it free of being determinable in its nature (Section 14(d))? If not, it cannot be enforced. If every answer is "yes", the contract is of a kind that the court shall enforce, provided the plaintiff clears the personal bars in Section 16. Force majeure is a French term meaning "superior force". In a contract, it is a clause that excuses or suspends performance when an extraordinary event (one beyond the ordinary), outside the parties' control, prevents it. The clause usually lists events, such as natural disasters, war, riots, strikes, epidemics and government orders, followed by general words such as "any other event beyond the reasonable control of the party". The Contract Act does not define the term. In Dhanrajamal Gobindram v. Shamji Kalidas and Co. (1961), the Supreme Court said: "The expression 'force majeure' is not a mere French version of the Latin expression ' vis major '." It is "a term of wider import". Vis major (an act of God) covers natural forces. Strikes and breakdown of machinery, which are normally not included in vis major, are included in force majeure. Was the event beyond the party's reasonable control? If no, the party could have prevented or avoided it, so there is no excuse. Did the event actually prevent performance? If no, the party may lose the protection. If all the tests are met, the effect is what the clause says. Under Section 56, the contract becomes void and advantages are restored (Section 65). The question this topic answers. Which contracts will a court order to be performed, and when does an event outside a party's control excuse it from performing? Why the law has this rule. Since 2018 the law treats performance as the normal remedy, so only contracts that a court cannot sensibly enforce are left out. Force majeure and frustration share the risk of events that no one could prevent, but they do not let a party escape a contract that has merely become a bad bargain.
keyPoints: After 2018, all contracts are enforceable except those barred by Section 11(2), Section 14 or Section 17. Land contracts are the standard case. Personal service, determinable and continuous-duty contracts are barred. Check the kind of contract first, then the plaintiff (Section 16). Force majeure is a clause. The Contract Act does not define it. Clause: Section 32. No clause: Section 56 ( Energy Watchdog ). Show: fit with the clause, beyond control, causal link, notice and mitigation. A rise in cost is hardship, not force majeure. Covid-19 was not an automatic excuse ( Standard Retail ; Halliburton ). Force majeure is wider than vis major ( Dhanrajamal Gobindram ).

caseLaws.name: Adcon Electronics v
caseLaws.facts: Daulat (2001) Facts. Buyers of Vithal Bhavan, Indore, under an agreement of 12 July 1986 for ₹53,75,000, sued in the Bombay High Court for specific performance, without claiming possession. Principle. A suit only for specific performance of a sale agreement is not a suit for land. Section 22(2) bars a decree for possession unless it is specifically claimed. (2001) 7 SCC 698 : AIR 2001 SC 3712. Why it matters. It shows how Section 22 shapes a suit on a land contract. Percept D'Mark v. Zaheer Khan (2006) Facts. A sports agency had a promotion agreement with a cricketer for 30 October 2000 to 29 October 2003, and claimed under clause 31(b) a right to match third-party offers after the term. Principle. Enforcing it would be "tantamount to ordering specific performance of this contract of personal services", which is barred. (2006) 4 SCC 227 : AIR 2006 SC 3426. Why it matters. It is the leading case for the personal-service bar. Indian Oil Corporation v. Amritsar Gas Service (1991) Facts. A distributorship agreement allowed either side to end it by thirty days' notice under clause 28. An arbitrator ordered the distributorship to be restored. Principle. The agreement was determinable in its nature and could not be specifically enforced (Section 14). The only relief was compensation for the 30-day notice period. (1991) 1 SCC 533. Why it matters. It is the standard authority for Section 14(d). Energy Watchdog v. CERC (2017) Facts. Adani Power won bids in 2007 to supply power at non-escalable energy charges. It said that a change in Indonesian law in 2010 and 2011 raised coal prices. Principle. Force majeure is governed by the Contract Act: Section 32 where there is a clause, Section 56 outside the contract (para 32). A rise in the price of coal is neither frustration nor force majeure (paras 38, 40). (2017) 14 SCC 80. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's leading modern statement of the law. Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur (1953) Facts. A land company agreed to sell plots after building roads and drains. During the war, the Government requisitioned part of the land. The company pleaded frustration. Principle. "Impossible" in Section 56 is read in a practical, not a literal, sense. A contract with its own term for discharge falls under Section 32. The requisition was temporary, so the contract was not frustrated. [1954] SCR 310 : AIR 1954 SC 44. Why it matters. It settles the meaning of impossibility in India. Taylor v. Caldwell (1863) Facts. The Surrey Gardens music hall, hired for four concert days at £100 a day, burned down before the concerts. Principle. The contract was discharged because the thing on which it depended was destroyed without fault. (1863) 3 B & S 826. Why it matters. It is the origin of the doctrine in Section 56. Dhanrajamal Gobindram v. Shamji Kalidas and Co. (1961) Facts. A contract for 500 bales of African raw cotton at ₹1,401 a candy was "subject to the usual Force Majeure Clause". The buyers said the contract was void for vagueness. Principle. "Force majeure" is "not a mere French version" of vis major. It is "a term of wider import" and includes strikes. The contract was not void, and the appeal was dismissed. AIR 1961 SC 1285 : [1961] 3 SCR 1029. Why it matters. It supports a wide reading of force majeure. Halliburton Offshore Services Inc. v. Vedanta Ltd. (2020) Facts. A contractor relied on the lockdown to stop the encashment of bank guarantees. An ad interim order of 20 April 2020 was vacated on 29 May 2020 (Delhi High Court). Principle. "The Contractor in this case was in breach in September, 2019 itself." Past non-performance "cannot be condoned due to the COVID-19 lockdown". O.M.P.(I)(COMM.) 88/2020. Why it matters. It shows that Covid-19 is not an automatic excuse.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a contract of personal service be specifically enforced?
selfTest.a: No. Section 14(c) bars it.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case holds that a distributorship terminable on notice cannot be enforced?
selfTest.a: Indian Oil Corporation v. Amritsar Gas Service (1991).

selfTest.q: 4. Which section governs a force majeure clause in a contract?
selfTest.a: Section 32 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, read with Chapter III on contingent contracts ( Energy Watchdog ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a sharp rise in the price of inputs force majeure?
selfTest.a: No. It is commercial hardship ( Energy Watchdog ).

selfTest.q: 6. What four things must a party relying on force majeure usually show?
selfTest.a: That the event fits the clause, was beyond reasonable control, actually prevented performance, and that notice and mitigation were given.

legalProvision: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 10. Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 11. Cases in which specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforceable. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, specific performance of a contract shall, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust. (2) A contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 12. Specific performance of part of contract. (1) Except as otherwise hereinafter provided in this section, the court shall not direct the specific performance of a part of a contract. (2) Where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, but the part which must be left unperformed be a only a small proportion to the whole in value and admits of compensation in money, the court may, at the suit of either party, direct the specific performance of so much of the contract as can be performed, and award compensation in money for the deficiency. (3) Where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, and the part which must be left unperformed either— (a) forms a considerable part of the whole, though admitting of compensation in money; or (b) does not admit of compensation in money; he is not entitled to obtain a decree for specific performance; but the court may, at the suit of the other party, direct the party in default to perform specifically so much of his part of the contract as he can perform, if the other party— (i) in a case falling under clause (a), pays or has paid the agreed consideration for the whole of the contract reduced by the consideration for the part which must be left unperformed and in a case falling under clause (b) pays or has paid the consideration for the whole of the contract without any abatement; and (ii) in either case, relinquishes all claims to the performance of the remaining part of the contract and all right to compensation, either for the deficiency or for the loss or damage sustained by him through the default of the defendant. (4) When a part of a contract which, taken by itself, can and ought to be specifically performed, stands on a separate and independent footing from another part of the same contract which cannot or ought not to be specifically performed, the court may direct specific performance of the former part. Explanation. —For the purposes of this section, a party to a contract shall be deemed to be unable to perform the whole of his part of it if a portion of its subject-matter existing at the date of the contract has ceased to exist at the time of its performance.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— (a) where a party to the contract has obtained substituted performance of contract in accordance with the provisions of section 20; (b) a contract, the performance of which involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 17. Contract to sell or let property by one who has no title, not specifically enforceable. (1) A contract to sell or let any immovable property cannot be specifically enforced in favour of a vendor or lessor— (a) who, knowing himself not to have any title to the property, has contracted to sell or let the property; (b) who, though he entered into the contract believing that he had a good title to the property, cannot at the time fixed by the parties or by the court for the completion of the sale or letting, give the purchaser or lessee a title free from reasonable doubt. (2) The provisions of sub-section (1) shall also apply, as far as may be, to contracts for the sale or hire of movable property. Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 32. Enforcement of contracts contingent on an event happening. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced by law unless and until that event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.

Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 56. Agreement to do impossible act. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. Contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful.—A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Compensation for loss through non-performance of act known to be impossible or unlawful.— Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or, with reasonable diligence, might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must make compensation to such promisee for any loss which such promisee sustains through the non- performance of the promise.

Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it.
సంక్షిప్తంగా:

సెక్షన్ 10: సెక్షన్ 11(2), సెక్షన్ 14, సెక్షన్ 16 కు లోబడి కోర్టు నిర్దిష్ట అమలు చేయిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 11: ట్రస్టుకు సంబంధించిన కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 11(1)). తన అధికారాలకు మించి లేదా ట్రస్టును ఉల్లంఘించి ట్రస్టీ చేసిన కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయించరు (సెక్షన్ 11(2)). సెక్షన్ 12: కాంట్రాక్టులో కొంత భాగాన్ని ఆ సెక్షన్ చెప్పిన సందర్భాల్లో మాత్రమే అమలు చేయిస్తారు. సెక్షన్ 14: అమలు చేయించలేనివి: (a) ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు ఇప్పటికే పొందినప్పుడు; (b) కోర్టు పర్యవేక్షించలేని (గమనిస్తూ ఆదేశాలు ఇవ్వలేని) నిరంతర బాధ్యత; (c) పక్షాల వ్యక్తిగత అర్హతలపై ఎంతగా ఆధారపడిందంటే దాని ముఖ్య నిబంధనలను కోర్టు అమలు చేయించలేని కాంట్రాక్టు; (d) స్వభావరీత్యా రద్దు చేయదగిన (ఇష్టం వచ్చినప్పుడు ముగించగల) కాంట్రాక్టు. సెక్షన్ 17: హక్కు (title) లేని అమ్మకందారు (ఆస్తి అమ్మే వ్యక్తి) లేదా కౌలుకు ఇచ్చే వ్యక్తి అమ్మకం లేదా కౌలు కాంట్రాక్టును అమలు చేయించలేడు. కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 32: షరతులతో కూడిన కాంట్రాక్టు (అనిశ్చిత సంఘటనపై ఆధారపడినది) ఆ సంఘటన జరిగే వరకు అమలు కాదు. ఆ సంఘటన అసాధ్యమైతే కాంట్రాక్టు చెల్లనిది (void) అవుతుంది. కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 56, రెండో పేరా: ఒక పనిని చేయాలన్న కాంట్రాక్టు, తర్వాత ఆ పని అసాధ్యమైనప్పుడు, లేదా వాగ్దానం చేసిన వ్యక్తి ఆపలేని సంఘటనతో చట్టవిరుద్ధమైనప్పుడు, చెల్లనిది అవుతుంది. కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 65: చెల్లనిదిగా మారిన కాంట్రాక్టు కింద ప్రయోజనం పొందిన వ్యక్తి దాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి, లేదా దానికి పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి.

క్లాజు లేకపోతే, ఆ సంఘటన పనిని అసాధ్యం లేదా చట్టవిరుద్ధం చేస్తుందా (సెక్షన్ 56)? కాకపోతే, మినహాయింపు లేదు. ఆ సంఘటన ఆ పక్షం సహేతుక నియంత్రణకు బయట ఉందా? లేకపోతే, ఆ పక్షం దాన్ని ఆపగలిగేవాడు లేదా తప్పించుకోగలిగేవాడు, కాబట్టి మినహాయింపు లేదు. ఆ సంఘటన నిజంగా నెరవేర్పును ఆపిందా? అది నెరవేర్పును కష్టతరం లేదా ఖరీదైనదిగా మాత్రమే చేస్తే, అది కష్టం (hardship) మాత్రమే, మినహాయింపు లేదు. క్లాజు కోరిన నోటీసు ఇచ్చి, ప్రభావాన్ని తగ్గించడానికి సహేతుక చర్యలు తీసుకున్నాడా? లేకపోతే, ఆ రక్షణ కోల్పోవచ్చు. అన్ని పరీక్షలు నెరవేరితే, ఫలితం క్లాజు చెప్పినట్లు ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 56 కింద కాంట్రాక్టు చెల్లనిది అవుతుంది, పొందిన ప్రయోజనాలు తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి (సెక్షన్ 65). ఈ అంశం జవాబిచ్చే ప్రశ్న. కోర్టు ఏ కాంట్రాక్టులను నెరవేర్చమని ఆదేశిస్తుంది, ఒక పక్షం నియంత్రణకు బయటి సంఘటన అతన్ని నెరవేర్చడం నుంచి ఎప్పుడు మినహాయిస్తుంది? చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. 2018 నుంచి చట్టం నెరవేర్పునే మామూలు పరిహారంగా చూస్తుంది; కోర్టు సమంజసంగా అమలు చేయించలేని కాంట్రాక్టులను మాత్రమే వదిలేస్తుంది. ఎవరూ ఆపలేని సంఘటనల నష్టాన్ని ఫోర్స్ మెజ్యూర్, ఫ్రస్ట్రేషన్ పంచుతాయి; కానీ కేవలం నష్టదాయక బేరంగా మారిన కాంట్రాక్టు నుంచి తప్పించుకోవడానికి అవి అనుమతించవు.

hi.inOneMinute: Two linked questions are asked together. First, which kinds of contract can the court enforce? Since 1 October 2018 the answer is almost all of them. Only the contracts listed in Sections 11(2), 14 and 17 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 are barred. Second, what if an event beyond a party's control stops it from performing? Floods, wars, strikes, government bans and pandemics can do this. A force majeure clause (Section 32 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) or Section 56 of the Contract Act then decides the result, and higher cost alone never counts. In exams, go through the kinds of contract one by one, with the section and an example. Then separate the clause route from the no-clause route, list what must be shown, and add the Covid-19 cases.
legalProvision: Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 10. Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 11. Cases in which specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforceable. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, specific performance of a contract shall, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust. (2) A contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 12. Specific performance of part of contract. (1) Except as otherwise hereinafter provided in this section, the court shall not direct the specific performance of a part of a contract. (2) Where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, but the part which must be left unperformed be a only a small proportion to the whole in value and admits of compensation in money, the court may, at the suit of either party, direct the specific performance of so much of the contract as can be performed, and award compensation in money for the deficiency. (3) Where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, and the part which must be left unperformed either— (a) forms a considerable part of the whole, though admitting of compensation in money; or (b) does not admit of compensation in money; he is not entitled to obtain a decree for specific performance; but the court may, at the suit of the other party, direct the party in default to perform specifically so much of his part of the contract as he can perform, if the other party— (i) in a case falling under clause (a), pays or has paid the agreed consideration for the whole of the contract reduced by the consideration for the part which must be left unperformed and in a case falling under clause (b) pays or has paid the consideration for the whole of the contract without any abatement; and (ii) in either case, relinquishes all claims to the performance of the remaining part of the contract and all right to compensation, either for the deficiency or for the loss or damage sustained by him through the default of the defendant. (4) When a part of a contract which, taken by itself, can and ought to be specifically performed, stands on a separate and independent footing from another part of the same contract which cannot or ought not to be specifically performed, the court may direct specific performance of the former part. Explanation. —For the purposes of this section, a party to a contract shall be deemed to be unable to perform the whole of his part of it if a portion of its subject-matter existing at the date of the contract has ceased to exist at the time of its performance.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— (a) where a party to the contract has obtained substituted performance of contract in accordance with the provisions of section 20; (b) a contract, the performance of which involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 17. Contract to sell or let property by one who has no title, not specifically enforceable. (1) A contract to sell or let any immovable property cannot be specifically enforced in favour of a vendor or lessor— (a) who, knowing himself not to have any title to the property, has contracted to sell or let the property; (b) who, though he entered into the contract believing that he had a good title to the property, cannot at the time fixed by the parties or by the court for the completion of the sale or letting, give the purchaser or lessee a title free from reasonable doubt. (2) The provisions of sub-section (1) shall also apply, as far as may be, to contracts for the sale or hire of movable property. Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 32. Enforcement of contracts contingent on an event happening. Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced by law unless and until that event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.

Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 56. Agreement to do impossible act. An agreement to do an act impossible in itself is void. Contract to do an act afterwards becoming impossible or unlawful.—A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Compensation for loss through non-performance of act known to be impossible or unlawful.— Where one person has promised to do something which he knew, or, with reasonable diligence, might have known, and which the promisee did not know, to be impossible or unlawful, such promisor must make compensation to such promisee for any loss which such promisee sustains through the non- performance of the promise.

Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it.
In short:

Section 10: specific performance shall be enforced, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16. Section 11: a contract connected with a trust is enforced (Section 11(1)). A trustee 's contract in excess of his powers or in breach of trust is not (Section 11(2)). Section 12: part of a contract is enforced only in the cases the section lists. Section 14: not enforceable: (a) substituted performance obtained; (b) a continuous duty the court cannot supervise (watch over and direct); (c) so dependent on personal qualifications that the court cannot enforce its material terms; (d) a contract determinable (capable of being ended at will) in its nature. Section 17: a vendor (seller of property) or lessor with no title cannot enforce a contract to sell or let. Contract Act, Section 32: a contingent contract (one depending on an uncertain event) cannot be enforced until the event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, the contract becomes void. Contract Act, Section 56, second paragraph: a contract to do an act which later becomes impossible, or unlawful by an event the promisor could not prevent, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful. Contract Act, Section 65: a person who has received an advantage under a contract that becomes void must restore it or make compensation for it.

Force majeure is a French term meaning "superior force". In a contract, it is a clause that excuses or suspends performance when an extraordinary event (one beyond the ordinary), outside the parties' control, prevents it. The clause usually lists events, such as natural disasters, war, riots, strikes, epidemics and government orders, followed by general words such as "any other event beyond the reasonable control of the party". The Contract Act does not define the term. In Dhanrajamal Gobindram v. Shamji Kalidas and Co. (1961), the Supreme Court said: "The expression 'force majeure' is not a mere French version of the Latin expression ' vis major '." It is "a term of wider import". Vis major (an act of God) covers natural forces. Strikes and breakdown of machinery, which are normally not included in vis major, are included in force majeure. The question this topic answers. Which contracts will a court order to be performed, and when does an event outside a party's control excuse it from performing? Why the law has this rule. Since 2018 the law treats performance as the normal remedy, so only contracts that a court cannot sensibly enforce are left out. Force majeure and frustration share the risk of events that no one could prevent, but they do not let a party escape a contract that has merely become a bad bargain.
keyPoints: After 2018, all contracts are enforceable except those barred by Section 11(2), Section 14 or Section 17. Land contracts are the standard case. Personal service, determinable and continuous-duty contracts are barred. Check the kind of contract first, then the plaintiff (Section 16). Force majeure is a clause. The Contract Act does not define it. Clause: Section 32. No clause: Section 56 ( Energy Watchdog ). Show: fit with the clause, beyond control, causal link, notice and mitigation. A rise in cost is hardship, not force majeure. Covid-19 was not an automatic excuse ( Standard Retail ; Halliburton ). Force majeure is wider than vis major ( Dhanrajamal Gobindram ).

caseLaws.name: Adcon Electronics v
caseLaws.facts: Daulat (2001) Facts. Buyers of Vithal Bhavan, Indore, under an agreement of 12 July 1986 for ₹53,75,000, sued in the Bombay High Court for specific performance, without claiming possession. Principle. A suit only for specific performance of a sale agreement is not a suit for land. Section 22(2) bars a decree for possession unless it is specifically claimed. (2001) 7 SCC 698 : AIR 2001 SC 3712. Why it matters. It shows how Section 22 shapes a suit on a land contract. Percept D'Mark v. Zaheer Khan (2006) Facts. A sports agency had a promotion agreement with a cricketer for 30 October 2000 to 29 October 2003, and claimed under clause 31(b) a right to match third-party offers after the term. Principle. Enforcing it would be "tantamount to ordering specific performance of this contract of personal services", which is barred. (2006) 4 SCC 227 : AIR 2006 SC 3426. Why it matters. It is the leading case for the personal-service bar. Indian Oil Corporation v. Amritsar Gas Service (1991) Facts. A distributorship agreement allowed either side to end it by thirty days' notice under clause 28. An arbitrator ordered the distributorship to be restored. Principle. The agreement was determinable in its nature and could not be specifically enforced (Section 14). The only relief was compensation for the 30-day notice period. (1991) 1 SCC 533. Why it matters. It is the standard authority for Section 14(d). Energy Watchdog v. CERC (2017) Facts. Adani Power won bids in 2007 to supply power at non-escalable energy charges. It said that a change in Indonesian law in 2010 and 2011 raised coal prices. Principle. Force majeure is governed by the Contract Act: Section 32 where there is a clause, Section 56 outside the contract (para 32). A rise in the price of coal is neither frustration nor force majeure (paras 38, 40). (2017) 14 SCC 80. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's leading modern statement of the law. Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur (1953) Facts. A land company agreed to sell plots after building roads and drains. During the war, the Government requisitioned part of the land. The company pleaded frustration. Principle. "Impossible" in Section 56 is read in a practical, not a literal, sense. A contract with its own term for discharge falls under Section 32. The requisition was temporary, so the contract was not frustrated. [1954] SCR 310 : AIR 1954 SC 44. Why it matters. It settles the meaning of impossibility in India. Taylor v. Caldwell (1863) Facts. The Surrey Gardens music hall, hired for four concert days at £100 a day, burned down before the concerts. Principle. The contract was discharged because the thing on which it depended was destroyed without fault. (1863) 3 B & S 826. Why it matters. It is the origin of the doctrine in Section 56. Dhanrajamal Gobindram v. Shamji Kalidas and Co. (1961) Facts. A contract for 500 bales of African raw cotton at ₹1,401 a candy was "subject to the usual Force Majeure Clause". The buyers said the contract was void for vagueness. Principle. "Force majeure" is "not a mere French version" of vis major. It is "a term of wider import" and includes strikes. The contract was not void, and the appeal was dismissed. AIR 1961 SC 1285 : [1961] 3 SCR 1029. Why it matters. It supports a wide reading of force majeure. Halliburton Offshore Services Inc. v. Vedanta Ltd. (2020) Facts. A contractor relied on the lockdown to stop the encashment of bank guarantees. An ad interim order of 20 April 2020 was vacated on 29 May 2020 (Delhi High Court). Principle. "The Contractor in this case was in breach in September, 2019 itself." Past non-performance "cannot be condoned due to the COVID-19 lockdown". O.M.P.(I)(COMM.) 88/2020. Why it matters. It shows that Covid-19 is not an automatic excuse.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a contract of personal service be specifically enforced?
selfTest.a: No. Section 14(c) bars it.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case holds that a distributorship terminable on notice cannot be enforced?
selfTest.a: Indian Oil Corporation v. Amritsar Gas Service (1991).

selfTest.q: 4. Which section governs a force majeure clause in a contract?
selfTest.a: Section 32 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, read with Chapter III on contingent contracts ( Energy Watchdog ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a sharp rise in the price of inputs force majeure?
selfTest.a: No. It is commercial hardship ( Energy Watchdog ).

selfTest.q: 6. What four things must a party relying on force majeure usually show?
selfTest.a: That the event fits the clause, was beyond reasonable control, actually prevented performance, and that notice and mitigation were given.

family-law-i-u1-t2.subtitle: Who is governed by the Hindu Acts: section 2 and the three groups of persons

en.inOneMinute: The four Hindu Acts do not define "Hindu" in one sentence. They list who is covered. Three groups are covered: Hindus by religion in any form; Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs; and any other person who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew, unless it is proved that Hindu law would not have governed that person. An Explanation adds children and converts. A child of two Hindu parents is a Hindu; a child of one Hindu parent is a Hindu if brought up in that parent's community or family; a convert or re-convert is a Hindu. Members of Scheduled Tribes are outside the Acts unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. Exams ask for the three groups, the Explanation, the Scheduled Tribe exclusion, the meaning of Hindu religion ( Yagnapurushdasji ), and the effect of conversion on a Hindu marriage ( Sarla Mudgal , Lily Thomas ).
legalProvision: The same application section appears in all four Acts. It is Section 2 of the Hindu Marriage Act, the Hindu Succession Act and the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, and Section 3 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act. The Hindu Marriage Act text is quoted.

Section 2, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Application of Act. (1) This Act applies— (a) to any person who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms or developments, including a Virashaiva, a Lingayat or a follower of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj, (b) to any person who is a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion, and (c) to any other person domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion, unless it is proved that any such person would not have been governed by the Hindu law or by any custom or usage as part of that law in respect of any of the matters dealt with herein if this Act had not been passed. Explanation. —The following persons are Hindus, Buddhists, Jainas or Sikhs by religion, as the case may be:— (a) any child, legitimate or illegitimate, both of whose parents are Hindus, Buddhists, Jainas or Sikhs by religion; (b) any child, legitimate or illegitimate, one of whose parents is a Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion and who is brought up as a member of the tribe, community, group or family to which such parent belongs or belonged; and (c) any person who is a convert or re-convert to the Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh religion. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), nothing contained in this Act shall apply to the members of any Scheduled Tribe within the meaning of clause (25) of article 366 of the Constitution unless the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, otherwise directs. (3) The expression "Hindu" in any portion of this Act shall be construed as if it included a person who, though not a Hindu by religion, is, nevertheless, a person to whom this Act applies by virtue of the provisions contained in this section.
Section 1(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. It extends to the whole of India, and applies also to Hindus domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends who are outside the said territories.

Explanation (bb), Section 2, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. any child, legitimate or illegitimate, who has been abandoned both by his father and mother or whose parentage is not known and who in either case is brought up as a Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh;
In simple words

Clause (a): a Hindu by religion in any form or development, including a Virashaiva, a Lingayat, and a follower of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj. Clause (b): a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion. Clause (c): anyone else who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew. He is covered unless someone proves that, without the Act, Hindu law or Hindu custom would not have governed him. The Marriage Act and the Minority and Guardianship Act add that he must be domiciled in the territories to which the Act extends. The Succession Act and the Adoptions and Maintenance Act do not have this domicile condition. Explanation: children of two Hindu (or Buddhist, Jaina, Sikh) parents; children of one such parent brought up in that parent's tribe, community, group or family; and converts or re-converts. Sub-section (2): members of a Scheduled Tribe are outside the Act unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. Sub-section (3): wherever the Act says "Hindu", it includes a person who is not a Hindu by religion but to whom the Act applies under this section. Section 1(2): the Marriage Act covers the whole of India, and also Hindus domiciled in India who live outside it. The Minority and Guardianship Act has the same clause. Explanation (bb), Adoptions and Maintenance Act only: an abandoned child, or a child of unknown parentage, brought up as a Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh.
en.meaning:
Scope means the reach of Hindu law: to whom, and where, it applies. Application means the test a court uses to decide whether a particular person is governed by the Hindu Acts. The Acts do not define "Hindu" in a positive sentence. They list who is covered and then use a residuary (left-over) group that works by exclusion. This keeps the law wide: anyone without another personal law of marriage and succession falls under Hindu law. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Section 2(1) covers three groups; Scheduled Tribes are outside unless notified. flowchart TD S["Section 2(1): the Act applies to"] S --> A["(a) Hindus by religion in any form
incl. Virashaiva, Lingayat,
Brahmo, Prarthana, Arya Samaj"] S --> B["(b) Buddhists, Jainas, Sikhs"] S --> C["(c) Anyone not Muslim, Christian,
Parsi or Jew, unless proved
outside Hindu law or custom"] X["Section 2(2): Scheduled Tribes
outside unless notified"] S -.-> X Text description Section 2(1) applies the Act to (a) Hindus by religion in any form, including Virashaiva, Lingayat, Brahmo, Prarthana and Arya Samaj; (b) Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs; (c) any other person who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew, unless proved outside Hindu law or custom. Section 2(2) excludes Scheduled Tribes unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. The question this topic answers. Is this person governed by the Hindu Acts? If yes, the Hindu Marriage Act decides the validity of his marriage, the Hindu Succession Act decides who inherits from him, and so on. Why the law has this rule. Before 1955, Hindu law applied to a person because of religion and custom. The Acts kept that wide reach, brought in Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs, who had always been governed by Hindu law in family matters, and left out only those with their own personal laws.
keyPoints: Section 2(1) covers Hindus by religion, Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs, and a residuary group. The residuary group is anyone not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew, unless proved outside Hindu law or custom. The Explanation covers children of two Hindu parents, children of one Hindu parent brought up in that parent's group, and converts. Scheduled Tribes are excluded unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. Hindu religion "may broadly be described as a way of life and nothing more" ( Yagnapurushadji ). Conversion does not end a Hindu marriage; a second marriage is void ( Sarla Mudgal , Lily Thomas ). Domicile in clause (c) only in the Marriage and Minority-Guardianship Acts; clause (bb) only in the Adoptions and Maintenance Act. A migrating family carries its personal law with it unless it adopts the new law (Mulla, section 14).

caseLaws.name: Sastri Yagnapurushadji v
caseLaws.facts: Muldas Bhudardas Vaishya (1966) Facts. Followers of the Swaminarayan sect (Satsangis) sued for a declaration that the temple entry law did not apply to their temples, because their religion was distinct from Hindu religion, and to keep non-Satsangi Harijans out. Principle. Hindu religion "may broadly be described as a way of life and nothing more"; Tilak's formula was accepted; the Swaminarayan sect is not distinct from Hindu religion, so its temples fell within the 1956 Act. Appeal dismissed with costs. AIR 1966 SC 1119 : (1966) 3 SCR 242. Why it matters. It is the leading case on what Hindu religion means and why the Acts are drawn so widely. Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) Facts. Hindu husbands with living wives converted to Islam and married again. Principle. Conversion does not dissolve the Hindu marriage. The second marriage without dissolving the first is void in terms of Section 494 IPC, and the husband is guilty of that offence. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It shows that leaving Hinduism does not take a person out of an existing Hindu marriage. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) Facts. Sushmita Ghosh, married by Hindu rites in 1984, said her husband told her in 1992 that he had embraced Islam, asked her to agree to a divorce, and planned to marry another woman. Review of Sarla Mudgal was also sought. Principle. Conversion "does not automatically dissolve a marriage already solemnized under the Hindu Marriage Act. It only provides a ground for divorce under Section 13." A second marriage is void and punishable under Section 494 IPC. Sarla Mudgal gave no direction to enact a common civil code. (2000) 6 SCC 224 : AIR 2000 SC 1650. Why it matters. It confirms Sarla Mudgal and settles the effect of conversion.

selfTest.q: 1. Are Sikhs and Jainas Hindus by religion?
selfTest.a: No. The Acts apply to them under clause (b), and sub-section (3) reads "Hindu" to include them.

selfTest.q: 2. Which sub-section excludes Scheduled Tribes?
selfTest.a: Section 2(2) (Section 3(2) of the Minority and Guardianship Act).

selfTest.q: 3. Which case describes Hindu religion as a way of life?
selfTest.a: Sastri Yagnapurushadji v. Muldas Bhudardas Vaishya (1966).

selfTest.q: 4. Does a husband's conversion to Islam end his Hindu marriage?
selfTest.a: No. It gives the wife a ground for divorce under Section 13(1)(ii). The marriage continues until a decree, and a second marriage is void.

selfTest.q: 5. A child has one Hindu parent and one Christian parent. When is the child a Hindu?
selfTest.a: When brought up as a member of the tribe, community, group or family of the Hindu parent (Explanation (b)).

selfTest.q: 6. Which Act covers an abandoned child brought up as a Hindu?
selfTest.a: The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, Explanation (bb) to Section 2.

క్లాజ్ (a): ఏ రూపంలోనైనా, ఏ వికాసంలోనైనా మతం ప్రకారం హిందువు; వీరశైవ, లింగాయత, బ్రహ్మ, ప్రార్థన, ఆర్య సమాజ అనుచరులు కూడా. క్లాజ్ (b): మతం ప్రకారం బౌద్ధుడు, జైనుడు, సిక్కు. క్లాజ్ (c): ముస్లిం, క్రైస్తవ, పార్సీ, యూదు కాని ఇతర ఎవరైనా. చట్టం లేకపోతే హిందూ చట్టం గానీ హిందూ ఆచారం గానీ అతన్ని పాలించేది కాదని ఎవరైనా రుజువు చేస్తే తప్ప అతను కవర్ అవుతాడు. వివాహ చట్టం, మైనారిటీ-సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టం అతను చట్టం విస్తరించిన భూభాగాల్లో డొమిసైల్ (శాశ్వత నివాసం) కలిగి ఉండాలని చేరుస్తాయి. వారసత్వ చట్టం, దత్తత-భరణ చట్టాలలో ఈ డొమిసైల్ షరతు లేదు. Explanation: ఇద్దరు హిందూ (లేదా బౌద్ధ, జైన, సిక్కు) తల్లిదండ్రుల పిల్లలు; అలాంటి ఒక తల్లి/తండ్రి పిల్లలు, ఆ తల్లి/తండ్రి తెగ, సమాజం, గుంపు లేదా కుటుంబంలో పెరిగితే; మతం మారినవారు లేదా తిరిగి వచ్చినవారు. ఉప-సెక్షన్ (2): కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం వేరే విధంగా నోటిఫై చేస్తే తప్ప, షెడ్యూల్డ్ తెగ సభ్యులు చట్టం బయట ఉంటారు. ఉప-సెక్షన్ (3): చట్టం "హిందువు" అన్న ప్రతిచోటా, మతం ప్రకారం హిందువు కాకపోయినా ఈ సెక్షన్ కింద చట్టం వర్తించే వ్యక్తి కూడా అందులో ఉంటాడు. సెక్షన్ 1(2): వివాహ చట్టం భారతదేశమంతటికీ, అలాగే భారతదేశంలో డొమిసైల్ ఉండి బయట నివసించే హిందువులకూ వర్తిస్తుంది. మైనారిటీ-సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టంలోనూ ఇదే క్లాజ్ ఉంది. Explanation (bb), దత్తత-భరణ చట్టంలో మాత్రమే: వదిలివేయబడిన బిడ్డ, లేదా తల్లిదండ్రులు తెలియని బిడ్డ, హిందువుగా, బౌద్ధుడిగా, జైనుడిగా లేదా సిక్కుగా పెరిగితే.

selfTest.q: 2. ఏ ఉప-సెక్షన్ షెడ్యూల్డ్ తెగలను మినహాయిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 2(2) (మైనారిటీ-సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టంలో సెక్షన్ 3(2)).

selfTest.q: 3. హిందూ మతాన్ని జీవన విధానంగా ఏ కేసు వర్ణిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: Sastri Yagnapurushadji v. Muldas Bhudardas Vaishya (1966).

selfTest.q: 4. భర్త ఇస్లాంలోకి మారితే అతని హిందూ వివాహం ముగుస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అది సెక్షన్ 13(1)(ii) కింద భార్యకు విడాకుల కారణం ఇస్తుంది. డిక్రీ వచ్చే వరకు వివాహం కొనసాగుతుంది, రెండవ పెళ్లి శూన్యం.

selfTest.q: 5. ఒక బిడ్డకు ఒక హిందూ, ఒక క్రైస్తవ తల్లి/తండ్రి ఉన్నారు. ఆ బిడ్డ ఎప్పుడు హిందువు?

selfTest.q: 6. హిందువుగా పెరిగిన వదిలివేయబడిన బిడ్డను ఏ చట్టం కవర్ చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: హిందూ దత్తత మరియు భరణ చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 2 Explanation (bb).

hi.inOneMinute: The four Hindu Acts do not define "Hindu" in one sentence. They list who is covered. Three groups are covered: Hindus by religion in any form; Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs; and any other person who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew, unless it is proved that Hindu law would not have governed that person. An Explanation adds children and converts. A child of two Hindu parents is a Hindu; a child of one Hindu parent is a Hindu if brought up in that parent's community or family; a convert or re-convert is a Hindu. Members of Scheduled Tribes are outside the Acts unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. Exams ask for the three groups, the Explanation, the Scheduled Tribe exclusion, the meaning of Hindu religion ( Yagnapurushdasji ), and the effect of conversion on a Hindu marriage ( Sarla Mudgal , Lily Thomas ).
legalProvision: The same application section appears in all four Acts. It is Section 2 of the Hindu Marriage Act, the Hindu Succession Act and the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, and Section 3 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act. The Hindu Marriage Act text is quoted.

Section 2, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Application of Act. (1) This Act applies— (a) to any person who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms or developments, including a Virashaiva, a Lingayat or a follower of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj, (b) to any person who is a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion, and (c) to any other person domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion, unless it is proved that any such person would not have been governed by the Hindu law or by any custom or usage as part of that law in respect of any of the matters dealt with herein if this Act had not been passed. Explanation. —The following persons are Hindus, Buddhists, Jainas or Sikhs by religion, as the case may be:— (a) any child, legitimate or illegitimate, both of whose parents are Hindus, Buddhists, Jainas or Sikhs by religion; (b) any child, legitimate or illegitimate, one of whose parents is a Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion and who is brought up as a member of the tribe, community, group or family to which such parent belongs or belonged; and (c) any person who is a convert or re-convert to the Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh religion. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), nothing contained in this Act shall apply to the members of any Scheduled Tribe within the meaning of clause (25) of article 366 of the Constitution unless the Central Government, by notification in the Official Gazette, otherwise directs. (3) The expression "Hindu" in any portion of this Act shall be construed as if it included a person who, though not a Hindu by religion, is, nevertheless, a person to whom this Act applies by virtue of the provisions contained in this section.
Section 1(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. It extends to the whole of India, and applies also to Hindus domiciled in the territories to which this Act extends who are outside the said territories.

Explanation (bb), Section 2, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. any child, legitimate or illegitimate, who has been abandoned both by his father and mother or whose parentage is not known and who in either case is brought up as a Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh;
In simple words

Clause (a): a Hindu by religion in any form or development, including a Virashaiva, a Lingayat, and a follower of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj. Clause (b): a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion. Clause (c): anyone else who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew. He is covered unless someone proves that, without the Act, Hindu law or Hindu custom would not have governed him. The Marriage Act and the Minority and Guardianship Act add that he must be domiciled in the territories to which the Act extends. The Succession Act and the Adoptions and Maintenance Act do not have this domicile condition. Explanation: children of two Hindu (or Buddhist, Jaina, Sikh) parents; children of one such parent brought up in that parent's tribe, community, group or family; and converts or re-converts. Sub-section (2): members of a Scheduled Tribe are outside the Act unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. Sub-section (3): wherever the Act says "Hindu", it includes a person who is not a Hindu by religion but to whom the Act applies under this section. Section 1(2): the Marriage Act covers the whole of India, and also Hindus domiciled in India who live outside it. The Minority and Guardianship Act has the same clause. Explanation (bb), Adoptions and Maintenance Act only: an abandoned child, or a child of unknown parentage, brought up as a Hindu, Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh.
hi.meaning:
Scope means the reach of Hindu law: to whom, and where, it applies. Application means the test a court uses to decide whether a particular person is governed by the Hindu Acts. The Acts do not define "Hindu" in a positive sentence. They list who is covered and then use a residuary (left-over) group that works by exclusion. This keeps the law wide: anyone without another personal law of marriage and succession falls under Hindu law. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. outside unless notified"] S -.-> X Text description Section 2(1) applies the Act to (a) Hindus by religion in any form, including Virashaiva, Lingayat, Brahmo, Prarthana and Arya Samaj; (b) Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs; (c) any other person who is not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew, unless proved outside Hindu law or custom. Section 2(2) excludes Scheduled Tribes unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. The question this topic answers. Is this person governed by the Hindu Acts? If yes, the Hindu Marriage Act decides the validity of his marriage, the Hindu Succession Act decides who inherits from him, and so on. Why the law has this rule. Before 1955, Hindu law applied to a person because of religion and custom. The Acts kept that wide reach, brought in Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs, who had always been governed by Hindu law in family matters, and left out only those with their own personal laws.
keyPoints: Section 2(1) covers Hindus by religion, Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs, and a residuary group. The residuary group is anyone not a Muslim, Christian, Parsi or Jew, unless proved outside Hindu law or custom. The Explanation covers children of two Hindu parents, children of one Hindu parent brought up in that parent's group, and converts. Scheduled Tribes are excluded unless the Central Government notifies otherwise. Hindu religion "may broadly be described as a way of life and nothing more" ( Yagnapurushadji ). Conversion does not end a Hindu marriage; a second marriage is void ( Sarla Mudgal , Lily Thomas ). Domicile in clause (c) only in the Marriage and Minority-Guardianship Acts; clause (bb) only in the Adoptions and Maintenance Act. A migrating family carries its personal law with it unless it adopts the new law (Mulla, section 14).

caseLaws.name: Sastri Yagnapurushadji v
caseLaws.facts: Muldas Bhudardas Vaishya (1966) Facts. Followers of the Swaminarayan sect (Satsangis) sued for a declaration that the temple entry law did not apply to their temples, because their religion was distinct from Hindu religion, and to keep non-Satsangi Harijans out. Principle. Hindu religion "may broadly be described as a way of life and nothing more"; Tilak's formula was accepted; the Swaminarayan sect is not distinct from Hindu religion, so its temples fell within the 1956 Act. Appeal dismissed with costs. AIR 1966 SC 1119 : (1966) 3 SCR 242. Why it matters. It is the leading case on what Hindu religion means and why the Acts are drawn so widely. Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) Facts. Hindu husbands with living wives converted to Islam and married again. Principle. Conversion does not dissolve the Hindu marriage. The second marriage without dissolving the first is void in terms of Section 494 IPC, and the husband is guilty of that offence. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It shows that leaving Hinduism does not take a person out of an existing Hindu marriage. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) Facts. Sushmita Ghosh, married by Hindu rites in 1984, said her husband told her in 1992 that he had embraced Islam, asked her to agree to a divorce, and planned to marry another woman. Review of Sarla Mudgal was also sought. Principle. Conversion "does not automatically dissolve a marriage already solemnized under the Hindu Marriage Act. It only provides a ground for divorce under Section 13." A second marriage is void and punishable under Section 494 IPC. Sarla Mudgal gave no direction to enact a common civil code. (2000) 6 SCC 224 : AIR 2000 SC 1650. Why it matters. It confirms Sarla Mudgal and settles the effect of conversion.

selfTest.q: 1. Are Sikhs and Jainas Hindus by religion?
selfTest.a: No. The Acts apply to them under clause (b), and sub-section (3) reads "Hindu" to include them.

selfTest.q: 2. Which sub-section excludes Scheduled Tribes?
selfTest.a: Section 2(2) (Section 3(2) of the Minority and Guardianship Act).

selfTest.q: 3. Which case describes Hindu religion as a way of life?
selfTest.a: Sastri Yagnapurushadji v. Muldas Bhudardas Vaishya (1966).

selfTest.q: 4. Does a husband's conversion to Islam end his Hindu marriage?
selfTest.a: No. It gives the wife a ground for divorce under Section 13(1)(ii). The marriage continues until a decree, and a second marriage is void.

selfTest.q: 5. A child has one Hindu parent and one Christian parent. When is the child a Hindu?
selfTest.a: When brought up as a member of the tribe, community, group or family of the Hindu parent (Explanation (b)).

selfTest.q: 6. Which Act covers an abandoned child brought up as a Hindu?
selfTest.a: The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, Explanation (bb) to Section 2.

family-law-i-u1-t3.subtitle: Why Hindu law has two schools, where each applies, and the four Mitakshara sub-schools

en.inOneMinute: A school of Hindu law is a body of rules built on one leading commentary and followed in one part of India. There are only two schools: the Mitakshara and the Dayabhaga . The Dayabhaga prevails in Bengal (and Assam). The Mitakshara prevails in the rest of India. The Mitakshara school has four sub-schools: Benares, Mithila, Maharashtra or Bombay, and Dravida or Madras. They all accept the Mitakshara as supreme and differ only in details, mainly of adoption and inheritance. The two schools differ mainly on inheritance and the joint family. Today the Hindu Acts apply to both schools alike, so the difference matters mainly for joint family property. Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act speaks only of a family "governed by the Mitakshara law". Exams ask why the schools arose, the two schools and their regions, the four sub-schools with their regions and leading works, and what the schools mean today ( Vineeta Sharma , Surjit Lal Chhabda ).
legalProvision: No Act creates or lists the schools. They come from the commentaries and the courts. The Acts refer to them in a few places.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: ...

Section 4(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,― (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to apply to Hindus in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 3(1), Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (a pre-1956 Act, quoted to show how statutes used the schools). When a Hindu governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law dies intestate leaving any property, and when a Hindu governed by any other school of Hindu law or by customary law dies intestate leaving separate property, his widow ... shall ... be entitled ... to the same share as a son: ...
In simple words

Section 6(1): the daughter's birthright as a coparcener applies only in a joint Hindu family "governed by the Mitakshara law". A Dayabhaga family is outside these words. Section 4(1): on every matter the Succession Act covers, the old texts and interpretations of each school stop having effect. A school's rules survive only on matters the Act does not cover. The other three Acts have the same clause (Hindu Marriage Act s. 4; Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act s. 4; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act s. 5). Section 3(a), Hindu Marriage Act: a custom that is ancient, certain, reasonable and not against public policy has the force of law. A local rule of a sub-school can therefore survive as custom where the Act saves custom. 1937 Act: before codification, statutes named the schools and gave different rules to a Dayabhaga Hindu and to a Hindu of "any other school". On matters the 1956 Act covers, such earlier law ceased to apply under Section 4(1)(b).
en.meaning:
A school of Hindu law is a system of rules built on one authoritative commentary and followed in a particular region. The schools share the same ancient sources, the Smritis. They differ because each region accepted a different commentator's reading of those texts. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. One set of Smritis, two schools, and four Mitakshara sub-schools with their regions. flowchart TD S["Smritis: common to all schools"] S --> M["Mitakshara school
Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya
All India except Bengal"] S --> D["Dayabhaga school
Jimutavahana, digest of all Codes
Bengal and Assam"] M --> B1["Benares
Northern India"] M --> B2["Mithila
Tirhoot, north Bihar"] M --> B3["Maharashtra or Bombay
Western India"] M --> B4["Dravida or Madras
Southern India"] Text description The Smritis are common to all schools. Commentaries gave rise to two schools: the Mitakshara (Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya, all India except Bengal) and the Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana, digest, Bengal and Assam). The Mitakshara has four sub-schools: Benares (Northern India), Mithila (Tirhoot and north Bihar), Maharashtra or Bombay (Western India), Dravida or Madras (Southern India). The question this topic answers. Which body of Hindu law governs this family? The answer still matters for joint family property and coparcenary rights, and for any matter the Acts do not cover. Why the law has this rule. The Smritis sometimes conflicted. Commentators settled the conflicts in different ways. A commentator's view accepted in one region and rejected in another became the law of the region that accepted it. Courts then followed what each region had accepted.
keyPoints: The Smritis are common to all schools; the schools arose from commentaries accepted in different regions. Only two schools: Mitakshara (Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya) and Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana, digest of all Codes). Dayabhaga: Bengal and Assam. Mitakshara: the rest of India. The schools differ mainly on inheritance and the joint family system. Four Mitakshara sub-schools: Benares, Mithila, Maharashtra or Bombay, Dravida or Madras. Sub-school works supplement the Mitakshara; first ask what the Mitakshara says. The Mayukha overrules the Mitakshara only in Gujarat, the Island of Bombay and the North Konkan. The Hindu Acts apply to both schools alike; Section 6 of the Succession Act speaks only of the Mitakshara.

caseLaws.name: Collector of Madura v
caseLaws.facts: Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868) Facts. Known as the Ramnad case, it concerned the validity of an adoption made by a widow. Mulla records that the Privy Council first laid down in it the rule on the consent of the husband's sapindas to such an adoption. Principle. The Smritis are common to all schools; commentaries received in one region and rejected in another gave rise to schools with conflicting doctrines. (1868) 12 M.I.A. 397. Why it matters. It is the classic explanation of how the schools arose (quoted in Mulla, section 11(1)). Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter is a coparcener under the amended Section 6 if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. The Court set out the two schools, the four Mitakshara sub-schools and their regions (paras 18–20), and held that the daughter is a coparcener by birth whether or not her father was alive on that date. (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's recent statement of the schools and their regions. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. A man governed by the Mitakshara claimed that he, his wife and his unmarried daughter formed a Hindu undivided family for income tax. Principle. The schools differ on the coparcener's birthright and on inheritance, but a Dayabhaga family, like a Mitakshara family, is normally joint in food, worship and estate, and the basic idea of who can be a member of a Hindu undivided family is the same. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It shows what the two schools have in common.

selfTest.q: 1. Who wrote the Mitakshara, and on which Smriti?
selfTest.a: Vijnaneswara, as a running commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti.

selfTest.q: 3. Where does the Dayabhaga prevail?
selfTest.a: In Bengal and Assam (the Bengali-speaking areas).

selfTest.q: 4. Do the schools still decide succession to a Hindu's property?
selfTest.a: No. The Hindu Succession Act applies to both schools alike, and its Section 4 overrides the old rules on matters it covers.

selfTest.q: 5. Where does the Vyavahara Mayukha overrule the Mitakshara?
selfTest.a: In Gujarat, the Island of Bombay and the North Konkan (Mulla, section 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. On what two main points do the schools differ?
selfTest.a: The law of inheritance and the joint family system (Mulla, section 11(6)).

సెక్షన్ 6(1): కూతురికి కోపార్సినర్ ‌గా జన్మహక్కు "governed by the Mitakshara law" అయిన ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం లో మాత్రమే వర్తిస్తుంది. దాయభాగ కుటుంబం ఈ పదాల బయట ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 4(1): వారసత్వ చట్టం కవర్ చేసే ప్రతి విషయంలోనూ, ప్రతి శాఖ పాత గ్రంథాలు, వ్యాఖ్యానాలు అమలు కావడం ఆగిపోతాయి. చట్టం కవర్ చేయని విషయాల్లో మాత్రమే శాఖ నియమాలు మిగులుతాయి. మిగతా మూడు చట్టాల్లోనూ ఇదే క్లాజ్ ఉంది (హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం సె. 4; హిందూ దత్తత మరియు భరణ చట్టం సె. 4; హిందూ మైనారిటీ మరియు సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టం సె. 5). హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 3(a): ప్రాచీనమైన, నిర్దిష్టమైన, సహేతుకమైన, ప్రజా విధానానికి విరుద్ధం కాని ఆచారానికి చట్టబలం ఉంటుంది. కాబట్టి చట్టం ఆచారాన్ని కాపాడిన చోట, ఒక ఉప-శాఖ స్థానిక నియమం ఆచారంగా మిగలవచ్చు. 1937 చట్టం: క్రోడీకరణకు ముందు, చట్టాలు శాఖల పేర్లు చెప్పి, దాయభాగ హిందువుకు ఒక నియమం, "any other school" హిందువుకు మరో నియమం ఇచ్చాయి. 1956 చట్టం కవర్ చేసే విషయాల్లో అలాంటి పాత చట్టం సెక్షన్ 4(1)(b) కింద వర్తించడం ఆగిపోయింది.

selfTest.q: 1. మితాక్షరను ఎవరు రాశారు, ఏ స్మృతిపై?
selfTest.a: విజ్ఞానేశ్వరుడు, యాజ్ఞవల్క్య స్మృతిపై వరుస వ్యాఖ్యానంగా.

selfTest.q: 3. దాయభాగ ఎక్కడ అమలులో ఉంది?
selfTest.a: బెంగాల్, అస్సాంలో (బెంగాలీ మాట్లాడే ప్రాంతాల్లో).

selfTest.q: 4. హిందువు ఆస్తి వారసత్వాన్ని ఇప్పటికీ శాఖలే నిర్ణయిస్తాయా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం రెండు శాఖలకూ ఒకేలా వర్తిస్తుంది; అది కవర్ చేసే విషయాల్లో దాని సెక్షన్ 4 పాత నియమాలను అధిగమిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 5. వ్యవహార మయూఖ ఎక్కడ మితాక్షరను అధిగమిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: గుజరాత్, బొంబాయి ద్వీపం, ఉత్తర కొంకణ్‌లో (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. శాఖలు ఏ రెండు ముఖ్య అంశాల్లో విభేదిస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: వారసత్వ చట్టం, ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ వ్యవస్థ (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 11(6)).
