hi.inOneMinute: A school of Hindu law is a body of rules built on one leading commentary and followed in one part of India. There are only two schools: the Mitakshara and the Dayabhaga . The Dayabhaga prevails in Bengal (and Assam). The Mitakshara prevails in the rest of India. The Mitakshara school has four sub-schools: Benares, Mithila, Maharashtra or Bombay, and Dravida or Madras. They all accept the Mitakshara as supreme and differ only in details, mainly of adoption and inheritance. The two schools differ mainly on inheritance and the joint family. Today the Hindu Acts apply to both schools alike, so the difference matters mainly for joint family property. Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act speaks only of a family "governed by the Mitakshara law". Exams ask why the schools arose, the two schools and their regions, the four sub-schools with their regions and leading works, and what the schools mean today ( Vineeta Sharma , Surjit Lal Chhabda ).
legalProvision: No Act creates or lists the schools. They come from the commentaries and the courts. The Acts refer to them in a few places.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: ...

Section 4(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,― (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to apply to Hindus in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 3(1), Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (a pre-1956 Act, quoted to show how statutes used the schools). When a Hindu governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law dies intestate leaving any property, and when a Hindu governed by any other school of Hindu law or by customary law dies intestate leaving separate property, his widow ... shall ... be entitled ... to the same share as a son: ...
In simple words

Section 6(1): the daughter's birthright as a coparcener applies only in a joint Hindu family "governed by the Mitakshara law". A Dayabhaga family is outside these words. Section 4(1): on every matter the Succession Act covers, the old texts and interpretations of each school stop having effect. A school's rules survive only on matters the Act does not cover. The other three Acts have the same clause (Hindu Marriage Act s. 4; Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act s. 4; Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act s. 5). Section 3(a), Hindu Marriage Act: a custom that is ancient, certain, reasonable and not against public policy has the force of law. A local rule of a sub-school can therefore survive as custom where the Act saves custom. 1937 Act: before codification, statutes named the schools and gave different rules to a Dayabhaga Hindu and to a Hindu of "any other school". On matters the 1956 Act covers, such earlier law ceased to apply under Section 4(1)(b).
hi.meaning:
A school of Hindu law is a system of rules built on one authoritative commentary and followed in a particular region. The schools share the same ancient sources, the Smritis. They differ because each region accepted a different commentator's reading of those texts. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. One set of Smritis, two schools, and four Mitakshara sub-schools with their regions. flowchart TD S["Smritis: common to all schools"] S --> M["Mitakshara school
Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya
All India except Bengal"] S --> D["Dayabhaga school
Jimutavahana, digest of all Codes
Bengal and Assam"] M --> B1["Benares
Northern India"] M --> B2["Mithila
Tirhoot, north Bihar"] M --> B3["Maharashtra or Bombay
Western India"] M --> B4["Dravida or Madras
Southern India"] Text description The Smritis are common to all schools. Commentaries gave rise to two schools: the Mitakshara (Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya, all India except Bengal) and the Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana, digest, Bengal and Assam). The Mitakshara has four sub-schools: Benares (Northern India), Mithila (Tirhoot and north Bihar), Maharashtra or Bombay (Western India), Dravida or Madras (Southern India). The question this topic answers. Which body of Hindu law governs this family? The answer still matters for joint family property and coparcenary rights, and for any matter the Acts do not cover. Why the law has this rule. The Smritis sometimes conflicted. Commentators settled the conflicts in different ways. A commentator's view accepted in one region and rejected in another became the law of the region that accepted it. Courts then followed what each region had accepted.
keyPoints: The Smritis are common to all schools; the schools arose from commentaries accepted in different regions. Only two schools: Mitakshara (Vijnaneswara, commentary on Yajnavalkya) and Dayabhaga (Jimutavahana, digest of all Codes). Dayabhaga: Bengal and Assam. Mitakshara: the rest of India. The schools differ mainly on inheritance and the joint family system. Four Mitakshara sub-schools: Benares, Mithila, Maharashtra or Bombay, Dravida or Madras. Sub-school works supplement the Mitakshara; first ask what the Mitakshara says. The Mayukha overrules the Mitakshara only in Gujarat, the Island of Bombay and the North Konkan. The Hindu Acts apply to both schools alike; Section 6 of the Succession Act speaks only of the Mitakshara.

caseLaws.name: Collector of Madura v
caseLaws.facts: Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868) Facts. Known as the Ramnad case, it concerned the validity of an adoption made by a widow. Mulla records that the Privy Council first laid down in it the rule on the consent of the husband's sapindas to such an adoption. Principle. The Smritis are common to all schools; commentaries received in one region and rejected in another gave rise to schools with conflicting doctrines. (1868) 12 M.I.A. 397. Why it matters. It is the classic explanation of how the schools arose (quoted in Mulla, section 11(1)). Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter is a coparcener under the amended Section 6 if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. The Court set out the two schools, the four Mitakshara sub-schools and their regions (paras 18–20), and held that the daughter is a coparcener by birth whether or not her father was alive on that date. (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's recent statement of the schools and their regions. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. A man governed by the Mitakshara claimed that he, his wife and his unmarried daughter formed a Hindu undivided family for income tax. Principle. The schools differ on the coparcener's birthright and on inheritance, but a Dayabhaga family, like a Mitakshara family, is normally joint in food, worship and estate, and the basic idea of who can be a member of a Hindu undivided family is the same. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It shows what the two schools have in common.

selfTest.q: 1. Who wrote the Mitakshara, and on which Smriti?
selfTest.a: Vijnaneswara, as a running commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti.

selfTest.q: 3. Where does the Dayabhaga prevail?
selfTest.a: In Bengal and Assam (the Bengali-speaking areas).

selfTest.q: 4. Do the schools still decide succession to a Hindu's property?
selfTest.a: No. The Hindu Succession Act applies to both schools alike, and its Section 4 overrides the old rules on matters it covers.

selfTest.q: 5. Where does the Vyavahara Mayukha overrule the Mitakshara?
selfTest.a: In Gujarat, the Island of Bombay and the North Konkan (Mulla, section 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. On what two main points do the schools differ?
selfTest.a: The law of inheritance and the joint family system (Mulla, section 11(6)).

family-law-i-u1-t5.subtitle: Joint Hindu family, coparcenary, ancestral and blended property, and separate property

en.inOneMinute: A joint Hindu family is a wide group of relatives descended from a common ancestor, with their wives and unmarried daughters. Membership is a status that comes by birth, marriage or adoption. The family need not own any property. A coparcenary is a smaller body inside it. Its members, the coparceners , get an interest in the ancestral property by birth and can demand partition. Traditionally it was the holder of the property and three generations of male descendants; since 2005 daughters are coparceners too. Joint family property and coparcenary property mean the same thing: ancestral property, property bought with joint funds, and separate property thrown into the common stock. A member's own earnings are self-acquired property and stay separate. Exams ask you to keep these ideas apart, to list the incidents of a coparcenary ( Ghamandi Ram ), to explain blending ( Surjit Lal Chhabda ), and to say what changed after 1956 ( Chander Sen ) and 2005 ( Vineeta Sharma ).
legalProvision: No Act defines "joint family" or " coparcenary ". Both come from the Mitakshara and from court decisions. The Hindu Succession Act changes how coparcenary property passes.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(2). Any property to which a female Hindu becomes entitled by virtue of sub-section (1) shall be held by her with the incidents of coparcenary ownership and shall be regarded, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any other law for the time being in force, as property capable of being disposed of by her by testamentary disposition.

Section 6(3) (first part). Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, ...

Explanation to Section 30. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property ... shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 3, Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975. Birth in family not to give rise to rights in property. On and after the commencement of this Act, no right to claim any interest in any property of an ancestor during his or her lifetime which is founded on the mere fact that the claimant was born in the family of the ancestor shall be recognised in any court.
In simple words

Section 6(1): in a Mitakshara joint family, a daughter of a coparcener is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Partitions and dispositions before 20 December 2004 are saved. Section 6(2): what she gets she holds as coparcenary property, and she can leave it by will . Section 6(3): when a coparcener dies after 9 September 2005, his interest passes by will or by succession, not by survivorship . Section 30, Explanation: a male Hindu can leave his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will. Section 8: the property of a Hindu male who dies intestate (without a will) goes to his heirs under the Act. Chander Sen shows what this means for property a son inherits from his father. Kerala Act, Section 3: in Kerala no one gets a right in an ancestor's property merely by being born in the family.
en.meaning:
Joint Hindu family . "A Joint Hindu family consists of all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, and includes their wives and unmarried daughters. A daughter ceases to be a member of her father's family on marriage, and becomes a member of her husband's family" (Mulla, section 212(1)). It is a status, not a contract. Coparcenary. "The coparcenary consists of only those persons who have taken by birth an interest in the property of the holder and who can enforce a partition whenever they like. It is a narrower body than a joint family" ( Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash (1988), quoted in Vineeta Sharma , para 27). Mulla describes it as "a common male ancestor with his lineal descendants in the male line within four degrees counting from and inclusive of such ancestor (or three degrees exclusive of the ancestor)" (section 214(1)). Since 2005, daughters are coparceners by birth. Joint family property or coparcenary property. Mulla says the two terms are synonymous (section 220). It is property in which every coparcener has a joint interest and joint possession (section 221). Separate property. Property that belongs to one member alone. It includes self-acquired property (Mulla, sections 220, 222). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The joint family is the widest group; the coparcenary sits inside it; coparcenary property is what the coparcenary owns. Separate property stays outside. flowchart TD subgraph JF["Joint Hindu family: a status (sapindaship); wives and unmarried daughters belong"] direction TB SP[" "] SP ~~~ CP subgraph CP["Coparcenary: holder and three generations; daughters since 2005"] SQ["
"] SQ ~~~ P P["Coparcenary property
ancestral, joint acquisitions,
income, blended property"] end end S["Separate or self-acquired property
of a member"] S -. "blending" .-> P classDef hide fill:none,stroke:none,color:transparent class SP,SQ hide Text description Outer box: joint Hindu family, a status based on sapindaship, including wives and unmarried daughters. Inside it: the coparcenary, the holder and three generations of descendants, and daughters since 2005. Inside that: coparcenary property, which is ancestral property, joint acquisitions with its aid, income, and blended property. Outside, linked by a dotted line marked "blending": a member's separate or self-acquired property. The question this topic answers. Who belongs to the family, who among them has rights in the property, and which property is shared? Why the law has this rule. "The cord that knits the members of the family is not property but the relationship of one another" ( Sunil Kumar , quoted in Vineeta Sharma , para 27). Rights in property, however, belong only to the smaller group who take by birth.
keyPoints: A joint Hindu family is a status based on sapindaship and needs no property. A coparcenary is a creature of law and is smaller than the joint family; a stranger enters only by adoption. The test of a coparcener is the right to demand partition ( Vineeta Sharma , para 25). Since 2005 daughters are coparceners by birth (Section 6(1)). Joint family property and coparcenary property are synonyms: ancestral, joint acquisitions with its aid, income, blended. Self-acquired property stays separate unless blended by clear intention. A son who inherits from his father under Section 8 holds it as his own ( Chander Sen ). Kerala Act, 1975: the joint family system among Hindus is abolished; birthright ends and coparcenary property is held as tenancy in common.

caseLaws.name: Surjit Lal Chhabda v
caseLaws.facts: Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. Surjit Lal, with no son, swore before a Presidency Magistrate in 1956 that he had thrown his self-acquired Kathoke Lodge into the family hotchpot of himself, his wife and unmarried daughter, and claimed the rent was the family's income. Principle. A joint Hindu family can consist of one male, his wife and unmarried daughter; but property he throws into the common stock is still really his in the eye of Hindu law until a son is born, so its income is his individual income. Appeal dismissed. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It separates the joint family from the coparcenary and shows the limits of blending by a man with no son. State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969) Facts. The karta of a joint family firm that had traded in what became Pakistan claimed the surplus in its bank account; the question was whether the firm was an "individual" under a Pakistan notification . Principle. A Mitakshara coparcenary is a creature of law holding property in a quasi-corporate capacity; the Court listed its six incidents and held the firm a body of individuals. Bank's appeal allowed. AIR 1969 SC 1330. Why it matters. It is the standard source for the incidents of a coparcenary. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died in 1965, leaving his son Chander Sen and grandsons; ₹1,85,043 stood to his credit in the firm. The Revenue treated it as the property of Chander Sen's joint family with his sons. Principle. A son who inherits his father's property under Section 8 takes it in his individual capacity; his sons get no right by birth in it. (1986) 3 SCC 567 : AIR 1986 SC 1753. Why it matters. It shows that property inherited from a father after 1956 is not ancestral property in the old sense. Sitabai v. Ramchandra (1969) Facts. Sitabai, widow of Bhagirath, adopted a son on 4 March 1958; Bhagirath's brother Dulichand, the sole surviving coparcener, died on 13 March 1958. Dulichand's illegitimate son took possession of the family property. Principle. Joint family property does not lose its character in the hands of a sole surviving coparcener while a widow entitled to maintenance is alive; a son adopted by a widow under the 1956 Act becomes a coparcener with her husband's surviving brother. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It shows that a joint family can continue with a single coparcener and revive through adoption. Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963) Facts. Chimpirayya's will said he was a divided member and left his property to his grandson and a granddaughter. The question was whether the will severed his joint status although it was not communicated to his grandson's guardian before his death. Principle. A clear, unequivocal, unilateral declaration is enough to sever joint status, but it takes effect only when it reaches the members affected. Appeal dismissed with costs. AIR 1964 SC 136. Why it matters. It shows how the joint status of a coparcener ends. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter is a coparcener if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. The Court described the joint family, the coparcenary and coparcenary property (paras 22–35) and held that a daughter is a coparcener by birth, whether or not her father was alive on that date. (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It is the current Supreme Court statement of the whole topic.

selfTest.q: 1. Can a joint family exist without property?
selfTest.a: Yes. It is a status, and the family need not own anything (Mulla, section 212(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. Can members create a coparcenary by agreement?
selfTest.a: No. It is created by law. A stranger joins only by adoption.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the doctrine of blending?
selfTest.a: A coparcener voluntarily throws his separate property into the common stock, giving up his separate claim; it becomes joint family property.

selfTest.q: 4. Is property inherited from a maternal grandfather coparcenary property?
selfTest.a: No. Only property inherited from the father, grandfather or great-grandfather is ( Vineeta Sharma , para 24; Mulla, section 218).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a married daughter a coparcener today?
selfTest.a: Yes. She leaves her father's joint family on marriage, but Section 6(1) speaks of "the daughter of a coparcener" without distinguishing married and unmarried daughters, and Vineeta Sharma (para 129(i)) applies it to daughters born before or after 2005.

selfTest.q: 6. In Surjit Lal Chhabda , why was the rent taxed as Surjit Lal's own income?
selfTest.a: He had no son. Though he threw the lodge into the common stock, in the eye of Hindu law it remained really his, with full power to sell or give it away.

legalProvision: ఏ చట్టమూ "ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబం" లేదా " కోపార్సినరీ " ని నిర్వచించదు. రెండూ మితాక్షర నుంచి, కోర్టు తీర్పుల నుంచి వచ్చాయి. కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తి ఎలా వెళ్తుందో హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం మారుస్తుంది.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(2). Any property to which a female Hindu becomes entitled by virtue of sub-section (1) shall be held by her with the incidents of coparcenary ownership and shall be regarded, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any other law for the time being in force, as property capable of being disposed of by her by testamentary disposition.

Section 6(3) (first part). Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, ...

Explanation to Section 30. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property ... shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 3, Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975. Birth in family not to give rise to rights in property. On and after the commencement of this Act, no right to claim any interest in any property of an ancestor during his or her lifetime which is founded on the mere fact that the claimant was born in the family of the ancestor shall be recognised in any court.
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 6(1): మితాక్షర ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబంలో కోపార్సినర్ కూతురు పుట్టుకతోనే కోపార్సినర్; కొడుకుతో సమాన హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలు. 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన విభజన లు, అన్యాక్రాంతాలు కాపాడబడతాయి. సెక్షన్ 6(2): ఆమె పొందినదాన్ని కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిగా కలిగి ఉంటుంది; వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 6(3): 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాత కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే, అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా కాకుండా వీలునామా లేదా వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 30, Explanation: పురుష హిందువు మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిలో తన హక్కును వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 8: వీలునామా లేకుండా మరణించిన హిందూ పురుషుని ఆస్తి చట్టం కింద అతని వారసులకు వెళ్తుంది. కొడుకు తండ్రి నుంచి పొందిన ఆస్తికి దీని అర్థం ఏమిటో Chander Sen చూపిస్తుంది. కేరళ చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 3: కేరళలో కుటుంబంలో పుట్టినంత మాత్రాన ఎవరికీ పూర్వీకుని ఆస్తిలో హక్కు రాదు.
te.meaning:
ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం . "A Joint Hindu family consists of all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, and includes their wives and unmarried daughters. A daughter ceases to be a member of her father's family on marriage, and becomes a member of her husband's family" (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 212(1)). ఇది ఒప్పందం కాదు, హోదా. కోపార్సినరీ. "The coparcenary consists of only those persons who have taken by birth an interest in the property of the holder and who can enforce a partition whenever they like. It is a narrower body than a joint family" ( Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash (1988), Vineeta Sharma para 27 లో ఉటంకించినది). ముల్లా దీన్ని "a common male ancestor with his lineal descendants in the male line within four degrees counting from and inclusive of such ancestor (or three degrees exclusive of the ancestor)" అని వర్ణిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 214(1)). 2005 నుంచి కూతుళ్లు పుట్టుకతోనే కోపార్సినర్లు. ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తి లేదా కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తి. ఈ రెండు పదాలు పర్యాయపదాలని ముల్లా చెబుతారు (సెక్షన్ 220). ప్రతి కోపార్సినర్‌కు ఉమ్మడి హక్కు, ఉమ్మడి స్వాధీనం ఉన్న ఆస్తి ఇది (సెక్షన్ 221). ప్రత్యేక ఆస్తి. ఒక్క సభ్యునికి మాత్రమే చెందిన ఆస్తి. స్వార్జిత ఆస్తి దీనిలో భాగం (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్లు 220, 222). "కలపడం" .-> P classDef hide fill:none,stroke:none,color:transparent class SP,SQ hide వచన వివరణ బయటి పెట్టె: ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం, సపిండత్వంపై ఆధారపడిన హోదా, భార్యలు, పెళ్లికాని కూతుళ్లు సహా. దాని లోపల: కోపార్సినరీ, ఆస్తి కలిగినవారు, మూడు తరాల వంశస్థులు, 2005 నుంచి కూతుళ్లు. దాని లోపల: కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తి, అంటే పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తి, దాని సహాయంతో సంపాదించినది, ఆదాయం, కలిపిన ఆస్తి. బయట, "కలపడం" అని గుర్తించిన చుక్కల గీతతో కలిపి: సభ్యుని ప్రత్యేక లేదా స్వార్జిత ఆస్తి. ఈ అంశం జవాబిచ్చే ప్రశ్న. కుటుంబంలో ఎవరు ఉంటారు, వారిలో ఎవరికి ఆస్తిలో హక్కులు ఉంటాయి, ఏ ఆస్తి ఉమ్మడి? చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు ఉంది. "The cord that knits the members of the family is not property but the relationship of one another" ( Sunil Kumar , Vineeta Sharma para 27 లో). అయితే ఆస్తిలో హక్కులు పుట్టుకతో పొందే చిన్న సమూహానికే చెందుతాయి.

selfTest.q: 1. ఆస్తి లేకుండా ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబం ఉండగలదా?
selfTest.a: అవును. అది హోదా; కుటుంబానికి ఏమీ ఉండనక్కర్లేదు (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 212(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. సభ్యులు ఒప్పందం ద్వారా కోపార్సినరీని సృష్టించగలరా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అది చట్టం ద్వారా ఏర్పడుతుంది. అపరిచితుడు దత్తత ద్వారా మాత్రమే చేరతాడు.

selfTest.q: 3. బ్లెండింగ్ సిద్ధాంతం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: కోపార్సినర్ తన ప్రత్యేక హక్కును వదులుకుని, తన ప్రత్యేక ఆస్తిని స్వచ్ఛందంగా ఉమ్మడి నిల్వలో కలపడం; అది ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తి అవుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. తల్లి తండ్రి నుంచి వచ్చిన ఆస్తి కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. తండ్రి, తాత లేదా ముత్తాత నుంచి వచ్చిన ఆస్తి మాత్రమే ( Vineeta Sharma , para 24; ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 218).

selfTest.q: 5. ఈరోజు పెళ్లయిన కూతురు కోపార్సినరా?
selfTest.a: అవును. పెళ్లితో ఆమె తండ్రి ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబాన్ని వదులుతుంది; కానీ సెక్షన్ 6(1) పెళ్లయిన, కాని కూతుళ్ల మధ్య తేడా చూపకుండా "the daughter of a coparcener" అంటుంది; 2005 కు ముందు లేదా తర్వాత పుట్టిన కూతుళ్లకు Vineeta Sharma (para 129(i)) దాన్ని వర్తింపజేస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 6. Surjit Lal Chhabda లో అద్దెపై సుర్జిత్ లాల్ సొంత ఆదాయంగా ఎందుకు పన్ను వేశారు?
selfTest.a: అతనికి కొడుకు లేడు. లాడ్జిని ఉమ్మడి నిల్వలో కలిపినా, హిందూ చట్టం దృష్టిలో అది నిజానికి అతనిదే; దాన్ని అమ్మడానికి, దానం చేయడానికి అతనికి పూర్తి అధికారం ఉంది.

hi.inOneMinute: A joint Hindu family is a wide group of relatives descended from a common ancestor, with their wives and unmarried daughters. Membership is a status that comes by birth, marriage or adoption. The family need not own any property. A coparcenary is a smaller body inside it. Its members, the coparceners , get an interest in the ancestral property by birth and can demand partition. Traditionally it was the holder of the property and three generations of male descendants; since 2005 daughters are coparceners too. Joint family property and coparcenary property mean the same thing: ancestral property, property bought with joint funds, and separate property thrown into the common stock. A member's own earnings are self-acquired property and stay separate. Exams ask you to keep these ideas apart, to list the incidents of a coparcenary ( Ghamandi Ram ), to explain blending ( Surjit Lal Chhabda ), and to say what changed after 1956 ( Chander Sen ) and 2005 ( Vineeta Sharma ).
legalProvision: No Act defines "joint family" or " coparcenary ". Both come from the Mitakshara and from court decisions. The Hindu Succession Act changes how coparcenary property passes.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(2). Any property to which a female Hindu becomes entitled by virtue of sub-section (1) shall be held by her with the incidents of coparcenary ownership and shall be regarded, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any other law for the time being in force, as property capable of being disposed of by her by testamentary disposition.

Section 6(3) (first part). Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, ...

Explanation to Section 30. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property ... shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 3, Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975. Birth in family not to give rise to rights in property. On and after the commencement of this Act, no right to claim any interest in any property of an ancestor during his or her lifetime which is founded on the mere fact that the claimant was born in the family of the ancestor shall be recognised in any court.
In simple words

Section 6(1): in a Mitakshara joint family, a daughter of a coparcener is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Partitions and dispositions before 20 December 2004 are saved. Section 6(2): what she gets she holds as coparcenary property, and she can leave it by will . Section 6(3): when a coparcener dies after 9 September 2005, his interest passes by will or by succession, not by survivorship . Section 30, Explanation: a male Hindu can leave his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will. Section 8: the property of a Hindu male who dies intestate (without a will) goes to his heirs under the Act. Chander Sen shows what this means for property a son inherits from his father. Kerala Act, Section 3: in Kerala no one gets a right in an ancestor's property merely by being born in the family.
hi.meaning:
Joint Hindu family . "A Joint Hindu family consists of all persons lineally descended from a common ancestor, and includes their wives and unmarried daughters. A daughter ceases to be a member of her father's family on marriage, and becomes a member of her husband's family" (Mulla, section 212(1)). It is a status, not a contract. Coparcenary. "The coparcenary consists of only those persons who have taken by birth an interest in the property of the holder and who can enforce a partition whenever they like. It is a narrower body than a joint family" ( Sunil Kumar v. Ram Parkash (1988), quoted in Vineeta Sharma , para 27). Mulla describes it as "a common male ancestor with his lineal descendants in the male line within four degrees counting from and inclusive of such ancestor (or three degrees exclusive of the ancestor)" (section 214(1)). Since 2005, daughters are coparceners by birth. Joint family property or coparcenary property. Mulla says the two terms are synonymous (section 220). It is property in which every coparcener has a joint interest and joint possession (section 221). Separate property. Property that belongs to one member alone. It includes self-acquired property (Mulla, sections 220, 222). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The joint family is the widest group; the coparcenary sits inside it; coparcenary property is what the coparcenary owns. Inside it: the coparcenary, the holder and three generations of descendants, and daughters since 2005. Inside that: coparcenary property, which is ancestral property, joint acquisitions with its aid, income, and blended property. Outside, linked by a dotted line marked "blending": a member's separate or self-acquired property. The question this topic answers. Who belongs to the family, who among them has rights in the property, and which property is shared? Why the law has this rule. "The cord that knits the members of the family is not property but the relationship of one another" ( Sunil Kumar , quoted in Vineeta Sharma , para 27). Rights in property, however, belong only to the smaller group who take by birth.
keyPoints: A joint Hindu family is a status based on sapindaship and needs no property. A coparcenary is a creature of law and is smaller than the joint family; a stranger enters only by adoption. The test of a coparcener is the right to demand partition ( Vineeta Sharma , para 25). Since 2005 daughters are coparceners by birth (Section 6(1)). Joint family property and coparcenary property are synonyms: ancestral, joint acquisitions with its aid, income, blended. Self-acquired property stays separate unless blended by clear intention. A son who inherits from his father under Section 8 holds it as his own ( Chander Sen ). Kerala Act, 1975: the joint family system among Hindus is abolished; birthright ends and coparcenary property is held as tenancy in common.

caseLaws.name: Surjit Lal Chhabda v
caseLaws.facts: Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. Surjit Lal, with no son, swore before a Presidency Magistrate in 1956 that he had thrown his self-acquired Kathoke Lodge into the family hotchpot of himself, his wife and unmarried daughter, and claimed the rent was the family's income. Principle. A joint Hindu family can consist of one male, his wife and unmarried daughter; but property he throws into the common stock is still really his in the eye of Hindu law until a son is born, so its income is his individual income. Appeal dismissed. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It separates the joint family from the coparcenary and shows the limits of blending by a man with no son. State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969) Facts. The karta of a joint family firm that had traded in what became Pakistan claimed the surplus in its bank account; the question was whether the firm was an "individual" under a Pakistan notification . Principle. A Mitakshara coparcenary is a creature of law holding property in a quasi-corporate capacity; the Court listed its six incidents and held the firm a body of individuals. Bank's appeal allowed. AIR 1969 SC 1330. Why it matters. It is the standard source for the incidents of a coparcenary. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died in 1965, leaving his son Chander Sen and grandsons; ₹1,85,043 stood to his credit in the firm. The Revenue treated it as the property of Chander Sen's joint family with his sons. Principle. A son who inherits his father's property under Section 8 takes it in his individual capacity; his sons get no right by birth in it. (1986) 3 SCC 567 : AIR 1986 SC 1753. Why it matters. It shows that property inherited from a father after 1956 is not ancestral property in the old sense. Sitabai v. Ramchandra (1969) Facts. Sitabai, widow of Bhagirath, adopted a son on 4 March 1958; Bhagirath's brother Dulichand, the sole surviving coparcener, died on 13 March 1958. Dulichand's illegitimate son took possession of the family property. Principle. Joint family property does not lose its character in the hands of a sole surviving coparcener while a widow entitled to maintenance is alive; a son adopted by a widow under the 1956 Act becomes a coparcener with her husband's surviving brother. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It shows that a joint family can continue with a single coparcener and revive through adoption. Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963) Facts. Chimpirayya's will said he was a divided member and left his property to his grandson and a granddaughter. The question was whether the will severed his joint status although it was not communicated to his grandson's guardian before his death. Principle. A clear, unequivocal, unilateral declaration is enough to sever joint status, but it takes effect only when it reaches the members affected. Appeal dismissed with costs. AIR 1964 SC 136. Why it matters. It shows how the joint status of a coparcener ends. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter is a coparcener if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. The Court described the joint family, the coparcenary and coparcenary property (paras 22–35) and held that a daughter is a coparcener by birth, whether or not her father was alive on that date. (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It is the current Supreme Court statement of the whole topic.

selfTest.q: 1. Can a joint family exist without property?
selfTest.a: Yes. It is a status, and the family need not own anything (Mulla, section 212(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. Can members create a coparcenary by agreement?
selfTest.a: No. It is created by law. A stranger joins only by adoption.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the doctrine of blending?
selfTest.a: A coparcener voluntarily throws his separate property into the common stock, giving up his separate claim; it becomes joint family property.

selfTest.q: 4. Is property inherited from a maternal grandfather coparcenary property?
selfTest.a: No. Only property inherited from the father, grandfather or great-grandfather is ( Vineeta Sharma , para 24; Mulla, section 218).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a married daughter a coparcener today?
selfTest.a: Yes. She leaves her father's joint family on marriage, but Section 6(1) speaks of "the daughter of a coparcener" without distinguishing married and unmarried daughters, and Vineeta Sharma (para 129(i)) applies it to daughters born before or after 2005.

selfTest.q: 6. In Surjit Lal Chhabda , why was the rent taxed as Surjit Lal's own income?
selfTest.a: He had no son. Though he threw the lodge into the common stock, in the eye of Hindu law it remained really his, with full power to sell or give it away.

family-law-i-u1-t6.subtitle: Who the Karta is, how the office arises, and the limits on his power

en.inOneMinute: The Karta is the manager of a joint Hindu family . By default he is the father or, in his absence, the senior-most coparcener . The office comes from law and seniority, not from a contract or an election. The Supreme Court has said that managership goes to a person by birth and is regulated by seniority ( Tribhovandas Haribhai Tamboli , 1991). A junior member can act as manager only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional situations. Only a coparcener can be Karta ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills , 1966). The Karta has no larger share than any other member. His one special power is to deal with the whole family property for purposes the law accepts, such as legal necessity . If members dislike his management, their remedy is partition . Since 2005 a daughter is a coparcener by birth. In Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015) the Delhi High Court held that the eldest coparcener, though a woman, is the Karta.
legalProvision: No Act creates or defines the office of Karta . It is part of uncodified Mitakshara law. Three statutes touch it.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: ...

Section 4(1)(a), Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,― (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act;

Section 6, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (opening words). The natural guardians of a Hindu minor, in respect of the minor's person as well as in respect of the minor's property (excluding his or her undivided interest in joint family property), are― ...

Section 12, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. Where a minor has an undivided interest in joint family property and the property is under the management of an adult member of the family, no guardian shall be appointed for the minor in respect of such undivided interest: Provided that nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect the jurisdiction of a High Court to appoint a guardian in respect of such interest.
In simple words

Section 6(1) makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Since coparcenership is the qualification for the office, this is the basis for a woman becoming Karta. Section 4(1)(a) ends old Hindu law rules only on matters the Act provides for. The Act says nothing about who manages the family, so the classical rules on the Karta continue, read with the new Section 6. Sections 6 and 12 of the Guardianship Act keep a minor's undivided interest in joint family property out of the hands of a guardian. That interest is managed by the adult member who manages the family, which is the Karta.
en.meaning:
Mulla states the rule this way (section 236): "Property belonging to a joint family is ordinarily managed by the father or other senior member for the time being of the family. The manager of a joint family is called karta. The father is in all cases naturally, and in the case of minor sons necessarily, the manager of the joint family property." So the Karta is the member who manages the joint family and its property and represents it in dealings with outsiders. The family does not need to appoint him. The office falls on the senior member who is a coparcener. The Karta manages the joint family, which is wider than the coparcenary . Wives, widows and unmarried daughters are members of the family. But the person who holds the office must be a coparcener. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The office goes to the senior-most coparcener; a junior member acts only in the exceptions; a non-coparcener cannot hold it. flowchart TD Q1{"Is the person a coparcener?

while the Karta is available"] Text description Is the person a coparcener? If no (for example a widow or wife), the person cannot be Karta. If yes, is the person the father or the senior-most coparcener? If yes, the person is Karta by birth and seniority, presumed to be manager. If no, a junior member can act as manager only if the Karta gives up the office, in distress or calamity affecting the family in his absence, or if the father is missing or far away and not expected back.
keyPoints: The Karta is the manager of the joint Hindu family; no Act creates the office. The father, or else the senior-most coparcener, is Karta by birth and seniority; the senior member is presumed to be manager. A junior member acts only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional circumstances ( Tribhovandas ). Coparcenership is a necessary qualification ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills ). Since 2005 a daughter is a coparcener, so the eldest coparcener can be Karta though a woman ( Sujata Sharma ); a widow or wife cannot. The Karta has no larger share; he is not an agent; the members' remedy is partition. He accounts on partition only for what he received, unless there is fraud or misappropriation. He cannot alienate except for necessity ( Brij Narain ); he does not manage separate property or Section 8 inheritance ( Chander Sen ).

caseLaws.name: Sujata Sharma v
caseLaws.facts: Manu Gupta (2015) Facts. Sujata Sharma, the eldest coparcener of D.R. Gupta & Sons (HUF), sued for a declaration that she was its Karta. The defendants argued that Section 6 deals with inheritance, not management. Principle. After the 2005 amendment, a woman who is the eldest coparcener can be Karta; her marriage does not alter this. Delhi High Court, Najmi Waziri J., CS(OS) 2011/2006, decided 22.12.2015, paras 25, 27 and 29. Why it matters. It is the leading authority that a woman can be Karta. Commissioner of Income Tax v. Seth Govindram Sugar Mills (1966) Facts. The question was whether a widow, who is a member of the joint family but not a coparcener, could be its manager. The Nagpur High Court had allowed a mother to act as manager; the Madras High Court had not. Principle. Coparcenership is a necessary qualification for managership; a woman who is not a coparcener cannot be the manager. AIR 1966 SC 24 (as quoted in Sujata Sharma , para 26). Why it matters. It fixes the qualification for the office, which is why Sujata Sharma turned on Section 6. Tribhovandas Haribhai Tamboli v. Gujarat Revenue Tribunal (1991) Facts. The question was the position of a junior member who deals with joint family property while the Karta is available. (Only the passages quoted in Sujata Sharma were checked.) Principle. Managership goes by birth and seniority; a junior member acts only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional circumstances. AIR 1991 SC 1538 (as quoted in Sujata Sharma , paras 6 and 15). Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court statement of how the office arises. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. A man with no son threw his house into the family hotchpot and claimed its rent should be taxed as income of the HUF of himself, his wife and unmarried daughter. Principle. Such a family is a joint Hindu family, but until a son is born the property "is really his"; the rent is his individual income. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. Calling oneself Karta does not turn one's own property into family property for all purposes. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Chander Sen inherited ₹1,85,043 standing to his father's credit in their firm. The Revenue treated it as the wealth of Chander Sen's joint family with his sons. Principle. A son inherits under Section 8 in his individual capacity, not as Karta of his own family. (1986) 3 SCC 567 : AIR 1986 SC 1753. Why it matters. It limits the property a Karta manages. Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged family property for Rs. 11,000 in 1908 to pay off two earlier mortgages. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding. Principle. "The managing co-parcener of a joint undivided estate cannot alienate or burden the estate qua manager except for purposes of necessity" (para 17). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It states the basic limit on the Karta's power.

selfTest.q: 1. Who is the Karta by default?
selfTest.a: The father; in his absence, the senior-most coparcener (Mulla, section 236; Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 2. When can a junior member act as manager while the Karta is alive?
selfTest.a: If the Karta gives up the office, in distress or calamity affecting the family in the Karta's absence, or if the father is missing or far away and not expected back soon ( Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 3. Why could a widow not be Karta, and can she be one today?
selfTest.a: Because coparcenership is a necessary qualification and she is not a coparcener ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills ). Section 6(1) makes daughters, not widows, coparceners, so she still cannot.

selfTest.q: 4. Which case held that a woman can be Karta, and which court decided it?
selfTest.a: Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015), a single judge of the Delhi High Court.

selfTest.q: 5. A coparcener is unhappy with the Karta's spending on family ceremonies. What is his remedy?
selfTest.a: To demand partition (Mulla, section 237). The Karta need not economise like a trustee while he spends for family purposes.

selfTest.q: 6. Is a guardian appointed for a minor coparcener's undivided interest?
selfTest.a: No, where an adult member manages the joint family property (Section 12, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act); a High Court's power is saved.

Where a minor has an undivided interest in joint family property and the property is under the management of an adult member of the family, no guardian shall be appointed for the minor in respect of such undivided interest: Provided that nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect the jurisdiction of a High Court to appoint a guardian in respect of such interest.
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 6(1) కూతురిని పుట్టుకతో కోపార్సినర్ ‌గా చేస్తుంది; కొడుకుకు ఉన్న హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలే ఆమెకూ ఉంటాయి. కర్త పదవికి అర్హత కోపార్సినర్‌గా ఉండటమే కాబట్టి, స్త్రీ కర్త కావడానికి ఇదే ఆధారం. సెక్షన్ 4(1)(a) చట్టం ఏ విషయాలకు నిబంధన చేసిందో ఆ విషయాల్లో మాత్రమే పాత హిందూ చట్ట నియమాలను రద్దు చేస్తుంది. కుటుంబాన్ని ఎవరు నిర్వహించాలో చట్టం ఏమీ చెప్పలేదు. కాబట్టి కర్త గురించిన సంప్రదాయ నియమాలు కొత్త సెక్షన్ 6 తో కలిపి చదివి కొనసాగుతాయి. సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టంలోని సెక్షన్లు 6, 12 ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిలో మైనర్ అవిభక్త వాటాను సంరక్షకుని చేతుల్లో పెట్టవు. కుటుంబాన్ని నిర్వహించే వయోజన సభ్యుడు, అంటే కర్త, ఆ వాటాను నిర్వహిస్తాడు.

ముల్లా ఈ నియమాన్ని ఇలా చెబుతారు (సెక్షన్ 236): "Property belonging to a joint family is ordinarily managed by the father or other senior member for the time being of the family. The manager of a joint family is called karta. The father is in all cases naturally, and in the case of minor sons necessarily, the manager of the joint family property." అంటే కర్త ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబాన్ని, దాని ఆస్తిని నిర్వహించి, బయటివారితో వ్యవహారాల్లో కుటుంబానికి ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహించే సభ్యుడు. కుటుంబం అతన్ని నియమించనక్కర్లేదు. కోపార్సినర్ అయిన పెద్ద సభ్యునిపై ఆ పదవి పడుతుంది. కర్త ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబాన్ని నిర్వహిస్తాడు; అది కోపార్సినరీ కంటే విస్తృతం. భార్యలు, వితంతువులు, పెళ్లికాని కూతుళ్లు కుటుంబ సభ్యులు. కానీ పదవి చేపట్టే వ్యక్తి కోపార్సినర్ అయి ఉండాలి. Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. పదవి అందరికంటే పెద్ద కోపార్సినర్‌కు వెళ్తుంది; మినహాయింపుల్లో మాత్రమే చిన్న సభ్యుడు వ్యవహరిస్తాడు; కోపార్సినర్ కానివారు చేపట్టలేరు. flowchart TD Q1{"ఆ వ్యక్తి కోపార్సినరా?

నిర్వాహకుడిగా వ్యవహరించలేడు"] వచన వివరణ ఆ వ్యక్తి కోపార్సినరా? కాకపోతే (ఉదాహరణకు వితంతువు లేదా భార్య) కర్త కాలేరు. అవును అయితే, తండ్రి లేదా అందరికంటే పెద్ద కోపార్సినరా? అవును అయితే పుట్టుక, పెద్దరికంతో కర్త; నిర్వాహకుడని ఊహ. కాకపోతే, కర్త పదవి వదులుకుంటే, అతను లేనప్పుడు కుటుంబానికి ఆపద లేదా విపత్తు వస్తే, లేదా తండ్రి కనిపించకపోయినా దూరంగా ఉండి తిరిగి వస్తాడని ఆశించలేకపోయినా మాత్రమే చిన్న సభ్యుడు నిర్వాహకుడిగా వ్యవహరించవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. సాధారణంగా కర్త ఎవరు?
selfTest.a: తండ్రి; ఆయన లేనప్పుడు అందరికంటే పెద్ద కోపార్సినర్ (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 236; Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 2. కర్త బతికి ఉండగా చిన్న సభ్యుడు నిర్వాహకుడిగా ఎప్పుడు వ్యవహరించవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: కర్త పదవి వదులుకుంటే; కర్త లేనప్పుడు కుటుంబాన్ని ప్రభావితం చేసే ఆపద లేదా విపత్తులో; తండ్రి కనిపించకపోతే లేదా దూరంగా ఉండి త్వరలో తిరిగి వస్తాడని ఆశించలేకపోతే ( Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 3. వితంతువు ఎందుకు కర్త కాలేకపోయేది?
selfTest.a: ఈరోజు కాగలదా? కోపార్సినర్‌గా ఉండటం తప్పనిసరి అర్హత, ఆమె కోపార్సినర్ కాదు ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills ). సెక్షన్ 6(1) కూతుళ్లను కోపార్సినర్లుగా చేసింది, వితంతువులను కాదు; కాబట్టి ఇప్పటికీ కాలేదు.

selfTest.q: 4. స్త్రీ కర్త కావచ్చని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది, ఏ కోర్టు?
selfTest.a: Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015), ఢిల్లీ హైకోర్టు ఏకసభ్య ధర్మాసనం.

selfTest.q: 5. కుటుంబ కర్మలకు కర్త చేసే ఖర్చుపై ఒక కోపార్సినర్‌కు అసంతృప్తి. అతని పరిష్కారం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: విభజన కోరడం (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 237). కుటుంబ అవసరాలకు ఖర్చు చేస్తున్నంతకాలం కర్త ట్రస్టీ లాగా పొదుపు చేయనక్కర్లేదు.

selfTest.q: 6. మైనర్ కోపార్సినర్ అవిభక్త వాటాకు సంరక్షకుడిని నియమిస్తారా?
selfTest.a: వయోజన సభ్యుడు ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని నిర్వహిస్తున్నప్పుడు నియమించరు (హిందూ మైనారిటీ, సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 12); హైకోర్టు అధికారం మాత్రం కాపాడబడింది.

hi.inOneMinute: The Karta is the manager of a joint Hindu family . By default he is the father or, in his absence, the senior-most coparcener . The office comes from law and seniority, not from a contract or an election. The Supreme Court has said that managership goes to a person by birth and is regulated by seniority ( Tribhovandas Haribhai Tamboli , 1991). A junior member can act as manager only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional situations. Only a coparcener can be Karta ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills , 1966). The Karta has no larger share than any other member. His one special power is to deal with the whole family property for purposes the law accepts, such as legal necessity . If members dislike his management, their remedy is partition . Since 2005 a daughter is a coparcener by birth. In Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015) the Delhi High Court held that the eldest coparcener, though a woman, is the Karta.
legalProvision: No Act creates or defines the office of Karta . It is part of uncodified Mitakshara law. Three statutes touch it.

Section 6(1), Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: ...

Section 4(1)(a), Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,― (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act;

Section 6, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (opening words). The natural guardians of a Hindu minor, in respect of the minor's person as well as in respect of the minor's property (excluding his or her undivided interest in joint family property), are― ...

Section 12, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. Where a minor has an undivided interest in joint family property and the property is under the management of an adult member of the family, no guardian shall be appointed for the minor in respect of such undivided interest: Provided that nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect the jurisdiction of a High Court to appoint a guardian in respect of such interest.
In simple words

Section 6(1) makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Since coparcenership is the qualification for the office, this is the basis for a woman becoming Karta. Section 4(1)(a) ends old Hindu law rules only on matters the Act provides for. The Act says nothing about who manages the family, so the classical rules on the Karta continue, read with the new Section 6. Sections 6 and 12 of the Guardianship Act keep a minor's undivided interest in joint family property out of the hands of a guardian. That interest is managed by the adult member who manages the family, which is the Karta.
hi.meaning:
Mulla states the rule this way (section 236): "Property belonging to a joint family is ordinarily managed by the father or other senior member for the time being of the family. The manager of a joint family is called karta. The father is in all cases naturally, and in the case of minor sons necessarily, the manager of the joint family property." So the Karta is the member who manages the joint family and its property and represents it in dealings with outsiders. The family does not need to appoint him. The office falls on the senior member who is a coparcener. The Karta manages the joint family, which is wider than the coparcenary . Wives, widows and unmarried daughters are members of the family. But the person who holds the office must be a coparcener. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The office goes to the senior-most coparcener; a junior member acts only in the exceptions; a non-coparcener cannot hold it. flowchart TD Q1{"Is the person a coparcener?
(daughters since 2005)"} Q1 -- "No: widow, wife" --> N["Cannot be Karta
(Seth Govindram Sugar Mills)"] Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"Father, or the senior-most
coparcener?"} Q2 -- "Yes" --> K["Karta by birth and seniority;
presumed to be manager"] Q2 -- "No: junior member" --> J{"Karta gave up the office, distress
or calamity in his absence, or father
missing or far away?"} J -- "Yes" --> M["May act as manager
(Tribhovandas)"] J -- "No" --> X["Cannot act as manager
while the Karta is available"] Text description Is the person a coparcener? If no (for example a widow or wife), the person cannot be Karta. If yes, is the person the father or the senior-most coparcener? If yes, the person is Karta by birth and seniority, presumed to be manager. If no, a junior member can act as manager only if the Karta gives up the office, in distress or calamity affecting the family in his absence, or if the father is missing or far away and not expected back.
keyPoints: The Karta is the manager of the joint Hindu family; no Act creates the office. The father, or else the senior-most coparcener, is Karta by birth and seniority; the senior member is presumed to be manager. A junior member acts only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional circumstances ( Tribhovandas ). Coparcenership is a necessary qualification ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills ). Since 2005 a daughter is a coparcener, so the eldest coparcener can be Karta though a woman ( Sujata Sharma ); a widow or wife cannot. The Karta has no larger share; he is not an agent; the members' remedy is partition. He accounts on partition only for what he received, unless there is fraud or misappropriation. He cannot alienate except for necessity ( Brij Narain ); he does not manage separate property or Section 8 inheritance ( Chander Sen ).

caseLaws.name: Sujata Sharma v
caseLaws.facts: Manu Gupta (2015) Facts. Sujata Sharma, the eldest coparcener of D.R. Gupta & Sons (HUF), sued for a declaration that she was its Karta. The defendants argued that Section 6 deals with inheritance, not management. Principle. After the 2005 amendment, a woman who is the eldest coparcener can be Karta; her marriage does not alter this. Delhi High Court, Najmi Waziri J., CS(OS) 2011/2006, decided 22.12.2015, paras 25, 27 and 29. Why it matters. It is the leading authority that a woman can be Karta. Commissioner of Income Tax v. Seth Govindram Sugar Mills (1966) Facts. The question was whether a widow, who is a member of the joint family but not a coparcener, could be its manager. The Nagpur High Court had allowed a mother to act as manager; the Madras High Court had not. Principle. Coparcenership is a necessary qualification for managership; a woman who is not a coparcener cannot be the manager. AIR 1966 SC 24 (as quoted in Sujata Sharma , para 26). Why it matters. It fixes the qualification for the office, which is why Sujata Sharma turned on Section 6. Tribhovandas Haribhai Tamboli v. Gujarat Revenue Tribunal (1991) Facts. The question was the position of a junior member who deals with joint family property while the Karta is available. (Only the passages quoted in Sujata Sharma were checked.) Principle. Managership goes by birth and seniority; a junior member acts only if the Karta gives up the office or in exceptional circumstances. AIR 1991 SC 1538 (as quoted in Sujata Sharma , paras 6 and 15). Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court statement of how the office arises. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. A man with no son threw his house into the family hotchpot and claimed its rent should be taxed as income of the HUF of himself, his wife and unmarried daughter. Principle. Such a family is a joint Hindu family, but until a son is born the property "is really his"; the rent is his individual income. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. Calling oneself Karta does not turn one's own property into family property for all purposes. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Chander Sen inherited ₹1,85,043 standing to his father's credit in their firm. The Revenue treated it as the wealth of Chander Sen's joint family with his sons. Principle. A son inherits under Section 8 in his individual capacity, not as Karta of his own family. (1986) 3 SCC 567 : AIR 1986 SC 1753. Why it matters. It limits the property a Karta manages. Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged family property for Rs. 11,000 in 1908 to pay off two earlier mortgages. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding. Principle. "The managing co-parcener of a joint undivided estate cannot alienate or burden the estate qua manager except for purposes of necessity" (para 17). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It states the basic limit on the Karta's power.

selfTest.q: 1. Who is the Karta by default?
selfTest.a: The father; in his absence, the senior-most coparcener (Mulla, section 236; Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 2. When can a junior member act as manager while the Karta is alive?
selfTest.a: If the Karta gives up the office, in distress or calamity affecting the family in the Karta's absence, or if the father is missing or far away and not expected back soon ( Tribhovandas ).

selfTest.q: 3. Why could a widow not be Karta, and can she be one today?
selfTest.a: Because coparcenership is a necessary qualification and she is not a coparcener ( Seth Govindram Sugar Mills ). Section 6(1) makes daughters, not widows, coparceners, so she still cannot.

selfTest.q: 4. Which case held that a woman can be Karta, and which court decided it?
selfTest.a: Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015), a single judge of the Delhi High Court.

selfTest.q: 5. A coparcener is unhappy with the Karta's spending on family ceremonies. What is his remedy?
selfTest.a: To demand partition (Mulla, section 237). The Karta need not economise like a trustee while he spends for family purposes.

selfTest.q: 6. Is a guardian appointed for a minor coparcener's undivided interest?
selfTest.a: No, where an adult member manages the joint family property (Section 12, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act); a High Court's power is saved.

family-law-i-u1-t1.subtitle: Shruti, Smriti, commentaries, custom, legislation, precedent and equity

en.inOneMinute: The sources of Hindu law are the places its rules come from. The old sources are Shruti (the Vedas), Smriti (the ancient law books), the commentaries and digests written on the Smritis, and custom . The modern sources are Acts of Parliament, court decisions, and justice, equity and good conscience. Today the order is reversed. The Acts of 1955 and 1956 come first. Each Act says that the old texts and customs stop having effect on any matter the Act covers, unless the Act itself keeps them. Custom survives only where an Act saves it, for example customary marriage rites (Section 7) and customary divorce (Section 29(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act). Exams ask for the list of sources, the meaning of each, the test for a valid custom, and the rule that clear proof of usage outweighs the written text. Write both layers, old and modern, and end with how they rank today.
legalProvision: No single section lists the sources. These provisions decide what a custom is and how the sources rank.

Section 3(a), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. the expressions "custom" and "usage" signify any rule which, having been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, has obtained the force of law among Hindus in any local area, tribe, community, group or family: Provided that the rule is certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy; and Provided further that in the case of a rule applicable only to a family it has not been discontinued by the family;

Section 4, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 29(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Nothing contained in this Act shall be deemed to affect any right recognised by custom or conferred by any special enactment to obtain the dissolution of a Hindu marriage, whether solemnized before or after the commencement of this Act.
Article 13(3)(a), Constitution. "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law;
Article 141, Constitution. The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.
In simple words

Section 3(a): a custom is a rule that has been followed continuously and in the same way for a long time, so that it has become law for Hindus of a local area, tribe, community, group or family. It must be certain, and not unreasonable or against public policy. A family custom must not have been given up by the family. Section 3(1)(d) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gives the same definition. Section 4: on any matter the Act deals with, the old texts, their interpretation and any custom stop having effect. Any other earlier law stops having effect where it clashes with the Act. Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, and Section 5 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, say the same thing. Both limbs start with "Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act", so an express saving in the Act survives. Section 29(2): the Act does not take away a right, recognised by custom or given by a special law, to obtain a divorce. Article 13(3)(a): custom having the force of law is "law" for Part III, so it must respect the fundamental rights. Article 141: what the Supreme Court declares as law binds every court in India.
en.meaning:
A source of law is the origin of a legal rule: the place a judge looks to find it. Hindu law grew over many centuries, so its sources come in two layers. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Hindu law has an ancient layer and a modern layer of sources. flowchart TD S["Sources of Hindu law"] S --> A["Ancient sources"] S --> M["Modern sources"] A --> A1["Shruti
(the Vedas)"] A --> A2["Smriti
(Manu, Yajnavalkya, Narada)"] A --> A3["Commentaries and digests
(Mitakshara, Dayabhaga)"] A --> A4["Custom"] M --> M1["Legislation
(Acts of 1955-56)"] M --> M2["Judicial precedent
(Article 141)"] M --> M3["Justice, equity and
good conscience"] Text description Sources of Hindu law divide into ancient sources (Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, custom) and modern sources (legislation, judicial precedent, and justice, equity and good conscience). Ancient sources: Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, and custom. Mulla (Principles of Hindu Law, 14th ed., section 8) names the three main sources of Hindu law as the Sruti, the Smriti and custom. For practical purposes he divides them into the original texts, the commentaries and digests, and custom. Modern sources: legislation, judicial decisions, and justice, equity and good conscience . Mulla (section 8) says these must be added "for all practical purposes" to the main sources. The question this topic answers. Where does a court find a rule of Hindu law, and which source wins when two of them differ? Why it matters. The old texts were written for a very different society. The Acts of 1955 and 1956 changed much of the law. A student must know which source still governs a matter, which one has been displaced, and where custom is still allowed.
keyPoints: Ancient sources: Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, custom. Modern sources: legislation, precedent, justice, equity and good conscience. Shruti = that which was heard; Smriti = that which was remembered. Three principal Smritis: Manu, Yajnavalkya, Narada. Mitakshara: commentary on Yajnavalkya by Vijnaneswara. Dayabhaga: digest of all Codes by Jimutavahana. "Clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text of the law" ( Collector of Madura ). Section 3(a): custom must be continuous, uniform, long, certain, reasonable and not against public policy; a family custom must not be discontinued. Section 4 of each Act ends old text and custom on matters the Act covers, unless the Act expressly saves them. Custom saved by the Hindu Marriage Act: Sections 5(iv), 5(v), 7(1), 29(2). Hindu law today, apart from codified branches, is "Judge-made law" ( Surjit Lal Chhabda ).

caseLaws.name: Collector of Madura v
caseLaws.facts: Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868) Facts. Known as the Ramnad case, it concerned the validity of an adoption made by a widow. Mulla records that the Privy Council first laid down in it the rule on the consent of the husband's sapindas to such an adoption. Principle. Courts must follow the rules in the commentaries even if they seem to rest on a wrong reading of the Smritis, because "clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text of the law". (1868) 12 M.I.A. 397 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It is the classic authority that custom and the commentaries, not the bare Smriti text, decide the law. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. Surjit Lal threw his self-acquired house, Kathoke Lodge, into the family hotchpot in 1956. His family was himself, his wife and an unmarried daughter. He claimed the rent should be taxed as income of a Hindu undivided family. Principle. Hindu law today, apart from its codified branches, "is Judge-made law", though the Smritis keep their juristic weight. The Court held that the property remained, in the eye of Hindu law, his own, and dismissed the appeal. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It places judicial decisions beside the old texts as a working source. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter becomes a coparcener under the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. Basic Hindu law emanates from the Vedas and past shrutis and smritis (para 18). Custom, equity, justice, conscience and judicial decisions also acted as sources, and the law "was not static but always progressive" (para 21). (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court summary of the sources and of codification. Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) Facts. Hindu husbands converted to Islam and married again without dissolving their Hindu marriages. Principle. The conduct of a converting spouse is judged by justice, equity and good conscience. The second marriage, violating that rule, "would be void on that ground also" and attracts Section 494 IPC. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It shows justice, equity and good conscience still working as a source of decision. Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) Facts. Two commercial pilots obtained a "marriage certificate" from the Vadik Jankalyan Samiti and then a registration certificate, without performing any marriage ceremony. The family ceremony was fixed for a later date. Principle. A Hindu marriage must be solemnized with the rites and ceremonies under Section 7. Without them there is no Hindu marriage, and the certificates were declared null and void. 2024 INSC 355. Why it matters. It shows that custom, through Section 7, still decides how a Hindu marriage is performed.

selfTest.q: 1. What do "Shruti" and "Smriti" literally mean?
selfTest.a: Shruti means "that which was heard"; Smriti means "that which was remembered" (Mulla, section 8).

selfTest.q: 2. Who wrote the Mitakshara, and on which Smriti is it a commentary?
selfTest.a: Vijnaneswara, in the latter part of the eleventh century; it is a running commentary on the Code of Yajnavalkya.

selfTest.q: 3. What must a custom satisfy under Section 3(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act?
selfTest.a: It must have been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time and obtained the force of law; it must be certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy; a family custom must not have been discontinued.

selfTest.q: 4. Which provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act still allow custom?
selfTest.a: Sections 5(iv), 5(v), 7(1) and 29(2), and the residuary rule in Section 2(1)(c).

selfTest.q: 5. Which case says that clear proof of usage outweighs the written text?
selfTest.a: Collector of Madura v. Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868), the Ramnad case.

selfTest.q: 6. In which sub-school does Mulla place the Nirnayasindhu?
selfTest.a: In the Benares sub-school and the Maharashtra or Bombay sub-school, not in Mithila.
