legalProvision: ఆధారాల జాబితా ఇచ్చే ఒక్క సెక్షన్ కూడా లేదు. ఆచారం అంటే ఏమిటో, ఆధారాలు ఏ క్రమంలో ఉంటాయో ఈ నిబంధనలు నిర్ణయిస్తాయి.

Section 3(a), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. the expressions "custom" and "usage" signify any rule which, having been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, has obtained the force of law among Hindus in any local area, tribe, community, group or family: Provided that the rule is certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy; and Provided further that in the case of a rule applicable only to a family it has not been discontinued by the family;

Section 4, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 29(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Nothing contained in this Act shall be deemed to affect any right recognised by custom or conferred by any special enactment to obtain the dissolution of a Hindu marriage, whether solemnized before or after the commencement of this Act.
Article 13(3)(a), Constitution. "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law;
Article 141, Constitution. The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 3(a): చాలా కాలంగా నిరంతరంగా, ఒకే విధంగా పాటించడం వల్ల ఒక ప్రాంతం, తెగ, సమాజం, గుంపు లేదా కుటుంబంలోని హిందువులకు చట్టంగా మారిన నియమమే ఆచారం. అది నిశ్చితంగా ఉండాలి; అసమంజసంగా గానీ, ప్రజా విధానానికి విరుద్ధంగా గానీ ఉండకూడదు. కుటుంబ ఆచారాన్ని ఆ కుటుంబం వదిలేసి ఉండకూడదు. హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం, 1956 సెక్షన్ 3(1)(d) కూడా ఇదే నిర్వచనం ఇస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 4: చట్టం వ్యవహరించే ఏ విషయంపైనైనా ప్రాచీన గ్రంథాలు, వాటి వ్యాఖ్యానం, ఏ ఆచారమైనా అమలులో ఉండవు. ఇతర ఏ పాత చట్టమైనా ఈ చట్టంతో విరుద్ధంగా ఉన్నంత మేరకు అమలులో ఉండదు. హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం, 1956 సెక్షన్ 4, హిందూ దత్తత మరియు భరణ చట్టం, 1956 సెక్షన్ 4, హిందూ మైనారిటీ మరియు సంరక్షకత్వ చట్టం, 1956 సెక్షన్ 5 కూడా ఇదే చెబుతాయి. రెండు భాగాలూ "Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act" తో మొదలవుతాయి కాబట్టి, చట్టంలోని స్పష్టమైన మినహాయింపు నిలుస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 29(2): ఆచారం గుర్తించిన, లేదా ప్రత్యేక చట్టం ఇచ్చిన, విడాకులు పొందే హక్కును ఈ చట్టం తీసివేయదు. ఆర్టికల్ 13(3)(a): చట్ట బలం ఉన్న ఆచారం Part III కోసం "చట్టమే"; కాబట్టి అది ప్రాథమిక హక్కులను గౌరవించాలి. ఆర్టికల్ 141: సుప్రీంకోర్టు ప్రకటించిన చట్టం భారతదేశంలోని ప్రతి కోర్టునూ బంధిస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
చట్టపు ఆధారం అంటే ఒక చట్ట నియమం పుట్టిన మూలం: ఆ నియమాన్ని కనుగొనడానికి న్యాయమూర్తి చూసే చోటు. హిందూ చట్టం అనేక శతాబ్దాలుగా పెరిగింది, కాబట్టి దాని ఆధారాలు రెండు పొరలుగా ఉంటాయి. Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. హిందూ చట్టానికి ప్రాచీన పొర, ఆధునిక పొర అనే రెండు పొరల ఆధారాలు ఉన్నాయి. flowchart TD S["హిందూ చట్టపు ఆధారాలు"] S --> A["ప్రాచీన ఆధారాలు"] S --> M["ఆధునిక ఆధారాలు"] A --> A1["శ్రుతి
(వేదాలు)"] A --> A2["స్మృతి
(మను, యాజ్ఞవల్క్య, నారద)"] A --> A3["వ్యాఖ్యానాలు, డైజెస్ట్‌లు
(మితాక్షర, దాయభాగ)"] A --> A4["ఆచారం"] M --> M1["శాసనం
(1955-56 చట్టాలు)"] M --> M2["న్యాయ పూర్వనిర్ణయం
(ఆర్టికల్ 141)"] M --> M3["న్యాయం, సమన్యాయం,
మంచి మనస్సాక్షి"] వచన వివరణ హిందూ చట్టపు ఆధారాలు ప్రాచీన ఆధారాలు (శ్రుతి, స్మృతి, వ్యాఖ్యానాలు మరియు డైజెస్ట్‌లు, ఆచారం), ఆధునిక ఆధారాలు (శాసనం, న్యాయ పూర్వనిర్ణయం, న్యాయం-సమన్యాయం-మంచి మనస్సాక్షి) గా విభజించబడతాయి. ప్రాచీన ఆధారాలు: శ్రుతి, స్మృతి, వ్యాఖ్యానాలు మరియు డైజెస్ట్‌లు, ఆచారం. ముల్లా (Principles of Hindu Law, 14వ ఎడిషన్, సెక్షన్ 8) హిందూ చట్టానికి మూడు ప్రధాన ఆధారాలు శ్రుతి, స్మృతి, ఆచారం అని చెబుతారు. ఆచరణ కోసం వాటిని మూల గ్రంథాలు, వ్యాఖ్యానాలు మరియు డైజెస్ట్‌లు, ఆచారం అని విభజిస్తారు. ఆధునిక ఆధారాలు: శాసనం, కోర్టు తీర్పులు, మరియు న్యాయం, సమన్యాయం, మంచి మనస్సాక్షి. ప్రధాన ఆధారాలకు ఇవి "for all practical purposes" జతచేయాలని ముల్లా (సెక్షన్ 8) చెబుతారు. ఈ అంశం జవాబిచ్చే ప్రశ్న. హిందూ చట్ట నియమాన్ని కోర్టు ఎక్కడ కనుగొంటుంది? రెండు ఆధారాలు భిన్నంగా చెబితే ఏది గెలుస్తుంది? ఇది ఎందుకు ముఖ్యం. ప్రాచీన గ్రంథాలు చాలా భిన్నమైన సమాజం కోసం రాయబడ్డాయి. 1955, 1956 చట్టాలు చాలా చట్టాన్ని మార్చాయి. ఏ విషయాన్ని ఇంకా ఏ ఆధారం పాలిస్తుందో, ఏది తొలగిపోయిందో, ఆచారానికి ఎక్కడ ఇంకా అనుమతి ఉందో విద్యార్థి తెలుసుకోవాలి.

selfTest.q: 1. "శ్రుతి", "స్మృతి" అక్షరాలా అర్థం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: శ్రుతి అంటే "విన్నది"; స్మృతి అంటే "జ్ఞాపకం ఉంచుకున్నది" (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 8).

selfTest.q: 2. మితాక్షరను ఎవరు రాశారు, అది ఏ స్మృతిపై వ్యాఖ్యానం?
selfTest.a: విజ్ఞానేశ్వరుడు, పదకొండవ శతాబ్దం చివరి భాగంలో; అది యాజ్ఞవల్క్య స్మృతిపై వరుస వ్యాఖ్యానం.

selfTest.q: 3. హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 3(a) కింద ఆచారం ఏమి సంతృప్తిపరచాలి?
selfTest.a: చాలా కాలం నిరంతరంగా, ఏకరీతిగా పాటించి చట్ట బలం పొంది ఉండాలి; నిశ్చితంగా ఉండాలి, అసమంజసం గానీ ప్రజా విధానానికి విరుద్ధం గానీ కాకూడదు; కుటుంబ ఆచారం ఆగిపోయి ఉండకూడదు.

selfTest.q: 4. హిందూ వివాహ చట్టంలోని ఏ నిబంధనలు ఇంకా ఆచారానికి అనుమతిస్తాయి?
5. వాడుకకు స్పష్టమైన రుజువు రాతపూర్వక గ్రంథాన్ని మించిపోతుందని ఏ కేసు చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: Collector of Madura v. Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868), రామనాడ్ కేసు.

selfTest.q: 6. ముల్లా నిర్ణయసింధును ఏ ఉప-శాఖలో ఉంచారు?
selfTest.a: బనారస్ ఉప-శాఖలో, మహారాష్ట్ర లేదా బొంబాయి ఉప-శాఖలో; మిథిలలో కాదు.

hi.inOneMinute: The sources of Hindu law are the places its rules come from. The old sources are Shruti (the Vedas), Smriti (the ancient law books), the commentaries and digests written on the Smritis, and custom . The modern sources are Acts of Parliament, court decisions, and justice, equity and good conscience. Today the order is reversed. The Acts of 1955 and 1956 come first. Each Act says that the old texts and customs stop having effect on any matter the Act covers, unless the Act itself keeps them. Custom survives only where an Act saves it, for example customary marriage rites (Section 7) and customary divorce (Section 29(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act). Exams ask for the list of sources, the meaning of each, the test for a valid custom, and the rule that clear proof of usage outweighs the written text. Write both layers, old and modern, and end with how they rank today.
legalProvision: No single section lists the sources. These provisions decide what a custom is and how the sources rank.

Section 3(a), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. the expressions "custom" and "usage" signify any rule which, having been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, has obtained the force of law among Hindus in any local area, tribe, community, group or family: Provided that the rule is certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy; and Provided further that in the case of a rule applicable only to a family it has not been discontinued by the family;

Section 4, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 29(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Nothing contained in this Act shall be deemed to affect any right recognised by custom or conferred by any special enactment to obtain the dissolution of a Hindu marriage, whether solemnized before or after the commencement of this Act.
Article 13(3)(a), Constitution. "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law;
Article 141, Constitution. The law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all courts within the territory of India.
In simple words

Section 3(a): a custom is a rule that has been followed continuously and in the same way for a long time, so that it has become law for Hindus of a local area, tribe, community, group or family. It must be certain, and not unreasonable or against public policy. A family custom must not have been given up by the family. Section 3(1)(d) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 gives the same definition. Section 4: on any matter the Act deals with, the old texts, their interpretation and any custom stop having effect. Any other earlier law stops having effect where it clashes with the Act. Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, and Section 5 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, say the same thing. Both limbs start with "Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act", so an express saving in the Act survives. Section 29(2): the Act does not take away a right, recognised by custom or given by a special law, to obtain a divorce. Article 13(3)(a): custom having the force of law is "law" for Part III, so it must respect the fundamental rights. Article 141: what the Supreme Court declares as law binds every court in India.
hi.meaning:
A source of law is the origin of a legal rule: the place a judge looks to find it. Hindu law grew over many centuries, so its sources come in two layers. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Hindu law has an ancient layer and a modern layer of sources. flowchart TD S["Sources of Hindu law"] S --> A["Ancient sources"] S --> M["Modern sources"] A --> A1["Shruti
(the Vedas)"] A --> A2["Smriti
(Manu, Yajnavalkya, Narada)"] A --> A3["Commentaries and digests
(Mitakshara, Dayabhaga)"] A --> A4["Custom"] M --> M1["Legislation
(Acts of 1955-56)"] M --> M2["Judicial precedent
(Article 141)"] M --> M3["Justice, equity and
good conscience"] Text description Sources of Hindu law divide into ancient sources (Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, custom) and modern sources (legislation, judicial precedent, and justice, equity and good conscience). Ancient sources: Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, and custom. Mulla (Principles of Hindu Law, 14th ed., section 8) names the three main sources of Hindu law as the Sruti, the Smriti and custom. For practical purposes he divides them into the original texts, the commentaries and digests, and custom. Modern sources: legislation, judicial decisions, and justice, equity and good conscience . Mulla (section 8) says these must be added "for all practical purposes" to the main sources. The question this topic answers. Where does a court find a rule of Hindu law, and which source wins when two of them differ? Why it matters. The old texts were written for a very different society. The Acts of 1955 and 1956 changed much of the law. A student must know which source still governs a matter, which one has been displaced, and where custom is still allowed.
keyPoints: Ancient sources: Shruti, Smriti, commentaries and digests, custom. Modern sources: legislation, precedent, justice, equity and good conscience. Shruti = that which was heard; Smriti = that which was remembered. Three principal Smritis: Manu, Yajnavalkya, Narada. Mitakshara: commentary on Yajnavalkya by Vijnaneswara. Dayabhaga: digest of all Codes by Jimutavahana. "Clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text of the law" ( Collector of Madura ). Section 3(a): custom must be continuous, uniform, long, certain, reasonable and not against public policy; a family custom must not be discontinued. Section 4 of each Act ends old text and custom on matters the Act covers, unless the Act expressly saves them. Custom saved by the Hindu Marriage Act: Sections 5(iv), 5(v), 7(1), 29(2). Hindu law today, apart from codified branches, is "Judge-made law" ( Surjit Lal Chhabda ).

caseLaws.name: Collector of Madura v
caseLaws.facts: Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868) Facts. Known as the Ramnad case, it concerned the validity of an adoption made by a widow. Mulla records that the Privy Council first laid down in it the rule on the consent of the husband's sapindas to such an adoption. Principle. Courts must follow the rules in the commentaries even if they seem to rest on a wrong reading of the Smritis, because "clear proof of usage will outweigh the written text of the law". (1868) 12 M.I.A. 397 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It is the classic authority that custom and the commentaries, not the bare Smriti text, decide the law. Surjit Lal Chhabda v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1975) Facts. Surjit Lal threw his self-acquired house, Kathoke Lodge, into the family hotchpot in 1956. His family was himself, his wife and an unmarried daughter. He claimed the rent should be taxed as income of a Hindu undivided family. Principle. Hindu law today, apart from its codified branches, "is Judge-made law", though the Smritis keep their juristic weight. The Court held that the property remained, in the eye of Hindu law, his own, and dismissed the appeal. (1976) 3 SCC 142 : AIR 1976 SC 109. Why it matters. It places judicial decisions beside the old texts as a working source. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. The question was whether a daughter becomes a coparcener under the amended Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. Basic Hindu law emanates from the Vedas and past shrutis and smritis (para 18). Custom, equity, justice, conscience and judicial decisions also acted as sources, and the law "was not static but always progressive" (para 21). (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court summary of the sources and of codification. Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) Facts. Hindu husbands converted to Islam and married again without dissolving their Hindu marriages. Principle. The conduct of a converting spouse is judged by justice, equity and good conscience. The second marriage, violating that rule, "would be void on that ground also" and attracts Section 494 IPC. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It shows justice, equity and good conscience still working as a source of decision. Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) Facts. Two commercial pilots obtained a "marriage certificate" from the Vadik Jankalyan Samiti and then a registration certificate, without performing any marriage ceremony. The family ceremony was fixed for a later date. Principle. A Hindu marriage must be solemnized with the rites and ceremonies under Section 7. Without them there is no Hindu marriage, and the certificates were declared null and void. 2024 INSC 355. Why it matters. It shows that custom, through Section 7, still decides how a Hindu marriage is performed.

selfTest.q: 1. What do "Shruti" and "Smriti" literally mean?
selfTest.a: Shruti means "that which was heard"; Smriti means "that which was remembered" (Mulla, section 8).

selfTest.q: 2. Who wrote the Mitakshara, and on which Smriti is it a commentary?
selfTest.a: Vijnaneswara, in the latter part of the eleventh century; it is a running commentary on the Code of Yajnavalkya.

selfTest.q: 3. What must a custom satisfy under Section 3(a) of the Hindu Marriage Act?
selfTest.a: It must have been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time and obtained the force of law; it must be certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy; a family custom must not have been discontinued.

selfTest.q: 4. Which provisions of the Hindu Marriage Act still allow custom?
selfTest.a: Sections 5(iv), 5(v), 7(1) and 29(2), and the residuary rule in Section 2(1)(c).

selfTest.q: 5. Which case says that clear proof of usage outweighs the written text?
selfTest.a: Collector of Madura v. Moottoo Ramalinga Sathupathy (1868), the Ramnad case.

selfTest.q: 6. In which sub-school does Mulla place the Nirnayasindhu?
selfTest.a: In the Benares sub-school and the Maharashtra or Bombay sub-school, not in Mithila.

family-law-i-u1-t4.subtitle: Birthright and fluctuating shares in the Mitakshara against defined shares in the Dayabhaga

en.inOneMinute: The Mitakshara and the Dayabhaga are the two schools of Hindu law. They differ most on how a family holds property. Under the Mitakshara, a son gets an interest in ancestral property at birth. No one has a fixed share until partition, and on a death the interest passes to the others by survivorship . Under the Dayabhaga, a son gets nothing by birth. A coparcenary begins only on the father's death, each coparcener holds a defined share, and that share passes to his own heirs. They also differ on the basis of inheritance: nearness of blood in the Mitakshara, spiritual benefit in the Dayabhaga. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 changed the Mitakshara side. Since 2005, Section 6 makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, replaces survivorship with succession, and ends the sons' pious obligation for new debts. Exams ask for the points of difference, the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary ( Ghamandi Ram ), and how Section 6 changed the law ( Gurupad , Vineeta Sharma ).
legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. (1) On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. ... (3) Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenery property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,― (a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; ... Explanation. ―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. (4) After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: [proviso saves debts contracted before the 2005 Act] (5) Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation. ―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.

Explanation to Section 30, Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as originally enacted, quoted in Gurupad ). When a male Hindu dies after the commencement of this Act, having at the time of his death an interest in a Mitakshara coparcenary property, his interest in the property shall devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with this Act: Provided that, if the deceased had left him surviving a female relative specified in class I of the Schedule or a male relative specified in that class who claims through such a female relative, the interest of the deceased in the Mitakshara coparcenary property shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship. Explanation 1. —For the purposes of this section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. ...
In simple words

Section 6(1): in a Mitakshara joint family, a daughter is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Dispositions and partitions made before 20 December 2004 are not disturbed. Section 6(3): when a coparcener dies after 9 September 2005, his interest goes by will or by succession under the Act, not by survivorship . To find his interest, a partition is assumed just before his death, and the daughter gets the same share as a son. Section 6(4): for debts after 2005, no court lets a creditor proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson only on the ground of pious obligation. Debts contracted before 2005 are saved, and for that saving "son, grandson or great-grandson" means one born or adopted before the 2005 Act (Explanation to Section 6(4)). Section 6(5): Section 6 does not touch a partition made before 20 December 2004, and "partition" means only a registered partition deed or a court decree. Section 30, Explanation: a male Hindu can dispose of his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will. Section 6 as enacted in 1956: survivorship was the normal rule, but if the deceased left a female Class I heir (or a male Class I heir claiming through her), his interest passed by succession, and his share was worked out by assuming a partition just before his death.
en.meaning:
Mitakshara is Vijnaneswara's running commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, written in the latter part of the eleventh century. Its family law rests on the son's birthright in ancestral property. Dayabhaga is Jimutavahana's digest of all the Smriti Codes, written about the beginning of the twelfth century. Its family law rests on ownership by the father and defined shares (Mulla, section 11(3)). "The conception of a coparcenary and of coparcenary property according to the Dayabhaga law is entirely distinct from that according to the Mitakshara law" (Mulla, section 272). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Mitakshara: interest at birth, survivorship (now succession). Dayabhaga: nothing at birth, defined shares that pass to heirs. flowchart TD subgraph M["Mitakshara"] M1["Son is born"] --> M2["At once a coparcener
with his father"] M2 --> M3["Interest fluctuates
with births and deaths"] M3 --> M4["On a death: survivorship
after 2005: succession, s. 6(3)"] end subgraph D["Dayabhaga"] D1["Son is born"] --> D2["No interest while
father lives"] D2 --> D3["Father dies: sons inherit
defined shares as coparceners"] D3 --> D4["On a death: share passes
to his own heirs"] end Text description Mitakshara: a son is born and at once becomes a coparcener with his father; his interest fluctuates with births and deaths; on a coparcener's death his interest passed by survivorship, and after 2005 passes by succession under Section 6(3). Dayabhaga: a son gets nothing while the father lives; on the father's death the sons inherit as heirs and hold defined shares as coparceners; on a coparcener's death his share passes to his own heirs. The question this topic answers. How does a member hold joint family property, and what happens to his interest when he or another member is born or dies? Why the two schools differ. The Dayabhaga school did not accept the Mitakshara view that a son becomes an owner at birth. For the Dayabhaga, property passes only on the owner's death. Every other difference on the joint family follows from this.
keyPoints: Mitakshara: right by birth, unity of ownership, fluctuating interest, survivorship (now replaced by succession). Dayabhaga: no birthright, defined shares, unity of possession but no unity of ownership, shares pass to heirs. A Dayabhaga coparcenary begins only on the father's death; there is none between father and sons. A Dayabhaga father has absolute power over ancestral property. Ghamandi Ram : six incidents; the coparcenary is a creature of law. Section 6(1): daughters are Mitakshara coparceners by birth; 6(3): succession replaces survivorship after 2005; 6(4): no pious obligation for new debts; 6(5): only a registered deed or a decree counts as partition. Gurupad : widow's 7/24 share under the old Section 6. Vineeta Sharma : father need not be alive on 9 September 2005; the test of a coparcener is the right to demand partition.

caseLaws.name: State Bank of India v
caseLaws.facts: Ghamandi Ram (1969) Facts. The karta of a joint Hindu family firm that had traded in what became Pakistan claimed the surplus left in the firm's bank account after Partition. The question was whether the family firm was an "individual" or a "body of individuals" under a Pakistan notification . Principle. A Mitakshara coparcenary holds property in collective ownership in a quasi-corporate capacity; the Court listed its six incidents and held it is "a creature of law". The firm was a body of individuals, the amount had vested in the Custodian in Pakistan, and the Bank's appeal was allowed. AIR 1969 SC 1330. Why it matters. It is the standard statement of the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench was asked whether a daughter is a coparcener under the amended Section 6 if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener by birth, born before or after the amendment; the father need not be alive on 9 September 2005; the old notional partition did not disrupt the coparcenary; oral partition is not accepted except in exceptional cases (para 129). (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It places daughters inside the Mitakshara coparcenary on the same footing as sons and overrules Prakash v. Phulavati . Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960 leaving his widow, two sons and three daughters, and Mitakshara joint family property. The widow sued for a 7/24 share. Principle. Under Explanation 1 to the original Section 6, the assumed partition just before death must be worked out fully; the widow takes her share on that partition (1/4) plus her share in the deceased's interest (1/24). Appeal dismissed with costs. (1978) 3 SCC 383 : AIR 1978 SC 1239. Why it matters. It shows how the 1956 Act displaced survivorship before 2005. Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. Sita Ram, managing ancestral property for himself and his two minor sons, mortgaged it in 1908 to pay off two earlier mortgages. The sons sued to have the mortgage declared not binding on them. Principle. A manager cannot burden the estate except for necessity; a father's mortgage binds the sons only if it pays an antecedent debt, "antecedent in fact as well as in time". The mortgage here paid earlier debts, so it bound the estate; appeal allowed. Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It shows the Mitakshara limits on the manager and the father's power over ancestral property, which the Dayabhaga does not have.

selfTest.q: 1. In which school does a son get a right by birth?
selfTest.a: The Mitakshara.

selfTest.q: 2. Does a Dayabhaga coparcener's share rise or fall with births and deaths?
selfTest.a: No. Each coparcener takes a defined share that does not fluctuate ( Vineeta Sharma , para 35).

selfTest.q: 3. Which case lists the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary?
selfTest.a: State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969).

selfTest.q: 4. What did Section 6(4) do to the pious obligation?
selfTest.a: For debts after 2005, no court recognises proceedings against a son, grandson or great-grandson solely on that ground. Earlier debts are saved.

selfTest.q: 5. In Gurupad , how did the widow get 7/24?
selfTest.a: 1/4 on the assumed partition between her husband and two sons, plus 1/6 of her husband's 1/4 (that is, 1/24) as one of six Class I heirs.

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Dayabhaga son demand partition from his father?
selfTest.a: No. The father is the sole owner of the ancestral property (Mulla, section 275).

legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. (1) On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. ... (3) Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenery property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,― (a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; ... Explanation. ―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. (4) After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: [proviso saves debts contracted before the 2005 Act] (5) Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation. ―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.

Explanation to Section 30, Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as originally enacted, quoted in Gurupad ). When a male Hindu dies after the commencement of this Act, having at the time of his death an interest in a Mitakshara coparcenary property, his interest in the property shall devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with this Act: Provided that, if the deceased had left him surviving a female relative specified in class I of the Schedule or a male relative specified in that class who claims through such a female relative, the interest of the deceased in the Mitakshara coparcenary property shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship. Explanation 1. —For the purposes of this section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. ...
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 6(1): మితాక్షర ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబంలో కూతురు పుట్టుకతోనే కోపార్సినర్ ; కొడుకుతో సమాన హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలు. 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన అన్యాక్రాంతాలు, విభజన లను ఇది కదిలించదు. సెక్షన్ 6(3): 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాత కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే, అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా కాకుండా వీలునామా ద్వారా లేదా చట్టం కింది వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్తుంది. అతని హక్కును తెలుసుకోవడానికి మరణానికి ముందు విభజన జరిగినట్టు భావిస్తారు; కూతురికి కొడుకుతో సమాన వాటా వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(4): 2005 తర్వాతి అప్పులకు, పవిత్ర బాధ్యత ఆధారంగా మాత్రమే కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడిపై రుణదాత చర్య తీసుకోవడాన్ని ఏ కోర్టూ అనుమతించదు. 2005 కు ముందు చేసిన అప్పులకు మినహాయింపు ఉంది; ఆ మినహాయింపు కోసం "కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడు" అంటే 2005 చట్టానికి ముందు పుట్టినవారు లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్నవారు (సెక్షన్ 6(4) Explanation). సెక్షన్ 6(5): 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన విభజనను సెక్షన్ 6 తాకదు; "విభజన" అంటే రిజిస్టర్డ్ విభజన దస్తావేజు లేదా కోర్టు డిక్రీ మాత్రమే. సెక్షన్ 30, Explanation: పురుష హిందువు మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిలో తన హక్కును వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. 1956 లో అసలు సెక్షన్ 6: సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ సాధారణ నియమం; కానీ మరణించినవారికి Class I స్త్రీ వారసురాలు (లేదా ఆమె ద్వారా క్లెయిమ్ చేసే Class I పురుష వారసుడు) ఉంటే, అతని హక్కు వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్ళేది; మరణానికి ముందు విభజన జరిగినట్టు భావించి అతని వాటాను లెక్కించేవారు.

మితాక్షర అంటే పదకొండో శతాబ్దం చివరి భాగంలో విజ్ఞానేశ్వరుడు యాజ్ఞవల్క్య స్మృతిపై రాసిన వరుస వ్యాఖ్యానం. దాని కుటుంబ చట్టం పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తిలో కొడుకు జన్మహక్కుపై ఆధారపడుతుంది. దాయభాగ అంటే సుమారు పన్నెండో శతాబ్దం ప్రారంభంలో జీమూతవాహనుడు రాసిన అన్ని స్మృతుల డైజెస్ట్. దాని కుటుంబ చట్టం తండ్రి యాజమాన్యం, నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలపై ఆధారపడుతుంది (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 11(3)). "The conception of a coparcenary and of coparcenary property according to the Dayabhaga law is entirely distinct from that according to the Mitakshara law" (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 272). Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. మితాక్షర: పుట్టుకతో హక్కు, సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ (ఇప్పుడు వారసత్వం). దాయభాగ: పుట్టుకతో ఏమీ లేదు, వారసులకు వెళ్ళే నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలు. flowchart TD subgraph M["మితాక్షర"] M1["కొడుకు పుడతాడు"] --> M2["వెంటనే తండ్రితో
కోపార్సినర్"] M2 --> M3["జననాలు, మరణాలతో
హక్కు మారుతుంది"] M3 --> M4["మరణంపై: సర్వైవర్‌షిప్
2005 తర్వాత: వారసత్వం, సె. 6(3)"] end subgraph D["దాయభాగ"] D1["కొడుకు పుడతాడు"] --> D2["తండ్రి బతికి ఉండగా
హక్కు లేదు"] D2 --> D3["తండ్రి మరణం: కొడుకులు కోపార్సినర్లుగా
నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలు పొందుతారు"] D3 --> D4["మరణంపై: వాటా అతని
సొంత వారసులకు"] end వచన వివరణ మితాక్షర: కొడుకు పుట్టగానే తండ్రితో కోపార్సినర్ అవుతాడు; అతని హక్కు జననాలు, మరణాలతో మారుతుంది; కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా వెళ్ళేది, 2005 తర్వాత సెక్షన్ 6(3) కింద వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్తుంది. దాయభాగ: తండ్రి బతికి ఉండగా కొడుకుకు ఏమీ రాదు; తండ్రి మరణిస్తే కొడుకులు వారసులుగా తీసుకుని కోపార్సినర్లుగా నిర్దిష్ట వాటాలు కలిగి ఉంటారు; కోపార్సినర్ మరణిస్తే అతని వాటా అతని సొంత వారసులకు వెళ్తుంది. ఈ అంశం జవాబిచ్చే ప్రశ్న. ఒక సభ్యుడు ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని ఎలా కలిగి ఉంటాడు, అతను లేదా మరో సభ్యుడు పుట్టినప్పుడు, మరణించినప్పుడు అతని హక్కుకు ఏమవుతుంది? రెండు శాఖలు ఎందుకు విభేదిస్తాయి. కొడుకు పుట్టుకతోనే యజమాని అవుతాడనే మితాక్షర అభిప్రాయాన్ని దాయభాగ శాఖ అంగీకరించలేదు. దాయభాగ ప్రకారం యజమాని మరణించినప్పుడే ఆస్తి వెళ్తుంది. ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబంపై మిగతా తేడాలన్నీ దీని నుంచే వస్తాయి.

selfTest.q: 1. ఏ శాఖలో కొడుకుకు పుట్టుకతో హక్కు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: మితాక్షర.

selfTest.q: 2. దాయభాగ కోపార్సినర్ వాటా జననాలు, మరణాలతో పెరుగుతుందా, తగ్గుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ప్రతి కోపార్సినర్‌కు మారని నిర్దిష్ట వాటా ఉంటుంది ( Vineeta Sharma , para 35).

selfTest.q: 3. మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ లక్షణాలను ఏ కేసు జాబితా చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969).

selfTest.q: 4. సెక్షన్ 6(4) పవిత్ర బాధ్యతను ఏం చేసింది?
selfTest.a: 2005 తర్వాతి అప్పులకు, ఆ కారణంతో మాత్రమే కొడుకు, మనవడు, మునిమనవడిపై చర్యను ఏ కోర్టూ గుర్తించదు. పాత అప్పులకు మినహాయింపు ఉంది.

selfTest.q: 5. Gurupad లో భార్యకు 7/24 ఎలా వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: భర్త, ఇద్దరు కొడుకుల మధ్య ఊహించిన విభజనలో 1/4, దానికి తోడు ఆరుగురు Class I వారసుల్లో ఒకరిగా భర్త 1/4 లో 1/6 (అంటే 1/24).

selfTest.q: 6. దాయభాగ కొడుకు తండ్రి నుంచి విభజన కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తికి తండ్రే ఏకైక యజమాని (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 275).

hi.inOneMinute: The Mitakshara and the Dayabhaga are the two schools of Hindu law. They differ most on how a family holds property. Under the Mitakshara, a son gets an interest in ancestral property at birth. No one has a fixed share until partition, and on a death the interest passes to the others by survivorship . Under the Dayabhaga, a son gets nothing by birth. A coparcenary begins only on the father's death, each coparcener holds a defined share, and that share passes to his own heirs. They also differ on the basis of inheritance: nearness of blood in the Mitakshara, spiritual benefit in the Dayabhaga. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 changed the Mitakshara side. Since 2005, Section 6 makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, replaces survivorship with succession, and ends the sons' pious obligation for new debts. Exams ask for the points of difference, the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary ( Ghamandi Ram ), and how Section 6 changed the law ( Gurupad , Vineeta Sharma ).
legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as substituted in 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. (1) On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,― (a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenery property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenery property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004. ... (3) Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenery property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,― (a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; ... Explanation. ―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. (4) After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: [proviso saves debts contracted before the 2005 Act] (5) Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation. ―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.

Explanation to Section 30, Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.

Section 6, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as originally enacted, quoted in Gurupad ). When a male Hindu dies after the commencement of this Act, having at the time of his death an interest in a Mitakshara coparcenary property, his interest in the property shall devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with this Act: Provided that, if the deceased had left him surviving a female relative specified in class I of the Schedule or a male relative specified in that class who claims through such a female relative, the interest of the deceased in the Mitakshara coparcenary property shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship. Explanation 1. —For the purposes of this section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. ...
In simple words

Section 6(1): in a Mitakshara joint family, a daughter is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Dispositions and partitions made before 20 December 2004 are not disturbed. Section 6(3): when a coparcener dies after 9 September 2005, his interest goes by will or by succession under the Act, not by survivorship . To find his interest, a partition is assumed just before his death, and the daughter gets the same share as a son. Section 6(4): for debts after 2005, no court lets a creditor proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson only on the ground of pious obligation. Debts contracted before 2005 are saved, and for that saving "son, grandson or great-grandson" means one born or adopted before the 2005 Act (Explanation to Section 6(4)). Section 6(5): Section 6 does not touch a partition made before 20 December 2004, and "partition" means only a registered partition deed or a court decree. Section 30, Explanation: a male Hindu can dispose of his interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property by will. Section 6 as enacted in 1956: survivorship was the normal rule, but if the deceased left a female Class I heir (or a male Class I heir claiming through her), his interest passed by succession, and his share was worked out by assuming a partition just before his death.
hi.meaning:
Mitakshara is Vijnaneswara's running commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, written in the latter part of the eleventh century. Its family law rests on the son's birthright in ancestral property. Dayabhaga is Jimutavahana's digest of all the Smriti Codes, written about the beginning of the twelfth century. Its family law rests on ownership by the father and defined shares (Mulla, section 11(3)). "The conception of a coparcenary and of coparcenary property according to the Dayabhaga law is entirely distinct from that according to the Mitakshara law" (Mulla, section 272). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Mitakshara: interest at birth, survivorship (now succession). Dayabhaga: nothing at birth, defined shares that pass to heirs. flowchart TD subgraph M["Mitakshara"] M1["Son is born"] --> M2["At once a coparcener
with his father"] M2 --> M3["Interest fluctuates
with births and deaths"] M3 --> M4["On a death: survivorship
after 2005: succession, s. 6(3)"] end subgraph D["Dayabhaga"] D1["Son is born"] --> D2["No interest while
father lives"] D2 --> D3["Father dies: sons inherit
defined shares as coparceners"] D3 --> D4["On a death: share passes
to his own heirs"] end Text description Mitakshara: a son is born and at once becomes a coparcener with his father; his interest fluctuates with births and deaths; on a coparcener's death his interest passed by survivorship, and after 2005 passes by succession under Section 6(3). Dayabhaga: a son gets nothing while the father lives; on the father's death the sons inherit as heirs and hold defined shares as coparceners; on a coparcener's death his share passes to his own heirs. The question this topic answers. How does a member hold joint family property, and what happens to his interest when he or another member is born or dies? Why the two schools differ. The Dayabhaga school did not accept the Mitakshara view that a son becomes an owner at birth. For the Dayabhaga, property passes only on the owner's death. Every other difference on the joint family follows from this.
keyPoints: Mitakshara: right by birth, unity of ownership, fluctuating interest, survivorship (now replaced by succession). Dayabhaga: no birthright, defined shares, unity of possession but no unity of ownership, shares pass to heirs. A Dayabhaga coparcenary begins only on the father's death; there is none between father and sons. A Dayabhaga father has absolute power over ancestral property. Ghamandi Ram : six incidents; the coparcenary is a creature of law. Section 6(1): daughters are Mitakshara coparceners by birth; 6(3): succession replaces survivorship after 2005; 6(4): no pious obligation for new debts; 6(5): only a registered deed or a decree counts as partition. Gurupad : widow's 7/24 share under the old Section 6. Vineeta Sharma : father need not be alive on 9 September 2005; the test of a coparcener is the right to demand partition.

caseLaws.name: State Bank of India v
caseLaws.facts: Ghamandi Ram (1969) Facts. The karta of a joint Hindu family firm that had traded in what became Pakistan claimed the surplus left in the firm's bank account after Partition. The question was whether the family firm was an "individual" or a "body of individuals" under a Pakistan notification . Principle. A Mitakshara coparcenary holds property in collective ownership in a quasi-corporate capacity; the Court listed its six incidents and held it is "a creature of law". The firm was a body of individuals, the amount had vested in the Custodian in Pakistan, and the Bank's appeal was allowed. AIR 1969 SC 1330. Why it matters. It is the standard statement of the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench was asked whether a daughter is a coparcener under the amended Section 6 if her father died before 9 September 2005. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener by birth, born before or after the amendment; the father need not be alive on 9 September 2005; the old notional partition did not disrupt the coparcenary; oral partition is not accepted except in exceptional cases (para 129). (2020) 9 SCC 1 : [2020] 10 SCR. Why it matters. It places daughters inside the Mitakshara coparcenary on the same footing as sons and overrules Prakash v. Phulavati . Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960 leaving his widow, two sons and three daughters, and Mitakshara joint family property. The widow sued for a 7/24 share. Principle. Under Explanation 1 to the original Section 6, the assumed partition just before death must be worked out fully; the widow takes her share on that partition (1/4) plus her share in the deceased's interest (1/24). Appeal dismissed with costs. (1978) 3 SCC 383 : AIR 1978 SC 1239. Why it matters. It shows how the 1956 Act displaced survivorship before 2005. Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. Sita Ram, managing ancestral property for himself and his two minor sons, mortgaged it in 1908 to pay off two earlier mortgages. The sons sued to have the mortgage declared not binding on them. Principle. A manager cannot burden the estate except for necessity; a father's mortgage binds the sons only if it pays an antecedent debt, "antecedent in fact as well as in time". The mortgage here paid earlier debts, so it bound the estate; appeal allowed. Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It shows the Mitakshara limits on the manager and the father's power over ancestral property, which the Dayabhaga does not have.

selfTest.q: 1. In which school does a son get a right by birth?
selfTest.a: The Mitakshara.

selfTest.q: 2. Does a Dayabhaga coparcener's share rise or fall with births and deaths?
selfTest.a: No. Each coparcener takes a defined share that does not fluctuate ( Vineeta Sharma , para 35).

selfTest.q: 3. Which case lists the incidents of a Mitakshara coparcenary?
selfTest.a: State Bank of India v. Ghamandi Ram (1969).

selfTest.q: 4. What did Section 6(4) do to the pious obligation?
selfTest.a: For debts after 2005, no court recognises proceedings against a son, grandson or great-grandson solely on that ground. Earlier debts are saved.

selfTest.q: 5. In Gurupad , how did the widow get 7/24?
selfTest.a: 1/4 on the assumed partition between her husband and two sons, plus 1/6 of her husband's 1/4 (that is, 1/24) as one of six Class I heirs.

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Dayabhaga son demand partition from his father?
selfTest.a: No. The father is the sole owner of the ancestral property (Mulla, section 275).

family-law-i-u1-t7.subtitle: Management, debts and alienation of joint family property, with Brij Narain

en.inOneMinute: The Karta manages the joint family and its property. His powers are wide in day-to-day matters: he controls income and spending, runs the family business, contracts debts for family purposes, makes contracts, gives receipts, compromises and refers disputes to arbitration, and sues and is sued for the family. His power to sell or mortgage family property is limited. The Privy Council in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) held that a managing coparcener "cannot alienate or burden the estate qua manager except for purposes of necessity". Mulla adds a second ground: benefit of the estate. An alienation outside these grounds is voidable at the option of the other coparceners. A father who is Karta has an extra power. He may, by a debt not incurred for an immoral purpose, lay the estate open to execution for that debt. A mortgage binds the estate only if it pays off an antecedent debt , antecedent "in fact as well as in time". His functions are the duties that go with the office: maintaining the members, meeting marriage and ceremony expenses, keeping the property, and accounting when the family divides. Exams ask for the Brij Narain propositions, the meaning of legal necessity , and the father's special power.
legalProvision: The Karta 's powers are not in an Act. They come from Mitakshara law and court decisions. Three provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 bear on them.

Section 6(1), proviso (as substituted in 2005). Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(4). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005).

Section 30, Explanation. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.
In simple words

Section 6(1) makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, so she can be Karta and exercise all the powers in this note ( Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta , Delhi High Court, 2015). The proviso to Section 6(1) protects any sale, mortgage, gift, partition or will made before 20 December 2004. A Karta's earlier valid alienation therefore stands against a daughter's claim. Section 6(4) ends the pious obligation for debts taken after 9 September 2005 (the commencement of the 2005 Act). For debts taken before that date, a creditor's rights against sons, grandsons and great-grandsons born or adopted before that date are saved. Vineeta Sharma (para 61) adds that a daughter is equally bound by the pious obligation in the same way as a son. The Section 30 Explanation lets a coparcener dispose of his own undivided interest by will. That is a power of every coparcener over his own interest, not a power of the Karta over the whole property.
en.meaning:
The Karta's powers are the legal capacities that let him act for the joint family as its manager and bind the other members. His functions are the duties that come with the office. Two ideas fix the limits. First, no coparcener can claim a precise share while the property is undivided, because the interest "is fluctuating" and "increases and diminishes by death and birth in the family" ( Vineeta Sharma , para 26). So the Karta, too, holds no separate share he can deal with as his own. Second, one of the incidents of a coparcenary is "that there can be no alienation of the property without the concurrence of the other coparceners unless it be for legal necessity " ( Vineeta Sharma , para 30, quoting Controller of Estate Duty v. Alladi Kuppuswamy on Ghamandi Ram ). Mulla (section 236) puts it this way: the manager has no larger interest than any other member; "The only respect in which he has a superior right is that he has a power of disposition for causes recognised as just and proper under Hindu law of the whole family property, including the interest of the junior members." See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A test for any sale or mortgage of joint family property by the Karta. flowchart TD Q1{"For legal necessity or
benefit of the estate?"} Q1 -- "Yes" --> A["Binds all coparceners,
adults and minors"] Q1 -- "No" --> Q2{"All other coparceners
adults and consented?"} Q2 -- "Yes" --> B["Valid in its entirety"] Q2 -- "No" --> Q3{"Karta is the father, and mortgage
pays his antecedent debt
not for an immoral purpose?"} Q3 -- "Yes" --> C["Binds the sons' interests
(Brij Narain; s. 6(4) for debts
after 9.9.2005)"] Q3 -- "No" --> D["Voidable at the option of
the other coparceners"] Text description Was it for legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate? If yes, it binds all coparceners, adults and minors. If no, did all the other coparceners, all adults, consent? If yes, it is valid in its entirety. If no, is the Karta the father, and was it a mortgage to discharge his antecedent debt not for an immoral purpose? If yes, it binds the sons' interests (debts after 9 September 2005 cannot be recovered from sons solely on pious obligation). If no, it is voidable at the option of the other coparceners.
keyPoints: The Karta manages the family and represents it ( Tribhovandas ). He controls income; members who dislike his spending can only seek partition (Mulla s. 237). His debts for family purposes bind the family property, not other members' separate property (Mulla s. 240). He may contract, give receipts, compromise, refer to arbitration and give discharges, but cannot give up a family debt (Mulla ss. 241–250). He cannot alienate or burden the estate except for necessity ( Brij Narain , para 17) or benefit of the estate (Mulla s. 242); otherwise the alienation is voidable. A father may lay the estate open to execution for his debt not for an immoral purpose; a mortgage binds only for an antecedent debt, antecedent in fact as well as in time. Section 6(4): no recovery from sons solely on pious obligation for debts after 9 September 2005. A sole surviving coparcener may dispose of the property; the alienation stands after a son's birth ( Vineeta Sharma , para 28).

caseLaws.name: Brij Narain v
caseLaws.facts: Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. In 1908 Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged ancestral property for Rs. 11,000 to repay two earlier mortgages. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding on them. Principle. A managing coparcener cannot burden the estate except for necessity; a father may lay the estate open to execution for his non-immoral debt; a mortgage binds only if it discharges an antecedent debt (para 17). The earlier mortgages were antecedent debts, so the mortgage bound the estate and the mortgagee 's appeal was allowed (paras 18–19). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It states the limits on a manager's power and the father's special power. Hunoomanpersaud Panday v. Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree (1856) Facts. A mother, as manager of her minor son's estate, mortgaged it (as described in Mulla, section 242). Principle. The power to charge an estate not one's own "can only be exercised rightly in a case of need, or for the benefit of the estate"; a lender who inquires and acts honestly is protected. (1856) 6 Moo IA 393. Why it matters. Mulla treats it as the leading case on alienation for necessity, and a Karta's power is analogous. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench heard a reference on how the substituted Section 6 applies to daughters. Principle. No coparcener can claim a precise share (para 26); a sole coparcener may dispose of the property (para 28); no alienation without the concurrence of the coparceners unless for legal necessity (para 30); a daughter is bound by the pious obligation like a son (para 61). Why it matters. It shows the Karta's power as an exception to joint ownership. Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015) Facts. The eldest coparcener of a Hindu undivided family, a woman, claimed to be its Karta. Principle. The Delhi High Court held that she could be Karta (para 27). The powers in this note belong to her as to any Karta. Why it matters. Women Kartas now exercise the same powers.

selfTest.q: 1. On what grounds can a Karta alienate joint family property?
selfTest.a: For legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate ( Brij Narain , para 17; Mulla, section 242).

selfTest.q: 2. When does a mortgage by a father bind the estate?
selfTest.a: Only if it discharges an antecedent debt ( Brij Narain , para 17(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. What does "antecedent" mean?
selfTest.a: Antecedent in fact as well as in time: the debt must be truly independent and not part of the transaction challenged ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)).

selfTest.q: 4. Is an alienation without legal necessity void?
selfTest.a: No. It is voidable at the option of the other coparceners; a creditor cannot repudiate it (Mulla, section 242(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can the bank that lent to the Karta for the family business reach the separate property of another coparcener?
selfTest.a: No, unless that coparcener was a party to the loan or later ratified it. It can reach the family property, including that member's share in it (Mulla, section 240).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Karta write off a debt owed to the family?
selfTest.a: No. He has no power to give up a debt due to the joint family (Mulla, section 250), though he may compromise it bona fide for the family's benefit (section 248).

legalProvision: కర్త అధికారాలు ఏ చట్టంలోనూ లేవు. అవి మితాక్షర చట్టం, కోర్టు తీర్పుల నుంచి వస్తాయి. హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం, 1956 లోని మూడు నిబంధనలు వీటిని తాకుతాయి.

Section 6(1), proviso (as substituted in 2005). Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(4). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005).

Section 30, Explanation. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.
సరళమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 6(1) కూతురిని పుట్టుకతో కోపార్సినర్ ‌గా చేస్తుంది; కాబట్టి ఆమె కర్త కాగలదు, ఈ నోట్‌లోని అన్ని అధికారాలనూ వినియోగించగలదు ( Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta , ఢిల్లీ హైకోర్టు, 2015). 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కు ముందు జరిగిన అమ్మకం, తాకట్టు, దానం, విభజన , వీలునామా లను సెక్షన్ 6(1) నిబంధన ( proviso ) కాపాడుతుంది. కాబట్టి కర్త అంతకుముందు చేసిన చెల్లుబాటయ్యే అన్యాక్రాంతం కూతురి క్లెయిమ్‌కు వ్యతిరేకంగా నిలుస్తుంది. 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 (2005 చట్టం అమల్లోకి వచ్చిన తేదీ) తర్వాత చేసిన అప్పులకు సెక్షన్ 6(4) పవిత్ర బాధ్యత (pious obligation) ను ముగిస్తుంది. ఆ తేదీకి ముందు చేసిన అప్పుల విషయంలో, ఆ తేదీకి ముందు పుట్టిన లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్న కొడుకులు, మనవళ్లు, మునిమనవళ్లపై రుణదాత హక్కులు కాపాడబడ్డాయి. కూతురు కూడా కొడుకు లాగే పవిత్ర బాధ్యతకు బద్ధురాలని Vineeta Sharma (para 61) చెబుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 30 Explanation ప్రకారం కోపార్సినర్ తన అవిభక్త వాటాను వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. అది ప్రతి కోపార్సినర్‌కు తన వాటాపై ఉన్న అధికారం; మొత్తం ఆస్తిపై కర్త అధికారం కాదు.

కర్త అధికారాలు అంటే నిర్వాహకుడిగా కుటుంబం తరఫున వ్యవహరించి ఇతర సభ్యులను బంధించడానికి అతనికి ఉన్న చట్టపరమైన సామర్థ్యాలు. అతని విధులు అంటే ఆ పదవితో వచ్చే బాధ్యతలు. రెండు ఆలోచనలు పరిమితులను నిర్ణయిస్తాయి. మొదటిది, ఆస్తి అవిభక్తంగా ఉన్నంతకాలం ఏ కోపార్సినరూ ఖచ్చితమైన వాటాను చెప్పలేడు; ఎందుకంటే హక్కు "is fluctuating", "increases and diminishes by death and birth in the family" ( Vineeta Sharma , para 26). కాబట్టి కర్తకు కూడా తన సొంతంగా వ్యవహరించగల ప్రత్యేక వాటా ఉండదు. రెండోది, కోపార్సినరీ లక్షణాల్లో ఒకటి "that there can be no alienation of the property without the concurrence of the other coparceners unless it be for legal necessity " ( Vineeta Sharma , para 30, Ghamandi Ram పై Controller of Estate Duty v. Alladi Kuppuswamy విశ్లేషణను ఉటంకిస్తూ). ముల్లా (సెక్షన్ 236) ఇలా చెబుతారు: నిర్వాహకుడికి ఇతర సభ్యుల కంటే ఎక్కువ హక్కు లేదు; "The only respect in which he has a superior right is that he has a power of disposition for causes recognised as just and proper under Hindu law of the whole family property, including the interest of the junior members." Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. కర్త చేసిన ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తి అమ్మకం లేదా తాకట్టుకు ఒక పరీక్ష. flowchart TD Q1{"చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేదా
ఎస్టేట్ ప్రయోజనం కోసమా?"} Q1 -- "అవును" --> A["వయోజన, మైనర్
కోపార్సినర్లందరినీ బంధిస్తుంది"] Q1 -- "కాదు" --> Q2{"ఇతర కోపార్సినర్లందరూ వయోజనులై
అంగీకరించారా?"} Q2 -- "అవును" --> B["పూర్తిగా చెల్లుతుంది"] Q2 -- "కాదు" --> Q3{"కర్త తండ్రా, అనైతికం కాని అతని
పూర్వపు అప్పు తీర్చడానికి తాకట్టా?"} Q3 -- "అవును" --> C["కొడుకుల వాటాలను బంధిస్తుంది
(Brij Narain; 9.9.2005 తర్వాత
అప్పులకు సె. 6(4))"] Q3 -- "కాదు" --> D["ఇతర కోపార్సినర్ల ఇష్టం మేరకు
రద్దు చేయదగినది"] వచన వివరణ అది చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేదా ఎస్టేట్ ప్రయోజనం కోసమా? అవును అయితే వయోజన, మైనర్ కోపార్సినర్లందరినీ బంధిస్తుంది. కాకపోతే, ఇతర కోపార్సినర్లందరూ వయోజనులై అంగీకరించారా? అవును అయితే పూర్తిగా చెల్లుతుంది. కాకపోతే, కర్త తండ్రా, అనైతికం కాని అతని పూర్వపు అప్పు తీర్చడానికి తాకట్టా? అవును అయితే కొడుకుల వాటాలను బంధిస్తుంది (9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 తర్వాత అప్పులను కేవలం పవిత్ర బాధ్యతపై కొడుకుల నుంచి వసూలు చేయలేరు). కాకపోతే ఇతర కోపార్సినర్ల ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది.

selfTest.q: 1. కర్త ఏ కారణాలపై ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని అన్యాక్రాంతం చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేదా ఎస్టేట్ ప్రయోజనం కోసం ( Brij Narain , para 17; ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 242).

selfTest.q: 2. తండ్రి చేసిన తాకట్టు ఎస్టేట్‌ను ఎప్పుడు బంధిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: పూర్వపు అప్పు తీర్చడానికి అయితేనే ( Brij Narain , para 17(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. "Antecedent" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సమయంలోనూ, వాస్తవంలోనూ ముందుది: అప్పు నిజంగా స్వతంత్రమైనదై, సవాలు చేసిన లావాదేవీలో భాగం కాకూడదు ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)).

selfTest.q: 4. చట్టబద్ధమైన అవసరం లేని అన్యాక్రాంతం శూన్యమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అది ఇతర కోపార్సినర్ల ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది; రుణదాత తిరస్కరించలేడు (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 242(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. కుటుంబ వ్యాపారం కోసం కర్తకు అప్పు ఇచ్చిన బ్యాంకు మరో కోపార్సినర్ ప్రత్యేక ఆస్తిని చేరుకోగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు, ఆ కోపార్సినర్ అప్పులో పక్షం కాకపోతే లేదా తర్వాత ఆమోదించకపోతే. ఆ సభ్యుని వాటాతో సహా కుటుంబ ఆస్తిని చేరుకోవచ్చు (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 240).

selfTest.q: 6. కుటుంబానికి రావాల్సిన అప్పును కర్త మాఫీ చేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబానికి రావాల్సిన అప్పును వదులుకునే అధికారం అతనికి లేదు (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 250); అయితే కుటుంబ ప్రయోజనం కోసం మంచి ఉద్దేశంతో రాజీ చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 248).

hi.inOneMinute: The Karta manages the joint family and its property. His powers are wide in day-to-day matters: he controls income and spending, runs the family business, contracts debts for family purposes, makes contracts, gives receipts, compromises and refers disputes to arbitration, and sues and is sued for the family. His power to sell or mortgage family property is limited. The Privy Council in Brij Narain v. Mangla Prasad (1923) held that a managing coparcener "cannot alienate or burden the estate qua manager except for purposes of necessity". Mulla adds a second ground: benefit of the estate. An alienation outside these grounds is voidable at the option of the other coparceners. A father who is Karta has an extra power. He may, by a debt not incurred for an immoral purpose, lay the estate open to execution for that debt. A mortgage binds the estate only if it pays off an antecedent debt , antecedent "in fact as well as in time". His functions are the duties that go with the office: maintaining the members, meeting marriage and ceremony expenses, keeping the property, and accounting when the family divides. Exams ask for the Brij Narain propositions, the meaning of legal necessity , and the father's special power.
legalProvision: The Karta 's powers are not in an Act. They come from Mitakshara law and court decisions. Three provisions of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 bear on them.

Section 6(1), proviso (as substituted in 2005). Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(4). After the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), no court shall recognise any right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for the recovery of any debt due from his father, grandfather or great-grandfather solely on the ground of the pious obligation under the Hindu law, of such son, grandson or great-grandson to discharge any such debt: Provided that in the case of any debt contracted before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005), nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect― (a) the right of any creditor to proceed against the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be; or (b) any alienation made in respect of or in satisfaction of, any such debt, and any such right or alienation shall be enforceable under the rule of pious obligation in the same manner and to the same extent as it would have been enforceable as if the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005) had not been enacted. Explanation.―For the purposes of clause (a), the expression "son", "grandson" or "great-grandson" shall be deemed to refer to the son, grandson or great-grandson, as the case may be, who was born or adopted prior to the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (39 of 2005).

Section 30, Explanation. The interest of a male Hindu in a Mitakshara coparcenary property or the interest of a member of a tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru in the property of the tarwad, tavazhi, illom, kutumba or kavaru shall, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force, be deemed to be property capable of being disposed of by him or by her within the meaning of this section.
In simple words

Section 6(1) makes a daughter a coparcener by birth, so she can be Karta and exercise all the powers in this note ( Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta , Delhi High Court, 2015). The proviso to Section 6(1) protects any sale, mortgage, gift, partition or will made before 20 December 2004. A Karta's earlier valid alienation therefore stands against a daughter's claim. Section 6(4) ends the pious obligation for debts taken after 9 September 2005 (the commencement of the 2005 Act). For debts taken before that date, a creditor's rights against sons, grandsons and great-grandsons born or adopted before that date are saved. Vineeta Sharma (para 61) adds that a daughter is equally bound by the pious obligation in the same way as a son. The Section 30 Explanation lets a coparcener dispose of his own undivided interest by will. That is a power of every coparcener over his own interest, not a power of the Karta over the whole property.
hi.meaning:
The Karta's powers are the legal capacities that let him act for the joint family as its manager and bind the other members. His functions are the duties that come with the office. Two ideas fix the limits. First, no coparcener can claim a precise share while the property is undivided, because the interest "is fluctuating" and "increases and diminishes by death and birth in the family" ( Vineeta Sharma , para 26). So the Karta, too, holds no separate share he can deal with as his own. Second, one of the incidents of a coparcenary is "that there can be no alienation of the property without the concurrence of the other coparceners unless it be for legal necessity " ( Vineeta Sharma , para 30, quoting Controller of Estate Duty v. Alladi Kuppuswamy on Ghamandi Ram ). Mulla (section 236) puts it this way: the manager has no larger interest than any other member; "The only respect in which he has a superior right is that he has a power of disposition for causes recognised as just and proper under Hindu law of the whole family property, including the interest of the junior members." See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A test for any sale or mortgage of joint family property by the Karta. flowchart TD Q1{"For legal necessity or
benefit of the estate?"} Q1 -- "Yes" --> A["Binds all coparceners,
adults and minors"] Q1 -- "No" --> Q2{"All other coparceners
adults and consented?"} Q2 -- "Yes" --> B["Valid in its entirety"] Q2 -- "No" --> Q3{"Karta is the father, and mortgage
pays his antecedent debt
not for an immoral purpose?"} Q3 -- "Yes" --> C["Binds the sons' interests
(Brij Narain; s. 6(4) for debts
after 9.9.2005)"] Q3 -- "No" --> D["Voidable at the option of
the other coparceners"] Text description Was it for legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate? If yes, it binds all coparceners, adults and minors. If no, did all the other coparceners, all adults, consent? If yes, it is valid in its entirety. If no, is the Karta the father, and was it a mortgage to discharge his antecedent debt not for an immoral purpose? If yes, it binds the sons' interests (debts after 9 September 2005 cannot be recovered from sons solely on pious obligation). If no, it is voidable at the option of the other coparceners.
keyPoints: The Karta manages the family and represents it ( Tribhovandas ). He controls income; members who dislike his spending can only seek partition (Mulla s. 237). His debts for family purposes bind the family property, not other members' separate property (Mulla s. 240). He may contract, give receipts, compromise, refer to arbitration and give discharges, but cannot give up a family debt (Mulla ss. 241–250). He cannot alienate or burden the estate except for necessity ( Brij Narain , para 17) or benefit of the estate (Mulla s. 242); otherwise the alienation is voidable. A father may lay the estate open to execution for his debt not for an immoral purpose; a mortgage binds only for an antecedent debt, antecedent in fact as well as in time. Section 6(4): no recovery from sons solely on pious obligation for debts after 9 September 2005. A sole surviving coparcener may dispose of the property; the alienation stands after a son's birth ( Vineeta Sharma , para 28).

caseLaws.name: Brij Narain v
caseLaws.facts: Mangla Prasad (1923) Facts. In 1908 Sita Ram, manager of a joint family with his two minor sons, mortgaged ancestral property for Rs. 11,000 to repay two earlier mortgages. The sons, through their mother, sued to have it declared not binding on them. Principle. A managing coparcener cannot burden the estate except for necessity; a father may lay the estate open to execution for his non-immoral debt; a mortgage binds only if it discharges an antecedent debt (para 17). The earlier mortgages were antecedent debts, so the mortgage bound the estate and the mortgagee 's appeal was allowed (paras 18–19). Privy Council, (1924) 26 Bom LR 500. Why it matters. It states the limits on a manager's power and the father's special power. Hunoomanpersaud Panday v. Mussumat Babooee Munraj Koonweree (1856) Facts. A mother, as manager of her minor son's estate, mortgaged it (as described in Mulla, section 242). Principle. The power to charge an estate not one's own "can only be exercised rightly in a case of need, or for the benefit of the estate"; a lender who inquires and acts honestly is protected. (1856) 6 Moo IA 393. Why it matters. Mulla treats it as the leading case on alienation for necessity, and a Karta's power is analogous. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-judge bench heard a reference on how the substituted Section 6 applies to daughters. Principle. No coparcener can claim a precise share (para 26); a sole coparcener may dispose of the property (para 28); no alienation without the concurrence of the coparceners unless for legal necessity (para 30); a daughter is bound by the pious obligation like a son (para 61). Why it matters. It shows the Karta's power as an exception to joint ownership. Sujata Sharma v. Manu Gupta (2015) Facts. The eldest coparcener of a Hindu undivided family, a woman, claimed to be its Karta. Principle. The Delhi High Court held that she could be Karta (para 27). The powers in this note belong to her as to any Karta. Why it matters. Women Kartas now exercise the same powers.

selfTest.q: 1. On what grounds can a Karta alienate joint family property?
selfTest.a: For legal necessity or for the benefit of the estate ( Brij Narain , para 17; Mulla, section 242).

selfTest.q: 2. When does a mortgage by a father bind the estate?
selfTest.a: Only if it discharges an antecedent debt ( Brij Narain , para 17(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. What does "antecedent" mean?
selfTest.a: Antecedent in fact as well as in time: the debt must be truly independent and not part of the transaction challenged ( Brij Narain , para 17(4)).

selfTest.q: 4. Is an alienation without legal necessity void?
selfTest.a: No. It is voidable at the option of the other coparceners; a creditor cannot repudiate it (Mulla, section 242(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can the bank that lent to the Karta for the family business reach the separate property of another coparcener?
selfTest.a: No, unless that coparcener was a party to the loan or later ratified it. It can reach the family property, including that member's share in it (Mulla, section 240).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Karta write off a debt owed to the family?
selfTest.a: No. He has no power to give up a debt due to the joint family (Mulla, section 250), though he may compromise it bona fide for the family's benefit (section 248).
