(Dolly Rani)"] Text description The parties perform the customary rites of either side under section 7(1). If the saptapadi is part of the rites, the marriage is complete at the seventh step under section 7(2). The marriage may then be entered in the Hindu Marriage Register under section 8. The entry is evidence of the marriage; it does not create or cure the marriage. If no rites were performed, a certificate or registration has no effect (Dolly Rani).
keyPoints: Section 7: customary rites of either party; the Act prescribes no fixed ceremony. Saptapadi: where part of the rites, the marriage is complete at the seventh step. Essential rites in a ceremonial marriage: invocation before the sacred fire and saptapadi, unless a proved custom changes them ( Bhaurao ; Mulla s. 437). Custom must be proved by definite evidence, not by what was done at one wedding. Bigamy needs a properly solemnized second marriage; admission is not proof ( Priya Bala Ghosh ). Section 8(5): non-registration does not affect validity; fine up to ₹25 where compulsory. Registration does not create a marriage ( Dolly Rani ). Seema : marriages of all religions to be compulsorily registrable; registration has great evidentiary value. Special Marriage Act, 1954: thirty days' notice, three witnesses, conclusive certificate; an earlier marriage can be registered under Sections 15 to 18.

caseLaws.name: Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v
caseLaws.facts: State of Maharashtra (1965) Facts. Bhaurao married Indubai in about 1956 and, while she was alive, went through a "Gandharva" marriage with Kamlabai in February 1962 by an exchange of garlands and touching of foreheads, without homa or saptapadi. He was convicted under Section 494 IPC and his brother of abetment . Principle. A marriage is "solemnized" only when celebrated with proper ceremonies and in due form; invocation before the sacred fire and saptapadi are essential even in a Gandharva marriage unless a proved custom has changed them, and a practice of five or seven years is not a custom under Section 3(a); the convictions were set aside. AIR 1965 SC 1564 : (1965) 2 SCR 837. Why it matters. It defines "solemnize" and sets what must be proved to show a marriage, especially a second marriage in a bigamy case. Priya Bala Ghosh v. Suresh Chandra Ghosh (1971) Facts. A wife prosecuted her husband for bigamy. The courts found no evidence that homa and saptapadi, essential rites in the parties' community, were performed at the second marriage; she relied on his earlier admission that he had married again. Principle. The prosecution must prove that the second marriage was duly performed with the essential rites of the parties' law and custom; an admission of marriage by the accused is no evidence of the marriage in a bigamy case. Appeal dismissed. [1971] 3 SCR 961 : AIR 1971 SC 1153. Why it matters. It confirms Bhaurao and shows how strictly the ceremonies must be proved. Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006) Facts. In a transfer petition the Supreme Court noticed that many people deny their marriages because there is no official record. It heard the States, the Union Territories and the National Commission for Women on registration. Principle. Registration is not per se proof of a valid marriage but has great evidentiary value; marriages of all citizens of India, of all religions, should be compulsorily registrable in the State where solemnized; the States must notify the procedure within three months. Decided 14 February 2006. Why it matters. It explains the place of registration and led to compulsory registration rules. Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) Facts. Two commercial pilots, engaged on 7 March 2021, obtained on 7 July 2021 a certificate from a society and a registration certificate under the Uttar Pradesh Marriage Registration Rules, 2017, without any ceremony; the families fixed a ceremony for 25 October 2022 that was never held. Principle. Without the ceremonies of Section 7 there is no Hindu marriage, and registration under Section 8 confers no status; on their joint application under Article 142 the Court declared both certificates null and void and quashed the divorce, maintenance and criminal cases between them. 2024 INSC 355. Why it matters. Registration only proves a marriage that has taken place; it cannot create one.

selfTest.q: 1. When is a marriage with saptapadi complete?
selfTest.a: When the seventh step is taken (Section 7(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. Does failure to register invalidate a Hindu marriage?
selfTest.a: No. Section 8(5), even where registration is compulsory.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case held that a certificate without ceremonies has no effect?
selfTest.a: Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024).

selfTest.q: 4. In a bigamy case, can the second marriage be proved by the accused's own admission?
selfTest.a: No. The ceremonies must be proved ( Priya Bala Ghosh , following Bhaurao ).

selfTest.q: 5. Witnesses say a priest was not needed at a Gandharva wedding in their community. Does that prove a custom dispensing with saptapadi?
selfTest.a: No. Evidence of what was done is not evidence of the custom ( Bhaurao ).

selfTest.q: 6. What is the evidentiary value of a certificate under the Special Marriage Act?
selfTest.a: It is conclusive evidence that the marriage was solemnized under that Act (Section 13(2)).

legalProvision: Section 7, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Ceremonies for a Hindu marriage. (1) A Hindu marriage may be solemnized in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies of either party thereto. (2) Where such rites and ceremonies include the Saptapadi (that is, the taking of seven steps by the bridegroom and the bride jointly before the sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.

Section 8. Registration of Hindu marriages. (1) For the purpose of facilitating the proof of Hindu marriages, the State Government may make rules providing that the parties to any such marriage may have the particulars relating to their marriage entered in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed in a Hindu Marriage Register kept for the purpose. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the State Government may, if it is of opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do, provide that the entering of the particulars referred to in sub-section (1) shall be compulsory in the State or in any part thereof, whether in all cases or in such cases as may be specified, and where any such direction has been issued, any person contravening any rule made in this behalf shall be punishable with fine which may extend to twenty-five rupees. (3) All rules made under this section shall be laid before the State Legislature, as soon as may be, after they are made. (4) The Hindu Marriage Register shall at all reasonable times be open for inspection, and shall be admissible as evidence of the statements therein contained and certified extracts therefrom shall, on application, be given by the Registrar on payment to him of the prescribed fee. (5) Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the validity of any Hindu marriage shall in no way be affected by the omission to make the entry.

సెక్షన్ 7(1): HMA వేడుకల జాబితా ఇవ్వదు. వధువు వైపు లేదా వరుడి వైపు ఆచార కర్మలను అంగీకరిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 7(2): ఆ కర్మల్లో సప్తపది ఉంటే, ఏడవ అడుగుతో వివాహం పూర్తవుతుంది, అంతకుముందు కాదు. సెక్షన్ 8(1)–(3): హిందూ వివాహ రిజిస్టర్ కోసం రాష్ట్రం నియమాలు చేస్తుంది. నియమాలు రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభ ముందు ఉంచాలి. సెక్షన్ 8(2): రాష్ట్రం నమోదును తప్పనిసరి చేయవచ్చు; అలాంటి నియమాన్ని ఉల్లంఘిస్తే ₹25 వరకు జరిమానా మాత్రమే. సెక్షన్ 8(4): ఎవరైనా రిజిస్టర్‌ను తనిఖీ చేయవచ్చు; దాని నమోదులు సాక్ష్యంగా ఆమోదయోగ్యం; ఫీజు చెల్లిస్తే సర్టిఫైడ్ కాపీలు ఇస్తారు. సెక్షన్ 8(5): రిజిస్టర్ కాని వివాహం కూడా చెల్లుబాటవుతుంది.

వివాహ నిర్వహణ (Solemnisation) . వివాహాన్ని " solemnize " చేయడం అంటే "to celebrate the marriage with proper ceremonies and in due form" ( Bhaurao , Shorter Oxford Dictionary ఆధారంగా). "Merely going through certain ceremonies with the intention that the parties be taken to be married, will not make them ceremonies prescribed by law or approved by any established custom." ఆచార కర్మలు, వేడుకలు. వధువు లేదా వరుడి సమాజపు ఆచారం ముఖ్యమైనవిగా భావించే కర్మలు. ఆచారం సెక్షన్ 3(a) ని నెరవేర్చాలి: చాలా కాలంగా నిరంతరంగా, ఒకే విధంగా పాటించబడాలి; నిశ్చితంగా ఉండాలి; అసమంజసంగా లేదా ప్రజా విధానానికి విరుద్ధంగా ఉండకూడదు; కుటుంబ ఆచారం అయితే నిలిపివేయబడి ఉండకూడదు. రిజిస్ట్రేషన్. రాష్ట్ర నియమాల కింద ఉంచే హిందూ వివాహ రిజిస్టర్‌లో వివాహ వివరాల నమోదు. ఇది వివాహాన్ని రుజువు చేయడానికి సహాయపడే రికార్డు. ఈ అంశం రెండు ప్రశ్నలకు జవాబిస్తుంది: ఏ వేడుకలు హిందూ వివాహాన్ని సృష్టిస్తాయి, రిజిస్ట్రేషన్ పాత్ర ఏమిటి. selfTest.q: 1. సప్తపది ఉన్న వివాహం ఎప్పుడు పూర్తవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: ఏడవ అడుగు వేసినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 7(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. రిజిస్టర్ చేయకపోతే హిందూ వివాహం చెల్లకుండా పోతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. రిజిస్ట్రేషన్ తప్పనిసరి అయిన చోట కూడా సెక్షన్ 8(5).

selfTest.q: 3. వేడుకలు లేని సర్టిఫికెట్‌కు ప్రభావం లేదని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది?
selfTest.a: Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024).

selfTest.q: 4. ద్విభార్యత్వ కేసులో రెండో వివాహాన్ని నిందితుడి సొంత ఒప్పుకోలుతో రుజువు చేయవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. వేడుకలను రుజువు చేయాలి ( Priya Bala Ghosh , Bhaurao ను అనుసరించి).

selfTest.q: 5. తమ సమాజంలో గాంధర్వ పెళ్లికి పురోహితుడు అవసరం లేదని సాక్షులు చెప్పారు. సప్తపదిని అవసరం లేకుండా చేసిన ఆచారం రుజువైనట్లా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. ఏమి జరిగిందనే సాక్ష్యం ఆచారానికి సాక్ష్యం కాదు ( Bhaurao ).

selfTest.q: 6. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం కింద సర్టిఫికెట్ సాక్ష్య విలువ ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఆ చట్టం కింద వివాహం జరిగిందని అది నిర్ణయాత్మక సాక్ష్యం (సెక్షన్ 13(2)).

hi.inOneMinute: Ceremonies make the marriage. Under Section 7 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA), a Hindu marriage may be solemnized in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies of either party. Where those rites include the saptapadi (seven steps taken jointly by the bride and bridegroom before the sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken. Registration only proves the marriage. Section 8 lets the State make rules for entering marriages in a Hindu Marriage Register "for the purpose of facilitating the proof of Hindu marriages". Failure to register does not affect validity (Section 8(5)). Registration cannot create a marriage. In Dolly Rani (2024) the Supreme Court held that a certificate or registration without the ceremonies of Section 7 has no legal consequence; the couple never became husband and wife. Proof in bigamy cases. In Bhaurao (1965) the Supreme Court held that a second marriage is "solemnized" only if performed with the proper ceremonies; without proof of the essential ceremonies there is no bigamy. Alternative. Two Hindus may instead marry, or register an earlier ceremonial marriage, under the Special Marriage Act, 1954.
legalProvision: Section 7, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Ceremonies for a Hindu marriage. (1) A Hindu marriage may be solemnized in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies of either party thereto. (2) Where such rites and ceremonies include the Saptapadi (that is, the taking of seven steps by the bridegroom and the bride jointly before the sacred fire), the marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.

Section 8. Registration of Hindu marriages. (1) For the purpose of facilitating the proof of Hindu marriages, the State Government may make rules providing that the parties to any such marriage may have the particulars relating to their marriage entered in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed in a Hindu Marriage Register kept for the purpose. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the State Government may, if it is of opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do, provide that the entering of the particulars referred to in sub-section (1) shall be compulsory in the State or in any part thereof, whether in all cases or in such cases as may be specified, and where any such direction has been issued, any person contravening any rule made in this behalf shall be punishable with fine which may extend to twenty-five rupees. (3) All rules made under this section shall be laid before the State Legislature, as soon as may be, after they are made. (4) The Hindu Marriage Register shall at all reasonable times be open for inspection, and shall be admissible as evidence of the statements therein contained and certified extracts therefrom shall, on application, be given by the Registrar on payment to him of the prescribed fee. (5) Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, the validity of any Hindu marriage shall in no way be affected by the omission to make the entry.
In simple words:

Section 7(1): the HMA does not list the ceremonies. It accepts the customary rites of the bride's side or the bridegroom's side. Section 7(2): if those rites include the saptapadi , the marriage is complete at the seventh step, not before. Section 8(1)–(3): the State makes the rules for a Hindu Marriage Register. The rules go before the State Legislature. Section 8(2): the State may make the entry compulsory; breaking such a rule is punishable with a fine of up to ₹25 only. Section 8(4): anyone may inspect the Register; its entries are admissible in evidence; certified copies are given on payment of a fee. Section 8(5): an unregistered marriage is still valid.
hi.meaning:
Solemnisation . To " solemnize " a marriage is "to celebrate the marriage with proper ceremonies and in due form" ( Bhaurao , adopting the Shorter Oxford Dictionary). "Merely going through certain ceremonies with the intention that the parties be taken to be married, will not make them ceremonies prescribed by law or approved by any established custom." Customary rites and ceremonies. The rites that the custom of the bride's or the bridegroom's community treats as essential. A custom must meet Section 3(a): continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, certain, not unreasonable or opposed to public policy, and, for a family custom, not discontinued. Registration. The entry of the particulars of a marriage in the Hindu Marriage Register kept under the State's rules. It is a record that helps prove the marriage. The topic answers two questions: what ceremonies create a Hindu marriage, and what part registration plays. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. (Dolly Rani)"] Text description The parties perform the customary rites of either side under section 7(1). If the saptapadi is part of the rites, the marriage is complete at the seventh step under section 7(2). The marriage may then be entered in the Hindu Marriage Register under section 8. The entry is evidence of the marriage; it does not create or cure the marriage. If no rites were performed, a certificate or registration has no effect (Dolly Rani).
keyPoints: Section 7: customary rites of either party; the Act prescribes no fixed ceremony. Saptapadi: where part of the rites, the marriage is complete at the seventh step. Essential rites in a ceremonial marriage: invocation before the sacred fire and saptapadi, unless a proved custom changes them ( Bhaurao ; Mulla s. 437). Custom must be proved by definite evidence, not by what was done at one wedding. Bigamy needs a properly solemnized second marriage; admission is not proof ( Priya Bala Ghosh ). Section 8(5): non-registration does not affect validity; fine up to ₹25 where compulsory. Registration does not create a marriage ( Dolly Rani ). Seema : marriages of all religions to be compulsorily registrable; registration has great evidentiary value. Special Marriage Act, 1954: thirty days' notice, three witnesses, conclusive certificate; an earlier marriage can be registered under Sections 15 to 18.

caseLaws.name: Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v
caseLaws.facts: State of Maharashtra (1965) Facts. Bhaurao married Indubai in about 1956 and, while she was alive, went through a "Gandharva" marriage with Kamlabai in February 1962 by an exchange of garlands and touching of foreheads, without homa or saptapadi. He was convicted under Section 494 IPC and his brother of abetment . Principle. A marriage is "solemnized" only when celebrated with proper ceremonies and in due form; invocation before the sacred fire and saptapadi are essential even in a Gandharva marriage unless a proved custom has changed them, and a practice of five or seven years is not a custom under Section 3(a); the convictions were set aside. AIR 1965 SC 1564 : (1965) 2 SCR 837. Why it matters. It defines "solemnize" and sets what must be proved to show a marriage, especially a second marriage in a bigamy case. Priya Bala Ghosh v. Suresh Chandra Ghosh (1971) Facts. A wife prosecuted her husband for bigamy. The courts found no evidence that homa and saptapadi, essential rites in the parties' community, were performed at the second marriage; she relied on his earlier admission that he had married again. Principle. The prosecution must prove that the second marriage was duly performed with the essential rites of the parties' law and custom; an admission of marriage by the accused is no evidence of the marriage in a bigamy case. Appeal dismissed. [1971] 3 SCR 961 : AIR 1971 SC 1153. Why it matters. It confirms Bhaurao and shows how strictly the ceremonies must be proved. Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006) Facts. In a transfer petition the Supreme Court noticed that many people deny their marriages because there is no official record. It heard the States, the Union Territories and the National Commission for Women on registration. Principle. Registration is not per se proof of a valid marriage but has great evidentiary value; marriages of all citizens of India, of all religions, should be compulsorily registrable in the State where solemnized; the States must notify the procedure within three months. Decided 14 February 2006. Why it matters. It explains the place of registration and led to compulsory registration rules. Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) Facts. Two commercial pilots, engaged on 7 March 2021, obtained on 7 July 2021 a certificate from a society and a registration certificate under the Uttar Pradesh Marriage Registration Rules, 2017, without any ceremony; the families fixed a ceremony for 25 October 2022 that was never held. Principle. Without the ceremonies of Section 7 there is no Hindu marriage, and registration under Section 8 confers no status; on their joint application under Article 142 the Court declared both certificates null and void and quashed the divorce, maintenance and criminal cases between them. 2024 INSC 355. Why it matters. Registration only proves a marriage that has taken place; it cannot create one.

selfTest.q: 1. When is a marriage with saptapadi complete?
selfTest.a: When the seventh step is taken (Section 7(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. Does failure to register invalidate a Hindu marriage?
selfTest.a: No. Section 8(5), even where registration is compulsory.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case held that a certificate without ceremonies has no effect?
selfTest.a: Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024).

selfTest.q: 4. In a bigamy case, can the second marriage be proved by the accused's own admission?
selfTest.a: No. The ceremonies must be proved ( Priya Bala Ghosh , following Bhaurao ).

selfTest.q: 5. Witnesses say a priest was not needed at a Gandharva wedding in their community. Does that prove a custom dispensing with saptapadi?
selfTest.a: No. Evidence of what was done is not evidence of the custom ( Bhaurao ).

selfTest.q: 6. What is the evidentiary value of a certificate under the Special Marriage Act?
selfTest.a: It is conclusive evidence that the marriage was solemnized under that Act (Section 13(2)).

family-law-i-u2-t5.subtitle: One spouse at a time: section 5(i), void second marriage and bigamy

en.inOneMinute: One spouse at a time. Monogamy means having only one spouse at a time. Section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) allows a marriage only if neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage. Civil result. A second marriage during the life of the first spouse is void (Sections 11 and 17). The second "spouse" gets no status as husband or wife. Criminal result. Section 17 applies the bigamy offence of Sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). These are now Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS): up to seven years and fine, and up to ten years and fine if the first marriage was hidden from the new partner. A proper second ceremony is needed. There is bigamy only if the second marriage was " solemnized " with the essential ceremonies ( Bhaurao , 1965). Conversion is no escape. A Hindu who converts to another religion and marries again, without first ending the Hindu marriage, commits bigamy ( Sarla Mudgal , 1995; Lily Thomas , 2000). History. Before 1955 a Hindu man could marry any number of wives, except where State anti-bigamy Acts applied (Mulla). Monogamy is the outstanding feature of the HMA.
legalProvision: Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Conditions for a Hindu marriage. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; …

Section 11. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 17. Punishment of bigamy. Any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after the commencement of this Act is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living; and the provisions of sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860), shall apply accordingly.

Section 82, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife. (1) Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Exception. —This sub-section does not extend to any person whose marriage with such husband or wife has been declared void by a Court of competent jurisdiction, nor to any person who contracts a marriage during the life of a former husband or wife, if such husband or wife, at the time of the subsequent marriage, shall have been continually absent from such person for the space of seven years, and shall not have been heard of by such person as being alive within that time provided the person contracting such subsequent marriage shall, before such marriage takes place, inform the person with whom such marriage is contracted of the real state of facts so far as the same are within his or her knowledge. (2) Whoever commits the offence under sub-section (1) having concealed from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
In simple words:

Section 5(i): on the wedding day, neither the bride nor the bridegroom may have a living husband or wife. Section 11: a marriage that breaks clause (i) is void. Either party may ask the court for a decree of nullity against the other. Section 17: a marriage between two Hindus is void if either party had a living spouse on that date, and the IPC bigamy sections (now BNS Section 82) apply. BNS Section 82(1): marrying again in the life of a spouse, where the new marriage is void for that reason: up to seven years and fine. BNS Section 82(2): the same offence after hiding the first marriage from the new partner: up to ten years and fine.
en.meaning:
Monogamy . The rule that a person may have only one spouse at a time. Bigamy. Marrying again while the first spouse is alive and the first marriage still subsists (continues). "Spouse living". A husband or wife of a marriage that still subsists on the date of the new marriage. A person whose marriage has been ended by death, by a divorce decree, or by a decree of nullity has no spouse living for Section 5(i). Void marriage . A marriage that has no legal effect from the start. A marriage in breach of Section 5(i) is void, not merely voidable. The topic answers two questions: what happens to the second marriage in civil law, and when the person who marries again commits a crime. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A second marriage while the first subsists is void; if it was properly solemnized, it is also bigamy. flowchart TD A{"Spouse living on the date
of the new marriage?"} A -->|"No"| OK["s. 5(i) satisfied"] A -->|"Yes"| B{"Earlier marriage ended by death,
divorce decree or nullity decree?"} B -->|"Yes"| OK B -->|"No"| V["New marriage VOID

up to 7 years + fine"] BG --> BG2["First marriage concealed:
s. 82(2), up to 10 years + fine"] Text description Ask whether either party had a spouse living on the date of the new marriage. If no, section 5(i) is satisfied. If yes, ask whether the earlier marriage had been ended by death, a divorce decree or a decree of nullity. If it had, there is no spouse living. If not, the new marriage is void under sections 11 and 17. Then ask whether the new marriage was solemnized with the essential ceremonies. If not, there is no bigamy (Bhaurao). If it was, ask whether an exception applies: an earlier marriage declared void, or seven years' absence with disclosure. If an exception applies, there is no offence. Otherwise it is bigamy under BNS section 82(1), up to seven years and fine, or section 82(2), up to ten years and fine, if the first marriage was concealed.
keyPoints: Section 5(i): no spouse living at the time of marriage. A breach makes the marriage void (Sections 11 and 17) and punishable (Section 17; BNS Section 82). BNS Section 82: up to seven years and fine; up to ten years and fine with concealment. The second ceremony must be proved for bigamy ( Bhaurao ). Exceptions: earlier marriage declared void; spouse absent and unheard of for seven years, with disclosure. Conversion does not dissolve the first marriage ( Sarla Mudgal ; Lily Thomas ). Before 1955 a Hindu man could marry any number of wives (Mulla, Section 430), except under State Acts such as the Bombay Act, 1946 and the Madras Act, 1949. The Special Marriage Act, 1954 also bars a second marriage (Sections 4(a), 43, 44).

caseLaws.name: Sarla Mudgal v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (1995) Facts. Four petitions under Article 32 came from first wives (Meena Mathur, Geeta Rani, Sushmita Ghosh) and from a second wife (Sunita alias Fathima) of Hindu husbands who converted to Islam and married again without ending the first marriage. Principle. The first Hindu marriage continues after conversion until dissolved under the Act; the second marriage is invalid, void for Section 494 IPC, and the husband is guilty of bigamy. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It closed the conversion route to a second marriage. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) Facts. A review petition and writ petitions asked the Court to clarify Sarla Mudgal . Sushmita Ghosh said her husband, married to her on 10 May 1984, got a certificate of conversion dated 17 June 1992 only to remarry. Principle. Mere conversion does not end the first marriage without a divorce decree; a second marriage is void under Sections 11 and 17 and punishable under Section 494 IPC; Sarla Mudgal gave no direction for a common civil code. (2000) 6 SCC 224 : AIR 2000 SC 1650. Why it matters. It confirms Sarla Mudgal and states its scope. Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v. State of Maharashtra (1965) Facts. Bhaurao, married to Indubai in about 1956, went through a "Gandharva" marriage with Kamlabai in February 1962 by an exchange of garlands and touching of foreheads, without homa or saptapadi. He was convicted under Section 494 IPC. Principle. "Whoever … marries" in Section 494 means whoever marries validly; a marriage is void under Section 17 only if it was solemnized with the proper ceremonies; the conviction was set aside. AIR 1965 SC 1564 : (1965) 2 SCR 837. Why it matters. The second marriage must be proved to have been properly solemnized before there can be bigamy.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a second marriage during the life of the first spouse void or voidable?
selfTest.a: Void (Sections 11 and 17).

selfTest.q: 2. Which BNS section punishes bigamy?
selfTest.a: Section 82.

selfTest.q: 3. Does conversion end the first Hindu marriage?
selfTest.a: No. See Sarla Mudgal and Lily Thomas .

selfTest.q: 4. What is the punishment if the first marriage was hidden from the new partner?
selfTest.a: Up to ten years and fine (BNS Section 82(2)).

selfTest.q: 5. A husband's wife has been missing and unheard of for eight years. He tells his new partner everything and marries her. Is it bigamy?
selfTest.a: No. The Exception to BNS Section 82(1) covers him.

selfTest.q: 6. Did Sarla Mudgal direct the enactment of a uniform civil code?
selfTest.a: No. Lily Thomas clarified that it gave no such direction.

సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే:

సెక్షన్ 5(i): పెళ్లి రోజున వధువుకు గానీ వరుడికి గానీ జీవించి ఉన్న భర్త లేదా భార్య ఉండకూడదు. సెక్షన్ 11: క్లాజ్ (i) ను ఉల్లంఘించిన వివాహం శూన్యం. ఏ పక్షమైనా మరో పక్షంపై శూన్యత డిక్రీ కోసం కోర్టును అడగవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 17: ఆ తేదీన ఏ పక్షానికైనా జీవించి ఉన్న జీవిత భాగస్వామి ఉంటే ఇద్దరు హిందువుల మధ్య వివాహం శూన్యం; IPC ద్విభార్యత్వ సెక్షన్లు (ఇప్పుడు BNS సెక్షన్ 82) వర్తిస్తాయి. BNS సెక్షన్ 82(1): జీవిత భాగస్వామి జీవించి ఉండగా, ఆ కారణంగా శూన్యమయ్యే మరో వివాహం చేసుకోవడం: ఏడేళ్ల వరకు జైలు, జరిమానా. BNS సెక్షన్ 82(2): కొత్త భాగస్వామి నుంచి మొదటి వివాహాన్ని దాచి అదే నేరం చేయడం: పదేళ్ల వరకు జైలు, జరిమానా.

ఏకపత్నీత్వం . ఒక వ్యక్తికి ఒకే సమయంలో ఒకే జీవిత భాగస్వామి ఉండాలనే నియమం. ద్విభార్యత్వం . మొదటి జీవిత భాగస్వామి జీవించి ఉండి, మొదటి వివాహం ఇంకా కొనసాగుతుండగా మళ్ళీ పెళ్లి చేసుకోవడం. "జీవించి ఉన్న జీవిత భాగస్వామి" (spouse living). కొత్త వివాహం తేదీన ఇంకా కొనసాగుతున్న వివాహంలోని భర్త లేదా భార్య. మరణం, విడాకుల డిక్రీ, లేదా శూన్యత డిక్రీతో వివాహం ముగిసిన వ్యక్తికి సెక్షన్ 5(i) కోసం జీవించి ఉన్న జీవిత భాగస్వామి లేరు. శూన్య వివాహం . మొదటి నుంచే చట్టపరంగా ప్రభావం లేని వివాహం. సెక్షన్ 5(i) ఉల్లంఘించిన వివాహం శూన్యం; కేవలం రద్దు చేయదగినది కాదు. ఈ అంశం రెండు ప్రశ్నలకు సమాధానం ఇస్తుంది: సివిల్ చట్టంలో రెండో వివాహానికి ఏమవుతుంది, మళ్ళీ పెళ్లి చేసుకునే వ్యక్తి ఎప్పుడు నేరం చేస్తాడు. selfTest.a: లేదు. Sarla Mudgal , Lily Thomas చూడండి.

selfTest.q: 5. ఒక భర్త భార్య ఎనిమిదేళ్లుగా కనిపించకుండా, ఏ వార్తా లేకుండా ఉంది. అతను కొత్త భాగస్వామికి అంతా చెప్పి ఆమెను పెళ్లి చేసుకున్నాడు. ఇది ద్విభార్యత్వమా?

selfTest.q: 6. ఉమ్మడి పౌర స్మృతి చేయమని Sarla Mudgal ఆదేశించిందా?

hi.inOneMinute: One spouse at a time. Monogamy means having only one spouse at a time. Section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) allows a marriage only if neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage. Civil result. A second marriage during the life of the first spouse is void (Sections 11 and 17). The second "spouse" gets no status as husband or wife. Criminal result. Section 17 applies the bigamy offence of Sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). These are now Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS): up to seven years and fine, and up to ten years and fine if the first marriage was hidden from the new partner. A proper second ceremony is needed. There is bigamy only if the second marriage was " solemnized " with the essential ceremonies ( Bhaurao , 1965). Conversion is no escape. A Hindu who converts to another religion and marries again, without first ending the Hindu marriage, commits bigamy ( Sarla Mudgal , 1995; Lily Thomas , 2000). History. Before 1955 a Hindu man could marry any number of wives, except where State anti-bigamy Acts applied (Mulla). Monogamy is the outstanding feature of the HMA.
legalProvision: Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Conditions for a Hindu marriage. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; …

Section 11. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 17. Punishment of bigamy. Any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after the commencement of this Act is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living; and the provisions of sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860), shall apply accordingly.

Section 82, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife. (1) Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Exception. —This sub-section does not extend to any person whose marriage with such husband or wife has been declared void by a Court of competent jurisdiction, nor to any person who contracts a marriage during the life of a former husband or wife, if such husband or wife, at the time of the subsequent marriage, shall have been continually absent from such person for the space of seven years, and shall not have been heard of by such person as being alive within that time provided the person contracting such subsequent marriage shall, before such marriage takes place, inform the person with whom such marriage is contracted of the real state of facts so far as the same are within his or her knowledge. (2) Whoever commits the offence under sub-section (1) having concealed from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
In simple words:

Section 5(i): on the wedding day, neither the bride nor the bridegroom may have a living husband or wife. Section 11: a marriage that breaks clause (i) is void. Either party may ask the court for a decree of nullity against the other. Section 17: a marriage between two Hindus is void if either party had a living spouse on that date, and the IPC bigamy sections (now BNS Section 82) apply. BNS Section 82(1): marrying again in the life of a spouse, where the new marriage is void for that reason: up to seven years and fine. BNS Section 82(2): the same offence after hiding the first marriage from the new partner: up to ten years and fine.
hi.meaning:
Monogamy . The rule that a person may have only one spouse at a time. Bigamy. Marrying again while the first spouse is alive and the first marriage still subsists (continues). "Spouse living". A husband or wife of a marriage that still subsists on the date of the new marriage. A person whose marriage has been ended by death, by a divorce decree, or by a decree of nullity has no spouse living for Section 5(i). Void marriage . A marriage that has no legal effect from the start. A marriage in breach of Section 5(i) is void, not merely voidable. The topic answers two questions: what happens to the second marriage in civil law, and when the person who marries again commits a crime. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. s. 82(2), up to 10 years + fine"] Text description Ask whether either party had a spouse living on the date of the new marriage. If no, section 5(i) is satisfied. If yes, ask whether the earlier marriage had been ended by death, a divorce decree or a decree of nullity. If it had, there is no spouse living. If not, the new marriage is void under sections 11 and 17. Then ask whether the new marriage was solemnized with the essential ceremonies. If not, there is no bigamy (Bhaurao). If it was, ask whether an exception applies: an earlier marriage declared void, or seven years' absence with disclosure. If an exception applies, there is no offence. Otherwise it is bigamy under BNS section 82(1), up to seven years and fine, or section 82(2), up to ten years and fine, if the first marriage was concealed.
keyPoints: Section 5(i): no spouse living at the time of marriage. A breach makes the marriage void (Sections 11 and 17) and punishable (Section 17; BNS Section 82). BNS Section 82: up to seven years and fine; up to ten years and fine with concealment. The second ceremony must be proved for bigamy ( Bhaurao ). Exceptions: earlier marriage declared void; spouse absent and unheard of for seven years, with disclosure. Conversion does not dissolve the first marriage ( Sarla Mudgal ; Lily Thomas ). Before 1955 a Hindu man could marry any number of wives (Mulla, Section 430), except under State Acts such as the Bombay Act, 1946 and the Madras Act, 1949. The Special Marriage Act, 1954 also bars a second marriage (Sections 4(a), 43, 44).

caseLaws.name: Sarla Mudgal v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (1995) Facts. Four petitions under Article 32 came from first wives (Meena Mathur, Geeta Rani, Sushmita Ghosh) and from a second wife (Sunita alias Fathima) of Hindu husbands who converted to Islam and married again without ending the first marriage. Principle. The first Hindu marriage continues after conversion until dissolved under the Act; the second marriage is invalid, void for Section 494 IPC, and the husband is guilty of bigamy. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It closed the conversion route to a second marriage. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) Facts. A review petition and writ petitions asked the Court to clarify Sarla Mudgal . Sushmita Ghosh said her husband, married to her on 10 May 1984, got a certificate of conversion dated 17 June 1992 only to remarry. Principle. Mere conversion does not end the first marriage without a divorce decree; a second marriage is void under Sections 11 and 17 and punishable under Section 494 IPC; Sarla Mudgal gave no direction for a common civil code. (2000) 6 SCC 224 : AIR 2000 SC 1650. Why it matters. It confirms Sarla Mudgal and states its scope. Bhaurao Shankar Lokhande v. State of Maharashtra (1965) Facts. Bhaurao, married to Indubai in about 1956, went through a "Gandharva" marriage with Kamlabai in February 1962 by an exchange of garlands and touching of foreheads, without homa or saptapadi. He was convicted under Section 494 IPC. Principle. "Whoever … marries" in Section 494 means whoever marries validly; a marriage is void under Section 17 only if it was solemnized with the proper ceremonies; the conviction was set aside. AIR 1965 SC 1564 : (1965) 2 SCR 837. Why it matters. The second marriage must be proved to have been properly solemnized before there can be bigamy.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a second marriage during the life of the first spouse void or voidable?
selfTest.a: Void (Sections 11 and 17).

selfTest.q: 2. Which BNS section punishes bigamy?
selfTest.a: Section 82.

selfTest.q: 3. Does conversion end the first Hindu marriage?
selfTest.a: No. See Sarla Mudgal and Lily Thomas .

selfTest.q: 4. What is the punishment if the first marriage was hidden from the new partner?
selfTest.a: Up to ten years and fine (BNS Section 82(2)).

selfTest.q: 5. A husband's wife has been missing and unheard of for eight years. He tells his new partner everything and marries her. Is it bigamy?
selfTest.a: No. The Exception to BNS Section 82(1) covers him.

selfTest.q: 6. Did Sarla Mudgal direct the enactment of a uniform civil code?
selfTest.a: No. Lily Thomas clarified that it gave no such direction.

family-law-i-u2-t3.subtitle: The five conditions of section 5 and what follows when each is broken

en.inOneMinute: Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) says a marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus if five conditions are met: No living spouse – neither party has a husband or wife living (clause (i)). Mental capacity – neither party is of unsound mind, mentally unfit for marriage and procreation, or subject to recurrent attacks of insanity (clause (ii)). Age – the bridegroom has completed 21 years and the bride 18 years (clause (iii)). No prohibited relationship – unless the custom of each party permits (clause (iv)). Not sapindas – unless the custom of each party permits (clause (v)). The results of a breach are not the same, and exams test this: Breach of clause (i), (iv) or (v): the marriage is void (Section 11). Breach of clause (i) is also the offence of bigamy (Section 17). Breach of clause (ii): the marriage is voidable (Section 12(1)(b)). Breach of clause (iii): the marriage stays valid under the HMA, but the person who procured it is punishable (Section 18(a)). The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (PCMA) separately lets the party who was a child have it annulled (PCMA Section 3). There was once a clause (vi) (consent of the bride's guardian). It was omitted in 1978. Same gotra, same pravara and different castes are no longer bars.
legalProvision: Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Conditions for a Hindu marriage. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; (ii) at the time of the marriage, neither party— (a) is incapable of giving a valid consent to it in consequence of unsoundness of mind; or (b) though capable of giving a valid consent, has been suffering from mental disorder of such a kind or to such an extent as to be unfit for marriage and the procreation of children; or (c) has been subject to recurrent attacks of insanity; (iii) the bridegroom has completed the age of twenty-one years and the bride, the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage; (iv) the parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two; (v) the parties are not sapindas of each other, unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two;

Notes from the bare Act: clause (ii) was substituted by Act 68 of 1976. The words "or epilepsy" were omitted from clause (ii)(c) by Act 39 of 1999 (from 29 December 1999). In clause (iii) the ages were "eighteen" and "fifteen" until Act 2 of 1978 raised them to twenty-one and eighteen (from 1 October 1978). Clause (vi) was omitted by the same Act of 1978.

Section 3(a). the expressions "custom" and "usage" signify any rule which, having been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, has obtained the force of law among Hindus in any local area, tribe, community, group or family: Provided that the rule is certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy; and Provided further that in the case of a rule applicable only to a family it has not been discontinued by the family;

Section 3(f). (i) "sapinda relationship" with reference to any person extends as far as the third generation (inclusive) in the line of ascent through the mother, and the fifth (inclusive) in the line of ascent through the father, the line being traced upwards in each case from the person concerned, who is to be counted as the first generation; (ii) two persons are said to be "sapindas" of each other if one is a lineal ascendant of the other within the limits of sapinda relationship, or if they have a common lineal ascendant who is within the limits of sapinda relationship with reference to each of them;

Section 3(g). "degrees of prohibited relationship"—two persons are said to be within the "degrees of prohibited relationship"— (i) if one is a lineal ascendant of the other; or (ii) if one was the wife or husband of a lineal ascendant or descendant of the other; or (iii) if one was the wife of the brother or of the father's or mother's brother or of the grandfather's or grandmother's brother of the other; or (iv) if the two are brother and sister, uncle and niece, aunt and nephew, or children of brother and sister or of two brothers or of two sisters; Explanation. —For the purposes of clauses (f) and (g), relationship includes— (i) relationship by half or uterine blood as well as by full blood; (ii) illegitimate blood relationship as well as legitimate; (iii) relationship by adoption as well as by blood; and all terms of relationship in those clauses shall be construed accordingly.

Section 11. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 12(1)(b). Voidable marriages. Any marriage solemnised, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be voidable and may be annulled by a decree of nullity on any of the following grounds, namely:— … (b) that the marriage is in contravention of the condition specified in clause (ii) of section 5;

Section 17. Punishment of bigamy. Any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after the commencement of this Act is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living; and the provisions of sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860), shall apply accordingly.

Section 18. Punishment for contravention of certain other conditions for a Hindu marriage. Every person who procures a marriage of himself or herself to be solemnized under this Act in contravention of the conditions specified in clauses (iii), (iv), and (v) of section 5 shall be punishable— (a) in the case of contravention of the condition specified in clause (iii) of section 5, with rigorous imprisonment which may extend to two years or with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both. (b) in the case of a contravention of the condition specified in clause (iv) or clause (v) of section 5, with simple imprisonment which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both;
Clause (a) of Section 18 was substituted by Section 20 of the PCMA (from 30 October 2007). A former clause (c), on the guardian's consent, was omitted in 1978.

In simple words: Section 5 lists what the two persons must satisfy on the wedding day. Sections 3(a), (f) and (g) explain the words used. Sections 11, 12, 17 and 18 say what happens if a condition is broken. The ceremonies themselves are a separate requirement (Section 7, covered in "Ceremonies and Registration").
en.meaning:
The conditions of a Hindu marriage are the legal requirements that the two parties must satisfy at the time of the marriage . A marriage that satisfies them, and is solemnized with the ceremonies required by Section 7, is a valid Hindu marriage. Three points come straight from the words of Section 5: "between any two Hindus". Both parties must be persons to whom the Act applies (Section 2). If one party is not a Hindu, a marriage under the HMA is not possible; the parties may marry under the Special Marriage Act, 1954. "at the time of the marriage". Each condition is tested on the date of the wedding. A spouse who dies a week after a second wedding does not make that wedding valid. Not every condition has the same weight. Breach of some conditions destroys the marriage (void), breach of one makes it open to challenge (voidable), and breach of the age condition only attracts punishment. See Diagram 1 for the step-by-step test. Diagram 1. Test the five conditions in this order; the first "Yes" gives the result. flowchart TD Q1{"Either party had a

no custom of each permitting?

punishable: s. 18(b)"] Q3 -->|"No"| Q4{"Groom under 21 or
bride under 18? s. 5(iii)"} Q4 -->|"Yes"| V4["VALID but punishable: s. 18(a)
voidable at child's option:
PCMA s. 3"] Q4 -->|"No"| V5["VALID, if s. 7
ceremonies performed"] Text description First ask whether either party had a living spouse; if yes, the marriage is void and bigamy is punishable under sections 11 and 17. If no, ask whether either party lacked mental capacity; if yes, it is voidable under section 12(1)(b). If no, ask whether the parties are within prohibited degrees or are sapindas with no custom of each permitting it; if yes, it is void under section 11 and punishable under section 18(b). If no, ask whether the groom is under 21 or the bride under 18; if yes, it is valid but punishable under section 18(a), and voidable at the child's option under PCMA section 3. If no, and the section 7 ceremonies were performed, the marriage is valid. Mulla (notes to Sections 3(g) and 5) explains that clauses (iv) and (v) are based on the old principle of exogamy, and that the Act aims at "uniformity and certainty" on prohibited degrees, which had varied widely across India.
keyPoints: Five conditions: no living spouse, mental capacity, age (21 and 18, completed), no prohibited relationship, no sapinda relationship. Breach of clauses (i), (iv), (v): void (Section 11). Clause (i) is also bigamy (Section 17; now BNS Section 82). Breach of clause (ii): voidable (Section 12(1)(b)). Breach of clause (iii): valid but punishable (Section 18(a)); voidable at the child's option under PCMA Section 3. Custom can save only clauses (iv) and (v), and must govern each party. Sapinda: five generations through the father, three through the mother, counting the person as the first. PCMA 2006: petition before completing two years of attaining majority; offences cognizable and non-bailable; CMRA 1929 repealed. Same gotra, pravara or caste is no bar (Section 5 has none; Section 29(1) saves older marriages). Yamunabai : a bigamous marriage is void, and the woman is not a wife for maintenance; Badshah : except where the man hid his first marriage.

caseLaws.name: Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v
caseLaws.facts: Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week, alleging ill-treatment, and in 1976 claimed maintenance as his wife under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Principle. A marriage in breach of Section 5(i) is null and void under Section 11, "void ipso jure", and need not be declared so by a court in advance; Section 12 does not apply to it, and because of Section 4 no earlier law or custom can save it; estoppel cannot defeat the Act, so she was not a "wife" under Section 125. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. It is the leading case on breach of the monogamy condition and on the difference between void and voidable marriages. Badshah v. Urmila Badshah Godse (2013) Facts. A man already married to Shobha married Urmila in 2005 with Hindu rites, hiding his first marriage. She and their daughter claimed maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Principle. Yamunabai applies only where the woman married with full knowledge of the subsisting first marriage; a man who duped her by hiding it cannot take advantage of his own wrong, and for Section 125 she is treated as his wife. (2014) 1 SCC 188 : AIR 2014 SC 869. Why it matters. It limits the harsh result of a void bigamous marriage for a deceived woman.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the result of breaking Section 5(i)?
selfTest.a: The marriage is void under Sections 11 and 17, and bigamy is punishable.

selfTest.q: 2. Is a marriage below the minimum age void under the HMA?
selfTest.a: No. It is valid under the HMA and punishable under Section 18(a). The child party may have it annulled under PCMA Section 3.

selfTest.q: 3. Which clauses can a custom save?
selfTest.a: Clauses (iv) and (v), and only if the custom governs each party.

selfTest.q: 4. A and B share a great-great-grandfather through their fathers. Are they sapindas?
selfTest.a: Yes. The great-great-grandfather is the fifth generation through the father for each of them, which is within the limit.

selfTest.q: 5. Sunil married at 19. By when must he file a petition under PCMA Section 3?
selfTest.a: Before he completes two years of attaining majority, that is, before he turns 20.

selfTest.q: 6. Can a man marry his deceased wife's sister?
selfTest.a: Yes. Relationship by marriage is not a bar unless Section 3(g)(ii) or (iii) names it (Mulla).

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 5(i) ఉల్లంఘన ఫలితం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్లు 11, 17 కింద వివాహం శూన్యం; ద్విభార్యత్వం శిక్షార్హం.

selfTest.q: 2. కనీస వయస్సు లోపు జరిగిన వివాహం HMA కింద శూన్యమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. HMA కింద చెల్లుబాటవుతుంది, సెక్షన్ 18(a) కింద శిక్షార్హం. PCMA సెక్షన్ 3 కింద child పక్షం దానిని రద్దు చేయించుకోవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 3. ఆచారం ఏ క్లాజులను కాపాడగలదు?
selfTest.a: క్లాజులు (iv), (v); అదీ ఆచారం ప్రతి పక్షాన్నీ నియంత్రిస్తేనే.

selfTest.q: 4. A, B లకు తండ్రుల ద్వారా ఒకే ముత్తాత తండ్రి ఉన్నాడు. వారు సపిండులా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ఇద్దరిలో ప్రతి ఒక్కరికీ ముత్తాత తండ్రి, తండ్రి ద్వారా ఐదవ తరం; అది పరిమితిలోనే ఉంది.

selfTest.q: 5. సునీల్ 19 ఏళ్లకు పెళ్లి చేసుకున్నాడు. PCMA సెక్షన్ 3 కింద ఎప్పటిలోగా పిటిషన్ వేయాలి?
selfTest.a: మెజారిటీ వచ్చిన రెండేళ్లు పూర్తయ్యేలోపు, అంటే 20 ఏళ్లు రాకముందే.

selfTest.q: 6. ఒక పురుషుడు మరణించిన భార్య సోదరిని పెళ్లి చేసుకోవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. సెక్షన్ 3(g)(ii) లేదా (iii) పేర్కొంటే తప్ప, పెళ్లి ద్వారా వచ్చిన బంధుత్వం అడ్డంకి కాదు (ముల్లా).

hi.inOneMinute: Section 5 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) says a marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus if five conditions are met: No living spouse – neither party has a husband or wife living (clause (i)). Mental capacity – neither party is of unsound mind, mentally unfit for marriage and procreation, or subject to recurrent attacks of insanity (clause (ii)). Age – the bridegroom has completed 21 years and the bride 18 years (clause (iii)). No prohibited relationship – unless the custom of each party permits (clause (iv)). Not sapindas – unless the custom of each party permits (clause (v)). The results of a breach are not the same, and exams test this: Breach of clause (i), (iv) or (v): the marriage is void (Section 11). Breach of clause (i) is also the offence of bigamy (Section 17). Breach of clause (ii): the marriage is voidable (Section 12(1)(b)). Breach of clause (iii): the marriage stays valid under the HMA, but the person who procured it is punishable (Section 18(a)). The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (PCMA) separately lets the party who was a child have it annulled (PCMA Section 3). There was once a clause (vi) (consent of the bride's guardian). It was omitted in 1978. Same gotra, same pravara and different castes are no longer bars.
legalProvision: Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Conditions for a Hindu marriage. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; (ii) at the time of the marriage, neither party— (a) is incapable of giving a valid consent to it in consequence of unsoundness of mind; or (b) though capable of giving a valid consent, has been suffering from mental disorder of such a kind or to such an extent as to be unfit for marriage and the procreation of children; or (c) has been subject to recurrent attacks of insanity; (iii) the bridegroom has completed the age of twenty-one years and the bride, the age of eighteen years at the time of the marriage; (iv) the parties are not within the degrees of prohibited relationship unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two; (v) the parties are not sapindas of each other, unless the custom or usage governing each of them permits of a marriage between the two;

Notes from the bare Act: clause (ii) was substituted by Act 68 of 1976. The words "or epilepsy" were omitted from clause (ii)(c) by Act 39 of 1999 (from 29 December 1999). In clause (iii) the ages were "eighteen" and "fifteen" until Act 2 of 1978 raised them to twenty-one and eighteen (from 1 October 1978). Clause (vi) was omitted by the same Act of 1978.

Section 3(a). the expressions "custom" and "usage" signify any rule which, having been continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, has obtained the force of law among Hindus in any local area, tribe, community, group or family: Provided that the rule is certain and not unreasonable or opposed to public policy; and Provided further that in the case of a rule applicable only to a family it has not been discontinued by the family;

Section 3(f). (i) "sapinda relationship" with reference to any person extends as far as the third generation (inclusive) in the line of ascent through the mother, and the fifth (inclusive) in the line of ascent through the father, the line being traced upwards in each case from the person concerned, who is to be counted as the first generation; (ii) two persons are said to be "sapindas" of each other if one is a lineal ascendant of the other within the limits of sapinda relationship, or if they have a common lineal ascendant who is within the limits of sapinda relationship with reference to each of them;

Section 3(g). "degrees of prohibited relationship"—two persons are said to be within the "degrees of prohibited relationship"— (i) if one is a lineal ascendant of the other; or (ii) if one was the wife or husband of a lineal ascendant or descendant of the other; or (iii) if one was the wife of the brother or of the father's or mother's brother or of the grandfather's or grandmother's brother of the other; or (iv) if the two are brother and sister, uncle and niece, aunt and nephew, or children of brother and sister or of two brothers or of two sisters; Explanation. —For the purposes of clauses (f) and (g), relationship includes— (i) relationship by half or uterine blood as well as by full blood; (ii) illegitimate blood relationship as well as legitimate; (iii) relationship by adoption as well as by blood; and all terms of relationship in those clauses shall be construed accordingly.

Section 11. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 12(1)(b). Voidable marriages. Any marriage solemnised, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be voidable and may be annulled by a decree of nullity on any of the following grounds, namely:— … (b) that the marriage is in contravention of the condition specified in clause (ii) of section 5;

Section 17. Punishment of bigamy. Any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after the commencement of this Act is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living; and the provisions of sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860), shall apply accordingly.

Section 18. Punishment for contravention of certain other conditions for a Hindu marriage. Every person who procures a marriage of himself or herself to be solemnized under this Act in contravention of the conditions specified in clauses (iii), (iv), and (v) of section 5 shall be punishable— (a) in the case of contravention of the condition specified in clause (iii) of section 5, with rigorous imprisonment which may extend to two years or with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both. (b) in the case of a contravention of the condition specified in clause (iv) or clause (v) of section 5, with simple imprisonment which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both;
Clause (a) of Section 18 was substituted by Section 20 of the PCMA (from 30 October 2007). A former clause (c), on the guardian's consent, was omitted in 1978.

In simple words: Section 5 lists what the two persons must satisfy on the wedding day. Sections 3(a), (f) and (g) explain the words used. Sections 11, 12, 17 and 18 say what happens if a condition is broken. The ceremonies themselves are a separate requirement (Section 7, covered in "Ceremonies and Registration").
hi.meaning:
The conditions of a Hindu marriage are the legal requirements that the two parties must satisfy at the time of the marriage . A marriage that satisfies them, and is solemnized with the ceremonies required by Section 7, is a valid Hindu marriage. Three points come straight from the words of Section 5: "between any two Hindus". Both parties must be persons to whom the Act applies (Section 2). If one party is not a Hindu, a marriage under the HMA is not possible; the parties may marry under the Special Marriage Act, 1954. "at the time of the marriage". Each condition is tested on the date of the wedding. A spouse who dies a week after a second wedding does not make that wedding valid. Not every condition has the same weight. Breach of some conditions destroys the marriage (void), breach of one makes it open to challenge (voidable), and breach of the age condition only attracts punishment. ceremonies performed"] Text description First ask whether either party had a living spouse; if yes, the marriage is void and bigamy is punishable under sections 11 and 17. If no, ask whether either party lacked mental capacity; if yes, it is voidable under section 12(1)(b). If no, ask whether the parties are within prohibited degrees or are sapindas with no custom of each permitting it; if yes, it is void under section 11 and punishable under section 18(b). If no, ask whether the groom is under 21 or the bride under 18; if yes, it is valid but punishable under section 18(a), and voidable at the child's option under PCMA section 3. If no, and the section 7 ceremonies were performed, the marriage is valid. Mulla (notes to Sections 3(g) and 5) explains that clauses (iv) and (v) are based on the old principle of exogamy, and that the Act aims at "uniformity and certainty" on prohibited degrees, which had varied widely across India.
keyPoints: Five conditions: no living spouse, mental capacity, age (21 and 18, completed), no prohibited relationship, no sapinda relationship. Breach of clauses (i), (iv), (v): void (Section 11). Clause (i) is also bigamy (Section 17; now BNS Section 82). Breach of clause (ii): voidable (Section 12(1)(b)). Breach of clause (iii): valid but punishable (Section 18(a)); voidable at the child's option under PCMA Section 3. Custom can save only clauses (iv) and (v), and must govern each party. Sapinda: five generations through the father, three through the mother, counting the person as the first. PCMA 2006: petition before completing two years of attaining majority; offences cognizable and non-bailable; CMRA 1929 repealed. Same gotra, pravara or caste is no bar (Section 5 has none; Section 29(1) saves older marriages). Yamunabai : a bigamous marriage is void, and the woman is not a wife for maintenance; Badshah : except where the man hid his first marriage.

caseLaws.name: Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v
caseLaws.facts: Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week, alleging ill-treatment, and in 1976 claimed maintenance as his wife under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Principle. A marriage in breach of Section 5(i) is null and void under Section 11, "void ipso jure", and need not be declared so by a court in advance; Section 12 does not apply to it, and because of Section 4 no earlier law or custom can save it; estoppel cannot defeat the Act, so she was not a "wife" under Section 125. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. It is the leading case on breach of the monogamy condition and on the difference between void and voidable marriages. Badshah v. Urmila Badshah Godse (2013) Facts. A man already married to Shobha married Urmila in 2005 with Hindu rites, hiding his first marriage. She and their daughter claimed maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Principle. Yamunabai applies only where the woman married with full knowledge of the subsisting first marriage; a man who duped her by hiding it cannot take advantage of his own wrong, and for Section 125 she is treated as his wife. (2014) 1 SCC 188 : AIR 2014 SC 869. Why it matters. It limits the harsh result of a void bigamous marriage for a deceived woman.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the result of breaking Section 5(i)?
selfTest.a: The marriage is void under Sections 11 and 17, and bigamy is punishable.

selfTest.q: 2. Is a marriage below the minimum age void under the HMA?
selfTest.a: No. It is valid under the HMA and punishable under Section 18(a). The child party may have it annulled under PCMA Section 3.

selfTest.q: 3. Which clauses can a custom save?
selfTest.a: Clauses (iv) and (v), and only if the custom governs each party.

selfTest.q: 4. A and B share a great-great-grandfather through their fathers. Are they sapindas?
selfTest.a: Yes. The great-great-grandfather is the fifth generation through the father for each of them, which is within the limit.

selfTest.q: 5. Sunil married at 19. By when must he file a petition under PCMA Section 3?
selfTest.a: Before he completes two years of attaining majority, that is, before he turns 20.

selfTest.q: 6. Can a man marry his deceased wife's sister?
selfTest.a: Yes. Relationship by marriage is not a bar unless Section 3(g)(ii) or (iii) names it (Mulla).

family-law-i-u2-t7.subtitle: Live-in relationships, choice of spouse, inter-caste marriage and same-sex marriage

en.inOneMinute: The gap. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) was not written with live-in couples, inter-caste elopements or same-sex couples in mind. Courts have built answers for each. Presumption. Long, open cohabitation as husband and wife raises a strong but rebuttable presumption of marriage ( Badri Prasad , 1978). Live-in relationships. A woman in a relationship in the nature of marriage gets the reliefs of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (DV Act), if the tests in Velusamy (2010) and Indra Sarma (2013) are met. Right to choose. Adults have a constitutional right to choose a spouse under Articles 19 and 21 ( Lata Singh , Shakti Vahini , Shafin Jahan ). Same-sex marriage. In Supriyo (2023) the Supreme Court held that there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry and left the recognition of same-sex unions to Parliament. Legislation. Many changes, from widow remarriage to the ban on child marriage, came through Acts of the legislatures ( Supriyo ).
legalProvision: Section 2(f), Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. "domestic relationship" means a relationship between two persons who live or have, at any point of time, lived together in a shared household, when they are related by consanguinity, marriage, or through a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption or are family members living together as a joint family;

Section 2(s). "shared household" means a household where the person aggrieved lives or at any stage has lived in a domestic relationship either singly or along with the respondent and includes such a household whether owned or tenanted either jointly by the aggrieved person and the respondent, or owned or tenanted by either of them …

Section 17(1). Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, every woman in a domestic relationship shall have the right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has any right, title or beneficial interest in the same.
In simple words:

Articles 19 and 21, Constitution. They protect the freedom of adults to choose a life partner ( Shakti Vahini ; Shafin Jahan ). DV Act, Section 2(f). A " domestic relationship " includes persons who live or have lived together in a household when related by marriage or "through a relationship in the nature of marriage ". DV Act, Section 17. A woman in a domestic relationship may live in the shared household even if she does not own it. HMA, Sections 5 and 7. They still decide who can marry under the Act and how. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA). Dolly Rani (2024) notes that it is not restricted to Hindus: any man and woman, whatever their race, caste or creed, can become husband and wife under it.
en.meaning:
Recent trends. The changes made by courts and legislatures to fit marriage law to present society. Presumption of marriage . The rule that a man and woman who have lived together for a long time as husband and wife are taken to be validly married unless it is disproved. It is a rebuttable presumption . Relationship in the nature of marriage. A live-in relationship akin to a common law marriage , which the DV Act protects ( Velusamy ). Live-in relationship. Living together without marriage. Not every live-in relationship is "in the nature of marriage". Four fronts matter in this subject. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Long, open cohabitation raises a rebuttable presumption of marriage ( Badri Prasad ). Velusamy : four-part test for a relationship in the nature of marriage, plus a shared household. Indra Sarma : eight guidelines; a woman who knows her partner is married is outside the Act. Chanmuniya : questions on maintenance referred to a larger Bench. The right to choose a spouse is protected by Articles 19 and 21 ( Shakti Vahini ; Shafin Jahan ); inter-caste marriage is not barred ( Lata Singh ). Supriyo : no unqualified right to marry; same-sex recognition left to Parliament; a Cabinet Secretary committee to define entitlements. DV Act: right to reside, protection, residence, monetary, custody and compensation orders; "adult male" struck down from Section 2(q).

caseLaws.name: Badri Prasad v
caseLaws.facts: Deputy Director of Consolidation (1978) Facts. A man and a woman lived together as husband and wife for about fifty years; the petitioner challenged the fact of their marriage, saying no priest or witness of the ceremony was examined. Principle. Long cohabitation as husband and wife raises a strong presumption of marriage; it is rebuttable, but a heavy burden lies on the person who denies it; the petitions were dismissed. (1978) 3 SCC 527 : AIR 1978 SC 1557. Why it matters. It protects long-term couples who cannot prove a ceremony. D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010) Facts. A woman claimed maintenance under Section 125 CrPC as the appellant's wife; he said he was already married to Lakshmi in 1980. Principle. A relationship in the nature of marriage is akin to a common law marriage and needs the four-part test and a shared household; the case went back to the Family Court. Decided 21 October 2010. Why it matters. Not every live-in relationship is covered by the DV Act. Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013) Facts. From 1992 an unmarried woman lived with a married man who had two children; she knew of his marriage and later claimed relief under the DV Act. Principle. The Court gave eight guidelines and held that her relationship was not in the nature of marriage, so she was not in a "domestic relationship"; the appeal was dismissed. Decided 26 November 2013. Why it matters. It built on Velusamy and called for legislation. Chanmuniya v. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha (2010) Facts. A widow said she was married by Katha and Sindur to her late husband's younger brother; the High Court held that the essentials of Section 7 were not performed. Principle. The Bench favoured a broad meaning of "wife" in Section 125 CrPC but referred three questions to a larger Bench. (2011) 1 SCC 141. Why it matters. It is a reference order, not a final ruling. Lata Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2006) Facts. Lata Singh, a major, married outside her caste at an Arya Samaj Mandir in Delhi on 2 November 2000; her brothers lodged a missing person report and a kidnapping case against her husband's relatives. Principle. No offence was committed; a major can marry anyone, and inter-caste marriage is not barred; the case was quashed and proceedings were ordered against the brothers. (2006) 5 SCC 475. Why it matters. It began the protection of the right to choose a spouse. Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018) Facts. An NGO asked the Court to stop honour killings and Khap interference with the marriages of consenting adults. Principle. The choice of a life partner by two adults is recognised under Articles 19 and 21; Khap panchayats have no authority; the Court issued preventive, remedial and punitive directions. (2018) 7 SCC 192. Why it matters. It gave binding guidelines against honour crimes. Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (2018) Facts. An adult woman, Hadiya, converted to Islam and married a man of her choice; the High Court annulled the marriage on her father's habeas corpus petition. Principle. The High Court should not have annulled the marriage in a habeas corpus petition; parens patriae does not apply to an adult with capacity; the right to marry a person of one's choice is integral to Article 21. Order 8 March 2018; reasons 9 April 2018. Why it matters. It protects an adult's choice of faith and spouse from judicial overreach. Supriyo v. Union of India (2023) Facts. Same-sex couples and others filed connected petitions seeking a right to marry; a five-judge Bench heard them. Principle. There is no unqualified fundamental right to marry, and the SMA cannot be read to include same-sex couples (unanimous); by 3 to 2 the Court declined to order civil unions or joint adoption. Decided 17 October 2023. Why it matters. It marks the limit of judicial power on marriage reform.

selfTest.q: 1. Which case gave the four-part test for live-in relationships?
selfTest.a: D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010).

selfTest.q: 2. Does Hindu law recognise same-sex marriage after Supriyo?
selfTest.a: No. The Court left it to Parliament.

selfTest.q: 3. Which Articles protect the right to choose a spouse?
selfTest.a: Articles 19 and 21.

selfTest.q: 4. A couple have lived together as husband and wife for forty years. A relative says no ceremony was proved. Who must prove what?
selfTest.a: A strong presumption of marriage arises; the relative must rebut it ( Badri Prasad ).

selfTest.q: 5. Did Chanmuniya finally decide that a live-in partner is a "wife" under Section 125 CrPC?
selfTest.a: No. It referred the questions to a larger Bench.

selfTest.q: 6. Can a woman under the DV Act claim to live in the shared household though she does not own it?
selfTest.a: Yes (Section 17).

సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే:

ఆర్టికల్స్ 19, 21, రాజ్యాంగం. జీవిత భాగస్వామిని ఎంచుకునే వయోజనుల స్వేచ్ఛను రక్షిస్తాయి ( Shakti Vahini ; Shafin Jahan ). hi.inOneMinute: The gap. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) was not written with live-in couples, inter-caste elopements or same-sex couples in mind. Courts have built answers for each. Presumption. Long, open cohabitation as husband and wife raises a strong but rebuttable presumption of marriage ( Badri Prasad , 1978). Live-in relationships. A woman in a relationship in the nature of marriage gets the reliefs of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (DV Act), if the tests in Velusamy (2010) and Indra Sarma (2013) are met. Right to choose. Adults have a constitutional right to choose a spouse under Articles 19 and 21 ( Lata Singh , Shakti Vahini , Shafin Jahan ). Same-sex marriage. In Supriyo (2023) the Supreme Court held that there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry and left the recognition of same-sex unions to Parliament. Legislation. Many changes, from widow remarriage to the ban on child marriage, came through Acts of the legislatures ( Supriyo ).
legalProvision: Section 2(f), Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. "domestic relationship" means a relationship between two persons who live or have, at any point of time, lived together in a shared household, when they are related by consanguinity, marriage, or through a relationship in the nature of marriage, adoption or are family members living together as a joint family;

Section 2(s). "shared household" means a household where the person aggrieved lives or at any stage has lived in a domestic relationship either singly or along with the respondent and includes such a household whether owned or tenanted either jointly by the aggrieved person and the respondent, or owned or tenanted by either of them …

Section 17(1). Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, every woman in a domestic relationship shall have the right to reside in the shared household, whether or not she has any right, title or beneficial interest in the same.
In simple words:

Articles 19 and 21, Constitution. They protect the freedom of adults to choose a life partner ( Shakti Vahini ; Shafin Jahan ). DV Act, Section 2(f). A " domestic relationship " includes persons who live or have lived together in a household when related by marriage or "through a relationship in the nature of marriage ". DV Act, Section 17. A woman in a domestic relationship may live in the shared household even if she does not own it. HMA, Sections 5 and 7. They still decide who can marry under the Act and how. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA). Dolly Rani (2024) notes that it is not restricted to Hindus: any man and woman, whatever their race, caste or creed, can become husband and wife under it.
hi.meaning:
Recent trends. The changes made by courts and legislatures to fit marriage law to present society. Presumption of marriage . The rule that a man and woman who have lived together for a long time as husband and wife are taken to be validly married unless it is disproved. It is a rebuttable presumption . Relationship in the nature of marriage. A live-in relationship akin to a common law marriage , which the DV Act protects ( Velusamy ). Live-in relationship. Living together without marriage. Not every live-in relationship is "in the nature of marriage". Four fronts matter in this subject. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1.
