(Supriyo)"] Text description Recent trends in marriage have four fronts. Presumption of marriage from long open cohabitation: Badri Prasad. Live-in relationships under the Domestic Violence Act: Velusamy and Indra Sarma. Right to choose a spouse under Articles 19 and 21: Lata Singh, Shakti Vahini and Shafin Jahan. Same-sex marriage: Supriyo, which left the matter to Parliament. Front Leading cases Presumption of marriage Badri Prasad ; Chanmuniya (reference) Live-in relationships under the DV Act Velusamy ; Indra Sarma Right to choose a spouse Lata Singh ; Shakti Vahini ; Shafin Jahan Same-sex marriage Supriyo : left to Parliament
keyPoints: Long, open cohabitation raises a rebuttable presumption of marriage ( Badri Prasad ). Velusamy : four-part test for a relationship in the nature of marriage, plus a shared household. Indra Sarma : eight guidelines; a woman who knows her partner is married is outside the Act. Chanmuniya : questions on maintenance referred to a larger Bench. The right to choose a spouse is protected by Articles 19 and 21 ( Shakti Vahini ; Shafin Jahan ); inter-caste marriage is not barred ( Lata Singh ). Supriyo : no unqualified right to marry; same-sex recognition left to Parliament; a Cabinet Secretary committee to define entitlements. DV Act: right to reside, protection, residence, monetary, custody and compensation orders; "adult male" struck down from Section 2(q).

caseLaws.name: Badri Prasad v
caseLaws.facts: Deputy Director of Consolidation (1978) Facts. A man and a woman lived together as husband and wife for about fifty years; the petitioner challenged the fact of their marriage, saying no priest or witness of the ceremony was examined. Principle. Long cohabitation as husband and wife raises a strong presumption of marriage; it is rebuttable, but a heavy burden lies on the person who denies it; the petitions were dismissed. (1978) 3 SCC 527 : AIR 1978 SC 1557. Why it matters. It protects long-term couples who cannot prove a ceremony. D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010) Facts. A woman claimed maintenance under Section 125 CrPC as the appellant's wife; he said he was already married to Lakshmi in 1980. Principle. A relationship in the nature of marriage is akin to a common law marriage and needs the four-part test and a shared household; the case went back to the Family Court. Decided 21 October 2010. Why it matters. Not every live-in relationship is covered by the DV Act. Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013) Facts. From 1992 an unmarried woman lived with a married man who had two children; she knew of his marriage and later claimed relief under the DV Act. Principle. The Court gave eight guidelines and held that her relationship was not in the nature of marriage, so she was not in a "domestic relationship"; the appeal was dismissed. Decided 26 November 2013. Why it matters. It built on Velusamy and called for legislation. Chanmuniya v. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha (2010) Facts. A widow said she was married by Katha and Sindur to her late husband's younger brother; the High Court held that the essentials of Section 7 were not performed. Principle. The Bench favoured a broad meaning of "wife" in Section 125 CrPC but referred three questions to a larger Bench. (2011) 1 SCC 141. Why it matters. It is a reference order, not a final ruling. Lata Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2006) Facts. Lata Singh, a major, married outside her caste at an Arya Samaj Mandir in Delhi on 2 November 2000; her brothers lodged a missing person report and a kidnapping case against her husband's relatives. Principle. No offence was committed; a major can marry anyone, and inter-caste marriage is not barred; the case was quashed and proceedings were ordered against the brothers. (2006) 5 SCC 475. Why it matters. It began the protection of the right to choose a spouse. Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018) Facts. An NGO asked the Court to stop honour killings and Khap interference with the marriages of consenting adults. Principle. The choice of a life partner by two adults is recognised under Articles 19 and 21; Khap panchayats have no authority; the Court issued preventive, remedial and punitive directions. (2018) 7 SCC 192. Why it matters. It gave binding guidelines against honour crimes. Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (2018) Facts. An adult woman, Hadiya, converted to Islam and married a man of her choice; the High Court annulled the marriage on her father's habeas corpus petition. Principle. The High Court should not have annulled the marriage in a habeas corpus petition; parens patriae does not apply to an adult with capacity; the right to marry a person of one's choice is integral to Article 21. Order 8 March 2018; reasons 9 April 2018. Why it matters. It protects an adult's choice of faith and spouse from judicial overreach. Supriyo v. Union of India (2023) Facts. Same-sex couples and others filed connected petitions seeking a right to marry; a five-judge Bench heard them. Principle. There is no unqualified fundamental right to marry, and the SMA cannot be read to include same-sex couples (unanimous); by 3 to 2 the Court declined to order civil unions or joint adoption. Decided 17 October 2023. Why it matters. It marks the limit of judicial power on marriage reform.

selfTest.q: 1. Which case gave the four-part test for live-in relationships?
selfTest.a: D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010).

selfTest.q: 2. Does Hindu law recognise same-sex marriage after Supriyo?
selfTest.a: No. The Court left it to Parliament.

selfTest.q: 3. Which Articles protect the right to choose a spouse?
selfTest.a: Articles 19 and 21.

selfTest.q: 4. A couple have lived together as husband and wife for forty years. A relative says no ceremony was proved. Who must prove what?
selfTest.a: A strong presumption of marriage arises; the relative must rebut it ( Badri Prasad ).

selfTest.q: 5. Did Chanmuniya finally decide that a live-in partner is a "wife" under Section 125 CrPC?
selfTest.a: No. It referred the questions to a larger Bench.

selfTest.q: 6. Can a woman under the DV Act claim to live in the shared household though she does not own it?
selfTest.a: Yes (Section 17).

family-law-i-u2-t6.subtitle: Plural marriage before 1955, its abolition for Hindus, and its legal and social effects

en.inOneMinute: Meaning. Polygamy means having more than one spouse at the same time. Polygyny is one husband with several wives; polyandry is one wife with several husbands. Before 1955. Hindu law allowed a man to marry any number of wives, except where State anti-bigamy Acts applied. A woman could have only one husband at a time (Mulla, Sections 430 and 431). Abolished in 1955. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) ended polygamy for Hindus through Section 5(i). A second marriage during the first is now void (Sections 11 and 17) and a crime (now Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)). Children are protected. A child of a void marriage is legitimate (Section 16(1)) and has rights in the property of the parents only (Section 16(3)), including the parent's share in joint family property worked out on a notional partition ( Revanasiddappa , 2023). Exams ask for the legal effects and the social effects of polygamy, and for the reasons it was abolished.
legalProvision: Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; …

Section 11. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 13(2)(i). A wife may also present a petition for the dissolution of her marriage by a decree of divorce on the ground,— (i) in the case of any marriage solemnized before the commencement of this Act, that the husband had married again before such commencement or that any other wife of the husband married before such commencement was alive at the time of the solemnization of the marriage of the petitioner: Provided that in either case the other wife is alive at the time of the presentation of the petition;

Section 15. Divorced persons when may marry again. When a marriage has been dissolved by a decree of divorce and either there is no right of appeal against the decree or, if there is such a right of appeal, the time for appealing has expired without an appeal having been presented, or an appeal has been presented but has been dismissed, it shall be lawful for either party to the marriage to marry again.

Section 16. Legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages. (1) Notwithstanding that a marriage is null and void under section 11, any child of such marriage who would have been legitimate if the marriage had been valid, shall be legitimate, whether such child is born before or after the commencement of the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 (68 of 1976), and whether or not a decree of nullity is granted in respect of that marriage under this Act and whether or not the marriage is held to be void otherwise than on a petition under this Act. (2) Where a decree of nullity is granted in respect of a voidable marriage under section 12, any child begotten or conceived before the decree is made, who would have been the legitimate child of the parties to the marriage if at the date of the decree it had been dissolved instead of being annulled, shall be deemed to be their legitimate child notwithstanding the decree of nullity. (3) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall be construed as conferring upon any child of a marriage which is null and void or which is annulled by a decree of nullity under section 12, any rights in or to the property of any person, other than the parents, in any case where, but for the passing of this Act, such child would have been incapable of possessing or acquiring any such rights by reason of his not being the legitimate child of his parents.

Section 17. Punishment of bigamy. Any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after the commencement of this Act is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living; and the provisions of sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860), shall apply accordingly.
In simple words:

Section 5(i): neither party may have a spouse living at the time of the marriage. Sections 11 and 17: a marriage in breach is void, and the bigamy provisions apply (now BNS Section 82). Section 13(2)(i): a wife of a polygamous marriage made before the Act may seek divorce, if the other wife is still alive when she files the petition. Section 15: after a divorce decree, either party may marry again once the time for appeal has expired, or the appeal has been dismissed. Section 16(1) and (2): a child of a void marriage is legitimate; so is a child begotten or conceived before the decree in a voidable marriage. Section 16(3): such a child gets rights only in the property of the parents, not of any other person.
en.meaning:
Polygamy . The state of having more than one spouse at one time. It has two forms: Polygyny: one husband with several wives. Polyandry: one wife with several husbands. Monogamy . One spouse at a time; the only form now allowed for Hindus. Bigamy . The offence of marrying again while the first spouse is alive and the first marriage subsists. Polygamy is the state; bigamy is the crime committed in creating it after 1955. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. s. 5(i); later marriage void + crime"] A1 --> N Text description Polygamy has two forms. Polygyny is one husband with several wives; in classical law a Hindu man could marry any number of wives (Mulla section 430). Polyandry is one wife with several husbands; in classical law a woman could not marry another man while her husband was alive (Mulla section 431). Since the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, section 5(i) allows one spouse at a time to everyone; a later marriage is void and a crime.
keyPoints: Polygamy: more than one spouse at a time (polygyny and polyandry). Banned for Hindus by Section 5(i) of the 1955 Act. A second marriage is void and a crime (Sections 11, 17; BNS Section 82). Pre-1955 plural marriages stay valid; the wife may seek divorce under Section 13(2)(i). Children are legitimate (Section 16); they share only in the parents' property, including the parent's share on a notional partition, and are not coparceners by birth ( Revanasiddappa ). Classical law: a man could have many wives, a woman only one husband (Mulla, Sections 430 and 431). A divorced person may remarry after the appeal time (Section 15). Conversion is no escape ( Sarla Mudgal ; Lily Thomas ).

caseLaws.name: Sarla Mudgal v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (1995) Facts. First wives (Meena Mathur, Geeta Rani, Sushmita Ghosh), and a second wife (Sunita alias Fathima), of Hindu husbands who converted to Islam and married again filed four petitions under Article 32. Principle. The first Hindu marriage continues after conversion until dissolved under the Act; the second marriage is invalid, and the husband is guilty of bigamy under Section 494 IPC. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It closed the conversion route to polygamy. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) Facts. A review petition and writ petitions asked the Court to clarify Sarla Mudgal . Sushmita Ghosh said her husband got a certificate of conversion dated 17 June 1992 only to remarry. Principle. Mere conversion does not end the first marriage without a divorce decree; the second marriage is void under Sections 11 and 17 and punishable under Section 494 IPC. (2000) 6 SCC 224 : AIR 2000 SC 1650. Why it matters. It confirms Sarla Mudgal and states its scope. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v. Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week and claimed maintenance as his wife. Principle. The marriage was void from the start; she was not a "wife" under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and her plea that she was not told of the first marriage failed because estoppel cannot defeat the Act. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. It shows the harm a void plural marriage does to the second wife; Badshah (2013) later limited it to a woman who knew of the first marriage. Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun (2023) Facts. A two-judge Bench doubted Jinia Keotin and later cases that denied children of void marriages any share in joint family property, and referred the question of their rights under Section 16(3) to a larger Bench. Principle. Such a child is not a coparcener by birth, but on the parent's death takes a share, with the other heirs, in the parent's share of the coparcenary property worked out on a notional partition immediately before death; the child has no right in the property of anyone other than the parents. Decided 1 September 2023 by a three-judge Bench (Chandrachud CJI, Pardiwala and Misra JJ). Why it matters. It states the present law on the property rights of children of void and voidable marriages.

selfTest.q: 1. What are polygyny and polyandry?
selfTest.a: One husband with several wives, and one wife with several husbands.

selfTest.q: 2. Are children of a void second marriage legitimate?
selfTest.a: Yes, under Section 16(1).

selfTest.q: 3. Which section lets a divorced person remarry?
selfTest.a: Section 15.

selfTest.q: 4. A Hindu married two wives in 1950, both alive. Is the second marriage void under the HMA?
selfTest.a: No. Section 17 applies only to marriages after the Act. The wife may seek divorce under Section 13(2)(i).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a child of a void marriage claim a share in the grandfather's property?
selfTest.a: No. Section 16(3) limits the child to the parents' property; the child shares in the parent's share on a notional partition ( Revanasiddappa ).

selfTest.q: 6. Is a woman who knowingly lives with a married man in a "relationship in the nature of marriage"?
selfTest.a: No ( Indra Sarma ).

సెక్షన్ 5(i): వివాహ సమయంలో ఏ పక్షానికీ జీవించి ఉన్న జీవిత భాగస్వామి ఉండకూడదు. సెక్షన్లు 11, 17: ఉల్లంఘించిన వివాహం శూన్యం; ద్విభార్యత్వ నిబంధనలు (ఇప్పుడు BNS సెక్షన్ 82) వర్తిస్తాయి. సెక్షన్ 13(2)(i): చట్టానికి ముందు జరిగిన బహుభార్యత్వ వివాహంలోని భార్య, పిటిషన్ వేసే సమయానికి మరో భార్య జీవించి ఉంటే, విడాకులు కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 15: విడాకుల డిక్రీ తర్వాత, అప్పీలు గడువు ముగిసినా, అప్పీలు కొట్టివేయబడినా, ఏ పక్షమైనా మళ్ళీ పెళ్లి చేసుకోవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 16(1), (2): శూన్య వివాహపు బిడ్డ చట్టబద్ధుడు; రద్దు చేయదగిన వివాహంలో డిక్రీకి ముందు పుట్టిన లేదా గర్భంలో ఉన్న బిడ్డ కూడా. సెక్షన్ 16(3): అలాంటి బిడ్డకు తల్లిదండ్రుల ఆస్తిలో మాత్రమే హక్కులు; ఇతరుల ఆస్తిలో కాదు.

బహుభార్యత్వం (Polygamy) . ఒకే సమయంలో ఒకరికంటే ఎక్కువ జీవిత భాగస్వాములు ఉండే స్థితి. దీనికి రెండు రూపాలు: Polygyny (బహుభార్యత్వం): ఒక భర్తకు అనేక భార్యలు. Polyandry (బహుభర్తృత్వం): ఒక భార్యకు అనేక భర్తలు. ఏకపత్నీత్వం . ఒకసారి ఒకే జీవిత భాగస్వామి; ఇప్పుడు హిందువులకు అనుమతించిన ఏకైక రూపం. ద్విభార్యత్వం . మొదటి జీవిత భాగస్వామి జీవించి ఉండి, మొదటి వివాహం కొనసాగుతుండగా మళ్ళీ పెళ్లి చేసుకునే నేరం. బహుభార్యత్వం ఒక స్థితి; 1955 తర్వాత ఆ స్థితిని సృష్టించడంలో చేసే నేరం ద్విభార్యత్వం. selfTest.a: లేదు ( Indra Sarma ).

hi.inOneMinute: Meaning. Polygamy means having more than one spouse at the same time. Polygyny is one husband with several wives; polyandry is one wife with several husbands. Before 1955. Hindu law allowed a man to marry any number of wives, except where State anti-bigamy Acts applied. A woman could have only one husband at a time (Mulla, Sections 430 and 431). Abolished in 1955. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) ended polygamy for Hindus through Section 5(i). A second marriage during the first is now void (Sections 11 and 17) and a crime (now Section 82 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)). Children are protected. A child of a void marriage is legitimate (Section 16(1)) and has rights in the property of the parents only (Section 16(3)), including the parent's share in joint family property worked out on a notional partition ( Revanasiddappa , 2023). Exams ask for the legal effects and the social effects of polygamy, and for the reasons it was abolished.
legalProvision: Section 5, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. A marriage may be solemnized between any two Hindus, if the following conditions are fulfilled, namely:— (i) neither party has a spouse living at the time of the marriage; …

Section 11. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 13(2)(i). A wife may also present a petition for the dissolution of her marriage by a decree of divorce on the ground,— (i) in the case of any marriage solemnized before the commencement of this Act, that the husband had married again before such commencement or that any other wife of the husband married before such commencement was alive at the time of the solemnization of the marriage of the petitioner: Provided that in either case the other wife is alive at the time of the presentation of the petition;

Section 15. Divorced persons when may marry again. When a marriage has been dissolved by a decree of divorce and either there is no right of appeal against the decree or, if there is such a right of appeal, the time for appealing has expired without an appeal having been presented, or an appeal has been presented but has been dismissed, it shall be lawful for either party to the marriage to marry again.

Section 16. Legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages. (1) Notwithstanding that a marriage is null and void under section 11, any child of such marriage who would have been legitimate if the marriage had been valid, shall be legitimate, whether such child is born before or after the commencement of the Marriage Laws (Amendment) Act, 1976 (68 of 1976), and whether or not a decree of nullity is granted in respect of that marriage under this Act and whether or not the marriage is held to be void otherwise than on a petition under this Act. (2) Where a decree of nullity is granted in respect of a voidable marriage under section 12, any child begotten or conceived before the decree is made, who would have been the legitimate child of the parties to the marriage if at the date of the decree it had been dissolved instead of being annulled, shall be deemed to be their legitimate child notwithstanding the decree of nullity. (3) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall be construed as conferring upon any child of a marriage which is null and void or which is annulled by a decree of nullity under section 12, any rights in or to the property of any person, other than the parents, in any case where, but for the passing of this Act, such child would have been incapable of possessing or acquiring any such rights by reason of his not being the legitimate child of his parents.

Section 17. Punishment of bigamy. Any marriage between two Hindus solemnized after the commencement of this Act is void if at the date of such marriage either party had a husband or wife living; and the provisions of sections 494 and 495 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860), shall apply accordingly.
In simple words:

Section 5(i): neither party may have a spouse living at the time of the marriage. Sections 11 and 17: a marriage in breach is void, and the bigamy provisions apply (now BNS Section 82). Section 13(2)(i): a wife of a polygamous marriage made before the Act may seek divorce, if the other wife is still alive when she files the petition. Section 15: after a divorce decree, either party may marry again once the time for appeal has expired, or the appeal has been dismissed. Section 16(1) and (2): a child of a void marriage is legitimate; so is a child begotten or conceived before the decree in a voidable marriage. Section 16(3): such a child gets rights only in the property of the parents, not of any other person.
hi.meaning:
Polygamy . The state of having more than one spouse at one time. It has two forms: Polygyny: one husband with several wives. Polyandry: one wife with several husbands. Monogamy . One spouse at a time; the only form now allowed for Hindus. Bigamy . The offence of marrying again while the first spouse is alive and the first marriage subsists. Polygamy is the state; bigamy is the crime committed in creating it after 1955. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Polygyny is one husband with several wives; in classical law a Hindu man could marry any number of wives (Mulla section 430). Polyandry is one wife with several husbands; in classical law a woman could not marry another man while her husband was alive (Mulla section 431). Since the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, section 5(i) allows one spouse at a time to everyone; a later marriage is void and a crime.
keyPoints: Polygamy: more than one spouse at a time (polygyny and polyandry). Banned for Hindus by Section 5(i) of the 1955 Act. A second marriage is void and a crime (Sections 11, 17; BNS Section 82). Pre-1955 plural marriages stay valid; the wife may seek divorce under Section 13(2)(i). Children are legitimate (Section 16); they share only in the parents' property, including the parent's share on a notional partition, and are not coparceners by birth ( Revanasiddappa ). Classical law: a man could have many wives, a woman only one husband (Mulla, Sections 430 and 431). A divorced person may remarry after the appeal time (Section 15). Conversion is no escape ( Sarla Mudgal ; Lily Thomas ).

caseLaws.name: Sarla Mudgal v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (1995) Facts. First wives (Meena Mathur, Geeta Rani, Sushmita Ghosh), and a second wife (Sunita alias Fathima), of Hindu husbands who converted to Islam and married again filed four petitions under Article 32. Principle. The first Hindu marriage continues after conversion until dissolved under the Act; the second marriage is invalid, and the husband is guilty of bigamy under Section 494 IPC. (1995) 3 SCC 635 : AIR 1995 SC 1531. Why it matters. It closed the conversion route to polygamy. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2000) Facts. A review petition and writ petitions asked the Court to clarify Sarla Mudgal . Sushmita Ghosh said her husband got a certificate of conversion dated 17 June 1992 only to remarry. Principle. Mere conversion does not end the first marriage without a divorce decree; the second marriage is void under Sections 11 and 17 and punishable under Section 494 IPC. (2000) 6 SCC 224 : AIR 2000 SC 1650. Why it matters. It confirms Sarla Mudgal and states its scope. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v. Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week and claimed maintenance as his wife. Principle. The marriage was void from the start; she was not a "wife" under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and her plea that she was not told of the first marriage failed because estoppel cannot defeat the Act. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. It shows the harm a void plural marriage does to the second wife; Badshah (2013) later limited it to a woman who knew of the first marriage. Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun (2023) Facts. A two-judge Bench doubted Jinia Keotin and later cases that denied children of void marriages any share in joint family property, and referred the question of their rights under Section 16(3) to a larger Bench. Principle. Such a child is not a coparcener by birth, but on the parent's death takes a share, with the other heirs, in the parent's share of the coparcenary property worked out on a notional partition immediately before death; the child has no right in the property of anyone other than the parents. Decided 1 September 2023 by a three-judge Bench (Chandrachud CJI, Pardiwala and Misra JJ). Why it matters. It states the present law on the property rights of children of void and voidable marriages.

selfTest.q: 1. What are polygyny and polyandry?
selfTest.a: One husband with several wives, and one wife with several husbands.

selfTest.q: 2. Are children of a void second marriage legitimate?
selfTest.a: Yes, under Section 16(1).

selfTest.q: 3. Which section lets a divorced person remarry?
selfTest.a: Section 15.

selfTest.q: 4. A Hindu married two wives in 1950, both alive. Is the second marriage void under the HMA?
selfTest.a: No. Section 17 applies only to marriages after the Act. The wife may seek divorce under Section 13(2)(i).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a child of a void marriage claim a share in the grandfather's property?
selfTest.a: No. Section 16(3) limits the child to the parents' property; the child shares in the parent's share on a notional partition ( Revanasiddappa ).

selfTest.q: 6. Is a woman who knowingly lives with a married man in a "relationship in the nature of marriage"?
selfTest.a: No ( Indra Sarma ).

en.meaning:
Which section of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 deals with restitution of conjugal rights?

Explanation. Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides the remedy of restitution of conjugal rights.

What must the petitioner prove to succeed under Section 9?

Explanation. The core requirement under Section 9 is withdrawal from society without reasonable excuse.

Once withdrawal from society is proved, on whom does the burden shift to prove a reasonable excuse?

Explanation. The burden shifts to the respondent once withdrawal from society is established.

In T. Sareetha v. T. Venkata Subbaiah (1983), which court declared Section 9 unconstitutional?

hi.meaning: Which section of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 deals with restitution of conjugal rights? Explanation. Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides the remedy of restitution of conjugal rights. What must the petitioner prove to succeed under Section 9? Explanation. The core requirement under Section 9 is withdrawal from society without reasonable excuse. Once withdrawal from society is proved, on whom does the burden shift to prove a reasonable excuse? Explanation. The burden shifts to the respondent once withdrawal from society is established. In T. Sareetha v. T. Venkata Subbaiah (1983), which court declared Section 9 unconstitutional?

family-law-i-u3-t1.subtitle: The six remedies, the court, common bars to relief and the ancillary orders

en.inOneMinute: Four main remedies. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) gives four main matrimonial remedies: restitution of conjugal rights (Section 9), judicial separation (Section 10), a decree of nullity (Sections 11 and 12) and divorce (Sections 13, 13A, 13B and 14). Ancillary reliefs. Alongside these, the court can order maintenance pendente lite and costs (Section 24), permanent alimony (Section 25), custody of children (Section 26) and disposal of joint property (Section 27). The court. Every petition goes to the district court (Section 19). Where a Family Court has been set up, it alone hears these cases (Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7 and 8). Section 23 conditions. Relief is granted only if a ground exists and the bars in Section 23(1) do not apply: own wrong, connivance or condonation , consent obtained by force or fraud, collusion , delay, or any other legal ground. Reconciliation first. The court must first try to reconcile the parties (Section 23(2)); a Family Court must first try to settle the dispute (Family Courts Act, Section 9). Appeals. An appeal under the HMA lies within ninety days (Section 28(4)). An appeal from a Family Court lies to the High Court within thirty days (Family Courts Act, Section 19(3)).
legalProvision: Section 9, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Restitution of conjugal rights. When either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply, by petition to the district court, for restitution of conjugal rights and the court, on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted, may decree restitution of conjugal rights accordingly. Explanation. —Where a question arises whether there has been reasonable excuse for withdrawal from the society, the burden of proving reasonable excuse shall be on the person who has withdrawn from the society.

Section 10(1). Judicial separation. Either party to a marriage, whether solemnised before or after the commencement of this Act, may present a petition praying for a decree for judicial separation on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (1) of section 13, and in the case of a wife also on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (2) thereof, as grounds on which a petition for divorce might have been presented.

Section 23(1). Decree in proceedings. In any proceeding under this Act, whether defended or not, if the court is satisfied that— (a) any of the grounds for granting relief exists and the petitioner except in cases where the relief is sought by him on the ground specified in sub-clause (a), sub-clause (b) or sub-clause (c) of clause (ii) of section 5 is not in any way taking advantage of his or her own wrong or disability for the purpose of such relief, and (b) where the ground of the petition is the ground specified … in clause (i) of sub-section (1) of section 13, the petitioner has not in any manner been accessory to or connived at or condoned the act or acts complained of, or where the ground of the petition is cruelty the petitioner has not in any manner condoned the cruelty, and (bb) when a divorce is sought on the ground of mutual consent, such consent has not been obtained by force, fraud or undue influence, and (c) the petition (not being a petition presented under section 11) is not presented or prosecuted in collusion with the respondent, and (d) there has not been any unnecessary or improper delay in instituting the proceeding, and (e) there is no other legal ground why relief should not be granted, then, and in such a case, but not otherwise, the court shall decree such relief accordingly.

Section 23(2). Before proceeding to grant any relief under this Act, it shall be the duty of the court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible so to do consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation between the parties: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall apply to any proceeding wherein relief is sought on any of the grounds specified in clause (ii), clause (iii), clause (iv), clause (v), clause (vi) or clause (vii) of sub-section (1) of section 13.

Section 9(1), Family Courts Act, 1984. Duty of Family Court to make efforts for settlement. In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding …
The other sections, in short:

Sections 11 and 12: nullity of void and voidable marriages . Sections 13, 13A, 13B and 14: divorce, alternative relief of judicial separation, divorce by mutual consent, and no divorce petition within one year of marriage. Sections 15 and 16: remarriage after divorce, and legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages. Section 19: the court in which the petition is presented. Sections 20, 21, 21A, 21B and 21C: contents of the petition, the Code of Civil Procedure, rival petitions, speedy trial, and documents not barred for want of stamp or registration. Section 22: proceedings in camera ; no printing or publishing. Section 23A: counter-claim by the respondent . Sections 24 to 27: maintenance pendente lite , permanent alimony, custody of children, disposal of property. Sections 28 and 28A: appeals (ninety days) and enforcement. Section 29(2) and (4): customary and special-law divorces saved; the Special Marriage Act, 1954 untouched. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 19 and 20: jurisdiction , exclusion of other courts, settlement, procedure, in camera, experts, no lawyer as of right, appeal, overriding effect. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 22 to 39A: the matching remedies for marriages under that Act.

A matrimonial remedy is a relief that a court gives to a spouse in respect of the marriage itself. Each remedy does one of four things to the marriage (see Diagram 1 ): Diagram 1. custody s. 26; property s. 27"] Text description Matrimonial remedies under the Hindu Marriage Act. Keep the marriage: restitution of conjugal rights, section 9. Suspend cohabitation: judicial separation, section 10. Declare invalid: nullity of void and voidable marriages, sections 11 and 12. End the marriage: divorce, sections 13, 13A and 13B. Ancillary reliefs: maintenance pendente lite and costs, section 24; permanent alimony, section 25; custody of children, section 26; property, section 27. What it does to the marriage Remedy Section Keeps it together Restitution of conjugal rights 9 Suspends the duty to live together Judicial separation 10 Declares or makes it invalid Nullity: void marriage or voidable marriage 11, 12 Ends a valid marriage Divorce 13, 13A, 13B The ancillary reliefs (Sections 24 to 27) do not act on the marriage. They protect a spouse and the children while the case is pending and after the decree: money for support and costs, alimony, custody and property.
keyPoints: Four main remedies: restitution, judicial separation, nullity, divorce. Ancillary reliefs: Sections 24 to 27. Section 23 conditions apply to every relief; the court must first try reconciliation (Section 23(2)). Standard of proof: preponderance of probabilities ( Dastane ). Proceedings are in camera (Section 22; Family Courts Act, Section 11). A Family Court hears these petitions where one exists (Family Courts Act, Sections 7 and 8), and must first try to settle (Section 9). Appeal: ninety days under the HMA (Section 28(4)); thirty days from a Family Court (Family Courts Act, Section 19(3)); none from a consent decree of a Family Court. The Special Marriage Act has matching remedies in Sections 22 to 39A.

caseLaws.name: Saroj Rani v
caseLaws.facts: Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. The wife got a consent decree for restitution on 28 March 1978. A year later the husband sought divorce under Section 13(1A) because there was no cohabitation; the High Court granted it. The wife relied on T. Sareetha (Andhra Pradesh High Court), which had struck down Section 9. Principle. Section 9 does not violate Article 14 or 21; T. Sareetha was overruled . A consent decree in matrimonial matters is not collusive by itself. The divorce was upheld, with maintenance for the wife and daughter. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It settles that restitution is constitutional, and that a consent decree is not barred as collusive. Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008 and settled all disputes. They asked for the six-month wait under Section 13B(2) to be waived . Principle. The six-month period is directory, not mandatory . The court may waive it if the separation period is already over, mediation has failed, all issues are settled, and waiting would only prolong their agony. Decided 12 September 2017. Why it matters. It makes the cooling-off period under Section 13B flexible. Dastane v. Dastane (1975) Facts. A husband sought annulment for fraud, divorce for unsoundness of mind, and judicial separation for cruelty. Only judicial separation for cruelty reached the Supreme Court. Principle. Matrimonial facts are proved on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt. The wife was cruel, but the husband condoned the cruelty and her later conduct did not revive it; the appeal was dismissed. (1975) 2 SCC 326 : AIR 1975 SC 1534. Why it matters. It explains the standard of proof and the Section 23 bar of condonation.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2).

selfTest.q: 2. Does judicial separation end the marriage?
selfTest.a: No. It ends only the duty to cohabit (Section 10(2)).

selfTest.q: 3. What is the appeal period under Section 28?
selfTest.a: Ninety days (Section 28(4)).

selfTest.q: 4. A wife living in Guntur wants to file for divorce against a husband living in Hyderabad. They married and lived together in Nellore. Where can she file?
selfTest.a: Nellore (place of marriage and last residence together), Hyderabad (respondent's residence) or Guntur (her own residence, Section 19(iiia)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a party appeal against a consent decree of a Family Court?
selfTest.a: No (Family Courts Act, Section 19(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. Is a consent decree for restitution collusive by itself?
selfTest.a: No ( Saroj Rani ).

సంరక్షణ సె. 26; ఆస్తి సె. 27"] వచన వివరణ హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం కింద వైవాహిక పరిష్కారాలు. వివాహాన్ని నిలపడం: దాంపత్య హక్కుల పునరుద్ధరణ, సెక్షన్ 9. సహజీవనాన్ని నిలిపివేయడం: న్యాయ విభజన, సెక్షన్ 10. చెల్లదని ప్రకటించడం: శూన్య, రద్దు చేయదగిన వివాహాల శూన్యత, సెక్షన్లు 11, 12. వివాహాన్ని ముగించడం: విడాకులు, సెక్షన్లు 13, 13A, 13B. అనుబంధ ఉపశమనాలు: కేసు నడుస్తున్నప్పుడు భరణం, ఖర్చులు, సెక్షన్ 24; శాశ్వత భరణం, సెక్షన్ 25; పిల్లల సంరక్షణ, సెక్షన్ 26; ఆస్తి, సెక్షన్ 27. వివాహానికి ఏమి చేస్తుంది పరిష్కారం సెక్షన్ కలిపి ఉంచుతుంది దాంపత్య హక్కుల పునరుద్ధరణ 9 కలిసి జీవించే బాధ్యతను నిలిపివేస్తుంది న్యాయ విభజన 10 చెల్లదని ప్రకటిస్తుంది లేదా రద్దు చేస్తుంది శూన్యత: శూన్య వివాహం లేదా రద్దు చేయదగిన వివాహం 11, 12 చెల్లుబాటయ్యే వివాహాన్ని ముగిస్తుంది విడాకులు 13, 13A, 13B అనుబంధ ఉపశమనాలు (సెక్షన్లు 24 నుంచి 27) వివాహంపై పని చేయవు. కేసు నడుస్తున్నప్పుడు, డిక్రీ తర్వాత అవి జీవిత భాగస్వామిని, పిల్లలను కాపాడతాయి: పోషణ, ఖర్చులకు డబ్బు, భరణం, సంరక్షణ, ఆస్తి.

selfTest.q: 1. సయోధ్యకు ప్రయత్నించమని కోర్టును ఏ సెక్షన్ కోరుతుంది?
2. న్యాయ విభజన వివాహాన్ని ముగిస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కలిసి జీవించే బాధ్యతను మాత్రమే ముగిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 10(2)).

selfTest.q: 3. సెక్షన్ 28 కింద అప్పీలు గడువు ఎంత?
4. గుంటూరులో నివసించే భార్య, హైదరాబాద్‌లో నివసించే భర్తపై విడాకుల పిటిషన్ వేయాలనుకుంటుంది. వారు నెల్లూరులో పెళ్లి చేసుకుని, అక్కడే కలిసి జీవించారు. ఆమె ఎక్కడ వేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: నెల్లూరు (పెళ్లి జరిగిన, చివరిగా కలిసి జీవించిన చోటు), హైదరాబాద్ (ప్రతివాది నివాసం), లేదా గుంటూరు (ఆమె సొంత నివాసం, సెక్షన్ 19(iiia)).

selfTest.q: 5. కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానం సమ్మతి డిక్రీపై అప్పీలు చేయవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు (కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానాల చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 19(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. పునరుద్ధరణకు సమ్మతి డిక్రీ దానంతట అదే కుమ్మక్కా?
selfTest.a: కాదు ( Saroj Rani ).

hi.inOneMinute: Four main remedies. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) gives four main matrimonial remedies: restitution of conjugal rights (Section 9), judicial separation (Section 10), a decree of nullity (Sections 11 and 12) and divorce (Sections 13, 13A, 13B and 14). Ancillary reliefs. Alongside these, the court can order maintenance pendente lite and costs (Section 24), permanent alimony (Section 25), custody of children (Section 26) and disposal of joint property (Section 27). The court. Every petition goes to the district court (Section 19). Where a Family Court has been set up, it alone hears these cases (Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7 and 8). Section 23 conditions. Relief is granted only if a ground exists and the bars in Section 23(1) do not apply: own wrong, connivance or condonation , consent obtained by force or fraud, collusion , delay, or any other legal ground. Reconciliation first. The court must first try to reconcile the parties (Section 23(2)); a Family Court must first try to settle the dispute (Family Courts Act, Section 9). Appeals. An appeal under the HMA lies within ninety days (Section 28(4)). An appeal from a Family Court lies to the High Court within thirty days (Family Courts Act, Section 19(3)).
legalProvision: Section 9, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Restitution of conjugal rights. When either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply, by petition to the district court, for restitution of conjugal rights and the court, on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted, may decree restitution of conjugal rights accordingly. Explanation. —Where a question arises whether there has been reasonable excuse for withdrawal from the society, the burden of proving reasonable excuse shall be on the person who has withdrawn from the society.

Section 10(1). Judicial separation. Either party to a marriage, whether solemnised before or after the commencement of this Act, may present a petition praying for a decree for judicial separation on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (1) of section 13, and in the case of a wife also on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (2) thereof, as grounds on which a petition for divorce might have been presented.

Section 23(1). Decree in proceedings. In any proceeding under this Act, whether defended or not, if the court is satisfied that— (a) any of the grounds for granting relief exists and the petitioner except in cases where the relief is sought by him on the ground specified in sub-clause (a), sub-clause (b) or sub-clause (c) of clause (ii) of section 5 is not in any way taking advantage of his or her own wrong or disability for the purpose of such relief, and (b) where the ground of the petition is the ground specified … in clause (i) of sub-section (1) of section 13, the petitioner has not in any manner been accessory to or connived at or condoned the act or acts complained of, or where the ground of the petition is cruelty the petitioner has not in any manner condoned the cruelty, and (bb) when a divorce is sought on the ground of mutual consent, such consent has not been obtained by force, fraud or undue influence, and (c) the petition (not being a petition presented under section 11) is not presented or prosecuted in collusion with the respondent, and (d) there has not been any unnecessary or improper delay in instituting the proceeding, and (e) there is no other legal ground why relief should not be granted, then, and in such a case, but not otherwise, the court shall decree such relief accordingly.

Section 23(2). Before proceeding to grant any relief under this Act, it shall be the duty of the court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible so to do consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation between the parties: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall apply to any proceeding wherein relief is sought on any of the grounds specified in clause (ii), clause (iii), clause (iv), clause (v), clause (vi) or clause (vii) of sub-section (1) of section 13.

Section 9(1), Family Courts Act, 1984. Duty of Family Court to make efforts for settlement. In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding …
The other sections, in short:

Sections 11 and 12: nullity of void and voidable marriages . Sections 13, 13A, 13B and 14: divorce, alternative relief of judicial separation, divorce by mutual consent, and no divorce petition within one year of marriage. Sections 15 and 16: remarriage after divorce, and legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages. Section 19: the court in which the petition is presented. Sections 20, 21, 21A, 21B and 21C: contents of the petition, the Code of Civil Procedure, rival petitions, speedy trial, and documents not barred for want of stamp or registration. Section 22: proceedings in camera ; no printing or publishing. Section 23A: counter-claim by the respondent . Sections 24 to 27: maintenance pendente lite , permanent alimony, custody of children, disposal of property. Sections 28 and 28A: appeals (ninety days) and enforcement. Section 29(2) and (4): customary and special-law divorces saved; the Special Marriage Act, 1954 untouched. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 19 and 20: jurisdiction , exclusion of other courts, settlement, procedure, in camera, experts, no lawyer as of right, appeal, overriding effect. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 22 to 39A: the matching remedies for marriages under that Act.

custody s. 26; property s. 27"] Text description Matrimonial remedies under the Hindu Marriage Act. Keep the marriage: restitution of conjugal rights, section 9. Suspend cohabitation: judicial separation, section 10. Declare invalid: nullity of void and voidable marriages, sections 11 and 12. End the marriage: divorce, sections 13, 13A and 13B. Ancillary reliefs: maintenance pendente lite and costs, section 24; permanent alimony, section 25; custody of children, section 26; property, section 27. What it does to the marriage Remedy Section Keeps it together Restitution of conjugal rights 9 Suspends the duty to live together Judicial separation 10 Declares or makes it invalid Nullity: void marriage or voidable marriage 11, 12 Ends a valid marriage Divorce 13, 13A, 13B The ancillary reliefs (Sections 24 to 27) do not act on the marriage. They protect a spouse and the children while the case is pending and after the decree: money for support and costs, alimony, custody and property.
keyPoints: Four main remedies: restitution, judicial separation, nullity, divorce. Ancillary reliefs: Sections 24 to 27. Section 23 conditions apply to every relief; the court must first try reconciliation (Section 23(2)). Standard of proof: preponderance of probabilities ( Dastane ). Proceedings are in camera (Section 22; Family Courts Act, Section 11). A Family Court hears these petitions where one exists (Family Courts Act, Sections 7 and 8), and must first try to settle (Section 9). Appeal: ninety days under the HMA (Section 28(4)); thirty days from a Family Court (Family Courts Act, Section 19(3)); none from a consent decree of a Family Court. The Special Marriage Act has matching remedies in Sections 22 to 39A.

caseLaws.name: Saroj Rani v
caseLaws.facts: Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. The wife got a consent decree for restitution on 28 March 1978. A year later the husband sought divorce under Section 13(1A) because there was no cohabitation; the High Court granted it. The wife relied on T. Sareetha (Andhra Pradesh High Court), which had struck down Section 9. Principle. Section 9 does not violate Article 14 or 21; T. Sareetha was overruled . A consent decree in matrimonial matters is not collusive by itself. The divorce was upheld, with maintenance for the wife and daughter. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It settles that restitution is constitutional, and that a consent decree is not barred as collusive. Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008 and settled all disputes. They asked for the six-month wait under Section 13B(2) to be waived . Principle. The six-month period is directory, not mandatory . The court may waive it if the separation period is already over, mediation has failed, all issues are settled, and waiting would only prolong their agony. Decided 12 September 2017. Why it matters. It makes the cooling-off period under Section 13B flexible. Dastane v. Dastane (1975) Facts. A husband sought annulment for fraud, divorce for unsoundness of mind, and judicial separation for cruelty. Only judicial separation for cruelty reached the Supreme Court. Principle. Matrimonial facts are proved on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt. The wife was cruel, but the husband condoned the cruelty and her later conduct did not revive it; the appeal was dismissed. (1975) 2 SCC 326 : AIR 1975 SC 1534. Why it matters. It explains the standard of proof and the Section 23 bar of condonation.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2).

selfTest.q: 2. Does judicial separation end the marriage?
selfTest.a: No. It ends only the duty to cohabit (Section 10(2)).

selfTest.q: 3. What is the appeal period under Section 28?
selfTest.a: Ninety days (Section 28(4)).

selfTest.q: 4. A wife living in Guntur wants to file for divorce against a husband living in Hyderabad. They married and lived together in Nellore. Where can she file?
selfTest.a: Nellore (place of marriage and last residence together), Hyderabad (respondent's residence) or Guntur (her own residence, Section 19(iiia)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a party appeal against a consent decree of a Family Court?
selfTest.a: No (Family Courts Act, Section 19(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. Is a consent decree for restitution collusive by itself?
selfTest.a: No ( Saroj Rani ).

family-law-i-u3-t2.subtitle: Section 9: withdrawal from society, reasonable excuse, enforcement and the link to divorce

en.inOneMinute: The remedy. If a spouse leaves the other without reasonable excuse, the aggrieved spouse may ask the district court for a decree that the other return and live together. This is restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). Burden. The spouse who left must prove the reasonable excuse (Explanation to Section 9). Enforcement. The court cannot force anyone to live together. A wilfully disobeyed decree is enforced only by attaching the property of the disobedient spouse (Order XXI Rule 32, Code of Civil Procedure). Road to divorce. If there is no restitution for one year or more after the decree, either spouse may seek divorce (Section 13(1A)(ii)). Valid. The Andhra Pradesh High Court struck Section 9 down in T. Sareetha (1983). The Delhi High Court upheld it in Harvinder Kaur (1983), and the Supreme Court upheld it in Saroj Rani (1984).
legalProvision: Section 9, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Restitution of conjugal rights. When either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply, by petition to the district court, for restitution of conjugal rights and the court, on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted, may decree restitution of conjugal rights accordingly. Explanation. —Where a question arises whether there has been reasonable excuse for withdrawal from the society, the burden of proving reasonable excuse shall be on the person who has withdrawn from the society.

Section 13(1A). Either party to a marriage, whether solemnized before or after the commencement of this Act, may also present a petition for the dissolution of the marriage by a decree of divorce on the ground— … (ii) that there has been no restitution of conjugal rights as between the parties to the marriage for a period of one year or upwards after the passing of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights in a proceeding to which they were parties.

Order XXI Rule 32(1), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (as quoted in Saroj Rani ). Where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights or for an injunction, has been passed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced in the case of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for an injunction by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property, or by both.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 23, HMA: conditions for any relief (own wrong, collusion , delay, other legal ground) and the duty to try reconciliation. Section 23A, HMA: counter-claim on the petitioner 's adultery, cruelty or desertion. Sections 19 and 20, HMA: the court and the petition. Order XXI Rule 32(3), (4) and Rule 33, Code of Civil Procedure: sale of attached property after six months; periodical payments where the decree is against a husband. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7(1) Explanation (a) and 9: a Family Court hears the petition where one exists and first tries settlement. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 22, 23(1)(b) and 27(2)(ii): the same remedy for marriages under that Act.
en.meaning:
Conjugal rights are the rights of husband and wife to each other's society: living together, companionship and marital life. Saroj Rani treated this right as " inherent in the very institution of marriage itself", not a mere creation of statute. Restitution of conjugal rights is a decree that orders a spouse who has left, without reasonable excuse , to return to the other and resume married life. It is available to the husband and the wife alike. It is the only remedy in the HMA that aims at keeping the marriage together ( Harvinder Kaur ). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The petitioner proves withdrawal; the respondent must prove a reasonable excuse; Section 23 and reconciliation come before the decree. flowchart TD A{"Respondent withdrew from
petitioner's society?"} A -->|"No"| F["Petition fails"] A -->|"Yes"| B{"Respondent proved a
reasonable excuse?

delay, other legal ground"} C -->|"Yes"| F C -->|"No"| R["Court tries reconciliation

s. 9"] Text description First ask whether the respondent withdrew from the petitioner's society; if not, the petition fails. Then ask whether the respondent proved a reasonable excuse; the burden is on the respondent; if proved, the petition fails. Then check the Section 23 bars: own wrong, collusion, delay, other legal ground; if any applies, the petition fails. Then the court tries reconciliation. If it fails, the court decrees restitution.
keyPoints: Section 9: remedy when a spouse withdraws from the other's society without reasonable excuse. The burden of proving reasonable excuse lies on the spouse who left. The decree is enforced by attachment of property, not by force or arrest (Order XXI Rule 32); against a husband, also by periodical payments (Rule 33). No restitution for one year allows either party to seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii). Mere non-compliance is not a "wrong" under Section 23(1)(a) ( Dharmendra Kumar ). Saroj Rani : Section 9 is valid; T. Sareetha overruled. Special Marriage Act: Section 22 repeats Section 9, and Section 27(2)(ii) repeats Section 13(1A)(ii).

caseLaws.name: Saroj Rani v
caseLaws.facts: Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. The wife obtained a consent decree for restitution on 28 March 1978. There was no cohabitation afterwards, and on 19 April 1979 the husband sought divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii). The District Judge refused; the High Court granted divorce. Principle. Section 9 does not violate Article 14 or 21; its only sanction is attachment of property, meant to induce reconciliation; T. Sareetha overruled. A consent decree is not collusive by itself. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It is the binding authority that Section 9 is valid. T. Sareetha v. T. Venkata Subbaiah (1983) Facts. A film actress, married at about sixteen at Tirupathi on 13 December 1975, had lived apart from her husband for over five years. He petitioned for restitution at Cuddapah, and she filed a civil revision. Principle. The Andhra Pradesh High Court declared Section 9 void under Articles 14 and 21, as it coerced an unwilling spouse into sexual cohabitation; the petition was held incompetent. AIR 1983 AP 356. Why it matters. It tested Section 9 against privacy and dignity. The Supreme Court overruled it in Saroj Rani . Harvinder Kaur v. Harmander Singh Choudhry (1983) Facts. The parties married on 10 October 1976. The wife left the matrimonial home in 1978, and the husband petitioned in February 1979. The trial court granted the decree, and the wife appealed. Principle. The Delhi High Court held Section 9 valid under Articles 14 and 21: the decree enforces cohabitation, not sexual intercourse. The wife proved no reasonable excuse, and the appeal was dismissed. AIR 1984 Del 66. Why it matters. It rejected the T. Sareetha view, and the Supreme Court approved it in Saroj Rani . Dharmendra Kumar v. Usha Kumari (1977) Facts. The wife got a restitution decree on 27 August 1973. The husband said he wrote registered letters asking her to live with him and she never replied. In 1975 she sought divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii), and he said she was taking advantage of her own wrong. Principle. Mere non-compliance with the decree is not a "wrong" under Section 23(1)(a); the conduct must be serious misconduct, more than a disinclination to agree to reunion. Decided 19 August 1977. Why it matters. Either party, even the one who did not obey, can usually get a divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii).

selfTest.q: 1. Who must prove reasonable excuse?
selfTest.a: The spouse who withdrew (Explanation to Section 9).

selfTest.q: 2. How is a restitution decree enforced?
selfTest.a: By attachment of property (Order XXI Rule 32(1)); the property may be sold after six months (Rule 32(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. Which case upheld Section 9?
selfTest.a: Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984).

selfTest.q: 4. Which section of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 matches Section 9?
selfTest.a: Section 22.

selfTest.q: 5. A wife obtains a restitution decree, but the husband does not return for fourteen months. Who can seek divorce?
selfTest.a: Either of them (Section 13(1A)(ii)); the husband's mere non-compliance is not a "wrong" ( Dharmendra Kumar ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a court send a disobedient spouse to civil prison?
selfTest.a: No. For a restitution decree, Rule 32(1) allows only attachment of property.

selfTest.a: ఆస్తి జప్తు ద్వారా (ఆర్డర్ XXI రూల్ 32(1)); ఆరు నెలల తర్వాత ఆస్తిని అమ్మవచ్చు (రూల్ 32(3)).

selfTest.a: Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984).

selfTest.q: 4. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం, 1954 లో సెక్షన్ 9 కు సరిపోయే సెక్షన్ ఏది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 22.

selfTest.q: 5. భార్య పునరుద్ధరణ డిక్రీ పొందింది, కానీ భర్త పద్నాలుగు నెలలు తిరిగి రాలేదు. విడాకులు ఎవరు కోరవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: ఇద్దరిలో ఎవరైనా (సెక్షన్ 13(1A)(ii)); భర్త కేవలం పాటించకపోవడం "తప్పు" కాదు ( Dharmendra Kumar ).

selfTest.q: 6. డిక్రీని పాటించని జీవిత భాగస్వామిని కోర్టు సివిల్ జైలుకు పంపగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పునరుద్ధరణ డిక్రీకి రూల్ 32(1) ఆస్తి జప్తును మాత్రమే అనుమతిస్తుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: The remedy. If a spouse leaves the other without reasonable excuse, the aggrieved spouse may ask the district court for a decree that the other return and live together. This is restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). Burden. The spouse who left must prove the reasonable excuse (Explanation to Section 9). Enforcement. The court cannot force anyone to live together. A wilfully disobeyed decree is enforced only by attaching the property of the disobedient spouse (Order XXI Rule 32, Code of Civil Procedure). Road to divorce. If there is no restitution for one year or more after the decree, either spouse may seek divorce (Section 13(1A)(ii)). Valid. The Andhra Pradesh High Court struck Section 9 down in T. Sareetha (1983). The Delhi High Court upheld it in Harvinder Kaur (1983), and the Supreme Court upheld it in Saroj Rani (1984).
legalProvision: Section 9, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Restitution of conjugal rights. When either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply, by petition to the district court, for restitution of conjugal rights and the court, on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted, may decree restitution of conjugal rights accordingly. Explanation. —Where a question arises whether there has been reasonable excuse for withdrawal from the society, the burden of proving reasonable excuse shall be on the person who has withdrawn from the society.

Section 13(1A). Either party to a marriage, whether solemnized before or after the commencement of this Act, may also present a petition for the dissolution of the marriage by a decree of divorce on the ground— … (ii) that there has been no restitution of conjugal rights as between the parties to the marriage for a period of one year or upwards after the passing of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights in a proceeding to which they were parties.

Order XXI Rule 32(1), Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (as quoted in Saroj Rani ). Where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights or for an injunction, has been passed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced in the case of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for an injunction by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property, or by both.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 23, HMA: conditions for any relief (own wrong, collusion , delay, other legal ground) and the duty to try reconciliation. Section 23A, HMA: counter-claim on the petitioner 's adultery, cruelty or desertion. Sections 19 and 20, HMA: the court and the petition. Order XXI Rule 32(3), (4) and Rule 33, Code of Civil Procedure: sale of attached property after six months; periodical payments where the decree is against a husband. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7(1) Explanation (a) and 9: a Family Court hears the petition where one exists and first tries settlement. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 22, 23(1)(b) and 27(2)(ii): the same remedy for marriages under that Act.
hi.meaning:
Conjugal rights are the rights of husband and wife to each other's society: living together, companionship and marital life. Saroj Rani treated this right as " inherent in the very institution of marriage itself", not a mere creation of statute. Restitution of conjugal rights is a decree that orders a spouse who has left, without reasonable excuse , to return to the other and resume married life. It is available to the husband and the wife alike. It is the only remedy in the HMA that aims at keeping the marriage together ( Harvinder Kaur ). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The petitioner proves withdrawal; the respondent must prove a reasonable excuse; Section 23 and reconciliation come before the decree. flowchart TD A{"Respondent withdrew from

s. 9"] Text description First ask whether the respondent withdrew from the petitioner's society; if not, the petition fails. Then ask whether the respondent proved a reasonable excuse; the burden is on the respondent; if proved, the petition fails. Then check the Section 23 bars: own wrong, collusion, delay, other legal ground; if any applies, the petition fails. Then the court tries reconciliation. If it fails, the court decrees restitution.
keyPoints: Section 9: remedy when a spouse withdraws from the other's society without reasonable excuse. The burden of proving reasonable excuse lies on the spouse who left. The decree is enforced by attachment of property, not by force or arrest (Order XXI Rule 32); against a husband, also by periodical payments (Rule 33). No restitution for one year allows either party to seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii). Mere non-compliance is not a "wrong" under Section 23(1)(a) ( Dharmendra Kumar ). Saroj Rani : Section 9 is valid; T. Sareetha overruled. Special Marriage Act: Section 22 repeats Section 9, and Section 27(2)(ii) repeats Section 13(1A)(ii).

caseLaws.name: Saroj Rani v
caseLaws.facts: Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. The wife obtained a consent decree for restitution on 28 March 1978. There was no cohabitation afterwards, and on 19 April 1979 the husband sought divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii). The District Judge refused; the High Court granted divorce. Principle. Section 9 does not violate Article 14 or 21; its only sanction is attachment of property, meant to induce reconciliation; T. Sareetha overruled. A consent decree is not collusive by itself. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It is the binding authority that Section 9 is valid. T. Sareetha v. T. Venkata Subbaiah (1983) Facts. A film actress, married at about sixteen at Tirupathi on 13 December 1975, had lived apart from her husband for over five years. He petitioned for restitution at Cuddapah, and she filed a civil revision. Principle. The Andhra Pradesh High Court declared Section 9 void under Articles 14 and 21, as it coerced an unwilling spouse into sexual cohabitation; the petition was held incompetent. AIR 1983 AP 356. Why it matters. It tested Section 9 against privacy and dignity. The Supreme Court overruled it in Saroj Rani . Harvinder Kaur v. Harmander Singh Choudhry (1983) Facts. The parties married on 10 October 1976. The wife left the matrimonial home in 1978, and the husband petitioned in February 1979. The trial court granted the decree, and the wife appealed. Principle. The Delhi High Court held Section 9 valid under Articles 14 and 21: the decree enforces cohabitation, not sexual intercourse. The wife proved no reasonable excuse, and the appeal was dismissed. AIR 1984 Del 66. Why it matters. It rejected the T. Sareetha view, and the Supreme Court approved it in Saroj Rani . Dharmendra Kumar v. Usha Kumari (1977) Facts. The wife got a restitution decree on 27 August 1973. The husband said he wrote registered letters asking her to live with him and she never replied. In 1975 she sought divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii), and he said she was taking advantage of her own wrong. Principle. Mere non-compliance with the decree is not a "wrong" under Section 23(1)(a); the conduct must be serious misconduct, more than a disinclination to agree to reunion. Decided 19 August 1977. Why it matters. Either party, even the one who did not obey, can usually get a divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii).

selfTest.q: 1. Who must prove reasonable excuse?
selfTest.a: The spouse who withdrew (Explanation to Section 9).

selfTest.q: 2. How is a restitution decree enforced?
selfTest.a: By attachment of property (Order XXI Rule 32(1)); the property may be sold after six months (Rule 32(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. Which case upheld Section 9?
selfTest.a: Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984).

selfTest.q: 4. Which section of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 matches Section 9?
selfTest.a: Section 22.

selfTest.q: 5. A wife obtains a restitution decree, but the husband does not return for fourteen months. Who can seek divorce?
selfTest.a: Either of them (Section 13(1A)(ii)); the husband's mere non-compliance is not a "wrong" ( Dharmendra Kumar ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a court send a disobedient spouse to civil prison?
selfTest.a: No. For a restitution decree, Rule 32(1) allows only attachment of property.

en.meaning:
A marriage is void under Section 11 if it contravenes conditions in Section 5 relating to:

Explanation. Section 11 makes a marriage void if it contravenes Sec. 5(i) bigamy, 5(iv) prohibited relationship, or 5(v) sapinda relationship.

Explanation. A void marriage never had legal existence from the very moment it was performed.

Which of the following is a ground for a voidable marriage under Section 12?

Explanation. Impotence preventing consummation is a Section 12 ground for a voidable marriage.

A voidable marriage remains valid:

Explanation. A voidable marriage is fully valid and subsisting until a competent court annuls it by decree.

family-law-i-u3-t3.subtitle: Void marriages (section 11), voidable marriages (section 12) and the children of both

en.inOneMinute: What it is. A decree of nullity says that a marriage was not valid. A void marriage (Section 11) is invalid from the start. A voidable marriage (Section 12) is valid until a court annuls it on the petition of the party entitled on the ground. Void grounds. A living spouse, a prohibited relationship, or a sapinda relationship (Section 5 clauses (i), (iv) and (v)); custom can save the last two. Voidable grounds. Non- consummation owing to impotence, the mental conditions of Section 5(ii), consent obtained by force or fraud, and pregnancy by another person at the time of the marriage. Time limits. Force or fraud: within one year of the force ending or the fraud being discovered. Pregnancy: within one year of the marriage (Section 12(2)). Age. Under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA), an under-age marriage is neither void nor voidable, only punishable (Section 18). The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (PCMA) separately makes it voidable at the option of the child party. Children. Children of void and voidable marriages are legitimate (Section 16), with rights only in their parents' property (Section 16(3)).
legalProvision: Section 11, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 12(1). Voidable marriages. Any marriage solemnised, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be voidable and may be annulled by a decree of nullity on any of the following grounds, namely:— (a) that the marriage has not been consummated owing to the impotence of the respondent; or (b) that the marriage is in contravention of the condition specified in clause (ii) of section 5; or (c) that the consent of the petitioner, or where the consent of the guardian in marriage of the petitioner was required under section 5 as it stood immediately before the commencement of the Child Marriage Restraint (Amendment) Act, 1978 (2 of 1978), the consent of such guardian was obtained by force or by fraud as to the nature of the ceremony or as to any material fact or circumstances concerning the respondent; or (d) that the respondent was at the time of the marriage pregnant by some person other than the petitioner.

Section 12(2). Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), no petition for annulling a marriage— (a) on the ground specified in clause (c) of sub-section (1) shall be entertained if— (i) the petition is presented more than one year after the force had ceased to operate or, as the case may be, the fraud had been discovered; or (ii) the petitioner has, with his or her full consent, lived with the other party to the marriage as husband or wife after the force had ceased to operate or, as the case may be, the fraud had been discovered; (b) on the ground specified in clause (d) of sub-section (1) shall be entertained unless the court is satisfied— (i) that the petitioner was at the time of the marriage ignorant of the facts alleged; (ii) that proceedings have been instituted in the case of a marriage solemnised before the commencement of this Act within one year of such commencement and in the case of marriages solemnised after such commencement within one year from the date of the marriage; and (iii) that marital intercourse with the consent of the petitioner has not taken place since the discovery by the petitioner of the existence of the said ground.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 3(a), (f), (g): custom and usage ; sapinda relationship ; degrees of prohibited relationship. Section 5: conditions for a Hindu marriage. Section 7: ceremonies. Section 16: legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages. Sections 17 and 18: punishment of bigamy ; punishment for breach of Section 5(iii), (iv) and (v). Sections 20(1) and 23(1)(c): no collusion statement or bar for a Section 11 petition. Sections 24 and 25: maintenance and alimony in these proceedings, as in any proceeding under the Act. Section 29(1): pre-Act marriages not invalid for gotra, pravara, religion or caste. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), Section 82: bigamy. PCMA Sections 3 and 12: child marriage voidable at the child's option; void in certain cases. Family Courts Act, 1984, Section 7(1) Explanation (a), (b), (e). Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 4, 24, 25 and 26.
en.meaning:
A decree of nullity is a court decree that declares a marriage void, or annuls a voidable one. A void marriage has no legal effect from the start. It is invalid even without a decree; a decree gives a clear record and proof. A voidable marriage is valid unless and until it is annulled . Only the party entitled on the ground can petition. If no one petitions, it remains a valid marriage. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Void, section 11: a living spouse, section 5(i); prohibited relationship, section 5(iv); sapinda relationship, section 5(v); custom can save the last two. Voidable, section 12: not consummated owing to impotence; mental condition under section 5(ii); consent by force or fraud; pregnancy by another person at the marriage. keyPoints: Void (Section 11): Section 5(i), (iv), (v). Invalid from the start; either party may petition. Voidable (Section 12): impotence, mental condition, force or fraud, pregnancy by another. Valid until annulled. Breach of Section 5(iii) (age): neither void nor voidable under the HMA, but punishable (Section 18); voidable at the child's option under the PCMA. Section 12(2): force or fraud within one year of the end of force or discovery of fraud; pregnancy within one year of the marriage. Section 16: children of void and voidable marriages are legitimate, with rights only in their parents' property. Special Marriage Act: Section 24 (void) and Section 25 (voidable); age and mental condition make a marriage void there.

caseLaws.name: Jinia Keotin v
caseLaws.facts: Kumar Sitaram Manjhi (2003) Facts. In a suit for partition of ancestral property, the children of Sahadeo Manjhi by his void marriage with Jinia Keotin claimed shares in the coparcenary property along with the other heirs. Principle. Section 16(3) limits their rights to the property of their parents; they are not entitled to a share in the coparcenary property, "though they may claim to be entitled to their due share in the property of their parents". Decided 20 December 2002; appeal dismissed. Why it matters. It shows how far Section 16 goes and what it leaves out; Revanasiddappa (2023) later fixed how the parent's share is worked out. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v. Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week and claimed maintenance as his wife. Principle. The marriage was void from the start under Sections 5(i) and 11; she was not a "wife" under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and estoppel cannot defeat the Act. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. It shows the effect of a void marriage on the second spouse. Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) Facts. Two commercial pilots, engaged on 7 March 2021, obtained on 7 July 2021 a certificate from a society and a State registration certificate without any wedding ceremony. Principle. A Hindu marriage needs the ceremonies of Section 7; registration without them confers no status. The Court declared both certificates null and void and held that no Hindu marriage had taken place. 2024 INSC 355. Why it matters. It separates a marriage that never happened from a void or voidable one. Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun (2023) Facts. A two-judge Bench doubted Jinia Keotin and later cases that denied children of void marriages any share in joint family property, and referred the question under Section 16(3) to a larger Bench. Principle. Such a child is not a coparcener by birth, but on the parent's death takes a share, with the other heirs, in the parent's share worked out on a notional partition immediately before death. Decided 1 September 2023 (Chandrachud CJI, Pardiwala and Misra JJ). Why it matters. It states the present law on the property rights of children of void and voidable marriages.

selfTest.q: 1. Which clauses of Section 5 make a marriage void?
selfTest.a: Clauses (i), (iv) and (v).

selfTest.q: 2. Who can seek annulment of a voidable marriage?
selfTest.a: The party entitled on the ground under Section 12.

selfTest.q: 3. Are children of a void marriage legitimate?
selfTest.a: Yes, under Section 16(1).

selfTest.q: 4. Is a marriage under the Special Marriage Act void if the bride is under 18?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 4(c) is one of the conditions whose breach makes it void under Section 24.

selfTest.q: 5. A husband learns three years after the marriage that his wife was pregnant by another man at the wedding. Can he get a decree under Section 12(1)(d)?
selfTest.a: No. The petition had to be filed within one year of the marriage (Section 12(2)(b)(ii)).

selfTest.q: 6. Is a Hindu marriage of a 17-year-old bride void?
selfTest.a: No. It is valid under the HMA (punishable under Section 18(a)), but voidable at her option under PCMA Section 3.
