selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 5 లోని ఏ క్లాజులు వివాహాన్ని శూన్యం చేస్తాయి?
2. రద్దు చేయదగిన వివాహం రద్దును ఎవరు కోరవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 12 కింద ఆధారంపై హక్కు ఉన్న పక్షం.

selfTest.q: 3. శూన్య వివాహ పిల్లలు చట్టబద్ధమైనవారా?
4. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం కింద వధువుకు 18 లోపు ఉంటే వివాహం శూన్యమా?
selfTest.a: అవును. సెక్షన్ 24 కింద ఉల్లంఘిస్తే శూన్యం చేసే షరతుల్లో సెక్షన్ 4(c) ఒకటి.

selfTest.q: 5. పెళ్లి సమయంలో భార్య మరొకరి వల్ల గర్భవతి అని భర్తకు పెళ్లైన మూడేళ్ల తర్వాత తెలిసింది. సెక్షన్ 12(1)(d) కింద అతనికి డిక్రీ వస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: రాదు. పెళ్లైన ఒక సంవత్సరంలోనే పిటిషన్ వేయాలి (సెక్షన్ 12(2)(b)(ii)).

selfTest.q: 6. 17 ఏళ్ల వధువు హిందూ వివాహం శూన్యమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. HMA కింద అది చెల్లుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 18(a) కింద శిక్షార్హం), కానీ PCMA సెక్షన్ 3 కింద ఆమె ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది.

hi.inOneMinute: What it is. A decree of nullity says that a marriage was not valid. A void marriage (Section 11) is invalid from the start. A voidable marriage (Section 12) is valid until a court annuls it on the petition of the party entitled on the ground. Void grounds. A living spouse, a prohibited relationship, or a sapinda relationship (Section 5 clauses (i), (iv) and (v)); custom can save the last two. Voidable grounds. Non- consummation owing to impotence, the mental conditions of Section 5(ii), consent obtained by force or fraud, and pregnancy by another person at the time of the marriage. Time limits. Force or fraud: within one year of the force ending or the fraud being discovered. Pregnancy: within one year of the marriage (Section 12(2)). Age. Under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA), an under-age marriage is neither void nor voidable, only punishable (Section 18). The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 (PCMA) separately makes it voidable at the option of the child party. Children. Children of void and voidable marriages are legitimate (Section 16), with rights only in their parents' property (Section 16(3)).
legalProvision: Section 11, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Void marriages. Any marriage solemnised after the commencement of this Act shall be null and void and may, on a petition presented by either party thereto against the other party, be so declared by a decree of nullity if it contravenes any one of the conditions specified in clauses (i), (iv) and (v) of section 5.

Section 12(1). Voidable marriages. Any marriage solemnised, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be voidable and may be annulled by a decree of nullity on any of the following grounds, namely:— (a) that the marriage has not been consummated owing to the impotence of the respondent; or (b) that the marriage is in contravention of the condition specified in clause (ii) of section 5; or (c) that the consent of the petitioner, or where the consent of the guardian in marriage of the petitioner was required under section 5 as it stood immediately before the commencement of the Child Marriage Restraint (Amendment) Act, 1978 (2 of 1978), the consent of such guardian was obtained by force or by fraud as to the nature of the ceremony or as to any material fact or circumstances concerning the respondent; or (d) that the respondent was at the time of the marriage pregnant by some person other than the petitioner.

Section 12(2). Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), no petition for annulling a marriage— (a) on the ground specified in clause (c) of sub-section (1) shall be entertained if— (i) the petition is presented more than one year after the force had ceased to operate or, as the case may be, the fraud had been discovered; or (ii) the petitioner has, with his or her full consent, lived with the other party to the marriage as husband or wife after the force had ceased to operate or, as the case may be, the fraud had been discovered; (b) on the ground specified in clause (d) of sub-section (1) shall be entertained unless the court is satisfied— (i) that the petitioner was at the time of the marriage ignorant of the facts alleged; (ii) that proceedings have been instituted in the case of a marriage solemnised before the commencement of this Act within one year of such commencement and in the case of marriages solemnised after such commencement within one year from the date of the marriage; and (iii) that marital intercourse with the consent of the petitioner has not taken place since the discovery by the petitioner of the existence of the said ground.

Section 16: legitimacy of children of void and voidable marriages. Sections 17 and 18: punishment of bigamy ; punishment for breach of Section 5(iii), (iv) and (v). Sections 20(1) and 23(1)(c): no collusion statement or bar for a Section 11 petition. Sections 24 and 25: maintenance and alimony in these proceedings, as in any proceeding under the Act. Section 29(1): pre-Act marriages not invalid for gotra, pravara, religion or caste. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), Section 82: bigamy. PCMA Sections 3 and 12: child marriage voidable at the child's option; void in certain cases. Family Courts Act, 1984, Section 7(1) Explanation (a), (b), (e). Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 4, 24, 25 and 26.
hi.meaning:
A decree of nullity is a court decree that declares a marriage void, or annuls a voidable one. A void marriage has no legal effect from the start. It is invalid even without a decree; a decree gives a clear record and proof. A voidable marriage is valid unless and until it is annulled . Only the party entitled on the ground can petition. If no one petitions, it remains a valid marriage. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Void (Section 11): Section 5(i), (iv), (v). Invalid from the start; either party may petition. Voidable (Section 12): impotence, mental condition, force or fraud, pregnancy by another. Valid until annulled. Breach of Section 5(iii) (age): neither void nor voidable under the HMA, but punishable (Section 18); voidable at the child's option under the PCMA. Section 12(2): force or fraud within one year of the end of force or discovery of fraud; pregnancy within one year of the marriage. Section 16: children of void and voidable marriages are legitimate, with rights only in their parents' property. Special Marriage Act: Section 24 (void) and Section 25 (voidable); age and mental condition make a marriage void there.

caseLaws.name: Jinia Keotin v
caseLaws.facts: Kumar Sitaram Manjhi (2003) Facts. In a suit for partition of ancestral property, the children of Sahadeo Manjhi by his void marriage with Jinia Keotin claimed shares in the coparcenary property along with the other heirs. Principle. Section 16(3) limits their rights to the property of their parents; they are not entitled to a share in the coparcenary property, "though they may claim to be entitled to their due share in the property of their parents". Decided 20 December 2002; appeal dismissed. Why it matters. It shows how far Section 16 goes and what it leaves out; Revanasiddappa (2023) later fixed how the parent's share is worked out. Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v. Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week and claimed maintenance as his wife. Principle. The marriage was void from the start under Sections 5(i) and 11; she was not a "wife" under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and estoppel cannot defeat the Act. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. It shows the effect of a void marriage on the second spouse. Dolly Rani v. Manish Kumar Chanchal (2024) Facts. Two commercial pilots, engaged on 7 March 2021, obtained on 7 July 2021 a certificate from a society and a State registration certificate without any wedding ceremony. Principle. A Hindu marriage needs the ceremonies of Section 7; registration without them confers no status. The Court declared both certificates null and void and held that no Hindu marriage had taken place. 2024 INSC 355. Why it matters. It separates a marriage that never happened from a void or voidable one. Revanasiddappa v. Mallikarjun (2023) Facts. A two-judge Bench doubted Jinia Keotin and later cases that denied children of void marriages any share in joint family property, and referred the question under Section 16(3) to a larger Bench. Principle. Such a child is not a coparcener by birth, but on the parent's death takes a share, with the other heirs, in the parent's share worked out on a notional partition immediately before death. Decided 1 September 2023 (Chandrachud CJI, Pardiwala and Misra JJ). Why it matters. It states the present law on the property rights of children of void and voidable marriages.

selfTest.q: 1. Which clauses of Section 5 make a marriage void?
selfTest.a: Clauses (i), (iv) and (v).

selfTest.q: 2. Who can seek annulment of a voidable marriage?
selfTest.a: The party entitled on the ground under Section 12.

selfTest.q: 3. Are children of a void marriage legitimate?
selfTest.a: Yes, under Section 16(1).

selfTest.q: 4. Is a marriage under the Special Marriage Act void if the bride is under 18?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 4(c) is one of the conditions whose breach makes it void under Section 24.

selfTest.q: 5. A husband learns three years after the marriage that his wife was pregnant by another man at the wedding. Can he get a decree under Section 12(1)(d)?
selfTest.a: No. The petition had to be filed within one year of the marriage (Section 12(2)(b)(ii)).

selfTest.q: 6. Is a Hindu marriage of a 17-year-old bride void?
selfTest.a: No. It is valid under the HMA (punishable under Section 18(a)), but voidable at her option under PCMA Section 3.

family-law-i-u3-t7.subtitle: Why the law makes the court try for settlement first: section 23(2), cooling-off and family courts

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Conciliation means helping the spouses to settle their dispute and, where possible, save the marriage. Duty of the court. Before granting any relief under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA), the court must make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation, where the nature of the case allows (Section 23(2)). It may adjourn up to fifteen days and refer the parties to a person for this (Section 23(3)). Exceptions. The duty does not apply where relief is sought on conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation or presumed death ( proviso to Section 23(2)). Family Courts. The Family Courts Act, 1984 was passed "with a view to promote conciliation"; a Family Court must first try to assist and persuade the parties to settle (Section 9). Why it matters. Breakdown of a marriage harms children and families. The six-month wait in a mutual-consent divorce and the duty to reconcile serve the same aim: peace first, decree last.
legalProvision: Section 23(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Before proceeding to grant any relief under this Act, it shall be the duty of the court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible so to do consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation between the parties: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall apply to any proceeding wherein relief is sought on any of the grounds specified in clause (ii), clause (iii), clause (iv), clause (v), clause (vi) or clause (vii) of sub-section (1) of section 13. (3) For the purpose of aiding the court in bringing about such reconciliation, the court may, if the parties so desire or if the court thinks it just and proper so to do, adjourn the proceedings for a reasonable period not exceeding fifteen days and refer the matter to any person named by the parties in this behalf or to any person nominated by the court if the parties fail to name any person, with directions to report to the court as to whether reconciliation can be and has been, effected and the court shall in disposing of the proceeding have due regard to the report.

Section 9(1), Family Courts Act, 1984. In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding and for this purpose a Family Court may, subject to any rules made by the High Court, follow such procedure as it may deem fit.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 13B(2): the second motion in a mutual-consent divorce comes six to eighteen months after the petition. Family Courts Act, 1984 (FCA): long title; Sections 4(4), 5, 6, 9(2), (3), 10(3), 11, 12, 13 and 21(2)(c). Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC): Order XXXIIA, Rules 1 to 5. Mediation Act, 2023: Sections 5(1), 6(1), 7, 22 and 27, and the First Schedule. Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996: Sections 61, 74 and 75. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA): Section 34(2) and (3).
en.meaning:
Conciliation is a process in which the court or a neutral person helps the spouses to settle their dispute by agreement. It is not a ruling: the parties remain free to accept or reject the suggestions. In matrimonial law its first aim is reconciliation (the spouses live together again); if that fails, a fair settlement of maintenance, custody and property. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Before any relief the court checks the ground; on most grounds it must try reconciliation, with an optional fifteen-day reference; a Family Court also tries settlement under Section 9. flowchart TD P["Petition under the
Hindu Marriage Act"] --> FC["In a Family Court:
first try settlement
FCA s. 9"] FC --> G{"Ground in
s. 13(1)(ii) to (vii)?"} G -->|"Yes"| T["No s. 23(2) duty
trial proceeds"] G -->|"No"| R["Court must try reconciliation
s. 23(2)"] R --> A["May adjourn up to 15 days
and refer to a person who reports
s. 23(3)"] A -->|"Reconciled"| E["Case ends"] A -->|"Fails"| D["Trial and decree"] Text description A petition under the Hindu Marriage Act is filed. If a Family Court hears it, the Family Court first tries to assist and persuade the parties to settle under Section 9. Then the court asks whether relief is sought on a ground in Section 13(1)(ii) to (vii). If yes, the Section 23(2) duty does not apply and the case goes to trial. If no, the court must try reconciliation; it may adjourn up to fifteen days and refer the parties to a person who reports back (Section 23(3)). If reconciliation succeeds, the case ends. If it fails, the case goes to trial and decree. Stage Who acts Provision Before any relief The court tries reconciliation HMA s. 23(2) Reference for up to fifteen days A person named by the parties or the court HMA s. 23(3) First step in every Family Court case The Family Court assists and persuades the parties to settle FCA s. 9(1) Waiting period in mutual consent The parties themselves, with time to rethink HMA s. 13B(2)
keyPoints: Section 23(2): the court must try reconciliation before granting relief. Adjournment up to fifteen days and reference to a person (Section 23(3)). Duty excluded for conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation and presumed death. Section 9, Family Courts Act: the Family Court must first assist and persuade the parties to settle, and may adjourn for that purpose. Amardeep Singh (para 18) lists Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA among the conciliation efforts that must fail before waiver. The Section 13B waiting period gives time to reconcile and is directory. Order XXXIIA CPC and the Mediation Act, 2023 support settlement of family disputes.

caseLaws.name: Amardeep Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008. They settled all disputes and sought waiver of the six months under Section 13B(2). Principle. The period is directory; it exists for a rethink and reconciliation, and may be waived only if conciliation efforts (including Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA) have failed and the other conditions are met. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It treats the waiting period as a chance for conciliation, not a rigid delay. Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023) Facts. A Constitution Bench answered questions on the Supreme Court's power under Article 142 in matrimonial cases, decided on 1 May 2023. Principle. Public policy in family matters is to encourage mutual settlement (Section 89 CPC, Section 23(2) HMA, Section 9 FCA); a settlement must be free of pressure, fraud or undue influence. [2023] 5 SCR 165. Why it matters. It places conciliation at the centre of matrimonial law at the highest level.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act.

selfTest.q: 2. For how long may the court adjourn to reconcile under Section 23(3)?
selfTest.a: Up to fifteen days.

selfTest.q: 3. What does Section 9(1) of the Family Courts Act require?
selfTest.a: The Family Court must first try, where possible, to assist and persuade the parties to settle.

selfTest.q: 4. Which provisions does Amardeep Singh list among the conciliation efforts?
selfTest.a: Order XXXIIA Rule 3 CPC, Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 of the Family Courts Act (para 18, condition (ii)).

selfTest.q: 5. Must the court attempt reconciliation in a divorce petition on the ground of desertion?
selfTest.a: Yes. Desertion (Section 13(1)(ib)) is not among the excluded grounds.

selfTest.q: 6. Under the Family Courts Act, for how long may the Family Court adjourn for settlement?
selfTest.a: For such period as it thinks fit (Section 9(2)).

hi.inOneMinute: What it is. Conciliation means helping the spouses to settle their dispute and, where possible, save the marriage. Duty of the court. Before granting any relief under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA), the court must make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation, where the nature of the case allows (Section 23(2)). It may adjourn up to fifteen days and refer the parties to a person for this (Section 23(3)). Exceptions. The duty does not apply where relief is sought on conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation or presumed death ( proviso to Section 23(2)). Family Courts. The Family Courts Act, 1984 was passed "with a view to promote conciliation"; a Family Court must first try to assist and persuade the parties to settle (Section 9). Why it matters. Breakdown of a marriage harms children and families. The six-month wait in a mutual-consent divorce and the duty to reconcile serve the same aim: peace first, decree last.
legalProvision: Section 23(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Before proceeding to grant any relief under this Act, it shall be the duty of the court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible so to do consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation between the parties: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall apply to any proceeding wherein relief is sought on any of the grounds specified in clause (ii), clause (iii), clause (iv), clause (v), clause (vi) or clause (vii) of sub-section (1) of section 13. (3) For the purpose of aiding the court in bringing about such reconciliation, the court may, if the parties so desire or if the court thinks it just and proper so to do, adjourn the proceedings for a reasonable period not exceeding fifteen days and refer the matter to any person named by the parties in this behalf or to any person nominated by the court if the parties fail to name any person, with directions to report to the court as to whether reconciliation can be and has been, effected and the court shall in disposing of the proceeding have due regard to the report.

Section 9(1), Family Courts Act, 1984. In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding and for this purpose a Family Court may, subject to any rules made by the High Court, follow such procedure as it may deem fit.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 13B(2): the second motion in a mutual-consent divorce comes six to eighteen months after the petition. Family Courts Act, 1984 (FCA): long title; Sections 4(4), 5, 6, 9(2), (3), 10(3), 11, 12, 13 and 21(2)(c). Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC): Order XXXIIA, Rules 1 to 5. Mediation Act, 2023: Sections 5(1), 6(1), 7, 22 and 27, and the First Schedule. Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996: Sections 61, 74 and 75. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA): Section 34(2) and (3).
hi.meaning:
Conciliation is a process in which the court or a neutral person helps the spouses to settle their dispute by agreement. It is not a ruling: the parties remain free to accept or reject the suggestions. In matrimonial law its first aim is reconciliation (the spouses live together again); if that fails, a fair settlement of maintenance, custody and property. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Before any relief the court checks the ground; on most grounds it must try reconciliation, with an optional fifteen-day reference; a Family Court also tries settlement under Section 9. flowchart TD P["Petition under the

If a Family Court hears it, the Family Court first tries to assist and persuade the parties to settle under Section 9. Then the court asks whether relief is sought on a ground in Section 13(1)(ii) to (vii). If yes, the Section 23(2) duty does not apply and the case goes to trial. If no, the court must try reconciliation; it may adjourn up to fifteen days and refer the parties to a person who reports back (Section 23(3)). If reconciliation succeeds, the case ends. If it fails, the case goes to trial and decree. keyPoints: Section 23(2): the court must try reconciliation before granting relief. Adjournment up to fifteen days and reference to a person (Section 23(3)). Duty excluded for conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation and presumed death. Section 9, Family Courts Act: the Family Court must first assist and persuade the parties to settle, and may adjourn for that purpose. Amardeep Singh (para 18) lists Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA among the conciliation efforts that must fail before waiver. The Section 13B waiting period gives time to reconcile and is directory. Order XXXIIA CPC and the Mediation Act, 2023 support settlement of family disputes.

caseLaws.name: Amardeep Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008. They settled all disputes and sought waiver of the six months under Section 13B(2). Principle. The period is directory; it exists for a rethink and reconciliation, and may be waived only if conciliation efforts (including Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA) have failed and the other conditions are met. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It treats the waiting period as a chance for conciliation, not a rigid delay. Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023) Facts. A Constitution Bench answered questions on the Supreme Court's power under Article 142 in matrimonial cases, decided on 1 May 2023. Principle. Public policy in family matters is to encourage mutual settlement (Section 89 CPC, Section 23(2) HMA, Section 9 FCA); a settlement must be free of pressure, fraud or undue influence. [2023] 5 SCR 165. Why it matters. It places conciliation at the centre of matrimonial law at the highest level.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act.

selfTest.q: 2. For how long may the court adjourn to reconcile under Section 23(3)?
selfTest.a: Up to fifteen days.

selfTest.q: 3. What does Section 9(1) of the Family Courts Act require?
selfTest.a: The Family Court must first try, where possible, to assist and persuade the parties to settle.

selfTest.q: 4. Which provisions does Amardeep Singh list among the conciliation efforts?
selfTest.a: Order XXXIIA Rule 3 CPC, Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 of the Family Courts Act (para 18, condition (ii)).

selfTest.q: 5. Must the court attempt reconciliation in a divorce petition on the ground of desertion?
selfTest.a: Yes. Desertion (Section 13(1)(ib)) is not among the excluded grounds.

selfTest.q: 6. Under the Family Courts Act, for how long may the Family Court adjourn for settlement?
selfTest.a: For such period as it thinks fit (Section 9(2)).

Explanation. Section 13(2) gives a wife four more grounds: pre-1955 polygamy of the husband, rape, sodomy or bestiality by him, non-cohabitation for a year after a maintenance decree, and repudiation of a marriage solemnized before she was fifteen.

family-law-i-u3-t6.subtitle: Section 24: interim maintenance and expenses, with a comparison to permanent alimony under section 25

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Maintenance pendente lite is interim support that the court orders while a matrimonial case is pending, together with the expenses of the case (Section 24). Who may claim. Either the wife or the husband, in any proceeding under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). The test. The applicant has no independent income sufficient for his or her support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding. Speed. The application is to be decided, as far as possible, within sixty days of service of notice ( proviso to Section 24). After the case. The order ends with the proceeding. At or after the decree, the court may grant permanent alimony under Section 25.
legalProvision: Section 24, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings. Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the court to be reasonable: Provided that the application for the payment of the expenses of the proceeding and such monthly sum during the proceeding, shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the wife or the husband, as the case may be.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 25: permanent alimony and maintenance at or after the decree. HMA Section 26: custody, maintenance and education of minor children, with a sixty-day target for interim maintenance and education. HMA Sections 21B, 28 and 28A: speedy trial, appeals and enforcement. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 36, 37 and 38. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7 and 9. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Section 144 (earlier Section 125, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA), Sections 18(1) and 23(2). Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), Sections 12, 20, 23 and 26.
en.meaning:
Maintenance pendente lite means maintenance while the suit is pending (" pendente lite " means "while the litigation is pending"). It lets a spouse with no means live during the case and carry on the case on fair terms. The order is temporary. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A proceeding under the Act, an application by the wife or the husband, and no sufficient independent income lead to an order for expenses and a monthly sum, decided within sixty days as far as possible. flowchart TD A{"Proceeding under the
Hindu Marriage Act pending?"} A -->|"No"| N["Section 24 does not apply"] A -->|"Yes"| B["Application by
wife or husband"] B --> C{"Independent income sufficient
for support and expenses?"} C -->|"Yes"| F["Application fails"] C -->|"No"| O["Order: expenses of proceeding
+ reasonable monthly sum
(both incomes considered)"] O --> T["Decided within 60 days
of notice, as far as possible"] T --> E["Lasts until the
proceeding ends"] Text description First ask whether a proceeding under the Hindu Marriage Act is pending; if not, Section 24 does not apply. Then ask whether the wife or the husband has applied. Then ask whether the applicant has independent income sufficient for support and the expenses of the proceeding; if yes, the application fails. If no, the court orders the other spouse to pay the expenses of the proceeding and a reasonable monthly sum, having regard to both incomes, deciding as far as possible within sixty days of notice. The order lasts until the proceeding ends. Element What Section 24 says Proceeding Any proceeding under the Act Applicant The wife or the husband Condition No independent income sufficient for support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding What is ordered Expenses of the proceeding, and a monthly sum during the proceeding Measure Reasonable, having regard to the applicant's own income and the other spouse's income Time As far as possible, within sixty days of service of notice
keyPoints: Section 24: interim maintenance and expenses during any proceeding under the Act. Wife or husband may claim; the test is no independent income sufficient. Disposal within sixty days of notice, as far as possible. Section 25: permanent alimony at or after the decree, variable under Section 25(2) and (3). BNSS Section 144 also allows interim maintenance, within sixty days as far as possible. Special Marriage Act, 1954: interim maintenance (Section 36) and permanent alimony (Section 37) are for the wife only. Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 20: monetary relief, including maintenance, from a Magistrate.

caseLaws.name: Saroj Rani v
caseLaws.facts: Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. In the wife's restitution case the Sub-Judge on 21 March 1978 granted ₹185 a month as maintenance pendente lite and ₹300 as litigation expenses; a consent decree followed on 28 March 1978. The husband later got divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii). Principle. The Supreme Court directed that maintenance continue after the divorce: ₹200 a month to the wife until she remarries and ₹300 a month to the daughter until her marriage. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It shows interim maintenance and expenses during a case, and continuing maintenance at the decree stage.

selfTest.q: 1. Can a husband claim maintenance pendente lite?
selfTest.a: Yes. The section says wife or husband.

selfTest.q: 2. What is the target time to decide a Section 24 application?
selfTest.a: Sixty days from service of notice, as far as possible.

selfTest.q: 3. Which section gives permanent alimony?
selfTest.a: Section 25.

selfTest.q: 4. Who may claim alimony pendente lite under Section 36 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954?
selfTest.a: The wife only.

selfTest.q: 5. Under which section is interim maintenance for minor children ordered?
selfTest.a: Section 26.

selfTest.q: 6. Does a Section 24 order continue after the decree?
selfTest.a: No. It runs during the proceeding; after the decree, Section 25 applies.

Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the court to be reasonable: Provided that the application for the payment of the expenses of the proceeding and such monthly sum during the proceeding, shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the wife or the husband, as the case may be.
ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

HMA సెక్షన్ 25: డిక్రీ సమయంలో లేదా తర్వాత శాశ్వత భరణం, పోషణ. HMA సెక్షన్ 26: మైనర్ పిల్లల సంరక్షణ, పోషణ, చదువు; తాత్కాలిక పోషణ, చదువుకు అరవై రోజుల లక్ష్యం. HMA సెక్షన్లు 21B, 28, 28A: వేగవంతమైన విచారణ, అప్పీళ్లు, అమలు. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం, 1954 (SMA), సెక్షన్లు 36, 37, 38. కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానాల చట్టం, 1984, సెక్షన్లు 7, 9. భారతీయ నాగరిక సురక్ష సంహిత, 2023 (BNSS), సెక్షన్ 144 (గతంలో క్రిమినల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1973, సెక్షన్ 125). హిందూ దత్తత, భరణ చట్టం, 1956 (HAMA), సెక్షన్లు 18(1), 23(2). గృహ హింస నుంచి మహిళల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2005 (PWDVA), సెక్షన్లు 12, 20, 23, 26.
te.meaning:
Maintenance pendente lite అంటే దావా పెండింగ్‌లో ఉన్నప్పుడు భరణం (" pendente lite " అంటే "వ్యాజ్యం పెండింగ్‌లో ఉన్నప్పుడు"). ఆర్థిక వనరులు లేని జీవిత భాగస్వామి కేసు సమయంలో జీవించడానికి, న్యాయమైన పరిస్థితుల్లో కేసు నడపడానికి ఇది వీలిస్తుంది. ఉత్తర్వు తాత్కాలికం. Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. చట్టం కింద కేసు, భార్య లేదా భర్త దరఖాస్తు, సరిపడా స్వతంత్ర ఆదాయం లేకపోవడం ఉంటే, సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు అరవై రోజుల్లో, ఖర్చులు, నెలవారీ మొత్తానికి ఉత్తర్వు. flowchart TD A{"హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం కింద
కేసు పెండింగ్‌లో ఉందా?"} A -->|"లేదు"| N["సెక్షన్ 24 వర్తించదు"] A -->|"అవును"| B["భార్య లేదా భర్త

అమలులో"] వచన వివరణ మొదట హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం కింద కేసు పెండింగ్‌లో ఉందా అని అడగండి; లేకపోతే సెక్షన్ 24 వర్తించదు. తర్వాత భార్య లేదా భర్త దరఖాస్తు చేశారా. తర్వాత దరఖాస్తుదారుకు పోషణకు, కేసు ఖర్చులకు సరిపడా స్వతంత్ర ఆదాయం ఉందా; ఉంటే దరఖాస్తు విఫలం. లేకపోతే, రెండు ఆదాయాలను పరిగణించి, కేసు ఖర్చులు, సహేతుక నెలవారీ మొత్తం చెల్లించాలని కోర్టు మరో జీవిత భాగస్వామిని ఆదేశిస్తుంది; సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు నోటీసు నుంచి అరవై రోజుల్లో నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. కేసు ముగిసే వరకు ఉత్తర్వు అమలులో ఉంటుంది. అంశం సెక్షన్ 24 ఏమి చెబుతుంది కేసు చట్టం కింద ఏ కేసైనా దరఖాస్తుదారు భార్య లేదా భర్త షరతు పోషణకు, కేసు అవసరమైన ఖర్చులకు సరిపడా స్వతంత్ర ఆదాయం లేకపోవడం ఏమి ఆదేశిస్తారు కేసు ఖర్చులు, కేసు సమయంలో నెలవారీ మొత్తం కొలమానం దరఖాస్తుదారు సొంత ఆదాయం, మరో జీవిత భాగస్వామి ఆదాయం పరిగణించి సహేతుకం సమయం సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు, నోటీసు అందిన అరవై రోజుల్లో

selfTest.q: 1. భర్త కేసు పెండింగ్‌లో భరణం కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. సెక్షన్ భార్య లేదా భర్త అంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 24 దరఖాస్తును నిర్ణయించడానికి లక్ష్య సమయం ఎంత?
selfTest.a: సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు, నోటీసు అందిన అరవై రోజులు.

selfTest.q: 3. శాశ్వత భరణం ఏ సెక్షన్ ఇస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 25.

hi.inOneMinute: What it is. Maintenance pendente lite is interim support that the court orders while a matrimonial case is pending, together with the expenses of the case (Section 24). Who may claim. Either the wife or the husband, in any proceeding under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). The test. The applicant has no independent income sufficient for his or her support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding. Speed. The application is to be decided, as far as possible, within sixty days of service of notice ( proviso to Section 24). After the case. The order ends with the proceeding. At or after the decree, the court may grant permanent alimony under Section 25.
legalProvision: Section 24, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings. Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the court to be reasonable: Provided that the application for the payment of the expenses of the proceeding and such monthly sum during the proceeding, shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the wife or the husband, as the case may be.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 25: permanent alimony and maintenance at or after the decree. HMA Section 26: custody, maintenance and education of minor children, with a sixty-day target for interim maintenance and education. HMA Sections 21B, 28 and 28A: speedy trial, appeals and enforcement. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 36, 37 and 38. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7 and 9. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Section 144 (earlier Section 125, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA), Sections 18(1) and 23(2). Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), Sections 12, 20, 23 and 26.
hi.meaning:
Maintenance pendente lite means maintenance while the suit is pending (" pendente lite " means "while the litigation is pending"). It lets a spouse with no means live during the case and carry on the case on fair terms. The order is temporary. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A proceeding under the Act, an application by the wife or the husband, and no sufficient independent income lead to an order for expenses and a monthly sum, decided within sixty days as far as possible. flowchart TD A{"Proceeding under the
Hindu Marriage Act pending?"} A -->|"No"| N["Section 24 does not apply"] A -->|"Yes"| B["Application by
wife or husband"] B --> C{"Independent income sufficient
for support and expenses?"} C -->|"Yes"| F["Application fails"] C -->|"No"| O["Order: expenses of proceeding
+ reasonable monthly sum
(both incomes considered)"] O --> T["Decided within 60 days
of notice, as far as possible"] T --> E["Lasts until the
proceeding ends"] Text description First ask whether a proceeding under the Hindu Marriage Act is pending; if not, Section 24 does not apply. Then ask whether the wife or the husband has applied. Then ask whether the applicant has independent income sufficient for support and the expenses of the proceeding; if yes, the application fails. If no, the court orders the other spouse to pay the expenses of the proceeding and a reasonable monthly sum, having regard to both incomes, deciding as far as possible within sixty days of notice. The order lasts until the proceeding ends. Element What Section 24 says Proceeding Any proceeding under the Act Applicant The wife or the husband Condition No independent income sufficient for support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding What is ordered Expenses of the proceeding, and a monthly sum during the proceeding Measure Reasonable, having regard to the applicant's own income and the other spouse's income Time As far as possible, within sixty days of service of notice
keyPoints: Section 24: interim maintenance and expenses during any proceeding under the Act. Wife or husband may claim; the test is no independent income sufficient. Disposal within sixty days of notice, as far as possible. Section 25: permanent alimony at or after the decree, variable under Section 25(2) and (3). BNSS Section 144 also allows interim maintenance, within sixty days as far as possible. Special Marriage Act, 1954: interim maintenance (Section 36) and permanent alimony (Section 37) are for the wife only. Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 20: monetary relief, including maintenance, from a Magistrate.

caseLaws.name: Saroj Rani v
caseLaws.facts: Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. In the wife's restitution case the Sub-Judge on 21 March 1978 granted ₹185 a month as maintenance pendente lite and ₹300 as litigation expenses; a consent decree followed on 28 March 1978. The husband later got divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii). Principle. The Supreme Court directed that maintenance continue after the divorce: ₹200 a month to the wife until she remarries and ₹300 a month to the daughter until her marriage. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It shows interim maintenance and expenses during a case, and continuing maintenance at the decree stage.

selfTest.q: 1. Can a husband claim maintenance pendente lite?
selfTest.a: Yes. The section says wife or husband.

selfTest.q: 2. What is the target time to decide a Section 24 application?
selfTest.a: Sixty days from service of notice, as far as possible.

selfTest.q: 3. Which section gives permanent alimony?
selfTest.a: Section 25.

selfTest.q: 4. Who may claim alimony pendente lite under Section 36 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954?
selfTest.a: The wife only.

selfTest.q: 5. Under which section is interim maintenance for minor children ordered?
selfTest.a: Section 26.

selfTest.q: 6. Does a Section 24 order continue after the decree?
selfTest.a: No. It runs during the proceeding; after the decree, Section 25 applies.

family-law-i-u3-t4.subtitle: Section 10: grounds, effect, rescission and the route to divorce

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Judicial separation is a court decree that ends the duty of the spouses to live together. The marriage itself continues, so neither spouse can marry again. Grounds. Either spouse may petition on any ground on which a divorce could be sought under Section 13(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). A wife may also use her special grounds in Section 13(2) (Section 10(1)). Undoing it. The court may rescind the decree on the petition of either party if it is just and reasonable (Section 10(2)). Road to divorce. If the spouses do not resume cohabitation for one year or more after the decree, either may seek divorce (Section 13(1A)(i)). Instead of divorce. On a divorce petition, the court may grant judicial separation instead, except on conversion, renunciation of the world or presumed death (Section 13A).
legalProvision: Section 10, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Judicial separation. (1) Either party to a marriage, whether solemnised before or after the commencement of this Act, may present a petition praying for a decree for judicial separation on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (1) of section 13, and in the case of a wife also on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (2) thereof, as grounds on which a petition for divorce might have been presented. (2) Where a decree for judicial separation has been passed, it shall no longer be obligatory for the petitioner to cohabit with the respondent, but the court may, on the application by petition of either party and on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition, rescind the decree if it considers it just and reasonable to do so.

Section 13(1A). Either party to a marriage, whether solemnized before or after the commencement of this Act, may also present a petition for the dissolution of the marriage by a decree of divorce on the ground— (i) that there has been no resumption of cohabitation as between the parties to the marriage for a period of one year or upwards after the passing of a decree for judicial separation in a proceeding to which they were parties; …

Section 13A. Alternate relief in divorce proceedings. In any proceeding under this Act, on a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce, except in so far as the petition is founded on the grounds mentioned in clauses (ii), (vi) and (vii) of sub-section (1) of section 13, the court may, if it considers it just so to do having regard to the circumstances of the case, pass instead a decree for judicial separation.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 13(1) and (2), HMA: the grounds (and the Explanation on desertion ). Sections 14, 15, 19, 20, 21A, 21B, 23, 24, 25, 26, HMA: one-year bar (divorce only), remarriage, procedure, conditions and ancillary orders. Section 18(2), (3), Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA): a wife's right to live separately with maintenance. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7(1) Explanation (a) and 9. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 23, 27(1), (1A) and 27A.
en.meaning:
Judicial separation is a decree that allows the spouses to live apart without ending the marriage. It gives a breathing space, which may lead to reconciliation, or to divorce if it fails. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The decree ends the duty to cohabit but keeps the marriage alive; it can be rescinded, or lead to divorce after one year. flowchart TD P["Petition under s. 10
ground in s. 13(1)
(wife: also s. 13(2))"] --> D["Decree of
judicial separation"] D --> E1["Petitioner need not cohabit"] D --> E2["Marriage continues"] D --> E3["No remarriage (s. 15)"] D -->|"Parties reconcile"| R["Court may rescind
s. 10(2)"] D -->|"No cohabitation
1 year or more"| V["Either party may
seek divorce
s. 13(1A)(i)"] Text description A petition under Section 10 on a Section 13(1) ground, or a Section 13(2) ground for a wife, leads to a decree of judicial separation. The decree has three effects: the petitioner need not cohabit; the marriage continues; neither spouse can remarry. From the decree there are two paths: if the parties reconcile, the court may rescind the decree under Section 10(2); if there is no cohabitation for one year or more, either party may seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(i). Point Effect of the decree Duty to cohabit Ends for the petitioner (Section 10(2)) Marriage Continues Remarriage Not allowed; only a divorce decree permits it (Section 15) Can it be undone? Yes, by rescission (Section 10(2)) Next step Divorce after one year without resumed cohabitation (Section 13(1A)(i))
keyPoints: Section 10: the decree ends the duty to cohabit; the marriage continues. Grounds are those of divorce (Section 13(1)), and for a wife also Section 13(2). No remarriage after judicial separation. Rescission is possible under Section 10(2). No cohabitation for one year allows either party to seek divorce (Section 13(1A)(i)). Section 13A lets the court grant judicial separation instead of divorce. Special Marriage Act, 1954, Section 23: judicial separation on the grounds of Section 27 and on failure to obey a restitution decree.

caseLaws.name: Dastane v
caseLaws.facts: Dastane (1975) Facts. Dr. Dastane, married in 1956, sought annulment for fraud, divorce for unsoundness of mind, or judicial separation for cruelty. Only judicial separation for cruelty under the old Section 10(1)(b) reached the Supreme Court. Principle. Cruelty is proved on a preponderance of probabilities. The wife was cruel, but the husband condoned it and her later conduct did not revive it, so he lost. (1975) 2 SCC 326 : AIR 1975 SC 1534. Why it matters. It shows that the Section 23 bars apply to judicial separation. Savitri Pandey v. Prem Chandra Pandey (2002) Facts. The parties married on 6 May 1987 and lived together only till 21 June 1987. The wife sought divorce alleging cruelty and desertion. Principle. Neither was proved; desertion needs separation plus animus deserendi , and "there can be no desertion without previous cohabitation by the parties". The appeals were dismissed. (2002) 2 SCC 73 : AIR 2002 SC 591. Why it matters. It explains desertion and cruelty, which are grounds for both judicial separation and divorce.

selfTest.q: 1. Does judicial separation end a marriage?
selfTest.a: No.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a decree of judicial separation be undone?
selfTest.a: Yes, by rescission under Section 10(2).

selfTest.q: 3. What does Section 13(1A)(i) allow?
selfTest.a: Divorce, for either party, after one year without cohabitation following the decree.

selfTest.q: 4. Which section of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides judicial separation?
selfTest.a: Section 23.

selfTest.q: 5. Can a wife seek judicial separation six months after her marriage?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 14 bars only a divorce petition within one year.

selfTest.q: 6. On a divorce petition based on the husband's renunciation of the world, can the court grant judicial separation instead?
selfTest.a: No. Section 13A excludes Section 13(1)(vi).

legalProvision: Section 10, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Judicial separation. (1) Either party to a marriage, whether solemnised before or after the commencement of this Act, may present a petition praying for a decree for judicial separation on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (1) of section 13, and in the case of a wife also on any of the grounds specified in sub-section (2) thereof, as grounds on which a petition for divorce might have been presented. (2) Where a decree for judicial separation has been passed, it shall no longer be obligatory for the petitioner to cohabit with the respondent, but the court may, on the application by petition of either party and on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition, rescind the decree if it considers it just and reasonable to do so.

Section 13(1A). Either party to a marriage, whether solemnized before or after the commencement of this Act, may also present a petition for the dissolution of the marriage by a decree of divorce on the ground— (i) that there has been no resumption of cohabitation as between the parties to the marriage for a period of one year or upwards after the passing of a decree for judicial separation in a proceeding to which they were parties; …

Section 13A. Alternate relief in divorce proceedings. In any proceeding under this Act, on a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce, except in so far as the petition is founded on the grounds mentioned in clauses (ii), (vi) and (vii) of sub-section (1) of section 13, the court may, if it considers it just so to do having regard to the circumstances of the case, pass instead a decree for judicial separation.

hi.inOneMinute: What it is. Judicial separation is a court decree that ends the duty of the spouses to live together. The marriage itself continues, so neither spouse can marry again. Grounds. Either spouse may petition on any ground on which a divorce could be sought under Section 13(1) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). A wife may also use her special grounds in Section 13(2) (Section 10(1)). Undoing it. The court may rescind the decree on the petition of either party if it is just and reasonable (Section 10(2)). Road to divorce. If the spouses do not resume cohabitation for one year or more after the decree, either may seek divorce (Section 13(1A)(i)). Instead of divorce. On a divorce petition, the court may grant judicial separation instead, except on conversion, renunciation of the world or presumed death (Section 13A).

hi.meaning:
Judicial separation is a decree that allows the spouses to live apart without ending the marriage. It gives a breathing space, which may lead to reconciliation, or to divorce if it fails. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The decree ends the duty to cohabit but keeps the marriage alive; it can be rescinded, or lead to divorce after one year. flowchart TD P["Petition under s. 10
ground in s. 13(1)
(wife: also s. 13(2))"] --> D["Decree of
judicial separation"] D --> E1["Petitioner need not cohabit"] D --> E2["Marriage continues"] D --> E3["No remarriage (s. 15)"] D -->|"Parties reconcile"| R["Court may rescind
s. 10(2)"] D -->|"No cohabitation
1 year or more"| V["Either party may
seek divorce
s. 13(1A)(i)"] Text description A petition under Section 10 on a Section 13(1) ground, or a Section 13(2) ground for a wife, leads to a decree of judicial separation. The decree has three effects: the petitioner need not cohabit; the marriage continues; neither spouse can remarry. From the decree there are two paths: if the parties reconcile, the court may rescind the decree under Section 10(2); if there is no cohabitation for one year or more, either party may seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(i). Point Effect of the decree Duty to cohabit Ends for the petitioner (Section 10(2)) Marriage Continues Remarriage Not allowed; only a divorce decree permits it (Section 15) Can it be undone? Yes, by rescission (Section 10(2)) Next step Divorce after one year without resumed cohabitation (Section 13(1A)(i))
keyPoints: Section 10: the decree ends the duty to cohabit; the marriage continues. Grounds are those of divorce (Section 13(1)), and for a wife also Section 13(2). No remarriage after judicial separation. Rescission is possible under Section 10(2). No cohabitation for one year allows either party to seek divorce (Section 13(1A)(i)). Section 13A lets the court grant judicial separation instead of divorce. Special Marriage Act, 1954, Section 23: judicial separation on the grounds of Section 27 and on failure to obey a restitution decree.

caseLaws.name: Dastane v
caseLaws.facts: Dastane (1975) Facts. Dr. Dastane, married in 1956, sought annulment for fraud, divorce for unsoundness of mind, or judicial separation for cruelty. Only judicial separation for cruelty under the old Section 10(1)(b) reached the Supreme Court. Principle. Cruelty is proved on a preponderance of probabilities. The wife was cruel, but the husband condoned it and her later conduct did not revive it, so he lost. (1975) 2 SCC 326 : AIR 1975 SC 1534. Why it matters. It shows that the Section 23 bars apply to judicial separation. Savitri Pandey v. Prem Chandra Pandey (2002) Facts. The parties married on 6 May 1987 and lived together only till 21 June 1987. The wife sought divorce alleging cruelty and desertion. Principle. Neither was proved; desertion needs separation plus animus deserendi , and "there can be no desertion without previous cohabitation by the parties". The appeals were dismissed. (2002) 2 SCC 73 : AIR 2002 SC 591. Why it matters. It explains desertion and cruelty, which are grounds for both judicial separation and divorce.

selfTest.q: 1. Does judicial separation end a marriage?
selfTest.a: No.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a decree of judicial separation be undone?
selfTest.a: Yes, by rescission under Section 10(2).

selfTest.q: 3. What does Section 13(1A)(i) allow?
selfTest.a: Divorce, for either party, after one year without cohabitation following the decree.

selfTest.q: 4. Which section of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides judicial separation?
selfTest.a: Section 23.

selfTest.q: 5. Can a wife seek judicial separation six months after her marriage?
selfTest.a: Yes. Section 14 bars only a divorce petition within one year.

selfTest.q: 6. On a divorce petition based on the husband's renunciation of the world, can the court grant judicial separation instead?
selfTest.a: No. Section 13A excludes Section 13(1)(vi).

Which section of the Hindu Marriage Act makes it the court's duty to attempt reconciliation before granting relief?

Explanation. Section 23(2) makes it the court's duty to attempt reconciliation wherever possible.

Under Section 23(3), the court may adjourn proceedings for reconciliation for a period ordinarily not exceeding:

Explanation. Section 23(3) permits adjournment for reconciliation, ordinarily not exceeding fifteen days.

Under Section 13B(1), the parties must have been living separately for a period of:

Explanation. Section 13B(1) requires the parties to have been living separately for a period of one year or more.

family-law-i-u3-t5.subtitle: Fault grounds, wife's special grounds, mutual consent, waiting periods and irretrievable breakdown

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Divorce ends a valid marriage by a court decree. After it, and after the appeal time, either party may marry again (Section 15). Four routes. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) allows divorce on fault grounds (Section 13(1)), after a failed decree of judicial separation or restitution (Section 13(1A)), on four special grounds for a wife (Section 13(2)), and by mutual consent (Section 13B). Bars. No petition within one year of marriage without leave (Section 14). The petitioner must not take advantage of his or her own wrong, must not have condoned or connived at the fault, and must not collude or delay (Section 23). Mutual consent. Both spouses petition together after living apart for one year; the second motion comes six to eighteen months later; consent must continue till the decree ( Sureshta Devi ); the six months can be waived ( Amardeep Singh ). Irretrievable breakdown. It is not a ground in the Act. Only the Supreme Court can dissolve a marriage on it, under Article 142 ( Shilpa Sailesh , 2023).
legalProvision: Section 13(1), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Divorce. Any marriage solemnized, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, may, on a petition presented by either the husband or the wife, be dissolved by a decree of divorce on the ground that the other party— (i) has, after the solemnization of the marriage, had voluntary sexual intercourse with any person other than his or her spouse; or (ia) has, after the solemnization of the marriage, treated the petitioner with cruelty; or (ib) has deserted the petitioner for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition; or (ii) has ceased to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion; or (iii) has been incurably of unsound mind, or has been suffering continuously or intermittently from mental disorder of such a kind and to such an extent that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent. … (v) has … been suffering from venereal disease in a communicable form; or (vi) has renounced the world by entering any religious order; or (vii) has not been heard of as being alive for a period of seven years or more by those persons who would naturally have heard of it, had that party been alive.

Section 13B(1). … a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce may be presented to the district court by both the parties to a marriage together … on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved. (2) On the motion of both the parties made not earlier than six months after the date of the presentation of the petition … and not later than eighteen months after the said date, if the petition is not withdrawn in the meantime, the court shall, on being satisfied, after hearing the parties and after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, that a marriage has been solemnised and that the averments in the petition are true, pass a decree of divorce declaring the marriage to be dissolved with effect from the date of the decree.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 13(1A): divorce after a failed decree of judicial separation or restitution. HMA Section 13(2): a wife's four extra grounds. HMA Sections 13A, 14, 15, 16, 21A, 23, 23A, 24 to 28: alternative relief, the one-year bar, remarriage, legitimacy of children, rival petitions, bars to relief, counter-claim, ancillary orders and appeals. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7(1) Explanation (a), 9, 11 and 19. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 27, 27A, 28, 29, 30, 34 and 35. Constitution of India, Article 142(1): the Supreme Court's power to do "complete justice".
en.meaning:
Divorce is the dissolution of a valid marriage by a decree of the court. It differs from nullity, which declares that no valid marriage existed or annuls a voidable one, and from judicial separation , which keeps the marriage alive. The Act began with the fault theory of divorce : one spouse must prove a matrimonial wrong by the other. Later amendments added divorce after a failed decree (1964 and 1976) and divorce by mutual consent (1976). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Section 13(1): adultery, cruelty, desertion (two years), conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation, presumed death. Section 13(1A): one year without cohabitation or restitution after the earlier decree; either party. Section 13(2): four grounds for a wife. Section 13B: one year apart, two motions, six to eighteen months; waivable; consent must continue. Section 14: one-year bar. Section 23: bars and reconciliation. Irretrievable breakdown: only the Supreme Court, under Article 142. Special Marriage Act, 1954: divorce in Sections 27 and 28; no conversion or renunciation ground, but imprisonment for seven years.

caseLaws.name: Dastane v
caseLaws.facts: Dastane (1975) Facts. Dr. Dastane, married in 1956, sought annulment , divorce or judicial separation. Only judicial separation for cruelty under the old Section 10(1)(b) reached the Supreme Court. Principle. Cruelty is proved on a preponderance of probabilities; danger to life, limb or health is not needed; trivialities are ignored. The wife was cruel, but the husband condoned it and it was not revived. (1975) 2 SCC 326 : AIR 1975 SC 1534. Why it matters. It fixes the standard of proof and the test for cruelty, and shows how condonation bars relief. Savitri Pandey v. Prem Chandra Pandey (2002) Facts. The parties, married on 6 May 1987, lived together only till 21 June 1987. The wife sought divorce for cruelty and desertion. Principle. Neither was proved; desertion needs separation and animus deserendi , and there is no desertion without previous cohabitation; a spouse cannot take advantage of his or her own wrong. Appeals dismissed. (2002) 2 SCC 73 : AIR 2002 SC 591. Why it matters. It states the elements of cruelty and desertion. Shilpa Sailesh (2023) read it down on the Supreme Court's power under Article 142. Sureshta Devi v. Om Prakash (1991) Facts. Married in 1968, the spouses filed a Section 13B petition at Hamirpur on 8 January 1985. On 15 January 1985 the wife applied to withdraw, saying her statement was obtained under pressure. The High Court granted divorce. Principle. Mutual consent must continue till the decree; either party may withdraw it before then. Appeal allowed and the decree set aside. (1991) 2 SCC 25 : AIR 1992 SC 1904. Why it matters. It is the leading case on withdrawal of consent and the meaning of "living separately". Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. The parties married in 1994 and lived apart from 2008. They settled all disputes, including alimony of ₹2.75 crore and custody, and asked to waive the six months. Principle. The six-month period in Section 13B(2) is directory; the court may waive it on four conditions. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It makes the waiting period flexible where the marriage is clearly over and everything is settled. Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. The wife got a consent decree for restitution on 28 March 1978. With no cohabitation for over a year, the husband petitioned for divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii) on 19 April 1979. Principle. Divorce was granted; the consent decree was not collusive and the husband was not taking advantage of his own wrong. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It shows how a failed restitution decree leads to divorce. Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023) Facts. A transfer petition in which the Supreme Court referred questions on its power under Article 142 in matrimonial cases to a Constitution Bench, decided on 1 May 2023. Principle. The Supreme Court may dissolve a marriage on irretrievable breakdown, and may waive the Section 13B procedure on a settlement, but only with great care and caution. [2023] 5 SCR 165. Why it matters. It settles that irretrievable breakdown is a ground only before the Supreme Court, not before trial courts.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the period of desertion required?
selfTest.a: A continuous period of at least two years immediately before the petition.

selfTest.q: 2. Is the six-month period in Section 13B mandatory?
selfTest.a: No. It is directory ( Amardeep Singh ).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a spouse withdraw consent before the decree?
selfTest.a: Yes ( Sureshta Devi ).

selfTest.q: 4. Which section of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides divorce by mutual consent?
selfTest.a: Section 28.

selfTest.q: 5. Can the spouse against whom a restitution decree was passed seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii)?
selfTest.a: Yes. Either party may petition ( Saroj Rani ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Family Court grant divorce on irretrievable breakdown of marriage?
selfTest.a: No. It is not a ground in the Act; only the Supreme Court can do so under Article 142 ( Shilpa Sailesh ).

hi.inOneMinute: What it is. Divorce ends a valid marriage by a court decree. After it, and after the appeal time, either party may marry again (Section 15). Four routes. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) allows divorce on fault grounds (Section 13(1)), after a failed decree of judicial separation or restitution (Section 13(1A)), on four special grounds for a wife (Section 13(2)), and by mutual consent (Section 13B). Bars. No petition within one year of marriage without leave (Section 14). The petitioner must not take advantage of his or her own wrong, must not have condoned or connived at the fault, and must not collude or delay (Section 23). Mutual consent. Both spouses petition together after living apart for one year; the second motion comes six to eighteen months later; consent must continue till the decree ( Sureshta Devi ); the six months can be waived ( Amardeep Singh ). Irretrievable breakdown. It is not a ground in the Act. Only the Supreme Court can dissolve a marriage on it, under Article 142 ( Shilpa Sailesh , 2023).
legalProvision: Section 13(1), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Divorce. Any marriage solemnized, whether before or after the commencement of this Act, may, on a petition presented by either the husband or the wife, be dissolved by a decree of divorce on the ground that the other party— (i) has, after the solemnization of the marriage, had voluntary sexual intercourse with any person other than his or her spouse; or (ia) has, after the solemnization of the marriage, treated the petitioner with cruelty; or (ib) has deserted the petitioner for a continuous period of not less than two years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition; or (ii) has ceased to be a Hindu by conversion to another religion; or (iii) has been incurably of unsound mind, or has been suffering continuously or intermittently from mental disorder of such a kind and to such an extent that the petitioner cannot reasonably be expected to live with the respondent. … (v) has … been suffering from venereal disease in a communicable form; or (vi) has renounced the world by entering any religious order; or (vii) has not been heard of as being alive for a period of seven years or more by those persons who would naturally have heard of it, had that party been alive.

Section 13B(1). … a petition for dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce may be presented to the district court by both the parties to a marriage together … on the ground that they have been living separately for a period of one year or more, that they have not been able to live together and that they have mutually agreed that the marriage should be dissolved. (2) On the motion of both the parties made not earlier than six months after the date of the presentation of the petition … and not later than eighteen months after the said date, if the petition is not withdrawn in the meantime, the court shall, on being satisfied, after hearing the parties and after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, that a marriage has been solemnised and that the averments in the petition are true, pass a decree of divorce declaring the marriage to be dissolved with effect from the date of the decree.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 13(1A): divorce after a failed decree of judicial separation or restitution. HMA Section 13(2): a wife's four extra grounds. HMA Sections 13A, 14, 15, 16, 21A, 23, 23A, 24 to 28: alternative relief, the one-year bar, remarriage, legitimacy of children, rival petitions, bars to relief, counter-claim, ancillary orders and appeals. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7(1) Explanation (a), 9, 11 and 19. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 27, 27A, 28, 29, 30, 34 and 35. Constitution of India, Article 142(1): the Supreme Court's power to do "complete justice".
hi.meaning:
Divorce is the dissolution of a valid marriage by a decree of the court. It differs from nullity, which declares that no valid marriage existed or annuls a voidable one, and from judicial separation , which keeps the marriage alive. The Act began with the fault theory of divorce : one spouse must prove a matrimonial wrong by the other. Later amendments added divorce after a failed decree (1964 and 1976) and divorce by mutual consent (1976). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Section 13(1): adultery, cruelty, desertion (two years), conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation, presumed death. Section 13(1A): one year without cohabitation or restitution after the earlier decree; either party. Section 13(2): four grounds for a wife. Section 13B: one year apart, two motions, six to eighteen months; waivable; consent must continue. Section 14: one-year bar. Section 23: bars and reconciliation. Irretrievable breakdown: only the Supreme Court, under Article 142. Special Marriage Act, 1954: divorce in Sections 27 and 28; no conversion or renunciation ground, but imprisonment for seven years.

caseLaws.name: Dastane v
caseLaws.facts: Dastane (1975) Facts. Dr. Dastane, married in 1956, sought annulment , divorce or judicial separation. Only judicial separation for cruelty under the old Section 10(1)(b) reached the Supreme Court. Principle. Cruelty is proved on a preponderance of probabilities; danger to life, limb or health is not needed; trivialities are ignored. The wife was cruel, but the husband condoned it and it was not revived. (1975) 2 SCC 326 : AIR 1975 SC 1534. Why it matters. It fixes the standard of proof and the test for cruelty, and shows how condonation bars relief. Savitri Pandey v. Prem Chandra Pandey (2002) Facts. The parties, married on 6 May 1987, lived together only till 21 June 1987. The wife sought divorce for cruelty and desertion. Principle. Neither was proved; desertion needs separation and animus deserendi , and there is no desertion without previous cohabitation; a spouse cannot take advantage of his or her own wrong. Appeals dismissed. (2002) 2 SCC 73 : AIR 2002 SC 591. Why it matters. It states the elements of cruelty and desertion. Shilpa Sailesh (2023) read it down on the Supreme Court's power under Article 142. Sureshta Devi v. Om Prakash (1991) Facts. Married in 1968, the spouses filed a Section 13B petition at Hamirpur on 8 January 1985. On 15 January 1985 the wife applied to withdraw, saying her statement was obtained under pressure. The High Court granted divorce. Principle. Mutual consent must continue till the decree; either party may withdraw it before then. Appeal allowed and the decree set aside. (1991) 2 SCC 25 : AIR 1992 SC 1904. Why it matters. It is the leading case on withdrawal of consent and the meaning of "living separately". Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. The parties married in 1994 and lived apart from 2008. They settled all disputes, including alimony of ₹2.75 crore and custody, and asked to waive the six months. Principle. The six-month period in Section 13B(2) is directory; the court may waive it on four conditions. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It makes the waiting period flexible where the marriage is clearly over and everything is settled. Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. The wife got a consent decree for restitution on 28 March 1978. With no cohabitation for over a year, the husband petitioned for divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii) on 19 April 1979. Principle. Divorce was granted; the consent decree was not collusive and the husband was not taking advantage of his own wrong. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It shows how a failed restitution decree leads to divorce. Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023) Facts. A transfer petition in which the Supreme Court referred questions on its power under Article 142 in matrimonial cases to a Constitution Bench, decided on 1 May 2023. Principle. The Supreme Court may dissolve a marriage on irretrievable breakdown, and may waive the Section 13B procedure on a settlement, but only with great care and caution. [2023] 5 SCR 165. Why it matters. It settles that irretrievable breakdown is a ground only before the Supreme Court, not before trial courts.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the period of desertion required?
selfTest.a: A continuous period of at least two years immediately before the petition.

selfTest.q: 2. Is the six-month period in Section 13B mandatory?
selfTest.a: No. It is directory ( Amardeep Singh ).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a spouse withdraw consent before the decree?
selfTest.a: Yes ( Sureshta Devi ).

selfTest.q: 4. Which section of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides divorce by mutual consent?
selfTest.a: Section 28.

selfTest.q: 5. Can the spouse against whom a restitution decree was passed seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii)?
selfTest.a: Yes. Either party may petition ( Saroj Rani ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Family Court grant divorce on irretrievable breakdown of marriage?
selfTest.a: No. It is not a ground in the Act; only the Supreme Court can do so under Article 142 ( Shilpa Sailesh ).

family-law-i-u3-t8.subtitle: Settlement first: the Family Courts Act, 1984 (jurisdiction, duty to assist settlement, procedure, appeals), Hindu Marriage Act procedure, Order XXXIIA, maintenance and mediation

en.inOneMinute: Aim. The Family Courts Act, 1984 (FCA) provides for Family Courts "with a view to promote conciliation in, and secure speedy settlement of, disputes relating to marriage and family affairs" (long title). Who hears what. A Family Court takes over the matrimonial , family property, maintenance, legitimacy and custody suits of its area, and the maintenance cases of a Magistrate (Sections 7 and 8). Settlement first. It must first try to assist and persuade the parties to settle (Section 9). The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) (Section 23(2)) and Order XXXIIA of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) say the same for other courts. Simple procedure. Hearings in camera on request (Section 11), help of counsellors and experts (Sections 6 and 12), no lawyer as of right (Section 13), flexible evidence (Sections 14 to 16). Appeal. To the High Court within thirty days; none from a consent decree (Section 19).
legalProvision: Section 9, Family Courts Act, 1984. Duty of Family Court to make efforts for settlement. (1) In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding and for this purpose a Family Court may, subject to any rules made by the High Court, follow such procedure as it may deem fit. (2) If, in any suit or proceeding, at any stage, it appears to the Family Court that there is a reasonable possibility of a settlement between the parties, the Family Court may adjourn the proceedings for such period as it thinks fit to enable attempts to be made to effect such a settlement. (3) The power conferred by sub-section (2) shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other power of the Family Court to adjourn the proceedings.

Section 13. Right to legal representation. Notwithstanding anything contained in any law, no party to a suit or proceeding before a Family Court shall be entitled, as of right, to be represented by a legal practitioner: Provided that if the Family Court considers it necessary in the interest of justice, it may seek the assistance of a legal expert as amicus curiae.
The scheme of the Family Courts Act, 1984 (Act 66 of 1984):

Sections 1 and 2: short title, extent, commencement by notification , and definitions. Sections 3 to 6: establishment of Family Courts, Judges, social welfare agencies, counsellors and staff. Sections 7 and 8: jurisdiction , and exclusion of other courts with transfer of pending cases. Sections 9 to 18: settlement, procedure, in camera hearings, experts, lawyers, evidence, judgment and execution. Section 19: appeals and revision. Section 20: overriding effect. Sections 21 to 23: rules.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Sections 3(b), 19, 21A, 21B, 22, 23(2), (3), 24 to 28. CPC Order XXXIIA , Rules 1 to 6. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Section 144 (earlier Chapter IX of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), Section 26. Mediation Act, 2023, Section 7.
en.meaning:
A Family Court is a court established by the State Government under Section 3 of the Family Courts Act, 1984 (Section 2(d)). It is a specialised court for disputes about marriage and family affairs, built around conciliation and speed rather than a contest between lawyers. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. s. 19"] Text description A matrimonial, property, maintenance, legitimacy or custody case arises in an area that has a Family Court. The district court, subordinate civil court and Magistrate cannot hear it (Section 8); it goes to the Family Court (Section 7). The Family Court first assists and persuades the parties to settle, and may adjourn for that (Section 9), with counsellors and experts (Sections 6 and 12). If they settle, a consent decree or order follows and no appeal lies (Section 19(2)). If they do not settle, the court hears the case: in camera if desired (Section 11), no lawyer as of right (Section 13), evidence not bound by the Evidence Act (Sections 14 to 16). It gives a judgment (Section 17). Appeal lies to the High Court within thirty days (Section 19). keyPoints: Family Courts Act, 1984: the aim is conciliation and speedy settlement of marriage and family disputes. Section 3: a Family Court for every city or town above one million people. Section 7: nullity, restitution, judicial separation, divorce, property, injunction, legitimacy, maintenance, guardianship and custody, plus Chapter IX maintenance. Section 9: the Family Court first assists the parties to settle. Section 11: in camera if the Court or either party so desires. Section 13: no lawyer as of right. Section 19: appeal to the High Court within thirty days; none from a consent decree. Section 20: overriding effect. Section 23(2) HMA: the court must try reconciliation. Order XXXIIA Rule 3: assist the parties to settle first. HMA Section 28(4): appeal within ninety days. Mediation Act, Section 7: the parties are not bound to settle.

caseLaws.name: Amardeep Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008 and settled all disputes before the Family Court at Tis Hazari, Delhi. They asked to waive the six-month wait under Section 13B(2). Principle. The period is directory; waiver is allowed only if settlement efforts under Order XXXIIA Rule 3, Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA have failed and the other conditions are met. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It shows that a Family Court's duty to try settlement is a condition the court must check before relaxing the waiting period.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section of the Hindu Marriage Act requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2).

selfTest.q: 2. Which Order of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with suits about the family?
selfTest.a: Order XXXIIA.

selfTest.q: 3. Which section of the Family Courts Act makes the Court assist the parties to settle?
selfTest.a: Section 9. Amardeep Singh names it at para 18, condition (ii).

selfTest.q: 4. What is the time limit to appeal from a Family Court to the High Court?
selfTest.a: Thirty days from the judgment or order (Section 19(3)).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a party entitled to a lawyer as of right before a Family Court?
selfTest.a: No (Section 13). The Court may seek a legal expert as amicus curiae.

selfTest.q: 6. Once a Family Court is set up for an area, can a Magistrate there still hear a maintenance case under Chapter IX?
selfTest.a: No (Section 8(b)). The Family Court hears it (Section 7(2)(a)).
