hi.inOneMinute: Aim. The Family Courts Act, 1984 (FCA) provides for Family Courts "with a view to promote conciliation in, and secure speedy settlement of, disputes relating to marriage and family affairs" (long title). Who hears what. A Family Court takes over the matrimonial , family property, maintenance, legitimacy and custody suits of its area, and the maintenance cases of a Magistrate (Sections 7 and 8). Settlement first. It must first try to assist and persuade the parties to settle (Section 9). The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) (Section 23(2)) and Order XXXIIA of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) say the same for other courts. Simple procedure. Hearings in camera on request (Section 11), help of counsellors and experts (Sections 6 and 12), no lawyer as of right (Section 13), flexible evidence (Sections 14 to 16). Appeal. To the High Court within thirty days; none from a consent decree (Section 19).
legalProvision: Section 9, Family Courts Act, 1984. Duty of Family Court to make efforts for settlement. (1) In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding and for this purpose a Family Court may, subject to any rules made by the High Court, follow such procedure as it may deem fit. (2) If, in any suit or proceeding, at any stage, it appears to the Family Court that there is a reasonable possibility of a settlement between the parties, the Family Court may adjourn the proceedings for such period as it thinks fit to enable attempts to be made to effect such a settlement. (3) The power conferred by sub-section (2) shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other power of the Family Court to adjourn the proceedings.

Section 13. Right to legal representation. Notwithstanding anything contained in any law, no party to a suit or proceeding before a Family Court shall be entitled, as of right, to be represented by a legal practitioner: Provided that if the Family Court considers it necessary in the interest of justice, it may seek the assistance of a legal expert as amicus curiae.
The scheme of the Family Courts Act, 1984 (Act 66 of 1984):

Sections 1 and 2: short title, extent, commencement by notification , and definitions. Sections 3 to 6: establishment of Family Courts, Judges, social welfare agencies, counsellors and staff. Sections 7 and 8: jurisdiction , and exclusion of other courts with transfer of pending cases. Sections 9 to 18: settlement, procedure, in camera hearings, experts, lawyers, evidence, judgment and execution. Section 19: appeals and revision. Section 20: overriding effect. Sections 21 to 23: rules.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Sections 3(b), 19, 21A, 21B, 22, 23(2), (3), 24 to 28. CPC Order XXXIIA , Rules 1 to 6. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Section 144 (earlier Chapter IX of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), Section 26. Mediation Act, 2023, Section 7.

A Family Court is a court established by the State Government under Section 3 of the Family Courts Act, 1984 (Section 2(d)). It is a specialised court for disputes about marriage and family affairs, built around conciliation and speed rather than a contest between lawyers. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. s. 19"] Text description A matrimonial, property, maintenance, legitimacy or custody case arises in an area that has a Family Court. The district court, subordinate civil court and Magistrate cannot hear it (Section 8); it goes to the Family Court (Section 7). The Family Court first assists and persuades the parties to settle, and may adjourn for that (Section 9), with counsellors and experts (Sections 6 and 12). If they settle, a consent decree or order follows and no appeal lies (Section 19(2)). If they do not settle, the court hears the case: in camera if desired (Section 11), no lawyer as of right (Section 13), evidence not bound by the Evidence Act (Sections 14 to 16). It gives a judgment (Section 17). Appeal lies to the High Court within thirty days (Section 19). keyPoints: Family Courts Act, 1984: the aim is conciliation and speedy settlement of marriage and family disputes. Section 3: a Family Court for every city or town above one million people. Section 7: nullity, restitution, judicial separation, divorce, property, injunction, legitimacy, maintenance, guardianship and custody, plus Chapter IX maintenance. Section 9: the Family Court first assists the parties to settle. Section 11: in camera if the Court or either party so desires. Section 13: no lawyer as of right. Section 19: appeal to the High Court within thirty days; none from a consent decree. Section 20: overriding effect. Section 23(2) HMA: the court must try reconciliation. Order XXXIIA Rule 3: assist the parties to settle first. HMA Section 28(4): appeal within ninety days. Mediation Act, Section 7: the parties are not bound to settle.

caseLaws.name: Amardeep Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008 and settled all disputes before the Family Court at Tis Hazari, Delhi. They asked to waive the six-month wait under Section 13B(2). Principle. The period is directory; waiver is allowed only if settlement efforts under Order XXXIIA Rule 3, Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA have failed and the other conditions are met. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It shows that a Family Court's duty to try settlement is a condition the court must check before relaxing the waiting period.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section of the Hindu Marriage Act requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2).

selfTest.q: 2. Which Order of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with suits about the family?
selfTest.a: Order XXXIIA.

selfTest.q: 3. Which section of the Family Courts Act makes the Court assist the parties to settle?
selfTest.a: Section 9. Amardeep Singh names it at para 18, condition (ii).

selfTest.q: 4. What is the time limit to appeal from a Family Court to the High Court?
selfTest.a: Thirty days from the judgment or order (Section 19(3)).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a party entitled to a lawyer as of right before a Family Court?
selfTest.a: No (Section 13). The Court may seek a legal expert as amicus curiae.

selfTest.q: 6. Once a Family Court is set up for an area, can a Magistrate there still hear a maintenance case under Chapter IX?
selfTest.a: No (Section 8(b)). The Family Court hears it (Section 7(2)(a)).

family-law-i-u4-t1.subtitle: Meaning, requisites of a valid adoption, who may give and take, and the effects under the 1956 Act

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Adoption moves a child for good from the family of birth to the adoptive family. From the date of adoption the child is the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes (Section 12, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA)). Four requisites. The taker has the capacity and right to take, the giver has the capacity to give, the child can be adopted, and the other conditions of Chapter II are met (Section 6). Void if the Act is broken. An adoption made in breach of Chapter II is void; it creates no new rights in the adoptive family and takes away none in the family of birth (Section 5). Final. A valid adoption cannot be cancelled, and the child cannot go back to the birth family (Section 15). No payment. Giving or taking payment for an adoption is punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, or fine, or both (Section 17).
legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Requisites of a valid adoption. No adoption shall be valid unless— (i) the person adopting has the capacity, and also the right, to take in adoption; (ii) the person giving in adoption has the capacity to do so; (iii) the person adopted is capable of being taken in adoption; and (iv) the adoption is made in compliance with the other conditions mentioned in this Chapter.

Section 12. Effects of adoption. An adopted child shall be deemed to be the child of his or her adoptive father or mother for all purposes with effect from the date of the adoption and from such date all the ties of the child in the family of his or her birth shall be deemed to be severed and replaced by those created by the adoption in the adoptive family: Provided that— (a) the child cannot marry any person whom he or she could not have married if he or she had continued in the family of his or her birth; (b) any property which vested in the adopted child before the adoption shall continue to vest in such person subject to the obligations, if any, attaching to the ownership of such property, including the obligation to maintain relatives in the family of his or her birth; (c) the adopted child shall not divest any person of any estate which vested in him or her before the adoption.
Chapter II of HAMA ( Adoption ) at a glance:

Section 5: adoption only as Chapter II provides; an adoption in breach is void. Section 6: the four requisites. Sections 7 and 8: capacity of a male and a female Hindu to take in adoption, with the spouse's consent. Section 9: who may give a child in adoption. Section 10: who may be adopted. Section 11: other conditions, including actual giving and taking. Sections 12 to 17: effects, power to dispose of property, adoptive mother, no cancellation, presumption from registered documents, and prohibition of payments.
Other provisions used in this note:

HAMA Sections 2, 3 and 4: who is covered, definitions, overriding effect. Section 30: adoptions before the Act are saved. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act): Sections 2(2), 56, 61 and 63. Guardians and Wards Act, 1890: Sections 24 and 41 (for the contrast with guardianship).
en.meaning:
HAMA does not define adoption. Read together, Sections 6 to 12 show it: adoption is the legal act by which a child is given and taken, with the intent to transfer the child from the family of birth to the adoptive family, so that the child becomes the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes. The JJ Act, which has its own adoption system, defines it in Section 2(2) as "the process through which the adopted child is permanently separated from his biological parents and becomes the lawful child of his adoptive parents with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities that are attached to a biological child". A valid adoption must pass all four requisites of Section 6, one after the other. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Section 5: an adoption in breach of Chapter II is void. Section 6: four requisites. Spouse's consent is needed (Sections 7 and 8), with exceptions. The child must be a Hindu, unmarried, under fifteen and not already adopted, unless custom permits. Giving and taking is essential; datta homam is not. Section 12: an adopted child is the child of the adopters for all purposes. Section 16 only presumes a registered adoption to be valid; registration is not compulsory under the Act. A widow may adopt in her own right (Section 8); the child becomes her late husband's son too ( Sitabai ). The Act does not apply to Scheduled Tribes unless notified (Section 2(2)).

caseLaws.name: Sitabai v
caseLaws.facts: Ramchandra (1969) Facts. Sitabai's husband died in 1930. In March 1958, after the Act, she adopted Suresh Chandra. The question was whether he became a coparcener with her late husband's brother in the joint family property. Principle. Under Sections 11, 12 and 14, a child adopted by a widow is absorbed in the adoptive family to which she belonged and becomes the son of her deceased husband as well. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It explains the effect of Section 12 on adoption by a widow; the boy took the joint family property as sole surviving coparcener. Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963) Facts. A widow claimed that her husband had adopted his elder brother's only son in 1905. No document, invitation or expense entry supported it. Principle. A person who alleges adoption to displace natural succession must prove the fact of adoption and its validity. 1964 AIR 136; [1964] 2 SCR 933. Why it matters. It shows why proof of giving and taking matters; Section 16 now presumes in favour of registered documents. Supriyo v. Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which bars unmarried couples from adopting jointly. Principle. The Chief Justice noted that Section 12 of HAMA and Section 63 of the JJ Act deem an adopted child to be the adopters' child for all purposes (paras 337–338, his opinion). The majority did not strike down Regulation 5(3). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It restates the effect of adoption in Section 12.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the result of an adoption that breaks Chapter II?
selfTest.a: It is void (Section 5).

selfTest.q: 2. Is datta homam essential for a valid adoption?
selfTest.a: No. See the proviso to Section 11.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a valid adoption be cancelled?
selfTest.a: No (Section 15).

selfTest.q: 4. A woman aged 30 wants to adopt a boy aged 10. Is the age-gap rule met?
selfTest.a: No. The gap is 20 years; Section 11(iv) requires at least twenty-one.

selfTest.q: 5. Who gives a child of unknown parentage in adoption?
selfTest.a: The guardian, with the previous permission of the court (Section 9(4)).

selfTest.q: 6. Does the JJ Act, 2015 apply to an adoption made under HAMA?
selfTest.a: No (JJ Act, Section 56(3)).

HAMA అధ్యాయం II (దత్తత) ఒక్క చూపులో:

సెక్షన్ 5: అధ్యాయం II ప్రకారం మాత్రమే దత్తత; ఉల్లంఘించిన దత్తత శూన్యం. సెక్షన్ 6: నాలుగు అవసరాలు. సెక్షన్లు 7, 8: పురుష, స్త్రీ హిందువు దత్తత తీసుకునే సామర్థ్యం, జీవిత భాగస్వామి సమ్మతితో. సెక్షన్ 9: బిడ్డను దత్తతకు ఎవరు ఇవ్వగలరు. సెక్షన్ 10: ఎవరిని దత్తత తీసుకోవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 11: నిజంగా ఇవ్వడం, తీసుకోవడం సహా ఇతర షరతులు. సెక్షన్లు 12 నుంచి 17: ప్రభావాలు, ఆస్తిని అమ్మే లేదా ఇచ్చే అధికారం, దత్తత తల్లి, రద్దు లేదు, రిజిస్టర్డ్ పత్రాలపై ఊహ, డబ్బు చెల్లింపుల నిషేధం.
ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

HAMA సెక్షన్లు 2, 3, 4: ఎవరికి వర్తిస్తుంది, నిర్వచనాలు, ఆధిపత్య ప్రభావం. సెక్షన్ 30: చట్టానికి ముందు దత్తతలు కాపాడబడ్డాయి. బాల న్యాయ (పిల్లల సంరక్షణ, రక్షణ) చట్టం, 2015 (JJ Act): సెక్షన్లు 2(2), 56, 61, 63. సంరక్షకులు, సంరక్షితుల చట్టం, 1890: సెక్షన్లు 24, 41 (సంరక్షకత్వంతో తేడా కోసం).

hi.inOneMinute: What it is. Adoption moves a child for good from the family of birth to the adoptive family. From the date of adoption the child is the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes (Section 12, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA)). Four requisites. The taker has the capacity and right to take, the giver has the capacity to give, the child can be adopted, and the other conditions of Chapter II are met (Section 6). Void if the Act is broken. An adoption made in breach of Chapter II is void; it creates no new rights in the adoptive family and takes away none in the family of birth (Section 5). Final. A valid adoption cannot be cancelled, and the child cannot go back to the birth family (Section 15). No payment. Giving or taking payment for an adoption is punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, or fine, or both (Section 17).
legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Requisites of a valid adoption. No adoption shall be valid unless— (i) the person adopting has the capacity, and also the right, to take in adoption; (ii) the person giving in adoption has the capacity to do so; (iii) the person adopted is capable of being taken in adoption; and (iv) the adoption is made in compliance with the other conditions mentioned in this Chapter.

Section 12. Effects of adoption. An adopted child shall be deemed to be the child of his or her adoptive father or mother for all purposes with effect from the date of the adoption and from such date all the ties of the child in the family of his or her birth shall be deemed to be severed and replaced by those created by the adoption in the adoptive family: Provided that— (a) the child cannot marry any person whom he or she could not have married if he or she had continued in the family of his or her birth; (b) any property which vested in the adopted child before the adoption shall continue to vest in such person subject to the obligations, if any, attaching to the ownership of such property, including the obligation to maintain relatives in the family of his or her birth; (c) the adopted child shall not divest any person of any estate which vested in him or her before the adoption.
Chapter II of HAMA ( Adoption ) at a glance:

Section 5: adoption only as Chapter II provides; an adoption in breach is void. Section 6: the four requisites. Sections 7 and 8: capacity of a male and a female Hindu to take in adoption, with the spouse's consent. Section 9: who may give a child in adoption. Section 10: who may be adopted. Section 11: other conditions, including actual giving and taking. Sections 12 to 17: effects, power to dispose of property, adoptive mother, no cancellation, presumption from registered documents, and prohibition of payments.
Other provisions used in this note:

HAMA Sections 2, 3 and 4: who is covered, definitions, overriding effect. Section 30: adoptions before the Act are saved. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act): Sections 2(2), 56, 61 and 63. Guardians and Wards Act, 1890: Sections 24 and 41 (for the contrast with guardianship).
hi.meaning:
HAMA does not define adoption. Read together, Sections 6 to 12 show it: adoption is the legal act by which a child is given and taken, with the intent to transfer the child from the family of birth to the adoptive family, so that the child becomes the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes. The JJ Act, which has its own adoption system, defines it in Section 2(2) as "the process through which the adopted child is permanently separated from his biological parents and becomes the lawful child of his adoptive parents with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities that are attached to a biological child". A valid adoption must pass all four requisites of Section 6, one after the other. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Section 5: an adoption in breach of Chapter II is void. Section 6: four requisites. Spouse's consent is needed (Sections 7 and 8), with exceptions. The child must be a Hindu, unmarried, under fifteen and not already adopted, unless custom permits. Giving and taking is essential; datta homam is not. Section 12: an adopted child is the child of the adopters for all purposes. Section 16 only presumes a registered adoption to be valid; registration is not compulsory under the Act. A widow may adopt in her own right (Section 8); the child becomes her late husband's son too ( Sitabai ). The Act does not apply to Scheduled Tribes unless notified (Section 2(2)).

caseLaws.name: Sitabai v
caseLaws.facts: Ramchandra (1969) Facts. Sitabai's husband died in 1930. In March 1958, after the Act, she adopted Suresh Chandra. The question was whether he became a coparcener with her late husband's brother in the joint family property. Principle. Under Sections 11, 12 and 14, a child adopted by a widow is absorbed in the adoptive family to which she belonged and becomes the son of her deceased husband as well. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It explains the effect of Section 12 on adoption by a widow; the boy took the joint family property as sole surviving coparcener. Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963) Facts. A widow claimed that her husband had adopted his elder brother's only son in 1905. No document, invitation or expense entry supported it. Principle. A person who alleges adoption to displace natural succession must prove the fact of adoption and its validity. 1964 AIR 136; [1964] 2 SCR 933. Why it matters. It shows why proof of giving and taking matters; Section 16 now presumes in favour of registered documents. Supriyo v. Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which bars unmarried couples from adopting jointly. Principle. The Chief Justice noted that Section 12 of HAMA and Section 63 of the JJ Act deem an adopted child to be the adopters' child for all purposes (paras 337–338, his opinion). The majority did not strike down Regulation 5(3). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It restates the effect of adoption in Section 12.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the result of an adoption that breaks Chapter II?
selfTest.a: It is void (Section 5).

selfTest.q: 2. Is datta homam essential for a valid adoption?
selfTest.a: No. See the proviso to Section 11.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a valid adoption be cancelled?
selfTest.a: No (Section 15).

selfTest.q: 4. A woman aged 30 wants to adopt a boy aged 10. Is the age-gap rule met?
selfTest.a: No. The gap is 20 years; Section 11(iv) requires at least twenty-one.

selfTest.q: 5. Who gives a child of unknown parentage in adoption?
selfTest.a: The guardian, with the previous permission of the court (Section 9(4)).

selfTest.q: 6. Does the JJ Act, 2015 apply to an adoption made under HAMA?
selfTest.a: No (JJ Act, Section 56(3)).

family-law-i-u4-t3.subtitle: Eligibility under section 57 and Regulation 5, the effect of an adoption order and the guidelines noted in Supriyo

en.inOneMinute: Two routes. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA) covers adoption by Hindus. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act) is a separate system for orphan, abandoned and surrendered children, open to people of every religion, with eligibility rules in Section 57 and in Regulation 5 of the Adoption Regulations, 2022. In-country and inter-country. In-country adoption places a child with parents resident in India. Inter-country adoption sends a child from India to parents living abroad; Indian, non-resident Indian and overseas citizen of India parents get priority (Section 59). Who decides. Since the 2021 amendment, the District Magistrate, not a court, issues the adoption order (Section 61). The Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) frames the Regulations and acts as India's Central Authority under the Hague Convention, 1993 (Section 68). History. Bhat J. notes that guidelines pioneered in Laxmi Kant Pandey v. UOI helped inter-country adoptions, and executive instructions filled the vacuum to some extent ( Supriyo , para 25).
legalProvision: Section 57, Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. Eligibility of prospective adoptive parents. (1) The prospective adoptive parents shall be physically fit, financially sound, mentally alert and highly motivated to adopt a child for providing a good upbringing to him. (2) In case of a couple, the consent of both the spouses for the adoption shall be required. (3) A single or divorced person can also adopt, subject to fulfilment of the criteria and in accordance with the provisions of adoption regulations framed by the Authority. (4) A single male is not eligible to adopt a girl child. (5) Any other criteria that may be specified in the adoption regulations framed by the Authority.

Section 59(1). If an orphan or abandoned or surrendered child could not be placed with an Indian or non-resident Indian prospective adoptive parent despite the joint effort of the Specialised Adoption Agency and State Agency within sixty days from the date the child has been declared legally free for adoption, such child shall be free for inter-country adoption: Provided that children with physical and mental disability, siblings and children above five years of age may be given preference over other children for such inter-country adoption, in accordance with the adoption regulations, as may be framed by the Authority.
Other provisions used in this note:

JJ Act Section 2(49): " prospective adoptive parents" means the person or persons eligible to adopt under Section 57. Section 63: an adoption order makes the child the child of the adoptive parents ( Supriyo , Chandrachud CJI, para 337). Sections 2(3) and 68(c): the Authority is CARA, which frames the Adoption Regulations. Sections 35, 38, 56 to 62, 65 to 68, 80 and 101(6): surrender, legal freedom, the adoption scheme, the roles of the Specialised Adoption Agency and the District Magistrate (since the 2021 amendment), CARA, the offence of unlawful adoption and the appeal. Adoption Regulations, 2022 (G.S.R. 726(E), 23 September 2022): principles, eligible children, eligibility, availability, registration, referral, timelines, inter-country steps, relative and step-parent adoption, grievances, and HAMA adoptions that go abroad. Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption, 1993: Articles 1, 2, 4 to 7, 15 to 17, 19, 21, 23, 24 and 32, summarised below.
en.meaning:
Inter-country adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents living in another. In-country adoption is the adoption of a child within India by parents resident in India. Under the JJ Act, "adoption" is the process through which the child is permanently separated from the biological parents and becomes the lawful child of the adoptive parents, with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities of a biological child (Section 2(2)). Eligibility to adopt under the JJ Act is checked in layers: the Act first, then the Regulations. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Two routes: HAMA, 1956 and the JJ Act, 2015. Section 57: eligibility; both spouses consent; a single male cannot adopt a girl. Regulation 5(3): two years of stable marital relationship for couples; Supriyo (3:2) did not read it down. Regulation 5(4): age limits by the child's age; at least twenty-five years' gap. Indians first: sixty days for a child below five, thirty for older children and siblings (Regulation 8; Section 59(1)). The District Magistrate issues the adoption order; appeal to the Divisional Commissioner within thirty days. An adoption order makes the child the adopters' child (Section 63). Bhat J. notes the Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines on inter-country adoption (para 25). The Authority under Section 2(3) is CARA, India's Central Authority under the Hague Convention (Section 68(d)).

caseLaws.name: Supriyo v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which allows a couple to adopt only after two years of stable marital relationship. Principle. By 3:2, the Court did not read down Regulation 5(3). Bhat J. held that Section 57(2) of the Act contemplates joint adoption only by married couples (paras 120–123); the Chief Justice would have read down "marital" (paras 299–317). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's latest word on who may adopt jointly under the Act.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section bars a single male from adopting a girl child?
selfTest.a: Section 57(4).

selfTest.q: 2. What does Section 63 do to an adopted child's status?
selfTest.a: It makes the child the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes, including intestacy ( Supriyo , para 337).

selfTest.q: 3. Which 2023 case decided on joint adoption by unmarried couples?
selfTest.a: Supriyo v. Union of India : by 3:2 the Court did not read down Regulation 5(3).

selfTest.q: 4. A couple's composite age is 98. Can they adopt a child of three?
selfTest.a: No. For a child above two and up to four the limit is 90; they can adopt a child above four and up to eight (limit 100) (Regulation 5(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. When does a normal child below five become available to foreign parents?
selfTest.a: Only after sixty days for Indian, NRI and OCI parents and seven more days for them regardless of seniority (Regulation 8; Section 59(1)).

selfTest.q: 6. Which certificate does CARA issue under Article 23 of the Hague Convention?
selfTest.a: The Conformity Certificate (Regulation 19(1)).

Status today Replaced by the 2015 Guidelines Made under the repealed 2000 Act; superseded by the 2017 Regulations Current; read with the 2015 Act as amended in 2021
Eligibility Guideline 5 follows Section 41(6) of the 2000 Act: an individual irrespective of marital status, or parents adopting a child of the same sex irrespective of living biological children, or a childless couple. Guideline 6 adds two years of stable marital relationship for a couple. Live-in couples not eligible. A single male cannot adopt a girl. Guideline 5: physically, mentally and emotionally stable, financially capable, motivated, no life-threatening medical condition. A single female may adopt a child of any gender; a single male may not adopt a girl. Both spouses consent. Two years of stable marital relationship. Couples with more than four children not considered. Regulation 5: the same core rules on capability, consent, single female, single male and two years of stable marital relationship. A couple with two or more children is considered only for special needs and hard-to-place children, unless relatives or step-parents (Regulation 5(7)).
Age rules Composite age of couple: 90 years for a child of 0 to 3 years and 105 above 3 (Guideline 6(3), (4)). Single parent 30 to 50 years, at most 45 for a child of 0 to 3 (Guideline 6(5)). A table fixes age limits by the age of the child (Guideline 5); its figures are not legible in the copy used. Minimum age gap twenty-five years. Regulation 5(4): composite 85, 90, 100 or 110 years and single 40, 45, 50 or 55 years, by child age bands up to 2, above 2 to 4, above 4 to 8 and above 8 to 18. Gap at least twenty-five years.
Priority Preference to in-country adoption (Guideline 3(b)). In-country to inter-country ratio 80:20 of the total processed annually by a Recognised Indian Placement Agency, excluding special needs children (Guideline 8(5)). Inter-country order: NRI, OCI, PIO, foreign nationals (Guideline 8(6)). Preference to Indian citizens, with regard to the child's socio-cultural environment (Guideline 3(b)). NRIs at par with Indians living in India (Guideline 15). Preference to Indian citizens (Regulation 3(b)). Time windows reserve a child first for resident Indian, NRI and OCI cardholder parents (Regulation 8). NRI and OCI cardholders at par with resident Indians (Regulation 15).
Role of CARA Nodal body; frames rules and guidelines, regulates and monitors adoptions, keeps a database (Guideline 77). Nodal body; frames rules and guidelines, promotes in-country adoption, facilitates inter-State adoption, monitors the programme, issues the No Objection Certificate for inter-country adoption (Guideline 38). The Authority under Section 2(3); frames the Regulations under Section 68(c); issues the No Objection Certificate (Regulation 17(1)) and the Conformity Certificate (Regulation 19(1)).

legalProvision: Section 57, Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. Eligibility of prospective adoptive parents. (1) The prospective adoptive parents shall be physically fit, financially sound, mentally alert and highly motivated to adopt a child for providing a good upbringing to him. (2) In case of a couple, the consent of both the spouses for the adoption shall be required. (3) A single or divorced person can also adopt, subject to fulfilment of the criteria and in accordance with the provisions of adoption regulations framed by the Authority. (4) A single male is not eligible to adopt a girl child. (5) Any other criteria that may be specified in the adoption regulations framed by the Authority.

Section 59(1). If an orphan or abandoned or surrendered child could not be placed with an Indian or non-resident Indian prospective adoptive parent despite the joint effort of the Specialised Adoption Agency and State Agency within sixty days from the date the child has been declared legally free for adoption, such child shall be free for inter-country adoption: Provided that children with physical and mental disability, siblings and children above five years of age may be given preference over other children for such inter-country adoption, in accordance with the adoption regulations, as may be framed by the Authority.

JJ Act సెక్షన్ 2(49): "కాబోయే దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రులు" అంటే సెక్షన్ 57 కింద దత్తతకు అర్హులైన వ్యక్తి లేదా వ్యక్తులు. సెక్షన్ 63: దత్తత ఉత్తర్వు బిడ్డను దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రుల బిడ్డగా చేస్తుంది ( Supriyo , Chandrachud CJI, పేరా 337). సెక్షన్లు 2(3), 68(c): అధికార సంస్థ CARA, అది Adoption Regulations రూపొందిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్లు 35, 38, 56 నుంచి 62, 65 నుంచి 68, 80, 101(6): అప్పగింత, చట్టపరమైన స్వేచ్ఛ, దత్తత పథకం, ప్రత్యేక దత్తత సంస్థ, జిల్లా మేజిస్ట్రేట్ (2021 సవరణ నుంచి) పాత్రలు, CARA, అక్రమ దత్తత నేరం, అప్పీలు. Adoption Regulations, 2022 (G.S.R. 726(E), 23 సెప్టెంబర్ 2022): సూత్రాలు, అర్హులైన పిల్లలు, అర్హత, లభ్యత, రిజిస్ట్రేషన్, రిఫరల్, కాల పరిమితులు, అంతర్ దేశ దశలు, బంధువులు, సవతి తల్లిదండ్రుల దత్తత, ఫిర్యాదులు, విదేశాలకు వెళ్లే HAMA దత్తతలు. అంతర్ దేశ దత్తతపై హేగ్ కన్వెన్షన్, 1993: అధికరణలు 1, 2, 4 నుంచి 7, 15 నుంచి 17, 19, 21, 23, 24, 32, కింద సంక్షిప్తంగా.

అంతర్ దేశ దత్తత అంటే ఒక దేశంలోని బిడ్డను మరో దేశంలో నివసించే తల్లిదండ్రులు దత్తత తీసుకోవడం. దేశంలో దత్తత అంటే భారతదేశంలో నివసించే తల్లిదండ్రులు భారతదేశంలోనే బిడ్డను దత్తత తీసుకోవడం. JJ Act కింద, "దత్తత" అంటే బిడ్డ జీవసంబంధమైన తల్లిదండ్రుల నుంచి శాశ్వతంగా వేరై, జీవసంబంధమైన బిడ్డకు ఉండే అన్ని హక్కులు, ప్రయోజనాలు, బాధ్యతలతో దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రుల చట్టబద్ధమైన బిడ్డ అయ్యే ప్రక్రియ (సెక్షన్ 2(2)). JJ Act కింద దత్తత అర్హతను పొరలుగా చూస్తారు: మొదట చట్టం, తర్వాత Regulations. Diagram 1 చూడండి. Diagram 1. అర్హతను పొరలుగా చూస్తారు: మొదట చట్టం (సెక్షన్ 57), తర్వాత Regulations (Regulation 5); తర్వాత దత్తత ఉత్తర్వు బిడ్డను దత్తత తీసుకున్నవారి బిడ్డగా చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 63). flowchart TD A["వ్యక్తి లేదా జంట

దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రుల బిడ్డ"] వచన వివరణ ప్రారంభం: వ్యక్తి లేదా జంట JJ Act కింద దత్తత తీసుకోవాలనుకుంటున్నారు (సెక్షన్లు 56, 58, 59). సెక్షన్ 57 చూడండి: దృఢత్వం, ఆర్థిక స్థిరత్వం, చురుకుదనం, కోరిక; భార్యాభర్తలు ఇద్దరి సమ్మతి; ఒంటరి పురుషుడు అమ్మాయిని దత్తత తీసుకోలేడు. నెరవేరకపోతే అర్హులు కారు. నెరవేరితే Regulation 5 చూడండి: ఆరోగ్యం, శిక్ష లేకపోవడం; జంటకు రెండేళ్ల స్థిరమైన వైవాహిక సంబంధం; వయసు పరిమితులు, 25 సంవత్సరాల తేడా. నెరవేరకపోతే అర్హులు కారు. నెరవేరితే జిల్లా మేజిస్ట్రేట్ దత్తత ఉత్తర్వు; సెక్షన్ 63 కింద బిడ్డ అన్ని ప్రయోజనాలకూ దత్తత తీసుకున్నవారి బిడ్డ. దశ ప్రశ్న నిబంధన 1 వ్యక్తి లేదా జంట JJ Act కింద దత్తత తీసుకోవాలనుకుంటున్నారా? సెక్షన్లు 56, 58, 59 2 సెక్షన్ 57 లోని లక్షణాలు, భార్యాభర్తలు ఇద్దరి సమ్మతి ఉన్నాయా? సెక్షన్ 57 3 Regulation 5 (ఆరోగ్యం, రికార్డు, వైవాహిక స్థితి, లింగం, వయసు) నెరవేరుతుందా? Regulation 5 ఫలితం దత్తత ఉత్తర్వు బిడ్డను దత్తత తీసుకున్నవారి బిడ్డగా చేస్తుంది సెక్షన్ 63

selfTest.q: 1. ఒంటరి పురుషుడు అమ్మాయిని దత్తత తీసుకోవడాన్ని ఏ సెక్షన్ నిషేధిస్తుంది?
2. దత్తత బిడ్డ హోదాపై సెక్షన్ 63 ఏమి చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: వారసత్వం సహా అన్ని ప్రయోజనాలకూ బిడ్డను దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రుల బిడ్డగా చేస్తుంది ( Supriyo , పేరా 337).

selfTest.q: 3. పెళ్లికాని జంటల ఉమ్మడి దత్తతపై ఏ 2023 కేసు నిర్ణయించింది?
selfTest.a: Supriyo v. Union of India : 3:2 తో కోర్టు Regulation 5(3) ను పరిమితం చేసి చదవలేదు.

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక జంట ఉమ్మడి వయసు 98. వారు మూడేళ్ల బిడ్డను దత్తత తీసుకోవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. 2 పైన 4 వరకు బిడ్డకు పరిమితి 90; వారు 4 పైన 8 వరకు బిడ్డను దత్తత తీసుకోవచ్చు (పరిమితి 100) (Regulation 5(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. ఐదేళ్ల లోపు సాధారణ బిడ్డ విదేశీ తల్లిదండ్రులకు ఎప్పుడు అందుబాటులోకి వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: భారతీయ, NRI, OCI తల్లిదండ్రులకు అరవై రోజులు, సీనియారిటీతో సంబంధం లేకుండా వారికే మరో ఏడు రోజుల తర్వాత మాత్రమే (Regulation 8; సెక్షన్ 59(1)).

selfTest.q: 6. హేగ్ కన్వెన్షన్ అధికరణ 23 కింద CARA ఏ సర్టిఫికెట్ జారీ చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: అనుగుణత సర్టిఫికెట్ (Conformity Certificate) (Regulation 19(1)).

hi.inOneMinute: Two routes. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA) covers adoption by Hindus. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act) is a separate system for orphan, abandoned and surrendered children, open to people of every religion, with eligibility rules in Section 57 and in Regulation 5 of the Adoption Regulations, 2022. In-country and inter-country. In-country adoption places a child with parents resident in India. Inter-country adoption sends a child from India to parents living abroad; Indian, non-resident Indian and overseas citizen of India parents get priority (Section 59). Who decides. Since the 2021 amendment, the District Magistrate, not a court, issues the adoption order (Section 61). The Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) frames the Regulations and acts as India's Central Authority under the Hague Convention, 1993 (Section 68). History. Bhat J. notes that guidelines pioneered in Laxmi Kant Pandey v. UOI helped inter-country adoptions, and executive instructions filled the vacuum to some extent ( Supriyo , para 25).
legalProvision: Section 57, Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. Eligibility of prospective adoptive parents. (1) The prospective adoptive parents shall be physically fit, financially sound, mentally alert and highly motivated to adopt a child for providing a good upbringing to him. (2) In case of a couple, the consent of both the spouses for the adoption shall be required. (3) A single or divorced person can also adopt, subject to fulfilment of the criteria and in accordance with the provisions of adoption regulations framed by the Authority. (4) A single male is not eligible to adopt a girl child. (5) Any other criteria that may be specified in the adoption regulations framed by the Authority.

Section 59(1). If an orphan or abandoned or surrendered child could not be placed with an Indian or non-resident Indian prospective adoptive parent despite the joint effort of the Specialised Adoption Agency and State Agency within sixty days from the date the child has been declared legally free for adoption, such child shall be free for inter-country adoption: Provided that children with physical and mental disability, siblings and children above five years of age may be given preference over other children for such inter-country adoption, in accordance with the adoption regulations, as may be framed by the Authority.
Other provisions used in this note:

JJ Act Section 2(49): " prospective adoptive parents" means the person or persons eligible to adopt under Section 57. Section 63: an adoption order makes the child the child of the adoptive parents ( Supriyo , Chandrachud CJI, para 337). Sections 2(3) and 68(c): the Authority is CARA, which frames the Adoption Regulations. Sections 35, 38, 56 to 62, 65 to 68, 80 and 101(6): surrender, legal freedom, the adoption scheme, the roles of the Specialised Adoption Agency and the District Magistrate (since the 2021 amendment), CARA, the offence of unlawful adoption and the appeal. Adoption Regulations, 2022 (G.S.R. 726(E), 23 September 2022): principles, eligible children, eligibility, availability, registration, referral, timelines, inter-country steps, relative and step-parent adoption, grievances, and HAMA adoptions that go abroad. Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption, 1993: Articles 1, 2, 4 to 7, 15 to 17, 19, 21, 23, 24 and 32, summarised below.
hi.meaning:
Inter-country adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents living in another. In-country adoption is the adoption of a child within India by parents resident in India. Under the JJ Act, "adoption" is the process through which the child is permanently separated from the biological parents and becomes the lawful child of the adoptive parents, with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities of a biological child (Section 2(2)). Eligibility to adopt under the JJ Act is checked in layers: the Act first, then the Regulations. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Two routes: HAMA, 1956 and the JJ Act, 2015. Section 57: eligibility; both spouses consent; a single male cannot adopt a girl. Regulation 5(3): two years of stable marital relationship for couples; Supriyo (3:2) did not read it down. Regulation 5(4): age limits by the child's age; at least twenty-five years' gap. Indians first: sixty days for a child below five, thirty for older children and siblings (Regulation 8; Section 59(1)). The District Magistrate issues the adoption order; appeal to the Divisional Commissioner within thirty days. An adoption order makes the child the adopters' child (Section 63). Bhat J. notes the Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines on inter-country adoption (para 25). The Authority under Section 2(3) is CARA, India's Central Authority under the Hague Convention (Section 68(d)).

caseLaws.name: Supriyo v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which allows a couple to adopt only after two years of stable marital relationship. Principle. By 3:2, the Court did not read down Regulation 5(3). Bhat J. held that Section 57(2) of the Act contemplates joint adoption only by married couples (paras 120–123); the Chief Justice would have read down "marital" (paras 299–317). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's latest word on who may adopt jointly under the Act.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section bars a single male from adopting a girl child?
selfTest.a: Section 57(4).

selfTest.q: 2. What does Section 63 do to an adopted child's status?
selfTest.a: It makes the child the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes, including intestacy ( Supriyo , para 337).

selfTest.q: 3. Which 2023 case decided on joint adoption by unmarried couples?
selfTest.a: Supriyo v. Union of India : by 3:2 the Court did not read down Regulation 5(3).

selfTest.q: 4. A couple's composite age is 98. Can they adopt a child of three?
selfTest.a: No. For a child above two and up to four the limit is 90; they can adopt a child above four and up to eight (limit 100) (Regulation 5(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. When does a normal child below five become available to foreign parents?
selfTest.a: Only after sixty days for Indian, NRI and OCI parents and seven more days for them regardless of seniority (Regulation 8; Section 59(1)).

selfTest.q: 6. Which certificate does CARA issue under Article 23 of the Hague Convention?
selfTest.a: The Conformity Certificate (Regulation 19(1)).

family-law-i-u4-t2.subtitle: From custom and personal law to the 1956 Act and the Juvenile Justice Act, as recorded in the Act and in Supriyo

en.inOneMinute: Classical law. Hindu adoption came from the texts, two special works (the Dattaka Mimamsa and the Dattaka Chandrika), and custom and usage . Its objects were religious (a son to offer funeral cakes and water) and secular (an heir) (Mulla, Section 447). Only a boy could be adopted, and a woman could not adopt to herself. The 1956 Act. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA) put Hindu adoption into a statute. It ends any old text, rule, interpretation, custom or usage on a matter it covers (Section 4), allows a son or a daughter to be adopted, and saves adoptions made before it (Section 30). Other children. Court guidelines on inter-country adoption ( Laxmi Kant Pandey ) came first, then executive instructions, then the Juvenile Justice Act, which enables adoption among members of all faiths and communities ( Supriyo , Bhat J., para 25). Today. The Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, as amended in 2021, with the Adoption Regulations, 2022, governs adoption outside HAMA; the District Magistrate issues the adoption order.
legalProvision: Section 4, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to apply to Hindus in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 30. Savings. Nothing contained in this Act shall affect any adoption made before the commencement of this Act, and the validity and effect of any such adoption shall be determined as if this Act had not been passed.
Other provisions used in this note:

HAMA, Chapter II (Sections 5 to 17): the statutory law of Hindu adoption . HAMA Section 3(a): "custom" and "usage" mean a rule continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, which has obtained the force of law among Hindus in a local area, tribe, community, group or family. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act): Sections 2(2), 56, 63, 68(c), 101(6), (7) and 111(1). Supriyo records Section 63 (Chandrachud CJI, para 337). Bhat J. refers to Section 41 of the Juvenile Justice Act (Section 41 of the 2000 Act), which enables adoption among members of all faiths and communities (para 25). Guardians and Wards Act, 1890: Section 7.
en.meaning:
The historical perspective traces how the law of adoption moved from old texts, custom and usage to a statute for Hindus, and then to a law open to members of all faiths. The classical rules are those described in Mulla's Principles of Hindu Law (14th edition); the modern rules are in HAMA and the JJ Act. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Hindu adoption moved from texts and custom to the 1956 Act; adoption for all faiths moved from court guidelines to the Juvenile Justice Act. flowchart TD A["Before 1956

District Magistrate orders"] Text description Before 1956: texts, the Dattaka Mimamsa and Dattaka Chandrika, custom and usage; dattaka and kritrima forms. Branch one, for Hindus: the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (Sections 4 and 30), amended in 1962 and 2010. Branch two, for all faiths: Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines and executive instructions; the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000 with the 2011 and 2015 Guidelines; the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 with the 2017 Regulations; the 2021 amendment and the 2022 Regulations, with the District Magistrate issuing orders. Stage Source of law What it allowed Before 1956 Texts, the Dattaka Mimamsa and Dattaka Chandrika, custom and usage Adoption of a boy, mainly in the dattaka form; kritrima in Mithila 1956 HAMA, Chapter II Adoption of a son or a daughter by a Hindu man or woman From 1984 Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines, then executive instructions Inter-country adoption under court supervision 2000 to now JJ Act 2000, then JJ Act 2015 (amended 2021); CARA Guidelines and Regulations Adoption among members of all faiths and communities
keyPoints: Classical objects: religious (funeral offerings) and secular (an heir) (Mulla, Section 447). Dattaka prevailed all over India; kritrima in Mithila. Classical law: only a boy, of the same caste; a woman could not adopt to herself in dattaka form. Section 4: old texts, rules, interpretations, custom and usage cease on matters the Act covers. HAMA: statutory adoption of sons and daughters; Section 12 gives full status. Section 30 saves adoptions made before the Act. Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines on inter-country adoption (noted in Supriyo , para 25). Juvenile Justice Act: adoption among members of all faiths and communities (Bhat J., para 25). Shabnam Hashmi : the right to adopt was not raised to a fundamental right (quoted in Supriyo , para 307). Since 2021 the District Magistrate issues JJ Act adoption orders; the Adoption Regulations, 2022 are current.

caseLaws.name: Supriyo v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which bars unmarried couples from adopting jointly. Principle. Bhat J. traced the law: court guidelines on inter-country adoption, then executive instructions, then the Juvenile Justice Act for all faiths (para 25). The Court also quoted Shabnam Hashmi (Chandrachud CJI, paras 307–308). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It records the route open to all faiths in the Supreme Court's own words. Sitabai v. Ramchandra (1969) Facts. A widow whose husband had died in 1930 adopted a son in March 1958, after HAMA. Principle. Under Sections 11, 12 and 14, the adopted child is absorbed in the adoptive family and becomes her deceased husband's son too. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It shows the full status HAMA gives to an adopted child, even through a widow, which classical law in Mithila would have denied.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 4 of HAMA do to old texts and custom?
selfTest.a: They cease to have effect on any matter for which the Act makes provision.

selfTest.q: 2. Which Act made Hindu adoption statutory?
selfTest.a: The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case pioneered the guidelines for inter-country adoption?
selfTest.a: Laxmi Kant Pandey v. Union of India , as noted in Supriyo v. Union of India (para 25, Bhat J.).

selfTest.q: 4. Could a widow in Mithila adopt under classical law?
selfTest.a: No, not even with her husband's express authority (Mulla, Section 452(1)).

selfTest.q: 5. Which form of adoption let a woman adopt a son to herself?
selfTest.a: The kritrima form (Mulla, Section 515).

selfTest.q: 6. Who now issues an adoption order under the JJ Act, and where does an appeal lie?
selfTest.a: The District Magistrate; an appeal lies to the Divisional Commissioner within thirty days (Section 101(6)).

selfTest.q: 2. హిందూ దత్తతను శాసనంగా మార్చిన చట్టం ఏది?
selfTest.a: హిందూ దత్తత, భరణ చట్టం, 1956.

selfTest.q: 3. అంతర్ దేశ దత్తతకు మార్గదర్శకాలను మొదట రూపొందించిన కేసు ఏది?

selfTest.a: లేదు, భర్త స్పష్టమైన అధికారం ఉన్నా కాదు (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 452(1)).

selfTest.q: 5. ఏ రూపం స్త్రీ తనకు తానే కొడుకును దత్తత తీసుకోవడానికి అనుమతించింది?
selfTest.a: కృత్రిమ రూపం (ముల్లా, సెక్షన్ 515).

selfTest.q: 6. ఇప్పుడు JJ Act కింద దత్తత ఉత్తర్వు ఎవరు ఇస్తారు, అప్పీలు ఎక్కడికి?

hi.inOneMinute: Classical law. Hindu adoption came from the texts, two special works (the Dattaka Mimamsa and the Dattaka Chandrika), and custom and usage . Its objects were religious (a son to offer funeral cakes and water) and secular (an heir) (Mulla, Section 447). Only a boy could be adopted, and a woman could not adopt to herself. The 1956 Act. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA) put Hindu adoption into a statute. It ends any old text, rule, interpretation, custom or usage on a matter it covers (Section 4), allows a son or a daughter to be adopted, and saves adoptions made before it (Section 30). Other children. Court guidelines on inter-country adoption ( Laxmi Kant Pandey ) came first, then executive instructions, then the Juvenile Justice Act, which enables adoption among members of all faiths and communities ( Supriyo , Bhat J., para 25). Today. The Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, as amended in 2021, with the Adoption Regulations, 2022, governs adoption outside HAMA; the District Magistrate issues the adoption order.
legalProvision: Section 4, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to apply to Hindus in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 30. Savings. Nothing contained in this Act shall affect any adoption made before the commencement of this Act, and the validity and effect of any such adoption shall be determined as if this Act had not been passed.
Other provisions used in this note:

HAMA, Chapter II (Sections 5 to 17): the statutory law of Hindu adoption . HAMA Section 3(a): "custom" and "usage" mean a rule continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, which has obtained the force of law among Hindus in a local area, tribe, community, group or family. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act): Sections 2(2), 56, 63, 68(c), 101(6), (7) and 111(1). Supriyo records Section 63 (Chandrachud CJI, para 337). Bhat J. refers to Section 41 of the Juvenile Justice Act (Section 41 of the 2000 Act), which enables adoption among members of all faiths and communities (para 25). Guardians and Wards Act, 1890: Section 7.
hi.meaning:
The historical perspective traces how the law of adoption moved from old texts, custom and usage to a statute for Hindus, and then to a law open to members of all faiths. The classical rules are those described in Mulla's Principles of Hindu Law (14th edition); the modern rules are in HAMA and the JJ Act. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Branch one, for Hindus: the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (Sections 4 and 30), amended in 1962 and 2010. Branch two, for all faiths: Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines and executive instructions; the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000 with the 2011 and 2015 Guidelines; the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 with the 2017 Regulations; the 2021 amendment and the 2022 Regulations, with the District Magistrate issuing orders. keyPoints: Classical objects: religious (funeral offerings) and secular (an heir) (Mulla, Section 447). Dattaka prevailed all over India; kritrima in Mithila. Classical law: only a boy, of the same caste; a woman could not adopt to herself in dattaka form. Section 4: old texts, rules, interpretations, custom and usage cease on matters the Act covers. HAMA: statutory adoption of sons and daughters; Section 12 gives full status. Section 30 saves adoptions made before the Act. Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines on inter-country adoption (noted in Supriyo , para 25). Juvenile Justice Act: adoption among members of all faiths and communities (Bhat J., para 25). Shabnam Hashmi : the right to adopt was not raised to a fundamental right (quoted in Supriyo , para 307). Since 2021 the District Magistrate issues JJ Act adoption orders; the Adoption Regulations, 2022 are current.

caseLaws.name: Supriyo v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which bars unmarried couples from adopting jointly. Principle. Bhat J. traced the law: court guidelines on inter-country adoption, then executive instructions, then the Juvenile Justice Act for all faiths (para 25). The Court also quoted Shabnam Hashmi (Chandrachud CJI, paras 307–308). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It records the route open to all faiths in the Supreme Court's own words. Sitabai v. Ramchandra (1969) Facts. A widow whose husband had died in 1930 adopted a son in March 1958, after HAMA. Principle. Under Sections 11, 12 and 14, the adopted child is absorbed in the adoptive family and becomes her deceased husband's son too. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It shows the full status HAMA gives to an adopted child, even through a widow, which classical law in Mithila would have denied.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 4 of HAMA do to old texts and custom?
selfTest.a: They cease to have effect on any matter for which the Act makes provision.

selfTest.q: 2. Which Act made Hindu adoption statutory?
selfTest.a: The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case pioneered the guidelines for inter-country adoption?
selfTest.a: Laxmi Kant Pandey v. Union of India , as noted in Supriyo v. Union of India (para 25, Bhat J.).

selfTest.q: 4. Could a widow in Mithila adopt under classical law?
selfTest.a: No, not even with her husband's express authority (Mulla, Section 452(1)).

selfTest.q: 5. Which form of adoption let a woman adopt a son to herself?
selfTest.a: The kritrima form (Mulla, Section 515).

selfTest.q: 6. Who now issues an adoption order under the JJ Act, and where does an appeal lie?
selfTest.a: The District Magistrate; an appeal lies to the Divisional Commissioner within thirty days (Section 101(6)).

family-law-i-u4-t4.subtitle: Who can claim maintenance under the 1956 Act and other laws, and how the amount is fixed

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Maintenance is the support that the law makes one person pay to another. Under Chapter III (Sections 18 to 28) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA), a Hindu wife, a widowed daughter-in-law, children, aged or infirm parents and certain dependants of a dead person can claim it. How much. The court fixes the amount by the status of the parties, the claimant's reasonable wants and means, and the other factors in Section 23. A claimant who ceases to be a Hindu by conversion loses the claim under this Act (Section 24). Other laws. Maintenance is also given by Sections 24 and 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (in matrimonial cases), by Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which takes the place of Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. Nature. In V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy the Supreme Court held that a Hindu woman's right to maintenance is a pre-existing right , not a mere gift.
legalProvision: Section 3(b), Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. "maintenance" includes― (i) in all cases, provision for food, clothing, residence, education and medical attendance and treatment; (ii) in the case of an unmarried daughter, also the reasonable expenses of and incident to her marriage;

Section 18(1). Subject to the provisions of this section, a Hindu wife, whether married before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be entitled to be maintained by her husband during her life time.
Section 22(1). Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), the heirs of a deceased Hindu are bound to maintain the dependants of the deceased out of the estate inherited by them from the deceased.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 18(2) and (3): the wife's right to live separately without losing maintenance, and when she loses it. Section 19: widowed daughter-in-law, from her father-in-law. Section 20: children and aged or infirm parents. Sections 21 and 22: the nine classes of dependants, and the heirs' duty. Sections 23 to 28: amount; claimant must be a Hindu; alteration; debts first; charge only if created; transfer of the estate. Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Sections 24 and 25: maintenance pendente lite and permanent alimony . BNSS, Sections 144 to 147: maintenance of wives, children and parents by order of a Magistrate; Section 531 repeals the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Sections 2(a), 2(b), 2(f), 12, 17, 20 to 23, 26 and 36.
en.meaning:
Maintenance is the provision of the basic needs of a person who cannot meet them, by a person whom the law binds to provide them. Section 3(b) says it includes food, clothing, residence, education, and medical attendance and treatment, and for an unmarried daughter also the reasonable expenses of her marriage. Under the Act it is a personal obligation of a living person (wife, widowed daughter-in-law, children, parents), and for dependants an obligation of the heirs, payable out of the estate they inherit. A dependant's claim is a charge on the estate only if one is created (Section 27). Who can claim under the 1956 Act. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Chapter III of the 1956 Act groups claimants by who must pay: a living person, or the heirs out of a dead person's estate. flowchart TD A["Maintenance under Chapter III
HAMA, 1956"] --> L["From a living person"] A --> D["From the estate of a dead person"] L --> L1["Wife, from husband
s. 18"] L --> L2["Widowed daughter-in-law,
from father-in-law, s. 19"] L --> L3["Children and aged or
infirm parents, s. 20"] D --> D1["Nine classes of dependants
from the heirs, ss. 21 and 22"] L1 --> C["Common rules, ss. 23 to 28
amount, Hindu claimant, alteration,
debts, charge, transfer"] L2 --> C L3 --> C D1 --> C Text description Top: maintenance under Chapter III of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Branch one, from a living person: wife from husband (Section 18); widowed daughter-in-law from father-in-law (Section 19); children and aged or infirm parents (Section 20). Branch two, from the estate of a dead person: the nine classes of dependants, from the heirs (Sections 21 and 22). Common rules for both: Sections 23 to 28. Who pays Who can claim Section A living husband His wife 18 A living father-in-law His widowed daughter-in-law 19 A living Hindu His or her children and aged or infirm parents 20 The heirs of a dead Hindu, out of the estate The dead person's dependants 21 and 22
keyPoints: Section 3(b): food, clothing, residence, education, medical care; for an unmarried daughter, marriage expenses. Section 18: wife; may live apart for justified reasons; loses it if unchaste or she converts. Section 19: widowed daughter-in-law, from the father-in-law; ends on remarriage. Section 20: children (while minors) and aged or infirm parents; includes a childless step-mother. Sections 21 and 22: nine classes of dependants; heirs pay out of the estate, in proportion to their shares. Section 23: factors for the amount. Section 24: claimant must be a Hindu. Section 27: a dependant's claim is a charge only if created. Section 28: enforceable against a transferee with notice or a donee. Section 144 BNSS speaks of "any person having sufficient means"; a Magistrate of the first class orders a monthly allowance and may order interim maintenance. Hindu Marriage Act Sections 24 and 25: interim and permanent maintenance between spouses. Tulasamma : maintenance is a pre-existing right.

caseLaws.name: Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v
caseLaws.facts: Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week and claimed maintenance as his wife under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Principle. The marriage was void under Sections 5(i) and 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, a complete nullity, so she was not a "wife" under Section 125. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. The claim to maintenance as a wife depends on a valid marriage. Chanmuniya v. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha (2010) Facts. A widow said she was married by Katha and Sindur to her late husband's younger brother; the High Court held that the essentials of marriage were not performed. Principle. The two-Judge Bench favoured a broad meaning of "wife" in Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but could not depart from earlier two-Judge decisions, and referred three questions to a larger Bench. (2011) 1 SCC 141. Why it matters. It is a reference order, not a final ruling, and shows the debate on who is a wife for maintenance. D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010) Facts. A woman claimed maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as the appellant 's wife; he said he was already married to Lakshmi in 1980. Principle. A relationship in the nature of marriage under the Domestic Violence Act is akin to a common law marriage and needs four conditions and a shared household; the case went back to the Family Court. (2010) 10 SCC 469. Why it matters. It extends relief to women in relationships in the nature of marriage, but not to every live-in relationship. Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013) Facts. From 1992 an unmarried woman lived with a married man who had two children; she knew of his marriage and later claimed relief, including maintenance, under the Domestic Violence Act. Principle. The Court gave eight guidelines and held that her relationship was not in the nature of marriage, so she was not in a "domestic relationship"; the appeal was dismissed, and the Court asked Parliament to legislate. Decided 26 November 2013. Why it matters. It sets limits on maintenance claims by live-in partners. V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) Facts. A widow, whose husband died in 1931 in a joint family, got a decree for maintenance; in execution, a compromise gave her properties for her life in lieu of maintenance. Principle. Her right to maintenance is a pre-existing right in property; property given in lieu of it falls under Section 14(1), not 14(2), of the Hindu Succession Act, so she became full owner. AIR 1977 SC 1944 : (1977) 3 SCC 99. Why it matters. It shows maintenance as a real right in Hindu law that can ripen into ownership.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section gives a Hindu wife maintenance from her husband?
selfTest.a: Section 18.

selfTest.q: 2. Is a dependant's claim a charge on the estate?
selfTest.a: Not unless one is created by will, decree, agreement or otherwise (Section 27).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a person who converts claim under the 1956 Act?
selfTest.a: No (Section 24).

selfTest.q: 4. Two heirs take ₹12,00,000 and ₹4,00,000 of an estate. Maintenance of a dependant is fixed at ₹8,000 a month. How much does each pay?
selfTest.a: In proportion to their shares (Section 22(3)): the heir with ₹12,00,000 holds three-quarters of ₹16,00,000 and pays ₹6,000; the heir with ₹4,00,000 holds one-quarter and pays ₹2,000.

selfTest.q: 5. Within what time must an application to levy unpaid maintenance under Section 144 of the BNSS be made?
selfTest.a: Within one year from the date the amount became due (proviso to Section 144(3)).

selfTest.q: 6. In Tulasamma , why did the widow become full owner of property given in lieu of maintenance?
selfTest.a: Because her right to maintenance was a pre-existing right, so Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act applied, not Section 14(2).

భరణం అంటే తమ ప్రాథమిక అవసరాలు తీర్చుకోలేని వ్యక్తికి, వాటిని అందించాలని చట్టం బాధ్యత పెట్టిన వ్యక్తి అందించడం. ఆహారం, దుస్తులు, నివాసం, విద్య, వైద్య సంరక్షణ, చికిత్స, పెళ్లికాని కూతురికి ఆమె పెళ్లి సహేతుక ఖర్చులు కూడా ఇందులో ఉంటాయని సెక్షన్ 3(b) చెబుతుంది. చట్టం కింద ఇది జీవించి ఉన్న వ్యక్తి వ్యక్తిగత బాధ్యత (భార్య, వితంతువైన కోడలు, పిల్లలు, తల్లిదండ్రులు), ఆశ్రితుల విషయంలో వారసులు పొందిన ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లించాల్సిన బాధ్యత. ఆశ్రితుడి దావా సృష్టిస్తేనే ఆస్తిపై భారం అవుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 27). 1956 చట్టం కింద ఎవరు దావా వేయవచ్చు. selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 18.

selfTest.q: 2. ఆశ్రితుడి దావా ఆస్తిపై భారమా?
selfTest.a: వీలునామా, డిక్రీ, ఒప్పందం, లేదా మరో విధంగా సృష్టిస్తే తప్ప కాదు (సెక్షన్ 27).

selfTest.q: 3. మతం మారిన వ్యక్తి 1956 చట్టం కింద దావా వేయవచ్చా?
4. ఇద్దరు వారసులు ఆస్తిలో ₹12,00,000 మరియు ₹4,00,000 తీసుకుంటారు. ఒక ఆశ్రితుడి భరణం నెలకు ₹8,000 గా నిర్ణయించారు. ప్రతి ఒక్కరూ ఎంత చెల్లిస్తారు?
5. BNSS సెక్షన్ 144 కింద చెల్లించని భరణం వసూలుకు ఎంత సమయంలో దరఖాస్తు చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: మొత్తం బకాయి అయిన తేదీ నుంచి ఒక సంవత్సరంలో (సెక్షన్ 144(3) నిబంధన).

selfTest.q: 6. Tulasamma లో భరణానికి బదులుగా ఇచ్చిన ఆస్తికి వితంతువు పూర్తి యజమాని ఎందుకు అయింది?
selfTest.a: ఆమె భరణ హక్కు ముందే ఉన్న హక్కు కాబట్టి, హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 14(2) కాదు, సెక్షన్ 14(1) వర్తించింది.

hi.inOneMinute: What it is. Maintenance is the support that the law makes one person pay to another. Under Chapter III (Sections 18 to 28) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA), a Hindu wife, a widowed daughter-in-law, children, aged or infirm parents and certain dependants of a dead person can claim it. How much. The court fixes the amount by the status of the parties, the claimant's reasonable wants and means, and the other factors in Section 23. A claimant who ceases to be a Hindu by conversion loses the claim under this Act (Section 24). Other laws. Maintenance is also given by Sections 24 and 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (in matrimonial cases), by Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which takes the place of Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. Nature. In V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy the Supreme Court held that a Hindu woman's right to maintenance is a pre-existing right , not a mere gift.
legalProvision: Section 3(b), Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. "maintenance" includes― (i) in all cases, provision for food, clothing, residence, education and medical attendance and treatment; (ii) in the case of an unmarried daughter, also the reasonable expenses of and incident to her marriage;

Section 18(1). Subject to the provisions of this section, a Hindu wife, whether married before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be entitled to be maintained by her husband during her life time.
Section 22(1). Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), the heirs of a deceased Hindu are bound to maintain the dependants of the deceased out of the estate inherited by them from the deceased.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 18(2) and (3): the wife's right to live separately without losing maintenance, and when she loses it. Section 19: widowed daughter-in-law, from her father-in-law. Section 20: children and aged or infirm parents. Sections 21 and 22: the nine classes of dependants, and the heirs' duty. Sections 23 to 28: amount; claimant must be a Hindu; alteration; debts first; charge only if created; transfer of the estate. Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Sections 24 and 25: maintenance pendente lite and permanent alimony . BNSS, Sections 144 to 147: maintenance of wives, children and parents by order of a Magistrate; Section 531 repeals the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Sections 2(a), 2(b), 2(f), 12, 17, 20 to 23, 26 and 36.
hi.meaning:
Maintenance is the provision of the basic needs of a person who cannot meet them, by a person whom the law binds to provide them. Section 3(b) says it includes food, clothing, residence, education, and medical attendance and treatment, and for an unmarried daughter also the reasonable expenses of her marriage. Under the Act it is a personal obligation of a living person (wife, widowed daughter-in-law, children, parents), and for dependants an obligation of the heirs, payable out of the estate they inherit. A dependant's claim is a charge on the estate only if one is created (Section 27). Who can claim under the 1956 Act. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Chapter III of the 1956 Act groups claimants by who must pay: a living person, or the heirs out of a dead person's estate. flowchart TD A["Maintenance under Chapter III
HAMA, 1956"] --> L["From a living person"] A --> D["From the estate of a dead person"] L --> L1["Wife, from husband
s. 18"] L --> L2["Widowed daughter-in-law,
from father-in-law, s. 19"] L --> L3["Children and aged or
infirm parents, s. 20"] D --> D1["Nine classes of dependants
from the heirs, ss. 21 and 22"] L1 --> C["Common rules, ss. 23 to 28
amount, Hindu claimant, alteration,
debts, charge, transfer"] L2 --> C L3 --> C D1 --> C Text description Top: maintenance under Chapter III of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Branch one, from a living person: wife from husband (Section 18); widowed daughter-in-law from father-in-law (Section 19); children and aged or infirm parents (Section 20). Branch two, from the estate of a dead person: the nine classes of dependants, from the heirs (Sections 21 and 22). Common rules for both: Sections 23 to 28. Who pays Who can claim Section A living husband His wife 18 A living father-in-law His widowed daughter-in-law 19 A living Hindu His or her children and aged or infirm parents 20 The heirs of a dead Hindu, out of the estate The dead person's dependants 21 and 22
keyPoints: Section 3(b): food, clothing, residence, education, medical care; for an unmarried daughter, marriage expenses. Section 18: wife; may live apart for justified reasons; loses it if unchaste or she converts. Section 19: widowed daughter-in-law, from the father-in-law; ends on remarriage. Section 20: children (while minors) and aged or infirm parents; includes a childless step-mother. Sections 21 and 22: nine classes of dependants; heirs pay out of the estate, in proportion to their shares. Section 23: factors for the amount. Section 24: claimant must be a Hindu. Section 27: a dependant's claim is a charge only if created. Section 28: enforceable against a transferee with notice or a donee. Section 144 BNSS speaks of "any person having sufficient means"; a Magistrate of the first class orders a monthly allowance and may order interim maintenance. Hindu Marriage Act Sections 24 and 25: interim and permanent maintenance between spouses. Tulasamma : maintenance is a pre-existing right.

caseLaws.name: Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v
caseLaws.facts: Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week and claimed maintenance as his wife under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Principle. The marriage was void under Sections 5(i) and 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, a complete nullity, so she was not a "wife" under Section 125. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. The claim to maintenance as a wife depends on a valid marriage. Chanmuniya v. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha (2010) Facts. A widow said she was married by Katha and Sindur to her late husband's younger brother; the High Court held that the essentials of marriage were not performed. Principle. The two-Judge Bench favoured a broad meaning of "wife" in Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but could not depart from earlier two-Judge decisions, and referred three questions to a larger Bench. (2011) 1 SCC 141. Why it matters. It is a reference order, not a final ruling, and shows the debate on who is a wife for maintenance. D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010) Facts. A woman claimed maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as the appellant 's wife; he said he was already married to Lakshmi in 1980. Principle. A relationship in the nature of marriage under the Domestic Violence Act is akin to a common law marriage and needs four conditions and a shared household; the case went back to the Family Court. (2010) 10 SCC 469. Why it matters. It extends relief to women in relationships in the nature of marriage, but not to every live-in relationship. Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013) Facts. From 1992 an unmarried woman lived with a married man who had two children; she knew of his marriage and later claimed relief, including maintenance, under the Domestic Violence Act. Principle. The Court gave eight guidelines and held that her relationship was not in the nature of marriage, so she was not in a "domestic relationship"; the appeal was dismissed, and the Court asked Parliament to legislate. Decided 26 November 2013. Why it matters. It sets limits on maintenance claims by live-in partners. V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) Facts. A widow, whose husband died in 1931 in a joint family, got a decree for maintenance; in execution, a compromise gave her properties for her life in lieu of maintenance. Principle. Her right to maintenance is a pre-existing right in property; property given in lieu of it falls under Section 14(1), not 14(2), of the Hindu Succession Act, so she became full owner. AIR 1977 SC 1944 : (1977) 3 SCC 99. Why it matters. It shows maintenance as a real right in Hindu law that can ripen into ownership.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section gives a Hindu wife maintenance from her husband?
selfTest.a: Section 18.

selfTest.q: 2. Is a dependant's claim a charge on the estate?
selfTest.a: Not unless one is created by will, decree, agreement or otherwise (Section 27).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a person who converts claim under the 1956 Act?
selfTest.a: No (Section 24).

selfTest.q: 4. Two heirs take ₹12,00,000 and ₹4,00,000 of an estate. Maintenance of a dependant is fixed at ₹8,000 a month. How much does each pay?
selfTest.a: In proportion to their shares (Section 22(3)): the heir with ₹12,00,000 holds three-quarters of ₹16,00,000 and pays ₹6,000; the heir with ₹4,00,000 holds one-quarter and pays ₹2,000.

selfTest.q: 5. Within what time must an application to levy unpaid maintenance under Section 144 of the BNSS be made?
selfTest.a: Within one year from the date the amount became due (proviso to Section 144(3)).

selfTest.q: 6. In Tulasamma , why did the widow become full owner of property given in lieu of maintenance?
selfTest.a: Because her right to maintenance was a pre-existing right, so Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act applied, not Section 14(2).

family-law-i-u4-t7.subtitle: Scheme of the Act: extent, link to the Guardians and Wards Act, application, definitions, overriding effect and sections 6 to 13

en.inOneMinute: What it is. The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (HMGA) is one of the four Hindu Acts of 1955–56. It deals with the guardianship of Hindu minors in only 13 sections. Supplemental Act. It is in addition to the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, and does not replace it (Section 2). Both Acts work together for a Hindu minor. Who is a minor. A person who has not completed eighteen years (Section 4(a)). Extent. It extends to the whole of India and also to Hindus domiciled in India who are outside it (Section 1(2)). Core rules. Sections 6 to 13 name the natural guardians , limit their powers over the minor's property, allow testamentary guardians , end the powers of a de facto guardian , and make the welfare of the minor the paramount consideration. Scope of this note. The scheme of the Act as a whole. Sections 6 to 13 are explained in detail in the note on the Law of Guardianship.
legalProvision: Long title. An Act to amend and codify certain parts of the law relating to minority and guardianship among Hindus.

Section 2. Act to be supplemental to Act 8 of 1890. ―The provisions of this Act shall be in addition to, and not, save as hereinafter expressly provided, in derogation of, the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (8 of 1890).

Section 5. Over-riding effect of Act. ―Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,― (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu Law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 1: short title, and extent to the whole of India, including Hindus domiciled in India who are outside it. Section 3: application to Hindus by religion in any form, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs and the residuary group, with the Explanation on children and converts. Section 3(2) excludes Scheduled Tribes unless notified. Section 3(2A) excludes the Renoncants of Pondicherry. Section 4: definitions of "minor", "guardian" and "natural guardian". Sections 6 to 13: the working rules on guardians.
en.meaning:
The Act is a codifying statute , but only in part: its long title says it codifies "certain parts" of the law on minority and guardianship among Hindus. Mulla notes that it does not codify the whole law of guardianship, and that rules on matters for which the Act makes no provision are not overridden by it. Section 4 gives three definitions. "Minor" (Section 4(a)): a person who has not completed the age of eighteen years. "Guardian" (Section 4(b)): a person having the care of the person of a minor, or of his property, or of both. It includes four kinds: (i) a natural guardian; (ii) a guardian appointed by the will of the minor's father or mother; (iii) a guardian appointed or declared by a court; (iv) a person empowered to act as such by or under any enactment relating to any Court of Wards. "Natural guardian" (Section 4(c)): any of the guardians mentioned in Section 6. Kinds of guardian under Section 4(b). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1.
