keyPoints: Male: class I, class II, agnates, cognates (Section 8). Class I heirs take together and exclude all others (Section 9). Section 10: widow one share; each son, daughter and the mother one share; branches of pre-deceased children one share each. Female: five stages (Section 15). The source of property can send it back to the father's or husband's heirs (Section 15(2)). Degrees are counted inclusive of the intestate (Section 13). The Schedule has sixteen class I heirs and nine class II entries. Uterine brothers and sisters are excluded from "brother" and "sister". Before 1956, the 1929 Act added the son's daughter, daughter's daughter, sister and sister's son as Mitakshara heirs, after the father's father and before the father's brother. Section 14(1): a female Hindu holds property possessed by her as full owner. Section 14(2) saves restricted estates created by a gift, will, instrument, decree, order or award.

caseLaws.name: Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v
caseLaws.facts: Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died on 17 July 1965, leaving his only son Chander Sen. The Revenue taxed ₹1,85,043 standing to Rangi Lal's credit in the firm's books as joint family property of Chander Sen and his sons. Principle. Under Section 8, the son takes his father's property in his individual capacity, and his sons get no right by birth in it. AIR 1986 SC 1753 : (1986) 3 SCC 567. Why it matters. It is the leading case on the effect of Section 8 on a son who inherits. Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died on 27 June 1960, leaving a widow, two sons and three daughters. The widow sued for a 7/24 share in the joint family property. Principle. A notional partition is assumed immediately before the death; the widow takes the 1/4 share she would have got on that partition plus her 1/24 share in Khandappa's interest, making 7/24. AIR 1978 SC 1239 : (1978) 3 SCC 383. Why it matters. It shows how shares are worked out where a male coparcener dies leaving female class I heirs. V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) Facts. A widow got properties for life, with no power to alienate, under a compromise in lieu of maintenance certified on 30 July 1949. She sold and leased some of them in 1960 and 1961. Principle. Section 14(1) applied, so she held the properties as full owner, because the grant only recognised her pre-existing right to maintenance; Section 14(2) covers only a grant that creates a new title. AIR 1977 SC 1944 : (1977) 3 SCC 99. Why it matters. It shows that Section 14(1) is wide and that Section 14(2) is a narrow proviso.

selfTest.q: 1. Who comes first in the male scheme?
selfTest.a: Class I heirs (Section 8).

selfTest.q: 2. Where does property a woman inherited from her husband go if she has no child?
selfTest.a: To the heirs of the husband (Section 15(2)(b)).

selfTest.q: 3. How are degrees counted?
selfTest.a: Inclusive of the intestate, one degree for each generation (Section 13).

selfTest.q: 4. A man leaves ₹90 lakh, a widow, his mother and two daughters. What does each get?
selfTest.a: Four heirs, one share each under Section 10, Rules 1 and 2: ₹22.5 lakh each.

selfTest.q: 5. A man leaves only his father and his brother. Who takes?
selfTest.a: The father alone. He is in class II, Entry I; the brother is in Entry II, and an earlier entry is preferred (Section 9).

selfTest.q: 6. A woman dies leaving her husband and the two children of a pre-deceased daughter. How is her estate divided?
selfTest.a: The husband takes one share; the two grandchildren together take the share their mother would have taken (Section 16, Rule 2). So the husband gets half and each grandchild one-fourth.

family-law-i-u5-t2.subtitle: General rules for property of a Hindu who dies without a will: shares, unborn child, simultaneous deaths, disqualified heirs and failure of heirs

en.inOneMinute: Meaning. A Hindu is intestate in respect of a property if he or she dies without a valid will for that property. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 then fixes who inherits. This note. It covers the general rules that apply to every intestate estate (Sections 18 to 29). Sharing rules. Full blood is preferred to half blood (Section 18). Heirs who succeed together take per capita and as tenants-in-common (Section 19). Special cases. A child in the womb can inherit (Section 20). In simultaneous deaths the younger is presumed to have survived the elder (Section 21). Shut out. A murderer is disqualified (Section 25), and so are a convert's later-born children (Section 26). No heir. If there is no heir, the property goes to the Government ( escheat , Section 29).
legalProvision: Section 19. Mode of succession of two or more heirs. ―If two or more heirs succeed together to the property of an intestate, they shall take the property,― (a) save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, per capita and not per stirpes; and (b) as tenants-in-common and not as joint tenants.

Section 25. Murderer disqualified. ―A person who commits murder or abets the commission of murder shall be disqualified from inheriting the property of the person murdered, or any other property in furtherance of the succession to which he or she committed or abetted the commission of the murder.
Section 27. Succession when heir disqualified. ―If any person is disqualified from inheriting any property under this Act, it shall devolve as if such person had died before the intestate.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 18: heirs by full blood are preferred to heirs by half blood, if the nature of the relationship is the same in every other respect. Section 20: a child in the womb at the death, born alive later, inherits as if born before the death. Section 21: when two persons die and it is uncertain who survived, the younger is presumed to have survived the elder. Section 22: class I heirs have a preferential right to acquire a co-heir's interest in immovable property or a business. Sections 24 to 28: disqualifications (Section 24 now omitted). Section 29: failure of heirs.
en.meaning:
Under Section 3(1)(g), a person is deemed to die intestate in respect of property of which he or she has not made a testamentary disposition capable of taking effect. The rules in this note work after the heirs are known (Sections 8 to 17 and the Schedule). They fix how the heirs share, who is shut out, and what happens if no one qualifies. keyPoints: Section 18: full blood before half blood, if the relationship is otherwise the same. Section 19: per capita, and as tenants-in-common. Section 20: the child in the womb inherits. Section 21: the younger is presumed to survive. Section 22: class I heirs may buy out a co-heir; the highest offer wins. Section 25: murderer disqualified. Section 27: treated as dead before the intestate. Section 26: a convert's later-born children are barred unless Hindus when succession opens. Section 29: the Government takes if there is no heir. Section 28: disease, defect or deformity never disqualify. Section 24 (remarried widows) was omitted on 9 September 2005. Uterine brothers and sisters are not class II heirs as brothers and sisters.

caseLaws.name: Vellikannu v
caseLaws.facts: R. Singaperumal (2005) Facts. On 10 October 1972 a son murdered his father, Ramasami Konar, was convicted and later released. His wife sued to inherit the father's estate, saying her husband was disqualified and must be deemed to have predeceased his father. Principle. Disqualification under Section 25 read with Section 27 is total: the murderer is treated as non-existent and not as the stock of a fresh line of descent, so his wife can have no better claim through him. (2005) 6 SCC 622. Why it matters. It links Section 25 with the legal fiction in Section 27 and stops claims made through a disqualified murderer. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died on 17 July 1965, leaving his only son Chander Sen. The Wealth-tax Officer included ₹1,85,043 standing to Rangi Lal's credit in the firm's books as property of the joint family of Chander Sen and his sons. Principle. Under Section 8 read with Section 4, a son takes his father's property in his individual capacity, and his sons get no right by birth in it. AIR 1986 SC 1753 : (1986) 3 SCC 567. Why it matters. The reasoning draws on Section 19 (heirs take as tenants-in-common, not joint tenants) to support the break from the old law.

selfTest.q: 1. How do heirs hold under Section 19?
selfTest.a: As tenants-in-common, and per capita.

selfTest.q: 2. What does Section 27 say?
selfTest.a: A disqualified person's share goes as if that person died before the intestate.

selfTest.q: 3. Who takes if there is no heir?
selfTest.a: The Government, with the liabilities an heir would bear (Section 29).

selfTest.q: 4. A Hindu's estate of ₹45 lakh goes to his widow, son and a daughter born two months after his death; his mother is dead. What does each get?
selfTest.a: ₹15 lakh each. The posthumous daughter inherits as if born before his death (Section 20), and the three take equally under Section 10, Rules 1 and 2.

selfTest.q: 5. Is a Hindu who converts to another religion barred from inheriting from his Hindu father?
selfTest.a: Not by Section 26. That section bars only his children born after the conversion and their descendants.

selfTest.q: 6. Two class I heirs both want to buy a co-heir's share of a shop. Who is preferred?
selfTest.a: The one who offers the highest consideration (Section 22(3)).

legalProvision: Section 19. Mode of succession of two or more heirs. ―If two or more heirs succeed together to the property of an intestate, they shall take the property,― (a) save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, per capita and not per stirpes; and (b) as tenants-in-common and not as joint tenants.

Section 25. Murderer disqualified. ―A person who commits murder or abets the commission of murder shall be disqualified from inheriting the property of the person murdered, or any other property in furtherance of the succession to which he or she committed or abetted the commission of the murder.
Section 27. Succession when heir disqualified. ―If any person is disqualified from inheriting any property under this Act, it shall devolve as if such person had died before the intestate.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 19 కింద వారసులు ఎలా పట్టుకుంటారు?
selfTest.a: ఉమ్మడి యజమానులుగా, తలసరిగా.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 27 ఏమి చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: అనర్హుడైన వ్యక్తి వాటా, ఆ వ్యక్తి వీలునామా లేకుండా మరణించినవారి కంటే ముందే మరణించినట్లుగా చేరుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 3. వారసుడు లేకపోతే ఎవరు తీసుకుంటారు?
selfTest.a: వారసుడు భరించే బాధ్యతలతో ప్రభుత్వం (సెక్షన్ 29).

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక హిందువు ₹45 లక్షల ఎస్టేట్ అతని వితంతువు, కొడుకు, అతని మరణానికి రెండు నెలల తర్వాత పుట్టిన కూతురికి చేరుతుంది; అతని తల్లి మరణించారు. ఒక్కొక్కరికి ఎంత?
selfTest.a: ఒక్కొక్కరికి ₹15 లక్షలు. మరణం తర్వాత పుట్టిన కూతురు అతని మరణానికి ముందే పుట్టినట్లుగా వారసత్వం పొందుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 20); సెక్షన్ 10, నియమాలు 1, 2 కింద ముగ్గురూ సమానంగా పొందుతారు.

selfTest.q: 5. వేరే మతంలోకి మారిన హిందువు తన హిందూ తండ్రి నుంచి వారసత్వం పొందకుండా నిషేధించబడతాడా?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 26 ద్వారా కాదు. ఆ సెక్షన్ మతం మారిన తర్వాత పుట్టిన అతని పిల్లలను, వారి సంతతిని మాత్రమే నిషేధిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 6. ఇద్దరు క్లాస్ I వారసులు ఒక దుకాణంలో సహ-వారసుడి వాటాను కొనాలనుకుంటున్నారు. ఎవరికి ప్రాధాన్యం?
selfTest.a: అత్యధిక ప్రతిఫలం ఇచ్చేవారికి (సెక్షన్ 22(3)).

hi.inOneMinute: Meaning. A Hindu is intestate in respect of a property if he or she dies without a valid will for that property. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 then fixes who inherits. This note. It covers the general rules that apply to every intestate estate (Sections 18 to 29). Sharing rules. Full blood is preferred to half blood (Section 18). Heirs who succeed together take per capita and as tenants-in-common (Section 19). Special cases. A child in the womb can inherit (Section 20). In simultaneous deaths the younger is presumed to have survived the elder (Section 21). Shut out. A murderer is disqualified (Section 25), and so are a convert's later-born children (Section 26). No heir. If there is no heir, the property goes to the Government ( escheat , Section 29).
legalProvision: Section 19. Mode of succession of two or more heirs. ―If two or more heirs succeed together to the property of an intestate, they shall take the property,― (a) save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, per capita and not per stirpes; and (b) as tenants-in-common and not as joint tenants.

Section 25. Murderer disqualified. ―A person who commits murder or abets the commission of murder shall be disqualified from inheriting the property of the person murdered, or any other property in furtherance of the succession to which he or she committed or abetted the commission of the murder.
Section 27. Succession when heir disqualified. ―If any person is disqualified from inheriting any property under this Act, it shall devolve as if such person had died before the intestate.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 18: heirs by full blood are preferred to heirs by half blood, if the nature of the relationship is the same in every other respect. Section 20: a child in the womb at the death, born alive later, inherits as if born before the death. Section 21: when two persons die and it is uncertain who survived, the younger is presumed to have survived the elder. Section 22: class I heirs have a preferential right to acquire a co-heir's interest in immovable property or a business. Sections 24 to 28: disqualifications (Section 24 now omitted). Section 29: failure of heirs.
hi.meaning:
Under Section 3(1)(g), a person is deemed to die intestate in respect of property of which he or she has not made a testamentary disposition capable of taking effect. The rules in this note work after the heirs are known (Sections 8 to 17 and the Schedule). They fix how the heirs share, who is shut out, and what happens if no one qualifies. General rules for an intestate estate. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Section 18: full blood before half blood, if the relationship is otherwise the same. Section 19: per capita, and as tenants-in-common. Section 20: the child in the womb inherits. Section 21: the younger is presumed to survive. Section 22: class I heirs may buy out a co-heir; the highest offer wins. Section 25: murderer disqualified. Section 27: treated as dead before the intestate. Section 26: a convert's later-born children are barred unless Hindus when succession opens. Section 29: the Government takes if there is no heir. Section 28: disease, defect or deformity never disqualify. Section 24 (remarried widows) was omitted on 9 September 2005. Uterine brothers and sisters are not class II heirs as brothers and sisters.

caseLaws.name: Vellikannu v
caseLaws.facts: R. Singaperumal (2005) Facts. On 10 October 1972 a son murdered his father, Ramasami Konar, was convicted and later released. His wife sued to inherit the father's estate, saying her husband was disqualified and must be deemed to have predeceased his father. Principle. Disqualification under Section 25 read with Section 27 is total: the murderer is treated as non-existent and not as the stock of a fresh line of descent, so his wife can have no better claim through him. (2005) 6 SCC 622. Why it matters. It links Section 25 with the legal fiction in Section 27 and stops claims made through a disqualified murderer. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v. Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died on 17 July 1965, leaving his only son Chander Sen. The Wealth-tax Officer included ₹1,85,043 standing to Rangi Lal's credit in the firm's books as property of the joint family of Chander Sen and his sons. Principle. Under Section 8 read with Section 4, a son takes his father's property in his individual capacity, and his sons get no right by birth in it. AIR 1986 SC 1753 : (1986) 3 SCC 567. Why it matters. The reasoning draws on Section 19 (heirs take as tenants-in-common, not joint tenants) to support the break from the old law.

selfTest.q: 1. How do heirs hold under Section 19?
selfTest.a: As tenants-in-common, and per capita.

selfTest.q: 2. What does Section 27 say?
selfTest.a: A disqualified person's share goes as if that person died before the intestate.

selfTest.q: 3. Who takes if there is no heir?
selfTest.a: The Government, with the liabilities an heir would bear (Section 29).

selfTest.q: 4. A Hindu's estate of ₹45 lakh goes to his widow, son and a daughter born two months after his death; his mother is dead. What does each get?
selfTest.a: ₹15 lakh each. The posthumous daughter inherits as if born before his death (Section 20), and the three take equally under Section 10, Rules 1 and 2.

selfTest.q: 5. Is a Hindu who converts to another religion barred from inheriting from his Hindu father?
selfTest.a: Not by Section 26. That section bars only his children born after the conversion and their descendants.

selfTest.q: 6. Two class I heirs both want to buy a co-heir's share of a shop. Who is preferred?
selfTest.a: The one who offers the highest consideration (Section 22(3)).

family-law-i-u5-t6.subtitle: The assumed partition just before a coparcener's death, under the old section 6 and under section 6(3) after 2005

en.inOneMinute: Meaning. A notional partition is a partition the law assumes to have taken place immediately before a coparcener's death. It is used only to find out the share of the deceased in Mitakshara coparcenary property. Where the share goes. That share then goes to his heirs by succession, not by survivorship . Where the rule is. Before 2005 it was in Explanation 1 to Section 6. After 2005 it is in the Explanation to Section 6(3). What it does not do. It does not actually divide the family property, which stays joint (Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma, paras 101, 129(iv)).
legalProvision: Section 6(3) (as substituted by Act 39 of 2005). ―Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenary property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,―(a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; (b) the share of the pre-deceased son or a pre-deceased daughter, as they would have got had they been alive at the time of partition, shall be allotted to the surviving child of such pre-deceased son or of such pre-deceased daughter; and (c) the share of the pre-deceased child of a pre-deceased son or of a pre-deceased daughter, as such child would have got had he or she been alive at the time of the partition, shall be allotted to the child of such pre-deceased child of the pre-deceased son or a pre-deceased daughter, as the case may be. Explanation.―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not.

Old Section 6, Explanation 1 (as quoted in Gurupad). ―For the purposes of this section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not.
Other provisions used in this note:

Old Section 6, proviso : if the deceased left a female relative in class I of the Schedule, or a male relative in that class who claims through such a female relative, his interest devolved by will or intestate succession under the Act and not by survivorship . Old Section 6, Explanation 2: a person who had separated from the coparcenary before the death, or any of his heirs, could not claim a share on intestacy in that interest. Sections 8, 9 and 10: class I heirs take together and exclude all others. The widow, each son, each daughter and the mother take one share each (Section 10, Rules 1 and 2). These sections give the heirs' shares in the deceased's interest once the assumed partition has fixed that interest. Explanation to Section 30: the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property is deemed to be property he can dispose of by will. Section 6(5) and its Explanation, 2005: Section 6(5) saves a partition made before 20 December 2004. "Partition" means a registered deed or a court decree. The assumed partition is not that kind of partition (see part 7 below).
en.meaning:
Mitakshara coparcenary property is held jointly. A coparcener has no fixed share until partition; his share keeps changing with births and deaths in the family ( Vineeta Sharma , para 66). When a coparcener dies, the law needs a way to find his share. It does this by a legal fiction . It assumes that a partition took place just before his death and gives him the share he would then have received. Assumed, not real. No deed, decree or division happens. The law only pretends one did. Just before death. The moment of the assumed partition is immediately before the death. Any coparcener. It applies whether or not he could himself claim partition, for example a minor coparcener (Explanation; Mulla, 14th ed., s. 6). How a notional partition works. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The law assumes a partition only to find the dead coparcener's share; nothing is actually divided. flowchart TD D["Coparcener dies"] --> A["1. Assume a partition
just before his death"] A --> F["2. Find the share
he would have received"] F --> P["3. That share devolves on his heirs
by will or intestate succession"] P --> N["4. Nothing divided
the coparcenary continues"] Text description A coparcener dies. Step 1: assume a partition just before his death. Step 2: find the share he would have received. Step 3: that share devolves on his heirs by will or intestate succession. Step 4: the family property is not in fact divided; the coparcenary continues. Step What happens 1. Assume A partition is assumed just before the coparcener's death 2. Find the share Find the share he would have received on that partition 3. Pass it on That share devolves on his heirs by will or intestate succession 4. Nothing divided The family property is not in fact divided
keyPoints: A notional partition is a partition assumed just before a coparcener's death. It fixes only the deceased's share; the coparcenary is not divided. Gurupad : widow's share is 1/4 plus 1/24, which is 7/24. Section 6(3), after 2005: succession, not survivorship. Daughter gets the same share as a son (Section 6(3)(a)). It is not a Section 6(5) partition and does not end the coparcenary ( Prakash , paras 18, 22; Vineeta Sharma , para 101).

caseLaws.name: Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v
caseLaws.facts: Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960, leaving a widow, two sons and three daughters. The widow sued for 7/24th of the joint family property. Principle. The assumed partition under Explanation 1 must be carried to the end. The widow gets her assumed-partition share plus her share in his interest: 7/24th. AIR 1978 SC 1239 : (1978) 3 SCC 383. Why it matters. Leading case on working out the assumed partition. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-Judge Bench answered a reference on amended Section 6 on 11 August 2020. Principle. The deemed partition under old Section 6 only fixes the deceased's share. It does not disrupt the coparcenary (paras 66, 97, 101, 129(iv)). (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It limits what the assumed partition does. Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) Facts. Phulavati's father died on 18 February 1988. The trial court gave her a share on the assumed partition at his death. Principle. A statutory notional partition is not covered by the proviso, Section 6(5) or its Explanation (paras 17, 18, 22). (2016) 2 SCC 36. Why it matters. Its treatment of the fiction was rejected in Vineeta Sharma (para 106).

selfTest.q: 1. What does a notional partition find?
selfTest.a: The share of a coparcener who has died.

selfTest.q: 2. What was the widow's share in Gurupad?
3. Does the notional partition divide the family property?
selfTest.a: No. It only fixes the deceased's share.

selfTest.q: 4. What did Explanation 2 to old Section 6 say?
selfTest.a: A person who had separated before the death, or his heir, could not claim a share on intestacy.

selfTest.q: 5. A Hindu dies in 2010 leaving a wife, a son and a daughter, with ₹12 lakh of coparcenary property. What does each get?
selfTest.a: ₹4 lakh each: ₹3 lakh on the assumed partition plus ₹1 lakh from his ₹3 lakh.

selfTest.q: 6. Must a notional partition be by registered deed or decree?
selfTest.a: No. It arises by operation of law ( Prakash , para 17).

ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

పాత సెక్షన్ 6, proviso : మరణించిన వ్యక్తి షెడ్యూల్ క్లాస్ I లోని స్త్రీ బంధువును, లేదా అలాంటి స్త్రీ ద్వారా క్లెయిమ్ చేసే ఆ క్లాస్‌లోని పురుష బంధువును వదిలితే, అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా కాకుండా చట్టం కింద వీలునామా లేదా వీలునామా లేని వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్లింది. పాత సెక్షన్ 6, Explanation 2: మరణానికి ముందు కోపార్సినరీ నుంచి వేరుపడిన వ్యక్తి గానీ, అతని వారసులు గానీ ఆ హక్కులో వీలునామా లేని వారసత్వ వాటా క్లెయిమ్ చేయలేరు. సెక్షన్లు 8, 9, 10: క్లాస్ I వారసులు కలిసి పొంది మిగతా అందరినీ మినహాయిస్తారు. వితంతువు, ప్రతి కొడుకు, ప్రతి కూతురు, తల్లి ఒక్కొక్క వాటా పొందుతారు (సెక్షన్ 10, Rules 1, 2). ఊహాత్మక విభజన మరణించిన వ్యక్తి హక్కును నిర్ణయించిన తర్వాత, ఆ హక్కులో వారసుల వాటాలను ఈ సెక్షన్లు ఇస్తాయి. సెక్షన్ 30 Explanation: మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిలో హిందూ పురుషుడి హక్కు అతను వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వగల ఆస్తిగా భావించబడుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(5), దాని Explanation, 2005: 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కి ముందు జరిగిన విభజనను సెక్షన్ 6(5) కాపాడుతుంది. మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తి ఉమ్మడిగా ఉంటుంది. విభజన వరకు కోపార్సినర్ ‌కు నిర్దిష్ట వాటా ఉండదు; కుటుంబంలో పుట్టుకలు, మరణాలతో అతని వాటా మారుతూ ఉంటుంది ( Vineeta Sharma , పేరా 66). కోపార్సినర్ మరణించినప్పుడు, అతని వాటాను కనుగొనడానికి చట్టానికి ఒక మార్గం కావాలి. అది ఒక చట్టపరమైన కల్పన ద్వారా దీనిని చేస్తుంది. అతని మరణానికి కొంచెం ముందు విభజన జరిగినట్లు భావించి, అప్పుడు అతనికి వచ్చే వాటాను అతనికి ఇస్తుంది. భావించినది, వాస్తవం కాదు. ఏ దస్తావేజూ, డిక్రీ, పంపకమూ జరగదు. జరిగినట్లు చట్టం భావిస్తుంది మాత్రమే. మరణానికి కొంచెం ముందు. ఊహాత్మక విభజన సమయం మరణానికి వెంటనే ముందు. ఏ కోపార్సినర్‌కైనా. అతను స్వయంగా విభజన కోరగలడా లేదా అనేదానితో సంబంధం లేకుండా వర్తిస్తుంది, ఉదాహరణకు మైనర్ కోపార్సినర్ (Explanation; Mulla, 14వ ఎడిషన్, సెక్షన్ 6). ఊహాత్మక విభజన ఎలా పనిచేస్తుంది. hi.inOneMinute: Meaning. A notional partition is a partition the law assumes to have taken place immediately before a coparcener's death. It is used only to find out the share of the deceased in Mitakshara coparcenary property. Where the share goes. That share then goes to his heirs by succession, not by survivorship . Where the rule is. Before 2005 it was in Explanation 1 to Section 6. After 2005 it is in the Explanation to Section 6(3). What it does not do. It does not actually divide the family property, which stays joint (Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma, paras 101, 129(iv)).
legalProvision: Section 6(3) (as substituted by Act 39 of 2005). ―Where a Hindu dies after the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, his interest in the property of a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, shall devolve by testamentary or intestate succession, as the case may be, under this Act and not by survivorship, and the coparcenary property shall be deemed to have been divided as if a partition had taken place and,―(a) the daughter is allotted the same share as is allotted to a son; (b) the share of the pre-deceased son or a pre-deceased daughter, as they would have got had they been alive at the time of partition, shall be allotted to the surviving child of such pre-deceased son or of such pre-deceased daughter; and (c) the share of the pre-deceased child of a pre-deceased son or of a pre-deceased daughter, as such child would have got had he or she been alive at the time of the partition, shall be allotted to the child of such pre-deceased child of the pre-deceased son or a pre-deceased daughter, as the case may be. Explanation.―For the purposes of this sub-section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not.

Old Section 6, Explanation 1 (as quoted in Gurupad). ―For the purposes of this section, the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to be the share in the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of the property had taken place immediately before his death, irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not.
Other provisions used in this note:

Old Section 6, proviso : if the deceased left a female relative in class I of the Schedule, or a male relative in that class who claims through such a female relative, his interest devolved by will or intestate succession under the Act and not by survivorship . Old Section 6, Explanation 2: a person who had separated from the coparcenary before the death, or any of his heirs, could not claim a share on intestacy in that interest. Sections 8, 9 and 10: class I heirs take together and exclude all others. The widow, each son, each daughter and the mother take one share each (Section 10, Rules 1 and 2). These sections give the heirs' shares in the deceased's interest once the assumed partition has fixed that interest. Explanation to Section 30: the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property is deemed to be property he can dispose of by will. Section 6(5) and its Explanation, 2005: Section 6(5) saves a partition made before 20 December 2004. "Partition" means a registered deed or a court decree. The assumed partition is not that kind of partition (see part 7 below).
hi.meaning:
Mitakshara coparcenary property is held jointly. A coparcener has no fixed share until partition; his share keeps changing with births and deaths in the family ( Vineeta Sharma , para 66). When a coparcener dies, the law needs a way to find his share. It does this by a legal fiction . It assumes that a partition took place just before his death and gives him the share he would then have received. Assumed, not real. No deed, decree or division happens. The law only pretends one did. Just before death. The moment of the assumed partition is immediately before the death. Any coparcener. It applies whether or not he could himself claim partition, for example a minor coparcener (Explanation; Mulla, 14th ed., s. 6). How a notional partition works. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The law assumes a partition only to find the dead coparcener's share; nothing is actually divided. flowchart TD D["Coparcener dies"] --> A["1. Assume a partition
just before his death"] A --> F["2. Find the share
he would have received"] F --> P["3. That share devolves on his heirs
by will or intestate succession"] P --> N["4. Nothing divided
the coparcenary continues"] Text description A coparcener dies. Step 1: assume a partition just before his death. Step 2: find the share he would have received. Step 3: that share devolves on his heirs by will or intestate succession. Step 4: the family property is not in fact divided; the coparcenary continues. Step What happens 1. Assume A partition is assumed just before the coparcener's death 2. Find the share Find the share he would have received on that partition 3. Pass it on That share devolves on his heirs by will or intestate succession 4. Nothing divided The family property is not in fact divided
keyPoints: A notional partition is a partition assumed just before a coparcener's death. It fixes only the deceased's share; the coparcenary is not divided. Gurupad : widow's share is 1/4 plus 1/24, which is 7/24. Section 6(3), after 2005: succession, not survivorship. Daughter gets the same share as a son (Section 6(3)(a)). It is not a Section 6(5) partition and does not end the coparcenary ( Prakash , paras 18, 22; Vineeta Sharma , para 101).

caseLaws.name: Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v
caseLaws.facts: Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960, leaving a widow, two sons and three daughters. The widow sued for 7/24th of the joint family property. Principle. The assumed partition under Explanation 1 must be carried to the end. The widow gets her assumed-partition share plus her share in his interest: 7/24th. AIR 1978 SC 1239 : (1978) 3 SCC 383. Why it matters. Leading case on working out the assumed partition. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. A three-Judge Bench answered a reference on amended Section 6 on 11 August 2020. Principle. The deemed partition under old Section 6 only fixes the deceased's share. It does not disrupt the coparcenary (paras 66, 97, 101, 129(iv)). (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It limits what the assumed partition does. Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) Facts. Phulavati's father died on 18 February 1988. The trial court gave her a share on the assumed partition at his death. Principle. A statutory notional partition is not covered by the proviso, Section 6(5) or its Explanation (paras 17, 18, 22). (2016) 2 SCC 36. Why it matters. Its treatment of the fiction was rejected in Vineeta Sharma (para 106).

selfTest.q: 1. What does a notional partition find?
selfTest.a: The share of a coparcener who has died.

selfTest.q: 2. What was the widow's share in Gurupad?
3. Does the notional partition divide the family property?
selfTest.a: No. It only fixes the deceased's share.

selfTest.q: 4. What did Explanation 2 to old Section 6 say?
selfTest.a: A person who had separated before the death, or his heir, could not claim a share on intestacy.

selfTest.q: 5. A Hindu dies in 2010 leaving a wife, a son and a daughter, with ₹12 lakh of coparcenary property. What does each get?
selfTest.a: ₹4 lakh each: ₹3 lakh on the assumed partition plus ₹1 lakh from his ₹3 lakh.

selfTest.q: 6. Must a notional partition be by registered deed or decree?
selfTest.a: No. It arises by operation of law ( Prakash , para 17).

family-law-i-u5-t5.subtitle: History of the Act and its two amendments: the 1986 Andhra Pradesh law on daughters and the 2005 central law that changed section 6 and removed sections 23 and 24

en.inOneMinute: Two amendments on daughters. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 has been amended twice on the point of daughters. The Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 added Sections 29A to 29C for Andhra Pradesh, deemed in force from 5 September 1985. It made the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth, twenty years before the central law. The central law. The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (Act 39 of 2005) did the same for the whole of India from 9 September 2005 by substituting a new Section 6. It also omitted Sections 4(2), 23 and 24, amended Section 30 and added four class I heirs. The settled meaning. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) held that a daughter is a coparcener by birth, whether born before or after 2005, and that her father need not have been alive on 9 September 2005. What is saved. Dispositions, alienations, partitions and wills before 20 December 2004 are saved (Section 6(1), proviso ). Only a partition by registered deed or court decree counts (Section 6(5), Explanation).
legalProvision: Section 29-A (Andhra Pradesh, Act 13 of 1986). Equal rights to daughter in coparcenary property. ―Notwithstanding anything contained in section 6 of this Act―(i) in a Joint Hindu Family governed by Mitakshara Law, the daughter of a coparcener shall by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son and have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son, inclusive of the right to claim by survivorship; and shall be subject to the same liabilities and disabilities in respect thereto as the son; … (iv) Nothing in clause (ii) shall apply to a daughter married prior to or to a partition which had been effected before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986.

Section 6(1) (as substituted by Act 39 of 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. ―On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,―(a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenary property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(5). ―Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation.―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.
The amending provisions used in this note:

Andhra Pradesh Act 13 of 1986: inserted Chapter II-A (Sections 29A, 29B and 29C) after Chapter II, for Andhra Pradesh, deemed in force from 5 September 1985 (Section 1(3); Vineeta Sharma , para 52). Hindu Succession (Maharashtra Amendment) Act, 1994 (Maharashtra Act 40 of 1994): inserted a new Chapter I-A (Sections 29-A, 29-B and 29-C) after Section 29, for Maharashtra, deemed in force from 22 June 1994. Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975: a separate State Act that abolishes the joint family system among Hindus in Kerala. Its text does not amend the 1956 Act. Act 39 of 2005, Section 2: omitted Section 4(2). Act 39 of 2005, Section 3: substituted a new Section 6. Act 39 of 2005, Sections 4 and 5: omitted Sections 23 and 24. Act 39 of 2005, Section 6: in Section 30, "disposed of by him" became "disposed of by him or by her". Act 39 of 2005, Section 7: added four more class I heirs to the Schedule.
en.meaning:
Under the old Mitakshara rule, only sons, grandsons and great-grandsons were coparceners by birth. A daughter was not a coparcener. The two amendments changed that. Section 6 now makes the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth, in her own right and in the same manner as a son. "Daughter of a coparcener". Section 6(1) gives the status to the daughter of a coparcener in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law. Any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener in law now includes her. "By birth". The right comes from birth, not from inheritance. So it does not depend on the father dying after 2005 ( Vineeta Sharma , para 129(iii)). " Partition " for Section 6. Only a partition by a registered deed of partition or by a court decree (Section 6(5), Explanation). How the law on daughters changed. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Andhra Pradesh Amendment, 1986 (Act 13 of 1986): Sections 29A to 29C, deemed in force from 5 September 1985. Other State laws before 2005: Tamil Nadu (1989), Karnataka Section 6A (1994), Maharashtra Act 40 of 1994 (Chapter I-A, Sections 29-A to 29-C, deemed in force from 22 June 1994), Kerala Act (1975, abolishes the joint family system). Act 39 of 2005: new Section 6 from 9 September 2005; Sections 4(2), 23 and 24 omitted; Section 30 amended; four class I heirs added. Cut-off for saved partitions: 20 December 2004, by registered deed or court decree (Section 6(5)). Section 6(4) ends the pious obligation for later debts. Section 6(3): on a coparcener's death after the Amendment, a deemed partition gives the daughter the same share as a son. Vineeta Sharma (2020): the daughter is a coparcener by birth; the father need not be alive.

caseLaws.name: Vineeta Sharma v
caseLaws.facts: Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. Two Supreme Court Benches had given conflicting views on amended Section 6. A three-Judge Bench heard the reference and decided it on 11 August 2020. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener by birth. She claims her rights from 9 September 2005 whether born before or after it, and her father need not have been alive on that date (para 129). (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It settled the meaning of the 2005 Amendment and overruled the contrary views in Prakash v. Phulavati and Mangammal (para 130). Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) Facts. Phulavati sued in 1992 at Belgaum for partition. Her father died on 18 February 1988. The Karnataka High Court applied the 2005 Amendment to her pending claim. Principle. The Supreme Court held that the rights under the Amendment apply to living daughters of living coparceners as on 9 September 2005, and set aside the High Court's order (paras 23, 24). (2016) 2 SCC 36. Why it matters. Vineeta Sharma (2020) overruled this view and held that the father need not be alive. Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960, leaving a widow, two sons and three daughters. The widow sued for 7/24th of the joint family property. Principle. A notional partition is assumed immediately before the death, and the heir gets that share plus her share in the deceased's interest. AIR 1978 SC 1239 : (1978) 3 SCC 383. Why it matters. It explains the old Section 6 that the 2005 Amendment replaced.

selfTest.q: 1. When did the Andhra Pradesh Amendment take effect?
selfTest.a: It is deemed to have come into force on 5 September 1985.

selfTest.q: 2. Which sections did the 2005 Amendment omit?
selfTest.a: Sections 4(2), 23 and 24.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the cut-off date for saved partitions?
selfTest.a: 20 December 2004 (Section 6(5)).

selfTest.q: 4. Does a daughter born in 1980 get coparcenary rights under the 2005 Amendment?
selfTest.a: Yes, from 9 September 2005 ( Vineeta Sharma , para 129(ii)).

selfTest.q: 5. Ravi dies in 2010 leaving a son and a daughter as coparceners with him in ₹90 lakh of coparcenary property. What does the daughter get?
selfTest.a: ₹45 lakh: ₹30 lakh on the deemed partition, plus ₹15 lakh as Ravi's class I heir.

selfTest.q: 6. Which partition counts under Section 6(5)?
selfTest.a: A partition by a registered deed of partition or by a court decree.

hi.inOneMinute: Two amendments on daughters. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 has been amended twice on the point of daughters. The Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 added Sections 29A to 29C for Andhra Pradesh, deemed in force from 5 September 1985. It made the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth, twenty years before the central law. The central law. The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 (Act 39 of 2005) did the same for the whole of India from 9 September 2005 by substituting a new Section 6. It also omitted Sections 4(2), 23 and 24, amended Section 30 and added four class I heirs. The settled meaning. Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020) held that a daughter is a coparcener by birth, whether born before or after 2005, and that her father need not have been alive on 9 September 2005. What is saved. Dispositions, alienations, partitions and wills before 20 December 2004 are saved (Section 6(1), proviso ). Only a partition by registered deed or court decree counts (Section 6(5), Explanation).
legalProvision: Section 29-A (Andhra Pradesh, Act 13 of 1986). Equal rights to daughter in coparcenary property. ―Notwithstanding anything contained in section 6 of this Act―(i) in a Joint Hindu Family governed by Mitakshara Law, the daughter of a coparcener shall by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son and have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son, inclusive of the right to claim by survivorship; and shall be subject to the same liabilities and disabilities in respect thereto as the son; … (iv) Nothing in clause (ii) shall apply to a daughter married prior to or to a partition which had been effected before the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986.

Section 6(1) (as substituted by Act 39 of 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. ―On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,―(a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenary property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(5). ―Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation.―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.
The amending provisions used in this note:

Andhra Pradesh Act 13 of 1986: inserted Chapter II-A (Sections 29A, 29B and 29C) after Chapter II, for Andhra Pradesh, deemed in force from 5 September 1985 (Section 1(3); Vineeta Sharma , para 52). Hindu Succession (Maharashtra Amendment) Act, 1994 (Maharashtra Act 40 of 1994): inserted a new Chapter I-A (Sections 29-A, 29-B and 29-C) after Section 29, for Maharashtra, deemed in force from 22 June 1994. Kerala Joint Hindu Family System (Abolition) Act, 1975: a separate State Act that abolishes the joint family system among Hindus in Kerala. Its text does not amend the 1956 Act. Act 39 of 2005, Section 2: omitted Section 4(2). Act 39 of 2005, Section 3: substituted a new Section 6. Act 39 of 2005, Sections 4 and 5: omitted Sections 23 and 24. Act 39 of 2005, Section 6: in Section 30, "disposed of by him" became "disposed of by him or by her". Act 39 of 2005, Section 7: added four more class I heirs to the Schedule.
hi.meaning:
Under the old Mitakshara rule, only sons, grandsons and great-grandsons were coparceners by birth. A daughter was not a coparcener. The two amendments changed that. Section 6 now makes the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth, in her own right and in the same manner as a son. "Daughter of a coparcener". Section 6(1) gives the status to the daughter of a coparcener in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law. Any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener in law now includes her. "By birth". The right comes from birth, not from inheritance. So it does not depend on the father dying after 2005 ( Vineeta Sharma , para 129(iii)). " Partition " for Section 6. Only a partition by a registered deed of partition or by a court decree (Section 6(5), Explanation). How the law on daughters changed. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Andhra Pradesh Amendment, 1986 (Act 13 of 1986): Sections 29A to 29C, deemed in force from 5 September 1985. Other State laws before 2005: Tamil Nadu (1989), Karnataka Section 6A (1994), Maharashtra Act 40 of 1994 (Chapter I-A, Sections 29-A to 29-C, deemed in force from 22 June 1994), Kerala Act (1975, abolishes the joint family system). Act 39 of 2005: new Section 6 from 9 September 2005; Sections 4(2), 23 and 24 omitted; Section 30 amended; four class I heirs added. Cut-off for saved partitions: 20 December 2004, by registered deed or court decree (Section 6(5)). Section 6(4) ends the pious obligation for later debts. Section 6(3): on a coparcener's death after the Amendment, a deemed partition gives the daughter the same share as a son. Vineeta Sharma (2020): the daughter is a coparcener by birth; the father need not be alive.

caseLaws.name: Vineeta Sharma v
caseLaws.facts: Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. Two Supreme Court Benches had given conflicting views on amended Section 6. A three-Judge Bench heard the reference and decided it on 11 August 2020. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener by birth. She claims her rights from 9 September 2005 whether born before or after it, and her father need not have been alive on that date (para 129). (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It settled the meaning of the 2005 Amendment and overruled the contrary views in Prakash v. Phulavati and Mangammal (para 130). Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) Facts. Phulavati sued in 1992 at Belgaum for partition. Her father died on 18 February 1988. The Karnataka High Court applied the 2005 Amendment to her pending claim. Principle. The Supreme Court held that the rights under the Amendment apply to living daughters of living coparceners as on 9 September 2005, and set aside the High Court's order (paras 23, 24). (2016) 2 SCC 36. Why it matters. Vineeta Sharma (2020) overruled this view and held that the father need not be alive. Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978) Facts. Khandappa died in 1960, leaving a widow, two sons and three daughters. The widow sued for 7/24th of the joint family property. Principle. A notional partition is assumed immediately before the death, and the heir gets that share plus her share in the deceased's interest. AIR 1978 SC 1239 : (1978) 3 SCC 383. Why it matters. It explains the old Section 6 that the 2005 Amendment replaced.

selfTest.q: 1. When did the Andhra Pradesh Amendment take effect?
selfTest.a: It is deemed to have come into force on 5 September 1985.

selfTest.q: 2. Which sections did the 2005 Amendment omit?
selfTest.a: Sections 4(2), 23 and 24.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the cut-off date for saved partitions?
selfTest.a: 20 December 2004 (Section 6(5)).

selfTest.q: 4. Does a daughter born in 1980 get coparcenary rights under the 2005 Amendment?
selfTest.a: Yes, from 9 September 2005 ( Vineeta Sharma , para 129(ii)).

selfTest.q: 5. Ravi dies in 2010 leaving a son and a daughter as coparceners with him in ₹90 lakh of coparcenary property. What does the daughter get?
selfTest.a: ₹45 lakh: ₹30 lakh on the deemed partition, plus ₹15 lakh as Ravi's class I heir.

selfTest.q: 6. Which partition counts under Section 6(5)?
selfTest.a: A partition by a registered deed of partition or by a court decree.

family-law-i-u5-t9.subtitle: A daughter as coparcener by birth under section 6: Prakash v. Phulavati, Danamma and Vineeta Sharma, saved partitions and the other changes of 2005

en.inOneMinute: The rule. Since 9 September 2005, Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 makes the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth. She has the same rights and liabilities as a son. Father need not be alive. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), a three-Judge Bench held that her father need not have been alive on that date. Saved partitions. The right does not reopen a partition made before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed or a court decree. An oral partition is accepted only in exceptional cases. The cases. Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) had required a living father; Danamma (2018) gave daughters a share though the father died in 2001. Vineeta Sharma settled the conflict.
legalProvision: Section 6(1) (as substituted by Act 39 of 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. ―On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,―(a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenary property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(5). ―Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation.―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 6(1): from the commencement of the 2005 Amendment, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right, in the same manner as the son. She has the same rights and the same liabilities. Any reference to a Mitakshara coparcener includes the daughter of a coparcener. Proviso to Section 6(1): it saves any disposition, alienation, partition or testamentary disposition made before 20 December 2004. Section 6(2): property she gets under Section 6(1) is held with the incidents of coparcenary ownership. She can dispose of it by will . Section 6(3): on a Hindu's death after the Amendment, his interest devolves by will or intestate succession and not by survivorship . A partition is deemed to have taken place, and the daughter gets the same share as a son. Section 6(4): after the Amendment, no court recognises a right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for his father's, grandfather's or great-grandfather's debt solely on the ground of pious obligation . The proviso keeps the creditor's right, and any alienation made for such a debt, for debts contracted before the Amendment. The Explanation limits "son", "grandson" and "great-grandson" in that proviso to those born or adopted before the Amendment. Section 6(5): the section does not apply to a partition effected before 20 December 2004. "Partition" means a partition by a registered deed or by a court decree. Explanation to Section 30: the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property is property he can dispose of by will. The 2005 Amendment made Section 30 read "disposed of by him or by her". State laws: the Act text prints Karnataka Sections 6A to 6C and Tamil Nadu Sections 29-A to 29-C. Both give daughters coparcenary rights from their own dates. Karnataka Section 6A(d) denies the clause (b) share on partition to a daughter married before the Hindu Succession (Karnataka Amendment) Act, 1990. Tamil Nadu Section 29-A(iv) excludes a daughter married before the Tamil Nadu Act. Both State Acts save partitions made before their commencement. The Maharashtra Act, 1994 and the Kerala Act, 1975 are described below from their own texts.
en.meaning:
Ancestral property here means Mitakshara coparcenary property held by a joint Hindu family , which gives its members a right from birth. A coparcener has a birthright interest in it. Before 2005, only sons were coparceners by birth. Now a daughter is one too, with the same rights and liabilities, and no rule in Section 6 excludes a married daughter. Coparcener by birth. Her right comes from birth, not from anyone's death. This is the old idea of unobstructed heritage , now applied to daughters ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 55, 63). Right to partition. A coparcener is one who can claim partition. The daughter can claim partition from 9 September 2005 (para 79). Retroactive. Section 6 is a retroactive statute : it operates from 9 September 2005, but on the basis of an earlier event, her birth (paras 55 to 57). Daughters' right to ancestral property. See Diagram 1 . Question 1: was there a partition before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed that was acted upon, or by a final court decree? Yes: the partition is saved (Section 6(5)). No: question 2: is only an oral partition alleged? Yes: it counts only in exceptional cases, on cogent public documents (paras 127, 128). No: she is a coparcener by birth from 9 September 2005, with the same rights and liabilities as a son, whether born before or after 2005 and whether or not her father was alive (Vineeta Sharma). keyPoints: Section 6(1): the daughter of a coparcener is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Vineeta Sharma (2020): the father need not be alive on 9 September 2005. The amendment is retroactive, not retrospective (paras 55-56). Saved partitions: registered deed or court decree before 20 December 2004. Oral partition only in exceptional cases. Prakash and Mangammal are overruled; Danamma is partly overruled. Preliminary decree is not a partition; daughters claim a share in pending final decree proceedings and appeals (para 129(iv)). Section 6 makes no distinction between married and unmarried daughters. Pending matters to be decided within six months, as far as possible (para 130).

caseLaws.name: Vineeta Sharma v
caseLaws.facts: Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. Two Supreme Court benches gave conflicting views on amended Section 6. A three-Judge Bench heard the reference with connected matters and decided on 11 August 2020. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener by birth. She claims her rights from 9 September 2005 whether born before or after it, and whether or not her father was alive. Saved partitions are only those made before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed or a court decree. (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It is the leading authority on the daughter's coparcenary right. Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) Facts. Phulavati sued for partition. Her father died on 18 February 1988. The Karnataka High Court applied the 2005 Amendment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal. Principle. The 2005 rights apply to living daughters of living coparceners on 9 September 2005, whenever the daughters were born. (2016) 2 SCC 36. Why it matters. Overruled in this part by Vineeta Sharma . Danamma @ Suman Surpur v. Amar (2018) Facts. Gurulingappa Savadi died in 2001, leaving two daughters, two sons and a widow. A partition suit was pending when Section 6 was amended. Principle. The amended Section 6 confers full rights on a daughter coparcener. Each of the daughters, sons and widow got a 1/5th share. (2018) 3 SCC 343 : [2018] 2 S.C.R. 553. Why it matters. It differed from Prakash and was partly overruled by Vineeta Sharma (para 130).

selfTest.q: 1. Is a daughter a coparcener by birth?
selfTest.a: Yes, under Section 6(1), from 9 September 2005.

selfTest.q: 2. Must her father be alive on 9 September 2005?
selfTest.a: No ( Vineeta Sharma ).

selfTest.q: 3. Which partitions are saved?
selfTest.a: Those made before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed or a court decree.

selfTest.q: 4. Does a preliminary decree stop the daughter?
selfTest.a: No. Only a final decree effects partition ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 128, 129(iv)).

selfTest.q: 5. Why is the amendment called retroactive?
selfTest.a: It operates from 9 September 2005 but rests on the antecedent event of birth (paras 55 to 57).

selfTest.q: 6. A father dies in 2010 leaving ₹90 lakh of ancestral land, a son and a daughter, with no earlier partition. What does the daughter get?
selfTest.a: ₹45 lakh: ₹30 lakh as a coparcener and ₹15 lakh from her father's share, the same as the son.

ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

సెక్షన్ 6(1): 2005 సవరణ ప్రారంభం నుండి, మితాక్షర చట్టం వర్తించే ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం లో, కోపార్సినర్ కుమార్తె కుమారుడిలాగే తన సొంత హక్కుతో పుట్టుకతోనే కోపార్సినర్ అవుతుంది. ఆమెకు అవే హక్కులు, అవే బాధ్యతలు ఉంటాయి. మితాక్షర కోపార్సినర్ అనే ప్రతి ప్రస్తావనలో కోపార్సినర్ కుమార్తె కూడా వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(1) నిబంధన ( proviso ): 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కి ముందు జరిగిన ఏ బదిలీ, అన్యాక్రాంతం, విభజన లేదా వీలునామా ఏర్పాటునైనా ఇది కాపాడుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(2): సెక్షన్ 6(1) కింద ఆమె పొందిన ఆస్తి కోపార్సినరీ యాజమాన్య లక్షణాలతో ఉంటుంది. ఆమె దానిని వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 6(3): సవరణ తర్వాత ఒక హిందువు మరణిస్తే, అతని హక్కు సర్వైవర్‌షిప్ ద్వారా కాకుండా వీలునామా లేదా వీలునామా లేని వారసత్వం ద్వారా వెళ్తుంది. విభజన జరిగినట్లు భావించబడుతుంది, కుమార్తెకు కుమారుడితో సమాన వాటా వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(4): సవరణ తర్వాత, కేవలం పవిత్ర బాధ్యత ఆధారంగా తండ్రి, తాత లేదా ముత్తాత అప్పు కోసం కుమారుడు, మనవడు లేదా మునిమనవడిపై చర్య తీసుకునే హక్కును ఏ కోర్టూ గుర్తించదు. సవరణకు ముందు చేసిన అప్పులకు రుణదాత హక్కును, అలాంటి అప్పు కోసం జరిగిన బదిలీని proviso కాపాడుతుంది. ఆ proviso లోని "son", "grandson", "great-grandson" ను సవరణకు ముందు పుట్టినవారు లేదా దత్తత తీసుకున్నవారికి Explanation పరిమితం చేస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(5): 20 డిసెంబర్ 2004 కి ముందు జరిగిన విభజనకు ఈ సెక్షన్ వర్తించదు. "విభజన" అంటే రిజిస్టర్డ్ దస్తావేజు లేదా కోర్టు డిక్రీ ద్వారా జరిగిన విభజన. సెక్షన్ 30 Explanation: మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తిలో పురుష హిందువు హక్కు అతను వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వగల ఆస్తి. 2005 సవరణ సెక్షన్ 30 ను "disposed of by him or by her" అని చదివేలా చేసింది. రాష్ట్ర చట్టాలు: చట్టం పాఠం కర్ణాటక సెక్షన్లు 6A నుండి 6C, తమిళనాడు సెక్షన్లు 29-A నుండి 29-C ను ముద్రిస్తుంది. రెండూ తమ తమ తేదీల నుండి కుమార్తెలకు కోపార్సినరీ హక్కులు ఇస్తాయి. Hindu Succession (Karnataka Amendment) Act, 1990 కి ముందు వివాహమైన కుమార్తెకు కర్ణాటక సెక్షన్ 6A(d) విభజనలో clause (b) వాటాను నిరాకరిస్తుంది. తమిళనాడు చట్టానికి ముందు వివాహమైన కుమార్తెను తమిళనాడు సెక్షన్ 29-A(iv) మినహాయిస్తుంది. రెండు రాష్ట్ర చట్టాలూ తమ ప్రారంభానికి ముందటి విభజనలను కాపాడుతాయి. మహారాష్ట్ర చట్టం, 1994, కేరళ చట్టం, 1975 వాటి సొంత పాఠాల నుండి కింద వివరించబడ్డాయి.

ఇక్కడ పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తి అంటే మితాక్షర కోపార్సినరీ ఆస్తి, అంటే ఒక ఉమ్మడి హిందూ కుటుంబం కలిగి ఉన్న ఆస్తి; అది దాని సభ్యులకు పుట్టుకతో వచ్చే హక్కును ఇస్తుంది. కోపార్సినర్‌కు దానిలో పుట్టుకతో వచ్చే హక్కు ఉంటుంది. 2005 కి ముందు కుమారులు మాత్రమే పుట్టుకతో కోపార్సినర్లు. ఇప్పుడు కుమార్తె కూడా అదే హక్కులు, బాధ్యతలతో కోపార్సినర్; వివాహమైన కుమార్తెను మినహాయించే నియమం సెక్షన్ 6 లో ఏదీ లేదు. పుట్టుకతో కోపార్సినర్. ఆమె హక్కు పుట్టుక నుండి వస్తుంది, ఎవరి మరణం నుండీ కాదు. ఇది పాత అప్రతిబంధ దాయ భావన, ఇప్పుడు కుమార్తెలకూ వర్తిస్తుంది ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 55, 63). విభజన హక్కు. విభజన కోరగలిగినవాడే కోపార్సినర్. 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 నుండి కుమార్తె విభజన కోరవచ్చు (para 79). Retroactive. సెక్షన్ 6 ఒక retroactive చట్టం : అది 9 సెప్టెంబర్ 2005 నుండి పనిచేస్తుంది, కానీ అంతకు ముందటి సంఘటన అయిన ఆమె పుట్టుక ఆధారంగా (paras 55 నుండి 57). పూర్వీకుల ఆస్తిలో కుమార్తెల హక్కు. hi.inOneMinute: The rule. Since 9 September 2005, Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 makes the daughter of a coparcener a coparcener by birth. She has the same rights and liabilities as a son. Father need not be alive. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), a three-Judge Bench held that her father need not have been alive on that date. Saved partitions. The right does not reopen a partition made before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed or a court decree. An oral partition is accepted only in exceptional cases. The cases. Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) had required a living father; Danamma (2018) gave daughters a share though the father died in 2001. Vineeta Sharma settled the conflict.
legalProvision: Section 6(1) (as substituted by Act 39 of 2005). Devolution of interest in coparcenary property. ―On and from the commencement of the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener shall,―(a) by birth become a coparcener in her own right in the same manner as the son; (b) have the same rights in the coparcenary property as she would have had if she had been a son; (c) be subject to the same liabilities in respect of the said coparcenary property as that of a son, and any reference to a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener shall be deemed to include a reference to a daughter of a coparcener: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall affect or invalidate any disposition or alienation including any partition or testamentary disposition of property which had taken place before the 20th day of December, 2004.

Section 6(5). ―Nothing contained in this section shall apply to a partition, which has been effected before the 20th day of December, 2004. Explanation.―For the purposes of this section "partition" means any partition made by execution of a deed of partition duly registered under the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) or partition effected by a decree of a court.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 6(1): from the commencement of the 2005 Amendment, in a Joint Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law, the daughter of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth in her own right, in the same manner as the son. She has the same rights and the same liabilities. Any reference to a Mitakshara coparcener includes the daughter of a coparcener. Proviso to Section 6(1): it saves any disposition, alienation, partition or testamentary disposition made before 20 December 2004. Section 6(2): property she gets under Section 6(1) is held with the incidents of coparcenary ownership. She can dispose of it by will . Section 6(3): on a Hindu's death after the Amendment, his interest devolves by will or intestate succession and not by survivorship . A partition is deemed to have taken place, and the daughter gets the same share as a son. Section 6(4): after the Amendment, no court recognises a right to proceed against a son, grandson or great-grandson for his father's, grandfather's or great-grandfather's debt solely on the ground of pious obligation . The proviso keeps the creditor's right, and any alienation made for such a debt, for debts contracted before the Amendment. The Explanation limits "son", "grandson" and "great-grandson" in that proviso to those born or adopted before the Amendment. Section 6(5): the section does not apply to a partition effected before 20 December 2004. "Partition" means a partition by a registered deed or by a court decree. Explanation to Section 30: the interest of a male Hindu in Mitakshara coparcenary property is property he can dispose of by will. The 2005 Amendment made Section 30 read "disposed of by him or by her". State laws: the Act text prints Karnataka Sections 6A to 6C and Tamil Nadu Sections 29-A to 29-C. Both give daughters coparcenary rights from their own dates. Karnataka Section 6A(d) denies the clause (b) share on partition to a daughter married before the Hindu Succession (Karnataka Amendment) Act, 1990. Tamil Nadu Section 29-A(iv) excludes a daughter married before the Tamil Nadu Act. Both State Acts save partitions made before their commencement. The Maharashtra Act, 1994 and the Kerala Act, 1975 are described below from their own texts.
hi.meaning:
Ancestral property here means Mitakshara coparcenary property held by a joint Hindu family , which gives its members a right from birth. A coparcener has a birthright interest in it. Before 2005, only sons were coparceners by birth. Now a daughter is one too, with the same rights and liabilities, and no rule in Section 6 excludes a married daughter. Coparcener by birth. Her right comes from birth, not from anyone's death. This is the old idea of unobstructed heritage , now applied to daughters ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 55, 63). Right to partition. A coparcener is one who can claim partition. The daughter can claim partition from 9 September 2005 (para 79). Retroactive. Section 6 is a retroactive statute : it operates from 9 September 2005, but on the basis of an earlier event, her birth (paras 55 to 57). Daughters' right to ancestral property. See Diagram 1 . Question 1: was there a partition before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed that was acted upon, or by a final court decree? Yes: the partition is saved (Section 6(5)). No: question 2: is only an oral partition alleged? Yes: it counts only in exceptional cases, on cogent public documents (paras 127, 128). No: she is a coparcener by birth from 9 September 2005, with the same rights and liabilities as a son, whether born before or after 2005 and whether or not her father was alive (Vineeta Sharma). Point Rule Status Coparcener by birth, in her own right Rights and liabilities Same as a son's Saved transactions Registered partition deed or court decree before 20 December 2004 Disposal She can leave her share by will (Section 6(2))
keyPoints: Section 6(1): the daughter of a coparcener is a coparcener by birth, with the same rights and liabilities as a son. Vineeta Sharma (2020): the father need not be alive on 9 September 2005. The amendment is retroactive, not retrospective (paras 55-56). Saved partitions: registered deed or court decree before 20 December 2004. Oral partition only in exceptional cases. Prakash and Mangammal are overruled; Danamma is partly overruled. Preliminary decree is not a partition; daughters claim a share in pending final decree proceedings and appeals (para 129(iv)). Section 6 makes no distinction between married and unmarried daughters. Pending matters to be decided within six months, as far as possible (para 130).

caseLaws.name: Vineeta Sharma v
caseLaws.facts: Rakesh Sharma (2020) Facts. Two Supreme Court benches gave conflicting views on amended Section 6. A three-Judge Bench heard the reference with connected matters and decided on 11 August 2020. Principle. A daughter is a coparcener by birth. She claims her rights from 9 September 2005 whether born before or after it, and whether or not her father was alive. Saved partitions are only those made before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed or a court decree. (2020) 9 SCC 1. Why it matters. It is the leading authority on the daughter's coparcenary right. Prakash v. Phulavati (2015) Facts. Phulavati sued for partition. Her father died on 18 February 1988. The Karnataka High Court applied the 2005 Amendment. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal. Principle. The 2005 rights apply to living daughters of living coparceners on 9 September 2005, whenever the daughters were born. (2016) 2 SCC 36. Why it matters. Overruled in this part by Vineeta Sharma . Danamma @ Suman Surpur v. Amar (2018) Facts. Gurulingappa Savadi died in 2001, leaving two daughters, two sons and a widow. A partition suit was pending when Section 6 was amended. Principle. The amended Section 6 confers full rights on a daughter coparcener. Each of the daughters, sons and widow got a 1/5th share. (2018) 3 SCC 343 : [2018] 2 S.C.R. 553. Why it matters. It differed from Prakash and was partly overruled by Vineeta Sharma (para 130).

selfTest.q: 1. Is a daughter a coparcener by birth?
selfTest.a: Yes, under Section 6(1), from 9 September 2005.

selfTest.q: 2. Must her father be alive on 9 September 2005?
selfTest.a: No ( Vineeta Sharma ).

selfTest.q: 3. Which partitions are saved?
selfTest.a: Those made before 20 December 2004 by a registered deed or a court decree.

selfTest.q: 4. Does a preliminary decree stop the daughter?
selfTest.a: No. Only a final decree effects partition ( Vineeta Sharma , paras 128, 129(iv)).

selfTest.q: 5. Why is the amendment called retroactive?
selfTest.a: It operates from 9 September 2005 but rests on the antecedent event of birth (paras 55 to 57).

selfTest.q: 6. A father dies in 2010 leaving ₹90 lakh of ancestral land, a son and a daughter, with no earlier partition. What does the daughter get?
selfTest.a: ₹45 lakh: ₹30 lakh as a coparcener and ₹15 lakh from her father's share, the same as the son.

family-law-i-u5-t8.subtitle: Section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956: property of a Hindu woman becomes her full property; the narrow exception in section 14(2); Tulasamma

en.inOneMinute: The old law. Under the old law, a Hindu woman who inherited property usually held only a limited estate . On her death it went to the reversioners , not to her own heirs. Section 14(1). The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 changed this. Any property possessed by a female Hindu, acquired before or after the Act, is held by her as full owner and not as a limited owner. Section 14(2). It is a narrow exception for grants that themselves prescribe a restricted estate . Tulasamma. In V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977), the Supreme Court held that the exception does not apply where the grant only gives effect to a right she already had , such as maintenance. Now. In Tej Bhan v. Ram Kishan (2024), the Supreme Court referred the interplay of Sections 14(1) and 14(2) to a larger bench.
legalProvision: Section 14. Property of a female Hindu to be her absolute property. ―(1) Any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be held by her as full owner thereof and not as a limited owner. Explanation.―In this sub-section, "property" includes both movable and immovable property acquired by a female Hindu by inheritance or devise, or at a partition, or in lieu of maintenance or arrears of maintenance, or by gift from any person, whether a relative or not, before, at or after her marriage, or by her own skill or exertion, or by purchase or by prescription, or in any other manner whatsoever, and also any such property held by her as stridhana immediately before the commencement of this Act. (2) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) shall apply to any property acquired by way of gift or under a will or any other instrument or under a decree or order of a civil court or under an award where the terms of the gift, will or other instrument or the decree, order or award prescribe a restricted estate in such property.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 15(1): when a female Hindu dies intestate, her property goes firstly to her sons and daughters (including the children of a pre-deceased son or daughter) and her husband, secondly to the husband's heirs, thirdly to her mother and father, fourthly to the father's heirs, and lastly to the mother's heirs. Section 15(2): property she inherited from her father or mother goes, if she leaves no child (or child of a pre-deceased child), to the father's heirs. Property she inherited from her husband or father-in-law goes in the same case to the husband's heirs. Kerala (Act 17 of 2016) adds property inherited from a pre-deceased son, which goes to that son's heirs. Section 30: any Hindu may dispose of property by will under the Indian Succession Act, 1925. Section 14(2) refers to a "will" as one of the instruments that may prescribe a restricted estate . Section 31 (repeal): the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 is repealed , without affecting rights already acquired (Mulla, 14th ed.).
en.meaning:
A "limited estate" is an interest that a Hindu woman held for her own life, without full power to dispose of it. Section 14(1) turns such an interest into full ownership by force of the statute. No court order or new document is needed. Stridhan she already held is also covered by the Explanation. Limited owner. She enjoys the whole income but cannot alienate the corpus except for legal necessity , benefit of the estate or with the reversioners' consent (Mulla, 14th ed., § 176). Full owner. She can sell, give or will the property, and on her death it goes to her own heirs under Section 15. Reversioner. The heir of the last full owner who would take on the limited heir's death. His interest is a mere chance of succession (spes successionis), not a vested interest (Mulla, § 175). What Section 14 does. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Section 14(1) turns a woman's limited estate into full ownership; Section 14(2) is a narrow exception. flowchart TD O["Before 1956: woman's estate

that itself prescribes a restricted estate"] X --> XR["Restriction stays"] Text description Before 1956: a woman's estate; no alienation of the corpus without legal necessity, benefit of the estate or reversioners' consent; on her death it goes to the reversioners. Section 14(1): property possessed by a female Hindu, acquired before or after the Act in any manner, including stridhana, is held as full owner. On her death it goes to her own heirs under Section 15. Exception, Section 14(2): a gift, will, instrument, decree, order or award that itself prescribes a restricted estate; the restriction stays. Part Rule Section 14(1) Property possessed by a female Hindu is held as full owner, not as a limited owner Explanation Covers property acquired in any manner, including stridhana Section 14(2) Exception: a grant that itself prescribes a restricted estate Tulasamma test A grant that gives effect to a pre-existing right falls under Section 14(1)
keyPoints: Section 14(1): property possessed by a Hindu woman, acquired before or after the Act, is her full property. The Explanation covers property acquired in any manner, including stridhana. Before 1956 a widow's estate was limited: no sale of the corpus without legal necessity, benefit of the estate or reversioners' consent. The 1937 Act gave the widow a son's share as a Hindu woman's estate (Mulla, 14th ed.). Section 14(2) is a narrow exception for grants that prescribe a restricted estate. Tulasamma : a grant giving effect to a pre-existing right falls under Section 14(1). Section 14 decides the kind of ownership; Section 15 decides the heirs. "Possessed" includes constructive possession; the possession must rest on some right or title. Tej Bhan (December 2024) refers the Section 14(1) and 14(2) conflict to a larger bench.

caseLaws.name: V
caseLaws.facts: Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) Facts. Tulasamma's husband died in 1931. A 1949 compromise of her maintenance claim gave her a limited interest in properties. She sold some after 1956. Sesha Reddy sued, saying the sales did not bind him. Principle. Property given to satisfy a right she already had, such as maintenance, is held under Section 14(1) whatever the document says. Section 14(2) covers only new titles. AIR 1977 SC 1944 : (1977) 3 SCC 99. Why it matters. Foundational authority on Sections 14(1) and 14(2). Tej Bhan v. Ram Kishan (2024), reference order Facts. A widow had a life estate under her husband's will of 1965 and sold the land in 1981. Principle. Tulasamma 's principles "substantially hold the field", but inconsistent decisions exist. The matter goes to a larger bench. 2024 INSC 945. Why it matters. It shows the present uncertainty on Section 14(2).

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 14(1) do?
selfTest.a: It makes property possessed by a female Hindu her full property, not a limited estate.

selfTest.q: 2. When does Section 14(2) apply?
selfTest.a: Only where the document is the sole source of a wholly new, restricted title.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case set the pre-existing right test?
selfTest.a: V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977).

selfTest.q: 4. Is "restricted estate" the same as "limited interest"?
selfTest.a: No. It is wider and covers any restriction ( Tulasamma ).

selfTest.q: 5. What happened in Tej Bhan v. Ram Kishan (2024)?
selfTest.a: The bench found the cases inconsistent and referred Section 14 to a larger bench.

selfTest.q: 6. A widow took ₹10 lakh under the 1937 Act in 1950 and was in possession in 1956. What is her estate now?
selfTest.a: Full ownership of the ₹10 lakh, by Section 14(1), from the commencement of the Act.
