"పరిమిత ఎస్టేట్" అంటే హిందూ స్త్రీ తన జీవితకాలం పాటు, అమ్మే పూర్తి అధికారం లేకుండా కలిగి ఉన్న హక్కు. సెక్షన్ 14(1) చట్టం యొక్క బలంతో ఈ హక్కును పూర్తి యాజమాన్యంగా మారుస్తుంది. కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు గానీ కొత్త పత్రం గానీ అవసరం లేదు. ఆమె అప్పటికే కలిగి ఉన్న స్త్రీధనం కూడా Explanation లో వస్తుంది. పరిమిత యజమాని. ఆమె మొత్తం ఆదాయాన్ని అనుభవిస్తుంది, కానీ చట్టపరమైన అవసరం , ఎస్టేట్ ప్రయోజనం లేదా రివర్షనర్ల సమ్మతి ఉంటేనే మూలధనాన్ని బదిలీ చేయగలదు (Mulla, 14th ed., § 176). పూర్తి యజమాని. ఆమె ఆస్తిని అమ్మవచ్చు, దానం చేయవచ్చు, వీలునామా రాయవచ్చు; ఆమె మరణించాక అది సెక్షన్ 15 ప్రకారం ఆమె సొంత వారసులకు వెళ్తుంది. రివర్షనర్. పరిమిత వారసురాలు మరణించాక ఆస్తిని తీసుకునే, చివరి పూర్తి యజమాని యొక్క వారసుడు. అతని హక్కు వారసత్వం పొందే ఒక అవకాశం మాత్రమే (spes successionis), స్థిరపడిన హక్కు కాదు (Mulla, § 175). సెక్షన్ 14 ఏమి చేస్తుంది. selfTest.a: హిందూ స్త్రీ స్వాధీనంలోని ఆస్తిని పరిమిత ఎస్టేట్‌గా కాకుండా ఆమె పూర్తి ఆస్తిగా చేస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 14(2) ఎప్పుడు వర్తిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: పత్రమే పూర్తిగా కొత్త, నిర్బంధిత టైటిల్‌కు ఏకైక మూలం అయినప్పుడు మాత్రమే.

selfTest.q: 3. ముందే ఉన్న హక్కు పరీక్షను ఏ కేసు నిర్ణయించింది?
selfTest.a: V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977).

selfTest.q: 4. "Restricted estate", "limited interest" ఒకటేనా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అది విస్తృతమైనది, ఏ పరిమితినైనా కవర్ చేస్తుంది ( Tulasamma ).

selfTest.q: 5. Tej Bhan v. Ram Kishan (2024) లో ఏమి జరిగింది?
selfTest.a: కేసులు పరస్పర విరుద్ధంగా ఉన్నాయని ధర్మాసనం భావించి, సెక్షన్ 14 ను పెద్ద ధర్మాసనానికి పంపింది.

selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 14(1) ద్వారా, చట్టం ప్రారంభం నుండి ఆ ₹10 లక్షలకు పూర్తి యాజమాన్యం.

hi.inOneMinute: The old law. Under the old law, a Hindu woman who inherited property usually held only a limited estate . On her death it went to the reversioners , not to her own heirs. Section 14(1). The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 changed this. Any property possessed by a female Hindu, acquired before or after the Act, is held by her as full owner and not as a limited owner. Section 14(2). It is a narrow exception for grants that themselves prescribe a restricted estate . Tulasamma. In V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977), the Supreme Court held that the exception does not apply where the grant only gives effect to a right she already had , such as maintenance. Now. In Tej Bhan v. Ram Kishan (2024), the Supreme Court referred the interplay of Sections 14(1) and 14(2) to a larger bench.
legalProvision: Section 14. Property of a female Hindu to be her absolute property. ―(1) Any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be held by her as full owner thereof and not as a limited owner. Explanation.―In this sub-section, "property" includes both movable and immovable property acquired by a female Hindu by inheritance or devise, or at a partition, or in lieu of maintenance or arrears of maintenance, or by gift from any person, whether a relative or not, before, at or after her marriage, or by her own skill or exertion, or by purchase or by prescription, or in any other manner whatsoever, and also any such property held by her as stridhana immediately before the commencement of this Act. (2) Nothing contained in sub-section (1) shall apply to any property acquired by way of gift or under a will or any other instrument or under a decree or order of a civil court or under an award where the terms of the gift, will or other instrument or the decree, order or award prescribe a restricted estate in such property.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 15(1): when a female Hindu dies intestate, her property goes firstly to her sons and daughters (including the children of a pre-deceased son or daughter) and her husband, secondly to the husband's heirs, thirdly to her mother and father, fourthly to the father's heirs, and lastly to the mother's heirs. Section 15(2): property she inherited from her father or mother goes, if she leaves no child (or child of a pre-deceased child), to the father's heirs. Property she inherited from her husband or father-in-law goes in the same case to the husband's heirs. Kerala (Act 17 of 2016) adds property inherited from a pre-deceased son, which goes to that son's heirs. Section 30: any Hindu may dispose of property by will under the Indian Succession Act, 1925. Section 14(2) refers to a "will" as one of the instruments that may prescribe a restricted estate . Section 31 (repeal): the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 is repealed , without affecting rights already acquired (Mulla, 14th ed.).
hi.meaning:
A "limited estate" is an interest that a Hindu woman held for her own life, without full power to dispose of it. Section 14(1) turns such an interest into full ownership by force of the statute. No court order or new document is needed. Stridhan she already held is also covered by the Explanation. Limited owner. She enjoys the whole income but cannot alienate the corpus except for legal necessity , benefit of the estate or with the reversioners' consent (Mulla, 14th ed., § 176). Full owner. She can sell, give or will the property, and on her death it goes to her own heirs under Section 15. Reversioner. The heir of the last full owner who would take on the limited heir's death. His interest is a mere chance of succession (spes successionis), not a vested interest (Mulla, § 175). What Section 14 does. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. that itself prescribes a restricted estate"] X --> XR["Restriction stays"] Text description Before 1956: a woman's estate; no alienation of the corpus without legal necessity, benefit of the estate or reversioners' consent; on her death it goes to the reversioners. Section 14(1): property possessed by a female Hindu, acquired before or after the Act in any manner, including stridhana, is held as full owner. On her death it goes to her own heirs under Section 15. Exception, Section 14(2): a gift, will, instrument, decree, order or award that itself prescribes a restricted estate; the restriction stays. Part Rule Section 14(1) Property possessed by a female Hindu is held as full owner, not as a limited owner Explanation Covers property acquired in any manner, including stridhana Section 14(2) Exception: a grant that itself prescribes a restricted estate Tulasamma test A grant that gives effect to a pre-existing right falls under Section 14(1)
keyPoints: Section 14(1): property possessed by a Hindu woman, acquired before or after the Act, is her full property. The Explanation covers property acquired in any manner, including stridhana. Before 1956 a widow's estate was limited: no sale of the corpus without legal necessity, benefit of the estate or reversioners' consent. The 1937 Act gave the widow a son's share as a Hindu woman's estate (Mulla, 14th ed.). Section 14(2) is a narrow exception for grants that prescribe a restricted estate. Tulasamma : a grant giving effect to a pre-existing right falls under Section 14(1). Section 14 decides the kind of ownership; Section 15 decides the heirs. "Possessed" includes constructive possession; the possession must rest on some right or title. Tej Bhan (December 2024) refers the Section 14(1) and 14(2) conflict to a larger bench.

caseLaws.name: V
caseLaws.facts: Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) Facts. Tulasamma's husband died in 1931. A 1949 compromise of her maintenance claim gave her a limited interest in properties. She sold some after 1956. Sesha Reddy sued, saying the sales did not bind him. Principle. Property given to satisfy a right she already had, such as maintenance, is held under Section 14(1) whatever the document says. Section 14(2) covers only new titles. AIR 1977 SC 1944 : (1977) 3 SCC 99. Why it matters. Foundational authority on Sections 14(1) and 14(2). Tej Bhan v. Ram Kishan (2024), reference order Facts. A widow had a life estate under her husband's will of 1965 and sold the land in 1981. Principle. Tulasamma 's principles "substantially hold the field", but inconsistent decisions exist. The matter goes to a larger bench. 2024 INSC 945. Why it matters. It shows the present uncertainty on Section 14(2).

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 14(1) do?
selfTest.a: It makes property possessed by a female Hindu her full property, not a limited estate.

selfTest.q: 2. When does Section 14(2) apply?
selfTest.a: Only where the document is the sole source of a wholly new, restricted title.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case set the pre-existing right test?
selfTest.a: V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977).

selfTest.q: 4. Is "restricted estate" the same as "limited interest"?
selfTest.a: No. It is wider and covers any restriction ( Tulasamma ).

selfTest.q: 5. What happened in Tej Bhan v. Ram Kishan (2024)?
selfTest.a: The bench found the cases inconsistent and referred Section 14 to a larger bench.

selfTest.q: 6. A widow took ₹10 lakh under the 1937 Act in 1950 and was in possession in 1956. What is her estate now?
selfTest.a: Full ownership of the ₹10 lakh, by Section 14(1), from the commencement of the Act.

family-law-i-u5-t7.subtitle: The Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956: sixteen class I heirs, nine entries of class II heirs, and how agnates and cognates follow

en.inOneMinute: Two classes in the Schedule. The Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 lists the heirs of a male Hindu in two classes. Class I has sixteen heirs, such as the son, daughter, widow and mother. Class II has nine entries, beginning with the father. Order. Class I heirs take together and shut out everyone else. Class II comes next, entry by entry. After class II come agnates and then cognates (Section 8). Sharing. Class I heirs share by the four rules of Section 10. Heirs in one class II entry share equally (Section 11). Agnates and cognates are chosen by degrees (Sections 12 and 13).
legalProvision: Section 9. Order of succession among heirs in the Schedule. ―Among the heirs specified in the Schedule, those in class I shall take simultaneously and to the exclusion of all other heirs; those in the first entry in class II shall be preferred to those in the second entry; those in the second entry shall be preferred to those in the third entry; and so on in succession.

Section 12. Order of succession among agnates and cognates. ―The order of succession among agnates or cognates, as the case may be, shall be determined in accordance with the rules of preference laid down hereunder:― Rule 1.―Of two heirs, the one who has fewer or no degrees of ascent is preferred. Rule 2.―Where the number of degrees of ascent is the same or none, that heir is preferred who has fewer or no degrees of descent. Rule 3.―Where neither heir is entitled to be preferred to the other under Rule 1 or Rule 2 they take simultaneously.

Section 13. Computation of degrees. ―(1) For the purposes of determining the order of succession among agnates or cognates, relationship shall be reckoned from the intestate to the heir in terms of degrees of ascent or degrees of descent or both, as the case may be. (2) Degrees of ascent and degrees of descent shall be computed inclusive of the intestate. (3) Every generation constitutes a degree either ascending or descending.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 8: property of a male Hindu goes firstly to class I of the Schedule, secondly to class II, thirdly to agnates, lastly to cognates. Section 10: shares among class I heirs (Rules 1 to 4). Section 11: heirs in one class II entry share equally. Section 3(1)(a) and (c): definitions of agnate and cognate . Section 3(1)(e): full blood, half blood and uterine blood. Section 3(1)(f), (g) and (j): "heir" is any person, male or female, entitled to succeed to the property of an intestate under the Act. A person dies "intestate" in respect of property not disposed of by a will capable of taking effect. "Related" means related by legitimate kinship. Illegitimate children are related to their mother and to one another, and their legitimate descendants are related to them. Section 2: the Act applies to Hindus in any form, including Virashaivas, Lingayats and followers of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj, to Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs, and to others who are not Muslims, Christians, Parsis or Jews unless shown not to be governed by Hindu law. It does not apply to members of a Scheduled Tribe unless the Central Government notifies otherwise (Section 2(2)). Section 4: any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law, or custom, in force before the Act ceases to have effect on a matter the Act provides for. The Schedule: the lists of class I and class II heirs, with the Explanation on uterine brothers and sisters.
en.meaning:
Class I heirs are the closest relatives: the deceased's children, widow, mother and certain later generations. Class II heirs are the next group, such as the father, brothers, sisters and some grandchildren. An agnate is related wholly through males. A cognate is related, but not wholly through males. Heir. Any person, male or female, entitled to succeed to the property of an intestate under the Act (Section 3(1)(f)). Class. A list in the Schedule. Class I is one group; class II is nine groups called entries. Agnate and cognate. Relatives outside the Schedule, used only when the Schedule has no heir (Section 8). Order of the classes. keyPoints: Class I has sixteen heirs, four of them added in 2005. Class II has nine entries. Class I heirs take together and shut out all others (Section 9). The mother is in class I; the father is in class II, Entry I. Class II: an earlier entry beats a later entry; one entry shares equally (Sections 9 and 11). Brother or sister in the Schedule does not include uterine brother or sister. Section 10: widow(s) one share; each son, daughter and the mother one share; each pre-deceased child's branch one share. Agnates before cognates; fewer degrees of ascent, then fewer degrees of descent (Sections 12, 13). Chander Sen : a son inheriting under Section 8 takes individually, not as karta.

caseLaws.name: Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v
caseLaws.facts: Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died intestate on 17 July 1965. His only son, Chander Sen, inherited Rs.1,85,043 from the firm account. The Wealth-tax Officer counted it as joint family wealth. Principle. Under Section 8, a class I heir takes his father's separate property in his individual capacity, not as karta. AIR 1986 SC 1753 : (1986) 3 SCC 567. Why it matters. It shows the effect of being a class I heir. Vellikannu v. R. Singaperumal (2005) Facts. A son murdered his father in 1972, was convicted and was released in 1975. His wife sued to inherit the father's estate through him. Principle. A disqualified murderer is treated as non-existent and not as the stock of a fresh line of descent. His wife cannot claim through him (Sections 25, 27). (2005) 6 SCC 622. Why it matters. It shows that a class I heir can be disqualified, and that no claim can pass through him.

selfTest.q: 1. How many class I heirs are there?
selfTest.a: Sixteen. The last four were added in 2005.

selfTest.q: 2. Where is the father in the Schedule?
selfTest.a: Class II, Entry I.

selfTest.q: 3. What happens if there is a class I heir?
selfTest.a: Class I heirs take together and shut out everyone else (Section 9).

selfTest.q: 4. How does Section 12 choose between two agnates?
selfTest.a: The one with fewer or no degrees of ascent; then fewer or no degrees of descent; if neither, they take together.

selfTest.q: 5. How does a son who inherits under Section 8 hold the property?
selfTest.a: In his individual capacity, not as karta ( Chander Sen ).

selfTest.q: 6. A man leaves ₹90 lakh, a widow, a son and a pre-deceased son's widow and two children. What does the pre-deceased son's widow get?
selfTest.a: ₹10 lakh: one-third of ₹30 lakh, the branch's share.

సెక్షన్ 8: హిందూ పురుషుడి ఆస్తి మొదట షెడ్యూల్ క్లాస్ I కు, రెండోది క్లాస్ II కు, మూడోది అగ్నేట్లకు, చివరగా కాగ్నేట్లకు వెళ్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 10: క్లాస్ I వారసుల మధ్య వాటాలు (Rules 1 నుంచి 4). సెక్షన్ 11: క్లాస్ II లో ఒకే ఎంట్రీలోని వారసులు సమానంగా పంచుకుంటారు. సెక్షన్ 3(1)(a), (c): అగ్నేట్, కాగ్నేట్ నిర్వచనాలు. సెక్షన్ 3(1)(e): పూర్తి రక్తం, అర్ధ రక్తం, గర్భ రక్తం. సెక్షన్ 3(1)(f), (g), (j): "వారసుడు" అంటే చట్టం కింద వీలునామా లేకుండా మరణించిన వ్యక్తి ఆస్తికి వారసత్వం పొందే అర్హత ఉన్న ఏ వ్యక్తి అయినా, పురుషుడు లేదా స్త్రీ. అమలయ్యే వీలునామా ద్వారా ఇవ్వని ఆస్తి విషయంలో వ్యక్తి "వీలునామా లేకుండా" మరణించినట్లు. "సంబంధం" అంటే చట్టబద్ధ బంధుత్వం. అక్రమ సంతానం తమ తల్లితో, ఒకరితో ఒకరు సంబంధం కలిగి ఉంటారు; వారి చట్టబద్ధ వంశీయులు వారితో సంబంధం కలిగి ఉంటారు. సెక్షన్ 2: చట్టం ఏ రూపంలోనైనా హిందువులకు, వీరశైవులు, లింగాయతులు, బ్రహ్మో, ప్రార్థన, ఆర్య సమాజ అనుచరులతో సహా; బౌద్ధులు, జైనులు, సిక్కులకు; హిందూ చట్టం వర్తించదని రుజువు కాకపోతే ముస్లింలు, క్రైస్తవులు, పార్సీలు, యూదులు కాని ఇతరులకు వర్తిస్తుంది. కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం వేరే విధంగా నోటిఫై చేస్తే తప్ప షెడ్యూల్డ్ తెగల సభ్యులకు వర్తించదు (సెక్షన్ 2(2)). సెక్షన్ 4: చట్టానికి ముందు అమలులో ఉన్న హిందూ చట్టపు ఏ పాఠం, నియమం, వ్యాఖ్యానం లేదా ఆచారమైనా, చట్టం నిబంధన చేసిన విషయంలో ప్రభావం కోల్పోతుంది. షెడ్యూల్: క్లాస్ I, క్లాస్ II వారసుల జాబితాలు, గర్భ రక్త సోదర సోదరీలపై Explanation తో.

క్లాస్ I వారసులు అత్యంత దగ్గరి బంధువులు: మరణించిన వ్యక్తి పిల్లలు, వితంతువు, తల్లి, కొన్ని తర్వాతి తరాలు. క్లాస్ II వారసులు తర్వాతి గుంపు, తండ్రి, సోదరులు, సోదరీలు, కొందరు మనవలు వంటివారు. అగ్నేట్ పూర్తిగా పురుషుల ద్వారా సంబంధం ఉన్నవారు. కాగ్నేట్ సంబంధం ఉన్నా, పూర్తిగా పురుషుల ద్వారా కాదు. వారసుడు. చట్టం కింద వీలునామా లేకుండా మరణించిన వ్యక్తి ఆస్తికి వారసత్వం పొందే అర్హత ఉన్న ఏ వ్యక్తి అయినా, పురుషుడు లేదా స్త్రీ (సెక్షన్ 3(1)(f)). తరగతి. షెడ్యూల్‌లోని ఒక జాబితా. క్లాస్ I ఒక గుంపు; క్లాస్ II ఎంట్రీలు అనే తొమ్మిది గుంపులు. అగ్నేట్, కాగ్నేట్. షెడ్యూల్ బయటి బంధువులు; షెడ్యూల్‌లో వారసుడు లేనప్పుడే వస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 8). తరగతుల క్రమం. selfTest.q: 1. క్లాస్ I వారసులు ఎంతమంది?
selfTest.a: పదహారు మంది. చివరి నలుగురిని 2005 లో చేర్చారు.

selfTest.q: 2. షెడ్యూల్‌లో తండ్రి ఎక్కడ ఉన్నాడు?
selfTest.a: క్లాస్ II, ఎంట్రీ I.

selfTest.q: 3. క్లాస్ I వారసుడు ఉంటే ఏమవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: క్లాస్ I వారసులు కలిసి పొంది మిగతా అందరినీ మినహాయిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 9).

selfTest.q: 4. ఇద్దరు అగ్నేట్ల మధ్య సెక్షన్ 12 ఎలా ఎంచుకుంటుంది?
selfTest.a: తక్కువ లేదా అసలు ఆరోహణ డిగ్రీలు లేనివారు; తర్వాత తక్కువ లేదా అసలు అవరోహణ డిగ్రీలు లేనివారు; ఎవరికీ కాకపోతే కలిసి పొందుతారు.

selfTest.q: 5. సెక్షన్ 8 కింద వారసత్వం పొందే కొడుకు ఆస్తిని ఎలా కలిగి ఉంటాడు?
selfTest.a: కర్తగా కాకుండా వ్యక్తిగత హోదాలో ( Chander Sen ).

selfTest.q: 6. ఒక వ్యక్తి ₹90 లక్షలు, వితంతువు, కొడుకు, ముందే మరణించిన కొడుకు వితంతువు, ఇద్దరు పిల్లలను వదిలాడు. ముందే మరణించిన కొడుకు వితంతువుకు ఎంత వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: ₹10 లక్షలు: శాఖ వాటా అయిన ₹30 లక్షలలో మూడో వంతు.

hi.inOneMinute: Two classes in the Schedule. The Schedule to the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 lists the heirs of a male Hindu in two classes. Class I has sixteen heirs, such as the son, daughter, widow and mother. Class II has nine entries, beginning with the father. Order. Class I heirs take together and shut out everyone else. Class II comes next, entry by entry. After class II come agnates and then cognates (Section 8). Sharing. Class I heirs share by the four rules of Section 10. Heirs in one class II entry share equally (Section 11). Agnates and cognates are chosen by degrees (Sections 12 and 13).
legalProvision: Section 9. Order of succession among heirs in the Schedule. ―Among the heirs specified in the Schedule, those in class I shall take simultaneously and to the exclusion of all other heirs; those in the first entry in class II shall be preferred to those in the second entry; those in the second entry shall be preferred to those in the third entry; and so on in succession.

Section 12. Order of succession among agnates and cognates. ―The order of succession among agnates or cognates, as the case may be, shall be determined in accordance with the rules of preference laid down hereunder:― Rule 1.―Of two heirs, the one who has fewer or no degrees of ascent is preferred. Rule 2.―Where the number of degrees of ascent is the same or none, that heir is preferred who has fewer or no degrees of descent. Rule 3.―Where neither heir is entitled to be preferred to the other under Rule 1 or Rule 2 they take simultaneously.

Section 13. Computation of degrees. ―(1) For the purposes of determining the order of succession among agnates or cognates, relationship shall be reckoned from the intestate to the heir in terms of degrees of ascent or degrees of descent or both, as the case may be. (2) Degrees of ascent and degrees of descent shall be computed inclusive of the intestate. (3) Every generation constitutes a degree either ascending or descending.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 8: property of a male Hindu goes firstly to class I of the Schedule, secondly to class II, thirdly to agnates, lastly to cognates. Section 10: shares among class I heirs (Rules 1 to 4). Section 11: heirs in one class II entry share equally. Section 3(1)(a) and (c): definitions of agnate and cognate . Section 3(1)(e): full blood, half blood and uterine blood. Section 3(1)(f), (g) and (j): "heir" is any person, male or female, entitled to succeed to the property of an intestate under the Act. A person dies "intestate" in respect of property not disposed of by a will capable of taking effect. "Related" means related by legitimate kinship. Illegitimate children are related to their mother and to one another, and their legitimate descendants are related to them. Section 2: the Act applies to Hindus in any form, including Virashaivas, Lingayats and followers of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj, to Buddhists, Jainas and Sikhs, and to others who are not Muslims, Christians, Parsis or Jews unless shown not to be governed by Hindu law. It does not apply to members of a Scheduled Tribe unless the Central Government notifies otherwise (Section 2(2)). Section 4: any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law, or custom, in force before the Act ceases to have effect on a matter the Act provides for. The Schedule: the lists of class I and class II heirs, with the Explanation on uterine brothers and sisters.
hi.meaning:
Class I heirs are the closest relatives: the deceased's children, widow, mother and certain later generations. Class II heirs are the next group, such as the father, brothers, sisters and some grandchildren. An agnate is related wholly through males. A cognate is related, but not wholly through males. Heir. Any person, male or female, entitled to succeed to the property of an intestate under the Act (Section 3(1)(f)). Class. A list in the Schedule. Class I is one group; class II is nine groups called entries. Agnate and cognate. Relatives outside the Schedule, used only when the Schedule has no heir (Section 8). Order of the classes. equal within an entry (s. 11)"] C2 -- "none" --> A["3. Agnates
related wholly through males"] A -- "none" --> C["4. Cognates
related, not wholly through males"] Text description Heirs of a male Hindu. First: class I, 16 heirs, who take together and shut out all other heirs. If none: class II, 9 entries, Entry I first, then Entry II and so on, equal within an entry. If none: agnates, related wholly through males. If none: cognates, related but not wholly through males. Order Group How they take 1 Class I (16 heirs) Together; shut out all other heirs (Section 9) 2 Class II (9 entries) Entry I first, then Entry II, and so on; equal within an entry (Sections 9, 11) 3 Agnates Related wholly through males; Section 12 rules 4 Cognates Related, but not wholly through males; Section 12 rules
keyPoints: Class I has sixteen heirs, four of them added in 2005. Class II has nine entries. Class I heirs take together and shut out all others (Section 9). The mother is in class I; the father is in class II, Entry I. Class II: an earlier entry beats a later entry; one entry shares equally (Sections 9 and 11). Brother or sister in the Schedule does not include uterine brother or sister. Section 10: widow(s) one share; each son, daughter and the mother one share; each pre-deceased child's branch one share. Agnates before cognates; fewer degrees of ascent, then fewer degrees of descent (Sections 12, 13). Chander Sen : a son inheriting under Section 8 takes individually, not as karta.

caseLaws.name: Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Kanpur v
caseLaws.facts: Chander Sen (1986) Facts. Rangi Lal died intestate on 17 July 1965. His only son, Chander Sen, inherited Rs.1,85,043 from the firm account. The Wealth-tax Officer counted it as joint family wealth. Principle. Under Section 8, a class I heir takes his father's separate property in his individual capacity, not as karta. AIR 1986 SC 1753 : (1986) 3 SCC 567. Why it matters. It shows the effect of being a class I heir. Vellikannu v. R. Singaperumal (2005) Facts. A son murdered his father in 1972, was convicted and was released in 1975. His wife sued to inherit the father's estate through him. Principle. A disqualified murderer is treated as non-existent and not as the stock of a fresh line of descent. His wife cannot claim through him (Sections 25, 27). (2005) 6 SCC 622. Why it matters. It shows that a class I heir can be disqualified, and that no claim can pass through him.

selfTest.q: 1. How many class I heirs are there?
selfTest.a: Sixteen. The last four were added in 2005.

selfTest.q: 2. Where is the father in the Schedule?
selfTest.a: Class II, Entry I.

selfTest.q: 3. What happens if there is a class I heir?
selfTest.a: Class I heirs take together and shut out everyone else (Section 9).

selfTest.q: 4. How does Section 12 choose between two agnates?
selfTest.a: The one with fewer or no degrees of ascent; then fewer or no degrees of descent; if neither, they take together.

selfTest.q: 5. How does a son who inherits under Section 8 hold the property?
selfTest.a: In his individual capacity, not as karta ( Chander Sen ).

selfTest.q: 6. A man leaves ₹90 lakh, a widow, a son and a pre-deceased son's widow and two children. What does the pre-deceased son's widow get?
selfTest.a: ₹10 lakh: one-third of ₹30 lakh, the branch's share.

family-law-i-u5-t18.subtitle: Sourced from actual Osmania University LL.B. question papers (2016–2026), cross-checked against the official Unit 5 syllabus — every question here is answerable entirely from what's already published on this site. Part A — Short Answer Write a short note on intestate succession. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 as amended by the Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 & the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 Write a short note on notional partition. Explained through Gurupad Khandappa Magdum v. Hirabai Khandappa Magdum (1978). Succession to the property of Hindu Male and Female Part B — Long Answer Discuss the general rules of succession to the property of a Hindu male who dies intestate. Succession to the property of Hindu Male and Female Explain the coparcenary rights of daughters under the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005. Daughter’s right to inherit ancestral property and impact of recent changes in law What are the changes brought about by the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005? The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 as amended by the Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 & the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 Daughter’s right to inherit ancestral property and impact of recent changes in law Write a note on Hindu women's property rights under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Enlargement of limited estate of women into their absolute estate Daughter’s right to inherit ancestral property and impact of recent changes in law Explain the major developments in succession law under the Hindu Succession Act since 1956. Adapted from the original OU question, which read "since 1986" — almost certainly a printing error for "1956"; this version covers the real developments, from the 1956 Act through the 2005 Amendment. The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 as amended by the Hindu Succession (Andhra Pradesh Amendment) Act, 1986 & the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 Daughter’s right to inherit ancestral property and impact of recent changes in law Part C — Problem / Case-Study Questions 'A' has murdered his maternal grandfather with a view to inherit the property. His mother — the grandfather's own daughter — is alive. Discuss the succession rights of A. Intestate succession Succession to the property of Hindu Male and Female A and B, two brothers, were members of a Mitakshara coparcenary, having inherited property from their maternal grandfather. A dies, leaving behind his widow. Can the surviving brother B claim the interest of the deceased A? Succession to the property of Hindu Male and Female Daughter’s right to inherit ancestral property and impact of recent changes in law X dies intestate, leaving his widows W1 and W2, his mother M, two sons S1 and S2, and two daughters D1 and D2. Who is entitled to X's property under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and to what extent? Succession to the property of Hindu Male and Female On A's death, his property devolved upon his mother M as a limited estate holder. R, the next reversioner, murdered M and was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment. Can R take A's property? Can R's sister claim it? "Reversioner" is pre-1956 terminology — under current law, M's limited estate would first mature into full ownership under Section 14 while she was alive, and R's disqualification for her murder would then be assessed under Section 25. Intestate succession Enlargement of limited estate of women into their absolute estate A son murdered his aged parents in order to inherit their property. Their granddaughter is alive. State the son's rights under the succession laws. Intestate succession A Hindu dies intestate, survived by his widow U, his mother M, his married daughter D1 and his unmarried daughter D2, leaving property worth ₹40,00,000. Distribute the property according to law. Succession to the property of Hindu Male and Female Questions are drawn from previous Osmania University LL.B. examination papers for study and revision purposes only.

constitutional-law-i-u1-t2.subtitle: From Magna Carta to the written constitutions of the twentieth century, and what India took from them

en.inOneMinute: A modern constitution is a written constitution : one document, made by a special body (a constituent assembly or convention), which stands above ordinary law, limits government and declares the rights of the people. It grew in stages. England never made one written constitution; its Parliament can "make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country". But English charters and statutes (Magna Carta, Petition of Right, Bill of Rights, Act of Settlement) planted the ideas of rights, rule of law and independent judges. America (1787) made the first great written, federal, republican constitution at the Philadelphia Convention, and later added a Bill of Rights (the first ten amendments). France (1789) called the first Constituent Assembly in Europe and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man. The American model was followed by Canada (1867), Australia (1900) and South Africa (1909) . The 20th century added new ideas: the Weimar Constitution's emergency powers (a warning), the Irish Constitution's Directive Principles, the Japanese Constitution's "procedure established by law". India's Constitution (1949–50) came at the end of this line and consciously borrowed from all of them. Dr. Ambedkar said: "There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing."
legalProvision: There is no Article that describes the history of constitutions. The Constitution of India shows the end-point of this evolution in its own text. (Text: The Constitution of India , Government of India, Legislative Department, edition as on 1 May 2026.)
Preamble (closing words)
IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
Article 21 – No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
Article 32(1) – The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.

Article 37 – The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.

Article 368(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.
In simple words

India's Constitution was made by its own Constituent Assembly (Preamble) – the "constituent assembly" method that began in America and France. It has a written list of rights with a guaranteed court remedy (Part III, Art. 32) – the "bill of rights" idea. Its Directive Principles are not enforceable in court but are "fundamental in the governance of the country" (Art. 37) – the Irish idea. Art. 21's words "procedure established by law" came from the Japanese Constitution of 1946 ( A.K. Gopalan , Kania C.J.). It has its own amendment procedure (Art. 368) – a feature of every rigid written constitution. It replaced the British-made framework (Art. 395).
en.meaning:
1. What "modern constitution" means here. A modern constitution is a deliberately made, usually written, basic law that (a) is framed by a body chosen for that purpose, (b) sets up and limits the organs of government, (c) declares the rights of the people, and (d) can be changed only by a special method. "Evolution" means the step-by-step growth of these features from the English charters to the post-war constitutions of the 20th century.

2. The British contrast. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, temporary Chairman, said on the first day of the Constituent Assembly (9 December 1946): "under the British Constitution, there is no such thing as a constituent law, it being a cherished privilege of the British Parliament, as the sole sovereign authority, to make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country."

3. Why later constitutions look alike. Dr. Ambedkar (4 November 1948): "More than hundred years have rolled over when the first written Constitution was drafted. It has been followed by many countries reducing their Constitutions to writing. What the scope of a Constitution should be has long been settled. Similarly what are the fundamentals of a Constitution are recognized all over the world. Given these facts, all Constitutions in their main provisions must look similar."
keyPoints: Britain: no constituent law; Parliament can "make and unmake all laws" (Sinha, 9 Dec 1946). Magna Carta ch. 39: "by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land". U.S.: Philadelphia Convention, 25 May – 17 Sept 1787; Bill of Rights = first ten amendments. France: first Constituent Assembly, 1789; Declaration of the Rights of Man. Canada: Quebec 1864, 33 delegates, 74 resolutions, BNA Act 1867. Australia: law on 9 July 1900; South Africa: law on 20 Sept 1909. Weimar art. 48 – emergency powers misused (H.V. Kamath). Ireland – directive principles (Ambedkar); Japan 1946 art. 31 – "procedure established by law" ( A.K. Gopalan ). Ambedkar: "There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing."

caseLaws.facts: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , AIR 1950 SC 27; 1950 SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained in Madras jail under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, applied under Art. 32 for habeas corpus, arguing that his detention broke Arts. 19, 21 and 22. Principle: Kania C.J.: "The phrase 'procedure established by law' seems to be borrowed from article 31 of the Japanese Constitution"; the Court contrasted it with the American "due process of law". Why it matters: It shows, in a judgment, how a key Indian provision came from another modern constitution and why its wording mattered.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (as amended) and the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments. Principle: In discussing how a constitution must be read, Chandrachud J contrasted India's Constitution, built "in the hope that it will last", with the French Third Republic Constitution of 1875, framed "in the hope that it will fail"; the majority held that Art. 368 "does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution". Why it matters: It uses the history of other constitutions to explain why a modern constitution must be durable and protected from destruction.

selfTest.q: Why did Sinha say the British had no "constituent law"?
selfTest.a: Answer: Because the British Parliament, as sole sovereign authority, can make and unmake all laws, including constitutional law. When did the Philadelphia Convention meet and finish? Answer: 25 May 1787 to 17 September 1787 (about four months). What is the American Bill of Rights? Answer: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution. From which constitution did India take the idea of directive principles? Answer: The Irish Constitution (Irish Free State / 1937). Which case says "procedure established by law" was borrowed from the Japanese Constitution? Answer: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), Kania C.J. How many delegates and resolutions did the Quebec Convention have? Answer: 33 delegates; 74 resolutions. Which article of the Weimar Constitution was given as a warning about emergency powers? Answer: Article 48. Complete Ambedkar's line: "Nobody holds any patent rights in ..." Answer: "... the fundamental ideas of a Constitution."

te.inOneMinute: ఆధునిక రాజ్యాంగం అంటే లిఖిత రాజ్యాంగం : ఒకే పత్రం, ప్రత్యేక సంస్థ ( రాజ్యాంగ సభ లేదా కన్వెన్షన్) రూపొందించినది, సాధారణ చట్టం కంటే పైన ఉండేది, ప్రభుత్వాన్ని పరిమితం చేసేది, ప్రజల హక్కులను ప్రకటించేది. ఇది దశలవారీగా ఎదిగింది. ఇంగ్లండ్ ఒకే లిఖిత రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ఎప్పుడూ చేయలేదు; దాని పార్లమెంటు "రాజ్యాంగ చట్టంతో సహా అన్ని చట్టాలను చేయగలదు, రద్దు చేయగలదు". కానీ ఆంగ్ల చార్టర్లు, చట్టాలు (మాగ్నా కార్టా, పిటిషన్ ఆఫ్ రైట్, బిల్ ఆఫ్ రైట్స్, యాక్ట్ ఆఫ్ సెటిల్‌మెంట్) హక్కులు, చట్ట పాలన, స్వతంత్ర న్యాయమూర్తుల భావనలను నాటాయి. అమెరికా (1787) ఫిలడెల్ఫియా కన్వెన్షన్‌లో మొదటి గొప్ప లిఖిత, సమాఖ్య, గణతంత్ర రాజ్యాంగాన్ని రూపొందించింది; తర్వాత హక్కుల పత్రం (Bill of Rights) – మొదటి పది సవరణలు – చేర్చింది. ఫ్రాన్స్ (1789) యూరప్‌లో మొదటి రాజ్యాంగ సభను పిలిచి, మానవ హక్కుల ప్రకటన (Declaration of the Rights of Man) చేసింది. అమెరికా నమూనాను కెనడా (1867), ఆస్ట్రేలియా (1900), దక్షిణాఫ్రికా (1909) అనుసరించాయి. 20వ శతాబ్దం కొత్త భావనలు తెచ్చింది: వైమార్ రాజ్యాంగ అత్యవసర అధికారాలు (ఒక హెచ్చరిక), ఐరిష్ రాజ్యాంగ ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలు, జపాన్ రాజ్యాంగంలోని "procedure established by law". భారత రాజ్యాంగం (1949–50) ఈ పరంపర చివరలో వచ్చి, వీటన్నింటి నుండి తెలిసి తెలిసి తీసుకుంది. డా. అంబేద్కర్: "There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing." (తీసుకోవడంలో సిగ్గుపడవలసింది ఏమీ లేదు.)
te.meaning:
1. ఇక్కడ "ఆధునిక రాజ్యాంగం" అంటే. ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా తయారు చేసిన, సాధారణంగా లిఖితమైన ప్రాథమిక చట్టం: (a) ఆ ఉద్దేశం కోసం ఎంపికైన సంస్థ రూపొందిస్తుంది, (b) ప్రభుత్వ వ్యవస్థలను ఏర్పాటు చేసి పరిమితం చేస్తుంది, (c) ప్రజల హక్కులను ప్రకటిస్తుంది, (d) ప్రత్యేక పద్ధతిలో మాత్రమే మారుతుంది. "పరిణామం" అంటే ఆంగ్ల చార్టర్ల నుండి 20వ శతాబ్దపు యుద్ధానంతర రాజ్యాంగాల వరకు ఈ లక్షణాలు దశలవారీగా ఎదగడం.

2. బ్రిటిష్ వ్యత్యాసం. రాజ్యాంగ సభ మొదటి రోజు (9 డిసెంబర్ 1946) తాత్కాలిక అధ్యక్షుడు డా. సచ్చిదానంద సిన్హా ఇలా అన్నారు: "under the British Constitution, there is no such thing as a constituent law, it being a cherished privilege of the British Parliament, as the sole sovereign authority, to make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country." అర్థం: బ్రిటిష్ రాజ్యాంగంలో "రాజ్యాంగ నిర్మాణ చట్టం" అనేదే లేదు; ఏకైక సార్వభౌమ అధికారంగా బ్రిటిష్ పార్లమెంటు దేశపు రాజ్యాంగ చట్టంతో సహా అన్ని చట్టాలను చేయగలదు, రద్దు చేయగలదు.

3. తర్వాతి రాజ్యాంగాలు ఎందుకు ఒకేలా కనిపిస్తాయి. డా. అంబేద్కర్ (4 నవంబర్ 1948): "More than hundred years have rolled over when the first written Constitution was drafted. It has been followed by many countries reducing their Constitutions to writing. What the scope of a Constitution should be has long been settled. Similarly what are the fundamentals of a Constitution are recognized all over the world. Given these facts, all Constitutions in their main provisions must look similar." అర్థం: మొదటి లిఖిత రాజ్యాంగ ం వచ్చి వంద సంవత్సరాలు దాటింది; చాలా దేశాలు తమ రాజ్యాంగాలను రాతలో పెట్టాయి. రాజ్యాంగ పరిధి, దాని ప్రాథమికాంశాలు ప్రపంచమంతా గుర్తించబడ్డాయి. కాబట్టి అన్ని రాజ్యాంగాలు ముఖ్య నిబంధనల్లో ఒకేలా కనిపించాలి.

hi.inOneMinute: A modern constitution is a written constitution : one document, made by a special body (a constituent assembly or convention), which stands above ordinary law, limits government and declares the rights of the people. It grew in stages. England never made one written constitution; its Parliament can "make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country". But English charters and statutes (Magna Carta, Petition of Right, Bill of Rights, Act of Settlement) planted the ideas of rights, rule of law and independent judges. America (1787) made the first great written, federal, republican constitution at the Philadelphia Convention, and later added a Bill of Rights (the first ten amendments). France (1789) called the first Constituent Assembly in Europe and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man. The American model was followed by Canada (1867), Australia (1900) and South Africa (1909) . The 20th century added new ideas: the Weimar Constitution's emergency powers (a warning), the Irish Constitution's Directive Principles, the Japanese Constitution's "procedure established by law". India's Constitution (1949–50) came at the end of this line and consciously borrowed from all of them. Dr. Ambedkar said: "There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing."
legalProvision: There is no Article that describes the history of constitutions. The Constitution of India shows the end-point of this evolution in its own text. (Text: The Constitution of India , Government of India, Legislative Department, edition as on 1 May 2026.)
Preamble (closing words)
IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
Article 21 – No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
Article 32(1) – The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.

Article 37 – The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.

Article 368(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.
In simple words

India's Constitution was made by its own Constituent Assembly (Preamble) – the "constituent assembly" method that began in America and France. It has a written list of rights with a guaranteed court remedy (Part III, Art. 32) – the "bill of rights" idea. Its Directive Principles are not enforceable in court but are "fundamental in the governance of the country" (Art. 37) – the Irish idea. Art. 21's words "procedure established by law" came from the Japanese Constitution of 1946 ( A.K. Gopalan , Kania C.J.). It has its own amendment procedure (Art. 368) – a feature of every rigid written constitution. It replaced the British-made framework (Art. 395).
hi.meaning: 1. What "modern constitution" means here. A modern constitution is a deliberately made, usually written, basic law that (a) is framed by a body chosen for that purpose, (b) sets up and limits the organs of government, (c) declares the rights of the people, and (d) can be changed only by a special method. "Evolution" means the step-by-step growth of these features from the English charters to the post-war constitutions of the 20th century. 2. The British contrast. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, temporary Chairman, said on the first day of the Constituent Assembly (9 December 1946): "under the British Constitution, there is no such thing as a constituent law, it being a cherished privilege of the British Parliament, as the sole sovereign authority, to make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country." 3. Why later constitutions look alike. Dr. Ambedkar (4 November 1948): "More than hundred years have rolled over when the first written Constitution was drafted. It has been followed by many countries reducing their Constitutions to writing. What the scope of a Constitution should be has long been settled. Similarly what are the fundamentals of a Constitution are recognized all over the world. Given these facts, all Constitutions in their main provisions must look similar."
keyPoints: Britain: no constituent law; Parliament can "make and unmake all laws" (Sinha, 9 Dec 1946). Magna Carta ch. 39: "by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land". U.S.: Philadelphia Convention, 25 May – 17 Sept 1787; Bill of Rights = first ten amendments. France: first Constituent Assembly, 1789; Declaration of the Rights of Man. Canada: Quebec 1864, 33 delegates, 74 resolutions, BNA Act 1867. Australia: law on 9 July 1900; South Africa: law on 20 Sept 1909. Weimar art. 48 – emergency powers misused (H.V. Kamath). Ireland – directive principles (Ambedkar); Japan 1946 art. 31 – "procedure established by law" ( A.K. Gopalan ). Ambedkar: "There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing."

caseLaws.facts: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , AIR 1950 SC 27; 1950 SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained in Madras jail under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, applied under Art. 32 for habeas corpus, arguing that his detention broke Arts. 19, 21 and 22. Principle: Kania C.J.: "The phrase 'procedure established by law' seems to be borrowed from article 31 of the Japanese Constitution"; the Court contrasted it with the American "due process of law". Why it matters: It shows, in a judgment, how a key Indian provision came from another modern constitution and why its wording mattered.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 (as amended) and the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments. Principle: In discussing how a constitution must be read, Chandrachud J contrasted India's Constitution, built "in the hope that it will last", with the French Third Republic Constitution of 1875, framed "in the hope that it will fail"; the majority held that Art. 368 "does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution". Why it matters: It uses the history of other constitutions to explain why a modern constitution must be durable and protected from destruction.

selfTest.q: Why did Sinha say the British had no "constituent law"?
selfTest.a: Answer: Because the British Parliament, as sole sovereign authority, can make and unmake all laws, including constitutional law. When did the Philadelphia Convention meet and finish? Answer: 25 May 1787 to 17 September 1787 (about four months). What is the American Bill of Rights? Answer: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution. From which constitution did India take the idea of directive principles? Answer: The Irish Constitution (Irish Free State / 1937). Which case says "procedure established by law" was borrowed from the Japanese Constitution? Answer: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950), Kania C.J. How many delegates and resolutions did the Quebec Convention have? Answer: 33 delegates; 74 resolutions. Which article of the Weimar Constitution was given as a warning about emergency powers? Answer: Article 48. Complete Ambedkar's line: "Nobody holds any patent rights in ..." Answer: "... the fundamental ideas of a Constitution."

constitutional-law-i-u1-t4.subtitle: Written or unwritten, rigid or flexible, federal or unitary, parliamentary or presidential, and where India stands

en.inOneMinute: Constitutions are grouped ("classified") by asking a few simple questions about them. Each question gives one pair of types: Is it in one document? Written or unwritten . How hard is it to change? Rigid or flexible . How is power divided between the centre and the regions? Federal or unitary . Who really runs the executive? Parliamentary or presidential . Who is the head of State? Republic (elected head) or monarchy ( hereditary head). One constitution is placed in one box of each pair. Britain: unwritten, flexible, unitary, parliamentary, monarchy. USA: written, rigid, federal, presidential, republic. India: written; partly rigid and partly flexible; federal with strong unitary features ("dual polity with a single citizenship", Ambedkar); parliamentary; republic (Preamble, Arts. 52, 54). Ambedkar (4 Nov 1948): the Indian Constitution "can be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances", and "Its distinguishing feature is that it is a flexible federation."
legalProvision: "Classification of constitutions" is a way of studying constitutions; no Article uses the phrase. The Articles below show where the Constitution of India stands on each test. (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)
Federal or unitary
Article 1(1) – India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.

Article 246(1) – Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "Union List").

Article 246(2) – Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "Concurrent List").

Article 246(3) – Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "State List").
Article 248(1) – Subject to article 246A, Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List.

Article 249(1) (main words) – if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest that Parliament should make laws with respect to ... any matter enumerated in the State List specified in the resolution, it shall be lawful for Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to that matter while the resolution remains in force.

Article 250(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament shall, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, have power to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to goods and services tax provided under article 246A or any of the matters enumerated in the State List.

Article 353(a) – While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, ... notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to any State as to the manner in which the executive power thereof is to be exercised.
Rigid or flexible

Article 368(2) (main words) – An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill.

Proviso to Article 368(2) (summary of its list) – if the amendment seeks to make any change in Arts. 54, 55, 73, 162, 241 or 279A; Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI or Chapter I of Part XI; any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule; the representation of States in Parliament; or the provisions of Art. 368 itself, "the amendment shall also require to be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States".

Article 4(2) – No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368. (Similar words appear in Art. 169(3), para 7(2) of the Fifth Schedule and para 21(2) of the Sixth Schedule.)
Parliamentary or presidential

Article 53(1) – The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution.

Article 74(1) – There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice.
Article 75(3) – The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.
Republic
Preamble (opening words) – WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC ...
Article 52 – There shall be a President of India.

Article 54 – The President shall be elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of— (a) the elected members of both Houses of Parliament; and (b) the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States.
In simple words:

Arts. 1, 246 and 248 create two levels of government (Union and States) with their own lists of subjects, but give the Union the bigger share, including the leftover ("residuary") subjects. Arts. 249, 250 and 353 let the Union move into State subjects in the national interest or in an emergency. Art. 368 makes some parts of the Constitution harder to change (special majority, and for federal parts also half the States). Art. 4(2) and similar clauses let Parliament change some matters by an ordinary law. Art. 53(1) gives executive power to the President, but Art. 74(1) makes the President act on the advice of Ministers, who answer to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)). That is the parliamentary system. Arts. 52 and 54 give India an elected head of State, so India is a republic.
en.meaning: Classification means sorting constitutions into types according to their main features, so that one constitution can be compared with another. Each test below is a separate question. A constitution gets one answer for each question, so a full description of a constitution is a string of answers (for example, "written, rigid, federal, presidential, republican"). Ambedkar's definitions (CAD, 4 Nov 1948): "The two essential characteristics of a Unitary Constitution are: (1) the supremacy of the Central Polity and (2) the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities." "a Federal Constitution is marked: (1) by the existence of a Central polity and subsidiary polities side by side, and (2) by each being sovereign in the field assigned to it. In other words, Federation means the establishment of a Dual Polity." On the executive: "A democratic executive must satisfy two conditions - (1) It must be a stable executive and (2) it must be a responsible executive." The American and Swiss systems "give more stability but less responsibility"; the British system "gives you more responsibility but less stability". Written / unwritten: a written constitution is one where the main rules are put together in one document made at one time by a body such as a Constituent Assembly . An unwritten constitution is one where the rules are spread across ordinary laws, court decisions and practices that grew over time. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, Provisional Chairman of the Constituent Assembly, said (9 Dec 1946) that "under the British Constitution, there is no such thing as a constituent law, it being a cherished privilege of the British Parliament, as the sole sovereign authority, to make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country." Rigid / flexible: a rigid constitution needs a special, harder procedure to change it; a flexible constitution can be changed like an ordinary law. Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava (30 Aug 1947) put the test simply: "no flexible constitution has any such rule. If today any body in England wishes to make changes in the Law, he can do so; for the Legislature has the power to make such changes by a bare majority vote in the House of Commons."
keyPoints: Five tests: written/unwritten; rigid/flexible; federal/unitary; parliamentary/presidential; republic/monarchy. India: written; partly rigid, partly flexible; federal with unitary features; parliamentary; republic. Ambedkar (4 Nov 1948): unitary = "supremacy of the Central Polity" + "absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities"; federal = "Dual Polity". India = "a dual polity with a single citizenship"; "a flexible federation"; can be "both unitary as well as federal". India preferred "more responsibility to more stability" (parliamentary system). Three amending levels: simple majority (Art. 4(2)); special majority (Art. 368(2)); special majority + half the States (proviso). Cases: State of West Bengal (1962), S.R. Bommai (1994), Minerva Mills (1980).

caseLaws.facts: State of West Bengal v. Union of India , AIR 1963 SC 1241; [1964] 1 SCR 371 (6-judge Bench, decided 21 December 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, made by Parliament, the
caseLaws.facts: The State sued, saying the Act did not apply to land vested in or owned by the State, and that if it did, Parliament had no power to make it. Principle: By majority (Subba Rao J dissenting), the Act was valid and applied to State land too. "The Constitution of India is not truly Federal in character"; only powers concerned with local problems are vested in the States, and the residue, especially powers that "maintain the economic industrial and commercial unity of the country", are left to the Union; it is not correct to say that full sovereignty is vested in the States (headnote). Why it matters: It is the leading case for India's strong-centre character: Indian States are not sovereign units.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By a Proclamation dated 21 April 1989 under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356, the President dismissed the Karnataka Government of Chief Minister S.R. Bommai and dissolved the Assembly, giving no reasons except his satisfaction; Proclamations for Meghalaya, Nagaland, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan were also challenged. Principle: "Federalism envisaged in the Constitution of India is a basic feature" (K. Ramaswamy J); "federal structure ... and judicial review are basic features of the constitution" (headnote to his opinion). "while creating a federation, the founding fathers wished to establish a strong centre" (B.P. Jeevan Reddy J, for himself and S.C. Agrawal J). Whether a Ministry has lost the confidence of the House is to be decided "on the floor of the House", not by the Governor's own view; the Proclamation is open to judicial review. Ramaswamy J also recalled that in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab ([1975] 1 SCR 814) the Court "held that parliamentary system of quasi-federalism was accepted rejecting the substance of Presidential style of executive", and quoted Ambedkar's "both unitary as well as federal". Why it matters: It places India exactly in the classification: federal (a basic feature), with a strong centre, and parliamentary, not presidential. It also limits the unitary use of Art. 356.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , (1980) 3 SCC 625; AIR 1980 SC 1789 (5-judge Bench, decided 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A nationalised textile company challenged ss
caseLaws.facts: 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which tried to make the amending power unlimited and amendments immune from courts. Principle: "a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution"; "The power to destroy is not a power to amend." Why it matters: It shows that India's rigid/flexible amending procedure works inside an outer limit: the basic structure.

selfTest.q: Name the five main tests for classifying constitutions. Answer: Written/unwritten; rigid/flexible; federal/unitary; parliamentary/presidential; republic/monarchy. Give Ambedkar's two essential characteristics of a unitary constitution. Answer: "(1) the supremacy of the Central Polity and (2) the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities." Why did Ambedkar call India "a dual polity with a single citizenship"?
selfTest.a: Answer: There are two levels of government (Union and States) but only one citizenship, Indian citizenship; no State citizenship. Which Indian provisions can be changed by a simple majority? Answer: Laws under Arts. 2 and 3 (Art. 4(2)); Legislative Councils (Art. 169(3)); Fifth Schedule (para 7(2)); Sixth Schedule (para 21(2)). Which amendments need ratification by half the States? Answer: Those listed in the proviso to Art. 368(2), e.g., the Seventh Schedule Lists, representation of States in Parliament, election of the President, Art. 368 itself. Is India presidential because it has a President? Give two Articles. Answer: No; it is parliamentary. Art. 74(1) (President acts on advice of Ministers) and Art. 75(3) (collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha). Why did India prefer the parliamentary system? Answer: It "preferred more responsibility to more stability" because Parliament can check the executive daily (Ambedkar). Which Articles make India a republic? Answer: Preamble ("REPUBLIC"), Art. 52 (President), Art. 54 (election of President). Name two unitary features that come into play in an emergency. Answer: Parliament can legislate on State subjects (Art. 250); the Union can give directions to States (Art. 353(a)). Which case held federalism to be a basic feature? Answer: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994).

This Is not the same as Why
Written Rigid Usually go together, but they answer different questions (form vs ease of change). India is written but parts are flexible.
Unwritten Having no constitution Britain has a constitution; it is just not in one document.
Federal Two separate countries joined loosely In a federation both levels work under one constitution; Ambedkar said India is "not a league of States".
Single citizenship (India) Dual citizenship (USA) In the USA there is "a citizenship of the U.S.A." and "also a citizenship of the State"; India has only Indian citizenship.

te.inOneMinute: రాజ్యాంగాలను కొన్ని సరళమైన ప్రశ్నలు అడిగి రకాలుగా విభజిస్తారు ("వర్గీకరణ"). ప్రతి ప్రశ్న ఒక జత రకాలను ఇస్తుంది: ఒకే పత్రంలో ఉందా? లిఖిత లేదా అలిఖిత . మార్చడం ఎంత కష్టం? దృఢ లేదా సరళ (వశ్య) . కేంద్రం, ప్రాంతాల మధ్య అధికారం ఎలా పంచబడింది? సమాఖ్య లేదా ఏకకేంద్ర . కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థను నిజంగా ఎవరు నడుపుతారు? పార్లమెంటరీ లేదా అధ్యక్ష . దేశాధినేత ఎవరు? గణతంత్రం (ఎన్నికైన అధినేత) లేదా రాజరికం (వంశపారంపర్య అధినేత). ఒక రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ప్రతి జతలో ఒక పెట్టెలో ఉంచుతారు. బ్రిటన్: అలిఖిత, సరళ, ఏకకేంద్ర, పార్లమెంటరీ, రాజరికం. అమెరికా: లిఖిత, దృఢ, సమాఖ్య, అధ్యక్ష, గణతంత్రం. భారతదేశం: లిఖిత; కొంత దృఢ, కొంత సరళ; బలమైన ఏకకేంద్ర లక్షణాలతో కూడిన సమాఖ్య ("dual polity with a single citizenship" – అంబేద్కర్); పార్లమెంటరీ; గణతంత్రం (ప్రవేశిక, అ. 52, 54). అంబేద్కర్ (4 నవంబర్ 1948): భారత రాజ్యాంగం "can be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances" (అర్థం: కాలం, పరిస్థితుల అవసరాన్ని బట్టి ఏకకేంద్రంగానూ, సమాఖ్యగానూ పనిచేయగలదు); "Its distinguishing feature is that it is a flexible federation." (అర్థం: దీని ప్రత్యేక లక్షణం – ఇది వశ్య సమాఖ్య).
te.meaning: వర్గీకరణ అంటే రాజ్యాంగాలను వాటి ముఖ్య లక్షణాల ఆధారంగా రకాలుగా విభజించడం; దీనివల్ల ఒక రాజ్యాంగాన్ని మరొకదానితో పోల్చవచ్చు. క్రింది ప్రతి పరీక్ష ఒక వేరు ప్రశ్న. ఒక రాజ్యాంగానికి ప్రతి ప్రశ్నకు ఒక సమాధానం వస్తుంది; కాబట్టి రాజ్యాంగం పూర్తి వర్ణన సమాధానాల వరుస (ఉదా: "లిఖిత, దృఢ, సమాఖ్య, అధ్యక్ష, గణతంత్ర"). అంబేద్కర్ నిర్వచనాలు (CAD, 4 నవంబర్ 1948): "The two essential characteristics of a Unitary Constitution are: (1) the supremacy of the Central Polity and (2) the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities." (అర్థం: ఏకకేంద్ర రాజ్యాంగానికి రెండు ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు – (1) కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వ ఆధిపత్యం, (2) సార్వభౌమాధికారం గల ఉప-ప్రభుత్వాలు లేకపోవడం.) "a Federal Constitution is marked: (1) by the existence of a Central polity and subsidiary polities side by side, and (2) by each being sovereign in the field assigned to it. In other words, Federation means the establishment of a Dual Polity." (అర్థం: సమాఖ్య రాజ్యాంగంలో (1) కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం, ఉప-ప్రభుత్వాలు పక్కపక్కనే ఉంటాయి, (2) ప్రతిదీ తనకు కేటాయించిన రంగంలో సార్వభౌమం. అంటే సమాఖ్య = ద్వంద్వ ప్రభుత్వ వ్యవస్థ.) కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థపై: "A democratic executive must satisfy two conditions - (1) It must be a stable executive and (2) it must be a responsible executive." (అర్థం: ప్రజాస్వామ్య కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థ (1) స్థిరంగా, (2) జవాబుదారీగా ఉండాలి.) అమెరికా, స్విస్ వ్యవస్థలు "give more stability but less responsibility" (ఎక్కువ స్థిరత్వం, తక్కువ జవాబుదారీతనం); బ్రిటిష్ వ్యవస్థ "gives you more responsibility but less stability" (ఎక్కువ జవాబుదారీతనం, తక్కువ స్థిరత్వం). లిఖిత / అలిఖిత: ముఖ్య నియమాలన్నీ ఒకే పత్రంలో, ఒకే సమయంలో, రాజ్యాంగ సభ వంటి సంస్థ ద్వారా రూపొందితే అది లిఖిత రాజ్యాంగం. నియమాలు సాధారణ చట్టాలు, కోర్టు తీర్పులు, కాలక్రమేణా పెరిగిన ఆచారాల్లో చెల్లాచెదురుగా ఉంటే అది అలిఖిత రాజ్యాంగ ం. రాజ్యాంగ సభ తాత్కాలిక అధ్యక్షుడు (Provisional Chairman) డా. సచ్చిదానంద సిన్హా (9 డిసెంబర్ 1946) ఇలా అన్నారు: "under the British Constitution, there is no such thing as a constituent law, it being a cherished privilege of the British Parliament, as the sole sovereign authority, to make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country." (అర్థం: బ్రిటిష్ రాజ్యాంగంలో ప్రత్యేక రాజ్యాంగ చట్టం అనేదే లేదు; రాజ్యాంగ చట్టంతో సహా అన్ని చట్టాలను చేయడం, రద్దు చేయడం ఏకైక సార్వభౌమ సంస్థ అయిన బ్రిటిష్ పార్లమెంటు ప్రత్యేక హక్కు.) దృఢ / సరళ: మార్చడానికి సాధారణ చట్టం కంటే కష్టమైన ప్రత్యేక విధానం అవసరమైతే దృఢ రాజ్యాంగ ం; సాధారణ చట్టంలాగే మార్చగలిగితే సరళ రాజ్యాంగం. పండిత్ ఠాకూర్ దాస్ భార్గవ (30 ఆగస్టు 1947): "no flexible constitution has any such rule. If today any body in England wishes to make changes in the Law, he can do so; for the Legislature has the power to make such changes by a bare majority vote in the House of Commons." (అర్థం: సరళ రాజ్యాంగంలో అలాంటి ప్రత్యేక నియమం ఉండదు; ఇంగ్లాండ్‌లో హౌస్ ఆఫ్ కామన్స్‌లో సాధారణ మెజారిటీతోనే చట్టాన్ని మార్చవచ్చు.)
keyPoints: ఐదు పరీక్షలు: లిఖిత/అలిఖిత; దృఢ/సరళ; సమాఖ్య/ఏకకేంద్ర; పార్లమెంటరీ/అధ్యక్ష; గణతంత్రం/రాజరికం. భారతదేశం: లిఖిత; కొంత దృఢ, కొంత సరళ; ఏకకేంద్ర లక్షణాలతో సమాఖ్య; పార్లమెంటరీ; గణతంత్రం. అంబేద్కర్ (4 నవంబర్ 1948): ఏకకేంద్ర = "supremacy of the Central Polity" + "absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities"; సమాఖ్య = "Dual Polity". భారతదేశం = "a dual polity with a single citizenship"; "a flexible federation"; "both unitary as well as federal" కాగలదు. భారతదేశం "more responsibility to more stability" ప్రాధాన్యం ఇచ్చింది (పార్లమెంటరీ వ్యవస్థ). మూడు సవరణ స్థాయిలు: సాధారణ మెజారిటీ (అ. 4(2)); ప్రత్యేక మెజారిటీ (అ. 368(2)); ప్రత్యేక మెజారిటీ + సగం రాష్ట్రాలు (నిబంధన). కేసులు: State of West Bengal (1962), S.R. Bommai (1994), Minerva Mills (1980).

selfTest.q: రాజ్యాంగాల వర్గీకరణకు ఐదు ప్రధాన పరీక్షలు పేర్కొనండి. జవాబు: లిఖిత/అలిఖిత; దృఢ/సరళ; సమాఖ్య/ఏకకేంద్ర; పార్లమెంటరీ/అధ్యక్ష; గణతంత్రం/రాజరికం. ఏకకేంద్ర రాజ్యాంగానికి అంబేద్కర్ చెప్పిన రెండు ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: "(1) the supremacy of the Central Polity and (2) the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities." అంబేద్కర్ భారతదేశాన్ని "a dual polity with a single citizenship" అని ఎందుకు అన్నారు? జవాబు: రెండు స్థాయిల ప్రభుత్వం (కేంద్రం, రాష్ట్రాలు) ఉంది, కానీ పౌరసత్వం ఒక్కటే – భారత పౌరసత్వం; రాష్ట్ర పౌరసత్వం లేదు. ఏ భారత నిబంధనలను సాధారణ మెజారిటీతో మార్చవచ్చు? జవాబు: అ. 2, 3 కింద చట్టాలు (అ. 4(2)); శాసన మండళ్లు (అ. 169(3)); ఐదవ షెడ్యూల్ (పేరా 7(2)); ఆరవ షెడ్యూల్ (పేరా 21(2)). ఏ సవరణలకు సగం రాష్ట్రాల ఆమోదం కావాలి? జవాబు: అ. 368(2) నిబంధనలో పేర్కొన్నవి – ఉదా: ఏడవ షెడ్యూల్ జాబితాలు, పార్లమెంటులో రాష్ట్రాల ప్రాతినిధ్యం, రాష్ట్రపతి ఎన్నిక, అ. 368 స్వయంగా. రాష్ట్రపతి ఉన్నారు కాబట్టి భారతదేశం అధ్యక్ష వ్యవస్థా? రెండు అనుచ్ఛేదాలు ఇవ్వండి. జవాబు: కాదు; పార్లమెంటరీ. అ. 74(1) (మంత్రుల సలహా మేరకు రాష్ట్రపతి), అ. 75(3) (లోక్‌సభకు సమష్టి జవాబుదారీతనం). భారతదేశం పార్లమెంటరీ వ్యవస్థను ఎందుకు ఎంచుకుంది? జవాబు: పార్లమెంటు కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థను రోజూ తనిఖీ చేయగలదు కాబట్టి, అది "preferred more responsibility to more stability" (అంబేద్కర్). భారతదేశాన్ని గణతంత్రంగా చేసే నిబంధనలు? జవాబు: ప్రవేశిక ("REPUBLIC"), అ. 52 (రాష్ట్రపతి), అ. 54 (రాష్ట్రపతి ఎన్నిక). అత్యవసర పరిస్థితిలో అమలయ్యే రెండు ఏకకేంద్ర లక్షణాలు? జవాబు: రాష్ట్ర విషయాలపై పార్లమెంటు చట్టాలు చేయగలదు (అ. 250); కేంద్రం రాష్ట్రాలకు ఆదేశాలు ఇవ్వగలదు (అ. 353(a)). సమాఖ్య వ్యవస్థ మౌలిక లక్షణమని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది? జవాబు: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994).
