లిఖిత దృఢ సాధారణంగా కలిసి ఉంటాయి, కానీ వేర్వేరు ప్రశ్నలకు సమాధానాలు (రూపం vs మార్పు సౌలభ్యం). భారతదేశం లిఖితం, కానీ కొన్ని భాగాలు సరళం.
అలిఖిత రాజ్యాంగమే లేకపోవడం బ్రిటన్‌కు రాజ్యాంగం ఉంది; అది ఒకే పత్రంలో లేదు అంతే.
సమాఖ్య వదులుగా కలిసిన రెండు వేర్వేరు దేశాలు సమాఖ్యలో రెండు స్థాయిలూ ఒకే రాజ్యాంగం కింద పనిచేస్తాయి; భారతదేశం "not a league of States" (రాష్ట్రాల కూటమి కాదు) అని అంబేద్కర్ అన్నారు.
ఏక పౌరసత్వం (భారతదేశం) ద్వంద్వ పౌరసత్వం (అమెరికా) అమెరికాలో "a citizenship of the U.S.A." తో పాటు "also a citizenship of the State" ఉంది; భారతదేశంలో భారత పౌరసత్వం ఒక్కటే.
దేశాధినేత (భారత రాష్ట్రపతి) కార్యనిర్వాహక అధిపతి (ప్రధానమంత్రి, మంత్రిమండలి) రాష్ట్రపతి "represents the Nation but does not rule the Nation" (అంబేద్కర్).
గణతంత్రం ప్రజాస్వామ్యం గణతంత్రం అంటే ఎన్నికైన దేశాధినేత; బ్రిటన్ ప్రజాస్వామ్యం, కానీ గణతంత్రం కాదు.
అ. 4(2) చట్టం అ. 368 కింద రాజ్యాంగ సవరణ అలాంటి చట్టం "deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368" కాదని అ. 4(2) చెబుతుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: Constitutions are grouped ("classified") by asking a few simple questions about them. Each question gives one pair of types: Is it in one document? Written or unwritten . How hard is it to change? Rigid or flexible . How is power divided between the centre and the regions? Federal or unitary . Who really runs the executive? Parliamentary or presidential . Who is the head of State? Republic (elected head) or monarchy ( hereditary head). One constitution is placed in one box of each pair. Britain: unwritten, flexible, unitary, parliamentary, monarchy. USA: written, rigid, federal, presidential, republic. India: written; partly rigid and partly flexible; federal with strong unitary features ("dual polity with a single citizenship", Ambedkar); parliamentary; republic (Preamble, Arts. 52, 54). Ambedkar (4 Nov 1948): the Indian Constitution "can be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances", and "Its distinguishing feature is that it is a flexible federation."
legalProvision: "Classification of constitutions" is a way of studying constitutions; no Article uses the phrase. The Articles below show where the Constitution of India stands on each test. (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)
Federal or unitary
Article 1(1) – India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.

Article 246(1) – Notwithstanding anything in clauses (2) and (3), Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "Union List").

Article 246(2) – Notwithstanding anything in clause (3), Parliament, and, subject to clause (1), the Legislature of any State also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "Concurrent List").

Article 246(3) – Subject to clauses (1) and (2), the Legislature of any State has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II in the Seventh Schedule (in this Constitution referred to as the "State List").
Article 248(1) – Subject to article 246A, Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List.

Article 249(1) (main words) – if the Council of States has declared by resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the national interest that Parliament should make laws with respect to ... any matter enumerated in the State List specified in the resolution, it shall be lawful for Parliament to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to that matter while the resolution remains in force.

Article 250(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, Parliament shall, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, have power to make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India with respect to goods and services tax provided under article 246A or any of the matters enumerated in the State List.

Article 353(a) – While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, ... notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the executive power of the Union shall extend to the giving of directions to any State as to the manner in which the executive power thereof is to be exercised.
Rigid or flexible

Article 368(2) (main words) – An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill.

Proviso to Article 368(2) (summary of its list) – if the amendment seeks to make any change in Arts. 54, 55, 73, 162, 241 or 279A; Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI or Chapter I of Part XI; any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule; the representation of States in Parliament; or the provisions of Art. 368 itself, "the amendment shall also require to be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States".

Article 4(2) – No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368. (Similar words appear in Art. 169(3), para 7(2) of the Fifth Schedule and para 21(2) of the Sixth Schedule.)
Parliamentary or presidential

Article 53(1) – The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with this Constitution.

Article 74(1) – There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice.
Article 75(3) – The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.
Republic
Preamble (opening words) – WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC ...
Article 52 – There shall be a President of India.

Article 54 – The President shall be elected by the members of an electoral college consisting of— (a) the elected members of both Houses of Parliament; and (b) the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States.
In simple words:

Arts. 1, 246 and 248 create two levels of government (Union and States) with their own lists of subjects, but give the Union the bigger share, including the leftover ("residuary") subjects. Arts. 249, 250 and 353 let the Union move into State subjects in the national interest or in an emergency. Art. 368 makes some parts of the Constitution harder to change (special majority, and for federal parts also half the States). Art. 4(2) and similar clauses let Parliament change some matters by an ordinary law. Art. 53(1) gives executive power to the President, but Art. 74(1) makes the President act on the advice of Ministers, who answer to the Lok Sabha (Art. 75(3)). That is the parliamentary system. Arts. 52 and 54 give India an elected head of State, so India is a republic.
hi.meaning: Classification means sorting constitutions into types according to their main features, so that one constitution can be compared with another. Each test below is a separate question. A constitution gets one answer for each question, so a full description of a constitution is a string of answers (for example, "written, rigid, federal, presidential, republican"). Ambedkar's definitions (CAD, 4 Nov 1948): "The two essential characteristics of a Unitary Constitution are: (1) the supremacy of the Central Polity and (2) the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities." "a Federal Constitution is marked: (1) by the existence of a Central polity and subsidiary polities side by side, and (2) by each being sovereign in the field assigned to it. In other words, Federation means the establishment of a Dual Polity." On the executive: "A democratic executive must satisfy two conditions - (1) It must be a stable executive and (2) it must be a responsible executive." The American and Swiss systems "give more stability but less responsibility"; the British system "gives you more responsibility but less stability". Written / unwritten: a written constitution is one where the main rules are put together in one document made at one time by a body such as a Constituent Assembly . An unwritten constitution is one where the rules are spread across ordinary laws, court decisions and practices that grew over time. Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha, Provisional Chairman of the Constituent Assembly, said (9 Dec 1946) that "under the British Constitution, there is no such thing as a constituent law, it being a cherished privilege of the British Parliament, as the sole sovereign authority, to make and unmake all laws, including the constitutional law of the country." Rigid / flexible: a rigid constitution needs a special, harder procedure to change it; a flexible constitution can be changed like an ordinary law. Pandit Thakur Das Bhargava (30 Aug 1947) put the test simply: "no flexible constitution has any such rule. If today any body in England wishes to make changes in the Law, he can do so; for the Legislature has the power to make such changes by a bare majority vote in the House of Commons."
keyPoints: Five tests: written/unwritten; rigid/flexible; federal/unitary; parliamentary/presidential; republic/monarchy. India: written; partly rigid, partly flexible; federal with unitary features; parliamentary; republic. Ambedkar (4 Nov 1948): unitary = "supremacy of the Central Polity" + "absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities"; federal = "Dual Polity". India = "a dual polity with a single citizenship"; "a flexible federation"; can be "both unitary as well as federal". India preferred "more responsibility to more stability" (parliamentary system). Three amending levels: simple majority (Art. 4(2)); special majority (Art. 368(2)); special majority + half the States (proviso). Cases: State of West Bengal (1962), S.R. Bommai (1994), Minerva Mills (1980).

caseLaws.facts: State of West Bengal v. Union of India , AIR 1963 SC 1241; [1964] 1 SCR 371 (6-judge Bench, decided 21 December 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, made by Parliament, the
caseLaws.facts: The State sued, saying the Act did not apply to land vested in or owned by the State, and that if it did, Parliament had no power to make it. Principle: By majority (Subba Rao J dissenting), the Act was valid and applied to State land too. "The Constitution of India is not truly Federal in character"; only powers concerned with local problems are vested in the States, and the residue, especially powers that "maintain the economic industrial and commercial unity of the country", are left to the Union; it is not correct to say that full sovereignty is vested in the States (headnote). Why it matters: It is the leading case for India's strong-centre character: Indian States are not sovereign units.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By a Proclamation dated 21 April 1989 under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356, the President dismissed the Karnataka Government of Chief Minister S.R. Bommai and dissolved the Assembly, giving no reasons except his satisfaction; Proclamations for Meghalaya, Nagaland, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan were also challenged. Principle: "Federalism envisaged in the Constitution of India is a basic feature" (K. Ramaswamy J); "federal structure ... and judicial review are basic features of the constitution" (headnote to his opinion). "while creating a federation, the founding fathers wished to establish a strong centre" (B.P. Jeevan Reddy J, for himself and S.C. Agrawal J). Whether a Ministry has lost the confidence of the House is to be decided "on the floor of the House", not by the Governor's own view; the Proclamation is open to judicial review. Ramaswamy J also recalled that in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab ([1975] 1 SCR 814) the Court "held that parliamentary system of quasi-federalism was accepted rejecting the substance of Presidential style of executive", and quoted Ambedkar's "both unitary as well as federal". Why it matters: It places India exactly in the classification: federal (a basic feature), with a strong centre, and parliamentary, not presidential. It also limits the unitary use of Art. 356.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , (1980) 3 SCC 625; AIR 1980 SC 1789 (5-judge Bench, decided 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A nationalised textile company challenged ss
caseLaws.facts: 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which tried to make the amending power unlimited and amendments immune from courts. Principle: "a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution"; "The power to destroy is not a power to amend." Why it matters: It shows that India's rigid/flexible amending procedure works inside an outer limit: the basic structure.

selfTest.q: Name the five main tests for classifying constitutions. Answer: Written/unwritten; rigid/flexible; federal/unitary; parliamentary/presidential; republic/monarchy. Give Ambedkar's two essential characteristics of a unitary constitution. Answer: "(1) the supremacy of the Central Polity and (2) the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities." Why did Ambedkar call India "a dual polity with a single citizenship"?
selfTest.a: Answer: There are two levels of government (Union and States) but only one citizenship, Indian citizenship; no State citizenship. Which Indian provisions can be changed by a simple majority? Answer: Laws under Arts. 2 and 3 (Art. 4(2)); Legislative Councils (Art. 169(3)); Fifth Schedule (para 7(2)); Sixth Schedule (para 21(2)). Which amendments need ratification by half the States? Answer: Those listed in the proviso to Art. 368(2), e.g., the Seventh Schedule Lists, representation of States in Parliament, election of the President, Art. 368 itself. Is India presidential because it has a President? Give two Articles. Answer: No; it is parliamentary. Art. 74(1) (President acts on advice of Ministers) and Art. 75(3) (collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha). Why did India prefer the parliamentary system? Answer: It "preferred more responsibility to more stability" because Parliament can check the executive daily (Ambedkar). Which Articles make India a republic? Answer: Preamble ("REPUBLIC"), Art. 52 (President), Art. 54 (election of President). Name two unitary features that come into play in an emergency. Answer: Parliament can legislate on State subjects (Art. 250); the Union can give directions to States (Art. 353(a)). Which case held federalism to be a basic feature? Answer: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994).

Written Rigid Usually go together, but they answer different questions (form vs ease of change). India is written but parts are flexible.
Unwritten Having no constitution Britain has a constitution; it is just not in one document.
Federal Two separate countries joined loosely In a federation both levels work under one constitution; Ambedkar said India is "not a league of States".

constitutional-law-i-u1-t5.subtitle: What the document is: adoption, commencement, and how its Parts, Articles and Schedules are arranged

en.inOneMinute: The Constitution of India (Art. 393) is the supreme law of India. It was made by the Constituent Assembly and given by the people to themselves: "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA ... do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION" (Preamble). Key dates: adopted 26 November 1949 ; signed by members on 24 January 1950 ; came fully into force on 26 January 1950 (Art. 394). A few Articles (on citizenship, elections, interim provisions) came into force at once on 26 Nov 1949. Size when passed: 395 Articles and 8 Schedules (Rajendra Prasad, 26 Nov 1949). Today it has a Preamble, 22 Parts (some with letters, e.g. IVA, IXA), 12 Schedules and appendices; new Articles are added with letters (e.g. Art. 21A, Art. 51A), so the last Article is still Art. 395. Break with British law: Art. 395 repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935. From 26 Jan 1950 India's legal system rests on this Constitution, not on any British Act. It is a living document : it can be amended (Art. 368), but not so as to destroy its basic structure ( Kesavananda Bharati ; Minerva Mills ). Ambedkar (25 Nov 1949): "however good a Constitution may be, it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it, happen to be a bad lot."
legalProvision: (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)
Preamble (closing words) – IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
Article 393 – This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.

Article 394 – This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution.

Article 394A(1) (main words) – The President shall cause to be published under his authority,— (a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, ... and (b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of this Constitution made in the English language. [Inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987, w.e.f. 9-12-1987.]

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

Article 245(1) – Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.
Article 343(1) – The official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script.

Article 368(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.
In simple words:

The Preamble says who made the Constitution (the people, through their Constituent Assembly) and when (26 Nov 1949). Art. 393 gives its name. Art. 394 says it started in two steps: some Articles at once, the rest on 26 Jan 1950. Art. 394A provides for an authoritative Hindi text. Art. 395 ends the old British Acts. Art. 245(1) shows that even Parliament makes laws "subject to" the Constitution, so the Constitution is above every other law. Art. 368(1) allows the Constitution to be changed by Parliament under its special procedure.
en.meaning: The Indian Constitution is the written document, adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950, that creates the organs of the Indian State (Union and States; legislature, executive, judiciary), gives them their powers, limits those powers, and guarantees the rights of the people. Its official name is "the Constitution of India" (Art. 393). Its source of authority is the people. The Preamble says the people "adopt, enact and give to ourselves" this Constitution. Its authority does not come from the British Parliament (Art. 395 repealed the British Acts). Its rank is the highest. Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void (Art. 13); Parliament and State Legislatures make laws "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution" (Art. 245(1)).
keyPoints: Name: Constitution of India (Art. 393). Adopted 26 Nov 1949; signed 24 Jan 1950 (284 members); in force 26 Jan 1950 (Art. 394). Articles in force on 26 Nov 1949: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394. Sizes: Rau's draft 243 Articles + 13 Schedules; Draft 315 + 8; as passed 395 + 8; now 12 Schedules. Art. 395 repealed the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the GoI Act 1935 (Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949 saved). Art. 394A – authoritative Hindi text (58th Amendment, 1987). Amendable (Art. 368) but basic structure cannot be destroyed.

caseLaws.facts: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner ( Writ Petition No
caseLaws.facts: 135 of 1970, under Art. 32) challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended in 1969 and 1971; the case then turned on the validity of the 24th, 25th and 29th Constitutional Amendments. Principle: By majority, "The power to amend does not include the power to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution so as to change its identity" (headnote). Khanna J (para 1480): it would not be competent "under the garb of amendment ... to change the democratic government into dictatorship or hereditary monarchy"; Art. 368 cannot "provide sanction for what may perhaps be called its lawful harakiri". Why it matters: It decides what the Indian Constitution is at its core: an amendable document with a basic structure that Parliament cannot destroy.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , (1980) 3 SCC 625; AIR 1980 SC 1789 (5-judge Bench, decided 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A nationalised textile company challenged ss
caseLaws.facts: 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which tried to make the amending power unlimited and amendments immune from courts. Principle: "a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution"; "The power to destroy is not a power to amend." Why it matters: It confirms that the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme.
In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves , [1960] 3 SCR 250 (8-judge Bench, Presidential Reference under Art. 143, opinion given 14 March 1960)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The President asked whether an agreement with Pakistan to transfer part of the Berubari Union
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Agreement involved cession of Indian territory, so the law to implement it had to be passed under Art. 368, not under Art. 3. The Preamble is "a key to open the mind of the makers", but "the preamble is not a part of the Constitution" and is not "the source of any substantive power" (Gajendragadkar J for the Court). (The later view in Kesavananda Bharati that the Preamble is part of the Constitution is covered in Preamble to Indian Constitution .) Why it matters: It shows that the Constitution's own procedure must be followed for basic changes, such as changing India's territory.

selfTest.q: On what date was the Constitution adopted, and where is that date written?
selfTest.a: Answer: 26 November 1949; in the Preamble. Name five Articles that came into force on 26 Nov 1949. Answer: Any five of Arts. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394. What does Art. 394 call 26 January 1950? Answer: "the commencement of this Constitution". Which Acts did Art. 395 repeal, and which Act did it save? Answer: Repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935; saved the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949. How many Articles and Schedules did the Constitution have when passed? Answer: 395 Articles and 8 Schedules. Which Amendments added the Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules? Answer: First (1951), Fifty-second (1985), Seventy-third (1992), Seventy-fourth (1992). Why did Ambedkar include details of administration in the Constitution? Answer: Because the Constitution could be perverted by changing the form of administration, and constitutional morality could not yet be assumed; so it was "wiser not to trust the Legislature to prescribe forms of administration". Who prepared the first draft and how many Articles did it have? Answer: B.N. Rau; 243 Articles and 13 Schedules. Can Parliament amend any part of the Constitution? Answer: Yes under Art. 368, but not so as to destroy the basic structure ( Kesavananda Bharati ; Minerva Mills ). Complete Ambedkar: "however good a Constitution may be, ..." Answer: "it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it, happen to be a bad lot."

te.inOneMinute: భారత రాజ్యాంగం (అ. 393) భారతదేశ సర్వోన్నత చట్టం. దీన్ని రాజ్యాంగ సభ రూపొందించింది; ప్రజలు దీన్ని తమకు తామే ఇచ్చుకున్నారు: "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA ... do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION" (ప్రవేశిక) (అర్థం: భారత ప్రజలమైన మేము ఈ రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ఆమోదించి, శాసనంగా చేసి, మాకు మేమే ఇచ్చుకుంటున్నాం). ముఖ్య తేదీలు: ఆమోదం 26 నవంబర్ 1949 ; సభ్యుల సంతకాలు 24 జనవరి 1950 ; పూర్తిగా అమలు 26 జనవరి 1950 (అ. 394). కొన్ని అనుచ్ఛేదాలు (పౌరసత్వం, ఎన్నికలు, తాత్కాలిక ఏర్పాట్లు) 26 నవంబర్ 1949నే అమలులోకి వచ్చాయి. ఆమోదించినప్పుడు పరిమాణం: 395 అనుచ్ఛేదాలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లు (రాజేంద్ర ప్రసాద్, 26 నవంబర్ 1949). నేడు ప్రవేశిక, 22 భాగాలు (కొన్ని అక్షరాలతో, ఉదా: IVA, IXA), 12 షెడ్యూళ్లు, అనుబంధాలు ఉన్నాయి; కొత్త అనుచ్ఛేదాలను అక్షరాలతో చేర్చారు (ఉదా: అ. 21A, అ. 51A), కాబట్టి చివరి అనుచ్ఛేదం ఇప్పటికీ అ. 395. బ్రిటిష్ చట్టంతో తెగతెంపు: అ. 395 భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం, 1947 మరియు భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1935ను రద్దు చేసింది. 26 జనవరి 1950 నుంచి భారత న్యాయ వ్యవస్థ ఏ బ్రిటిష్ చట్టం మీద కాక, ఈ రాజ్యాంగం మీదే ఆధారపడుతుంది. ఇది సజీవ పత్రం : దీన్ని సవరించవచ్చు (అ. 368), కానీ దాని మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని నాశనం చేసేలా కాదు ( కేశవానంద భారతి ; మినర్వా మిల్స్ ). అంబేద్కర్ (25 నవంబర్ 1949): "however good a Constitution may be, it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it, happen to be a bad lot." (అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగం ఎంత మంచిదైనా, దాన్ని అమలు చేసేవారు చెడ్డవారైతే అది చెడ్డదిగానే మారుతుంది.)
te.meaning: భారత రాజ్యాంగం అంటే – 26 నవంబర్ 1949న రాజ్యాంగ సభ ఆమోదించి, 26 జనవరి 1950 నుంచి అమలులో ఉన్న లిఖిత పత్రం; ఇది భారత రాజ్య అంగాలను (కేంద్రం, రాష్ట్రాలు; శాసన, కార్యనిర్వాహక, న్యాయ వ్యవస్థలు) సృష్టిస్తుంది, వాటికి అధికారాలు ఇస్తుంది, ఆ అధికారాలను పరిమితం చేస్తుంది, ప్రజల హక్కులకు హామీ ఇస్తుంది. అధికారిక పేరు "the Constitution of India" (అ. 393). అధికార మూలం ప్రజలు. ప్రజలు ఈ రాజ్యాంగాన్ని "adopt, enact and give to ourselves" అని ప్రవేశిక చెబుతుంది. దీని అధికారం బ్రిటిష్ పార్లమెంటు నుంచి రాదు (అ. 395 బ్రిటిష్ చట్టాలను రద్దు చేసింది). స్థానం అత్యున్నతం. ప్రాథమిక హక్కు లకు విరుద్ధమైన చట్టాలు శూన్యం (అ. 13); పార్లమెంటు, రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభలు "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution" చట్టాలు చేస్తాయి (అ. 245(1)).
keyPoints: పేరు: భారత రాజ్యాంగం (అ. 393). ఆమోదం 26 నవంబర్ 1949; సంతకాలు 24 జనవరి 1950 (284 మంది); అమలు 26 జనవరి 1950 (అ. 394). 26 నవంబర్ 1949న అమలులోకి వచ్చిన అనుచ్ఛేదాలు: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394. పరిమాణాలు: రావు ముసాయిదా 243 అనుచ్ఛేదాలు + 13 షెడ్యూళ్లు; ముసాయిదా 315 + 8; ఆమోదించినప్పుడు 395 + 8; ఇప్పుడు 12 షెడ్యూళ్లు. అ. 395 భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం 1947, భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం 1935ను రద్దు చేసింది (Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949 మినహాయింపు). అ. 394A – అధికారిక హిందీ పాఠం (58వ సవరణ, 1987). సవరించవచ్చు (అ. 368), కానీ మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని నాశనం చేయలేరు.

selfTest.q: రాజ్యాంగం ఏ తేదీన ఆమోదించబడింది, ఆ తేదీ ఎక్కడ రాసి ఉంది?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: 26 నవంబర్ 1949; ప్రవేశికలో. 26 నవంబర్ 1949న అమలులోకి వచ్చిన ఐదు అనుచ్ఛేదాలు పేర్కొనండి. జవాబు: అ. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394లో ఏవైనా ఐదు. అ. 394 26 జనవరి 1950ని ఏమని పిలుస్తుంది? జవాబు: "the commencement of this Constitution". అ. 395 ఏ చట్టాలను రద్దు చేసింది, దేన్ని మినహాయించింది? జవాబు: భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం, 1947, భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1935ను రద్దు చేసింది; Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949ని మినహాయించింది. ఆమోదించినప్పుడు రాజ్యాంగంలో ఎన్ని అనుచ్ఛేదాలు, షెడ్యూళ్లు ఉన్నాయి? జవాబు: 395 అనుచ్ఛేదాలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లు. 9, 10, 11, 12 షెడ్యూళ్లను ఏ సవరణలు చేర్చాయి? జవాబు: మొదటి (1951), 52వ (1985), 73వ (1992), 74వ (1992). అంబేద్కర్ పరిపాలన వివరాలను రాజ్యాంగంలో ఎందుకు చేర్చారు? జవాబు: పరిపాలన రూపాన్ని మార్చడం ద్వారా రాజ్యాంగాన్ని వక్రీకరించవచ్చు; రాజ్యాంగ నైతికతను ఇంకా ఊహించలేం; కాబట్టి "wiser not to trust the Legislature to prescribe forms of administration". మొదటి ముసాయిదా ఎవరు తయారుచేశారు, దానిలో ఎన్ని అనుచ్ఛేదాలు? జవాబు: బి.ఎన్. రావు; 243 అనుచ్ఛేదాలు, 13 షెడ్యూళ్లు. పార్లమెంటు రాజ్యాంగంలోని ఏ భాగాన్నైనా సవరించగలదా? జవాబు: అ. 368 కింద అవును; కానీ మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని నాశనం చేసేలా కాదు ( కేశవానంద భారతి ; మినర్వా మిల్స్ ). అంబేద్కర్ మాట పూర్తి చేయండి: "however good a Constitution may be, ..." జవాబు: "it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it, happen to be a bad lot."

hi.inOneMinute: The Constitution of India (Art. 393) is the supreme law of India. It was made by the Constituent Assembly and given by the people to themselves: "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA ... do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION" (Preamble). Key dates: adopted 26 November 1949 ; signed by members on 24 January 1950 ; came fully into force on 26 January 1950 (Art. 394). A few Articles (on citizenship, elections, interim provisions) came into force at once on 26 Nov 1949. Size when passed: 395 Articles and 8 Schedules (Rajendra Prasad, 26 Nov 1949). Today it has a Preamble, 22 Parts (some with letters, e.g. IVA, IXA), 12 Schedules and appendices; new Articles are added with letters (e.g. Art. 21A, Art. 51A), so the last Article is still Art. 395. Break with British law: Art. 395 repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935. From 26 Jan 1950 India's legal system rests on this Constitution, not on any British Act. It is a living document : it can be amended (Art. 368), but not so as to destroy its basic structure ( Kesavananda Bharati ; Minerva Mills ). Ambedkar (25 Nov 1949): "however good a Constitution may be, it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it, happen to be a bad lot."
legalProvision: (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)
Preamble (closing words) – IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
Article 393 – This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.

Article 394 – This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution.

Article 394A(1) (main words) – The President shall cause to be published under his authority,— (a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, ... and (b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of this Constitution made in the English language. [Inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987, w.e.f. 9-12-1987.]

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

Article 245(1) – Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.
Article 343(1) – The official language of the Union shall be Hindi in Devanagari script.

Article 368(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.
In simple words:

The Preamble says who made the Constitution (the people, through their Constituent Assembly) and when (26 Nov 1949). Art. 393 gives its name. Art. 394 says it started in two steps: some Articles at once, the rest on 26 Jan 1950. Art. 394A provides for an authoritative Hindi text. Art. 395 ends the old British Acts. Art. 245(1) shows that even Parliament makes laws "subject to" the Constitution, so the Constitution is above every other law. Art. 368(1) allows the Constitution to be changed by Parliament under its special procedure.
hi.meaning: The Indian Constitution is the written document, adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950, that creates the organs of the Indian State (Union and States; legislature, executive, judiciary), gives them their powers, limits those powers, and guarantees the rights of the people. Its official name is "the Constitution of India" (Art. 393). Its source of authority is the people. The Preamble says the people "adopt, enact and give to ourselves" this Constitution. Its authority does not come from the British Parliament (Art. 395 repealed the British Acts). Its rank is the highest. Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void (Art. 13); Parliament and State Legislatures make laws "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution" (Art. 245(1)).
keyPoints: Name: Constitution of India (Art. 393). Adopted 26 Nov 1949; signed 24 Jan 1950 (284 members); in force 26 Jan 1950 (Art. 394). Articles in force on 26 Nov 1949: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394. Sizes: Rau's draft 243 Articles + 13 Schedules; Draft 315 + 8; as passed 395 + 8; now 12 Schedules. Art. 395 repealed the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the GoI Act 1935 (Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act 1949 saved). Art. 394A – authoritative Hindi text (58th Amendment, 1987). Amendable (Art. 368) but basic structure cannot be destroyed.

caseLaws.facts: 135 of 1970, under Art. 32) challenged the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended in 1969 and 1971; the case then turned on the validity of the 24th, 25th and 29th Constitutional Amendments. Principle: By majority, "The power to amend does not include the power to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution so as to change its identity" (headnote). Khanna J (para 1480): it would not be competent "under the garb of amendment ... to change the democratic government into dictatorship or hereditary monarchy"; Art. 368 cannot "provide sanction for what may perhaps be called its lawful harakiri". Why it matters: It decides what the Indian Constitution is at its core: an amendable document with a basic structure that Parliament cannot destroy.

Principle: "a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution"; "The power to destroy is not a power to amend." Why it matters: It confirms that the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The President asked whether an agreement with Pakistan to transfer part of the Berubari Union
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Agreement involved cession of Indian territory, so the law to implement it had to be passed under Art. 368, not under Art. 3. The Preamble is "a key to open the mind of the makers", but "the preamble is not a part of the Constitution" and is not "the source of any substantive power" (Gajendragadkar J for the Court). (The later view in Kesavananda Bharati that the Preamble is part of the Constitution is covered in Preamble to Indian Constitution .) Why it matters: It shows that the Constitution's own procedure must be followed for basic changes, such as changing India's territory.

selfTest.q: On what date was the Constitution adopted, and where is that date written?
selfTest.a: Answer: 26 November 1949; in the Preamble. Name five Articles that came into force on 26 Nov 1949. Answer: Any five of Arts. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394. What does Art. 394 call 26 January 1950? Answer: "the commencement of this Constitution". Which Acts did Art. 395 repeal, and which Act did it save? Answer: Repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935; saved the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949. How many Articles and Schedules did the Constitution have when passed? Answer: 395 Articles and 8 Schedules. Which Amendments added the Ninth, Tenth, Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules? Answer: First (1951), Fifty-second (1985), Seventy-third (1992), Seventy-fourth (1992). Why did Ambedkar include details of administration in the Constitution? Answer: Because the Constitution could be perverted by changing the form of administration, and constitutional morality could not yet be assumed; so it was "wiser not to trust the Legislature to prescribe forms of administration". Who prepared the first draft and how many Articles did it have? Answer: B.N. Rau; 243 Articles and 13 Schedules. Can Parliament amend any part of the Constitution? Answer: Yes under Art. 368, but not so as to destroy the basic structure ( Kesavananda Bharati ; Minerva Mills ). Complete Ambedkar: "however good a Constitution may be, ..." Answer: "it is sure to turn out bad because those who are called to work it, happen to be a bad lot."

constitutional-law-i-u1-t3.subtitle: Limited government in practice, Ambedkar's idea of constitutional morality, and how the Supreme Court uses it

en.inOneMinute: Constitutionalism is the idea of limited government : power must be controlled so that it "does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based" ( I.R. Coelho , 2007). Its tools are checks and balances, separation of powers , independent courts, judicial review and fundamental rights. Having a constitution is not the same as having constitutionalism. A country can keep the form of a constitution and still slide into dictatorship (Ambedkar, 25 Nov 1949). Constitutional morality is the habit and attitude needed to work a constitution: "a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution", obedience to authority acting within those forms, combined with free speech and open criticism of those in power (Grote, quoted by Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Ambedkar warned: "Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." Today the Supreme Court uses constitutional morality to test laws against the values of the Constitution, not against popular or majority opinion ( Navtej Singh Johar , 2018).
legalProvision: Neither word appears in the Constitution of India. The Constitution puts constitutionalism into practice through the provisions below, and constitutional morality is the attitude with which they are to be worked. (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)

Article 13(2) – The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void.
Article 14 – The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
Article 32(1) – The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.
Article 50 – The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
Article 75(3) – The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.

Article 124(4) – A Judge of the Supreme Court shall not be removed from his office except by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

Article 245(1) – Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.

Article 324(1) (opening words) – The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Parliament and to the Legislature of every State and of elections to the offices of President and Vice-President held under this Constitution shall be vested in a Commission (referred to in this Constitution as the Election Commission).
Article 51A(a) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
In simple words

Laws cannot take away fundamental rights (Art. 13(2)); everyone is equal before the law (Art. 14). Courts can be approached to enforce rights (Art. 32). Judiciary is to be kept separate from the executive (Art. 50), and judges cannot be removed easily (Art. 124(4)). The government is answerable to the elected House (Art. 75(3)) and elections are run by an independent Election Commission (Art. 324). Legislatures act only within the Constitution (Art. 245). Citizens must abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions (Art. 51A(a)) – the citizen's side of constitutional morality.
en.meaning:
1. Constitutionalism – definition from the Supreme Court. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the nine-judge Bench said: "The principle of constitutionalism is now a legal principle which requires control over the exercise of Governmental power to ensure that it does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based. These democratic principles include the protection of fundamental rights. The principle of constitutionalism advocates a check and balance model of the separation of powers, it requires a diffusion of powers, necessitating different independent centers of decision making."

2. Constitutionalism in simple words. Government must be (a) limited by law, (b) divided among different organs that check each other, (c) answerable to the people and to the courts, and (d) respectful of fundamental rights .

3. Constitutional morality – definition from the Constituent Assembly . Dr. Ambedkar (4 November 1948) quoted the historian Grote: "By constitutional morality Grote meant 'a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution, enforcing obedience to authority acting under and within these forms yet combined with the habit of open speech, of action subject only to definite legal control, and unrestrained censure of those very authorities as to all their public acts combined too with a perfect confidence in the bosom of every citizen amidst the bitterness of party contest that the forms of the Constitution will not be less sacred in the eyes of his opponents than in his own.'"

4. Constitutional morality – definition from the Supreme Court. In Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India , as quoted in Navtej Singh Johar (2018): "Constitutional morality, appositely understood, means the morality that has inherent elements in the constitutional norms and the conscience of the Constitution."

5. In simple words. Constitutionalism is what the system must be (limited and checked government). Constitutional morality is how people in and out of power must behave so that the system works (respect for the rules and the values of the Constitution, even when they are inconvenient).

See Diagram 1 .

Diagram 1. Structure and spirit flowchart TD C["Constitution (the text)"] --> CM["Constitutionalism: limited, checked government (I.R. Coelho)"] C --> MO["Constitutional morality: reverence for forms + open criticism (Grote via Ambedkar)"] CM --> T1["Separation of powers (Art. 50, Art. 75(3))"] CM --> T2["Independent judges and judicial review (Art. 124(4), Art. 32, Art. 226)"] CM --> T3["Fundamental rights and rule of law (Part III, Art. 14)"] CM --> T4["Free elections (Art. 324)"] MO --> M1["Constitutional methods only - no 'Grammar of Anarchy'"] MO --> M2["No hero-worship"] MO --> M3["Not popular sentiment (Navtej)"] MO --> M4["Citizens abide by the Constitution (Art. 51A(a))"] Text description Diagram text, in the order drawn: Constitution (the text) | Constitutionalism: limited, checked government (I.R. Coelho) | Constitutional morality: reverence for forms + open criticism (Grote via Ambedkar) | Separation of powers (Art. 50, Art. 75(3)) | Independent judges and judicial review (Art. 124(4), Art. 32, Art. 226) | Fundamental rights and rule of law (Part III, Art. 14) | Free elections (Art. 324) | Constitutional methods only - no 'Grammar of Anarchy' | No hero-worship | Not popular sentiment (Navtej) | Citizens abide by the Constitution (Art. 51A(a))
keyPoints: Constitutionalism = limited, checked government ( I.R. Coelho , 2007). Tools: separation of powers (Art. 50), responsible government (Art. 75(3)), independent judges (Art. 124(4)), judicial review (Arts. 32, 226), rights (Part III), elections (Art. 324). Constitutional morality = Grote's "paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution" + open speech and censure. Ambedkar: "not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." Ambedkar (25 Nov 1949): constitutional methods; "Grammar of Anarchy"; no hero-worship; social democracy. Navtej (2018): constitutional morality is not popular sentiment; transformative constitutionalism.

selfTest.q: Define constitutionalism in the words of I.R. Coelho . Answer: "a legal principle which requires control over the exercise of Governmental power to ensure that it does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based." Whom did Ambedkar quote for the meaning of constitutional morality?
selfTest.a: Answer: The historian Grote. Complete: "Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. ..." Answer: "It has to be cultivated." What did Ambedkar call unconstitutional methods where constitutional methods are open? Answer: "the Grammar of Anarchy". Which case said constitutional morality must not be equated with popular sentiment? Answer: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018). Name four Articles that show constitutionalism in India. Answer: Any four of Arts. 13, 14, 32, 50, 75(3), 124(4), 245, 324. Can a country have a constitution without constitutionalism? Answer: Yes; Ambedkar warned democracy may "retain its form but give place to dictatorship in fact".

visuals.html:
This Is not the same as Why
Constitution Constitutionalism A constitution is the document; constitutionalism is the principle that power is limited. A country can keep the form and lose the substance (Ambedkar, 25 Nov 1949).
Constitutional morality Popular / social morality Constitutional morality is not "the popular sentiment prevalent at a particular point of time" (Navtej).
Constitutional morality Obedience only Grote's idea combines obedience with "open speech" and "unrestrained censure" of authorities.
Majority rule Constitutionalism The majority governs, but within limits; fundamental rights and judicial review restrain it.
Transformative constitutionalism Ordinary constitutionalism The transformative idea adds a duty to move society in a "democratic egalitarian direction" (Navtej).

te.inOneMinute: రాజ్యాంగవాదం అంటే పరిమిత ప్రభుత్వం అనే భావన: అధికారం "does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based" (దాని పునాది అయిన ప్రజాస్వామ్య సూత్రాలను నాశనం చేయకుండా) నియంత్రించబడాలి ( ఐ.ఆర్. కొయెల్హో , 2007). దాని సాధనాలు: తనిఖీలు-సమతుల్యతలు, అధికార విభజన , స్వతంత్ర న్యాయస్థానాలు, న్యాయ సమీక్ష, ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు. రాజ్యాంగం ఉండటం, రాజ్యాంగవాదం ఉండటం ఒకటి కాదు. ఒక దేశం రాజ్యాంగ రూపాన్ని ఉంచుకుని కూడా నియంతృత్వంలోకి జారిపోవచ్చు (అంబేద్కర్, 25 నవం. 1949). రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత అంటే రాజ్యాంగాన్ని నడపడానికి కావలసిన అలవాటు, దృక్పథం: "a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution" (రాజ్యాంగ రూపాల పట్ల అత్యున్నత గౌరవం), ఆ రూపాల లోపల పనిచేసే అధికారానికి విధేయత, దానితో పాటు స్వేచ్ఛగా మాట్లాడటం, అధికారంలో ఉన్నవారిని బహిరంగంగా విమర్శించడం (గ్రోట్, అంబేద్కర్ ఉదహరించారు, 4 నవం. 1948). అంబేద్కర్ హెచ్చరిక: "Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." (రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత సహజ భావన కాదు. దాన్ని పెంపొందించాలి.) ఈ రోజు సుప్రీంకోర్టు చట్టాలను ప్రజాభిప్రాయం లేదా మెజారిటీ అభిప్రాయంతో కాకుండా, రాజ్యాంగ విలువలతో పరీక్షించడానికి రాజ్యాంగ నైతికతను వాడుతుంది ( నవతేజ్ సింగ్ జోహార్ , 2018).
te.meaning:
1. రాజ్యాంగవాదం – సుప్రీంకోర్టు నిర్వచనం. ఐ.ఆర్. కొయెల్హో v. తమిళనాడు రాష్ట్రం (2007) లో తొమ్మిది మంది న్యాయమూర్తుల ధర్మాసనం: "The principle of constitutionalism is now a legal principle which requires control over the exercise of Governmental power to ensure that it does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based. These democratic principles include the protection of fundamental rights. The principle of constitutionalism advocates a check and balance model of the separation of powers, it requires a diffusion of powers, necessitating different independent centers of decision making." అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగవాదం ఇప్పుడు ఒక చట్టపరమైన సూత్రం; ప్రభుత్వ అధికార వినియోగం దాని పునాది అయిన ప్రజాస్వామ్య సూత్రాలను నాశనం చేయకుండా నియంత్రణ కోరుతుంది. ఆ సూత్రాల్లో ప్రాథమిక హక్కు ల రక్షణ ఉంది. ఇది తనిఖీలు-సమతుల్యతల అధికార విభజన నమూనాను సమర్థిస్తుంది; అధికారం వేర్వేరు స్వతంత్ర నిర్ణయ కేంద్రాల్లో పంచబడాలని కోరుతుంది.

2. సరళంగా రాజ్యాంగవాదం. ప్రభుత్వం (a) చట్టంతో పరిమితం , (b) ఒకదానినొకటి తనిఖీ చేసే వేర్వేరు వ్యవస్థల మధ్య విభజితం , (c) ప్రజలకు, న్యాయస్థానాలకు జవాబుదారీ , (d) ప్రాథమిక హక్కులను గౌరవించేది అయి ఉండాలి.

3. రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత – రాజ్యాంగ సభ నిర్వచనం. డా. అంబేద్కర్ (4 నవంబర్ 1948) చరిత్రకారుడు గ్రోట్‌ను ఉదహరించారు: "By constitutional morality Grote meant 'a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution, enforcing obedience to authority acting under and within these forms yet combined with the habit of open speech, of action subject only to definite legal control, and unrestrained censure of those very authorities as to all their public acts combined too with a perfect confidence in the bosom of every citizen amidst the bitterness of party contest that the forms of the Constitution will not be less sacred in the eyes of his opponents than in his own.'" అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగ రూపాల పట్ల అత్యున్నత గౌరవం; ఆ రూపాల లోపల పనిచేసే అధికారానికి విధేయత; దానితో పాటు స్వేచ్ఛగా మాట్లాడే అలవాటు, స్పష్టమైన చట్ట నియంత్రణకు మాత్రమే లోబడిన చర్య, అదే అధికారుల ప్రజా చర్యలన్నింటినీ నిర్భయంగా విమర్శించడం; పార్టీ పోరాటాల చేదులో కూడా, తన ప్రత్యర్థులకు కూడా రాజ్యాంగ రూపాలు తనకున్నంత పవిత్రమేనని ప్రతి పౌరునికి పూర్తి నమ్మకం.

4. రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత – సుప్రీంకోర్టు నిర్వచనం. గవర్నమెంట్ ఆఫ్ ఎన్.సి.టి. ఆఫ్ ఢిల్లీ v. యూనియన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా కేసులో, నవతేజ్ సింగ్ జోహార్ (2018) లో ఉదహరించినట్లు: "Constitutional morality, appositely understood, means the morality that has inherent elements in the constitutional norms and the conscience of the Constitution." అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత అంటే రాజ్యాంగ ప్రమాణాల్లో, రాజ్యాంగ అంతరాత్మలో అంతర్లీనంగా ఉన్న నైతికత.

5. సరళంగా. రాజ్యాంగవాదం వ్యవస్థ ఎలా ఉండాలో (పరిమిత, తనిఖీ చేయబడిన ప్రభుత్వం) చెబుతుంది. రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత వ్యవస్థ పనిచేయడానికి అధికారంలో ఉన్నవారు, లేనివారు ఎలా ప్రవర్తించాలో (అసౌకర్యంగా ఉన్నా రాజ్యాంగ నియమాలను, విలువలను గౌరవించడం) చెబుతుంది.

డయాగ్రామ్ 1 చూడండి.

Diagram 1. నిర్మాణం, స్ఫూర్తి flowchart TD C["రాజ్యాంగం (పాఠం)"] --> CM["రాజ్యాంగవాదం: పరిమిత, తనిఖీ చేయబడిన ప్రభుత్వం (ఐ.ఆర్. కొయెల్హో)"] C --> MO["రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత: రూపాల పట్ల గౌరవం + బహిరంగ విమర్శ (గ్రోట్ – అంబేద్కర్)"] CM --> T1["అధికార విభజన (అ. 50, అ. 75(3))"] CM --> T2["స్వతంత్ర న్యాయమూర్తులు, న్యాయ సమీక్ష (అ. 124(4), అ. 32, అ. 226)"] CM --> T3["ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు, చట్ట పాలన (భాగం III, అ. 14)"] CM --> T4["స్వేచ్ఛాయుత ఎన్నికలు (అ. 324)"] MO --> M1["రాజ్యాంగ పద్ధతులు మాత్రమే – #quot;అరాచకపు వ్యాకరణం#quot; వద్దు"] MO --> M2["వ్యక్తి పూజ వద్దు"] MO --> M3["ప్రజాభిప్రాయం కాదు (నవతేజ్)"] MO --> M4["పౌరులు రాజ్యాంగానికి కట్టుబడాలి (అ. 51A(a))"] వచన వివరణ చిత్రంలోని పాఠ్యం, గీసిన క్రమంలో: రాజ్యాంగం (పాఠం) | రాజ్యాంగవాదం: పరిమిత, తనిఖీ చేయబడిన ప్రభుత్వం (ఐ.ఆర్. కొయెల్హో) | రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత: రూపాల పట్ల గౌరవం + బహిరంగ విమర్శ (గ్రోట్ – అంబేద్కర్) | అధికార విభజన (అ. 50, అ. 75(3)) | స్వతంత్ర న్యాయమూర్తులు, న్యాయ సమీక్ష (అ. 124(4), అ. 32, అ. 226) | ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు, చట్ట పాలన (భాగం III, అ. 14) | స్వేచ్ఛాయుత ఎన్నికలు (అ. 324) | రాజ్యాంగ పద్ధతులు మాత్రమే – "అరాచకపు వ్యాకరణం" వద్దు | వ్యక్తి పూజ వద్దు | ప్రజాభిప్రాయం కాదు (నవతేజ్) | పౌరులు రాజ్యాంగానికి కట్టుబడాలి (అ. 51A(a))
keyPoints: రాజ్యాంగవాదం = పరిమిత, తనిఖీ చేయబడిన ప్రభుత్వం ( ఐ.ఆర్. కొయెల్హో , 2007). సాధనాలు: అధికార విభజన (అ. 50), బాధ్యతాయుత ప్రభుత్వం (అ. 75(3)), స్వతంత్ర న్యాయమూర్తులు (అ. 124(4)), న్యాయ సమీక్ష (అ. 32, 226), హక్కులు (భాగం III), ఎన్నికలు (అ. 324). రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత = గ్రోట్ "paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution" + బహిరంగ మాట, విమర్శ. అంబేద్కర్: "not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." అంబేద్కర్ (25 నవం. 1949): రాజ్యాంగ పద్ధతులు; "Grammar of Anarchy"; వ్యక్తి పూజ వద్దు; సామాజిక ప్రజాస్వామ్యం. నవతేజ్ (2018): రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత ప్రజాభిప్రాయం కాదు; పరివర్తనాత్మక రాజ్యాంగవాదం.

selfTest.q: ఐ.ఆర్. కొయెల్హో మాటల్లో రాజ్యాంగవాదాన్ని నిర్వచించండి. జవాబు: "a legal principle which requires control over the exercise of Governmental power to ensure that it does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based." రాజ్యాంగ నైతికత అర్థానికి అంబేద్కర్ ఎవరిని ఉదహరించారు?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: చరిత్రకారుడు గ్రోట్. పూర్తి చేయండి: "Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. ..." జవాబు: "It has to be cultivated." రాజ్యాంగ పద్ధతులు తెరిచి ఉన్నప్పుడు రాజ్యాంగేతర పద్ధతులను అంబేద్కర్ ఏమన్నారు? జవాబు: "the Grammar of Anarchy" (అరాచకపు వ్యాకరణం). రాజ్యాంగ నైతికతను ప్రజాభిప్రాయంతో సమానం చేయకూడదని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది? జవాబు: నవతేజ్ సింగ్ జోహార్ v. యూనియన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా (2018). భారతదేశంలో రాజ్యాంగవాదాన్ని చూపే నాలుగు అధికరణలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: అ. 13, 14, 32, 50, 75(3), 124(4), 245, 324 లో ఏవైనా నాలుగు. రాజ్యాంగవాదం లేకుండా రాజ్యాంగం ఉండగలదా? జవాబు: ఉండగలదు; ప్రజాస్వామ్యం "retain its form but give place to dictatorship in fact" అని అంబేద్కర్ హెచ్చరించారు.

hi.inOneMinute: Constitutionalism is the idea of limited government : power must be controlled so that it "does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based" ( I.R. Coelho , 2007). Its tools are checks and balances, separation of powers , independent courts, judicial review and fundamental rights. Having a constitution is not the same as having constitutionalism. A country can keep the form of a constitution and still slide into dictatorship (Ambedkar, 25 Nov 1949). Constitutional morality is the habit and attitude needed to work a constitution: "a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution", obedience to authority acting within those forms, combined with free speech and open criticism of those in power (Grote, quoted by Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Ambedkar warned: "Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." Today the Supreme Court uses constitutional morality to test laws against the values of the Constitution, not against popular or majority opinion ( Navtej Singh Johar , 2018).
legalProvision: Neither word appears in the Constitution of India. The Constitution puts constitutionalism into practice through the provisions below, and constitutional morality is the attitude with which they are to be worked. (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)

Article 13(2) – The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void.
Article 14 – The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
Article 32(1) – The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed.
Article 50 – The State shall take steps to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
Article 75(3) – The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.

Article 124(4) – A Judge of the Supreme Court shall not be removed from his office except by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

Article 245(1) – Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.

Article 324(1) (opening words) – The superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Parliament and to the Legislature of every State and of elections to the offices of President and Vice-President held under this Constitution shall be vested in a Commission (referred to in this Constitution as the Election Commission).
Article 51A(a) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
In simple words

Laws cannot take away fundamental rights (Art. 13(2)); everyone is equal before the law (Art. 14). Courts can be approached to enforce rights (Art. 32). Judiciary is to be kept separate from the executive (Art. 50), and judges cannot be removed easily (Art. 124(4)). The government is answerable to the elected House (Art. 75(3)) and elections are run by an independent Election Commission (Art. 324). Legislatures act only within the Constitution (Art. 245). Citizens must abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions (Art. 51A(a)) – the citizen's side of constitutional morality.
hi.meaning: 1. Constitutionalism – definition from the Supreme Court. In I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), the nine-judge Bench said: "The principle of constitutionalism is now a legal principle which requires control over the exercise of Governmental power to ensure that it does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based. These democratic principles include the protection of fundamental rights. The principle of constitutionalism advocates a check and balance model of the separation of powers, it requires a diffusion of powers, necessitating different independent centers of decision making." 2. Constitutionalism in simple words. Government must be (a) limited by law, (b) divided among different organs that check each other, (c) answerable to the people and to the courts, and (d) respectful of fundamental rights . 3. Constitutional morality – definition from the Constituent Assembly . Dr. Ambedkar (4 November 1948) quoted the historian Grote: "By constitutional morality Grote meant 'a paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution, enforcing obedience to authority acting under and within these forms yet combined with the habit of open speech, of action subject only to definite legal control, and unrestrained censure of those very authorities as to all their public acts combined too with a perfect confidence in the bosom of every citizen amidst the bitterness of party contest that the forms of the Constitution will not be less sacred in the eyes of his opponents than in his own.'" 4. Constitutional morality – definition from the Supreme Court. In Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India , as quoted in Navtej Singh Johar (2018): "Constitutional morality, appositely understood, means the morality that has inherent elements in the constitutional norms and the conscience of the Constitution." 5. In simple words. Constitutionalism is what the system must be (limited and checked government). Constitutional morality is how people in and out of power must behave so that the system works (respect for the rules and the values of the Constitution, even when they are inconvenient). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Structure and spirit flowchart TD C["Constitution (the text)"] --> CM["Constitutionalism: limited, checked government (I.R. Coelho)"] C --> MO["Constitutional morality: reverence for forms + open criticism (Grote via Ambedkar)"] CM --> T1["Separation of powers (Art. 50, Art. 75(3))"] CM --> T2["Independent judges and judicial review (Art. 124(4), Art. 32, Art. 226)"] CM --> T3["Fundamental rights and rule of law (Part III, Art. 14)"] CM --> T4["Free elections (Art. 324)"] MO --> M1["Constitutional methods only - no 'Grammar of Anarchy'"] MO --> M2["No hero-worship"] MO --> M3["Not popular sentiment (Navtej)"] MO --> M4["Citizens abide by the Constitution (Art. 51A(a))"] Text description Diagram text, in the order drawn: Constitution (the text) | Constitutionalism: limited, checked government (I.R. Coelho) | Constitutional morality: reverence for forms + open criticism (Grote via Ambedkar) | Separation of powers (Art. 50, Art. 75(3)) | Independent judges and judicial review (Art. 124(4), Art. 32, Art. 226) | Fundamental rights and rule of law (Part III, Art. 14) | Free elections (Art. 324) | Constitutional methods only - no 'Grammar of Anarchy' | No hero-worship | Not popular sentiment (Navtej) | Citizens abide by the Constitution (Art. 51A(a))
keyPoints: Constitutionalism = limited, checked government ( I.R. Coelho , 2007). Tools: separation of powers (Art. 50), responsible government (Art. 75(3)), independent judges (Art. 124(4)), judicial review (Arts. 32, 226), rights (Part III), elections (Art. 324). Constitutional morality = Grote's "paramount reverence for the forms of the Constitution" + open speech and censure. Ambedkar: "not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." Ambedkar (25 Nov 1949): constitutional methods; "Grammar of Anarchy"; no hero-worship; social democracy. Navtej (2018): constitutional morality is not popular sentiment; transformative constitutionalism.

Answer: "a legal principle which requires control over the exercise of Governmental power to ensure that it does not destroy the democratic principles upon which it is based." Whom did Ambedkar quote for the meaning of constitutional morality?
selfTest.a: Answer: The historian Grote. Complete: "Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. ..." Answer: "It has to be cultivated." What did Ambedkar call unconstitutional methods where constitutional methods are open? Answer: "the Grammar of Anarchy". Which case said constitutional morality must not be equated with popular sentiment? Answer: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018). Name four Articles that show constitutionalism in India. Answer: Any four of Arts. 13, 14, 32, 50, 75(3), 124(4), 245, 324. Can a country have a constitution without constitutionalism? Answer: Yes; Ambedkar warned democracy may "retain its form but give place to dictatorship in fact".

constitutional-law-i-u1-t6.subtitle: The path from Company rule to the Indian Councils Act, 1909, and what the Constitution inherited from it

en.inOneMinute: India's Constitution did not start in 1946. For about 175 years before it, Acts of the British Parliament built up, step by step, the government of India: a central executive, a legislature, courts, civil services and, slowly, Indian representation. Company rule under Parliament's control (1773–1858): Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Acts 1813, 1833 and 1853. Crown rule (1858–1947): Government of India Act 1858; Indian Councils Acts 1861, 1892 and 1909; Government of India Acts 1919 and 1935 (separate syllabus topics). Transfer of power (1940s): Cripps proposals, Cabinet Mission plan (1946), Indian Independence Act 1947, Constituent Assembly. Three long trends: (1) power moved from the Company to the Crown; (2) law-making moved from the executive to a separate and slowly more representative legislature; (3) a unitary, centralised system slowly moved towards provincial autonomy and federation. Many features of today's Constitution have roots here, e.g. ordinances (1861 → Art. 123), suits against the Government (1858 s. 65 → Art. 300), open competitive examinations (1853 → Art. 320), and no bar to office on grounds of religion, birth or descent (1833 s. 87 → Art. 16(2)).
legalProvision: This topic is about history. The present Constitution links back to it in these provisions. (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

Article 300(1) (opening words) – The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may ... sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted.

Article 123(1) – If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.

Article 16(2) – No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State.
In simple words:

Art. 395 closes the British period: it repeals the last two British Acts that governed India. Art. 300 keeps an old rule alive: the Government can be sued "in the like cases" as before. The Supreme Court has traced this chain back to s. 65 of the Government of India Act, 1858 ( State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati ). Art. 123 (ordinances) and Art. 16(2) (no bar on grounds of religion, birth, descent) have earlier versions in the Acts of 1861 and 1833.

Old Acts used in this note (texts from the bare Act PDFs): Regulating Act, 1773; Pitt's India Act, 1784; Charter Act, 1813; Charter Act, 1833; Charter Act, 1853; Government of India Act, 1858; Indian Councils Act, 1861; Indian Councils Act, 1892; Indian Councils Act, 1909. Section numbers below are from those texts.
en.meaning: "Historical perspectives" means studying how the system of government in India grew through earlier laws and events, so that the present Constitution can be understood as the result of that growth. Constitutional development means the gradual change in (a) who holds supreme power, (b) how laws are made, (c) how far Indians take part, and (d) how power is divided between the centre and the provinces. The Regulating Act of 1773 explains why Parliament stepped in: the powers in the Company's charters had "been found, by experience, not to have sufficient force and efficacy to prevent various abuses which have prevailed in the government and administration of the affairs of the said united company" ( Preamble ). So the history of statutory government in India begins with Parliament controlling a trading company.
keyPoints: 1773: Governor-General + 4 councillors (s. 7); Warren Hastings first (s. 10); Supreme Court at Calcutta, CJ + 3 judges (s. 13). 1784: Board of Control, up to 6 commissioners (s. 1); dual control. 1813: monopoly ended except China and tea (s. 2); Rs 1 lakh a year for education (s. 43). 1833: Governor-General of India in Council (s. 39); law member (s. 40); Law Commission (s. 53); no disability (s. 87). 1853: Legislative Councillors (s. 22); open examination (s. 37). 1858: Crown rule (ss. 1–2); Secretary of State (s. 3); Council of India of 15 (s. 7); suits (s. 65 → Art. 300). 1861: 6–12 additional members, half non-official (s. 10); ordinances for 6 months (s. 23 → Art. 123). 1892: budget discussion and questions (s. 2). 1909: elected members (s. 1); "any matter of general public interest" (s. 5). Constitution repealed the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the GoI Act 1935 (Art. 395).

caseLaws.facts: State of Rajasthan v. Mst. Vidhyawati , AIR 1962 SC 933; 1962 Supp (2) SCR 989 (5-judge Bench, decided 2 February 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 11 February 1952 a Government jeep, being driven rashly and negligently by a State employe
caseLaws.facts: His widow and minor child sued the State for damages. Principle: The State's liability for a tort of its servant in the course of employment was the same as that of any other employer. Art. 300 is to be traced back: "by the chain of enactments, beginning with the Act of 1858 and ending with the Constitution", s. 65 applies to the Government of a State as it applied to the East India Company (Sinha C.J.). Why it matters: It shows directly how the Government of India Act, 1858 still shapes the law under the Constitution.
Kasturilal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh , AIR 1965 SC 1039; [1965] 1 SCR 375 (5-judge Bench, decided 29 September 1964)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Police officers seized gold from the appellant under their statutory powers but were negligen
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Powers to arrest, search and seize are "sovereign powers"; though the police were negligent, the claim failed because the act was in exercise of sovereign power. The Court approved The P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. The Secretary of State for India (decided by the Supreme Court of Calcutta under s. 65 of the 1858 Act) and distinguished Vidyawati ; it suggested that the legislature should regulate the State's liability. Why it matters: It shows that a rule worked out under the 1858 Act (the sovereign/non-sovereign distinction from the P. & O. case) continued after the Constitution.

selfTest.q: Which Act first set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta, and how many judges?
selfTest.a: Answer: Regulating Act, 1773 (s. 13): a chief justice and three other judges. What was the Board of Control? Answer: Up to six Privy Councillors appointed as "commissioners for the affairs of India" under Pitt's India Act, 1784, with control over the Company's political affairs. Which Act first used the title "Governor General of India"? Answer: Charter Act, 1833 (s. 39). Which provision of 1833 is the ancestor of Art. 16(2)? Answer: s. 87 – no native disabled from office "by reason only of his Religion, Place of Birth, Descent, Colour". What did the Charter Act, 1853 do for the civil services? Answer: Allowed any natural-born subject to be examined as a candidate (s. 37) – recruitment by examination. Name four changes made by the Government of India Act, 1858. Answer: Crown rule (s. 1); India governed in the Queen's name (s. 2); Secretary of State (s. 3); Council of India of 15 (s. 7); suits against Secretary of State in Council (s. 65). Which Act first gave the Governor-General power to make ordinances, and for how long did they last? Answer: Indian Councils Act, 1861 (s. 23); not more than six months. What new rights did members get in 1892? Answer: Discussion of the annual financial statement and asking questions (s. 2), but no resolutions or votes on them. Which Act first provided for elected members of the Legislative Councils? Answer: Indian Councils Act, 1909 (s. 1). How did the Supreme Court use the 1858 Act in Vidyawati ? Answer: It traced Art. 300 back through a "chain of enactments" to s. 65 of the 1858 Act to decide the State's liability for its driver's negligence .

te.inOneMinute: భారత రాజ్యాంగం 1946లో మొదలవలేదు. దానికి ముందు సుమారు 175 సంవత్సరాల పాటు బ్రిటిష్ పార్లమెంటు చట్టాలు దశలవారీగా భారత ప్రభుత్వాన్ని నిర్మించాయి: కేంద్ర కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థ, శాసనసభ, న్యాయస్థానాలు, సివిల్ సర్వీసులు, నెమ్మదిగా భారతీయుల ప్రాతినిధ్యం. పార్లమెంటు నియంత్రణలో కంపెనీ పాలన (1773–1858): రెగ్యులేటింగ్ చట్టం 1773, పిట్స్ ఇండియా చట్టం 1784, చార్టర్ చట్టాలు 1813, 1833, 1853. బ్రిటిష్ రాజు/రాణి (Crown) పాలన (1858–1947): భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం 1858; ఇండియన్ కౌన్సిల్స్ చట్టాలు 1861, 1892, 1909; భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టాలు 1919, 1935 (వేరే సిలబస్ అంశాలు). అధికార బదిలీ (1940లు): క్రిప్స్ ప్రతిపాదనలు, క్యాబినెట్ మిషన్ ప్రణాళిక (1946), భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం 1947, రాజ్యాంగ సభ. మూడు దీర్ఘకాలిక ధోరణులు: (1) అధికారం కంపెనీ నుంచి క్రౌన్‌కు మారింది; (2) చట్టాల రూపకల్పన కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థ నుంచి వేరైన, నెమ్మదిగా మరింత ప్రాతినిధ్యం గల శాసనసభకు మారింది; (3) ఏకకేంద్ర, కేంద్రీకృత వ్యవస్థ నెమ్మదిగా ప్రాంతీయ స్వయంప్రతిపత్తి, సమాఖ్య వైపు కదిలింది. నేటి రాజ్యాంగంలోని చాలా లక్షణాలకు మూలాలు ఇక్కడే ఉన్నాయి – ఉదా: ఆర్డినెన్సులు (1861 → అ. 123), ప్రభుత్వంపై దావాలు (1858 సె. 65 → అ. 300), బహిరంగ పోటీ పరీక్షలు (1853 → అ. 320), మతం, జన్మస్థలం, వంశం కారణంగా పదవికి అడ్డు లేకపోవడం (1833 సె. 87 → అ. 16(2)).
te.meaning: "చారిత్రక దృక్పథాలు" అంటే – భారతదేశంలో ప్రభుత్వ వ్యవస్థ పూర్వపు చట్టాలు, సంఘటనల ద్వారా ఎలా పెరిగిందో అధ్యయనం చేయడం; దీనివల్ల ప్రస్తుత రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ఆ పెరుగుదల ఫలితంగా అర్థం చేసుకోవచ్చు. రాజ్యాంగ అభివృద్ధి అంటే – (a) సర్వోన్నత అధికారం ఎవరిది, (b) చట్టాలు ఎలా తయారవుతాయి, (c) భారతీయులు ఎంతవరకు పాల్గొంటారు, (d) కేంద్రం, ప్రావిన్సుల మధ్య అధికారం ఎలా పంచబడింది – వీటిలో క్రమక్రమ మార్పు. పార్లమెంటు ఎందుకు జోక్యం చేసుకుందో రెగ్యులేటింగ్ చట్టం, 1773 వివరిస్తుంది: కంపెనీ చార్టర్లలోని అధికారాలు "been found, by experience, not to have sufficient force and efficacy to prevent various abuses which have prevailed in the government and administration of the affairs of the said united company" ( ప్రవేశిక ) (అర్థం: కంపెనీ వ్యవహారాల పాలనలో జరుగుతున్న అనేక దుర్వినియోగాలను అడ్డుకోవడానికి అవి సరిపోవని అనుభవంలో తేలింది). కాబట్టి భారతదేశంలో చట్టబద్ధ పాలన చరిత్ర ఒక వ్యాపార కంపెనీని పార్లమెంటు నియంత్రించడంతో మొదలవుతుంది.
keyPoints: 1773: గవర్నర్ జనరల్ + 4 కౌన్సిలర్లు (సె. 7); మొదటి వారు వారెన్ హేస్టింగ్స్ (సె. 10); కలకత్తాలో సుప్రీంకోర్టు, ప్ర.న్యా. + 3 న్యాయమూర్తులు (సె. 13). 1784: బోర్డ్ ఆఫ్ కంట్రోల్, 6 వరకు కమిషనర్లు (సె. 1); ద్వంద్వ నియంత్రణ. 1813: చైనా, తేయాకు తప్ప గుత్తాధిపత్యం ముగింపు (సె. 2); విద్యకు ఏటా రూ. 1 లక్ష (సె. 43). 1833: భారత గవర్నర్ జనరల్ ఇన్ కౌన్సిల్ (సె. 39); న్యాయ సభ్యుడు (సె. 40); లా కమిషన్ (సె. 53); అనర్హత లేదు (సె. 87). 1853: లెజిస్లేటివ్ కౌన్సిలర్లు (సె. 22); బహిరంగ పరీక్ష (సె. 37). 1858: క్రౌన్ పాలన (సె. 1–2); సెక్రటరీ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ (సె. 3); 15 మందితో కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా (సె. 7); దావాలు (సె. 65 → అ. 300). 1861: 6–12 అదనపు సభ్యులు, సగం అధికారేతరులు (సె. 10); 6 నెలల ఆర్డినెన్సులు (సె. 23 → అ. 123). 1892: బడ్జెట్ చర్చ, ప్రశ్నలు (సె. 2). 1909: ఎన్నికైన సభ్యులు (సె. 1); "any matter of general public interest" (సె. 5). రాజ్యాంగం భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం 1947, భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం 1935ను రద్దు చేసింది (అ. 395).

selfTest.q: కలకత్తాలో సుప్రీంకోర్టును మొదట ఏ చట్టం ఏర్పాటు చేసింది, ఎంత మంది న్యాయమూర్తులు?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: రెగ్యులేటింగ్ చట్టం, 1773 (సె. 13): ఒక ప్రధాన న్యాయమూర్తి, ముగ్గురు ఇతర న్యాయమూర్తులు. బోర్డ్ ఆఫ్ కంట్రోల్ అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: పిట్స్ ఇండియా చట్టం, 1784 కింద "commissioners for the affairs of India"గా నియమించిన ఆరుగురు వరకు ప్రివీ కౌన్సిలర్లు; కంపెనీ రాజకీయ వ్యవహారాలపై నియంత్రణ. "Governor General of India" అనే పదవిని మొదట ఏ చట్టం వాడింది? జవాబు: చార్టర్ చట్టం, 1833 (సె. 39). 1833లోని ఏ నిబంధన అ. 16(2)కు పూర్వరూపం? జవాబు: సె. 87 – "by reason only of his Religion, Place of Birth, Descent, Colour" కారణంగా ఏ స్థానికుడూ పదవికి అనర్హుడు కాడు. చార్టర్ చట్టం, 1853 సివిల్ సర్వీసులకు ఏమి చేసింది? జవాబు: ఏ సహజ పౌరుడైనా అభ్యర్థిగా పరీక్షకు హాజరుకావచ్చు (సె. 37) – పరీక్ష ద్వారా నియామకం. భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1858 చేసిన నాలుగు మార్పులు? జవాబు: క్రౌన్ పాలన (సె. 1); రాణి పేరుతో పాలన (సె. 2); సెక్రటరీ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ (సె. 3); 15 మందితో కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా (సె. 7); సెక్రటరీ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ ఇన్ కౌన్సిల్‌పై దావాలు (సె. 65). గవర్నర్ జనరల్‌కు ఆర్డినెన్సులు చేసే అధికారం మొదట ఏ చట్టం ఇచ్చింది, అవి ఎంతకాలం? జవాబు: ఇండియన్ కౌన్సిల్స్ చట్టం, 1861 (సె. 23); ఆరు నెలలకు మించకుండా. 1892లో సభ్యులకు వచ్చిన కొత్త హక్కులు? జవాబు: వార్షిక ఆర్థిక నివేదికపై చర్చ, ప్రశ్నలు అడగడం (సె. 2); కానీ వాటిపై తీర్మానాలు, ఓటింగ్ లేవు. శాసన మండళ్లలో ఎన్నికైన సభ్యులకు మొదట ఏ చట్టం ఏర్పాటు చేసింది? జవాబు: ఇండియన్ కౌన్సిల్స్ చట్టం, 1909 (సె. 1). Vidyawati లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు 1858 చట్టాన్ని ఎలా ఉపయోగించింది? జవాబు: డ్రైవర్ నిర్లక్ష్యానికి రాష్ట్ర బాధ్యతను నిర్ణయించడానికి అ. 300ను "chain of enactments" ద్వారా 1858 చట్టం సె. 65 వరకు వెనక్కి గుర్తించింది.
