hi.inOneMinute: India's Constitution did not start in 1946. For about 175 years before it, Acts of the British Parliament built up, step by step, the government of India: a central executive, a legislature, courts, civil services and, slowly, Indian representation. Company rule under Parliament's control (1773–1858): Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Acts 1813, 1833 and 1853. Crown rule (1858–1947): Government of India Act 1858; Indian Councils Acts 1861, 1892 and 1909; Government of India Acts 1919 and 1935 (separate syllabus topics). Transfer of power (1940s): Cripps proposals, Cabinet Mission plan (1946), Indian Independence Act 1947, Constituent Assembly. Three long trends: (1) power moved from the Company to the Crown; (2) law-making moved from the executive to a separate and slowly more representative legislature; (3) a unitary, centralised system slowly moved towards provincial autonomy and federation. Many features of today's Constitution have roots here, e.g. ordinances (1861 → Art. 123), suits against the Government (1858 s. 65 → Art. 300), open competitive examinations (1853 → Art. 320), and no bar to office on grounds of religion, birth or descent (1833 s. 87 → Art. 16(2)).
legalProvision: This topic is about history. The present Constitution links back to it in these provisions. (Text: The Constitution of India , Legislative Department, as on 1 May 2026.)

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

Article 300(1) (opening words) – The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may ... sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted.

Article 123(1) – If at any time, except when both Houses of Parliament are in session, the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action, he may promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require.

Article 16(2) – No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State.
In simple words:

Art. 395 closes the British period: it repeals the last two British Acts that governed India. Art. 300 keeps an old rule alive: the Government can be sued "in the like cases" as before. The Supreme Court has traced this chain back to s. 65 of the Government of India Act, 1858 ( State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati ). Art. 123 (ordinances) and Art. 16(2) (no bar on grounds of religion, birth, descent) have earlier versions in the Acts of 1861 and 1833.

Old Acts used in this note (texts from the bare Act PDFs): Regulating Act, 1773; Pitt's India Act, 1784; Charter Act, 1813; Charter Act, 1833; Charter Act, 1853; Government of India Act, 1858; Indian Councils Act, 1861; Indian Councils Act, 1892; Indian Councils Act, 1909. Section numbers below are from those texts.
hi.meaning: "Historical perspectives" means studying how the system of government in India grew through earlier laws and events, so that the present Constitution can be understood as the result of that growth. Constitutional development means the gradual change in (a) who holds supreme power, (b) how laws are made, (c) how far Indians take part, and (d) how power is divided between the centre and the provinces. The Regulating Act of 1773 explains why Parliament stepped in: the powers in the Company's charters had "been found, by experience, not to have sufficient force and efficacy to prevent various abuses which have prevailed in the government and administration of the affairs of the said united company" ( Preamble ). So the history of statutory government in India begins with Parliament controlling a trading company.
keyPoints: 1773: Governor-General + 4 councillors (s. 7); Warren Hastings first (s. 10); Supreme Court at Calcutta, CJ + 3 judges (s. 13). 1784: Board of Control, up to 6 commissioners (s. 1); dual control. 1813: monopoly ended except China and tea (s. 2); Rs 1 lakh a year for education (s. 43). 1833: Governor-General of India in Council (s. 39); law member (s. 40); Law Commission (s. 53); no disability (s. 87). 1853: Legislative Councillors (s. 22); open examination (s. 37). 1858: Crown rule (ss. 1–2); Secretary of State (s. 3); Council of India of 15 (s. 7); suits (s. 65 → Art. 300). 1861: 6–12 additional members, half non-official (s. 10); ordinances for 6 months (s. 23 → Art. 123). 1892: budget discussion and questions (s. 2). 1909: elected members (s. 1); "any matter of general public interest" (s. 5). Constitution repealed the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the GoI Act 1935 (Art. 395).

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 11 February 1952 a Government jeep, being driven rashly and negligently by a State employe
caseLaws.facts: His widow and minor child sued the State for damages. Principle: The State's liability for a tort of its servant in the course of employment was the same as that of any other employer. Art. 300 is to be traced back: "by the chain of enactments, beginning with the Act of 1858 and ending with the Constitution", s. 65 applies to the Government of a State as it applied to the East India Company (Sinha C.J.). Why it matters: It shows directly how the Government of India Act, 1858 still shapes the law under the Constitution.
Kasturilal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh , AIR 1965 SC 1039; [1965] 1 SCR 375 (5-judge Bench, decided 29 September 1964)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Police officers seized gold from the appellant under their statutory powers but were negligen
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Powers to arrest, search and seize are "sovereign powers"; though the police were negligent, the claim failed because the act was in exercise of sovereign power. The Court approved The P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. The Secretary of State for India (decided by the Supreme Court of Calcutta under s. 65 of the 1858 Act) and distinguished Vidyawati ; it suggested that the legislature should regulate the State's liability. Why it matters: It shows that a rule worked out under the 1858 Act (the sovereign/non-sovereign distinction from the P. & O. case) continued after the Constitution.

selfTest.q: Which Act first set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta, and how many judges?
selfTest.a: Answer: Regulating Act, 1773 (s. 13): a chief justice and three other judges. What was the Board of Control? Answer: Up to six Privy Councillors appointed as "commissioners for the affairs of India" under Pitt's India Act, 1784, with control over the Company's political affairs. Which Act first used the title "Governor General of India"? Answer: Charter Act, 1833 (s. 39). Which provision of 1833 is the ancestor of Art. 16(2)? Answer: s. 87 – no native disabled from office "by reason only of his Religion, Place of Birth, Descent, Colour". What did the Charter Act, 1853 do for the civil services? Answer: Allowed any natural-born subject to be examined as a candidate (s. 37) – recruitment by examination. Name four changes made by the Government of India Act, 1858. Answer: Crown rule (s. 1); India governed in the Queen's name (s. 2); Secretary of State (s. 3); Council of India of 15 (s. 7); suits against Secretary of State in Council (s. 65). Which Act first gave the Governor-General power to make ordinances, and for how long did they last? Answer: Indian Councils Act, 1861 (s. 23); not more than six months. What new rights did members get in 1892? Answer: Discussion of the annual financial statement and asking questions (s. 2), but no resolutions or votes on them. Which Act first provided for elected members of the Legislative Councils? Answer: Indian Councils Act, 1909 (s. 1). How did the Supreme Court use the 1858 Act in Vidyawati ? Answer: It traced Art. 300 back through a "chain of enactments" to s. 65 of the 1858 Act to decide the State's liability for its driver's negligence .

constitutional-law-i-u1-t1.subtitle: What a constitution is, the two senses of the word, and why the Indian Constitution is the supreme law

en.inOneMinute: A constitution is the basic law of a country. It creates the main organs of the State (Legislature, Executive, Judiciary), gives them their powers, limits those powers, and protects the rights of the people. Every other law gets its authority from the Constitution. In India, Parliament and the State Legislatures can make laws only "subject to the provisions of this Constitution" (Article 245). If an ordinary law goes against the Constitution, the Constitution wins. A law that takes away Fundamental Rights is void to that extent (Article 13). The courts enforce this supremacy through judicial review : any person can go to the Supreme Court (Art. 32) or a High Court (Art. 226) when a law or an action breaks the Constitution. Even Parliament's power to change the Constitution is limited. It cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution ( Kesavananda Bharati , 1973; Minerva Mills , 1980). Its significance: it is the supreme law, the source of all State power, the shield of the people's rights, the divider of power between the Union and the States, and the record of the ideals the people chose for themselves in the Preamble .
legalProvision: The Constitution of India has no single article that defines the word "constitution". Its meaning and its importance come from the text as a whole. The provisions below show what the Constitution is and why it matters. (Text from The Constitution of India , Government of India, Legislative Department, edition as on 1 May 2026.)
Preamble

WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
(The words "SOCIALIST SECULAR" and "and integrity" were added by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, w.e.f. 3-1-1977.)
Article 1(1) – India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
Article 13 – Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights.

(1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. (2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. (3) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law; ... (4) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368.
(Clause (4) was inserted by the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, w.e.f. 5-11-1971.)

Article 32(1), (2) – (1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed. (2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.
Article 52 – There shall be a President of India.
Article 79 – There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People.

Article 83(2) (main part) – The House of the People, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer and the expiration of the said period of five years shall operate as a dissolution of the House.

(Official footnote: "five years" was substituted by "six years" by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 17 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977), and "five years" was restored by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 13 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).)
Article 124(1) – There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges.
(Official footnote: the number of other Judges is now "thirty-three" under the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019.)

Article 226(1) – Notwithstanding anything in article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.

Article 245(1) – Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.

Article 368(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.

Article 368(2) (main part) – An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill.

(Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, inserted by section 55 of the Forty-second Amendment, are still printed in the official text, but the official footnote says: "This section has been declared invalid by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. and Others Vs. Union of India and Others AIR 1980 SC 1789.")
Article 51A(a) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
Article 60 (President's oath, relevant words) – "... will to the best of my ability preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law ..."

Third Schedule, Form IV (Judges of the Supreme Court, relevant words) – "... I will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established ... and that I will uphold the Constitution and the laws."
Article 393 – This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.

Article 394 – This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution.

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.
In simple words

The people of India, through the Constituent Assembly, gave themselves this Constitution (Preamble). The Constitution creates India as a Union of States (Art. 1). Parliament and State Legislatures make laws only within the limits the Constitution sets (Art. 245). Any law that takes away Fundamental Rights is void to that extent (Art. 13). "Law" here is wide: it covers Ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and even custom or usage that has the force of law (Art. 13(3)(a)). Art. 13 does not apply to amendments of the Constitution made under Art. 368 (Art. 13(4)); amendments are tested instead against the basic structure. The Constitution itself creates the President (Art. 52), Parliament (Art. 79) and the Supreme Court (Art. 124), and fixes the term of the Lok Sabha (Art. 83(2)). Anyone whose Fundamental Rights are broken can go straight to the Supreme Court (Art. 32) or to a High Court (Art. 226). The Constitution itself can be changed only in the way it lays down (Art. 368), and the courts have held that this power cannot be used to destroy its basic structure. The highest office-holders swear to protect and uphold it (Art. 60, Third Schedule), and every citizen has a duty to abide by it (Art. 51A(a)). It took full effect on 26 January 1950 and ended the old colonial framework by repealing the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935 (Arts. 394, 395).
en.meaning:
1. Working definition. A constitution is the basic and highest law of a country. It sets up the organs of the State, gives each of them its powers, fixes the limits of those powers, and sets out the rights of the people and their relationship with the State.

2. What Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said about it. In his last speech in the Constituent Assembly (25 November 1949) he said: "The Constitution can provide only the organs of State such as the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary. The factors on which the working of those organs of the State depend are the people and the political parties they will set up as their instruments to carry out their wishes and their politics."

3. A constitution binds even those who made it. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), Mathew J quoted K.C. Wheare ( Modern Constitutions , 1966, p. 62): once the Constitution is enacted, "it binds thereafter, not only the institutions which it establishes, but also the people themselves. They may amend the Constitution, if at all, only by the method which the Constitution itself provides."

4. A constitution is not an ordinary Act. In the same case, Chandrachud J quoted Higgins J of Australia: we must "remember that it is a Constitution, a mechanism under which laws are to be made and not a mere Act which declares what the law is to be". He also quoted Sir Maurice Gwyer C.J. that "a Constitution of government is a living and organic thing".

5. Two senses of the word "constitution".

Narrow sense – the document. The written text called "the Constitution of India" (Art. 393): the Preamble , the Articles and the Schedules. When a question asks "Is this law against the Constitution?", the word is used in this narrow sense. Wide sense – the whole framework of government. The document plus the laws, rules and practices through which the State actually works under it. For example, the Constitution itself says only that Parliament may increase the number of Supreme Court Judges by law (Art. 124(1)); the actual number today is fixed by an ordinary Act of Parliament. In the wide sense, such laws are also part of how the country is "constituted". For exams on the Indian Constitution, use the narrow sense unless the question asks about the system of government as a whole.

6. Four parts of the meaning (remember as C-E-L-P):

C reates – the organs of the State and the State itself (Art. 1: India is a Union of States). E mpowers – gives each organ its powers (e.g., Art. 245 law-making power). L imits – fixes the boundaries of those powers (Art. 13, "subject to the provisions of this Constitution" in Art. 245, limited amending power). P rotects – secures the rights of the people (Part III, made effective by Art. 13).

See Diagram 1 .

Diagram 1. What a constitution does (C-E-L-P) flowchart TD A["Constitution: basic and highest law"] --> C["Creates the State and its organs (Art. 1)"] A --> E["Empowers each organ (Art. 245)"] A --> L["Limits those powers (Art. 13, Art. 245, limited Art. 368)"] A --> P["Protects the rights of the people (Part III)"] C --> O1["Parliament (Art. 79)"] C --> O2["President (Art. 52)"] C --> O3["Supreme Court (Art. 124)"] P --> RM["Remedy: writs (Art. 32, Art. 226)"] Text description Diagram text, in the order drawn: Constitution: basic and highest law | Creates the State and its organs (Art. 1) | Empowers each organ (Art. 245) | Limits those powers (Art. 13, Art. 245, limited Art. 368) | Protects the rights of the people (Part III) | Parliament (Art. 79) | President (Art. 52) | Supreme Court (Art. 124) | Remedy: writs (Art. 32, Art. 226)
keyPoints: Constitution = basic and highest law; it Creates, Empowers, Limits and Protects. Adopted 26 Nov 1949 (Preamble); fully in force 26 Jan 1950 (Art. 394). Art. 245: law-making power is "subject to the provisions of this Constitution". Art. 13: laws against Fundamental Rights are void "to the extent" of the conflict. Art. 13(3)(a): "law" includes Ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, custom or usage. Art. 13(4) (24th Amendment, 1971): Art. 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments. Arts. 32 and 226: Supreme Court and High Courts enforce the Constitution (judicial review); Ambedkar called Art. 32 "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it". Arts. 52, 79, 124: the Constitution creates the President, Parliament and the Supreme Court; Art. 83(2) fixes the Lok Sabha's five-year term. Art. 368: special majority; amending power is limited. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Art. 368 cannot alter the basic structure; supremacy of the Constitution is a basic feature (Sikri C.J.). Minerva Mills (1980): a limited amending power is itself a basic feature; Art. 368(4) and (5) struck down; "The power to destroy is not a power to amend". Art. 60 and Third Schedule: office-holders swear to protect and uphold the Constitution. Art. 51A(a): every citizen must abide by the Constitution. Art. 395: repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The view of the majority was that "Art. 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution"; Sikri C.J. listed "Supremacy of the Constitution" first among the basic features. Why it matters: It shows that the Constitution stands above every organ it creates, including Parliament when it amends the Constitution.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , (1980) 3 SCC 625; AIR 1980 SC 1789 (5-judge Bench, decided 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Minerva Mills, a textile undertaking in Karnataka, was nationalised under the Sick Textile Un
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Since the Constitution had conferred a limited amending power on the Parliament, the Parliament cannot under the exercise of that limited power enlarge that very power into an absolute power. Indeed, a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution" (Chandrachud C.J.). He added: "The power to destroy is not a power to amend." Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 were struck down. Why it matters: It confirms that the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme, and that no organ can make itself the master of the Constitution.

selfTest.q: Name the four things a constitution does (C-E-L-P). Answer: Creates the organs of the State, Empowers them, Limits their powers, Protects the rights of the people. Which article says Parliament and State Legislatures make laws "subject to the provisions of this Constitution"?
selfTest.a: Answer: Article 245(1). Is a law that abridges a Fundamental Right wholly void? Answer: No. It is void "to the extent of the contravention" (Art. 13(2)). On what date did the Constitution come fully into force, and which article says so? Answer: 26 January 1950; Article 394. A House has 300 members; 240 are present and voting. What is the minimum vote for an amendment Bill? Answer: Majority of total membership = 151; two-thirds of 240 = 160. Minimum = 160. Which case held that a limited amending power is a basic feature of the Constitution? Answer: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980). Which two Acts did Article 395 repeal? Answer: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935. Who said that a constitution is sure to turn out bad if those who work it are a bad lot, and when? Answer: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, in the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949. Does Article 13 apply to an amendment of the Constitution? Answer: No. Article 13(4), inserted by the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971), excludes it. Give an example to show that an ordinary law can be changed easily but a constitutional provision cannot. Answer: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 was changed by ordinary amending Acts (e.g., 2019); the five-year term of the Lok Sabha (Art. 83(2)) needed the 42nd and 44th Amendments to change it. Which articles give the Supreme Court and High Courts the power to issue writs? Answer: Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts).

# Function How the Constitution of India does it
1 Creates the organs of the State "There shall be a President of India" (Art. 52); "There shall be a Parliament" (Art. 79); "There shall be a Supreme Court of India" (Art. 124(1))
2 Fixes their structure and tenure Parliament = President + two Houses (Art. 79); Lok Sabha lasts five years unless sooner dissolved (Art. 83(2))
3 Gives them powers Law-making power (Art. 245); executive power of the Union in the President (Art. 53(1)); writ powers of courts (Arts. 32, 226)
4 Divides power between Union and States Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Art. 246, Seventh Schedule)
5 Limits power "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution" (Art. 245); laws against Fundamental Rights void (Art. 13)
6 Guarantees rights Fundamental Rights (Part III)
7 Provides remedies Right to move the Supreme Court (Art. 32); High Court writs (Art. 226)
8 Provides for its own change Amendment procedure (Art. 368)
9 States ideals and aims Preamble
10 Lays down duties Fundamental duties (Art. 51A)

visuals.html:
This Is not the same as Why
Constitution Ordinary law (Act of Parliament or State) An ordinary law is made under the Constitution and must obey it (Art. 245). The Constitution is the higher law.
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (ordinary law) Article 83(2) (part of the Constitution) The Act was changed by ordinary amending Acts (e.g., 2019); the Lok Sabha's term in Art. 83(2) could be changed only by constitutional amendments (42nd, 44th).
Constitution in the narrow sense (the document) Constitution in the wide sense (the whole working framework) The narrow sense is the text (Art. 393); the wide sense adds the laws and practices made under it.
Article 32 Article 226 Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and lies only for Part III rights; Art. 226 lies in a High Court for Part III rights "and for any other purpose".
Amending the Constitution (Art. 368) Making an ordinary law (Art. 245) Amendment uses constituent power and a special majority; ordinary law uses legislative power and a simple majority.
Amending the Constitution Destroying it Parliament may add, vary or repeal provisions, but not alter the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati).
Constitution (the document and its rules) Constitutionalism (the idea of limited government) The meaning of constitutionalism is a separate syllabus topic: Constitutionalism and Constitutional Morality.
Preamble The whole Constitution The Preamble states who gave the Constitution and its aims; the Articles and Schedules contain the operative rules.

te.inOneMinute: రాజ్యాంగం అనేది ఒక దేశపు ప్రాథమిక చట్టం. ఇది రాజ్యపు ముఖ్య వ్యవస్థలను (శాసన వ్యవస్థ, కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థ, న్యాయ వ్యవస్థ) సృష్టిస్తుంది , వాటికి అధికారాలు ఇస్తుంది , ఆ అధికారాలను పరిమితం చేస్తుంది , ప్రజల హక్కులను రక్షిస్తుంది . మిగతా ప్రతి చట్టానికీ అధికారం రాజ్యాంగం నుండే వస్తుంది. భారతదేశంలో పార్లమెంటు, రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభలు "ఈ రాజ్యాంగ నిబంధనలకు లోబడి" (subject to the provisions of this Constitution) మాత్రమే చట్టాలు చేయగలవు (అధికరణ 245). సాధారణ చట్టం రాజ్యాంగానికి విరుద్ధంగా ఉంటే రాజ్యాంగమే గెలుస్తుంది. ప్రాథమిక హక్కులను తీసివేసే చట్టం ఆ మేరకు శూన్యం (అధికరణ 13). న్యాయస్థానాలు ఈ ఆధిపత్యాన్ని న్యాయ సమీక్ష ద్వారా అమలు చేస్తాయి: ఒక చట్టం లేదా చర్య రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ఉల్లంఘిస్తే ఎవరైనా సుప్రీంకోర్టుకు (అ. 32) లేదా హైకోర్టుకు (అ. 226) వెళ్ళవచ్చు. రాజ్యాంగాన్ని మార్చే పార్లమెంటు అధికారానికి కూడా పరిమితి ఉంది. అది రాజ్యాంగపు మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని నాశనం చేయలేదు ( కేశవానంద భారతి , 1973; మినర్వా మిల్స్ , 1980). ప్రాముఖ్యత: ఇది అత్యున్నత చట్టం, రాజ్యపు అన్ని అధికారాలకు మూలం, ప్రజల హక్కులకు కవచం, కేంద్రం–రాష్ట్రాల మధ్య అధికార విభజనకర్త, ప్రజలు తమకు తామే ఎంచుకున్న ఆదర్శాల రికార్డు ( ప్రవేశిక ).
te.meaning:
1. పని నిర్వచనం. రాజ్యాంగం అనేది ఒక దేశపు ప్రాథమిక మరియు అత్యున్నత చట్టం. ఇది రాజ్య వ్యవస్థలను ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది, ఒక్కో వ్యవస్థకు దాని అధికారాలు ఇస్తుంది, ఆ అధికారాల హద్దులు నిర్ణయిస్తుంది, ప్రజల హక్కులను మరియు రాజ్యంతో వారి సంబంధాన్ని తెలియజేస్తుంది.

2. డా. బి.ఆర్. అంబేద్కర్ చెప్పినది. రాజ్యాంగ సభ లో తన చివరి ప్రసంగంలో (25 నవంబర్ 1949) ఆయన ఇలా అన్నారు: "The Constitution can provide only the organs of State such as the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary. The factors on which the working of those organs of the State depend are the people and the political parties they will set up as their instruments to carry out their wishes and their politics." అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగం శాసన వ్యవస్థ, కార్యనిర్వాహక వ్యవస్థ, న్యాయ వ్యవస్థ వంటి రాజ్య వ్యవస్థలను మాత్రమే ఇవ్వగలదు. అవి ఎలా పనిచేస్తాయన్నది ప్రజలపై, వారు తమ కోరికలు నెరవేర్చుకోవడానికి ఏర్పాటు చేసుకునే రాజకీయ పార్టీలపై ఆధారపడి ఉంటుంది.

3. రాజ్యాంగం దానిని చేసిన వారినీ కట్టుబడి ఉంచుతుంది. కేశవానంద భారతి v. కేరళ రాష్ట్రం (1973) కేసులో జస్టిస్ మాథ్యూ, కె.సి. వేర్ (K.C. Wheare, Modern Constitutions , 1966, పేజీ 62) మాటలను ఉదహరించారు: రాజ్యాంగం ఒకసారి అమలైన తర్వాత "it binds thereafter, not only the institutions which it establishes, but also the people themselves. They may amend the Constitution, if at all, only by the method which the Constitution itself provides." అర్థం: అది తాను ఏర్పాటు చేసిన వ్యవస్థలనే కాదు, ప్రజలను కూడా కట్టుబడి ఉంచుతుంది. దానిని సవరించాలంటే, రాజ్యాంగమే చెప్పిన పద్ధతిలో మాత్రమే సవరించాలి.

4. రాజ్యాంగం సాధారణ చట్టం కాదు. అదే కేసులో జస్టిస్ చంద్రచూడ్, ఆస్ట్రేలియా న్యాయమూర్తి హిగ్గిన్స్ మాటలను ఉదహరించారు: "remember that it is a Constitution, a mechanism under which laws are to be made and not a mere Act which declares what the law is to be". సర్ మారిస్ గ్వయర్ (ప్రధాన న్యాయమూర్తి) మాటను కూడా ఉదహరించారు: "a Constitution of government is a living and organic thing". అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగం అనేది చట్టాలు ఏ పద్ధతిలో తయారు కావాలో చెప్పే యంత్రాంగం; చట్టం ఏమిటో మాత్రమే చెప్పే సాధారణ చట్టం కాదు. అది సజీవమైన, ఎదిగే వ్యవస్థ.

5. "రాజ్యాంగం" అనే పదానికి రెండు అర్థాలు.

సంకుచిత అర్థం – పత్రం. "భారత రాజ్యాంగం" అనే లిఖిత పాఠం (అ. 393): ప్రవేశిక , అధికరణలు, షెడ్యూళ్లు. "ఈ చట్టం రాజ్యాంగానికి విరుద్ధమా?" అని అడిగినప్పుడు ఈ సంకుచిత అర్థంలో వాడతాం. విస్తృత అర్థం – మొత్తం ప్రభుత్వ చట్రం. పత్రం మరియు దాని క్రింద రాజ్యం నిజంగా పనిచేసే చట్టాలు, నియమాలు, పద్ధతులు. ఉదాహరణకు, పార్లమెంటు చట్టం ద్వారా సుప్రీంకోర్టు న్యాయమూర్తుల సంఖ్యను పెంచవచ్చని మాత్రమే రాజ్యాంగం చెబుతుంది (అ. 124(1)); ఈ రోజు ఉన్న సంఖ్యను పార్లమెంటు సాధారణ చట్టం నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. విస్తృత అర్థంలో అలాంటి చట్టాలు కూడా దేశం ఎలా "ఏర్పాటైంది" అనే దానిలో భాగమే. భారత రాజ్యాంగంపై పరీక్ష ప్రశ్నల్లో, ప్రశ్న మొత్తం ప్రభుత్వ వ్యవస్థ గురించి అడిగితే తప్ప, సంకుచిత అర్థాన్నే వాడండి.

6. అర్థంలో నాలుగు భాగాలు (C-E-L-P గా గుర్తుంచుకోండి):

C reates (సృష్టిస్తుంది) – రాజ్యాన్ని, దాని వ్యవస్థలను (అ. 1: భారతదేశం రాష్ట్రాల సమాఖ్య). E mpowers (అధికారం ఇస్తుంది) – ఒక్కో వ్యవస్థకు అధికారాలు (ఉదా. అ. 245 చట్టాలు చేసే అధికారం). L imits (పరిమితం చేస్తుంది) – ఆ అధికారాల హద్దులు (అ. 13; అ. 245 లోని "ఈ రాజ్యాంగ నిబంధనలకు లోబడి"; పరిమిత సవరణ అధికారం). P rotects (రక్షిస్తుంది) – ప్రజల హక్కులు (భాగం III, అ. 13 ద్వారా అమలు).

డయాగ్రామ్ 1 చూడండి.

Diagram 1. రాజ్యాంగం చేసే పని (C-E-L-P) flowchart TD A["రాజ్యాంగం: ప్రాథమిక మరియు అత్యున్నత చట్టం"] --> C["సృష్టిస్తుంది (అ. 1)"] A --> E["అధికారం ఇస్తుంది (అ. 245)"] A --> L["అధికారాలను పరిమితం చేస్తుంది (అ. 13, అ. 245, పరిమిత అ. 368)"] A --> P["ప్రజల హక్కులను రక్షిస్తుంది (భాగం III)"] C --> O1["పార్లమెంటు (అ. 79)"] C --> O2["రాష్ట్రపతి (అ. 52)"] C --> O3["సుప్రీంకోర్టు (అ. 124)"] P --> RM["పరిష్కారం: రిట్లు (అ. 32, అ. 226)"] వచన వివరణ చిత్రంలోని పాఠ్యం, గీసిన క్రమంలో: రాజ్యాంగం: ప్రాథమిక మరియు అత్యున్నత చట్టం | సృష్టిస్తుంది (అ. 1) | అధికారం ఇస్తుంది (అ. 245) | అధికారాలను పరిమితం చేస్తుంది (అ. 13, అ. 245, పరిమిత అ. 368) | ప్రజల హక్కులను రక్షిస్తుంది (భాగం III) | పార్లమెంటు (అ. 79) | రాష్ట్రపతి (అ. 52) | సుప్రీంకోర్టు (అ. 124) | పరిష్కారం: రిట్లు (అ. 32, అ. 226)
keyPoints: రాజ్యాంగం = ప్రాథమిక మరియు అత్యున్నత చట్టం; అది సృష్టిస్తుంది, అధికారం ఇస్తుంది, పరిమితం చేస్తుంది, రక్షిస్తుంది. ఆమోదం 26 నవం. 1949 (ప్రవేశిక); పూర్తి అమలు 26 జన. 1950 (అ. 394). అ. 245: చట్టాలు చేసే అధికారం "ఈ రాజ్యాంగ నిబంధనలకు లోబడి" ఉంటుంది. అ. 13: ప్రాథమిక హక్కులకు విరుద్ధమైన చట్టాలు విరోధం "మేరకు" శూన్యం. అ. 13(3)(a): "చట్టం" లో ఆర్డినెన్సులు, ఉత్తర్వులు, ఉప-చట్టాలు, నియమాలు, నిబంధనలు, ప్రకటనలు, ఆచారం లేదా వాడుక ఉంటాయి. అ. 13(4) (24వ సవరణ, 1971): రాజ్యాంగ సవరణలకు అ. 13 వర్తించదు. అ. 32, 226: సుప్రీంకోర్టు, హైకోర్టులు రాజ్యాంగాన్ని అమలు చేస్తాయి (న్యాయ సమీక్ష); అంబేద్కర్ అ. 32 ను "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" అన్నారు. అ. 52, 79, 124: రాజ్యాంగం రాష్ట్రపతి, పార్లమెంటు, సుప్రీంకోర్టులను సృష్టిస్తుంది; అ. 83(2) లోక్‌సభకు ఐదేళ్ల కాలపరిమితి నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. అ. 368: ప్రత్యేక మెజారిటీ; సవరణ అధికారం పరిమితం. కేశవానంద భారతి (1973): అ. 368 మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని మార్చలేదు; రాజ్యాంగ ఆధిపత్యం ఒక మౌలిక లక్షణం (ప్రధాన న్యాయమూర్తి సిక్రీ). మినర్వా మిల్స్ (1980): పరిమిత సవరణ అధికారమే ఒక మౌలిక లక్షణం; అ. 368(4), (5) రద్దు; "The power to destroy is not a power to amend". అ. 60, మూడవ షెడ్యూలు: పదవిలో ఉన్నవారు రాజ్యాంగాన్ని రక్షిస్తామని, సమర్థిస్తామని ప్రమాణం చేస్తారు. అ. 51A(a): ప్రతి పౌరుడూ రాజ్యాంగానికి కట్టుబడి ఉండాలి. అ. 395: భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం, 1947, భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1935 రద్దు.

selfTest.q: రాజ్యాంగం చేసే నాలుగు పనులు చెప్పండి (C-E-L-P). జవాబు: రాజ్య వ్యవస్థలను సృష్టిస్తుంది, వాటికి అధికారం ఇస్తుంది, వాటి అధికారాలను పరిమితం చేస్తుంది, ప్రజల హక్కులను రక్షిస్తుంది. పార్లమెంటు, రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభలు "ఈ రాజ్యాంగ నిబంధనలకు లోబడి" చట్టాలు చేస్తాయని ఏ అధికరణ చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: అధికరణ 245(1). ప్రాథమిక హక్కును తగ్గించే చట్టం పూర్తిగా శూన్యమా? జవాబు: కాదు. "ఉల్లంఘించిన మేరకు" మాత్రమే శూన్యం (అ. 13(2)). రాజ్యాంగం ఏ తేదీన పూర్తిగా అమలులోకి వచ్చింది, ఏ అధికరణ ఆ విషయం చెబుతుంది? జవాబు: 26 జనవరి 1950; అధికరణ 394. ఒక సభలో మొత్తం 300 మంది సభ్యులు; 240 మంది హాజరై ఓటు వేశారు. సవరణ బిల్లుకు కనీసం ఎన్ని ఓట్లు కావాలి? జవాబు: మొత్తం సభ్యత్వంలో మెజారిటీ = 151; 240లో మూడింట రెండు వంతులు = 160. కనీసం = 160. పరిమిత సవరణ అధికారం రాజ్యాంగపు మౌలిక లక్షణమని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది? జవాబు: మినర్వా మిల్స్ లిమిటెడ్ v. భారత ప్రభుత్వం (1980). అధికరణ 395 ఏ రెండు చట్టాలను రద్దు చేసింది? జవాబు: భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం, 1947 మరియు భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1935. రాజ్యాంగాన్ని నడిపేవారు చెడ్డవారైతే అది తప్పకుండా చెడుగా మారుతుందని ఎవరు, ఎప్పుడు అన్నారు? జవాబు: డా. బి.ఆర్. అంబేద్కర్, రాజ్యాంగ సభలో 25 నవంబర్ 1949న. రాజ్యాంగ సవరణకు అధికరణ 13 వర్తిస్తుందా? జవాబు: లేదు. 24వ సవరణ (1971) చేర్చిన అధికరణ 13(4) దానిని మినహాయిస్తుంది. సాధారణ చట్టాన్ని సులభంగా మార్చవచ్చు కానీ రాజ్యాంగ నిబంధనను కాదు అని చూపే ఉదాహరణ ఇవ్వండి. జవాబు: మోటారు వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 ను సాధారణ సవరణ చట్టాలతో మార్చారు (ఉదా. 2019); లోక్‌సభ ఐదేళ్ల కాలపరిమితిని (అ. 83(2)) మార్చడానికి 42వ, 44వ సవరణలు కావలసి వచ్చాయి. సుప్రీంకోర్టు, హైకోర్టులకు రిట్లు జారీ చేసే అధికారం ఏ అధికరణలు ఇస్తాయి? జవాబు: అధికరణ 32 (సుప్రీంకోర్టు), అధికరణ 226 (హైకోర్టులు).

# విధి భారత రాజ్యాంగం దానిని ఎలా చేస్తుంది
1 రాజ్య వ్యవస్థలను సృష్టిస్తుంది "There shall be a President of India" (అ. 52); "There shall be a Parliament" (అ. 79); "There shall be a Supreme Court of India" (అ. 124(1))
2 వాటి నిర్మాణం, కాలపరిమితి నిర్ణయిస్తుంది పార్లమెంటు = రాష్ట్రపతి + రెండు సభలు (అ. 79); ముందే రద్దు కాకపోతే లోక్‌సభ ఐదేళ్లు (అ. 83(2))
3 వాటికి అధికారాలు ఇస్తుంది చట్టాలు చేసే అధికారం (అ. 245); కేంద్ర కార్యనిర్వాహక అధికారం రాష్ట్రపతిలో (అ. 53(1)); న్యాయస్థానాల రిట్ అధికారాలు (అ. 32, 226)
4 కేంద్రం, రాష్ట్రాల మధ్య అధికారాన్ని విభజిస్తుంది కేంద్ర, రాష్ట్ర, ఉమ్మడి జాబితాలు (అ. 246, ఏడవ షెడ్యూలు)
5 అధికారాన్ని పరిమితం చేస్తుంది "ఈ రాజ్యాంగ నిబంధనలకు లోబడి" (అ. 245); ప్రాథమిక హక్కులకు విరుద్ధమైన చట్టాలు శూన్యం (అ. 13)
6 హక్కులకు హామీ ఇస్తుంది ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు (భాగం III)
7 పరిష్కారాలు (remedies) ఇస్తుంది సుప్రీంకోర్టును ఆశ్రయించే హక్కు (అ. 32); హైకోర్టు రిట్లు (అ. 226)
8 తన మార్పుకు మార్గం చూపుతుంది సవరణ పద్ధతి (అ. 368)
9 ఆదర్శాలు, లక్ష్యాలు పేర్కొంటుంది ప్రవేశిక
10 కర్తవ్యాలు నిర్దేశిస్తుంది ప్రాథమిక కర్తవ్యాలు (అ. 51A)

అంశం అర్థం ఆధారం
అర్థం సృష్టించే, అధికారం ఇచ్చే, పరిమితం చేసే, రక్షించే ప్రాథమిక మరియు అత్యున్నత చట్టం అంబేద్కర్, రాజ్యాంగ సభ 25 నవం. 1949; కేశవానంద భారతి
ఎవరు ఇచ్చారు "భారత ప్రజలమైన మేము", రాజ్యాంగ సభ ద్వారా, 26 నవం. 1949 ప్రవేశిక
పూర్తి అమలు 26 జనవరి 1950 అ. 394
ఆధిపత్యం ప్రాథమిక హక్కులకు విరుద్ధమైన చట్టాలు ఆ మేరకు శూన్యం అ. 13
అ. 13 లో "చట్టం" ఆర్డినెన్సులు, ఉత్తర్వులు, ఉప-చట్టాలు, నియమాలు, నిబంధనలు, ప్రకటనలు, ఆచారం లేదా వాడుక అ. 13(3)(a)
సవరణలు మరియు అ. 13 సవరణలకు అ. 13 వర్తించదు; వాటిని మౌలిక నిర్మాణంతో పరీక్షిస్తారు అ. 13(4) (24వ సవరణ, 1971); కేశవానంద భారతి
పరిష్కారం సుప్రీంకోర్టు రిట్లు; హైకోర్టు రిట్లు అ. 32, 226
వ్యవస్థల సృష్టి రాష్ట్రపతి, పార్లమెంటు, సుప్రీంకోర్టు అ. 52, 79, 124
చట్టాలు చేసే అధికారం "ఈ రాజ్యాంగ నిబంధనలకు లోబడి" మాత్రమే అ. 245
సవరణ ప్రత్యేక మెజారిటీ; మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని నాశనం చేయలేదు అ. 368; కేశవానంద భారతి; మినర్వా మిల్స్

hi.inOneMinute: A constitution is the basic law of a country. It creates the main organs of the State (Legislature, Executive, Judiciary), gives them their powers, limits those powers, and protects the rights of the people. Every other law gets its authority from the Constitution. In India, Parliament and the State Legislatures can make laws only "subject to the provisions of this Constitution" (Article 245). If an ordinary law goes against the Constitution, the Constitution wins. A law that takes away Fundamental Rights is void to that extent (Article 13). The courts enforce this supremacy through judicial review : any person can go to the Supreme Court (Art. 32) or a High Court (Art. 226) when a law or an action breaks the Constitution. Even Parliament's power to change the Constitution is limited. It cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution ( Kesavananda Bharati , 1973; Minerva Mills , 1980). Its significance: it is the supreme law, the source of all State power, the shield of the people's rights, the divider of power between the Union and the States, and the record of the ideals the people chose for themselves in the Preamble .
legalProvision: The Constitution of India has no single article that defines the word "constitution". Its meaning and its importance come from the text as a whole. The provisions below show what the Constitution is and why it matters. (Text from The Constitution of India , Government of India, Legislative Department, edition as on 1 May 2026.)
Preamble

WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
(The words "SOCIALIST SECULAR" and "and integrity" were added by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, w.e.f. 3-1-1977.)
Article 1(1) – India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
Article 13 – Laws inconsistent with or in derogation of the fundamental rights.

(1) All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void. (2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void. (3) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "law" includes any Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage having in the territory of India the force of law; ... (4) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 368.
(Clause (4) was inserted by the Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1971, w.e.f. 5-11-1971.)

Article 32(1), (2) – (1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed. (2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.
Article 52 – There shall be a President of India.
Article 79 – There shall be a Parliament for the Union which shall consist of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People.

Article 83(2) (main part) – The House of the People, unless sooner dissolved, shall continue for five years from the date appointed for its first meeting and no longer and the expiration of the said period of five years shall operate as a dissolution of the House.

(Official footnote: "five years" was substituted by "six years" by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 17 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977), and "five years" was restored by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 13 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).)
Article 124(1) – There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges.
(Official footnote: the number of other Judges is now "thirty-three" under the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019.)

Article 226(1) – Notwithstanding anything in article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose.

Article 245(1) – Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State.

Article 368(1) – Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.

Article 368(2) (main part) – An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting, it shall be presented to the President who shall give his assent to the Bill and thereupon the Constitution shall stand amended in accordance with the terms of the Bill.

(Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368, inserted by section 55 of the Forty-second Amendment, are still printed in the official text, but the official footnote says: "This section has been declared invalid by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. and Others Vs. Union of India and Others AIR 1980 SC 1789.")
Article 51A(a) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
Article 60 (President's oath, relevant words) – "... will to the best of my ability preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law ..."

Third Schedule, Form IV (Judges of the Supreme Court, relevant words) – "... I will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established ... and that I will uphold the Constitution and the laws."
Article 393 – This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India.

Article 394 – This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution.

Article 395 – The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.
In simple words

The people of India, through the Constituent Assembly, gave themselves this Constitution (Preamble). The Constitution creates India as a Union of States (Art. 1). Parliament and State Legislatures make laws only within the limits the Constitution sets (Art. 245). Any law that takes away Fundamental Rights is void to that extent (Art. 13). "Law" here is wide: it covers Ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, and even custom or usage that has the force of law (Art. 13(3)(a)). Art. 13 does not apply to amendments of the Constitution made under Art. 368 (Art. 13(4)); amendments are tested instead against the basic structure. The Constitution itself creates the President (Art. 52), Parliament (Art. 79) and the Supreme Court (Art. 124), and fixes the term of the Lok Sabha (Art. 83(2)). Anyone whose Fundamental Rights are broken can go straight to the Supreme Court (Art. 32) or to a High Court (Art. 226). The Constitution itself can be changed only in the way it lays down (Art. 368), and the courts have held that this power cannot be used to destroy its basic structure. The highest office-holders swear to protect and uphold it (Art. 60, Third Schedule), and every citizen has a duty to abide by it (Art. 51A(a)). It took full effect on 26 January 1950 and ended the old colonial framework by repealing the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935 (Arts. 394, 395).
hi.meaning: 1. Working definition. A constitution is the basic and highest law of a country. It sets up the organs of the State, gives each of them its powers, fixes the limits of those powers, and sets out the rights of the people and their relationship with the State. 2. What Dr. B.R. Ambedkar said about it. In his last speech in the Constituent Assembly (25 November 1949) he said: "The Constitution can provide only the organs of State such as the Legislature, the Executive and the Judiciary. The factors on which the working of those organs of the State depend are the people and the political parties they will set up as their instruments to carry out their wishes and their politics." 3. A constitution binds even those who made it. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), Mathew J quoted K.C. Wheare ( Modern Constitutions , 1966, p. 62): once the Constitution is enacted, "it binds thereafter, not only the institutions which it establishes, but also the people themselves. They may amend the Constitution, if at all, only by the method which the Constitution itself provides." 4. A constitution is not an ordinary Act. In the same case, Chandrachud J quoted Higgins J of Australia: we must "remember that it is a Constitution, a mechanism under which laws are to be made and not a mere Act which declares what the law is to be". He also quoted Sir Maurice Gwyer C.J. that "a Constitution of government is a living and organic thing". 5. Two senses of the word "constitution". Narrow sense – the document. The written text called "the Constitution of India" (Art. 393): the Preamble , the Articles and the Schedules. When a question asks "Is this law against the Constitution?", the word is used in this narrow sense. Wide sense – the whole framework of government. The document plus the laws, rules and practices through which the State actually works under it. For example, the Constitution itself says only that Parliament may increase the number of Supreme Court Judges by law (Art. 124(1)); the actual number today is fixed by an ordinary Act of Parliament. In the wide sense, such laws are also part of how the country is "constituted". For exams on the Indian Constitution, use the narrow sense unless the question asks about the system of government as a whole. 6. Four parts of the meaning (remember as C-E-L-P): C reates – the organs of the State and the State itself (Art. 1: India is a Union of States). E mpowers – gives each organ its powers (e.g., Art. 245 law-making power). L imits – fixes the boundaries of those powers (Art. 13, "subject to the provisions of this Constitution" in Art. 245, limited amending power). P rotects – secures the rights of the people (Part III, made effective by Art. 13). See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. What a constitution does (C-E-L-P) flowchart TD A["Constitution: basic and highest law"] --> C["Creates the State and its organs (Art. 1)"] A --> E["Empowers each organ (Art. 245)"] A --> L["Limits those powers (Art. 13, Art. 245, limited Art. 368)"] A --> P["Protects the rights of the people (Part III)"] C --> O1["Parliament (Art. 79)"] C --> O2["President (Art. 52)"] C --> O3["Supreme Court (Art. 124)"] P --> RM["Remedy: writs (Art. 32, Art. 226)"] Text description Diagram text, in the order drawn: Constitution: basic and highest law | Creates the State and its organs (Art. 1) | Empowers each organ (Art. 245) | Limits those powers (Art. 13, Art. 245, limited Art. 368) | Protects the rights of the people (Part III) | Parliament (Art. 79) | President (Art. 52) | Supreme Court (Art. 124) | Remedy: writs (Art. 32, Art. 226)
keyPoints: Constitution = basic and highest law; it Creates, Empowers, Limits and Protects. Adopted 26 Nov 1949 (Preamble); fully in force 26 Jan 1950 (Art. 394). Art. 245: law-making power is "subject to the provisions of this Constitution". Art. 13: laws against Fundamental Rights are void "to the extent" of the conflict. Art. 13(3)(a): "law" includes Ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, custom or usage. Art. 13(4) (24th Amendment, 1971): Art. 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments. Arts. 32 and 226: Supreme Court and High Courts enforce the Constitution (judicial review); Ambedkar called Art. 32 "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it". Arts. 52, 79, 124: the Constitution creates the President, Parliament and the Supreme Court; Art. 83(2) fixes the Lok Sabha's five-year term. Art. 368: special majority; amending power is limited. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Art. 368 cannot alter the basic structure; supremacy of the Constitution is a basic feature (Sikri C.J.). Minerva Mills (1980): a limited amending power is itself a basic feature; Art. 368(4) and (5) struck down; "The power to destroy is not a power to amend". Art. 60 and Third Schedule: office-holders swear to protect and uphold the Constitution. Art. 51A(a): every citizen must abide by the Constitution. Art. 395: repealed the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935.

Why it matters: It shows that the Constitution stands above every organ it creates, including Parliament when it amends the Constitution.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , (1980) 3 SCC 625; AIR 1980 SC 1789 (5-judge Bench, decided 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Minerva Mills, a textile undertaking in Karnataka, was nationalised under the Sick Textile Un
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Since the Constitution had conferred a limited amending power on the Parliament, the Parliament cannot under the exercise of that limited power enlarge that very power into an absolute power. Indeed, a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution" (Chandrachud C.J.). He added: "The power to destroy is not a power to amend." Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 were struck down. Why it matters: It confirms that the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme, and that no organ can make itself the master of the Constitution.

selfTest.q: Name the four things a constitution does (C-E-L-P). Answer: Creates the organs of the State, Empowers them, Limits their powers, Protects the rights of the people. Which article says Parliament and State Legislatures make laws "subject to the provisions of this Constitution"?
selfTest.a: Answer: Article 245(1). Is a law that abridges a Fundamental Right wholly void? Answer: No. It is void "to the extent of the contravention" (Art. 13(2)). On what date did the Constitution come fully into force, and which article says so? Answer: 26 January 1950; Article 394. A House has 300 members; 240 are present and voting. What is the minimum vote for an amendment Bill? Answer: Majority of total membership = 151; two-thirds of 240 = 160. Minimum = 160. Which case held that a limited amending power is a basic feature of the Constitution? Answer: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980). Which two Acts did Article 395 repeal? Answer: The Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Government of India Act, 1935. Who said that a constitution is sure to turn out bad if those who work it are a bad lot, and when? Answer: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, in the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949. Does Article 13 apply to an amendment of the Constitution? Answer: No. Article 13(4), inserted by the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971), excludes it. Give an example to show that an ordinary law can be changed easily but a constitutional provision cannot. Answer: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 was changed by ordinary amending Acts (e.g., 2019); the five-year term of the Lok Sabha (Art. 83(2)) needed the 42nd and 44th Amendments to change it. Which articles give the Supreme Court and High Courts the power to issue writs? Answer: Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts).

1 Creates the organs of the State "There shall be a President of India" (Art. 52); "There shall be a Parliament" (Art. 79); "There shall be a Supreme Court of India" (Art. 124(1))

5 Limits power "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution" (Art. 245); laws against Fundamental Rights void (Art. 13)
6 Guarantees rights Fundamental Rights (Part III)
7 Provides remedies Right to move the Supreme Court (Art. 32); High Court writs (Art. 226)
8 Provides for its own change Amendment procedure (Art. 368)
9 States ideals and aims Preamble
10 Lays down duties Fundamental duties (Art. 51A)

This Is not the same as Why
Constitution Ordinary law (Act of Parliament or State) An ordinary law is made under the Constitution and must obey it (Art. 245). The Constitution is the higher law.
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (ordinary law) Article 83(2) (part of the Constitution) The Act was changed by ordinary amending Acts (e.g., 2019); the Lok Sabha's term in Art. 83(2) could be changed only by constitutional amendments (42nd, 44th).
Constitution in the narrow sense (the document) Constitution in the wide sense (the whole working framework) The narrow sense is the text (Art. 393); the wide sense adds the laws and practices made under it.
Article 32 Article 226 Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right and lies only for Part III rights; Art. 226 lies in a High Court for Part III rights "and for any other purpose".
Amending the Constitution (Art. 368) Making an ordinary law (Art. 245) Amendment uses constituent power and a special majority; ordinary law uses legislative power and a simple majority.
Amending the Constitution Destroying it Parliament may add, vary or repeal provisions, but not alter the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati).
Constitution (the document and its rules) Constitutionalism (the idea of limited government) The meaning of constitutionalism is a separate syllabus topic: Constitutionalism and Constitutional Morality.
Preamble The whole Constitution The Preamble states who gave the Constitution and its aims; the Articles and Schedules contain the operative rules.

en.meaning:
Who introduced the idea of constitutional morality into the Constituent Assembly debates, quoting George Grote?

Explanation. Ambedkar did so in his speech on the draft Constitution on 4 November 1948.

Grote described constitutional morality as:

constitutional-law-i-u1-t8.subtitle: Provincial autonomy, the planned federation, the three Lists and what the Constitution took from the Act

en.inOneMinute: The Government of India Act, 1935 (26 Geo. 5, Ch. 2; Royal Assent 2 August 1935) was the longest and last full constitution made for India by the British Parliament: 321 sections and 10 Schedules. It repealed the earlier "Government of India Act" (s. 321). It planned an all-India federation of the British Indian Provinces and the Indian States (s. 5). The States were to join by an Instrument of Accession (s. 6). The States never joined in enough numbers, so the federal part never came into force ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). Provincial autonomy: dyarchy in the provinces ended. All provincial subjects were run by the Governor with a council of ministers (s. 50), and each Province got its own legislative field (List II). Six Provinces had two Houses (s. 60). Three legislative lists in the Seventh Schedule: Federal (List I, 59 entries), Provincial (List II, 54 entries) and Concurrent (List III, 36 entries) (s. 100). The Governor-General could give residuary powers to either level (s. 104). Dyarchy at the centre (planned): defence, ecclesiastical affairs, external affairs and tribal areas were to be in the Governor-General's discretion (s. 11); other subjects with ministers. Safeguards: "special responsibilities" (ss. 12, 52), individual judgment , ordinances (ss. 42–43, 88–89), "Governor-General's Acts" (s. 44), and Proclamations when constitutional machinery failed (ss. 45, 93). It set up a Federal Court (s. 200), Public Service Commissions for the Federation and each Province (s. 264), a Federal Railway Authority, and an Auditor-General of India (s. 166). It separated Burma (s. 46(2)) and created Sind and Orissa (s. 289). The Constitution of India repealed it (Art. 395), but kept much of its framework. Dr. Ambedkar: "As to the accusation that the Draft Constitution has produced a good part of the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, I make no apologies." The Supreme Court: "The Constitution of India was erected on the foundations of the Government of India Act, 1935".
legalProvision: Source: Government of India Act, 1935 (bare Act PDF). Long title: "An Act to make further provision for the government of India." [2nd August 1935.]

Section 5(1) (Proclamation of Federation) – His Majesty may, on an address from each House of Parliament and if the condition in s. 5(2) is satisfied, "declare by Proclamation that as from the day therein appointed there shall be united in a Federation under the Crown, by the name of the Federation of India,— (a) the Provinces hereinafter called Governors' Provinces; and (b) the Indian States which have acceded or may thereafter accede to the Federation".

Section 5(2) (the condition) – States whose Rulers are entitled to choose "not less than fifty-two members of the Council of State" and whose population "amounts to at least one-half of the total population of the States" must have acceded.

Section 50(1) – "There shall be a council of ministers to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions, except in so far as he is by or under this Act required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion".

Section 100(1)–(3) – The Federal Legislature "has, and a Provincial Legislature has not," power over List I (the "Federal Legislative List"); both have power over List III (the "Concurrent Legislative List"); the Provincial Legislature "has, and the Federal Legislature has not," power over List II (the "Provincial Legislative List").

Section 93(1) – "If at any time the Governor of a Province is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the Province cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Act, he may by Proclamation— (a) declare that his functions shall, to such extent as may be specified in the Proclamation, be exercised by him in his discretion; (b) assume to himself all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by any Provincial body or authority".

Article 395 of the Constitution – "The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed."
In simple words:

The Act offered a federation, but only if enough Indian States signed up. Without them, only the provincial part worked. In the provinces, ministers now ran the government on all provincial subjects, but the Governor kept "discretion" and "individual judgment" powers. The Act divided law-making into three lists – the model for today's Seventh Schedule. If the government of a province broke down, the Governor could take over (s. 93) – the model for today's Art. 356. The Constitution repealed the Act in 1950, but carried over a large part of its structure.
en.meaning: Government of India Act, 1935: an Act of the British Parliament that replaced the earlier Government of India Act (s. 321) and laid down a new constitution for British India, with a plan for federation . Federation of India: the union, "under the Crown", of the Governors' Provinces and the Indian States that acceded , with the Chief Commissioners' Provinces included (s. 5(1)). Instrument of Accession : the document by which a Ruler accepted the Federation and specified "the matters which the Ruler accepts as matters with respect to which the Federal Legislature may make laws for his State" (s. 6(1)–(2)). Provincial autonomy : each Province's executive authority extended "to the matters with respect to which the Legislature of the Province has power to make laws" (s. 49(2)), with ministers responsible for them (s. 50). The words "provincial autonomy" are not used in the Act; members of the Constituent Assembly used them for this system (e.g. "Provincial Autonomy which had been introduced by the Act of 1935"). "In his discretion": matters on which the Governor-General or Governor acted on his own, without consulting ministers (e.g. s. 11). "Individual judgment": matters on which he consulted ministers but could act against their advice, e.g. where a "special responsibility" was involved (s. 12(2)). Special responsibilities: duties listed in s. 12 (Governor-General) and s. 52 (Governor), such as "the prevention of any grave menace to the peace or tranquillity" and "the safeguarding of the legitimate interests of minorities".
keyPoints: 26 Geo. 5, Ch. 2; Royal Assent 2 August 1935; 321 sections, 10 Schedules. s. 5: Federation of Provinces and acceding States – condition 52 Council of State seats and half the States' population; never came into force. s. 9: ≤ 10 federal ministers; s. 11: defence, ecclesiastical, external affairs, tribal areas in discretion. ss. 12, 52: special responsibilities; individual judgment. s. 18: Council of State 156 + ≤ 104 (permanent); Federal Assembly 250 + ≤ 125 (5 years). s. 46: 11 Governors' Provinces; Burma separated; s. 289: Sind and Orissa. s. 50: council of ministers in Provinces – end of provincial dyarchy. s. 60: bicameral in Madras, Bombay, Bengal, UP, Bihar, Assam. s. 100: Lists I (59), II (54), III (36); s. 104: residuary by Governor-General. ss. 45, 93: breakdown Proclamations → Art. 356. s. 200: Federal Court (CJ + ≤ 6); ss. 204, 205, 213. s. 240: pleasure + reasonable opportunity; s. 264: PSCs. ss. 298, 299: no disability; property by authority of law. s. 321: repeal; 1919 Preamble saved. Art. 395 repealed the 1935 Act.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, the Union proposed to a
caseLaws.facts: West Bengal sued, claiming the Union could not acquire land vested in a State because the States were sovereign in their own field. Principle: The majority (Sinha C.J.) traced the history: "The aim of the Government of India Act, 1935 was to unite the Provinces and Indian States into a federation, but that could be achieved only if a substantial number of the Indian States agreed to join"; "For diverse reasons the Indian States never joined the proposed federation and the part dealing with federation never became effective"; and "The Constitution of India was erected on the foundations of the Government of India Act, 1935; the basic structure was not altered in many important matters, and a large number of provisions were incorporated verbatim from the earlier Constitution." The suit was dismissed. Why it matters: It is the Supreme Court's own account of what the 1935 Act planned, what actually came into force, and how much the Constitution took from it.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to Proclamations under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing several State governments. Principle: Jeevan Reddy J.: "Both the Indian and Pakistani provisions appear to be inspired by Section 45 and Section 93 of the Government of India Act, 1935. Article 356, however, is qualitatively different"; he also noted that Dr. Ambedkar wanted a provision "analogous to provisions contained in Section 93 of the 1935 Act". Sawant J. noted that provisions identical to Art. 74(2) "were contained in Sections 10(4) and 51(4) of the Government of India Act, 1935". The Court held Art. 356 Proclamations open to judicial review. Why it matters: It shows how 1935 provisions survive in the Constitution and how the Constitution changes them – under the 1935 Act the Governor acted in his discretion; under the Constitution the power is subject to judicial review.
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , [1950] SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, challenged the Act under Arts. 19, 21 and 22. Principle: Kania C.J. noted that the structure of the Supreme Court in Arts. 124 to 147 "follows the pattern of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the previous Constitution of the Government of India". Mahajan J. noted that "The Government of India Act, 1935, conferred authority on the Central and Provincial Legislatures to enact laws on this subject [preventive detention] for the first time". (The detention law was upheld by majority.) Why it matters: It shows that the first Supreme Court read the new Constitution against the 1935 Act – both for the court system and for the legislative Lists (preventive detention was in the 1935 Concurrent List, entry 34).

selfTest.q: What was the condition for establishing the Federation of India?
selfTest.a: Answer: Accession by States whose Rulers could choose at least 52 members of the Council of State and whose population was at least half of the States' total population (s. 5(2)). Did the federation come into force? Answer: No. The Indian States never joined in sufficient numbers; the federal part "never became effective" ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). What is provincial autonomy? Answer: Provinces got their own legislative field (List II) and executive authority over it, run by a council of ministers (ss. 49–50), ending dyarchy. Which subjects were in the Governor-General's discretion under s. 11? Answer: Defence, ecclesiastical affairs, external affairs (except relations with His Majesty's dominions) and tribal areas. Distinguish "discretion" and "individual judgment". Answer: Discretion – he acts without consulting ministers; individual judgment – he consults them but may act against their advice (e.g. special responsibilities, s. 12(2)). How many entries were there in each List? Answer: Federal 59, Provincial 54, Concurrent 36. Who held the residuary power? Answer: The Governor-General, in his discretion, could empower either the Federal or a Provincial Legislature (s. 104). Which Provinces had bicameral legislatures? Answer: Madras, Bombay, Bengal, the United Provinces, Bihar and Assam (s. 60). What did s. 93 provide, and which Article corresponds to it? Answer: Governor's Proclamation when provincial government cannot be carried on; Art. 356. What jurisdictions did the Federal Court have? Answer: Original (s. 204), appellate (s. 205) and advisory (s. 213); appeals lay to the Privy Council (s. 208). Which section is the ancestor of Art. 300A? Answer: s. 299(1): "No person shall be deprived of his property in British India save by authority of law." What did Ambedkar say about borrowing from the 1935 Act? Answer: "I make no apologies. There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing"; he regretted that the borrowed provisions related mostly to details of administration.

Government of India Act, 1935 Indian Independence Act, 1947 1935 gave the constitutional framework; 1947 ended British rule and made the 1935 Act (as adapted) the interim constitution. Art. 395 repealed both.

te.inOneMinute: భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1935 (26 Geo. 5, Ch. 2; రాజ ఆమోదం 2 ఆగస్టు 1935) బ్రిటిష్ పార్లమెంటు భారతదేశానికి చేసిన అతి పెద్ద, చివరి పూర్తి రాజ్యాంగం: 321 సెక్షన్లు, 10 షెడ్యూళ్లు. ఇది ముందటి "Government of India Act" ను రద్దు చేసింది (సె. 321). బ్రిటిష్ ఇండియా ప్రావిన్సులు, భారతీయ సంస్థానాలతో అఖిల భారత సమాఖ్య ను ఇది ప్రణాళిక చేసింది (సె. 5). సంస్థానాలు విలీన పత్రం (Instrument of Accession ) ద్వారా చేరాలి (సె. 6). తగినన్ని సంస్థానాలు చేరలేదు, కాబట్టి సమాఖ్య భాగం ఎప్పుడూ అమలులోకి రాలేదు ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). ప్రాంతీయ స్వయంప్రతిపత్తి: ప్రావిన్సుల్లో ద్వంద్వ పాలన ముగిసింది. అన్ని ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలను మంత్రుల మండలి తో గవర్నర్ నడిపారు (సె. 50); ప్రతి ప్రావిన్సుకు సొంత శాసన రంగం (జాబితా II) వచ్చింది. ఆరు ప్రావిన్సుల్లో రెండు సభలు (సె. 60). ఏడో షెడ్యూల్‌లో మూడు శాసన జాబితాలు : సమాఖ్య (జాబితా I, 59 అంశాలు), ప్రాంతీయ (జాబితా II, 54 అంశాలు), ఉమ్మడి (జాబితా III, 36 అంశాలు) (సె. 100). అవశిష్ట అధికారాలను గవర్నర్ జనరల్ ఏ స్థాయికైనా ఇవ్వవచ్చు (సె. 104). కేంద్రంలో ద్వంద్వ పాలన (ప్రణాళిక): రక్షణ, మతసంబంధ వ్యవహారాలు, విదేశీ వ్యవహారాలు, గిరిజన ప్రాంతాలు గవర్నర్ జనరల్ విచక్షణ లో (సె. 11); మిగిలినవి మంత్రులతో. రక్షణలు (safeguards): "ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యతలు" (సె. 12, 52), వ్యక్తిగత నిర్ణయం , ఆర్డినెన్సులు (సె. 42–43, 88–89), "గవర్నర్ జనరల్ చట్టాలు" (సె. 44), రాజ్యాంగ యంత్రాంగం విఫలమైనప్పుడు ప్రకటనలు (సె. 45, 93). ఇది ఫెడరల్ కోర్టు (సె. 200), సమాఖ్యకు, ప్రతి ప్రావిన్సుకు పబ్లిక్ సర్వీస్ కమిషన్లు (సె. 264), ఫెడరల్ రైల్వే అథారిటీ, భారత ఆడిటర్ జనరల్ (సె. 166) ఏర్పాటు చేసింది. బర్మాను వేరు చేసింది (సె. 46(2)), సింధ్, ఒరిస్సాలను సృష్టించింది (సె. 289). భారత రాజ్యాంగం దీన్ని రద్దు చేసింది (అ. 395), కానీ దాని చట్రంలో చాలా భాగాన్ని ఉంచుకుంది. డా. అంబేద్కర్: "As to the accusation that the Draft Constitution has produced a good part of the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, I make no apologies." (ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగం 1935 చట్టంలోని చాలా నిబంధనలను తీసుకుందనే ఆరోపణకు నేను క్షమాపణ చెప్పను.) సుప్రీంకోర్టు: "The Constitution of India was erected on the foundations of the Government of India Act, 1935" (భారత రాజ్యాంగం 1935 చట్టం పునాదులపై నిర్మించబడింది).
te.meaning: భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1935: ముందటి భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టాన్ని (సె. 321) రద్దు చేసి, సమాఖ్య ప్రణాళికతో బ్రిటిష్ ఇండియాకు కొత్త రాజ్యాంగాన్ని నిర్దేశించిన బ్రిటిష్ పార్లమెంటు చట్టం. Federation of India (భారత సమాఖ్య): గవర్నర్ ప్రావిన్సులు, చేరిన భారతీయ సంస్థానాల "under the Crown" (క్రౌన్ కింద) సమైక్యత; చీఫ్ కమిషనర్ ప్రావిన్సులు అందులో చేర్చబడ్డాయి (సె. 5(1)). విలీన పత్రం ( Instrument of Accession ): పాలకుడు సమాఖ్యను అంగీకరించి, "the matters which the Ruler accepts as matters with respect to which the Federal Legislature may make laws for his State" (తన సంస్థానానికి సమాఖ్య శాసనసభ చట్టాలు చేయగల విషయాలుగా పాలకుడు అంగీకరించేవి) పేర్కొనే పత్రం (సె. 6(1)–(2)). ప్రాంతీయ స్వయంప్రతిపత్తి : ప్రతి ప్రావిన్సు కార్యనిర్వాహక అధికారం "to the matters with respect to which the Legislature of the Province has power to make laws" (ప్రావిన్సు శాసనసభ చట్టాలు చేయగల విషయాలకు) విస్తరించింది (సె. 49(2)); వాటికి మంత్రులు బాధ్యులు (సె. 50). "Provincial autonomy" అనే పదాలు చట్టంలో లేవు; రాజ్యాంగ సభ సభ్యులు ఈ వ్యవస్థకు వాటిని వాడారు (ఉదా. "Provincial Autonomy which had been introduced by the Act of 1935" – 1935 చట్టం ప్రవేశపెట్టిన ప్రాంతీయ స్వయంప్రతిపత్తి). "తన విచక్షణతో" (In his discretion ): మంత్రులను సంప్రదించకుండా గవర్నర్ జనరల్ లేదా గవర్నర్ స్వయంగా వ్యవహరించే విషయాలు (ఉదా. సె. 11). "వ్యక్తిగత నిర్ణయం" (Individual judgment): మంత్రులను సంప్రదించి, వారి సలహాకు భిన్నంగా వ్యవహరించగల విషయాలు – ఉదా. "ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యత" ఉన్నప్పుడు (సె. 12(2)). ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యతలు (Special responsibilities): సె. 12 (గవర్నర్ జనరల్), సె. 52 (గవర్నర్) లో పేర్కొన్న విధులు – ఉదా. "the prevention of any grave menace to the peace or tranquillity" (శాంతి, ప్రశాంతతకు తీవ్ర ముప్పు నివారణ), "the safeguarding of the legitimate interests of minorities" ( మైనారిటీ ల న్యాయమైన ప్రయోజనాల రక్షణ).
keyPoints: 26 Geo. 5, Ch. 2; రాజ ఆమోదం 2 ఆగస్టు 1935; 321 సెక్షన్లు, 10 షెడ్యూళ్లు. సె. 5: ప్రావిన్సులు, చేరిన సంస్థానాల సమాఖ్య – షరతు 52 కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ స్థానాలు, సంస్థానాల జనాభాలో సగం; ఎప్పుడూ అమలులోకి రాలేదు. సె. 9: ≤ 10 సమాఖ్య మంత్రులు; సె. 11: రక్షణ, మతసంబంధ, విదేశీ వ్యవహారాలు, గిరిజన ప్రాంతాలు విచక్షణలో. సె. 12, 52: ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యతలు; వ్యక్తిగత నిర్ణయం. సె. 18: కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ 156 + ≤ 104 (శాశ్వతం); ఫెడరల్ అసెంబ్లీ 250 + ≤ 125 (5 ఏళ్లు). సె. 46: 11 గవర్నర్ ప్రావిన్సులు; బర్మా వేరు; సె. 289: సింధ్, ఒరిస్సా. సె. 50: ప్రావిన్సుల్లో మంత్రుల మండలి – ప్రాంతీయ ద్వంద్వ పాలన ముగింపు. సె. 60: మద్రాస్, బొంబాయి, బెంగాల్, యూపీ, బీహార్, అస్సాంలో రెండు సభలు. సె. 100: జాబితాలు I (59), II (54), III (36); సె. 104: అవశిష్టం గవర్నర్ జనరల్ ద్వారా. సె. 45, 93: వైఫల్య ప్రకటనలు → అ. 356. సె. 200: ఫెడరల్ కోర్టు (ప్రధాన న్యాయమూర్తి + ≤ 6); సె. 204, 205, 213. సె. 240: ఇష్టానుసారం + సహేతుక అవకాశం; సె. 264: PSCలు. సె. 298, 299: అనర్హత లేదు; చట్ట అధికారం ద్వారానే ఆస్తి హరణ. సె. 321: రద్దు; 1919 ప్రవేశిక కొనసాగింది. అ. 395 1935 చట్టాన్ని రద్దు చేసింది.

selfTest.q: భారత సమాఖ్య ఏర్పాటుకు షరతు ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్‌లో కనీసం 52 మందిని ఎన్నుకోగల, సంస్థానాల మొత్తం జనాభాలో కనీసం సగం జనాభా ఉన్న సంస్థానాల విలీనం (సె. 5(2)). సమాఖ్య అమలులోకి వచ్చిందా? జవాబు: లేదు. తగినన్ని సంస్థానాలు చేరలేదు; సమాఖ్య భాగం "never became effective" ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). ప్రాంతీయ స్వయంప్రతిపత్తి అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: ప్రావిన్సులకు సొంత శాసన రంగం (జాబితా II), దానిపై మంత్రుల మండలి నడిపే కార్యనిర్వాహక అధికారం వచ్చాయి (సె. 49–50); ద్వంద్వ పాలన ముగిసింది. సె. 11 కింద గవర్నర్ జనరల్ విచక్షణలో ఏ విషయాలు ఉన్నాయి? జవాబు: రక్షణ, మతసంబంధ వ్యవహారాలు, విదేశీ వ్యవహారాలు (రాజు డొమినియన్లతో సంబంధాలు తప్ప), గిరిజన ప్రాంతాలు. "విచక్షణ", "వ్యక్తిగత నిర్ణయం" మధ్య తేడా చెప్పండి. జవాబు: విచక్షణ – మంత్రులను సంప్రదించకుండా వ్యవహరిస్తారు; వ్యక్తిగత నిర్ణయం – సంప్రదించి, వారి సలహాకు భిన్నంగా వ్యవహరించవచ్చు (ఉదా. ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యతలు, సె. 12(2)). ఒక్కో జాబితాలో ఎన్ని అంశాలు ఉన్నాయి? జవాబు: సమాఖ్య 59, ప్రాంతీయ 54, ఉమ్మడి 36. అవశిష్ట అధికారం ఎవరి వద్ద ఉంది? జవాబు: గవర్నర్ జనరల్ తన విచక్షణతో సమాఖ్య లేదా ప్రాంతీయ శాసనసభకు అధికారం ఇవ్వవచ్చు (సె. 104). ఏ ప్రావిన్సుల్లో రెండు సభలు ఉన్నాయి? జవాబు: మద్రాస్, బొంబాయి, బెంగాల్, యునైటెడ్ ప్రావిన్సెస్, బీహార్, అస్సాం (సె. 60). సె. 93 ఏమి చెప్పింది, దానికి ఏ అనుచ్ఛేదం సరిపోతుంది? జవాబు: ప్రావిన్సు ప్రభుత్వాన్ని నడపలేనప్పుడు గవర్నర్ ప్రకటన; అ. 356. ఫెడరల్ కోర్టుకు ఏ అధికార పరిధులు ఉన్నాయి? జవాబు: అసలు (సె. 204), అప్పీలు (సె. 205), సలహా (సె. 213); ప్రివీ కౌన్సిల్‌కు అప్పీళ్లు ఉండేవి (సె. 208). అ. 300A కు పూర్వరూపమైన సెక్షన్ ఏది? జవాబు: సె. 299(1): "No person shall be deprived of his property in British India save by authority of law." 1935 చట్టం నుంచి తీసుకోవడంపై అంబేద్కర్ ఏమన్నారు? జవాబు: "I make no apologies. There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing" (నేను క్షమాపణ చెప్పను. తీసుకోవడంలో సిగ్గుపడాల్సింది లేదు); తీసుకున్న నిబంధనలు ఎక్కువగా పరిపాలనా వివరాలకు సంబంధించినవి కావడం పట్ల విచారం వ్యక్తం చేశారు.
