hi.inOneMinute: The Government of India Act, 1935 (26 Geo. 5, Ch. 2; Royal Assent 2 August 1935) was the longest and last full constitution made for India by the British Parliament: 321 sections and 10 Schedules. It repealed the earlier "Government of India Act" (s. 321). It planned an all-India federation of the British Indian Provinces and the Indian States (s. 5). The States were to join by an Instrument of Accession (s. 6). The States never joined in enough numbers, so the federal part never came into force ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). Provincial autonomy: dyarchy in the provinces ended. All provincial subjects were run by the Governor with a council of ministers (s. 50), and each Province got its own legislative field (List II). Six Provinces had two Houses (s. 60). Three legislative lists in the Seventh Schedule: Federal (List I, 59 entries), Provincial (List II, 54 entries) and Concurrent (List III, 36 entries) (s. 100). The Governor-General could give residuary powers to either level (s. 104). Dyarchy at the centre (planned): defence, ecclesiastical affairs, external affairs and tribal areas were to be in the Governor-General's discretion (s. 11); other subjects with ministers. Safeguards: "special responsibilities" (ss. 12, 52), individual judgment , ordinances (ss. 42–43, 88–89), "Governor-General's Acts" (s. 44), and Proclamations when constitutional machinery failed (ss. 45, 93). It set up a Federal Court (s. 200), Public Service Commissions for the Federation and each Province (s. 264), a Federal Railway Authority, and an Auditor-General of India (s. 166). It separated Burma (s. 46(2)) and created Sind and Orissa (s. 289). The Constitution of India repealed it (Art. 395), but kept much of its framework. Dr. Ambedkar: "As to the accusation that the Draft Constitution has produced a good part of the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, I make no apologies." The Supreme Court: "The Constitution of India was erected on the foundations of the Government of India Act, 1935".
legalProvision: Source: Government of India Act, 1935 (bare Act PDF). Long title: "An Act to make further provision for the government of India." [2nd August 1935.]

Section 5(1) (Proclamation of Federation) – His Majesty may, on an address from each House of Parliament and if the condition in s. 5(2) is satisfied, "declare by Proclamation that as from the day therein appointed there shall be united in a Federation under the Crown, by the name of the Federation of India,— (a) the Provinces hereinafter called Governors' Provinces; and (b) the Indian States which have acceded or may thereafter accede to the Federation".

Section 5(2) (the condition) – States whose Rulers are entitled to choose "not less than fifty-two members of the Council of State" and whose population "amounts to at least one-half of the total population of the States" must have acceded.

Section 50(1) – "There shall be a council of ministers to aid and advise the Governor in the exercise of his functions, except in so far as he is by or under this Act required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion".

Section 100(1)–(3) – The Federal Legislature "has, and a Provincial Legislature has not," power over List I (the "Federal Legislative List"); both have power over List III (the "Concurrent Legislative List"); the Provincial Legislature "has, and the Federal Legislature has not," power over List II (the "Provincial Legislative List").

Section 93(1) – "If at any time the Governor of a Province is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the Province cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Act, he may by Proclamation— (a) declare that his functions shall, to such extent as may be specified in the Proclamation, be exercised by him in his discretion; (b) assume to himself all or any of the powers vested in or exercisable by any Provincial body or authority".

Article 395 of the Constitution – "The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed."
In simple words:

The Act offered a federation, but only if enough Indian States signed up. Without them, only the provincial part worked. In the provinces, ministers now ran the government on all provincial subjects, but the Governor kept "discretion" and "individual judgment" powers. The Act divided law-making into three lists – the model for today's Seventh Schedule. If the government of a province broke down, the Governor could take over (s. 93) – the model for today's Art. 356. The Constitution repealed the Act in 1950, but carried over a large part of its structure.
hi.meaning: Government of India Act, 1935: an Act of the British Parliament that replaced the earlier Government of India Act (s. 321) and laid down a new constitution for British India, with a plan for federation . Federation of India: the union, "under the Crown", of the Governors' Provinces and the Indian States that acceded , with the Chief Commissioners' Provinces included (s. 5(1)). Instrument of Accession : the document by which a Ruler accepted the Federation and specified "the matters which the Ruler accepts as matters with respect to which the Federal Legislature may make laws for his State" (s. 6(1)–(2)). Provincial autonomy : each Province's executive authority extended "to the matters with respect to which the Legislature of the Province has power to make laws" (s. 49(2)), with ministers responsible for them (s. 50). The words "provincial autonomy" are not used in the Act; members of the Constituent Assembly used them for this system (e.g. "Provincial Autonomy which had been introduced by the Act of 1935"). "In his discretion": matters on which the Governor-General or Governor acted on his own, without consulting ministers (e.g. s. 11). "Individual judgment": matters on which he consulted ministers but could act against their advice, e.g. where a "special responsibility" was involved (s. 12(2)). Special responsibilities: duties listed in s. 12 (Governor-General) and s. 52 (Governor), such as "the prevention of any grave menace to the peace or tranquillity" and "the safeguarding of the legitimate interests of minorities".
keyPoints: 26 Geo. 5, Ch. 2; Royal Assent 2 August 1935; 321 sections, 10 Schedules. s. 5: Federation of Provinces and acceding States – condition 52 Council of State seats and half the States' population; never came into force. s. 9: ≤ 10 federal ministers; s. 11: defence, ecclesiastical, external affairs, tribal areas in discretion. ss. 12, 52: special responsibilities; individual judgment. s. 18: Council of State 156 + ≤ 104 (permanent); Federal Assembly 250 + ≤ 125 (5 years). s. 46: 11 Governors' Provinces; Burma separated; s. 289: Sind and Orissa. s. 50: council of ministers in Provinces – end of provincial dyarchy. s. 60: bicameral in Madras, Bombay, Bengal, UP, Bihar, Assam. s. 100: Lists I (59), II (54), III (36); s. 104: residuary by Governor-General. ss. 45, 93: breakdown Proclamations → Art. 356. s. 200: Federal Court (CJ + ≤ 6); ss. 204, 205, 213. s. 240: pleasure + reasonable opportunity; s. 264: PSCs. ss. 298, 299: no disability; property by authority of law. s. 321: repeal; 1919 Preamble saved. Art. 395 repealed the 1935 Act.

caseLaws.facts: West Bengal sued, claiming the Union could not acquire land vested in a State because the States were sovereign in their own field. Principle: The majority (Sinha C.J.) traced the history: "The aim of the Government of India Act, 1935 was to unite the Provinces and Indian States into a federation, but that could be achieved only if a substantial number of the Indian States agreed to join"; "For diverse reasons the Indian States never joined the proposed federation and the part dealing with federation never became effective"; and "The Constitution of India was erected on the foundations of the Government of India Act, 1935; the basic structure was not altered in many important matters, and a large number of provisions were incorporated verbatim from the earlier Constitution." The suit was dismissed. Why it matters: It is the Supreme Court's own account of what the 1935 Act planned, what actually came into force, and how much the Constitution took from it.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to Proclamations under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing several State governments. Principle: Jeevan Reddy J.: "Both the Indian and Pakistani provisions appear to be inspired by Section 45 and Section 93 of the Government of India Act, 1935. Article 356, however, is qualitatively different"; he also noted that Dr. Ambedkar wanted a provision "analogous to provisions contained in Section 93 of the 1935 Act". Sawant J. noted that provisions identical to Art. 74(2) "were contained in Sections 10(4) and 51(4) of the Government of India Act, 1935". The Court held Art. 356 Proclamations open to judicial review. Why it matters: It shows how 1935 provisions survive in the Constitution and how the Constitution changes them – under the 1935 Act the Governor acted in his discretion; under the Constitution the power is subject to judicial review.
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , [1950] SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, challenged the Act under Arts. 19, 21 and 22. Principle: Kania C.J. noted that the structure of the Supreme Court in Arts. 124 to 147 "follows the pattern of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the previous Constitution of the Government of India". Mahajan J. noted that "The Government of India Act, 1935, conferred authority on the Central and Provincial Legislatures to enact laws on this subject [preventive detention] for the first time". (The detention law was upheld by majority.) Why it matters: It shows that the first Supreme Court read the new Constitution against the 1935 Act – both for the court system and for the legislative Lists (preventive detention was in the 1935 Concurrent List, entry 34).

selfTest.q: What was the condition for establishing the Federation of India?
selfTest.a: Answer: Accession by States whose Rulers could choose at least 52 members of the Council of State and whose population was at least half of the States' total population (s. 5(2)). Did the federation come into force? Answer: No. The Indian States never joined in sufficient numbers; the federal part "never became effective" ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). What is provincial autonomy? Answer: Provinces got their own legislative field (List II) and executive authority over it, run by a council of ministers (ss. 49–50), ending dyarchy. Which subjects were in the Governor-General's discretion under s. 11? Answer: Defence, ecclesiastical affairs, external affairs (except relations with His Majesty's dominions) and tribal areas. Distinguish "discretion" and "individual judgment". Answer: Discretion – he acts without consulting ministers; individual judgment – he consults them but may act against their advice (e.g. special responsibilities, s. 12(2)). How many entries were there in each List? Answer: Federal 59, Provincial 54, Concurrent 36. Who held the residuary power? Answer: The Governor-General, in his discretion, could empower either the Federal or a Provincial Legislature (s. 104). Which Provinces had bicameral legislatures? Answer: Madras, Bombay, Bengal, the United Provinces, Bihar and Assam (s. 60). What did s. 93 provide, and which Article corresponds to it? Answer: Governor's Proclamation when provincial government cannot be carried on; Art. 356. What jurisdictions did the Federal Court have? Answer: Original (s. 204), appellate (s. 205) and advisory (s. 213); appeals lay to the Privy Council (s. 208). Which section is the ancestor of Art. 300A? Answer: s. 299(1): "No person shall be deprived of his property in British India save by authority of law." What did Ambedkar say about borrowing from the 1935 Act? Answer: "I make no apologies. There is nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing"; he regretted that the borrowed provisions related mostly to details of administration.

constitutional-law-i-u1-t7.subtitle: The Montagu-Chelmsford reforms: dyarchy in the provinces, a two-house central legislature and their limits

en.inOneMinute: The Government of India Act, 1919 (9 & 10 Geo. 5, Ch. 101; Royal Assent 23 December 1919) is the Act that carried out what the Constituent Assembly members called the Montagu-Chelmsford or "Montford" Reforms . Its Preamble declared, for the first time in an Act, the aim of the "progressive realisation of responsible government in British India", to be reached "by successive stages". In the provinces it brought in dyarchy (dual government): provincial subjects were split into transferred subjects , run by the Governor with Indian ministers answerable to the legislature, and reserved subjects , run by the Governor with his executive council (s. 3). At the centre it created a bicameral Indian legislature : the Governor-General, the Council of State (up to 60 members) and the Legislative Assembly (140 members, 100 of them elected) (ss. 17–19). The central executive stayed answerable to Parliament in Britain, not to this legislature. Subjects were divided into central and provincial (s. 1), with separate provincial revenues: the first clear division of power and money between the centre and the provinces. It also provided for a Public Service Commission (s. 38), an Auditor-General (s. 39), a High Commissioner for India in London (s. 35) and a Statutory Commission after ten years (s. 41). The Governor and Governor-General kept strong over-riding powers (certification of Bills, restoring refused grants, emergency spending). Members of the Constituent Assembly later said dyarchy "miserably failed". Many features of today's Constitution have early versions here: ministers who must enter the legislature within six months (Arts. 75(5), 164(4)), demands for grants and charged expenditure (Arts. 112–113, 202–203), freedom of speech in the legislature (Arts. 105, 194), reservation of Bills (Arts. 200, 201), and the Public Service Commission (Art. 315).
legalProvision: Source: Government of India Act, 1919 (bare Act PDF). The Act amended the Government of India Act, 1915 (called in it "the principal Act"); s. 45 and the Second Schedule inserted its provisions into the principal Act.

Preamble (main part) – "WHEREAS it is the declared policy of Parliament to provide for the increasing association of Indians in every branch of Indian administration, and for the gradual development of self-governing institutions, with a view to the progressive realisation of responsible government in British India as an integral part of the empire: And whereas progress in giving effect to this policy can only be achieved by successive stages, and it is expedient that substantial steps in this direction should now be taken: And whereas the time and manner of each advance can be determined only by Parliament, upon whom responsibility lies for the welfare and advancement of the Indian peoples ..."

Section 3(1) (revised system of government in the provinces) – the presidencies and provinces named "shall each be governed, in relation to reserved subjects, by a governor in council, and in relation to transferred subjects (save as otherwise provided by this Act) by the governor acting with ministers appointed under this Act."

Section 4(3) – "In relation to transferred subjects, the governor shall be guided by the advice of his ministers, unless he sees sufficient cause to dissent from their opinion, in which case he may require action to be taken otherwise than in accordance with that advice".
Section 17 – "Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Indian legislature shall consist of the Governor-General and two chambers, namely, the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly."
In simple words:

The Preamble set a goal (responsible government), a method (step by step) and a judge of progress (the British Parliament alone). In each major province, some subjects were handed to Indian ministers (transferred); the rest stayed with the Governor and his officials (reserved). That split is dyarchy. On transferred subjects the Governor was normally to follow his ministers, but he could over-rule them. At the centre there were now two houses, but the Government of India itself was not made responsible to them.
en.meaning: Government of India Act, 1919: an Act of the British Parliament "to make further provision with respect to the government of India" (long title). It did not replace the 1915 Act; it amended it (s. 45). Montagu-Chelmsford (Montford) Reforms: the name used in the Constituent Assembly for the reforms of 1919 (e.g. S. Radhakrishnan, 11 December 1946: "We had after that the Montford Reforms and then the 1935 Act"). The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati refers to the "Montague-Chelmsford Report" that came before the Act. Central subjects and provincial subjects: subjects classified by rules under s. 1(1)(a) "for the purpose of distinguishing the functions of local governments and local legislatures from the functions of the Governor-General in Council and the Indian legislature". Transferred subjects: provincial subjects transferred "to the administration of the governor acting with ministers appointed under this Act" (s. 1(1)(d)). Reserved subjects: "Provincial subjects, other than transferred subjects, are in this Act referred to as 'reserved subjects'" (s. 1(4)). Dyarchy (diarchy) : "rule by two". The word is not used in the Act; it is the name given to the s. 3 system, under which one province had two executives side by side – the governor in council (reserved side) and the governor with ministers (transferred side). Responsible government : a government whose ministers hold office as long as they keep the support of an elected legislature and answer to it. The 1919 Act gave only a part of this, and only in the provinces. Official / non-official: "a person who is or is not in the civil or military service of the Crown in India" (s. 46).
keyPoints: Act: 9 & 10 Geo. 5, Ch. 101; Royal Assent 23 December 1919; amended the GoI Act, 1915. Preamble: "progressive realisation of responsible government" by "successive stages"; Parliament decides. s. 1: central / provincial subjects; transferred / reserved (s. 1(4)). s. 3: dyarchy in 8 governor's provinces. s. 4: ministers – non-officials, pleasure, six-month rule, advice with power to dissent. s. 7: provincial councils ≤ 20% officials, ≥ 70% elected; communal electorates by rules. ss. 11, 25: demands for grants; non-votable heads; restoration; emergency spending. ss. 13, 26: certification of Bills. ss. 17–19: Indian legislature = Governor-General + Council of State (≤ 60) + Legislative Assembly (140; 100 elected; 26 officials). s. 21: Council of State 5 years; Assembly 3 years. s. 35: High Commissioner for India in the UK; s. 38: Public Service Commission (≤ 5 members, 5 years); s. 39: Auditor-General. s. 41: Statutory Commission after ten years. State of West Bengal v. UoI : Government "did not cease to be unitary".

caseLaws.name: Facts: Under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, the Union proposed to a
caseLaws.facts: West Bengal sued, arguing that the Union could not acquire land belonging to a State, because the States were sovereign in their own field. Principle: The majority (Sinha C.J.) rejected the claim to State sovereignty and reviewed the history: British India was "unitary and highly centralized"; under the Government of India Act, 1919, there was decentralisation, "but that was only for the purpose of decentralization of the Governmental power but on that account the Government did not cease to be unitary"; the Central Government "as it was originally constituted under the Government of India Act, 1919, with some modification continued to function" after 1935. Why it matters: The Supreme Court itself describes the 1919 Act as devolution within a unitary state – the right way to describe dyarchy in an exam.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to Proclamations under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing State governments; one question was whether courts could look at the material behind the President's decision despite Art. 74(2). Principle: Sawant J. (for himself and Kuldip Singh J.) traced the history of Art. 74(2) to "the Government of India Act, 1915, as amended by the Act of 1919", quoting the rule that "In relation to the transferred subjects the governor shall be guided by the advice of his Ministers, unless he sees sufficient cause to dissent". Jeevan Reddy J. described the Governor-General's emergency ordinance power under the Act (as amended in 1919), lasting "not more than six months", and the Privy Council's ruling in Bhagat Singh v. King Emperor (1931) that the Governor-General "alone" judged whether an emergency existed. Why it matters: It shows that the 1919 rules on ministerial advice and ordinances are part of the history the Supreme Court uses to read today's Articles 74 and 356.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973) – para 684 (Hegde and Mukherjea JJ.)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Tracing the origins of Fundamental Rights , the judges noted that "After the publication of the Montague-Chelmsford Report, the Indian National Congress at its special session held in Bombay in August 1918 demanded that the new Government of India Act should contain 'Declaration of Rights of the people of India as British citizens'". Why it matters: It links the 1919 reforms to the long Indian demand for guaranteed rights, which the 1919 Act itself did not contain and which Part III of the Constitution later met.

selfTest.q: What policy did the Preamble of the 1919 Act declare?
selfTest.a: Answer: Increasing association of Indians in administration, gradual development of self-governing institutions, and "progressive realisation of responsible government in British India", by successive stages, with Parliament deciding each advance. What is dyarchy? Answer: Dual government in the governor's provinces: reserved subjects under the Governor in council and transferred subjects under the Governor acting with ministers (s. 3). What were "reserved subjects"? Answer: Provincial subjects other than transferred subjects (s. 1(4)). What happened to a minister who was not a member of the legislature? Answer: He could not hold office for more than six months unless he became a member (s. 4(2)) – compare Arts. 75(5), 164(4). Could the Governor over-rule his ministers? Answer: Yes. He was "guided by the advice" but could dissent if he saw "sufficient cause" (s. 4(3)). What was the composition of the Legislative Assembly? Answer: 140 members: 100 elected, 40 non-elected of whom 26 officials; at least five-sevenths elected (s. 19). What was the term of the Council of State and of the Legislative Assembly? Answer: Five years and three years respectively (s. 21). Name three heads of central expenditure not put to the vote. Answer: Any three of: loan charges; expenditure fixed by law; salaries and pensions of persons appointed by His Majesty or the Secretary of State; salaries of chief commissioners and judicial commissioners; expenditure classified as ecclesiastical, political or defence (s. 25(3)). Which section provided for a Public Service Commission? Answer: s. 38 – not more than five members including a chairman, appointed by the Secretary of State in Council, five-year term. What did s. 41 provide? Answer: A Statutory Commission, after ten years, to inquire into the working of the system and report whether responsible government should be established, extended, modified or restricted. How did the Supreme Court describe the 1919 Act in State of West Bengal v. Union of India ? Answer: It decentralised governmental power, "but on that account the Government did not cease to be unitary".

Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto) Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford) 1909 added elected members to councils; 1919 brought dyarchy and a two-chamber central legislature with an elected majority.
Statutory Commission (s. 41) Constituent Assembly The commission was to be appointed by the British side to review the system; the Constituent Assembly was the Indians' own constitution-making body (1946).

te.inOneMinute: భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1919 (9 & 10 Geo. 5, Ch. 101; రాజ ఆమోదం 23 డిసెంబర్ 1919) – రాజ్యాంగ సభ సభ్యులు మాంటేగు-చెమ్స్‌ఫోర్డ్ లేదా "మాంట్‌ఫోర్డ్" సంస్కరణలు అని పిలిచిన వాటిని అమలు చేసిన చట్టం. దాని ప్రవేశిక, ఒక చట్టంలో మొదటిసారిగా, "progressive realisation of responsible government in British India" (బ్రిటిష్ ఇండియాలో బాధ్యతాయుత ప్రభుత్వాన్ని క్రమంగా సాధించడం) లక్ష్యమని, అది "by successive stages" (వరుస దశల్లో) చేరాలని ప్రకటించింది. ప్రావిన్సుల్లో అది ద్వంద్వ పాలన (డయార్కీ) తెచ్చింది: ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలను బదిలీ చేసిన విషయాలు – శాసనసభకు జవాబుదారీ అయిన భారతీయ మంత్రులతో కలిసి గవర్నర్ నడిపేవి – మరియు రిజర్వ్డ్ విషయాలు – తన కార్యనిర్వాహక మండలితో గవర్నర్ నడిపేవి – అని విభజించింది (సె. 3). కేంద్రంలో అది రెండు సభల భారత శాసనసభను సృష్టించింది: గవర్నర్ జనరల్, కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ (60 వరకు సభ్యులు), లెజిస్లేటివ్ అసెంబ్లీ (140 సభ్యులు, వారిలో 100 మంది ఎన్నికైనవారు) (సె. 17–19). కేంద్ర కార్యనిర్వాహక వర్గం ఈ శాసనసభకు కాకుండా బ్రిటన్ పార్లమెంటుకే జవాబుదారీగా ఉంది. విషయాలను కేంద్ర , ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలుగా విభజించారు (సె. 1); ప్రావిన్సులకు వేరైన ఆదాయాలు ఇచ్చారు: కేంద్రం, ప్రావిన్సుల మధ్య అధికారం, ధనం మొదటి స్పష్ట విభజన ఇదే. అది పబ్లిక్ సర్వీస్ కమిషన్ (సె. 38), ఆడిటర్ జనరల్ (సె. 39), లండన్‌లో భారత హైకమిషనర్ (సె. 35), పదేళ్ల తర్వాత చట్టబద్ధ కమిషన్ (సె. 41) ఏర్పాటుకు కూడా నిబంధనలు చేసింది. గవర్నర్, గవర్నర్ జనరల్ బలమైన అధిగమించే అధికారాలు ఉంచుకున్నారు (బిల్లుల ధ్రువీకరణ, తిరస్కరించిన గ్రాంట్ల పునరుద్ధరణ, అత్యవసర వ్యయం). ద్వంద్వ పాలన "miserably failed" (ఘోరంగా విఫలమైంది) అని తర్వాత రాజ్యాంగ సభ సభ్యులు అన్నారు. నేటి రాజ్యాంగంలోని చాలా అంశాలకు ఇక్కడ తొలి రూపాలు ఉన్నాయి: ఆరు నెలల్లో శాసనసభ సభ్యులు కావలసిన మంత్రులు (అ. 75(5), 164(4)), గ్రాంట్ల డిమాండ్లు, చార్జ్‌డ్ వ్యయం (అ. 112–113, 202–203), శాసనసభలో వాక్ స్వాతంత్ర్యం (అ. 105, 194), బిల్లుల రిజర్వేషన్ (అ. 200, 201), పబ్లిక్ సర్వీస్ కమిషన్ (అ. 315).
te.meaning: భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం, 1919: "to make further provision with respect to the government of India" (భారత ప్రభుత్వానికి సంబంధించి మరిన్ని నిబంధనలు చేయడానికి) చేసిన బ్రిటిష్ పార్లమెంటు చట్టం (దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక). ఇది 1915 చట్టాన్ని రద్దు చేయలేదు; దాన్ని సవరించింది (సె. 45). మాంటేగు-చెమ్స్‌ఫోర్డ్ (మాంట్‌ఫోర్డ్) సంస్కరణలు: 1919 సంస్కరణలకు రాజ్యాంగ సభ లో వాడిన పేరు (ఉదా. ఎస్. రాధాకృష్ణన్, 11 డిసెంబర్ 1946: "We had after that the Montford Reforms and then the 1935 Act" – ఆ తర్వాత మాంట్‌ఫోర్డ్ సంస్కరణలు, తర్వాత 1935 చట్టం వచ్చాయి). చట్టానికి ముందు వచ్చిన "Montague-Chelmsford Report" ను Kesavananda Bharati లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు ప్రస్తావించింది. కేంద్ర విషయాలు, ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలు: "for the purpose of distinguishing the functions of local governments and local legislatures from the functions of the Governor-General in Council and the Indian legislature" (ప్రాంతీయ ప్రభుత్వాలు, శాసనసభల విధులను గవర్నర్ జనరల్ ఇన్ కౌన్సిల్, భారత శాసనసభ విధుల నుంచి వేరు చేయడానికి) సె. 1(1)(ఎ) కింద నియమాల ద్వారా వర్గీకరించిన విషయాలు. బదిలీ చేసిన విషయాలు: "to the administration of the governor acting with ministers appointed under this Act" (ఈ చట్టం కింద నియమించిన మంత్రులతో కలిసి వ్యవహరించే గవర్నర్ పరిపాలనకు) బదిలీ చేసిన ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలు (సె. 1(1)(డి)). రిజర్వ్డ్ విషయాలు: "Provincial subjects, other than transferred subjects, are in this Act referred to as 'reserved subjects'" (బదిలీ చేసిన విషయాలు కాని ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలను ఈ చట్టంలో "రిజర్వ్డ్ విషయాలు" అంటారు) (సె. 1(4)). ద్వంద్వ పాలన (డయార్కీ): "ఇద్దరి పాలన". ఈ పదం చట్టంలో లేదు; సె. 3 వ్యవస్థకు ఇచ్చిన పేరు. దాని ప్రకారం ఒక ప్రావిన్సులో పక్కపక్కనే రెండు కార్యనిర్వాహక వర్గాలు ఉండేవి – గవర్నర్ ఇన్ కౌన్సిల్ (రిజర్వ్డ్ వైపు), మంత్రులతో గవర్నర్ (బదిలీ వైపు). బాధ్యతాయుత ప్రభుత్వం : ఎన్నికైన శాసనసభ మద్దతు ఉన్నంతవరకే మంత్రులు పదవిలో ఉండి, దానికి జవాబుదారీగా ఉండే ప్రభుత్వం. 1919 చట్టం దీనిలో ఒక భాగాన్ని మాత్రమే, అదీ ప్రావిన్సుల్లో మాత్రమే ఇచ్చింది. అధికారి / అధికారేతరుడు: "a person who is or is not in the civil or military service of the Crown in India" (భారతదేశంలో క్రౌన్ పౌర లేదా సైనిక సేవలో ఉన్న / లేని వ్యక్తి) (సె. 46).
keyPoints: చట్టం: 9 & 10 Geo. 5, Ch. 101; రాజ ఆమోదం 23 డిసెంబర్ 1919; 1915 భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టాన్ని సవరించింది. ప్రవేశిక: "progressive realisation of responsible government" "successive stages" లో; పార్లమెంటు నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. సె. 1: కేంద్ర / ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలు; బదిలీ / రిజర్వ్డ్ (సె. 1(4)). సె. 3: 8 గవర్నర్ ప్రావిన్సుల్లో ద్వంద్వ పాలన. సె. 4: మంత్రులు – అధికారేతరులు, ఇష్టానుసారం, ఆరు నెలల నియమం, విభేదించే అధికారంతో సలహా. సె. 7: ప్రాంతీయ మండళ్లు ≤ 20% అధికారులు, ≥ 70% ఎన్నికైనవారు; నియమాల ద్వారా మతపరమైన నియోజకవర్గాలు. సె. 11, 25: గ్రాంట్ల డిమాండ్లు; ఓటుకు రాని పద్దులు; పునరుద్ధరణ; అత్యవసర వ్యయం. సె. 13, 26: బిల్లుల ధ్రువీకరణ. సె. 17–19: భారత శాసనసభ = గవర్నర్ జనరల్ + కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ (≤ 60) + లెజిస్లేటివ్ అసెంబ్లీ (140; 100 ఎన్నికైనవారు; 26 అధికారులు). సె. 21: కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ 5 ఏళ్లు; అసెంబ్లీ 3 ఏళ్లు. సె. 35: UKలో భారత హైకమిషనర్; సె. 38: పబ్లిక్ సర్వీస్ కమిషన్ (≤ 5 సభ్యులు, 5 ఏళ్లు); సె. 39: ఆడిటర్ జనరల్. సె. 41: పదేళ్ల తర్వాత చట్టబద్ధ కమిషన్. State of West Bengal v. UoI : ప్రభుత్వం "did not cease to be unitary" (ఏకకేంద్రంగా ఉండటం మానలేదు).

selfTest.q: 1919 చట్టం ప్రవేశిక ఏ విధానాన్ని ప్రకటించింది?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: పరిపాలనలో భారతీయుల భాగస్వామ్యం పెంపు, స్వపరిపాలన సంస్థల క్రమాభివృద్ధి, "progressive realisation of responsible government in British India" – వరుస దశల్లో, ప్రతి అడుగును పార్లమెంటు నిర్ణయిస్తూ. ద్వంద్వ పాలన అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: గవర్నర్ ప్రావిన్సుల్లో రెండు రకాల ప్రభుత్వం: రిజర్వ్డ్ విషయాలు గవర్నర్ ఇన్ కౌన్సిల్ కింద, బదిలీ విషయాలు మంత్రులతో వ్యవహరించే గవర్నర్ కింద (సె. 3). "రిజర్వ్డ్ విషయాలు" అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: బదిలీ చేసిన విషయాలు కాని ప్రాంతీయ విషయాలు (సె. 1(4)). శాసనసభ సభ్యుడు కాని మంత్రికి ఏమవుతుంది? జవాబు: సభ్యుడు కాకపోతే ఆరు నెలలకు మించి పదవిలో ఉండలేడు (సె. 4(2)) – అ. 75(5), 164(4) తో పోల్చండి. గవర్నర్ మంత్రులను అధిగమించగలరా? జవాబు: అవును. ఆయన "guided by the advice" (సలహా ప్రకారం నడుచుకోవాలి), కానీ "sufficient cause" (తగిన కారణం) చూస్తే విభేదించవచ్చు (సె. 4(3)). లెజిస్లేటివ్ అసెంబ్లీ కూర్పు ఏమిటి? జవాబు: 140 సభ్యులు: 100 ఎన్నికైనవారు, 40 ఎన్నిక కానివారు, వారిలో 26 అధికారులు; కనీసం ఏడింట ఐదు వంతులు ఎన్నికైనవారు (సె. 19). కౌన్సిల్ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్, లెజిస్లేటివ్ అసెంబ్లీ కాలపరిమితి ఎంత? జవాబు: వరుసగా ఐదేళ్లు, మూడేళ్లు (సె. 21). ఓటుకు రాని మూడు కేంద్ర వ్యయ పద్దులు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: ఈ క్రింది వాటిలో ఏవైనా మూడు: రుణ భారాలు; చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన వ్యయం; రాజు లేదా సెక్రటరీ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ నియమించిన వారి జీతాలు, పెన్షన్లు; చీఫ్ కమిషనర్లు, జుడీషియల్ కమిషనర్ల జీతాలు; మతసంబంధ, రాజకీయ, రక్షణగా వర్గీకరించిన వ్యయం (సె. 25(3)). పబ్లిక్ సర్వీస్ కమిషన్‌కు ఏ సెక్షన్ నిబంధన చేసింది? జవాబు: సె. 38 – చైర్మన్‌తో సహా ఐదుగురికి మించని సభ్యులు, సెక్రటరీ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్ ఇన్ కౌన్సిల్ నియామకం, ఐదేళ్ల పదవీకాలం. సె. 41 ఏమి చెప్పింది? జవాబు: పదేళ్ల తర్వాత, వ్యవస్థ పనితీరుపై విచారించి, బాధ్యతాయుత ప్రభుత్వాన్ని స్థాపించాలా, విస్తరించాలా, మార్చాలా, పరిమితం చేయాలా అని నివేదించే చట్టబద్ధ కమిషన్. State of West Bengal v. Union of India లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు 1919 చట్టాన్ని ఎలా వర్ణించింది? జవాబు: అది ప్రభుత్వ అధికారాన్ని వికేంద్రీకరించింది, "but on that account the Government did not cease to be unitary" (కానీ దాని వల్ల ప్రభుత్వం ఏకకేంద్రంగా ఉండటం మానలేదు).

చట్టబద్ధ కమిషన్ (సె. 41) రాజ్యాంగ సభ వ్యవస్థను సమీక్షించడానికి బ్రిటిష్ వైపు నియమించే కమిషన్ అది; రాజ్యాంగ సభ భారతీయుల స్వంత రాజ్యాంగ రచనా సంస్థ (1946).

hi.inOneMinute: The Government of India Act, 1919 (9 & 10 Geo. 5, Ch. 101; Royal Assent 23 December 1919) is the Act that carried out what the Constituent Assembly members called the Montagu-Chelmsford or "Montford" Reforms . Its Preamble declared, for the first time in an Act, the aim of the "progressive realisation of responsible government in British India", to be reached "by successive stages". In the provinces it brought in dyarchy (dual government): provincial subjects were split into transferred subjects , run by the Governor with Indian ministers answerable to the legislature, and reserved subjects , run by the Governor with his executive council (s. 3). At the centre it created a bicameral Indian legislature : the Governor-General, the Council of State (up to 60 members) and the Legislative Assembly (140 members, 100 of them elected) (ss. 17–19). The central executive stayed answerable to Parliament in Britain, not to this legislature. Subjects were divided into central and provincial (s. 1), with separate provincial revenues: the first clear division of power and money between the centre and the provinces. It also provided for a Public Service Commission (s. 38), an Auditor-General (s. 39), a High Commissioner for India in London (s. 35) and a Statutory Commission after ten years (s. 41). The Governor and Governor-General kept strong over-riding powers (certification of Bills, restoring refused grants, emergency spending). Members of the Constituent Assembly later said dyarchy "miserably failed". Many features of today's Constitution have early versions here: ministers who must enter the legislature within six months (Arts. 75(5), 164(4)), demands for grants and charged expenditure (Arts. 112–113, 202–203), freedom of speech in the legislature (Arts. 105, 194), reservation of Bills (Arts. 200, 201), and the Public Service Commission (Art. 315).
legalProvision: Source: Government of India Act, 1919 (bare Act PDF). The Act amended the Government of India Act, 1915 (called in it "the principal Act"); s. 45 and the Second Schedule inserted its provisions into the principal Act.

Preamble (main part) – "WHEREAS it is the declared policy of Parliament to provide for the increasing association of Indians in every branch of Indian administration, and for the gradual development of self-governing institutions, with a view to the progressive realisation of responsible government in British India as an integral part of the empire: And whereas progress in giving effect to this policy can only be achieved by successive stages, and it is expedient that substantial steps in this direction should now be taken: And whereas the time and manner of each advance can be determined only by Parliament, upon whom responsibility lies for the welfare and advancement of the Indian peoples ..."

Section 3(1) (revised system of government in the provinces) – the presidencies and provinces named "shall each be governed, in relation to reserved subjects, by a governor in council, and in relation to transferred subjects (save as otherwise provided by this Act) by the governor acting with ministers appointed under this Act."

Section 4(3) – "In relation to transferred subjects, the governor shall be guided by the advice of his ministers, unless he sees sufficient cause to dissent from their opinion, in which case he may require action to be taken otherwise than in accordance with that advice".
Section 17 – "Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Indian legislature shall consist of the Governor-General and two chambers, namely, the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly."
In simple words:

The Preamble set a goal (responsible government), a method (step by step) and a judge of progress (the British Parliament alone). In each major province, some subjects were handed to Indian ministers (transferred); the rest stayed with the Governor and his officials (reserved). That split is dyarchy. On transferred subjects the Governor was normally to follow his ministers, but he could over-rule them. At the centre there were now two houses, but the Government of India itself was not made responsible to them.
hi.meaning: Government of India Act, 1919: an Act of the British Parliament "to make further provision with respect to the government of India" (long title). It did not replace the 1915 Act; it amended it (s. 45). Montagu-Chelmsford (Montford) Reforms: the name used in the Constituent Assembly for the reforms of 1919 (e.g. S. Radhakrishnan, 11 December 1946: "We had after that the Montford Reforms and then the 1935 Act"). The Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati refers to the "Montague-Chelmsford Report" that came before the Act. Central subjects and provincial subjects: subjects classified by rules under s. 1(1)(a) "for the purpose of distinguishing the functions of local governments and local legislatures from the functions of the Governor-General in Council and the Indian legislature". Transferred subjects: provincial subjects transferred "to the administration of the governor acting with ministers appointed under this Act" (s. 1(1)(d)). Reserved subjects: "Provincial subjects, other than transferred subjects, are in this Act referred to as 'reserved subjects'" (s. 1(4)). Dyarchy (diarchy) : "rule by two". The word is not used in the Act; it is the name given to the s. 3 system, under which one province had two executives side by side – the governor in council (reserved side) and the governor with ministers (transferred side). Responsible government : a government whose ministers hold office as long as they keep the support of an elected legislature and answer to it. The 1919 Act gave only a part of this, and only in the provinces. Official / non-official: "a person who is or is not in the civil or military service of the Crown in India" (s. 46).
keyPoints: Act: 9 & 10 Geo. 5, Ch. 101; Royal Assent 23 December 1919; amended the GoI Act, 1915. Preamble: "progressive realisation of responsible government" by "successive stages"; Parliament decides. s. 1: central / provincial subjects; transferred / reserved (s. 1(4)). s. 3: dyarchy in 8 governor's provinces. s. 4: ministers – non-officials, pleasure, six-month rule, advice with power to dissent. s. 7: provincial councils ≤ 20% officials, ≥ 70% elected; communal electorates by rules. ss. 11, 25: demands for grants; non-votable heads; restoration; emergency spending. ss. 13, 26: certification of Bills. ss. 17–19: Indian legislature = Governor-General + Council of State (≤ 60) + Legislative Assembly (140; 100 elected; 26 officials). s. 21: Council of State 5 years; Assembly 3 years. s. 35: High Commissioner for India in the UK; s. 38: Public Service Commission (≤ 5 members, 5 years); s. 39: Auditor-General. s. 41: Statutory Commission after ten years. State of West Bengal v. UoI : Government "did not cease to be unitary".

caseLaws.name: Facts: Under the Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, the Union proposed to a
caseLaws.facts: West Bengal sued, arguing that the Union could not acquire land belonging to a State, because the States were sovereign in their own field. Principle: The majority (Sinha C.J.) rejected the claim to State sovereignty and reviewed the history: British India was "unitary and highly centralized"; under the Government of India Act, 1919, there was decentralisation, "but that was only for the purpose of decentralization of the Governmental power but on that account the Government did not cease to be unitary"; the Central Government "as it was originally constituted under the Government of India Act, 1919, with some modification continued to function" after 1935. Why it matters: The Supreme Court itself describes the 1919 Act as devolution within a unitary state – the right way to describe dyarchy in an exam.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing State governments; one question was whether courts could look at the material behind the President's decision despite Art. 74(2). Principle: Sawant J. (for himself and Kuldip Singh J.) traced the history of Art. 74(2) to "the Government of India Act, 1915, as amended by the Act of 1919", quoting the rule that "In relation to the transferred subjects the governor shall be guided by the advice of his Ministers, unless he sees sufficient cause to dissent". Jeevan Reddy J. described the Governor-General's emergency ordinance power under the Act (as amended in 1919), lasting "not more than six months", and the Privy Council's ruling in Bhagat Singh v. King Emperor (1931) that the Governor-General "alone" judged whether an emergency existed. Why it matters: It shows that the 1919 rules on ministerial advice and ordinances are part of the history the Supreme Court uses to read today's Articles 74 and 356.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973) – para 684 (Hegde and Mukherjea JJ.)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Tracing the origins of Fundamental Rights , the judges noted that "After the publication of the Montague-Chelmsford Report, the Indian National Congress at its special session held in Bombay in August 1918 demanded that the new Government of India Act should contain 'Declaration of Rights of the people of India as British citizens'". Why it matters: It links the 1919 reforms to the long Indian demand for guaranteed rights, which the 1919 Act itself did not contain and which Part III of the Constitution later met.

selfTest.q: What policy did the Preamble of the 1919 Act declare?
selfTest.a: Answer: Increasing association of Indians in administration, gradual development of self-governing institutions, and "progressive realisation of responsible government in British India", by successive stages, with Parliament deciding each advance. What is dyarchy? Answer: Dual government in the governor's provinces: reserved subjects under the Governor in council and transferred subjects under the Governor acting with ministers (s. 3). What were "reserved subjects"? Answer: Provincial subjects other than transferred subjects (s. 1(4)). What happened to a minister who was not a member of the legislature? Answer: He could not hold office for more than six months unless he became a member (s. 4(2)) – compare Arts. 75(5), 164(4). Could the Governor over-rule his ministers? Answer: Yes. He was "guided by the advice" but could dissent if he saw "sufficient cause" (s. 4(3)). What was the composition of the Legislative Assembly? Answer: 140 members: 100 elected, 40 non-elected of whom 26 officials; at least five-sevenths elected (s. 19). What was the term of the Council of State and of the Legislative Assembly? Answer: Five years and three years respectively (s. 21). Name three heads of central expenditure not put to the vote. Answer: Any three of: loan charges; expenditure fixed by law; salaries and pensions of persons appointed by His Majesty or the Secretary of State; salaries of chief commissioners and judicial commissioners; expenditure classified as ecclesiastical, political or defence (s. 25(3)). Which section provided for a Public Service Commission? Answer: s. 38 – not more than five members including a chairman, appointed by the Secretary of State in Council, five-year term. What did s. 41 provide? Answer: A Statutory Commission, after ten years, to inquire into the working of the system and report whether responsible government should be established, extended, modified or restricted. How did the Supreme Court describe the 1919 Act in State of West Bengal v. Union of India ? Answer: It decentralised governmental power, "but on that account the Government did not cease to be unitary".

This Is not the same as Why
Dyarchy in the provinces (1919) Responsible government at the centre In 1919 only the transferred half of provincial government was handed to ministers; the central executive stayed answerable to Parliament in Britain.
Transferred subjects Reserved subjects Transferred: Governor with Indian ministers. Reserved: Governor with his executive council (s. 3).

Council of State (1919) Council of States / Rajya Sabha (Art. 80) The 1919 Council of State was partly nominated and partly official; the Rajya Sabha represents the States.
Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto) Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford) 1909 added elected members to councils; 1919 brought dyarchy and a two-chamber central legislature with an elected majority.

constitutional-law-i-u1-t9.subtitle: How the Constituent Assembly was formed, how it worked from 1946 to 1949, and when the Constitution began

en.inOneMinute: The Constitution of India was framed by a Constituent Assembly , a body of Indian representatives set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan announced on 16 May 1946. Its members were elected indirectly by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies in July–August 1946. Planned strength: 389 (292 from Provinces + 93 from Indian States + 4 from Chief Commissioners' Provinces). After Partition (Mountbatten Plan, 3 June 1947), a separate Assembly was set up for Pakistan and the strength fell to 299. First meeting: 9 December 1946 , with Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary Chairman. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent Chairman on 11 December 1946. The Muslim League stayed away. On 13 December 1946 Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution . It was adopted on 22 January 1947 , "all members standing". It became the basis of the Preamble. The Assembly worked through committees (Union Powers, Union Constitution, Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, States, and others). The Constitutional Adviser B. N. Rau prepared the first draft. A Drafting Committee under Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was set up on 29 August 1947 and produced the Draft Constitution (315 Articles, 8 Schedules). The Indian Independence Act, 1947 (s. 8) gave the Assembly legal power to make the Constitution. From the midnight of 14 August 1947 it also worked as the legislature of independent India. The Draft went through three readings : Ambedkar moved it on 4 November 1948; clause-by-clause consideration followed from 15 November 1948; the third reading began on 17 November 1949. 7,635 amendments were tabled and 2,473 were moved. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (Preamble: "IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949"), signed on 24 January 1950 by 284 members, and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Art. 394). It then had 395 Articles and 8 Schedules. Total time: 2 years, 11 months, 17 days; 11 sessions; 165 days of sitting, 114 of them on the Draft. The Assembly then became the Provisional Parliament until the new Parliament was constituted in 1952.
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF).
Preamble (last words) – "IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION."
Article 393 (Short title) – "This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India."

Article 394 (Commencement) – "This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution."

Article 394A (Authoritative text in the Hindi language) – inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987. The President shall publish "the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly", and that translation is "deemed to be, for all purposes, the authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language".

Article 395 (Repeals) – "The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed."

Indian Independence Act, 1947, ss. 6 and 8 (as explained by the Supreme Court, Kesavananda Bharati , para 1160, Jaganmohan Reddy J.) – "Sections 6 and 8 of which conferred on the Constituent Assembly the power to enact a Constitution".
In simple words:

The Constitution says about itself that it was adopted by the people "in our Constituent Assembly" on 26 November 1949. A few Articles (citizenship, elections, interpretation, transitional matters, the President's oath, short title) started on 26 November 1949 itself, because they were needed before the new system began. All the rest started on 26 January 1950. The Constitution ended the two British Acts that had governed India till then (Art. 395). The legal power to make the Constitution came from the Indian Independence Act, 1947; but the Constitution itself claims its authority from "the people of India".
en.meaning: Framing of the Constitution: the whole process by which the Constitution of India was prepared, debated, adopted and brought into force – from the setting up of the Constituent Assembly (1946) to the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950). Constituent Assembly: a body of representatives whose task is to make a constitution. Dr. Sinha's inaugural address (9 December 1946) traces the demand to the 1934 resolution: "the only method of applying that principle is to convene a Constituent Assembly, representative of all sections of the Indian people, to frame an acceptable constitution." Cabinet Mission Plan : the plan of the British Cabinet Mission "announced on May 16, 1946" ( Kesavananda , para 515), under which the Provincial Legislative Assemblies elected the members of the Constituent Assembly. Objectives Resolution : the resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947, laying down the aims of the Constitution; it was the Assembly's "terms of reference" (Dr. Rajendra Prasad, 26 November 1949). Drafting Committee: the committee appointed on 29 August 1947, under Dr. Ambedkar, to prepare the Draft Constitution from the Assembly's decisions (details in Role of Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly ). Readings: the stages of consideration of the Draft – general discussion on the motion to take it into consideration; clause-by-clause consideration (which Dr. Prasad called "the second reading stage"); and the "third reading", on the motion "That the Constitution as settled by the Assembly be passed." Adoption, signing and commencement: adoption is the passing of the Constitution (26 November 1949); signing is the members putting their signatures (24 January 1950); commencement is the date it came into force (26 January 1950, Art. 394). Provisional Parliament: the Constituent Assembly acting as Parliament after 26 January 1950, until "a new Parliament was constituted in 1952" (Lok Sabha note in the CAD).
keyPoints: Idea: Gandhi 1922; Swaraj Party and Congress 1934; Faizpur 1936; CWC 1939. Cabinet Mission Plan, 16 May 1946; elections July–August 1946; indirect; limited franchise (~15%). 389 = 292 + 93 + 4; 299 after Partition (229 + 70). 9 December 1946: first sitting; 207 present, 9 women; Sinha temporary Chairman. 11 December 1946: Prasad elected permanent Chairman. 13 December 1946: Objectives Resolution moved; 22 January 1947 adopted. 14 August 1947 midnight: Assembly took over as Legislative Assembly. s. 8, Indian Independence Act, 1947: legal authority. 29 August 1947: Drafting Committee (Ambedkar). B. N. Rau: 243 articles, 13 schedules → Draft 315 Articles, 8 Schedules → final 395 articles, 8 schedules. 4 November 1948 Draft moved; 9 November 1948 motion adopted; 15 November 1948 clause-by-clause; 17 November 1949 third reading. 7,635 amendments tabled; 2,473 moved. 26 November 1949 adopted; 24 January 1950 signed by 284; 26 January 1950 in force. 2 years 11 months 17 days; 11 sessions; 165 days (114 on Draft); Rs. 63,96,729. Art. 394 (commencement), 394A (Hindi text), 395 (repeals).

caseLaws.facts: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner filed a writ petition on 21 March 1970 challenging the Kerala Land Reforms Act
caseLaws.facts: The petitions raised the validity of the Twenty-fourth, Twenty-fifth and Twenty-ninth Amendments, i.e. the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Art. 368. Principle: In answering it, the judges examined the framing of the Constitution. Shelat and Grover JJ. (para 515): the Cabinet Mission plan was "announced on May 16, 1946"; the Assembly was "elected between July-August 1946"; "It was by virtue of Section 8 of the Indian Independence Act 1947 that the Constituent Assembly was vested with the legal authority to frame a Constitution for India." Hegde and Mukherjea JJ. (para 686): the Objectives Resolution "is a definite landmark. It is a precursor to the preamble to our Constitution." Jaganmohan Reddy J. (paras 1159–1162): the members "were not elected on adult franchise"; "The Constitution was not ratified by the people but it came into force, by virtue of Article 394". Why it matters: It is the Supreme Court's own account of how the Constitution was framed, and it shows that the history of framing is used to interpret the Constitution (here, the amending power and the basic structure ).
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , [1950] SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, challenged the Act under Arts. 19, 21 and 22. The Court was referred to the Constituent Assembly debates and the Drafting Committee's report on the wording of Art. 21, to show that the expression "due process of law" had been considered and not adopted. Principle: Kania C.J.: "while it is not proper to take into consideration the individual opinions of Members of Parliament or Convention to construe the meaning of the particular clause, when a question is raised whether a certain phrase or expression was up for consideration at all or not, a reference to the debates may be permitted." Mukherjea J.: "these debates are of doubtful value" as an aid to the meaning of words; headnote: "a higher value may be placed on the report of the Drafting Committee." Why it matters: It decides how the record of framing (debates, committee reports) may be used in court – with caution, mainly to see what was considered.

selfTest.q: Under which plan was the Constituent Assembly set up, and how were its members chosen?
selfTest.a: Answer: The Cabinet Mission Plan of 16 May 1946; indirectly, by members of the Provincial Legislative Assemblies. Show how the figure 389 is made up. Answer: 292 (Provinces) + 93 (Indian States) + 4 (Chief Commissioners' Provinces) = 389. Why did the strength fall to 299? Answer: Partition under the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947; a separate Assembly for Pakistan. Who presided on 9 December 1946, and who was elected on 11 December 1946? Answer: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha (temporary Chairman); Dr. Rajendra Prasad (permanent Chairman). When was the Objectives Resolution moved and adopted? Answer: Moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946; adopted on 22 January 1947. Which law gave the Assembly legal authority to frame the Constitution? Answer: Section 8 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 ( Kesavananda , para 515). How many articles and schedules did B. N. Rau's draft, the Draft Constitution and the final Constitution have? Answer: 243/13; 315/8; 395/8. Distinguish adoption, signing and commencement. Answer: Adopted 26 November 1949; signed 24 January 1950 (284 members); in force 26 January 1950. Name any four Articles that came into force on 26 November 1949. Answer: Any four of Arts. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394. How many amendments were tabled and moved? Answer: 7,635 tabled; 2,473 moved. What did A.K. Gopalan say about using the Assembly debates? Answer: Individual speeches cannot fix the meaning of a clause, but the debates may be referred to on whether a phrase was considered at all (Kania C.J.); they are "of doubtful value" (Mukherjea J.). What were Dr. Prasad's two regrets? Answer: No qualifications were laid down for legislators; the Constitution could not be drawn up in an Indian language.

te.inOneMinute: భారత రాజ్యాంగాన్ని రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు (Constituent Assembly) రూపొందించింది. ఇది 16 మే 1946న ప్రకటించిన కేబినెట్ మిషన్ ప్రణాళిక ప్రకారం ఏర్పడిన భారతీయ ప్రతినిధుల సభ. జూలై–ఆగస్టు 1946లో ప్రాంతీయ శాసనసభలు దీని సభ్యులను పరోక్షంగా ఎన్నుకున్నాయి. ప్రణాళిక ప్రకారం సభ్యులు: 389 (ప్రావిన్సుల నుండి 292 + భారతీయ సంస్థానాల నుండి 93 + చీఫ్ కమిషనర్ ప్రావిన్సుల నుండి 4). దేశ విభజన తర్వాత (మౌంట్‌బాటన్ ప్రణాళిక, 3 జూన్ 1947) పాకిస్తాన్‌కు ప్రత్యేక సభ ఏర్పడి, సభ్యత్వం 299కి తగ్గింది. మొదటి సమావేశం: 9 డిసెంబర్ 1946 ; డా. సచ్చిదానంద సిన్హా తాత్కాలిక అధ్యక్షుడు (temporary Chairman). 11 డిసెంబర్ 1946న డా. రాజేంద్ర ప్రసాద్ శాశ్వత అధ్యక్షుడిగా ఎన్నికయ్యారు. ముస్లిం లీగ్ హాజరు కాలేదు. 13 డిసెంబర్ 1946న జవహర్‌లాల్ నెహ్రూ లక్ష్యాల తీర్మానం (Objectives Resolution) ప్రతిపాదించారు. అది 22 జనవరి 1947 న "all members standing" (సభ్యులందరూ నిలబడి) ఆమోదించబడింది. ఇదే ప్రవేశిక (Preamble) కు ఆధారం. సభ కమిటీల ద్వారా పని చేసింది (యూనియన్ అధికారాల కమిటీ, యూనియన్ రాజ్యాంగ కమిటీ, ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు–మైనారిటీలపై సలహా కమిటీ, సంస్థానాల కమిటీ మొదలైనవి). రాజ్యాంగ సలహాదారు బి. ఎన్. రావు మొదటి ముసాయిదా తయారు చేశారు. 29 ఆగస్టు 1947న డా. బి. ఆర్. అంబేద్కర్ అధ్యక్షతన ముసాయిదా కమిటీ ఏర్పడి, ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగాన్ని (315 అధికరణలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లు) సిద్ధం చేసింది. భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం, 1947 (సె. 8) సభకు రాజ్యాంగం చేసే చట్టపరమైన అధికారం ఇచ్చింది. 14 ఆగస్టు 1947 అర్ధరాత్రి నుండి అది స్వతంత్ర భారత శాసనసభగా కూడా పనిచేసింది. ముసాయిదా మూడు పఠనాల ద్వారా సాగింది: 4 నవంబర్ 1948న అంబేద్కర్ దాన్ని ప్రతిపాదించారు; 15 నవంబర్ 1948 నుండి అధికరణాల వారీగా పరిశీలన; 17 నవంబర్ 1949న మూడవ పఠనం మొదలైంది. 7,635 సవరణలు ప్రతిపాదనకు వచ్చాయి (tabled); 2,473 సభలో ప్రవేశపెట్టబడ్డాయి (moved). రాజ్యాంగం 26 నవంబర్ 1949న ఆమోదించబడింది (ప్రవేశిక: "IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949" – అర్థం: "మా రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తులో 1949 నవంబర్ ఇరవై ఆరవ తేదీన"), 24 జనవరి 1950న 284 మంది సభ్యులు సంతకం చేశారు , 26 జనవరి 1950 నుండి అమలులోకి వచ్చింది (అ. 394). అప్పటికి అందులో 395 అధికరణలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లు ఉన్నాయి. మొత్తం సమయం: 2 సంవత్సరాలు, 11 నెలలు, 17 రోజులు; 11 సమావేశాలు (sessions); 165 రోజుల సభ, వాటిలో 114 రోజులు ముసాయిదాపై. ఆ తర్వాత 1952లో కొత్త పార్లమెంటు ఏర్పడే వరకు సభ తాత్కాలిక పార్లమెంటు గా పనిచేసింది.
te.meaning: రాజ్యాంగ రూపకల్పన (Framing of the Constitution): భారత రాజ్యాంగాన్ని సిద్ధం చేసి, చర్చించి, ఆమోదించి, అమలులోకి తెచ్చిన మొత్తం ప్రక్రియ – రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు ఏర్పాటు (1946) నుండి రాజ్యాంగ ప్రారంభం (26 జనవరి 1950) వరకు. రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు: రాజ్యాంగం తయారు చేయడమే పనిగా ఉన్న ప్రతినిధుల సభ. డా. సిన్హా ప్రారంభ ఉపన్యాసం (9 డిసెంబర్ 1946) ఈ డిమాండ్‌ను 1934 తీర్మానం వరకు గుర్తించింది: "the only method of applying that principle is to convene a Constituent Assembly, representative of all sections of the Indian people, to frame an acceptable constitution." ( అర్థం: ఆ సూత్రాన్ని అమలు చేసే ఏకైక మార్గం – భారత ప్రజల అన్ని వర్గాలకు ప్రాతినిధ్యం ఉన్న రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తును సమావేశపరచి, ఆమోదయోగ్యమైన రాజ్యాంగాన్ని రూపొందించడం.) కేబినెట్ మిషన్ ప్రణాళిక : "announced on May 16, 1946" ( అర్థం: 16 మే 1946న ప్రకటించబడిన) బ్రిటిష్ కేబినెట్ మిషన్ ప్రణాళిక ( కేశవానంద , పేరా 515); దీని ప్రకారం ప్రాంతీయ శాసనసభలు రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు సభ్యులను ఎన్నుకున్నాయి. లక్ష్యాల తీర్మానం : 13 డిసెంబర్ 1946న నెహ్రూ ప్రతిపాదించి, 22 జనవరి 1947న ఆమోదించిన, రాజ్యాంగ లక్ష్యాలను తెలిపిన తీర్మానం; ఇది సభ యొక్క "terms of reference" ( అర్థం: పని పరిధి) అని డా. రాజేంద్ర ప్రసాద్ (26 నవంబర్ 1949) అన్నారు. ముసాయిదా కమిటీ (Drafting Committee): సభ నిర్ణయాల ఆధారంగా ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగం తయారు చేయడానికి 29 ఆగస్టు 1947న డా. అంబేద్కర్ అధ్యక్షతన నియమించిన కమిటీ (వివరాలు Role of Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly అంశంలో). పఠనాలు (Readings): ముసాయిదా పరిశీలన దశలు – పరిశీలన తీర్మానంపై సాధారణ చర్చ; అధికరణాల వారీగా పరిశీలన (డా. ప్రసాద్ దీనిని "the second reading stage" – రెండవ పఠన దశ – అన్నారు); "That the Constitution as settled by the Assembly be passed." ( అర్థం: సభ నిర్ణయించిన రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ఆమోదించాలి) అనే తీర్మానంపై "మూడవ పఠనం" (third reading). ఆమోదం, సంతకం, ప్రారంభం: ఆమోదం అంటే రాజ్యాంగాన్ని పాస్ చేయడం (26 నవంబర్ 1949); సంతకం అంటే సభ్యులు సంతకాలు చేయడం (24 జనవరి 1950); ప్రారంభం అంటే అమలులోకి వచ్చిన రోజు (26 జనవరి 1950, అ. 394). తాత్కాలిక పార్లమెంటు: 26 జనవరి 1950 తర్వాత "a new Parliament was constituted in 1952" ( అర్థం: 1952లో కొత్త పార్లమెంటు ఏర్పడే) వరకు పార్లమెంటుగా పనిచేసిన రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు (CAD లోని లోక్‌సభ నోట్).

selfTest.q: రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు ఏ ప్రణాళిక కింద ఏర్పడింది?
selfTest.a: సభ్యులను ఎలా ఎన్నుకున్నారు? సమాధానం: 16 మే 1946 కేబినెట్ మిషన్ ప్రణాళిక; ప్రాంతీయ శాసనసభ సభ్యుల ద్వారా పరోక్షంగా. 389 సంఖ్య ఎలా వచ్చిందో చూపండి. సమాధానం: 292 (ప్రావిన్సులు) + 93 (భారతీయ సంస్థానాలు) + 4 (చీఫ్ కమిషనర్ ప్రావిన్సులు) = 389. సభ్యత్వం 299కి ఎందుకు తగ్గింది? సమాధానం: 3 జూన్ 1947 మౌంట్‌బాటన్ ప్రణాళిక కింద దేశ విభజన; పాకిస్తాన్‌కు ప్రత్యేక సభ. 9 డిసెంబర్ 1946న ఎవరు అధ్యక్షత వహించారు? 11 డిసెంబర్ 1946న ఎవరు ఎన్నికయ్యారు? సమాధానం: డా. సచ్చిదానంద సిన్హా (తాత్కాలిక అధ్యక్షుడు); డా. రాజేంద్ర ప్రసాద్ (శాశ్వత అధ్యక్షుడు). లక్ష్యాల తీర్మానం ఎప్పుడు ప్రతిపాదించబడింది, ఎప్పుడు ఆమోదించబడింది? సమాధానం: 13 డిసెంబర్ 1946న నెహ్రూ ప్రతిపాదన; 22 జనవరి 1947న ఆమోదం. రాజ్యాంగం రూపొందించే చట్టపరమైన అధికారం సభకు ఏ చట్టం ఇచ్చింది? సమాధానం: భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య చట్టం, 1947 సెక్షన్ 8 ( కేశవానంద , పేరా 515). బి. ఎన్. రావు ముసాయిదా, ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగం, తుది రాజ్యాంగంలో ఎన్ని అధికరణలు, షెడ్యూళ్లు? సమాధానం: 243/13; 315/8; 395/8. ఆమోదం, సంతకం, ప్రారంభం మధ్య తేడా చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: ఆమోదం 26 నవంబర్ 1949; సంతకాలు 24 జనవరి 1950 (284 మంది); అమలు 26 జనవరి 1950. 26 నవంబర్ 1949న అమలులోకి వచ్చిన ఏవైనా నాలుగు అధికరణలు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: అ. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394 లో ఏవైనా నాలుగు. ఎన్ని సవరణలు ప్రతిపాదనకు వచ్చాయి, ఎన్ని ప్రవేశపెట్టబడ్డాయి? సమాధానం: 7,635 ప్రతిపాదనకు; 2,473 ప్రవేశపెట్టబడ్డాయి. సభ చర్చల ఉపయోగంపై ఎ. కె. గోపాలన్ ఏమి చెప్పింది? సమాధానం: వ్యక్తిగత ప్రసంగాలు నిబంధన అర్థాన్ని నిర్ణయించవు; కానీ ఒక పదం అసలు పరిశీలనకు వచ్చిందా అనే విషయంలో చర్చలను చూడవచ్చు (కానియా ప్ర.న్యా.); అవి "of doubtful value" ( విలువ సందేహాస్పదం ) (ముఖర్జియా న్యా.). డా. ప్రసాద్ రెండు విచారాలు ఏమిటి? సమాధానం: శాసనకర్తలకు అర్హతలు నిర్ణయించలేదు; మొదటి రాజ్యాంగాన్ని భారతీయ భాషలో రూపొందించలేకపోయాం.

వయోజన ఓటు హక్కుపై ఎన్నిక కాలేదు; పూర్తి ప్రాతినిధ్యం లేదు నిజమే – సుమారు 15% పరిమిత ఓటు హక్కు (జగన్మోహన్ రెడ్డి న్యా.). అంబేద్కర్: "the Constituent Assembly though elected on limited franchise can be trusted to pass the Constitution by simple majority" (పరిమిత ఓటు హక్కుతో ఎన్నికైనా, సాధారణ మెజారిటీతో రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ఆమోదించడానికి రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తును నమ్మవచ్చు), ఎందుకంటే దానికి "no partisan motive" (పక్షపాత ఉద్దేశం లేదు). సభ క్రమంగా "became fully representative of the various communities and interests" (వివిధ వర్గాలు, ప్రయోజనాలకు పూర్తి ప్రాతినిధ్యం పొందింది) అని సుప్రీంకోర్టు (షెలాట్, గ్రోవర్ న్యా., పేరా 515).
ప్రజలు ధృవీకరించలేదు (ratification లేదు) "The Constitution was not ratified by the people but it came into force, by virtue of Article 394" (రాజ్యాంగాన్ని ప్రజలు ధృవీకరించలేదు, కానీ అది అధికరణ 394 వల్ల అమలులోకి వచ్చింది) (జగన్మోహన్ రెడ్డి న్యా., పేరా 1161).
చాలా ఆలస్యం, ఖరీదు ప్రసాద్: ఆ సమయం సంస్థానాలు, మత సమస్యల పరిష్కారానికి తోడ్పడింది; 22 నవంబర్ 1949 వరకు ఖర్చు రూ. 63,96,729.
చాలా పెద్దది ప్రసాద్: "If the provisions have been well thought out, the bulk need not disturb the equanimity of our mind." (నిబంధనలు బాగా ఆలోచించి చేసినవైతే, పరిమాణం మన మనశ్శాంతిని భంగపరచనవసరం లేదు.)
1935 చట్టం నుండి తీసుకున్నారు అంబేద్కర్: "I make no apologies" (నేను క్షమాపణ చెప్పను) (Government of India Act 1935 చూడండి).
భారతీయ భాషలో లేదు ప్రసాద్ విచారం; హిందీ అనువాదం 24 జనవరి 1950 నాటికి సిద్ధమైంది; ఇప్పుడు అదే ప్రామాణిక హిందీ పాఠం (అ. 394A).
శాసనకర్తలకు అర్హతలు లేవు ప్రసాద్ మరో విచారం.

hi.inOneMinute: The Constitution of India was framed by a Constituent Assembly , a body of Indian representatives set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan announced on 16 May 1946. Its members were elected indirectly by the Provincial Legislative Assemblies in July–August 1946. Planned strength: 389 (292 from Provinces + 93 from Indian States + 4 from Chief Commissioners' Provinces). After Partition (Mountbatten Plan, 3 June 1947), a separate Assembly was set up for Pakistan and the strength fell to 299. First meeting: 9 December 1946 , with Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary Chairman. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent Chairman on 11 December 1946. The Muslim League stayed away. On 13 December 1946 Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution . It was adopted on 22 January 1947 , "all members standing". It became the basis of the Preamble. The Assembly worked through committees (Union Powers, Union Constitution, Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities, States, and others). The Constitutional Adviser B. N. Rau prepared the first draft. A Drafting Committee under Dr. B. R. Ambedkar was set up on 29 August 1947 and produced the Draft Constitution (315 Articles, 8 Schedules). The Indian Independence Act, 1947 (s. 8) gave the Assembly legal power to make the Constitution. From the midnight of 14 August 1947 it also worked as the legislature of independent India. The Draft went through three readings : Ambedkar moved it on 4 November 1948; clause-by-clause consideration followed from 15 November 1948; the third reading began on 17 November 1949. 7,635 amendments were tabled and 2,473 were moved. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (Preamble: "IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949"), signed on 24 January 1950 by 284 members, and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Art. 394). It then had 395 Articles and 8 Schedules. Total time: 2 years, 11 months, 17 days; 11 sessions; 165 days of sitting, 114 of them on the Draft. The Assembly then became the Provisional Parliament until the new Parliament was constituted in 1952.
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF).
Preamble (last words) – "IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION."
Article 393 (Short title) – "This Constitution may be called the Constitution of India."

Article 394 (Commencement) – "This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution as the commencement of this Constitution."

Article 394A (Authoritative text in the Hindi language) – inserted by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987. The President shall publish "the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly", and that translation is "deemed to be, for all purposes, the authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language".

Article 395 (Repeals) – "The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed."

Indian Independence Act, 1947, ss. 6 and 8 (as explained by the Supreme Court, Kesavananda Bharati , para 1160, Jaganmohan Reddy J.) – "Sections 6 and 8 of which conferred on the Constituent Assembly the power to enact a Constitution".
In simple words:

The Constitution says about itself that it was adopted by the people "in our Constituent Assembly" on 26 November 1949. A few Articles (citizenship, elections, interpretation, transitional matters, the President's oath, short title) started on 26 November 1949 itself, because they were needed before the new system began. All the rest started on 26 January 1950. The Constitution ended the two British Acts that had governed India till then (Art. 395). The legal power to make the Constitution came from the Indian Independence Act, 1947; but the Constitution itself claims its authority from "the people of India".
hi.meaning: Framing of the Constitution: the whole process by which the Constitution of India was prepared, debated, adopted and brought into force – from the setting up of the Constituent Assembly (1946) to the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950). Constituent Assembly: a body of representatives whose task is to make a constitution. Dr. Sinha's inaugural address (9 December 1946) traces the demand to the 1934 resolution: "the only method of applying that principle is to convene a Constituent Assembly, representative of all sections of the Indian people, to frame an acceptable constitution." Cabinet Mission Plan : the plan of the British Cabinet Mission "announced on May 16, 1946" ( Kesavananda , para 515), under which the Provincial Legislative Assemblies elected the members of the Constituent Assembly. Objectives Resolution : the resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947, laying down the aims of the Constitution; it was the Assembly's "terms of reference" (Dr. Rajendra Prasad, 26 November 1949). Drafting Committee: the committee appointed on 29 August 1947, under Dr. Ambedkar, to prepare the Draft Constitution from the Assembly's decisions (details in Role of Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly ). Readings: the stages of consideration of the Draft – general discussion on the motion to take it into consideration; clause-by-clause consideration (which Dr. Prasad called "the second reading stage"); and the "third reading", on the motion "That the Constitution as settled by the Assembly be passed." Adoption, signing and commencement: adoption is the passing of the Constitution (26 November 1949); signing is the members putting their signatures (24 January 1950); commencement is the date it came into force (26 January 1950, Art. 394). Provisional Parliament: the Constituent Assembly acting as Parliament after 26 January 1950, until "a new Parliament was constituted in 1952" (Lok Sabha note in the CAD).
keyPoints: Idea: Gandhi 1922; Swaraj Party and Congress 1934; Faizpur 1936; CWC 1939. Cabinet Mission Plan, 16 May 1946; elections July–August 1946; indirect; limited franchise (~15%). 389 = 292 + 93 + 4; 299 after Partition (229 + 70). 9 December 1946: first sitting; 207 present, 9 women; Sinha temporary Chairman. 11 December 1946: Prasad elected permanent Chairman. 13 December 1946: Objectives Resolution moved; 22 January 1947 adopted. 14 August 1947 midnight: Assembly took over as Legislative Assembly. s. 8, Indian Independence Act, 1947: legal authority. 29 August 1947: Drafting Committee (Ambedkar). B. N. Rau: 243 articles, 13 schedules → Draft 315 Articles, 8 Schedules → final 395 articles, 8 schedules. 4 November 1948 Draft moved; 9 November 1948 motion adopted; 15 November 1948 clause-by-clause; 17 November 1949 third reading. 7,635 amendments tabled; 2,473 moved. 26 November 1949 adopted; 24 January 1950 signed by 284; 26 January 1950 in force. 2 years 11 months 17 days; 11 sessions; 165 days (114 on Draft); Rs. 63,96,729. Art. 394 (commencement), 394A (Hindi text), 395 (repeals).

caseLaws.facts: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner filed a writ petition on 21 March 1970 challenging the Kerala Land Reforms Act
caseLaws.facts: The petitions raised the validity of the Twenty-fourth, Twenty-fifth and Twenty-ninth Amendments, i.e. the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Art. 368. Principle: In answering it, the judges examined the framing of the Constitution. Shelat and Grover JJ. (para 515): the Cabinet Mission plan was "announced on May 16, 1946"; the Assembly was "elected between July-August 1946"; "It was by virtue of Section 8 of the Indian Independence Act 1947 that the Constituent Assembly was vested with the legal authority to frame a Constitution for India." Hegde and Mukherjea JJ. (para 686): the Objectives Resolution "is a definite landmark. It is a precursor to the preamble to our Constitution." Jaganmohan Reddy J. (paras 1159–1162): the members "were not elected on adult franchise"; "The Constitution was not ratified by the people but it came into force, by virtue of Article 394". Why it matters: It is the Supreme Court's own account of how the Constitution was framed, and it shows that the history of framing is used to interpret the Constitution (here, the amending power and the basic structure ).
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , [1950] SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, challenged the Act under Arts. 19, 21 and 22. The Court was referred to the Constituent Assembly debates and the Drafting Committee's report on the wording of Art. 21, to show that the expression "due process of law" had been considered and not adopted. Principle: Kania C.J.: "while it is not proper to take into consideration the individual opinions of Members of Parliament or Convention to construe the meaning of the particular clause, when a question is raised whether a certain phrase or expression was up for consideration at all or not, a reference to the debates may be permitted." Mukherjea J.: "these debates are of doubtful value" as an aid to the meaning of words; headnote: "a higher value may be placed on the report of the Drafting Committee." Why it matters: It decides how the record of framing (debates, committee reports) may be used in court – with caution, mainly to see what was considered.

selfTest.q: Under which plan was the Constituent Assembly set up, and how were its members chosen?
selfTest.a: Answer: The Cabinet Mission Plan of 16 May 1946; indirectly, by members of the Provincial Legislative Assemblies. Show how the figure 389 is made up. Answer: 292 (Provinces) + 93 (Indian States) + 4 (Chief Commissioners' Provinces) = 389. Why did the strength fall to 299? Answer: Partition under the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947; a separate Assembly for Pakistan. Who presided on 9 December 1946, and who was elected on 11 December 1946? Answer: Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha (temporary Chairman); Dr. Rajendra Prasad (permanent Chairman). When was the Objectives Resolution moved and adopted? Answer: Moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946; adopted on 22 January 1947. Which law gave the Assembly legal authority to frame the Constitution? Answer: Section 8 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 ( Kesavananda , para 515). How many articles and schedules did B. N. Rau's draft, the Draft Constitution and the final Constitution have? Answer: 243/13; 315/8; 395/8. Distinguish adoption, signing and commencement. Answer: Adopted 26 November 1949; signed 24 January 1950 (284 members); in force 26 January 1950. Name any four Articles that came into force on 26 November 1949. Answer: Any four of Arts. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60, 324, 366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392, 393, 394. How many amendments were tabled and moved? Answer: 7,635 tabled; 2,473 moved. What did A.K. Gopalan say about using the Assembly debates? Answer: Individual speeches cannot fix the meaning of a clause, but the debates may be referred to on whether a phrase was considered at all (Kania C.J.); they are "of doubtful value" (Mukherjea J.). What were Dr. Prasad's two regrets? Answer: No qualifications were laid down for legislators; the Constitution could not be drawn up in an Indian language.

Criticism Reply / record
Not elected on adult franchise; not fully representative True – limited franchise of about 15% (Jaganmohan Reddy J.). Ambedkar: "the Constituent Assembly though elected on limited franchise can be trusted to pass the Constitution by simple majority" because it "has no partisan motive". The Supreme Court notes it gradually "became fully representative of the various communities and interests" (Shelat and Grover JJ., para 515).
Not ratified by the people "The Constitution was not ratified by the people but it came into force, by virtue of Article 394" (Jaganmohan Reddy J., para 1161).
Too slow and costly Prasad: the time helped solve the States and communal problems; cost Rs. 63,96,729 till 22 November 1949.
Too bulky Prasad: "If the provisions have been well thought out, the bulk need not disturb the equanimity of our mind."
Borrowed from the 1935 Act Ambedkar: "I make no apologies" (see Government of India Act 1935).
Not in an Indian language Prasad's regret; the Hindi translation was ready by 24 January 1950 and is now the authoritative Hindi text (Art. 394A).
No qualifications for legislators Prasad's other regret.

This Is not the same as Why
Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee The Assembly (299 members) debated and adopted the Constitution; the Drafting Committee was one of its committees that prepared the Draft.
Date of adoption (26 November 1949) Date of commencement (26 January 1950) Adopted = passed; commencement = came into force (Art. 394). Some Articles started on 26 November 1949.
Signing (24 January 1950) Adoption (26 November 1949) Signing came two months after adoption.
Objectives Resolution Preamble The Resolution (1947) was the "precursor"; the Preamble is part of the Constitution.
Temporary Chairman (Sinha) President of the Assembly (Prasad) Sinha presided only until Prasad was elected on 11 December 1946.
Prasad as President of the Constituent Assembly Prasad as President of India He was elected President of India on 24 January 1950.
B. N. Rau (Constitutional Adviser) Member of the Drafting Committee Rau prepared the original draft as adviser; the Drafting Committee was chaired by Ambedkar.

en.meaning:
Who first formally proposed a constitution framed by Indians for India, in 1934?

Explanation. M.N. Roy first proposed a Constituent Assembly in 1934; the Indian National Congress officially demanded one in 1935.

The scheme by which the Constituent Assembly was actually elected and constituted came from:

Explanation. The Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946 provided that members from the provinces were chosen indirectly by the provincial legislative assemblies, and that the Indian States sent their own representatives.

The Constituent Assembly's original strength was 389 members. After Partition, this was reduced to:

Explanation. The Assembly was meant to have 389 members: 296 from British India and 93 from the Indian States. After the division of the country in August 1947, the strength became 299.

Who was elected the Constituent Assembly's permanent President, on 11 December 1946?

te.meaning: Who first formally proposed a constitution framed by Indians for India, in 1934? Explanation. M.N. Roy first proposed a Constituent Assembly in 1934; the Indian National Congress officially demanded one in 1935. The scheme by which the Constituent Assembly was actually elected and constituted came from: Explanation. The Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946 provided that members from the provinces were chosen indirectly by the provincial legislative assemblies, and that the Indian States sent their own representatives. The Constituent Assembly's original strength was 389 members. After Partition, this was reduced to: Explanation. The Assembly was meant to have 389 members: 296 from British India and 93 from the Indian States. After the division of the country in August 1947, the strength became 299. Who was elected the Constituent Assembly's permanent President, on 11 December 1946?
