constitutional-law-i-u1-t10.subtitle: Who sat on the Drafting Committee, what it did with B.N. Rau's draft, and Ambedkar's part in it

en.inOneMinute: The Drafting Committee was appointed by a resolution of the Constituent Assembly on 29 August 1947 , moved by Shri Satyanarayan Sinha. The mover called it "purely an expert committee". Seven members: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, K. M. Munshi, Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, Sir B. L. Mitter and D. P. Khaitan. The Committee elected Dr. Ambedkar as its Chairman . Later, N. Madhava Rau and T. T. Krishnamachari also served on it (Khaitan had died). Task (as amended on 29 August 1947): "to scrutinise the draft of the text of the Constitution of India prepared by the Constitutional Adviser giving effect to the decisions taken already in the Assembly and including all matters which are ancillary thereto ... and to submit to the Assembly for consideration the text of the draft Constitution as revised by the Committee." It first met on 30 August 1947 and sat for 141 days . It worked on the Constitutional Adviser B. N. Rau's draft (243 articles, 13 Schedules) and produced the Draft Constitution (315 Articles, 8 Schedules), sent with Ambedkar's letter of 21 February 1948 explaining its "departures" and "alternatives". The Committee made real choices of drafting: e.g. the word "Union" in Art. 1 (no right to secede); "procedure established by law" instead of "due process of law" in Art. 21 ( A.K. Gopalan ); the shape of the Preamble and the amendment provisions ( Kesavananda ). In the Assembly it piloted the Draft: Ambedkar moved it on 4 November 1948, answered criticism, accepted or withdrew amendments, presented a revised report on 14 November 1949 and moved the third reading on 17 November 1949. The Constitution was passed on 26 November 1949 with 395 articles and 8 Schedules. Limits: it followed the Assembly's decisions. Ambedkar: on minority safeguards "the Drafting Committee has no responsibility. It follows the decisions of the Constituent Assembly." Credit: Ambedkar shared it with B. N. Rau, the other members, the Chief Draftsman S. N. Mukherjee, and the discipline of the Congress Party. Dr. Rajendra Prasad: "We could never make a decision which was or could be ever so right as when we put him on the Drafting Committee and made him its Chairman."
legalProvision: There is no Article on the Drafting Committee; it was created by a resolution of the Constituent Assembly. Its work is now the text of the Constitution.

Resolution of 29 August 1947 (as moved) – "This Assembly resolves that a Committee consisting of-(1) Shri Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, (2) Shri N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, (3) The Honourable Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, (4) Shri K. M. Munshi, (5) Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, (6) Sir B. L. Mitter, (7) Shri D. P. Khaitan, be appointed to scrutinise and to suggest necessary amendment to the draft Constitution of India prepared in the Office of the Assembly on the basis of the decisions taken in, the Assembly."

B. G. Kher's amendment (adopted the same day) – the words of the task were replaced by: "to scrutinise the draft of the text of the Constitution of India prepared by the Constitutional Adviser giving effect to the decisions taken already in the Assembly and including all matters which are ancillary thereto or which have to be provided in such a Constitution, and to submit to the Assembly for consideration the text of the draft Constitution as revised by the Committee."
Article 1(1) of the Constitution – "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."
Article 21 of the Constitution – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
In simple words:

The Drafting Committee was not the body that decided the Constitution's principles; the Assembly did that through its committees. Its job was to take the Constitutional Adviser's draft, put the Assembly's decisions into proper legal words, fill in the matters "ancillary" (connected) to them, and give the Assembly a complete revised Draft. The Assembly kept full power to change anything in that Draft. Arts. 1 and 21 are two examples of words chosen by the Drafting Committee that the Assembly accepted.
en.meaning: Drafting Committee: the seven-member committee of the Constituent Assembly appointed on 29 August 1947 to scrutinise the Constitutional Adviser's draft and submit a revised Draft Constitution. Constitutional Adviser: Sir B. N. Rau, who "prepared a rough draft of the Constitution for the consideration of the Drafting Committee" (Ambedkar, 25 November 1949). Draft Constitution: the text "as settled by the Drafting Committee" (315 Articles, 8 Schedules), which Ambedkar moved for consideration on 4 November 1948. "Ancillary" matters: matters connected with the Assembly's decisions, or which "have to be provided in such a Constitution", but which the Assembly had not yet decided (Kher's amendment). Chief Draftsman: S. N. Mukherjee, Joint Secretary and Draftsman, whose "ability to put the most intricate proposals in the simplest and clearest legal form can rarely be equalled" (Ambedkar).
keyPoints: 29 August 1947: resolution moved by Satyanarayan Sinha; "purely an expert committee". Members: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, B. R. Ambedkar, K. M. Munshi, Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, B. L. Mitter, D. P. Khaitan. Chairman Ambedkar – elected by the Committee. Task widened by B. G. Kher's amendment. First meeting 30 August 1947; sat 141 days. B. N. Rau's draft 243/13 → Draft 315/8 → 386 → final 395/8. Letter of 21 February 1948 (departures and alternatives). Khaitan died (announced 4 November 1948); later members N. Madhava Rau, T. T. Krishnamachari. Draft moved 4 November 1948; revised report 14 November 1949; third reading 17 November 1949. "Union" (Art. 1) – no right to secede; "procedure established by law" (Art. 21). "Drifting Committee" (Naziruddin Ahmad) – "drift with mastery" (Ambedkar). Credit: Rau, members, S. N. Mukherjee, Congress Party discipline. A.K. Gopalan : report has higher value than debates.

caseLaws.facts: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , [1950] SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, challenged the Act under Arts. 19, 21 and 22. The Attorney-General placed before the Court the Assembly debates "centering round the adoption of this recommendation of the Drafting Committee" on Art. 21. Principle: Mukherjea J.: draft article 15 read "without due process of law"; "The Drafting Committee in their report recommended a change" to "procedure established by law", "the reason given being that the former expression was more specific"; "when that form was abandoned and another was deliberately substituted in its place, it is not possible to say that in spite of the difference in the language and expression, they should mean the same thing". Headnote: "a higher value may be placed on the report of the Drafting Committee." Kania C.J.: the report "may be read not to control the meaning of the article, but may be seen in case of ambiguity." (The detention law was upheld by majority.) Why it matters: It shows that the Drafting Committee's choice of words changed the law, and that its report is a recognised aid to interpretation.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.facts: 368. Principle: The judges traced the Drafting Committee's work. Shelat and Grover JJ. (para 541): in February 1948 the Committee "omitted that part of the Objectives Resolution which declared that the territories of India would retain the status of automonous units with residuary powers" and limited the Preamble to "the essential features of the new State and its basic socio-political objectives". A.N. Ray J. (para 924): in February 1948 it "made three material changes in the provisions made by the Constitution Adviser" on amendment. Why it matters: It shows the Committee shaped both the Preamble and the amending power, and that its work is studied in deciding major constitutional questions.

selfTest.q: When and on whose motion was the Drafting Committee appointed?
selfTest.a: Answer: 29 August 1947, on the motion of Shri Satyanarayan Sinha. Name the seven original members. Answer: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, B. R. Ambedkar, K. M. Munshi, Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, B. L. Mitter, D. P. Khaitan. Who elected Ambedkar Chairman? Answer: The Drafting Committee itself ("the Drafting Committee elected me to be its Chairman"). What was the Committee's task after Kher's amendment? Answer: To scrutinise the Constitutional Adviser's draft giving effect to the Assembly's decisions, include ancillary matters, and submit the revised Draft. How many days did the Committee sit? Answer: 141 days (first meeting 30 August 1947). Give the article/schedule counts at each stage. Answer: 243/13 (Rau) → 315/8 (Draft) → 386 (end of consideration) → 395/8 (final). Why did the Committee use the word "Union"? Answer: To show the federation was not the result of an agreement, so no State could secede (Ambedkar). What change did the Committee make in draft article 15 (now Art. 21)? Answer: Added "personal" before "liberty" and replaced "due process of law" with "procedure established by law" as "more specific" ( A.K. Gopalan ). What did T. T. Krishnamachari say on 5 November 1948? Answer: Of seven members one resigned and was replaced, one died and was not replaced, one was in America, one was engaged in State affairs; the burden fell on Ambedkar. How did Ambedkar answer the "Drifting Committee" jibe? Answer: There is a difference between "drift without mastery and drift with mastery"; withdrawing faulty amendments showed honesty and courage. To whom did Ambedkar give the credit? Answer: B. N. Rau, the members, S. N. Mukherjee (Chief Draftsman), and the Congress Party's discipline. What weight does the Drafting Committee's report have in courts? Answer: A "higher value" than the debates; it may be seen in case of ambiguity ( A.K. Gopalan ).

te.inOneMinute: ముసాయిదా కమిటీ (Drafting Committee) ను 29 ఆగస్టు 1947 న రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు తీర్మానం ద్వారా నియమించారు; తీర్మానాన్ని శ్రీ సత్యనారాయణ్ సిన్హా ప్రతిపాదించారు. ఆయన దానిని "purely an expert committee" ( పూర్తిగా నిపుణుల కమిటీ ) అన్నారు. ఏడుగురు సభ్యులు: అల్లాడి కృష్ణస్వామి అయ్యర్, ఎన్. గోపాలస్వామి అయ్యంగార్, డా. బి. ఆర్. అంబేద్కర్, కె. ఎం. మున్షీ, సయ్యద్ మొహమ్మద్ సాదుల్లా, సర్ బి. ఎల్. మిట్టర్, డి. పి. ఖైతాన్. కమిటీ డా. అంబేద్కర్‌ను అధ్యక్షుడిగా ఎన్నుకుంది. తర్వాత ఎన్. మాధవరావు, టి. టి. కృష్ణమాచారి కూడా సభ్యులుగా ఉన్నారు (ఖైతాన్ మరణించారు). పని (29 ఆగస్టు 1947న సవరించినట్లు): "to scrutinise the draft of the text of the Constitution of India prepared by the Constitutional Adviser giving effect to the decisions taken already in the Assembly and including all matters which are ancillary thereto ... and to submit to the Assembly for consideration the text of the draft Constitution as revised by the Committee." ( అర్థం: సభ ఇప్పటికే తీసుకున్న నిర్ణయాలను అమలు చేస్తూ రాజ్యాంగ సలహాదారు తయారు చేసిన ముసాయిదా పాఠాన్ని పరిశీలించడం, వాటికి అనుబంధమైన అన్ని విషయాలు చేర్చడం, కమిటీ సవరించిన ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగ పాఠాన్ని సభ పరిశీలనకు సమర్పించడం.) అది 30 ఆగస్టు 1947న మొదట సమావేశమై 141 రోజులు పనిచేసింది. రాజ్యాంగ సలహాదారు బి. ఎన్. రావు ముసాయిదా (243 అధికరణలు, 13 షెడ్యూళ్లు) పై పనిచేసి ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగం (315 అధికరణలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లు) తయారు చేసింది; దాని "departures" ( మార్పులు ), "alternatives" ( ప్రత్యామ్నాయాలు ) ను వివరిస్తూ అంబేద్కర్ 21 ఫిబ్రవరి 1948 లేఖ పంపారు. కమిటీ నిజమైన ముసాయిదా ఎంపికలు చేసింది: ఉదా. అ. 1లో "Union" ( యూనియన్ ) అనే పదం (విడిపోయే హక్కు లేదు); అ. 21లో "due process of law" కు బదులు "procedure established by law" ( చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన ప్రక్రియ ) ( ఎ. కె. గోపాలన్ ); ప్రవేశిక, సవరణ నిబంధనల రూపం ( కేశవానంద ). సభలో ముసాయిదాను నడిపించింది: 4 నవంబర్ 1948న అంబేద్కర్ దాన్ని ప్రతిపాదించారు, విమర్శలకు సమాధానం ఇచ్చారు, సవరణలను అంగీకరించారు లేదా ఉపసంహరించారు, 14 నవంబర్ 1949న సవరించిన నివేదిక సమర్పించారు, 17 నవంబర్ 1949న మూడవ పఠనం ప్రతిపాదించారు. 26 నవంబర్ 1949న 395 అధికరణలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లతో రాజ్యాంగం ఆమోదించబడింది. పరిమితులు: అది సభ నిర్ణయాలను అనుసరించింది. అంబేద్కర్: మైనారిటీ రక్షణలపై "the Drafting Committee has no responsibility. It follows the decisions of the Constituent Assembly." ( ముసాయిదా కమిటీకి బాధ్యత లేదు; అది రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు నిర్ణయాలను అనుసరిస్తుంది. ) ఘనత: అంబేద్కర్ దానిని బి. ఎన్. రావు, ఇతర సభ్యులు, ప్రధాన ముసాయిదాకారుడు ఎస్. ఎన్. ముఖర్జీ, కాంగ్రెస్ పార్టీ క్రమశిక్షణతో పంచుకున్నారు. డా. రాజేంద్ర ప్రసాద్: "We could never make a decision which was or could be ever so right as when we put him on the Drafting Committee and made him its Chairman." ( ఆయనను ముసాయిదా కమిటీలో పెట్టి, దాని అధ్యక్షుడిని చేసినప్పటి నిర్ణయం కంటే సరైన నిర్ణయం మనం ఎప్పుడూ తీసుకోలేదు. )
te.meaning: ముసాయిదా కమిటీ: రాజ్యాంగ సలహాదారు ముసాయిదాను పరిశీలించి సవరించిన ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగాన్ని సమర్పించడానికి 29 ఆగస్టు 1947న నియమించిన రాజ్యాంగ పరిషత్తు ఏడుగురు సభ్యుల కమిటీ. రాజ్యాంగ సలహాదారు: సర్ బి. ఎన్. రావు; ఆయన "prepared a rough draft of the Constitution for the consideration of the Drafting Committee" ( ముసాయిదా కమిటీ పరిశీలనకు రాజ్యాంగ ప్రాథమిక ముసాయిదా తయారు చేశారు ) (అంబేద్కర్, 25 నవంబర్ 1949). ముసాయిదా రాజ్యాంగం: "as settled by the Drafting Committee" ( ముసాయిదా కమిటీ నిర్ణయించిన ) పాఠం (315 అధికరణలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లు); 4 నవంబర్ 1948న అంబేద్కర్ దానిని పరిశీలనకు ప్రతిపాదించారు. "Ancillary" (అనుబంధ) విషయాలు: సభ నిర్ణయాలకు సంబంధించిన, లేదా "have to be provided in such a Constitution" ( అటువంటి రాజ్యాంగంలో తప్పక ఉండాల్సిన ), కానీ సభ ఇంకా నిర్ణయించని విషయాలు (ఖేర్ సవరణ). ప్రధాన ముసాయిదాకారుడు (Chief Draftsman): ఎస్. ఎన్. ముఖర్జీ, జాయింట్ సెక్రటరీ మరియు డ్రాఫ్ట్స్‌మన్; ఆయన "ability to put the most intricate proposals in the simplest and clearest legal form can rarely be equalled" ( అత్యంత సంక్లిష్ట ప్రతిపాదనలను అత్యంత సరళమైన, స్పష్టమైన చట్ట రూపంలో పెట్టే ఆయన సామర్థ్యానికి సాటి అరుదు ) (అంబేద్కర్).

selfTest.q: ముసాయిదా కమిటీని ఎప్పుడు, ఎవరి తీర్మానంపై నియమించారు?
selfTest.a: సమాధానం: 29 ఆగస్టు 1947, శ్రీ సత్యనారాయణ్ సిన్హా తీర్మానంపై. ఏడుగురు అసలు సభ్యుల పేర్లు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: అల్లాడి కృష్ణస్వామి అయ్యర్, ఎన్. గోపాలస్వామి అయ్యంగార్, బి. ఆర్. అంబేద్కర్, కె. ఎం. మున్షీ, సయ్యద్ మొహమ్మద్ సాదుల్లా, బి. ఎల్. మిట్టర్, డి. పి. ఖైతాన్. అంబేద్కర్‌ను అధ్యక్షుడిగా ఎవరు ఎన్నుకున్నారు? సమాధానం: ముసాయిదా కమిటీయే ("the Drafting Committee elected me to be its Chairman"). ఖేర్ సవరణ తర్వాత కమిటీ పని ఏమిటి? సమాధానం: సభ నిర్ణయాలను అమలు చేసే రాజ్యాంగ సలహాదారు ముసాయిదాను పరిశీలించడం, అనుబంధ విషయాలు చేర్చడం, సవరించిన ముసాయిదా సమర్పించడం. కమిటీ ఎన్ని రోజులు కూర్చుంది? సమాధానం: 141 రోజులు (మొదటి సమావేశం 30 ఆగస్టు 1947). ప్రతి దశలో అధికరణలు/షెడ్యూళ్ల సంఖ్య చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: 243/13 (రావు) → 315/8 (ముసాయిదా) → 386 (పరిశీలన చివర) → 395/8 (తుది). కమిటీ "Union" పదాన్ని ఎందుకు వాడింది? సమాధానం: సమాఖ్య ఒప్పందం ఫలితం కాదని, కాబట్టి ఏ రాష్ట్రమూ విడిపోలేదని చూపడానికి (అంబేద్కర్). ముసాయిదా అధికరణ 15 (ఇప్పుడు అ. 21) లో కమిటీ ఏ మార్పు చేసింది? సమాధానం: "liberty" ముందు "personal" చేర్చి, "due process of law" కు బదులు "procedure established by law" పెట్టింది – "more specific" కాబట్టి ( ఎ. కె. గోపాలన్ ). 5 నవంబర్ 1948న టి. టి. కృష్ణమాచారి ఏమన్నారు? సమాధానం: ఏడుగురిలో ఒకరు రాజీనామా చేసి భర్తీ అయ్యారు, ఒకరు మరణించి భర్తీ కాలేదు, ఒకరు అమెరికాలో, ఒకరు రాష్ట్ర వ్యవహారాల్లో; భారం అంబేద్కర్‌పై పడింది. "Drifting Committee" వ్యంగ్యానికి అంబేద్కర్ ఎలా సమాధానం ఇచ్చారు? సమాధానం: "drift without mastery and drift with mastery" ( నియంత్రణ లేకుండా, నియంత్రణతో ) మధ్య తేడా ఉంది; లోపమున్న సవరణలను ఉపసంహరించడం నిజాయితీ, ధైర్యం. అంబేద్కర్ ఘనతను ఎవరికి ఇచ్చారు? సమాధానం: బి. ఎన్. రావు, సభ్యులు, ఎస్. ఎన్. ముఖర్జీ (ప్రధాన ముసాయిదాకారుడు), కాంగ్రెస్ పార్టీ క్రమశిక్షణ. కోర్టుల్లో ముసాయిదా కమిటీ నివేదికకు ఎంత విలువ? సమాధానం: చర్చల కంటే "higher value" ( ఎక్కువ విలువ ); అస్పష్టత ఉన్నప్పుడు చూడవచ్చు ( ఎ. కె. గోపాలన్ ).

hi.inOneMinute: The Drafting Committee was appointed by a resolution of the Constituent Assembly on 29 August 1947 , moved by Shri Satyanarayan Sinha. The mover called it "purely an expert committee". Seven members: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, K. M. Munshi, Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, Sir B. L. Mitter and D. P. Khaitan. The Committee elected Dr. Ambedkar as its Chairman . Later, N. Madhava Rau and T. T. Krishnamachari also served on it (Khaitan had died). Task (as amended on 29 August 1947): "to scrutinise the draft of the text of the Constitution of India prepared by the Constitutional Adviser giving effect to the decisions taken already in the Assembly and including all matters which are ancillary thereto ... and to submit to the Assembly for consideration the text of the draft Constitution as revised by the Committee." It first met on 30 August 1947 and sat for 141 days . It worked on the Constitutional Adviser B. N. Rau's draft (243 articles, 13 Schedules) and produced the Draft Constitution (315 Articles, 8 Schedules), sent with Ambedkar's letter of 21 February 1948 explaining its "departures" and "alternatives". The Committee made real choices of drafting: e.g. the word "Union" in Art. 1 (no right to secede); "procedure established by law" instead of "due process of law" in Art. 21 ( A.K. Gopalan ); the shape of the Preamble and the amendment provisions ( Kesavananda ). In the Assembly it piloted the Draft: Ambedkar moved it on 4 November 1948, answered criticism, accepted or withdrew amendments, presented a revised report on 14 November 1949 and moved the third reading on 17 November 1949. The Constitution was passed on 26 November 1949 with 395 articles and 8 Schedules. Limits: it followed the Assembly's decisions. Ambedkar: on minority safeguards "the Drafting Committee has no responsibility. It follows the decisions of the Constituent Assembly." Credit: Ambedkar shared it with B. N. Rau, the other members, the Chief Draftsman S. N. Mukherjee, and the discipline of the Congress Party. Dr. Rajendra Prasad: "We could never make a decision which was or could be ever so right as when we put him on the Drafting Committee and made him its Chairman."
legalProvision: There is no Article on the Drafting Committee; it was created by a resolution of the Constituent Assembly. Its work is now the text of the Constitution.

Resolution of 29 August 1947 (as moved) – "This Assembly resolves that a Committee consisting of-(1) Shri Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, (2) Shri N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, (3) The Honourable Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, (4) Shri K. M. Munshi, (5) Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, (6) Sir B. L. Mitter, (7) Shri D. P. Khaitan, be appointed to scrutinise and to suggest necessary amendment to the draft Constitution of India prepared in the Office of the Assembly on the basis of the decisions taken in, the Assembly."

B. G. Kher's amendment (adopted the same day) – the words of the task were replaced by: "to scrutinise the draft of the text of the Constitution of India prepared by the Constitutional Adviser giving effect to the decisions taken already in the Assembly and including all matters which are ancillary thereto or which have to be provided in such a Constitution, and to submit to the Assembly for consideration the text of the draft Constitution as revised by the Committee."
Article 1(1) of the Constitution – "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."
Article 21 of the Constitution – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
In simple words:

The Drafting Committee was not the body that decided the Constitution's principles; the Assembly did that through its committees. Its job was to take the Constitutional Adviser's draft, put the Assembly's decisions into proper legal words, fill in the matters "ancillary" (connected) to them, and give the Assembly a complete revised Draft. The Assembly kept full power to change anything in that Draft. Arts. 1 and 21 are two examples of words chosen by the Drafting Committee that the Assembly accepted.
hi.meaning: Drafting Committee: the seven-member committee of the Constituent Assembly appointed on 29 August 1947 to scrutinise the Constitutional Adviser's draft and submit a revised Draft Constitution. Constitutional Adviser: Sir B. N. Rau, who "prepared a rough draft of the Constitution for the consideration of the Drafting Committee" (Ambedkar, 25 November 1949). Draft Constitution: the text "as settled by the Drafting Committee" (315 Articles, 8 Schedules), which Ambedkar moved for consideration on 4 November 1948. "Ancillary" matters: matters connected with the Assembly's decisions, or which "have to be provided in such a Constitution", but which the Assembly had not yet decided (Kher's amendment). Chief Draftsman: S. N. Mukherjee, Joint Secretary and Draftsman, whose "ability to put the most intricate proposals in the simplest and clearest legal form can rarely be equalled" (Ambedkar).
keyPoints: 29 August 1947: resolution moved by Satyanarayan Sinha; "purely an expert committee". Members: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, B. R. Ambedkar, K. M. Munshi, Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, B. L. Mitter, D. P. Khaitan. Chairman Ambedkar – elected by the Committee. Task widened by B. G. Kher's amendment. First meeting 30 August 1947; sat 141 days. B. N. Rau's draft 243/13 → Draft 315/8 → 386 → final 395/8. Letter of 21 February 1948 (departures and alternatives). Khaitan died (announced 4 November 1948); later members N. Madhava Rau, T. T. Krishnamachari. Draft moved 4 November 1948; revised report 14 November 1949; third reading 17 November 1949. "Union" (Art. 1) – no right to secede; "procedure established by law" (Art. 21). "Drifting Committee" (Naziruddin Ahmad) – "drift with mastery" (Ambedkar). Credit: Rau, members, S. N. Mukherjee, Congress Party discipline. A.K. Gopalan : report has higher value than debates.

caseLaws.facts: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras , [1950] SCR 88 (6-judge Bench, decided 19 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, challenged the Act under Arts. 19, 21 and 22. The Attorney-General placed before the Court the Assembly debates "centering round the adoption of this recommendation of the Drafting Committee" on Art. 21. Principle: Mukherjea J.: draft article 15 read "without due process of law"; "The Drafting Committee in their report recommended a change" to "procedure established by law", "the reason given being that the former expression was more specific"; "when that form was abandoned and another was deliberately substituted in its place, it is not possible to say that in spite of the difference in the language and expression, they should mean the same thing". Headnote: "a higher value may be placed on the report of the Drafting Committee." Kania C.J.: the report "may be read not to control the meaning of the article, but may be seen in case of ambiguity." (The detention law was upheld by majority.) Why it matters: It shows that the Drafting Committee's choice of words changed the law, and that its report is a recognised aid to interpretation.

caseLaws.facts: 368. Principle: The judges traced the Drafting Committee's work. Shelat and Grover JJ. (para 541): in February 1948 the Committee "omitted that part of the Objectives Resolution which declared that the territories of India would retain the status of automonous units with residuary powers" and limited the Preamble to "the essential features of the new State and its basic socio-political objectives". A.N. Ray J. (para 924): in February 1948 it "made three material changes in the provisions made by the Constitution Adviser" on amendment. Why it matters: It shows the Committee shaped both the Preamble and the amending power, and that its work is studied in deciding major constitutional questions.

selfTest.q: When and on whose motion was the Drafting Committee appointed?
selfTest.a: Answer: 29 August 1947, on the motion of Shri Satyanarayan Sinha. Name the seven original members. Answer: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, B. R. Ambedkar, K. M. Munshi, Saiyid Mohd. Saadulla, B. L. Mitter, D. P. Khaitan. Who elected Ambedkar Chairman? Answer: The Drafting Committee itself ("the Drafting Committee elected me to be its Chairman"). What was the Committee's task after Kher's amendment? Answer: To scrutinise the Constitutional Adviser's draft giving effect to the Assembly's decisions, include ancillary matters, and submit the revised Draft. How many days did the Committee sit? Answer: 141 days (first meeting 30 August 1947). Give the article/schedule counts at each stage. Answer: 243/13 (Rau) → 315/8 (Draft) → 386 (end of consideration) → 395/8 (final). Why did the Committee use the word "Union"? Answer: To show the federation was not the result of an agreement, so no State could secede (Ambedkar). What change did the Committee make in draft article 15 (now Art. 21)? Answer: Added "personal" before "liberty" and replaced "due process of law" with "procedure established by law" as "more specific" ( A.K. Gopalan ). What did T. T. Krishnamachari say on 5 November 1948? Answer: Of seven members one resigned and was replaced, one died and was not replaced, one was in America, one was engaged in State affairs; the burden fell on Ambedkar. How did Ambedkar answer the "Drifting Committee" jibe? Answer: There is a difference between "drift without mastery and drift with mastery"; withdrawing faulty amendments showed honesty and courage. To whom did Ambedkar give the credit? Answer: B. N. Rau, the members, S. N. Mukherjee (Chief Draftsman), and the Congress Party's discipline. What weight does the Drafting Committee's report have in courts? Answer: A "higher value" than the debates; it may be seen in case of ambiguity ( A.K. Gopalan ).

Which Article empowers Parliament to admit or establish new States into the Union?

Explanation. Article 2 empowers Parliament to admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms as it thinks fit.

Under Article 3, whose consent is required before Parliament can alter a State's boundaries?

Explanation. The affected State Legislature must be given a chance to express its views, but its views are not binding on Parliament.

In Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay (1960), the Supreme Court held that:

Explanation. Once the original Bill has been referred, Parliament need not refer an amended version back to the State Legislature again.

According to In Re: The Berubari Union (1960), what is needed to cede Indian territory to a foreign country?

en.meaning:
Under Article 5, a person who has been ordinarily resident in India for how many years immediately before the Constitution's commencement could become a citizen?

Explanation. Article 5(c) required not less than five years' ordinary residence in India immediately preceding the Constitution's commencement.

A person who migrated from Pakistan to India on or after 19 July 1948 needed to:

Explanation. Migrants after 19 July 1948 needed to be registered as citizens, having been resident for at least six months immediately before the application.

Does the Constitution of India permit dual citizenship?

Explanation. Article 9 says that a person who has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State is not a citizen under Articles 5, 6 or 8. Section 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955 terminates Indian citizenship on such acquisition.

Which Article gives Parliament the power to make laws regulating citizenship after the Constitution's commencement?

constitutional-law-i-u2-t1.subtitle: A written, detailed and partly rigid Constitution: federal with a strong Centre, parliamentary, secular, with enforceable rights and judicial review

en.inOneMinute: Nature: India's Constitution sets up a federal system with strong unitary features. Dr. Ambedkar: it "can be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances". The Supreme Court calls it a federation "with a bias in favour of the centre" ( S.R. Bommai ), or quasi-federal (Ahmadi J., Bommai ); it "was not true to, any traditional pattern of federation" ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). Salient (main) features: Written, detailed constitution (395 articles and 8 Schedules when adopted; now 12 Schedules), drawn from many sources. Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic (Preamble). Parliamentary form of government – President acts on ministers' advice (Art. 74(1)); ministers collectively responsible to the House of the People (Art. 75(3)). Federal division of powers (Arts. 245–246, Seventh Schedule) with unitary features: residuary power with Parliament (Art. 248), Parliament's power over State List in certain cases (Arts. 249, 250, 252, 253), emergency powers (Arts. 352, 356, 360). Single citizenship for the whole country. Single integrated and independent judiciary ; uniform basic laws; All-India Services (Art. 312). Fundamental Rights (Part III) with judicial review (Arts. 13, 32, 226). Directive Principles (Part IV) – "not ... enforceable by any court" but "fundamental in the governance of the country" (Art. 37). Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A, added in 1976). Secular State (Arts. 25–28; "Secularism is one of the basic features", Bommai ). Universal adult suffrage (Art. 326). Partly rigid, partly flexible amendment (Art. 368; some changes by simple law, e.g. Arts. 4(2), 169(3)); amending power limited by the basic structure ( Kesavananda , Minerva Mills ). Independent bodies – Election Commission (Art. 324), Comptroller and Auditor-General (Art. 148), Public Service Commissions (Art. 315), Finance Commission (Art. 280). Special provisions for Scheduled Areas and Tribes (Fifth and Sixth Schedules); local self-government (Parts IX and IXA).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Preamble – "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a [SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC] ..." ("SOCIALIST SECULAR" substituted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, for "SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC").
Article 1(1) – "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."

Article 74(1) – "There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice".
Article 75(3) – "The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People."
Article 248(1) – "Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List." (Words "Subject to article 246A" added later.)

Article 37 – "The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws."
Article 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed."

Article 326 – elections to the House of the People and State Legislative Assemblies "shall be on the basis of adult suffrage", i.e. every citizen "not less than eighteen years of age" who is not disqualified.

Article 368(2) – an amendment Bill must be passed in each House "by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting"; changes in matters listed in the proviso (e.g. "any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule", "the representation of States in Parliament") also need ratification "by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States".
In simple words:

The people of India gave themselves the Constitution; it creates a republic with an elected head. Real executive power is with ministers who answer to the elected House. Power is divided between the Union and the States, but the Union is stronger. Citizens' rights can be enforced in court; the State's welfare goals guide law-making but cannot be enforced in court. The Constitution can be changed, sometimes easily and sometimes with difficulty, but its basic structure cannot be destroyed.
en.meaning: Nature of a constitution: the type to which it belongs – written or unwritten, federal or unitary, rigid or flexible, parliamentary or presidential. Salient features: the main, distinctive characteristics of the Constitution. Federal constitution: Ambedkar (4 November 1948): "Federation means the establishment of a Dual Polity" – a Central polity and subsidiary polities "each being sovereign in the field assigned to it". A unitary constitution has "the supremacy of the Central Polity" and "the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities". Quasi-federal : "a mixture of the federal and unitary elements, leaning more towards the latter" (Ahmadi J., S.R. Bommai ). Parliamentary government: a system where the executive comes from and is responsible to the legislature; the head of State acts on ministers' advice (Arts. 74, 75). Basic structure : the essential features of the Constitution that cannot be destroyed by amendment under Art. 368 ( Kesavananda ; Minerva Mills ).
keyPoints: Ambedkar: "both unitary as well as federal"; "a flexible federation"; "dual polity with a single citizenship". Prasad: "I do not attach any importance to the label". West Bengal : no compact; "not true to, any traditional pattern of federation". Bommai : "federation but with a bias in favour of the centre"; "quasi-federal" (Ahmadi J.); federalism and secularism are basic features. Parliamentary: Art. 74(1), Art. 75(3); "more responsibility to more stability". Single judiciary, uniform laws, All-India Services (Art. 312). Rights (Part III) + judicial review (Arts. 13, 32, 226); DPSP (Art. 37); Duties (Art. 51A, 1976). Adult suffrage (Art. 326, 18 years). Amendment: simple / special / special + ratification (Art. 368); basic structure limit. Emergency: Arts. 352, 356, 360. Independent bodies: Arts. 148, 280, 315, 324. "SOCIALIST SECULAR" added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

caseLaws.facts: State of West Bengal v. Union of India , AIR 1963 SC 1241; [1964] 1 SCR 371 (6-judge Bench, decided 21 December 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Union proposed to acquire coal-bearing land vested in West Bengal under the Coal Bearing
caseLaws.facts: The State sued, arguing that it was sovereign in its field and its property could not be acquired by Parliament's law. Principle: Sinha C.J. (majority) listed the marks of a true federation – (a) a compact between sovereign units, (b) supremacy of a constitution alterable only by the units, (c) distribution of powers, (d) supreme authority of courts – and held: "In our Constitution characteristic (d) is to be found in full force, (a) and (b) are absent"; "Our Constitution was not the result of any such compact or agreement"; it "was not true to, any traditional pattern of federation". The suit was dismissed. Why it matters: The leading statement that India is federal in some respects but not a classic federation, and that States are not sovereign.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to Kerala land reform laws and to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments; the question
caseLaws.facts: 368. Principle: Sikri C.J. (para 316): "every provision of the Constitution can be amended provided in the result the basic foundation and structure of the Constitution remains the same." The basic structure includes: "(1) Supremacy of the Constitution; (2) Republican and Democratic form of Government. (3) Secular character of the Constitution; (4) Separation of powers between the Legislature, the executive and the judiciary; (5) Federal character of the Constitution." It is "built on the basic foundation, i.e., the dignity and freedom of the individual" (para 317). Why it matters: It turns the salient features into a legal limit on amendment.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , AIR 1980 SC 1789; (1980) 3 SCC 625 (5-judge Bench, decided 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Minerva Mills was nationalised under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 197
caseLaws.facts: The owners challenged that Act and ss. 4 and 55 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 (which widened Art. 31C and added Art. 368(4)–(5)). Principle: Chandrachud C.J. (majority): "a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution and therefore, the limitations on that power cannot be destroyed"; and "the Indian Constitution is founded on the bed-rock of the balance between Parts III and IV ... This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution." Sections 4 and 55 were held void. Why it matters: It adds two features to the basic structure – limited amending power and the balance between Rights and Directive Principles.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to Proclamations under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing State governments in several States. Principle: Jeevan Reddy J.: "The Constitution of India has created a federation but with a bias in favour of the centre. Within the sphere allotted to the States, they are supreme"; "Secularism is one of the basic features of the Constitution." Sawant J.: "Democracy and federalism are the essential features of our Constitution and are part of its basic structure." Ahmadi J.: the Constitution is "more appropriately" described as "'quasi-federal' because it is a mixture of the federal and unitary elements, leaning more towards the latter". Art. 356 Proclamations are subject to judicial review. Why it matters: The Court's most direct statement on the nature of Indian federalism and on secularism as basic features.

selfTest.q: What did Ambedkar mean by "dual polity"?
selfTest.a: Answer: A Union at the centre and States at the periphery, each with sovereign powers in the field assigned by the Constitution. Name two ways in which Indian federalism differs from the American. Answer: Single citizenship; no separate State constitutions (one frame for Union and States). (Also: no compact of States.) Which marks of a true federation did West Bengal find absent? Answer: (a) a compact of sovereign units and (b) a constitution alterable only by the units. Give three unitary features. Answer: Residuary power with Parliament (Art. 248); Parliament's power over State List (Arts. 249–253); emergency provisions (Arts. 352, 356, 360). (Also single citizenship, Art. 3.) Why did the framers choose the parliamentary system? Answer: It gives "more responsibility" through daily and periodic assessment; they "preferred more responsibility to more stability". Which Article makes Directive Principles non-enforceable? Answer: Art. 37. When were "socialist" and "secular" added? Answer: By the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976. Name the three methods of amendment. Answer: Simple majority (e.g. Arts. 4(2), 169(3)); special majority (Art. 368(2)); special majority plus ratification by half the States (proviso). List the five basic features named by Sikri C.J. Answer: Supremacy of the Constitution; republican and democratic government; secular character; separation of powers ; federal character. What did Minerva Mills add? Answer: Limited amending power, and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, are basic features. How many voters did Prasad expect under adult suffrage, and how? Answer: About 160 million – about 50% of a population of about 320 million. Name four independent constitutional bodies. Answer: Election Commission (Art. 324), CAG (Art. 148), Public Service Commissions (Art. 315), Finance Commission (Art. 280).

Federal (India) Federal (U.S.A.) U.S.: compact of States, dual citizenship, State constitutions; India: no compact, single citizenship, one Constitution (Ambedkar; West Bengal).
Quasi-federal Unitary States are "supreme" in their sphere (Bommai); a unitary State has no subsidiary sovereign polities.

Fundamental Rights Directive Principles Rights are enforceable (Art. 32); Principles are not (Art. 37) but are fundamental in governance.

te.inOneMinute: స్వభావం: భారత రాజ్యాంగం బలమైన ఏకకేంద్ర (unitary) లక్షణాలతో కూడిన సమాఖ్య వ్యవస్థను ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది. డా. అంబేద్కర్: అది "can be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances" ( కాలం, పరిస్థితుల అవసరాలను బట్టి ఏకకేంద్రంగానూ, సమాఖ్యగానూ ఉండగలదు ). సుప్రీంకోర్టు దానిని "with a bias in favour of the centre" ( కేంద్రం వైపు మొగ్గుతో ) సమాఖ్య ( ఎస్. ఆర్. బొమ్మై ) అని, లేదా అర్ధ-సమాఖ్య (quasi-federal) (అహ్మదీ న్యా., బొమ్మై ) అని అంది; అది "was not true to, any traditional pattern of federation" ( ఏ సంప్రదాయ సమాఖ్య నమూనాకూ సరిగ్గా సరిపోదు ) ( స్టేట్ ఆఫ్ వెస్ట్ బెంగాల్ v. యూనియన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా ). ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు: లిఖిత, వివరమైన రాజ్యాంగం (ఆమోదించినప్పుడు 395 అధికరణలు, 8 షెడ్యూళ్లు; ఇప్పుడు 12 షెడ్యూళ్లు); అనేక మూలాల నుండి తీసుకున్నది. సార్వభౌమ, సామ్యవాద, లౌకిక, ప్రజాస్వామ్య గణతంత్రం (ప్రవేశిక). పార్లమెంటరీ ప్రభుత్వం – రాష్ట్రపతి మంత్రుల సలహాపై వ్యవహరిస్తారు (అ. 74(1)); మంత్రులు సమష్టిగా లోక్‌సభకు బాధ్యులు (అ. 75(3)). సమాఖ్య అధికార విభజన (అ. 245–246, ఏడవ షెడ్యూల్) + ఏకకేంద్ర లక్షణాలు: అవశిష్ట అధికారం పార్లమెంటుకు (అ. 248), కొన్ని సందర్భాల్లో రాష్ట్ర జాబితాపై పార్లమెంటు అధికారం (అ. 249, 250, 252, 253), అత్యవసర అధికారాలు (అ. 352, 356, 360). దేశమంతటికీ ఏక పౌరసత్వం . ఏకీకృత, స్వతంత్ర న్యాయవ్యవస్థ ; ఏకరీతి మౌలిక చట్టాలు; అఖిల భారత సర్వీసులు (అ. 312). ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు (భాగం III) + న్యాయ సమీక్ష (అ. 13, 32, 226). ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలు (భాగం IV) – "not ... enforceable by any court" ( ఏ కోర్టు ద్వారానూ అమలు చేయించలేము ) కానీ "fundamental in the governance of the country" ( దేశ పాలనలో మౌలికమైనవి ) (అ. 37). ప్రాథమిక విధులు (అ. 51A, 1976లో చేర్చబడింది). లౌకిక రాజ్యం (అ. 25–28; "Secularism is one of the basic features" – లౌకికవాదం మౌలిక లక్షణాల్లో ఒకటి , బొమ్మై ). సార్వత్రిక వయోజన ఓటు హక్కు (అ. 326). పాక్షికంగా దృఢం, పాక్షికంగా సరళమైన సవరణ (అ. 368; కొన్ని మార్పులు సాధారణ చట్టంతోనే, ఉదా. అ. 4(2), 169(3)); సవరణాధికారానికి మౌలిక నిర్మాణం పరిమితి ( కేశవానంద , మినర్వా మిల్స్ ). స్వతంత్ర సంస్థలు – ఎన్నికల సంఘం (అ. 324), కాగ్ (అ. 148), పబ్లిక్ సర్వీస్ కమిషన్లు (అ. 315), ఆర్థిక సంఘం (అ. 280). షెడ్యూల్డ్ ప్రాంతాలు, తెగలకు ప్రత్యేక నిబంధనలు (ఐదవ, ఆరవ షెడ్యూళ్లు); స్థానిక స్వపరిపాలన (భాగాలు IX, IXA).
te.meaning: రాజ్యాంగ స్వభావం: అది ఏ రకానికి చెందినదో – లిఖిత/అలిఖిత, సమాఖ్య /ఏకకేంద్ర, దృఢ/సరళ, పార్లమెంటరీ/అధ్యక్ష తరహా. ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు (Salient features): రాజ్యాంగ ప్రధాన, విలక్షణ లక్షణాలు. సమాఖ్య రాజ్యాంగం: అంబేద్కర్ (4 నవంబర్ 1948): "Federation means the establishment of a Dual Polity" ( సమాఖ్య అంటే ద్వంద్వ రాజ్య వ్యవస్థ ఏర్పాటు ) – కేంద్ర వ్యవస్థ, ఉప వ్యవస్థలు, "each being sovereign in the field assigned to it" ( ప్రతిదీ తనకు కేటాయించిన రంగంలో సార్వభౌమం ). ఏకకేంద్ర రాజ్యాంగంలో "the supremacy of the Central Polity" ( కేంద్ర వ్యవస్థ ఆధిపత్యం ), "the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities" ( సార్వభౌమ ఉప వ్యవస్థలు లేకపోవడం ) ఉంటాయి. అర్ధ-సమాఖ్య : "a mixture of the federal and unitary elements, leaning more towards the latter" ( సమాఖ్య, ఏకకేంద్ర అంశాల మిశ్రమం, ఏకకేంద్రం వైపు ఎక్కువ మొగ్గు ) (అహ్మదీ న్యా., ఎస్. ఆర్. బొమ్మై ). పార్లమెంటరీ ప్రభుత్వం: కార్యనిర్వాహక వర్గం శాసనసభ నుండి వచ్చి దానికి బాధ్యత వహించే వ్యవస్థ; దేశాధినేత మంత్రుల సలహాపై వ్యవహరిస్తారు (అ. 74, 75). మౌలిక నిర్మాణం : అ. 368 కింద సవరణ ద్వారా నాశనం చేయలేని రాజ్యాంగ ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు ( కేశవానంద ; మినర్వా మిల్స్ ).

selfTest.q: "ద్వంద్వ రాజ్య వ్యవస్థ" అంటే అంబేద్కర్ ఉద్దేశం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సమాధానం: కేంద్రంలో యూనియన్, చుట్టూ రాష్ట్రాలు – ప్రతిదానికీ రాజ్యాంగం కేటాయించిన రంగంలో సార్వభౌమ అధికారాలు. భారత సమాఖ్య అమెరికా సమాఖ్యకు భిన్నమైన రెండు విధాలు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: ఏక పౌరసత్వం; రాష్ట్రాలకు వేర్వేరు రాజ్యాంగాలు లేవు (యూనియన్, రాష్ట్రాలకు ఒకే చట్రం). (రాష్ట్రాల ఒప్పందం కూడా లేదు.) వెస్ట్ బెంగాల్ నిజమైన సమాఖ్య లక్షణాల్లో ఏవి లేవని చెప్పింది? సమాధానం: (a) సార్వభౌమ యూనిట్ల ఒప్పందం, (b) యూనిట్లు మాత్రమే మార్చగల రాజ్యాంగం. మూడు ఏకకేంద్ర లక్షణాలు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: అవశిష్ట అధికారం పార్లమెంటుకు (అ. 248); రాష్ట్ర జాబితాపై పార్లమెంటు అధికారం (అ. 249–253); అత్యవసర నిబంధనలు (అ. 352, 356, 360). (ఏక పౌరసత్వం, అ. 3 కూడా.) ఫ్రేమర్లు పార్లమెంటరీ వ్యవస్థను ఎందుకు ఎంచుకున్నారు? సమాధానం: రోజువారీ, కాలానుగుణ పరీక్షల ద్వారా "more responsibility" ( ఎక్కువ బాధ్యత ) వస్తుంది; వారు "preferred more responsibility to more stability". ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలను అమలు చేయించలేమని చెప్పే అధికరణ ఏది? సమాధానం: అ. 37. "సామ్యవాద", "లౌకిక" ఎప్పుడు చేర్చారు? సమాధానం: రాజ్యాంగ (నలభై రెండవ సవరణ) చట్టం, 1976 ద్వారా. సవరణ మూడు పద్ధతులు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: సాధారణ మెజారిటీ (ఉదా. అ. 4(2), 169(3)); ప్రత్యేక మెజారిటీ (అ. 368(2)); ప్రత్యేక మెజారిటీ + సగం రాష్ట్రాల ఆమోదం (నిబంధన). సిక్రీ ప్ర.న్యా. చెప్పిన ఐదు మౌలిక లక్షణాలు ఏవి? సమాధానం: రాజ్యాంగ సర్వోన్నతత్వం; గణతంత్ర, ప్రజాస్వామ్య ప్రభుత్వం; లౌకిక స్వభావం; అధికార విభజన; సమాఖ్య స్వభావం. మినర్వా మిల్స్ ఏమి జోడించింది? సమాధానం: పరిమిత సవరణాధికారం, ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు-ఆదేశిక సూత్రాల సమతుల్యత మౌలిక లక్షణాలు. వయోజన ఓటు హక్కుతో ప్రసాద్ ఎంతమంది ఓటర్లను ఊహించారు, ఎలా? సమాధానం: సుమారు 16 కోట్లు – సుమారు 32 కోట్ల జనాభాలో సుమారు 50%. నాలుగు స్వతంత్ర రాజ్యాంగ సంస్థల పేర్లు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: ఎన్నికల సంఘం (అ. 324), కాగ్ (అ. 148), పబ్లిక్ సర్వీస్ కమిషన్లు (అ. 315), ఆర్థిక సంఘం (అ. 280).

hi.inOneMinute: Nature: India's Constitution sets up a federal system with strong unitary features. Dr. Ambedkar: it "can be both unitary as well as federal according to the requirements of time and circumstances". The Supreme Court calls it a federation "with a bias in favour of the centre" ( S.R. Bommai ), or quasi-federal (Ahmadi J., Bommai ); it "was not true to, any traditional pattern of federation" ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ). Salient (main) features: Written, detailed constitution (395 articles and 8 Schedules when adopted; now 12 Schedules), drawn from many sources. Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic (Preamble). Parliamentary form of government – President acts on ministers' advice (Art. 74(1)); ministers collectively responsible to the House of the People (Art. 75(3)). Federal division of powers (Arts. 245–246, Seventh Schedule) with unitary features: residuary power with Parliament (Art. 248), Parliament's power over State List in certain cases (Arts. 249, 250, 252, 253), emergency powers (Arts. 352, 356, 360). Single citizenship for the whole country. Single integrated and independent judiciary ; uniform basic laws; All-India Services (Art. 312). Fundamental Rights (Part III) with judicial review (Arts. 13, 32, 226). Directive Principles (Part IV) – "not ... enforceable by any court" but "fundamental in the governance of the country" (Art. 37). Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A, added in 1976). Secular State (Arts. 25–28; "Secularism is one of the basic features", Bommai ). Universal adult suffrage (Art. 326). Partly rigid, partly flexible amendment (Art. 368; some changes by simple law, e.g. Arts. 4(2), 169(3)); amending power limited by the basic structure ( Kesavananda , Minerva Mills ). Independent bodies – Election Commission (Art. 324), Comptroller and Auditor-General (Art. 148), Public Service Commissions (Art. 315), Finance Commission (Art. 280). Special provisions for Scheduled Areas and Tribes (Fifth and Sixth Schedules); local self-government (Parts IX and IXA).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Preamble – "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a [SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC] ..." ("SOCIALIST SECULAR" substituted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, for "SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC").
Article 1(1) – "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."

Article 74(1) – "There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice".
Article 75(3) – "The Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People."
Article 248(1) – "Parliament has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List." (Words "Subject to article 246A" added later.)

Article 37 – "The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws."
Article 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed."

Article 326 – elections to the House of the People and State Legislative Assemblies "shall be on the basis of adult suffrage", i.e. every citizen "not less than eighteen years of age" who is not disqualified.

Article 368(2) – an amendment Bill must be passed in each House "by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting"; changes in matters listed in the proviso (e.g. "any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule", "the representation of States in Parliament") also need ratification "by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States".
In simple words:

The people of India gave themselves the Constitution; it creates a republic with an elected head. Real executive power is with ministers who answer to the elected House. Power is divided between the Union and the States, but the Union is stronger. Citizens' rights can be enforced in court; the State's welfare goals guide law-making but cannot be enforced in court. The Constitution can be changed, sometimes easily and sometimes with difficulty, but its basic structure cannot be destroyed.
hi.meaning: Nature of a constitution: the type to which it belongs – written or unwritten, federal or unitary, rigid or flexible, parliamentary or presidential. Salient features: the main, distinctive characteristics of the Constitution. Federal constitution: Ambedkar (4 November 1948): "Federation means the establishment of a Dual Polity" – a Central polity and subsidiary polities "each being sovereign in the field assigned to it". A unitary constitution has "the supremacy of the Central Polity" and "the absence of subsidiary Sovereign polities". Quasi-federal : "a mixture of the federal and unitary elements, leaning more towards the latter" (Ahmadi J., S.R. Bommai ). Parliamentary government: a system where the executive comes from and is responsible to the legislature; the head of State acts on ministers' advice (Arts. 74, 75). Basic structure : the essential features of the Constitution that cannot be destroyed by amendment under Art. 368 ( Kesavananda ; Minerva Mills ).
keyPoints: Ambedkar: "both unitary as well as federal"; "a flexible federation"; "dual polity with a single citizenship". Prasad: "I do not attach any importance to the label". West Bengal : no compact; "not true to, any traditional pattern of federation". Bommai : "federation but with a bias in favour of the centre"; "quasi-federal" (Ahmadi J.); federalism and secularism are basic features. Parliamentary: Art. 74(1), Art. 75(3); "more responsibility to more stability". Single judiciary, uniform laws, All-India Services (Art. 312). Rights (Part III) + judicial review (Arts. 13, 32, 226); DPSP (Art. 37); Duties (Art. 51A, 1976). Adult suffrage (Art. 326, 18 years). Amendment: simple / special / special + ratification (Art. 368); basic structure limit. Emergency: Arts. 352, 356, 360. Independent bodies: Arts. 148, 280, 315, 324. "SOCIALIST SECULAR" added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

caseLaws.facts: State of West Bengal v. Union of India , AIR 1963 SC 1241; [1964] 1 SCR 371 (6-judge Bench, decided 21 December 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Union proposed to acquire coal-bearing land vested in West Bengal under the Coal Bearing
caseLaws.facts: The State sued, arguing that it was sovereign in its field and its property could not be acquired by Parliament's law. Principle: Sinha C.J. (majority) listed the marks of a true federation – (a) a compact between sovereign units, (b) supremacy of a constitution alterable only by the units, (c) distribution of powers, (d) supreme authority of courts – and held: "In our Constitution characteristic (d) is to be found in full force, (a) and (b) are absent"; "Our Constitution was not the result of any such compact or agreement"; it "was not true to, any traditional pattern of federation". The suit was dismissed. Why it matters: The leading statement that India is federal in some respects but not a classic federation, and that States are not sovereign.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to Kerala land reform laws and to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments; the question
caseLaws.facts: 368. Principle: Sikri C.J. (para 316): "every provision of the Constitution can be amended provided in the result the basic foundation and structure of the Constitution remains the same." The basic structure includes: "(1) Supremacy of the Constitution; (2) Republican and Democratic form of Government. (3) Secular character of the Constitution; (4) Separation of powers between the Legislature, the executive and the judiciary; (5) Federal character of the Constitution." It is "built on the basic foundation, i.e., the dignity and freedom of the individual" (para 317). Why it matters: It turns the salient features into a legal limit on amendment.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , AIR 1980 SC 1789; (1980) 3 SCC 625 (5-judge Bench, decided 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Minerva Mills was nationalised under the Sick Textile Undertakings (Nationalisation) Act, 197
caseLaws.facts: The owners challenged that Act and ss. 4 and 55 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 (which widened Art. 31C and added Art. 368(4)–(5)). Principle: Chandrachud C.J. (majority): "a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution and therefore, the limitations on that power cannot be destroyed"; and "the Indian Constitution is founded on the bed-rock of the balance between Parts III and IV ... This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution." Sections 4 and 55 were held void. Why it matters: It adds two features to the basic structure – limited amending power and the balance between Rights and Directive Principles.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to Proclamations under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing State governments in several States. Principle: Jeevan Reddy J.: "The Constitution of India has created a federation but with a bias in favour of the centre. Within the sphere allotted to the States, they are supreme"; "Secularism is one of the basic features of the Constitution." Sawant J.: "Democracy and federalism are the essential features of our Constitution and are part of its basic structure." Ahmadi J.: the Constitution is "more appropriately" described as "'quasi-federal' because it is a mixture of the federal and unitary elements, leaning more towards the latter". Art. 356 Proclamations are subject to judicial review. Why it matters: The Court's most direct statement on the nature of Indian federalism and on secularism as basic features.

selfTest.q: What did Ambedkar mean by "dual polity"?
selfTest.a: Answer: A Union at the centre and States at the periphery, each with sovereign powers in the field assigned by the Constitution. Name two ways in which Indian federalism differs from the American. Answer: Single citizenship; no separate State constitutions (one frame for Union and States). (Also: no compact of States.) Which marks of a true federation did West Bengal find absent? Answer: (a) a compact of sovereign units and (b) a constitution alterable only by the units. Give three unitary features. Answer: Residuary power with Parliament (Art. 248); Parliament's power over State List (Arts. 249–253); emergency provisions (Arts. 352, 356, 360). (Also single citizenship, Art. 3.) Why did the framers choose the parliamentary system? Answer: It gives "more responsibility" through daily and periodic assessment; they "preferred more responsibility to more stability". Which Article makes Directive Principles non-enforceable? Answer: Art. 37. When were "socialist" and "secular" added? Answer: By the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976. Name the three methods of amendment. Answer: Simple majority (e.g. Arts. 4(2), 169(3)); special majority (Art. 368(2)); special majority plus ratification by half the States (proviso). List the five basic features named by Sikri C.J. Answer: Supremacy of the Constitution; republican and democratic government; secular character; separation of powers ; federal character. What did Minerva Mills add? Answer: Limited amending power, and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, are basic features. How many voters did Prasad expect under adult suffrage, and how? Answer: About 160 million – about 50% of a population of about 320 million. Name four independent constitutional bodies. Answer: Election Commission (Art. 324), CAG (Art. 148), Public Service Commissions (Art. 315), Finance Commission (Art. 280).

constitutional-law-i-u2-t3.subtitle: Articles 1 to 4: the name and territory of India, new States, changes to States, and Union territories

en.inOneMinute: Part I (Arts. 1–4) of the Constitution deals with "The Union and its Territory". Art. 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." Ambedkar: the word "Union" was used because the federation is not the result of an agreement among States, so "no State has the right to secede from it". Territory of India (Art. 1(3)) = (a) territories of the States + (b) Union territories in the First Schedule + (c) "such other territories as may be acquired". The First Schedule lists the States and Union territories. As on 1 May 2026 it lists 28 States and 8 Union territories . Art. 2: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish , new States. Art. 3: Parliament may by law form a new State, increase or diminish the area, alter the boundaries, or alter the name of any State. The Bill needs the President's recommendation , and if it affects a State, it must be referred to that State's Legislature for its views . The views are not binding ( Babulal Parate , as followed in In re Article 370 ). Art. 4(2): such a law is not an amendment of the Constitution for Art. 368, so a simple majority is enough. Cession of Indian territory to a foreign country cannot be done under Art. 3; it needs an amendment under Art. 368 ( Berubari , 1960). There is "no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States" ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 1 – Name and territory of the Union

(1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. (2) The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule. (3) The territory of India shall comprise— (a) the territories of the States; (b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and (c) such other territories as may be acquired.
(Cl. (2) and sub-cl. (3)(b) were substituted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, w.e.f. 1-11-1956.)
Article 2 – Admission or establishment of new States
Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
(Art. 2A, "Sikkim to be associated with the Union", inserted by the 35th Amendment, 1974, was omitted by the 36th Amendment, 1975, w.e.f. 26-4-1975.)
Article 3 – Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States

Parliament may by law— (a) form a new State by separation of territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State; (b) increase the area of any State; (c) diminish the area of any State; (d) alter the boundaries of any State; (e) alter the name of any State: Provided that no Bill for the purpose shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President and unless, where the proposal contained in the Bill affects the area, boundaries or name of any of the States, the Bill has been referred by the President to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views thereon within such period as may be specified in the reference or within such further period as the President may allow and the period so specified or allowed has expired. Explanation I.—In this article, in clauses (a) to (e), "State" includes a Union territory, but in the proviso, "State" does not include a Union territory. Explanation II.—The power conferred on Parliament by clause (a) includes the power to form a new State or Union territory by uniting a part of any State or Union territory to any other State or Union territory.
(Proviso substituted by the 5th Amendment, 1955; Explanations I and II inserted by the 18th Amendment, 1966.)
Article 4 – Laws under Arts. 2 and 3

(1) Any law referred to in article 2 or article 3 shall contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law and may also contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to representation in Parliament and in the Legislature or Legislatures of the State or States affected by such law) as Parliament may deem necessary. (2) No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
In simple words:

India is one Union made of States. States cannot leave. India's territory = States + Union territories + any land India acquires later. Parliament can bring new States into India (Art. 2) and can redraw, merge, split or rename States (Art. 3) by an ordinary law. The State concerned is only asked for its views; Parliament need not follow them. Such a law automatically changes the First Schedule (list of States) and Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats), and it is not treated as a constitutional amendment.
en.meaning: Union of States : India as one indestructible whole divided into States "for convenience of administration" (Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Territory of India: the area described in Art. 1(3) – States, Union territories and acquired territories. State: a constituent unit listed in Part I of the First Schedule, with its own Governor, Legislature and Government under Part VI. Union territory : a unit listed in Part II of the First Schedule, administered by the President through an Administrator (Art. 239). In re Article 370 : "States are governed by their own governments and are directly accountable to the citizenry whereas Union territories are governed by the Union Government." Cession of territory : transfer of a part of India's territory to a foreign State. Berubari : it "amounts in law to a transfer of sovereignty". Acquired territory (Art. 1(3)(c)): territory that India gets in the exercise of its sovereign rights. Berubari : Art. 1(3)(c) "confers no power to acquire foreign territories but merely recognises automatic absorption of such territories as may be acquired".
keyPoints: Art. 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." "Union" – no agreement, no right to secede; "indestructible" (Ambedkar). Art. 1(3): States + UTs + acquired territories. First Schedule (1 May 2026): 28 States, 8 UTs. Art. 2: admit/establish new States (Sikkim, 1975). Art. 3: form, increase, diminish, alter boundaries, alter name. Proviso: President's recommendation + reference for views; views not binding ( Babulal Parate ). Explanation I: proviso not for UTs; Explanation II: new State or UT by uniting parts. Art. 4(2): not an Art. 368 amendment – simple majority. Berubari : cession needs Art. 368. West Bengal : "no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States". In re Article 370 : Ladakh valid under Art. 3(a) + Expl. I; conversion of whole State left open.

caseLaws.facts: The President asked the Court under Art. 143(1) whether legislation was needed and of what kind. Principle: The Agreement involved "cession of a part of India's territory". Art. 3 deals with "territorial adjustment inter se of the Constituent States" and is not "wide enough to cover cession of national territory". Hence "the Agreement cannot be implemented by a law relatable to Art. 3 and legislation relatable to Art. 368 would be inevitable." Why it matters: Draws the line between Art. 3 (internal reorganisation) and Art. 368 (giving away Indian territory).

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Union proposed to acquire coal-bearing land belonging to West Bengal under the Coal Beari
caseLaws.facts: The State claimed that, being sovereign, its property could not be acquired. Principle: Sinha C.J.: "There is no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States"; Parliament can "diminish its area so as even to destroy a State"; a Parliament competent to destroy a State can also acquire its property. The suit was dismissed. Why it matters: Shows that Arts. 2 and 3 make States subject to Parliament's power, a key reason Indian States are not sovereign.

caseLaws.facts: After a Joint Select Committee, it was changed to one composite State of Bombay and passed. A petitioner argued that the Bombay Legislature had no chance to give views on the changed proposal. Principle: "Nor is there anything in the proviso to indicate that Parliament must accept or act upon the views of the State Legislature"; a fresh reference for every amendment "might result in an interminable process". The views are only recommendatory. Why it matters: Leading rule on the nature of the proviso to Art. 3.
In re Article 370 of the Constitution , [2023] 16 SCR 1; 2023 INSC 1058 (5-judge Bench, decided 11 December 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Article 370 was made inoperative by Constitutional Orders 272 and 273, and the Jammu and Kash
caseLaws.facts: 356 and Parliament gave the "views" in place of the State Legislature. Principle: Chandrachud C.J. (for himself, Gavai and Surya Kant JJ.): the views under the first proviso to Art. 3 "are recommendatory"; Parliament's exercise of the power under the Proclamation was valid and not mala fide ; the carving out of Ladakh is valid under "Article 3(a) read with Explanation I"; whether a whole State can be converted into UTs "is left open". Elections were directed by 30 September 2024, and statehood restored "at the earliest". Why it matters: Latest Constitution Bench ruling on the scope of Art. 3 and the place of States and Union territories in the federal structure.

selfTest.q: What does Art. 1(1) say?
selfTest.a: Answer: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." Why did the Drafting Committee use "Union"? Answer: To show the federation was not the result of an agreement and no State can secede. What are the three parts of the territory of India? Answer: Territories of the States, Union territories in the First Schedule, and territories acquired later. How many States and Union territories are in the First Schedule as on 1 May 2026? Answer: 28 States and 8 Union territories. Give the five powers under Art. 3. Answer: Form a new State; increase area; diminish area; alter boundaries; alter name. What are the two conditions in the proviso to Art. 3? Answer: President's recommendation; reference to the affected State Legislature for its views within the time fixed. Are the State Legislature's views binding? Answer: No ( Babulal Parate ; In re Article 370 ). Does an Art. 3 law need a special majority? Answer: No; Art. 4(2) says it is not an amendment for Art. 368. Can India cede territory to another country by a law under Art. 3? Answer: No; an Art. 368 amendment is needed ( Berubari ). What did West Bengal say about State boundaries? Answer: "There is no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States." Under which provisions was the UT of Ladakh upheld? Answer: Art. 3(a) read with Explanation I. In a Lok Sabha sitting with 400 members present and voting, how many votes pass an Art. 3 Bill? Answer: A simple majority – 201.

te.inOneMinute: రాజ్యాంగంలోని భాగం I (అ. 1–4) "The Union and its Territory" ( యూనియన్, దాని భూభాగం ) గురించి చెబుతుంది. అ. 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." ( భారతదేశం, అంటే భారత్, రాష్ట్రాల యూనియన్‌గా ఉంటుంది. ) అంబేద్కర్: సమాఖ్య రాష్ట్రాల ఒప్పందం ఫలితం కాదు కాబట్టి "Union" అనే పదం వాడారు; అందువల్ల "no State has the right to secede from it" ( దాని నుండి విడిపోయే హక్కు ఏ రాష్ట్రానికీ లేదు ). భారత భూభాగం (అ. 1(3)) = (a) రాష్ట్రాల భూభాగాలు + (b) మొదటి షెడ్యూల్‌లోని కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాలు + (c) "such other territories as may be acquired" ( తర్వాత సంపాదించే ఇతర భూభాగాలు ). మొదటి షెడ్యూల్ రాష్ట్రాలు, కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాల జాబితా. 1 మే 2026 నాటికి అందులో 28 రాష్ట్రాలు , 8 కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాలు ఉన్నాయి. అ. 2: పార్లమెంటు చట్టం ద్వారా కొత్త రాష్ట్రాలను యూనియన్‌లోకి చేర్చుకోవచ్చు లేదా ఏర్పాటు చేయవచ్చు. అ. 3: పార్లమెంటు చట్టం ద్వారా కొత్త రాష్ట్రం ఏర్పాటు, విస్తీర్ణం పెంపు లేదా తగ్గింపు, సరిహద్దుల మార్పు, పేరు మార్పు చేయవచ్చు. బిల్లుకు రాష్ట్రపతి సిఫార్సు కావాలి; అది ఏదైనా రాష్ట్రాన్ని ప్రభావితం చేస్తే, ఆ రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభ అభిప్రాయం కోసం పంపాలి . ఆ అభిప్రాయం కట్టుబడి ఉండదు ( బాబూలాల్ పరాటే , In re Article 370 అనుసరించినట్లు). అ. 4(2): అలాంటి చట్టం అ. 368 ప్రయోజనాలకు రాజ్యాంగ సవరణ కాదు ; సాధారణ మెజారిటీ చాలు. విదేశీ దేశానికి భారత భూభాగం అప్పగింత అ. 3 కింద చేయలేము; అ. 368 కింద సవరణ కావాలి ( బెరుబారి , 1960). "no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States" ( రాష్ట్రాల సరిహద్దుల మార్పుకు వ్యతిరేకంగా రాజ్యాంగ హామీ లేదు ) ( స్టేట్ ఆఫ్ వెస్ట్ బెంగాల్ v. యూనియన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా ).
te.meaning: రాష్ట్రాల యూనియన్ : "for convenience of administration" ( పరిపాలన సౌలభ్యం కోసం ) రాష్ట్రాలుగా విభజించబడిన, నాశనం చేయలేని ఒకే సంపూర్ణ దేశం భారత్ (అంబేద్కర్, 4 నవంబర్ 1948). భారత భూభాగం: అ. 1(3) లో చెప్పిన ప్రాంతం – రాష్ట్రాలు, కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంత ాలు, సంపాదించిన భూభాగాలు. రాష్ట్రం: మొదటి షెడ్యూల్ భాగం Iలో ఉన్న, భాగం VI కింద సొంత గవర్నర్, శాసనసభ, ప్రభుత్వం గల యూనిట్. కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతం: మొదటి షెడ్యూల్ భాగం IIలో ఉన్న, రాష్ట్రపతి ఒక పరిపాలకుడి ద్వారా పాలించే (అ. 239) యూనిట్. In re Article 370 : "States are governed by their own governments and are directly accountable to the citizenry whereas Union territories are governed by the Union Government." ( రాష్ట్రాలను వాటి సొంత ప్రభుత్వాలు పాలిస్తాయి, అవి నేరుగా పౌరులకు జవాబుదారీ; కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాలను యూనియన్ ప్రభుత్వం పాలిస్తుంది. ) భూభాగ అప్పగింత : భారత భూభాగంలో కొంత భాగాన్ని విదేశీ రాజ్యానికి బదిలీ చేయడం. బెరుబారి : అది "amounts in law to a transfer of sovereignty" ( చట్టపరంగా సార్వభౌమత్వ బదిలీ ). సంపాదించిన భూభాగం (అ. 1(3)(c)): భారత్ తన సార్వభౌమ హక్కులతో పొందే భూభాగం. బెరుబారి : అ. 1(3)(c) "confers no power to acquire foreign territories but merely recognises automatic absorption of such territories as may be acquired" ( విదేశీ భూభాగాలను సంపాదించే అధికారం ఇవ్వదు; సంపాదించిన భూభాగాల స్వయంచాలక విలీనాన్ని గుర్తిస్తుంది మాత్రమే ).

selfTest.a: సమాధానం: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." ( భారతదేశం, అంటే భారత్, రాష్ట్రాల యూనియన్‌గా ఉంటుంది. ) ముసాయిదా కమిటీ "యూనియన్" ఎందుకు వాడింది? సమాధానం: సమాఖ్య ఒప్పందం ఫలితం కాదని, ఏ రాష్ట్రమూ విడిపోలేదని చూపడానికి. భారత భూభాగంలోని మూడు భాగాలు ఏవి? సమాధానం: రాష్ట్రాల భూభాగాలు, మొదటి షెడ్యూల్‌లోని కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాలు, తర్వాత సంపాదించిన భూభాగాలు. 1 మే 2026 నాటికి మొదటి షెడ్యూల్‌లో ఎన్ని రాష్ట్రాలు, కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాలు ఉన్నాయి? సమాధానం: 28 రాష్ట్రాలు, 8 కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాలు. అ. 3 కింది ఐదు అధికారాలు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: కొత్త రాష్ట్ర ఏర్పాటు; విస్తీర్ణం పెంపు; తగ్గింపు; సరిహద్దు మార్పు; పేరు మార్పు. అ. 3 నిబంధనలోని రెండు షరతులు ఏవి? సమాధానం: రాష్ట్రపతి సిఫార్సు; నిర్ణీత గడువులో అభిప్రాయం కోసం ప్రభావిత రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభకు రిఫరెన్స్. రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభ అభిప్రాయం కట్టుబడి ఉంటుందా? సమాధానం: లేదు ( బాబూలాల్ పరాటే ; In re Article 370 ). అ. 3 చట్టానికి ప్రత్యేక మెజారిటీ కావాలా? సమాధానం: లేదు; అ. 4(2) ప్రకారం అది అ. 368 ప్రయోజనాలకు సవరణ కాదు. అ. 3 కింది చట్టంతో భారత్ మరో దేశానికి భూభాగం అప్పగించవచ్చా? సమాధానం: లేదు; అ. 368 సవరణ కావాలి ( బెరుబారి ). రాష్ట్ర సరిహద్దుల గురించి వెస్ట్ బెంగాల్ ఏమి చెప్పింది? సమాధానం: "There is no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States." లడఖ్ కేంద్రపాలిత ప్రాంతాన్ని ఏ నిబంధనల కింద సమర్థించారు? సమాధానం: అ. 3(a), వివరణ I తో కలిపి. 400 మంది హాజరై ఓటు వేసిన లోక్‌సభలో అ. 3 బిల్లు ఆమోదానికి ఎన్ని ఓట్లు కావాలి? సమాధానం: సాధారణ మెజారిటీ – 201.
