hi.inOneMinute: Part I (Arts. 1–4) of the Constitution deals with "The Union and its Territory". Art. 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." Ambedkar: the word "Union" was used because the federation is not the result of an agreement among States, so "no State has the right to secede from it". Territory of India (Art. 1(3)) = (a) territories of the States + (b) Union territories in the First Schedule + (c) "such other territories as may be acquired". The First Schedule lists the States and Union territories. As on 1 May 2026 it lists 28 States and 8 Union territories . Art. 2: Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish , new States. Art. 3: Parliament may by law form a new State, increase or diminish the area, alter the boundaries, or alter the name of any State. The Bill needs the President's recommendation , and if it affects a State, it must be referred to that State's Legislature for its views . The views are not binding ( Babulal Parate , as followed in In re Article 370 ). Art. 4(2): such a law is not an amendment of the Constitution for Art. 368, so a simple majority is enough. Cession of Indian territory to a foreign country cannot be done under Art. 3; it needs an amendment under Art. 368 ( Berubari , 1960). There is "no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States" ( State of West Bengal v. Union of India ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 1 – Name and territory of the Union

(1) India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States. (2) The States and the territories thereof shall be as specified in the First Schedule. (3) The territory of India shall comprise— (a) the territories of the States; (b) the Union territories specified in the First Schedule; and (c) such other territories as may be acquired.
(Cl. (2) and sub-cl. (3)(b) were substituted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, w.e.f. 1-11-1956.)
Article 2 – Admission or establishment of new States
Parliament may by law admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
(Art. 2A, "Sikkim to be associated with the Union", inserted by the 35th Amendment, 1974, was omitted by the 36th Amendment, 1975, w.e.f. 26-4-1975.)
Article 3 – Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States

Parliament may by law— (a) form a new State by separation of territory from any State or by uniting two or more States or parts of States or by uniting any territory to a part of any State; (b) increase the area of any State; (c) diminish the area of any State; (d) alter the boundaries of any State; (e) alter the name of any State: Provided that no Bill for the purpose shall be introduced in either House of Parliament except on the recommendation of the President and unless, where the proposal contained in the Bill affects the area, boundaries or name of any of the States, the Bill has been referred by the President to the Legislature of that State for expressing its views thereon within such period as may be specified in the reference or within such further period as the President may allow and the period so specified or allowed has expired. Explanation I.—In this article, in clauses (a) to (e), "State" includes a Union territory, but in the proviso, "State" does not include a Union territory. Explanation II.—The power conferred on Parliament by clause (a) includes the power to form a new State or Union territory by uniting a part of any State or Union territory to any other State or Union territory.
(Proviso substituted by the 5th Amendment, 1955; Explanations I and II inserted by the 18th Amendment, 1966.)
Article 4 – Laws under Arts. 2 and 3

(1) Any law referred to in article 2 or article 3 shall contain such provisions for the amendment of the First Schedule and the Fourth Schedule as may be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the law and may also contain such supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions (including provisions as to representation in Parliament and in the Legislature or Legislatures of the State or States affected by such law) as Parliament may deem necessary. (2) No such law as aforesaid shall be deemed to be an amendment of this Constitution for the purposes of article 368.
In simple words:

India is one Union made of States. States cannot leave. India's territory = States + Union territories + any land India acquires later. Parliament can bring new States into India (Art. 2) and can redraw, merge, split or rename States (Art. 3) by an ordinary law. The State concerned is only asked for its views; Parliament need not follow them. Such a law automatically changes the First Schedule (list of States) and Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats), and it is not treated as a constitutional amendment.
hi.meaning: Union of States : India as one indestructible whole divided into States "for convenience of administration" (Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Territory of India: the area described in Art. 1(3) – States, Union territories and acquired territories. State: a constituent unit listed in Part I of the First Schedule, with its own Governor, Legislature and Government under Part VI. Union territory : a unit listed in Part II of the First Schedule, administered by the President through an Administrator (Art. 239). In re Article 370 : "States are governed by their own governments and are directly accountable to the citizenry whereas Union territories are governed by the Union Government." Cession of territory : transfer of a part of India's territory to a foreign State. Berubari : it "amounts in law to a transfer of sovereignty". Acquired territory (Art. 1(3)(c)): territory that India gets in the exercise of its sovereign rights. Berubari : Art. 1(3)(c) "confers no power to acquire foreign territories but merely recognises automatic absorption of such territories as may be acquired".
keyPoints: Art. 1(1): "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." "Union" – no agreement, no right to secede; "indestructible" (Ambedkar). Art. 1(3): States + UTs + acquired territories. First Schedule (1 May 2026): 28 States, 8 UTs. Art. 2: admit/establish new States (Sikkim, 1975). Art. 3: form, increase, diminish, alter boundaries, alter name. Proviso: President's recommendation + reference for views; views not binding ( Babulal Parate ). Explanation I: proviso not for UTs; Explanation II: new State or UT by uniting parts. Art. 4(2): not an Art. 368 amendment – simple majority. Berubari : cession needs Art. 368. West Bengal : "no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States". In re Article 370 : Ladakh valid under Art. 3(a) + Expl. I; conversion of whole State left open.

caseLaws.facts: In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves , [1960] 3 SCR 250 (8-judge Bench; opinion of 14 March 1960)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Indo-Pakistan Agreement of 10 September 1958 provided for dividing Berubari Union (then i
caseLaws.facts: The President asked the Court under Art. 143(1) whether legislation was needed and of what kind. Principle: The Agreement involved "cession of a part of India's territory". Art. 3 deals with "territorial adjustment inter se of the Constituent States" and is not "wide enough to cover cession of national territory". Hence "the Agreement cannot be implemented by a law relatable to Art. 3 and legislation relatable to Art. 368 would be inevitable." Why it matters: Draws the line between Art. 3 (internal reorganisation) and Art. 368 (giving away Indian territory).
State of West Bengal v. Union of India , AIR 1963 SC 1241; [1964] 1 SCR 371 (6-judge Bench, decided 21 December 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Union proposed to acquire coal-bearing land belonging to West Bengal under the Coal Beari
caseLaws.facts: The State claimed that, being sovereign, its property could not be acquired. Principle: Sinha C.J.: "There is no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States"; Parliament can "diminish its area so as even to destroy a State"; a Parliament competent to destroy a State can also acquire its property. The suit was dismissed. Why it matters: Shows that Arts. 2 and 3 make States subject to Parliament's power, a key reason Indian States are not sovereign.
Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay , AIR 1960 SC 51 (5-judge Bench) – as summarised and quoted in In re Article 370

caseLaws.name: Facts: The States Reorganisation Bill, 1956 first proposed three units (Bombay as a UT, Maharashtra,
caseLaws.facts: After a Joint Select Committee, it was changed to one composite State of Bombay and passed. A petitioner argued that the Bombay Legislature had no chance to give views on the changed proposal. Principle: "Nor is there anything in the proviso to indicate that Parliament must accept or act upon the views of the State Legislature"; a fresh reference for every amendment "might result in an interminable process". The views are only recommendatory. Why it matters: Leading rule on the nature of the proviso to Art. 3.
In re Article 370 of the Constitution , [2023] 16 SCR 1; 2023 INSC 1058 (5-judge Bench, decided 11 December 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Article 370 was made inoperative by Constitutional Orders 272 and 273, and the Jammu and Kash
caseLaws.facts: 356 and Parliament gave the "views" in place of the State Legislature. Principle: Chandrachud C.J. (for himself, Gavai and Surya Kant JJ.): the views under the first proviso to Art. 3 "are recommendatory"; Parliament's exercise of the power under the Proclamation was valid and not mala fide ; the carving out of Ladakh is valid under "Article 3(a) read with Explanation I"; whether a whole State can be converted into UTs "is left open". Elections were directed by 30 September 2024, and statehood restored "at the earliest". Why it matters: Latest Constitution Bench ruling on the scope of Art. 3 and the place of States and Union territories in the federal structure.

selfTest.q: What does Art. 1(1) say?
selfTest.a: Answer: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." Why did the Drafting Committee use "Union"? Answer: To show the federation was not the result of an agreement and no State can secede. What are the three parts of the territory of India? Answer: Territories of the States, Union territories in the First Schedule, and territories acquired later. How many States and Union territories are in the First Schedule as on 1 May 2026? Answer: 28 States and 8 Union territories. Give the five powers under Art. 3. Answer: Form a new State; increase area; diminish area; alter boundaries; alter name. What are the two conditions in the proviso to Art. 3? Answer: President's recommendation; reference to the affected State Legislature for its views within the time fixed. Are the State Legislature's views binding? Answer: No ( Babulal Parate ; In re Article 370 ). Does an Art. 3 law need a special majority? Answer: No; Art. 4(2) says it is not an amendment for Art. 368. Can India cede territory to another country by a law under Art. 3? Answer: No; an Art. 368 amendment is needed ( Berubari ). What did West Bengal say about State boundaries? Answer: "There is no constitutional guarantee against alteration of the boundaries of the States." Under which provisions was the UT of Ladakh upheld? Answer: Art. 3(a) read with Explanation I. In a Lok Sabha sitting with 400 members present and voting, how many votes pass an Art. 3 Bill? Answer: A simple majority – 201.

constitutional-law-i-u2-t4.subtitle: Articles 5 to 11 at the start of the Constitution, the Citizenship Act, 1955 and the rights that depend on citizenship

en.inOneMinute: Citizenship is full legal membership of the State. Some rights in the Constitution belong only to citizens (e.g. Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30, voting under Art. 326, and the offices of President, Judge and MP/MLA). India has single citizenship : "There is only one citizenship for the whole of India. It is Indian citizenship. There is no State citizenship" (Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Part II (Arts. 5–11) only decides who was a citizen at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950): Art. 5: persons with domicile in India who were born in India, or whose parent was born in India, or who lived in India for 5 years before 26 Jan 1950. Art. 6: migrants from Pakistan (before 19 July 1948 – automatic if resident since; on or after – registration). Art. 7: migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 are not citizens, unless they returned under a resettlement permit. Art. 8: persons of Indian origin living abroad – by registration with Indian diplomatic or consular representative. Art. 9: voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship – no citizenship under Arts. 5, 6, 8. Art. 10: citizenship continues, subject to Parliament's law. Art. 11: Parliament may make any law on acquisition, termination and all other matters of citizenship. Under Art. 11, Parliament made the Citizenship Act, 1955 . It provides five ways to acquire citizenship (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation , incorporation of territory), special provisions (ss. 6A, 6B), the Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder scheme (ss. 7A–7D), and three ways to lose it (renunciation, termination, deprivation – ss. 8, 9, 10). Non-citizens (foreigners) still have rights given to "persons", such as Arts. 14, 20, 21 and 22 ( Chandrima Das ), but not Art. 19 ( Louis De Raedt ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026); Citizenship Act, 1955 (bare Act PDF, as on 15 April 2026).
Article 5 – Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution

At the commencement of this Constitution, every person who has his domicile in the territory of India and— (a) who was born in the territory of India; or (b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; or (c) who has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding such commencement, shall be a citizen of India.
Article 6 – Migrants from Pakistan (summary of text): "Notwithstanding anything in article 5", a person who migrated from the territory now in Pakistan is deemed a citizen if—

(a) he or either parent or any grandparent was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted); and (b)(i) if he migrated before 19 July 1948 , he has been ordinarily resident in India since migration; or (b)(ii) if he migrated on or after 19 July 1948 , he has been registered as a citizen by an officer of the Dominion Government on an application made before the commencement, and "no person shall be so registered unless he has been resident in the territory of India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of his application".

Article 7 – Migrants to Pakistan: "Notwithstanding anything in articles 5 and 6, a person who has after the first day of March, 1947, migrated from the territory of India to the territory now included in Pakistan shall not be deemed to be a citizen of India". Proviso: this does not apply to a person who returned "under a permit for resettlement or permanent return"; such a person is treated as having migrated to India after 19 July 1948 (so Art. 6(b)(ii) applies).

Article 8 – Persons of Indian origin residing outside India: a person who, or either of whose parents or any of whose grandparents, was born in India (as defined in the 1935 Act), and who ordinarily resides outside India, is deemed a citizen "if he has been registered as a citizen of India by the diplomatic or consular representative of India in the country where he is for the time being residing".

Article 9: "No person shall be a citizen of India by virtue of article 5, or be deemed to be a citizen of India by virtue of article 6 or article 8, if he has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign State."

Article 10: "Every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen of India under any of the foregoing provisions of this Part shall, subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament, continue to be such citizen."

Article 11: "Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship."
Article 394: Arts. 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 (with some others) "shall come into force at once", i.e. on 26 November 1949.
In simple words:

On 26 January 1950, the Constitution itself decided who were India's first citizens. After that, Parliament makes the rules on how people become, or stop being, citizens – mainly through the Citizenship Act, 1955.
en.meaning: Citizenship : the legal status of being a full member of the Indian State, with rights (some given only to citizens) and duties (e.g. Art. 51A applies to "every citizen of India"). Single citizenship: one Indian citizenship for the whole country; no separate State citizenship (Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Domicile : the place a person treats as his permanent home. Louis De Raedt : "for acquisition of a domicile of choice one of the necessary conditions is the intention to remain there permanently". Domicile of origin is received at birth; it is "retained and cannot be divested until the acquisition of the domicile of choice". Alien / foreigner: a person who is not a citizen of India. "Person" in the Citizenship Act: s. 2(1)(f) – "'person' does not include any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not". Illegal migrant: s. 2(1)(b) – a foreigner who entered India without a valid passport or travel documents, or with them but "remains therein beyond the permitted period of time" (subject to the proviso added in 2019). Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder: a person registered as such by the Central Government under s. 7A (s. 2(1)(ee)). An OCI Cardholder is not a citizen of India.
keyPoints: Single citizenship; no State citizenship (Ambedkar). Arts. 5–9 in force on 26 Nov 1949 (Art. 394); deal only with the commencement. Art. 5: domicile + (born / parent born / 5 years). Art. 6: 19 July 1948 dividing date; 6 months' residence for registration. Art. 7: 1 March 1947; resettlement permit exception. Art. 8: Indians abroad – registration. Art. 11: Parliament's full power → Citizenship Act, 1955. Acquisition: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation. Naturalisation: 12 months + 11 of 14 years (5 years for the s. 2(1)(b) proviso class). Loss: renunciation (s. 8), termination (s. 9), deprivation (s. 10). OCI is not citizenship (s. 7B(2)). Louis De Raedt : domicile needs intention; foreigners have Art. 21, not Art. 19(1)(e). Chandrima Das : Art. 21 protects non-citizens.

caseLaws.facts: Louis De Raedt v. Union of India , (1991) 3 SCC 554; AIR 1991 SC 1886; [1991] 3 SCR 149 (2-judge Bench: L. M. Sharma and J. S. Verma JJ., decided 24 July 1991)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Foreign Christian missionaries had lived in India since before Independence on foreign passpo
caseLaws.facts: In 1987 they were ordered to leave India. They claimed citizenship under Art. 5(c) because they had lived in India for more than five years before 26 January 1950. Principle: Art. 5 requires domicile; a domicile of choice needs "animus manendi" (intention to stay permanently). "Residence alone, unaccompanied by this state of mind, is insufficient." The burden of proof is on the claimant. A foreigner's fundamental right "is confined to Article 21 for life and liberty and does not include the right to reside and settle in this country". The Government's power to expel foreigners "is absolute and unlimited" (relying on Hans Muller of Nurenburg ). The writ petitions were dismissed. Why it matters: Leading case on domicile under Art. 5 and the rights of foreigners.
Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das , (2000) 2 SCC 465; AIR 2000 SC 988 (2-judge Bench: R. P. Sethi and S. Saghir Ahmad JJ., decided 28 January 2000)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Hanuffa Khatoon, a Bangladeshi national, was gang-raped by persons including railway employee
caseLaws.facts: The Calcutta High Court awarded compensation; the Railways appealed, arguing in part that she was a foreign national. Principle: Arts. 15, 16 and 19 are only for citizens, but Art. 21 "will be available not only to every citizen of this country, but also to a 'person' who may not be a citizen of the country". "Just as the State is under an obligation to protect the life of every citizen in this country, so also the State is under an obligation to protect the life of the persons who are not citizens." The appeal was dismissed and the compensation was to be paid through the High Commissioner for Bangladesh. Why it matters: Shows the difference between citizen-only rights and rights of all persons.
State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer , AIR 1963 SC 1811; (1964) 4 SCR 99 – as summarised in Chandrima Das

caseLaws.name: Facts: (Not set out in the source used
caseLaws.facts: ) The question was whether a corporation could claim Art. 19 rights as a "citizen". Principle: The word "citizen" in Art. 19 "has not been used in a sense different from that in which it has been used in Part II of the Constitution dealing with 'citizenship'"; "the words 'all citizens' have been deliberately used to keep out all 'non-citizens' which would include 'aliens'". Why it matters: Corporations are not citizens and cannot claim citizen-only rights.

selfTest.q: What did Ambedkar say about State citizenship?
selfTest.a: Answer: "There is no State citizenship." India has one citizenship. Name the two conditions under Art. 5. Answer: Domicile in India, and one of: born in India; a parent born in India; 5 years' ordinary residence before 26 Jan 1950. What is the significance of 19 July 1948? Answer: The permit system began; migrants from Pakistan before it became citizens by residence, after it only by registration. Who is excluded by Art. 7? Answer: Persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947, unless they returned under a resettlement or permanent-return permit. Which Article gives Parliament power over citizenship? Answer: Art. 11. Name the five modes of acquisition under the 1955 Act. Answer: Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory. A child is born in India in 2010; father is Indian, mother an illegal migrant. Citizen by birth? Answer: No – after 3-12-2004, both parents must be citizens, or one a citizen and the other not an illegal migrant (s. 3(1)(c)). What residence is needed for naturalisation? Answer: Throughout the 12 months before applying, and at least 11 years in the 14 years before that. Name the three modes of loss. Answer: Renunciation (s. 8), termination (s. 9), deprivation (s. 10). Can an OCI Cardholder vote? Answer: No (s. 7B(2)(f)). Does a foreigner have the right to reside and settle in India? Answer: No; Art. 19(1)(e) is only for citizens ( Louis De Raedt ). Is a company a citizen? Answer: No ( State Trading Corporation ; s. 2(1)(f)).

Mode Section How
Renunciation s. 8 A citizen of full age and capacity makes a declaration; on registration he ceases to be a citizen. During war, registration may be withheld. Minor children also cease, but may resume within one year after full age.
Termination s. 9 A citizen who "voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country" ceases to be a citizen (subject to a war-time exception). Questions on when or how foreign citizenship was acquired are decided by the prescribed authority (s. 9(2)).
Deprivation s. 10 Central Government's order against a citizen by naturalisation, by Art. 5(c) only, or by registration (with exceptions). Grounds: fraud; disloyalty or disaffection to the Constitution; trading with the enemy in war; sentence of 2+ years within 5 years of registration or naturalisation; 7 years' continuous residence abroad without annual registration (with exceptions). Only if continued citizenship is "not conducive to the public good"; notice and a Committee of Inquiry (chairman with 10 years' judicial office).

te.inOneMinute: పౌరసత్వం అంటే రాజ్యంలో పూర్తి చట్టపరమైన సభ్యత్వం. రాజ్యాంగంలోని కొన్ని హక్కులు పౌరులకు మాత్రమే (ఉదా. అ. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30, అ. 326 కింద ఓటు, రాష్ట్రపతి, న్యాయమూర్తి, MP/MLA పదవులు). భారతదేశంలో ఏక పౌరసత్వం : "There is only one citizenship for the whole of India. It is Indian citizenship. There is no State citizenship" (అంబేడ్కర్, 4 నవంబర్ 1948). ( అర్థం: దేశమంతటికీ ఒకే పౌరసత్వం – భారత పౌరసత్వం. రాష్ట్ర పౌరసత్వం లేదు.) భాగం II (అ. 5–11) రాజ్యాంగం ప్రారంభమైన రోజున (26 జనవరి 1950) ఎవరు పౌరులో మాత్రమే నిర్ణయిస్తుంది: అ. 5: భారతదేశంలో నివాసస్థానం (domicile) ఉండి, భారతదేశంలో పుట్టినవారు, లేదా తల్లిదండ్రుల్లో ఒకరు ఇక్కడ పుట్టినవారు, లేదా 26 జనవరి 1950కి ముందు 5 ఏళ్లు ఇక్కడ నివసించినవారు. అ. 6: పాకిస్తాన్ నుండి వలస వచ్చినవారు (19 జులై 1948కి ముందు – అప్పటి నుండి నివాసం ఉంటే స్వయంచాలకంగా; ఆ రోజు లేదా తర్వాత – నమోదు ద్వారా). అ. 7: 1 మార్చి 1947 తర్వాత పాకిస్తాన్‌కు వలస వెళ్లినవారు పౌరులు కారు – పునరావాస అనుమతి (permit)తో తిరిగి వస్తే తప్ప. అ. 8: విదేశాల్లో నివసించే భారత సంతతి వారు – భారత దౌత్య/కాన్సులర్ ప్రతినిధి వద్ద నమోదు ద్వారా. అ. 9: స్వచ్ఛందంగా విదేశీ పౌరసత్వం తీసుకుంటే – అ. 5, 6, 8 కింద పౌరసత్వం లేదు. అ. 10: పౌరసత్వం కొనసాగుతుంది, పార్లమెంటు చట్టానికి లోబడి. అ. 11: పౌరసత్వం పొందడం, ముగియడం, మిగతా అన్ని విషయాలపై పార్లమెంటు ఏ చట్టమైనా చేయవచ్చు. అ. 11 కింద పార్లమెంటు పౌరసత్వ చట్టం, 1955 చేసింది. ఇందులో పౌరసత్వం పొందే ఐదు మార్గాలు (జన్మ, వంశం, నమోదు, సహజీకరణ, భూభాగ విలీనం), ప్రత్యేక నిబంధనలు (సె. 6A, 6B), ఓవర్సీస్ సిటిజన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా కార్డుదారు పథకం (సె. 7A–7D), పౌరసత్వం కోల్పోయే మూడు మార్గాలు (పరిత్యాగం, ముగింపు, హరణ – సె. 8, 9, 10) ఉన్నాయి. పౌరులు కానివారికి (విదేశీయులకు) కూడా "వ్యక్తుల"కు ఇచ్చిన హక్కులు ఉంటాయి – అ. 14, 20, 21, 22 ( చంద్రిమా దాస్ ), కానీ అ. 19 కాదు ( లూయిస్ డి రేడ్ట్ ).
te.meaning: పౌరసత్వం : భారత రాజ్యంలో పూర్తి సభ్యుడిగా ఉండే చట్టపరమైన హోదా; హక్కులు (కొన్ని పౌరులకు మాత్రమే) మరియు విధులు (ఉదా. అ. 51A "every citizen of India"కు వర్తిస్తుంది). ఏక పౌరసత్వం: దేశమంతటికీ ఒకే భారత పౌరసత్వం; వేరే రాష్ట్ర పౌరసత్వం లేదు (అంబేడ్కర్, 4 నవంబర్ 1948). నివాసస్థానం (domicile) : వ్యక్తి తన శాశ్వత ఇల్లుగా భావించే ప్రదేశం. లూయిస్ డి రేడ్ట్ : "for acquisition of a domicile of choice one of the necessary conditions is the intention to remain there permanently" ( అర్థం: ఎంచుకున్న నివాసస్థానం పొందడానికి అవసరమైన షరతుల్లో ఒకటి అక్కడ శాశ్వతంగా ఉండాలనే ఉద్దేశం). జన్మ నివాసస్థానం (domicile of origin) పుట్టుకతో వస్తుంది; అది ఎంచుకున్న నివాసస్థానం పొందే వరకు "retained and cannot be divested" ( అర్థం: కొనసాగుతుంది, తొలగించబడదు). విదేశీయుడు (alien / foreigner): భారత పౌరుడు కాని వ్యక్తి. పౌరసత్వ చట్టంలో "వ్యక్తి": సె. 2(1)(f) – "'person' does not include any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not" ( అర్థం: 'వ్యక్తి'లో ఏ కంపెనీ, సంఘం లేదా వ్యక్తుల సమూహం – నమోదైనా కాకపోయినా – చేరదు). అక్రమ వలసదారు (illegal migrant): సె. 2(1)(b) – చెల్లుబాటు అయ్యే పాస్‌పోర్ట్ లేదా ప్రయాణ పత్రాలు లేకుండా భారతదేశంలోకి వచ్చిన విదేశీయుడు, లేదా అవి ఉండి "remains therein beyond the permitted period of time" ( అర్థం: అనుమతించిన కాలం దాటి ఇక్కడే ఉండిపోయినవాడు) (2019లో చేర్చిన నిబంధనకు లోబడి). ఓవర్సీస్ సిటిజన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా కార్డుదారు: సె. 7A కింద కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం అలా నమోదు చేసిన వ్యక్తి (సె. 2(1)(ee)). OCI కార్డుదారు భారత పౌరుడు కాడు .
keyPoints: ఏక పౌరసత్వం; రాష్ట్ర పౌరసత్వం లేదు (అంబేడ్కర్). అ. 5–9 26 నవంబర్ 1949న అమల్లోకి (అ. 394); ప్రారంభానికి మాత్రమే సంబంధించినవి. అ. 5: నివాసస్థానం + (జన్మ / తల్లిదండ్రుల జన్మ / 5 ఏళ్లు). అ. 6: 19 జులై 1948 విభజన తేదీ; నమోదుకు 6 నెలల నివాసం. అ. 7: 1 మార్చి 1947; పునరావాస అనుమతి మినహాయింపు. అ. 8: విదేశాల్లోని భారతీయులు – నమోదు. అ. 11: పార్లమెంటుకు పూర్తి అధికారం → పౌరసత్వ చట్టం, 1955. పొందడం: జన్మ, వంశం, నమోదు, సహజీకరణ, విలీనం. సహజీకరణ: 12 నెలలు + 14లో 11 ఏళ్లు (సె. 2(1)(b) నిబంధన వర్గానికి 5 ఏళ్లు). కోల్పోవడం: పరిత్యాగం (సె. 8), ముగింపు (సె. 9), హరణ (సె. 10). OCI పౌరసత్వం కాదు (సె. 7B(2)). లూయిస్ డి రేడ్ట్ : నివాసస్థానానికి ఉద్దేశం కావాలి; విదేశీయులకు అ. 21 ఉంది, అ. 19(1)(e) లేదు. చంద్రిమా దాస్ : అ. 21 పౌరులు కానివారినీ రక్షిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: రాష్ట్ర పౌరసత్వం గురించి అంబేడ్కర్ ఏమన్నారు?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: "There is no State citizenship." ( అర్థం: రాష్ట్ర పౌరసత్వం లేదు.) భారతదేశానికి ఒకే పౌరసత్వం. అ. 5 కింద రెండు షరతులు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: భారతదేశంలో నివాసస్థానం; మరియు వీటిలో ఒకటి: భారతదేశంలో జన్మ; తల్లిదండ్రుల్లో ఒకరి జన్మ భారతదేశంలో; 26 జనవరి 1950కి ముందు 5 ఏళ్ల సాధారణ నివాసం. 19 జులై 1948 ప్రాముఖ్యం ఏమిటి? జవాబు: అనుమతి వ్యవస్థ మొదలైంది; అంతకు ముందు పాకిస్తాన్ నుండి వచ్చినవారు నివాసం ద్వారా, తర్వాత వచ్చినవారు నమోదు ద్వారా మాత్రమే పౌరులయ్యారు. అ. 7 ఎవరిని మినహాయిస్తుంది? జవాబు: 1 మార్చి 1947 తర్వాత పాకిస్తాన్‌కు వలస వెళ్లినవారిని – పునరావాస లేదా శాశ్వతంగా తిరిగి రావడానికి అనుమతితో తిరిగి వస్తే తప్ప. పౌరసత్వంపై పార్లమెంటుకు అధికారం ఇచ్చే అనుచ్ఛేదం ఏది? జవాబు: అ. 11. 1955 చట్టం కింద పౌరసత్వం పొందే ఐదు మార్గాలు? జవాబు: జన్మ, వంశం, నమోదు, సహజీకరణ, భూభాగ విలీనం. 2010లో భారతదేశంలో ఒక బిడ్డ పుట్టింది; తండ్రి భారతీయుడు, తల్లి అక్రమ వలసదారు. జన్మతః పౌరుడా? జవాబు: కాదు – 3-12-2004 తర్వాత తల్లిదండ్రులు ఇద్దరూ పౌరులు కావాలి, లేదా ఒకరు పౌరుడు, మరొకరు అక్రమ వలసదారు కాకూడదు (సె. 3(1)(c)). సహజీకరణకు ఎంత నివాసం కావాలి? జవాబు: దరఖాస్తుకు ముందు 12 నెలలు నిరంతరం, దానికి ముందు 14 ఏళ్లలో కనీసం 11 ఏళ్లు. కోల్పోయే మూడు మార్గాలు? జవాబు: పరిత్యాగం (సె. 8), ముగింపు (సె. 9), హరణ (సె. 10). OCI కార్డుదారు ఓటు వేయగలడా? జవాబు: లేదు (సె. 7B(2)(f)). విదేశీయుడికి భారతదేశంలో నివసించే, స్థిరపడే హక్కు ఉందా? జవాబు: లేదు; అ. 19(1)(e) పౌరులకు మాత్రమే ( లూయిస్ డి రేడ్ట్ ). కంపెనీ పౌరుడా? జవాబు: కాదు ( స్టేట్ ట్రేడింగ్ కార్పొరేషన్ ; సె. 2(1)(f)).

OCI కార్డుదారు పౌరుడు (ద్వంద్వ పౌరసత్వం) OCI కార్డుదారులు నోటిఫై చేసిన హక్కులున్న విదేశీ పౌరులు; అ. 16, ఓటు, పదవుల హక్కులు లేవు (సె. 7B(2)).
ముగింపు (సె. 9) హరణ (సె. 10) విదేశీ పౌరసత్వం స్వచ్ఛందంగా తీసుకుంటే ముగింపు స్వయంచాలకం; హరణ కారణాలపై ప్రభుత్వ ఉత్తర్వుతో.

hi.inOneMinute: Citizenship is full legal membership of the State. Some rights in the Constitution belong only to citizens (e.g. Arts. 15, 16, 19, 29, 30, voting under Art. 326, and the offices of President, Judge and MP/MLA). India has single citizenship : "There is only one citizenship for the whole of India. It is Indian citizenship. There is no State citizenship" (Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Part II (Arts. 5–11) only decides who was a citizen at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950): Art. 5: persons with domicile in India who were born in India, or whose parent was born in India, or who lived in India for 5 years before 26 Jan 1950. Art. 6: migrants from Pakistan (before 19 July 1948 – automatic if resident since; on or after – registration). Art. 7: migrants to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 are not citizens, unless they returned under a resettlement permit. Art. 8: persons of Indian origin living abroad – by registration with Indian diplomatic or consular representative. Art. 9: voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship – no citizenship under Arts. 5, 6, 8. Art. 10: citizenship continues, subject to Parliament's law. Art. 11: Parliament may make any law on acquisition, termination and all other matters of citizenship. Under Art. 11, Parliament made the Citizenship Act, 1955 . It provides five ways to acquire citizenship (birth, descent, registration, naturalisation , incorporation of territory), special provisions (ss. 6A, 6B), the Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder scheme (ss. 7A–7D), and three ways to lose it (renunciation, termination, deprivation – ss. 8, 9, 10). Non-citizens (foreigners) still have rights given to "persons", such as Arts. 14, 20, 21 and 22 ( Chandrima Das ), but not Art. 19 ( Louis De Raedt ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026); Citizenship Act, 1955 (bare Act PDF, as on 15 April 2026).
Article 5 – Citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution

At the commencement of this Constitution, every person who has his domicile in the territory of India and— (a) who was born in the territory of India; or (b) either of whose parents was born in the territory of India; or (c) who has been ordinarily resident in the territory of India for not less than five years immediately preceding such commencement, shall be a citizen of India.
Article 6 – Migrants from Pakistan (summary of text): "Notwithstanding anything in article 5", a person who migrated from the territory now in Pakistan is deemed a citizen if—

(a) he or either parent or any grandparent was born in India as defined in the Government of India Act, 1935 (as originally enacted); and (b)(i) if he migrated before 19 July 1948 , he has been ordinarily resident in India since migration; or (b)(ii) if he migrated on or after 19 July 1948 , he has been registered as a citizen by an officer of the Dominion Government on an application made before the commencement, and "no person shall be so registered unless he has been resident in the territory of India for at least six months immediately preceding the date of his application".

Article 7 – Migrants to Pakistan: "Notwithstanding anything in articles 5 and 6, a person who has after the first day of March, 1947, migrated from the territory of India to the territory now included in Pakistan shall not be deemed to be a citizen of India". Proviso: this does not apply to a person who returned "under a permit for resettlement or permanent return"; such a person is treated as having migrated to India after 19 July 1948 (so Art. 6(b)(ii) applies).

Article 8 – Persons of Indian origin residing outside India: a person who, or either of whose parents or any of whose grandparents, was born in India (as defined in the 1935 Act), and who ordinarily resides outside India, is deemed a citizen "if he has been registered as a citizen of India by the diplomatic or consular representative of India in the country where he is for the time being residing".

Article 9: "No person shall be a citizen of India by virtue of article 5, or be deemed to be a citizen of India by virtue of article 6 or article 8, if he has voluntarily acquired the citizenship of any foreign State."

Article 10: "Every person who is or is deemed to be a citizen of India under any of the foregoing provisions of this Part shall, subject to the provisions of any law that may be made by Parliament, continue to be such citizen."

Article 11: "Nothing in the foregoing provisions of this Part shall derogate from the power of Parliament to make any provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship."
Article 394: Arts. 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 (with some others) "shall come into force at once", i.e. on 26 November 1949.
In simple words:

On 26 January 1950, the Constitution itself decided who were India's first citizens. After that, Parliament makes the rules on how people become, or stop being, citizens – mainly through the Citizenship Act, 1955.
hi.meaning: Citizenship : the legal status of being a full member of the Indian State, with rights (some given only to citizens) and duties (e.g. Art. 51A applies to "every citizen of India"). Single citizenship: one Indian citizenship for the whole country; no separate State citizenship (Ambedkar, 4 Nov 1948). Domicile : the place a person treats as his permanent home. Louis De Raedt : "for acquisition of a domicile of choice one of the necessary conditions is the intention to remain there permanently". Domicile of origin is received at birth; it is "retained and cannot be divested until the acquisition of the domicile of choice". Alien / foreigner: a person who is not a citizen of India. "Person" in the Citizenship Act: s. 2(1)(f) – "'person' does not include any company or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not". Illegal migrant: s. 2(1)(b) – a foreigner who entered India without a valid passport or travel documents, or with them but "remains therein beyond the permitted period of time" (subject to the proviso added in 2019). Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder: a person registered as such by the Central Government under s. 7A (s. 2(1)(ee)). An OCI Cardholder is not a citizen of India.
keyPoints: Single citizenship; no State citizenship (Ambedkar). Arts. 5–9 in force on 26 Nov 1949 (Art. 394); deal only with the commencement. Art. 5: domicile + (born / parent born / 5 years). Art. 6: 19 July 1948 dividing date; 6 months' residence for registration. Art. 7: 1 March 1947; resettlement permit exception. Art. 8: Indians abroad – registration. Art. 11: Parliament's full power → Citizenship Act, 1955. Acquisition: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation. Naturalisation: 12 months + 11 of 14 years (5 years for the s. 2(1)(b) proviso class). Loss: renunciation (s. 8), termination (s. 9), deprivation (s. 10). OCI is not citizenship (s. 7B(2)). Louis De Raedt : domicile needs intention; foreigners have Art. 21, not Art. 19(1)(e). Chandrima Das : Art. 21 protects non-citizens.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Foreign Christian missionaries had lived in India since before Independence on foreign passpo
caseLaws.facts: In 1987 they were ordered to leave India. They claimed citizenship under Art. 5(c) because they had lived in India for more than five years before 26 January 1950. Principle: Art. 5 requires domicile; a domicile of choice needs "animus manendi" (intention to stay permanently). "Residence alone, unaccompanied by this state of mind, is insufficient." The burden of proof is on the claimant. A foreigner's fundamental right "is confined to Article 21 for life and liberty and does not include the right to reside and settle in this country". The Government's power to expel foreigners "is absolute and unlimited" (relying on Hans Muller of Nurenburg ). The writ petitions were dismissed. Why it matters: Leading case on domicile under Art. 5 and the rights of foreigners.
Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das , (2000) 2 SCC 465; AIR 2000 SC 988 (2-judge Bench: R. P. Sethi and S. Saghir Ahmad JJ., decided 28 January 2000)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Hanuffa Khatoon, a Bangladeshi national, was gang-raped by persons including railway employee
caseLaws.facts: The Calcutta High Court awarded compensation; the Railways appealed, arguing in part that she was a foreign national. Principle: Arts. 15, 16 and 19 are only for citizens, but Art. 21 "will be available not only to every citizen of this country, but also to a 'person' who may not be a citizen of the country". "Just as the State is under an obligation to protect the life of every citizen in this country, so also the State is under an obligation to protect the life of the persons who are not citizens." The appeal was dismissed and the compensation was to be paid through the High Commissioner for Bangladesh. Why it matters: Shows the difference between citizen-only rights and rights of all persons.
State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer , AIR 1963 SC 1811; (1964) 4 SCR 99 – as summarised in Chandrima Das

caseLaws.name: Facts: (Not set out in the source used
caseLaws.facts: ) The question was whether a corporation could claim Art. 19 rights as a "citizen". Principle: The word "citizen" in Art. 19 "has not been used in a sense different from that in which it has been used in Part II of the Constitution dealing with 'citizenship'"; "the words 'all citizens' have been deliberately used to keep out all 'non-citizens' which would include 'aliens'". Why it matters: Corporations are not citizens and cannot claim citizen-only rights.

selfTest.q: What did Ambedkar say about State citizenship?
selfTest.a: Answer: "There is no State citizenship." India has one citizenship. Name the two conditions under Art. 5. Answer: Domicile in India, and one of: born in India; a parent born in India; 5 years' ordinary residence before 26 Jan 1950. What is the significance of 19 July 1948? Answer: The permit system began; migrants from Pakistan before it became citizens by residence, after it only by registration. Who is excluded by Art. 7? Answer: Persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947, unless they returned under a resettlement or permanent-return permit. Which Article gives Parliament power over citizenship? Answer: Art. 11. Name the five modes of acquisition under the 1955 Act. Answer: Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory. A child is born in India in 2010; father is Indian, mother an illegal migrant. Citizen by birth? Answer: No – after 3-12-2004, both parents must be citizens, or one a citizen and the other not an illegal migrant (s. 3(1)(c)). What residence is needed for naturalisation? Answer: Throughout the 12 months before applying, and at least 11 years in the 14 years before that. Name the three modes of loss. Answer: Renunciation (s. 8), termination (s. 9), deprivation (s. 10). Can an OCI Cardholder vote? Answer: No (s. 7B(2)(f)). Does a foreigner have the right to reside and settle in India? Answer: No; Art. 19(1)(e) is only for citizens ( Louis De Raedt ). Is a company a citizen? Answer: No ( State Trading Corporation ; s. 2(1)(f)).

Renunciation s. 8 A citizen of full age and capacity makes a declaration; on registration he ceases to be a citizen. During war, registration may be withheld. Minor children also cease, but may resume within one year after full age.
Termination s. 9 A citizen who "voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country" ceases to be a citizen (subject to a war-time exception). Questions on when or how foreign citizenship was acquired are decided by the prescribed authority (s. 9(2)).
Deprivation s. 10 Central Government's order against a citizen by naturalisation, by Art. 5(c) only, or by registration (with exceptions). Which Article of the Constitution declares that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void?

Explanation. Article 13 declares that any law inconsistent with Part III is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

The "doctrine of eclipse" applies to:

Explanation. The doctrine of eclipse applies only to pre-Constitution laws under Article 13(1) — such a law is dormant, not void, and can revive.

In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court held that "procedure established by law" under Article 21 must be:

Explanation. Maneka Gandhi held that the procedure under Article 21 must itself be fair, just, and reasonable, not arbitrary or oppressive.

Which case established that Fundamental Rights cannot be waived by an individual, even voluntarily?

en.inOneMinute: The Preamble is the opening statement of the Constitution. It answers four questions: Who gave the Constitution? "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA" – the source of authority is the people ( popular sovereignty ). What kind of State? A "SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC". What are its aims? JUSTICE (social, economic, political); LIBERTY (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship); EQUALITY (of status and of opportunity); FRATERNITY (assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation). When was it adopted? "this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949". The words "SOCIALIST SECULAR" and "and integrity" were added by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 (from 3 January 1977). This is the only amendment of the Preamble so far. The Constituent Assembly took up the Preamble last , on 17 October 1949, and adopted the motion "That the Preamble stand part of the Constitution". Is it part of the Constitution? Berubari (1960): a "key to open the mind of the makers", but "not a part of the Constitution". Kesavananda Bharati (1973): it is a part of the Constitution. It can be amended under Art. 368, but not so as to destroy the basic structure. Use in court: it is not a source of power or of prohibitions. It helps to interpret an Article when the words are ambiguous, and it shows the basic structure .
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

PREAMBLE WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a [SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC] and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the [unity and integrity of the Nation]; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
Footnotes in the bare Act:

"SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC" was substituted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 2, for "SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC" (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). "unity and integrity of the Nation" was substituted by s. 2, ibid., for "unity of the Nation" (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).
Articles that carry out the Preamble's promises (examples):

Art. 38(1): "The State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life." Art. 51A(e): the duty of every citizen "to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities". Art. 326: elections "on the basis of adult suffrage". Arts. 14–18 (equality), 19 and 25 (liberty), 25–28 (secularism).
In simple words:

The people of India made this Constitution and gave it to themselves. India is free to decide its own affairs (sovereign), aims at a fair sharing of wealth (socialist), treats all religions equally (secular), is ruled by elected representatives (democratic) and has an elected head (republic). The State must try to give every citizen justice, freedom, equality and a feeling of brotherhood.
en.meaning: Preamble : the introductory statement placed before the Articles. It states the source, the nature of the State, the objectives, and the date of adoption. Key to the mind of the makers: Berubari , quoting Story: the Preamble is "a key to open the mind of the makers" which "may show the general purposes for which they made the several provisions in the Constitution". Popular sovereignty: the final authority belongs to the people. Ambedkar (17 Oct 1949): the Preamble shows "that this Constitution should have its root, its authority, its sovereignty, from the people. That it has." Part of the Constitution? Khanna J. ( Kesavananda , para 1524): "I am unable to accept the contention that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution."
keyPoints: Text: "SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC"; JUSTICE, LIBERTY, EQUALITY, FRATERNITY. 42nd Amendment, 1976 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977): "SOCIALIST SECULAR" and "integrity" added – the only amendment. Adopted last: 17 Oct 1949; "God" amendment lost 41 to 68. Ambedkar: sovereignty "from the people"; three parts – declaratory, descriptive, objective. Berubari : key to the mind; not part; not a source of power. Kesavananda : part of the Constitution; amendable except basic structure. Bommai : integral part; secularism implicit before 1976. Randhir Singh : "socialist" must mean at least equal pay for equal work. Ambedkar's trinity: liberty, equality, fraternity cannot be divorced. Use: interpretation of ambiguous words; guide to basic features.

caseLaws.facts: The President referred to the Court under Art. 143(1) how the Agreement could be carried out. It was argued that the Preamble made India's territory untouchable. Principle: The Preamble is "a key to open the mind of the makers", "but nevertheless the preamble is not a part of the Constitution"; it is not "the source of any substantive power", and "What is true about the powers is equally true about the prohibitions and limitations." It may help only if an Article is "ambiguous or ... capable of two meanings". The Agreement "cannot be implemented by a law relatable to Art. 3 and legislation relatable to Art. 368 would be inevitable." Why it matters: First major ruling on the Preamble's legal status; its "not a part" view was later rejected, but the rule that the Preamble is not a source of power still stands.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to Kerala land reform laws and to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments; the scope of
caseLaws.facts: 368 was in question. Principle: The Preamble is part of the Constitution: "It was expressly voted to be a part of the Constitution" (Sikri C.J., para 105); Khanna J. (para 1524) relied on the motion "the Preamble stands part of the Constitution". It can be amended, but not its basic-structure part (Khanna J., para 1526 and conclusion (x)). It shows the basic features: "one has only to look to the preamble" (Hegde and Mukherjea JJ., para 700). Why it matters: Settled the Preamble's status and linked it to the basic-structure limit on amendment.
Randhir Singh v. Union of India , AIR 1982 SC 879; (1982) 1 SCC 618 (3-judge Bench, decided 22 February 1982)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A driver-constable in the Delhi Police got a lower pay scale than drivers doing the same work
caseLaws.facts: He filed a writ petition under Art. 32. Principle: Chinnappa Reddy J.: "the word 'Socialist' must mean something. Even if it does not mean 'To each according to his need', it must atleast mean 'equal pay for equal work'." Reading Arts. 14 and 16 "in the light of the Preamble and Art.39(d)", the principle of equal pay for equal work was applied. The petition was allowed. Why it matters: Shows how the word "socialist" in the Preamble is used to interpret Fundamental Rights .
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to proclamations under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing several State Governments; one question was whether "secularism" could be a ground. Principle: Jeevan Reddy J.: the view that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution "is no longer extent [extant]"; the words "the provisions of this Constitution" in Art. 356 "take in all the provisions including the Preamble"; "the 42nd Amendment merely made explicit what was implicit". Headnote: "The preamble of the Constitution is an integral part of the Constitution." Why it matters: Confirms the Preamble's status and that secularism , stated in it, is a basic feature.
LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre , [1995] Supp. 1 SCR 349 (2-judge Bench, decided 10 May 1995)

caseLaws.name: Facts: LIC offered a cheap term policy only to persons employed in government, quasi-government or r
caseLaws.facts: This was challenged as arbitrary . Principle: K. Ramaswamy J.: "The Preamble, the arch of the Constitution, assures socio-economic justice to all the Indian citizen in matters of equality of status and of opportunity with assurance to dignity of the individual"; "the touchstone of the Directive Principles of the State policy in the light of the Preamble provides yardstick". The restriction was held unconstitutional under Art. 14; LIC's appeals were dismissed. Why it matters: Shows the Preamble being used, with Part IV, to test State action.

selfTest.q: Name the four parts of the Preamble. Answer: Source (We, the people), nature of the State, objectives, date of adoption. Which words were added by the 42nd Amendment?
selfTest.a: Answer: "SOCIALIST", "SECULAR" and "integrity" (in "unity and integrity of the Nation"). On which date did the Assembly adopt the Preamble, and why was it taken up last? Answer: 17 October 1949; so that it would conform to the Constitution already accepted. What happened to Kamath's "In the name of God" amendment? Answer: Negatived by show of hands, 41 for and 68 against. What did Berubari say about the Preamble? Answer: A key to open the mind of the makers, but not a part of the Constitution and not a source of power or limitations. Which case held the Preamble is a part of the Constitution? Answer: Kesavananda Bharati (1973); confirmed in Bommai (1994). Can the Preamble be amended? Answer: Yes, under Art. 368, except the part relating to the basic structure (Khanna J.). Why did Ambedkar oppose adding "socialist" in 1948? Answer: The people should decide their social and economic organisation; and the Directive Principles were already socialistic. What did Randhir Singh say "socialist" must at least mean? Answer: Equal pay for equal work. When can a court use the Preamble to interpret an Article? Answer: Only when the words of the Article are ambiguous or capable of two meanings. Complete Ambedkar's line: "Without equality, liberty would ..." Answer: "... produce the supremacy of the few over the many." Which Article repeats the Preamble's "justice, social, economic and political"? Answer: Art. 38(1).

te.inOneMinute: ప్రవేశిక రాజ్యాంగ ప్రారంభ ప్రకటన. అది నాలుగు ప్రశ్నలకు సమాధానం ఇస్తుంది: రాజ్యాంగం ఎవరు ఇచ్చారు? "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA" ( భారత ప్రజలమైన మేము ) – అధికారానికి మూలం ప్రజలు ( ప్రజా సార్వభౌమాధికారం ). ఎలాంటి రాజ్యం? "SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC" ( సార్వభౌమ సామ్యవాద లౌకిక ప్రజాస్వామ్య గణతంత్రం ). దాని లక్ష్యాలు ఏమిటి? న్యాయం (సామాజిక, ఆర్థిక, రాజకీయ); స్వేచ్ఛ (ఆలోచన, భావ ప్రకటన, నమ్మకం, విశ్వాసం, ఆరాధన); సమానత్వం (హోదా, అవకాశం); సౌభ్రాతృత్వం (వ్యక్తి గౌరవం, దేశ ఐక్యత, సమగ్రతకు హామీ). ఎప్పుడు ఆమోదించారు? "this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949" ( 1949 నవంబర్ ఇరవై ఆరవ తేదీ ). "SOCIALIST SECULAR", "and integrity" పదాలను రాజ్యాంగ (నలభై రెండవ సవరణ) చట్టం, 1976 చేర్చింది (3 జనవరి 1977 నుండి). ఇప్పటివరకు ప్రవేశికకు జరిగిన సవరణ ఇదొక్కటే. రాజ్యాంగ సభ ప్రవేశికను చివరగా , 17 అక్టోబర్ 1949న చేపట్టి, "That the Preamble stand part of the Constitution" ( ప్రవేశిక రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగంగా ఉండాలి ) అనే తీర్మానాన్ని ఆమోదించింది. ఇది రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగమా? బెరుబారి (1960): "key to open the mind of the makers" ( నిర్మాతల మనసును తెరిచే తాళంచెవి ), కానీ "not a part of the Constitution" ( రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగం కాదు ). కేశవానంద భారతి (1973): ఇది రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగమే . అ. 368 కింద సవరించవచ్చు, కానీ మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని నాశనం చేసేలా కాదు. కోర్టులో ఉపయోగం: ఇది అధికారానికి గానీ నిషేధాలకు గానీ మూలం కాదు. అధికరణ పదాలు అస్పష్టంగా ఉన్నప్పుడు వ్యాఖ్యానానికి సహాయపడుతుంది; మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని చూపిస్తుంది.
te.meaning: ప్రవేశిక : అధికరణలకు ముందు ఉండే పరిచయ ప్రకటన. ఇది మూలం, రాజ్య స్వభావం, లక్ష్యాలు, ఆమోద తేదీని తెలుపుతుంది. నిర్మాతల మనసుకు తాళంచెవి: బెరుబారి , స్టోరీని ఉటంకిస్తూ: ప్రవేశిక "a key to open the mind of the makers" ( నిర్మాతల మనసును తెరిచే తాళంచెవి ); అది "may show the general purposes for which they made the several provisions in the Constitution" ( రాజ్యాంగంలోని వివిధ నిబంధనలను ఏ సాధారణ ఉద్దేశాలతో చేశారో చూపవచ్చు ). ప్రజా సార్వభౌమాధికారం: అంతిమ అధికారం ప్రజలదే. అంబేద్కర్ (17 అక్టోబర్ 1949): ప్రవేశిక చూపేది "that this Constitution should have its root, its authority, its sovereignty, from the people. That it has." ( ఈ రాజ్యాంగానికి మూలం, అధికారం, సార్వభౌమత్వం ప్రజల నుండే రావాలి. అదే ఉంది. ) రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగమా? ఖన్నా న్యా. ( కేశవానంద , పేరా 1524): "I am unable to accept the contention that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution." ( ప్రవేశిక రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగం కాదనే వాదనను నేను అంగీకరించలేను. )

selfTest.q: ప్రవేశికలోని నాలుగు భాగాలు చెప్పండి. సమాధానం: మూలం (భారత ప్రజలమైన మేము), రాజ్య స్వభావం, లక్ష్యాలు, ఆమోద తేదీ. 42వ సవరణ ఏ పదాలను చేర్చింది?
selfTest.a: సమాధానం: "SOCIALIST", "SECULAR", "integrity" ("unity and integrity of the Nation" లో). సభ ప్రవేశికను ఏ తేదీన ఆమోదించింది, చివరగా ఎందుకు చేపట్టింది? సమాధానం: 17 అక్టోబర్ 1949; ఇప్పటికే ఆమోదించిన రాజ్యాంగానికి అనుగుణంగా ఉండేందుకు. కామత్ "దేవుని పేరిట" సవరణ ఏమైంది? సమాధానం: చేతులెత్తి ఓటింగ్‌లో 41 అనుకూలం, 68 వ్యతిరేకంతో తిరస్కరించబడింది. బెరుబారి ప్రవేశిక గురించి ఏమి చెప్పింది? సమాధానం: నిర్మాతల మనసును తెరిచే తాళంచెవి, కానీ రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగం కాదు; అధికారానికి గానీ పరిమితులకు గానీ మూలం కాదు. ప్రవేశిక రాజ్యాంగంలో భాగమని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది? సమాధానం: కేశవానంద భారతి (1973); బొమ్మై (1994) లో ధృవీకరణ. ప్రవేశికను సవరించవచ్చా? సమాధానం: అవును, అ. 368 కింద, మౌలిక నిర్మాణానికి సంబంధించిన భాగం తప్ప (ఖన్నా న్యా.). 1948లో "సామ్యవాద" చేర్చడాన్ని అంబేద్కర్ ఎందుకు వ్యతిరేకించారు? సమాధానం: సామాజిక, ఆర్థిక వ్యవస్థను ప్రజలే నిర్ణయించుకోవాలి; ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలు ఇప్పటికే సామ్యవాదపూరితం. "సామ్యవాద" కనీసం ఏమి అర్థం కావాలని రణధీర్ సింగ్ చెప్పింది? సమాధానం: సమాన పనికి సమాన వేతనం. ఒక అధికరణను వ్యాఖ్యానించడానికి కోర్టు ప్రవేశికను ఎప్పుడు వాడవచ్చు? సమాధానం: అధికరణ పదాలు అస్పష్టంగా లేదా రెండు అర్థాలు కలిగి ఉన్నప్పుడు మాత్రమే. అంబేద్కర్ వాక్యం పూర్తి చేయండి: "Without equality, liberty would ..." సమాధానం: "... produce the supremacy of the few over the many." ( ... చాలా మందిపై కొద్దిమంది ఆధిపత్యాన్ని తెస్తుంది. ) ప్రవేశికలోని "justice, social, economic and political" ను ఏ అధికరణ పునరావృతం చేస్తుంది? సమాధానం: అ. 38(1).

hi.inOneMinute: The Preamble is the opening statement of the Constitution. It answers four questions: Who gave the Constitution? "WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA" – the source of authority is the people ( popular sovereignty ). What kind of State? A "SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC". What are its aims? JUSTICE (social, economic, political); LIBERTY (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship); EQUALITY (of status and of opportunity); FRATERNITY (assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation). When was it adopted? "this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949". The words "SOCIALIST SECULAR" and "and integrity" were added by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 (from 3 January 1977). This is the only amendment of the Preamble so far. The Constituent Assembly took up the Preamble last , on 17 October 1949, and adopted the motion "That the Preamble stand part of the Constitution". Is it part of the Constitution? Berubari (1960): a "key to open the mind of the makers", but "not a part of the Constitution". Kesavananda Bharati (1973): it is a part of the Constitution. It can be amended under Art. 368, but not so as to destroy the basic structure. Use in court: it is not a source of power or of prohibitions. It helps to interpret an Article when the words are ambiguous, and it shows the basic structure .
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

PREAMBLE WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a [SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC] and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE, social, economic and political; LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; EQUALITY of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the [unity and integrity of the Nation]; IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.
Footnotes in the bare Act:

"SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC" was substituted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 2, for "SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC" (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). "unity and integrity of the Nation" was substituted by s. 2, ibid., for "unity of the Nation" (w.e.f. 3-1-1977).
Articles that carry out the Preamble's promises (examples):

Art. 38(1): "The State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, shall inform all the institutions of the national life." Art. 51A(e): the duty of every citizen "to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities". Art. 326: elections "on the basis of adult suffrage". Arts. 14–18 (equality), 19 and 25 (liberty), 25–28 (secularism).
In simple words:

The people of India made this Constitution and gave it to themselves. India is free to decide its own affairs (sovereign), aims at a fair sharing of wealth (socialist), treats all religions equally (secular), is ruled by elected representatives (democratic) and has an elected head (republic). The State must try to give every citizen justice, freedom, equality and a feeling of brotherhood.
hi.meaning: Preamble : the introductory statement placed before the Articles. It states the source, the nature of the State, the objectives, and the date of adoption. Key to the mind of the makers: Berubari , quoting Story: the Preamble is "a key to open the mind of the makers" which "may show the general purposes for which they made the several provisions in the Constitution". Popular sovereignty: the final authority belongs to the people. Ambedkar (17 Oct 1949): the Preamble shows "that this Constitution should have its root, its authority, its sovereignty, from the people. That it has." Part of the Constitution? Khanna J. ( Kesavananda , para 1524): "I am unable to accept the contention that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution."
keyPoints: Text: "SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC"; JUSTICE, LIBERTY, EQUALITY, FRATERNITY. 42nd Amendment, 1976 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977): "SOCIALIST SECULAR" and "integrity" added – the only amendment. Adopted last: 17 Oct 1949; "God" amendment lost 41 to 68. Ambedkar: sovereignty "from the people"; three parts – declaratory, descriptive, objective. Berubari : key to the mind; not part; not a source of power. Kesavananda : part of the Constitution; amendable except basic structure. Bommai : integral part; secularism implicit before 1976. Randhir Singh : "socialist" must mean at least equal pay for equal work. Ambedkar's trinity: liberty, equality, fraternity cannot be divorced. Use: interpretation of ambiguous words; guide to basic features.

caseLaws.facts: In re Berubari Union and Exchange of Enclaves , [1960] 3 SCR 250 (8-judge Bench; opinion of 14 March 1960, delivered by Gajendragadkar J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By the Indo-Pakistan Agreement of 10 September 1958, half of Berubari Union and certain Cooch
caseLaws.facts: The President referred to the Court under Art. 143(1) how the Agreement could be carried out. It was argued that the Preamble made India's territory untouchable. Principle: The Preamble is "a key to open the mind of the makers", "but nevertheless the preamble is not a part of the Constitution"; it is not "the source of any substantive power", and "What is true about the powers is equally true about the prohibitions and limitations." It may help only if an Article is "ambiguous or ... capable of two meanings". The Agreement "cannot be implemented by a law relatable to Art. 3 and legislation relatable to Art. 368 would be inevitable." Why it matters: First major ruling on the Preamble's legal status; its "not a part" view was later rejected, but the rule that the Preamble is not a source of power still stands.
Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13-judge Bench, decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to Kerala land reform laws and to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments; the scope of
caseLaws.facts: 368 was in question. Principle: The Preamble is part of the Constitution: "It was expressly voted to be a part of the Constitution" (Sikri C.J., para 105); Khanna J. (para 1524) relied on the motion "the Preamble stands part of the Constitution". It can be amended, but not its basic-structure part (Khanna J., para 1526 and conclusion (x)). It shows the basic features: "one has only to look to the preamble" (Hegde and Mukherjea JJ., para 700). Why it matters: Settled the Preamble's status and linked it to the basic-structure limit on amendment.
Randhir Singh v. Union of India , AIR 1982 SC 879; (1982) 1 SCC 618 (3-judge Bench, decided 22 February 1982)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A driver-constable in the Delhi Police got a lower pay scale than drivers doing the same work
caseLaws.facts: He filed a writ petition under Art. 32. Principle: Chinnappa Reddy J.: "the word 'Socialist' must mean something. Even if it does not mean 'To each according to his need', it must atleast mean 'equal pay for equal work'." Reading Arts. 14 and 16 "in the light of the Preamble and Art.39(d)", the principle of equal pay for equal work was applied. The petition was allowed. Why it matters: Shows how the word "socialist" in the Preamble is used to interpret Fundamental Rights .
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India , [1994] 2 SCR 644 (9-judge Bench, decided 11 March 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to proclamations under Art
caseLaws.facts: 356 dismissing several State Governments; one question was whether "secularism" could be a ground. Principle: Jeevan Reddy J.: the view that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution "is no longer extent [extant]"; the words "the provisions of this Constitution" in Art. 356 "take in all the provisions including the Preamble"; "the 42nd Amendment merely made explicit what was implicit". Headnote: "The preamble of the Constitution is an integral part of the Constitution." Why it matters: Confirms the Preamble's status and that secularism , stated in it, is a basic feature.
LIC of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre , [1995] Supp. 1 SCR 349 (2-judge Bench, decided 10 May 1995)

caseLaws.name: Facts: LIC offered a cheap term policy only to persons employed in government, quasi-government or r
caseLaws.facts: This was challenged as arbitrary . Principle: K. Ramaswamy J.: "The Preamble, the arch of the Constitution, assures socio-economic justice to all the Indian citizen in matters of equality of status and of opportunity with assurance to dignity of the individual"; "the touchstone of the Directive Principles of the State policy in the light of the Preamble provides yardstick". The restriction was held unconstitutional under Art. 14; LIC's appeals were dismissed. Why it matters: Shows the Preamble being used, with Part IV, to test State action.

selfTest.q: Name the four parts of the Preamble. Answer: Source (We, the people), nature of the State, objectives, date of adoption. Which words were added by the 42nd Amendment?
selfTest.a: Answer: "SOCIALIST", "SECULAR" and "integrity" (in "unity and integrity of the Nation"). On which date did the Assembly adopt the Preamble, and why was it taken up last? Answer: 17 October 1949; so that it would conform to the Constitution already accepted. What happened to Kamath's "In the name of God" amendment? Answer: Negatived by show of hands, 41 for and 68 against. What did Berubari say about the Preamble? Answer: A key to open the mind of the makers, but not a part of the Constitution and not a source of power or limitations. Which case held the Preamble is a part of the Constitution? Answer: Kesavananda Bharati (1973); confirmed in Bommai (1994). Can the Preamble be amended? Answer: Yes, under Art. 368, except the part relating to the basic structure (Khanna J.). Why did Ambedkar oppose adding "socialist" in 1948? Answer: The people should decide their social and economic organisation; and the Directive Principles were already socialistic. What did Randhir Singh say "socialist" must at least mean? Answer: Equal pay for equal work. When can a court use the Preamble to interpret an Article? Answer: Only when the words of the Article are ambiguous or capable of two meanings. Complete Ambedkar's line: "Without equality, liberty would ..." Answer: "... produce the supremacy of the few over the many." Which Article repeats the Preamble's "justice, social, economic and political"? Answer: Art. 38(1).

constitutional-law-i-u2-t7.subtitle: How courts test laws and executive action against the Constitution, the Articles behind it, and its limits: Minerva Mills, I.R. Coelho and Chandra Kumar

en.inOneMinute: Judicial review is the power of the Supreme Court and the High Courts to examine laws, constitutional amendments and executive action, and to declare them void if they go beyond the Constitution. The Constitution gives this power expressly : Art. 13 – laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void; Art. 32 – the right to move the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights is itself "guaranteed"; Art. 226 – High Courts may issue writs "for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose". Das J. in A. K. Gopalan (1950): "In India the position of the Judiciary is somewhere in between the Courts in England and the United States" – the Court checks whether a constitutional limitation "has been transgressed", but "has no authority to question the wisdom or policy of the law". Grounds: (1) lack of legislative competence (Arts. 245, 246); (2) violation of Fundamental Rights (Art. 13); (3) breach of other constitutional limits; (4) for constitutional amendments – damage to the basic structure ( Kesavananda , 1973). Judicial review is itself part of the basic structure: Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art. 368(4) and (5), which tried to bar courts from questioning amendments; L. Chandra Kumar (1997): the power under Arts. 226 and 32 "is an integral and essential feature of the Constitution, constituting part of its basic structure"; I. R. Coelho (2007): laws put in the Ninth Schedule on or after 24 April 1973 can be tested against the basic structure.
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Article 13(2): "The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void."
Article 32(1)–(2):

(1) The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed. (2) The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part.

Article 226(1) (extract): "every High Court shall have power ... to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government ... directions, orders or writs ... for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose."

Article 245(1): "Subject to the provisions of this Constitution, Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of the territory of India, and the Legislature of a State may make laws for the whole or any part of the State."
Article 368(4) and (5) (inserted by the 42nd Amendment, s. 55, w.e.f. 3-1-1977):

(4) No amendment of this Constitution (including the provisions of Part III) made or purporting to have been made under this article ... shall be called in question in any court on any ground. (5) For the removal of doubts, it is hereby declared that there shall be no limitation whatever on the constituent power of Parliament to amend ...
Footnote in the bare Act: "This section has been declared invalid by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. and Others Vs. Union of India and Others AIR 1980 SC 1789."
In simple words:

Parliament and State Legislatures can make laws only within the limits the Constitution sets. If they cross those limits, the Supreme Court (Art. 32) and the High Courts (Art. 226) can declare the law void. Even Parliament's power to amend the Constitution has a limit – the basic structure – and courts check that too.
en.meaning: Judicial review : the power of the superior courts to test the validity of legislative and executive action (and constitutional amendments) against the Constitution, and to declare invalid action void. L. Chandra Kumar : Judges of the superior courts "have been entrusted with the task of upholding the Constitution and to this end, have been conferred the power to interpret it". Ultra vires : "beyond the powers" – a law or action outside the authority given by the Constitution or the parent law. Basic structure : the essential features of the Constitution which Parliament cannot "alter" by amendment ( Kesavananda : "Art. 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution"). Constitutional supremacy : the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme. Patanjali Sastri J. in A. K. Gopalan : "It is not correct to say that the Constitution has adopted the doctrine of Parliamentary supremacy."
keyPoints: Judicial review = power to declare laws, amendments and actions void if unconstitutional. Sources: Arts. 13, 32, 226, 245. India: "somewhere in between" England and the U.S.A. ( Gopalan , Das J.). Courts do not question wisdom or policy. Amendments: basic structure test ( Kesavananda , 24-4-1973). Art. 368(4), (5) (42nd Amendment) struck down ( Minerva Mills , 1980). Judicial review under Arts. 226, 32 = basic structure ( L. Chandra Kumar , 1997). Ninth Schedule laws after 24-4-1973 reviewable ( I. R. Coelho , 2007).

caseLaws.name: Facts: A
caseLaws.facts: K. Gopalan, detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, applied under Art. 32 for habeas corpus, challenging the Act under Arts. 19, 21 and 22. Principle: On judicial review, Das J.: "In India the position of the Judiciary is somewhere in between the Courts in England and the United States"; the Court will "courageously declare the law unconstitutional" where a limitation is transgressed , but "has no authority to question the wisdom or policy of the law". Patanjali Sastri J.: the Constitution has not "adopted the doctrine of Parliamentary supremacy". Why it matters: Early explanation of the nature and limits of judicial review in India.
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala , (1973) 4 SCC 225; AIR 1973 SC 1461 (13 judges; decided 24 April 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to the 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments and Kerala land reform laws
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "The view by the majority": "Art. 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution"; the part of Art. 31C barring courts from questioning the declaration "is invalid". Why it matters: Basis of judicial review of constitutional amendments.
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India , AIR 1980 SC 1789; [1981] 1 SCR 206 (5 judges; majority judgment by Y. V. Chandrachud C.J.; order 9 May 1980, reasons 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.facts: 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment (amending Art. 31C and adding Art. 368(4), (5)). Principle: "Section 55 of the Constitution 42nd Amendment Act is beyond the amending power of the Parliament and is void since it removes all limitations on the power of the Parliament to amend the Constitution"; "a limited amending power is one of the basic features of our Constitution". Why it matters: Parliament cannot shut out judicial review of amendments.
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India , AIR 1997 SC 1125; (1997) 3 SCC 261; [1997] 2 SCR 1186 (7 judges; A. M. Ahmadi C.J.I.; decided 18 March 1997)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Arts
caseLaws.facts: 323A and 323B, inserted by the 42nd Amendment, and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 excluded the jurisdiction of the High Courts in matters given to tribunals. This was challenged. Principle: Judicial review under Arts. 226 and 32 "is an integral and essential feature of the Constitution, constituting part of its basic structure"; the exclusion clauses were unconstitutional to that extent; tribunals' decisions go to a Division Bench of the High Court. Why it matters: Confirms judicial review of the High Courts and the Supreme Court as basic structure.
I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu , Civil Appeal Nos. 1344–45 of 1976 (9 judges; Y. K. Sabharwal C.J.I.; decided 11 January 2007)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Reference on the nature of protection given by Art
caseLaws.facts: 31B to laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973. Principle: Such laws "shall have to be tested on the touchstone of the basic or essential features of the Constitution as reflected in Article 21 read with Article 14, Article 19"; the "rights test" applies; earlier-upheld laws and finalized transactions not reopened. Why it matters: The Ninth Schedule cannot be used to escape judicial review after Kesavananda .

selfTest.q: Which three Articles expressly give judicial review over Fundamental Rights?
selfTest.a: Answer: Arts. 13, 32 and 226. How did Das J. describe India's position? Answer: "Somewhere in between the Courts in England and the United States". Can courts strike down a law as unwise? Answer: No; they cannot question the wisdom or policy of a law. What did Art. 368(4) say? Answer: No amendment "shall be called in question in any court on any ground". Why was Art. 368(5) struck down? Answer: It removed all limits on the amending power; "a limited amending power is one of the basic features". What did L. Chandra Kumar hold about Arts. 226 and 32? Answer: Judicial review under them is part of the basic structure. Can tribunals decide validity of laws? Answer: Yes (except their parent Act), subject to scrutiny by a High Court Division Bench. Which Ninth Schedule laws are open to basic-structure review? Answer: Those added on or after 24 April 1973 ( I. R. Coelho ). What was the majority in Kesavananda as stated in L. Chandra Kumar ? Answer: 7:6. Is a constitutional amendment tested under Art. 13? Answer: No (Arts. 13(4), 368(3)); it is tested against the basic structure.
