constitutional-law-i-u3-t7.subtitle: Article 21A: free and compulsory education for children of six to fourteen, how the Court built it from Article 21, and the Act that carries it out

en.inOneMinute: Text: Art. 21A: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." Origin: in 1950, education up to 14 was only a Directive Principle (old Art. 45, "within a period of ten years"). Courts first: Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) read the right to education into Art. 21. Unni Krishnan limited it: free education until the child "completes the age of fourteen years"; after that, it depends on the State's "economic capacity and development". Constitution next: the 86th Amendment (in force 1-4-2010) inserted Art. 21A, replaced Art. 45 (now early childhood care below six) and added the duty in Art. 51A(k). The law: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act), in force 1-4-2010, gives every child of 6–14 the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until elementary education (class I to VIII) is complete. Key RTE rules: 25% seats in class I of private unaided schools for weaker and disadvantaged children; no capitation fee and no screening; no physical punishment; no expulsion till class VIII.
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026); RTE Act, 2009 (bare Act PDF).

Article 21A – "Right to education." "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." (Ins. by the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, s. 2, w.e.f. 1-4-2010.)

Article 45 (as substituted by the 86th Amendment, s. 3, w.e.f. 1-4-2010) – "Provision for early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years." "The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years."

Article 51A(k) (Ins. by the 86th Amendment, s. 4, w.e.f. 1-4-2010): it is the duty of every citizen "who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years."

Article 41 (Directive Principle): "The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance…"

Old Article 45 (1950 to 2010) , as quoted in Unni Krishnan : "the State shall endeavour to provide, within a period of ten years from the commencement of this Constitution, for free and compulsory education for all children until they complete the age of fourteen years."
RTE Act, 2009 – main sections:

s. 2(c): "child" means a male or female child of the age of six to fourteen years. s. 2(f): "elementary education" means the education from first class to eighth class. s. 3(1): every child of six to fourteen "shall have the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school till the completion of his or her elementary education." s. 3(2): no child shall be liable to pay "any kind of fee or charges or expenses which may prevent him or her from pursuing and completing the elementary education." s. 8(a), Explanation: "compulsory education" means the obligation of the appropriate Government to provide free elementary education and "ensure compulsory admission, attendance and completion of elementary education". s. 10: duty of every parent or guardian to admit the child to elementary education in the neighbourhood school. s. 12(1)(c): unaided and specified-category schools "shall admit in class I, to the extent of at least twenty-five per cent. of the strength of that class, children belonging to weaker section and disadvantaged group in the neighbourhood". s. 13: no capitation fee and no screening procedure. s. 14(2): "No child shall be denied admission in a school for lack of age proof." s. 16 (as substituted w.e.f. 1-3-2019): regular examination in class 5 and class 8; re-examination within two months; holding back may be allowed; "No child shall be expelled from a school till the completion of elementary education." s. 17(1): "No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment." s. 1(4)–(5) (ins. w.e.f. 1-8-2012): the Act applies "Subject to the provisions of articles 29 and 30"; it does not apply to "Madrasas, Vedic Pathsalas and educational institutions primarily imparting religious instruction."
en.meaning: Right to education (Art. 21A): a fundamental right of every child of 6 to 14 years to receive free and compulsory education from the State, in the manner fixed by law (the RTE Act). Free and compulsory education: Free : no fee, charge or expense that may prevent the child from completing elementary education (RTE s. 3(2)). Compulsory : the Government must ensure "compulsory admission, attendance and completion" (RTE s. 8(a), Explanation). The duty is on the State, not a punishment of the child. Elementary education: class I to class VIII (RTE s. 2(f)). Neighbourhood school: a school within the area or limits of neighbourhood prescribed by rules; the Government must set one up within three years where none exists (RTE s. 6). Capitation fee: "any kind of donation or contribution or payment other than the fee notified by the school" (RTE s. 2(b)).
keyPoints: Art. 21A: 6–14; free and compulsory; manner by law; w.e.f. 1-4-2010. 86th Amendment: Art. 21A (s. 2), new Art. 45 (s. 3), Art. 51A(k) (s. 4). CAD 23-11-1948: "Every citizen is entitled to free primary education" deleted. Unni Krishnan (1993): free education up to 14; after that, economic capacity. T. M. A. Pai (2002): scheme struck down; fundamental right to primary education kept. RTE Act: class I–VIII; neighbourhood school; 25% (s. 12(1)(c)); no capitation fee or screening (s. 13); no denial for lack of age proof (s. 14); no physical punishment (s. 17).

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The right to education flows from Art. 21, but free education is a right only until the child "completes the age of fourteen years"; beyond that it depends on the State's economic capacity. Why it matters: Laid the base for Art. 21A.
T. M. A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka , [2002] Supp. 3 SCR; (2002) 8 SCC 481 (11 judges; B. N. Kirpal C.J.; decided 31 October 2002)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Unni Krishnan scheme was unconstitutional "except where it holds that primary education is a fundamental right"; capitation fee and profiteering remain impermissible. Why it matters: Kept the fundamental right to primary education alive.
Miss Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka , (1992) 3 SCC 666; [1992] 3 SCR 658

caseLaws.name: Facts: (As described in Unni Krishnan ; Kuldip Singh and R
caseLaws.facts: M. Sahai JJ.) A challenge to capitation fees charged by State-recognised private educational institutions. Principle: Every citizen has a right to education under the Constitution; charging capitation fee was "a patent denial of a citizen's right to education" and permitting it was arbitrary under Art. 14. Why it matters: First to read education into Art. 21; partly overruled in Unni Krishnan .
Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India , (2012) 6 SCC 1; [2012] 2 SCR 715

caseLaws.name: Facts: (As described in Janhit Abhiyan
caseLaws.facts: ) Unaided non-minority schools challenged the RTE Act's application to them. Principle: Art. 21 "covers access to education"; Art. 21A works through the 2009 Act, which is "child-centric and not institution-centric" (Kapadia C.J. for the majority). Why it matters: Explains how Art. 21A and the RTE Act fit together.

selfTest.q: Quote Art. 21A. Answer: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." When did Art. 21A come into force?
selfTest.a: Answer: 1 April 2010. What does Art. 45 cover now? Answer: Early childhood care and education for children until they complete six years. Which case limited free education to children up to 14? Answer: Unni Krishnan (1993). Did T. M. A. Pai overrule the right to primary education? Answer: No; it struck down the Unni Krishnan scheme "except where it holds that primary education is a fundamental right". What is "elementary education" under the RTE Act? Answer: Class I to class VIII (s. 2(f)). A class I has 80 seats. How many must a private unaided school give under s. 12(1)(c)? Answer: At least 20 (25% of 80). A school takes a Rs. 20,000 capitation fee. What is the maximum fine? Answer: Rs. 2,00,000 (ten times). Can a school refuse a child for lack of a birth certificate? Answer: No (s. 14(2)). Which fundamental duty matches Art. 21A? Answer: Art. 51A(k).

te.inOneMinute: పాఠం: అధికరణ 21A: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." ( అర్థం: ఆరు నుండి పద్నాలుగు సంవత్సరాల వయస్సు గల పిల్లలందరికీ, రాజ్యం చట్టం ద్వారా నిర్ణయించే విధంగా, రాజ్యం ఉచిత మరియు నిర్బంధ విద్యను అందించాలి.) మూలం: 1950లో 14 ఏళ్ల వరకు విద్య కేవలం ఆదేశిక సూత్రం మాత్రమే (పాత అధికరణ 45, "within a period of ten years" ( అర్థం: పది సంవత్సరాల వ్యవధిలోపు)). ముందు కోర్టులు: Mohini Jain (1992), Unni Krishnan (1993) విద్యా హక్కును అధికరణ 21లో చదివాయి. Unni Krishnan దానిని పరిమితం చేసింది: పిల్లవాడు "completes the age of fourteen years" ( అర్థం: పద్నాలుగు సంవత్సరాలు పూర్తి చేసే) వరకు ఉచిత విద్య; ఆ తర్వాత రాజ్యం "economic capacity and development" ( అర్థం: ఆర్థిక సామర్థ్యం, అభివృద్ధి)పై ఆధారపడుతుంది. తర్వాత రాజ్యాంగం: 86వ సవరణ (1-4-2010 నుండి అమలు) అధికరణ 21Aను చేర్చింది, అధికరణ 45ను మార్చింది (ఇప్పుడు ఆరేళ్ల లోపు బాల్య సంరక్షణ), అధికరణ 51A(k)లో విధిని జోడించింది. చట్టం: ఉచిత మరియు నిర్బంధ విద్యకు పిల్లల హక్కు చట్టం, 2009 (RTE చట్టం), 1-4-2010 నుండి అమలు, 6–14 ఏళ్ల ప్రతి బిడ్డకు ప్రాథమిక విద్య (I నుండి VIII తరగతి) పూర్తయ్యే వరకు పొరుగు పాఠశాల లో ఉచిత మరియు నిర్బంధ విద్య హక్కు ఇస్తుంది. RTE ముఖ్య నియమాలు: ప్రైవేట్ అన్‌ఎయిడెడ్ పాఠశాలల్లో I తరగతిలో 25% సీట్లు బలహీన, వెనుకబడిన వర్గాల పిల్లలకు; క్యాపిటేషన్ ఫీజు , స్క్రీనింగ్ నిషేధం; శారీరక శిక్ష నిషేధం; VIII తరగతి వరకు బహిష్కరణ లేదు.
te.meaning: విద్యా హక్కు (అధికరణ 21A): 6 నుండి 14 ఏళ్ల ప్రతి బిడ్డ, చట్టం (RTE చట్టం) నిర్ణయించిన విధంగా, రాజ్యం నుండి ఉచిత మరియు నిర్బంధ విద్య పొందే ప్రాథమిక హక్కు. ఉచిత మరియు నిర్బంధ విద్య: ఉచిత : బిడ్డ ప్రాథమిక విద్య పూర్తి చేయకుండా అడ్డుకునే ఏ ఫీజు, ఛార్జీ, ఖర్చూ ఉండదు (RTE సెక్షన్ 3(2)). నిర్బంధ : ప్రభుత్వం "compulsory admission, attendance and completion" ( అర్థం: నిర్బంధ ప్రవేశం, హాజరు, పూర్తి చేయడం) నిర్ధారించాలి (RTE సెక్షన్ 8(a), వివరణ). బాధ్యత రాజ్యంపై ఉంటుంది; ఇది బిడ్డకు శిక్ష కాదు. ప్రాథమిక విద్య: I తరగతి నుండి VIII తరగతి వరకు (RTE సెక్షన్ 2(f)). పొరుగు పాఠశాల: నియమాలు నిర్దేశించిన పొరుగు ప్రాంతం లేదా పరిమితుల్లోని పాఠశాల; లేని చోట ప్రభుత్వం మూడు సంవత్సరాల్లో ఏర్పాటు చేయాలి (RTE సెక్షన్ 6). క్యాపిటేషన్ ఫీజు: "any kind of donation or contribution or payment other than the fee notified by the school" ( అర్థం: పాఠశాల ప్రకటించిన ఫీజు కాకుండా ఏ రకమైన విరాళం, చందా లేదా చెల్లింపు) (RTE సెక్షన్ 2(b)).
keyPoints: అధికరణ 21A: 6–14; ఉచిత, నిర్బంధ; విధానం చట్టం ద్వారా; 1-4-2010 నుండి. 86వ సవరణ: అధికరణ 21A (సెక్షన్ 2), కొత్త అధికరణ 45 (సెక్షన్ 3), అధికరణ 51A(k) (సెక్షన్ 4). CAD 23-11-1948: "Every citizen is entitled to free primary education" ( అర్థం: ప్రతి పౌరుడు ఉచిత ప్రాథమిక విద్యకు అర్హుడు) తొలగించబడింది. Unni Krishnan (1993): 14 వరకు ఉచిత విద్య; ఆ తర్వాత ఆర్థిక సామర్థ్యం. T. M. A. Pai (2002): పథకం కొట్టివేత; ప్రాథమిక విద్యకు ప్రాథమిక హక్కు నిలిచింది. RTE చట్టం: I–VIII తరగతి; పొరుగు పాఠశాల; 25% (సెక్షన్ 12(1)(c)); క్యాపిటేషన్ ఫీజు, స్క్రీనింగ్ లేదు (సెక్షన్ 13); వయస్సు రుజువు లేదని నిరాకరణ లేదు (సెక్షన్ 14); శారీరక శిక్ష లేదు (సెక్షన్ 17).

selfTest.q: అధికరణ 21Aను ఉదహరించండి. జవాబు: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." ( అర్థం: ఆరు నుండి పద్నాలుగు సంవత్సరాల వయస్సు గల పిల్లలందరికీ, రాజ్యం చట్టం ద్వారా నిర్ణయించే విధంగా, రాజ్యం ఉచిత మరియు నిర్బంధ విద్యను అందించాలి.) అధికరణ 21A ఎప్పుడు అమలులోకి వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: 1 ఏప్రిల్ 2010. ఇప్పుడు అధికరణ 45 దేనిని కవర్ చేస్తుంది? జవాబు: పిల్లలు ఆరేళ్లు పూర్తి చేసే వరకు బాల్య సంరక్షణ, విద్య. ఉచిత విద్యను 14 ఏళ్ల వరకు పిల్లలకు పరిమితం చేసిన కేసు ఏది? జవాబు: Unni Krishnan (1993). T. M. A. Pai ప్రాథమిక విద్యా హక్కును రద్దు చేసిందా? జవాబు: లేదు; Unni Krishnan పథకాన్ని "except where it holds that primary education is a fundamental right" ( అర్థం: ప్రాథమిక విద్య ప్రాథమిక హక్కు అని చెప్పిన చోట తప్ప) కొట్టివేసింది. RTE చట్టం కింద "ప్రాథమిక విద్య" అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: I తరగతి నుండి VIII తరగతి వరకు (సెక్షన్ 2(f)). ఒక I తరగతిలో 80 సీట్లు ఉన్నాయి. సెక్షన్ 12(1)(c) కింద ప్రైవేట్ అన్‌ఎయిడెడ్ పాఠశాల ఎన్ని ఇవ్వాలి? జవాబు: కనీసం 20 (80లో 25%). ఒక పాఠశాల Rs. 20,000 క్యాపిటేషన్ ఫీజు తీసుకుంది. గరిష్ట జరిమానా ఎంత? జవాబు: Rs. 2,00,000 (పది రెట్లు). జనన ధృవీకరణ పత్రం లేదని పాఠశాల బిడ్డను నిరాకరించవచ్చా? జవాబు: లేదు (సెక్షన్ 14(2)). అధికరణ 21Aకు సరిపోయే ప్రాథమిక విధి ఏది? జవాబు: అధికరణ 51A(k).

hi.inOneMinute: Text: Art. 21A: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." Origin: in 1950, education up to 14 was only a Directive Principle (old Art. 45, "within a period of ten years"). Courts first: Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) read the right to education into Art. 21. Unni Krishnan limited it: free education until the child "completes the age of fourteen years"; after that, it depends on the State's "economic capacity and development". Constitution next: the 86th Amendment (in force 1-4-2010) inserted Art. 21A, replaced Art. 45 (now early childhood care below six) and added the duty in Art. 51A(k). The law: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act), in force 1-4-2010, gives every child of 6–14 the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until elementary education (class I to VIII) is complete. Key RTE rules: 25% seats in class I of private unaided schools for weaker and disadvantaged children; no capitation fee and no screening; no physical punishment; no expulsion till class VIII.
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026); RTE Act, 2009 (bare Act PDF).

Article 21A – "Right to education." "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." (Ins. by the Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, s. 2, w.e.f. 1-4-2010.)

Article 45 (as substituted by the 86th Amendment, s. 3, w.e.f. 1-4-2010) – "Provision for early childhood care and education to children below the age of six years." "The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years."

Article 51A(k) (Ins. by the 86th Amendment, s. 4, w.e.f. 1-4-2010): it is the duty of every citizen "who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of six and fourteen years."

Article 41 (Directive Principle): "The State shall, within the limits of its economic capacity and development, make effective provision for securing the right to work, to education and to public assistance…"

Old Article 45 (1950 to 2010) , as quoted in Unni Krishnan : "the State shall endeavour to provide, within a period of ten years from the commencement of this Constitution, for free and compulsory education for all children until they complete the age of fourteen years."
RTE Act, 2009 – main sections:

s. 2(c): "child" means a male or female child of the age of six to fourteen years. s. 2(f): "elementary education" means the education from first class to eighth class. s. 3(1): every child of six to fourteen "shall have the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school till the completion of his or her elementary education." s. 3(2): no child shall be liable to pay "any kind of fee or charges or expenses which may prevent him or her from pursuing and completing the elementary education." s. 8(a), Explanation: "compulsory education" means the obligation of the appropriate Government to provide free elementary education and "ensure compulsory admission, attendance and completion of elementary education". s. 10: duty of every parent or guardian to admit the child to elementary education in the neighbourhood school. s. 12(1)(c): unaided and specified-category schools "shall admit in class I, to the extent of at least twenty-five per cent. of the strength of that class, children belonging to weaker section and disadvantaged group in the neighbourhood". s. 13: no capitation fee and no screening procedure. s. 14(2): "No child shall be denied admission in a school for lack of age proof." s. 16 (as substituted w.e.f. 1-3-2019): regular examination in class 5 and class 8; re-examination within two months; holding back may be allowed; "No child shall be expelled from a school till the completion of elementary education." s. 17(1): "No child shall be subjected to physical punishment or mental harassment." s. 1(4)–(5) (ins. w.e.f. 1-8-2012): the Act applies "Subject to the provisions of articles 29 and 30"; it does not apply to "Madrasas, Vedic Pathsalas and educational institutions primarily imparting religious instruction."
hi.meaning: Right to education (Art. 21A): a fundamental right of every child of 6 to 14 years to receive free and compulsory education from the State, in the manner fixed by law (the RTE Act). Free and compulsory education: Free : no fee, charge or expense that may prevent the child from completing elementary education (RTE s. 3(2)). Compulsory : the Government must ensure "compulsory admission, attendance and completion" (RTE s. 8(a), Explanation). The duty is on the State, not a punishment of the child. Elementary education: class I to class VIII (RTE s. 2(f)). Neighbourhood school: a school within the area or limits of neighbourhood prescribed by rules; the Government must set one up within three years where none exists (RTE s. 6). Capitation fee: "any kind of donation or contribution or payment other than the fee notified by the school" (RTE s. 2(b)).
keyPoints: Art. 21A: 6–14; free and compulsory; manner by law; w.e.f. 1-4-2010. 86th Amendment: Art. 21A (s. 2), new Art. 45 (s. 3), Art. 51A(k) (s. 4). CAD 23-11-1948: "Every citizen is entitled to free primary education" deleted. Unni Krishnan (1993): free education up to 14; after that, economic capacity. T. M. A. Pai (2002): scheme struck down; fundamental right to primary education kept. RTE Act: class I–VIII; neighbourhood school; 25% (s. 12(1)(c)); no capitation fee or screening (s. 13); no denial for lack of age proof (s. 14); no physical punishment (s. 17).

selfTest.q: Quote Art. 21A. Answer: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine." When did Art. 21A come into force?
selfTest.a: Answer: 1 April 2010. What does Art. 45 cover now? Answer: Early childhood care and education for children until they complete six years. Which case limited free education to children up to 14? Answer: Unni Krishnan (1993). Did T. M. A. Pai overrule the right to primary education? Answer: No; it struck down the Unni Krishnan scheme "except where it holds that primary education is a fundamental right". What is "elementary education" under the RTE Act? Answer: Class I to class VIII (s. 2(f)). A class I has 80 seats. How many must a private unaided school give under s. 12(1)(c)? Answer: At least 20 (25% of 80). A school takes a Rs. 20,000 capitation fee. What is the maximum fine? Answer: Rs. 2,00,000 (ten times). Can a school refuse a child for lack of a birth certificate? Answer: No (s. 14(2)). Which fundamental duty matches Art. 21A? Answer: Art. 51A(k).

constitutional-law-i-u3-t1.subtitle: Equality before law, discrimination, public employment, untouchability and titles, with the tests of classification and arbitrariness

en.inOneMinute: Arts. 14 to 18 form the "Right to Equality" in Part III. Art. 14: equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws , for any person . Art. 15: no discrimination by the State against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; with special provisions allowed for women and children, backward classes, SCs/STs and EWS. Art. 16: equality of opportunity in public employment ; reservation allowed for backward classes, SCs/STs (also in promotion) and EWS. Art. 17: "Untouchability" is abolished; its practice is an offence. Art. 18: the State shall confer no title, except military or academic distinctions. Art. 14 does not forbid reasonable classification . The classification must rest on an intelligible differentia with a rational relation to the object of the law ( Budhan Choudhry , 1954; Ram Krishna Dalmia , 1958). Art. 14 also strikes at arbitrariness : "equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies" ( E. P. Royappa , 1973). Reservation ( Indra Sawhney , 1992): Art. 16(4) is not an exception to Art. 16(1); the creamy layer must be excluded; reservation under Art. 16(4) should not exceed 50% (save extraordinary situations). Economically weaker sections (Arts. 15(6), 16(6), up to 10%) were upheld 3:2 in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 14 – Equality before law: "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
Article 15 – Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth:

(1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to— (a) access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or (b) the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children. (4) Nothing in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.

Cl. (4) was added by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 (w.e.f. 18-6-1951). Cl. (5) (93rd Amendment, w.e.f. 20-1-2006): special provision, by law, for socially and educationally backward classes or SCs/STs in admission to educational institutions , including private ones, aided or unaided, "other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30". Cl. (6) (103rd Amendment, w.e.f. 14-1-2019): special provision for "economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5)", including admission to educational institutions, "subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the total seats in each category", "in addition to the existing reservations". Explanation: "economically weaker sections" are those notified by the State "on the basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage".
Article 16 – Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment:

(1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing ... any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment. (4) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State.

Cl. (4A) (77th Amendment, w.e.f. 17-6-1995; words "with consequential seniority" by the 85th Amendment): reservation "in matters of promotion, with consequential seniority" for SCs and STs not adequately represented. Cl. (4B) (81st Amendment, w.e.f. 9-6-2000): unfilled reserved vacancies of a year may be carried forward as a separate class, not counted "for determining the ceiling of fifty per cent. reservation on total number of vacancies of that year". Cl. (5): offices of a religious or denominational institution may be kept for persons of that religion or denomination. Cl. (6) (103rd Amendment, w.e.f. 14-1-2019): reservation for economically weaker sections (other than cl. (4) classes), "in addition to the existing reservation and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the posts in each category".

Article 17 – Abolition of Untouchability: "'Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of 'Untouchability' shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law."
Article 18 – Abolition of titles:

(1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State. (2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State. (3) No person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State. (4) No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State shall, without the consent of the President, accept any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.
Article 35(a)(ii) (connected): Parliament, and not a State Legislature, has power to make laws "for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under this Part".
In simple words:

Art. 14 is the general rule of equality for everyone. Arts. 15 and 16 apply it to particular areas (discrimination in general; public jobs) and allow special help for groups that need it. Arts. 17 and 18 remove two old forms of inequality: untouchability and titles.
en.meaning: Equality before the law: no person is above the law; the same law applies to all. Patanjali Sastri C.J. ( Anwar Ali Sarkar ): it is "a declaration of equality of the civil rights of all persons within the territories of India". Equal protection of the laws: equal laws for persons in equal situations. Patanjali Sastri C.J., quoting a U.S. case: "it is a pledge of the protection of equal laws", that is, "laws that operate alike on all persons under like circumstances". Reasonable classification : Art. 14 "forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation" ( Budhan Choudhry , headnote). Arbitrariness : action without reason or principle. "Where an act is arbitrary it is implicit in it that it is unequal ... and is therefore violative of Art. 14" ( E. P. Royappa ). Backward classes : classes of citizens whom the State may help under Arts. 15(4) and 16(4). "A caste can be and quite often is a social class in India", but a backward class "cannot be identified only and exclusively with reference to economic criteria" ( Indra Sawhney ). Creamy layer : the socially advanced members of a backward class, who are excluded from reservation ( Indra Sawhney ). Economically weaker sections: sections notified by the State on the basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage (Explanation to Art. 15). Untouchability : the caste-based practice abolished by Art. 17. The Constitution does not define the word (see Detailed explanation 6).
keyPoints: Art. 14: any person; equality before law + equal protection of laws. Classification test: intelligible differentia + rational nexus ( Budhan , 1954). Arbitrariness is against equality ( Royappa , 1973); manifest arbitrariness can strike down a law ( Shayara Bano , 2017). Art. 15: citizens; grounds "only"; 15(3) women/children; 15(4) added 1951 after Champakam . "Sex" includes gender identity ( NALSA , 2014). Art. 16(4) is not an exception; creamy layer out; 50% per year ( Indra Sawhney , 1992). Promotion: Art. 16(4A); no backwardness data needed for SCs/STs ( Jarnail Singh , 2018). EWS 10% upheld 3:2 ( Janhit Abhiyan , 2022). Art. 17 binds everyone ( PUDR ); Art. 18 – awards are not titles ( Balaji Raghavan ).

caseLaws.facts: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar , AIR 1952 SC 75; [1952] 1 SCR 284 (7 judges; decided 11 January 1952)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The respondent and 49 others were tried by a Special Court for an armed raid on the Jessop fa
caseLaws.facts: The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, s. 5(1), let the State Government send any case to the Special Court, which used a shorter procedure. Principle: The unguided power violated Art. 14; the appeals were dismissed (Patanjali Sastri C.J. would have allowed them). Das J. applied the test: the classification "must be founded on an intelligible differentia ... and that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Act". Why it matters: Art. 14 forbids arbitrary laws and arbitrary application of laws, including procedural laws.
Budhan Choudhry v. State of Bihar , [1955] 1 SCR 1045 (7 judges; Das J.; decided 2 December 1954)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Appellants convicted by a magistrate empowered under s
caseLaws.facts: 30 CrPC challenged that section under Art. 14. Principle: Art. 14 "forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification"; the two conditions are intelligible differentia and rational relation to the object. s. 30 was valid. Why it matters: The standard statement of the classification test.
Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S. R. Tendolkar , AIR 1958 SC 538; 1959 SCR 279 (5 judges; S. R. Das C.J.; decided 28 March 1958)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A notification under the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 appointed a commission to inquire i
caseLaws.facts: 14. Principle: Restated the Budhan test and added principles (a)–(f): a single person may be a class; presumption of constitutionality ; burden on the challenger. Why it matters: The fullest list of Art. 14 classification principles.
E. P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu , AIR 1974 SC 555; (1974) 4 SCC 3; 1974 SCR (2) 348 (5 judges; decided 23 November 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An IAS officer was moved from the post of Chief Secretary to non-cadre posts; he claimed viol
caseLaws.facts: 14 and 16. Principle: Petition dismissed. Bhagwati J. (for himself, Chandrachud and Krishna Iyer JJ.): "equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies"; "Where an act is arbitrary it is implicit in it that it is unequal". Why it matters: Start of the non-arbitrariness doctrine under Art. 14.
State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan , AIR 1951 SC 226; 1951 SCR 525 (7 judges; decided 9 April 1951)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Communal G
caseLaws.facts: O. allotted medical and engineering college seats community-wise (6, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1 out of every 14). Principle: It violated Art. 29(2) and was void under Art. 13; Directive Principles cannot override Fundamental Rights. Why it matters: Led to Art. 15(4) (First Amendment, 1951).
M. R. Balaji v. State of Mysore , [1963] Supp 1 SCR 439 (5 judges; Gajendragadkar J.; decided 28 September 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Mysore reserved 68% of seats in engineering and medical colleges for backward classes, SCs an
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The order was "a fraud on the constitutional power" under Art. 15(4); caste cannot be the sole basis; "Speaking generally and in a broad way, a special provision should be less than 50%." Why it matters: Origin of the 50% limit.
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India , AIR 1993 SC 477; 1992 Supp (3) SCC 217 (9 judges; leading judgment by B. P. Jeevan Reddy J.; decided 16 November 1992)

caseLaws.name: Facts: O
caseLaws.facts: M. of 13-8-1990 reserved 27% of central government posts for SEBCs (Mandal Commission); O.M. of 25-9-1991 added preference for poorer sections and 10% for other economically backward sections. Principle: Art. 16(4) not an exception to 16(1); caste can be a class; creamy layer excluded; not economic criterion alone; 50% per year; no reservation in promotions under Art. 16(4) (prospective); the 10% economic reservation struck down. Why it matters: The leading case on reservation.
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India , AIR 2007 SC 71; (2006) 8 SCC 212 (5 judges; Kapadia J.; decided 19 October 2006)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments (Arts
caseLaws.facts: 16(4A), 16(4B), proviso to Art. 335) were challenged as against the basic structure. Principle: Amendments valid; 50% ceiling, creamy layer, backwardness, inadequacy of representation and efficiency remain "constitutional requirements"; quantifiable data needed. Why it matters: Conditions for reservation in promotion (later modified by Jarnail Singh ).
Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta , [2018] 10 SCR 663 (5 judges; decided 26 September 2018)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Reference on whether Nagaraj needed reconsideration by seven judges
caseLaws.facts: Principle: No reference needed, but Nagaraj 's requirement of quantifiable data showing backwardness of SCs/STs was "contrary to the nine-Judge Bench in Indra Sawhney" and invalid to that extent; creamy layer principle applies. Why it matters: Current law on SC/ST promotion reservation.
Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India , W.P. (C) No. 55 of 2019 (5 judges; decided 7 November 2022)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 103rd Amendment (EWS reservation, Arts
caseLaws.facts: 15(6), 16(6)) was challenged as violating the basic structure. Principle: Upheld 3:2; economic criteria alone, exclusion of SEBCs/SCs/STs, and 10% over 50% do not breach the basic structure (Maheshwari J.); Bhat J. (with Lalit C.J.I.) dissented. Why it matters: Current law on EWS reservation.
National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India , W.P. (C) No. 400 of 2012 (Radhakrishnan and Sikri JJ.; decided 15 April 2014)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Petition for recognition and rights of transgender persons
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "'sex' under Articles 15 and 16 ... includes discrimination on the ground of gender identity". Why it matters: Widens the "sex" ground.
Joseph Shine v. Union of India , W.P. (Crl.) No. 194 of 2017 (5 judges; decided 27 September 2018)

caseLaws.name: Facts: s
caseLaws.facts: 497 IPC punished only a man for adultery with another man's wife, and treated the wife as not liable; it was challenged under Arts. 14, 15, 21. Principle: s. 497 struck down; Chandrachud J.: Art. 15(3) "does not protect a statutory provision that entrenches patriarchal notions in the garb of protecting women". Why it matters: Limits of Art. 15(3).
People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India , [1983] 1 SCR 456 (Bhagwati and Baharul Islam JJ.; decided 18 September 1982)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Labour law violations against workers on the Asiad (Asian Games) projects were raised by lett
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Some Fundamental Rights "are enforceable against the whole world and they are to be found inter alia in Articles 17, 23 and 24." Why it matters: Art. 17 binds private persons.
Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India , [1995] Supp 6 SCR (5 judges; A. M. Ahmadi C.J.; decided 15 December 1995)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Petitions sought to stop the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards as "titles" under Art
caseLaws.facts: 18(1). Principle: National Awards are not "titles" and must not be used as prefixes or suffixes; selection guidelines must be improved. Why it matters: Meaning of "title" in Art. 18.

selfTest.q: Who is protected by Art. 14, and who by Arts. 15 and 16?
selfTest.a: Answer: Art. 14 – any person; Arts. 15, 16 – citizens. State the two conditions of reasonable classification. Answer: Intelligible differentia; rational relation to the object of the law. What did Royappa say about arbitrariness? Answer: "Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies"; an arbitrary act is unequal and violates Art. 14. Why was Art. 15(4) inserted? Answer: After Champakam (1951) struck down the Communal G.O. What did Balaji say about percentage? Answer: Generally, a special provision should be less than 50%. Is Art. 16(4) an exception to Art. 16(1)? Answer: No – an instance of classification inherent in Art. 16(1) ( Indra Sawhney ). To what period does the 50% rule apply? Answer: To each year. What did Jarnail Singh change in Nagaraj ? Answer: No need for quantifiable data showing backwardness of SCs/STs. What was the vote in Janhit Abhiyan ? Answer: 3:2 upholding the 103rd Amendment. Can a private person violate Art. 17? Answer: Yes; Art. 17 is enforceable against the whole world ( PUDR ).

te.inOneMinute: భాగం IIIలోని అ. 14 నుండి 18 వరకు "సమానత్వ హక్కు". అ. 14: ఏ వ్యక్తికైనా చట్టం ముందు సమానత్వం , చట్టాల సమాన రక్షణ . అ. 15: మతం, జాతి, కులం, లింగం, జన్మస్థలం అనే ఆధారాలపై మాత్రమే రాజ్యం పౌరుల పట్ల వివక్ష చూపకూడదు; మహిళలు, పిల్లలు, వెనుకబడిన తరగతులు, ఎస్‌సి/ఎస్‌టిలు, ఈడబ్ల్యూఎస్‌కు ప్రత్యేక నిబంధనలు అనుమతించబడ్డాయి. అ. 16: ప్రభుత్వ ఉద్యోగాల్లో అవకాశ సమానత్వం; వెనుకబడిన తరగతులు, ఎస్‌సి/ఎస్‌టిలు (పదోన్నతుల్లో కూడా), ఈడబ్ల్యూఎస్‌కు రిజర్వేషన్ అనుమతి. అ. 17: "అంటరానితనం" రద్దు; దాన్ని పాటించడం నేరం. అ. 18: సైనిక లేదా విద్యా విశిష్టతలు తప్ప రాజ్యం ఏ బిరుదూ ఇవ్వకూడదు. అ. 14 సహేతుక వర్గీకరణ ను నిషేధించదు. వర్గీకరణ గుర్తించదగిన భేదం ( intelligible differentia ) మీద ఆధారపడి, చట్టం లక్ష్యంతో హేతుబద్ధ సంబంధం కలిగి ఉండాలి ( బుధన్ చౌధ్రీ , 1954; రామ్ కృష్ణ దాల్మియా , 1958). అ. 14 ఏకపక్షత ను కూడా దెబ్బతీస్తుంది: "equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies" ( అర్థం: సమానత్వం, ఏకపక్షత బద్ధ శత్రువులు) ( ఇ. పి. రోయప్ప , 1973). రిజర్వేషన్ ( ఇంద్రా సాహ్నీ , 1992): అ. 16(4) అ. 16(1)కు మినహాయింపు కాదు; క్రీమీ లేయర్ ను మినహాయించాలి; అ. 16(4) కింద రిజర్వేషన్ 50% మించకూడదు (అసాధారణ పరిస్థితులు తప్ప). ఆర్థికంగా బలహీన వర్గాలు (అ. 15(6), 16(6), 10% వరకు) – జన్‌హిత్ అభియాన్ (2022)లో 3:2తో సమర్థించబడ్డాయి.
te.meaning: చట్టం ముందు సమానత్వం: ఎవరూ చట్టానికి అతీతులు కారు; అందరికీ ఒకే చట్టం. పతంజలి శాస్త్రి ప్ర.న్యా. ( అన్వర్ అలీ సర్కార్ ): ఇది "a declaration of equality of the civil rights of all persons within the territories of India" ( అర్థం: భారత భూభాగంలోని వ్యక్తులందరి పౌర హక్కుల సమానత్వ ప్రకటన). చట్టాల సమాన రక్షణ: సమాన పరిస్థితుల్లోని వ్యక్తులకు సమాన చట్టాలు. పతంజలి శాస్త్రి ప్ర.న్యా., ఒక అమెరికా కేసును ఉటంకిస్తూ: "it is a pledge of the protection of equal laws" ( అర్థం: ఇది సమాన చట్టాల రక్షణ వాగ్దానం), అంటే "laws that operate alike on all persons under like circumstances" ( అర్థం: ఒకే విధమైన పరిస్థితుల్లోని వ్యక్తులందరిపై ఒకేలా పనిచేసే చట్టాలు). సహేతుక వర్గీకరణ : అ. 14 "forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation" ( అర్థం: వర్గ శాసనాన్ని నిషేధిస్తుంది, శాసన ప్రయోజనాల కోసం సహేతుక వర్గీకరణను నిషేధించదు) ( బుధన్ చౌధ్రీ , హెడ్‌నోట్). ఏకపక్షత : కారణం లేదా సూత్రం లేని చర్య. "Where an act is arbitrary it is implicit in it that it is unequal ... and is therefore violative of Art. 14" ( అర్థం: ఒక చర్య ఏకపక్షమైతే అది అసమానమైనదని అందులోనే ఇమిడి ఉంది ... అందువల్ల అ. 14ను ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది) ( ఇ. పి. రోయప్ప ). వెనుకబడిన తరగతులు : అ. 15(4), 16(4) కింద రాజ్యం సహాయం చేయగల పౌర తరగతులు. "A caste can be and quite often is a social class in India" ( అర్థం: భారతదేశంలో కులం ఒక సామాజిక తరగతి కావచ్చు, తరచుగా అవుతుంది), కానీ వెనుకబడిన తరగతిని "cannot be identified only and exclusively with reference to economic criteria" ( అర్థం: కేవలం, ప్రత్యేకంగా ఆర్థిక ప్రమాణాల ఆధారంగా గుర్తించలేరు) ( ఇంద్రా సాహ్నీ ). క్రీమీ లేయర్ : వెనుకబడిన తరగతిలోని సామాజికంగా అభివృద్ధి చెందిన సభ్యులు; వారిని రిజర్వేషన్ నుండి మినహాయిస్తారు ( ఇంద్రా సాహ్నీ ). ఆర్థికంగా బలహీన వర్గాలు: కుటుంబ ఆదాయం, ఆర్థిక ప్రతికూలత ఇతర సూచికల ఆధారంగా రాజ్యం నోటిఫై చేసే వర్గాలు (అ. 15 వివరణ). అంటరానితనం : అ. 17 రద్దు చేసిన కుల ఆధారిత ఆచారం. రాజ్యాంగం ఈ పదాన్ని నిర్వచించలేదు (వివరణాత్మక వివరణ 6 చూడండి).
keyPoints: అ. 14: ఏ వ్యక్తికైనా; చట్టం ముందు సమానత్వం + చట్టాల సమాన రక్షణ. వర్గీకరణ పరీక్ష: గుర్తించదగిన భేదం + హేతుబద్ధ సంబంధం ( బుధన్ , 1954). ఏకపక్షత సమానత్వానికి వ్యతిరేకం ( రోయప్ప , 1973); స్పష్టమైన ఏకపక్షత చట్టాన్ని రద్దు చేయగలదు ( షాయరా బానో , 2017). అ. 15: పౌరులు; "మాత్రమే" ఆధారాలు; 15(3) మహిళలు/పిల్లలు; చంపకం తర్వాత 1951లో 15(4). "లింగం"లో లింగ గుర్తింపు ఉంది ( నల్సా , 2014). అ. 16(4) మినహాయింపు కాదు; క్రీమీ లేయర్ బయట; సంవత్సరానికి 50% ( ఇంద్రా సాహ్నీ , 1992). పదోన్నతి: అ. 16(4A); ఎస్‌సి/ఎస్‌టిలకు వెనుకబాటుతన గణాంకాలు అవసరం లేదు ( జర్నైల్ సింగ్ , 2018). ఈడబ్ల్యూఎస్ 10% 3:2తో సమర్థన ( జన్‌హిత్ అభియాన్ , 2022). అ. 17 అందరినీ బంధిస్తుంది ( పీయూడీఆర్ ); అ. 18 – పురస్కారాలు బిరుదులు కావు ( బాలాజీ రాఘవన్ ).

selfTest.q: అ. 14 ఎవరిని రక్షిస్తుంది, అ. 15, 16 ఎవరిని?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: అ. 14 – ఏ వ్యక్తినైనా; అ. 15, 16 – పౌరులను. సహేతుక వర్గీకరణ రెండు షరతులు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: గుర్తించదగిన భేదం; చట్టం లక్ష్యంతో హేతుబద్ధ సంబంధం. ఏకపక్షత గురించి రోయప్ప ఏమి చెప్పింది? జవాబు: "Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies" ( అర్థం: సమానత్వం, ఏకపక్షత బద్ధ శత్రువులు); ఏకపక్ష చర్య అసమానం, అ. 14ను ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది. అ. 15(4) ఎందుకు చేర్చారు? జవాబు: కమ్యూనల్ జి.ఓ.ను చంపకం (1951) రద్దు చేసిన తర్వాత. శాతం గురించి బాలాజీ ఏమి చెప్పింది? జవాబు: సాధారణంగా, ప్రత్యేక నిబంధన 50% కంటే తక్కువ ఉండాలి. అ. 16(4) అ. 16(1)కు మినహాయింపా? జవాబు: కాదు – అ. 16(1)లో అంతర్లీన వర్గీకరణకు ఉదాహరణ ( ఇంద్రా సాహ్నీ ). 50% నియమం ఏ కాలానికి వర్తిస్తుంది? జవాబు: ప్రతి సంవత్సరానికి. నాగరాజ్ లో జర్నైల్ సింగ్ ఏమి మార్చింది? జవాబు: ఎస్‌సి/ఎస్‌టిల వెనుకబాటుతనాన్ని చూపే లెక్కించదగిన గణాంకాలు అవసరం లేదు. జన్‌హిత్ అభియాన్ లో ఓటు ఎంత? జవాబు: 103వ సవరణను సమర్థిస్తూ 3:2. ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తి అ. 17ను ఉల్లంఘించగలరా? జవాబు: అవును; అ. 17 ప్రపంచం మొత్తానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా అమలు చేయదగినది ( పీయూడీఆర్ ).

ఇది దీనితో సమానం కాదు ఎందుకు
చట్టం ముందు సమానత్వం చట్టాల సమాన రక్షణ మొదటిది: ఎవరూ చట్టానికి అతీతులు కారు; రెండోది: సమానులను సమానంగా చూడటం.

hi.inOneMinute: Arts. 14 to 18 form the "Right to Equality" in Part III. Art. 14: equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws , for any person . Art. 15: no discrimination by the State against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth; with special provisions allowed for women and children, backward classes, SCs/STs and EWS. Art. 16: equality of opportunity in public employment ; reservation allowed for backward classes, SCs/STs (also in promotion) and EWS. Art. 17: "Untouchability" is abolished; its practice is an offence. Art. 18: the State shall confer no title, except military or academic distinctions. Art. 14 does not forbid reasonable classification . The classification must rest on an intelligible differentia with a rational relation to the object of the law ( Budhan Choudhry , 1954; Ram Krishna Dalmia , 1958). Art. 14 also strikes at arbitrariness : "equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies" ( E. P. Royappa , 1973). Reservation ( Indra Sawhney , 1992): Art. 16(4) is not an exception to Art. 16(1); the creamy layer must be excluded; reservation under Art. 16(4) should not exceed 50% (save extraordinary situations). Economically weaker sections (Arts. 15(6), 16(6), up to 10%) were upheld 3:2 in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 14 – Equality before law: "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India."
Article 15 – Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth:

(1) The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to— (a) access to shops, public restaurants, hotels and places of public entertainment; or (b) the use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads and places of public resort maintained wholly or partly out of State funds or dedicated to the use of the general public. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any special provision for women and children. (4) Nothing in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes.

Cl. (4) was added by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 (w.e.f. 18-6-1951). Cl. (5) (93rd Amendment, w.e.f. 20-1-2006): special provision, by law, for socially and educationally backward classes or SCs/STs in admission to educational institutions , including private ones, aided or unaided, "other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30". Cl. (6) (103rd Amendment, w.e.f. 14-1-2019): special provision for "economically weaker sections of citizens other than the classes mentioned in clauses (4) and (5)", including admission to educational institutions, "subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the total seats in each category", "in addition to the existing reservations". Explanation: "economically weaker sections" are those notified by the State "on the basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage".
Article 16 – Equality of opportunity in matters of public employment:

(1) There shall be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. (2) No citizen shall, on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them, be ineligible for, or discriminated against in respect of, any employment or office under the State. (3) Nothing in this article shall prevent Parliament from making any law prescribing ... any requirement as to residence within that State or Union territory prior to such employment or appointment. (4) Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from making any provision for the reservation of appointments or posts in favour of any backward class of citizens which, in the opinion of the State, is not adequately represented in the services under the State.

Cl. (4A) (77th Amendment, w.e.f. 17-6-1995; words "with consequential seniority" by the 85th Amendment): reservation "in matters of promotion, with consequential seniority" for SCs and STs not adequately represented. Cl. (4B) (81st Amendment, w.e.f. 9-6-2000): unfilled reserved vacancies of a year may be carried forward as a separate class, not counted "for determining the ceiling of fifty per cent. reservation on total number of vacancies of that year". Cl. (5): offices of a religious or denominational institution may be kept for persons of that religion or denomination. Cl. (6) (103rd Amendment, w.e.f. 14-1-2019): reservation for economically weaker sections (other than cl. (4) classes), "in addition to the existing reservation and subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the posts in each category".

Article 17 – Abolition of Untouchability: "'Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of 'Untouchability' shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law."
Article 18 – Abolition of titles:

(1) No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State. (2) No citizen of India shall accept any title from any foreign State. (3) No person who is not a citizen of India shall, while he holds any office of profit or trust under the State, accept without the consent of the President any title from any foreign State. (4) No person holding any office of profit or trust under the State shall, without the consent of the President, accept any present, emolument, or office of any kind from or under any foreign State.
Article 35(a)(ii) (connected): Parliament, and not a State Legislature, has power to make laws "for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under this Part".
In simple words:

Art. 14 is the general rule of equality for everyone. Arts. 15 and 16 apply it to particular areas (discrimination in general; public jobs) and allow special help for groups that need it. Arts. 17 and 18 remove two old forms of inequality: untouchability and titles.
hi.meaning: Equality before the law: no person is above the law; the same law applies to all. Patanjali Sastri C.J. ( Anwar Ali Sarkar ): it is "a declaration of equality of the civil rights of all persons within the territories of India". Equal protection of the laws: equal laws for persons in equal situations. Patanjali Sastri C.J., quoting a U.S. case: "it is a pledge of the protection of equal laws", that is, "laws that operate alike on all persons under like circumstances". Reasonable classification : Art. 14 "forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification for the purposes of legislation" ( Budhan Choudhry , headnote). Arbitrariness : action without reason or principle. "Where an act is arbitrary it is implicit in it that it is unequal ... and is therefore violative of Art. 14" ( E. P. Royappa ). Backward classes : classes of citizens whom the State may help under Arts. 15(4) and 16(4). "A caste can be and quite often is a social class in India", but a backward class "cannot be identified only and exclusively with reference to economic criteria" ( Indra Sawhney ). Creamy layer : the socially advanced members of a backward class, who are excluded from reservation ( Indra Sawhney ). Economically weaker sections: sections notified by the State on the basis of family income and other indicators of economic disadvantage (Explanation to Art. 15). Untouchability : the caste-based practice abolished by Art. 17. The Constitution does not define the word (see Detailed explanation 6).
keyPoints: Art. 14: any person; equality before law + equal protection of laws. Classification test: intelligible differentia + rational nexus ( Budhan , 1954). Arbitrariness is against equality ( Royappa , 1973); manifest arbitrariness can strike down a law ( Shayara Bano , 2017). Art. 15: citizens; grounds "only"; 15(3) women/children; 15(4) added 1951 after Champakam . "Sex" includes gender identity ( NALSA , 2014). Art. 16(4) is not an exception; creamy layer out; 50% per year ( Indra Sawhney , 1992). Promotion: Art. 16(4A); no backwardness data needed for SCs/STs ( Jarnail Singh , 2018). EWS 10% upheld 3:2 ( Janhit Abhiyan , 2022). Art. 17 binds everyone ( PUDR ); Art. 18 – awards are not titles ( Balaji Raghavan ).

caseLaws.facts: State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar , AIR 1952 SC 75; [1952] 1 SCR 284 (7 judges; decided 11 January 1952)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The respondent and 49 others were tried by a Special Court for an armed raid on the Jessop fa
caseLaws.facts: The West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, s. 5(1), let the State Government send any case to the Special Court, which used a shorter procedure. Principle: The unguided power violated Art. 14; the appeals were dismissed (Patanjali Sastri C.J. would have allowed them). Das J. applied the test: the classification "must be founded on an intelligible differentia ... and that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Act". Why it matters: Art. 14 forbids arbitrary laws and arbitrary application of laws, including procedural laws.
Budhan Choudhry v. State of Bihar , [1955] 1 SCR 1045 (7 judges; Das J.; decided 2 December 1954)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Appellants convicted by a magistrate empowered under s
caseLaws.facts: 30 CrPC challenged that section under Art. 14. Principle: Art. 14 "forbids class legislation, it does not forbid reasonable classification"; the two conditions are intelligible differentia and rational relation to the object. s. 30 was valid. Why it matters: The standard statement of the classification test.
Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Justice S. R. Tendolkar , AIR 1958 SC 538; 1959 SCR 279 (5 judges; S. R. Das C.J.; decided 28 March 1958)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A notification under the Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952 appointed a commission to inquire i
caseLaws.facts: 14. Principle: Restated the Budhan test and added principles (a)–(f): a single person may be a class; presumption of constitutionality ; burden on the challenger. Why it matters: The fullest list of Art. 14 classification principles.
E. P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu , AIR 1974 SC 555; (1974) 4 SCC 3; 1974 SCR (2) 348 (5 judges; decided 23 November 1973)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An IAS officer was moved from the post of Chief Secretary to non-cadre posts; he claimed viol
caseLaws.facts: 14 and 16. Principle: Petition dismissed. Bhagwati J. (for himself, Chandrachud and Krishna Iyer JJ.): "equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies"; "Where an act is arbitrary it is implicit in it that it is unequal". Why it matters: Start of the non-arbitrariness doctrine under Art. 14.
State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan , AIR 1951 SC 226; 1951 SCR 525 (7 judges; decided 9 April 1951)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Communal G
caseLaws.facts: O. allotted medical and engineering college seats community-wise (6, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1 out of every 14). Principle: It violated Art. 29(2) and was void under Art. 13; Directive Principles cannot override Fundamental Rights. Why it matters: Led to Art. 15(4) (First Amendment, 1951).
M. R. Balaji v. State of Mysore , [1963] Supp 1 SCR 439 (5 judges; Gajendragadkar J.; decided 28 September 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Mysore reserved 68% of seats in engineering and medical colleges for backward classes, SCs an
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The order was "a fraud on the constitutional power" under Art. 15(4); caste cannot be the sole basis; "Speaking generally and in a broad way, a special provision should be less than 50%." Why it matters: Origin of the 50% limit.
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India , AIR 1993 SC 477; 1992 Supp (3) SCC 217 (9 judges; leading judgment by B. P. Jeevan Reddy J.; decided 16 November 1992)

caseLaws.name: Facts: O
caseLaws.facts: M. of 13-8-1990 reserved 27% of central government posts for SEBCs (Mandal Commission); O.M. of 25-9-1991 added preference for poorer sections and 10% for other economically backward sections. Principle: Art. 16(4) not an exception to 16(1); caste can be a class; creamy layer excluded; not economic criterion alone; 50% per year; no reservation in promotions under Art. 16(4) (prospective); the 10% economic reservation struck down. Why it matters: The leading case on reservation.
M. Nagaraj v. Union of India , AIR 2007 SC 71; (2006) 8 SCC 212 (5 judges; Kapadia J.; decided 19 October 2006)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th Amendments (Arts
caseLaws.facts: 16(4A), 16(4B), proviso to Art. 335) were challenged as against the basic structure. Principle: Amendments valid; 50% ceiling, creamy layer, backwardness, inadequacy of representation and efficiency remain "constitutional requirements"; quantifiable data needed. Why it matters: Conditions for reservation in promotion (later modified by Jarnail Singh ).
Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta , [2018] 10 SCR 663 (5 judges; decided 26 September 2018)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Reference on whether Nagaraj needed reconsideration by seven judges
caseLaws.facts: Principle: No reference needed, but Nagaraj 's requirement of quantifiable data showing backwardness of SCs/STs was "contrary to the nine-Judge Bench in Indra Sawhney" and invalid to that extent; creamy layer principle applies. Why it matters: Current law on SC/ST promotion reservation.
Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India , W.P. (C) No. 55 of 2019 (5 judges; decided 7 November 2022)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 103rd Amendment (EWS reservation, Arts
caseLaws.facts: 15(6), 16(6)) was challenged as violating the basic structure. Principle: Upheld 3:2; economic criteria alone, exclusion of SEBCs/SCs/STs, and 10% over 50% do not breach the basic structure (Maheshwari J.); Bhat J. (with Lalit C.J.I.) dissented. Why it matters: Current law on EWS reservation.
National Legal Services Authority v. Union of India , W.P. (C) No. 400 of 2012 (Radhakrishnan and Sikri JJ.; decided 15 April 2014)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Petition for recognition and rights of transgender persons
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "'sex' under Articles 15 and 16 ... includes discrimination on the ground of gender identity". Why it matters: Widens the "sex" ground.
Joseph Shine v. Union of India , W.P. (Crl.) No. 194 of 2017 (5 judges; decided 27 September 2018)

Principle: s. 497 struck down; Chandrachud J.: Art. 15(3) "does not protect a statutory provision that entrenches patriarchal notions in the garb of protecting women". Why it matters: Limits of Art. 15(3).
People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India , [1983] 1 SCR 456 (Bhagwati and Baharul Islam JJ.; decided 18 September 1982)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Labour law violations against workers on the Asiad (Asian Games) projects were raised by lett
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Some Fundamental Rights "are enforceable against the whole world and they are to be found inter alia in Articles 17, 23 and 24." Why it matters: Art. 17 binds private persons.
Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India , [1995] Supp 6 SCR (5 judges; A. M. Ahmadi C.J.; decided 15 December 1995)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Petitions sought to stop the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards as "titles" under Art
caseLaws.facts: 18(1). Principle: National Awards are not "titles" and must not be used as prefixes or suffixes; selection guidelines must be improved. Why it matters: Meaning of "title" in Art. 18.

selfTest.q: Who is protected by Art. 14, and who by Arts. 15 and 16?
selfTest.a: Answer: Art. 14 – any person; Arts. 15, 16 – citizens. State the two conditions of reasonable classification. Answer: Intelligible differentia; rational relation to the object of the law. What did Royappa say about arbitrariness? Answer: "Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies"; an arbitrary act is unequal and violates Art. 14. Why was Art. 15(4) inserted? Answer: After Champakam (1951) struck down the Communal G.O. What did Balaji say about percentage? Answer: Generally, a special provision should be less than 50%. Is Art. 16(4) an exception to Art. 16(1)? Answer: No – an instance of classification inherent in Art. 16(1) ( Indra Sawhney ). To what period does the 50% rule apply? Answer: To each year. What did Jarnail Singh change in Nagaraj ? Answer: No need for quantifiable data showing backwardness of SCs/STs. What was the vote in Janhit Abhiyan ? Answer: 3:2 upholding the 103rd Amendment. Can a private person violate Art. 17? Answer: Yes; Art. 17 is enforceable against the whole world ( PUDR ).

constitutional-law-i-u3-t8.subtitle: Article 22: the safeguards for a person arrested, the separate rules for preventive detention, and the guidelines of Joginder Kumar and D.K. Basu

en.inOneMinute: Article 22 has two parts: Ordinary arrest – clauses (1) and (2): the arrested person must be told the grounds "as soon as may be", may consult and be defended by a lawyer of his choice, and must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours (journey time excluded). Preventive detention – clauses (3) to (7): clauses (1) and (2) do not apply; instead the detenu gets the grounds "as soon as may be", the "earliest opportunity" of making a representation, and an Advisory Board review before detention goes beyond three months . Enemy aliens get neither set of protections under clauses (1) and (2) (Art. 22(3)(a)). Preventive vs punitive: preventive detention is "not a punitive but a precautionary measure" – it aims to stop a person before he acts ( A. K. Gopalan , Mukherjea J.). Courts added safeguards from Arts. 21 and 22(1): the right to have a friend or relative told of the arrest ( Joginder Kumar , 1994); 11 requirements including a memo of arrest ( D. K. Basu , 1996). The BNSS, 2023 now contains most of them (ss. 35–38, 47, 48, 53, 58). 44th Amendment (1978) would reduce three months to two months, but s. 3 is not yet in force ; the Court would not compel the Government to notify it ( A. K. Roy , 1981).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 22 – "Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases."

(1) "No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice." (2) "Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate." (3) "Nothing in clauses (1) and (2) shall apply— (a) to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or (b) to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention." (4) "No law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless— (a) an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention: Provided that nothing in this sub-clause shall authorise the detention of any person beyond the maximum period prescribed by any law made by Parliament under sub-clause (b) of clause (7); or (b) such person is detained in accordance with the provisions of any law made by Parliament under sub-clauses (a) and (b) of clause (7)." (5) "When any person is detained in pursuance of an order made under any law providing for preventive detention, the authority making the order shall, as soon as may be, communicate to such person the grounds on which the order has been made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order." (6) "Nothing in clause (5) shall require the authority making any such order as is referred to in that clause to disclose facts which such authority considers to be against the public interest to disclose." (7) Parliament may by law prescribe— (a) the circumstances and classes of cases in which a person may be detained for longer than three months without an Advisory Board opinion; (b) "the maximum period for which any person may in any class or classes of cases be detained"; (c) the procedure of an Advisory Board.

Footnote in the Constitution (44th Amendment, s. 3, "date yet to be notified"): cl. (4) "shall stand substituted" by a new clause – maximum two months without an Advisory Board report; the Board to be constituted "in accordance with the recommendations of the Chief Justice of the appropriate High Court", with a Chairman who is "a serving Judge of the appropriate High Court"; and cl. (7)(a) to be omitted.
Power to make preventive detention laws (Seventh Schedule):

List I, Entry 9: "Preventive detention for reasons connected with Defence, Foreign Affairs, or the security of India; persons subjected to such detention." List III, Entry 3: "Preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State, the maintenance of public order, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community; persons subjected to such detention."
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (statutory safeguards on arrest):

s. 35(3)–(6): where arrest is not required, the police "shall… issue a notice" to appear; a person who complies "shall not be arrested… unless, for reasons to be recorded". s. 36: officer must bear "an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name"; prepare a memorandum of arrest attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee; inform the arrestee of the right to have a relative or friend informed. s. 37: police control room in every district and at State level; designated officer to display names of arrested persons. s. 38: the arrested person "shall be entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation." s. 47(1): the officer "shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest"; s. 47(2): if the offence is bailable, inform him of the right to bail. s. 48: inform a relative or friend and the designated officer "forthwith"; entry in a book; the Magistrate must satisfy himself that this was done. s. 53(1): medical examination soon after arrest. s. 58: no detention without warrant beyond 24 hours (journey excluded) without a Magistrate's special order under s. 187.
en.meaning: Arrest: taking a person into custody under legal authority, usually for an offence. Art. 22(1)–(2) protects such a person. Preventive detention : detention without trial to prevent a person from acting in a harmful way in future. "The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept him before he does it and to prevent him from doing it. No offence is proved, nor any charge formulated; and the justification of such detention is suspicion or reasonable probability and not criminal conviction" ( A. K. Gopalan , Mukherjea J.). Punitive detention: detention after a trial and conviction, as punishment for an offence already committed. Advisory Board : a body of persons who are, have been, or are qualified to be High Court Judges, which must report "sufficient cause" before preventive detention can go beyond three months (Art. 22(4)(a)). Detenu: a person held under a preventive detention order. Memo of arrest : a written record made at the time of arrest, attested by a witness (family member or respectable local person), countersigned by the arrestee, and showing the time and date of arrest ( D. K. Basu , requirement 2; BNSS s. 36(b)). Enemy alien: Art. 22(3)(a) uses the words "enemy alien" without defining them; for such a person, "for the time being", Art. 22(1)–(2) do not apply.
keyPoints: Art. 22(1): grounds "as soon as may be"; lawyer of choice. Art. 22(2): Magistrate within 24 hours, journey excluded. Art. 22(3): not for enemy aliens or preventive detainees. Art. 22(4): Advisory Board before 3 months. Art. 22(5): grounds and earliest opportunity of representation; (6) public-interest facts may be withheld. Art. 22(7): Parliament may allow longer detention without a Board and fix maximum period. 44th Amendment s. 3 (2 months) not in force ( A. K. Roy ). Joginder Kumar (1994); D. K. Basu (1996, 11 requirements).

selfTest.q: Within what time must an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate?
selfTest.a: Answer: 24 hours, excluding journey time (Art. 22(2)). To whom do Art. 22(1) and (2) not apply? Answer: Enemy aliens and persons under preventive detention laws (Art. 22(3)). What is the maximum detention without an Advisory Board report (as in force)? Answer: Three months (Art. 22(4)(a)), unless a law under Art. 22(7)(a) applies. Why is the two-month limit not in force? Answer: Section 3 of the 44th Amendment has not been notified; A. K. Roy refused mandamus. Can a detenu be represented by a lawyer before the Board? Answer: Not as of right; only if the Government uses a lawyer; a friend may assist ( A. K. Roy ). Which case said "No arrest can be made because it is lawful for the police officer to do so"? Answer: Joginder Kumar (1994). Arrest at 8 p.m.; journey 4 hours. Latest time for production? Answer: Midnight the next day (8 p.m. + 24 h + 4 h). How often must an arrestee be medically examined under D. K. Basu ? Answer: Every 48 hours. Under which List and Entry can States make preventive detention laws for public order? Answer: List III, Entry 3. When was Art. 22 (as draft Art. 15A) adopted by the Constituent Assembly? Answer: 16 September 1949.

te.inOneMinute: అధికరణ 22 కు రెండు భాగాలు ఉన్నాయి: సాధారణ అరెస్టు – క్లాజులు (1), (2): అరెస్టయిన వ్యక్తికి కారణాలు "as soon as may be" ( అర్థం: వీలైనంత త్వరగా) చెప్పాలి; తనకు నచ్చిన న్యాయవాదిని సంప్రదించవచ్చు, ఆయన ద్వారా వాదించుకోవచ్చు; 24 గంటల లోపు (ప్రయాణ సమయం మినహా) సమీప మేజిస్ట్రేట్ ముందు హాజరుపరచాలి. నివారక నిర్బంధం – క్లాజులు (3) నుండి (7): క్లాజులు (1), (2) వర్తించవు; బదులుగా నిర్బంధితునికి "as soon as may be" ( అర్థం: వీలైనంత త్వరగా) కారణాలు, ప్రాతినిధ్యం చేయడానికి "earliest opportunity" ( అర్థం: తొలి అవకాశం), నిర్బంధం మూడు నెలలు దాటే ముందు సలహా మండలి సమీక్ష లభిస్తాయి. శత్రు విదేశీయులకు క్లాజులు (1), (2) కింద ఈ రక్షణలు లేవు (అధికరణ 22(3)(a)). నివారక vs శిక్షాత్మక: నివారక నిర్బంధం "not a punitive but a precautionary measure" ( అర్థం: శిక్ష కాదు, ముందు జాగ్రత్త చర్య) – వ్యక్తి చర్య చేయకముందే ఆపడం దీని లక్ష్యం ( A. K. Gopalan , ముఖర్జియా న్యాయమూర్తి). కోర్టులు అధికరణలు 21, 22(1) నుండి రక్షణలు జోడించాయి: అరెస్టు గురించి స్నేహితుడు లేదా బంధువుకు తెలియజేసే హక్కు ( Joginder Kumar , 1994); అరెస్టు మెమో తో సహా 11 అవసరాలు ( D. K. Basu , 1996). వీటిలో చాలా భాగం ఇప్పుడు BNSS, 2023లో ఉంది (సెక్షన్లు 35–38, 47, 48, 53, 58). 44వ సవరణ (1978) మూడు నెలలను రెండు నెలలకు తగ్గిస్తుంది, కానీ సెక్షన్ 3 ఇంకా అమలులోకి రాలేదు ; దానిని నోటిఫై చేయమని కోర్టు ప్రభుత్వాన్ని బలవంతం చేయలేదు ( A. K. Roy , 1981).
te.meaning: అరెస్టు: చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం కింద, సాధారణంగా ఒక నేరం కోసం, ఒక వ్యక్తిని కస్టడీలోకి తీసుకోవడం. అధికరణ 22(1)–(2) అలాంటి వ్యక్తిని రక్షిస్తుంది. నివారక నిర్బంధం : భవిష్యత్తులో హానికరంగా ప్రవర్తించకుండా ఆపడానికి విచారణ లేకుండా నిర్బంధించడం. "The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept him before he does it and to prevent him from doing it. No offence is proved, nor any charge formulated; and the justification of such detention is suspicion or reasonable probability and not criminal conviction" ( అర్థం: ఏదో చేసినందుకు శిక్షించడం లక్ష్యం కాదు; చేయకముందే అడ్డుకుని, చేయకుండా ఆపడం లక్ష్యం. ఏ నేరమూ రుజువు కాదు, ఏ అభియోగమూ ఉండదు; ఈ నిర్బంధానికి సమర్థన అనుమానం లేదా సహేతుక సంభావ్యత, నేర నిర్ధారణ కాదు) ( A. K. Gopalan , ముఖర్జియా న్యాయమూర్తి). శిక్షాత్మక నిర్బంధం: విచారణ, నేర నిర్ధారణ తర్వాత, ఇప్పటికే చేసిన నేరానికి శిక్షగా నిర్బంధం. సలహా మండలి : హైకోర్టు న్యాయమూర్తులుగా ఉన్న, ఉండిన, లేదా అర్హులైన వ్యక్తుల మండలి; నివారక నిర్బంధం మూడు నెలలు దాటే ముందు "sufficient cause" ( అర్థం: తగిన కారణం) ఉందని నివేదించాలి (అధికరణ 22(4)(a)). నిర్బంధితుడు ( Detenu ): నివారక నిర్బంధ ఉత్తర్వు కింద ఉంచబడిన వ్యక్తి. అరెస్టు మెమో : అరెస్టు సమయంలో తయారు చేసే లిఖిత నమోదు; సాక్షి (కుటుంబ సభ్యుడు లేదా స్థానిక గౌరవనీయ వ్యక్తి) ధృవీకరించి, అరెస్టయిన వ్యక్తి ప్రతి సంతకం చేసి, అరెస్టు సమయం, తేదీ ఉంటాయి ( D. K. Basu , అవసరం 2; BNSS సెక్షన్ 36(b)). శత్రు విదేశీయుడు: అధికరణ 22(3)(a) "enemy alien" అనే మాటను నిర్వచించకుండా వాడుతుంది; అలాంటి వ్యక్తికి "for the time being" ( అర్థం: ప్రస్తుతానికి) అధికరణ 22(1)–(2) వర్తించవు.
keyPoints: అధికరణ 22(1): కారణాలు "as soon as may be" ( అర్థం: వీలైనంత త్వరగా); నచ్చిన న్యాయవాది. అధికరణ 22(2): 24 గంటల్లో మేజిస్ట్రేట్, ప్రయాణం మినహా. అధికరణ 22(3): శత్రు విదేశీయులకు, నివారక నిర్బంధితులకు వర్తించదు. అధికరణ 22(4): 3 నెలల ముందు సలహా మండలి. అధికరణ 22(5): కారణాలు, ప్రాతినిధ్యానికి తొలి అవకాశం; (6) ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వాస్తవాలు దాచవచ్చు. అధికరణ 22(7): మండలి లేకుండా ఎక్కువ నిర్బంధాన్ని పార్లమెంటు అనుమతించవచ్చు, గరిష్ట కాలం నిర్ణయించవచ్చు. 44వ సవరణ సెక్షన్ 3 (2 నెలలు) అమలులో లేదు ( A. K. Roy ). Joginder Kumar (1994); D. K. Basu (1996, 11 అవసరాలు).

selfTest.q: అరెస్టయిన వ్యక్తిని ఎంత సమయంలో మేజిస్ట్రేట్ ముందు హాజరుపరచాలి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: ప్రయాణ సమయం మినహా 24 గంటలు (అధికరణ 22(2)). అధికరణ 22(1), (2) ఎవరికి వర్తించవు? జవాబు: శత్రు విదేశీయులకు, నివారక నిర్బంధ చట్టాల కింద ఉన్నవారికి (అధికరణ 22(3)). సలహా మండలి నివేదిక లేకుండా గరిష్ట నిర్బంధం (అమలులో ఉన్నట్లు) ఎంత? జవాబు: మూడు నెలలు (అధికరణ 22(4)(a)), అధికరణ 22(7)(a) కింద చట్టం వర్తిస్తే తప్ప. రెండు నెలల పరిమితి ఎందుకు అమలులో లేదు? జవాబు: 44వ సవరణ సెక్షన్ 3 నోటిఫై కాలేదు; A. K. Roy మాండమస్ నిరాకరించింది. మండలి ముందు నిర్బంధితుని తరఫున న్యాయవాది ఉండవచ్చా? జవాబు: హక్కుగా కాదు; ప్రభుత్వం న్యాయవాదిని వాడితేనే; స్నేహితుడు సహాయం చేయవచ్చు ( A. K. Roy ). "No arrest can be made because it is lawful for the police officer to do so" ( అర్థం: పోలీసు అధికారికి చట్టబద్ధంగా వీలుంది అనే కారణంతో అరెస్టు చేయరాదు) అని ఏ కేసు చెప్పింది? జవాబు: Joginder Kumar (1994). రాత్రి 8 గంటలకు అరెస్టు; ప్రయాణం 4 గంటలు. హాజరుకు చివరి సమయం? జవాబు: మరుసటి రోజు అర్ధరాత్రి (రాత్రి 8 + 24 గంటలు + 4 గంటలు). D. K. Basu ప్రకారం అరెస్టయిన వ్యక్తికి ఎంత తరచుగా వైద్య పరీక్ష చేయాలి? జవాబు: ప్రతి 48 గంటలకు. ప్రజా శాంతి కోసం నివారక నిర్బంధ చట్టాలను రాష్ట్రాలు ఏ జాబితా, ఎంట్రీ కింద చేయవచ్చు? జవాబు: జాబితా III, ఎంట్రీ 3. అధికరణ 22 (ముసాయిదా అధికరణ 15Aగా) రాజ్యాంగ సభలో ఎప్పుడు ఆమోదించబడింది? జవాబు: 16 సెప్టెంబర్ 1949.

visuals.html:
