hi.inOneMinute: Article 22 has two parts: Ordinary arrest – clauses (1) and (2): the arrested person must be told the grounds "as soon as may be", may consult and be defended by a lawyer of his choice, and must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours (journey time excluded). Preventive detention – clauses (3) to (7): clauses (1) and (2) do not apply; instead the detenu gets the grounds "as soon as may be", the "earliest opportunity" of making a representation, and an Advisory Board review before detention goes beyond three months . Enemy aliens get neither set of protections under clauses (1) and (2) (Art. 22(3)(a)). Preventive vs punitive: preventive detention is "not a punitive but a precautionary measure" – it aims to stop a person before he acts ( A. K. Gopalan , Mukherjea J.). Courts added safeguards from Arts. 21 and 22(1): the right to have a friend or relative told of the arrest ( Joginder Kumar , 1994); 11 requirements including a memo of arrest ( D. K. Basu , 1996). The BNSS, 2023 now contains most of them (ss. 35–38, 47, 48, 53, 58). 44th Amendment (1978) would reduce three months to two months, but s. 3 is not yet in force ; the Court would not compel the Government to notify it ( A. K. Roy , 1981).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 22 – "Protection against arrest and detention in certain cases."

(1) "No person who is arrested shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest nor shall he be denied the right to consult, and to be defended by, a legal practitioner of his choice." (2) "Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court of the magistrate and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate." (3) "Nothing in clauses (1) and (2) shall apply— (a) to any person who for the time being is an enemy alien; or (b) to any person who is arrested or detained under any law providing for preventive detention." (4) "No law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless— (a) an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention: Provided that nothing in this sub-clause shall authorise the detention of any person beyond the maximum period prescribed by any law made by Parliament under sub-clause (b) of clause (7); or (b) such person is detained in accordance with the provisions of any law made by Parliament under sub-clauses (a) and (b) of clause (7)." (5) "When any person is detained in pursuance of an order made under any law providing for preventive detention, the authority making the order shall, as soon as may be, communicate to such person the grounds on which the order has been made and shall afford him the earliest opportunity of making a representation against the order." (6) "Nothing in clause (5) shall require the authority making any such order as is referred to in that clause to disclose facts which such authority considers to be against the public interest to disclose." (7) Parliament may by law prescribe— (a) the circumstances and classes of cases in which a person may be detained for longer than three months without an Advisory Board opinion; (b) "the maximum period for which any person may in any class or classes of cases be detained"; (c) the procedure of an Advisory Board.

Footnote in the Constitution (44th Amendment, s. 3, "date yet to be notified"): cl. (4) "shall stand substituted" by a new clause – maximum two months without an Advisory Board report; the Board to be constituted "in accordance with the recommendations of the Chief Justice of the appropriate High Court", with a Chairman who is "a serving Judge of the appropriate High Court"; and cl. (7)(a) to be omitted.
Power to make preventive detention laws (Seventh Schedule):

List I, Entry 9: "Preventive detention for reasons connected with Defence, Foreign Affairs, or the security of India; persons subjected to such detention." List III, Entry 3: "Preventive detention for reasons connected with the security of a State, the maintenance of public order, or the maintenance of supplies and services essential to the community; persons subjected to such detention."
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (statutory safeguards on arrest):

s. 35(3)–(6): where arrest is not required, the police "shall… issue a notice" to appear; a person who complies "shall not be arrested… unless, for reasons to be recorded". s. 36: officer must bear "an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name"; prepare a memorandum of arrest attested by a witness and countersigned by the arrestee; inform the arrestee of the right to have a relative or friend informed. s. 37: police control room in every district and at State level; designated officer to display names of arrested persons. s. 38: the arrested person "shall be entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout interrogation." s. 47(1): the officer "shall forthwith communicate to him full particulars of the offence for which he is arrested or other grounds for such arrest"; s. 47(2): if the offence is bailable, inform him of the right to bail. s. 48: inform a relative or friend and the designated officer "forthwith"; entry in a book; the Magistrate must satisfy himself that this was done. s. 53(1): medical examination soon after arrest. s. 58: no detention without warrant beyond 24 hours (journey excluded) without a Magistrate's special order under s. 187.
hi.meaning: Arrest: taking a person into custody under legal authority, usually for an offence. Art. 22(1)–(2) protects such a person. Preventive detention : detention without trial to prevent a person from acting in a harmful way in future. "The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept him before he does it and to prevent him from doing it. No offence is proved, nor any charge formulated; and the justification of such detention is suspicion or reasonable probability and not criminal conviction" ( A. K. Gopalan , Mukherjea J.). Punitive detention: detention after a trial and conviction, as punishment for an offence already committed. Advisory Board : a body of persons who are, have been, or are qualified to be High Court Judges, which must report "sufficient cause" before preventive detention can go beyond three months (Art. 22(4)(a)). Detenu: a person held under a preventive detention order. Memo of arrest : a written record made at the time of arrest, attested by a witness (family member or respectable local person), countersigned by the arrestee, and showing the time and date of arrest ( D. K. Basu , requirement 2; BNSS s. 36(b)). Enemy alien: Art. 22(3)(a) uses the words "enemy alien" without defining them; for such a person, "for the time being", Art. 22(1)–(2) do not apply.
keyPoints: Art. 22(1): grounds "as soon as may be"; lawyer of choice. Art. 22(2): Magistrate within 24 hours, journey excluded. Art. 22(3): not for enemy aliens or preventive detainees. Art. 22(4): Advisory Board before 3 months. Art. 22(5): grounds and earliest opportunity of representation; (6) public-interest facts may be withheld. Art. 22(7): Parliament may allow longer detention without a Board and fix maximum period. 44th Amendment s. 3 (2 months) not in force ( A. K. Roy ). Joginder Kumar (1994); D. K. Basu (1996, 11 requirements).

selfTest.q: Within what time must an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate?
selfTest.a: Answer: 24 hours, excluding journey time (Art. 22(2)). To whom do Art. 22(1) and (2) not apply? Answer: Enemy aliens and persons under preventive detention laws (Art. 22(3)). What is the maximum detention without an Advisory Board report (as in force)? Answer: Three months (Art. 22(4)(a)), unless a law under Art. 22(7)(a) applies. Why is the two-month limit not in force? Answer: Section 3 of the 44th Amendment has not been notified; A. K. Roy refused mandamus. Can a detenu be represented by a lawyer before the Board? Answer: Not as of right; only if the Government uses a lawyer; a friend may assist ( A. K. Roy ). Which case said "No arrest can be made because it is lawful for the police officer to do so"? Answer: Joginder Kumar (1994). Arrest at 8 p.m.; journey 4 hours. Latest time for production? Answer: Midnight the next day (8 p.m. + 24 h + 4 h). How often must an arrestee be medically examined under D. K. Basu ? Answer: Every 48 hours. Under which List and Entry can States make preventive detention laws for public order? Answer: List III, Entry 3. When was Art. 22 (as draft Art. 15A) adopted by the Constituent Assembly? Answer: 16 September 1949.

en.meaning:
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002), makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for children of what age group?

Explanation. Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years, in such manner as the State may, by law, determine.

Parliament gave effect to Article 21A by enacting which statute?

Explanation. The RTE Act, 2009 operationalises Article 21A, laying down norms for schools, teacher qualifications, prohibition of screening tests/capitation fees, and a 25% reservation for economically weaker/disadvantaged children in private unaided schools.

In Society for Un-aided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2012), the Supreme Court upheld the RTE Act's 25% reservation for economically weaker sections in:

Explanation. A three-Judge Bench upheld the 25 per cent rule as a reasonable restriction on the trade and profession of private schools. The majority exempted unaided minority schools, whose right comes from Article 30(1).

In Society for Un-aided Private Schools of Rajasthan, Radhakrishnan J. dissented, holding that the RTE Act should not bind:

constitutional-law-i-u3-t2.subtitle: The six freedoms of citizens, the grounds on which each can be restricted, and the cases on speech, sedition, the internet and the anthem

en.inOneMinute: Six freedoms for citizens: Art. 19(1) gives all citizens six freedoms: (a) freedom of speech and expression ; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of India; (g) to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business. Sub-clause (f) (property) was omitted by the 44th Amendment (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). The restrictions: each freedom may be limited only by a law imposing reasonable restrictions on the grounds listed in its own clause, Art. 19(2) to (6). Speech has eight grounds in Art. 19(2), and they are exhaustive ( Kaushal Kishor , 2023). Romesh Thappar (1950): "freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, and that freedom is ensured by the freedom of circulation." Meaning of "reasonable": not "arbitrary or of an excessive nature" ( Chintaman Rao , as quoted in Shreya Singhal ). Shreya Singhal (2015): only incitement , not mere discussion or advocacy, can be restricted. S. 66A of the IT Act was struck down. Effect, not form: the test is the direct and inevitable effect of State action ( Bennett Coleman , 1972; Maneka Gandhi , 1978). Internet and proportionality: speech and trade over the internet are protected. Restrictions must satisfy proportionality ( Anuradha Bhasin , 2020).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 19(1): "All citizens shall have the right—

(a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (f) * * * (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business."
"or co-operative societies" was inserted by the 97th Amendment, w.e.f. 8-2-2012. Sub-clause (f) was omitted by the 44th Amendment, w.e.f. 20-6-1979.

Article 19(2) (substituted by the First Amendment, 1951, "with retrospective effect"): "Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence."
"the sovereignty and integrity of India" was inserted by the 16th Amendment, w.e.f. 5-10-1963.
Article 19(3): reasonable restrictions on (b) "in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order".
Article 19(4): reasonable restrictions on (c) "in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order or morality".
Article 19(5): reasonable restrictions on (d) and (e) "either in the interests of the general public or for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe".
Article 19(6): reasonable restrictions on (g) "in the interests of the general public". In particular, nothing in (g) affects any law relating to:

(i) the professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade or business; or (ii) the carrying on by the State, or by a corporation owned or controlled by the State, of any trade, business, industry or service, whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.
In simple words:
Every citizen has six freedoms. The State can limit each one only by a law, only for the reasons written in that freedom's own clause, and only by a restriction that is reasonable.
en.meaning: Freedom of speech and expression: the right to express one's views by word, writing, print, picture or any other medium. It includes propagation and circulation of ideas ( Romesh Thappar ), freedom of the press ( Brij Bhushan ; Bennett Coleman ) and expression over the internet ( Anuradha Bhasin ). Reasonable restriction : "the limitation imposed on a person in enjoyment of the right should not be arbitrary or of an excessive nature, beyond what is required in the interests of the public" ( Chintaman Rao , quoted in Shreya Singhal ). Public order : a ground in Arts. 19(2)–(4). Of the "three concentric circles", "Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State" ( Ram Manohar Lohia , quoted in Shreya Singhal ). Direct and inevitable effect: the Court looks at "the direct and inevitable consequence or effect of the impugned state action on the fundamental right", not only its object or form ( Maneka Gandhi , headnote of Bhagwati J.'s opinion). Proportionality: a restriction must not go beyond what is necessary for its purpose. Restrictions on internet speech and trade must be "in consonance with the mandate under Article 19 (2) and (6) of the Constitution, inclusive of the test of proportionality" ( Anuradha Bhasin ). Chilling effect : a vague or wide law makes people afraid to speak even lawful speech. S. 66A "has a chilling effect on the freedom of speech and expression" ( Shreya Singhal ).
keyPoints: Six freedoms for citizens; (f) omitted w.e.f. 20-6-1979. Each freedom has its own restriction clause: 19(2) for (a), 19(3) for (b), 19(4) for (c), 19(5) for (d) and (e), 19(6) for (g). Eight speech grounds; exhaustive ( Kaushal Kishor , 2023). Circulation ( Romesh Thappar ); no pre-censorship ( Brij Bhushan ). "Public order" added in 1951 after Romesh Thappar . Discussion, advocacy, incitement ( Shreya Singhal , 2015). Reasonable = not arbitrary or excessive ( Chintaman Rao ). Effect test ( Bennett Coleman ; Maneka Gandhi ). Internet: proportionate and temporary ( Anuradha Bhasin , 2020).

caseLaws.facts: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras , AIR 1950 SC 124; [1950] SCR 594 (6 judges; decided 26 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Madras banned the entry and circulation of the Bombay weekly Cross Roads under s
caseLaws.facts: 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949. Principle: Freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation. A law for the wider purpose of "public safety or the maintenance of public order" fell outside the original Art. 19(2) and was void (Fazl Ali J. dissenting). Why it matters: Led to the First Amendment (1951) adding "public order"; over-wide laws are wholly void.
Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi , [1950] SCR 605 (decided 26 May 1950; Patanjali Sastri J. for the majority)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Chief Commissioner of Delhi ordered pre-censorship of the English weekly Organizer under
caseLaws.facts: 7(1)(c) of the East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949. Principle: "the imposition of pre-censorship on a journal is a restriction on the liberty of the press which is an essential part of the right to freedom of speech and expression". Why it matters: Freedom of the press is part of Art. 19(1)(a).
Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar , 1962 AIR 955; 1962 Supp (2) SCR 769 (5 judges; Sinha C.J.; decided 20 January 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The appellant was convicted under ss
caseLaws.facts: 124A and 505 IPC for a speech; the sections were challenged under Art. 19(1)(a). Principle: s. 124A is valid only when limited "to acts involving intention or tendency to create disorder, or disturbance of law and order, or incitement to violence"; strong criticism of Government is not sedition. Why it matters: Reading down a speech offence to fit Art. 19(2).
Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India , [1973] 2 SCR 757 (5 judges; decided 30 October 1972)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The newsprint policy for 1972–73 fixed a 10-page limit and barred new newspapers and editions
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Majority (Sikri C.J., Ray and Jaganmohan Reddy JJ.; Beg J. concurring; Mathew J. dissenting): the direct effect of the policy infringed Art. 19(1)(a); shareholders can claim for the company. Why it matters: Effect test; economic controls on the press.
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India , 1978 AIR 597; 1978 SCR (2) 621; (1978) 1 SCC 248 (7 judges; decided 25 January 1978)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded under s
caseLaws.facts: 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 without reasons or hearing. Principle (Bhagwati J.'s opinion, headnote): Art. 19(1)(a) has no geographical limits; the test is the "direct and inevitable consequence" of State action; the right to go abroad is not itself an Art. 19(1) right. Why it matters: Effect test; scope of Art. 19 beyond India.
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala , 1987 AIR 748; 1986 SCR (3) 518; (1986) 3 SCC 615 (O. Chinnappa Reddy and M. M. Dutt JJ.; decided 11 August 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Three Jehovah's Witness children stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem, and
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Expulsion violated Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25(1); a restriction needs a law, not an executive instruction. Why it matters: Freedom of speech includes the freedom to remain silent respectfully.
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India , AIR 2015 SC 1523 (J. Chelameswar and R. F. Nariman JJ.; decided 24 March 2015)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Writ petitions under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 challenged s. 66A of the IT Act, 2000 (added w.e.f. 27-10-2009), which punished sending "grossly offensive" or annoying messages by computer or communication device. Principle: Only incitement can be restricted; s. 66A is vague, has a chilling effect, and was struck down in its entirety. Why it matters: The modern test for speech restrictions.
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India , W.P. (C) No. 1031 of 2019 (N. V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy, B. R. Gavai JJ.; decided 10 January 2020)

caseLaws.name: Facts: From 04-08-2019, mobile networks, internet and movement were restricted in Jammu and Kashmir;
caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: Speech and trade over the internet are protected by Arts. 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); restrictions must meet proportionality; indefinite internet suspension is impermissible. Why it matters: Applies Art. 19 to the internet.
Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. , W.P. (Crl.) No. 113 of 2016 (5 judges; decided 3 January 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Statements of a Minister about a crime victim led to questions on limits of free speech
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Majority: the Art. 19(2) grounds are exhaustive; no additional restrictions can be imposed by invoking other rights; Arts. 19/21 can be enforced against non-State persons. Why it matters: Closes the list of speech restrictions.
T. M. A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka , [2002] Supp 3 SCR (11 judges; Kirpal C.J.; decided 31 October 2002)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Questions about the rights of private and minority educational institutions

selfTest.q: Who can claim Art. 19 freedoms?
selfTest.a: Answer: Citizens only (shareholders through a company, Bennett Coleman ). How many freedoms are in Art. 19(1) today? Answer: Six; (f) was omitted by the 44th Amendment. Name the eight grounds in Art. 19(2). Answer: Sovereignty and integrity; security of State; friendly relations; public order; decency or morality; contempt of court; defamation; incitement to an offence. Can a court add a new ground for restricting speech? Answer: No; the grounds are exhaustive ( Kaushal Kishor ). What did Romesh Thappar say about circulation? Answer: Freedom of speech is ensured by freedom of circulation. What are the three concepts in Shreya Singhal ? Answer: Discussion, advocacy, incitement; only incitement can be restricted. What is a "reasonable" restriction? Answer: One that is not arbitrary or excessive, and strikes a proper balance ( Chintaman Rao ). Can the internet be suspended indefinitely? Answer: No ( Anuradha Bhasin ). Is running a school an "occupation"? Answer: Yes ( T. M. A. Pai ). Does Art. 19(1)(a) allow a loudspeaker at midnight? Answer: No; it cannot defeat Art. 21 ( Noise Pollution ).

te.inOneMinute: పౌరులకు ఆరు స్వేచ్ఛలు: అ. 19(1) పౌరులందరికీ ఆరు స్వేచ్ఛలు ఇస్తుంది: (a) వాక్, భావ ప్రకటనా స్వేచ్ఛ ; (b) శాంతియుతంగా, ఆయుధాలు లేకుండా సమావేశమయ్యే స్వేచ్ఛ; (c) సంఘాలు, యూనియన్లు లేదా సహకార సంఘాలు ఏర్పాటు చేసే స్వేచ్ఛ; (d) భారతదేశం అంతటా స్వేచ్ఛగా సంచరించే స్వేచ్ఛ; (e) భారతదేశంలో ఎక్కడైనా నివసించే, స్థిరపడే స్వేచ్ఛ; (g) ఏ వృత్తినైనా చేపట్టే లేదా ఏ ఉపాధి, వ్యాపారం, వాణిజ్యాన్నైనా నిర్వహించే స్వేచ్ఛ. ఉప-ఖండం (f) (ఆస్తి)ను 44వ సవరణ తొలగించింది (20-6-1979 నుండి). ఆంక్షలు: ప్రతి స్వేచ్ఛను ఒక చట్టం ద్వారా, ఆ స్వేచ్ఛకు సంబంధించిన ఖండంలో (అ. 19(2) నుండి (6)) పేర్కొన్న ఆధారాలపై మాత్రమే సహేతుక ఆంక్షలు విధించి పరిమితం చేయవచ్చు. వాక్ స్వేచ్ఛకు అ. 19(2)లో ఎనిమిది ఆధారాలు ఉన్నాయి; అవి సమగ్రమైనవి ( కౌశల్ కిషోర్ , 2023). రొమేష్ థాపర్ (1950): "freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, and that freedom is ensured by the freedom of circulation." ( అర్థం: వాక్, భావ ప్రకటనా స్వేచ్ఛలో భావాల ప్రచార స్వేచ్ఛ ఉంది, ఆ స్వేచ్ఛ పంపిణీ స్వేచ్ఛ ద్వారా నిర్ధారించబడుతుంది.) "సహేతుక" అర్థం: "arbitrary or of an excessive nature" ( అర్థం: ఏకపక్షమైనది లేదా అతిగా ఉండేది) కాకూడదు ( చింతామణ్ రావు , శ్రేయా సింఘాల్ లో ఉటంకించినట్టు). శ్రేయా సింఘాల్ (2015): చర్చ లేదా సమర్థన కాదు, ప్రేరేపణ మాత్రమే పరిమితం చేయవచ్చు. ఐటీ చట్టం సె. 66A రద్దు చేయబడింది. రూపం కాదు, ప్రభావం: రాజ్య చర్య ప్రత్యక్ష, అనివార్య ప్రభావమే పరీక్ష ( బెన్నెట్ కోల్‌మన్ , 1972; మేనకా గాంధీ , 1978). ఇంటర్నెట్, అనుపాతత: ఇంటర్నెట్ ద్వారా వాక్ స్వేచ్ఛ, వాణిజ్యం రక్షించబడ్డాయి. ఆంక్షలు అనుపాతత పరీక్షను నెరవేర్చాలి ( అనురాధా భాసిన్ , 2020).
te.meaning: వాక్, భావ ప్రకటనా స్వేచ్ఛ: మాట, రాత, ముద్రణ, చిత్రం లేదా మరే మాధ్యమం ద్వారానైనా తన అభిప్రాయాలను వ్యక్తం చేసే హక్కు. ఇందులో భావాల ప్రచారం, పంపిణీ ( రొమేష్ థాపర్ ), పత్రికా స్వేచ్ఛ ( బ్రిజ్ భూషణ్ ; బెన్నెట్ కోల్‌మన్ ), ఇంటర్నెట్ ద్వారా భావ ప్రకటన ( అనురాధా భాసిన్ ) ఉన్నాయి. సహేతుక ఆంక్ష : "the limitation imposed on a person in enjoyment of the right should not be arbitrary or of an excessive nature, beyond what is required in the interests of the public" ( అర్థం: హక్కు అనుభవంలో ఒక వ్యక్తిపై విధించే పరిమితి ఏకపక్షంగా గానీ, ప్రజా ప్రయోజనాలకు అవసరమైన దానికంటే అతిగా గానీ ఉండకూడదు) ( చింతామణ్ రావు , శ్రేయా సింఘాల్ లో ఉటంకించినట్టు). ప్రజా శాంతిభద్రతలు (public order) : అ. 19(2)–(4)లోని ఒక ఆధారం. "మూడు ఏకకేంద్ర వృత్తాల్లో", "Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State" ( అర్థం: శాంతిభద్రతలు (law and order) అతిపెద్ద వృత్తం, దాని లోపల ప్రజా శాంతిభద్రతలు (public order) వృత్తం, అతిచిన్న వృత్తం రాజ్య భద్రత ) ( రామ్ మనోహర్ లోహియా , శ్రేయా సింఘాల్ లో ఉటంకించినట్టు). ప్రత్యక్ష, అనివార్య ప్రభావం: కోర్టు రాజ్య చర్య లక్ష్యం లేదా రూపాన్ని మాత్రమే కాక, "the direct and inevitable consequence or effect of the impugned state action on the fundamental right" ( అర్థం: సవాలు చేసిన రాజ్య చర్య ప్రాథమిక హక్కు పై చూపే ప్రత్యక్ష, అనివార్య పరిణామం లేదా ప్రభావం) చూస్తుంది ( మేనకా గాంధీ , భగవతి జె. అభిప్రాయ హెడ్‌నోట్). అనుపాతత: ఆంక్ష దాని ఉద్దేశానికి అవసరమైన దానికంటే మించకూడదు. ఇంటర్నెట్ వాక్, వాణిజ్యంపై ఆంక్షలు "in consonance with the mandate under Article 19 (2) and (6) of the Constitution, inclusive of the test of proportionality" ( అర్థం: అనుపాతత పరీక్షతో సహా, రాజ్యాంగ అ. 19(2), (6) ఆదేశానికి అనుగుణంగా) ఉండాలి ( అనురాధా భాసిన్ ). భయపెట్టే ప్రభావం (chilling effect) : అస్పష్టమైన లేదా విస్తృతమైన చట్టం వల్ల చట్టబద్ధమైన మాట కూడా మాట్లాడటానికి ప్రజలు భయపడతారు. సె. 66A "has a chilling effect on the freedom of speech and expression" ( అర్థం: వాక్, భావ ప్రకటనా స్వేచ్ఛపై భయపెట్టే ప్రభావం చూపుతుంది) ( శ్రేయా సింఘాల్ ).
keyPoints: పౌరులకు ఆరు స్వేచ్ఛలు; (f) 20-6-1979 నుండి తొలగింపు. ప్రతి స్వేచ్ఛకు సొంత ఆంక్ష ఖండం: (a)కు 19(2), (b)కు 19(3), (c)కు 19(4), (d), (e)కు 19(5), (g)కు 19(6). ఎనిమిది వాక్ ఆధారాలు; సమగ్రం ( కౌశల్ కిషోర్ , 2023). పంపిణీ ( రొమేష్ థాపర్ ); ముందస్తు సెన్సార్‌షిప్ లేదు ( బ్రిజ్ భూషణ్ ). రొమేష్ థాపర్ తర్వాత 1951లో "public order" చేర్పు. చర్చ, సమర్థన, ప్రేరేపణ ( శ్రేయా సింఘాల్ , 2015). సహేతుకం = ఏకపక్షం లేదా అతి కాదు ( చింతామణ్ రావు ). ప్రభావ పరీక్ష ( బెన్నెట్ కోల్‌మన్ ; మేనకా గాంధీ ). ఇంటర్నెట్: అనుపాతం, తాత్కాలికం ( అనురాధా భాసిన్ , 2020).

selfTest.q: అ. 19 స్వేచ్ఛలను ఎవరు కోరవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: పౌరులు మాత్రమే (కంపెనీ ద్వారా వాటాదారులు, బెన్నెట్ కోల్‌మన్ ). ఇప్పుడు అ. 19(1)లో ఎన్ని స్వేచ్ఛలు ఉన్నాయి? జవాబు: ఆరు; (f)ను 44వ సవరణ తొలగించింది. అ. 19(2)లోని ఎనిమిది ఆధారాలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: సార్వభౌమత్వం, సమగ్రత; రాజ్య భద్రత; స్నేహ సంబంధాలు; ప్రజా శాంతిభద్రతలు; మర్యాద లేదా నైతికత; కోర్టు ధిక్కారం; పరువు నష్టం; నేరానికి ప్రేరేపణ. వాక్ స్వేచ్ఛను పరిమితం చేయడానికి కోర్టు కొత్త ఆధారం చేర్చగలదా? జవాబు: లేదు; ఆధారాలు సమగ్రమైనవి ( కౌశల్ కిషోర్ ). పంపిణీ గురించి రొమేష్ థాపర్ ఏమి చెప్పింది? జవాబు: వాక్ స్వేచ్ఛ పంపిణీ స్వేచ్ఛ ద్వారా నిర్ధారించబడుతుంది. శ్రేయా సింఘాల్ లోని మూడు భావనలు ఏవి? జవాబు: చర్చ, సమర్థన, ప్రేరేపణ; ప్రేరేపణను మాత్రమే పరిమితం చేయవచ్చు. "సహేతుక" ఆంక్ష అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: ఏకపక్షం లేదా అతి కానిది, సరైన సమతుల్యత పాటించేది ( చింతామణ్ రావు ). ఇంటర్నెట్‌ను నిరవధికంగా నిలిపివేయవచ్చా? జవాబు: లేదు ( అనురాధా భాసిన్ ). పాఠశాల నడపడం "ఉపాధి"నా? జవాబు: అవును ( టి. ఎం. ఎ. పై ). అ. 19(1)(a) అర్ధరాత్రి లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్‌ను అనుమతిస్తుందా? జవాబు: లేదు; అది అ. 21ను ఓడించలేదు ( నాయిస్ పొల్యూషన్ ).

hi.inOneMinute: Six freedoms for citizens: Art. 19(1) gives all citizens six freedoms: (a) freedom of speech and expression ; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of India; (g) to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business. Sub-clause (f) (property) was omitted by the 44th Amendment (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). The restrictions: each freedom may be limited only by a law imposing reasonable restrictions on the grounds listed in its own clause, Art. 19(2) to (6). Speech has eight grounds in Art. 19(2), and they are exhaustive ( Kaushal Kishor , 2023). Romesh Thappar (1950): "freedom of speech and expression includes freedom of propagation of ideas, and that freedom is ensured by the freedom of circulation." Meaning of "reasonable": not "arbitrary or of an excessive nature" ( Chintaman Rao , as quoted in Shreya Singhal ). Shreya Singhal (2015): only incitement , not mere discussion or advocacy, can be restricted. S. 66A of the IT Act was struck down. Effect, not form: the test is the direct and inevitable effect of State action ( Bennett Coleman , 1972; Maneka Gandhi , 1978). Internet and proportionality: speech and trade over the internet are protected. Restrictions must satisfy proportionality ( Anuradha Bhasin , 2020).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 19(1): "All citizens shall have the right—

(a) to freedom of speech and expression; (b) to assemble peaceably and without arms; (c) to form associations or unions or co-operative societies; (d) to move freely throughout the territory of India; (e) to reside and settle in any part of the territory of India; and (f) * * * (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business."
"or co-operative societies" was inserted by the 97th Amendment, w.e.f. 8-2-2012. Sub-clause (f) was omitted by the 44th Amendment, w.e.f. 20-6-1979.

Article 19(2) (substituted by the First Amendment, 1951, "with retrospective effect"): "Nothing in sub-clause (a) of clause (1) shall affect the operation of any existing law, or prevent the State from making any law, in so far as such law imposes reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence."
"the sovereignty and integrity of India" was inserted by the 16th Amendment, w.e.f. 5-10-1963.
Article 19(3): reasonable restrictions on (b) "in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order".
Article 19(4): reasonable restrictions on (c) "in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order or morality".
Article 19(5): reasonable restrictions on (d) and (e) "either in the interests of the general public or for the protection of the interests of any Scheduled Tribe".
Article 19(6): reasonable restrictions on (g) "in the interests of the general public". In particular, nothing in (g) affects any law relating to:

(i) the professional or technical qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade or business; or (ii) the carrying on by the State, or by a corporation owned or controlled by the State, of any trade, business, industry or service, whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.
In simple words:
Every citizen has six freedoms. The State can limit each one only by a law, only for the reasons written in that freedom's own clause, and only by a restriction that is reasonable.
hi.meaning: Freedom of speech and expression: the right to express one's views by word, writing, print, picture or any other medium. It includes propagation and circulation of ideas ( Romesh Thappar ), freedom of the press ( Brij Bhushan ; Bennett Coleman ) and expression over the internet ( Anuradha Bhasin ). Reasonable restriction : "the limitation imposed on a person in enjoyment of the right should not be arbitrary or of an excessive nature, beyond what is required in the interests of the public" ( Chintaman Rao , quoted in Shreya Singhal ). Public order : a ground in Arts. 19(2)–(4). Of the "three concentric circles", "Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State" ( Ram Manohar Lohia , quoted in Shreya Singhal ). Direct and inevitable effect: the Court looks at "the direct and inevitable consequence or effect of the impugned state action on the fundamental right", not only its object or form ( Maneka Gandhi , headnote of Bhagwati J.'s opinion). Proportionality: a restriction must not go beyond what is necessary for its purpose. Restrictions on internet speech and trade must be "in consonance with the mandate under Article 19 (2) and (6) of the Constitution, inclusive of the test of proportionality" ( Anuradha Bhasin ). Chilling effect : a vague or wide law makes people afraid to speak even lawful speech. S. 66A "has a chilling effect on the freedom of speech and expression" ( Shreya Singhal ).
keyPoints: Six freedoms for citizens; (f) omitted w.e.f. 20-6-1979. Each freedom has its own restriction clause: 19(2) for (a), 19(3) for (b), 19(4) for (c), 19(5) for (d) and (e), 19(6) for (g). Eight speech grounds; exhaustive ( Kaushal Kishor , 2023). Circulation ( Romesh Thappar ); no pre-censorship ( Brij Bhushan ). "Public order" added in 1951 after Romesh Thappar . Discussion, advocacy, incitement ( Shreya Singhal , 2015). Reasonable = not arbitrary or excessive ( Chintaman Rao ). Effect test ( Bennett Coleman ; Maneka Gandhi ). Internet: proportionate and temporary ( Anuradha Bhasin , 2020).

caseLaws.facts: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras , AIR 1950 SC 124; [1950] SCR 594 (6 judges; decided 26 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Madras banned the entry and circulation of the Bombay weekly Cross Roads under s
caseLaws.facts: 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949. Principle: Freedom of speech includes freedom of circulation. A law for the wider purpose of "public safety or the maintenance of public order" fell outside the original Art. 19(2) and was void (Fazl Ali J. dissenting). Why it matters: Led to the First Amendment (1951) adding "public order"; over-wide laws are wholly void.
Brij Bhushan v. State of Delhi , [1950] SCR 605 (decided 26 May 1950; Patanjali Sastri J. for the majority)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Chief Commissioner of Delhi ordered pre-censorship of the English weekly Organizer under
caseLaws.facts: 7(1)(c) of the East Punjab Public Safety Act, 1949. Principle: "the imposition of pre-censorship on a journal is a restriction on the liberty of the press which is an essential part of the right to freedom of speech and expression". Why it matters: Freedom of the press is part of Art. 19(1)(a).
Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar , 1962 AIR 955; 1962 Supp (2) SCR 769 (5 judges; Sinha C.J.; decided 20 January 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The appellant was convicted under ss
caseLaws.facts: 124A and 505 IPC for a speech; the sections were challenged under Art. 19(1)(a). Principle: s. 124A is valid only when limited "to acts involving intention or tendency to create disorder, or disturbance of law and order, or incitement to violence"; strong criticism of Government is not sedition. Why it matters: Reading down a speech offence to fit Art. 19(2).
Bennett Coleman & Co. v. Union of India , [1973] 2 SCR 757 (5 judges; decided 30 October 1972)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The newsprint policy for 1972–73 fixed a 10-page limit and barred new newspapers and editions
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Majority (Sikri C.J., Ray and Jaganmohan Reddy JJ.; Beg J. concurring; Mathew J. dissenting): the direct effect of the policy infringed Art. 19(1)(a); shareholders can claim for the company. Why it matters: Effect test; economic controls on the press.
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India , 1978 AIR 597; 1978 SCR (2) 621; (1978) 1 SCC 248 (7 judges; decided 25 January 1978)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded under s
caseLaws.facts: 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 without reasons or hearing. Principle (Bhagwati J.'s opinion, headnote): Art. 19(1)(a) has no geographical limits; the test is the "direct and inevitable consequence" of State action; the right to go abroad is not itself an Art. 19(1) right. Why it matters: Effect test; scope of Art. 19 beyond India.
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala , 1987 AIR 748; 1986 SCR (3) 518; (1986) 3 SCC 615 (O. Chinnappa Reddy and M. M. Dutt JJ.; decided 11 August 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Three Jehovah's Witness children stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem, and
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Expulsion violated Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25(1); a restriction needs a law, not an executive instruction. Why it matters: Freedom of speech includes the freedom to remain silent respectfully.
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India , AIR 2015 SC 1523 (J. Chelameswar and R. F. Nariman JJ.; decided 24 March 2015)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Writ petitions under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 challenged s. 66A of the IT Act, 2000 (added w.e.f. 27-10-2009), which punished sending "grossly offensive" or annoying messages by computer or communication device. Principle: Only incitement can be restricted; s. 66A is vague, has a chilling effect, and was struck down in its entirety. Why it matters: The modern test for speech restrictions.
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India , W.P. (C) No. 1031 of 2019 (N. V. Ramana, R. Subhash Reddy, B. R. Gavai JJ.; decided 10 January 2020)

caseLaws.name: Facts: From 04-08-2019, mobile networks, internet and movement were restricted in Jammu and Kashmir;
caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: Speech and trade over the internet are protected by Arts. 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g); restrictions must meet proportionality; indefinite internet suspension is impermissible. Why it matters: Applies Art. 19 to the internet.
Kaushal Kishor v. State of U.P. , W.P. (Crl.) No. 113 of 2016 (5 judges; decided 3 January 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Statements of a Minister about a crime victim led to questions on limits of free speech
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Majority: the Art. 19(2) grounds are exhaustive; no additional restrictions can be imposed by invoking other rights; Arts. 19/21 can be enforced against non-State persons. Why it matters: Closes the list of speech restrictions.
T. M. A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka , [2002] Supp 3 SCR (11 judges; Kirpal C.J.; decided 31 October 2002)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Questions about the rights of private and minority educational institutions
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Establishing and running an educational institution is an "occupation" under Art. 19(1)(g), even without profit. Why it matters: Width of Art. 19(1)(g).
In re Noise Pollution , [2005] Supp 1 SCR (R. C. Lahoti C.J. and Ashok Bhan J.; decided 18 July 2005)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Matters on noise from loudspeakers, sound systems and fire-crackers
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Art. 19(1)(a) "cannot be pressed to defeat Art. 21"; no sound amplifiers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. except in public emergencies. Why it matters: Balancing speech with Art. 21.

selfTest.q: Who can claim Art. 19 freedoms?
selfTest.a: Answer: Citizens only (shareholders through a company, Bennett Coleman ). How many freedoms are in Art. 19(1) today? Answer: Six; (f) was omitted by the 44th Amendment. Name the eight grounds in Art. 19(2). Answer: Sovereignty and integrity; security of State; friendly relations; public order; decency or morality; contempt of court; defamation; incitement to an offence. Can a court add a new ground for restricting speech? Answer: No; the grounds are exhaustive ( Kaushal Kishor ). What did Romesh Thappar say about circulation? Answer: Freedom of speech is ensured by freedom of circulation. What are the three concepts in Shreya Singhal ? Answer: Discussion, advocacy, incitement; only incitement can be restricted. What is a "reasonable" restriction? Answer: One that is not arbitrary or excessive, and strikes a proper balance ( Chintaman Rao ). Can the internet be suspended indefinitely? Answer: No ( Anuradha Bhasin ). Is running a school an "occupation"? Answer: Yes ( T. M. A. Pai ). Does Art. 19(1)(a) allow a loudspeaker at midnight? Answer: No; it cannot defeat Art. 21 ( Noise Pollution ).

Article 22(1) and 22(2) guarantee a person arrested under ordinary law the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice, and to be produced before the nearest magistrate within:

Explanation. Article 22(2) requires production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding travel time, and prohibits detention beyond that period without the magistrate's authority.

Article 22(3) creates an important exception, under which the safeguards in Article 22(1)-(2) do NOT apply to:

Explanation. Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and persons detained under preventive detention laws from the ordinary-arrest safeguards of clauses (1) and (2) — preventive detention instead has its own separate, more limited safeguards under clauses (4) to (7).

Under Article 22(4) (as it originally stands and continues to operate, since the 44th Amendment's changes to it were never brought into force), a person cannot be detained under a preventive detention law for longer than __ months without obtaining the opinion of an Advisory Board:

Explanation. As confirmed in A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982), the 44th Amendment's changes to Article 22(4) — which would reduce this period to two months and change the Board, have never been brought into force, so the original three-month rule continues to govern preventive detention.

constitutional-law-i-u4-t2.subtitle: Articles 25 to 28: conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, the rights of religious denominations, no tax for a religion, and no forced religious instruction

en.inOneMinute: Four Articles (Arts. 25–28): Art. 25 – every person: freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion. Art. 26 – every religious denomination : manage its own affairs in matters of religion, own and administer property. Art. 27 – no person can be compelled to pay a tax whose proceeds are specifically appropriated to promote a particular religion. Art. 28 – no religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds; no compulsion to attend religious instruction or worship without consent. Limits: Arts. 25 and 26 are both "subject to public order, morality and health"; Art. 25 is also subject "to the other provisions of this Part", and Art. 25(2) lets the State regulate secular activities linked with religion and make laws for social welfare and reform. What is protected: not only belief but "acts done in pursuance of a religion"; only the essential part of religion is protected ( Shirur Mutt , 1954). Propagate ≠ convert: Art. 25 gives the right to spread one's religion, not a right to convert another person ( Rev. Stainislaus , 1977). Recent tests: Sabarimala (2018, 4:1) – exclusion of women aged 10 to 50 from the temple held unconstitutional; Shayara Bano (2017, 3:2) – triple talaq set aside.
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Art. 25 – "Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion."

(1) "Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice and propagate religion." (2) "Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law— (a) regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice; (b) providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus." Explanation I: "The wearing and carrying of kirpans shall be deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion." Explanation II: in clause (2)(b), "the reference to Hindus shall be construed as including a reference to persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion".
Art. 26 – "Freedom to manage religious affairs." "Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right—

(a) to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes; (b) to manage its own affairs in matters of religion; (c) to own and acquire movable and immovable property; and (d) to administer such property in accordance with law."

Art. 27 – "Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion." "No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination."
Art. 28 – "Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions."

(1) "No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds." (2) Clause (1) does not apply to an institution "administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution". (3) "No person attending any educational institution recognised by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction ... or to attend any religious worship ... unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto."
Related:

Preamble: "LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship"; the word "SECULAR" was added by the 42nd Amendment, s. 2 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 28: "Charities and charitable institutions, charitable and religious endowments and religious institutions."
en.meaning: Freedom of conscience : the inner freedom of a person to hold any belief, or none. Every person has a right "not merely to entertain such religious belief as may be approved of by his judgment or conscience but to exhibit his belief and ideas in such overt acts as are enjoined or sanctioned by his religion and further to propagate his religious views for the edification of others" ( Ratilal , 1954). Religion: "Religion is certainly a matter of faith with individuals or communities and it is not necessarily theistic." Buddhism and Jainism "do not believe in God or in any Intelligent First Cause" ( Shirur Mutt ). Profess, practise, propagate: profess = declare one's faith openly; practise = perform its rites; propagate = "to transmit or spread one's religion by an exposition of its tenets" ( Rev. Stainislaus ). Religious denomination : the Oxford Dictionary meaning adopted in Shirur Mutt : "a collection of individuals classed together under the same name: a religious sect or body having a common faith and organisation and designated by a distinctive name." Essential religious practice : a practice that forms an essential part of the religion; "what constitutes the essential part of a religion is primarily to be ascertained with reference to the doctrines of that religion itself" ( Shirur Mutt ).
keyPoints: Art. 25: all persons; conscience; profess, practise, propagate. Arts. 25 and 26: subject to public order, morality and health. Religion need not be theistic ( Shirur Mutt ). Acts, rituals, food and dress can be part of religion ( Shirur Mutt ). Only essential practices are protected; secular activities may be regulated. Propagate ≠ convert ( Rev. Stainislaus , 1977). Denomination: common faith, common organisation, distinctive name. Art. 26(d): property administration can be regulated, not taken away altogether. Art. 27: tax for one religion barred; supervision levy is not for "promotion". Art. 28: no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions; consent needed in recognised or aided ones.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The head (Mathadhipati) of the Shirur Math at Udipi challenged the Madras Hindu Religious and
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Religion covers rituals and practices, not only belief; the essential part is judged by the religion's own doctrines; a denomination has complete autonomy in matters of religion, and its property can be regulated but not taken away. Why it matters: The first full statement of Arts. 25 and 26; source of the essential practices test.
Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay , [1954] SCR 1055 (5 judges; Mukherjea J. for the Court; decided 18 March 1954)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The manager of a Jain temple and the trustees of the Parsi Punchayet funds challenged the Bom
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Art. 25 covers every person; religious practices are as much part of religion as belief; the Charity Commissioner cannot be made trustee of a religious trust or divert its funds. Why it matters: Applied Shirur Mutt to Jain and Parsi trusts.
Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh , 1977 AIR 908; [1977] 2 SCR 611; (1977) 1 SCC 677 (A. N. Ray C.J. and four judges; decided 17 January 1977)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Madhya Pradesh and Orissa laws banning conversion by force, allurement or fraud were chal
caseLaws.facts: 25. Principle: "Propagate" means to spread by exposition; there is no fundamental right to convert; the laws protect public order. Why it matters: The leading case on conversion.
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala , [1986] 3 SCR 518 (O. Chinnappa Reddy and M. M. Dutt JJ.; decided 11 August 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Three children, Jehovah's Witnesses, stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem;
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A genuinely and conscientiously held belief is protected by Art. 25; the expulsion violated Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25(1). Why it matters: "our tradition teaches tolerance; our philosophy preaches tolerance; our constitution practices tolerance; let us not dilute it."
Church of God (Full Gospel) in India v. K.K.R. Majestic Colony Welfare Association (M. B. Shah and S. N. Phukan JJ.; decided 30 August 2000)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents complained that prayers in a church in Chennai were recited with loudspeakers, drum
caseLaws.facts: Principle: No religion prescribes prayers by disturbing others' peace; noise rules must be enforced. Why it matters: Shows the "public order" and "health" limits on Arts. 25 and 26.
Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala ( Sabarimala ), [2018] 9 SCR 561 (5 judges; 4:1, Indu Malhotra J. dissenting; decided 28 September 2018)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965 p
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The majority held rule 3(b) invalid; the devotees of Lord Ayyappa are not a separate denomination; the exclusion is not an essential practice and violates women's right under Art. 25(1). Why it matters: Restated the essential practices test; the dissent held that "Notions of rationality cannot be invoked in matters of religion by courts".
Shayara Bano v. Union of India , [2017] 9 SCR 797 (5 judges; decided 22 August 2017)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A Muslim woman challenged talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq)
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "by a majority of 3:2 the practice of 'talaq-e-biddat' – triple talaq is set aside." Nariman J. (for himself and Lalit J.) held it manifestly arbitrary under Art. 14; Kurian Joseph J. held it not an integral part of religious practice; Khehar C.J. and Nazeer J. (minority) held it part of personal law protected by Art. 25. Why it matters: Shows that a long-standing practice is not protected merely because it is old.

selfTest.q: Who can claim Art. 25?
selfTest.a: Answer: All persons, not only citizens ( Ratilal ). Is religion necessarily belief in God? Answer: No; "it is not necessarily theistic" ( Shirur Mutt ). Does Art. 25 give a right to convert? Answer: No; only to propagate ( Rev. Stainislaus ). What three marks make a religious denomination? Answer: Common faith, common organisation, distinctive name ( Shirur Mutt ). Can the State take a denomination's property administration away altogether? Answer: No; that violates Art. 26(d) ( Shirur Mutt ). A temple earns Rs. 30,00,000. What is the most it could pay under a 5% levy like s. 76 of the Madras Act? Answer: Rs. 1,50,000. Can a wholly State-funded college hold compulsory daily worship of one religion? Answer: No; Art. 28(1). In an aided school, 40 students of another religion attend; guardians of 25 consent. How many cannot be required to attend religious instruction? Answer: 40 − 25 = 15. Why did the children in Bijoe Emmanuel win? Answer: Their belief was genuinely and conscientiously held, and they stood respectfully; expulsion violated Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25(1). By what majority was triple talaq set aside? Answer: 3:2 ( Shayara Bano , 2017).

te.inOneMinute: నాలుగు అధికరణలు (అధికరణలు 25–28): అధికరణ 25 – ప్రతి వ్యక్తికి: అంతరాత్మ స్వేచ్ఛ , మతాన్ని స్వేచ్ఛగా ప్రకటించే, ఆచరించే, ప్రచారం చేసే హక్కు. అధికరణ 26 – ప్రతి మత శాఖ కు: మత విషయాల్లో తన వ్యవహారాలను నిర్వహించుకోవడం, ఆస్తిని కలిగి ఉండడం, నిర్వహించడం. అధికరణ 27 – ఒక ప్రత్యేక మతాన్ని ప్రోత్సహించడానికి ప్రత్యేకంగా కేటాయించిన పన్నును చెల్లించమని ఎవరినీ బలవంతం చేయరాదు. అధికరణ 28 – పూర్తిగా రాజ్య నిధులతో నడిచే సంస్థల్లో మత బోధన ఉండరాదు; సమ్మతి లేకుండా మత బోధనకు లేదా ప్రార్థనకు హాజరు కావాలని బలవంతం చేయరాదు. పరిమితులు: అధికరణలు 25, 26 రెండూ "subject to public order, morality and health" ( అర్థం: ప్రజా శాంతిభద్రతలు, నైతికత, ఆరోగ్యానికి లోబడి); అధికరణ 25 అదనంగా "to the other provisions of this Part" ( అర్థం: ఈ భాగంలోని ఇతర నిబంధనలకు) లోబడి ఉంటుంది; మతంతో ముడిపడిన లౌకిక కార్యకలాపాలను నియంత్రించడానికి, సామాజిక సంక్షేమం, సంస్కరణల కోసం చట్టాలు చేయడానికి అధికరణ 25(2) రాజ్యానికి అనుమతిస్తుంది. ఏది రక్షించబడుతుంది: నమ్మకం మాత్రమే కాదు, "acts done in pursuance of a religion" ( అర్థం: మతాన్ని అనుసరించి చేసే చర్యలు) కూడా; మతంలోని ముఖ్యమైన భాగం మాత్రమే రక్షించబడుతుంది ( Shirur Mutt , 1954). ప్రచారం ≠ మతమార్పిడి: అధికరణ 25 తన మతాన్ని వ్యాప్తి చేసే హక్కును ఇస్తుంది, మరొకరిని మతం మార్చే హక్కును కాదు ( Rev. Stainislaus , 1977). ఇటీవలి పరీక్షలు: Sabarimala (2018, 4:1) – 10 నుండి 50 ఏళ్ల మహిళలను ఆలయం నుండి మినహాయించడం రాజ్యాంగ విరుద్ధం; Shayara Bano (2017, 3:2) – ట్రిపుల్ తలాఖ్ రద్దు.
te.meaning: అంతరాత్మ స్వేచ్ఛ : ఏ నమ్మకాన్నైనా కలిగి ఉండే, లేదా ఏ నమ్మకమూ లేకుండా ఉండే వ్యక్తి అంతర స్వేచ్ఛ. ప్రతి వ్యక్తికి "not merely to entertain such religious belief as may be approved of by his judgment or conscience but to exhibit his belief and ideas in such overt acts as are enjoined or sanctioned by his religion and further to propagate his religious views for the edification of others" ( అర్థం: తన వివేకం లేదా అంతరాత్మ ఆమోదించే మత నమ్మకాన్ని కలిగి ఉండడమే కాకుండా, తన మతం ఆదేశించే లేదా అనుమతించే బహిరంగ చర్యల్లో తన నమ్మకాన్ని, భావాలను ప్రదర్శించడానికి, ఇతరుల జ్ఞానోదయం కోసం తన మత అభిప్రాయాలను ప్రచారం చేయడానికి) హక్కు ఉంది ( Ratilal , 1954). మతం: "Religion is certainly a matter of faith with individuals or communities and it is not necessarily theistic." ( అర్థం: మతం నిశ్చయంగా వ్యక్తుల లేదా సమాజాల విశ్వాసానికి సంబంధించినది, అది తప్పనిసరిగా దైవ విశ్వాసంతో కూడినది కాదు.) బౌద్ధం, జైనం "do not believe in God or in any Intelligent First Cause" ( అర్థం: దేవుడిని లేదా ఏ మేధావంతమైన ప్రథమ కారణాన్నీ నమ్మవు) ( Shirur Mutt ). ప్రకటించడం, ఆచరించడం, ప్రచారం చేయడం: ప్రకటించడం = తన విశ్వాసాన్ని బహిరంగంగా చెప్పడం; ఆచరించడం = దాని ఆచారాలను పాటించడం; ప్రచారం = "to transmit or spread one's religion by an exposition of its tenets" ( అర్థం: తన మత సిద్ధాంతాలను వివరించడం ద్వారా తన మతాన్ని అందజేయడం లేదా వ్యాప్తి చేయడం) ( Rev. Stainislaus ). మత శాఖ : Shirur Mutt స్వీకరించిన ఆక్స్‌ఫర్డ్ నిఘంటువు అర్థం: "a collection of individuals classed together under the same name: a religious sect or body having a common faith and organisation and designated by a distinctive name." ( అర్థం: ఒకే పేరుతో వర్గీకరించబడిన వ్యక్తుల సమూహం: ఉమ్మడి విశ్వాసం, సంస్థ కలిగి, ఒక విలక్షణమైన పేరుతో పిలువబడే మత శాఖ లేదా సంఘం.) ముఖ్యమైన మత ఆచారం : మతంలో ముఖ్యమైన భాగంగా ఉండే ఆచారం; "what constitutes the essential part of a religion is primarily to be ascertained with reference to the doctrines of that religion itself" ( అర్థం: మతంలో ముఖ్యమైన భాగం ఏమిటో ప్రధానంగా ఆ మతం సిద్ధాంతాలను బట్టే నిర్ణయించాలి) ( Shirur Mutt ).
keyPoints: అధికరణ 25: వ్యక్తులందరూ; అంతరాత్మ; ప్రకటించడం, ఆచరించడం, ప్రచారం చేయడం. అధికరణలు 25, 26: శాంతిభద్రతలు, నైతికత, ఆరోగ్యానికి లోబడి. మతం దైవ విశ్వాసంతో కూడినదే కానవసరం లేదు ( Shirur Mutt ). చర్యలు, ఆచారాలు, ఆహారం, దుస్తులు మతంలో భాగం కావచ్చు ( Shirur Mutt ). ముఖ్యమైన ఆచారాలకే రక్షణ; లౌకిక కార్యకలాపాలను నియంత్రించవచ్చు. ప్రచారం ≠ మతమార్పిడి ( Rev. Stainislaus , 1977). మత శాఖ: ఉమ్మడి విశ్వాసం, ఉమ్మడి సంస్థ, విలక్షణ పేరు. అధికరణ 26(d): ఆస్తి నిర్వహణను నియంత్రించవచ్చు, పూర్తిగా తీసివేయలేము. అధికరణ 27: ఒక మతం కోసం పన్ను నిషేధం; పర్యవేక్షణ లెవీ "ప్రోత్సాహం" కోసం కాదు. అధికరణ 28: పూర్తిగా రాజ్య నిధుల సంస్థల్లో మత బోధన లేదు; గుర్తించిన లేదా సహాయం పొందే వాటిలో సమ్మతి అవసరం.

selfTest.q: అధికరణ 25ను ఎవరు కోరవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: వ్యక్తులందరూ, పౌరులు మాత్రమే కాదు ( Ratilal ). మతం అంటే తప్పనిసరిగా దేవుడిపై నమ్మకమా? జవాబు: కాదు; "it is not necessarily theistic" ( అర్థం: అది తప్పనిసరిగా దైవ విశ్వాసంతో కూడినది కాదు) ( Shirur Mutt ). అధికరణ 25 మతమార్పిడి హక్కు ఇస్తుందా? జవాబు: లేదు; ప్రచారం చేసే హక్కు మాత్రమే ( Rev. Stainislaus ). ఏ మూడు లక్షణాలు మత శాఖను ఏర్పరుస్తాయి? జవాబు: ఉమ్మడి విశ్వాసం, ఉమ్మడి సంస్థ, విలక్షణ పేరు ( Shirur Mutt ). మత శాఖ ఆస్తి నిర్వహణను రాజ్యం పూర్తిగా తీసివేయవచ్చా? జవాబు: లేదు; అది అధికరణ 26(d) ఉల్లంఘన ( Shirur Mutt ). ఒక ఆలయం ఆదాయం Rs. 30,00,000. మద్రాస్ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 76 వంటి 5% లెవీ కింద గరిష్టంగా ఎంత చెల్లించాలి? జవాబు: Rs. 1,50,000. పూర్తిగా రాజ్య నిధులతో నడిచే కళాశాల ఒక మతం యొక్క తప్పనిసరి రోజువారీ ఆరాధన నిర్వహించవచ్చా? జవాబు: లేదు; అధికరణ 28(1). సహాయం పొందే పాఠశాలలో మరొక మతానికి చెందిన 40 మంది విద్యార్థులు ఉన్నారు; 25 మంది సంరక్షకులు సమ్మతిస్తారు. ఎంత మందిని మత బోధనకు హాజరు కావాలని కోరరాదు? జవాబు: 40 − 25 = 15. Bijoe Emmanuel లో పిల్లలు ఎందుకు గెలిచారు? జవాబు: వారి నమ్మకం నిజాయితీగా, అంతరాత్మపూర్వకంగా కలిగి ఉన్నది, వారు గౌరవంగా నిలబడ్డారు; బహిష్కరణ అధికరణలు 19(1)(a), 25(1) ఉల్లంఘన. ట్రిపుల్ తలాఖ్ ఏ మెజారిటీతో రద్దు చేయబడింది? జవాబు: 3:2 ( Shayara Bano , 2017).

సంస్థ మత బోధన?
పూర్తిగా రాజ్య నిధులతో నిర్వహించేది అనుమతి లేదు (28(1))
రాజ్యం నిర్వహిస్తుంది కానీ దానిని కోరే దానం లేదా ట్రస్టు కింద స్థాపించబడింది అనుమతి ఉంది (28(2))
రాజ్యం గుర్తించినది, లేదా రాజ్య సహాయం పొందేది అనుమతి ఉంది, కానీ సమ్మతి లేకుండా ఎవరినీ హాజరు కావాలని కోరరాదు (మైనర్‌కు సంరక్షకుని సమ్మతి) (28(3))
సహాయం లేని, గుర్తింపు లేనిది అధికరణ 28 పరిధిలో లేదు

నియమం చెప్పిన మూలం
నమ్మకమే కాదు, మతాన్ని అనుసరించి చేసే చర్యలకూ రక్షణ ఆస్ట్రేలియా రాజ్యాంగ సెక్షన్ 116పై ఆస్ట్రేలియా హైకోర్టు ప్రధాన న్యాయమూర్తి లాథమ్ (Adelaide Company v. The Commonwealth), Shirur Mutt లో ఉదహరించబడింది
"denomination" (అర్థం: మత శాఖ) అర్థం ఆక్స్‌ఫర్డ్ నిఘంటువు, Shirur Mutt లో ఉదహరించబడింది
అధికరణ 25లో "propagate" (అర్థం: ప్రచారం చేయడం) నిలుపుదల మైనారిటీల కమిటీలో రాజీ, కె. ఎం. మున్షీ చెప్పినట్లు (CAD, 6 డిసెంబర్ 1948)
మత స్థాపన నిషేధం / మతానికి దానం నిషేధం క్లాజు అమెరికా తరహా నమూనాలో ("make no law respecting an establishment of religion" (అర్థం: మత స్థాపనకు సంబంధించి ఏ చట్టమూ చేయరాదు)), హెచ్. వి. కామత్ ప్రతిపాదించారు; రెండూ తిరస్కరించబడ్డాయి (CAD, 6 డిసెంబర్ 1948)
"propagate" (అర్థం: ప్రచారం చేయడం) అర్థం నిఘంటువు అర్థాలు, Rev. Stainislaus

అధికరణ హక్కు ఎవరిది ఏమి ఇస్తుంది ప్రధాన పరిమితి
25 వ్యక్తులందరూ అంతరాత్మ; ప్రకటించడం, ఆచరించడం, ప్రచారం చేయడం శాంతిభద్రతలు, నైతికత, ఆరోగ్యం; భాగం IIIలోని ఇతర నిబంధనలు; 25(2) చట్టాలు
26 మత శాఖలు లేదా విభాగాలు సంస్థలు; మత విషయాలు; ఆస్తి; నిర్వహణ శాంతిభద్రతలు, నైతికత, ఆరోగ్యం; ఆస్తి "in accordance with law" (అర్థం: చట్ట ప్రకారం)
27 వ్యక్తులందరూ ఒక మతానికి ప్రత్యేకంగా కేటాయించిన పన్ను లేదు —

hi.inOneMinute: Four Articles (Arts. 25–28): Art. 25 – every person: freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion. Art. 26 – every religious denomination : manage its own affairs in matters of religion, own and administer property. Art. 27 – no person can be compelled to pay a tax whose proceeds are specifically appropriated to promote a particular religion. Art. 28 – no religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds; no compulsion to attend religious instruction or worship without consent. Limits: Arts. 25 and 26 are both "subject to public order, morality and health"; Art. 25 is also subject "to the other provisions of this Part", and Art. 25(2) lets the State regulate secular activities linked with religion and make laws for social welfare and reform. What is protected: not only belief but "acts done in pursuance of a religion"; only the essential part of religion is protected ( Shirur Mutt , 1954). Propagate ≠ convert: Art. 25 gives the right to spread one's religion, not a right to convert another person ( Rev. Stainislaus , 1977). Recent tests: Sabarimala (2018, 4:1) – exclusion of women aged 10 to 50 from the temple held unconstitutional; Shayara Bano (2017, 3:2) – triple talaq set aside.
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Art. 25 – "Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion."

(1) "Subject to public order, morality and health and to the other provisions of this Part, all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practice and propagate religion." (2) "Nothing in this article shall affect the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from making any law— (a) regulating or restricting any economic, financial, political or other secular activity which may be associated with religious practice; (b) providing for social welfare and reform or the throwing open of Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus." Explanation I: "The wearing and carrying of kirpans shall be deemed to be included in the profession of the Sikh religion." Explanation II: in clause (2)(b), "the reference to Hindus shall be construed as including a reference to persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion".
Art. 26 – "Freedom to manage religious affairs." "Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious denomination or any section thereof shall have the right—

(a) to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes; (b) to manage its own affairs in matters of religion; (c) to own and acquire movable and immovable property; and (d) to administer such property in accordance with law."

Art. 27 – "Freedom as to payment of taxes for promotion of any particular religion." "No person shall be compelled to pay any taxes, the proceeds of which are specifically appropriated in payment of expenses for the promotion or maintenance of any particular religion or religious denomination."
Art. 28 – "Freedom as to attendance at religious instruction or religious worship in certain educational institutions."

(1) "No religious instruction shall be provided in any educational institution wholly maintained out of State funds." (2) Clause (1) does not apply to an institution "administered by the State but has been established under any endowment or trust which requires that religious instruction shall be imparted in such institution". (3) "No person attending any educational institution recognised by the State or receiving aid out of State funds shall be required to take part in any religious instruction ... or to attend any religious worship ... unless such person or, if such person is a minor, his guardian has given his consent thereto."
Related:

Preamble: "LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship"; the word "SECULAR" was added by the 42nd Amendment, s. 2 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 28: "Charities and charitable institutions, charitable and religious endowments and religious institutions."
hi.meaning: Freedom of conscience : the inner freedom of a person to hold any belief, or none. Every person has a right "not merely to entertain such religious belief as may be approved of by his judgment or conscience but to exhibit his belief and ideas in such overt acts as are enjoined or sanctioned by his religion and further to propagate his religious views for the edification of others" ( Ratilal , 1954). Religion: "Religion is certainly a matter of faith with individuals or communities and it is not necessarily theistic." Buddhism and Jainism "do not believe in God or in any Intelligent First Cause" ( Shirur Mutt ). Profess, practise, propagate: profess = declare one's faith openly; practise = perform its rites; propagate = "to transmit or spread one's religion by an exposition of its tenets" ( Rev. Stainislaus ). Religious denomination : the Oxford Dictionary meaning adopted in Shirur Mutt : "a collection of individuals classed together under the same name: a religious sect or body having a common faith and organisation and designated by a distinctive name." Essential religious practice : a practice that forms an essential part of the religion; "what constitutes the essential part of a religion is primarily to be ascertained with reference to the doctrines of that religion itself" ( Shirur Mutt ).
keyPoints: Art. 25: all persons; conscience; profess, practise, propagate. Arts. 25 and 26: subject to public order, morality and health. Religion need not be theistic ( Shirur Mutt ). Acts, rituals, food and dress can be part of religion ( Shirur Mutt ). Only essential practices are protected; secular activities may be regulated. Propagate ≠ convert ( Rev. Stainislaus , 1977). Denomination: common faith, common organisation, distinctive name. Art. 26(d): property administration can be regulated, not taken away altogether. Art. 27: tax for one religion barred; supervision levy is not for "promotion". Art. 28: no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions; consent needed in recognised or aided ones.

caseLaws.facts: Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt , [1954] SCR 1005 (7 judges; Mukherjea J. for the Court; decided 16 March 1954)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The head (Mathadhipati) of the Shirur Math at Udipi challenged the Madras Hindu Religious and
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Religion covers rituals and practices, not only belief; the essential part is judged by the religion's own doctrines; a denomination has complete autonomy in matters of religion, and its property can be regulated but not taken away. Why it matters: The first full statement of Arts. 25 and 26; source of the essential practices test.
Ratilal Panachand Gandhi v. State of Bombay , [1954] SCR 1055 (5 judges; Mukherjea J. for the Court; decided 18 March 1954)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The manager of a Jain temple and the trustees of the Parsi Punchayet funds challenged the Bom
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Art. 25 covers every person; religious practices are as much part of religion as belief; the Charity Commissioner cannot be made trustee of a religious trust or divert its funds. Why it matters: Applied Shirur Mutt to Jain and Parsi trusts.
Rev. Stainislaus v. State of Madhya Pradesh , 1977 AIR 908; [1977] 2 SCR 611; (1977) 1 SCC 677 (A. N. Ray C.J. and four judges; decided 17 January 1977)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Madhya Pradesh and Orissa laws banning conversion by force, allurement or fraud were chal
caseLaws.facts: 25. Principle: "Propagate" means to spread by exposition; there is no fundamental right to convert; the laws protect public order. Why it matters: The leading case on conversion.
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala , [1986] 3 SCR 518 (O. Chinnappa Reddy and M. M. Dutt JJ.; decided 11 August 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Three children, Jehovah's Witnesses, stood respectfully but did not sing the National Anthem;
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A genuinely and conscientiously held belief is protected by Art. 25; the expulsion violated Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25(1). Why it matters: "our tradition teaches tolerance; our philosophy preaches tolerance; our constitution practices tolerance; let us not dilute it."
Church of God (Full Gospel) in India v. K.K.R. Majestic Colony Welfare Association (M. B. Shah and S. N. Phukan JJ.; decided 30 August 2000)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents complained that prayers in a church in Chennai were recited with loudspeakers, drum
caseLaws.facts: Principle: No religion prescribes prayers by disturbing others' peace; noise rules must be enforced. Why it matters: Shows the "public order" and "health" limits on Arts. 25 and 26.
Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala ( Sabarimala ), [2018] 9 SCR 561 (5 judges; 4:1, Indu Malhotra J. dissenting; decided 28 September 2018)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965 p
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The majority held rule 3(b) invalid; the devotees of Lord Ayyappa are not a separate denomination; the exclusion is not an essential practice and violates women's right under Art. 25(1). Why it matters: Restated the essential practices test; the dissent held that "Notions of rationality cannot be invoked in matters of religion by courts".
Shayara Bano v. Union of India , [2017] 9 SCR 797 (5 judges; decided 22 August 2017)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A Muslim woman challenged talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq)
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "by a majority of 3:2 the practice of 'talaq-e-biddat' – triple talaq is set aside." Nariman J. (for himself and Lalit J.) held it manifestly arbitrary under Art. 14; Kurian Joseph J. held it not an integral part of religious practice; Khehar C.J. and Nazeer J. (minority) held it part of personal law protected by Art. 25. Why it matters: Shows that a long-standing practice is not protected merely because it is old.

selfTest.q: Who can claim Art. 25?
selfTest.a: Answer: All persons, not only citizens ( Ratilal ). Is religion necessarily belief in God? Answer: No; "it is not necessarily theistic" ( Shirur Mutt ). Does Art. 25 give a right to convert? Answer: No; only to propagate ( Rev. Stainislaus ). What three marks make a religious denomination? Answer: Common faith, common organisation, distinctive name ( Shirur Mutt ). Can the State take a denomination's property administration away altogether? Answer: No; that violates Art. 26(d) ( Shirur Mutt ). A temple earns Rs. 30,00,000. What is the most it could pay under a 5% levy like s. 76 of the Madras Act? Answer: Rs. 1,50,000. Can a wholly State-funded college hold compulsory daily worship of one religion? Answer: No; Art. 28(1). In an aided school, 40 students of another religion attend; guardians of 25 consent. How many cannot be required to attend religious instruction? Answer: 40 − 25 = 15. Why did the children in Bijoe Emmanuel win? Answer: Their belief was genuinely and conscientiously held, and they stood respectfully; expulsion violated Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25(1). By what majority was triple talaq set aside? Answer: 3:2 ( Shayara Bano , 2017).

en.meaning:
What right does Article 29(1) guarantee to any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture?

Explanation. Article 29(1) guarantees any section of citizens with a distinct language, script or culture the right to conserve it.

Is the right under Article 29(1) available only to religious minorities?

Explanation. Article 29(1) is not confined to religious minorities; it extends to any section of citizens, including linguistic groups, whether majority or minority in a given area.

What does Article 29(2) prohibit?

Explanation. Article 29(2) prohibits denying admission to any State-maintained or State-aided educational institution on grounds only of religion, race, caste, or language.

In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), what did the Supreme Court hold about the Communal Government Order fixing caste-based admission quotas?

Does Article 25(1) protect purely secular activities that happen to be associated with a religious practice?

te.meaning: Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practise and propagate religion to whom? Explanation. Article 25(1) guarantees this freedom to 'all persons', not just citizens, subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III. What test did the Supreme Court lay down in the Shirur Mutt case (1954) to determine what religious practices are protected under Article 25? Explanation. Shirur Mutt (Commissioner, HRE v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar) held that only practices genuinely essential and integral to a religion are constitutionally protected under Article 25. Does Article 25(1) protect purely secular activities that happen to be associated with a religious practice? Explanation. Article 25(2)(a) allows the State to regulate or restrict any economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religious practice. What does Article 25(2)(b) permit the State to do?

en.meaning:
Who told the Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1948 that without Article 32 the Constitution would be a dead letter?

Explanation. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1948 that without Article 32 the Constitution would be a dead letter.

Which court(s) have original jurisdiction to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32?

Explanation. Article 32 vests the Supreme Court with original jurisdiction to issue directions or writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

Which writ is issued to secure the release of a person unlawfully detained?

Explanation. Habeas corpus ('to have the body') is issued to produce a detained person before the court and secure release if the detention is unlawful.

Which writ commands a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed to perform?
