constitutional-law-i-u4-t1.subtitle: Articles 23 and 24: no traffic in human beings, begar or forced labour, and no child below fourteen in a factory, mine or hazardous work

en.inOneMinute: Two Articles: Art. 23 prohibits " Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour "; any contravention is an offence. The State may still impose compulsory service for public purposes , without discrimination "on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class". Art. 24: "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment." Against everyone, not only the State: Arts. 23 and 24 (like Art. 17) are "enforceable against the whole world" ( PUDR , 1982). Wide meaning of "force": paying less than the minimum wage is presumed to be forced labour, because "force" includes "compulsion arising from hunger and poverty, want and destitution" ( PUDR ). Bonded labour: when a labourer is shown to give forced labour, the Court presumes he is a bonded labourer ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , 1983). Child labour: M. C. Mehta (1996) directed Rs. 20,000 compensation per child from the offending employer, plus Rs. 5,000 from the Government (or a job for an adult), into a welfare fund. Punishment: only Parliament can prescribe punishment for offences declared in Part III (Art. 35(a)(ii)); the BNS, 2023 punishes trafficking (s. 143) and unlawful compulsory labour (s. 146).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 23 – "Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour."

(1) "Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law." (2) "Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them."

Article 24 – "Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc." "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment."

Article 35(a)(ii): Parliament, and not a State Legislature, has power to make laws "for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under this Part", and shall make such laws "as soon as may be after the commencement of this Constitution".
Related Directive Principles:

Art. 39(e): "the health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused and that citizens are not forced by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age or strength". Art. 39(f): children are to be given opportunities to develop "in conditions of freedom and dignity" and "childhood and youth are protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment."
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023:

s. 143(1): whoever, "for the purpose of exploitation", recruits, transports, harbours, transfers or receives a person by threats, force or coercion, abduction, fraud or deception, abuse of power, or inducement, "commits the offence of trafficking". Explanation 1: "exploitation" includes "physical exploitation or any form of sexual exploitation, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude, beggary or forced removal of organs." Explanation 2: "The consent of the victim is immaterial". Punishment: 7 to 10 years (s. 143(2)); more than one person – 10 years to life (s. 143(3)); a child – 10 years to life (s. 143(4)); more than one child – 14 years to life (s. 143(5)). s. 145: habitual dealing in slaves – imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and fine. s. 146: "Whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person" – up to one year, or fine, or both.
en.meaning: Traffic in human beings: dealing in human beings like goods – recruiting, moving, keeping or receiving persons for exploitation (see BNS s. 143). Begar: "a word of Indian origin"; "a form of forced labour under which a person is compelled to work without receiving any remuneration" ( PUDR ). Forced labour : labour or service a person is forced to provide. "Force" may be physical, legal (e.g. threat of prison or fine), or "compulsion arising from hunger and poverty, want and destitution" ( PUDR ). Bonded labour: forced labour in return for an advance or other economic consideration, where the labourer loses freedom of employment or movement ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , describing the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976). Hazardous employment (Art. 24): work dangerous to a child's life or health; besides factories and mines, it includes construction work ( PUDR ).
keyPoints: Art. 23(1): traffic, begar, similar forced labour prohibited; offence. Art. 23(2): compulsory public service allowed; no discrimination on religion, race, caste or class only. Art. 24: no child below 14 in factory, mine or hazardous work. Arts. 17, 23, 24 bind private persons ( PUDR ). Below minimum wage = forced labour ( PUDR ). Forced labour shown → bonded labour presumed ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). M. C. Mehta (1996): Rs. 20,000 + Rs. 5,000 = Rs. 25,000 per child. Art. 35(a)(ii): only Parliament prescribes punishment.

caseLaws.facts: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India , [1983] 1 SCR 456 (P. N. Bhagwati and Baharul Islam JJ.; decided 18 September 1982)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter to Bhagwati J
caseLaws.facts: complained that workers on Asian Games projects in Delhi were paid less than the minimum wage through Jamadars and that children below 14 were employed. Principle: Arts. 23 and 24 bind private persons; work for less than the minimum wage is forced labour; construction is hazardous employment for Art. 24. Why it matters: Gave Art. 23 its wide meaning.
Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India , [1984] 2 SCR 67 (P. N. Bhagwati, R. S. Pathak and A. N. Sen JJ.; decided 16 December 1983)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter alleged that bonded labourers worked in inhuman conditions in Faridabad stone quarri
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Once forced labour is shown, the Court presumes bonded labour; the State must identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers. Why it matters: Made the Bonded Labour Act effective through Art. 23.
M. C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu , [1996] Supp. 9 SCR 726 (Kuldip Singh, B. L. Hansaria and S. B. Majmudar JJ.; decided 10 December 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A PIL about children employed in hazardous match and fireworks factories of Sivakasi
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Rs. 20,000 per child from the offending employer, plus a job for an adult or Rs. 5,000 from the Government, into a welfare fund; benefits tied to the child's education. Why it matters: Practical scheme to enforce Art. 24.

selfTest.q: Quote Art. 24. Answer: "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment." What is begar?
selfTest.a: Answer: Forced labour without any remuneration ( PUDR ). Is paying less than the minimum wage forced labour? Answer: Yes, it is presumed to be, because of economic compulsion ( PUDR ). Can Art. 23 be enforced against a private contractor? Answer: Yes ( PUDR ). What may the State do under Art. 23(2)? Answer: Impose compulsory service for public purposes, without discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class. What presumption did Bandhua Mukti Morcha lay down? Answer: Once forced labour is shown, the labourer is presumed to be a bonded labourer. A factory employs 8 children. Total employer compensation under M. C. Mehta ? Answer: 8 × Rs. 20,000 = Rs. 1,60,000. Who can make laws punishing offences under Art. 23? Answer: Parliament only (Art. 35(a)(ii)). Is consent a defence to trafficking under the BNS? Answer: No; "The consent of the victim is immaterial" (s. 143, Explanation 2). When were draft Arts. 17 and 18 adopted? Answer: 3 December 1948.

te.inOneMinute: రెండు అధికరణలు: అధికరణ 23 " Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour " ( అర్థం: మానవ అక్రమ రవాణా, వెట్టిచాకిరీ, ఇతర సారూప్య బలవంతపు శ్రమ)ను నిషేధిస్తుంది; ఉల్లంఘన నేరం. అయినా "religion, race, caste or class" ( అర్థం: మతం, జాతి, కులం లేదా వర్గం) ఆధారంగా మాత్రమే వివక్ష చూపకుండా, రాజ్యం ప్రజా ప్రయోజనాల కోసం నిర్బంధ సేవ ను విధించవచ్చు. అధికరణ 24: "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment." ( అర్థం: పద్నాలుగు సంవత్సరాల లోపు ఏ బిడ్డనూ ఏ కర్మాగారంలో లేదా గనిలో పనికి పెట్టరాదు, లేదా మరే ఇతర ప్రమాదకర ఉపాధిలో నియమించరాదు.) రాజ్యానికే కాదు, అందరికీ వ్యతిరేకంగా: అధికరణలు 23, 24 (అధికరణ 17 లాగే) "enforceable against the whole world" ( అర్థం: ప్రపంచం మొత్తానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా అమలు చేయదగినవి) ( PUDR , 1982). "బలం"కు విస్తృత అర్థం: కనీస వేతనం కంటే తక్కువ చెల్లించడం బలవంతపు శ్రమగా భావించబడుతుంది, ఎందుకంటే "force"లో "compulsion arising from hunger and poverty, want and destitution" ( అర్థం: ఆకలి, పేదరికం, లేమి, నిరాశ్రయత నుండి వచ్చే బలవంతం) ఉంది ( PUDR ). వెట్టి కార్మికులు: ఒక కార్మికుడు బలవంతపు శ్రమ చేస్తున్నట్లు చూపితే, అతను వెట్టి కార్మికుడని కోర్టు భావిస్తుంది ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , 1983). బాల కార్మికులు: M. C. Mehta (1996) – నేరస్తుడైన యజమాని ప్రతి బిడ్డకు Rs. 20,000 పరిహారం, ప్రభుత్వం Rs. 5,000 (లేదా వయోజనుడికి ఉద్యోగం) సంక్షేమ నిధిలో జమ చేయాలని ఆదేశించింది. శిక్ష: భాగం IIIలో ప్రకటించిన నేరాలకు శిక్ష నిర్దేశించే చట్టం పార్లమెంటు మాత్రమే చేయగలదు (అధికరణ 35(a)(ii)); BNS, 2023 అక్రమ రవాణా (సెక్షన్ 143), చట్టవిరుద్ధ నిర్బంధ శ్రమ (సెక్షన్ 146)ను శిక్షిస్తుంది.
te.meaning: మానవ అక్రమ రవాణా: మనుషులతో వస్తువుల్లా వ్యాపారం – దోపిడీ కోసం వ్యక్తులను నియమించడం, తరలించడం, ఉంచడం లేదా స్వీకరించడం (BNS సెక్షన్ 143 చూడండి). వెట్టిచాకిరీ (Begar): "a word of Indian origin" ( అర్థం: భారతీయ మూలం గల మాట); "a form of forced labour under which a person is compelled to work without receiving any remuneration" ( అర్థం: ఏ ప్రతిఫలమూ పొందకుండా పని చేయమని ఒక వ్యక్తిని బలవంతం చేసే బలవంతపు శ్రమ రూపం) ( PUDR ). బలవంతపు శ్రమ: ఒక వ్యక్తి బలవంతంగా అందించే శ్రమ లేదా సేవ. "బలం" శారీరకమైనది, చట్టపరమైనది (ఉదా. జైలు లేదా జరిమానా బెదిరింపు), లేదా "compulsion arising from hunger and poverty, want and destitution" ( అర్థం: ఆకలి, పేదరికం, లేమి, నిరాశ్రయత నుండి వచ్చే బలవంతం) కావచ్చు ( PUDR ). వెట్టి శ్రమ (Bonded labour): అడ్వాన్స్ లేదా ఇతర ఆర్థిక ప్రతిఫలానికి బదులుగా బలవంతపు శ్రమ; కార్మికుడు ఉపాధి లేదా సంచార స్వేచ్ఛను కోల్పోతాడు ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , వెట్టి కార్మిక వ్యవస్థ (రద్దు) చట్టం, 1976ను వివరిస్తూ). ప్రమాదకర ఉపాధి (అధికరణ 24): బిడ్డ ప్రాణానికి లేదా ఆరోగ్యానికి ప్రమాదకరమైన పని; కర్మాగారాలు, గనులతో పాటు నిర్మాణ పని కూడా ఇందులో ఉంది ( PUDR ).
keyPoints: అధికరణ 23(1): అక్రమ రవాణా, వెట్టిచాకిరీ, సారూప్య బలవంతపు శ్రమ నిషేధం; నేరం. అధికరణ 23(2): నిర్బంధ ప్రజా సేవ అనుమతి; మతం, జాతి, కులం లేదా వర్గం ఆధారంగా మాత్రమే వివక్ష లేదు. అధికరణ 24: 14 లోపు బిడ్డ కర్మాగారం, గని, ప్రమాదకర పనిలో ఉండరాదు. అధికరణలు 17, 23, 24 ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తులకు వర్తిస్తాయి ( PUDR ). కనీస వేతనం కంటే తక్కువ = బలవంతపు శ్రమ ( PUDR ). బలవంతపు శ్రమ చూపితే → వెట్టి శ్రమ భావన ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). M. C. Mehta (1996): ప్రతి బిడ్డకు Rs. 20,000 + Rs. 5,000 = Rs. 25,000. అధికరణ 35(a)(ii): పార్లమెంటు మాత్రమే శిక్ష నిర్దేశిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: అధికరణ 24ను ఉదహరించండి. జవాబు: "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment." ( అర్థం: పద్నాలుగు సంవత్సరాల లోపు ఏ బిడ్డనూ ఏ కర్మాగారంలో లేదా గనిలో పనికి పెట్టరాదు, లేదా మరే ఇతర ప్రమాదకర ఉపాధిలో నియమించరాదు.) వెట్టిచాకిరీ అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: ఏ ప్రతిఫలమూ లేని బలవంతపు శ్రమ ( PUDR ). కనీస వేతనం కంటే తక్కువ చెల్లించడం బలవంతపు శ్రమా? జవాబు: అవును, ఆర్థిక బలవంతం కారణంగా అలా భావించబడుతుంది ( PUDR ). అధికరణ 23ను ప్రైవేట్ కాంట్రాక్టర్‌కు వ్యతిరేకంగా అమలు చేయవచ్చా? జవాబు: అవును ( PUDR ). అధికరణ 23(2) కింద రాజ్యం ఏమి చేయవచ్చు? జవాబు: మతం, జాతి, కులం లేదా వర్గం ఆధారంగా మాత్రమే వివక్ష లేకుండా ప్రజా ప్రయోజనాల కోసం నిర్బంధ సేవ విధించవచ్చు. Bandhua Mukti Morcha ఏ భావనను నిర్దేశించింది? జవాబు: బలవంతపు శ్రమ చూపిన తర్వాత, ఆ కార్మికుడు వెట్టి కార్మికుడని భావించబడతాడు. ఒక కర్మాగారం 8 మంది పిల్లలను పనిలో పెట్టింది. M. C. Mehta కింద యజమాని మొత్తం పరిహారం? జవాబు: 8 × Rs. 20,000 = Rs. 1,60,000. అధికరణ 23 కింద నేరాలను శిక్షించే చట్టాలు ఎవరు చేయవచ్చు? జవాబు: పార్లమెంటు మాత్రమే (అధికరణ 35(a)(ii)). BNS కింద అక్రమ రవాణాకు సమ్మతి రక్షణా? జవాబు: కాదు; "The consent of the victim is immaterial" ( అర్థం: బాధితుని సమ్మతి అప్రస్తుతం) (సెక్షన్ 143, వివరణ 2). ముసాయిదా అధికరణలు 17, 18 ఎప్పుడు ఆమోదించబడ్డాయి? జవాబు: 3 డిసెంబర్ 1948.

hi.inOneMinute: Two Articles: Art. 23 prohibits " Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour "; any contravention is an offence. The State may still impose compulsory service for public purposes , without discrimination "on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class". Art. 24: "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment." Against everyone, not only the State: Arts. 23 and 24 (like Art. 17) are "enforceable against the whole world" ( PUDR , 1982). Wide meaning of "force": paying less than the minimum wage is presumed to be forced labour, because "force" includes "compulsion arising from hunger and poverty, want and destitution" ( PUDR ). Bonded labour: when a labourer is shown to give forced labour, the Court presumes he is a bonded labourer ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , 1983). Child labour: M. C. Mehta (1996) directed Rs. 20,000 compensation per child from the offending employer, plus Rs. 5,000 from the Government (or a job for an adult), into a welfare fund. Punishment: only Parliament can prescribe punishment for offences declared in Part III (Art. 35(a)(ii)); the BNS, 2023 punishes trafficking (s. 143) and unlawful compulsory labour (s. 146).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Article 23 – "Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour."

(1) "Traffic in human beings and begar and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited and any contravention of this provision shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law." (2) "Nothing in this article shall prevent the State from imposing compulsory service for public purposes, and in imposing such service the State shall not make any discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class or any of them."

Article 24 – "Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc." "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment."

Article 35(a)(ii): Parliament, and not a State Legislature, has power to make laws "for prescribing punishment for those acts which are declared to be offences under this Part", and shall make such laws "as soon as may be after the commencement of this Constitution".
Related Directive Principles:

Art. 39(e): "the health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused and that citizens are not forced by economic necessity to enter avocations unsuited to their age or strength". Art. 39(f): children are to be given opportunities to develop "in conditions of freedom and dignity" and "childhood and youth are protected against exploitation and against moral and material abandonment."
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023:

s. 143(1): whoever, "for the purpose of exploitation", recruits, transports, harbours, transfers or receives a person by threats, force or coercion, abduction, fraud or deception, abuse of power, or inducement, "commits the offence of trafficking". Explanation 1: "exploitation" includes "physical exploitation or any form of sexual exploitation, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude, beggary or forced removal of organs." Explanation 2: "The consent of the victim is immaterial". Punishment: 7 to 10 years (s. 143(2)); more than one person – 10 years to life (s. 143(3)); a child – 10 years to life (s. 143(4)); more than one child – 14 years to life (s. 143(5)). s. 145: habitual dealing in slaves – imprisonment for life or up to ten years, and fine. s. 146: "Whoever unlawfully compels any person to labour against the will of that person" – up to one year, or fine, or both.
hi.meaning: Traffic in human beings: dealing in human beings like goods – recruiting, moving, keeping or receiving persons for exploitation (see BNS s. 143). Begar: "a word of Indian origin"; "a form of forced labour under which a person is compelled to work without receiving any remuneration" ( PUDR ). Forced labour : labour or service a person is forced to provide. "Force" may be physical, legal (e.g. threat of prison or fine), or "compulsion arising from hunger and poverty, want and destitution" ( PUDR ). Bonded labour: forced labour in return for an advance or other economic consideration, where the labourer loses freedom of employment or movement ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , describing the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976). Hazardous employment (Art. 24): work dangerous to a child's life or health; besides factories and mines, it includes construction work ( PUDR ).
keyPoints: Art. 23(1): traffic, begar, similar forced labour prohibited; offence. Art. 23(2): compulsory public service allowed; no discrimination on religion, race, caste or class only. Art. 24: no child below 14 in factory, mine or hazardous work. Arts. 17, 23, 24 bind private persons ( PUDR ). Below minimum wage = forced labour ( PUDR ). Forced labour shown → bonded labour presumed ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). M. C. Mehta (1996): Rs. 20,000 + Rs. 5,000 = Rs. 25,000 per child. Art. 35(a)(ii): only Parliament prescribes punishment.

caseLaws.facts: People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India , [1983] 1 SCR 456 (P. N. Bhagwati and Baharul Islam JJ.; decided 18 September 1982)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter to Bhagwati J
caseLaws.facts: complained that workers on Asian Games projects in Delhi were paid less than the minimum wage through Jamadars and that children below 14 were employed. Principle: Arts. 23 and 24 bind private persons; work for less than the minimum wage is forced labour; construction is hazardous employment for Art. 24. Why it matters: Gave Art. 23 its wide meaning.
Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India , [1984] 2 SCR 67 (P. N. Bhagwati, R. S. Pathak and A. N. Sen JJ.; decided 16 December 1983)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter alleged that bonded labourers worked in inhuman conditions in Faridabad stone quarri
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Once forced labour is shown, the Court presumes bonded labour; the State must identify, release and rehabilitate bonded labourers. Why it matters: Made the Bonded Labour Act effective through Art. 23.
M. C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu , [1996] Supp. 9 SCR 726 (Kuldip Singh, B. L. Hansaria and S. B. Majmudar JJ.; decided 10 December 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A PIL about children employed in hazardous match and fireworks factories of Sivakasi
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Rs. 20,000 per child from the offending employer, plus a job for an adult or Rs. 5,000 from the Government, into a welfare fund; benefits tied to the child's education. Why it matters: Practical scheme to enforce Art. 24.

selfTest.q: Quote Art. 24. Answer: "No child below the age of fourteen years shall be employed to work in any factory or mine or engaged in any other hazardous employment." What is begar?
selfTest.a: Answer: Forced labour without any remuneration ( PUDR ). Is paying less than the minimum wage forced labour? Answer: Yes, it is presumed to be, because of economic compulsion ( PUDR ). Can Art. 23 be enforced against a private contractor? Answer: Yes ( PUDR ). What may the State do under Art. 23(2)? Answer: Impose compulsory service for public purposes, without discrimination on grounds only of religion, race, caste or class. What presumption did Bandhua Mukti Morcha lay down? Answer: Once forced labour is shown, the labourer is presumed to be a bonded labourer. A factory employs 8 children. Total employer compensation under M. C. Mehta ? Answer: 8 × Rs. 20,000 = Rs. 1,60,000. Who can make laws punishing offences under Art. 23? Answer: Parliament only (Art. 35(a)(ii)). Is consent a defence to trafficking under the BNS? Answer: No; "The consent of the victim is immaterial" (s. 143, Explanation 2). When were draft Arts. 17 and 18 adopted? Answer: 3 December 1948.

constitutional-law-i-u4-t3.subtitle: Articles 29 and 30: a section's right to conserve its language, script or culture, equal admission to State schools, and the right of minorities to run their own institutions

en.inOneMinute: Two Articles under the heading "Cultural and Educational Rights": Art. 29(1) – any section of citizens with "a distinct language, script or culture of its own" has the right to conserve it. Art. 29(2) – no citizen can be denied admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution "on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them". Art. 30(1) – all minorities , "whether based on religion or language", have the right to establish and administer educational institutions "of their choice". Art. 30(1A) – if the State compulsorily acquires the property of a minority educational institution , the amount must not "restrict or abrogate" the Art. 30(1) right. Art. 30(2) – the State shall not discriminate in granting aid on the ground that an institution is under minority management. Four distinct rights: Arts. 29 and 30 "confer four distinct rights" ( St. Xavier's College , 1974). Minority is decided State-wise: "the unit will be the State and not the whole of India" ( T.M.A. Pai , 2002). Not absolute: the State may regulate standards, but cannot take away the right to administer; there is no fundamental right to affiliation , yet affiliation conditions cannot destroy the Art. 30 right ( St. Xavier's ). Unaided institutions: the State cannot force its reservation policy or a quota on unaided minority or non-minority institutions ( P. A. Inamdar , 2005).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Art. 29 – "Protection of interests of minorities."

(1) "Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same." (2) "No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them."
Art. 30 – "Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions."

(1) "All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice." (1A) "In making any law providing for the compulsory acquisition of any property of an educational institution established and administered by a minority, referred to in clause (1), the State shall ensure that the amount fixed by or determined under such law for the acquisition of such property is such as would not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under that clause." Inserted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 4 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). (2) "The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language."
Related:

Art. 15(5) (Ninety-third Amendment, 2005, s. 2, w.e.f. 20-1-2006): special provisions for admission of backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to private educational institutions, "other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30". Art. 350A (Seventh Amendment, 1956, s. 21, w.e.f. 1-11-1956): every State shall endeavour "to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children belonging to linguistic minority groups".
en.meaning: Minority : the Constitution does not define it. Art. 30 covers "Linguistic and religious minorities"; "for the purpose of determining the minority, the unit will be the State and not the whole of India" ( T.M.A. Pai ). Section of citizens (Art. 29(1)): any group of citizens – majority or minority – with a distinct language, script or culture. "Article 29 confers the fundamental right on any section of the citizens which will include the majority section whereas Article 30(1) confers the right on all minorities" ( St. Xavier's ). Minority educational institution: an educational institution established and administered by a religious or linguistic minority under Art. 30(1). "Of their choice" means "even professional educational institutions would be covered by Article 30" ( T.M.A. Pai ). Education / educational institution: "education" "means and includes education at all levels from the primary school level upto the post-graduate level. It includes professional education" ( T.M.A. Pai ). Affiliation / recognition: linking a college to a university (or school to a board) so that its students can take the university's examinations and degrees. "There is no fundamental right to affiliation. But recognition or affiliation is necessary for a meaningful exercise of the right to establish and administer educational institutions" ( St. Xavier's , headnote).
keyPoints: Art. 29(1): any section of citizens; language, script or culture. Art. 29(2): individual citizen; State-maintained or aided institutions; religion, race, caste, language. Art. 30(1): religious and linguistic minorities; institutions of their choice. Minority status: the State is the unit ( T.M.A. Pai ). Four distinct rights ( St. Xavier's ). No fundamental right to affiliation, but affiliation conditions cannot destroy Art. 30. Aided minority institution: reasonable extent of non-minority students. Unaided: no State quota or reservation; NRI seats ≤ 15% ( P. A. Inamdar ). Art. 30(1A): 44th Amendment; fair amount on acquisition. Art. 30(2): no discrimination in aid; aid itself is not a right.

caseLaws.facts: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan , [1951] SCR 525 (7 judges; S. R. Das J. for the Court; decided 9 April 1951)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Communal G
caseLaws.facts: O. allotted college seats by community (6 of every 14 to Non-Brahmin Hindus, 2 to Brahmins, and so on); two Brahmin applicants challenged it. Principle: Admission based on religion, race or caste only violates Art. 29(2); Directive Principles cannot override Fundamental Rights. Why it matters: Led to the First Amendment adding Art. 15(4).
Ahmedabad St. Xavier's College Society v. State of Gujarat , [1975] 1 SCR 173 (9 judges; leading judgment by Ray C.J.; decided 26 April 1974)

caseLaws.name: Facts: St
caseLaws.facts: Xavier's College, Ahmedabad, established in June 1955 by the Society of Jesus, challenged provisions of the Gujarat University Act, 1949 placing University nominees on its governing body and making colleges constituent colleges. Principle: Arts. 29 and 30 are not mutually exclusive; Art. 30 covers general secular education; there is no fundamental right to affiliation, but affiliation conditions cannot take away administration; ss. 33A, 40 and 41 cannot apply compulsorily to minority colleges. Why it matters: Set out the "four distinct rights" and the line between regulation and control.
T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka , [2002] Supp. 3 SCR 587; (2002) 8 SCC 481 (11 judges; Kirpal C.J. for the majority; decided 31 October 2002)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A large group of cases on how far the State can regulate private and minority educational ins
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Minority status is decided State-wise; Art. 30 covers professional education; the right is not absolute; aided minority institutions must admit a reasonable extent of non-minority students; the Unni Krishnan scheme was unconstitutional. Why it matters: The leading case on Art. 30, answering eleven questions.
P. A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra , [2005] Supp. 2 SCR 603 (7 judges, Lahoti C.J. presiding; decided 12 August 2005)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Doubts arose on how T
caseLaws.facts: M.A. Pai and Islamic Academy applied to admissions and fees in unaided professional colleges. Principle: No State reservation or quota in unaided minority or non-minority institutions; admission may be by a credible common entrance test; NRI seats up to 15%; no capitation fee or profiteering. Why it matters: Islamic Academy was partly overruled; the rules for unaided colleges were settled.

selfTest.q: Can the majority community claim Art. 29(1)?
selfTest.a: Answer: Yes; it is for "any section of the citizens" ( St. Xavier's ). Is minority status decided on all-India figures? Answer: No; the State is the unit ( T.M.A. Pai ). Under the Communal G.O., how many seats out of 14 went to Brahmins, and what percentage is that? Answer: 2 of 14 ≈ 14.3%. Does Art. 30 cover a minority-run engineering college? Answer: Yes; "of their choice" includes professional education ( T.M.A. Pai ). Is there a fundamental right to affiliation? Answer: No, but affiliation conditions cannot take away the Art. 30 right ( St. Xavier's ). An unaided college has 120 seats. What is the most it can give to NRIs? Answer: 15% of 120 = 18 seats ( P. A. Inamdar ). Can the State impose its reservation policy on an unaided minority college? Answer: No ( P. A. Inamdar ); Art. 15(5) also excludes minority institutions. Must an aided minority college admit non-minority students? Answer: Yes, to a reasonable extent ( T.M.A. Pai ). Which Amendment inserted Art. 30(1A)? Answer: The Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978, s. 4 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). Why did Dr. Ambedkar drop the word "minority" from draft Art. 23(1)? Answer: To protect cultural minorities in the wider sense, such as people from Madras settled in Bombay.

te.inOneMinute: "Cultural and Educational Rights" ( అర్థం: సాంస్కృతిక మరియు విద్యా హక్కులు) శీర్షిక కింద రెండు అధికరణలు: అధికరణ 29(1) – "a distinct language, script or culture of its own" ( అర్థం: తనదైన విలక్షణ భాష, లిపి లేదా సంస్కృతి) ఉన్న పౌరుల ఏ విభాగానికైనా దానిని సంరక్షించుకునే హక్కు ఉంది. అధికరణ 29(2) – రాజ్యం నిర్వహించే లేదా సహాయం పొందే విద్యా సంస్థలో "on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them" ( అర్థం: మతం, జాతి, కులం, భాష లేదా వాటిలో ఏదైనా ఆధారంగా మాత్రమే) ఏ పౌరుడికీ ప్రవేశం నిరాకరించరాదు. అధికరణ 30(1) – "whether based on religion or language" ( అర్థం: మతం ఆధారంగా లేదా భాష ఆధారంగా) అన్ని మైనారిటీలకు "of their choice" ( అర్థం: తమకు నచ్చిన) విద్యా సంస్థలను స్థాపించి నిర్వహించే హక్కు ఉంది. అధికరణ 30(1A) – మైనారిటీ విద్యా సంస్థ ఆస్తిని రాజ్యం నిర్బంధంగా స్వాధీనం చేసుకుంటే, ఆ మొత్తం అధికరణ 30(1) హక్కును "restrict or abrogate" ( అర్థం: పరిమితం చేయరాదు లేదా రద్దు చేయరాదు). అధికరణ 30(2) – ఒక సంస్థ మైనారిటీ నిర్వహణలో ఉందన్న కారణంగా సహాయం ఇవ్వడంలో రాజ్యం వివక్ష చూపరాదు. నాలుగు వేర్వేరు హక్కులు: అధికరణలు 29, 30 "confer four distinct rights" ( అర్థం: నాలుగు వేర్వేరు హక్కులను ఇస్తాయి) ( St. Xavier's College , 1974). మైనారిటీని రాష్ట్రాల వారీగా నిర్ణయిస్తారు: "the unit will be the State and not the whole of India" ( అర్థం: యూనిట్ రాష్ట్రమే, మొత్తం భారతదేశం కాదు) ( T.M.A. Pai , 2002). సంపూర్ణం కాదు: రాజ్యం ప్రమాణాలను నియంత్రించవచ్చు, కానీ నిర్వహించే హక్కును తీసివేయలేదు; అనుబంధం పొందడానికి ప్రాథమిక హక్కు లేదు, అయినా అనుబంధ షరతులు అధికరణ 30 హక్కును నాశనం చేయరాదు ( St. Xavier's ). సహాయం లేని సంస్థలు: సహాయం లేని మైనారిటీ లేదా మైనారిటీ కాని సంస్థలపై రాజ్యం తన రిజర్వేషన్ విధానాన్ని లేదా కోటాను బలవంతంగా విధించలేదు ( P. A. Inamdar , 2005).
te.meaning: మైనారిటీ : రాజ్యాంగం దీనిని నిర్వచించలేదు. అధికరణ 30 "Linguistic and religious minorities" ( అర్థం: భాషా, మత మైనారిటీలు)కు వర్తిస్తుంది; "for the purpose of determining the minority, the unit will be the State and not the whole of India" ( అర్థం: మైనారిటీని నిర్ణయించడానికి యూనిట్ రాష్ట్రమే, మొత్తం భారతదేశం కాదు) ( T.M.A. Pai ). పౌరుల విభాగం (అధికరణ 29(1)): విలక్షణ భాష, లిపి లేదా సంస్కృతి ఉన్న పౌరుల ఏ సమూహమైనా – మెజారిటీ అయినా మైనారిటీ అయినా. "Article 29 confers the fundamental right on any section of the citizens which will include the majority section whereas Article 30(1) confers the right on all minorities" ( అర్థం: అధికరణ 29 మెజారిటీ విభాగంతో సహా పౌరుల ఏ విభాగానికైనా ప్రాథమిక హక్కు ను ఇస్తుంది, అధికరణ 30(1) అన్ని మైనారిటీలకు హక్కును ఇస్తుంది) ( St. Xavier's ). మైనారిటీ విద్యా సంస్థ: అధికరణ 30(1) కింద మత లేదా భాషా మైనారిటీ స్థాపించి నిర్వహించే విద్యా సంస్థ. "Of their choice" ( అర్థం: తమకు నచ్చిన) అంటే "even professional educational institutions would be covered by Article 30" ( అర్థం: వృత్తి విద్యా సంస్థలు కూడా అధికరణ 30 పరిధిలోకి వస్తాయి) ( T.M.A. Pai ). విద్య / విద్యా సంస్థ: "education" ( అర్థం: విద్య) అంటే "means and includes education at all levels from the primary school level upto the post-graduate level. It includes professional education" ( అర్థం: ప్రాథమిక పాఠశాల స్థాయి నుండి పోస్ట్-గ్రాడ్యుయేట్ స్థాయి వరకు అన్ని స్థాయిల విద్య. ఇందులో వృత్తి విద్య కూడా ఉంది) ( T.M.A. Pai ). అనుబంధం / గుర్తింపు: ఒక కళాశాలను విశ్వవిద్యాలయంతో (లేదా పాఠశాలను బోర్డుతో) అనుసంధానించడం, తద్వారా దాని విద్యార్థులు ఆ విశ్వవిద్యాలయ పరీక్షలు రాసి డిగ్రీలు పొందగలుగుతారు. "There is no fundamental right to affiliation. But recognition or affiliation is necessary for a meaningful exercise of the right to establish and administer educational institutions" ( అర్థం: అనుబంధానికి ప్రాథమిక హక్కు లేదు. కానీ విద్యా సంస్థలను స్థాపించి నిర్వహించే హక్కును అర్థవంతంగా వినియోగించుకోవడానికి గుర్తింపు లేదా అనుబంధం అవసరం) ( St. Xavier's , హెడ్‌నోట్).
keyPoints: అధికరణ 29(1): పౌరుల ఏ విభాగమైనా; భాష, లిపి లేదా సంస్కృతి. అధికరణ 29(2): వ్యక్తిగత పౌరుడు; రాజ్యం నిర్వహించే లేదా సహాయం పొందే సంస్థలు; మతం, జాతి, కులం, భాష. అధికరణ 30(1): మత, భాషా మైనారిటీలు; నచ్చిన సంస్థలు. మైనారిటీ హోదా: రాష్ట్రమే యూనిట్ ( T.M.A. Pai ). నాలుగు వేర్వేరు హక్కులు ( St. Xavier's ). అనుబంధానికి ప్రాథమిక హక్కు లేదు, కానీ అనుబంధ షరతులు అధికరణ 30ని నాశనం చేయరాదు. సహాయం పొందే మైనారిటీ సంస్థ: సహేతుక మేరకు మైనారిటీ కాని విద్యార్థులు. సహాయం లేనివి: రాజ్య కోటా లేదా రిజర్వేషన్ లేదు; ఎన్‌ఆర్‌ఐ సీట్లు ≤ 15% ( P. A. Inamdar ). అధికరణ 30(1A): 44వ సవరణ; స్వాధీనంపై న్యాయమైన మొత్తం. అధికరణ 30(2): సహాయంలో వివక్ష లేదు; సహాయం స్వయంగా హక్కు కాదు.

selfTest.q: మెజారిటీ సమాజం అధికరణ 29(1)ను కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: అవును; అది "any section of the citizens" ( అర్థం: పౌరుల ఏ విభాగానికైనా) ( St. Xavier's ). మైనారిటీ హోదాను అఖిల భారత గణాంకాలపై నిర్ణయిస్తారా? జవాబు: లేదు; రాష్ట్రమే యూనిట్ ( T.M.A. Pai ). కమ్యూనల్ జి.ఒ. కింద 14 సీట్లలో బ్రాహ్మణులకు ఎన్ని, అది ఎంత శాతం? జవాబు: 14లో 2 ≈ 14.3%. మైనారిటీ నడిపే ఇంజినీరింగ్ కళాశాలకు అధికరణ 30 వర్తిస్తుందా? జవాబు: అవును; "of their choice" ( అర్థం: తమకు నచ్చిన)లో వృత్తి విద్య ఉంది ( T.M.A. Pai ). అనుబంధానికి ప్రాథమిక హక్కు ఉందా? జవాబు: లేదు, కానీ అనుబంధ షరతులు అధికరణ 30 హక్కును తీసివేయలేవు ( St. Xavier's ). సహాయం లేని ఒక కళాశాలలో 120 సీట్లు ఉన్నాయి. ఎన్‌ఆర్‌ఐలకు గరిష్టంగా ఎన్ని ఇవ్వవచ్చు? జవాబు: 120లో 15% = 18 సీట్లు ( P. A. Inamdar ). సహాయం లేని మైనారిటీ కళాశాలపై రాజ్యం తన రిజర్వేషన్ విధానాన్ని విధించవచ్చా? జవాబు: లేదు ( P. A. Inamdar ); అధికరణ 15(5) కూడా మైనారిటీ సంస్థలను మినహాయిస్తుంది. సహాయం పొందే మైనారిటీ కళాశాల మైనారిటీ కాని విద్యార్థులను చేర్చుకోవాలా? జవాబు: అవును, సహేతుక మేరకు ( T.M.A. Pai ). అధికరణ 30(1A)ను ఏ సవరణ చేర్చింది? జవాబు: నలభై నాలుగో సవరణ, 1978, సెక్షన్ 4 (20-6-1979 నుండి). ముసాయిదా అధికరణ 23(1) నుండి డాక్టర్ అంబేద్కర్ "minority" ( అర్థం: మైనారిటీ) అనే మాటను ఎందుకు తొలగించారు? జవాబు: బొంబాయిలో స్థిరపడిన మద్రాసు ప్రజల వంటి విస్తృత అర్థంలోని సాంస్కృతిక మైనారిటీలను రక్షించడానికి.

hi.inOneMinute: Two Articles under the heading "Cultural and Educational Rights": Art. 29(1) – any section of citizens with "a distinct language, script or culture of its own" has the right to conserve it. Art. 29(2) – no citizen can be denied admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution "on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them". Art. 30(1) – all minorities , "whether based on religion or language", have the right to establish and administer educational institutions "of their choice". Art. 30(1A) – if the State compulsorily acquires the property of a minority educational institution , the amount must not "restrict or abrogate" the Art. 30(1) right. Art. 30(2) – the State shall not discriminate in granting aid on the ground that an institution is under minority management. Four distinct rights: Arts. 29 and 30 "confer four distinct rights" ( St. Xavier's College , 1974). Minority is decided State-wise: "the unit will be the State and not the whole of India" ( T.M.A. Pai , 2002). Not absolute: the State may regulate standards, but cannot take away the right to administer; there is no fundamental right to affiliation , yet affiliation conditions cannot destroy the Art. 30 right ( St. Xavier's ). Unaided institutions: the State cannot force its reservation policy or a quota on unaided minority or non-minority institutions ( P. A. Inamdar , 2005).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).
Art. 29 – "Protection of interests of minorities."

(1) "Any section of the citizens residing in the territory of India or any part thereof having a distinct language, script or culture of its own shall have the right to conserve the same." (2) "No citizen shall be denied admission into any educational institution maintained by the State or receiving aid out of State funds on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language or any of them."
Art. 30 – "Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions."

(1) "All minorities, whether based on religion or language, shall have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice." (1A) "In making any law providing for the compulsory acquisition of any property of an educational institution established and administered by a minority, referred to in clause (1), the State shall ensure that the amount fixed by or determined under such law for the acquisition of such property is such as would not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed under that clause." Inserted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 4 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). (2) "The State shall not, in granting aid to educational institutions, discriminate against any educational institution on the ground that it is under the management of a minority, whether based on religion or language."
Related:

Art. 15(5) (Ninety-third Amendment, 2005, s. 2, w.e.f. 20-1-2006): special provisions for admission of backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to private educational institutions, "other than the minority educational institutions referred to in clause (1) of article 30". Art. 350A (Seventh Amendment, 1956, s. 21, w.e.f. 1-11-1956): every State shall endeavour "to provide adequate facilities for instruction in the mother-tongue at the primary stage of education to children belonging to linguistic minority groups".
hi.meaning: Minority : the Constitution does not define it. Art. 30 covers "Linguistic and religious minorities"; "for the purpose of determining the minority, the unit will be the State and not the whole of India" ( T.M.A. Pai ). Section of citizens (Art. 29(1)): any group of citizens – majority or minority – with a distinct language, script or culture. "Article 29 confers the fundamental right on any section of the citizens which will include the majority section whereas Article 30(1) confers the right on all minorities" ( St. Xavier's ). Minority educational institution: an educational institution established and administered by a religious or linguistic minority under Art. 30(1). "Of their choice" means "even professional educational institutions would be covered by Article 30" ( T.M.A. Pai ). Education / educational institution: "education" "means and includes education at all levels from the primary school level upto the post-graduate level. It includes professional education" ( T.M.A. Pai ). Affiliation / recognition: linking a college to a university (or school to a board) so that its students can take the university's examinations and degrees. "There is no fundamental right to affiliation. But recognition or affiliation is necessary for a meaningful exercise of the right to establish and administer educational institutions" ( St. Xavier's , headnote).
keyPoints: Art. 29(1): any section of citizens; language, script or culture. Art. 29(2): individual citizen; State-maintained or aided institutions; religion, race, caste, language. Art. 30(1): religious and linguistic minorities; institutions of their choice. Minority status: the State is the unit ( T.M.A. Pai ). Four distinct rights ( St. Xavier's ). No fundamental right to affiliation, but affiliation conditions cannot destroy Art. 30. Aided minority institution: reasonable extent of non-minority students. Unaided: no State quota or reservation; NRI seats ≤ 15% ( P. A. Inamdar ). Art. 30(1A): 44th Amendment; fair amount on acquisition. Art. 30(2): no discrimination in aid; aid itself is not a right.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Communal G
caseLaws.facts: O. allotted college seats by community (6 of every 14 to Non-Brahmin Hindus, 2 to Brahmins, and so on); two Brahmin applicants challenged it. Principle: Admission based on religion, race or caste only violates Art. 29(2); Directive Principles cannot override Fundamental Rights. Why it matters: Led to the First Amendment adding Art. 15(4).
Ahmedabad St. Xavier's College Society v. State of Gujarat , [1975] 1 SCR 173 (9 judges; leading judgment by Ray C.J.; decided 26 April 1974)

caseLaws.name: Facts: St
caseLaws.facts: Xavier's College, Ahmedabad, established in June 1955 by the Society of Jesus, challenged provisions of the Gujarat University Act, 1949 placing University nominees on its governing body and making colleges constituent colleges. Principle: Arts. 29 and 30 are not mutually exclusive; Art. 30 covers general secular education; there is no fundamental right to affiliation, but affiliation conditions cannot take away administration; ss. 33A, 40 and 41 cannot apply compulsorily to minority colleges. Why it matters: Set out the "four distinct rights" and the line between regulation and control.
T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka , [2002] Supp. 3 SCR 587; (2002) 8 SCC 481 (11 judges; Kirpal C.J. for the majority; decided 31 October 2002)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A large group of cases on how far the State can regulate private and minority educational ins
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Minority status is decided State-wise; Art. 30 covers professional education; the right is not absolute; aided minority institutions must admit a reasonable extent of non-minority students; the Unni Krishnan scheme was unconstitutional. Why it matters: The leading case on Art. 30, answering eleven questions.
P. A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra , [2005] Supp. 2 SCR 603 (7 judges, Lahoti C.J. presiding; decided 12 August 2005)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Doubts arose on how T
caseLaws.facts: M.A. Pai and Islamic Academy applied to admissions and fees in unaided professional colleges. Principle: No State reservation or quota in unaided minority or non-minority institutions; admission may be by a credible common entrance test; NRI seats up to 15%; no capitation fee or profiteering. Why it matters: Islamic Academy was partly overruled; the rules for unaided colleges were settled.

selfTest.q: Can the majority community claim Art. 29(1)?
selfTest.a: Answer: Yes; it is for "any section of the citizens" ( St. Xavier's ). Is minority status decided on all-India figures? Answer: No; the State is the unit ( T.M.A. Pai ). Under the Communal G.O., how many seats out of 14 went to Brahmins, and what percentage is that? Answer: 2 of 14 ≈ 14.3%. Does Art. 30 cover a minority-run engineering college? Answer: Yes; "of their choice" includes professional education ( T.M.A. Pai ). Is there a fundamental right to affiliation? Answer: No, but affiliation conditions cannot take away the Art. 30 right ( St. Xavier's ). An unaided college has 120 seats. What is the most it can give to NRIs? Answer: 15% of 120 = 18 seats ( P. A. Inamdar ). Can the State impose its reservation policy on an unaided minority college? Answer: No ( P. A. Inamdar ); Art. 15(5) also excludes minority institutions. Must an aided minority college admit non-minority students? Answer: Yes, to a reasonable extent ( T.M.A. Pai ). Which Amendment inserted Art. 30(1A)? Answer: The Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978, s. 4 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). Why did Dr. Ambedkar drop the word "minority" from draft Art. 23(1)? Answer: To protect cultural minorities in the wider sense, such as people from Madras settled in Bombay.

en.meaning:
In Basheshar Nath v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1959), what did the Supreme Court hold about a citizen's ability to waive a Fundamental Right?

Explanation. Basheshar Nath held that Fundamental Rights cannot be waived even by voluntary consent, since fundamental rights rest on public policy and there can be no estoppel against the Constitution.

What is the doctrine of severability, as applied to a law that partly violates a Fundamental Right?

Explanation. Under the doctrine of severability, only the offending, unconstitutional portion of a statute is struck down, provided it can be separated from the valid remainder without changing the law's essential character.

What is Article 13(2) of the Constitution's core mandate?

Explanation. Article 13(2) bars the State from making laws that take away or abridge Fundamental Rights, rendering any contravening law void to the extent of the contravention.

Under Article 19(2)-(6), restrictions on the freedoms guaranteed by Article 19(1) must satisfy which standard?

constitutional-law-i-u4-t4.subtitle: Article 32: the guaranteed right to move the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights, the five writs, compensation, and how Article 226 differs

en.inOneMinute: Art. 32 is the remedy for all other Fundamental Rights. Art. 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Art. 32(2) – the Supreme Court can issue directions or orders or writs , including habeas corpus , mandamus , prohibition , quo warranto and certiorari . Art. 32(3) – Parliament may empower any other court to exercise these powers within its local limits. Art. 32(4) – the right "shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution". Itself a Fundamental Right: the remedial right "is itself made a fundamental right by being included in Part III" ( Romesh Thappar , 1950). So a person may come straight to the Supreme Court without going to the High Court first. Dr. Ambedkar called it "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" (CAD, 9 December 1948). Who can move the Court: not only the injured person. In public interest litigation , "any member of the public acting bona fide" can move the Court for poor or disadvantaged persons, "even by addressing a letter to the court" ( PUDR , 1982; Bandhua Mukti Morcha , 1983). Compensation: the Court can order the State to pay money for violation of Art. 21 ( Rudul Sah , 1983; Nilabati Behera , 1993). Art. 226: every High Court can issue the same writs "for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose" – wider than Art. 32. Basic structure: judicial review under Arts. 226 and 32 is part of the "inviolable basic structure" ( L. Chandra Kumar , 1997).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026). Heading in Part III: "Right to Constitutional Remedies".
Art. 32 – "Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part."

(1) "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." (2) "The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part." (3) "Without prejudice to the powers conferred on the Supreme Court by clauses (1) and (2), Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under clause (2)." (4) "The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution."
Art. 32A ("Constitutional validity of State laws not to be considered in proceedings under article 32") – omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 3 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978).

Art. 33 – Parliament may by law decide how far the rights in Part III shall, for members of the Armed Forces, forces "charged with the maintenance of public order", intelligence or counter-intelligence organisations, and connected telecommunication staff, "be restricted or abrogated so as to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them" (substituted by the Fiftieth Amendment, 1984, s. 2, w.e.f. 11-9-1984).
Art. 226 – "Power of High Courts to issue certain writs."

(1) "Notwithstanding anything in article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose." (2) The power may also be used by any High Court within whose territory "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises", even if the Government, authority or person is located elsewhere. (3) If an interim order is passed without giving the other party copies and a hearing, and that party applies to vacate it, the High Court must decide the application "within a period of two weeks"; otherwise the interim order "shall ... stand vacated". (4) "The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32." Art. 226 was substituted by the Forty-second Amendment, 1976, s. 38 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977); the writs part was again substituted by the Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978, s. 30 (w.e.f. 1-8-1979).
Art. 139 – Parliament may by law give the Supreme Court power to issue the same writs "for any purposes other than those mentioned in clause (2) of article 32."

Related: Art. 359(1) – during a Proclamation of Emergency, the President may by order suspend "the right to move any court for the enforcement of such of the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21)" as are mentioned in the order. This is the main case of "otherwise provided" in Art. 32(4).
en.meaning: Constitutional remedy: a way given by the Constitution itself to get a Fundamental Right enforced by a court. Art. 32 makes this way a Fundamental Right. "Appropriate proceedings" (Art. 32(1)): "It should be a proceeding which can appropriately lead to an adjudication of the claim made for the enforcement of a fundamental right and can result in the grant of effective relief" ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). "Appropriate" refers to the purpose of the proceeding, not to any particular form. Writ : a formal written order of a court commanding a person or authority to do, or not to do, something. Art. 32(2) names five writs, but the power is wider: "even if the conditions for issue of any of these high prerogative writs are not fulfilled", the Supreme Court can issue "any direction, order or writ" ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , headnote). The five writs (plain meaning): Habeas corpus ("have the body") – orders the person holding someone in custody to produce that person before the Court, so the Court can see whether the detention is lawful. "The person to whom it is directed is under a legal obligation to produce the body of the person alleged to be unlawfully detained before the Court" ( Sebastian M. Hongray ). Mandamus ("we command") – orders a public authority to perform a public duty it is legally bound to perform. Prohibition – orders a lower court, tribunal or authority to stop proceeding in a matter outside its jurisdiction , before it decides. Certiorari – calls up the record of a decision already made by a lower court, tribunal or authority and quashes it if it was made without jurisdiction or is otherwise illegal. Quo warranto ("by what authority") – asks a person holding a public office to show by what legal authority he or she holds it; if none, the person is removed. Locus standi : the right to come before a court. The traditional rule allowed only the person whose legal right was hurt. In PIL, that rule "has now been jettisoned by the Supreme Court" ( PUDR , headnote). Public interest litigation (PIL): a case brought by a public-spirited person or body, acting bona fide, for persons who cannot come to court "by reason of poverty, disability or socially or economically disadvantaged position" ( PUDR ).
keyPoints: Art. 32(1): the right to move the Supreme Court is "guaranteed". Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right; no need to go to the High Court first ( Romesh Thappar ). Five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari – plus any direction or order ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). Dr. Ambedkar: "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" (9 December 1948). PIL: any bona fide member of the public, even by letter ( PUDR ; Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). Compensation for Art. 21 violations: Rudul Sah , Sebastian M. Hongray , Bhim Singh , Nilabati Behera . No sovereign immunity in public law compensation ( Nilabati Behera ). Art. 226: Part III rights "and for any other purpose"; not in derogation of Art. 32. Judicial review under Arts. 32 and 226 is basic structure ( L. Chandra Kumar ). Art. 32(4): suspension only as the Constitution provides – Art. 359; never Arts. 20 and 21.

caseLaws.facts: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras , [1950] SCR 594 (Kania C.J., Fazl Ali, Patanjali Sastri, Mahajan, Mukherjea and Das JJ.; decided 26 May 1950)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Madras banned the entry and circulation of the petitioner's journal Cross Roads ; he came dir
caseLaws.facts: 32. The State objected that he should first go to the Madras High Court. Principle: Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right; the Supreme Court is "the protector and guarantor of fundamental rights" and cannot refuse a petition because the High Court was not approached first. Why it matters: Established direct access to the Supreme Court for Fundamental Rights.
Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India , [1984] 2 SCR 67 (Bhagwati J.; Pathak J. concurring; decided 16 December 1983)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An organisation wrote a letter about bonded labourers working in inhuman conditions in stone
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Appropriate proceedings" means appropriate to the purpose, not a particular form; a bona fide member of the public may move the Court by letter for the poor; the Court may issue any direction or order, beyond the five writs. Why it matters: The leading statement on PIL and the width of Art. 32.
Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar , [1983] 3 SCR 508 (Chandrachud C.J., A. N. Sen and Ranganath Misra JJ.; decided 1 August 1983)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Acquitted on 3 June 1968, Rudul Sah stayed in jail until 16 October 1982 – over 14 years; he
caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: Under Art. 32 the Court can order monetary compensation for violation of Art. 21; release alone is not enough. Why it matters: First award of compensation under Art. 32 (Rs. 30,000 more, besides Rs. 5,000 paid).
Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa , [1993] 2 SCR 581 (Verma, Anand and Venkatachala JJ.; decided 24 March 1993)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A 22-year-old taken into police custody on 1 December 1987 was found dead on a railway track
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Compensation under Arts. 32/226 is a public law remedy based on strict liability; sovereign immunity does not apply; Kasturilal distinguished. Why it matters: Gave the legal basis for constitutional compensation (Rs. 1,50,000 awarded).
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India , [1997] 2 SCR 1186 (7 judges; Ahmadi C.J. for the Court; decided 18 March 1997)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to Arts
caseLaws.facts: 323A(2)(d) and 323B(3)(d) and tribunal laws that excluded the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts. Principle: Judicial review under Arts. 226 and 32 is part of the "inviolable basic structure"; the exclusion clauses are unconstitutional to that extent; tribunal decisions go to a High Court Division Bench. Why it matters: Art. 32 and Art. 226 cannot be taken away even by constitutional amendment.

selfTest.q: Must a petitioner go to the High Court before using Art. 32?
selfTest.a: Answer: No ( Romesh Thappar ). Name the five writs in Art. 32(2). Answer: Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari. Which writ stops a lower tribunal before it decides, and which quashes its decision afterwards? Answer: Prohibition stops it before; certiorari quashes after. Can a letter be treated as a writ petition? Answer: Yes, when written bona fide for persons unable to approach the Court ( PUDR ; Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). How long was Rudul Sah in jail after acquittal? Answer: 3 June 1968 to 16 October 1982 = 14 years, 4 months and 13 days. Does sovereign immunity bar compensation under Art. 32? Answer: No; it is a public law remedy based on strict liability ( Nilabati Behera ). A person is arrested at 6 a.m. on Monday and produced before a Magistrate at 6 p.m. on Tuesday; the journey took 4 hours. Is Art. 22(2) breached? Answer: 36 hours − 4 hours = 32 hours > 24 hours → yes. Can Art. 226 be used for a right that is not a Fundamental Right? Answer: Yes, "for any other purpose". Which case held judicial review under Arts. 32 and 226 is basic structure? Answer: L. Chandra Kumar (1997). Can the President suspend enforcement of Art. 21 during an Emergency? Answer: No; Art. 359(1) excludes Arts. 20 and 21.

te.inOneMinute: మిగతా అన్ని ప్రాథమిక హక్కులకు పరిహారం అధికరణ 32. అధికరణ 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." ( అర్థం: ఈ భాగం ఇచ్చిన హక్కుల అమలు కోసం తగిన విచారణల ద్వారా సుప్రీం కోర్టును ఆశ్రయించే హక్కు హామీ ఇవ్వబడింది.) అధికరణ 32(2) – సుప్రీం కోర్టు ఆదేశాలు, ఉత్తర్వులు లేదా రిట్‌లు జారీ చేయవచ్చు; వాటిలో హెబియస్ కార్పస్ , మాండమస్ , ప్రొహిబిషన్ , కో వారంటో , సెర్షియోరరి ఉన్నాయి. అధికరణ 32(3) – పార్లమెంటు ఏ ఇతర కోర్టుకైనా తన స్థానిక పరిధిలో ఈ అధికారాలను ఇవ్వవచ్చు. అధికరణ 32(4) – ఈ హక్కు "shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution" ( అర్థం: ఈ రాజ్యాంగం వేరే విధంగా నిర్దేశించిన సందర్భంలో తప్ప నిలిపివేయబడదు). ఇది స్వయంగా ప్రాథమిక హక్కు: పరిహార హక్కు "is itself made a fundamental right by being included in Part III" ( అర్థం: భాగం IIIలో చేర్చడం ద్వారా స్వయంగా ప్రాథమిక హక్కుగా చేయబడింది) ( Romesh Thappar , 1950). కాబట్టి ముందుగా హైకోర్టుకు వెళ్లకుండా నేరుగా సుప్రీం కోర్టుకు రావచ్చు. డా. అంబేడ్కర్ దీనిని "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" ( అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగానికి ఆత్మ, దాని హృదయం) అన్నారు (రాజ్యాంగ సభ చర్చలు, 9 డిసెంబర్ 1948). కోర్టును ఎవరు ఆశ్రయించవచ్చు: హాని పొందిన వ్యక్తి మాత్రమే కాదు. ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం లో పేదలు లేదా వెనుకబడిన వారి కోసం "any member of the public acting bona fide" ( అర్థం: సద్భావనతో వ్యవహరించే ప్రజల్లో ఎవరైనా) కోర్టును ఆశ్రయించవచ్చు, "even by addressing a letter to the court" ( అర్థం: కోర్టుకు ఉత్తరం రాయడం ద్వారా కూడా) ( PUDR , 1982; Bandhua Mukti Morcha , 1983). పరిహారం (డబ్బు): అధికరణ 21 ఉల్లంఘనకు రాజ్యం డబ్బు చెల్లించాలని కోర్టు ఆదేశించవచ్చు ( Rudul Sah , 1983; Nilabati Behera , 1993). అధికరణ 226: ప్రతి హైకోర్టు అవే రిట్‌లను "for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose" ( అర్థం: భాగం III ఇచ్చిన ఏ హక్కుల అమలు కోసమైనా మరియు మరే ఇతర ప్రయోజనం కోసమైనా) జారీ చేయవచ్చు – ఇది అధికరణ 32 కంటే విస్తృతం. మౌలిక నిర్మాణం: అధికరణలు 226, 32 కింద న్యాయ సమీక్ష "inviolable basic structure" ( అర్థం: ఉల్లంఘించరాని మౌలిక నిర్మాణం)లో భాగం ( L. Chandra Kumar , 1997).
te.meaning: రాజ్యాంగ పరిహారం: ప్రాథమిక హక్కు ను కోర్టు ద్వారా అమలు చేయించుకోవడానికి రాజ్యాంగమే ఇచ్చిన మార్గం. అధికరణ 32 ఈ మార్గాన్నే ప్రాథమిక హక్కుగా చేసింది. "Appropriate proceedings" ( అర్థం: తగిన విచారణలు) (అధికరణ 32(1)): "It should be a proceeding which can appropriately lead to an adjudication of the claim made for the enforcement of a fundamental right and can result in the grant of effective relief" ( అర్థం: అది ప్రాథమిక హక్కు అమలు కోసం చేసిన దావాపై తగిన విధంగా తీర్పుకు దారి తీసి, సమర్థవంతమైన ఉపశమనం ఇవ్వగల విచారణ అయి ఉండాలి) ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). "తగిన" అనేది విచారణ ఉద్దేశానికి సంబంధించినది, ఏదో ఒక నిర్దిష్ట రూపానికి కాదు. రిట్ : ఒక వ్యక్తి లేదా అధికారి ఏదైనా చేయాలని లేదా చేయరాదని ఆదేశించే కోర్టు అధికారిక లిఖిత ఉత్తర్వు. అధికరణ 32(2) ఐదు రిట్‌లను పేర్కొంటుంది, కానీ అధికారం ఇంకా విస్తృతం: "even if the conditions for issue of any of these high prerogative writs are not fulfilled" ( అర్థం: ఈ ఉన్నత ప్రత్యేకాధికార రిట్‌లలో ఏదైనా జారీ చేసే షరతులు నెరవేరకపోయినా), సుప్రీం కోర్టు "any direction, order or writ" ( అర్థం: ఏ ఆదేశం, ఉత్తర్వు లేదా రిట్ అయినా) జారీ చేయవచ్చు ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , హెడ్‌నోట్). ఐదు రిట్‌లు (సరళ అర్థం): హెబియస్ కార్పస్ ("have the body" ( అర్థం: శరీరాన్ని హాజరుపరచండి)) – ఒకరిని నిర్బంధంలో ఉంచిన వ్యక్తి ఆ వ్యక్తిని కోర్టు ముందు హాజరుపరచాలని ఆదేశిస్తుంది; నిర్బంధం చట్టబద్ధమా కాదా అని కోర్టు చూస్తుంది. "The person to whom it is directed is under a legal obligation to produce the body of the person alleged to be unlawfully detained before the Court" ( అర్థం: ఎవరికి రిట్ జారీ అయిందో ఆ వ్యక్తి, చట్టవిరుద్ధంగా నిర్బంధించబడినట్లు ఆరోపించబడిన వ్యక్తిని కోర్టు ముందు హాజరుపరచాల్సిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత కలిగి ఉంటాడు) ( Sebastian M. Hongray ). మాండమస్ ("we command" ( అర్థం: మేము ఆదేశిస్తున్నాము)) – ఒక ప్రభుత్వ అధికారి చట్టప్రకారం తప్పనిసరిగా చేయాల్సిన ప్రజా విధిని చేయమని ఆదేశిస్తుంది. ప్రొహిబిషన్ – తన అధికార పరిధి కి వెలుపల ఉన్న విషయంలో, నిర్ణయం తీసుకోకముందే, విచారణ ఆపమని దిగువ కోర్టు, ట్రిబ్యునల్ లేదా అధికారిని ఆదేశిస్తుంది. సెర్షియోరరి – దిగువ కోర్టు, ట్రిబ్యునల్ లేదా అధికారి ఇప్పటికే తీసుకున్న నిర్ణయ రికార్డును తెప్పించి, అది అధికార పరిధి లేకుండా లేదా ఇతరత్రా చట్టవిరుద్ధంగా ఉంటే రద్దు చేస్తుంది. కో వారంటో ("by what authority" ( అర్థం: ఏ అధికారంతో)) – ప్రజా పదవిలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తిని ఏ చట్టపరమైన అధికారంతో ఆ పదవిలో ఉన్నారో చూపమని అడుగుతుంది; అధికారం లేకపోతే ఆ వ్యక్తిని తొలగిస్తారు. లోకస్ స్టాండీ : కోర్టు ముందుకు రావడానికి గల హక్కు. సాంప్రదాయ నియమం ప్రకారం చట్టపరమైన హక్కుకు హాని పొందిన వ్యక్తి మాత్రమే రావచ్చు. ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యంలో ఆ నియమం "has now been jettisoned by the Supreme Court" ( అర్థం: ఇప్పుడు సుప్రీం కోర్టు ద్వారా విడిచిపెట్టబడింది) ( PUDR , హెడ్‌నోట్). ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం (PIL): "by reason of poverty, disability or socially or economically disadvantaged position" ( అర్థం: పేదరికం, అశక్తత లేదా సామాజికంగా లేదా ఆర్థికంగా వెనుకబడిన స్థితి కారణంగా) కోర్టుకు రాలేని వారి కోసం సద్భావనతో వ్యవహరించే ప్రజాహిత వ్యక్తి లేదా సంస్థ తెచ్చే కేసు ( PUDR ).
keyPoints: అధికరణ 32(1): సుప్రీం కోర్టును ఆశ్రయించే హక్కు "guaranteed" ( అర్థం: హామీ ఇవ్వబడింది). అధికరణ 32 స్వయంగా ప్రాథమిక హక్కు; ముందుగా హైకోర్టుకు వెళ్లాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు ( Romesh Thappar ). ఐదు రిట్‌లు: హెబియస్ కార్పస్, మాండమస్, ప్రొహిబిషన్, కో వారంటో, సెర్షియోరరి – అదనంగా ఏ ఆదేశమైనా, ఉత్తర్వైనా ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). డా. అంబేడ్కర్: "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" ( అర్థం: రాజ్యాంగానికి ఆత్మ, దాని హృదయం) (9 డిసెంబర్ 1948). PIL: సద్భావనతో వ్యవహరించే ప్రజల్లో ఎవరైనా, ఉత్తరం ద్వారా కూడా ( PUDR ; Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). అధికరణ 21 ఉల్లంఘనలకు పరిహారం: Rudul Sah , Sebastian M. Hongray , Bhim Singh , Nilabati Behera . ప్రజా చట్ట పరిహారంలో సార్వభౌమ రక్షణ లేదు ( Nilabati Behera ). అధికరణ 226: భాగం III హక్కులు "and for any other purpose" ( అర్థం: మరియు మరే ఇతర ప్రయోజనం కోసమైనా); అధికరణ 32కు భంగం కలిగించదు. అధికరణలు 32, 226 కింద న్యాయ సమీక్ష మౌలిక నిర్మాణం ( L. Chandra Kumar ). అధికరణ 32(4): రాజ్యాంగం నిర్దేశించినట్లు మాత్రమే నిలిపివేత – అధికరణ 359; అధికరణలు 20, 21 ఎప్పుడూ కాదు.

selfTest.q: అధికరణ 32ను వాడే ముందు పిటిషనర్ హైకోర్టుకు వెళ్లాలా?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: అవసరం లేదు ( Romesh Thappar ). అధికరణ 32(2)లోని ఐదు రిట్‌లను చెప్పండి. జవాబు: హెబియస్ కార్పస్, మాండమస్, ప్రొహిబిషన్, కో వారంటో, సెర్షియోరరి. దిగువ ట్రిబ్యునల్‌ను నిర్ణయానికి ముందే ఆపే రిట్ ఏది, తర్వాత దాని నిర్ణయాన్ని రద్దు చేసే రిట్ ఏది? జవాబు: ముందు ప్రొహిబిషన్ ఆపుతుంది; తర్వాత సెర్షియోరరి రద్దు చేస్తుంది. ఉత్తరాన్ని రిట్ పిటిషన్‌గా పరిగణించవచ్చా? జవాబు: అవును, కోర్టును ఆశ్రయించలేని వ్యక్తుల కోసం సద్భావనతో రాసినప్పుడు ( PUDR ; Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). నిర్దోషిగా తేలిన తర్వాత రుదుల్ సా ఎంత కాలం జైలులో ఉన్నాడు? జవాబు: 3 జూన్ 1968 నుండి 16 అక్టోబర్ 1982 వరకు = 14 సంవత్సరాల 4 నెలల 13 రోజులు. అధికరణ 32 కింద పరిహారాన్ని సార్వభౌమ రక్షణ అడ్డుకుంటుందా? జవాబు: లేదు; అది కఠిన బాధ్యతపై ఆధారపడిన ప్రజా చట్ట పరిహారం ( Nilabati Behera ). ఒక వ్యక్తిని సోమవారం ఉదయం 6 గంటలకు అరెస్టు చేసి మంగళవారం సాయంత్రం 6 గంటలకు మేజిస్ట్రేట్ ముందు హాజరుపరిచారు; ప్రయాణానికి 4 గంటలు పట్టింది. అధికరణ 22(2) ఉల్లంఘన జరిగిందా? జవాబు: 36 గంటలు − 4 గంటలు = 32 గంటలు > 24 గంటలు → అవును. ప్రాథమిక హక్కు కాని హక్కు కోసం అధికరణ 226ను వాడవచ్చా? జవాబు: అవును, "for any other purpose" ( అర్థం: మరే ఇతర ప్రయోజనం కోసమైనా). అధికరణలు 32, 226 కింద న్యాయ సమీక్ష మౌలిక నిర్మాణమని ఏ కేసు తేల్చింది? జవాబు: L. Chandra Kumar (1997). అత్యవసర పరిస్థితిలో అధికరణ 21 అమలును రాష్ట్రపతి నిలిపివేయగలరా? జవాబు: లేదు; అధికరణ 359(1) అధికరణలు 20, 21లను మినహాయిస్తుంది.

అధికరణ 32 అధికరణ 226 అధికరణ 32 భాగం III హక్కులకు మాత్రమే, స్వయంగా ప్రాథమిక హక్కు; అధికరణ 226 "any other purpose" (అర్థం: మరే ఇతర ప్రయోజనం)ను కూడా కవర్ చేస్తుంది.

హెబియస్ కార్పస్ మాండమస్ హెబియస్ కార్పస్ నిర్బంధిత వ్యక్తిని హాజరుపరచడానికి; మాండమస్ ప్రభుత్వ అధికారి తన ప్రజా విధిని చేసేలా చేయడానికి.
అధికరణ 32 కింద పరిహారం సివిల్ దావాలో నష్టపరిహారం అధికరణ 32 పరిహారం కఠిన బాధ్యతపై ప్రజా చట్ట పరిహారం, సార్వభౌమ రక్షణ లేదు; టార్ట్‌లో దావా వేసే హక్కు అలాగే ఉంటుంది (Nilabati Behera; Rudul Sah).
అధికరణ 32(3) అధికరణ 139 అధికరణ 32(3): ఇతర కోర్టులకు అధికరణ 32(2) అధికారాలు ఇవ్వవచ్చు; అధికరణ 139: ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు కాని ప్రయోజనాల కోసం సుప్రీం కోర్టుకు రిట్ అధికారం ఇవ్వవచ్చు.

hi.inOneMinute: Art. 32 is the remedy for all other Fundamental Rights. Art. 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Art. 32(2) – the Supreme Court can issue directions or orders or writs , including habeas corpus , mandamus , prohibition , quo warranto and certiorari . Art. 32(3) – Parliament may empower any other court to exercise these powers within its local limits. Art. 32(4) – the right "shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution". Itself a Fundamental Right: the remedial right "is itself made a fundamental right by being included in Part III" ( Romesh Thappar , 1950). So a person may come straight to the Supreme Court without going to the High Court first. Dr. Ambedkar called it "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" (CAD, 9 December 1948). Who can move the Court: not only the injured person. In public interest litigation , "any member of the public acting bona fide" can move the Court for poor or disadvantaged persons, "even by addressing a letter to the court" ( PUDR , 1982; Bandhua Mukti Morcha , 1983). Compensation: the Court can order the State to pay money for violation of Art. 21 ( Rudul Sah , 1983; Nilabati Behera , 1993). Art. 226: every High Court can issue the same writs "for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose" – wider than Art. 32. Basic structure: judicial review under Arts. 226 and 32 is part of the "inviolable basic structure" ( L. Chandra Kumar , 1997).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026). Heading in Part III: "Right to Constitutional Remedies".
Art. 32 – "Remedies for enforcement of rights conferred by this Part."

(1) "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." (2) "The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part." (3) "Without prejudice to the powers conferred on the Supreme Court by clauses (1) and (2), Parliament may by law empower any other court to exercise within the local limits of its jurisdiction all or any of the powers exercisable by the Supreme Court under clause (2)." (4) "The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution."
Art. 32A ("Constitutional validity of State laws not to be considered in proceedings under article 32") – omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 3 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978).

Art. 33 – Parliament may by law decide how far the rights in Part III shall, for members of the Armed Forces, forces "charged with the maintenance of public order", intelligence or counter-intelligence organisations, and connected telecommunication staff, "be restricted or abrogated so as to ensure the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them" (substituted by the Fiftieth Amendment, 1984, s. 2, w.e.f. 11-9-1984).
Art. 226 – "Power of High Courts to issue certain writs."

(1) "Notwithstanding anything in article 32, every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose." (2) The power may also be used by any High Court within whose territory "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises", even if the Government, authority or person is located elsewhere. (3) If an interim order is passed without giving the other party copies and a hearing, and that party applies to vacate it, the High Court must decide the application "within a period of two weeks"; otherwise the interim order "shall ... stand vacated". (4) "The power conferred on a High Court by this article shall not be in derogation of the power conferred on the Supreme Court by clause (2) of article 32." Art. 226 was substituted by the Forty-second Amendment, 1976, s. 38 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977); the writs part was again substituted by the Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978, s. 30 (w.e.f. 1-8-1979).
Art. 139 – Parliament may by law give the Supreme Court power to issue the same writs "for any purposes other than those mentioned in clause (2) of article 32."

Related: Art. 359(1) – during a Proclamation of Emergency, the President may by order suspend "the right to move any court for the enforcement of such of the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21)" as are mentioned in the order. This is the main case of "otherwise provided" in Art. 32(4).
hi.meaning: Constitutional remedy: a way given by the Constitution itself to get a Fundamental Right enforced by a court. Art. 32 makes this way a Fundamental Right. "Appropriate proceedings" (Art. 32(1)): "It should be a proceeding which can appropriately lead to an adjudication of the claim made for the enforcement of a fundamental right and can result in the grant of effective relief" ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). "Appropriate" refers to the purpose of the proceeding, not to any particular form. Writ : a formal written order of a court commanding a person or authority to do, or not to do, something. Art. 32(2) names five writs, but the power is wider: "even if the conditions for issue of any of these high prerogative writs are not fulfilled", the Supreme Court can issue "any direction, order or writ" ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , headnote). The five writs (plain meaning): Habeas corpus ("have the body") – orders the person holding someone in custody to produce that person before the Court, so the Court can see whether the detention is lawful. "The person to whom it is directed is under a legal obligation to produce the body of the person alleged to be unlawfully detained before the Court" ( Sebastian M. Hongray ). Mandamus ("we command") – orders a public authority to perform a public duty it is legally bound to perform. Prohibition – orders a lower court, tribunal or authority to stop proceeding in a matter outside its jurisdiction , before it decides. Certiorari – calls up the record of a decision already made by a lower court, tribunal or authority and quashes it if it was made without jurisdiction or is otherwise illegal. Quo warranto ("by what authority") – asks a person holding a public office to show by what legal authority he or she holds it; if none, the person is removed. Locus standi : the right to come before a court. The traditional rule allowed only the person whose legal right was hurt. In PIL, that rule "has now been jettisoned by the Supreme Court" ( PUDR , headnote). Public interest litigation (PIL): a case brought by a public-spirited person or body, acting bona fide, for persons who cannot come to court "by reason of poverty, disability or socially or economically disadvantaged position" ( PUDR ).
keyPoints: Art. 32(1): the right to move the Supreme Court is "guaranteed". Art. 32 is itself a Fundamental Right; no need to go to the High Court first ( Romesh Thappar ). Five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari – plus any direction or order ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). Dr. Ambedkar: "the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it" (9 December 1948). PIL: any bona fide member of the public, even by letter ( PUDR ; Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). Compensation for Art. 21 violations: Rudul Sah , Sebastian M. Hongray , Bhim Singh , Nilabati Behera . No sovereign immunity in public law compensation ( Nilabati Behera ). Art. 226: Part III rights "and for any other purpose"; not in derogation of Art. 32. Judicial review under Arts. 32 and 226 is basic structure ( L. Chandra Kumar ). Art. 32(4): suspension only as the Constitution provides – Art. 359; never Arts. 20 and 21.

selfTest.q: Must a petitioner go to the High Court before using Art. 32?
selfTest.a: Answer: No ( Romesh Thappar ). Name the five writs in Art. 32(2). Answer: Habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari. Which writ stops a lower tribunal before it decides, and which quashes its decision afterwards? Answer: Prohibition stops it before; certiorari quashes after. Can a letter be treated as a writ petition? Answer: Yes, when written bona fide for persons unable to approach the Court ( PUDR ; Bandhua Mukti Morcha ). How long was Rudul Sah in jail after acquittal? Answer: 3 June 1968 to 16 October 1982 = 14 years, 4 months and 13 days. Does sovereign immunity bar compensation under Art. 32? Answer: No; it is a public law remedy based on strict liability ( Nilabati Behera ). A person is arrested at 6 a.m. on Monday and produced before a Magistrate at 6 p.m. on Tuesday; the journey took 4 hours. Is Art. 22(2) breached? Answer: 36 hours − 4 hours = 32 hours > 24 hours → yes. Can Art. 226 be used for a right that is not a Fundamental Right? Answer: Yes, "for any other purpose". Which case held judicial review under Arts. 32 and 226 is basic structure? Answer: L. Chandra Kumar (1997). Can the President suspend enforcement of Art. 21 during an Emergency? Answer: No; Art. 359(1) excludes Arts. 20 and 21.
