hi.inOneMinute: Application by the State: Art. 37 makes it "the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws". Parliament and the State Legislatures carry them out through laws and amendments. Application by courts – four uses, one limit: Support for laws and classifications – Art. 46 helps uphold SC/ST concessions under Art. 16 ( N. M. Thomas , 1975). Content for Arts. 14 and 16 – equal pay for equal work, Art. 39(d) ( Randhir Singh , 1982). Content for Art. 21 – livelihood ( Olga Tellis , 1985), humane conditions for bonded labour ( Bandhua Mukti Morcha , 1983), education up to 14 ( Unni Krishnan , 1993), medical aid ( Paschim Banga , 1996), clean environment ( Vellore Citizens , 1996). Directions where a law already exists – e.g. an authority under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 ( Vellore Citizens ); a request for an affidavit on Art. 44 ( Sarla Mudgal , 1995). Limit: no order to make a new law; Part IV goals must be reached "without the abrogation of the means provided for by Part III" ( Minerva Mills ). The journey: from "subsidiary" ( Champakam , 1951) to "supplementary and complementary" ( Unni Krishnan , 1993).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Art. 37: "The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws." Articles most used by courts: Art. 39(a): "the right to an adequate means of livelihood". Art. 39(d): "equal pay for equal work for both men and women". Art. 39(e): "that the health and strength of workers, men and women, and the tender age of children are not abused". Art. 41: "the right to work, to education and to public assistance". Art. 44: "a uniform civil code". Art. 45 (as it stood till 2010): free and compulsory education "until they complete the age of fourteen years" (quoted in Unni Krishnan ). Art. 46: "the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people". Art. 47: "the improvement of public health". Art. 48A: "protect and improve the environment". Rights through which they are applied: Art. 14 (equality before law), Art. 16 (equality of opportunity in public employment), Art. 21 ("No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.").
hi.meaning: Application (of Directive Principles): carrying out Part IV – by the State in making laws and policy, and by courts in deciding cases. Judicial interpretation (of Directive Principles): the ways courts read Part IV and use it to give meaning to other parts of the Constitution, especially Part III. Right to livelihood : the right to earn a living, held part of the right to life under Art. 21, read with Arts. 39(a) and 41 ( Olga Tellis ). Precautionary principle : State measures "must anticipate, prevent and attack the causes of environmental degradation"; lack of scientific certainty is no reason to postpone them; the "Onus of proof" is on the actor or developer ( Vellore Citizens ). Polluter pays principle : the polluter pays the cost to sufferers and "the cost of reversing the damaged ecology" ( Vellore Citizens ).
keyPoints: Art. 37: State's duty to apply Part IV in making laws. Champakam (1951): subsidiary. N. M. Thomas (1975): Art. 46 shapes Art. 16; 184 of 8,780 = 2%. Randhir Singh (1982): Art. 39(d) through Arts. 14, 16. Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1983): Art. 21 from Arts. 39(e), (f), 41, 42; no order to legislate. Olga Tellis (1985): livelihood; not compellable to give work. Unni Krishnan (1993): education to 14; complementary. Sarla Mudgal (1995): Art. 44 – affidavit requested. Paschim Banga (1996): Art. 47 – medical aid; Rs. 25,000. Vellore Citizens (1996): Art. 48A – polluter pays; Rs. 10,000 per tannery.

caseLaws.facts: O. reserved college seats community-wise; the State relied on Art. 46. Principle: Directive Principles "cannot override the provisions found in Part III"; they "run as subsidiary to the Chapter of Fundamental Rights". Why it matters: Starting point of judicial interpretation – strict separation.
Randhir Singh v. Union of India , [1982] 3 SCR 298 (3 judges; Chinnappa Reddy J.; decided 22 February 1982)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A Delhi Police driver-constable (Rs
caseLaws.facts: 210-270 / 225-308) claimed parity with Railway Protection Force drivers (Rs. 260-400). Principle: "Directive Principles have to be read into the fundamental rights as a matter of interpretation"; equal pay for equal work enforced through Arts. 14 and 16 (headnote). Why it matters: First clear use of a Directive Principle to give content to equality.
Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation , [1985] Supp. 2 SCR 51 (5 judges; Chandrachud C.J.; decided 10 July 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Pavement and slum dwellers in Bombay faced forcible eviction under the Bombay Municipal Corpo
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 39(a) and 41 are "equally fundamental" in interpreting Fundamental Rights; the right to life includes the right to livelihood; but the State "may not ... be compellable" to provide work. Why it matters: Model of how Part IV enters Art. 21 – with its limit.
Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh , [1993] 1 SCR (5 judges; decided 4 February 1993)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenges to capitation fees and admission rules in private professional colleges
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The right to education flows from Art. 21, its content fixed "in the light of Articles 45 and 41"; Parts III and IV are "supplementary and complementary" (headnote). Why it matters: The fullest statement of the complementary approach.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India , decided 28 August 1996 (3 judges; Kuldip Singh, Faizan Uddin, K. Venkataswami JJ.)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Read with Arts. 21, 47, 48A and 51A(g), the precautionary and polluter pays principles are "part of the law of the land"; authority under s. 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Rs. 10,000 fine on each tannery. Why it matters: Shows Part IV applied through Art. 21 and existing law, with concrete directions.

selfTest.q: Which Article puts the duty of applying Part IV on the State?
selfTest.a: Answer: Art. 37. Which case first called Part IV subsidiary? Answer: Champakam Dorairajan (1951). Through which Articles was Art. 39(d) applied in Randhir Singh ? Answer: Arts. 14 and 16. Which Directive Principles did Olga Tellis read into Art. 21? Answer: Arts. 39(a) and 41. What can a court not do under Bandhua Mukti Morcha ? Answer: Compel the State to make a new law for Arts. 39(e), (f), 41, 42. What share of non-gazetted posts did SC/ST hold in N. M. Thomas ? Answer: 11,437 of 1,62,784 = 7%. Up to what age is education free under Unni Krishnan ? Answer: 14. What did Sarla Mudgal ask the government to file? Answer: An affidavit on steps taken towards a uniform civil code. What fine was imposed on each tannery in Vellore Citizens ? Answer: Rs. 10,000. How long after his fall was Hakim Seikh refused at Calcutta Medical College Hospital? Answer: 7.45 p.m. to 12.20 a.m. = 4 hours 35 minutes.

constitutional-law-i-u5-t6.subtitle: From Champakam to Minerva Mills: how Parts III and IV clash, how the amending power and Article 31C were fought over, and where the balance now stands

en.inOneMinute: The tension: Part III is enforceable (Art. 32); Part IV is not (Art. 37). What if a law made to carry out Part IV restricts a right in Part III? Five stages: Part III prevails (1951): Directive Principles "run as subsidiary to the Chapter of Fundamental Rights" ( Champakam ). Parliament replied with Art. 15(4) (First Amendment, 1951). Rights cannot be amended away (1967): "If it is the duty of Parliament to enforce directive principles it is equally its duty to enforce them without infringing the fundamental rights" ( Golaknath , 6:5). Art. 31C and the basic structure (1972–73): the 25th Amendment protected laws for Art. 39(b) and (c) from Arts. 14, 19 and 31; Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Art. 31C and struck down the second. Balance is part of the basic structure (1980): the 42nd Amendment extended Art. 31C to "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV"; Minerva Mills struck this down – "To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution." Harmonious construction (1975 onwards): Parts III and IV are "supplementary and complementary" ( Unni Krishnan ); "neither part being superior to the other" ( N. M. Thomas ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Art. 13(2): "The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void." Art. 32(1): "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Art. 37: "The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws." Art. 15(4) (First Amendment, 1951, s. 2, w.e.f. 18-6-1951): "Nothing in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes." Art. 31C (25th Amendment, 1971, s. 3, w.e.f. 20-4-1972), as printed today: "Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by article 14 or article 19; and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy". Proviso: a State law needs to be "reserved for the consideration of the President" and to have "received his assent". Footnotes: the words "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" were substituted by the 42nd Amendment, s. 4, for "the principles specified in clause (b) or clause (c) of article 39"; "Section 4 has been declared invalid by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills"; "article 14 or article 19" was substituted by the 44th Amendment, s. 8, for "article 14, article 19 or article 31"; the declaration words (in italics in the official text) were "struck down by the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati". Art. 39(b) and (c): ownership and control of "the material resources of the community" to "subserve the common good"; no "concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment".
en.meaning: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles: how Part III (enforceable rights of individuals) and Part IV (non-enforceable directions to the State) fit together, and which prevails when they seem to pull apart. Basic structure : the essential features of the Constitution which even a constitutional amendment cannot damage or destroy ( Kesavananda Bharati ). Minerva Mills added: "This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution." Harmonious construction : reading two provisions so that both work, instead of letting one cancel the other. Here: reading Part III in the light of Part IV, and pursuing Part IV without destroying Part III.
keyPoints: Art. 32 guarantees Part III; Art. 37 makes Part IV non-enforceable. Champakam (1951): subsidiary → Art. 15(4). Golaknath (1967, 6:5): enforce Part IV "without infringing the fundamental rights". Art. 31C (25th Amendment, 20-4-1972): Art. 39(b), (c). Kesavananda Bharati (1973): first part valid (8:5), declaration clause invalid (7:6). 42nd Amendment s. 4 (1977): all of Part IV → struck down in Minerva Mills (1980, 4:1). 44th Amendment s. 8: Art. 31 dropped from Art. 31C. "two wheels of a chariot"; "harmony and balance" is basic structure. N. M. Thomas : neither superior; Unni Krishnan : complementary.

selfTest.q: Which Article guarantees the enforcement of Part III?
selfTest.a: Answer: Art. 32. Which Amendment answered Champakam ? Answer: The First Amendment, 1951 (Art. 15(4)). What was the vote in Golaknath ? Answer: 6:5. Which Directive Principles did Art. 31C originally protect? Answer: Art. 39(b) and (c). Which part of Art. 31C was struck down in Kesavananda Bharati ? Answer: The declaration clause (no court may question the declaration). How many judges upheld the first part of Art. 31C? Answer: 8 of 13. Which section of the 42nd Amendment did Minerva Mills strike down on this topic? Answer: Section 4. Which judge in Minerva Mills would have upheld s. 4? Answer: Bhagwati J. Which Amendment removed Art. 31 from Art. 31C? Answer: The 44th Amendment (s. 8). In the Sundarpur ceiling example, how many families get 3 acres each from 30 surplus acres? Answer: 30 ÷ 3 = 10.

te.inOneMinute: ఘర్షణ: భాగం III అమలు చేయించదగినది (అధికరణ 32); భాగం IV కాదు (అధికరణ 37). భాగం IVను అమలు చేయడానికి చేసిన చట్టం భాగం IIIలోని హక్కును పరిమితం చేస్తే ఏమవుతుంది? ఐదు దశలు: భాగం III పైచేయి (1951): ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలు "run as subsidiary to the Chapter of Fundamental Rights" ( అర్థం: ప్రాథమిక హక్కుల అధ్యాయానికి లోబడి నడుస్తాయి) ( Champakam ). పార్లమెంటు అధికరణ 15(4)తో జవాబిచ్చింది (మొదటి సవరణ, 1951). సవరణ ద్వారా హక్కులను తొలగించలేరు (1967): "If it is the duty of Parliament to enforce directive principles it is equally its duty to enforce them without infringing the fundamental rights" ( అర్థం: ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలను అమలు చేయడం పార్లమెంటు విధి అయితే, ప్రాథమిక హక్కులను ఉల్లంఘించకుండా వాటిని అమలు చేయడం కూడా అంతే దాని విధి) ( Golaknath , 6:5). అధికరణ 31C, మౌలిక నిర్మాణం (1972–73): 25వ సవరణ అధికరణ 39(b), (c) కోసం చేసిన చట్టాలను అధికరణలు 14, 19, 31 నుండి రక్షించింది; Kesavananda Bharati అధికరణ 31C మొదటి భాగాన్ని సమర్థించి, రెండవ భాగాన్ని కొట్టివేసింది. సమతుల్యం మౌలిక నిర్మాణంలో భాగం (1980): 42వ సవరణ అధికరణ 31Cని "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" ( అర్థం: భాగం IVలో నిర్దేశించిన సూత్రాలన్నింటికీ లేదా వాటిలో దేనికైనా) విస్తరించింది; Minerva Mills దీనిని కొట్టివేసింది – "To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution." ( అర్థం: ఒకదానికి మరొకదానిపై సంపూర్ణ ప్రాధాన్యం ఇవ్వడం రాజ్యాంగ సామరస్యాన్ని భంగపరచడమే.) సామరస్య వ్యాఖ్యానం (1975 నుండి): భాగాలు III, IV "supplementary and complementary" ( అర్థం: అనుబంధమైనవి, పూరకమైనవి) ( Unni Krishnan ); "neither part being superior to the other" ( అర్థం: ఏ భాగమూ మరొకదాని కంటే ఉన్నతమైనది కాదు) ( N. M. Thomas ).
te.meaning: ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు మరియు ఆదేశిక సూత్రాల మధ్య సంబంధం: భాగం III (వ్యక్తుల అమలు చేయించదగిన హక్కులు), భాగం IV (రాజ్యానికి అమలు చేయించలేని ఆదేశాలు) ఎలా కలిసి పనిచేస్తాయి, అవి వేర్వేరు దిశల్లో లాగినట్లు కనిపించినప్పుడు ఏది పైచేయి సాధిస్తుంది. మౌలిక నిర్మాణం : రాజ్యాంగ సవరణ కూడా దెబ్బతీయలేని లేదా నాశనం చేయలేని రాజ్యాంగ ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు ( Kesavananda Bharati ). Minerva Mills ఇలా జోడించింది: "This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution." ( అర్థం: ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు, ఆదేశిక సూత్రాల మధ్య ఈ సామరస్యం, సమతుల్యం రాజ్యాంగ మౌలిక నిర్మాణంలో ముఖ్య లక్షణం.) సామరస్య వ్యాఖ్యానం : ఒక నిబంధన మరొకదాన్ని రద్దు చేయకుండా, రెండూ పనిచేసేలా చదవడం. ఇక్కడ: భాగం IV వెలుగులో భాగం IIIని చదవడం, భాగం IIIని నాశనం చేయకుండా భాగం IVను సాధించడం.
keyPoints: అధికరణ 32 భాగం IIIకి హామీ ఇస్తుంది; అధికరణ 37 భాగం IVను అమలు చేయించలేనిదిగా చేస్తుంది. Champakam (1951): లోబడినవి → అధికరణ 15(4). Golaknath (1967, 6:5): భాగం IVను "without infringing the fundamental rights" ( అర్థం: ప్రాథమిక హక్కులను ఉల్లంఘించకుండా) అమలు చేయాలి. అధికరణ 31C (25వ సవరణ, 20-4-1972): అధికరణ 39(b), (c). Kesavananda Bharati (1973): మొదటి భాగం చెల్లుతుంది (8:5), ప్రకటన క్లాజు చెల్లదు (7:6). 42వ సవరణ సె. 4 (1977): భాగం IV మొత్తం → Minerva Mills ‌లో కొట్టివేత (1980, 4:1). 44వ సవరణ సె. 8: అధికరణ 31C నుండి అధికరణ 31 తొలగింపు. "two wheels of a chariot" ( అర్థం: రథానికి రెండు చక్రాలు); "harmony and balance" ( అర్థం: సామరస్యం, సమతుల్యం) మౌలిక నిర్మాణం. N. M. Thomas : ఏదీ ఉన్నతం కాదు; Unni Krishnan : పూరకమైనవి.

selfTest.q: భాగం III అమలుకు ఏ అధికరణ హామీ ఇస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: అధికరణ 32. Champakam ‌కు ఏ సవరణ జవాబిచ్చింది? జవాబు: మొదటి సవరణ, 1951 (అధికరణ 15(4)). Golaknath ‌లో ఓట్ల లెక్క ఏమిటి? జవాబు: 6:5. అధికరణ 31C మొదట ఏ ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలను రక్షించింది? జవాబు: అధికరణ 39(b), (c). Kesavananda Bharati ‌లో అధికరణ 31C ఏ భాగాన్ని కొట్టివేశారు? జవాబు: ప్రకటన క్లాజు (ప్రకటనను ఏ కోర్టూ ప్రశ్నించకూడదు అనేది). అధికరణ 31C మొదటి భాగాన్ని ఎంతమంది న్యాయమూర్తులు సమర్థించారు? జవాబు: 13లో 8. ఈ అంశంపై Minerva Mills 42వ సవరణలోని ఏ సెక్షన్‌ను కొట్టివేసింది? జవాబు: సెక్షన్ 4. Minerva Mills ‌లో సె. 4ను సమర్థించే న్యాయమూర్తి ఎవరు? జవాబు: భగవతి J. అధికరణ 31C నుండి అధికరణ 31ను ఏ సవరణ తొలగించింది? జవాబు: 44వ సవరణ (సె. 8). సుందర్‌పూర్ పరిమితి ఉదాహరణలో 30 మిగులు ఎకరాల నుండి ఒక్కొక్కటి 3 ఎకరాలు ఎన్ని కుటుంబాలకు లభిస్తాయి? జవాబు: 30 ÷ 3 = 10.

hi.inOneMinute: The tension: Part III is enforceable (Art. 32); Part IV is not (Art. 37). What if a law made to carry out Part IV restricts a right in Part III? Five stages: Part III prevails (1951): Directive Principles "run as subsidiary to the Chapter of Fundamental Rights" ( Champakam ). Parliament replied with Art. 15(4) (First Amendment, 1951). Rights cannot be amended away (1967): "If it is the duty of Parliament to enforce directive principles it is equally its duty to enforce them without infringing the fundamental rights" ( Golaknath , 6:5). Art. 31C and the basic structure (1972–73): the 25th Amendment protected laws for Art. 39(b) and (c) from Arts. 14, 19 and 31; Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Art. 31C and struck down the second. Balance is part of the basic structure (1980): the 42nd Amendment extended Art. 31C to "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV"; Minerva Mills struck this down – "To give absolute primacy to one over the other is to disturb the harmony of the Constitution." Harmonious construction (1975 onwards): Parts III and IV are "supplementary and complementary" ( Unni Krishnan ); "neither part being superior to the other" ( N. M. Thomas ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Art. 13(2): "The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void." Art. 32(1): "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Art. 37: "The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws." Art. 15(4) (First Amendment, 1951, s. 2, w.e.f. 18-6-1951): "Nothing in this article or in clause (2) of article 29 shall prevent the State from making any special provision for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens or for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes." Art. 31C (25th Amendment, 1971, s. 3, w.e.f. 20-4-1972), as printed today: "Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by article 14 or article 19; and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy". Proviso: a State law needs to be "reserved for the consideration of the President" and to have "received his assent". Footnotes: the words "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" were substituted by the 42nd Amendment, s. 4, for "the principles specified in clause (b) or clause (c) of article 39"; "Section 4 has been declared invalid by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills"; "article 14 or article 19" was substituted by the 44th Amendment, s. 8, for "article 14, article 19 or article 31"; the declaration words (in italics in the official text) were "struck down by the Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati". Art. 39(b) and (c): ownership and control of "the material resources of the community" to "subserve the common good"; no "concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment".
hi.meaning: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles: how Part III (enforceable rights of individuals) and Part IV (non-enforceable directions to the State) fit together, and which prevails when they seem to pull apart. Basic structure : the essential features of the Constitution which even a constitutional amendment cannot damage or destroy ( Kesavananda Bharati ). Minerva Mills added: "This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution." Harmonious construction : reading two provisions so that both work, instead of letting one cancel the other. Here: reading Part III in the light of Part IV, and pursuing Part IV without destroying Part III.
keyPoints: Art. 32 guarantees Part III; Art. 37 makes Part IV non-enforceable. Champakam (1951): subsidiary → Art. 15(4). Golaknath (1967, 6:5): enforce Part IV "without infringing the fundamental rights". Art. 31C (25th Amendment, 20-4-1972): Art. 39(b), (c). Kesavananda Bharati (1973): first part valid (8:5), declaration clause invalid (7:6). 42nd Amendment s. 4 (1977): all of Part IV → struck down in Minerva Mills (1980, 4:1). 44th Amendment s. 8: Art. 31 dropped from Art. 31C. "two wheels of a chariot"; "harmony and balance" is basic structure. N. M. Thomas : neither superior; Unni Krishnan : complementary.

selfTest.q: Which Article guarantees the enforcement of Part III?
selfTest.a: Answer: Art. 32. Which Amendment answered Champakam ? Answer: The First Amendment, 1951 (Art. 15(4)). What was the vote in Golaknath ? Answer: 6:5. Which Directive Principles did Art. 31C originally protect? Answer: Art. 39(b) and (c). Which part of Art. 31C was struck down in Kesavananda Bharati ? Answer: The declaration clause (no court may question the declaration). How many judges upheld the first part of Art. 31C? Answer: 8 of 13. Which section of the 42nd Amendment did Minerva Mills strike down on this topic? Answer: Section 4. Which judge in Minerva Mills would have upheld s. 4? Answer: Bhagwati J. Which Amendment removed Art. 31 from Art. 31C? Answer: The 44th Amendment (s. 8). In the Sundarpur ceiling example, how many families get 3 acres each from 30 surplus acres? Answer: 30 ÷ 3 = 10.

constitutional-law-i-u5-t9.subtitle: How courts treat the Fundamental Duties: not enforceable alone, but used to support rights, read statutes and justify directions

en.inOneMinute: The text: Art. 51A lists 11 duties of "every citizen of India". It says nothing about enforcement – so how much the duties mean in law has come from the courts. Five things courts have done with Art. 51A (as seen in the sources): Read duties with rights, not against them – standing respectfully for the Anthem is enough ( Bijoe Emmanuel , 1986). Read the State's duty and the citizen's duty together on the environment – Kinkri Devi (HP HC, 1987), Virender Gaur (1994), Ganesh Wood Products (1995), Barkati (Cal HC, 1998). Give directions to Government – environment lessons in schools ( M. C. Mehta , 1988). Interpret statutes and support State action – untouchability ( Appa Balu Ingale , 1992), National Awards ( Balaji Raghavan , 1995), animal welfare ( Animal Welfare Board , 2014). Shape the use of rights, within Art. 19(2) – fraternity and clause (e) ( Kaushal Kishor , 2023). The line courts hold: a duty does not cut down a Fundamental Right beyond what the Constitution allows ( Bijoe Emmanuel ; Kaushal Kishor ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Art. 51A: "It shall be the duty of every citizen of India—" followed by clauses (a) to (k). Clauses most interpreted by courts: (a) "to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem". (e) "to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women". (g) "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". (h) "to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform". (j) "to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement". Provisions read with them: Art. 19(1)(a) and 19(2); Art. 21; Art. 25(1); Art. 18(1); Art. 48A ("The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country."). Footnotes: Part IVA – Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 11 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977); clause (k) – Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, s. 4 (w.e.f. 1-4-2010).
en.meaning: Judicial interpretation (of Fundamental Duties ): the ways courts read Art. 51A and use it – with rights, with Directive Principles and with statutes – in deciding cases. Sustainable development : development that keeps the balance with forests and ecology; in Ganesh Wood Products it meant that "a proper assessment should be made of the forest wealth" before forest-based industries are allowed. Inter-generational equity : "Inter-generational equity means the concern for the generations to come. The present generation has no right to imperil the safety and well-being of the next generation or the generations to come thereafter." ( Ganesh Wood Products ). Reading down / reading with: a court does not enforce Art. 51A alone; it reads a law or a right "along with" a duty ( Animal Welfare Board : ss. 3 and 11 of the PCA Act "have to be read along with Art. 51A(g)&(h)").
keyPoints: Art. 51A is silent on enforcement; courts read it with rights, Part IV and statutes. Bijoe Emmanuel (1986): clause (a); standing respectfully is respect. Kinkri Devi (1987, HP HC): pointer to State, duty of citizens. M. C. Mehta (1988): 1 hour a week, first ten classes. Appa Balu Ingale (1992): duties guide the PCR Act. Virender Gaur (1994): duty of every citizen too; pull down in 4 weeks. Ganesh Wood Products (1995): no absolute right to forest industry; inter-generational equity. Balaji Raghavan (1995): awards for excellence; not titles. Barkati (1998, Cal HC): loudspeakers not essential to Azan. Animal Welfare Board (2014): "magna carta of animal rights"; 5 freedoms (OIE). Kaushal Kishor (2023): fraternity; Art. 19(2) exhaustive.

selfTest.q: Does Art. 51A say how it is to be enforced?
selfTest.a: Answer: No. Which clause was interpreted in Bijoe Emmanuel ? Answer: Clause (a). What did Bijoe Emmanuel say shows proper respect to the Anthem? Answer: Standing up when it is sung. In Virender Gaur , within how many weeks was the construction to be pulled down? Answer: Four weeks. What percentage of her land had the first appellant surrendered in Virender Gaur ? Answer: 25%. Which industry was involved in Ganesh Wood Products ? Answer: Katha (from khair trees). Which High Court decided Barkati ? Answer: Calcutta High Court (1998). How many freedoms for animals (OIE guidelines) did Animal Welfare Board rely on? Answer: Five. Which clauses were called the "magna carta of animal rights"? Answer: Art. 51A(g) and (h). What limit did Kaushal Kishor set on using duties against speech? Answer: Art. 19(2) grounds are exhaustive.

te.inOneMinute: పాఠం: అధికరణ 51A "every citizen of India" ( అర్థం: భారతదేశంలోని ప్రతి పౌరుడు) యొక్క 11 విధులను జాబితా చేస్తుంది. అమలు గురించి అది ఏమీ చెప్పదు – కాబట్టి చట్టంలో విధులకు ఎంత అర్థం ఉందో కోర్టుల నుండే వచ్చింది. అధికరణ 51Aతో కోర్టులు చేసిన ఐదు పనులు (మూలాల్లో కనిపించినట్లు): విధులను హక్కులతో కలిపి చదవడం, వాటికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కాదు – జాతీయ గీతానికి గౌరవంగా నిలబడడం చాలు ( Bijoe Emmanuel , 1986). పర్యావరణంపై రాజ్యం విధిని, పౌరుని విధిని కలిపి చదవడం – Kinkri Devi (HP హైకోర్టు, 1987), Virender Gaur (1994), Ganesh Wood Products (1995), Barkati (కలకత్తా హైకోర్టు, 1998). ప్రభుత్వానికి ఆదేశాలు ఇవ్వడం – పాఠశాలల్లో పర్యావరణ పాఠాలు ( M. C. Mehta , 1988). చట్టాలను వ్యాఖ్యానించడం, రాజ్య చర్యను సమర్థించడం – అంటరానితనం ( Appa Balu Ingale , 1992), జాతీయ పురస్కారాలు ( Balaji Raghavan , 1995), జంతు సంక్షేమం ( Animal Welfare Board , 2014). అధికరణ 19(2) పరిధిలోనే హక్కుల వినియోగాన్ని తీర్చిదిద్దడం – సౌభ్రాతృత్వం, ఖండం (e) ( Kaushal Kishor , 2023). కోర్టులు పాటించే గీత: రాజ్యాంగం అనుమతించిన దానికి మించి ఒక విధి ప్రాథమిక హక్కును తగ్గించదు ( Bijoe Emmanuel ; Kaushal Kishor ).
te.meaning: న్యాయ వ్యాఖ్యానం (ప్రాథమిక విధుల): కేసులను నిర్ణయించేటప్పుడు కోర్టులు అధికరణ 51Aను చదివే, వాడే విధానాలు – హక్కులతో, ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలతో, చట్టాలతో. సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి : అడవులు, పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యతను కాపాడే అభివృద్ధి; Ganesh Wood Products ‌లో అటవీ ఆధారిత పరిశ్రమలను అనుమతించే ముందు "a proper assessment should be made of the forest wealth" ( అర్థం: అటవీ సంపదను సరిగ్గా అంచనా వేయాలి) అని దాని అర్థం. తరాల మధ్య సమన్యాయం : "Inter-generational equity means the concern for the generations to come. The present generation has no right to imperil the safety and well-being of the next generation or the generations to come thereafter." ( అర్థం: తరాల మధ్య సమన్యాయం అంటే రాబోయే తరాల పట్ల శ్రద్ధ. తర్వాతి తరం లేదా ఆ తర్వాత వచ్చే తరాల భద్రతను, శ్రేయస్సును ప్రమాదంలో పెట్టే హక్కు ప్రస్తుత తరానికి లేదు.) ( Ganesh Wood Products ). కలిపి చదవడం: కోర్టు అధికరణ 51Aను ఒంటరిగా అమలు చేయించదు; ఒక చట్టాన్ని లేదా హక్కును ఒక విధితో "along with" ( అర్థం: కలిపి) చదువుతుంది ( Animal Welfare Board : PCA చట్టం సె. 3, 11 "have to be read along with Art. 51A(g)&(h)" ( అర్థం: అధికరణ 51A(g), (h)తో కలిపి చదవాలి)).
keyPoints: అధికరణ 51A అమలు గురించి మౌనంగా ఉంది; కోర్టులు దానిని హక్కులు, భాగం IV, చట్టాలతో కలిపి చదువుతాయి. Bijoe Emmanuel (1986): ఖండం (a); గౌరవంగా నిలబడడమే గౌరవం. Kinkri Devi (1987, HP హైకోర్టు): రాజ్యానికి సూచిక, పౌరులకు విధి. M. C. Mehta (1988): వారానికి 1 గంట, మొదటి పది తరగతులు. Appa Balu Ingale (1992): విధులు PCR చట్టానికి మార్గదర్శి. Virender Gaur (1994): ప్రతి పౌరుని విధి కూడా; 4 వారాల్లో కూల్చివేత. Ganesh Wood Products (1995): అటవీ పరిశ్రమకు సంపూర్ణ హక్కు లేదు; తరాల మధ్య సమన్యాయం. Balaji Raghavan (1995): శ్రేష్ఠతకు పురస్కారాలు; బిరుదులు కావు. Barkati (1998, కలకత్తా హైకోర్టు): లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్లు అజాన్‌కు ముఖ్యం కాదు. Animal Welfare Board (2014): "magna carta of animal rights" ( అర్థం: జంతు హక్కుల మాగ్నా కార్టా); 5 స్వేచ్ఛలు (OIE). Kaushal Kishor (2023): సౌభ్రాతృత్వం; అధికరణ 19(2) సంపూర్ణం.

selfTest.q: అధికరణ 51A దానిని ఎలా అమలు చేయాలో చెబుతుందా?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: లేదు. Bijoe Emmanuel ‌లో ఏ ఖండాన్ని వ్యాఖ్యానించారు? జవాబు: ఖండం (a). జాతీయ గీతానికి సరైన గౌరవం ఏది అని Bijoe Emmanuel చెప్పింది? జవాబు: అది పాడుతున్నప్పుడు లేచి నిలబడడం. Virender Gaur ‌లో ఎన్ని వారాల్లో నిర్మాణాన్ని కూల్చివేయాలి? జవాబు: నాలుగు వారాలు. Virender Gaur ‌లో మొదటి అప్పీలుదారు తన భూమిలో ఎంత శాతం అప్పగించారు? జవాబు: 25%. Ganesh Wood Products ‌లో ఏ పరిశ్రమ ఉంది? జవాబు: కథ (ఖైర్ చెట్ల నుండి). Barkati ‌ను ఏ హైకోర్టు నిర్ణయించింది? జవాబు: కలకత్తా హైకోర్టు (1998). జంతువులకు సంబంధించిన ఎన్ని స్వేచ్ఛలపై (OIE మార్గదర్శకాలు) Animal Welfare Board ఆధారపడింది? జవాబు: ఐదు (5). ఏ ఖండాలను "magna carta of animal rights" ( అర్థం: జంతు హక్కుల మాగ్నా కార్టా) అని పిలిచారు? జవాబు: అధికరణ 51A(g), (h). వాక్కుకు వ్యతిరేకంగా విధులను వాడడంపై Kaushal Kishor ఏ పరిమితి పెట్టింది? జవాబు: అధికరణ 19(2) కారణాలు సంపూర్ణమైనవి.

hi.inOneMinute: The text: Art. 51A lists 11 duties of "every citizen of India". It says nothing about enforcement – so how much the duties mean in law has come from the courts. Five things courts have done with Art. 51A (as seen in the sources): Read duties with rights, not against them – standing respectfully for the Anthem is enough ( Bijoe Emmanuel , 1986). Read the State's duty and the citizen's duty together on the environment – Kinkri Devi (HP HC, 1987), Virender Gaur (1994), Ganesh Wood Products (1995), Barkati (Cal HC, 1998). Give directions to Government – environment lessons in schools ( M. C. Mehta , 1988). Interpret statutes and support State action – untouchability ( Appa Balu Ingale , 1992), National Awards ( Balaji Raghavan , 1995), animal welfare ( Animal Welfare Board , 2014). Shape the use of rights, within Art. 19(2) – fraternity and clause (e) ( Kaushal Kishor , 2023). The line courts hold: a duty does not cut down a Fundamental Right beyond what the Constitution allows ( Bijoe Emmanuel ; Kaushal Kishor ).
legalProvision: Source: Constitution of India (bare Act PDF, as on 1 May 2026).

Art. 51A: "It shall be the duty of every citizen of India—" followed by clauses (a) to (k). Clauses most interpreted by courts: (a) "to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem". (e) "to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women". (g) "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". (h) "to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform". (j) "to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement". Provisions read with them: Art. 19(1)(a) and 19(2); Art. 21; Art. 25(1); Art. 18(1); Art. 48A ("The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country."). Footnotes: Part IVA – Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 11 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977); clause (k) – Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2002, s. 4 (w.e.f. 1-4-2010).
hi.meaning: Judicial interpretation (of Fundamental Duties ): the ways courts read Art. 51A and use it – with rights, with Directive Principles and with statutes – in deciding cases. Sustainable development : development that keeps the balance with forests and ecology; in Ganesh Wood Products it meant that "a proper assessment should be made of the forest wealth" before forest-based industries are allowed. Inter-generational equity : "Inter-generational equity means the concern for the generations to come. The present generation has no right to imperil the safety and well-being of the next generation or the generations to come thereafter." ( Ganesh Wood Products ). Reading down / reading with: a court does not enforce Art. 51A alone; it reads a law or a right "along with" a duty ( Animal Welfare Board : ss. 3 and 11 of the PCA Act "have to be read along with Art. 51A(g)&(h)").
keyPoints: Art. 51A is silent on enforcement; courts read it with rights, Part IV and statutes. Bijoe Emmanuel (1986): clause (a); standing respectfully is respect. Kinkri Devi (1987, HP HC): pointer to State, duty of citizens. M. C. Mehta (1988): 1 hour a week, first ten classes. Appa Balu Ingale (1992): duties guide the PCR Act. Virender Gaur (1994): duty of every citizen too; pull down in 4 weeks. Ganesh Wood Products (1995): no absolute right to forest industry; inter-generational equity. Balaji Raghavan (1995): awards for excellence; not titles. Barkati (1998, Cal HC): loudspeakers not essential to Azan. Animal Welfare Board (2014): "magna carta of animal rights"; 5 freedoms (OIE). Kaushal Kishor (2023): fraternity; Art. 19(2) exhaustive.

caseLaws.facts: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala , [1986] 3 SCR 518 (O. Chinnappa Reddy and M. M. Dutt JJ.; decided 11 August 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Three Jehovah's Witness children stood in respectful silence during the National Anthem but d
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Proper respect is shown to the National Anthem by standing up when the National Anthem is sung."; Arts. 19(1)(a) and 25(1) infringed; children to be re-admitted. Why it matters: Leading case on clause (a); a duty is read with Fundamental Rights , not used to cut them down.
M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (Ganga – Kanpur municipal bodies), 1988 SCR (2) 530; (1988) 1 SCC 471 (E. S. Venkataramiah and K. N. Singh JJ.; decided 12 January 1988)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Pollution of the Ganga by Kanpur; case against the Kanpur Nagar Mahapalika and others
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Protecting the environment is "one of the fundamental duties under the Constitution"; Government to direct lessons "at least for one hour in a week" "in the first ten classes". Why it matters: First major use of clause (g) to issue directions.
Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana , [1994] Supp. 6 SCR (K. Ramaswamy and N. Venkatachala JJ.; decided 24 November 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land in Thanesar vested in the Municipality and reserved as open space under a town planning
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Read with Arts. 48A, 47 and 51A(g): "not only the duty of the State but also the duty of every citizen to maintain hygienic environment"; allotment invalid; construction to be pulled down within four weeks. Why it matters: Clause (g) used with Art. 21 to protect open spaces in towns.
State of Himachal Pradesh v. Ganesh Wood Products , [1995] Supp. 3 SCR (B. P. Jeevan Reddy and M. K. Mukherjee JJ.; decided 11 September 1995)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Approvals for new katha units (using khair trees) were refused by the Government; the High Co
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Referring to Art. 51-A, "there is no absolute or unrestricted right to establish industries" based on forests; sustainable development and inter-generational equity apply; the appeals were allowed. Why it matters: Shows clause (g) used to support State limits on industry.
Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja , [2014] 6 SCR 646 (K. S. Radhakrishnan and Pinaki Chandra Ghose JJ.; decided 7 May 2014)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Jallikattu and bullock-cart races in Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra
caseLaws.facts: Principle: ss. 3 and 11 of the PCA Act "have to be read along with Art. 51A(g)&(h) of the Constitution, which is the magna carta of animal rights"; the Tamil Nadu Act was "declared unconstitutional and void". Why it matters: The widest reading of clauses (g) and (h) – compassion and humanism – to protect animals.

selfTest.q: Does Art. 51A say how it is to be enforced?
selfTest.a: Answer: No. Which clause was interpreted in Bijoe Emmanuel ? Answer: Clause (a). What did Bijoe Emmanuel say shows proper respect to the Anthem? Answer: Standing up when it is sung. In Virender Gaur , within how many weeks was the construction to be pulled down? Answer: Four weeks. What percentage of her land had the first appellant surrendered in Virender Gaur ? Answer: 25%. Which industry was involved in Ganesh Wood Products ? Answer: Katha (from khair trees). Which High Court decided Barkati ? Answer: Calcutta High Court (1998). How many freedoms for animals (OIE guidelines) did Animal Welfare Board rely on? Answer: Five. Which clauses were called the "magna carta of animal rights"? Answer: Art. 51A(g) and (h). What limit did Kaushal Kishor set on using duties against speech? Answer: Art. 19(2) grounds are exhaustive.

en.meaning:
In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court held that Parliament:

Explanation. By a 6:5 majority, the Court held Parliament cannot amend Part III so as to take away or abridge Fundamental Rights — a ruling later overruled in Kesavananda Bharati.

Which amendment directly reversed Golaknath by amending Articles 368 and 13?

Explanation. The 24th Amendment, 1971 restored Parliament's express power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.

Article 31C, as originally inserted by the 25th Amendment, protected laws implementing which provisions from Article 14/19 challenge?

Explanation. Article 31C originally protected only laws genuinely implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c).

How many Judges heard Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)?

In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (12 January 1988, AIR 1988 SC 1115, the Kanpur Nagar Mahapalika case), the Supreme Court relied on Article 51A(g) for which direction?

Explanation. The Court called protecting the natural environment one of the fundamental duties under Article 51A(g). It used that for the direction on environment lessons in schools.

Which of the following best describes how Article 51A(g) operated in the M.C. Mehta judgment of 12 January 1988?

Explanation. The judgment uses Article 51A(g) only for the environment education direction. It does not use Articles 21 or 51A(g) to close any industry.

For how long each week did the Court direct that lessons on protecting the natural environment be taught in the first ten classes?

Explanation. The Court directed teaching of at least one hour in a week, with free text books and a consideration of short training courses for teachers.

law-of-torts-u1-t2.subtitle: Section 2(m) of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the definitions of Salmond, Winfield and Fraser

en.inOneMinute: No single definition of tort is perfect, because torts are of many kinds. Each definition tries to mark off tort from crime , breach of contract and breach of trust . Indian statute: "tort" means "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m)). Salmond: a civil wrong for which the remedy is a common-law action for unliquidated damages , and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or of a trust or other merely equitable obligation. (Remedy-based definition.) Winfield: tortious liability arises from the breach of a duty primarily fixed by law ; the duty is towards persons generally ; its breach is redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. (Duty-based definition.) Fraser: a tort is an infringement of a right in rem of a private individual, giving a right of compensation at the suit of the injured party. (Right-based definition.) Putting them together: a tort is (1) a civil wrong , (2) arising from breach of a duty fixed by law , (3) usually owed to people generally , (4) violating a private legal right , (5) remedied mainly by unliquidated damages , and (6) not only a breach of contract or trust.
legalProvision: Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

In simple words: in Indian statute law, a tort is defined by two parts: (a) it is a civil wrong (not a crime), and (b) it is not exclusively a breach of contract or of trust. The word "exclusively" means the same act may also be a breach of contract and still be a tort.

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 19 (shows the kinds of wrongs the law treats as civil wrongs) – "Where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property ..., the suit may be instituted at the option of the plaintiff in either of the said Courts." Illustration (b): "A, residing in Delhi, publishes in Calcutta statements defamatory of B. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi."
In simple words: the CPC itself treats "wrong done to the person or to movable property" (for example beating, defamation) as a subject of a civil suit "for compensation" – the core of tort.
en.meaning: Statutory definition (India): "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, s. 2(m)). The same definition is used in Indian law generally when the word "tort" has to be understood. Salmond (in substance): a tort is a civil wrong for which the remedy is a common-law action for unliquidated damages , and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust or other merely equitable obligation. Winfield (in substance): tortious liability arises from the breach of a duty primarily fixed by the law; this duty is towards persons generally and its breach is redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. Fraser (in substance): a tort is an infringement of a right in rem of a private individual, giving a right of compensation at the suit of the injured party. Clerk and Lindsell (in substance): a tort is a wrong independent of contract, for which the appropriate remedy is a common-law action. Working definition for answers: A tort is a civil wrong, other than a mere breach of contract or trust, arising from breach of a duty fixed by law and owed to persons generally, which violates a private legal right and is remedied by an action for unliquidated damages (and, where suitable, an injunction ).
keyPoints: s. 2(m) Limitation Act: civil wrong, not exclusively breach of contract or trust. Salmond = remedy (unliquidated damages); Winfield = duty (fixed by law, persons generally); Fraser = right in rem. Criticisms: Salmond circular; both ignore injunction; Winfield's "primarily" is important. Tort is the residue of civil wrongs after contract and trust. Ashby v. White – right violated without loss is a tort; Bradford v. Pickles – loss without right violated is not.

selfTest.q: Quote the statutory definition of tort in India. Answer: "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m)). Why is the word "exclusively" important?
selfTest.a: Answer: It allows an act that is a breach of contract to be a tort also, if it violates a duty under general law. Which jurist defines tort by its remedy? Answer: Salmond – a civil wrong remedied by a common-law action for unliquidated damages. What are the three parts of Winfield's definition? Answer: Duty primarily fixed by law; towards persons generally; breach redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. What is a right in rem? Answer: A right good against the whole world, such as the right to reputation or to bodily safety. Give one criticism common to Salmond's and Winfield's definitions. Answer: Both treat unliquidated damages as the remedy and leave out injunction. Is breach of trust a tort? Answer: Not if it is merely a breach of trust; it is remedied in equity. Which case shows that loss without violation of a legal right is not a tort? Answer: Mayor of Bradford v. Pickles [1895] AC 587. Which case shows that a tort duty exists without contract? Answer: Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562. Late completion of a building contract – tort or not? Answer: Not a tort; it is exclusively a breach of contract.

visuals.caption: Comparison Table
visuals.html:
This Is not the same as Why
Right in rem Right in personam In rem: good against the whole world (reputation, body, property). In personam: against a particular person (rights under a contract).
Duty fixed by law Duty fixed by agreement Tort duties come from law; contract duties come from the parties' agreement.
Unliquidated damages Liquidated damages / debt Unliquidated: assessed by the court. Liquidated: a sum fixed beforehand.
Civil wrong Tort Every tort is a civil wrong, but civil wrongs also include breach of contract and breach of trust.
"Not exclusively" a breach of contract "Not" a breach of contract The statute allows an act to be both; it excludes only acts that are only breaches of contract.
Equitable obligation (trust) Tort duty Breach of trust is remedied in equity; it is excluded from tort if it is merely a breach of trust.

te.inOneMinute: అపకృత్యాలు అనేక రకాలు కాబట్టి ఏ ఒక్క నిర్వచనమూ పరిపూర్ణం కాదు. ప్రతి నిర్వచనం అపకృత్యాన్ని నేరం , ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన , ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి వేరు చేయడానికి ప్రయత్నిస్తుంది. భారత చట్టం: "tort" means "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (పరిమితి చట్టం, 1963, సె. 2(m)) – కేవలం ఒప్పంద లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. సాల్మండ్: అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం (unliquidated damages) కోసం కామన్ లా దావాయే పరిహారంగా ఉండే పౌర తప్పిదం; అది కేవలం ఒప్పంద, ట్రస్ట్ లేదా ఇతర కేవల సమత (equitable) బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన కాదు. (పరిహారం ఆధారిత నిర్వచనం.) విన్‌ఫీల్డ్: చట్టం ప్రధానంగా నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల అపకృత్య బాధ్యత పుడుతుంది; ఆ బాధ్యత ప్రజలందరి పట్ల ; దాని ఉల్లంఘనకు అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహార దావా ద్వారా పరిష్కారం. (బాధ్యత ఆధారిత నిర్వచనం.) ఫ్రేజర్: ఒక ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తి యొక్క సర్వజన హక్కు (right in rem) ను ఉల్లంఘించడం; నష్టపోయిన పక్షం దావా ద్వారా పరిహారం పొందే హక్కు ఇస్తుంది. (హక్కు ఆధారిత నిర్వచనం.) అన్నీ కలిపి: అపకృత్యం అంటే (1) పౌర తప్పిదం , (2) చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల, (3) సాధారణంగా ప్రజలందరి పట్ల , (4) ఒక ప్రైవేట్ చట్టబద్ధ హక్కును ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది, (5) ప్రధానంగా అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం ద్వారా పరిష్కారం, (6) కేవలం ఒప్పంద లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాదు.
te.meaning: చట్టబద్ధ నిర్వచనం (భారతదేశం): "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (పరిమితి చట్టం, సె. 2(m)). "tort" అనే పదాన్ని అర్థం చేసుకోవలసినప్పుడు భారత చట్టంలో సాధారణంగా ఇదే నిర్వచనం ఉపయోగిస్తారు. సాల్మండ్ (సారాంశం): అపకృత్యం ఒక పౌర తప్పిదం; దానికి పరిహారం అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం కోసం కామన్ లా దావా; అది కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన , ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన లేదా ఇతర కేవల సమత బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన కాదు. విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ (సారాంశం): చట్టం ప్రధానంగా నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల అపకృత్య బాధ్యత పుడుతుంది; ఈ బాధ్యత ప్రజలందరి పట్ల; దాని ఉల్లంఘనకు అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహార దావా ద్వారా పరిష్కారం. ఫ్రేజర్ (సారాంశం): అపకృత్యం అంటే ఒక ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తి సర్వజన హక్కు (right in rem) ఉల్లంఘన; నష్టపోయిన పక్షం దావా ద్వారా పరిహారం పొందే హక్కు ఇస్తుంది. క్లర్క్ అండ్ లిండ్సెల్ (సారాంశం): అపకృత్యం ఒప్పందంతో సంబంధం లేని తప్పిదం; దానికి తగిన పరిహారం కామన్ లా దావా. జవాబులకు పని నిర్వచనం: అపకృత్యం అంటే – కేవలం ఒప్పంద లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాని పౌర తప్పిదం; చట్టం నిర్ణయించి ప్రజలందరి పట్ల ఉండే బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల పుడుతుంది; ఒక ప్రైవేట్ చట్టబద్ధ హక్కును ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది; అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహార దావా (తగిన చోట నిషేధాజ్ఞ ) ద్వారా పరిష్కారం.
keyPoints: పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 2(m): పౌర తప్పిదం, కేవలం ఒప్పంద లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాదు. సాల్మండ్ = పరిహారం (అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం); విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ = బాధ్యత (చట్టం నిర్ణయించినది, ప్రజలందరి పట్ల); ఫ్రేజర్ = సర్వజన హక్కు. విమర్శలు: సాల్మండ్ వృత్తాకారం; రెండూ నిషేధాజ్ఞను విస్మరిస్తాయి; విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ "primarily" ముఖ్యం. ఒప్పందం, ట్రస్ట్ తీసేశాక మిగిలిన పౌర తప్పిదాలే అపకృత్యం. ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ – నష్టం లేకుండా హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన అపకృత్యం; బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ – హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన లేని నష్టం అపకృత్యం కాదు.

selfTest.q: భారతదేశంలో అపకృత్యానికి చట్టబద్ధ నిర్వచనం ఉల్లేఖించండి. జవాబు: "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (పరిమితి చట్టం, 1963, సె. 2(m)). "exclusively" పదం ఎందుకు ముఖ్యం?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన అయిన చర్య, సాధారణ చట్టం కింద బాధ్యతను కూడా ఉల్లంఘిస్తే, అపకృత్యం కూడా కావడానికి అనుమతిస్తుంది. ఏ న్యాయశాస్త్రవేత్త అపకృత్యాన్ని దాని పరిహారంతో నిర్వచిస్తారు? జవాబు: సాల్మండ్ – అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం కోసం కామన్ లా దావాతో పరిష్కరించబడే పౌర తప్పిదం. విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ నిర్వచనంలోని మూడు భాగాలు ఏమిటి? జవాబు: చట్టం ప్రధానంగా నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత; ప్రజలందరి పట్ల; ఉల్లంఘనకు అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహార దావా ద్వారా పరిష్కారం. సర్వజన హక్కు (right in rem) అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: ప్రపంచమంతటికీ వ్యతిరేకంగా ఉండే హక్కు – పరువు లేదా శారీరక భద్రత హక్కు వంటిది. సాల్మండ్, విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ నిర్వచనాలకు ఉమ్మడి విమర్శ ఒకటి చెప్పండి. జవాబు: రెండూ అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారాన్నే పరిహారంగా తీసుకుని నిషేధాజ్ఞను వదిలేస్తాయి. ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన అపకృత్యమా? జవాబు: కేవలం ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన అయితే కాదు; దానికి సమతలో పరిష్కారం. చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన లేని నష్టం అపకృత్యం కాదని చూపే కేసు ఏది? జవాబు: మేయర్ ఆఫ్ బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ [1895] AC 587. ఒప్పందం లేకుండానే అపకృత్య బాధ్యత ఉంటుందని చూపే కేసు ఏది? జవాబు: డోనోఘ్యూ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ [1932] AC 562. భవన నిర్మాణ ఒప్పందాన్ని ఆలస్యంగా పూర్తి చేయడం – అపకృత్యమా? జవాబు: కాదు; అది కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన.

సర్వజన హక్కు (right in rem) వ్యక్తిగత హక్కు (right in personam) In rem: ప్రపంచమంతటికీ వ్యతిరేకంగా (పరువు, శరీరం, ఆస్తి). In personam: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా (ఒప్పందం కింద హక్కులు).
చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత ఒప్పందం నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత అపకృత్య బాధ్యతలు చట్టం నుంచి; ఒప్పంద బాధ్యతలు పక్షాల ఒప్పందం నుంచి.
అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం నిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం / అప్పు అనిర్ధారితం: కోర్టు అంచనా. నిర్ధారితం: ముందుగా నిర్ణయించిన మొత్తం.
పౌర తప్పిదం అపకృత్యం ప్రతి అపకృత్యం పౌర తప్పిదమే; కానీ పౌర తప్పిదాల్లో ఒప్పంద, ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘనలు కూడా ఉన్నాయి.
"కేవలం" ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన కాదు ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన "కాదు" చట్టం ఒక చర్య రెండూ కావడాన్ని అనుమతిస్తుంది; కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘనలను మాత్రమే మినహాయిస్తుంది.
సమత బాధ్యత (ట్రస్ట్) అపకృత్య బాధ్యత ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘనకు సమతలో పరిష్కారం; కేవలం ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన అయితే అపకృత్యం నుంచి మినహాయించబడింది.

hi.inOneMinute: No single definition of tort is perfect, because torts are of many kinds. Each definition tries to mark off tort from crime , breach of contract and breach of trust . Indian statute: "tort" means "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m)). Salmond: a civil wrong for which the remedy is a common-law action for unliquidated damages , and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or of a trust or other merely equitable obligation. (Remedy-based definition.) Winfield: tortious liability arises from the breach of a duty primarily fixed by law ; the duty is towards persons generally ; its breach is redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. (Duty-based definition.) Fraser: a tort is an infringement of a right in rem of a private individual, giving a right of compensation at the suit of the injured party. (Right-based definition.) Putting them together: a tort is (1) a civil wrong , (2) arising from breach of a duty fixed by law , (3) usually owed to people generally , (4) violating a private legal right , (5) remedied mainly by unliquidated damages , and (6) not only a breach of contract or trust.
legalProvision: Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

In simple words: in Indian statute law, a tort is defined by two parts: (a) it is a civil wrong (not a crime), and (b) it is not exclusively a breach of contract or of trust. The word "exclusively" means the same act may also be a breach of contract and still be a tort.

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 19 (shows the kinds of wrongs the law treats as civil wrongs) – "Where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property ..., the suit may be instituted at the option of the plaintiff in either of the said Courts." Illustration (b): "A, residing in Delhi, publishes in Calcutta statements defamatory of B. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi."
In simple words: the CPC itself treats "wrong done to the person or to movable property" (for example beating, defamation) as a subject of a civil suit "for compensation" – the core of tort.
hi.meaning: Statutory definition (India): "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, s. 2(m)). The same definition is used in Indian law generally when the word "tort" has to be understood. Salmond (in substance): a tort is a civil wrong for which the remedy is a common-law action for unliquidated damages , and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust or other merely equitable obligation. Winfield (in substance): tortious liability arises from the breach of a duty primarily fixed by the law; this duty is towards persons generally and its breach is redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. Fraser (in substance): a tort is an infringement of a right in rem of a private individual, giving a right of compensation at the suit of the injured party. Clerk and Lindsell (in substance): a tort is a wrong independent of contract, for which the appropriate remedy is a common-law action. Working definition for answers: A tort is a civil wrong, other than a mere breach of contract or trust, arising from breach of a duty fixed by law and owed to persons generally, which violates a private legal right and is remedied by an action for unliquidated damages (and, where suitable, an injunction ).
keyPoints: s. 2(m) Limitation Act: civil wrong, not exclusively breach of contract or trust. Salmond = remedy (unliquidated damages); Winfield = duty (fixed by law, persons generally); Fraser = right in rem. Criticisms: Salmond circular; both ignore injunction; Winfield's "primarily" is important. Tort is the residue of civil wrongs after contract and trust. Ashby v. White – right violated without loss is a tort; Bradford v. Pickles – loss without right violated is not.

selfTest.q: Quote the statutory definition of tort in India. Answer: "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m)). Why is the word "exclusively" important?
selfTest.a: Answer: It allows an act that is a breach of contract to be a tort also, if it violates a duty under general law. Which jurist defines tort by its remedy? Answer: Salmond – a civil wrong remedied by a common-law action for unliquidated damages. What are the three parts of Winfield's definition? Answer: Duty primarily fixed by law; towards persons generally; breach redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. What is a right in rem? Answer: A right good against the whole world, such as the right to reputation or to bodily safety. Give one criticism common to Salmond's and Winfield's definitions. Answer: Both treat unliquidated damages as the remedy and leave out injunction. Is breach of trust a tort? Answer: Not if it is merely a breach of trust; it is remedied in equity. Which case shows that loss without violation of a legal right is not a tort? Answer: Mayor of Bradford v. Pickles [1895] AC 587. Which case shows that a tort duty exists without contract? Answer: Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562. Late completion of a building contract – tort or not? Answer: Not a tort; it is exclusively a breach of contract.

law-of-torts-u1-t3.subtitle: Wrongful act or omission, legal damage and legal remedy, with the remedies in tort

en.inOneMinute: To succeed in a tort action, the plaintiff must usually prove three essentials : a wrongful act or omission by the defendant; which causes legal damage – that is, the violation of a legal right of the plaintiff ( injuria ); and the wrong must be of a kind that gives rise to a legal remedy (an action for damages, injunction, etc.). The act must be wrongful in law , not only morally wrong. An omission is a tort only if there was a legal duty to act ( Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti , 1966: failure to inspect and maintain a clock tower that collapsed). "Legal damage" does not mean money loss. It means injury to a legal right . So: injury to a right without money loss is actionable ( Ashby v. White , 1703) – injuria sine damno; money loss without injury to a right is not ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895; Mogul Steamship , 1891; Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal , 1974) – damnum sine injuria. "Where there is a right, there is a remedy" – ubi jus ibi remedium . In Ashby v. White the House of Lords resolved that, as an "Incident inseparable to that Right, he must have a Remedy to assert and maintain it." Motive and the defendant's mental state are generally not separate elements, but they matter in some torts (malice in malicious prosecution; intention in assault).
legalProvision: There is no statute listing the elements of tort. The elements are taken from the definition and from case law.
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 23 – "In the case of a suit for compensation for an act which does not give rise to a cause of action unless some specific injury actually results therefrom, the period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the injury results."

In simple words: s. 2(m) gives the first elements (a civil wrong ). Section 23 shows that some acts are actionable only when actual injury results (for example slander not actionable per se , or negligence) – in such torts, damage itself is part of the cause of action. In other torts (trespass, libel) the violation of the right is enough.
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 9 – "The Courts shall ... have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred."
In simple words: once a legal right is violated, the civil court is open to the injured person – this is the "remedy" element in procedural form.
en.meaning: Elements (essentials) of tort are the conditions that must exist before the law holds a person liable in tort. Wrongful act – an act or omission that violates a legal right of another, or is a breach of a duty imposed by law. "Wrongful" means contrary to law ( in jus , against right), not merely harmful or immoral. Omission – failure to do an act. In tort, an omission counts only where the law imposes a duty to act. Legal damage (injuria) – infringement of a legal right vested in the plaintiff. It is different from damnum (actual loss or harm, usually money loss). Legal remedy – the right to bring an action in court for damages, injunction or other relief. Expressed in the maxim ubi jus ibi remedium .
keyPoints: Three essentials: wrongful act/omission + legal damage (injuria) + legal remedy. Omission = tort only where legal duty to act ( MCD v. Subhagwanti ). Injuria sine damno – actionable ( Ashby v. White ; Bhim Singh ₹50,000). Damnum sine injuria – not actionable ( Bradford ; Mogul ; Town Area Committee ). Ubi jus ibi remedium – Ashby : "no such Notion ... as a Right without a Remedy." Actionable per se (trespass, assault, battery, false imprisonment, libel) vs on proof of damage (negligence, nuisance, slander mostly). Limitation Act s. 23: where specific injury is needed, time runs from when it results.

selfTest.q: Name the three essentials of a tort. Answer: Wrongful act or omission; legal damage (injury to a legal right); legal remedy. When is an omission a tort?
selfTest.a: Answer: When the defendant had a legal duty to act and failed to do so. What is the difference between injuria and damnum? Answer: Injuria is violation of a legal right; damnum is actual loss or harm. Give an Indian case of injuria sine damno. Answer: Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) – illegal detention of an MLA; ₹50,000 awarded. Why did the plaintiffs lose in Mogul Steamship ? Answer: The defendants used lawful means of competition; loss without legal injury. What was held in Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal ? Answer: Demolition of an illegally built structure is not injuria; no compensation though loss was suffered. State the maxim about rights and remedies. Answer: Ubi jus ibi remedium – where there is a right, there is a remedy. Name two torts actionable per se. Answer: Any two of trespass to land, assault, battery, false imprisonment, libel. Is malice a general element of tort? Answer: No; it is an element only in some torts, such as malicious prosecution. What does s. 23 of the Limitation Act provide? Answer: For acts actionable only when specific injury results, limitation runs from when the injury results.

te.inOneMinute: అపకృత్య దావాలో గెలవాలంటే వాది సాధారణంగా మూడు ముఖ్యాంశాలను నిరూపించాలి: ప్రతివాది చేసిన తప్పుడు చర్య లేదా లోపం (wrongful act or omission) ; దాని వల్ల చట్టపరమైన నష్టం (legal damage) – అంటే వాది యొక్క చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన ( ఇంజూరియా (injuria) ); మరియు ఆ తప్పిదం చట్టపరమైన పరిహారం (legal remedy) ఇచ్చే రకమైనదై ఉండాలి (నష్టపరిహార దావా, నిషేధాజ్ఞ మొదలైనవి). చర్య కేవలం నైతికంగా తప్పు కాక, చట్టపరంగా తప్పు అయి ఉండాలి. లోపం (omission) అపకృత్యం కావాలంటే చర్య తీసుకోవలసిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత ఉండాలి ( మున్సిపల్ కార్పొరేషన్ ఆఫ్ ఢిల్లీ v. సుభాగ్‌వంతి , 1966: కూలిపోయిన గడియార స్తంభాన్ని పరిశీలించి నిర్వహించకపోవడం). "చట్టపరమైన నష్టం" అంటే డబ్బు నష్టం కాదు. చట్టబద్ధ హక్కుకు గాయం అని అర్థం. కాబట్టి: డబ్బు నష్టం లేకుండా హక్కుకు గాయం – దావా యోగ్యం ( ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ , 1703) – injuria sine damno; హక్కుకు గాయం లేకుండా డబ్బు నష్టం – దావా యోగ్యం కాదు ( బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ , 1895; మొగల్ స్టీమ్‌షిప్ , 1891; టౌన్ ఏరియా కమిటీ v. ప్రభు దయాళ్ , 1974) – damnum sine injuria. "హక్కు ఉన్నచోట పరిహారం ఉంటుంది" – ఉబి జస్ ఇబి రెమెడియం (ubi jus ibi remedium) . ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ లో హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్ తీర్మానించింది: "Incident inseparable to that Right, he must have a Remedy to assert and maintain it." (ఆ హక్కు నుంచి విడదీయలేని అంశంగా, దాన్ని నిలబెట్టుకోవడానికి అతనికి పరిహారం ఉండాలి.) ఉద్దేశం (motive), ప్రతివాది మానసిక స్థితి సాధారణంగా వేరే అంశాలు కావు ; కానీ కొన్ని అపకృత్యాల్లో ముఖ్యం (దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్‌లో దురుద్దేశం; దాడిలో ఉద్దేశం).
te.meaning: అపకృత్యం అంశాలు (ముఖ్యాంశాలు) అంటే ఒక వ్యక్తిని అపకృత్యంలో బాధ్యుడిగా చట్టం పరిగణించే ముందు ఉండవలసిన షరతులు. తప్పుడు చర్య – మరొకరి చట్టబద్ధ హక్కును ఉల్లంఘించే లేదా చట్టం విధించిన బాధ్యతను ఉల్లంఘించే చర్య లేదా లోపం. "తప్పుడు" అంటే చట్టానికి విరుద్ధం ( in jus , హక్కుకు వ్యతిరేకం); కేవలం హానికరం లేదా అనైతికం కాదు. లోపం (omission) – ఒక చర్యను చేయకపోవడం. అపకృత్యంలో, చట్టం చర్య తీసుకోవలసిన బాధ్యత విధించినచోట మాత్రమే లోపం లెక్కలోకి వస్తుంది. చట్టపరమైన నష్టం (injuria) – వాదికి ఉన్న చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన. ఇది డామ్నమ్ (damnum) (వాస్తవ నష్టం లేదా హాని, సాధారణంగా డబ్బు నష్టం) కంటే భిన్నమైనది. చట్టపరమైన పరిహారం – నష్టపరిహారం, నిషేధాజ్ఞ లేదా ఇతర ఉపశమనం కోసం కోర్టులో దావా వేసే హక్కు. ubi jus ibi remedium అనే సూత్రంలో వ్యక్తమవుతుంది.
keyPoints: మూడు ముఖ్యాంశాలు: తప్పుడు చర్య/లోపం + చట్టపరమైన నష్టం (injuria) + చట్టపరమైన పరిహారం. చర్య తీసుకోవలసిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత ఉన్నచోట మాత్రమే లోపం = అపకృత్యం ( MCD v. సుభాగ్‌వంతి ). Injuria sine damno – దావా యోగ్యం ( ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ ; భీమ్ సింగ్ ₹50,000). Damnum sine injuria – దావా యోగ్యం కాదు ( బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ ; మొగల్ ; టౌన్ ఏరియా కమిటీ ). Ubi jus ibi remedium – ఆష్బీ : "no such Notion ... as a Right without a Remedy." స్వతఃసిద్ధంగా దావా యోగ్యం (అతిక్రమణ, దాడి, కొట్టడం, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, libel) vs నష్టం నిరూపిస్తే (నిర్లక్ష్యం, ఉపద్రవం, ఎక్కువగా slander). పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 23: నిర్దిష్ట గాయం అవసరమైనచోట, అది జరిగినప్పటి నుంచి కాలం.

selfTest.q: అపకృత్యం మూడు ముఖ్యాంశాలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: తప్పుడు చర్య లేదా లోపం; చట్టపరమైన నష్టం (చట్టబద్ధ హక్కుకు గాయం); చట్టపరమైన పరిహారం. లోపం ఎప్పుడు అపకృత్యం అవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: ప్రతివాదికి చర్య తీసుకోవలసిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత ఉండి, అతను విఫలమైనప్పుడు. Injuria, damnum మధ్య తేడా ఏమిటి? జవాబు: Injuria చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన; damnum వాస్తవ నష్టం లేదా హాని. Injuria sine damnoకు ఒక భారతీయ కేసు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: భీమ్ సింగ్ v. స్టేట్ ఆఫ్ J&K (1985) – MLA అక్రమ నిర్బంధం; ₹50,000 ఇచ్చారు. మొగల్ స్టీమ్‌షిప్ లో వాదులు ఎందుకు ఓడిపోయారు? జవాబు: ప్రతివాదులు చట్టబద్ధమైన పోటీ మార్గాలు వాడారు; చట్టపరమైన గాయం లేని నష్టం. టౌన్ ఏరియా కమిటీ v. ప్రభు దయాళ్ లో ఏమి తీర్పు ఇచ్చారు? జవాబు: అక్రమంగా కట్టిన నిర్మాణం కూల్చివేత injuria కాదు; నష్టం జరిగినా పరిహారం లేదు. హక్కులు, పరిహారాల గురించిన సూత్రం చెప్పండి. జవాబు: Ubi jus ibi remedium – హక్కు ఉన్నచోట పరిహారం ఉంటుంది. స్వతఃసిద్ధంగా దావా యోగ్యమైన రెండు అపకృత్యాలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ, దాడి, కొట్టడం, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, libelలో ఏవైనా రెండు. దురుద్దేశం అపకృత్యానికి సాధారణ అంశమా? జవాబు: కాదు; దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ వంటి కొన్ని అపకృత్యాల్లో మాత్రమే అంశం. పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 23 ఏమి చెబుతుంది? జవాబు: నిర్దిష్ట గాయం జరిగితేనే దావా యోగ్యమయ్యే చర్యలకు, గాయం జరిగినప్పటి నుంచి పరిమితి కాలం.

hi.inOneMinute: To succeed in a tort action, the plaintiff must usually prove three essentials : a wrongful act or omission by the defendant; which causes legal damage – that is, the violation of a legal right of the plaintiff ( injuria ); and the wrong must be of a kind that gives rise to a legal remedy (an action for damages, injunction, etc.). The act must be wrongful in law , not only morally wrong. An omission is a tort only if there was a legal duty to act ( Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti , 1966: failure to inspect and maintain a clock tower that collapsed). "Legal damage" does not mean money loss. It means injury to a legal right . So: injury to a right without money loss is actionable ( Ashby v. White , 1703) – injuria sine damno; money loss without injury to a right is not ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895; Mogul Steamship , 1891; Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal , 1974) – damnum sine injuria. "Where there is a right, there is a remedy" – ubi jus ibi remedium . In Ashby v. White the House of Lords resolved that, as an "Incident inseparable to that Right, he must have a Remedy to assert and maintain it." Motive and the defendant's mental state are generally not separate elements, but they matter in some torts (malice in malicious prosecution; intention in assault).
legalProvision: There is no statute listing the elements of tort. The elements are taken from the definition and from case law.
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 23 – "In the case of a suit for compensation for an act which does not give rise to a cause of action unless some specific injury actually results therefrom, the period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the injury results."

In simple words: s. 2(m) gives the first elements (a civil wrong ). Section 23 shows that some acts are actionable only when actual injury results (for example slander not actionable per se , or negligence) – in such torts, damage itself is part of the cause of action. In other torts (trespass, libel) the violation of the right is enough.
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 9 – "The Courts shall ... have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred."
In simple words: once a legal right is violated, the civil court is open to the injured person – this is the "remedy" element in procedural form.
hi.meaning: Elements (essentials) of tort are the conditions that must exist before the law holds a person liable in tort. Wrongful act – an act or omission that violates a legal right of another, or is a breach of a duty imposed by law. "Wrongful" means contrary to law ( in jus , against right), not merely harmful or immoral. Omission – failure to do an act. In tort, an omission counts only where the law imposes a duty to act. Legal damage (injuria) – infringement of a legal right vested in the plaintiff. It is different from damnum (actual loss or harm, usually money loss). Legal remedy – the right to bring an action in court for damages, injunction or other relief. Expressed in the maxim ubi jus ibi remedium .
keyPoints: Three essentials: wrongful act/omission + legal damage (injuria) + legal remedy. Omission = tort only where legal duty to act ( MCD v. Subhagwanti ). Injuria sine damno – actionable ( Ashby v. White ; Bhim Singh ₹50,000). Damnum sine injuria – not actionable ( Bradford ; Mogul ; Town Area Committee ). Ubi jus ibi remedium – Ashby : "no such Notion ... as a Right without a Remedy." Actionable per se (trespass, assault, battery, false imprisonment, libel) vs on proof of damage (negligence, nuisance, slander mostly). Limitation Act s. 23: where specific injury is needed, time runs from when it results.

selfTest.q: Name the three essentials of a tort. Answer: Wrongful act or omission; legal damage (injury to a legal right); legal remedy. When is an omission a tort?
selfTest.a: Answer: When the defendant had a legal duty to act and failed to do so. What is the difference between injuria and damnum? Answer: Injuria is violation of a legal right; damnum is actual loss or harm. Give an Indian case of injuria sine damno. Answer: Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) – illegal detention of an MLA; ₹50,000 awarded. Why did the plaintiffs lose in Mogul Steamship ? Answer: The defendants used lawful means of competition; loss without legal injury. What was held in Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal ? Answer: Demolition of an illegally built structure is not injuria; no compensation though loss was suffered. State the maxim about rights and remedies. Answer: Ubi jus ibi remedium – where there is a right, there is a remedy. Name two torts actionable per se. Answer: Any two of trespass to land, assault, battery, false imprisonment, libel. Is malice a general element of tort? Answer: No; it is an element only in some torts, such as malicious prosecution. What does s. 23 of the Limitation Act provide? Answer: For acts actionable only when specific injury results, limitation runs from when the injury results.
