law-of-torts-u1-t4.subtitle: From the medieval writs to negligence in England, and from the 1726 Charter to absolute liability in India

en.inOneMinute: England: the law of torts grew out of the medieval writ system . The writ of trespass covered direct, forcible injuries; the action on the case covered indirect harm. Most modern torts (nuisance, defamation, negligence, deceit, conversion) grew from the action on the case. The forms of action were abolished in the 19th century, and the law became a body of principles built by judges: strict liability ( Rylands v. Fletcher , 1868), the duty of care ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932), negligent misstatement ( Hedley Byrne , 1964), remoteness ( Wagon Mound , 1961), wider vicarious liability ( Lister , 2001; Mohamud , 2016). Statutes filled gaps: at common law "the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury" ( Baker v. Bolton , 1808), which statute later changed. India: English tort law came with British courts. It was applied as "justice, equity and good conscience" , only so far as it suited Indian conditions. Indian statutes added to it: the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 , whose preamble says that before it "no action or suit is now maintainable" against a person who caused another's death; later the Employee's Compensation Act, 1923, Motor Vehicles Acts, Consumer Protection Acts (1986, 2019), and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991. State liability passed from the East India Company to the Secretary of State (GoI Act 1858, s. 65), then to the Federation and Provinces (GoI Act 1935, s. 176) and to the Union and States ( Constitution, Art. 300 ). Cases: State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati (1962), Kasturilal (1964). After 1950 the law continues under Art. 372 , and Indian courts have moved away from English rules where needed: absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta , 1987: "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order"), constitutional torts ( Rudul Sah , 1983; Bhim Singh , 1985; Nilabati Behera , 1993). Tort litigation in India has remained small in volume compared with England, because of cost, delay and low awards; much compensation law now works through special forums (Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals, Consumer Commissions).
legalProvision: Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 (Act 13 of 1855), Preamble – "WHEREAS no action or suit is now maintainable in any Court against a person who, by his wrongful act, neglect or default, may have caused the death of another person, and it is often-times right and expedient that the wrong-doer in such case should be answerable in damages for the injury so caused by him."

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A (main words) – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensued) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages ... Every such action or suit shall be for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child, if any, of the person whose death shall have been so caused".

In simple words: before 1855, in India as in England, a wrongdoer who killed a person could not be sued by the family. The 1855 Act changed this: the family can sue if the deceased could have sued had he lived.

Government of India Act, 1858, s. 65 (main words) – "The Secretary of State in Council shall and may sue and be sued as well in India as in England ... and all Persons and Bodies Politic shall and may have and take the same Suits, Remedies, and Proceedings, legal and equitable, against the Secretary of State in Council of India as they could have done against the said Company".

Government of India Act, 1935, s. 176(1) (main words) – the Federation and Provinces "may ... sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Secretary of State in Council might have sued or been sued if this Act had not been passed."

Constitution of India, Art. 300(1) (main words) – "The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may ... sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted."

In simple words: the liability of the Government in tort in India today goes back, step by step, to the liability of the East India Company. Art. 300 keeps the old position unless Parliament or a State Legislature makes a law.

Constitution of India, Art. 372(1) (main words) – "all the law in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other competent authority."
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1)–(2) (main words, as amended) – the owner or insurer "shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt"; "the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish" fault. (The earlier no-fault provision, s. 140, was omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2022.)
In simple words: modern Indian statutes have moved some tort claims (road accidents) to a no-fault basis.
en.meaning: Development of the law of torts means the historical growth of the rules about civil wrongs: where they came from, how they were enforced, and how they changed to meet new social needs. Writ – in medieval England, a written order from the King's Chancery that started an action in the royal courts. Each kind of claim needed its own writ (a "form of action"). Trespass (writ of trespass) – an action for direct and forcible injury to person, land or goods. Action on the case (trespass on the case) – an action for injury that was indirect or consequential, or not forcible; it allowed the courts to give remedies for new kinds of harm. Justice, equity and good conscience – the rule under which courts in British India decided cases where no Indian statute or personal law applied, often by borrowing English rules that suited Indian conditions.
keyPoints: Trespass = direct, forcible injury; action on the case = indirect harm → negligence, nuisance, defamation. Forms of action abolished 1852–75 → principles. Baker v. Bolton (1808): death not actionable at common law → Fatal Accidents Act 1846 (Eng.), 1855 (India). India: English law through British courts; justice, equity and good conscience; selective. State liability: GoI Act 1858 s. 65 → GoI Act 1935 s. 176 → Art. 300; P. & O. (1861); Vidyawati (1962); Kasturilal (1964). Indian innovations: absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta , 1987); constitutional torts ( Rudul Sah , Bhim Singh , Nilabati ). MV Act s. 164: no-fault ₹5 lakh (death) / ₹2.5 lakh (grievous hurt).

caseLaws.name: Facts: A husband and wife were travelling on a stage-coach that overturned; the wife died about a mo
caseLaws.facts: The husband sued the coach proprietors. Principle: Lord Ellenborough: "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury"; damages only up to the time of death (verdict £100). Why it matters: Explains why Fatal Accidents Acts (1846 England; 1855 India) were needed.
Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) LR 3 HL 330

caseLaws.name: Facts: Defendants' reservoir, built over old filled-up mine shafts, burst through them and flooded t
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A person who brings and keeps on his land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage caused by its escape, without proof of negligence. Why it matters: Shows how industrial risks produced new rules of liability.
Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562

caseLaws.name: Facts: Ginger-beer with a decomposed snail in an opaque bottle; the consumer had no contract with th
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle – a general duty of reasonable care. Why it matters: Made negligence the leading modern tort in England and in India.
State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati AIR 1962 SC 933 (5 judges, 2 Feb 1962)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 11 Feb 1952, a Government jeep driven rashly and negligently by a State employee knocked d
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "the liability of the State for damages in respect of a tortious act committed by its servant within the scope of his employment and functioning as such was the same as that of any other employer" (headnote). The Court traced the history through Art. 300, GoI Act 1935 s. 176, and the P. & O. case. Why it matters: Shows the historical line of State liability in India and the post-1950 approach.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) 1 SCC 395; AIR 1987 SC 1086

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas leaked from Shriram's Delhi plant on 4 and 6 Dec 1985; compensation claims were mad
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Absolute and non-delegable duty of hazardous enterprises; "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order." Why it matters: Marks India's independent development of tort law.
Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) 4 SCC 141; AIR 1983 SC 1086

caseLaws.name: Facts: Detention for over 14 years after acquittal
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Compensation under Art. 32 for violation of Art. 21; the State "must repair the damage done by its officers". Why it matters: Starts the Indian line of constitutional torts.

selfTest.q: What was the difference between trespass and action on the case?
selfTest.a: Answer: Trespass covered direct and forcible injury; action on the case covered indirect or consequential harm. Which modern tort grew mainly from the action on the case? Answer: Negligence (also nuisance, defamation, deceit). What did Baker v. Bolton decide? Answer: That at common law the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury in a civil court. Which Indian Act first allowed families to sue for death caused by wrongful act? Answer: The Fatal Accidents Act, 1855. Under what principle was English tort law applied in British India? Answer: Justice, equity and good conscience – where suitable to Indian conditions. Trace the provisions on suits against the Government from 1858 to today. Answer: GoI Act 1858 s. 65 → GoI Act 1935 s. 176 → Constitution Art. 300. What did Vidyawati hold? Answer: The State is liable for torts of its servants in the course of employment like any other employer (on the facts: a Government jeep accident). Which case created absolute liability in India? Answer: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987). Name one reason why tort litigation remained limited in India. Answer: Any one: high court fees, delay, cost, poverty and low awareness, low awards, preference for criminal remedies. Which section of the MV Act now gives no-fault compensation, and how much? Answer: Section 164: ₹5 lakh on death; ₹2.5 lakh on grievous hurt.

te.inOneMinute: ఇంగ్లాండ్: అపకృత్యాల చట్టం మధ్యయుగపు రిట్ వ్యవస్థ ( writ system) నుంచి పెరిగింది. అతిక్రమణ (trespass) రిట్ ప్రత్యక్ష, బలప్రయోగ గాయాలను కవర్ చేసింది; ఆక్షన్ ఆన్ ది కేస్ (action on the case) పరోక్ష హానిని కవర్ చేసింది. ఆధునిక అపకృత్యాల్లో చాలావరకు (ఉపద్రవం, పరువు నష్టం, నిర్లక్ష్యం, మోసం, మార్పిడి) action on the case నుంచి పెరిగాయి. 19వ శతాబ్దంలో forms of action రద్దయ్యాయి; న్యాయమూర్తులు నిర్మించిన సూత్రాల సమూహంగా చట్టం మారింది: కఠిన బాధ్యత ( రైలాండ్స్ v. ఫ్లెచర్ , 1868), జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత ( డోనోఘ్యూ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ , 1932), నిర్లక్ష్యపు తప్పుడు ప్రకటన ( హెడ్లీ బైర్న్ , 1964), దూరత్వం ( వేగన్ మౌండ్ , 1961), విస్తృత ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత ( లిస్టర్ , 2001; మొహముద్ , 2016). ఖాళీలను చట్టాలు నింపాయి: కామన్ లాలో "the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury" ( బేకర్ v. బోల్టన్ , 1808) (మనిషి మరణాన్ని గాయంగా ఫిర్యాదు చేయలేం); తర్వాత చట్టం దీన్ని మార్చింది. భారతదేశం: బ్రిటిష్ కోర్టులతో ఇంగ్లీష్ అపకృత్యాల చట్టం వచ్చింది. భారత పరిస్థితులకు సరిపోయినంత వరకు మాత్రమే "justice, equity and good conscience" (న్యాయం, సమత, మంచి మనస్సాక్షి)గా అన్వయించబడింది. భారత చట్టాలు దానికి తోడయ్యాయి: ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం (Fatal Accidents Act), 1855 – దాని ప్రవేశిక చెబుతుంది, దానికి ముందు మరొకరి మరణానికి కారణమైన వ్యక్తిపై "no action or suit is now maintainable" (ఏ దావా వేయడానికీ వీలు లేదు); తర్వాత ఉద్యోగుల పరిహార చట్టం 1923, మోటారు వాహనాల చట్టాలు, వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టాలు (1986, 2019), ప్రజా బాధ్యత బీమా చట్టం 1991. రాజ్యం (State) బాధ్యత ఈస్ట్ ఇండియా కంపెనీ నుంచి సెక్రటరీ ఆఫ్ స్టేట్‌కు (భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం 1858, సె. 65), తర్వాత ఫెడరేషన్, ప్రావిన్సులకు (భారత ప్రభుత్వ చట్టం 1935, సె. 176), యూనియన్, రాష్ట్రాలకు ( రాజ్యాంగం, అ. 300 ) వచ్చింది. కేసులు: స్టేట్ ఆఫ్ రాజస్థాన్ v. విద్యావతి (1962), కస్తూరిలాల్ (1964). 1950 తర్వాత చట్టం అ. 372 కింద కొనసాగుతోంది; అవసరమైనచోట భారత కోర్టులు ఇంగ్లీష్ నియమాల నుంచి దూరం జరిగాయి: సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( ఎం.సి. మెహతా , 1987: "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order"), రాజ్యాంగ అపకృత్యాలు ( రుదుల్ సాహ్ , 1983; భీమ్ సింగ్ , 1985; నీలాబతి బెహెరా , 1993). ఇంగ్లాండ్‌తో పోలిస్తే భారతదేశంలో అపకృత్య వ్యాజ్యాలు తక్కువగానే ఉన్నాయి – ఖర్చు, ఆలస్యం, తక్కువ పరిహారాల కారణంగా; ఇప్పుడు చాలా పరిహార చట్టం ప్రత్యేక వేదికల ద్వారా పనిచేస్తుంది (మోటారు ప్రమాద క్లెయిమ్స్ ట్రిబ్యునల్స్, వినియోగదారుల కమిషన్లు).
te.meaning: అపకృత్యాల చట్టం అభివృద్ధి అంటే పౌర తప్పిదాల నియమాల చారిత్రక పెరుగుదల: అవి ఎక్కడి నుంచి వచ్చాయి, ఎలా అమలు చేయబడ్డాయి, కొత్త సామాజిక అవసరాలకు తగ్గట్లు ఎలా మారాయి. రిట్ (writ) – మధ్యయుగ ఇంగ్లాండ్‌లో, రాజు చాన్సరీ నుంచి వచ్చే లిఖిత ఆదేశం; దానితో రాజ కోర్టుల్లో దావా మొదలయ్యేది. ప్రతి రకం దావాకు దాని సొంత రిట్ ("form of action") కావాలి. అతిక్రమణ (writ of trespass) – వ్యక్తికి, భూమికి లేదా వస్తువులకు ప్రత్యక్ష, బలప్రయోగ గాయానికి దావా. ఆక్షన్ ఆన్ ది కేస్ (trespass on the case) – పరోక్ష లేదా పర్యవసాన గాయానికి, లేదా బలప్రయోగం లేని గాయానికి దావా; కొత్త రకాల హానికి కోర్టులు పరిహారం ఇవ్వడానికి వీలు కల్పించింది. Justice, equity and good conscience – బ్రిటిష్ ఇండియాలో భారత చట్టం గానీ, వ్యక్తిగత చట్టం గానీ వర్తించని చోట కోర్టులు కేసులు నిర్ణయించిన నియమం; తరచుగా భారత పరిస్థితులకు సరిపోయే ఇంగ్లీష్ నియమాలను స్వీకరించడం ద్వారా.
keyPoints: అతిక్రమణ = ప్రత్యక్ష, బలప్రయోగ గాయం; action on the case = పరోక్ష హాని → నిర్లక్ష్యం, ఉపద్రవం, పరువు నష్టం. Forms of action 1852–75లో రద్దు → సూత్రాలు. బేకర్ v. బోల్టన్ (1808): కామన్ లాలో మరణం దావా యోగ్యం కాదు → ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం 1846 (ఇంగ్లాండ్), 1855 (భారత్). భారత్: బ్రిటిష్ కోర్టుల ద్వారా ఇంగ్లీష్ చట్టం; justice, equity and good conscience; ఎంపిక చేసి. రాజ్యం బాధ్యత: భా.ప్ర. చట్టం 1858 సె. 65 → 1935 సె. 176 → అ. 300; పి. & ఓ. (1861); విద్యావతి (1962); కస్తూరిలాల్ (1964). భారత నవీకరణలు: సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( ఎం.సి. మెహతా , 1987); రాజ్యాంగ అపకృత్యాలు ( రుదుల్ సాహ్ , భీమ్ సింగ్ , నీలాబతి ). MV చట్టం సె. 164: తప్పు లేని ₹5 లక్షలు (మరణం) / ₹2.5 లక్షలు (తీవ్ర గాయం).

selfTest.q: అతిక్రమణ, action on the case మధ్య తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: అతిక్రమణ ప్రత్యక్ష, బలప్రయోగ గాయాన్ని కవర్ చేసింది; action on the case పరోక్ష లేదా పర్యవసాన హానిని కవర్ చేసింది. ఏ ఆధునిక అపకృత్యం ప్రధానంగా action on the case నుంచి పెరిగింది? జవాబు: నిర్లక్ష్యం (ఉపద్రవం, పరువు నష్టం, మోసం కూడా). బేకర్ v. బోల్టన్ ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? జవాబు: కామన్ లాలో సివిల్ కోర్టులో మనిషి మరణాన్ని గాయంగా ఫిర్యాదు చేయలేమని. తప్పుడు చర్య వల్ల మరణానికి కుటుంబాలు దావా వేయడాన్ని మొదట అనుమతించిన భారత చట్టం ఏది? జవాబు: ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం, 1855. బ్రిటిష్ ఇండియాలో ఇంగ్లీష్ అపకృత్యాల చట్టం ఏ సూత్రం కింద అన్వయించబడింది? జవాబు: Justice, equity and good conscience – భారత పరిస్థితులకు సరిపోయినచోట. 1858 నుంచి నేటి వరకు ప్రభుత్వంపై దావాల నిబంధనలను గుర్తించండి. జవాబు: భా.ప్ర. చట్టం 1858 సె. 65 → భా.ప్ర. చట్టం 1935 సె. 176 → రాజ్యాంగం అ. 300. విద్యావతి ఏమి తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది? జవాబు: ఉద్యోగ పరిధిలో తన ఉద్యోగుల అపకృత్యాలకు రాజ్యం ఏ ఇతర యజమాని లాగే బాధ్యురాలు (వాస్తవాలు: ప్రభుత్వ జీపు ప్రమాదం). భారతదేశంలో సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యతను సృష్టించిన కేసు ఏది? జవాబు: ఎం.సి. మెహతా v. యూనియన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా (1987). భారతదేశంలో అపకృత్య వ్యాజ్యాలు పరిమితంగా ఉండటానికి ఒక కారణం చెప్పండి. జవాబు: ఏదైనా ఒకటి: అధిక కోర్టు రుసుము, ఆలస్యం, ఖర్చు, పేదరికం, తక్కువ అవగాహన, తక్కువ పరిహారాలు, నేర పరిహారాలకు ప్రాధాన్యం. MV చట్టంలో ఇప్పుడు తప్పు లేని పరిహారం ఏ సెక్షన్‌లో ఉంది, ఎంత? జవాబు: సెక్షన్ 164: మరణానికి ₹5 లక్షలు; తీవ్ర గాయానికి ₹2.5 లక్షలు.

hi.inOneMinute: England: the law of torts grew out of the medieval writ system . The writ of trespass covered direct, forcible injuries; the action on the case covered indirect harm. Most modern torts (nuisance, defamation, negligence, deceit, conversion) grew from the action on the case. The forms of action were abolished in the 19th century, and the law became a body of principles built by judges: strict liability ( Rylands v. Fletcher , 1868), the duty of care ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932), negligent misstatement ( Hedley Byrne , 1964), remoteness ( Wagon Mound , 1961), wider vicarious liability ( Lister , 2001; Mohamud , 2016). Statutes filled gaps: at common law "the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury" ( Baker v. Bolton , 1808), which statute later changed. India: English tort law came with British courts. It was applied as "justice, equity and good conscience" , only so far as it suited Indian conditions. Indian statutes added to it: the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 , whose preamble says that before it "no action or suit is now maintainable" against a person who caused another's death; later the Employee's Compensation Act, 1923, Motor Vehicles Acts, Consumer Protection Acts (1986, 2019), and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991. State liability passed from the East India Company to the Secretary of State (GoI Act 1858, s. 65), then to the Federation and Provinces (GoI Act 1935, s. 176) and to the Union and States ( Constitution, Art. 300 ). Cases: State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati (1962), Kasturilal (1964). After 1950 the law continues under Art. 372 , and Indian courts have moved away from English rules where needed: absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta , 1987: "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order"), constitutional torts ( Rudul Sah , 1983; Bhim Singh , 1985; Nilabati Behera , 1993). Tort litigation in India has remained small in volume compared with England, because of cost, delay and low awards; much compensation law now works through special forums (Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals, Consumer Commissions).
legalProvision: Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 (Act 13 of 1855), Preamble – "WHEREAS no action or suit is now maintainable in any Court against a person who, by his wrongful act, neglect or default, may have caused the death of another person, and it is often-times right and expedient that the wrong-doer in such case should be answerable in damages for the injury so caused by him."

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A (main words) – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensued) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages ... Every such action or suit shall be for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child, if any, of the person whose death shall have been so caused".

In simple words: before 1855, in India as in England, a wrongdoer who killed a person could not be sued by the family. The 1855 Act changed this: the family can sue if the deceased could have sued had he lived.

Government of India Act, 1858, s. 65 (main words) – "The Secretary of State in Council shall and may sue and be sued as well in India as in England ... and all Persons and Bodies Politic shall and may have and take the same Suits, Remedies, and Proceedings, legal and equitable, against the Secretary of State in Council of India as they could have done against the said Company".

Government of India Act, 1935, s. 176(1) (main words) – the Federation and Provinces "may ... sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Secretary of State in Council might have sued or been sued if this Act had not been passed."

Constitution of India, Art. 300(1) (main words) – "The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may ... sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted."

In simple words: the liability of the Government in tort in India today goes back, step by step, to the liability of the East India Company. Art. 300 keeps the old position unless Parliament or a State Legislature makes a law.

Constitution of India, Art. 372(1) (main words) – "all the law in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other competent authority."
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1)–(2) (main words, as amended) – the owner or insurer "shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt"; "the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish" fault. (The earlier no-fault provision, s. 140, was omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2022.)
In simple words: modern Indian statutes have moved some tort claims (road accidents) to a no-fault basis.
hi.meaning: Development of the law of torts means the historical growth of the rules about civil wrongs: where they came from, how they were enforced, and how they changed to meet new social needs. Writ – in medieval England, a written order from the King's Chancery that started an action in the royal courts. Each kind of claim needed its own writ (a "form of action"). Trespass (writ of trespass) – an action for direct and forcible injury to person, land or goods. Action on the case (trespass on the case) – an action for injury that was indirect or consequential, or not forcible; it allowed the courts to give remedies for new kinds of harm. Justice, equity and good conscience – the rule under which courts in British India decided cases where no Indian statute or personal law applied, often by borrowing English rules that suited Indian conditions.
keyPoints: Trespass = direct, forcible injury; action on the case = indirect harm → negligence, nuisance, defamation. Forms of action abolished 1852–75 → principles. Baker v. Bolton (1808): death not actionable at common law → Fatal Accidents Act 1846 (Eng.), 1855 (India). India: English law through British courts; justice, equity and good conscience; selective. State liability: GoI Act 1858 s. 65 → GoI Act 1935 s. 176 → Art. 300; P. & O. (1861); Vidyawati (1962); Kasturilal (1964). Indian innovations: absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta , 1987); constitutional torts ( Rudul Sah , Bhim Singh , Nilabati ). MV Act s. 164: no-fault ₹5 lakh (death) / ₹2.5 lakh (grievous hurt).

selfTest.q: What was the difference between trespass and action on the case?
selfTest.a: Answer: Trespass covered direct and forcible injury; action on the case covered indirect or consequential harm. Which modern tort grew mainly from the action on the case? Answer: Negligence (also nuisance, defamation, deceit). What did Baker v. Bolton decide? Answer: That at common law the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury in a civil court. Which Indian Act first allowed families to sue for death caused by wrongful act? Answer: The Fatal Accidents Act, 1855. Under what principle was English tort law applied in British India? Answer: Justice, equity and good conscience – where suitable to Indian conditions. Trace the provisions on suits against the Government from 1858 to today. Answer: GoI Act 1858 s. 65 → GoI Act 1935 s. 176 → Constitution Art. 300. What did Vidyawati hold? Answer: The State is liable for torts of its servants in the course of employment like any other employer (on the facts: a Government jeep accident). Which case created absolute liability in India? Answer: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987). Name one reason why tort litigation remained limited in India. Answer: Any one: high court fees, delay, cost, poverty and low awareness, low awards, preference for criminal remedies. Which section of the MV Act now gives no-fault compensation, and how much? Answer: Section 164: ₹5 lakh on death; ₹2.5 lakh on grievous hurt.

law-of-torts-u1-t5.subtitle: Legal damage, the two maxims, and damages: kinds, assessment and remoteness

en.inOneMinute: A tort needs a wrongful act (an act or omission that violates a legal right or breaks a legal duty) and legal damage (the violation of a legal right of the plaintiff). Two Latin words: injuria = violation of a legal right; damnum = actual loss or harm (money, comfort, health). Injuria sine damno (violation of a right without actual loss) – actionable . Ashby v. White (1703): a voter wrongly refused his vote could sue though his candidates won. Holt CJ: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it." Indian examples: Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) – ₹50,000; Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983). Damnum sine injuria (actual loss without violation of a right) – not actionable . Gloucester Grammar School case (1410): a rival school took pupils; Mogul Steamship (1891): fair trade competition; Bradford v. Pickles (1895): lawful use of one's own land even with bad motive; Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974): demolition of an illegal building. The test is injury to a legal right, not loss . Where injuria is proved without loss, the court gives at least nominal damages .
legalProvision: There is no statute that states these maxims; they come from case law. Related statutory provisions:
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 23 – "In the case of a suit for compensation for an act which does not give rise to a cause of action unless some specific injury actually results therefrom, the period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the injury results."
In simple words: s. 23 recognises that some torts need actual damage (damnum) before the cause of action arises; others (actionable per se) arise as soon as the right is violated.
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Art. 76 – slander: one year from "When the words are spoken, or, if the words are not actionable in themselves, when the special damage complained of results."
In simple words: the Act itself distinguishes words "actionable in themselves" (injuria enough) from words actionable only on "special damage" (damnum also needed).
en.meaning: Wrongful act – an act or omission that is contrary to law: it infringes a legal right of another or breaks a duty imposed by law. A merely harmful, unfair or immoral act is not "wrongful" in this sense. Legal damage – the infringement of a legal right of the plaintiff. It is "damage" in the eye of law, whether or not money is lost. Injuria – Latin for "wrong" ( in jus , contrary to right): violation of a legal right. Damnum – Latin for "loss": actual harm, usually money loss, also loss of comfort, health or service. Injuria sine damno – legal injury without actual loss. Actionable. Damnum sine injuria (also damnum absque injuria ) – actual loss without legal injury. Not actionable. Damage vs damages – "damage" is the harm suffered; "damages" is the money the court awards for it.
keyPoints: Injuria = violation of legal right; damnum = actual loss. Injuria sine damno – actionable – Ashby v. White (1703); Bhim Singh (₹50,000); Rudul Sah . Damnum sine injuria – not actionable – Gloucester Grammar School (1410); Mogul Steamship (1891); Bradford v. Pickles (1895); Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974). Holt CJ: "every Injury imports Damage". Bad motive does not make a lawful act wrongful. Injuria without loss → nominal damages at least.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Holt CJ: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it"; the House of Lords "reversed the Judgement; and gave Judgement, That the Plaintiff should recover." Why it matters: The leading authority for injuria sine damno.
Gloucester Grammar School case (1410) YB 11 Hen IV 47

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Setting up a competing school is lawful; loss from competition gives no action. Why it matters: The classic early example of damnum sine injuria.
Mogul Steamship Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. [1892] AC 25 (House of Lords, 18 Dec 1891)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Associated shipowners cut freights and offered a 5% rebate to shippers using only their ships
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Acts done "with the lawful object of protecting and extending their trade", without unlawful means, give "no cause of action". Why it matters: Loss caused by lawful trade competition is damnum sine injuria.
Mayor of Bradford v. Pickles [1895] AC 587 (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A landowner drained percolating water under his land, reducing the Corporation's water supply
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A lawful use of property does not become unlawful because of a malicious motive. Why it matters: Damnum sine injuria; motive irrelevant.
Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal AIR 1975 All 132

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "There is no right to enjoy property not legally obtained or constructed"; no injuria, so no compensation. Why it matters: Indian example of damnum sine injuria.
Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) 4 SCC 677; AIR 1986 SC 494

caseLaws.name: Facts: An MLA was arrested on his way to the Assembly and not produced before a magistrate in time
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Gross violation of Arts. 21 and 22(2); State directed to pay ₹50,000. Why it matters: Indian example of injuria being compensated even without proof of money loss.

selfTest.q: What do "injuria" and "damnum" mean?
selfTest.a: Answer: Injuria – violation of a legal right; damnum – actual loss or harm. Is injuria sine damno actionable? Give a case. Answer: Yes – Ashby v. White (1703). Is damnum sine injuria actionable? Give a case. Answer: No – Gloucester Grammar School case (1410) or Bradford v. Pickles (1895). What happened to the King's Bench decision in Ashby v. White ? Answer: The House of Lords reversed it and gave judgment for the plaintiff. Why did the plaintiffs fail in Mogul Steamship ? Answer: The defendants used lawful means of competition to protect and extend their trade. Can a bad motive turn a lawful act into a tort? Answer: No, in general ( Bradford v. Pickles ); except torts where malice is an element. Give an Indian case of damnum sine injuria. Answer: Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974) – demolition of an illegally built structure. What damages are given for injuria without loss? Answer: At least nominal damages. Distinguish damage from damages. Answer: Damage is the harm; damages is the money the court awards. How does the Limitation Act recognise the difference between injuria alone and injuria with damage? Answer: s. 23 (time runs from when specific injury results) and Art. 76 (slander: words "not actionable in themselves" – from when special damage results).

Damage Damages Damage = harm; damages = money awarded by court.
Legal damage Actual damage Legal damage = violation of right; actual damage = loss.

te.inOneMinute: అపకృత్యానికి తప్పుడు చర్య (చట్టబద్ధ హక్కును ఉల్లంఘించే లేదా చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యతను భంగపరిచే చర్య లేదా లోపం), చట్టపరమైన నష్టం (వాది చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన) కావాలి. రెండు లాటిన్ పదాలు: ఇంజూరియా (injuria) = చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన; డామ్నమ్ (damnum) = వాస్తవ నష్టం లేదా హాని (డబ్బు, సౌకర్యం, ఆరోగ్యం). ఇంజూరియా సైన్ డామ్నో (injuria sine damno) (వాస్తవ నష్టం లేకుండా హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన) – దావా యోగ్యం . ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ (1703): అక్రమంగా ఓటు నిరాకరించబడిన ఓటరు, అతని అభ్యర్థులు గెలిచినా దావా వేయగలిగాడు. హోల్ట్ CJ: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it." భారతీయ ఉదాహరణలు: భీమ్ సింగ్ v. స్టేట్ ఆఫ్ J&K (1985) – ₹50,000; రుదుల్ సాహ్ v. స్టేట్ ఆఫ్ బిహార్ (1983). డామ్నమ్ సైన్ ఇంజూరియా (damnum sine injuria) (హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన లేకుండా వాస్తవ నష్టం) – దావా యోగ్యం కాదు . గ్లౌసెస్టర్ గ్రామర్ స్కూల్ కేసు (1410): ప్రత్యర్థి పాఠశాల విద్యార్థులను తీసుకుంది; మొగల్ స్టీమ్‌షిప్ (1891): న్యాయమైన వ్యాపార పోటీ; బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ (1895): చెడు ఉద్దేశంతోనైనా తన భూమిని చట్టబద్ధంగా వాడుకోవడం; టౌన్ ఏరియా కమిటీ v. ప్రభు దయాళ్ (1974): అక్రమ భవనం కూల్చివేత. పరీక్ష నష్టం కాదు, చట్టబద్ధ హక్కుకు గాయం . నష్టం లేకుండా injuria నిరూపితమైతే కోర్టు కనీసం నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం (nominal damages) ఇస్తుంది.
te.meaning: తప్పుడు చర్య (wrongful act) – చట్టానికి విరుద్ధమైన చర్య లేదా లోపం: మరొకరి చట్టబద్ధ హక్కును ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది లేదా చట్టం విధించిన బాధ్యతను భంగపరుస్తుంది. కేవలం హానికరమైన, అన్యాయమైన లేదా అనైతికమైన చర్య ఈ అర్థంలో "తప్పుడు" కాదు. చట్టపరమైన నష్టం (legal damage) – వాది చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన. డబ్బు పోయినా పోకపోయినా అది చట్టం దృష్టిలో "నష్టం". ఇంజూరియా (injuria) – లాటిన్‌లో "తప్పు" ( in jus , హక్కుకు విరుద్ధం): చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన. డామ్నమ్ (damnum) – లాటిన్‌లో "నష్టం": వాస్తవ హాని, సాధారణంగా డబ్బు నష్టం; సౌకర్యం, ఆరోగ్యం లేదా సేవ నష్టం కూడా. ఇంజూరియా సైన్ డామ్నో – వాస్తవ నష్టం లేని చట్టపరమైన గాయం. దావా యోగ్యం. డామ్నమ్ సైన్ ఇంజూరియా ( damnum absque injuria అని కూడా) – చట్టపరమైన గాయం లేని వాస్తవ నష్టం. దావా యోగ్యం కాదు. Damage vs damages – "damage" జరిగిన హాని; "damages" దానికి కోర్టు ఇచ్చే డబ్బు (నష్టపరిహారం).
keyPoints: Injuria = చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన; damnum = వాస్తవ నష్టం. Injuria sine damno – దావా యోగ్యం – ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ (1703); భీమ్ సింగ్ (₹50,000); రుదుల్ సాహ్ . Damnum sine injuria – దావా యోగ్యం కాదు – గ్లౌసెస్టర్ గ్రామర్ స్కూల్ (1410); మొగల్ స్టీమ్‌షిప్ (1891); బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ (1895); టౌన్ ఏరియా కమిటీ v. ప్రభు దయాళ్ (1974). హోల్ట్ CJ: "every Injury imports Damage". చెడు ఉద్దేశం చట్టబద్ధ చర్యను తప్పుడుగా చేయదు. నష్టం లేని injuria → కనీసం నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం.

selfTest.q: "Injuria", "damnum" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: Injuria – చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన; damnum – వాస్తవ నష్టం లేదా హాని. Injuria sine damno దావా యోగ్యమా? ఒక కేసు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: అవును – ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ (1703). Damnum sine injuria దావా యోగ్యమా? ఒక కేసు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: కాదు – గ్లౌసెస్టర్ గ్రామర్ స్కూల్ కేసు (1410) లేదా బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ (1895). ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ లో కింగ్స్ బెంచ్ తీర్పుకు ఏమైంది? జవాబు: హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్ దాన్ని తిరగరాసి వాదికి అనుకూలంగా తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది. మొగల్ స్టీమ్‌షిప్ లో వాదులు ఎందుకు విఫలమయ్యారు? జవాబు: ప్రతివాదులు తమ వ్యాపారాన్ని రక్షించి విస్తరించుకోవడానికి చట్టబద్ధ పోటీ మార్గాలు వాడారు. చెడు ఉద్దేశం చట్టబద్ధ చర్యను అపకృత్యంగా మార్చగలదా? జవాబు: సాధారణంగా కాదు ( బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ ); దురుద్దేశం అంశంగా ఉన్న అపకృత్యాలు తప్ప. Damnum sine injuriaకు ఒక భారతీయ కేసు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: టౌన్ ఏరియా కమిటీ v. ప్రభు దయాళ్ (1974) – అక్రమంగా కట్టిన నిర్మాణం కూల్చివేత. నష్టం లేని injuriaకు ఏ నష్టపరిహారం ఇస్తారు? జవాబు: కనీసం నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం. Damage, damages మధ్య తేడా చెప్పండి. జవాబు: Damage జరిగిన హాని; damages కోర్టు ఇచ్చే డబ్బు. Injuria మాత్రమే, injuria + నష్టం మధ్య తేడాను పరిమితి చట్టం ఎలా గుర్తిస్తుంది? జవాబు: సె. 23 (నిర్దిష్ట గాయం జరిగినప్పటి నుంచి కాలం), అ. 76 (slander: "not actionable in themselves" మాటలు – ప్రత్యేక నష్టం జరిగినప్పటి నుంచి).

hi.inOneMinute: A tort needs a wrongful act (an act or omission that violates a legal right or breaks a legal duty) and legal damage (the violation of a legal right of the plaintiff). Two Latin words: injuria = violation of a legal right; damnum = actual loss or harm (money, comfort, health). Injuria sine damno (violation of a right without actual loss) – actionable . Ashby v. White (1703): a voter wrongly refused his vote could sue though his candidates won. Holt CJ: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it." Indian examples: Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) – ₹50,000; Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983). Damnum sine injuria (actual loss without violation of a right) – not actionable . Gloucester Grammar School case (1410): a rival school took pupils; Mogul Steamship (1891): fair trade competition; Bradford v. Pickles (1895): lawful use of one's own land even with bad motive; Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974): demolition of an illegal building. The test is injury to a legal right, not loss . Where injuria is proved without loss, the court gives at least nominal damages .
legalProvision: There is no statute that states these maxims; they come from case law. Related statutory provisions:
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 23 – "In the case of a suit for compensation for an act which does not give rise to a cause of action unless some specific injury actually results therefrom, the period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the injury results."
In simple words: s. 23 recognises that some torts need actual damage (damnum) before the cause of action arises; others (actionable per se) arise as soon as the right is violated.
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Art. 76 – slander: one year from "When the words are spoken, or, if the words are not actionable in themselves, when the special damage complained of results."
In simple words: the Act itself distinguishes words "actionable in themselves" (injuria enough) from words actionable only on "special damage" (damnum also needed).
hi.meaning: Wrongful act – an act or omission that is contrary to law: it infringes a legal right of another or breaks a duty imposed by law. A merely harmful, unfair or immoral act is not "wrongful" in this sense. Legal damage – the infringement of a legal right of the plaintiff. It is "damage" in the eye of law, whether or not money is lost. Injuria – Latin for "wrong" ( in jus , contrary to right): violation of a legal right. Damnum – Latin for "loss": actual harm, usually money loss, also loss of comfort, health or service. Injuria sine damno – legal injury without actual loss. Actionable. Damnum sine injuria (also damnum absque injuria ) – actual loss without legal injury. Not actionable. Damage vs damages – "damage" is the harm suffered; "damages" is the money the court awards for it.
keyPoints: Injuria = violation of legal right; damnum = actual loss. Injuria sine damno – actionable – Ashby v. White (1703); Bhim Singh (₹50,000); Rudul Sah . Damnum sine injuria – not actionable – Gloucester Grammar School (1410); Mogul Steamship (1891); Bradford v. Pickles (1895); Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974). Holt CJ: "every Injury imports Damage". Bad motive does not make a lawful act wrongful. Injuria without loss → nominal damages at least.

selfTest.q: What do "injuria" and "damnum" mean?
selfTest.a: Answer: Injuria – violation of a legal right; damnum – actual loss or harm. Is injuria sine damno actionable? Give a case. Answer: Yes – Ashby v. White (1703). Is damnum sine injuria actionable? Give a case. Answer: No – Gloucester Grammar School case (1410) or Bradford v. Pickles (1895). What happened to the King's Bench decision in Ashby v. White ? Answer: The House of Lords reversed it and gave judgment for the plaintiff. Why did the plaintiffs fail in Mogul Steamship ? Answer: The defendants used lawful means of competition to protect and extend their trade. Can a bad motive turn a lawful act into a tort? Answer: No, in general ( Bradford v. Pickles ); except torts where malice is an element. Give an Indian case of damnum sine injuria. Answer: Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974) – demolition of an illegally built structure. What damages are given for injuria without loss? Answer: At least nominal damages. Distinguish damage from damages. Answer: Damage is the harm; damages is the money the court awards. How does the Limitation Act recognise the difference between injuria alone and injuria with damage? Answer: s. 23 (time runs from when specific injury results) and Art. 76 (slander: words "not actionable in themselves" – from when special damage results).

law-of-torts-u1-t1.subtitle: Meaning, features, objects and scope of the law of torts

en.inOneMinute: A tort is a civil wrong that is not only a breach of contract or a breach of trust. The Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) defines it in exactly this way. The wrongdoer is called the tortfeasor . The injured person sues him in a civil court (CPC, s. 9). The main remedy is money compensation that the court fixes after the harm: unliquidated damages . The court can also grant an injunction . The duty broken in a tort is fixed by law itself , not by agreement. It is owed to people in general (for example, everyone must not hit, defame or carelessly injure anyone). The law of torts in India is mostly judge-made . It came from English common law, was applied by Indian courts as "justice, equity and good conscience", and continues as "law in force" under Art. 372 of the Constitution. Statutes (Fatal Accidents Act 1855, Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Consumer Protection Act 2019, Limitation Act 1963) add to it. It is a growing law: courts keep recognising new wrongs and new rules, for example the duty of care in Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932), absolute liability in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), and compensation for violation of Art. 21 in Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983). Its aims are to compensate the injured, protect rights ( Ashby v. White : "every Injury imports Damage"), deter careless or wrongful conduct and restore the injured person, as far as money can, to the position before the wrong.
legalProvision: There is no single "Torts Act" in India. The nature of tort law is seen from the following provisions.
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

In simple words: a tort is a wrong for which a civil action lies. If the wrong is only a breach of contract or only a breach of trust, it is not a tort. If the same act is also a wrong under the general law (for example a doctor who is paid under a contract but injures the patient by carelessness), it can be a tort as well.
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Part VII – "Suits relating to tort" (Arts. 72–91) – fixes time limits for tort suits. Examples:

Art. 73: false imprisonment – one year – "When the imprisonment ends." Art. 74: malicious prosecution – one year – "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated." Art. 75: libel – one year – "When the libel is published." Art. 76: slander – one year – "When the words are spoken, or, if the words are not actionable in themselves, when the special damage complained of results." Art. 82: suit by representatives under the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 – two years – "The date of the death of the person killed." Art. 87: trespass upon immovable property – three years – "The date of the trespass." Art. 91: wrongful taking, detaining or injuring of movable property – three years. Art. 113 (residuary): "Any suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in this Schedule" – three years – "When the right to sue accrues." (A suit for negligence causing personal injury, which has no special Article, falls here.)

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 22 – "In the case of a continuing breach of contract or in the case of a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues."

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 9 – "The Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred."

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 19 – "Where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property, if the wrong was done within the local limits of the jurisdiction of one Court and the defendant resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of another Court, the suit may be instituted at the option of the plaintiff in either of the said Courts." Illustration (a): "A, residing in Delhi, beats B in Calcutta. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi."

Constitution of India, Art. 372(1) (main words) – "all the law in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other competent authority."

In simple words: tort claims are civil suits, tried by ordinary civil courts, filed where the wrong happened or where the defendant lives, within the time the Limitation Act allows. The rules of tort that existed before 1950 continue under Art. 372 until a legislature changes them.
en.meaning:
Word origin. "Tort" comes from the Latin tortum , meaning "twisted" or "crooked". In French, tort simply means "wrong". In law it means conduct that is "twisted" away from what is lawful. Statutory meaning (India). "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, s. 2(m)). Salmond's definition (standard text). A tort is a civil wrong for which the remedy is a common-law action for unliquidated damages , and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust or other merely equitable obligation. Winfield's definition (standard text). Tortious liability arises from the breach of a duty primarily fixed by law; this duty is towards persons generally and its breach is redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. Law of torts is the branch of civil law that tells us (a) which interests of a person the law protects (body, liberty, reputation, property, business and so on), (b) which acts or omissions infringe those interests, (c) who is liable, and (d) what remedies the injured person gets.

(The full study of these definitions, with their elements, is in the topics Definition of Tort and Elements of Tort .)
keyPoints: Tort = civil wrong, not exclusively breach of contract or trust (Limitation Act s. 2(m)). Origin: Latin tortum (twisted); French tort (wrong). Duty fixed by law; owed to persons generally; remedy mainly unliquidated damages. Ashby v. White : "every Injury imports Damage" – injuria sine damno actionable. Bradford v. Pickles : lawful act + bad motive = no tort; damnum sine injuria. Winfield: law of tort (general principle); Salmond: law of torts (pigeon-hole). India: judge-made; Art. 372 keeps pre-1950 law; statutes add; M.C. Mehta : "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order." Limitation: Arts. 72–91; Art. 113 residuary (3 years); s. 22 continuing tort. CPC s. 19: suit for wrong to person or movables – where wrong done or where defendant resides.

caseLaws.facts: Donoghue drank ginger-beer, bought for her by a friend, from an opaque bottle that contained the decomposed remains of a snail; she alleged shock and gastro-enteritis. She had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle: Lord Atkin: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour." Why it matters: Shows that tort duties exist without contract and that courts can state new general principles – the law of torts grows.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas escaped from a unit of Shriram Foods and Fertilizer Industries in Delhi on 4 and 6
caseLaws.facts: Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry "owes an absolute and nondelegable duty to the community"; it is "absolutely liable" and cannot plead reasonable care. The Court said: "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order." Why it matters: Shows that Indian tort law is not frozen in English rules; Indian courts develop it to meet Indian conditions.
Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) 4 SCC 141; AIR 1983 SC 1086

caseLaws.name: Facts: Rudul Sah remained in jail for over 14 years after his acquittal; he filed a habeas corpus pe
caseLaws.facts: 32 and asked for compensation. Principle: Art. 21 would be "denuded of its significant content" if the Court could only order release; the State must "repair the damage done by its officers"; the State was ordered to pay ₹30,000 more, in addition to ₹5,000 already paid, without prejudice to a regular suit. Why it matters: Shows the extension of the tort idea of compensation into constitutional law in India.

selfTest.q: Give the statutory definition of tort in India. Answer: Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m): "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust". What does the word "tort" literally mean?
selfTest.a: Answer: From Latin tortum , twisted; French tort , wrong. What are unliquidated damages? Answer: Compensation whose amount the court fixes after the harm, not fixed in advance by the parties. To whom is a tort duty owed? Answer: To persons generally – everyone who may be affected – not only to a contracting party. State the principle of Ashby v. White . Answer: Violation of a legal right is actionable even without money loss; "every Injury imports Damage". Why did the Corporation lose in Bradford v. Pickles ? Answer: Pickles' act was lawful; a bad motive cannot make a lawful act unlawful, so there was loss without legal injury. Explain the pigeon-hole theory. Answer: Salmond's view that there is no general principle of liability, only specific named torts; a claim must fit one of them. How does the law of torts apply in India without a code? Answer: As common law applied on justice, equity and good conscience, continued as "law in force" by Art. 372, and supplemented by statutes. What is the limitation period for a suit for libel and when does it start? Answer: One year, from when the libel is published (Art. 75). What does s. 22 of the Limitation Act say about a continuing tort? Answer: A fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment during which the tort continues.

Tort Breach of contract Contract duty is created by agreement and owed to the other party; tort duty is fixed by law and owed to persons generally.
Unliquidated damages Liquidated damages Unliquidated: fixed by the court after the harm. Liquidated: fixed in advance by the parties.
Injuria sine damno Damnum sine injuria First: legal right violated without loss – actionable. Second: loss without violation of a legal right – not actionable.
Law of tort (Winfield) Law of torts (Salmond) Winfield: general principle of liability; Salmond: a closed list of specific torts.
Tortfeasor Plaintiff Tortfeasor is the wrongdoer (defendant); plaintiff is the injured person who sues.
Constitutional tort (compensation under Art. 32/226) Ordinary tort suit First is a public-law remedy against the State for violation of fundamental rights; second is a private civil suit.

te.inOneMinute: అపకృత్యం (టార్ట్) అంటే ఒక పౌర తప్పిదం (civil wrong) ; అది కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన గానీ, కేవలం ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన గానీ కాదు. పరిమితి చట్టం (Limitation Act), 1963, సె. 2(m) సరిగ్గా ఇలాగే నిర్వచిస్తుంది. తప్పు చేసినవాడిని అపకృత్యకారి (tortfeasor) అంటారు. నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తి అతనిపై సివిల్ కోర్టులో దావా వేస్తాడు (CPC, సె. 9). ప్రధాన పరిహారం – నష్టం జరిగిన తర్వాత కోర్టు నిర్ణయించే డబ్బు పరిహారం: అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం (unliquidated damages) . కోర్టు నిషేధాజ్ఞ (injunction) కూడా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. అపకృత్యంలో ఉల్లంఘించిన బాధ్యత (duty) చట్టమే నిర్ణయించినది ; ఒప్పందం ద్వారా వచ్చింది కాదు. అది సాధారణంగా ప్రజలందరి పట్ల ఉంటుంది (ఉదా: ఎవరినీ కొట్టకూడదు, ఎవరి పరువూ తీయకూడదు, నిర్లక్ష్యంతో ఎవరికీ హాని చేయకూడదు). భారతదేశంలో అపకృత్యాల చట్టం ఎక్కువగా న్యాయమూర్తులు రూపొందించినది (judge-made) . అది ఇంగ్లీష్ కామన్ లా నుంచి వచ్చింది; భారత కోర్టులు దాన్ని "justice, equity and good conscience" (న్యాయం, సమత, మంచి మనస్సాక్షి) సూత్రంగా అన్వయించాయి; రాజ్యాంగంలోని అ. 372 కింద "law in force" (అమలులో ఉన్న చట్టం)గా కొనసాగుతోంది. చట్టాలు (ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం 1855, మోటారు వాహనాల చట్టం 1988, వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం 2019, పరిమితి చట్టం 1963) దానికి తోడవుతాయి. ఇది పెరుగుతున్న (growing) చట్టం: కోర్టులు కొత్త తప్పిదాలను, కొత్త నియమాలను గుర్తిస్తూ ఉంటాయి – ఉదా: డోనోఘ్యూ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ (1932)లో జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత (duty of care); ఎం.సి. మెహతా v. యూనియన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా (1987)లో సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత (absolute liability); రుదుల్ సాహ్ v. స్టేట్ ఆఫ్ బిహార్ (1983)లో అ. 21 ఉల్లంఘనకు పరిహారం. దీని లక్ష్యాలు: నష్టపోయినవారికి పరిహారం ఇవ్వడం, హక్కులను రక్షించడం ( ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ : "every Injury imports Damage" – అంటే ప్రతి హక్కు ఉల్లంఘనలోనూ నష్టం ఇమిడి ఉంటుంది), నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా తప్పుడు ప్రవర్తనను నిరోధించడం ( deterrence ) , డబ్బు ద్వారా సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు నష్టపోయినవారిని తప్పిదానికి ముందున్న స్థితికి తిరిగి తేవడం .
te.meaning:
పద మూలం. "Tort" అనే పదం లాటిన్ tortum నుంచి వచ్చింది; దాని అర్థం "మెలితిప్పిన" లేదా "వంకర". ఫ్రెంచ్‌లో tort అంటే "తప్పు". చట్టంలో దాని అర్థం – చట్టబద్ధమైన మార్గం నుంచి "వంకరగా" తప్పిన ప్రవర్తన. చట్టబద్ధ అర్థం (భారతదేశం). "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (పరిమితి చట్టం, సె. 2(m)) – కేవలం ఒప్పంద లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. సాల్మండ్ నిర్వచనం (ప్రామాణిక గ్రంథం). అపకృత్యం అంటే ఒక పౌర తప్పిదం; దానికి పరిహారం అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం కోసం కామన్ లా దావా; అది కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన గానీ, ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన గానీ, ఇతర కేవల సమత (equitable) బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన గానీ కాదు. విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ నిర్వచనం (ప్రామాణిక గ్రంథం). చట్టం ప్రధానంగా నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల అపకృత్య బాధ్యత పుడుతుంది; ఈ బాధ్యత సాధారణంగా ప్రజలందరి పట్ల ఉంటుంది; దాని ఉల్లంఘనకు అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహార దావా ద్వారా పరిష్కారం లభిస్తుంది. అపకృత్యాల చట్టం అనేది సివిల్ చట్టంలోని ఒక శాఖ. అది (a) వ్యక్తి యొక్క ఏ ప్రయోజనాలను చట్టం రక్షిస్తుంది (శరీరం, స్వేచ్ఛ, పరువు, ఆస్తి, వ్యాపారం మొదలైనవి), (b) ఏ చర్యలు లేదా లోపాలు వాటిని ఉల్లంఘిస్తాయి, (c) ఎవరు బాధ్యులు, (d) నష్టపోయినవారికి ఏ పరిహారాలు లభిస్తాయి – అనేవి చెబుతుంది.

(ఈ నిర్వచనాల పూర్తి అధ్యయనం, వాటి అంశాలతో సహా, ఈ అంశాల్లో ఉంది: Definition of Tort , Elements of Tort .)
keyPoints: అపకృత్యం = కేవలం ఒప్పంద లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాని పౌర తప్పిదం (పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 2(m)). మూలం: లాటిన్ tortum (మెలితిప్పిన); ఫ్రెంచ్ tort (తప్పు). చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత; ప్రజలందరి పట్ల; పరిహారం ప్రధానంగా అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం. ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ : "every Injury imports Damage" – injuria sine damno దావా యోగ్యం. బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ : చట్టబద్ధ చర్య + చెడు ఉద్దేశం = అపకృత్యం కాదు; damnum sine injuria. విన్‌ఫీల్డ్: law of tort (సాధారణ సూత్రం); సాల్మండ్: law of torts (గూళ్లు). భారతదేశం: న్యాయమూర్తుల రూపకల్పన; అ. 372 1950కి ముందు చట్టాన్ని కొనసాగిస్తుంది; చట్టాలు తోడవుతాయి; ఎం.సి. మెహతా : "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order." కాలపరిమితి: అ. 72–91; అ. 113 అవశేషం (3 సంవత్సరాలు); సె. 22 కొనసాగే అపకృత్యం. CPC సె. 19: వ్యక్తికి లేదా చరాస్తికి తప్పిదం – తప్పు జరిగిన చోట లేదా ప్రతివాది నివసించే చోట దావా.

selfTest.q: భారతదేశంలో అపకృత్యానికి చట్టబద్ధ నిర్వచనం ఇవ్వండి. జవాబు: పరిమితి చట్టం, 1963, సె. 2(m): "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust". "Tort" పదానికి అక్షరార్థం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: లాటిన్ tortum – మెలితిప్పిన; ఫ్రెంచ్ tort – తప్పు. అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: పక్షాలు ముందుగా నిర్ణయించకుండా, హాని తర్వాత కోర్టు మొత్తం నిర్ణయించే పరిహారం. అపకృత్య బాధ్యత ఎవరి పట్ల ఉంటుంది? జవాబు: ప్రజలందరి పట్ల – ప్రభావితమయ్యే ప్రతి ఒక్కరి పట్ల – ఒప్పంద పక్షం పట్ల మాత్రమే కాదు. ఆష్బీ v. వైట్ సూత్రం చెప్పండి. జవాబు: డబ్బు నష్టం లేకపోయినా చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘనకు దావా వేయవచ్చు; "every Injury imports Damage". బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ లో కార్పొరేషన్ ఎందుకు ఓడిపోయింది? జవాబు: పికిల్స్ చర్య చట్టబద్ధమైనది; చెడు ఉద్దేశం చట్టబద్ధ చర్యను చట్టవిరుద్ధం చేయదు; కాబట్టి చట్టపరమైన గాయం లేని నష్టం. పావురాల గూళ్ల సిద్ధాంతాన్ని వివరించండి. జవాబు: బాధ్యతకు సాధారణ సూత్రం లేదు, నిర్దిష్ట పేరున్న అపకృత్యాలు మాత్రమే ఉన్నాయి; దావా వాటిలో ఒకదానిలో సరిపోవాలి – అని సాల్మండ్ అభిప్రాయం. కోడ్ లేకుండా భారతదేశంలో అపకృత్యాల చట్టం ఎలా వర్తిస్తుంది? జవాబు: justice, equity and good conscience ఆధారంగా అన్వయించిన కామన్ లాగా, అ. 372 ద్వారా "law in force"గా కొనసాగి, చట్టాల తోడుతో. libel దావాకు కాలపరిమితి ఎంత, ఎప్పటి నుంచి మొదలవుతుంది? జవాబు: ఒక సంవత్సరం, libel ప్రచురించినప్పటి నుంచి (అ. 75). కొనసాగే అపకృత్యం గురించి పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 22 ఏమి చెబుతుంది? జవాబు: అపకృత్యం కొనసాగుతున్న ప్రతి క్షణం కొత్త పరిమితి కాలం మొదలవుతుంది.

లక్షణం అర్థం ఆధారం
పౌర తప్పిదం సివిల్ దావా ద్వారా పరిహారం; శిక్ష కాదు పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 2(m); CPC సె. 9
కేవలం ఒప్పంద/ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాదు అదే చర్య ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన కూడా కావచ్చు పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 2(m)
చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత ఒప్పందం ద్వారా సృష్టించినది కాదు విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ నిర్వచనం
ప్రజలందరి పట్ల బాధ్యత ప్రభావితమయ్యే అందరి పట్ల డోనోఘ్యూ v. స్టీవెన్సన్
అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం హాని తర్వాత కోర్టు మొత్తం నిర్ణయిస్తుంది సాల్మండ్, విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ నిర్వచనాలు

hi.inOneMinute: A tort is a civil wrong that is not only a breach of contract or a breach of trust. The Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) defines it in exactly this way. The wrongdoer is called the tortfeasor . The injured person sues him in a civil court (CPC, s. 9). The main remedy is money compensation that the court fixes after the harm: unliquidated damages . The court can also grant an injunction . The duty broken in a tort is fixed by law itself , not by agreement. It is owed to people in general (for example, everyone must not hit, defame or carelessly injure anyone). The law of torts in India is mostly judge-made . It came from English common law, was applied by Indian courts as "justice, equity and good conscience", and continues as "law in force" under Art. 372 of the Constitution. Statutes (Fatal Accidents Act 1855, Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Consumer Protection Act 2019, Limitation Act 1963) add to it. It is a growing law: courts keep recognising new wrongs and new rules, for example the duty of care in Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932), absolute liability in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), and compensation for violation of Art. 21 in Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983). Its aims are to compensate the injured, protect rights ( Ashby v. White : "every Injury imports Damage"), deter careless or wrongful conduct and restore the injured person, as far as money can, to the position before the wrong.
legalProvision: There is no single "Torts Act" in India. The nature of tort law is seen from the following provisions.
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

In simple words: a tort is a wrong for which a civil action lies. If the wrong is only a breach of contract or only a breach of trust, it is not a tort. If the same act is also a wrong under the general law (for example a doctor who is paid under a contract but injures the patient by carelessness), it can be a tort as well.
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Part VII – "Suits relating to tort" (Arts. 72–91) – fixes time limits for tort suits. Examples:

Art. 73: false imprisonment – one year – "When the imprisonment ends." Art. 74: malicious prosecution – one year – "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated." Art. 75: libel – one year – "When the libel is published." Art. 76: slander – one year – "When the words are spoken, or, if the words are not actionable in themselves, when the special damage complained of results." Art. 82: suit by representatives under the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 – two years – "The date of the death of the person killed." Art. 87: trespass upon immovable property – three years – "The date of the trespass." Art. 91: wrongful taking, detaining or injuring of movable property – three years. Art. 113 (residuary): "Any suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in this Schedule" – three years – "When the right to sue accrues." (A suit for negligence causing personal injury, which has no special Article, falls here.)

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 22 – "In the case of a continuing breach of contract or in the case of a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues."

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 9 – "The Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred."

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 19 – "Where a suit is for compensation for wrong done to the person or to movable property, if the wrong was done within the local limits of the jurisdiction of one Court and the defendant resides, or carries on business, or personally works for gain, within the local limits of the jurisdiction of another Court, the suit may be instituted at the option of the plaintiff in either of the said Courts." Illustration (a): "A, residing in Delhi, beats B in Calcutta. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi."

Constitution of India, Art. 372(1) (main words) – "all the law in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended by a competent Legislature or other competent authority."

In simple words: tort claims are civil suits, tried by ordinary civil courts, filed where the wrong happened or where the defendant lives, within the time the Limitation Act allows. The rules of tort that existed before 1950 continue under Art. 372 until a legislature changes them.
hi.meaning: Word origin. "Tort" comes from the Latin tortum , meaning "twisted" or "crooked". In French, tort simply means "wrong". In law it means conduct that is "twisted" away from what is lawful. Statutory meaning (India). "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, s. 2(m)). Salmond's definition (standard text). A tort is a civil wrong for which the remedy is a common-law action for unliquidated damages , and which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust or other merely equitable obligation. Winfield's definition (standard text). Tortious liability arises from the breach of a duty primarily fixed by law; this duty is towards persons generally and its breach is redressible by an action for unliquidated damages. Law of torts is the branch of civil law that tells us (a) which interests of a person the law protects (body, liberty, reputation, property, business and so on), (b) which acts or omissions infringe those interests, (c) who is liable, and (d) what remedies the injured person gets. (The full study of these definitions, with their elements, is in the topics Definition of Tort and Elements of Tort .)
keyPoints: Tort = civil wrong, not exclusively breach of contract or trust (Limitation Act s. 2(m)). Origin: Latin tortum (twisted); French tort (wrong). Duty fixed by law; owed to persons generally; remedy mainly unliquidated damages. Ashby v. White : "every Injury imports Damage" – injuria sine damno actionable. Bradford v. Pickles : lawful act + bad motive = no tort; damnum sine injuria. Winfield: law of tort (general principle); Salmond: law of torts (pigeon-hole). India: judge-made; Art. 372 keeps pre-1950 law; statutes add; M.C. Mehta : "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order." Limitation: Arts. 72–91; Art. 113 residuary (3 years); s. 22 continuing tort. CPC s. 19: suit for wrong to person or movables – where wrong done or where defendant resides.

Principle: Art. 21 would be "denuded of its significant content" if the Court could only order release; the State must "repair the damage done by its officers"; the State was ordered to pay ₹30,000 more, in addition to ₹5,000 already paid, without prejudice to a regular suit. Why it matters: Shows the extension of the tort idea of compensation into constitutional law in India.

selfTest.q: Give the statutory definition of tort in India. Answer: Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m): "a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust". What does the word "tort" literally mean?
selfTest.a: Answer: From Latin tortum , twisted; French tort , wrong. What are unliquidated damages? Answer: Compensation whose amount the court fixes after the harm, not fixed in advance by the parties. To whom is a tort duty owed? Answer: To persons generally – everyone who may be affected – not only to a contracting party. State the principle of Ashby v. White . Answer: Violation of a legal right is actionable even without money loss; "every Injury imports Damage". Why did the Corporation lose in Bradford v. Pickles ? Answer: Pickles' act was lawful; a bad motive cannot make a lawful act unlawful, so there was loss without legal injury. Explain the pigeon-hole theory. Answer: Salmond's view that there is no general principle of liability, only specific named torts; a claim must fit one of them. How does the law of torts apply in India without a code? Answer: As common law applied on justice, equity and good conscience, continued as "law in force" by Art. 372, and supplemented by statutes. What is the limitation period for a suit for libel and when does it start? Answer: One year, from when the libel is published (Art. 75). What does s. 22 of the Limitation Act say about a continuing tort? Answer: A fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment during which the tort continues.

law-of-torts-u1-t7.subtitle: The conditions that make a person liable in tort, and the bases of liability: intention, negligence and no fault

en.inOneMinute: A person is liable in tort when: (1) he does a wrongful act or omission – a breach of a duty fixed by law; (2) it violates a legal right of the plaintiff ( injuria ); (3) where the tort needs it, actual damage results; (4) the act caused the damage and the damage is not too remote; and (5) no defence applies. There are two broad bases of liability : fault (the defendant acted intentionally or negligently) and no-fault (liability imposed even though the defendant was careful – strict liability under Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), absolute liability under M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1986), and statutory no-fault liability such as Motor Vehicles Act s. 164). The mental element varies by tort: intention (assault, battery, deceit), negligence, or none (strict and absolute liability). Motive is generally irrelevant: a lawful act does not become a tort because of a bad motive, and an unlawful act is not excused by a good one ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895). Remoteness: the defendant is liable only for damage "of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen" ( The Wagon Mound , 1961), which replaced the older "direct consequences" test of Re Polemis (1921). If the kind of harm was foreseeable, the defendant is liable even if its extent or manner was not ( Hughes v. Lord Advocate , 1963). Liability may also be for another's tort (vicarious liability), shared (joint tortfeasors), or of the State (Art. 300) – each is a separate syllabus topic.
legalProvision: There is no statute that sets out the general principles of tortious liability; they come from judgments. Statutes recognise them in parts:
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 23 – "In the case of a suit for compensation for an act which does not give rise to a cause of action unless some specific injury actually results therefrom, the period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the injury results."
In simple words: some torts are complete as soon as the right is violated; others need actual damage (s. 23). The law of liability must therefore ask, for each tort, whether damage is an ingredient.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1) – "Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or instrument having the force of law, the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be."

MV Act s. 164(2) – "In any claim for compensation under sub-section (1), the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person."
In simple words: Parliament can create liability without fault : the claimant need not prove any wrongful act or negligence.
en.meaning: Liability – the legal obligation of a wrongdoer to pay damages or obey an injunction because he has committed a tort . Fault – blameworthy conduct: doing harm intentionally, or failing to take the care a reasonable person would take ( negligence ). No-fault liability – liability imposed by law without proof of intention or negligence (strict, absolute, statutory). Intention – the defendant desires the consequence, or knows it is substantially certain to follow. Negligence – failure to take reasonable care where there is a duty to take care, causing damage. Motive – the reason or purpose behind an act (e.g., spite, gain, revenge). Causation – the link between the defendant's act and the plaintiff's damage. Remoteness of damage – the limit beyond which consequences, though caused by the act, are too remote for liability.
keyPoints: Liability = wrongful act + injuria + (damage where needed) + causation + not too remote + no defence. Fault: intention / negligence ( Donoghue ). No-fault: Rylands (1868), M.C. Mehta (1986), MV Act s. 164. Motive generally irrelevant ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895). Omission → liability only with a duty to act ( Subhagwanti , 1966). Remoteness: foreseeable kind of damage ( Wagon Mound , 1961); extent need not be foreseen ( Hughes , 1963); Re Polemis rejected.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Pickles drew off percolating water on his land, reducing the Corporation's supply, allegedly
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "If it was a lawful act, however ill the motive might be, he had a right to do it." Why it matters: motive is generally irrelevant to liability.
Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v. Morts Dock & Engineering Co. (The Wagon Mound) [1961] AC 388 (Privy Council, 18 Jan 1961)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Furnace oil discharged from the appellants' ship spread across the bay and later caught fire,
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Re Polemis is "no longer ... good law"; liability depends on "whether the damage is of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen." Why it matters: the modern test of remoteness.
Hughes v. Lord Advocate (House of Lords, 21 Feb 1963)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A boy was burned when a paraffin lamp left by Post Office workmen at an unattended open manho
caseLaws.facts: Principle: liable if the kind of damage was foreseeable, even if its extent or the way it happened was not. Why it matters: refines The Wagon Mound : kind, not extent or manner.
Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti AIR 1966 SC 1750 (24 Feb 1966)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The clock tower in Chandni Chowk, under the Corporation's control, collapsed; heirs of three
caseLaws.facts: Principle: the Corporation was bound to maintain the tower safely; its failure was negligence (an omission where there was a duty); the maxim res ipsa loquitur applied. Why it matters: an omission creates liability where there is a legal duty to act.

selfTest.q: List the elements of tortious liability. Answer: Wrongful act/omission, legal damage, actual damage where required, causation and remoteness, absence of defence. What are the two broad bases of liability?
selfTest.a: Answer: Fault (intention/negligence) and no-fault (strict, absolute, statutory). Give a statutory example of no-fault liability. Answer: MV Act s. 164 – ₹5 lakh on death, ₹2.5 lakh on grievous hurt. Is motive relevant in tort? Answer: Generally no ( Bradford v. Pickles ), except where malice is an ingredient (e.g., malicious prosecution). When does an omission create liability? Answer: Only where there is a legal duty to act ( MCD v. Subhagwanti ). What was the rule in Re Polemis ? Answer: Liability for all direct consequences, foreseeable or not. Which case replaced Re Polemis and with what test? Answer: The Wagon Mound (1961) – foreseeability of the kind of damage. What did Hughes v. Lord Advocate add? Answer: The extent or manner need not be foreseen if the kind of damage was. Difference between strict and absolute liability? Answer: Strict allows exceptions ( Rylands ); absolute does not ( M.C. Mehta ). Name two ways liability can be extinguished. Answer: Release; accord and satisfaction (also waiver, limitation, death in some cases).

visuals.html:
This Is not the same as Why
Intention Motive Intention is the desire to do the act / bring about the result; motive is the reason why. Motive is generally irrelevant.
Strict liability Absolute liability Strict (Rylands) allows exceptions; absolute (M.C. Mehta) allows none of those exceptions.
Causation Remoteness Causation asks whether the act caused the harm; remoteness asks whether the harm is too remote even though caused.
Re Polemis (direct consequences) The Wagon Mound (foreseeability) Polemis was rejected; foreseeability of the kind of damage is the test.
Extent of damage Kind of damage Unforeseeable extent does not excuse; only an unforeseeable kind does (Hughes).

te.inOneMinute: ఒక వ్యక్తి అపకృత్యంలో బాధ్యుడయ్యేది: (1) అతను తప్పుడు చర్య లేదా లోపం చేసినప్పుడు – చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన; (2) అది వాది చట్టబద్ధ హక్కును ఉల్లంఘించినప్పుడు ( ఇంజూరియా (injuria) ); (3) ఆ అపకృత్యానికి అవసరమైతే, వాస్తవ నష్టం జరిగినప్పుడు; (4) ఆ చర్య నష్టానికి కారణమై , నష్టం మరీ దూరమైనది కానప్పుడు; (5) ఏ రక్షణ (defence) వర్తించనప్పుడు. బాధ్యతకు రెండు విస్తృత ఆధారాలు : తప్పు (fault) (ప్రతివాది ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా లేదా నిర్లక్ష్యంగా వ్యవహరించాడు), తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత (ప్రతివాది జాగ్రత్తగా ఉన్నా విధించే బాధ్యత – రైలాండ్స్ v. ఫ్లెచర్ (1868) కింద కఠిన బాధ్యత, ఎం.సి. మెహతా v. యూనియన్ ఆఫ్ ఇండియా (1986) కింద సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత, మోటారు వాహనాల చట్టం సె. 164 వంటి చట్టబద్ధ తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత). మానసిక అంశం అపకృత్యాన్ని బట్టి మారుతుంది: ఉద్దేశం (దాడి, కొట్టడం, మోసం), నిర్లక్ష్యం, లేదా ఏదీ అవసరం లేదు (కఠిన, సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత). ప్రేరణ (motive) సాధారణంగా అప్రస్తుతం: చెడు ప్రేరణ వల్ల చట్టబద్ధ చర్య అపకృత్యం కాదు, మంచి ప్రేరణ చట్టవిరుద్ధ చర్యను క్షమించదు ( బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ , 1895). దూరత్వం (remoteness): "of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen" (సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ముందుగా ఊహించవలసిన రకమైన) నష్టానికి మాత్రమే ప్రతివాది బాధ్యుడు ( ది వాగన్ మౌండ్ , 1961); ఇది రీ పోలెమిస్ (1921) పాత "ప్రత్యక్ష పర్యవసానాల" పరీక్షను భర్తీ చేసింది. హాని రకం ఊహించదగినదైతే, దాని పరిమాణం లేదా జరిగిన తీరు ఊహించలేకపోయినా ప్రతివాది బాధ్యుడే ( హ్యూస్ v. లార్డ్ అడ్వకేట్ , 1963). బాధ్యత ఇతరుల అపకృత్యానికి (ప్రతినిధి బాధ్యత), ఉమ్మడిగా (ఉమ్మడి అపకృత్యకారులు), లేదా రాజ్యానిది (అ. 300) కూడా కావచ్చు – ప్రతిదీ వేరే సిలబస్ అంశం.
te.meaning: బాధ్యత (liability) – అపకృత్యం చేసినందుకు నష్టపరిహారం చెల్లించడానికి లేదా నిషేధాజ్ఞను పాటించడానికి తప్పు చేసినవాడికి ఉన్న చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత. తప్పు (fault) – నిందార్హమైన ప్రవర్తన: ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా హాని చేయడం, లేదా సహేతుక వ్యక్తి తీసుకునే జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోకపోవడం ( నిర్లక్ష్యం ). తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత – ఉద్దేశం లేదా నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేకుండా చట్టం విధించే బాధ్యత (కఠిన, సంపూర్ణ, చట్టబద్ధ). ఉద్దేశం (intention) – ప్రతివాది ఫలితాన్ని కోరుకుంటాడు, లేదా అది దాదాపు ఖచ్చితంగా జరుగుతుందని తెలుసు. నిర్లక్ష్యం (negligence) – జాగ్రత్త వహించే బాధ్యత ఉన్నచోట సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోకపోవడం, దాని వల్ల నష్టం. ప్రేరణ (motive) – చర్య వెనుక కారణం లేదా ప్రయోజనం (ఉదా: ద్వేషం, లాభం, ప్రతీకారం). కారణత్వం (causation) – ప్రతివాది చర్యకు, వాది నష్టానికి మధ్య సంబంధం. నష్టం దూరత్వం (remoteness of damage) – చర్య వల్ల కలిగినప్పటికీ, బాధ్యతకు మరీ దూరమైన పర్యవసానాల పరిమితి.
keyPoints: బాధ్యత = తప్పుడు చర్య + injuria + (అవసరమైనచోట నష్టం) + కారణత్వం + మరీ దూరం కాకపోవడం + రక్షణ లేకపోవడం. తప్పు: ఉద్దేశం / నిర్లక్ష్యం ( డోనోఘ్ ). తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత: రైలాండ్స్ (1868), ఎం.సి. మెహతా (1986), MV చట్టం సె. 164. ప్రేరణ సాధారణంగా అప్రస్తుతం ( బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ , 1895). లోపం → చర్య తీసుకోవలసిన బాధ్యత ఉంటేనే బాధ్యత ( సుభాగ్‌వంతి , 1966). దూరత్వం: ఊహించదగిన రకమైన నష్టం ( వాగన్ మౌండ్ , 1961); పరిమాణం ఊహించనవసరం లేదు ( హ్యూస్ , 1963); రీ పోలెమిస్ తిరస్కరించబడింది.

selfTest.q: అపకృత్య బాధ్యత అంశాలను పేర్కొనండి. జవాబు: తప్పుడు చర్య/లోపం, చట్టపరమైన నష్టం, అవసరమైనచోట వాస్తవ నష్టం, కారణత్వం, దూరత్వం, రక్షణ లేకపోవడం. బాధ్యతకు రెండు విస్తృత ఆధారాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: తప్పు (ఉద్దేశం/నిర్లక్ష్యం), తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత (కఠిన, సంపూర్ణ, చట్టబద్ధ). తప్పు లేని బాధ్యతకు ఒక చట్టబద్ధ ఉదాహరణ ఇవ్వండి. జవాబు: MV చట్టం సె. 164 – మరణానికి ₹5 లక్షలు, తీవ్ర గాయానికి ₹2.5 లక్షలు. అపకృత్యంలో ప్రేరణ ప్రస్తుతమా? జవాబు: సాధారణంగా కాదు ( బ్రాడ్‌ఫోర్డ్ v. పికిల్స్ ), దురుద్దేశం అంశంగా ఉన్నచోట తప్ప (ఉదా: దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్). లోపం ఎప్పుడు బాధ్యతను సృష్టిస్తుంది? జవాబు: చర్య తీసుకోవలసిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత ఉన్నప్పుడే ( MCD v. సుభాగ్‌వంతి ). రీ పోలెమిస్ నియమం ఏమిటి? జవాబు: ఊహించదగినవైనా కాకపోయినా అన్ని ప్రత్యక్ష పర్యవసానాలకు బాధ్యత. రీ పోలెమిస్ ను ఏ కేసు, ఏ పరీక్షతో భర్తీ చేసింది? జవాబు: ది వాగన్ మౌండ్ (1961) – నష్టం రకం యొక్క ముందుచూపు. హ్యూస్ v. లార్డ్ అడ్వకేట్ ఏమి జోడించింది? జవాబు: నష్టం రకం ఊహించదగినదైతే పరిమాణం లేదా తీరు ఊహించనవసరం లేదు. కఠిన, సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత మధ్య తేడా? జవాబు: కఠిన బాధ్యత మినహాయింపులను అనుమతిస్తుంది ( రైలాండ్స్ ); సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత అనుమతించదు ( ఎం.సి. మెహతా ). బాధ్యత ముగిసే రెండు మార్గాలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: విడుదల (release); ఒప్పందం–సంతృప్తి (accord and satisfaction) (మాఫీ, కాలపరిమితి, కొన్ని సందర్భాల్లో మరణం కూడా).
