ఇది దీనితో సమానం కాదు ఎందుకు
ఉద్దేశం ప్రేరణ ఉద్దేశం – చర్య చేయాలనే / ఫలితం తేవాలనే కోరిక; ప్రేరణ – ఎందుకు అనే కారణం. ప్రేరణ సాధారణంగా అప్రస్తుతం.
కఠిన బాధ్యత సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత కఠిన (రైలాండ్స్) మినహాయింపులను అనుమతిస్తుంది; సంపూర్ణ (ఎం.సి. మెహతా) ఆ మినహాయింపులను అనుమతించదు.
కారణత్వం దూరత్వం కారణత్వం – చర్య హాని కలిగించిందా; దూరత్వం – కలిగించినా హాని మరీ దూరమైనదా.
రీ పోలెమిస్ (ప్రత్యక్ష పర్యవసానాలు) ది వాగన్ మౌండ్ (ముందుచూపు) పోలెమిస్ తిరస్కరించబడింది; నష్టం రకం యొక్క ముందుచూపే పరీక్ష.
నష్టం పరిమాణం నష్టం రకం ఊహించలేని పరిమాణం మినహాయింపు ఇవ్వదు; ఊహించలేని రకం మాత్రమే ఇస్తుంది (హ్యూస్).

hi.inOneMinute: A person is liable in tort when: (1) he does a wrongful act or omission – a breach of a duty fixed by law; (2) it violates a legal right of the plaintiff ( injuria ); (3) where the tort needs it, actual damage results; (4) the act caused the damage and the damage is not too remote; and (5) no defence applies. There are two broad bases of liability : fault (the defendant acted intentionally or negligently) and no-fault (liability imposed even though the defendant was careful – strict liability under Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), absolute liability under M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1986), and statutory no-fault liability such as Motor Vehicles Act s. 164). The mental element varies by tort: intention (assault, battery, deceit), negligence, or none (strict and absolute liability). Motive is generally irrelevant: a lawful act does not become a tort because of a bad motive, and an unlawful act is not excused by a good one ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895). Remoteness: the defendant is liable only for damage "of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen" ( The Wagon Mound , 1961), which replaced the older "direct consequences" test of Re Polemis (1921). If the kind of harm was foreseeable, the defendant is liable even if its extent or manner was not ( Hughes v. Lord Advocate , 1963). Liability may also be for another's tort (vicarious liability), shared (joint tortfeasors), or of the State (Art. 300) – each is a separate syllabus topic.
legalProvision: There is no statute that sets out the general principles of tortious liability; they come from judgments. Statutes recognise them in parts:
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

Limitation Act, 1963, s. 23 – "In the case of a suit for compensation for an act which does not give rise to a cause of action unless some specific injury actually results therefrom, the period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the injury results."
In simple words: some torts are complete as soon as the right is violated; others need actual damage (s. 23). The law of liability must therefore ask, for each tort, whether damage is an ingredient.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1) – "Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or instrument having the force of law, the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be."

MV Act s. 164(2) – "In any claim for compensation under sub-section (1), the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person."
In simple words: Parliament can create liability without fault : the claimant need not prove any wrongful act or negligence.
hi.meaning: Liability – the legal obligation of a wrongdoer to pay damages or obey an injunction because he has committed a tort . Fault – blameworthy conduct: doing harm intentionally, or failing to take the care a reasonable person would take ( negligence ). No-fault liability – liability imposed by law without proof of intention or negligence (strict, absolute, statutory). Intention – the defendant desires the consequence, or knows it is substantially certain to follow. Negligence – failure to take reasonable care where there is a duty to take care, causing damage. Motive – the reason or purpose behind an act (e.g., spite, gain, revenge). Causation – the link between the defendant's act and the plaintiff's damage. Remoteness of damage – the limit beyond which consequences, though caused by the act, are too remote for liability.
keyPoints: Liability = wrongful act + injuria + (damage where needed) + causation + not too remote + no defence. Fault: intention / negligence ( Donoghue ). No-fault: Rylands (1868), M.C. Mehta (1986), MV Act s. 164. Motive generally irrelevant ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895). Omission → liability only with a duty to act ( Subhagwanti , 1966). Remoteness: foreseeable kind of damage ( Wagon Mound , 1961); extent need not be foreseen ( Hughes , 1963); Re Polemis rejected.

selfTest.q: List the elements of tortious liability. Answer: Wrongful act/omission, legal damage, actual damage where required, causation and remoteness, absence of defence. What are the two broad bases of liability?
selfTest.a: Answer: Fault (intention/negligence) and no-fault (strict, absolute, statutory). Give a statutory example of no-fault liability. Answer: MV Act s. 164 – ₹5 lakh on death, ₹2.5 lakh on grievous hurt. Is motive relevant in tort? Answer: Generally no ( Bradford v. Pickles ), except where malice is an ingredient (e.g., malicious prosecution). When does an omission create liability? Answer: Only where there is a legal duty to act ( MCD v. Subhagwanti ). What was the rule in Re Polemis ? Answer: Liability for all direct consequences, foreseeable or not. Which case replaced Re Polemis and with what test? Answer: The Wagon Mound (1961) – foreseeability of the kind of damage. What did Hughes v. Lord Advocate add? Answer: The extent or manner need not be foreseen if the kind of damage was. Difference between strict and absolute liability? Answer: Strict allows exceptions ( Rylands ); absolute does not ( M.C. Mehta ). Name two ways liability can be extinguished. Answer: Release; accord and satisfaction (also waiver, limitation, death in some cases).

law-of-torts-u1-t11.subtitle: Negligence as a ground of tortious liability: the meaning of carelessness and the standard of the reasonable person

en.inOneMinute: Negligence is the most common basis of liability in tort. It means failing to take the care that the law requires, so that harm is caused to someone to whom that care was owed. It has three essentials : (1) a duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff; (2) breach of that duty – falling below the standard of a reasonable person; (3) damage to the plaintiff caused by the breach and not too remote. Lord Macmillan in Bourhill v. Young (1942): the plaintiff "must show that he owed her a duty of care which he failed to observe and that as a result of this failure in duty on his part she suffered". Duty – the neighbour principle: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932). The duty is owed only to persons who can reasonably be foreseen as likely to be injured ( Bourhill : a woman 45–50 feet away, out of sight of the collision, was not owed a duty). Two theories of negligence: the subjective theory (negligence is a state of mind – carelessness or indifference) and the objective theory (negligence is conduct – failure to meet the standard of the reasonable person). The law follows the objective theory. Negligence is both an independent tort (since Donoghue ) and a mode of committing other torts (e.g., negligent trespass or nuisance). Indian statutes rely on it: MV Act claims (ss. 165–166), Fatal Accidents Act ("wrongful act, neglect or default"), BNS s. 106 (causing death by negligence).
legalProvision: No Indian statute defines negligence for the law of torts. Statutes use the idea:

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensured) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured ..." ("ensured" is as printed in the official text.)
In simple words: where a death is caused by "neglect", the family can sue the negligent person as the deceased could have done.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 166(1) – "An application for compensation arising out of an accident of the nature specified in sub-section (1) of section 165 may be made— (a) by the person who has sustained the injury; or (b) by the owner of the property; or (c) where death has resulted from the accident, by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased; ..."
In simple words: most motor-accident claims before the Claims Tribunal are claims in negligence (fault of the driver), apart from the no-fault and strict-liability routes.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 106(1) (comparison) – "Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine ..."
In simple words: the same negligent act can be a crime as well as the tort of negligence (see Tort distinguished from Crime and Breach of Contract ).
en.meaning: Negligence (as a tort ) – breach of a legal duty to take care, owed by the defendant to the plaintiff, which results in damage to the plaintiff. Negligence (as a state of mind – subjective theory) – inadvertence or indifference to the consequences of one's conduct. Negligence (as conduct – objective theory) – failure to do what a reasonable person would do, or doing what a reasonable person would not do, in the circumstances. Duty of care – a legal obligation to take reasonable care to avoid causing foreseeable harm to persons within the range of foreseeable danger. Standard of care – the care a reasonable person would take in the same circumstances. Neighbour principle – the test of Donoghue v. Stevenson for who is owed a duty: "persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation".
keyPoints: Negligence = duty + breach + damage ( Bourhill v. Young , 1942). Duty: neighbour principle ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932). Duty owed to foreseeable plaintiffs only ( Bourhill : 45–50 feet away – no duty). Objective test – reasonable person ( Wagon Mound ). Not actionable per se – damage must be proved; remoteness by foreseeability. Statutes: FAA s. 1A ("neglect"); MV Act s. 166; BNS s. 106.

selfTest.q: What are the three essentials of negligence?
selfTest.a: Answer: Duty of care, breach of duty, consequent damage. State the neighbour principle. Answer: Take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour ( Donoghue ). Who is a "neighbour"? Answer: Persons so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation. Why did the plaintiff fail in Bourhill v. Young ? Answer: She was not within the range of persons to whom injury could reasonably be anticipated; no duty was owed to her. Which theory of negligence does the law follow? Answer: The objective theory – the reasonable person standard. Is negligence actionable per se? Answer: No – actual damage must be proved. Which case fixes the remoteness test in negligence? Answer: The Wagon Mound (1961). What is meant by "take the victim as he finds him"? Answer: Once a wrong is established, the wrongdoer is liable for the full harm even if the victim was unusually vulnerable (Lord Wright, Bourhill ). Name an Indian statute that bases liability on "neglect". Answer: Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A. Can the same negligent act be a crime? Answer: Yes – e.g., causing death by negligence under BNS s. 106.

Civil negligence Criminal negligence (BNS s. 106) Civil: compensation, balance of probabilities; criminal: punishment, proof beyond reasonable doubt.

te.inOneMinute: నిర్లక్ష్యం (negligence) అపకృత్యంలో బాధ్యతకు అత్యంత సాధారణ ఆధారం. చట్టం కోరే జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోకపోవడం, దాని వల్ల ఆ జాగ్రత్త రావలసిన వ్యక్తికి హాని కలగడం దీని అర్థం. దీనికి మూడు ముఖ్యాంశాలు : (1) ప్రతివాది వాది పట్ల కలిగి ఉన్న జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత (duty of care) ; (2) ఆ బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన – సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ప్రమాణం కంటే తక్కువగా ప్రవర్తించడం; (3) ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల కలిగిన, మరీ దూరం కాని నష్టం . బోర్‌హిల్ v. యంగ్ (1942)లో లార్డ్ మాక్‌మిలన్: వాది "must show that he owed her a duty of care which he failed to observe and that as a result of this failure in duty on his part she suffered" (అతను ఆమె పట్ల జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత కలిగి ఉన్నాడని, దాన్ని పాటించలేదని, ఆ వైఫల్యం ఫలితంగా ఆమె బాధపడిందని చూపాలి). బాధ్యత – పొరుగువారి సూత్రం (neighbour principle): "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" (మీ పొరుగువారిని గాయపరిచే అవకాశం ఉందని మీరు సహేతుకంగా ఊహించగల చర్యలు లేదా లోపాలను నివారించడానికి సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాలి) ( డోనోఘ్ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ , 1932). గాయపడే అవకాశం ఉందని సహేతుకంగా ఊహించగల వ్యక్తుల పట్ల మాత్రమే బాధ్యత ఉంటుంది ( బోర్‌హిల్ : ఢీకొన్న చోటు కనిపించని, 45–50 అడుగుల దూరంలో ఉన్న మహిళ పట్ల బాధ్యత లేదు). నిర్లక్ష్యానికి రెండు సిద్ధాంతాలు: వ్యక్తిగత (subjective) సిద్ధాంతం (నిర్లక్ష్యం ఒక మానసిక స్థితి – అజాగ్రత్త లేదా ఉదాసీనత), వస్తుగత (objective) సిద్ధాంతం (నిర్లక్ష్యం ప్రవర్తన – సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ప్రమాణాన్ని అందుకోకపోవడం). చట్టం వస్తుగత సిద్ధాంతాన్ని అనుసరిస్తుంది. నిర్లక్ష్యం స్వతంత్ర అపకృత్యం ( డోనోఘ్ నుంచి) కూడా, ఇతర అపకృత్యాలు చేసే విధానం (ఉదా: నిర్లక్ష్యపు అతిక్రమణ లేదా ఉపద్రవం) కూడా. భారతీయ చట్టాలు దీనిపై ఆధారపడతాయి: MV చట్టం క్లెయిమ్‌లు (సె. 165–166), ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం ("wrongful act, neglect or default"), BNS సె. 106 (నిర్లక్ష్యంతో మరణం కలిగించడం).
te.meaning: నిర్లక్ష్యం ( అపకృత్యంగా ) – ప్రతివాది వాది పట్ల కలిగి ఉన్న జాగ్రత్త వహించే చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన, దాని వల్ల వాదికి నష్టం. నిర్లక్ష్యం (మానసిక స్థితిగా – వ్యక్తిగత సిద్ధాంతం) – తన ప్రవర్తన పర్యవసానాల పట్ల ఏమరుపాటు లేదా ఉదాసీనత. నిర్లక్ష్యం (ప్రవర్తనగా – వస్తుగత సిద్ధాంతం) – పరిస్థితుల్లో సహేతుక వ్యక్తి చేసేది చేయకపోవడం, లేదా సహేతుక వ్యక్తి చేయనిది చేయడం. జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత (duty of care) – ఊహించదగిన ప్రమాద పరిధిలోని వ్యక్తులకు ఊహించదగిన హాని కలగకుండా సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవలసిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత. జాగ్రత్త ప్రమాణం (standard of care) – అదే పరిస్థితుల్లో సహేతుక వ్యక్తి తీసుకునే జాగ్రత్త. పొరుగువారి సూత్రం – ఎవరి పట్ల బాధ్యత ఉందో చెప్పే డోనోఘ్ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ పరీక్ష: "persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation" (నా చర్య వల్ల ఎంత దగ్గరగా, నేరుగా ప్రభావితమవుతారో, వారిని నేను సహేతుకంగా దృష్టిలో ఉంచుకోవలసిన వ్యక్తులు).
keyPoints: నిర్లక్ష్యం = బాధ్యత + ఉల్లంఘన + నష్టం ( బోర్‌హిల్ v. యంగ్ , 1942). బాధ్యత: పొరుగువారి సూత్రం ( డోనోఘ్ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ , 1932). ఊహించదగిన వాదుల పట్ల మాత్రమే బాధ్యత ( బోర్‌హిల్ : 45–50 అడుగుల దూరం – బాధ్యత లేదు). వస్తుగత పరీక్ష – సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ( వాగన్ మౌండ్ ). స్వతఃసిద్ధంగా దావా యోగ్యం కాదు – నష్టం రుజువు చేయాలి; ముందుచూపుతో దూరత్వం. చట్టాలు: FAA సె. 1A ("neglect"); MV చట్టం సె. 166; BNS సె. 106.

selfTest.q: నిర్లక్ష్యానికి మూడు ముఖ్యాంశాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత, బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన, ఫలితంగా నష్టం. పొరుగువారి సూత్రాన్ని చెప్పండి. జవాబు: మీ పొరుగువారిని గాయపరిచే అవకాశం ఉందని సహేతుకంగా ఊహించగల చర్యలు లేదా లోపాలను నివారించడానికి సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాలి ( డోనోఘ్ ). "పొరుగువారు" ఎవరు? జవాబు: నా చర్య వల్ల ఎంత దగ్గరగా, నేరుగా ప్రభావితమవుతారో, వారిని నేను సహేతుకంగా దృష్టిలో ఉంచుకోవలసిన వ్యక్తులు. బోర్‌హిల్ v. యంగ్ ‌లో వాది ఎందుకు ఓడిపోయింది? జవాబు: గాయం సహేతుకంగా ఊహించగల వ్యక్తుల పరిధిలో ఆమె లేదు; ఆమె పట్ల బాధ్యత లేదు. చట్టం నిర్లక్ష్యానికి ఏ సిద్ధాంతాన్ని అనుసరిస్తుంది? జవాబు: వస్తుగత సిద్ధాంతం – సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ప్రమాణం. నిర్లక్ష్యం స్వతఃసిద్ధంగా దావా యోగ్యమా? జవాబు: కాదు – వాస్తవ నష్టాన్ని రుజువు చేయాలి. నిర్లక్ష్యంలో దూరత్వ పరీక్షను ఏ కేసు నిర్ణయిస్తుంది? జవాబు: ది వాగన్ మౌండ్ (1961). "బాధితుడిని ఉన్నట్లుగానే స్వీకరించాలి" అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: తప్పు నిరూపితమైన తరువాత, బాధితుడు అసాధారణంగా బలహీనుడైనా తప్పు చేసినవాడు పూర్తి హానికి బాధ్యుడు (లార్డ్ రైట్, బోర్‌హిల్ ). "neglect" మీద బాధ్యతను ఆధారపరిచే ఒక భారతీయ చట్టం చెప్పండి. జవాబు: ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం, 1855, సె. 1A. అదే నిర్లక్ష్యపు చర్య నేరం కాగలదా? జవాబు: అవును – ఉదా: BNS సె. 106 కింద నిర్లక్ష్యంతో మరణం కలిగించడం.

నిర్లక్ష్యం (అపకృత్యం) నిర్లక్ష్యం (మరో అపకృత్య విధానం) అపకృత్యానికి బాధ్యత–ఉల్లంఘన–నష్టం కావాలి; విధానంగా, అజాగ్రత్త మరో అపకృత్యం (ఉదా: అతిక్రమణ) చేసే మార్గం.
జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత జాగ్రత్త ప్రమాణం బాధ్యత: ఈ వాది పట్ల జాగ్రత్త రావాలా; ప్రమాణం: ఎంత జాగ్రత్త.
వస్తుగత సిద్ధాంతం వ్యక్తిగత సిద్ధాంతం వస్తుగతం: సహేతుక వ్యక్తితో ప్రవర్తన పోలిక (చట్టం); వ్యక్తిగతం: మానసిక స్థితి.
నిర్లక్ష్యం నిర్లక్ష్యపు తెగింపు తెగింపు: తెలిసిన ప్రమాదాన్ని స్పృహతో విస్మరించడం; నిర్లక్ష్యం: జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోకపోవడం, అవగాహన అవసరం లేదు.
పౌర నిర్లక్ష్యం నేర నిర్లక్ష్యం (BNS సె. 106) పౌర: పరిహారం, సంభావ్యతల సమతుల్యత; నేర: శిక్ష, సహేతుక సందేహానికి అతీతంగా రుజువు.

hi.inOneMinute: Negligence is the most common basis of liability in tort. It means failing to take the care that the law requires, so that harm is caused to someone to whom that care was owed. It has three essentials : (1) a duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff; (2) breach of that duty – falling below the standard of a reasonable person; (3) damage to the plaintiff caused by the breach and not too remote. Lord Macmillan in Bourhill v. Young (1942): the plaintiff "must show that he owed her a duty of care which he failed to observe and that as a result of this failure in duty on his part she suffered". Duty – the neighbour principle: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932). The duty is owed only to persons who can reasonably be foreseen as likely to be injured ( Bourhill : a woman 45–50 feet away, out of sight of the collision, was not owed a duty). Two theories of negligence: the subjective theory (negligence is a state of mind – carelessness or indifference) and the objective theory (negligence is conduct – failure to meet the standard of the reasonable person). The law follows the objective theory. Negligence is both an independent tort (since Donoghue ) and a mode of committing other torts (e.g., negligent trespass or nuisance). Indian statutes rely on it: MV Act claims (ss. 165–166), Fatal Accidents Act ("wrongful act, neglect or default"), BNS s. 106 (causing death by negligence).
legalProvision: No Indian statute defines negligence for the law of torts. Statutes use the idea:

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensured) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured ..." ("ensured" is as printed in the official text.)
In simple words: where a death is caused by "neglect", the family can sue the negligent person as the deceased could have done.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 166(1) – "An application for compensation arising out of an accident of the nature specified in sub-section (1) of section 165 may be made— (a) by the person who has sustained the injury; or (b) by the owner of the property; or (c) where death has resulted from the accident, by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased; ..."
In simple words: most motor-accident claims before the Claims Tribunal are claims in negligence (fault of the driver), apart from the no-fault and strict-liability routes.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 106(1) (comparison) – "Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine ..."
In simple words: the same negligent act can be a crime as well as the tort of negligence (see Tort distinguished from Crime and Breach of Contract ).
hi.meaning: Negligence (as a tort ) – breach of a legal duty to take care, owed by the defendant to the plaintiff, which results in damage to the plaintiff. Negligence (as a state of mind – subjective theory) – inadvertence or indifference to the consequences of one's conduct. Negligence (as conduct – objective theory) – failure to do what a reasonable person would do, or doing what a reasonable person would not do, in the circumstances. Duty of care – a legal obligation to take reasonable care to avoid causing foreseeable harm to persons within the range of foreseeable danger. Standard of care – the care a reasonable person would take in the same circumstances. Neighbour principle – the test of Donoghue v. Stevenson for who is owed a duty: "persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation".
keyPoints: Negligence = duty + breach + damage ( Bourhill v. Young , 1942). Duty: neighbour principle ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932). Duty owed to foreseeable plaintiffs only ( Bourhill : 45–50 feet away – no duty). Objective test – reasonable person ( Wagon Mound ). Not actionable per se – damage must be proved; remoteness by foreseeability. Statutes: FAA s. 1A ("neglect"); MV Act s. 166; BNS s. 106.

selfTest.q: What are the three essentials of negligence?
selfTest.a: Answer: Duty of care, breach of duty, consequent damage. State the neighbour principle. Answer: Take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour ( Donoghue ). Who is a "neighbour"? Answer: Persons so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation. Why did the plaintiff fail in Bourhill v. Young ? Answer: She was not within the range of persons to whom injury could reasonably be anticipated; no duty was owed to her. Which theory of negligence does the law follow? Answer: The objective theory – the reasonable person standard. Is negligence actionable per se? Answer: No – actual damage must be proved. Which case fixes the remoteness test in negligence? Answer: The Wagon Mound (1961). What is meant by "take the victim as he finds him"? Answer: Once a wrong is established, the wrongdoer is liable for the full harm even if the victim was unusually vulnerable (Lord Wright, Bourhill ). Name an Indian statute that bases liability on "neglect". Answer: Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A. Can the same negligent act be a crime? Answer: Yes – e.g., causing death by negligence under BNS s. 106.

law-of-torts-u1-t6.subtitle: How a tort differs from a crime and from a breach of contract, and when one act is more than one wrong

en.inOneMinute: A tort is a civil wrong "which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m)). Its remedy is an action for unliquidated damages or an injunction, brought by the injured person. A crime is a public wrong: an act "made punishable" by law (BNS, 2023, s. 2(24)). The State prosecutes; the aim is punishment (BNS s. 4: death, imprisonment, forfeiture , fine, community service). A breach of contract is failure to perform a duty that the parties themselves fixed by agreement. Only a party to the contract can sue ( privity of contract ); compensation follows Contract Act s. 73. Tort vs crime: private vs public wrong; victim sues vs State prosecutes; compensation vs punishment; parties can settle a tort, but only listed offences can be compounded (BNSS s. 359). Tort vs contract: duty fixed by law vs duty fixed by the parties; duty owed to persons generally ( right in rem ) vs to the other party only ( right in personam ); no privity needed in tort ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932). Overlap: one act can be all three. A police beating can be a crime and a tort at the same time ( Saheli v. Commissioner of Police , 1989: ₹75,000 compensation while prosecution was pending). A negligent taxi driver can breach his contract with the passenger and commit a tort against him.
legalProvision: There is no single section that distinguishes the three. The distinctions come from the statutes that govern each:
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

In simple words: a tort is a civil (not criminal) wrong. If the wrong is only a breach of contract, it is not a tort; but if it also breaks a duty imposed by law, it is a tort too ("not exclusively").
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 2(24) – "offence" ... means a thing made punishable by this Sanhita ...

BNS, s. 4 – "The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Sanhita are— (a) Death; (b) Imprisonment for life; (c) Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:— (1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; (d) Forfeiture of property; (e) Fine; (f) Community Service."
In simple words: a crime is defined by the State making it punishable; its consequence is punishment, not compensation to the victim.
Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 2(h) – "An agreement enforceable by law is a contract;"

Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 73 – "When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach."

In simple words: in contract, the duty comes from the agreement, the claim belongs to "the party who suffers", and compensation is limited to loss that arose naturally or was in the parties' contemplation.

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 395(1)(b) and (5) – a criminal court imposing a fine may order it to be applied "in the payment to any person of compensation for any loss or injury caused by the offence, when compensation is, in the opinion of the Court, recoverable by such person in a Civil Court"; and "At the time of awarding compensation in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter, the Court shall take into account any sum paid or recovered as compensation under this section."

In simple words: the law itself accepts that one act can be both a crime and a civil wrong; a criminal court may give some compensation, and a later civil (tort) suit can still be filed, with the amount already paid taken into account.
en.meaning: Tort – a civil wrong, other than a mere breach of contract or trust, for which the remedy is an action for unliquidated damages (or an injunction ) by the injured person. Crime (offence) – an act or omission that the law makes punishable (BNS s. 2(24)); a wrong against society as a whole, prosecuted by the State. Breach of contract – failure, without lawful excuse, to perform a promise contained in an agreement enforceable by law (Contract Act s. 2(h)). Right in rem – a right available against people in general (e.g., the right not to be assaulted). Tort protects such rights. Right in personam – a right available against a particular person (e.g., the right of a buyer against the seller to get delivery). Contract creates such rights. Privity of contract – only the parties to a contract can sue on it. Unliquidated damages – an amount not fixed in advance, assessed by the court.
keyPoints: Tort: s. 2(m) Limitation Act; offence: BNS s. 2(24); punishments: BNS s. 4; contract: Contract Act s. 2(h); compensation for breach: s. 73. Tort = private wrong → compensation; crime = public wrong → punishment; contract = agreed duty → compensation. Compounding only under BNSS s. 359; tort suits can be settled freely. One act can be crime + tort ( Saheli , ₹75,000; BNSS s. 395(5)). One act can be contract + tort ("not exclusively"; Hedley Byrne ). No privity in tort ( Donoghue v. Stevenson ). Contract suit: 3 years (Art. 55); minor offences: BNSS s. 514.

caseLaws.facts: She had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle: Lord Atkin – a manufacturer who sells products intending them to reach "the ultimate consumer in the form in which they left him with no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care. Why it matters: a duty in tort exists without any contract; privity is not needed – a key difference between tort and contract.

Why it matters: tort duties can exist alongside or without a contract – basis of concurrent liability.
Saheli, A Women's Resources Centre v. Commissioner of Police, Delhi (1990) 1 SCC 422; AIR 1990 SC 513 (decided 14 December 1989)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Police beat a woman and her nine-year-old son, who died; a criminal case under s
caseLaws.facts: 304/34 IPC was registered against police officials. Principle: "An action for damages lies for bodily harm which includes battery, assault, false imprisonment, physical injuries and death"; the State is responsible for the tortious acts of its employees; ₹75,000 awarded, without affecting the pending criminal prosecution. Why it matters: the same act was a crime and a tort; both remedies ran side by side.
Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) 2 SCC 746; AIR 1993 SC 1960

caseLaws.name: Facts: A youth died in police custody; his mother sought compensation under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: public-law compensation for violation of fundamental rights is "distinct from, and in addition to, the remedy in private law for damages for the tort"; ₹1,50,000 awarded. Why it matters: shows that one act (custodial death) can lead to criminal prosecution, a private tort claim, and a public-law claim – each with its own purpose.

selfTest.q: How does the Limitation Act define "tort"?
selfTest.a: Answer: A civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust (s. 2(m)). How does the BNS define "offence"? Answer: A thing made punishable by the Sanhita (s. 2(24)). Who brings proceedings in tort and in crime? Answer: Tort – the injured person; crime – the State. Can a tort claim be settled privately? Can a crime? Answer: A tort claim, yes; a crime only if compoundable under BNSS s. 359. Name a case where the same act was treated as both a crime and a tort. Answer: Saheli v. Commissioner of Police (1989). Which provision lets a criminal court give compensation to the victim? Answer: BNSS s. 395 (and the victim compensation scheme in s. 396). Which case shows that a tort claim needs no contract? Answer: Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932). Which word in s. 2(m) shows that a breach of contract may also be a tort? Answer: "exclusively". What is the time limit for a suit for breach of contract generally? Answer: Three years from when the contract is broken (Limitation Act Art. 55). Distinguish right in rem and right in personam. Answer: In rem – against people generally (tort); in personam – against a particular person (contract).

Breach of contract that is also a tort Pure breach of contract If a duty imposed by law is also broken, it is a tort too; if only the agreed promise is broken, it is only a contract claim.

te.inOneMinute: అపకృత్యం (tort) ఒక పౌర తప్పు, "which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కానిది) (పరిమితి చట్టం, 1963, సె. 2(m)). దీని పరిహారం అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం (unliquidated damages) లేదా నిషేధాజ్ఞ; బాధితుడే దావా వేస్తాడు. నేరం (crime) ప్రజా తప్పు: చట్టం "made punishable" (శిక్షార్హం చేసిన) చర్య (BNS, 2023, సె. 2(24)). రాజ్యం ప్రాసిక్యూట్ చేస్తుంది; లక్ష్యం శిక్ష (BNS సె. 4: మరణశిక్ష, జైలు, ఆస్తి జప్తు, జరిమానా, సమాజ సేవ). ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన అంటే పక్షాలు తమ ఒప్పందం ద్వారా నిర్ణయించుకున్న బాధ్యతను నెరవేర్చకపోవడం. ఒప్పందంలో పక్షం మాత్రమే దావా వేయగలడు ( ఒప్పంద సంబంధం (privity of contract) ); పరిహారం ఒప్పంద చట్టం సె. 73 ప్రకారం. అపకృత్యం vs నేరం: వ్యక్తిగత తప్పు vs ప్రజా తప్పు; బాధితుడు దావా vs రాజ్యం ప్రాసిక్యూషన్; పరిహారం vs శిక్ష; అపకృత్య దావాను పక్షాలు రాజీ చేసుకోవచ్చు, కానీ జాబితాలోని నేరాలను మాత్రమే రాజీ (compound) చేయవచ్చు (BNSS సె. 359). అపకృత్యం vs ఒప్పందం: చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత vs పక్షాలు నిర్ణయించిన బాధ్యత; అందరి పట్ల బాధ్యత ( సర్వజన హక్కు (right in rem) ) vs అవతలి పక్షం పట్ల మాత్రమే ( వ్యక్తిగత హక్కు (right in personam) ); అపకృత్యానికి ఒప్పంద సంబంధం అవసరం లేదు ( డోనోఘ్ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ , 1932). కలయిక: ఒకే చర్య మూడూ కావచ్చు. పోలీసులు కొట్టడం ఒకేసారి నేరం, అపకృత్యం కావచ్చు ( సహేలి v. కమిషనర్ ఆఫ్ పోలీస్ , 1989: ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ కొనసాగుతుండగానే ₹75,000 పరిహారం). నిర్లక్ష్యపు టాక్సీ డ్రైవర్ ప్రయాణికుడితో ఒప్పందాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించి, అతని పట్ల అపకృత్యం కూడా చేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning: అపకృత్యం – కేవలం ఒప్పంద లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాని పౌర తప్పు; బాధితుడు అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం (లేదా నిషేధాజ్ఞ ) కోసం దావా వేస్తాడు. నేరం (offence) – చట్టం శిక్షార్హం చేసిన చర్య లేదా లోపం (BNS సె. 2(24)); సమాజం మొత్తానికి వ్యతిరేకమైన తప్పు, రాజ్యం ప్రాసిక్యూట్ చేస్తుంది. ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన – చట్టం ద్వారా అమలు చేయగల ఒప్పందంలోని వాగ్దానాన్ని, చట్టబద్ధ కారణం లేకుండా నెరవేర్చకపోవడం (ఒప్పంద చట్టం సె. 2(h)). సర్వజన హక్కు (right in rem) – సాధారణంగా అందరికీ వ్యతిరేకంగా ఉండే హక్కు (ఉదా: దాడికి గురి కాకుండా ఉండే హక్కు). అపకృత్య చట్టం ఇలాంటి హక్కులను రక్షిస్తుంది. వ్యక్తిగత హక్కు (right in personam ) – ఒక నిర్దిష్ట వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా ఉండే హక్కు (ఉదా: సరుకు డెలివరీ కోసం కొనుగోలుదారుకు విక్రేతపై హక్కు). ఒప్పందం ఇలాంటి హక్కులను సృష్టిస్తుంది. ఒప్పంద సంబంధం ( privity of contract ) – ఒప్పందంలోని పక్షాలు మాత్రమే దానిపై దావా వేయగలరు. అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం – ముందుగా నిర్ణయించని, కోర్టు అంచనా వేసే మొత్తం.
keyPoints: అపకృత్యం: పరిమితి చట్టం సె. 2(m); నేరం: BNS సె. 2(24); శిక్షలు: BNS సె. 4; ఒప్పందం: ఒప్పంద చట్టం సె. 2(h); ఉల్లంఘనకు పరిహారం: సె. 73. అపకృత్యం = వ్యక్తిగత తప్పు → పరిహారం; నేరం = ప్రజా తప్పు → శిక్ష; ఒప్పందం = ఒప్పుకున్న బాధ్యత → పరిహారం. రాజీ (compounding) BNSS సె. 359 కింద మాత్రమే; అపకృత్య దావాలను స్వేచ్ఛగా రాజీ చేసుకోవచ్చు. ఒకే చర్య నేరం + అపకృత్యం కావచ్చు ( సహేలి , ₹75,000; BNSS సె. 395(5)). ఒకే చర్య ఒప్పందం + అపకృత్యం కావచ్చు ("not exclusively"; హెడ్లీ బైర్న్ ). అపకృత్యంలో ఒప్పంద సంబంధం అవసరం లేదు ( డోనోఘ్ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ ). ఒప్పంద దావా: 3 సంవత్సరాలు (అ. 55); చిన్న నేరాలు: BNSS సె. 514.

selfTest.q: పరిమితి చట్టం "tort"ను ఎలా నిర్వచిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కాని పౌర తప్పు (సె. 2(m)). BNS "offence"ను ఎలా నిర్వచిస్తుంది? జవాబు: సంహిత శిక్షార్హం చేసినది (సె. 2(24)). అపకృత్యంలో, నేరంలో విచారణ ఎవరు ప్రారంభిస్తారు? జవాబు: అపకృత్యం – బాధితుడు; నేరం – రాజ్యం. అపకృత్య దావాను ప్రైవేటుగా రాజీ చేసుకోవచ్చా? నేరాన్ని? జవాబు: అపకృత్య దావాను అవును; నేరాన్ని BNSS సె. 359 కింద రాజీ చేయదగినదైతేనే. ఒకే చర్యను నేరం, అపకృత్యం రెండింటిగా చూసిన కేసు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: సహేలి v. కమిషనర్ ఆఫ్ పోలీస్ (1989). బాధితుడికి పరిహారం ఇవ్వడానికి నేర న్యాయస్థానానికి ఏ నిబంధన అధికారం ఇస్తుంది? జవాబు: BNSS సె. 395 (సె. 396 లోని బాధితుల పరిహార పథకం కూడా). అపకృత్య దావాకు ఒప్పందం అవసరం లేదని చూపే కేసు ఏది? జవాబు: డోనోఘ్ v. స్టీవెన్సన్ (1932). ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన అపకృత్యం కూడా కావచ్చని సె. 2(m)లోని ఏ పదం చూపిస్తుంది? జవాబు: "exclusively". ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన దావాకు సాధారణ కాలపరిమితి ఎంత? జవాబు: ఒప్పందం ఉల్లంఘించబడినప్పటి నుంచి మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (పరిమితి చట్టం అ. 55). సర్వజన హక్కు, వ్యక్తిగత హక్కు మధ్య తేడా చెప్పండి. జవాబు: In rem – సాధారణంగా అందరికీ వ్యతిరేకంగా (అపకృత్యం); in personam – నిర్దిష్ట వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా (ఒప్పందం).

నిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం అనిర్ధారిత నష్టపరిహారం నిర్ధారితం: ఒప్పందంలో ముందే నిర్ణయించినది; అనిర్ధారితం: కోర్టు అంచనా వేసేది (అపకృత్యం).
అపకృత్యం కూడా అయిన ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన కేవలం ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన చట్టం విధించిన బాధ్యత కూడా భంగమైతే అది అపకృత్యం కూడా; ఒప్పుకున్న వాగ్దానం మాత్రమే భంగమైతే ఒప్పంద దావా మాత్రమే.

hi.inOneMinute: A tort is a civil wrong "which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust" (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m)). Its remedy is an action for unliquidated damages or an injunction, brought by the injured person. A crime is a public wrong: an act "made punishable" by law (BNS, 2023, s. 2(24)). The State prosecutes; the aim is punishment (BNS s. 4: death, imprisonment, forfeiture , fine, community service). A breach of contract is failure to perform a duty that the parties themselves fixed by agreement. Only a party to the contract can sue ( privity of contract ); compensation follows Contract Act s. 73. Tort vs crime: private vs public wrong; victim sues vs State prosecutes; compensation vs punishment; parties can settle a tort, but only listed offences can be compounded (BNSS s. 359). Tort vs contract: duty fixed by law vs duty fixed by the parties; duty owed to persons generally ( right in rem ) vs to the other party only ( right in personam ); no privity needed in tort ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932). Overlap: one act can be all three. A police beating can be a crime and a tort at the same time ( Saheli v. Commissioner of Police , 1989: ₹75,000 compensation while prosecution was pending). A negligent taxi driver can breach his contract with the passenger and commit a tort against him.
legalProvision: There is no single section that distinguishes the three. The distinctions come from the statutes that govern each:
Limitation Act, 1963, s. 2(m) – "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.

In simple words: a tort is a civil (not criminal) wrong. If the wrong is only a breach of contract, it is not a tort; but if it also breaks a duty imposed by law, it is a tort too ("not exclusively").
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 2(24) – "offence" ... means a thing made punishable by this Sanhita ...

BNS, s. 4 – "The punishments to which offenders are liable under the provisions of this Sanhita are— (a) Death; (b) Imprisonment for life; (c) Imprisonment, which is of two descriptions, namely:— (1) Rigorous, that is, with hard labour; (2) Simple; (d) Forfeiture of property; (e) Fine; (f) Community Service."
In simple words: a crime is defined by the State making it punishable; its consequence is punishment, not compensation to the victim.
Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 2(h) – "An agreement enforceable by law is a contract;"

Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 73 – "When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach."

In simple words: in contract, the duty comes from the agreement, the claim belongs to "the party who suffers", and compensation is limited to loss that arose naturally or was in the parties' contemplation.

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 395(1)(b) and (5) – a criminal court imposing a fine may order it to be applied "in the payment to any person of compensation for any loss or injury caused by the offence, when compensation is, in the opinion of the Court, recoverable by such person in a Civil Court"; and "At the time of awarding compensation in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter, the Court shall take into account any sum paid or recovered as compensation under this section."

In simple words: the law itself accepts that one act can be both a crime and a civil wrong; a criminal court may give some compensation, and a later civil (tort) suit can still be filed, with the amount already paid taken into account.
hi.meaning: Tort – a civil wrong, other than a mere breach of contract or trust, for which the remedy is an action for unliquidated damages (or an injunction ) by the injured person. Crime (offence) – an act or omission that the law makes punishable (BNS s. 2(24)); a wrong against society as a whole, prosecuted by the State. Breach of contract – failure, without lawful excuse, to perform a promise contained in an agreement enforceable by law (Contract Act s. 2(h)). Right in rem – a right available against people in general (e.g., the right not to be assaulted). Tort protects such rights. Right in personam – a right available against a particular person (e.g., the right of a buyer against the seller to get delivery). Contract creates such rights. Privity of contract – only the parties to a contract can sue on it. Unliquidated damages – an amount not fixed in advance, assessed by the court.
keyPoints: Tort: s. 2(m) Limitation Act; offence: BNS s. 2(24); punishments: BNS s. 4; contract: Contract Act s. 2(h); compensation for breach: s. 73. Tort = private wrong → compensation; crime = public wrong → punishment; contract = agreed duty → compensation. Compounding only under BNSS s. 359; tort suits can be settled freely. One act can be crime + tort ( Saheli , ₹75,000; BNSS s. 395(5)). One act can be contract + tort ("not exclusively"; Hedley Byrne ). No privity in tort ( Donoghue v. Stevenson ). Contract suit: 3 years (Art. 55); minor offences: BNSS s. 514.

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 26 August 1928 Mrs Donoghue drank a bottle of ginger beer which a friend had bought from a
caseLaws.facts: She had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle: Lord Atkin – a manufacturer who sells products intending them to reach "the ultimate consumer in the form in which they left him with no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care. Why it matters: a duty in tort exists without any contract; privity is not needed – a key difference between tort and contract.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Bankers gave a careless favourable reference about a customer's credit, "without responsibili
caseLaws.facts: Principle: a duty of care arises where a person with special skill undertakes, "quite irrespective of contract", to apply it for another who relies on it (Lord Morris); on the facts the disclaimer excluded liability. Why it matters: tort duties can exist alongside or without a contract – basis of concurrent liability.
Saheli, A Women's Resources Centre v. Commissioner of Police, Delhi (1990) 1 SCC 422; AIR 1990 SC 513 (decided 14 December 1989)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Police beat a woman and her nine-year-old son, who died; a criminal case under s
caseLaws.facts: 304/34 IPC was registered against police officials. Principle: "An action for damages lies for bodily harm which includes battery, assault, false imprisonment, physical injuries and death"; the State is responsible for the tortious acts of its employees; ₹75,000 awarded, without affecting the pending criminal prosecution. Why it matters: the same act was a crime and a tort; both remedies ran side by side.
Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) 2 SCC 746; AIR 1993 SC 1960

caseLaws.name: Facts: A youth died in police custody; his mother sought compensation under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: public-law compensation for violation of fundamental rights is "distinct from, and in addition to, the remedy in private law for damages for the tort"; ₹1,50,000 awarded. Why it matters: shows that one act (custodial death) can lead to criminal prosecution, a private tort claim, and a public-law claim – each with its own purpose.

selfTest.q: How does the Limitation Act define "tort"?
selfTest.a: Answer: A civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust (s. 2(m)). How does the BNS define "offence"? Answer: A thing made punishable by the Sanhita (s. 2(24)). Who brings proceedings in tort and in crime? Answer: Tort – the injured person; crime – the State. Can a tort claim be settled privately? Can a crime? Answer: A tort claim, yes; a crime only if compoundable under BNSS s. 359. Name a case where the same act was treated as both a crime and a tort. Answer: Saheli v. Commissioner of Police (1989). Which provision lets a criminal court give compensation to the victim? Answer: BNSS s. 395 (and the victim compensation scheme in s. 396). Which case shows that a tort claim needs no contract? Answer: Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932). Which word in s. 2(m) shows that a breach of contract may also be a tort? Answer: "exclusively". What is the time limit for a suit for breach of contract generally? Answer: Three years from when the contract is broken (Limitation Act Art. 55). Distinguish right in rem and right in personam. Answer: In rem – against people generally (tort); in personam – against a particular person (contract).

law-of-torts-u1-t8.subtitle: Fault as a basis of liability in tort: its forms, the fault theory, and proof of fault

en.inOneMinute: Fault means blameworthy conduct: the defendant either intended the harmful act (or its result) or was negligent – he failed to take the care that a reasonable person would have taken. The fault principle says: as a general rule, a person is liable in tort only if the harm was caused by his fault. Liability rests on the idea that a person should answer for harm he could have avoided. Fault is judged by an objective standard – "the standard of the reasonable man" ( The Wagon Mound , 1961) – not by what the defendant personally thought or could do. The plaintiff must prove fault ; but under res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself") the facts may raise "a presumption of fault" that the defendant must rebut ( MCD v. Subhagwanti , 1966: collapse of an 80-year-old clock tower). Fault is not always needed . Courts and Parliament have created liability without fault: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), M.C. Mehta (1986), MV Act s. 164, and Kaushnuma Begum (2001), which spoke of the worldwide move to make motor accident liability "a liability without fault".
legalProvision: No statute defines "fault" for the law of torts; the idea comes from judgments. The statutes that come closest show where fault is required and where it is not:

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(2) – "In any claim for compensation under sub-section (1), the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person."

In simple words: in ordinary tort claims, the plaintiff must prove "wrongful act or neglect or default" (fault). Section 164 removes that requirement for its fixed no-fault compensation, which shows that fault is the normal rule and no-fault is an exception made by law.

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensured) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured ..." (the word "ensured" appears in the official text as printed)
In simple words: the right of a family to sue for a death depends on "wrongful act, neglect or default" – i.e., on fault (or other tortious liability) of the defendant.
en.meaning: Fault – conduct that the law regards as blameworthy: intentional wrongdoing or negligence . Intention – the defendant desires the consequence of his act, or knows it is substantially certain to follow. Recklessness – the defendant knows of a risk and goes ahead without caring whether harm results (treated like intention for many torts ; it is a form of fault). Negligence (as fault) – failure to take reasonable care where there is a duty to take care. Fault principle – "no liability without fault": liability in tort generally depends on proof of fault. Objective standard – fault is measured against what a reasonable person would have done, not against the defendant's own ability. Res ipsa loquitur – "the thing speaks for itself": where the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence and the thing was under the defendant's control, negligence is presumed .
keyPoints: Fault = intention (incl. recklessness) or negligence. Fault principle: no liability without fault – moral basis, freedom of action, deterrence. Objective standard: reasonable man ( Wagon Mound ). Burden on plaintiff; res ipsa loquitur raises "a presumption of fault" ( Subhagwanti , 1966). Inevitable accident: no fault, no liability (under the fault principle). Exceptions: Rylands (1868), M.C. Mehta (1986), MV Act s. 164, Kaushnuma (2001).

Fletcher applies to motor accident claims; a victim can get compensation without proving negligence unless an exception applies; s. 140 no-fault liability is a separate statutory liability. Why it matters: shows the Indian move away from fault in motor accidents.

selfTest.q: What are the two main forms of fault?
selfTest.a: Answer: Intention (including recklessness) and negligence. State the fault principle. Answer: As a general rule, there is no liability in tort without fault. Give two reasons for the fault principle. Answer: It is morally fair; it leaves people free to act reasonably (also deterrence). Is fault judged subjectively or objectively? Answer: Objectively – by the standard of the reasonable man ( The Wagon Mound ). Who must prove fault? Answer: The plaintiff, in the first instance. What is res ipsa loquitur? Answer: "The thing speaks for itself" – facts raise a presumption of fault that the defendant must rebut ( Subhagwanti ). What is an inevitable accident? Answer: An accident that reasonable care could not have avoided; no fault, so no liability under the fault principle. Name a case of liability without fault. Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) (also M.C. Mehta , 1986). What did Kaushnuma Begum decide? Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher applies to motor accident claims; compensation without proof of negligence unless an exception applies. Which statute removes the need to prove fault for fixed compensation? Answer: MV Act s. 164(2).

te.inOneMinute: తప్పు (fault) అంటే నిందార్హమైన ప్రవర్తన: ప్రతివాది హానికరమైన చర్యను (లేదా దాని ఫలితాన్ని) ఉద్దేశించాడు , లేదా నిర్లక్ష్యంగా ఉన్నాడు – సహేతుక వ్యక్తి తీసుకునే జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోలేదు. తప్పు సూత్రం (fault principle) చెప్పేది: సాధారణ నియమంగా, హాని తన తప్పు వల్ల కలిగితేనే వ్యక్తి అపకృత్యంలో బాధ్యుడు. తాను తప్పించగలిగిన హానికి వ్యక్తి జవాబుదారుడనే భావనపై ఈ బాధ్యత ఆధారపడుతుంది. తప్పును వస్తుగత ప్రమాణం (objective standard) ద్వారా అంచనా వేస్తారు – "the standard of the reasonable man" (సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ప్రమాణం) ( ది వాగన్ మౌండ్ , 1961) – ప్రతివాది వ్యక్తిగతంగా ఏమనుకున్నాడు లేదా ఏం చేయగలడు అనే దాని ద్వారా కాదు. తప్పును వాది రుజువు చేయాలి ; కానీ రెస్ ఇప్సా లోక్విటర్ (res ipsa loquitur) ("వస్తువే చెబుతుంది") కింద వాస్తవాలు "a presumption of fault" (తప్పు ఊహ) కలిగించవచ్చు, దాన్ని ప్రతివాది తిప్పికొట్టాలి ( MCD v. సుభాగ్‌వంతి , 1966: 80 ఏళ్ల గడియార స్తంభం కూలిపోవడం). తప్పు ఎప్పుడూ అవసరం కాదు . కోర్టులు, పార్లమెంటు తప్పు లేని బాధ్యతను సృష్టించాయి: రైలాండ్స్ v. ఫ్లెచర్ (1868), ఎం.సి. మెహతా (1986), MV చట్టం సె. 164, మోటారు ప్రమాద బాధ్యతను "a liability without fault" (తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత)గా చేసే ప్రపంచవ్యాప్త ఉద్యమం గురించి మాట్లాడిన కౌష్నుమా బేగం (2001).
te.meaning: తప్పు (fault) – చట్టం నిందార్హంగా భావించే ప్రవర్తన: ఉద్దేశపూర్వక తప్పు లేదా నిర్లక్ష్యం . ఉద్దేశం (intention) – ప్రతివాది తన చర్య పర్యవసానాన్ని కోరుకుంటాడు, లేదా అది దాదాపు ఖచ్చితంగా జరుగుతుందని తెలుసు. నిర్లక్ష్యపు తెగింపు ( recklessness ) – ప్రమాదం ఉందని తెలిసి, హాని జరుగుతుందా లేదా అని పట్టించుకోకుండా ముందుకు వెళ్లడం (చాలా అపకృత్యాలకు ఉద్దేశంలాగే పరిగణిస్తారు; ఇదీ తప్పు రూపమే). నిర్లక్ష్యం (తప్పుగా) – జాగ్రత్త వహించే బాధ్యత ఉన్నచోట సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోకపోవడం. తప్పు సూత్రం – "no liability without fault" (తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత లేదు): అపకృత్య బాధ్యత సాధారణంగా తప్పు రుజువుపై ఆధారపడుతుంది. వస్తుగత ప్రమాణం – ప్రతివాది స్వంత సామర్థ్యంతో కాకుండా, సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ఏం చేసేవాడో దానితో తప్పును కొలుస్తారు. రెస్ ఇప్సా లోక్విటర్ – "వస్తువే చెబుతుంది": నిర్లక్ష్యం లేకుండా సాధారణంగా జరగని ప్రమాదం, వస్తువు ప్రతివాది అదుపులో ఉన్నప్పుడు, నిర్లక్ష్యాన్ని ఊహిస్తారు.
keyPoints: తప్పు = ఉద్దేశం (నిర్లక్ష్యపు తెగింపుతో సహా) లేదా నిర్లక్ష్యం. తప్పు సూత్రం: తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత లేదు – నైతిక ఆధారం, చర్య స్వేచ్ఛ, నిరోధం. వస్తుగత ప్రమాణం: సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ( వాగన్ మౌండ్ ). భారం వాదిపై; రెస్ ఇప్సా లోక్విటర్ "a presumption of fault" కలిగిస్తుంది ( సుభాగ్‌వంతి , 1966). అనివార్య ప్రమాదం: తప్పు లేదు, బాధ్యత లేదు (తప్పు సూత్రం కింద). మినహాయింపులు: రైలాండ్స్ (1868), ఎం.సి. మెహతా (1986), MV చట్టం సె. 164, కౌష్నుమా (2001).

selfTest.q: తప్పుకు రెండు ముఖ్య రూపాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: ఉద్దేశం (నిర్లక్ష్యపు తెగింపుతో సహా), నిర్లక్ష్యం. తప్పు సూత్రాన్ని చెప్పండి. జవాబు: సాధారణ నియమంగా, తప్పు లేకుండా అపకృత్యంలో బాధ్యత లేదు. తప్పు సూత్రానికి రెండు కారణాలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: నైతికంగా న్యాయం; సహేతుకంగా వ్యవహరించే స్వేచ్ఛ ఇస్తుంది (నిరోధం కూడా). తప్పును వ్యక్తిగతంగానా, వస్తుగతంగానా అంచనా వేస్తారు? జవాబు: వస్తుగతంగా – సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ప్రమాణంతో ( ది వాగన్ మౌండ్ ). తప్పును ఎవరు రుజువు చేయాలి? జవాబు: మొదట వాది. రెస్ ఇప్సా లోక్విటర్ అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: "వస్తువే చెబుతుంది" – వాస్తవాలు తప్పు ఊహను కలిగిస్తాయి, దాన్ని ప్రతివాది తిప్పికొట్టాలి ( సుభాగ్‌వంతి ). అనివార్య ప్రమాదం అంటే ఏమిటి? జవాబు: సహేతుక జాగ్రత్తతో తప్పించలేని ప్రమాదం; తప్పు లేదు, కాబట్టి తప్పు సూత్రం కింద బాధ్యత లేదు. తప్పు లేని బాధ్యతకు ఒక కేసు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: రైలాండ్స్ v. ఫ్లెచర్ (1868) ( ఎం.సి. మెహతా , 1986 కూడా). కౌష్నుమా బేగం ఏం నిర్ణయించింది? జవాబు: మోటారు ప్రమాద క్లెయిమ్‌లకు రైలాండ్స్ v. ఫ్లెచర్ వర్తిస్తుంది; మినహాయింపు వర్తిస్తే తప్ప నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేకుండా పరిహారం. నిర్ణీత పరిహారానికి తప్పు రుజువు అవసరాన్ని ఏ చట్టం తొలగిస్తుంది? జవాబు: MV చట్టం సె. 164(2).

hi.inOneMinute: Fault means blameworthy conduct: the defendant either intended the harmful act (or its result) or was negligent – he failed to take the care that a reasonable person would have taken. The fault principle says: as a general rule, a person is liable in tort only if the harm was caused by his fault. Liability rests on the idea that a person should answer for harm he could have avoided. Fault is judged by an objective standard – "the standard of the reasonable man" ( The Wagon Mound , 1961) – not by what the defendant personally thought or could do. The plaintiff must prove fault ; but under res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself") the facts may raise "a presumption of fault" that the defendant must rebut ( MCD v. Subhagwanti , 1966: collapse of an 80-year-old clock tower). Fault is not always needed . Courts and Parliament have created liability without fault: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), M.C. Mehta (1986), MV Act s. 164, and Kaushnuma Begum (2001), which spoke of the worldwide move to make motor accident liability "a liability without fault".
legalProvision: No statute defines "fault" for the law of torts; the idea comes from judgments. The statutes that come closest show where fault is required and where it is not:

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(2) – "In any claim for compensation under sub-section (1), the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person."

In simple words: in ordinary tort claims, the plaintiff must prove "wrongful act or neglect or default" (fault). Section 164 removes that requirement for its fixed no-fault compensation, which shows that fault is the normal rule and no-fault is an exception made by law.

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensured) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured ..." (the word "ensured" appears in the official text as printed)
In simple words: the right of a family to sue for a death depends on "wrongful act, neglect or default" – i.e., on fault (or other tortious liability) of the defendant.
hi.meaning: Fault – conduct that the law regards as blameworthy: intentional wrongdoing or negligence . Intention – the defendant desires the consequence of his act, or knows it is substantially certain to follow. Recklessness – the defendant knows of a risk and goes ahead without caring whether harm results (treated like intention for many torts ; it is a form of fault). Negligence (as fault) – failure to take reasonable care where there is a duty to take care. Fault principle – "no liability without fault": liability in tort generally depends on proof of fault. Objective standard – fault is measured against what a reasonable person would have done, not against the defendant's own ability. Res ipsa loquitur – "the thing speaks for itself": where the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence and the thing was under the defendant's control, negligence is presumed .
keyPoints: Fault = intention (incl. recklessness) or negligence. Fault principle: no liability without fault – moral basis, freedom of action, deterrence. Objective standard: reasonable man ( Wagon Mound ). Burden on plaintiff; res ipsa loquitur raises "a presumption of fault" ( Subhagwanti , 1966). Inevitable accident: no fault, no liability (under the fault principle). Exceptions: Rylands (1868), M.C. Mehta (1986), MV Act s. 164, Kaushnuma (2001).

selfTest.q: What are the two main forms of fault?
selfTest.a: Answer: Intention (including recklessness) and negligence. State the fault principle. Answer: As a general rule, there is no liability in tort without fault. Give two reasons for the fault principle. Answer: It is morally fair; it leaves people free to act reasonably (also deterrence). Is fault judged subjectively or objectively? Answer: Objectively – by the standard of the reasonable man ( The Wagon Mound ). Who must prove fault? Answer: The plaintiff, in the first instance. What is res ipsa loquitur? Answer: "The thing speaks for itself" – facts raise a presumption of fault that the defendant must rebut ( Subhagwanti ). What is an inevitable accident? Answer: An accident that reasonable care could not have avoided; no fault, so no liability under the fault principle. Name a case of liability without fault. Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) (also M.C. Mehta , 1986). What did Kaushnuma Begum decide? Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher applies to motor accident claims; compensation without proof of negligence unless an exception applies. Which statute removes the need to prove fault for fixed compensation? Answer: MV Act s. 164(2).

law-of-torts-u1-t12.subtitle: Strict, absolute, statutory and vicarious liability: when the law makes a person pay without proof of fault

en.inOneMinute: Liability without fault (no-fault liability) means a person is held liable for harm even though he was neither intentional nor negligent – even though he "had taken all reasonable care". It is an exception to the general rule "no liability without fault" (see Fault ). Its basis is the risk of the activity, not the blame of the actor: the person who creates or profits from a dangerous risk should bear its cost. Main forms: Strict liability – Rylands v. Fletcher (1868): one who keeps on his land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes "must keep it in at his peril"; some exceptions (e.g., act of God, act of a stranger, plaintiff's default, consent, statutory authority). Absolute liability – M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1986): a hazardous or inherently dangerous enterprise is liable and "it should be no answer to the enterprise to say that it had taken all reasonable care"; not subject to the Rylands exceptions. Statutory no-fault liability – MV Act, 1988 s. 164 (₹5 lakh death / ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt); Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 s. 3; Employee's Compensation Act, 1923 s. 3. Vicarious liability – an employer is liable for his employee's tort without any fault of his own (see Vicarious Liability ). Indian courts apply it widely: electricity lines ( M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari , 2002), motor accidents ( Kaushnuma Begum , 2001), toxic waste ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action , 1996).
legalProvision: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1)–(2) – the owner or insurer "shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt"; and "the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt ... was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person."

Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3(1)–(2) – "Where death or injury to any person (other than a workman) or damage to any property has resulted from an accident, the owner shall be liable to reimburse such amount, or provide such other relief as may be prescribed, for— (a) death due to fatal accident; (b) medical expenses incurred due to total or partial disability; (c) loss of wages due to partial disability; (d) other injury or sickness; (e) damage to private property; ..." and "the claimant shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person." (The section heading reads: "Liability to give relief in certain cases on principle of no fault.")

Employee's Compensation Act, 1923, s. 3(1) – "If personal injury is caused to a [employee] by accident arising out of and in the course of his employment, his employer shall be liable to pay compensation in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter ..."

In simple words: Parliament has created several no-fault schemes. The victim need not prove anyone's "wrongful act, neglect or default"; liability follows from the accident itself (motor vehicle use, handling hazardous substances, employment).
en.meaning: Liability without fault – legal liability for harm imposed without proof of intention or negligence . Strict liability – liability for the escape of a dangerous thing brought on to land, without proof of negligence, but subject to recognised exceptions ( Rylands v. Fletcher ). Absolute liability – liability of a hazardous or inherently dangerous enterprise for harm caused by its activity, with none of the Rylands exceptions ( M.C. Mehta ). Statutory no-fault liability – fixed or limited compensation payable under a statute without proof of fault. Vicarious liability – liability of one person for the tort of another because of their relationship (mainly employer–employee).
keyPoints: No-fault liability: liable though all reasonable care was taken. Rylands (1868): strict, with exceptions; M.C. Mehta (1986): absolute, no exceptions. Shail Kumari (2002): electricity; act of stranger rejected. Kaushnuma (2001): Rylands in motor accidents. MV Act s. 164: ₹5 lakh / ₹2.5 lakh; PLI Act s. 3; EC Act s. 3. Basis: risk + profit + difficulty of proof.

selfTest.q: What is liability without fault?
selfTest.a: Answer: Liability imposed without proof of intention or negligence. Name the case that founded strict liability. Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). How does absolute liability differ from strict liability? Answer: It allows none of the Rylands exceptions ( M.C. Mehta ). Give two reasons for no-fault liability. Answer: The person who creates and profits from a risk should bear its cost; victims cannot prove negligence inside a hazardous process. What did Shail Kumari decide about "act of stranger"? Answer: It fails where the stranger's act should reasonably have been anticipated or its consequences prevented. What did Kaushnuma Begum decide? Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher applies to motor accident claims. How much is payable under MV Act s. 164? Answer: ₹5 lakh on death; ₹2.5 lakh on grievous hurt. Which Act gives no-fault relief for accidents involving hazardous substances? Answer: Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3. Is vicarious liability a form of liability without fault? Answer: Yes – the employer is liable without personal fault. Which case says public-law compensation rests on strict liability? Answer: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993).

te.inOneMinute: తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత (no-fault liability) అంటే ఒక వ్యక్తికి ఉద్దేశం గానీ, నిర్లక్ష్యం గానీ లేకపోయినా – "అన్ని సహేతుక జాగ్రత్తలు తీసుకున్నా" – కలిగిన హానికి బాధ్యత విధించడం. ఇది "తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత లేదు" అనే సాధారణ నియమానికి మినహాయింపు ( Fault చూడండి). దీని ఆధారం చేసిన వ్యక్తి యొక్క తప్పు కాదు, చేసే కార్యకలాపంలోని ప్రమాదం (risk) : ప్రమాదకర రిస్క్‌ను సృష్టించి లాభం పొందేవారే దాని ఖర్చు భరించాలి. ప్రధాన రూపాలు: కఠిన బాధ్యత – Rylands v. Fletcher (1868): తప్పించుకుంటే హాని చేసే వస్తువును తన భూమిపై ఉంచేవాడు "must keep it in at his peril" (అర్థం: తన బాధ్యతపైనే దానిని లోపల ఉంచాలి); కొన్ని మినహాయింపులు ఉన్నాయి (దైవ చర్య, అపరిచితుని చర్య, వాది తప్పు, సమ్మతి, చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం మొదలైనవి). సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత – M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1986): ప్రమాదకర లేదా స్వాభావికంగా ప్రమాదకర సంస్థ బాధ్యురాలు; "it should be no answer to the enterprise to say that it had taken all reasonable care" (అర్థం: అన్ని సహేతుక జాగ్రత్తలు తీసుకున్నామని చెప్పడం సంస్థకు జవాబు కాదు); Rylands మినహాయింపులు వర్తించవు. చట్టపరమైన no-fault బాధ్యత – MV Act, 1988 s. 164 (మరణానికి ₹5 లక్షలు / తీవ్ర గాయానికి ₹2.5 లక్షలు); Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 s. 3; Employee's Compensation Act, 1923 s. 3. ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత (vicarious liability) – యజమాని తన తప్పు ఏమీ లేకుండానే ఉద్యోగి చేసిన టార్ట్‌కు బాధ్యుడు ( Vicarious Liability చూడండి). భారత న్యాయస్థానాలు దీనిని విస్తృతంగా వర్తింపజేస్తాయి: విద్యుత్ తీగలు ( M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari , 2002), మోటారు ప్రమాదాలు ( Kaushnuma Begum , 2001), విషపూరిత వ్యర్థాలు ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action , 1996).
te.meaning: తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత – ఉద్దేశం లేదా నిర్లక్ష్యం నిరూపించకుండానే హానికి విధించే చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత. కఠిన బాధ్యత ( strict liability ) – భూమిపైకి తెచ్చిన ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు తప్పించుకుంటే నిర్లక్ష్యం నిరూపణ లేకుండానే బాధ్యత, కానీ గుర్తింపు పొందిన మినహాయింపులకు లోబడి ( Rylands v. Fletcher ). సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( absolute liability ) – ప్రమాదకర లేదా స్వాభావికంగా ప్రమాదకర సంస్థ తన కార్యకలాపం వల్ల కలిగిన హానికి, Rylands మినహాయింపులు ఏవీ లేకుండా బాధ్యత ( M.C. Mehta ). చట్టపరమైన no-fault బాధ్యత – తప్పు నిరూపణ లేకుండా చట్టం ప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సిన స్థిర లేదా పరిమిత పరిహారం. ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత – సంబంధం కారణంగా (ముఖ్యంగా యజమాని–ఉద్యోగి) ఒకరి టార్ట్‌కు మరొకరి బాధ్యత.
keyPoints: No-fault బాధ్యత: అన్ని సహేతుక జాగ్రత్తలు తీసుకున్నా బాధ్యుడు. Rylands (1868): మినహాయింపులతో కఠిన; M.C. Mehta (1986): మినహాయింపులు లేని సంపూర్ణ. Shail Kumari (2002): విద్యుత్; అపరిచితుని చర్య తిరస్కరణ. Kaushnuma (2001): మోటారు ప్రమాదాల్లో Rylands . MV Act s. 164: ₹5 లక్షలు / ₹2.5 లక్షలు; PLI Act s. 3; EC Act s. 3. ఆధారం: రిస్క్ + లాభం + నిరూపణ కష్టం.

selfTest.q: తప్పు లేకుండా బాధ్యత అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: ఉద్దేశం లేదా నిర్లక్ష్యం నిరూపించకుండా విధించే బాధ్యత. కఠిన బాధ్యతకు పునాది వేసిన కేసు ఏది? జవాబు: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత కఠిన బాధ్యత నుంచి ఎలా భిన్నం? జవాబు: దానిలో Rylands మినహాయింపులు ఏవీ ఉండవు ( M.C. Mehta ). No-fault బాధ్యతకు రెండు కారణాలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: రిస్క్‌ను సృష్టించి లాభం పొందేవారే ఖర్చు భరించాలి; ప్రమాదకర ప్రక్రియ లోపల నిర్లక్ష్యాన్ని బాధితులు నిరూపించలేరు. "అపరిచితుని చర్య" గురించి Shail Kumari ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? జవాబు: అపరిచితుని చర్యను సహేతుకంగా ఊహించి ఉండాల్సి ఉంటే లేదా దాని పరిణామాలను నివారించి ఉండాల్సి ఉంటే ఆ మినహాయింపు విఫలం. Kaushnuma Begum ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? జవాబు: మోటారు ప్రమాద దావాలకు Rylands v. Fletcher వర్తిస్తుంది. hi.inOneMinute: Liability without fault (no-fault liability) means a person is held liable for harm even though he was neither intentional nor negligent – even though he "had taken all reasonable care". It is an exception to the general rule "no liability without fault" (see Fault ). Its basis is the risk of the activity, not the blame of the actor: the person who creates or profits from a dangerous risk should bear its cost. Main forms: Strict liability – Rylands v. Fletcher (1868): one who keeps on his land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes "must keep it in at his peril"; some exceptions (e.g., act of God, act of a stranger, plaintiff's default, consent, statutory authority). Absolute liability – M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1986): a hazardous or inherently dangerous enterprise is liable and "it should be no answer to the enterprise to say that it had taken all reasonable care"; not subject to the Rylands exceptions. Statutory no-fault liability – MV Act, 1988 s. 164 (₹5 lakh death / ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt); Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 s. 3; Employee's Compensation Act, 1923 s. 3. Vicarious liability – an employer is liable for his employee's tort without any fault of his own (see Vicarious Liability ). Indian courts apply it widely: electricity lines ( M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari , 2002), motor accidents ( Kaushnuma Begum , 2001), toxic waste ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action , 1996).
legalProvision: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1)–(2) – the owner or insurer "shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt"; and "the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt ... was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person."

Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3(1)–(2) – "Where death or injury to any person (other than a workman) or damage to any property has resulted from an accident, the owner shall be liable to reimburse such amount, or provide such other relief as may be prescribed, for— (a) death due to fatal accident; (b) medical expenses incurred due to total or partial disability; (c) loss of wages due to partial disability; (d) other injury or sickness; (e) damage to private property; ..." and "the claimant shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person." (The section heading reads: "Liability to give relief in certain cases on principle of no fault.")

Employee's Compensation Act, 1923, s. 3(1) – "If personal injury is caused to a [employee] by accident arising out of and in the course of his employment, his employer shall be liable to pay compensation in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter ..."

In simple words: Parliament has created several no-fault schemes. The victim need not prove anyone's "wrongful act, neglect or default"; liability follows from the accident itself (motor vehicle use, handling hazardous substances, employment).
hi.meaning: Liability without fault – legal liability for harm imposed without proof of intention or negligence . Strict liability – liability for the escape of a dangerous thing brought on to land, without proof of negligence, but subject to recognised exceptions ( Rylands v. Fletcher ). Absolute liability – liability of a hazardous or inherently dangerous enterprise for harm caused by its activity, with none of the Rylands exceptions ( M.C. Mehta ). Statutory no-fault liability – fixed or limited compensation payable under a statute without proof of fault. Vicarious liability – liability of one person for the tort of another because of their relationship (mainly employer–employee).
keyPoints: No-fault liability: liable though all reasonable care was taken. Rylands (1868): strict, with exceptions; M.C. Mehta (1986): absolute, no exceptions. Shail Kumari (2002): electricity; act of stranger rejected. Kaushnuma (2001): Rylands in motor accidents. MV Act s. 164: ₹5 lakh / ₹2.5 lakh; PLI Act s. 3; EC Act s. 3. Basis: risk + profit + difficulty of proof.

selfTest.q: What is liability without fault?
selfTest.a: Answer: Liability imposed without proof of intention or negligence. Name the case that founded strict liability. Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). How does absolute liability differ from strict liability? Answer: It allows none of the Rylands exceptions ( M.C. Mehta ). Give two reasons for no-fault liability. Answer: The person who creates and profits from a risk should bear its cost; victims cannot prove negligence inside a hazardous process. What did Shail Kumari decide about "act of stranger"? Answer: It fails where the stranger's act should reasonably have been anticipated or its consequences prevented. What did Kaushnuma Begum decide? Answer: Rylands v. Fletcher applies to motor accident claims. How much is payable under MV Act s. 164? Answer: ₹5 lakh on death; ₹2.5 lakh on grievous hurt. Which Act gives no-fault relief for accidents involving hazardous substances? Answer: Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3. Is vicarious liability a form of liability without fault? Answer: Yes – the employer is liable without personal fault. Which case says public-law compensation rests on strict liability? Answer: Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993).

law-of-torts-u1-t10.subtitle: Malice in law and malice in fact, and where malice matters in the law of torts

en.inOneMinute: "Malice" is used in two senses in the law of torts: Malice in law – a wrongful act "done intentionally without just cause or excuse" ( Bromage v. Prosser , per Bayley J, as relied on in Mogul and Quinn ). No spite is needed: "This wilful injuria is in law malicious" ( Wilkinson v. Downton , 1897). Malice in fact (express malice) – spite, ill-will, or any improper motive. General rule: malice in fact (bad motive) is irrelevant . A lawful act does not become a tort because it is done maliciously ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895; Allen v. Flood , as explained in Quinn v. Leathem , 1901); and an unlawful act is not excused because it is done without malice. Exceptions – where malice is an essential ingredient: malicious prosecution; injurious (malicious) falsehood ( Ratcliffe v. Evans , 1892); conspiracy to injure ( Quinn v. Leathem ); defamation, where malice defeats qualified privilege and fair comment; and in nuisance, where a malicious purpose can make a use of land unreasonable. Malice may also increase damages ( aggravated or exemplary damages).
legalProvision: No statute defines malice for the law of torts. The idea is judge-made. One statute recognises a tort in which malice is an essential part:
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Art. 74 – "For compensation for a malicious prosecution" – one year – "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated."
In simple words: Indian statute law itself recognises "malicious prosecution" as a tort with its own time limit – a tort in which malice must be proved.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 356(1) (comparison) – "Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes in any manner, any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person."

In simple words: the criminal offence of defamation turns on an intention to harm or knowledge that harm will result. In the civil wrong of defamation, malice becomes important mainly where the defendant pleads a privilege or fair comment (see Defamation ).
en.meaning: Malice in law (implied malice) – the intentional doing of a wrongful act without just cause or excuse. It is a legal label for a deliberate wrong; it does not mean ill-will. Malice in fact (express or actual malice) – an improper motive: spite, ill-will, revenge, or any purpose other than the one for which the law gives a right or privilege. Motive – the reason for an act. Malice in fact is a bad motive. Intention – what the defendant means to do. A person can act intentionally without malice in fact (e.g., a "joke" in Wilkinson ).
keyPoints: Malice in law: wrongful act "done intentionally without just cause or excuse" ( Bromage v. Prosser ). Malice in fact: spite / improper motive. General rule: malice irrelevant ( Bradford v. Pickles , 1895; Allen v. Flood ). Exceptions: malicious prosecution; injurious falsehood ( Ratcliffe v. Evans , 1892); conspiracy ( Quinn , 1901); privilege/fair comment; nuisance. Wilkinson : "wilful injuria is in law malicious". Malicious prosecution: one year from acquittal (Limitation Act Art. 74).

selfTest.q: What are the two meanings of malice?
selfTest.a: Answer: Malice in law (intentional wrongful act without just cause) and malice in fact (spite / improper motive). Who gave the classic definition of malice in law? Answer: Bayley J in Bromage v. Prosser . State the general rule about malice. Answer: A lawful act does not become a tort because it is done with a bad motive ( Bradford v. Pickles ). Is ill-will needed for malice in law? Answer: No. Name three torts where malice is an ingredient. Answer: Malicious prosecution, injurious falsehood, conspiracy to injure. What did Lord Brampton say about malicious prosecution in Quinn ? Answer: Absence of reasonable cause plus a malicious motive turns a justifiable act into an actionable wrong. What did Ratcliffe v. Evans decide? Answer: A malicious untrue statement about a business causing general loss of trade is actionable. How do Quinn and Mogul differ? Answer: Quinn – purpose to injure (actionable); Mogul – purpose to advance own trade (not actionable). How does malice affect defamation defences? Answer: It defeats qualified privilege and fair comment. Within what time must a suit for malicious prosecution be filed? Answer: One year from acquittal or termination of the prosecution (Art. 74).
