te.inOneMinute: ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత అంటే ఒక వ్యక్తి (A) స్వయంగా ఏ తప్పూ చేయకపోయినా, వారి మధ్య ఉన్న సంబంధం కారణంగా మరొకరు (B) చేసిన టార్ట్‌కు బాధ్యుడు కావడం. రెండు సూక్తులు దీనిని వివరిస్తాయి: qui facit per alium facit per se ("మరొకరి ద్వారా చేసేవాడు స్వయంగా చేసినట్లే") మరియు respondeat superior ("పై అధికారి జవాబు చెప్పాలి"). రెండు అంశాలు చూపించాలి ( Mohamud v. Morrison , 2016; Barclays Bank v. Various Claimants , 2020): ప్రతివాది మరియు తప్పు చేసినవాడి మధ్య సంబంధం – ఉద్యోగం, లేదా "akin to employment" (అర్థం: ఉద్యోగం లాంటి) సంబంధం ( Cox v. Ministry of Justice , 2016); ప్రిన్సిపల్–ఏజెంట్, భాగస్వాములు కూడా; ఆ సంబంధానికి మరియు తప్పుకు మధ్య సంబంధం (connection) – సంప్రదాయంగా టార్ట్ ఉద్యోగ క్రమంలో జరగాలి; ఈరోజు ఉద్యోగంతో "close connection" (అర్థం: సన్నిహిత సంబంధం) ( Lister v. Hesley Hall , 2001). యజమాని బాధ్యుడు: అనుమతించిన చర్యను అనుమతి లేని విధంగా చేసినప్పుడు ( State of Maharashtra v. Kanchanmala , 1995), ఉద్యోగ క్రమంలో చేసిన మోసం లేదా నేరానికి ( SBI v. Shyama Devi , 1978), ఉద్యోగంతో సంబంధం ఉంటే ఆదేశాలకు విరుద్ధంగా చేసిన చర్యలకు కూడా. యజమాని బాధ్యుడు కాదు: సేవకుడు తన ఉద్యోగానికి బయట "frolic of his own" (అర్థం: తన సొంత వినోదం/పని) చేసినప్పుడు ( Shyama Devi – ఉద్యోగి వినియోగదారుడి ఏజెంట్‌గా వ్యవహరించాడు); సాధారణంగా స్వతంత్ర కాంట్రాక్టర్ కు ( Barclays , 2020), విధి ఇతరులకు అప్పగించలేనిది లేదా కార్యకలాపం ప్రమాదకరమైనది అయితే తప్ప. తప్పు చేసినవాడు స్వయంగా బాధ్యుడిగానే ఉంటాడు; యజమాని మరియు ఉద్యోగి సంయుక్తంగా బాధ్యులు.
te.meaning: ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత – మొదటి వ్యక్తి సొంత తప్పు నుంచి కాకుండా, వారి సంబంధం నుంచి ఉత్పన్నమయ్యే, మరొకరి టార్ట్‌కు ఒక వ్యక్తి బాధ్యత. Qui facit per alium facit per se – మరొకరి ద్వారా చర్య చేసేవాడు దానిని స్వయంగా చేసినట్లుగా భావించబడతాడు. Respondeat superior – ప్రిన్సిపల్ (పై అధికారి) బాధ్యుడు కావాలి. సేవకుడు / ఉద్యోగి – సేవా ఒప్పందం ( contract of service ) కింద నియమించబడి, తన పని యజమాని వ్యాపారంలో భాగంగా, అతడి ఆదేశాలకు లోబడి ఉండే వ్యక్తి. స్వతంత్ర కాంట్రాక్టర్ – తన సొంత ఖాతాపై వ్యాపారం చేస్తూ, తన సొంత పద్ధతులతో ఒక ఫలితాన్ని ఇవ్వడానికి అంగీకరించే వ్యక్తి. ఉద్యోగ క్రమం – ఉద్యోగి పని పరిధి; Salmond సూత్రం: "(a) a wrongful act authorised by the master, or (b) a wrongful and unauthorised mode of doing some act authorised by the master" (అర్థం: (a) యజమాని అనుమతించిన తప్పుడు చర్య, లేదా (b) యజమాని అనుమతించిన ఏదైనా చర్యను తప్పుగా, అనుమతి లేని విధంగా చేయడం) ( Lister లో ఉదహరించబడింది).
keyPoints: ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత = సొంత తప్పు లేకుండా మరొకరి టార్ట్‌కు బాధ్యత. సంబంధం + connection ( Mohamud ; Barclays ). ఉద్యోగం లాంటిది వర్తిస్తుంది ( Cox ); స్వతంత్ర కాంట్రాక్టర్ కాదు ( Barclays ). Salmond పరీక్ష; అనుమతించిన చర్య అనుమతి లేని విధానంలో ( Kanchanmala ). సన్నిహిత సంబంధం ( Lister ); seamless episode ( Mohamud ). క్రమంలో మోసం/నేరం → బాధ్యుడు ( Shyama Devi ). భాగస్వాములు s. 26; ఏజెంట్లు s. 238.

selfTest.q: ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: సంబంధం కారణంగా మరొకరి టార్ట్‌కు ఒక వ్యక్తి బాధ్యత. "qui facit per alium facit per se" ను అనువదించండి. జవాబు: మరొకరి ద్వారా చేసేవాడు స్వయంగా చేసినట్లే. ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత రెండు అంశాలు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: ప్రతివాది, తప్పు చేసినవాడి మధ్య సంబంధం; ఆ సంబంధానికి, తప్పుకు మధ్య connection. Salmond పరీక్ష ఏమిటి? జవాబు: యజమాని అనుమతించిన తప్పుడు చర్య, లేదా అనుమతించిన చర్యను తప్పుగా, అనుమతి లేని విధంగా చేయడం. "సన్నిహిత సంబంధ" పరీక్షను ఏ కేసు ప్రవేశపెట్టింది? జవాబు: Lister v. Hesley Hall (2001). Mohamud లో సూపర్‌మార్కెట్ బాధ్యురాలా? జవాబు: అవును – దాడి అటెండెంట్ ఉద్యోగంలో విరామం లేని ఒకే సంఘటన. స్వతంత్ర కాంట్రాక్టర్‌కు యజమాని బాధ్యుడా? జవాబు: సాధారణంగా కాదు ( Barclays , 2020), అప్పగించలేని విధులు మొదలైన సందర్భాలు తప్ప. Kanchanmala ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? జవాబు: అనుమతించిన చర్య (కార్యాలయ పనికి జీప్ ఉపయోగం) అనుమతి లేని విధంగా (క్లర్క్ నడపడం) చేయబడినందుకు రాజ్యం బాధ్యురాలు. సేవకుడి సొంత ప్రయోజనం కోసం చేసిన మోసానికి యజమాని బాధ్యుడా? జవాబు: అవును, ఉద్యోగ క్రమంలో చేస్తే ( Shyama Devi ). భాగస్వామి తప్పుడు చర్యకు సంస్థను బాధ్యురాలిని చేసే సెక్షన్ ఏది? జవాబు: Partnership Act, 1932, s. 26.

hi.inOneMinute: Vicarious liability means that one person (A) is liable for a tort committed by another (B), because of the relationship between them, even though A himself did nothing wrong. Two maxims explain it: qui facit per alium facit per se ("he who acts through another acts himself") and respondeat superior ("let the superior answer"). Two elements must be shown ( Mohamud v. Morrison , 2016; Barclays Bank v. Various Claimants , 2020): a relationship between the defendant and the wrongdoer – employment, or one "akin to employment" ( Cox v. Ministry of Justice , 2016); also principal–agent and partners; a connection between that relationship and the wrong – traditionally, the tort must be committed in the course of employment ; today, a "close connection" with the job ( Lister v. Hesley Hall , 2001). Employer liable: for an authorised act done in an unauthorised manner ( State of Maharashtra v. Kanchanmala , 1995), for fraud or crime committed in the course of employment ( SBI v. Shyama Devi , 1978), and even for acts done against orders if connected with the job. Employer not liable: where the servant acts on a "frolic of his own", outside his job ( Shyama Devi – employee acting as the customer's agent); and generally for an independent contractor ( Barclays , 2020), unless the duty is non- delegable or the activity hazardous. The wrongdoer remains personally liable; employer and employee are jointly liable.
legalProvision: There is no general statute on vicarious liability; it is judge-made. Statutes apply it in particular relationships:

Indian Partnership Act, 1932, s. 26 – "Where, by the wrongful act or omission of a partner acting in the ordinary course of the business of a firm, or with the authority of his partners, loss or injury is caused to any third party, or any penalty is incurred, the firm is liable therefor to the same extent as the partner."

Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 238 – "Misrepresentation made, or frauds committed, by agents acting in the course of their business for their principals, have the same effect on agreements made by such agents as if such misrepresentations or frauds had been made or committed by the principals; but misrepresentations made, or frauds committed, by agents, in matters which do not fall within their authority, do not affect their principals."

Law Reform (Personal Injuries) Act, 1948 (United Kingdom), s. 1(1) – "It shall not be a defence to an employer who is sued in respect of personal injuries caused by the negligence of a person employed by him, that that person was at the time the injuries were caused in common employment with the person injured."

In simple words: a firm answers for its partner, a principal for its agent, and an employer for its employee, when the wrong is done in the course of the business or employment. The old English defence of "common employment" (that the injured worker and the negligent worker had the same employer) was abolished in England in 1948.
hi.meaning: Vicarious liability – liability of one person for the tort of another, arising from their relationship and not from the first person's own fault. Qui facit per alium facit per se – he who does an act through another is deemed to do it himself. Respondeat superior – let the principal (superior) be liable. Servant / employee – a person employed under a contract of service , whose work is part of the employer's business and subject to his direction. Independent contractor – a person who carries on business on his own account and agrees to produce a result, using his own methods. Course of employment – the scope of the employee's job; Salmond's formula: "(a) a wrongful act authorised by the master, or (b) a wrongful and unauthorised mode of doing some act authorised by the master" (quoted in Lister ).
keyPoints: Vicarious liability = liability for another's tort, without own fault. Relationship + connection ( Mohamud ; Barclays ). Akin to employment counts ( Cox ); independent contractor does not ( Barclays ). Salmond test; authorised act in unauthorised manner ( Kanchanmala ). Close connection ( Lister ); seamless episode ( Mohamud ). Fraud/crime in course → liable ( Shyama Devi ). Partners s. 26; agents s. 238.

selfTest.q: What is vicarious liability?
selfTest.a: Answer: Liability of one person for the tort of another because of their relationship. Translate "qui facit per alium facit per se". Answer: He who acts through another acts himself. Name the two elements of vicarious liability. Answer: A relationship between defendant and wrongdoer, and a connection between that relationship and the wrong. What is Salmond's test? Answer: A wrongful act authorised by the master, or a wrongful and unauthorised mode of doing an authorised act. Which case introduced the "close connection" test? Answer: Lister v. Hesley Hall (2001). Was the supermarket liable in Mohamud ? Answer: Yes – the attack was a seamless episode within the attendant's job. Is an employer liable for an independent contractor? Answer: Generally no ( Barclays , 2020), except for non-delegable duties and similar cases. What did Kanchanmala decide? Answer: The State was liable for an authorised act (using the jeep for office work) done in an unauthorised manner (driven by a clerk). Is a master liable for a servant's fraud for the servant's own benefit? Answer: Yes, if committed in the course of employment ( Shyama Devi ). Which section makes a firm liable for a partner's wrongful act? Answer: Partnership Act, 1932, s. 26.

law-of-torts-u2-t1.subtitle: Volenti non fit injuria, plaintiff the wrongdoer, inevitable accident, act of God, private defence, necessity and statutory authority

en.inOneMinute: A general defence is a ground that defeats (or reduces) liability for many torts , even when the plaintiff proves all the ingredients of the tort. A specific defence belongs to one tort only (e.g., truth in defamation). The main general defences are: Volenti non fit injuria – the plaintiff freely consented to the harm or the risk of it. Plaintiff the wrongdoer – a person cannot sue for harm suffered while doing an illegal act, where the claim rests on that illegality. Inevitable accident – an accident that could not have been prevented by reasonable care. Act of God (vis major) – "circumstances which no human foresight can provide against" ( Kaushnuma Begum , 2001). Private defence – reasonable force to protect person or property. Mistake – generally no defence; it helps only in a few torts. Necessity – harm done to prevent a greater harm. Statutory authority – an act authorised by statute, done without negligence. In strict liability ( Rylands ), the recognised exceptions are consent, common benefit, act of stranger, statutory authority, act of God, plaintiff's default and remoteness (listed in Kaushnuma Begum ). In absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ), none of these apply. The burden of proving a defence is on the defendant (e.g., inevitable accident – Pushpabai v. Ranjit Ginning , 1977).
legalProvision: There is no single statute listing defences in tort; they come from judgments. Courts and statutes give guidance:

Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance (2001) , listing the defences to Rylands v. Fletcher : "(1) Consent of the plaintiff i.e. volenti non fit injuria. (2) Common benefit ... (3) Act of stranger i.e. if the escape was caused by the unforeseeable act of a stranger, the rule does not apply. (4) Exercise of statutory authority i.e. the rule will stand excluded either when the act was done under a statutory duty or when a statute provides otherwise. (5) Act of God or vis major i.e. circumstances which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility. (6) Default of the plaintiff i.e. if the damage is caused solely by the act or default of the plaintiff himself, the rule will not apply. (7) Remoteness of consequences ..."

Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), Blackburn J – the defendant "can excuse himself by shewing that the escape was owing to the Plaintiff's default; or, perhaps, that the escape was the consequence of vis major, or the act of God".
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (criminal law, used here only for comparison):

s. 19 – "Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property." (necessity) s. 34 – "Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence." s. 37(2) – "The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence." s. 28(a) – consent is not valid "if the consent is given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact" and the doer knows or has reason to believe it.

In simple words: tort law has its own judge-made defences. The BNS sections show the same ideas in criminal law – necessity, private defence within limits, and consent that must be free – and help explain the tort defences, but they do not by themselves decide a tort case.
en.meaning: General defence – a defence available against many torts . Volenti non fit injuria – "to one who is willing, no wrong is done": free and informed consent to the harm or risk. Plaintiff the wrongdoer ( ex turpi causa non oritur actio ) – no action arises from a base cause: a plaintiff whose claim depends on his own illegal act may fail. Inevitable accident – an accident that could not have been avoided by the exercise of ordinary care, caution and skill. Act of God / vis major – an extraordinary natural event, "which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility" ( Kaushnuma ). Private defence – using reasonable and proportionate force to defend one's person, others, or property. Mistake – acting under an honest but wrong belief of fact or law. Necessity – intentionally causing harm to prevent a greater harm to persons or property. Statutory authority – the defence that the act was authorised by a statute.
keyPoints: Defences are pleaded and proved by the defendant. Volenti: knowledge + free consent; scienti non fit injuria. Inevitable accident: no negligence; Pushpabai (burden), Subhagwanti (rejected). Act of God: extraordinary natural event ( Kaushnuma ). Private defence: proportionate; necessity: prevent greater harm to others. Mistake: generally no defence. Statutory authority: inevitable harm only; never negligence. Rylands has seven exceptions; M.C. Mehta none.

caseLaws.facts: Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. [2001] 1 SCR 8 (3 Jan 2001)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A jeep's front tyre burst; the capsizing jeep hit and killed a pedestrian, Haji Mohammad Hani
caseLaws.facts: The Tribunal and High Court dismissed the claim for want of negligence. Principle: Rylands v. Fletcher applies to motor accidents; the Court listed seven defences – consent, common benefit, act of stranger, statutory authority, act of God, plaintiff's default, remoteness – and held that compensation is payable "unless any one of the exceptions would apply". Why it matters: the Supreme Court's own list and definitions of the defences.
Pushpabai Purshottam Udeshi v. Ranjit Ginning & Pressing Co. (1977) 2 SCC 745; AIR 1977 SC 1735 (25 Mar 1977)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Purshottam Udeshi was travelling in a car driven by the company's Manager; it dashed against
caseLaws.facts: The company pleaded inevitable accident. Principle: res ipsa loquitur applied; "the burden was on the respondents to prove the inevitable accident"; they did not. Why it matters: the defendant must prove inevitable accident.
Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti AIR 1966 SC 1750 (24 Feb 1966)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Clock Tower in Chandni Chowk, about 80 years old and under the Corporation's control, col
caseLaws.facts: Principle: the plea that the fall "was due to an inevitable accident which could not have been prevented by the exercise of reasonable care" was rejected; the Corporation should have inspected the structure. Why it matters: inevitable accident fails where reasonable care could have found the danger.
M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari (2002) 2 SCC 162; AIR 2002 SC 551 (11 Jan 2002)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A cyclist was electrocuted by a live wire on a flooded road; the Board blamed a third person'
caseLaws.facts: Principle: the act-of-stranger exception was not available because the act "should reasonably have been anticipated or at any rate its consequences should have been prevented". Why it matters: limits the act-of-stranger defence.
N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. [1994] Supp. 3 SCR 144 (6 Sep 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Seized foodgrains and fertiliser deteriorated in State custody
caseLaws.facts: Principle: the State is liable for its officers' negligence in discharging statutory duties. Why it matters: statutory authority does not protect negligent performance.

selfTest.q: What is a general defence?
selfTest.a: Answer: A defence available against many torts, as opposed to one tort only. Translate "volenti non fit injuria". Answer: "To one who is willing, no wrong is done." Is knowledge of a risk enough for volenti? Answer: No – free agreement to bear it is needed (scienti non fit injuria). Who must prove inevitable accident? Answer: The defendant ( Pushpabai , 1977). How did the Supreme Court define act of God in Kaushnuma ? Answer: "Circumstances which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility." Is ordinary monsoon rain an act of God? Answer: No; it is foreseeable. How does necessity differ from private defence? Answer: Necessity harms an innocent person to avoid greater harm; private defence is against a wrongdoer. Is mistake a defence in trespass? Answer: Generally no. Does statutory authority protect negligent acts? Answer: No ( Nagendra Rao ). Name the seven exceptions to Rylands listed in Kaushnuma . Answer: Consent, common benefit, act of stranger, statutory authority, act of God, plaintiff's default, remoteness.

te.inOneMinute: సాధారణ రక్షణ (general defence) అంటే వాది టార్ట్ యొక్క అన్ని అంశాలను నిరూపించినా, అనేక టార్ట్‌లలో బాధ్యతను తొలగించే (లేదా తగ్గించే) కారణం. ప్రత్యేక రక్షణ ఒకే టార్ట్‌కు చెందుతుంది (ఉదా: పరువు నష్టంలో సత్యం). ప్రధాన సాధారణ రక్షణలు: వోలెంటి నాన్ ఫిట్ ఇంజురియా – వాది ఆ హానికి లేదా దాని రిస్క్‌కు స్వేచ్ఛగా సమ్మతించాడు. వాదే తప్పు చేసినవాడు – దావా అక్రమ చర్యపై ఆధారపడినప్పుడు, అక్రమ చర్య చేస్తూ పొందిన హానికి వ్యక్తి దావా వేయలేడు. అనివార్య ప్రమాదం – సహేతుక జాగ్రత్తతో నివారించలేని ప్రమాదం. దైవ చర్య (vis major) – "circumstances which no human foresight can provide against" (అర్థం: ఏ మానవ దూరదృష్టీ ముందుగా కాపాడలేని పరిస్థితులు) ( Kaushnuma Begum , 2001). స్వీయ రక్షణ (private defence) – వ్యక్తిని లేదా ఆస్తిని కాపాడటానికి సహేతుక బలం. పొరపాటు – సాధారణంగా రక్షణ కాదు; కొన్ని టార్ట్‌లలో మాత్రమే సహాయపడుతుంది. ఆవశ్యకత (necessity) – ఎక్కువ హానిని నివారించడానికి చేసిన హాని. చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం – చట్టం అనుమతించిన, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేకుండా చేసిన చర్య. కఠిన బాధ్యతలో ( Rylands ) గుర్తింపు పొందిన మినహాయింపులు: సమ్మతి, ఉమ్మడి ప్రయోజనం, అపరిచితుని చర్య, చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం, దైవ చర్య, వాది తప్పు, దూరత్వం ( Kaushnuma Begum లో జాబితా). సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యతలో ( M.C. Mehta ) ఇవేవీ వర్తించవు. రక్షణను నిరూపించే భారం ప్రతివాదిపై ఉంటుంది (ఉదా: అనివార్య ప్రమాదం – Pushpabai v. Ranjit Ginning , 1977).
te.meaning: సాధారణ రక్షణ – అనేక టార్ట్‌లకు వ్యతిరేకంగా అందుబాటులో ఉండే రక్షణ. వోలెంటి నాన్ ఫిట్ ఇంజురియా – "ఇష్టపడిన వ్యక్తికి ఏ తప్పూ జరగదు": హానికి లేదా రిస్క్‌కు స్వేచ్ఛాయుత, తెలిసిన సమ్మతి. వాదే తప్పు చేసినవాడు ( ex turpi causa non oritur actio ) – హీన కారణం నుంచి దావా పుట్టదు: తన సొంత అక్రమ చర్యపై ఆధారపడిన వాది దావా విఫలం కావచ్చు. అనివార్య ప్రమాదం – సాధారణ జాగ్రత్త, మెలకువ, నైపుణ్యంతో నివారించలేని ప్రమాదం. దైవ చర్య / vis major – అసాధారణ సహజ సంఘటన, "which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility" ( Kaushnuma ). స్వీయ రక్షణ – తన శరీరం, ఇతరుల శరీరం లేదా ఆస్తిని కాపాడటానికి సహేతుక, అనుపాత బలాన్ని ఉపయోగించడం. పొరపాటు – వాస్తవం లేదా చట్టం గురించి నిజాయితీగా కానీ తప్పుగా నమ్మి వ్యవహరించడం. ఆవశ్యకత – ఎక్కువ హానిని నివారించడానికి ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా హాని చేయడం. చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం – ఆ చర్యను చట్టం అనుమతించిందనే రక్షణ.
keyPoints: రక్షణలను ప్రతివాది వాదించి నిరూపించాలి. వోలెంటి: తెలియడం + స్వేచ్ఛాయుత సమ్మతి; scienti non fit injuria. అనివార్య ప్రమాదం: నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదు; Pushpabai (భారం), Subhagwanti (తిరస్కరణ). దైవ చర్య: అసాధారణ సహజ సంఘటన ( Kaushnuma ). స్వీయ రక్షణ: అనుపాతం; ఆవశ్యకత: ఇతరులకు ఎక్కువ హాని నివారణ. పొరపాటు: సాధారణంగా రక్షణ కాదు. చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం: అనివార్య హాని మాత్రమే; నిర్లక్ష్యం ఎప్పుడూ కాదు. Rylands కు ఏడు మినహాయింపులు; M.C. Mehta లో ఏవీ లేవు.

selfTest.q: సాధారణ రక్షణ అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: జవాబు: ఒకే టార్ట్‌కు కాకుండా, అనేక టార్ట్‌లకు వ్యతిరేకంగా అందుబాటులో ఉండే రక్షణ. "volenti non fit injuria" ను అనువదించండి. జవాబు: "ఇష్టపడిన వ్యక్తికి ఏ తప్పూ జరగదు." వోలెంటికి రిస్క్ తెలియడం సరిపోతుందా? జవాబు: లేదు – దానిని భరించడానికి స్వేచ్ఛాయుత అంగీకారం కావాలి (scienti non fit injuria). అనివార్య ప్రమాదాన్ని ఎవరు నిరూపించాలి? జవాబు: ప్రతివాది ( Pushpabai , 1977). Kaushnuma లో సుప్రీం కోర్టు దైవ చర్యను ఎలా నిర్వచించింది? జవాబు: "Circumstances which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility." సాధారణ వర్షాకాల వర్షం దైవ చర్యా? జవాబు: కాదు; అది ఊహించదగినది. ఆవశ్యకత స్వీయ రక్షణ నుంచి ఎలా భిన్నం? జవాబు: ఆవశ్యకత ఎక్కువ హానిని తప్పించడానికి నిర్దోషికి హాని చేస్తుంది; స్వీయ రక్షణ తప్పు చేసినవాడికి వ్యతిరేకంగా. అతిక్రమణలో పొరపాటు రక్షణా? జవాబు: సాధారణంగా కాదు. చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం నిర్లక్ష్యపు చర్యలను కాపాడుతుందా? జవాబు: లేదు ( Nagendra Rao ). Kaushnuma లో జాబితా చేసిన Rylands కు ఏడు మినహాయింపులు చెప్పండి. జవాబు: సమ్మతి, ఉమ్మడి ప్రయోజనం, అపరిచితుని చర్య, చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం, దైవ చర్య, వాది తప్పు, దూరత్వం.

hi.inOneMinute: A general defence is a ground that defeats (or reduces) liability for many torts , even when the plaintiff proves all the ingredients of the tort. A specific defence belongs to one tort only (e.g., truth in defamation). The main general defences are: Volenti non fit injuria – the plaintiff freely consented to the harm or the risk of it. Plaintiff the wrongdoer – a person cannot sue for harm suffered while doing an illegal act, where the claim rests on that illegality. Inevitable accident – an accident that could not have been prevented by reasonable care. Act of God (vis major) – "circumstances which no human foresight can provide against" ( Kaushnuma Begum , 2001). Private defence – reasonable force to protect person or property. Mistake – generally no defence; it helps only in a few torts. Necessity – harm done to prevent a greater harm. Statutory authority – an act authorised by statute, done without negligence. In strict liability ( Rylands ), the recognised exceptions are consent, common benefit, act of stranger, statutory authority, act of God, plaintiff's default and remoteness (listed in Kaushnuma Begum ). In absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ), none of these apply. The burden of proving a defence is on the defendant (e.g., inevitable accident – Pushpabai v. Ranjit Ginning , 1977).
legalProvision: There is no single statute listing defences in tort; they come from judgments. Courts and statutes give guidance:

Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance (2001) , listing the defences to Rylands v. Fletcher : "(1) Consent of the plaintiff i.e. volenti non fit injuria. (2) Common benefit ... (3) Act of stranger i.e. if the escape was caused by the unforeseeable act of a stranger, the rule does not apply. (4) Exercise of statutory authority i.e. the rule will stand excluded either when the act was done under a statutory duty or when a statute provides otherwise. (5) Act of God or vis major i.e. circumstances which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility. (6) Default of the plaintiff i.e. if the damage is caused solely by the act or default of the plaintiff himself, the rule will not apply. (7) Remoteness of consequences ..."

Rylands v. Fletcher (1868), Blackburn J – the defendant "can excuse himself by shewing that the escape was owing to the Plaintiff's default; or, perhaps, that the escape was the consequence of vis major, or the act of God".
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (criminal law, used here only for comparison):

s. 19 – "Nothing is an offence merely by reason of its being done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause harm, if it be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and in good faith for the purpose of preventing or avoiding other harm to person or property." (necessity) s. 34 – "Nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence." s. 37(2) – "The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence." s. 28(a) – consent is not valid "if the consent is given by a person under fear of injury, or under a misconception of fact" and the doer knows or has reason to believe it.

In simple words: tort law has its own judge-made defences. The BNS sections show the same ideas in criminal law – necessity, private defence within limits, and consent that must be free – and help explain the tort defences, but they do not by themselves decide a tort case.
hi.meaning: General defence – a defence available against many torts . Volenti non fit injuria – "to one who is willing, no wrong is done": free and informed consent to the harm or risk. Plaintiff the wrongdoer ( ex turpi causa non oritur actio ) – no action arises from a base cause: a plaintiff whose claim depends on his own illegal act may fail. Inevitable accident – an accident that could not have been avoided by the exercise of ordinary care, caution and skill. Act of God / vis major – an extraordinary natural event, "which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility" ( Kaushnuma ). Private defence – using reasonable and proportionate force to defend one's person, others, or property. Mistake – acting under an honest but wrong belief of fact or law. Necessity – intentionally causing harm to prevent a greater harm to persons or property. Statutory authority – the defence that the act was authorised by a statute.
keyPoints: Defences are pleaded and proved by the defendant. Volenti: knowledge + free consent; scienti non fit injuria. Inevitable accident: no negligence; Pushpabai (burden), Subhagwanti (rejected). Act of God: extraordinary natural event ( Kaushnuma ). Private defence: proportionate; necessity: prevent greater harm to others. Mistake: generally no defence. Statutory authority: inevitable harm only; never negligence. Rylands has seven exceptions; M.C. Mehta none.

selfTest.q: What is a general defence?
selfTest.a: Answer: A defence available against many torts, as opposed to one tort only. Translate "volenti non fit injuria". Answer: "To one who is willing, no wrong is done." Is knowledge of a risk enough for volenti? Answer: No – free agreement to bear it is needed (scienti non fit injuria). Who must prove inevitable accident? Answer: The defendant ( Pushpabai , 1977). How did the Supreme Court define act of God in Kaushnuma ? Answer: "Circumstances which no human foresight can provide against and of which human prudence is not bound to recognise the possibility." Is ordinary monsoon rain an act of God? Answer: No; it is foreseeable. How does necessity differ from private defence? Answer: Necessity harms an innocent person to avoid greater harm; private defence is against a wrongdoer. Is mistake a defence in trespass? Answer: Generally no. Does statutory authority protect negligent acts? Answer: No ( Nagendra Rao ). Name the seven exceptions to Rylands listed in Kaushnuma . Answer: Consent, common benefit, act of stranger, statutory authority, act of God, plaintiff's default, remoteness.

law-of-torts-u2-t3.subtitle: Article 300, sovereign and non-sovereign functions, the decline of sovereign immunity, and public law compensation

en.inOneMinute: The State acts only through its servants (police, drivers, clerks, doctors). When a servant commits a tort in the course of employment, the question is: is the State vicariously liable? In England the old rule was "the King can do no wrong", so the Crown could not be sued in tort until the Crown Proceedings Act, 1947 . India never adopted that rule fully. The State's liability comes from a chain of statutes: Government of India Act, 1858 s. 65 → Government of India Act, 1935 s. 176 → Constitution, Art. 300(1) . Each says the Government may be sued "in the like cases" as its predecessor (finally, the East India Company). P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State (1861) drew the line: no liability for acts done in exercise of sovereign functions ; liability for acts that "might be carried on by private individuals" ( non-sovereign functions ). State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati (1962): State liable for a Government jeep driver's negligence. Kasturi Lal v. State of U.P. (1965): State not liable for police losing seized gold, because the power to seize is a sovereign power. This defence is called sovereign immunity . N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. (1994) narrowed the defence to true sovereign acts (defence, war, treaties). Today immunity survives only for these. Separately, for violation of fundamental rights the Supreme Court and High Courts award public law compensation under Arts. 32 and 226, where sovereign immunity does not apply ( Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera , Chandrima Das ).
legalProvision: Constitution of India, Art. 300(1) – "The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of such State enacted by virtue of powers conferred by this Constitution, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted."

Government of India Act, 1935, s. 176(1) – "The Federation may sue or be sued by the name of the Federation of India and a Provincial Government may sue or be sued by the name of the Province, and, without prejudice to the subsequent provisions of this chapter, may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of the Federal or a Provincial Legislature enacted by virtue of powers conferred on that Legislature by this Act, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Secretary of State in Council might have sued or been sued if this Act had not been passed."

Government of India Act, 1858, s. 65 (LXV) – "The Secretary of State in Council shall and may sue and be sued as well in India as in England by the Name of the Secretary of State in Council as a Body Corporate; and all Persons and Bodies Politic shall and may have and take the same Suits, Remedies, and Proceedings, legal and equitable, against the Secretary of State in Council of India as they could have done against the said Company..."

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 80(1) – no suit "shall be instituted against the Government ... or against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done by such public officer in his official capacity, until the expiration of two months next after notice in writing has been delivered to, or left at the office of" the specified officer.

Constitution, Arts. 32 and 226 – the Supreme Court and High Courts may issue directions, orders or writs; these are the basis of public law compensation for breach of fundamental rights (especially Art. 21).
en.meaning: Liability of the State for torts – the liability of the Union or a State Government to pay damages for torts committed by its servants in the course of their employment. It is a form of vicarious liability . Sovereign immunity – the defence that the State is not liable for a tort committed by its servant while exercising a sovereign power of the State. Sovereign function – a function that only the State, as sovereign, can perform, and that a private person cannot carry on: e.g. defence of the country, making war and peace, treaties. Kasturi Lal also treated statutory powers of arrest, search and seizure as sovereign. Non-sovereign function – an activity that "might be carried on by private individuals" (e.g. running a dockyard, driving vehicles, trade, public works). The State is liable for torts in these like any employer. Public law compensation – money ordered by the Supreme Court (Art. 32) or a High Court (Art. 226) against the State for violation of a fundamental right. Nilabati Behera calls it a remedy "based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply".
keyPoints: Art. 300(1): the State may be sued "in the like cases" as before 1950; the chain goes back to the 1858 Act and the East India Company. P. & O. (1861): sovereign acts immune; acts a private person could do are not. Vidyawati (1962): State liable for a jeep driver's negligence. Kasturi Lal (1965): seizure by police held sovereign; State immune. Nagendra Rao (1994): only core sovereign acts (defence, war, treaties) immune. Chandrima Das (2000): Kasturi Lal 's theory "no longer available in a welfare State". Public law compensation ( Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera ): sovereign immunity does not apply. CPC s. 80: two months' notice before suing the Government.

Why it matters: first Supreme Court ruling that the State is liable for non-sovereign torts of its servants.

Why it matters: clearest statement that sovereign immunity is no answer to a fundamental-rights claim.
N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. [1994] Supp. 3 SCR 144 (6 Sep 1994)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Any watertight compartmentalisation of the functions of the State as 'sovereign and non-sovereign' ... is not sound"; immunity only for acts like defence and war; "But there the immunity ends." The State was liable. Why it matters: modern test; Kasturi Lal confined.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Hanuffa Khatoon, a Bangladeshi national, was gang-raped by Railway employees in a room at Yat
caseLaws.facts: The Calcutta High Court awarded ₹10 lacs. Principle: Art. 21 protects non-citizens too; the Railways were liable; Kasturi Lal 's sovereign-power theory "is no longer available in a welfare State". Appeal dismissed. Why it matters: latest word: sovereign immunity cannot shield the State from serious wrongs by its employees.

selfTest.q: Which Article lets the Union and States be sued?
selfTest.a: Art. 300(1). What phrase in Art. 300(1) links it to earlier law? "in the like cases". Which section of the 1858 Act was the starting point? Section 65. State the P. & O. test. Sovereign acts immune; acts that private individuals could do are not. Why was the State liable in Vidyawati ? Driving a jeep back from repairs was not a sovereign act. Why did Kasturi Lal fail? Arrest, search and seizure were held to be sovereign powers. What English Act did Kasturi Lal suggest copying? Crown Proceedings Act, 1947. Which acts remain immune after Nagendra Rao ? Core sovereign acts like defence, raising armed forces, making war and peace. Does sovereign immunity apply to compensation under Art. 32? No (Nilabati Behera). What notice is needed before suing the Government? Two months' written notice under CPC s. 80.

te.inOneMinute: రాజ్యం (State) తన ఉద్యోగుల ద్వారా మాత్రమే పనిచేస్తుంది (పోలీసులు, డ్రైవర్లు, క్లర్కులు, డాక్టర్లు). ఉద్యోగి తన ఉద్యోగ పరిధిలో టార్ట్ చేస్తే, రాజ్యం ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత (vicarious liability) వహిస్తుందా? అనేదే ప్రశ్న. ఇంగ్లండ్‌లో పాత నియమం "the King can do no wrong" (అర్థం: రాజు తప్పు చేయలేడు). కాబట్టి Crown Proceedings Act, 1947 వచ్చేవరకు Crown పై టార్ట్ దావా వేయలేరు. భారతదేశం ఆ నియమాన్ని పూర్తిగా స్వీకరించలేదు. రాజ్యం బాధ్యత ఒక చట్టాల గొలుసు నుండి వస్తుంది: Government of India Act, 1858 s. 65 → Government of India Act, 1935 s. 176 → రాజ్యాంగం Art. 300(1) . ప్రతి ఒక్కటీ ప్రభుత్వంపై "in the like cases" (అర్థం: అదే రకమైన కేసుల్లో) దాని ముందున్న దానిపై లాగే దావా వేయవచ్చని చెబుతుంది (చివరికి East India Company). P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State (1861) గీత గీసింది: సార్వభౌమ విధుల నిర్వహణలో చేసిన చర్యలకు బాధ్యత లేదు; "might be carried on by private individuals" (అర్థం: ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తులు కూడా నిర్వహించగలిగే) చర్యలకు బాధ్యత ఉంది ( సార్వభౌమేతర విధులు ). State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati (1962): ప్రభుత్వ జీప్ డ్రైవర్ నిర్లక్ష్యానికి రాజ్యం బాధ్యత వహించింది. Kasturi Lal v. State of U.P. (1965): స్వాధీనం చేసుకున్న బంగారాన్ని పోలీసులు పోగొట్టినందుకు రాజ్యం బాధ్యత వహించలేదు , ఎందుకంటే స్వాధీనం చేసుకునే అధికారం సార్వభౌమ అధికారం. ఈ రక్షణను సార్వభౌమ మినహాయింపు అంటారు. N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. (1994) ఈ రక్షణను నిజమైన సార్వభౌమ చర్యలకు (రక్షణ, యుద్ధం, ఒప్పందాలు) మాత్రమే పరిమితం చేసింది. నేడు మినహాయింపు వీటికి మాత్రమే మిగిలింది. దీనికి వేరుగా, ప్రాథమిక హక్కుల ఉల్లంఘనకు సుప్రీంకోర్టు, హైకోర్టులు Arts. 32, 226 కింద ప్రజా చట్ట పరిహారం ఇస్తాయి; అక్కడ సార్వభౌమ మినహాయింపు వర్తించదు ( Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera , Chandrima Das ).
te.meaning: టార్ట్‌లకు రాజ్యం బాధ్యత – తన ఉద్యోగులు ఉద్యోగ పరిధిలో చేసిన టార్ట్‌లకు కేంద్ర లేదా రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం నష్టపరిహారం చెల్లించే బాధ్యత. ఇది ప్రాతినిధ్య బాధ్యత యొక్క ఒక రూపం. సార్వభౌమ మినహాయింపు – రాజ్యపు సార్వభౌమ అధికారం వినియోగిస్తూ ఉద్యోగి చేసిన టార్ట్‌కు రాజ్యం బాధ్యత వహించదనే రక్షణ. సార్వభౌమ విధి – సార్వభౌముడిగా రాజ్యం మాత్రమే చేయగలిగిన, ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తి చేయలేని విధి: ఉదా. దేశ రక్షణ, యుద్ధం మరియు శాంతి, ఒప్పందాలు. Kasturi Lal అరెస్ట్, సోదా, స్వాధీన చట్టబద్ధ అధికారాలను కూడా సార్వభౌమంగా పరిగణించింది. సార్వభౌమేతర విధి – "might be carried on by private individuals" (అర్థం: ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తులు కూడా నిర్వహించగలిగే) కార్యకలాపం (ఉదా. డాక్‌యార్డ్ నడపడం, వాహనాలు నడపడం, వ్యాపారం, ప్రజా పనులు). వీటిలో టార్ట్‌లకు రాజ్యం ఏ యజమానిలాగే బాధ్యత వహిస్తుంది. ప్రజా చట్ట పరిహారం – ప్రాథమిక హక్కు ఉల్లంఘనకు సుప్రీంకోర్టు (Art. 32) లేదా హైకోర్టు (Art. 226) రాజ్యంపై విధించే డబ్బు. Nilabati Behera దీనిని "based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply" (అర్థం: ప్రాథమిక హక్కుల ఉల్లంఘనకు కఠిన బాధ్యతపై ఆధారపడినది, దీనికి సార్వభౌమ మినహాయింపు సూత్రం వర్తించదు) అని చెప్పింది.
keyPoints: Art. 300(1): 1950 ముందులాగే "in the like cases" (అర్థం: అదే రకమైన కేసుల్లో) రాజ్యంపై దావా వేయవచ్చు; ఆ గొలుసు 1858 Act, East India Company వరకు వెళ్తుంది. P. & O. (1861): సార్వభౌమ చర్యలకు మినహాయింపు; ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తి చేయగలిగే చర్యలకు లేదు. Vidyawati (1962): జీప్ డ్రైవర్ నిర్లక్ష్యానికి రాజ్యం బాధ్యత. Kasturi Lal (1965): పోలీసు స్వాధీనం సార్వభౌమంగా పరిగణన; రాజ్యానికి మినహాయింపు. Nagendra Rao (1994): కేంద్ర సార్వభౌమ చర్యలకు (రక్షణ, యుద్ధం, ఒప్పందాలు) మాత్రమే మినహాయింపు. Chandrima Das (2000): Kasturi Lal సిద్ధాంతం "no longer available in a welfare State" (అర్థం: సంక్షేమ రాజ్యంలో ఇక అందుబాటులో లేదు). ప్రజా చట్ట పరిహారం ( Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera ): సార్వభౌమ మినహాయింపు వర్తించదు. CPC s. 80: ప్రభుత్వంపై దావాకు ముందు రెండు నెలల నోటీసు.

selfTest.q: కేంద్రం, రాష్ట్రాలపై దావా వేయడానికి ఏ Article అనుమతిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: Art. 300(1). Art. 300(1) లో ఏ పదబంధం దానిని పాత చట్టంతో కలుపుతుంది? "in the like cases" (అర్థం: అదే రకమైన కేసుల్లో). 1858 Act లోని ఏ సెక్షన్ ప్రారంభ బిందువు? సెక్షన్ 65. P. & O. పరీక్షను చెప్పండి. సార్వభౌమ చర్యలకు మినహాయింపు; ప్రైవేట్ వ్యక్తులు చేయగలిగే చర్యలకు లేదు. Vidyawati లో రాజ్యం ఎందుకు బాధ్యత వహించింది? మరమ్మతుల తర్వాత జీప్ తిరిగి నడపడం సార్వభౌమ చర్య కాదు. Kasturi Lal ఎందుకు విఫలమైంది? అరెస్ట్, సోదా, స్వాధీనం సార్వభౌమ అధికారాలుగా పరిగణించారు. Kasturi Lal ఏ ఇంగ్లీష్ చట్టాన్ని అనుసరించాలని సూచించింది? Crown Proceedings Act, 1947. Nagendra Rao తర్వాత ఏ చర్యలకు మినహాయింపు మిగిలింది? రక్షణ, సైన్య ఏర్పాటు, యుద్ధం మరియు శాంతి వంటి కేంద్ర సార్వభౌమ చర్యలు. Art. 32 కింద పరిహారానికి సార్వభౌమ మినహాయింపు వర్తిస్తుందా? లేదు (Nilabati Behera). ప్రభుత్వంపై దావాకు ముందు ఏ నోటీసు అవసరం? CPC s. 80 కింద రెండు నెలల లిఖితపూర్వక నోటీసు.

hi.inOneMinute: The State acts only through its servants (police, drivers, clerks, doctors). When a servant commits a tort in the course of employment, the question is: is the State vicariously liable? In England the old rule was "the King can do no wrong", so the Crown could not be sued in tort until the Crown Proceedings Act, 1947 . India never adopted that rule fully. The State's liability comes from a chain of statutes: Government of India Act, 1858 s. 65 → Government of India Act, 1935 s. 176 → Constitution, Art. 300(1) . Each says the Government may be sued "in the like cases" as its predecessor (finally, the East India Company). P. & O. Steam Navigation Co. v. Secretary of State (1861) drew the line: no liability for acts done in exercise of sovereign functions ; liability for acts that "might be carried on by private individuals" ( non-sovereign functions ). State of Rajasthan v. Vidyawati (1962): State liable for a Government jeep driver's negligence. Kasturi Lal v. State of U.P. (1965): State not liable for police losing seized gold, because the power to seize is a sovereign power. This defence is called sovereign immunity . N. Nagendra Rao & Co. v. State of A.P. (1994) narrowed the defence to true sovereign acts (defence, war, treaties). Today immunity survives only for these. Separately, for violation of fundamental rights the Supreme Court and High Courts award public law compensation under Arts. 32 and 226, where sovereign immunity does not apply ( Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera , Chandrima Das ).
legalProvision: Constitution of India, Art. 300(1) – "The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of such State enacted by virtue of powers conferred by this Constitution, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted."

Government of India Act, 1935, s. 176(1) – "The Federation may sue or be sued by the name of the Federation of India and a Provincial Government may sue or be sued by the name of the Province, and, without prejudice to the subsequent provisions of this chapter, may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of the Federal or a Provincial Legislature enacted by virtue of powers conferred on that Legislature by this Act, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Secretary of State in Council might have sued or been sued if this Act had not been passed."

Government of India Act, 1858, s. 65 (LXV) – "The Secretary of State in Council shall and may sue and be sued as well in India as in England by the Name of the Secretary of State in Council as a Body Corporate; and all Persons and Bodies Politic shall and may have and take the same Suits, Remedies, and Proceedings, legal and equitable, against the Secretary of State in Council of India as they could have done against the said Company..."

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 80(1) – no suit "shall be instituted against the Government ... or against a public officer in respect of any act purporting to be done by such public officer in his official capacity, until the expiration of two months next after notice in writing has been delivered to, or left at the office of" the specified officer.

Constitution, Arts. 32 and 226 – the Supreme Court and High Courts may issue directions, orders or writs; these are the basis of public law compensation for breach of fundamental rights (especially Art. 21).
hi.meaning: Liability of the State for torts – the liability of the Union or a State Government to pay damages for torts committed by its servants in the course of their employment. It is a form of vicarious liability . Sovereign immunity – the defence that the State is not liable for a tort committed by its servant while exercising a sovereign power of the State. Sovereign function – a function that only the State, as sovereign, can perform, and that a private person cannot carry on: e.g. defence of the country, making war and peace, treaties. Kasturi Lal also treated statutory powers of arrest, search and seizure as sovereign. Non-sovereign function – an activity that "might be carried on by private individuals" (e.g. running a dockyard, driving vehicles, trade, public works). The State is liable for torts in these like any employer. Public law compensation – money ordered by the Supreme Court (Art. 32) or a High Court (Art. 226) against the State for violation of a fundamental right. Nilabati Behera calls it a remedy "based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply".
keyPoints: Art. 300(1): the State may be sued "in the like cases" as before 1950; the chain goes back to the 1858 Act and the East India Company. P. & O. (1861): sovereign acts immune; acts a private person could do are not. Vidyawati (1962): State liable for a jeep driver's negligence. Kasturi Lal (1965): seizure by police held sovereign; State immune. Nagendra Rao (1994): only core sovereign acts (defence, war, treaties) immune. Chandrima Das (2000): Kasturi Lal 's theory "no longer available in a welfare State". Public law compensation ( Rudul Sah , Nilabati Behera ): sovereign immunity does not apply. CPC s. 80: two months' notice before suing the Government.

caseLaws.facts: The Calcutta High Court awarded ₹10 lacs. Why it matters: latest word: sovereign immunity cannot shield the State from serious wrongs by its employees.

selfTest.q: Which Article lets the Union and States be sued?
selfTest.a: Art. 300(1). What phrase in Art. 300(1) links it to earlier law? "in the like cases". Which section of the 1858 Act was the starting point? Section 65. State the P. & O. test. Sovereign acts immune; acts that private individuals could do are not. Why was the State liable in Vidyawati ? Driving a jeep back from repairs was not a sovereign act. Why did Kasturi Lal fail? Arrest, search and seizure were held to be sovereign powers. What English Act did Kasturi Lal suggest copying? Crown Proceedings Act, 1947. Which acts remain immune after Nagendra Rao ? Core sovereign acts like defence, raising armed forces, making war and peace. Does sovereign immunity apply to compensation under Art. 32? No (Nilabati Behera). What notice is needed before suing the Government? Two months' written notice under CPC s. 80.

law-of-torts-u2-t7.subtitle: The duty of an occupier of premises to people who enter them, children and the public on the highway

en.inOneMinute: Occupiers' liability is the liability of the person in control of premises (the occupier ) for injury caused to people who enter the premises, because of the state of the premises or things done on them. The occupier is the person who controls the premises, not necessarily the owner. A tenant in possession is usually the occupier; the landlord usually is not. The common law grouped entrants into invitees (enter on business of common interest), licensees (enter with permission only), trespassers (no permission), and persons entering as of right (e.g. a public park). The duty was highest to invitees and lowest to trespassers. Children get special protection. An "object of attraction" in a frequented place "may well constitute a trap" ( Glasgow Corporation v. Taylor , 1921: a seven-year-old died after eating poisonous berries in a public park). An owner of a structure beside a highway has a "special obligation" for its safety; it is "no defence" that the defect was latent ( MCD v. Subhagwanti , 1966: Clock Tower collapse in Chandni Chowk). India has no occupiers' liability statute . Indian courts apply the common law and the general duty of care in negligence ( Donoghue v. Stevenson ).
legalProvision: There is no Indian statute on occupiers' liability. The law is judge-made, drawn from:

the common law rules on invitees, licensees and trespassers, and on children; the general law of negligence: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932); the special rule for structures beside a highway ( MCD v. Subhagwanti , 1966).

For comparison only: in England, the Occupiers' Liability Act, 1957 replaced the invitee/licensee distinction with a single "common duty of care" to all lawful visitors, and the Occupiers' Liability Act, 1984 set out the duty to trespassers. These Acts do not apply in India.
en.meaning: Occupiers' liability – liability of an occupier for harm suffered by persons on the premises because of the dangerous condition of the premises or of things on them. Occupier – the person who has control over the premises and so can decide who enters and can make them safe. Ownership is not necessary; more than one person can be an occupier. Premises – land and buildings, and also structures and things on them (e.g. a lift, a scaffold, a swimming pool, a clock tower). Invitee – a person who enters on business in which he and the occupier share an interest (a customer in a shop, a patient in a clinic). Licensee – a person who enters with the occupier's permission, express or implied, but for his own purpose (a guest at home, a person taking a short cut with permission). Trespasser – a person who enters without any permission or right. Entrant as of right – a person who enters under a legal right, e.g. a member of the public in a public park. Glasgow Corporation : the child was in the gardens "not merely as a licensee but as of right".
keyPoints: Occupier = person in control, not necessarily the owner. Duty is reasonable care; varies with the type of entrant at common law. Invitee: unusual dangers; licensee: concealed dangers known; trespasser: no intentional or reckless harm. Children: allurement may be a trap ( Glasgow Corporation ). Familiar and obvious dangers: owner may rely on parents (Lord Shaw). Highway structures: special obligation; latent defect no defence ( Subhagwanti ). Defences: warning, volenti, contributory negligence. India has no occupiers' liability statute; the English Acts of 1957 and 1984 are not Indian law.

Why it matters: the leading Indian case on an occupier's duty to passers-by.

selfTest.q: Who is an occupier?
selfTest.a: The person in control of the premises. Is the landlord of a let house usually the occupier? No, the tenant in possession is. Define an invitee. A person entering on business of common interest with the occupier. What duty is owed to a licensee? To warn of concealed dangers the occupier knows of. What happened in Glasgow Corporation v. Taylor ? A seven-year-old died after eating poisonous berries in a public park. What did Lord Shaw say about familiar and obvious dangers? The owner may assume reasonable parents will protect their children from them. What is the rule for structures beside a highway? Special obligation; owner liable even for latent defects (Subhagwanti). Which doctrine of evidence did Subhagwanti apply? Res ipsa loquitur. Name two defences. Adequate warning; volenti non fit injuria (also contributory negligence). Does India have an occupiers' liability statute? No.

te.inOneMinute: ఆక్రమణదారుల బాధ్యత అంటే ఆవరణ స్థితి వల్ల లేదా దానిపై చేసిన పనుల వల్ల, ఆవరణలోకి ప్రవేశించే వ్యక్తులకు కలిగే గాయానికి ఆవరణపై నియంత్రణ ఉన్న వ్యక్తి ( ఆక్రమణదారు ) బాధ్యత. ఆక్రమణదారు అంటే ఆవరణను నియంత్రించే వ్యక్తి; తప్పనిసరిగా యజమాని కాదు. స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న అద్దెదారు సాధారణంగా ఆక్రమణదారు; భూస్వామి సాధారణంగా కాదు. కామన్ లా ప్రవేశించేవారిని ఇలా విభజించింది: ఆహ్వానితులు (ఉమ్మడి ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యాపారంపై వచ్చేవారు), అనుమతిదారులు (కేవలం అనుమతితో వచ్చేవారు), అతిక్రమణదారులు (అనుమతి లేనివారు), హక్కుగా ప్రవేశించేవారు (ఉదా. ప్రజా పార్కు). విధి ఆహ్వానితులకు ఎక్కువ, అతిక్రమణదారులకు తక్కువ. పిల్లలకు ప్రత్యేక రక్షణ ఉంది. జనం తిరిగే ప్రదేశంలో ఒక "object of attraction" (అర్థం: ఆకర్షించే వస్తువు) "may well constitute a trap" (అర్థం: ఉచ్చు కావచ్చు) ( Glasgow Corporation v. Taylor , 1921: ఒక ప్రజా పార్కులో విషపు పండ్లు తిని ఏడేళ్ల బాలుడు మరణించాడు). రహదారి పక్కన కట్టడం ఉన్న యజమానికి దాని భద్రతపై "special obligation" (అర్థం: ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యత) ఉంది; లోపం దాగి ఉన్నదని చెప్పడం "no defence" (అర్థం: రక్షణ కాదు) ( MCD v. Subhagwanti , 1966: చాందినీ చౌక్ క్లాక్ టవర్ కూలిపోవడం). భారతదేశంలో ఆక్రమణదారుల బాధ్యతపై చట్టం లేదు . భారత కోర్టులు కామన్ లా ను, నిర్లక్ష్యంలోని సాధారణ జాగ్రత్త విధిని ( Donoghue v. Stevenson ) అన్వయిస్తాయి.
te.meaning: ఆక్రమణదారుల బాధ్యత – ఆవరణ లేదా దానిపై ఉన్న వస్తువుల ప్రమాదకర స్థితి వల్ల ఆవరణలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తులకు కలిగే హానికి ఆక్రమణదారు బాధ్యత. ఆక్రమణదారు – ఆవరణపై నియంత్రణ ఉండి, ఎవరు ప్రవేశించాలో నిర్ణయించగల, దానిని సురక్షితంగా చేయగల వ్యక్తి. యాజమాన్యం అవసరం లేదు; ఒకరికి మించి ఆక్రమణదారులు ఉండవచ్చు. ఆవరణ – భూమి, భవనాలు, వాటిపై ఉన్న కట్టడాలు, వస్తువులు (ఉదా. లిఫ్ట్, పరంజా, ఈత కొలను, క్లాక్ టవర్). ఆహ్వానితుడు – తనకూ ఆక్రమణదారుకూ ఉమ్మడి ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యాపారంపై ప్రవేశించే వ్యక్తి (దుకాణంలో కస్టమర్, క్లినిక్‌లో రోగి). అనుమతిదారుడు – ఆక్రమణదారు అనుమతితో (స్పష్టమైన లేదా సూచించిన), కానీ తన స్వంత ప్రయోజనం కోసం ప్రవేశించే వ్యక్తి (ఇంట్లో అతిథి, అనుమతితో షార్ట్‌కట్ తీసుకునే వ్యక్తి). అతిక్రమణదారుడు – ఏ అనుమతి లేదా హక్కు లేకుండా ప్రవేశించే వ్యక్తి. హక్కుగా ప్రవేశించేవాడు – చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు కింద ప్రవేశించే వ్యక్తి, ఉదా. ప్రజా పార్కులో ప్రజా సభ్యుడు. Glasgow Corporation : బాలుడు తోటల్లో "not merely as a licensee but as of right" (అర్థం: కేవలం అనుమతిదారుడిగా కాదు, హక్కుగా) ఉన్నాడు.
keyPoints: ఆక్రమణదారు = నియంత్రణ ఉన్న వ్యక్తి, తప్పనిసరిగా యజమాని కాదు. విధి సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త; కామన్ లా లో ప్రవేశకుడి రకాన్ని బట్టి మారుతుంది. ఆహ్వానితుడు: అసాధారణ ప్రమాదాలు; అనుమతిదారుడు: తెలిసిన దాగి ఉన్న ప్రమాదాలు; అతిక్రమణదారుడు: ఉద్దేశపూర్వక లేదా బేఖాతరు హాని కూడదు. పిల్లలు: ఆకర్షణ ఉచ్చు కావచ్చు ( Glasgow Corporation ). సుపరిచిత, స్పష్టమైన ప్రమాదాలు: యజమాని తల్లిదండ్రులపై ఆధారపడవచ్చు (Lord Shaw). రహదారి కట్టడాలు: ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యత; దాగి ఉన్న లోపం రక్షణ కాదు ( Subhagwanti ). రక్షణలు: హెచ్చరిక, volenti, సహకార నిర్లక్ష్యం. భారతదేశంలో ఆక్రమణదారుల బాధ్యత చట్టం లేదు; 1957, 1984 ఇంగ్లీష్ చట్టాలు భారత చట్టం కాదు.

selfTest.q: ఆక్రమణదారు ఎవరు?
selfTest.a: ఆవరణపై నియంత్రణ ఉన్న వ్యక్తి. అద్దెకిచ్చిన ఇంటి భూస్వామి సాధారణంగా ఆక్రమణదారా? కాదు, స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న అద్దెదారు. ఆహ్వానితుడిని నిర్వచించండి. ఆక్రమణదారుతో ఉమ్మడి ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యాపారంపై ప్రవేశించే వ్యక్తి. అనుమతిదారుడి పట్ల ఏ విధి ఉంది? ఆక్రమణదారుకు తెలిసిన దాగి ఉన్న ప్రమాదాల గురించి హెచ్చరించడం. Glasgow Corporation v. Taylor లో ఏమి జరిగింది? ఒక ప్రజా పార్కులో విషపు పండ్లు తిని ఏడేళ్ల బాలుడు మరణించాడు. సుపరిచిత, స్పష్టమైన ప్రమాదాల గురించి Lord Shaw ఏమి చెప్పారు? సహేతుక తల్లిదండ్రులు వాటి నుండి పిల్లలను కాపాడతారని యజమాని భావించవచ్చు. రహదారి పక్కన కట్టడాలకు నియమం ఏమిటి? ప్రత్యేక బాధ్యత; దాగి ఉన్న లోపాలకు కూడా యజమాని బాధ్యుడు (Subhagwanti). Subhagwanti ఏ సాక్ష్య సిద్ధాంతాన్ని అన్వయించింది? Res ipsa loquitur. రెండు రక్షణలు చెప్పండి. తగిన హెచ్చరిక; volenti non fit injuria (సహకార నిర్లక్ష్యం కూడా). భారతదేశంలో ఆక్రమణదారుల బాధ్యత చట్టం ఉందా? లేదు.

hi.inOneMinute: Occupiers' liability is the liability of the person in control of premises (the occupier ) for injury caused to people who enter the premises, because of the state of the premises or things done on them. The occupier is the person who controls the premises, not necessarily the owner. A tenant in possession is usually the occupier; the landlord usually is not. The common law grouped entrants into invitees (enter on business of common interest), licensees (enter with permission only), trespassers (no permission), and persons entering as of right (e.g. a public park). The duty was highest to invitees and lowest to trespassers. Children get special protection. An "object of attraction" in a frequented place "may well constitute a trap" ( Glasgow Corporation v. Taylor , 1921: a seven-year-old died after eating poisonous berries in a public park). An owner of a structure beside a highway has a "special obligation" for its safety; it is "no defence" that the defect was latent ( MCD v. Subhagwanti , 1966: Clock Tower collapse in Chandni Chowk). India has no occupiers' liability statute . Indian courts apply the common law and the general duty of care in negligence ( Donoghue v. Stevenson ).
legalProvision: There is no Indian statute on occupiers' liability. The law is judge-made, drawn from:

the common law rules on invitees, licensees and trespassers, and on children; the general law of negligence: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932); the special rule for structures beside a highway ( MCD v. Subhagwanti , 1966).

For comparison only: in England, the Occupiers' Liability Act, 1957 replaced the invitee/licensee distinction with a single "common duty of care" to all lawful visitors, and the Occupiers' Liability Act, 1984 set out the duty to trespassers. These Acts do not apply in India.
hi.meaning: Occupiers' liability – liability of an occupier for harm suffered by persons on the premises because of the dangerous condition of the premises or of things on them. Occupier – the person who has control over the premises and so can decide who enters and can make them safe. Ownership is not necessary; more than one person can be an occupier. Premises – land and buildings, and also structures and things on them (e.g. a lift, a scaffold, a swimming pool, a clock tower). Invitee – a person who enters on business in which he and the occupier share an interest (a customer in a shop, a patient in a clinic). Licensee – a person who enters with the occupier's permission, express or implied, but for his own purpose (a guest at home, a person taking a short cut with permission). Trespasser – a person who enters without any permission or right. Entrant as of right – a person who enters under a legal right, e.g. a member of the public in a public park. Glasgow Corporation : the child was in the gardens "not merely as a licensee but as of right".
keyPoints: Occupier = person in control, not necessarily the owner. Duty is reasonable care; varies with the type of entrant at common law. Invitee: unusual dangers; licensee: concealed dangers known; trespasser: no intentional or reckless harm. Children: allurement may be a trap ( Glasgow Corporation ). Familiar and obvious dangers: owner may rely on parents (Lord Shaw). Highway structures: special obligation; latent defect no defence ( Subhagwanti ). Defences: warning, volenti, contributory negligence. India has no occupiers' liability statute; the English Acts of 1957 and 1984 are not Indian law.

selfTest.q: Who is an occupier?
selfTest.a: The person in control of the premises. Is the landlord of a let house usually the occupier? No, the tenant in possession is. Define an invitee. A person entering on business of common interest with the occupier. What duty is owed to a licensee? To warn of concealed dangers the occupier knows of. What happened in Glasgow Corporation v. Taylor ? A seven-year-old died after eating poisonous berries in a public park. What did Lord Shaw say about familiar and obvious dangers? The owner may assume reasonable parents will protect their children from them. What is the rule for structures beside a highway? Special obligation; owner liable even for latent defects (Subhagwanti). Which doctrine of evidence did Subhagwanti apply? Res ipsa loquitur. Name two defences. Adequate warning; volenti non fit injuria (also contributory negligence). Does India have an occupiers' liability statute? No.

law-of-torts-u2-t5.subtitle: The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher: its elements, its defences, and its place in Indian law

en.inOneMinute: Strict liability means liability without proof of negligence . The defendant is liable even if he took every care. It comes from Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). Blackburn J.'s rule: a person who "for his own purposes, brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril". Essentials: (1) a dangerous thing brought and kept on land, (2) a non-natural use of land, (3) escape of the thing, (4) damage that is the natural consequence of the escape. Seven exceptions (listed in Kaushnuma Begum , 2001): consent of the plaintiff; common benefit; act of a stranger; statutory authority; act of God (vis major); default of the plaintiff; remoteness of consequences. In India the rule is applied to electricity supply ( M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari , 2002) and motor accidents ( Kaushnuma Begum ). For hazardous industries India goes further: absolute liability with no exceptions ( M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , 1987). See Rule of Absolute Liability (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India) .
legalProvision: The rule of strict liability is a common law rule made by judges; no Indian statute enacts it. Indian courts apply it as part of the law of torts.
Related statutory rules that work on the same idea (liability without proof of fault):

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1) – "Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or instrument having the force of law, the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be." Under s. 164(2) the claimant need not plead or prove negligence.
Note: Kaushnuma Begum (2001) referred to the old s. 140 ("no fault liability"). Section 140 has since been omitted from the Act; the fixed-sum no-fault scheme is now in s. 164.
en.meaning: Strict liability – liability imposed without proof of negligence or intention, for harm caused by the escape of a dangerous thing kept by the defendant; subject to recognised exceptions. Shail Kumari : the defendant "is held liable irrespective of whether he could have avoided the particular harm by taking precautions." The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher (Blackburn J., approved by the House of Lords) – "the person who, for his own purposes, brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril; and if he does not do so, is primâ facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape." Non-natural use – Lord Cairns: using land "for the purpose of introducing into the close that which in its natural condition was not in or upon it". Later understood as a special use that brings increased danger to others, not the ordinary use of land. Escape – the dangerous thing moves from the place under the defendant's control to a place outside it.
keyPoints: Strict liability = liability without proof of negligence. Origin: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). Essentials: dangerous thing, non-natural use, escape, damage. Seven exceptions: consent, common benefit, act of stranger, statutory authority, act of God, plaintiff's default, remoteness. Act of stranger fails if the act was foreseeable ( Shail Kumari ). Kaushnuma : rule applies to motor accidents. MV Act s. 164 now holds the statutory no-fault scheme (old s. 140 omitted). M.C. Mehta : hazardous industry → absolute liability, no exceptions.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: One who brings and keeps on his land "anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril"; liable "however careful he may have been". Possible excuses: plaintiff's default, vis major or act of God. Why it matters: the origin of strict liability.
Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. [2001] 1 SCR 8; (2001) 2 SCC 9 (3 Jan 2001; K.T. Thomas and R.P. Sethi JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: At about 7 p
caseLaws.facts: m. on 20 March 1986 a jeep's front tyre burst; as it capsized it hit and killed Haji Mohammad Hanif, a pedestrian. The Tribunal found no negligence and refused compensation. Principle: The rule in Rylands applies to motor accident claims; the victim "is entitled to get compensation from a Tribunal unless any one of the exceptions would apply". Lists the seven exceptions. Why it matters: Indian adoption of the rule and its exceptions.
M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari (2002) 2 SCC 162; AIR 2002 SC 551 (11 Jan 2002)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A factory workman cycling home at night was electrocuted by a live wire lying on a rain-flood
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A person carrying on a hazardous activity is liable "irrespective of any negligence or carelessness"; the act-of-stranger exception fails where the act "should reasonably have been anticipated". Why it matters: narrows the act-of-stranger exception; applies strict liability to electricity supply.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Constitution Bench, 20 Dec 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas leaked from Shriram's plant in Delhi
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A hazardous enterprise is "strictly and absolutely liable"; such liability "is not subject to any of the exceptions to the principle of strict liability under the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher" (as quoted in Shail Kumari ). Why it matters: marks the limit of Rylands in India and the move to absolute liability.

selfTest.q: What is strict liability?
selfTest.a: Liability without proof of negligence. Who stated the rule in Rylands ? Blackburn J., approved by the House of Lords. Name the four essentials. Dangerous thing; non-natural use; escape; damage. Were the defendants in Rylands personally negligent? No; the engineer and contractor had not taken reasonable care. What is "common benefit"? Source of danger kept for both plaintiff and defendant; no liability. When does the act-of-stranger exception fail? When the act should reasonably have been anticipated (Shail Kumari). Define act of God. Circumstances no human foresight can provide against. Does Rylands apply to motor accidents in India? Yes (Kaushnuma Begum). Which MV Act section now gives fixed no-fault compensation? Section 164. How does absolute liability differ? No exceptions at all (M.C. Mehta).

te.inOneMinute: కఠిన బాధ్యత అంటే నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేకుండానే బాధ్యత. ప్రతివాది అన్ని జాగ్రత్తలు తీసుకున్నా బాధ్యుడే. ఇది Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) నుండి వచ్చింది. Blackburn J. నియమం: "for his own purposes, brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril" (అర్థం: తన స్వంత ప్రయోజనాల కోసం, తప్పించుకుంటే హాని చేయగల ఏదైనా వస్తువును తన భూమిపైకి తెచ్చి, సేకరించి, ఉంచే వ్యక్తి దానిని తన స్వంత ప్రమాదంపై లోపల ఉంచాలి). ముఖ్య అంశాలు: (1) భూమిపైకి తెచ్చి ఉంచిన ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు, (2) భూమి యొక్క అసహజ వినియోగం , (3) ఆ వస్తువు తప్పించుకోవడం , (4) తప్పించుకోవడం యొక్క సహజ పర్యవసానమైన నష్టం. ఏడు మినహాయింపులు ( Kaushnuma Begum , 2001 లో జాబితా): వాది సమ్మతి; ఉమ్మడి ప్రయోజనం; అపరిచితుని చర్య; చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం; దైవ చర్య (vis major); వాది తప్పు; పర్యవసానాల దూరత్వం. భారతదేశంలో ఈ నియమాన్ని విద్యుత్ సరఫరాకు ( M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari , 2002), మోటార్ ప్రమాదాలకు ( Kaushnuma Begum ) అన్వయిస్తారు. ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమలకు భారత్ ఇంకా ముందుకెళ్తుంది: మినహాయింపులు లేని సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , 1987). Rule of Absolute Liability (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India) చూడండి.
te.meaning: కఠిన బాధ్యత – ప్రతివాది ఉంచిన ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు తప్పించుకోవడం వల్ల కలిగిన హానికి, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా ఉద్దేశ్యం రుజువు లేకుండా విధించే బాధ్యత; గుర్తించిన మినహాయింపులకు లోబడి. Shail Kumari : ప్రతివాది "is held liable irrespective of whether he could have avoided the particular harm by taking precautions." (అర్థం: జాగ్రత్తలు తీసుకుని ఆ హానిని నివారించగలిగేవాడా లేదా అనే దానితో సంబంధం లేకుండా బాధ్యుడిగా పరిగణించబడతాడు.) Rylands v. Fletcher నియమం (Blackburn J., House of Lords ఆమోదించింది) – "the person who, for his own purposes, brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril; and if he does not do so, is primâ facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape." (అర్థం: తన స్వంత ప్రయోజనాల కోసం, తప్పించుకుంటే హాని చేయగల ఏదైనా వస్తువును తన భూమిపైకి తెచ్చి, సేకరించి, ఉంచే వ్యక్తి దానిని తన ప్రమాదంపై లోపల ఉంచాలి; అలా చేయకపోతే, దాని తప్పించుకోవడం యొక్క సహజ పర్యవసానమైన మొత్తం నష్టానికి ప్రథమదృష్ట్యా బాధ్యుడు.) అసహజ వినియోగం – Lord Cairns: భూమిని "for the purpose of introducing into the close that which in its natural condition was not in or upon it" (అర్థం: సహజ స్థితిలో ఆ భూమిలో లేదా దానిపై లేనిదాన్ని దానిలోకి తీసుకురావడం కోసం) వినియోగించడం. తర్వాత దీనిని భూమి యొక్క సాధారణ వినియోగం కాకుండా, ఇతరులకు పెరిగిన ప్రమాదాన్ని తెచ్చే ప్రత్యేక వినియోగంగా అర్థం చేసుకున్నారు. తప్పించుకోవడం – ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు ప్రతివాది నియంత్రణలోని ప్రదేశం నుండి దాని బయట ఉన్న ప్రదేశానికి వెళ్లడం.
keyPoints: కఠిన బాధ్యత = నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేని బాధ్యత. మూలం: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). ముఖ్య అంశాలు: ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు, అసహజ వినియోగం, తప్పించుకోవడం, నష్టం. ఏడు మినహాయింపులు: సమ్మతి, ఉమ్మడి ప్రయోజనం, అపరిచితుని చర్య, చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం, దైవ చర్య, వాది తప్పు, దూరత్వం. చర్య ఊహించగలిగినదైతే అపరిచితుని చర్య విఫలమవుతుంది ( Shail Kumari ). Kaushnuma : నియమం మోటార్ ప్రమాదాలకు వర్తిస్తుంది. MV Act s. 164 ఇప్పుడు చట్టబద్ధ తప్పు-రహిత పథకాన్ని కలిగి ఉంది (పాత s. 140 తొలగించబడింది). M.C. Mehta : ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమ → సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత, మినహాయింపులు లేవు.

selfTest.q: కఠిన బాధ్యత అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేకుండా బాధ్యత. Rylands లో నియమాన్ని ఎవరు చెప్పారు? Blackburn J., House of Lords ఆమోదించింది. నాలుగు ముఖ్య అంశాలు చెప్పండి. ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు; అసహజ వినియోగం; తప్పించుకోవడం; నష్టం. Rylands లో ప్రతివాదులు వ్యక్తిగతంగా నిర్లక్ష్యం చేశారా? లేదు; ఇంజనీర్, కాంట్రాక్టర్ తగిన జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోలేదు. "ఉమ్మడి ప్రయోజనం" అంటే ఏమిటి? వాది, ప్రతివాది ఇద్దరి కోసం ప్రమాద మూలాన్ని ఉంచడం; బాధ్యత లేదు. అపరిచితుని చర్య మినహాయింపు ఎప్పుడు విఫలమవుతుంది? చర్యను సహేతుకంగా ఊహించి ఉండాల్సినప్పుడు (Shail Kumari). దైవ చర్యను నిర్వచించండి. ఏ మానవ ముందుచూపూ నివారించలేని పరిస్థితులు. భారతదేశంలో Rylands మోటార్ ప్రమాదాలకు వర్తిస్తుందా? అవును (Kaushnuma Begum). నిర్ణీత తప్పు-రహిత పరిహారాన్ని ఇప్పుడు MV Act లోని ఏ సెక్షన్ ఇస్తుంది? సెక్షన్ 164. సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ఎలా వేరు? మినహాయింపులు అసలే లేవు (M.C. Mehta).

hi.inOneMinute: Strict liability means liability without proof of negligence . The defendant is liable even if he took every care. It comes from Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). Blackburn J.'s rule: a person who "for his own purposes, brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril". Essentials: (1) a dangerous thing brought and kept on land, (2) a non-natural use of land, (3) escape of the thing, (4) damage that is the natural consequence of the escape. Seven exceptions (listed in Kaushnuma Begum , 2001): consent of the plaintiff; common benefit; act of a stranger; statutory authority; act of God (vis major); default of the plaintiff; remoteness of consequences. In India the rule is applied to electricity supply ( M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari , 2002) and motor accidents ( Kaushnuma Begum ). For hazardous industries India goes further: absolute liability with no exceptions ( M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , 1987). See Rule of Absolute Liability (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India) .
legalProvision: The rule of strict liability is a common law rule made by judges; no Indian statute enacts it. Indian courts apply it as part of the law of torts.
Related statutory rules that work on the same idea (liability without proof of fault):

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 164(1) – "Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or instrument having the force of law, the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be." Under s. 164(2) the claimant need not plead or prove negligence.
Note: Kaushnuma Begum (2001) referred to the old s. 140 ("no fault liability"). Section 140 has since been omitted from the Act; the fixed-sum no-fault scheme is now in s. 164.
hi.meaning: Strict liability – liability imposed without proof of negligence or intention, for harm caused by the escape of a dangerous thing kept by the defendant; subject to recognised exceptions. Shail Kumari : the defendant "is held liable irrespective of whether he could have avoided the particular harm by taking precautions." The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher (Blackburn J., approved by the House of Lords) – "the person who, for his own purposes, brings on his land and collects and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes, must keep it in at his peril; and if he does not do so, is primâ facie answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape." Non-natural use – Lord Cairns: using land "for the purpose of introducing into the close that which in its natural condition was not in or upon it". Later understood as a special use that brings increased danger to others, not the ordinary use of land. Escape – the dangerous thing moves from the place under the defendant's control to a place outside it.
keyPoints: Strict liability = liability without proof of negligence. Origin: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868). Essentials: dangerous thing, non-natural use, escape, damage. Seven exceptions: consent, common benefit, act of stranger, statutory authority, act of God, plaintiff's default, remoteness. Act of stranger fails if the act was foreseeable ( Shail Kumari ). Kaushnuma : rule applies to motor accidents. MV Act s. 164 now holds the statutory no-fault scheme (old s. 140 omitted). M.C. Mehta : hazardous industry → absolute liability, no exceptions.

selfTest.q: What is strict liability?
selfTest.a: Liability without proof of negligence. Who stated the rule in Rylands ? Blackburn J., approved by the House of Lords. Name the four essentials. Dangerous thing; non-natural use; escape; damage. Were the defendants in Rylands personally negligent? No; the engineer and contractor had not taken reasonable care. What is "common benefit"? Source of danger kept for both plaintiff and defendant; no liability. When does the act-of-stranger exception fail? When the act should reasonably have been anticipated (Shail Kumari). Define act of God. Circumstances no human foresight can provide against. Does Rylands apply to motor accidents in India? Yes (Kaushnuma Begum). Which MV Act section now gives fixed no-fault compensation? Section 164. How does absolute liability differ? No exceptions at all (M.C. Mehta).

law-of-torts-u2-t6.subtitle: The Indian rule of absolute liability for hazardous industry: its basis, its scope and how it differs from the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher

en.inOneMinute: Absolute liability is an Indian rule laid down by a Constitution Bench in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987), the Oleum Gas Leak case . An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes "an absolute and nondelegable duty to the community to ensure that no harm results to anyone". If harm results, the enterprise is "strictly and absolutely liable", and the liability "is not subject to any of the exceptions" of Rylands v. Fletcher . Reasonable care is no answer. The amount of compensation must be "co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise" so that it has a deterrent effect. Rylands was rejected for such cases because it "evolved in the 19th Century" and "cannot afford any guidance" for a modern industrial economy. The rule was confirmed in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996). Parliament built on it in the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 and the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (s. 17(3): "principle of no fault").
legalProvision: Absolute liability is a judge-made rule of the Supreme Court. It was laid down in proceedings under Art. 32 for enforcement of Art. 21. Statutes now carry the same idea:

Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3(1) – "Where death or injury to any person (other than a workman) or damage to any property has resulted from an accident, the owner shall be liable to reimburse such amount, or provide such other relief as may be prescribed, for— (a) death due to fatal accident; (b) medical expenses incurred due to total or partial disability; (c) loss of wages due to partial disability; (d) other injury or sickness; (e) damage to private property; or (f) such other loss or damage, as may be prescribed."

PLI Act, s. 3(2) – "the claimant shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person."
PLI Act, s. 4(1) – "Every owner of any undertaking shall take out, before he starts handling any hazardous substance, one or more insurance policies" against this liability.

National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, s. 17(1) – where death, injury or damage to property or environment "has resulted from an accident or the adverse impact of an activity or operation or process, under any enactment specified in Schedule I, the person responsible shall be liable to pay such relief or compensation".
NGT Act, s. 17(3) – "The Tribunal shall, in case of an accident, apply the principle of no fault."
en.meaning: Absolute liability – the liability of an enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity to compensate everyone harmed by an accident in that activity, without proof of negligence and without any of the Rylands exceptions. Hazardous or inherently dangerous activity – an activity "which poses a potential threat to the health and safety of the persons working in the factory and residing in the surrounding areas" ( M.C. Mehta ), e.g. manufacture of toxic chemicals or gases. Non-delegable duty – a duty that the enterprise cannot pass on to anyone else (a contractor, a supplier). If the duty is broken, the enterprise is liable even if someone else did the work.
keyPoints: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987): Oleum Gas Leak; Constitution Bench; 20 Dec 1986. Hazardous enterprise owes an "absolute and nondelegable duty". No Rylands exceptions; reasonable care is no defence. Compensation linked to "magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". Rylands "evolved in the 19th Century" and gives no guidance for modern industry. Union Carbide (1991) called it obiter; Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) disagreed and applied it. PLI Act 1991 s. 3: no-fault relief; s. 4: compulsory insurance. NGT Act 2010 s. 17(3): "principle of no fault" in accidents.

selfTest.q: Which case laid down absolute liability?
selfTest.a: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak case). When did the oleum gas leak happen? 4 and 6 December 1985. What duty does a hazardous enterprise owe? An absolute and nondelegable duty to the community. Which Rylands exceptions apply? None. Is reasonable care a defence? No. How is compensation measured? Co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise, to deter. Why was Rylands rejected? It evolved in the 19th century and cannot guide modern industrial liability. Which case confirmed the rule and rejected the obiter view? Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996). Under the PLI Act, must the claimant prove negligence? No (s. 3(2)). What principle does NGT Act s. 17(3) apply in accidents? The principle of no fault.
