hi.inOneMinute: Release is one way a tort liability comes to an end. The injured person, the only one entitled to sue, gives up his right of action against the wrongdoer, wholly or in part. Once validly released, the claim cannot be sued on. (See Diagram 1 .) A release is a matter of agreement and consent . In India, the Indian Contract Act, 1872 supplies the rules: a person entitled to performance "may dispense with or remit, wholly or in part" what is due to him (s. 63); the consent must be free , that is, not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake (s. 14); a release obtained without free consent is voidable at the option of the injured person (ss. 19, 19A); the person releasing must be competent : of majority and sound mind (s. 11). Once a suit is filed, an adjustment or satisfaction of the claim, in writing and signed by the parties, is recorded and a decree passed on it (Order XXIII, rule 3, Code of Civil Procedure). For a minor , the next friend or guardian cannot compromise without the court's leave (Order XXXII, rule 7). Release gives up the claim. Accord and satisfaction replaces the claim with something else that is actually given and accepted.
legalProvision: No statute deals with "release" of a tort claim as such. It works through the general law of agreement:
Indian Contract Act, 1872

Section 63: "Every promisee may dispense with or remit, wholly or in part, the performance of the promise made to him, or may extend the time for such performance, or may accept instead of it any satisfaction which he thinks fit." Illustration (a): "A promises to paint a picture for B. B afterwards forbids him to do so. A is no longer bound to perform the promise." Section 11: "Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject." Section 14: consent is free when it is not caused by coercion (s. 15), undue influence (s. 16), fraud (s. 17), misrepresentation (s. 18) or mistake (ss. 20–22). Section 19: "When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused." Section 19A: "When consent to an agreement is caused by undue influence, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused."
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

Order XXIII, rule 3: "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise in writing and signed by the parties, or where the defendant satisfied the plaintiff in respect to the whole or any part of the subject-matter of the suit, the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded, and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith". Order XXXII, rule 7(1): "No next friend or guardian for the suit shall, without the leave of the Court, expressly recorded in the proceedings, enter into any agreement or compromise on behalf of a minor with reference to the suit in which he acts as next friend or guardian."
hi.meaning: Release – the injured person's giving up of his right of action in tort , wholly or in part, so that the wrongdoer's liability ends to that extent. Right of action – the injured person's right to sue the wrongdoer for the tort. Release extinguishes it. Free consent – consent not caused by coercion , undue influence , fraud, misrepresentation or mistake (s. 14, Contract Act). A release must rest on free consent. Voidable – valid until the person whose consent was not free chooses to avoid it (ss. 19, 19A). A release obtained by fraud or pressure is voidable, not automatically void. Remission – giving up, wholly or in part, what is due (s. 63). A release of a tort claim is a remission of the right to compensation.
keyPoints: Release: the injured person gives up his right of action. s. 63: "dispense with or remit, wholly or in part" – remission. Total or partial. Needs competence (s. 11) and free consent (s. 14). Without free consent: voidable (ss. 19, 19A). Pending suit: written, signed compromise recorded; decree (O. XXIII r. 3). Minor's suit: court leave (O. XXXII r. 7). Release needs no substitute; accord and satisfaction does.

law-of-torts-u2-t12.subtitle: The effect of death on claims in tort: survival of actions, and compensation to dependants for a death caused by a wrong

en.inOneMinute: Death affects tort liability in two ways. (1) Death of a party: what happens to a tort claim when the injured person or the wrongdoer dies? (2) Death as the harm: can anyone sue when a wrongful act kills a person? The old common law answer to (1) was the maxim actio personalis moritur cum persona : "a personal action dies with the person". The old answer to (2) was Baker v. Bolton (1808): "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury". In India both answers have been changed by statute. The Supreme Court in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy (2026) held that the maxim "in India has been statutorily modified by various statutory instruments such as Fatal Accidents' Act of 1855, Legal representatives' Suits Act of 1855, Indian Succession Act of 1925". Survival of causes of action (Indian Succession Act, 1925 s. 306): all rights of action for or against a person survive to or against his executors or administrators, except defamation, assault and other personal injuries not causing death. In short: "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive" ( Kumud Lall ). Death caused by a wrong (Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 s. 1A): the wrongdoer is liable to the family (wife, husband, parent, child) for the loss caused by the death. For motor accidents, the claim is made by the legal representatives under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 s. 166, a wider group ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai , 1987). A pending suit does not abate on a party's death "if the right to sue survives" (CPC Order XXII r. 1); the legal representative must be brought on record within ninety days (Limitation Act Art. 120).
legalProvision: Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall ) – "All demands whatsoever and all rights to prosecute or defend any action or special proceeding existing in favour of or against a person at the time of his decease, survive to and against his executors or administrators; except causes of action for defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860) or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party; and except also cases where, after the death of the party, the relief sought could not be enjoyed or granting it would be nugatory." Illustration (i): a railway passenger "is severely hurt, but not so as to cause death. He afterwards dies without having brought any action. The cause of action does not survive."

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensued) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured". Every such suit "shall be for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child, if any, of the person whose death shall have been so caused, and shall be brought by and in the name of the executor, administrator or representative of the person deceased". The court gives damages "proportioned to the loss resulting from such death" and divides them among those persons.

s. 2: "not more than one action or suit shall be brought for, and in respect of the same subject-matter of complaint"; but the representative "may insert a claim for, and recover any pecuniary loss to the estate of the deceased", which becomes part of the estate. s. 4: "parent" includes grandfather and grandmother; "child" includes grandson, grand-daughter, step-son and step-daughter.

Legal Representatives' Suits Act, 1855, ss. 1–2 (as quoted in Kumud Lall ) – executors, administrators or representatives may sue "for any wrong committed in the time of such person, which has occasioned pecuniary loss to his estate", if the wrong was committed "within one year before his death"; and a suit may be brought against the representatives of a deceased wrongdoer "for any wrong committed by him in his lifetime", again if committed within one year before his death. "No action commenced under the provisions of this Act shall abate by reason of the death of either party".

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII r. 1 – "The death of a plaintiff or defendant shall not cause the suit to abate if the right to sue survives." Rules 3 and 4: on an application, the court brings the legal representative of the deceased plaintiff or defendant on record; if no application is made in time, the suit abates as to that party.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 – s. 166(1)(c): where death has resulted from the accident, the claim may be made "by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased". s. 155: "Notwithstanding anything contained in section 306 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925", the death of the insured person after the accident "shall not be a bar to the survival of any cause of action arising out of such event against his estate or against the insurer."

Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule – Art. 81 (suit by representatives under the Legal Representatives' Suits Act): one year from the death of the person wronged; Art. 82 (suit under the Fatal Accidents Act): two years from the death of the person killed; Art. 83 (suit under the Legal Representatives' Suits Act against a representative): two years from when the wrong is done; Art. 120 (application to bring a legal representative on record): ninety days from the date of death.
en.meaning: Actio personalis moritur cum persona – "a personal right of action dies with the person" (commentary quoted in Kumud Lall ). Under the old rule a tort claim ended when either the injured person or the wrongdoer died. Survival of causes of action – the rule that a right to sue (or a liability to be sued) existing at a person's death passes to or against his executors , administrators or other legal representatives (ISA s. 306). In Melepurath Sankunni v. Thekittil Geopalankutty Nair (1986), quoted in Kumud Lall , the Court said other legal representatives "cannot in law be in better or worse position than executors and administrators". Legal representative – the person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person (executor, administrator, heir or person in possession of the estate). Under the Motor Vehicles Act this group is wider than the four relations named in the Fatal Accidents Act ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai ). Abatement – the ending of a pending suit or appeal because a party has died and either the right to sue does not survive, or the legal representative was not brought on record in time (CPC Order XXII rr. 3(2), 4(3)).
keyPoints: Actio personalis moritur cum persona is "statutorily modified" in India ( Kumud Lall ). Baker v. Bolton : at common law death was not an injury in a civil court. ISA s. 306: claims survive, except defamation, assault and personal injuries not causing death. "Personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive." FAA s. 1A: claim for the family (wife, husband, parent, child); one suit; estate loss can be added. Motor accident deaths: all legal representatives can claim ( Gujarat SRTC ; MV Act s. 166). MV Act s. 155: death of the insured does not end the claim against his estate or the insurer. CPC O. XXII r. 1: no abatement if the right to sue survives; substitute within ninety days (Art. 120).

Principle: "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury"; damages "must stop with the period of her existence". Verdict for £100 only for the period before her death. Why it matters: States the old common law rule that the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 was passed to change.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The brothers of a man killed in a motor vehicle accident claimed compensation under s
caseLaws.facts: 110-A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The Tribunal awarded ₹32,000. The Corporation argued that only the wife, husband, parent and child could claim under the Fatal Accidents Act. Principle: The motor accident provisions "are not merely procedural provisions. They substantively affect the rights of the parties"; the brother of a person who dies in a motor accident can claim if he is a legal representative. Why it matters: Widens the group of claimants in motor accident deaths beyond the Fatal Accidents Act.
Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026; J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ)

selfTest.q: What does actio personalis moritur cum persona mean?
selfTest.a: A personal action dies with the person. What did Baker v. Bolton hold? Death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury in a civil court. Which section is the general survival rule? Indian Succession Act, 1925 s. 306. Name the s. 306 exceptions. Defamation, assault, other personal injuries not causing death; and cases where the relief could not be enjoyed. Who benefits under the Fatal Accidents Act? Wife, husband, parent and child (with grandparents, grandchildren, step-children). How many suits under the FAA? Only one (s. 2). Who can claim for a motor accident death? All or any of the legal representatives (s. 166(1)(c); Gujarat SRTC). Limitation for an FAA suit? Two years from the death (Art. 82). Time to bring a legal representative on record? Ninety days from death (Art. 120). In Kumud Lall , what survived the doctor's death? Claims against his estate, not personal claims.

te.inOneMinute: మరణం టార్ట్ బాధ్యతను రెండు విధాలుగా ప్రభావితం చేస్తుంది. (1) ఒక పక్షం మరణం: గాయపడిన వ్యక్తి లేదా తప్పిదారుడు మరణిస్తే టార్ట్ దావా ఏమవుతుంది? (2) మరణమే హాని: తప్పుడు చర్య ఒక వ్యక్తిని చంపితే ఎవరైనా దావా వేయగలరా? (1) కి పాత కామన్ లా జవాబు actio personalis moritur cum persona సూత్రం: "a personal action dies with the person" (అర్థం: వ్యక్తిగత దావా వ్యక్తితోనే చనిపోతుంది). (2) కి పాత జవాబు Baker v. Bolton (1808): "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury" (అర్థం: సివిల్ కోర్టులో మనిషి మరణాన్ని హానిగా ఫిర్యాదు చేయలేరు). భారతదేశంలో ఈ రెండు జవాబులనూ చట్టం మార్చింది. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy (2026) లో సుప్రీం కోర్టు ఈ సూత్రం "in India has been statutorily modified by various statutory instruments such as Fatal Accidents' Act of 1855, Legal representatives' Suits Act of 1855, Indian Succession Act of 1925" (అర్థం: భారతదేశంలో Fatal Accidents Act 1855, Legal Representatives' Suits Act 1855, Indian Succession Act 1925 వంటి చట్టాల ద్వారా మార్చబడింది) అని తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది. దావా కారణం కొనసాగడం (Indian Succession Act, 1925 s. 306): ఒక వ్యక్తికి అనుకూలంగా లేదా వ్యతిరేకంగా ఉన్న అన్ని దావా హక్కులు అతని executors లేదా administrators కు లేదా వారికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కొనసాగుతాయి; మినహాయింపు: పరువు నష్టం, దాడి, మరణానికి కారణం కాని ఇతర వ్యక్తిగత గాయాలు. సంక్షిప్తంగా: "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive" (అర్థం: వ్యక్తిగత గాయాల దావాలు రద్దవుతాయి, మృతుని ఆస్తికి అనుకూలంగా లేదా వ్యతిరేకంగా ఉన్న దావాలు కొనసాగుతాయి) ( Kumud Lall ). తప్పు వల్ల మరణం (Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 s. 1A): మరణం వల్ల కుటుంబానికి (భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లలు) కలిగిన నష్టానికి తప్పిదారుడు బాధ్యుడు. మోటారు ప్రమాదాల్లో, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 s. 166 కింద చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులు దావా వేస్తారు; ఇది విస్తృత సమూహం ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai , 1987). ఒక పక్షం మరణించినా, "if the right to sue survives" (అర్థం: దావా హక్కు కొనసాగితే) పెండింగ్ దావా రద్దు కాదు (CPC Order XXII r. 1); చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధిని తొంభై రోజుల్లో రికార్డులోకి తీసుకురావాలి (Limitation Act Art. 120).
te.meaning: Actio personalis moritur cum persona – "a personal right of action dies with the person" (అర్థం: వ్యక్తిగత దావా హక్కు వ్యక్తితోనే చనిపోతుంది) ( Kumud Lall లో ఉటంకించిన వ్యాఖ్యానం). పాత నియమం ప్రకారం గాయపడిన వ్యక్తి లేదా తప్పిదారుడు మరణిస్తే టార్ట్ దావా ముగిసేది. దావా కారణం కొనసాగడం – ఒక వ్యక్తి మరణ సమయంలో ఉన్న దావా హక్కు (లేదా దావాకు గురయ్యే బాధ్యత) అతని executors , administrators లేదా ఇతర చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులకు, లేదా వారికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కొనసాగుతుందనే నియమం (ISA s. 306). Melepurath Sankunni v. Thekittil Geopalankutty Nair (1986) లో ( Kumud Lall లో ఉటంకించినది) ఇతర చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులు "cannot in law be in better or worse position than executors and administrators" (అర్థం: చట్టంలో executors, administrators కంటే మెరుగైన లేదా అధ్వాన్న స్థితిలో ఉండలేరు) అని కోర్టు చెప్పింది. చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధి – చట్టంలో మృతుని ఆస్తికి ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహించే వ్యక్తి (executor, administrator, వారసుడు లేదా ఆస్తిని స్వాధీనంలో ఉంచుకున్న వ్యక్తి). Motor Vehicles Act కింద ఈ సమూహం Fatal Accidents Act లో పేర్కొన్న నలుగురు బంధువుల కంటే విస్తృతం ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai ). దావా రద్దు – ఒక పక్షం మరణించి, దావా హక్కు కొనసాగకపోవడం వల్ల, లేదా చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధిని సమయంలో రికార్డులోకి తీసుకురాకపోవడం వల్ల పెండింగ్ దావా లేదా అప్పీల్ ముగిసిపోవడం (CPC Order XXII rr. 3(2), 4(3)).
keyPoints: Actio personalis moritur cum persona భారతదేశంలో "statutorily modified" (అర్థం: చట్టం ద్వారా మార్చబడింది) ( Kumud Lall ). Baker v. Bolton : కామన్ లాలో సివిల్ కోర్టులో మరణం హాని కాదు. ISA s. 306: దావాలు కొనసాగుతాయి, పరువు నష్టం, దాడి, మరణానికి కారణం కాని వ్యక్తిగత గాయాలు తప్ప. "Personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive." (అర్థం: వ్యక్తిగత గాయాల దావాలు రద్దవుతాయి, ఆస్తికి సంబంధించిన దావాలు కొనసాగుతాయి.) FAA s. 1A: కుటుంబానికి (భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లలు) దావా; ఒకే దావా; ఆస్తి నష్టం చేర్చవచ్చు. మోటారు ప్రమాద మరణాలు: చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులందరూ దావా వేయవచ్చు ( Gujarat SRTC ; MV Act s. 166). MV Act s. 155: బీమా ఉన్న వ్యక్తి మరణం అతని ఆస్తి లేదా బీమా సంస్థపై దావాను ముగించదు. CPC O. XXII r. 1: దావా హక్కు కొనసాగితే రద్దు కాదు; తొంభై రోజుల్లో ప్రత్యామ్నాయం (Art. 120).

selfTest.q: actio personalis moritur cum persona అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: వ్యక్తిగత దావా వ్యక్తితోనే చనిపోతుంది. Baker v. Bolton ఏమి తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది? సివిల్ కోర్టులో మనిషి మరణాన్ని హానిగా ఫిర్యాదు చేయలేరు. సాధారణ కొనసాగింపు నియమం ఏ సెక్షన్? Indian Succession Act, 1925 s. 306. s. 306 మినహాయింపులు చెప్పండి. పరువు నష్టం, దాడి, మరణానికి కారణం కాని ఇతర వ్యక్తిగత గాయాలు; ఉపశమనం అనుభవించలేని సందర్భాలు. Fatal Accidents Act కింద ఎవరికి ప్రయోజనం? భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లలు (తాత-నాయనమ్మలు, మనవలు, సవతి పిల్లలతో). FAA కింద ఎన్ని దావాలు? ఒక్కటే (s. 2). మోటారు ప్రమాద మరణానికి ఎవరు దావా వేయవచ్చు? చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులందరూ లేదా ఎవరైనా (s. 166(1)(c); Gujarat SRTC). FAA దావాకు కాలపరిమితి? మరణం నుండి రెండు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 82). చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధిని రికార్డులోకి తీసుకురావడానికి సమయం? మరణం నుండి తొంభై రోజులు (Art. 120). Kumud Lall లో డాక్టర్ మరణం తర్వాత ఏమి కొనసాగింది? అతని ఆస్తిపై దావాలు, వ్యక్తిగత దావాలు కాదు.

పరిస్థితి వర్తించే చట్టం దావా కొనసాగుతుందా? ఎవరు దావా వేస్తారు / ఎవరిపై కాలపరిమితి
గాయపడిన వ్యక్తి మరణిస్తాడు, గాయం మరణానికి కారణం కాదు ISA s. 306; LR Suits Act s. 1 వ్యక్తిగత గాయాల దావా (నొప్పి, అవమానం, దాడి, పరువు నష్టం) రద్దవుతుంది; ఆస్తి నష్టం కొనసాగుతుంది ఆస్తి ప్రతినిధులు దావా వేస్తారు LR Suits Act దావాలకు Art. 81 (మరణం నుండి ఒక సంవత్సరం)
తప్పు వల్ల గాయపడిన వ్యక్తి మరణిస్తాడు Fatal Accidents Act ss. 1A, 2; MV Act s. 166 అవును: కుటుంబానికి కొత్త దావా, ఆస్తి నష్టంతో పాటు భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లల కోసం ప్రతినిధి; మోటారు కేసుల్లో చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులందరూ Art. 82 (మరణం నుండి రెండు సంవత్సరాలు); MV Act s. 166(3)
తప్పిదారుడు మరణిస్తాడు ISA s. 306; LR Suits Act s. 1; MV Act s. 155 అవును, ఆస్తిపై, వ్యక్తిగత గాయాల మినహాయింపులు తప్ప; బీమా ఉన్న వ్యక్తి విషయంలో మోటారు దావాలు ఆస్తి, బీమా సంస్థపై కొనసాగుతాయి బాధితుడు తప్పిదారుని చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులపై దావా వేస్తాడు (ఆస్తి మేరకు బాధ్యులు) LR Suits Act దావాలకు Art. 83 (తప్పు నుండి రెండు సంవత్సరాలు)
దావా పెండింగ్‌లో ఉండగా పక్షం మరణిస్తాడు CPC O. XXII; ISA s. 306 దావా హక్కు కొనసాగితే దావా కొనసాగుతుంది చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధిని ప్రత్యామ్నాయంగా చేర్చుతారు Art. 120 (తొంభై రోజులు)

hi.inOneMinute: Death affects tort liability in two ways. (1) Death of a party: what happens to a tort claim when the injured person or the wrongdoer dies? (2) Death as the harm: can anyone sue when a wrongful act kills a person? The old common law answer to (1) was the maxim actio personalis moritur cum persona : "a personal action dies with the person". The old answer to (2) was Baker v. Bolton (1808): "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury". In India both answers have been changed by statute. The Supreme Court in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy (2026) held that the maxim "in India has been statutorily modified by various statutory instruments such as Fatal Accidents' Act of 1855, Legal representatives' Suits Act of 1855, Indian Succession Act of 1925". Survival of causes of action (Indian Succession Act, 1925 s. 306): all rights of action for or against a person survive to or against his executors or administrators, except defamation, assault and other personal injuries not causing death. In short: "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive" ( Kumud Lall ). Death caused by a wrong (Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 s. 1A): the wrongdoer is liable to the family (wife, husband, parent, child) for the loss caused by the death. For motor accidents, the claim is made by the legal representatives under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 s. 166, a wider group ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai , 1987). A pending suit does not abate on a party's death "if the right to sue survives" (CPC Order XXII r. 1); the legal representative must be brought on record within ninety days (Limitation Act Art. 120).
legalProvision: Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall ) – "All demands whatsoever and all rights to prosecute or defend any action or special proceeding existing in favour of or against a person at the time of his decease, survive to and against his executors or administrators; except causes of action for defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860) or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party; and except also cases where, after the death of the party, the relief sought could not be enjoyed or granting it would be nugatory." Illustration (i): a railway passenger "is severely hurt, but not so as to cause death. He afterwards dies without having brought any action. The cause of action does not survive."

Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensued) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured". Every such suit "shall be for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child, if any, of the person whose death shall have been so caused, and shall be brought by and in the name of the executor, administrator or representative of the person deceased". The court gives damages "proportioned to the loss resulting from such death" and divides them among those persons.

s. 2: "not more than one action or suit shall be brought for, and in respect of the same subject-matter of complaint"; but the representative "may insert a claim for, and recover any pecuniary loss to the estate of the deceased", which becomes part of the estate. s. 4: "parent" includes grandfather and grandmother; "child" includes grandson, grand-daughter, step-son and step-daughter.

Legal Representatives' Suits Act, 1855, ss. 1–2 (as quoted in Kumud Lall ) – executors, administrators or representatives may sue "for any wrong committed in the time of such person, which has occasioned pecuniary loss to his estate", if the wrong was committed "within one year before his death"; and a suit may be brought against the representatives of a deceased wrongdoer "for any wrong committed by him in his lifetime", again if committed within one year before his death. "No action commenced under the provisions of this Act shall abate by reason of the death of either party".

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXII r. 1 – "The death of a plaintiff or defendant shall not cause the suit to abate if the right to sue survives." Rules 3 and 4: on an application, the court brings the legal representative of the deceased plaintiff or defendant on record; if no application is made in time, the suit abates as to that party.

Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 – s. 166(1)(c): where death has resulted from the accident, the claim may be made "by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased". s. 155: "Notwithstanding anything contained in section 306 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925", the death of the insured person after the accident "shall not be a bar to the survival of any cause of action arising out of such event against his estate or against the insurer."

Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule – Art. 81 (suit by representatives under the Legal Representatives' Suits Act): one year from the death of the person wronged; Art. 82 (suit under the Fatal Accidents Act): two years from the death of the person killed; Art. 83 (suit under the Legal Representatives' Suits Act against a representative): two years from when the wrong is done; Art. 120 (application to bring a legal representative on record): ninety days from the date of death.
hi.meaning: Actio personalis moritur cum persona – "a personal right of action dies with the person" (commentary quoted in Kumud Lall ). Under the old rule a tort claim ended when either the injured person or the wrongdoer died. Survival of causes of action – the rule that a right to sue (or a liability to be sued) existing at a person's death passes to or against his executors , administrators or other legal representatives (ISA s. 306). In Melepurath Sankunni v. Thekittil Geopalankutty Nair (1986), quoted in Kumud Lall , the Court said other legal representatives "cannot in law be in better or worse position than executors and administrators". Legal representative – the person who in law represents the estate of a deceased person (executor, administrator, heir or person in possession of the estate). Under the Motor Vehicles Act this group is wider than the four relations named in the Fatal Accidents Act ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai ). Abatement – the ending of a pending suit or appeal because a party has died and either the right to sue does not survive, or the legal representative was not brought on record in time (CPC Order XXII rr. 3(2), 4(3)).
keyPoints: Actio personalis moritur cum persona is "statutorily modified" in India ( Kumud Lall ). Baker v. Bolton : at common law death was not an injury in a civil court. ISA s. 306: claims survive, except defamation, assault and personal injuries not causing death. "Personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive." FAA s. 1A: claim for the family (wife, husband, parent, child); one suit; estate loss can be added. Motor accident deaths: all legal representatives can claim ( Gujarat SRTC ; MV Act s. 166). MV Act s. 155: death of the insured does not end the claim against his estate or the insurer. CPC O. XXII r. 1: no abatement if the right to sue survives; substitute within ninety days (Art. 120).

caseLaws.facts: He claimed for the loss of her "comfort, fellowship, and assistance". Principle: "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury"; damages "must stop with the period of her existence". Verdict for £100 only for the period before her death. Why it matters: States the old common law rule that the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 was passed to change.
Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation v. Ramanbhai Prabhatbhai [1987] 3 SCR 404 (11 May 1987; E.S. Venkataramiah and K.N. Singh JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The brothers of a man killed in a motor vehicle accident claimed compensation under s
caseLaws.facts: 110-A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The Tribunal awarded ₹32,000. The Corporation argued that only the wife, husband, parent and child could claim under the Fatal Accidents Act. Principle: The motor accident provisions "are not merely procedural provisions. They substantively affect the rights of the parties"; the brother of a person who dies in a motor accident can claim if he is a legal representative. Why it matters: Widens the group of claimants in motor accident deaths beyond the Fatal Accidents Act.
Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026; J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ)

Why it matters: The latest Supreme Court statement of Indian law on the effect of death on tort and negligence claims.

selfTest.q: What does actio personalis moritur cum persona mean?
selfTest.a: A personal action dies with the person. What did Baker v. Bolton hold? Death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury in a civil court. Which section is the general survival rule? Indian Succession Act, 1925 s. 306. Name the s. 306 exceptions. Defamation, assault, other personal injuries not causing death; and cases where the relief could not be enjoyed. Who benefits under the Fatal Accidents Act? Wife, husband, parent and child (with grandparents, grandchildren, step-children). How many suits under the FAA? Only one (s. 2). Who can claim for a motor accident death? All or any of the legal representatives (s. 166(1)(c); Gujarat SRTC). Limitation for an FAA suit? Two years from the death (Art. 82). Time to bring a legal representative on record? Ninety days from death (Art. 120). In Kumud Lall , what survived the doctor's death? Claims against his estate, not personal claims.

visuals.html:
Inside the idea Just outside it
Survival claim: the deceased's own claim, passed to his estate (ISA s. 306) Fatal accident claim: a new claim of the family for its own loss (FAA s. 1A)
Personal injury not causing death: abates Personal injury causing death: family claims under FAA
Loss to the estate: survives Pain, insult, injury to feelings: dies with the person

FAA beneficiaries: wife, husband, parent, child MV Act claimants: all legal representatives, e.g. brothers

The maxim volenti non fit injuria means:

Explanation. Volenti non fit injuria means no injury is done to one who consents to a known risk.

For volenti non fit injuria to succeed as a defence, the plaintiff must have had:

en.meaning:
Who is an occupier of premises for the law of occupiers' liability?

Explanation. Control, not ownership, decides. A tenant, a hotel manager or a school management can be an occupier, and more than one person can occupy the same premises.

The English Occupiers' Liability Act, 1957 states, for lawful visitors:

Explanation. The 1957 Act states the common duty of care: reasonable care that the visitor is reasonably safe in using the premises for the purpose for which he is allowed to be there. Indian courts treat it as persuasive.

Res ipsa loquitur applies where:

Explanation. Res ipsa loquitur raises an inference of negligence where an accident of this kind would not ordinarily happen without it, and the cause was in the defendant's exclusive control.

In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti (1966), the Supreme Court applied res ipsa loquitur to:

en.meaning:
What does the maxim actio personalis moritur cum persona mean?

Explanation. The maxim literally means a personal action dies with the person — at early common law, this extinguished purely personal tort claims on the death of either party.

What was the first aspect of the actio personalis rule, concerning the death of the wrongdoer?

Explanation. At common law, a claim in tort ended when either the wrongdoer or the injured person died, so it could not be continued against the wrongdoer's estate. Section 306 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 now saves most claims.

In Baker v Bolton (1808), what did Lord Ellenborough hold regarding a claim for the death of the plaintiff's wife?

Explanation. Lord Ellenborough held that the jury could consider only the husband's own bruises, the loss of his wife's society and his distress, from the accident until her death. The damages as to the wife stopped with the period of her existence.

What anomaly did the rule in Baker v Bolton famously create?

Occupier's Liability and Extinction of Liability Part C — Problem / Case-Study Questions Some military personnel found firewood lying by the side of a river. They took away the wood under the impression that it belonged to the Government and used it as fuel in the camp. The plaintiff, the real owner of the firewood, brought a suit against the Government. Is the Government liable, and if so, under which tort? Liability of the State for Torts – Defense of Sovereign Immunity Two strangers voluntarily took a lift in a jeep and were injured, one of them subsequently dying, due to an accident caused because the right wheel suddenly went off the jeep. Is the owner of the jeep liable for the death and injuries? General Defences to an action in Torts Padmavati v. Dugganaika (1975) A driver of a goods truck, in contravention of a statutory provision, gave a lift to an unauthorized passenger in the truck. Due to the driver's negligence, the passenger was killed in an accident. Can the owner of the truck be held liable? Vicarious Liability X constructed an artificial water reservoir fed by a natural stream. There was a breach of the reservoir due to a very heavy rainfall, which was quite exceptional, and lands belonging to Y were damaged. Decide the liability of X. Rule of Strict Liability (Rylands v. Fletcher) Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) (Landmark Case) The driver of an omnibus allowed the conductor to drive the bus, and in doing so the conductor injured a pedestrian. Is the owner of the bus liable to pay damages to the injured pedestrian? Vicarious Liability A tourist passenger, knowing that the cab driver was drunk and that the chances of an accident were great, chose to travel by that cab. He was injured in an accident caused by the drunkenness of the driver. Is the injured passenger entitled to claim damages? General Defences to an action in Torts Hall v. Brooklands Auto Racing Club (1933) While a bus of Z was being reversed at a bus stand, a person standing at the back was knocked down. Can the respondents be held liable? Vicarious Liability A lady was arrested believing that she was aiding a group which was against the State. Immediately she was released after confirming that she was not the lady whom they were searching for. State what wrong the police committed, and advise the lady. Liability of the State for Torts – Defense of Sovereign Immunity Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1965) (Landmark Case) A drunken driver, driving a car at high speed, caused the death of the car's own driver and of a passerby on the road. Who is responsible for the death of the passerby — the legal representative of the deceased driver, or the owner of the car? Who will pay the damages? law-of-torts-u3-t2.subtitle: Wrongs to body, liberty, mind and name: how assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution and nervous shock fit together

en.inOneMinute: Torts affecting the person protect a human being's own self: his body , his freedom from fear of violence , his liberty , his freedom from unjust legal proceedings and his mental health . The syllabus names five: assault (threat of immediate force), battery (actual application of force), false imprisonment (unlawful total restraint), malicious prosecution (an unjust prosecution brought with malice), and nervous shock (psychiatric harm). Assault, battery and false imprisonment together form trespass to the person : direct, intentional interferences that are actionable without proof of loss. Malicious prosecution and nervous shock need proof of damage. The law also recognises liability where a person wilfully does an act calculated to cause physical harm and it does so, even without force ( Wilkinson v. Downton , 1897). When police or other officials commit these torts, the victim can also claim public law compensation under Arts. 21 and 32/226, in addition to a civil suit ( D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal , 1996; Bhim Singh v. State of J&K , 1985). Custodial violence "strikes a blow at the Rule of Law" ( D.K. Basu ). Common defences: consent , self-defence (private defence), lawful authority (e.g. a lawful arrest), and statutory authority .
legalProvision: There is no Indian statute that codifies the torts affecting the person; they are common law torts. But Indian statutes define the matching wrongs and limit official power:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (criminal definitions often used to explain the torts)

s. 130 (Assault): "Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault." Explanation: "Mere words do not amount to an assault." s. 128 (Force) and s. 129 (Criminal force): force is causing motion, change of motion or cessation of motion that brings a substance "into contact with any part of that other's body"; criminal force is force used intentionally "without that person's consent" to cause "injury, fear or annoyance". s. 127(1) (Wrongful confinement): "Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said 'wrongfully to confine' that person."
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

s. 43(1)–(2): in making an arrest the officer "shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody"; if the person "forcibly resists ... or attempts to evade the arrest", the officer "may use all means necessary to effect the arrest". s. 43(4): this does not give "a right to cause the death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for life." s. 58: no person arrested without warrant shall be detained for longer than is reasonable, and not beyond "twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey" without a Magistrate's special order.
Constitution of India

Art. 21: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Art. 22(2): "Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest ... and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate."

Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule – Art. 73 (false imprisonment): one year "When the imprisonment ends"; Art. 74 (malicious prosecution): one year "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated"; assault, battery and nervous shock: Art. 113, three years "When the right to sue accrues".
en.meaning: Torts affecting the person – civil wrongs that injure a person's body, liberty, mental well-being or freedom from unjust prosecution, as opposed to torts against property, reputation or business. Trespass to the person – the group of torts ( assault , battery , false imprisonment ) in which the defendant directly and (usually) intentionally interferes with the plaintiff's person; actionable per se . Intentional infliction of harm – the principle in Wilkinson v. Downton : a defendant who has "wilfully done an act calculated to cause physical harm to the plaintiff—that is to say, to infringe her legal right to personal safety, and has in fact thereby caused physical harm to her" is liable, "there being no justification alleged for the act". Custodial violence – violence, torture or death of a person in police or other official custody; in D.K. Basu the Court said it "strikes a blow at the Rule of Law, which demands that the powers of the executive should not only be derived from law but also that the same should be limited by law."
keyPoints: Torts affecting the person protect body, liberty, mind and freedom from unjust prosecution. Assault, battery and false imprisonment are forms of trespass to the person; actionable per se. Assault is the threat; battery is the contact. False imprisonment needs total restraint; no force is required. Malicious prosecution and nervous shock need damage. Wilkinson v. Downton : wilful act calculated to cause harm is actionable. Arrest powers are limited: BNSS ss. 43, 58; Art. 22(2). Public law compensation is in addition to tort damages ( D.K. Basu ; Bhim Singh : ₹50,000).

caseLaws.facts: Wilkinson v. Downton [1897] 2 QB 57 (Wright J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: As a practical joke, the defendant falsely told the plaintiff that her husband had met with a
caseLaws.facts: She believed it and suffered a violent nervous shock that made her ill. Principle: A person who has "wilfully done an act calculated to cause physical harm to the plaintiff ... and has in fact thereby caused physical harm to her" is liable, "there being no justification alleged for the act." Judgment for the plaintiff. Why it matters: Extends protection of the person to harm caused without force or contact.
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1996) Supp. 10 SCR; (1997) 1 SCC 416 (18 Dec 1996; Kuldip Singh and Dr. A.S. Anand JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Executive Chairman of Legal Aid Services, West Bengal, wrote to the Chief Justice of Indi
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Custodial violence, including torture and death in the lock ups, strikes a blow at the Rule of Law"; public law compensation for violation of Art. 21 "is a claim based on strict liability and is in addition to the claim available in private law for damages for tortious acts of the public servants." Requirements for arrest (name tags, memo of arrest, etc.) were laid down. Why it matters: Shows how torts against the person by police are answered by both tort law and constitutional law.
Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) 4 SCC 677; AIR 1986 SC 494 (22 Nov 1985; O. Chinnappa Reddy and V. Khalid JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An MLA was arrested at about 3 a
caseLaws.facts: m. on 10 September 1985 on his way to Srinagar, apparently to keep him away from the Assembly session; he was not produced before a Magistrate on 11th or the Sub Judge on 13th. Principle: "When a person comes to us with the complaint that he has been arrested and imprisoned with mischievous or malicious intent and that his constitutional and legal rights were invaded, the mischief or malice and the invasion may not be washed away or wished away by his being set free." The State was directed to pay ₹50,000. Why it matters: Unlawful detention is compensated even after release.

selfTest.q: Name the five torts affecting the person in the syllabus. Assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock. What is trespass to the person?
selfTest.a: Direct, intentional interference with the person: assault, battery, false imprisonment. Do mere words amount to assault? No (BNS s. 130 Explanation), though words can give meaning to gestures. Is physical force needed for false imprisonment? No; restraint by authority or threat is enough. Which torts affecting the person need proof of damage? Malicious prosecution and nervous shock. What did Wilkinson v. Downton decide? A wilful false statement calculated to cause harm, which caused illness, is actionable. Within what time must an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate? Twenty-four hours, excluding journey time (Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58). Does a writ award bar a civil suit? No; it is without prejudice to it (D.K. Basu). How much was awarded in Bhim Singh ? ₹50,000. Limitation for false imprisonment? One year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73).

te.inOneMinute: వ్యక్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు ఒక మనిషి స్వంత ఉనికిని కాపాడతాయి: అతని శరీరం , హింస భయం నుండి స్వేచ్ఛ , స్వేచ్ఛ , అన్యాయ చట్ట ప్రక్రియల నుండి రక్షణ , మానసిక ఆరోగ్యం . సిలబస్ ఐదింటిని పేర్కొంటుంది: దాడి (assault) (తక్షణ బలప్రయోగ బెదిరింపు), దెబ్బ (battery) (వాస్తవంగా బలప్రయోగం), అక్రమ నిర్బంధం (చట్టవిరుద్ధ సంపూర్ణ నిర్బంధం), దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ (దురుద్దేశంతో వేసిన అన్యాయ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్), మానసిక ఆఘాతం (మానసిక వ్యాధి). దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం కలిసి వ్యక్తిపై అతిక్రమణ అవుతాయి: నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండానే దావా యోగ్యమైన, ప్రత్యక్ష, ఉద్దేశపూర్వక జోక్యాలు. దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, మానసిక ఆఘాతానికి నష్టం రుజువు అవసరం. ఒక వ్యక్తి శారీరక హాని కలిగించేలా ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా ఒక చర్య చేసి , అది హాని కలిగిస్తే, బలప్రయోగం లేకపోయినా చట్టం బాధ్యతను గుర్తిస్తుంది ( Wilkinson v. Downton , 1897). పోలీసులు లేదా ఇతర అధికారులు ఈ టార్ట్‌లు చేసినప్పుడు, బాధితుడు సివిల్ దావాతో పాటు Arts. 21, 32/226 కింద ప్రజా చట్ట నష్టపరిహారం కూడా కోరవచ్చు ( D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal , 1996; Bhim Singh v. State of J&K , 1985). కస్టడీ హింస "strikes a blow at the Rule of Law" (అర్థం: చట్టబద్ధ పాలనపై దెబ్బ కొడుతుంది) ( D.K. Basu ). సాధారణ రక్షణలు: సమ్మతి , ఆత్మరక్షణ (ప్రైవేట్ రక్షణ), చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం (ఉదా. చట్టబద్ధ అరెస్ట్), చట్టపరమైన అధికారం .
te.meaning: వ్యక్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు – ఆస్తి, ప్రతిష్ఠ లేదా వ్యాపారంపై టార్ట్‌లకు భిన్నంగా, ఒక వ్యక్తి శరీరం, స్వేచ్ఛ, మానసిక శ్రేయస్సు లేదా అన్యాయ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ నుండి రక్షణను దెబ్బతీసే సివిల్ తప్పులు. వ్యక్తిపై అతిక్రమణ – ప్రతివాది వాది వ్యక్తిపై ప్రత్యక్షంగా , (సాధారణంగా) ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా జోక్యం చేసుకునే టార్ట్‌ల సమూహం ( దాడి , దెబ్బ , అక్రమ నిర్బంధం ); స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం. ఉద్దేశపూర్వక హాని కలిగించడం – Wilkinson v. Downton సూత్రం: "wilfully done an act calculated to cause physical harm to the plaintiff—that is to say, to infringe her legal right to personal safety, and has in fact thereby caused physical harm to her" (అర్థం: వాదికి శారీరక హాని కలిగించేలా – అంటే ఆమె వ్యక్తిగత భద్రత చట్టపరమైన హక్కును ఉల్లంఘించేలా – ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా చర్య చేసి, దాని ద్వారా వాస్తవంగా ఆమెకు శారీరక హాని కలిగించిన) ప్రతివాది, "there being no justification alleged for the act" (అర్థం: ఆ చర్యకు ఏ సమర్థనా చెప్పనప్పుడు) బాధ్యుడు. కస్టడీ హింస – పోలీసు లేదా ఇతర అధికార కస్టడీలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తిపై హింస, హింసించడం లేదా మరణం; D.K. Basu లో కోర్టు ఇది "strikes a blow at the Rule of Law, which demands that the powers of the executive should not only be derived from law but also that the same should be limited by law" (అర్థం: కార్యనిర్వాహక అధికారాలు చట్టం నుండి రావడమే కాకుండా చట్టం ద్వారా పరిమితం కావాలని కోరే చట్టబద్ధ పాలనపై దెబ్బ కొడుతుంది) అని చెప్పింది.
keyPoints: వ్యక్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు శరీరం, స్వేచ్ఛ, మనస్సు, అన్యాయ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ నుండి రక్షణను కాపాడతాయి. దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం వ్యక్తిపై అతిక్రమణ రూపాలు; స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం. దాడి బెదిరింపు; దెబ్బ స్పర్శ. అక్రమ నిర్బంధానికి సంపూర్ణ నిర్బంధం అవసరం; బలం అవసరం లేదు. దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, మానసిక ఆఘాతానికి నష్టం అవసరం. Wilkinson v. Downton : హాని కలిగించేలా చేసిన ఉద్దేశపూర్వక చర్య దావా యోగ్యం. అరెస్ట్ అధికారాలు పరిమితం: BNSS ss. 43, 58; Art. 22(2). ప్రజా చట్ట నష్టపరిహారం టార్ట్ నష్టపరిహారానికి అదనం ( D.K. Basu ; Bhim Singh : ₹50,000).

selfTest.q: సిలబస్‌లో వ్యక్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే ఐదు టార్ట్‌లు చెప్పండి. దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, మానసిక ఆఘాతం. వ్యక్తిపై అతిక్రమణ అంటే?
selfTest.a: వ్యక్తిపై ప్రత్యక్ష, ఉద్దేశపూర్వక జోక్యం: దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం. కేవలం మాటలు దాడి అవుతాయా? కావు (BNS s. 130 Explanation), అయితే మాటలు సైగలకు అర్థం ఇవ్వవచ్చు. అక్రమ నిర్బంధానికి భౌతిక బలం అవసరమా? లేదు; అధికారం లేదా బెదిరింపు ద్వారా నిరోధం చాలు. వ్యక్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే ఏ టార్ట్‌లకు నష్టం రుజువు అవసరం? దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, మానసిక ఆఘాతం. Wilkinson v. Downton ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? హాని కలిగించేలా చెప్పిన ఉద్దేశపూర్వక అబద్ధం, అనారోగ్యం కలిగిస్తే, దావా యోగ్యం. అరెస్ట్ అయిన వ్యక్తిని ఎంత సమయంలో Magistrate ముందు హాజరుపరచాలి? ఇరవై నాలుగు గంటలు, ప్రయాణ సమయం మినహా (Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58). రిట్ పరిహారం సివిల్ దావాను నిషేధిస్తుందా? లేదు; దానికి భంగం కలిగించదు (D.K. Basu). Bhim Singh లో ఎంత ఇచ్చారు? ₹50,000. అక్రమ నిర్బంధానికి కాలపరిమితి? నిర్బంధం ముగిసినప్పటి నుండి ఒక సంవత్సరం (Art. 73).

hi.inOneMinute: Torts affecting the person protect a human being's own self: his body , his freedom from fear of violence , his liberty , his freedom from unjust legal proceedings and his mental health . The syllabus names five: assault (threat of immediate force), battery (actual application of force), false imprisonment (unlawful total restraint), malicious prosecution (an unjust prosecution brought with malice), and nervous shock (psychiatric harm). Assault, battery and false imprisonment together form trespass to the person : direct, intentional interferences that are actionable without proof of loss. Malicious prosecution and nervous shock need proof of damage. The law also recognises liability where a person wilfully does an act calculated to cause physical harm and it does so, even without force ( Wilkinson v. Downton , 1897). When police or other officials commit these torts, the victim can also claim public law compensation under Arts. 21 and 32/226, in addition to a civil suit ( D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal , 1996; Bhim Singh v. State of J&K , 1985). Custodial violence "strikes a blow at the Rule of Law" ( D.K. Basu ). Common defences: consent , self-defence (private defence), lawful authority (e.g. a lawful arrest), and statutory authority .
legalProvision: There is no Indian statute that codifies the torts affecting the person; they are common law torts. But Indian statutes define the matching wrongs and limit official power:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (criminal definitions often used to explain the torts)

s. 130 (Assault): "Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault." Explanation: "Mere words do not amount to an assault." s. 128 (Force) and s. 129 (Criminal force): force is causing motion, change of motion or cessation of motion that brings a substance "into contact with any part of that other's body"; criminal force is force used intentionally "without that person's consent" to cause "injury, fear or annoyance". s. 127(1) (Wrongful confinement): "Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said 'wrongfully to confine' that person."
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

s. 43(1)–(2): in making an arrest the officer "shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody"; if the person "forcibly resists ... or attempts to evade the arrest", the officer "may use all means necessary to effect the arrest". s. 43(4): this does not give "a right to cause the death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for life." s. 58: no person arrested without warrant shall be detained for longer than is reasonable, and not beyond "twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey" without a Magistrate's special order.
Constitution of India

Art. 21: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Art. 22(2): "Every person who is arrested and detained in custody shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest ... and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate."

Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule – Art. 73 (false imprisonment): one year "When the imprisonment ends"; Art. 74 (malicious prosecution): one year "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated"; assault, battery and nervous shock: Art. 113, three years "When the right to sue accrues".
hi.meaning: Torts affecting the person – civil wrongs that injure a person's body, liberty, mental well-being or freedom from unjust prosecution, as opposed to torts against property, reputation or business. Trespass to the person – the group of torts ( assault , battery , false imprisonment ) in which the defendant directly and (usually) intentionally interferes with the plaintiff's person; actionable per se . Intentional infliction of harm – the principle in Wilkinson v. Downton : a defendant who has "wilfully done an act calculated to cause physical harm to the plaintiff—that is to say, to infringe her legal right to personal safety, and has in fact thereby caused physical harm to her" is liable, "there being no justification alleged for the act". Custodial violence – violence, torture or death of a person in police or other official custody; in D.K. Basu the Court said it "strikes a blow at the Rule of Law, which demands that the powers of the executive should not only be derived from law but also that the same should be limited by law."
keyPoints: Torts affecting the person protect body, liberty, mind and freedom from unjust prosecution. Assault, battery and false imprisonment are forms of trespass to the person; actionable per se. Assault is the threat; battery is the contact. False imprisonment needs total restraint; no force is required. Malicious prosecution and nervous shock need damage. Wilkinson v. Downton : wilful act calculated to cause harm is actionable. Arrest powers are limited: BNSS ss. 43, 58; Art. 22(2). Public law compensation is in addition to tort damages ( D.K. Basu ; Bhim Singh : ₹50,000).

caseLaws.facts: Wilkinson v. Downton [1897] 2 QB 57 (Wright J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: As a practical joke, the defendant falsely told the plaintiff that her husband had met with a
caseLaws.facts: She believed it and suffered a violent nervous shock that made her ill. Principle: A person who has "wilfully done an act calculated to cause physical harm to the plaintiff ... and has in fact thereby caused physical harm to her" is liable, "there being no justification alleged for the act." Judgment for the plaintiff. Why it matters: Extends protection of the person to harm caused without force or contact.
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1996) Supp. 10 SCR; (1997) 1 SCC 416 (18 Dec 1996; Kuldip Singh and Dr. A.S. Anand JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Executive Chairman of Legal Aid Services, West Bengal, wrote to the Chief Justice of Indi
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Custodial violence, including torture and death in the lock ups, strikes a blow at the Rule of Law"; public law compensation for violation of Art. 21 "is a claim based on strict liability and is in addition to the claim available in private law for damages for tortious acts of the public servants." Requirements for arrest (name tags, memo of arrest, etc.) were laid down. Why it matters: Shows how torts against the person by police are answered by both tort law and constitutional law.
Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) 4 SCC 677; AIR 1986 SC 494 (22 Nov 1985; O. Chinnappa Reddy and V. Khalid JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An MLA was arrested at about 3 a
caseLaws.facts: m. on 10 September 1985 on his way to Srinagar, apparently to keep him away from the Assembly session; he was not produced before a Magistrate on 11th or the Sub Judge on 13th. Principle: "When a person comes to us with the complaint that he has been arrested and imprisoned with mischievous or malicious intent and that his constitutional and legal rights were invaded, the mischief or malice and the invasion may not be washed away or wished away by his being set free." The State was directed to pay ₹50,000. Why it matters: Unlawful detention is compensated even after release.

selfTest.q: Name the five torts affecting the person in the syllabus. Assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock. What is trespass to the person?
selfTest.a: Direct, intentional interference with the person: assault, battery, false imprisonment. Do mere words amount to assault? No (BNS s. 130 Explanation), though words can give meaning to gestures. Is physical force needed for false imprisonment? No; restraint by authority or threat is enough. Which torts affecting the person need proof of damage? Malicious prosecution and nervous shock. What did Wilkinson v. Downton decide? A wilful false statement calculated to cause harm, which caused illness, is actionable. Within what time must an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate? Twenty-four hours, excluding journey time (Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58). Does a writ award bar a civil suit? No; it is without prejudice to it (D.K. Basu). How much was awarded in Bhim Singh ? ₹50,000. Limitation for false imprisonment? One year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73).

law-of-torts-u3-t3.subtitle: The tort of making another person expect that force is about to be used on them

en.inOneMinute: Assault is an act of the defendant that makes the plaintiff reasonably apprehend that force is about to be applied to him immediately . No contact is needed. Raising a fist, aiming a stick, or rushing at someone can each be an assault. The key element is the plaintiff's reasonable apprehension of immediate force, together with the defendant's apparent present ability to carry it out. In Stephens v. Myers (1830) a man advancing with a clenched fist was stopped before he could reach the chairman; it was still an assault, because "within a second or two of time, he would have reached the plaintiff". Mere words are not an assault (BNS s. 130 Explanation), but words may give a gesture the meaning of a threat ("I will give you a beating" while lifting a stick), and words may also take the threat away. Assault is a form of trespass to the person . It is actionable per se : the plaintiff need not prove any loss (in Stephens v. Myers the damages were one shilling). Assault and battery differ: assault is the threat; battery is the touch. Each can exist without the other. Defences: consent, self-defence (private defence), lawful authority. Limitation: three years (Limitation Act Art. 113).
legalProvision: Assault in tort is a common law wrong. Indian criminal law gives a close definition that courts and students use to explain it:

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 130 – "Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault."

Explanation: "Mere words do not amount to an assault. But the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparation such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault." Illustration (a): "A shakes his fist at Z, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that A is about to strike Z. A has committed an assault." Illustration (b): "A begins to unloose the muzzle of a ferocious dog, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that he is about to cause the dog to attack Z. A has committed an assault upon Z." Illustration (c): "A takes up a stick, saying to Z, 'I will give you a beating'. Here, though the words used by A could in no case amount to an assault, and though the mere gesture, unaccompanied by any other circumstances, might not amount to an assault, the gesture explained by the words may amount to an assault."

BNS s. 35 – "Every person has a right, subject to the restrictions contained in section 37, to defend— (a) his own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body". s. 37(2): "The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence."

Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy , 2026) – a cause of action for "assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code" does not survive the death of the party.
Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – "Any suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in this Schedule": three years "When the right to sue accrues". (Assault has no separate Article.)
en.meaning: Assault ( tort ) – an act by the defendant which causes the plaintiff to reasonably apprehend the immediate application of force to his person, where the defendant has (or appears to have) the present ability to apply it. Reasonable apprehension – the plaintiff must actually expect the force, and a reasonable person in his position would also expect it. Fear in the sense of being frightened is not essential; it is enough that the plaintiff expects contact. Tindal C.J. in Stephens v. Myers : "It is not every threat, when there is no actual personal violence, that constitutes an assault, there must, in all cases, be the means of carrying the threat into effect." Immediacy – the force must appear to be about to happen now or almost at once, not at some future time. Stephens v. Myers : "within a second or two of time".
keyPoints: Assault = reasonable apprehension of immediate force; no contact needed. Present ability (actual or apparent) is required ( Stephens v. Myers ). Immediacy: "within a second or two of time". Mere words are not assault; words can colour a gesture (BNS s. 130). Actionable per se: damages of one shilling in Stephens v. Myers . Assault is the threat; battery is the touch. Defences: consent; reasonable private defence (BNS ss. 35, 37(2)); lawful authority. Limitation: three years (Art. 113); the claim does not survive death (ISA s. 306).

caseLaws.facts: Stephens v. Myers (1830) 172 ER 735; 4 C & P 349 (Tindal C.J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: At a parish meeting a vote was carried to turn the defendant out
caseLaws.facts: He said he would rather pull the chairman out of the chair and advanced with his fist clenched towards him, but was stopped by the churchwarden before he was near enough to strike. Principle: "there must, in all cases, be the means of carrying the threat into effect"; but "If he was so advancing, that, within a second or two of time, he would have reached the plaintiff, it seems to me it is an assault in law." Verdict for the plaintiff; damages one shilling. Why it matters: The leading illustration of assault without contact, and of the present ability and immediacy requirements.
Wilkinson v. Downton [1897] 2 QB 57 (Wright J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: As a practical joke, the defendant falsely told the plaintiff that her husband had both legs
caseLaws.facts: She suffered a violent nervous shock and became ill. There was no gesture or threat of force. Principle: A person who has "wilfully done an act calculated to cause physical harm to the plaintiff ... and has in fact thereby caused physical harm to her" is liable. Why it matters: Shows the boundary of assault: harm caused by words without any threat of immediate force is not assault, but may be a separate wrong.

selfTest.q: Define assault. An act causing reasonable apprehension of immediate force to the plaintiff. Is contact needed?
selfTest.a: No. Which case says there must be "the means of carrying the threat into effect"? Stephens v. Myers. In Stephens v. Myers , why was there an assault though the defendant was stopped? He would have reached the chairman within a second or two. Do mere words amount to assault? No (BNS s. 130 Explanation). Give the BNS illustration where words make a gesture an assault. Taking up a stick and saying "I will give you a beating". What damages were awarded in Stephens v. Myers ? One shilling. Can there be battery without assault? Yes, e.g. a blow from behind. What limits private defence? It cannot inflict more harm than necessary (BNS s. 37(2)). Limitation for a suit for assault? Three years (Art. 113).

te.inOneMinute: దాడి (assault) అంటే తనపై వెంటనే బలప్రయోగం జరగబోతోందని వాది సహేతుకంగా భయపడేలా చేసే ప్రతివాది చర్య. స్పర్శ అవసరం లేదు. పిడికిలి ఎత్తడం, కర్ర గురిపెట్టడం, ఎవరిపైకైనా దూసుకెళ్లడం – ప్రతి ఒక్కటీ దాడి కావచ్చు. ముఖ్య అంశం: తక్షణ బలప్రయోగం గురించి వాది సహేతుక భయం , దానితో పాటు దానిని అమలు చేయడానికి ప్రతివాదికి కనిపించే ప్రస్తుత సామర్థ్యం . Stephens v. Myers (1830) లో పిడికిలి బిగించి ముందుకు వస్తున్న వ్యక్తిని అధ్యక్షుని చేరకముందే ఆపేశారు; అయినా అది దాడి, ఎందుకంటే "within a second or two of time, he would have reached the plaintiff" (అర్థం: ఒకటి రెండు క్షణాల్లో అతను వాదిని చేరుకునేవాడు). కేవలం మాటలు దాడి కావు (BNS s. 130 Explanation), కానీ మాటలు ఒక సైగకు బెదిరింపు అర్థాన్ని ఇవ్వవచ్చు (కర్ర ఎత్తుతూ "నిన్ను కొడతా" అనడం), మాటలు బెదిరింపును తొలగించనూవచ్చు. దాడి వ్యక్తిపై అతిక్రమణ యొక్క ఒక రూపం. అది స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం : వాది ఏ నష్టమూ రుజువు చేయనక్కర్లేదు ( Stephens v. Myers లో నష్టపరిహారం ఒక షిల్లింగ్). దాడి, దెబ్బ వేర్వేరు: దాడి బెదిరింపు; దెబ్బ స్పర్శ. ఒకటి లేకుండా మరొకటి ఉండవచ్చు. రక్షణలు: సమ్మతి, ఆత్మరక్షణ (ప్రైవేట్ రక్షణ), చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం. కాలపరిమితి: మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Limitation Act Art. 113).
te.meaning: దాడి ( టార్ట్ ) – ప్రతివాదికి బలప్రయోగం చేసే ప్రస్తుత సామర్థ్యం ఉన్న (లేదా ఉన్నట్లు కనిపించే) సందర్భంలో, తన శరీరంపై తక్షణ బలప్రయోగం జరుగుతుందని వాది సహేతుకంగా భయపడేలా చేసే ప్రతివాది చర్య. సహేతుక భయం – వాది వాస్తవంగా బలప్రయోగాన్ని ఆశించాలి, అతని స్థానంలోని సహేతుక వ్యక్తి కూడా ఆశించాలి. భయపడటం అనే అర్థంలో భయం తప్పనిసరి కాదు; వాది స్పర్శను ఆశిస్తే చాలు. Stephens v. Myers లో Tindal C.J.: "It is not every threat, when there is no actual personal violence, that constitutes an assault, there must, in all cases, be the means of carrying the threat into effect." (అర్థం: వాస్తవ వ్యక్తిగత హింస లేనప్పుడు ప్రతి బెదిరింపూ దాడి కాదు; అన్ని సందర్భాల్లో బెదిరింపును అమలు చేసే సాధనాలు ఉండాలి.) తక్షణత – బలప్రయోగం ఇప్పుడే లేదా దాదాపు వెంటనే జరగబోతున్నట్లు కనిపించాలి, భవిష్యత్తులో కాదు. Stephens v. Myers : "within a second or two of time" (అర్థం: ఒకటి రెండు క్షణాల్లో).
keyPoints: దాడి = తక్షణ బలప్రయోగంపై సహేతుక భయం; స్పర్శ అవసరం లేదు. ప్రస్తుత సామర్థ్యం (వాస్తవ లేదా కనిపించే) అవసరం ( Stephens v. Myers ). తక్షణత: "within a second or two of time" (అర్థం: ఒకటి రెండు క్షణాల్లో). కేవలం మాటలు దాడి కావు; మాటలు సైగకు అర్థం ఇవ్వగలవు (BNS s. 130). స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం: Stephens v. Myers లో ఒక షిల్లింగ్ నష్టపరిహారం. దాడి బెదిరింపు; దెబ్బ స్పర్శ. రక్షణలు: సమ్మతి; సహేతుక ప్రైవేట్ రక్షణ (BNS ss. 35, 37(2)); చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం. కాలపరిమితి: మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 113); మరణం తర్వాత దావా కొనసాగదు (ISA s. 306).

selfTest.q: దాడిని నిర్వచించండి. తక్షణ బలప్రయోగంపై వాదికి సహేతుక భయం కలిగించే చర్య. స్పర్శ అవసరమా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. "the means of carrying the threat into effect" ఉండాలని ఏ కేసు చెబుతుంది? Stephens v. Myers. Stephens v. Myers లో ప్రతివాదిని ఆపినా దాడి ఎందుకు? ఒకటి రెండు క్షణాల్లో అతను అధ్యక్షుని చేరుకునేవాడు. కేవలం మాటలు దాడి అవుతాయా? కావు (BNS s. 130 Explanation). మాటలు సైగను దాడిగా మార్చే BNS ఉదాహరణ ఇవ్వండి. కర్ర తీసుకుని "నిన్ను కొడతా" అనడం. Stephens v. Myers లో ఎంత నష్టపరిహారం ఇచ్చారు? ఒక షిల్లింగ్. దాడి లేకుండా దెబ్బ ఉండవచ్చా? ఉండవచ్చు, ఉదా. వెనుక నుండి దెబ్బ. ప్రైవేట్ రక్షణను ఏది పరిమితం చేస్తుంది? అవసరమైన దానికంటే ఎక్కువ హాని కలిగించకూడదు (BNS s. 37(2)). దాడి దావాకు కాలపరిమితి? మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 113).

hi.inOneMinute: Assault is an act of the defendant that makes the plaintiff reasonably apprehend that force is about to be applied to him immediately . No contact is needed. Raising a fist, aiming a stick, or rushing at someone can each be an assault. The key element is the plaintiff's reasonable apprehension of immediate force, together with the defendant's apparent present ability to carry it out. In Stephens v. Myers (1830) a man advancing with a clenched fist was stopped before he could reach the chairman; it was still an assault, because "within a second or two of time, he would have reached the plaintiff". Mere words are not an assault (BNS s. 130 Explanation), but words may give a gesture the meaning of a threat ("I will give you a beating" while lifting a stick), and words may also take the threat away. Assault is a form of trespass to the person . It is actionable per se : the plaintiff need not prove any loss (in Stephens v. Myers the damages were one shilling). Assault and battery differ: assault is the threat; battery is the touch. Each can exist without the other. Defences: consent, self-defence (private defence), lawful authority. Limitation: three years (Limitation Act Art. 113).
legalProvision: Assault in tort is a common law wrong. Indian criminal law gives a close definition that courts and students use to explain it:

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 130 – "Whoever makes any gesture, or any preparation intending or knowing it to be likely that such gesture or preparation will cause any person present to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person, is said to commit an assault."

Explanation: "Mere words do not amount to an assault. But the words which a person uses may give to his gestures or preparation such a meaning as may make those gestures or preparations amount to an assault." Illustration (a): "A shakes his fist at Z, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that A is about to strike Z. A has committed an assault." Illustration (b): "A begins to unloose the muzzle of a ferocious dog, intending or knowing it to be likely that he may thereby cause Z to believe that he is about to cause the dog to attack Z. A has committed an assault upon Z." Illustration (c): "A takes up a stick, saying to Z, 'I will give you a beating'. Here, though the words used by A could in no case amount to an assault, and though the mere gesture, unaccompanied by any other circumstances, might not amount to an assault, the gesture explained by the words may amount to an assault."

BNS s. 35 – "Every person has a right, subject to the restrictions contained in section 37, to defend— (a) his own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body". s. 37(2): "The right of private defence in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence."

Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy , 2026) – a cause of action for "assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code" does not survive the death of the party.
Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – "Any suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in this Schedule": three years "When the right to sue accrues". (Assault has no separate Article.)
hi.meaning: Assault ( tort ) – an act by the defendant which causes the plaintiff to reasonably apprehend the immediate application of force to his person, where the defendant has (or appears to have) the present ability to apply it. Reasonable apprehension – the plaintiff must actually expect the force, and a reasonable person in his position would also expect it. Fear in the sense of being frightened is not essential; it is enough that the plaintiff expects contact. Tindal C.J. in Stephens v. Myers : "It is not every threat, when there is no actual personal violence, that constitutes an assault, there must, in all cases, be the means of carrying the threat into effect." Immediacy – the force must appear to be about to happen now or almost at once, not at some future time. Stephens v. Myers : "within a second or two of time".
keyPoints: Assault = reasonable apprehension of immediate force; no contact needed. Present ability (actual or apparent) is required ( Stephens v. Myers ). Immediacy: "within a second or two of time". Mere words are not assault; words can colour a gesture (BNS s. 130). Actionable per se: damages of one shilling in Stephens v. Myers . Assault is the threat; battery is the touch. Defences: consent; reasonable private defence (BNS ss. 35, 37(2)); lawful authority. Limitation: three years (Art. 113); the claim does not survive death (ISA s. 306).

caseLaws.facts: Stephens v. Myers (1830) 172 ER 735; 4 C & P 349 (Tindal C.J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: At a parish meeting a vote was carried to turn the defendant out
caseLaws.facts: He said he would rather pull the chairman out of the chair and advanced with his fist clenched towards him, but was stopped by the churchwarden before he was near enough to strike. Principle: "there must, in all cases, be the means of carrying the threat into effect"; but "If he was so advancing, that, within a second or two of time, he would have reached the plaintiff, it seems to me it is an assault in law." Verdict for the plaintiff; damages one shilling. Why it matters: The leading illustration of assault without contact, and of the present ability and immediacy requirements.
Wilkinson v. Downton [1897] 2 QB 57 (Wright J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: As a practical joke, the defendant falsely told the plaintiff that her husband had both legs
caseLaws.facts: She suffered a violent nervous shock and became ill. There was no gesture or threat of force. Principle: A person who has "wilfully done an act calculated to cause physical harm to the plaintiff ... and has in fact thereby caused physical harm to her" is liable. Why it matters: Shows the boundary of assault: harm caused by words without any threat of immediate force is not assault, but may be a separate wrong.

selfTest.q: Define assault. An act causing reasonable apprehension of immediate force to the plaintiff. Is contact needed?
selfTest.a: No. Which case says there must be "the means of carrying the threat into effect"? Stephens v. Myers. In Stephens v. Myers , why was there an assault though the defendant was stopped? He would have reached the chairman within a second or two. Do mere words amount to assault? No (BNS s. 130 Explanation). Give the BNS illustration where words make a gesture an assault. Taking up a stick and saying "I will give you a beating". What damages were awarded in Stephens v. Myers ? One shilling. Can there be battery without assault? Yes, e.g. a blow from behind. What limits private defence? It cannot inflict more harm than necessary (BNS s. 37(2)). Limitation for a suit for assault? Three years (Art. 113).
