law-of-torts-u3-t1.subtitle: The named torts and the interests they protect: person, property, reputation, business and family

en.inOneMinute: A specific tort is a named civil wrong with its own fixed elements, such as assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, trespass to land or nuisance. Each protects a particular interest of the plaintiff: his body, his liberty, his mind, his land, his reputation, and so on. Units 1 and 2 taught the general principles (wrongful act, legal damage, fault, defences). Specific torts apply those principles to particular kinds of harm. To win, the plaintiff must prove every element of the particular tort he sues for. The syllabus divides them by the interest protected. The first group covers torts affecting the person (assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock), digital torts , and torts affecting immovable property (trespass to land, nuisance). The second group covers movable property, accidents, defamation, negligence, business relations and family relations. Some specific torts are actionable per se (the wrong itself is enough; no loss need be proved), e.g. trespass to land, assault, battery, false imprisonment. Others need proof of special damage (actual loss), e.g. malicious prosecution, private nuisance, nervous shock. Indian statute law names many specific torts. Part VII of the Limitation Act, 1963 Schedule is headed "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" and lists, among others, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, libel, slander and trespass upon immovable property, each with its own time limit.
legalProvision: There is no single code of torts in India. The specific torts are mainly common law wrongs applied by Indian courts, but several statutes recognise them by name.
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Part VII – "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" (examples):

Article Suit Period Time runs from 73 "For compensation for false imprisonment" One year "When the imprisonment ends" 74 "For compensation for a malicious prosecution" One year "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated" 75 "For compensation for libel" One year "When the libel is published" 76 "For compensation for slander" One year When the words are spoken, or, if not actionable in themselves, "when the special damage complained of results" 85 "For compensation for obstructing a way or a water-course" Three years "The date of the obstruction" 87 "For compensation for trespass upon immovable property" Three years "The date of the trespass" 113 "Any suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere" (e.g. assault, battery, nuisance) Three years "When the right to sue accrues"

Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(3) – "When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction", among other cases, "where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief". s. 40(1): damages may be claimed "either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction".

Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy , 2026) – names "defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 ... or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party" as causes of action that do not survive death.

Constitution of India, Art. 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Many torts affecting the person (false imprisonment, battery by officials) also violate this right.
en.meaning: Specific tort – a particular, named civil wrong for which the law gives damages or an injunction , with its own elements that the plaintiff must prove (for example, assault needs a threat of immediate force; malicious prosecution needs a prosecution ended in the plaintiff's favour, without reasonable cause and with malice ). Actionable per se – a tort that can be sued on without proof of actual loss; the violation of the right is itself the injury. In Ashby v. White the reasons given in the House of Lords put it this way: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it. If a Man pick a Lock, and come into an House without the Consent of the Owner, perhaps there is no Pecuniary Damage done to the Value of a Farthing, yet the Owner shall have an Action against him". Special damage – actual, provable loss (money, property, health, or similar harm) that must be shown before certain torts are complete (e.g. malicious prosecution, private nuisance , slander not actionable in itself: Limitation Act Art. 76).
keyPoints: A specific tort is a named wrong with its own elements. Specific torts are classified by the interest protected. First group: assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock, digital torts, trespass to land, nuisance. Trespass forms are actionable per se ( Entick ; Stephens v. Myers ). Malicious prosecution, private nuisance and nervous shock need damage. Limitation Act Part VII is headed "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" (Arts. 72–91). Many specific torts are also crimes; both proceedings can run. Remedies: damages and injunction (SRA ss. 38(3), 40).

caseLaws.facts: Entick v. Carrington (1765) 95 ER 807 (King's Bench)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The King's messengers, acting under a general warrant from the Secretary of State, broke into
caseLaws.facts: The jury assessed damages at £300. Principle: "no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all"; the warrant was "wholly illegal and void". Why it matters: Shows that trespass to land is actionable per se and that even officials need legal authority for an entry.
Stephens v. Myers (1830) 172 ER 735; 4 C & P 349 (Tindal C.J.)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "If he was so advancing, that, within a second or two of time, he would have reached the plaintiff, it seems to me it is an assault in law." Verdict for the plaintiff, "Damages 1s." Why it matters: Assault needs no contact and no loss; it is actionable per se.
Ashby v. White (1703) (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A returning officer wrongfully refused Ashby's vote at a parliamentary election
caseLaws.facts: The Queen's Bench gave judgment for the officer; the House of Lords reversed it and gave judgment "That the Plaintiff should recover." Principle: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it"; a person denied his right may sue even without money loss. Why it matters: Explains why some specific torts are actionable per se.

selfTest.q: What is a specific tort?
selfTest.a: A named civil wrong with its own elements. On what basis are specific torts classified? The interest protected. Name the torts affecting the person in the first group. Assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock. Name the torts affecting immovable property in the first group. Trespass to land and nuisance. What does "actionable per se" mean? Actionable without proof of loss. Which case says no man can set foot on his neighbour's land without leave? Entick v. Carrington. What damages were awarded in Stephens v. Myers ? One shilling. Limitation for false imprisonment? One year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73). Limitation for trespass upon immovable property? Three years from the trespass (Art. 87). Which provision allows an injunction against invasion of property rights? Specific Relief Act s. 38(3).

te.inOneMinute: నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్ అంటే దాని స్వంత స్థిర అంశాలు కలిగిన, పేరున్న సివిల్ తప్పు; ఉదా. దాడి (assault), దెబ్బ (battery), అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ, న్యూసెన్స్. ప్రతి ఒక్కటి వాది యొక్క ఒక ప్రత్యేక ప్రయోజనాన్ని కాపాడుతుంది: అతని శరీరం, స్వేచ్ఛ, మనస్సు, భూమి, ప్రతిష్ఠ మొదలైనవి. Units 1, 2 సాధారణ సూత్రాలను (తప్పుడు చర్య, చట్టపరమైన నష్టం, తప్పిదం, రక్షణలు) నేర్పాయి. నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్‌లు ఆ సూత్రాలను ప్రత్యేక రకాల హానికి అన్వయిస్తాయి. గెలవడానికి, వాది తాను దావా వేసిన ఆ టార్ట్ యొక్క ప్రతి అంశాన్నీ రుజువు చేయాలి. సిలబస్ వీటిని కాపాడే ప్రయోజనం ఆధారంగా విభజిస్తుంది. మొదటి వర్గంలో వ్యక్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు (దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, మానసిక ఆఘాతం), డిజిటల్ టార్ట్‌లు , స్థిరాస్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు (భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ, న్యూసెన్స్) ఉన్నాయి. రెండవ వర్గం చరాస్తి, ప్రమాదాలు, పరువు నష్టం, నిర్లక్ష్యం, వ్యాపార సంబంధాలు, కుటుంబ సంబంధాలను కవర్ చేస్తుంది. కొన్ని నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్‌లు స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం (తప్పు జరిగితే చాలు; నష్టం రుజువు అవసరం లేదు), ఉదా. భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ, దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం. మరికొన్నింటికి ప్రత్యేక నష్టం (వాస్తవ నష్టం) రుజువు అవసరం, ఉదా. దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, ప్రైవేట్ న్యూసెన్స్, మానసిక ఆఘాతం. భారతీయ చట్టం అనేక నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్‌లకు పేరు పెడుతుంది. Limitation Act, 1963 Schedule లోని Part VII శీర్షిక "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" (అర్థం: టార్ట్‌కు సంబంధించిన దావాలు); అది అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, libel, slander, స్థిరాస్తిపై అతిక్రమణ మొదలైనవాటిని, ఒక్కొక్కదానికి దాని కాలపరిమితితో, జాబితా చేస్తుంది.
te.meaning: నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్ – చట్టం నష్టపరిహారం లేదా నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇచ్చే, పేరున్న ఒక ప్రత్యేక సివిల్ తప్పు; వాది రుజువు చేయాల్సిన దాని స్వంత అంశాలతో (ఉదా. దాడికి తక్షణ బలప్రయోగ బెదిరింపు అవసరం; దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్‌కు వాదికి అనుకూలంగా ముగిసిన, సహేతుక కారణం లేని, దురుద్దేశంతో చేసిన ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ అవసరం). స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం – వాస్తవ నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండానే దావా వేయగల టార్ట్ ; హక్కు ఉల్లంఘనే హాని. Ashby v. White లో House of Lords లో ఇచ్చిన కారణాలు ఇలా చెప్పాయి: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it. If a Man pick a Lock, and come into an House without the Consent of the Owner, perhaps there is no Pecuniary Damage done to the Value of a Farthing, yet the Owner shall have an Action against him" (అర్థం: ప్రతి హానిలోనూ స్వభావంగా నష్టం ఉంటుంది. ఒక వ్యక్తి తాళం తెరిచి యజమాని సమ్మతి లేకుండా ఇంట్లోకి వస్తే, బహుశా ఒక పైసా విలువైన ఆర్థిక నష్టం కూడా జరగకపోవచ్చు, అయినా యజమాని అతనిపై దావా వేయవచ్చు). ప్రత్యేక నష్టం – కొన్ని టార్ట్‌లు పూర్తి కావడానికి చూపించాల్సిన వాస్తవ, రుజువు చేయగల నష్టం (డబ్బు, ఆస్తి, ఆరోగ్యం లేదా అలాంటి హాని) (ఉదా. దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, ప్రైవేట్ న్యూసెన్స్ , స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం కాని slander : Limitation Act Art. 76).
keyPoints: నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్ అంటే దాని స్వంత అంశాలు కలిగిన పేరున్న తప్పు. నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్‌లను కాపాడే ప్రయోజనం ఆధారంగా వర్గీకరిస్తారు. మొదటి వర్గం: దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, మానసిక ఆఘాతం, డిజిటల్ టార్ట్‌లు, భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ, న్యూసెన్స్. అతిక్రమణ రూపాలు స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం ( Entick ; Stephens v. Myers ). దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, ప్రైవేట్ న్యూసెన్స్, మానసిక ఆఘాతానికి నష్టం అవసరం. Limitation Act Part VII శీర్షిక "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" (అర్థం: టార్ట్‌కు సంబంధించిన దావాలు) (Arts. 72–91). అనేక నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్‌లు నేరాలు కూడా; రెండు ప్రక్రియలూ సాగవచ్చు. పరిహారాలు: నష్టపరిహారం, నిషేధాజ్ఞ (SRA ss. 38(3), 40).

selfTest.q: నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్ అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: దాని స్వంత అంశాలు కలిగిన పేరున్న సివిల్ తప్పు. నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్‌లను ఏ ఆధారంగా వర్గీకరిస్తారు? కాపాడే ప్రయోజనం. మొదటి వర్గంలో వ్యక్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లను పేర్కొనండి. దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్, మానసిక ఆఘాతం. మొదటి వర్గంలో స్థిరాస్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లను పేర్కొనండి. భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ, న్యూసెన్స్. "స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం" అంటే? నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండానే దావా యోగ్యం. పొరుగువాని అనుమతి లేకుండా అతని భూమిపై కాలు పెట్టలేరని ఏ కేసు చెబుతుంది? Entick v. Carrington. Stephens v. Myers లో ఎంత నష్టపరిహారం ఇచ్చారు? ఒక షిల్లింగ్. అక్రమ నిర్బంధానికి కాలపరిమితి? నిర్బంధం ముగిసినప్పటి నుండి ఒక సంవత్సరం (Art. 73). స్థిరాస్తిపై అతిక్రమణకు కాలపరిమితి? అతిక్రమణ నుండి మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 87). ఆస్తి హక్కుల ఆక్రమణపై నిషేధాజ్ఞను ఏ నిబంధన అనుమతిస్తుంది? Specific Relief Act s. 38(3).

hi.inOneMinute: A specific tort is a named civil wrong with its own fixed elements, such as assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, trespass to land or nuisance. Each protects a particular interest of the plaintiff: his body, his liberty, his mind, his land, his reputation, and so on. Units 1 and 2 taught the general principles (wrongful act, legal damage, fault, defences). Specific torts apply those principles to particular kinds of harm. To win, the plaintiff must prove every element of the particular tort he sues for. The syllabus divides them by the interest protected. The first group covers torts affecting the person (assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock), digital torts , and torts affecting immovable property (trespass to land, nuisance). The second group covers movable property, accidents, defamation, negligence, business relations and family relations. Some specific torts are actionable per se (the wrong itself is enough; no loss need be proved), e.g. trespass to land, assault, battery, false imprisonment. Others need proof of special damage (actual loss), e.g. malicious prosecution, private nuisance, nervous shock. Indian statute law names many specific torts. Part VII of the Limitation Act, 1963 Schedule is headed "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" and lists, among others, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, libel, slander and trespass upon immovable property, each with its own time limit.
legalProvision: There is no single code of torts in India. The specific torts are mainly common law wrongs applied by Indian courts, but several statutes recognise them by name.
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Part VII – "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" (examples):

Article Suit Period Time runs from 73 "For compensation for false imprisonment" One year "When the imprisonment ends" 74 "For compensation for a malicious prosecution" One year "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated" 75 "For compensation for libel" One year "When the libel is published" 76 "For compensation for slander" One year When the words are spoken, or, if not actionable in themselves, "when the special damage complained of results" 85 "For compensation for obstructing a way or a water-course" Three years "The date of the obstruction" 87 "For compensation for trespass upon immovable property" Three years "The date of the trespass" 113 "Any suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere" (e.g. assault, battery, nuisance) Three years "When the right to sue accrues"

Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(3) – "When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction", among other cases, "where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief". s. 40(1): damages may be claimed "either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction".

Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy , 2026) – names "defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 ... or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party" as causes of action that do not survive death.

Constitution of India, Art. 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Many torts affecting the person (false imprisonment, battery by officials) also violate this right.
hi.meaning: Specific tort – a particular, named civil wrong for which the law gives damages or an injunction , with its own elements that the plaintiff must prove (for example, assault needs a threat of immediate force; malicious prosecution needs a prosecution ended in the plaintiff's favour, without reasonable cause and with malice ). Actionable per se – a tort that can be sued on without proof of actual loss; the violation of the right is itself the injury. In Ashby v. White the reasons given in the House of Lords put it this way: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it. If a Man pick a Lock, and come into an House without the Consent of the Owner, perhaps there is no Pecuniary Damage done to the Value of a Farthing, yet the Owner shall have an Action against him". Special damage – actual, provable loss (money, property, health, or similar harm) that must be shown before certain torts are complete (e.g. malicious prosecution, private nuisance , slander not actionable in itself: Limitation Act Art. 76).
keyPoints: A specific tort is a named wrong with its own elements. Specific torts are classified by the interest protected. First group: assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock, digital torts, trespass to land, nuisance. Trespass forms are actionable per se ( Entick ; Stephens v. Myers ). Malicious prosecution, private nuisance and nervous shock need damage. Limitation Act Part VII is headed "SUITS RELATING TO TORT" (Arts. 72–91). Many specific torts are also crimes; both proceedings can run. Remedies: damages and injunction (SRA ss. 38(3), 40).

caseLaws.facts: The jury assessed damages at £300. Principle: "no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all"; the warrant was "wholly illegal and void". Why it matters: Shows that trespass to land is actionable per se and that even officials need legal authority for an entry.

caseLaws.name: Facts: A returning officer wrongfully refused Ashby's vote at a parliamentary election
caseLaws.facts: The Queen's Bench gave judgment for the officer; the House of Lords reversed it and gave judgment "That the Plaintiff should recover." Principle: "every Injury imports Damage in the Nature of it"; a person denied his right may sue even without money loss. Why it matters: Explains why some specific torts are actionable per se.

selfTest.q: What is a specific tort?
selfTest.a: A named civil wrong with its own elements. On what basis are specific torts classified? The interest protected. Name the torts affecting the person in the first group. Assault, battery, false imprisonment, malicious prosecution, nervous shock. Name the torts affecting immovable property in the first group. Trespass to land and nuisance. What does "actionable per se" mean? Actionable without proof of loss. Which case says no man can set foot on his neighbour's land without leave? Entick v. Carrington. What damages were awarded in Stephens v. Myers ? One shilling. Limitation for false imprisonment? One year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73). Limitation for trespass upon immovable property? Three years from the trespass (Art. 87). Which provision allows an injunction against invasion of property rights? Specific Relief Act s. 38(3).

law-of-torts-u3-t4.subtitle: Using force on another person's body without lawful justification

en.inOneMinute: Battery is the intentional and direct application of force to another person's body without lawful justification . Any touch can be enough: a slap, a push, spitting on someone, throwing water at him, pulling a chair away so he falls. No injury is needed. Battery is a form of trespass to the person and is actionable per se : the law protects the body for its own sake. The Supreme Court in Saheli v. Commissioner of Police (1989) said: "In cases of assault, battery and false imprisonment, the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity, loss of liberty and death." "Force" is wide. BNS s. 128 counts motion that brings a substance into contact with a person's body, with "anything which that other is wearing or carrying", or with anything so placed "that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling". Directness: the force must follow directly from the defendant's act (a stone thrown at the plaintiff). Indirect harm (leaving a stone on the road over which someone trips) is negligence, not battery. Defences: consent (including informed consent to medical treatment), private defence, lawful arrest or other legal authority, and the ordinary touching of daily life. Battery by the State's officers also violates Art. 21; the Supreme Court has awarded compensation for custodial beatings and deaths ( Saheli : ₹75,000; Nilabati Behera : ₹1,50,000).
legalProvision: Battery in tort is a common law wrong. Indian criminal law defines the matching ideas of "force" and "criminal force":

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 128 (Force) – "A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other's body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling". The motion may be caused "(a) by his own bodily power; (b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion ... takes place without any further act on his part ...; or (c) by inducing any animal to move".

BNS s. 129 (Criminal force) – "Whoever intentionally uses force to any person, without that person's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used, is said to use criminal force to that other."
BNS ss. 35, 37(2) – right of private defence of the body, which "in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence."

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 43(1)–(2), (4) – an arresting officer "shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody"; against forcible resistance he "may use all means necessary to effect the arrest"; but this does not give "a right to cause the death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for life."
Constitution of India, Art. 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – three years "When the right to sue accrues" (no separate Article for battery).
en.meaning: Battery – the intentional (or at least voluntary) and direct application of force to the body of another without his consent or other lawful justification. Force – any physical contact, however slight, including contact through an object or with things the plaintiff is wearing or carrying (compare BNS s. 128). It need not cause pain or injury. Informed consent – a patient's agreement to a particular medical procedure, given with knowledge of its nature; treatment beyond or without such consent can be battery (standard doctrine). Solatium – compensation for mental pain, distress and indignity, as opposed to money loss. Saheli : in battery cases "the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity".
keyPoints: Battery = intentional, direct application of force without lawful justification. Any touch is enough; injury is not needed. Force includes contact through objects and with things worn or carried (BNS s. 128). Indirect harm is negligence, not battery. Consent must cover the act done; treatment without consent is battery. Private defence must not exceed what is necessary (BNS s. 37(2)). Saheli : battery damages are "large" and a "solatium" (₹75,000). Custodial beatings: tort damages and Art. 21 compensation ( Nilabati Behera : ₹1,50,000).

caseLaws.facts: Saheli, A Women's Resources Centre v. Commissioner of Police, Delhi (1990) 1 SCC 422; AIR 1990 SC 513 (14 Dec 1989; B.C. Ray and S.R. Pandian JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A landlord's son, accompanied by the Station House Officer and other police, severely beat a
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "An action for damages lies for bodily harm which includes battery, assault, false imprisonment, physical injuries and death. In cases of assault, battery and false imprisonment, the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity, loss of liberty and death." ₹75,000 was directed to be paid to the mother. Why it matters: The Supreme Court expressly recognises battery as a tort and explains the nature of damages for it.
Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) 2 SCC 746

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner's son, about 22, was taken into police custody at about 8 a
caseLaws.facts: m. on 1.12.1987 for investigation of a theft; next day his dead body was found on a railway track with multiple injuries. Principle: Death caused by injuries inflicted in police custody violates Art. 21; the State must pay compensation in public law, in addition to any private law remedy. ₹1,50,000 was awarded. Why it matters: Shows the most serious form of battery by officials and the constitutional remedy for it.
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (24 Aug 2017; nine-judge bench)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to the Aadhaar scheme led to a reference on whether privacy is a fundamental right
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Privacy is protected by Art. 21; Dr D.Y. Chandrachud J.: "The integrity of the body and the sanctity of the mind can exist on the foundation that each individual possesses an inalienable ability and right to preserve a private space in which the human personality can develop." Why it matters: Bodily integrity, which battery protects in private law, is also a constitutional value.

selfTest.q: Define battery. Intentional, direct application of force to another's body without lawful justification. Must the plaintiff prove injury?
selfTest.a: No; it is actionable per se. Is touching a person's bag while he carries it battery? Yes, if unjustified (compare BNS s. 128). Is leaving a banana peel on which someone slips battery? No; it is indirect (negligence). Which case says battery damages are "a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity"? Saheli v. Commissioner of Police. How much was awarded in Saheli ? ₹75,000. Is surgery without consent battery? Yes, except in an emergency where consent cannot be obtained (standard doctrine). What limits force in arrest? Only "all means necessary" against resistance (BNSS s. 43(2)); no right to cause death except as allowed (s. 43(4)). What did Puttaswamy say about the body? "The integrity of the body and the sanctity of the mind" rest on a right to a private space. Limitation for battery? Three years (Art. 113).

te.inOneMinute: దెబ్బ (battery) అంటే చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా మరొక వ్యక్తి శరీరంపై ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా, ప్రత్యక్షంగా బలప్రయోగం చేయడం. ఏ స్పర్శ అయినా సరిపోవచ్చు: చెంపదెబ్బ, తోపు, ఎవరిపైనైనా ఉమ్మివేయడం, నీళ్లు విసరడం, కుర్చీ లాగేసి పడేయడం. గాయం అవసరం లేదు. దెబ్బ వ్యక్తిపై అతిక్రమణ రూపం, స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం : చట్టం శరీరాన్ని దానికోసమే కాపాడుతుంది. Saheli v. Commissioner of Police (1989) లో సుప్రీం కోర్టు చెప్పింది: "In cases of assault, battery and false imprisonment, the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity, loss of liberty and death." (అర్థం: దాడి, దెబ్బ, అక్రమ నిర్బంధం సందర్భాల్లో నష్టపరిహారం పెద్దది, మానసిక వేదన, బాధ, అవమానం, స్వేచ్ఛ కోల్పోవడం, మరణానికి ఊరట రూపం.) "బలం" విస్తృతమైనది. ఒక వ్యక్తి శరీరంతో, "anything which that other is wearing or carrying" (అర్థం: అవతలి వ్యక్తి ధరించిన లేదా మోస్తున్న ఏదైనా) తో, లేదా "that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling" (అర్థం: ఆ స్పర్శ అవతలి వ్యక్తి స్పర్శ జ్ఞానాన్ని ప్రభావితం చేసేలా) ఉంచిన దేనితోనైనా ఒక పదార్థం తాకేలా చేసే చలనాన్ని BNS s. 128 బలంగా లెక్కిస్తుంది. ప్రత్యక్షత: బలం ప్రతివాది చర్య నుండి నేరుగా రావాలి (వాదిపై విసిరిన రాయి). పరోక్ష హాని (రోడ్డుపై రాయి వదిలేస్తే ఎవరో తడబడటం) నిర్లక్ష్యం, దెబ్బ కాదు. రక్షణలు: సమ్మతి (వైద్య చికిత్సకు సమాచారంతో కూడిన సమ్మతి తో సహా), ప్రైవేట్ రక్షణ, చట్టబద్ధ అరెస్ట్ లేదా ఇతర చట్టపరమైన అధికారం, దైనందిన జీవితంలో సాధారణ స్పర్శ. ప్రభుత్వ అధికారులు చేసే దెబ్బ Art. 21 ను కూడా ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది; కస్టడీలో కొట్టడం, మరణాలకు సుప్రీం కోర్టు నష్టపరిహారం ఇప్పించింది ( Saheli : ₹75,000; Nilabati Behera : ₹1,50,000).
te.meaning: దెబ్బ – మరొకరి సమ్మతి లేదా ఇతర చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా అతని శరీరంపై ఉద్దేశపూర్వక (లేదా కనీసం స్వచ్ఛంద), ప్రత్యక్ష బలప్రయోగం. బలం – ఎంత స్వల్పమైనదైనా ఏ భౌతిక స్పర్శ అయినా; ఒక వస్తువు ద్వారా స్పర్శ, వాది ధరించిన లేదా మోస్తున్న వస్తువులతో స్పర్శతో సహా (BNS s. 128 తో పోల్చండి). నొప్పి లేదా గాయం కలిగించాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు. సమాచారంతో కూడిన సమ్మతి – ఒక నిర్దిష్ట వైద్య ప్రక్రియ స్వభావం తెలిసి రోగి ఇచ్చే అంగీకారం; అటువంటి సమ్మతిని మించిన లేదా అది లేని చికిత్స దెబ్బ కావచ్చు (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం). Solatium (ఊరట నష్టపరిహారం) – డబ్బు నష్టానికి భిన్నంగా, మానసిక వేదన, బాధ, అవమానానికి నష్టపరిహారం. Saheli : దెబ్బ కేసుల్లో "the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity" (అర్థం: నష్టపరిహారం పెద్దది, మానసిక వేదన, బాధ, అవమానానికి ఊరట రూపం).
keyPoints: దెబ్బ = చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా ఉద్దేశపూర్వక, ప్రత్యక్ష బలప్రయోగం. ఏ స్పర్శ అయినా చాలు; గాయం అవసరం లేదు. బలంలో వస్తువుల ద్వారా, ధరించిన లేదా మోస్తున్న వస్తువులతో స్పర్శ చేరుతుంది (BNS s. 128). పరోక్ష హాని నిర్లక్ష్యం, దెబ్బ కాదు. సమ్మతి చేసిన చర్యకు వర్తించాలి; సమ్మతి లేని చికిత్స దెబ్బ. ప్రైవేట్ రక్షణ అవసరమైన దానికి మించకూడదు (BNS s. 37(2)). Saheli : దెబ్బ నష్టపరిహారం "large" (అర్థం: పెద్దది), ఒక "solatium" (అర్థం: ఊరట) (₹75,000). కస్టడీలో కొట్టడం: టార్ట్ నష్టపరిహారం, Art. 21 నష్టపరిహారం ( Nilabati Behera : ₹1,50,000).

selfTest.q: దెబ్బను నిర్వచించండి. చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా మరొకరి శరీరంపై ఉద్దేశపూర్వక, ప్రత్యక్ష బలప్రయోగం. వాది గాయం రుజువు చేయాలా?
selfTest.a: లేదు; అది స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం. ఒక వ్యక్తి మోస్తున్న బ్యాగ్‌ను తాకడం దెబ్బా? అవును, సమర్థన లేకపోతే (BNS s. 128 తో పోల్చండి). ఎవరో జారే అరటి తొక్కను వదిలేయడం దెబ్బా? కాదు; అది పరోక్షం (నిర్లక్ష్యం). దెబ్బ నష్టపరిహారం "a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity" అని ఏ కేసు చెబుతుంది? Saheli v. Commissioner of Police. Saheli లో ఎంత ఇచ్చారు? ₹75,000. సమ్మతి లేని శస్త్రచికిత్స దెబ్బా? అవును, సమ్మతి పొందలేని అత్యవసర పరిస్థితి తప్ప (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం). అరెస్ట్‌లో బలాన్ని ఏది పరిమితం చేస్తుంది? ప్రతిఘటనకు వ్యతిరేకంగా "all means necessary" మాత్రమే (BNSS s. 43(2)); అనుమతించిన చోట తప్ప మరణం కలిగించే హక్కు లేదు (s. 43(4)). శరీరం గురించి Puttaswamy ఏమి చెప్పింది? "శరీర సమగ్రత, మనస్సు పవిత్రత" ప్రైవేట్ ప్రదేశ హక్కుపై ఆధారపడతాయి. దెబ్బకు కాలపరిమితి? మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 113).

hi.inOneMinute: Battery is the intentional and direct application of force to another person's body without lawful justification . Any touch can be enough: a slap, a push, spitting on someone, throwing water at him, pulling a chair away so he falls. No injury is needed. Battery is a form of trespass to the person and is actionable per se : the law protects the body for its own sake. The Supreme Court in Saheli v. Commissioner of Police (1989) said: "In cases of assault, battery and false imprisonment, the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity, loss of liberty and death." "Force" is wide. BNS s. 128 counts motion that brings a substance into contact with a person's body, with "anything which that other is wearing or carrying", or with anything so placed "that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling". Directness: the force must follow directly from the defendant's act (a stone thrown at the plaintiff). Indirect harm (leaving a stone on the road over which someone trips) is negligence, not battery. Defences: consent (including informed consent to medical treatment), private defence, lawful arrest or other legal authority, and the ordinary touching of daily life. Battery by the State's officers also violates Art. 21; the Supreme Court has awarded compensation for custodial beatings and deaths ( Saheli : ₹75,000; Nilabati Behera : ₹1,50,000).
legalProvision: Battery in tort is a common law wrong. Indian criminal law defines the matching ideas of "force" and "criminal force":

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 128 (Force) – "A person is said to use force to another if he causes motion, change of motion, or cessation of motion to that other, or if he causes to any substance such motion, or change of motion, or cessation of motion as brings that substance into contact with any part of that other's body, or with anything which that other is wearing or carrying, or with anything so situated that such contact affects that other's sense of feeling". The motion may be caused "(a) by his own bodily power; (b) by disposing any substance in such a manner that the motion ... takes place without any further act on his part ...; or (c) by inducing any animal to move".

BNS s. 129 (Criminal force) – "Whoever intentionally uses force to any person, without that person's consent, in order to the committing of any offence, or intending by the use of such force to cause, or knowing it to be likely that by the use of such force he will cause injury, fear or annoyance to the person to whom the force is used, is said to use criminal force to that other."
BNS ss. 35, 37(2) – right of private defence of the body, which "in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence."

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 43(1)–(2), (4) – an arresting officer "shall actually touch or confine the body of the person to be arrested, unless there be a submission to the custody"; against forcible resistance he "may use all means necessary to effect the arrest"; but this does not give "a right to cause the death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or with imprisonment for life."
Constitution of India, Art. 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – three years "When the right to sue accrues" (no separate Article for battery).
hi.meaning: Battery – the intentional (or at least voluntary) and direct application of force to the body of another without his consent or other lawful justification. Force – any physical contact, however slight, including contact through an object or with things the plaintiff is wearing or carrying (compare BNS s. 128). It need not cause pain or injury. Informed consent – a patient's agreement to a particular medical procedure, given with knowledge of its nature; treatment beyond or without such consent can be battery (standard doctrine). Solatium – compensation for mental pain, distress and indignity, as opposed to money loss. Saheli : in battery cases "the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity".
keyPoints: Battery = intentional, direct application of force without lawful justification. Any touch is enough; injury is not needed. Force includes contact through objects and with things worn or carried (BNS s. 128). Indirect harm is negligence, not battery. Consent must cover the act done; treatment without consent is battery. Private defence must not exceed what is necessary (BNS s. 37(2)). Saheli : battery damages are "large" and a "solatium" (₹75,000). Custodial beatings: tort damages and Art. 21 compensation ( Nilabati Behera : ₹1,50,000).

caseLaws.facts: Saheli, A Women's Resources Centre v. Commissioner of Police, Delhi (1990) 1 SCC 422; AIR 1990 SC 513 (14 Dec 1989; B.C. Ray and S.R. Pandian JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A landlord's son, accompanied by the Station House Officer and other police, severely beat a
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "An action for damages lies for bodily harm which includes battery, assault, false imprisonment, physical injuries and death. In cases of assault, battery and false imprisonment, the damages are large and represent a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity, loss of liberty and death." ₹75,000 was directed to be paid to the mother. Why it matters: The Supreme Court expressly recognises battery as a tort and explains the nature of damages for it.
Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) 2 SCC 746

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner's son, about 22, was taken into police custody at about 8 a
caseLaws.facts: m. on 1.12.1987 for investigation of a theft; next day his dead body was found on a railway track with multiple injuries. Principle: Death caused by injuries inflicted in police custody violates Art. 21; the State must pay compensation in public law, in addition to any private law remedy. ₹1,50,000 was awarded. Why it matters: Shows the most serious form of battery by officials and the constitutional remedy for it.
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (24 Aug 2017; nine-judge bench)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Challenge to the Aadhaar scheme led to a reference on whether privacy is a fundamental right
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Privacy is protected by Art. 21; Dr D.Y. Chandrachud J.: "The integrity of the body and the sanctity of the mind can exist on the foundation that each individual possesses an inalienable ability and right to preserve a private space in which the human personality can develop." Why it matters: Bodily integrity, which battery protects in private law, is also a constitutional value.

selfTest.q: Define battery. Intentional, direct application of force to another's body without lawful justification. Must the plaintiff prove injury?
selfTest.a: No; it is actionable per se. Is touching a person's bag while he carries it battery? Yes, if unjustified (compare BNS s. 128). Is leaving a banana peel on which someone slips battery? No; it is indirect (negligence). Which case says battery damages are "a solatium for the mental pain, distress, indignity"? Saheli v. Commissioner of Police. How much was awarded in Saheli ? ₹75,000. Is surgery without consent battery? Yes, except in an emergency where consent cannot be obtained (standard doctrine). What limits force in arrest? Only "all means necessary" against resistance (BNSS s. 43(2)); no right to cause death except as allowed (s. 43(4)). What did Puttaswamy say about the body? "The integrity of the body and the sanctity of the mind" rest on a right to a private space. Limitation for battery? Three years (Art. 113).

law-of-torts-u3-t5.subtitle: The tort of totally restraining a person's liberty without lawful justification

en.inOneMinute: False imprisonment is the total restraint of a person's liberty, for any time however short, without lawful justification . "False" means wrongful, not untrue. No prison, no force and no touching is needed. Locking a person in a room, keeping him in a police station, or making him stay by a show of authority can each be false imprisonment. The restraint must be total . In Bird v. Jones (1845) the plaintiff was stopped from going forward along a bridge footway but was free to go back or another way; this was not imprisonment. Patteson J.: "imprisonment is ... a total restraint of the liberty of the person, for however short a time, and not a partial obstruction of his will". It is a form of trespass to the person and is actionable per se : no loss need be proved. Lawful authority is the main defence (lawful arrest, detention by court order). But detention beyond the time allowed (twenty-four hours without a Magistrate's order: Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58), or after the authority ends, is false imprisonment. In Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) a man kept in jail for over 14 years after his acquittal was awarded compensation. Limitation: one year "When the imprisonment ends" (Limitation Act Art. 73).
legalProvision: False imprisonment in tort is a common law wrong. The following statutory provisions are closely connected:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

s. 126(1) (Wrongful restraint): "Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person." s. 127(1) (Wrongful confinement): "Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said 'wrongfully to confine' that person." Illustration (a): "A causes Z to go within a walled space, and locks Z in." Illustration (b): "A places men with firearms at the outlets of a building, and tells Z that they will fire at Z if Z attempts to leave the building. A wrongfully confines Z." The distinction between restraint (s. 126: blocking one direction) and confinement (s. 127: prevented from going beyond limits) matches the tort rule in Bird v. Jones : only confinement is false imprisonment.
Constitution of India

Art. 21: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Art. 22(1): no arrested person "shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest". Art. 22(2): every arrested person "shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey ... and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate."

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 58 – no police officer shall detain a person arrested without warrant "for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable", and not beyond "twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey" without a Magistrate's special order.
Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 73 – "For compensation for false imprisonment": one year from "When the imprisonment ends".
en.meaning: False imprisonment – the unlawful, total restraint of a person's freedom of movement, by the defendant's direct act, for any period. Patteson J. in Bird v. Jones approved the definition: "False imprisonment is a restraint on the liberty of the person without lawful cause; either by confinement in prison, stocks, house, etc., or even by forcibly detaining the party in the streets, against his will." Total restraint – the plaintiff is prevented from leaving an area bounded on all sides (large or small, fixed or moving). Coleridge J. in Bird v. Jones : "A prison may have its boundary large or narrow, visible and tangible, or, though real, still in the conception only; it may itself be moveable or fixed: but a boundary it must have". Lawful justification – legal authority for the restraint, such as a lawful arrest within the time limits, a court's order of remand , or detention under a valid statute.
keyPoints: False imprisonment = total restraint of liberty without lawful justification. Any duration is enough: "for however short a time". Total, not partial: Bird v. Jones . "A boundary it must have", but it may be "large or narrow", "moveable or fixed". No force or touch is needed. Actionable per se. Detention beyond 24 hours without a Magistrate's order is unlawful (Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58). Rudul Sah : 14 years after acquittal – compensation; Bhim Singh : ₹50,000. Limitation: one year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73).

caseLaws.facts: Bird v. Jones (1845) 7 QB 742; 115 ER 668 (Queen's Bench; Coleridge, Williams, Patteson JJ.; Lord Denman C.J. dissenting)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Part of Hammersmith Bridge footway was fenced off for regatta seats
caseLaws.facts: Two policemen stopped the plaintiff from going forward along the footway; he was told he could go back and use the carriage way. He stayed over half an hour. Principle: "imprisonment is ... a total restraint of the liberty of the person, for however short a time, and not a partial obstruction of his will" (Patteson J.); "a boundary it must have" (Coleridge J.). No imprisonment; rule absolute. Why it matters: The leading authority that restraint must be total.
Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar [1983] 3 SCR 508 (1 Aug 1983; Y.V. Chandrachud C.J., Amarendra Nath Sen and Ranganath Misra JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner was kept in prison for over 14 years after his acquittal
caseLaws.facts: He filed a habeas corpus petition; by the hearing he had been released. Principle: Art. 21 "will be denuded of its significant content if the power of this Court were limited to passing orders of release from illegal detention"; the State must pay compensation – a further ₹30,000 in addition to ₹5,000. Why it matters: Unlawful detention by the State is compensated, not merely ended.
Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) 4 SCC 677; AIR 1986 SC 494 (22 Nov 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An MLA was arrested at about 3 a
caseLaws.facts: m. on 10 September 1985 and was not produced before the Magistrate on 11th or the Sub Judge on 13th. Principle: The "invasion may not be washed away or wished away by his being set free"; the State was directed to pay ₹50,000. Why it matters: Detention in breach of the production requirement (Art. 22(2)) is unlawful and compensable .

selfTest.q: Define false imprisonment. Total restraint of a person's liberty without lawful justification. Does "false" mean the charge was untrue?
selfTest.a: No; it means wrongful. What did Bird v. Jones decide? Blocking one direction while others are open is not imprisonment. Who dissented in Bird v. Jones ? Lord Denman C.J. Is physical force required? No. Must the plaintiff prove loss? No; it is actionable per se. Which BNS section matches false imprisonment? s. 127 (wrongful confinement). Within what time must an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate? Twenty-four hours, excluding journey time (Art. 22(2)). How long was Rudul Sah kept in jail after acquittal? Over 14 years. Limitation for false imprisonment? One year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73).

te.inOneMinute: అక్రమ నిర్బంధం (false imprisonment) అంటే చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా , ఎంత తక్కువ సమయమైనా, ఒక వ్యక్తి స్వేచ్ఛను సంపూర్ణంగా నిరోధించడం . "False" అంటే తప్పుడు (అక్రమ), అబద్ధం కాదు. జైలు, బలం, స్పర్శ అవసరం లేదు. ఒక వ్యక్తిని గదిలో బంధించడం, పోలీస్ స్టేషన్‌లో ఉంచడం, అధికార ప్రదర్శనతో ఉండిపోయేలా చేయడం – ప్రతి ఒక్కటీ అక్రమ నిర్బంధం కావచ్చు. నిరోధం సంపూర్ణంగా ఉండాలి. Bird v. Jones (1845) లో వాదిని ఒక వంతెన కాలిబాటపై ముందుకు వెళ్లకుండా ఆపారు, కానీ వెనక్కి లేదా మరో దారిలో వెళ్లడానికి స్వేచ్ఛ ఉంది; ఇది నిర్బంధం కాదు . Patteson J.: "imprisonment is ... a total restraint of the liberty of the person, for however short a time, and not a partial obstruction of his will" (అర్థం: నిర్బంధం అంటే ఎంత తక్కువ సమయమైనా వ్యక్తి స్వేచ్ఛను సంపూర్ణంగా నిరోధించడం, అతని ఇష్టాన్ని పాక్షికంగా అడ్డుకోవడం కాదు). ఇది వ్యక్తిపై అతిక్రమణ రూపం, స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం : నష్టం రుజువు అవసరం లేదు. చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం ప్రధాన రక్షణ (చట్టబద్ధ అరెస్ట్, కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు ద్వారా నిర్బంధం). కానీ అనుమతించిన సమయం దాటి (Magistrate ఉత్తర్వు లేకుండా ఇరవై నాలుగు గంటలు: Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58), లేదా అధికారం ముగిసిన తర్వాత నిర్బంధించడం అక్రమ నిర్బంధం. Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) లో నిర్దోషిగా విడుదలైన తర్వాత 14 ఏళ్లకు పైగా జైలులో ఉంచిన వ్యక్తికి నష్టపరిహారం ఇప్పించారు. కాలపరిమితి: "When the imprisonment ends" (అర్థం: నిర్బంధం ముగిసినప్పుడు) నుండి ఒక సంవత్సరం (Limitation Act Art. 73).
te.meaning: అక్రమ నిర్బంధం – ప్రతివాది ప్రత్యక్ష చర్య ద్వారా, ఏ కాలానికైనా, ఒక వ్యక్తి సంచార స్వేచ్ఛను చట్టవిరుద్ధంగా, సంపూర్ణంగా నిరోధించడం. Bird v. Jones లో Patteson J. ఈ నిర్వచనాన్ని ఆమోదించారు: "False imprisonment is a restraint on the liberty of the person without lawful cause; either by confinement in prison, stocks, house, etc., or even by forcibly detaining the party in the streets, against his will." (అర్థం: అక్రమ నిర్బంధం అంటే చట్టబద్ధ కారణం లేకుండా వ్యక్తి స్వేచ్ఛపై నిరోధం; జైలు, stocks, ఇల్లు మొదలైన వాటిలో బంధించడం ద్వారా, లేదా అతని ఇష్టానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా వీధుల్లో బలవంతంగా ఆపడం ద్వారా కూడా.) సంపూర్ణ నిరోధం – అన్ని వైపులా సరిహద్దు ఉన్న ప్రదేశం (పెద్దదైనా చిన్నదైనా, స్థిరమైనా కదిలేదైనా) నుండి వాది బయటకు వెళ్లకుండా ఆపబడతాడు. Bird v. Jones లో Coleridge J.: "A prison may have its boundary large or narrow, visible and tangible, or, though real, still in the conception only; it may itself be moveable or fixed: but a boundary it must have" (అర్థం: ఒక జైలుకు సరిహద్దు పెద్దది లేదా చిన్నది, కనిపించేది, తాకగలిగేది, లేదా వాస్తవమైనా భావనలో మాత్రమే ఉండవచ్చు; అది కదిలేది లేదా స్థిరమైనది కావచ్చు: కానీ దానికి ఒక సరిహద్దు ఉండాలి). చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన – నిరోధానికి చట్టపరమైన అధికారం; ఉదా. కాల పరిమితుల్లో చట్టబద్ధ అరెస్ట్, కోర్టు remand ఉత్తర్వు , చెల్లుబాటైన చట్టం కింద నిర్బంధం.
keyPoints: అక్రమ నిర్బంధం = చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా స్వేచ్ఛపై సంపూర్ణ నిరోధం. ఏ కాలవ్యవధి అయినా చాలు: "for however short a time" (అర్థం: ఎంత తక్కువ సమయమైనా). సంపూర్ణం, పాక్షికం కాదు: Bird v. Jones . "A boundary it must have" (అర్థం: దానికి సరిహద్దు ఉండాలి), కానీ అది "large or narrow" (అర్థం: పెద్దది లేదా చిన్నది), "moveable or fixed" (అర్థం: కదిలేది లేదా స్థిరమైనది) కావచ్చు. బలం లేదా స్పర్శ అవసరం లేదు. స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం. Magistrate ఉత్తర్వు లేకుండా 24 గంటలు దాటిన నిర్బంధం చట్టవిరుద్ధం (Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58). Rudul Sah : విడుదల తర్వాత 14 ఏళ్లు – నష్టపరిహారం; Bhim Singh : ₹50,000. కాలపరిమితి: నిర్బంధం ముగిసినప్పటి నుండి ఒక సంవత్సరం (Art. 73).

selfTest.q: అక్రమ నిర్బంధాన్ని నిర్వచించండి. చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా ఒక వ్యక్తి స్వేచ్ఛపై సంపూర్ణ నిరోధం. "False" అంటే ఆరోపణ అబద్ధమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు; అక్రమం అని అర్థం. Bird v. Jones ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? ఇతర దారులు తెరిచి ఉండగా ఒక దిశను అడ్డుకోవడం నిర్బంధం కాదు. Bird v. Jones లో భిన్నాభిప్రాయం ఎవరిది? Lord Denman C.J. భౌతిక బలం అవసరమా? లేదు. వాది నష్టం రుజువు చేయాలా? లేదు; స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం. అక్రమ నిర్బంధానికి సరిపోలే BNS సెక్షన్? s. 127 (wrongful confinement). అరెస్ట్ అయిన వ్యక్తిని ఎంత సమయంలో Magistrate ముందు హాజరుపరచాలి? ప్రయాణ సమయం మినహా ఇరవై నాలుగు గంటలు (Art. 22(2)). Rudul Sah ను విడుదల తర్వాత ఎంత కాలం జైలులో ఉంచారు? 14 ఏళ్లకు పైగా. అక్రమ నిర్బంధానికి కాలపరిమితి? నిర్బంధం ముగిసినప్పటి నుండి ఒక సంవత్సరం (Art. 73).

hi.inOneMinute: False imprisonment is the total restraint of a person's liberty, for any time however short, without lawful justification . "False" means wrongful, not untrue. No prison, no force and no touching is needed. Locking a person in a room, keeping him in a police station, or making him stay by a show of authority can each be false imprisonment. The restraint must be total . In Bird v. Jones (1845) the plaintiff was stopped from going forward along a bridge footway but was free to go back or another way; this was not imprisonment. Patteson J.: "imprisonment is ... a total restraint of the liberty of the person, for however short a time, and not a partial obstruction of his will". It is a form of trespass to the person and is actionable per se : no loss need be proved. Lawful authority is the main defence (lawful arrest, detention by court order). But detention beyond the time allowed (twenty-four hours without a Magistrate's order: Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58), or after the authority ends, is false imprisonment. In Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) a man kept in jail for over 14 years after his acquittal was awarded compensation. Limitation: one year "When the imprisonment ends" (Limitation Act Art. 73).
legalProvision: False imprisonment in tort is a common law wrong. The following statutory provisions are closely connected:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

s. 126(1) (Wrongful restraint): "Whoever voluntarily obstructs any person so as to prevent that person from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed, is said wrongfully to restrain that person." s. 127(1) (Wrongful confinement): "Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said 'wrongfully to confine' that person." Illustration (a): "A causes Z to go within a walled space, and locks Z in." Illustration (b): "A places men with firearms at the outlets of a building, and tells Z that they will fire at Z if Z attempts to leave the building. A wrongfully confines Z." The distinction between restraint (s. 126: blocking one direction) and confinement (s. 127: prevented from going beyond limits) matches the tort rule in Bird v. Jones : only confinement is false imprisonment.
Constitution of India

Art. 21: "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Art. 22(1): no arrested person "shall be detained in custody without being informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds for such arrest". Art. 22(2): every arrested person "shall be produced before the nearest magistrate within a period of twenty-four hours of such arrest excluding the time necessary for the journey ... and no such person shall be detained in custody beyond the said period without the authority of a magistrate."

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 58 – no police officer shall detain a person arrested without warrant "for a longer period than under all the circumstances of the case is reasonable", and not beyond "twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey" without a Magistrate's special order.
Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 73 – "For compensation for false imprisonment": one year from "When the imprisonment ends".
hi.meaning: False imprisonment – the unlawful, total restraint of a person's freedom of movement, by the defendant's direct act, for any period. Patteson J. in Bird v. Jones approved the definition: "False imprisonment is a restraint on the liberty of the person without lawful cause; either by confinement in prison, stocks, house, etc., or even by forcibly detaining the party in the streets, against his will." Total restraint – the plaintiff is prevented from leaving an area bounded on all sides (large or small, fixed or moving). Coleridge J. in Bird v. Jones : "A prison may have its boundary large or narrow, visible and tangible, or, though real, still in the conception only; it may itself be moveable or fixed: but a boundary it must have". Lawful justification – legal authority for the restraint, such as a lawful arrest within the time limits, a court's order of remand , or detention under a valid statute.
keyPoints: False imprisonment = total restraint of liberty without lawful justification. Any duration is enough: "for however short a time". Total, not partial: Bird v. Jones . "A boundary it must have", but it may be "large or narrow", "moveable or fixed". No force or touch is needed. Actionable per se. Detention beyond 24 hours without a Magistrate's order is unlawful (Art. 22(2); BNSS s. 58). Rudul Sah : 14 years after acquittal – compensation; Bhim Singh : ₹50,000. Limitation: one year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73).

caseLaws.facts: Bird v. Jones (1845) 7 QB 742; 115 ER 668 (Queen's Bench; Coleridge, Williams, Patteson JJ.; Lord Denman C.J. dissenting)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Part of Hammersmith Bridge footway was fenced off for regatta seats
caseLaws.facts: Two policemen stopped the plaintiff from going forward along the footway; he was told he could go back and use the carriage way. He stayed over half an hour. Principle: "imprisonment is ... a total restraint of the liberty of the person, for however short a time, and not a partial obstruction of his will" (Patteson J.); "a boundary it must have" (Coleridge J.). No imprisonment; rule absolute. Why it matters: The leading authority that restraint must be total.
Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar [1983] 3 SCR 508 (1 Aug 1983; Y.V. Chandrachud C.J., Amarendra Nath Sen and Ranganath Misra JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner was kept in prison for over 14 years after his acquittal
caseLaws.facts: He filed a habeas corpus petition; by the hearing he had been released. Principle: Art. 21 "will be denuded of its significant content if the power of this Court were limited to passing orders of release from illegal detention"; the State must pay compensation – a further ₹30,000 in addition to ₹5,000. Why it matters: Unlawful detention by the State is compensated, not merely ended.
Bhim Singh v. State of J&K (1985) 4 SCC 677; AIR 1986 SC 494 (22 Nov 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An MLA was arrested at about 3 a
caseLaws.facts: m. on 10 September 1985 and was not produced before the Magistrate on 11th or the Sub Judge on 13th. Principle: The "invasion may not be washed away or wished away by his being set free"; the State was directed to pay ₹50,000. Why it matters: Detention in breach of the production requirement (Art. 22(2)) is unlawful and compensable .

selfTest.q: Define false imprisonment. Total restraint of a person's liberty without lawful justification. Does "false" mean the charge was untrue?
selfTest.a: No; it means wrongful. What did Bird v. Jones decide? Blocking one direction while others are open is not imprisonment. Who dissented in Bird v. Jones ? Lord Denman C.J. Is physical force required? No. Must the plaintiff prove loss? No; it is actionable per se. Which BNS section matches false imprisonment? s. 127 (wrongful confinement). Within what time must an arrested person be produced before a Magistrate? Twenty-four hours, excluding journey time (Art. 22(2)). How long was Rudul Sah kept in jail after acquittal? Over 14 years. Limitation for false imprisonment? One year from when the imprisonment ends (Art. 73).

en.meaning:
In Stephens v. Myers (1830), the defendant was liable for assault even though he:

Explanation. The defendant advanced with a clenched fist but was stopped before making contact — his liability rested on the apprehension of imminent contact created, not on any actual touching.

According to Cole v. Turner (1704), what degree of force is required for battery?

Explanation. Cole v. Turner established that "the least touching of another in anger is a battery" — the degree of force is irrelevant so long as it is unwanted and intentional.

What is the key difference between assault and battery?

Explanation. Assault protects against the apprehension of imminent unlawful contact; battery is the actual unwanted physical contact itself.

Are assault and battery in tort law independent of any criminal proceedings for the same conduct?

law-of-torts-u3-t6.subtitle: The tort of starting a criminal case maliciously and without reasonable and probable cause

en.inOneMinute: Malicious prosecution is the tort of setting the law in motion against a person maliciously and without reasonable and probable cause , where the proceeding ends in that person's favour and causes him damage . (See Diagram 1 .) The law balances two interests: every citizen is "entitled though not always bound" to report a crime he has reasonable cause to believe was committed; but no one may misuse courts to harass another. The Supreme Court described the essentials in West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray (2006): "no probable cause existed for instituting the prosecution or suit complained of"; "such prosecution or suit terminated in some way favorably" to the person prosecuted; malice means "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right"; "if the defendant had reasonable or probable cause of launching the criminal prosecution no amount of malice will make him liable"; "the onus rests on the plaintiff to prove them". Related law: false charge with intent to injure is an offence (s. 248, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023); a Magistrate may order compensation for an accusation without reasonable ground (s. 273, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023); the civil suit must be filed within one year from acquittal or other termination of the prosecution (Art. 74, Limitation Act, 1963).
legalProvision: Malicious prosecution is a common law tort; no Act defines it. Statutes that touch it:

Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Article 74: for compensation "for a malicious prosecution", the period is "One year", running from "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated". Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 248: "Whoever, with intent to cause injury to any person, institutes or causes to be instituted any criminal proceeding against that person, or falsely charges any person with having committed an offence, knowing that there is no just or lawful ground for such proceeding or charge against that person" is punishable: (a) with imprisonment up to five years, or fine up to two lakh rupees, or both; (b) up to ten years and fine, if the false charge is of an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or ten years or more. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 273: (1)–(2) where a Magistrate discharges or acquits an accused and is of opinion "that there was no reasonable ground for making the accusation", he may, after hearing the complainant or informant and recording reasons, order him to pay compensation "not exceeding the amount of fine he is empowered to impose"; (5) such an order does not exempt him "from any civil or criminal liability", but "any amount paid to an accused person under this section shall be taken into account in awarding compensation to such person in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter". Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 35A: a court may award compensatory costs where a claim or defence is "false or vexatious to the knowledge of the party by whom it has been put forward".
en.meaning: Malicious prosecution – in the words quoted in Dilip Kumar Ray , "A prosecution begun in malice, without probable cause to believe that it can succeed and which finally ends in failure". The term "imports a causeless as well as an ill-intended prosecution". Malice (in this tort ) – "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right. It need not necessarily be a feeling of enmity, spite or ill-will. It may be due to a desire to obtain a collateral advantage" ( Dilip Kumar Ray ). Reasonable and probable cause – a ground that "would operate on the mind of a discreet and reasonable man" to believe the person guilty ( Dilip Kumar Ray ). Abuse of process – "the employment of legal process for some purpose other than that which it was intended by the law to effect". It differs from malicious prosecution, which "consists in maliciously causing process to be issued" ( Dilip Kumar Ray , quoting American Jurisprudence).
keyPoints: Malicious prosecution: prosecution + favourable termination + no reasonable cause + malice + damage. Malice: improper or indirect motive; spite not necessary. Reasonable and probable cause: would satisfy a discreet and reasonable man; with it, malice does not matter. State of mind judged at the start of the proceeding; onus on the plaintiff. Honest informants are protected even if the accused is acquitted. Abuse of process is a different wrong. Limitation: 1 year from acquittal or termination (Art. 74). s. 273 BNSS compensation counted in the civil suit; s. 248 BNS punishes false charges. Dilip Kumar Ray : vague pleadings and no evidence mean no damages.

caseLaws.facts: West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray, (2006) Supp. 9 SCR 553 (24 November 2006) Facts: A Superintending Engineer was suspended and faced disciplinary proceedings. The High Court quashed them for denial of a reasonable hearing. He then sued the Board for damages. The trial court awarded ₹50,000 for harassment and ₹50,000 for loss of reputation; the High Court upheld this, treating the harassment award as damages for malicious prosecution. Bench: Arijit Pasayat and Lokeshwar Singh Panta JJ. Principle: Malice is "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right". "if the defendant had reasonable or probable cause of launching the criminal prosecution no amount of malice will make him liable". Malice and want of reasonable cause relate to the defendant's state of mind "at the date of the initiation of criminal proceedings and the onus rests on the plaintiff to prove them". On the facts, there was "no specific averment regarding any malicious prosecution", no issue was framed and no evidence was led. The High Court's judgment was "indefensible and is set aside". Why it matters: It is the leading Indian statement of the meaning of malice and malicious prosecution. It shows that each element must be pleaded and proved. 2. Quinn v. Leathem [1901] UKHL 2 (House of Lords, 5 August 1901) Facts: A conspiracy case. Trade-union officials induced customers and servants to stop dealing with the plaintiff butcher. In discussing when a malicious motive makes an act wrongful, Lord Brampton took malicious prosecution as "the familiar instance". Principle: It is not wrongful for a person "who honestly believes that he has reasonable and probable cause, though he has it not in fact, to put the criminal law in motion against another". But where malice is added to the absence of reasonable and probable cause, the act "becomes with malice wrongful and actionable" (Lord Brampton). Why it matters: It explains why malicious prosecution needs both want of reasonable cause and malice. Honest prosecutors are protected.

selfTest.q: List the essentials of malicious prosecution. What is "malice" in this tort?
selfTest.a: Can a person with reasonable cause be liable if he also had ill will? On whom is the burden of proof ? What is the limitation period , and from when does it run? How does s. 273 BNSS affect a later civil suit?

te.inOneMinute: దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ అంటే ఒక వ్యక్తిపై దురుద్దేశంతో , సహేతుకమైన, సంభావ్యమైన కారణం లేకుండా చట్టాన్ని కదిలించడం; ఆ విచారణ ఆ వ్యక్తికి అనుకూలంగా ముగిసి , అతనికి నష్టం కలిగించే టార్ట్. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) చట్టం రెండు ప్రయోజనాలను సమతుల్యం చేస్తుంది: జరిగిందని సహేతుకంగా నమ్మడానికి కారణం ఉన్న నేరాన్ని నివేదించడానికి ప్రతి పౌరుడు "entitled though not always bound" (అర్థం: హక్కు కలిగి ఉంటాడు, కానీ ఎల్లప్పుడూ బాధ్యుడు కాదు); కానీ మరొకరిని వేధించడానికి ఎవరూ కోర్టులను దుర్వినియోగం చేయకూడదు. West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray (2006)లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు మూలాంశాలను వివరించింది: "no probable cause existed for instituting the prosecution or suit complained of" (అర్థం: ఫిర్యాదు చేసిన ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ లేదా దావా ప్రారంభించడానికి సంభావ్య కారణం లేదు); "such prosecution or suit terminated in some way favorably" (అర్థం: ఆ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ లేదా దావా ఏదో విధంగా అనుకూలంగా ముగిసింది) – ప్రాసిక్యూట్ చేయబడిన వ్యక్తికి; దురుద్దేశం అంటే "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right" (అర్థం: ప్రజా న్యాయాన్ని లేదా ప్రైవేటు హక్కును నిలబెట్టాలనే కోరిక కాకుండా అనుచితమైన లేదా పరోక్ష ఉద్దేశం); "if the defendant had reasonable or probable cause of launching the criminal prosecution no amount of malice will make him liable" (అర్థం: క్రిమినల్ ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ ప్రారంభించడానికి ప్రతివాదికి సహేతుక లేదా సంభావ్య కారణం ఉంటే, ఎంత దురుద్దేశం ఉన్నా అతను బాధ్యుడు కాడు); "the onus rests on the plaintiff to prove them" (అర్థం: వాటిని రుజువు చేసే భారం వాదిపై ఉంటుంది). సంబంధిత చట్టం: గాయపరచాలనే ఉద్దేశంతో తప్పుడు ఆరోపణ నేరం (భారతీయ న్యాయ సంహిత, 2023 సెక్షన్ 248); సహేతుక ఆధారం లేని ఆరోపణకు మేజిస్ట్రేట్ నష్టపరిహారం ఆదేశించవచ్చు (భారతీయ నాగరిక సురక్ష సంహిత, 2023 సెక్షన్ 273); సివిల్ దావాను ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ నుండి నిర్దోషిగా విడుదలైన లేదా అది మరో విధంగా ముగిసిన ఒక సంవత్సరంలోపు వేయాలి (పరిమితి చట్టం, 1963 ఆర్టికల్ 74).
te.meaning: దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ – Dilip Kumar Ray లో ఉదహరించిన మాటల్లో, "A prosecution begun in malice, without probable cause to believe that it can succeed and which finally ends in failure" (అర్థం: విజయం సాధిస్తుందని నమ్మడానికి సంభావ్య కారణం లేకుండా, దురుద్దేశంతో ప్రారంభించి, చివరకు విఫలమైన ప్రాసిక్యూషన్). ఈ పదం "imports a causeless as well as an ill-intended prosecution" (అర్థం: కారణం లేని, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్‌ను సూచిస్తుంది). దురుద్దేశం (malice) (ఈ టార్ట్‌లో ) – "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right. It need not necessarily be a feeling of enmity, spite or ill-will. It may be due to a desire to obtain a collateral advantage" (అర్థం: ప్రజా న్యాయాన్ని లేదా ప్రైవేటు హక్కును నిలబెట్టాలనే కోరిక కాకుండా అనుచితమైన లేదా పరోక్ష ఉద్దేశం. ఇది తప్పనిసరిగా శత్రుత్వం, ద్వేషం లేదా దుర్భావన కానవసరం లేదు. అనుబంధ ప్రయోజనం పొందాలనే కోరిక వల్ల కూడా కావచ్చు) ( Dilip Kumar Ray ). సహేతుకమైన, సంభావ్యమైన కారణం (reasonable and probable cause) – ఆ వ్యక్తి దోషి అని నమ్మడానికి "would operate on the mind of a discreet and reasonable man" (అర్థం: వివేకవంతుడైన, సహేతుకమైన వ్యక్తి మనసుపై ప్రభావం చూపే) ఆధారం ( Dilip Kumar Ray ). ప్రక్రియ దుర్వినియోగం (abuse of process) – "the employment of legal process for some purpose other than that which it was intended by the law to effect" (అర్థం: చట్టం ఉద్దేశించిన ప్రయోజనం కాకుండా మరో ప్రయోజనం కోసం చట్టపరమైన ప్రక్రియను ఉపయోగించడం). "consists in maliciously causing process to be issued" (అర్థం: దురుద్దేశంతో ప్రక్రియ జారీ చేయించడంలో ఉంటుంది) అయిన దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ నుండి ఇది భిన్నం ( Dilip Kumar Ray , American Jurisprudence ఉదహరిస్తూ).
keyPoints: దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్: ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ + అనుకూల ముగింపు + సహేతుక కారణం లేకపోవడం + దురుద్దేశం + నష్టం. దురుద్దేశం: అనుచిత లేదా పరోక్ష ఉద్దేశం; ద్వేషం అవసరం లేదు. సహేతుకమైన, సంభావ్యమైన కారణం: వివేకవంతుడైన, సహేతుకమైన వ్యక్తిని సంతృప్తిపరుస్తుంది; అది ఉంటే దురుద్దేశం పట్టింపు లేదు. మనస్థితిని విచారణ ప్రారంభం నాటికి నిర్ణయిస్తారు; భారం వాదిపై. నిందితుడు నిర్దోషిగా విడుదలైనా నిజాయితీగా సమాచారం ఇచ్చినవారికి రక్షణ ఉంటుంది. ప్రక్రియ దుర్వినియోగం వేరే తప్పు. పరిమితి: నిర్దోషిత్వం లేదా ముగింపు నుండి 1 సంవత్సరం (ఆర్టికల్ 74). BNSS సెక్షన్ 273 నష్టపరిహారాన్ని సివిల్ దావాలో పరిగణిస్తారు; BNS సెక్షన్ 248 తప్పుడు ఆరోపణలను శిక్షిస్తుంది. Dilip Kumar Ray : అస్పష్ట వాదనలు, సాక్ష్యం లేకపోవడం అంటే నష్టపరిహారం లేదు.

selfTest.q: దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ మూలాంశాలను పేర్కొనండి. ఈ టార్ట్‌లో "దురుద్దేశం" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సహేతుక కారణం ఉన్న వ్యక్తికి దుర్భావన కూడా ఉంటే అతను బాధ్యుడవుతాడా? రుజువు భారం ఎవరిపై ఉంటుంది? పరిమితి కాలం ఎంత, అది ఎప్పటి నుండి నడుస్తుంది? BNSS సెక్షన్ 273 తర్వాతి సివిల్ దావాను ఎలా ప్రభావితం చేస్తుంది?

Flowchart Diagram
Comparison Table
visuals.html:
మూలాంశం వాది ఏమి రుజువు చేయాలి గమనించాల్సిన అంశం
1. ప్రతివాది ప్రాసిక్యూషన్ ప్రతివాది చట్టాన్ని కదిలించాడు (ఫిర్యాదు, విచారణకు దారితీసిన పోలీసు సమాచారం) నిజాయితీగా సమాచారం ఇవ్వడం మాత్రమే సరిపోదు

hi.inOneMinute: Malicious prosecution is the tort of setting the law in motion against a person maliciously and without reasonable and probable cause , where the proceeding ends in that person's favour and causes him damage . (See Diagram 1 .) The law balances two interests: every citizen is "entitled though not always bound" to report a crime he has reasonable cause to believe was committed; but no one may misuse courts to harass another. The Supreme Court described the essentials in West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray (2006): "no probable cause existed for instituting the prosecution or suit complained of"; "such prosecution or suit terminated in some way favorably" to the person prosecuted; malice means "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right"; "if the defendant had reasonable or probable cause of launching the criminal prosecution no amount of malice will make him liable"; "the onus rests on the plaintiff to prove them". Related law: false charge with intent to injure is an offence (s. 248, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023); a Magistrate may order compensation for an accusation without reasonable ground (s. 273, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023); the civil suit must be filed within one year from acquittal or other termination of the prosecution (Art. 74, Limitation Act, 1963).
legalProvision: Malicious prosecution is a common law tort; no Act defines it. Statutes that touch it:

Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule, Article 74: for compensation "for a malicious prosecution", the period is "One year", running from "When the plaintiff is acquitted or the prosecution is otherwise terminated". Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 248: "Whoever, with intent to cause injury to any person, institutes or causes to be instituted any criminal proceeding against that person, or falsely charges any person with having committed an offence, knowing that there is no just or lawful ground for such proceeding or charge against that person" is punishable: (a) with imprisonment up to five years, or fine up to two lakh rupees, or both; (b) up to ten years and fine, if the false charge is of an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or ten years or more. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 273: (1)–(2) where a Magistrate discharges or acquits an accused and is of opinion "that there was no reasonable ground for making the accusation", he may, after hearing the complainant or informant and recording reasons, order him to pay compensation "not exceeding the amount of fine he is empowered to impose"; (5) such an order does not exempt him "from any civil or criminal liability", but "any amount paid to an accused person under this section shall be taken into account in awarding compensation to such person in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter". Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 35A: a court may award compensatory costs where a claim or defence is "false or vexatious to the knowledge of the party by whom it has been put forward".
hi.meaning: Malicious prosecution – in the words quoted in Dilip Kumar Ray , "A prosecution begun in malice, without probable cause to believe that it can succeed and which finally ends in failure". The term "imports a causeless as well as an ill-intended prosecution". Malice (in this tort ) – "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right. It need not necessarily be a feeling of enmity, spite or ill-will. It may be due to a desire to obtain a collateral advantage" ( Dilip Kumar Ray ). Reasonable and probable cause – a ground that "would operate on the mind of a discreet and reasonable man" to believe the person guilty ( Dilip Kumar Ray ). Abuse of process – "the employment of legal process for some purpose other than that which it was intended by the law to effect". It differs from malicious prosecution, which "consists in maliciously causing process to be issued" ( Dilip Kumar Ray , quoting American Jurisprudence).
keyPoints: Malicious prosecution: prosecution + favourable termination + no reasonable cause + malice + damage. Malice: improper or indirect motive; spite not necessary. Reasonable and probable cause: would satisfy a discreet and reasonable man; with it, malice does not matter. State of mind judged at the start of the proceeding; onus on the plaintiff. Honest informants are protected even if the accused is acquitted. Abuse of process is a different wrong. Limitation: 1 year from acquittal or termination (Art. 74). s. 273 BNSS compensation counted in the civil suit; s. 248 BNS punishes false charges. Dilip Kumar Ray : vague pleadings and no evidence mean no damages.

caseLaws.facts: West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray, (2006) Supp. 9 SCR 553 (24 November 2006) Facts: A Superintending Engineer was suspended and faced disciplinary proceedings. The High Court quashed them for denial of a reasonable hearing. He then sued the Board for damages. The trial court awarded ₹50,000 for harassment and ₹50,000 for loss of reputation; the High Court upheld this, treating the harassment award as damages for malicious prosecution. Bench: Arijit Pasayat and Lokeshwar Singh Panta JJ. Principle: Malice is "an improper or indirect motive other than a desire to vindicate public justice or a private right". "if the defendant had reasonable or probable cause of launching the criminal prosecution no amount of malice will make him liable". Malice and want of reasonable cause relate to the defendant's state of mind "at the date of the initiation of criminal proceedings and the onus rests on the plaintiff to prove them". On the facts, there was "no specific averment regarding any malicious prosecution", no issue was framed and no evidence was led. The High Court's judgment was "indefensible and is set aside". Why it matters: It is the leading Indian statement of the meaning of malice and malicious prosecution. It shows that each element must be pleaded and proved. 2. Quinn v. Leathem [1901] UKHL 2 (House of Lords, 5 August 1901) Facts: A conspiracy case. Trade-union officials induced customers and servants to stop dealing with the plaintiff butcher. In discussing when a malicious motive makes an act wrongful, Lord Brampton took malicious prosecution as "the familiar instance". Principle: It is not wrongful for a person "who honestly believes that he has reasonable and probable cause, though he has it not in fact, to put the criminal law in motion against another". But where malice is added to the absence of reasonable and probable cause, the act "becomes with malice wrongful and actionable" (Lord Brampton). Why it matters: It explains why malicious prosecution needs both want of reasonable cause and malice. Honest prosecutors are protected.

selfTest.q: List the essentials of malicious prosecution. What is "malice" in this tort?
selfTest.a: Can a person with reasonable cause be liable if he also had ill will? On whom is the burden of proof ? What is the limitation period , and from when does it run? How does s. 273 BNSS affect a later civil suit?
