law-of-torts-u3-t8.subtitle: Civil wrongs committed through computers and the internet: hacking, data, defamation, privacy and platform liability

en.inOneMinute: A digital tort is a civil wrong committed through a computer, mobile phone, the internet or other electronic means, for which the injured person can claim damages or an injunction. Examples are hacking, damaging data, spreading a virus, online defamation, publishing private images, identity theft, and failing to protect personal data. "Digital tort" is a descriptive name, not a term defined in any Act. The law comes from two sources: (1) the ordinary torts (defamation, trespass, negligence, privacy) applied to the online world; and (2) statutes , mainly the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) . IT Act s. 43: anyone who, "without permission of the owner", accesses, downloads, introduces a virus into, damages or disrupts a computer system "shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected". This is the main statutory digital tort. IT Act s. 43A: a body corporate that is "negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices" for sensitive personal data and thereby causes wrongful loss must pay compensation. The DPDP Act s. 44(2)(a) will omit s. 43A when that sub-section comes into force (18 months from 13 November 2025). Claims up to ₹5 crore go to an adjudicating officer under the IT Act (s. 46(1A)); above that, to the "competent court". A civil court cannot entertain a suit on a matter the adjudicating officer can decide (s. 61). An intermediary (such as a social media platform or internet service provider) is protected by safe harbour under s. 79 for third-party content, but loses it if it fails to remove unlawful material after "actual knowledge". In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) the Supreme Court read "actual knowledge" to mean knowledge from a court order or a government notification , and struck down s. 66A "in its entirety". In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) nine judges held privacy to be a fundamental right and said: "The dangers to privacy in an age of information can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well."
legalProvision: Information Technology Act, 2000

s. 2(1)(w) – "intermediary", "with respect to any particular electronic records, means any person who on behalf of another person receives, stores or transmits that record or provides any service with respect to that record and includes telecom service providers, network service providers, internet service providers, web-hosting service providers, search engines, online payment sites, online-auction sites, online-market places and cyber cafes". s. 43 – penalty and compensation for damage to computer, computer system, etc. If any person "without permission of the owner or any other person who is in charge of a computer, computer system or computer network" does any of the acts in clauses (a) to (j) (for example (a) "accesses or secures access", (b) "downloads, copies or extracts any data", (c) "introduces or causes to be introduced any computer contaminant or computer virus", (d) "damages or causes to be damaged", (e) "disrupts", (f) "denies or causes the denial of access", (h) charges services to another's account by tampering, (i) "destroys, deletes or alters any information", (j) steals or alters source code), "he shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected." s. 43A – compensation for failure to protect data (quoted in the Detailed explanation). s. 46(1A) – the adjudicating officer has jurisdiction where "the claim for damage does not exceed rupees five crore"; above that, "the jurisdiction ... shall vest with the competent court". s. 47 – in fixing compensation the adjudicating officer considers "(a) the amount of gain of unfair advantage ... (b) the amount of loss caused to any person ... (c) the repetitive nature of the default." s. 61 – "No court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which an adjudicating officer ... is empowered by or under this Act to determine". s. 79 – exemption from liability of intermediary (quoted in the Detailed explanation). Related offences (criminal, not torts, but often on the same facts): s. 66C (identity theft), s. 66D (cheating by personation using a computer resource), s. 66E (violation of privacy by capturing or publishing images of a private area without consent).
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

s. 2(i) – "Data Fiduciary" means any person who "determines the purpose and means of processing of personal data"; s. 2(j) – "Data Principal" means "the individual to whom the personal data relates"; s. 2(t) – "personal data" means "any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to such data"; s. 2(u) – "personal data breach" (quoted below). s. 8(5) – a Data Fiduciary shall protect personal data "by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach"; s. 8(6) – it must inform the Board and "each affected Data Principal" of a breach. s. 33 and the Schedule – penalty imposed by the Data Protection Board, which "may extend to two hundred and fifty crore rupees" for failure to take reasonable security safeguards; s. 34 – penalties are credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. s. 39 – no civil court can entertain a suit on a matter the Board is empowered to decide. Commencement: G.S.R. 843(E) dated 13 November 2025 – ss. 2, 18 to 26, 35 to 43 and s. 44(1), (3) from 13 November 2025; ss. 3 to 5, 7 to 17, 28 to 34, 36, 37 and s. 44(2) after eighteen months from 13 November 2025.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 – s. 356 (defamation, "by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations"); s. 78(1)(ii) (stalking includes a man who "monitors the use by a woman of the internet, e-mail or any other form of electronic communication").
Limitation Act, 1963 – Art. 75 (libel: one year from publication); Art. 76 (slander: one year); Art. 113 (other suits: three years).
en.meaning: Digital tort – a civil wrong done by or against a computer resource or through electronic communication, causing harm to a person's property (data, systems, money), reputation, privacy or mind. It is a class of torts , not a single tort. Intermediary – a person who, on behalf of another, receives, stores or transmits electronic records or provides a service with respect to them (IT Act s. 2(1)(w)), such as a social media platform, search engine, internet service provider or online marketplace. Safe harbour – the protection in IT Act s. 79(1) that "an intermediary shall not be liable for any third party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by him", if the conditions of s. 79(2) are met and s. 79(3) does not apply. Personal data breach – "any unauthorised processing of personal data or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access to personal data, that compromises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data" (DPDP Act s. 2(u)).
keyPoints: Digital tort = civil wrong through computers/internet; not defined by statute. IT Act s. 43: unauthorised access, download, virus, damage → compensation. IT Act s. 43A: negligent body corporate → compensation; to be omitted by DPDP s. 44(2)(a). Adjudicating officer up to ₹5 crore; civil court barred (s. 61). DPDP Act: s. 8(5) security safeguards; s. 8(6) breach notice; penalties up to ₹250 crore to the Consolidated Fund. Section 79 safe harbour; lost on actual knowledge from a court order or government notice ( Shreya Singhal ). Section 66A struck down (2015). Privacy is a fundamental right; non-state actors also threaten it ( Puttaswamy , 2017).

Principle: "Section 66A ... is struck down in its entirety being violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved under Article 19(2)"; s. 69A is valid; s. 79 is valid subject to s. 79(3)(b) "being read down to mean that an intermediary upon receiving actual knowledge from a court order or on being notified by the appropriate government or its agency" fails to remove material. Why it matters: Fixes when a platform loses its safe harbour, and removes a vague offence that chilled online speech.

selfTest.q: Is "digital tort" defined in any Act?
selfTest.a: No. Which IT Act section gives compensation for hacking? Section 43. Up to what amount does the adjudicating officer decide claims? ₹5 crore. What does s. 43A cover? A body corporate's negligence in protecting sensitive personal data. Which provision will omit s. 43A? DPDP Act s. 44(2)(a). Who is an intermediary? A person who receives, stores or transmits records for another, e.g. ISPs, search engines, marketplaces. When does an intermediary lose s. 79 protection after Shreya Singhal ? If it fails to remove material after a court order or government notification. What happened to s. 66A? Struck down in its entirety. What is the maximum DPDP penalty for failing to take security safeguards? ₹250 crore. Which case said privacy dangers can come from non-state actors? K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

te.inOneMinute: డిజిటల్ టార్ట్ (Digital tort) అంటే కంప్యూటర్, మొబైల్ ఫోన్, ఇంటర్నెట్ లేదా ఇతర ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ మార్గాల ద్వారా చేసిన పౌర తప్పు; దీనికి బాధితుడు నష్టపరిహారం లేదా నిషేధాజ్ఞ (injunction) కోరవచ్చు. ఉదాహరణలు: hacking, డేటాను నాశనం చేయడం, వైరస్ పంపడం, ఆన్‌లైన్ పరువు నష్టం, వ్యక్తిగత చిత్రాలను ప్రచురించడం, గుర్తింపు దొంగతనం, వ్యక్తిగత డేటాను కాపాడడంలో వైఫల్యం. "డిజిటల్ టార్ట్" అనేది వర్ణనాత్మక పేరు; ఏ చట్టంలోనూ నిర్వచించిన పదం కాదు. చట్టం రెండు మూలాల నుండి వస్తుంది: (1) ఆన్‌లైన్ ప్రపంచానికి వర్తింపజేసిన సాధారణ టార్ట్‌లు (పరువు నష్టం, అతిక్రమణ, నిర్లక్ష్యం, గోప్యత); (2) చట్టాలు , ముఖ్యంగా సమాచార సాంకేతిక చట్టం, 2000 (IT Act) మరియు డిజిటల్ వ్యక్తిగత డేటా రక్షణ చట్టం, 2023 (DPDP Act) . IT Act s. 43: "without permission of the owner" (యజమాని అనుమతి లేకుండా) కంప్యూటర్ వ్యవస్థను access చేసినా, download చేసినా, వైరస్ ప్రవేశపెట్టినా, నాశనం చేసినా లేదా అంతరాయం కలిగించినా, అతను "shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected" (ప్రభావితుడైన వ్యక్తికి పరిహారం రూపంలో నష్టపరిహారం చెల్లించాలి). ఇదే ప్రధాన చట్టబద్ధ డిజిటల్ టార్ట్. IT Act s. 43A: సున్నితమైన వ్యక్తిగత డేటాకు "negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices" (సహేతుక భద్రతా పద్ధతులను అమలు చేయడంలో, నిర్వహించడంలో నిర్లక్ష్యం) చూపి తప్పుడు నష్టం కలిగించిన body corporate పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి. DPDP Act s. 44(2)(a) ఆ ఉప-విభాగం అమలులోకి వచ్చినప్పుడు (13 నవంబర్ 2025 నుండి 18 నెలల తర్వాత) s. 43A ను తొలగిస్తుంది. ₹5 కోట్ల వరకు దావాలు IT Act కింద న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి ( adjudicating officer) వద్దకు వెళ్తాయి (s. 46(1A)); అంతకు మించితే "competent court" (సమర్థ న్యాయస్థానం) కు. న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి నిర్ణయించగల విషయంపై సివిల్ కోర్టు దావా స్వీకరించదు (s. 61). మధ్యవర్తి (Intermediary – సోషల్ మీడియా వేదిక, ఇంటర్నెట్ సేవా ప్రదాత వంటివి) మూడవ పక్షం కంటెంట్‌కు s. 79 కింద సురక్షిత ఆశ్రయం (safe harbour) పొందుతుంది; కానీ "actual knowledge" (వాస్తవ జ్ఞానం) తర్వాత చట్టవిరుద్ధ విషయాన్ని తొలగించకపోతే అది పోతుంది. Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు "actual knowledge" ను కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు లేదా ప్రభుత్వ నోటిఫికేషన్ ద్వారా వచ్చిన జ్ఞానంగా చదివింది, s. 66A ను "in its entirety" (పూర్తిగా) కొట్టివేసింది. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) లో తొమ్మిది మంది న్యాయమూర్తులు గోప్యతను ప్రాథమిక హక్కుగా ప్రకటించి ఇలా అన్నారు: "The dangers to privacy in an age of information can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well." (అర్థం: సమాచార యుగంలో గోప్యతకు ప్రమాదాలు ప్రభుత్వం నుండే కాక ప్రభుత్వేతర వ్యక్తుల నుండి కూడా రావచ్చు).
te.meaning: డిజిటల్ టార్ట్ – కంప్యూటర్ వనరు ద్వారా లేదా దానిపై, లేదా ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ సంభాషణ ద్వారా చేసిన పౌర తప్పు; ఇది ఒక వ్యక్తి ఆస్తి (డేటా, వ్యవస్థలు, డబ్బు), పరువు, గోప్యత లేదా మనసుకు హాని కలిగిస్తుంది. ఇది ఒకే టార్ట్ కాదు, టార్ట్‌ల వర్గం. మధ్యవర్తి – మరొకరి తరఫున ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ రికార్డులను స్వీకరించే, నిల్వ చేసే లేదా పంపే, లేదా వాటికి సంబంధించిన సేవ అందించే వ్యక్తి (IT Act s. 2(1)(w)); ఉదా: సోషల్ మీడియా వేదిక, సెర్చ్ ఇంజిన్, ఇంటర్నెట్ సేవా ప్రదాత, ఆన్‌లైన్ మార్కెట్. సురక్షిత ఆశ్రయం – IT Act s. 79(1) లోని రక్షణ: "an intermediary shall not be liable for any third party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by him" (అర్థం: తాను అందుబాటులో ఉంచిన లేదా hosting చేసిన మూడవ పక్షపు సమాచారం, డేటా లేదా లింక్‌కు మధ్యవర్తి బాధ్యుడు కాదు), s. 79(2) షరతులు నెరవేరి, s. 79(3) వర్తించకపోతే. వ్యక్తిగత డేటా ఉల్లంఘన – "any unauthorised processing of personal data or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access to personal data, that compromises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data" (DPDP Act s. 2(u)) (అర్థం: వ్యక్తిగత డేటా గోప్యత, సమగ్రత లేదా లభ్యతకు భంగం కలిగించే అనధికార ప్రాసెసింగ్, లేదా ప్రమాదవశాత్తు బహిర్గతం, సంపాదన, పంచుకోవడం, వినియోగం, మార్పు, నాశనం లేదా ప్రవేశం కోల్పోవడం).
keyPoints: డిజిటల్ టార్ట్ = కంప్యూటర్లు/ఇంటర్నెట్ ద్వారా పౌర తప్పు; చట్టంలో నిర్వచనం లేదు. IT Act s. 43: అనధికార ప్రవేశం, download, వైరస్, నష్టం → పరిహారం. IT Act s. 43A: నిర్లక్ష్యపు body corporate → పరిహారం; DPDP s. 44(2)(a) ద్వారా తొలగించబడుతుంది. ₹5 కోట్ల వరకు న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి; సివిల్ కోర్టుకు నిషేధం (s. 61). DPDP Act: s. 8(5) భద్రతా రక్షణలు; s. 8(6) ఉల్లంఘన నోటీసు; ₹250 కోట్ల వరకు జరిమానాలు సంఘటిత నిధికి. Section 79 సురక్షిత ఆశ్రయం; కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు లేదా ప్రభుత్వ నోటీసు ద్వారా వాస్తవ జ్ఞానం వచ్చాక పోతుంది ( Shreya Singhal ). Section 66A కొట్టివేయబడింది (2015). గోప్యత ప్రాథమిక హక్కు; ప్రభుత్వేతర వ్యక్తులు కూడా దానికి ప్రమాదం ( Puttaswamy , 2017).

selfTest.q: "డిజిటల్ టార్ట్" ఏ చట్టంలోనైనా నిర్వచించబడిందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. Hacking కు పరిహారం ఇచ్చే IT Act సెక్షన్ ఏది? Section 43. న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి ఎంత మొత్తం వరకు దావాలు నిర్ణయిస్తారు? ₹5 కోట్లు. s. 43A దేనిని కవర్ చేస్తుంది? సున్నితమైన వ్యక్తిగత డేటా రక్షణలో body corporate నిర్లక్ష్యం. s. 43A ను ఏ నిబంధన తొలగిస్తుంది? DPDP Act s. 44(2)(a). మధ్యవర్తి ఎవరు? మరొకరి కోసం రికార్డులను స్వీకరించే, నిల్వ చేసే లేదా పంపే వ్యక్తి; ఉదా: ISPs, సెర్చ్ ఇంజిన్లు, మార్కెట్ సైట్లు. Shreya Singhal తర్వాత మధ్యవర్తి s. 79 రక్షణ ఎప్పుడు కోల్పోతుంది? కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు లేదా ప్రభుత్వ నోటిఫికేషన్ తర్వాత విషయాన్ని తొలగించకపోతే. s. 66A కు ఏమైంది? పూర్తిగా కొట్టివేయబడింది. భద్రతా రక్షణలు తీసుకోకపోతే గరిష్ఠ DPDP జరిమానా ఎంత? ₹250 కోట్లు. గోప్యతకు ప్రమాదాలు ప్రభుత్వేతర వ్యక్తుల నుండి రావచ్చని చెప్పిన కేసు ఏది? K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

hi.inOneMinute: A digital tort is a civil wrong committed through a computer, mobile phone, the internet or other electronic means, for which the injured person can claim damages or an injunction. Examples are hacking, damaging data, spreading a virus, online defamation, publishing private images, identity theft, and failing to protect personal data. "Digital tort" is a descriptive name, not a term defined in any Act. The law comes from two sources: (1) the ordinary torts (defamation, trespass, negligence, privacy) applied to the online world; and (2) statutes , mainly the Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) . IT Act s. 43: anyone who, "without permission of the owner", accesses, downloads, introduces a virus into, damages or disrupts a computer system "shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected". This is the main statutory digital tort. IT Act s. 43A: a body corporate that is "negligent in implementing and maintaining reasonable security practices" for sensitive personal data and thereby causes wrongful loss must pay compensation. The DPDP Act s. 44(2)(a) will omit s. 43A when that sub-section comes into force (18 months from 13 November 2025). Claims up to ₹5 crore go to an adjudicating officer under the IT Act (s. 46(1A)); above that, to the "competent court". A civil court cannot entertain a suit on a matter the adjudicating officer can decide (s. 61). An intermediary (such as a social media platform or internet service provider) is protected by safe harbour under s. 79 for third-party content, but loses it if it fails to remove unlawful material after "actual knowledge". In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) the Supreme Court read "actual knowledge" to mean knowledge from a court order or a government notification , and struck down s. 66A "in its entirety". In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) nine judges held privacy to be a fundamental right and said: "The dangers to privacy in an age of information can originate not only from the state but from non-state actors as well."
legalProvision: Information Technology Act, 2000

s. 2(1)(w) – "intermediary", "with respect to any particular electronic records, means any person who on behalf of another person receives, stores or transmits that record or provides any service with respect to that record and includes telecom service providers, network service providers, internet service providers, web-hosting service providers, search engines, online payment sites, online-auction sites, online-market places and cyber cafes". s. 43 – penalty and compensation for damage to computer, computer system, etc. If any person "without permission of the owner or any other person who is in charge of a computer, computer system or computer network" does any of the acts in clauses (a) to (j) (for example (a) "accesses or secures access", (b) "downloads, copies or extracts any data", (c) "introduces or causes to be introduced any computer contaminant or computer virus", (d) "damages or causes to be damaged", (e) "disrupts", (f) "denies or causes the denial of access", (h) charges services to another's account by tampering, (i) "destroys, deletes or alters any information", (j) steals or alters source code), "he shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected." s. 43A – compensation for failure to protect data (quoted in the Detailed explanation). s. 46(1A) – the adjudicating officer has jurisdiction where "the claim for damage does not exceed rupees five crore"; above that, "the jurisdiction ... shall vest with the competent court". s. 47 – in fixing compensation the adjudicating officer considers "(a) the amount of gain of unfair advantage ... (b) the amount of loss caused to any person ... (c) the repetitive nature of the default." s. 61 – "No court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which an adjudicating officer ... is empowered by or under this Act to determine". s. 79 – exemption from liability of intermediary (quoted in the Detailed explanation). Related offences (criminal, not torts, but often on the same facts): s. 66C (identity theft), s. 66D (cheating by personation using a computer resource), s. 66E (violation of privacy by capturing or publishing images of a private area without consent).
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

s. 2(i) – "Data Fiduciary" means any person who "determines the purpose and means of processing of personal data"; s. 2(j) – "Data Principal" means "the individual to whom the personal data relates"; s. 2(t) – "personal data" means "any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to such data"; s. 2(u) – "personal data breach" (quoted below). s. 8(5) – a Data Fiduciary shall protect personal data "by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach"; s. 8(6) – it must inform the Board and "each affected Data Principal" of a breach. s. 33 and the Schedule – penalty imposed by the Data Protection Board, which "may extend to two hundred and fifty crore rupees" for failure to take reasonable security safeguards; s. 34 – penalties are credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. s. 39 – no civil court can entertain a suit on a matter the Board is empowered to decide. Commencement: G.S.R. 843(E) dated 13 November 2025 – ss. 2, 18 to 26, 35 to 43 and s. 44(1), (3) from 13 November 2025; ss. 3 to 5, 7 to 17, 28 to 34, 36, 37 and s. 44(2) after eighteen months from 13 November 2025.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 – s. 356 (defamation, "by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations"); s. 78(1)(ii) (stalking includes a man who "monitors the use by a woman of the internet, e-mail or any other form of electronic communication").
Limitation Act, 1963 – Art. 75 (libel: one year from publication); Art. 76 (slander: one year); Art. 113 (other suits: three years).
hi.meaning: Digital tort – a civil wrong done by or against a computer resource or through electronic communication, causing harm to a person's property (data, systems, money), reputation, privacy or mind. It is a class of torts , not a single tort. Intermediary – a person who, on behalf of another, receives, stores or transmits electronic records or provides a service with respect to them (IT Act s. 2(1)(w)), such as a social media platform, search engine, internet service provider or online marketplace. Safe harbour – the protection in IT Act s. 79(1) that "an intermediary shall not be liable for any third party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by him", if the conditions of s. 79(2) are met and s. 79(3) does not apply. Personal data breach – "any unauthorised processing of personal data or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access to personal data, that compromises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data" (DPDP Act s. 2(u)).
keyPoints: Digital tort = civil wrong through computers/internet; not defined by statute. IT Act s. 43: unauthorised access, download, virus, damage → compensation. IT Act s. 43A: negligent body corporate → compensation; to be omitted by DPDP s. 44(2)(a). Adjudicating officer up to ₹5 crore; civil court barred (s. 61). DPDP Act: s. 8(5) security safeguards; s. 8(6) breach notice; penalties up to ₹250 crore to the Consolidated Fund. Section 79 safe harbour; lost on actual knowledge from a court order or government notice ( Shreya Singhal ). Section 66A struck down (2015). Privacy is a fundamental right; non-state actors also threaten it ( Puttaswamy , 2017).

Why it matters: Fixes when a platform loses its safe harbour, and removes a vague offence that chilled online speech.

Why it matters: Foundation of data protection law and of privacy claims in the digital world.

selfTest.q: Is "digital tort" defined in any Act?
selfTest.a: No. Which IT Act section gives compensation for hacking? Section 43. Up to what amount does the adjudicating officer decide claims? ₹5 crore. What does s. 43A cover? A body corporate's negligence in protecting sensitive personal data. Which provision will omit s. 43A? DPDP Act s. 44(2)(a). Who is an intermediary? A person who receives, stores or transmits records for another, e.g. ISPs, search engines, marketplaces. When does an intermediary lose s. 79 protection after Shreya Singhal ? If it fails to remove material after a court order or government notification. What happened to s. 66A? Struck down in its entirety. What is the maximum DPDP penalty for failing to take security safeguards? ₹250 crore. Which case said privacy dangers can come from non-state actors? K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

law-of-torts-u3-t7.subtitle: Liability for psychiatric injury caused by shock: Wilkinson v. Downton, Bourhill v. Young and Alcock

en.inOneMinute: Nervous shock is the legal name for psychiatric illness caused by a sudden shock from the defendant's wrongful act, as when a person suffers a breakdown after seeing an accident. In the words of Lord Denning M.R. in Hinz v. Berry [1970] 2 QB 40, quoted in Alcock (1991): "Damages are ... recoverable for nervous shock, or, to put it in medical terms, for any recognisable psychiatric illness caused by the breach of duty by the defendant". Ordinary grief, fear or sorrow is not enough. Hidden J., the trial judge in Alcock , said psychiatric illness "is something more than the sad, but inevitable, human emotions of grief, sorrow, compassion and anxiety which occur in all bereavements ... For these emotions, however, the law gives no compensation." A medically recognised illness must be proved. No physical impact is needed. Lord Macmillan in Bourhill v. Young (1942): "The crude view that the law should take cognizance only of physical injury resulting from actual impact has been discarded". Claims usually arise in negligence . The claimant must show that psychiatric harm to a person in his position was reasonably foreseeable . In Bourhill v. Young a pregnant fishwife who heard a crash 45–50 feet away and later saw blood on the road failed: she was not within "the area of potential danger". A primary victim is someone within the range of physical danger. A secondary victim is someone who suffers shock from seeing harm to another. Alcock v. Chief Constable of South Yorkshire (Hillsborough disaster, 15 April 1989) set strict controls for secondary victims: close ties of love and affection; presence at the event or its immediate aftermath ; and perception with one's own senses (live TV was not enough). A wilful act calculated to cause shock is also actionable ( Wilkinson v. Downton , 1897).
legalProvision: There is no Indian statute that defines nervous shock. It is a common law head of damage (mainly in negligence), followed by Indian courts. Related provisions:

Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – no specific Article; three years "When the right to sue accrues". Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 166(1)(a) – a claim for compensation may be made "by the person who has sustained the injury"; psychiatric injury caused by a motor accident can form part of such a claim before the Claims Tribunal (general practice; no Indian judgment on nervous shock was available). Consumer Protection Act, 2019 – "deficiency" in service, including medical service, may cause mental agony for which compensation is awarded (studied in the consumer protection topics).
en.meaning: Nervous shock – a recognisable psychiatric illness (for example, post-traumatic stress disorder, clinical depression, or pathological grief) caused by the defendant's wrongful act, usually through a sudden shock to the senses. It must go beyond "ordinary human grief or anguish" (Burbury C.J. in the Tasmanian case Storm v. Geeves (1965), quoted in Alcock : a relative "is only entitled to damages if it is established by acceptable evidence that he or she has suffered from some form of medically recognisable neurosis or damage to the mind going beyond ordinary human grief or anguish"). Primary victim – a person who was himself within the range of foreseeable physical injury (or reasonably believed he was) and suffers psychiatric harm. Secondary victim – a person who was not himself in danger but suffers psychiatric harm from witnessing death, injury or danger to another. Immediate aftermath – the scene of the accident or its direct consequences seen very soon after the event (for example, at the hospital within hours, before the victims have been cleaned up). Lord Ackner in Alcock stated the established law: the shock must have "come about through the sight or hearing of the event, or its immediate aftermath".
keyPoints: Nervous shock = recognisable psychiatric illness caused by shock. Grief and sorrow alone are not compensated. No physical impact is needed ( Bourhill v. Young ). Duty depends on foreseeability; ordinary fortitude ("customary phlegm") is assumed. Bourhill v. Young : claimant outside "the area of potential danger" – no duty. Alcock controls for secondary victims: close tie, presence at event or immediate aftermath, own senses. Live television is not "sight or hearing" ( Alcock ). Wilful shock is actionable ( Wilkinson v. Downton ).

selfTest.q: What is nervous shock in law?
selfTest.a: A recognisable psychiatric illness caused by shock. Is grief alone compensated? No. Is physical impact needed? No (Bourhill v. Young). Why did the claimant fail in Bourhill v. Young ? She was outside the area of potential danger; no duty was owed. What is "customary phlegm"? The ordinary fortitude a defendant may assume in others (Lord Porter). Who is a secondary victim? A person who suffers shock from seeing harm to another. Name the Alcock controls. Close tie of love and affection; proximity in time and space; perception by own senses. Was watching live TV enough in Alcock ? No. How many died at Hillsborough? 95. Which case allows recovery for shock from a deliberate false statement? Wilkinson v. Downton.

te.inOneMinute: నాడీ ఆఘాతం (Nervous shock) అంటే ప్రతివాది తప్పుడు చర్య వల్ల కలిగిన ఆకస్మిక షాక్‌తో వచ్చే మానసిక వ్యాధి (psychiatric illness) . ఉదా: ప్రమాదాన్ని చూసి ఒక వ్యక్తి మానసికంగా కుప్పకూలడం. Hinz v. Berry [1970] 2 QB 40 లో Lord Denning M.R. మాటలు, Alcock (1991) లో ఉదహరించబడ్డాయి: "Damages are ... recoverable for nervous shock, or, to put it in medical terms, for any recognisable psychiatric illness caused by the breach of duty by the defendant" (అర్థం: నాడీ ఆఘాతానికి, అంటే వైద్య భాషలో, ప్రతివాది విధి ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల కలిగిన ఏదైనా గుర్తించదగిన మానసిక వ్యాధికి, నష్టపరిహారం పొందవచ్చు). సాధారణ దుఃఖం, భయం, బాధ సరిపోవు. Alcock లో ట్రయల్ జడ్జి Hidden J. ఇలా అన్నారు: మానసిక వ్యాధి "is something more than the sad, but inevitable, human emotions of grief, sorrow, compassion and anxiety which occur in all bereavements ... For these emotions, however, the law gives no compensation." (అర్థం: ప్రతి మరణంలోనూ కలిగే దుఃఖం, విచారం, కరుణ, ఆందోళన అనే అనివార్య భావాల కంటే ఇది ఎక్కువ; ఈ భావాలకు చట్టం పరిహారం ఇవ్వదు). వైద్యపరంగా గుర్తించిన వ్యాధి రుజువు కావాలి. శారీరక తాకిడి (impact) అవసరం లేదు. Bourhill v. Young (1942) లో Lord Macmillan: "The crude view that the law should take cognizance only of physical injury resulting from actual impact has been discarded" (అర్థం: అసలు తాకిడి వల్ల కలిగిన శారీరక గాయాన్నే చట్టం పరిగణించాలన్న మొరటు అభిప్రాయం విడిచిపెట్టబడింది). సాధారణంగా ఈ దావాలు నిర్లక్ష్యం (negligence) లో వస్తాయి. హక్కుదారు స్థానంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తికి మానసిక హాని జరగడం సహేతుకంగా ఊహించదగినది అని చూపాలి. Bourhill v. Young లో 45–50 అడుగుల దూరంలో ప్రమాదం శబ్దం విని, తర్వాత రోడ్డుపై రక్తం చూసిన గర్భిణి చేపల వ్యాపారి ఓడిపోయింది: ఆమె "the area of potential danger" (సంభావ్య ప్రమాద పరిధి) లో లేదు. ప్రాథమిక బాధితుడు (Primary victim) అంటే శారీరక ప్రమాద పరిధిలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి. ద్వితీయ బాధితుడు (Secondary victim) అంటే మరొకరికి హాని జరగడం చూసి షాక్‌కు గురైన వ్యక్తి. Alcock v. Chief Constable of South Yorkshire (Hillsborough దుర్ఘటన, 15 ఏప్రిల్ 1989) ద్వితీయ బాధితులకు కఠిన నియంత్రణలు పెట్టింది: ప్రేమానురాగాల దగ్గరి బంధం; సంఘటన వద్ద లేదా దాని తక్షణ పరిణామం (immediate aftermath) వద్ద ఉండటం; స్వంత ఇంద్రియాలతో గ్రహించడం (ప్రత్యక్ష TV ప్రసారం సరిపోలేదు). షాక్ కలిగించేలా ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా చేసిన చర్య కూడా దావాకు అర్హం ( Wilkinson v. Downton , 1897).
te.meaning: నాడీ ఆఘాతం – ప్రతివాది తప్పుడు చర్య వల్ల, సాధారణంగా ఇంద్రియాలకు కలిగిన ఆకస్మిక షాక్ ద్వారా వచ్చిన గుర్తించదగిన మానసిక వ్యాధి (ఉదా: post-traumatic stress disorder, క్లినికల్ డిప్రెషన్, రోగలక్షణ దుఃఖం). ఇది "ordinary human grief or anguish" (సాధారణ మానవ దుఃఖం లేదా వేదన) కంటే ఎక్కువగా ఉండాలి. Tasmania కేసు Storm v. Geeves (1965) లో Burbury C.J. మాటలు, Alcock లో ఉదహరించబడ్డాయి: బంధువు "is only entitled to damages if it is established by acceptable evidence that he or she has suffered from some form of medically recognisable neurosis or damage to the mind going beyond ordinary human grief or anguish" (అర్థం: సాధారణ దుఃఖం లేదా వేదనకు మించిన, వైద్యపరంగా గుర్తించదగిన నరాల వ్యాధి లేదా మనసుకు హాని కలిగిందని ఆమోదయోగ్య సాక్ష్యంతో రుజువైతేనే నష్టపరిహారానికి అర్హుడు). ప్రాథమిక బాధితుడు – తానే ఊహించదగిన శారీరక గాయ పరిధిలో ఉన్న (లేదా ఉన్నానని సహేతుకంగా నమ్మిన) వ్యక్తి, మానసిక హానికి గురైనవాడు. ద్వితీయ బాధితుడు – తాను ప్రమాదంలో లేకపోయినా, మరొకరి మరణం, గాయం లేదా ప్రమాదాన్ని చూసి మానసిక హానికి గురైన వ్యక్తి. తక్షణ పరిణామం – ప్రమాద స్థలం లేదా దాని ప్రత్యక్ష పరిణామాలను సంఘటన జరిగిన కొద్దిసేపటికే చూడటం (ఉదా: కొన్ని గంటల్లోనే ఆసుపత్రిలో, బాధితులను శుభ్రం చేయకముందే). Alcock లో Lord Ackner స్థిరపడిన చట్టాన్ని ఇలా చెప్పారు: షాక్ "come about through the sight or hearing of the event, or its immediate aftermath" (అర్థం: సంఘటనను లేదా దాని తక్షణ పరిణామాన్ని చూడటం లేదా వినడం ద్వారా కలిగి ఉండాలి).
keyPoints: నాడీ ఆఘాతం = షాక్ వల్ల కలిగిన గుర్తించదగిన మానసిక వ్యాధి. కేవలం దుఃఖం, విచారానికి పరిహారం లేదు. శారీరక తాకిడి అవసరం లేదు ( Bourhill v. Young ). విధి ఊహించదగినతపై ఆధారపడుతుంది; సాధారణ ధైర్యం ("customary phlegm") ను భావిస్తారు. Bourhill v. Young : హక్కుదారు "the area of potential danger" (సంభావ్య ప్రమాద పరిధి) బయట – విధి లేదు. ద్వితీయ బాధితులకు Alcock నియంత్రణలు: దగ్గరి బంధం, సంఘటన లేదా తక్షణ పరిణామం వద్ద ఉనికి, స్వంత ఇంద్రియాలు. ప్రత్యక్ష టెలివిజన్ "sight or hearing" (చూపు లేదా వినికిడి) కాదు ( Alcock ). ఉద్దేశపూర్వక షాక్ దావాకు అర్హం ( Wilkinson v. Downton ).

selfTest.q: చట్టంలో నాడీ ఆఘాతం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: షాక్ వల్ల కలిగిన గుర్తించదగిన మానసిక వ్యాధి. కేవలం దుఃఖానికి పరిహారం ఉందా? లేదు. శారీరక తాకిడి అవసరమా? లేదు (Bourhill v. Young). Bourhill v. Young లో హక్కుదారు ఎందుకు ఓడిపోయింది? ఆమె సంభావ్య ప్రమాద పరిధి బయట ఉంది; విధి లేదు. "customary phlegm" అంటే ఏమిటి? ఇతరులకు ఉంటుందని ప్రతివాది భావించగల సాధారణ ధైర్యం (Lord Porter). ద్వితీయ బాధితుడు ఎవరు? మరొకరికి హాని జరగడం చూసి షాక్‌కు గురైన వ్యక్తి. Alcock నియంత్రణలు చెప్పండి. ప్రేమానురాగాల దగ్గరి బంధం; కాలం, స్థలంలో సామీప్యం; స్వంత ఇంద్రియాలతో గ్రహణం. Alcock లో ప్రత్యక్ష TV చూడటం సరిపోయిందా? లేదు. Hillsborough లో ఎంతమంది చనిపోయారు? 95. ఉద్దేశపూర్వక అబద్ధపు మాట వల్ల కలిగిన షాక్‌కు పరిహారం అనుమతించిన కేసు ఏది? Wilkinson v. Downton.

hi.inOneMinute: Nervous shock is the legal name for psychiatric illness caused by a sudden shock from the defendant's wrongful act, as when a person suffers a breakdown after seeing an accident. In the words of Lord Denning M.R. in Hinz v. Berry [1970] 2 QB 40, quoted in Alcock (1991): "Damages are ... recoverable for nervous shock, or, to put it in medical terms, for any recognisable psychiatric illness caused by the breach of duty by the defendant". Ordinary grief, fear or sorrow is not enough. Hidden J., the trial judge in Alcock , said psychiatric illness "is something more than the sad, but inevitable, human emotions of grief, sorrow, compassion and anxiety which occur in all bereavements ... For these emotions, however, the law gives no compensation." A medically recognised illness must be proved. No physical impact is needed. Lord Macmillan in Bourhill v. Young (1942): "The crude view that the law should take cognizance only of physical injury resulting from actual impact has been discarded". Claims usually arise in negligence . The claimant must show that psychiatric harm to a person in his position was reasonably foreseeable . In Bourhill v. Young a pregnant fishwife who heard a crash 45–50 feet away and later saw blood on the road failed: she was not within "the area of potential danger". A primary victim is someone within the range of physical danger. A secondary victim is someone who suffers shock from seeing harm to another. Alcock v. Chief Constable of South Yorkshire (Hillsborough disaster, 15 April 1989) set strict controls for secondary victims: close ties of love and affection; presence at the event or its immediate aftermath ; and perception with one's own senses (live TV was not enough). A wilful act calculated to cause shock is also actionable ( Wilkinson v. Downton , 1897).
legalProvision: There is no Indian statute that defines nervous shock. It is a common law head of damage (mainly in negligence), followed by Indian courts. Related provisions:

Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – no specific Article; three years "When the right to sue accrues". Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 166(1)(a) – a claim for compensation may be made "by the person who has sustained the injury"; psychiatric injury caused by a motor accident can form part of such a claim before the Claims Tribunal (general practice; no Indian judgment on nervous shock was available). Consumer Protection Act, 2019 – "deficiency" in service, including medical service, may cause mental agony for which compensation is awarded (studied in the consumer protection topics).
hi.meaning: Nervous shock – a recognisable psychiatric illness (for example, post-traumatic stress disorder, clinical depression, or pathological grief) caused by the defendant's wrongful act, usually through a sudden shock to the senses. It must go beyond "ordinary human grief or anguish" (Burbury C.J. in the Tasmanian case Storm v. Geeves (1965), quoted in Alcock : a relative "is only entitled to damages if it is established by acceptable evidence that he or she has suffered from some form of medically recognisable neurosis or damage to the mind going beyond ordinary human grief or anguish"). Primary victim – a person who was himself within the range of foreseeable physical injury (or reasonably believed he was) and suffers psychiatric harm. Secondary victim – a person who was not himself in danger but suffers psychiatric harm from witnessing death, injury or danger to another. Immediate aftermath – the scene of the accident or its direct consequences seen very soon after the event (for example, at the hospital within hours, before the victims have been cleaned up). Lord Ackner in Alcock stated the established law: the shock must have "come about through the sight or hearing of the event, or its immediate aftermath".
keyPoints: Nervous shock = recognisable psychiatric illness caused by shock. Grief and sorrow alone are not compensated. No physical impact is needed ( Bourhill v. Young ). Duty depends on foreseeability; ordinary fortitude ("customary phlegm") is assumed. Bourhill v. Young : claimant outside "the area of potential danger" – no duty. Alcock controls for secondary victims: close tie, presence at event or immediate aftermath, own senses. Live television is not "sight or hearing" ( Alcock ). Wilful shock is actionable ( Wilkinson v. Downton ).

caseLaws.facts: Principle: No duty was owed; she "was not within the area of potential danger which the cyclist should reasonably have had in view" (Lord Thankerton). Lord Macmillan: the "crude view" requiring "actual impact has been discarded". Why it matters: Nervous shock needs no impact, but there must be a duty of care based on foreseeability; ordinary fortitude ("customary phlegm") is assumed.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: In addition to foreseeability there must be "a requisite relationship of proximity" (Lord Keith); the three elements are the class of persons, proximity "in time and space", and "the means by which the shock has been caused" (Lord Ackner); live television "cannot be equated with the 'sight or hearing of the event or its immediate aftermath'". All claims failed. Why it matters: The leading statement of the controls on secondary victims.

selfTest.q: What is nervous shock in law?
selfTest.a: A recognisable psychiatric illness caused by shock. Is grief alone compensated? No. Is physical impact needed? No (Bourhill v. Young). Why did the claimant fail in Bourhill v. Young ? She was outside the area of potential danger; no duty was owed. What is "customary phlegm"? The ordinary fortitude a defendant may assume in others (Lord Porter). Who is a secondary victim? A person who suffers shock from seeing harm to another. Name the Alcock controls. Close tie of love and affection; proximity in time and space; perception by own senses. Was watching live TV enough in Alcock ? No. How many died at Hillsborough? 95. Which case allows recovery for shock from a deliberate false statement? Wilkinson v. Downton.

law-of-torts-u3-t10.subtitle: The tort of directly and wrongfully entering, remaining on or placing things on land in another's possession

en.inOneMinute: Trespass to land is the direct and unjustified interference with land in the possession of another, for example by entering it, remaining on it, or putting things on it. It is actionable per se : no damage need be proved. In Entick v. Carrington (1765) the court said: "our law holds the property of every man so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all; if he will tread upon his neighbour's ground, he must justify it by law." Elements: (1) the plaintiff is in possession; (2) the defendant directly interferes (entry, remaining, placing objects, damaging); (3) the act is voluntary; (4) there is no lawful justification. Main defences: a licence (permission) of the possessor (Easements Act, 1882, s. 52), authority of law (a valid warrant or statutory power), and an easement. In Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974) the demolition of a building put up without sanction, under a statutory power, gave no claim, even if the officers acted with malice. A licensee who stays after the licence is revoked becomes a trespasser, but he gets "a reasonable time to leave" (s. 63). Remedies: damages (nominal if no loss), mesne profits for wrongful occupation (CPC s. 2(12)), injunction, recovery of possession (Specific Relief Act ss. 5, 6), and reasonable self-help. Limitation: "For compensation for trespass upon immovable property" – three years from "The date of the trespass" (Limitation Act Art. 87); a continuing trespass gives "a fresh period of limitation" every moment it continues (s. 22).
legalProvision: There is no statutory definition of trespass to land as a tort. The tort is from common law. Related provisions:

Indian Easements Act, 1882 s. 52 – "Where one person grants to another, or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would, in the absence of such right, be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a license." s. 54 – a licence may be "express or implied from the conduct of the grantor". s. 60 – "A license may be revoked by the grantor, unless— (a) it is coupled with a transfer of property and such transfer is in force; (b) the licensee, acting upon the license, has executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses in the execution." s. 61 – revocation "may be express or implied". Illustration (a): A, who allowed B to use a path, "with intent to revoke the license, locks a gate across the path. The license is revoked." s. 63 – on revocation "the licensee is entitled to a reasonable time to leave the property affected thereby and to remove any goods which he has been allowed to place on such property." s. 64 – a licensee for consideration who "without any fault of his own, is evicted by the grantor before he has fully enjoyed" the right "is entitled to recover compensation from the grantor." Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 2(12) – "mesne profits" of property means "those profits which the person in wrongful possession of such property actually received or might with ordinary diligence have received therefrom, together with interest on such profits, but shall not include profits due to improvements made by the person in wrongful possession". Specific Relief Act, 1963 – s. 5 (recovery of immovable property under the CPC); s. 6 (suit within six months by a person "dispossessed without his consent ... otherwise than in due course of law"); ss. 37–40 (injunctions; damages in addition or substitution). Limitation Act, 1963 – Art. 87 (compensation for trespass: three years from the date of the trespass); s. 22 ("In the case of ... a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the ... tort ... continues"); Arts. 64, 65 (possession: twelve years). Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 329(1) – criminal trespass: whoever "enters into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession", or, having lawfully entered, "unlawfully remains there" with such intent. s. 329(2) – house-trespass (entering or remaining in a building used as a human dwelling, place of worship or place for custody of property).
en.meaning: Trespass to land – the intentional (voluntary) and direct entry upon, remaining upon, or interference with land in the possession of another, without lawful justification. Actionable per se – a wrong for which the plaintiff can sue without proving actual damage; the violation of the right is itself the injury. Licence – permission from the person in possession to do something on his land that would otherwise be unlawful, which does not create an easement or an interest in the land (Easements Act s. 52). A licensee is not a trespasser while the licence lasts. Mesne profits – the profits that a person in wrongful possession actually received, or might with ordinary diligence have received, from the property, with interest, but not profits from his own improvements (CPC s. 2(12)).
keyPoints: Trespass to land = direct, unjustified interference with land in another's possession. Actionable per se: "though he does no damage at all" ( Entick ). The person in possession sues. Forms: entry, remaining, placing things, damaging, airspace and subsoil. Licence (s. 52) is revocable (s. 60); reasonable time to leave (s. 63); compensation for wrongful eviction of a paid licensee (s. 64). Lawful statutory action is a justification even if malicious ( Prabhu Dayal ). Mesne profits: CPC s. 2(12). Limitation: 3 years (Art. 87); continuing trespass – s. 22.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "our law holds the property of every man so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all; if he will tread upon his neighbour's ground, he must justify it by law." The warrant was not lawful and judgment was given for the plaintiff. Why it matters: Trespass to land is actionable per se and every entry, even by State officers, must be justified by law.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff built 16 shops on old foundations without the notice (s
caseLaws.facts: 178) and sanction (s. 180) required by the U.P. Municipalities Act; after notices, the Town Area Committee demolished them under s. 186. He sued for ₹1,000 damages, alleging malice. Principle: "A legal act, though motivated by malice, will not make the actor liable to pay damages"; demolition of an illegal building by municipal authorities is not "injuria"; "No person has the right to enjoy the fruits of an act which is an offence under law." The suit failed. Why it matters: Lawful statutory authority is a complete justification for interference with land, and malice does not change this.

selfTest.q: Is damage needed for trespass to land?
selfTest.a: No. Who can sue? The person in possession. Is smoke drifting onto land trespass? No, it is nuisance. Where is "licence" defined? Easements Act, 1882, s. 52. When is a licence irrevocable ? When coupled with a transfer of property in force, or when the licensee has executed a permanent work and incurred expenses (s. 60). What does s. 63 give a licensee? A reasonable time to leave and remove his goods. Why were the defendants liable in Entick ? Their warrant was not lawful, so the entry was not justified by law. Did malice make the demolition actionable in Prabhu Dayal ? No. Define mesne profits. Profits the wrongful possessor received or might with ordinary diligence have received, with interest, excluding profits from his improvements (CPC s. 2(12)). What is the limitation for compensation for trespass? Three years from the date of the trespass (Art. 87).

te.inOneMinute: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ (Trespass to land) అంటే మరొకరి స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న భూమిలో ప్రత్యక్షంగా, సమర్థన లేకుండా జోక్యం చేసుకోవడం; ఉదా: దానిలోకి ప్రవేశించడం, దానిపై ఉండిపోవడం, దానిపై వస్తువులు పెట్టడం. ఇది స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం (actionable per se): నష్టం రుజువు అవసరం లేదు. Entick v. Carrington (1765) లో కోర్టు: "our law holds the property of every man so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all; if he will tread upon his neighbour's ground, he must justify it by law." (అర్థం: మన చట్టం ప్రతి మనిషి ఆస్తిని ఎంత పవిత్రంగా భావిస్తుందంటే అనుమతి లేకుండా ఎవరూ పొరుగువాడి స్థలంలో అడుగు పెట్టకూడదు; పెడితే, ఏ నష్టం చేయకపోయినా అతను అతిక్రమణదారుడే; పొరుగువాడి నేలపై నడవాలంటే దాన్ని చట్టం ద్వారా సమర్థించుకోవాలి). అంశాలు: (1) వాది స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్నాడు; (2) ప్రతివాది ప్రత్యక్షంగా జోక్యం చేసుకున్నాడు (ప్రవేశం, ఉండిపోవడం, వస్తువులు ఉంచడం, నష్టం); (3) చర్య స్వచ్ఛందం; (4) చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేదు. ప్రధాన ప్రతివాదనలు (defences): స్వాధీనదారుడి లైసెన్స్ (అనుమతి) (Easements Act, 1882, s. 52), చట్ట అధికారం (చెల్లుబాటైన warrant లేదా చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం), సౌలభ్య హక్కు. Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974) లో అనుమతి లేకుండా కట్టిన భవనాన్ని చట్టబద్ధ అధికారం కింద కూల్చడం, అధికారులు దురుద్దేశంతో వ్యవహరించినా, దావాకు దారి తీయలేదు. లైసెన్స్ రద్దైన తర్వాత ఉండిపోయే లైసెన్సీ అతిక్రమణదారుడు అవుతాడు, కానీ అతనికి "a reasonable time to leave" (వెళ్లిపోవడానికి సహేతుక సమయం) లభిస్తుంది (s. 63). పరిష్కారాలు: నష్టపరిహారం (నష్టం లేకపోతే నామమాత్రం), తప్పుడు ఆక్రమణకు మధ్యంతర లాభాలు (mesne profits) (CPC s. 2(12)), నిషేధాజ్ఞ, స్వాధీనం తిరిగి పొందడం (Specific Relief Act ss. 5, 6), సహేతుక స్వయం సహాయం. పరిమితి: "For compensation for trespass upon immovable property" (స్థిరాస్తిపై అతిక్రమణకు పరిహారం) – "The date of the trespass" (అతిక్రమణ తేదీ) నుండి మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Limitation Act Art. 87); కొనసాగే అతిక్రమణ కొనసాగే ప్రతి క్షణం "a fresh period of limitation" (కొత్త పరిమితి కాలం) ఇస్తుంది (s. 22).
te.meaning: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ – మరొకరి స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న భూమిలోకి చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా ఉద్దేశపూర్వక (స్వచ్ఛంద), ప్రత్యక్ష ప్రవేశం, దానిపై ఉండిపోవడం లేదా దానిలో జోక్యం. స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం – వాస్తవ నష్టం రుజువు చేయకుండానే వాది దావా వేయగల తప్పు; హక్కు ఉల్లంఘనే హాని. లైసెన్స్ – స్వాధీనదారుడి నుండి, లేకపోతే చట్టవిరుద్ధమయ్యే పనిని అతని భూమిపై చేయడానికి అనుమతి; ఇది సౌలభ్య హక్కును గానీ భూమిలో ఆసక్తిని గానీ సృష్టించదు (Easements Act s. 52). లైసెన్స్ ఉన్నంత వరకు లైసెన్సీ అతిక్రమణదారుడు కాదు. మధ్యంతర లాభాలు – తప్పుడు స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి ఆస్తి నుండి వాస్తవంగా పొందిన, లేదా సాధారణ శ్రద్ధతో పొందగలిగిన లాభాలు, వడ్డీతో సహా; అతని స్వంత మెరుగుదలల లాభాలు కాదు (CPC s. 2(12)).
keyPoints: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ = మరొకరి స్వాధీనంలోని భూమిలో ప్రత్యక్ష, సమర్థన లేని జోక్యం. స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం: "though he does no damage at all" (ఏ నష్టం చేయకపోయినా) ( Entick ). స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి దావా వేస్తాడు. రూపాలు: ప్రవేశం, ఉండిపోవడం, వస్తువులు ఉంచడం, నష్టం, గగనతలం, భూగర్భం. లైసెన్స్ (s. 52) రద్దు చేయదగినది (s. 60); వెళ్లడానికి సహేతుక సమయం (s. 63); డబ్బు చెల్లించిన లైసెన్సీని తప్పుగా ఖాళీ చేయిస్తే పరిహారం (s. 64). దురుద్దేశం ఉన్నా చట్టబద్ధ అధికార చర్య సమర్థనే ( Prabhu Dayal ). మధ్యంతర లాభాలు: CPC s. 2(12). పరిమితి: 3 సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 87); కొనసాగే అతిక్రమణ – s. 22.

selfTest.q: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణకు నష్టం అవసరమా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ఎవరు దావా వేయవచ్చు? స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి. భూమిపైకి పొగ వ్యాపించడం అతిక్రమణా? కాదు, అది ఉపద్రవం. "licence" ఎక్కడ నిర్వచించబడింది? Easements Act, 1882, s. 52. లైసెన్స్ ఎప్పుడు రద్దు చేయలేనిది? అమలులో ఉన్న ఆస్తి బదిలీతో కలిసి ఉన్నప్పుడు, లేదా లైసెన్సీ శాశ్వత పని చేసి ఖర్చు పెట్టినప్పుడు (s. 60). s. 63 లైసెన్సీకి ఏమి ఇస్తుంది? వెళ్లిపోవడానికి, వస్తువులు తొలగించడానికి సహేతుక సమయం. Entick లో ప్రతివాదులు ఎందుకు బాధ్యులయ్యారు? వారి warrant చట్టబద్ధం కాదు, కాబట్టి ప్రవేశం చట్టం ద్వారా సమర్థించబడలేదు. Prabhu Dayal లో దురుద్దేశం కూల్చివేతను దావా యోగ్యం చేసిందా? లేదు. మధ్యంతర లాభాలను నిర్వచించండి. తప్పుడు స్వాధీనదారుడు పొందిన లేదా సాధారణ శ్రద్ధతో పొందగలిగిన లాభాలు, వడ్డీతో సహా, అతని మెరుగుదలల లాభాలు తప్ప (CPC s. 2(12)). అతిక్రమణకు పరిహారం పరిమితి ఎంత? అతిక్రమణ తేదీ నుండి మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 87).

hi.inOneMinute: Trespass to land is the direct and unjustified interference with land in the possession of another, for example by entering it, remaining on it, or putting things on it. It is actionable per se : no damage need be proved. In Entick v. Carrington (1765) the court said: "our law holds the property of every man so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all; if he will tread upon his neighbour's ground, he must justify it by law." Elements: (1) the plaintiff is in possession; (2) the defendant directly interferes (entry, remaining, placing objects, damaging); (3) the act is voluntary; (4) there is no lawful justification. Main defences: a licence (permission) of the possessor (Easements Act, 1882, s. 52), authority of law (a valid warrant or statutory power), and an easement. In Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1974) the demolition of a building put up without sanction, under a statutory power, gave no claim, even if the officers acted with malice. A licensee who stays after the licence is revoked becomes a trespasser, but he gets "a reasonable time to leave" (s. 63). Remedies: damages (nominal if no loss), mesne profits for wrongful occupation (CPC s. 2(12)), injunction, recovery of possession (Specific Relief Act ss. 5, 6), and reasonable self-help. Limitation: "For compensation for trespass upon immovable property" – three years from "The date of the trespass" (Limitation Act Art. 87); a continuing trespass gives "a fresh period of limitation" every moment it continues (s. 22).
legalProvision: There is no statutory definition of trespass to land as a tort. The tort is from common law. Related provisions:

Indian Easements Act, 1882 s. 52 – "Where one person grants to another, or to a definite number of other persons, a right to do, or continue to do, in or upon the immovable property of the grantor, something which would, in the absence of such right, be unlawful, and such right does not amount to an easement or an interest in the property, the right is called a license." s. 54 – a licence may be "express or implied from the conduct of the grantor". s. 60 – "A license may be revoked by the grantor, unless— (a) it is coupled with a transfer of property and such transfer is in force; (b) the licensee, acting upon the license, has executed a work of a permanent character and incurred expenses in the execution." s. 61 – revocation "may be express or implied". Illustration (a): A, who allowed B to use a path, "with intent to revoke the license, locks a gate across the path. The license is revoked." s. 63 – on revocation "the licensee is entitled to a reasonable time to leave the property affected thereby and to remove any goods which he has been allowed to place on such property." s. 64 – a licensee for consideration who "without any fault of his own, is evicted by the grantor before he has fully enjoyed" the right "is entitled to recover compensation from the grantor." Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 2(12) – "mesne profits" of property means "those profits which the person in wrongful possession of such property actually received or might with ordinary diligence have received therefrom, together with interest on such profits, but shall not include profits due to improvements made by the person in wrongful possession". Specific Relief Act, 1963 – s. 5 (recovery of immovable property under the CPC); s. 6 (suit within six months by a person "dispossessed without his consent ... otherwise than in due course of law"); ss. 37–40 (injunctions; damages in addition or substitution). Limitation Act, 1963 – Art. 87 (compensation for trespass: three years from the date of the trespass); s. 22 ("In the case of ... a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the ... tort ... continues"); Arts. 64, 65 (possession: twelve years). Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 329(1) – criminal trespass: whoever "enters into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession", or, having lawfully entered, "unlawfully remains there" with such intent. s. 329(2) – house-trespass (entering or remaining in a building used as a human dwelling, place of worship or place for custody of property).
hi.meaning: Trespass to land – the intentional (voluntary) and direct entry upon, remaining upon, or interference with land in the possession of another, without lawful justification. Actionable per se – a wrong for which the plaintiff can sue without proving actual damage; the violation of the right is itself the injury. Licence – permission from the person in possession to do something on his land that would otherwise be unlawful, which does not create an easement or an interest in the land (Easements Act s. 52). A licensee is not a trespasser while the licence lasts. Mesne profits – the profits that a person in wrongful possession actually received, or might with ordinary diligence have received, from the property, with interest, but not profits from his own improvements (CPC s. 2(12)).
keyPoints: Trespass to land = direct, unjustified interference with land in another's possession. Actionable per se: "though he does no damage at all" ( Entick ). The person in possession sues. Forms: entry, remaining, placing things, damaging, airspace and subsoil. Licence (s. 52) is revocable (s. 60); reasonable time to leave (s. 63); compensation for wrongful eviction of a paid licensee (s. 64). Lawful statutory action is a justification even if malicious ( Prabhu Dayal ). Mesne profits: CPC s. 2(12). Limitation: 3 years (Art. 87); continuing trespass – s. 22.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff built 16 shops on old foundations without the notice (s
caseLaws.facts: 178) and sanction (s. 180) required by the U.P. Municipalities Act; after notices, the Town Area Committee demolished them under s. 186. He sued for ₹1,000 damages, alleging malice. Principle: "A legal act, though motivated by malice, will not make the actor liable to pay damages"; demolition of an illegal building by municipal authorities is not "injuria"; "No person has the right to enjoy the fruits of an act which is an offence under law." The suit failed. Why it matters: Lawful statutory authority is a complete justification for interference with land, and malice does not change this.

selfTest.q: Is damage needed for trespass to land?
selfTest.a: No. Who can sue? The person in possession. Is smoke drifting onto land trespass? No, it is nuisance. Where is "licence" defined? Easements Act, 1882, s. 52. When is a licence irrevocable ? When coupled with a transfer of property in force, or when the licensee has executed a permanent work and incurred expenses (s. 60). What does s. 63 give a licensee? A reasonable time to leave and remove his goods. Why were the defendants liable in Entick ? Their warrant was not lawful, so the entry was not justified by law. Did malice make the demolition actionable in Prabhu Dayal ? No. Define mesne profits. Profits the wrongful possessor received or might with ordinary diligence have received, with interest, excluding profits from his improvements (CPC s. 2(12)). What is the limitation for compensation for trespass? Three years from the date of the trespass (Art. 87).

law-of-torts-u3-t9.subtitle: Wrongs to land and what is attached to it: trespass, nuisance, easements and dispossession

en.inOneMinute: Immovable property "shall include land, benefits to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth" (General Clauses Act, 1897, s. 3(26)). The law of torts protects a person's possession and enjoyment of land against interference by others. The main torts affecting immovable property are: Trespass to land – a direct, unjustified entry on, or interference with, land in another's possession. It is actionable without proof of damage. The court in Entick v. Carrington (1765): "our law holds the property of every man so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all". Nuisance – an unlawful, indirect interference with the use or enjoyment of land (smoke, noise, fumes, water), or with a public right. Disturbance of an easement – obstructing a right of way, light, air or support that one owner has over another's land (Easements Act, 1882, s. 33). Dispossession – wrongfully putting a person out of possession; he can recover possession under Specific Relief Act, 1963, ss. 5 and 6. These torts rest on the owner's natural rights in his land, stated in Easements Act s. 7 (for example, that air shall not be unreasonably polluted and that physical comfort shall not be materially interfered with by noise). Remedies: damages , injunction (Specific Relief Act ss. 38(3), 39, 40), recovery of possession (ss. 5, 6), and limited self-help . Limitation: trespass compensation 3 years from the trespass (Limitation Act Art. 87); possession on previous possession 12 years (Art. 64); possession on title 12 years (Art. 65); s. 6 suit 6 months (SRA s. 6(2)(a)).
legalProvision: There is no single code of torts affecting land. The rules come from common law, applied with these statutes:

General Clauses Act, 1897, s. 3(26) – definition of "immovable property" (quoted above). Indian Easements Act, 1882 s. 4 – "An easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own." The benefited land is the "dominant heritage"; the burdened land is the "servient heritage". s. 7 – easements are restrictions of two natural rights of every owner: (a) the "exclusive right ... to enjoy and dispose of" his immovable property; (b) the right to enjoy without disturbance by another "the natural advantages arising from its situation". Illustrations include: (b) "The right of every owner of land that the air passing thereto shall not be unreasonably polluted by other persons"; (c) "The right of every owner of a house that his physical comfort shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration caused by any other person"; (e) the right to "the support naturally rendered by the subjacent and adjacent soil"; (g) the right "to collect and dispose within his own limits of all water under the land which does not pass in a defined channel"; (h) the right to the flow of a natural stream "without interruption and without material alteration". s. 33 – the dominant owner or occupier "may institute a suit for compensation for the disturbance of the easement ... provided that the disturbance has actually caused substantial damage to the plaintiff." s. 34 – removal of support gives a right to compensation only when "substantial damage is actually sustained". s. 35 – injunction to restrain disturbance of an easement, actual or threatened. Specific Relief Act, 1963 s. 5 – "A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908". s. 6(1) – "If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit." s. 6(2) : no suit "(a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government." s. 6(3) : no appeal or review. s. 6(4) : anyone may still sue on title. s. 38(3) – perpetual injunction "When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property", where (b) there is no standard for ascertaining the damage, (c) "compensation in money would not afford adequate relief", or (d) to prevent "a multiplicity of judicial proceedings". s. 39 – mandatory injunction (for example, to remove a structure); s. 40 – damages in addition to, or in substitution for, an injunction. Limitation Act, 1963 – Art. 64 (possession based on previous possession: 12 years from dispossession); Art. 65 (possession based on title: 12 years from when the defendant's possession becomes adverse); Art. 87 ("For compensation for trespass upon immovable property": 3 years from "The date of the trespass"); Art. 89 ("To restrain waste": 3 years from "When the waste begins"). Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 329 – criminal trespass (entry with intent to commit an offence or to "intimidate, insult or annoy"); this is a crime, separate from the tort.
en.meaning: Immovable property – land, benefits to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to such things (General Clauses Act s. 3(26)). Houses, walls, trees and buildings are included. Possession – actual control of land with the intention to hold it. Torts to land protect possession, so even a tenant or a person in possession without title can sue a stranger who disturbs him (see Specific Relief Act s. 6(1): "notwithstanding any other title"). Easement – a right of the owner or occupier of one land (dominant heritage) over another's land (servient heritage) for the beneficial enjoyment of his own land, such as a right of way or of light (Easements Act s. 4). Natural rights – rights that every owner of land has by law without any grant, such as exclusive enjoyment, support from neighbouring soil, freedom from unreasonable pollution of air and water, and freedom from material and unreasonable noise (Easements Act s. 7 and Illustrations). Torts affecting immovable property – civil wrongs that interfere with a person's possession, use or enjoyment of land or of rights connected with land.
keyPoints: Immovable property includes land, benefits from land and things attached to the earth. Torts to land protect possession, enjoyment and easements. Trespass: direct; actionable per se ( Entick ). Nuisance: indirect; damage needed ( St. Helen's ). Easement disturbance: substantial damage needed (s. 33); no self-abatement (s. 36). SRA s. 6: dispossessed person recovers possession within 6 months, regardless of title. Bad motive does not make a lawful act a tort ( Bradford v. Pickles ). Limitation: Art. 87 (trespass, 3 years); Arts. 64, 65 (possession, 12 years).

Why it matters: There is no tort affecting land without infringement of a legal right; damage without legal injury is not actionable.

selfTest.q: Where is "immovable property" defined?
selfTest.a: General Clauses Act, 1897, s. 3(26). Name four torts affecting immovable property. Trespass to land, nuisance, disturbance of easement, dispossession. Is damage needed for trespass to land? No. What must be proved under Easements Act s. 33? Substantial damage. Can a dominant owner pull down an obstruction himself? No (s. 36). Within what time must a s. 6 SRA suit be filed? Six months from dispossession. Is title relevant in a s. 6 suit? No. What did Bradford v. Pickles decide? A lawful act on one's own land is not made unlawful by a malicious motive. Limitation for compensation for trespass? Three years from the trespass (Art. 87). What injury did St. Helen's involve? Material injury to trees and crops by smelting vapours.

te.inOneMinute: స్థిరాస్తి (Immovable property) "shall include land, benefits to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth" (అర్థం: భూమి, భూమి నుండి వచ్చే ప్రయోజనాలు, భూమికి అతికి ఉన్న వస్తువులు, లేదా భూమికి అతికి ఉన్న దేనికైనా శాశ్వతంగా బిగించిన వస్తువులు ఇందులో ఉంటాయి) (General Clauses Act, 1897, s. 3(26)). ఇతరుల జోక్యం నుండి ఒక వ్యక్తి భూమిపై స్వాధీనం (possession) మరియు అనుభవాన్ని టార్ట్‌ల చట్టం రక్షిస్తుంది. స్థిరాస్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే ప్రధాన టార్ట్‌లు: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ (Trespass to land) – మరొకరి స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న భూమిలోకి సమర్థన లేకుండా ప్రత్యక్ష ప్రవేశం లేదా జోక్యం. నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండానే దావా యోగ్యం. Entick v. Carrington (1765) లో కోర్టు: "our law holds the property of every man so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all" (అర్థం: మన చట్టం ప్రతి మనిషి ఆస్తిని ఎంత పవిత్రంగా భావిస్తుందంటే, అనుమతి లేకుండా ఎవరూ పొరుగువాడి స్థలంలో అడుగు పెట్టకూడదు; పెడితే, ఏ నష్టం చేయకపోయినా అతను అతిక్రమణదారుడే). ఉపద్రవం (Nuisance) – భూమి వినియోగం లేదా అనుభవంలో (పొగ, శబ్దం, వాయువులు, నీరు), లేదా ప్రజా హక్కులో చట్టవిరుద్ధమైన పరోక్ష జోక్యం. సౌలభ్య హక్కు (Easement) భంగం – ఒక యజమానికి మరొకరి భూమిపై ఉన్న దారి, వెలుతురు, గాలి లేదా ఆధారం హక్కును అడ్డుకోవడం (Easements Act, 1882, s. 33). స్వాధీనం నుండి తొలగింపు ( Dispossession ) – ఒక వ్యక్తిని తప్పుగా స్వాధీనం నుండి బయటకు నెట్టడం; అతను Specific Relief Act, 1963, ss. 5, 6 కింద స్వాధీనం తిరిగి పొందవచ్చు. ఈ టార్ట్‌లు యజమానికి తన భూమిపై ఉన్న సహజ హక్కుల (natural rights) పై ఆధారపడతాయి; అవి Easements Act s. 7 లో ఉన్నాయి (ఉదా: గాలి అసమంజసంగా కలుషితం కాకూడదు; శబ్దంతో శారీరక సౌఖ్యానికి గణనీయంగా భంగం కలగకూడదు). పరిష్కారాలు: నష్టపరిహారం , నిషేధాజ్ఞ (injunction) (Specific Relief Act ss. 38(3), 39, 40), స్వాధీనం తిరిగి పొందడం (ss. 5, 6), పరిమితమైన స్వయం సహాయం (self-help) . పరిమితి: అతిక్రమణ పరిహారానికి అతిక్రమణ నుండి 3 సంవత్సరాలు (Limitation Act Art. 87); పూర్వ స్వాధీనం ఆధారంగా స్వాధీనానికి 12 సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 64); హక్కు (title) ఆధారంగా స్వాధీనానికి 12 సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 65); s. 6 దావాకు 6 నెలలు (SRA s. 6(2)(a)).
te.meaning: స్థిరాస్తి – భూమి, భూమి నుండి వచ్చే ప్రయోజనాలు, భూమికి అతికి ఉన్న లేదా అటువంటి వాటికి శాశ్వతంగా బిగించిన వస్తువులు (General Clauses Act s. 3(26)). ఇళ్లు, గోడలు, చెట్లు, భవనాలు ఇందులో ఉంటాయి. స్వాధీనం – భూమిని తన వద్ద ఉంచుకునే ఉద్దేశంతో దానిపై వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ. భూమికి సంబంధించిన టార్ట్‌లు స్వాధీనాన్ని రక్షిస్తాయి; కాబట్టి అద్దెదారు లేదా హక్కు లేకుండా స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తి కూడా తనను భంగపరిచిన అపరిచితుడిపై దావా వేయవచ్చు (Specific Relief Act s. 6(1): "notwithstanding any other title" (మరే హక్కు ఉన్నప్పటికీ) చూడండి). సౌలభ్య హక్కు – ఒక భూమి (ప్రబల భూమి) యజమాని లేదా ఆక్రమణదారుకు, తన భూమి ప్రయోజనకర అనుభవం కోసం మరొకరి భూమి (సేవక భూమి) పై ఉన్న హక్కు; ఉదా: దారి హక్కు, వెలుతురు హక్కు (Easements Act s. 4). సహజ హక్కులు – ఏ మంజూరు లేకుండానే చట్టం ద్వారా ప్రతి భూయజమానికి ఉన్న హక్కులు; ఉదా: ప్రత్యేక అనుభవం, పొరుగు నేల నుండి ఆధారం, గాలి, నీరు అసమంజసంగా కలుషితం కాకుండా ఉండటం, గణనీయమైన, అసమంజసమైన శబ్దం నుండి రక్షణ (Easements Act s. 7 మరియు ఉదాహరణలు). స్థిరాస్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు – ఒక వ్యక్తి భూమి స్వాధీనం, వినియోగం లేదా అనుభవంలో, లేదా భూమికి సంబంధించిన హక్కులలో జోక్యం చేసుకునే పౌర తప్పులు.
keyPoints: స్థిరాస్తిలో భూమి, భూమి నుండి ప్రయోజనాలు, భూమికి అతికిన వస్తువులు ఉంటాయి. భూమికి సంబంధించిన టార్ట్‌లు స్వాధీనం, అనుభవం, సౌలభ్య హక్కులను రక్షిస్తాయి. అతిక్రమణ: ప్రత్యక్షం; స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం ( Entick ). ఉపద్రవం: పరోక్షం; నష్టం అవసరం ( St. Helen's ). సౌలభ్య హక్కు భంగం: గణనీయమైన నష్టం అవసరం (s. 33); స్వయంగా తొలగించకూడదు (s. 36). SRA s. 6: తొలగించబడిన వ్యక్తి హక్కుతో సంబంధం లేకుండా 6 నెలల్లో స్వాధీనం తిరిగి పొందుతాడు. దురుద్దేశం చట్టబద్ధ చర్యను టార్ట్‌గా మార్చదు ( Bradford v. Pickles ). పరిమితి: Art. 87 (అతిక్రమణ, 3 సంవత్సరాలు); Arts. 64, 65 (స్వాధీనం, 12 సంవత్సరాలు).

selfTest.q: "immovable property" ఎక్కడ నిర్వచించబడింది?
selfTest.a: General Clauses Act, 1897, s. 3(26). స్థిరాస్తిని ప్రభావితం చేసే నాలుగు టార్ట్‌లు చెప్పండి. భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ, ఉపద్రవం, సౌలభ్య హక్కు భంగం, స్వాధీనం నుండి తొలగింపు. భూమిపై అతిక్రమణకు నష్టం అవసరమా? లేదు. Easements Act s. 33 కింద ఏమి రుజువు చేయాలి? గణనీయమైన నష్టం. ప్రబల యజమాని అడ్డంకిని తానే కూల్చగలడా? లేదు (s. 36). SRA s. 6 దావా ఎంత కాలంలో వేయాలి? తొలగింపు నుండి ఆరు నెలల్లో. s. 6 దావాలో హక్కు (title) ప్రస్తుతమా? కాదు. Bradford v. Pickles ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? తన భూమిపై చట్టబద్ధ చర్య దురుద్దేశం వల్ల చట్టవిరుద్ధం కాదు. అతిక్రమణకు పరిహారం పరిమితి ఎంత? అతిక్రమణ నుండి మూడు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 87). St. Helen's లో ఏ హాని ఉంది? కరిగించే కర్మాగార ఆవిరులతో చెట్లు, పంటలకు గణనీయమైన హాని.

hi.inOneMinute: Immovable property "shall include land, benefits to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth, or permanently fastened to anything attached to the earth" (General Clauses Act, 1897, s. 3(26)). The law of torts protects a person's possession and enjoyment of land against interference by others. The main torts affecting immovable property are: Trespass to land – a direct, unjustified entry on, or interference with, land in another's possession. It is actionable without proof of damage. The court in Entick v. Carrington (1765): "our law holds the property of every man so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all". Nuisance – an unlawful, indirect interference with the use or enjoyment of land (smoke, noise, fumes, water), or with a public right. Disturbance of an easement – obstructing a right of way, light, air or support that one owner has over another's land (Easements Act, 1882, s. 33). Dispossession – wrongfully putting a person out of possession; he can recover possession under Specific Relief Act, 1963, ss. 5 and 6. These torts rest on the owner's natural rights in his land, stated in Easements Act s. 7 (for example, that air shall not be unreasonably polluted and that physical comfort shall not be materially interfered with by noise). Remedies: damages , injunction (Specific Relief Act ss. 38(3), 39, 40), recovery of possession (ss. 5, 6), and limited self-help . Limitation: trespass compensation 3 years from the trespass (Limitation Act Art. 87); possession on previous possession 12 years (Art. 64); possession on title 12 years (Art. 65); s. 6 suit 6 months (SRA s. 6(2)(a)).
legalProvision: There is no single code of torts affecting land. The rules come from common law, applied with these statutes:

General Clauses Act, 1897, s. 3(26) – definition of "immovable property" (quoted above). Indian Easements Act, 1882 s. 4 – "An easement is a right which the owner or occupier of certain land possesses, as such, for the beneficial enjoyment of that land, to do and continue to do something, or to prevent and continue to prevent something being done, in or upon, or in respect of, certain other land not his own." The benefited land is the "dominant heritage"; the burdened land is the "servient heritage". s. 7 – easements are restrictions of two natural rights of every owner: (a) the "exclusive right ... to enjoy and dispose of" his immovable property; (b) the right to enjoy without disturbance by another "the natural advantages arising from its situation". Illustrations include: (b) "The right of every owner of land that the air passing thereto shall not be unreasonably polluted by other persons"; (c) "The right of every owner of a house that his physical comfort shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration caused by any other person"; (e) the right to "the support naturally rendered by the subjacent and adjacent soil"; (g) the right "to collect and dispose within his own limits of all water under the land which does not pass in a defined channel"; (h) the right to the flow of a natural stream "without interruption and without material alteration". s. 33 – the dominant owner or occupier "may institute a suit for compensation for the disturbance of the easement ... provided that the disturbance has actually caused substantial damage to the plaintiff." s. 34 – removal of support gives a right to compensation only when "substantial damage is actually sustained". s. 35 – injunction to restrain disturbance of an easement, actual or threatened. Specific Relief Act, 1963 s. 5 – "A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908". s. 6(1) – "If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit." s. 6(2) : no suit "(a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government." s. 6(3) : no appeal or review. s. 6(4) : anyone may still sue on title. s. 38(3) – perpetual injunction "When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property", where (b) there is no standard for ascertaining the damage, (c) "compensation in money would not afford adequate relief", or (d) to prevent "a multiplicity of judicial proceedings". s. 39 – mandatory injunction (for example, to remove a structure); s. 40 – damages in addition to, or in substitution for, an injunction. Limitation Act, 1963 – Art. 64 (possession based on previous possession: 12 years from dispossession); Art. 65 (possession based on title: 12 years from when the defendant's possession becomes adverse); Art. 87 ("For compensation for trespass upon immovable property": 3 years from "The date of the trespass"); Art. 89 ("To restrain waste": 3 years from "When the waste begins"). Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 329 – criminal trespass (entry with intent to commit an offence or to "intimidate, insult or annoy"); this is a crime, separate from the tort.
hi.meaning: Immovable property – land, benefits to arise out of land, and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to such things (General Clauses Act s. 3(26)). Houses, walls, trees and buildings are included. Possession – actual control of land with the intention to hold it. Torts to land protect possession, so even a tenant or a person in possession without title can sue a stranger who disturbs him (see Specific Relief Act s. 6(1): "notwithstanding any other title"). Easement – a right of the owner or occupier of one land (dominant heritage) over another's land (servient heritage) for the beneficial enjoyment of his own land, such as a right of way or of light (Easements Act s. 4). Natural rights – rights that every owner of land has by law without any grant, such as exclusive enjoyment, support from neighbouring soil, freedom from unreasonable pollution of air and water, and freedom from material and unreasonable noise (Easements Act s. 7 and Illustrations). Torts affecting immovable property – civil wrongs that interfere with a person's possession, use or enjoyment of land or of rights connected with land.
keyPoints: Immovable property includes land, benefits from land and things attached to the earth. Torts to land protect possession, enjoyment and easements. Trespass: direct; actionable per se ( Entick ). Nuisance: indirect; damage needed ( St. Helen's ). Easement disturbance: substantial damage needed (s. 33); no self-abatement (s. 36). SRA s. 6: dispossessed person recovers possession within 6 months, regardless of title. Bad motive does not make a lawful act a tort ( Bradford v. Pickles ). Limitation: Art. 87 (trespass, 3 years); Arts. 64, 65 (possession, 12 years).
