law-of-torts-u4-t3.subtitle: The tort of publishing a false statement that lowers a person in the estimation of right-thinking people

en.inOneMinute: Defamation is the publication of a false imputation about a person that harms his reputation, that is, lowers him in the estimation of others. As Shreya Singhal (2015) put it, "for something to be defamatory, injury to reputation is a basic ingredient". It is both a tort (the victim sues for damages or an injunction) and a crime (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 ("BNS"), s. 356). There is no separate civil statute; civil courts apply the common law, and the BNS definition and Exceptions are a useful guide (standard doctrine). Two forms: Libel – defamation in a permanent form (writing, print, picture, video, online post). Actionable without proof of special damage. Slander – defamation in a passing form (spoken words, gestures). Usually needs proof of special damage, unless the words are "actionable in themselves" (Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 76). The plaintiff must prove: (1) a defamatory statement, (2) that refers to him, (3) published to at least one person other than him (standard doctrine; BNS s. 356(1) uses "makes or publishes ... any imputation concerning any person"). Main defences: truth (justification) , fair comment on public matters, privilege (absolute or qualified), and consent. Reputation is part of the right to life under Article 21 ( Puttaswamy , 2017), and defamation is a ground on which free speech can be restricted (Article 19(2)). Time limit: one year (Limitation Act Arts. 75, 76).
legalProvision: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 356

s. 356(1) – "Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes in any manner, any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person." Explanation 1 – "It may amount to defamation to impute anything to a deceased person, if the imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living, and is intended to be hurtful to the feelings of his family or other near relatives." Explanation 2 – "It may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company or an association or collection of persons as such." Explanation 3 – "An imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically, may amount to defamation." Explanation 4 – "No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or indirectly, in the estimation of others, lowers the moral or intellectual character of that person, or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person, or causes it to be believed that the body of that person is in a loathsome state, or in a state generally considered as disgraceful." Illustration (a) – A says "Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch", "intending to cause it to be believed that Z did steal B's watch. This is defamation, unless it falls within one of the exceptions." The ten Exceptions (in short): Truth, "if it be for the public good that the imputation should be made or published". Good-faith opinion on "the conduct of a public servant in the discharge of his public functions". Good-faith opinion on the conduct of any person "touching any public question". Publishing a "substantially true report of the proceedings of a Court". Good-faith opinion on the merits of a decided case, or the conduct of a party, witness or agent in it. Good-faith opinion on "the merits of any performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public" (a book, a public speech, a stage performance). Good-faith censure by a person having lawful authority over another (judge over witness, parent over child, master over servant). Good-faith accusation to a person having lawful authority over the accused (complaint to a Magistrate, to an employer). Imputation made in good faith "for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good". A caution conveyed in good faith for the good of the person cautioned or for the public good. s. 356(2)–(4) – punishment: "simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service"; the same limit (without community service) for printing or selling defamatory matter knowingly.

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 222(1) – "No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence". For the President, Vice-President, Governors, Ministers and public servants in respect of public functions, a Court of Session may take cognizance on a written complaint by the Public Prosecutor, with sanction, within six months (s. 222(2), (4), (5)).
Constitution of India

Article 19(2) – free speech may be reasonably restricted "in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence". Article 105(2) – "No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof, and no person shall be so liable in respect of the publication by or under the authority of either House of Parliament of any report, paper, votes or proceedings." Article 194(2) gives the same protection in State Legislatures. Article 361A(1) – "No person shall be liable to any proceedings, civil or criminal, in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly ... unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice". It does not cover a "secret sitting" (proviso) and extends to broadcasts (cl. (2)).
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule

Art. 75 – "For compensation for libel" – one year – "When the libel is published." Art. 76 – "For compensation for slander" – one year – "When the words are spoken, or, if the words are not actionable in themselves, when the special damage complained of results."
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 19, Illustration (b) – "A, residing in Delhi, publishes in Calcutta statements defamatory of B. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi."
Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(1) – "a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication."

Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall , 2026) – all rights of action survive to and against executors or administrators "except causes of action for defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860) or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party".

Information Technology Act, 2000, s. 79(1) – "an intermediary shall not be liable for any third party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by him", subject to conditions; the protection is lost if, "upon receiving actual knowledge, or on being notified by the appropriate Government", it "fails to expeditiously remove or disable access" (s. 79(3)(b)).
en.meaning: Defamation – the publication of a statement about a person, without lawful justification, which tends to lower him in the estimation of right-thinking members of society, or makes them shun or avoid him (standard common law meaning). BNS s. 356, Explanation 4, lists the same harms: lowering a person's moral or intellectual character, his character as to caste or calling, his credit, or suggesting a loathsome or disgraceful bodily state. Reputation – the opinion that others hold of a person. It is different from self-esteem: "the right to honor relates to self-esteem and self-worth, while reputation refers to the opinion that others have of a person" (as quoted in Puttaswamy , Chandrachud J.). Libel – defamation in a permanent form. Slander – defamation in a transient form. Innuendo – a hidden or secondary meaning in words that look innocent, which people who know the extra facts would understand as defamatory. BNS Illustration (a) ("Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch") is an example. Privilege – an occasion on which the law allows a person to make a statement even if it is defamatory: absolute (no action at all, even if false and malicious) or qualified (protected unless made with malice ).
keyPoints: Injury to reputation is the core of defamation. Elements: defamatory statement, reference to plaintiff, publication to a third person. Libel = permanent, actionable per se; slander = transient, usually needs special damage. Truth is a full defence in tort; in crime it must also be for the public good. Fair comment protects honest opinion on public matters. Absolute privilege: Parliament, Legislatures (Arts. 105(2), 194(2)), courts. Qualified privilege is lost if malice is proved. Reputation is part of Article 21. Limitation: one year. A defamation action does not survive death (ISA s. 306).

caseLaws.facts: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1; AIR 2015 SC 1523 (24 Mar 2015; J. Chelameswar and R.F. Nariman JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Section 66A of the IT Act, which punished online messages that were "grossly offensive" or ca
caseLaws.facts: The Court examined whether it could be saved under any Article 19(2) ground, including defamation. Principle: "for something to be defamatory, injury to reputation is a basic ingredient. Section 66A does not concern itself with injury to reputation"; and s. 79(3)(b) was read down so that an intermediary must act on "actual knowledge that a court order has been passed". Why it matters: It fixes injury to reputation as the core of defamation and sets the limit of platform liability for online defamation.
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (24 Aug 2017; nine-judge bench; Chandrachud J.'s opinion)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A challenge to the Aadhaar scheme led to a reference on whether privacy is a fundamental righ
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Among the rights "held to flow out of Article 21", the opinion lists "(xiv) Right to reputation"; it also quotes that "reputation refers to the opinion that others have of a person". Why it matters: The interest that the tort of defamation protects is a constitutional right.
Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (3 Jan 2023; Constitution Bench; V. Ramasubramanian J. for himself, S. Abdul Nazeer, B.R. Gavai and A.S. Bopanna JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A Minister called a gang-rape incident a "political conspiracy"; the Court was asked whether
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court described R. Rajagopal as "reading down the restrictions (in the form of defamation) ... in its application to public officials and public figures in larger public interest", and recorded that in Subramanian Swamy the argument that free speech "was a higher right than the right to reputation under Article 21 was rejected". Why it matters: It summarises how Indian courts balance free speech and reputation, especially for public figures.
Melepurath Sankunni Ezhuthassan v. Thekittil Geopalankutty Nair (1986) 1 SCC 118; AIR 1986 SC 411 (as quoted in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy , 2026 INSC 443, 4 May 2026)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A plaintiff's defamation suit was dismissed; he appealed and died while the appeal was pendin
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "this right does not survive his death, his legal representative has no right to be brought on the record"; but where the suit "has resulted in a decree in favour of the plaintiff ... the cause of action has merged in the decree and the decretal debt forms part of his estate". Why it matters: A defamation action is personal and dies with the person, unless a decree has already been obtained.
West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray [2006] Supp. 9 SCR (24 Nov 2006; Arijit Pasayat and Lokeshwar Singh Panta JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An engineer whose suspension was quashed sued the Board; the trial court awarded ₹50,000 for
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The awards were set aside because the averments were "extremely vague and lacking in details"; the Court noted that "to rebut a plea of privilage in defamation, malice in fact has to be proved". Why it matters: Damages for loss of reputation need proper pleading and proof, and malice is what defeats a privileged occasion.

selfTest.q: What is the basic ingredient of defamation according to Shreya Singhal?
selfTest.a: Injury to reputation. Name the three elements of defamation. Defamatory statement, reference to the plaintiff, publication. Which form needs proof of special damage? Slander (usually). What is the limitation for a libel suit? One year from publication (Art. 75). Is truth alone a defence in a civil suit? Yes (standard doctrine); in the crime it must also be for the public good. Which Articles give absolute privilege to legislators? Articles 105(2) and 194(2). What defeats qualified privilege? Malice. Can a company be defamed? Yes (BNS Explanation 2). Does a defamation suit survive the plaintiff's death? No, unless a decree has already been passed in his favour. When does a platform lose IT Act s. 79 protection? When it fails to remove material after actual knowledge of a court order (or government notification ). Where can a suit be filed if the defendant lives in Delhi and published in Calcutta? Either place (CPC s. 19, Ill. (b)). Which Article protects true newspaper reports of legislative proceedings? Article 361A.

te.inOneMinute: పరువు నష్టం అంటే ఒక వ్యక్తి గురించి అబద్ధపు ఆరోపణను ప్రచురించి అతని ప్రతిష్ఠను దెబ్బతీయడం, అంటే ఇతరుల దృష్టిలో అతన్ని తక్కువ చేయడం. Shreya Singhal (2015) చెప్పినట్లు, "for something to be defamatory, injury to reputation is a basic ingredient" (అర్థం: ఏదైనా పరువు నష్టం కావాలంటే ప్రతిష్ఠకు హాని ప్రాథమిక అంశం). ఇది టార్ట్ కూడా (బాధితుడు నష్టపరిహారం లేదా నిషేధాజ్ఞ కోసం దావా వేస్తాడు), నేరం కూడా (భారతీయ న్యాయ సంహిత, 2023 ("BNS"), s. 356). ప్రత్యేక సివిల్ చట్టం లేదు; సివిల్ కోర్టులు కామన్ లా వర్తింపజేస్తాయి, BNS నిర్వచనం, మినహాయింపులు ఉపయోగకర మార్గదర్శి (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం). రెండు రూపాలు: లిఖిత పరువు నష్టం (Libel) – శాశ్వత రూపంలో (రాత, ముద్రణ, చిత్రం, వీడియో, ఆన్‌లైన్ పోస్ట్). ప్రత్యేక నష్టం నిరూపించకుండానే దావా వేయవచ్చు. మౌఖిక పరువు నష్టం (Slander) – తాత్కాలిక రూపంలో (మాటలు, సైగలు). సాధారణంగా ప్రత్యేక నష్టం నిరూపించాలి, మాటలు "actionable in themselves" (అర్థం: స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం) అయితే తప్ప (పరిమితి చట్టం, 1963, Art. 76). వాది నిరూపించాలి: (1) పరువు నష్టం కలిగించే ప్రకటన, (2) అది అతన్నే సూచిస్తుంది, (3) అతను కాకుండా కనీసం ఒక వ్యక్తికి ప్రచురించబడింది (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం; BNS s. 356(1) "makes or publishes ... any imputation concerning any person" (అర్థం: ఏ వ్యక్తి గురించైనా ఆరోపణ చేయడం లేదా ప్రచురించడం) అని వాడుతుంది). ప్రధాన రక్షణలు: సత్యం (సమర్థన) , ప్రజా విషయాలపై న్యాయమైన వ్యాఖ్య , విశేషాధికారం (సంపూర్ణ లేదా పరిమిత), సమ్మతి. ప్రతిష్ఠ ఆర్టికల్ 21 కింద జీవించే హక్కులో భాగం ( Puttaswamy , 2017); పరువు నష్టం వాక్ స్వాతంత్ర్యాన్ని పరిమితం చేయగల ఒక ఆధారం (ఆర్టికల్ 19(2)). కాల పరిమితి: ఒక సంవత్సరం (పరిమితి చట్టం Arts. 75, 76).
te.meaning: పరువు నష్టం – చట్టబద్ధ సమర్థన లేకుండా, ఒక వ్యక్తిని సమాజంలోని సరైన ఆలోచనాపరుల దృష్టిలో తక్కువ చేసే, లేదా వారు అతన్ని దూరంగా ఉంచేలా చేసే ప్రకటనను ప్రచురించడం (ప్రామాణిక కామన్ లా అర్థం). BNS s. 356, Explanation 4 అవే హానులను చెబుతుంది: నైతిక లేదా మేధో స్వభావం, కులం లేదా వృత్తి విషయంలో స్వభావం, పరపతి తగ్గించడం, లేదా అసహ్యకర లేదా అవమానకర శారీరక స్థితిని సూచించడం. ప్రతిష్ఠ – ఇతరులు ఒక వ్యక్తి గురించి కలిగి ఉన్న అభిప్రాయం. ఇది ఆత్మగౌరవం కంటే భిన్నం: "the right to honor relates to self-esteem and self-worth, while reputation refers to the opinion that others have of a person" (అర్థం: గౌరవ హక్కు ఆత్మగౌరవానికి, స్వీయ విలువకు సంబంధించినది; ప్రతిష్ఠ అంటే ఇతరులకు ఆ వ్యక్తిపై ఉన్న అభిప్రాయం) ( Puttaswamy లో Chandrachud J. ఉటంకించినట్లు). లిఖిత పరువు నష్టం (Libel) – శాశ్వత రూపంలో పరువు నష్టం. మౌఖిక పరువు నష్టం (Slander) – తాత్కాలిక రూపంలో పరువు నష్టం. గూఢార్థం (Innuendo) – నిర్దోషంగా కనిపించే మాటల్లో దాగి ఉన్న రెండో అర్థం; అదనపు వాస్తవాలు తెలిసినవారు దాన్ని పరువు నష్టంగా అర్థం చేసుకుంటారు. BNS Illustration (a) ("Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch") ఒక ఉదాహరణ. విశేషాధికారం (Privilege) – ప్రకటన పరువు నష్టం కలిగించేదైనా చేయడానికి చట్టం అనుమతించే సందర్భం: సంపూర్ణ (అబద్ధమైనా, దురుద్దేశంతో చేసినా దావా లేదు) లేదా పరిమిత (దురుద్దేశంతో చేయకపోతే రక్షణ).
keyPoints: ప్రతిష్ఠకు హాని పరువు నష్టం కేంద్రం. అంశాలు: పరువు నష్టకర ప్రకటన, వాదిని సూచించడం, మూడో వ్యక్తికి ప్రచురణ. లిఖిత = శాశ్వతం, స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం; మౌఖిక = తాత్కాలికం, సాధారణంగా ప్రత్యేక నష్టం అవసరం. టార్ట్‌లో సత్యం పూర్తి రక్షణ; నేరంలో ప్రజా శ్రేయస్సు కోసం కూడా కావాలి. న్యాయమైన వ్యాఖ్య ప్రజా విషయాలపై నిజాయితీ అభిప్రాయాన్ని కాపాడుతుంది. సంపూర్ణ విశేషాధికారం: పార్లమెంటు, శాసనసభలు (Arts. 105(2), 194(2)), కోర్టులు. దురుద్దేశం నిరూపిస్తే పరిమిత విశేషాధికారం పోతుంది. ప్రతిష్ఠ ఆర్టికల్ 21 లో భాగం. పరిమితి: ఒక సంవత్సరం. పరువు నష్ట దావా మరణం తర్వాత కొనసాగదు (ISA s. 306).

selfTest.q: Shreya Singhal ప్రకారం పరువు నష్టం ప్రాథమిక అంశం ఏది?
selfTest.a: ప్రతిష్ఠకు హాని. పరువు నష్టం మూడు అంశాలు చెప్పండి. పరువు నష్టకర ప్రకటన, వాదిని సూచించడం, ప్రచురణ. ఏ రూపానికి ప్రత్యేక నష్టం నిరూపణ అవసరం? మౌఖిక (సాధారణంగా). లిఖిత పరువు నష్ట దావాకు పరిమితి ఎంత? ప్రచురణ నుంచి ఒక సంవత్సరం (Art. 75). సివిల్ దావాలో సత్యం ఒక్కటే రక్షణా? అవును (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం); నేరంలో ప్రజా శ్రేయస్సు కోసం కూడా కావాలి. శాసనసభ్యులకు సంపూర్ణ విశేషాధికారం ఇచ్చే ఆర్టికల్స్ ఏవి? ఆర్టికల్స్ 105(2), 194(2). పరిమిత విశేషాధికారాన్ని ఏది ఓడిస్తుంది? దురుద్దేశం. కంపెనీ పరువు తీయవచ్చా? అవును (BNS Explanation 2). వాది మరణం తర్వాత పరువు నష్ట దావా కొనసాగుతుందా? లేదు, అతనికి అనుకూల డిక్రీ ఇప్పటికే వచ్చి ఉంటే తప్ప. ప్లాట్‌ఫారం IT Act s. 79 రక్షణ ఎప్పుడు కోల్పోతుంది? కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు (లేదా ప్రభుత్వ నోటిఫికేషన్) గురించి వాస్తవ జ్ఞానం వచ్చిన తర్వాత విషయాన్ని తొలగించకపోతే. ప్రతివాది ఢిల్లీలో నివసిస్తూ కలకత్తాలో ప్రచురిస్తే దావా ఎక్కడ వేయవచ్చు? ఏ చోటైనా (CPC s. 19, Ill. (b)). శాసనసభ విచారణల నిజమైన వార్తాపత్రిక నివేదికలను ఏ ఆర్టికల్ కాపాడుతుంది? ఆర్టికల్ 361A.

hi.inOneMinute: Defamation is the publication of a false imputation about a person that harms his reputation, that is, lowers him in the estimation of others. As Shreya Singhal (2015) put it, "for something to be defamatory, injury to reputation is a basic ingredient". It is both a tort (the victim sues for damages or an injunction) and a crime (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 ("BNS"), s. 356). There is no separate civil statute; civil courts apply the common law, and the BNS definition and Exceptions are a useful guide (standard doctrine). Two forms: Libel – defamation in a permanent form (writing, print, picture, video, online post). Actionable without proof of special damage. Slander – defamation in a passing form (spoken words, gestures). Usually needs proof of special damage, unless the words are "actionable in themselves" (Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 76). The plaintiff must prove: (1) a defamatory statement, (2) that refers to him, (3) published to at least one person other than him (standard doctrine; BNS s. 356(1) uses "makes or publishes ... any imputation concerning any person"). Main defences: truth (justification) , fair comment on public matters, privilege (absolute or qualified), and consent. Reputation is part of the right to life under Article 21 ( Puttaswamy , 2017), and defamation is a ground on which free speech can be restricted (Article 19(2)). Time limit: one year (Limitation Act Arts. 75, 76).
legalProvision: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 356

s. 356(1) – "Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes in any manner, any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person." Explanation 1 – "It may amount to defamation to impute anything to a deceased person, if the imputation would harm the reputation of that person if living, and is intended to be hurtful to the feelings of his family or other near relatives." Explanation 2 – "It may amount to defamation to make an imputation concerning a company or an association or collection of persons as such." Explanation 3 – "An imputation in the form of an alternative or expressed ironically, may amount to defamation." Explanation 4 – "No imputation is said to harm a person's reputation, unless that imputation directly or indirectly, in the estimation of others, lowers the moral or intellectual character of that person, or lowers the character of that person in respect of his caste or of his calling, or lowers the credit of that person, or causes it to be believed that the body of that person is in a loathsome state, or in a state generally considered as disgraceful." Illustration (a) – A says "Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch", "intending to cause it to be believed that Z did steal B's watch. This is defamation, unless it falls within one of the exceptions." The ten Exceptions (in short): Truth, "if it be for the public good that the imputation should be made or published". Good-faith opinion on "the conduct of a public servant in the discharge of his public functions". Good-faith opinion on the conduct of any person "touching any public question". Publishing a "substantially true report of the proceedings of a Court". Good-faith opinion on the merits of a decided case, or the conduct of a party, witness or agent in it. Good-faith opinion on "the merits of any performance which its author has submitted to the judgment of the public" (a book, a public speech, a stage performance). Good-faith censure by a person having lawful authority over another (judge over witness, parent over child, master over servant). Good-faith accusation to a person having lawful authority over the accused (complaint to a Magistrate, to an employer). Imputation made in good faith "for the protection of the interests of the person making it, or of any other person, or for the public good". A caution conveyed in good faith for the good of the person cautioned or for the public good. s. 356(2)–(4) – punishment: "simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both, or with community service"; the same limit (without community service) for printing or selling defamatory matter knowingly.

Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, s. 222(1) – "No Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 except upon a complaint made by some person aggrieved by the offence". For the President, Vice-President, Governors, Ministers and public servants in respect of public functions, a Court of Session may take cognizance on a written complaint by the Public Prosecutor, with sanction, within six months (s. 222(2), (4), (5)).
Constitution of India

Article 19(2) – free speech may be reasonably restricted "in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence". Article 105(2) – "No member of Parliament shall be liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in Parliament or any committee thereof, and no person shall be so liable in respect of the publication by or under the authority of either House of Parliament of any report, paper, votes or proceedings." Article 194(2) gives the same protection in State Legislatures. Article 361A(1) – "No person shall be liable to any proceedings, civil or criminal, in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly ... unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice". It does not cover a "secret sitting" (proviso) and extends to broadcasts (cl. (2)).
Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule

Art. 75 – "For compensation for libel" – one year – "When the libel is published." Art. 76 – "For compensation for slander" – one year – "When the words are spoken, or, if the words are not actionable in themselves, when the special damage complained of results."
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, s. 19, Illustration (b) – "A, residing in Delhi, publishes in Calcutta statements defamatory of B. B may sue A either in Calcutta or in Delhi."
Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(1) – "a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication."

Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall , 2026) – all rights of action survive to and against executors or administrators "except causes of action for defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860) or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party".

Information Technology Act, 2000, s. 79(1) – "an intermediary shall not be liable for any third party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by him", subject to conditions; the protection is lost if, "upon receiving actual knowledge, or on being notified by the appropriate Government", it "fails to expeditiously remove or disable access" (s. 79(3)(b)).
hi.meaning: Defamation – the publication of a statement about a person, without lawful justification, which tends to lower him in the estimation of right-thinking members of society, or makes them shun or avoid him (standard common law meaning). BNS s. 356, Explanation 4, lists the same harms: lowering a person's moral or intellectual character, his character as to caste or calling, his credit, or suggesting a loathsome or disgraceful bodily state. Reputation – the opinion that others hold of a person. It is different from self-esteem: "the right to honor relates to self-esteem and self-worth, while reputation refers to the opinion that others have of a person" (as quoted in Puttaswamy , Chandrachud J.). Libel – defamation in a permanent form. Slander – defamation in a transient form. Innuendo – a hidden or secondary meaning in words that look innocent, which people who know the extra facts would understand as defamatory. BNS Illustration (a) ("Z is an honest man; he never stole B's watch") is an example. Privilege – an occasion on which the law allows a person to make a statement even if it is defamatory: absolute (no action at all, even if false and malicious) or qualified (protected unless made with malice ).
keyPoints: Injury to reputation is the core of defamation. Elements: defamatory statement, reference to plaintiff, publication to a third person. Libel = permanent, actionable per se; slander = transient, usually needs special damage. Truth is a full defence in tort; in crime it must also be for the public good. Fair comment protects honest opinion on public matters. Absolute privilege: Parliament, Legislatures (Arts. 105(2), 194(2)), courts. Qualified privilege is lost if malice is proved. Reputation is part of Article 21. Limitation: one year. A defamation action does not survive death (ISA s. 306).

caseLaws.facts: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1; AIR 2015 SC 1523 (24 Mar 2015; J. Chelameswar and R.F. Nariman JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Section 66A of the IT Act, which punished online messages that were "grossly offensive" or ca
caseLaws.facts: The Court examined whether it could be saved under any Article 19(2) ground, including defamation. Principle: "for something to be defamatory, injury to reputation is a basic ingredient. Section 66A does not concern itself with injury to reputation"; and s. 79(3)(b) was read down so that an intermediary must act on "actual knowledge that a court order has been passed". Why it matters: It fixes injury to reputation as the core of defamation and sets the limit of platform liability for online defamation.
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (24 Aug 2017; nine-judge bench; Chandrachud J.'s opinion)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A challenge to the Aadhaar scheme led to a reference on whether privacy is a fundamental righ
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Among the rights "held to flow out of Article 21", the opinion lists "(xiv) Right to reputation"; it also quotes that "reputation refers to the opinion that others have of a person". Why it matters: The interest that the tort of defamation protects is a constitutional right.
Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh (3 Jan 2023; Constitution Bench; V. Ramasubramanian J. for himself, S. Abdul Nazeer, B.R. Gavai and A.S. Bopanna JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A Minister called a gang-rape incident a "political conspiracy"; the Court was asked whether
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court described R. Rajagopal as "reading down the restrictions (in the form of defamation) ... in its application to public officials and public figures in larger public interest", and recorded that in Subramanian Swamy the argument that free speech "was a higher right than the right to reputation under Article 21 was rejected". Why it matters: It summarises how Indian courts balance free speech and reputation, especially for public figures.
Melepurath Sankunni Ezhuthassan v. Thekittil Geopalankutty Nair (1986) 1 SCC 118; AIR 1986 SC 411 (as quoted in Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy , 2026 INSC 443, 4 May 2026)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A plaintiff's defamation suit was dismissed; he appealed and died while the appeal was pendin
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "this right does not survive his death, his legal representative has no right to be brought on the record"; but where the suit "has resulted in a decree in favour of the plaintiff ... the cause of action has merged in the decree and the decretal debt forms part of his estate". Why it matters: A defamation action is personal and dies with the person, unless a decree has already been obtained.
West Bengal State Electricity Board v. Dilip Kumar Ray [2006] Supp. 9 SCR (24 Nov 2006; Arijit Pasayat and Lokeshwar Singh Panta JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An engineer whose suspension was quashed sued the Board; the trial court awarded ₹50,000 for
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The awards were set aside because the averments were "extremely vague and lacking in details"; the Court noted that "to rebut a plea of privilage in defamation, malice in fact has to be proved". Why it matters: Damages for loss of reputation need proper pleading and proof, and malice is what defeats a privileged occasion.

selfTest.q: What is the basic ingredient of defamation according to Shreya Singhal?
selfTest.a: Injury to reputation. Name the three elements of defamation. Defamatory statement, reference to the plaintiff, publication. Which form needs proof of special damage? Slander (usually). What is the limitation for a libel suit? One year from publication (Art. 75). Is truth alone a defence in a civil suit? Yes (standard doctrine); in the crime it must also be for the public good. Which Articles give absolute privilege to legislators? Articles 105(2) and 194(2). What defeats qualified privilege? Malice. Can a company be defamed? Yes (BNS Explanation 2). Does a defamation suit survive the plaintiff's death? No, unless a decree has already been passed in his favour. When does a platform lose IT Act s. 79 protection? When it fails to remove material after actual knowledge of a court order (or government notification ). Where can a suit be filed if the defendant lives in Delhi and published in Calcutta? Either place (CPC s. 19, Ill. (b)). Which Article protects true newspaper reports of legislative proceedings? Article 361A.

law-of-torts-u4-t7.subtitle: Liability for careless words or advice that cause loss to a person who relied on them

en.inOneMinute: Negligent misstatement is liability in tort for careless (not dishonest) statements – information or advice – on which another person reasonably relies and so suffers loss, usually financial loss . Before 1963 the law said a person was liable for a false statement only if it was fraudulent ( Derry v. Peek , 1889) or made under a contract or fiduciary relationship. An honest but careless statement gave no claim. Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (House of Lords, 28 May 1963) changed this. Where there is a special relationship , a duty of care in making statements arises. Lord Morris: "if someone possessed of a special skill undertakes, quite irrespective of contract, to apply that skill for the assistance of another person who relies upon such skill, a duty of care will arise. The fact that the service is to be given by means of or by the instrumentality of words can make no difference." Elements (See Diagram 1 ): a special relationship – the speaker has (or claims) skill or knowledge, and knows or ought to know the hearer will rely on him; an assumption of responsibility by the speaker; reasonable reliance by the plaintiff; the statement was made carelessly ; and loss caused by the reliance. A clear disclaimer can prevent the duty arising. In Hedley Byrne itself the bank's reference was given "without responsibility", so the plaintiffs lost. In India, careless advice by a professional for payment can also be a "deficiency" in service under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(11).
legalProvision: There is no statute creating this tort in India; it is a common law tort. The related provisions are:

Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 17 – "Fraud" means and includes certain acts "committed by a party to a contract ... with intent to deceive another party thereto ... or to induce him to enter into the contract", including "(1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true". Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 18 – "Misrepresentation" means and includes "(1) the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true". Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 19 – "When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused." A party whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation "may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true." Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(11) – "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance ... in relation to any service and includes— (i) any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer". Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – residuary article: three years from "When the right to sue accrues".
(The Contract Act sections apply only between parties to a contract; the tort of negligent misstatement applies even where there is no contract.)
en.meaning: Negligent misstatement – an honest but careless statement of fact, information or advice, made in breach of a duty of care , on which the plaintiff reasonably relies to his loss. Special relationship – a relationship in which "the party seeking information or advice was trusting the other to exercise such a degree of care as the circumstances required, where it was reasonable for him to do that, and where the other gave the information or advice when he knew or ought to have known that the enquirer was relying on him" (Lord Reid, Hedley Byrne ). Assumption of responsibility – the speaker's voluntary undertaking, express or implied, to take care in giving the information or advice; Lord Devlin, using Lord Shaw's words in Nocton v. Ashburton , described relationships "equivalent to contract", "where there is an assumption of responsibility in circumstances in which, but for the absence of consideration, there would be a contract". Disclaimer – words such as "without responsibility" by which the speaker makes clear he accepts no duty of care; in Hedley Byrne it meant that the bank "never undertook any duty to exercise care" (Lord Reid). Deceit – the tort of fraud: a false representation made "knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly, without caring whether it be true or false" ( Derry v. Peek ).
keyPoints: Negligent misstatement = honest but careless statement causing loss through reliance. Derry v. Peek : deceit needs fraud. Hedley Byrne : duty of care for statements in a special relationship. Lord Reid: knew or ought to have known of reliance; three choices for the speaker. Lord Morris: special skill + reliance = duty, "irrespective of contract". Lord Devlin: relationship "equivalent to contract"; payment is very good evidence of reliance. Disclaimer can prevent the duty ( Hedley Byrne plaintiffs lost). Candler was wrongly decided. Contract Act s. 18 applies between contracting parties only. Paid professional advice can be a deficiency in service (CPA 2019).

caseLaws.facts: Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. [1964] AC 465 (House of Lords, 28 May 1963; Lords Reid, Morris of Borth-y-Gest, Hodson, Devlin and Pearce)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Advertising agents, through their own bank, asked Easipower's bankers for a credit reference
caseLaws.facts: The reply, marked "without responsibility", said Easipower was "considered good for its ordinary business engagements". Relying on it, the agents lost over £17,000 when Easipower went into liquidation. Principle: "if someone possessed of a special skill undertakes, quite irrespective of contract, to apply that skill for the assistance of another person who relies upon such skill, a duty of care will arise" (Lord Morris); but the bank's disclaimer meant it "never undertook any duty to exercise care" (Lord Reid). Appeal dismissed. Why it matters: Created liability for negligent misstatement causing financial loss, based on a special relationship and assumption of responsibility.
Derry v. Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (House of Lords, 1 July 1889)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tramway company directors stated in a prospectus that the company had the right to use steam
caseLaws.facts: The Board of Trade's consent was needed and was refused; the company was wound up. A shareholder sued the directors in deceit. Principle: "Fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly, without caring whether it be true or false"; a false statement made "in the honest belief that it is true, is not fraudulent" (headnote). Why it matters: Defines deceit and shows why a separate tort was needed for honest but careless statements.
Candler v. Crane, Christmas & Co. [1951] 2 KB 164 – as described in Hedley Byrne

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff wanted to see a company's accounts before investing; the company's accountants,
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court of Appeal majority held there was no duty of care without a contract (Lord Denning dissenting); Lord Reid in Hedley Byrne said it "was wrongly decided". Why it matters: Shows the law before Hedley Byrne , and that accountants who know their work will be relied on by a particular person can owe a duty.

selfTest.q: What is negligent misstatement?
selfTest.a: Liability for an honest but careless statement relied on by the plaintiff to his loss, where a special relationship exists. What did Derry v. Peek decide? Deceit needs fraud; an honest belief in a false statement is not fraud. What was the reference in Hedley Byrne about? The creditworthiness of Easipower Ltd. Why did Hedley Byrne lose? The reference was given "without responsibility", so no duty was undertaken. State Lord Morris's principle. A person with special skill who undertakes, irrespective of contract, to apply it for another who relies on it owes a duty of care. What did Lord Devlin say about payment? It is very good evidence that the advice is being relied upon and that the adviser knows it. Is a contract needed? No. Which earlier case did Lord Reid say was wrongly decided? Candler v. Crane, Christmas & Co. Which section of the Contract Act defines misrepresentation? Section 18. How much did Hedley Byrne lose? Over £17,000.

te.inOneMinute: నిర్లక్ష్య తప్పు ప్రకటన అంటే మరొకరు సహేతుకంగా ఆధారపడి నష్టపోయే – సాధారణంగా ఆర్థిక నష్టం – అజాగ్రత్త (నిజాయితీ లేనిది కాదు) ప్రకటనలకు – సమాచారం లేదా సలహాకు – టార్ట్ బాధ్యత. 1963 కు ముందు, ప్రకటన మోసపూరితమైతే ( Derry v. Peek , 1889) లేదా ఒప్పందం లేదా విశ్వాస ( fiduciary ) సంబంధం కింద చేస్తేనే తప్పుడు ప్రకటనకు బాధ్యత అని చట్టం చెప్పింది. నిజాయితీ కానీ అజాగ్రత్త ప్రకటనకు దావా లేదు. Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్, 28 మే 1963) దీన్ని మార్చింది. ప్రత్యేక సంబంధం ఉన్నచోట ప్రకటనలు చేయడంలో జాగ్రత్త విధి ఏర్పడుతుంది. Lord Morris: "if someone possessed of a special skill undertakes, quite irrespective of contract, to apply that skill for the assistance of another person who relies upon such skill, a duty of care will arise. The fact that the service is to be given by means of or by the instrumentality of words can make no difference." (అర్థం: ప్రత్యేక నైపుణ్యం ఉన్న వ్యక్తి, ఒప్పందంతో సంబంధం లేకుండా, ఆ నైపుణ్యంపై ఆధారపడే మరొకరి సహాయం కోసం దాన్ని వినియోగించడానికి పూనుకుంటే, జాగ్రత్త విధి ఏర్పడుతుంది. సేవ మాటల ద్వారా అందించబడుతుందనే వాస్తవం తేడా చేయదు.) అంశాలు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): ప్రత్యేక సంబంధం – మాట్లాడేవారికి నైపుణ్యం లేదా జ్ఞానం ఉంది (లేదా ఉందని చెప్పుకుంటాడు), వినేవారు తనపై ఆధారపడతారని తెలుసు లేదా తెలియాలి ; మాట్లాడేవారి బాధ్యత స్వీకరణ ; వాది సహేతుక ఆధారపడటం ; ప్రకటన అజాగ్రత్తగా చేయబడింది ; మరియు ఆధారపడటం వల్ల నష్టం . స్పష్టమైన బాధ్యత నిరాకరణ విధి ఏర్పడకుండా ఆపగలదు. Hedley Byrne లోనే బ్యాంకు రిఫరెన్స్ "without responsibility" (అర్థం: బాధ్యత లేకుండా) ఇవ్వబడింది, కాబట్టి వాదులు ఓడిపోయారు. భారతదేశంలో, డబ్బు తీసుకుని నిపుణుడు ఇచ్చే అజాగ్రత్త సలహా వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019, s. 2(11) కింద సేవలో "deficiency" (అర్థం: లోపం) కూడా కావచ్చు.
te.meaning: నిర్లక్ష్య తప్పు ప్రకటన – జాగ్రత్త విధిని ఉల్లంఘించి చేసిన, వాస్తవం, సమాచారం లేదా సలహా గురించిన నిజాయితీ కానీ అజాగ్రత్త ప్రకటన; దానిపై వాది సహేతుకంగా ఆధారపడి నష్టపోతాడు. ప్రత్యేక సంబంధం – "the party seeking information or advice was trusting the other to exercise such a degree of care as the circumstances required, where it was reasonable for him to do that, and where the other gave the information or advice when he knew or ought to have known that the enquirer was relying on him" (అర్థం: సమాచారం లేదా సలహా కోరే పక్షం, పరిస్థితులు కోరినంత జాగ్రత్త మరొకరు తీసుకుంటారని నమ్మి, అలా నమ్మడం సహేతుకమై, అడిగేవారు తనపై ఆధారపడుతున్నారని మరొకరికి తెలిసి లేదా తెలియాల్సి ఉండి సమాచారం లేదా సలహా ఇచ్చిన) సంబంధం (Lord Reid, Hedley Byrne ). బాధ్యత స్వీకరణ – సమాచారం లేదా సలహా ఇవ్వడంలో జాగ్రత్త తీసుకుంటానని మాట్లాడేవారు స్పష్టంగా లేదా సూచనగా స్వచ్ఛందంగా చేసే పూనిక; Nocton v. Ashburton లో Lord Shaw మాటలను ఉపయోగిస్తూ Lord Devlin "equivalent to contract" (అర్థం: ఒప్పందానికి సమానమైన) సంబంధాలను, "where there is an assumption of responsibility in circumstances in which, but for the absence of consideration, there would be a contract" (అర్థం: ప్రతిఫలం లేకపోవడం తప్ప ఒప్పందమే అయ్యే పరిస్థితుల్లో బాధ్యత స్వీకరణ ఉన్నచోట) వర్ణించారు. బాధ్యత నిరాకరణ – మాట్లాడేవారు జాగ్రత్త విధిని అంగీకరించడం లేదని స్పష్టం చేసే "without responsibility" వంటి మాటలు; Hedley Byrne లో దాని వల్ల బ్యాంకు "never undertook any duty to exercise care" (అర్థం: జాగ్రత్త తీసుకునే విధిని ఎప్పుడూ స్వీకరించలేదు) (Lord Reid). మోసం ( Deceit ) – మోసపు టార్ట్ : "knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly, without caring whether it be true or false" (అర్థం: తెలిసి, లేదా నిజమని నమ్మకుండా, లేదా నిజమో కాదో పట్టించుకోకుండా నిర్లక్ష్యంగా ) చేసిన తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం ( Derry v. Peek ).
keyPoints: నిర్లక్ష్య తప్పు ప్రకటన = ఆధారపడటం ద్వారా నష్టం కలిగించే నిజాయితీ కానీ అజాగ్రత్త ప్రకటన. Derry v. Peek : మోసపు దావాకు మోసం అవసరం. Hedley Byrne : ప్రత్యేక సంబంధంలో ప్రకటనలకు జాగ్రత్త విధి. Lord Reid: ఆధారపడటం తెలుసు లేదా తెలియాలి; మాట్లాడేవారికి మూడు మార్గాలు. Lord Morris: ప్రత్యేక నైపుణ్యం + ఆధారపడటం = విధి, "irrespective of contract" (అర్థం: ఒప్పందంతో సంబంధం లేకుండా). Lord Devlin: "equivalent to contract" సంబంధం; చెల్లింపు ఆధారపడటానికి చాలా మంచి సాక్ష్యం. బాధ్యత నిరాకరణ విధిని ఆపగలదు ( Hedley Byrne వాదులు ఓడిపోయారు). Candler తప్పుగా నిర్ణయించబడింది. ఒప్పంద చట్టం s. 18 ఒప్పంద పక్షాల మధ్యే వర్తిస్తుంది. చెల్లింపు నిపుణుల సలహా సేవలో లోపం కావచ్చు (CPA 2019).

selfTest.q: నిర్లక్ష్య తప్పు ప్రకటన అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ప్రత్యేక సంబంధం ఉన్నచోట, వాది ఆధారపడి నష్టపోయిన నిజాయితీ కానీ అజాగ్రత్త ప్రకటనకు బాధ్యత. Derry v. Peek ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది? మోసపు దావాకు మోసం అవసరం; తప్పుడు ప్రకటనపై నిజాయితీ నమ్మకం మోసం కాదు. Hedley Byrne లో రిఫరెన్స్ దేని గురించి? Easipower Ltd. క్రెడిట్ యోగ్యత గురించి. Hedley Byrne ఎందుకు ఓడిపోయారు? రిఫరెన్స్ "without responsibility" అని ఇవ్వబడింది, కాబట్టి ఏ విధీ స్వీకరించబడలేదు. Lord Morris సూత్రం చెప్పండి. ప్రత్యేక నైపుణ్యం ఉన్న వ్యక్తి, ఒప్పందంతో సంబంధం లేకుండా, దానిపై ఆధారపడే మరొకరి కోసం దాన్ని వినియోగించడానికి పూనుకుంటే జాగ్రత్త విధి ఉంటుంది. చెల్లింపు గురించి Lord Devlin ఏమన్నారు? సలహాపై ఆధారపడుతున్నారని, అది సలహాదారుకు తెలుసని చెప్పడానికి అది చాలా మంచి సాక్ష్యం. ఒప్పందం అవసరమా? లేదు. ఏ పాత కేసు తప్పుగా నిర్ణయించబడిందని Lord Reid అన్నారు? Candler v. Crane, Christmas & Co. ఒప్పంద చట్టంలో తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యాన్ని నిర్వచించే సెక్షన్ ఏది? Section 18. Hedley Byrne ఎంత నష్టపోయారు? £17,000 కు పైగా.

hi.inOneMinute: Negligent misstatement is liability in tort for careless (not dishonest) statements – information or advice – on which another person reasonably relies and so suffers loss, usually financial loss . Before 1963 the law said a person was liable for a false statement only if it was fraudulent ( Derry v. Peek , 1889) or made under a contract or fiduciary relationship. An honest but careless statement gave no claim. Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (House of Lords, 28 May 1963) changed this. Where there is a special relationship , a duty of care in making statements arises. Lord Morris: "if someone possessed of a special skill undertakes, quite irrespective of contract, to apply that skill for the assistance of another person who relies upon such skill, a duty of care will arise. The fact that the service is to be given by means of or by the instrumentality of words can make no difference." Elements (See Diagram 1 ): a special relationship – the speaker has (or claims) skill or knowledge, and knows or ought to know the hearer will rely on him; an assumption of responsibility by the speaker; reasonable reliance by the plaintiff; the statement was made carelessly ; and loss caused by the reliance. A clear disclaimer can prevent the duty arising. In Hedley Byrne itself the bank's reference was given "without responsibility", so the plaintiffs lost. In India, careless advice by a professional for payment can also be a "deficiency" in service under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(11).
legalProvision: There is no statute creating this tort in India; it is a common law tort. The related provisions are:

Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 17 – "Fraud" means and includes certain acts "committed by a party to a contract ... with intent to deceive another party thereto ... or to induce him to enter into the contract", including "(1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true". Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 18 – "Misrepresentation" means and includes "(1) the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true". Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 19 – "When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused." A party whose consent was caused by fraud or misrepresentation "may, if he thinks fit, insist that the contract shall be performed, and that he shall be put in the position in which he would have been if the representations made had been true." Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(11) – "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance ... in relation to any service and includes— (i) any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer". Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – residuary article: three years from "When the right to sue accrues".
(The Contract Act sections apply only between parties to a contract; the tort of negligent misstatement applies even where there is no contract.)
hi.meaning: Negligent misstatement – an honest but careless statement of fact, information or advice, made in breach of a duty of care , on which the plaintiff reasonably relies to his loss. Special relationship – a relationship in which "the party seeking information or advice was trusting the other to exercise such a degree of care as the circumstances required, where it was reasonable for him to do that, and where the other gave the information or advice when he knew or ought to have known that the enquirer was relying on him" (Lord Reid, Hedley Byrne ). Assumption of responsibility – the speaker's voluntary undertaking, express or implied, to take care in giving the information or advice; Lord Devlin, using Lord Shaw's words in Nocton v. Ashburton , described relationships "equivalent to contract", "where there is an assumption of responsibility in circumstances in which, but for the absence of consideration, there would be a contract". Disclaimer – words such as "without responsibility" by which the speaker makes clear he accepts no duty of care; in Hedley Byrne it meant that the bank "never undertook any duty to exercise care" (Lord Reid). Deceit – the tort of fraud: a false representation made "knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly, without caring whether it be true or false" ( Derry v. Peek ).
keyPoints: Negligent misstatement = honest but careless statement causing loss through reliance. Derry v. Peek : deceit needs fraud. Hedley Byrne : duty of care for statements in a special relationship. Lord Reid: knew or ought to have known of reliance; three choices for the speaker. Lord Morris: special skill + reliance = duty, "irrespective of contract". Lord Devlin: relationship "equivalent to contract"; payment is very good evidence of reliance. Disclaimer can prevent the duty ( Hedley Byrne plaintiffs lost). Candler was wrongly decided. Contract Act s. 18 applies between contracting parties only. Paid professional advice can be a deficiency in service (CPA 2019).

caseLaws.facts: Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. [1964] AC 465 (House of Lords, 28 May 1963; Lords Reid, Morris of Borth-y-Gest, Hodson, Devlin and Pearce)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Advertising agents, through their own bank, asked Easipower's bankers for a credit reference
caseLaws.facts: The reply, marked "without responsibility", said Easipower was "considered good for its ordinary business engagements". Relying on it, the agents lost over £17,000 when Easipower went into liquidation. Principle: "if someone possessed of a special skill undertakes, quite irrespective of contract, to apply that skill for the assistance of another person who relies upon such skill, a duty of care will arise" (Lord Morris); but the bank's disclaimer meant it "never undertook any duty to exercise care" (Lord Reid). Appeal dismissed. Why it matters: Created liability for negligent misstatement causing financial loss, based on a special relationship and assumption of responsibility.
Derry v. Peek (1889) 14 App Cas 337 (House of Lords, 1 July 1889)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tramway company directors stated in a prospectus that the company had the right to use steam
caseLaws.facts: The Board of Trade's consent was needed and was refused; the company was wound up. A shareholder sued the directors in deceit. Principle: "Fraud is proved when it is shewn that a false representation has been made knowingly, or without belief in its truth, or recklessly, without caring whether it be true or false"; a false statement made "in the honest belief that it is true, is not fraudulent" (headnote). Why it matters: Defines deceit and shows why a separate tort was needed for honest but careless statements.
Candler v. Crane, Christmas & Co. [1951] 2 KB 164 – as described in Hedley Byrne

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff wanted to see a company's accounts before investing; the company's accountants,
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court of Appeal majority held there was no duty of care without a contract (Lord Denning dissenting); Lord Reid in Hedley Byrne said it "was wrongly decided". Why it matters: Shows the law before Hedley Byrne , and that accountants who know their work will be relied on by a particular person can owe a duty.

selfTest.q: What is negligent misstatement?
selfTest.a: Liability for an honest but careless statement relied on by the plaintiff to his loss, where a special relationship exists. What did Derry v. Peek decide? Deceit needs fraud; an honest belief in a false statement is not fraud. What was the reference in Hedley Byrne about? The creditworthiness of Easipower Ltd. Why did Hedley Byrne lose? The reference was given "without responsibility", so no duty was undertaken. State Lord Morris's principle. A person with special skill who undertakes, irrespective of contract, to apply it for another who relies on it owes a duty of care. What did Lord Devlin say about payment? It is very good evidence that the advice is being relied upon and that the adviser knows it. Is a contract needed? No. Which earlier case did Lord Reid say was wrongly decided? Candler v. Crane, Christmas & Co. Which section of the Contract Act defines misrepresentation? Section 18. How much did Hedley Byrne lose? Over £17,000.

law-of-torts-u4-t2.subtitle: Fault liability, no-fault compensation, Claims Tribunals, just compensation and compulsory insurance after a road accident

en.inOneMinute: A road accident is a tort case: the driver who causes harm by negligence is liable, and the owner is liable for the driver's act in the course of employment ( Oriental Insurance v. Meena Variyal , 2007). The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("MV Act") builds a special system on top of the law of torts: Compulsory third-party insurance – no vehicle may be used in a public place without it (s. 146), so that the victim gets paid by an insurer (ss. 147, 150). Three bases of liability – (a) fault (negligence) for full "just" compensation under s. 166 ( Minu B. Mehta , 1977); (b) strict liability under the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher , applied to motor accidents by Kaushnuma Begum (2001); (c) no-fault liability – a fixed ₹5 lakh for death or ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt without proving any fault (s. 164). Hit and run victims get ₹2 lakh (death) or ₹50,000 (grievous hurt) from a Central Government scheme (s. 161). Claims Tribunals (s. 165) decide all such claims; civil courts are barred (s. 175). Time limit: claim within six months of the accident, extendable by up to twelve more months for sufficient cause (s. 166(3) and proviso). Appeal to the High Court within 90 days (s. 173).
legalProvision: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended up to Act 8 of 2026)

s. 2(28) – "motor vehicle" means "any mechanically propelled vehicle adapted for use upon roads ... and includes a chassis to which a body has not been attached and a trailer; but does not include a vehicle running upon fixed rails or a vehicle of a special type adapted for use only in a factory or in any other enclosed premises ...". s. 145(d) – "hit and run motor accident" means "an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle or motor vehicles the identity whereof cannot be ascertained in spite of reasonable efforts for the purpose". s. 146(1) – "No person shall use, except as a passenger, or cause or allow any other person to use, a motor vehicle in a public place, unless there is in force ... a policy of insurance complying with the requirements of this Chapter". Government vehicles not used for commerce are exempt (s. 146(2)); local authorities and State transport undertakings may be exempted if they keep a fund (s. 146(3)). s. 147(1)(b) – the policy must insure "(i) against any liability which may be incurred by him in respect of the death of or bodily injury to any person including owner of the goods or his authorised representative carried in the motor vehicle or damage to any property of a third party caused by or arising out of the use of the motor vehicle in a public place; (ii) against the death of or bodily injury to any passenger of a transport vehicle, except gratuitous passengers of a goods vehicle ...". Explanation – the harm is deemed to arise out of use in a public place "notwithstanding that the person who is dead or injured or the property which is damaged was not in a public place at the time of the accident, if the act or omission which led to the accident occurred in a public place". s. 149 – on information of the accident the insurer must "designate an officer to settle the claims"; the officer may offer a settlement "within thirty days"; if the claimant accepts, the Tribunal records it as "settled by consent" and the insurer pays "within a maximum period of thirty days"; if the claimant rejects, the Tribunal hears the claim on merits. s. 150(1) – once a certificate of insurance is issued and an award is obtained against the insured, the insurer "shall ... pay to the person entitled to the benefit of the award ... as if that person were the decree holder", even if it "may be entitled to avoid or cancel" the policy. s. 150(2) – the insurer, after notice, may defend only on these grounds: (a) breach of a specified condition: use for hire or reward without a permit, "organised racing and speed testing", use not allowed by the permit, a two-wheeler without side-car where required; driving "by any person who is not duly licenced" or a disqualified person or "driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs as laid down in section 185"; war, civil war, riot or civil commotion; (b) policy obtained by non-disclosure or false representation of a material fact; (c) "non-receipt of premium" under s. 64VB, Insurance Act, 1938. s. 150(4) – any other restriction in the policy is "of no effect" for the compulsory cover. s. 150(6) – if the claimant does not know the insurer, "it shall be the duty of the owner of the vehicle" to tell the Tribunal. s. 155 – the death of the insured after the accident "shall not be a bar to the survival of any cause of action ... against his estate or against the insurer". s. 159 – the police officer must prepare an "accident information report" within three months and send it to the Claims Tribunal. s. 161(2) – hit and run: "(a) in respect of the death ... a fixed sum of two lakh rupees or such higher amount as may be prescribed by the Central Government; (b) in respect of grievous hurt ... a fixed sum of fifty thousand rupees or such higher amount as may be prescribed ...". s. 162 – insurers must provide for treatment of road accident victims "including during the golden hour"; the Central Government "shall make a scheme for the cashless treatment of victims of the accident during the golden hour". s. 163 – compensation paid under s. 161 must be refunded to the insurer out of any later compensation for the same death or grievous hurt. s. 164(1) – "the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be." s. 164(2) – "the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt ... was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person." s. 164(3), (4) – compensation paid under any other law is reduced from this amount, but "ex gratia payments ... shall not be liable to be reduced". Explanation – "grievous hurt" has the meaning in s. 116, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. s. 164A – Central Government schemes for "interim relief to claimants". s. 164B – the "Motor Vehicle Accident Fund", used for golden hour treatment (s. 162), hit and run compensation (s. 161) and other prescribed compensation. s. 165(1) – Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals decide "claims for compensation in respect of accidents involving the death of, or bodily injury to, persons arising out of the use of motor vehicles, or damages to any property of a third party so arising, or both". The Explanation says this includes claims under s. 164. s. 166(1) – who may apply: "(a) by the person who has sustained the injury; or (b) by the owner of the property; or (c) where death has resulted from the accident, by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased; or (d) by any agent duly authorised ...". Legal representatives who do not join are made respondents (first proviso). If a person "accepts compensation under section 164 in accordance with the procedure provided under section 149, his claims petition before the Claims Tribunal shall lapse" (second proviso). s. 166(2) – the claim may be filed where the accident occurred, or where the claimant resides or carries on business, or where the defendant resides. s. 166(3) – "No application for compensation shall be entertained unless it is made within six months of the occurrence of the accident." Proviso – the Tribunal may entertain it "within a further period not exceeding twelve months" if "the applicant was prevented by sufficient cause". s. 166(4) – the Tribunal "shall treat any report of accidents forwarded to it under section 159 as an application for compensation". s. 166(5) – the injured person's right to claim "shall, upon the death of the person injured, survive to his legal representatives, irrespective of whether the cause of death is relatable to or had any nexus with the injury or not". s. 167 – where a claim lies under this Act and under the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 (now titled the Employee's Compensation Act, 1923), the person "may ... claim such compensation under either of those Acts but not under both". s. 168(1) – after notice to the insurer and a hearing, the Tribunal makes an award of compensation "which appears to it to be just" and specifies "the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them". s. 169 – the Tribunal may follow a summary procedure and has the powers of a civil court for evidence and witnesses. s. 171 – the Tribunal may award "simple interest ... from such date not earlier than the date of making the claim". s. 172 – special costs where the policy was obtained by false representation or a party puts forward "a false or vexatious claim or defence". s. 173 – appeal to the High Court "within ninety days from the date of the award"; a person who must pay must first deposit "twenty-five thousand rupees or fifty per cent. of the amount so awarded, whichever is less"; no appeal if "the amount in dispute in the appeal is less than one lakh rupees". s. 174 – amounts due under an award are recovered by the Collector "as an arrear of land revenue". s. 175 – "no Civil Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any question relating to any claim for compensation which may be adjudicated upon by the Claims Tribunal". s. 196 – driving an uninsured vehicle in contravention of s. 146: penalty of "three times the base premium ... or five thousand rupees, whichever is higher" for the first contravention.

Related criminal provision: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 106(1) – "Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine".
en.meaning: Accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle – an unintended event causing death, bodily injury or damage to property in which a motor vehicle (s. 2(28)) is in use. Both ss. 147 and 164 use the words "arising out of the use of the motor vehicle". Third-party insurance – insurance that covers the owner's liability to other persons (the "third party") for death, bodily injury or property damage caused by the use of the vehicle in a public place (ss. 146, 147). The insurer and the insured are the first two parties; the victim is the third. No-fault liability – liability to pay a fixed sum where the claimant "shall not be required to plead or establish" any "wrongful act or neglect or default" (s. 164(2)). Hit and run motor accident – "an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle or motor vehicles the identity whereof cannot be ascertained in spite of reasonable efforts for the purpose" (s. 145(d)). Claims Tribunal – a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal constituted by the State Government under s. 165; its members are, or have been, High Court Judges or District Judges, or are qualified to be (s. 165(3)). Legal representative – a person who in law represents the estate of the deceased; this is not limited to spouse, parents and children, and a brother may claim ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai , 1987).
keyPoints: Insurance against third-party risks is compulsory (s. 146). Fault claim needs proof of negligence ( Minu B. Mehta ); strict liability also applies ( Kaushnuma ). s. 164: ₹5 lakh death, ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt, no proof of fault. s. 161: hit and run, ₹2 lakh death, ₹50,000 grievous hurt. Insurer must pay the award; defences only under s. 150(2). Licence defence is narrow; pay and recover ( Swaran Singh ). Claim within six months, plus up to twelve months for sufficient cause (s. 166(3)). Brothers can be legal representatives ( Ramanbhai ). Civil courts barred (s. 175); appeal to High Court in 90 days (s. 173). Old ss. 140 and 163A omitted from 1-4-2022.

caseLaws.facts: Minu B. Mehta v. Balkrishna Ramchandra Nayan [1977] 2 SCR 886 (28 Jan 1977; A.N. Ray C.J., M.H. Beg and P.S. Kailasam JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A truck collided with the respondent's car
caseLaws.facts: The High Court held that compensation was payable irrespective of negligence. Principle: "Proof of negligence is necessary before the owner or the insurer could be held liable for payment of compensation in motor vehicle accident claims." Why it matters: It is the base rule for the fault-based claim; later statutes and cases added no-fault and strict liability around it.
Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation v. Ramanbhai Prabhatbhai [1987] 3 SCR (11 May 1987; E.S. Venkataramiah and K.N. Singh JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The brothers of a man killed in a bus accident claimed under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 and
caseLaws.facts: The corporation argued that brothers could not claim. Principle: "The brother of the person who dies in a motor vehicle accident is entitled to maintain a petition ... if he is a legal representative of the deceased"; a pedestrian killed "whether negligently or not" should recover "if the principle of social justice should have any meaning at all". Why it matters: It widened who may claim and supported liability without fault for road victims.
Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. [2001] 1 SCR (3 Jan 2001; K.T. Thomas and R.P. Sethi JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 20
caseLaws.facts: 3.1986 a jeep's front tyre burst and it capsized, killing a pedestrian aged 35 earning ₹1,500 a month. The Tribunal found no negligence and gave only ₹50,000 under old s. 140. Principle: The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher applies to motor accident claims; "even apart from Section 140 ... a victim ... is entitled to get compensation from a Tribunal unless any one of the exceptions would apply". The Court fixed ₹1,80,000 with 9% interest. Why it matters: Full compensation can be given without proof of negligence, unless the owner proves an exception.
National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh [2004] 1 SCR; [2004] 3 SCC 297 (5 Jan 2004; V.N. Khare C.J., D.M. Dharmadhikari and S.B. Sinha JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A batch of appeals in which insurers refused to pay because drivers had no licence, fake lice
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Mere absence, fake or invalid driving licence or disqualification of the driver ... are not in themselves defences available to the insurer"; the breach must be "so fundamental as are found to have contributed to the cause of the accident"; the Tribunal can direct "that the insurer is liable to be reimbursed by the insured". Why it matters: It created the "pay and recover" approach and narrowed the licence defence (now s. 150(2)).
Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal [2007] 4 SCR (2 Apr 2007; C.K. Thakker and P.K. Balasubramanyan JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A company's Regional Manager was himself driving the company's insured car and died in an acc
caseLaws.facts: His family claimed against the insurer. Principle: "Ordinarily, a contract of insurance is a contract of indemnity"; "Once the driver is liable, the owner of the vehicle becomes vicariously liable ... It is this vicarious liability of the owner that is indemnified by the insurance company"; a Tribunal must not "ignore all basic principles of law". Why it matters: The insurer pays only to indemnify the owner's liability; it was not liable on these facts.

selfTest.q: Which section makes third-party insurance compulsory?
selfTest.a: Section 146. What did Minu B. Mehta hold? Proof of negligence is necessary for owner or insurer liability. How much is payable under s. 164 for death? ₹5 lakh; ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt. Must the claimant prove fault under s. 164? No (s. 164(2)). What is paid for death in a hit and run accident? ₹2 lakh or a higher prescribed sum (s. 161(2)(a)). Which case applied Rylands v. Fletcher to motor accidents? Kaushnuma Begum (2001). Is a fake licence by itself a defence for the insurer? No (Swaran Singh). What is the time limit for a claim? Six months, extendable by up to twelve months for sufficient cause. Can a claim be filed in a civil court? No (s. 175). Within how many days does an appeal lie to the High Court? Ninety days (s. 173). What happens to the claim petition if the s. 164 settlement is accepted under s. 149? It lapses. Can a brother of the deceased claim? Yes, if he is a legal representative (Ramanbhai).

te.inOneMinute: రోడ్డు ప్రమాదం ఒక టార్ట్ కేసు: నిర్లక్ష్యంతో హాని చేసిన డ్రైవర్ బాధ్యుడు; ఉద్యోగ క్రమంలో డ్రైవర్ చేసిన చర్యకు యజమాని బాధ్యుడు ( Oriental Insurance v. Meena Variyal , 2007). మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 ("MV Act") టార్ట్ చట్టం పైన ఒక ప్రత్యేక వ్యవస్థను నిర్మిస్తుంది: తప్పనిసరి థర్డ్ పార్టీ బీమా – అది లేకుండా ఏ వాహనాన్నీ బహిరంగ ప్రదేశంలో ఉపయోగించకూడదు (s. 146); దీంతో బాధితుడికి బీమా సంస్థ చెల్లిస్తుంది (ss. 147, 150). బాధ్యతకు మూడు ఆధారాలు – (a) తప్పు (నిర్లక్ష్యం): s. 166 కింద పూర్తి "న్యాయమైన" పరిహారం ( Minu B. Mehta , 1977); (b) కఠిన బాధ్యత : Rylands v. Fletcher నియమం, దీన్ని Kaushnuma Begum (2001) మోటార్ ప్రమాదాలకు వర్తింపజేసింది; (c) తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత – ఏ తప్పూ నిరూపించకుండానే మరణానికి నిర్ణీత ₹5 లక్షలు, తీవ్ర గాయానికి ₹2.5 లక్షలు (s. 164). హిట్ అండ్ రన్ బాధితులకు కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వ పథకం నుంచి ₹2 లక్షలు (మరణం) లేదా ₹50,000 (తీవ్ర గాయం) (s. 161). క్లెయిమ్స్ ట్రిబ్యునల్స్ (s. 165) ఇలాంటి అన్ని క్లెయిమ్‌లను నిర్ణయిస్తాయి; సివిల్ కోర్టులకు అధికారం లేదు (s. 175). కాల పరిమితి: ప్రమాదం జరిగిన ఆరు నెలల్లో క్లెయిమ్; తగిన కారణం ఉంటే మరో పన్నెండు నెలల వరకు పొడిగించవచ్చు (s. 166(3), proviso). హైకోర్టుకు అప్పీల్ 90 రోజుల్లో (s. 173).
te.meaning: మోటార్ వాహన వాడకం వల్ల కలిగే ప్రమాదం – మోటార్ వాహనం (s. 2(28)) వాడకంలో ఉండగా మరణం, శారీరక గాయం లేదా ఆస్తి నష్టం కలిగించే అనుకోని సంఘటన. ss. 147, 164 రెండూ "arising out of the use of the motor vehicle" (అర్థం: మోటార్ వాహన వాడకం వల్ల కలిగే) అనే మాటలు వాడతాయి. థర్డ్ పార్టీ బీమా – బహిరంగ ప్రదేశంలో వాహన వాడకం వల్ల ఇతర వ్యక్తులకు ("మూడో వ్యక్తి") కలిగే మరణం, శారీరక గాయం, ఆస్తి నష్టానికి యజమాని బాధ్యతను కవర్ చేసే బీమా (ss. 146, 147). బీమా సంస్థ, బీమాదారుడు మొదటి రెండు పక్షాలు; బాధితుడు మూడో పక్షం. తప్పు లేని బాధ్యత – క్లెయిమెంట్ ఏ "wrongful act or neglect or default" (అర్థం: తప్పుడు చర్య, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా లోపం) ను "shall not be required to plead or establish" (అర్థం: వాదించాల్సిన లేదా నిరూపించాల్సిన అవసరం లేని) నిర్ణీత మొత్తం చెల్లించే బాధ్యత (s. 164(2)). హిట్ అండ్ రన్ మోటార్ ప్రమాదం – "an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle or motor vehicles the identity whereof cannot be ascertained in spite of reasonable efforts for the purpose" (అర్థం: సహేతుక ప్రయత్నాలు చేసినా వాహన గుర్తింపు తెలియని ప్రమాదం) (s. 145(d)). క్లెయిమ్స్ ట్రిబ్యునల్ – s. 165 కింద రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఏర్పాటు చేసే మోటార్ ప్రమాద క్లెయిమ్స్ ట్రిబ్యునల్; సభ్యులు హైకోర్టు న్యాయమూర్తులు లేదా జిల్లా న్యాయమూర్తులు (ప్రస్తుత లేదా మాజీ), లేదా అందుకు అర్హులు (s. 165(3)). చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధి – మృతుడి ఆస్తికి చట్టపరంగా ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహించే వ్యక్తి; భార్య/భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లలకే పరిమితం కాదు; సోదరుడు కూడా క్లెయిమ్ చేయవచ్చు ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai , 1987).
keyPoints: థర్డ్ పార్టీ బీమా తప్పనిసరి (s. 146). తప్పు క్లెయిమ్‌కు నిర్లక్ష్య నిరూపణ అవసరం ( Minu B. Mehta ); కఠిన బాధ్యత కూడా వర్తిస్తుంది ( Kaushnuma ). s. 164: మరణం ₹5 లక్షలు, తీవ్ర గాయం ₹2.5 లక్షలు, తప్పు నిరూపణ అవసరం లేదు. s. 161: హిట్ అండ్ రన్, మరణం ₹2 లక్షలు, తీవ్ర గాయం ₹50,000. బీమా సంస్థ అవార్డు చెల్లించాలి; రక్షణలు s. 150(2) కింద మాత్రమే. లైసెన్స్ రక్షణ సంకుచితం; చెల్లించి వసూలు ( Swaran Singh ). ఆరు నెలల్లో క్లెయిమ్, తగిన కారణంతో మరో పన్నెండు నెలల వరకు (s. 166(3)). సోదరులు చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులు కావచ్చు ( Ramanbhai ). సివిల్ కోర్టులకు అధికారం లేదు (s. 175); 90 రోజుల్లో హైకోర్టుకు అప్పీల్ (s. 173). పాత ss. 140, 163A 1-4-2022 నుంచి తొలగించబడ్డాయి.

selfTest.q: థర్డ్ పార్టీ బీమాను ఏ సెక్షన్ తప్పనిసరి చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 146. Minu B. Mehta ఏం తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది? యజమాని లేదా బీమా సంస్థ బాధ్యతకు నిర్లక్ష్య నిరూపణ అవసరం. s. 164 కింద మరణానికి ఎంత? ₹5 లక్షలు; తీవ్ర గాయానికి ₹2.5 లక్షలు. s. 164 కింద క్లెయిమెంట్ తప్పు నిరూపించాలా? లేదు (s. 164(2)). హిట్ అండ్ రన్ ప్రమాదంలో మరణానికి ఎంత? ₹2 లక్షలు లేదా నిర్దేశిత ఎక్కువ మొత్తం (s. 161(2)(a)). Rylands v. Fletcher ను మోటార్ ప్రమాదాలకు ఏ కేసు వర్తింపజేసింది? Kaushnuma Begum (2001). నకిలీ లైసెన్స్ స్వతహాగా బీమా సంస్థకు రక్షణా? కాదు (Swaran Singh). క్లెయిమ్‌కు కాల పరిమితి ఎంత? ఆరు నెలలు; తగిన కారణంతో మరో పన్నెండు నెలల వరకు. సివిల్ కోర్టులో క్లెయిమ్ వేయవచ్చా? లేదు (s. 175). ఎన్ని రోజుల్లో హైకోర్టుకు అప్పీల్? తొంభై రోజులు (s. 173). s. 149 కింద s. 164 పరిష్కారాన్ని అంగీకరిస్తే క్లెయిమ్ పిటిషన్ ఏమవుతుంది? రద్దవుతుంది. మృతుడి సోదరుడు క్లెయిమ్ చేయవచ్చా? అవును, అతను చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధి అయితే (Ramanbhai).
