hi.inOneMinute: A road accident is a tort case: the driver who causes harm by negligence is liable, and the owner is liable for the driver's act in the course of employment ( Oriental Insurance v. Meena Variyal , 2007). The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("MV Act") builds a special system on top of the law of torts: Compulsory third-party insurance – no vehicle may be used in a public place without it (s. 146), so that the victim gets paid by an insurer (ss. 147, 150). Three bases of liability – (a) fault (negligence) for full "just" compensation under s. 166 ( Minu B. Mehta , 1977); (b) strict liability under the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher , applied to motor accidents by Kaushnuma Begum (2001); (c) no-fault liability – a fixed ₹5 lakh for death or ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt without proving any fault (s. 164). Hit and run victims get ₹2 lakh (death) or ₹50,000 (grievous hurt) from a Central Government scheme (s. 161). Claims Tribunals (s. 165) decide all such claims; civil courts are barred (s. 175). Time limit: claim within six months of the accident, extendable by up to twelve more months for sufficient cause (s. 166(3) and proviso). Appeal to the High Court within 90 days (s. 173).
legalProvision: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended up to Act 8 of 2026)

s. 2(28) – "motor vehicle" means "any mechanically propelled vehicle adapted for use upon roads ... and includes a chassis to which a body has not been attached and a trailer; but does not include a vehicle running upon fixed rails or a vehicle of a special type adapted for use only in a factory or in any other enclosed premises ...". s. 145(d) – "hit and run motor accident" means "an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle or motor vehicles the identity whereof cannot be ascertained in spite of reasonable efforts for the purpose". s. 146(1) – "No person shall use, except as a passenger, or cause or allow any other person to use, a motor vehicle in a public place, unless there is in force ... a policy of insurance complying with the requirements of this Chapter". Government vehicles not used for commerce are exempt (s. 146(2)); local authorities and State transport undertakings may be exempted if they keep a fund (s. 146(3)). s. 147(1)(b) – the policy must insure "(i) against any liability which may be incurred by him in respect of the death of or bodily injury to any person including owner of the goods or his authorised representative carried in the motor vehicle or damage to any property of a third party caused by or arising out of the use of the motor vehicle in a public place; (ii) against the death of or bodily injury to any passenger of a transport vehicle, except gratuitous passengers of a goods vehicle ...". Explanation – the harm is deemed to arise out of use in a public place "notwithstanding that the person who is dead or injured or the property which is damaged was not in a public place at the time of the accident, if the act or omission which led to the accident occurred in a public place". s. 149 – on information of the accident the insurer must "designate an officer to settle the claims"; the officer may offer a settlement "within thirty days"; if the claimant accepts, the Tribunal records it as "settled by consent" and the insurer pays "within a maximum period of thirty days"; if the claimant rejects, the Tribunal hears the claim on merits. s. 150(1) – once a certificate of insurance is issued and an award is obtained against the insured, the insurer "shall ... pay to the person entitled to the benefit of the award ... as if that person were the decree holder", even if it "may be entitled to avoid or cancel" the policy. s. 150(2) – the insurer, after notice, may defend only on these grounds: (a) breach of a specified condition: use for hire or reward without a permit, "organised racing and speed testing", use not allowed by the permit, a two-wheeler without side-car where required; driving "by any person who is not duly licenced" or a disqualified person or "driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs as laid down in section 185"; war, civil war, riot or civil commotion; (b) policy obtained by non-disclosure or false representation of a material fact; (c) "non-receipt of premium" under s. 64VB, Insurance Act, 1938. s. 150(4) – any other restriction in the policy is "of no effect" for the compulsory cover. s. 150(6) – if the claimant does not know the insurer, "it shall be the duty of the owner of the vehicle" to tell the Tribunal. s. 155 – the death of the insured after the accident "shall not be a bar to the survival of any cause of action ... against his estate or against the insurer". s. 159 – the police officer must prepare an "accident information report" within three months and send it to the Claims Tribunal. s. 161(2) – hit and run: "(a) in respect of the death ... a fixed sum of two lakh rupees or such higher amount as may be prescribed by the Central Government; (b) in respect of grievous hurt ... a fixed sum of fifty thousand rupees or such higher amount as may be prescribed ...". s. 162 – insurers must provide for treatment of road accident victims "including during the golden hour"; the Central Government "shall make a scheme for the cashless treatment of victims of the accident during the golden hour". s. 163 – compensation paid under s. 161 must be refunded to the insurer out of any later compensation for the same death or grievous hurt. s. 164(1) – "the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer shall be liable to pay in the case of death or grievous hurt due to any accident arising out of the use of motor vehicle, a compensation, of a sum of five lakh rupees in case of death or of two and a half lakh rupees in case of grievous hurt to the legal heirs or the victim, as the case may be." s. 164(2) – "the claimant shall not be required to plead or establish that the death or grievous hurt ... was due to any wrongful act or neglect or default of the owner of the vehicle or of the vehicle concerned or of any other person." s. 164(3), (4) – compensation paid under any other law is reduced from this amount, but "ex gratia payments ... shall not be liable to be reduced". Explanation – "grievous hurt" has the meaning in s. 116, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. s. 164A – Central Government schemes for "interim relief to claimants". s. 164B – the "Motor Vehicle Accident Fund", used for golden hour treatment (s. 162), hit and run compensation (s. 161) and other prescribed compensation. s. 165(1) – Motor Accidents Claims Tribunals decide "claims for compensation in respect of accidents involving the death of, or bodily injury to, persons arising out of the use of motor vehicles, or damages to any property of a third party so arising, or both". The Explanation says this includes claims under s. 164. s. 166(1) – who may apply: "(a) by the person who has sustained the injury; or (b) by the owner of the property; or (c) where death has resulted from the accident, by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased; or (d) by any agent duly authorised ...". Legal representatives who do not join are made respondents (first proviso). If a person "accepts compensation under section 164 in accordance with the procedure provided under section 149, his claims petition before the Claims Tribunal shall lapse" (second proviso). s. 166(2) – the claim may be filed where the accident occurred, or where the claimant resides or carries on business, or where the defendant resides. s. 166(3) – "No application for compensation shall be entertained unless it is made within six months of the occurrence of the accident." Proviso – the Tribunal may entertain it "within a further period not exceeding twelve months" if "the applicant was prevented by sufficient cause". s. 166(4) – the Tribunal "shall treat any report of accidents forwarded to it under section 159 as an application for compensation". s. 166(5) – the injured person's right to claim "shall, upon the death of the person injured, survive to his legal representatives, irrespective of whether the cause of death is relatable to or had any nexus with the injury or not". s. 167 – where a claim lies under this Act and under the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 (now titled the Employee's Compensation Act, 1923), the person "may ... claim such compensation under either of those Acts but not under both". s. 168(1) – after notice to the insurer and a hearing, the Tribunal makes an award of compensation "which appears to it to be just" and specifies "the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them". s. 169 – the Tribunal may follow a summary procedure and has the powers of a civil court for evidence and witnesses. s. 171 – the Tribunal may award "simple interest ... from such date not earlier than the date of making the claim". s. 172 – special costs where the policy was obtained by false representation or a party puts forward "a false or vexatious claim or defence". s. 173 – appeal to the High Court "within ninety days from the date of the award"; a person who must pay must first deposit "twenty-five thousand rupees or fifty per cent. of the amount so awarded, whichever is less"; no appeal if "the amount in dispute in the appeal is less than one lakh rupees". s. 174 – amounts due under an award are recovered by the Collector "as an arrear of land revenue". s. 175 – "no Civil Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any question relating to any claim for compensation which may be adjudicated upon by the Claims Tribunal". s. 196 – driving an uninsured vehicle in contravention of s. 146: penalty of "three times the base premium ... or five thousand rupees, whichever is higher" for the first contravention.

Related criminal provision: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 106(1) – "Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine".
hi.meaning: Accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle – an unintended event causing death, bodily injury or damage to property in which a motor vehicle (s. 2(28)) is in use. Both ss. 147 and 164 use the words "arising out of the use of the motor vehicle". Third-party insurance – insurance that covers the owner's liability to other persons (the "third party") for death, bodily injury or property damage caused by the use of the vehicle in a public place (ss. 146, 147). The insurer and the insured are the first two parties; the victim is the third. No-fault liability – liability to pay a fixed sum where the claimant "shall not be required to plead or establish" any "wrongful act or neglect or default" (s. 164(2)). Hit and run motor accident – "an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle or motor vehicles the identity whereof cannot be ascertained in spite of reasonable efforts for the purpose" (s. 145(d)). Claims Tribunal – a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal constituted by the State Government under s. 165; its members are, or have been, High Court Judges or District Judges, or are qualified to be (s. 165(3)). Legal representative – a person who in law represents the estate of the deceased; this is not limited to spouse, parents and children, and a brother may claim ( Gujarat SRTC v. Ramanbhai , 1987).
keyPoints: Insurance against third-party risks is compulsory (s. 146). Fault claim needs proof of negligence ( Minu B. Mehta ); strict liability also applies ( Kaushnuma ). s. 164: ₹5 lakh death, ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt, no proof of fault. s. 161: hit and run, ₹2 lakh death, ₹50,000 grievous hurt. Insurer must pay the award; defences only under s. 150(2). Licence defence is narrow; pay and recover ( Swaran Singh ). Claim within six months, plus up to twelve months for sufficient cause (s. 166(3)). Brothers can be legal representatives ( Ramanbhai ). Civil courts barred (s. 175); appeal to High Court in 90 days (s. 173). Old ss. 140 and 163A omitted from 1-4-2022.

caseLaws.facts: Minu B. Mehta v. Balkrishna Ramchandra Nayan [1977] 2 SCR 886 (28 Jan 1977; A.N. Ray C.J., M.H. Beg and P.S. Kailasam JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A truck collided with the respondent's car
caseLaws.facts: The High Court held that compensation was payable irrespective of negligence. Principle: "Proof of negligence is necessary before the owner or the insurer could be held liable for payment of compensation in motor vehicle accident claims." Why it matters: It is the base rule for the fault-based claim; later statutes and cases added no-fault and strict liability around it.
Gujarat State Road Transport Corporation v. Ramanbhai Prabhatbhai [1987] 3 SCR (11 May 1987; E.S. Venkataramiah and K.N. Singh JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The brothers of a man killed in a bus accident claimed under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 and
caseLaws.facts: The corporation argued that brothers could not claim. Principle: "The brother of the person who dies in a motor vehicle accident is entitled to maintain a petition ... if he is a legal representative of the deceased"; a pedestrian killed "whether negligently or not" should recover "if the principle of social justice should have any meaning at all". Why it matters: It widened who may claim and supported liability without fault for road victims.
Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. [2001] 1 SCR (3 Jan 2001; K.T. Thomas and R.P. Sethi JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 20
caseLaws.facts: 3.1986 a jeep's front tyre burst and it capsized, killing a pedestrian aged 35 earning ₹1,500 a month. The Tribunal found no negligence and gave only ₹50,000 under old s. 140. Principle: The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher applies to motor accident claims; "even apart from Section 140 ... a victim ... is entitled to get compensation from a Tribunal unless any one of the exceptions would apply". The Court fixed ₹1,80,000 with 9% interest. Why it matters: Full compensation can be given without proof of negligence, unless the owner proves an exception.
National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh [2004] 1 SCR; [2004] 3 SCC 297 (5 Jan 2004; V.N. Khare C.J., D.M. Dharmadhikari and S.B. Sinha JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A batch of appeals in which insurers refused to pay because drivers had no licence, fake lice
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Mere absence, fake or invalid driving licence or disqualification of the driver ... are not in themselves defences available to the insurer"; the breach must be "so fundamental as are found to have contributed to the cause of the accident"; the Tribunal can direct "that the insurer is liable to be reimbursed by the insured". Why it matters: It created the "pay and recover" approach and narrowed the licence defence (now s. 150(2)).
Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Meena Variyal [2007] 4 SCR (2 Apr 2007; C.K. Thakker and P.K. Balasubramanyan JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A company's Regional Manager was himself driving the company's insured car and died in an acc
caseLaws.facts: His family claimed against the insurer. Principle: "Ordinarily, a contract of insurance is a contract of indemnity"; "Once the driver is liable, the owner of the vehicle becomes vicariously liable ... It is this vicarious liability of the owner that is indemnified by the insurance company"; a Tribunal must not "ignore all basic principles of law". Why it matters: The insurer pays only to indemnify the owner's liability; it was not liable on these facts.

selfTest.q: Which section makes third-party insurance compulsory?
selfTest.a: Section 146. What did Minu B. Mehta hold? Proof of negligence is necessary for owner or insurer liability. How much is payable under s. 164 for death? ₹5 lakh; ₹2.5 lakh for grievous hurt. Must the claimant prove fault under s. 164? No (s. 164(2)). What is paid for death in a hit and run accident? ₹2 lakh or a higher prescribed sum (s. 161(2)(a)). Which case applied Rylands v. Fletcher to motor accidents? Kaushnuma Begum (2001). Is a fake licence by itself a defence for the insurer? No (Swaran Singh). What is the time limit for a claim? Six months, extendable by up to twelve months for sufficient cause. Can a claim be filed in a civil court? No (s. 175). Within how many days does an appeal lie to the High Court? Ninety days (s. 173). What happens to the claim petition if the s. 164 settlement is accepted under s. 149? It lapses. Can a brother of the deceased claim? Yes, if he is a legal representative (Ramanbhai).

law-of-torts-u4-t8.subtitle: The tort that protects a trader's goodwill and the public against a rival who passes off his goods as the trader's

en.inOneMinute: Passing off is a business tort. A trader commits it when he sells his goods or offers his services in a way that leads the public to think they are another trader's. The action protects the plaintiff's goodwill and also the public . The Supreme Court said it is "an action not only to preserve the reputation of the plaintiff but also to safeguard the public" ( Satyam Infoway , 2004). Three elements ( Satyam Infoway ): (See Diagram 1 .) the plaintiff's goodwill or reputation in the name or mark; misrepresentation by the defendant to the public, causing likelihood of confusion; loss, or the likelihood of it. Passing off is available even for an unregistered mark. The Trade Marks Act, 1999 keeps this action alive (s. 27(2)), but registration is needed to sue for infringement (s. 27(1)). Remedies: injunction, and at the plaintiff's option damages or an account of profits (s. 135). The suit must be filed in a District Court or higher (s. 134(1)(c)).
legalProvision: Passing off is a common law tort. The Trade Marks Act, 1999 does not define it, but refers to it in these provisions:

Section 27(1): "No person shall be entitled to institute any proceeding to prevent, or to recover damages for, the infringement of an unregistered trade mark." Section 27(2): "Nothing in this Act shall be deemed to affect rights of action against any person for passing off goods or services as the goods of another person or as services provided by another person, or the remedies in respect thereof." Section 134(1)(c): no suit "for passing off arising out of the use by the defendant of any trade mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to the plaintiff's trade mark, whether registered or unregistered" shall be instituted "in any court inferior to a District Court having jurisdiction to try the suit". Section 135(1): relief in a suit for passing off "includes injunction (subject to such terms, if any, as the court thinks fit) and at the option of the plaintiff, either damages or an account of profits, together with or without any order for the delivery-up of the infringing labels and marks for destruction or erasure." Section 135(2): the injunction may include an ex parte or interlocutory order for discovery of documents, preserving infringing goods and evidence, and restraining the defendant from disposing of assets. Section 2(1)(h): "A mark shall be deemed to be deceptively similar to another mark if it so nearly resembles that other mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion". Section 2(1)(m): "mark" "includes a device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging or combination of colours or any combination thereof".
en.meaning: Passing off – the tort of a trader who represents, by name, mark, get-up or otherwise, that his goods or services are those of another trader, so that the public is likely to be deceived. Goodwill – the attractive force of a trader's name or mark that brings customers. Satyam Infoway : a passing off action "is based on the goodwill that a trader has in his name". Misrepresentation – conduct of the defendant likely to make actual or potential customers think his goods or services are the plaintiff's. No dishonest intention is required. Deceptive similarity – a mark "so nearly resembles that other mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion" (s. 2(1)(h)). Infringement – violation of a registered trade mark; a statutory action available only to the registered proprietor (s. 27(1); s. 28(1)).
keyPoints: Passing off: selling goods or services as another's. Protects goodwill and the public. Elements: goodwill, misrepresentation, damage. No need to prove mala fide intention; likelihood of confusion is enough. Deceptive similarity: s. 2(1)(h); Cadila factors. Stricter test for medicines ( Cadila ). Unregistered marks: passing off yes (s. 27(2)), infringement no (s. 27(1)). Domain names can found a passing off action ( Satyam Infoway ). Court: District Court or higher (s. 134(1)(c)); relief: s. 135.

caseLaws.facts: Satyam Infoway Ltd. v. Sifynet Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (2004) 6 SCC 145; [2004] Supp. (2) SCR 465 – decided 6 May 2004 (judgment by Ruma Pal J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The appellant used the coined word "Sify" in its business and in domain names registered in 1
caseLaws.facts: The respondent later began an internet business as "Siffynet". The City Civil Court granted a temporary injunction ; the High Court set it aside. Principle: Passing off has three elements: goodwill in the plaintiff's name, misrepresentation causing likelihood of confusion, and loss or its likelihood. A domain name "may have all the characteristics of a trademark and could found an action for passing off". The respondent's adoption of "Siffy" was found, prima facie , to be dishonest; the injunction was restored. Why it matters: It is the leading Supreme Court statement of the elements of passing off and extends the action to domain names and internet services.
Cadila Health Care Ltd. v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd. (2001) 5 SCC 73; AIR 2001 SC 1952 – decided 26 March 2001 (judgment by Kirpal J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The appellant sold an anti-malaria drug as "Falcigo"; the respondent later sold one as "Falci
caseLaws.facts: The trial court refused an interim injunction and the High Court upheld that. The Supreme Court did not interfere, but directed early disposal of the suit and laid down the governing principles. Principle: Deceptive similarity in a passing off action on an unregistered mark is decided by factors such as the nature of the marks, degree of resemblance, nature of goods, class of purchasers and mode of purchase. For medicinal products the test must be applied strictly, as confusion can have disastrous results. Why it matters: It gives the factors used in every passing off case and the stricter rule for medicines.

selfTest.q: What are the three elements of passing off?
selfTest.a: Can the owner of an unregistered mark sue for passing off? Must the plaintiff prove the defendant's dishonest intention? Name four Cadila factors. Why is a stricter test applied to medicines? Can a domain name be protected by a passing off action?

te.inOneMinute: పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ (Passing off) ఒక వ్యాపార టార్ట్. ఒక వ్యాపారి తన వస్తువులను అమ్మే లేదా సేవలను అందించే విధానం వల్ల, అవి మరొక వ్యాపారివని ప్రజలు అనుకునేలా చేస్తే అతను ఈ టార్ట్ చేసినట్లు. ఈ దావా వాది గుడ్‌విల్ ‌ను, ప్రజలను కూడా రక్షిస్తుంది. సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఇది "an action not only to preserve the reputation of the plaintiff but also to safeguard the public" (అర్థం: వాది ప్రతిష్ఠను కాపాడటానికి మాత్రమే కాక ప్రజలను రక్షించడానికి కూడా ఉన్న దావా) అని చెప్పింది ( Satyam Infoway , 2004). మూడు అంశాలు ( Satyam Infoway ): ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) పేరు లేదా మార్క్‌లో వాదికి ఉన్న గుడ్‌విల్ లేదా ప్రతిష్ఠ; ప్రతివాది ప్రజలకు చేసిన తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం, దాంతో గందరగోళం కలిగే అవకాశం; నష్టం, లేదా నష్టం కలిగే అవకాశం. నమోదు కాని మార్క్‌కు కూడా పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ దావా అందుబాటులో ఉంటుంది. ట్రేడ్ మార్క్స్ చట్టం, 1999 ఈ దావాను నిలబెడుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 27(2)), కానీ ఉల్లంఘన (infringement) దావాకు నమోదు అవసరం (సెక్షన్ 27(1)). పరిహారాలు: నిషేధాజ్ఞ (injunction), వాది ఎంపిక మేరకు నష్టపరిహారం లేదా లాభాల లెక్క (సెక్షన్ 135). దావాను జిల్లా కోర్టు లేదా అంతకంటే పై కోర్టులో వేయాలి (సెక్షన్ 134(1)(c)).
te.meaning: పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ (Passing off) – పేరు, మార్క్, రూపురేఖలు (get-up) లేదా ఇతర విధంగా తన వస్తువులు లేదా సేవలు మరొక వ్యాపారివని చూపించి, ప్రజలు మోసపోయే అవకాశం కలిగించే వ్యాపారి టార్ట్ . గుడ్‌విల్ (Goodwill) – వినియోగదారులను తీసుకొచ్చే వ్యాపారి పేరు లేదా మార్క్ ఆకర్షణ శక్తి. Satyam Infoway : పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ దావా "is based on the goodwill that a trader has in his name" (అర్థం: ఒక వ్యాపారికి తన పేరులో ఉన్న గుడ్‌విల్‌పై ఆధారపడి ఉంటుంది). తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం (Misrepresentation) – ప్రతివాది వస్తువులు లేదా సేవలు వాదివేనని వాస్తవ లేదా సంభావ్య వినియోగదారులు అనుకునేలా చేసే ప్రతివాది ప్రవర్తన. దురుద్దేశం అవసరం లేదు. మోసపూరిత పోలిక ( Deceptive similarity) – ఒక మార్క్ "so nearly resembles that other mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion" (అర్థం: మోసగించేలా లేదా గందరగోళం కలిగించేలా మరొక మార్క్‌ను అంత దగ్గరగా పోలి ఉండటం) (సెక్షన్ 2(1)(h)). ఉల్లంఘన (Infringement) – నమోదైన ట్రేడ్ మార్క్ ఉల్లంఘన; నమోదైన యజమానికి మాత్రమే అందుబాటులో ఉండే చట్టబద్ధ దావా (సెక్షన్ 27(1); సెక్షన్ 28(1)).
keyPoints: పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్: వస్తువులు లేదా సేవలను మరొకరివిగా అమ్మడం. గుడ్‌విల్‌ను, ప్రజలను రక్షిస్తుంది. అంశాలు: గుడ్‌విల్, తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం, నష్టం. దురుద్దేశం రుజువు చేయనక్కర్లేదు; గందరగోళం కలిగే అవకాశం చాలు. మోసపూరిత పోలిక: సెక్షన్ 2(1)(h); Cadila అంశాలు. మందులకు కఠిన పరీక్ష ( Cadila ). నమోదు కాని మార్కులు: పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ అవును (సెక్షన్ 27(2)), ఉల్లంఘన కాదు (సెక్షన్ 27(1)). డొమైన్ పేర్లు పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ దావాకు ఆధారం కావచ్చు ( Satyam Infoway ). కోర్టు: జిల్లా కోర్టు లేదా పైన (సెక్షన్ 134(1)(c)); ఉపశమనం: సెక్షన్ 135.

selfTest.a: నమోదు కాని మార్క్ యజమాని పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ దావా వేయవచ్చా? ప్రతివాది దురుద్దేశాన్ని వాది రుజువు చేయాలా? Cadila అంశాల్లో నాలుగు చెప్పండి. మందులకు కఠిన పరీక్ష ఎందుకు? డొమైన్ పేరును పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్ దావా ద్వారా రక్షించవచ్చా?

hi.inOneMinute: Passing off is a business tort. A trader commits it when he sells his goods or offers his services in a way that leads the public to think they are another trader's. The action protects the plaintiff's goodwill and also the public . The Supreme Court said it is "an action not only to preserve the reputation of the plaintiff but also to safeguard the public" ( Satyam Infoway , 2004). Three elements ( Satyam Infoway ): (See Diagram 1 .) the plaintiff's goodwill or reputation in the name or mark; misrepresentation by the defendant to the public, causing likelihood of confusion; loss, or the likelihood of it. Passing off is available even for an unregistered mark. The Trade Marks Act, 1999 keeps this action alive (s. 27(2)), but registration is needed to sue for infringement (s. 27(1)). Remedies: injunction, and at the plaintiff's option damages or an account of profits (s. 135). The suit must be filed in a District Court or higher (s. 134(1)(c)).
legalProvision: Passing off is a common law tort. The Trade Marks Act, 1999 does not define it, but refers to it in these provisions:

Section 27(1): "No person shall be entitled to institute any proceeding to prevent, or to recover damages for, the infringement of an unregistered trade mark." Section 27(2): "Nothing in this Act shall be deemed to affect rights of action against any person for passing off goods or services as the goods of another person or as services provided by another person, or the remedies in respect thereof." Section 134(1)(c): no suit "for passing off arising out of the use by the defendant of any trade mark which is identical with or deceptively similar to the plaintiff's trade mark, whether registered or unregistered" shall be instituted "in any court inferior to a District Court having jurisdiction to try the suit". Section 135(1): relief in a suit for passing off "includes injunction (subject to such terms, if any, as the court thinks fit) and at the option of the plaintiff, either damages or an account of profits, together with or without any order for the delivery-up of the infringing labels and marks for destruction or erasure." Section 135(2): the injunction may include an ex parte or interlocutory order for discovery of documents, preserving infringing goods and evidence, and restraining the defendant from disposing of assets. Section 2(1)(h): "A mark shall be deemed to be deceptively similar to another mark if it so nearly resembles that other mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion". Section 2(1)(m): "mark" "includes a device, brand, heading, label, ticket, name, signature, word, letter, numeral, shape of goods, packaging or combination of colours or any combination thereof".
hi.meaning: Passing off – the tort of a trader who represents, by name, mark, get-up or otherwise, that his goods or services are those of another trader, so that the public is likely to be deceived. Goodwill – the attractive force of a trader's name or mark that brings customers. Satyam Infoway : a passing off action "is based on the goodwill that a trader has in his name". Misrepresentation – conduct of the defendant likely to make actual or potential customers think his goods or services are the plaintiff's. No dishonest intention is required. Deceptive similarity – a mark "so nearly resembles that other mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion" (s. 2(1)(h)). Infringement – violation of a registered trade mark; a statutory action available only to the registered proprietor (s. 27(1); s. 28(1)).
keyPoints: Passing off: selling goods or services as another's. Protects goodwill and the public. Elements: goodwill, misrepresentation, damage. No need to prove mala fide intention; likelihood of confusion is enough. Deceptive similarity: s. 2(1)(h); Cadila factors. Stricter test for medicines ( Cadila ). Unregistered marks: passing off yes (s. 27(2)), infringement no (s. 27(1)). Domain names can found a passing off action ( Satyam Infoway ). Court: District Court or higher (s. 134(1)(c)); relief: s. 135.

caseLaws.facts: Satyam Infoway Ltd. v. Sifynet Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (2004) 6 SCC 145; [2004] Supp. (2) SCR 465 – decided 6 May 2004 (judgment by Ruma Pal J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The appellant used the coined word "Sify" in its business and in domain names registered in 1
caseLaws.facts: The respondent later began an internet business as "Siffynet". The City Civil Court granted a temporary injunction ; the High Court set it aside. Principle: Passing off has three elements: goodwill in the plaintiff's name, misrepresentation causing likelihood of confusion, and loss or its likelihood. A domain name "may have all the characteristics of a trademark and could found an action for passing off". The respondent's adoption of "Siffy" was found, prima facie , to be dishonest; the injunction was restored. Why it matters: It is the leading Supreme Court statement of the elements of passing off and extends the action to domain names and internet services.
Cadila Health Care Ltd. v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd. (2001) 5 SCC 73; AIR 2001 SC 1952 – decided 26 March 2001 (judgment by Kirpal J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The appellant sold an anti-malaria drug as "Falcigo"; the respondent later sold one as "Falci
caseLaws.facts: The trial court refused an interim injunction and the High Court upheld that. The Supreme Court did not interfere, but directed early disposal of the suit and laid down the governing principles. Principle: Deceptive similarity in a passing off action on an unregistered mark is decided by factors such as the nature of the marks, degree of resemblance, nature of goods, class of purchasers and mode of purchase. For medicinal products the test must be applied strictly, as confusion can have disastrous results. Why it matters: It gives the factors used in every passing off case and the stricter rule for medicines.

law-of-torts-u4-t5.subtitle: How the law protects trade, goodwill and economic interests: injurious falsehood, negligent misstatement, passing off and conspiracy

en.inOneMinute: Torts against business relations (also called economic or business torts) protect a person's freedom to trade, to work and to deal with others. They make a defendant liable when he intentionally damages the plaintiff's business or contracts by means the law treats as wrongful. The starting point is freedom of trade. A trader in a free country may, "in all matters not contrary to law", regulate his trade "according to his own discretion and choice" ( Mogul Steamship , 1891, Lord Halsbury L.C., adopting Alderson B.). In India, Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution guarantees the right "to carry on any occupation, trade or business". Competition is not a tort. Hard competition that ruins a rival is lawful if the motive is one's own gain and the means are lawful ( Mogul Steamship ). A bad motive alone does not make a lawful act wrongful ( Allen v. Flood , 1898, as explained in Quinn v. Leathem , 1901). Liability arises where the defendant uses unlawful means . Lord Halsbury listed them: "Intimidation, violence, molestation, or the procuring of people to break their contracts, are all of them unlawful acts". The main torts under this heading: Inducing breach of contract ( Lumley v. Gye , 1853, approved in Quinn v. Leathem ); Intimidation and interference with trade by unlawful means ( Quinn v. Leathem ); Conspiracy, injurious falsehood, passing off and negligent misstatement – each a separate syllabus topic, summarised here and studied in its own note (See Diagram 1 ). Justification is a defence; a registered trade union has a statutory immunity for acts in furtherance of an industrial dispute (Industrial Relations Code, 2020, s. 16). Remedies: damages and injunction; for anti-competitive conduct there is also a statutory route under the Competition Act, 2002.
legalProvision: There is no single statute on these torts; they are common law torts applied in India. The related provisions are:

Constitution of India, Article 19(1)(g) – "All citizens shall have the right— ... (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business." (Subject to reasonable restrictions under Art. 19(6).) Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 27 – "Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void." (Exception 1 saves a reasonable agreement by the seller of goodwill not to carry on a similar business within specified local limits.) Industrial Relations Code, 2020, s. 16(1) – "No suit or other legal proceeding shall be maintainable in any civil court against any registered Trade Union or any office-bearer or member thereof in respect of any act done in contemplation or furtherance of an industrial dispute to which a member of the Trade Union is a party on the ground only that such act induces some other person to break a contract of employment or that it is an interference with the trade, business, or employment of some other person or with the right of some other person to dispose of his capital or of his labour as he wills." Under s. 16(2), the union is not liable for a "tortuous act" of its agent done without the knowledge of, or contrary to express instructions given by, the union's executive. Competition Act, 2002: s. 3(1) – no enterprise or person "shall enter into any agreement in respect of production, supply, distribution, storage, acquisition or control of goods or provision of services, which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India"; such an agreement is void (s. 3(2)). s. 4(1) – "No enterprise or group shall abuse its dominant position." s. 53N(1) – any enterprise or person may apply to the Appellate Tribunal for "compensation ... for any loss or damage shown to have been suffered ... as a result of any contravention of the provisions of Chapter II". Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(1) – "a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication."
en.meaning: Torts against business relations – a group of intentional torts that protect a person's trade, business, employment and contractual relations from deliberate interference by wrongful means. Inducing breach of contract – knowingly and intentionally persuading or procuring a party to a contract to break it, without sufficient justification, causing loss to the other party. Lord Macnaghten: "a violation of legal right committed knowingly is a cause of action, and ... it is a violation of legal right to interfere with contractual relations recognised by law if there be no sufficient justification for the interference" ( Quinn v. Leathem ). Unlawful means – acts the law already treats as wrongful, such as intimidation, violence, molestation , fraud, or procuring breaches of contract ( Mogul Steamship , Lord Halsbury). Intimidation – coercing a person, by a threat to do something unlawful or wrongful, into acting (or not acting) to the plaintiff's harm. Lord Lindley: "coercion by threats, open or disguised, not only of bodily harm but of serious annoyance and damage, is primâ facie, at all events, a wrong" ( Quinn v. Leathem ). Justification – a lawful reason which excuses an interference with another's contract or trade (Lord Macnaghten's "sufficient justification"). Malice (in these torts) – in Lumley v. Gye as quoted by the Court of Appeal in Jones Bros. v. Stevens (1955): "For this purpose maliciously means no more than knowingly" (quoted in WBSEB v. Dilip Kumar Ray , 2006).
keyPoints: Business torts protect trade, business, employment and contracts. Competition by lawful means is not a tort ( Mogul ). A bad motive alone does not create liability ( Allen v. Flood ). Unlawful means: intimidation, violence, molestation, procuring breaches of contract ( Mogul ). Inducing breach: contract, knowledge, intentional inducement, breach, damage, no justification. "Maliciously" in Lumley v. Gye means "knowingly". Leaving after due notice is not a breach ( Quinn ). Coercion by threats of serious annoyance and damage is a wrong ( Quinn ). Trade unions have limited immunity in industrial disputes (IR Code s. 16). Competition Act s. 53N gives a statutory compensation route.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Shipowners in the China tea trade (Hankow to London) formed an association, gave a 5 per cent
caseLaws.facts: The excluded plaintiffs sued for conspiracy. Principle: Since the defendants acted "with the lawful object of protecting and extending their trade" and "had not employed any unlawful means", there was no cause of action (headnote). Lord Morris: "It is not illegal for a trader to aim at driving a competitor out of trade, provided the motive be his own gain ... and the means he uses be lawful weapons." Why it matters: Draws the line between lawful competition and unlawful interference.
Quinn v. Leathem [1901] UKHL 2 (House of Lords, 5 August 1901)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Union officials demanded that Leathem, a butcher at Lisburn, dismiss non-union assistants
caseLaws.facts: He refused, though he offered to pay their fines to get them admitted. They threatened to call out the workmen of his customer Munce, who then stopped buying his meat; they also published "black lists" and induced an assistant to leave without notice. The jury awarded £200 (and £50 on the black lists). Principle: Lumley v. Gye was right because "a violation of legal right committed knowingly is a cause of action" and interfering with contractual relations without "sufficient justification" is such a violation (Lord Macnaghten); "coercion by threats ... of serious annoyance and damage" is prima facie a wrong (Lord Lindley). Why it matters: Leading authority on inducing breach of contract, intimidation and the limits of Allen v. Flood .
Allen v. Flood [1898] AC 1 (House of Lords) – as explained in Quinn v. Leathem

caseLaws.name: Facts: A union official told an iron company that its workmen would leave if two other workmen were
caseLaws.facts: There was no conspiracy, intimidation or breach of contract before the House. Principle: Allen "had done nothing which he had no legal right to do", and acting "maliciously and with intent to injure" did not, "without more", give a cause of action (Lord Lindley's account). Why it matters: A lawful act does not become a tort because of a bad motive.
Lumley v. Gye (1853) 2 E & B 216 – as quoted in Jones Bros. v. Stevens (1955), in WBSEB v. Dilip Kumar Ray [2006] Supp. 9 SCR

caseLaws.facts: Principle: A person who "wrongfully and maliciously, or, which is the same thing, with notice, interrupts the relation of master and servant ... commits a wrongful act" (Crompton J.); "maliciously means no more than knowingly". Why it matters: The origin of the tort of inducing breach of contract; the Supreme Court has quoted its meaning of "maliciously".

selfTest.q: Is it a tort to drive a competitor out of trade?
selfTest.a: Not if the motive is one's own gain and the means are lawful (Mogul). Which case says a bad motive alone does not make a lawful act actionable? Allen v. Flood (as explained in Quinn v. Leathem). List the unlawful acts named by Lord Halsbury in Mogul . Intimidation, violence, molestation, procuring people to break their contracts. What does "maliciously" mean in Lumley v. Gye ? Knowingly. Name the elements of inducing breach of contract. Contract, knowledge, intentional inducement, actual breach, damage, no justification. Why could Leathem not sue for the two servants who left? They gave due notice, so no contract was broken. How did the union pressure Munce? By threatening to call out his workmen if Leathem's beef arrived. Which provision gives trade unions immunity? Industrial Relations Code, 2020, s. 16. Which Constitutional right supports freedom of trade? Article 19(1)(g). Under which section can compensation be claimed for anti-competitive conduct? Competition Act, 2002, s. 53N.

te.inOneMinute: వ్యాపార సంబంధాలకు వ్యతిరేకమైన టార్ట్‌లు (ఆర్థిక లేదా వ్యాపార టార్ట్‌లు అని కూడా అంటారు) వ్యక్తి వ్యాపారం చేసే, పని చేసే, ఇతరులతో వ్యవహరించే స్వేచ్ఛను రక్షిస్తాయి. చట్టం తప్పుగా భావించే మార్గాల ద్వారా ప్రతివాది ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా వాది వ్యాపారానికి లేదా ఒప్పందాలకు నష్టం కలిగిస్తే బాధ్యుడవుతాడు. ప్రారంభ సూత్రం వ్యాపార స్వేచ్ఛ. స్వేచ్ఛా దేశంలో వ్యాపారి "in all matters not contrary to law" (అర్థం: చట్టానికి విరుద్ధం కాని అన్ని విషయాల్లో) తన వ్యాపారాన్ని "according to his own discretion and choice" (అర్థం: తన విచక్షణ, ఎంపిక ప్రకారం) నిర్వహించుకోవచ్చు ( Mogul Steamship , 1891, Lord Halsbury L.C., Alderson B. మాటలను స్వీకరిస్తూ). భారతదేశంలో రాజ్యాంగం Art. 19(1)(g) "to carry on any occupation, trade or business" (అర్థం: ఏదైనా వృత్తి, వ్యాపారం లేదా వ్యవహారం నిర్వహించే) హక్కును హామీ ఇస్తుంది. పోటీ టార్ట్ కాదు. ప్రత్యర్థిని నాశనం చేసే గట్టి పోటీ కూడా, ఉద్దేశం స్వలాభం, మార్గాలు చట్టబద్ధమైతే చట్టబద్ధమే ( Mogul Steamship ). దురుద్దేశం మాత్రమే చట్టబద్ధ చర్యను తప్పుగా మార్చదు ( Allen v. Flood , 1898, Quinn v. Leathem , 1901 లో వివరించినట్లు). ప్రతివాది చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాలు ఉపయోగిస్తే బాధ్యత వస్తుంది. Lord Halsbury వాటిని పేర్కొన్నారు: "Intimidation, violence, molestation, or the procuring of people to break their contracts, are all of them unlawful acts" (అర్థం: బెదిరింపు, హింస, వేధింపు, లేదా ఒప్పందాలను ఉల్లంఘించేలా వ్యక్తులను ప్రేరేపించడం – ఇవన్నీ చట్టవిరుద్ధ చర్యలే). ఈ శీర్షిక కింద ప్రధాన టార్ట్‌లు: ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘనకు ప్రేరేపణ ( Lumley v. Gye , 1853, Quinn v. Leathem లో ఆమోదించారు); బెదిరింపు , చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాలతో వ్యాపారంలో జోక్యం ( Quinn v. Leathem ); కుట్ర, హానికర అసత్యం, పాసింగ్ ఆఫ్, నిర్లక్ష్య తప్పు ప్రకటన – ఒక్కొక్కటి ప్రత్యేక సిలబస్ అంశం; ఇక్కడ సంక్షిప్తంగా, తమ స్వంత నోట్‌లో పూర్తిగా ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి). సమర్థన ఒక రక్షణ; నమోదిత ట్రేడ్ యూనియన్‌కు పారిశ్రామిక వివాదానికి సంబంధించిన చర్యలకు చట్టబద్ధ రక్షణ ఉంది (పారిశ్రామిక సంబంధాల కోడ్, 2020, s. 16). పరిష్కారాలు: నష్టపరిహారం, నిషేధాజ్ఞ; పోటీ వ్యతిరేక ప్రవర్తనకు పోటీ చట్టం, 2002 కింద చట్టబద్ధ మార్గం కూడా ఉంది.
te.meaning: వ్యాపార సంబంధాలకు వ్యతిరేకమైన టార్ట్‌లు – తప్పుడు మార్గాలతో చేసే ఉద్దేశపూర్వక జోక్యం నుంచి వ్యక్తి వ్యాపారం, వ్యవహారం, ఉద్యోగం, ఒప్పంద సంబంధాలను రక్షించే ఉద్దేశపూర్వక టార్ట్‌ల సమూహం. ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘనకు ప్రేరేపణ – తగిన సమర్థన లేకుండా, ఒప్పంద పక్షాన్ని దాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించేలా తెలిసి, ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా ఒప్పించడం లేదా ప్రేరేపించడం, దాని వల్ల మరో పక్షానికి నష్టం. Lord Macnaghten: "a violation of legal right committed knowingly is a cause of action, and ... it is a violation of legal right to interfere with contractual relations recognised by law if there be no sufficient justification for the interference" (అర్థం: తెలిసి చేసిన చట్టపరమైన హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన దావా కారణం; తగిన సమర్థన లేకుండా చట్టం గుర్తించిన ఒప్పంద సంబంధాలలో జోక్యం చేసుకోవడం చట్టపరమైన హక్కు ఉల్లంఘనే) ( Quinn v. Leathem ). చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాలు – బెదిరింపు, హింస, వేధింపు, మోసం, లేదా ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘనలకు ప్రేరేపణ వంటి, చట్టం ఇప్పటికే తప్పుగా భావించే చర్యలు ( Mogul Steamship , Lord Halsbury). బెదిరింపు – చట్టవిరుద్ధమైన లేదా తప్పుడు పని చేస్తానని బెదిరించి, ఒక వ్యక్తి వాదికి హాని కలిగేలా ప్రవర్తించేలా (లేదా ప్రవర్తించకుండా) బలవంతం చేయడం. Lord Lindley: "coercion by threats, open or disguised, not only of bodily harm but of serious annoyance and damage, is primâ facie, at all events, a wrong" (అర్థం: శారీరక హాని గురించే కాకుండా, తీవ్రమైన ఇబ్బంది, నష్టం గురించి బహిరంగంగా లేదా ముసుగులో చేసే బెదిరింపులతో బలవంతం చేయడం ప్రాథమికంగా తప్పే) ( Quinn v. Leathem ). సమర్థన – మరొకరి ఒప్పందం లేదా వ్యాపారంలో జోక్యాన్ని క్షమించే చట్టబద్ధ కారణం (Lord Macnaghten చెప్పిన "sufficient justification" (అర్థం: తగిన సమర్థన)). దురుద్దేశం (ఈ టార్ట్‌లలో) – Jones Bros. v. Stevens (1955) లో అప్పీల్ కోర్టు ఉటంకించిన Lumley v. Gye ప్రకారం: "For this purpose maliciously means no more than knowingly" (అర్థం: ఈ ప్రయోజనం కోసం "దురుద్దేశంతో" అంటే "తెలిసి" అని మాత్రమే) ( WBSEB v. Dilip Kumar Ray , 2006 లో ఉటంకించారు).
keyPoints: వ్యాపార టార్ట్‌లు వ్యాపారం, వ్యవహారం, ఉద్యోగం, ఒప్పందాలను రక్షిస్తాయి. చట్టబద్ధ మార్గాలతో పోటీ టార్ట్ కాదు ( Mogul ). దురుద్దేశం మాత్రమే బాధ్యతను సృష్టించదు ( Allen v. Flood ). చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాలు: బెదిరింపు, హింస, వేధింపు, ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘనలకు ప్రేరేపణ ( Mogul ). ఉల్లంఘనకు ప్రేరేపణ: ఒప్పందం, జ్ఞానం, ఉద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రేరేపణ, ఉల్లంఘన, నష్టం, సమర్థన లేకపోవడం. Lumley v. Gye లో "maliciously" అంటే "తెలిసి". సరైన నోటీసుతో వెళ్లడం ఉల్లంఘన కాదు ( Quinn ). తీవ్రమైన ఇబ్బంది, నష్టం గురించి బెదిరింపులతో బలవంతం తప్పు ( Quinn ). పారిశ్రామిక వివాదాల్లో ట్రేడ్ యూనియన్లకు పరిమిత రక్షణ ఉంది (IR కోడ్ s. 16). పోటీ చట్టం s. 53N చట్టబద్ధ పరిహార మార్గాన్ని ఇస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: పోటీదారుని వ్యాపారం నుంచి తరిమివేయడం టార్టా?
selfTest.a: ఉద్దేశం స్వలాభం, మార్గాలు చట్టబద్ధమైతే కాదు (Mogul). దురుద్దేశం మాత్రమే చట్టబద్ధ చర్యను దావా యోగ్యం చేయదని చెప్పిన కేసు ఏది? Allen v. Flood (Quinn v. Leathem లో వివరించినట్లు). Mogul లో Lord Halsbury పేర్కొన్న చట్టవిరుద్ధ చర్యలు ఏవి? బెదిరింపు, హింస, వేధింపు, ఒప్పందాలు ఉల్లంఘించేలా వ్యక్తులను ప్రేరేపించడం. Lumley v. Gye లో "maliciously" అర్థం ఏమిటి? తెలిసి. ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘనకు ప్రేరేపణ అంశాలు చెప్పండి. ఒప్పందం, జ్ఞానం, ఉద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రేరేపణ, నిజమైన ఉల్లంఘన, నష్టం, సమర్థన లేకపోవడం. వెళ్లిపోయిన ఇద్దరు సేవకుల కోసం Leathem ఎందుకు దావా వేయలేకపోయాడు? వారు సరైన నోటీసు ఇచ్చారు, కాబట్టి ఏ ఒప్పందమూ ఉల్లంఘించబడలేదు. యూనియన్ Munce పై ఎలా ఒత్తిడి తెచ్చింది? Leathem మాంసం వస్తే అతని కార్మికులను పని ఆపిస్తామని బెదిరించడం ద్వారా. ట్రేడ్ యూనియన్లకు రక్షణ ఇచ్చే నిబంధన ఏది? పారిశ్రామిక సంబంధాల కోడ్, 2020, s. 16. వ్యాపార స్వేచ్ఛకు ఆధారమైన రాజ్యాంగ హక్కు ఏది? Article 19(1)(g). పోటీ వ్యతిరేక ప్రవర్తనకు ఏ సెక్షన్ కింద పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు? పోటీ చట్టం, 2002, s. 53N.

hi.inOneMinute: Torts against business relations (also called economic or business torts) protect a person's freedom to trade, to work and to deal with others. They make a defendant liable when he intentionally damages the plaintiff's business or contracts by means the law treats as wrongful. The starting point is freedom of trade. A trader in a free country may, "in all matters not contrary to law", regulate his trade "according to his own discretion and choice" ( Mogul Steamship , 1891, Lord Halsbury L.C., adopting Alderson B.). In India, Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution guarantees the right "to carry on any occupation, trade or business". Competition is not a tort. Hard competition that ruins a rival is lawful if the motive is one's own gain and the means are lawful ( Mogul Steamship ). A bad motive alone does not make a lawful act wrongful ( Allen v. Flood , 1898, as explained in Quinn v. Leathem , 1901). Liability arises where the defendant uses unlawful means . Lord Halsbury listed them: "Intimidation, violence, molestation, or the procuring of people to break their contracts, are all of them unlawful acts". The main torts under this heading: Inducing breach of contract ( Lumley v. Gye , 1853, approved in Quinn v. Leathem ); Intimidation and interference with trade by unlawful means ( Quinn v. Leathem ); Conspiracy, injurious falsehood, passing off and negligent misstatement – each a separate syllabus topic, summarised here and studied in its own note (See Diagram 1 ). Justification is a defence; a registered trade union has a statutory immunity for acts in furtherance of an industrial dispute (Industrial Relations Code, 2020, s. 16). Remedies: damages and injunction; for anti-competitive conduct there is also a statutory route under the Competition Act, 2002.
legalProvision: There is no single statute on these torts; they are common law torts applied in India. The related provisions are:

Constitution of India, Article 19(1)(g) – "All citizens shall have the right— ... (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business." (Subject to reasonable restrictions under Art. 19(6).) Indian Contract Act, 1872, s. 27 – "Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void." (Exception 1 saves a reasonable agreement by the seller of goodwill not to carry on a similar business within specified local limits.) Industrial Relations Code, 2020, s. 16(1) – "No suit or other legal proceeding shall be maintainable in any civil court against any registered Trade Union or any office-bearer or member thereof in respect of any act done in contemplation or furtherance of an industrial dispute to which a member of the Trade Union is a party on the ground only that such act induces some other person to break a contract of employment or that it is an interference with the trade, business, or employment of some other person or with the right of some other person to dispose of his capital or of his labour as he wills." Under s. 16(2), the union is not liable for a "tortuous act" of its agent done without the knowledge of, or contrary to express instructions given by, the union's executive. Competition Act, 2002: s. 3(1) – no enterprise or person "shall enter into any agreement in respect of production, supply, distribution, storage, acquisition or control of goods or provision of services, which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India"; such an agreement is void (s. 3(2)). s. 4(1) – "No enterprise or group shall abuse its dominant position." s. 53N(1) – any enterprise or person may apply to the Appellate Tribunal for "compensation ... for any loss or damage shown to have been suffered ... as a result of any contravention of the provisions of Chapter II". Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(1) – "a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication."
hi.meaning: Torts against business relations – a group of intentional torts that protect a person's trade, business, employment and contractual relations from deliberate interference by wrongful means. Inducing breach of contract – knowingly and intentionally persuading or procuring a party to a contract to break it, without sufficient justification, causing loss to the other party. Lord Macnaghten: "a violation of legal right committed knowingly is a cause of action, and ... it is a violation of legal right to interfere with contractual relations recognised by law if there be no sufficient justification for the interference" ( Quinn v. Leathem ). Unlawful means – acts the law already treats as wrongful, such as intimidation, violence, molestation , fraud, or procuring breaches of contract ( Mogul Steamship , Lord Halsbury). Intimidation – coercing a person, by a threat to do something unlawful or wrongful, into acting (or not acting) to the plaintiff's harm. Lord Lindley: "coercion by threats, open or disguised, not only of bodily harm but of serious annoyance and damage, is primâ facie, at all events, a wrong" ( Quinn v. Leathem ). Justification – a lawful reason which excuses an interference with another's contract or trade (Lord Macnaghten's "sufficient justification"). Malice (in these torts) – in Lumley v. Gye as quoted by the Court of Appeal in Jones Bros. v. Stevens (1955): "For this purpose maliciously means no more than knowingly" (quoted in WBSEB v. Dilip Kumar Ray , 2006).
keyPoints: Business torts protect trade, business, employment and contracts. Competition by lawful means is not a tort ( Mogul ). A bad motive alone does not create liability ( Allen v. Flood ). Unlawful means: intimidation, violence, molestation, procuring breaches of contract ( Mogul ). Inducing breach: contract, knowledge, intentional inducement, breach, damage, no justification. "Maliciously" in Lumley v. Gye means "knowingly". Leaving after due notice is not a breach ( Quinn ). Coercion by threats of serious annoyance and damage is a wrong ( Quinn ). Trade unions have limited immunity in industrial disputes (IR Code s. 16). Competition Act s. 53N gives a statutory compensation route.

caseLaws.facts: The excluded plaintiffs sued for conspiracy. Principle: Since the defendants acted "with the lawful object of protecting and extending their trade" and "had not employed any unlawful means", there was no cause of action (headnote). Lord Morris: "It is not illegal for a trader to aim at driving a competitor out of trade, provided the motive be his own gain ... and the means he uses be lawful weapons." Why it matters: Draws the line between lawful competition and unlawful interference.
Quinn v. Leathem [1901] UKHL 2 (House of Lords, 5 August 1901)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Union officials demanded that Leathem, a butcher at Lisburn, dismiss non-union assistants
caseLaws.facts: He refused, though he offered to pay their fines to get them admitted. They threatened to call out the workmen of his customer Munce, who then stopped buying his meat; they also published "black lists" and induced an assistant to leave without notice. The jury awarded £200 (and £50 on the black lists). Principle: Lumley v. Gye was right because "a violation of legal right committed knowingly is a cause of action" and interfering with contractual relations without "sufficient justification" is such a violation (Lord Macnaghten); "coercion by threats ... of serious annoyance and damage" is prima facie a wrong (Lord Lindley). Why it matters: Leading authority on inducing breach of contract, intimidation and the limits of Allen v. Flood .
Allen v. Flood [1898] AC 1 (House of Lords) – as explained in Quinn v. Leathem

selfTest.q: Is it a tort to drive a competitor out of trade?
selfTest.a: Not if the motive is one's own gain and the means are lawful (Mogul). Which case says a bad motive alone does not make a lawful act actionable? Allen v. Flood (as explained in Quinn v. Leathem). List the unlawful acts named by Lord Halsbury in Mogul . Intimidation, violence, molestation, procuring people to break their contracts. What does "maliciously" mean in Lumley v. Gye ? Knowingly. Name the elements of inducing breach of contract. Contract, knowledge, intentional inducement, actual breach, damage, no justification. Why could Leathem not sue for the two servants who left? They gave due notice, so no contract was broken. How did the union pressure Munce? By threatening to call out his workmen if Leathem's beef arrived. Which provision gives trade unions immunity? Industrial Relations Code, 2020, s. 16. Which Constitutional right supports freedom of trade? Article 19(1)(g). Under which section can compensation be claimed for anti-competitive conduct? Competition Act, 2002, s. 53N.

law-of-torts-u4-t9.subtitle: The tort of combining with others to injure a person, or to use unlawful means against him, causing him damage

en.inOneMinute: Civil conspiracy is a tort committed when two or more persons combine to injure the plaintiff and damage results. It is both a crime and a tort; as a tort, actual damage must be proved. Lord Brampton in Quinn v. Leathem (1901): "A conspiracy consists of an unlawful combination of two or more persons to do that which is contrary to law, or to do that which is wrongful and harmful towards another person. It may be punished criminally by indictment, or civilly by an action on the case in the nature of conspiracy if damage has been occasioned to the person against whom it is directed." Two kinds (See Diagram 1 ): Lawful-means conspiracy – the combination uses acts that would be lawful if done by one person, but its purpose is to injure the plaintiff, not to advance the combiners ' own legitimate interests ( Quinn v. Leathem ). Unlawful-means conspiracy – the combination uses unlawful means (intimidation, violence, procuring breaches of contract) to damage the plaintiff ( Mogul Steamship , Lord Halsbury). Why numbers matter: "numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not" (Lord Lindley, Quinn ). Defence of legitimate interest: a combination to protect or extend one's own trade is lawful even if it ruins a rival, so long as the means are lawful ( Mogul Steamship , 1891). The loss is then damnum sine injuria – damage without legal injury (Lord Watson). In India, criminal conspiracy is defined in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 61; the tort is a common law tort. Agreements between competitors ( cartels ) are also controlled by the Competition Act, 2002, s. 3.
legalProvision: There is no statute creating the tort of conspiracy in India; it is a common law tort. The related provisions are:

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 61(1) – "When two or more persons agree with the common object to do, or cause to be done— (a) an illegal act; or (b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof." Explanation: "It is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of such agreement, or is merely incidental to that object." BNS, s. 61(2) – punishment: for a conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment of two years or more, as if the party had abetted the offence (where no express provision exists); otherwise, imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both. Competition Act, 2002, s. 3(1) – no enterprise or person "shall enter into any agreement ... which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India"; s. 3(3) applies to agreements between enterprises or persons "including cartels, engaged in identical or similar" trade; s. 2(c) – "cartel" includes "an association of producers, sellers, distributors, traders or service providers" (definition opening words). Competition Act, 2002, s. 53N(1) – compensation "for any loss or damage shown to have been suffered ... as a result of any contravention of the provisions of Chapter II". Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – residuary article: three years from "When the right to sue accrues".
en.meaning: Civil conspiracy – an agreement or combination of two or more persons to injure the plaintiff, carried out and causing him damage, either (a) by lawful means with the purpose of injuring him, or (b) by unlawful means. Combination – an agreement of two or more persons; Willes J. in Mulcahy v. R. (quoted by Lord Brampton): "A conspiracy consists not merely in the intention of two or more, but in the agreement of two or more to do an unlawful act, or to do a lawful act by unlawful means ... The number and the compact give weight and cause danger." Lawful-means conspiracy – a combination using acts lawful in themselves, but "in pursuit merely of a malicious purpose to injure another" (Lord Shand, Quinn ). Unlawful-means conspiracy – a combination "to carry out an object not in itself unlawful by unlawful means" (Lord Brampton, Quinn ), or to procure unlawful acts: "a combination to procure people to do such acts is a conspiracy and unlawful" (Lord Halsbury, Mogul ). Damnum sine injuria – loss without the infringement of a legal right; not actionable. Lord Watson in Mogul : if "neither the end contemplated by the agreement, nor the means used for its attainment were contrary to law, the loss suffered by the appellants was damnum sine injuria."
keyPoints: Conspiracy needs two or more persons in agreement. As a tort, damage must be proved. Lawful-means conspiracy: purpose to injure, not to advance own interest ( Quinn ). Unlawful-means conspiracy: unlawful means used ( Mogul , Lord Halsbury). Combining to advance one's own trade by lawful means is lawful ( Mogul ). Loss without legal injury is damnum sine injuria. "Numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not." Allen v. Flood : no combination, own-interest purpose – no tort. Criminal conspiracy: BNS s. 61. Cartels: Competition Act s. 3.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Union officials, after Leathem refused to dismiss non-union assistants, combined to stop his
caseLaws.facts: The jury found a conspiracy to injure and awarded £200. Principle: "A conspiracy consists of an unlawful combination of two or more persons to do that which is contrary to law, or to do that which is wrongful and harmful towards another person" (Lord Brampton); a combination "for the sole purpose of injuring the plaintiff in his trade" is unlawful (Lord Shand); "numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not" (Lord Lindley). Why it matters: The leading authority on civil conspiracy to injure.
Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. [1892] AC 25 (House of Lords, decided 18 December 1891)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Shipowners combined to keep the Hankow tea trade, using rebates to loyal shippers, extra ship
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The plaintiffs had to show "either that the object of the agreement was unlawful, or that illegal methods were resorted to"; neither was shown, so the loss "was damnum sine injuria" (Lord Watson). A combination to procure intimidation, violence, molestation or breaches of contract would be "a conspiracy and unlawful" (Lord Halsbury). Why it matters: A combination to advance one's own trade by lawful means is not a conspiracy.
Scottish Co-operative Society v. Glasgow Fleshers' Association – as described by Lord Lindley in Quinn v. Leathem

caseLaws.name: Facts: Butchers threatened salesmen that they would not buy from them if they sold meat to the plain
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "There was nothing unlawful in this"; no cause of action, though the defendants "were acting in concert". Why it matters: Shows that a combined threat to do a lawful act, for one's own trade interest, is not actionable.

selfTest.q: Define civil conspiracy. A combination of two or more persons to injure the plaintiff, by lawful means with a purpose to injure, or by unlawful means, causing damage. Who defined conspiracy in Quinn v. Leathem?
selfTest.a: Lord Brampton. Why did the plaintiffs lose in Mogul ? The object (advancing their own trade) and the means were lawful. What is damnum sine injuria? Loss without violation of a legal right; not actionable. What was the purpose of the defendants in Quinn ? To injure Leathem in his trade. What did Lord Lindley say about numbers? Numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not. Must damage be proved in civil conspiracy? Yes. Which BNS section defines criminal conspiracy? Section 61. Was the butchers' threat in Scottish Co-operative Society actionable? No; there was nothing unlawful in it. Can one person alone commit conspiracy? No.

te.inOneMinute: సివిల్ కుట్ర అంటే ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది కలిసి వాదికి హాని చేయడానికి ఒప్పుకుని, నష్టం కలిగించినప్పుడు జరిగే టార్ట్. ఇది నేరమూ, టార్ట్ కూడా; టార్ట్‌గా వాస్తవ నష్టం నిరూపించాలి. Quinn v. Leathem (1901) లో Lord Brampton: "A conspiracy consists of an unlawful combination of two or more persons to do that which is contrary to law, or to do that which is wrongful and harmful towards another person. It may be punished criminally by indictment, or civilly by an action on the case in the nature of conspiracy if damage has been occasioned to the person against whom it is directed." (అర్థం: చట్టానికి విరుద్ధమైనది, లేదా మరొకరికి తప్పుడు, హానికరమైనది చేయడానికి ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది చట్టవిరుద్ధ కలయికే కుట్ర. దీన్ని నేరపరంగా అభియోగంతో శిక్షించవచ్చు, లేదా ఎవరిపై నిర్దేశించబడిందో ఆ వ్యక్తికి నష్టం కలిగితే కుట్ర స్వభావంలోని దావాతో సివిల్‌గా శిక్షించవచ్చు.) రెండు రకాలు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): చట్టబద్ధ మార్గాల కుట్ర – ఒక్కరు చేస్తే చట్టబద్ధమైన చర్యలనే కలయిక ఉపయోగిస్తుంది, కానీ దాని ఉద్దేశం వాదికి హాని చేయడం , కలిసినవారి స్వంత న్యాయమైన ప్రయోజనాలను ముందుకు తీసుకెళ్లడం కాదు ( Quinn v. Leathem ). చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాల కుట్ర – వాదికి నష్టం కలిగించడానికి కలయిక చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాలు (బెదిరింపు, హింస, ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘనలకు ప్రేరేపణ) ఉపయోగిస్తుంది ( Mogul Steamship , Lord Halsbury). సంఖ్య ఎందుకు ముఖ్యం: "numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not" (అర్థం: ఒక్కరు చేయలేని చోట అనేకులు వేధించి బలవంతం చేయగలరు) (Lord Lindley, Quinn ). న్యాయమైన ప్రయోజన రక్షణ: మార్గాలు చట్టబద్ధమైనంత కాలం, ప్రత్యర్థిని నాశనం చేసినా, తమ స్వంత వ్యాపారాన్ని రక్షించుకోవడానికి లేదా విస్తరించుకోవడానికి కలయిక చట్టబద్ధమే ( Mogul Steamship , 1891). అప్పుడు నష్టం చట్టపరమైన హాని లేని నష్టం (damnum sine injuria) – చట్టపరమైన గాయం లేని నష్టం (Lord Watson). భారతదేశంలో, నేరపూరిత కుట్రను భారతీయ న్యాయ సంహిత, 2023, s. 61 నిర్వచిస్తుంది; టార్ట్ కామన్ లా టార్ట్. పోటీదారుల మధ్య ఒప్పందాలను (కార్టెల్‌లు) పోటీ చట్టం, 2002, s. 3 కూడా నియంత్రిస్తుంది.
te.meaning: సివిల్ కుట్ర – వాదికి హాని చేయడానికి ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది చేసుకున్న ఒప్పందం లేదా కలయిక, అమలు చేయబడి అతనికి నష్టం కలిగించడం: (a) హాని చేయాలనే ఉద్దేశంతో చట్టబద్ధ మార్గాల ద్వారా, లేదా (b) చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాల ద్వారా. కలయిక – ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది ఒప్పందం; Mulcahy v. R. లో Willes J. (Lord Brampton ఉటంకించారు): "A conspiracy consists not merely in the intention of two or more, but in the agreement of two or more to do an unlawful act, or to do a lawful act by unlawful means ... The number and the compact give weight and cause danger." (అర్థం: కుట్ర అంటే ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది ఉద్దేశం మాత్రమే కాదు, చట్టవిరుద్ధ చర్య చేయడానికి, లేదా చట్టబద్ధ చర్యను చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాలతో చేయడానికి ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది ఒప్పందం ... సంఖ్య, ఒప్పందం బలాన్ని ఇచ్చి ప్రమాదాన్ని కలిగిస్తాయి.) చట్టబద్ధ మార్గాల కుట్ర – స్వతహాగా చట్టబద్ధమైన చర్యలను ఉపయోగించే, కానీ "in pursuit merely of a malicious purpose to injure another" (అర్థం: మరొకరికి హాని చేయాలనే దురుద్దేశాన్ని మాత్రమే అనుసరిస్తూ) ఉన్న కలయిక (Lord Shand, Quinn ). చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాల కుట్ర – "to carry out an object not in itself unlawful by unlawful means" (అర్థం: స్వతహాగా చట్టవిరుద్ధం కాని లక్ష్యాన్ని చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాలతో సాధించడానికి) కలయిక (Lord Brampton, Quinn ), లేదా చట్టవిరుద్ధ చర్యలకు ప్రేరేపణ: "a combination to procure people to do such acts is a conspiracy and unlawful" (అర్థం: అలాంటి చర్యలు చేయించడానికి కలయిక కుట్ర, చట్టవిరుద్ధం) (Lord Halsbury, Mogul ). చట్టపరమైన హాని లేని నష్టం – చట్టపరమైన హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన లేకుండా నష్టం; దావా యోగ్యం కాదు. Mogul లో Lord Watson: "neither the end contemplated by the agreement, nor the means used for its attainment were contrary to law" (అర్థం: ఒప్పందం లక్ష్యంగా పెట్టుకున్న ఫలితం గానీ, దాన్ని సాధించడానికి ఉపయోగించిన మార్గాలు గానీ చట్టానికి విరుద్ధం కాకపోతే), "the loss suffered by the appellants was damnum sine injuria" (అర్థం: అప్పీలుదారులు అనుభవించిన నష్టం చట్టపరమైన హాని లేని నష్టం).
keyPoints: కుట్రకు ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది ఒప్పందం అవసరం. టార్ట్‌గా నష్టం నిరూపించాలి. చట్టబద్ధ మార్గాల కుట్ర: హాని చేసే ఉద్దేశం, స్వంత ప్రయోజనం కాదు ( Quinn ). చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాల కుట్ర: చట్టవిరుద్ధ మార్గాల వినియోగం ( Mogul , Lord Halsbury). చట్టబద్ధ మార్గాలతో స్వంత వ్యాపారాన్ని ముందుకు తీసుకెళ్లడానికి కలవడం చట్టబద్ధం ( Mogul ). చట్టపరమైన హాని లేని నష్టం damnum sine injuria. "Numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not." Allen v. Flood : కలయిక లేదు, స్వంత ప్రయోజన ఉద్దేశం – టార్ట్ లేదు. నేరపూరిత కుట్ర: BNS s. 61. కార్టెల్‌లు: పోటీ చట్టం s. 3.

selfTest.a: Lord Brampton. Mogul లో వాదులు ఎందుకు ఓడిపోయారు? లక్ష్యం (స్వంత వ్యాపారాన్ని ముందుకు తీసుకెళ్లడం), మార్గాలు చట్టబద్ధమైనవి. Damnum sine injuria అంటే ఏమిటి? చట్టపరమైన హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన లేని నష్టం; దావా యోగ్యం కాదు. Quinn లో ప్రతివాదుల ఉద్దేశం ఏమిటి? Leathem కు అతని వ్యాపారంలో హాని చేయడం. సంఖ్య గురించి Lord Lindley ఏమన్నారు? ఒక్కరు చేయలేని చోట అనేకులు వేధించి బలవంతం చేయగలరు. సివిల్ కుట్రలో నష్టం నిరూపించాలా? అవును. నేరపూరిత కుట్రను నిర్వచించే BNS సెక్షన్ ఏది? Section 61. Scottish Co-operative Society లో కసాయి వ్యాపారుల బెదిరింపు దావా యోగ్యమా? కాదు; అందులో చట్టవిరుద్ధం ఏమీ లేదు. ఒక్కరే కుట్ర చేయగలరా? లేదు.

hi.inOneMinute: Civil conspiracy is a tort committed when two or more persons combine to injure the plaintiff and damage results. It is both a crime and a tort; as a tort, actual damage must be proved. Lord Brampton in Quinn v. Leathem (1901): "A conspiracy consists of an unlawful combination of two or more persons to do that which is contrary to law, or to do that which is wrongful and harmful towards another person. It may be punished criminally by indictment, or civilly by an action on the case in the nature of conspiracy if damage has been occasioned to the person against whom it is directed." Two kinds (See Diagram 1 ): Lawful-means conspiracy – the combination uses acts that would be lawful if done by one person, but its purpose is to injure the plaintiff, not to advance the combiners ' own legitimate interests ( Quinn v. Leathem ). Unlawful-means conspiracy – the combination uses unlawful means (intimidation, violence, procuring breaches of contract) to damage the plaintiff ( Mogul Steamship , Lord Halsbury). Why numbers matter: "numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not" (Lord Lindley, Quinn ). Defence of legitimate interest: a combination to protect or extend one's own trade is lawful even if it ruins a rival, so long as the means are lawful ( Mogul Steamship , 1891). The loss is then damnum sine injuria – damage without legal injury (Lord Watson). In India, criminal conspiracy is defined in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 61; the tort is a common law tort. Agreements between competitors ( cartels ) are also controlled by the Competition Act, 2002, s. 3.
legalProvision: There is no statute creating the tort of conspiracy in India; it is a common law tort. The related provisions are:

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 61(1) – "When two or more persons agree with the common object to do, or cause to be done— (a) an illegal act; or (b) an act which is not illegal by illegal means, such an agreement is designated a criminal conspiracy: Provided that no agreement except an agreement to commit an offence shall amount to a criminal conspiracy unless some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties to such agreement in pursuance thereof." Explanation: "It is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of such agreement, or is merely incidental to that object." BNS, s. 61(2) – punishment: for a conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment of two years or more, as if the party had abetted the offence (where no express provision exists); otherwise, imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both. Competition Act, 2002, s. 3(1) – no enterprise or person "shall enter into any agreement ... which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India"; s. 3(3) applies to agreements between enterprises or persons "including cartels, engaged in identical or similar" trade; s. 2(c) – "cartel" includes "an association of producers, sellers, distributors, traders or service providers" (definition opening words). Competition Act, 2002, s. 53N(1) – compensation "for any loss or damage shown to have been suffered ... as a result of any contravention of the provisions of Chapter II". Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 113 – residuary article: three years from "When the right to sue accrues".
hi.meaning: Civil conspiracy – an agreement or combination of two or more persons to injure the plaintiff, carried out and causing him damage, either (a) by lawful means with the purpose of injuring him, or (b) by unlawful means. Combination – an agreement of two or more persons; Willes J. in Mulcahy v. R. (quoted by Lord Brampton): "A conspiracy consists not merely in the intention of two or more, but in the agreement of two or more to do an unlawful act, or to do a lawful act by unlawful means ... The number and the compact give weight and cause danger." Lawful-means conspiracy – a combination using acts lawful in themselves, but "in pursuit merely of a malicious purpose to injure another" (Lord Shand, Quinn ). Unlawful-means conspiracy – a combination "to carry out an object not in itself unlawful by unlawful means" (Lord Brampton, Quinn ), or to procure unlawful acts: "a combination to procure people to do such acts is a conspiracy and unlawful" (Lord Halsbury, Mogul ). Damnum sine injuria – loss without the infringement of a legal right; not actionable. Lord Watson in Mogul : if "neither the end contemplated by the agreement, nor the means used for its attainment were contrary to law, the loss suffered by the appellants was damnum sine injuria."
keyPoints: Conspiracy needs two or more persons in agreement. As a tort, damage must be proved. Lawful-means conspiracy: purpose to injure, not to advance own interest ( Quinn ). Unlawful-means conspiracy: unlawful means used ( Mogul , Lord Halsbury). Combining to advance one's own trade by lawful means is lawful ( Mogul ). Loss without legal injury is damnum sine injuria. "Numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not." Allen v. Flood : no combination, own-interest purpose – no tort. Criminal conspiracy: BNS s. 61. Cartels: Competition Act s. 3.

caseLaws.facts: Quinn v. Leathem [1901] UKHL 2 (House of Lords, 5 August 1901)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Union officials, after Leathem refused to dismiss non-union assistants, combined to stop his
caseLaws.facts: The jury found a conspiracy to injure and awarded £200. Principle: "A conspiracy consists of an unlawful combination of two or more persons to do that which is contrary to law, or to do that which is wrongful and harmful towards another person" (Lord Brampton); a combination "for the sole purpose of injuring the plaintiff in his trade" is unlawful (Lord Shand); "numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not" (Lord Lindley). Why it matters: The leading authority on civil conspiracy to injure.
Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. [1892] AC 25 (House of Lords, decided 18 December 1891)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Shipowners combined to keep the Hankow tea trade, using rebates to loyal shippers, extra ship
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The plaintiffs had to show "either that the object of the agreement was unlawful, or that illegal methods were resorted to"; neither was shown, so the loss "was damnum sine injuria" (Lord Watson). A combination to procure intimidation, violence, molestation or breaches of contract would be "a conspiracy and unlawful" (Lord Halsbury). Why it matters: A combination to advance one's own trade by lawful means is not a conspiracy.
Scottish Co-operative Society v. Glasgow Fleshers' Association – as described by Lord Lindley in Quinn v. Leathem

caseLaws.name: Facts: Butchers threatened salesmen that they would not buy from them if they sold meat to the plain
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "There was nothing unlawful in this"; no cause of action, though the defendants "were acting in concert". Why it matters: Shows that a combined threat to do a lawful act, for one's own trade interest, is not actionable.

selfTest.q: Define civil conspiracy. A combination of two or more persons to injure the plaintiff, by lawful means with a purpose to injure, or by unlawful means, causing damage. Who defined conspiracy in Quinn v. Leathem?
selfTest.a: Lord Brampton. Why did the plaintiffs lose in Mogul ? The object (advancing their own trade) and the means were lawful. What is damnum sine injuria? Loss without violation of a legal right; not actionable. What was the purpose of the defendants in Quinn ? To injure Leathem in his trade. What did Lord Lindley say about numbers? Numbers may annoy and coerce where one may not. Must damage be proved in civil conspiracy? Yes. Which BNS section defines criminal conspiracy? Section 61. Was the butchers' threat in Scottish Co-operative Society actionable? No; there was nothing unlawful in it. Can one person alone commit conspiracy? No.

en.meaning:
What are the three essentials of the tort of negligence?

Explanation. Negligence requires: (1) a duty of care owed by the defendant to the plaintiff, (2) breach of that duty by falling below the standard of care, and (3) damage caused to the plaintiff by that breach.

In Donoghue v Stevenson (1932), Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle' established that a duty of care is owed to

Explanation. Lord Atkin's neighbour principle extended the duty of care beyond contractual relationships to anyone reasonably foreseeable as likely to be affected by the defendant's acts or omissions.

Why did the manufacturer in Donoghue v Stevenson owe a duty of care to the consumer despite no contract between them?

Explanation. The House of Lords held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer where the product reaches them in the form it left the manufacturer, without reasonable possibility of intermediate examination.

What legal test did Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington Hospital Management Committee (1969) apply to determine causation?
