law-of-torts-u4-t6.subtitle: The tort of making a false statement, with malice, that causes loss to another's trade, goods or property interests

en.inOneMinute: Injurious falsehood (also called malicious falsehood) is a false statement, made maliciously, about the plaintiff's goods, property or business, which causes him actual loss. It protects a person's business and economic interests , not his personal reputation. The statement need not be defamatory at all. The leading case is Ratcliffe v. Evans (1892), where Bowen L.J. said that "an action will lie for written or oral falsehoods, not actionable per se nor even defamatory, where they are maliciously published, where they are calculated in the ordinary course of things to produce, and where they do produce, actual damage". Three elements (See Diagram 1 ): a false statement about the plaintiff's goods, property or business; published maliciously – "without just occasion or excuse"; actual damage to the plaintiff ("damage is the gist of the action"). Main forms: slander of title (false statements about a person's title to property), slander of goods (false statements about the quality of goods), and other false statements about a business (as in Ratcliffe , where a newspaper falsely said the plaintiff's firm no longer existed). Damage: the plaintiff must prove special damage – actual loss – but where the nature of the statement makes it impossible to name lost customers, a general loss of business may be proved ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ). In India, false statements disparaging a rival's goods or trade are also an "unfair trade practice" under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(47)(i)(j).
legalProvision: There is no statute creating this tort in India; it is a common law tort. The related provisions are:

Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(47) – "unfair trade practice" means a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice, including "(i) making any statement, whether orally or in writing or by visible representation including by means of electronic record, which— ... (j) gives false or misleading facts disparaging the goods, services or trade of another person." Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(28) – "misleading advertisement" includes an advertisement which "(iii) conveys an express or implied representation which, if made by the manufacturer or seller or service provider thereof, would constitute an unfair trade practice". Trade Marks Act, 1999, s. 29(8) – a registered trade mark is infringed by any advertising of that trade mark if such advertising "(a) takes unfair advantage of and is contrary to honest practices in industrial or commercial matters; or (b) is detrimental to its distinctive character; or (c) is against the reputation of the trade mark." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(1) – "a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication."
en.meaning: Injurious falsehood – an action "for damage wilfully and intentionally done without just occasion or excuse" by a false statement about the plaintiff's goods or business; "not one of libel or of slander, but an action on the case ... analogous to an action for slander of title" ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ). Slander of title – a false and malicious statement denying or casting doubt on the plaintiff's title to property (land or goods), causing loss – for example, at an auction ( Hargrave v. Le Breton , as described in Ratcliffe ). Slander of goods – a false and malicious statement about the quality or nature of the plaintiff's goods, causing loss (standard doctrine; Ratcliffe speaks of falsehoods "about a man's goods or business"). Malice (here) – publishing the statement without just occasion or excuse, for example knowing it to be false or not caring whether it is true, or with an improper motive (standard doctrine). In the legal sense, malice "means a wrongful act done intentionally without just cause or excuse" ( WBSEB v. Dilip Kumar Ray , 2006). Special damage – in this tort , "the actual and temporal loss which has, in fact, occurred" ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ), as opposed to general damage which the law presumes.
keyPoints: Injurious falsehood protects business and property, not personal reputation. Elements: false statement, malice, actual damage. The statement need not be defamatory ( Ratcliffe ). Oral or written makes no difference. Plaintiff proves falsity and malice. Actual damage is the gist; general loss of business may be proved where appropriate. Forms: slander of title, slander of goods, other business falsehoods. Puffing is not actionable. Disparaging false facts are an unfair trade practice (CPA 2019 s. 2(47)(i)(j)). Remedies: damages and injunction.

caseLaws.facts: Ratcliffe v. Evans [1892] 2 QB 524 (Court of Appeal, 26 May 1892; Lord Esher M.R., Bowen and Fry L.JJ.; judgment of the Court read by Bowen L.J.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff carried on business at Hawarden as engineer and boiler-maker under the name "Ra
caseLaws.facts: The defendant's newspaper, the County Herald , falsely stated that he had ceased business and that the firm no longer existed. The jury found the words were not libellous but not published bona fide, and that the business suffered £120 of injury; the plaintiff proved only a general loss of business. Principle: "an action will lie for written or oral falsehoods, not actionable per se nor even defamatory, where they are maliciously published, where they are calculated in the ordinary course of things to produce, and where they do produce, actual damage"; evidence of a general decline of business is admissible where the falsehood is by its nature likely to cause it. Why it matters: The leading statement of the elements of injurious falsehood and of how damage may be proved.
Hargrave v. Le Breton (1769) 4 Burr 2422 – as described in Ratcliffe v. Evans

selfTest.q: What are the elements of injurious falsehood?
selfTest.a: A false statement about the plaintiff's goods or business, published maliciously, causing actual damage. Must the statement be defamatory? No (Ratcliffe v. Evans). What did the newspaper say in Ratcliffe v. Evans ? That the plaintiff had ceased business and the firm Ratcliffe & Sons no longer existed. How much did the jury award in Ratcliffe ? £120. Can general loss of business be proved? Yes, where the falsehood by its nature is likely to cause a general loss and lost customers cannot be named. What is slander of title? A false and malicious statement about the plaintiff's title to property, causing loss. Who must prove falsity? The plaintiff. Is a trader's boast that his goods are best actionable? No; it is puffing. Which CPA 2019 provision covers disparaging a rival's goods? Section 2(47)(i)(j). How does injurious falsehood differ from passing off? It is a false statement about the plaintiff's goods; passing off is presenting one's goods as the plaintiff's.

te.inOneMinute: హానికర అసత్యం (దురుద్దేశపూర్వక అసత్యం అని కూడా అంటారు) అంటే వాది వస్తువులు, ఆస్తి లేదా వ్యాపారం గురించి దురుద్దేశంతో చేసిన తప్పుడు ప్రకటన, దాని వల్ల అతనికి వాస్తవ నష్టం. ఇది వ్యక్తి వ్యాపార, ఆర్థిక ప్రయోజనాలను రక్షిస్తుంది, వ్యక్తిగత ప్రతిష్ఠను కాదు. ప్రకటన పరువు నష్టకరం కావాల్సిన అవసరమే లేదు. ప్రముఖ కేసు Ratcliffe v. Evans (1892); Bowen L.J. ఇలా అన్నారు: "an action will lie for written or oral falsehoods, not actionable per se nor even defamatory, where they are maliciously published, where they are calculated in the ordinary course of things to produce, and where they do produce, actual damage" (అర్థం: స్వతహాగా దావా యోగ్యం కాని, పరువు నష్టకరం కూడా కాని రాతపూర్వక లేదా మౌఖిక అసత్యాలు దురుద్దేశంతో ప్రచురించబడి, సాధారణ క్రమంలో వాస్తవ నష్టం కలిగించేలా ఉండి, నిజంగా నష్టం కలిగిస్తే దావా వేయవచ్చు). మూడు అంశాలు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): వాది వస్తువులు, ఆస్తి లేదా వ్యాపారం గురించి తప్పుడు ప్రకటన; దురుద్దేశంతో ప్రచురణ – "without just occasion or excuse" (అర్థం: న్యాయమైన సందర్భం లేదా సాకు లేకుండా); వాదికి వాస్తవ నష్టం ("damage is the gist of the action" (అర్థం: నష్టమే దావా సారాంశం)). ప్రధాన రూపాలు: హక్కుపై అపవాదు (ఆస్తిపై వ్యక్తి హక్కు గురించి తప్పుడు ప్రకటనలు), వస్తువులపై అపవాదు (వస్తువుల నాణ్యత గురించి తప్పుడు ప్రకటనలు), వ్యాపారం గురించి ఇతర తప్పుడు ప్రకటనలు ( Ratcliffe లో వాది సంస్థ ఇక లేదని ఒక వార్తాపత్రిక తప్పుగా చెప్పినట్లు). నష్టం: వాది ప్రత్యేక నష్టం – వాస్తవ నష్టం – నిరూపించాలి; కానీ ప్రకటన స్వభావం వల్ల కోల్పోయిన కస్టమర్ల పేర్లు చెప్పడం అసాధ్యమైనచోట, వ్యాపారంలో సాధారణ నష్టం నిరూపించవచ్చు ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ). భారతదేశంలో, ప్రత్యర్థి వస్తువులు లేదా వ్యాపారాన్ని కించపరిచే తప్పుడు ప్రకటనలు వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019, s. 2(47)(i)(j) కింద "unfair trade practice" (అర్థం: అన్యాయ వాణిజ్య పద్ధతి) కూడా.
te.meaning: హానికర అసత్యం – వాది వస్తువులు లేదా వ్యాపారం గురించి తప్పుడు ప్రకటనతో "for damage wilfully and intentionally done without just occasion or excuse" (అర్థం: న్యాయమైన సందర్భం లేదా సాకు లేకుండా ఇష్టపూర్వకంగా, ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా కలిగించిన నష్టానికి) దావా; ఇది "not one of libel or of slander, but an action on the case ... analogous to an action for slander of title" (అర్థం: లిఖిత లేదా మౌఖిక పరువు నష్ట దావా కాదు, హక్కుపై అపవాదు దావాకు సమానమైన action on the case) ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ). హక్కుపై అపవాదు – వాదికి ఆస్తి (భూమి లేదా వస్తువులు) పై ఉన్న హక్కును తిరస్కరించే లేదా దానిపై సందేహం కలిగించే తప్పుడు, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రకటన, నష్టం కలిగించడం – ఉదా: వేలంలో ( Hargrave v. Le Breton , Ratcliffe లో వర్ణించినట్లు). వస్తువులపై అపవాదు – వాది వస్తువుల నాణ్యత లేదా స్వభావం గురించి తప్పుడు, దురుద్దేశపూర్వక ప్రకటన, నష్టం కలిగించడం (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం; Ratcliffe "about a man's goods or business" (అర్థం: ఒకరి వస్తువులు లేదా వ్యాపారం గురించి) అసత్యాల గురించి మాట్లాడుతుంది). దురుద్దేశం (ఇక్కడ) – న్యాయమైన సందర్భం లేదా సాకు లేకుండా ప్రకటన ప్రచురించడం, ఉదా: అది అబద్ధమని తెలిసి, లేదా నిజమో కాదో పట్టించుకోకుండా, లేదా అనుచిత ఉద్దేశంతో (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం). చట్టపరమైన అర్థంలో దురుద్దేశం "means a wrongful act done intentionally without just cause or excuse" (అర్థం: న్యాయమైన కారణం లేదా సాకు లేకుండా ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా చేసిన తప్పుడు చర్య) ( WBSEB v. Dilip Kumar Ray , 2006). ప్రత్యేక నష్టం – ఈ టార్ట్‌లో "the actual and temporal loss which has, in fact, occurred" (అర్థం: నిజంగా జరిగిన వాస్తవ, భౌతిక నష్టం) ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ); చట్టం ఊహించే సాధారణ నష్టానికి భిన్నం.
keyPoints: హానికర అసత్యం వ్యాపారాన్ని, ఆస్తిని రక్షిస్తుంది, వ్యక్తిగత ప్రతిష్ఠను కాదు. అంశాలు: తప్పుడు ప్రకటన, దురుద్దేశం, వాస్తవ నష్టం. ప్రకటన పరువు నష్టకరం కానవసరం లేదు ( Ratcliffe ). మౌఖికమా, రాతపూర్వకమా అనేదానిలో తేడా లేదు. వాది అసత్యాన్ని, దురుద్దేశాన్ని నిరూపిస్తాడు. వాస్తవ నష్టమే సారాంశం; సరైనచోట వ్యాపారంలో సాధారణ నష్టం నిరూపించవచ్చు. రూపాలు: హక్కుపై అపవాదు, వస్తువులపై అపవాదు, ఇతర వ్యాపార అసత్యాలు. గొప్పలు దావా యోగ్యం కావు. కించపరిచే తప్పుడు వాస్తవాలు అన్యాయ వాణిజ్య పద్ధతి (CPA 2019 s. 2(47)(i)(j)). పరిష్కారాలు: నష్టపరిహారం, నిషేధాజ్ఞ.

selfTest.q: హానికర అసత్యం అంశాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: వాది వస్తువులు లేదా వ్యాపారం గురించి తప్పుడు ప్రకటన, దురుద్దేశంతో ప్రచురణ, వాస్తవ నష్టం. ప్రకటన పరువు నష్టకరం కావాలా? అవసరం లేదు (Ratcliffe v. Evans). Ratcliffe v. Evans లో వార్తాపత్రిక ఏమి చెప్పింది? వాది వ్యాపారం ఆపేశాడని, Ratcliffe & Sons సంస్థ ఇక లేదని. hi.inOneMinute: Injurious falsehood (also called malicious falsehood) is a false statement, made maliciously, about the plaintiff's goods, property or business, which causes him actual loss. It protects a person's business and economic interests , not his personal reputation. The statement need not be defamatory at all. The leading case is Ratcliffe v. Evans (1892), where Bowen L.J. said that "an action will lie for written or oral falsehoods, not actionable per se nor even defamatory, where they are maliciously published, where they are calculated in the ordinary course of things to produce, and where they do produce, actual damage". Three elements (See Diagram 1 ): a false statement about the plaintiff's goods, property or business; published maliciously – "without just occasion or excuse"; actual damage to the plaintiff ("damage is the gist of the action"). Main forms: slander of title (false statements about a person's title to property), slander of goods (false statements about the quality of goods), and other false statements about a business (as in Ratcliffe , where a newspaper falsely said the plaintiff's firm no longer existed). Damage: the plaintiff must prove special damage – actual loss – but where the nature of the statement makes it impossible to name lost customers, a general loss of business may be proved ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ). In India, false statements disparaging a rival's goods or trade are also an "unfair trade practice" under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(47)(i)(j).
legalProvision: There is no statute creating this tort in India; it is a common law tort. The related provisions are:

Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(47) – "unfair trade practice" means a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice, including "(i) making any statement, whether orally or in writing or by visible representation including by means of electronic record, which— ... (j) gives false or misleading facts disparaging the goods, services or trade of another person." Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(28) – "misleading advertisement" includes an advertisement which "(iii) conveys an express or implied representation which, if made by the manufacturer or seller or service provider thereof, would constitute an unfair trade practice". Trade Marks Act, 1999, s. 29(8) – a registered trade mark is infringed by any advertising of that trade mark if such advertising "(a) takes unfair advantage of and is contrary to honest practices in industrial or commercial matters; or (b) is detrimental to its distinctive character; or (c) is against the reputation of the trade mark." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(1) – "a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication."
hi.meaning: Injurious falsehood – an action "for damage wilfully and intentionally done without just occasion or excuse" by a false statement about the plaintiff's goods or business; "not one of libel or of slander, but an action on the case ... analogous to an action for slander of title" ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ). Slander of title – a false and malicious statement denying or casting doubt on the plaintiff's title to property (land or goods), causing loss – for example, at an auction ( Hargrave v. Le Breton , as described in Ratcliffe ). Slander of goods – a false and malicious statement about the quality or nature of the plaintiff's goods, causing loss (standard doctrine; Ratcliffe speaks of falsehoods "about a man's goods or business"). Malice (here) – publishing the statement without just occasion or excuse, for example knowing it to be false or not caring whether it is true, or with an improper motive (standard doctrine). In the legal sense, malice "means a wrongful act done intentionally without just cause or excuse" ( WBSEB v. Dilip Kumar Ray , 2006). Special damage – in this tort , "the actual and temporal loss which has, in fact, occurred" ( Ratcliffe v. Evans ), as opposed to general damage which the law presumes.
keyPoints: Injurious falsehood protects business and property, not personal reputation. Elements: false statement, malice, actual damage. The statement need not be defamatory ( Ratcliffe ). Oral or written makes no difference. Plaintiff proves falsity and malice. Actual damage is the gist; general loss of business may be proved where appropriate. Forms: slander of title, slander of goods, other business falsehoods. Puffing is not actionable. Disparaging false facts are an unfair trade practice (CPA 2019 s. 2(47)(i)(j)). Remedies: damages and injunction.

The jury found the words were not libellous but not published bona fide, and that the business suffered £120 of injury; the plaintiff proved only a general loss of business. Principle: "an action will lie for written or oral falsehoods, not actionable per se nor even defamatory, where they are maliciously published, where they are calculated in the ordinary course of things to produce, and where they do produce, actual damage"; evidence of a general decline of business is admissible where the falsehood is by its nature likely to cause it. Why it matters: The leading statement of the elements of injurious falsehood and of how damage may be proved.

selfTest.q: What are the elements of injurious falsehood?
selfTest.a: A false statement about the plaintiff's goods or business, published maliciously, causing actual damage. Must the statement be defamatory? No (Ratcliffe v. Evans). What did the newspaper say in Ratcliffe v. Evans ? That the plaintiff had ceased business and the firm Ratcliffe & Sons no longer existed. How much did the jury award in Ratcliffe ? £120. Can general loss of business be proved? Yes, where the falsehood by its nature is likely to cause a general loss and lost customers cannot be named. What is slander of title? A false and malicious statement about the plaintiff's title to property, causing loss. Who must prove falsity? The plaintiff. Is a trader's boast that his goods are best actionable? No; it is puffing. Which CPA 2019 provision covers disparaging a rival's goods? Section 2(47)(i)(j). How does injurious falsehood differ from passing off? It is a false statement about the plaintiff's goods; passing off is presenting one's goods as the plaintiff's.

law-of-torts-u4-t10.subtitle: Old actions for loss of services and consortium, enticement and harbouring, and claims when a family member is killed

en.inOneMinute: Torts affecting family relations are wrongs which harm a person through injury to, death of, or interference with a member of his family – a spouse, child or parent. Old common law actions (See Diagram 1 ): Loss of services ( per quod servitium amisit ) – a parent (or master) could sue a person who injured, seduced or enticed away a child (or servant), for the loss of the child's services. Loss of consortium ( per quod consortium amisit ) – a husband could sue for the loss of his wife's company, help and comfort caused by injury to her. Enticement and harbouring – persuading a wife or child to leave the home, or keeping them away. These rest on "ancient and now outmoded concepts of the quasi-proprietorial rights of husbands over their wives, parents over their children or employers over their menial servants" (Lord Oliver, Alcock , 1991); in England they were abolished by the Administration of Justice Act 1982. Death of a family member: at common law, "the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury" ( Baker v. Bolton , 1808). In India the family can claim under the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 , s. 1A – "for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child" – and, for road accidents, under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 , s. 166 by the dependants who are legal representatives. Today , consortium survives mainly as a head of compensation in death claims (for example, "Consortium expenses were added as INR 25,000" by the Tribunal in Sushilaben Indravadan Gandhi , 2020), and the criminal law punishes enticing a married woman with criminal intent (BNS s. 84).
legalProvision: Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensued) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured". "Every such action or suit shall be for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child, if any, of the person whose death shall have been so caused, and shall be brought by and in the name of the executor, administrator or representative of the person deceased"; the Court "may give such damages as it may think proportioned to the loss resulting from such death to the parties respectively". Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 2 – "not more than one action or suit shall be brought for, and in respect of the same subject-matter of complaint"; the representative "may insert a claim for, and recover any pecuniary loss to the estate of the deceased". Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 166(1) – an application for compensation may be made "(a) by the person who has sustained the injury; or (b) by the owner of the property; or (c) where death has resulted from the accident, by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased; or (d) by any agent duly authorised". Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall , 2026) – rights of action survive to and against executors or administrators, "except causes of action for defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860) or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party". Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 84 – "Whoever takes or entices away any woman who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of any other man, with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person, or conceals or detains with that intent any such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both." Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 82 – suit under the Fatal Accidents Act: two years from "The date of the death of the person killed".
en.meaning: Torts affecting family relations – torts by which a person suffers loss because a member of his family is injured, killed, seduced, enticed away or harboured. Loss of services ( per quod servitium amisit – "whereby he lost the service") – the old action of a master or parent for the loss of the services of a servant or child caused by a wrong done to that servant or child. Loss of consortium ( per quod consortium amisit – "whereby he lost the consortium") – loss of the company, affection, help and comfort of a spouse. In Baker v. Bolton , the husband pleaded the loss of "the comfort, fellowship, and assistance of his said wife". Enticement – persuading or inducing a wife or child to leave the home of the husband or parent, without justification; harbouring is keeping them away after they have left (standard doctrine). Dependants – family members who depended on the deceased; under the Fatal Accidents Act, the "wife, husband, parent and child"; under the MV Act, the "legal representatives" who claim.
keyPoints: These torts harm a person through his family members. Old actions: loss of services, loss of consortium, enticement, harbouring, seduction. Basis: quasi-proprietorial ideas, now outmoded (Lord Oliver). Abolished in England by the Administration of Justice Act 1982. No common law claim for death ( Baker v. Bolton ). Fatal Accidents Act s. 1A: claim for wife, husband, parent and child. One suit only; estate claim may be added (s. 2). MV Act s. 166(1)(c): legal representatives claim. Consortium is now a head of compensation. Fatal Accidents Act suit: 2 years from death.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff and his wife were travelling on top of the defendants' stage-coach, which overt
caseLaws.facts: He claimed for the loss of "the comfort, fellowship, and assistance of his said wife". Principle: "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury"; damages "as to the plaintiff's wife, must stop with the period of her existence". Verdict £100. Why it matters: States the common law bar on claims for death and the old idea of a husband's claim for loss of his wife's society, which the Fatal Accidents Act changed.
Alcock v. Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police [1992] 1 AC 310 (House of Lords, 28 November 1991) – Lord Oliver's speech

caseLaws.name: Facts: Relatives of victims of the Hillsborough stadium disaster claimed for nervous shock (see "Ner
caseLaws.facts: Lord Oliver discussed when third parties can claim for harm to others. Principle: The common law has in general refused claims by third parties for consequential injuries, except old actions "based upon some ancient and now outmoded concepts of the quasi-proprietorial rights of husbands over their wives, parents over their children or employers over their menial servants"; these were "abolished by the Administration of Justice Act 1982". Why it matters: Explains the basis of the old family-relation torts and why they are now viewed as outdated.
Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. [2001] 1 SCR (Supreme Court, 3 January 2001; K.T. Thomas and R.P. Sethi JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A jeep's tyre burst, it capsized and crushed a pedestrian, Haji Mohammad Hanif, aged about 35
caseLaws.facts: His widow and children claimed compensation. Principle: The Court fixed compensation itself using the structured formula in the Second Schedule to the MV Act as "a safer guidance": ₹2,70,000 less one-third, i.e. ₹1,80,000, with 9% interest from the date of claim. Why it matters: Shows how a family (widow and children) recovers for the death of the earning member.
Sushilaben Indravadan Gandhi v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. [2020] 9 SCR 32 (15 April 2020; R.F. Nariman and S. Ravindra Bhat JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A surgeon died in a motor accident; his family claimed compensation
caseLaws.facts: Principle: As recorded by the Supreme Court, the Tribunal computed loss of dependency (₹37,28,100) and added "Consortium expenses ... as INR 25,000" and funeral expenses ₹10,000. Why it matters: Shows consortium surviving as a head of compensation for the family in death claims.

selfTest.q: What did Baker v. Bolton decide?
selfTest.a: At common law, death could not be complained of as an injury in a civil court. What is per quod servitium amisit ? An action for loss of services of a servant or child. What is loss of consortium? Loss of a spouse's company, help and comfort. Who benefits under the Fatal Accidents Act? Wife, husband, parent and child of the deceased. How many suits may be brought under the Fatal Accidents Act for the same death? Only one. What did Lord Oliver call the basis of the old family actions? Ancient and now outmoded concepts of quasi-proprietorial rights. Which MV Act clause lets legal representatives claim? Section 166(1)(c). How much was awarded in Kaushnuma Begum ? ₹1,80,000 with 9% interest. Which BNS section punishes enticing a married woman with criminal intent? Section 84. What is the limitation for a Fatal Accidents Act suit? Two years from the date of death (Art. 82).

te.inOneMinute: కుటుంబ సంబంధాలను ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు అంటే కుటుంబ సభ్యుడికి – భార్య/భర్త, బిడ్డ లేదా తల్లిదండ్రులకు – గాయం, మరణం లేదా వారితో జోక్యం ద్వారా ఒక వ్యక్తికి హాని చేసే తప్పులు. పాత కామన్ లా దావాలు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): సేవల నష్టం ( per quod servitium amisit ) – బిడ్డ (లేదా సేవకుడి) ని గాయపరిచిన, మోసగించిన లేదా ప్రలోభపెట్టి తీసుకెళ్లిన వ్యక్తిపై, బిడ్డ సేవల నష్టం కోసం తల్లిదండ్రి (లేదా యజమాని) దావా వేయవచ్చు. సాహచర్య నష్టం ( per quod consortium amisit ) – భార్యకు గాయం వల్ల ఆమె సాంగత్యం, సహాయం, ఓదార్పు కోల్పోయినందుకు భర్త దావా వేయవచ్చు. ప్రలోభపెట్టడం , ఆశ్రయం ఇవ్వడం – భార్యను లేదా బిడ్డను ఇల్లు వదిలేలా ఒప్పించడం, లేదా వారిని దూరంగా ఉంచడం. ఇవి "ancient and now outmoded concepts of the quasi-proprietorial rights of husbands over their wives, parents over their children or employers over their menial servants" (అర్థం: భార్యలపై భర్తలకు, పిల్లలపై తల్లిదండ్రులకు, సేవకులపై యజమానులకు ఉండే దాదాపు యాజమాన్య హక్కులనే పురాతన, ఇప్పుడు కాలం చెల్లిన భావనల) పై ఆధారపడినవి (Lord Oliver, Alcock , 1991); ఇంగ్లాండ్‌లో Administration of Justice Act 1982 వీటిని రద్దు చేసింది. కుటుంబ సభ్యుడి మరణం: కామన్ లా ప్రకారం "the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury" (అర్థం: ఒక మనిషి మరణాన్ని గాయంగా ఫిర్యాదు చేయలేము) ( Baker v. Bolton , 1808). భారతదేశంలో కుటుంబం ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం, 1855 , s. 1A కింద – "for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child" (అర్థం: భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లల ప్రయోజనం కోసం) – క్లెయిమ్ చేయవచ్చు; రోడ్డు ప్రమాదాలకు మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 , s. 166 కింద చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులైన ఆధారితులు క్లెయిమ్ చేయవచ్చు. నేడు , సాహచర్యం ప్రధానంగా మరణ క్లెయిమ్‌లలో పరిహారంలో ఒక అంశంగా మిగిలి ఉంది (ఉదా: Sushilaben Indravadan Gandhi , 2020 లో ట్రిబ్యునల్ "Consortium expenses were added as INR 25,000" (అర్థం: సాహచర్య ఖర్చులుగా ₹25,000 జోడించారు)), నేరపూరిత ఉద్దేశంతో వివాహిత స్త్రీని ప్రలోభపెట్టడాన్ని నేర చట్టం శిక్షిస్తుంది (BNS s. 84).
te.meaning: కుటుంబ సంబంధాలను ప్రభావితం చేసే టార్ట్‌లు – కుటుంబ సభ్యుడు గాయపడటం, మరణించడం, మోసగించబడటం, ప్రలోభపెట్టి తీసుకెళ్లబడటం లేదా ఆశ్రయం పొందటం వల్ల ఒక వ్యక్తికి నష్టం కలిగించే టార్ట్‌లు. సేవల నష్టం ( per quod servitium amisit – "దీని వల్ల అతను సేవను కోల్పోయాడు") – సేవకుడు లేదా బిడ్డకు చేసిన తప్పు వల్ల వారి సేవలు కోల్పోయినందుకు యజమాని లేదా తల్లిదండ్రి వేసే పాత దావా. సాహచర్య నష్టం ( per quod consortium amisit – "దీని వల్ల అతను సాహచర్యాన్ని కోల్పోయాడు") – భార్య/భర్త సాంగత్యం, ప్రేమ, సహాయం, ఓదార్పు నష్టం. Baker v. Bolton లో భర్త "the comfort, fellowship, and assistance of his said wife" (అర్థం: తన భార్య ఓదార్పు, సాంగత్యం, సహాయం) కోల్పోయానని వాదించాడు. ప్రలోభపెట్టడం – సమర్థన లేకుండా భార్య లేదా బిడ్డను భర్త లేదా తల్లిదండ్రి ఇల్లు వదిలేలా ఒప్పించడం లేదా ప్రేరేపించడం; ఆశ్రయం ఇవ్వడం అంటే వెళ్లిపోయిన తర్వాత వారిని దూరంగా ఉంచడం (ప్రామాణిక సిద్ధాంతం). ఆధారితులు – మరణించినవారిపై ఆధారపడిన కుటుంబ సభ్యులు; ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం కింద "wife, husband, parent and child" (అర్థం: భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లలు); MV చట్టం కింద క్లెయిమ్ చేసే "legal representatives" (అర్థం: చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులు).
keyPoints: ఈ టార్ట్‌లు కుటుంబ సభ్యుల ద్వారా ఒక వ్యక్తికి హాని చేస్తాయి. పాత దావాలు: సేవల నష్టం, సాహచర్య నష్టం, ప్రలోభపెట్టడం, ఆశ్రయం ఇవ్వడం, మోసగించడం. ఆధారం: దాదాపు యాజమాన్య భావనలు, ఇప్పుడు కాలం చెల్లినవి (Lord Oliver). ఇంగ్లాండ్‌లో Administration of Justice Act 1982 రద్దు చేసింది. కామన్ లాలో మరణానికి క్లెయిమ్ లేదు ( Baker v. Bolton ). ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం s. 1A: భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లలకు క్లెయిమ్. ఒకే దావా; ఆస్తి క్లెయిమ్ జోడించవచ్చు (s. 2). MV Act s. 166(1)(c): చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులు క్లెయిమ్ చేస్తారు. సాహచర్యం ఇప్పుడు పరిహారంలో ఒక అంశం. ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం దావా: మరణం నుంచి 2 సంవత్సరాలు.

selfTest.q: Baker v. Bolton ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది?
selfTest.a: కామన్ లా ప్రకారం సివిల్ కోర్టులో మరణాన్ని గాయంగా ఫిర్యాదు చేయలేము. Per quod servitium amisit అంటే ఏమిటి? సేవకుడు లేదా బిడ్డ సేవల నష్టానికి దావా. సాహచర్య నష్టం అంటే ఏమిటి? భార్య/భర్త సాంగత్యం, సహాయం, ఓదార్పు నష్టం. ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం కింద లబ్ధిదారులు ఎవరు? మరణించినవారి భార్య, భర్త, తల్లిదండ్రులు, పిల్లలు. ఒకే మరణానికి ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం కింద ఎన్ని దావాలు వేయవచ్చు? ఒకటి మాత్రమే. పాత కుటుంబ దావాల ఆధారాన్ని Lord Oliver ఏమన్నారు? దాదాపు యాజమాన్య హక్కులనే పురాతన, ఇప్పుడు కాలం చెల్లిన భావనలు. చట్టపరమైన ప్రతినిధులు క్లెయిమ్ చేయడానికి అనుమతించే MV చట్ట నిబంధన ఏది? Section 166(1)(c). Kaushnuma Begum లో ఎంత ఇచ్చారు? 9% వడ్డీతో ₹1,80,000. నేరపూరిత ఉద్దేశంతో వివాహిత స్త్రీని ప్రలోభపెట్టడాన్ని శిక్షించే BNS సెక్షన్ ఏది? Section 84. ప్రాణాంతక ప్రమాదాల చట్టం దావాకు పరిమితి ఎంత? మరణ తేదీ నుంచి రెండు సంవత్సరాలు (Art. 82).

hi.inOneMinute: Torts affecting family relations are wrongs which harm a person through injury to, death of, or interference with a member of his family – a spouse, child or parent. Old common law actions (See Diagram 1 ): Loss of services ( per quod servitium amisit ) – a parent (or master) could sue a person who injured, seduced or enticed away a child (or servant), for the loss of the child's services. Loss of consortium ( per quod consortium amisit ) – a husband could sue for the loss of his wife's company, help and comfort caused by injury to her. Enticement and harbouring – persuading a wife or child to leave the home, or keeping them away. These rest on "ancient and now outmoded concepts of the quasi-proprietorial rights of husbands over their wives, parents over their children or employers over their menial servants" (Lord Oliver, Alcock , 1991); in England they were abolished by the Administration of Justice Act 1982. Death of a family member: at common law, "the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury" ( Baker v. Bolton , 1808). In India the family can claim under the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 , s. 1A – "for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child" – and, for road accidents, under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 , s. 166 by the dependants who are legal representatives. Today , consortium survives mainly as a head of compensation in death claims (for example, "Consortium expenses were added as INR 25,000" by the Tribunal in Sushilaben Indravadan Gandhi , 2020), and the criminal law punishes enticing a married woman with criminal intent (BNS s. 84).
legalProvision: Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 1A – "Whenever the death of a person shall be caused by wrongful act, neglect or default, and the act, neglect or default is such as would (if death had not ensued) have entitled the party injured to maintain an action and recover damages in respect thereof, the party who would have been liable if death had not ensued, shall be liable to an action or suit for damages, notwithstanding the death of the person injured". "Every such action or suit shall be for the benefit of the wife, husband, parent and child, if any, of the person whose death shall have been so caused, and shall be brought by and in the name of the executor, administrator or representative of the person deceased"; the Court "may give such damages as it may think proportioned to the loss resulting from such death to the parties respectively". Fatal Accidents Act, 1855, s. 2 – "not more than one action or suit shall be brought for, and in respect of the same subject-matter of complaint"; the representative "may insert a claim for, and recover any pecuniary loss to the estate of the deceased". Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, s. 166(1) – an application for compensation may be made "(a) by the person who has sustained the injury; or (b) by the owner of the property; or (c) where death has resulted from the accident, by all or any of the legal representatives of the deceased; or (d) by any agent duly authorised". Indian Succession Act, 1925, s. 306 (as quoted in Kumud Lall , 2026) – rights of action survive to and against executors or administrators, "except causes of action for defamation, assault, as defined in the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (45 of 1860) or other personal injuries not causing the death of the party". Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 84 – "Whoever takes or entices away any woman who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of any other man, with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person, or conceals or detains with that intent any such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both." Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 82 – suit under the Fatal Accidents Act: two years from "The date of the death of the person killed".
hi.meaning: Torts affecting family relations – torts by which a person suffers loss because a member of his family is injured, killed, seduced, enticed away or harboured. Loss of services ( per quod servitium amisit – "whereby he lost the service") – the old action of a master or parent for the loss of the services of a servant or child caused by a wrong done to that servant or child. Loss of consortium ( per quod consortium amisit – "whereby he lost the consortium") – loss of the company, affection, help and comfort of a spouse. In Baker v. Bolton , the husband pleaded the loss of "the comfort, fellowship, and assistance of his said wife". Enticement – persuading or inducing a wife or child to leave the home of the husband or parent, without justification; harbouring is keeping them away after they have left (standard doctrine). Dependants – family members who depended on the deceased; under the Fatal Accidents Act, the "wife, husband, parent and child"; under the MV Act, the "legal representatives" who claim.
keyPoints: These torts harm a person through his family members. Old actions: loss of services, loss of consortium, enticement, harbouring, seduction. Basis: quasi-proprietorial ideas, now outmoded (Lord Oliver). Abolished in England by the Administration of Justice Act 1982. No common law claim for death ( Baker v. Bolton ). Fatal Accidents Act s. 1A: claim for wife, husband, parent and child. One suit only; estate claim may be added (s. 2). MV Act s. 166(1)(c): legal representatives claim. Consortium is now a head of compensation. Fatal Accidents Act suit: 2 years from death.

caseLaws.facts: He claimed for the loss of "the comfort, fellowship, and assistance of his said wife". Principle: "In a civil Court, the death of a human being could not be complained of as an injury"; damages "as to the plaintiff's wife, must stop with the period of her existence". Verdict £100. Why it matters: States the common law bar on claims for death and the old idea of a husband's claim for loss of his wife's society, which the Fatal Accidents Act changed.

caseLaws.facts: Lord Oliver discussed when third parties can claim for harm to others. Principle: The common law has in general refused claims by third parties for consequential injuries, except old actions "based upon some ancient and now outmoded concepts of the quasi-proprietorial rights of husbands over their wives, parents over their children or employers over their menial servants"; these were "abolished by the Administration of Justice Act 1982". Why it matters: Explains the basis of the old family-relation torts and why they are now viewed as outdated.
Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. [2001] 1 SCR (Supreme Court, 3 January 2001; K.T. Thomas and R.P. Sethi JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A jeep's tyre burst, it capsized and crushed a pedestrian, Haji Mohammad Hanif, aged about 35
caseLaws.facts: His widow and children claimed compensation. Principle: The Court fixed compensation itself using the structured formula in the Second Schedule to the MV Act as "a safer guidance": ₹2,70,000 less one-third, i.e. ₹1,80,000, with 9% interest from the date of claim. Why it matters: Shows how a family (widow and children) recovers for the death of the earning member.
Sushilaben Indravadan Gandhi v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. [2020] 9 SCR 32 (15 April 2020; R.F. Nariman and S. Ravindra Bhat JJ.)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A surgeon died in a motor accident; his family claimed compensation
caseLaws.facts: Principle: As recorded by the Supreme Court, the Tribunal computed loss of dependency (₹37,28,100) and added "Consortium expenses ... as INR 25,000" and funeral expenses ₹10,000. Why it matters: Shows consortium surviving as a head of compensation for the family in death claims.

selfTest.q: What did Baker v. Bolton decide?
selfTest.a: At common law, death could not be complained of as an injury in a civil court. What is per quod servitium amisit ? An action for loss of services of a servant or child. What is loss of consortium? Loss of a spouse's company, help and comfort. Who benefits under the Fatal Accidents Act? Wife, husband, parent and child of the deceased. How many suits may be brought under the Fatal Accidents Act for the same death? Only one. What did Lord Oliver call the basis of the old family actions? Ancient and now outmoded concepts of quasi-proprietorial rights. Which MV Act clause lets legal representatives claim? Section 166(1)(c). How much was awarded in Kaushnuma Begum ? ₹1,80,000 with 9% interest. Which BNS section punishes enticing a married woman with criminal intent? Section 84. What is the limitation for a Fatal Accidents Act suit? Two years from the date of death (Art. 82).

What is the primary interest protected by the tort of injurious falsehood, as distinct from defamation?

Explanation. Injurious falsehood (trade libel/malicious falsehood) protects a plaintiff's economic or trade interests from false statements, unlike defamation, which protects personal reputation.

What did Ratcliffe v Evans (1892) establish regarding proof of damage in injurious falsehood?

Explanation. Bowen LJ held that where a false statement injures a class of business generally, general evidence of a decline in trade suffices — the plaintiff need not identify specific customers lost.

What are the essentials of the tort of injurious falsehood?

Explanation. Injurious falsehood requires a false statement made with malice, causing special (pecuniary) damage to the plaintiff's trade, business, or property interests.

In Armory v. Delamirie (1722), the court held that a finder of a lost item:

Explanation. A finder's possession is good against everyone except someone with a better title, such as the true owner.

Why did the court in Armory v. Delamirie award damages assessed at the highest possible value of the jewel?

Explanation. The Chief Justice directed that, unless the defendant produced the jewel and showed it was not of the finest water, the jury should presume the strongest against him.

What distinguishes conversion from trespass to goods?

Explanation. Conversion involves treating goods as one's own to such an extent that it denies the owner's rights entirely, whereas trespass to goods is a more limited direct interference.

en.meaning:
How are remedies in the law of torts broadly divided?

Explanation. Remedies in tort are broadly divided into judicial remedies, which require court intervention, and extra-judicial (self-help) remedies, which can be exercised without going to court.

Which of the following is a judicial remedy in tort law?

Explanation. Damages, awarded through court proceedings, is a judicial remedy — the other three options are all extra-judicial (self-help) remedies.

What is 'expulsion of trespasser' as an extra-judicial remedy?

Explanation. Expulsion of trespasser allows a lawful occupier to use reasonable force, without breach of the peace, to remove a trespasser from their land, without first obtaining a court order.

What limits the lawful exercise of the extra-judicial remedy of re-entry on land?

en.meaning:
How many persons are required, at minimum, for the tort of conspiracy?

Explanation. Conspiracy, by its very nature, requires a combination of two or more persons — a single individual cannot conspire alone.

What are the essentials of the tort of conspiracy?

Explanation. The essentials are: a combination or agreement between two or more persons, an overt act done in pursuance of it, and actual damage suffered by the plaintiff — conspiracy is not actionable per se.

In a claim for conspiracy to injure by lawful means, what must the plaintiff prove about the defendants' purpose?

Explanation. Lawful means conspiracy requires proof that the combination's predominant purpose was to injure the plaintiff, since each individual act involved is otherwise lawful.

In conspiracy by unlawful means, why is it unnecessary to prove the defendants' predominant purpose?

en.meaning:
What does the action for 'loss of consortium' historically compensate?

Explanation. Loss of consortium compensates a spouse for the loss of the other spouse's companionship, society, and services, where a third party's tort injures that other spouse.

In Best v Samuel Fox & Co Ltd (1952), why was the wife's claim for loss of consortium rejected?

Explanation. The House of Lords held that at common law, the action for loss of consortium was historically available only to a husband for injury to his wife, not vice versa — illustrating the doctrine's outdated, gender-asymmetric origins.

What is 'enticement' as a tort affecting family relations?

Explanation. Enticement refers to inducing one spouse to leave the other, historically recognised as a tort affecting the marital relationship.

What is 'criminal conversation' as historically recognised in the law of torts?

en.meaning:
Explanation. An injunction is a judicial order — prohibitory (restraining an act) or mandatory (compelling an act) — aimed at preventing or remedying an ongoing or threatened wrong, rather than merely compensating past loss.

What is the distinction between a 'prohibitory' and a 'mandatory' injunction?

Explanation. A prohibitory injunction restrains the defendant from doing (or continuing to do) something; a mandatory injunction compels the defendant to take positive action, such as removing an obstruction.

A builder keeps dumping debris on Nirmala's plot. After a full trial, the court orders him to stop for good. This is:

Explanation. A prohibitory injunction forbids a continuing or repeated wrong. A perpetual injunction is granted at the end of the trial. The court may also award damages.

In American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd (1975), what was the first stage of Lord Diplock's test for granting an interim injunction?

Explanation. The first stage of the American Cyanamid test asks only whether there is a serious question to be tried — the court does not, at this stage, assess the relative strength of the parties' cases in detail.

en.meaning:
What does the principle of restitutio in integrum mean in the context of assessing damages?

Explanation. Restitutio in integrum is the general principle that damages should, as far as money can achieve it, restore the plaintiff to the position they would have occupied had the tort not been committed.

What are 'exemplary' or 'punitive' damages intended to do?

Explanation. Exemplary (punitive) damages go beyond compensating the plaintiff — they are awarded to punish and deter particularly egregious, malicious, or oppressive conduct by the defendant.

What is the 'once and for all' rule regarding assessment of damages?

Explanation. The 'once and for all' rule requires that damages be assessed in a single lump sum at the time of judgment, covering both past and anticipated future loss, without any later reopening of the assessment.

What was the 'directness' test for remoteness of damage, laid down in Re Polemis, and later rejected in the Wagon Mound?

Negligence 'Z' lured a young girl to have sexual relations under the promise to marry her. Later the girl became pregnant, and the man refused to marry her. What is the remedy available to the girl? Torts Affecting Family Relations The plaintiff was a student of X University who had applied for revaluation. The results were declared by the University after an unduly long delay. He claimed damages for mental distress and psychiatric trauma. Discuss whether, and under what tort, the plaintiff will get relief. Negligence A house surgeon negligently injected a patient with cocaine instead of procaine, a mild, harmless local anaesthetic. The patient died because of the cocaine injection. Is the hospital liable? Negligence Barnett v. Chelsea & Kensington Hospital Management Committee (1969) 'Y' was travelling by railway. While the train was crossing another train, his elbow, resting at the window, was injured. Whether the railway is liable or not. Negligence 'A' parked his car by the roadside and left a dog inside the car. The dog jumped about and smashed a glass panel. A splinter from the glass injured 'B' while he was walking past the car. Is there any negligence on the part of 'A'? Discuss. Negligence Questions are drawn from previous Osmania University LL.B. examination papers for study and revision purposes only.

law-of-torts-u5-t1.subtitle: How the common law protected buyers and patients through the duty of care before any consumer statute existed

en.inOneMinute: Before consumer statutes, a consumer who was harmed by goods or services had two routes at common law: an action in contract (only against the person he contracted with) and an action in tort for negligence (against anyone who owed him a duty). The contract route was blocked by privity of contract : a person who had not bought from the maker could not sue the maker in contract. In Winterbottom v. Wright , as Lord Buckmaster described it in Donoghue , a stranger injured by a negligently built carriage "had no cause of action either in tort or arising out of contract". Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 opened the tort route (See Diagram 1 ): The neighbour principle (Lord Atkin): "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour." The manufacturer's rule : a manufacturer who sends out products to reach "the ultimate consumer" with "no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care". Liability for negligence needs three things: a duty of care , its breach , and damage caused by the breach. "Negligence must be both averred and proved" (Lord Macmillan). The duty extends to services and advice : Hedley Byrne v. Heller (1963) – a person with special skill who gives advice knowing another will rely on it owes a duty of care; doctors owe "a duty of care" in deciding whether to undertake a case, what treatment to give and in giving it (quoted in V.P. Shantha ). Common law remedies were slow and costly, and the consumer had to prove negligence. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) builds on the common law: "deficiency" includes "any act of negligence" (s. 2(11)); a product manufacturer is liable "even if he proves that he was not negligent" (s. 84(2)); and the common law action remains (s. 100). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: There is no single statute for this topic; the common law of negligence is judge-made. The leading authorities are:

Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) – Lord Atkin's neighbour principle; the manufacturer's duty to the ultimate consumer; Lord Macmillan's "The categories of negligence are never closed." Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (House of Lords, 28 May 1963) – duty of care for negligent statements and advice where a person relies on special skill. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) 6 SCC 651 – deficiency in medical service is judged by "the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence". Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka [2009] 9 SCR 313 – burden of proof in medical negligence; adequate compensation.
How the statute now uses the common law – Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019):

s. 2(10): "defect" means "any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods or product". s. 2(11): "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service and includes— (i) any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer; and (ii) deliberate withholding of relevant information by such person to the consumer". s. 39(1)(d): compensation "for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party", with power "to grant punitive damages". s. 84(1)–(2): a product manufacturer is liable in a product liability action for a manufacturing defect, design defect, deviation from specifications, non-conformity with express warranty, or lack of adequate instructions or warnings; and "A product manufacturer shall be liable in a product liability action even if he proves that he was not negligent or fraudulent in making the express warranty of a product." s. 85(b): a product service provider is liable if "there was an act of omission or commission or negligence or conscious withholding any information which caused harm". s. 100: "The provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law for the time being in force."
en.meaning: Common law – law made by judges through decided cases, as distinct from statute. The law of negligence is mainly common law. Consumer (in this topic) – the person who finally uses or consumes goods or services, whether or not he bought them himself. Mrs Donoghue drank ginger-beer that "a friend had bought from a retailer and given to her". Duty of care – a legal obligation to take reasonable care to avoid causing foreseeable harm to persons closely and directly affected by one's acts. Neighbour (Lord Atkin) – "persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation as being so affected when I am directing my mind to the acts or omissions which are called in question". Negligence – as a tort , breach of a duty of care that causes damage. Lord Macmillan: the party complained of "should owe to the party complaining a duty to take care", and the party complaining must "prove that he has suffered damage in consequence of a breach of that duty". Privity of contract – the rule that only the parties to a contract can sue on it.
keyPoints: Privity barred contract claims by non-buyers. Donoghue (1932): neighbour principle; manufacturer's duty to ultimate consumer; 3:2. Elements: duty of care, breach, damage; negligence "averred and proved". "The categories of negligence are never closed." Hedley Byrne (1963): duty for advice by a person with special skill relied on by another. Doctors: reasonable skill and care; Bolam standard. V.P. Shantha : deficiency judged by negligence test. Nizam's : onus shifts after prima facie negligence. CPA 2019: deficiency includes negligence (s. 2(11)); s. 39(1)(d); s. 84(2) no-fault; s. 100 keeps common law. Users and beneficiaries are consumers – no privity needed. Neighbour principle is the general test; privity of contract is what Donoghue got around.

caseLaws.facts: Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) Facts: On 26 August 1928 the appellant drank ginger-beer made by the respondent and bought for her by a friend. The opaque bottle contained "the decomposed remains of a snail"; she alleged shock and severe gastro-enteritis. The Scottish court held the manufacturer owed her no duty. Principle: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" (Lord Atkin). A manufacturer who intends products to reach the ultimate consumer with "no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care." "The categories of negligence are never closed" (Lord Macmillan). Appeal allowed 3:2. Why it matters: It is the foundation of the consumer's right to sue a manufacturer in negligence without a contract. 2. Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (House of Lords, 28 May 1963) Facts: Advertising agents asked, through their bank, about a client's credit-worthiness. The client's bankers gave a favourable reference "without responsibility". Relying on it, the agents did not cancel orders and lost money when the client failed. Principle: "if someone possessed of a special skill undertakes, quite irrespective of contract, to apply that skill for the assistance of another person who relies upon such skill, a duty of care will arise" (Lord Morris of Borth-y-Gest). On the facts, the disclaimer meant no duty was assumed, and the appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It extends the duty of care from products to advice and information – the basis of consumer claims against professionals and service providers. 3. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: The question was whether medical services fall under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and how deficiency in such service is judged. A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) decided. Principle: "A determination about deficiency in service for the purpose of Section 2(1)(g) has, therefore, to be made by applying the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence"; a practitioner "must bring to his task a reasonable degree of skill and knowledge and must exercise a reasonable degree of care". Why it matters: It joins the common law duty of care to the statutory idea of deficiency in service. 4. Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A twenty-year-old student became paraplegic after surgery to remove a tumour; the National Commission found negligence and both sides appealed (B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ.). Principle: "once the initial burden has been discharged by the complainant by making out a case of negligence on the part of the hospital or the doctor concerned, the onus then shifts on to the hospital or to the attending doctors" (para 32). Compensation was raised to ₹1 crore with interest. Why it matters: It eases the consumer's common law burden of proof in negligence cases before Consumer Commissions.

selfTest.q: Why could a person who received goods as a gift not sue the manufacturer in contract?
selfTest.a: State Lord Atkin's neighbour principle. What were the facts of Donoghue v. Stevenson , and what was the majority? What are the elements of the tort of negligence? How did Hedley Byrne extend the duty of care, and why did the plaintiffs lose? How did V.P. Shantha link deficiency in service to negligence? Must a consumer prove negligence to make a manufacturer liable under CPA 2019?

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల చట్టాలు రాకముందు, వస్తువులు లేదా సేవల వల్ల హాని పొందిన వినియోగదారుడికి సాధారణ చట్టంలో రెండు మార్గాలు ఉండేవి: ఒప్పందం పై దావా (తాను ఒప్పందం చేసుకున్న వ్యక్తిపై మాత్రమే), నిర్లక్ష్యానికి టార్ట్ ‌లో దావా (తన పట్ల బాధ్యత ఉన్న ఎవరిపైనైనా). ఒప్పంద మార్గాన్ని ఒప్పంద సంబంధం (privity of contract) అడ్డుకుంది: తయారీదారు నుండి కొనని వ్యక్తి తయారీదారుపై ఒప్పందంలో దావా వేయలేడు. Donoghue లో Lord Buckmaster వివరించినట్లు Winterbottom v. Wright లో, నిర్లక్ష్యంగా తయారు చేసిన బండి వల్ల గాయపడిన అపరిచితుడికి "had no cause of action either in tort or arising out of contract" (అర్థం: టార్ట్‌లో గానీ ఒప్పందం నుండి గానీ దావా కారణం లేదు). Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 టార్ట్ మార్గాన్ని తెరిచింది ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): పొరుగువారి సూత్రం (Lord Atkin): "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour." (అర్థం: మీ పొరుగువారిని గాయపరిచే అవకాశం ఉందని మీరు సహేతుకంగా ఊహించగల చర్యలు లేదా లోపాలను నివారించడానికి మీరు సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాలి). తయారీదారు నియమం : "the ultimate consumer" (అర్థం: చివరి వినియోగదారుడు)కు "no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" (అర్థం: మధ్యలో పరిశీలనకు సహేతుక అవకాశం లేకుండా) చేరేలా ఉత్పత్తులు పంపే తయారీదారు "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care" (అర్థం: ఆ సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాల్సిన బాధ్యత వినియోగదారుడి పట్ల కలిగి ఉంటాడు). నిర్లక్ష్యానికి బాధ్యత కు మూడు అవసరం: జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత , దాని ఉల్లంఘన , ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల నష్టం . "Negligence must be both averred and proved" (అర్థం: నిర్లక్ష్యాన్ని ఆరోపించాలి, రుజువు కూడా చేయాలి) (Lord Macmillan). బాధ్యత సేవలు, సలహా లకు విస్తరిస్తుంది: Hedley Byrne v. Heller (1963) – మరొకరు ఆధారపడతారని తెలిసి సలహా ఇచ్చే ప్రత్యేక నైపుణ్యం గల వ్యక్తికి జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత ఉంటుంది; కేసును చేపట్టాలా వద్దా, ఏ చికిత్స ఇవ్వాలి, దానిని ఇవ్వడంలో డాక్టర్లకు "a duty of care" (అర్థం: జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత) ఉంది ( V.P. Shantha లో ఉదహరించినది). సాధారణ చట్ట పరిష్కారాలు నెమ్మదిగా, ఖరీదుగా ఉండేవి, వినియోగదారుడే నిర్లక్ష్యాన్ని రుజువు చేయాల్సి వచ్చేది. వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019) సాధారణ చట్టంపై నిర్మించబడింది: "deficiency" (సేవా లోపం)లో "any act of negligence" (అర్థం: ఏ నిర్లక్ష్య చర్య అయినా) చేరుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 2(11)); ఉత్పత్తి తయారీదారు "even if he proves that he was not negligent" (అర్థం: తాను నిర్లక్ష్యంగా లేనని రుజువు చేసినా) బాధ్యుడు (సెక్షన్ 84(2)); సాధారణ చట్ట దావా కొనసాగుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 100). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: సాధారణ చట్టం (common law) – చట్టసభ చేసిన చట్టం కాకుండా, తీర్పుల ద్వారా న్యాయమూర్తులు రూపొందించిన చట్టం. నిర్లక్ష్యం చట్టం ప్రధానంగా సాధారణ చట్టమే. వినియోగదారుడు (ఈ అంశంలో) – వస్తువులు లేదా సేవలను చివరకు వాడే లేదా వినియోగించే వ్యక్తి, తానే కొన్నా కొనకపోయినా. Mrs Donoghue తాగిన జింజర్-బీర్‌ను "a friend had bought from a retailer and given to her" (అర్థం: ఒక స్నేహితురాలు రిటైలర్ నుండి కొని ఆమెకు ఇచ్చింది). జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత – తన చర్యల వల్ల దగ్గరగా, నేరుగా ప్రభావితమయ్యే వ్యక్తులకు ఊహించగల హాని కలగకుండా సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాల్సిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత. పొరుగువారు (Lord Atkin) – "persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation as being so affected when I am directing my mind to the acts or omissions which are called in question" (అర్థం: ప్రశ్నార్థకమైన చర్యలు లేదా లోపాల గురించి ఆలోచిస్తున్నప్పుడు, నా చర్య వల్ల అంత దగ్గరగా, నేరుగా ప్రభావితమవుతారని నేను సహేతుకంగా దృష్టిలో ఉంచుకోవాల్సిన వ్యక్తులు). నిర్లక్ష్యం – టార్ట్‌గా , నష్టం కలిగించే జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన. Lord Macmillan: ఫిర్యాదుకు గురైన పక్షం "should owe to the party complaining a duty to take care" (అర్థం: ఫిర్యాదు చేసే పక్షం పట్ల జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత కలిగి ఉండాలి), ఫిర్యాదు చేసే పక్షం "prove that he has suffered damage in consequence of a breach of that duty" (అర్థం: ఆ బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన పర్యవసానంగా తనకు నష్టం కలిగిందని రుజువు చేయాలి). ఒప్పంద సంబంధం ( privity of contract ) – ఒప్పందంలోని పక్షాలు మాత్రమే దానిపై దావా వేయగలరనే నియమం.
keyPoints: కొనుగోలుదారు కాని వారి ఒప్పంద దావాలను ఒప్పంద సంబంధం అడ్డుకుంది. Donoghue (1932): పొరుగువారి సూత్రం; చివరి వినియోగదారుడి పట్ల తయారీదారు బాధ్యత; 3:2. అంశాలు: జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత, ఉల్లంఘన, నష్టం; నిర్లక్ష్యం "averred and proved" (అర్థం: ఆరోపించి రుజువు చేయాలి). "The categories of negligence are never closed." (అర్థం: నిర్లక్ష్యం వర్గాలు ఎప్పుడూ మూసుకుపోవు). Hedley Byrne (1963): మరొకరు ఆధారపడే ప్రత్యేక నైపుణ్యం గల వ్యక్తి సలహాకు బాధ్యత. డాక్టర్లు: సహేతుక నైపుణ్యం, జాగ్రత్త; Bolam ప్రమాణం. V.P. Shantha : సేవా లోపాన్ని నిర్లక్ష్య పరీక్షతో నిర్ణయించాలి. Nizam's : ప్రాథమిక నిర్లక్ష్యం తర్వాత భారం మారుతుంది. CPA 2019: సేవా లోపంలో నిర్లక్ష్యం చేరుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 2(11)); సెక్షన్ 39(1)(d); సెక్షన్ 84(2) దోషం లేని బాధ్యత; సెక్షన్ 100 సాధారణ చట్టాన్ని కాపాడుతుంది. వాడేవారు, లబ్ధిదారులు వినియోగదారులే – ఒప్పంద సంబంధం అవసరం లేదు. పొరుగువారి సూత్రం సాధారణ పరీక్ష; Donoghue అధిగమించినది ఒప్పంద సంబంధం.

selfTest.a: Lord Atkin పొరుగువారి సూత్రాన్ని చెప్పండి. Donoghue v. Stevenson వాస్తవాలు ఏమిటి, మెజారిటీ ఎంత? నిర్లక్ష్యం టార్ట్ అంశాలు ఏమిటి? Hedley Byrne జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యతను ఎలా విస్తరించింది, దావాదారులు ఎందుకు ఓడిపోయారు? V.P. Shantha సేవా లోపాన్ని నిర్లక్ష్యంతో ఎలా కలిపింది? CPA 2019 కింద తయారీదారును బాధ్యుడిని చేయడానికి వినియోగదారుడు నిర్లక్ష్యాన్ని రుజువు చేయాలా?

hi.inOneMinute: Before consumer statutes, a consumer who was harmed by goods or services had two routes at common law: an action in contract (only against the person he contracted with) and an action in tort for negligence (against anyone who owed him a duty). The contract route was blocked by privity of contract : a person who had not bought from the maker could not sue the maker in contract. In Winterbottom v. Wright , as Lord Buckmaster described it in Donoghue , a stranger injured by a negligently built carriage "had no cause of action either in tort or arising out of contract". Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 opened the tort route (See Diagram 1 ): The neighbour principle (Lord Atkin): "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour." The manufacturer's rule : a manufacturer who sends out products to reach "the ultimate consumer" with "no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care". Liability for negligence needs three things: a duty of care , its breach , and damage caused by the breach. "Negligence must be both averred and proved" (Lord Macmillan). The duty extends to services and advice : Hedley Byrne v. Heller (1963) – a person with special skill who gives advice knowing another will rely on it owes a duty of care; doctors owe "a duty of care" in deciding whether to undertake a case, what treatment to give and in giving it (quoted in V.P. Shantha ). Common law remedies were slow and costly, and the consumer had to prove negligence. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) builds on the common law: "deficiency" includes "any act of negligence" (s. 2(11)); a product manufacturer is liable "even if he proves that he was not negligent" (s. 84(2)); and the common law action remains (s. 100). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: There is no single statute for this topic; the common law of negligence is judge-made. The leading authorities are:

Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) – Lord Atkin's neighbour principle; the manufacturer's duty to the ultimate consumer; Lord Macmillan's "The categories of negligence are never closed." Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (House of Lords, 28 May 1963) – duty of care for negligent statements and advice where a person relies on special skill. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) 6 SCC 651 – deficiency in medical service is judged by "the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence". Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka [2009] 9 SCR 313 – burden of proof in medical negligence; adequate compensation.
How the statute now uses the common law – Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019):

s. 2(10): "defect" means "any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods or product". s. 2(11): "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service and includes— (i) any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer; and (ii) deliberate withholding of relevant information by such person to the consumer". s. 39(1)(d): compensation "for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party", with power "to grant punitive damages". s. 84(1)–(2): a product manufacturer is liable in a product liability action for a manufacturing defect, design defect, deviation from specifications, non-conformity with express warranty, or lack of adequate instructions or warnings; and "A product manufacturer shall be liable in a product liability action even if he proves that he was not negligent or fraudulent in making the express warranty of a product." s. 85(b): a product service provider is liable if "there was an act of omission or commission or negligence or conscious withholding any information which caused harm". s. 100: "The provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law for the time being in force."
hi.meaning: Common law – law made by judges through decided cases, as distinct from statute. The law of negligence is mainly common law. Consumer (in this topic) – the person who finally uses or consumes goods or services, whether or not he bought them himself. Mrs Donoghue drank ginger-beer that "a friend had bought from a retailer and given to her". Duty of care – a legal obligation to take reasonable care to avoid causing foreseeable harm to persons closely and directly affected by one's acts. Neighbour (Lord Atkin) – "persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation as being so affected when I am directing my mind to the acts or omissions which are called in question". Negligence – as a tort , breach of a duty of care that causes damage. Lord Macmillan: the party complained of "should owe to the party complaining a duty to take care", and the party complaining must "prove that he has suffered damage in consequence of a breach of that duty". Privity of contract – the rule that only the parties to a contract can sue on it.
keyPoints: Privity barred contract claims by non-buyers. Donoghue (1932): neighbour principle; manufacturer's duty to ultimate consumer; 3:2. Elements: duty of care, breach, damage; negligence "averred and proved". "The categories of negligence are never closed." Hedley Byrne (1963): duty for advice by a person with special skill relied on by another. Doctors: reasonable skill and care; Bolam standard. V.P. Shantha : deficiency judged by negligence test. Nizam's : onus shifts after prima facie negligence. CPA 2019: deficiency includes negligence (s. 2(11)); s. 39(1)(d); s. 84(2) no-fault; s. 100 keeps common law. Users and beneficiaries are consumers – no privity needed. Neighbour principle is the general test; privity of contract is what Donoghue got around.

caseLaws.facts: Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) Facts: On 26 August 1928 the appellant drank ginger-beer made by the respondent and bought for her by a friend. The opaque bottle contained "the decomposed remains of a snail"; she alleged shock and severe gastro-enteritis. The Scottish court held the manufacturer owed her no duty. Principle: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour" (Lord Atkin). A manufacturer who intends products to reach the ultimate consumer with "no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care." "The categories of negligence are never closed" (Lord Macmillan). Appeal allowed 3:2. Why it matters: It is the foundation of the consumer's right to sue a manufacturer in negligence without a contract. 2. Hedley Byrne & Co. Ltd. v. Heller & Partners Ltd. (House of Lords, 28 May 1963) Facts: Advertising agents asked, through their bank, about a client's credit-worthiness. The client's bankers gave a favourable reference "without responsibility". Relying on it, the agents did not cancel orders and lost money when the client failed. Principle: "if someone possessed of a special skill undertakes, quite irrespective of contract, to apply that skill for the assistance of another person who relies upon such skill, a duty of care will arise" (Lord Morris of Borth-y-Gest). On the facts, the disclaimer meant no duty was assumed, and the appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It extends the duty of care from products to advice and information – the basis of consumer claims against professionals and service providers. 3. Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: The question was whether medical services fall under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and how deficiency in such service is judged. A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) decided. Principle: "A determination about deficiency in service for the purpose of Section 2(1)(g) has, therefore, to be made by applying the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence"; a practitioner "must bring to his task a reasonable degree of skill and knowledge and must exercise a reasonable degree of care". Why it matters: It joins the common law duty of care to the statutory idea of deficiency in service. 4. Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A twenty-year-old student became paraplegic after surgery to remove a tumour; the National Commission found negligence and both sides appealed (B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ.). Principle: "once the initial burden has been discharged by the complainant by making out a case of negligence on the part of the hospital or the doctor concerned, the onus then shifts on to the hospital or to the attending doctors" (para 32). Compensation was raised to ₹1 crore with interest. Why it matters: It eases the consumer's common law burden of proof in negligence cases before Consumer Commissions.

selfTest.q: Why could a person who received goods as a gift not sue the manufacturer in contract?
selfTest.a: State Lord Atkin's neighbour principle. What were the facts of Donoghue v. Stevenson , and what was the majority? What are the elements of the tort of negligence? How did Hedley Byrne extend the duty of care, and why did the plaintiffs lose? How did V.P. Shantha link deficiency in service to negligence? Must a consumer prove negligence to make a manufacturer liable under CPA 2019?
