law-of-torts-u5-t2.subtitle: The movement and policy that protect consumers' interests and rights, and how Indian law gives effect to them

en.inOneMinute: Consumerism , in consumer protection law, means the movement and the policy that protect the interests and rights of consumers against sellers, manufacturers and service providers. These are parties who usually know more and bargain from a stronger position. No Indian statute defines "consumerism". The idea is built into the law through: the long titles of the Consumer Protection Acts; the list of consumer rights (s. 2(9), CPA 2019); the bodies that promote and enforce them. Three stages (See Diagram 1 ): the common law gave only slow, fault-based remedies ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932); the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 set up councils and quasi-judicial forums, against the background of the UN General Assembly resolution of 9 April 1985 (as recorded in V.P. Shantha ); the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 repealed the 1986 Act (s. 107). It added a regulator (the Central Consumer Protection Authority), product liability, mediation and online transactions. Six consumer rights (s. 2(9)): safety; information; choice; to be heard; redressal; consumer awareness. The Act protects "consumers as a class", not only the person who pays ( V.P. Shantha ). The Central Authority's job is to "promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class" (s. 10(1)).
legalProvision: There is no section defining "consumerism". The law that gives it effect:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Long title: "An Act to provide for protection of the interests of consumers and for the said purpose, to establish authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto." Section 1(4): "Save as otherwise expressly provided by the Central Government, by notification, this Act shall apply to all goods and services." Section 2(9): "consumer rights" includes: "(i) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property;" "(ii) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices;" "(iii) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices;" "(iv) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora;" "(v) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and" "(vi) the right to consumer awareness;" Section 2(5)(ii): a "complainant" includes "any voluntary consumer association registered under any law for the time being in force". Section 3: the Central Consumer Protection Council, "an advisory council", chaired by the Minister in charge of Consumer Affairs. Section 5: its object is "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act". State Councils (s. 6) and District Councils (s. 8) follow. Section 10(1): the Central Consumer Protection Authority, "to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class". Section 107(1): "The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (68 of 1986) is hereby repealed." Commencement: most of the Act came into force on 20 July 2020; ss. 10 to 27 (the Central Authority) and some definitions came into force on 24 July 2020 (footnote to s. 1(3)).
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986, dated 24 December 1986)

Long title: "An Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith." Section 6: the Central Council's object was "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers". It listed six rights. The sixth was "the right to consumer education".
en.meaning: Consumerism – the organised effort, by consumers , their associations and the State, to protect consumers' interests and rights. It covers safety, fair information, choice, a voice in policy, redress for wrongs, and awareness. The word is not defined in any Act; this meaning is drawn from what the Consumer Protection Acts set out to do. Consumer – the person who buys goods or avails of services for consideration , other than for resale or commercial purpose, together with the approved user or beneficiary (s. 2(7), CPA 2019). Consumer rights – the six rights listed in s. 2(9), CPA 2019. Voluntary consumer association – an association of consumers registered under any law, which can itself file a complaint (s. 2(5)(ii)). Consumer awareness – the sixth right in s. 2(9). Consumers should know their rights and remedies. The 1986 Act called this "consumer education".
keyPoints: Consumerism: movement and policy protecting consumers; not defined by statute. UN General Assembly resolution, 9 April 1985 ( V.P. Shantha ). CPA 1986 dated 24 December 1986; repealed by s. 107(1) CPA 2019. CPA 2019 in force mainly from 20 July 2020; Central Authority provisions from 24 July 2020. Six consumer rights (s. 2(9)): safety, information, choice, hearing, redressal, awareness. Consumer awareness replaced "consumer education". Voluntary consumer association can complain (s. 2(5)(ii)). Councils advise; the Central Authority regulates; Commissions decide. Consumers protected "as a class" ( V.P. Shantha ; s. 10(1)).

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: The question was whether services of doctors and hospitals fall under the 1986 Act, including free services in hospitals that charge others. Bench: S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ. Principle: The Act was enacted "in the background of the guidelines contained in the Consumer Protection Resolution passed by the U.N. General Assembly on April 9, 1985", and "The protection that is envisaged by the Act is, therefore, protection for consumers as a class." Why it matters: It ties Indian consumer law to the international consumer movement. It also explains why the Act is read widely in favour of consumers. 2. Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) Facts: A woman drank ginger-beer bought by a friend; the opaque bottle held "the decomposed remains of a snail"; she alleged illness. There was no contract between her and the manufacturer. Principle: A manufacturer whose products reach "the ultimate consumer" with no reasonable chance of examination "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care" (Lord Atkin, 3:2 majority). Why it matters: It is the common law starting point of consumer protection. Its limits, that negligence must be proved in a court action, show why statutory consumerism was needed.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టంలో కన్స్యూమరిజం (వినియోగదారుల ఉద్యమం) అంటే అమ్మకందారులు, తయారీదారులు, సేవా ప్రదాతల నుండి వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాలు, హక్కుల ను కాపాడే ఉద్యమం, విధానం. ఈ పక్షాలకు సాధారణంగా ఎక్కువ తెలుసు, బలమైన స్థితి నుండి బేరం చేస్తాయి. ఏ భారతీయ చట్టమూ "consumerism"ను నిర్వచించలేదు. ఈ భావన చట్టంలో వీటి ద్వారా నిర్మితమైంది: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టాల దీర్ఘ శీర్షికలు (long titles); వినియోగదారుల హక్కుల జాబితా (CPA 2019 సెక్షన్ 2(9)); వాటిని ప్రోత్సహించి అమలు చేసే సంస్థలు. మూడు దశలు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): సాధారణ చట్టం నెమ్మదిగా, దోష ఆధారిత పరిష్కారాలు మాత్రమే ఇచ్చింది ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932); వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 1986 9 ఏప్రిల్ 1985 నాటి ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి సాధారణ సభ తీర్మానం నేపథ్యంలో మండళ్లు, అర్ధ-న్యాయ వేదికలను ఏర్పాటు చేసింది ( V.P. Shantha లో నమోదు చేసినట్లు); వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 1986 చట్టాన్ని రద్దు చేసింది (సెక్షన్ 107). ఇది ఒక నియంత్రణ సంస్థ (కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ అథారిటీ), ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత, మధ్యవర్తిత్వం, ఆన్‌లైన్ లావాదేవీలను చేర్చింది. ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)): భద్రత; సమాచారం; ఎంపిక; వినిపించుకునే హక్కు; పరిష్కారం; వినియోగదారుల అవగాహన. చట్టం చెల్లించే వ్యక్తిని మాత్రమే కాకుండా "consumers as a class" (అర్థం: ఒక వర్గంగా వినియోగదారులను) రక్షిస్తుంది ( V.P. Shantha ). కేంద్ర అథారిటీ పని "promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class" (అర్థం: ఒక వర్గంగా వినియోగదారుల హక్కులను ప్రోత్సహించడం, రక్షించడం, అమలు చేయడం) (సెక్షన్ 10(1)).
te.meaning: కన్స్యూమరిజం ( వినియోగదారుల ఉద్యమం ) – వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాలు, హక్కులను కాపాడడానికి వినియోగదారులు, వారి సంఘాలు, ప్రభుత్వం చేసే వ్యవస్థీకృత ప్రయత్నం. ఇందులో భద్రత, సరైన సమాచారం, ఎంపిక, విధానంలో గొంతు, అన్యాయాలకు పరిష్కారం, అవగాహన ఉంటాయి. ఈ పదం ఏ చట్టంలోనూ నిర్వచించబడలేదు; ఈ అర్థం వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టాలు సాధించాలనుకున్న దాని నుండి తీసుకున్నది. వినియోగదారుడు – తిరిగి అమ్మకం లేదా వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనానికి కాకుండా, ప్రతిఫలానికి వస్తువులు కొనే లేదా సేవలు పొందే వ్యక్తి; ఆమోదం పొందిన వాడకందారు లేదా లబ్ధిదారుతో సహా (CPA 2019 సెక్షన్ 2(7)). వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు – CPA 2019 సెక్షన్ 2(9)లో పేర్కొన్న ఆరు హక్కులు. స్వచ్ఛంద వినియోగదారుల సంఘం – ఏ చట్టం కిందైనా రిజిస్టర్ అయిన వినియోగదారుల సంఘం; అది స్వయంగా ఫిర్యాదు వేయగలదు (సెక్షన్ 2(5)(ii)). వినియోగదారుల అవగాహన – సెక్షన్ 2(9)లో ఆరవ హక్కు. వినియోగదారులు తమ హక్కులు, పరిష్కారాలు తెలుసుకోవాలి. 1986 చట్టం దీనిని "consumer education" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల విద్య) అంది.
keyPoints: వినియోగదారుల ఉద్యమం: వినియోగదారులను రక్షించే ఉద్యమం, విధానం; చట్టంలో నిర్వచనం లేదు. ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి సాధారణ సభ తీర్మానం, 9 ఏప్రిల్ 1985 ( V.P. Shantha ). CPA 1986 తేదీ 24 డిసెంబర్ 1986; CPA 2019 సెక్షన్ 107(1) దానిని రద్దు చేసింది. CPA 2019 ప్రధానంగా 20 జూలై 2020 నుండి అమలు; కేంద్ర అథారిటీ నిబంధనలు 24 జూలై 2020 నుండి. ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)): భద్రత, సమాచారం, ఎంపిక, వినిపించుకోవడం, పరిష్కారం, అవగాహన. వినియోగదారుల అవగాహన "consumer education" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల విద్య) స్థానంలో వచ్చింది. స్వచ్ఛంద వినియోగదారుల సంఘం ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 2(5)(ii)). మండళ్లు సలహా ఇస్తాయి; కేంద్ర అథారిటీ నియంత్రిస్తుంది; కమిషన్లు నిర్ణయిస్తాయి. వినియోగదారులకు "as a class" (అర్థం: ఒక వర్గంగా) రక్షణ ( V.P. Shantha ; సెక్షన్ 10(1)).

selfTest.q: వినియోగదారుల ఉద్యమం (consumerism) అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 2(9)లోని ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు చెప్పండి. V.P. Shantha 1986 చట్టంతో ఏ అంతర్జాతీయ పత్రాన్ని కలిపింది, దాని తేదీ ఏమిటి? కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ మండలి పాత్ర ఏమిటి? 2019 చట్టంలో ఏ హక్కు పేరు మారింది? వినియోగదారులకు సాధారణ చట్ట పరిష్కారం ఎందుకు సరిపోదు?

hi.inOneMinute: Consumerism , in consumer protection law, means the movement and the policy that protect the interests and rights of consumers against sellers, manufacturers and service providers. These are parties who usually know more and bargain from a stronger position. No Indian statute defines "consumerism". The idea is built into the law through: the long titles of the Consumer Protection Acts; the list of consumer rights (s. 2(9), CPA 2019); the bodies that promote and enforce them. Three stages (See Diagram 1 ): the common law gave only slow, fault-based remedies ( Donoghue v. Stevenson , 1932); the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 set up councils and quasi-judicial forums, against the background of the UN General Assembly resolution of 9 April 1985 (as recorded in V.P. Shantha ); the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 repealed the 1986 Act (s. 107). It added a regulator (the Central Consumer Protection Authority), product liability, mediation and online transactions. Six consumer rights (s. 2(9)): safety; information; choice; to be heard; redressal; consumer awareness. The Act protects "consumers as a class", not only the person who pays ( V.P. Shantha ). The Central Authority's job is to "promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class" (s. 10(1)).
legalProvision: There is no section defining "consumerism". The law that gives it effect:
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Long title: "An Act to provide for protection of the interests of consumers and for the said purpose, to establish authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto." Section 1(4): "Save as otherwise expressly provided by the Central Government, by notification, this Act shall apply to all goods and services." Section 2(9): "consumer rights" includes: "(i) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property;" "(ii) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices;" "(iii) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices;" "(iv) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora;" "(v) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and" "(vi) the right to consumer awareness;" Section 2(5)(ii): a "complainant" includes "any voluntary consumer association registered under any law for the time being in force". Section 3: the Central Consumer Protection Council, "an advisory council", chaired by the Minister in charge of Consumer Affairs. Section 5: its object is "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act". State Councils (s. 6) and District Councils (s. 8) follow. Section 10(1): the Central Consumer Protection Authority, "to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class". Section 107(1): "The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (68 of 1986) is hereby repealed." Commencement: most of the Act came into force on 20 July 2020; ss. 10 to 27 (the Central Authority) and some definitions came into force on 24 July 2020 (footnote to s. 1(3)).
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986, dated 24 December 1986)

Long title: "An Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith." Section 6: the Central Council's object was "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers". It listed six rights. The sixth was "the right to consumer education".
hi.meaning: Consumerism – the organised effort, by consumers , their associations and the State, to protect consumers' interests and rights. It covers safety, fair information, choice, a voice in policy, redress for wrongs, and awareness. The word is not defined in any Act; this meaning is drawn from what the Consumer Protection Acts set out to do. Consumer – the person who buys goods or avails of services for consideration , other than for resale or commercial purpose, together with the approved user or beneficiary (s. 2(7), CPA 2019). Consumer rights – the six rights listed in s. 2(9), CPA 2019. Voluntary consumer association – an association of consumers registered under any law, which can itself file a complaint (s. 2(5)(ii)). Consumer awareness – the sixth right in s. 2(9). Consumers should know their rights and remedies. The 1986 Act called this "consumer education".
keyPoints: Consumerism: movement and policy protecting consumers; not defined by statute. UN General Assembly resolution, 9 April 1985 ( V.P. Shantha ). CPA 1986 dated 24 December 1986; repealed by s. 107(1) CPA 2019. CPA 2019 in force mainly from 20 July 2020; Central Authority provisions from 24 July 2020. Six consumer rights (s. 2(9)): safety, information, choice, hearing, redressal, awareness. Consumer awareness replaced "consumer education". Voluntary consumer association can complain (s. 2(5)(ii)). Councils advise; the Central Authority regulates; Commissions decide. Consumers protected "as a class" ( V.P. Shantha ; s. 10(1)).

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: The question was whether services of doctors and hospitals fall under the 1986 Act, including free services in hospitals that charge others. Bench: S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ. Principle: The Act was enacted "in the background of the guidelines contained in the Consumer Protection Resolution passed by the U.N. General Assembly on April 9, 1985", and "The protection that is envisaged by the Act is, therefore, protection for consumers as a class." Why it matters: It ties Indian consumer law to the international consumer movement. It also explains why the Act is read widely in favour of consumers. 2. Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) Facts: A woman drank ginger-beer bought by a friend; the opaque bottle held "the decomposed remains of a snail"; she alleged illness. There was no contract between her and the manufacturer. Principle: A manufacturer whose products reach "the ultimate consumer" with no reasonable chance of examination "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care" (Lord Atkin, 3:2 majority). Why it matters: It is the common law starting point of consumer protection. Its limits, that negligence must be proved in a court action, show why statutory consumerism was needed.

law-of-torts-u5-t3.subtitle: The main features of the Act that created consumer rights, Consumer Councils and a three-tier forum

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986, CPA 1986) was passed on 24 December 1986 "to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers" through consumer councils and "other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes" (long title). Its main features (See Diagram 1 ): Wide coverage: "all goods and services" unless the Central Government excludes them (s. 1(4)); a wide meaning of consumer (s. 2(1)(d)). Clear grounds of complaint: unfair or restrictive trade practice, defect in goods, deficiency in services, excess price, hazardous goods and services (s. 2(1)(c)). Six consumer rights promoted by Consumer Protection Councils at Central, State and District level (ss. 4 to 8B). A three-tier machinery of quasi-judicial bodies – the District Forum , the State Commission and the National Commission (s. 9) – with jurisdiction based on value (ss. 11, 17, 21). Simple, quick procedure with fixed time limits and powers of a civil court (s. 13). A wide list of reliefs (s. 14), appeals (ss. 15, 19, 23), limitation of two years (s. 24A), enforcement (s. 25), costs for frivolous complaints (s. 26) and penalties (ss. 27, 27A). An additional remedy: the Act is "in addition to and not in derogation of" other laws (s. 3). It was repealed by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 107(1), with savings for things done under it (s. 107(2)). Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) described this structure and held that paid medical services are "service" under the Act.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 1986

Long title – "An Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith." s. 1(2) – "It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir." s. 1(4) – "Save as otherwise expressly provided by the Central Government by notification, this Act shall apply to all goods and services." Chapters I, II and IV came into force on 15 April 1987 and Chapter III on 1 July 1987 (footnote to s. 1(3)). s. 2(1)(b) – "complainant" means a consumer; a registered voluntary consumer association; the Central Government or any State Government; "one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest"; and, on the death of a consumer, "his legal heir or representative". s. 2(1)(c) – "complaint" means an allegation in writing that an unfair or restrictive trade practice has been adopted; goods suffer from defects; services suffer from deficiency; excess price has been charged; or hazardous goods or services are offered – "with a view to obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act". s. 2(1)(d) – "consumer" means any person who "(i) buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment" (including a user with the buyer's approval), "but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose"; or "(ii) hires or avails of any services for a consideration" (including a beneficiary with approval) "but does not include a person who avails of such services for any commercial purpose". Explanation – "commercial purpose" does not include goods or services used "exclusively for the purposes of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment". s. 2(1)(f) – "defect" means "any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard" required by law, by contract, or "as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods". s. 2(1)(g) – "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service". s. 2(1)(nnn) – "restrictive trade practice" means a trade practice which "tends to bring about manipulation of price or its conditions of delivery or to affect flow of supplies in the market ... in such a manner as to impose on the consumers unjustified costs or restrictions", including delay in supply leading to a rise in price, and tie-in conditions. s. 2(1)(o) – "service" means "service of any description which is made available to potential users", including banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, board or lodging, housing construction, entertainment, amusement and the purveying of news or other information, "but does not include the rendering of any service free of charge or under a contract of personal service". s. 2(1)(r) – "unfair trade practice" – a trade practice which, for promoting sale, use or supply of goods or provision of services, "adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice", including false representations, bargain-price advertisements, gifts and prizes, contests, goods below safety standards, hoarding and spurious goods. s. 3 – "The provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law for the time being in force." s. 6 – the objects of the Central Council are to promote and protect the rights of consumers such as: "(a) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods and services which are hazardous to life and property; (b) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods or services ...; (c) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices; (d) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumers' interests will receive due consideration at appropriate forums; (e) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and (f) the right to consumer education." ss. 7, 8 (State Council) and 8A, 8B (District Council) provide the same objects at those levels. s. 9 – establishes (a) a District Forum in each district (more than one if the State Government deems fit), (b) a State Commission, and (c) a National Commission. s. 10(1) – the District Forum consists of "a person who is, or has been, or is qualified to be a District Judge, who shall be its President" and "two other members, one of whom shall be a woman". s. 11(1) – District Forum: complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation claimed "does not exceed rupees twenty lakhs". s. 17(1)(a) – State Commission: over twenty lakhs up to one crore, appeals from District Fora, and (s. 17(1)(b)) revision. s. 21 – National Commission: over one crore, appeals from State Commissions, and revision. (Figures as amended in 2002, w.e.f. 15 March 2003; the District Forum limit earlier was five lakhs.) s. 12(1) – a complaint may be filed by the consumer, any recognised consumer association, one or more consumers with permission on behalf of numerous consumers having the same interest, or the Central or State Government. s. 13 – the opposite party is given a copy within twenty-one days of admission and must give his version within thirty days (extendable by fifteen days) (s. 13(1)(a), (2)(a)); goods needing analysis are sent to an "appropriate laboratory" for a report within forty-five days (s. 13(1)(c)); the Forum may proceed ex parte (s. 13(2)(b)(ii)); proceedings following this procedure cannot be challenged on the ground of natural justice (s. 13(3)); a complaint should be decided within three months, or five months if testing is needed (s. 13(3A)); interim orders (s. 13(3B)); powers of a civil court for summons, discovery, affidavits, laboratory reports and commissions (s. 13(4)). s. 14(1) – reliefs: remove defect, replace goods, return price, compensation (with punitive damages), remove defects or deficiencies, discontinue unfair or restrictive trade practice, withdraw hazardous goods, cease manufacture of hazardous goods, a sum of not less than five per cent. for unidentified consumers, corrective advertisement, and costs. ss. 15, 19, 23 – appeals within thirty days to the State Commission, the National Commission and the Supreme Court, with a deposit of fifty per cent. or ₹25,000, ₹35,000 and ₹50,000 respectively, whichever is less. s. 22(2) – review by the National Commission "when there is an error apparent on the face of record"; s. 22A – setting aside ex parte orders. s. 24 – orders not appealed are final. s. 24A(1) – complaint "within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen", with condonation for sufficient cause (s. 24A(2)). s. 25 – where an interim order is not complied with, the property of the person may be attached, and after three months sold (s. 25(1), (2)); an amount due may be recovered by a certificate to the Collector "in the same manner as arrears of land revenue" (s. 25(3)). s. 26 – a "frivolous or vexatious" complaint shall be dismissed with costs to the opposite party "not exceeding ten thousand rupees". s. 27(1) – failure to comply with an order is punishable with imprisonment "not less than one month but which may extend to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than two thousand rupees but which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both"; the Forum or Commission has the powers of a Judicial Magistrate of first class (s. 27(2)) and may try offences summarily (s. 27(3)). s. 27A – appeal on facts and law within thirty days.

Consumer Protection Act, 2019 – s. 107(1) – "The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (68 of 1986) is hereby repealed." s. 107(2) – anything done or action taken under the repealed Act, "in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act", is deemed done under the corresponding provisions of the 2019 Act.
en.meaning: Salient features – the main and distinctive points of a statute: its aim, coverage, institutions, procedure and remedies. Consumer – a person who buys goods or hires or avails of services for consideration , including the approved user or beneficiary , but not one who buys for resale or commercial purpose (s. 2(1)(d)). Defect – a fault, imperfection or shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard of goods (s. 2(1)(f)). Deficiency – a fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance of a service (s. 2(1)(g)). District Forum – the Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum at the district level, presided over by a person qualified to be a District Judge (ss. 2(1)(h), 9(a), 10). Three-tier machinery – the District Forum, State Commission and National Commission , each with a pecuniary limit and appeals upward (ss. 9, 11, 17, 21).
keyPoints: Act 68 of 1986; 24 December 1986; in force 1987. All goods and services (s. 1(4)). Consumer excludes resale and commercial purpose; self-employment saved. Service excludes free service and contract of personal service. Six rights as Council objects (s. 6). Three tiers: District Forum (₹20 lakh), State Commission (₹1 crore), National Commission (above). (See Diagram 2 .) District Forum: President qualified to be District Judge + two members, one a woman. s. 13: 21 / 30 + 15 / 45 days; 3 or 5 months. Reliefs s. 14; appeals 30 days; limitation 2 years. Enforcement s. 25; frivolous complaint s. 26; penalty s. 27. s. 3: additional remedy; repealed by CPA 2019, s. 107. (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors and hospitals argued that medical services were outside the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and that the summary procedure of the consumer bodies was unsuitable for complicated negligence cases. The Supreme Court (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) heard appeals and writ petitions on the question. Principle: Service rendered by a medical practitioner by "consultation, diagnosis and treatment, both medicinal and surgical" falls within "service" in s. 2(1)(o), except where it is free of charge to every patient or under a contract of personal service; disciplinary control of the Medical Council does not exclude it. The Court also explained the Act's three-tier structure, its civil-court powers and that s. 3 "preserves the right of the consumer to approach the civil court". Why it matters: It is the leading judgment that both describes the salient features of the 1986 Act and widens its reach to the medical profession.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 1986 (1986 చట్టం నం. 68, CPA 1986) 24 డిసెంబర్ 1986న, వినియోగదారుల మండళ్ళు, "other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల వివాదాల పరిష్కారానికి ఇతర సంస్థలు) ద్వారా "to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాలకు మెరుగైన రక్షణ కల్పించడానికి) చేయబడింది (దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక). దీని ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): విస్తృత పరిధి: కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం మినహాయిస్తే తప్ప "all goods and services" (అర్థం: అన్ని వస్తువులు, సేవలు) (సెక్షన్ 1(4)); వినియోగదారుడు అనే పదానికి విస్తృత అర్థం (సెక్షన్ 2(1)(d)). స్పష్టమైన ఫిర్యాదు కారణాలు: అన్యాయ లేదా నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి, వస్తువుల్లో లోపం, సేవల్లో లోపం (deficiency) , అధిక ధర, ప్రమాదకర వస్తువులు, సేవలు (సెక్షన్ 2(1)(c)). కేంద్ర, రాష్ట్ర, జిల్లా స్థాయి వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ మండళ్ళు ప్రోత్సహించే ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు (సెక్షన్లు 4 నుండి 8B). పాక్షిక న్యాయ సంస్థల మూడంచెల వ్యవస్థ – జిల్లా ఫోరం , రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్, జాతీయ కమిషన్ (సెక్షన్ 9) – విలువ ఆధారంగా అధికార పరిధి (సెక్షన్లు 11, 17, 21). నిర్ణీత కాలపరిమితులు, సివిల్ కోర్టు అధికారాలతో సరళమైన, వేగవంతమైన ప్రక్రియ (సెక్షన్ 13). విస్తృత ఉపశమనాల జాబితా (సెక్షన్ 14), అప్పీళ్ళు (సెక్షన్లు 15, 19, 23), రెండు సంవత్సరాల కాలపరిమితి (సెక్షన్ 24A), అమలు (సెక్షన్ 25), నిరర్థక ఫిర్యాదులకు ఖర్చులు (సెక్షన్ 26), శిక్షలు (సెక్షన్లు 27, 27A). అదనపు పరిష్కారం: ఈ చట్టం ఇతర చట్టాలకు "in addition to and not in derogation of" (అర్థం: అదనంగా, వాటిని తగ్గించకుండా) ఉంటుంది (సెక్షన్ 3). వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 సెక్షన్ 107(1) దీనిని రద్దు చేసింది; దీని కింద చేసిన పనులకు రక్షణ ఉంది (సెక్షన్ 107(2)). Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) ఈ నిర్మాణాన్ని వివరించి, డబ్బు చెల్లించే వైద్య సేవలు చట్టం కింద "సేవ" అని తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది.
te.meaning: ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు (Salient features) – ఒక చట్టంలోని ప్రధాన, విశిష్ట అంశాలు: దాని లక్ష్యం, పరిధి, సంస్థలు, ప్రక్రియ, పరిష్కారాలు. వినియోగదారుడు – ప్రతిఫలానికి వస్తువులు కొనే లేదా సేవలు పొందే వ్యక్తి, అనుమతి పొందిన వాడకందారు లేదా లబ్ధిదారుతో సహా; తిరిగి అమ్మడానికి లేదా వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం కోసం కొనేవారు కాదు (సెక్షన్ 2(1)(d)). లోపం (Defect) – వస్తువుల నాణ్యత, పరిమాణం, శక్తి, స్వచ్ఛత లేదా ప్రమాణంలో తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత లేదా లోటు (సెక్షన్ 2(1)(f)). లోపం (deficiency) – ఒక సేవ పనితీరు నాణ్యత, స్వభావం, విధానంలో తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత, లోటు లేదా సరిపోకపోవడం (సెక్షన్ 2(1)(g)). జిల్లా ఫోరం – జిల్లా జడ్జిగా అర్హత ఉన్న వ్యక్తి అధ్యక్షత వహించే జిల్లా స్థాయి వినియోగదారుల వివాద పరిష్కార ఫోరం (సెక్షన్లు 2(1)(h), 9(a), 10). మూడంచెల వ్యవస్థ – జిల్లా ఫోరం, రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్ , జాతీయ కమిషన్ ; ప్రతి దానికి విలువ పరిమితి, పై స్థాయికి అప్పీళ్ళు (సెక్షన్లు 9, 11, 17, 21).
keyPoints: 1986 చట్టం నం. 68; 24 డిసెంబర్ 1986; 1987లో అమలు. అన్ని వస్తువులు, సేవలు (సెక్షన్ 1(4)). వినియోగదారుడు – తిరిగి అమ్మకం, వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం మినహాయింపు; స్వయం ఉపాధికి రక్షణ. సేవ – ఉచిత సేవ, వ్యక్తిగత సేవా ఒప్పందం మినహాయింపు. మండళ్ళ లక్ష్యాలుగా ఆరు హక్కులు (సెక్షన్ 6). మూడు అంచెలు: జిల్లా ఫోరం (₹20 లక్షలు), రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్ (₹1 కోటి), జాతీయ కమిషన్ (పైన). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) జిల్లా ఫోరం: జిల్లా జడ్జిగా అర్హత ఉన్న అధ్యక్షుడు + ఇద్దరు సభ్యులు, ఒకరు మహిళ. సెక్షన్ 13: 21 / 30 + 15 / 45 రోజులు; 3 లేదా 5 నెలలు. ఉపశమనాలు సెక్షన్ 14; అప్పీళ్ళు 30 రోజులు; కాలపరిమితి 2 సంవత్సరాలు. అమలు సెక్షన్ 25; నిరర్థక ఫిర్యాదు సెక్షన్ 26; శిక్ష సెక్షన్ 27. సెక్షన్ 3: అదనపు పరిష్కారం; CPA 2019 సెక్షన్ 107 రద్దు చేసింది. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)

selfTest.q: 1986 చట్టపు దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 6లోని ఆరు హక్కులు చెప్పండి. 2002 తర్వాత మూడు అంచెలు, వాటి విలువ పరిమితులు చెప్పండి. 1986 చట్టం కింద ఎవరు ఫిర్యాదు చేయగలరు? కాలపరిమితి ఎంత? నిరర్థక ఫిర్యాదుకు ఏమవుతుంది? 1986 చట్టాన్ని ఏ చట్టం, ఏ సెక్షన్ కింద రద్దు చేసింది?

hi.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986, CPA 1986) was passed on 24 December 1986 "to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers" through consumer councils and "other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes" (long title). Its main features (See Diagram 1 ): Wide coverage: "all goods and services" unless the Central Government excludes them (s. 1(4)); a wide meaning of consumer (s. 2(1)(d)). Clear grounds of complaint: unfair or restrictive trade practice, defect in goods, deficiency in services, excess price, hazardous goods and services (s. 2(1)(c)). Six consumer rights promoted by Consumer Protection Councils at Central, State and District level (ss. 4 to 8B). A three-tier machinery of quasi-judicial bodies – the District Forum , the State Commission and the National Commission (s. 9) – with jurisdiction based on value (ss. 11, 17, 21). Simple, quick procedure with fixed time limits and powers of a civil court (s. 13). A wide list of reliefs (s. 14), appeals (ss. 15, 19, 23), limitation of two years (s. 24A), enforcement (s. 25), costs for frivolous complaints (s. 26) and penalties (ss. 27, 27A). An additional remedy: the Act is "in addition to and not in derogation of" other laws (s. 3). It was repealed by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 107(1), with savings for things done under it (s. 107(2)). Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) described this structure and held that paid medical services are "service" under the Act.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 1986

Long title – "An Act to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumer councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith." s. 1(2) – "It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir." s. 1(4) – "Save as otherwise expressly provided by the Central Government by notification, this Act shall apply to all goods and services." Chapters I, II and IV came into force on 15 April 1987 and Chapter III on 1 July 1987 (footnote to s. 1(3)). s. 2(1)(b) – "complainant" means a consumer; a registered voluntary consumer association; the Central Government or any State Government; "one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest"; and, on the death of a consumer, "his legal heir or representative". s. 2(1)(c) – "complaint" means an allegation in writing that an unfair or restrictive trade practice has been adopted; goods suffer from defects; services suffer from deficiency; excess price has been charged; or hazardous goods or services are offered – "with a view to obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act". s. 2(1)(d) – "consumer" means any person who "(i) buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment" (including a user with the buyer's approval), "but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose"; or "(ii) hires or avails of any services for a consideration" (including a beneficiary with approval) "but does not include a person who avails of such services for any commercial purpose". Explanation – "commercial purpose" does not include goods or services used "exclusively for the purposes of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment". s. 2(1)(f) – "defect" means "any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard" required by law, by contract, or "as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods". s. 2(1)(g) – "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service". s. 2(1)(nnn) – "restrictive trade practice" means a trade practice which "tends to bring about manipulation of price or its conditions of delivery or to affect flow of supplies in the market ... in such a manner as to impose on the consumers unjustified costs or restrictions", including delay in supply leading to a rise in price, and tie-in conditions. s. 2(1)(o) – "service" means "service of any description which is made available to potential users", including banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, board or lodging, housing construction, entertainment, amusement and the purveying of news or other information, "but does not include the rendering of any service free of charge or under a contract of personal service". s. 2(1)(r) – "unfair trade practice" – a trade practice which, for promoting sale, use or supply of goods or provision of services, "adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice", including false representations, bargain-price advertisements, gifts and prizes, contests, goods below safety standards, hoarding and spurious goods. s. 3 – "The provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law for the time being in force." s. 6 – the objects of the Central Council are to promote and protect the rights of consumers such as: "(a) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods and services which are hazardous to life and property; (b) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods or services ...; (c) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices; (d) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumers' interests will receive due consideration at appropriate forums; (e) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and (f) the right to consumer education." ss. 7, 8 (State Council) and 8A, 8B (District Council) provide the same objects at those levels. s. 9 – establishes (a) a District Forum in each district (more than one if the State Government deems fit), (b) a State Commission, and (c) a National Commission. s. 10(1) – the District Forum consists of "a person who is, or has been, or is qualified to be a District Judge, who shall be its President" and "two other members, one of whom shall be a woman". s. 11(1) – District Forum: complaints where the value of the goods or services and the compensation claimed "does not exceed rupees twenty lakhs". s. 17(1)(a) – State Commission: over twenty lakhs up to one crore, appeals from District Fora, and (s. 17(1)(b)) revision. s. 21 – National Commission: over one crore, appeals from State Commissions, and revision. (Figures as amended in 2002, w.e.f. 15 March 2003; the District Forum limit earlier was five lakhs.) s. 12(1) – a complaint may be filed by the consumer, any recognised consumer association, one or more consumers with permission on behalf of numerous consumers having the same interest, or the Central or State Government. s. 13 – the opposite party is given a copy within twenty-one days of admission and must give his version within thirty days (extendable by fifteen days) (s. 13(1)(a), (2)(a)); goods needing analysis are sent to an "appropriate laboratory" for a report within forty-five days (s. 13(1)(c)); the Forum may proceed ex parte (s. 13(2)(b)(ii)); proceedings following this procedure cannot be challenged on the ground of natural justice (s. 13(3)); a complaint should be decided within three months, or five months if testing is needed (s. 13(3A)); interim orders (s. 13(3B)); powers of a civil court for summons, discovery, affidavits, laboratory reports and commissions (s. 13(4)). s. 14(1) – reliefs: remove defect, replace goods, return price, compensation (with punitive damages), remove defects or deficiencies, discontinue unfair or restrictive trade practice, withdraw hazardous goods, cease manufacture of hazardous goods, a sum of not less than five per cent. for unidentified consumers, corrective advertisement, and costs. ss. 15, 19, 23 – appeals within thirty days to the State Commission, the National Commission and the Supreme Court, with a deposit of fifty per cent. or ₹25,000, ₹35,000 and ₹50,000 respectively, whichever is less. s. 22(2) – review by the National Commission "when there is an error apparent on the face of record"; s. 22A – setting aside ex parte orders. s. 24 – orders not appealed are final. s. 24A(1) – complaint "within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen", with condonation for sufficient cause (s. 24A(2)). s. 25 – where an interim order is not complied with, the property of the person may be attached, and after three months sold (s. 25(1), (2)); an amount due may be recovered by a certificate to the Collector "in the same manner as arrears of land revenue" (s. 25(3)). s. 26 – a "frivolous or vexatious" complaint shall be dismissed with costs to the opposite party "not exceeding ten thousand rupees". s. 27(1) – failure to comply with an order is punishable with imprisonment "not less than one month but which may extend to three years, or with fine which shall not be less than two thousand rupees but which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both"; the Forum or Commission has the powers of a Judicial Magistrate of first class (s. 27(2)) and may try offences summarily (s. 27(3)). s. 27A – appeal on facts and law within thirty days.

Consumer Protection Act, 2019 – s. 107(1) – "The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (68 of 1986) is hereby repealed." s. 107(2) – anything done or action taken under the repealed Act, "in so far as it is not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act", is deemed done under the corresponding provisions of the 2019 Act.
hi.meaning: Salient features – the main and distinctive points of a statute: its aim, coverage, institutions, procedure and remedies. Consumer – a person who buys goods or hires or avails of services for consideration , including the approved user or beneficiary , but not one who buys for resale or commercial purpose (s. 2(1)(d)). Defect – a fault, imperfection or shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard of goods (s. 2(1)(f)). Deficiency – a fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance of a service (s. 2(1)(g)). District Forum – the Consumer Disputes Redressal Forum at the district level, presided over by a person qualified to be a District Judge (ss. 2(1)(h), 9(a), 10). Three-tier machinery – the District Forum, State Commission and National Commission , each with a pecuniary limit and appeals upward (ss. 9, 11, 17, 21).
keyPoints: Act 68 of 1986; 24 December 1986; in force 1987. All goods and services (s. 1(4)). Consumer excludes resale and commercial purpose; self-employment saved. Service excludes free service and contract of personal service. Six rights as Council objects (s. 6). Three tiers: District Forum (₹20 lakh), State Commission (₹1 crore), National Commission (above). (See Diagram 2 .) District Forum: President qualified to be District Judge + two members, one a woman. s. 13: 21 / 30 + 15 / 45 days; 3 or 5 months. Reliefs s. 14; appeals 30 days; limitation 2 years. Enforcement s. 25; frivolous complaint s. 26; penalty s. 27. s. 3: additional remedy; repealed by CPA 2019, s. 107. (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors and hospitals argued that medical services were outside the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and that the summary procedure of the consumer bodies was unsuitable for complicated negligence cases. The Supreme Court (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) heard appeals and writ petitions on the question. Principle: Service rendered by a medical practitioner by "consultation, diagnosis and treatment, both medicinal and surgical" falls within "service" in s. 2(1)(o), except where it is free of charge to every patient or under a contract of personal service; disciplinary control of the Medical Council does not exclude it. The Court also explained the Act's three-tier structure, its civil-court powers and that s. 3 "preserves the right of the consumer to approach the civil court". Why it matters: It is the leading judgment that both describes the salient features of the 1986 Act and widens its reach to the medical profession.

law-of-torts-u5-t4.subtitle: The Act that replaced the 1986 law: a regulator, product liability, mediation, e-commerce rules and e-filing

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019, CPA 2019) received assent on 9 August 2019. Most of it came into force on 20 July 2020 and the Central Authority provisions on 24 July 2020. It repealed the 1986 Act (s. 107). Its aim: "protection of the interests of consumers" and "authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes" (long title). It has eight Chapters (See Diagram 1 ): Preliminary – definitions, including e-commerce , unfair contract , product liability and "consumer rights" (s. 2). Consumer Protection Councils (ss. 3 to 9). Central Authority – the Central Consumer Protection Authority, a regulator for consumers "as a class" (ss. 10 to 27). Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions – District Commission , State Commission, National Commission (ss. 28 to 73). Mediation (ss. 74 to 81). Product liability (ss. 82 to 87). Offences and penalties (ss. 88 to 93). Miscellaneous – e-commerce measures (s. 94), rules, repeal (ss. 94 to 107). New features compared to 1986: online and teleshopping buyers expressly covered; complaint where the complainant resides; e-filing; unfair contracts; a regulator; mediation; product liability; heavier penalties. Pecuniary limits in the Act are ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore (ss. 34, 47, 58), but the 2021 Rules fixed them at ₹50 lakh and ₹2 crore.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

Long title – "An Act to provide for protection of the interests of consumers and for the said purpose, to establish authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto." s. 1(2) – "It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir" (footnote: by S.O. 3912(E) dated 30 October 2019 the Act was made applicable to the Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh). s. 1(4) – "Save as otherwise expressly provided by the Central Government, by notification, this Act shall apply to all goods and services." Commencement (footnote to s. 1(3)) – most provisions from 20 July 2020 (S.O. 2351(E)); clauses (4), (13), (14), (16), (40) of s. 2, ss. 10 to 27, s. 58(1)(a)(iv), ss. 88, 89, 92, 93, 94, 96, 97, 99 and 104 from 24 July 2020 (S.O. 2421(E)). s. 2(5) – "complainant" includes a consumer; a voluntary consumer association; the Central or any State Government; "the Central Authority"; one or more consumers with the same interest; "in case of death of a consumer, his legal heir or legal representative"; and "in case of a consumer being a minor, his parent or legal guardian". s. 2(7) – "consumer" means any person who buys goods or hires or avails of a service for consideration (including the approved user or beneficiary), "but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose". Explanation (a) – "commercial purpose" does not include goods "bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood, by means of self-employment". Explanation (b) – "the expressions 'buys any goods' and 'hires or avails any services' includes offline or online transactions through electronic means or by teleshopping or direct selling or multi-level marketing". s. 2(9) – "consumer rights" includes: (i) protection against marketing of hazardous goods, products or services; (ii) the right to be informed; (iii) access to a variety at competitive prices; (iv) the right to be heard; (v) the right to seek redressal; and "(vi) the right to consumer awareness". s. 2(16) – "'e-commerce' means buying or selling of goods or services including digital products over digital or electronic network". s. 2(34) – "product liability" means the responsibility of a product manufacturer or product seller to compensate for harm caused by a defective product or deficient service relating to it. s. 2(46) – "unfair contract" means a contract between a manufacturer, trader or service provider and a consumer "having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer", including: "(i) requiring manifestly excessive security deposits"; "(ii) imposing any penalty on the consumer, for the breach of contract thereof which is wholly disproportionate to the loss"; "(iii) refusing to accept early repayment of debts on payment of applicable penalty"; "(iv) entitling a party to the contract to terminate such contract unilaterally, without reasonable cause"; "(v) permitting ... one party to assign the contract to the detriment of the other party who is a consumer, without his consent"; "(vi) imposing on the consumer any unreasonable charge, obligation or condition which puts such consumer to disadvantage". s. 2(47) – "unfair trade practice" – any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice for promoting sale, use or supply of goods or provision of services, including false representations "including by means of electronic record" and other listed practices. ss. 3 to 9 – Central, State and District Consumer Protection Councils. s. 10(1) – the Central Government shall establish the Central Consumer Protection Authority "to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class". s. 18(1)(a) – it shall "protect, promote and enforce the rights of consumers as a class, and prevent violation of consumers rights under this Act". s. 28(1) – the State Government shall establish "a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, to be known as the District Commission, in each district of the State"; s. 28(2) – a President and "not less than two" members. ss. 42, 53 – State and National Commissions. s. 34(1) – District Commission: complaints where "the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees", with a proviso that the Central Government may prescribe another value. s. 34(2)(d) – a complaint may be instituted where "the complainant resides or personally works for gain". s. 47(1)(a)(i) – State Commission: above ₹1 crore up to ₹10 crore; s. 47(1)(a)(ii) – complaints against unfair contracts up to ₹10 crore. s. 58(1)(a)(i), (ii) – National Commission: above ₹10 crore, and unfair contracts above ₹10 crore; s. 58(1)(a)(iv) – appeals against orders of the Central Authority. s. 35(1) – a complaint may be filed by the consumer, a recognised consumer association, one or more consumers for numerous consumers with the same interest, or "the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government"; proviso – "the complaint under this sub-section may be filed electronically in such manner as may be prescribed". s. 36(2), (3) – admissibility "shall ordinarily be decided within twenty-one days"; if not decided in that time, the complaint "shall be deemed to have been admitted". s. 38(6) – every complaint shall be heard "on the basis of affidavit and documentary evidence placed on record", with hearing in person or "through video conferencing" allowed for sufficient cause. s. 38(7) – decide within three months (five months if testing is needed). s. 37; ss. 74 to 81 – mediation. ss. 82 to 87 – product liability. ss. 88 to 93 – offences. s. 94 – the Central Government may take measures to prevent unfair trade practices "in e-commerce, direct selling". s. 100 – the Act is "in addition to and not in derogation of" other laws. s. 107(1) – "The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (68 of 1986) is hereby repealed."

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021) – made under the provisos to ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i) and 58(1)(a)(i): r. 3 – District Commission: value of goods or services paid as consideration "does not exceed fifty lakh rupees"; r. 4 – State Commission: "exceeds fifty lakh but does not exceed two crore rupees"; r. 5 – National Commission: "exceeds two crore rupees". They came into force on publication (r. 1(2)).
en.meaning: Consumer (s. 2(7)) – a buyer of goods or hirer of services for consideration , including online, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing transactions; not one who buys for resale or commercial purpose. E-commerce – buying or selling of goods or services, including digital products, over a digital or electronic network (s. 2(16)). Unfair contract – a contract with a consumer whose terms "cause significant change in the rights of such consumer", such as excessive deposits, disproportionate penalties or one-sided termination (s. 2(46)). Central Authority – the Central Consumer Protection Authority established under s. 10 to regulate violations of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements, and to protect consumers as a class (s. 2(4)). District Commission – the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established in each district under s. 28 (the "District Forum" of the 1986 Act). Consumer rights (s. 2(9)) – the six rights: safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and consumer awareness.
keyPoints: Act 35 of 2019; assent 9 August 2019; in force 20 July 2020 / 24 July 2020. Eight Chapters; 107 sections. Consumer includes online, teleshopping, direct selling, multi-level marketing. Six consumer rights; sixth is awareness. Unfair contract (s. 2(46)) – only State and National Commissions. Central Authority (s. 10) – consumers as a class. Limits: Act ₹1 crore / ₹10 crore; Rules 2021 ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore. (See Diagram 2 .) File where complainant resides; e-filing; deemed admission in 21 days. Mediation, product liability, penalties. s. 107: 1986 Act repealed. (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: A complaint of medical negligence against an eye surgeon was pending in revision before the National Commission when the doctor died. The National Commission brought his wife and son on record, and they appealed (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.). Principle: "in view of the preceding discussion and the statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act, we conclude that upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; personal injury claims abate but claims against the estate survive. Why it matters: It shows that the 2019 Act continues the 1986 framework (including the application of Order XXII CPC, now s. 38(12)), so remedies under the old Act are carried forward. Note: No other judgment interpreting the new features of the 2019 Act was available for this note.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (2019 చట్టం నం. 35, CPA 2019) 9 ఆగస్టు 2019న ఆమోదం పొందింది. చాలా భాగం 20 జూలై 2020న, కేంద్ర అథారిటీ నిబంధనలు 24 జూలై 2020న అమలులోకి వచ్చాయి. ఇది 1986 చట్టాన్ని రద్దు చేసింది (సెక్షన్ 107). దీని లక్ష్యం: "protection of the interests of consumers" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాల రక్షణ), "authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల వివాదాల సకాల, సమర్థ నిర్వహణ, పరిష్కారానికి సంస్థలు) (దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక). ఇందులో ఎనిమిది అధ్యాయాలు ఉన్నాయి ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): ప్రాథమికం – ఇ-కామర్స్ , అన్యాయ ఒప్పందం , ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత, "consumer rights" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు) సహా నిర్వచనాలు (సెక్షన్ 2). వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ మండళ్ళు (సెక్షన్లు 3 నుండి 9). కేంద్ర అథారిటీ – వినియోగదారులకు "as a class" (అర్థం: ఒక వర్గంగా) నియంత్రణ సంస్థ అయిన కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ అథారిటీ (సెక్షన్లు 10 నుండి 27). వినియోగదారుల వివాద పరిష్కార కమిషన్లు – జిల్లా కమిషన్ , రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్, జాతీయ కమిషన్ (సెక్షన్లు 28 నుండి 73). మధ్యవర్తిత్వం (సెక్షన్లు 74 నుండి 81). ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత (సెక్షన్లు 82 నుండి 87). నేరాలు, శిక్షలు (సెక్షన్లు 88 నుండి 93). ఇతరాలు – ఇ-కామర్స్ చర్యలు (సెక్షన్ 94), నియమాలు, రద్దు (సెక్షన్లు 94 నుండి 107). 1986తో పోలిస్తే కొత్త లక్షణాలు: ఆన్‌లైన్, టెలిషాపింగ్ కొనుగోలుదారులకు స్పష్టంగా వర్తింపు; ఫిర్యాదుదారు నివసించే చోట ఫిర్యాదు; ఇ-ఫైలింగ్; అన్యాయ ఒప్పందాలు; నియంత్రణ సంస్థ; మధ్యవర్తిత్వం; ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత; కఠిన శిక్షలు. చట్టంలో విలువ పరిమితులు ₹1 కోటి, ₹10 కోట్లు (సెక్షన్లు 34, 47, 58), కానీ 2021 నియమాలు వాటిని ₹50 లక్షలు, ₹2 కోట్లుగా నిర్ణయించాయి.
te.meaning: వినియోగదారుడు (సెక్షన్ 2(7)) – ప్రతిఫలానికి వస్తువులు కొనేవారు లేదా సేవలు పొందేవారు; ఆన్‌లైన్, టెలిషాపింగ్, ప్రత్యక్ష అమ్మకం, బహుళ స్థాయి మార్కెటింగ్ లావాదేవీలతో సహా; తిరిగి అమ్మకం లేదా వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం కోసం కొనేవారు కాదు. ఇ-కామర్స్ – డిజిటల్ లేదా ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ నెట్‌వర్క్ ద్వారా డిజిటల్ ఉత్పత్తులతో సహా వస్తువులు లేదా సేవలు కొనడం లేదా అమ్మడం (సెక్షన్ 2(16)). అన్యాయ ఒప్పందం – షరతులు "cause significant change in the rights of such consumer" (అర్థం: ఆ వినియోగదారుడి హక్కుల్లో గణనీయమైన మార్పు కలిగించే) వినియోగదారుడితో ఒప్పందం ; ఉదాహరణకు అధిక డిపాజిట్లు, అసమాన జరిమానాలు, ఏకపక్ష రద్దు (సెక్షన్ 2(46)). కేంద్ర అథారిటీ – వినియోగదారుల హక్కుల ఉల్లంఘనలు, అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతులు , తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటనలను నియంత్రించడానికి, వినియోగదారులను ఒక వర్గంగా రక్షించడానికి సెక్షన్ 10 కింద ఏర్పాటైన కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ అథారిటీ (సెక్షన్ 2(4)). జిల్లా కమిషన్ – సెక్షన్ 28 కింద ప్రతి జిల్లాలో ఏర్పాటైన జిల్లా వినియోగదారుల వివాద పరిష్కార కమిషన్ (1986 చట్టపు "జిల్లా ఫోరం"). వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)) – ఆరు హక్కులు: భద్రత, సమాచారం, ఎంపిక, వినిపించుకోవడం, పరిష్కారం, వినియోగదారుల అవగాహన.
keyPoints: 2019 చట్టం నం. 35; ఆమోదం 9 ఆగస్టు 2019; అమలు 20 జూలై 2020 / 24 జూలై 2020. ఎనిమిది అధ్యాయాలు; 107 సెక్షన్లు. వినియోగదారుడిలో ఆన్‌లైన్, టెలిషాపింగ్, ప్రత్యక్ష అమ్మకం, బహుళ స్థాయి మార్కెటింగ్. ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు; ఆరవది అవగాహన. అన్యాయ ఒప్పందం (సెక్షన్ 2(46)) – రాష్ట్ర, జాతీయ కమిషన్లు మాత్రమే. కేంద్ర అథారిటీ (సెక్షన్ 10) – వినియోగదారులు ఒక వర్గంగా. పరిమితులు: చట్టం ₹1 కోటి / ₹10 కోట్లు; నియమాలు 2021 ₹50 లక్షలు / ₹2 కోట్లు. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) ఫిర్యాదుదారు నివసించే చోట ఫిర్యాదు; ఇ-ఫైలింగ్; 21 రోజుల్లో స్వీకరించినట్లు భావన. మధ్యవర్తిత్వం, ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత, శిక్షలు. సెక్షన్ 107: 1986 చట్టం రద్దు. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)

selfTest.q: 2019 చట్టంలో చాలా భాగం ఎప్పుడు అమలులోకి వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 2(7) వివరణ (b) ఏ లావాదేవీలను "ఏవైనా వస్తువులు కొనడం"లోకి తెస్తుంది? "ఇ-కామర్స్" నిర్వచించండి. అన్యాయ ఒప్పందానికి ఏవైనా మూడు ఉదాహరణలు ఇవ్వండి. మూడు కమిషన్ల ప్రస్తుత విలువ పరిమితులు ఏమిటి? సెక్షన్ 34(2) కింద వినియోగదారుడు ఎక్కడ ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు? జిల్లా కమిషన్ ఇరవై ఒక్క రోజుల్లో స్వీకార్యత నిర్ణయించకపోతే ఏమవుతుంది?

hi.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019, CPA 2019) received assent on 9 August 2019. Most of it came into force on 20 July 2020 and the Central Authority provisions on 24 July 2020. It repealed the 1986 Act (s. 107). Its aim: "protection of the interests of consumers" and "authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes" (long title). It has eight Chapters (See Diagram 1 ): Preliminary – definitions, including e-commerce , unfair contract , product liability and "consumer rights" (s. 2). Consumer Protection Councils (ss. 3 to 9). Central Authority – the Central Consumer Protection Authority, a regulator for consumers "as a class" (ss. 10 to 27). Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions – District Commission , State Commission, National Commission (ss. 28 to 73). Mediation (ss. 74 to 81). Product liability (ss. 82 to 87). Offences and penalties (ss. 88 to 93). Miscellaneous – e-commerce measures (s. 94), rules, repeal (ss. 94 to 107). New features compared to 1986: online and teleshopping buyers expressly covered; complaint where the complainant resides; e-filing; unfair contracts; a regulator; mediation; product liability; heavier penalties. Pecuniary limits in the Act are ₹1 crore and ₹10 crore (ss. 34, 47, 58), but the 2021 Rules fixed them at ₹50 lakh and ₹2 crore.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

Long title – "An Act to provide for protection of the interests of consumers and for the said purpose, to establish authorities for timely and effective administration and settlement of consumers' disputes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto." s. 1(2) – "It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir" (footnote: by S.O. 3912(E) dated 30 October 2019 the Act was made applicable to the Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh). s. 1(4) – "Save as otherwise expressly provided by the Central Government, by notification, this Act shall apply to all goods and services." Commencement (footnote to s. 1(3)) – most provisions from 20 July 2020 (S.O. 2351(E)); clauses (4), (13), (14), (16), (40) of s. 2, ss. 10 to 27, s. 58(1)(a)(iv), ss. 88, 89, 92, 93, 94, 96, 97, 99 and 104 from 24 July 2020 (S.O. 2421(E)). s. 2(5) – "complainant" includes a consumer; a voluntary consumer association; the Central or any State Government; "the Central Authority"; one or more consumers with the same interest; "in case of death of a consumer, his legal heir or legal representative"; and "in case of a consumer being a minor, his parent or legal guardian". s. 2(7) – "consumer" means any person who buys goods or hires or avails of a service for consideration (including the approved user or beneficiary), "but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose". Explanation (a) – "commercial purpose" does not include goods "bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood, by means of self-employment". Explanation (b) – "the expressions 'buys any goods' and 'hires or avails any services' includes offline or online transactions through electronic means or by teleshopping or direct selling or multi-level marketing". s. 2(9) – "consumer rights" includes: (i) protection against marketing of hazardous goods, products or services; (ii) the right to be informed; (iii) access to a variety at competitive prices; (iv) the right to be heard; (v) the right to seek redressal; and "(vi) the right to consumer awareness". s. 2(16) – "'e-commerce' means buying or selling of goods or services including digital products over digital or electronic network". s. 2(34) – "product liability" means the responsibility of a product manufacturer or product seller to compensate for harm caused by a defective product or deficient service relating to it. s. 2(46) – "unfair contract" means a contract between a manufacturer, trader or service provider and a consumer "having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer", including: "(i) requiring manifestly excessive security deposits"; "(ii) imposing any penalty on the consumer, for the breach of contract thereof which is wholly disproportionate to the loss"; "(iii) refusing to accept early repayment of debts on payment of applicable penalty"; "(iv) entitling a party to the contract to terminate such contract unilaterally, without reasonable cause"; "(v) permitting ... one party to assign the contract to the detriment of the other party who is a consumer, without his consent"; "(vi) imposing on the consumer any unreasonable charge, obligation or condition which puts such consumer to disadvantage". s. 2(47) – "unfair trade practice" – any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice for promoting sale, use or supply of goods or provision of services, including false representations "including by means of electronic record" and other listed practices. ss. 3 to 9 – Central, State and District Consumer Protection Councils. s. 10(1) – the Central Government shall establish the Central Consumer Protection Authority "to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class". s. 18(1)(a) – it shall "protect, promote and enforce the rights of consumers as a class, and prevent violation of consumers rights under this Act". s. 28(1) – the State Government shall establish "a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, to be known as the District Commission, in each district of the State"; s. 28(2) – a President and "not less than two" members. ss. 42, 53 – State and National Commissions. s. 34(1) – District Commission: complaints where "the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees", with a proviso that the Central Government may prescribe another value. s. 34(2)(d) – a complaint may be instituted where "the complainant resides or personally works for gain". s. 47(1)(a)(i) – State Commission: above ₹1 crore up to ₹10 crore; s. 47(1)(a)(ii) – complaints against unfair contracts up to ₹10 crore. s. 58(1)(a)(i), (ii) – National Commission: above ₹10 crore, and unfair contracts above ₹10 crore; s. 58(1)(a)(iv) – appeals against orders of the Central Authority. s. 35(1) – a complaint may be filed by the consumer, a recognised consumer association, one or more consumers for numerous consumers with the same interest, or "the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government"; proviso – "the complaint under this sub-section may be filed electronically in such manner as may be prescribed". s. 36(2), (3) – admissibility "shall ordinarily be decided within twenty-one days"; if not decided in that time, the complaint "shall be deemed to have been admitted". s. 38(6) – every complaint shall be heard "on the basis of affidavit and documentary evidence placed on record", with hearing in person or "through video conferencing" allowed for sufficient cause. s. 38(7) – decide within three months (five months if testing is needed). s. 37; ss. 74 to 81 – mediation. ss. 82 to 87 – product liability. ss. 88 to 93 – offences. s. 94 – the Central Government may take measures to prevent unfair trade practices "in e-commerce, direct selling". s. 100 – the Act is "in addition to and not in derogation of" other laws. s. 107(1) – "The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (68 of 1986) is hereby repealed."

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021) – made under the provisos to ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i) and 58(1)(a)(i): r. 3 – District Commission: value of goods or services paid as consideration "does not exceed fifty lakh rupees"; r. 4 – State Commission: "exceeds fifty lakh but does not exceed two crore rupees"; r. 5 – National Commission: "exceeds two crore rupees". They came into force on publication (r. 1(2)).
hi.meaning: Consumer (s. 2(7)) – a buyer of goods or hirer of services for consideration , including online, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing transactions; not one who buys for resale or commercial purpose. E-commerce – buying or selling of goods or services, including digital products, over a digital or electronic network (s. 2(16)). Unfair contract – a contract with a consumer whose terms "cause significant change in the rights of such consumer", such as excessive deposits, disproportionate penalties or one-sided termination (s. 2(46)). Central Authority – the Central Consumer Protection Authority established under s. 10 to regulate violations of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements, and to protect consumers as a class (s. 2(4)). District Commission – the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established in each district under s. 28 (the "District Forum" of the 1986 Act). Consumer rights (s. 2(9)) – the six rights: safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and consumer awareness.
keyPoints: Act 35 of 2019; assent 9 August 2019; in force 20 July 2020 / 24 July 2020. Eight Chapters; 107 sections. Consumer includes online, teleshopping, direct selling, multi-level marketing. Six consumer rights; sixth is awareness. Unfair contract (s. 2(46)) – only State and National Commissions. Central Authority (s. 10) – consumers as a class. Limits: Act ₹1 crore / ₹10 crore; Rules 2021 ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore. (See Diagram 2 .) File where complainant resides; e-filing; deemed admission in 21 days. Mediation, product liability, penalties. s. 107: 1986 Act repealed. (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: A complaint of medical negligence against an eye surgeon was pending in revision before the National Commission when the doctor died. The National Commission brought his wife and son on record, and they appealed (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.). Principle: "in view of the preceding discussion and the statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act, we conclude that upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; personal injury claims abate but claims against the estate survive. Why it matters: It shows that the 2019 Act continues the 1986 framework (including the application of Order XXII CPC, now s. 38(12)), so remedies under the old Act are carried forward. Note: No other judgment interpreting the new features of the 2019 Act was available for this note.

law-of-torts-u5-t6.subtitle: The six consumer rights in section 2(9) of the 2019 Act and how each is protected

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) defines consumer rights in s. 2(9). There are six (See Diagram 1 ): Right to safety – protection against marketing of goods, products or services "hazardous to life and property". Right to be informed – about "quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price", to protect against unfair trade practices. Right to choose – access, wherever possible, to "a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices". Right to be heard – consumers' interests "will receive due consideration at appropriate fora". Right to redressal – against unfair trade practice, restrictive trade practices or "unscrupulous exploitation of consumers". Right to consumer awareness . The definition says "includes", so the list is not closed. (See Diagram 3 .) Each right is backed by machinery in the Act (See Diagram 2 ): Councils advise on them (ss. 5, 7, 9); the Central Authority protects them for consumers "as a class" (ss. 10, 18, 20, 21); Commissions give individual redress (ss. 34 to 73); and product liability and offences protect safety (ss. 82 to 93). Under the 1986 Act the same six rights (with "consumer education" in place of "awareness") were only the objects of the Councils (s. 6).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 2(9) – "'consumer rights' includes,— (i) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property; (ii) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices; (iii) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices; (iv) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora; (v) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and (vi) the right to consumer awareness". s. 5 – "The objects of the Central Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act." s. 7 (State Council) and s. 9 (District Council, "within the district") – the same objects at their levels. Each Council is "an advisory council" (ss. 3(2), 6(2), 8(2)). s. 10(1) – the Central Authority is established "to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements ... and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class". s. 18(1)(a) – the Central Authority shall "protect, promote and enforce the rights of consumers as a class, and prevent violation of consumers rights under this Act". s. 18(2) – it may, among other things, "(a) inquire or cause an inquiry or investigation to be made into violations of consumer rights or unfair trade practices, either suo motu or on a complaint"; "(b) file complaints before the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission"; "(c) intervene in any proceedings"; "(d) review the matters relating to, and the factors inhibiting enjoyment of, consumer rights"; "(f) undertake and promote research in the field of consumer rights"; "(g) spread and promote awareness on consumer rights"; "(j) issue safety notices to alert consumers against dangerous or hazardous or unsafe goods or services". s. 20 – on sufficient evidence of "violation of consumer rights or unfair trade practice", the Central Authority may order "(a) recalling of goods or withdrawal of services which are dangerous, hazardous or unsafe; (b) reimbursement of the prices of goods or services so recalled to purchasers ...; and (c) discontinuation of practices which are unfair and prejudicial to consumers' interest", after giving "an opportunity of being heard". s. 21 – directions and penalties against false or misleading advertisements. s. 2(6) – a "complaint" may allege an unfair contract or unfair or restrictive trade practice, defective goods, deficient services, excess price, hazardous goods or services, or a product liability claim. s. 2(41) – "restrictive trade practice" – a practice which manipulates price or conditions of delivery or affects flow of supplies "in such a manner as to impose on the consumers unjustified costs or restrictions". s. 2(47) – "unfair trade practice" – any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice for promoting sale or supply. s. 39(1) – reliefs a Commission may order (refund, compensation, withdrawal of hazardous goods, corrective advertisement and others).

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (for comparison) – s. 6 – the objects of the Central Council were "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers such as" the same first five rights and "(f) the right to consumer education".
en.meaning: Consumer rights – the rights listed in s. 2(9) of CPA 2019; the word "includes" shows the list is illustrative. Right to safety – the right to be protected against goods, products or services that are "hazardous to life and property" (s. 2(9)(i)). Right to be informed – the right to know the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price, so that unfair trade practices do not mislead (s. 2(9)(ii)). Right to choose – the right to be assured, wherever possible, of access to a variety at competitive prices (s. 2(9)(iii)). Right to be heard – the right that consumer interests receive due consideration "at appropriate fora" (s. 2(9)(iv)). Right to redressal – the right to seek a remedy against unfair or restrictive trade practices or exploitation (s. 2(9)(v)). Right to consumer awareness – the right to know one's rights and remedies (s. 2(9)(vi)).
keyPoints: s. 2(9): six rights; "includes". (See Diagram 1 .) Safety, information, choice ("wherever possible"), being heard, redressal, awareness. 1986: s. 6, Council objects; sixth was "education". Councils advise (ss. 5, 7, 9). Central Authority: rights of consumers "as a class" (ss. 10, 18(1)(a)); recall (s. 20); awareness (s. 18(2)(g)); safety notices (s. 18(2)(j)). Commissions: individual redressal (s. 39). V.P. Shantha : UN guidelines – safety and effective redress. Nizam's Institute : adequate compensation. (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors and hospitals argued that medical services were outside the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, so patients could not use the consumer fora. The Supreme Court (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) decided the question. Principle: Paid medical service by "consultation, diagnosis and treatment, both medicinal and surgical" is "service" under the Act (except free service to all and contracts of personal service). The Court traced the Act to UN guidelines aimed at "the protection of consumers from hazards to their health and safety and availability of effective consumer redress". Why it matters: It links the rights to safety and redressal to the purpose of the Act and extends the right to redressal to patients. 2. Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A young engineering student became paraplegic after negligent surgery; the National Commission awarded ₹14 lakh. Both sides appealed (B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ.). Principle: "if a case is made out, the Court must not be chary of awarding adequate compensation"; the award was raised to ₹1 crore with interest. Why it matters: The right to redressal means real, adequate redress, not a token sum.
