te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019) సెక్షన్ 2(9)లో వినియోగదారుల హక్కుల ను నిర్వచిస్తుంది. అవి ఆరు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): భద్రత హక్కు – "hazardous to life and property" (అర్థం: ప్రాణానికి, ఆస్తికి ప్రమాదకరమైన) వస్తువులు, ఉత్పత్తులు లేదా సేవల మార్కెటింగ్ నుండి రక్షణ. సమాచారం పొందే హక్కు – అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతుల నుండి రక్షణ కోసం "quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price" (అర్థం: నాణ్యత, పరిమాణం, శక్తి, స్వచ్ఛత, ప్రమాణం, ధర) గురించి. ఎంపిక హక్కు – సాధ్యమైన చోట "a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices" (అర్థం: పోటీ ధరలకు వివిధ వస్తువులు, ఉత్పత్తులు లేదా సేవలు) అందుబాటు. వినిపించుకునే హక్కు – వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాలు "will receive due consideration at appropriate fora" (అర్థం: తగిన వేదికల్లో తగిన ప్రాధాన్యం పొందుతాయి). పరిష్కారం కోరే హక్కు – అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి, నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతులు లేదా "unscrupulous exploitation of consumers" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల నిర్లజ్జ దోపిడీ)కి వ్యతిరేకంగా. వినియోగదారుల అవగాహన హక్కు . నిర్వచనం "includes" (అర్థం: కలిగి ఉంటుంది) అని చెబుతుంది, కాబట్టి జాబితా మూసివేసినది కాదు. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) ప్రతి హక్కుకు చట్టంలో యంత్రాంగం ఉంది ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి): మండళ్ళు వాటిపై సలహా ఇస్తాయి (సెక్షన్లు 5, 7, 9); కేంద్ర అథారిటీ వినియోగదారులను "as a class" (అర్థం: ఒక వర్గంగా) రక్షిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్లు 10, 18, 20, 21); కమిషన్లు వ్యక్తిగత పరిష్కారం ఇస్తాయి (సెక్షన్లు 34 నుండి 73); ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత, నేరాలు భద్రతను కాపాడతాయి (సెక్షన్లు 82 నుండి 93). 1986 చట్టం కింద ఇవే ఆరు హక్కులు ("అవగాహన" బదులు "consumer education" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల విద్య)తో) మండళ్ళ లక్ష్యాలు మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 6).
te.meaning: వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు – CPA 2019 సెక్షన్ 2(9)లో పేర్కొన్న హక్కులు; "includes" (అర్థం: కలిగి ఉంటుంది) అనే పదం జాబితా ఉదాహరణాత్మకమని చూపుతుంది. భద్రత హక్కు – "hazardous to life and property" (అర్థం: ప్రాణానికి, ఆస్తికి ప్రమాదకరమైన) వస్తువులు, ఉత్పత్తులు లేదా సేవల నుండి రక్షణ పొందే హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)(i)). సమాచారం పొందే హక్కు – అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతులు తప్పుదారి పట్టించకుండా ఉండేందుకు నాణ్యత, పరిమాణం, శక్తి, స్వచ్ఛత, ప్రమాణం, ధర తెలుసుకునే హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)(ii)). ఎంపిక హక్కు – సాధ్యమైన చోట పోటీ ధరలకు వివిధ వాటి అందుబాటుపై హామీ పొందే హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)(iii)). వినిపించుకునే హక్కు – వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాలు "at appropriate fora" (అర్థం: తగిన వేదికల్లో) తగిన ప్రాధాన్యం పొందే హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)(iv)). పరిష్కారం కోరే హక్కు – అన్యాయ లేదా నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతులు లేదా దోపిడీకి వ్యతిరేకంగా పరిష్కారం కోరే హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)(v)). వినియోగదారుల అవగాహన హక్కు – తన హక్కులు, పరిష్కారాలు తెలుసుకునే హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)(vi)).
keyPoints: సెక్షన్ 2(9): ఆరు హక్కులు; "includes" (అర్థం: కలిగి ఉంటుంది). ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) భద్రత, సమాచారం, ఎంపిక ("సాధ్యమైన చోట"), వినిపించుకోవడం, పరిష్కారం, అవగాహన. 1986: సెక్షన్ 6, మండలి లక్ష్యాలు; ఆరవది "విద్య". మండళ్ళు సలహా ఇస్తాయి (సెక్షన్లు 5, 7, 9). కేంద్ర అథారిటీ: వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు "as a class" (అర్థం: ఒక వర్గంగా) (సెక్షన్లు 10, 18(1)(a)); రీకాల్ (సెక్షన్ 20); అవగాహన (సెక్షన్ 18(2)(g)); భద్రతా నోటీసులు (సెక్షన్ 18(2)(j)). కమిషన్లు: వ్యక్తిగత పరిష్కారం (సెక్షన్ 39). V.P. Shantha : UN మార్గదర్శకాలు – భద్రత, సమర్థ పరిష్కారం. Nizam's Institute : తగిన నష్టపరిహారం. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)

selfTest.q: CPA 2019లోని ఏ సెక్షన్‌లో వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు నిర్వచించబడ్డాయి?
selfTest.a: ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు చెప్పండి. 1986 చట్టం కింద ఆరవ హక్కును ఏమని పిలిచారు? వినియోగదారుల హక్కులను ఒక వర్గంగా ఏ సంస్థ రక్షిస్తుంది? కేంద్ర అథారిటీ యొక్క ఏ అధికారాలు భద్రత హక్కును రక్షిస్తాయి? సెక్షన్ 2(9)లోని జాబితా సమగ్రమా?

హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 2(9)) అర్థం చట్టం ఎలా రక్షిస్తుంది
(i) భద్రత ప్రమాదకర వస్తువులు, ఉత్పత్తులు లేదా సేవల నుండి రక్షణ భద్రతా నోటీసులు (సెక్షన్ 18(2)(j)); రీకాల్, డబ్బు వాపసు (సెక్షన్ 20); ప్రమాదకర వస్తువులు లేదా సేవలపై ఫిర్యాదు (సెక్షన్ 2(6)(v), (vi)); ఉపసంహరణ, తయారీ ఆపడం (సెక్షన్ 39(1)(h)–(j)); ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత (సెక్షన్లు 82 నుండి 87); కల్తీ, నకిలీ వస్తువుల నేరాలు (సెక్షన్లు 90, 91)
(ii) సమాచారం నాణ్యత, పరిమాణం, శక్తి, స్వచ్ఛత, ప్రమాణం, ధర తెలుసుకోవడం అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతిలో తప్పుడు ప్రాతినిధ్యం (సెక్షన్ 2(47)); తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటన (సెక్షన్ 21); సరిదిద్దే ప్రకటన (సెక్షన్ 39(1)(l)); అధిక ధర ఫిర్యాదు కారణం (సెక్షన్ 2(6)(iv))
(iii) ఎంపిక పోటీ ధరలకు వివిధ వస్తువులు నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి – ముడిపెట్టిన అమ్మకాలు, ధర పెరుగుదలకు దారితీసే ఆలస్యం (సెక్షన్ 2(41)); నిలిపివేత ఉత్తర్వు (సెక్షన్ 39(1)(g))
(iv) వినిపించుకోవడం తగిన వేదికల్లో వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాల పరిశీలన ఫిర్యాదు దాఖలు హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 35); వినియోగదారుల సభ్యులతో మండళ్ళు (సెక్షన్లు 3, 6, 8); కేంద్ర అథారిటీ విచారణల్లో జోక్యం (సెక్షన్ 18(2)(c)); ఫిర్యాదు తిరస్కరణకు ముందు విచారణ (సెక్షన్ 36(2) నిబంధన)
(v) పరిష్కారం అన్యాయ పద్ధతులు, దోపిడీకి పరిష్కారం మూడు కమిషన్లు (సెక్షన్లు 28 నుండి 73); ఉపశమనాలు (సెక్షన్ 39); మధ్యవర్తిత్వం (సెక్షన్ 37); అప్పీళ్ళు (సెక్షన్లు 41, 51, 67)
(vi) అవగాహన హక్కులు, పరిష్కారాలు తెలుసుకోవడం కేంద్ర అథారిటీ "spread and promote awareness" (అర్థం: అవగాహన వ్యాప్తి చేయాలి, ప్రోత్సహించాలి) (సెక్షన్ 18(2)(g)); హక్కుల ప్రోత్సాహంపై మండళ్ళ సలహా (సెక్షన్లు 5, 7, 9)

hi.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) defines consumer rights in s. 2(9). There are six (See Diagram 1 ): Right to safety – protection against marketing of goods, products or services "hazardous to life and property". Right to be informed – about "quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price", to protect against unfair trade practices. Right to choose – access, wherever possible, to "a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices". Right to be heard – consumers' interests "will receive due consideration at appropriate fora". Right to redressal – against unfair trade practice, restrictive trade practices or "unscrupulous exploitation of consumers". Right to consumer awareness . The definition says "includes", so the list is not closed. (See Diagram 3 .) Each right is backed by machinery in the Act (See Diagram 2 ): Councils advise on them (ss. 5, 7, 9); the Central Authority protects them for consumers "as a class" (ss. 10, 18, 20, 21); Commissions give individual redress (ss. 34 to 73); and product liability and offences protect safety (ss. 82 to 93). Under the 1986 Act the same six rights (with "consumer education" in place of "awareness") were only the objects of the Councils (s. 6).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 2(9) – "'consumer rights' includes,— (i) the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property; (ii) the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices; (iii) the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices; (iv) the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora; (v) the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers; and (vi) the right to consumer awareness". s. 5 – "The objects of the Central Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act." s. 7 (State Council) and s. 9 (District Council, "within the district") – the same objects at their levels. Each Council is "an advisory council" (ss. 3(2), 6(2), 8(2)). s. 10(1) – the Central Authority is established "to regulate matters relating to violation of rights of consumers, unfair trade practices and false or misleading advertisements ... and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a class". s. 18(1)(a) – the Central Authority shall "protect, promote and enforce the rights of consumers as a class, and prevent violation of consumers rights under this Act". s. 18(2) – it may, among other things, "(a) inquire or cause an inquiry or investigation to be made into violations of consumer rights or unfair trade practices, either suo motu or on a complaint"; "(b) file complaints before the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission"; "(c) intervene in any proceedings"; "(d) review the matters relating to, and the factors inhibiting enjoyment of, consumer rights"; "(f) undertake and promote research in the field of consumer rights"; "(g) spread and promote awareness on consumer rights"; "(j) issue safety notices to alert consumers against dangerous or hazardous or unsafe goods or services". s. 20 – on sufficient evidence of "violation of consumer rights or unfair trade practice", the Central Authority may order "(a) recalling of goods or withdrawal of services which are dangerous, hazardous or unsafe; (b) reimbursement of the prices of goods or services so recalled to purchasers ...; and (c) discontinuation of practices which are unfair and prejudicial to consumers' interest", after giving "an opportunity of being heard". s. 21 – directions and penalties against false or misleading advertisements. s. 2(6) – a "complaint" may allege an unfair contract or unfair or restrictive trade practice, defective goods, deficient services, excess price, hazardous goods or services, or a product liability claim. s. 2(41) – "restrictive trade practice" – a practice which manipulates price or conditions of delivery or affects flow of supplies "in such a manner as to impose on the consumers unjustified costs or restrictions". s. 2(47) – "unfair trade practice" – any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice for promoting sale or supply. s. 39(1) – reliefs a Commission may order (refund, compensation, withdrawal of hazardous goods, corrective advertisement and others).

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (for comparison) – s. 6 – the objects of the Central Council were "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers such as" the same first five rights and "(f) the right to consumer education".
hi.meaning: Consumer rights – the rights listed in s. 2(9) of CPA 2019; the word "includes" shows the list is illustrative. Right to safety – the right to be protected against goods, products or services that are "hazardous to life and property" (s. 2(9)(i)). Right to be informed – the right to know the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price, so that unfair trade practices do not mislead (s. 2(9)(ii)). Right to choose – the right to be assured, wherever possible, of access to a variety at competitive prices (s. 2(9)(iii)). Right to be heard – the right that consumer interests receive due consideration "at appropriate fora" (s. 2(9)(iv)). Right to redressal – the right to seek a remedy against unfair or restrictive trade practices or exploitation (s. 2(9)(v)). Right to consumer awareness – the right to know one's rights and remedies (s. 2(9)(vi)).
keyPoints: s. 2(9): six rights; "includes". (See Diagram 1 .) Safety, information, choice ("wherever possible"), being heard, redressal, awareness. 1986: s. 6, Council objects; sixth was "education". Councils advise (ss. 5, 7, 9). Central Authority: rights of consumers "as a class" (ss. 10, 18(1)(a)); recall (s. 20); awareness (s. 18(2)(g)); safety notices (s. 18(2)(j)). Commissions: individual redressal (s. 39). V.P. Shantha : UN guidelines – safety and effective redress. Nizam's Institute : adequate compensation. (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors and hospitals argued that medical services were outside the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, so patients could not use the consumer fora. The Supreme Court (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) decided the question. Principle: Paid medical service by "consultation, diagnosis and treatment, both medicinal and surgical" is "service" under the Act (except free service to all and contracts of personal service). The Court traced the Act to UN guidelines aimed at "the protection of consumers from hazards to their health and safety and availability of effective consumer redress". Why it matters: It links the rights to safety and redressal to the purpose of the Act and extends the right to redressal to patients. 2. Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A young engineering student became paraplegic after negligent surgery; the National Commission awarded ₹14 lakh. Both sides appealed (B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ.). Principle: "if a case is made out, the Court must not be chary of awarding adequate compensation"; the award was raised to ₹1 crore with interest. Why it matters: The right to redressal means real, adequate redress, not a token sum.

law-of-torts-u5-t7.subtitle: What counts as a defect in goods or a deficiency in service under the 2019 Act, how it is proved and the leading cases

en.inOneMinute: A consumer may complain that goods bought "suffer from one or more defects" (s. 2(6)(ii)) or that services availed of "suffer from any deficiency" (s. 2(6)(iii)) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Defect (s. 2(10)) is for goods or products . It means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard . The required standard can come from three sources (See Diagram 1 ): any law in force; any contract, express or implied; what the trader claims "in any manner whatsoever". Deficiency (s. 2(11)) is for services . It means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance . The required standard comes from: any law in force; or what the provider undertook to do under a contract "or otherwise". Deficiency includes two things: any act of negligence , omission or commission that causes loss or injury; deliberate withholding of relevant information . If a defect needs testing, the District Commission sends a sealed sample to an appropriate laboratory , which reports in 45 days (s. 38(2)(c)). Services complaints are decided on evidence (s. 38(3)). Remedies include: remove the defect; replace the goods; refund the price with interest; compensation for negligence, with punitive damages; remove deficiencies in services (s. 39(1)). For medical services, deficiency is judged by "the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence" ( V.P. Shantha ).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 2(10): "defect" means "any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods or product and the expression "defective" shall be construed accordingly". Section 2(11): "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service and includes— (i) any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer; and (ii) deliberate withholding of relevant information by such person to the consumer". Section 2(6)(ii), (iii): a "complaint" includes an allegation that "the goods bought by him or agreed to be bought by him suffer from one or more defects" or that "the services hired or availed of or agreed to be hired or availed of by him suffer from any deficiency". Section 2(45): "trader", in relation to goods, means a person who sells or distributes goods for sale "and includes the manufacturer thereof", and for packaged goods "includes the packer thereof". Section 2(2): "appropriate laboratory" means a laboratory or organisation recognised by the Central Government, or by a State Government subject to Central guidelines, or established by or under any law and maintained, financed or aided by the Central or a State Government, "for carrying out analysis or test of any goods with a view to determining whether such goods suffer from any defect". Section 38(2)(c): if the complaint "alleges a defect in the goods which cannot be determined without proper analysis or test of the goods", the District Commission shall obtain a sample, seal and authenticate it, and refer it to the appropriate laboratory, which reports "within a period of forty-five days of the receipt of the reference or within such extended period as may be granted by it". Under s. 38(2)(d), the complainant first deposits the laboratory fee. Section 38(3): if the goods procedure cannot be followed, "or if the complaint relates to any services", the Commission refers the complaint to the opposite party for his version in 30 days (extendable by up to 15 days), and then decides on the evidence of both parties, or ex parte. Section 39(1): the orders include: (a) "to remove the defect pointed out by the appropriate laboratory from the goods in question"; (b) "to replace the goods with new goods of similar description which shall be free from any defect"; (c) "to return to the complainant the price, or, as the case may be, the charges paid by the complainant along with such interest on such price or charges as may be decided"; (d) compensation "for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party", with power "to grant punitive damages"; (f) "to remove the defects in goods or deficiencies in the services in question".

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now repealed): s. 2(1)(f) "defect" had the same core words, but applied only "in relation to any goods". s. 2(1)(g) "deficiency" had the same core words, but no "includes" clause on negligence and withholding information. "Goods" meant goods as defined in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (s. 2(1)(i)).
en.meaning: Defect – a fault, imperfection or shortcoming in goods, measured against a standard set by law, by contract (express or implied), or by the trader's own claim (s. 2(10)). Deficiency – a fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in how a service is performed, measured against a standard set by law or undertaken by the provider; it includes negligence and deliberate withholding of relevant information (s. 2(11)). Trader – a seller or distributor of goods, including the manufacturer and, for packaged goods, the packer (s. 2(45)). His claims about the goods set a standard for "defect". Appropriate laboratory – a government-recognised or government-supported laboratory that tests goods to find whether they suffer from a defect (s. 2(2)).
keyPoints: Defect = goods; deficiency = services. Defect: fault, imperfection, shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard. Defect standard: law, contract (express or implied), or the trader's claim. Deficiency: fault, imperfection, shortcoming, inadequacy in quality, nature, manner of performance. Deficiency includes negligence causing loss or injury and deliberate withholding of information. Test needed? Sample to an appropriate laboratory; report in 45 days. Services: version in 30 + 15 days; decide on evidence. s. 39(1): remove defect, replace, refund with interest, compensate, remove deficiency. V.P. Shantha : medical deficiency judged by negligence test. Nizam's : onus shifts after a case of negligence is made out.

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Appeals and a writ petition raised whether doctors and hospitals render "service" under the 1986 Act and how deficiency in such service is to be judged. Bench: S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ. Principle: "A determination about deficiency in service for the purpose of Section 2(1)(g) has, therefore, to be made by applying the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence." The standard is that of "the ordinary skilled man exercising and professing to have that special skill". Why it matters: It fixes the test for deficiency in professional services. The 2019 Act now says expressly that deficiency includes negligence (s. 2(11)(i)). 2. Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A twenty-year-old engineering student had a tumour removed at the hospital and developed "acute paraplegia" right after the surgery. The National Commission found "negligence and deficiency in service" at the pre-operative, operative and post-operative stages and awarded ₹14 lakhs, plus ₹1.5 lakhs to his parents jointly. Both sides appealed. Bench: B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ. Principle: Once the complainant makes out a case of negligence, "the onus then shifts on to the hospital or to the attending doctors" (para 32). Compensation was raised to Rs. One Crore plus interest. Why it matters: It shows deficiency in medical service being found through negligence, and how the burden of proof shifts before a Consumer Commission. Note: No judgment on a defect in goods was in the available set. The "defect" part of this note is explained from the bare words of the Act.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 కింద, కొన్న వస్తువులు "suffer from one or more defects" (అర్థం: ఒకటి లేదా ఎక్కువ లోపాలతో ఉన్నాయి) (సెక్షన్ 2(6)(ii)) అని, లేదా పొందిన సేవలు "suffer from any deficiency" (అర్థం: ఏదైనా సేవా లోపంతో ఉన్నాయి) (సెక్షన్ 2(6)(iii)) అని వినియోగదారుడు ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు. లోపం (defect) (సెక్షన్ 2(10)) వస్తువులు లేదా ఉత్పత్తుల కోసం. అంటే నాణ్యత, పరిమాణం, శక్తి, స్వచ్ఛత లేదా ప్రమాణం లో ఏ తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత లేదా కొరత అయినా. అవసరమైన ప్రమాణం మూడు మూలాల నుండి రావచ్చు ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): అమలులో ఉన్న ఏ చట్టం అయినా; వ్యక్త లేదా అవ్యక్త ఏ ఒప్పందం అయినా; వ్యాపారి "in any manner whatsoever" (అర్థం: ఏ విధంగానైనా) చెప్పుకున్నది. సేవా లోపం (deficiency) (సెక్షన్ 2(11)) సేవల కోసం. అంటే పనితీరు నాణ్యత, స్వభావం, పద్ధతి లో ఏ తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత, కొరత లేదా అసమర్థత అయినా. అవసరమైన ప్రమాణం: అమలులో ఉన్న ఏ చట్టం అయినా; లేదా ఒప్పందం ప్రకారం "or otherwise" (అర్థం: లేదా మరో విధంగా) సేవా ప్రదాత చేస్తానని చేపట్టినది. సేవా లోపంలో రెండు చేరతాయి : నష్టం లేదా గాయం కలిగించే ఏ నిర్లక్ష్యం , లోపం లేదా చర్య అయినా; సంబంధిత సమాచారాన్ని ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా దాచడం . లోపాన్ని పరీక్షించాల్సి వస్తే, జిల్లా కమిషన్ సీలు చేసిన నమూనాను తగిన ప్రయోగశాల కు పంపుతుంది; అది 45 రోజుల్లో నివేదిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 38(2)(c)). సేవల ఫిర్యాదులు సాక్ష్యాధారాలపై నిర్ణయించబడతాయి (సెక్షన్ 38(3)). పరిష్కారాలు: లోపాన్ని తొలగించడం; వస్తువులను మార్చడం; వడ్డీతో ధర తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం; నిర్లక్ష్యానికి నష్టపరిహారం, శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారంతో; సేవల్లో లోపాలను తొలగించడం (సెక్షన్ 39(1)). వైద్య సేవలకు, సేవా లోపాన్ని "the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence" (అర్థం: నిర్లక్ష్యానికి నష్టపరిహార దావాలో వర్తించే అదే పరీక్ష)తో నిర్ణయిస్తారు ( V.P. Shantha ).
te.meaning: లోపం (defect) – చట్టం, ఒప్పందం (వ్యక్త లేదా అవ్యక్త) లేదా వ్యాపారి సొంత ప్రకటన నిర్ణయించిన ప్రమాణంతో పోల్చి చూసే, వస్తువుల్లోని తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత లేదా కొరత (సెక్షన్ 2(10)). సేవా లోపం (deficiency) – చట్టం నిర్ణయించిన లేదా సేవా ప్రదాత చేపట్టిన ప్రమాణంతో పోల్చి చూసే, సేవ నిర్వహించే విధానంలోని తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత, కొరత లేదా అసమర్థత; ఇందులో నిర్లక్ష్యం , సంబంధిత సమాచారాన్ని ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా దాచడం చేరతాయి (సెక్షన్ 2(11)). వ్యాపారి (trader) – వస్తువులు అమ్మే లేదా పంపిణీ చేసే వ్యక్తి; తయారీదారు, ప్యాకేజ్ వస్తువులకు ప్యాక్ చేసేవారు కూడా (సెక్షన్ 2(45)). అతను వస్తువుల గురించి చెప్పేది "లోపం"కు ఒక ప్రమాణం అవుతుంది. తగిన ప్రయోగశాల (appropriate laboratory) – వస్తువుల్లో లోపం ఉందో లేదో పరీక్షించే, ప్రభుత్వం గుర్తించిన లేదా ప్రభుత్వ మద్దతు ఉన్న ప్రయోగశాల (సెక్షన్ 2(2)).
keyPoints: లోపం = వస్తువులు; సేవా లోపం = సేవలు. లోపం: నాణ్యత, పరిమాణం, శక్తి, స్వచ్ఛత, ప్రమాణంలో తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత, కొరత. లోపం ప్రమాణం: చట్టం, ఒప్పందం (వ్యక్త లేదా అవ్యక్త), లేదా వ్యాపారి ప్రకటన. సేవా లోపం: పనితీరు నాణ్యత, స్వభావం, పద్ధతిలో తప్పు, అసంపూర్ణత, కొరత, అసమర్థత. సేవా లోపంలో నష్టం లేదా గాయం కలిగించే నిర్లక్ష్యం, సమాచారాన్ని ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా దాచడం చేరతాయి. పరీక్ష అవసరమా? నమూనాను తగిన ప్రయోగశాలకు; 45 రోజుల్లో నివేదిక. సేవలు: 30 + 15 రోజుల్లో వాదన; సాక్ష్యంపై నిర్ణయం. సెక్షన్ 39(1): లోపం తొలగింపు, మార్పు, వడ్డీతో వాపసు, నష్టపరిహారం, సేవా లోపం తొలగింపు. V.P. Shantha : వైద్య సేవా లోపాన్ని నిర్లక్ష్య పరీక్షతో నిర్ణయించాలి. Nizam's : నిర్లక్ష్య కేసు చూపిన తర్వాత రుజువు భారం మారుతుంది.

selfTest.q: "లోపం" నిర్వచనంలోని ఐదు లక్షణాలు చెప్పండి. లోపానికి ప్రమాణం వచ్చే మూడు మూలాలు ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: 2019 చట్టం కింద "సేవా లోపం"లో ఏమి చేరతాయి? జిల్లా కమిషన్ వస్తువులను ఎప్పుడు ప్రయోగశాలకు పంపుతుంది, నివేదికకు ఎంత సమయం? సేవా లోపం, నిర్లక్ష్యం ఒకటేనా? వస్తువుల్లో లోపానికి కమిషన్ ఏ పరిష్కారాలు ఇవ్వగలదు?

hi.inOneMinute: A consumer may complain that goods bought "suffer from one or more defects" (s. 2(6)(ii)) or that services availed of "suffer from any deficiency" (s. 2(6)(iii)) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Defect (s. 2(10)) is for goods or products . It means any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard . The required standard can come from three sources (See Diagram 1 ): any law in force; any contract, express or implied; what the trader claims "in any manner whatsoever". Deficiency (s. 2(11)) is for services . It means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance . The required standard comes from: any law in force; or what the provider undertook to do under a contract "or otherwise". Deficiency includes two things: any act of negligence , omission or commission that causes loss or injury; deliberate withholding of relevant information . If a defect needs testing, the District Commission sends a sealed sample to an appropriate laboratory , which reports in 45 days (s. 38(2)(c)). Services complaints are decided on evidence (s. 38(3)). Remedies include: remove the defect; replace the goods; refund the price with interest; compensation for negligence, with punitive damages; remove deficiencies in services (s. 39(1)). For medical services, deficiency is judged by "the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence" ( V.P. Shantha ).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 2(10): "defect" means "any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in the quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or under any contract, express or implied or as is claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever in relation to any goods or product and the expression "defective" shall be construed accordingly". Section 2(11): "deficiency" means "any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance which is required to be maintained by or under any law for the time being in force or has been undertaken to be performed by a person in pursuance of a contract or otherwise in relation to any service and includes— (i) any act of negligence or omission or commission by such person which causes loss or injury to the consumer; and (ii) deliberate withholding of relevant information by such person to the consumer". Section 2(6)(ii), (iii): a "complaint" includes an allegation that "the goods bought by him or agreed to be bought by him suffer from one or more defects" or that "the services hired or availed of or agreed to be hired or availed of by him suffer from any deficiency". Section 2(45): "trader", in relation to goods, means a person who sells or distributes goods for sale "and includes the manufacturer thereof", and for packaged goods "includes the packer thereof". Section 2(2): "appropriate laboratory" means a laboratory or organisation recognised by the Central Government, or by a State Government subject to Central guidelines, or established by or under any law and maintained, financed or aided by the Central or a State Government, "for carrying out analysis or test of any goods with a view to determining whether such goods suffer from any defect". Section 38(2)(c): if the complaint "alleges a defect in the goods which cannot be determined without proper analysis or test of the goods", the District Commission shall obtain a sample, seal and authenticate it, and refer it to the appropriate laboratory, which reports "within a period of forty-five days of the receipt of the reference or within such extended period as may be granted by it". Under s. 38(2)(d), the complainant first deposits the laboratory fee. Section 38(3): if the goods procedure cannot be followed, "or if the complaint relates to any services", the Commission refers the complaint to the opposite party for his version in 30 days (extendable by up to 15 days), and then decides on the evidence of both parties, or ex parte. Section 39(1): the orders include: (a) "to remove the defect pointed out by the appropriate laboratory from the goods in question"; (b) "to replace the goods with new goods of similar description which shall be free from any defect"; (c) "to return to the complainant the price, or, as the case may be, the charges paid by the complainant along with such interest on such price or charges as may be decided"; (d) compensation "for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party", with power "to grant punitive damages"; (f) "to remove the defects in goods or deficiencies in the services in question".

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now repealed): s. 2(1)(f) "defect" had the same core words, but applied only "in relation to any goods". s. 2(1)(g) "deficiency" had the same core words, but no "includes" clause on negligence and withholding information. "Goods" meant goods as defined in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (s. 2(1)(i)).
hi.meaning: Defect – a fault, imperfection or shortcoming in goods, measured against a standard set by law, by contract (express or implied), or by the trader's own claim (s. 2(10)). Deficiency – a fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in how a service is performed, measured against a standard set by law or undertaken by the provider; it includes negligence and deliberate withholding of relevant information (s. 2(11)). Trader – a seller or distributor of goods, including the manufacturer and, for packaged goods, the packer (s. 2(45)). His claims about the goods set a standard for "defect". Appropriate laboratory – a government-recognised or government-supported laboratory that tests goods to find whether they suffer from a defect (s. 2(2)).
keyPoints: Defect = goods; deficiency = services. Defect: fault, imperfection, shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard. Defect standard: law, contract (express or implied), or the trader's claim. Deficiency: fault, imperfection, shortcoming, inadequacy in quality, nature, manner of performance. Deficiency includes negligence causing loss or injury and deliberate withholding of information. Test needed? Sample to an appropriate laboratory; report in 45 days. Services: version in 30 + 15 days; decide on evidence. s. 39(1): remove defect, replace, refund with interest, compensate, remove deficiency. V.P. Shantha : medical deficiency judged by negligence test. Nizam's : onus shifts after a case of negligence is made out.

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Appeals and a writ petition raised whether doctors and hospitals render "service" under the 1986 Act and how deficiency in such service is to be judged. Bench: S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ. Principle: "A determination about deficiency in service for the purpose of Section 2(1)(g) has, therefore, to be made by applying the same test as is applied in an action for damages for negligence." The standard is that of "the ordinary skilled man exercising and professing to have that special skill". Why it matters: It fixes the test for deficiency in professional services. The 2019 Act now says expressly that deficiency includes negligence (s. 2(11)(i)). 2. Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A twenty-year-old engineering student had a tumour removed at the hospital and developed "acute paraplegia" right after the surgery. The National Commission found "negligence and deficiency in service" at the pre-operative, operative and post-operative stages and awarded ₹14 lakhs, plus ₹1.5 lakhs to his parents jointly. Both sides appealed. Bench: B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ. Principle: Once the complainant makes out a case of negligence, "the onus then shifts on to the hospital or to the attending doctors" (para 32). Compensation was raised to Rs. One Crore plus interest. Why it matters: It shows deficiency in medical service being found through negligence, and how the burden of proof shifts before a Consumer Commission. Note: No judgment on a defect in goods was in the available set. The "defect" part of this note is explained from the bare words of the Act.

selfTest.a: What does "deficiency" include under the 2019 Act? When does the District Commission send goods to a laboratory, and how long does it have to report? Is deficiency the same as negligence? What remedies can the Commission give for a defect in goods?

law-of-torts-u5-t10.subtitle: The advisory Councils at Central, State and District level that promote and protect consumer rights

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019), Chapter II (ss. 3 to 9), sets up Consumer Protection Councils at three levels: the Central Council , a State Council in every State, and a District Council in every district (See Diagram 1 ). Each Council is expressly "an advisory council". Its object is "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act" (s. 5); the State and District Councils do the same "within the State" (s. 7) and "within the district" (s. 9). Chairpersons: Central Council – the Minister-in-charge of the Department of Consumer Affairs in the Central Government (s. 3(2)(a)); State Council – the Minister-in-charge of Consumer Affairs in the State Government (s. 6(2)(a)); District Council – the Collector of the district (s. 8(2)(a)). Meetings: Central Council – "at least one meeting" every year (s. 4(1)); State and District Councils – "not less than two meetings" every year (ss. 6(3), 8(3)). The consumer rights on which they advise are the six rights in s. 2(9): safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and consumer awareness. A Council does not decide complaints and has no power to punish . Complaints go to the Consumer Commissions; enforcement of consumer rights as a class is for the Central Consumer Protection Authority (s. 18) (See Diagram 3 ). The Councils continue the Councils of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (ss. 4 to 8B), which had a wider-worded object: "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers" (See Diagram 2 ).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Chapter II – "Consumer Protection Councils" (in force from 20 July 2020, by Notification S.O. 2351(E) dated 15 July 2020, which brought "s. 3 to 9 (both inclusive)" into force).

s. 3(1) – "The Central Government shall, by notification, establish with effect from such date as it may specify in that notification, the Central Consumer Protection Council to be known as the Central Council." s. 3(2) – "The Central Council shall be an advisory council and consist of the following members, namely:— (a) the Minister-in-charge of the Department of Consumer Affairs in the Central Government, who shall be the Chairperson; and (b) such number of other official or non-official members representing such interests as may be prescribed." s. 4(1) – "The Central Council shall meet as and when necessary, but at least one meeting of the Council shall be held every year." s. 4(2) – the Central Council meets "at such time and place as the Chairperson may think fit" and follows the procedure "as may be prescribed". s. 5 – "The objects of the Central Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act." s. 6(1) – "Every State Government shall, by notification, establish ... a State Consumer Protection Council for such State to be known as the State Council." s. 6(2) – "The State Council shall be an advisory council and consist of the following members, namely:— (a) the Minister-in-charge of Consumer Affairs in the State Government who shall be the Chairperson; (b) such number of other official or non-official members representing such interests as may be prescribed; (c) such number of other official or non-official members, not exceeding ten, as may be nominated by the Central Government." s. 6(3) – "The State Council shall meet as and when necessary but not less than two meetings shall be held every year." s. 6(4) – time, place and procedure as the Chairperson thinks fit and "as may be prescribed". s. 7 – "The objects of every State Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of consumer rights under this Act within the State." s. 8(1) – "The State Government shall, by notification, establish for every District ... a District Consumer Protection Council to be known as the District Council." s. 8(2) – "The District Council shall be an advisory council and consist of the following members, namely:— (a) the Collector of the district (by whatever name called), who shall be the Chairperson; and (b) such number of other official and non-official members representing such interests as may be prescribed." s. 8(3) – "not less than two meetings shall be held every year." s. 8(4) – meetings "at such time and place within the district as the Chairperson may think fit". s. 9 – "The objects of every District Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of consumer rights under this Act within the district." s. 2(9) – "consumer rights" includes (i) "the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property"; (ii) "the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices"; (iii) "the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices"; (iv) "the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora"; (v) "the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers"; and (vi) "the right to consumer awareness". s. 2(32) – " prescribed " means "prescribed by rules made by the Central Government, or, as the case may be, the State Government". s. 101(2)(d), (e) – Central rules may provide for the number of other members of the Central Council and the time, place and procedure of its meetings. s. 102(2)(c) to (f) – State rules may provide for the number of other members of the State Council and the District Council, and the time, place and procedure of their meetings. The proviso to s. 102(1) allows the Central Government to frame model rules, which apply until the State makes its own. s. 107(1), (2) – the 1986 Act "is hereby repealed"; anything done under it, so far as not inconsistent, is "deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of this Act".

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (repealed) – for comparison: s. 4 (Central Council, chaired by "the Minister in charge of consumer affairs in the Central Government"); s. 5 ("at least one meeting" every year, substituted in 1993 for "not less than three meetings"); s. 6 (objects: "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers such as" (a) to (f), ending with "(f) the right to consumer education"); s. 7 (State Council; members nominated by the Centre "not exceeding ten", inserted in 2002); s. 8 (objects of the State Council); s. 8A and s. 8B (District Council, inserted by Act 62 of 2002 with effect from 15 March 2003).
en.meaning: Consumer Protection Council – a body set up by notification under CPA 2019, ss. 3, 6 or 8, at the Central, State or District level, whose object is to render advice on the promotion and protection of consumer rights. Advisory body – a body that gives advice to the government and does not itself decide disputes or issue binding orders. The Act says of each Council that it "shall be an advisory council" (ss. 3(2), 6(2), 8(2)). Consumer rights – the six rights listed in s. 2(9). The word "includes" shows that the list is inclusive. Official and non-official members – officials are government servants; non-official members are persons outside government (for example, persons representing consumer interests). The Act leaves their number and the interests they represent to be fixed by rules (ss. 3(2)(b), 6(2)(b), 8(2)(b)). Chairperson – the person who presides over the Council and fixes the time and place of its meetings (ss. 4(2), 6(4), 8(4)). Notification – "a notification published in the Official Gazette" (s. 2(30)). Each Council comes into existence only on the date stated in its notification.
keyPoints: CPA 2019, Chapter II: ss. 3–5 Central; ss. 6–7 State; ss. 8–9 District. All three are "advisory" councils. Object: "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights". Chairs: Union Consumer Affairs Minister; State Consumer Affairs Minister; Collector. Meetings: Central at least one a year; State and District not less than two. State Council: up to ten members nominated by the Central Government. Other members: as prescribed (Central rules s. 101; State rules s. 102). Six consumer rights: s. 2(9)(i)–(vi). 1986 Act: ss. 4–8B; District Council added in 2002; repealed by s. 107. In force from 20 July 2020.

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651; AIR 1996 SC 550 (13 November 1995) Facts: The question was whether services of medical practitioners and hospitals are "service" under the 1986 Act. While answering it, the Court explained the background and scheme of the Act. Principle: The Act was passed in the light of UN Resolution No. 39/248 (9 April 1985) "to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumers councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes". The Court also noted the Act's three-tier structure of redressal agencies. Why it matters: It shows that the Councils are one of the two arms of the consumer law scheme: Councils for promotion and advice, redressal agencies for disputes. Note: No judgment interpreting the Council provisions (CPA 2019, ss. 3 to 9, or CPA 1986, ss. 4 to 8B) was found among the judgments available for this note. The topic is answered from the text of the Act.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019), అధ్యాయం II (సెక్షన్లు 3 నుండి 9), మూడు స్థాయిలలో వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ మండళ్ల ను ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది: కేంద్ర మండలి , ప్రతి రాష్ట్రంలో రాష్ట్ర మండలి , ప్రతి జిల్లాలో జిల్లా మండలి ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి). ప్రతి మండలి స్పష్టంగా "an advisory council" (అర్థం: ఒక సలహా మండలి). దాని లక్ష్యం "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act" (అర్థం: ఈ చట్టం కింద వినియోగదారుల హక్కుల ప్రోత్సాహం మరియు రక్షణపై సలహా ఇవ్వడం) (సెక్షన్ 5); రాష్ట్ర, జిల్లా మండళ్లు ఇదే పనిని "within the State" (అర్థం: రాష్ట్రం లోపల) (సెక్షన్ 7), "within the district" (అర్థం: జిల్లా లోపల) (సెక్షన్ 9) చేస్తాయి. అధ్యక్షులు: కేంద్ర మండలి – కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వ వినియోగదారుల వ్యవహారాల శాఖ ఇన్‌చార్జి మంత్రి (సెక్షన్ 3(2)(a)); రాష్ట్ర మండలి – రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వ వినియోగదారుల వ్యవహారాల ఇన్‌చార్జి మంత్రి (సెక్షన్ 6(2)(a)); జిల్లా మండలి – జిల్లా కలెక్టర్ (సెక్షన్ 8(2)(a)). సమావేశాలు: కేంద్ర మండలి – ప్రతి సంవత్సరం "at least one meeting" (అర్థం: కనీసం ఒక సమావేశం) (సెక్షన్ 4(1)); రాష్ట్ర, జిల్లా మండళ్లు – ప్రతి సంవత్సరం "not less than two meetings" (అర్థం: రెండు కంటే తక్కువ కాని సమావేశాలు) (సెక్షన్లు 6(3), 8(3)). మండళ్లు సలహా ఇచ్చే వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు సెక్షన్ 2(9)లోని ఆరు హక్కులు: భద్రత, సమాచారం, ఎంపిక, తమ మాట వినిపించుకోవడం, పరిహారం పొందడం, వినియోగదారుల అవగాహన. మండలి ఫిర్యాదులను నిర్ణయించదు, శిక్షించే అధికారం లేదు . ఫిర్యాదులు వినియోగదారుల కమిషన్లకు వెళ్తాయి; వినియోగదారులందరి (తరగతిగా) హక్కుల అమలు కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ ప్రాధికార సంస్థ పని (సెక్షన్ 18) ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి). ఈ మండళ్లు వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 1986 (సెక్షన్లు 4 నుండి 8B) నాటి మండళ్లకు కొనసాగింపు. ఆ చట్టంలో లక్ష్యం విస్తృత పదాలలో ఉండేది: "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల హక్కులను ప్రోత్సహించడం, రక్షించడం) ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి).
te.meaning: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ మండలి – CPA 2019 సెక్షన్లు 3, 6 లేదా 8 కింద నోటిఫికేషన్ ద్వారా కేంద్ర, రాష్ట్ర లేదా జిల్లా స్థాయిలో ఏర్పాటు చేయబడిన సంస్థ; వినియోగదారుల హక్కుల ప్రోత్సాహం, రక్షణపై సలహా ఇవ్వడం దాని లక్ష్యం. సలహా సంస్థ – ప్రభుత్వానికి సలహా ఇచ్చే సంస్థ; అది స్వయంగా వివాదాలను నిర్ణయించదు, కట్టుబడి ఉండాల్సిన ఉత్తర్వులు ఇవ్వదు. ప్రతి మండలి గురించి చట్టం "shall be an advisory council" (అర్థం: ఒక సలహా మండలిగా ఉండాలి) అంటుంది (సెక్షన్లు 3(2), 6(2), 8(2)). వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు – సెక్షన్ 2(9)లో పేర్కొన్న ఆరు హక్కులు. "includes" (అర్థం: కలిగి ఉంటుంది) అనే పదం ఈ జాబితా పూర్తి జాబితా కాదని (inclusive అని) చూపిస్తుంది. అధికార, అనధికార సభ్యులు – అధికార సభ్యులు ప్రభుత్వ ఉద్యోగులు; అనధికార సభ్యులు ప్రభుత్వం బయటి వ్యక్తులు (ఉదాహరణకు, వినియోగదారుల ప్రయోజనాలకు ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహించేవారు). వారి సంఖ్య, వారు ప్రాతినిధ్యం వహించే ప్రయోజనాలను నియమాలు నిర్ణయించేలా చట్టం వదిలేసింది (సెక్షన్లు 3(2)(b), 6(2)(b), 8(2)(b)). అధ్యక్షులు (Chairperson) – మండలికి అధ్యక్షత వహించి, దాని సమావేశాల సమయం, స్థలం నిర్ణయించే వ్యక్తి (సెక్షన్లు 4(2), 6(4), 8(4)). నోటిఫికేషన్ – "a notification published in the Official Gazette" (అర్థం: అధికారిక గెజిట్‌లో ప్రచురించిన నోటిఫికేషన్) (సెక్షన్ 2(30)). ప్రతి మండలి తన నోటిఫికేషన్‌లో పేర్కొన్న తేదీ నుండి మాత్రమే ఉనికిలోకి వస్తుంది.
keyPoints: CPA 2019, అధ్యాయం II: సెక్షన్లు 3–5 కేంద్ర; 6–7 రాష్ట్ర; 8–9 జిల్లా. మూడూ "advisory" (అర్థం: సలహా) మండళ్లు. లక్ష్యం: "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights" (అర్థం: వినియోగదారుల హక్కుల ప్రోత్సాహం, రక్షణపై సలహా ఇవ్వడం). అధ్యక్షులు: కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల వ్యవహారాల మంత్రి; రాష్ట్ర వినియోగదారుల వ్యవహారాల మంత్రి; కలెక్టర్. సమావేశాలు: కేంద్ర సంవత్సరానికి కనీసం ఒకటి; రాష్ట్ర, జిల్లా రెండు కంటే తక్కువ కాకుండా. రాష్ట్ర మండలి: కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం నామినేట్ చేసే పది మంది వరకు సభ్యులు. ఇతర సభ్యులు: నియమాల ప్రకారం (కేంద్ర నియమాలు సెక్షన్ 101; రాష్ట్ర నియమాలు సెక్షన్ 102). ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు: సెక్షన్ 2(9)(i)–(vi). 1986 చట్టం: సెక్షన్లు 4–8B; 2002లో జిల్లా మండలి చేర్చబడింది; సెక్షన్ 107 ద్వారా రద్దు. 20 జూలై 2020 నుండి అమలు.

selfTest.q: CPA 2019 కింద మూడు వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ మండళ్లు, వాటి సెక్షన్లు చెప్పండి. (a) కేంద్ర మండలి, (b) రాష్ట్ర మండలి, (c) జిల్లా మండలి అధ్యక్షులు ఎవరు?
selfTest.a: ప్రతి మండలి సంవత్సరానికి ఎన్ని సమావేశాలు నిర్వహించాలి? సెక్షన్ 5 కింద కేంద్ర మండలి లక్ష్యం ఏమిటి? రాష్ట్ర మండలికి కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఎంత మంది సభ్యులను నామినేట్ చేయవచ్చు? సెక్షన్ 2(9)లోని ఆరు వినియోగదారుల హక్కులు రాయండి. జిల్లా మండలి నష్టపరిహారం ఇప్పించగలదా? కారణాలు చెప్పండి. 1986 చట్టం, 2019 చట్టం కింద మండళ్ల మధ్య రెండు తేడాలు చెప్పండి.

hi.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019), Chapter II (ss. 3 to 9), sets up Consumer Protection Councils at three levels: the Central Council , a State Council in every State, and a District Council in every district (See Diagram 1 ). Each Council is expressly "an advisory council". Its object is "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act" (s. 5); the State and District Councils do the same "within the State" (s. 7) and "within the district" (s. 9). Chairpersons: Central Council – the Minister-in-charge of the Department of Consumer Affairs in the Central Government (s. 3(2)(a)); State Council – the Minister-in-charge of Consumer Affairs in the State Government (s. 6(2)(a)); District Council – the Collector of the district (s. 8(2)(a)). Meetings: Central Council – "at least one meeting" every year (s. 4(1)); State and District Councils – "not less than two meetings" every year (ss. 6(3), 8(3)). The consumer rights on which they advise are the six rights in s. 2(9): safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and consumer awareness. A Council does not decide complaints and has no power to punish . Complaints go to the Consumer Commissions; enforcement of consumer rights as a class is for the Central Consumer Protection Authority (s. 18) (See Diagram 3 ). The Councils continue the Councils of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (ss. 4 to 8B), which had a wider-worded object: "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers" (See Diagram 2 ).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019, Chapter II – "Consumer Protection Councils" (in force from 20 July 2020, by Notification S.O. 2351(E) dated 15 July 2020, which brought "s. 3 to 9 (both inclusive)" into force).

s. 3(1) – "The Central Government shall, by notification, establish with effect from such date as it may specify in that notification, the Central Consumer Protection Council to be known as the Central Council." s. 3(2) – "The Central Council shall be an advisory council and consist of the following members, namely:— (a) the Minister-in-charge of the Department of Consumer Affairs in the Central Government, who shall be the Chairperson; and (b) such number of other official or non-official members representing such interests as may be prescribed." s. 4(1) – "The Central Council shall meet as and when necessary, but at least one meeting of the Council shall be held every year." s. 4(2) – the Central Council meets "at such time and place as the Chairperson may think fit" and follows the procedure "as may be prescribed". s. 5 – "The objects of the Central Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights under this Act." s. 6(1) – "Every State Government shall, by notification, establish ... a State Consumer Protection Council for such State to be known as the State Council." s. 6(2) – "The State Council shall be an advisory council and consist of the following members, namely:— (a) the Minister-in-charge of Consumer Affairs in the State Government who shall be the Chairperson; (b) such number of other official or non-official members representing such interests as may be prescribed; (c) such number of other official or non-official members, not exceeding ten, as may be nominated by the Central Government." s. 6(3) – "The State Council shall meet as and when necessary but not less than two meetings shall be held every year." s. 6(4) – time, place and procedure as the Chairperson thinks fit and "as may be prescribed". s. 7 – "The objects of every State Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of consumer rights under this Act within the State." s. 8(1) – "The State Government shall, by notification, establish for every District ... a District Consumer Protection Council to be known as the District Council." s. 8(2) – "The District Council shall be an advisory council and consist of the following members, namely:— (a) the Collector of the district (by whatever name called), who shall be the Chairperson; and (b) such number of other official and non-official members representing such interests as may be prescribed." s. 8(3) – "not less than two meetings shall be held every year." s. 8(4) – meetings "at such time and place within the district as the Chairperson may think fit". s. 9 – "The objects of every District Council shall be to render advice on promotion and protection of consumer rights under this Act within the district." s. 2(9) – "consumer rights" includes (i) "the right to be protected against the marketing of goods, products or services which are hazardous to life and property"; (ii) "the right to be informed about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, products or services, as the case may be, so as to protect the consumer against unfair trade practices"; (iii) "the right to be assured, wherever possible, access to a variety of goods, products or services at competitive prices"; (iv) "the right to be heard and to be assured that consumer's interests will receive due consideration at appropriate fora"; (v) "the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practices or unscrupulous exploitation of consumers"; and (vi) "the right to consumer awareness". s. 2(32) – " prescribed " means "prescribed by rules made by the Central Government, or, as the case may be, the State Government". s. 101(2)(d), (e) – Central rules may provide for the number of other members of the Central Council and the time, place and procedure of its meetings. s. 102(2)(c) to (f) – State rules may provide for the number of other members of the State Council and the District Council, and the time, place and procedure of their meetings. The proviso to s. 102(1) allows the Central Government to frame model rules, which apply until the State makes its own. s. 107(1), (2) – the 1986 Act "is hereby repealed"; anything done under it, so far as not inconsistent, is "deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of this Act".

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (repealed) – for comparison: s. 4 (Central Council, chaired by "the Minister in charge of consumer affairs in the Central Government"); s. 5 ("at least one meeting" every year, substituted in 1993 for "not less than three meetings"); s. 6 (objects: "to promote and protect the rights of the consumers such as" (a) to (f), ending with "(f) the right to consumer education"); s. 7 (State Council; members nominated by the Centre "not exceeding ten", inserted in 2002); s. 8 (objects of the State Council); s. 8A and s. 8B (District Council, inserted by Act 62 of 2002 with effect from 15 March 2003).
hi.meaning: Consumer Protection Council – a body set up by notification under CPA 2019, ss. 3, 6 or 8, at the Central, State or District level, whose object is to render advice on the promotion and protection of consumer rights. Advisory body – a body that gives advice to the government and does not itself decide disputes or issue binding orders. The Act says of each Council that it "shall be an advisory council" (ss. 3(2), 6(2), 8(2)). Consumer rights – the six rights listed in s. 2(9). The word "includes" shows that the list is inclusive. Official and non-official members – officials are government servants; non-official members are persons outside government (for example, persons representing consumer interests). The Act leaves their number and the interests they represent to be fixed by rules (ss. 3(2)(b), 6(2)(b), 8(2)(b)). Chairperson – the person who presides over the Council and fixes the time and place of its meetings (ss. 4(2), 6(4), 8(4)). Notification – "a notification published in the Official Gazette" (s. 2(30)). Each Council comes into existence only on the date stated in its notification.
keyPoints: CPA 2019, Chapter II: ss. 3–5 Central; ss. 6–7 State; ss. 8–9 District. All three are "advisory" councils. Object: "to render advice on promotion and protection of the consumers' rights". Chairs: Union Consumer Affairs Minister; State Consumer Affairs Minister; Collector. Meetings: Central at least one a year; State and District not less than two. State Council: up to ten members nominated by the Central Government. Other members: as prescribed (Central rules s. 101; State rules s. 102). Six consumer rights: s. 2(9)(i)–(vi). 1986 Act: ss. 4–8B; District Council added in 2002; repealed by s. 107. In force from 20 July 2020.

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651; AIR 1996 SC 550 (13 November 1995) Facts: The question was whether services of medical practitioners and hospitals are "service" under the 1986 Act. While answering it, the Court explained the background and scheme of the Act. Principle: The Act was passed in the light of UN Resolution No. 39/248 (9 April 1985) "to provide for the better protection of the interests of consumers and for that purpose to make provision for the establishment of consumers councils and other authorities for the settlement of consumers' disputes". The Court also noted the Act's three-tier structure of redressal agencies. Why it matters: It shows that the Councils are one of the two arms of the consumer law scheme: Councils for promotion and advice, redressal agencies for disputes. Note: No judgment interpreting the Council provisions (CPA 2019, ss. 3 to 9, or CPA 1986, ss. 4 to 8B) was found among the judgments available for this note. The topic is answered from the text of the Act.

law-of-torts-u5-t5.subtitle: Who is a consumer under section 2(7) of the 2019 Act: buyers, users, beneficiaries, and who is left out

en.inOneMinute: Only a "consumer" (or another "complainant" listed in s. 2(5)) can file a consumer complaint. So the definition in s. 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is the gateway to every remedy under the Act. A consumer is a person who: buys goods for consideration, or hires or avails of services for consideration. Consideration may be paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or under a system of deferred payment . The definition also covers users of goods and beneficiaries of services, if the buyer or hirer approves the use. It excludes : a person who obtains goods for resale or for any commercial purpose , and a person who avails of services for any commercial purpose . Two Explanations: (a) use of goods bought and used exclusively to earn a livelihood by self-employment is not a "commercial purpose"; (b) buying goods or hiring services includes online, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing transactions. A "service" does not include service free of charge or under a contract of personal service (s. 2(42)). Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) applied this to doctors and hospitals. (See Diagram 1 .)
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 2(7): "consumer" means any person who— "(i) buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment and includes any user of such goods other than the person who buys such goods for consideration paid or promised or partly paid or partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment, when such use is made with the approval of such person, but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose; or" "(ii) hires or avails of any service for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment and includes any beneficiary of such service other than the person who hires or avails of the services for consideration paid or promised, or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment, when such services are availed of with the approval of the first mentioned person, but does not include a person who avails of such service for any commercial purpose." Explanation (a): "the expression "commercial purpose" does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood, by means of self-employment;" Explanation (b): "the expressions "buys any goods" and "hires or avails any services" includes offline or online transactions through electronic means or by teleshopping or direct selling or multi-level marketing;" Section 2(21): "goods" means "every kind of movable property and includes "food" as defined in clause (j) of sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006". Section 2(31): "person" includes an individual; a firm, whether registered or not; a Hindu undivided family; a co-operative society; an association of persons, whether registered or not; any corporation, company or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not; and any other artificial juridical person. Section 2(42): "service" means "service of any description which is made available to potential users". It includes facilities in connection with banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, telecom, boarding or lodging or both, housing construction, entertainment, amusement and the purveying of news or other information. It ends with "but does not include the rendering of any service free of charge or under a contract of personal service". Section 2(5): "complainant" means a consumer, a registered voluntary consumer association, the Central or a State Government, the Central Authority, one or more consumers having the same interest, the legal heir or legal representative of a dead consumer, or the parent or legal guardian of a minor consumer.

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now repealed) – s. 2(1)(d): the same two limbs (buyer and user; hirer and beneficiary). Its Explanation said "commercial purpose" does not include use of "goods bought and used by him and services availed by him exclusively for the purposes of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment". It had no Explanation on online transactions.
en.meaning: Consumer – the person who buys goods or hires or avails of services for consideration , for himself and not for resale or commercial purpose, together with the approved user or beneficiary (s. 2(7)). Consideration – the price for the goods or service. It may be paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or under a system of deferred payment (for example, instalments ). User of goods – anyone other than the buyer who uses the goods "with the approval of" the buyer, for example a family member or a friend who receives the goods as a gift. Beneficiary of a service – anyone other than the hirer who gets the benefit of the service, when the service is availed of "with the approval of the first mentioned person", for example a patient whose treatment is paid for by an insurer or an employer. Commercial purpose – the Act does not define it. It only says what it does not include: use of goods bought and used exclusively to earn a livelihood by self-employment (Explanation (a)). Contract of personal service – a contract of employment (master and servant). A service rendered under such a contract is not a "service" (s. 2(42)). It is different from a "contract for personal services", such as a patient engaging a doctor, which is covered ( V.P. Shantha ).
keyPoints: s. 2(7): buyer of goods or hirer of services, for consideration. Consideration: paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or deferred payment. Includes the user of goods and the beneficiary of services, with the payer's approval. Excludes resale and commercial purpose. Explanation (a): goods used exclusively for livelihood by self-employment are not commercial purpose. Explanation (b): online, teleshopping, direct selling, multi-level marketing are included. s. 2(42): no "service" if free of charge or under a contract of personal service. V.P. Shantha : doctors covered; free-to-all excluded; free patients in paying hospitals covered; insurer- or employer-paid treatment covered. "Person" is wide (s. 2(31)). A consumer is one of the "complainants" in s. 2(5).

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Several appeals and writ petitions raised a common question: whether medical practitioners, and government and private hospitals and nursing homes, render "service" under s. 2(1)(o) of the 1986 Act, so that patients are consumers. The bench was S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ. Principle: A doctor's consultation, diagnosis and treatment is "service", except where the doctor renders service free of charge to every patient or under a contract of personal service. In the absence of master and servant, the patient–doctor relationship is a "contract for personal services", not a "contract of personal service". Where some pay and others are treated free, "Free service, would also be "service" and the recipient a "consumer" under the Act." Service paid for by an insurer or by an employer is not free. Why it matters: It is the leading case on who is a consumer of services, on the free-service exclusion and on the personal-service exclusion. These words are repeated in s. 2(42) of the 2019 Act. (See Diagram 3 .) 2. Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) Facts: The appellant drank a ginger-beer that "a friend had bought from a retailer and given to her". The opaque bottle held "the decomposed remains of a snail", and she alleged that she fell ill. Principle: A manufacturer who sends out goods meant to reach "the ultimate consumer" without "reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care" (Lord Atkin). The duty was owed to her though she had no contract. Why it matters: It shows the common law idea that the ultimate user , not only the buyer, needs protection. Section 2(7)(i) gives the same person a statutory remedy, as a "user of such goods" with the buyer's approval. Note: No judgment in the available set deals with the meaning of "commercial purpose" or the self-employment Explanation. The note therefore explains these from the bare words of the Act only.

te.inOneMinute: "వినియోగదారుడు" (లేదా సెక్షన్ 2(5)లో చెప్పిన మరో "ఫిర్యాదుదారు") మాత్రమే వినియోగదారుల ఫిర్యాదు వేయగలడు. కాబట్టి వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 సెక్షన్ 2(7) లోని నిర్వచనమే చట్టంలోని ప్రతి పరిష్కారానికి ప్రవేశ ద్వారం. వినియోగదారుడు అంటే: ప్రతిఫలానికి వస్తువులు కొనే వ్యక్తి, లేదా ప్రతిఫలానికి సేవలను అద్దెకు తీసుకునే లేదా పొందే వ్యక్తి. ప్రతిఫలం చెల్లించినది, వాగ్దానం చేసినది, కొంత చెల్లించి కొంత వాగ్దానం చేసినది, లేదా వాయిదా చెల్లింపు పద్ధతిలో ఉండవచ్చు. కొనుగోలుదారు లేదా సేవ పొందిన వ్యక్తి ఆమోదం ఉంటే, వస్తువుల వాడకందారులు , సేవల లబ్ధిదారులు కూడా నిర్వచనంలోకి వస్తారు. ఇది మినహాయిస్తుంది : తిరిగి అమ్మడానికి లేదా ఏ వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనానికైనా వస్తువులు పొందే వ్యక్తిని, ఏ వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనానికైనా సేవలు పొందే వ్యక్తిని. రెండు వివరణలు (Explanations): (a) స్వయం ఉపాధి ద్వారా జీవనోపాధి సంపాదించడానికి మాత్రమే కొని వాడే వస్తువుల వాడకం "వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం" కాదు; (b) వస్తువులు కొనడం లేదా సేవలు పొందడంలో ఆన్‌లైన్, టెలీషాపింగ్, డైరెక్ట్ సెల్లింగ్, మల్టీ-లెవెల్ మార్కెటింగ్ లావాదేవీలు చేరతాయి. ఉచితంగా అందించే సేవ లేదా వ్యక్తిగత సేవా ఒప్పందం కింద అందించే సేవ "సేవ" కాదు (సెక్షన్ 2(42)). Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) దీనిని డాక్టర్లు, ఆసుపత్రులకు వర్తింపజేసింది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: వినియోగదారుడు – తిరిగి అమ్మడానికి లేదా వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనానికి కాకుండా, తన కోసం ప్రతిఫలానికి వస్తువులు కొనే లేదా సేవలు పొందే వ్యక్తి; ఆమోదం పొందిన వాడకందారు లేదా లబ్ధిదారుతో సహా (సెక్షన్ 2(7)). ప్రతిఫలం (consideration) – వస్తువులు లేదా సేవకు ధర. ఇది చెల్లించినది, వాగ్దానం చేసినది, కొంత చెల్లించి కొంత వాగ్దానం చేసినది, లేదా వాయిదా చెల్లింపు పద్ధతిలో (ఉదాహరణకు వాయిదాలు) ఉండవచ్చు. వస్తువుల వాడకందారు – కొనుగోలుదారు "with the approval of" (అర్థం: ఆమోదంతో) వస్తువులు వాడే, కొనుగోలుదారు కాని ఏ వ్యక్తి అయినా; ఉదాహరణకు కుటుంబ సభ్యుడు లేదా బహుమతిగా వస్తువులు పొందిన స్నేహితుడు. సేవ లబ్ధిదారు – "with the approval of the first mentioned person" (అర్థం: మొదట చెప్పిన వ్యక్తి ఆమోదంతో) సేవ పొందినప్పుడు, సేవ తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తి కాకుండా దాని ప్రయోజనం పొందే ఏ వ్యక్తి అయినా; ఉదాహరణకు బీమా సంస్థ లేదా యజమాని చికిత్స ఖర్చు చెల్లించిన రోగి. వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం – చట్టం దీనిని నిర్వచించలేదు. దీనిలో ఏది చేరదో మాత్రమే చెబుతుంది: స్వయం ఉపాధి ద్వారా జీవనోపాధి సంపాదించడానికి మాత్రమే కొని వాడే వస్తువుల వాడకం (వివరణ (a)). వ్యక్తిగత సేవా ఒప్పందం – ఉద్యోగ ఒప్పందం (యజమాని, సేవకుడు). అటువంటి ఒప్పందం కింద అందించే సేవ "సేవ" కాదు (సెక్షన్ 2(42)). ఇది రోగి డాక్టర్‌ను నియమించుకోవడం వంటి "వ్యక్తిగత సేవల కోసం ఒప్పందం" నుండి భిన్నం; అది చట్ట పరిధిలోకి వస్తుంది ( V.P. Shantha ).
keyPoints: సెక్షన్ 2(7): ప్రతిఫలానికి వస్తువుల కొనుగోలుదారు లేదా సేవలు పొందినవారు. ప్రతిఫలం: చెల్లించినది, వాగ్దానం చేసినది, కొంత చెల్లించి కొంత వాగ్దానం, లేదా వాయిదా చెల్లింపు. చెల్లించినవారి ఆమోదంతో వస్తువుల వాడకందారు, సేవల లబ్ధిదారు చేరతారు. తిరిగి అమ్మకం, వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం మినహాయింపు. వివరణ (a): స్వయం ఉపాధి ద్వారా జీవనోపాధికి మాత్రమే వాడే వస్తువులు వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం కాదు. వివరణ (b): ఆన్‌లైన్, టెలీషాపింగ్, డైరెక్ట్ సెల్లింగ్, మల్టీ-లెవెల్ మార్కెటింగ్ చేరతాయి. సెక్షన్ 2(42): ఉచితంగా లేదా వ్యక్తిగత సేవా ఒప్పందం కింద అయితే "సేవ" కాదు. V.P. Shantha : డాక్టర్లు పరిధిలోకి; అందరికీ ఉచితం మినహాయింపు; చెల్లించే ఆసుపత్రుల్లో ఉచిత రోగులు పరిధిలోకి; బీమా సంస్థ లేదా యజమాని చెల్లించే చికిత్స పరిధిలోకి. "వ్యక్తి" విస్తృతం (సెక్షన్ 2(31)). సెక్షన్ 2(5)లోని "ఫిర్యాదుదారుల్లో" వినియోగదారుడు ఒకరు.

selfTest.q: సెక్షన్ 2(7) రెండు భాగాలు చెప్పండి. వస్తువుల "వాడకందారు" ఎవరు, అతను ఏ షరతు తీర్చాలి?
selfTest.a: వాణిజ్య ప్రయోజనం గురించి వివరణ (a) ఏం చెబుతుంది? సెక్షన్ 2(42) మినహాయించే రెండు రకాల సేవలు చెప్పండి. ఇతర రోగుల నుండి ఛార్జీ తీసుకునే ప్రైవేటు ఆసుపత్రిలో ఉచితంగా చికిత్స పొందిన పేద రోగి వినియోగదారుడా? ఆన్‌లైన్ లావాదేవీల గురించి 2019 చట్టం ఏం చేర్చింది? 2019 జీవనోపాధి వివరణ 1986 వివరణ నుండి ఎలా భిన్నం?

అనిల్ తన కోసం ఆన్‌లైన్‌లో ₹42,000 ఫోన్ కొన్నాడు అవును ప్రతిఫలానికి కొనుగోలుదారు; ఆన్‌లైన్ చేరుతుంది (వివరణ (b))
అనిల్ తల్లి అనిల్ ఇచ్చిన ఫోన్ వాడుతోంది అవును కొనుగోలుదారు ఆమోదంతో వాడకందారు
రవి మొబైల్స్ అమ్మడానికి ఒక్కొక్కటి ₹38,000 చొప్పున 100 ఫోన్లు (₹38 లక్షలు) కొన్నది కాదు తిరిగి అమ్మడానికి పొందింది
మీనా 24 నెలవారీ వాయిదాలపై (ఒక్కొక్కటి సుమారు ₹13,333) ₹3,20,000 ఆటో-రిక్షా కొని, తన జీవనం కోసం తానే నడుపుతోంది అవును వాయిదా చెల్లింపు; స్వయం ఉపాధి ద్వారా జీవనోపాధికి మాత్రమే వాడకం (వివరణ (a))
కిరణ్ ₹10 నమోదు రుసుము చెల్లించాక, ఎవరి దగ్గరా ఛార్జీ తీసుకోని ప్రభుత్వ ఆసుపత్రిలో ఉచిత చికిత్స కాదు అందరికీ ఉచిత సేవ; నామమాత్రపు నమోదు రుసుము దీనిని మార్చదు
లక్ష్మి ప్రైవేటు ఆసుపత్రిలో ఆమె ₹1,50,000 శస్త్రచికిత్స బిల్లును బీమా సంస్థ చెల్లించింది అవును లబ్ధిదారు; సేవ ఉచితం కాదు (V.P. Shantha)
డా. రావు కంపెనీ సిబ్బందికి చికిత్స చేసే, కంపెనీ నియమించిన వైద్యాధికారి కంపెనీకి ఇది సేవ కాదు వ్యక్తిగత సేవా ఒప్పందం

hi.inOneMinute: Only a "consumer" (or another "complainant" listed in s. 2(5)) can file a consumer complaint. So the definition in s. 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is the gateway to every remedy under the Act. A consumer is a person who: buys goods for consideration, or hires or avails of services for consideration. Consideration may be paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or under a system of deferred payment . The definition also covers users of goods and beneficiaries of services, if the buyer or hirer approves the use. It excludes : a person who obtains goods for resale or for any commercial purpose , and a person who avails of services for any commercial purpose . Two Explanations: (a) use of goods bought and used exclusively to earn a livelihood by self-employment is not a "commercial purpose"; (b) buying goods or hiring services includes online, teleshopping, direct selling and multi-level marketing transactions. A "service" does not include service free of charge or under a contract of personal service (s. 2(42)). Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha (1995) applied this to doctors and hospitals. (See Diagram 1 .)
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 2(7): "consumer" means any person who— "(i) buys any goods for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment and includes any user of such goods other than the person who buys such goods for consideration paid or promised or partly paid or partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment, when such use is made with the approval of such person, but does not include a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose; or" "(ii) hires or avails of any service for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment and includes any beneficiary of such service other than the person who hires or avails of the services for consideration paid or promised, or partly paid and partly promised, or under any system of deferred payment, when such services are availed of with the approval of the first mentioned person, but does not include a person who avails of such service for any commercial purpose." Explanation (a): "the expression "commercial purpose" does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood, by means of self-employment;" Explanation (b): "the expressions "buys any goods" and "hires or avails any services" includes offline or online transactions through electronic means or by teleshopping or direct selling or multi-level marketing;" Section 2(21): "goods" means "every kind of movable property and includes "food" as defined in clause (j) of sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006". Section 2(31): "person" includes an individual; a firm, whether registered or not; a Hindu undivided family; a co-operative society; an association of persons, whether registered or not; any corporation, company or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not; and any other artificial juridical person. Section 2(42): "service" means "service of any description which is made available to potential users". It includes facilities in connection with banking, financing, insurance, transport, processing, supply of electrical or other energy, telecom, boarding or lodging or both, housing construction, entertainment, amusement and the purveying of news or other information. It ends with "but does not include the rendering of any service free of charge or under a contract of personal service". Section 2(5): "complainant" means a consumer, a registered voluntary consumer association, the Central or a State Government, the Central Authority, one or more consumers having the same interest, the legal heir or legal representative of a dead consumer, or the parent or legal guardian of a minor consumer.

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now repealed) – s. 2(1)(d): the same two limbs (buyer and user; hirer and beneficiary). Its Explanation said "commercial purpose" does not include use of "goods bought and used by him and services availed by him exclusively for the purposes of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment". It had no Explanation on online transactions.
hi.meaning: Consumer – the person who buys goods or hires or avails of services for consideration , for himself and not for resale or commercial purpose, together with the approved user or beneficiary (s. 2(7)). Consideration – the price for the goods or service. It may be paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or under a system of deferred payment (for example, instalments ). User of goods – anyone other than the buyer who uses the goods "with the approval of" the buyer, for example a family member or a friend who receives the goods as a gift. Beneficiary of a service – anyone other than the hirer who gets the benefit of the service, when the service is availed of "with the approval of the first mentioned person", for example a patient whose treatment is paid for by an insurer or an employer. Commercial purpose – the Act does not define it. It only says what it does not include: use of goods bought and used exclusively to earn a livelihood by self-employment (Explanation (a)). Contract of personal service – a contract of employment (master and servant). A service rendered under such a contract is not a "service" (s. 2(42)). It is different from a "contract for personal services", such as a patient engaging a doctor, which is covered ( V.P. Shantha ).
keyPoints: s. 2(7): buyer of goods or hirer of services, for consideration. Consideration: paid, promised, partly paid and partly promised, or deferred payment. Includes the user of goods and the beneficiary of services, with the payer's approval. Excludes resale and commercial purpose. Explanation (a): goods used exclusively for livelihood by self-employment are not commercial purpose. Explanation (b): online, teleshopping, direct selling, multi-level marketing are included. s. 2(42): no "service" if free of charge or under a contract of personal service. V.P. Shantha : doctors covered; free-to-all excluded; free patients in paying hospitals covered; insurer- or employer-paid treatment covered. "Person" is wide (s. 2(31)). A consumer is one of the "complainants" in s. 2(5).

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Several appeals and writ petitions raised a common question: whether medical practitioners, and government and private hospitals and nursing homes, render "service" under s. 2(1)(o) of the 1986 Act, so that patients are consumers. The bench was S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ. Principle: A doctor's consultation, diagnosis and treatment is "service", except where the doctor renders service free of charge to every patient or under a contract of personal service. In the absence of master and servant, the patient–doctor relationship is a "contract for personal services", not a "contract of personal service". Where some pay and others are treated free, "Free service, would also be "service" and the recipient a "consumer" under the Act." Service paid for by an insurer or by an employer is not free. Why it matters: It is the leading case on who is a consumer of services, on the free-service exclusion and on the personal-service exclusion. These words are repeated in s. 2(42) of the 2019 Act. (See Diagram 3 .) 2. Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords, 26 May 1932) Facts: The appellant drank a ginger-beer that "a friend had bought from a retailer and given to her". The opaque bottle held "the decomposed remains of a snail", and she alleged that she fell ill. Principle: A manufacturer who sends out goods meant to reach "the ultimate consumer" without "reasonable possibility of intermediate examination" "owes a duty to the consumer to take that reasonable care" (Lord Atkin). The duty was owed to her though she had no contract. Why it matters: It shows the common law idea that the ultimate user , not only the buyer, needs protection. Section 2(7)(i) gives the same person a statutory remedy, as a "user of such goods" with the buyer's approval. Note: No judgment in the available set deals with the meaning of "commercial purpose" or the self-employment Explanation. The note therefore explains these from the bare words of the Act only.
