law-of-torts-u5-t9.subtitle: The agencies that settle consumer disputes: three Commissions, mediation cells and the regulator

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) sets up a three-level system of quasi-judicial bodies to decide consumer disputes (See Diagram 1 ): District Commission – set up by the State Government in each district (s. 28). State Commission – set up by the State Government in the State (s. 42). National Commission – set up by the Central Government (s. 53). Above them is the Supreme Court , to which an appeal lies from an original order of the National Commission (s. 67). Each Commission has a President and members : District – at least two members (s. 28(2)); State – at least four (s. 42(3)); National – at least four (s. 54). Which Commission hears a complaint depends on the value of the goods or services paid as consideration (ss. 34, 47, 58). Under the Consumer Protection ( Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 the limits are: District – up to ₹50 lakh; State – above ₹50 lakh up to ₹2 crore; National – above ₹2 crore. Orders move up the ladder by appeal (ss. 41, 51, 67) and are corrected by revision (ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). (See Diagram 2 .) Supporting parts of the machinery: a consumer mediation cell attached to every Commission (s. 74); the Central Consumer Protection Authority (s. 10), whose orders are appealable to the National Commission (s. 58(1)(a)(iv)); and the advisory Consumer Protection Councils (ss. 3–9). Under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (CPA 1986) the same three levels were the District Forum, the State Commission and the National Commission (s. 9).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019) – Chapter IV, "Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission" (ss. 28–73).
District Commission

s. 28(1): "The State Government shall, by notification, establish a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, to be known as the District Commission, in each district of the State". Proviso: the State Government "may, if it deems fit, establish more than one District Commission in a district." s. 28(2): "Each District Commission shall consist of— (a) a President; and (b) not less than two and not more than such number of members as may be prescribed, in consultation with the Central Government." s. 29: the Central Government makes rules on qualifications, method of recruitment, procedure for appointment, term of office, resignation and removal. s. 30: the State Government makes rules on salaries, allowances and other service conditions. s. 31: persons already in office when the Act began continue till the end of their term. s. 32: if there is a vacancy in the office of the President or a member, the State Government may by notification direct another District Commission to exercise jurisdiction for that district also, or direct the President or a member of another District Commission to act for that Commission also. s. 33: the State Government provides officers and employees, who work "under the general superintendence of the President". s. 34(1): jurisdiction where the value of goods or services paid as consideration "does not exceed one crore rupees"; proviso: the Central Government may prescribe another value. s. 34(2): territorial jurisdiction – where the opposite party resides, carries on business, has a branch office or personally works for gain; where the cause of action arises wholly or in part; or where "the complainant resides or personally works for gain". s. 34(3): the District Commission "shall ordinarily function in the district headquarters". s. 36(1): every proceeding is conducted by "the President of that Commission and atleast one member thereof, sitting together".
State Commission

s. 42(1)–(2): established by the State Government by notification; "shall ordinarily function at the State capital"; proviso: regional benches may be set up. s. 42(3): "Each State Commission shall consist of— (a) a President; and (b) not less than four or not more than such number of members as may be prescribed in consultation with the Central Government." ss. 43–46: qualifications etc. (Central rules), salaries (State rules), transitional provision, officers and employees. s. 47(1)(a): original complaints above ₹1 crore up to ₹10 crore (value may be changed by the Central Government); complaints against unfair contracts up to ₹10 crore; appeals against orders of any District Commission in the State. s. 47(1)(b): revision – calling for records where a District Commission "has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or has failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested or has acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity". s. 47(2)–(3): benches constituted by the President, "the senior-most member shall preside over the Bench"; majority decides; if members are equally divided, the point goes to the President, and the opinion on the referred point is given "within a period of one month". s. 48: the State Commission may transfer a complaint from one District Commission to another within the State "if the interest of justice so requires".
National Commission

s. 53: established by the Central Government; "shall ordinarily function at the National Capital Region"; proviso: regional Benches may be set up. s. 54: "The National Commission shall consist of— (a) a President; and (b) not less than four and not more than such number of members as may be prescribed." s. 55(1): Central rules on qualifications, appointment, term, salaries etc.; term "not exceeding five years", with eligibility for re-appointment; age limit not exceeding "seventy years" for the President and "sixty-seven years" for any other member. s. 55(1A) (inserted by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026, w.e.f. 25 August 2026): these service matters "shall be governed by the provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026". s. 55(2): salary and service conditions cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment. s. 58(1)(a): original complaints above ₹10 crore; complaints against unfair contracts above ₹10 crore; appeals against orders of any State Commission; "appeals against the orders of the Central Authority". s. 58(1)(b): revision over State Commissions on the same grounds as s. 47(1)(b). s. 58(2)–(3): benches, senior-most member presides; on an equal division the referred point is answered "within a period of two months". s. 62: the National Commission may transfer a complaint from a District Commission of one State to a District Commission of another State, or from one State Commission to another. s. 63: if the President's office is vacant, the senior-most member performs the duties; but a member who is a retired High Court Judge or has been a Judicial Member presides in the President's absence.
Provisions common to all three

s. 64: "No act or proceeding of the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall be invalid by reason only of the existence of any vacancy amongst its members or any defect in the constitution thereof." s. 65: service of notices (registered post with acknowledgment, speed post, approved courier, or electronic means); s. 65(2) allows service on the nodal officer of an electronic service provider. s. 66: where a matter "involves the larger interest of consumers", the National or State Commission may direct any individual, organisation or expert to assist it. ss. 41, 51, 67: appeals – District to State (45 days), State to National (30 days), National to Supreme Court (30 days); each needs a deposit of fifty per cent. of the amount ordered. s. 68: an order not appealed is final. s. 69: complaint within two years of the cause of action; delay condonable for sufficient cause with recorded reasons. s. 70: administrative control – the National Commission over State Commissions (periodical returns on institution, disposal and pendency; inquiry into allegations against the President and members; instructions on uniform procedure, English translation of judgments and speedy copies; oversight by inspection); s. 70(2) a monitoring cell; s. 70(3) the State Commission over District Commissions. s. 71: every order is enforced "as if it were a decree" under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. s. 72: punishment for non-compliance. s. 74(1)–(2): "The State Government shall establish, by notification, a consumer mediation cell to be attached to each of the District Commissions and the State Commissions of that State"; the Central Government establishes one for the National Commission and each of its regional Benches.

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 – G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021, made under the provisos to ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i) and 58(1)(a)(i). They fix the limits at: District Commission – not exceeding ₹50 lakh; State Commission – exceeding ₹50 lakh but not exceeding ₹2 crore; National Commission – exceeding ₹2 crore.

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986) – s. 9 (three agencies: District Forum, State Commission, National Commission); s. 10 (District Forum: President "a person who is, or has been, or is qualified to be a District Judge" and two other members, "one of whom shall be a woman"); s. 16 (State Commission: President "a person who is or has been a Judge of a High Court"); s. 20 (National Commission: President "a person who is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court"); ss. 11, 17, 21 (jurisdiction, finally ₹20 lakh / ₹1 crore, counting "the value of the goods or services and compensation, if any, claimed").
en.meaning: Redressal machinery means the bodies that the Act creates to hear and decide consumer disputes and to give relief. The Act does not use the word "machinery"; it uses "Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission" (Chapter IV). District Commission – "a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 28" (s. 2(15)). State Commission – "a State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 42" (s. 2(44)). National Commission – "the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 53" (s. 2(29)). Consumer dispute – "a dispute where the person against whom a complaint has been made, denies or disputes the allegations contained in the complaint" (s. 2(8)). This is what the machinery decides. The Commissions are quasi-judicial : they are not civil courts, but they have certain civil court powers (s. 38(9)), and their proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings (s. 38(10)).
keyPoints: Three tiers: District (s. 28), State (s. 42), National (s. 53) + Supreme Court (s. 67). Members: District ≥ 2; State ≥ 4; National ≥ 4; plus a President. Qualifications: Central rules (ss. 29, 43, 55). National: term ≤ 5 years; age ≤ 70 (President), ≤ 67 (members); s. 55(1A) Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026. Limits (2021 Rules): ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore; test is value paid. Unfair contracts: State ≤ ₹10 crore; National > ₹10 crore. Complainant may file where he resides or works for gain. Appeal 45 / 30 / 30 days; revision ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b). Transfer: s. 48 (within State), s. 62 (across States). s. 64: vacancy does not invalidate; s. 66: experts; s. 70: administrative control. Consumer mediation cell with every Commission (s. 74). (See Diagram 3 .) CPA 1986: District Forum, State Commission, National Commission (s. 9).

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors and hospitals argued that they were outside the CPA 1986 and that the District Forum, State Commission and National Commission, whose members need not have medical knowledge, could not decide complicated questions of medical negligence . A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) heard the matters. Principle: The Court described the Act as one that "sets up a three-tier structure for the redressal of consumer grievances" (s. 9) and rejected the objection to composition: "the presence of a person well versed in law as the President will have a bearing on the deliberations of these Agencies and their decisions"; requiring members to have expertise in every field "would lead to impossible situations". Why it matters: It confirms that the three-tier Commissions are competent to decide even technical disputes such as medical negligence. 2. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: A medical negligence complaint filed in 1997 went from the District Forum (award of ₹2.6 lakh) to the State Commission (award set aside) and then in revision to the National Commission, where the doctor died in 2009 and his legal heirs were brought on record. The Supreme Court (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.) examined the 1986 and 2019 Acts. Principle: Read with the "statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act", "upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; the case was sent back to the National Commission to be decided within six months. Why it matters: It shows the three tiers at work, one after another, and confirms the National Commission's revisional role and that the machinery can continue a case against the estate after a party dies.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019) వినియోగదారుల వివాదాలను నిర్ణయించడానికి మూడు స్థాయిల అర్ధ-న్యాయ ( quasi-judicial ) సంస్థలను ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): జిల్లా కమిషన్ – ప్రతి జిల్లాలో రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 28). రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్ – రాష్ట్రంలో రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 42). జాతీయ కమిషన్ – కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 53). వీటి పైన సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఉంది; జాతీయ కమిషన్ అసలు ఉత్తర్వుపై అప్పీలు అక్కడికి వెళ్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 67). ప్రతి కమిషన్‌లో అధ్యక్షుడు, సభ్యులు ఉంటారు: జిల్లా – కనీసం ఇద్దరు సభ్యులు (సెక్షన్ 28(2)); రాష్ట్రం – కనీసం నలుగురు (సెక్షన్ 42(3)); జాతీయం – కనీసం నలుగురు (సెక్షన్ 54). ఫిర్యాదు ఏ కమిషన్ విచారిస్తుందో ప్రతిఫలంగా చెల్లించిన వస్తువులు లేదా సేవల విలువ నిర్ణయిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్లు 34, 47, 58). Consumer Protection ( Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 ప్రకారం పరిమితులు: జిల్లా – ₹50 లక్షల వరకు; రాష్ట్రం – ₹50 లక్షలు దాటి ₹2 కోట్ల వరకు; జాతీయం – ₹2 కోట్లు దాటితే. ఉత్తర్వులు అప్పీలు ద్వారా పై స్థాయికి వెళ్తాయి (సెక్షన్లు 41, 51, 67), రివిజన్ ద్వారా సరిదిద్దబడతాయి (సెక్షన్లు 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) సహాయక భాగాలు: ప్రతి కమిషన్‌కు అనుబంధంగా వినియోగదారుల మధ్యవర్తిత్వ సెల్ (సెక్షన్ 74); కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ అథారిటీ (సెక్షన్ 10), దాని ఉత్తర్వులపై జాతీయ కమిషన్‌కు అప్పీలు (సెక్షన్ 58(1)(a)(iv)); సలహా ఇచ్చే వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ మండళ్లు (సెక్షన్లు 3–9). వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 1986 (CPA 1986) కింద ఇవే మూడు స్థాయిలు జిల్లా ఫోరం, రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్, జాతీయ కమిషన్ (సెక్షన్ 9).
te.meaning: వివాద పరిష్కార యంత్రాంగం అంటే వినియోగదారుల వివాదాలను విని, నిర్ణయించి, ఉపశమనం ఇవ్వడానికి చట్టం ఏర్పాటు చేసిన సంస్థలు. చట్టం "machinery" (యంత్రాంగం) అనే పదం వాడదు; "Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission" అని వాడుతుంది (అధ్యాయం IV). జిల్లా కమిషన్ – "a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 28" (అర్థం: సెక్షన్ 28 ఉప-సెక్షన్ (1) కింద ఏర్పాటైన జిల్లా వినియోగదారుల వివాదాల పరిష్కార కమిషన్) (సెక్షన్ 2(15)). రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్ – "a State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 42" (అర్థం: సెక్షన్ 42 ఉప-సెక్షన్ (1) కింద ఏర్పాటైన రాష్ట్ర వినియోగదారుల వివాదాల పరిష్కార కమిషన్) (సెక్షన్ 2(44)). జాతీయ కమిషన్ – "the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 53" (అర్థం: సెక్షన్ 53 ఉప-సెక్షన్ (1) కింద ఏర్పాటైన జాతీయ వినియోగదారుల వివాదాల పరిష్కార కమిషన్) (సెక్షన్ 2(29)). వినియోగదారుల వివాదం – "a dispute where the person against whom a complaint has been made, denies or disputes the allegations contained in the complaint" (అర్థం: ఎవరిపై ఫిర్యాదు చేయబడిందో ఆ వ్యక్తి ఫిర్యాదులోని ఆరోపణలను నిరాకరించే లేదా వివాదించే వివాదం) (సెక్షన్ 2(8)). యంత్రాంగం నిర్ణయించేది ఇదే. కమిషన్లు అర్ధ-న్యాయ సంస్థలు: అవి సివిల్ కోర్టులు కావు, కానీ కొన్ని సివిల్ కోర్టు అధికారాలు ఉన్నాయి (సెక్షన్ 38(9)), వాటి విచారణలు న్యాయ విచారణలుగా భావించబడతాయి (సెక్షన్ 38(10)).
keyPoints: మూడు స్థాయిలు: జిల్లా (సెక్షన్ 28), రాష్ట్రం (సెక్షన్ 42), జాతీయం (సెక్షన్ 53) + సుప్రీంకోర్టు (సెక్షన్ 67). సభ్యులు: జిల్లా ≥ 2; రాష్ట్రం ≥ 4; జాతీయం ≥ 4; అదనంగా అధ్యక్షుడు. అర్హతలు: కేంద్ర నియమాలు (సెక్షన్లు 29, 43, 55). జాతీయం: పదవీకాలం ≤ 5 సంవత్సరాలు; వయస్సు ≤ 70 (అధ్యక్షుడు), ≤ 67 (సభ్యులు); సెక్షన్ 55(1A) ట్రిబ్యునల్స్ సంస్కరణల చట్టం, 2026. పరిమితులు (2021 నియమాలు): ₹50 లక్షలు / ₹2 కోట్లు; పరీక్ష చెల్లించిన విలువ. అన్యాయ ఒప్పందాలు: రాష్ట్రం ≤ ₹10 కోట్లు; జాతీయం > ₹10 కోట్లు. ఫిర్యాదుదారు తాను నివసించే లేదా లాభం కోసం పని చేసే చోట దాఖలు చేయవచ్చు. అప్పీలు 45 / 30 / 30 రోజులు; రివిజన్ సెక్షన్లు 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b). బదిలీ: సెక్షన్ 48 (రాష్ట్రంలోపల), సెక్షన్ 62 (రాష్ట్రాల మధ్య). సెక్షన్ 64: ఖాళీ ఉత్తర్వును రద్దు చేయదు; సెక్షన్ 66: నిపుణులు; సెక్షన్ 70: పరిపాలనా నియంత్రణ. ప్రతి కమిషన్‌తో వినియోగదారుల మధ్యవర్తిత్వ సెల్ (సెక్షన్ 74). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) CPA 1986: జిల్లా ఫోరం, రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్, జాతీయ కమిషన్ (సెక్షన్ 9).

selfTest.q: జిల్లా కమిషన్‌ను ఎవరు ఏర్పాటు చేస్తారు, దానిలో ఎంత మంది సభ్యులు ఉండాలి?
selfTest.a: మూడు కమిషన్ల ప్రస్తుత ఆర్థిక పరిమితులు ఏమిటి? ఒక వినియోగదారుడు ₹40 లక్షలు చెల్లించి ₹1 కోటి కోరుతున్నాడు. ఏ కమిషన్? అన్యాయ ఒప్పందాలపై ఫిర్యాదులను ఏ కమిషన్లు వినగలవు? జాతీయ కమిషన్ బెంచి సభ్యులు సమానంగా విడిపోతే ఏమవుతుంది? కమిషన్‌లో ఖాళీ ఉంటే దాని ఉత్తర్వు చెల్లకుండా పోతుందా? కేంద్ర అథారిటీ ఉత్తర్వుపై అప్పీలును ఎవరు వింటారు?

hi.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) sets up a three-level system of quasi-judicial bodies to decide consumer disputes (See Diagram 1 ): District Commission – set up by the State Government in each district (s. 28). State Commission – set up by the State Government in the State (s. 42). National Commission – set up by the Central Government (s. 53). Above them is the Supreme Court , to which an appeal lies from an original order of the National Commission (s. 67). Each Commission has a President and members : District – at least two members (s. 28(2)); State – at least four (s. 42(3)); National – at least four (s. 54). Which Commission hears a complaint depends on the value of the goods or services paid as consideration (ss. 34, 47, 58). Under the Consumer Protection ( Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 the limits are: District – up to ₹50 lakh; State – above ₹50 lakh up to ₹2 crore; National – above ₹2 crore. Orders move up the ladder by appeal (ss. 41, 51, 67) and are corrected by revision (ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). (See Diagram 2 .) Supporting parts of the machinery: a consumer mediation cell attached to every Commission (s. 74); the Central Consumer Protection Authority (s. 10), whose orders are appealable to the National Commission (s. 58(1)(a)(iv)); and the advisory Consumer Protection Councils (ss. 3–9). Under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (CPA 1986) the same three levels were the District Forum, the State Commission and the National Commission (s. 9).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019) – Chapter IV, "Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission" (ss. 28–73).
District Commission

s. 28(1): "The State Government shall, by notification, establish a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, to be known as the District Commission, in each district of the State". Proviso: the State Government "may, if it deems fit, establish more than one District Commission in a district." s. 28(2): "Each District Commission shall consist of— (a) a President; and (b) not less than two and not more than such number of members as may be prescribed, in consultation with the Central Government." s. 29: the Central Government makes rules on qualifications, method of recruitment, procedure for appointment, term of office, resignation and removal. s. 30: the State Government makes rules on salaries, allowances and other service conditions. s. 31: persons already in office when the Act began continue till the end of their term. s. 32: if there is a vacancy in the office of the President or a member, the State Government may by notification direct another District Commission to exercise jurisdiction for that district also, or direct the President or a member of another District Commission to act for that Commission also. s. 33: the State Government provides officers and employees, who work "under the general superintendence of the President". s. 34(1): jurisdiction where the value of goods or services paid as consideration "does not exceed one crore rupees"; proviso: the Central Government may prescribe another value. s. 34(2): territorial jurisdiction – where the opposite party resides, carries on business, has a branch office or personally works for gain; where the cause of action arises wholly or in part; or where "the complainant resides or personally works for gain". s. 34(3): the District Commission "shall ordinarily function in the district headquarters". s. 36(1): every proceeding is conducted by "the President of that Commission and atleast one member thereof, sitting together".
State Commission

s. 42(1)–(2): established by the State Government by notification; "shall ordinarily function at the State capital"; proviso: regional benches may be set up. s. 42(3): "Each State Commission shall consist of— (a) a President; and (b) not less than four or not more than such number of members as may be prescribed in consultation with the Central Government." ss. 43–46: qualifications etc. (Central rules), salaries (State rules), transitional provision, officers and employees. s. 47(1)(a): original complaints above ₹1 crore up to ₹10 crore (value may be changed by the Central Government); complaints against unfair contracts up to ₹10 crore; appeals against orders of any District Commission in the State. s. 47(1)(b): revision – calling for records where a District Commission "has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or has failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested or has acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity". s. 47(2)–(3): benches constituted by the President, "the senior-most member shall preside over the Bench"; majority decides; if members are equally divided, the point goes to the President, and the opinion on the referred point is given "within a period of one month". s. 48: the State Commission may transfer a complaint from one District Commission to another within the State "if the interest of justice so requires".
National Commission

s. 53: established by the Central Government; "shall ordinarily function at the National Capital Region"; proviso: regional Benches may be set up. s. 54: "The National Commission shall consist of— (a) a President; and (b) not less than four and not more than such number of members as may be prescribed." s. 55(1): Central rules on qualifications, appointment, term, salaries etc.; term "not exceeding five years", with eligibility for re-appointment; age limit not exceeding "seventy years" for the President and "sixty-seven years" for any other member. s. 55(1A) (inserted by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026, w.e.f. 25 August 2026): these service matters "shall be governed by the provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026". s. 55(2): salary and service conditions cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment. s. 58(1)(a): original complaints above ₹10 crore; complaints against unfair contracts above ₹10 crore; appeals against orders of any State Commission; "appeals against the orders of the Central Authority". s. 58(1)(b): revision over State Commissions on the same grounds as s. 47(1)(b). s. 58(2)–(3): benches, senior-most member presides; on an equal division the referred point is answered "within a period of two months". s. 62: the National Commission may transfer a complaint from a District Commission of one State to a District Commission of another State, or from one State Commission to another. s. 63: if the President's office is vacant, the senior-most member performs the duties; but a member who is a retired High Court Judge or has been a Judicial Member presides in the President's absence.
Provisions common to all three

s. 64: "No act or proceeding of the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall be invalid by reason only of the existence of any vacancy amongst its members or any defect in the constitution thereof." s. 65: service of notices (registered post with acknowledgment, speed post, approved courier, or electronic means); s. 65(2) allows service on the nodal officer of an electronic service provider. s. 66: where a matter "involves the larger interest of consumers", the National or State Commission may direct any individual, organisation or expert to assist it. ss. 41, 51, 67: appeals – District to State (45 days), State to National (30 days), National to Supreme Court (30 days); each needs a deposit of fifty per cent. of the amount ordered. s. 68: an order not appealed is final. s. 69: complaint within two years of the cause of action; delay condonable for sufficient cause with recorded reasons. s. 70: administrative control – the National Commission over State Commissions (periodical returns on institution, disposal and pendency; inquiry into allegations against the President and members; instructions on uniform procedure, English translation of judgments and speedy copies; oversight by inspection); s. 70(2) a monitoring cell; s. 70(3) the State Commission over District Commissions. s. 71: every order is enforced "as if it were a decree" under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. s. 72: punishment for non-compliance. s. 74(1)–(2): "The State Government shall establish, by notification, a consumer mediation cell to be attached to each of the District Commissions and the State Commissions of that State"; the Central Government establishes one for the National Commission and each of its regional Benches.

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 – G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021, made under the provisos to ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i) and 58(1)(a)(i). They fix the limits at: District Commission – not exceeding ₹50 lakh; State Commission – exceeding ₹50 lakh but not exceeding ₹2 crore; National Commission – exceeding ₹2 crore.

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986) – s. 9 (three agencies: District Forum, State Commission, National Commission); s. 10 (District Forum: President "a person who is, or has been, or is qualified to be a District Judge" and two other members, "one of whom shall be a woman"); s. 16 (State Commission: President "a person who is or has been a Judge of a High Court"); s. 20 (National Commission: President "a person who is or has been a Judge of the Supreme Court"); ss. 11, 17, 21 (jurisdiction, finally ₹20 lakh / ₹1 crore, counting "the value of the goods or services and compensation, if any, claimed").
hi.meaning: Redressal machinery means the bodies that the Act creates to hear and decide consumer disputes and to give relief. The Act does not use the word "machinery"; it uses "Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission" (Chapter IV). District Commission – "a District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 28" (s. 2(15)). State Commission – "a State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 42" (s. 2(44)). National Commission – "the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission established under sub-section (1) of section 53" (s. 2(29)). Consumer dispute – "a dispute where the person against whom a complaint has been made, denies or disputes the allegations contained in the complaint" (s. 2(8)). This is what the machinery decides. The Commissions are quasi-judicial : they are not civil courts, but they have certain civil court powers (s. 38(9)), and their proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings (s. 38(10)).
keyPoints: Three tiers: District (s. 28), State (s. 42), National (s. 53) + Supreme Court (s. 67). Members: District ≥ 2; State ≥ 4; National ≥ 4; plus a President. Qualifications: Central rules (ss. 29, 43, 55). National: term ≤ 5 years; age ≤ 70 (President), ≤ 67 (members); s. 55(1A) Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026. Limits (2021 Rules): ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore; test is value paid. Unfair contracts: State ≤ ₹10 crore; National > ₹10 crore. Complainant may file where he resides or works for gain. Appeal 45 / 30 / 30 days; revision ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b). Transfer: s. 48 (within State), s. 62 (across States). s. 64: vacancy does not invalidate; s. 66: experts; s. 70: administrative control. Consumer mediation cell with every Commission (s. 74). (See Diagram 3 .) CPA 1986: District Forum, State Commission, National Commission (s. 9).

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors and hospitals argued that they were outside the CPA 1986 and that the District Forum, State Commission and National Commission, whose members need not have medical knowledge, could not decide complicated questions of medical negligence . A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) heard the matters. Principle: The Court described the Act as one that "sets up a three-tier structure for the redressal of consumer grievances" (s. 9) and rejected the objection to composition: "the presence of a person well versed in law as the President will have a bearing on the deliberations of these Agencies and their decisions"; requiring members to have expertise in every field "would lead to impossible situations". Why it matters: It confirms that the three-tier Commissions are competent to decide even technical disputes such as medical negligence. 2. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: A medical negligence complaint filed in 1997 went from the District Forum (award of ₹2.6 lakh) to the State Commission (award set aside) and then in revision to the National Commission, where the doctor died in 2009 and his legal heirs were brought on record. The Supreme Court (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.) examined the 1986 and 2019 Acts. Principle: Read with the "statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act", "upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; the case was sent back to the National Commission to be decided within six months. Why it matters: It shows the three tiers at work, one after another, and confirms the National Commission's revisional role and that the machinery can continue a case against the estate after a party dies.

law-of-torts-u5-t8.subtitle: Restrictive trade practices, unfair trade practices and unfair contracts under the 2019 Act, with the full list of unfair practices

en.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) treats two kinds of wrongful trade conduct as grounds of complaint (s. 2(6)(i)) (See Diagram 1 ): Restrictive trade practice (s. 2(41)) – a practice that manipulates price or delivery conditions, or affects supply, so as to impose "unjustified costs or restrictions" on consumers. It includes (i) delay in supply beyond the agreed period leading to a rise in price, and (ii) forcing a consumer to buy one thing as a condition for buying another. Unfair trade practice (s. 2(47)) – any "unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice" to promote sales, including nine listed groups: false or misleading statements; false bargain price advertisements; gifts, prizes and contests; sale of goods below safety standards; hoarding or destruction to raise prices; spurious goods and deceptive services; not issuing a bill; refusing to take back defective goods within thirty days; and disclosing a consumer's personal information. Remedies: a complaint to a Commission (ss. 2(6)(i), 35), which may order the practice to be discontinued and not repeated (s. 39(1)(g)) with compensation; and action by the Central Authority for consumers as a class – inquiry, discontinuation, and penalties for misleading advertisements (ss. 18, 20, 21). A consumer who merely "alleges unfair trade practice" may complain, even without being the buyer in that transaction (s. 35(1)(a)(ii)).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 2(41) – "'restrictive trade practice' means a trade practice which tends to bring about manipulation of price or its conditions of delivery or to affect flow of supplies in the market relating to goods or services in such a manner as to impose on the consumers unjustified costs or restrictions and shall include— (i) delay beyond the period agreed to by a trader in supply of such goods or in providing the services which has led or is likely to lead to rise in the price; (ii) any trade practice which requires a consumer to buy, hire or avail of any goods or, as the case may be, services as condition precedent for buying, hiring or availing of other goods or services". s. 2(47) – "'unfair trade practice' means a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice including any of the following practices, namely:— (i) making any statement, whether orally or in writing or by visible representation including by means of electronic record, which— (a) falsely represents that the goods are of a particular standard, quality, quantity, grade, composition, style or model; (b) falsely represents that the services are of a particular standard, quality or grade; (c) falsely represents any re-built, second-hand, renovated, reconditioned or old goods as new goods; (d) represents that the goods or services have sponsorship, approval, performance, characteristics, accessories, uses or benefits which such goods or services do not have; (e) represents that the seller or the supplier has a sponsorship or approval or affiliation which such seller or supplier does not have; (f) makes a false or misleading representation concerning the need for, or the usefulness of, any goods or services; (g) gives to the public any warranty or guarantee of the performance, efficacy or length of life of a product or of any goods that is not based on an adequate or proper test thereof" – with the proviso that where a defence is raised that it was based on adequate or proper test, "the burden of proof of such defence shall lie on the person raising such defence"; (h) makes to the public a representation purporting to be a warranty or guarantee, or a promise to replace, maintain or repair, "if such purported warranty or guarantee or promise is materially misleading or if there is no reasonable prospect that such warranty, guarantee or promise will be carried out"; (i) "materially misleads the public concerning the price at which a product or like products or goods or services, have been or are, ordinarily sold or provided"; (j) "gives false or misleading facts disparaging the goods, services or trade of another person". Explanation – a statement on an article, its wrapper or container, or on anything attached to or accompanying it, or made available to the public, is deemed to be a statement made to the public by the person who caused it to be made. (ii) permitting the publication of any advertisement, "including by way of electronic record, for the sale or supply at a bargain price of goods or services that are not intended to be offered for sale or supply at the bargain price, or for a period that is, and in quantities that are, reasonable". Explanation – "bargain price" means "(A) a price that is stated in any advertisement to be a bargain price, by reference to an ordinary price or otherwise; or (B) a price that a person who reads, hears or sees the advertisement, would reasonably understand to be a bargain price". (iii) permitting "(a) the offering of gifts, prizes or other items with the intention of not providing them as offered or creating impression that something is being given or offered free of charge when it is fully or partly covered by the amount charged"; "(b) the conduct of any contest, lottery, game of chance or skill, for the purpose of promoting ... the sale, use or supply of any product or any business interest, except such contest ... as may be prescribed"; "(c) withholding from the participants of any scheme offering gifts, prizes or other items free of charge on its closure, the information about final results of the scheme" (results published within a reasonable time, prominently in the same newspaper, are deemed informed). (iv) permitting the sale or supply of goods "knowing or having reason to believe that the goods do not comply with the standards prescribed by the competent authority relating to performance, composition, contents, design, constructions, finishing or packaging as are necessary to prevent or reduce the risk of injury". (v) "permitting the hoarding or destruction of goods, or refusal to sell the goods or to make them available for sale or to provide any service, if such hoarding or destruction or refusal raises or tends to raise or is intended to raise, the cost of those or other similar goods or services". (vi) "manufacturing of spurious goods or offering such goods for sale or adopting deceptive practices in the provision of services". (vii) "not issuing bill or cash memo or receipt for the goods sold or services rendered in such manner as may be prescribed". (viii) "refusing, after selling goods or rendering services, to take back or withdraw defective goods or to withdraw or discontinue deficient services and to refund the consideration thereof, if paid, within the period stipulated in the bill or cash memo or receipt or in the absence of such stipulation, within a period of thirty days". (ix) "disclosing to other person any personal information given in confidence by the consumer unless such disclosure is made in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force". s. 2(43) – "'spurious goods' means such goods which are falsely claimed to be genuine". s. 2(6)(i) – a "complaint" may allege that "an unfair contract or unfair trade practice or a restrictive trade practice has been adopted by any trader or service provider". s. 35(1)(a) – a complaint may be filed by the consumer "(i) to whom such goods are sold ... or such service is provided ...; or (ii) who alleges unfair trade practice in respect of such goods or service". s. 39(1)(g) – the Commission may order the opposite party "to discontinue the unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice and not to repeat them"; also compensation (d), corrective advertisement (l), cease and desist (n). s. 18(2)(a) – the Central Authority may "inquire or cause an inquiry or investigation to be made into violations of consumer rights or unfair trade practices, either suo motu or on a complaint". s. 20(c) – it may order "discontinuation of practices which are unfair and prejudicial to consumers' interest". s. 21 – directions and penalties for false or misleading advertisements. s. 94 – the Central Government may take measures "for the purposes of preventing unfair trade practices in e-commerce, direct selling".

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (for comparison) – s. 2(1)(nnn) defined restrictive trade practice in the same words; s. 2(1)(r) defined unfair trade practice with clauses (1) to (6) (statements, bargain price, gifts and contests, unsafe goods, hoarding, spurious goods), without the 2019 additions of electronic records, no-bill, refusal to take back, and disclosure of personal information.

Competition Act, 2002 (for contrast) – s. 3(1) – "No enterprise or association of enterprises or person or association of persons shall enter into any agreement ... which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India." This deals with competition in the market as a whole, not with an individual consumer's complaint.
en.meaning: Trade practice – a method or practice adopted by a trader or service provider in the course of business. Restrictive trade practice – a practice that manipulates price or delivery conditions, or affects supply, so as to impose unjustified costs or restrictions on consumers (s. 2(41)). Unfair trade practice – a practice that, to promote sales or services, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice (s. 2(47)). Bargain price – a price advertised as a bargain, or one which a reasonable reader, listener or viewer would understand to be a bargain (s. 2(47)(ii), Explanation). Spurious goods – goods "which are falsely claimed to be genuine" (s. 2(43)). Condition precedent (tie-in) – making the purchase of one item a condition for buying another (s. 2(41)(ii)).
keyPoints: RTP s. 2(41): price/delivery/supply manipulation → unjustified costs or restrictions; delay with price rise; tie-in. (See Diagram 2 .) UTP s. 2(47): unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice; nine groups. (i) false statements incl. electronic record; (ii) bargain price; (iii) gifts, contests, results; (iv) unsafe goods; (v) hoarding; (vi) spurious goods; (vii) no bill; (viii) no return in 30 days; (ix) personal information. Untested warranty – burden on trader. Complaint: s. 2(6)(i); s. 35(1)(a)(ii). Relief: s. 39(1)(g) discontinue and not repeat. (See Diagram 3 .) Central Authority: ss. 18(2)(a), 20(c), 21. (See Diagram 1 .)

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019) రెండు రకాల తప్పుడు వ్యాపార ప్రవర్తనను ఫిర్యాదు కారణాలుగా పరిగణిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 2(6)(i)) ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి (సెక్షన్ 2(41)) – వినియోగదారులపై "unjustified costs or restrictions" (అర్థం: అన్యాయమైన ఖర్చులు లేదా ఆంక్షలు) విధించేలా ధర లేదా డెలివరీ షరతులను తారుమారు చేసే, లేదా సరఫరాను ప్రభావితం చేసే పద్ధతి. ఇందులో (i) అంగీకరించిన కాలానికి మించిన సరఫరా ఆలస్యం వల్ల ధర పెరగడం, (ii) మరొకటి కొనడానికి షరతుగా ఒకటి కొనమని బలవంతం చేయడం ఉంటాయి. అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి (సెక్షన్ 2(47)) – అమ్మకాలను ప్రోత్సహించడానికి ఏదైనా "unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice" (అర్థం: అన్యాయ పద్ధతి లేదా అన్యాయ లేదా మోసపూరిత పద్ధతి); ఇందులో తొమ్మిది వర్గాలు: తప్పుడు లేదా తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటనలు; తప్పుడు బేరం ధర ప్రకటనలు; బహుమతులు, పోటీలు; భద్రతా ప్రమాణాలకు తక్కువ వస్తువుల అమ్మకం; ధరలు పెంచడానికి నిల్వ దాచడం లేదా నాశనం చేయడం; నకిలీ వస్తువులు , మోసపూరిత సేవలు; బిల్లు ఇవ్వకపోవడం; ముప్పై రోజుల్లో లోపభూయిష్ట వస్తువులను తిరిగి తీసుకోకపోవడం; వినియోగదారుడి వ్యక్తిగత సమాచారం వెల్లడించడం. పరిష్కారాలు: కమిషన్‌కు ఫిర్యాదు (సెక్షన్లు 2(6)(i), 35); కమిషన్ ఆ పద్ధతిని ఆపి, మళ్ళీ చేయకూడదని (సెక్షన్ 39(1)(g)), నష్టపరిహారంతో ఆదేశించవచ్చు; వినియోగదారుల వర్గం కోసం కేంద్ర అథారిటీ చర్య – విచారణ, నిలిపివేత, తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటనలకు జరిమానాలు (సెక్షన్లు 18, 20, 21). కేవలం "alleges unfair trade practice" (అర్థం: అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతిని ఆరోపించే) వినియోగదారుడు ఆ లావాదేవీలో కొనుగోలుదారు కాకపోయినా ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 35(1)(a)(ii)).
te.meaning: వ్యాపార పద్ధతి – వ్యాపారి లేదా సేవా ప్రదాత వ్యాపారంలో అనుసరించే విధానం లేదా పద్ధతి. నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి – వినియోగదారులపై అన్యాయమైన ఖర్చులు లేదా ఆంక్షలు విధించేలా ధర లేదా డెలివరీ షరతులను తారుమారు చేసే, లేదా సరఫరాను ప్రభావితం చేసే పద్ధతి (సెక్షన్ 2(41)). అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి – అమ్మకాలు లేదా సేవలను ప్రోత్సహించడానికి ఏదైనా అన్యాయ పద్ధతి లేదా అన్యాయ లేదా మోసపూరిత పద్ధతిని అనుసరించడం (సెక్షన్ 2(47)). బేరం ధర – బేరం అని ప్రకటించిన ధర, లేదా సహేతుకమైన పాఠకుడు, శ్రోత లేదా వీక్షకుడు బేరంగా అర్థం చేసుకునే ధర (సెక్షన్ 2(47)(ii), వివరణ). నకిలీ వస్తువులు – "falsely claimed to be genuine" (అర్థం: అసలైనవని తప్పుగా చెప్పుకునే) వస్తువులు (సెక్షన్ 2(43)). ముందస్తు షరతు (ముడిపెట్టిన అమ్మకం) – మరొకటి కొనడానికి ఒక వస్తువు కొనడాన్ని షరతుగా పెట్టడం (సెక్షన్ 2(41)(ii)).
keyPoints: నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి సెక్షన్ 2(41): ధర/డెలివరీ/సరఫరా తారుమారు → అన్యాయమైన ఖర్చులు లేదా ఆంక్షలు; ధర పెరుగుదలతో ఆలస్యం; ముడిపెట్టిన అమ్మకం. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి సెక్షన్ 2(47): అన్యాయ పద్ధతి లేదా అన్యాయ లేదా మోసపూరిత పద్ధతి; తొమ్మిది వర్గాలు. (i) ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ రికార్డుతో సహా తప్పుడు ప్రకటనలు; (ii) బేరం ధర; (iii) బహుమతులు, పోటీలు, ఫలితాలు; (iv) సురక్షితం కాని వస్తువులు; (v) నిల్వ దాచడం; (vi) నకిలీ వస్తువులు; (vii) బిల్లు లేదు; (viii) 30 రోజుల్లో వాపసు లేదు; (ix) వ్యక్తిగత సమాచారం. పరీక్షించని వారంటీ – భారం వ్యాపారిపై. ఫిర్యాదు: సెక్షన్ 2(6)(i); సెక్షన్ 35(1)(a)(ii). ఉపశమనం: సెక్షన్ 39(1)(g) ఆపడం, మళ్ళీ చేయకపోవడం. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) కేంద్ర అథారిటీ: సెక్షన్లు 18(2)(a), 20(c), 21. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.)

selfTest.q: నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతిని నిర్వచించండి. సెక్షన్ 2(41) స్పష్టంగా చేర్చిన రెండు పద్ధతులు చెప్పండి. "బేరం ధర" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: 1986 చట్టంలో లేని, 2019లో చేర్చిన మూడు అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతులు చెప్పండి. వారంటీ సరైన పరీక్ష ఆధారంగా ఇచ్చారని రుజువు చేసే భారం ఎవరిది? సెక్షన్ 39(1)(g) కింద కమిషన్ ఏ ఉత్తర్వు ఇవ్వవచ్చు?

క్లాజు పద్ధతి ఉదాహరణ
(i) తప్పుడు లేదా తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటనలు (నోటితో, రాతతో, దృశ్యంగా, ఎలక్ట్రానిక్) – ప్రమాణం, నాణ్యత, పాతవి కొత్తవిగా, తప్పుడు ఆమోదం, తప్పుడు అవసరం, పరీక్షించని గ్యారంటీ, తప్పుదారి పట్టించే వారంటీ, తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ధర, ప్రత్యర్థిని కించపరచడం "100% స్వచ్ఛమైన తేనె" అని తప్పుగా లేబుల్
(ii) సహేతుక పరిమాణం, కాలంలో ఆ ధరకు అమ్మే ఉద్దేశం లేకుండా బేరం ధర ప్రకటన రెండు ముక్కలు మాత్రమే ఉన్నప్పుడు "సగం ధర" ఆఫర్
(iii) చెప్పినట్లు ఇవ్వని బహుమతులు; ధరలో కలిపిన "ఉచిత" వస్తువులు; ప్రోత్సాహక పోటీలు, లాటరీలు (నిర్దేశించినవి తప్ప); బహుమతి పథకం తుది ఫలితాలు దాచడం ధర బిల్లులో కలిపిన "ఉచిత బహుమతి"
(iv) భద్రతా ప్రమాణాలు పాటించవని తెలిసి వస్తువులు అమ్మడం నిర్దేశించిన ప్రమాణంలో విఫలమైన హెల్మెట్లు
(v) ధరలు పెంచడానికి నిల్వ దాచడం, నాశనం చేయడం, అమ్మడానికి నిరాకరించడం ధర పెంచడానికి ఉల్లిపాయలు నిల్వ దాచడం
(vi) నకిలీ వస్తువులు; సేవల్లో మోసపూరిత పద్ధతులు నకిలీ బ్రాండెడ్ మందులు
(vii) నిర్దేశించిన విధంగా బిల్లు, క్యాష్ మెమో లేదా రసీదు ఇవ్వకపోవడం బిల్లు ఇవ్వడానికి నిరాకరించే దుకాణం
(viii) నిర్ణీత కాలంలో లేదా ముప్పై రోజుల్లో లోపభూయిష్ట వస్తువులను తిరిగి తీసుకోకపోవడం లేదా లోపభూయిష్ట సేవలను ఉపసంహరించి డబ్బు ఇవ్వకపోవడం విరిగిన వస్తువు తిరిగి తీసుకోవడానికి నిరాకరించే ఆన్‌లైన్ విక్రేత
(ix) చట్టం అనుమతిస్తే తప్ప, నమ్మకంతో ఇచ్చిన వ్యక్తిగత సమాచారం వెల్లడించడం కస్టమర్ ఫోన్ నంబర్లను మార్కెటర్లకు అమ్మడం

hi.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) treats two kinds of wrongful trade conduct as grounds of complaint (s. 2(6)(i)) (See Diagram 1 ): Restrictive trade practice (s. 2(41)) – a practice that manipulates price or delivery conditions, or affects supply, so as to impose "unjustified costs or restrictions" on consumers. It includes (i) delay in supply beyond the agreed period leading to a rise in price, and (ii) forcing a consumer to buy one thing as a condition for buying another. Unfair trade practice (s. 2(47)) – any "unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice" to promote sales, including nine listed groups: false or misleading statements; false bargain price advertisements; gifts, prizes and contests; sale of goods below safety standards; hoarding or destruction to raise prices; spurious goods and deceptive services; not issuing a bill; refusing to take back defective goods within thirty days; and disclosing a consumer's personal information. Remedies: a complaint to a Commission (ss. 2(6)(i), 35), which may order the practice to be discontinued and not repeated (s. 39(1)(g)) with compensation; and action by the Central Authority for consumers as a class – inquiry, discontinuation, and penalties for misleading advertisements (ss. 18, 20, 21). A consumer who merely "alleges unfair trade practice" may complain, even without being the buyer in that transaction (s. 35(1)(a)(ii)).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 2(41) – "'restrictive trade practice' means a trade practice which tends to bring about manipulation of price or its conditions of delivery or to affect flow of supplies in the market relating to goods or services in such a manner as to impose on the consumers unjustified costs or restrictions and shall include— (i) delay beyond the period agreed to by a trader in supply of such goods or in providing the services which has led or is likely to lead to rise in the price; (ii) any trade practice which requires a consumer to buy, hire or avail of any goods or, as the case may be, services as condition precedent for buying, hiring or availing of other goods or services". s. 2(47) – "'unfair trade practice' means a trade practice which, for the purpose of promoting the sale, use or supply of any goods or for the provision of any service, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice including any of the following practices, namely:— (i) making any statement, whether orally or in writing or by visible representation including by means of electronic record, which— (a) falsely represents that the goods are of a particular standard, quality, quantity, grade, composition, style or model; (b) falsely represents that the services are of a particular standard, quality or grade; (c) falsely represents any re-built, second-hand, renovated, reconditioned or old goods as new goods; (d) represents that the goods or services have sponsorship, approval, performance, characteristics, accessories, uses or benefits which such goods or services do not have; (e) represents that the seller or the supplier has a sponsorship or approval or affiliation which such seller or supplier does not have; (f) makes a false or misleading representation concerning the need for, or the usefulness of, any goods or services; (g) gives to the public any warranty or guarantee of the performance, efficacy or length of life of a product or of any goods that is not based on an adequate or proper test thereof" – with the proviso that where a defence is raised that it was based on adequate or proper test, "the burden of proof of such defence shall lie on the person raising such defence"; (h) makes to the public a representation purporting to be a warranty or guarantee, or a promise to replace, maintain or repair, "if such purported warranty or guarantee or promise is materially misleading or if there is no reasonable prospect that such warranty, guarantee or promise will be carried out"; (i) "materially misleads the public concerning the price at which a product or like products or goods or services, have been or are, ordinarily sold or provided"; (j) "gives false or misleading facts disparaging the goods, services or trade of another person". Explanation – a statement on an article, its wrapper or container, or on anything attached to or accompanying it, or made available to the public, is deemed to be a statement made to the public by the person who caused it to be made. (ii) permitting the publication of any advertisement, "including by way of electronic record, for the sale or supply at a bargain price of goods or services that are not intended to be offered for sale or supply at the bargain price, or for a period that is, and in quantities that are, reasonable". Explanation – "bargain price" means "(A) a price that is stated in any advertisement to be a bargain price, by reference to an ordinary price or otherwise; or (B) a price that a person who reads, hears or sees the advertisement, would reasonably understand to be a bargain price". (iii) permitting "(a) the offering of gifts, prizes or other items with the intention of not providing them as offered or creating impression that something is being given or offered free of charge when it is fully or partly covered by the amount charged"; "(b) the conduct of any contest, lottery, game of chance or skill, for the purpose of promoting ... the sale, use or supply of any product or any business interest, except such contest ... as may be prescribed"; "(c) withholding from the participants of any scheme offering gifts, prizes or other items free of charge on its closure, the information about final results of the scheme" (results published within a reasonable time, prominently in the same newspaper, are deemed informed). (iv) permitting the sale or supply of goods "knowing or having reason to believe that the goods do not comply with the standards prescribed by the competent authority relating to performance, composition, contents, design, constructions, finishing or packaging as are necessary to prevent or reduce the risk of injury". (v) "permitting the hoarding or destruction of goods, or refusal to sell the goods or to make them available for sale or to provide any service, if such hoarding or destruction or refusal raises or tends to raise or is intended to raise, the cost of those or other similar goods or services". (vi) "manufacturing of spurious goods or offering such goods for sale or adopting deceptive practices in the provision of services". (vii) "not issuing bill or cash memo or receipt for the goods sold or services rendered in such manner as may be prescribed". (viii) "refusing, after selling goods or rendering services, to take back or withdraw defective goods or to withdraw or discontinue deficient services and to refund the consideration thereof, if paid, within the period stipulated in the bill or cash memo or receipt or in the absence of such stipulation, within a period of thirty days". (ix) "disclosing to other person any personal information given in confidence by the consumer unless such disclosure is made in accordance with the provisions of any law for the time being in force". s. 2(43) – "'spurious goods' means such goods which are falsely claimed to be genuine". s. 2(6)(i) – a "complaint" may allege that "an unfair contract or unfair trade practice or a restrictive trade practice has been adopted by any trader or service provider". s. 35(1)(a) – a complaint may be filed by the consumer "(i) to whom such goods are sold ... or such service is provided ...; or (ii) who alleges unfair trade practice in respect of such goods or service". s. 39(1)(g) – the Commission may order the opposite party "to discontinue the unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice and not to repeat them"; also compensation (d), corrective advertisement (l), cease and desist (n). s. 18(2)(a) – the Central Authority may "inquire or cause an inquiry or investigation to be made into violations of consumer rights or unfair trade practices, either suo motu or on a complaint". s. 20(c) – it may order "discontinuation of practices which are unfair and prejudicial to consumers' interest". s. 21 – directions and penalties for false or misleading advertisements. s. 94 – the Central Government may take measures "for the purposes of preventing unfair trade practices in e-commerce, direct selling".

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (for comparison) – s. 2(1)(nnn) defined restrictive trade practice in the same words; s. 2(1)(r) defined unfair trade practice with clauses (1) to (6) (statements, bargain price, gifts and contests, unsafe goods, hoarding, spurious goods), without the 2019 additions of electronic records, no-bill, refusal to take back, and disclosure of personal information.

Competition Act, 2002 (for contrast) – s. 3(1) – "No enterprise or association of enterprises or person or association of persons shall enter into any agreement ... which causes or is likely to cause an appreciable adverse effect on competition within India." This deals with competition in the market as a whole, not with an individual consumer's complaint.
hi.meaning: Trade practice – a method or practice adopted by a trader or service provider in the course of business. Restrictive trade practice – a practice that manipulates price or delivery conditions, or affects supply, so as to impose unjustified costs or restrictions on consumers (s. 2(41)). Unfair trade practice – a practice that, to promote sales or services, adopts any unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice (s. 2(47)). Bargain price – a price advertised as a bargain, or one which a reasonable reader, listener or viewer would understand to be a bargain (s. 2(47)(ii), Explanation). Spurious goods – goods "which are falsely claimed to be genuine" (s. 2(43)). Condition precedent (tie-in) – making the purchase of one item a condition for buying another (s. 2(41)(ii)).
keyPoints: RTP s. 2(41): price/delivery/supply manipulation → unjustified costs or restrictions; delay with price rise; tie-in. (See Diagram 2 .) UTP s. 2(47): unfair method or unfair or deceptive practice; nine groups. (i) false statements incl. electronic record; (ii) bargain price; (iii) gifts, contests, results; (iv) unsafe goods; (v) hoarding; (vi) spurious goods; (vii) no bill; (viii) no return in 30 days; (ix) personal information. Untested warranty – burden on trader. Complaint: s. 2(6)(i); s. 35(1)(a)(ii). Relief: s. 39(1)(g) discontinue and not repeat. (See Diagram 3 .) Central Authority: ss. 18(2)(a), 20(c), 21. (See Diagram 1 .)

law-of-torts-u5-t13.subtitle: The reliefs a Consumer Commission can give under section 39, with interest, compensation, punitive damages and enforcement

en.inOneMinute: A consumer who has a grievance under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) gets these remedies (See Diagram 1 ): Final reliefs – the Commission's order under s. 39(1)(a) to (n): remove the defect, replace, refund with interest, compensation (with punitive damages), product liability compensation, stop unfair or restrictive trade practices, withdraw or stop making hazardous goods, a sum of at least 25% of value for unidentified consumers, corrective advertisement, costs, and stop misleading advertisement. Interim order – while the case is pending, "such interim order as is just and proper" (s. 38(8)). Mediation – a settlement through the consumer mediation cell (s. 37; Chapter V). Challenge to an order (See Diagram 2 ) – review by the same Commission for an "error apparent on the face of the record" within 30 days (ss. 40, 50, 60); appeal to the next level (s. 41: 45 days; ss. 51, 67: 30 days), after a pre-deposit of 50% of the amount ordered; revision by the State or National Commission (ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)); setting aside an ex parte order of the National Commission (s. 61). Enforcement – the order is executed as a decree (s. 71), and non-compliance is punishable (s. 72). Other remedies remain: a civil suit in tort, or criminal law, because the Act is "in addition to and not in derogation of" other laws (s. 100). Nizam's Institute (2009) shows how compensation is measured; Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy (2026) shows what happens to the remedy when the opposite party dies (See Diagram 3 ).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 39(1) – where the District Commission is satisfied that the goods suffer from defects, or that allegations about the services or any unfair trade practices, "or claims for compensation under product liability are proved, it shall issue an order to the opposite party directing him to do one or more of the following, namely:— (a) to remove the defect pointed out by the appropriate laboratory from the goods in question; (b) to replace the goods with new goods of similar description which shall be free from any defect; (c) to return to the complainant the price, or, as the case may be, the charges paid by the complainant along with such interest on such price or charges as may be decided; (d) to pay such amount as may be awarded by it as compensation to the consumer for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party: Provided that the District Commission shall have the power to grant punitive damages in such circumstances as it deems fit; (e) to pay such amount as may be awarded by it as compensation in a product liability action under Chapter VI; (f) to remove the defects in goods or deficiencies in the services in question; (g) to discontinue the unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice and not to repeat them; (h) not to offer the hazardous or unsafe goods for sale; (i) to withdraw the hazardous goods from being offered for sale; (j) to cease manufacture of hazardous goods and to desist from offering services which are hazardous in nature; (k) to pay such sum as may be determined by it, if it is of the opinion that loss or injury has been suffered by a large number of consumers who are not identifiable conveniently: Provided that the minimum amount of sum so payable shall not be less than twenty-five per cent. of the value of such defective goods sold or service provided, as the case may be, to such consumers; (l) to issue corrective advertisement to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement at the cost of the opposite party responsible for issuing such misleading advertisement; (m) to provide for adequate costs to parties; and (n) to cease and desist from issuing any misleading advertisement." s. 39(2) – "Any amount obtained under sub-section (1) shall be credited to such fund and utilised in such manner as may be prescribed." ss. 49(1), 59(1) – the same provisions apply to complaints before the State Commission and the National Commission. s. 38(8) – "Where during the pendency of any proceeding before the District Commission, if it appears necessary, it may pass such interim order as is just and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case." s. 38(12) – on the death of a complainant who is a consumer, or of the opposite party, "the provisions of Order XXII of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908) shall apply". s. 37 – reference of the dispute to mediation where there are elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties. s. 40 (District), s. 50 (State), s. 60 (National) – each Commission "shall have the power to review any of the order passed by it if there is an error apparent on the face of the record, either of its own motion or on an application made by any of the parties within thirty days of such order". s. 41 – "Any person aggrieved by an order made by the District Commission may prefer an appeal against such order to the State Commission on the grounds of facts or law within a period of forty-five days from the date of the order". Provisos: delay may be condoned for "sufficient cause"; no appeal by a person required to pay an amount "unless the appellant has deposited fifty per cent. of that amount"; "no appeal shall lie from any order passed under sub-section (1) of section 81 by the District Commission pursuant to a settlement by mediation under section 80". s. 51(1) – appeal against an order of the State Commission in its original jurisdiction to the National Commission "within a period of thirty days", with the same 50% deposit. s. 51(2) – an appeal lies to the National Commission from an order passed in appeal by a State Commission only "if the National Commission is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law". s. 67 – appeal against an order of the National Commission in its original jurisdiction "to the Supreme Court within a period of thirty days", with the same 50% deposit. s. 47(1)(b) and s. 58(1)(b) – the State Commission (over District Commissions) and the National Commission (over State Commissions) may "call for the records and pass appropriate orders" where the lower Commission "has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or has failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested or has acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity". s. 61 – "Where an order is passed by the National Commission ex parte, the aggrieved party may make an application to the Commission for setting aside such order." s. 68 – an order "shall, if no appeal has been preferred against such order under the provisions of this Act, be final". s. 69(1) – a complaint must be "filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen"; s. 69(2) – delay may be condoned for sufficient cause, with reasons recorded. s. 71 – every order "shall be enforced by it in the same manner as if it were a decree made by a Court in a suit before it and the provisions of Order XXI of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908) shall, as far as may be, applicable". s. 72(1) – whoever fails to comply with an order of a Commission is punishable with imprisonment from one month to three years, or fine from ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh, or both. s. 100 – "The provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law for the time being in force."

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (for comparison) – s. 14(1) listed the reliefs of the District Forum: (a) remove defect; (b) replace; (c) return the price or charges; (d) compensation for negligence, with punitive damages (proviso inserted in 2003); (e) remove defects or deficiencies; (f) discontinue unfair or restrictive trade practice; (g), (h) not offer, and withdraw, hazardous goods; (ha) cease manufacture of hazardous goods; (hb) a sum for unidentified consumers, "not be less than five per cent." of the value; (hc) corrective advertisement; (i) costs. Appeals: s. 15 (to the State Commission within thirty days; deposit of "fifty per cent. of that amount or twenty-five thousand rupees, whichever is less"), s. 19 and s. 23 (thirty days; deposit of 50% or ₹35,000 and 50% or ₹50,000, whichever is less).
en.meaning: Remedy – the relief that the law gives to a person whose right has been violated. Under CPA 2019 it is mainly an order of a Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. Interim order – a temporary order passed while the case is pending, to protect the complainant until the final decision (s. 38(8)). Review – re-examination of an order by the same Commission that passed it, only where there is "an error apparent on the face of the record" (ss. 40, 50, 60). Appeal – a challenge to a higher Commission or the Supreme Court, on facts and law (ss. 41, 51, 67). Revision – supervisory power of the State or National Commission to call for records and correct a lower Commission's jurisdictional error, illegality or material irregularity (ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). Pre-deposit – the condition that a person ordered to pay must first deposit fifty per cent. of that amount before an appeal is entertained (provisos to ss. 41, 51(1), 67).
keyPoints: s. 39(1): 14 reliefs; "one or more". Punitive damages: proviso to s. 39(1)(d). Unidentified consumers: at least 25% (1986: 5%). Interim order: s. 38(8). Review: ss. 40, 50, 60; 30 days; error apparent. Appeals: s. 41 (45 days), s. 51 (30 days), s. 67 (30 days); 50% pre-deposit. Second appeal to National Commission only on a substantial question of law (s. 51(2)). Revision: ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b). No appeal from mediated settlement order. Finality s. 68; limitation s. 69 (two years). Enforcement: ss. 71, 72. Death of party: s. 38(12); Kumud Lall . (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A twenty-year-old engineering student became paraplegic after surgery to remove a tumour at the appellant hospital. The National Commission found negligence before, during and after the operation and awarded ₹14 lakh (and ₹1.5 lakh to the parents). Both sides appealed to the Supreme Court (B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ.). Principle: The Court must "strike a balance between the inflated and unreasonable demands of a victim and the equally untenable claim of the opposite party saying that nothing is payable"; "if a case is made out, the Court must not be chary of awarding adequate compensation". It awarded ₹1 crore with interest at 6% from 1 March 1999. Why it matters: It is the leading guide on how a Consumer Commission should measure the compensation remedy – adequate and realistic, not token. 2. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: A patient's husband complained (1997) that an eye surgeon's wrong operation had cost her the sight of one eye. The District Forum awarded ₹2.6 lakh; the State Commission set the award aside. While the complainant's revision was pending before the National Commission, the doctor died (2009), and the National Commission brought his wife and son on record. They appealed to the Supreme Court (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.). Principle: "upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; under s. 306 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive". The matter was remitted to the National Commission to decide negligence and the surviving claims against the estate within six months. Why it matters: The consumer's remedy does not end with the opposite party's death; it continues against the estate, but only for claims that survive.

selfTest.q: Name the four groups of reliefs under s. 39(1). Within what time can a District Commission's order be appealed?
selfTest.a: What must an appellant who is ordered to pay money do before the appeal is heard? On what ground can a Commission review its own order? When does an appeal lie to the National Commission from an appellate order of a State Commission? What is the minimum sum payable where many unidentifiable consumers have suffered loss? What happens to a medical negligence complaint if the doctor dies during the case?

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019) కింద ఫిర్యాదు ఉన్న వినియోగదారుడికి ఈ పరిష్కారాలు లభిస్తాయి ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): తుది ఉపశమనాలు – సెక్షన్ 39(1)(a) నుండి (n) కింద కమిషన్ ఉత్తర్వు: లోపం తొలగించడం, మార్చడం, వడ్డీతో డబ్బు తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం, నష్టపరిహారం (శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారంతో), ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత నష్టపరిహారం, అన్యాయ లేదా నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతులు ఆపడం, ప్రమాదకర వస్తువులను ఉపసంహరించడం లేదా తయారీ ఆపడం, గుర్తించలేని వినియోగదారుల కోసం విలువలో కనీసం 25% మొత్తం, సరిదిద్దే ప్రకటన, ఖర్చులు, తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటన ఆపడం. మధ్యంతర ఉత్తర్వు – కేసు పెండింగ్‌లో ఉండగా "such interim order as is just and proper" (అర్థం: న్యాయమైన, సరైన మధ్యంతర ఉత్తర్వు) (సెక్షన్ 38(8)). మధ్యవర్తిత్వం – వినియోగదారుల మధ్యవర్తిత్వ సెల్ ద్వారా రాజీ (సెక్షన్ 37; అధ్యాయం V). ఉత్తర్వును సవాలు చేయడం ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి) – అదే కమిషన్ ద్వారా పునఃసమీక్ష , "error apparent on the face of the record" (అర్థం: రికార్డులో స్పష్టంగా కనిపించే తప్పు) ఉంటే 30 రోజుల్లో (సెక్షన్లు 40, 50, 60); తదుపరి స్థాయికి అప్పీలు (సెక్షన్ 41: 45 రోజులు; సెక్షన్లు 51, 67: 30 రోజులు), ఆదేశించిన మొత్తంలో 50% ముందస్తు డిపాజిట్ చేసిన తర్వాత; రాష్ట్ర లేదా జాతీయ కమిషన్ ద్వారా రివిజన్ (సెక్షన్లు 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)); జాతీయ కమిషన్ ఏకపక్ష ఉత్తర్వును రద్దు చేయించుకోవడం (సెక్షన్ 61). అమలు – ఉత్తర్వు డిక్రీలాగా అమలవుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 71), పాటించకపోవడం శిక్షార్హం (సెక్షన్ 72). ఇతర పరిష్కారాలూ ఉంటాయి: టార్ట్‌లో సివిల్ దావా, లేదా నేర చట్టం; ఎందుకంటే ఈ చట్టం ఇతర చట్టాలకు "in addition to and not in derogation of" (అర్థం: అదనంగా, వాటిని తగ్గించకుండా) ఉంటుంది (సెక్షన్ 100). Nizam's Institute (2009) నష్టపరిహారం ఎలా లెక్కించాలో చూపుతుంది; Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy (2026) ఎదుటి పక్షం మరణిస్తే పరిష్కారానికి ఏమవుతుందో చూపుతుంది ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి).
te.meaning: పరిష్కారం (Remedy) – హక్కు ఉల్లంఘించబడిన వ్యక్తికి చట్టం ఇచ్చే ఉపశమనం. CPA 2019 కింద ఇది ప్రధానంగా వినియోగదారుల వివాద పరిష్కార కమిషన్ ఉత్తర్వు. మధ్యంతర ఉత్తర్వు – తుది నిర్ణయం వచ్చే వరకు ఫిర్యాదుదారుని రక్షించడానికి, కేసు పెండింగ్‌లో ఉండగా ఇచ్చే తాత్కాలిక ఉత్తర్వు (సెక్షన్ 38(8)). పునఃసమీక్ష – ఉత్తర్వు ఇచ్చిన అదే కమిషన్ దానిని మళ్ళీ పరిశీలించడం; "an error apparent on the face of the record" (అర్థం: రికార్డులో స్పష్టంగా కనిపించే తప్పు) ఉన్నప్పుడు మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్లు 40, 50, 60). అప్పీలు – ఉన్నత కమిషన్‌కు లేదా సుప్రీంకోర్టుకు, వాస్తవాలు, చట్టంపై సవాలు (సెక్షన్లు 41, 51, 67). రివిజన్ – రికార్డులు తెప్పించుకుని దిగువ కమిషన్ అధికార పరిధి తప్పు, చట్టవిరుద్ధత లేదా గణనీయమైన అక్రమతను సరిదిద్దే రాష్ట్ర లేదా జాతీయ కమిషన్ పర్యవేక్షణ అధికారం (సెక్షన్లు 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). ముందస్తు డిపాజిట్ – డబ్బు చెల్లించమని ఆదేశించబడిన వ్యక్తి అప్పీలు స్వీకరించబడే ముందు ఆ మొత్తంలో యాభై శాతం డిపాజిట్ చేయాలనే షరతు (సెక్షన్లు 41, 51(1), 67 నిబంధనలు).
keyPoints: సెక్షన్ 39(1): 14 ఉపశమనాలు; "one or more" (అర్థం: ఒకటి లేదా ఎక్కువ). శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారం: సెక్షన్ 39(1)(d) నిబంధన. గుర్తించలేని వినియోగదారులు: కనీసం 25% (1986: 5%). మధ్యంతర ఉత్తర్వు: సెక్షన్ 38(8). పునఃసమీక్ష: సెక్షన్లు 40, 50, 60; 30 రోజులు; స్పష్టమైన తప్పు. అప్పీళ్ళు: సెక్షన్ 41 (45 రోజులు), సెక్షన్ 51 (30 రోజులు), సెక్షన్ 67 (30 రోజులు); 50% ముందస్తు డిపాజిట్. జాతీయ కమిషన్‌కు రెండో అప్పీలు గణనీయమైన చట్ట ప్రశ్నపై మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 51(2)). రివిజన్: సెక్షన్లు 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b). మధ్యవర్తిత్వ రాజీ ఉత్తర్వుపై అప్పీలు లేదు. అంతిమత్వం సెక్షన్ 68; కాలపరిమితి సెక్షన్ 69 (రెండు సంవత్సరాలు). అమలు: సెక్షన్లు 71, 72. పక్షం మరణం: సెక్షన్ 38(12); Kumud Lall . ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)

selfTest.q: సెక్షన్ 39(1) కింద ఉపశమనాల నాలుగు వర్గాలు చెప్పండి. జిల్లా కమిషన్ ఉత్తర్వుపై ఎంత సమయంలో అప్పీలు చేయవచ్చు?
