law-of-torts-u5-t15.subtitle: Step by step: who may complain, where, within what time, how the Commission admits and decides the complaint

en.inOneMinute: A consumer dispute starts with a complaint – "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act" (s. 2(6), Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019)). The steps are (See Diagram 1 ): Who files – a complainant : the consumer, a recognised consumer association, one or more consumers for many with the same interest (with permission), the Central Government, the Central Authority or a State Government (s. 35(1)); also a legal heir on a consumer's death, and a parent or guardian of a minor (s. 2(5)). When – within two years from the date the cause of action arose; later only if the delay is condoned with reasons (s. 69). Where – the right Commission by value paid (2021 Rules: ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore) and place (s. 34(2)). (See Diagram 2 .) How – in writing, with the prescribed fee; it "may be filed electronically" (s. 35(1) proviso, s. 35(2)). Admission of complaint – decided ordinarily within twenty-one days; otherwise "deemed to have been admitted" (s. 36). Mediation if a settlement seems possible (s. 37). Notice to the opposite party – his version within thirty days (plus up to fifteen) (s. 38(2)–(3)). Hearing – on affidavits and documents; testing of goods if needed; ex parte if the opposite party does not appear (s. 38). Order – s. 39 reliefs; aim to decide within three months (five if testing is needed) (s. 38(7)). Fee (rule 7(2) of the Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2020, Table substituted by G.S.R. 606(E), 17 August 2023): nil up to ₹5 lakh , rising in slabs to ₹7,500 above ₹10 crore.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

s. 2(5): "complainant" means "(i) a consumer; or (ii) any voluntary consumer association registered under any law for the time being in force; or (iii) the Central Government or any State Government; or (iv) the Central Authority; or (v) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest; or (vi) in case of death of a consumer, his legal heir or legal representative; or (vii) in case of a consumer being a minor, his parent or legal guardian". s. 2(6): "complaint" means "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act, that—" (i) an unfair contract or unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice has been adopted; (ii) goods suffer from defects; (iii) services suffer from deficiency; (iv) a price in excess of the price fixed by law, displayed on the goods or package, displayed on the price list, or agreed between the parties has been charged; (v) hazardous goods are offered for sale in contravention of safety standards or with knowledge that they are unsafe; (vi) hazardous services are offered with knowledge; (vii) a claim for product liability action lies. s. 2(8): "consumer dispute" means "a dispute where the person against whom a complaint has been made, denies or disputes the allegations contained in the complaint". s. 34(2): place of filing – where the opposite party ordinarily resides, carries on business, has a branch office or personally works for gain; any one of several opposite parties (with permission); where "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises"; or where "the complainant resides or personally works for gain". s. 35(1): "A complaint, in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided, may be filed with a District Commission by— (a) the consumer,— (i) to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or such service is provided or agreed to be provided; or (ii) who alleges unfair trade practice in respect of such goods or service; (b) any recognised consumer association, whether the consumer … is a member of such association or not; (c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest, with the permission of the District Commission, on behalf of, or for the benefit of, all consumers so interested; or (d) the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government, as the case may be". Proviso: "the complaint under this sub-section may be filed electronically in such manner as may be prescribed." Explanation: "recognised consumer association" means "any voluntary consumer association registered under any law for the time being in force". s. 35(2): "Every complaint filed under sub-section (1) shall be accompanied with such fee and payable in such manner, including electronic form, as may be prescribed." s. 36(2)–(3): the District Commission "may, by order, admit the complaint for being proceeded with or reject the same"; no rejection "unless an opportunity of being heard has been given to the complainant"; "the admissibility of the complaint shall ordinarily be decided within twenty-one days from the date on which the complaint was filed"; if not decided within that period, the complaint "shall be deemed to have been admitted". s. 37: at the first hearing after admission or later, if "there exists elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties", the Commission may direct them to give written consent to mediation "within five days"; on consent, it refers the matter to mediation within five days. s. 38(1): the Commission proceeds with the complaint on admission, or when mediation fails. s. 38(2): goods – a copy of the admitted complaint goes to the opposite party "within twenty-one days from the date of its admission", directing him to give his version "within a period of thirty days or such extended period not exceeding fifteen days"; where a defect cannot be found without test, a sealed sample goes to the appropriate laboratory, which reports within forty-five days; the complainant deposits the laboratory fee; objections and hearing on the report. s. 38(3): services (or goods that cannot be tested) – version within thirty days plus up to fifteen; decision on both sides' evidence, or "ex parte" on the complainant's evidence if the opposite party fails to act; decision "on merits if the complainant fails to appear on the date of hearing". s. 38(6): hearing "on the basis of affidavit and documentary evidence placed on record"; in person or by video conferencing on sufficient cause, with reasons. s. 38(7): endeavour to decide within three months from the opposite party's receipt of notice (five months if testing is needed); adjournments only for sufficient cause with reasons; costs; reasons for delay to be recorded. s. 38(8): interim orders; s. 38(9): civil court powers; s. 38(11): Order I Rule 8 CPC for complaints by numerous consumers; s. 38(12): Order XXII CPC on death of a party. s. 39: findings and reliefs; split opinion referred to another member (s. 39(3)); order signed (s. 39(4)). s. 49(1), s. 59(1): ss. 35 to 39 apply to complaints before the State and National Commissions, with necessary modifications. s. 69: "(1) The District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), a complaint may be entertained after the period specified in sub-section (1), if the complainant satisfies the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, that he had sufficient cause for not filing the complaint within such period: Provided that no such complaint shall be entertained unless the District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, records its reasons for condoning such delay."

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021): District – value paid "does not exceed fifty lakh rupees" (r. 3); State – "exceeds fifty lakh but does not exceed two crore rupees" (r. 4); National – "exceeds two crore rupees" (r. 5).

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986) – s. 2(1)(b) (complainant); s. 12(1) (complaint by the consumer, a recognised consumer association, one or more consumers with the same interest with permission, or "the Central Government or the State Government"); s. 12(2) (fee as prescribed); s. 12(3) (admissibility "ordinarily … decided within twenty-one days from the date on which the complaint was received"); s. 13 (procedure); s. 24A (limitation: two years, delay condonable with reasons).
en.meaning: Procedure for filing means the steps a person must follow to bring a consumer dispute before a Consumer Commission and get it decided. Complainant – the person entitled to file (s. 2(5)). A trader or service provider is not a complainant. Opposite party – the person against whom the complaint is made (the trader, manufacturer, seller or service provider). The Act uses the term (for example, ss. 34(2), 38(2)) but does not define it. Complaint – a written allegation on one of the seven grounds in s. 2(6), made to obtain relief under the Act. Admission of complaint – the Commission's decision to proceed with the complaint (s. 36(2)); if not decided within twenty-one days, it is deemed admitted (s. 36(3)). Cause of action – the facts that give the right to complain (for example, the date the defect appeared or service was refused). Limitation runs from this date (s. 69).
keyPoints: Complaint = written allegation on s. 2(6) grounds. Complainants: s. 2(5)(i)–(vii); s. 35(1)(a)–(d). Limitation period: two years from cause of action; condonation with reasons (s. 69). Commission: ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore by value paid. Place: includes complainant's residence or work (s. 34(2)(d)). Fee: nil up to ₹5 lakh; ₹200 up to ₹10 lakh; … ₹7,500 above ₹10 crore. E-filing allowed (s. 35(1) proviso). Admission: 21 days; deemed admission (s. 36). Mediation: consent in 5 days; referral in 5 days (s. 37). Version: 30 + 15 days; lab report 45 days (s. 38). Decide in 3 / 5 months (s. 38(7)). (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors argued that consumer bodies under the 1986 Act, which decide on affidavits by a summary procedure, could not try medical negligence complaints. A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) examined who may complain and how complaints are tried. Principle: "The expression "complainant", as defined in Section 2(1)(b), is comprehensive" – it covers the consumer, a registered voluntary consumer association, the Central or State Government, or one or more consumers with the same interest. The summary procedure suits simple cases such as "leaving inside the patient swabs", which "can be speedily disposed of"; in complicated cases "the complainant can be asked to approach the civil court". Why it matters: It shows the breadth of persons who may file and the nature of the procedure – quick and mainly on affidavits – that a complainant must prepare for. 2. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: A husband filed a complaint on 13 August 1997 that an eye operation had cost his wife the sight of one eye. The District Forum awarded ₹2,60,000; the State Commission set it aside on 2 December 2005; during the revision the doctor died on 4 August 2009. The Supreme Court (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.) decided whether the complaint could go on. Principle: Under the "statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act", "upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive" (para 64(vi)). Why it matters: It shows what happens to a filed complaint when a party dies (s. 38(12), Order XXII CPC) and why a complainant should claim reliefs that can survive against the estate.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల వివాదం ఫిర్యాదు తో మొదలవుతుంది – "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act" (అర్థం: ఈ చట్టం ద్వారా లేదా దాని కింద అందించే ఉపశమనం పొందడానికి ఫిర్యాదుదారు లిఖితంగా చేసే ఏ ఆరోపణ అయినా) (సెక్షన్ 2(6), వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019)). దశలు ఇవి ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): ఎవరు దాఖలు చేస్తారు – ఫిర్యాదుదారు : వినియోగదారుడు, గుర్తింపు పొందిన వినియోగదారుల సంఘం, ఒకే ప్రయోజనం ఉన్న అనేకమంది కోసం ఒకరు లేదా ఎక్కువ వినియోగదారులు (అనుమతితో), కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం, కేంద్ర అథారిటీ లేదా రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం (సెక్షన్ 35(1)); వినియోగదారుడు మరణిస్తే చట్టపరమైన వారసుడు, మైనర్ అయితే తల్లిదండ్రి లేదా సంరక్షకుడు కూడా (సెక్షన్ 2(5)). ఎప్పుడు – దావా కారణం ఏర్పడిన తేదీ నుండి రెండు సంవత్సరాల్లో ; తర్వాత అయితే కారణాలతో ఆలస్యం మన్నిస్తేనే (సెక్షన్ 69). ఎక్కడ – చెల్లించిన విలువ (2021 నియమాలు: ₹50 లక్షలు / ₹2 కోట్లు), స్థలం (సెక్షన్ 34(2)) ఆధారంగా సరైన కమిషన్. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) ఎలా – లిఖితంగా, నిర్దేశించిన రుసుముతో; "may be filed electronically" (అర్థం: ఎలక్ట్రానిక్‌గా దాఖలు చేయవచ్చు) (సెక్షన్ 35(1) నిబంధన, సెక్షన్ 35(2)). ఫిర్యాదు స్వీకరణ – సాధారణంగా ఇరవై ఒక్క రోజుల్లో నిర్ణయం; లేకపోతే "deemed to have been admitted" (అర్థం: స్వీకరించినట్లుగా భావించబడుతుంది) (సెక్షన్ 36). రాజీ సాధ్యమనిపిస్తే మధ్యవర్తిత్వం (సెక్షన్ 37). ప్రతిపక్షి కి నోటీసు – ముప్పై రోజుల్లో (అదనంగా పదిహేను వరకు) అతని వివరణ (సెక్షన్ 38(2)–(3)). విచారణ – అఫిడవిట్లు, పత్రాలపై; అవసరమైతే వస్తువుల పరీక్ష; ప్రతిపక్షి హాజరు కాకపోతే ఏకపక్షం (సెక్షన్ 38). ఉత్తర్వు – సెక్షన్ 39 ఉపశమనాలు; మూడు నెలల్లో (పరీక్ష అవసరమైతే ఐదు) నిర్ణయించే లక్ష్యం (సెక్షన్ 38(7)). రుసుము (Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2020 నియమం 7(2), G.S.R. 606(E), 17 ఆగస్టు 2023 ద్వారా మార్చిన పట్టిక): ₹5 లక్షల వరకు రుసుము లేదు , శ్లాబులుగా పెరిగి ₹10 కోట్లు దాటితే ₹7,500.
te.meaning: దాఖలు ప్రక్రియ అంటే వినియోగదారుల కమిషన్ ముందు వివాదాన్ని తెచ్చి నిర్ణయం పొందడానికి వ్యక్తి పాటించాల్సిన దశలు. ఫిర్యాదుదారు – దాఖలు చేయడానికి అర్హత ఉన్న వ్యక్తి (సెక్షన్ 2(5)). వ్యాపారి లేదా సేవా ప్రదాత ఫిర్యాదుదారు కాదు. ప్రతిపక్షి – ఎవరిపై ఫిర్యాదు చేయబడిందో ఆ వ్యక్తి (వ్యాపారి, తయారీదారు, అమ్మకందారు లేదా సేవా ప్రదాత). చట్టం ఈ పదాన్ని వాడుతుంది (ఉదాహరణకు సెక్షన్లు 34(2), 38(2)) కానీ నిర్వచించదు. ఫిర్యాదు – చట్టం కింద ఉపశమనం పొందడానికి, సెక్షన్ 2(6)లోని ఏడు కారణాలలో ఒకదానిపై చేసే లిఖిత ఆరోపణ. ఫిర్యాదు స్వీకరణ – ఫిర్యాదుతో ముందుకు సాగాలనే కమిషన్ నిర్ణయం (సెక్షన్ 36(2)); ఇరవై ఒక్క రోజుల్లో నిర్ణయించకపోతే స్వీకరించినట్లు భావన (సెక్షన్ 36(3)). దావా కారణం – ఫిర్యాదు చేసే హక్కు ఇచ్చే వాస్తవాలు (ఉదాహరణకు లోపం కనిపించిన లేదా సేవ నిరాకరించిన తేదీ). కాల పరిమితి ఈ తేదీ నుండి మొదలవుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 69).
keyPoints: ఫిర్యాదు = సెక్షన్ 2(6) కారణాలపై లిఖిత ఆరోపణ. ఫిర్యాదుదారులు: సెక్షన్ 2(5)(i)–(vii); సెక్షన్ 35(1)(a)–(d). కాల పరిమితి: దావా కారణం నుండి రెండు సంవత్సరాలు; కారణాలతో మన్నింపు (సెక్షన్ 69). కమిషన్: చెల్లించిన విలువ ఆధారంగా ₹50 లక్షలు / ₹2 కోట్లు. స్థలం: ఫిర్యాదుదారు నివాసం లేదా పని కూడా (సెక్షన్ 34(2)(d)). రుసుము: ₹5 లక్షల వరకు లేదు; ₹10 లక్షల వరకు ₹200; … ₹10 కోట్లు దాటితే ₹7,500. ఇ-ఫైలింగ్ అనుమతి (సెక్షన్ 35(1) నిబంధన). స్వీకరణ: 21 రోజులు; స్వీకరించినట్లు భావన (సెక్షన్ 36). మధ్యవర్తిత్వం: 5 రోజుల్లో సమ్మతి; 5 రోజుల్లో పంపడం (సెక్షన్ 37). వివరణ: 30 + 15 రోజులు; ప్రయోగశాల నివేదిక 45 రోజులు (సెక్షన్ 38). 3 / 5 నెలల్లో నిర్ణయం (సెక్షన్ 38(7)). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)

selfTest.q: సెక్షన్ 2(5) కింద నాలుగు రకాల ఫిర్యాదుదారులను చెప్పండి. ఫిర్యాదును ఎంత సమయంలో, ఎప్పటి నుండి దాఖలు చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: చెల్లించిన విలువ ₹7 లక్షలు ఉన్న ఫిర్యాదుకు రుసుము ఎంత? ఇరవై ఒక్క రోజుల్లో స్వీకార యోగ్యత నిర్ణయించకపోతే ఏమవుతుంది? ప్రతిపక్షికి వివరణ ఇవ్వడానికి ఎంత సమయం ఉంటుంది? వస్తువుల పరీక్ష అవసరమైన ఫిర్యాదును కమిషన్ ఎంత సమయంలో నిర్ణయించడానికి ప్రయత్నించాలి? హైదరాబాద్‌లోని వినియోగదారుడు ఢిల్లీ అమ్మకందారుపై హైదరాబాద్‌లో దావా వేయగలడా?

hi.inOneMinute: A consumer dispute starts with a complaint – "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act" (s. 2(6), Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019)). The steps are (See Diagram 1 ): Who files – a complainant : the consumer, a recognised consumer association, one or more consumers for many with the same interest (with permission), the Central Government, the Central Authority or a State Government (s. 35(1)); also a legal heir on a consumer's death, and a parent or guardian of a minor (s. 2(5)). When – within two years from the date the cause of action arose; later only if the delay is condoned with reasons (s. 69). Where – the right Commission by value paid (2021 Rules: ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore) and place (s. 34(2)). (See Diagram 2 .) How – in writing, with the prescribed fee; it "may be filed electronically" (s. 35(1) proviso, s. 35(2)). Admission of complaint – decided ordinarily within twenty-one days; otherwise "deemed to have been admitted" (s. 36). Mediation if a settlement seems possible (s. 37). Notice to the opposite party – his version within thirty days (plus up to fifteen) (s. 38(2)–(3)). Hearing – on affidavits and documents; testing of goods if needed; ex parte if the opposite party does not appear (s. 38). Order – s. 39 reliefs; aim to decide within three months (five if testing is needed) (s. 38(7)). Fee (rule 7(2) of the Consumer Protection (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions) Rules, 2020, Table substituted by G.S.R. 606(E), 17 August 2023): nil up to ₹5 lakh , rising in slabs to ₹7,500 above ₹10 crore.
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

s. 2(5): "complainant" means "(i) a consumer; or (ii) any voluntary consumer association registered under any law for the time being in force; or (iii) the Central Government or any State Government; or (iv) the Central Authority; or (v) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest; or (vi) in case of death of a consumer, his legal heir or legal representative; or (vii) in case of a consumer being a minor, his parent or legal guardian". s. 2(6): "complaint" means "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act, that—" (i) an unfair contract or unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice has been adopted; (ii) goods suffer from defects; (iii) services suffer from deficiency; (iv) a price in excess of the price fixed by law, displayed on the goods or package, displayed on the price list, or agreed between the parties has been charged; (v) hazardous goods are offered for sale in contravention of safety standards or with knowledge that they are unsafe; (vi) hazardous services are offered with knowledge; (vii) a claim for product liability action lies. s. 2(8): "consumer dispute" means "a dispute where the person against whom a complaint has been made, denies or disputes the allegations contained in the complaint". s. 34(2): place of filing – where the opposite party ordinarily resides, carries on business, has a branch office or personally works for gain; any one of several opposite parties (with permission); where "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises"; or where "the complainant resides or personally works for gain". s. 35(1): "A complaint, in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided, may be filed with a District Commission by— (a) the consumer,— (i) to whom such goods are sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or such service is provided or agreed to be provided; or (ii) who alleges unfair trade practice in respect of such goods or service; (b) any recognised consumer association, whether the consumer … is a member of such association or not; (c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest, with the permission of the District Commission, on behalf of, or for the benefit of, all consumers so interested; or (d) the Central Government, the Central Authority or the State Government, as the case may be". Proviso: "the complaint under this sub-section may be filed electronically in such manner as may be prescribed." Explanation: "recognised consumer association" means "any voluntary consumer association registered under any law for the time being in force". s. 35(2): "Every complaint filed under sub-section (1) shall be accompanied with such fee and payable in such manner, including electronic form, as may be prescribed." s. 36(2)–(3): the District Commission "may, by order, admit the complaint for being proceeded with or reject the same"; no rejection "unless an opportunity of being heard has been given to the complainant"; "the admissibility of the complaint shall ordinarily be decided within twenty-one days from the date on which the complaint was filed"; if not decided within that period, the complaint "shall be deemed to have been admitted". s. 37: at the first hearing after admission or later, if "there exists elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties", the Commission may direct them to give written consent to mediation "within five days"; on consent, it refers the matter to mediation within five days. s. 38(1): the Commission proceeds with the complaint on admission, or when mediation fails. s. 38(2): goods – a copy of the admitted complaint goes to the opposite party "within twenty-one days from the date of its admission", directing him to give his version "within a period of thirty days or such extended period not exceeding fifteen days"; where a defect cannot be found without test, a sealed sample goes to the appropriate laboratory, which reports within forty-five days; the complainant deposits the laboratory fee; objections and hearing on the report. s. 38(3): services (or goods that cannot be tested) – version within thirty days plus up to fifteen; decision on both sides' evidence, or "ex parte" on the complainant's evidence if the opposite party fails to act; decision "on merits if the complainant fails to appear on the date of hearing". s. 38(6): hearing "on the basis of affidavit and documentary evidence placed on record"; in person or by video conferencing on sufficient cause, with reasons. s. 38(7): endeavour to decide within three months from the opposite party's receipt of notice (five months if testing is needed); adjournments only for sufficient cause with reasons; costs; reasons for delay to be recorded. s. 38(8): interim orders; s. 38(9): civil court powers; s. 38(11): Order I Rule 8 CPC for complaints by numerous consumers; s. 38(12): Order XXII CPC on death of a party. s. 39: findings and reliefs; split opinion referred to another member (s. 39(3)); order signed (s. 39(4)). s. 49(1), s. 59(1): ss. 35 to 39 apply to complaints before the State and National Commissions, with necessary modifications. s. 69: "(1) The District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), a complaint may be entertained after the period specified in sub-section (1), if the complainant satisfies the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, that he had sufficient cause for not filing the complaint within such period: Provided that no such complaint shall be entertained unless the District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, records its reasons for condoning such delay."

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021): District – value paid "does not exceed fifty lakh rupees" (r. 3); State – "exceeds fifty lakh but does not exceed two crore rupees" (r. 4); National – "exceeds two crore rupees" (r. 5).

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986) – s. 2(1)(b) (complainant); s. 12(1) (complaint by the consumer, a recognised consumer association, one or more consumers with the same interest with permission, or "the Central Government or the State Government"); s. 12(2) (fee as prescribed); s. 12(3) (admissibility "ordinarily … decided within twenty-one days from the date on which the complaint was received"); s. 13 (procedure); s. 24A (limitation: two years, delay condonable with reasons).
hi.meaning: Procedure for filing means the steps a person must follow to bring a consumer dispute before a Consumer Commission and get it decided. Complainant – the person entitled to file (s. 2(5)). A trader or service provider is not a complainant. Opposite party – the person against whom the complaint is made (the trader, manufacturer, seller or service provider). The Act uses the term (for example, ss. 34(2), 38(2)) but does not define it. Complaint – a written allegation on one of the seven grounds in s. 2(6), made to obtain relief under the Act. Admission of complaint – the Commission's decision to proceed with the complaint (s. 36(2)); if not decided within twenty-one days, it is deemed admitted (s. 36(3)). Cause of action – the facts that give the right to complain (for example, the date the defect appeared or service was refused). Limitation runs from this date (s. 69).
keyPoints: Complaint = written allegation on s. 2(6) grounds. Complainants: s. 2(5)(i)–(vii); s. 35(1)(a)–(d). Limitation period: two years from cause of action; condonation with reasons (s. 69). Commission: ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore by value paid. Place: includes complainant's residence or work (s. 34(2)(d)). Fee: nil up to ₹5 lakh; ₹200 up to ₹10 lakh; … ₹7,500 above ₹10 crore. E-filing allowed (s. 35(1) proviso). Admission: 21 days; deemed admission (s. 36). Mediation: consent in 5 days; referral in 5 days (s. 37). Version: 30 + 15 days; lab report 45 days (s. 38). Decide in 3 / 5 months (s. 38(7)). (See Diagram 3 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors argued that consumer bodies under the 1986 Act, which decide on affidavits by a summary procedure, could not try medical negligence complaints. A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) examined who may complain and how complaints are tried. Principle: "The expression "complainant", as defined in Section 2(1)(b), is comprehensive" – it covers the consumer, a registered voluntary consumer association, the Central or State Government, or one or more consumers with the same interest. The summary procedure suits simple cases such as "leaving inside the patient swabs", which "can be speedily disposed of"; in complicated cases "the complainant can be asked to approach the civil court". Why it matters: It shows the breadth of persons who may file and the nature of the procedure – quick and mainly on affidavits – that a complainant must prepare for. 2. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: A husband filed a complaint on 13 August 1997 that an eye operation had cost his wife the sight of one eye. The District Forum awarded ₹2,60,000; the State Commission set it aside on 2 December 2005; during the revision the doctor died on 4 August 2009. The Supreme Court (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.) decided whether the complaint could go on. Principle: Under the "statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act", "upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive" (para 64(vi)). Why it matters: It shows what happens to a filed complaint when a party dies (s. 38(12), Order XXII CPC) and why a complainant should claim reliefs that can survive against the estate.

law-of-torts-u5-t14.subtitle: Pecuniary, territorial, appellate and revisional jurisdiction of the three Commissions, and the powers they exercise

en.inOneMinute: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) there are three Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: the District Commission (s. 28), the State Commission (s. 42) and the National Commission (s. 53). Jurisdiction means which Commission can hear which matter. It has these kinds (See Diagram 1 ): Original jurisdiction over complaints, fixed by pecuniary jurisdiction (value of goods or services paid as consideration) and territorial jurisdiction (place of filing) (ss. 34, 47, 58). Original jurisdiction over unfair contract complaints – only the State Commission (up to ₹10 crore) and the National Commission (above ₹10 crore). Appellate jurisdiction – State over District (s. 47(1)(a)(iii)); National over State (s. 58(1)(a)(iii)) and over the Central Authority (s. 58(1)(a)(iv)); Supreme Court over National (s. 67). Revisional jurisdiction – State over District (s. 47(1)(b)); National over State (s. 58(1)(b)). Present pecuniary limits (Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021): District – up to ₹50 lakh; State – above ₹50 lakh up to ₹2 crore; National – above ₹2 crore. Powers (See Diagram 2 ): admit or reject a complaint (s. 36); refer to mediation (s. 37); call for the opposite party's version, send goods to a laboratory, decide ex parte (s. 38(2)–(3)); civil court powers (s. 38(9)); interim orders (s. 38(8)); final orders under s. 39(1)(a)–(n), including punitive damages; declare unfair contract terms "null and void" (ss. 49(2), 59(2)); review (ss. 40, 50, 60); transfer (ss. 48, 62); enforce orders as decrees (s. 71); punish non-compliance with powers of a Judicial Magistrate of the first class (s. 72).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)
Jurisdiction

s. 34(1): the District Commission has "jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees"; proviso: the Central Government may prescribe another value. s. 34(2): "A complaint shall be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction,— (a) the opposite party or each of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, at the time of the institution of the complaint, ordinarily resides or carries on business or has a branch office or personally works for gain; or (b) any of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, … provided that in such case the permission of the District Commission is given; or (c) the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises; or (d) the complainant resides or personally works for gain." s. 47(1): the State Commission has jurisdiction "(a) to entertain— (i) complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration, exceeds rupees one crore, but does not exceed rupees ten crore … (ii) complaints against unfair contracts, where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed ten crore rupees; (iii) appeals against the orders of any District Commission within the State; and (b) to call for the records and pass appropriate orders in any consumer dispute which is pending before or has been decided by any District Commission within the State, where it appears to the State Commission that such District Commission has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or has failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested or has acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity." s. 47(4): the same four territorial grounds as s. 34(2) apply to complaints in the State Commission. s. 58(1): the National Commission has jurisdiction "(a) to entertain— (i) complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration exceeds rupees ten crore … (ii) complaints against unfair contracts, where the value of goods or services paid as consideration exceeds ten crore rupees; (iii) appeals against the orders of any State Commission; (iv) appeals against the orders of the Central Authority; and (b)" revision over any State Commission on the same grounds as s. 47(1)(b). s. 69(1): a Commission "shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen"; s. 69(2): delay may be condoned for sufficient cause, with reasons recorded.

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021), made under the provisos to ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i) and 58(1)(a)(i):

r. 3: the District Commission entertains complaints "where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees". r. 4: the State Commission – value "exceeds fifty lakh but does not exceed two crore rupees". r. 5: the National Commission – value "exceeds two crore rupees".
Powers

s. 36(2)–(3): the District Commission may admit or reject a complaint; it shall not reject without hearing the complainant; admissibility "shall ordinarily be decided within twenty-one days"; if not decided in that time, the complaint "shall be deemed to have been admitted". s. 37(1): at the first hearing after admission or at any later stage, if there is scope for settlement acceptable to the parties, the Commission may, with their written consent, refer the dispute to mediation. s. 38(2): for goods – send the complaint to the opposite party within twenty-one days for his version within thirty days (extendable by not more than fifteen days); where a defect cannot be found without testing, send a sealed sample to the appropriate laboratory, which reports within forty-five days; the complainant deposits the laboratory fee; parties may object to the report and are heard. s. 38(3): for services, or goods that cannot be tested – call for the opposite party's version; decide on the evidence of both sides, or "ex parte on the basis of evidence brought to its notice by the complainant" if the opposite party does not act; and "decide the complaint on merits if the complainant fails to appear on the date of hearing". s. 38(4): may require an electronic service provider to give information, documents or records. s. 38(5): proceedings that follow sub-sections (2) and (3) cannot be challenged on the ground that natural justice was not followed. s. 38(6): "Every complaint shall be heard by the District Commission on the basis of affidavit and documentary evidence placed on record"; hearing or examination in person or by video conferencing may be allowed for sufficient cause, with reasons. s. 38(7): endeavour to decide "within a period of three months from the date of receipt of notice by opposite party where the complaint does not require analysis or testing of commodities and within five months if it requires analysis or testing"; no adjournment ordinarily unless sufficient cause is shown and reasons recorded; costs of adjournment; reasons to be recorded for delay. s. 38(8): "such interim order as is just and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case". s. 38(9): "the same powers as are vested in a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 … while trying a suit in respect of the following matters, namely:— (a) the summoning and enforcing the attendance of any defendant or witness and examining the witness on oath; (b) requiring the discovery and production of any document or other material object as evidence; (c) receiving of evidence on affidavits; (d) the requisitioning of the report of the concerned analysis or test from the appropriate laboratory or from any other relevant source; (e) issuing of commissions for the examination of any witness, or document; and (f) any other matter which may be prescribed by the Central Government." s. 38(10): every proceeding "shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code", and the Commission is deemed a criminal court for s. 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. s. 38(11): for a complaint by one or more consumers having the same interest, Order I Rule 8 CPC (representative suit) applies. s. 38(12): on the death of the complainant or the opposite party, Order XXII CPC applies. s. 39(1): where the allegations are proved, an order directing "one or more" of reliefs (a) to (n) – remove defect, replace, refund with interest, compensation for negligence (with power "to grant punitive damages"), product liability compensation, remove defects or deficiencies, discontinue unfair or restrictive trade practices, stop or withdraw hazardous goods, a sum not less than 25% of value for unidentifiable consumers, corrective advertisement, costs, and cease misleading advertisement. s. 39(3)–(4): if the President and member differ, the point goes to another member, who gives an opinion within one month; the majority opinion is the order; every order is signed. ss. 49, 59: ss. 35 to 39 apply to the State and National Commissions with necessary changes; and each "may also declare any terms of contract, which is unfair to any consumer, to be null and void" (ss. 49(2), 59(2)). ss. 40, 50, 60: review for "an error apparent on the face of the record", of its own motion or on an application within thirty days. s. 52: appeals to be heard expeditiously, with an endeavour to dispose of them within ninety days of admission. s. 61: a party may apply to the National Commission to set aside its ex parte order. ss. 48, 62: transfer of complaints – within a State (State Commission) and across States (National Commission). s. 66: in matters of "the larger interest of consumers", the State or National Commission may direct an individual, organisation or expert to assist it. s. 70: administrative control of the National Commission over State Commissions, and of each State Commission over District Commissions. s. 71: every order "shall be enforced by it in the same manner as if it were a decree made by a Court in a suit before it", under Order XXI CPC. s. 72(1): non-compliance is punishable with imprisonment "not … less than one month, but which may extend to three years", or fine "not … less than twenty-five thousand rupees, but which may extend to one lakh rupees", or both. s. 72(2)–(3): the Commissions have "the power of a Judicial Magistrate of first class" and try these offences summarily. s. 73: appeals against an order under s. 72(1) lie on facts and law – District to State, State to National, National to Supreme Court – within thirty days.

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986) – ss. 11, 17, 21 (jurisdiction, finally ₹20 lakh / ₹1 crore, on "the value of the goods or services and compensation, if any, claimed"); s. 13 (procedure; s. 13(3A) three / five months; s. 13(3B) interim orders; s. 13(4) civil court powers; s. 13(7) death of a party); s. 14 (reliefs); s. 22A (setting aside ex parte orders, National Commission); s. 25 (enforcement); s. 26 (frivolous or vexatious complaint dismissed with costs "not exceeding ten thousand rupees"); s. 27 (penalty: one month to three years, or fine "not be less than two thousand rupees but which may extend to ten thousand rupees", or both).
en.meaning: Jurisdiction is the authority of a Commission to hear and decide a matter. If a Commission acts without jurisdiction, its order can be corrected in revision (ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). Pecuniary jurisdiction – the limit by money value. Under CPA 2019 the test is "the value of the goods or services paid as consideration" (ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i), 58(1)(a)(i)). Territorial jurisdiction – the limit by place: where the opposite party is, where the cause of action arose, or where the complainant resides or personally works for gain (ss. 34(2), 47(4)). Complaint – "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act" about an unfair contract , unfair or restrictive trade practice , defect in goods , deficiency in services , excess price, hazardous goods or services, or a product liability claim (s. 2(6)). Unfair contract – "a contract between a manufacturer or trader or service provider on one hand, and a consumer on the other, having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer", including the terms listed in s. 2(46)(i)–(vi) (for example, "manifestly excessive security deposits"). Powers – what a Commission can do while hearing and after deciding: procedural powers (ss. 36–38), relief-granting powers (s. 39), corrective powers (review, set-aside, revision), and enforcement powers (ss. 71–72).
keyPoints: Test: value of goods or services paid as consideration – not compensation. 2021 Rules: ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore (rr. 3–5). Unfair contracts: State ≤ ₹10 crore; National > ₹10 crore; void declaration ss. 49(2), 59(2). Territorial: four grounds; complainant's residence or work (s. 34(2)(d)). Limitation: two years (s. 69). Appeal 45 / 30 / 30 days; 50% deposit; revision three grounds. Admission in twenty-one days, else deemed admitted (s. 36). Civil court powers s. 38(9); interim s. 38(8); death of party s. 38(12). Decide in three / five months (s. 38(7)). Enforcement s. 71; punishment s. 72 (₹25,000–₹1 lakh; one month–three years); appeal s. 73. (See Diagram 2 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors argued that medical negligence cases were too complicated for the summary procedure of the consumer bodies under the 1986 Act. A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) examined their jurisdiction and powers. Principle: The bodies have "the same power as are vested in a civil court" for summons, discovery, affidavits, laboratory reports and commissions (s. 13 of the 1986 Act), and the jurisdiction "is based on the pecuniary limit of the claim made by the complainant" under that Act. Simple cases such as "leaving inside the patient swabs" can be "speedily disposed of"; in complicated cases "the complainant can be asked to approach the civil court", since the Act "preserves the right of the consumer to approach the civil court". Why it matters: It explains how the Commissions' powers and summary procedure fit complicated disputes, and it confirms that the consumer forum is an additional, not exclusive, remedy. 2. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: In a medical negligence revision pending before the National Commission, the doctor (opposite party) died in 2009 and his widow and son were brought on record. The Supreme Court (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.) considered whether the case could continue, looking at s. 13(7) of the 1986 Act and s. 38(12) of the 2019 Act, both of which apply Order XXII CPC. Principle: "in view of the preceding discussion and the statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act, we conclude that upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive" (para 64(vi)). The case was remitted to the National Commission to decide within six months. Why it matters: It shows the Commission's power under s. 38(12) to bring legal heirs on record and continue a case, and the limit of that power: only claims against the estate survive.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 (CPA 2019) కింద మూడు వినియోగదారుల వివాదాల పరిష్కార కమిషన్లు ఉన్నాయి: జిల్లా కమిషన్ (సెక్షన్ 28), రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్ (సెక్షన్ 42), జాతీయ కమిషన్ (సెక్షన్ 53). అధికార పరిధి అంటే ఏ కమిషన్ ఏ విషయాన్ని విచారించగలదు అనేది. దీనిలో ఈ రకాలు ఉన్నాయి ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): ఫిర్యాదులపై అసలు అధికార పరిధి – దీనిని ఆర్థిక అధికార పరిధి (ప్రతిఫలంగా చెల్లించిన వస్తువులు లేదా సేవల విలువ), ప్రాదేశిక అధికార పరిధి (దాఖలు చేసే స్థలం) నిర్ణయిస్తాయి (సెక్షన్లు 34, 47, 58). అన్యాయ ఒప్పందం ఫిర్యాదులపై అసలు అధికార పరిధి – రాష్ట్ర కమిషన్ (₹10 కోట్ల వరకు), జాతీయ కమిషన్ (₹10 కోట్లు దాటితే) మాత్రమే. అప్పీలు అధికార పరిధి – జిల్లాపై రాష్ట్రం (సెక్షన్ 47(1)(a)(iii)); రాష్ట్రంపై (సెక్షన్ 58(1)(a)(iii)), కేంద్ర అథారిటీపై (సెక్షన్ 58(1)(a)(iv)) జాతీయం; జాతీయంపై సుప్రీంకోర్టు (సెక్షన్ 67). రివిజన్ అధికార పరిధి – జిల్లాపై రాష్ట్రం (సెక్షన్ 47(1)(b)); రాష్ట్రంపై జాతీయం (సెక్షన్ 58(1)(b)). ప్రస్తుత ఆర్థిక పరిమితులు (Consumer Protection ( Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021): జిల్లా – ₹50 లక్షల వరకు; రాష్ట్రం – ₹50 లక్షలు దాటి ₹2 కోట్ల వరకు; జాతీయం – ₹2 కోట్లు దాటితే. అధికారాలు ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి): ఫిర్యాదును స్వీకరించడం లేదా తిరస్కరించడం (సెక్షన్ 36); మధ్యవర్తిత్వానికి పంపడం (సెక్షన్ 37); ప్రతిపక్షి వివరణ కోరడం, వస్తువులను ప్రయోగశాలకు పంపడం, ఏకపక్షంగా నిర్ణయించడం (సెక్షన్ 38(2)–(3)); సివిల్ కోర్టు అధికారాలు (సెక్షన్ 38(9)); మధ్యంతర ఉత్తర్వులు (సెక్షన్ 38(8)); శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారం సహా సెక్షన్ 39(1)(a)–(n) కింద తుది ఉత్తర్వులు; అన్యాయ ఒప్పంద షరతులను "null and void" (అర్థం: శూన్యమైనవి, చెల్లనివి) అని ప్రకటించడం (సెక్షన్లు 49(2), 59(2)); పునఃసమీక్ష (సెక్షన్లు 40, 50, 60); బదిలీ (సెక్షన్లు 48, 62); ఉత్తర్వులను డిక్రీలుగా అమలు చేయడం (సెక్షన్ 71); ప్రథమ శ్రేణి జ్యుడీషియల్ మేజిస్ట్రేట్ అధికారాలతో పాటించకపోవడాన్ని శిక్షించడం (సెక్షన్ 72).
te.meaning: అధికార పరిధి అంటే ఒక విషయాన్ని విని నిర్ణయించే కమిషన్ అధికారం. అధికార పరిధి లేకుండా కమిషన్ వ్యవహరిస్తే, దాని ఉత్తర్వును రివిజన్‌లో సరిచేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్లు 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). ఆర్థిక అధికార పరిధి – డబ్బు విలువ ఆధారిత పరిమితి. CPA 2019 కింద పరీక్ష "the value of the goods or services paid as consideration" (అర్థం: ప్రతిఫలంగా చెల్లించిన వస్తువులు లేదా సేవల విలువ) (సెక్షన్లు 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i), 58(1)(a)(i)). ప్రాదేశిక అధికార పరిధి – స్థల ఆధారిత పరిమితి: ప్రతిపక్షి ఉన్న చోట, దావా కారణం ఏర్పడిన చోట, లేదా ఫిర్యాదుదారు నివసించే లేదా స్వయంగా లాభం కోసం పని చేసే చోట (సెక్షన్లు 34(2), 47(4)). ఫిర్యాదు – "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act" (అర్థం: ఈ చట్టం ద్వారా లేదా దాని కింద అందించే ఉపశమనం పొందడానికి ఫిర్యాదుదారు లిఖితంగా చేసే ఏ ఆరోపణ అయినా) – అన్యాయ ఒప్పందం , అన్యాయ లేదా నిర్బంధ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి , వస్తువుల్లో లోపం , సేవల్లో లోపం , అధిక ధర, ప్రమాదకర వస్తువులు లేదా సేవలు, లేదా ఉత్పత్తి బాధ్యత క్లెయిమ్ గురించి (సెక్షన్ 2(6)). అన్యాయ ఒప్పందం – "a contract between a manufacturer or trader or service provider on one hand, and a consumer on the other, having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer" (అర్థం: ఒకవైపు తయారీదారు లేదా వ్యాపారి లేదా సేవా ప్రదాత, మరోవైపు వినియోగదారుడి మధ్య, ఆ వినియోగదారుడి హక్కుల్లో గణనీయమైన మార్పు కలిగించే షరతులు ఉన్న ఒప్పందం), సెక్షన్ 2(46)(i)–(vi)లో చెప్పిన షరతులతో సహా (ఉదాహరణకు "manifestly excessive security deposits" (అర్థం: స్పష్టంగా అధికమైన సెక్యూరిటీ డిపాజిట్లు)). అధికారాలు – విచారణ సమయంలో, నిర్ణయం తర్వాత కమిషన్ చేయగలిగేవి: ప్రక్రియా అధికారాలు (సెక్షన్లు 36–38), ఉపశమనం ఇచ్చే అధికారాలు (సెక్షన్ 39), సరిదిద్దే అధికారాలు (పునఃసమీక్ష, రద్దు, రివిజన్), అమలు అధికారాలు (సెక్షన్లు 71–72).
keyPoints: పరీక్ష: ప్రతిఫలంగా చెల్లించిన వస్తువులు లేదా సేవల విలువ – నష్టపరిహారం కాదు. 2021 నియమాలు: ₹50 లక్షలు / ₹2 కోట్లు (నియమాలు 3–5). అన్యాయ ఒప్పందాలు: రాష్ట్రం ≤ ₹10 కోట్లు; జాతీయం > ₹10 కోట్లు; శూన్య ప్రకటన సెక్షన్లు 49(2), 59(2). ప్రాదేశిక: నాలుగు కారణాలు; ఫిర్యాదుదారుని నివాసం లేదా పని (సెక్షన్ 34(2)(d)). కాల పరిమితి: రెండు సంవత్సరాలు (సెక్షన్ 69). అప్పీలు 45 / 30 / 30 రోజులు; 50% డిపాజిట్; రివిజన్ మూడు కారణాలు. ఇరవై ఒక్క రోజుల్లో స్వీకరణ, లేకపోతే స్వీకరించినట్లు భావన (సెక్షన్ 36). సివిల్ కోర్టు అధికారాలు సెక్షన్ 38(9); మధ్యంతర సెక్షన్ 38(8); పక్షం మరణం సెక్షన్ 38(12). మూడు / ఐదు నెలల్లో నిర్ణయం (సెక్షన్ 38(7)). అమలు సెక్షన్ 71; శిక్ష సెక్షన్ 72 (₹25,000–₹1 లక్ష; ఒక నెల–మూడు సంవత్సరాలు); అప్పీలు సెక్షన్ 73. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.)

selfTest.q: CPA 2019 కింద ఆర్థిక అధికార పరిధికి పరీక్ష ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఒక వినియోగదారుడు కారుకు ₹60 లక్షలు చెల్లించి ₹1.5 కోట్లు కోరుతున్నాడు. ఏ కమిషన్? అన్యాయ ఒప్పంద షరతును శూన్యమని ఏ కమిషన్ ప్రకటించగలదు? రివిజన్ మూడు కారణాలు చెప్పండి. జిల్లా కమిషన్ ఇరవై ఒక్క రోజుల్లో స్వీకార యోగ్యత నిర్ణయించకపోతే ఏమవుతుంది? కమిషన్ ఉత్తర్వును పాటించకపోతే శిక్ష ఏమిటి? కమిషన్‌కు ఏ సివిల్ కోర్టు అధికారాలు ఉన్నాయి?

ఆర్థిక పరీక్ష వస్తువులు లేదా సేవల విలువ "and compensation, if any, claimed" (అర్థం: కోరిన నష్టపరిహారం ఏదైనా ఉంటే అది కూడా) (సెక్షన్లు 11, 17, 21) "value of the goods or services paid as consideration" (అర్థం: ప్రతిఫలంగా చెల్లించిన వస్తువులు లేదా సేవల విలువ) (సెక్షన్లు 34, 47, 58)
చివరి పరిమితులు ₹20 లక్షలు / ₹1 కోటి 2021 నియమాలు: ₹50 లక్షలు / ₹2 కోట్లు
ఫిర్యాదుదారుని స్థలం కారణం కాదు కారణం (సెక్షన్ 34(2)(d))
అన్యాయ ఒప్పందాలు అటువంటి అధికార పరిధి లేదు రాష్ట్ర, జాతీయ కమిషన్లు; షరతులను శూన్యమైనవిగా ప్రకటించడం (సెక్షన్లు 47(1)(a)(ii), 49(2), 58(1)(a)(ii), 59(2))
నియంత్రణ సంస్థ నుండి అప్పీళ్లు నియంత్రణ సంస్థ లేదు కేంద్ర అథారిటీ నుండి అప్పీళ్లను జాతీయ కమిషన్ వింటుంది (సెక్షన్ 58(1)(a)(iv))
స్వీకరణ సాధారణంగా ఇరవై ఒక్క రోజుల్లో నిర్ణయం (సెక్షన్ 12(3)); స్వీకరించినట్లు భావన కనబడలేదు అదే కాల పరిమితి; నిర్ణయించకపోతే స్వీకరించినట్లు భావన (సెక్షన్ 36(2)–(3))
మధ్యవర్తిత్వం లేదు సెక్షన్ 37
వీడియో కాన్ఫరెన్సింగ్; ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ సేవా ప్రదాతలు ఇవ్వలేదు సెక్షన్లు 38(4), 38(6)
పునఃసమీక్ష జాతీయ కమిషన్ మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 22(2)) మూడు కమిషన్లూ (సెక్షన్లు 40, 50, 60)
శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారం సెక్షన్ 14(1)(d) నిబంధన సెక్షన్ 39(1)(d) నిబంధన

hi.inOneMinute: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) there are three Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: the District Commission (s. 28), the State Commission (s. 42) and the National Commission (s. 53). Jurisdiction means which Commission can hear which matter. It has these kinds (See Diagram 1 ): Original jurisdiction over complaints, fixed by pecuniary jurisdiction (value of goods or services paid as consideration) and territorial jurisdiction (place of filing) (ss. 34, 47, 58). Original jurisdiction over unfair contract complaints – only the State Commission (up to ₹10 crore) and the National Commission (above ₹10 crore). Appellate jurisdiction – State over District (s. 47(1)(a)(iii)); National over State (s. 58(1)(a)(iii)) and over the Central Authority (s. 58(1)(a)(iv)); Supreme Court over National (s. 67). Revisional jurisdiction – State over District (s. 47(1)(b)); National over State (s. 58(1)(b)). Present pecuniary limits (Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021): District – up to ₹50 lakh; State – above ₹50 lakh up to ₹2 crore; National – above ₹2 crore. Powers (See Diagram 2 ): admit or reject a complaint (s. 36); refer to mediation (s. 37); call for the opposite party's version, send goods to a laboratory, decide ex parte (s. 38(2)–(3)); civil court powers (s. 38(9)); interim orders (s. 38(8)); final orders under s. 39(1)(a)–(n), including punitive damages; declare unfair contract terms "null and void" (ss. 49(2), 59(2)); review (ss. 40, 50, 60); transfer (ss. 48, 62); enforce orders as decrees (s. 71); punish non-compliance with powers of a Judicial Magistrate of the first class (s. 72).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)
Jurisdiction

s. 34(1): the District Commission has "jurisdiction to entertain complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed one crore rupees"; proviso: the Central Government may prescribe another value. s. 34(2): "A complaint shall be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction,— (a) the opposite party or each of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, at the time of the institution of the complaint, ordinarily resides or carries on business or has a branch office or personally works for gain; or (b) any of the opposite parties, where there are more than one, … provided that in such case the permission of the District Commission is given; or (c) the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises; or (d) the complainant resides or personally works for gain." s. 47(1): the State Commission has jurisdiction "(a) to entertain— (i) complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration, exceeds rupees one crore, but does not exceed rupees ten crore … (ii) complaints against unfair contracts, where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed ten crore rupees; (iii) appeals against the orders of any District Commission within the State; and (b) to call for the records and pass appropriate orders in any consumer dispute which is pending before or has been decided by any District Commission within the State, where it appears to the State Commission that such District Commission has exercised a jurisdiction not vested in it by law, or has failed to exercise a jurisdiction so vested or has acted in exercise of its jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity." s. 47(4): the same four territorial grounds as s. 34(2) apply to complaints in the State Commission. s. 58(1): the National Commission has jurisdiction "(a) to entertain— (i) complaints where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration exceeds rupees ten crore … (ii) complaints against unfair contracts, where the value of goods or services paid as consideration exceeds ten crore rupees; (iii) appeals against the orders of any State Commission; (iv) appeals against the orders of the Central Authority; and (b)" revision over any State Commission on the same grounds as s. 47(1)(b). s. 69(1): a Commission "shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen"; s. 69(2): delay may be condoned for sufficient cause, with reasons recorded.

Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021 (G.S.R. 912(E), 30 December 2021), made under the provisos to ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i) and 58(1)(a)(i):

r. 3: the District Commission entertains complaints "where the value of the goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed fifty lakh rupees". r. 4: the State Commission – value "exceeds fifty lakh but does not exceed two crore rupees". r. 5: the National Commission – value "exceeds two crore rupees".
Powers

s. 36(2)–(3): the District Commission may admit or reject a complaint; it shall not reject without hearing the complainant; admissibility "shall ordinarily be decided within twenty-one days"; if not decided in that time, the complaint "shall be deemed to have been admitted". s. 37(1): at the first hearing after admission or at any later stage, if there is scope for settlement acceptable to the parties, the Commission may, with their written consent, refer the dispute to mediation. s. 38(2): for goods – send the complaint to the opposite party within twenty-one days for his version within thirty days (extendable by not more than fifteen days); where a defect cannot be found without testing, send a sealed sample to the appropriate laboratory, which reports within forty-five days; the complainant deposits the laboratory fee; parties may object to the report and are heard. s. 38(3): for services, or goods that cannot be tested – call for the opposite party's version; decide on the evidence of both sides, or "ex parte on the basis of evidence brought to its notice by the complainant" if the opposite party does not act; and "decide the complaint on merits if the complainant fails to appear on the date of hearing". s. 38(4): may require an electronic service provider to give information, documents or records. s. 38(5): proceedings that follow sub-sections (2) and (3) cannot be challenged on the ground that natural justice was not followed. s. 38(6): "Every complaint shall be heard by the District Commission on the basis of affidavit and documentary evidence placed on record"; hearing or examination in person or by video conferencing may be allowed for sufficient cause, with reasons. s. 38(7): endeavour to decide "within a period of three months from the date of receipt of notice by opposite party where the complaint does not require analysis or testing of commodities and within five months if it requires analysis or testing"; no adjournment ordinarily unless sufficient cause is shown and reasons recorded; costs of adjournment; reasons to be recorded for delay. s. 38(8): "such interim order as is just and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case". s. 38(9): "the same powers as are vested in a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 … while trying a suit in respect of the following matters, namely:— (a) the summoning and enforcing the attendance of any defendant or witness and examining the witness on oath; (b) requiring the discovery and production of any document or other material object as evidence; (c) receiving of evidence on affidavits; (d) the requisitioning of the report of the concerned analysis or test from the appropriate laboratory or from any other relevant source; (e) issuing of commissions for the examination of any witness, or document; and (f) any other matter which may be prescribed by the Central Government." s. 38(10): every proceeding "shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code", and the Commission is deemed a criminal court for s. 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. s. 38(11): for a complaint by one or more consumers having the same interest, Order I Rule 8 CPC (representative suit) applies. s. 38(12): on the death of the complainant or the opposite party, Order XXII CPC applies. s. 39(1): where the allegations are proved, an order directing "one or more" of reliefs (a) to (n) – remove defect, replace, refund with interest, compensation for negligence (with power "to grant punitive damages"), product liability compensation, remove defects or deficiencies, discontinue unfair or restrictive trade practices, stop or withdraw hazardous goods, a sum not less than 25% of value for unidentifiable consumers, corrective advertisement, costs, and cease misleading advertisement. s. 39(3)–(4): if the President and member differ, the point goes to another member, who gives an opinion within one month; the majority opinion is the order; every order is signed. ss. 49, 59: ss. 35 to 39 apply to the State and National Commissions with necessary changes; and each "may also declare any terms of contract, which is unfair to any consumer, to be null and void" (ss. 49(2), 59(2)). ss. 40, 50, 60: review for "an error apparent on the face of the record", of its own motion or on an application within thirty days. s. 52: appeals to be heard expeditiously, with an endeavour to dispose of them within ninety days of admission. s. 61: a party may apply to the National Commission to set aside its ex parte order. ss. 48, 62: transfer of complaints – within a State (State Commission) and across States (National Commission). s. 66: in matters of "the larger interest of consumers", the State or National Commission may direct an individual, organisation or expert to assist it. s. 70: administrative control of the National Commission over State Commissions, and of each State Commission over District Commissions. s. 71: every order "shall be enforced by it in the same manner as if it were a decree made by a Court in a suit before it", under Order XXI CPC. s. 72(1): non-compliance is punishable with imprisonment "not … less than one month, but which may extend to three years", or fine "not … less than twenty-five thousand rupees, but which may extend to one lakh rupees", or both. s. 72(2)–(3): the Commissions have "the power of a Judicial Magistrate of first class" and try these offences summarily. s. 73: appeals against an order under s. 72(1) lie on facts and law – District to State, State to National, National to Supreme Court – within thirty days.

Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (Act 68 of 1986) – ss. 11, 17, 21 (jurisdiction, finally ₹20 lakh / ₹1 crore, on "the value of the goods or services and compensation, if any, claimed"); s. 13 (procedure; s. 13(3A) three / five months; s. 13(3B) interim orders; s. 13(4) civil court powers; s. 13(7) death of a party); s. 14 (reliefs); s. 22A (setting aside ex parte orders, National Commission); s. 25 (enforcement); s. 26 (frivolous or vexatious complaint dismissed with costs "not exceeding ten thousand rupees"); s. 27 (penalty: one month to three years, or fine "not be less than two thousand rupees but which may extend to ten thousand rupees", or both).
hi.meaning: Jurisdiction is the authority of a Commission to hear and decide a matter. If a Commission acts without jurisdiction, its order can be corrected in revision (ss. 47(1)(b), 58(1)(b)). Pecuniary jurisdiction – the limit by money value. Under CPA 2019 the test is "the value of the goods or services paid as consideration" (ss. 34(1), 47(1)(a)(i), 58(1)(a)(i)). Territorial jurisdiction – the limit by place: where the opposite party is, where the cause of action arose, or where the complainant resides or personally works for gain (ss. 34(2), 47(4)). Complaint – "any allegation in writing, made by a complainant for obtaining any relief provided by or under this Act" about an unfair contract , unfair or restrictive trade practice , defect in goods , deficiency in services , excess price, hazardous goods or services, or a product liability claim (s. 2(6)). Unfair contract – "a contract between a manufacturer or trader or service provider on one hand, and a consumer on the other, having such terms which cause significant change in the rights of such consumer", including the terms listed in s. 2(46)(i)–(vi) (for example, "manifestly excessive security deposits"). Powers – what a Commission can do while hearing and after deciding: procedural powers (ss. 36–38), relief-granting powers (s. 39), corrective powers (review, set-aside, revision), and enforcement powers (ss. 71–72).
keyPoints: Test: value of goods or services paid as consideration – not compensation. 2021 Rules: ₹50 lakh / ₹2 crore (rr. 3–5). Unfair contracts: State ≤ ₹10 crore; National > ₹10 crore; void declaration ss. 49(2), 59(2). Territorial: four grounds; complainant's residence or work (s. 34(2)(d)). Limitation: two years (s. 69). Appeal 45 / 30 / 30 days; 50% deposit; revision three grounds. Admission in twenty-one days, else deemed admitted (s. 36). Civil court powers s. 38(9); interim s. 38(8); death of party s. 38(12). Decide in three / five months (s. 38(7)). Enforcement s. 71; punishment s. 72 (₹25,000–₹1 lakh; one month–three years); appeal s. 73. (See Diagram 2 .)

caseLaws.facts: Indian Medical Association v. V.P. Shantha, (1995) 6 SCC 651 (13 November 1995) Facts: Doctors argued that medical negligence cases were too complicated for the summary procedure of the consumer bodies under the 1986 Act. A three-judge bench (S.C. Agrawal, Kuldip Singh and B.L. Hansaria JJ.) examined their jurisdiction and powers. Principle: The bodies have "the same power as are vested in a civil court" for summons, discovery, affidavits, laboratory reports and commissions (s. 13 of the 1986 Act), and the jurisdiction "is based on the pecuniary limit of the claim made by the complainant" under that Act. Simple cases such as "leaving inside the patient swabs" can be "speedily disposed of"; in complicated cases "the complainant can be asked to approach the civil court", since the Act "preserves the right of the consumer to approach the civil court". Why it matters: It explains how the Commissions' powers and summary procedure fit complicated disputes, and it confirms that the consumer forum is an additional, not exclusive, remedy. 2. Kumud Lall v. Suresh Chandra Roy, 2026 INSC 443 (4 May 2026) Facts: In a medical negligence revision pending before the National Commission, the doctor (opposite party) died in 2009 and his widow and son were brought on record. The Supreme Court (J.K. Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar JJ.) considered whether the case could continue, looking at s. 13(7) of the 1986 Act and s. 38(12) of the 2019 Act, both of which apply Order XXII CPC. Principle: "in view of the preceding discussion and the statutory framework provided in 1986 Act as well as 2019 Act, we conclude that upon the death of the alleged medically negligent doctor, his/her legal heirs can be impleaded and brought on record"; "personal injury claims abate, while claims for or against the estate of the deceased survive" (para 64(vi)). The case was remitted to the National Commission to decide within six months. Why it matters: It shows the Commission's power under s. 38(12) to bring legal heirs on record and continue a case, and the limit of that power: only claims against the estate survive.

law-of-torts-u5-t17.subtitle: When a consumer wrong goes on day after day, and how the two-year limitation of section 69 applies

en.inOneMinute: A consumer complaint must be filed "within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen" (s. 69(1), Consumer Protection Act, 2019). A late complaint can still be entertained only if the Commission: is satisfied there was "sufficient cause"; and records its reasons for condoning the delay (s. 69(2)). So the key question is when the cause of action arose . A continuous (continuing) cause of action arises where the wrong itself goes on day after day. The Limitation Act, 1963 states the rule for a continuing breach of contract and a continuing tort: "a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues" (s. 22). (See Diagram 1 .) Three situations must be kept apart: a single completed wrong , even if its harm lasts: time runs from the wrong; a continuing wrong : time runs afresh while the wrong continues; recurring separate wrongs : each gives its own cause of action. The cause of action also fixes place . A complaint may be filed where "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises" (ss. 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 69(1): "The District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen." Section 69(2): "Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), a complaint may be entertained after the period specified in sub-section (1), if the complainant satisfies the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, that he had sufficient cause for not filing the complaint within such period:" Proviso: "Provided that no such complaint shall be entertained unless the District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, records its reasons for condoning such delay." Section 34(2)(c): a complaint may be instituted in the District Commission within whose local limits "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises". Section 47(4)(c) says the same for the State Commission.
Limitation Act, 1963 (Act 36 of 1963)

Section 22 – Continuing breaches and torts: "In the case of a continuing breach of contract or in the case of a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues." Section 29(2): where "any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed by the Schedule", ss. 4 to 24 apply "only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law".
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now repealed) – s. 24A: the same two-year rule from the date the cause of action arose, with the same power to condone delay for sufficient cause and recorded reasons.
en.meaning: Cause of action – the facts that give a person the right to complain or sue. Neither the 2019 Act nor the 1986 Act defines it. The Act uses the phrase for time (s. 69) and place (ss. 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)). Continuing wrong – a breach or tort that is not over once done but goes on. In the words of s. 22, it is a breach or tort that "continues". While it continues, a fresh period of limitation runs "at every moment". Limitation period – the time within which a complaint must be filed: two years from the date the cause of action arose (s. 69(1)). Condonation of delay – the Commission's power to entertain a late complaint if the complainant shows "sufficient cause", with reasons recorded (s. 69(2)).
keyPoints: Two years "from the date on which the cause of action has arisen" (s. 69(1)). Condonation of delay: sufficient cause + reasons recorded (s. 69(2)). s. 22 Limitation Act: fresh limitation period every moment a breach or tort continues. A continuing wrong is a breach or tort that goes on, not a wrong whose harm lasts. Recurring wrongs: each is separate. s. 29(2) Limitation Act: ss. 4–24 apply to special-law periods unless expressly excluded. Cause of action also decides the place of filing (ss. 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)). 1986 Act s. 24A: same rule.

te.inOneMinute: వినియోగదారుల ఫిర్యాదును "within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen" (అర్థం: దావా కారణం ఏర్పడిన తేదీ నుండి రెండు సంవత్సరాల్లోపు) దాఖలు చేయాలి (వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 సెక్షన్ 69(1)). ఆలస్యమైన ఫిర్యాదును కమిషన్ ఈ రెండూ ఉంటేనే స్వీకరిస్తుంది: "sufficient cause" (అర్థం: తగిన కారణం) ఉందని కమిషన్ సంతృప్తి చెందాలి; మరియు ఆలస్యాన్ని మన్నించడానికి కారణాలను నమోదు చేయాలి (సెక్షన్ 69(2)). కాబట్టి ముఖ్య ప్రశ్న: దావా కారణం ఎప్పుడు ఏర్పడింది . తప్పు రోజు తర్వాత రోజు కొనసాగుతూ ఉంటే నిరంతర (కొనసాగే) దావా కారణం ఏర్పడుతుంది. కొనసాగే ఒప్పంద ఉల్లంఘన, కొనసాగే టార్ట్‌కు పరిమితి చట్టం, 1963 నియమం చెబుతుంది: "a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues" (అర్థం: ఉల్లంఘన లేదా టార్ట్ కొనసాగుతున్న కాలంలో ప్రతి క్షణం కొత్త పరిమితి కాలం మొదలవుతుంది) (సెక్షన్ 22). ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) మూడు పరిస్థితులను వేరుగా ఉంచాలి: హాని కొనసాగినా, ఒకేసారి పూర్తయిన తప్పు : కాలం తప్పు జరిగిన తేదీ నుండి లెక్కిస్తారు; కొనసాగే తప్పు : తప్పు కొనసాగుతున్నంత కాలం కొత్తగా కాలం మొదలవుతుంది; పునరావృతమయ్యే వేర్వేరు తప్పులు : ప్రతిదానికీ సొంత దావా కారణం. దావా కారణం స్థలాన్ని కూడా నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises" (అర్థం: దావా కారణం పూర్తిగా లేదా పాక్షికంగా ఏర్పడిన) చోట ఫిర్యాదు వేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్లు 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)).
te.meaning: దావా కారణం (cause of action) – ఒక వ్యక్తికి ఫిర్యాదు చేసే లేదా దావా వేసే హక్కు ఇచ్చే వాస్తవాలు. 2019 చట్టం గానీ 1986 చట్టం గానీ దీనిని నిర్వచించలేదు. చట్టం ఈ పదాన్ని కాలం (సెక్షన్ 69), స్థలం (సెక్షన్లు 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)) కోసం వాడుతుంది. కొనసాగే తప్పు (continuing wrong) – ఒకసారి చేసి ముగిసిపోకుండా కొనసాగే ఉల్లంఘన లేదా టార్ట్ . సెక్షన్ 22 మాటల్లో, "continues" (అర్థం: కొనసాగుతుంది) అయ్యే ఉల్లంఘన లేదా టార్ట్. అది కొనసాగుతున్నంత కాలం "at every moment" (అర్థం: ప్రతి క్షణం) కొత్త పరిమితి కాలం మొదలవుతుంది. పరిమితి కాలం (limitation period) – ఫిర్యాదు దాఖలు చేయాల్సిన గడువు: దావా కారణం ఏర్పడిన తేదీ నుండి రెండు సంవత్సరాలు (సెక్షన్ 69(1)). ఆలస్యం మన్నింపు (condonation of delay) – ఫిర్యాదుదారు "sufficient cause" (అర్థం: తగిన కారణం) చూపితే, కారణాలు నమోదు చేసి, ఆలస్యమైన ఫిర్యాదును స్వీకరించే కమిషన్ అధికారం (సెక్షన్ 69(2)).
keyPoints: "దావా కారణం ఏర్పడిన తేదీ నుండి" రెండు సంవత్సరాలు (సెక్షన్ 69(1)). ఆలస్యం మన్నింపు: తగిన కారణం + కారణాల నమోదు (సెక్షన్ 69(2)). పరిమితి చట్టం సెక్షన్ 22: ఉల్లంఘన లేదా టార్ట్ కొనసాగుతున్న ప్రతి క్షణం కొత్త పరిమితి కాలం. కొనసాగే తప్పు అంటే కొనసాగే ఉల్లంఘన లేదా టార్ట్, హాని మాత్రమే కొనసాగే తప్పు కాదు. పునరావృత తప్పులు: ప్రతిదీ వేరే. పరిమితి చట్టం సెక్షన్ 29(2): స్పష్టంగా మినహాయించకపోతే ప్రత్యేక చట్టాల కాలాలకు సెక్షన్లు 4–24 వర్తిస్తాయి. దావా కారణం దాఖలు స్థలాన్ని కూడా నిర్ణయిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్లు 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)). 1986 చట్టం సెక్షన్ 24A: అదే నియమం.

hi.inOneMinute: A consumer complaint must be filed "within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen" (s. 69(1), Consumer Protection Act, 2019). A late complaint can still be entertained only if the Commission: is satisfied there was "sufficient cause"; and records its reasons for condoning the delay (s. 69(2)). So the key question is when the cause of action arose . A continuous (continuing) cause of action arises where the wrong itself goes on day after day. The Limitation Act, 1963 states the rule for a continuing breach of contract and a continuing tort: "a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues" (s. 22). (See Diagram 1 .) Three situations must be kept apart: a single completed wrong , even if its harm lasts: time runs from the wrong; a continuing wrong : time runs afresh while the wrong continues; recurring separate wrongs : each gives its own cause of action. The cause of action also fixes place . A complaint may be filed where "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises" (ss. 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 69(1): "The District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen." Section 69(2): "Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), a complaint may be entertained after the period specified in sub-section (1), if the complainant satisfies the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, that he had sufficient cause for not filing the complaint within such period:" Proviso: "Provided that no such complaint shall be entertained unless the District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, records its reasons for condoning such delay." Section 34(2)(c): a complaint may be instituted in the District Commission within whose local limits "the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises". Section 47(4)(c) says the same for the State Commission.
Limitation Act, 1963 (Act 36 of 1963)

Section 22 – Continuing breaches and torts: "In the case of a continuing breach of contract or in the case of a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues." Section 29(2): where "any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed by the Schedule", ss. 4 to 24 apply "only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or local law".
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (now repealed) – s. 24A: the same two-year rule from the date the cause of action arose, with the same power to condone delay for sufficient cause and recorded reasons.
hi.meaning: Cause of action – the facts that give a person the right to complain or sue. Neither the 2019 Act nor the 1986 Act defines it. The Act uses the phrase for time (s. 69) and place (ss. 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)). Continuing wrong – a breach or tort that is not over once done but goes on. In the words of s. 22, it is a breach or tort that "continues". While it continues, a fresh period of limitation runs "at every moment". Limitation period – the time within which a complaint must be filed: two years from the date the cause of action arose (s. 69(1)). Condonation of delay – the Commission's power to entertain a late complaint if the complainant shows "sufficient cause", with reasons recorded (s. 69(2)).
keyPoints: Two years "from the date on which the cause of action has arisen" (s. 69(1)). Condonation of delay: sufficient cause + reasons recorded (s. 69(2)). s. 22 Limitation Act: fresh limitation period every moment a breach or tort continues. A continuing wrong is a breach or tort that goes on, not a wrong whose harm lasts. Recurring wrongs: each is separate. s. 29(2) Limitation Act: ss. 4–24 apply to special-law periods unless expressly excluded. Cause of action also decides the place of filing (ss. 34(2)(c), 47(4)(c)). 1986 Act s. 24A: same rule.
