hi.inOneMinute: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA 2019) makes a wrongdoer answerable in two ways (See Diagram 1 ): Civil liability – an order of a Consumer Commission to remove a defect, replace goods, refund the price with interest, pay compensation (including punitive damages ), pay product liability compensation, stop unfair practices, withdraw hazardous goods, pay a sum for unidentified consumers, issue a corrective advertisement and pay costs (s. 39(1)(a)–(n)). Orders are enforced like a civil court decree (s. 71). Criminal liability – offences tried by a court (or, for s. 72, by the Commission itself) and punished with imprisonment and fine: s. 72 – non-compliance with a Commission's order: imprisonment 1 month to 3 years, or fine ₹25,000 to ₹1 lakh, or both; s. 88 – non-compliance with the Central Authority's directions: up to 6 months, or fine up to ₹20 lakh, or both; s. 89 – false or misleading advertisement: up to 2 years and fine up to ₹10 lakh (later: 5 years and ₹50 lakh); s. 90 – product containing an adulterant : from 6 months and ₹1 lakh (no injury) to not less than 7 years up to life and fine not less than ₹10 lakh (death); s. 91 – spurious goods : from 1 year and ₹3 lakh (simple injury) to not less than 7 years up to life and fine not less than ₹10 lakh (death); s. 93 – vexatious search by an officer: up to 1 year, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both. Both can run together: s. 100 says the Act is "in addition to and not in derogation of" other laws, so the general criminal law (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) and the tort action also remain. Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka (2009): on civil liability, the Supreme Court raised a Consumer Commission award from ₹14 lakh to ₹1 crore with interest, saying a court "must not be chary of awarding adequate compensation".
legalProvision: Civil liability – Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 39(1) – where the District Commission is satisfied that goods suffer from defects, or allegations about services or unfair trade practices, "or claims for compensation under product liability are proved", it "shall issue an order to the opposite party directing him to do one or more of the following": "(a) to remove the defect pointed out by the appropriate laboratory from the goods in question; (b) to replace the goods with new goods of similar description which shall be free from any defect; (c) to return to the complainant the price, or, as the case may be, the charges paid by the complainant along with such interest on such price or charges as may be decided; (d) to pay such amount as may be awarded by it as compensation to the consumer for any loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party: Provided that the District Commission shall have the power to grant punitive damages in such circumstances as it deems fit; (e) to pay such amount as may be awarded by it as compensation in a product liability action under Chapter VI; (f) to remove the defects in goods or deficiencies in the services in question; (g) to discontinue the unfair trade practice or restrictive trade practice and not to repeat them; (h) not to offer the hazardous or unsafe goods for sale; (i) to withdraw the hazardous goods from being offered for sale; (j) to cease manufacture of hazardous goods and to desist from offering services which are hazardous in nature; (k) to pay such sum as may be determined by it, if it is of the opinion that loss or injury has been suffered by a large number of consumers who are not identifiable conveniently: Provided that the minimum amount of sum so payable shall not be less than twenty-five per cent. of the value of such defective goods sold or service provided, as the case may be, to such consumers; (l) to issue corrective advertisement to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement at the cost of the opposite party responsible for issuing such misleading advertisement; (m) to provide for adequate costs to parties; and (n) to cease and desist from issuing any misleading advertisement." s. 39(2) – "Any amount obtained under sub-section (1) shall be credited to such fund and utilised in such manner as may be prescribed." ss. 49(1), 59(1) – these provisions apply to complaints before the State and National Commissions. s. 71 – "Every order made by a District Commission, State Commission or the National Commission shall be enforced by it in the same manner as if it were a decree made by a Court in a suit before it and the provisions of Order XXI of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908) shall, as far as may be, applicable". ss. 82 to 87 – product liability of manufacturers, service providers and sellers (see that topic).
Criminal liability – Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 72(1) – "Whoever fails to comply with any order made by the District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one month, but which may extend to three years, or with fine, which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees, but which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both." s. 72(2) – the Commission "shall have the power of a Judicial Magistrate of first class for the trial of offences under sub-section (1)". s. 72(3) – such offences "shall be tried summarily". s. 73 – appeal against an order under s. 72(1), "both on facts and on law", from the District Commission to the State Commission, from the State Commission to the National Commission, and from the National Commission to the Supreme Court, within thirty days (delay may be condoned for sufficient cause). s. 88 – "Whoever, fails to comply with any direction of the Central Authority under sections 20 and 21, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with fine which may extend to twenty lakh rupees, or with both." s. 89 – "Any manufacturer or service provider who causes a false or misleading advertisement to be made which is prejudicial to the interest of consumers shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees; and for every subsequent offence, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years and with fine which may extend to fifty lakh rupees." s. 90(1) – "Whoever, by himself or by any other person on his behalf, manufactures for sale or stores or sells or distributes or imports any product containing an adulterant shall be punished, if such act— (a) does not result in any injury to the consumer, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months and with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees; (b) causing injury not amounting to grievous hurt to the consumer, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and with fine which may extend to three lakh rupees; (c) causing injury resulting in grievous hurt to the consumer, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees; and (d) results in the death of a consumer, with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life and with fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees." s. 90(2) – offences under clauses (c) and (d) "shall be cognizable and non-bailable". s. 90(3) – the court may, on first conviction, "suspend any licence ... for a period up to two years, and in case of second or subsequent conviction, cancel the licence". Explanation – "adulterant" means "any material including extraneous matter which is employed or used for making a product unsafe"; "grievous hurt" has the meaning in s. 320 of the Indian Penal Code. s. 91(1) – whoever manufactures for sale, stores, sells, distributes or imports any spurious goods: "(a) causing injury not amounting to grievous hurt to the consumer, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and with fine which may extend to three lakh rupees; (b) causing injury resulting in grievous hurt to the consumer, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years and with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees; (c) results in the death of a consumer, with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years, but may extend to imprisonment for life and with fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees". s. 91(2) – clauses (b) and (c) are cognizable and non-bailable. s. 91(3) – licence suspension (first conviction, up to two years) or cancellation (second or subsequent). s. 2(43) – "spurious goods" means "such goods which are falsely claimed to be genuine". s. 92 – no cognizance of offences under ss. 88 and 89 "except on a complaint filed by the Central Authority or any officer authorised by it in this behalf". s. 93 – an officer exercising s. 22 powers who, knowing there are no reasonable grounds, searches premises or seizes records: "imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees or with both". s. 96 – offences under ss. 88 and 89 may be compounded. s. 100 – "The provisions of this Act shall be in addition to and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law for the time being in force."

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (general criminal law, for comparison): s. 274 – adulteration of food or drink intended for sale, making it noxious: imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to five thousand rupees, or both; ss. 275 to 278 – sale of noxious food or drink, adulteration and sale of adulterated drugs, and sale of a drug as a different drug.
hi.meaning: Civil liability – liability to repair the wrong to the consumer : to put right, replace, refund or pay compensation. Its aim is redress . Criminal liability – liability to punishment (imprisonment, fine, licence suspension) for an offence. Its aim is punishment and deterrence . Compensation – money to make good the "loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the negligence of the opposite party" (s. 39(1)(d)), or for "harm" in a product liability action (s. 39(1)(e)). Punitive damages – damages beyond actual loss, to punish and deter; the Commission may grant them "in such circumstances as it deems fit" (proviso to s. 39(1)(d)). Adulterant – "any material including extraneous matter which is employed or used for making a product unsafe" (s. 90, Explanation (a)). Spurious goods – "goods which are falsely claimed to be genuine" (s. 2(43)). Cognizable and non-bailable – the police may arrest without warrant, and bail is not a matter of right (used for the serious clauses of ss. 90 and 91).
keyPoints: s. 39(1): 14 civil reliefs; punitive damages in proviso to (d); 25% minimum in (k). s. 71: orders enforced as decrees. s. 72: non-compliance – 1 month–3 years, or ₹25,000–₹1 lakh; Commission as JMFC; summary trial. s. 73: appeal in 30 days; NCDRC to Supreme Court. (See Diagram 3 .) s. 88: 6 months / ₹20 lakh; s. 89: 2 years + ₹10 lakh (5 years + ₹50 lakh). s. 90: adulterant – four grades; death: 7 years–life + ≥ ₹10 lakh. s. 91: spurious goods – three grades. ss. 90(2), 91(2): serious grades cognizable and non-bailable; licence suspension or cancellation. s. 92: ss. 88, 89 only on Authority's complaint; s. 96: compounding of ss. 88, 89 only, not for a repeat within three years. s. 100: Act is in addition to other laws.

caseLaws.facts: Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences v. Prasanth S. Dhananka, [2009] 9 SCR 313 (14 May 2009) Facts: A twenty-year-old engineering student underwent surgery at the appellant hospital to remove a tumour. Immediately after the operation he developed acute paraplegia. The National Commission found negligence and deficiency of service before, during and after the operation and awarded ₹14 lakh (plus ₹1.5 lakh to his parents). Both sides appealed (B.N. Agrawal, Harjit Singh Bedi and G.S. Singhvi JJ.). Principle: The Court must "strike a balance between the inflated and unreasonable demands of a victim and the equally untenable claim of the opposite party saying that nothing is payable"; "if a case is made out, the Court must not be chary of awarding adequate compensation". It rejected the multiplier method as unsuitable for this kind of damage and awarded ₹1 crore with interest at 6% from 1 March 1999, refusing a "hypothetical" claim of ₹2 crore for future treatment. Why it matters: It shows how civil liability under consumer law is measured – full, realistic compensation for actual and future loss, not a token sum. Note: No judgment applying the offence provisions of CPA 2019 (ss. 72, 88 to 93) was found among the judgments available for this note.

en.meaning:
What best describes 'consumerism'?

Explanation. Consumerism is a collective, organised movement — through associations, advocacy, and legislative lobbying — not merely individual shopping caution.

Why couldn't ordinary tort remedies alone correct market-wide consumer harms such as adulteration or false advertising?

Explanation. Tort remedies compensate one injured consumer at a time, long after harm occurs, and only if that consumer can afford to litigate — inadequate for correcting market-wide problems.

The doctrine of caveat emptor means

Explanation. Caveat emptor, 'let the buyer beware', historically placed the responsibility of examining goods before purchase on the buyer, with limited seller disclosure duties.

Consumerism pushed the law towards a philosophy closer to which principle?

hi.meaning: What best describes 'consumerism'? Explanation. Consumerism is a collective, organised movement — through associations, advocacy, and legislative lobbying — not merely individual shopping caution. Why couldn't ordinary tort remedies alone correct market-wide consumer harms such as adulteration or false advertising? Explanation. Tort remedies compensate one injured consumer at a time, long after harm occurs, and only if that consumer can afford to litigate — inadequate for correcting market-wide problems. The doctrine of caveat emptor means Explanation. Caveat emptor, 'let the buyer beware', historically placed the responsibility of examining goods before purchase on the buyer, with limited seller disclosure duties. Consumerism pushed the law towards a philosophy closer to which principle?

en.meaning:
Under section 34(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the District Commission hears complaints where the consideration paid does not exceed:

Explanation. Section 34(1) fixes the limit at Rs 1 crore and lets the Central Government prescribe another value. The 2021 Rules prescribed Rs 50 lakh. Section 107 repealed the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.

What is the single most significant structural innovation of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?

Explanation. The CCPA is a dedicated regulatory body that can investigate and act on its own initiative, without waiting for an individual consumer complaint — something the 1986 Act had no equivalent of.

How does the 2019 Act treat product liability differently from the position under the 1986 Act?

Explanation. The 2019 Act, for the first time, gives product liability its own dedicated statutory chapter with defined standards, instead of requiring reliance purely on common-law negligence.

law-of-torts-u5-t19.subtitle: Settling consumer disputes by agreement: mediation under the 2019 Act and the place of other alternative dispute resolution

en.inOneMinute: ADR (alternative dispute resolution) means settling a dispute outside the usual contested trial, with the parties' agreement. Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure lists four modes (See Diagram 1 ): arbitration; conciliation ; judicial settlement, including Lok Adalat; mediation. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 builds one ADR method, mediation , into consumer cases. The 1986 Act had no such provision. How it works: At the first hearing after admission, or later, a Commission that sees "elements of a settlement" may ask the parties to consent in writing to mediation within five days (s. 37(1)). On consent, it refers the matter within five days (s. 37(2)). Mediation is held in the consumer mediation cell attached to the Commission, before an empanelled mediator (ss. 74–79). A settlement, full or partial, is put in writing and signed (s. 80). The Commission records it by order within seven days of the settlement report (s. 81). No appeal lies against that order (s. 41, third proviso). Not for mediation (rule 4, Consumer Protection (Mediation) Rules, 2020): medical negligence resulting in grievous injury or death; serious allegations of fraud, forgery and the like; criminal non-compoundable offences; matters of public interest or of numerous persons not before the Commission; and matters where compounding of offences is sought. If settled, the complainant gets back the full complaint fee (rule 5).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 2(25): "mediation" means "the process by which a mediator mediates the consumer disputes". Section 2(26): "mediator" means a mediator referred to in s. 75. Section 37(1): "At the first hearing of the complaint after its admission, or at any later stage, if it appears to the District Commission that there exists elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, except in such cases as may be prescribed, it may direct the parties to give in writing, within five days, consent to have their dispute settled by mediation in accordance with the provisions of Chapter V." Section 37(2): "Where the parties agree for settlement by mediation and give their consent in writing, the District Commission shall, within five days of receipt of such consent, refer the matter for mediation, and in such case, the provisions of Chapter V, relating to mediation, shall apply." Sections 49(1) and 59(1): ss. 35 to 39, including s. 37, apply "with such modifications as may be necessary" to complaints before the State and National Commissions. Section 74: a consumer mediation cell is attached to each District and State Commission (by the State Government) and to the National Commission and each regional Bench (by the Central Government). It maintains: a list of empanelled mediators; a list of cases; the record of proceedings; a quarterly report to its Commission. Section 75: a panel of mediators is prepared on the recommendation of a selection committee of "the President and a member of that Commission". It is valid for five years. Section 77: the mediator must disclose any personal, professional or financial interest, and circumstances giving rise to "a justifiable doubt as to his independence or impartiality". Section 79(2): the mediator "shall have regard to the rights and obligations of the parties, the usages of trade, if any, the circumstances giving rise to the consumer dispute and such other relevant factors", and "shall be guided by the principles of natural justice". Section 80: an agreement on all or some issues "shall be reduced to writing accordingly, and signed by the parties". The mediator sends a settlement report. If there is no agreement, he reports that. Section 81: (1) the Commission shall, "within seven days of the receipt of the settlement report, pass suitable order recording such settlement of consumer dispute and dispose of the matter accordingly"; (2) where only part is settled, it records that part and hears the rest; (3) where nothing is settled, it hears all issues. Section 41, third proviso: "no appeal shall lie from any order passed under sub-section (1) of section 81 by the District Commission pursuant to a settlement by mediation under section 80."
Consumer Protection (Mediation) Rules, 2020 (G.S.R. 450(E), 15 July 2020)

Rule 4: matters "not to be referred to mediation": (a) "proceedings in respect of medical negligence resulting in grievous injury or death"; (b) defaults or offences for which compounding has been applied for; (c) "serious and specific allegations of fraud, fabrication of documents, forgery, impersonation, coercion"; (d) "prosecution for criminal and non-compoundable offences"; (e) "cases which involve public interest or the interest of numerous persons who are not parties before the Commission". Proviso: even in other cases, the Commission may decline to refer if "no elements of a settlement exist" or mediation "is otherwise not appropriate". Rule 5: if settlement is reached, the complainant "shall be entitled to receive full amount of application fee paid in respect of such complaint". Rule 6: the parties shall not start arbitral or judicial proceedings on a matter that is the subject of the mediation.

Consumer Protection (Mediation) Regulations, 2020 – regulation 11(2): mediation "shall stand terminated on expiry of three months from the date of first appearance before the mediator", unless the Commission extends the time.

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 – Section 89(1): where "there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties", the court may refer the dispute for "(a) arbitration; (b) conciliation; (c) judicial settlement including settlement through Lok Adalat; or (d) mediation".
en.meaning: Alternative dispute resolution – methods of settling a dispute outside a contested hearing, with the help of a neutral person and the consent of the parties. Section 89 CPC lists arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement (including Lok Adalat) and mediation . Mediation – under the CPA 2019, "the process by which a mediator mediates the consumer disputes" (s. 2(25)). The mediator helps the parties reach their own agreement; he does not decide the dispute. Consumer mediation cell – the unit attached to each Commission (and regional Bench of the National Commission ) where mediation is held and records are kept (ss. 74, 79(1)). Settlement agreement – the written, signed terms the parties agree on in mediation, on all or some of the issues (s. 80(1)). The Commission records it by order (s. 81).
keyPoints: Alternative dispute resolution: arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement / Lok Adalat, mediation (s. 89 CPC). CPA 2019 provides mediation only; the 1986 Act had none. s. 37: consent in 5 days; reference in 5 days; applies to all three Commissions (ss. 49(1), 59(1)). Consumer mediation cell attached to each Commission (s. 74). Panel for 5 years (s. 75); disclosure (s. 77); natural justice (s. 79). Settlement agreement written and signed (s. 80); order in 7 days (s. 81). No appeal from the settlement order (s. 41, third proviso). Rule 4 exclusions; rule 5 full fee refund. Mediation ends 3 months after first appearance unless extended. Mediation Act, 2023 s. 65 will replace the scheme when brought into force.

te.inOneMinute: ADR (ప్రత్యామ్నాయ వివాద పరిష్కారం) అంటే పక్షాల అంగీకారంతో, సాధారణ వాదోపవాద విచారణకు బయట వివాదాన్ని పరిష్కరించడం. సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్ సెక్షన్ 89 నాలుగు పద్ధతులను పేర్కొంటుంది ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): ఆర్బిట్రేషన్ (మధ్యవర్తి తీర్పు); కన్సిలియేషన్ (సామరస్య పరిష్కారం); లోక్ అదాలత్‌తో సహా న్యాయ పరిష్కారం; మీడియేషన్ (మధ్యవర్తిత్వం). వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 ఒక ADR పద్ధతిని, మధ్యవర్తిత్వాన్ని , వినియోగదారుల కేసుల్లో చేర్చింది. 1986 చట్టంలో అలాంటి నిబంధన లేదు. ఇది ఎలా పనిచేస్తుంది: స్వీకరణ తర్వాత మొదటి విచారణలో, లేదా తర్వాత, "elements of a settlement" (అర్థం: పరిష్కారానికి అవకాశాలు) కనిపిస్తే కమిషన్ ఐదు రోజుల్లో మధ్యవర్తిత్వానికి లిఖిత సమ్మతి ఇవ్వమని పక్షాలను కోరవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 37(1)). సమ్మతి వస్తే, ఐదు రోజుల్లో విషయాన్ని మధ్యవర్తిత్వానికి పంపుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 37(2)). కమిషన్‌కు అనుబంధంగా ఉన్న వినియోగదారుల మధ్యవర్తిత్వ కేంద్రం లో, ప్యానెల్‌లోని మధ్యవర్తి ముందు మధ్యవర్తిత్వం జరుగుతుంది (సెక్షన్లు 74–79). పూర్తి లేదా పాక్షిక పరిష్కారాన్ని లిఖితంగా రాసి సంతకం చేస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 80). పరిష్కార నివేదిక అందిన ఏడు రోజుల్లో కమిషన్ ఉత్తర్వు ద్వారా దానిని నమోదు చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 81). ఆ ఉత్తర్వుపై అప్పీలు ఉండదు (సెక్షన్ 41, మూడవ నిబంధన). మధ్యవర్తిత్వానికి పంపకూడనివి (నియమం 4, వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ (మధ్యవర్తిత్వం) నియమాలు, 2020): తీవ్ర గాయం లేదా మరణానికి దారితీసిన వైద్య నిర్లక్ష్యం; మోసం, ఫోర్జరీ వంటి తీవ్ర ఆరోపణలు; నేరపూరిత, రాజీ చేయలేని నేరాలు; ప్రజా ప్రయోజనం లేదా కమిషన్ ముందు లేని అనేక మంది ప్రయోజనం ఉన్న విషయాలు; నేరాల రాజీ ( compounding ) కోరిన విషయాలు. పరిష్కారం కుదిరితే, ఫిర్యాదుదారుకు పూర్తి ఫిర్యాదు రుసుము తిరిగి వస్తుంది (నియమం 5).
te.meaning: ప్రత్యామ్నాయ వివాద పరిష్కారం – తటస్థ వ్యక్తి సహాయంతో, పక్షాల సమ్మతితో, వాదోపవాద విచారణకు బయట వివాదాన్ని పరిష్కరించే పద్ధతులు. CPC సెక్షన్ 89 ఆర్బిట్రేషన్, కన్సిలియేషన్, న్యాయ పరిష్కారం (లోక్ అదాలత్‌తో సహా), మధ్యవర్తిత్వాన్ని పేర్కొంటుంది. మధ్యవర్తిత్వం – CPA 2019 కింద "the process by which a mediator mediates the consumer disputes" (అర్థం: మధ్యవర్తి వినియోగదారుల వివాదాలకు మధ్యవర్తిత్వం చేసే ప్రక్రియ) (సెక్షన్ 2(25)). మధ్యవర్తి పక్షాలు తమ సొంత ఒప్పందానికి రావడానికి సహాయం చేస్తాడు; అతను వివాదాన్ని నిర్ణయించడు. వినియోగదారుల మధ్యవర్తిత్వ కేంద్రం – మధ్యవర్తిత్వం జరిగే, రికార్డులు ఉంచే, ప్రతి కమిషన్‌కు ( జాతీయ కమిషన్ ప్రాంతీయ బెంచ్‌కు) అనుబంధంగా ఉన్న విభాగం (సెక్షన్లు 74, 79(1)). పరిష్కార ఒప్పందం – మధ్యవర్తిత్వంలో అన్ని లేదా కొన్ని అంశాలపై పక్షాలు అంగీకరించిన, లిఖితంగా రాసి సంతకం చేసిన షరతులు (సెక్షన్ 80(1)). కమిషన్ దానిని ఉత్తర్వు ద్వారా నమోదు చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 81).
keyPoints: ప్రత్యామ్నాయ వివాద పరిష్కారం: ఆర్బిట్రేషన్, కన్సిలియేషన్, న్యాయ పరిష్కారం / లోక్ అదాలత్, మధ్యవర్తిత్వం (CPC సెక్షన్ 89). CPA 2019 మధ్యవర్తిత్వం మాత్రమే అందిస్తుంది; 1986 చట్టంలో ఏదీ లేదు. సెక్షన్ 37: 5 రోజుల్లో సమ్మతి; 5 రోజుల్లో పంపడం; మూడు కమిషన్లకూ వర్తిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్లు 49(1), 59(1)). వినియోగదారుల మధ్యవర్తిత్వ కేంద్రం ప్రతి కమిషన్‌కు అనుబంధం (సెక్షన్ 74). 5 సంవత్సరాల ప్యానెల్ (సెక్షన్ 75); వెల్లడి (సెక్షన్ 77); సహజ న్యాయం (సెక్షన్ 79). పరిష్కార ఒప్పందం లిఖితం, సంతకం (సెక్షన్ 80); 7 రోజుల్లో ఉత్తర్వు (సెక్షన్ 81). పరిష్కార ఉత్తర్వుపై అప్పీలు లేదు (సెక్షన్ 41, మూడవ నిబంధన). నియమం 4 మినహాయింపులు; నియమం 5 పూర్తి రుసుము వాపసు. పొడిగించకపోతే మొదటి హాజరు నుండి 3 నెలల్లో మధ్యవర్తిత్వం ముగుస్తుంది. మధ్యవర్తిత్వ చట్టం, 2023 సెక్షన్ 65 అమలులోకి వచ్చినప్పుడు ఈ పథకాన్ని భర్తీ చేస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: CPC సెక్షన్ 89లోని ADR పద్ధతులు పేర్కొనండి. వినియోగదారుల కమిషన్ కేసును ఎప్పుడు, ఎలా మధ్యవర్తిత్వానికి పంపగలదు?
selfTest.a: మధ్యవర్తిత్వానికి పంపలేని మూడు రకాల కేసులు చెప్పండి. మధ్యవర్తిత్వం కొన్ని అంశాలను మాత్రమే పరిష్కరిస్తే ఏమవుతుంది? మధ్యవర్తిత్వ పరిష్కారాన్ని నమోదు చేసిన ఉత్తర్వుపై అప్పీలు ఉందా? పరిష్కారంపై ఫిర్యాదుదారుకు ఏ ప్రయోజనం లభిస్తుంది?

hi.inOneMinute: ADR (alternative dispute resolution) means settling a dispute outside the usual contested trial, with the parties' agreement. Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure lists four modes (See Diagram 1 ): arbitration; conciliation ; judicial settlement, including Lok Adalat; mediation. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 builds one ADR method, mediation , into consumer cases. The 1986 Act had no such provision. How it works: At the first hearing after admission, or later, a Commission that sees "elements of a settlement" may ask the parties to consent in writing to mediation within five days (s. 37(1)). On consent, it refers the matter within five days (s. 37(2)). Mediation is held in the consumer mediation cell attached to the Commission, before an empanelled mediator (ss. 74–79). A settlement, full or partial, is put in writing and signed (s. 80). The Commission records it by order within seven days of the settlement report (s. 81). No appeal lies against that order (s. 41, third proviso). Not for mediation (rule 4, Consumer Protection (Mediation) Rules, 2020): medical negligence resulting in grievous injury or death; serious allegations of fraud, forgery and the like; criminal non-compoundable offences; matters of public interest or of numerous persons not before the Commission; and matters where compounding of offences is sought. If settled, the complainant gets back the full complaint fee (rule 5).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act 35 of 2019)

Section 2(25): "mediation" means "the process by which a mediator mediates the consumer disputes". Section 2(26): "mediator" means a mediator referred to in s. 75. Section 37(1): "At the first hearing of the complaint after its admission, or at any later stage, if it appears to the District Commission that there exists elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, except in such cases as may be prescribed, it may direct the parties to give in writing, within five days, consent to have their dispute settled by mediation in accordance with the provisions of Chapter V." Section 37(2): "Where the parties agree for settlement by mediation and give their consent in writing, the District Commission shall, within five days of receipt of such consent, refer the matter for mediation, and in such case, the provisions of Chapter V, relating to mediation, shall apply." Sections 49(1) and 59(1): ss. 35 to 39, including s. 37, apply "with such modifications as may be necessary" to complaints before the State and National Commissions. Section 74: a consumer mediation cell is attached to each District and State Commission (by the State Government) and to the National Commission and each regional Bench (by the Central Government). It maintains: a list of empanelled mediators; a list of cases; the record of proceedings; a quarterly report to its Commission. Section 75: a panel of mediators is prepared on the recommendation of a selection committee of "the President and a member of that Commission". It is valid for five years. Section 77: the mediator must disclose any personal, professional or financial interest, and circumstances giving rise to "a justifiable doubt as to his independence or impartiality". Section 79(2): the mediator "shall have regard to the rights and obligations of the parties, the usages of trade, if any, the circumstances giving rise to the consumer dispute and such other relevant factors", and "shall be guided by the principles of natural justice". Section 80: an agreement on all or some issues "shall be reduced to writing accordingly, and signed by the parties". The mediator sends a settlement report. If there is no agreement, he reports that. Section 81: (1) the Commission shall, "within seven days of the receipt of the settlement report, pass suitable order recording such settlement of consumer dispute and dispose of the matter accordingly"; (2) where only part is settled, it records that part and hears the rest; (3) where nothing is settled, it hears all issues. Section 41, third proviso: "no appeal shall lie from any order passed under sub-section (1) of section 81 by the District Commission pursuant to a settlement by mediation under section 80."
Consumer Protection (Mediation) Rules, 2020 (G.S.R. 450(E), 15 July 2020)

Rule 4: matters "not to be referred to mediation": (a) "proceedings in respect of medical negligence resulting in grievous injury or death"; (b) defaults or offences for which compounding has been applied for; (c) "serious and specific allegations of fraud, fabrication of documents, forgery, impersonation, coercion"; (d) "prosecution for criminal and non-compoundable offences"; (e) "cases which involve public interest or the interest of numerous persons who are not parties before the Commission". Proviso: even in other cases, the Commission may decline to refer if "no elements of a settlement exist" or mediation "is otherwise not appropriate". Rule 5: if settlement is reached, the complainant "shall be entitled to receive full amount of application fee paid in respect of such complaint". Rule 6: the parties shall not start arbitral or judicial proceedings on a matter that is the subject of the mediation.

Consumer Protection (Mediation) Regulations, 2020 – regulation 11(2): mediation "shall stand terminated on expiry of three months from the date of first appearance before the mediator", unless the Commission extends the time.

Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 – Section 89(1): where "there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties", the court may refer the dispute for "(a) arbitration; (b) conciliation; (c) judicial settlement including settlement through Lok Adalat; or (d) mediation".
hi.meaning: Alternative dispute resolution – methods of settling a dispute outside a contested hearing, with the help of a neutral person and the consent of the parties. Section 89 CPC lists arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement (including Lok Adalat) and mediation . Mediation – under the CPA 2019, "the process by which a mediator mediates the consumer disputes" (s. 2(25)). The mediator helps the parties reach their own agreement; he does not decide the dispute. Consumer mediation cell – the unit attached to each Commission (and regional Bench of the National Commission ) where mediation is held and records are kept (ss. 74, 79(1)). Settlement agreement – the written, signed terms the parties agree on in mediation, on all or some of the issues (s. 80(1)). The Commission records it by order (s. 81).
keyPoints: Alternative dispute resolution: arbitration, conciliation, judicial settlement / Lok Adalat, mediation (s. 89 CPC). CPA 2019 provides mediation only; the 1986 Act had none. s. 37: consent in 5 days; reference in 5 days; applies to all three Commissions (ss. 49(1), 59(1)). Consumer mediation cell attached to each Commission (s. 74). Panel for 5 years (s. 75); disclosure (s. 77); natural justice (s. 79). Settlement agreement written and signed (s. 80); order in 7 days (s. 81). No appeal from the settlement order (s. 41, third proviso). Rule 4 exclusions; rule 5 full fee refund. Mediation ends 3 months after first appearance unless extended. Mediation Act, 2023 s. 65 will replace the scheme when brought into force.

en.meaning:
Under Section 2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a 'consumer' is a person who buys goods or avails a service for consideration, but excludes a person acting for a

Explanation. A person who buys goods or avails a service for a 'commercial purpose' is excluded from the definition of 'consumer' under Section 2(7).

Which of the following buyers is NOT excluded from being a 'consumer', despite the commercial-purpose exclusion?

Explanation. The Act expressly carves out goods bought and used exclusively for earning one's livelihood through self-employment from the commercial-purpose exclusion.

Besides the person who actually pays for goods or a service, who else does the definition of 'consumer' include?

Explanation. The definition extends to a user of goods with the buyer's approval and a beneficiary of a service with the hirer's approval, even if they did not personally pay.

How many consumer rights does the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 expressly recognise?

law-of-torts-u5-t20.subtitle: What counts as a misleading advertisement, and the penalties the Central Authority and the courts can impose

en.inOneMinute: A misleading advertisement (CPA 2019, s. 2(28)) is one which (i) falsely describes a product or service; (ii) gives a false guarantee or is likely to mislead about its nature, substance, quantity or quality; (iii) conveys a representation that would be an unfair trade practice if made by the manufacturer, seller or service provider; or (iv) "deliberately conceals important information". The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 attacks such advertisements on three tracks (See Diagram 1 ): Administrative penalty by the Central Consumer Protection Authority (s. 21): directions to stop or modify; penalty on a manufacturer or endorser up to ₹10 lakh (every subsequent contravention up to ₹50 lakh ); ban on an endorser up to one year (subsequent: three years ); penalty on a publisher up to ₹10 lakh . Criminal punishment by a court (s. 89): a manufacturer or service provider who causes a false or misleading advertisement prejudicial to consumers – imprisonment up to two years and fine up to ₹10 lakh ; every subsequent offence – up to five years and fine up to ₹50 lakh . Cognizance only on the Central Authority's complaint (s. 92). Disobeying the Authority's directions is a separate offence (s. 88: up to six months, or fine up to ₹20 lakh, or both). Civil relief by a Consumer Commission (s. 39(1)(l), (n)): a corrective advertisement at the advertiser's cost, and an order to "cease and desist". Defences: an endorser who exercised due diligence escapes the s. 21 penalty and ban (s. 21(5)); a person who published "in the ordinary course of his business" escapes, unless he already knew of the Authority's order (s. 21(6)). Hearing is compulsory before a s. 21 order (s. 21(8)); appeal to the National Commission within thirty days (s. 24).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 2(1) – "advertisement" means "any audio or visual publicity, representation, endorsement or pronouncement made by means of light, sound, smoke, gas, print, electronic media, internet or website and includes any notice, circular, label, wrapper, invoice or such other documents". s. 2(18) – " endorsement ", in relation to an advertisement, means "(i) any message, verbal statement, demonstration; or (ii) depiction of the name, signature, likeness or other identifiable personal characteristics of an individual; or (iii) depiction of the name or seal of any institution or organisation, which makes the consumer to believe that it reflects the opinion, finding or experience of the person making such endorsement". s. 2(28) – "misleading advertisement" in relation to any product or service, means an advertisement, which— "(i) falsely describes such product or service; or (ii) gives a false guarantee to, or is likely to mislead the consumers as to the nature, substance, quantity or quality of such product or service; or (iii) conveys an express or implied representation which, if made by the manufacturer or seller or service provider thereof, would constitute an unfair trade practice; or (iv) deliberately conceals important information". s. 2(47)(i) – unfair trade practices include false statements about standard or quality of goods or services (cl. (a), (b)), representing benefits that goods or services "do not have" (cl. (d)), "a false or misleading representation concerning the need for, or the usefulness of, any goods or services" (cl. (f)), and a "warranty or guarantee of the performance, efficacy or length of life of a product ... that is not based on an adequate or proper test thereof" (cl. (g)); under the proviso to cl. (g), "the burden of proof of such defence shall lie on the person raising such defence". s. 10(1) – the Central Authority is set up "to regulate matters relating to ... false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers". s. 18(1)(c), (d) – the Central Authority shall "ensure that no false or misleading advertisement is made of any goods or services" and "ensure that no person takes part in the publication of any advertisement which is false or misleading". s. 21(1) – "Where the Central Authority is satisfied after investigation that any advertisement is false or misleading and is prejudicial to the interest of any consumer or is in contravention of consumer rights, it may, by order, issue directions to the concerned trader or manufacturer or endorser or advertiser or publisher, as the case may be, to discontinue such advertisement or to modify the same in such manner and within such time as may be specified in that order." s. 21(2) – "Notwithstanding the order passed under sub-section (1), if the Central Authority is of the opinion that it is necessary to impose a penalty in respect of such false or misleading advertisement, by a manufacturer or an endorser, it may, by order, impose on manufacturer or endorser a penalty which may extend to ten lakh rupees: Provided that the Central Authority may, for every subsequent contravention by a manufacturer or endorser, impose a penalty, which may extend to fifty lakh rupees." s. 21(3) – the Authority "may, by order, prohibit the endorser of a false or misleading advertisement from making endorsement of any product or service for a period which may extend to one year: Provided that the Central Authority may, for every subsequent contravention, prohibit such endorser from making endorsement in respect of any product or service for a period which may extend to three years." s. 21(4) – "Where the Central Authority is satisfied after investigation that any person is found to publish, or is a party to the publication of, a misleading advertisement, it may impose on such person a penalty which may extend to ten lakh rupees." s. 21(5) – "No endorser shall be liable to a penalty under sub-sections (2) and (3) if he has exercised due diligence to verify the veracity of the claims made in the advertisement regarding the product or service being endorsed by him." s. 21(6) – "No person shall be liable to such penalty if he proves that he had published or arranged for the publication of such advertisement in the ordinary course of his business: Provided that no such defence shall be available to such person if he had previous knowledge of the order passed by the Central Authority for withdrawal or modification of such advertisement." s. 21(7) – "While determining the penalty under this section, regard shall be had to the following, namely:— (a) the population and the area impacted or affected by such offence; (b) the frequency and duration of such offence; (c) the vulnerability of the class of persons likely to be adversely affected by such offence; and (d) the gross revenue from the sales effected by virtue of such offence." s. 21(8) – "The Central Authority shall give the person an opportunity of being heard before an order under this section is passed." s. 24 – appeal against an order under ss. 20 and 21 "to the National Commission within a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of such order". s. 39(1)(l) – the District Commission may order the opposite party "to issue corrective advertisement to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement at the cost of the opposite party responsible for issuing such misleading advertisement"; s. 39(1)(n) – "to cease and desist from issuing any misleading advertisement". (The State and National Commissions have the same powers when hearing complaints, through ss. 49(1) and 59(1).) s. 88 – "Whoever, fails to comply with any direction of the Central Authority under sections 20 and 21, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with fine which may extend to twenty lakh rupees, or with both." s. 89 – "Any manufacturer or service provider who causes a false or misleading advertisement to be made which is prejudicial to the interest of consumers shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees; and for every subsequent offence, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years and with fine which may extend to fifty lakh rupees." s. 92 – "No cognizance shall be taken by a competent court of any offence under sections 88 and 89 except on a complaint filed by the Central Authority or any officer authorised by it in this behalf." s. 96 – offences under ss. 88 and 89 may be compounded, before or after prosecution, on payment of the prescribed amount, with leave of the court where a complaint is filed; the sum cannot exceed the maximum fine; compounding is not available for the same or a similar offence within three years of an earlier compounding (s. 96(3)). s. 97 – "The penalty collected under section 21 and the amount collected under section 96 shall be credited to such fund as may be prescribed."
en.meaning: Advertisement – any audio or visual publicity, representation, endorsement or pronouncement, in any medium including internet and website; it includes labels, wrappers and invoices (s. 2(1)). So a statement on a product's label is an advertisement. Misleading advertisement – an advertisement falling within any of the four clauses of s. 2(28). One clause is enough (See Diagram 2 ). False advertisement – the Act uses the words "false or misleading" in ss. 10, 18, 21 and 89 but defines only "misleading advertisement". A false advertisement is one whose statement is untrue; it will usually also fall within s. 2(28)(i). Endorsement – a message, statement or demonstration, or the depiction of an individual's name or likeness, or an institution's name or seal, that makes the consumer believe it reflects the endorser's "opinion, finding or experience" (s. 2(18)). The endorser is the person who gives it. Due diligence – reasonable care taken to "verify the veracity of the claims" before endorsing (s. 21(5)). Corrective advertisement – an advertisement ordered by a Consumer Commission "to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement", paid for by the party responsible (s. 39(1)(l)). Subsequent contravention / offence – a repeat violation after the first; the Act raises the maximum penalty or punishment for it (s. 21(2) proviso, (3) proviso; s. 89).
keyPoints: s. 2(28): four kinds of misleading advertisement; "likely to mislead" is enough. s. 2(1): advertisement includes label, wrapper, invoice; internet and website. s. 21(2): manufacturer or endorser – ₹10 lakh; subsequent ₹50 lakh. s. 21(3): endorser ban – 1 year; subsequent 3 years. s. 21(4): publisher – ₹10 lakh. s. 21(5): endorser's due diligence; s. 21(6): ordinary course of business. s. 21(7): four factors; s. 21(8): hearing. s. 89: 2 years and ₹10 lakh; subsequent 5 years and ₹50 lakh. s. 88: disobeying directions – 6 months or ₹20 lakh, or both. s. 92: prosecution only on Authority's complaint. s. 39(1)(l), (n): corrective advertisement; cease and desist. s. 24: appeal to National Commission, 30 days.

Challenge Appeal to National Commission in 30 days (s. 24) Ordinary criminal appeal
Settlement – Compounding under s. 96

te.inOneMinute: తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటన (CPA 2019, సెక్షన్ 2(28)) అంటే (i) ఉత్పత్తి లేదా సేవను తప్పుగా వర్ణించేది; (ii) తప్పుడు హామీ ఇచ్చేది లేదా దాని స్వభావం, సారం, పరిమాణం లేదా నాణ్యత గురించి తప్పుదారి పట్టించే అవకాశం ఉన్నది; (iii) తయారీదారు, విక్రేత లేదా సేవా ప్రదాత చేస్తే అన్యాయ వ్యాపార పద్ధతి అయ్యే ప్రాతినిధ్యాన్ని తెలిపేది; లేదా (iv) "deliberately conceals important information" (అర్థం: ముఖ్యమైన సమాచారాన్ని ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా దాచేది). వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019 అలాంటి ప్రకటనలపై మూడు మార్గాలలో చర్య తీసుకుంటుంది ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి): కేంద్ర వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ ప్రాధికార సంస్థ విధించే పరిపాలనా జరిమానా (సెక్షన్ 21): ఆపమని లేదా మార్చమని ఆదేశాలు; తయారీదారు లేదా ఎండార్సర్‌పై ₹10 లక్షల వరకు జరిమానా (ప్రతి తర్వాతి ఉల్లంఘనకు ₹50 లక్షల వరకు); ఎండార్సర్‌పై ఒక సంవత్సరం వరకు నిషేధం (తర్వాత: మూడు సంవత్సరాలు ); ప్రచురణకర్తపై ₹10 లక్షల వరకు జరిమానా. కోర్టు విధించే క్రిమినల్ శిక్ష (సెక్షన్ 89): వినియోగదారులకు హానికరమైన తప్పుడు లేదా తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటన చేయించే తయారీదారు లేదా సేవా ప్రదాతకు – రెండు సంవత్సరాల వరకు జైలు మరియు ₹10 లక్షల వరకు జరిమానా; ప్రతి తర్వాతి నేరానికి – ఐదు సంవత్సరాల వరకు మరియు ₹50 లక్షల వరకు జరిమానా. కేంద్ర ప్రాధికార సంస్థ ఫిర్యాదుపై మాత్రమే కోర్టు స్వీకరణ (సెక్షన్ 92). ప్రాధికార సంస్థ ఆదేశాలను పాటించకపోవడం వేరే నేరం (సెక్షన్ 88: ఆరు నెలల వరకు, లేదా ₹20 లక్షల వరకు జరిమానా, లేదా రెండూ). వినియోగదారుల కమిషన్ ఇచ్చే సివిల్ ఉపశమనం (సెక్షన్ 39(1)(l), (n)): ప్రకటనదారు ఖర్చుతో సవరణ ప్రకటన , "cease and desist" (అర్థం: నిలిపివేసి మానుకోవాలి) అనే ఉత్తర్వు. రక్షణలు: తగిన శ్రద్ధ (due diligence) వహించిన ఎండార్సర్ సెక్షన్ 21 జరిమానా, నిషేధం నుండి తప్పించుకుంటాడు (సెక్షన్ 21(5)); "in the ordinary course of his business" (అర్థం: తన సాధారణ వ్యాపార క్రమంలో) ప్రచురించిన వ్యక్తి తప్పించుకుంటాడు, ప్రాధికార సంస్థ ఉత్తర్వు గురించి ముందే తెలిసి ఉంటే తప్ప (సెక్షన్ 21(6)). సెక్షన్ 21 ఉత్తర్వుకు ముందు విచారణ అవకాశం తప్పనిసరి (సెక్షన్ 21(8)); ముప్పై రోజుల్లో జాతీయ కమిషన్‌కు అప్పీల్ (సెక్షన్ 24).
te.meaning: ప్రకటన (Advertisement) – ఇంటర్నెట్, వెబ్‌సైట్‌తో సహా ఏ మాధ్యమంలోనైనా శ్రవ్య లేదా దృశ్య ప్రచారం, ప్రాతినిధ్యం, ఎండార్స్‌మెంట్ లేదా ప్రకటన; లేబుల్‌లు, రేపర్‌లు, ఇన్‌వాయిస్‌లు కూడా ఇందులోకి వస్తాయి (సెక్షన్ 2(1)). కాబట్టి ఉత్పత్తి లేబుల్ మీద ఉన్న వాక్యం కూడా ప్రకటనే. తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటన – సెక్షన్ 2(28)లోని నాలుగు క్లాజులలో ఏదో ఒకదాని కిందికి వచ్చే ప్రకటన. ఒక క్లాజు చాలు ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి). తప్పుడు ప్రకటన (False advertisement) – చట్టం సెక్షన్లు 10, 18, 21, 89లో "false or misleading" (అర్థం: తప్పుడు లేదా తప్పుదారి పట్టించే) అనే పదాలు వాడుతుంది, కానీ "misleading advertisement" ను మాత్రమే నిర్వచిస్తుంది. తప్పుడు ప్రకటన అంటే దాని వాక్యం అసత్యమైనది; అది సాధారణంగా సెక్షన్ 2(28)(i) కిందికి కూడా వస్తుంది. ఎండార్స్‌మెంట్ (సమర్థన) – ఎండార్సర్ "opinion, finding or experience" (అర్థం: అభిప్రాయం, పరిశీలన లేదా అనుభవం) ను ప్రతిబింబిస్తుందని వినియోగదారు నమ్మేలా చేసే సందేశం, వాక్యం లేదా ప్రదర్శన, లేదా ఒక వ్యక్తి పేరు లేదా రూపం, లేదా ఒక సంస్థ పేరు లేదా ముద్ర చిత్రణ (సెక్షన్ 2(18)). దానిని ఇచ్చే వ్యక్తే ఎండార్సర్. తగిన శ్రద్ధ (due diligence) – ఎండార్స్ చేసే ముందు "verify the veracity of the claims" (అర్థం: వాదనల నిజానిజాలను ధృవీకరించడానికి) తీసుకునే సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త (సెక్షన్ 21(5)). సవరణ ప్రకటన – "to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement" (అర్థం: తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటన ప్రభావాన్ని తటస్థీకరించడానికి) వినియోగదారుల కమిషన్ ఆదేశించే ప్రకటన; ఖర్చు బాధ్యుడైన పక్షమే భరిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 39(1)(l)). తర్వాతి ఉల్లంఘన / నేరం – మొదటిదాని తర్వాత మళ్లీ చేసే ఉల్లంఘన; దానికి చట్టం గరిష్ఠ జరిమానా లేదా శిక్షను పెంచుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 21(2) నిబంధన, (3) నిబంధన; సెక్షన్ 89).
keyPoints: సెక్షన్ 2(28): నాలుగు రకాల తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటనలు; "likely to mislead" (అర్థం: తప్పుదారి పట్టించే అవకాశం) చాలు. సెక్షన్ 2(1): ప్రకటనలో లేబుల్, రేపర్, ఇన్‌వాయిస్; ఇంటర్నెట్, వెబ్‌సైట్ ఉన్నాయి. సెక్షన్ 21(2): తయారీదారు లేదా ఎండార్సర్ – ₹10 లక్షలు; తర్వాత ₹50 లక్షలు. సెక్షన్ 21(3): ఎండార్సర్ నిషేధం – 1 సంవత్సరం; తర్వాత 3 సంవత్సరాలు. సెక్షన్ 21(4): ప్రచురణకర్త – ₹10 లక్షలు. సెక్షన్ 21(5): ఎండార్సర్ తగిన శ్రద్ధ; సెక్షన్ 21(6): సాధారణ వ్యాపార క్రమం. సెక్షన్ 21(7): నాలుగు అంశాలు; సెక్షన్ 21(8): విచారణ అవకాశం. సెక్షన్ 89: 2 సంవత్సరాలు మరియు ₹10 లక్షలు; తర్వాత 5 సంవత్సరాలు మరియు ₹50 లక్షలు. సెక్షన్ 88: ఆదేశాలు పాటించకపోవడం – 6 నెలలు లేదా ₹20 లక్షలు, లేదా రెండూ. సెక్షన్ 92: ప్రాధికార సంస్థ ఫిర్యాదుపై మాత్రమే ప్రాసిక్యూషన్. సెక్షన్ 39(1)(l), (n): సవరణ ప్రకటన; నిలిపివేసి మానుకోవడం. సెక్షన్ 24: జాతీయ కమిషన్‌కు అప్పీల్, 30 రోజులు.

selfTest.q: సెక్షన్ 2(28)లోని నాలుగు క్లాజులు రాయండి. "advertisement" ఉత్పత్తి లేబుల్‌ను కవర్ చేస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: మొదటి, తర్వాతి ఉల్లంఘనకు సెక్షన్ 21(2) కింద గరిష్ఠ జరిమానా ఎంత? ఎండార్సర్‌ను ఎంత కాలం నిషేధించవచ్చు? ఎండార్సర్ రక్షణ ఏమిటి? సెక్షన్ 89 కింద శిక్ష చెప్పండి. సెక్షన్ 89 కింద నేరానికి ఎవరు ఫిర్యాదు దాఖలు చేయవచ్చు? తప్పుదారి పట్టించే ప్రకటనపై వినియోగదారుల కమిషన్ ఏ పరిష్కారాలు ఇవ్వగలదు?

hi.inOneMinute: A misleading advertisement (CPA 2019, s. 2(28)) is one which (i) falsely describes a product or service; (ii) gives a false guarantee or is likely to mislead about its nature, substance, quantity or quality; (iii) conveys a representation that would be an unfair trade practice if made by the manufacturer, seller or service provider; or (iv) "deliberately conceals important information". The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 attacks such advertisements on three tracks (See Diagram 1 ): Administrative penalty by the Central Consumer Protection Authority (s. 21): directions to stop or modify; penalty on a manufacturer or endorser up to ₹10 lakh (every subsequent contravention up to ₹50 lakh ); ban on an endorser up to one year (subsequent: three years ); penalty on a publisher up to ₹10 lakh . Criminal punishment by a court (s. 89): a manufacturer or service provider who causes a false or misleading advertisement prejudicial to consumers – imprisonment up to two years and fine up to ₹10 lakh ; every subsequent offence – up to five years and fine up to ₹50 lakh . Cognizance only on the Central Authority's complaint (s. 92). Disobeying the Authority's directions is a separate offence (s. 88: up to six months, or fine up to ₹20 lakh, or both). Civil relief by a Consumer Commission (s. 39(1)(l), (n)): a corrective advertisement at the advertiser's cost, and an order to "cease and desist". Defences: an endorser who exercised due diligence escapes the s. 21 penalty and ban (s. 21(5)); a person who published "in the ordinary course of his business" escapes, unless he already knew of the Authority's order (s. 21(6)). Hearing is compulsory before a s. 21 order (s. 21(8)); appeal to the National Commission within thirty days (s. 24).
legalProvision: Consumer Protection Act, 2019

s. 2(1) – "advertisement" means "any audio or visual publicity, representation, endorsement or pronouncement made by means of light, sound, smoke, gas, print, electronic media, internet or website and includes any notice, circular, label, wrapper, invoice or such other documents". s. 2(18) – " endorsement ", in relation to an advertisement, means "(i) any message, verbal statement, demonstration; or (ii) depiction of the name, signature, likeness or other identifiable personal characteristics of an individual; or (iii) depiction of the name or seal of any institution or organisation, which makes the consumer to believe that it reflects the opinion, finding or experience of the person making such endorsement". s. 2(28) – "misleading advertisement" in relation to any product or service, means an advertisement, which— "(i) falsely describes such product or service; or (ii) gives a false guarantee to, or is likely to mislead the consumers as to the nature, substance, quantity or quality of such product or service; or (iii) conveys an express or implied representation which, if made by the manufacturer or seller or service provider thereof, would constitute an unfair trade practice; or (iv) deliberately conceals important information". s. 2(47)(i) – unfair trade practices include false statements about standard or quality of goods or services (cl. (a), (b)), representing benefits that goods or services "do not have" (cl. (d)), "a false or misleading representation concerning the need for, or the usefulness of, any goods or services" (cl. (f)), and a "warranty or guarantee of the performance, efficacy or length of life of a product ... that is not based on an adequate or proper test thereof" (cl. (g)); under the proviso to cl. (g), "the burden of proof of such defence shall lie on the person raising such defence". s. 10(1) – the Central Authority is set up "to regulate matters relating to ... false or misleading advertisements which are prejudicial to the interests of public and consumers". s. 18(1)(c), (d) – the Central Authority shall "ensure that no false or misleading advertisement is made of any goods or services" and "ensure that no person takes part in the publication of any advertisement which is false or misleading". s. 21(1) – "Where the Central Authority is satisfied after investigation that any advertisement is false or misleading and is prejudicial to the interest of any consumer or is in contravention of consumer rights, it may, by order, issue directions to the concerned trader or manufacturer or endorser or advertiser or publisher, as the case may be, to discontinue such advertisement or to modify the same in such manner and within such time as may be specified in that order." s. 21(2) – "Notwithstanding the order passed under sub-section (1), if the Central Authority is of the opinion that it is necessary to impose a penalty in respect of such false or misleading advertisement, by a manufacturer or an endorser, it may, by order, impose on manufacturer or endorser a penalty which may extend to ten lakh rupees: Provided that the Central Authority may, for every subsequent contravention by a manufacturer or endorser, impose a penalty, which may extend to fifty lakh rupees." s. 21(3) – the Authority "may, by order, prohibit the endorser of a false or misleading advertisement from making endorsement of any product or service for a period which may extend to one year: Provided that the Central Authority may, for every subsequent contravention, prohibit such endorser from making endorsement in respect of any product or service for a period which may extend to three years." s. 21(4) – "Where the Central Authority is satisfied after investigation that any person is found to publish, or is a party to the publication of, a misleading advertisement, it may impose on such person a penalty which may extend to ten lakh rupees." s. 21(5) – "No endorser shall be liable to a penalty under sub-sections (2) and (3) if he has exercised due diligence to verify the veracity of the claims made in the advertisement regarding the product or service being endorsed by him." s. 21(6) – "No person shall be liable to such penalty if he proves that he had published or arranged for the publication of such advertisement in the ordinary course of his business: Provided that no such defence shall be available to such person if he had previous knowledge of the order passed by the Central Authority for withdrawal or modification of such advertisement." s. 21(7) – "While determining the penalty under this section, regard shall be had to the following, namely:— (a) the population and the area impacted or affected by such offence; (b) the frequency and duration of such offence; (c) the vulnerability of the class of persons likely to be adversely affected by such offence; and (d) the gross revenue from the sales effected by virtue of such offence." s. 21(8) – "The Central Authority shall give the person an opportunity of being heard before an order under this section is passed." s. 24 – appeal against an order under ss. 20 and 21 "to the National Commission within a period of thirty days from the date of receipt of such order". s. 39(1)(l) – the District Commission may order the opposite party "to issue corrective advertisement to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement at the cost of the opposite party responsible for issuing such misleading advertisement"; s. 39(1)(n) – "to cease and desist from issuing any misleading advertisement". (The State and National Commissions have the same powers when hearing complaints, through ss. 49(1) and 59(1).) s. 88 – "Whoever, fails to comply with any direction of the Central Authority under sections 20 and 21, shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months or with fine which may extend to twenty lakh rupees, or with both." s. 89 – "Any manufacturer or service provider who causes a false or misleading advertisement to be made which is prejudicial to the interest of consumers shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with fine which may extend to ten lakh rupees; and for every subsequent offence, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years and with fine which may extend to fifty lakh rupees." s. 92 – "No cognizance shall be taken by a competent court of any offence under sections 88 and 89 except on a complaint filed by the Central Authority or any officer authorised by it in this behalf." s. 96 – offences under ss. 88 and 89 may be compounded, before or after prosecution, on payment of the prescribed amount, with leave of the court where a complaint is filed; the sum cannot exceed the maximum fine; compounding is not available for the same or a similar offence within three years of an earlier compounding (s. 96(3)). s. 97 – "The penalty collected under section 21 and the amount collected under section 96 shall be credited to such fund as may be prescribed."
hi.meaning: Advertisement – any audio or visual publicity, representation, endorsement or pronouncement, in any medium including internet and website; it includes labels, wrappers and invoices (s. 2(1)). So a statement on a product's label is an advertisement. Misleading advertisement – an advertisement falling within any of the four clauses of s. 2(28). One clause is enough (See Diagram 2 ). False advertisement – the Act uses the words "false or misleading" in ss. 10, 18, 21 and 89 but defines only "misleading advertisement". A false advertisement is one whose statement is untrue; it will usually also fall within s. 2(28)(i). Endorsement – a message, statement or demonstration, or the depiction of an individual's name or likeness, or an institution's name or seal, that makes the consumer believe it reflects the endorser's "opinion, finding or experience" (s. 2(18)). The endorser is the person who gives it. Due diligence – reasonable care taken to "verify the veracity of the claims" before endorsing (s. 21(5)). Corrective advertisement – an advertisement ordered by a Consumer Commission "to neutralise the effect of misleading advertisement", paid for by the party responsible (s. 39(1)(l)). Subsequent contravention / offence – a repeat violation after the first; the Act raises the maximum penalty or punishment for it (s. 21(2) proviso, (3) proviso; s. 89).
keyPoints: s. 2(28): four kinds of misleading advertisement; "likely to mislead" is enough. s. 2(1): advertisement includes label, wrapper, invoice; internet and website. s. 21(2): manufacturer or endorser – ₹10 lakh; subsequent ₹50 lakh. s. 21(3): endorser ban – 1 year; subsequent 3 years. s. 21(4): publisher – ₹10 lakh. s. 21(5): endorser's due diligence; s. 21(6): ordinary course of business. s. 21(7): four factors; s. 21(8): hearing. s. 89: 2 years and ₹10 lakh; subsequent 5 years and ₹50 lakh. s. 88: disobeying directions – 6 months or ₹20 lakh, or both. s. 92: prosecution only on Authority's complaint. s. 39(1)(l), (n): corrective advertisement; cease and desist. s. 24: appeal to National Commission, 30 days.

en.meaning:
Under Section 2(10) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, 'defect' applies to

Explanation. 'Defect' under Section 2(10) is defined specifically in relation to goods or products.

A trader advertises a claim about a product's performance that the product does not actually meet, even though no separate law or contract required that specific standard. Can this still amount to a 'defect'?

Explanation. 'Defect' under Section 2(10) expressly includes a shortfall against a standard 'claimed by the trader in any manner whatsoever' about the goods.

Under Section 2(11), 'deficiency' in a service expressly includes

Explanation. Section 2(11) expressly writes negligence and deliberate withholding of relevant information into the definition of 'deficiency'.

How does proof of a defect in goods usually differ from proof of a deficiency in a service?

en.meaning:
How many tiers of Consumer Protection Councils does the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 establish?

Explanation. The Act establishes a three-tier structure of Consumer Protection Councils — Central, State, and District.

Who chairs the Central Consumer Protection Council?

Explanation. The Central Consumer Protection Council is chaired by the Union Minister in charge of Consumer Affairs.

Who chairs the District Consumer Protection Council?

Explanation. The District Consumer Protection Council is chaired by the District Collector or an equivalent officer.

What is the core object of every Consumer Protection Council, regardless of level?

en.meaning:
Under which section of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 is the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) established?

Explanation. Section 10 empowers the Central Government to establish the CCPA by notification.

What is the key difference between the CCPA and the District/State/National Commissions?

Explanation. The CCPA's mandate is regulatory/preventive protection of consumers as a class, distinct from the Commissions' role of adjudicating individual complaints.

On what basis can the CCPA initiate an inquiry or investigation?

Explanation. The CCPA can act suo motu (on its own initiative), on a complaint, or on the direction of the Central Government.

Who heads the CCPA's Investigation Wing?

en.meaning:
Which chapter of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 introduces the formal mediation mechanism?

Explanation. Chapter V, Sections 74 to 81, introduces the formal statutory mediation mechanism under the 2019 Act.

Under Section 74, where are consumer mediation cells attached?

Explanation. Section 74 requires mediation cells attached to District Commissions, State Commissions, the National Commission, and its regional Benches.

How are mediators selected under Sections 75-76?

Explanation. Mediators are empanelled by the Commission, and for each dispute referred to mediation, one is nominated from that empanelled panel.

What must a mediator disclose under Section 77?

law-of-torts-u5-t34.subtitle: Sourced from actual OU question papers (August/September 2013, May/June 2016, August/September 2016, March/April 2017 Code 564, May/June 2017, March/April 2018, June 2018, February 2026) — every question here is answerable entirely from what's already published on this site. This unit's Consumer Protection Act topic draws far fewer Part C problem questions from these papers than the pure-tort units, since the papers allocate most case-study questions to torts and motor-vehicle fact patterns rather than consumer-law scenarios; only two genuine Consumer Protection Act problem questions were found across all papers checked, and both are included below. Question 14 also completes the negligence question from this subject's Unit 4 Important Questions post, which answered only the negligence portion and deferred the Consumer Protection Law portion to this unit. Part A — Short Answer Consumer. Definition of Consumer Rights of the consumer. Rights of Consumers Unfair trade practices. Restrictive and Unfair Trade Practices Consumerism. Consumerism District Forum. (now the "District Commission" under the 2019 Act) Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: Jurisdiction and Powers Caveat emptor Rule. Consumerism Product liability. Liability of the Service Providers, Manufacturers and Traders under the Act- Product Liability Part B — Long Answer Discuss the Redressal Machinery under Consumer Protection Act. Redressal Machinery under the Consumer Protection Act Explain the importance and significance of consumer forums in the present global market. Redressal Machinery under the Consumer Protection Act Discuss the composition, jurisdiction, power and functions of consumer disputes redressal agencies. Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: Jurisdiction and Powers Redressal Machinery under the Consumer Protection Act Explain the law relating to composition and jurisdiction of District Consumer Forum. Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: Jurisdiction and Powers Explain the composition of State Commission. Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions: Jurisdiction and Powers Explain consumer rights and remedies under the Consumer Protection Act. Rights of Consumers Remedies Explain the term 'Negligence'. Analyse professional liability due to negligence with special reference to Consumer Protection Law. What is the fundamental character of civil liability under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?

Explanation. Civil liability under the Act is compensatory — refund, replacement, compensation, and discontinuation orders — not punitive.

Can civil liability and criminal liability under the Act arise from the same underlying conduct?

Explanation. Civil liability (before a Commission) and criminal liability (before a criminal court) can both arise from the same conduct, serving different purposes through different processes.

Under Section 89, the punishment for a first offence of causing a false or misleading advertisement prejudicial to consumers is

Explanation. Section 89 prescribes imprisonment up to two years and a fine up to ten lakh rupees for a first offence.

Under Section 89, what is the punishment for a subsequent (repeat) offence?

environmental-law-u1-t2.subtitle: The science of how living things relate to their surroundings, and why environmental law depends on it

en.inOneMinute: Ecology is the study of the relationships between living organisms and their environment. The word was coined by the German zoologist Ernst Haeckel as Ökologie , from the Greek oikos ("house, dwelling place") and -logia ("study of"). So ecology is the study of the "home" of living things. (See Diagram 1 .) Ecology studies living things at several levels: individual organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere. (See Diagram 2 .) Two main branches: autecology – the ecology of a single species; synecology – the ecology of communities of many species. Ecological balance is the stable state in which living things and their surroundings support each other. Human activity (mining, deforestation, pollution) can upset it. Indian courts protect ecological balance: RLEK (1985) was described as "the first case of its kind in the country involving issues relating to environment and ecological balance"; quarries were closed. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". The word "inter-relationship" brings the ecological idea into the law. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 21 – the courts read the right to a healthy environment and ecological balance into the right to life ( Virender Gaur : environment brings within its ambit "hygienic atmosphere and ecological balance").
en.meaning: Ecology – the "branch of science dealing with the relationship of living things to their environments" (etymological dictionary); "the study of the relationships between organisms and their environment" (encyclopaedia definition). Autecology – population ecology, which "examines single species". Synecology – community ecology, which "considers the ecology of communities, the set of species found in a particular place". Ecological balance – a stable state of a natural system in which the numbers of living things and the supply of air, water, food and space remain in a working balance over time.
keyPoints: Ecology: study of relationships between living things and their environment. Coined by Ernst Haeckel; oikos (house) + -logia (study). Autecology: one species. Synecology: communities. Levels: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, biosphere. Ecological balance is protected by courts ( RLEK , 1985). EP Act s. 2(a) "inter-relationship" reflects ecology in law.

caseLaws.facts: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. (1985) 2 SCC 431; AIR 1985 SC 652 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati CJ, A.N. Sen and R. Misra JJ; order of 12 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter from an organisation in Dehradun complained that limestone quarrying in the Dehradun
caseLaws.facts: The letter was treated as a writ petition. An expert committee (the Bhargav Committee) placed the quarries in categories A, B and C. Principle: The Court said this was "the first case of its kind in the country involving issues relating to environment and ecological balance" and ordered the closure of the most harmful quarries, accepting that the loss was "a price that has to be paid" for a healthy environment. Why it matters: It is the starting point of ecological protection by Indian courts.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur tanneries) (1987) 4 SCC 463 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J, K.N. Singh J concurring; 22 September 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries at Kanpur discharged untreated effluent into the Ganga
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A tannery that does not set up even a primary treatment plant "cannot be permitted to continue"; financial capacity is irrelevant. K.N. Singh J: "life, health and ecology have greater importance". Why it matters: It puts ecology above private profit and local economic loss.
Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal AIR 1987 SC 1109; (1987) 2 SCC 295 (Supreme Court; O. Chinnappa Reddy J, Khalid J concurring; 11 February 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land from the Alipore zoo area in Calcutta was given for a five-star hotel; it was challenged
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A". The appeal was dismissed on the facts. Why it matters: It makes ecology a constitutional consideration in every such case.

te.inOneMinute: జీవావరణ శాస్త్రం (Ecology) అంటే జీవులకు, వాటి పర్యావరణానికి మధ్య ఉన్న సంబంధాల అధ్యయనం. ఈ పదాన్ని జర్మన్ జంతుశాస్త్రవేత్త Ernst Haeckel Ökologie గా సృష్టించారు; గ్రీకు oikos ("ఇల్లు, నివాస స్థలం"), -logia ("అధ్యయనం") నుండి. కాబట్టి జీవావరణ శాస్త్రం అంటే జీవుల "ఇంటి" అధ్యయనం. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) జీవావరణ శాస్త్రం జీవులను అనేక స్థాయిల్లో అధ్యయనం చేస్తుంది: వ్యక్తిగత జీవి, జనాభా, సముదాయం, పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ, బయోమ్, జీవ మండలం. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) రెండు ముఖ్య శాఖలు: ఆటెకాలజీ (autecology) – ఒకే జాతి జీవావరణం; సినెకాలజీ (synecology) – అనేక జాతుల సముదాయాల జీవావరణం. పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యత (Ecological balance) అంటే జీవులు, వాటి పరిసరాలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఆధారంగా నిలిచే స్థిర స్థితి. మానవ కార్యకలాపాలు (గనుల తవ్వకం, అడవుల నరికివేత, కాలుష్యం) దానిని దెబ్బతీయవచ్చు. భారత కోర్టులు పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యతను రక్షిస్తాయి: RLEK (1985) ను "the first case of its kind in the country involving issues relating to environment and ecological balance" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణం, పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యతకు సంబంధించిన సమస్యలపై దేశంలో ఈ రకమైన మొదటి కేసు) అని వర్ణించారు; క్వారీలు మూసివేయబడ్డాయి. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: జీవావరణ శాస్త్రం (Ecology) – "branch of science dealing with the relationship of living things to their environments" (అర్థం: జీవులకు వాటి పర్యావరణాలతో ఉన్న సంబంధం గురించి వ్యవహరించే శాస్త్ర శాఖ) (పద వ్యుత్పత్తి నిఘంటువు); "the study of the relationships between organisms and their environment" (అర్థం: జీవులు, వాటి పర్యావరణం మధ్య సంబంధాల అధ్యయనం) (విజ్ఞాన సర్వస్వ నిర్వచనం). ఆటెకాలజీ (Autecology) – జనాభా జీవావరణ శాస్త్రం; ఇది "examines single species" (అర్థం: ఒకే జాతిని పరిశీలిస్తుంది). సినెకాలజీ (Synecology) – సముదాయ జీవావరణ శాస్త్రం; ఇది "considers the ecology of communities, the set of species found in a particular place" (అర్థం: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట ప్రదేశంలో కనిపించే జాతుల సమూహమైన సముదాయాల జీవావరణాన్ని పరిశీలిస్తుంది). పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యత (Ecological balance) – జీవుల సంఖ్య, గాలి, నీరు, ఆహారం, స్థలం సరఫరా కాలక్రమేణా పనిచేసే సమతుల్యంలో ఉండే సహజ వ్యవస్థ స్థిర స్థితి.
keyPoints: జీవావరణ శాస్త్రం: జీవులకు, వాటి పర్యావరణానికి మధ్య సంబంధాల అధ్యయనం. Ernst Haeckel సృష్టించారు; oikos (ఇల్లు) + -logia (అధ్యయనం). ఆటెకాలజీ: ఒక జాతి. సినెకాలజీ: సముదాయాలు. స్థాయిలు: జీవి, జనాభా, సముదాయం, పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ, బయోమ్, జీవ మండలం. పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యత ను కోర్టులు రక్షిస్తాయి ( RLEK , 1985). EP Act s. 2(a) లోని "inter-relationship" చట్టంలో జీవావరణాన్ని ప్రతిబింబిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: జీవావరణ శాస్త్రాన్ని నిర్వచించండి. ఈ పదాన్ని ఎవరు సృష్టించారు, ఏ గ్రీకు మూలాల నుండి?
selfTest.a: ఆటెకాలజీకి, సినెకాలజీకి తేడా ఏమిటి? జీవావరణ శాస్త్రంలో వ్యవస్థీకరణ స్థాయిలను పేర్కొనండి. EP Act s. 2(a) లోని ఏ భాగం జీవావరణ భావనను ప్రతిబింబిస్తుంది? పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యతపై "the first case of its kind" (అర్థం: ఈ రకమైన మొదటి కేసు) అని పిలవబడిన కేసు ఏది?

hi.inOneMinute: Ecology is the study of the relationships between living organisms and their environment. The word was coined by the German zoologist Ernst Haeckel as Ökologie , from the Greek oikos ("house, dwelling place") and -logia ("study of"). So ecology is the study of the "home" of living things. (See Diagram 1 .) Ecology studies living things at several levels: individual organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome and biosphere. (See Diagram 2 .) Two main branches: autecology – the ecology of a single species; synecology – the ecology of communities of many species. Ecological balance is the stable state in which living things and their surroundings support each other. Human activity (mining, deforestation, pollution) can upset it. Indian courts protect ecological balance: RLEK (1985) was described as "the first case of its kind in the country involving issues relating to environment and ecological balance"; quarries were closed. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". The word "inter-relationship" brings the ecological idea into the law. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 21 – the courts read the right to a healthy environment and ecological balance into the right to life ( Virender Gaur : environment brings within its ambit "hygienic atmosphere and ecological balance").
hi.meaning: Ecology – the "branch of science dealing with the relationship of living things to their environments" (etymological dictionary); "the study of the relationships between organisms and their environment" (encyclopaedia definition). Autecology – population ecology, which "examines single species". Synecology – community ecology, which "considers the ecology of communities, the set of species found in a particular place". Ecological balance – a stable state of a natural system in which the numbers of living things and the supply of air, water, food and space remain in a working balance over time.
keyPoints: Ecology: study of relationships between living things and their environment. Coined by Ernst Haeckel; oikos (house) + -logia (study). Autecology: one species. Synecology: communities. Levels: organism, population, community, ecosystem, biome, biosphere. Ecological balance is protected by courts ( RLEK , 1985). EP Act s. 2(a) "inter-relationship" reflects ecology in law.

caseLaws.facts: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. (1985) 2 SCC 431; AIR 1985 SC 652 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati CJ, A.N. Sen and R. Misra JJ; order of 12 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter from an organisation in Dehradun complained that limestone quarrying in the Dehradun
caseLaws.facts: The letter was treated as a writ petition. An expert committee (the Bhargav Committee) placed the quarries in categories A, B and C. Principle: The Court said this was "the first case of its kind in the country involving issues relating to environment and ecological balance" and ordered the closure of the most harmful quarries, accepting that the loss was "a price that has to be paid" for a healthy environment. Why it matters: It is the starting point of ecological protection by Indian courts.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur tanneries) (1987) 4 SCC 463 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J, K.N. Singh J concurring; 22 September 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries at Kanpur discharged untreated effluent into the Ganga
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A tannery that does not set up even a primary treatment plant "cannot be permitted to continue"; financial capacity is irrelevant. K.N. Singh J: "life, health and ecology have greater importance". Why it matters: It puts ecology above private profit and local economic loss.
Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal AIR 1987 SC 1109; (1987) 2 SCC 295 (Supreme Court; O. Chinnappa Reddy J, Khalid J concurring; 11 February 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land from the Alipore zoo area in Calcutta was given for a five-star hotel; it was challenged
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A". The appeal was dismissed on the facts. Why it matters: It makes ecology a constitutional consideration in every such case.
