en.meaning:
Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Rules of 2021 made under section 34, the District Commission has pecuniary jurisdiction where the value of goods/services paid as consideration is

Explanation. Section 34 fixes Rs 1 crore unless the Central Government prescribes another value. The 2021 Rules prescribed up to fifty lakh rupees for the District Commission.

Under the 2021 Rules, the State Commission has pecuniary jurisdiction where the consideration paid is

Explanation. The State Commission's pecuniary jurisdiction covers consideration exceeding fifty lakh rupees but not exceeding two crore rupees.

What is the correct order of appeal under the three-tier Commission structure?

Explanation. The correct appellate chain is District Commission → State Commission → National Commission → Supreme Court.

Besides the opposite party's location and where the cause of action arose, where else may a complaint under the 2019 Act be filed?

environmental-law-u1-t3.subtitle: Producers, consumers and decomposers, one-way energy flow and recycled nutrients

en.inOneMinute: An ecosystem is "the complex of living organisms, their physical environment, and all their interrelationships" in a particular area. The word dates from 1935 and is believed to have been coined by the English ecologist Sir Arthur George Tansley . Every ecosystem has two parts: (See Diagram 1 .) abiotic (non-living): minerals, climate, soil, water, sunlight; biotic (living): producers (green plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria, fungi). Two main processes keep an ecosystem working: the flow of energy (from the sun, through food chains) and the cycling of nutrients . (See Diagram 2 .) Ecosystems may be natural (forest, pond, river, sea, grassland, desert) or man-made (crop field, garden, reservoir). Courts protect ecosystems such as tanks and village ponds: Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi (2006) and Jagpal Singh (2011). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". This "inter-relationship" is the legal form of the ecosystem idea. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Forests, lakes and rivers are all ecosystems. Article 21 – the courts have brought the protection of the environment under the right to life ( Intellectuals Forum ).
en.meaning: Ecosystem – "the complex of living organisms, their physical environment, and all their interrelationships" (encyclopaedia definition), in a particular area. Producer – a green plant or other autotroph that makes its own food from sunlight (the "producer level"). Consumer – a heterotroph ; consumers "cannot make their own food" and eat plants or other animals. Decomposer – "those heterotrophs that break down dead organisms and organic wastes", returning nutrients to the soil. Food chain – the path by which food energy passes from producers to a series of consumers.
keyPoints: Ecosystem: living organisms + physical environment + interrelationships. Term from 1935; perhaps coined by Tansley. Producer → consumers → decomposer. Energy flows one way through the food chain; nutrients cycle. Kinds: terrestrial, aquatic, man-made. Courts protect tanks and ponds ( Intellectuals Forum , 2006; Jagpal Singh , 2011).

caseLaws.facts: Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v. State of A.P. AIR 2006 SC 1350; (2006) 3 SCC 549 (Supreme Court; Ruma Pal and Dr. AR. Lakshmanan JJ; judgment by Dr. AR. Lakshmanan J; 23 February 2006)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Two historic tanks near Tirupati, Peruru and Avilala, said to exist since about 1500 A
caseLaws.facts: D., were given by government orders for building (Peruru tank bed to TTD; Avilala land to the Housing Board/TUDA). An expert committee reported on reviving them. Principle: The tank is "a communal property and the State authorities are trustees"; "The state is the trustee of all natural resources which are by nature meant for public use and enjoyment"; development must follow "a principle of sustainable development". The Court did not order complete restoration but directed "No further constructions", a percolation tank, rainwater harvesting and a ban on borewells. Why it matters: It applies the public trust doctrine and sustainable development to protect water-body ecosystems.
Jagpal Singh v. State of Punjab, Civil Appeal No. 1132 of 2011 (Supreme Court; Markandey Katju and Gyan Sudha Mishra JJ; 28 January 2011)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The village pond "has been used for the common purpose of the villagers and cannot be allowed to be encroached upon". All Chief Secretaries were directed to "prepare schemes for eviction" of encroachers on common village lands; regularisation "should only be permitted in exceptional cases". Why it matters: It protects small village water ecosystems all over India.
Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. (1985) 2 SCC 431; AIR 1985 SC 652 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati CJ, A.N. Sen and R. Misra JJ; order of 12 March 1985)

te.inOneMinute: పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ (Ecosystem) అంటే ఒక నిర్దిష్ట ప్రాంతంలో "the complex of living organisms, their physical environment, and all their interrelationships" (అర్థం: జీవులు, వాటి భౌతిక పర్యావరణం, వాటి మధ్య ఉన్న అన్ని పరస్పర సంబంధాల సముదాయం). ఈ పదం 1935 నాటిది; దీనిని ఆంగ్ల జీవావరణ శాస్త్రవేత్త Sir Arthur George Tansley సృష్టించి ఉండవచ్చని భావిస్తారు. ప్రతి పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థకు రెండు భాగాలు: ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) నిర్జీవ ( abiotic ) : ఖనిజాలు, వాతావరణం, మట్టి, నీరు, సూర్యరశ్మి; జీవ ( biotic ) : ఉత్పాదకులు (పచ్చని మొక్కలు), వినియోగదారులు (జంతువులు), విచ్ఛిన్నకారులు (బ్యాక్టీరియా, శిలీంధ్రాలు). పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థను పనిచేయించే రెండు ముఖ్య ప్రక్రియలు: శక్తి ప్రవాహం (సూర్యుని నుండి, ఆహార గొలుసుల ద్వారా), పోషకాల చక్రం . ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థలు సహజమైనవి (అడవి, చెరువు, నది, సముద్రం, గడ్డి మైదానం, ఎడారి) లేదా మానవ నిర్మితమైనవి (పంట పొలం, తోట, జలాశయం) కావచ్చు. చెరువులు, గ్రామ కుంటలు వంటి పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థలను కోర్టులు రక్షిస్తాయి: Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi (2006), Jagpal Singh (2011). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ (Ecosystem) – ఒక నిర్దిష్ట ప్రాంతంలో "the complex of living organisms, their physical environment, and all their interrelationships" (అర్థం: జీవులు, వాటి భౌతిక పర్యావరణం , వాటి మధ్య ఉన్న అన్ని పరస్పర సంబంధాల సముదాయం) (విజ్ఞాన సర్వస్వ నిర్వచనం). ఉత్పాదకుడు (Producer) – సూర్యరశ్మి నుండి తన ఆహారాన్ని తానే తయారు చేసుకునే పచ్చని మొక్క లేదా ఇతర స్వయంపోషి ("producer level" – ఉత్పాదక స్థాయి). వినియోగదారు (Consumer) – పరపోషి; వినియోగదారులు "cannot make their own food" (అర్థం: తమ ఆహారాన్ని తాము తయారు చేసుకోలేవు); మొక్కలను లేదా ఇతర జంతువులను తింటాయి. విచ్ఛిన్నకారి (Decomposer) – "those heterotrophs that break down dead organisms and organic wastes" (అర్థం: చనిపోయిన జీవులను, సేంద్రియ వ్యర్థాలను విచ్ఛిన్నం చేసే పరపోషులు); పోషకాలను మళ్లీ మట్టికి చేరుస్తాయి. ఆహార గొలుసు (Food chain) – ఆహార శక్తి ఉత్పాదకుల నుండి వరుస వినియోగదారులకు చేరే మార్గం.
keyPoints: పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ: జీవులు + భౌతిక పర్యావరణం + పరస్పర సంబంధాలు. పదం 1935 నాటిది; Tansley సృష్టించి ఉండవచ్చు. ఉత్పాదకుడు → వినియోగదారులు → విచ్ఛిన్నకారి. శక్తి ఆహార గొలుసు ద్వారా ఒకే దిశలో ప్రవహిస్తుంది; పోషకాలు చక్రంలో తిరుగుతాయి. రకాలు: భూ, జల, మానవ నిర్మిత. కోర్టులు చెరువులు, కుంటలను రక్షిస్తాయి ( Intellectuals Forum , 2006; Jagpal Singh , 2011).

selfTest.q: పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థను నిర్వచించండి. ఈ పదాన్ని ఎవరు, ఎప్పుడు సృష్టించారని భావిస్తారు?
selfTest.a: పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థలోని మూడు రకాల జీవ సభ్యులను పేర్కొనండి. శక్తి ప్రవహిస్తుందని, పోషకాలు చక్రంలో తిరుగుతాయని ఎందుకు అంటారు? రెండు మానవ నిర్మిత పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థలు చెప్పండి. గ్రామ కుంటల గురించి Jagpal Singh ఏం చెప్పింది?

hi.inOneMinute: An ecosystem is "the complex of living organisms, their physical environment, and all their interrelationships" in a particular area. The word dates from 1935 and is believed to have been coined by the English ecologist Sir Arthur George Tansley . Every ecosystem has two parts: (See Diagram 1 .) abiotic (non-living): minerals, climate, soil, water, sunlight; biotic (living): producers (green plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria, fungi). Two main processes keep an ecosystem working: the flow of energy (from the sun, through food chains) and the cycling of nutrients . (See Diagram 2 .) Ecosystems may be natural (forest, pond, river, sea, grassland, desert) or man-made (crop field, garden, reservoir). Courts protect ecosystems such as tanks and village ponds: Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi (2006) and Jagpal Singh (2011). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". This "inter-relationship" is the legal form of the ecosystem idea. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Forests, lakes and rivers are all ecosystems. Article 21 – the courts have brought the protection of the environment under the right to life ( Intellectuals Forum ).
hi.meaning: Ecosystem – "the complex of living organisms, their physical environment, and all their interrelationships" (encyclopaedia definition), in a particular area. Producer – a green plant or other autotroph that makes its own food from sunlight (the "producer level"). Consumer – a heterotroph ; consumers "cannot make their own food" and eat plants or other animals. Decomposer – "those heterotrophs that break down dead organisms and organic wastes", returning nutrients to the soil. Food chain – the path by which food energy passes from producers to a series of consumers.
keyPoints: Ecosystem: living organisms + physical environment + interrelationships. Term from 1935; perhaps coined by Tansley. Producer → consumers → decomposer. Energy flows one way through the food chain; nutrients cycle. Kinds: terrestrial, aquatic, man-made. Courts protect tanks and ponds ( Intellectuals Forum , 2006; Jagpal Singh , 2011).

caseLaws.name: Facts: Two historic tanks near Tirupati, Peruru and Avilala, said to exist since about 1500 A
caseLaws.facts: D., were given by government orders for building (Peruru tank bed to TTD; Avilala land to the Housing Board/TUDA). An expert committee reported on reviving them. Principle: The tank is "a communal property and the State authorities are trustees"; "The state is the trustee of all natural resources which are by nature meant for public use and enjoyment"; development must follow "a principle of sustainable development". The Court did not order complete restoration but directed "No further constructions", a percolation tank, rainwater harvesting and a ban on borewells. Why it matters: It applies the public trust doctrine and sustainable development to protect water-body ecosystems.
Jagpal Singh v. State of Punjab, Civil Appeal No. 1132 of 2011 (Supreme Court; Markandey Katju and Gyan Sudha Mishra JJ; 28 January 2011)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The village pond "has been used for the common purpose of the villagers and cannot be allowed to be encroached upon". All Chief Secretaries were directed to "prepare schemes for eviction" of encroachers on common village lands; regularisation "should only be permitted in exceptional cases". Why it matters: It protects small village water ecosystems all over India.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court called it "the first case of its kind in the country involving issues relating to environment and ecological balance" and ordered closure of the most harmful quarries. Why it matters: It protects a hill ecosystem even at economic cost.

environmental-law-u1-t1.subtitle: Section 2(a) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: water, air, land and their links with living beings and property

en.inOneMinute: Environment means everything that surrounds a living being: air, water, land, plants, animals, micro-organisms, and the things people make. The word comes from the French environner , "to surround, enclose, encircle". (See Diagram 1 .) It has two kinds of parts: abiotic (non-living): air, water, land, sunlight, temperature; biotic (living): human beings, animals, plants, micro-organisms. Legal definition: s. 2(a) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 says environment "includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". (See Diagram 2 .) The definition is inclusive and stresses the inter-relationship among the parts, not only the parts themselves. The Supreme Court has said: "The word 'environment' is of broad spectrum" and brings within it "hygienic atmosphere and ecological balance" ( Virender Gaur , 1994). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property. Section 2(b) – "environmental pollutant" means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to environment. Section 2(c) – "environmental pollution" means the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant. Section 2(e) – "hazardous substance" means any substance or preparation which, by reason of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling, is liable to cause harm to human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism, property or the environment. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures".
en.meaning: Ordinary meaning – the surroundings or conditions in which a person, animal or plant lives. The word "environment" was used in English by about 1600 for "state of being environed"; the sense "the aggregate of the conditions in which a person or thing lives" is recorded by 1827. Scientific meaning – the sum of physical (abiotic) and biological (biotic) factors around an organism, and the interactions among them. Legal meaning – the inclusive definition in s. 2(a) of the EP Act, 1986, covering water, air, land, living beings, property and the inter-relationship among them. Abiotic component – the non-living part of the environment : air, water, soil and land, sunlight, temperature, minerals. Biotic component – the living part of the environment: human beings, animals, plants and micro-organisms.
keyPoints: Environment means "that which surrounds"; from Old French environer . Abiotic component: air, water, land, sunlight, temperature. Biotic component: human beings, animals, plants, micro-organisms. EP Act s. 2(a): water, air, land, living beings, property and their inter-relationship; inclusive. Environmental pollution is the presence of an environmental pollutant (s. 2(c)). Virender Gaur : environment is of "broad spectrum".

caseLaws.facts: Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) 2 SCC 577 (Supreme Court; K. Ramaswamy and N. Venkatachala JJ; 24 November 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land kept as open space in a Thanesar town planning scheme was leased to a sabha to build a d
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "The word 'environment' is of broad spectrum" which brings within its ambit "hygienic atmosphere and ecological balance"; Art. 21 protects the right to life, and the State must protect the environment. The lease was quashed and the construction ordered to be demolished. Why it matters: It is the leading judicial statement on the wide meaning of "environment".
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar AIR 1991 SC 420; (1991) 1 SCC 598 (Supreme Court; K.N. Singh J with N.D. Ojha J; reasons given on 9 January 1991)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A petition alleged that slurry from TISCO's coal washeries was polluting the Bokaro river
caseLaws.facts: The Court found the petitioner was acting from personal interest. Principle: The right to life under Art. 21 "includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life". The petition was dismissed with costs. Why it matters: It ties the basic parts of the environment (water and air) to the right to life.
Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal AIR 1987 SC 1109; (1987) 2 SCC 295 (Supreme Court; O. Chinnappa Reddy J, Khalid J concurring; 11 February 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land from the Alipore zoo area in Calcutta was given for building a five-star hotel; the deci
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A". The appeal was dismissed on the facts. Why it matters: It shows that the constitutional meaning of environment guides courts in every environmental case.

te.inOneMinute: పర్యావరణం (Environment) అంటే ఒక జీవి చుట్టూ ఉన్నదంతా: గాలి, నీరు, భూమి, మొక్కలు, జంతువులు, సూక్ష్మజీవులు, మనుషులు తయారు చేసిన వస్తువులు. ఈ పదం ఫ్రెంచ్ environner నుండి వచ్చింది – "to surround, enclose, encircle" (అర్థం: చుట్టుముట్టడం, ఆవరించడం, చుట్టూ వలయంగా ఉండడం). ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) దీనికి రెండు రకాల భాగాలు ఉన్నాయి: నిర్జీవ ( abiotic ) : గాలి, నీరు, భూమి, సూర్యరశ్మి, ఉష్ణోగ్రత; జీవ ( biotic ) : మనుషులు, జంతువులు, మొక్కలు, సూక్ష్మజీవులు. చట్టపరమైన నిర్వచనం: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 s. 2(a) ప్రకారం పర్యావరణం "includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property" (అర్థం: నీరు, గాలి, భూమి, మరియు నీరు, గాలి, భూమికి – మనుషులు, ఇతర జీవులు, మొక్కలు, సూక్ష్మజీవులు, ఆస్తికి మధ్య ఉన్న పరస్పర సంబంధాన్ని కలిగి ఉంటుంది). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) ఈ నిర్వచనం సమ్మిళితమైనది (inclusive) ; భాగాలతో పాటు వాటి మధ్య పరస్పర సంబంధాన్ని నొక్కి చెబుతుంది. సుప్రీంకోర్టు: "The word 'environment' is of broad spectrum" (అర్థం: 'పర్యావరణం' అనే పదం విస్తృత పరిధి గలది); దానిలో "hygienic atmosphere and ecological balance" (అర్థం: ఆరోగ్యకరమైన వాతావరణం, పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యత) వస్తాయి ( Virender Gaur , 1994). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: సాధారణ అర్థం – ఒక మనిషి, జంతువు లేదా మొక్క నివసించే పరిసరాలు లేదా పరిస్థితులు. ఆంగ్లంలో "environment" అనే పదం సుమారు 1600 నాటికి "state of being environed" (అర్థం: ఆవరించబడిన స్థితి) అనే అర్థంలో వాడబడింది; "the aggregate of the conditions in which a person or thing lives" (అర్థం: ఒక వ్యక్తి లేదా వస్తువు జీవించే పరిస్థితుల సమాహారం) అనే అర్థం 1827 నాటికి నమోదైంది. శాస్త్రీయ అర్థం – ఒక జీవి చుట్టూ ఉన్న భౌతిక (నిర్జీవ), జీవ కారకాల మొత్తం, వాటి మధ్య పరస్పర చర్యలు. చట్టపరమైన అర్థం – EP Act, 1986 s. 2(a) లోని సమ్మిళిత నిర్వచనం; నీరు, గాలి, భూమి, జీవులు, ఆస్తి, వాటి మధ్య పరస్పర సంబంధం. నిర్జీవ భాగం (Abiotic component) – పర్యావరణంలోని జీవం లేని భాగం: గాలి, నీరు, మట్టి, భూమి, సూర్యరశ్మి, ఉష్ణోగ్రత, ఖనిజాలు. జీవ భాగం (Biotic component) – పర్యావరణంలోని జీవం ఉన్న భాగం: మనుషులు, జంతువులు, మొక్కలు, సూక్ష్మజీవులు.
keyPoints: పర్యావరణం అంటే "చుట్టూ ఉన్నది"; పాత ఫ్రెంచ్ environer నుండి. నిర్జీవ భాగం: గాలి, నీరు, భూమి, సూర్యరశ్మి, ఉష్ణోగ్రత. జీవ భాగం: మనుషులు, జంతువులు, మొక్కలు, సూక్ష్మజీవులు. EP Act s. 2(a): నీరు, గాలి, భూమి, జీవులు, ఆస్తి, వాటి పరస్పర సంబంధం; సమ్మిళితం. పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యం అంటే పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యకారకం ఉండడం (s. 2(c)). Virender Gaur : పర్యావరణం "broad spectrum" (అర్థం: విస్తృత పరిధి) గలది.

selfTest.q: "Environment" అనే పదానికి అక్షరార్థం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: EP Act, 1986 s. 2(a) ను ఉటంకించండి. s. 2(a) లో "includes" అనే పదం ఎందుకు ముఖ్యం? పర్యావరణంలోని నాలుగు మండలాలు చెప్పండి. పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యకారకానికి, పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యానికి తేడా ఏమిటి? Virender Gaur లో "environment" అనే పదం గురించి సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఏం చెప్పింది?

hi.inOneMinute: Environment means everything that surrounds a living being: air, water, land, plants, animals, micro-organisms, and the things people make. The word comes from the French environner , "to surround, enclose, encircle". (See Diagram 1 .) It has two kinds of parts: abiotic (non-living): air, water, land, sunlight, temperature; biotic (living): human beings, animals, plants, micro-organisms. Legal definition: s. 2(a) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 says environment "includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". (See Diagram 2 .) The definition is inclusive and stresses the inter-relationship among the parts, not only the parts themselves. The Supreme Court has said: "The word 'environment' is of broad spectrum" and brings within it "hygienic atmosphere and ecological balance" ( Virender Gaur , 1994). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property. Section 2(b) – "environmental pollutant" means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to environment. Section 2(c) – "environmental pollution" means the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant. Section 2(e) – "hazardous substance" means any substance or preparation which, by reason of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling, is liable to cause harm to human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism, property or the environment. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures".
hi.meaning: Ordinary meaning – the surroundings or conditions in which a person, animal or plant lives. The word "environment" was used in English by about 1600 for "state of being environed"; the sense "the aggregate of the conditions in which a person or thing lives" is recorded by 1827. Scientific meaning – the sum of physical (abiotic) and biological (biotic) factors around an organism, and the interactions among them. Legal meaning – the inclusive definition in s. 2(a) of the EP Act, 1986, covering water, air, land, living beings, property and the inter-relationship among them. Abiotic component – the non-living part of the environment : air, water, soil and land, sunlight, temperature, minerals. Biotic component – the living part of the environment: human beings, animals, plants and micro-organisms.
keyPoints: Environment means "that which surrounds"; from Old French environer . Abiotic component: air, water, land, sunlight, temperature. Biotic component: human beings, animals, plants, micro-organisms. EP Act s. 2(a): water, air, land, living beings, property and their inter-relationship; inclusive. Environmental pollution is the presence of an environmental pollutant (s. 2(c)). Virender Gaur : environment is of "broad spectrum".

caseLaws.facts: The Court found the petitioner was acting from personal interest. Why it matters: It ties the basic parts of the environment (water and air) to the right to life.
Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal AIR 1987 SC 1109; (1987) 2 SCC 295 (Supreme Court; O. Chinnappa Reddy J, Khalid J concurring; 11 February 1987)

en.inOneMinute: A biome is "the largest geographic biotic unit, a major community of plants and animals with similar life forms and environmental conditions". A biome is named after its main type of vegetation, such as grassland or coniferous forest. The word dates from 1916 (Greek bios , "life", + -ome ) and was probably coined by the U.S. ecologist Frederic E. Clements . (See Diagram 1 .) Biomes are shaped mainly by climate – temperature and rainfall – and by soil and height above sea level. Main land biomes: tropical rainforest, tropical deciduous forest, savanna, desert, grassland, temperate forest, taiga (coniferous forest) and tundra. Water biomes: freshwater and marine. (See Diagram 2 .) India has many biomes: rainforests of the Western Ghats and North-East, deciduous forests, the Thar desert, grasslands, mangroves of the Sundarbans and alpine areas of the Himalaya. Law protects biomes through forest, wild life and coastal laws; courts have protected forests "irrespective of the ownership" ( Godavarman , 1996) and mangroves (Bombay High Court, 2018). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (now called the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980) – prior approval of the Central Government is needed for using forest land for non-forest purposes; the Supreme Court has applied this to all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification thereof" ( Godavarman , 1996). Article 21 – "The destruction of mangroves offends the fundamental rights of the citizens under Article 21" (Bombay High Court, 2018, as reported). Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air, land and living beings and their inter-relationship; this covers every biome.
en.meaning: Biome – the largest geographic biotic unit; a major community of plants and animals with similar life forms and environmental conditions, named after its dominant vegetation. Biome type – "Several similar biomes constitute a biome type" (for example, all tropical rainforests of the world). Major life zone – the European phrase for the North American idea of a biome. Tundra – a cold, treeless biome with short summers, found near the poles and on high mountains. Mangrove – salt-tolerant trees and shrubs growing in coastal tidal areas; mangrove forests form a distinct coastal biome.
keyPoints: Biome: largest geographic biotic unit; named after main vegetation. Word from 1916; probably coined by Clements. Several similar biomes make a biome type. Decided by temperature, rainfall, soil and altitude. Tundra is cold and treeless; mangrove forests grow in tidal coastal areas. Courts protect forests ( Godavarman ) and mangroves (Bombay High Court, 2018).

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The word "forest" "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning"; the Forest (Conservation) Act applies to all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification thereof"; "prior approval of the Central Government is required for any non-forest activity within the area of any 'forest'"; felling was suspended except under approved Working Plans. Why it matters: It protects the forest biome all over India, including privately owned forests.

te.inOneMinute: బయోమ్ (Biome) అంటే "the largest geographic biotic unit, a major community of plants and animals with similar life forms and environmental conditions" (అర్థం: అతిపెద్ద భౌగోళిక జీవ యూనిట్; ఒకే రకమైన జీవ రూపాలు, పర్యావరణ పరిస్థితులు గల మొక్కలు, జంతువుల ప్రధాన సముదాయం). బయోమ్‌కు దాని ప్రధాన వృక్షసంపద రకం పేరు పెడతారు, ఉదా. గడ్డి మైదానం లేదా శృంగాకార అడవి. ఈ పదం 1916 నాటిది (గ్రీకు bios , "జీవం", + -ome ); దీనిని అమెరికన్ జీవావరణ శాస్త్రవేత్త Frederic E. Clements సృష్టించి ఉండవచ్చు. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) బయోమ్‌లు ప్రధానంగా వాతావరణం – ఉష్ణోగ్రత, వర్షపాతం – మరియు మట్టి, సముద్ర మట్టం నుండి ఎత్తు ద్వారా రూపొందుతాయి. ప్రధాన భూ బయోమ్‌లు: ఉష్ణమండల వర్షారణ్యం, ఉష్ణమండల ఆకురాల్చే అడవి, సవన్నా, ఎడారి, గడ్డి మైదానం, సమశీతోష్ణ అడవి, టైగా (శృంగాకార అడవి), టండ్రా. జల బయోమ్‌లు: మంచినీరు, సముద్రం. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) భారతదేశంలో అనేక బయోమ్‌లు ఉన్నాయి: పశ్చిమ కనుమలు, ఈశాన్య ప్రాంతాల వర్షారణ్యాలు, ఆకురాల్చే అడవులు, థార్ ఎడారి, గడ్డి మైదానాలు, సుందర్‌బన్స్ మడ అడవులు, హిమాలయాల ఆల్పైన్ ప్రాంతాలు. అటవీ, వన్యప్రాణి, తీర చట్టాల ద్వారా చట్టం బయోమ్‌లను రక్షిస్తుంది; కోర్టులు అడవులను "irrespective of the ownership" (అర్థం: యాజమాన్యంతో సంబంధం లేకుండా) రక్షించాయి ( Godavarman , 1996); మడ అడవులను రక్షించాయి (బాంబే హైకోర్టు, 2018). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: బయోమ్ (Biome) – అతిపెద్ద భౌగోళిక జీవ యూనిట్; ఒకే రకమైన జీవ రూపాలు, పర్యావరణ పరిస్థితులు గల మొక్కలు, జంతువుల ప్రధాన సముదాయం; దాని ప్రధాన వృక్షసంపద పేరు పెడతారు. బయోమ్ రకం (Biome type) – "Several similar biomes constitute a biome type" (అర్థం: అనేక సారూప్య బయోమ్‌లు కలిసి ఒక బయోమ్ రకం అవుతాయి) (ఉదా. ప్రపంచంలోని అన్ని ఉష్ణమండల వర్షారణ్యాలు). ప్రధాన జీవ మండలం (Major life zone) – ఉత్తర అమెరికా బయోమ్ భావనకు యూరోపియన్ పదం. టండ్రా (Tundra) – ధ్రువాల దగ్గర, ఎత్తైన పర్వతాలపై కనిపించే, చిన్న వేసవి గల చల్లని, చెట్లు లేని బయోమ్. మడ అడవి (Mangrove) – తీర పోటు ప్రాంతాల్లో పెరిగే ఉప్పును తట్టుకునే చెట్లు, పొదలు; మడ అడవులు ఒక ప్రత్యేక తీర బయోమ్.
keyPoints: బయోమ్: అతిపెద్ద భౌగోళిక జీవ యూనిట్; ప్రధాన వృక్షసంపద పేరు. పదం 1916 నాటిది; బహుశా Clements సృష్టించారు. అనేక సారూప్య బయోమ్‌లు కలిసి ఒక బయోమ్ రకం. ఉష్ణోగ్రత, వర్షపాతం, మట్టి, ఎత్తు ద్వారా నిర్ణయించబడుతుంది. టండ్రా చల్లని, చెట్లు లేనిది; మడ అడవి తీర పోటు ప్రాంతాల్లో పెరుగుతుంది. కోర్టులు అడవులను ( Godavarman ), మడ అడవులను (బాంబే హైకోర్టు, 2018) రక్షిస్తాయి.

hi.inOneMinute: A biome is "the largest geographic biotic unit, a major community of plants and animals with similar life forms and environmental conditions". A biome is named after its main type of vegetation, such as grassland or coniferous forest. The word dates from 1916 (Greek bios , "life", + -ome ) and was probably coined by the U.S. ecologist Frederic E. Clements . (See Diagram 1 .) Biomes are shaped mainly by climate – temperature and rainfall – and by soil and height above sea level. Main land biomes: tropical rainforest, tropical deciduous forest, savanna, desert, grassland, temperate forest, taiga (coniferous forest) and tundra. Water biomes: freshwater and marine. (See Diagram 2 .) India has many biomes: rainforests of the Western Ghats and North-East, deciduous forests, the Thar desert, grasslands, mangroves of the Sundarbans and alpine areas of the Himalaya. Law protects biomes through forest, wild life and coastal laws; courts have protected forests "irrespective of the ownership" ( Godavarman , 1996) and mangroves (Bombay High Court, 2018). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (now called the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980) – prior approval of the Central Government is needed for using forest land for non-forest purposes; the Supreme Court has applied this to all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification thereof" ( Godavarman , 1996). Article 21 – "The destruction of mangroves offends the fundamental rights of the citizens under Article 21" (Bombay High Court, 2018, as reported). Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air, land and living beings and their inter-relationship; this covers every biome.
hi.meaning: Biome – the largest geographic biotic unit; a major community of plants and animals with similar life forms and environmental conditions, named after its dominant vegetation. Biome type – "Several similar biomes constitute a biome type" (for example, all tropical rainforests of the world). Major life zone – the European phrase for the North American idea of a biome. Tundra – a cold, treeless biome with short summers, found near the poles and on high mountains. Mangrove – salt-tolerant trees and shrubs growing in coastal tidal areas; mangrove forests form a distinct coastal biome.
keyPoints: Biome: largest geographic biotic unit; named after main vegetation. Word from 1916; probably coined by Clements. Several similar biomes make a biome type. Decided by temperature, rainfall, soil and altitude. Tundra is cold and treeless; mangrove forests grow in tidal coastal areas. Courts protect forests ( Godavarman ) and mangroves (Bombay High Court, 2018).

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition sought protection of forests across India from illegal felling and non-forest
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The word "forest" "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning"; the Forest (Conservation) Act applies to all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification thereof"; "prior approval of the Central Government is required for any non-forest activity within the area of any 'forest'"; felling was suspended except under approved Working Plans. Why it matters: It protects the forest biome all over India, including privately owned forests.
Bombay Environmental Action Group v. State of Maharashtra (Bombay High Court; A.S. Oka and R.I. Chagla JJ; September 2018)

environmental-law-u1-t4.subtitle: The thin zone of the Earth where life exists, the threats it faces and how law protects it

en.inOneMinute: The biosphere is the "relatively thin life-supporting stratum of Earth's surface, extending from a few kilometres into the atmosphere to the deep-sea vents of the ocean". It is "a global ecosystem" made of living organisms and the non-living factors from which they get energy and nutrients. The word was coined in German ( Biosphäre ) in 1875 by the geologist Eduard Suess . (See Diagram 1 .) The biosphere is where three non-living spheres meet and support life: the lithosphere (rock and soil), the hydrosphere (water) and the atmosphere (air). It works by "the continuous cycling of matter and an accompanying flow of solar energy". (See Diagram 2 .) Biosphere reserves protect large representative areas. India has 18 notified biosphere reserves, of which 13 are in UNESCO's World Network under the Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme ; the first was Nilgiri (1986). (See Diagram 3 .) The Supreme Court has said "our approach should be eco-centric and not anthropocentric" ( Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-I , 2013).
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 21 – "conservation and protection of environment is an inseparable part of right to life" ( Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-I , 2013, para 41). Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship among them and "human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". This covers the whole biosphere. Biosphere reserves – there is no separate Act for biosphere reserves; they are notified by the Government of India and recognised internationally under UNESCO's MAB Programme. Their core areas usually include national parks and sanctuaries protected under wild life and forest laws.
en.meaning: Biosphere – the thin layer of the earth where life exists, from a few kilometres up in the air to the deep-sea vents; a global ecosystem of living things and the non-living factors that support them. Biosphere reserve – a large area notified to conserve biodiversity together with the sustainable use of resources by local people, divided into core, buffer and transition zones. Core zone – the most strictly protected inner area of a biosphere reserve. Eco-centrism – "Eco-centrism is nature-centred, where humans are part of nature and non-humans have intrinsic value" ( WWF-I , para 39).
keyPoints: Biosphere: thin layer of life on earth; global ecosystem. Coined by Eduard Suess (1875). Matter cycles; solar energy flows. India: 18 biosphere reserves; 13 in UNESCO network; Nilgiri first (1986). Zones: core zone, buffer, transition. WWF-I (2013): eco-centrism, "not anthropocentric".

caseLaws.facts: Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-I v. Union of India, I.A. No. 100 in W.P. (C) No. 337 of 1995 (Supreme Court; K.S. Radhakrishnan and Chandramauli Kr. Prasad JJ; judgment by K.S. Radhakrishnan J; 15 April 2013)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Asiatic lion survived only in the Gir forest of Gujarat
caseLaws.facts: Experts found Kuno Wildlife Sanctuary (Kuno Palpur) the most suitable site for re-introduction, and the question was whether lions should be moved there. The Ministry had also ordered African cheetahs to be brought to Kuno. Principle: "our approach should be eco-centric and not anthropocentric"; "species has equal rights to exist on this earth"; Art. 21 casts "an obligation on human beings to protect and preserve a specie becoming extinct". The cheetah order was quashed , and the Ministry was directed to take urgent steps "for re-introduction of Asiatic lion from Gir forests to Kuno". Why it matters: It brings the whole biosphere, not only humans, into the centre of Indian environmental law.
Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v. State of A.P. AIR 2006 SC 1350; (2006) 3 SCC 549 (Supreme Court; Ruma Pal and Dr. AR. Lakshmanan JJ; 23 February 2006)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Historic tanks near Tirupati were given away for building; residents challenged it
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court relied on Principle 2 of the Stockholm Declaration (protect "especially representative samples of natural ecosystems") and held that "The state is the trustee of all natural resources which are by nature meant for public use and enjoyment"; it stopped further construction. Why it matters: It links the protection of natural resources (parts of the biosphere) to the State's duty as trustee .
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries polluted the Palar river and the land around it in Tamil Nadu
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". Why it matters: Sustainable development keeps human use within the limits the biosphere can bear.

te.inOneMinute: జీవ మండలం (Biosphere) అంటే "relatively thin life-supporting stratum of Earth's surface, extending from a few kilometres into the atmosphere to the deep-sea vents of the ocean" (అర్థం: వాతావరణంలో కొన్ని కిలోమీటర్ల ఎత్తు నుండి సముద్రపు లోతైన బిలాల వరకు విస్తరించిన, జీవానికి ఆధారమైన భూ ఉపరితలంలోని సాపేక్షంగా పలుచని పొర). ఇది జీవులు, అవి శక్తి, పోషకాలను పొందే నిర్జీవ కారకాలతో కూడిన "a global ecosystem" (అర్థం: ప్రపంచ పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ). ఈ పదాన్ని జర్మన్‌లో ( Biosphäre ) 1875 లో భూగర్భ శాస్త్రవేత్త Eduard Suess సృష్టించారు. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) జీవ మండలం అంటే మూడు నిర్జీవ మండలాలు కలిసి జీవానికి ఆధారమయ్యే ప్రదేశం: శిలా మండలం (lithosphere) (రాళ్లు, మట్టి), జల మండలం (hydrosphere) (నీరు), వాతావరణ మండలం (atmosphere) (గాలి). ఇది "the continuous cycling of matter and an accompanying flow of solar energy" (అర్థం: పదార్థం నిరంతర చక్రం, దానితో పాటు సౌర శక్తి ప్రవాహం) ద్వారా పనిచేస్తుంది. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) జీవ మండల రిజర్వులు (Biosphere reserves) పెద్ద ప్రాతినిధ్య ప్రాంతాలను రక్షిస్తాయి. భారతదేశంలో 18 నోటిఫై చేసిన జీవ మండల రిజర్వులు ఉన్నాయి; వాటిలో 13 Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme కింద UNESCO ప్రపంచ నెట్‌వర్క్‌లో ఉన్నాయి; మొదటిది నీలగిరి (1986). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) సుప్రీంకోర్టు: "our approach should be eco-centric and not anthropocentric" (అర్థం: మన దృక్పథం మానవ కేంద్రితం కాకుండా పర్యావరణ కేంద్రితంగా ఉండాలి) ( Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-I , 2013).
te.meaning: జీవ మండలం ( Biosphere ) – గాలిలో కొన్ని కిలోమీటర్ల ఎత్తు నుండి లోతైన సముద్ర బిలాల వరకు జీవం ఉన్న భూమి పలుచని పొర; జీవులు, వాటికి ఆధారమైన నిర్జీవ కారకాలతో కూడిన ప్రపంచ పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ . జీవ మండల రిజర్వు ( Biosphere reserve ) – స్థానిక ప్రజల సుస్థిర వనరుల వినియోగంతో పాటు జీవవైవిధ్యాన్ని సంరక్షించడానికి నోటిఫై చేసిన పెద్ద ప్రాంతం; కోర్, బఫర్, ట్రాన్సిషన్ మండలాలుగా విభజించబడుతుంది. కోర్ మండలం (Core zone) – జీవ మండల రిజర్వులో అత్యంత కఠినంగా రక్షించబడే లోపలి ప్రాంతం. పర్యావరణ కేంద్రితవాదం (Eco-centrism) – "Eco-centrism is nature-centred, where humans are part of nature and non-humans have intrinsic value" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణ కేంద్రితవాదం ప్రకృతి కేంద్రితమైనది; దీనిలో మనుషులు ప్రకృతిలో భాగం, మానవేతరులకు స్వాభావిక విలువ ఉంది) ( WWF-I , para 39).
keyPoints: జీవ మండలం: భూమిపై జీవ పలుచని పొర; ప్రపంచ పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ. Eduard Suess సృష్టించారు (1875). పదార్థం చక్రంలో తిరుగుతుంది; సౌర శక్తి ప్రవహిస్తుంది. భారతదేశం: 18 జీవ మండల రిజర్వు లు; UNESCO నెట్‌వర్క్‌లో 13; నీలగిరి మొదటిది (1986). మండలాలు: కోర్ మండలం, బఫర్, ట్రాన్సిషన్. WWF-I (2013): పర్యావరణ కేంద్రితవాదం, "not anthropocentric" (అర్థం: మానవ కేంద్రితం కాదు).

hi.inOneMinute: The biosphere is the "relatively thin life-supporting stratum of Earth's surface, extending from a few kilometres into the atmosphere to the deep-sea vents of the ocean". It is "a global ecosystem" made of living organisms and the non-living factors from which they get energy and nutrients. The word was coined in German ( Biosphäre ) in 1875 by the geologist Eduard Suess . (See Diagram 1 .) The biosphere is where three non-living spheres meet and support life: the lithosphere (rock and soil), the hydrosphere (water) and the atmosphere (air). It works by "the continuous cycling of matter and an accompanying flow of solar energy". (See Diagram 2 .) Biosphere reserves protect large representative areas. India has 18 notified biosphere reserves, of which 13 are in UNESCO's World Network under the Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme ; the first was Nilgiri (1986). (See Diagram 3 .) The Supreme Court has said "our approach should be eco-centric and not anthropocentric" ( Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-I , 2013).
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 21 – "conservation and protection of environment is an inseparable part of right to life" ( Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-I , 2013, para 41). Section 2(a), Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – "environment" includes water, air and land and the inter-relationship among them and "human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". This covers the whole biosphere. Biosphere reserves – there is no separate Act for biosphere reserves; they are notified by the Government of India and recognised internationally under UNESCO's MAB Programme. Their core areas usually include national parks and sanctuaries protected under wild life and forest laws.
hi.meaning: Biosphere – the thin layer of the earth where life exists, from a few kilometres up in the air to the deep-sea vents; a global ecosystem of living things and the non-living factors that support them. Biosphere reserve – a large area notified to conserve biodiversity together with the sustainable use of resources by local people, divided into core, buffer and transition zones. Core zone – the most strictly protected inner area of a biosphere reserve. Eco-centrism – "Eco-centrism is nature-centred, where humans are part of nature and non-humans have intrinsic value" ( WWF-I , para 39).
keyPoints: Biosphere: thin layer of life on earth; global ecosystem. Coined by Eduard Suess (1875). Matter cycles; solar energy flows. India: 18 biosphere reserves; 13 in UNESCO network; Nilgiri first (1986). Zones: core zone, buffer, transition. WWF-I (2013): eco-centrism, "not anthropocentric".

caseLaws.facts: Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-I v. Union of India, I.A. No. 100 in W.P. (C) No. 337 of 1995 (Supreme Court; K.S. Radhakrishnan and Chandramauli Kr. Prasad JJ; judgment by K.S. Radhakrishnan J; 15 April 2013)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Asiatic lion survived only in the Gir forest of Gujarat
caseLaws.facts: Experts found Kuno Wildlife Sanctuary (Kuno Palpur) the most suitable site for re-introduction, and the question was whether lions should be moved there. The Ministry had also ordered African cheetahs to be brought to Kuno. Principle: "our approach should be eco-centric and not anthropocentric"; "species has equal rights to exist on this earth"; Art. 21 casts "an obligation on human beings to protect and preserve a specie becoming extinct". The cheetah order was quashed , and the Ministry was directed to take urgent steps "for re-introduction of Asiatic lion from Gir forests to Kuno". Why it matters: It brings the whole biosphere, not only humans, into the centre of Indian environmental law.
Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v. State of A.P. AIR 2006 SC 1350; (2006) 3 SCC 549 (Supreme Court; Ruma Pal and Dr. AR. Lakshmanan JJ; 23 February 2006)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Historic tanks near Tirupati were given away for building; residents challenged it
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court relied on Principle 2 of the Stockholm Declaration (protect "especially representative samples of natural ecosystems") and held that "The state is the trustee of all natural resources which are by nature meant for public use and enjoyment"; it stopped further construction. Why it matters: It links the protection of natural resources (parts of the biosphere) to the State's duty as trustee .
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries polluted the Palar river and the land around it in Tamil Nadu
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". Why it matters: Sustainable development keeps human use within the limits the biosphere can bear.

environmental-law-u1-t6.subtitle: Thinning of the stratospheric ozone layer, its causes, effects and the legal response

en.inOneMinute: Ozone depletion is the "gradual thinning of Earth's ozone layer in the upper atmosphere", caused by the release of chlorine or bromine compounds. The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, some 15 to 35 km above the earth. It shields life from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays; when it thins, more UV radiation reaches the surface. (See Diagram 1 .) Main culprits are ozone depleting substances (ODS) : chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, HCFCs and methyl bromide. Their chlorine and bromine "break ozone molecules apart by stripping away one of the three oxygen atoms". (See Diagram 2 .) The Antarctic ozone hole was first documented in 1985 by British Antarctic Survey scientists (Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin). Effects: more skin cancer, eye cataracts , damage to genes and the immune system. Law: the Montreal Protocol (adopted 16 September 1987) controls ODS; the Kigali Amendment (October 2016) adds the phase-down of HFCs. India became a Party to the Montreal Protocol on 19 June 1992 and made the Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 under the EP Act. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 – S.O. 670(E), dated 19 July 2000, made under "sections 6, 8 and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986". Rule 2(i) – "ozone depleting substance" means the substances specified in column (2) of Schedule I, "whether existing by itself or in a mixture". Rule 2(m) – "protocol" means the Montreal Protocol "adopted on 16th September 1987". Rule 3(1) – "No person shall produce or cause to produce any ozone depleting substance after the date specified in column (5)" of the relevant Schedule. Rule 4 – prohibition on export to or import from countries not specified in Schedule VI. Rule 5(1) – import or export with Schedule VI countries only "under a licence" issued by the authority. Rule 9(1) – "No person shall establish or expand or cause to establish or expand any manufacturing facility for production" of ODS (prohibition on new investment). Sections 6, 8 and 25, EP Act, 1986 – power of the Central Government to make rules to regulate environmental pollution, and the duty to handle hazardous substances only in accordance with procedure. Article 51(c) of the Constitution – the State shall endeavour to "foster respect for international law and treaty obligations". Article 21 – right to life includes the right to pollution-free air ( Subhash Kumar , 1991).

te.inOneMinute: ఓజోన్ క్షీణత (Ozone depletion) అంటే "gradual thinning of Earth's ozone layer in the upper atmosphere" (అర్థం: ఎగువ వాతావరణంలోని భూమి ఓజోన్ పొర క్రమంగా పలుచబడడం); క్లోరిన్ లేదా బ్రోమిన్ సమ్మేళనాల విడుదల దీనికి కారణం. ఓజోన్ పొర భూమికి సుమారు 15 నుండి 35 కి.మీ. ఎత్తులో, స్ట్రాటోస్ఫియర్‌లో ఉంటుంది. ఇది హానికర అతినీలలోహిత (UV) కిరణాల నుండి జీవులను కాపాడుతుంది; అది పలుచబడితే ఎక్కువ UV కిరణాలు భూ ఉపరితలానికి చేరతాయి. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ముఖ్య కారకాలు ఓజోన్ క్షీణింపజేసే పదార్థాలు (ODS) : క్లోరోఫ్లోరోకార్బన్‌లు (CFCs), హాలోన్‌లు, కార్బన్ టెట్రాక్లోరైడ్, మిథైల్ క్లోరోఫామ్, HCFCs, మిథైల్ బ్రోమైడ్. వాటిలోని క్లోరిన్, బ్రోమిన్ "break ozone molecules apart by stripping away one of the three oxygen atoms" (అర్థం: మూడు ఆక్సిజన్ అణువుల్లో ఒకదాన్ని లాగేసి ఓజోన్ అణువులను విడగొడతాయి). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) అంటార్కిటిక్ ఓజోన్ రంధ్రం ను 1985 లో British Antarctic Survey శాస్త్రవేత్తలు (Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin) మొదటిసారి నమోదు చేశారు. ప్రభావాలు: చర్మ క్యాన్సర్, కంటి శుక్లాలు పెరగడం, జన్యువులు, రోగనిరోధక వ్యవస్థకు నష్టం. చట్టం: Montreal Protocol (16 సెప్టెంబర్ 1987 న ఆమోదం) ODS ను నియంత్రిస్తుంది; Kigali Amendment (అక్టోబర్ 2016) HFCs తగ్గింపును చేరుస్తుంది. భారతదేశం 19 జూన్ 1992 న Montreal Protocol లో పక్షమైంది; EP Act కింద Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 రూపొందించింది. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: ఓజోన్ (Ozone) – మూడు ఆక్సిజన్ అణువులు గల అణువు ఉన్న వాయువు (O₃). ఓజోన్ పొర (Ozone layer) – భూమికి సుమారు 15 నుండి 35 కి.మీ. ఎత్తులో స్ట్రాటోస్ఫియర్‌లో ఉండే, సూర్యుని హానికర UV కిరణాలలో అధిక భాగాన్ని పీల్చుకునే ఓజోన్ పొర. ఓజోన్ క్షీణత ( Ozone depletion ) – మానవ కార్యకలాపాల వల్ల విడుదలైన క్లోరిన్ లేదా బ్రోమిన్ సమ్మేళనాల వల్ల ఎగువ వాతావరణంలో ఓజోన్ పొర క్రమంగా పలుచబడడం. ఓజోన్ క్షీణింపజేసే పదార్థం (ODS) – 2000 Rules Schedule I లో పేర్కొన్న, స్వయంగా లేదా మిశ్రమంలో, స్ట్రాటోస్ఫియర్ ఓజోన్‌ను నాశనం చేసే పదార్థం. క్లోరోఫ్లోరోకార్బన్ (CFC) – క్లోరిన్, ఫ్లోరిన్, కార్బన్‌తో కూడిన మానవ నిర్మిత సమ్మేళనం; ఒకప్పుడు రిఫ్రిజిరేటర్లు, ఏసీలు, ఏరోసోల్ స్ప్రేలు, ఫోమ్‌లలో విస్తృతంగా వాడబడింది; ప్రధాన ODS.
keyPoints: ఓజోన్ పొర స్ట్రాటోస్ఫియర్‌లో, 15–35 కి.మీ. ఎత్తులో ఉంది; హానికర UV ని అడ్డుకుంటుంది. క్లోరోఫ్లోరోకార్బన్ లు, ఇతర ODS క్లోరిన్/బ్రోమిన్‌ను విడుదల చేసి ఓజోన్‌ను నాశనం చేస్తాయి. అంటార్కిటిక్ ఓజోన్ రంధ్రం 1985 లో నమోదైంది. Montreal Protocol (16-9-1987); HFCs కోసం Kigali Amendment (2016). భారతదేశం: 19-6-1992 నుండి పక్షం; ODS Rules, 2000 Schedule I ద్వారా ఓజోన్ క్షీణింపజేసే పదార్థం ను నిర్వచిస్తాయి. కోర్టులు: ముందుజాగ్రత్త సూత్రం, రుజువు భారం ( Vellore ; Nayudu ).

hi.inOneMinute: Ozone depletion is the "gradual thinning of Earth's ozone layer in the upper atmosphere", caused by the release of chlorine or bromine compounds. The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, some 15 to 35 km above the earth. It shields life from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays; when it thins, more UV radiation reaches the surface. (See Diagram 1 .) Main culprits are ozone depleting substances (ODS) : chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, HCFCs and methyl bromide. Their chlorine and bromine "break ozone molecules apart by stripping away one of the three oxygen atoms". (See Diagram 2 .) The Antarctic ozone hole was first documented in 1985 by British Antarctic Survey scientists (Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin). Effects: more skin cancer, eye cataracts , damage to genes and the immune system. Law: the Montreal Protocol (adopted 16 September 1987) controls ODS; the Kigali Amendment (October 2016) adds the phase-down of HFCs. India became a Party to the Montreal Protocol on 19 June 1992 and made the Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 under the EP Act. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Ozone Depleting Substances (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 – S.O. 670(E), dated 19 July 2000, made under "sections 6, 8 and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986". Rule 2(i) – "ozone depleting substance" means the substances specified in column (2) of Schedule I, "whether existing by itself or in a mixture". Rule 2(m) – "protocol" means the Montreal Protocol "adopted on 16th September 1987". Rule 3(1) – "No person shall produce or cause to produce any ozone depleting substance after the date specified in column (5)" of the relevant Schedule. Rule 4 – prohibition on export to or import from countries not specified in Schedule VI. Rule 5(1) – import or export with Schedule VI countries only "under a licence" issued by the authority. Rule 9(1) – "No person shall establish or expand or cause to establish or expand any manufacturing facility for production" of ODS (prohibition on new investment). Sections 6, 8 and 25, EP Act, 1986 – power of the Central Government to make rules to regulate environmental pollution, and the duty to handle hazardous substances only in accordance with procedure. Article 51(c) of the Constitution – the State shall endeavour to "foster respect for international law and treaty obligations". Article 21 – right to life includes the right to pollution-free air ( Subhash Kumar , 1991).

environmental-law-u1-t7.subtitle: The rise in the Earth's average surface temperature caused by greenhouse gases

en.inOneMinute: Global warming is "the phenomenon of rising average air temperatures near Earth's surface over the past 100 to 200 years". It is caused mainly by human activity: "Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature reaching 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020" (IPCC, 2023). Greenhouse effect: gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide "absorb some of the infrared radiation produced by Earth's surface". Without them the earth would be about 33 °C colder. Burning fossil fuels adds more of these gases and strengthens the effect (the enhanced greenhouse effect ). (See Diagram 1 .) Effects: rising seas (0.20 m between 1901 and 2018), more extreme weather, heat, droughts, floods, melting ice, harm to health and food supply. (See Diagram 2 .) Law: UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto Protocol (in force 16 February 2005) and Paris Agreement (adopted 12 December 2015; aim: "well below 2°C" and efforts for 1.5°C). (See Diagram 3 .) India: there is "no single or umbrella legislation in India which relates to climate change", but the Supreme Court has recognised "a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change" under Arts. 14 and 21 ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
legalProvision: Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Read with Art. 14, it includes "a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , para 27). Article 14 – "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". UNFCCC, 1992, Article 2 – objective: "stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system". UNFCCC, Article 3(1) – Parties act "in accordance with their common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities"; "the developed country Parties should take the lead in combating climate change".
en.meaning: Global warming – the rise in average air temperatures near the earth's surface over the past 100 to 200 years, caused mainly by human emissions of greenhouse gases . Greenhouse effect – the warming of the earth because certain gases in the air absorb some of the heat (infrared radiation) given off by the earth's surface. Greenhouse gas – a gas that traps heat in this way, mainly carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O); also water vapour and fluorinated gases. Climate change (UNFCCC, Art. 1(2)) – "a change of climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods".
keyPoints: Global warming: rising average surface air temperatures over 100–200 years. IPCC: human activities "unequivocally caused" it; 1.1 °C above 1850–1900. Enhanced greenhouse effect from fossil fuels. Main greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O. UNFCCC: common but differentiated responsibilities; Paris: "well below 2°C", efforts for 1.5°C. M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): right to be free from adverse effects of climate change (Arts. 14, 21).

Principle: "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change", recognised by Arts. 14 and 21 (paras 24, 27). The 2021 directions were recalled and substituted, and an Expert Committee was formed to balance "the preservation of the GIB which is non-negotiable" with sustainable development (paras 61, 64, 72). Why it matters: It is the first clear recognition of a constitutional right against climate change in India.

te.inOneMinute: భూతాపం (Global warming) అంటే "the phenomenon of rising average air temperatures near Earth's surface over the past 100 to 200 years" (అర్థం: గత 100 నుండి 200 సంవత్సరాలలో భూ ఉపరితలం దగ్గర సగటు గాలి ఉష్ణోగ్రతలు పెరుగుతున్న దృగ్విషయం). ఇది ప్రధానంగా మానవ కార్యకలాపాల వల్ల: "Human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature reaching 1.1°C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020" (అర్థం: ప్రధానంగా హరితగృహ వాయువుల ఉద్గారాల ద్వారా మానవ కార్యకలాపాలు నిస్సందేహంగా భూతాపానికి కారణమయ్యాయి; 2011-2020 లో ప్రపంచ ఉపరితల ఉష్ణోగ్రత 1850-1900 కంటే 1.1°C ఎక్కువకు చేరింది) (IPCC, 2023). హరితగృహ ప్రభావం: కార్బన్ డయాక్సైడ్, మీథేన్, నైట్రస్ ఆక్సైడ్ వంటి వాయువులు "absorb some of the infrared radiation produced by Earth's surface" (అర్థం: భూ ఉపరితలం విడుదల చేసే పరారుణ వికిరణంలో కొంత భాగాన్ని పీల్చుకుంటాయి). అవి లేకపోతే భూమి సుమారు 33 °C చల్లగా ఉండేది. శిలాజ ఇంధనాలను మండించడం ఈ వాయువులను పెంచి, ప్రభావాన్ని బలపరుస్తుంది ( వృద్ధి చెందిన హరితగృహ ప్రభావం ). ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ప్రభావాలు: సముద్ర మట్టం పెరగడం (1901 నుండి 2018 మధ్య 0.20 మీ.), తీవ్ర వాతావరణ సంఘటనలు, వేడి, కరువులు, వరదలు, మంచు కరగడం, ఆరోగ్యం, ఆహార సరఫరాకు హాని. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) చట్టం: UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto Protocol (16 ఫిబ్రవరి 2005 నుండి అమలు), Paris Agreement (12 డిసెంబర్ 2015 న ఆమోదం; లక్ష్యం: "well below 2°C" (అర్థం: 2°C కంటే బాగా తక్కువ), 1.5°C కోసం ప్రయత్నాలు). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) భారతదేశం: "no single or umbrella legislation in India which relates to climate change" (అర్థం: వాతావరణ మార్పుకు సంబంధించి భారతదేశంలో ఏకైక లేదా సమగ్ర చట్టం లేదు), కానీ సుప్రీంకోర్టు Arts. 14, 21 కింద "a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change" (అర్థం: వాతావరణ మార్పు దుష్ప్రభావాల నుండి విముక్తి పొందే హక్కు) ను గుర్తించింది ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
te.meaning: భూతాపం ( Global warming ) – ప్రధానంగా మానవ హరితగృహ వాయు ఉద్గారాల వల్ల గత 100 నుండి 200 సంవత్సరాలలో భూ ఉపరితలం దగ్గర సగటు గాలి ఉష్ణోగ్రతలు పెరగడం. హరితగృహ ప్రభావం (Greenhouse effect) – భూ ఉపరితలం విడుదల చేసే వేడి (పరారుణ వికిరణం) లో కొంత భాగాన్ని గాలిలోని కొన్ని వాయువులు పీల్చుకోవడం వల్ల భూమి వేడెక్కడం. హరితగృహ వాయువు (Greenhouse gas) – ఈ విధంగా వేడిని బంధించే వాయువు; ప్రధానంగా కార్బన్ డయాక్సైడ్ (CO₂), మీథేన్ (CH₄), నైట్రస్ ఆక్సైడ్ (N₂O); నీటి ఆవిరి, ఫ్లోరినేటెడ్ వాయువులు కూడా. వాతావరణ మార్పు (Climate change) (UNFCCC, Art. 1(2)) – "a change of climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods" (అర్థం: ప్రపంచ వాతావరణ కూర్పును మార్చే మానవ కార్యకలాపాలకు ప్రత్యక్షంగా లేదా పరోక్షంగా ఆపాదించబడే, పోల్చదగిన కాలాల్లో గమనించిన సహజ వాతావరణ వైవిధ్యానికి అదనంగా ఉండే వాతావరణ మార్పు).
keyPoints: భూతాపం: 100–200 సంవత్సరాలలో సగటు ఉపరితల గాలి ఉష్ణోగ్రతల పెరుగుదల. IPCC: మానవ కార్యకలాపాలు "unequivocally caused" (అర్థం: నిస్సందేహంగా కారణమయ్యాయి); 1850–1900 కంటే 1.1 °C. శిలాజ ఇంధనాల వల్ల వృద్ధి చెందిన హరితగృహ ప్రభావం. ప్రధాన హరితగృహ వాయువు లు: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O. UNFCCC: ఉమ్మడి కానీ విభిన్న బాధ్యతలు; Paris: "well below 2°C" (అర్థం: 2°C కంటే బాగా తక్కువ), 1.5°C కోసం ప్రయత్నాలు. M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): వాతావరణ మార్పు దుష్ప్రభావాల నుండి విముక్తి హక్కు (Arts. 14, 21).

selfTest.q: భూతాపాన్ని నిర్వచించండి. హరితగృహ ప్రభావాన్ని నాలుగు దశల్లో వివరించండి. మూడు ప్రధాన హరితగృహ వాయువులను పేర్కొనండి. Paris Agreement ఉష్ణోగ్రత లక్ష్యం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: "common but differentiated responsibilities" అంటే ఏమిటి? M.K. Ranjitsinh లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఏ హక్కును గుర్తించింది?

Read with Art. 14, it includes "a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , para 27). Article 14 – "The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". UNFCCC, 1992, Article 2 – objective: "stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system". UNFCCC, Article 3(1) – Parties act "in accordance with their common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities"; "the developed country Parties should take the lead in combating climate change".
hi.meaning: Global warming – the rise in average air temperatures near the earth's surface over the past 100 to 200 years, caused mainly by human emissions of greenhouse gases . Greenhouse effect – the warming of the earth because certain gases in the air absorb some of the heat (infrared radiation) given off by the earth's surface. Greenhouse gas – a gas that traps heat in this way, mainly carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O); also water vapour and fluorinated gases. Climate change (UNFCCC, Art. 1(2)) – "a change of climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods".
keyPoints: Global warming: rising average surface air temperatures over 100–200 years. IPCC: human activities "unequivocally caused" it; 1.1 °C above 1850–1900. Enhanced greenhouse effect from fossil fuels. Main greenhouse gases: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O. UNFCCC: common but differentiated responsibilities; Paris: "well below 2°C", efforts for 1.5°C. M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): right to be free from adverse effects of climate change (Arts. 14, 21).

caseLaws.facts: M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280; W.P. (C) No. 838 of 2019 (Supreme Court; Dr D.Y. Chandrachud CJI, J.B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra JJ; judgment by Chandrachud CJI; 21 March 2024)

caseLaws.name: Facts: To protect the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard, an order of 19 April 2021 restrict
caseLaws.facts: km of the bird's habitat. The Union Ministries of Environment, Power and New and Renewable Energy sought modification of the order, as it affected renewable energy transmission. Principle: "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change", recognised by Arts. 14 and 21 (paras 24, 27). The 2021 directions were recalled and substituted, and an Expert Committee was formed to balance "the preservation of the GIB which is non-negotiable" with sustainable development (paras 61, 64, 72). Why it matters: It is the first clear recognition of a constitutional right against climate change in India.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries polluted the Palar river in Tamil Nadu
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". Why it matters: These principles guide climate law: act early, and polluters (emitters) bear the cost.
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar AIR 1991 SC 420; (1991) 1 SCC 598 (Supreme Court; K.N. Singh J with N.D. Ojha J; reasons given on 9 January 1991)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A petition about slurry from coal washeries polluting the Bokaro river
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Art. 21 "includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life". Why it matters: It is the base on which the later climate right was built.

environmental-law-u1-t8.subtitle: Long-term shifts in weather patterns, and the UNFCCC meaning of climate change

en.inOneMinute: Climate means the "conditions of the atmosphere at a particular location over a long period of time"; weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere. Climate change is the "periodic modification of Earth's climate brought about as a result of changes in the atmosphere" and its interactions with other natural factors. In law, the UNFCCC uses a narrower meaning: a change of climate "attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere", in addition to natural variability. (See Diagram 1 .) Natural causes: changes in the sun's output, volcanic eruptions, changes in the earth's orbit (Milankovitch variations) and tectonic activity. Human causes: above all, "fossil-fuel combustion since the Industrial Revolution", and deforestation and land-use change. (See Diagram 2 .) Responses: mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions) and adaptation (adjusting to the changes). (See Diagram 3 .) Courts: the Supreme Court recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024); the NGT held that "climate change is certainly a matter covered in the process of impact assessment" ( Ridhima Pandey , 2019).
legalProvision: UNFCCC, 1992, Article 1(2) – "Climate change" means "a change of climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods". UNFCCC, Article 2 – objective: "stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system". UNFCCC, Article 3(1) – "common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities"; developed countries "should take the lead". Articles 14 and 21 – together recognise "a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , paras 24, 27). Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – environmental impact assessment of projects is done under this Act; climate change is "a matter covered in the process of impact assessment" ( Ridhima Pandey , NGT, 2019).
en.meaning: Weather – the state of the atmosphere (temperature, rain, wind) at a place over a short time. Climate – the long-term summation of the atmospheric elements, which over short periods make up weather; it "is not just the 'average weather'". Climatic change – a long-lasting change in the climate of a region or of the whole earth, whether from natural causes or human activity. Mitigation – action to reduce the sources or increase the sinks of greenhouse gases (for example, renewable energy, forests). Adaptation – adjusting human and natural systems to actual or expected climate change so as to reduce harm (for example, flood defences, drought-resistant crops).
keyPoints: Climate: long-term conditions of the atmosphere at a place; weather is short-term. Climate change (UNFCCC Art. 1(2)): due to human activity, in addition to natural variability. Natural causes: sun, volcanoes, Milankovitch, tectonics. Human: fossil fuels, deforestation. Mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation reduces harm. M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): right against adverse effects of climate change. Ridhima Pandey (NGT, 2019): climate change is covered in impact assessment.

Principle: "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change", recognised by Arts. 14 and 21 (paras 24, 27); the 2021 directions were substituted and an Expert Committee formed to balance GIB conservation with sustainable development. Why it matters: It makes protection from climatic change a constitutional right in India.

caseLaws.name: Facts: A young applicant sought directions to assess climate-related issues while appraising project
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "The issue of climate change is certainly a matter covered in the process of impact assessment"; there was "no reason to presume that Paris Agreement and other international protocols are not reflected" in government policy or clearances. The application was disposed of without further directions. Why it matters: It confirms that climate change is part of environmental clearance law, though the Tribunal declined to order a separate climate plan.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

te.inOneMinute: శీతోష్ణస్థితి (Climate) అంటే "conditions of the atmosphere at a particular location over a long period of time" (అర్థం: ఒక ప్రదేశంలో దీర్ఘకాలం పాటు ఉండే వాతావరణ పరిస్థితులు); వాతావరణం (Weather) అంటే తక్కువ కాలపు వాతావరణ స్థితి. శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు (Climate change) అంటే "periodic modification of Earth's climate brought about as a result of changes in the atmosphere" (అర్థం: వాతావరణంలో మార్పుల ఫలితంగా భూమి శీతోష్ణస్థితిలో కాలానుగుణంగా వచ్చే మార్పు), ఇతర సహజ అంశాలతో దాని పరస్పర చర్యలతో సహా. చట్టంలో UNFCCC సన్నని అర్థం ఇస్తుంది: "attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere" (అర్థం: ప్రపంచ వాతావరణ కూర్పును మార్చే మానవ కార్యకలాపాల వల్ల ప్రత్యక్షంగా లేదా పరోక్షంగా వచ్చిన) శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు, సహజ మార్పులకు అదనంగా. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) సహజ కారణాలు: సూర్యుని శక్తిలో మార్పులు, అగ్నిపర్వత విస్ఫోటనాలు, భూమి కక్ష్యలో మార్పులు (మిలాంకోవిచ్ మార్పులు), భూఫలకాల కదలికలు. మానవ కారణాలు: ముఖ్యంగా "fossil-fuel combustion since the Industrial Revolution" (అర్థం: పారిశ్రామిక విప్లవం నుండి శిలాజ ఇంధనాల దహనం), అడవుల నరికివేత మరియు భూవినియోగ మార్పులు. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) ప్రతిస్పందనలు: ఉపశమనం (Mitigation) (హరితగృహ వాయువుల విడుదల తగ్గించడం) మరియు అనుసరణ (Adaptation) (మార్పులకు తగ్గట్టు సర్దుకోవడం). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) న్యాయస్థానాలు: శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు దుష్ప్రభావాల నుండి విముక్తి హక్కును సుప్రీంకోర్టు గుర్తించింది ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024); "climate change is certainly a matter covered in the process of impact assessment" (అర్థం: శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు ప్రభావ అంచనా ప్రక్రియలో తప్పక భాగమే) అని NGT చెప్పింది ( Ridhima Pandey , 2019).
te.meaning: వాతావరణం (Weather) – ఒక ప్రదేశంలో తక్కువ కాలంలో ఉండే వాతావరణ స్థితి (ఉష్ణోగ్రత, వర్షం, గాలి). శీతోష్ణస్థితి (Climate) – వాతావరణ అంశాల దీర్ఘకాలిక సమ్మేళనం; తక్కువ కాలంలో ఇవే వాతావరణం అవుతాయి; ఇది "is not just the 'average weather'" (అర్థం: కేవలం 'సగటు వాతావరణం' మాత్రమే కాదు). శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు (Climatic change) – ఒక ప్రాంతం లేదా మొత్తం భూమి శీతోష్ణస్థితిలో దీర్ఘకాలం నిలిచే మార్పు; సహజ కారణాల వల్ల గానీ, మానవ కార్యకలాపాల వల్ల గానీ. ఉపశమనం (Mitigation) – హరితగృహ వాయువుల మూలాలను తగ్గించే లేదా వాటిని పీల్చుకునే వనరులను (sinks) పెంచే చర్య (ఉదా: పునరుత్పాదక శక్తి, అడవులు). అనుసరణ (Adaptation) – నష్టం తగ్గించడానికి, ఇప్పటికే వచ్చిన లేదా రాబోయే శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పుకు మానవ, సహజ వ్యవస్థలను సర్దుబాటు చేయడం (ఉదా: వరద రక్షణ కట్టడాలు, కరువును తట్టుకునే పంటలు).
keyPoints: శీతోష్ణస్థితి: ఒక ప్రదేశంలో దీర్ఘకాలపు వాతావరణ పరిస్థితులు; వాతావరణం తక్కువ కాలానిది. శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు (UNFCCC ఆర్టి. 1(2)): మానవ కార్యకలాపాల వల్ల, సహజ మార్పులకు అదనంగా. సహజ కారణాలు: సూర్యుడు, అగ్నిపర్వతాలు, మిలాంకోవిచ్, భూఫలకాలు. మానవ: శిలాజ ఇంధనాలు, అడవుల నరికివేత. ఉపశమనం విడుదలలను తగ్గిస్తుంది; అనుసరణ నష్టాన్ని తగ్గిస్తుంది. M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు దుష్ప్రభావాల నుండి విముక్తి హక్కు. Ridhima Pandey (NGT, 2019): ప్రభావ అంచనాలో శీతోష్ణస్థితి మార్పు భాగం.

hi.inOneMinute: Climate means the "conditions of the atmosphere at a particular location over a long period of time"; weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere. Climate change is the "periodic modification of Earth's climate brought about as a result of changes in the atmosphere" and its interactions with other natural factors. In law, the UNFCCC uses a narrower meaning: a change of climate "attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere", in addition to natural variability. (See Diagram 1 .) Natural causes: changes in the sun's output, volcanic eruptions, changes in the earth's orbit (Milankovitch variations) and tectonic activity. Human causes: above all, "fossil-fuel combustion since the Industrial Revolution", and deforestation and land-use change. (See Diagram 2 .) Responses: mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions) and adaptation (adjusting to the changes). (See Diagram 3 .) Courts: the Supreme Court recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024); the NGT held that "climate change is certainly a matter covered in the process of impact assessment" ( Ridhima Pandey , 2019).
legalProvision: UNFCCC, 1992, Article 1(2) – "Climate change" means "a change of climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods". UNFCCC, Article 2 – objective: "stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system". UNFCCC, Article 3(1) – "common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities"; developed countries "should take the lead". Articles 14 and 21 – together recognise "a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , paras 24, 27). Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – environmental impact assessment of projects is done under this Act; climate change is "a matter covered in the process of impact assessment" ( Ridhima Pandey , NGT, 2019).
hi.meaning: Weather – the state of the atmosphere (temperature, rain, wind) at a place over a short time. Climate – the long-term summation of the atmospheric elements, which over short periods make up weather; it "is not just the 'average weather'". Climatic change – a long-lasting change in the climate of a region or of the whole earth, whether from natural causes or human activity. Mitigation – action to reduce the sources or increase the sinks of greenhouse gases (for example, renewable energy, forests). Adaptation – adjusting human and natural systems to actual or expected climate change so as to reduce harm (for example, flood defences, drought-resistant crops).
keyPoints: Climate: long-term conditions of the atmosphere at a place; weather is short-term. Climate change (UNFCCC Art. 1(2)): due to human activity, in addition to natural variability. Natural causes: sun, volcanoes, Milankovitch, tectonics. Human: fossil fuels, deforestation. Mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation reduces harm. M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): right against adverse effects of climate change. Ridhima Pandey (NGT, 2019): climate change is covered in impact assessment.

caseLaws.facts: M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280; W.P. (C) No. 838 of 2019 (Supreme Court; Dr D.Y. Chandrachud CJI, J.B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra JJ; 21 March 2024)

Principle: "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change", recognised by Arts. 14 and 21 (paras 24, 27); the 2021 directions were substituted and an Expert Committee formed to balance GIB conservation with sustainable development. Why it matters: It makes protection from climatic change a constitutional right in India.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "The issue of climate change is certainly a matter covered in the process of impact assessment"; there was "no reason to presume that Paris Agreement and other international protocols are not reflected" in government policy or clearances. The application was disposed of without further directions. Why it matters: It confirms that climate change is part of environmental clearance law, though the Tribunal declined to order a separate climate plan.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". Why it matters: These principles guide action against climatic change before full harm occurs.
