te.inOneMinute: రెండు నియమాలూ నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేకుండానే కాలుష్యకారుడిని బాధ్యుడిని చేస్తాయి. కఠిన బాధ్యత (Strict liability) – Rylands v. Fletcher (1868): "likely to do mischief if it escapes" (అర్థం: బయటకు వస్తే హాని చేసే అవకాశం ఉన్న) దేనినైనా తన భూమిపైకి తెచ్చి ఉంచే వ్యక్తి దాన్ని "at his peril" (అర్థం: తన బాధ్యతపై) లోపల ఉంచాలి. ఆ ఉపయోగం అసహజ (non-natural) ఉపయోగం కావాలని హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్ జోడించింది. ఈ నియమానికి మినహాయింపులు ఉన్నాయి (వాది సొంత తప్పు, దైవ చర్య లేదా vis major, అపరిచితుడి చర్య, మరికొన్ని). సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత (Absolute liability) – M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (ఓలియం గ్యాస్ లీక్, 1986): ప్రమాదకర లేదా స్వాభావికంగా ప్రమాదకర చర్యలో నిమగ్నమైన సంస్థ ప్రమాదం వల్ల కలిగిన హానికి "strictly and absolutely liable" (అర్థం: కఠినంగా, సంపూర్ణంగా బాధ్యురాలు); ఆ బాధ్యత Rylands కింద ఉన్న "not subject to any of the exceptions" (అర్థం: ఏ మినహాయింపుకూ లోబడదు). నష్టపరిహారం "co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise" (అర్థం: సంస్థ పరిమాణం, సామర్థ్యంతో ముడిపడి) ఉండాలి. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యతను, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రాన్ని (polluter pays principle) అన్వయించింది: నష్టాన్ని సరిచేసే ఖర్చు కాలుష్యకారుడే భరించాలి. పర్యావరణ (పరిరక్షణ) చట్టం, 1986 సెక్షన్లు 3, 5 కింద కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం సరిచేసే ఖర్చులను వసూలు చేయవచ్చు. ప్రజా బాధ్యత బీమా చట్టం, 1991 ప్రమాదకర పదార్థాలతో జరిగే ప్రమాదాలకు తక్షణ తప్పు లేని (no-fault) ఉపశమనం ఇస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 3(2)). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: కఠిన బాధ్యత ( Strict liability ) – భూమి అసహజ ఉపయోగంలో ఉంచిన ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు బయటకు రావడం వల్ల కలిగిన నష్టానికి, గుర్తించబడిన మినహాయింపులకు లోబడి, నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేని బాధ్యత ( Rylands ). సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( Absolute liability ) – ప్రమాదకర లేదా స్వాభావికంగా ప్రమాదకర చర్యలో నిమగ్నమైన సంస్థకు ఆ చర్యలో ప్రమాదం వల్ల కలిగిన అన్ని హానులకు, ఏ మినహాయింపూ లేని బాధ్యత ( M.C. Mehta ). అసహజ ఉపయోగం (Non-natural use) – సహజంగా లేని, బయటకు వస్తే ప్రమాదకరమైనదాన్ని భూమిపైకి తెచ్చే ఉపయోగం, ఉదా. పెద్ద నీటి జలాశయం ( Rylands , Lord Cairns). బయటకు రావడం (Escape) – ప్రమాదకర వస్తువు ప్రతివాది భూమి లేదా నియంత్రణ నుంచి హాని జరిగిన చోటికి బయటకు రావాలి. కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం (Polluter pays principle) – కాలుష్యం వల్ల కలిగిన నష్టాన్ని నివారించే లేదా సరిచేసే ఆర్థిక ఖర్చులు దాన్ని కలిగించిన సంస్థలపైనే ఉంటాయి ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action ).
keyPoints: కఠిన బాధ్యత: తన బాధ్యతపై లోపల ఉంచాలి ( Rylands ). అసహజ ఉపయోగం అవసరం (Lord Cairns). మినహాయింపులు: వాది సొంత తప్పు, దైవ చర్య, అపరిచితుడి చర్య, ఇతరాలు. సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత: ప్రమాదకర చర్య, మినహాయింపులు లేవు ( M.C. Mehta ). నష్టపరిహారం సంస్థ పరిమాణం, సామర్థ్యంతో ముడిపడి ఉంటుంది. కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం, EPA సెక్షన్లు 3, 5 కింద సరిచేసే ఖర్చులు ( ICELA ). PLI చట్టం: తప్పు లేని ఉపశమనం (సెక్షన్ 3(2)); తర్వాతి నష్టపరిహారాన్ని తగ్గిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 8(2)).

selfTest.q: Rylands v. Fletcher నియమాన్ని చెప్పండి. Lord Cairns ఏం జోడించారు?
selfTest.a: కఠిన బాధ్యతకు మూడు మినహాయింపులు చెప్పండి. M.C. Mehta చట్టాన్ని ఎలా మార్చింది? భారతదేశంలో Rylands గురించి ICELA ఏం చెప్పింది? PLI చట్టం కింద దావాదారుడు తప్పు రుజువు చేయాలా?

hi.inOneMinute: Both rules make a polluter liable without proof of negligence . Strict liability – Rylands v. Fletcher (1868): a person who brings on his land and keeps there anything "likely to do mischief if it escapes" must keep it in "at his peril". The House of Lords added that the use must be a non-natural use. The rule has exceptions (plaintiff's default, act of God or vis major, act of a stranger, and others). Absolute liability – M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak, 1986): an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is "strictly and absolutely liable" for harm from an accident, and the liability "is not subject to any of the exceptions" under Rylands . Compensation must be "co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) applied absolute liability and the polluter pays principle : the polluter bears the cost of remedying the damage. The Central Government can recover remedial costs under ss. 3 and 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. The Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 gives immediate no-fault relief for accidents involving hazardous substances (s. 3(2)). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Strict and absolute liability are judge-made rules. Statutory support:

Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3(1) – "Where death or injury to any person (other than a workman) or damage to any property has resulted from an accident, the owner shall be liable to reimburse such amount, or provide such other relief as may be prescribed", for death, medical expenses, loss of wages, other injury or sickness, damage to private property, and other prescribed loss. Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3(2) – "the claimant shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person." Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 2(d) – "hazardous substance" means any substance or preparation "defined as hazardous substance under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (29 of 1986), and exceeding such quantity as may be specified, by notification, by the Central Government". Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 8 – relief is "in addition to any other right to claim compensation" (s. 8(1)); compensation under any other law is "reduced by the amount of relief paid under this Act" (s. 8(2)). Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, ss. 3 and 5 – as read in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996), the Central Government's powers to take measures and issue directions include "the power to impose the cost of remedial measures on the offending industry".
hi.meaning: Strict liability – liability without proof of negligence for damage from the escape of a dangerous thing kept on land in the course of a non-natural use , subject to recognised exceptions ( Rylands ). Absolute liability – liability of an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity for all harm from an accident in that activity, with no exceptions ( M.C. Mehta ). Non-natural use – a use of land that brings on it something not naturally there and dangerous if it escapes, such as a large reservoir of water ( Rylands , Lord Cairns). Escape – the dangerous thing must get out from the defendant's land or control to the place where the harm occurs. Polluter pays principle – the financial costs of preventing or remedying damage caused by pollution lie with the undertakings that cause it ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action ).
keyPoints: Strict liability: keep it in at your peril ( Rylands ). Non-natural use needed (Lord Cairns). Exceptions: plaintiff's default, act of God, act of stranger, others. Absolute liability: hazardous activity, no exceptions ( M.C. Mehta ). Compensation linked to the enterprise's magnitude and capacity. Polluter pays principle and remedial costs under EPA ss. 3, 5 ( ICELA ). PLI Act: no-fault relief (s. 3(2)); reduces later compensation (s. 8(2)).

caseLaws.facts: Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) LR 3 HL 330 (House of Lords: Lord Cairns LC, Lord Cranworth)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The defendants' reservoir, built over old disused mine shafts, burst through them and flooded
caseLaws.facts: The defendants were not personally negligent. Principle: A person who brings and keeps on his land anything likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it in at his peril; Lord Cairns added the non-natural use requirement. Judgment of the Exchequer Chamber for the plaintiff was affirmed. Why it matters: It is the root of no-fault liability for the escape of dangerous substances, including pollutants.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak) (1987) 1 SCC 395; AIR 1987 SC 1086 – decided 20 December 1986 (P.N. Bhagwati CJ for a five-judge bench)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas escaped on 4 and 6 December 1985 from a unit of Shriram in Delhi
caseLaws.facts: Applications for compensation were referred to a five-judge bench. Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity is strictly and absolutely liable for harm from an accident, without any Rylands exception; compensation must be linked to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise. Why it matters: It created absolute liability, the Indian rule for industrial pollution disasters.
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) 3 SCC 212; AIR 1996 SC 1446 – decided 13 February 1996 (B.P. Jeevan Reddy J; bench with B.N. Kirpal J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Chemical units at Bichhri, Rajasthan, making 'H' acid, discharged toxic effluent and dumped s
caseLaws.facts: Principle: M.C. Mehta absolute liability is binding and Rylands is unsuitable for India; the polluter pays principle applies, and the cost of remedial measures can be imposed on the polluting industry under EPA ss. 3 and 5. Why it matters: It extended absolute liability to the cost of restoring the environment.
M.P. Electricity Board v. Shail Kumari AIR 2002 SC 551 – decided 11 January 2002 (K.T. Thomas J, with S.N. Phukan J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A cyclist was electrocuted at night by a live wire lying on a rain-flooded road
caseLaws.facts: The Board blamed a stranger's illegal tapping. Principle: Strict liability applied; the act-of-stranger exception was not available because the act should reasonably have been anticipated or its consequences prevented. The appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It shows Rylands strict liability still applied in India, and how narrowly its exceptions are read.

environmental-law-u2-t1.subtitle: The ordinary civil and criminal law a person can use when pollution harms them, side by side with special pollution statutes

en.inOneMinute: Long before pollution statutes, a person harmed by smoke, fumes, effluent, dust, noise or vibration could sue in tort . These are the common law remedies against pollution. The torts used are: private nuisance – unreasonable interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land; public nuisance – a nuisance that affects the public or a class of people; trespass – direct physical entry of a substance onto another's land; negligence – harm caused by failure to take reasonable care; strict liability ( Rylands v. Fletcher ) and absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta , 1986) – liability for escape of dangerous things or for hazardous industry, without proof of fault. (See Diagram 1 .) The reliefs are damages , an injunction (temporary, perpetual or mandatory : Specific Relief Act, 1963, ss. 36–40) and, in some cases, abatement . For a public nuisance, a civil suit may be brought by the Advocate-General , or by two or more persons with the leave of the Court even without special damage (s. 91, CPC). A magistrate can also order removal of a public nuisance (s. 152, BNSS), as in Municipal Council, Ratlam (1980).
legalProvision: Common law torts are judge-made. In India they are applied with these statutory supports:
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

Section 91(1): "In the case of a public nuisance or other wrongful act affecting, or likely to affect, the public, a suit for a declaration and injunction or for such other relief as may be appropriate in the circumstances of the case, may be instituted,— (a) by the Advocate-General, or (b) with the leave of the Court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons by reason of such public nuisance or other wrongful act." Section 91(2): "Nothing in this section shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any right of suit which may exist independently of its provisions."
Specific Relief Act, 1963

Section 36: "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." Section 37(2): a perpetual injunction "can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit". Section 38(1): a perpetual injunction "may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication"; s. 38(3) covers a defendant who "invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property". Section 39: where it is necessary "to compel the performance of certain acts", the court may grant a mandatory injunction. Section 40(1): the plaintiff "may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction".
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

BNS s. 270: a person is guilty of a public nuisance "who does any act or is guilty of an illegal omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity". BNSS s. 152(1)(b): a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or specially empowered Executive Magistrate may act where "the conduct of any trade or occupation, or the keeping of any goods or merchandise, is injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community".
en.meaning: Common law remedies – remedies developed by courts in tort cases, as distinct from remedies created by pollution statutes. Private nuisance – unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or some right over it, such as by smoke, smell, noise or vibration. Public nuisance – a nuisance that "materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of life of a class of Her Majesty's subjects" ( A.G. v. P.Y.A. Quarries , Romer LJ); in Indian criminal law, see BNS s. 270. Injunction – a court order restraining a person from doing an act (prohibitory) or requiring him to do an act (mandatory) (Specific Relief Act, ss. 36–39). Special damage – damage to the plaintiff over and above that suffered by the public in general. A private person suing alone for public nuisance needs it; under s. 91(1)(b) CPC two or more persons may sue with leave without it.
keyPoints: Common law remedies: tort actions against polluters. Private nuisance: locality matters for discomfort, not for material injury ( St. Helen's ). Public nuisance: affects a class; representative cross-section enough ( P.Y.A. Quarries ). s. 91 CPC: A-G, or two or more persons with leave, without special damage. Injunction: temporary, perpetual, mandatory (ss. 36–39 SRA); damages with or instead (s. 40). BNS s. 270; BNSS s. 152; Ratlam : abatement is a mandatory duty. Absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ): no exceptions; compensation linked to the enterprise's capacity.

caseLaws.facts: St. Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping (1865) 11 HLC 642; 11 ER 1483 (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff bought an estate about a mile and a half from large copper smelting works
caseLaws.facts: Fumes damaged his trees and crops. The jury found the works were not carried on in a proper place and awarded £361 18s. 4½d. Principle: Lord Westbury separated "material injury to the property" from "sensible personal discomfort". Locality matters for discomfort, but not in the same way for material injury. Why it matters: It is the basic authority for using private nuisance against industrial air pollution.
Attorney-General v. P.Y.A. Quarries Ltd. [1958] EWCA Civ 1 (Court of Appeal, Denning, Romer and Parker LJJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A quarry near Pontardawe threw out stones and splinters and caused dust and vibration
caseLaws.facts: The trial judge granted an injunction; the company appealed only against the dust and vibration part. Principle: A nuisance is public if it "materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of life of a class of Her Majesty's subjects" (Romer LJ); a representative cross-section is enough. The appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It gives the test for public nuisance used in pollution cases such as dust and vibration.
Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Shri Vardhichand (1980) – AIR 1980 SC 1622; 1981 SCR (1) 97; decided 29 July 1980 (Krishna Iyer J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents complained under s
caseLaws.facts: 133 CrPC (now s. 152 BNSS) that the municipality failed to provide drains and sanitation and that an alcohol plant discharged foul fluids into the street. The magistrate ordered the municipality to abate the nuisance. Principle: The provision made the abatement of public nuisance "a mandatory duty"; a municipality cannot plead lack of funds to avoid it. Why it matters: It shows a public nuisance remedy being used to force a public body to stop pollution.

te.inOneMinute: కాలుష్య చట్టాలు రాకముందే, పొగ, విష వాయువులు, మురుగు నీరు, ధూళి, శబ్దం లేదా కంపనల వల్ల హాని పొందిన వ్యక్తి టార్ట్ ‌లో దావా వేయగలిగేవాడు. ఇవే కాలుష్యానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా సాధారణ చట్ట (common law) పరిహారాలు . ఉపయోగించే టార్ట్‌లు: ప్రైవేట్ న్యూసెన్స్ (private nuisance) – ఒక వ్యక్తి తన భూమిని ఉపయోగించుకోవడంలో లేదా అనుభవించడంలో అసమంజస జోక్యం; పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్ (public nuisance) – ప్రజలను లేదా ఒక వర్గం ప్రజలను ప్రభావితం చేసే న్యూసెన్స్; అతిక్రమణ (trespass) – ఒక పదార్థం నేరుగా భౌతికంగా మరొకరి భూమిలోకి ప్రవేశించడం; నిర్లక్ష్యం (negligence) – సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోకపోవడం వల్ల కలిగిన హాని; కఠిన బాధ్యత (strict liability) ( Rylands v. Fletcher ), సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత (absolute liability) ( M.C. Mehta , 1986) – ప్రమాదకర వస్తువులు బయటకు రావడం లేదా ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమ వల్ల, తప్పు రుజువు లేకుండానే బాధ్యత. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ఉపశమనాలు: నష్టపరిహారం , నిషేధాజ్ఞ (injunction) (తాత్కాలిక, శాశ్వత లేదా ఆదేశాత్మక: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం, 1963, సెక్షన్లు 36–40), కొన్ని సందర్భాల్లో స్వయంగా తొలగించడం ( abatement ) . పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్‌కు సివిల్ దావాను అడ్వకేట్ జనరల్ , లేదా ప్రత్యేక నష్టం లేకపోయినా కోర్టు అనుమతితో ఇద్దరు లేదా అంతకంటే ఎక్కువ మంది వేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 91, CPC). మేజిస్ట్రేట్ కూడా పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్ తొలగింపుకు ఆదేశించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 152, BNSS), Municipal Council, Ratlam (1980)లో లాగా.
te.meaning: సాధారణ చట్ట పరిహారాలు – కాలుష్య చట్టాలు సృష్టించిన పరిహారాలకు భిన్నంగా, టార్ట్ కేసుల్లో కోర్టులు అభివృద్ధి చేసిన పరిహారాలు. ప్రైవేట్ న్యూసెన్స్ (Private nuisance ) – పొగ, వాసన, శబ్దం లేదా కంపన వంటి వాటి ద్వారా ఒక వ్యక్తి తన భూమిని లేదా దానిపై హక్కును ఉపయోగించుకోవడంలో లేదా అనుభవించడంలో చట్టవిరుద్ధ జోక్యం. పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్ (Public nuisance) – "materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of life of a class of Her Majesty's subjects" (అర్థం: ఒక వర్గం ప్రజల జీవితంలో సహేతుక సౌకర్యాన్ని, సదుపాయాన్ని గణనీయంగా ప్రభావితం చేసే) న్యూసెన్స్ ( A.G. v. P.Y.A. Quarries , Romer LJ); భారతీయ క్రిమినల్ చట్టంలో BNS సెక్షన్ 270 చూడండి. నిషేధాజ్ఞ ( Injunction ) – ఒక చర్య చేయకుండా నిరోధించే (నిషేధాత్మక) లేదా ఒక చర్య చేయమని ఆదేశించే (ఆదేశాత్మక) కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు (నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం, సెక్షన్లు 36–39). ప్రత్యేక నష్టం (Special damage) – సాధారణ ప్రజలు పొందిన నష్టానికి మించి వాదికి కలిగిన నష్టం. పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్ కోసం ఒంటరిగా దావా వేసే వ్యక్తికి ఇది అవసరం; సెక్షన్ 91(1)(b) CPC కింద ఇద్దరు లేదా అంతకంటే ఎక్కువ మంది అనుమతితో అది లేకుండానే దావా వేయవచ్చు.
keyPoints: సాధారణ చట్ట పరిహారాలు: కాలుష్యకారులపై టార్ట్ దావాలు. ప్రైవేట్ న్యూసెన్స్: అసౌకర్యానికి ప్రదేశం ముఖ్యం, భౌతిక గాయానికి కాదు ( St. Helen's ). పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్: ఒక వర్గాన్ని ప్రభావితం చేస్తుంది; ప్రాతినిధ్య భాగం చాలు ( P.Y.A. Quarries ). సెక్షన్ 91 CPC: అడ్వకేట్ జనరల్, లేదా ప్రత్యేక నష్టం లేకుండా అనుమతితో ఇద్దరు లేదా ఎక్కువ మంది. నిషేధాజ్ఞ: తాత్కాలిక, శాశ్వత, ఆదేశాత్మక (సెక్షన్లు 36–39 SRA); దానితో లేదా బదులుగా నష్టపరిహారం (సెక్షన్ 40). BNS సెక్షన్ 270; BNSS సెక్షన్ 152; Ratlam : తొలగింపు తప్పనిసరి విధి. సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( M.C. Mehta ): మినహాయింపులు లేవు; నష్టపరిహారం సంస్థ సామర్థ్యంతో ముడిపడి ఉంటుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: Long before pollution statutes, a person harmed by smoke, fumes, effluent, dust, noise or vibration could sue in tort . These are the common law remedies against pollution. The torts used are: private nuisance – unreasonable interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land; public nuisance – a nuisance that affects the public or a class of people; trespass – direct physical entry of a substance onto another's land; negligence – harm caused by failure to take reasonable care; strict liability ( Rylands v. Fletcher ) and absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta , 1986) – liability for escape of dangerous things or for hazardous industry, without proof of fault. (See Diagram 1 .) The reliefs are damages , an injunction (temporary, perpetual or mandatory : Specific Relief Act, 1963, ss. 36–40) and, in some cases, abatement . For a public nuisance, a civil suit may be brought by the Advocate-General , or by two or more persons with the leave of the Court even without special damage (s. 91, CPC). A magistrate can also order removal of a public nuisance (s. 152, BNSS), as in Municipal Council, Ratlam (1980).
legalProvision: Common law torts are judge-made. In India they are applied with these statutory supports:
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

Section 91(1): "In the case of a public nuisance or other wrongful act affecting, or likely to affect, the public, a suit for a declaration and injunction or for such other relief as may be appropriate in the circumstances of the case, may be instituted,— (a) by the Advocate-General, or (b) with the leave of the Court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons by reason of such public nuisance or other wrongful act." Section 91(2): "Nothing in this section shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect any right of suit which may exist independently of its provisions."
Specific Relief Act, 1963

Section 36: "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." Section 37(2): a perpetual injunction "can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit". Section 38(1): a perpetual injunction "may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication"; s. 38(3) covers a defendant who "invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property". Section 39: where it is necessary "to compel the performance of certain acts", the court may grant a mandatory injunction. Section 40(1): the plaintiff "may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction".
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

BNS s. 270: a person is guilty of a public nuisance "who does any act or is guilty of an illegal omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity". BNSS s. 152(1)(b): a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or specially empowered Executive Magistrate may act where "the conduct of any trade or occupation, or the keeping of any goods or merchandise, is injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community".
hi.meaning: Common law remedies – remedies developed by courts in tort cases, as distinct from remedies created by pollution statutes. Private nuisance – unlawful interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land, or some right over it, such as by smoke, smell, noise or vibration. Public nuisance – a nuisance that "materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of life of a class of Her Majesty's subjects" ( A.G. v. P.Y.A. Quarries , Romer LJ); in Indian criminal law, see BNS s. 270. Injunction – a court order restraining a person from doing an act (prohibitory) or requiring him to do an act (mandatory) (Specific Relief Act, ss. 36–39). Special damage – damage to the plaintiff over and above that suffered by the public in general. A private person suing alone for public nuisance needs it; under s. 91(1)(b) CPC two or more persons may sue with leave without it.
keyPoints: Common law remedies: tort actions against polluters. Private nuisance: locality matters for discomfort, not for material injury ( St. Helen's ). Public nuisance: affects a class; representative cross-section enough ( P.Y.A. Quarries ). s. 91 CPC: A-G, or two or more persons with leave, without special damage. Injunction: temporary, perpetual, mandatory (ss. 36–39 SRA); damages with or instead (s. 40). BNS s. 270; BNSS s. 152; Ratlam : abatement is a mandatory duty. Absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ): no exceptions; compensation linked to the enterprise's capacity.

caseLaws.facts: St. Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping (1865) 11 HLC 642; 11 ER 1483 (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The plaintiff bought an estate about a mile and a half from large copper smelting works
caseLaws.facts: Fumes damaged his trees and crops. The jury found the works were not carried on in a proper place and awarded £361 18s. 4½d. Principle: Lord Westbury separated "material injury to the property" from "sensible personal discomfort". Locality matters for discomfort, but not in the same way for material injury. Why it matters: It is the basic authority for using private nuisance against industrial air pollution.
Attorney-General v. P.Y.A. Quarries Ltd. [1958] EWCA Civ 1 (Court of Appeal, Denning, Romer and Parker LJJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A quarry near Pontardawe threw out stones and splinters and caused dust and vibration
caseLaws.facts: The trial judge granted an injunction; the company appealed only against the dust and vibration part. Principle: A nuisance is public if it "materially affects the reasonable comfort and convenience of life of a class of Her Majesty's subjects" (Romer LJ); a representative cross-section is enough. The appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It gives the test for public nuisance used in pollution cases such as dust and vibration.
Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Shri Vardhichand (1980) – AIR 1980 SC 1622; 1981 SCR (1) 97; decided 29 July 1980 (Krishna Iyer J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents complained under s
caseLaws.facts: 133 CrPC (now s. 152 BNSS) that the municipality failed to provide drains and sanitation and that an alcohol plant discharged foul fluids into the street. The magistrate ordered the municipality to abate the nuisance. Principle: The provision made the abatement of public nuisance "a mandatory duty"; a municipality cannot plead lack of funds to avoid it. Why it matters: It shows a public nuisance remedy being used to force a public body to stop pollution.

selfTest.q: Name five torts used against pollution. What distinction did Lord Westbury draw in St. Helen's?
selfTest.a: What is the test for public nuisance in P.Y.A. Quarries ? Who may file a civil suit for public nuisance under s. 91 CPC? Which section of the Specific Relief Act provides for mandatory injunctions? What did Ratlam decide about a municipality's lack of funds?

environmental-law-u2-t2.subtitle: Direct interference with possession of land, and when polluting matter amounts to it

en.inOneMinute: Trespass to land is an unjustified, direct physical interference with land in another person's possession. In pollution cases, trespass covers a polluter who directly puts a substance on another's land: dumping garbage, pumping effluent onto a field, spraying chemicals over a boundary, or piling debris on a neighbour's plot. (See Diagram 1 .) Trespass is actionable per se : the owner need not prove damage. Entick v. Carrington (1765): a person who sets foot on his neighbour's land without leave "is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all". If the polluting matter stays on the land, the trespass is continuing , and a fresh period of limitation runs every moment it continues (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 22). The ordinary period for compensation is three years from the trespass (Art. 87). Remedies: damages, an injunction ( perpetual : s. 38(3) Specific Relief Act; mandatory removal: s. 39), and removal by the possessor himself. (See Diagram 3 .) Trespass needs direct entry. Fumes, smoke or smells drifting across are usually treated as nuisance , not trespass.
legalProvision: Trespass to land is a common law tort; no statute defines it. These provisions support it:

Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7(a) – the "exclusive right of every owner of immovable property (subject to any law for the time being in force) to enjoy and dispose of the same and all products thereof and accessions thereto". Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 87 – "For compensation for trespass upon immovable property": three years from "The date of the trespass". Limitation Act, 1963, s. 22 – "In the case of a continuing breach of contract or in the case of a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(3) – a perpetual injunction may be granted when the defendant "invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property", including: "(b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion"; "(c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief"; "(d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 39 – a mandatory injunction "to compel performance of the requisite acts". Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 329(1) (criminal side) – "Whoever enters into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession of such property ... is said to commit criminal trespass."
en.meaning: Trespass to land – an unjustified, direct, physical interference with land in the possession of another. Actionable per se – a wrong for which a suit lies without proof of damage. Trespass is one. Direct interference – the defendant's act itself puts the person or substance on the land, as opposed to harm that follows indirectly (which is nuisance ). Continuing trespass – trespass that lasts as long as the thing wrongfully placed stays on the land; each moment is a fresh wrong (s. 22, Limitation Act). Possession – trespass protects the person in possession, not only the owner. Section 7(a) of the Easements Act states the owner's exclusive right to enjoy his property.
keyPoints: Trespass to land: direct, unjustified interference with land in possession. Actionable per se ( Entick ). Needs direct interference; drifting fumes are nuisance ( St. Helen's ). Continuing trespass: fresh limitation every moment (s. 22); otherwise three years (Art. 87). Remedies: damages; perpetual injunction (s. 38(3)); mandatory removal (s. 39); self-help removal. Criminal trespass: s. 329 BNS (needs specific intent).

caseLaws.facts: Entick v. Carrington [1765] EWHC KB J98; 95 ER 807 (judgment of the whole Court for the plaintiff)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The King's messengers broke into John Entick's house under a warrant from the Secretary of St
caseLaws.facts: Entick sued them in trespass. Principle: The law holds every man's property "so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all". Any entry must be justified by law. Why it matters: It establishes that trespass is actionable per se, so a polluter who directly puts waste on land is liable without proof of loss.
St. Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping (1865) 11 HLC 642; 11 ER 1483 (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Fumes from copper smelting works about a mile and a half away damaged the plaintiff's trees a
caseLaws.facts: The action was in nuisance, and the plaintiff won damages. Principle: Lord Westbury treated the injury from drifting fumes as nuisance and distinguished "material injury to the property" from "sensible personal discomfort". Why it matters: It shows the line between trespass and nuisance: airborne pollution reaching land indirectly is nuisance, not trespass.

selfTest.q: Define trespass to land. What does "actionable per se" mean?
selfTest.a: Is smoke drifting from a factory trespass or nuisance? What is the limitation period for compensation for trespass upon immovable property? How does s. 22 of the Limitation Act help in continuing trespass? Which section of the Specific Relief Act allows an order to remove dumped waste?

te.inOneMinute: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ (Trespass to land) అంటే మరొక వ్యక్తి స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న భూమిపై సమర్థన లేని, ప్రత్యక్ష భౌతిక జోక్యం. కాలుష్య కేసుల్లో, మరొకరి భూమిపై నేరుగా ఒక పదార్థాన్ని వేసే కాలుష్యకారుడిని అతిక్రమణ కవర్ చేస్తుంది: చెత్త పారవేయడం, పొలంలోకి మురుగు నీరు పంప్ చేయడం, సరిహద్దు మీదుగా రసాయనాలు చల్లడం, లేదా పొరుగువారి స్థలంలో శిథిలాలు పోయడం. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) అతిక్రమణ నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండానే దావాకు అర్హం (actionable per se) : యజమాని నష్టం రుజువు చేయనక్కర్లేదు. Entick v. Carrington (1765): అనుమతి లేకుండా పొరుగువారి భూమిపై అడుగుపెట్టిన వ్యక్తి "is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all" (అర్థం: ఏ నష్టమూ చేయకపోయినా అతిక్రమణదారే). కాలుష్య పదార్థం భూమిపై అలాగే ఉంటే, అతిక్రమణ కొనసాగుతుంది ; అది కొనసాగే ప్రతి క్షణం కొత్త కాలపరిమితి మొదలవుతుంది (కాలపరిమితి చట్టం, 1963, సెక్షన్ 22). నష్టపరిహారానికి సాధారణ కాలపరిమితి అతిక్రమణ జరిగిన తేదీ నుంచి మూడేళ్లు (ఆర్టికల్ 87). పరిహారాలు: నష్టపరిహారం, నిషేధాజ్ఞ (శాశ్వత: సెక్షన్ 38(3) నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం; తొలగించమని ఆదేశం: సెక్షన్ 39), స్వాధీనదారుడే స్వయంగా తొలగించడం. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) అతిక్రమణకు ప్రత్యక్ష ప్రవేశం అవసరం. గాలిలో వ్యాపించే విష వాయువులు, పొగ, వాసనలను సాధారణంగా న్యూసెన్స్ ‌గా పరిగణిస్తారు, అతిక్రమణగా కాదు.
te.meaning: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ ( Trespass to land ) – మరొకరి స్వాధీనంలోని భూమిపై సమర్థన లేని, ప్రత్యక్ష, భౌతిక జోక్యం. నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండా దావాకు అర్హం (Actionable per se ) – నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండానే దావా వేయగలిగే తప్పు. అతిక్రమణ అలాంటిది. ప్రత్యక్ష జోక్యం (Direct interference) – ప్రతివాది చర్యే వ్యక్తిని లేదా పదార్థాన్ని భూమిపై ఉంచడం; పరోక్షంగా కలిగే హాని ( న్యూసెన్స్ )కి భిన్నం. కొనసాగే అతిక్రమణ (Continuing trespass) – తప్పుగా ఉంచిన వస్తువు భూమిపై ఉన్నంత కాలం కొనసాగే అతిక్రమణ; ప్రతి క్షణం కొత్త తప్పు (సెక్షన్ 22, కాలపరిమితి చట్టం). స్వాధీనం (Possession) – అతిక్రమణ యజమానినే కాక స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తిని రక్షిస్తుంది. ఈజ్‌మెంట్స్ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 7(a) యజమాని తన ఆస్తిని అనుభవించే ప్రత్యేక హక్కును చెప్తుంది.
keyPoints: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణ: స్వాధీనంలోని భూమిపై ప్రత్యక్ష, సమర్థన లేని జోక్యం. నష్టం రుజువు లేకుండా దావాకు అర్హం ( Entick ). ప్రత్యక్ష జోక్యం అవసరం; వ్యాపించే విష వాయువులు న్యూసెన్స్ ( St. Helen's ). కొనసాగే అతిక్రమణ: ప్రతి క్షణం కొత్త కాలపరిమితి (సెక్షన్ 22); లేకపోతే మూడేళ్లు (ఆర్టికల్ 87). పరిహారాలు: నష్టపరిహారం; శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ (సెక్షన్ 38(3)); తొలగింపు ఆదేశం (సెక్షన్ 39); స్వయంగా తొలగించడం. క్రిమినల్ అతిక్రమణ: సెక్షన్ 329 BNS (ప్రత్యేక ఉద్దేశం అవసరం).

selfTest.q: భూమిపై అతిక్రమణను నిర్వచించండి. "Actionable per se" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఫ్యాక్టరీ నుంచి వ్యాపించే పొగ అతిక్రమణా లేదా న్యూసెన్సా? స్థిరాస్తిపై అతిక్రమణకు నష్టపరిహారం కోసం కాలపరిమితి ఎంత? కొనసాగే అతిక్రమణలో కాలపరిమితి చట్టం సెక్షన్ 22 ఎలా సహాయపడుతుంది? పారవేసిన వ్యర్థాల తొలగింపుకు ఆదేశించడానికి నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టంలోని ఏ సెక్షన్ అనుమతిస్తుంది?

hi.inOneMinute: Trespass to land is an unjustified, direct physical interference with land in another person's possession. In pollution cases, trespass covers a polluter who directly puts a substance on another's land: dumping garbage, pumping effluent onto a field, spraying chemicals over a boundary, or piling debris on a neighbour's plot. (See Diagram 1 .) Trespass is actionable per se : the owner need not prove damage. Entick v. Carrington (1765): a person who sets foot on his neighbour's land without leave "is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all". If the polluting matter stays on the land, the trespass is continuing , and a fresh period of limitation runs every moment it continues (Limitation Act, 1963, s. 22). The ordinary period for compensation is three years from the trespass (Art. 87). Remedies: damages, an injunction ( perpetual : s. 38(3) Specific Relief Act; mandatory removal: s. 39), and removal by the possessor himself. (See Diagram 3 .) Trespass needs direct entry. Fumes, smoke or smells drifting across are usually treated as nuisance , not trespass.
legalProvision: Trespass to land is a common law tort; no statute defines it. These provisions support it:

Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7(a) – the "exclusive right of every owner of immovable property (subject to any law for the time being in force) to enjoy and dispose of the same and all products thereof and accessions thereto". Limitation Act, 1963, Art. 87 – "For compensation for trespass upon immovable property": three years from "The date of the trespass". Limitation Act, 1963, s. 22 – "In the case of a continuing breach of contract or in the case of a continuing tort, a fresh period of limitation begins to run at every moment of the time during which the breach or the tort, as the case may be, continues." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 38(3) – a perpetual injunction may be granted when the defendant "invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property", including: "(b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion"; "(c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief"; "(d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 39 – a mandatory injunction "to compel performance of the requisite acts". Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, s. 329(1) (criminal side) – "Whoever enters into or upon property in the possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person in possession of such property ... is said to commit criminal trespass."
hi.meaning: Trespass to land – an unjustified, direct, physical interference with land in the possession of another. Actionable per se – a wrong for which a suit lies without proof of damage. Trespass is one. Direct interference – the defendant's act itself puts the person or substance on the land, as opposed to harm that follows indirectly (which is nuisance ). Continuing trespass – trespass that lasts as long as the thing wrongfully placed stays on the land; each moment is a fresh wrong (s. 22, Limitation Act). Possession – trespass protects the person in possession, not only the owner. Section 7(a) of the Easements Act states the owner's exclusive right to enjoy his property.
keyPoints: Trespass to land: direct, unjustified interference with land in possession. Actionable per se ( Entick ). Needs direct interference; drifting fumes are nuisance ( St. Helen's ). Continuing trespass: fresh limitation every moment (s. 22); otherwise three years (Art. 87). Remedies: damages; perpetual injunction (s. 38(3)); mandatory removal (s. 39); self-help removal. Criminal trespass: s. 329 BNS (needs specific intent).

caseLaws.facts: Entick v. Carrington [1765] EWHC KB J98; 95 ER 807 (judgment of the whole Court for the plaintiff)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The King's messengers broke into John Entick's house under a warrant from the Secretary of St
caseLaws.facts: Entick sued them in trespass. Principle: The law holds every man's property "so sacred, that no man can set his foot upon his neighbour's close without his leave; if he does he is a trespasser, though he does no damage at all". Any entry must be justified by law. Why it matters: It establishes that trespass is actionable per se, so a polluter who directly puts waste on land is liable without proof of loss.
St. Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping (1865) 11 HLC 642; 11 ER 1483 (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Fumes from copper smelting works about a mile and a half away damaged the plaintiff's trees a
caseLaws.facts: The action was in nuisance, and the plaintiff won damages. Principle: Lord Westbury treated the injury from drifting fumes as nuisance and distinguished "material injury to the property" from "sensible personal discomfort". Why it matters: It shows the line between trespass and nuisance: airborne pollution reaching land indirectly is nuisance, not trespass.

environmental-law-u2-t3.subtitle: Harm caused by failing to take the care the law requires, and how it applies to polluters

en.inOneMinute: Negligence is a common law remedy against pollution where the polluter failed to take reasonable care and that failure caused foreseeable harm. The claimant must prove four things: a duty of care , its breach , causation , and damage that is not too remote. (See Diagram 1 .) The duty comes from Lord Atkin's neighbour principle in Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932): "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour." The leading pollution cases are the two Wagon Mound cases on oil spilled into Sydney Harbour. Wagon Mound (No. 1) (1961): the polluter is liable only for damage "of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen". Polemis (liability for all direct consequences) "should no longer be regarded as good law". Wagon Mound (No. 2) (1966): a real risk , even a small one, must not be ignored if removing it costs nothing; the polluter was liable. Negligence has limits: the victim must prove fault. Strict liability, absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ) and no-fault relief under the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 remove that burden.
legalProvision: Negligence is a common law tort; no Indian statute defines it. Related statutory provisions:

Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3(2) – in a claim for relief for an accident involving a hazardous substance, "the claimant shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person." Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 8(1) – the right to relief under s. 3(1) "shall be in addition to any other right to claim compensation in respect thereof under any other law for the time being in force". So a negligence suit remains available. Specific Relief Act, 1963, ss. 38–40 – injunctions, and damages with or instead of an injunction, in a suit to stop a negligent polluting activity.
en.meaning: Negligence – failure to take the care that a reasonable person would take in the circumstances, causing damage to someone to whom a duty of care was owed. Duty of care – a legal duty to take reasonable care towards persons "so closely and directly affected" by one's act that one ought to have them in contemplation ( Donoghue , Lord Atkin). Breach of duty – falling below the standard of the reasonable person, for example by careless discharge or storage of pollutants. Reasonable foreseeability – what a reasonable person in the defendant's position would have foreseen as a real risk, not a far-fetched one. Remoteness of damage – the limit on recovery: only damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable is recoverable ( Wagon Mound (No. 1) ).
keyPoints: Negligence: duty of care, breach of duty, causation, damage. Neighbour principle ( Donoghue ). Real risk must be removed if easy ( Wagon Mound (No. 2) ). Reasonable foreseeability of the kind of damage. Remoteness of damage: Polemis rejected ( Wagon Mound (No. 1) ). PLI Act: no-fault relief (s. 3(2)); other claims preserved (s. 8(1)). Absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ) removes the need to prove fault for hazardous industries.

caseLaws.facts: Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A consumer fell ill after drinking ginger beer from an opaque bottle said to contain a decomp
caseLaws.facts: She had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle: reasonable care must be taken to avoid acts or omissions reasonably foreseeable as likely to injure one's neighbour. Why it matters: It is the source of the duty of care a polluter owes to those near its activities.
Overseas Tankship (U.K.) Ltd. v. Morts Dock & Engineering Co. Ltd. (The Wagon Mound (No. 1)) [1961] AC 388 (Privy Council; judgment delivered by Viscount Simonds, 18 January 1961)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oil overflowed from the "Wagon Mound" while bunkering in Sydney Harbour and drifted to the re
caseLaws.facts: The oil later caught fire and damaged the wharf. The trial judge found the defendant could not reasonably have known that the oil could be set afire when spread on water. Principle: "the essential factor in determining liability is whether the damage is of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen"; Polemis should no longer be regarded as good law. The negligence claim for fire damage failed; the nuisance issue was remitted . Why it matters: It sets the foreseeability test for remoteness in pollution damage claims.
Overseas Tankship (U.K.) Ltd. v. Miller Steamship Co. Pty. Ltd. (The Wagon Mound (No. 2)) (Privy Council; judgment delivered by Lord Reid, 25 May 1966)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Owners of two vessels damaged in the same fire sued in nuisance and negligence
caseLaws.facts: The trial judge awarded £80,000 and £1,000 in nuisance but rejected negligence. Principle: A person must be regarded as negligent if he does not take steps to eliminate a real risk, not a mere possibility; here there was no justification for discharging oil into the harbour. The judgment for £80,000 and £1,000 was affirmed, and the cross-appeal on negligence allowed. Why it matters: It shows that even a small but real risk of pollution damage must be guarded against when doing so is easy.

te.inOneMinute: నిర్లక్ష్యం (Negligence) అనేది కాలుష్యానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా ఒక సాధారణ చట్ట పరిహారం; కాలుష్యకారుడు సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోకపోవడం , ఆ లోపం ఊహించదగిన హాని కలిగించడం. దావాదారుడు నాలుగు విషయాలు రుజువు చేయాలి: జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత , దాని ఉల్లంఘన , కారణ సంబంధం , మరీ దూరం కాని నష్టం . ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) బాధ్యత Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932)లో Lord Atkin పొరుగువారి సూత్రం నుంచి వస్తుంది: "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour." (అర్థం: మీ పొరుగువారిని గాయపరిచే అవకాశం ఉందని మీరు సహేతుకంగా ఊహించగల చర్యలు లేదా విస్మరణలను నివారించడానికి మీరు సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాలి.) ప్రధాన కాలుష్య కేసులు సిడ్నీ హార్బర్‌లో చిందిన నూనెపై రెండు Wagon Mound కేసులు. Wagon Mound (No. 1) (1961): కాలుష్యకారుడు "of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen" (అర్థం: సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ఊహించాల్సిన రకమైన) నష్టానికి మాత్రమే బాధ్యుడు. Polemis (అన్ని ప్రత్యక్ష పరిణామాలకు బాధ్యత) "should no longer be regarded as good law" (అర్థం: ఇకపై మంచి చట్టంగా పరిగణించకూడదు). Wagon Mound (No. 2) (1966): తొలగించడానికి ఏ ఖర్చూ లేకపోతే, చిన్నదైనా వాస్తవ ప్రమాదాన్ని విస్మరించకూడదు; కాలుష్యకారుడు బాధ్యుడయ్యాడు. నిర్లక్ష్యానికి పరిమితులు ఉన్నాయి: బాధితుడు తప్పును రుజువు చేయాలి. కఠిన బాధ్యత, సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( M.C. Mehta ), ప్రజా బాధ్యత బీమా చట్టం, 1991 కింద తప్పు లేని ఉపశమనం ఆ భారాన్ని తొలగిస్తాయి.
te.meaning: నిర్లక్ష్యం (Negligence) – పరిస్థితుల్లో సహేతుక వ్యక్తి తీసుకునే జాగ్రత్తను తీసుకోకపోవడం, దాంతో జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యత ఉన్న వ్యక్తికి నష్టం కలగడం. జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత (Duty of care) – తన చర్య వల్ల "so closely and directly affected" (అర్థం: అంత దగ్గరగా, నేరుగా ప్రభావితమయ్యే) వ్యక్తులను దృష్టిలో ఉంచుకోవాల్సిన, వారి పట్ల సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాల్సిన చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత ( Donoghue , Lord Atkin). బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన (Breach of duty) – సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ప్రమాణం కంటే కిందకు పడటం, ఉదా. కాలుష్య పదార్థాలను అజాగ్రత్తగా విడుదల చేయడం లేదా నిల్వ చేయడం. సహేతుక ఊహాశక్తి (Reasonable foreseeability ) – ప్రతివాది స్థానంలో ఉన్న సహేతుక వ్యక్తి వాస్తవ ప్రమాదంగా ఊహించేది, అసంభవమైనది కాదు. నష్టం దూరత్వం ( Remoteness of damage ) – పరిహారంపై పరిమితి: సహేతుకంగా ఊహించదగిన రకమైన నష్టం మాత్రమే పొందవచ్చు ( Wagon Mound (No. 1) ).
keyPoints: నిర్లక్ష్యం: జాగ్రత్త వహించాల్సిన బాధ్యత, బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన, కారణ సంబంధం, నష్టం. పొరుగువారి సూత్రం ( Donoghue ). సులభమైతే వాస్తవ ప్రమాదాన్ని తొలగించాలి ( Wagon Mound (No. 2) ). నష్టం రకం సహేతుక ఊహాశక్తికి లోబడి ఉండాలి. నష్టం దూరత్వం: Polemis తిరస్కరణ ( Wagon Mound (No. 1) ). PLI చట్టం: తప్పు లేని ఉపశమనం (సెక్షన్ 3(2)); ఇతర దావాలు నిలుస్తాయి (సెక్షన్ 8(1)). ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమలకు సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( M.C. Mehta ) తప్పు రుజువు అవసరాన్ని తొలగిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: నిర్లక్ష్యం యొక్క నాలుగు అంశాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: Lord Atkin పొరుగువారి సూత్రాన్ని చెప్పండి. Polemis గురించి Wagon Mound (No. 1) ఏం నిర్ణయించింది? *Wagon Mound (No. 2)*లో ప్రతివాది ఎందుకు బాధ్యుడయ్యాడు? PLI చట్టం కింద దావాదారుడు నిర్లక్ష్యాన్ని రుజువు చేయాలా? PLI చట్టం ఉపశమనం కోరితే నిర్లక్ష్య దావా నిషిద్ధమా?

hi.inOneMinute: Negligence is a common law remedy against pollution where the polluter failed to take reasonable care and that failure caused foreseeable harm. The claimant must prove four things: a duty of care , its breach , causation , and damage that is not too remote. (See Diagram 1 .) The duty comes from Lord Atkin's neighbour principle in Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932): "You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour." The leading pollution cases are the two Wagon Mound cases on oil spilled into Sydney Harbour. Wagon Mound (No. 1) (1961): the polluter is liable only for damage "of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen". Polemis (liability for all direct consequences) "should no longer be regarded as good law". Wagon Mound (No. 2) (1966): a real risk , even a small one, must not be ignored if removing it costs nothing; the polluter was liable. Negligence has limits: the victim must prove fault. Strict liability, absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ) and no-fault relief under the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 remove that burden.
legalProvision: Negligence is a common law tort; no Indian statute defines it. Related statutory provisions:

Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 3(2) – in a claim for relief for an accident involving a hazardous substance, "the claimant shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person." Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991, s. 8(1) – the right to relief under s. 3(1) "shall be in addition to any other right to claim compensation in respect thereof under any other law for the time being in force". So a negligence suit remains available. Specific Relief Act, 1963, ss. 38–40 – injunctions, and damages with or instead of an injunction, in a suit to stop a negligent polluting activity.
hi.meaning: Negligence – failure to take the care that a reasonable person would take in the circumstances, causing damage to someone to whom a duty of care was owed. Duty of care – a legal duty to take reasonable care towards persons "so closely and directly affected" by one's act that one ought to have them in contemplation ( Donoghue , Lord Atkin). Breach of duty – falling below the standard of the reasonable person, for example by careless discharge or storage of pollutants. Reasonable foreseeability – what a reasonable person in the defendant's position would have foreseen as a real risk, not a far-fetched one. Remoteness of damage – the limit on recovery: only damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable is recoverable ( Wagon Mound (No. 1) ).
keyPoints: Negligence: duty of care, breach of duty, causation, damage. Neighbour principle ( Donoghue ). Real risk must be removed if easy ( Wagon Mound (No. 2) ). Reasonable foreseeability of the kind of damage. Remoteness of damage: Polemis rejected ( Wagon Mound (No. 1) ). PLI Act: no-fault relief (s. 3(2)); other claims preserved (s. 8(1)). Absolute liability ( M.C. Mehta ) removes the need to prove fault for hazardous industries.

caseLaws.facts: Donoghue v. Stevenson [1932] AC 562 (House of Lords)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A consumer fell ill after drinking ginger beer from an opaque bottle said to contain a decomp
caseLaws.facts: She had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle: reasonable care must be taken to avoid acts or omissions reasonably foreseeable as likely to injure one's neighbour. Why it matters: It is the source of the duty of care a polluter owes to those near its activities.
Overseas Tankship (U.K.) Ltd. v. Morts Dock & Engineering Co. Ltd. (The Wagon Mound (No. 1)) [1961] AC 388 (Privy Council; judgment delivered by Viscount Simonds, 18 January 1961)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oil overflowed from the "Wagon Mound" while bunkering in Sydney Harbour and drifted to the re
caseLaws.facts: The oil later caught fire and damaged the wharf. The trial judge found the defendant could not reasonably have known that the oil could be set afire when spread on water. Principle: "the essential factor in determining liability is whether the damage is of such a kind as the reasonable man should have foreseen"; Polemis should no longer be regarded as good law. The negligence claim for fire damage failed; the nuisance issue was remitted . Why it matters: It sets the foreseeability test for remoteness in pollution damage claims.
Overseas Tankship (U.K.) Ltd. v. Miller Steamship Co. Pty. Ltd. (The Wagon Mound (No. 2)) (Privy Council; judgment delivered by Lord Reid, 25 May 1966)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Owners of two vessels damaged in the same fire sued in nuisance and negligence
caseLaws.facts: The trial judge awarded £80,000 and £1,000 in nuisance but rejected negligence. Principle: A person must be regarded as negligent if he does not take steps to eliminate a real risk, not a mere possibility; here there was no justification for discharging oil into the harbour. The judgment for £80,000 and £1,000 was affirmed, and the cross-appeal on negligence allowed. Why it matters: It shows that even a small but real risk of pollution damage must be guarded against when doing so is easy.

selfTest.q: What are the four elements of negligence?
selfTest.a: State Lord Atkin's neighbour principle. What did Wagon Mound (No. 1) decide about Polemis ? Why was the defendant liable in Wagon Mound (No. 2) ? Under the PLI Act, must a claimant prove negligence? Is a negligence suit barred if PLI Act relief is claimed?

environmental-law-u2-t5.subtitle: Criminal and magistrate powers against pollution as public nuisance, with the civil route under the Code of Civil Procedure

en.inOneMinute: Pollution that harms the public is a public nuisance . Indian criminal law deals with it in two ways: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) makes public nuisance and certain polluting acts offences (ss. 270, 279, 280, 292, 293); the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) lets an Executive Magistrate order the nuisance removed quickly (ss. 152–163). (See Diagram 1 .) BNS s. 270 defines public nuisance: an act or illegal omission causing "common injury, danger or annoyance to the public". It is "not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage". BNS s. 279 : fouling the water of a public spring or reservoir. BNS s. 280 : making the atmosphere noxious to health. BNSS s. 152 : the Magistrate makes a conditional order to remove the nuisance or stop or regulate an injurious trade, or appear and show cause. If the person does not comply or show cause, the order is made absolute (s. 155). BNSS s. 163 gives power to make urgent orders , even ex parte, for up to two months. Municipal Council, Ratlam (1980) used the same power (then s. 133 CrPC) to make a municipality build drains and stop an alcohol plant's discharge, holding that lack of funds is no excuse.
legalProvision: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Section 270 (Public nuisance): "A person is guilty of a public nuisance who does any act or is guilty of an illegal omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity, or which must necessarily cause injury, obstruction, danger or annoyance to persons who may have occasion to use any public right but a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage." Section 279 (Fouling water of public spring or reservoir): "Whoever voluntarily corrupts or fouls the water of any public spring or reservoir, so as to render it less fit for the purpose for which it is ordinarily used, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both." Section 280 (Making atmosphere noxious to health): "Whoever voluntarily vitiates the atmosphere in any place so as to make it noxious to the health of persons in general dwelling or carrying on business in the neighbourhood or passing along a public way, shall be punished with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees." Section 286 (Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance): rash or negligent acts with any poisonous substance endangering human life, or negligent omission to guard against probable danger from it: up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Section 292: public nuisance "in any case not otherwise punishable by this Sanhita": fine up to ₹1,000. Section 293: "Whoever repeats or continues a public nuisance, having been enjoined by any public servant who has lawful authority to issue such injunction not to repeat or continue such nuisance": simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Section 223: disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant; under clause (b), where the disobedience "causes or tends to cause danger to human life, health or safety", imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both.
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

Section 152(1): a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or specially empowered Executive Magistrate, on a police report "or other information", may act where he considers, among other things: "(a) that any unlawful obstruction or nuisance should be removed from any public place or from any way, river or channel which is or may be lawfully used by the public"; or "(b) that the conduct of any trade or occupation, or the keeping of any goods or merchandise, is injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community"; or "(c) that the construction of any building, or, the disposal of any substance, as is likely to occasion conflagration or explosion, should be prevented or stopped". He may make a conditional order requiring the person, "within a time to be fixed in the order", to remove the nuisance, or "to desist from carrying on, or to remove or regulate" the trade, or to alter the disposal of the substance, or else to appear and "show cause ... why the order should not be made absolute". Section 152(2): "No order duly made by a Magistrate under this section shall be called in question in any Civil Court." Section 155: if the person neither performs the act nor shows cause, he is liable to the penalty in BNS s. 223 "and the order shall be made absolute". Section 157: if he shows cause, evidence is taken "as in a summons-case"; the order is made absolute if "reasonable and proper"; proceedings are to be completed "within a period of ninety days", extendable to 120 days with reasons. Section 158: the Magistrate may direct a local investigation or "summon and examine an expert". Section 160(2): if the act is not performed, the Magistrate "may cause it to be performed, and may recover the costs of performing it". Section 161(1): to prevent "imminent danger or injury of a serious kind to the public", the Magistrate may issue an injunction pending the inquiry. Section 162: a Magistrate "may order any person not to repeat or continue a public nuisance, as defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or any special or local law." Section 163: in urgent cases, a written order directing a person "to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to certain property", if likely to prevent "danger to human life, health or safety"; may be ex parte (s. 163(2)); in force not more than two months, extendable by the State Government up to six months (s. 163(4)).
en.meaning: Public nuisance – an act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to people in the vicinity (BNS s. 270). Conditional order – an order under BNSS s. 152 requiring the removal of the nuisance within a fixed time, or appearance to show cause. Order made absolute – the final, enforceable form of the conditional order, after default (s. 155) or after the inquiry (s. 157). Urgent order – an order under BNSS s. 163 for immediate prevention or speedy remedy, which may be ex parte and lasts up to two months. Abatement – putting an end to the nuisance, here by order of the Magistrate.
keyPoints: Public nuisance: BNS s. 270; convenience or advantage no excuse. Water: s. 279; air: s. 280; poisons: s. 286. BNSS s. 152: conditional order on police report or other information. Default or cause shown: order made absolute (ss. 155, 157); 90 days. Magistrate may do the work and recover costs (s. 160). Urgent order: s. 163; ex parte; two months. Ratlam : mandatory duty; no plea of lack of funds.

caseLaws.facts: Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Shri Vardhichand AIR 1980 SC 1622; 1981 SCR (1) 97 – decided 29 July 1980 (Krishna Iyer J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents complained under s
caseLaws.facts: 133 CrPC that the municipality failed to provide drains and public conveniences, and that an alcohol plant discharged foul fluids into the street. The Magistrate ordered the municipality to construct drains; the Sessions Court set this aside, but the High Court restored it. Principle: The "imperative tone" of s. 133 CrPC, read with the penalty for disobedience, makes abatement "a mandatory duty"; a municipality cannot plead financial inability; the Magistrate can fix time-limits and give specific directions. Why it matters: It is the leading authority for using the Magistrate's nuisance power (now BNSS s. 152) against pollution, including against public bodies.

caseLaws.name: Note: Ratlam was decided under CrPC s
caseLaws.facts: 133 and IPC s. 188. BNSS s. 152 and BNS s. 223 are their successors; no judgment under the new provisions was available.

te.inOneMinute: ప్రజలకు హాని చేసే కాలుష్యం పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్ (public nuisance) . భారతీయ క్రిమినల్ చట్టం దాన్ని రెండు విధాలుగా ఎదుర్కొంటుంది: భారతీయ న్యాయ సంహిత, 2023 (BNS) పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్‌ను, కొన్ని కాలుష్య చర్యలను నేరాలు గా చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్లు 270, 279, 280, 292, 293); భారతీయ నాగరిక్ సురక్ష సంహిత, 2023 (BNSS) ఎగ్జిక్యూటివ్ మేజిస్ట్రేట్ న్యూసెన్స్‌ను త్వరగా తొలగించమని ఆదేశించడానికి అనుమతిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్లు 152–163). ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) BNS సెక్షన్ 270 పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్‌ను నిర్వచిస్తుంది: "common injury, danger or annoyance to the public" (అర్థం: ప్రజలకు ఉమ్మడి గాయం, ప్రమాదం లేదా చికాకు) కలిగించే చర్య లేదా చట్టవిరుద్ధ విస్మరణ. అది "not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage" (అర్థం: కొంత సౌలభ్యం లేదా ప్రయోజనం కలిగిస్తుందనే కారణంతో క్షమించబడదు). BNS సెక్షన్ 279 : ప్రజా ఊట లేదా జలాశయం నీటిని కలుషితం చేయడం. BNS సెక్షన్ 280 : వాతావరణాన్ని ఆరోగ్యానికి హానికరంగా చేయడం. BNSS సెక్షన్ 152 : మేజిస్ట్రేట్ న్యూసెన్స్‌ను తొలగించమని లేదా హానికర వ్యాపారాన్ని ఆపమని లేదా నియంత్రించమని, లేదా హాజరై కారణం చూపమని షరతులతో కూడిన ఉత్తర్వు (conditional order) ఇస్తాడు. వ్యక్తి పాటించకపోతే లేదా కారణం చూపకపోతే ఉత్తర్వు సంపూర్ణం (made absolute) అవుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 155). BNSS సెక్షన్ 163 అత్యవసర ఉత్తర్వులు ఇచ్చే అధికారం ఇస్తుంది, ఏకపక్షంగా (ex parte) కూడా, రెండు నెలల వరకు. Municipal Council, Ratlam (1980) అదే అధికారాన్ని (అప్పటి సెక్షన్ 133 CrPC) ఉపయోగించి ఒక మున్సిపాలిటీని మురుగు కాలువలు నిర్మించమని, ఆల్కహాల్ ప్లాంట్ విడుదలను ఆపమని చేసింది; నిధుల కొరత సాకు కాదని చెప్పింది.
te.meaning: పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్ (Public nuisance ) – ప్రజలకు లేదా సమీపంలోని ప్రజలకు ఉమ్మడి గాయం, ప్రమాదం లేదా చికాకు కలిగించే చర్య లేదా చట్టవిరుద్ధ విస్మరణ (BNS సెక్షన్ 270). షరతులతో కూడిన ఉత్తర్వు (Conditional order) – నిర్ణీత సమయంలో న్యూసెన్స్‌ను తొలగించమని, లేదా హాజరై కారణం చూపమని కోరే BNSS సెక్షన్ 152 ఉత్తర్వు. సంపూర్ణం చేసిన ఉత్తర్వు (Order made absolute) – డిఫాల్ట్ తర్వాత (సెక్షన్ 155) లేదా విచారణ తర్వాత (సెక్షన్ 157) షరతులతో కూడిన ఉత్తర్వు యొక్క తుది, అమలు చేయదగిన రూపం. అత్యవసర ఉత్తర్వు (Urgent order) – తక్షణ నివారణ లేదా త్వరిత పరిహారం కోసం BNSS సెక్షన్ 163 కింద ఉత్తర్వు; ఏకపక్షంగా ఇవ్వవచ్చు, రెండు నెలల వరకు ఉంటుంది. తొలగింపు ( Abatement ) – న్యూసెన్స్‌ను అంతం చేయడం, ఇక్కడ మేజిస్ట్రేట్ ఉత్తర్వు ద్వారా.
keyPoints: పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్: BNS సెక్షన్ 270; సౌలభ్యం లేదా ప్రయోజనం సాకు కాదు. నీరు: సెక్షన్ 279; గాలి: సెక్షన్ 280; విషాలు: సెక్షన్ 286. BNSS సెక్షన్ 152: పోలీసు నివేదిక లేదా ఇతర సమాచారంపై షరతులతో కూడిన ఉత్తర్వు. డిఫాల్ట్ లేదా కారణం చూపిన తర్వాత: సంపూర్ణం చేసిన ఉత్తర్వు (సెక్షన్లు 155, 157); 90 రోజులు. మేజిస్ట్రేట్ పని చేయించి ఖర్చు వసూలు చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 160). అత్యవసర ఉత్తర్వు: సెక్షన్ 163; ఏకపక్షం; రెండు నెలలు. Ratlam : తప్పనిసరి విధి; నిధుల కొరత సాకు కాదు.

hi.inOneMinute: Pollution that harms the public is a public nuisance . Indian criminal law deals with it in two ways: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) makes public nuisance and certain polluting acts offences (ss. 270, 279, 280, 292, 293); the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) lets an Executive Magistrate order the nuisance removed quickly (ss. 152–163). (See Diagram 1 .) BNS s. 270 defines public nuisance: an act or illegal omission causing "common injury, danger or annoyance to the public". It is "not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage". BNS s. 279 : fouling the water of a public spring or reservoir. BNS s. 280 : making the atmosphere noxious to health. BNSS s. 152 : the Magistrate makes a conditional order to remove the nuisance or stop or regulate an injurious trade, or appear and show cause. If the person does not comply or show cause, the order is made absolute (s. 155). BNSS s. 163 gives power to make urgent orders , even ex parte, for up to two months. Municipal Council, Ratlam (1980) used the same power (then s. 133 CrPC) to make a municipality build drains and stop an alcohol plant's discharge, holding that lack of funds is no excuse.
legalProvision: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Section 270 (Public nuisance): "A person is guilty of a public nuisance who does any act or is guilty of an illegal omission which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity, or which must necessarily cause injury, obstruction, danger or annoyance to persons who may have occasion to use any public right but a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage." Section 279 (Fouling water of public spring or reservoir): "Whoever voluntarily corrupts or fouls the water of any public spring or reservoir, so as to render it less fit for the purpose for which it is ordinarily used, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both." Section 280 (Making atmosphere noxious to health): "Whoever voluntarily vitiates the atmosphere in any place so as to make it noxious to the health of persons in general dwelling or carrying on business in the neighbourhood or passing along a public way, shall be punished with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees." Section 286 (Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance): rash or negligent acts with any poisonous substance endangering human life, or negligent omission to guard against probable danger from it: up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Section 292: public nuisance "in any case not otherwise punishable by this Sanhita": fine up to ₹1,000. Section 293: "Whoever repeats or continues a public nuisance, having been enjoined by any public servant who has lawful authority to issue such injunction not to repeat or continue such nuisance": simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. Section 223: disobedience of an order duly promulgated by a public servant; under clause (b), where the disobedience "causes or tends to cause danger to human life, health or safety", imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both.
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023

Section 152(1): a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or specially empowered Executive Magistrate, on a police report "or other information", may act where he considers, among other things: "(a) that any unlawful obstruction or nuisance should be removed from any public place or from any way, river or channel which is or may be lawfully used by the public"; or "(b) that the conduct of any trade or occupation, or the keeping of any goods or merchandise, is injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community"; or "(c) that the construction of any building, or, the disposal of any substance, as is likely to occasion conflagration or explosion, should be prevented or stopped". He may make a conditional order requiring the person, "within a time to be fixed in the order", to remove the nuisance, or "to desist from carrying on, or to remove or regulate" the trade, or to alter the disposal of the substance, or else to appear and "show cause ... why the order should not be made absolute". Section 152(2): "No order duly made by a Magistrate under this section shall be called in question in any Civil Court." Section 155: if the person neither performs the act nor shows cause, he is liable to the penalty in BNS s. 223 "and the order shall be made absolute". Section 157: if he shows cause, evidence is taken "as in a summons-case"; the order is made absolute if "reasonable and proper"; proceedings are to be completed "within a period of ninety days", extendable to 120 days with reasons. Section 158: the Magistrate may direct a local investigation or "summon and examine an expert". Section 160(2): if the act is not performed, the Magistrate "may cause it to be performed, and may recover the costs of performing it". Section 161(1): to prevent "imminent danger or injury of a serious kind to the public", the Magistrate may issue an injunction pending the inquiry. Section 162: a Magistrate "may order any person not to repeat or continue a public nuisance, as defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or any special or local law." Section 163: in urgent cases, a written order directing a person "to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to certain property", if likely to prevent "danger to human life, health or safety"; may be ex parte (s. 163(2)); in force not more than two months, extendable by the State Government up to six months (s. 163(4)).
hi.meaning: Public nuisance – an act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to people in the vicinity (BNS s. 270). Conditional order – an order under BNSS s. 152 requiring the removal of the nuisance within a fixed time, or appearance to show cause. Order made absolute – the final, enforceable form of the conditional order, after default (s. 155) or after the inquiry (s. 157). Urgent order – an order under BNSS s. 163 for immediate prevention or speedy remedy, which may be ex parte and lasts up to two months. Abatement – putting an end to the nuisance, here by order of the Magistrate.
keyPoints: Public nuisance: BNS s. 270; convenience or advantage no excuse. Water: s. 279; air: s. 280; poisons: s. 286. BNSS s. 152: conditional order on police report or other information. Default or cause shown: order made absolute (ss. 155, 157); 90 days. Magistrate may do the work and recover costs (s. 160). Urgent order: s. 163; ex parte; two months. Ratlam : mandatory duty; no plea of lack of funds.

caseLaws.facts: Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Shri Vardhichand AIR 1980 SC 1622; 1981 SCR (1) 97 – decided 29 July 1980 (Krishna Iyer J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents complained under s
caseLaws.facts: 133 CrPC that the municipality failed to provide drains and public conveniences, and that an alcohol plant discharged foul fluids into the street. The Magistrate ordered the municipality to construct drains; the Sessions Court set this aside, but the High Court restored it. Principle: The "imperative tone" of s. 133 CrPC, read with the penalty for disobedience, makes abatement "a mandatory duty"; a municipality cannot plead financial inability; the Magistrate can fix time-limits and give specific directions. Why it matters: It is the leading authority for using the Magistrate's nuisance power (now BNSS s. 152) against pollution, including against public bodies.

environmental-law-u2-t9.subtitle: How artificial intelligence harms and helps the environment, and which existing Indian laws and principles apply

en.inOneMinute: Artificial intelligence (AI) affects the environment in two directions. It harms through energy use, emissions, water use, raw material extraction and electronic waste; it helps through pollution detection, climate prediction, disaster warning and resource efficiency. (See Diagram 1 .) The harm arises across the whole AI life cycle : making the hardware, building and running data centres , training models, using them, and discarding equipment. No Indian statute deals specifically with AI and the environment. Existing law applies: Article 21 (freedom from pollution is part of the right to life), Article 48A, Article 51A(g), the general environmental laws, and the polluter pays principle ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action , 1996). (See Diagram 2 .) Internationally, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (adopted 23 November 2021) makes "Environment and ecosystem flourishing" one of its four values and asks States to assess AI's "carbon footprint, energy consumption and the environmental impact of raw material extraction" (para. 84). The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) requires providers of general-purpose AI models to document "known or estimated energy consumption of the model" (Annex XI) and promotes energy-efficient AI (Arts. 40(2), 95(2)(b), 112(6)). Common law remedies (nuisance, negligence, injunction) remain available against a data centre's local pollution, such as generator noise or smoke. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Constitution of India, Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – a fundamental duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 21 – right to life; the Supreme Court in In re Noise Pollution (2005) recognised freedom from noise pollution as part of it. UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, 2021 (adopted 23 November 2021; not a treaty): Value 2, para. 17: "Environmental and ecosystem flourishing should be recognized, protected and promoted through the life cycle of AI systems." Para. 18: AI actors "should reduce the environmental impact of AI systems, including but not limited to its carbon footprint", and "prevent the unsustainable exploitation, use and transformation of natural resources". Policy Area 5, para. 84: Member States should "assess the direct and indirect environmental impact throughout the AI system life cycle", including "its carbon footprint, energy consumption and the environmental impact of raw material extraction", and should "reduce the environmental impact of AI systems and data infrastructures". They "should ensure compliance of all AI actors with environmental law, policies and practices." Para. 85: States should support "rights-based and ethical AI-powered solutions for disaster risk resilience" and "the monitoring, protection and regeneration of the environment and ecosystems", for example to "Detect pollutants or predict levels of pollution". Para. 86: AI actors should "favour data, energy and resource-efficient AI methods", and "in instances where there are disproportionate negative impacts on the environment, AI should not be used." EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (for comparison; it does not apply in India): Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(e): technical documentation of a general-purpose AI model must include "known or estimated energy consumption of the model"; if unknown, it "may be based on information about computational resources used". Art. 40(2): standardisation deliverables "to improve AI systems' resource performance, such as reducing the high-risk AI system's consumption of energy and of other resources during its lifecycle". Art. 95(2)(b): voluntary codes of conduct on "assessing and minimising the impact of AI systems on environmental sustainability, including as regards energy-efficient programming". Art. 112(6): "By 2 August 2028 and every four years thereafter", the Commission reports on standardisation for "the energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models", and assesses the need for further measures, "including binding measures". Polluter pays principle – adopted in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996): the "financial costs of preventing or remedying damage caused by pollution should lie with the undertakings which cause the pollution".
en.meaning: Artificial intelligence (AI) – computer systems that perform tasks such as prediction, recognition, language and decision support by learning from data. AI life cycle – all stages of an AI system: research and design, hardware manufacture, data collection, training, deployment and use, and disposal (UNESCO para. 84 speaks of the "AI system life cycle"). Data centre – a building housing servers, storage and networking equipment that train and run AI systems; it needs continuous electricity and cooling. Carbon footprint – the total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an activity, here by building and operating AI systems. Training and inference – training is the energy-intensive process of building a model from data; inference is using the trained model to answer queries. Polluter pays principle – the person who causes pollution must bear the cost of preventing and remedying it.
keyPoints: Impact is two-way: harms and benefits, across the AI life cycle. Harms: energy, carbon footprint, water, minerals, e-waste, local nuisance from the data centre. India: no AI-specific environmental law; Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g) and general laws apply. Polluter pays principle ( ICELA , 1996) applies to AI facilities. UNESCO 2021: value of "Environment and ecosystem flourishing"; Policy Area 5 (paras. 84–86). EU AI Act: energy consumption documented for general-purpose AI models (Annex XI).

caseLaws.facts: Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996) 3 SCC 212 (Supreme Court; Jeevan Reddy J; 13 February 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Chemical units at Bichhri, Rajasthan, producing 'H' acid let toxic untreated waste waters flo
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court applied the polluter pays principle: "the financial costs of preventing or remedying damage caused by pollution should lie with the undertakings which cause the pollution". Why it matters: The principle applies to any polluter, so an AI company whose data centre or hardware waste pollutes must bear the cost of prevention and remediation.
In re Noise Pollution, Writ Petition (Civil) 72 of 1998, decided 18 July 2005 (Supreme Court; R.C. Lahoti CJI and Ashok Bhan J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A public interest petition after a girl's cries for help "went unheard due to blaring noise o
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Freedom from noise pollution is part of the right to life under Article 21; the Court issued binding directions under Articles 141 and 142. Why it matters: It shows that pollution from any source, including the generators and cooling plant of an AI facility, can engage Article 21.
