te.inOneMinute: కృత్రిమ మేధ (Artificial intelligence – AI) పర్యావరణాన్ని రెండు దిశల్లో ప్రభావితం చేస్తుంది. శక్తి వినియోగం, ఉద్గారాలు, నీటి వినియోగం, ముడి పదార్థాల వెలికితీత, ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ వ్యర్థాల ద్వారా అది హాని చేస్తుంది; కాలుష్య గుర్తింపు, వాతావరణ అంచనా, విపత్తు హెచ్చరిక, వనరుల సమర్థ వినియోగం ద్వారా సహాయం చేస్తుంది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ఈ హాని మొత్తం AI జీవిత చక్రం అంతటా వస్తుంది: హార్డ్‌వేర్ తయారీ, డేటా సెంటర్ల నిర్మాణం, నిర్వహణ, మోడళ్ల శిక్షణ, వాటి వినియోగం, పరికరాల పారవేత. AI, పర్యావరణం గురించి ప్రత్యేకంగా ఏ భారతీయ చట్టమూ లేదు. ఉన్న చట్టమే వర్తిస్తుంది: ఆర్టికల్ 21 (కాలుష్యం నుంచి స్వేచ్ఛ జీవించే హక్కులో భాగం), ఆర్టికల్ 48A, ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g), సాధారణ పర్యావరణ చట్టాలు, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలనే సూత్రం (polluter pays principle) ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action , 1996). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) అంతర్జాతీయంగా, UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (23 నవంబర్ 2021న ఆమోదం) "Environment and ecosystem flourishing" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణం, పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థల వికాసం)ను నాలుగు విలువల్లో ఒకటిగా చేసి, AI "carbon footprint, energy consumption and the environmental impact of raw material extraction" (అర్థం: కార్బన్ పాదముద్ర, శక్తి వినియోగం, ముడి పదార్థాల వెలికితీత పర్యావరణ ప్రభావం)ను అంచనా వేయమని దేశాలను కోరుతుంది (పేరా 84). EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) సాధారణ ప్రయోజన AI మోడళ్ల ప్రొవైడర్లు "known or estimated energy consumption of the model" (అర్థం: మోడల్ తెలిసిన లేదా అంచనా వేసిన శక్తి వినియోగం)ను నమోదు చేయాలని కోరుతుంది (Annex XI); శక్తి-సమర్థ AIని ప్రోత్సహిస్తుంది (ఆర్టికల్స్ 40(2), 95(2)(b), 112(6)). డేటా సెంటర్ వల్ల స్థానిక కాలుష్యానికి (జనరేటర్ శబ్దం లేదా పొగ వంటివి) వ్యతిరేకంగా సాధారణ చట్ట పరిహారాలు (న్యూసెన్స్, నిర్లక్ష్యం, నిషేధాజ్ఞ) అందుబాటులో ఉంటాయి. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: కృత్రిమ మేధ (Artificial intelligence – AI) – డేటా నుంచి నేర్చుకుని అంచనా, గుర్తింపు, భాష, నిర్ణయ సహాయం వంటి పనులు చేసే కంప్యూటర్ వ్యవస్థలు. AI జీవిత చక్రం (AI life cycle) – AI వ్యవస్థ అన్ని దశలు: పరిశోధన, రూపకల్పన, హార్డ్‌వేర్ తయారీ, డేటా సేకరణ, శిక్షణ, అమలు, వినియోగం, పారవేత (UNESCO పేరా 84 "AI system life cycle" గురించి చెబుతుంది). డేటా సెంటర్ (Data centre) – AI వ్యవస్థలకు శిక్షణ ఇచ్చి నడిపే సర్వర్లు, నిల్వ, నెట్‌వర్కింగ్ పరికరాలు ఉండే భవనం; దీనికి నిరంతర విద్యుత్, శీతలీకరణ అవసరం. కార్బన్ పాదముద్ర (Carbon footprint) – ఒక కార్యకలాపం వల్ల కలిగే మొత్తం గ్రీన్‌హౌస్ వాయు ఉద్గారాలు; ఇక్కడ AI వ్యవస్థల నిర్మాణం, నిర్వహణ వల్ల. శిక్షణ, ఇన్ఫరెన్స్ (Training and inference ) – శిక్షణ అంటే డేటా నుంచి మోడల్ నిర్మించే అధిక శక్తి ప్రక్రియ; ఇన్ఫరెన్స్ అంటే శిక్షణ పొందిన మోడల్‌ను ప్రశ్నలకు జవాబులు ఇవ్వడానికి వాడడం. కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలనే సూత్రం (Polluter pays principle) – కాలుష్యం కలిగించిన వ్యక్తే దాని నివారణ, సరిదిద్దే ఖర్చు భరించాలి.
keyPoints: ప్రభావం రెండు దిశల్లో: AI జీవిత చక్రం అంతటా హానులు, ప్రయోజనాలు. హానులు: శక్తి, కార్బన్ పాదముద్ర, నీరు, ఖనిజాలు, ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ వ్యర్థాలు, డేటా సెంటర్ నుంచి స్థానిక న్యూసెన్స్. భారతదేశం: AI-ప్రత్యేక పర్యావరణ చట్టం లేదు; ఆర్టికల్స్ 21, 48A, 51A(g), సాధారణ చట్టాలు వర్తిస్తాయి. కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలనే సూత్రం ( ICELA , 1996) AI సదుపాయాలకు వర్తిస్తుంది. UNESCO 2021: "Environment and ecosystem flourishing" విలువ; విధాన రంగం 5 (పేరాలు 84–86). EU AI Act: సాధారణ ప్రయోజన AI మోడళ్ల శక్తి వినియోగం నమోదు (Annex XI).

selfTest.q: AI పర్యావరణానికి హాని చేసే నాలుగు మార్గాలు చెప్పండి. AI పర్యావరణానికి సహాయపడే రెండు మార్గాలు చెప్పండి. పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించమని రాజ్యాన్ని నిర్దేశించే రాజ్యాంగ ఆర్టికల్ ఏది?
selfTest.a: AI నైతికతపై UNESCO Recommendation ఎప్పుడు ఆమోదించబడింది? ఆ Recommendationలోని పేరా 84 దేశాలను ఏమి అంచనా వేయమంటుంది? సాధారణ ప్రయోజన AI మోడళ్లకు EU AI Act ఏ శక్తి సమాచారం కోరుతుంది? AI కంపెనీ తన సదుపాయం వల్ల కలిగే కాలుష్యానికి చెల్లించేలా చేసే సూత్రం ఏది?

ప్రభావం AI దాన్ని ఎలా కలిగిస్తుంది పర్యావరణ ఫలితం
శక్తి వినియోగం డేటా సెంటర్లలో మోడళ్ల శిక్షణ, నిర్వహణకు పెద్ద ఎత్తున నిరంతర విద్యుత్ అవసరం విద్యుత్ బొగ్గు, గ్యాస్ లేదా డీజిల్ నుంచి వస్తే గ్రీన్‌హౌస్ వాయు ఉద్గారాలు, గాలి కాలుష్యం పెరుగుతాయి
కార్బన్ పాదముద్ర విద్యుత్ ఉద్గారాలు, చిప్‌లు, భవనాల తయారీ ఉద్గారాలు వాతావరణ మార్పుకు దోహదం (UNESCO పేరా 18)
నీటి వినియోగం డేటా సెంటర్లు శీతలీకరణకు నీరు వాడతాయి స్థానిక నీటి వనరులపై ఒత్తిడి
ముడి పదార్థాల వెలికితీత చిప్‌లు, సర్వర్లు, బ్యాటరీలకు లోహాలు, ఖనిజాలు అవసరం గనుల తవ్వకం భూమి, అడవులు, నీటిని దెబ్బతీస్తుంది (UNESCO పేరా 84)
ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ వ్యర్థాలు హార్డ్‌వేర్ తక్కువ కాలంలో మార్చడం రీసైకిల్ చేయకపోతే చెత్తకుప్పల్లో విష లోహాలు
స్థానిక న్యూసెన్స్ బ్యాకప్ డీజిల్ జనరేటర్లు, శీతలీకరణ ఫ్యాన్లు, వేడి పొరుగువారికి శబ్దం, పొగ, వేడి
భూ వినియోగం డేటా సెంటర్ల కోసం పెద్ద క్యాంపస్‌లు వ్యవసాయ లేదా పచ్చని భూమి నష్టం

hi.inOneMinute: Artificial intelligence (AI) affects the environment in two directions. It harms through energy use, emissions, water use, raw material extraction and electronic waste; it helps through pollution detection, climate prediction, disaster warning and resource efficiency. (See Diagram 1 .) The harm arises across the whole AI life cycle : making the hardware, building and running data centres , training models, using them, and discarding equipment. No Indian statute deals specifically with AI and the environment. Existing law applies: Article 21 (freedom from pollution is part of the right to life), Article 48A, Article 51A(g), the general environmental laws, and the polluter pays principle ( Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action , 1996). (See Diagram 2 .) Internationally, the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (adopted 23 November 2021) makes "Environment and ecosystem flourishing" one of its four values and asks States to assess AI's "carbon footprint, energy consumption and the environmental impact of raw material extraction" (para. 84). The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) requires providers of general-purpose AI models to document "known or estimated energy consumption of the model" (Annex XI) and promotes energy-efficient AI (Arts. 40(2), 95(2)(b), 112(6)). Common law remedies (nuisance, negligence, injunction) remain available against a data centre's local pollution, such as generator noise or smoke. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Constitution of India, Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – a fundamental duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 21 – right to life; the Supreme Court in In re Noise Pollution (2005) recognised freedom from noise pollution as part of it. UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, 2021 (adopted 23 November 2021; not a treaty): Value 2, para. 17: "Environmental and ecosystem flourishing should be recognized, protected and promoted through the life cycle of AI systems." Para. 18: AI actors "should reduce the environmental impact of AI systems, including but not limited to its carbon footprint", and "prevent the unsustainable exploitation, use and transformation of natural resources". Policy Area 5, para. 84: Member States should "assess the direct and indirect environmental impact throughout the AI system life cycle", including "its carbon footprint, energy consumption and the environmental impact of raw material extraction", and should "reduce the environmental impact of AI systems and data infrastructures". They "should ensure compliance of all AI actors with environmental law, policies and practices." Para. 85: States should support "rights-based and ethical AI-powered solutions for disaster risk resilience" and "the monitoring, protection and regeneration of the environment and ecosystems", for example to "Detect pollutants or predict levels of pollution". Para. 86: AI actors should "favour data, energy and resource-efficient AI methods", and "in instances where there are disproportionate negative impacts on the environment, AI should not be used." EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (for comparison; it does not apply in India): Annex XI, Section 1, point 2(e): technical documentation of a general-purpose AI model must include "known or estimated energy consumption of the model"; if unknown, it "may be based on information about computational resources used". Art. 40(2): standardisation deliverables "to improve AI systems' resource performance, such as reducing the high-risk AI system's consumption of energy and of other resources during its lifecycle". Art. 95(2)(b): voluntary codes of conduct on "assessing and minimising the impact of AI systems on environmental sustainability, including as regards energy-efficient programming". Art. 112(6): "By 2 August 2028 and every four years thereafter", the Commission reports on standardisation for "the energy-efficient development of general-purpose AI models", and assesses the need for further measures, "including binding measures". Polluter pays principle – adopted in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (1996): the "financial costs of preventing or remedying damage caused by pollution should lie with the undertakings which cause the pollution".
hi.meaning: Artificial intelligence (AI) – computer systems that perform tasks such as prediction, recognition, language and decision support by learning from data. AI life cycle – all stages of an AI system: research and design, hardware manufacture, data collection, training, deployment and use, and disposal (UNESCO para. 84 speaks of the "AI system life cycle"). Data centre – a building housing servers, storage and networking equipment that train and run AI systems; it needs continuous electricity and cooling. Carbon footprint – the total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an activity, here by building and operating AI systems. Training and inference – training is the energy-intensive process of building a model from data; inference is using the trained model to answer queries. Polluter pays principle – the person who causes pollution must bear the cost of preventing and remedying it.
keyPoints: Impact is two-way: harms and benefits, across the AI life cycle. Harms: energy, carbon footprint, water, minerals, e-waste, local nuisance from the data centre. India: no AI-specific environmental law; Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g) and general laws apply. Polluter pays principle ( ICELA , 1996) applies to AI facilities. UNESCO 2021: value of "Environment and ecosystem flourishing"; Policy Area 5 (paras. 84–86). EU AI Act: energy consumption documented for general-purpose AI models (Annex XI).

Trespass to land is best described as:

Explanation. Trespass to land is a direct and unauthorised interference with a person's possession of land — directness is the key distinguishing feature.

Which statement about trespass is correct?

Explanation. Trespass is actionable per se — the mere fact of unauthorised direct entry is itself a wrong, without needing proof of damage.

A factory pipe discharges liquid waste directly onto a neighbour's field. This is:

Explanation. A direct discharge onto another's land is trespass, because the interference is the immediate result of the defendant's own act.

environmental-law-u2-t6.subtitle: Injunctions and damages under the Specific Relief Act, 1963 to stop a continuing wrong such as pollution

en.inOneMinute: A person harmed by pollution (smoke, effluent, dust, noise, vibration) usually wants the pollution stopped , not only money. The Specific Relief Act, 1963 (SRA) gives this through injunctions (Part III, ss. 36–42). Section 36: "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." (See Diagram 1 .) Temporary injunction (s. 37(1)): lasts until a specified time or further order; granted at any stage of the suit; governed by the CPC, Order XXXIX. Perpetual injunction (ss. 37(2), 38): granted only by the decree after hearing the suit on merits. Section 38(3) lists when it may be granted to protect property, for example where money is not adequate relief. Mandatory injunction (s. 39): orders the defendant to do something, such as remove a waste dump or install pollution-control equipment. Damages (s. 40): may be claimed in addition to, or in place of, the injunction, but must be claimed in the plaint . Refusal (s. 41): no injunction, for example, where it is not reasonably clear that the act will be a nuisance (cl. (f)), where the plaintiff has acquiesced (cl. (g)), or where the plaintiff has no personal interest (cl. (j)). (See Diagram 2 .)
legalProvision: SRA, s. 4 – "Specific relief can be granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights and not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law." SRA, s. 36 – "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." SRA, s. 37(1) – "Temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specific time, or until the further order of the court, and they may be granted at any stage of a suit, and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908". SRA, s. 37(2) – "A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit; the defendant is thereby perpetually enjoined from the assertion of a right, or from the commission of an act, which would be contrary to the rights of the plaintiff." SRA, s. 38(1) – a perpetual injunction may be granted "to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication." SRA, s. 38(3) – "When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings." SRA, s. 39 – "When, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts." SRA, s. 40(1) – the plaintiff in a suit for perpetual injunction under s. 38 or mandatory injunction under s. 39 "may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction and the court may, if it thinks fit, award such damages." SRA, s. 40(2) – "No relief for damages shall be granted under this section unless the plaintiff has claimed such relief in his plaint". The proviso: where damages were not claimed, the court "shall, at any stage of the proceedings, allow the plaintiff to amend the plaint on such terms as may be just for including such claim." SRA, s. 40(3) – "The dismissal of a suit to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff shall bar his right to sue for damages for such breach." SRA, s. 41 – "An injunction cannot be granted—" in clauses (a) to (j). The clauses that matter most in pollution cases: "(f) to prevent, on the ground of nuisance, an act of which it is not reasonably clear that it will be a nuisance;" "(g) to prevent a continuing breach in which the plaintiff has acquiesced;" "(h) when equally efficacious relief can certainly be obtained by any other usual mode of proceeding except in case of breach of trust;" "(ha) if it would impede or delay the progress or completion of any infrastructure project or interfere with the continued provision of relevant facility related thereto or services being the subject matter of such project." (Inserted by Act 18 of 2018, w.e.f. 1-10-2018.) "(i) when the conduct of the plaintiff or his agents has been such as to disentitle him to be the assistance of the court;" "(j) when the plaintiff has no personal interest in the matter." CPC, Order XXXIX, rule 1 – a temporary injunction may be granted where it is proved "by affidavit or otherwise" that property in dispute "is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated" (cl. (a)), or that the defendant threatens to "cause injury to the plaintiff in relation to any property in dispute in the suit" (cl. (c)). CPC, Order XXXIX, rule 2(1) – in a suit to restrain a "breach of contract or other injury of any kind, whether compensation is claimed in the suit or not", the plaintiff may apply "at any time after the commencement of the suit, and either before or after judgment" for a temporary injunction. CPC, Order XXXIX, rule 3 – notice of the application must be given to the opposite party, "except where it appears that the object of granting the injunction would be defeated by the delay"; then the court must record its reasons. CPC, s. 91(1) – for a public nuisance, a suit "for a declaration and injunction" may be filed "(a) by the Advocate-General, or (b) with the leave of the Court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons".
en.meaning: Injunction – an order of the court that forbids a person from doing an act, or (if mandatory) orders him to do an act. Temporary injunction – an injunction that lasts until a specified time or until further order; granted at any stage of the suit under the CPC (s. 37(1)). Perpetual injunction – an injunction granted by the final decree after a hearing on merits; it permanently restrains the defendant (s. 37(2)). Mandatory injunction – an injunction that compels the defendant to perform acts needed to prevent a breach (s. 39). Damages in lieu of injunction – money awarded instead of, or along with, an injunction under s. 40. Preventive relief – the SRA's name for injunctions (s. 36): relief that prevents a wrong rather than compensating for it.
keyPoints: Preventive relief is discretionary, by injunction (s. 36). Temporary injunction: until a set time or further order; CPC O. XXXIX (s. 37(1)). Perpetual injunction: only by decree on merits (s. 37(2)); grounds for property in s. 38(3)(a)–(d). Mandatory injunction: compels acts the court can enforce (s. 39). Damages in lieu of injunction or in addition: must be claimed in the plaint (s. 40). Refusal: s. 41, especially (f), (g), (ha), (j). Public nuisance: CPC s. 91.

caseLaws.facts: Sturges v. Bridgman (1879) 11 Ch D 852 (Court of Appeal; judgment of the Court by Thesiger LJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A confectioner had used heavy pestles and mortars in his kitchen for over twenty years
caseLaws.facts: In 1873 a physician built a consulting-room at the end of his garden, against the kitchen wall, and the noise and vibration then disturbed him. He sued for an injunction. Principle: The confectioner had acquired no easement to make the noise, because it was not an actionable nuisance until the consulting-room was built. Whether an act is a nuisance depends on its circumstances: "what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey". The Court of Appeal affirmed Jessel MR, and the injunction was granted. Why it matters: It shows an injunction being granted against a continuing noise and vibration nuisance, and shows that long use does not by itself give a polluter a right to continue.
Attorney-General v. P.Y.A. Quarries Ltd. [1958] EWCA Civ 1 (Court of Appeal; Romer and Denning LJJ, Parker LJ agreeing)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oliver J granted an injunction restraining a quarry from throwing stones and splinters beyond
caseLaws.facts: The action was brought by the Attorney-General on the relation of two local councils. The quarry appealed against the dust and vibration part. Principle: Dust and vibration affecting a class of the public were a public nuisance, and the injunction was upheld: "Appeal dismissed". Why it matters: It shows a court restraining the polluting manner of a lawful business, not the business itself, and a public nuisance suit brought by the law officer, as CPC s. 91 allows in India.

te.inOneMinute: కాలుష్యం (పొగ, మురుగు నీరు, దుమ్ము, శబ్దం, కంపనం) వల్ల నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తి సాధారణంగా డబ్బు మాత్రమే కాకుండా కాలుష్యం ఆగిపోవాలని కోరుకుంటాడు. నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం, 1963 (SRA) దీన్ని నిషేధాజ్ఞల (injunctions) ద్వారా ఇస్తుంది (భాగం III, సెక్షన్లు 36–42). సెక్షన్ 36: "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." (అర్థం: నివారణ ఉపశమనం కోర్టు విచక్షణ మేరకు, తాత్కాలిక లేదా శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ద్వారా ఇవ్వబడుతుంది.) ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ (సెక్షన్ 37(1)): నిర్దిష్ట సమయం వరకు లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వు వరకు ఉంటుంది; దావా ఏ దశలోనైనా ఇవ్వవచ్చు; CPC ఆర్డర్ XXXIX దీన్ని నియంత్రిస్తుంది. శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ (సెక్షన్లు 37(2), 38): దావాను మెరిట్స్‌పై విచారించిన తర్వాత ఇచ్చే డిక్రీ ద్వారా మాత్రమే. ఆస్తి రక్షణకు అది ఎప్పుడు ఇవ్వవచ్చో సెక్షన్ 38(3) చెబుతుంది; ఉదాహరణకు, డబ్బు తగిన ఉపశమనం కానప్పుడు. ఆదేశాత్మక నిషేధాజ్ఞ (సెక్షన్ 39): ప్రతివాది ఏదైనా చేయాలని ఆదేశిస్తుంది; ఉదాహరణకు వ్యర్థాల కుప్ప తొలగించడం లేదా కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ పరికరాలు అమర్చడం. నష్టపరిహారం (సెక్షన్ 40): నిషేధాజ్ఞతో పాటు, లేదా దానికి బదులుగా కోరవచ్చు; కానీ ప్లెయింట్‌లో కోరి ఉండాలి. నిరాకరణ (సెక్షన్ 41): ఉదాహరణకు, ఆ చర్య న్యూసెన్స్ అవుతుందని సహేతుకంగా స్పష్టం కానప్పుడు (క్లాజ్ (f)), వాది అంగీకరించి ఊరుకున్నప్పుడు (క్లాజ్ (g)), లేదా వాదికి వ్యక్తిగత ఆసక్తి లేనప్పుడు (క్లాజ్ (j)) నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వరు. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: నిషేధాజ్ఞ ( Injunction ) – ఒక వ్యక్తి ఒక చర్య చేయకుండా నిషేధించే, లేదా (ఆదేశాత్మకమైతే) ఒక చర్య చేయమని ఆదేశించే కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు. తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ( Temporary injunction ) – నిర్దిష్ట సమయం వరకు లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వు వరకు ఉండే నిషేధాజ్ఞ; CPC కింద దావా ఏ దశలోనైనా ఇవ్వబడుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 37(1)). శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ( Perpetual injunction ) – మెరిట్స్‌పై విచారణ తర్వాత తుది డిక్రీ ద్వారా ఇచ్చే నిషేధాజ్ఞ; ప్రతివాదిని శాశ్వతంగా నిరోధిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 37(2)). ఆదేశాత్మక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ( Mandatory injunction ) – ఉల్లంఘనను నివారించడానికి అవసరమైన చర్యలు చేయాలని ప్రతివాదిని బలవంతం చేసే నిషేధాజ్ఞ (సెక్షన్ 39). నిషేధాజ్ఞకు బదులు నష్టపరిహారం (Damages in lieu of injunction) – సెక్షన్ 40 కింద నిషేధాజ్ఞకు బదులుగా, లేదా దానితో పాటు ఇచ్చే డబ్బు. నివారణ ఉపశమనం ( Preventive relief ) – నిషేధాజ్ఞలకు SRA పెట్టిన పేరు (సెక్షన్ 36): తప్పుకు పరిహారం ఇవ్వడం కాకుండా తప్పును నివారించే ఉపశమనం.
keyPoints: నివారణ ఉపశమనం విచక్షణాధికారం, నిషేధాజ్ఞ ద్వారా (సెక్షన్ 36). తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ: నిర్దిష్ట సమయం లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వు వరకు; CPC ఆర్డర్ XXXIX (సెక్షన్ 37(1)). శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ: మెరిట్స్‌పై డిక్రీ ద్వారా మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 37(2)); ఆస్తికి కారణాలు సెక్షన్ 38(3)(a)–(d). ఆదేశాత్మక నిషేధాజ్ఞ: కోర్టు అమలు చేయగల చర్యలు చేయిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 39). నిషేధాజ్ఞకు బదులు నష్టపరిహారం లేదా అదనంగా: ప్లెయింట్‌లో కోరాలి (సెక్షన్ 40). నిరాకరణ: సెక్షన్ 41, ముఖ్యంగా (f), (g), (ha), (j). పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్: CPC సెక్షన్ 91.

selfTest.q: నివారణ ఉపశమనం కోర్టు విచక్షణ మేరకు ఇవ్వబడుతుందని ఏ సెక్షన్ చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఎప్పుడు ఇవ్వవచ్చు? సెక్షన్ 38(3)లోని నాలుగు సందర్భాలు చెప్పండి. ఆదేశాత్మక నిషేధాజ్ఞకు సెక్షన్ 39 పెట్టే రెండు షరతులు ఏమిటి? వాది ప్లెయింట్‌లో నష్టపరిహారం కోరకపోతే ఏమవుతుంది? న్యూసెన్స్ అవుతుందని సహేతుకంగా స్పష్టం కాని చర్యపై నిషేధాజ్ఞను సెక్షన్ 41లోని ఏ క్లాజ్ నిరోధిస్తుంది? 2018లో సెక్షన్ 41లో ఏ క్లాజ్ చేర్చబడింది, అది దేన్ని నిరోధిస్తుంది?

hi.inOneMinute: A person harmed by pollution (smoke, effluent, dust, noise, vibration) usually wants the pollution stopped , not only money. The Specific Relief Act, 1963 (SRA) gives this through injunctions (Part III, ss. 36–42). Section 36: "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." (See Diagram 1 .) Temporary injunction (s. 37(1)): lasts until a specified time or further order; granted at any stage of the suit; governed by the CPC, Order XXXIX. Perpetual injunction (ss. 37(2), 38): granted only by the decree after hearing the suit on merits. Section 38(3) lists when it may be granted to protect property, for example where money is not adequate relief. Mandatory injunction (s. 39): orders the defendant to do something, such as remove a waste dump or install pollution-control equipment. Damages (s. 40): may be claimed in addition to, or in place of, the injunction, but must be claimed in the plaint . Refusal (s. 41): no injunction, for example, where it is not reasonably clear that the act will be a nuisance (cl. (f)), where the plaintiff has acquiesced (cl. (g)), or where the plaintiff has no personal interest (cl. (j)). (See Diagram 2 .)
legalProvision: SRA, s. 4 – "Specific relief can be granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights and not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law." SRA, s. 36 – "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." SRA, s. 37(1) – "Temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specific time, or until the further order of the court, and they may be granted at any stage of a suit, and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908". SRA, s. 37(2) – "A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit; the defendant is thereby perpetually enjoined from the assertion of a right, or from the commission of an act, which would be contrary to the rights of the plaintiff." SRA, s. 38(1) – a perpetual injunction may be granted "to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication." SRA, s. 38(3) – "When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings." SRA, s. 39 – "When, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts." SRA, s. 40(1) – the plaintiff in a suit for perpetual injunction under s. 38 or mandatory injunction under s. 39 "may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction and the court may, if it thinks fit, award such damages." SRA, s. 40(2) – "No relief for damages shall be granted under this section unless the plaintiff has claimed such relief in his plaint". The proviso: where damages were not claimed, the court "shall, at any stage of the proceedings, allow the plaintiff to amend the plaint on such terms as may be just for including such claim." SRA, s. 40(3) – "The dismissal of a suit to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff shall bar his right to sue for damages for such breach." SRA, s. 41 – "An injunction cannot be granted—" in clauses (a) to (j). The clauses that matter most in pollution cases: "(f) to prevent, on the ground of nuisance, an act of which it is not reasonably clear that it will be a nuisance;" "(g) to prevent a continuing breach in which the plaintiff has acquiesced;" "(h) when equally efficacious relief can certainly be obtained by any other usual mode of proceeding except in case of breach of trust;" "(ha) if it would impede or delay the progress or completion of any infrastructure project or interfere with the continued provision of relevant facility related thereto or services being the subject matter of such project." (Inserted by Act 18 of 2018, w.e.f. 1-10-2018.) "(i) when the conduct of the plaintiff or his agents has been such as to disentitle him to be the assistance of the court;" "(j) when the plaintiff has no personal interest in the matter." CPC, Order XXXIX, rule 1 – a temporary injunction may be granted where it is proved "by affidavit or otherwise" that property in dispute "is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated" (cl. (a)), or that the defendant threatens to "cause injury to the plaintiff in relation to any property in dispute in the suit" (cl. (c)). CPC, Order XXXIX, rule 2(1) – in a suit to restrain a "breach of contract or other injury of any kind, whether compensation is claimed in the suit or not", the plaintiff may apply "at any time after the commencement of the suit, and either before or after judgment" for a temporary injunction. CPC, Order XXXIX, rule 3 – notice of the application must be given to the opposite party, "except where it appears that the object of granting the injunction would be defeated by the delay"; then the court must record its reasons. CPC, s. 91(1) – for a public nuisance, a suit "for a declaration and injunction" may be filed "(a) by the Advocate-General, or (b) with the leave of the Court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons".
hi.meaning: Injunction – an order of the court that forbids a person from doing an act, or (if mandatory) orders him to do an act. Temporary injunction – an injunction that lasts until a specified time or until further order; granted at any stage of the suit under the CPC (s. 37(1)). Perpetual injunction – an injunction granted by the final decree after a hearing on merits; it permanently restrains the defendant (s. 37(2)). Mandatory injunction – an injunction that compels the defendant to perform acts needed to prevent a breach (s. 39). Damages in lieu of injunction – money awarded instead of, or along with, an injunction under s. 40. Preventive relief – the SRA's name for injunctions (s. 36): relief that prevents a wrong rather than compensating for it.
keyPoints: Preventive relief is discretionary, by injunction (s. 36). Temporary injunction: until a set time or further order; CPC O. XXXIX (s. 37(1)). Perpetual injunction: only by decree on merits (s. 37(2)); grounds for property in s. 38(3)(a)–(d). Mandatory injunction: compels acts the court can enforce (s. 39). Damages in lieu of injunction or in addition: must be claimed in the plaint (s. 40). Refusal: s. 41, especially (f), (g), (ha), (j). Public nuisance: CPC s. 91.

caseLaws.facts: Sturges v. Bridgman (1879) 11 Ch D 852 (Court of Appeal; judgment of the Court by Thesiger LJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A confectioner had used heavy pestles and mortars in his kitchen for over twenty years
caseLaws.facts: In 1873 a physician built a consulting-room at the end of his garden, against the kitchen wall, and the noise and vibration then disturbed him. He sued for an injunction. Principle: The confectioner had acquired no easement to make the noise, because it was not an actionable nuisance until the consulting-room was built. Whether an act is a nuisance depends on its circumstances: "what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey". The Court of Appeal affirmed Jessel MR, and the injunction was granted. Why it matters: It shows an injunction being granted against a continuing noise and vibration nuisance, and shows that long use does not by itself give a polluter a right to continue.
Attorney-General v. P.Y.A. Quarries Ltd. [1958] EWCA Civ 1 (Court of Appeal; Romer and Denning LJJ, Parker LJ agreeing)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oliver J granted an injunction restraining a quarry from throwing stones and splinters beyond
caseLaws.facts: The action was brought by the Attorney-General on the relation of two local councils. The quarry appealed against the dust and vibration part. Principle: Dust and vibration affecting a class of the public were a public nuisance, and the injunction was upheld: "Appeal dismissed". Why it matters: It shows a court restraining the polluting manner of a lawful business, not the business itself, and a public nuisance suit brought by the law officer, as CPC s. 91 allows in India.

environmental-law-u2-t7.subtitle: The civil, criminal and statutory routes open to a person troubled by smoke or noise

en.inOneMinute: Smoke (with fumes, gases and dust) and noise (with vibration) are the classic forms of nuisance . They cross boundaries indirectly, so the law treats them as nuisance, not trespass. The owner's rights are stated in the Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7, Illustrations (b) and (c): air passing to his land "shall not be unreasonably polluted", and his physical comfort "shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration". Two kinds of harm ( St. Helen's Smelting v. Tipping , 1865): material injury to property (crops, trees, buildings) and sensible personal discomfort (sleep, health, quiet). Locality matters for the second, not for the first. (See Diagram 1 .) Reliefs come from four sources (See Diagram 2 .): civil : damages; temporary, perpetual and mandatory injunctions (Specific Relief Act, ss. 37–41); a public nuisance suit (CPC s. 91); criminal : BNS ss. 270, 280, 292, 293; magisterial : BNSS s. 152 (conditional order) and s. 163 (urgent order); writ : mandamus to make authorities enforce the law ( Rabin Mukherjee v. State of West Bengal , 1985). Coming to the nuisance and long use are not defences by themselves ( St. Helen's ; Sturges v. Bridgman , 1879).
legalProvision: Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7(b) – "The right of every owner of immovable property (subject to any law for the time being in force) to enjoy without disturbance by another the natural advantages arising from its situation." s. 7, Illustration (b) – "The right of every owner of land that the air passing thereto shall not be unreasonably polluted by other persons." s. 7, Illustration (c) – "The right of every owner of a house that his physical comfort shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration caused by any other person." Easements Act, s. 15 – an easement "peaceably and openly enjoyed ... as of right, without interruption, and for twenty years" becomes absolute. Explanation IV: "In the case of an easement to pollute water, the said period of twenty years begins when the pollution first prejudices perceptibly the servient heritage." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 36 – "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." SRA, s. 38(3) – perpetual injunction where the defendant "invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property", including "(c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief" and "(d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings." SRA, s. 39 – mandatory injunction "to compel performance of the requisite acts". SRA, s. 41(f) – no injunction "to prevent, on the ground of nuisance, an act of which it is not reasonably clear that it will be a nuisance". CPC, s. 91(1) – for a public nuisance, a suit "for a declaration and injunction" by "(a) the Advocate-General, or (b) with the leave of the Court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons". BNS, 2023, s. 270 – public nuisance: an act "which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity ... but a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage." BNS, s. 280 – "Whoever voluntarily vitiates the atmosphere in any place so as to make it noxious to the health of persons in general dwelling or carrying on business in the neighbourhood or passing along a public way, shall be punished with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees." BNS, s. 292 – public nuisance "not otherwise punishable": fine up to one thousand rupees. BNS, s. 293 – repeating or continuing a public nuisance after being enjoined by a public servant: simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to five thousand rupees, or both. BNSS, 2023, s. 152(1)(b) – the Magistrate may make a conditional order where "the conduct of any trade or occupation ... is injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community, and that in consequence such trade or occupation should be prohibited or regulated". BNSS, s. 163(1) – in urgent cases, a written order directing "any person to abstain from a certain act", to prevent "obstruction, annoyance or injury to any person lawfully employed, or danger to human life, health or safety". It may be ex parte (s. 163(2)) and may be directed "to the public generally" in a place (s. 163(3)); it lasts no more than two months unless extended (s. 163(4)).
en.meaning: Smoke nuisance – interference with a neighbour's land or comfort by smoke, fumes, gases, soot or dust coming from the defendant's premises. Noise nuisance – interference with a neighbour's physical comfort by noise or vibration that is material and unreasonable (Easements Act, s. 7, Illus. (c)). Material injury to property – physical, measurable damage to land, crops, trees or buildings. Locality is no answer to it. Sensible personal discomfort – interference with comfort, quiet, sleep or health. Whether it is a nuisance depends on "the circumstances of the place" ( St. Helen's ). Coming to the nuisance – the plaintiff moved near an existing source of smoke or noise. It is not a defence by itself. Prescriptive right – an easement acquired by twenty years' peaceable, open, uninterrupted enjoyment as of right (Easements Act, s. 15).
keyPoints: Smoke and noise are nuisance; rights in Easements Act s. 7, Illus. (b), (c). Material injury: locality no defence. Sensible personal discomfort: judged by the circumstances of the place. Coming to the nuisance is not a defence by itself ( St. Helen's ; Sturges ). Prescriptive right to make noise needs twenty years of actionable nuisance ( Sturges ; s. 15). Reliefs: civil (SRA, CPC s. 91), criminal (BNS ss. 270, 280, 292, 293), magisterial (BNSS ss. 152, 163), writ ( Rabin Mukherjee ).

caseLaws.facts: St. Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping (1865) 11 HLC 642; 11 ER 1483 (House of Lords; Lord Westbury LC)

caseLaws.name: Facts: In 1860 Tipping bought an estate near the company's copper smelting works
caseLaws.facts: Noxious gases and vapours from the works damaged his hedges, trees and crops. The jury found the business ordinary and properly conducted but not carried on in a proper place, and awarded £361 18s. 4½d. Principle: Lord Westbury distinguished a nuisance that "produces material injury to the property" from one "productive of sensible personal discomfort"; only the second "must undoubtedly depend greatly on the circumstances of the place". The verdict was upheld. Why it matters: It is the leading smoke case: locality is no defence to physical damage, and the fact that the works existed first did not defeat the claim.
Sturges v. Bridgman (1879) 11 Ch D 852 (Court of Appeal; judgment of the Court by Thesiger LJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A confectioner used heavy pestles and mortars for over twenty years
caseLaws.facts: When a physician built a consulting-room against the kitchen wall in 1873, the noise and vibration disturbed him, and he sued for an injunction. Principle: No easement to make the noise had been acquired, because the noise was not an actionable nuisance until the consulting-room was built. Nuisance depends on circumstances: "what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey". The injunction was granted. Why it matters: It is the leading noise case: long use does not give a right to make noise, and coming to the nuisance does not bar relief.
Rabin Mukherjee v. State of West Bengal AIR 1985 Cal 222 (Calcutta High Court; Bhagabati Prasad Banerjee J; 5 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition, also in public interest, complained of shrill air and electric horns on tran
caseLaws.facts: The authorities were not enforcing the rule. Principle: The Court held that sudden blowing of such horns "produces rude shock in the human system", and directed the State to enforce Rule 114(d), to notify operators to remove such horns within 15 days, and to refuse certificates of fitness to vehicles fitted with them. Why it matters: It shows writ relief against noise where a rule exists but is not enforced.

te.inOneMinute: పొగ (విష వాయువులు, వాయువులు, దుమ్ముతో సహా), శబ్దం (కంపనంతో సహా) న్యూసెన్స్ ‌కు సంప్రదాయ రూపాలు. అవి సరిహద్దులను పరోక్షంగా దాటుతాయి కాబట్టి చట్టం వాటిని అతిక్రమణగా కాకుండా న్యూసెన్స్‌గా పరిగణిస్తుంది. యజమాని హక్కులు భారతీయ ఈజ్‌మెంట్స్ చట్టం, 1882, సెక్షన్ 7, ఉదాహరణలు (b), (c)లో ఉన్నాయి: అతని భూమికి వచ్చే గాలి "shall not be unreasonably polluted" (అర్థం: అసమంజసంగా కలుషితం కాకూడదు), అతని శారీరక సౌకర్యం "shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration" (అర్థం: శబ్దం లేదా కంపనం ద్వారా గణనీయంగా, అసమంజసంగా భంగపడకూడదు). రెండు రకాల హాని ( St. Helen's Smelting v. Tipping , 1865): ఆస్తికి భౌతిక గాయం (material injury) (పంటలు, చెట్లు, భవనాలు), గమనించదగిన వ్యక్తిగత అసౌకర్యం (sensible personal discomfort) (నిద్ర, ఆరోగ్యం, ప్రశాంతత). ప్రదేశం (locality) రెండో దానికి ముఖ్యం, మొదటి దానికి కాదు. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ఉపశమనాలు నాలుగు మూలాల నుంచి వస్తాయి ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.): సివిల్ : నష్టపరిహారం; తాత్కాలిక, శాశ్వత, ఆదేశాత్మక నిషేధాజ్ఞలు (నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం, సెక్షన్లు 37–41); పబ్లిక్ న్యూసెన్స్ దావా (CPC సెక్షన్ 91); క్రిమినల్ : BNS సెక్షన్లు 270, 280, 292, 293; మేజిస్టీరియల్ : BNSS సెక్షన్ 152 (షరతులతో కూడిన ఉత్తర్వు), సెక్షన్ 163 (అత్యవసర ఉత్తర్వు); రిట్ : చట్టాన్ని అమలు చేయమని అధికారులకు మాండమస్ ( Rabin Mukherjee v. State of West Bengal , 1985). న్యూసెన్స్ దగ్గరికి రావడం, దీర్ఘకాల వినియోగం స్వయంగా ప్రతివాదనలు కావు ( St. Helen's ; Sturges v. Bridgman , 1879).
te.meaning: పొగ న్యూసెన్స్ (Smoke nuisance) – ప్రతివాది ఆవరణ నుంచి వచ్చే పొగ, విష వాయువులు, వాయువులు, మసి లేదా దుమ్ము ద్వారా పొరుగువారి భూమిలో లేదా సౌకర్యంలో జోక్యం. శబ్ద న్యూసెన్స్ (Noise nuisance) – గణనీయమైన, అసమంజసమైన శబ్దం లేదా కంపనం ద్వారా పొరుగువారి శారీరక సౌకర్యంలో జోక్యం (ఈజ్‌మెంట్స్ చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 7, ఉదా. (c)). ఆస్తికి భౌతిక గాయం (Material injury to property) – భూమి, పంటలు, చెట్లు లేదా భవనాలకు భౌతిక, కొలవదగిన నష్టం. ప్రదేశం దానికి సమాధానం కాదు. గమనించదగిన వ్యక్తిగత అసౌకర్యం (Sensible personal discomfort) – సౌకర్యం, ప్రశాంతత, నిద్ర లేదా ఆరోగ్యంలో జోక్యం. అది న్యూసెన్సా కాదా అనేది "the circumstances of the place" (అర్థం: ఆ ప్రదేశ పరిస్థితులు)పై ఆధారపడుతుంది ( St. Helen's ). న్యూసెన్స్ దగ్గరికి రావడం (Coming to the nuisance) – వాది ఇప్పటికే ఉన్న పొగ లేదా శబ్ద మూలం దగ్గరికి వచ్చాడు. అది స్వయంగా ప్రతివాదన కాదు. ప్రిస్క్రిప్టివ్ హక్కు (Prescriptive right) – హక్కుగా ఇరవై ఏళ్లు శాంతియుతంగా, బహిరంగంగా, అంతరాయం లేకుండా అనుభవించడం ద్వారా సంపాదించిన ఈజ్‌మెంట్ (ఈజ్‌మెంట్స్ చట్టం, సెక్షన్ 15).
keyPoints: పొగ, శబ్దం న్యూసెన్స్; హక్కులు ఈజ్‌మెంట్స్ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 7, ఉదా. (b), (c)లో. భౌతిక గాయం: ప్రదేశం ప్రతివాదన కాదు. గమనించదగిన వ్యక్తిగత అసౌకర్యం: ప్రదేశ పరిస్థితుల బట్టి నిర్ణయిస్తారు. న్యూసెన్స్ దగ్గరికి రావడం స్వయంగా ప్రతివాదన కాదు ( St. Helen's ; Sturges ). శబ్దం చేసే ప్రిస్క్రిప్టివ్ హక్కుకు దావాకు అర్హమైన న్యూసెన్స్ ఇరవై ఏళ్లు ఉండాలి ( Sturges ; సెక్షన్ 15). ఉపశమనాలు: సివిల్ (SRA, CPC సెక్షన్ 91), క్రిమినల్ (BNS సెక్షన్లు 270, 280, 292, 293), మేజిస్టీరియల్ (BNSS సెక్షన్లు 152, 163), రిట్ ( Rabin Mukherjee ).

selfTest.q: ఈజ్‌మెంట్స్ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 7లోని ఏ ఉదాహరణలు గాలి, శబ్దం గురించి చెబుతాయి?
selfTest.a: Lord Westbury ఏ రెండు రకాల న్యూసెన్స్‌ను వేరు చేశారు? విష వాయువులు పొరుగువారి చెట్లను చంపినప్పుడు ప్రదేశం ముఖ్యమా? Sturges లో మిఠాయి తయారీదారుకు శబ్దం చేసే హక్కు ఎందుకు రాలేదు? వాతావరణాన్ని ఆరోగ్యానికి హానికరం చేయడాన్ని BNSలోని ఏ సెక్షన్ శిక్షిస్తుంది? BNSS సెక్షన్ 163 కింద ఉత్తర్వు పొడిగింపు లేకుండా ఎంత కాలం అమలులో ఉండవచ్చు? Rabin Mukherjee లో కలకత్తా హైకోర్టు ఏమి ఆదేశించింది?

hi.inOneMinute: Smoke (with fumes, gases and dust) and noise (with vibration) are the classic forms of nuisance . They cross boundaries indirectly, so the law treats them as nuisance, not trespass. The owner's rights are stated in the Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7, Illustrations (b) and (c): air passing to his land "shall not be unreasonably polluted", and his physical comfort "shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration". Two kinds of harm ( St. Helen's Smelting v. Tipping , 1865): material injury to property (crops, trees, buildings) and sensible personal discomfort (sleep, health, quiet). Locality matters for the second, not for the first. (See Diagram 1 .) Reliefs come from four sources (See Diagram 2 .): civil : damages; temporary, perpetual and mandatory injunctions (Specific Relief Act, ss. 37–41); a public nuisance suit (CPC s. 91); criminal : BNS ss. 270, 280, 292, 293; magisterial : BNSS s. 152 (conditional order) and s. 163 (urgent order); writ : mandamus to make authorities enforce the law ( Rabin Mukherjee v. State of West Bengal , 1985). Coming to the nuisance and long use are not defences by themselves ( St. Helen's ; Sturges v. Bridgman , 1879).
legalProvision: Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7(b) – "The right of every owner of immovable property (subject to any law for the time being in force) to enjoy without disturbance by another the natural advantages arising from its situation." s. 7, Illustration (b) – "The right of every owner of land that the air passing thereto shall not be unreasonably polluted by other persons." s. 7, Illustration (c) – "The right of every owner of a house that his physical comfort shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration caused by any other person." Easements Act, s. 15 – an easement "peaceably and openly enjoyed ... as of right, without interruption, and for twenty years" becomes absolute. Explanation IV: "In the case of an easement to pollute water, the said period of twenty years begins when the pollution first prejudices perceptibly the servient heritage." Specific Relief Act, 1963, s. 36 – "Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual." SRA, s. 38(3) – perpetual injunction where the defendant "invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to, or enjoyment of, property", including "(c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief" and "(d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings." SRA, s. 39 – mandatory injunction "to compel performance of the requisite acts". SRA, s. 41(f) – no injunction "to prevent, on the ground of nuisance, an act of which it is not reasonably clear that it will be a nuisance". CPC, s. 91(1) – for a public nuisance, a suit "for a declaration and injunction" by "(a) the Advocate-General, or (b) with the leave of the Court, by two or more persons, even though no special damage has been caused to such persons". BNS, 2023, s. 270 – public nuisance: an act "which causes any common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity ... but a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage." BNS, s. 280 – "Whoever voluntarily vitiates the atmosphere in any place so as to make it noxious to the health of persons in general dwelling or carrying on business in the neighbourhood or passing along a public way, shall be punished with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees." BNS, s. 292 – public nuisance "not otherwise punishable": fine up to one thousand rupees. BNS, s. 293 – repeating or continuing a public nuisance after being enjoined by a public servant: simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to five thousand rupees, or both. BNSS, 2023, s. 152(1)(b) – the Magistrate may make a conditional order where "the conduct of any trade or occupation ... is injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community, and that in consequence such trade or occupation should be prohibited or regulated". BNSS, s. 163(1) – in urgent cases, a written order directing "any person to abstain from a certain act", to prevent "obstruction, annoyance or injury to any person lawfully employed, or danger to human life, health or safety". It may be ex parte (s. 163(2)) and may be directed "to the public generally" in a place (s. 163(3)); it lasts no more than two months unless extended (s. 163(4)).
hi.meaning: Smoke nuisance – interference with a neighbour's land or comfort by smoke, fumes, gases, soot or dust coming from the defendant's premises. Noise nuisance – interference with a neighbour's physical comfort by noise or vibration that is material and unreasonable (Easements Act, s. 7, Illus. (c)). Material injury to property – physical, measurable damage to land, crops, trees or buildings. Locality is no answer to it. Sensible personal discomfort – interference with comfort, quiet, sleep or health. Whether it is a nuisance depends on "the circumstances of the place" ( St. Helen's ). Coming to the nuisance – the plaintiff moved near an existing source of smoke or noise. It is not a defence by itself. Prescriptive right – an easement acquired by twenty years' peaceable, open, uninterrupted enjoyment as of right (Easements Act, s. 15).
keyPoints: Smoke and noise are nuisance; rights in Easements Act s. 7, Illus. (b), (c). Material injury: locality no defence. Sensible personal discomfort: judged by the circumstances of the place. Coming to the nuisance is not a defence by itself ( St. Helen's ; Sturges ). Prescriptive right to make noise needs twenty years of actionable nuisance ( Sturges ; s. 15). Reliefs: civil (SRA, CPC s. 91), criminal (BNS ss. 270, 280, 292, 293), magisterial (BNSS ss. 152, 163), writ ( Rabin Mukherjee ).

caseLaws.facts: St. Helen's Smelting Co. v. Tipping (1865) 11 HLC 642; 11 ER 1483 (House of Lords; Lord Westbury LC)

caseLaws.name: Facts: In 1860 Tipping bought an estate near the company's copper smelting works
caseLaws.facts: Noxious gases and vapours from the works damaged his hedges, trees and crops. The jury found the business ordinary and properly conducted but not carried on in a proper place, and awarded £361 18s. 4½d. Principle: Lord Westbury distinguished a nuisance that "produces material injury to the property" from one "productive of sensible personal discomfort"; only the second "must undoubtedly depend greatly on the circumstances of the place". The verdict was upheld. Why it matters: It is the leading smoke case: locality is no defence to physical damage, and the fact that the works existed first did not defeat the claim.
Sturges v. Bridgman (1879) 11 Ch D 852 (Court of Appeal; judgment of the Court by Thesiger LJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A confectioner used heavy pestles and mortars for over twenty years
caseLaws.facts: When a physician built a consulting-room against the kitchen wall in 1873, the noise and vibration disturbed him, and he sued for an injunction. Principle: No easement to make the noise had been acquired, because the noise was not an actionable nuisance until the consulting-room was built. Nuisance depends on circumstances: "what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey". The injunction was granted. Why it matters: It is the leading noise case: long use does not give a right to make noise, and coming to the nuisance does not bar relief.
Rabin Mukherjee v. State of West Bengal AIR 1985 Cal 222 (Calcutta High Court; Bhagabati Prasad Banerjee J; 5 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition, also in public interest, complained of shrill air and electric horns on tran
caseLaws.facts: The authorities were not enforcing the rule. Principle: The Court held that sudden blowing of such horns "produces rude shock in the human system", and directed the State to enforce Rule 114(d), to notify operators to remove such horns within 15 days, and to refuse certificates of fitness to vehicles fitted with them. Why it matters: It shows writ relief against noise where a rule exists but is not enforced.

selfTest.a: What two kinds of nuisance did Lord Westbury distinguish? Is locality relevant when fumes kill a neighbour's trees? Why did the confectioner in Sturges not acquire a right to make noise? Which BNS section punishes making the atmosphere noxious to health? How long can an order under BNSS s. 163 remain in force without extension? What did the Calcutta High Court direct in Rabin Mukherjee ?

environmental-law-u2-t8.subtitle: Unwanted or excessive sound as a pollutant: the Noise Rules, 2000, silence zones, loudspeaker limits and court decisions

en.inOneMinute: Noise pollution is unwanted sound, from loudspeakers, horns, fire crackers, machines, construction or generators, at levels that harm health, sleep or comfort. The main law is the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 , made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. They fix ambient noise standards for four zones (industrial, commercial, residential, silence), measured in dB(A) Leq . (See Diagram 1 .) Loudspeakers need written permission and cannot be used at night (10 p.m. to 6 a.m.) , except in closed premises or a public emergency. The State may relax this to midnight on festive occasions for up to 15 days a year (Rule 5). No horns in silence zones or at night in residential areas; no sound-emitting fire crackers in silence zones or at night (Rule 5A). A person may complain to the authority if noise exceeds the standard by 10 dB(A) or more (Rule 7); the authority can prohibit the noise by written order (Rule 8). (See Diagram 2 .) The Supreme Court in In re Noise Pollution (2005) recognised freedom from noise pollution as part of the right to life under Article 21. Article 19(1)(a) does not give a right to use loudspeakers, and religion is no shelter for noise. Older remedies still apply: nuisance (Easements Act s. 7, Illus. (c)), injunction, BNS s. 270, BNSS ss. 152, 163, and writs ( Rabin Mukherjee , 1985).
legalProvision: Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 (principal rules S.O. 123(E), 14-2-2000; amended in 2000, 2002, 2006 and 2010) – made under ss. 3(1), 3(2)(ii), 6(2)(b) and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Rule 2(c) – "authority" means "any authority or officer authorized by the Central Government, or as the case may be, the State Government", and includes "a District Magistrate, Police Commissioner, or any other officer not below the rank of the Deputy Superintendent of Police" designated for maintaining ambient noise standards. Rule 2(i) – "public place" means "any place to which the public have access, whether as of right or not" (for example auditoria, hotels, malls, cinema halls, open grounds). Rule 2(j) – "night time" means "the period between 10.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m.". Rule 3 – the Schedule sets the standards (r. 3(1)); the State Government categorises areas as industrial, commercial, residential or silence (r. 3(2)); takes measures for abatement, including vehicular noise, horns, fire crackers and loudspeakers, and must "ensure that the existing noise levels do not exceed the ambient air quality standards" (r. 3(3)); planning authorities must treat noise "as a parameter of quality of life" (r. 3(4)); "An area comprising not less than 100 metres around hospitals, educational institutions and courts" may be declared a silence zone (r. 3(5)). Rule 4 – noise in any area "shall not exceed the ambient air quality standards in respect of noise as specified in the Schedule" (r. 4(1)); the authority enforces (r. 4(2)). Rule 5 – loudspeakers / public address systems: r. 5(1): only with written permission of the authority; r. 5(2): not at night, except in closed premises for communication within (auditoria, conference rooms, community halls, banquet halls) or in a public emergency; r. 5(3): the State Government may permit use between 10 p.m. and 12 midnight on cultural or religious festive occasions "not exceeding fifteen days in all during a calendar year"; r. 5(4): noise at the boundary of a public place "shall not exceed 10 dB (A) above the ambient noise standards for the area" or 75 dB(A), whichever is lower; r. 5(5): a private sound system must not "exceed by more than 5 dB (A) the ambient noise standards specified for the area" at the boundary of the private place. Rule 5A – "No horn shall be used in silence zones or during night time in residential areas" except in a public emergency; sound-emitting fire crackers not in silence zones or at night; sound-emitting construction equipment not at night in residential areas or silence zones. Rule 6 – in a silence zone, playing music, using amplifiers, beating drums or blowing horns, crowd-drawing performances, bursting sound-emitting crackers or using a loudspeaker makes a person "liable for penalty under the provisions of the Act". Rule 7 – a person may complain if noise "exceeds the ambient noise standards by 10 dB (A) or more", or a night restriction is broken; "The authority shall act on the complaint and take action against the violator". Rule 8 – on a police report or other information, the authority may, "by a written order issue such directions as he may consider necessary" to prevent annoyance, disturbance or injury, including over music, instruments, horns, construction equipment, crackers and noisy trades; under r. 8(2) it may rescind or modify the order after hearing the applicant and the original complainant. The Schedule – ambient standards, dB(A) Leq:
Area code Category Day time Night time (A) Industrial area 75 70 (B) Commercial area 65 55 (C) Residential area 55 45 (D) Silence zone 50 40

Notes: day time is 6.00 a.m. to 10.00 p.m.; night time is 10.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m.; a silence zone is an area of not less than 100 metres around "hospitals, educational institutions, courts, religious places" or any other area declared by the competent authority; mixed categories may be declared as one of the four.

Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7, Illustration (c) – "The right of every owner of a house that his physical comfort shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration caused by any other person." BNS, 2023, s. 270 – public nuisance; "a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage." s. 292 – fine up to one thousand rupees. s. 293 – continuing after a public servant's injunction. BNSS, 2023, s. 152(1)(b) (trade "injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community") and s. 163 (urgent order to "abstain from a certain act").
en.meaning: Noise pollution – sound at a level or time that harms health, sleep, work or comfort, beyond what the law permits. Ambient noise standards – the maximum noise levels permitted in each category of area by day and by night, set in the Schedule to the 2000 Rules. dB(A) Leq – the unit of the standards: a time-weighted average sound level on the "A" scale, which matches the response of the human ear. Silence zone – an area of not less than 100 metres around hospitals, educational institutions and courts (Rule 3(5)); the Schedule note adds religious places. Night time – 10.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m. (Rule 2(j)). Authority – the officer designated to enforce the Rules, such as a District Magistrate, Police Commissioner or an officer not below the rank of DSP (Rule 2(c)).
keyPoints: Noise Rules, 2000 under EPA, 1986; four zones; limits in dB(A) Leq. Ambient noise standards: industrial 75/70, commercial 65/55, residential 55/45, silence 50/40. Silence zone: not less than 100 m around hospitals, educational institutions, courts (and religious places, Schedule note). Night time: 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.; loudspeakers barred, festive relaxation to midnight for 15 days a year. Complaint at +10 dB(A) (r. 7); prohibition order (r. 8). In re Noise Pollution (2005): Article 21 protects freedom from noise; no right to loudspeakers under Article 19(1)(a) or Article 25.

caseLaws.facts: In re Noise Pollution – Implementation of the Laws for restricting use of loudspeakers and high volume producing sound systems, Writ Petition (Civil) 72 of 1998, decided 18 July 2005 (Supreme Court; R.C. Lahoti CJI and Ashok Bhan J; judgment by Lahoti CJI)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petition was filed in public interest after a report that a 13-year-old girl was raped an
caseLaws.facts: It was heard with a civil appeal by the Forum, Prevention of Environment and Sound Pollution. Principle: Freedom from noise pollution is part of the right to life under Article 21. "Nobody can claim a fundamental right to create noise by amplifying the sound of his speech with the help of loudspeakers." The Court issued directions under Articles 141 and 142 on fire crackers, loudspeakers, horns, seizure and awareness. Why it matters: It is the leading Indian case on noise pollution, making noise control a fundamental-rights issue and adding binding directions to the 2000 Rules.
Rabin Mukherjee v. State of West Bengal AIR 1985 Cal 222 (Calcutta High Court; Bhagabati Prasad Banerjee J; 5 March 1985)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Such horns produce "rude shock in the human system"; the State was directed to enforce Rule 114(d), give operators 15 days to remove the horns, and refuse fitness certificates to vehicles fitted with them. Why it matters: An early Indian case treating vehicular noise as pollution and using mandamus to compel enforcement.
Sturges v. Bridgman (1879) 11 Ch D 852 (Court of Appeal; judgment of the Court by Thesiger LJ)

An injunction was granted. Why it matters: It shows the common law remedy for noise, which still runs alongside the Rules.

te.inOneMinute: శబ్ద కాలుష్యం అంటే లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్లు, హారన్లు, టపాసులు, యంత్రాలు, నిర్మాణం లేదా జనరేటర్ల నుంచి వచ్చే, ఆరోగ్యానికి, నిద్రకు లేదా సౌకర్యానికి హాని చేసే స్థాయిలోని అవాంఛిత శబ్దం. ప్రధాన చట్టం Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 (శబ్ద కాలుష్య (నియంత్రణ) నియమాలు, 2000); ఇవి పర్యావరణ (పరిరక్షణ) చట్టం, 1986 కింద రూపొందించబడ్డాయి. నాలుగు జోన్లకు (పారిశ్రామిక, వాణిజ్య, నివాస, నిశ్శబ్ద) పరిసర శబ్ద ప్రమాణాలు నిర్ణయిస్తాయి; వీటిని dB(A) Leq లో కొలుస్తారు. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్లకు లిఖిత అనుమతి అవసరం; రాత్రి (రాత్రి 10 నుంచి ఉదయం 6 వరకు) వాడకూడదు, మూసి ఉన్న ఆవరణలు లేదా ప్రజా అత్యవసర పరిస్థితి తప్ప. పండుగ సందర్భాల్లో ఏడాదికి 15 రోజుల వరకు అర్ధరాత్రి వరకు రాష్ట్రం సడలించవచ్చు (రూల్ 5). నిశ్శబ్ద జోన్లలో లేదా రాత్రి నివాస ప్రాంతాల్లో హారన్లు వద్దు; నిశ్శబ్ద జోన్లలో లేదా రాత్రి శబ్దం చేసే టపాసులు వద్దు (రూల్ 5A). శబ్దం ప్రమాణాన్ని 10 dB(A) లేదా అంతకంటే ఎక్కువ దాటితే ఎవరైనా అధికారి (authority) కి ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు (రూల్ 7); అధికారి లిఖిత ఉత్తర్వు ద్వారా శబ్దాన్ని నిషేధించవచ్చు (రూల్ 8). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) In re Noise Pollution (2005)లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు శబ్ద కాలుష్యం నుంచి స్వేచ్ఛను ఆర్టికల్ 21 కింద జీవించే హక్కులో భాగంగా గుర్తించింది. ఆర్టికల్ 19(1)(a) లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్లు వాడే హక్కు ఇవ్వదు; మతం శబ్దానికి ఆశ్రయం కాదు. పాత పరిహారాలు ఇంకా వర్తిస్తాయి: న్యూసెన్స్ (ఈజ్‌మెంట్స్ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 7, ఉదా. (c)), నిషేధాజ్ఞ, BNS సెక్షన్ 270, BNSS సెక్షన్లు 152, 163, రిట్లు ( Rabin Mukherjee , 1985).
te.meaning: శబ్ద కాలుష్యం ( Noise pollution ) – చట్టం అనుమతించే దానికి మించి, ఆరోగ్యానికి, నిద్రకు, పనికి లేదా సౌకర్యానికి హాని చేసే స్థాయిలో లేదా సమయంలో వచ్చే శబ్దం. పరిసర శబ్ద ప్రమాణాలు (Ambient noise standards) – 2000 నియమాల షెడ్యూల్‌లో ప్రతి ప్రాంత వర్గానికి పగలు, రాత్రి అనుమతించిన గరిష్ఠ శబ్ద స్థాయిలు. dB(A) Leq – ప్రమాణాల యూనిట్: మనిషి చెవి స్పందనకు సరిపోయే "A" స్కేల్‌పై, కాలంతో సగటు చేసిన శబ్ద స్థాయి. నిశ్శబ్ద జోన్ (Silence zone) – ఆసుపత్రులు, విద్యాసంస్థలు, కోర్టుల చుట్టూ 100 మీటర్లకు తగ్గని ప్రాంతం (రూల్ 3(5)); షెడ్యూల్ గమనిక మత స్థలాలను కూడా చేరుస్తుంది. రాత్రి సమయం (Night time) – రాత్రి 10.00 నుంచి ఉదయం 6.00 వరకు (రూల్ 2(j)). అధికారి (Authority) – నియమాలను అమలు చేయడానికి నియమించిన అధికారి; ఉదాహరణకు జిల్లా మేజిస్ట్రేట్, పోలీస్ కమిషనర్ లేదా DSP హోదాకు తగ్గని అధికారి (రూల్ 2(c)).
keyPoints: EPA, 1986 కింద శబ్ద నియమాలు, 2000; నాలుగు జోన్లు; dB(A) Leqలో పరిమితులు. పరిసర శబ్ద ప్రమాణాలు: పారిశ్రామిక 75/70, వాణిజ్య 65/55, నివాస 55/45, నిశ్శబ్ద 50/40. నిశ్శబ్ద జోన్: ఆసుపత్రులు, విద్యాసంస్థలు, కోర్టుల చుట్టూ 100 మీటర్లకు తగ్గకుండా (మత స్థలాలు, షెడ్యూల్ గమనిక). రాత్రి సమయం: రాత్రి 10 నుంచి ఉదయం 6; లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్లు నిషేధం, పండుగలకు ఏడాదికి 15 రోజులు అర్ధరాత్రి వరకు సడలింపు. +10 dB(A) వద్ద ఫిర్యాదు (రూల్ 7); నిషేధ ఉత్తర్వు (రూల్ 8). In re Noise Pollution (2005): ఆర్టికల్ 21 శబ్దం నుంచి స్వేచ్ఛను రక్షిస్తుంది; ఆర్టికల్ 19(1)(a) లేదా ఆర్టికల్ 25 కింద లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్ల హక్కు లేదు.

selfTest.q: శబ్ద నియమాలు, 2000 ఏ చట్టం కింద రూపొందించబడ్డాయి?
selfTest.a: నివాస ప్రాంతానికి పగటి, రాత్రి పరిమితులు చెప్పండి. నిశ్శబ్ద జోన్ అంటే ఏమిటి? నియమాల ప్రకారం రాత్రి సమయం ఏది? రాత్రి 10 నుంచి అర్ధరాత్రి 12 మధ్య లౌడ్‌స్పీకర్లు ఎప్పుడు వాడవచ్చు? రూల్ 7 కింద ఎప్పుడు ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు? ఆర్టికల్ 19(1)(a) గురించి In re Noise Pollution ఏమి చెప్పింది?

hi.inOneMinute: Noise pollution is unwanted sound, from loudspeakers, horns, fire crackers, machines, construction or generators, at levels that harm health, sleep or comfort. The main law is the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 , made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. They fix ambient noise standards for four zones (industrial, commercial, residential, silence), measured in dB(A) Leq . (See Diagram 1 .) Loudspeakers need written permission and cannot be used at night (10 p.m. to 6 a.m.) , except in closed premises or a public emergency. The State may relax this to midnight on festive occasions for up to 15 days a year (Rule 5). No horns in silence zones or at night in residential areas; no sound-emitting fire crackers in silence zones or at night (Rule 5A). A person may complain to the authority if noise exceeds the standard by 10 dB(A) or more (Rule 7); the authority can prohibit the noise by written order (Rule 8). (See Diagram 2 .) The Supreme Court in In re Noise Pollution (2005) recognised freedom from noise pollution as part of the right to life under Article 21. Article 19(1)(a) does not give a right to use loudspeakers, and religion is no shelter for noise. Older remedies still apply: nuisance (Easements Act s. 7, Illus. (c)), injunction, BNS s. 270, BNSS ss. 152, 163, and writs ( Rabin Mukherjee , 1985).
legalProvision: Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 (principal rules S.O. 123(E), 14-2-2000; amended in 2000, 2002, 2006 and 2010) – made under ss. 3(1), 3(2)(ii), 6(2)(b) and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. Rule 2(c) – "authority" means "any authority or officer authorized by the Central Government, or as the case may be, the State Government", and includes "a District Magistrate, Police Commissioner, or any other officer not below the rank of the Deputy Superintendent of Police" designated for maintaining ambient noise standards. Rule 2(i) – "public place" means "any place to which the public have access, whether as of right or not" (for example auditoria, hotels, malls, cinema halls, open grounds). Rule 2(j) – "night time" means "the period between 10.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m.". Rule 3 – the Schedule sets the standards (r. 3(1)); the State Government categorises areas as industrial, commercial, residential or silence (r. 3(2)); takes measures for abatement, including vehicular noise, horns, fire crackers and loudspeakers, and must "ensure that the existing noise levels do not exceed the ambient air quality standards" (r. 3(3)); planning authorities must treat noise "as a parameter of quality of life" (r. 3(4)); "An area comprising not less than 100 metres around hospitals, educational institutions and courts" may be declared a silence zone (r. 3(5)). Rule 4 – noise in any area "shall not exceed the ambient air quality standards in respect of noise as specified in the Schedule" (r. 4(1)); the authority enforces (r. 4(2)). Rule 5 – loudspeakers / public address systems: r. 5(1): only with written permission of the authority; r. 5(2): not at night, except in closed premises for communication within (auditoria, conference rooms, community halls, banquet halls) or in a public emergency; r. 5(3): the State Government may permit use between 10 p.m. and 12 midnight on cultural or religious festive occasions "not exceeding fifteen days in all during a calendar year"; r. 5(4): noise at the boundary of a public place "shall not exceed 10 dB (A) above the ambient noise standards for the area" or 75 dB(A), whichever is lower; r. 5(5): a private sound system must not "exceed by more than 5 dB (A) the ambient noise standards specified for the area" at the boundary of the private place. Rule 5A – "No horn shall be used in silence zones or during night time in residential areas" except in a public emergency; sound-emitting fire crackers not in silence zones or at night; sound-emitting construction equipment not at night in residential areas or silence zones. Rule 6 – in a silence zone, playing music, using amplifiers, beating drums or blowing horns, crowd-drawing performances, bursting sound-emitting crackers or using a loudspeaker makes a person "liable for penalty under the provisions of the Act". Rule 7 – a person may complain if noise "exceeds the ambient noise standards by 10 dB (A) or more", or a night restriction is broken; "The authority shall act on the complaint and take action against the violator". Rule 8 – on a police report or other information, the authority may, "by a written order issue such directions as he may consider necessary" to prevent annoyance, disturbance or injury, including over music, instruments, horns, construction equipment, crackers and noisy trades; under r. 8(2) it may rescind or modify the order after hearing the applicant and the original complainant. The Schedule – ambient standards, dB(A) Leq:
Area code Category Day time Night time (A) Industrial area 75 70 (B) Commercial area 65 55 (C) Residential area 55 45 (D) Silence zone 50 40

Notes: day time is 6.00 a.m. to 10.00 p.m.; night time is 10.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m.; a silence zone is an area of not less than 100 metres around "hospitals, educational institutions, courts, religious places" or any other area declared by the competent authority; mixed categories may be declared as one of the four.

Indian Easements Act, 1882, s. 7, Illustration (c) – "The right of every owner of a house that his physical comfort shall not be interfered with materially and unreasonably by noise or vibration caused by any other person." BNS, 2023, s. 270 – public nuisance; "a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage." s. 292 – fine up to one thousand rupees. s. 293 – continuing after a public servant's injunction. BNSS, 2023, s. 152(1)(b) (trade "injurious to the health or physical comfort of the community") and s. 163 (urgent order to "abstain from a certain act").
hi.meaning: Noise pollution – sound at a level or time that harms health, sleep, work or comfort, beyond what the law permits. Ambient noise standards – the maximum noise levels permitted in each category of area by day and by night, set in the Schedule to the 2000 Rules. dB(A) Leq – the unit of the standards: a time-weighted average sound level on the "A" scale, which matches the response of the human ear. Silence zone – an area of not less than 100 metres around hospitals, educational institutions and courts (Rule 3(5)); the Schedule note adds religious places. Night time – 10.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m. (Rule 2(j)). Authority – the officer designated to enforce the Rules, such as a District Magistrate, Police Commissioner or an officer not below the rank of DSP (Rule 2(c)).
keyPoints: Noise Rules, 2000 under EPA, 1986; four zones; limits in dB(A) Leq. Ambient noise standards: industrial 75/70, commercial 65/55, residential 55/45, silence 50/40. Silence zone: not less than 100 m around hospitals, educational institutions, courts (and religious places, Schedule note). Night time: 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.; loudspeakers barred, festive relaxation to midnight for 15 days a year. Complaint at +10 dB(A) (r. 7); prohibition order (r. 8). In re Noise Pollution (2005): Article 21 protects freedom from noise; no right to loudspeakers under Article 19(1)(a) or Article 25.

caseLaws.facts: In re Noise Pollution – Implementation of the Laws for restricting use of loudspeakers and high volume producing sound systems, Writ Petition (Civil) 72 of 1998, decided 18 July 2005 (Supreme Court; R.C. Lahoti CJI and Ashok Bhan J; judgment by Lahoti CJI)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petition was filed in public interest after a report that a 13-year-old girl was raped an
caseLaws.facts: It was heard with a civil appeal by the Forum, Prevention of Environment and Sound Pollution. Principle: Freedom from noise pollution is part of the right to life under Article 21. "Nobody can claim a fundamental right to create noise by amplifying the sound of his speech with the help of loudspeakers." The Court issued directions under Articles 141 and 142 on fire crackers, loudspeakers, horns, seizure and awareness. Why it matters: It is the leading Indian case on noise pollution, making noise control a fundamental-rights issue and adding binding directions to the 2000 Rules.
Rabin Mukherjee v. State of West Bengal AIR 1985 Cal 222 (Calcutta High Court; Bhagabati Prasad Banerjee J; 5 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition complained of air and electric horns on transport vehicles, contrary to Rule
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Such horns produce "rude shock in the human system"; the State was directed to enforce Rule 114(d), give operators 15 days to remove the horns, and refuse fitness certificates to vehicles fitted with them. Why it matters: An early Indian case treating vehicular noise as pollution and using mandamus to compel enforcement.
Sturges v. Bridgman (1879) 11 Ch D 852 (Court of Appeal; judgment of the Court by Thesiger LJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A confectioner's pestles and mortars, used for over twenty years, disturbed a physician after
caseLaws.facts: Principle: No right to make the noise had been acquired, since it was not an actionable nuisance until then; "what would be a nuisance in Belgrave Square would not necessarily be so in Bermondsey". An injunction was granted. Why it matters: It shows the common law remedy for noise, which still runs alongside the Rules.
