environmental-law-u2-t10.subtitle: How war damages the environment and which rules of international law protect it

en.inOneMinute: War damages the environment directly (bombing of land, forests, rivers, industrial plants, oil installations) and indirectly (toxic remnants, displaced people, collapse of environmental governance). (See Diagram 1 .) The Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 24: "Warfare is inherently destructive of sustainable development." Main rules of international law: Additional Protocol I, 1977 : Art. 35(3) prohibits methods or means of warfare intended or expected "to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment"; Art. 55 repeats the duty of care and bans reprisals against the environment. ENMOD Convention (signed 18 May 1977): no hostile use of environmental modification techniques "having widespread, long-lasting or severe effects". Rome Statute , Art. 8(2)(b)(iv): an attack causing such environmental damage that is clearly excessive to the military advantage is a war crime. ILC Draft Principles (2022) : 27 principles protecting the environment before, during and after armed conflict. The ICJ ( Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion , 1996): the environment "is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings"; it must be weighed in necessity and proportionality . (See Diagram 2 .) India: Art. 51(c) (respect for international law), Art. 253 (laws to implement treaties), Arts. 48A and 51A(g).
legalProvision: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, 1992: Principle 24: "Warfare is inherently destructive of sustainable development. States shall therefore respect international law providing protection for the environment in times of armed conflict and cooperate in its further development, as necessary." Principle 25: "Peace, development and environmental protection are interdependent and indivisible." Principle 26: "States shall resolve all their environmental disputes peacefully and by appropriate means in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations." Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions (8 June 1977): Art. 35(3): "it is prohibited to employ methods or means of warfare which are intended, or may be expected, to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment". Art. 55(1): "Care shall be taken in warfare to protect the natural environment against widespread, long-term and severe damage." The paragraph includes a prohibition of methods or means expected to cause such damage and thereby prejudice the health or survival of the population. Art. 55(2): "Attacks against the natural environment by way of reprisals are prohibited." ENMOD Convention (Convention on the Prohibition of Military or Any Other Hostile Use of Environmental Modification Techniques; signed at Geneva 18 May 1977; in force 5 October 1978): Art. I(1): each State Party "undertakes not to engage in military or any other hostile use of environmental modification techniques having widespread, long-lasting or severe effects as the means of destruction, damage or injury to any other State Party." Art. II: "environmental modification techniques" means any technique for changing, "through the deliberate manipulation of natural processes", the dynamics, composition or structure of the Earth or outer space. Understanding relating to Art. I: "widespread" means "encompassing an area on the scale of several hundred square kilometres"; "long-lasting" means "lasting for a period of months, or approximately a season"; "severe" means "involving serious or significant disruption or harm to human life, natural and economic resources or other assets." This meaning is "intended exclusively for this Convention". Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, 1998, Art. 8(2)(b)(iv) – the war crime of intentionally launching an attack knowing it will cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment which would be clearly excessive in relation to the concrete and direct overall military advantage anticipated. ILC Draft Principles on Protection of the Environment in relation to Armed Conflicts, 2022 (27 principles): Principle 4: "States should designate, by agreement or otherwise, areas of environmental importance as protected zones in the event of an armed conflict, including where those areas are of cultural importance." Principle 13(1): "The environment shall be respected and protected in accordance with applicable international law and, in particular, the law of armed conflict." Principle 13(2)(a): "care shall be taken to protect the environment against widespread, long-term and severe damage;" Principle 13(3): "No part of the environment may be attacked, unless it has become a military objective." Principle 26(1): "Parties to an armed conflict shall seek, as soon as possible, to remove or render harmless toxic or other hazardous remnants of war under their jurisdiction or control that are causing or risk causing damage to the environment." Principle 27: "States and relevant international organizations should cooperate to ensure that remnants of war at sea do not constitute a danger to the environment." UN Security Council Resolution 687 (1991) (adopted 3 April 1991, after the Gulf War) – decided that Iraq "is liable under international law for any direct loss, damage, including environmental damage" resulting from its unlawful invasion and occupation of Kuwait. Constitution of India: Art. 51(c): the State shall endeavour to "foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another". Art. 253: Parliament "has power to make any law ... for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference". Art. 48A: "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Art. 51A(g): the duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life".
en.meaning: Armed conflict – fighting between States (international armed conflict) or between a State and organised armed groups, or between such groups (non-international armed conflict). Natural environment – land, water, air, forests, wildlife and ecosystems , including their resources. Widespread, long-term and severe damage – the threshold in AP I Arts. 35(3) and 55 and the Rome Statute; the three conditions are joined by "and", so all must be met. Environmental modification technique – a technique that changes the Earth's natural processes by deliberate manipulation (ENMOD Art. II), for example causing floods or changing weather as a weapon. Protected zone – an area of environmental (and possibly cultural) importance designated, by agreement or otherwise, as protected in armed conflict (ILC Principle 4). Remnants of war – toxic or hazardous material left after conflict, such as unexploded ordnance or chemical residues (ILC Principles 26, 27).
keyPoints: Rio Principle 24: warfare destroys sustainable development. AP I Art. 35(3), 55: widespread, long-term and severe damage prohibited (all three needed); no reprisals. ENMOD: no hostile use of an environmental modification technique with widespread, long-lasting or severe effects (any one). Rome Statute Art. 8(2)(b)(iv): clearly excessive environmental damage is a war crime. ILC 2022: protected zone (Principle 4); protection in conflict (Principle 13); remnants of war (Principles 26, 27). ICJ 1996: environment weighed in necessity and proportionality; India: Arts. 51(c), 253.

te.inOneMinute: యుద్ధం పర్యావరణాన్ని ప్రత్యక్షంగా (భూమి, అడవులు, నదులు, పారిశ్రామిక ప్లాంట్లు, చమురు సదుపాయాలపై బాంబులు) మరియు పరోక్షంగా (విషపూరిత అవశేషాలు, నిర్వాసితులైన ప్రజలు, పర్యావరణ పాలన కుప్పకూలడం) దెబ్బతీస్తుంది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) రియో డిక్లరేషన్, 1992, సూత్రం 24: "Warfare is inherently destructive of sustainable development." (అర్థం: యుద్ధం స్వభావరీత్యా సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిని నాశనం చేస్తుంది.) అంతర్జాతీయ చట్టంలో ముఖ్య నియమాలు: అదనపు ప్రోటోకాల్ I, 1977 : ఆర్టికల్ 35(3) "to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment" (అర్థం: సహజ పర్యావరణానికి విస్తృతమైన, దీర్ఘకాలిక, తీవ్రమైన నష్టం కలిగించడానికి) ఉద్దేశించిన లేదా ఆశించిన యుద్ధ పద్ధతులు, సాధనాలను నిషేధిస్తుంది; ఆర్టికల్ 55 జాగ్రత్త బాధ్యతను పునరుద్ఘాటించి, పర్యావరణంపై ప్రతీకార దాడులను నిషేధిస్తుంది. ENMOD కన్వెన్షన్ (18 మే 1977న సంతకం): "having widespread, long-lasting or severe effects" (అర్థం: విస్తృతమైన, దీర్ఘకాలం ఉండే లేదా తీవ్రమైన ప్రభావాలు కలిగిన) పర్యావరణ మార్పు పద్ధతుల శత్రుపూరిత వినియోగం వద్దు. రోమ్ శాసనం , ఆర్టికల్ 8(2)(b)(iv): సైనిక ప్రయోజనంతో పోలిస్తే స్పష్టంగా అధికమైన అలాంటి పర్యావరణ నష్టం కలిగించే దాడి యుద్ధ నేరం. ILC ముసాయిదా సూత్రాలు (2022) : సాయుధ సంఘర్షణకు ముందు, సమయంలో, తర్వాత పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించే 27 సూత్రాలు. ICJ ( Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion , 1996): పర్యావరణం "is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings" (అర్థం: ఒక భావన మాత్రమే కాదు; అది మానవుల నివాస స్థలం, జీవన నాణ్యత, వారి ఆరోగ్యానికి ప్రతిరూపం); అవసరం, అనుపాతంలో దాన్ని తూకం వేయాలి. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) భారతదేశం: ఆర్టికల్ 51(c) (అంతర్జాతీయ చట్టం పట్ల గౌరవం), ఆర్టికల్ 253 (ఒప్పందాల అమలుకు చట్టాలు), ఆర్టికల్స్ 48A, 51A(g).
te.meaning: సాయుధ సంఘర్షణ (Armed conflict) – దేశాల మధ్య (అంతర్జాతీయ సాయుధ సంఘర్షణ), లేదా ఒక దేశం, వ్యవస్థీకృత సాయుధ సమూహాల మధ్య, లేదా అలాంటి సమూహాల మధ్య (అంతర్జాతీయేతర సాయుధ సంఘర్షణ) జరిగే పోరాటం. సహజ పర్యావరణం (Natural environment ) – భూమి, నీరు, గాలి, అడవులు, వన్యప్రాణులు, పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థలు , వాటి వనరులతో సహా. విస్తృతమైన, దీర్ఘకాలిక, తీవ్రమైన నష్టం (Widespread, long-term and severe damage) – AP I ఆర్టికల్స్ 35(3), 55, రోమ్ శాసనంలోని పరిమితి; మూడు షరతులు "and" (అర్థం: మరియు)తో కలపబడ్డాయి, కాబట్టి మూడూ నెరవేరాలి. పర్యావరణ మార్పు పద్ధతి (Environmental modification technique) – ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా మార్చడం ద్వారా భూమి సహజ ప్రక్రియలను మార్చే పద్ధతి (ENMOD ఆర్టికల్ II); ఉదాహరణకు ఆయుధంగా వరదలు సృష్టించడం లేదా వాతావరణాన్ని మార్చడం. రక్షిత జోన్ (Protected zone) – సాయుధ సంఘర్షణలో రక్షణ కోసం, ఒప్పందం ద్వారా లేదా మరో విధంగా, ప్రకటించిన పర్యావరణ (సాంస్కృతిక కూడా కావచ్చు) ప్రాముఖ్యత ఉన్న ప్రాంతం (ILC సూత్రం 4). యుద్ధ అవశేషాలు (Remnants of war) – సంఘర్షణ తర్వాత మిగిలే విషపూరిత లేదా ప్రమాదకర పదార్థాలు; ఉదాహరణకు పేలని మందుగుండు లేదా రసాయన అవశేషాలు (ILC సూత్రాలు 26, 27).
keyPoints: రియో సూత్రం 24: యుద్ధం సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిని నాశనం చేస్తుంది. AP I ఆర్టికల్స్ 35(3), 55: విస్తృతమైన, దీర్ఘకాలిక, తీవ్రమైన నష్టం నిషేధం (మూడూ అవసరం); ప్రతీకార దాడులు వద్దు. ENMOD: విస్తృతమైన, దీర్ఘకాలం ఉండే లేదా తీవ్రమైన ప్రభావాలు కలిగిన పర్యావరణ మార్పు పద్ధతి శత్రుపూరిత వినియోగం వద్దు (ఏదైనా ఒక్కటి). రోమ్ శాసనం ఆర్టికల్ 8(2)(b)(iv): స్పష్టంగా అధికమైన పర్యావరణ నష్టం యుద్ధ నేరం. ILC 2022: రక్షిత జోన్ (సూత్రం 4); సంఘర్షణలో రక్షణ (సూత్రం 13); యుద్ధ అవశేషాలు (సూత్రాలు 26, 27). ICJ 1996: అవసరం, అనుపాతంలో పర్యావరణం తూకం; భారతదేశం: ఆర్టికల్స్ 51(c), 253.

selfTest.q: యుద్ధం గురించి రియో సూత్రం 24 ఏమి చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: AP I ఆర్టికల్ 35(3)లోని పరిమితి చెప్పండి. ENMOD పరిమితి AP I నుంచి ఎలా భిన్నం? ENMOD అవగాహన ప్రకారం "widespread" అంటే ఏమిటి? పర్యావరణ నష్టాన్ని యుద్ధ నేరంగా చేసే రోమ్ శాసన నిబంధన ఏది? పర్యావరణం, అనుపాతం గురించి ICJ ఏమి చెప్పింది? సముద్రంలోని యుద్ధ అవశేషాల గురించి ఏ ILC ముసాయిదా సూత్రం చెబుతుంది?

hi.inOneMinute: War damages the environment directly (bombing of land, forests, rivers, industrial plants, oil installations) and indirectly (toxic remnants, displaced people, collapse of environmental governance). (See Diagram 1 .) The Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 24: "Warfare is inherently destructive of sustainable development." Main rules of international law: Additional Protocol I, 1977 : Art. 35(3) prohibits methods or means of warfare intended or expected "to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment"; Art. 55 repeats the duty of care and bans reprisals against the environment. ENMOD Convention (signed 18 May 1977): no hostile use of environmental modification techniques "having widespread, long-lasting or severe effects". Rome Statute , Art. 8(2)(b)(iv): an attack causing such environmental damage that is clearly excessive to the military advantage is a war crime. ILC Draft Principles (2022) : 27 principles protecting the environment before, during and after armed conflict. The ICJ ( Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion , 1996): the environment "is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings"; it must be weighed in necessity and proportionality . (See Diagram 2 .) India: Art. 51(c) (respect for international law), Art. 253 (laws to implement treaties), Arts. 48A and 51A(g).
legalProvision: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, 1992: Principle 24: "Warfare is inherently destructive of sustainable development. States shall therefore respect international law providing protection for the environment in times of armed conflict and cooperate in its further development, as necessary." Principle 25: "Peace, development and environmental protection are interdependent and indivisible." Principle 26: "States shall resolve all their environmental disputes peacefully and by appropriate means in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations." Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions (8 June 1977): Art. 35(3): "it is prohibited to employ methods or means of warfare which are intended, or may be expected, to cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment". Art. 55(1): "Care shall be taken in warfare to protect the natural environment against widespread, long-term and severe damage." The paragraph includes a prohibition of methods or means expected to cause such damage and thereby prejudice the health or survival of the population. Art. 55(2): "Attacks against the natural environment by way of reprisals are prohibited." ENMOD Convention (Convention on the Prohibition of Military or Any Other Hostile Use of Environmental Modification Techniques; signed at Geneva 18 May 1977; in force 5 October 1978): Art. I(1): each State Party "undertakes not to engage in military or any other hostile use of environmental modification techniques having widespread, long-lasting or severe effects as the means of destruction, damage or injury to any other State Party." Art. II: "environmental modification techniques" means any technique for changing, "through the deliberate manipulation of natural processes", the dynamics, composition or structure of the Earth or outer space. Understanding relating to Art. I: "widespread" means "encompassing an area on the scale of several hundred square kilometres"; "long-lasting" means "lasting for a period of months, or approximately a season"; "severe" means "involving serious or significant disruption or harm to human life, natural and economic resources or other assets." This meaning is "intended exclusively for this Convention". Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, 1998, Art. 8(2)(b)(iv) – the war crime of intentionally launching an attack knowing it will cause widespread, long-term and severe damage to the natural environment which would be clearly excessive in relation to the concrete and direct overall military advantage anticipated. ILC Draft Principles on Protection of the Environment in relation to Armed Conflicts, 2022 (27 principles): Principle 4: "States should designate, by agreement or otherwise, areas of environmental importance as protected zones in the event of an armed conflict, including where those areas are of cultural importance." Principle 13(1): "The environment shall be respected and protected in accordance with applicable international law and, in particular, the law of armed conflict." Principle 13(2)(a): "care shall be taken to protect the environment against widespread, long-term and severe damage;" Principle 13(3): "No part of the environment may be attacked, unless it has become a military objective." Principle 26(1): "Parties to an armed conflict shall seek, as soon as possible, to remove or render harmless toxic or other hazardous remnants of war under their jurisdiction or control that are causing or risk causing damage to the environment." Principle 27: "States and relevant international organizations should cooperate to ensure that remnants of war at sea do not constitute a danger to the environment." UN Security Council Resolution 687 (1991) (adopted 3 April 1991, after the Gulf War) – decided that Iraq "is liable under international law for any direct loss, damage, including environmental damage" resulting from its unlawful invasion and occupation of Kuwait. Constitution of India: Art. 51(c): the State shall endeavour to "foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised peoples with one another". Art. 253: Parliament "has power to make any law ... for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference". Art. 48A: "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Art. 51A(g): the duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life".
hi.meaning: Armed conflict – fighting between States (international armed conflict) or between a State and organised armed groups, or between such groups (non-international armed conflict). Natural environment – land, water, air, forests, wildlife and ecosystems , including their resources. Widespread, long-term and severe damage – the threshold in AP I Arts. 35(3) and 55 and the Rome Statute; the three conditions are joined by "and", so all must be met. Environmental modification technique – a technique that changes the Earth's natural processes by deliberate manipulation (ENMOD Art. II), for example causing floods or changing weather as a weapon. Protected zone – an area of environmental (and possibly cultural) importance designated, by agreement or otherwise, as protected in armed conflict (ILC Principle 4). Remnants of war – toxic or hazardous material left after conflict, such as unexploded ordnance or chemical residues (ILC Principles 26, 27).
keyPoints: Rio Principle 24: warfare destroys sustainable development. AP I Art. 35(3), 55: widespread, long-term and severe damage prohibited (all three needed); no reprisals. ENMOD: no hostile use of an environmental modification technique with widespread, long-lasting or severe effects (any one). Rome Statute Art. 8(2)(b)(iv): clearly excessive environmental damage is a war crime. ILC 2022: protected zone (Principle 4); protection in conflict (Principle 13); remnants of war (Principles 26, 27). ICJ 1996: environment weighed in necessity and proportionality; India: Arts. 51(c), 253.

en.meaning:
The rule in Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) applies when a person:

Explanation. Rylands v. Fletcher requires a non-natural use of land plus accumulation of something likely to cause mischief if it escapes.

Which of the following is NOT a recognised exception to strict liability under Rylands v. Fletcher?

Explanation. The five recognised exceptions are act of God, act of a stranger, plaintiff's default, statutory authority, and consent — enterprise profitability is not one of them.

The rule of absolute liability was laid down by the Supreme Court of India in:

Explanation. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1986), the Oleum Gas Leak Case, is where the Indian Supreme Court evolved the rule of absolute liability.

How many of the Rylands v. Fletcher exceptions are available as a defence to absolute liability?

Under Section 37 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, a perpetual injunction can only be granted:

Explanation. A perpetual injunction under Section 37 can only be granted by a decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit, unlike a temporary injunction.

Which section of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 allows a perpetual injunction to prevent the invasion of a property right?

Explanation. Section 38 allows a perpetual injunction to prevent the breach of an obligation, including the invasion of the plaintiff's property right.

A mandatory injunction under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 is used to:

Explanation. Section 39 allows the court to compel the performance of requisite acts (e.g., installing treatment equipment), not merely restrain future conduct.

en.meaning:
Public nuisance is defined under which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

Explanation. Section 270 BNS (earlier section 268 IPC) defines public nuisance as an act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or to people who live nearby.

Which BNS section punishes voluntarily fouling the water of a public spring or reservoir?

Explanation. Section 279 BNS (earlier section 277 IPC) punishes a person who deliberately fouls the water of a public spring or reservoir. The punishment is imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to Rs 5,000, or both.

Section 152 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (earlier section 133 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973) empowers:

Explanation. Section 152 BNSS continues section 133 CrPC. An Executive Magistrate acts on a police report or other information and makes a conditional order to remove or stop the nuisance.

environmental-law-u3-t1.subtitle: The Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980: central control over forest land

en.inOneMinute: Two main statutes: the Indian Forest Act, 1927 (classifies and polices forests) and the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 (formerly the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980), which stops forest land being diverted without the Central Government's prior approval. (See Diagram 1 .) Indian Forest Act: three classes of forest: reserved (s. 3), village (s. 28) and protected (s. 29); acts such as clearing, setting fire, felling and quarrying in a reserved forest are offences (s. 26). Van Adhiniyam, s. 2(1): no State Government or other authority shall, "except with the prior approval of the Central Government", de-reserve a reserved forest, use forest land for a "non-forest purpose", lease it to a private person or body, or clear naturally grown trees for reafforestation . (See Diagram 2 .) 2023 amendment (in force 1 December 2023): renamed the Act, added a preamble , s. 1A (which land is covered) and exemptions. Constitution: "Forests" is Entry 17A of the Concurrent List; Arts. 48A and 51A(g). Courts: "forest" "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning" and the Act applies to all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification" ( T.N. Godavarman , 1996); States must still follow this meaning ( Ashok Kumar Sharma , 2024). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 17A – "Forests" (inserted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976). Indian Forest Act, 1927: s. 3 – "The State Government may constitute any forest-land or waste-land which is the property of Government, or over which the Government has proprietary rights", "a reserved forest". s. 26(1) – prohibited acts in a reserved forest, including fresh clearing, setting fire, trespass or pasturing cattle, felling, girdling, lopping or burning trees, quarrying, removing forest-produce, clearing land for cultivation, and hunting, shooting, fishing or poisoning water contrary to rules; punishment: "imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both", plus compensation. s. 28 – the State Government "may assign to any village-community the rights of Government to or over any land" constituted a reserved forest: a village-forest . s. 29 – the State Government may "declare the provisions of this Chapter applicable to any forest-land or waste-land" that is not a reserved forest but is Government property: a "protected forest" . Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980: s. 1A(1) – applies to (a) land declared or notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 or any other law, and (b) land recorded in Government record as forest on or after 25 October 1980. s. 1A(2) – exempts, among others, small strips along railways and public roads (up to 0.10 hectare), plantations on other land, and certain strategic and security projects near borders and in notified areas. s. 2(1) – prior approval of the Central Government is needed for (i) de-reservation, (ii) use for a non-forest purpose, (iii) assignment by lease or otherwise to a private person or body, (iv) clearing naturally grown trees for reafforestation. Explanation to s. 2 – "non-forest purpose" means breaking up or clearing forest land for cultivating tea, coffee, spices, rubber, palms, oil-bearing plants, horticultural crops or medicinal plants, or for any purpose other than reafforestation; work ancillary to forest and wild life conservation (silviculture, fire lines, check-posts, fencing, waterholes, etc.) is excluded. s. 2A – appeal against orders under s. 2 to the National Green Tribunal. s. 3 – Advisory Committee to advise the Central Government. s. 3A – contravention of s. 2 "shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a period which may extend to fifteen days". s. 3B – offences by Government departments and authorities: the head of the department or the person in charge is deemed guilty, unless he shows lack of knowledge or due diligence.
en.meaning: Forest – no single statutory definition; the Supreme Court held that the word "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning" ( Godavarman , 1996). Reserved forest – Government forest-land or waste-land constituted as such under s. 3 of the Indian Forest Act; the strictest protection . Village forest – a reserved forest whose Government rights are assigned to a village community (s. 28). Protected forest – Government forest-land or waste-land, not reserved, to which Chapter IV is applied by notification (s. 29). Non-forest purpose – breaking up or clearing forest land for plantation crops or for any purpose other than reafforestation (Van Adhiniyam, Explanation to s. 2). Forest-produce – includes timber, charcoal, bark, lac, mahua flowers and seeds; and, when found in or brought from a forest, trees, leaves, flowers, fruits, grass, wild animals and their skins, tusks and horns, honey and wax, and minerals (IFA s. 2(4)).
keyPoints: IFA, 1927: reserved forest (s. 3), village forest (s. 28), protected forest (s. 29); offences s. 26. Van Adhiniyam s. 2(1): prior Central approval for four kinds of order. Non-forest purpose: clearing for plantations or any purpose other than reafforestation. 2023 amendment in force 1 December 2023; s. 1A. Godavarman (1996): dictionary meaning; any ownership. Ashok Kumar Sharma (2024): Godavarman meaning continues.

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition sought protection of forests across India from illegal felling and non-forest
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The word "forest" "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning"; the Act covers all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification thereof"; "prior approval of the Central Government is required for any non-forest activity within the area of any 'forest'"; felling was suspended except under approved Working Plans. Why it matters: It is the base case of Indian forest law and the start of continuing court supervision of forests.
Ashok Kumar Sharma v. Union of India, W.P. (C) No. 1164 of 2023 (Supreme Court; Dr D.Y. Chandrachud CJI, J.B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra JJ; interim order of 19 February 2024)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "the principles which are elucidated in the judgment of this Court in T N Godavarman (supra) must continue to be observed"; States and Union Territories must comply with the meaning of "forest" in Godavarman ; Expert Committee records of forests to be sent by 31 March 2024 and published by 15 April 2024; zoos and safaris in forest areas need the Court's prior permission. Why it matters: It keeps the wide meaning of "forest" alive after the 2023 amendment.

te.inOneMinute: రెండు ప్రధాన చట్టాలు: భారత అటవీ చట్టం, 1927 (అడవులను వర్గీకరించి పర్యవేక్షిస్తుంది), వన్ (సంరక్షణ్ ఏవం సంవర్ధన్) అధినియమ్, 1980 (గతంలో అటవీ (పరిరక్షణ) చట్టం, 1980), కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వ ముందస్తు ఆమోదం లేకుండా అటవీ భూమి మళ్లింపును ఇది ఆపుతుంది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) భారత అటవీ చట్టం: మూడు రకాల అడవులు: రిజర్వు (సె. 3), గ్రామ (సె. 28), రక్షిత (సె. 29); రిజర్వు అడవిలో భూమిని శుభ్రం చేయడం, నిప్పు పెట్టడం, చెట్లు నరకడం, క్వారీయింగ్ వంటివి నేరాలు (సె. 26). వన్ అధినియమ్, సె. 2(1): ఏ రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం గానీ, ఇతర అధికారి గానీ "except with the prior approval of the Central Government" (అర్థం: కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వ ముందస్తు ఆమోదంతో తప్ప) రిజర్వు అడవిని రిజర్వు నుండి తొలగించకూడదు, అటవీ భూమిని "non-forest purpose" (అర్థం: అటవీయేతర ప్రయోజనం) కోసం వాడకూడదు, ప్రైవేటు వ్యక్తికి లేదా సంస్థకు లీజుకు ఇవ్వకూడదు, తిరిగి అడవి పెంచడానికి సహజంగా పెరిగిన చెట్లను తొలగించకూడదు. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) 2023 సవరణ (1 డిసెంబర్ 2023 నుండి అమలు): చట్టం పేరు మార్చింది, ప్రవేశిక, సె. 1A (ఏ భూమికి వర్తిస్తుంది), మినహాయింపులు చేర్చింది. రాజ్యాంగం: "Forests" (అర్థం: అడవులు) ఉమ్మడి జాబితాలో ఎంట్రీ 17A; ఆర్టి. 48A, 51A(g). న్యాయస్థానాలు: "forest" (అర్థం: అడవి) "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning" (అర్థం: దాని నిఘంటు అర్థం ప్రకారం అర్థం చేసుకోవాలి), చట్టం అన్ని అడవులకు "irrespective of the ownership or classification" (అర్థం: యాజమాన్యం లేదా వర్గీకరణతో సంబంధం లేకుండా) వర్తిస్తుంది ( T.N. Godavarman , 1996); రాష్ట్రాలు ఇప్పటికీ ఈ అర్థాన్నే పాటించాలి ( Ashok Kumar Sharma , 2024). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: అడవి (Forest) – ఒకే చట్టపరమైన నిర్వచనం లేదు; ఆ పదం "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning" (అర్థం: దాని నిఘంటు అర్థం ప్రకారం అర్థం చేసుకోవాలి) అని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది ( Godavarman , 1996). రిజర్వు అడవి – భారత అటవీ చట్టం సె. 3 కింద ఏర్పాటు చేసిన ప్రభుత్వ అటవీ భూమి లేదా బంజరు భూమి; అత్యంత కఠిన రక్షణ . గ్రామ అడవి – ప్రభుత్వ హక్కులు గ్రామ సమాజానికి అప్పగించబడిన రిజర్వు అడవి (సె. 28). రక్షిత అడవి – రిజర్వు కాని ప్రభుత్వ అటవీ భూమి లేదా బంజరు భూమి, నోటిఫికేషన్ ద్వారా అధ్యాయం IV వర్తింపజేయబడినది (సె. 29). అటవీయేతర ప్రయోజనం – తోట పంటల కోసం, లేదా తిరిగి అడవి పెంచడం కాకుండా మరే ప్రయోజనం కోసమైనా అటవీ భూమిని పగలగొట్టడం లేదా శుభ్రం చేయడం (వన్ అధినియమ్, సె. 2 వివరణ). అటవీ ఉత్పత్తులు (Forest-produce) – కలప, బొగ్గు, బెరడు, లక్క, ఇప్ప పువ్వులు, గింజలు; అడవిలో దొరికినప్పుడు లేదా అడవి నుండి తెచ్చినప్పుడు, చెట్లు, ఆకులు, పువ్వులు, పండ్లు, గడ్డి, వన్యప్రాణులు, వాటి చర్మాలు, దంతాలు, కొమ్ములు, తేనె, మైనం, ఖనిజాలు (IFA సె. 2(4)).
keyPoints: IFA, 1927: రిజర్వు అడవి (సె. 3), గ్రామ అడవి (సె. 28), రక్షిత అడవి (సె. 29); నేరాలు సె. 26. వన్ అధినియమ్ సె. 2(1): నాలుగు రకాల ఉత్తర్వులకు ముందస్తు కేంద్ర ఆమోదం. అటవీయేతర ప్రయోజనం: తోటల కోసం లేదా తిరిగి అడవి పెంచడం కాకుండా మరే ప్రయోజనం కోసమైనా భూమిని శుభ్రం చేయడం. 2023 సవరణ 1 డిసెంబర్ 2023 నుండి అమలు; సె. 1A. Godavarman (1996): నిఘంటు అర్థం; ఏ యాజమాన్యమైనా. Ashok Kumar Sharma (2024): Godavarman అర్థం కొనసాగుతుంది.

selfTest.q: భారత అటవీ చట్టం కింద మూడు రకాల అడవుల పేర్లు చెప్పండి. 1980 చట్టం సె. 2(1) కింద ఏ నాలుగు ఉత్తర్వులకు ముందస్తు కేంద్ర ఆమోదం అవసరం?
selfTest.a: అటవీయేతర ప్రయోజనం అంటే ఏమిటి? సె. 3A కింద శిక్ష ఏమిటి? "అడవి" అర్థం గురించి Godavarman ఏమి చెప్పింది? 19 ఫిబ్రవరి 2024న సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఏమి ఆదేశించింది?

hi.inOneMinute: Two main statutes: the Indian Forest Act, 1927 (classifies and polices forests) and the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 (formerly the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980), which stops forest land being diverted without the Central Government's prior approval. (See Diagram 1 .) Indian Forest Act: three classes of forest: reserved (s. 3), village (s. 28) and protected (s. 29); acts such as clearing, setting fire, felling and quarrying in a reserved forest are offences (s. 26). Van Adhiniyam, s. 2(1): no State Government or other authority shall, "except with the prior approval of the Central Government", de-reserve a reserved forest, use forest land for a "non-forest purpose", lease it to a private person or body, or clear naturally grown trees for reafforestation . (See Diagram 2 .) 2023 amendment (in force 1 December 2023): renamed the Act, added a preamble , s. 1A (which land is covered) and exemptions. Constitution: "Forests" is Entry 17A of the Concurrent List; Arts. 48A and 51A(g). Courts: "forest" "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning" and the Act applies to all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification" ( T.N. Godavarman , 1996); States must still follow this meaning ( Ashok Kumar Sharma , 2024). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 17A – "Forests" (inserted by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976). Indian Forest Act, 1927: s. 3 – "The State Government may constitute any forest-land or waste-land which is the property of Government, or over which the Government has proprietary rights", "a reserved forest". s. 26(1) – prohibited acts in a reserved forest, including fresh clearing, setting fire, trespass or pasturing cattle, felling, girdling, lopping or burning trees, quarrying, removing forest-produce, clearing land for cultivation, and hunting, shooting, fishing or poisoning water contrary to rules; punishment: "imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five hundred rupees, or with both", plus compensation. s. 28 – the State Government "may assign to any village-community the rights of Government to or over any land" constituted a reserved forest: a village-forest . s. 29 – the State Government may "declare the provisions of this Chapter applicable to any forest-land or waste-land" that is not a reserved forest but is Government property: a "protected forest" . Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980: s. 1A(1) – applies to (a) land declared or notified as forest under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 or any other law, and (b) land recorded in Government record as forest on or after 25 October 1980. s. 1A(2) – exempts, among others, small strips along railways and public roads (up to 0.10 hectare), plantations on other land, and certain strategic and security projects near borders and in notified areas. s. 2(1) – prior approval of the Central Government is needed for (i) de-reservation, (ii) use for a non-forest purpose, (iii) assignment by lease or otherwise to a private person or body, (iv) clearing naturally grown trees for reafforestation. Explanation to s. 2 – "non-forest purpose" means breaking up or clearing forest land for cultivating tea, coffee, spices, rubber, palms, oil-bearing plants, horticultural crops or medicinal plants, or for any purpose other than reafforestation; work ancillary to forest and wild life conservation (silviculture, fire lines, check-posts, fencing, waterholes, etc.) is excluded. s. 2A – appeal against orders under s. 2 to the National Green Tribunal. s. 3 – Advisory Committee to advise the Central Government. s. 3A – contravention of s. 2 "shall be punishable with simple imprisonment for a period which may extend to fifteen days". s. 3B – offences by Government departments and authorities: the head of the department or the person in charge is deemed guilty, unless he shows lack of knowledge or due diligence.
hi.meaning: Forest – no single statutory definition; the Supreme Court held that the word "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning" ( Godavarman , 1996). Reserved forest – Government forest-land or waste-land constituted as such under s. 3 of the Indian Forest Act; the strictest protection . Village forest – a reserved forest whose Government rights are assigned to a village community (s. 28). Protected forest – Government forest-land or waste-land, not reserved, to which Chapter IV is applied by notification (s. 29). Non-forest purpose – breaking up or clearing forest land for plantation crops or for any purpose other than reafforestation (Van Adhiniyam, Explanation to s. 2). Forest-produce – includes timber, charcoal, bark, lac, mahua flowers and seeds; and, when found in or brought from a forest, trees, leaves, flowers, fruits, grass, wild animals and their skins, tusks and horns, honey and wax, and minerals (IFA s. 2(4)).
keyPoints: IFA, 1927: reserved forest (s. 3), village forest (s. 28), protected forest (s. 29); offences s. 26. Van Adhiniyam s. 2(1): prior Central approval for four kinds of order. Non-forest purpose: clearing for plantations or any purpose other than reafforestation. 2023 amendment in force 1 December 2023; s. 1A. Godavarman (1996): dictionary meaning; any ownership. Ashok Kumar Sharma (2024): Godavarman meaning continues.

caseLaws.name: Facts: A writ petition sought protection of forests across India from illegal felling and non-forest
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The word "forest" "must be understood according to its dictionary meaning"; the Act covers all forests "irrespective of the ownership or classification thereof"; "prior approval of the Central Government is required for any non-forest activity within the area of any 'forest'"; felling was suspended except under approved Working Plans. Why it matters: It is the base case of Indian forest law and the start of continuing court supervision of forests.
Ashok Kumar Sharma v. Union of India, W.P. (C) No. 1164 of 2023 (Supreme Court; Dr D.Y. Chandrachud CJI, J.B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra JJ; interim order of 19 February 2024)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "the principles which are elucidated in the judgment of this Court in T N Godavarman (supra) must continue to be observed"; States and Union Territories must comply with the meaning of "forest" in Godavarman ; Expert Committee records of forests to be sent by 31 March 2024 and published by 15 April 2024; zoos and safaris in forest areas need the Court's prior permission. Why it matters: It keeps the wide meaning of "forest" alive after the 2023 amendment.

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "the present generation has no right to deplete all the existing forests and leave nothing for the next and future generations"; the matter was sent back and a survey of khair availability ordered. environmental-law-u3-t3.subtitle: Laws that protect the sea, the coast, wetlands and lakes

en.inOneMinute: No single Act: marine life, coasts and lakes are protected mainly by rules made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 : the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification , 2019 and the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 . (See Diagram 1 .) CRZ: the land from the High Tide Line (HTL) up to "500 meters on the landward side along the sea front", the intertidal zone, the tidal water bodies, and the water and sea bed up to the territorial limit of 12 nautical miles (para 1). Four classes: CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive areas such as mangroves and corals, and the intertidal zone), CRZ-II (developed areas), CRZ-III (rural and undeveloped areas, with a No Development Zone of 50 m or 200 m) and CRZ-IV (the sea and tidal waters). (See Diagram 2 .) Prohibited in the CRZ (para 4): new industries, untreated discharges, dumping of waste, land reclamation, sand mining, plastic disposal and more. Lakes and wetlands: the 2017 Rules ban conversion, industries, waste dumping, untreated discharges, permanent construction near the flood level and poaching in notified wetlands and Ramsar sites (rule 4). (See Diagram 3 .) Courts: shrimp farms on the coast are "per se hazardous" to marine ecology ( S. Jagannath , 1996); buildings put up against the CRZ rules were ordered removed ( Maradu , 2019); a lake is held by the State as trustee ( Intellectuals Forum , 2006).
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". EP Act, 1986, s. 3(1) and s. 3(2)(v) – the Central Government's power to protect the environment and to restrict areas in which industries and processes may be carried on; the CRZ Notification, 2019 was issued under "sub-section (1) and clause (v) of subsection (2) of section 3". CRZ Notification, 2019 (G.S.R. 37(E), 18 January 2019) – it replaced the CRZ Notification, 2011 (which had replaced the 1991 notification). Para 1 – CRZ covers: (i) land from HTL "to 500 meters on the landward side along the sea front"; (ii) along tidal water bodies, land from HTL "to 50 meters or width of the creek, whichever is less"; (iii) the "land area between the HTL and the Low Tide Line"; (iv) "The water and the bed area between the LTL to the territorial water limit (12 Nm) in case of sea", and the water and bed of tidal water bodies. HTL – "the line on the land up to which the highest water line reaches during the spring tide". Para 2 – classification into CRZ-I A, I B, II, III A, III B, IV A and IV B. Para 4 – activities prohibited "within the entire CRZ". Paras 6 to 9 – Coastal Zone Management Plans (CZMPs), clearance and enforcement by the Coastal Zone Management Authorities (CZMAs). Para 10.2 – a CRZ of 20 m from HTL for inland islands in backwaters and islands along the mainland coast. Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 (G.S.R. 1203(E), 26 September 2017) – made under the EP Act; they replaced the Wetlands Rules, 2010. Rule 2(1)(g) – defines "wetland" (see below). Rule 3 – the Rules apply to Ramsar sites and to wetlands notified by the Central, State or Union Territory Government. Rule 4 – wetlands to be managed on the principle of "wise use"; prohibited activities listed in rule 4(2). Rule 5 – a State Wetlands Authority in each State; Rule 6 – a National Wetlands Committee. Ramsar Convention, 1971 – the Convention on wetlands signed at Ramsar, Iran (rule 2(1)(f)); India is a party. Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 – marine animals listed in its Schedules get the same protection against hunting and trade as land animals.
en.meaning: Marine life – the plants and animals of the sea: fish, corals, sea grass, turtles, horseshoe crabs, dolphins and others. Coastal ecosystem – the living systems where land meets sea: mangroves, coral reefs, sand dunes, mudflats , salt marshes, beaches, estuaries, creeks, backwaters and lagoons. Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) – the coastal land and water area declared in para 1 of the CRZ Notification, in which development is controlled. High Tide Line (HTL) – "the line on the land up to which the highest water line reaches during the spring tide" (CRZ Notification, para 1, Explanation); demarcated by the National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM). No Development Zone (NDZ) – a strip on the landward side of the HTL in CRZ-III where construction is generally not allowed: 50 m in CRZ-III A, 200 m in CRZ-III B. Wetland (rule 2(1)(g)) – "an area of marsh, fen, peatland or water; whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt, including areas of marine water the depth of which at low tide does not exceed six meters"; it does not include river channels, paddy fields, drinking-water tanks and structures built for aquaculture , salt production, recreation and irrigation. Lake – a body of standing water on land; a lake with its marshy edges is a wetland in the sense of the 2017 Rules if it is notified or is a Ramsar site.
keyPoints: Coastal Regulation Zone: HTL to 500 m landward, intertidal zone, tidal waters, sea to 12 Nm. High Tide Line: highest water line during the spring tide. No Development Zone: 50 m (CRZ-III A), 200 m (CRZ-III B). Para 4: new industries, untreated discharge, sand mining, plastic disposal prohibited. Wetland: rule 2(1)(g); prohibitions in rule 4(2). Cases: S. Jagannath (shrimp farms), Maradu (removal), Intellectuals Forum (trust).

caseLaws.name: Facts: A public interest petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 sought enforcement of the CRZ Notification of 19 February 1991 and a stop to intensive shrimp (prawn) farming along the coasts. Principle: Shrimp culture is not an activity "directly related to water front" or "directly needing foreshore facilities"; "The setting up of shrimp culture farms within the prohibited areas under the CRZ notification cannot be permitted"; such farms are "per se hazardous" and "bound to degrade the marine ecology". Why it matters: It is the leading case enforcing the CRZ to protect marine and coastal ecosystems.
Kerala State Coastal Zone Management Authority v. State of Kerala (Maradu Municipality), C.A. Nos. 4784-4785 of 2019 (Supreme Court; Arun Mishra and Navin Sinha JJ; order of 8 May 2019)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Permission granted by the Panchayat was illegal and void"; construction in notified CRZ areas can be allowed "only in consultation with and concurrence" of the CZMA; the Court ordered "let all the structures be removed forthwith within a period of one month". Why it matters: It shows that CRZ rules are binding and that illegal buildings on the coast and backwaters can be removed.
Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v. State of A.P. AIR 2006 SC 1350; (2006) 3 SCC 549 (Supreme Court; Ruma Pal and Dr. AR. Lakshmanan JJ; judgment by Dr. AR. Lakshmanan J; 23 February 2006)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The tank is "a communal property and the State authorities are trustees"; "The state is the trustee of all natural resources which are by nature meant for public use and enjoyment"; the Court directed "No further constructions", a percolation tank, rainwater harvesting and a ban on borewells. Why it matters: It applies the public trust doctrine to lakes and tanks.

te.inOneMinute: ఒకే చట్టం లేదు: సముద్ర జీవులు, తీరాలు, సరస్సులు ప్రధానంగా పర్యావరణ (రక్షణ) చట్టం, 1986 కింద చేసిన నియమాల ద్వారా రక్షించబడతాయి: తీర నియంత్రణ మండలం (CRZ) నోటిఫికేషన్, 2019 , చిత్తడి నేలల (పరిరక్షణ, నిర్వహణ) నియమాలు, 2017 . ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) CRZ: హై టైడ్ లైన్ (HTL) నుండి "500 meters on the landward side along the sea front" (అర్థం: సముద్రం ముందు భాగం వెంట భూమి వైపు 500 మీటర్లు) వరకు భూమి, అంతర్‌జ్వార మండలం, జ్వార ప్రభావిత జలాశయాలు, 12 నాటికల్ మైళ్ల ప్రాదేశిక పరిమితి వరకు నీరు, సముద్ర గర్భం (para 1). నాలుగు వర్గాలు: CRZ-I (మడ అడవులు, పగడాలు వంటి పర్యావరణపరంగా సున్నితమైన ప్రాంతాలు, అంతర్‌జ్వార మండలం), CRZ-II (అభివృద్ధి చెందిన ప్రాంతాలు), CRZ-III (గ్రామీణ, అభివృద్ధి చెందని ప్రాంతాలు; 50 మీ. లేదా 200 మీ. నిర్మాణ నిషేధ మండలం), CRZ-IV (సముద్రం, జ్వార జలాలు). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) CRZ లో నిషిద్ధం (para 4): కొత్త పరిశ్రమలు, శుద్ధి చేయని విడుదలలు, వ్యర్థాల పారబోత, భూమి పునరుద్ధరణ, ఇసుక తవ్వకం, ప్లాస్టిక్ పారబోత మొదలైనవి. సరస్సులు, చిత్తడి నేలలు: నోటిఫై చేసిన చిత్తడి నేలల్లో, రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశాల్లో మార్పిడి, పరిశ్రమలు, వ్యర్థాల పారబోత, శుద్ధి చేయని విడుదలలు, వరద మట్టం దగ్గర శాశ్వత నిర్మాణం, అక్రమ వేటను 2017 నియమాలు నిషేధిస్తాయి (rule 4). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) న్యాయస్థానాలు: తీరంపై రొయ్యల చెరువులు సముద్ర పర్యావరణానికి "per se hazardous" (అర్థం: స్వతహాగా ప్రమాదకరం) ( S. Jagannath , 1996); CRZ నియమాలకు వ్యతిరేకంగా కట్టిన భవనాలను తొలగించమని ఆదేశించారు ( Maradu , 2019); సరస్సును రాష్ట్రం ధర్మకర్తగా కలిగి ఉంటుంది ( Intellectuals Forum , 2006).
te.meaning: సముద్ర జీవులు – సముద్రంలోని మొక్కలు, జంతువులు: చేపలు, పగడాలు, సముద్ర గడ్డి, తాబేళ్లు, గుర్రపుడెక్క పీతలు, డాల్ఫిన్లు మొదలైనవి. తీర పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థ – భూమి సముద్రాన్ని కలిసే చోటి జీవ వ్యవస్థలు: మడ అడవులు, పగడపు దిబ్బలు, ఇసుక దిబ్బలు, బురద నేలలు, ఉప్పు చిత్తడి నేలలు , బీచ్‌లు, నదీ ముఖద్వారాలు, కాలువలు, బ్యాక్‌వాటర్స్, లగూన్‌లు. తీర నియంత్రణ మండలం (CRZ) – CRZ నోటిఫికేషన్ para 1 లో ప్రకటించిన తీర భూమి, నీటి ప్రాంతం; ఇక్కడ అభివృద్ధి నియంత్రించబడుతుంది. హై టైడ్ లైన్ (HTL) – "the line on the land up to which the highest water line reaches during the spring tide" (అర్థం: పౌర్ణమి-అమావాస్య పోటు సమయంలో అత్యధిక నీటి మట్టం చేరే భూమిపై గీత) (CRZ నోటిఫికేషన్, para 1, వివరణ); జాతీయ సుస్థిర తీర నిర్వహణ కేంద్రం (NCSCM) దీన్ని గుర్తిస్తుంది. నిర్మాణ నిషేధ మండలం (NDZ) – CRZ-III లో HTL కి భూమి వైపు ఉన్న పట్టీ; ఇక్కడ సాధారణంగా నిర్మాణం అనుమతించబడదు: CRZ-III A లో 50 మీ., CRZ-III B లో 200 మీ. చిత్తడి నేల (rule 2(1)(g)) – "an area of marsh, fen, peatland or water; whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt, including areas of marine water the depth of which at low tide does not exceed six meters" (అర్థం: చిత్తడి, ఫెన్, పీట్ నేల లేదా నీటి ప్రాంతం; సహజమైనది లేదా కృత్రిమమైనది, శాశ్వతమైనది లేదా తాత్కాలికమైనది, నిలిచిన లేదా ప్రవహించే, మంచి, ఉప్పుకలిసిన లేదా ఉప్పు నీటితో; ఆటుపోటులో ఆటు సమయంలో లోతు ఆరు మీటర్లు మించని సముద్ర జల ప్రాంతాలతో సహా); నదీ ప్రవాహ మార్గాలు, వరి పొలాలు, తాగునీటి ట్యాంకులు, ఆక్వాకల్చర్, ఉప్పు ఉత్పత్తి, వినోదం, నీటిపారుదల కోసం కట్టిన నిర్మాణాలు ఇందులో చేరవు. సరస్సు – భూమిపై నిలిచిన నీటి వనరు; దాని చిత్తడి అంచులతో కూడిన సరస్సు నోటిఫై అయినా లేదా రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశమైనా 2017 నియమాల అర్థంలో చిత్తడి నేల అవుతుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: No single Act: marine life, coasts and lakes are protected mainly by rules made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 : the Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification , 2019 and the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 . (See Diagram 1 .) CRZ: the land from the High Tide Line (HTL) up to "500 meters on the landward side along the sea front", the intertidal zone, the tidal water bodies, and the water and sea bed up to the territorial limit of 12 nautical miles (para 1). Four classes: CRZ-I (ecologically sensitive areas such as mangroves and corals, and the intertidal zone), CRZ-II (developed areas), CRZ-III (rural and undeveloped areas, with a No Development Zone of 50 m or 200 m) and CRZ-IV (the sea and tidal waters). (See Diagram 2 .) Prohibited in the CRZ (para 4): new industries, untreated discharges, dumping of waste, land reclamation, sand mining, plastic disposal and more. Lakes and wetlands: the 2017 Rules ban conversion, industries, waste dumping, untreated discharges, permanent construction near the flood level and poaching in notified wetlands and Ramsar sites (rule 4). (See Diagram 3 .) Courts: shrimp farms on the coast are "per se hazardous" to marine ecology ( S. Jagannath , 1996); buildings put up against the CRZ rules were ordered removed ( Maradu , 2019); a lake is held by the State as trustee ( Intellectuals Forum , 2006).
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". EP Act, 1986, s. 3(1) and s. 3(2)(v) – the Central Government's power to protect the environment and to restrict areas in which industries and processes may be carried on; the CRZ Notification, 2019 was issued under "sub-section (1) and clause (v) of subsection (2) of section 3". CRZ Notification, 2019 (G.S.R. 37(E), 18 January 2019) – it replaced the CRZ Notification, 2011 (which had replaced the 1991 notification). Para 1 – CRZ covers: (i) land from HTL "to 500 meters on the landward side along the sea front"; (ii) along tidal water bodies, land from HTL "to 50 meters or width of the creek, whichever is less"; (iii) the "land area between the HTL and the Low Tide Line"; (iv) "The water and the bed area between the LTL to the territorial water limit (12 Nm) in case of sea", and the water and bed of tidal water bodies. HTL – "the line on the land up to which the highest water line reaches during the spring tide". Para 2 – classification into CRZ-I A, I B, II, III A, III B, IV A and IV B. Para 4 – activities prohibited "within the entire CRZ". Paras 6 to 9 – Coastal Zone Management Plans (CZMPs), clearance and enforcement by the Coastal Zone Management Authorities (CZMAs). Para 10.2 – a CRZ of 20 m from HTL for inland islands in backwaters and islands along the mainland coast. Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 (G.S.R. 1203(E), 26 September 2017) – made under the EP Act; they replaced the Wetlands Rules, 2010. Rule 2(1)(g) – defines "wetland" (see below). Rule 3 – the Rules apply to Ramsar sites and to wetlands notified by the Central, State or Union Territory Government. Rule 4 – wetlands to be managed on the principle of "wise use"; prohibited activities listed in rule 4(2). Rule 5 – a State Wetlands Authority in each State; Rule 6 – a National Wetlands Committee. Ramsar Convention, 1971 – the Convention on wetlands signed at Ramsar, Iran (rule 2(1)(f)); India is a party. Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 – marine animals listed in its Schedules get the same protection against hunting and trade as land animals.
hi.meaning: Marine life – the plants and animals of the sea: fish, corals, sea grass, turtles, horseshoe crabs, dolphins and others. Coastal ecosystem – the living systems where land meets sea: mangroves, coral reefs, sand dunes, mudflats , salt marshes, beaches, estuaries, creeks, backwaters and lagoons. Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) – the coastal land and water area declared in para 1 of the CRZ Notification, in which development is controlled. High Tide Line (HTL) – "the line on the land up to which the highest water line reaches during the spring tide" (CRZ Notification, para 1, Explanation); demarcated by the National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management (NCSCM). No Development Zone (NDZ) – a strip on the landward side of the HTL in CRZ-III where construction is generally not allowed: 50 m in CRZ-III A, 200 m in CRZ-III B. Wetland (rule 2(1)(g)) – "an area of marsh, fen, peatland or water; whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt, including areas of marine water the depth of which at low tide does not exceed six meters"; it does not include river channels, paddy fields, drinking-water tanks and structures built for aquaculture , salt production, recreation and irrigation. Lake – a body of standing water on land; a lake with its marshy edges is a wetland in the sense of the 2017 Rules if it is notified or is a Ramsar site.
keyPoints: Coastal Regulation Zone: HTL to 500 m landward, intertidal zone, tidal waters, sea to 12 Nm. High Tide Line: highest water line during the spring tide. No Development Zone: 50 m (CRZ-III A), 200 m (CRZ-III B). Para 4: new industries, untreated discharge, sand mining, plastic disposal prohibited. Wetland: rule 2(1)(g); prohibitions in rule 4(2). Cases: S. Jagannath (shrimp farms), Maradu (removal), Intellectuals Forum (trust).

caseLaws.name: Facts: A public interest petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 sought enforcement of the CRZ Notification of 19 February 1991 and a stop to intensive shrimp (prawn) farming along the coasts. Principle: Shrimp culture is not an activity "directly related to water front" or "directly needing foreshore facilities"; "The setting up of shrimp culture farms within the prohibited areas under the CRZ notification cannot be permitted"; such farms are "per se hazardous" and "bound to degrade the marine ecology". Why it matters: It is the leading case enforcing the CRZ to protect marine and coastal ecosystems.
Kerala State Coastal Zone Management Authority v. State of Kerala (Maradu Municipality), C.A. Nos. 4784-4785 of 2019 (Supreme Court; Arun Mishra and Navin Sinha JJ; order of 8 May 2019)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Permission granted by the Panchayat was illegal and void"; construction in notified CRZ areas can be allowed "only in consultation with and concurrence" of the CZMA; the Court ordered "let all the structures be removed forthwith within a period of one month". Why it matters: It shows that CRZ rules are binding and that illegal buildings on the coast and backwaters can be removed.

environmental-law-u3-t4.subtitle: The Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960: duty of care, cruelty, experiments and performing animals

en.inOneMinute: Main statute: the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (PCA Act), made "to prevent the infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering on animals". (See Diagram 1 .) "Animal" means "any living creature other than a human being" (s. 2(a)). Duty (s. 3): every person in charge of an animal must "take all reasonable measures to ensure the well-being of such animal and to prevent the infliction upon such animal of unnecessary pain or suffering". Cruelty (s. 11(1)): fifteen kinds of cruelty, from beating and overloading to starving, abandoning and making animals fight; exceptions in s. 11(3) (dehorning and castration in the prescribed manner, destruction of stray dogs in lethal chambers, destruction under law, experiments, and killing for food without unnecessary suffering). (See Diagram 2 .) Bodies: the Animal Welfare Board of India (s. 4; functions s. 9) and a Committee for control and supervision of experiments on animals (s. 15). Other controls: experiments (Chapter IV), performing animals (Chapter V: registration, and animals the Central Government bans from being exhibited or trained, s. 22), and killing "in a manner required by the religion of any community" is not an offence (s. 28). Constitution: Art. 51A(g) ("compassion for living creatures"), Art. 48 and Entry 17 of the Concurrent List ("Prevention of cruelty to animals"). Courts: Jallikattu and bullock-cart races broke ss. 3 and 11 ( A. Nagaraja , 2014); the State amendments of 2017 that allowed them under rules were upheld ( Animal Welfare Board of India , 2023); the ban on training and exhibiting bears, monkeys, tigers, panthers and lions was upheld because "the welfare of the animals" is "of paramount consideration" ( N.R. Nair , 2001). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 51A(h) – duty "to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform". Article 48 – the State shall endeavour to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and to take steps for "preserving and improving the breeds, and prohibiting the slaughter, of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle". Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 17 – "Prevention of cruelty to animals." PCA Act, 1960, long title – "An Act to prevent the infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering on animals and for that purpose to amend the law relating to the prevention of cruelty to animals." s. 2(a) – "animal" means "any living creature other than a human being". s. 2(c) – "captive animal": an animal (not a domestic animal) "which is in captivity or confinement, whether permanent or temporary". s. 3 – duty of persons having charge of animals (quoted above). s. 4 – the Animal Welfare Board of India, established "For the promotion of animal welfare generally"; "a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal". s. 9 – functions of the Board. s. 11(1) – acts of cruelty, clauses (a) to (o). s. 11(1), punishment (as amended in 1982) – first offence: fine "not less than ten rupees but which may extend to fifty rupees"; second or later offence within three years: fine "not less than twenty-five rupees but which may extend to one hundred rupees", or imprisonment up to three months, or both. s. 11(3) – exceptions, clauses (a) to (e). s. 12 – "phooka" or "doom dev" (and, since 1982, any operation to improve lactation that harms the animal): fine up to Rs. 1,000, or imprisonment up to two years, or both; the animal is forfeited to Government. ss. 14 to 20 (Chapter IV) – experiments on animals are lawful for the purposes named (s. 14), under a Committee constituted by the Central Government (s. 15), whose rules must secure that "experiments on animals are avoided wherever it is possible to do so" (s. 17). ss. 21 to 27 (Chapter V) – performing animals; s. 22: "No person shall exhibit or train" (i) a performing animal "unless he is registered", or (ii) an animal that the Central Government, by notification, specifies "as an animal which shall not be exhibited or trained as a performing animal"; s. 27 exempts military and police training and zoos. s. 28 – "Nothing contained in this Act shall render it an offence to kill any animal in a manner required by the religion of any community." s. 31 – offences under s. 11(1)(l), (n), (o) and s. 12 are cognizable. s. 38 – Central Government's power to make rules. State amendments of 2017 – Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Karnataka amended the Act (with the President's assent under Art. 254(2)) to allow Jallikattu, bullock-cart races and Kambala under rules; Tamil Nadu added s. 2(dd) (meaning of "Jallikattu"), s. 3(2), s. 11(3)(f), a proviso to s. 22, s. 27(c) and s. 28A.
en.meaning: Animal – "any living creature other than a human being" (s. 2(a)); the widest definition, covering birds, fish and insects as well as domestic and wild animals. Cruelty – causing an animal unnecessary pain or suffering, by doing an act listed in s. 11(1) or by failing in the duty of care in s. 3. Unnecessary pain or suffering – pain that is not needed for a purpose the law allows; the Supreme Court has read the s. 11(3) exceptions as based on necessity, so entertainment is not such a purpose ( A. Nagaraja , as described in the 2023 judgment). Performing animal – an animal exhibited at an entertainment to which the public is admitted through sale of tickets, or trained for such exhibition (s. 21 read with s. 22). Animal welfare – the well-being of animals; the Animal Welfare Board exists "For the promotion of animal welfare generally" (s. 4(1)).
keyPoints: Animal: "any living creature other than a human being" (s. 2(a)). s. 3: duty of care. Cruelty: s. 11(1)(a)–(o); exceptions s. 11(3); s. 28 religion. Animal Welfare Board of India: s. 4; functions s. 9. Performing animal: Chapter V; s. 22(ii) bans; N.R. Nair . A. Nagaraja (2014); 2017 amendments upheld (2023).

caseLaws.facts: Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja (2014) 7 SCC 547; Civil Appeal No. 5387 of 2014 (Supreme Court; K.S. Radhakrishnan and Pinaki Chandra Ghose JJ; judgment by K.S. Radhakrishnan J; 7 May 2014)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Jallikattu in Tamil Nadu and bullock-cart races in Maharashtra were defended as custom and tr
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The events were contrary to ss. 3 and 11(1)(a) and (m); "All living creatures have inherent dignity and a right to live peacefully" (para 32); "every species has an inherent right to live and shall be protected by law, subject to the exception provided out of necessity" (para 51). Why it matters: It is the strongest statement of animals' rights under the PCA Act.

Animal Welfare Board of India v. Union of India, W.P. (C) No. 23 of 2016 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench; K.M. Joseph, Ajay Rastogi, Aniruddha Bose, Hrishikesh Roy and C.T. Ravikumar JJ; judgment by Aniruddha Bose J; 18 May 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 2017 amendments of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Karnataka, which allowed Jallikattu, bullo
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The amendments, read with their Rules, were upheld and must be strictly enforced; Art. 14 cannot "be invoked by any animal as a person"; "if a long lasting tradition goes against the law, the law Courts obviously would have to enforce the law". Why it matters: It is the present law on animal sports and shows that the legislature can regulate, rather than ban, such events.
N.R. Nair v. Union of India, Civil Appeal Nos. 3609-3620 of 2001; 2001 (3) SCR 353 (Supreme Court; B.N. Kirpal, U.C. Banerjee and Brijesh Kumar JJ; judgment by Kirpal J; 1 May 2001)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Circus owners challenged a notification of 14 October 1998 under s
caseLaws.facts: 22 that banned the training and exhibition of bears, monkeys, tigers, panthers and lions; the Kerala High Court had upheld it. Principle: The Government's satisfaction that training or exhibition causes unnecessary pain is "a pre-condition to the issuance of the Notification"; courts cannot go into the correctness of that decision; "it is the welfare of the animals which is of paramount consideration". Why it matters: It upholds the Central Government's power to ban cruel use of wild animals in circuses.

te.inOneMinute: ప్రధాన చట్టం: జంతువులపై క్రూరత్వ నివారణ చట్టం, 1960 (PCA చట్టం); "to prevent the infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering on animals" (అర్థం: జంతువులకు అనవసర నొప్పి లేదా బాధ కలిగించడాన్ని నివారించడానికి) చేయబడింది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) "జంతువు" అంటే "any living creature other than a human being" (అర్థం: మనిషి కాకుండా ఏ జీవి అయినా) (సె. 2(a)). విధి (సె. 3): జంతువు బాధ్యత ఉన్న ప్రతి వ్యక్తి "take all reasonable measures to ensure the well-being of such animal and to prevent the infliction upon such animal of unnecessary pain or suffering" (అర్థం: ఆ జంతువు శ్రేయస్సుకు, దానికి అనవసర నొప్పి లేదా బాధ కలగకుండా నివారించడానికి అన్ని సహేతుక చర్యలు తీసుకోవాలి). క్రూరత్వం (సె. 11(1)): కొట్టడం, అధిక బరువు నుండి ఆకలితో ఉంచడం, వదిలేయడం, జంతువులను పోట్లాడించడం వరకు పదిహేను రకాల క్రూరత్వం; సె. 11(3) లో మినహాయింపులు (నిర్దేశిత పద్ధతిలో కొమ్ములు తీయడం, వృషణాలు తీయడం, వీధి కుక్కలను ప్రాణాంతక గదుల్లో నాశనం చేయడం, చట్టం కింద నాశనం, ప్రయోగాలు, అనవసర బాధ లేకుండా ఆహారం కోసం చంపడం). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) సంస్థలు: భారత జంతు సంక్షేమ బోర్డు (సె. 4; విధులు సె. 9), జంతువులపై ప్రయోగాల నియంత్రణ, పర్యవేక్షణ కమిటీ (సె. 15). ఇతర నియంత్రణలు: ప్రయోగాలు (అధ్యాయం IV), ప్రదర్శన జంతువులు (అధ్యాయం V: నమోదు, ప్రదర్శించకూడదని లేదా శిక్షణ ఇవ్వకూడదని కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం నిషేధించే జంతువులు, సె. 22); "in a manner required by the religion of any community" (అర్థం: ఏదైనా సమాజ మతం కోరిన పద్ధతిలో) చంపడం నేరం కాదు (సె. 28). రాజ్యాంగం: ఆర్టి. 51A(g) ("compassion for living creatures" – అర్థం: జీవుల పట్ల కరుణ), ఆర్టి. 48, ఉమ్మడి జాబితా ఎంట్రీ 17 ("Prevention of cruelty to animals" – అర్థం: జంతువులపై క్రూరత్వ నివారణ). న్యాయస్థానాలు: జల్లికట్టు, ఎడ్ల బండి పందాలు సె. 3, 11 ను ఉల్లంఘించాయి ( A. Nagaraja , 2014); నియమాల కింద వాటిని అనుమతించిన 2017 రాష్ట్ర సవరణలు సమర్థించబడ్డాయి ( Animal Welfare Board of India , 2023); "the welfare of the animals" (అర్థం: జంతువుల సంక్షేమం) "of paramount consideration" (అర్థం: అత్యంత ప్రధాన పరిగణన) కాబట్టి ఎలుగుబంట్లు, కోతులు, పులులు, చిరుతలు, సింహాలకు శిక్షణ, ప్రదర్శనపై నిషేధం సమర్థించబడింది ( N.R. Nair , 2001). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: జంతువు – "any living creature other than a human being" (అర్థం: మనిషి కాకుండా ఏ జీవి అయినా) (సె. 2(a)); అత్యంత విస్తృత నిర్వచనం, పెంపుడు, వన్య జంతువులతో పాటు పక్షులు, చేపలు, కీటకాలను కూడా కవర్ చేస్తుంది. క్రూరత్వం – సె. 11(1) లో జాబితా చేసిన చర్య చేయడం ద్వారా లేదా సె. 3 లోని సంరక్షణ విధిలో విఫలం కావడం ద్వారా జంతువుకు అనవసర నొప్పి లేదా బాధ కలిగించడం. అనవసర నొప్పి లేదా బాధ – చట్టం అనుమతించే ప్రయోజనానికి అవసరం లేని నొప్పి; సె. 11(3) మినహాయింపులు అవసరం ఆధారంగా ఉన్నాయని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చదివింది, కాబట్టి వినోదం అలాంటి ప్రయోజనం కాదు (2023 తీర్పులో వర్ణించినట్లు A. Nagaraja ). ప్రదర్శన జంతువు – టికెట్ల అమ్మకం ద్వారా ప్రజలను అనుమతించే వినోదంలో ప్రదర్శించే, లేదా అలాంటి ప్రదర్శనకు శిక్షణ పొందిన జంతువు (సె. 21 తో కలిపి సె. 22). జంతు సంక్షేమం – జంతువుల శ్రేయస్సు; జంతు సంక్షేమ బోర్డు "For the promotion of animal welfare generally" (అర్థం: సాధారణంగా జంతు సంక్షేమాన్ని ప్రోత్సహించడానికి) ఉంది (సె. 4(1)).
keyPoints: జంతువు: "any living creature other than a human being" (అర్థం: మనిషి కాకుండా ఏ జీవి అయినా) (సె. 2(a)). సె. 3: సంరక్షణ విధి. క్రూరత్వం: సె. 11(1)(a)–(o); మినహాయింపులు సె. 11(3); సె. 28 మతం. భారత జంతు సంక్షేమ బోర్డు: సె. 4; విధులు సె. 9. ప్రదర్శన జంతువు: అధ్యాయం V; సె. 22(ii) నిషేధాలు; N.R. Nair . A. Nagaraja (2014); 2017 సవరణలు సమర్థించబడ్డాయి (2023).

hi.inOneMinute: Main statute: the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (PCA Act), made "to prevent the infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering on animals". (See Diagram 1 .) "Animal" means "any living creature other than a human being" (s. 2(a)). Duty (s. 3): every person in charge of an animal must "take all reasonable measures to ensure the well-being of such animal and to prevent the infliction upon such animal of unnecessary pain or suffering". Cruelty (s. 11(1)): fifteen kinds of cruelty, from beating and overloading to starving, abandoning and making animals fight; exceptions in s. 11(3) (dehorning and castration in the prescribed manner, destruction of stray dogs in lethal chambers, destruction under law, experiments, and killing for food without unnecessary suffering). (See Diagram 2 .) Bodies: the Animal Welfare Board of India (s. 4; functions s. 9) and a Committee for control and supervision of experiments on animals (s. 15). Other controls: experiments (Chapter IV), performing animals (Chapter V: registration, and animals the Central Government bans from being exhibited or trained, s. 22), and killing "in a manner required by the religion of any community" is not an offence (s. 28). Constitution: Art. 51A(g) ("compassion for living creatures"), Art. 48 and Entry 17 of the Concurrent List ("Prevention of cruelty to animals"). Courts: Jallikattu and bullock-cart races broke ss. 3 and 11 ( A. Nagaraja , 2014); the State amendments of 2017 that allowed them under rules were upheld ( Animal Welfare Board of India , 2023); the ban on training and exhibiting bears, monkeys, tigers, panthers and lions was upheld because "the welfare of the animals" is "of paramount consideration" ( N.R. Nair , 2001). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 51A(h) – duty "to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform". Article 48 – the State shall endeavour to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and to take steps for "preserving and improving the breeds, and prohibiting the slaughter, of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle". Seventh Schedule, List III, Entry 17 – "Prevention of cruelty to animals." PCA Act, 1960, long title – "An Act to prevent the infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering on animals and for that purpose to amend the law relating to the prevention of cruelty to animals." s. 2(a) – "animal" means "any living creature other than a human being". s. 2(c) – "captive animal": an animal (not a domestic animal) "which is in captivity or confinement, whether permanent or temporary". s. 3 – duty of persons having charge of animals (quoted above). s. 4 – the Animal Welfare Board of India, established "For the promotion of animal welfare generally"; "a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal". s. 9 – functions of the Board. s. 11(1) – acts of cruelty, clauses (a) to (o). s. 11(1), punishment (as amended in 1982) – first offence: fine "not less than ten rupees but which may extend to fifty rupees"; second or later offence within three years: fine "not less than twenty-five rupees but which may extend to one hundred rupees", or imprisonment up to three months, or both. s. 11(3) – exceptions, clauses (a) to (e). s. 12 – "phooka" or "doom dev" (and, since 1982, any operation to improve lactation that harms the animal): fine up to Rs. 1,000, or imprisonment up to two years, or both; the animal is forfeited to Government. ss. 14 to 20 (Chapter IV) – experiments on animals are lawful for the purposes named (s. 14), under a Committee constituted by the Central Government (s. 15), whose rules must secure that "experiments on animals are avoided wherever it is possible to do so" (s. 17). ss. 21 to 27 (Chapter V) – performing animals; s. 22: "No person shall exhibit or train" (i) a performing animal "unless he is registered", or (ii) an animal that the Central Government, by notification, specifies "as an animal which shall not be exhibited or trained as a performing animal"; s. 27 exempts military and police training and zoos. s. 28 – "Nothing contained in this Act shall render it an offence to kill any animal in a manner required by the religion of any community." s. 31 – offences under s. 11(1)(l), (n), (o) and s. 12 are cognizable. s. 38 – Central Government's power to make rules. State amendments of 2017 – Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Karnataka amended the Act (with the President's assent under Art. 254(2)) to allow Jallikattu, bullock-cart races and Kambala under rules; Tamil Nadu added s. 2(dd) (meaning of "Jallikattu"), s. 3(2), s. 11(3)(f), a proviso to s. 22, s. 27(c) and s. 28A.
hi.meaning: Animal – "any living creature other than a human being" (s. 2(a)); the widest definition, covering birds, fish and insects as well as domestic and wild animals. Cruelty – causing an animal unnecessary pain or suffering, by doing an act listed in s. 11(1) or by failing in the duty of care in s. 3. Unnecessary pain or suffering – pain that is not needed for a purpose the law allows; the Supreme Court has read the s. 11(3) exceptions as based on necessity, so entertainment is not such a purpose ( A. Nagaraja , as described in the 2023 judgment). Performing animal – an animal exhibited at an entertainment to which the public is admitted through sale of tickets, or trained for such exhibition (s. 21 read with s. 22). Animal welfare – the well-being of animals; the Animal Welfare Board exists "For the promotion of animal welfare generally" (s. 4(1)).
keyPoints: Animal: "any living creature other than a human being" (s. 2(a)). s. 3: duty of care. Cruelty: s. 11(1)(a)–(o); exceptions s. 11(3); s. 28 religion. Animal Welfare Board of India: s. 4; functions s. 9. Performing animal: Chapter V; s. 22(ii) bans; N.R. Nair . A. Nagaraja (2014); 2017 amendments upheld (2023).

caseLaws.name: Facts: Jallikattu in Tamil Nadu and bullock-cart races in Maharashtra were defended as custom and tr
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The events were contrary to ss. 3 and 11(1)(a) and (m); "All living creatures have inherent dignity and a right to live peacefully" (para 32); "every species has an inherent right to live and shall be protected by law, subject to the exception provided out of necessity" (para 51). Why it matters: It is the strongest statement of animals' rights under the PCA Act.

Animal Welfare Board of India v. Union of India, W.P. (C) No. 23 of 2016 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench; K.M. Joseph, Ajay Rastogi, Aniruddha Bose, Hrishikesh Roy and C.T. Ravikumar JJ; judgment by Aniruddha Bose J; 18 May 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 2017 amendments of Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Karnataka, which allowed Jallikattu, bullo
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The amendments, read with their Rules, were upheld and must be strictly enforced; Art. 14 cannot "be invoked by any animal as a person"; "if a long lasting tradition goes against the law, the law Courts obviously would have to enforce the law". Why it matters: It is the present law on animal sports and shows that the legislature can regulate, rather than ban, such events.
N.R. Nair v. Union of India, Civil Appeal Nos. 3609-3620 of 2001; 2001 (3) SCR 353 (Supreme Court; B.N. Kirpal, U.C. Banerjee and Brijesh Kumar JJ; judgment by Kirpal J; 1 May 2001)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Circus owners challenged a notification of 14 October 1998 under s
caseLaws.facts: 22 that banned the training and exhibition of bears, monkeys, tigers, panthers and lions; the Kerala High Court had upheld it. Principle: The Government's satisfaction that training or exhibition causes unnecessary pain is "a pre-condition to the issuance of the Notification"; courts cannot go into the correctness of that decision; "it is the welfare of the animals which is of paramount consideration". Why it matters: It upholds the Central Government's power to ban cruel use of wild animals in circuses.
