environmental-law-u3-t2.subtitle: The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972: schedules, protected areas and trade in endangered species

en.inOneMinute: Main statute: the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 (WPA). After the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (No. 18 of 2022, in force 1 April 2023), its long title speaks of the "conservation, protection and management of wild life". (See Diagram 1 .) Four tools of the Act: a ban on hunting (s. 9), except as allowed by ss. 11 and 12; protected areas: sanctuaries (s. 18), national parks (s. 35), conservation reserves (s. 36A), community reserves (s. 36C) and tiger reserves (s. 38V) (see Diagram 2 ); control of trade in wild animals and their articles (Chapters V, VA and, since 2022, Chapter VB on CITES); wild animals hunted or found dead in the cases named in s. 39 become "the property of the State Government". Endangered species: species at risk of extinction, such as the Asiatic lion, the tiger and the Great Indian Bustard (GIB), which the Supreme Court called "critically endangered" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024). Constitution: Art. 48A (State to "safeguard the forests and wild life"), Art. 51A(g) (citizen's duty) and Entry 17B of the Concurrent List ("Protection of wild animals and birds"). Courts: Art. 21 casts "an obligation on human beings to protect and preserve a specie becoming extinct" ( WWF-I , 2013); poaching and trade in tiger and leopard skins is "a serious offence" ( Sansar Chand , 2010). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Seventh Schedule, List III (Concurrent List), Entry 17B – "Protection of wild animals and birds." Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Read by the Supreme Court to protect species facing extinction ( WWF-I ). WPA, long title (as amended in 2022) – the words "protection of wild animals, birds and plants" were replaced by "conservation, protection and management of wild life". WPA, s. 9 – bans hunting of the wild animals listed in the Schedules, "except as provided under section 11 and section 12" (text before 2022; s. 9 was amended in 2022). WPA, s. 11(1)(a) – the Chief Wild Life Warden may permit the hunting of a Schedule I animal only if satisfied that it "has become dangerous to human life or is so disabled or diseased as to be beyond recovery"; since 2002 a proviso says no such animal shall be killed unless it cannot be captured, tranquilised or translocated. WPA, s. 18(1) – the State Government may, by notification, declare its intention to constitute any area, "other than an area comprised within any reserve forest or the territorial waters", as a sanctuary if it is of adequate ecological (and similar) significance. WPA, s. 35(1) – "Whenever it appears to the State Government that an area, whether within a sanctuary or not," is needed for the purpose, it may declare its intention to constitute that area as a National Park . WPA, s. 36A – conservation reserve , declared by the State Government after consultation with the local communities. WPA, s. 36C – community reserve , where a community or an individual has volunteered to conserve wild life and its habitat. WPA, s. 38V – tiger reserve , notified by the State Government on the recommendation of the Tiger Conservation Authority (Chapter IVB). WPA, s. 39(1) – a wild animal hunted or killed in the cases named there "shall be the property of the State Government". WPA, Chapter VA (s. 49B) – bans trade or commerce in scheduled animals, animal articles and trophies. WPA, Chapter VB (added in 2022) – gives effect to CITES (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora); a Management Authority and a Scientific Authority are appointed, trade in scheduled specimens is barred except as the Chapter allows, and every person holding a living specimen of a Schedule IV animal must report it and get it registered (s. 49M). WPA, s. 2(16A) and s. 62A (added in 2022) – define and deal with "invasive alien species". WPA, s. 51 – offences against the Act are punishable with imprisonment and fine; higher punishment applies to offences about the most protected animals (raised in 2002 and again in 2022).
en.meaning: Wild life – the wild animals, birds and plants of a country living in their natural state. The WPA's own definition of a wild animal (s. 2(36)) covers an animal "found wild in nature" and the animals listed in its Schedules. Hunting – under s. 2(16) it is a wide word: it includes "capturing, killing, poisoning, snaring and trapping" of a wild animal. Endangered species – a species whose numbers have fallen so low that it faces a real risk of extinction in the wild. "Critically endangered" is the most serious class below "extinct in the wild" (used in M.K. Ranjitsinh for the GIB and in Sansar Chand for the leopard). Protected area – an area set aside by notification under the WPA to protect wild life and its habitat ( sanctuary , national park, conservation reserve, community reserve, tiger reserve). CITES – the international treaty that controls trade across borders in endangered species; India is a signatory ( Sansar Chand , para 17).
keyPoints: Wild animal: found wild in nature or listed in the Schedules (s. 2(36)). Hunting banned (s. 9); exceptions ss. 11, 12. Sanctuary (s. 18) and national park (s. 35): declared by the State Government. s. 39: "the property of the State Government". 2022: new long title; Chapter VB (CITES); s. 62A invasive alien species. Endangered species: Art. 21 duty to protect ( WWF-I ); GIB "non-negotiable" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh ).

Why it matters: It treats wildlife trade as organised crime and supports strict enforcement.

te.inOneMinute: ప్రధాన చట్టం: వన్యప్రాణి (రక్షణ) చట్టం, 1972 (WPA). వన్యప్రాణి (రక్షణ) సవరణ చట్టం, 2022 (2022 లో No. 18, 1 ఏప్రిల్ 2023 నుండి అమలు) తర్వాత దాని దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక "conservation, protection and management of wild life" (అర్థం: వన్యప్రాణుల పరిరక్షణ, రక్షణ, నిర్వహణ) గురించి చెబుతుంది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) చట్టంలోని నాలుగు సాధనాలు: వేటపై నిషేధం (సె. 9), సె. 11, 12 అనుమతించినవి తప్ప; రక్షిత ప్రాంతాలు: అభయారణ్యాలు (సె. 18), జాతీయ ఉద్యానవనాలు (సె. 35), పరిరక్షణ రిజర్వులు (సె. 36A), సమాజ రిజర్వులు (సె. 36C), పులుల రిజర్వులు (సె. 38V) ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి); వన్యప్రాణులు, వాటి వస్తువుల వ్యాపారంపై నియంత్రణ (అధ్యాయాలు V, VA, 2022 నుండి CITES పై అధ్యాయం VB); సె. 39 లో పేర్కొన్న సందర్భాల్లో వేటాడబడిన లేదా చనిపోయి కనిపించిన వన్యప్రాణులు "the property of the State Government" (అర్థం: రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వ ఆస్తి) అవుతాయి. అంతరించిపోతున్న జాతులు: అంతరించిపోయే ప్రమాదంలో ఉన్న జాతులు; ఉదా. ఆసియా సింహం, పులి, గ్రేట్ ఇండియన్ బస్టర్డ్ (GIB). GIB ని సుప్రీంకోర్టు "critically endangered" (అర్థం: అత్యంత ప్రమాదంలో ఉన్న) అని పేర్కొంది ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024). రాజ్యాంగం: ఆర్టి. 48A (రాష్ట్రం "safeguard the forests and wild life" – అర్థం: అడవులను, వన్యప్రాణులను కాపాడాలి), ఆర్టి. 51A(g) (పౌరుల విధి), ఉమ్మడి జాబితా ఎంట్రీ 17B ("Protection of wild animals and birds" – అర్థం: వన్య జంతువులు, పక్షుల రక్షణ). న్యాయస్థానాలు: ఆర్టి. 21 "an obligation on human beings to protect and preserve a specie becoming extinct" (అర్థం: అంతరించిపోతున్న జాతిని రక్షించి కాపాడే బాధ్యతను మనుషులపై) మోపుతుంది ( WWF-I , 2013); పులి, చిరుతపులి చర్మాల వేట, వ్యాపారం "a serious offence" (అర్థం: తీవ్రమైన నేరం) ( Sansar Chand , 2010). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: వన్యప్రాణులు – ఒక దేశంలో సహజ స్థితిలో జీవించే వన్య జంతువులు, పక్షులు, మొక్కలు. WPA లోని వన్య జంతువు నిర్వచనం (సె. 2(36)) "found wild in nature" (అర్థం: ప్రకృతిలో వన్యంగా కనిపించే) జంతువును, దాని షెడ్యూళ్లలో జాబితా చేసిన జంతువులను కవర్ చేస్తుంది. వేట – సె. 2(16) కింద ఇది విస్తృత పదం: వన్య జంతువును "capturing, killing, poisoning, snaring and trapping" (అర్థం: పట్టుకోవడం, చంపడం, విషం పెట్టడం, ఉచ్చు వేయడం, బోనులో బంధించడం) దీనిలో చేరుతాయి. అంతరించిపోతున్న జాతి – సంఖ్య బాగా తగ్గిపోయి, అడవిలో అంతరించిపోయే నిజమైన ప్రమాదం ఎదుర్కొంటున్న జాతి. "Critically endangered" (అర్థం: అత్యంత ప్రమాదంలో ఉన్న) అనేది "extinct in the wild" (అర్థం: అడవిలో అంతరించిపోయిన) కంటే కిందటి అత్యంత తీవ్రమైన వర్గం ( M.K. Ranjitsinh లో GIB కి, Sansar Chand లో చిరుతపులికి వాడారు). రక్షిత ప్రాంతం – వన్యప్రాణులను, వాటి ఆవాసాన్ని రక్షించడానికి WPA కింద నోటిఫికేషన్ ద్వారా కేటాయించిన ప్రాంతం ( అభయారణ్యం , జాతీయ ఉద్యానవనం, పరిరక్షణ రిజర్వు, సమాజ రిజర్వు, పులుల రిజర్వు). CITES – అంతరించిపోతున్న జాతుల సరిహద్దులు దాటే వ్యాపారాన్ని నియంత్రించే అంతర్జాతీయ ఒడంబడిక; భారతదేశం దీనిపై సంతకం చేసింది ( Sansar Chand , para 17).
keyPoints: వన్య జంతువు: ప్రకృతిలో వన్యంగా కనిపించేది లేదా షెడ్యూళ్లలో జాబితా చేసినది (సె. 2(36)). వేట నిషేధం (సె. 9); మినహాయింపులు సె. 11, 12. అభయారణ్యం (సె. 18), జాతీయ ఉద్యానవనం (సె. 35): రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం ప్రకటిస్తుంది. సె. 39: "the property of the State Government" (అర్థం: రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వ ఆస్తి). 2022: కొత్త దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక; అధ్యాయం VB (CITES); సె. 62A ఆక్రమణశీల విదేశీ జాతులు. అంతరించిపోతున్న జాతి: రక్షించే విధి ఆర్టి. 21 కింద ( WWF-I ); GIB "non-negotiable" (అర్థం: బేరం చేయలేనిది) ( M.K. Ranjitsinh ).

hi.inOneMinute: Main statute: the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 (WPA). After the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (No. 18 of 2022, in force 1 April 2023), its long title speaks of the "conservation, protection and management of wild life". (See Diagram 1 .) Four tools of the Act: a ban on hunting (s. 9), except as allowed by ss. 11 and 12; protected areas: sanctuaries (s. 18), national parks (s. 35), conservation reserves (s. 36A), community reserves (s. 36C) and tiger reserves (s. 38V) (see Diagram 2 ); control of trade in wild animals and their articles (Chapters V, VA and, since 2022, Chapter VB on CITES); wild animals hunted or found dead in the cases named in s. 39 become "the property of the State Government". Endangered species: species at risk of extinction, such as the Asiatic lion, the tiger and the Great Indian Bustard (GIB), which the Supreme Court called "critically endangered" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024). Constitution: Art. 48A (State to "safeguard the forests and wild life"), Art. 51A(g) (citizen's duty) and Entry 17B of the Concurrent List ("Protection of wild animals and birds"). Courts: Art. 21 casts "an obligation on human beings to protect and preserve a specie becoming extinct" ( WWF-I , 2013); poaching and trade in tiger and leopard skins is "a serious offence" ( Sansar Chand , 2010). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Seventh Schedule, List III (Concurrent List), Entry 17B – "Protection of wild animals and birds." Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Read by the Supreme Court to protect species facing extinction ( WWF-I ). WPA, long title (as amended in 2022) – the words "protection of wild animals, birds and plants" were replaced by "conservation, protection and management of wild life". WPA, s. 9 – bans hunting of the wild animals listed in the Schedules, "except as provided under section 11 and section 12" (text before 2022; s. 9 was amended in 2022). WPA, s. 11(1)(a) – the Chief Wild Life Warden may permit the hunting of a Schedule I animal only if satisfied that it "has become dangerous to human life or is so disabled or diseased as to be beyond recovery"; since 2002 a proviso says no such animal shall be killed unless it cannot be captured, tranquilised or translocated. WPA, s. 18(1) – the State Government may, by notification, declare its intention to constitute any area, "other than an area comprised within any reserve forest or the territorial waters", as a sanctuary if it is of adequate ecological (and similar) significance. WPA, s. 35(1) – "Whenever it appears to the State Government that an area, whether within a sanctuary or not," is needed for the purpose, it may declare its intention to constitute that area as a National Park . WPA, s. 36A – conservation reserve , declared by the State Government after consultation with the local communities. WPA, s. 36C – community reserve , where a community or an individual has volunteered to conserve wild life and its habitat. WPA, s. 38V – tiger reserve , notified by the State Government on the recommendation of the Tiger Conservation Authority (Chapter IVB). WPA, s. 39(1) – a wild animal hunted or killed in the cases named there "shall be the property of the State Government". WPA, Chapter VA (s. 49B) – bans trade or commerce in scheduled animals, animal articles and trophies. WPA, Chapter VB (added in 2022) – gives effect to CITES (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora); a Management Authority and a Scientific Authority are appointed, trade in scheduled specimens is barred except as the Chapter allows, and every person holding a living specimen of a Schedule IV animal must report it and get it registered (s. 49M). WPA, s. 2(16A) and s. 62A (added in 2022) – define and deal with "invasive alien species". WPA, s. 51 – offences against the Act are punishable with imprisonment and fine; higher punishment applies to offences about the most protected animals (raised in 2002 and again in 2022).
hi.meaning: Wild life – the wild animals, birds and plants of a country living in their natural state. The WPA's own definition of a wild animal (s. 2(36)) covers an animal "found wild in nature" and the animals listed in its Schedules. Hunting – under s. 2(16) it is a wide word: it includes "capturing, killing, poisoning, snaring and trapping" of a wild animal. Endangered species – a species whose numbers have fallen so low that it faces a real risk of extinction in the wild. "Critically endangered" is the most serious class below "extinct in the wild" (used in M.K. Ranjitsinh for the GIB and in Sansar Chand for the leopard). Protected area – an area set aside by notification under the WPA to protect wild life and its habitat ( sanctuary , national park, conservation reserve, community reserve, tiger reserve). CITES – the international treaty that controls trade across borders in endangered species; India is a signatory ( Sansar Chand , para 17).
keyPoints: Wild animal: found wild in nature or listed in the Schedules (s. 2(36)). Hunting banned (s. 9); exceptions ss. 11, 12. Sanctuary (s. 18) and national park (s. 35): declared by the State Government. s. 39: "the property of the State Government". 2022: new long title; Chapter VB (CITES); s. 62A invasive alien species. Endangered species: Art. 21 duty to protect ( WWF-I ); GIB "non-negotiable" ( M.K. Ranjitsinh ).

environmental-law-u3-t5.subtitle: The Water Act, 1974: Pollution Control Boards, consent, directions and penalties

en.inOneMinute: Main statute: the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 (Water Act). Parliament made it under Art. 252 , after the Legislatures of several States passed resolutions; other States adopt it by resolution. (See Diagram 1 .) Pollution (s. 2(e)): contamination of water, or discharge of sewage or trade effluent into it, that may create a nuisance or make the water harmful to health, to its legitimate uses, or to animals, plants and aquatic organisms. Boards: a Central Pollution Control Board (s. 3) and a State Pollution Control Board in each State (s. 4); their functions are in ss. 16 and 17. Core controls: no one shall "knowingly cause or permit any poisonous, noxious or polluting matter" to enter a stream, well, sewer or land (s. 24); no new outlet or discharge "without the previous consent of the State Board" (s. 25); consent not decided in four months is deemed given (s. 25(7)). (See Diagram 2 .) Enforcement: sampling (s. 21), emergency measures (s. 32), court orders (s. 33) and binding directions, including "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry" and stopping electricity or water (s. 33A). Penalties: under the 1988 text, breach of ss. 24, 25 or 26 is punishable with imprisonment of 1½ to 6 years and fine (ss. 43, 44). The Water Amendment Act, 2024 (No. 5 of 2024), where it applies, replaces most imprisonment with penalties of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh imposed by an adjudicating officer, with appeal to the NGT; imprisonment remains for failing to follow ss. 25 and 26 (s. 45E). (See Diagram 3 .) Courts: tanneries without even a primary treatment plant "cannot be permitted to continue" ( M.C. Mehta , Kanpur, 1987); polluters must pay ( Vellore , 1996; Bichhri , 1996).
legalProvision: Article 252(1) – Parliament may make a law on a State subject for two or more States if their Legislatures pass resolutions; other States may adopt it by resolution. The Water Act's preamble records that "in pursuance of clause (1) of article 252 of the Constitution resolutions have been passed" by the Legislatures of twelve States. Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." It includes the right to pollution-free water ( Subhash Kumar , 1991). Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Water Act, s. 1(2) – it applied first to Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tripura, West Bengal and the Union Territories, and to any State that adopts it under Art. 252(1). s. 2(e) – "pollution" means "such contamination of water or such alteration of the physical, chemical or biological properties of water or such discharge of any sewage or trade effluent or of any other liquid, gaseous or solid substance into water (whether directly or indirectly) as may, or is likely to, create a nuisance or render such water harmful or injurious to public health or safety or to domestic, commercial, industrial, agricultural or other legitimate uses or to the life and health of animals or plants or of aquatic organisms". s. 3 – Central Pollution Control Board, a body corporate. s. 4 – State Pollution Control Board, constituted by the State Government; in a Union Territory the Central Board acts as the State Board (s. 4(4)). s. 16(1) – "the main function of the Central Board shall be to promote cleanliness of streams and wells in different areas of the States." s. 17(1)(a) – the State Board is "to plan a comprehensive programme for the prevention, control or abatement of pollution of streams and wells in the State". s. 21 – power to take samples; a sample "shall not be admissible in evidence in a legal proceeding unless" the procedure in s. 21(3) to (5) is followed. s. 24(1) – "no person shall knowingly cause or permit any poisonous, noxious or polluting matter" to enter any stream or well or sewer or on land, beyond the standards laid down by the State Board. s. 25(1) – "no person shall, without the previous consent of the State Board," establish an industry or process likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent, bring a new or altered outlet into use, or begin a new discharge. s. 25(4) – the Board may grant consent with conditions or refuse it "for reasons to be recorded in writing". s. 25(7) – consent "shall, unless given or refused earlier, be deemed to have been given unconditionally on the expiry of a period of four months" from a complete application. s. 26 – the provisions of s. 25 apply to a person already discharging when the Act came into force. s. 32 – emergency measures by the Board, including orders "immediately restraining or prohibiting" discharge. s. 33(1) – the Board may "make an application to a court, not inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate" or Judicial Magistrate of the first class, to restrain a likely polluter. s. 33A – the Board may "issue any directions in writing to any person, officer or authority", who "shall be bound to comply"; these include "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process" and "the stoppage or regulation of supply of electricity, water or any other service." ss. 41 to 45A (1988 text) – penalties; breach of s. 24 (s. 43) or of s. 25 or 26 (s. 44) "shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year and six months but which may extend to six years and with fine." s. 47 – offences by companies; s. 48 – offences by Government departments ("the Head of the Department shall be deemed to be guilty"). s. 49(1) – no court takes cognizance "except on a complaint made by" the Board (or its authorised officer) or by any person who has given notice of "not less than sixty days" to the Board. s. 58 – no civil court has jurisdiction over matters for which an appellate authority under the Act is empowered, and no injunction lies against action under the Act. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Amendment Act, 2024 (No. 5 of 2024; assent 15 February 2024) – applies "in the first instance" to Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and the Union Territories, and to other States that adopt it by resolution. Main changes: Central Government may "exempt certain categories of industrial plants" from s. 25(1) (proviso to s. 25(1)); Central guidelines on consent bind State Boards (s. 27A); penalties "not less than ten thousand rupees, but which may extend to fifteen lakh rupees", and Rs. 10,000 for every day a breach continues (ss. 41, 41A, 42, 43; up to Rs. 10,000 a day under s. 45A); an adjudicating officer "not below the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India or a Secretary to the State Government" (s. 45B); appeal to the National Green Tribunal within sixty days, after depositing ten per cent of the penalty (s. 45C); penalties credited to the Environmental Protection Fund under s. 16 of the EP Act (s. 45D); imprisonment of 1½ to 6 years kept for failure to comply with s. 25 or 26 (s. 45E); ss. 45 and 47 omitted; s. 48 now makes the Head of the Department pay a penalty of one month's basic salary.
en.meaning: Water pollution – the statutory meaning in s. 2(e): contamination or change in the properties of water, or discharge of any sewage, trade effluent or other substance into it, which may create a nuisance or harm health, legitimate uses, or animal, plant and aquatic life. Stream – the Act uses "stream" widely; with "well", "sewer" and "land" it marks the places into which polluting matter must not enter (s. 24). Consent – the previous permission of the State Board needed before setting up an industry or process that will discharge sewage or trade effluent, or before using a new outlet (s. 25). In practice it has two stages: consent to establish and consent to operate. Pollution Control Board – the expert body under the Act: the Central Board for the country, the State Board for each State. Adjudicating officer – an officer appointed under s. 45B (2024 amendment) to impose penalties after a hearing.
keyPoints: Water pollution: s. 2(e). State Pollution Control Board: s. 4; functions s. 17. s. 24: no polluting matter into stream, well, sewer or land. Consent: s. 25; deemed after four months; s. 26. s. 33A: closure and stoppage of electricity or water. Adjudicating officer: s. 45B (2024); penalties Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh; NGT appeal.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries at Kanpur discharged untreated effluent into the Ganga
caseLaws.facts: Principle: A tannery that does not set up even a primary treatment plant "cannot be permitted to continue"; financial capacity is irrelevant. K.N. Singh J: "life, health and ecology have greater importance". Why it matters: It shows the Court closing polluters of a river when the law was not being enforced.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar river and on land
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country"; an authority under s. 3(3) of the EP Act was ordered, and each tannery fined Rs. 10,000. Why it matters: It gives the principles that guide water pollution control.
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India (Bichhri) AIR 1996 SC 1446; (1996) 3 SCC 212 (Supreme Court; B.P. Jeevan Reddy and B.N. Kirpal JJ; 13 February 1996)

selfTest.a: Define "pollution" under s. 2(e). What does s. 25(7) provide? Name two directions a Board can issue under s. 33A. Who may file a complaint under s. 49? What did the 2024 amendment change about penalties?

te.inOneMinute: ప్రధాన చట్టం: నీటి (కాలుష్య నివారణ, నియంత్రణ) చట్టం, 1974 (నీటి చట్టం). అనేక రాష్ట్రాల శాసనసభలు తీర్మానాలు ఆమోదించిన తర్వాత పార్లమెంటు ఆర్టి. 252 కింద దీన్ని చేసింది; ఇతర రాష్ట్రాలు తీర్మానం ద్వారా దీన్ని స్వీకరిస్తాయి. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) కాలుష్యం (సె. 2(e)): నీటి కలుషితం, లేదా దానిలోకి మురుగు లేదా పారిశ్రామిక వ్యర్థ జలాల విడుదల; ఇది ఇబ్బంది కలిగించవచ్చు లేదా నీటిని ఆరోగ్యానికి, దాని చట్టబద్ధ ఉపయోగాలకు, జంతువులు, మొక్కలు, జలచరాలకు హానికరంగా మార్చవచ్చు. బోర్డులు: కేంద్ర కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ బోర్డు (సె. 3), ప్రతి రాష్ట్రంలో రాష్ట్ర కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ బోర్డు (సె. 4); వాటి విధులు సె. 16, 17 లో ఉన్నాయి. ముఖ్య నియంత్రణలు: ఎవరూ "knowingly cause or permit any poisonous, noxious or polluting matter" (అర్థం: తెలిసి ఏదైనా విషపూరిత, హానికర లేదా కాలుష్యకర పదార్థాన్ని కలిగించరాదు లేదా అనుమతించరాదు) ప్రవాహం, బావి, మురుగు కాలువ లేదా భూమిలోకి చేరేలా (సె. 24); "without the previous consent of the State Board" (అర్థం: రాష్ట్ర బోర్డు ముందస్తు సమ్మతి లేకుండా) కొత్త అవుట్‌లెట్ లేదా విడుదల లేదు (సె. 25); నాలుగు నెలల్లో నిర్ణయించని సమ్మతి ఇచ్చినట్లే భావించబడుతుంది (సె. 25(7)). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) అమలు: నమూనాల సేకరణ (సె. 21), అత్యవసర చర్యలు (సె. 32), కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వులు (సె. 33), "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry" (అర్థం: ఏదైనా పరిశ్రమ మూసివేత, నిషేధం లేదా నియంత్రణ), విద్యుత్ లేదా నీటి నిలిపివేతతో సహా బంధనకారి ఆదేశాలు (సె. 33A). శిక్షలు: 1988 పాఠం ప్రకారం సె. 24, 25 లేదా 26 ఉల్లంఘనకు 1½ నుండి 6 సంవత్సరాల జైలు, జరిమానా (సె. 43, 44). నీటి సవరణ చట్టం, 2024 (2024 లో No. 5) వర్తించే చోట, చాలా జైలు శిక్షల స్థానంలో న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి విధించే రూ. 10,000 నుండి రూ. 15 లక్షల వరకు పెనాల్టీలు వచ్చాయి, NGT కి అప్పీల్ ఉంది; సె. 25, 26 పాటించకపోతే జైలు శిక్ష కొనసాగుతుంది (సె. 45E). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.) న్యాయస్థానాలు: కనీసం ప్రాథమిక శుద్ధి ప్లాంటు కూడా లేని చర్మశుద్ధి కర్మాగారాలను "cannot be permitted to continue" (అర్థం: కొనసాగించడానికి అనుమతించరాదు) ( M.C. Mehta , కాన్పూర్, 1987); కాలుష్యకారులు చెల్లించాలి ( Vellore , 1996; Bichhri , 1996).
te.meaning: నీటి కాలుష్యం – సె. 2(e) లోని చట్టబద్ధ అర్థం: నీటి కలుషితం లేదా దాని లక్షణాల మార్పు, లేదా దానిలోకి ఏదైనా మురుగు, పారిశ్రామిక వ్యర్థ జలం లేదా ఇతర పదార్థ విడుదల; ఇది ఇబ్బంది కలిగించవచ్చు లేదా ఆరోగ్యానికి, చట్టబద్ధ ఉపయోగాలకు, జంతు, మొక్క, జలచర జీవానికి హాని చేయవచ్చు. ప్రవాహం (Stream) – చట్టం "stream" (అర్థం: ప్రవాహం) ను విస్తృతంగా వాడుతుంది; "well" (బావి), "sewer" (మురుగు కాలువ), "land" (భూమి) తో కలిసి, కాలుష్యకర పదార్థం చేరకూడని ప్రదేశాలను ఇది సూచిస్తుంది (సె. 24). సమ్మతి – మురుగు లేదా పారిశ్రామిక వ్యర్థ జలం విడుదల చేసే పరిశ్రమ లేదా ప్రక్రియను స్థాపించే ముందు, లేదా కొత్త అవుట్‌లెట్ వాడే ముందు అవసరమైన రాష్ట్ర బోర్డు ముందస్తు అనుమతి (సె. 25). ఆచరణలో దీనికి రెండు దశలు ఉన్నాయి: స్థాపనకు సమ్మతి , నిర్వహణకు సమ్మతి. కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ బోర్డు – చట్టం కింద నిపుణుల సంస్థ: దేశానికి కేంద్ర బోర్డు, ప్రతి రాష్ట్రానికి రాష్ట్ర బోర్డు. న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి – వినిపించుకునే అవకాశం ఇచ్చిన తర్వాత పెనాల్టీలు విధించడానికి సె. 45B (2024 సవరణ) కింద నియమించిన అధికారి.
keyPoints: నీటి కాలుష్యం: సె. 2(e). రాష్ట్ర కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ బోర్డు: సె. 4; విధులు సె. 17. సె. 24: ప్రవాహం, బావి, మురుగు కాలువ లేదా భూమిలోకి కాలుష్యకర పదార్థం వద్దు. సమ్మతి: సె. 25; నాలుగు నెలల తర్వాత ఇచ్చినట్లు భావన; సె. 26. సె. 33A: మూసివేత, విద్యుత్ లేదా నీటి నిలిపివేత. న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి: సె. 45B (2024); రూ. 10,000 నుండి రూ. 15 లక్షల పెనాల్టీలు; NGT అప్పీల్.

selfTest.q: రాజ్యాంగంలోని ఏ ఆర్టికల్ కింద నీటి చట్టం చేయబడింది?
selfTest.a: సె. 2(e) కింద "కాలుష్యం" ను నిర్వచించండి. సె. 25(7) ఏమి చెబుతుంది? సె. 33A కింద బోర్డు ఇవ్వగల రెండు ఆదేశాలను పేర్కొనండి. సె. 49 కింద ఎవరు ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు? 2024 సవరణ శిక్షల గురించి ఏమి మార్చింది?

hi.inOneMinute: Main statute: the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 (Water Act). Parliament made it under Art. 252 , after the Legislatures of several States passed resolutions; other States adopt it by resolution. (See Diagram 1 .) Pollution (s. 2(e)): contamination of water, or discharge of sewage or trade effluent into it, that may create a nuisance or make the water harmful to health, to its legitimate uses, or to animals, plants and aquatic organisms. Boards: a Central Pollution Control Board (s. 3) and a State Pollution Control Board in each State (s. 4); their functions are in ss. 16 and 17. Core controls: no one shall "knowingly cause or permit any poisonous, noxious or polluting matter" to enter a stream, well, sewer or land (s. 24); no new outlet or discharge "without the previous consent of the State Board" (s. 25); consent not decided in four months is deemed given (s. 25(7)). (See Diagram 2 .) Enforcement: sampling (s. 21), emergency measures (s. 32), court orders (s. 33) and binding directions, including "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry" and stopping electricity or water (s. 33A). Penalties: under the 1988 text, breach of ss. 24, 25 or 26 is punishable with imprisonment of 1½ to 6 years and fine (ss. 43, 44). The Water Amendment Act, 2024 (No. 5 of 2024), where it applies, replaces most imprisonment with penalties of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh imposed by an adjudicating officer, with appeal to the NGT; imprisonment remains for failing to follow ss. 25 and 26 (s. 45E). (See Diagram 3 .) Courts: tanneries without even a primary treatment plant "cannot be permitted to continue" ( M.C. Mehta , Kanpur, 1987); polluters must pay ( Vellore , 1996; Bichhri , 1996).
legalProvision: Article 252(1) – Parliament may make a law on a State subject for two or more States if their Legislatures pass resolutions; other States may adopt it by resolution. The Water Act's preamble records that "in pursuance of clause (1) of article 252 of the Constitution resolutions have been passed" by the Legislatures of twelve States. Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." It includes the right to pollution-free water ( Subhash Kumar , 1991). Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Water Act, s. 1(2) – it applied first to Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tripura, West Bengal and the Union Territories, and to any State that adopts it under Art. 252(1). s. 2(e) – "pollution" means "such contamination of water or such alteration of the physical, chemical or biological properties of water or such discharge of any sewage or trade effluent or of any other liquid, gaseous or solid substance into water (whether directly or indirectly) as may, or is likely to, create a nuisance or render such water harmful or injurious to public health or safety or to domestic, commercial, industrial, agricultural or other legitimate uses or to the life and health of animals or plants or of aquatic organisms". s. 3 – Central Pollution Control Board, a body corporate. s. 4 – State Pollution Control Board, constituted by the State Government; in a Union Territory the Central Board acts as the State Board (s. 4(4)). s. 16(1) – "the main function of the Central Board shall be to promote cleanliness of streams and wells in different areas of the States." s. 17(1)(a) – the State Board is "to plan a comprehensive programme for the prevention, control or abatement of pollution of streams and wells in the State". s. 21 – power to take samples; a sample "shall not be admissible in evidence in a legal proceeding unless" the procedure in s. 21(3) to (5) is followed. s. 24(1) – "no person shall knowingly cause or permit any poisonous, noxious or polluting matter" to enter any stream or well or sewer or on land, beyond the standards laid down by the State Board. s. 25(1) – "no person shall, without the previous consent of the State Board," establish an industry or process likely to discharge sewage or trade effluent, bring a new or altered outlet into use, or begin a new discharge. s. 25(4) – the Board may grant consent with conditions or refuse it "for reasons to be recorded in writing". s. 25(7) – consent "shall, unless given or refused earlier, be deemed to have been given unconditionally on the expiry of a period of four months" from a complete application. s. 26 – the provisions of s. 25 apply to a person already discharging when the Act came into force. s. 32 – emergency measures by the Board, including orders "immediately restraining or prohibiting" discharge. s. 33(1) – the Board may "make an application to a court, not inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate" or Judicial Magistrate of the first class, to restrain a likely polluter. s. 33A – the Board may "issue any directions in writing to any person, officer or authority", who "shall be bound to comply"; these include "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process" and "the stoppage or regulation of supply of electricity, water or any other service." ss. 41 to 45A (1988 text) – penalties; breach of s. 24 (s. 43) or of s. 25 or 26 (s. 44) "shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year and six months but which may extend to six years and with fine." s. 47 – offences by companies; s. 48 – offences by Government departments ("the Head of the Department shall be deemed to be guilty"). s. 49(1) – no court takes cognizance "except on a complaint made by" the Board (or its authorised officer) or by any person who has given notice of "not less than sixty days" to the Board. s. 58 – no civil court has jurisdiction over matters for which an appellate authority under the Act is empowered, and no injunction lies against action under the Act. Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Amendment Act, 2024 (No. 5 of 2024; assent 15 February 2024) – applies "in the first instance" to Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and the Union Territories, and to other States that adopt it by resolution. Main changes: Central Government may "exempt certain categories of industrial plants" from s. 25(1) (proviso to s. 25(1)); Central guidelines on consent bind State Boards (s. 27A); penalties "not less than ten thousand rupees, but which may extend to fifteen lakh rupees", and Rs. 10,000 for every day a breach continues (ss. 41, 41A, 42, 43; up to Rs. 10,000 a day under s. 45A); an adjudicating officer "not below the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India or a Secretary to the State Government" (s. 45B); appeal to the National Green Tribunal within sixty days, after depositing ten per cent of the penalty (s. 45C); penalties credited to the Environmental Protection Fund under s. 16 of the EP Act (s. 45D); imprisonment of 1½ to 6 years kept for failure to comply with s. 25 or 26 (s. 45E); ss. 45 and 47 omitted; s. 48 now makes the Head of the Department pay a penalty of one month's basic salary.
hi.meaning: Water pollution – the statutory meaning in s. 2(e): contamination or change in the properties of water, or discharge of any sewage, trade effluent or other substance into it, which may create a nuisance or harm health, legitimate uses, or animal, plant and aquatic life. Stream – the Act uses "stream" widely; with "well", "sewer" and "land" it marks the places into which polluting matter must not enter (s. 24). Consent – the previous permission of the State Board needed before setting up an industry or process that will discharge sewage or trade effluent, or before using a new outlet (s. 25). In practice it has two stages: consent to establish and consent to operate. Pollution Control Board – the expert body under the Act: the Central Board for the country, the State Board for each State. Adjudicating officer – an officer appointed under s. 45B (2024 amendment) to impose penalties after a hearing.
keyPoints: Water pollution: s. 2(e). State Pollution Control Board: s. 4; functions s. 17. s. 24: no polluting matter into stream, well, sewer or land. Consent: s. 25; deemed after four months; s. 26. s. 33A: closure and stoppage of electricity or water. Adjudicating officer: s. 45B (2024); penalties Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh; NGT appeal.

environmental-law-u3-t7.subtitle: How the general environment laws fit together

en.inOneMinute: What this topic covers: the whole body of Indian law that protects the environment: the Constitution, the statutes made by Parliament, the principles laid down by the courts, the regulators, and the remedies. (See Diagram 1 .) Constitution: Art. 21 (right to life, which the Supreme Court has read to include "the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air"); Art. 48A (duty of the State); Art. 51A(g) (duty of every citizen); Art. 252 and Art. 253 (powers of Parliament used to make the main pollution laws). Main statutes: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972; Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, now the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980; Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (EP Act), the umbrella law; Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991; Biological Diversity Act, 2002; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. Principles: sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle ( Vellore , 1996); absolute liability for hazardous industries ( M.C. Mehta , Oleum gas, 1986); no-fault liability (PLI Act, 1991; NGT Act, 2010). (See Diagram 2 .) Enforcement: Pollution Control Boards and authorities under the EP Act; money penalties by adjudicating officers after the 2023–2024 amendments; appeals and compensation cases before the National Green Tribunal (NGT) ; appeal from the NGT to the Supreme Court; writs under Arts. 32 and 226. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Constitution of India

Art. 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Art. 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Art. 51A(g) – it is the duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Art. 252 – Parliament may make a law on a State subject for two or more States if "resolutions to that effect are passed by all the Houses of the Legislatures of those States"; other States may adopt it. Art. 253 – Parliament "has power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other body".
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

Long title – "An Act to provide for the protection and improvement of environment and for matters connected therewith." Preamble – refers to the decisions "taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held at Stockholm in June, 1972". s. 2(a) – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". s. 3(1) – the Central Government may take all such measures "as it deems necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and improving the quality of the environment". s. 5 – the Central Government may "issue directions in writing to any person, officer or any authority", including "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process".
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991

s. 3(1) (as substituted by the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023, from 1 April 2024) – where death or injury to any person (other than a workman) or damage to any property has resulted from an accident, "the owner shall be liable to reimburse such amount, or provide such other relief as may be prescribed", for death, medical expenses, loss of wages, other injury or sickness, damage to private property and other prescribed loss. s. 3(2) – the claimant "shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person".
National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

s. 14(1) – the Tribunal has jurisdiction over "all civil cases where a substantial question relating to environment" is involved and the question arises out of the implementation of the Acts in Schedule I. s. 17(3) – "The Tribunal shall, in case of an accident, apply the principle of no fault." s. 20 – the Tribunal shall apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
en.meaning: Environment protection law means the rules of law that aim to prevent harm to the environment, control pollution , conserve natural resources and give relief when harm is done. The EP Act does not define "environment protection", but its long title speaks of "the protection and improvement of environment", and s. 2(a) gives a wide meaning of "environment": water, air, land and their inter-relationship with human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property. Two related definitions in the EP Act: s. 2(b) "environmental pollutant" means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to environment; s. 2(c) "environmental pollution" means the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant . In simple words, Indian environment protection law has five parts: (1) the Constitution, (2) statutes, (3) judge-made principles, (4) regulators, and (5) remedies (penalties, compensation, writs ).
keyPoints: Art. 21 includes pollution-free water and air; Arts. 48A, 51A(g) added in 1976. EP Act, 1986 is the umbrella law (ss. 2(a), 3, 5). Absolute liability: Oleum gas, 1986; no exceptions. No-fault liability: PLI Act s. 3(2); NGT Act s. 17(3). Precautionary principle and polluter pays principle: Vellore , 1996; NGT Act s. 20. NGT Act, 2010 repealed the NET Act, 1995 and NEAA Act, 1997 (s. 38).

caseLaws.facts: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum gas leak) AIR 1987 SC 1086; (1987) 1 SCC 395; W.P. (C) No. 12739 of 1985 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati CJ, Ranganath Misra, G.L. Oza, M.M. Dutt and K.N. Singh JJ; judgment by Bhagwati CJ; 20 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas escaped from a unit of Shriram Foods & Fertilizer Industries in Delhi on 4 and 6 De
caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry "is strictly and absolutely liable" for harm from an accident, and the liability "is not subject to any of the exceptions" under Rylands v. Fletcher ; compensation must be "co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". Why it matters: It created absolute liability, the base of India's liability law for hazardous industries.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh, Faizan Uddin and K. Venkataswami JJ; judgment by Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar river and onto land; abo
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country"; the Central Government was directed to set up an authority under s. 3(3) of the EP Act. Why it matters: It made these principles part of Indian law; s. 20 of the NGT Act now requires the NGT to apply them.
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 1446; (1996) 3 SCC 212 (Supreme Court; B.P. Jeevan Reddy and B.N. Kirpal JJ; 13 February 1996) (Bichhri case)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Chemical units at Bichhri, Udaipur district, Rajasthan, producing "H" acid left about 2400–25
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Applying the Oleum gas rule, "Respondents Nos.4 to 8 are absolutely liable"; "the responsibility for repairing the damage is that of the offending industry"; the Central Government may recover the cost of remedial measures under ss. 3 and 5 of the EP Act. Why it matters: It joined absolute liability with the polluter pays principle and used the EP Act to make the polluter pay.

te.inOneMinute: ఈ అంశంలో ఏముంది: భారతదేశంలో పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించే మొత్తం చట్ట వ్యవస్థ: రాజ్యాంగం, పార్లమెంటు చేసిన చట్టాలు, కోర్టులు నిర్ణయించిన సూత్రాలు, నియంత్రణ సంస్థలు, పరిష్కారాలు. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) రాజ్యాంగం: ఆర్టికల్ 21 (జీవించే హక్కు; దీనిలో "the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air" (అర్థం: కాలుష్యం లేని నీరు, గాలిని అనుభవించే హక్కు) ఉందని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది); ఆర్టికల్ 48A (రాజ్యం విధి); ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g) (ప్రతి పౌరుడి విధి); ఆర్టికల్ 252, ఆర్టికల్ 253 (ముఖ్య కాలుష్య చట్టాలు చేయడానికి వాడిన పార్లమెంటు అధికారాలు). ముఖ్య చట్టాలు: వన్యప్రాణి (రక్షణ) చట్టం, 1972; నీటి (కాలుష్య నివారణ, నియంత్రణ) చట్టం, 1974; అటవీ (సంరక్షణ) చట్టం, 1980; ఇప్పుడు వన్ (సంరక్షణ్ ఏవం సంవర్ధన్) అధినియం, 1980; వాయు (కాలుష్య నివారణ, నియంత్రణ) చట్టం, 1981; పర్యావరణ (రక్షణ) చట్టం, 1986 (EP చట్టం), సమగ్ర (గొడుగు) చట్టం; ప్రజా బాధ్యత బీమా చట్టం, 1991 (PLI చట్టం); జీవ వైవిధ్య చట్టం, 2002; జాతీయ హరిత ట్రిబ్యునల్ చట్టం, 2010 (NGT చట్టం). సూత్రాలు: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి, ముందుజాగ్రత్త సూత్రం, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం ( వెల్లూర్ , 1996); ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమలకు సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( M.C. మెహతా , ఓలియం వాయువు, 1986); తప్పులేని బాధ్యత (PLI చట్టం, 1991; NGT చట్టం, 2010). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) అమలు: కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ బోర్డులు, EP చట్టం కింది అధికార సంస్థలు; 2023–2024 సవరణల తర్వాత న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారులు విధించే ధన పెనాల్టీలు; జాతీయ హరిత ట్రిబ్యునల్ (NGT) ముందు అప్పీళ్లు, పరిహార కేసులు; NGT నుండి సుప్రీంకోర్టుకు అప్పీల్; ఆర్టికల్ 32, 226 కింద రిట్లు. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: పర్యావరణ రక్షణ చట్టం అంటే పర్యావరణానికి హానిని నివారించడం, కాలుష్యాన్ని నియంత్రించడం, సహజ వనరులను సంరక్షించడం, హాని జరిగినప్పుడు ఉపశమనం ఇవ్వడం లక్ష్యంగా ఉన్న చట్ట నియమాలు. EP చట్టం "పర్యావరణ రక్షణ" ను నిర్వచించలేదు; కానీ దాని దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక "the protection and improvement of environment" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణ రక్షణ, మెరుగుదల) గురించి చెబుతుంది; సె. 2(a) "పర్యావరణం" కు విస్తృత అర్థం ఇస్తుంది: నీరు, గాలి, భూమి, వాటికి మనుషులు, ఇతర జీవులు, మొక్కలు, సూక్ష్మజీవులు, ఆస్తితో ఉన్న పరస్పర సంబంధం. EP చట్టంలో సంబంధిత రెండు నిర్వచనాలు: సె. 2(b) "environmental pollutant" ( పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యకారకం ) అంటే పర్యావరణానికి హాని కలిగించే లేదా కలిగించే అవకాశం ఉన్న సాంద్రతలో ఉన్న ఏదైనా ఘన, ద్రవ లేదా వాయు పదార్థం; సె. 2(c) "environmental pollution" (పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యం ) అంటే పర్యావరణంలో ఏదైనా పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యకారకం ఉండడం. సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే, భారత పర్యావరణ రక్షణ చట్టానికి ఐదు భాగాలు: (1) రాజ్యాంగం, (2) చట్టాలు, (3) కోర్టులు చేసిన సూత్రాలు, (4) నియంత్రణ సంస్థలు, (5) పరిష్కారాలు (పెనాల్టీలు, పరిహారం, రిట్లు ).
keyPoints: ఆర్టికల్ 21 లో కాలుష్యం లేని నీరు, గాలి ఉన్నాయి; ఆర్టికల్ 48A, 51A(g) 1976 లో చేర్చబడ్డాయి. hi.inOneMinute: What this topic covers: the whole body of Indian law that protects the environment: the Constitution, the statutes made by Parliament, the principles laid down by the courts, the regulators, and the remedies. (See Diagram 1 .) Constitution: Art. 21 (right to life, which the Supreme Court has read to include "the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air"); Art. 48A (duty of the State); Art. 51A(g) (duty of every citizen); Art. 252 and Art. 253 (powers of Parliament used to make the main pollution laws). Main statutes: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972; Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, now the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980; Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (EP Act), the umbrella law; Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991; Biological Diversity Act, 2002; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. Principles: sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle ( Vellore , 1996); absolute liability for hazardous industries ( M.C. Mehta , Oleum gas, 1986); no-fault liability (PLI Act, 1991; NGT Act, 2010). (See Diagram 2 .) Enforcement: Pollution Control Boards and authorities under the EP Act; money penalties by adjudicating officers after the 2023–2024 amendments; appeals and compensation cases before the National Green Tribunal (NGT) ; appeal from the NGT to the Supreme Court; writs under Arts. 32 and 226. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Constitution of India

Art. 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Art. 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Art. 51A(g) – it is the duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Art. 252 – Parliament may make a law on a State subject for two or more States if "resolutions to that effect are passed by all the Houses of the Legislatures of those States"; other States may adopt it. Art. 253 – Parliament "has power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other body".
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

Long title – "An Act to provide for the protection and improvement of environment and for matters connected therewith." Preamble – refers to the decisions "taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held at Stockholm in June, 1972". s. 2(a) – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". s. 3(1) – the Central Government may take all such measures "as it deems necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and improving the quality of the environment". s. 5 – the Central Government may "issue directions in writing to any person, officer or any authority", including "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process".
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991

s. 3(1) (as substituted by the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023, from 1 April 2024) – where death or injury to any person (other than a workman) or damage to any property has resulted from an accident, "the owner shall be liable to reimburse such amount, or provide such other relief as may be prescribed", for death, medical expenses, loss of wages, other injury or sickness, damage to private property and other prescribed loss. s. 3(2) – the claimant "shall not be required to plead and establish that the death, injury or damage in respect of which the claim has been made was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of any person".
National Green Tribunal Act, 2010

s. 14(1) – the Tribunal has jurisdiction over "all civil cases where a substantial question relating to environment" is involved and the question arises out of the implementation of the Acts in Schedule I. s. 17(3) – "The Tribunal shall, in case of an accident, apply the principle of no fault." s. 20 – the Tribunal shall apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle.
hi.meaning: Environment protection law means the rules of law that aim to prevent harm to the environment, control pollution , conserve natural resources and give relief when harm is done. The EP Act does not define "environment protection", but its long title speaks of "the protection and improvement of environment", and s. 2(a) gives a wide meaning of "environment": water, air, land and their inter-relationship with human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property. Two related definitions in the EP Act: s. 2(b) "environmental pollutant" means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to environment; s. 2(c) "environmental pollution" means the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant . In simple words, Indian environment protection law has five parts: (1) the Constitution, (2) statutes, (3) judge-made principles, (4) regulators, and (5) remedies (penalties, compensation, writs ).
keyPoints: Art. 21 includes pollution-free water and air; Arts. 48A, 51A(g) added in 1976. EP Act, 1986 is the umbrella law (ss. 2(a), 3, 5). Absolute liability: Oleum gas, 1986; no exceptions. No-fault liability: PLI Act s. 3(2); NGT Act s. 17(3). Precautionary principle and polluter pays principle: Vellore , 1996; NGT Act s. 20. NGT Act, 2010 repealed the NET Act, 1995 and NEAA Act, 1997 (s. 38).

caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry "is strictly and absolutely liable" for harm from an accident, and the liability "is not subject to any of the exceptions" under Rylands v. Fletcher ; compensation must be "co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". Why it matters: It created absolute liability, the base of India's liability law for hazardous industries.

environmental-law-u3-t8.subtitle: The umbrella Act: general power to protect the environment, directions, standards and penalties

en.inOneMinute: What it is: Act No. 29 of 1986, assented to on 23 May 1986 and in force across India from 19 November 1986. Its long title: "An Act to provide for the protection and improvement of environment and for matters connected therewith." It implements decisions of the Stockholm Conference of June 1972. (See Diagram 1 .) Why it is called an umbrella Act: it covers the whole environment (water, air, land and their inter-relationship with living beings and property, s. 2(a)) and gives the Central Government very wide powers to take "all such measures" needed to protect and improve the environment (s. 3). Key powers: measures and standards (s. 3(2)); authorities (s. 3(3)); directions, including closure and stoppage of electricity or water (s. 5), with appeal to the NGT (s. 5A); rules (ss. 6, 25). Key duties: no discharge of pollutants beyond standards (s. 7); handling hazardous substances only under prescribed safeguards (s. 8); reporting and controlling accidents (s. 9). (See Diagram 2 .) Enforcement: entry and inspection (s. 10), samples (s. 11), laboratories and analysts (ss. 12–14). Penalties: as enacted, imprisonment up to five years or fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both (s. 15). From 1 April 2024 the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 replaced this with money penalties fixed by an adjudicating officer (ss. 14A to 15F), appeal to the NGT (s. 15D), and an Environmental Protection Fund (s. 16). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Preamble – recites that "decisions were taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held at Stockholm in June, 1972" for the protection and improvement of the human environment and "the prevention of hazards to human beings, other living creatures, plants and property", and that it is necessary to implement them. s. 2(a) – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". s. 2(b) – "environmental pollutant" means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to environment. s. 2(c) – "environmental pollution" means the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant. s. 2(e) – "hazardous substance" means any substance or preparation which, by reason of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling, is liable to cause harm (to human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms, property or the environment). s. 3(1) – the Central Government may take all such measures "as it deems necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and improving the quality of the environment" and for preventing, controlling and abating environmental pollution. s. 5 – the Central Government may "issue directions in writing to any person, officer or any authority" and they "shall be bound to comply"; the Explanation includes "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process" and the "stoppage or regulation of the supply of electricity or water or any other service". s. 7 – "No person carrying on any industry, operation or process shall discharge or emit" any environmental pollutant "in excess of such standards as may be prescribed". s. 8 – no person shall handle any hazardous substance "except in accordance with such procedure and after complying with such safeguards as may be prescribed". s. 14A (inserted 2023) – contravention of s. 7 or s. 8 attracts a penalty "which shall not be less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to fifteen lakh rupees", and Rs. 50,000 a day for a continuing contravention. s. 19 – no court shall take cognizance of an offence except on a complaint by the Central Government (or its authorised officer), the adjudicating officer (clause (aa), inserted 2023), or "any person who has given notice of not less than sixty days, in the manner prescribed". s. 24 (as substituted in 2023) – the Act and its rules "shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law".
en.meaning: The Act defines the main terms in s. 2 : (a) environment – water, air, land and their inter-relationship with human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property; (b) environmental pollutant – any solid, liquid or gaseous substance in a concentration that is or may be injurious to environment; (c) environmental pollution – the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant; (ca) Fund (inserted 2023) – the Environmental Protection Fund under s. 16; (d) handling – manufacture, processing, treatment, package, storage, transportation, use, collection, destruction, conversion, offering for sale, transfer or the like of a substance; (e) hazardous substance – a substance or preparation liable to cause harm because of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling; (f) occupier – the person who has control over the affairs of the factory or the premises; (g) prescribed – prescribed by rules under the Act. In simple words, the EP Act is a framework law : it states the goal (protect and improve the environment), gives the Central Government powers to act, makes a few general duties, and leaves details to rules and notifications.
keyPoints: Environment: s. 2(a), with "inter-relationship". Environmental pollutant: s. 2(b); s. 7 bans emission beyond standards. Hazardous substance: s. 2(e); s. 8 safeguards. s. 3(3) authority; s. 5 directions (closure, electricity, water); s. 5A appeal to NGT. Adjudicating officer: s. 15C; penalties ss. 14A–15A; NGT appeal s. 15D with 10% deposit. s. 19: citizen complaint after sixty days' notice.

te.inOneMinute: ఇది ఏమిటి: 1986 చట్టం నం. 29; 23 మే 1986 న ఆమోదం పొంది, 19 నవంబర్ 1986 నుండి భారతదేశమంతటా అమలులోకి వచ్చింది. దీర్ఘ శీర్షిక: "An Act to provide for the protection and improvement of environment and for matters connected therewith." (అర్థం: పర్యావరణ రక్షణ, మెరుగుదల, వాటికి సంబంధించిన విషయాల కోసం చేసిన చట్టం.) ఇది 1972 జూన్ స్టాక్‌హోమ్ సదస్సు నిర్ణయాలను అమలు చేస్తుంది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) దీన్ని గొడుగు (సమగ్ర) చట్టం అని ఎందుకు అంటారు: ఇది మొత్తం పర్యావరణాన్ని (నీరు, గాలి, భూమి, జీవులు, ఆస్తితో వాటి పరస్పర సంబంధం, సె. 2(a)) కవర్ చేస్తుంది; పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించి మెరుగుపరచడానికి అవసరమైన "all such measures" (అర్థం: అన్ని చర్యలు) తీసుకునే చాలా విస్తృత అధికారాలను కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వానికి ఇస్తుంది (సె. 3). ముఖ్య అధికారాలు: చర్యలు, ప్రమాణాలు (సె. 3(2)); అధికార సంస్థలు (సె. 3(3)); మూసివేత, విద్యుత్ లేదా నీటి నిలిపివేతతో సహా ఆదేశాలు (సె. 5); NGT కి అప్పీల్ (సె. 5A); నియమాలు (సె. 6, 25). ముఖ్య విధులు: ప్రమాణాలకు మించి కాలుష్యకారకాల విడుదల వద్దు (సె. 7); నిర్దేశించిన రక్షణలతో మాత్రమే ప్రమాదకర పదార్థాల నిర్వహణ (సె. 8); ప్రమాదాలను తెలియజేయడం, నియంత్రించడం (సె. 9). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) అమలు: ప్రవేశం, తనిఖీ (సె. 10), నమూనాలు (సె. 11), ప్రయోగశాలలు, విశ్లేషకులు (సె. 12–14). శిక్షలు: మొదట చేసినప్పుడు ఐదేళ్ల వరకు జైలు లేదా రూ. 1 లక్ష వరకు జరిమానా, లేదా రెండూ (సె. 15). 1 ఏప్రిల్ 2024 నుండి జన్ విశ్వాస్ (నిబంధనల సవరణ) చట్టం, 2023 దీని స్థానంలో న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి నిర్ణయించే ధన పెనాల్టీలు (సె. 14A నుండి 15F), NGT కి అప్పీల్ (సె. 15D), పర్యావరణ రక్షణ నిధి (సె. 16) తెచ్చింది. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: చట్టం సె. 2 లో ముఖ్య పదాలను నిర్వచిస్తుంది: (a) పర్యావరణం – నీరు, గాలి, భూమి, వాటికి మనుషులు, ఇతర జీవులు, మొక్కలు, సూక్ష్మజీవులు, ఆస్తితో ఉన్న పరస్పర సంబంధం; (b) పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యకారకం – పర్యావరణానికి హానికరమైన లేదా హానికరం కాగల సాంద్రతలో ఉన్న ఏదైనా ఘన, ద్రవ లేదా వాయు పదార్థం; (c) పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యం – పర్యావరణంలో ఏదైనా పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యకారకం ఉండడం; (ca) నిధి (2023 లో చేర్చబడింది) – సె. 16 కింది పర్యావరణ రక్షణ నిధి; (d) నిర్వహణ (handling) – ఒక పదార్థం తయారీ, ప్రాసెసింగ్, శుద్ధి, ప్యాకేజీ, నిల్వ, రవాణా, వినియోగం, సేకరణ, నాశనం, మార్పిడి, అమ్మకానికి పెట్టడం, బదిలీ లేదా అలాంటివి; (e) ప్రమాదకర పదార్థం – రసాయన లేదా భౌతిక-రసాయన లక్షణాల వల్ల లేదా నిర్వహణ వల్ల హాని కలిగించే అవకాశం ఉన్న పదార్థం లేదా మిశ్రమం; (f) ఆక్రమణదారు ( occupier ) – కర్మాగారం లేదా ఆవరణ వ్యవహారాలపై నియంత్రణ ఉన్న వ్యక్తి; (g) నిర్దేశించిన (prescribed) – చట్టం కింది నియమాల ద్వారా నిర్దేశించినది. సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే, EP చట్టం ఒక చట్రం (framework) చట్టం : లక్ష్యాన్ని (పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించి మెరుగుపరచడం) చెబుతుంది, చర్య తీసుకోవడానికి కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వానికి అధికారాలు ఇస్తుంది, కొన్ని సాధారణ విధులు విధిస్తుంది, వివరాలను నియమాలు, నోటిఫికేషన్లకు వదిలేస్తుంది.
keyPoints: పర్యావరణం: సె. 2(a), "inter-relationship" (పరస్పర సంబంధం) తో. పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యకారకం: సె. 2(b); సె. 7 ప్రమాణాలకు మించి విడుదలను నిషేధిస్తుంది. ప్రమాదకర పదార్థం: సె. 2(e); సె. 8 రక్షణలు. సె. 3(3) అధికార సంస్థ; సె. 5 ఆదేశాలు (మూసివేత, విద్యుత్, నీరు); సె. 5A NGT కి అప్పీల్. న్యాయనిర్ణయ అధికారి: సె. 15C; పెనాల్టీలు సె. 14A–15A; 10% జమతో NGT అప్పీల్ సె. 15D. సె. 19: అరవై రోజుల నోటీసు తర్వాత పౌరుడి ఫిర్యాదు.

selfTest.q: EP చట్టం ఎప్పుడు అమలులోకి వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: సె. 2(a) కింద "పర్యావరణం" ను నిర్వచించండి. అధికార సంస్థను ఏర్పాటు చేయడానికి కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వానికి ఏ సెక్షన్ అధికారం ఇస్తుంది? సె. 5 కింద ఇవ్వగల రెండు ఆదేశాలు చెప్పండి. సె. 7 ఉల్లంఘనకు ఇప్పుడు పెనాల్టీ ఎంత? సె. 19 కింద ఎవరు ఫిర్యాదు చేయవచ్చు?

hi.inOneMinute: What it is: Act No. 29 of 1986, assented to on 23 May 1986 and in force across India from 19 November 1986. Its long title: "An Act to provide for the protection and improvement of environment and for matters connected therewith." It implements decisions of the Stockholm Conference of June 1972. (See Diagram 1 .) Why it is called an umbrella Act: it covers the whole environment (water, air, land and their inter-relationship with living beings and property, s. 2(a)) and gives the Central Government very wide powers to take "all such measures" needed to protect and improve the environment (s. 3). Key powers: measures and standards (s. 3(2)); authorities (s. 3(3)); directions, including closure and stoppage of electricity or water (s. 5), with appeal to the NGT (s. 5A); rules (ss. 6, 25). Key duties: no discharge of pollutants beyond standards (s. 7); handling hazardous substances only under prescribed safeguards (s. 8); reporting and controlling accidents (s. 9). (See Diagram 2 .) Enforcement: entry and inspection (s. 10), samples (s. 11), laboratories and analysts (ss. 12–14). Penalties: as enacted, imprisonment up to five years or fine up to Rs. 1 lakh, or both (s. 15). From 1 April 2024 the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 replaced this with money penalties fixed by an adjudicating officer (ss. 14A to 15F), appeal to the NGT (s. 15D), and an Environmental Protection Fund (s. 16). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Preamble – recites that "decisions were taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held at Stockholm in June, 1972" for the protection and improvement of the human environment and "the prevention of hazards to human beings, other living creatures, plants and property", and that it is necessary to implement them. s. 2(a) – "environment" includes water, air and land "and the inter-relationship which exists among and between water, air and land, and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organism and property". s. 2(b) – "environmental pollutant" means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to environment. s. 2(c) – "environmental pollution" means the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant. s. 2(e) – "hazardous substance" means any substance or preparation which, by reason of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling, is liable to cause harm (to human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms, property or the environment). s. 3(1) – the Central Government may take all such measures "as it deems necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and improving the quality of the environment" and for preventing, controlling and abating environmental pollution. s. 5 – the Central Government may "issue directions in writing to any person, officer or any authority" and they "shall be bound to comply"; the Explanation includes "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or process" and the "stoppage or regulation of the supply of electricity or water or any other service". s. 7 – "No person carrying on any industry, operation or process shall discharge or emit" any environmental pollutant "in excess of such standards as may be prescribed". s. 8 – no person shall handle any hazardous substance "except in accordance with such procedure and after complying with such safeguards as may be prescribed". s. 14A (inserted 2023) – contravention of s. 7 or s. 8 attracts a penalty "which shall not be less than one lakh rupees but which may extend to fifteen lakh rupees", and Rs. 50,000 a day for a continuing contravention. s. 19 – no court shall take cognizance of an offence except on a complaint by the Central Government (or its authorised officer), the adjudicating officer (clause (aa), inserted 2023), or "any person who has given notice of not less than sixty days, in the manner prescribed". s. 24 (as substituted in 2023) – the Act and its rules "shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law".
hi.meaning: The Act defines the main terms in s. 2 : (a) environment – water, air, land and their inter-relationship with human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property; (b) environmental pollutant – any solid, liquid or gaseous substance in a concentration that is or may be injurious to environment; (c) environmental pollution – the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant; (ca) Fund (inserted 2023) – the Environmental Protection Fund under s. 16; (d) handling – manufacture, processing, treatment, package, storage, transportation, use, collection, destruction, conversion, offering for sale, transfer or the like of a substance; (e) hazardous substance – a substance or preparation liable to cause harm because of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling; (f) occupier – the person who has control over the affairs of the factory or the premises; (g) prescribed – prescribed by rules under the Act. In simple words, the EP Act is a framework law : it states the goal (protect and improve the environment), gives the Central Government powers to act, makes a few general duties, and leaves details to rules and notifications.
keyPoints: Environment: s. 2(a), with "inter-relationship". Environmental pollutant: s. 2(b); s. 7 bans emission beyond standards. Hazardous substance: s. 2(e); s. 8 safeguards. s. 3(3) authority; s. 5 directions (closure, electricity, water); s. 5A appeal to NGT. Adjudicating officer: s. 15C; penalties ss. 14A–15A; NGT appeal s. 15D with 10% deposit. s. 19: citizen complaint after sixty days' notice.

environmental-law-u3-t6.subtitle: The Air Act, 1981: control areas, consent, emission standards, directions and penalties

en.inOneMinute: Main statute: the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 (Air Act), made after the decisions "taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held in Stockholm in June, 1972" ( preamble ). (See Diagram 1 .) Air pollutant (s. 2(a)): any solid, liquid or gaseous substance "(including noise)" in the atmosphere in a concentration that may be injurious to human beings, other living creatures, plants, property or environment; air pollution (s. 2(b)) is the presence of any air pollutant in the atmosphere. Boards: the Pollution Control Boards under the Water Act also act as Boards under the Air Act (ss. 3, 4); the Central Board's main function is "to improve the quality of air" (s. 16). Core controls: the State Government declares air pollution control areas (s. 19); no one shall "establish or operate any industrial plant" there without the previous consent of the State Board (s. 21); the Board must decide within four months (s. 21(4)); no emission of any air pollutant in excess of the Board's standards (s. 22). (See Diagram 2 .) Enforcement: court orders (s. 22A), entry (s. 24), samples (s. 26), appeals (s. 31) and binding directions including closure and stoppage of electricity or water (s. 31A). Penalties: as enacted, imprisonment of 1½ to 6 years for breach of ss. 21, 22 or s. 31A directions (s. 37). The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 replaced most of this with penalties of Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh imposed by an adjudicating officer (ss. 37 to 39A), with appeal to the NGT (s. 39B), keeping imprisonment for failure to comply with s. 21 (s. 39D). (See Diagram 3 .) Courts: Delhi's bus fleet was converted to CNG, and "If there is a short supply of an essential commodity, then the priority must be of public health" ( M.C. Mehta , CNG, 2002); coal and coke-using industries near the Taj were made to shift to natural gas or relocate ( M.C. Mehta , Taj Trapezium, 1996); noise is controlled under Art. 21 ( In re Noise Pollution , 2005).
legalProvision: Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Freedom from noise pollution is part of it ( In re Noise Pollution ). Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – It shall be the duty of every citizen of India "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 253 – Parliament may make any law for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention, or any decision made at an international conference; the Air Act carries out the Stockholm decisions. Air Act, preamble – it records that "decisions were taken at the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held in Stockholm in June, 1972" to take steps to preserve the quality of air and control air pollution. s. 2(a) – "air pollutant" means "any solid, liquid or gaseous substance (including noise) present in the atmosphere in such concentration as may be or tend to be injurious to human beings or other living creatures or plants or property or environment". s. 2(b) – "air pollution" means the presence in the atmosphere of any air pollutant. s. 2(m) – "occupier", in relation to a factory or premises, means "the person who has control over the affairs of the factory or the premises". ss. 3, 4 – the Central and State Boards under the Water Act, 1974 act as the Boards under the Air Act; s. 5 lets a State constitute a State Board where none exists. s. 16(1) – "the main functions of the Central Board shall be to improve the quality of air" and to prevent, control or abate air pollution. s. 17(1)(g) – the State Board lays down "standards for emission of air pollutants into the atmosphere from industrial plants and automobiles". s. 19(1) – the State Government may declare "any area or areas within the State as air pollution control area or areas". s. 20 – the State Government instructs the motor-vehicle registering authority to enforce "the standards for emission of air pollutants from automobiles laid down by the State Board". s. 21(1) (as enacted) – "no person shall, without the previous consent of the State Board, establish or operate any industrial plant" in an air pollution control area; s. 21(4): the Board must grant or refuse consent "Within a period of four months after the receipt of the application". s. 22 – no person operating an industrial plant shall discharge "the emission of any air pollutant in excess of the standards laid down by the State Board". s. 22A – the Board may apply "to a court, not inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate" to restrain emissions. s. 23 – in an accident, the person in charge "shall forthwith intimate the fact of such occurrence or the apprehension of such occurrence to the State Board". s. 24 – power of entry and inspection; s. 26 – samples (analysis result "shall not be admissible in evidence in any legal proceeding unless" the procedure is followed); s. 31 – appeal within thirty days. s. 31A – the Board may "issue any directions in writing to any person, officer or authority", including "the closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry, operation or" process and "the stoppage or regulation of supply of electricity, water or any other service". ss. 37 to 39 (as enacted) – failure to comply with s. 21, s. 22 or s. 31A directions: imprisonment "not be less than one year and six months but which may extend to six years" and fine (s. 37(1)); 2 to 7 years if it continues for over a year after conviction (s. 37(2)); other offences: imprisonment up to three months or fine up to Rs. 10,000, or both (ss. 38, 39). ss. 40, 41 – offences by companies and Government departments; s. 43(1) – no court shall take cognizance "except on a complaint made by" the Board or its officer, or "any person who has given notice of not less than sixty days". Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 (No. 18 of 2023; assent 11 August 2023) – amends the Air Act: s. 21(1): "No person shall establish or operate any industrial plant in an air pollution control area unless the previous consent" of the State Board is obtained; the Central Government may exempt categories of plants; s. 21A: Central guidelines on consent; ss. 37, 38, 39: penalties "not less than ten thousand rupees, but which may extend to fifteen lakh rupees", with an additional daily penalty; s. 38A: Head of a Department liable to a penalty "equal to one month of his basic salary"; s. 39A: adjudicating officer "not below the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India or a Secretary to the State Government"; s. 39B: appeal to the NGT within sixty days, on depositing ten per cent of the penalty; s. 39C: penalties credited to the Environmental Protection Fund under s. 16 of the EP Act; s. 39D: failure to comply with s. 21 is punishable with imprisonment of 1½ to 6 years and fine; failure to pay a penalty within ninety days, up to three years; s. 43(1)(aa): the adjudicating officer may also complain.
en.meaning: Air pollutant – the statutory meaning in s. 2(a); it expressly includes noise. Air pollution – the presence of any air pollutant in the atmosphere (s. 2(b)). Air pollution control area – an area declared by the State Government under s. 19 in which the consent and emission controls of the Act apply. Emission standard – the limit, laid down by the State Board for industrial plants and automobiles, beyond which no air pollutant may be discharged (ss. 17(1)(g), 22). Adjudicating officer – the officer appointed under s. 39A (inserted in 2023) to impose penalties after an inquiry.
keyPoints: Air pollutant: s. 2(a), including noise. Air pollution: s. 2(b). Air pollution control area: s. 19; consent s. 21. s. 22: no emission beyond standards; s. 31A: closure, stoppage of electricity or water. Adjudicating officer: s. 39A (2023); penalties Rs. 10,000 to Rs. 15 lakh; NGT appeal s. 39B. Cases: CNG (2002), Taj (1996), Noise (2005).

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Noise is defined as unwanted sound"; "Nobody can claim a fundamental right to create noise by amplifying the sound of his speech"; no amplifiers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. except in public emergencies; no sound-emitting firecrackers between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. Why it matters: It treats noise, an air pollutant under the Air Act, as a threat to the right to life.
