hi.inOneMinute: "Pollution control mechanism" means the whole machinery the law uses to stop pollution before it happens and to act when it does happen. It has six working parts: Bodies: the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), the State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs), the Central Government and authorities set up under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (EP Act). Standards: limits on what may be discharged or emitted (EP Act ss. 3(2)(iii), (iv), 6, 7). Permission before starting: consent of the SPCB (Water Act s. 25; Air Act s. 21) and prior environmental clearance (EIA Notification , 2006). Directions: orders to close, stop or regulate an industry, including cutting off electricity or water (EP Act s. 5; Water Act s. 33A; Air Act s. 31A). Penalties: money penalties fixed by an adjudicating officer (after the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 and the Water Amendment Act, 2024), and prosecution for serious failures. Complaints and review: a citizen may complain to a court after 60 days' notice (EP Act s. 19(b); Water Act s. 49; Air Act s. 43), and appeals go to the National Green Tribunal (NGT). The Supreme Court has added two principles that guide the whole machinery: the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle ( Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum , 1996; A.P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu , 1999).
legalProvision: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974: ss. 3, 4 (Boards); ss. 16, 17 (functions); s. 25 (consent for new outlets and discharges); s. 26 (existing discharges); s. 27 (refusal or withdrawal of consent); s. 27A (Central guidelines on consent, added in 2024); s. 28 (appeal); s. 33A (directions); ss. 41 to 45C (penalties, adjudicating officer, appeal); s. 49 (cognizance). Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981: s. 5 (State Boards); ss. 16, 17 (functions); s. 21 (consent); s. 31 (appeal); s. 31A (directions); s. 31B (appeal to NGT); ss. 37 to 39D (penalties, adjudicating officer, offences); s. 43 (cognizance). Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: s. 3(1) (general power of the Central Government); s. 3(2) (list of measures); s. 3(3) (authorities); s. 5 (directions); s. 5A (appeal to NGT); s. 6 (rules on standards); s. 7 (no discharge in excess of standards); s. 10 (entry and inspection); ss. 14A to 15F (penalties, adjudicating officer, appeal); s. 19 (cognizance). EIA Notification, 2006 (S.O. 1533, 14-9-2006), made under EP Act s. 3(1) and s. 3(2)(v). National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: s. 16 (appeals), Schedule I (the Acts the NGT applies). Constitution: Art. 21 (right to life includes a clean environment), Art. 48A (State shall protect the environment), Art. 51A(g) (citizen's duty).
hi.meaning: No Act defines "pollution control mechanism". It is a study term for the bodies, powers and procedures that the Water Act, the Air Act and the EP Act together create. Water pollution (Water Act s. 2(e)) and air pollution (Air Act s. 2(b)) are defined in the two Acts; environmental pollution is defined in EP Act s. 2(c) as "the presence in the environment of any environmental pollutant". Consent: the written permission of the SPCB, without which no person shall establish or operate a polluting unit or outlet (Water Act s. 25(1); Air Act s. 21(1)). Environmental standards: the limits laid down by the Central Government for the quality of air, water or soil and for emissions or discharges (EP Act s. 3(2)(iii), (iv)). Prior environmental clearance : the clearance needed under the EIA Notification, 2006 for listed projects "before any construction work, or preparation of land" (para 2). Adjudicating officer : an officer appointed by the Central Government, "not below the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India or a Secretary to the State Government", to inquire and impose penalties (EP Act s. 15C; Air Act s. 39A; Water Act s. 45B).
keyPoints: Consent: Water s. 25, Air s. 21; four months; appeal Water s. 28, Air s. 31. Environmental standards: EP Act s. 3(2)(iii), (iv); s. 7 forbids discharge above them. Prior environmental clearance: EIA 2006; Category A to MoEFCC, Category B to SEIAA; four stages. Adjudicating officer: EP Act s. 15C, Air s. 39A, Water s. 45B; appeal to NGT in sixty days. Directions include closure and stopping electricity or water (EP Act s. 5; Water s. 33A; Air s. 31A). A citizen may complain after sixty days' notice (EP Act s. 19(b); Water s. 49; Air s. 43).

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar river; about 35,000 hect
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". The Court directed the Central Government to constitute an authority under EP Act s. 3(3) to deal with the tanneries. Why it matters: It shows how the Court uses s. 3(3) to create a special authority when the regular machinery fails, and it gave the mechanism its two guiding principles.
A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu , (1999) 2 SCC 718 (Supreme Court; S.B. Majmudar and M. Jagannadha Rao JJ; 27 January 1999)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Board refused consent to a castor oil derivatives unit (a "red category" industry) near t
caseLaws.facts: 28 allowed the unit's appeal. Principle: Under the precautionary principle "the burden of proof is to be placed on those attempting to alter the status quo"; the industry must prove it is safe. The Court noted that "Scientific conclusions are subject to perpetual revision" and asked for expert bodies in environmental cases. Why it matters: It is the leading case on how consent decisions must be made, and on placing the burden of proof on the polluter.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (CNG case), (2002) 4 SCC 356; AIR 2002 SC 1696 (Supreme Court; B.N. Kirpal, V.N. Khare and Ashok Bhan JJ; 5 April 2002)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Delhi's air was badly polluted by diesel buses
caseLaws.facts: On 28 July 1998 the Court ordered the city bus fleet to be converted to CNG, and an authority constituted under EP Act s. 3 (EPCA, the Bhure Lal Committee) worked out the steps. Principle: Directions of the authority under s. 3 are "final and binding"; public health has priority, and the Court imposed a daily charge per bus that ran on diesel after the deadline. Why it matters: It shows the mechanism in action: an EP Act authority, standards and directions, enforced by the Court.

environmental-law-u3-t13.subtitle: The National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: composition, original and appellate jurisdiction, relief and appeal

en.inOneMinute: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is a specialised court for environmental cases. It was created by the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (No. 19 of 2010). The Act came into force, and the Tribunal was established, on 18 October 2010. It has judges and experts sitting together. The number of Expert Members on a bench must equal the number of Judicial Members (s. 4(4)(c) proviso ). It has three kinds of jurisdiction : Original jurisdiction (s. 14): all civil cases involving a "substantial question relating to environment" arising out of the seven Acts in Schedule I. Relief and restitution (ss. 15, 17): compensation to victims and restoration of property and the environment, with no-fault liability for accidents. Appellate jurisdiction (s. 16): appeals against orders under the Water, Air, EP, Forest, Cess and Biological Diversity Acts, including grant or refusal of environmental clearance. It must apply "the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle" (s. 20). It is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure or the Evidence Act. It has civil court powers, including interim orders and cease-and- desist orders (s. 19). Appeal lies to the Supreme Court within ninety days (s. 22). Civil courts are barred (s. 29). The Supreme Court has held that the NGT can act suo motu ( Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha , 2021).
legalProvision: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: Preamble (Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992, Article 21). s. 2 (definitions: accident, environment, hazardous substance, person, substantial question relating to environment). s. 3 (establishment). s. 4 (composition). s. 5 (qualifications). ss. 6, 7 (appointment; term). s. 10A (selection and conditions of service, now governed by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026). s. 14 (original jurisdiction). s. 15 (relief, compensation and restitution). s. 16 (appellate jurisdiction). s. 17 (liability; no fault). s. 18 (who may apply). s. 19 (procedure and powers). s. 20 (principles to apply). ss. 21–25 (majority, appeal, costs, Environmental Relief Fund, execution). ss. 26–28, 30 (penalties and cognizance). s. 29 (bar of civil courts). s. 33 (overriding effect). s. 38 (repeal of the 1995 and 1997 Acts). Schedules I, II and III. Constitution: Article 21 (right to a healthy environment, as the preamble records).
en.meaning: Tribunal (s. 2(1)(n)): the National Green Tribunal established under s. 3. Substantial question relating to environment (s. 2(1)(m)): includes an instance where: there is "a direct violation of a specific statutory environmental obligation" by which (A) "the community at large other than an individual or group of individuals is affected or likely to be affected", or (B) "the gravity of damage to the environment or property is substantial", or (C) "the damage to public health is broadly measurable"; or "the environmental consequences relate to a specific activity or a point source of pollution". Accident (s. 2(1)(a)): a "fortuitous or sudden or unintended occurrence while handling any hazardous substance or equipment, or plant, or vehicle" causing death, injury or damage. It does not include an accident "by reason only of war or civil disturbance". Expert Member (s. 2(1)(d)): a member who holds the qualifications in s. 5(2) and "is not a Judicial Member". Restitution: restoring damaged property or "the environment for such area or areas, as the Tribunal may think fit" (s. 15(1)(b), (c)). Suo motu power: the power to start a case on the Tribunal's own motion, without an application, recognised in Ankita Sinha (2021).
keyPoints: Substantial question relating to environment: s. 2(1)(m); community affected, substantial damage, or measurable public health damage; Schedule I Acts only. Expert Member: 10–20; equal to Judicial Members on every bench (s. 4). Restitution: of property and the environment (s. 15); in addition to PLI relief; no fault for accidents (s. 17(3)). Suo motu power: recognised in Ankita Sinha (2021), within the environmental domain. Appeals under s. 16 (ten heads, thirty days); appeal to the Supreme Court in ninety days (s. 22). Section 20: sustainable development, precautionary principle , polluter pays principle.

caseLaws.facts: Bhopal Gas Peedith Mahila Udyog Sangathan v. Union of India, (2012) 8 SCC 326 (Supreme Court; S.H. Kapadia CJI, A.K. Patnaik and Swatanter Kumar JJ; 9 August 2012)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A petition concerned the toxic waste left at the Union Carbide factory in Bhopal after the ga
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Environmental matters covered by the NGT Act "should be instituted and litigated before the National Green Tribunal". This is to "avoid likelihood of conflict of orders between the High Courts and the NGT" and to give "expeditious and specialized justice". Why it matters: It made the NGT the main forum for environmental cases. (In 2014, in Adarsh Co-operative Housing Society , the Court said these paragraphs needed reconsideration.)

Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha, Civil Appeal Nos. 12122–12123 of 2018 and connected appeals (Supreme Court; A.M. Khanwilkar, Hrishikesh Roy and C.T. Ravikumar JJ; judgment by Hrishikesh Roy J; 7 October 2021)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The NGT took suo motu notice of a news report on the Deonar dumping ground in Mumbai and pass
caseLaws.facts: The corporation argued that the NGT had no suo motu power. Principle: The NGT has a "sui generis" character and, "even in the absence of an application, can self-ignite action". But it cannot "travel beyond its environmental domain" and has no "inherent power of residuary character". Why it matters: It settled that the NGT can act on its own, within the limits of the Act.
A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu , (1999) 2 SCC 718 (Supreme Court; S.B. Majmudar and M. Jagannadha Rao JJ; 27 January 1999)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Scientific questions arose about whether a castor oil derivatives unit endangered the reservo
caseLaws.facts: The Court found the existing tribunals inadequate. Principle: Environmental cases need courts of "one professional Judge and two experts". The Court asked for changes in the law to provide such bodies. Why it matters: It was a key step towards the NGT's design of Judicial and Expert Members sitting together in equal numbers.

te.inOneMinute: జాతీయ హరిత ట్రిబ్యునల్ (NGT) పర్యావరణ కేసుల కోసం ఒక ప్రత్యేక న్యాయస్థానం. దీనిని జాతీయ హరిత ట్రిబ్యునల్ చట్టం, 2010 (No. 19 of 2010) ఏర్పాటు చేసింది. చట్టం 18 అక్టోబర్ 2010 న అమలులోకి వచ్చింది, అదే రోజు ట్రిబ్యునల్ స్థాపించబడింది. ఇందులో న్యాయమూర్తులు, నిపుణులు కలిసి కూర్చుంటారు. ఒక బెంచ్‌లో నిపుణ సభ్యుల సంఖ్య జ్యుడీషియల్ సభ్యుల సంఖ్యకు సమానంగా ఉండాలి (సె. 4(4)(c) ప్రొవిసో). దీనికి మూడు రకాల అధికార పరిధి ఉంది: మూల అధికార పరిధి (సె. 14): షెడ్యూల్ I లోని ఏడు చట్టాల నుండి ఉత్పన్నమయ్యే "substantial question relating to environment" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణానికి సంబంధించిన గణనీయమైన ప్రశ్న) ఉన్న అన్ని సివిల్ కేసులు. ఉపశమనం, పునరుద్ధరణ (సె. 15, 17): బాధితులకు పరిహారం, ఆస్తి, పర్యావరణ పునరుద్ధరణ; ప్రమాదాలకు నో-ఫాల్ట్ బాధ్యత. అప్పీలేట్ అధికార పరిధి (సె. 16): పర్యావరణ అనుమతి మంజూరు లేదా తిరస్కరణతో సహా నీటి, వాయు, EP, అటవీ, సెస్, జీవ వైవిధ్య చట్టాల కింది ఉత్తర్వులపై అప్పీళ్లు. అది "the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle" (అర్థం: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి, ముందుజాగ్రత్త సూత్రం, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రాలు) వర్తింపజేయాలి (సె. 20). ఇది సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్‌కు లేదా సాక్ష్య చట్టానికి కట్టుబడి ఉండదు. మధ్యంతర ఉత్తర్వులు, ఆపివేత ఉత్తర్వులతో సహా సివిల్ కోర్టు అధికారాలు కలిగి ఉంది (సె. 19). తొంభై రోజుల్లో సుప్రీంకోర్టుకు అప్పీల్ (సె. 22). సివిల్ కోర్టులకు అధికారం లేదు (సె. 29). NGT స్వయంగా (suo motu) చర్య తీసుకోవచ్చని సుప్రీంకోర్టు తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది ( Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha , 2021).
te.meaning: ట్రిబ్యునల్ (సె. 2(1)(n)): సె. 3 కింద స్థాపించిన జాతీయ హరిత ట్రిబ్యునల్ . పర్యావరణానికి సంబంధించిన గణనీయమైన ప్రశ్న (సె. 2(1)(m)): ఈ సందర్భాలు ఇందులో ఉంటాయి: "a direct violation of a specific statutory environmental obligation" (అర్థం: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట చట్టబద్ధ పర్యావరణ బాధ్యత ప్రత్యక్ష ఉల్లంఘన) ఉండి, దాని వల్ల (A) "the community at large other than an individual or group of individuals is affected or likely to be affected" (అర్థం: ఒక వ్యక్తి లేదా వ్యక్తుల సమూహం కాకుండా సమాజం మొత్తం ప్రభావితమవుతుంది లేదా ప్రభావితమయ్యే అవకాశం ఉంది), లేదా (B) "the gravity of damage to the environment or property is substantial" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణానికి లేదా ఆస్తికి నష్టం తీవ్రత గణనీయంగా ఉంది), లేదా (C) "the damage to public health is broadly measurable" (అర్థం: ప్రజారోగ్యానికి నష్టాన్ని స్థూలంగా కొలవవచ్చు); లేదా "the environmental consequences relate to a specific activity or a point source of pollution" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణ పర్యవసానాలు ఒక నిర్దిష్ట కార్యకలాపానికి లేదా కాలుష్య బిందు మూలానికి సంబంధించినవి). ప్రమాదం (సె. 2(1)(a)): "fortuitous or sudden or unintended occurrence while handling any hazardous substance or equipment, or plant, or vehicle" (అర్థం: ఏదైనా ప్రమాదకర పదార్థం, పరికరం, ప్లాంట్ లేదా వాహనాన్ని హ్యాండిల్ చేస్తున్నప్పుడు యాదృచ్ఛికంగా, ఆకస్మికంగా లేదా అనుకోకుండా జరిగే సంఘటన), దాని వల్ల మరణం, గాయం లేదా నష్టం కలగాలి. "by reason only of war or civil disturbance" (అర్థం: కేవలం యుద్ధం లేదా పౌర అల్లర్ల కారణంగా) జరిగిన ప్రమాదం ఇందులో చేరదు. నిపుణ సభ్యుడు (సె. 2(1)(d)): సె. 5(2) లోని అర్హతలు కలిగి, "is not a Judicial Member" (అర్థం: జ్యుడీషియల్ సభ్యుడు కాని) సభ్యుడు. పునరుద్ధరణ: నష్టపోయిన ఆస్తిని లేదా "the environment for such area or areas, as the Tribunal may think fit" (అర్థం: ట్రిబ్యునల్ తగినదని భావించే ప్రాంతం లేదా ప్రాంతాల పర్యావరణాన్ని) పూర్వ స్థితికి తీసుకురావడం (సె. 15(1)(b), (c)). స్వయంచాలక ( suo motu ) అధికారం: దరఖాస్తు లేకుండానే ట్రిబ్యునల్ స్వయంగా కేసు ప్రారంభించే అధికారం; Ankita Sinha (2021) లో గుర్తించబడింది.
keyPoints: పర్యావరణానికి సంబంధించిన గణనీయమైన ప్రశ్న: సె. 2(1)(m); సమాజం ప్రభావితం, గణనీయమైన నష్టం, లేదా కొలవదగిన ప్రజారోగ్య నష్టం; షెడ్యూల్ I చట్టాలు మాత్రమే. నిపుణ సభ్యుడు: 10–20; ప్రతి బెంచ్‌లో జ్యుడీషియల్ సభ్యులకు సమానం (సె. 4). పునరుద్ధరణ: ఆస్తి, పర్యావరణం (సె. 15); PLI ఉపశమనానికి అదనం; ప్రమాదాలకు నో-ఫాల్ట్ (సె. 17(3)). స్వయంచాలక అధికారం: Ankita Sinha (2021) లో గుర్తించబడింది, పర్యావరణ పరిధిలోనే. సె. 16 కింద అప్పీళ్లు (పది శీర్షికలు, ముప్పై రోజులు); తొంభై రోజుల్లో సుప్రీంకోర్టుకు అప్పీల్ (సె. 22). సెక్షన్ 20: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి, ముందుజాగ్రత్త సూత్రం, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం.

selfTest.q: NGT ఎప్పుడు స్థాపించబడింది?
selfTest.a: సె. 14 కింద దరఖాస్తుకు కాల పరిమితి ఎంత? షెడ్యూల్ I లోని ఏవైనా నాలుగు చట్టాలను పేర్కొనండి. పర్యావరణ అనుమతి తిరస్కరణపై NGT అప్పీల్ వినగలదా? NGT ఏ మూడు సూత్రాలను వర్తింపజేయాలి? NGT స్వయంగా చర్య తీసుకోవచ్చని ఏ కేసు తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది?

hi.inOneMinute: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is a specialised court for environmental cases. It was created by the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010 (No. 19 of 2010). The Act came into force, and the Tribunal was established, on 18 October 2010. It has judges and experts sitting together. The number of Expert Members on a bench must equal the number of Judicial Members (s. 4(4)(c) proviso ). It has three kinds of jurisdiction : Original jurisdiction (s. 14): all civil cases involving a "substantial question relating to environment" arising out of the seven Acts in Schedule I. Relief and restitution (ss. 15, 17): compensation to victims and restoration of property and the environment, with no-fault liability for accidents. Appellate jurisdiction (s. 16): appeals against orders under the Water, Air, EP, Forest, Cess and Biological Diversity Acts, including grant or refusal of environmental clearance. It must apply "the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle" (s. 20). It is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure or the Evidence Act. It has civil court powers, including interim orders and cease-and- desist orders (s. 19). Appeal lies to the Supreme Court within ninety days (s. 22). Civil courts are barred (s. 29). The Supreme Court has held that the NGT can act suo motu ( Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha , 2021).
legalProvision: National Green Tribunal Act, 2010: Preamble (Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992, Article 21). s. 2 (definitions: accident, environment, hazardous substance, person, substantial question relating to environment). s. 3 (establishment). s. 4 (composition). s. 5 (qualifications). ss. 6, 7 (appointment; term). s. 10A (selection and conditions of service, now governed by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026). s. 14 (original jurisdiction). s. 15 (relief, compensation and restitution). s. 16 (appellate jurisdiction). s. 17 (liability; no fault). s. 18 (who may apply). s. 19 (procedure and powers). s. 20 (principles to apply). ss. 21–25 (majority, appeal, costs, Environmental Relief Fund, execution). ss. 26–28, 30 (penalties and cognizance). s. 29 (bar of civil courts). s. 33 (overriding effect). s. 38 (repeal of the 1995 and 1997 Acts). Schedules I, II and III. Constitution: Article 21 (right to a healthy environment, as the preamble records).
hi.meaning: Tribunal (s. 2(1)(n)): the National Green Tribunal established under s. 3. Substantial question relating to environment (s. 2(1)(m)): includes an instance where: there is "a direct violation of a specific statutory environmental obligation" by which (A) "the community at large other than an individual or group of individuals is affected or likely to be affected", or (B) "the gravity of damage to the environment or property is substantial", or (C) "the damage to public health is broadly measurable"; or "the environmental consequences relate to a specific activity or a point source of pollution". Accident (s. 2(1)(a)): a "fortuitous or sudden or unintended occurrence while handling any hazardous substance or equipment, or plant, or vehicle" causing death, injury or damage. It does not include an accident "by reason only of war or civil disturbance". Expert Member (s. 2(1)(d)): a member who holds the qualifications in s. 5(2) and "is not a Judicial Member". Restitution: restoring damaged property or "the environment for such area or areas, as the Tribunal may think fit" (s. 15(1)(b), (c)). Suo motu power: the power to start a case on the Tribunal's own motion, without an application, recognised in Ankita Sinha (2021).
keyPoints: Substantial question relating to environment: s. 2(1)(m); community affected, substantial damage, or measurable public health damage; Schedule I Acts only. Expert Member: 10–20; equal to Judicial Members on every bench (s. 4). Restitution: of property and the environment (s. 15); in addition to PLI relief; no fault for accidents (s. 17(3)). Suo motu power: recognised in Ankita Sinha (2021), within the environmental domain. Appeals under s. 16 (ten heads, thirty days); appeal to the Supreme Court in ninety days (s. 22). Section 20: sustainable development, precautionary principle , polluter pays principle.

caseLaws.facts: Bhopal Gas Peedith Mahila Udyog Sangathan v. Union of India, (2012) 8 SCC 326 (Supreme Court; S.H. Kapadia CJI, A.K. Patnaik and Swatanter Kumar JJ; 9 August 2012)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A petition concerned the toxic waste left at the Union Carbide factory in Bhopal after the ga
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Environmental matters covered by the NGT Act "should be instituted and litigated before the National Green Tribunal". This is to "avoid likelihood of conflict of orders between the High Courts and the NGT" and to give "expeditious and specialized justice". Why it matters: It made the NGT the main forum for environmental cases. (In 2014, in Adarsh Co-operative Housing Society , the Court said these paragraphs needed reconsideration.)

Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha, Civil Appeal Nos. 12122–12123 of 2018 and connected appeals (Supreme Court; A.M. Khanwilkar, Hrishikesh Roy and C.T. Ravikumar JJ; judgment by Hrishikesh Roy J; 7 October 2021)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The NGT took suo motu notice of a news report on the Deonar dumping ground in Mumbai and pass
caseLaws.facts: The corporation argued that the NGT had no suo motu power. Principle: The NGT has a "sui generis" character and, "even in the absence of an application, can self-ignite action". But it cannot "travel beyond its environmental domain" and has no "inherent power of residuary character". Why it matters: It settled that the NGT can act on its own, within the limits of the Act.
A.P. Pollution Control Board v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu , (1999) 2 SCC 718 (Supreme Court; S.B. Majmudar and M. Jagannadha Rao JJ; 27 January 1999)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Scientific questions arose about whether a castor oil derivatives unit endangered the reservo
caseLaws.facts: The Court found the existing tribunals inadequate. Principle: Environmental cases need courts of "one professional Judge and two experts". The Court asked for changes in the law to provide such bodies. Why it matters: It was a key step towards the NGT's design of Judicial and Expert Members sitting together in equal numbers.

Explanation. Since 'air' appears in no legislative list, Parliament used Article 253 (power to implement international agreements) to enact the Air Act following the Stockholm Conference, 1972.

Which body administers the Air Act, 1981 at the state level?

Explanation. Sections 3-5 of the Air Act do not create a new Board; the existing SPCB (and CPCB) from the Water Act, 1974 are given additional air-pollution functions.

Explanation. Section 19 empowers the State Government, after consulting the State Board, to declare an Air Pollution Control Area and restrict fuels/appliances within it.

en.meaning:
According to its Preamble, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 implements the decisions of which conference?

Explanation. The Preamble says the Act implements the decisions of the Stockholm Conference of June 1972 on protecting and improving the human environment. It is an umbrella Act, because it reaches every kind of pollution and not one medium alone.

Section 3 of the EPA, 1986 is significant because it:

Explanation. Section 3's broad, general power is the legal basis for the EIA Notification, CRZ Notifications, Hazardous Waste Rules, Plastic/Solid Waste Rules, and most other Indian environmental subordinate legislation.

How does the Central Government's Section 5 direction power differ from the State Board's powers under the Water/Air Acts?

Explanation. Section 5 is exercised directly by the Central Government (not a State Board) and is broader, not confined to a single pollution medium.

Section 8 of the EPA, 1986 is the statutory foundation for which set of rules?

en.meaning:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 implements India's obligations under which international instrument?

Explanation. The Act implements India's ratification of the Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992, adopted at the Rio Earth Summit.

Which body maintains the People's Biodiversity Register at the grassroots level?

Explanation. Biodiversity Management Committees, constituted by local bodies under Section 41, maintain People's Biodiversity Registers documenting local resources and traditional knowledge.

Under Section 7, an Indian citizen seeking to obtain a biological resource for commercial utilisation must:

Explanation. Section 7 requires only prior intimation to the State Biodiversity Board for Indian citizens/entities seeking commercial utilisation, a lighter requirement than Section 3's NBA approval for foreign entities.

Section 6 of the Act requires which approval before an IPR based on Indian biological resources can be granted?

en.meaning:
The National Green Tribunal hears civil cases involving a substantial environmental question under how many listed Acts?

Explanation. Section 14 gives the Tribunal jurisdiction over civil cases where a substantial environmental question arises from the Acts in Schedule I, which lists seven Acts.

The NGT's bench composition deliberately combines:

Explanation. The NGT combines Judicial Members with Expert Members qualified in environmental science/engineering, since environmental disputes routinely involve technical questions.

Which of the following is NOT listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act, and therefore outside the Tribunal's original jurisdiction for disputes arising purely under it?

Explanation. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 is NOT listed in Schedule I of the NGT Act — a frequently tested exclusion. Disputes purely under it go to the High Court or Supreme Court.

Under section 4 of the NGT Act, the Tribunal has a full-time Chairperson, ten to twenty full-time Judicial Members and:

environmental-law-u3-t25.subtitle: Previous Osmania University LL.B. exam questions for Environmental Law, Unit 3, each linked to the notes or case-law post that answers it. Sourced from actual OU Paper V: Environmental Law question papers — August/September 2013, February/March 2016, March/April 2017, September/October 2017, September/October 2021, and February 2026 (Code No. H-12005). environmental-law-u4-t2.subtitle: How the Supreme Court read a right to a clean environment into Article 21

en.inOneMinute: The Constitution has no Article that says in words "everyone has a right to a wholesome environment". The Supreme Court has read this right into Article 21 (protection of life and personal liberty), and read Article 21 together with Article 48A (State's duty) and Article 51A(g) (citizen's duty). (See Diagram 1 .) Three steps in the case law (See Diagram 2 .): Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. (1985): limestone quarries in the Mussoorie hills closed; hardship to lessees is "a price that has to be paid for protecting and safe-guarding the right of the people to live in healthy environment". Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991): the right to life under Art. 21 "includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life". Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1994): pollution of the environment "should be regarded as amounting to violation of Article 21"; a lease of open-space land was quashed . Because it is part of Art. 21, the right is a Fundamental Right : it can be enforced by writ under Art. 32 (Supreme Court) and Art. 226 (High Courts), often through public interest litigation.
legalProvision: Article 21 – "Protection of life and personal liberty.—No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – the duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Article 226(1) – every High Court may issue "directions, orders or writs" to any person or authority, including any Government, "for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose".
en.meaning: Right to life – the right in Art. 21. The Supreme Court reads "life" as more than mere survival: in Virender Gaur it spoke of the "right to life with human dignity". Wholesome environment – an environment fit for healthy human life: water and air free from pollution , sanitation, and ecological balance. The courts use phrases such as "healthy environment" ( RLEK ), "pollution free water and air" ( Subhash Kumar ) and "hygienic environment" ( Virender Gaur ). Ecological balance – the natural balance between living things and their surroundings (forests, water springs, soil), which human activity like mining can disturb. Public interest litigation (PIL) – a case brought to court for the benefit of the public or a section of it, not for the petitioner 's private gain. Derived right – a right not written in words but read by the courts into an existing Article (here, Art. 21).
keyPoints: The right to life under Art. 21 includes the right to a wholesome environment. Courts read Art. 21 with Arts. 48A and 51A(g) ( Virender Gaur ). RLEK (1985): right to live in a healthy environment with minimal disturbance of ecological balance. Subhash Kumar (1991): pollution-free water and air are part of Art. 21. Virender Gaur (1994): pollution amounts to violation of Art. 21. Enforced by writ under Arts. 32 and 226, often by public interest litigation, which must be genuine.

caseLaws.facts: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. AIR 1985 SC 652; (1985) 2 SCC 431 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati, A.N. Sen and Ranganath Misra JJ; order of 12 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter dated 2 July 1983 from RLEK, Dehra Dun, about illegal limestone mining in the Mussoo
caseLaws.facts: Quarrying affected "the perennial water springs". The Bhargav Committee classified the quarries into categories A, B and C. Principle: The Court closed category C quarries and many others, and allowed some category A quarries to work. Hardship to the lessees was "a price that has to be paid for protecting and safe-guarding the right of the people to live in healthy environment" "with minimal disturbance of ecological balance". Why it matters: Described by the Court as the first case of its kind on environment and ecological balance; it recognised the people's right to live in a healthy environment.
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar AIR 1991 SC 420; (1991) 1 SCC 598 (Supreme Court; K.N. Singh J for himself and N.D. Ojha J; reasons given on 9 January 1991)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner alleged that sludge and slurry from TISCO's washeries at Ghatotand were being
caseLaws.facts: He also asked to be allowed to collect the slurry himself. Principle: "Right to live is a fundamental right under Art 21 of the Constitution" and "it includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life." But PIL "cannot be invoked by a person or body or person to satisfy his or its personal grudge and enmity". The petition was filed "for the petitioner's personal interest" and was dismissed with costs of Rs. 5,000. Why it matters: It is the clearest early statement that pollution-free water and air are part of Art. 21, and also a warning against misuse of PIL.
Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) 2 SCC 577 (Supreme Court; K. Ramaswamy and N. Venkatachala JJ; decided 24 November 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land in Town Planning Scheme No
caseLaws.facts: 5 of Thanesar (Kurukshetra) was earmarked for open spaces. The Government allotted it to the Punjab Samaj Sabha, which began building a Dharamshala. Residents challenged it. Principle: Right to life with human dignity includes "the protection and preservation of environment, ecological balance free from pollution of air and water, sanitation"; environmental and pollution harm "should be regarded as amounting to violation of Article 21". The lease was "clearly without authority of law and jurisdiction"; the construction was to be pulled down. Why it matters: It reads Art. 21 together with Arts. 48A and 51A(g), and shows the right protecting open spaces and sanitation, not only clean water and air.

selfTest.q: Which Article is the right to a wholesome environment read into?
selfTest.a: What did Subhash Kumar say Art. 21 includes? Why was the petition in Subhash Kumar dismissed? What did the Court close in RLEK ? What did the Court order in Virender Gaur ? Under which Articles can the right be enforced?

te.inOneMinute: "ప్రతి ఒక్కరికీ ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణ హక్కు ఉంది" అని మాటల్లో చెప్పే ఆర్టికల్ రాజ్యాంగంలో లేదు. సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఈ హక్కును ఆర్టికల్ 21 (జీవితం, వ్యక్తిగత స్వేచ్ఛ రక్షణ)లో చదివింది; ఆర్టికల్ 21ను ఆర్టికల్ 48A (రాజ్యం విధి), ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g) (పౌరుడి విధి)తో కలిపి చదివింది. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) కేసు చట్టంలో మూడు దశలు ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.): Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. (1985): ముస్సోరీ కొండల్లోని సున్నపురాయి క్వారీలు మూసివేయబడ్డాయి; లీజుదారులకు కష్టం "a price that has to be paid for protecting and safe-guarding the right of the people to live in healthy environment" (అర్థం: ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణంలో జీవించే ప్రజల హక్కును రక్షించడానికి, కాపాడడానికి చెల్లించాల్సిన మూల్యం). Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991): ఆర్టికల్ 21 కింద జీవించే హక్కు "includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life" (అర్థం: జీవితాన్ని పూర్తిగా అనుభవించడానికి కాలుష్యం లేని నీరు, గాలిని అనుభవించే హక్కును కలిగి ఉంటుంది). Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1994): పర్యావరణ కాలుష్యం "should be regarded as amounting to violation of Article 21" (అర్థం: ఆర్టికల్ 21 ఉల్లంఘనగా పరిగణించాలి); బహిరంగ స్థల భూమి లీజు రద్దు చేయబడింది. ఇది ఆర్టికల్ 21లో భాగం కాబట్టి, ఈ హక్కు ఒక ప్రాథమిక హక్కు : ఆర్టికల్ 32 (సుప్రీంకోర్టు), ఆర్టికల్ 226 (హైకోర్టులు) కింద రిట్ ద్వారా, తరచుగా ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం ద్వారా అమలు చేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning: జీవించే హక్కు (Right to life) – ఆర్టికల్ 21లోని హక్కు. సుప్రీంకోర్టు "life" (అర్థం: జీవితం)ను కేవలం బతికి ఉండడం కంటే ఎక్కువగా చదువుతుంది: Virender Gaur లో అది "right to life with human dignity" (అర్థం: మానవ గౌరవంతో జీవించే హక్కు) గురించి మాట్లాడింది. ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణం ( Wholesome environment ) – ఆరోగ్యకరమైన మానవ జీవితానికి తగిన పర్యావరణం: కాలుష్యం లేని నీరు, గాలి, పారిశుద్ధ్యం, పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యత. కోర్టులు "healthy environment" (అర్థం: ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణం) ( RLEK ), "pollution free water and air" (అర్థం: కాలుష్యం లేని నీరు, గాలి) ( Subhash Kumar ), "hygienic environment" (అర్థం: పరిశుభ్రమైన పర్యావరణం) ( Virender Gaur ) వంటి పదాలు వాడతాయి. పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యత (Ecological balance) – జీవులకు, వాటి పరిసరాలకు (అడవులు, నీటి ఊటలు, నేల) మధ్య ఉన్న సహజ సమతుల్యత; మైనింగ్ వంటి మానవ కార్యకలాపాలు దీన్ని దెబ్బతీయగలవు. ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం ( Public interest litigation – PIL) – పిటిషనర్ స్వంత లాభం కోసం కాకుండా, ప్రజల లేదా వారిలో ఒక వర్గం ప్రయోజనం కోసం కోర్టుకు తెచ్చిన కేసు. ఉత్పన్న హక్కు (Derived right) – మాటల్లో రాయబడకపోయినా, కోర్టులు ఉన్న ఆర్టికల్‌లో (ఇక్కడ ఆర్టికల్ 21) చదివిన హక్కు.
keyPoints: ఆర్టికల్ 21 కింద జీవించే హక్కులో ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణం హక్కు ఉంది. కోర్టులు ఆర్టికల్ 21ను ఆర్టికల్స్ 48A, 51A(g)తో కలిపి చదువుతాయి ( Virender Gaur ). RLEK (1985): పర్యావరణ సమతుల్యతకు కనీస భంగంతో ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణంలో జీవించే హక్కు. Subhash Kumar (1991): కాలుష్యం లేని నీరు, గాలి ఆర్టికల్ 21లో భాగం. Virender Gaur (1994): కాలుష్యం ఆర్టికల్ 21 ఉల్లంఘనకు సమానం. ఆర్టికల్స్ 32, 226 కింద రిట్ ద్వారా, తరచుగా ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం ద్వారా అమలు; అది నిజమైనదై ఉండాలి.

hi.inOneMinute: The Constitution has no Article that says in words "everyone has a right to a wholesome environment". The Supreme Court has read this right into Article 21 (protection of life and personal liberty), and read Article 21 together with Article 48A (State's duty) and Article 51A(g) (citizen's duty). (See Diagram 1 .) Three steps in the case law (See Diagram 2 .): Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. (1985): limestone quarries in the Mussoorie hills closed; hardship to lessees is "a price that has to be paid for protecting and safe-guarding the right of the people to live in healthy environment". Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991): the right to life under Art. 21 "includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life". Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1994): pollution of the environment "should be regarded as amounting to violation of Article 21"; a lease of open-space land was quashed . Because it is part of Art. 21, the right is a Fundamental Right : it can be enforced by writ under Art. 32 (Supreme Court) and Art. 226 (High Courts), often through public interest litigation.
legalProvision: Article 21 – "Protection of life and personal liberty.—No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – the duty of every citizen "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Article 226(1) – every High Court may issue "directions, orders or writs" to any person or authority, including any Government, "for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose".
hi.meaning: Right to life – the right in Art. 21. The Supreme Court reads "life" as more than mere survival: in Virender Gaur it spoke of the "right to life with human dignity". Wholesome environment – an environment fit for healthy human life: water and air free from pollution , sanitation, and ecological balance. The courts use phrases such as "healthy environment" ( RLEK ), "pollution free water and air" ( Subhash Kumar ) and "hygienic environment" ( Virender Gaur ). Ecological balance – the natural balance between living things and their surroundings (forests, water springs, soil), which human activity like mining can disturb. Public interest litigation (PIL) – a case brought to court for the benefit of the public or a section of it, not for the petitioner 's private gain. Derived right – a right not written in words but read by the courts into an existing Article (here, Art. 21).
keyPoints: The right to life under Art. 21 includes the right to a wholesome environment. Courts read Art. 21 with Arts. 48A and 51A(g) ( Virender Gaur ). RLEK (1985): right to live in a healthy environment with minimal disturbance of ecological balance. Subhash Kumar (1991): pollution-free water and air are part of Art. 21. Virender Gaur (1994): pollution amounts to violation of Art. 21. Enforced by writ under Arts. 32 and 226, often by public interest litigation, which must be genuine.

caseLaws.facts: Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. AIR 1985 SC 652; (1985) 2 SCC 431 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati, A.N. Sen and Ranganath Misra JJ; order of 12 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter dated 2 July 1983 from RLEK, Dehra Dun, about illegal limestone mining in the Mussoo
caseLaws.facts: Quarrying affected "the perennial water springs". The Bhargav Committee classified the quarries into categories A, B and C. Principle: The Court closed category C quarries and many others, and allowed some category A quarries to work. Hardship to the lessees was "a price that has to be paid for protecting and safe-guarding the right of the people to live in healthy environment" "with minimal disturbance of ecological balance". Why it matters: Described by the Court as the first case of its kind on environment and ecological balance; it recognised the people's right to live in a healthy environment.
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar AIR 1991 SC 420; (1991) 1 SCC 598 (Supreme Court; K.N. Singh J for himself and N.D. Ojha J; reasons given on 9 January 1991)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner alleged that sludge and slurry from TISCO's washeries at Ghatotand were being
caseLaws.facts: He also asked to be allowed to collect the slurry himself. Principle: "Right to live is a fundamental right under Art 21 of the Constitution" and "it includes the right of enjoyment of pollution free water and air for full enjoyment of life." But PIL "cannot be invoked by a person or body or person to satisfy his or its personal grudge and enmity". The petition was filed "for the petitioner's personal interest" and was dismissed with costs of Rs. 5,000. Why it matters: It is the clearest early statement that pollution-free water and air are part of Art. 21, and also a warning against misuse of PIL.
Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) 2 SCC 577 (Supreme Court; K. Ramaswamy and N. Venkatachala JJ; decided 24 November 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land in Town Planning Scheme No
caseLaws.facts: 5 of Thanesar (Kurukshetra) was earmarked for open spaces. The Government allotted it to the Punjab Samaj Sabha, which began building a Dharamshala. Residents challenged it. Principle: Right to life with human dignity includes "the protection and preservation of environment, ecological balance free from pollution of air and water, sanitation"; environmental and pollution harm "should be regarded as amounting to violation of Article 21". The lease was "clearly without authority of law and jurisdiction"; the construction was to be pulled down. Why it matters: It reads Art. 21 together with Arts. 48A and 51A(g), and shows the right protecting open spaces and sanitation, not only clean water and air.

environmental-law-u4-t3.subtitle: The international claim to development and how Indian courts balance it with the environment

en.inOneMinute: The right to development means that every person and all peoples are entitled to take part in, contribute to and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development. It was declared by the UN General Assembly in the Declaration on the Right to Development, 1986 (G.A. res. 41/128): "The right to development is an inalienable human right". (See Diagram 1 .) Development can harm the environment, and protecting the environment can slow development. The Rio Declaration, 1992 joins the two: Principle 3: the right to development must meet "developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations". Principle 4: environmental protection "shall constitute an integral part of the development process". Indian courts answer the clash with sustainable development . In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996): "Sustainable Development is the answer." (See Diagram 2 .) So the right to development is real, but it does not include a right to destroy the environment.
legalProvision: Declaration on the Right to Development, 1986, Art. 1(1) – "The right to development is an inalienable human right" "by virtue of which every human person and all peoples are entitled to participate in" "contribute to, and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development" "in which all human rights and fundamental freedoms can be fully realized". Art. 2(1) – "The human person is the central subject of development" and "should be the active participant and beneficiary of the right to development". Art. 2(3) – "States have the right and the duty to formulate appropriate national development policies" "that aim at the constant improvement of the well-being of the entire population and of all individuals". Art. 8(1) – States "shall ensure, inter alia, equality of opportunity for all in their access to basic resources" "education, health services, food, housing, employment and the fair distribution of income". Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 3 – "The right to development must be fulfilled so as to equitably meet developmental and environmental needs" "of present and future generations". Rio Declaration, Principle 4 – "In order to achieve sustainable development, environmental protection shall constitute an integral part" "of the development process and cannot be considered in isolation from it." Constitution of India – Art. 21 (life), Art. 48A (State to protect and improve the environment), Art. 51A(g) (citizen's duty) are the provisions the courts weigh against development.
en.meaning: Right to development – the human right of every person and all peoples to take part in and enjoy development (Art. 1(1), 1986 Declaration). Sustainable development – as the Brundtland Report defined it, quoted in Vellore : "Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of the future generations" "to meet their own needs". Precautionary principle – where there is a threat of serious environmental harm, measures must be taken to anticipate and prevent it; Vellore treated it as an essential feature of sustainable development. Polluter pays principle – the one who causes pollution must bear the cost of repairing the damage; also an essential feature of sustainable development ( Vellore ). Inter-generational equity – the idea in Rio Principle 3 that development must meet the needs of "present and future generations".
keyPoints: The right to development is "an inalienable human right" (DRD 1986, Art. 1(1)). The human person is the central subject of development (Art. 2(1)). Rio Principle 3: present and future generations; Principle 4: environment is part of development. Vellore : "Sustainable Development is the answer"; sustainable development includes the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. Industry has no right to destroy the ecology ( Vellore ). Courts allow development with conditions ( Narmada : rehabilitation).

caseLaws.facts: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J for himself, Faizan Uddin and K. Venkataswami JJ; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent which reached the Palar river, the main
caseLaws.facts: A survey found nearly 35,000 hectares of farmland in the tannery belt partly or fully unfit for cultivation. Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer." The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are essential features of sustainable development and "part of the environmental law of the country". The Court directed the Central Government to set up an authority under s. 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, imposed a fine of Rs. 10,000 on each tannery, and provided for compensation and closure. Why it matters: It is the leading Indian case joining development and environment through sustainable development.
Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. AIR 1987 SC 359 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati and Ranganath Misra JJ; 18 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: In the Dehradun quarries case (begun on a 1983 letter), limestone quarrying in the Mussoorie
caseLaws.facts: The limestone was used by industry. Principle: The Court said that whether the deposits should be exploited at the cost of ecology "is for the Government and the Nation and not for the Court" to decide. It also referred to the "fundamental duty as enshrined in Article 51A(g) of the Constitution". Why it matters: It shows the court leaving the development choice to the Government while still protecting the ecology already at risk.
Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000) 10 SCC 664 (Supreme Court; judgment of B.N. Kirpal J; 18 October 2000)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner challenged the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada, including its 1987 environme
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court held the challenges belated; "When such projects are undertaken and hundreds of crores of public money is spent", late challenges cannot be allowed. "Dams play a vital role in providing irrigation for food security". Displacement "would not per se result in the violation of their fundamental or other rights"; the Court's concern was relief and rehabilitation under Art. 21. Why it matters: It shows the court supporting a large development project while insisting on the rights of displaced persons.

te.inOneMinute: అభివృద్ధి హక్కు అంటే ప్రతి వ్యక్తి, అన్ని ప్రజలు ఆర్థిక, సామాజిక, సాంస్కృతిక, రాజకీయ అభివృద్ధిలో పాల్గొనడానికి, తోడ్పడడానికి, దాన్ని అనుభవించడానికి అర్హులు. దీన్ని UN సాధారణ సభ అభివృద్ధి హక్కుపై ప్రకటన, 1986 (G.A. res. 41/128)లో ప్రకటించింది: "The right to development is an inalienable human right" (అర్థం: అభివృద్ధి హక్కు విడదీయలేని మానవ హక్కు). ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) అభివృద్ధి పర్యావరణానికి హాని చేయవచ్చు; పర్యావరణ రక్షణ అభివృద్ధిని నెమ్మదింపజేయవచ్చు. రియో ప్రకటన, 1992 రెండింటినీ జోడిస్తుంది: సూత్రం 3: అభివృద్ధి హక్కు "developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations" (అర్థం: ప్రస్తుత, భావి తరాల అభివృద్ధి, పర్యావరణ అవసరాలు)ను తీర్చాలి. సూత్రం 4: పర్యావరణ రక్షణ "shall constitute an integral part of the development process" (అర్థం: అభివృద్ధి ప్రక్రియలో అంతర్భాగంగా ఉండాలి). భారత కోర్టులు ఈ ఘర్షణకు సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి తో సమాధానం ఇస్తాయి. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996): "Sustainable Development is the answer." (అర్థం: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధే సమాధానం.) ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) కాబట్టి అభివృద్ధి హక్కు నిజమైనదే, కానీ అందులో పర్యావరణాన్ని నాశనం చేసే హక్కు లేదు.
te.meaning: అభివృద్ధి హక్కు ( Right to development ) – అభివృద్ధిలో పాల్గొని దాన్ని అనుభవించే ప్రతి వ్యక్తి, అన్ని ప్రజల మానవ హక్కు (1986 ప్రకటన, ఆర్టికల్ 1(1)). సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి ( Sustainable development ) – Vellore లో ఉటంకించిన బ్రండ్‌ట్‌లాండ్ నివేదిక నిర్వచనం: "Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of the future generations" "to meet their own needs" (అర్థం: భావి తరాలు తమ అవసరాలు తీర్చుకునే సామర్థ్యాన్ని దెబ్బతీయకుండా ప్రస్తుత అవసరాలను తీర్చే అభివృద్ధి). ముందు జాగ్రత్త సూత్రం ( Precautionary principle ) – తీవ్రమైన పర్యావరణ హాని ముప్పు ఉన్నప్పుడు, దాన్ని ముందుగానే ఊహించి నివారించే చర్యలు తీసుకోవాలి; Vellore దీన్ని సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి యొక్క ముఖ్య లక్షణంగా పరిగణించింది. కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం (Polluter pays principle) – కాలుష్యం కలిగించినవారే నష్టాన్ని సరిచేసే ఖర్చు భరించాలి; ఇది కూడా సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి ముఖ్య లక్షణం ( Vellore ). తరాల మధ్య న్యాయం ( Inter-generational equity ) – అభివృద్ధి "present and future generations" (అర్థం: ప్రస్తుత, భావి తరాలు) అవసరాలను తీర్చాలనే రియో సూత్రం 3లోని భావన.
keyPoints: అభివృద్ధి హక్కు "an inalienable human right" (అర్థం: విడదీయలేని మానవ హక్కు) (DRD 1986, ఆర్టికల్ 1(1)). మనిషే అభివృద్ధికి కేంద్ర బిందువు (ఆర్టికల్ 2(1)). రియో సూత్రం 3: ప్రస్తుత, భావి తరాలు; సూత్రం 4: పర్యావరణం అభివృద్ధిలో భాగం. Vellore : "Sustainable Development is the answer" (అర్థం: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధే సమాధానం); సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిలో ముందు జాగ్రత్త సూత్రం, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం ఉన్నాయి. పరిశ్రమకు పర్యావరణాన్ని నాశనం చేసే హక్కు లేదు ( Vellore ). కోర్టులు షరతులతో అభివృద్ధిని అనుమతిస్తాయి ( Narmada : పునరావాసం).

selfTest.q: ఏ UN సాధనం అభివృద్ధి హక్కును ప్రకటించింది, ఎప్పుడు?
selfTest.a: ఆ ప్రకటనలోని ఆర్టికల్ 2(1) ఏమి చెబుతుంది? రియో సూత్రాలు 3, 4 ఏమి చెబుతాయి? అభివృద్ధి, పర్యావరణం గురించి Vellore ఏమి చెప్పింది? Vellore ఏ రెండు సూత్రాలను భారత చట్టంలో భాగం చేసింది? Narmada Bachao Andolan లో కోర్టు దృష్టి దేనిపై ఉంది?

hi.inOneMinute: The right to development means that every person and all peoples are entitled to take part in, contribute to and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development. It was declared by the UN General Assembly in the Declaration on the Right to Development, 1986 (G.A. res. 41/128): "The right to development is an inalienable human right". (See Diagram 1 .) Development can harm the environment, and protecting the environment can slow development. The Rio Declaration, 1992 joins the two: Principle 3: the right to development must meet "developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations". Principle 4: environmental protection "shall constitute an integral part of the development process". Indian courts answer the clash with sustainable development . In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996): "Sustainable Development is the answer." (See Diagram 2 .) So the right to development is real, but it does not include a right to destroy the environment.
legalProvision: Declaration on the Right to Development, 1986, Art. 1(1) – "The right to development is an inalienable human right" "by virtue of which every human person and all peoples are entitled to participate in" "contribute to, and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development" "in which all human rights and fundamental freedoms can be fully realized". Art. 2(1) – "The human person is the central subject of development" and "should be the active participant and beneficiary of the right to development". Art. 2(3) – "States have the right and the duty to formulate appropriate national development policies" "that aim at the constant improvement of the well-being of the entire population and of all individuals". Art. 8(1) – States "shall ensure, inter alia, equality of opportunity for all in their access to basic resources" "education, health services, food, housing, employment and the fair distribution of income". Rio Declaration, 1992, Principle 3 – "The right to development must be fulfilled so as to equitably meet developmental and environmental needs" "of present and future generations". Rio Declaration, Principle 4 – "In order to achieve sustainable development, environmental protection shall constitute an integral part" "of the development process and cannot be considered in isolation from it." Constitution of India – Art. 21 (life), Art. 48A (State to protect and improve the environment), Art. 51A(g) (citizen's duty) are the provisions the courts weigh against development.
hi.meaning: Right to development – the human right of every person and all peoples to take part in and enjoy development (Art. 1(1), 1986 Declaration). Sustainable development – as the Brundtland Report defined it, quoted in Vellore : "Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of the future generations" "to meet their own needs". Precautionary principle – where there is a threat of serious environmental harm, measures must be taken to anticipate and prevent it; Vellore treated it as an essential feature of sustainable development. Polluter pays principle – the one who causes pollution must bear the cost of repairing the damage; also an essential feature of sustainable development ( Vellore ). Inter-generational equity – the idea in Rio Principle 3 that development must meet the needs of "present and future generations".
keyPoints: The right to development is "an inalienable human right" (DRD 1986, Art. 1(1)). The human person is the central subject of development (Art. 2(1)). Rio Principle 3: present and future generations; Principle 4: environment is part of development. Vellore : "Sustainable Development is the answer"; sustainable development includes the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle. Industry has no right to destroy the ecology ( Vellore ). Courts allow development with conditions ( Narmada : rehabilitation).

caseLaws.facts: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J for himself, Faizan Uddin and K. Venkataswami JJ; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent which reached the Palar river, the main
caseLaws.facts: A survey found nearly 35,000 hectares of farmland in the tannery belt partly or fully unfit for cultivation. Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer." The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are essential features of sustainable development and "part of the environmental law of the country". The Court directed the Central Government to set up an authority under s. 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, imposed a fine of Rs. 10,000 on each tannery, and provided for compensation and closure. Why it matters: It is the leading Indian case joining development and environment through sustainable development.
Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. AIR 1987 SC 359 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati and Ranganath Misra JJ; 18 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: In the Dehradun quarries case (begun on a 1983 letter), limestone quarrying in the Mussoorie
caseLaws.facts: The limestone was used by industry. Principle: The Court said that whether the deposits should be exploited at the cost of ecology "is for the Government and the Nation and not for the Court" to decide. It also referred to the "fundamental duty as enshrined in Article 51A(g) of the Constitution". Why it matters: It shows the court leaving the development choice to the Government while still protecting the ecology already at risk.
Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000) 10 SCC 664 (Supreme Court; judgment of B.N. Kirpal J; 18 October 2000)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The petitioner challenged the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada, including its 1987 environme
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court held the challenges belated; "When such projects are undertaken and hundreds of crores of public money is spent", late challenges cannot be allowed. "Dams play a vital role in providing irrigation for food security". Displacement "would not per se result in the violation of their fundamental or other rights"; the Court's concern was relief and rehabilitation under Art. 21. Why it matters: It shows the court supporting a large development project while insisting on the rights of displaced persons.

environmental-law-u4-t1.subtitle: The State's directive and the citizen's fundamental duty to protect the environment

en.inOneMinute: The original Constitution of 1950 had no express provision on the environment. The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 inserted two (both w.e.f. 3-1-1977): Article 48A (a Directive Principle, Part IV): a duty on the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g) (a Fundamental Duty, Part IVA): a duty on every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment and to have compassion for living creatures. (See Diagram 1 .) Neither is directly enforceable in a court (Art. 37 for Part IV; Part IVA has no enforcement clause). But courts use both to interpret laws and to give content to Article 21. Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal (1987): "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A". M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Municipalities, 1988): relying on Art. 51A(g), the Court directed environmental lessons in all educational institutions, at least one hour a week. (See Diagram 2 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life.—The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." (Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 10, w.e.f. 3-1-1977.) Article 51A(g) – "It shall be the duty of every citizen of India— ... (g) to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures;" (Part IVA ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 11, w.e.f. 3-1-1977.) Article 37 – "The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws." Article 36 – in Part IV, "the State" has the same meaning as in Part III (Art. 12). Article 253 – Parliament may make any law "for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference" (used for environmental laws following international conferences).
en.meaning: Directive Principle – a principle in Part IV that the State must apply in making laws; it is not enforceable by any court (Art. 37). Fundamental Duty – a duty of every citizen listed in Article 51A (Part IVA). Non-justiciable – not directly enforceable in a court; a person cannot sue only to enforce it. Natural environment – in Art. 51A(g), it expressly "including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life". "Endeavour" – Art. 48A asks the State to try to achieve the goal; it sets a direction, not a fixed result. "Protect and improve" – both provisions require more than avoiding harm; they ask for improvement of the environment.
keyPoints: Art. 48A (Directive Principle): State shall endeavour to protect and improve environment; safeguard forests and wild life. Art. 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty): every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment; compassion for living creatures. Both inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). Non-justiciable (Art. 37), but courts must bear them in mind ( Sachidananda Pandey ). M.C. Mehta (1988): environmental lessons one hour a week; free textbooks. M.C. Mehta (1987): tanneries without treatment plants must stop.

caseLaws.facts: Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal AIR 1987 SC 1109; (1987) 2 SCC 295 (Supreme Court; O. Chinnappa Reddy J, V. Khalid J concurring; 11 February 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: About four acres of Begumbari land, across the road from the Alipore Zoological Garden in Cal
caseLaws.facts: Citizens challenged it on ecological grounds, including the effect on migratory birds. Principle: "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A". The Court "is not to shrug its shoulders and say that priorities are a matter of policy", and "may always give necessary directions". On the facts, the government "was alive to the ecological considerations", and the appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It makes Art. 48A a binding consideration for courts in every ecology case, even though it is a Directive Principle.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Municipalities), W.P. 3727 of 1985, decided 12 January 1988 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Untreated sewage of about 274 million litres a day from Kanpur city was flowing into the Gang
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Referring to "protecting and improving the natural environment which is considered to be one of the fundamental duties" (Art. 51A(g)), the Court directed the Central Government to direct "all the educational institutions throughout India to teach at least for one hour in a week" lessons on protecting and improving the natural environment, and to have textbooks written and distributed "free of cost". Why it matters: It turned the citizen's duty under Art. 51A(g) into concrete steps for environmental education.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Tanneries) (1987) 4 SCC 463 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J, K.N. Singh J concurring; 22 September 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries at Jajmau near Kanpur discharged trade effluents into the Ganga without primary tre
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Quoting Arts. 48-A and 51-A and the Water Act, the Court held that "a tannery which cannot set up a primary treatment plant cannot be permitted to continue to be in existence"; financial capacity was "irrelevant". K.N. Singh J: "life, health and ecology have greater importance" than unemployment or loss of revenue. Why it matters: It shows Arts. 48A and 51A(g) supporting strict enforcement of pollution laws against industry.

selfTest.q: Which Amendment inserted Arts. 48A and 51A?
selfTest.a: Who bears the duty under Art. 48A, and who under Art. 51A(g)? What does Art. 37 say about Directive Principles? What did Sachidananda Pandey say about Art. 48A? What direction did the Court give in M.C. Mehta (1988) on education? What extra element does Art. 51A(g) contain that Art. 48A does not?

te.inOneMinute: 1950 నాటి అసలు రాజ్యాంగంలో పర్యావరణం గురించి స్పష్టమైన నిబంధన లేదు. రాజ్యాంగ (నలభై రెండవ సవరణ) చట్టం, 1976 రెండు నిబంధనలను చేర్చింది (రెండూ 3-1-1977 నుంచి అమలు): ఆర్టికల్ 48A (ఆదేశిక సూత్రం, భాగం IV): పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించి మెరుగుపరచాలని, అడవులను, వన్యప్రాణులను కాపాడాలని రాజ్యం పై బాధ్యత. ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g) (ప్రాథమిక విధి, భాగం IVA): సహజ పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించి మెరుగుపరచాలని, జీవుల పట్ల కరుణ చూపాలని ప్రతి పౌరుడి పై విధి. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ఏదీ కోర్టులో నేరుగా అమలు చేయదగినది కాదు (భాగం IVకి ఆర్టికల్ 37; భాగం IVAలో అమలు క్లాజ్ లేదు). కానీ కోర్టులు చట్టాలను వ్యాఖ్యానించడానికి, ఆర్టికల్ 21కి అర్థం ఇవ్వడానికి రెండింటినీ వాడతాయి. Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal (1987): "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణ సమస్య కోర్టు ముందుకు వచ్చినప్పుడల్లా, కోర్టు ఆర్టికల్ 48Aను దృష్టిలో ఉంచుకోవాల్సిందే). M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (కాన్పూర్ మునిసిపాలిటీలు, 1988): ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g)పై ఆధారపడి, అన్ని విద్యాసంస్థల్లో వారానికి కనీసం ఒక గంట పర్యావరణ పాఠాలు బోధించాలని కోర్టు ఆదేశించింది. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: ఆదేశిక సూత్రం (Directive Principle) – చట్టాలు చేసేటప్పుడు రాజ్యం వర్తింపజేయాల్సిన భాగం IVలోని సూత్రం; ఏ కోర్టూ దాన్ని అమలు చేయదు (ఆర్టికల్ 37). ప్రాథమిక విధి (Fundamental Duty) – ఆర్టికల్ 51A (భాగం IVA)లో పేర్కొన్న ప్రతి పౌరుడి విధి. న్యాయస్థానంలో అమలు చేయలేనిది (Non- justiciable ) – కోర్టులో నేరుగా అమలు చేయలేనిది; దాన్ని మాత్రమే అమలు చేయమని దావా వేయలేము. సహజ పర్యావరణం (Natural environment ) – ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g)లో ఇది స్పష్టంగా "including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life" (అర్థం: అడవులు, సరస్సులు, నదులు, వన్యప్రాణులతో సహా). "Endeavour" (అర్థం: కృషి చేయాలి) – లక్ష్యాన్ని సాధించడానికి ప్రయత్నించాలని ఆర్టికల్ 48A రాజ్యాన్ని కోరుతుంది; ఇది దిశను నిర్ణయిస్తుంది, నిర్దిష్ట ఫలితాన్ని కాదు. "Protect and improve" (అర్థం: రక్షించి మెరుగుపరచడం) – రెండు నిబంధనలూ హాని నివారించడం కంటే ఎక్కువ కోరతాయి; పర్యావరణ మెరుగుదలను కోరతాయి.
keyPoints: ఆర్టికల్ 48A (ఆదేశిక సూత్రం): పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించి మెరుగుపరచడానికి, అడవులు, వన్యప్రాణులను కాపాడడానికి రాజ్యం కృషి చేయాలి. ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g) (ప్రాథమిక విధి): ప్రతి పౌరుడు సహజ పర్యావరణంను రక్షించి మెరుగుపరచాలి; జీవుల పట్ల కరుణ. రెండూ 42వ సవరణ, 1976 ద్వారా చేర్చబడ్డాయి (3-1-1977 నుంచి). న్యాయస్థానంలో అమలు చేయలేనివి (ఆర్టికల్ 37), కానీ కోర్టులు దృష్టిలో ఉంచుకోవాలి ( Sachidananda Pandey ). M.C. Mehta (1988): వారానికి ఒక గంట పర్యావరణ పాఠాలు; ఉచిత పాఠ్యపుస్తకాలు. M.C. Mehta (1987): శుద్ధి ప్లాంట్లు లేని టానరీలు ఆపాలి.

selfTest.a: ఆర్టికల్ 48A కింద విధి ఎవరిది, ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g) కింద ఎవరిది? ఆదేశిక సూత్రాల గురించి ఆర్టికల్ 37 ఏమి చెబుతుంది? ఆర్టికల్ 48A గురించి Sachidananda Pandey ఏమి చెప్పింది? విద్యపై M.C. Mehta (1988)లో కోర్టు ఏ ఆదేశం ఇచ్చింది? ఆర్టికల్ 48Aలో లేని ఏ అదనపు అంశం ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g)లో ఉంది?

hi.inOneMinute: The original Constitution of 1950 had no express provision on the environment. The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 inserted two (both w.e.f. 3-1-1977): Article 48A (a Directive Principle, Part IV): a duty on the State to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g) (a Fundamental Duty, Part IVA): a duty on every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment and to have compassion for living creatures. (See Diagram 1 .) Neither is directly enforceable in a court (Art. 37 for Part IV; Part IVA has no enforcement clause). But courts use both to interpret laws and to give content to Article 21. Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal (1987): "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A". M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Municipalities, 1988): relying on Art. 51A(g), the Court directed environmental lessons in all educational institutions, at least one hour a week. (See Diagram 2 .)
legalProvision: Article 48A – "Protection and improvement of environment and safeguarding of forests and wild life.—The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." (Ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 10, w.e.f. 3-1-1977.) Article 51A(g) – "It shall be the duty of every citizen of India— ... (g) to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures;" (Part IVA ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 11, w.e.f. 3-1-1977.) Article 37 – "The provisions contained in this Part shall not be enforceable by any court, but the principles therein laid down are nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws." Article 36 – in Part IV, "the State" has the same meaning as in Part III (Art. 12). Article 253 – Parliament may make any law "for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference" (used for environmental laws following international conferences).
hi.meaning: Directive Principle – a principle in Part IV that the State must apply in making laws; it is not enforceable by any court (Art. 37). Fundamental Duty – a duty of every citizen listed in Article 51A (Part IVA). Non-justiciable – not directly enforceable in a court; a person cannot sue only to enforce it. Natural environment – in Art. 51A(g), it expressly "including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life". "Endeavour" – Art. 48A asks the State to try to achieve the goal; it sets a direction, not a fixed result. "Protect and improve" – both provisions require more than avoiding harm; they ask for improvement of the environment.
keyPoints: Art. 48A (Directive Principle): State shall endeavour to protect and improve environment; safeguard forests and wild life. Art. 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty): every citizen to protect and improve the natural environment; compassion for living creatures. Both inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (w.e.f. 3-1-1977). Non-justiciable (Art. 37), but courts must bear them in mind ( Sachidananda Pandey ). M.C. Mehta (1988): environmental lessons one hour a week; free textbooks. M.C. Mehta (1987): tanneries without treatment plants must stop.

caseLaws.facts: Sachidananda Pandey v. State of West Bengal AIR 1987 SC 1109; (1987) 2 SCC 295 (Supreme Court; O. Chinnappa Reddy J, V. Khalid J concurring; 11 February 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: About four acres of Begumbari land, across the road from the Alipore Zoological Garden in Cal
caseLaws.facts: Citizens challenged it on ecological grounds, including the effect on migratory birds. Principle: "Whenever a problem of ecology is brought before the Court, the Court is bound to bear in mind Art. 48 A". The Court "is not to shrug its shoulders and say that priorities are a matter of policy", and "may always give necessary directions". On the facts, the government "was alive to the ecological considerations", and the appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It makes Art. 48A a binding consideration for courts in every ecology case, even though it is a Directive Principle.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Municipalities), W.P. 3727 of 1985, decided 12 January 1988 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Untreated sewage of about 274 million litres a day from Kanpur city was flowing into the Gang
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Referring to "protecting and improving the natural environment which is considered to be one of the fundamental duties" (Art. 51A(g)), the Court directed the Central Government to direct "all the educational institutions throughout India to teach at least for one hour in a week" lessons on protecting and improving the natural environment, and to have textbooks written and distributed "free of cost". Why it matters: It turned the citizen's duty under Art. 51A(g) into concrete steps for environmental education.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Tanneries) (1987) 4 SCC 463 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J, K.N. Singh J concurring; 22 September 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries at Jajmau near Kanpur discharged trade effluents into the Ganga without primary tre
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Quoting Arts. 48-A and 51-A and the Water Act, the Court held that "a tannery which cannot set up a primary treatment plant cannot be permitted to continue to be in existence"; financial capacity was "irrelevant". K.N. Singh J: "life, health and ecology have greater importance" than unemployment or loss of revenue. Why it matters: It shows Arts. 48A and 51A(g) supporting strict enforcement of pollution laws against industry.
