environmental-law-u4-t4.subtitle: Article 19(1)(g) and Article 19(6): when a law can limit a business to protect the environment

en.inOneMinute: Article 19(1)(g) gives every citizen the right "to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business". The right is not absolute. Article 19(6) lets the State make laws imposing "reasonable restrictions" on it "in the interests of the general public". Protecting the environment and public health is in the interests of the general public. (See Diagram 1 .) So a factory, tannery, quarry or dyeing unit can be regulated, made to treat its waste, fined, or even closed, if it pollutes. Courts have said this clearly: Abhilash Textile v. Rajkot Municipal Corporation (Guj HC, 1987): "No one has a right to carry on business so as to cause nuisance to the society." M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Tanneries, 1987): a tannery that cannot set up a primary treatment plant "cannot be permitted to continue to be in existence". But the restriction must be reasonable . Closure is the last step; where other remedies work, courts may prefer them ( Sterlite Industries v. Union of India , 2013). (See Diagram 2 .)
legalProvision: Article 19(1)(g) – "All citizens shall have the right— ... (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business." Article 19(6) – "Nothing in sub-clause (g) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the general public, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause". Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Courts read it to include a healthy environment (see "Right to wholesome environment"). Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment". Example of a law imposing such a restriction: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, s. 376A, under which the Rajkot Municipal Commissioner ordered dyeing units to stop discharging dirty water or face closure ( Abhilash Textile ).
en.meaning: Freedom of trade – the right in Art. 19(1)(g) to practise a profession or carry on an occupation, trade or business. Reasonable restriction – a limit on a Fundamental Right that is imposed by law and is not arbitrary or excessive compared with its purpose. Interests of the general public – the ground in Art. 19(6) on which the freedom of trade may be restricted; it covers public health and the environment . Closure order – an order stopping an industry or unit from operating, the strongest restriction on the freedom of trade. Fundamental duty – Art. 51A(g) duty to protect the natural environment, which courts set against a claim to trade freely ( Abhilash Textile ).
keyPoints: Freedom of trade under Art. 19(1)(g) is subject to Art. 19(6). A reasonable restriction may be imposed by law in the interests of the general public, which include public health and the environment. Abhilash Textile : no right to carry on business so as to cause nuisance to society. M.C. Mehta (1987): financial capacity irrelevant; no treatment plant, no tannery. Sterlite (2013): a closure order is a last step; compensation may be ordered instead. Workers' interests are considered, but do not create a right to pollute.

caseLaws.facts: Abhilash Textile v. Rajkot Municipal Corporation AIR 1988 Guj 57 (Gujarat High Court; decided 5 August 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: 165 dyeing and printing units in Rajkot were discharging dirty water onto public roads and dr
caseLaws.facts: The Municipal Commissioner gave them notice under s. 376A of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, to stop within seven days or face closure. They relied on Art. 19(1)(g) and said they had no hearing. Principle: "No one has a right to carry on business so as to cause nuisance to the society." "The petitioners cannot assert their right, much less fundamental right, to carry on business without any regard to the fundamental duty." "The petitioners cannot be allowed to reap profit at the cost of the public health." The petitions were rejected. Why it matters: It is the clearest statement that Art. 19(1)(g) gives no right to carry on business in a way that harms public health.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Tanneries) (1987) 4 SCC 463 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J, K.N. Singh J concurring; 22 September 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries at Jajmau near Kanpur discharged effluent into the Ganga without primary treatment
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "a tannery which cannot set up a primary treatment plant cannot be permitted to continue to be in existence"; financial capacity is "irrelevant". K.N. Singh J: "life, health and ecology have greater importance" than unemployment and loss of revenue. Why it matters: It shows closure as a valid restriction on trade when an industry will not control pollution.
Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. v. Union of India (Civil Appeal Nos. 2776-2783 of 2013; Supreme Court; A.K. Patnaik J for himself and H.L. Gokhale J; 2 April 2013)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Madras High Court on 28 September 2010 ordered closure of Sterlite's copper smelter at Tu
caseLaws.facts: The company appealed. Principle: The Supreme Court set aside the closure order because the plant had taken remedial steps, but held the company "liable to compensate by paying damages" and ordered a deposit of Rs. 100 crores, saying the amount "must be corelated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". The Board could still issue directions, including closure, in future. Why it matters: It shows that a restriction must be proportionate: closure is not automatic where other remedies can protect the environment.

What did the Supreme Court order in Sterlite instead of closure? How did Abhilash Textile treat the cost of a purification plant?

te.inOneMinute: ఆర్టికల్ 19(1)(g) ప్రతి పౌరుడికి "to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business" (అర్థం: ఏ వృత్తినైనా చేపట్టడానికి, లేదా ఏ ఉపాధి, వ్యాపారం లేదా వాణిజ్యాన్నైనా నిర్వహించడానికి) హక్కు ఇస్తుంది. ఈ హక్కు సంపూర్ణం కాదు. ఆర్టికల్ 19(6) "in the interests of the general public" (అర్థం: సాధారణ ప్రజల ప్రయోజనాల దృష్ట్యా) దానిపై "reasonable restrictions" (అర్థం: సహేతుకమైన పరిమితులు) విధించే చట్టాలు చేయడానికి రాజ్యాన్ని అనుమతిస్తుంది. పర్యావరణం, ప్రజారోగ్య రక్షణ సాధారణ ప్రజల ప్రయోజనమే. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) కాబట్టి ఒక ఫ్యాక్టరీ, టానరీ, క్వారీ లేదా అద్దకం యూనిట్ కాలుష్యం చేస్తే, దాన్ని నియంత్రించవచ్చు, వ్యర్థాలను శుద్ధి చేయమని ఆదేశించవచ్చు, జరిమానా విధించవచ్చు, మూసివేయవచ్చు కూడా. కోర్టులు దీన్ని స్పష్టంగా చెప్పాయి: Abhilash Textile v. Rajkot Municipal Corporation (గుజరాత్ హైకోర్టు, 1987): "No one has a right to carry on business so as to cause nuisance to the society." (అర్థం: సమాజానికి ఇబ్బంది కలిగించే విధంగా వ్యాపారం చేసే హక్కు ఎవరికీ లేదు.) M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (కాన్పూర్ టానరీలు, 1987): ప్రాథమిక శుద్ధి ప్లాంట్ ఏర్పాటు చేయలేని టానరీ "cannot be permitted to continue to be in existence" (అర్థం: కొనసాగడానికి అనుమతించలేము). కానీ పరిమితి సహేతుకంగా ఉండాలి. మూసివేత చివరి మెట్టు; ఇతర పరిష్కారాలు పనిచేస్తే కోర్టులు వాటికి ప్రాధాన్యం ఇవ్వవచ్చు ( Sterlite Industries v. Union of India , 2013). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: వ్యాపార స్వేచ్ఛ (Freedom of trade) – వృత్తి చేపట్టడానికి లేదా ఉపాధి, వ్యాపారం, వాణిజ్యం నిర్వహించడానికి ఆర్టికల్ 19(1)(g)లోని హక్కు. సహేతుకమైన పరిమితి ( Reasonable restriction ) – చట్టం ద్వారా విధించిన, దాని ఉద్దేశంతో పోలిస్తే ఏకపక్షంగా లేదా అతిగా లేని ప్రాథమిక హక్కుపై పరిమితి. సాధారణ ప్రజల ప్రయోజనాలు (Interests of the general public) – వ్యాపార స్వేచ్ఛను పరిమితం చేయగల ఆర్టికల్ 19(6)లోని ఆధారం; ఇందులో ప్రజారోగ్యం, పర్యావరణం ఉన్నాయి. మూసివేత ఉత్తర్వు (Closure order) – ఒక పరిశ్రమను లేదా యూనిట్‌ను పనిచేయకుండా ఆపే ఉత్తర్వు; వ్యాపార స్వేచ్ఛపై అత్యంత బలమైన పరిమితి. ప్రాథమిక విధి (Fundamental duty) – సహజ పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించే ఆర్టికల్ 51A(g) విధి; స్వేచ్ఛగా వ్యాపారం చేసే వాదనకు ఎదురుగా కోర్టులు దీన్ని ఉంచుతాయి ( Abhilash Textile ).
keyPoints: ఆర్టికల్ 19(1)(g) కింద వ్యాపార స్వేచ్ఛ ఆర్టికల్ 19(6)కి లోబడి ఉంటుంది. సాధారణ ప్రజల ప్రయోజనాలు దృష్ట్యా చట్టం ద్వారా సహేతుకమైన పరిమితి విధించవచ్చు; అందులో ప్రజారోగ్యం, పర్యావరణం ఉన్నాయి. Abhilash Textile : సమాజానికి ఇబ్బంది కలిగించే విధంగా వ్యాపారం చేసే హక్కు లేదు. M.C. Mehta (1987): ఆర్థిక సామర్థ్యం అసంబద్ధం; శుద్ధి ప్లాంట్ లేకపోతే టానరీ లేదు. Sterlite (2013): మూసివేత ఉత్తర్వు చివరి మెట్టు; బదులుగా పరిహారం ఆదేశించవచ్చు. కార్మికుల ప్రయోజనాలు పరిగణించబడతాయి, కానీ కాలుష్యం చేసే హక్కును సృష్టించవు.

hi.inOneMinute: Article 19(1)(g) gives every citizen the right "to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business". The right is not absolute. Article 19(6) lets the State make laws imposing "reasonable restrictions" on it "in the interests of the general public". Protecting the environment and public health is in the interests of the general public. (See Diagram 1 .) So a factory, tannery, quarry or dyeing unit can be regulated, made to treat its waste, fined, or even closed, if it pollutes. Courts have said this clearly: Abhilash Textile v. Rajkot Municipal Corporation (Guj HC, 1987): "No one has a right to carry on business so as to cause nuisance to the society." M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Tanneries, 1987): a tannery that cannot set up a primary treatment plant "cannot be permitted to continue to be in existence". But the restriction must be reasonable . Closure is the last step; where other remedies work, courts may prefer them ( Sterlite Industries v. Union of India , 2013). (See Diagram 2 .)
legalProvision: Article 19(1)(g) – "All citizens shall have the right— ... (g) to practise any profession, or to carry on any occupation, trade or business." Article 19(6) – "Nothing in sub-clause (g) of the said clause shall affect the operation of any existing law in so far as it imposes, or prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interests of the general public, reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by the said sub-clause". Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Courts read it to include a healthy environment (see "Right to wholesome environment"). Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment". Example of a law imposing such a restriction: Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, s. 376A, under which the Rajkot Municipal Commissioner ordered dyeing units to stop discharging dirty water or face closure ( Abhilash Textile ).
hi.meaning: Freedom of trade – the right in Art. 19(1)(g) to practise a profession or carry on an occupation, trade or business. Reasonable restriction – a limit on a Fundamental Right that is imposed by law and is not arbitrary or excessive compared with its purpose. Interests of the general public – the ground in Art. 19(6) on which the freedom of trade may be restricted; it covers public health and the environment . Closure order – an order stopping an industry or unit from operating, the strongest restriction on the freedom of trade. Fundamental duty – Art. 51A(g) duty to protect the natural environment, which courts set against a claim to trade freely ( Abhilash Textile ).
keyPoints: Freedom of trade under Art. 19(1)(g) is subject to Art. 19(6). A reasonable restriction may be imposed by law in the interests of the general public, which include public health and the environment. Abhilash Textile : no right to carry on business so as to cause nuisance to society. M.C. Mehta (1987): financial capacity irrelevant; no treatment plant, no tannery. Sterlite (2013): a closure order is a last step; compensation may be ordered instead. Workers' interests are considered, but do not create a right to pollute.

caseLaws.facts: Abhilash Textile v. Rajkot Municipal Corporation AIR 1988 Guj 57 (Gujarat High Court; decided 5 August 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: 165 dyeing and printing units in Rajkot were discharging dirty water onto public roads and dr
caseLaws.facts: The Municipal Commissioner gave them notice under s. 376A of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, 1949, to stop within seven days or face closure. They relied on Art. 19(1)(g) and said they had no hearing. Principle: "No one has a right to carry on business so as to cause nuisance to the society." "The petitioners cannot assert their right, much less fundamental right, to carry on business without any regard to the fundamental duty." "The petitioners cannot be allowed to reap profit at the cost of the public health." The petitions were rejected. Why it matters: It is the clearest statement that Art. 19(1)(g) gives no right to carry on business in a way that harms public health.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Kanpur Tanneries) (1987) 4 SCC 463 (Supreme Court; E.S. Venkataramiah J, K.N. Singh J concurring; 22 September 1987)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries at Jajmau near Kanpur discharged effluent into the Ganga without primary treatment
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "a tannery which cannot set up a primary treatment plant cannot be permitted to continue to be in existence"; financial capacity is "irrelevant". K.N. Singh J: "life, health and ecology have greater importance" than unemployment and loss of revenue. Why it matters: It shows closure as a valid restriction on trade when an industry will not control pollution.
Sterlite Industries (India) Ltd. v. Union of India (Civil Appeal Nos. 2776-2783 of 2013; Supreme Court; A.K. Patnaik J for himself and H.L. Gokhale J; 2 April 2013)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Madras High Court on 28 September 2010 ordered closure of Sterlite's copper smelter at Tu
caseLaws.facts: The company appealed. Principle: The Supreme Court set aside the closure order because the plant had taken remedial steps, but held the company "liable to compensate by paying damages" and ordered a deposit of Rs. 100 crores, saying the amount "must be corelated to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". The Board could still issue directions, including closure, in future. Why it matters: It shows that a restriction must be proportionate: closure is not automatic where other remedies can protect the environment.

environmental-law-u4-t6.subtitle: Which legislature can make an environmental law: Article 246, the Seventh Schedule and Articles 252 to 254

en.inOneMinute: The Constitution divides law-making power between Parliament (the Centre) and the State Legislatures through Article 246 and three Lists in the Seventh Schedule : Union List (List I), State List (List II) and Concurrent List (List III). (See Diagram 1 .) "Environment" as a word is not an entry in any List. Its parts are spread across the Lists: State List: public health and sanitation (Entry 6), water (Entry 17), land (Entry 18), fisheries (Entry 21). Concurrent List: forests (Entry 17A) and protection of wild animals and birds (Entry 17B), both added by the 42nd Amendment; also factories (Entry 36). Union List: oilfields (Entry 53), mines (Entry 54), inter-State rivers (Entry 56), and the residuary Entry 97. Parliament also has special routes (See Diagram 2 .): Art. 252 : law on a State subject when two or more States pass resolutions. The Water Act, 1974 was made this way. Art. 253 : law to implement international agreements and decisions. The Air Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 recite the Stockholm Conference of 1972. Art. 248 : residuary power for matters not in List II or III. If a State law conflicts with a Central law on a Concurrent subject, Article 254 makes the Central law prevail (unless the State law has the President's assent ).
legalProvision: Article 246(1) – "Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule". Article 246(2) – Parliament, and the Legislature of any State "also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III". Article 246(3) – "the Legislature of any State ... has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II". Article 248(1) – Parliament "has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List". Article 249(1) – if the Council of States declares by resolution "supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting" that it is necessary "in the national interest", Parliament may make laws on a State List matter while the resolution is in force (Art. 249(2): up to one year at a time). Article 252(1) – if "resolutions to that effect are passed by all the Houses of the Legislatures of those States", Parliament may pass an Act regulating that matter, which applies to those States "and to any other State by which it is adopted afterwards by resolution". Article 253 – "Parliament has power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other body." Article 254(1) – if a State law "is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament", on a Concurrent List matter, "the law made by Parliament ... shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void." Art. 254(2) saves a State law reserved for and assented to by the President. Seventh Schedule entries relevant to the environment:

List Entry Words I 13 "Participation in international conferences, associations and other bodies and implementing of decisions made thereat." I 52 "Industries, the control of which by the Union is declared by Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest." Article 243W and the Twelfth Schedule – a State may by law give Municipalities powers on matters in the Twelfth Schedule, which include item 6 "Public health, sanitation conservancy and solid waste management" and item 8 "Urban forestry, protection of the environment and promotion of ecological aspects".
en.meaning: Union List – List I of the Seventh Schedule; only Parliament can make laws on it (Art. 246(1)). State List – List II; only the State Legislature can make laws on it (Art. 246(3)), subject to Arts. 249, 250, 252 and 253. Concurrent List – List III; both Parliament and the States can make laws on it (Art. 246(2)); the Central law prevails in a conflict (Art. 254). Residuary power – Parliament's power under Art. 248 and List I Entry 97 over matters not in List II or III. Repugnancy – a direct conflict between a State law and a Central law on the same Concurrent subject. Pith and substance – the test courts use to find which entry a law truly falls under, by looking at its main subject.
keyPoints: Art. 246: Union List, State List, Concurrent List. Forests (17A) and wild animals and birds (17B) are Concurrent since 1977. Water (Entry 17) and public health (Entry 6) are State subjects. Water Act, 1974: Art. 252; Air Act, 1981 and EP Act, 1986: Stockholm 1972 (Art. 253). Residuary power: Art. 248 and List I Entry 97 ( Municipal Corporation of Jullundur ). Art. 254: Central law prevails on Concurrent subjects, unless the President assents to the State law.

caseLaws.facts: Sukhivender Kaur Gill v. State of Uttarakhand (Special Appeal No. 466 of 2022; Uttarakhand High Court, Division Bench; Vipin Sanghi CJ and Manoj Kumar Tiwari J; 3 January 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A maker of non-woven plastic carry bags was fined Rs
caseLaws.facts: 5,00,000 by the State Pollution Control Board under the Uttarakhand Plastic and Other Non Biodegradable Garbage (Regulation of Use and Disposal) Act, 2013. He argued that the State had no power, as environment fell under List I Entry 13, and that the State ban was repugnant to the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016. Principle: "The subject of environment does not specifically find mention in any of the Entries"; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 "is not related to participation" in international conferences (Entry 13). The State Act fell within State Entries 5, 6, 17, 18 and "can also be traced to Entries 17A and 17B of List III-Concurrent List". A stricter State ban "does not create any repugnancy with the Plastic Waste Management Rules". The appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It shows how environmental laws are placed in the Lists by pith and substance, and how repugnancy is judged.
Municipal Corporation of Jullundur v. Union of India AIR 1981 P&H 287 (Punjab and Haryana High Court; J.V. Gupta J; 25 February 1981)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Municipal Corporation challenged the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Parliament was competent "under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of List-I"; "Even in the absence of the Act of 1974 the Parliament was competent to levy tax on the water consumption". Why it matters: It shows Parliament's residuary power supporting environmental legislation.

What did Sukhivender Kaur Gill say about "environment" in the Lists? When does a State law on a Concurrent subject prevail over a Central law?

te.inOneMinute: రాజ్యాంగం ఆర్టికల్ 246 , ఏడవ షెడ్యూల్ ‌లోని మూడు జాబితాల ద్వారా చట్టాలు చేసే అధికారాన్ని పార్లమెంటు (కేంద్రం), రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభల మధ్య విభజిస్తుంది: కేంద్ర జాబితా (జాబితా I), రాష్ట్ర జాబితా (జాబితా II), ఉమ్మడి జాబితా (జాబితా III). ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) "Environment" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణం) అనే పదం ఏ జాబితాలోనూ ఎంట్రీగా లేదు. దాని భాగాలు జాబితాల అంతటా విస్తరించి ఉన్నాయి: రాష్ట్ర జాబితా: ప్రజారోగ్యం, పారిశుద్ధ్యం (ఎంట్రీ 6), నీరు (ఎంట్రీ 17), భూమి (ఎంట్రీ 18), మత్స్య సంపద (ఎంట్రీ 21). ఉమ్మడి జాబితా: అడవులు (ఎంట్రీ 17A), వన్య జంతువులు, పక్షుల రక్షణ (ఎంట్రీ 17B) – రెండూ 42వ సవరణ ద్వారా చేర్చబడ్డాయి; ఫ్యాక్టరీలు (ఎంట్రీ 36) కూడా. కేంద్ర జాబితా: చమురు క్షేత్రాలు (ఎంట్రీ 53), గనులు (ఎంట్రీ 54), అంతర్రాష్ట్ర నదులు (ఎంట్రీ 56), అవశేష ఎంట్రీ 97. పార్లమెంటుకు ప్రత్యేక మార్గాలు కూడా ఉన్నాయి ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.): ఆర్టికల్ 252 : రెండు లేదా అంతకంటే ఎక్కువ రాష్ట్రాలు తీర్మానాలు చేసినప్పుడు రాష్ట్ర విషయంపై చట్టం. నీటి చట్టం, 1974 ఇలా చేయబడింది. ఆర్టికల్ 253 : అంతర్జాతీయ ఒప్పందాలు, నిర్ణయాలను అమలు చేసే చట్టం. వాయు చట్టం, 1981 , పర్యావరణ (రక్షణ) చట్టం, 1986 1972 స్టాక్‌హోమ్ సమావేశాన్ని ప్రస్తావిస్తాయి. ఆర్టికల్ 248 : జాబితా II లేదా IIIలో లేని విషయాలకు అవశేష అధికారం. ఉమ్మడి విషయంపై రాష్ట్ర చట్టం కేంద్ర చట్టంతో విభేదిస్తే, ఆర్టికల్ 254 కేంద్ర చట్టం చెల్లేలా చేస్తుంది (రాష్ట్ర చట్టానికి రాష్ట్రపతి ఆమోదం ఉంటే తప్ప).
te.meaning: కేంద్ర జాబితా (Union List) – ఏడవ షెడ్యూల్‌లోని జాబితా I; దానిపై పార్లమెంటు మాత్రమే చట్టాలు చేయగలదు (ఆర్టికల్ 246(1)). రాష్ట్ర జాబితా (State List) – జాబితా II; దానిపై రాష్ట్ర శాసనసభ మాత్రమే చట్టాలు చేయగలదు (ఆర్టికల్ 246(3)), ఆర్టికల్స్ 249, 250, 252, 253కి లోబడి. ఉమ్మడి జాబితా ( Concurrent List ) – జాబితా III; దానిపై పార్లమెంటు, రాష్ట్రాలు రెండూ చట్టాలు చేయగలవు (ఆర్టికల్ 246(2)); విభేదం ఉంటే కేంద్ర చట్టం చెల్లుతుంది (ఆర్టికల్ 254). అవశేష అధికారం ( Residuary power) – జాబితా II లేదా IIIలో లేని విషయాలపై ఆర్టికల్ 248, జాబితా I ఎంట్రీ 97 కింద పార్లమెంటు అధికారం. విరుద్ధత ( Repugnancy ) – ఒకే ఉమ్మడి విషయంపై రాష్ట్ర చట్టం, కేంద్ర చట్టం మధ్య ప్రత్యక్ష విభేదం. సారాంశ పరీక్ష ( Pith and substance ) – ఒక చట్టం నిజంగా ఏ ఎంట్రీ కిందకు వస్తుందో, దాని ప్రధాన విషయాన్ని చూసి కనుగొనడానికి కోర్టులు వాడే పరీక్ష.
keyPoints: ఆర్టికల్ 246: కేంద్ర జాబితా, రాష్ట్ర జాబితా, ఉమ్మడి జాబితా. అడవులు (17A), వన్య జంతువులు, పక్షులు (17B) 1977 నుంచి ఉమ్మడి. నీరు (ఎంట్రీ 17), ప్రజారోగ్యం (ఎంట్రీ 6) రాష్ట్ర విషయాలు. నీటి చట్టం, 1974: ఆర్టికల్ 252; వాయు చట్టం, 1981, పర్యావరణ (రక్షణ) చట్టం, 1986: స్టాక్‌హోమ్ 1972 (ఆర్టికల్ 253). అవశేష అధికారం: ఆర్టికల్ 248, జాబితా I ఎంట్రీ 97 ( Municipal Corporation of Jullundur ). ఆర్టికల్ 254: ఉమ్మడి విషయాలపై కేంద్ర చట్టం చెల్లుతుంది, రాష్ట్ర చట్టానికి రాష్ట్రపతి ఆమోదం ఉంటే తప్ప.

selfTest.q: ఏ ఆర్టికల్ చట్టాలు చేసే అధికారాన్ని విభజిస్తుంది, ఏ షెడ్యూల్ ద్వారా?
selfTest.a: అడవులను ఏ సవరణ ఉమ్మడి విషయం చేసింది? నీటి చట్టం, 1974 ఏ ఆర్టికల్ కింద చేయబడింది, ఎందుకు? వాయు చట్టం, పర్యావరణ (రక్షణ) చట్టం ప్రవేశికలు దేనిని ప్రస్తావిస్తాయి? జాబితాల్లో "environment" గురించి Sukhivender Kaur Gill ఏమి చెప్పింది? ఉమ్మడి విషయంపై రాష్ట్ర చట్టం కేంద్ర చట్టంపై ఎప్పుడు చెల్లుతుంది?

hi.inOneMinute: The Constitution divides law-making power between Parliament (the Centre) and the State Legislatures through Article 246 and three Lists in the Seventh Schedule : Union List (List I), State List (List II) and Concurrent List (List III). (See Diagram 1 .) "Environment" as a word is not an entry in any List. Its parts are spread across the Lists: State List: public health and sanitation (Entry 6), water (Entry 17), land (Entry 18), fisheries (Entry 21). Concurrent List: forests (Entry 17A) and protection of wild animals and birds (Entry 17B), both added by the 42nd Amendment; also factories (Entry 36). Union List: oilfields (Entry 53), mines (Entry 54), inter-State rivers (Entry 56), and the residuary Entry 97. Parliament also has special routes (See Diagram 2 .): Art. 252 : law on a State subject when two or more States pass resolutions. The Water Act, 1974 was made this way. Art. 253 : law to implement international agreements and decisions. The Air Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 recite the Stockholm Conference of 1972. Art. 248 : residuary power for matters not in List II or III. If a State law conflicts with a Central law on a Concurrent subject, Article 254 makes the Central law prevail (unless the State law has the President's assent ).
legalProvision: Article 246(1) – "Parliament has exclusive power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule". Article 246(2) – Parliament, and the Legislature of any State "also, have power to make laws with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List III". Article 246(3) – "the Legislature of any State ... has exclusive power to make laws for such State or any part thereof with respect to any of the matters enumerated in List II". Article 248(1) – Parliament "has exclusive power to make any law with respect to any matter not enumerated in the Concurrent List or State List". Article 249(1) – if the Council of States declares by resolution "supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting" that it is necessary "in the national interest", Parliament may make laws on a State List matter while the resolution is in force (Art. 249(2): up to one year at a time). Article 252(1) – if "resolutions to that effect are passed by all the Houses of the Legislatures of those States", Parliament may pass an Act regulating that matter, which applies to those States "and to any other State by which it is adopted afterwards by resolution". Article 253 – "Parliament has power to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any other country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other body." Article 254(1) – if a State law "is repugnant to any provision of a law made by Parliament", on a Concurrent List matter, "the law made by Parliament ... shall prevail and the law made by the Legislature of the State shall, to the extent of the repugnancy, be void." Art. 254(2) saves a State law reserved for and assented to by the President. Seventh Schedule entries relevant to the environment:

List Entry Words I 13 "Participation in international conferences, associations and other bodies and implementing of decisions made thereat." I 52 "Industries, the control of which by the Union is declared by Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest." I 53 "Regulation and development of oilfields and mineral oil resources ..." I 54 "Regulation of mines and mineral development" (to the extent declared by Parliament by law) I 56 "Regulation and development of inter-State rivers and river valleys" (to the extent declared by Parliament by law) I 57 "Fishing and fisheries beyond territorial waters." I 97 "Any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III" II 5 "Local government" II 6 "Public health and sanitation; hospitals and dispensaries." II 14 "Agriculture, including ... protection against pests and prevention of plant diseases." II 17 "Water, that is to say, water supplies, irrigation and canals, drainage and embankments, water storage and water power subject to the provisions of entry 56 of List I." II 18 "Land" II 21 "Fisheries." II 23 "Regulation of mines and mineral development subject to the provisions of List I" II 24 "Industries subject to the provisions of entries 7 and 52 of List I." III 17 "Prevention of cruelty to animals." III 17A "Forests." (ins. by 42nd Amendment, s. 57, w.e.f. 3-1-1977) III 17B "Protection of wild animals and birds." (same) III 20 "Economic and social planning." III 29 "Prevention of the extension from one State to another of infectious or contagious diseases or pests affecting men, animals or plants." III 36 "Factories" III 38 "Electricity."

Article 243W and the Twelfth Schedule – a State may by law give Municipalities powers on matters in the Twelfth Schedule, which include item 6 "Public health, sanitation conservancy and solid waste management" and item 8 "Urban forestry, protection of the environment and promotion of ecological aspects".
hi.meaning: Union List – List I of the Seventh Schedule; only Parliament can make laws on it (Art. 246(1)). State List – List II; only the State Legislature can make laws on it (Art. 246(3)), subject to Arts. 249, 250, 252 and 253. Concurrent List – List III; both Parliament and the States can make laws on it (Art. 246(2)); the Central law prevails in a conflict (Art. 254). Residuary power – Parliament's power under Art. 248 and List I Entry 97 over matters not in List II or III. Repugnancy – a direct conflict between a State law and a Central law on the same Concurrent subject. Pith and substance – the test courts use to find which entry a law truly falls under, by looking at its main subject.
keyPoints: Art. 246: Union List, State List, Concurrent List. Forests (17A) and wild animals and birds (17B) are Concurrent since 1977. Water (Entry 17) and public health (Entry 6) are State subjects. Water Act, 1974: Art. 252; Air Act, 1981 and EP Act, 1986: Stockholm 1972 (Art. 253). Residuary power: Art. 248 and List I Entry 97 ( Municipal Corporation of Jullundur ). Art. 254: Central law prevails on Concurrent subjects, unless the President assents to the State law.

caseLaws.name: Facts: A maker of non-woven plastic carry bags was fined Rs
caseLaws.facts: 5,00,000 by the State Pollution Control Board under the Uttarakhand Plastic and Other Non Biodegradable Garbage (Regulation of Use and Disposal) Act, 2013. He argued that the State had no power, as environment fell under List I Entry 13, and that the State ban was repugnant to the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016. Principle: "The subject of environment does not specifically find mention in any of the Entries"; the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 "is not related to participation" in international conferences (Entry 13). The State Act fell within State Entries 5, 6, 17, 18 and "can also be traced to Entries 17A and 17B of List III-Concurrent List". A stricter State ban "does not create any repugnancy with the Plastic Waste Management Rules". The appeal was dismissed. Why it matters: It shows how environmental laws are placed in the Lists by pith and substance, and how repugnancy is judged.
Municipal Corporation of Jullundur v. Union of India AIR 1981 P&H 287 (Punjab and Haryana High Court; J.V. Gupta J; 25 February 1981)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Parliament was competent "under Article 248 read with Entry 97 of List-I"; "Even in the absence of the Act of 1974 the Parliament was competent to levy tax on the water consumption". environmental-law-u4-t5.subtitle: What Article 31C protects, what the 42nd Amendment added and what Minerva Mills struck down

en.inOneMinute: Article 31C says that a law giving effect to certain Directive Principles "shall not be deemed to be void" on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges , the rights in Article 14 or Article 19 . Environment is a Directive Principle (Art. 48A). So the question is: is an environmental law immune from challenge under Arts. 14 and 19? The answer depends on the history of Art. 31C (See Diagram 1 .): 1971 (25th Amendment): Art. 31C covered only Art. 39(b) and (c). 1976 (42nd Amendment, s. 4): extended to "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV", which would include Art. 48A. 1980 ( Minerva Mills ): s. 4 of the 42nd Amendment was declared void. 2024 ( Property Owners Association ): Art. 31C survives in its earlier form, for Art. 39(b) and (c) only. So today an environmental law made only to give effect to Art. 48A is not protected by Art. 31C. It can be tested against Arts. 14 and 19 like any other law. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 31C (as printed today) – "Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing [all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV] shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by [article 14 or article 19;]". Proviso – "where such law is made by the Legislature of a State, the provisions of this article shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent." Footnotes to Art. 31C in the bare Act: Inserted by the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 3 (w.e.f. 20-4-1972). "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" substituted by the 42nd Amendment, s. 4, for "the principles specified in clause (b) or clause (c) of article 39"; "Section 4 has been declared invalid by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills". "article 14 or article 19" substituted by the 44th Amendment, s. 8, for "article 14, article 19 or article 31" (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). The last words, "and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy", were struck down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala , AIR 1973 SC 1461. Article 39(b) – "that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good". Article 39(c) – "that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment". Article 13(2) – "The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country."
en.meaning: Judicial scrutiny – the court's power to examine whether a law is valid, for example whether it violates a Fundamental Right (Art. 13(2)). Immunity – protection of a law from being declared void on a particular ground; under Art. 31C, the ground of inconsistency with Art. 14 or Art. 19. Basic structure – the essential features of the Constitution that Parliament cannot destroy even by amendment. In Minerva Mills , the balance between Parts III and IV was held to be such a feature. Material resources of the community – the resources referred to in Art. 39(b), whose ownership and control must be distributed for the common good. Declaration clause – the struck-down last part of Art. 31C, which tried to stop courts from asking whether a law really gives effect to the Directive Principle.
keyPoints: Art. 31C gives immunity only against Arts. 14 and 19. The 42nd Amendment extension to all of Part IV (including Art. 48A) was void ( Minerva Mills ): the balance of Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure. Kesavananda : declaration clause struck down; judicial scrutiny of whether the law serves the policy remains. Property Owners Association (2024): Art. 31C survives for Art. 39(b) and (c). Not every private resource is a material resource of the community. Environmental laws under Art. 48A are tested under Arts. 14 and 19(6).

caseLaws.facts: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India AIR 1980 SC 1789; (1980) 3 SCC 625 (Supreme Court, five judges; Chandrachud CJ for himself, A.C. Gupta, N.L. Untwalia and P.S. Kailasam JJ; Bhagwati J separate opinion; order 9 May 1980, reasons 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Minerva Mills, a textile undertaking in Karnataka, was taken over (1971) and then nationalise
caseLaws.facts: The owners also challenged ss. 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which extended Art. 31C to all of Part IV and limited review of amendments under Art. 368. Principle: "Section 4 of the Constitution 42nd Amendment Act is beyond the amending power of the Parliament and is void". "Parts III and IV are like two wheels of a chariot, one no less important than the other"; "This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure". The unamended Art. 31C was valid "to the extent to which it was upheld in Kesavananda Bharati". Why it matters: It is the reason environmental laws under Art. 48A do not get Art. 31C immunity.
Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3122 (Supreme Court, nine judges; Chandrachud CJI for the majority; decided 5 November 2024)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Property owners challenged Chapter VIII-A of the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Act
caseLaws.facts: The case raised whether Art. 31C survived after Minerva Mills and what "material resources of the community" in Art. 39(b) means. Principle: Unanimously, Art. 31C survives in the unamended form upheld in Kesavananda Bharati . By majority, not every resource owned by an individual is a "material resource of the community"; it depends on factors such as the nature of the resource, its impact on the community's well-being, its scarcity and the effect of private concentration. Why it matters: It settles that Art. 31C today covers only Art. 39(b) and (c), and gives the test for when a resource falls under Art. 39(b).
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala AIR 1973 SC 1461 (Supreme Court)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 25th Amendment, which inserted Art
caseLaws.facts: 31C, was among the amendments challenged. Principle: The first part of Art. 31C (laws giving effect to Art. 39(b) and (c)) was upheld; the declaration clause, which barred courts from asking whether a law really gave effect to that policy, was struck down (as recorded in the footnote to Art. 31C). Why it matters: It keeps judicial scrutiny alive even for laws Art. 31C protects.

selfTest.q: Which rights does Art. 31C exclude today?
selfTest.a: What did s. 4 of the 42nd Amendment do to Art. 31C? Why did Minerva Mills strike down s. 4? What part of Art. 31C was struck down in Kesavananda ? What did Property Owners Association (2024) hold about Art. 31C? Does an environmental law made under Art. 48A get Art. 31C immunity today?

te.inOneMinute: కొన్ని ఆదేశిక సూత్రాలను అమలు చేసే చట్టం ఆర్టికల్ 14 లేదా ఆర్టికల్ 19 హక్కులకు విరుద్ధంగా ఉందనే లేదా వాటిని హరిస్తుందనే కారణంతో "shall not be deemed to be void" (అర్థం: చెల్లనిదిగా పరిగణించబడదు) అని ఆర్టికల్ 31C చెబుతుంది. పర్యావరణం ఒక ఆదేశిక సూత్రం (ఆర్టికల్ 48A). కాబట్టి ప్రశ్న: పర్యావరణ చట్టానికి ఆర్టికల్స్ 14, 19 కింద సవాలు నుంచి రక్షణ ఉందా? జవాబు ఆర్టికల్ 31C చరిత్రపై ఆధారపడి ఉంటుంది ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.): 1971 (25వ సవరణ): ఆర్టికల్ 31C ఆర్టికల్ 39(b), (c)ని మాత్రమే కవర్ చేసింది. 1976 (42వ సవరణ, సెక్షన్ 4): "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" (అర్థం: భాగం IVలో పేర్కొన్న అన్ని లేదా ఏ సూత్రాలైనా)కు విస్తరించింది; అందులో ఆర్టికల్ 48A ఉంటుంది. 1980 ( Minerva Mills ): 42వ సవరణలోని సెక్షన్ 4 చెల్లనిదిగా ప్రకటించబడింది. 2024 ( Property Owners Association ): ఆర్టికల్ 31C దాని పూర్వ రూపంలో, ఆర్టికల్ 39(b), (c)కి మాత్రమే, కొనసాగుతుంది. కాబట్టి నేడు కేవలం ఆర్టికల్ 48Aను అమలు చేయడానికి చేసిన పర్యావరణ చట్టానికి ఆర్టికల్ 31C రక్షణ లేదు . ఇతర ఏ చట్టం లాగే దాన్ని ఆర్టికల్స్ 14, 19కి వ్యతిరేకంగా పరీక్షించవచ్చు. ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: న్యాయ సమీక్ష (Judicial scrutiny ) – ఒక చట్టం చెల్లుబాటును, ఉదాహరణకు అది ప్రాథమిక హక్కును ఉల్లంఘిస్తుందా అని పరిశీలించే కోర్టు అధికారం (ఆర్టికల్ 13(2)). రక్షణ / మినహాయింపు (Immunity) – ఒక నిర్దిష్ట కారణంపై చట్టం చెల్లనిదిగా ప్రకటించబడకుండా రక్షణ; ఆర్టికల్ 31C కింద, ఆర్టికల్ 14 లేదా ఆర్టికల్ 19కి విరుద్ధం అనే కారణం. మౌలిక నిర్మాణం (Basic structure) – సవరణ ద్వారా కూడా పార్లమెంటు నాశనం చేయలేని రాజ్యాంగ ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు. Minerva Mills లో భాగాలు III, IV మధ్య సమతుల్యత అలాంటి లక్షణంగా తీర్పు ఇవ్వబడింది. సమాజ భౌతిక వనరులు (Material resources of the community) – ఆర్టికల్ 39(b)లో పేర్కొన్న వనరులు; వాటి యాజమాన్యం, నియంత్రణ ఉమ్మడి మేలు కోసం పంపిణీ చేయబడాలి. ప్రకటన క్లాజు (Declaration clause) – ఒక చట్టం నిజంగా ఆదేశిక సూత్రాన్ని అమలు చేస్తుందా అని కోర్టులు అడగకుండా ఆపడానికి ప్రయత్నించిన, కొట్టివేయబడిన ఆర్టికల్ 31C చివరి భాగం.
keyPoints: ఆర్టికల్ 31C ఆర్టికల్స్ 14, 19 నుంచి మాత్రమే రక్షణ ఇస్తుంది. భాగం IV మొత్తానికి (ఆర్టికల్ 48Aతో సహా) 42వ సవరణ విస్తరణ చెల్లదు ( Minerva Mills ): భాగాలు III, IV సమతుల్యత మౌలిక నిర్మాణంలో భాగం. Kesavananda : ప్రకటన క్లాజు కొట్టివేత; చట్టం విధానానికి ఉపయోగపడుతుందో న్యాయ సమీక్ష కొనసాగుతుంది. Property Owners Association (2024): ఆర్టికల్ 39(b), (c) కోసం ఆర్టికల్ 31C కొనసాగుతుంది. ప్రతి ప్రైవేటు వనరూ సమాజ భౌతిక వనరు కాదు. ఆర్టికల్ 48A కింద పర్యావరణ చట్టాలను ఆర్టికల్స్ 14, 19(6) కింద పరీక్షిస్తారు.

selfTest.q: నేడు ఆర్టికల్ 31C ఏ హక్కులను మినహాయిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: 42వ సవరణ సెక్షన్ 4 ఆర్టికల్ 31Cకి ఏమి చేసింది? Minerva Mills సెక్షన్ 4ను ఎందుకు కొట్టివేసింది? Kesavananda లో ఆర్టికల్ 31Cలోని ఏ భాగం కొట్టివేయబడింది? ఆర్టికల్ 31C గురించి Property Owners Association (2024) ఏమి తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది? ఆర్టికల్ 48A కింద చేసిన పర్యావరణ చట్టానికి నేడు ఆర్టికల్ 31C రక్షణ ఉందా?

భాగం IV మొత్తానికి విస్తరణ చెల్లదు; మౌలిక నిర్మాణాన్ని ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది Minerva Mills (1980)
భాగాలు III, IV సమతుల్యత మౌలిక నిర్మాణంలో ముఖ్య లక్షణం Minerva Mills, పేరా 61
ప్రస్తుత పరిధి ఆర్టికల్ 39(b), (c) మాత్రమే Property Owners Association (2024)
పర్యావరణ చట్టం (ఆర్టికల్ 48A) ఆర్టికల్ 31C రక్షణ లేదు; ఆర్టికల్స్ 14, 19 కింద పరీక్ష పైవాటి విశ్లేషణ

hi.inOneMinute: Article 31C says that a law giving effect to certain Directive Principles "shall not be deemed to be void" on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges , the rights in Article 14 or Article 19 . Environment is a Directive Principle (Art. 48A). So the question is: is an environmental law immune from challenge under Arts. 14 and 19? The answer depends on the history of Art. 31C (See Diagram 1 .): 1971 (25th Amendment): Art. 31C covered only Art. 39(b) and (c). 1976 (42nd Amendment, s. 4): extended to "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV", which would include Art. 48A. 1980 ( Minerva Mills ): s. 4 of the 42nd Amendment was declared void. 2024 ( Property Owners Association ): Art. 31C survives in its earlier form, for Art. 39(b) and (c) only. So today an environmental law made only to give effect to Art. 48A is not protected by Art. 31C. It can be tested against Arts. 14 and 19 like any other law. (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 31C (as printed today) – "Notwithstanding anything contained in article 13, no law giving effect to the policy of the State towards securing [all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV] shall be deemed to be void on the ground that it is inconsistent with, or takes away or abridges any of the rights conferred by [article 14 or article 19;]". Proviso – "where such law is made by the Legislature of a State, the provisions of this article shall not apply thereto unless such law, having been reserved for the consideration of the President, has received his assent." Footnotes to Art. 31C in the bare Act: Inserted by the Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 3 (w.e.f. 20-4-1972). "all or any of the principles laid down in Part IV" substituted by the 42nd Amendment, s. 4, for "the principles specified in clause (b) or clause (c) of article 39"; "Section 4 has been declared invalid by the Supreme Court in Minerva Mills". "article 14 or article 19" substituted by the 44th Amendment, s. 8, for "article 14, article 19 or article 31" (w.e.f. 20-6-1979). The last words, "and no law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy", were struck down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala , AIR 1973 SC 1461. Article 39(b) – "that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are so distributed as best to subserve the common good". Article 39(c) – "that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment". Article 13(2) – "The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country."
hi.meaning: Judicial scrutiny – the court's power to examine whether a law is valid, for example whether it violates a Fundamental Right (Art. 13(2)). Immunity – protection of a law from being declared void on a particular ground; under Art. 31C, the ground of inconsistency with Art. 14 or Art. 19. Basic structure – the essential features of the Constitution that Parliament cannot destroy even by amendment. In Minerva Mills , the balance between Parts III and IV was held to be such a feature. Material resources of the community – the resources referred to in Art. 39(b), whose ownership and control must be distributed for the common good. Declaration clause – the struck-down last part of Art. 31C, which tried to stop courts from asking whether a law really gives effect to the Directive Principle.
keyPoints: Art. 31C gives immunity only against Arts. 14 and 19. The 42nd Amendment extension to all of Part IV (including Art. 48A) was void ( Minerva Mills ): the balance of Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure. Kesavananda : declaration clause struck down; judicial scrutiny of whether the law serves the policy remains. Property Owners Association (2024): Art. 31C survives for Art. 39(b) and (c). Not every private resource is a material resource of the community. Environmental laws under Art. 48A are tested under Arts. 14 and 19(6).

caseLaws.facts: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India AIR 1980 SC 1789; (1980) 3 SCC 625 (Supreme Court, five judges; Chandrachud CJ for himself, A.C. Gupta, N.L. Untwalia and P.S. Kailasam JJ; Bhagwati J separate opinion; order 9 May 1980, reasons 31 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Minerva Mills, a textile undertaking in Karnataka, was taken over (1971) and then nationalise
caseLaws.facts: The owners also challenged ss. 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment, which extended Art. 31C to all of Part IV and limited review of amendments under Art. 368. Principle: "Section 4 of the Constitution 42nd Amendment Act is beyond the amending power of the Parliament and is void". "Parts III and IV are like two wheels of a chariot, one no less important than the other"; "This harmony and balance between fundamental rights and directive principles is an essential feature of the basic structure". The unamended Art. 31C was valid "to the extent to which it was upheld in Kesavananda Bharati". Why it matters: It is the reason environmental laws under Art. 48A do not get Art. 31C immunity.
Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3122 (Supreme Court, nine judges; Chandrachud CJI for the majority; decided 5 November 2024)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Property owners challenged Chapter VIII-A of the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Act
caseLaws.facts: The case raised whether Art. 31C survived after Minerva Mills and what "material resources of the community" in Art. 39(b) means. Principle: Unanimously, Art. 31C survives in the unamended form upheld in Kesavananda Bharati . By majority, not every resource owned by an individual is a "material resource of the community"; it depends on factors such as the nature of the resource, its impact on the community's well-being, its scarcity and the effect of private concentration. Why it matters: It settles that Art. 31C today covers only Art. 39(b) and (c), and gives the test for when a resource falls under Art. 39(b).
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala AIR 1973 SC 1461 (Supreme Court)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The 25th Amendment, which inserted Art
caseLaws.facts: 31C, was among the amendments challenged. Principle: The first part of Art. 31C (laws giving effect to Art. 39(b) and (c)) was upheld; the declaration clause, which barred courts from asking whether a law really gave effect to that policy, was struck down (as recorded in the footnote to Art. 31C). Why it matters: It keeps judicial scrutiny alive even for laws Art. 31C protects.

selfTest.q: Which rights does Art. 31C exclude today?

environmental-law-u4-t7.subtitle: Articles 32 and 226: how environmental disputes reach the Supreme Court and the High Courts

en.inOneMinute: Writ jurisdiction is the power of the Supreme Court ( Art. 32 ) and the High Courts ( Art. 226 ) to issue directions, orders or writs to protect rights. In environmental cases it is the main way people reach the courts, because the right to a healthy environment is part of Art. 21 (see "Right to wholesome environment"). (See Diagram 1 .) The five writs named in the Constitution are habeas corpus, mandamus , prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari . Mandamus (an order to a public authority to do its legal duty) is the one used most in pollution cases, together with wide "directions". Courts have widened access: A letter can be treated as a writ petition ( RLEK , 1983–85; M.C. Mehta (oleum), 1986). (See Diagram 2 .) Public-spirited persons and groups may file, if they act genuinely for the community ( Subhash Kumar , 1991). Courts have also widened remedies: under Art. 32 the power is "not only injunctive in ambit" but "also remedial in scope", and includes compensation in appropriate cases ( M.C. Mehta , oleum gas case, 1986).
legalProvision: Article 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Article 32(2) – "The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part." Article 32(4) – "The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution." Article 226(1) – "every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose." Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
en.meaning: Writ – a formal written order of a court commanding a person or authority to do or not to do something. Mandamus – "we command"; a writ ordering a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed to perform (for example, a Pollution Control Board failing to act). Certiorari – a writ quashing an order of an authority made without jurisdiction or in breach of law (for example, an illegal permission). Prohibition – a writ stopping a lower court or tribunal from acting beyond its jurisdiction. Quo warranto – a writ asking a person "by what authority" he holds a public office. Habeas corpus – a writ to produce a detained person before the court; rarely relevant to environment cases. Locus standi – the right to approach the court. In public interest cases it is widened to any public-spirited person or group acting genuinely for others. Epistolary jurisdiction – the court's practice of treating a letter as a writ petition.
keyPoints: Art. 32: Supreme Court; Fundamental Rights; itself a Fundamental Right. Art. 226: High Court; Fundamental Rights "and for any other purpose". Five writs; mandamus and directions are used most in pollution cases. Epistolary jurisdiction: a letter can be a writ petition ( RLEK ; M.C. Mehta ). Wide locus standi for genuine public interest ( Subhash Kumar ). Art. 32 is remedial; compensation in appropriate cases ( M.C. Mehta , oleum gas).

caseLaws.facts: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (oleum gas case) AIR 1987 SC 1086; (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench; P.N. Bhagwati CJ for the Court; 20 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: In a writ petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 about the Shriram Foods and Fertiliser Industries plant in Delhi, oleum gas escaped from one of its units on 4 and 6 December 1985. The Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board and the Delhi Bar Association applied for compensation for those harmed. Principle: Art. 32 includes "the power to forge new remedies and fashion new strategies designed to enforce the fundamental rights". The power "is not only injunctive in ambit" but "also remedial in scope", and "may include the power to award compensation in appropriate cases". A letter to the Court can start a case. Why it matters: It shaped writ jurisdiction in environmental cases: wide access and wide remedies.
Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. AIR 1985 SC 652; (1985) 2 SCC 431 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati, A.N. Sen and Ranganath Misra JJ; order of 12 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter dated 2 July 1983 from RLEK, Dehra Dun, complaining of illegal limestone mining in t
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Acting under Art. 32, the Court stopped blasting by interim order, closed many quarries and allowed others under conditions, to protect "the right of the people to live in healthy environment". Why it matters: It shows a letter becoming a full environmental writ case with far-reaching directions.
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar AIR 1991 SC 420; (1991) 1 SCC 598 (Supreme Court; K.N. Singh J for himself and N.D. Ojha J; reasons 9 January 1991)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 alleged that TISCO's washeries were discharging slurry into the Bokaro river. Principle: A citizen may approach the Court under Art. 32 "for removing the pollution of water or air which may be detrimental to the quality of life"; the petition may be filed by "affected persons or even by a group of social workers or journalists", but not to satisfy "personal grudge and enmity". The petition was dismissed with costs because it was filed for personal interest. Why it matters: It sets both the reach and the limit of environmental writ petitions.

te.inOneMinute: రిట్ అధికార పరిధి అంటే హక్కులను కాపాడడానికి ఆదేశాలు, ఉత్తర్వులు లేదా రిట్‌లు జారీ చేసే సుప్రీంకోర్టు ( ఆర్టికల్ 32 ), హైకోర్టుల ( ఆర్టికల్ 226 ) అధికారం. ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణ హక్కు ఆర్టికల్ 21 లో భాగం కాబట్టి ("Right to wholesome environment" చూడండి), పర్యావరణ కేసుల్లో ప్రజలు కోర్టులను చేరుకునే ప్రధాన మార్గం ఇదే. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) రాజ్యాంగంలో పేర్కొన్న ఐదు రిట్‌లు: హేబియస్ కార్పస్, మాండమస్ , ప్రొహిబిషన్, కో వారంటో, సెర్షియోరరి. కాలుష్య కేసుల్లో విస్తృత "directions" (అర్థం: ఆదేశాలు)తో పాటు ఎక్కువగా వాడేది మాండమస్ (ప్రజా అధికార సంస్థ తన చట్టపరమైన విధిని నిర్వర్తించాలనే ఉత్తర్వు). కోర్టులు అందుబాటును విస్తరించాయి: ఒక లేఖ ను రిట్ పిటిషన్‌గా పరిగణించవచ్చు ( RLEK , 1983–85; M.C. Mehta (ఓలియం), 1986). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) సమాజం కోసం నిజాయితీగా వ్యవహరిస్తే ప్రజాసేవా భావం ఉన్న వ్యక్తులు, సంఘాలు పిటిషన్ వేయవచ్చు ( Subhash Kumar , 1991). కోర్టులు పరిష్కారాలను కూడా విస్తరించాయి: ఆర్టికల్ 32 కింద అధికారం "not only injunctive in ambit" (అర్థం: నిరోధక పరిధికి మాత్రమే పరిమితం కాదు), "also remedial in scope" (అర్థం: పరిహార స్వభావం కూడా కలిగి ఉంది); తగిన కేసుల్లో నష్టపరిహారం కూడా ఇందులో ఉంది ( M.C. Mehta , ఓలియం గ్యాస్ కేసు, 1986).
te.meaning: రిట్ (Writ) – ఏదైనా చేయమని లేదా చేయవద్దని ఒక వ్యక్తిని లేదా అధికార సంస్థను ఆదేశించే కోర్టు అధికారిక లిఖిత ఉత్తర్వు. మాండమస్ ( Mandamus ) – "మేము ఆదేశిస్తున్నాం"; ఒక ప్రజా అధికార సంస్థ నిర్వర్తించని ప్రజా విధిని నిర్వర్తించమని ఆదేశించే రిట్ (ఉదా. చర్య తీసుకోని కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ బోర్డు). సెర్షియోరరి ( Certiorari ) – అధికార పరిధి లేకుండా లేదా చట్ట ఉల్లంఘనతో చేసిన అధికార సంస్థ ఉత్తర్వును రద్దు చేసే రిట్ (ఉదా. చట్టవిరుద్ధ అనుమతి). ప్రొహిబిషన్ ( Prohibition ) – కింది కోర్టు లేదా ట్రిబ్యునల్ తన అధికార పరిధి మించి వ్యవహరించకుండా ఆపే రిట్. కో వారంటో ( Quo warranto ) – ఒక వ్యక్తి ప్రజా పదవిని "ఏ అధికారంతో" నిర్వహిస్తున్నాడని అడిగే రిట్. హేబియస్ కార్పస్ ( Habeas corpus ) – నిర్బంధంలో ఉన్న వ్యక్తిని కోర్టు ముందు హాజరుపరచమనే రిట్; పర్యావరణ కేసుల్లో అరుదుగా సంబంధం ఉంటుంది. వ్యాజ్య అర్హత (Locus standi) – కోర్టును ఆశ్రయించే హక్కు. ప్రజా ప్రయోజన కేసుల్లో ఇతరుల కోసం నిజాయితీగా వ్యవహరించే ఏ ప్రజాసేవా వ్యక్తికైనా లేదా సంఘానికైనా ఇది విస్తరించబడింది. లేఖా అధికార పరిధి ( Epistolary jurisdiction ) – ఒక లేఖను రిట్ పిటిషన్‌గా పరిగణించే కోర్టు పద్ధతి.
keyPoints: ఆర్టికల్ 32: సుప్రీంకోర్టు; ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు; స్వయంగా ప్రాథమిక హక్కు. ఆర్టికల్ 226: హైకోర్టు; ప్రాథమిక హక్కులు "and for any other purpose" (అర్థం: మరే ఇతర ప్రయోజనం కోసమైనా). ఐదు రిట్‌లు; కాలుష్య కేసుల్లో మాండమస్, ఆదేశాలు ఎక్కువగా వాడబడతాయి. లేఖా అధికార పరిధి: ఒక లేఖ రిట్ పిటిషన్ కాగలదు ( RLEK ; M.C. Mehta ). నిజమైన ప్రజా ప్రయోజనానికి విస్తృత వ్యాజ్య అర్హత ( Subhash Kumar ). ఆర్టికల్ 32 పరిహారాత్మకం; తగిన కేసుల్లో నష్టపరిహారం ( M.C. Mehta , ఓలియం గ్యాస్).

selfTest.q: సుప్రీంకోర్టు, హైకోర్టులకు రిట్ అధికార పరిధిని ఏ ఆర్టికల్స్ ఇస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: ఆర్టికల్ 226 ఆర్టికల్ 32 కంటే ఎందుకు విస్తృతమైనది? ఆర్టికల్ 32(2)లోని ఐదు రిట్‌లను పేర్కొనండి. కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ బోర్డును తన విధి నిర్వర్తించమని ఏ రిట్ ఆదేశిస్తుంది? ఆర్టికల్ 32 పరిహారాత్మకం అని M.C. Mehta (ఓలియం గ్యాస్) ఏమి చెప్పింది? Subhash Kumar ప్రకారం కాలుష్య పిటిషన్‌ను ఎవరు వేయవచ్చు?

hi.inOneMinute: Writ jurisdiction is the power of the Supreme Court ( Art. 32 ) and the High Courts ( Art. 226 ) to issue directions, orders or writs to protect rights. In environmental cases it is the main way people reach the courts, because the right to a healthy environment is part of Art. 21 (see "Right to wholesome environment"). (See Diagram 1 .) The five writs named in the Constitution are habeas corpus, mandamus , prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari . Mandamus (an order to a public authority to do its legal duty) is the one used most in pollution cases, together with wide "directions". Courts have widened access: A letter can be treated as a writ petition ( RLEK , 1983–85; M.C. Mehta (oleum), 1986). (See Diagram 2 .) Public-spirited persons and groups may file, if they act genuinely for the community ( Subhash Kumar , 1991). Courts have also widened remedies: under Art. 32 the power is "not only injunctive in ambit" but "also remedial in scope", and includes compensation in appropriate cases ( M.C. Mehta , oleum gas case, 1986).
legalProvision: Article 32(1) – "The right to move the Supreme Court by appropriate proceedings for the enforcement of the rights conferred by this Part is guaranteed." Article 32(2) – "The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, whichever may be appropriate, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part." Article 32(4) – "The right guaranteed by this article shall not be suspended except as otherwise provided for by this Constitution." Article 226(1) – "every High Court shall have power, throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction, to issue to any person or authority, including in appropriate cases, any Government, within those territories directions, orders or writs, including writs in the nature of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto and certiorari, or any of them, for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose." Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law."
hi.meaning: Writ – a formal written order of a court commanding a person or authority to do or not to do something. Mandamus – "we command"; a writ ordering a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed to perform (for example, a Pollution Control Board failing to act). Certiorari – a writ quashing an order of an authority made without jurisdiction or in breach of law (for example, an illegal permission). Prohibition – a writ stopping a lower court or tribunal from acting beyond its jurisdiction. Quo warranto – a writ asking a person "by what authority" he holds a public office. Habeas corpus – a writ to produce a detained person before the court; rarely relevant to environment cases. Locus standi – the right to approach the court. In public interest cases it is widened to any public-spirited person or group acting genuinely for others. Epistolary jurisdiction – the court's practice of treating a letter as a writ petition.
keyPoints: Art. 32: Supreme Court; Fundamental Rights; itself a Fundamental Right. Art. 226: High Court; Fundamental Rights "and for any other purpose". Five writs; mandamus and directions are used most in pollution cases. Epistolary jurisdiction: a letter can be a writ petition ( RLEK ; M.C. Mehta ). Wide locus standi for genuine public interest ( Subhash Kumar ). Art. 32 is remedial; compensation in appropriate cases ( M.C. Mehta , oleum gas).

caseLaws.facts: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (oleum gas case) AIR 1987 SC 1086; (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench; P.N. Bhagwati CJ for the Court; 20 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: In a writ petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 about the Shriram Foods and Fertiliser Industries plant in Delhi, oleum gas escaped from one of its units on 4 and 6 December 1985. The Delhi Legal Aid and Advice Board and the Delhi Bar Association applied for compensation for those harmed. Principle: Art. 32 includes "the power to forge new remedies and fashion new strategies designed to enforce the fundamental rights". The power "is not only injunctive in ambit" but "also remedial in scope", and "may include the power to award compensation in appropriate cases". A letter to the Court can start a case. Why it matters: It shaped writ jurisdiction in environmental cases: wide access and wide remedies.
Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of U.P. AIR 1985 SC 652; (1985) 2 SCC 431 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati, A.N. Sen and Ranganath Misra JJ; order of 12 March 1985)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A letter dated 2 July 1983 from RLEK, Dehra Dun, complaining of illegal limestone mining in t
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Acting under Art. 32, the Court stopped blasting by interim order, closed many quarries and allowed others under conditions, to protect "the right of the people to live in healthy environment". Why it matters: It shows a letter becoming a full environmental writ case with far-reaching directions.
Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar AIR 1991 SC 420; (1991) 1 SCC 598 (Supreme Court; K.N. Singh J for himself and N.D. Ojha J; reasons 9 January 1991)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A petition under Art
caseLaws.facts: 32 alleged that TISCO's washeries were discharging slurry into the Bokaro river. Principle: A citizen may approach the Court under Art. 32 "for removing the pollution of water or air which may be detrimental to the quality of life"; the petition may be filed by "affected persons or even by a group of social workers or journalists", but not to satisfy "personal grudge and enmity". The petition was dismissed with costs because it was filed for personal interest. Why it matters: It sets both the reach and the limit of environmental writ petitions.

environmental-law-u4-t8.subtitle: How the Supreme Court built rights, principles and procedures for environmental protection

en.inOneMinute: Indian environmental law has been built as much by the courts as by Parliament. The Supreme Court and High Courts have: opened the courts to the public through public interest litigation and letters; read a right to a healthy environment into Art. 21; created or adopted new doctrines : absolute liability, polluter pays, precautionary principle and sustainable development; used Arts. 48A and 51A(g) to guide decisions; given new remedies : closures, conditions, compensation, expert committees and special benches. (See Diagram 1 .) Key steps: Ratlam (1980): courts can compel a municipality to remove a public nuisance; lack of funds is no excuse. M.C. Mehta (oleum gas, 1986): absolute liability for hazardous industries. Vellore (1996): precautionary and polluter pays principles are "part of the environmental law of the country". (See Diagram 2 .) The courts also set limits: PIL must be genuine ( Subhash Kumar ), and development is not stopped as such ( Narmada Bachao Andolan ; Sterlite ). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Article 32(2) – "The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs ... for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part." Article 226(1) – High Courts may issue "directions, orders or writs ... for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 141 – the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India (which is why its environmental doctrines bind lower courts). Section 133, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (now s. 152, BNSS, 2023) – the Magistrate's power to order removal of a public nuisance, used in Ratlam .
en.meaning: Environmental jurisprudence – the body of legal principles on environmental protection developed through statutes and, especially in India, through court decisions. Judicial activism – courts going beyond the narrow resolution of a private dispute to protect rights and the public interest, by widening access, rights and remedies. Public interest litigation (PIL) – a case brought for the benefit of the public, often by a person not personally injured. Absolute liability – liability of an enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity for harm caused by it, without the exceptions allowed under Rylands v. Fletcher ( M.C. Mehta , 1986). Polluter pays principle – the polluter must bear the cost of preventing or remedying the damage it causes.
keyPoints: Judicial activism built Indian environmental jurisprudence. Ratlam (1980): from locus standi to public interest litigation; no excuse of funds. M.C. Mehta (1986): absolute liability; compensation linked to capacity. Subhash Kumar (1991): pollution-free water and air in Art. 21. ICELA and Vellore (1996): polluter pays principle and precautionary principle part of Indian law; sustainable development. Limits: genuine PIL; balancing with development ( Narmada ; Sterlite ).

caseLaws.facts: Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand AIR 1980 SC 1622 (Supreme Court; V.R. Krishna Iyer J for himself and O. Chinnappa Reddy J; 29 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents of Ward No
caseLaws.facts: 12, New Road, Ratlam suffered from open drains, filth and "malodorous fluids" discharged from an alcohol plant into the street. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate under s. 133 CrPC ordered the municipality to build drains; it pleaded lack of funds. Principle: "Decency and dignity are non-negotiable facets of human rights and are a first charge on local self-governing bodies." No statutory body may legally defy its duties "by urging in self-defence a self-created bankruptcy or perverted expenditure budget". Section 133 "is categoric, although reads discretionary". Why it matters: It began the judiciary's shift to public interest litigation and positive directions for environmental sanitation.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (oleum gas case) AIR 1987 SC 1086; (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench; P.N. Bhagwati CJ; 20 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas escaped from the Shriram Foods & Fertilizers plant in Delhi on 4 and 6 December 198
caseLaws.facts: 32. Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity "is strictly and absolutely liable" and the liability "is not subject to any of the exceptions" under Rylands v. Fletcher ; compensation must be "co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". Art. 32 is "remedial in scope". Why it matters: It created absolute liability, a uniquely Indian environmental doctrine.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar river, polluting wells a
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". The Court directed an authority under s. 3(3) of the EP Act and asked for a "Green Bench" in the Madras High Court. Why it matters: It brought international environmental principles into Indian law by judicial decision.

te.inOneMinute: భారత పర్యావరణ చట్టాన్ని పార్లమెంటు ఎంతగా నిర్మించిందో, కోర్టులు కూడా అంతగా నిర్మించాయి. సుప్రీంకోర్టు, హైకోర్టులు: ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం (PIL) , లేఖల ద్వారా కోర్టు తలుపులు ప్రజలకు తెరిచాయి; Art. 21 లో ఆరోగ్యకరమైన పర్యావరణ హక్కు ను చదివాయి; కొత్త సిద్ధాంతాలు సృష్టించాయి లేదా స్వీకరించాయి: సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి, ముందుజాగ్రత్త సూత్రం, సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి; నిర్ణయాలకు మార్గదర్శకంగా Arts. 48A, 51A(g) ను వాడాయి; కొత్త పరిష్కారాలు ఇచ్చాయి: మూసివేతలు, షరతులు, పరిహారం, నిపుణుల కమిటీలు, ప్రత్యేక బెంచ్‌లు. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ముఖ్యమైన దశలు: Ratlam (1980): ప్రజా ఉపద్రవాన్ని తొలగించమని మున్సిపాలిటీని కోర్టులు బలవంతం చేయగలవు; నిధుల కొరత సాకు కాదు. M.C. Mehta (ఓలియం గ్యాస్, 1986): ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమలకు సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత . Vellore (1996): ముందుజాగ్రత్త, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రాలు "part of the environmental law of the country" (అర్థం: దేశ పర్యావరణ చట్టంలో భాగం). ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) కోర్టులు పరిమితులు కూడా పెట్టాయి: PIL నిజాయితీగా ఉండాలి ( Subhash Kumar ); అభివృద్ధిని పూర్తిగా ఆపరు ( Narmada Bachao Andolan ; Sterlite ). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: పర్యావరణ న్యాయశాస్త్రం (Environmental jurisprudence ) – చట్టాల ద్వారా, ముఖ్యంగా భారతదేశంలో కోర్టు తీర్పుల ద్వారా, అభివృద్ధి చెందిన పర్యావరణ రక్షణ చట్ట సూత్రాల సమూహం. న్యాయ క్రియాశీలత (Judicial activism) – కోర్టులు కేవలం ఒక ప్రైవేటు వివాదాన్ని పరిష్కరించడం దాటి, కోర్టుకు ప్రవేశం, హక్కులు, పరిష్కారాలను విస్తరించి హక్కులను, ప్రజా ప్రయోజనాన్ని రక్షించడం. ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం (PIL) – ప్రజల మేలు కోసం, తరచుగా వ్యక్తిగతంగా నష్టపోని వ్యక్తి వేసే కేసు. సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత ( Absolute liability ) – ప్రమాదకర లేదా స్వాభావికంగా ప్రమాదకరమైన కార్యకలాపం చేసే సంస్థ, దాని వల్ల కలిగిన హానికి Rylands v. Fletcher కింద ఉన్న మినహాయింపులు లేకుండా బాధ్యత వహించడం ( M.C. Mehta , 1986). కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం (Polluter pays principle) – తాను కలిగించిన నష్టాన్ని నివారించే లేదా సరిచేసే ఖర్చును కాలుష్యకారుడే భరించాలి.
keyPoints: న్యాయ క్రియాశీలత భారత పర్యావరణ న్యాయశాస్త్రాన్ని నిర్మించింది. Ratlam (1980): locus standi నుండి ప్రజా ప్రయోజన వ్యాజ్యం వైపు; నిధుల సాకు చెల్లదు. M.C. Mehta (1986): సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత; సామర్థ్యానికి అనుగుణంగా పరిహారం. Subhash Kumar (1991): Art. 21 లో కాలుష్యం లేని నీరు, గాలి. ICELA , Vellore (1996): కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం, ముందుజాగ్రత్త సూత్రం భారత చట్టంలో భాగం; సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి. పరిమితులు: నిజాయితీ గల PIL; అభివృద్ధితో సమతుల్యం ( Narmada ; Sterlite ).

selfTest.q: మున్సిపాలిటీ నిధుల కొరత గురించి Ratlam ఏం చెప్పింది?
selfTest.a: M.C. Mehta (1986) ఏ కొత్త బాధ్యతను సృష్టించింది? సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత Rylands v. Fletcher నుండి ఎలా భిన్నం? ముందుజాగ్రత్త, కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రాలను భారత చట్టంలో భాగం చేసిన కేసు ఏది? పర్యావరణ కేసుల్లో కోర్టులు వాడిన రెండు కొత్త పరిష్కారాలు చెప్పండి. పర్యావరణ PIL పై కోర్టులు పెట్టిన ఒక పరిమితి చెప్పండి.

hi.inOneMinute: Indian environmental law has been built as much by the courts as by Parliament. The Supreme Court and High Courts have: opened the courts to the public through public interest litigation and letters; read a right to a healthy environment into Art. 21; created or adopted new doctrines : absolute liability, polluter pays, precautionary principle and sustainable development; used Arts. 48A and 51A(g) to guide decisions; given new remedies : closures, conditions, compensation, expert committees and special benches. (See Diagram 1 .) Key steps: Ratlam (1980): courts can compel a municipality to remove a public nuisance; lack of funds is no excuse. M.C. Mehta (oleum gas, 1986): absolute liability for hazardous industries. Vellore (1996): precautionary and polluter pays principles are "part of the environmental law of the country". (See Diagram 2 .) The courts also set limits: PIL must be genuine ( Subhash Kumar ), and development is not stopped as such ( Narmada Bachao Andolan ; Sterlite ). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Article 32(2) – "The Supreme Court shall have power to issue directions or orders or writs ... for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by this Part." Article 226(1) – High Courts may issue "directions, orders or writs ... for the enforcement of any of the rights conferred by Part III and for any other purpose." Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Article 141 – the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India (which is why its environmental doctrines bind lower courts). Section 133, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (now s. 152, BNSS, 2023) – the Magistrate's power to order removal of a public nuisance, used in Ratlam .
hi.meaning: Environmental jurisprudence – the body of legal principles on environmental protection developed through statutes and, especially in India, through court decisions. Judicial activism – courts going beyond the narrow resolution of a private dispute to protect rights and the public interest, by widening access, rights and remedies. Public interest litigation (PIL) – a case brought for the benefit of the public, often by a person not personally injured. Absolute liability – liability of an enterprise carrying on a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity for harm caused by it, without the exceptions allowed under Rylands v. Fletcher ( M.C. Mehta , 1986). Polluter pays principle – the polluter must bear the cost of preventing or remedying the damage it causes.
keyPoints: Judicial activism built Indian environmental jurisprudence. Ratlam (1980): from locus standi to public interest litigation; no excuse of funds. M.C. Mehta (1986): absolute liability; compensation linked to capacity. Subhash Kumar (1991): pollution-free water and air in Art. 21. ICELA and Vellore (1996): polluter pays principle and precautionary principle part of Indian law; sustainable development. Limits: genuine PIL; balancing with development ( Narmada ; Sterlite ).

caseLaws.facts: Municipal Council, Ratlam v. Vardhichand AIR 1980 SC 1622 (Supreme Court; V.R. Krishna Iyer J for himself and O. Chinnappa Reddy J; 29 July 1980)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Residents of Ward No
caseLaws.facts: 12, New Road, Ratlam suffered from open drains, filth and "malodorous fluids" discharged from an alcohol plant into the street. The Sub-Divisional Magistrate under s. 133 CrPC ordered the municipality to build drains; it pleaded lack of funds. Principle: "Decency and dignity are non-negotiable facets of human rights and are a first charge on local self-governing bodies." No statutory body may legally defy its duties "by urging in self-defence a self-created bankruptcy or perverted expenditure budget". Section 133 "is categoric, although reads discretionary". Why it matters: It began the judiciary's shift to public interest litigation and positive directions for environmental sanitation.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (oleum gas case) AIR 1987 SC 1086; (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench; P.N. Bhagwati CJ; 20 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas escaped from the Shriram Foods & Fertilizers plant in Delhi on 4 and 6 December 198

Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous activity "is strictly and absolutely liable" and the liability "is not subject to any of the exceptions" under Rylands v. Fletcher ; compensation must be "co-related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise". Art. 32 is "remedial in scope". Why it matters: It created absolute liability, a uniquely Indian environmental doctrine.
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh J; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Sustainable Development is the answer"; the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". The Court directed an authority under s. 3(3) of the EP Act and asked for a "Green Bench" in the Madras High Court. Why it matters: It brought international environmental principles into Indian law by judicial decision.
