environmental-law-u4-t9.subtitle: What a green belt is, why it is required and where the law uses it

en.inOneMinute: A green belt is land kept green (trees, shrubs, grass, open land) and protected from building. There are two common types: in town planning , a belt or area of open land kept free of development in the master plan; around industries , a strip of trees planted to absorb pollution, dust and noise. Purpose: to protect the natural environment, improve air quality, give people open space and stop cities from spreading without limit. (See Diagram 1 .) Advantages: it controls air pollution, dust and noise; prevents soil erosion ; keeps water in the soil; gives habitat to birds and animals; gives space for recreation; and leads to better land use. (See Diagram 2 .) Law: Arts. 21, 48A and 51A(g); master plans under town planning laws give a green belt "statutory force"; green belt conditions are attached to environmental clearances under the EP Act, 1986. Courts: a green belt cannot be changed to housing or other use in violation of Arts. 21, 48A and 51A(g) ( Lal Bahadur , 2017); a green belt reservation "has statutory force" and encroachers cannot get it regularised ( CIDCO v. Ekta Mahila Mandal , 2007). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." The courts read the right to pollution-free air and water into it ( Subhash Kumar , 1991), and Lal Bahadur applied this to green belts. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Town planning laws – master plans and development plans made under State town planning Acts reserve areas as green belts. Example: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 (CIDCO is a Special Planning Authority under s. 40, as noted in CIDCO v. Ekta Mahila Mandal ). Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – environmental clearances given under the EP Act framework carry green belt conditions. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) has issued Office Memoranda on the area of green belt (see "Detailed explanation" §5).
en.meaning: Green belt – a policy used in land use planning to retain areas of undeveloped, wild or agricultural land; also, a belt of trees and plants around a pollution source that acts as a barrier and sink for pollutants. Master plan – the statutory plan for a city that fixes the use of each area (residential, industrial, green belt, park, etc.). Public trust doctrine – the rule, applied by the Supreme Court in Lal Bahadur , that authorities hold green areas for the public and have a duty to maintain them as such. Pollution sink – something that absorbs or traps pollutants, such as trees trapping dust and gases.
keyPoints: A green belt is land kept green and free of building, or a belt of trees around a pollution source. Purpose: protect environment, air quality, open space, check urban spread, control pollution near industries. Advantages: air, dust, noise, soil, water, habitat, recreation, better land use. Trees are a pollution sink only within their tolerance limits. A green belt in the master plan has statutory force ( CIDCO ). Changing it to housing violated Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g); authorities hold it under the public trust doctrine ( Lal Bahadur ).

caseLaws.facts: Lal Bahadur v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 15 SCC 407; AIR 2018 SC 220 (Supreme Court; Arun Mishra and Mohan M. Shantanagoudar JJ; 14 September 2017)

caseLaws.name: Facts: About 266
caseLaws.facts: 661 hectares for the expansion of Gomti Nagar, Lucknow were shown as green belt in the 1995 master plan. The Master Plan 2021 (approved on 31 March 2005) changed it to residential, and land acquisition notifications followed. The area was later turned into the Janeshwar Mishra Park. Principle: The change from green belt to residential was "in flagrant violation" of Arts. 21, 48-A and 51-A(g); a green belt is "essential for fresh air", and authorities must maintain such areas "as per doctrine of public trust". The Court quashed the Master Plan 2021 change of use. Why it matters: It is the clearest Supreme Court ruling that a green belt is protected by the Constitution.
City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra v. Ekta Mahila Mandal (2007) 7 SCC 701 (Supreme Court; Arijit Pasayat and D.K. Jain JJ; 17 September 2007)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A 770 sq
caseLaws.facts: m plot in Sector N-7, Navi Mumbai was notified as green belt under the development plan. A trust built two rooms on it, used it as a playground, and asked for regularisation for educational use; the High Court allowed it. Principle: "The reservation for green belt notified under the development plan has statutory force." A good purpose "does not confer any right on an encroacher to seek regularization of encroachment". The High Court order was set aside. Why it matters: It shows that a green belt is binding law, not a mere planning wish.
Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) 2 SCC 577 (Supreme Court; K. Ramaswamy and N. Venkatachala JJ; 24 November 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land in a Thanesar town planning scheme reserved as open space was leased to a sabha to build
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The State must keep open spaces for the public's health and environment, linked to Art. 21; the lease was quashed and the construction ordered to be demolished. Why it matters: It protects open spaces in town planning, which is the core idea behind a green belt.

te.inOneMinute: హరిత వలయం (green belt) అంటే పచ్చగా (చెట్లు, పొదలు, గడ్డి, ఖాళీ భూమి) ఉంచి, నిర్మాణాల నుండి రక్షించిన భూమి. సాధారణంగా రెండు రకాలు: పట్టణ ప్రణాళిక లో, మాస్టర్ ప్లాన్‌లో అభివృద్ధి లేకుండా ఉంచిన ఖాళీ భూమి పట్టీ లేదా ప్రాంతం; పరిశ్రమల చుట్టూ, కాలుష్యం, దుమ్ము, శబ్దాన్ని పీల్చుకోవడానికి నాటిన చెట్ల పట్టీ. ఉద్దేశ్యం: సహజ పర్యావరణాన్ని రక్షించడం, గాలి నాణ్యత మెరుగుపరచడం, ప్రజలకు ఖాళీ ప్రదేశం ఇవ్వడం, నగరాలు హద్దులేకుండా విస్తరించకుండా ఆపడం. ( చిత్రం 1 చూడండి.) ప్రయోజనాలు: గాలి కాలుష్యం, దుమ్ము, శబ్దాన్ని నియంత్రిస్తుంది; నేల కోతను ఆపుతుంది; నేలలో నీటిని నిలుపుతుంది; పక్షులు, జంతువులకు ఆవాసం ఇస్తుంది; వినోదానికి స్థలం ఇస్తుంది; మెరుగైన భూ వినియోగానికి దారి తీస్తుంది. ( చిత్రం 2 చూడండి.) చట్టం: Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g); పట్టణ ప్రణాళిక చట్టాల కింద మాస్టర్ ప్లాన్‌లు హరిత వలయానికి "statutory force" (అర్థం: చట్టబద్ధ బలం) ఇస్తాయి; EP Act, 1986 కింద పర్యావరణ అనుమతులకు హరిత వలయ షరతులు జతచేస్తారు. కోర్టులు: Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g) ను ఉల్లంఘిస్తూ హరిత వలయాన్ని నివాస లేదా ఇతర వినియోగానికి మార్చలేరు ( Lal Bahadur , 2017); హరిత వలయ రిజర్వేషన్ "has statutory force" (అర్థం: చట్టబద్ధ బలం కలిగి ఉంది), ఆక్రమణదారులు దానిని క్రమబద్ధీకరించుకోలేరు ( CIDCO v. Ekta Mahila Mandal , 2007). ( చిత్రం 3 చూడండి.)
te.meaning: హరిత వలయం ( Green belt ) – అభివృద్ధి చేయని, సహజమైన లేదా వ్యవసాయ భూమిని అలాగే నిలుపుకోవడానికి భూ వినియోగ ప్రణాళికలో వాడే విధానం; అలాగే, కాలుష్య మూలం చుట్టూ అడ్డుగా, కాలుష్యాన్ని పీల్చుకునేదిగా పనిచేసే చెట్లు, మొక్కల పట్టీ. మాస్టర్ ప్లాన్ (Master plan) – ప్రతి ప్రాంత వినియోగాన్ని (నివాస, పారిశ్రామిక, హరిత వలయం, పార్కు మొదలైనవి) నిర్ణయించే నగర చట్టబద్ధ ప్రణాళిక. ప్రజా ట్రస్ట్ సిద్ధాంతం (Public trust doctrine) – అధికారులు హరిత ప్రాంతాలను ప్రజల కోసం కలిగి ఉంటారు, వాటిని అలాగే నిర్వహించే విధి వారికి ఉంది అనే నియమం; Lal Bahadur లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు అన్వయించింది. కాలుష్య శోషకం ( Pollution sink) – కాలుష్య కారకాలను పీల్చుకునే లేదా పట్టుకునేది, ఉదా. దుమ్ము, వాయువులను పట్టుకునే చెట్లు.
keyPoints: హరిత వలయం అంటే పచ్చగా, నిర్మాణాలు లేకుండా ఉంచిన భూమి, లేదా కాలుష్య మూలం చుట్టూ చెట్ల పట్టీ. ఉద్దేశ్యం: పర్యావరణం, గాలి నాణ్యత, ఖాళీ ప్రదేశం రక్షణ, పట్టణ విస్తరణ నియంత్రణ, పరిశ్రమల దగ్గర కాలుష్య నియంత్రణ. ప్రయోజనాలు: గాలి, దుమ్ము, శబ్దం, నేల, నీరు, ఆవాసం, వినోదం, మెరుగైన భూ వినియోగం. చెట్లు తమ సహన పరిమితుల లోపల మాత్రమే కాలుష్య శోషకం. మాస్టర్ ప్లాన్ లోని హరిత వలయానికి చట్టబద్ధ బలం ఉంది ( CIDCO ). దానిని నివాసంగా మార్చడం Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g) ఉల్లంఘన; అధికారులు దానిని ప్రజా ట్రస్ట్ సిద్ధాంతం కింద కలిగి ఉంటారు ( Lal Bahadur ).

selfTest.q: హరిత వలయంలో రెండు రకాలు చెప్పండి. హరిత వలయ అభివృద్ధి నాలుగు ఉద్దేశ్యాలు ఇవ్వండి. హరిత వలయం శబ్దాన్ని ఎలా నియంత్రిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: Lal Bahadur ఏం నిర్ణయించింది? హరిత వలయ రిజర్వేషన్ గురించి CIDCO v. Ekta Mahila Mandal ఏం చెప్పింది? హరిత వలయం మూలం వద్ద కాలుష్య నియంత్రణకు ఎందుకు ప్రత్యామ్నాయం కాదు?

hi.inOneMinute: A green belt is land kept green (trees, shrubs, grass, open land) and protected from building. There are two common types: in town planning , a belt or area of open land kept free of development in the master plan; around industries , a strip of trees planted to absorb pollution, dust and noise. Purpose: to protect the natural environment, improve air quality, give people open space and stop cities from spreading without limit. (See Diagram 1 .) Advantages: it controls air pollution, dust and noise; prevents soil erosion ; keeps water in the soil; gives habitat to birds and animals; gives space for recreation; and leads to better land use. (See Diagram 2 .) Law: Arts. 21, 48A and 51A(g); master plans under town planning laws give a green belt "statutory force"; green belt conditions are attached to environmental clearances under the EP Act, 1986. Courts: a green belt cannot be changed to housing or other use in violation of Arts. 21, 48A and 51A(g) ( Lal Bahadur , 2017); a green belt reservation "has statutory force" and encroachers cannot get it regularised ( CIDCO v. Ekta Mahila Mandal , 2007). (See Diagram 3 .)
legalProvision: Article 21 – "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." The courts read the right to pollution-free air and water into it ( Subhash Kumar , 1991), and Lal Bahadur applied this to green belts. Article 48A – "The State shall endeavour to protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wild life of the country." Article 51A(g) – citizen's duty "to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wild life, and to have compassion for living creatures". Town planning laws – master plans and development plans made under State town planning Acts reserve areas as green belts. Example: Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 (CIDCO is a Special Planning Authority under s. 40, as noted in CIDCO v. Ekta Mahila Mandal ). Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 – environmental clearances given under the EP Act framework carry green belt conditions. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) has issued Office Memoranda on the area of green belt (see "Detailed explanation" §5).
hi.meaning: Green belt – a policy used in land use planning to retain areas of undeveloped, wild or agricultural land; also, a belt of trees and plants around a pollution source that acts as a barrier and sink for pollutants. Master plan – the statutory plan for a city that fixes the use of each area (residential, industrial, green belt, park, etc.). Public trust doctrine – the rule, applied by the Supreme Court in Lal Bahadur , that authorities hold green areas for the public and have a duty to maintain them as such. Pollution sink – something that absorbs or traps pollutants, such as trees trapping dust and gases.
keyPoints: A green belt is land kept green and free of building, or a belt of trees around a pollution source. Purpose: protect environment, air quality, open space, check urban spread, control pollution near industries. Advantages: air, dust, noise, soil, water, habitat, recreation, better land use. Trees are a pollution sink only within their tolerance limits. A green belt in the master plan has statutory force ( CIDCO ). Changing it to housing violated Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g); authorities hold it under the public trust doctrine ( Lal Bahadur ).

caseLaws.facts: Lal Bahadur v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 15 SCC 407; AIR 2018 SC 220 (Supreme Court; Arun Mishra and Mohan M. Shantanagoudar JJ; 14 September 2017)

caseLaws.name: Facts: About 266
caseLaws.facts: 661 hectares for the expansion of Gomti Nagar, Lucknow were shown as green belt in the 1995 master plan. The Master Plan 2021 (approved on 31 March 2005) changed it to residential, and land acquisition notifications followed. The area was later turned into the Janeshwar Mishra Park. Principle: The change from green belt to residential was "in flagrant violation" of Arts. 21, 48-A and 51-A(g); a green belt is "essential for fresh air", and authorities must maintain such areas "as per doctrine of public trust". The Court quashed the Master Plan 2021 change of use. Why it matters: It is the clearest Supreme Court ruling that a green belt is protected by the Constitution.
City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra v. Ekta Mahila Mandal (2007) 7 SCC 701 (Supreme Court; Arijit Pasayat and D.K. Jain JJ; 17 September 2007)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A 770 sq
caseLaws.facts: m plot in Sector N-7, Navi Mumbai was notified as green belt under the development plan. A trust built two rooms on it, used it as a playground, and asked for regularisation for educational use; the High Court allowed it. Principle: "The reservation for green belt notified under the development plan has statutory force." A good purpose "does not confer any right on an encroacher to seek regularization of encroachment". The High Court order was set aside. Why it matters: It shows that a green belt is binding law, not a mere planning wish.
Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana (1995) 2 SCC 577 (Supreme Court; K. Ramaswamy and N. Venkatachala JJ; 24 November 1994)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Land in a Thanesar town planning scheme reserved as open space was leased to a sabha to build
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The State must keep open spaces for the public's health and environment, linked to Art. 21; the lease was quashed and the construction ordered to be demolished. Why it matters: It protects open spaces in town planning, which is the core idea behind a green belt.

en.meaning:
Article 32 empowers which court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights?

Explanation. Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

Article 226 gives every High Court writ power for:

Explanation. Article 226 covers both Fundamental Rights and any other legal right, making it wider in subject-matter than Article 32.

Which of the following correctly compares Article 226 with Article 32?

Explanation. Article 226 covers more subject-matter (Fundamental Rights + any other purpose) but is territorially confined to the High Court's jurisdiction, unlike Article 32's all-India reach.

Public interest litigation lets which persons approach the Court?

A green belt differs from ordinary afforestation because:

Explanation. A green belt is a deliberately maintained zone tied to a specific regulatory or planning condition, unlike voluntary afforestation.

Which of the following is NOT a typical function of a green belt?

Explanation. A green belt has no function of increasing industrial output; its recognised functions are environmental and planning-related.

environmental-law-u5-t3.subtitle: When a State answers in international law for environmental harm that crosses its border

en.inOneMinute: State liability in international environmental law means the duty of a State to answer, and to make good the loss, when environmental harm is caused to another State or its people by activities for which the State is answerable. It has two branches: State responsibility for wrongful acts. A State that breaches an international obligation (for example, the duty not to cause transboundary harm) must stop the breach and make full reparation . The rules are in the ILC Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, 2001. Liability for harm from lawful but hazardous activities. Even where no rule is broken, the loss from hazardous activities must be borne by someone. Some treaties make the State itself absolutely liable (the Space Liability Convention, 1972). The ILC Principles on the Allocation of Loss, 2006 place liability mainly on the operator , with the State ensuring that victims get prompt and adequate compensation. The basic article is: "Every internationally wrongful act of a State entails the international responsibility of that State." (ILC 2001, Art. 1) Stockholm Principle 22 (1972) and Rio Principle 13 (1992) ask States to develop the law on liability and compensation, which is still the weakest part of international environmental law. Leading examples: Trail Smelter (1938, 1941), Corfu Channel (1949), Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (1997) and the Cosmos 954 settlement between Canada and the USSR (1981).
legalProvision: ILC Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, 2001 (annexed to UN General Assembly resolution 56/83 of 12 December 2001): Arts 1, 2: responsibility and its two elements; Arts 4, 5, 8: attribution of conduct to the State; Arts 12, 14: breach; Arts 20–25, 27: circumstances precluding wrongfulness; Arts 30, 31, 34–37: cessation and reparation; Arts 42, 48: who may invoke responsibility. ILC Draft Principles on the Allocation of Loss in the Case of Transboundary Harm Arising out of Hazardous Activities, 2006: Principles 1–8. Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, 1972: Arts II, III, VIII–XII, XIV, XIX. Stockholm Declaration, 1972: Principles 21 and 22. Rio Declaration, 1992: Principles 2 and 13. India: Art. 253 of the Constitution (implementing treaties); M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) on absolute liability of hazardous enterprises.
en.meaning: State responsibility : the legal consequences that follow when a State commits an internationally wrongful act. "Every internationally wrongful act of a State entails the international responsibility of that State." (Art. 1) Internationally wrongful act (Art. 2): conduct "consisting of an action or omission" which (a) "Is attributable to the State under international law"; and (b) "Constitutes a breach of an international obligation of the State." Breach (Art. 12): an act of the State "is not in conformity with what is required of it by that obligation", "regardless of its origin or character". Reparation (Art. 31): "The responsible State is under an obligation to make full reparation for the injury caused by the internationally wrongful act." Injury includes any damage, "whether material or moral". State liability (in the narrow sense): the duty to compensate for harm caused by activities that are not unlawful, such as space launches or hazardous industries. It does not depend on breach. Absolute liability : liability without proof of fault, subject only to very narrow exceptions. Under the Space Liability Convention, the launching State is "absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth" or to aircraft in flight (Art. II). Operator (2006 Principles, Principle 2): the person in command or control of the hazardous activity at the time of the incident.
keyPoints: Internationally wrongful act: conduct attributable to the State + breach of an international obligation (ILC 2001, Art. 2). Attribution: State organs (Art. 4), governmental authority (Art. 5), instructions or control (Art. 8); otherwise the State answers for its own lack of due diligence. Full reparation: Art. 31; restitution, compensation and satisfaction, singly or in combination (Art. 34). Absolute liability: Space Liability Convention Art. II; Cosmos 954 settled for C$3,000,000 (1981); M.C. Mehta (1987) in India. Necessity (Art. 25): only way, essential interest, grave and imminent peril; not if the State contributed. Stockholm P22 and Rio P13: liability and compensation law still to be developed.

caseLaws.facts: Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v. Canada), decisions of 16 April 1938 and 11 March 1941 (Arbitral Tribunal under the Convention of 15 April 1935; 3 RIAA 1905)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Sulphur dioxide fumes from a privately run smelter at Trail, British Columbia, damaged land a
caseLaws.facts: The USA and Canada referred the matter to a three-member tribunal by the Ottawa Convention of 1935. Principle: No State has the right to use or permit the use of its territory so as to cause serious injury by fumes to another State, where the injury is proved by clear and convincing evidence. Canada was held responsible for the conduct of the smelter, and a regime was laid down to control its future emissions. Why it matters: It shows that a State is answerable internationally for transboundary harm from private activity in its territory, and that the remedy can include both payment and control of future conduct.
Corfu Channel Case (United Kingdom v. Albania), Merits, Judgment of 9 April 1949 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 22 October 1946, the British warships Saumarez and Volage struck mines in Albanian waters
caseLaws.facts: 45 men were killed and 42 wounded. Principle: Albania was held responsible (by 11 votes to 5) for the explosions and the resulting damage and loss of life, relying on "every State's obligation not to allow knowingly its territory to be used for acts contrary to the rights of other States". A separate judgment of 15 December 1949 assessed the compensation. Why it matters: A State is responsible for an omission: failing to prevent known harm from its territory. This is the basis of State responsibility for pollution.
Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros Project (Hungary/Slovakia), Judgment of 25 September 1997 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By a 1977 treaty, Hungary and Czechoslovakia agreed to build dams on the Danube
caseLaws.facts: "In 1989, Hungary suspended and subsequently abandoned completion of the project." Czechoslovakia put an alternative ("Variant C") into operation in October 1992. Principle: Both States were found in breach of their obligations. Hungary's notification of May 1992 did not end the treaty. The States "must negotiate in good faith", and "each Party must compensate the other Party" for the damage caused by its conduct. Why it matters: It applies the law of State responsibility to an environmental dispute: breach leads to a duty to compensate, alongside a duty to cooperate.

te.inOneMinute: అంతర్జాతీయ పర్యావరణ చట్టంలో దేశ బాధ్యత అంటే, ఒక దేశం జవాబుదారీగా ఉండే కార్యకలాపాల వల్ల మరో దేశానికి లేదా దాని ప్రజలకు పర్యావరణ హాని కలిగినప్పుడు, ఆ దేశం జవాబు చెప్పి, నష్టాన్ని భర్తీ చేయవలసిన విధి. దీనికి రెండు శాఖలు ఉన్నాయి: తప్పుడు చర్యలకు దేశ బాధ్యత (responsibility). ఒక అంతర్జాతీయ బాధ్యతను (ఉదా. సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని కలిగించకూడదనే విధి) ఉల్లంఘించిన దేశం ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపి పూర్తి నష్టపరిహారం చేయాలి. నియమాలు అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్యలకు దేశాల బాధ్యతపై ILC ఆర్టికల్స్, 2001 లో ఉన్నాయి. చట్టబద్ధమైన కానీ ప్రమాదకర కార్యకలాపాల నుండి హానికి బాధ్యత (liability). ఏ నియమమూ ఉల్లంఘించబడకపోయినా, ప్రమాదకర కార్యకలాపాల నష్టాన్ని ఎవరో భరించాలి. కొన్ని ఒప్పందాలు దేశాన్నే సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత వహించేలా చేస్తాయి (అంతరిక్ష బాధ్యత కన్వెన్షన్, 1972). నష్ట కేటాయింపుపై ILC సూత్రాలు, 2006 బాధ్యతను ప్రధానంగా నిర్వాహకుడి పై ఉంచుతాయి, బాధితులకు సత్వర, తగిన పరిహారం అందేలా దేశం చూస్తుంది. ప్రాథమిక ఆర్టికల్: "Every internationally wrongful act of a State entails the international responsibility of that State." (అర్థం: ఒక దేశం చేసే ప్రతి అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్య ఆ దేశ అంతర్జాతీయ బాధ్యతకు దారి తీస్తుంది.) (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 1) బాధ్యత, పరిహారంపై చట్టాన్ని అభివృద్ధి చేయాలని స్టాక్‌హోమ్ సూత్రం 22 (1972), రియో సూత్రం 13 (1992) దేశాలను కోరుతున్నాయి. ఇది ఇప్పటికీ అంతర్జాతీయ పర్యావరణ చట్టంలో అత్యంత బలహీనమైన భాగం. ప్రధాన ఉదాహరణలు: Trail Smelter (1938, 1941), Corfu Channel (1949), Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (1997), కెనడా, USSR మధ్య Cosmos 954 పరిష్కారం (1981).
te.meaning: దేశ బాధ్యత (responsibility) : ఒక దేశం అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్య చేసినప్పుడు కలిగే చట్టపరమైన పర్యవసానాలు. "Every internationally wrongful act of a State entails the international responsibility of that State." (అర్థం: ఒక దేశం చేసే ప్రతి అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్య ఆ దేశ అంతర్జాతీయ బాధ్యతకు దారి తీస్తుంది.) (ఆర్టికల్ 1) అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్య (ఆర్టికల్ 2): "consisting of an action or omission" (అర్థం: ఒక చర్య లేదా విస్మరణతో కూడిన) ప్రవర్తన, అది (a) "Is attributable to the State under international law" (అర్థం: అంతర్జాతీయ చట్టం కింద దేశానికి ఆపాదించదగినది); మరియు (b) "Constitutes a breach of an international obligation of the State." (అర్థం: దేశ అంతర్జాతీయ బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన అవుతుంది.) ఉల్లంఘన (ఆర్టికల్ 12): దేశ చర్య "is not in conformity with what is required of it by that obligation" (అర్థం: ఆ బాధ్యత దాని నుండి కోరే దానికి అనుగుణంగా లేదు), "regardless of its origin or character" (అర్థం: దాని మూలం లేదా స్వభావం ఏదైనా). నష్టపరిహారం (ఆర్టికల్ 31): "The responsible State is under an obligation to make full reparation for the injury caused by the internationally wrongful act." (అర్థం: అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్య వల్ల కలిగిన గాయానికి పూర్తి నష్టపరిహారం చేయవలసిన బాధ్యత బాధ్యుడైన దేశంపై ఉంది.) గాయంలో "whether material or moral" (అర్థం: భౌతికమైనా, నైతికమైనా) ఏ నష్టమైనా ఉంటుంది. దేశ బాధ్యత (సంకుచిత అర్థంలో, liability): అంతరిక్ష ప్రయోగాలు లేదా ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమల వంటి చట్టవిరుద్ధం కాని కార్యకలాపాల వల్ల కలిగిన హానికి పరిహారం చెల్లించే విధి. ఇది ఉల్లంఘనపై ఆధారపడదు. సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత : తప్పు రుజువు అవసరం లేని బాధ్యత, చాలా సంకుచిత మినహాయింపులకు మాత్రమే లోబడి ఉంటుంది. అంతరిక్ష బాధ్యత కన్వెన్షన్ కింద ప్రయోగ దేశం "absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth" (అర్థం: భూ ఉపరితలంపై తన అంతరిక్ష వస్తువు కలిగించిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం చెల్లించడానికి సంపూర్ణంగా బాధ్యత వహిస్తుంది), లేదా ఎగురుతున్న విమానానికి కలిగిన నష్టానికి (ఆర్టికల్ II). నిర్వాహకుడు (2006 సూత్రాలు, సూత్రం 2): సంఘటన జరిగిన సమయంలో ప్రమాదకర కార్యకలాపంపై ఆధిపత్యం లేదా నియంత్రణ కలిగిన వ్యక్తి.
keyPoints: అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్య: దేశానికి ఆపాదించదగిన ప్రవర్తన + అంతర్జాతీయ బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘన (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 2). ఆపాదన: దేశ అవయవాలు (ఆర్టికల్ 4), ప్రభుత్వ అధికారం (ఆర్టికల్ 5), సూచనలు లేదా నియంత్రణ (ఆర్టికల్ 8); లేకపోతే దేశం తన సొంత తగిన శ్రద్ధ లోపానికి జవాబు చెబుతుంది. పూర్తి నష్టపరిహారం: ఆర్టికల్ 31; పునరుద్ధరణ, పరిహారం, సంతృప్తి, విడిగా లేదా కలిపి (ఆర్టికల్ 34). సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత: అంతరిక్ష బాధ్యత కన్వెన్షన్ ఆర్టికల్ II; Cosmos 954 C$3,000,000 కు పరిష్కారం (1981); భారత్‌లో M.C. Mehta (1987). ఆవశ్యకత (ఆర్టికల్ 25): ఏకైక మార్గం, ముఖ్యమైన ప్రయోజనం, తీవ్రమైన, ఆసన్నమైన ప్రమాదం; దేశం దోహదం చేస్తే కాదు. స్టాక్‌హోమ్ సూ22, రియో సూ13: బాధ్యత, పరిహార చట్టం ఇంకా అభివృద్ధి చెందాలి.

selfTest.q: అంతర్జాతీయ తప్పుడు చర్య యొక్క రెండు అంశాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: నష్టపరిహారం యొక్క మూడు రూపాలను పేర్కొనండి. అంతరిక్ష బాధ్యత కన్వెన్షన్ కింద ప్రయోగ దేశం ఎప్పుడు సంపూర్ణంగా బాధ్యత వహిస్తుంది? Cosmos 954 విషయం ఎలా పరిష్కరించబడింది? పరిస్థితికి దోహదం చేసిన దేశం ఆవశ్యకతను వాదించగలదా? ILC 2006 సూత్రాలు బాధ్యతను ప్రధానంగా ఎవరిపై ఉంచుతాయి?

hi.inOneMinute: State liability in international environmental law means the duty of a State to answer, and to make good the loss, when environmental harm is caused to another State or its people by activities for which the State is answerable. It has two branches: State responsibility for wrongful acts. A State that breaches an international obligation (for example, the duty not to cause transboundary harm) must stop the breach and make full reparation . The rules are in the ILC Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, 2001. Liability for harm from lawful but hazardous activities. Even where no rule is broken, the loss from hazardous activities must be borne by someone. Some treaties make the State itself absolutely liable (the Space Liability Convention, 1972). The ILC Principles on the Allocation of Loss, 2006 place liability mainly on the operator , with the State ensuring that victims get prompt and adequate compensation. The basic article is: "Every internationally wrongful act of a State entails the international responsibility of that State." (ILC 2001, Art. 1) Stockholm Principle 22 (1972) and Rio Principle 13 (1992) ask States to develop the law on liability and compensation, which is still the weakest part of international environmental law. Leading examples: Trail Smelter (1938, 1941), Corfu Channel (1949), Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (1997) and the Cosmos 954 settlement between Canada and the USSR (1981).
legalProvision: ILC Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts, 2001 (annexed to UN General Assembly resolution 56/83 of 12 December 2001): Arts 1, 2: responsibility and its two elements; Arts 4, 5, 8: attribution of conduct to the State; Arts 12, 14: breach; Arts 20–25, 27: circumstances precluding wrongfulness; Arts 30, 31, 34–37: cessation and reparation; Arts 42, 48: who may invoke responsibility. ILC Draft Principles on the Allocation of Loss in the Case of Transboundary Harm Arising out of Hazardous Activities, 2006: Principles 1–8. Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, 1972: Arts II, III, VIII–XII, XIV, XIX. Stockholm Declaration, 1972: Principles 21 and 22. Rio Declaration, 1992: Principles 2 and 13. India: Art. 253 of the Constitution (implementing treaties); M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) on absolute liability of hazardous enterprises.
hi.meaning: State responsibility : the legal consequences that follow when a State commits an internationally wrongful act. "Every internationally wrongful act of a State entails the international responsibility of that State." (Art. 1) Internationally wrongful act (Art. 2): conduct "consisting of an action or omission" which (a) "Is attributable to the State under international law"; and (b) "Constitutes a breach of an international obligation of the State." Breach (Art. 12): an act of the State "is not in conformity with what is required of it by that obligation", "regardless of its origin or character". Reparation (Art. 31): "The responsible State is under an obligation to make full reparation for the injury caused by the internationally wrongful act." Injury includes any damage, "whether material or moral". State liability (in the narrow sense): the duty to compensate for harm caused by activities that are not unlawful, such as space launches or hazardous industries. It does not depend on breach. Absolute liability : liability without proof of fault, subject only to very narrow exceptions. Under the Space Liability Convention, the launching State is "absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth" or to aircraft in flight (Art. II). Operator (2006 Principles, Principle 2): the person in command or control of the hazardous activity at the time of the incident.
keyPoints: Internationally wrongful act: conduct attributable to the State + breach of an international obligation (ILC 2001, Art. 2). Attribution: State organs (Art. 4), governmental authority (Art. 5), instructions or control (Art. 8); otherwise the State answers for its own lack of due diligence. Full reparation: Art. 31; restitution, compensation and satisfaction, singly or in combination (Art. 34). Absolute liability: Space Liability Convention Art. II; Cosmos 954 settled for C$3,000,000 (1981); M.C. Mehta (1987) in India. Necessity (Art. 25): only way, essential interest, grave and imminent peril; not if the State contributed. Stockholm P22 and Rio P13: liability and compensation law still to be developed.

caseLaws.facts: Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v. Canada), decisions of 16 April 1938 and 11 March 1941 (Arbitral Tribunal under the Convention of 15 April 1935; 3 RIAA 1905)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Sulphur dioxide fumes from a privately run smelter at Trail, British Columbia, damaged land a
caseLaws.facts: The USA and Canada referred the matter to a three-member tribunal by the Ottawa Convention of 1935. Principle: No State has the right to use or permit the use of its territory so as to cause serious injury by fumes to another State, where the injury is proved by clear and convincing evidence. Canada was held responsible for the conduct of the smelter, and a regime was laid down to control its future emissions. Why it matters: It shows that a State is answerable internationally for transboundary harm from private activity in its territory, and that the remedy can include both payment and control of future conduct.
Corfu Channel Case (United Kingdom v. Albania), Merits, Judgment of 9 April 1949 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 22 October 1946, the British warships Saumarez and Volage struck mines in Albanian waters
caseLaws.facts: 45 men were killed and 42 wounded. Principle: Albania was held responsible (by 11 votes to 5) for the explosions and the resulting damage and loss of life, relying on "every State's obligation not to allow knowingly its territory to be used for acts contrary to the rights of other States". A separate judgment of 15 December 1949 assessed the compensation. Why it matters: A State is responsible for an omission: failing to prevent known harm from its territory. This is the basis of State responsibility for pollution.
Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros Project (Hungary/Slovakia), Judgment of 25 September 1997 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By a 1977 treaty, Hungary and Czechoslovakia agreed to build dams on the Danube
caseLaws.facts: "In 1989, Hungary suspended and subsequently abandoned completion of the project." Czechoslovakia put an alternative ("Variant C") into operation in October 1992. Principle: Both States were found in breach of their obligations. Hungary's notification of May 1992 did not end the treaty. The States "must negotiate in good faith", and "each Party must compensate the other Party" for the damage caused by its conduct. Why it matters: It applies the law of State responsibility to an environmental dispute: breach leads to a duty to compensate, alongside a duty to cooperate.

selfTest.a: Name the three forms of reparation. Under the Space Liability Convention, when is the launching State absolutely liable? How was the Cosmos 954 matter settled? Can a State plead necessity if it contributed to the situation? On whom do the ILC 2006 Principles mainly place liability?

environmental-law-u5-t5.subtitle: Why a parent company is hard to sue for a subsidiary's pollution, and the routes that have opened

en.inOneMinute: A multinational corporation (MNC) is a group of companies with a parent company in one country (the home State) and subsidiaries in other countries (host States). Many hazardous industries, mines and chemical plants are run by such groups. When an MNC's plant pollutes, three problems arise: Separate personality: the subsidiary is a separate company, so the parent says it is not liable (the corporate veil ). Forum: the victims are in the host State, but the money and control are with the parent in the home State. Courts may send the case back ( forum non conveniens ). Weak international law: traditional international law binds States, not companies. Answers developed so far: Host-State law: India's absolute liability rule for hazardous enterprises ( M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , 1987), the polluter pays principle and the NGT's no-fault rule. Home-State courts: a parent may owe a duty of care for its subsidiary's operations where it controls them ( Vedanta Resources v. Lungowe , UK Supreme Court, 2019). Soft law: the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, 2011 ("Protect, Respect and Remedy"), and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (1976; updated 2023). The Bhopal gas leak of December 1984 (Union Carbide) is the leading example. It ended in a settlement of US$470 million in 1989, upheld on review in 1991 ( Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India ).
legalProvision: Indian law: Art. 21 and Art. 32 of the Constitution (right to life; compensation in writ jurisdiction); M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , AIR 1987 SC 1086 (absolute liability); Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, s.17(3) (no-fault principle); Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991. International soft law: Rio Declaration, 1992: Principle 13 (liability and compensation law) and Principle 16 (polluter pays); UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, 2011 (UN document A/HRC/17/31, annex); OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (first 1976; latest update 2023), Chapter VI (Environment); ILC Principles on the Allocation of Loss, 2006: liability on the "operator".
en.meaning: Multinational corporation / multinational enterprise: a group of companies under common control, with a parent company in one State and subsidiaries or branches in other States. Parent company and subsidiary: the parent owns or controls the subsidiary. Each is a separate legal person . Corporate veil: the separate legal personality of a company, which normally keeps the parent's assets out of reach for the subsidiary's debts and wrongs. Absolute liability (Indian law): an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry is liable for harm caused by an accident in its operations, without proof of negligence and without the exceptions allowed under Rylands v. Fletcher ( M.C. Mehta , 1987). Forum non conveniens : a doctrine under which a court declines to hear a case because another country's courts are the more appropriate place. Human rights due diligence (UNGPs, Principle 17): an "ongoing" process by which a business assesses actual and potential impacts, acts on the findings, tracks responses and communicates how impacts are addressed.
keyPoints: Corporate veil: separate legal personality of the subsidiary; not a shield for a parent's own role. Parent company liability: duty of care where the parent controls the activity ( Vedanta , [2019] UKSC 20). Forum non conveniens: used by UCC in the US Bhopal litigation; in Vedanta , lack of substantial justice in Zambia allowed an English trial. Human rights due diligence: UNGPs P17: assess, integrate, track, communicate; "ongoing". Bhopal: US$470 million settlement (1989); review (1991) upheld it but restored criminal proceedings; Union of India to make good any shortfall. M.C. Mehta (1987): absolute liability; compensation related to magnitude and capacity.

caseLaws.facts: Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India, (1991) 4 SCC 584; AIR 1992 SC 248 (Supreme Court; judgment of 3 October 1991; majority opinion by M.N. Venkatachaliah J); settlement orders of 14 and 15 February 1989 and reasons of 4 May 1989, (1989) 2 SCC 540

caseLaws.name: Facts: On the night of 2 December 1984, Methyl Isocyanate gas leaked from UCIL's plant at Bhopal
caseLaws.facts: UCC, the US company, avoided trial in the US on forum non conveniens. The Union of India sued in Bhopal. In February 1989 the Supreme Court recorded a settlement of US$470 million with termination of all civil and criminal proceedings. Review petitions challenged it. Principle: The settlement was "not void" and not opposed to public policy , and was upheld. But "the quashing of the criminal proceedings was not justified", so that part was set aside. If the settlement fund proves insufficient, "the deficiency is to be made good by the Union of India". Why it matters: It is the main Indian case on the liability of an MNC for an industrial disaster, and shows the limits of settlement and the State's role as guarantor for victims.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak), AIR 1987 SC 1086; (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati CJ, Ranganath Misra, G.L. Oza, M.M. Dutt and K.N. Singh JJ; 20 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas leaked on 4 and 6 December 1985 from a plant of Shriram Foods and Fertiliser Indust
caseLaws.facts: The Court considered what liability an enterprise in a hazardous industry bears. Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry is absolutely liable to compensate all those affected by an accident, and the exceptions to Rylands v. Fletcher do not apply. Compensation must be related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise. Why it matters: It created the rule of absolute liability, decided just two years after Bhopal, which applies to every hazardous enterprise in India, including MNC subsidiaries.
Vedanta Resources PLC v. Lungowe [2019] UKSC 20 (UK Supreme Court; Lady Hale, Lord Wilson, Lord Hodge, Lady Black, Lord Briggs; judgment by Lord Briggs; 10 April 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: About 1,826 Zambian villagers sued Vedanta, the UK-domiciled parent, and KCM, its Zambian sub
caseLaws.facts: Principle: There was a real triable issue that the parent owed a duty of care, given its alleged control over KCM's health, safety and environmental standards. Zambia would otherwise be the proper place, but the villagers would not get substantial justice there, so the claim could proceed in England. Why it matters: It shows home-State courts can hold a parent to account for a subsidiary's pollution abroad, overcoming the corporate veil and forum objections.

What did the UK Supreme Court decide in Vedanta v. Lungowe ? What are the three pillars of the UN Guiding Principles?

te.inOneMinute: బహుళజాతి సంస్థ (MNC) అంటే ఒక దేశంలో (స్వదేశం) మాతృ కంపెనీ , ఇతర దేశాలలో (ఆతిథ్య దేశాలు) అనుబంధ కంపెనీలు ఉండే కంపెనీల సమూహం. అనేక ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమలు, గనులు, రసాయన ప్లాంట్లను ఇలాంటి సమూహాలు నడుపుతాయి. MNC ప్లాంట్ కాలుష్యం చేసినప్పుడు మూడు సమస్యలు వస్తాయి: వేరు వ్యక్తిత్వం: అనుబంధ కంపెనీ వేరే కంపెనీ, కాబట్టి తాను బాధ్యురాలిని కాదని మాతృ కంపెనీ అంటుంది ( కార్పొరేట్ ముసుగు ). వేదిక: బాధితులు ఆతిథ్య దేశంలో ఉంటారు, కానీ డబ్బు, నియంత్రణ స్వదేశంలోని మాతృ కంపెనీ వద్ద ఉంటాయి. న్యాయస్థానాలు కేసును తిరిగి పంపవచ్చు ( ఫోరమ్ నాన్ కన్వీనియెన్స్ ). బలహీన అంతర్జాతీయ చట్టం: సాంప్రదాయ అంతర్జాతీయ చట్టం దేశాలను బంధిస్తుంది, కంపెనీలను కాదు. ఇప్పటి వరకు వచ్చిన సమాధానాలు: ఆతిథ్య దేశ చట్టం: ప్రమాదకర సంస్థలకు భారత్ సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత నియమం ( M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , 1987), కాలుష్యకారుడే చెల్లించాలి సూత్రం, NGT తప్పు లేని నియమం. స్వదేశ న్యాయస్థానాలు: మాతృ కంపెనీ అనుబంధ కంపెనీ కార్యకలాపాలను నియంత్రిస్తే, వాటికి సంరక్షణ విధి ఉండవచ్చు ( Vedanta Resources v. Lungowe , UK సుప్రీంకోర్టు, 2019). సాఫ్ట్ లా: వ్యాపారం, మానవ హక్కులపై ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి మార్గదర్శక సూత్రాలు, 2011 ("రక్షించు, గౌరవించు, పరిష్కరించు"), బహుళజాతి సంస్థలకు OECD మార్గదర్శకాలు (1976; 2023 లో నవీకరణ). డిసెంబర్ 1984 భోపాల్ గ్యాస్ లీకేజీ (యూనియన్ కార్బైడ్) ప్రధాన ఉదాహరణ. ఇది 1989 లో US$470 మిలియన్ పరిష్కారంతో ముగిసింది, 1991 లో పునఃపరిశీలనలో సమర్థించబడింది ( Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India ).
te.meaning: బహుళజాతి సంస్థ: ఉమ్మడి నియంత్రణ కింద ఉండే, ఒక దేశంలో మాతృ కంపెనీ, ఇతర దేశాలలో అనుబంధ కంపెనీలు లేదా శాఖలు ఉండే కంపెనీల సమూహం. మాతృ కంపెనీ, అనుబంధ కంపెనీ: మాతృ కంపెనీ అనుబంధ కంపెనీని స్వంతం చేసుకుంటుంది లేదా నియంత్రిస్తుంది. ప్రతిదీ వేరు చట్టపరమైన వ్యక్తి . కార్పొరేట్ ముసుగు: కంపెనీ వేరు చట్టపరమైన వ్యక్తిత్వం, ఇది సాధారణంగా అనుబంధ కంపెనీ అప్పులు, తప్పులకు మాతృ కంపెనీ ఆస్తులను అందుబాటులో లేకుండా ఉంచుతుంది. సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత (భారత చట్టం): ప్రమాదకర లేదా స్వాభావికంగా ప్రమాదకరమైన పరిశ్రమలో నిమగ్నమైన సంస్థ తన కార్యకలాపాలలో ప్రమాదం వల్ల కలిగిన హానికి, నిర్లక్ష్యం రుజువు లేకుండా, Rylands v. Fletcher కింద అనుమతించిన మినహాయింపులు లేకుండా బాధ్యత వహిస్తుంది ( M.C. Mehta , 1987). ఫోరమ్ నాన్ కన్వీనియెన్స్ : మరో దేశ న్యాయస్థానాలు మరింత తగిన ప్రదేశం కాబట్టి ఒక న్యాయస్థానం కేసును విచారించడానికి నిరాకరించే సిద్ధాంతం. మానవ హక్కుల తగిన శ్రద్ధ (UNGPs, సూత్రం 17): వ్యాపారం వాస్తవ, సంభావ్య ప్రభావాలను అంచనా వేసి, ఫలితాలపై చర్య తీసుకుని, ప్రతిస్పందనలను పర్యవేక్షించి, ప్రభావాలను ఎలా పరిష్కరిస్తుందో తెలియజేసే "ongoing" (అర్థం: నిరంతర) ప్రక్రియ.
keyPoints: కార్పొరేట్ ముసుగు: అనుబంధ కంపెనీ వేరు చట్టపరమైన వ్యక్తిత్వం; మాతృ కంపెనీ సొంత పాత్రకు రక్షణ కాదు. మాతృ కంపెనీ బాధ్యత: మాతృ కంపెనీ కార్యకలాపాన్ని నియంత్రించినప్పుడు సంరక్షణ విధి ( Vedanta , [2019] UKSC 20). ఫోరమ్ నాన్ కన్వీనియెన్స్: అమెరికా భోపాల్ వ్యాజ్యంలో UCC ఉపయోగించింది; Vedanta లో జాంబియాలో గణనీయమైన న్యాయం లేకపోవడం ఇంగ్లాండ్‌లో విచారణకు అనుమతించింది. మానవ హక్కుల తగిన శ్రద్ధ: UNGPs సూ17: అంచనా, అమలు, పర్యవేక్షణ, తెలియజేయడం; "ongoing" (అర్థం: నిరంతర). భోపాల్: US$470 మిలియన్ పరిష్కారం (1989); పునఃపరిశీలన (1991) దానిని సమర్థించింది కానీ క్రిమినల్ విచారణలను పునరుద్ధరించింది; ఏ లోటునైనా భారత ప్రభుత్వం భర్తీ చేయాలి. M.C. Mehta (1987): సంపూర్ణ బాధ్యత; పరిహారం పరిమాణం, సామర్థ్యానికి సంబంధించి.

hi.inOneMinute: A multinational corporation (MNC) is a group of companies with a parent company in one country (the home State) and subsidiaries in other countries (host States). Many hazardous industries, mines and chemical plants are run by such groups. When an MNC's plant pollutes, three problems arise: Separate personality: the subsidiary is a separate company, so the parent says it is not liable (the corporate veil ). Forum: the victims are in the host State, but the money and control are with the parent in the home State. Courts may send the case back ( forum non conveniens ). Weak international law: traditional international law binds States, not companies. Answers developed so far: Host-State law: India's absolute liability rule for hazardous enterprises ( M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , 1987), the polluter pays principle and the NGT's no-fault rule. Home-State courts: a parent may owe a duty of care for its subsidiary's operations where it controls them ( Vedanta Resources v. Lungowe , UK Supreme Court, 2019). Soft law: the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, 2011 ("Protect, Respect and Remedy"), and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (1976; updated 2023). The Bhopal gas leak of December 1984 (Union Carbide) is the leading example. It ended in a settlement of US$470 million in 1989, upheld on review in 1991 ( Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India ).
legalProvision: Indian law: Art. 21 and Art. 32 of the Constitution (right to life; compensation in writ jurisdiction); M.C. Mehta v. Union of India , AIR 1987 SC 1086 (absolute liability); Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, s.17(3) (no-fault principle); Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991. International soft law: Rio Declaration, 1992: Principle 13 (liability and compensation law) and Principle 16 (polluter pays); UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, 2011 (UN document A/HRC/17/31, annex); OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct (first 1976; latest update 2023), Chapter VI (Environment); ILC Principles on the Allocation of Loss, 2006: liability on the "operator".
hi.meaning: Multinational corporation / multinational enterprise: a group of companies under common control, with a parent company in one State and subsidiaries or branches in other States. Parent company and subsidiary: the parent owns or controls the subsidiary. Each is a separate legal person . Corporate veil: the separate legal personality of a company, which normally keeps the parent's assets out of reach for the subsidiary's debts and wrongs. Absolute liability (Indian law): an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry is liable for harm caused by an accident in its operations, without proof of negligence and without the exceptions allowed under Rylands v. Fletcher ( M.C. Mehta , 1987). Forum non conveniens : a doctrine under which a court declines to hear a case because another country's courts are the more appropriate place. Human rights due diligence (UNGPs, Principle 17): an "ongoing" process by which a business assesses actual and potential impacts, acts on the findings, tracks responses and communicates how impacts are addressed.
keyPoints: Corporate veil: separate legal personality of the subsidiary; not a shield for a parent's own role. Parent company liability: duty of care where the parent controls the activity ( Vedanta , [2019] UKSC 20). Forum non conveniens: used by UCC in the US Bhopal litigation; in Vedanta , lack of substantial justice in Zambia allowed an English trial. Human rights due diligence: UNGPs P17: assess, integrate, track, communicate; "ongoing". Bhopal: US$470 million settlement (1989); review (1991) upheld it but restored criminal proceedings; Union of India to make good any shortfall. M.C. Mehta (1987): absolute liability; compensation related to magnitude and capacity.

caseLaws.facts: Union Carbide Corporation v. Union of India, (1991) 4 SCC 584; AIR 1992 SC 248 (Supreme Court; judgment of 3 October 1991; majority opinion by M.N. Venkatachaliah J); settlement orders of 14 and 15 February 1989 and reasons of 4 May 1989, (1989) 2 SCC 540

caseLaws.name: Facts: On the night of 2 December 1984, Methyl Isocyanate gas leaked from UCIL's plant at Bhopal
caseLaws.facts: UCC, the US company, avoided trial in the US on forum non conveniens. The Union of India sued in Bhopal. In February 1989 the Supreme Court recorded a settlement of US$470 million with termination of all civil and criminal proceedings. Review petitions challenged it. Principle: The settlement was "not void" and not opposed to public policy , and was upheld. But "the quashing of the criminal proceedings was not justified", so that part was set aside. If the settlement fund proves insufficient, "the deficiency is to be made good by the Union of India". Why it matters: It is the main Indian case on the liability of an MNC for an industrial disaster, and shows the limits of settlement and the State's role as guarantor for victims.
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak), AIR 1987 SC 1086; (1987) 1 SCC 395 (Supreme Court; P.N. Bhagwati CJ, Ranganath Misra, G.L. Oza, M.M. Dutt and K.N. Singh JJ; 20 December 1986)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Oleum gas leaked on 4 and 6 December 1985 from a plant of Shriram Foods and Fertiliser Indust
caseLaws.facts: The Court considered what liability an enterprise in a hazardous industry bears. Principle: An enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently dangerous industry is absolutely liable to compensate all those affected by an accident, and the exceptions to Rylands v. Fletcher do not apply. Compensation must be related to the magnitude and capacity of the enterprise. Why it matters: It created the rule of absolute liability, decided just two years after Bhopal, which applies to every hazardous enterprise in India, including MNC subsidiaries.
Vedanta Resources PLC v. Lungowe [2019] UKSC 20 (UK Supreme Court; Lady Hale, Lord Wilson, Lord Hodge, Lady Black, Lord Briggs; judgment by Lord Briggs; 10 April 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: About 1,826 Zambian villagers sued Vedanta, the UK-domiciled parent, and KCM, its Zambian sub
caseLaws.facts: Principle: There was a real triable issue that the parent owed a duty of care, given its alleged control over KCM's health, safety and environmental standards. Zambia would otherwise be the proper place, but the villagers would not get substantial justice there, so the claim could proceed in England. Why it matters: It shows home-State courts can hold a parent to account for a subsidiary's pollution abroad, overcoming the corporate veil and forum objections.

environmental-law-u5-t2.subtitle: Pollution that starts in one State and harms another: the no-harm rule and the duties of the State of origin

en.inOneMinute: Transboundary pollution is pollution that starts in one State and causes harm in another State, or in areas beyond any State's jurisdiction such as the high seas. It travels through the air (smoke, acid rain), through water (shared rivers, the sea), through the movement of hazardous waste , and through accidents at industrial plants. The basic rule of international law is the no-harm rule . A State has the sovereign right to use its own resources, but it must ensure that activities within its jurisdiction or control do not damage the environment of other States (Stockholm Principle 21, 1972; Rio Principle 2, 1992). The rule began with the Trail Smelter arbitration (USA v. Canada, 1938 and 1941). It was supported by Corfu Channel (ICJ, 1949). The ICJ said in 1996 that it "is now part of the corpus of international law relating to the environment" ( Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion). The duties of the State where the activity takes place (the State of origin ) are: prevent harm; assess the risk; notify the State likely to be affected; consult with it; prepare for and report emergencies. These are set out in the ILC Draft Articles on Prevention of Transboundary Harm from Hazardous Activities, 2001. Main treaties: the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution, 1979 (LRTAP) and the Basel Convention, 1989 (hazardous wastes).
legalProvision: Stockholm Declaration, 1972: Principle 21: sovereign right over resources, with responsibility not to damage other States or areas beyond national jurisdiction. Principle 22: States shall cooperate to develop international law on liability and compensation for victims of pollution and other environmental damage caused beyond their jurisdiction. Rio Declaration, 1992: Principle 2: same rule as Stockholm Principle 21. Principle 13: "States shall develop national law regarding liability and compensation for the victims of pollution". Principle 18: "States shall immediately notify other States of any natural disasters or other emergencies" likely to produce sudden harmful effects on them. Principle 19: "States shall provide prior and timely notification and relevant information to potentially affected States" about activities that may have a significant adverse transboundary effect. Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution , Geneva, 13 November 1979; in force 16 March 1983. ILC Draft Articles on Prevention of Transboundary Harm from Hazardous Activities, 2001 (Arts 1–19). Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal , adopted 22 March 1989; in force 5 May 1992. India: Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
en.meaning: Transboundary pollution : pollution whose source is in one State and whose harmful effects are felt in another State or in areas beyond national jurisdiction . Air pollution (LRTAP Art. 1(a)): the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the air resulting in deleterious effects. Long-range transboundary air pollution (LRTAP Art. 1(b)): air pollution whose physical origin is wholly or partly within one State, and which has adverse effects in another State at such a distance that it is not generally possible to tell the contribution of individual sources. Harm (ILC 2001, Art. 2(b)): "harm caused to persons, property or the environment". Transboundary harm (ILC 2001, Art. 2(c)): harm caused in the territory of, or in other places under the jurisdiction or control of, a State other than the State of origin, "whether or not the States concerned share a common border". State of origin (ILC 2001, Art. 2(d)): the State in whose territory, or under whose jurisdiction or control, the activity is planned or carried out. State likely to be affected (ILC 2001, Art. 2(e)): the State in whose territory, or in a place under whose jurisdiction or control, there is a risk of significant transboundary harm. Risk of causing significant transboundary harm (ILC 2001, Art. 2(a)): includes a high probability of causing significant harm and also "a low probability of causing disastrous transboundary harm".
keyPoints: Transboundary harm: harm in another State or area under its control, whether or not the States share a border (ILC 2001, Art. 2(c)). State of origin: the State where the risky activity is planned or carried out; it carries the duties of prevention, assessment and notification. Due diligence: "all appropriate measures to prevent significant transboundary harm or at any event to minimize the risk thereof" (ILC 2001, Art. 3). Prior notification: Rio P19; ILC Art. 8; no authorisation decision for up to six months pending the reply. No-harm rule: Trail Smelter → Corfu Channel → Stockholm P21 → Rio P2 → Nuclear Weapons AO para. 29. LRTAP 1979: long-range air pollution; framework for cooperation; no liability rule. Basel 1989: hazardous waste; India ratified 24-6-1992.

caseLaws.facts: Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v. Canada), decisions of 16 April 1938 and 11 March 1941 (Arbitral Tribunal under the Convention of 15 April 1935; 3 RIAA 1905)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Sulphur dioxide fumes from a smelter at Trail, British Columbia, damaged land across the bord
caseLaws.facts: The USA and Canada set up a three-member tribunal by the Ottawa Convention of 1935 to decide the matter. Principle: No State has the right to use or permit the use of its territory so as to cause serious injury by fumes in or to the territory of another State, where the case has serious consequences and the injury is proved by clear and convincing evidence. Canada was held responsible, and a regime was laid down to control the smelter's future emissions. Why it matters: It is the first international decision on transboundary air pollution and the source of the no-harm rule.
Corfu Channel Case (United Kingdom v. Albania), Merits, Judgment of 9 April 1949 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 22 October 1946, the British warships Saumarez and Volage struck mines in Albanian waters
caseLaws.facts: 45 men were killed and 42 wounded. Principle: Albania was held responsible (by 11 votes to 5) for the explosions and the resulting damage and loss of life. The Court relied on "every State's obligation not to allow knowingly its territory to be used for acts contrary to the rights of other States". Why it matters: This general duty of a State over its territory is the basis of the duty to prevent transboundary pollution.
Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons, Advisory Opinion of 8 July 1996 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The UN General Assembly (resolution 49/75 K of 15 December 1994) asked the Court whether the
caseLaws.facts: The Court considered, among other things, the law protecting the environment. Principle: "the environment is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings, including generations unborn". The general obligation of States to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction and control respect the environment of other States or of areas beyond national control "is now part of the corpus of international law relating to the environment" (para. 29). Why it matters: The world court confirmed that the no-harm rule against transboundary environmental damage is part of general international law, binding all States.

selfTest.q: Define "transboundary harm" under the ILC Draft Articles, 2001. Which arbitration first laid down the rule against transboundary air pollution?

te.inOneMinute: సరిహద్దు దాటు కాలుష్యం అంటే ఒక దేశంలో మొదలై మరో దేశంలో, లేదా మహాసముద్రాల వంటి ఏ దేశ అధికార పరిధిలోనూ లేని ప్రాంతాలలో హాని కలిగించే కాలుష్యం. ఇది గాలి (పొగ, ఆమ్ల వర్షం), నీరు (ఉమ్మడి నదులు, సముద్రం), ప్రమాదకర వ్యర్థాల రవాణా , పారిశ్రామిక ప్లాంట్లలో ప్రమాదాల ద్వారా ప్రయాణిస్తుంది. అంతర్జాతీయ చట్టంలో ప్రాథమిక నియమం హాని చేయకూడదనే నియమం . ప్రతి దేశానికి తన వనరులను వినియోగించుకునే సార్వభౌమ హక్కు ఉంది, కానీ తన అధికార పరిధి లేదా నియంత్రణలోని కార్యకలాపాలు ఇతర దేశాల పర్యావరణానికి నష్టం కలిగించకుండా చూడాలి (స్టాక్‌హోమ్ సూత్రం 21, 1972; రియో సూత్రం 2, 1992). ఈ నియమం Trail Smelter మధ్యవర్తిత్వంతో (అమెరికా v. కెనడా, 1938, 1941) మొదలైంది. Corfu Channel (ICJ, 1949) దానికి బలం చేకూర్చింది. అది "is now part of the corpus of international law relating to the environment" (అర్థం: ఇప్పుడు పర్యావరణానికి సంబంధించిన అంతర్జాతీయ చట్ట సముదాయంలో భాగం) అని ICJ 1996 లో చెప్పింది ( Nuclear Weapons సలహా అభిప్రాయం). కార్యకలాపం జరిగే దేశం ( మూల దేశం ) విధులు: హానిని నివారించడం; ప్రమాదాన్ని అంచనా వేయడం; ప్రభావితమయ్యే అవకాశం ఉన్న దేశానికి తెలియజేయడం; ఆ దేశంతో సంప్రదించడం; అత్యవసర పరిస్థితులకు సిద్ధపడటం, వాటిని తెలియజేయడం. ఇవి ప్రమాదకర కార్యకలాపాల నుండి సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని నివారణపై ILC ముసాయిదా ఆర్టికల్స్, 2001 లో ఉన్నాయి. ప్రధాన ఒప్పందాలు: దీర్ఘ-శ్రేణి సరిహద్దు దాటు వాయు కాలుష్యంపై కన్వెన్షన్, 1979 (LRTAP), బాసెల్ కన్వెన్షన్, 1989 (ప్రమాదకర వ్యర్థాలు).
te.meaning: సరిహద్దు దాటు కాలుష్యం : మూలం ఒక దేశంలో ఉండి, హానికర ప్రభావాలు మరో దేశంలో లేదా జాతీయ అధికార పరిధికి అవతలి ప్రాంతాలలో కనిపించే కాలుష్యం. వాయు కాలుష్యం (LRTAP ఆర్టికల్ 1(a)): మనిషి ప్రత్యక్షంగా లేదా పరోక్షంగా పదార్థాలను లేదా శక్తిని గాలిలోకి ప్రవేశపెట్టడం, దాని ఫలితంగా దుష్ప్రభావాలు కలగడం. దీర్ఘ-శ్రేణి సరిహద్దు దాటు వాయు కాలుష్యం (LRTAP ఆర్టికల్ 1(b)): భౌతిక మూలం పూర్తిగా లేదా పాక్షికంగా ఒక దేశంలో ఉండి, ఎంత దూరంలో మరో దేశంలో దుష్ప్రభావాలు కలిగిస్తుందంటే వ్యక్తిగత మూలాల వాటాను సాధారణంగా గుర్తించలేని వాయు కాలుష్యం. హాని (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 2(b)): "harm caused to persons, property or the environment" (అర్థం: వ్యక్తులకు, ఆస్తికి లేదా పర్యావరణానికి కలిగిన హాని). సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 2(c)): మూల దేశం కాకుండా మరో దేశ భూభాగంలో, లేదా దాని అధికార పరిధి లేదా నియంత్రణలోని ఇతర ప్రదేశాలలో కలిగిన హాని, "whether or not the States concerned share a common border" (అర్థం: సంబంధిత దేశాలకు ఉమ్మడి సరిహద్దు ఉన్నా లేకపోయినా). మూల దేశం (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 2(d)): ఏ దేశ భూభాగంలో, లేదా ఏ దేశ అధికార పరిధి లేదా నియంత్రణలో కార్యకలాపం ప్రణాళిక చేయబడుతుందో లేదా జరుగుతుందో ఆ దేశం. ప్రభావితమయ్యే అవకాశం ఉన్న దేశం (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 2(e)): ఏ దేశ భూభాగంలో, లేదా ఏ దేశ అధికార పరిధి లేదా నియంత్రణలోని ప్రదేశంలో గణనీయమైన సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని ప్రమాదం ఉందో ఆ దేశం. గణనీయమైన సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని కలిగించే ప్రమాదం (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 2(a)): గణనీయమైన హాని కలిగించే అధిక సంభావ్యతతో పాటు "a low probability of causing disastrous transboundary harm" (అర్థం: విపత్కర సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని కలిగించే తక్కువ సంభావ్యత) కూడా ఇందులో ఉంటుంది.
keyPoints: సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని: దేశాలకు సరిహద్దు ఉన్నా లేకపోయినా, మరో దేశంలో లేదా దాని నియంత్రణలోని ప్రాంతంలో హాని (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 2(c)). మూల దేశం: ప్రమాదకర కార్యకలాపం ప్రణాళిక చేయబడే లేదా జరిగే దేశం; నివారణ, అంచనా, సమాచార విధులు దానివే. తగిన శ్రద్ధ: "all appropriate measures to prevent significant transboundary harm or at any event to minimize the risk thereof" (అర్థం: గణనీయమైన సరిహద్దు దాటు హానిని నివారించడానికి, లేదా ఏమైనా దాని ప్రమాదాన్ని కనిష్ఠం చేయడానికి తగిన అన్ని చర్యలు) (ILC 2001, ఆర్టికల్ 3). ముందస్తు సమాచారం: రియో సూ19; ILC ఆర్టికల్ 8; ప్రతిస్పందన కోసం ఆరు నెలల వరకు అనుమతి నిర్ణయం ఉండదు. హాని చేయకూడదనే నియమం: Trail Smelter → Corfu Channel → స్టాక్‌హోమ్ సూ21 → రియో సూ2 → Nuclear Weapons AO పేరా 29. LRTAP 1979: దీర్ఘ-శ్రేణి వాయు కాలుష్యం; సహకార చట్రం; బాధ్యత నియమం లేదు. బాసెల్ 1989: ప్రమాదకర వ్యర్థాలు; భారత్ ఆమోదం 24-6-1992.

selfTest.q: ILC ముసాయిదా ఆర్టికల్స్, 2001 ప్రకారం "సరిహద్దు దాటు హాని" ని నిర్వచించండి. సరిహద్దు దాటు వాయు కాలుష్యానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా మొదటిసారి నియమాన్ని నిర్దేశించిన మధ్యవర్తిత్వం ఏది?
selfTest.a: ప్రభావితమయ్యే అవకాశం ఉన్న దేశాలకు ముందస్తు, సకాల సమాచారం కోరే రియో సూత్రం ఏది? LRTAP కన్వెన్షన్ ఎప్పుడు కుదిరింది, ఎప్పుడు అమలులోకి వచ్చింది? ఇతర దేశాల పర్యావరణాన్ని గౌరవించే బాధ్యత గురించి ICJ 1996 లో ఏమి చెప్పింది? నష్టానికి దేశ బాధ్యతపై LRTAP కన్వెన్షన్‌లో నియమం ఉందా?

hi.inOneMinute: Transboundary pollution is pollution that starts in one State and causes harm in another State, or in areas beyond any State's jurisdiction such as the high seas. It travels through the air (smoke, acid rain), through water (shared rivers, the sea), through the movement of hazardous waste , and through accidents at industrial plants. The basic rule of international law is the no-harm rule . A State has the sovereign right to use its own resources, but it must ensure that activities within its jurisdiction or control do not damage the environment of other States (Stockholm Principle 21, 1972; Rio Principle 2, 1992). The rule began with the Trail Smelter arbitration (USA v. Canada, 1938 and 1941). It was supported by Corfu Channel (ICJ, 1949). The ICJ said in 1996 that it "is now part of the corpus of international law relating to the environment" ( Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion). The duties of the State where the activity takes place (the State of origin ) are: prevent harm; assess the risk; notify the State likely to be affected; consult with it; prepare for and report emergencies. These are set out in the ILC Draft Articles on Prevention of Transboundary Harm from Hazardous Activities, 2001. Main treaties: the Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution, 1979 (LRTAP) and the Basel Convention, 1989 (hazardous wastes).
legalProvision: Stockholm Declaration, 1972: Principle 21: sovereign right over resources, with responsibility not to damage other States or areas beyond national jurisdiction. Principle 22: States shall cooperate to develop international law on liability and compensation for victims of pollution and other environmental damage caused beyond their jurisdiction. Rio Declaration, 1992: Principle 2: same rule as Stockholm Principle 21. Principle 13: "States shall develop national law regarding liability and compensation for the victims of pollution". Principle 18: "States shall immediately notify other States of any natural disasters or other emergencies" likely to produce sudden harmful effects on them. Principle 19: "States shall provide prior and timely notification and relevant information to potentially affected States" about activities that may have a significant adverse transboundary effect. Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution , Geneva, 13 November 1979; in force 16 March 1983. ILC Draft Articles on Prevention of Transboundary Harm from Hazardous Activities, 2001 (Arts 1–19). Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal , adopted 22 March 1989; in force 5 May 1992. India: Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
hi.meaning: Transboundary pollution : pollution whose source is in one State and whose harmful effects are felt in another State or in areas beyond national jurisdiction . Air pollution (LRTAP Art. 1(a)): the introduction by man, directly or indirectly, of substances or energy into the air resulting in deleterious effects. Long-range transboundary air pollution (LRTAP Art. 1(b)): air pollution whose physical origin is wholly or partly within one State, and which has adverse effects in another State at such a distance that it is not generally possible to tell the contribution of individual sources. Harm (ILC 2001, Art. 2(b)): "harm caused to persons, property or the environment". Transboundary harm (ILC 2001, Art. 2(c)): harm caused in the territory of, or in other places under the jurisdiction or control of, a State other than the State of origin, "whether or not the States concerned share a common border". State of origin (ILC 2001, Art. 2(d)): the State in whose territory, or under whose jurisdiction or control, the activity is planned or carried out. State likely to be affected (ILC 2001, Art. 2(e)): the State in whose territory, or in a place under whose jurisdiction or control, there is a risk of significant transboundary harm. Risk of causing significant transboundary harm (ILC 2001, Art. 2(a)): includes a high probability of causing significant harm and also "a low probability of causing disastrous transboundary harm".
keyPoints: Transboundary harm: harm in another State or area under its control, whether or not the States share a border (ILC 2001, Art. 2(c)). State of origin: the State where the risky activity is planned or carried out; it carries the duties of prevention, assessment and notification. Due diligence: "all appropriate measures to prevent significant transboundary harm or at any event to minimize the risk thereof" (ILC 2001, Art. 3). Prior notification: Rio P19; ILC Art. 8; no authorisation decision for up to six months pending the reply. No-harm rule: Trail Smelter → Corfu Channel → Stockholm P21 → Rio P2 → Nuclear Weapons AO para. 29. LRTAP 1979: long-range air pollution; framework for cooperation; no liability rule. Basel 1989: hazardous waste; India ratified 24-6-1992.

caseLaws.facts: Trail Smelter Arbitration (United States v. Canada), decisions of 16 April 1938 and 11 March 1941 (Arbitral Tribunal under the Convention of 15 April 1935; 3 RIAA 1905)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Sulphur dioxide fumes from a smelter at Trail, British Columbia, damaged land across the bord
caseLaws.facts: The USA and Canada set up a three-member tribunal by the Ottawa Convention of 1935 to decide the matter. Principle: No State has the right to use or permit the use of its territory so as to cause serious injury by fumes in or to the territory of another State, where the case has serious consequences and the injury is proved by clear and convincing evidence. Canada was held responsible, and a regime was laid down to control the smelter's future emissions. Why it matters: It is the first international decision on transboundary air pollution and the source of the no-harm rule.
Corfu Channel Case (United Kingdom v. Albania), Merits, Judgment of 9 April 1949 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: On 22 October 1946, the British warships Saumarez and Volage struck mines in Albanian waters
caseLaws.facts: 45 men were killed and 42 wounded. Principle: Albania was held responsible (by 11 votes to 5) for the explosions and the resulting damage and loss of life. The Court relied on "every State's obligation not to allow knowingly its territory to be used for acts contrary to the rights of other States". Why it matters: This general duty of a State over its territory is the basis of the duty to prevent transboundary pollution.
Legality of the Threat or Use of Nuclear Weapons, Advisory Opinion of 8 July 1996 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The UN General Assembly (resolution 49/75 K of 15 December 1994) asked the Court whether the
caseLaws.facts: The Court considered, among other things, the law protecting the environment. Principle: "the environment is not an abstraction but represents the living space, the quality of life and the very health of human beings, including generations unborn". The general obligation of States to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction and control respect the environment of other States or of areas beyond national control "is now part of the corpus of international law relating to the environment" (para. 29). Why it matters: The world court confirmed that the no-harm rule against transboundary environmental damage is part of general international law, binding all States.

environmental-law-u5-t1.subtitle: The rules, treaties and institutions through which States protect the environment together

en.inOneMinute: Pollution and nature do not stop at borders. Smoke, rivers, the oceans, migratory birds and the climate are shared by many States. So States have built a body of international rules, institutions and procedures to protect the environment. This is the international environmental regime . It is made of: Treaties (conventions and protocols), for example the Ramsar Convention (1971), the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), the UNFCCC (1992), the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015). Customary international law , for example the duty not to cause harm to other States. Declarations and other "soft law" , for example the Stockholm Declaration (1972), the Rio Declaration (1992) and the Johannesburg Declaration (2002). Institutions , for example the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Conferences of the Parties (COPs) of each treaty. Judicial decisions , for example Trail Smelter (1941), Corfu Channel (1949) and Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros (1997). Its core principles are: the responsibility not to cause damage beyond one's borders, prevention, precaution, polluter pays, environmental impact assessment, sustainable development, and common but differentiated responsibilities. India takes part in this regime and implements it through Art. 51(c) and Art. 253 of the Constitution, through laws such as the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, and through Supreme Court judgments such as Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996).
legalProvision: Statute of the International Court of Justice, Art. 38(1): the sources of international law the Court applies. Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment, 1972: especially Principle 21. Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, 1992: especially Principles 2, 7, 10, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 27. Main treaties: Ramsar Convention, 1971; Bonn Convention, 1979; Vienna Convention, 1985 and Montreal Protocol, 1987; Basel Convention, 1989; Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992; UNFCCC, 1992; Kyoto Protocol, 1997; Paris Agreement, 2015. Constitution of India: Art. 51(c): the State shall endeavour to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations. Art. 253: Parliament may make laws to implement treaties and decisions made at international conferences. Art. 48A and Art. 51A(g): protection of the environment. Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: its preamble refers to the decisions of the Stockholm Conference, 1972.
en.meaning: Regime: a set of rules, principles, institutions and decision-making procedures that States accept in a particular area. No treaty defines "international environmental regime". It is a study term. International environmental law: the part of international law that deals with the protection of the environment . Sources (ICJ Statute Art. 38(1)): (a) "international conventions, whether general or particular, establishing rules expressly recognized by the contesting states"; (b) "international custom, as evidence of a general practice accepted as law"; (c) "the general principles of law recognized by civilized nations"; (d) judicial decisions and the teachings of the most highly qualified publicists , "as subsidiary means for the determination of rules of law". Soft law : declarations, resolutions, guidelines and action plans that are not binding treaties. They guide States and often later become treaty rules or custom. No-harm principle : a State's responsibility to ensure that activities within its jurisdiction or control do not damage the environment of other States or of areas beyond national jurisdiction (Stockholm Principle 21; Rio Principle 2). Sustainable development : development that meets present needs without harming future generations. Rio Principle 3 says the right to development must be fulfilled "so as to equitably meet developmental and environmental needs of present and future generations". Common but differentiated responsibilities : all States share responsibility for the global environment, but developed States carry a greater share (Rio Principle 7).
keyPoints: Soft law: Stockholm 1972, Rio 1992, Johannesburg 2002; not binding by itself but shapes treaties and judgments. No-harm principle: Stockholm P21, Rio P2; Trail Smelter ; part of the corpus of international environmental law (ICJ, 1996). Sustainable development: Rio P3, P4; Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros ; Vellore . Common but differentiated responsibilities: Rio P7; basis of the climate treaties. Rio P15 precaution, P16 polluter pays, P17 EIA, P10 participation, P13 liability. India implements the regime through Art. 253 and laws such as the EP Act, 1986 and the BD Act, 2002.

caseLaws.name: Facts: Sulphur dioxide fumes from a smelter at Trail, British Columbia, damaged crops, forests and l
caseLaws.facts: The two countries set up a three-member tribunal by the Ottawa Convention of 1935. Principle: No State has the right to use or permit the use of its territory in a way that causes serious injury by fumes to the territory of another State, where the case has serious consequences and the injury is proved by clear and convincing evidence. The tribunal held Canada responsible and laid down a regime to control the smelter's future emissions. Why it matters: It is the first international decision on transboundary pollution and the starting point of the no-harm principle.
Gabčíkovo-Nagymaros Project (Hungary/Slovakia), Judgment of 25 September 1997 (International Court of Justice)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By a 1977 treaty, Hungary and Czechoslovakia agreed to build dams on the Danube at Gabčíkovo
caseLaws.facts: "In 1989, Hungary suspended and subsequently abandoned completion of the project." Czechoslovakia put an alternative ("Variant C") into operation in October 1992. Principle: The Court found both States in breach of their obligations. The treaty remained in force. The two States "must negotiate in good faith", must look afresh at the environmental effects of the project, and must compensate each other for the damage caused. Why it matters: It shows that environmental concerns must be reconciled with treaty obligations and development through cooperation. It is a leading case on sustainable development.
Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India , AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh, Faizan Uddin and K. Venkataswami JJ; 28 August 1996)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar river, making about 35,0
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Sustainable development is part of customary international law. The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". The Court said "Sustainable Development is the answer". Why it matters: It shows how principles of the international environmental regime become part of Indian law through the courts.
