hi.inOneMinute: The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) was set up by the UN General Assembly by resolution 2997 (XXVII) of 15 December 1972 , as a result of the Stockholm Conference of June 1972. Its headquarters are in Nairobi, Kenya (resolution 3004 (XXVII), "Location of the environment secretariat", 15 December 1972). UNEP was "The first UN agency to be headquartered in a developing country". Resolution 2997 created four parts: a Governing Council of 58 States; a small secretariat headed by an Executive Director ; a voluntary Environment Fund ; an Environment Co-ordination Board . After Rio+20 (2012), the General Assembly gave the Governing Council universal membership (resolution 67/213, 21 December 2012) and renamed it the United Nations Environment Assembly (UNEA) (resolution 67/251, 13 March 2013). The first UNEA met in Nairobi from 23 to 27 June 2014. UNEP calls itself "the leading global environmental authority". Its role covers: setting the global environmental agenda; reviewing the state of the world environment; developing environmental law (the Montevideo Programme , since 1982); hosting the secretariats of many environmental treaties (Basel, CBD, CITES, CMS, Montreal Protocol and others); setting up the IPCC with the WMO (1988). India: Indian courts apply treaties that UNEP administers, such as the Basel Convention ( Research Foundation , 2003) and the CBD, CITES and CMS ( Centre for Environment Law, WWF-I , 2013).
legalProvision: UN General Assembly resolution 2997 (XXVII), 15 December 1972, "Institutional and financial arrangements for international environmental cooperation": Part I: Governing Council; Part II: Environment secretariat and Executive Director; Part III: Environment Fund; Part IV: Environment Co-ordination Board. Resolution 3004 (XXVII), 15 December 1972: location of the environment secretariat (adopted 128 votes to 0). Rio+20 outcome document "The future we want" (2012), paragraph 88: strengthen and upgrade UNEP (endorsed by GA resolution 66/288 of 27 July 2012). Resolution 67/213, 21 December 2012: universal membership of the Governing Council; reaffirms "the Nairobi headquarters location". Resolution 67/251, 13 March 2013: the Governing Council renamed the United Nations Environment Assembly of the United Nations Environment Programme. Treaties whose secretariats UNEP administers (examples): Vienna Convention and Montreal Protocol (ozone); Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions (chemicals and waste); Minamata Convention (mercury); CBD; CITES; CMS; regional seas conventions. India: Constitution Art. 253 (laws to implement treaties and decisions of international conferences); Art. 21; Art. 48A; Art. 51A(g).
hi.meaning: UNEP: the UN body for the environment , set up by the General Assembly in 1972. Its mission: "Our mission is to provide leadership and encourage partnership in caring for the environment" "by inspiring, informing, and enabling nations and peoples to improve their quality of life" "without compromising that of future generations." Role: UNEP describes itself as "the leading global environmental authority" that sets the global environmental agenda, promotes coherent implementation of the environmental dimension of sustainable development within the UN system, and serves as an authoritative advocate for the global environment. "Programme": UNEP was created by a General Assembly resolution, not by a treaty of its own. Its governing body reports to the General Assembly.
keyPoints: UNEP: GA resolution 2997 (XXVII), 15-12-1972; HQ Nairobi (resolution 3004 (XXVII)). Governing Council: 58 members, three-year terms; seven functions; renamed in 2013. UN Environment Assembly: universal membership (67/213, 2012); name change (67/251, 2013); 193 Member States; meets every second year; first session June 2014. Environment Fund: voluntary, from 1-1-1973; UNEP relies on voluntary contributions for about 95% of its income. Montevideo Programme: since 1982 (GC decision 10/21); Fifth Programme 2020–2029. Treaty secretariats: ozone, Basel/Rotterdam/Stockholm, Minamata, CBD, CITES, CMS, regional seas. IPCC with WMO, 1988.

caseLaws.facts: Research Foundation for Science, Technology and Natural Resource Policy v. Union of India, W.P. (C) No. 657 of 1995, order of 14 October 2003 (Supreme Court)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A public interest petition complained of the dumping of hazardous waste and its illegal impor
caseLaws.facts: A High Powered Committee chaired by Prof. M.G.K. Menon had reported on the problem. Principle: "The ratification of Basel Convention by India shows the commitment of our country". "The Basel Convention, it cannot be doubted, effectuates the fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 21." The precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are part of the law, and the right to information and community participation forms part of Art. 21. The Ministry "shall ensure that the agreement does not remain only on paper." Why it matters: It shows a UNEP-administered treaty being enforced by an Indian court: the Court ordered a ban on imports of listed wastes, re-export or destruction of waste oil at the importers' cost, and a Monitoring Committee.
Centre for Environment Law, WWF-I v. Union of India, I.A. No. 100 in W.P. (C) No. 337 of 1995 (Supreme Court; K.S. Radhakrishnan and Chandramauli Kr. Prasad JJ; 15 April 2013)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Asiatic lion, an endangered species , survived only in Gir (Gujarat)
caseLaws.facts: Expert bodies recommended a second home at Kuno in Madhya Pradesh. Gujarat objected, and the Ministry had also approved bringing African cheetahs to Kuno. Principle: "our approach should be eco-centric and not anthropocentric", applying the "species best interest standard". The Court relied on the Stockholm Declaration, the CBD, CITES (lion in Appendix I), the Bonn Convention and IUCN guidelines, and held: "MoEF is therefore directed to take urgent steps for re-introduction of Asiatic lion from Gir forests to Kuno." Why it matters: It shows Indian courts using nature treaties whose secretariats UNEP hosts (CBD, CITES, CMS) to protect a species.
Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India , AIR 1996 SC 2715; (1996) 5 SCC 647 (Supreme Court; Kuldip Singh, Faizan Uddin and K. Venkataswami JJ; 28 August 1996)

environmental-law-u5-t8.subtitle: The treaty on wetlands: the Ramsar List, wise use and the Montreux Record

en.inOneMinute: The Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat was adopted at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971 . It was amended in 1982 and 1987. It is the treaty for the protection of wetlands . It defines wetlands widely: "areas of marsh, fen, peatland or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary", fresh, brackish or salt, including sea water not deeper than six metres at low tide (Art. 1(1)). Each party must: designate at least one wetland for the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the "Ramsar List") (Art. 2); promote the conservation of listed wetlands and, as far as possible, the wise use of all its wetlands (Art. 3(1)); set up nature reserves on wetlands, listed or not (Art. 4(1)); consult other parties on shared wetlands and water systems (Art. 5). A party may delete or restrict a listed site only "because of its urgent national interests", and should then compensate for the loss (Arts 2(5), 4(2)). The Conference of the Contracting Parties meets at intervals of not more than three years (Art. 6). IUCN performs the bureau duties (Art. 8). Listed sites under threat can be put on the Montreux Record . India became a signatory on 1 February 1982. India's 100th Ramsar site was designated in 2026. In India, Ramsar sites are protected by the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 . 2 February is World Wetlands Day.
legalProvision: Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat (Ramsar, 2 February 1971), as amended in 1982 and 1987: Preamble; Art. 1: definitions of wetlands and waterfowl; Art. 2: the List; designation, criteria, sovereign rights, deletion; Art. 3: conservation and wise use; change in ecological character; Art. 4: nature reserves; compensation; Art. 5: international consultation; Arts 6–7: Conference of the Contracting Parties; Art. 8: bureau (IUCN); Arts 9–11: signature, entry into force, amendment, denunciation (UNESCO is the Depositary). India: Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 (G.S.R. 1203(E), 26 September 2017), made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: rules 2(1)(g), 3, 4, 5, 6; Constitution Arts 21, 48A, 51A(g) and 253.
en.meaning: Wetlands (Art. 1(1)): "areas of marsh, fen, peatland or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary" "with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt" "including areas of marine water the depth of which at low tide does not exceed six metres." Waterfowl (Art. 1(2)): "birds ecologically dependent on wetlands." Ramsar site: a wetland placed on the List of Wetlands of International Importance under Art. 2. Wise use : "At the centre of the Ramsar philosophy is the 'wise use' of wetlands." Under Art. 3(1), parties must promote, as far as possible, the wise use of wetlands in their territory, whether listed or not.
keyPoints: Ramsar, Iran, 2-2-1971; Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat. Art. 1(1): natural or artificial wetlands; marine water up to six metres at low tide. Ramsar List: at least one site per party; criteria in Art. 2(2); deletion only for urgent national interests. Wise use: Art. 3(1); rule 4(1) of the 2017 Rules. Ecological character: parties must know and report changes (Art. 3(2)). Montreux Record: threatened Ramsar sites; Keoladeo and Loktak in India. India: signatory 1-2-1982; 100th site 2026.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The State planned further reclamation of about 784 acres of the East Calcutta wetlands (fishi
caseLaws.facts: A citizens' group challenged it. Principle: "There shall have to be a proper balance between the development and the environment". The Court noted that "the wetlands purify the entire waste water through a natural process of oxidation" and that "India is a contracting party to the Ramsar Convention". It held that "wetland is precious" and restrained the State from reclaiming "any further wetland". Why it matters: It is the leading Indian case applying the idea of the Ramsar Convention to save a wetland from development.
M.K. Balakrishnan v. Union of India, W.P. (C) No. 230 of 2001, order of 4 October 2017 (Supreme Court; Madan B. Lokur, S. Abdul Nazeer and Deepak Gupta JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A public interest petition sought protection of India's wetlands, which were disappearing
caseLaws.facts: The Court took note of the 2017 Wetlands Rules, notified on 26 September 2017, and of objections that the Centre had left too much to the States. Principle: The Court observed that wetlands were diminishing "at a very fast rate" and ordered that the "2,01,503 wetlands that have been mapped by the Union of India should continue to remain protected on the same principles as were formulated in Rule 4" of the 2010 Rules. Why it matters: It extends protection beyond notified wetlands and Ramsar sites to every wetland mapped in the national inventory.
Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v. State of A.P., AIR 2006 SC 1350; (2006) 3 SCC 549 (Supreme Court; Ruma Pal and Dr. AR. Lakshmanan JJ; 23 February 2006)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Historic tanks near Tirupati were given away for building; residents challenged it
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court relied on Principle 2 of the Stockholm Declaration and held that "The state is the trustee of all natural resources which are by nature meant for public use and enjoyment"; it stopped further construction. Why it matters: It gives water bodies like tanks and lakes the protection of the public trust doctrine, which supports the wise use of wetlands.

te.inOneMinute: ముఖ్యంగా నీటిపక్షుల ఆవాసంగా అంతర్జాతీయ ప్రాముఖ్యత గల చిత్తడి నేలలపై కన్వెన్షన్ 2 ఫిబ్రవరి 1971 న ఇరాన్‌లోని రామ్‌సర్‌లో ఆమోదించబడింది. 1982, 1987 లో దానికి సవరణలు జరిగాయి. ఇది చిత్తడి నేలల (wetlands) రక్షణకు సంబంధించిన ఒప్పందం. ఇది చిత్తడి నేలలను విస్తృతంగా నిర్వచిస్తుంది: "areas of marsh, fen, peatland or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary" (అర్థం: సహజమైనవి లేదా కృత్రిమమైనవి, శాశ్వతమైనవి లేదా తాత్కాలికమైనవి అయిన బురద నేల, ఫెన్, పీట్ నేల లేదా నీటి ప్రాంతాలు), మంచి, ఉప్పుకలిసిన లేదా ఉప్పు నీటితో, అల్పపోటు సమయంలో ఆరు మీటర్ల కంటే లోతు లేని సముద్ర నీటితో సహా (ఆర్టికల్ 1(1)). ప్రతి భాగస్వామ్య దేశం తప్పక: అంతర్జాతీయ ప్రాముఖ్యత గల చిత్తడి నేలల జాబితా ("రామ్‌సర్ జాబితా") కు కనీసం ఒక చిత్తడి నేలను నియమించాలి (ఆర్టికల్ 2); జాబితాలోని చిత్తడి నేలల పరిరక్షణను, సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు తన అన్ని చిత్తడి నేలల వివేకవంతమైన వినియోగాన్ని ప్రోత్సహించాలి (ఆర్టికల్ 3(1)); జాబితాలో ఉన్నా లేకపోయినా, చిత్తడి నేలలపై ప్రకృతి రిజర్వులు ఏర్పాటు చేయాలి (ఆర్టికల్ 4(1)); ఉమ్మడి చిత్తడి నేలలు, నీటి వ్యవస్థలపై ఇతర భాగస్వాములతో సంప్రదించాలి (ఆర్టికల్ 5). జాబితాలోని ప్రదేశాన్ని ఒక దేశం "because of its urgent national interests" (అర్థం: తన అత్యవసర జాతీయ ప్రయోజనాల కారణంగా) మాత్రమే తొలగించవచ్చు లేదా పరిమితం చేయవచ్చు, తర్వాత నష్టానికి పరిహారం ఇవ్వాలి (ఆర్టికల్స్ 2(5), 4(2)). భాగస్వామ్య దేశాల సదస్సు మూడేళ్లకు మించని వ్యవధిలో సమావేశమవుతుంది (ఆర్టికల్ 6). బ్యూరో విధులను IUCN నిర్వహిస్తుంది (ఆర్టికల్ 8). ప్రమాదంలో ఉన్న జాబితా ప్రదేశాలను మాంట్రో రికార్డ్ (Montreux Record) లో చేర్చవచ్చు. భారత్ 1 ఫిబ్రవరి 1982 న సంతకం చేసింది. భారతదేశ 100వ రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశం 2026 లో నియమించబడింది. భారత్‌లో రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశాలను చిత్తడి నేలల (పరిరక్షణ, నిర్వహణ) నియమాలు, 2017 రక్షిస్తాయి. ఫిబ్రవరి 2 ప్రపంచ చిత్తడి నేలల దినోత్సవం.
te.meaning: చిత్తడి నేలలు (ఆర్టికల్ 1(1)): "areas of marsh, fen, peatland or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary" (అర్థం: సహజమైనవి లేదా కృత్రిమమైనవి, శాశ్వతమైనవి లేదా తాత్కాలికమైనవి అయిన బురద నేల, ఫెన్, పీట్ నేల లేదా నీటి ప్రాంతాలు) "with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt" (అర్థం: నిలకడగా ఉన్న లేదా ప్రవహించే, మంచి, ఉప్పుకలిసిన లేదా ఉప్పు నీటితో) "including areas of marine water the depth of which at low tide does not exceed six metres." (అర్థం: అల్పపోటు సమయంలో లోతు ఆరు మీటర్లు మించని సముద్ర నీటి ప్రాంతాలతో సహా.) నీటిపక్షులు (ఆర్టికల్ 1(2)): "birds ecologically dependent on wetlands." (అర్థం: పర్యావరణపరంగా చిత్తడి నేలలపై ఆధారపడే పక్షులు.) రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశం: ఆర్టికల్ 2 కింద అంతర్జాతీయ ప్రాముఖ్యత గల చిత్తడి నేలల జాబితాలో చేర్చిన చిత్తడి నేల. వివేకవంతమైన వినియోగం : "At the centre of the Ramsar philosophy is the 'wise use' of wetlands." (అర్థం: రామ్‌సర్ తత్వానికి కేంద్రం చిత్తడి నేలల 'వివేకవంతమైన వినియోగం'.) ఆర్టికల్ 3(1) కింద, జాబితాలో ఉన్నా లేకపోయినా, తమ భూభాగంలోని చిత్తడి నేలల వివేకవంతమైన వినియోగాన్ని భాగస్వాములు సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు ప్రోత్సహించాలి.
keyPoints: రామ్‌సర్, ఇరాన్, 2-2-1971; ముఖ్యంగా నీటిపక్షుల ఆవాసంగా అంతర్జాతీయ ప్రాముఖ్యత గల చిత్తడి నేలలపై కన్వెన్షన్. ఆర్టికల్ 1(1): సహజ లేదా కృత్రిమ చిత్తడి నేలలు; అల్పపోటులో ఆరు మీటర్ల వరకు సముద్ర నీరు. రామ్‌సర్ జాబితా: ప్రతి భాగస్వామికి కనీసం ఒక ప్రదేశం; ఆర్టికల్ 2(2) లో ప్రమాణాలు; అత్యవసర జాతీయ ప్రయోజనాల కోసం మాత్రమే తొలగింపు. వివేకవంతమైన వినియోగం: ఆర్టికల్ 3(1); 2017 నియమాలలో నియమం 4(1). పర్యావరణ స్వభావం: భాగస్వాములు మార్పులను తెలుసుకుని నివేదించాలి (ఆర్టికల్ 3(2)). మాంట్రో రికార్డ్: ప్రమాదంలో ఉన్న రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశాలు; భారత్‌లో కేవలాదేవ్, లోక్‌టక్. భారత్: సంతకం 1-2-1982; 100వ ప్రదేశం 2026.

selfTest.q: రామ్‌సర్ కన్వెన్షన్ ఎప్పుడు, ఎక్కడ ఆమోదించబడింది?
selfTest.a: ఆర్టికల్ 1(1) కింద "చిత్తడి నేలలు" ను నిర్వచించండి. ఏ కారణంపై భాగస్వామి రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశాన్ని తొలగించవచ్చు, తర్వాత ఏమి చేయాలి? మాంట్రో రికార్డ్ అంటే ఏమిటి? ఆర్టికల్ 8 కింద బ్యూరో విధులను ఏ సంస్థ నిర్వహిస్తుంది? ఏ భారత నియమాలు రామ్‌సర్ ప్రదేశాలను రక్షిస్తాయి, అవి ఏమి నిషేధిస్తాయి?

hi.inOneMinute: The Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat was adopted at Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971 . It was amended in 1982 and 1987. It is the treaty for the protection of wetlands . It defines wetlands widely: "areas of marsh, fen, peatland or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary", fresh, brackish or salt, including sea water not deeper than six metres at low tide (Art. 1(1)). Each party must: designate at least one wetland for the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the "Ramsar List") (Art. 2); promote the conservation of listed wetlands and, as far as possible, the wise use of all its wetlands (Art. 3(1)); set up nature reserves on wetlands, listed or not (Art. 4(1)); consult other parties on shared wetlands and water systems (Art. 5). A party may delete or restrict a listed site only "because of its urgent national interests", and should then compensate for the loss (Arts 2(5), 4(2)). The Conference of the Contracting Parties meets at intervals of not more than three years (Art. 6). IUCN performs the bureau duties (Art. 8). Listed sites under threat can be put on the Montreux Record . India became a signatory on 1 February 1982. India's 100th Ramsar site was designated in 2026. In India, Ramsar sites are protected by the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 . 2 February is World Wetlands Day.
legalProvision: Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat (Ramsar, 2 February 1971), as amended in 1982 and 1987: Preamble; Art. 1: definitions of wetlands and waterfowl; Art. 2: the List; designation, criteria, sovereign rights, deletion; Art. 3: conservation and wise use; change in ecological character; Art. 4: nature reserves; compensation; Art. 5: international consultation; Arts 6–7: Conference of the Contracting Parties; Art. 8: bureau (IUCN); Arts 9–11: signature, entry into force, amendment, denunciation (UNESCO is the Depositary). India: Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 (G.S.R. 1203(E), 26 September 2017), made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986: rules 2(1)(g), 3, 4, 5, 6; Constitution Arts 21, 48A, 51A(g) and 253.
hi.meaning: Wetlands (Art. 1(1)): "areas of marsh, fen, peatland or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary" "with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt" "including areas of marine water the depth of which at low tide does not exceed six metres." Waterfowl (Art. 1(2)): "birds ecologically dependent on wetlands." Ramsar site: a wetland placed on the List of Wetlands of International Importance under Art. 2. Wise use : "At the centre of the Ramsar philosophy is the 'wise use' of wetlands." Under Art. 3(1), parties must promote, as far as possible, the wise use of wetlands in their territory, whether listed or not.
keyPoints: Ramsar, Iran, 2-2-1971; Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat. Art. 1(1): natural or artificial wetlands; marine water up to six metres at low tide. Ramsar List: at least one site per party; criteria in Art. 2(2); deletion only for urgent national interests. Wise use: Art. 3(1); rule 4(1) of the 2017 Rules. Ecological character: parties must know and report changes (Art. 3(2)). Montreux Record: threatened Ramsar sites; Keoladeo and Loktak in India. India: signatory 1-2-1982; 100th site 2026.

caseLaws.facts: People United for Better Living in Calcutta v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1993 Cal 215 (Calcutta High Court; 24 September 1992)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The State planned further reclamation of about 784 acres of the East Calcutta wetlands (fishi
caseLaws.facts: A citizens' group challenged it. Principle: "There shall have to be a proper balance between the development and the environment". The Court noted that "the wetlands purify the entire waste water through a natural process of oxidation" and that "India is a contracting party to the Ramsar Convention". It held that "wetland is precious" and restrained the State from reclaiming "any further wetland". Why it matters: It is the leading Indian case applying the idea of the Ramsar Convention to save a wetland from development.
M.K. Balakrishnan v. Union of India, W.P. (C) No. 230 of 2001, order of 4 October 2017 (Supreme Court; Madan B. Lokur, S. Abdul Nazeer and Deepak Gupta JJ)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A public interest petition sought protection of India's wetlands, which were disappearing
caseLaws.facts: The Court took note of the 2017 Wetlands Rules, notified on 26 September 2017, and of objections that the Centre had left too much to the States. Principle: The Court observed that wetlands were diminishing "at a very fast rate" and ordered that the "2,01,503 wetlands that have been mapped by the Union of India should continue to remain protected on the same principles as were formulated in Rule 4" of the 2010 Rules. Why it matters: It extends protection beyond notified wetlands and Ramsar sites to every wetland mapped in the national inventory.
Intellectuals Forum, Tirupathi v. State of A.P., AIR 2006 SC 1350; (2006) 3 SCC 549 (Supreme Court; Ruma Pal and Dr. AR. Lakshmanan JJ; 23 February 2006)

caseLaws.name: Facts: Historic tanks near Tirupati were given away for building; residents challenged it
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court relied on Principle 2 of the Stockholm Declaration and held that "The state is the trustee of all natural resources which are by nature meant for public use and enjoyment"; it stopped further construction. Why it matters: It gives water bodies like tanks and lakes the protection of the public trust doctrine, which supports the wise use of wetlands.

environmental-law-u5-t12.subtitle: The first climate treaty with binding emission targets, and why they applied only to developed countries

en.inOneMinute: What it is: the Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change , a binding treaty adopted at Kyoto, Japan, on 11 December 1997 at the third session of the Conference of the Parties (COP3). It came into force on 16 February 2005 . Why: the UNFCCC (1992) only asks developed countries to adopt policies and report. The Protocol "operationalizes" the Convention by giving those countries binding targets to limit and reduce greenhouse gases. Who is bound: only developed countries and economies in transition ( Annex I Parties), with individual targets in Annex B . Developing countries such as India get no new commitments (Art. 10), following common but differentiated responsibilities . Main target (Art. 3(1)): Annex I emissions of six gases (Annex A) to fall "by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels in the commitment period 2008 to 2012". Three market mechanisms: Joint implementation (Art. 6) – between Annex I Parties; Clean Development Mechanism (Art. 12) – projects in developing countries; Emissions trading (Art. 17) – between Annex B Parties. Second period: the Doha Amendment (8 December 2012) for 2013–2020 , at least 18 per cent below 1990; in force on 31 December 2020. India: ratified on 26 August 2002; hosted many CDM projects. Indian tax law treats carbon credits from CDM projects as capital receipts ( CIT v. My Home Power Ltd , Andhra Pradesh High Court, 2014).
legalProvision: Kyoto Protocol, 1997 (28 Articles, Annexes A and B): Art. 1 – definitions ("Convention" means the UNFCCC adopted in New York on 9 May 1992; "Party included in Annex I"). Art. 2 – policies and measures by Annex I Parties "in order to promote sustainable development". Art. 3 – quantified emission limitation and reduction commitments; 3(1) "by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels in the commitment period 2008 to 2012"; 3(2) "demonstrable progress" by 2005; 3(3) forests; 3(7) assigned amounts; 3(9) later periods; 3(13) carry-over (banking). Art. 4 – joint fulfilment by a group of Parties. Art. 5 – national systems for estimating emissions; Arts. 7–8 – reporting and expert review. Art. 6 – transfer and acquisition of emission reduction units (joint implementation). Art. 10 – all Parties, "taking into account their common but differentiated responsibilities", "without introducing any new commitments for Parties not included in Annex I". Art. 12 – "A clean development mechanism is hereby defined." Art. 13 – the Conference of the Parties serves as the meeting of the Parties to the Protocol. Art. 17 – "The Parties included in Annex B may participate in emissions trading". Art. 18 – non-compliance procedures. Art. 24 – open for signature in New York "from 16 March 1998 to 15 March 1999". Art. 25(1) – entry into force on the ninetieth day after at least 55 Parties to the Convention, including Annex I Parties accounting for at least 55 per cent of the total carbon dioxide emissions for 1990 of Annex I Parties, have joined. Art. 26 – "No reservations may be made to this Protocol." Annex A – six greenhouse gases and the source sectors; Annex B – the target of each Party as a percentage of its base-year emissions. Doha Amendment, 2012 – second commitment period, 2013–2020. Constitution of India: Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
en.meaning: Kyoto Protocol: a protocol (an added treaty) to the UNFCCC that sets legally binding, quantified targets for developed countries to limit and reduce their greenhouse gas emissions within fixed commitment periods. Greenhouse gases (Annex A): carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6). Annex I Party: a Party listed in Annex I to the Convention, that is, developed countries and economies in transition. Annex B: the list in the Protocol giving each such Party's target as a percentage of base-year emissions (for example, European Community 92, United States 93, Japan 94, Russian Federation 100, Australia 108, Iceland 110). Assigned amount: the total quantity a Party may emit in the commitment period; under Art. 3(7), its Annex B percentage of 1990 emissions "multiplied by five" (for the five years 2008–2012). In simple words: rich countries promised, in a binding treaty, to cut greenhouse gases by fixed amounts, and were allowed to meet part of their promise by buying or earning reductions made elsewhere.
keyPoints: Adopted 11 December 1997 at Kyoto; in force 16 February 2005; 28 Articles, Annexes A and B. Commitment period: first 2008–2012 (at least 5 per cent below 1990); second 2013–2020 (Doha, at least 18 per cent). Assigned amount: Annex B percentage of 1990 emissions multiplied by five (Art. 3(7)). Clean Development Mechanism: projects in developing countries; voluntary, real and additional (Art. 12(5)). Emissions trading: between Annex B Parties, "supplemental to domestic actions" (Art. 17). Only Annex I bound; India ratified 26 August 2002 with no targets.

caseLaws.facts: Commissioner of Income Tax v. My Home Power Ltd, ITTA No. 60 of 2014, (2014) 365 ITR 82 (AP) (Andhra Pradesh High Court; 19 February 2014)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A power company earned carbon credits under the Kyoto Protocol's Clean Development Mechanism
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Carbon Credit is not an offshoot of business but an offshoot of environmental concerns"; it "is not even directly linked with power generation", and "it is capital receipt and it cannot be business receipt or income". The Tribunal it upheld had called a carbon credit "an entitlement" given "under the Kyoto Protocol". Why it matters: It shows a Kyoto mechanism (Art. 12) operating in India and the courts treating carbon credits as arising from world environmental concern, not ordinary trade.
State of the Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation, ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007, case 19/00135 (Supreme Court of the Netherlands; 20 December 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An environmental group sued the Dutch State to reduce greenhouse gas emissions; the lower cou
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Articles 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights require a State "to take suitable measures if a real and immediate risk to people's lives or welfare exists"; Annex I countries "would have to reduce their emissions in 2020 by 25-40%"; "Each country is thus responsible for its own share." The State's appeal was rejected. Why it matters: The Court used the Annex I framework of the UNFCCC and Kyoto, and the 25–40 per cent figure discussed at Doha, to make a State's climate duty enforceable through human rights.
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280 (Supreme Court; 21 March 2024)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 14 and 21 "are important sources of the right to a clean environment and the right against the adverse effects of climate change"; "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change." Why it matters: It gives India's climate commitments, which began under the UNFCCC and Kyoto, a constitutional base in Art. 21.

te.inOneMinute: ఇది ఏమిటి: వాతావరణ మార్పుపై ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి చట్రపు ఒడంబడికకు (UNFCCC) క్యోటో ప్రోటోకాల్ , పార్టీల సమావేశం మూడో సమావేశంలో (COP3) 11 డిసెంబర్ 1997 న జపాన్‌లోని క్యోటోలో ఆమోదించిన కట్టుబడి ఉండే ఒప్పందం. ఇది 16 ఫిబ్రవరి 2005 న అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది. ఎందుకు: UNFCCC (1992) అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలను విధానాలు చేపట్టి నివేదించమని మాత్రమే అడుగుతుంది. ఆ దేశాలకు హరితగృహ వాయువులను పరిమితం చేసి తగ్గించడానికి కట్టుబడి ఉండే లక్ష్యాలు ఇవ్వడం ద్వారా ప్రోటోకాల్ ఒడంబడికను "operationalizes" (అర్థం: ఆచరణలోకి తెస్తుంది). ఎవరు కట్టుబడి ఉంటారు: అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు, పరివర్తన దశలోని ఆర్థిక వ్యవస్థలు ( అనుబంధం I పక్షాలు) మాత్రమే, వాటి వ్యక్తిగత లక్ష్యాలు అనుబంధం B లో ఉన్నాయి. ఉమ్మడి కానీ విభిన్న బాధ్యతల ప్రకారం, భారతదేశం వంటి అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న దేశాలకు కొత్త బాధ్యతలు లేవు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 10). ప్రధాన లక్ష్యం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 3(1)): ఆరు వాయువుల (అనుబంధం A) అనుబంధం I ఉద్గారాలు "by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels in the commitment period 2008 to 2012" (అర్థం: 2008 నుండి 2012 వరకు నిబద్ధత కాలంలో 1990 స్థాయిల కంటే కనీసం 5 శాతం తక్కువకు) తగ్గాలి. మూడు మార్కెట్ యంత్రాంగాలు: ఉమ్మడి అమలు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 6) – అనుబంధం I పక్షాల మధ్య; స్వచ్ఛ అభివృద్ధి యంత్రాంగం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 12) – అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న దేశాలలో ప్రాజెక్టులు; ఉద్గారాల వ్యాపారం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 17) – అనుబంధం B పక్షాల మధ్య. రెండో కాలం: 2013–2020 కోసం దోహా సవరణ (8 డిసెంబర్ 2012), 1990 కంటే కనీసం 18 శాతం తక్కువ; 31 డిసెంబర్ 2020 న అమల్లోకి. భారతదేశం: 26 ఆగస్టు 2002 న ఆమోదించింది; అనేక CDM ప్రాజెక్టులకు ఆతిథ్యం ఇచ్చింది. భారతీయ పన్ను చట్టం CDM ప్రాజెక్టుల నుండి వచ్చే కార్బన్ క్రెడిట్లను మూలధన రసీదులుగా పరిగణిస్తుంది ( CIT v. My Home Power Ltd , ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ హైకోర్టు, 2014).
te.meaning: క్యోటో ప్రోటోకాల్: అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు నిర్ణీత నిబద్ధత కాలాల్లో తమ హరితగృహ వాయువు ఉద్గారాలను పరిమితం చేసి తగ్గించడానికి చట్టబద్ధంగా కట్టుబడి ఉండే, పరిమాణాత్మక లక్ష్యాలను నిర్ణయించే UNFCCC కి ప్రోటోకాల్ (అదనపు ఒప్పందం). హరితగృహ వాయువులు (అనుబంధం A): కార్బన్ డయాక్సైడ్ (CO2), మీథేన్ (CH4), నైట్రస్ ఆక్సైడ్ (N2O), హైడ్రోఫ్లోరోకార్బన్లు (HFCs), పెర్‌ఫ్లోరోకార్బన్లు (PFCs), సల్ఫర్ హెక్సాఫ్లోరైడ్ (SF6). అనుబంధం I పక్షం: ఒడంబడిక అనుబంధం I లో ఉన్న పక్షం, అంటే అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు, పరివర్తన దశలోని ఆర్థిక వ్యవస్థలు. అనుబంధం B: అలాంటి ప్రతి పక్షం లక్ష్యాన్ని మూల సంవత్సర ఉద్గారాల శాతంగా ఇచ్చే ప్రోటోకాల్‌లోని జాబితా (ఉదాహరణకు, యూరోపియన్ కమ్యూనిటీ 92, అమెరికా 93, జపాన్ 94, రష్యా 100, ఆస్ట్రేలియా 108, ఐస్‌లాండ్ 110). కేటాయించిన పరిమాణం: నిబద్ధత కాలంలో ఒక పక్షం విడుదల చేయగల మొత్తం పరిమాణం; అనుచ్ఛేదం 3(7) కింద, 1990 ఉద్గారాలలో దాని అనుబంధం B శాతం "multiplied by five" (అర్థం: ఐదుతో గుణించి) (2008–2012 ఐదు సంవత్సరాలకు). సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే: సంపన్న దేశాలు, కట్టుబడి ఉండే ఒప్పందంలో, హరితగృహ వాయువులను నిర్ణీత మొత్తాల్లో తగ్గిస్తామని వాగ్దానం చేశాయి, ఇతర చోట్ల చేసిన తగ్గింపులను కొనడం లేదా సంపాదించడం ద్వారా తమ వాగ్దానంలో కొంత భాగాన్ని నెరవేర్చుకోవడానికి వాటికి అనుమతి ఇచ్చారు.
keyPoints: 11 డిసెంబర్ 1997 న క్యోటోలో ఆమోదం; 16 ఫిబ్రవరి 2005 న అమలు; 28 అనుచ్ఛేదాలు, అనుబంధాలు A, B. నిబద్ధత కాలం: మొదటిది 2008–2012 (1990 కంటే కనీసం 5 శాతం తక్కువ); రెండోది 2013–2020 (దోహా, కనీసం 18 శాతం). కేటాయించిన పరిమాణం: 1990 ఉద్గారాలలో అనుబంధం B శాతం ఐదుతో గుణించి (అనుచ్ఛేదం 3(7)). స్వచ్ఛ అభివృద్ధి యంత్రాంగం: అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న దేశాల్లో ప్రాజెక్టులు; స్వచ్ఛందం, వాస్తవం, అదనపువి (అనుచ్ఛేదం 12(5)). ఉద్గారాల వ్యాపారం: అనుబంధం B పక్షాల మధ్య, "supplemental to domestic actions" (అర్థం: దేశీయ చర్యలకు అనుబంధంగా) (అనుచ్ఛేదం 17). అనుబంధం I మాత్రమే కట్టుబడి; భారతదేశం లక్ష్యాలు లేకుండా 26 ఆగస్టు 2002 న ఆమోదించింది.

selfTest.q: క్యోటో ప్రోటోకాల్ ఎప్పుడు ఆమోదించబడింది, ఎప్పుడు అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: మొదటి నిబద్ధత కాలం ప్రధాన లక్ష్యం ఏమిటి? భారతదేశానికి ఉద్గార లక్ష్యాలు ఎందుకు లేవు? మూడు క్యోటో యంత్రాంగాలను పేర్కొనండి. అనుచ్ఛేదం 12(5) కింద ధృవీకరించిన ఉద్గార తగ్గింపులకు మూడు షరతులను తెలపండి. దోహా సవరణ అంటే ఏమిటి? My Home Power లో ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్ హైకోర్టు ఏమి నిర్ణయించింది?

అంశం ఉమ్మడి అమలు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 6) స్వచ్ఛ అభివృద్ధి యంత్రాంగం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 12) ఉద్గారాల వ్యాపారం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 17)
ఎవరి మధ్య రెండు అనుబంధం I పక్షాలు ఒక అనుబంధం I పక్షం, ఒక అనుబంధం I కాని (అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న) పక్షం అనుబంధం B పక్షాలు
ఏమి బదిలీ అవుతుంది ప్రాజెక్టుల నుండి ఉద్గార తగ్గింపు యూనిట్లు ప్రాజెక్టుల నుండి ధృవీకరించిన ఉద్గార తగ్గింపులు కేటాయించిన పరిమాణాల భాగాలు, ఇతర యూనిట్లు

ముఖ్య షరతులు "supplemental to domestic actions" (అర్థం: దేశీయ చర్యలకు అనుబంధం) స్వచ్ఛంద ఆమోదం; వాస్తవ, కొలవదగిన, దీర్ఘకాలిక ప్రయోజనాలు; అదనపుత్వం "supplemental to domestic actions" (అర్థం: దేశీయ చర్యలకు అనుబంధం)
అనుకూలన వాటా రెండో కాలం నుండి 2 శాతం (దోహా) అనుకూలనానికి ఆదాయ వాటా (అనుచ్ఛేదం 12(8)) రెండో కాలం నుండి 2 శాతం (దోహా)

hi.inOneMinute: What it is: the Kyoto Protocol to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change , a binding treaty adopted at Kyoto, Japan, on 11 December 1997 at the third session of the Conference of the Parties (COP3). It came into force on 16 February 2005 . Why: the UNFCCC (1992) only asks developed countries to adopt policies and report. The Protocol "operationalizes" the Convention by giving those countries binding targets to limit and reduce greenhouse gases. Who is bound: only developed countries and economies in transition ( Annex I Parties), with individual targets in Annex B . Developing countries such as India get no new commitments (Art. 10), following common but differentiated responsibilities . Main target (Art. 3(1)): Annex I emissions of six gases (Annex A) to fall "by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels in the commitment period 2008 to 2012". Three market mechanisms: Joint implementation (Art. 6) – between Annex I Parties; Clean Development Mechanism (Art. 12) – projects in developing countries; Emissions trading (Art. 17) – between Annex B Parties. Second period: the Doha Amendment (8 December 2012) for 2013–2020 , at least 18 per cent below 1990; in force on 31 December 2020. India: ratified on 26 August 2002; hosted many CDM projects. Indian tax law treats carbon credits from CDM projects as capital receipts ( CIT v. My Home Power Ltd , Andhra Pradesh High Court, 2014).
legalProvision: Kyoto Protocol, 1997 (28 Articles, Annexes A and B): Art. 1 – definitions ("Convention" means the UNFCCC adopted in New York on 9 May 1992; "Party included in Annex I"). Art. 2 – policies and measures by Annex I Parties "in order to promote sustainable development". Art. 3 – quantified emission limitation and reduction commitments; 3(1) "by at least 5 per cent below 1990 levels in the commitment period 2008 to 2012"; 3(2) "demonstrable progress" by 2005; 3(3) forests; 3(7) assigned amounts; 3(9) later periods; 3(13) carry-over (banking). Art. 4 – joint fulfilment by a group of Parties. Art. 5 – national systems for estimating emissions; Arts. 7–8 – reporting and expert review. Art. 6 – transfer and acquisition of emission reduction units (joint implementation). Art. 10 – all Parties, "taking into account their common but differentiated responsibilities", "without introducing any new commitments for Parties not included in Annex I". Art. 12 – "A clean development mechanism is hereby defined." Art. 13 – the Conference of the Parties serves as the meeting of the Parties to the Protocol. Art. 17 – "The Parties included in Annex B may participate in emissions trading". Art. 18 – non-compliance procedures. Art. 24 – open for signature in New York "from 16 March 1998 to 15 March 1999". Art. 25(1) – entry into force on the ninetieth day after at least 55 Parties to the Convention, including Annex I Parties accounting for at least 55 per cent of the total carbon dioxide emissions for 1990 of Annex I Parties, have joined. Art. 26 – "No reservations may be made to this Protocol." Annex A – six greenhouse gases and the source sectors; Annex B – the target of each Party as a percentage of its base-year emissions. Doha Amendment, 2012 – second commitment period, 2013–2020. Constitution of India: Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
hi.meaning: Kyoto Protocol: a protocol (an added treaty) to the UNFCCC that sets legally binding, quantified targets for developed countries to limit and reduce their greenhouse gas emissions within fixed commitment periods. Greenhouse gases (Annex A): carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6). Annex I Party: a Party listed in Annex I to the Convention, that is, developed countries and economies in transition. Annex B: the list in the Protocol giving each such Party's target as a percentage of base-year emissions (for example, European Community 92, United States 93, Japan 94, Russian Federation 100, Australia 108, Iceland 110). Assigned amount: the total quantity a Party may emit in the commitment period; under Art. 3(7), its Annex B percentage of 1990 emissions "multiplied by five" (for the five years 2008–2012). In simple words: rich countries promised, in a binding treaty, to cut greenhouse gases by fixed amounts, and were allowed to meet part of their promise by buying or earning reductions made elsewhere.
keyPoints: Adopted 11 December 1997 at Kyoto; in force 16 February 2005; 28 Articles, Annexes A and B. Commitment period: first 2008–2012 (at least 5 per cent below 1990); second 2013–2020 (Doha, at least 18 per cent). Assigned amount: Annex B percentage of 1990 emissions multiplied by five (Art. 3(7)). Clean Development Mechanism: projects in developing countries; voluntary, real and additional (Art. 12(5)). Emissions trading: between Annex B Parties, "supplemental to domestic actions" (Art. 17). Only Annex I bound; India ratified 26 August 2002 with no targets.

caseLaws.facts: Commissioner of Income Tax v. My Home Power Ltd, ITTA No. 60 of 2014, (2014) 365 ITR 82 (AP) (Andhra Pradesh High Court; 19 February 2014)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A power company earned carbon credits under the Kyoto Protocol's Clean Development Mechanism
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "Carbon Credit is not an offshoot of business but an offshoot of environmental concerns"; it "is not even directly linked with power generation", and "it is capital receipt and it cannot be business receipt or income". The Tribunal it upheld had called a carbon credit "an entitlement" given "under the Kyoto Protocol". Why it matters: It shows a Kyoto mechanism (Art. 12) operating in India and the courts treating carbon credits as arising from world environmental concern, not ordinary trade.
State of the Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation, ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007, case 19/00135 (Supreme Court of the Netherlands; 20 December 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An environmental group sued the Dutch State to reduce greenhouse gas emissions; the lower cou
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Articles 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights require a State "to take suitable measures if a real and immediate risk to people's lives or welfare exists"; Annex I countries "would have to reduce their emissions in 2020 by 25-40%"; "Each country is thus responsible for its own share." The State's appeal was rejected. Why it matters: The Court used the Annex I framework of the UNFCCC and Kyoto, and the 25–40 per cent figure discussed at Doha, to make a State's climate duty enforceable through human rights.
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280 (Supreme Court; 21 March 2024)

caseLaws.name: Facts: In a case on protecting the Great Indian Bustard from power lines, the Union asked the Court
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 14 and 21 "are important sources of the right to a clean environment and the right against the adverse effects of climate change"; "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change." Why it matters: It gives India's climate commitments, which began under the UNFCCC and Kyoto, a constitutional base in Art. 21.

environmental-law-u5-t11.subtitle: The Convention on Biological Diversity: three objectives, sovereign rights over resources and benefit sharing

en.inOneMinute: Earth Summit: the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) , held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, from 3 to 14 June 1992 , on the 20th anniversary of the Stockholm Conference of 1972. Leaders, diplomats, scientists, the media and NGOs came "from 179 countries". What the Earth Summit produced: Agenda 21 (a voluntary programme of action); the Rio Declaration with 27 principles; the Forest Principles (a non-legally binding statement on forests); two treaties opened for signature: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) ; it also led to the Commission on Sustainable Development . The CBD is a binding treaty. It was opened for signature at Rio on 5 June 1992 and came into force on 29 December 1993 . It has 42 Articles and 2 Annexes , and no reservations are allowed (Art. 37). Three objectives (Art. 1): conservation of biological diversity; sustainable use of its components; fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of the use of genetic resources. Big ideas: conservation of biodiversity is "a common concern of humankind" ( preamble ); States have sovereign rights over their biological resources (preamble, Art. 3, Art. 15); access to genetic resources needs the prior informed consent of the providing State and mutually agreed terms (Art. 15). Protocols: the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) on living modified organisms, and the Nagoya Protocol (2010) on access and benefit sharing. India: the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 was made to give effect to the CBD. Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India (2018) applied it to Indian companies too.
legalProvision: Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992: Preamble – "Conscious of the intrinsic value of biological diversity"; "Affirming that the conservation of biological diversity is a common concern of humankind"; "Reaffirming that States have sovereign rights over their own biological resources". Art. 1 (Objectives) – conservation, sustainable use of components, and "the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilization of genetic resources", including by appropriate access, transfer of technology and funding. Art. 2 (Use of Terms) – definitions of biological diversity, biological resources, in-situ and ex-situ conservation, sustainable use, genetic resources, country of origin, biotechnology. Art. 3 (Principle) – States have "the sovereign right to exploit their own resources pursuant to their own environmental policies", and a responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not cause damage to the environment of other States or of areas beyond national jurisdiction. Arts. 6–14 – national measures: strategies (Art. 6), identification and monitoring (Art. 7), in-situ conservation (Art. 8), ex-situ conservation (Art. 9), sustainable use (Art. 10), environmental impact assessment (Art. 14). Art. 15 – access to genetic resources. Art. 16 – access to and transfer of technology. Art. 19(3) – the Parties to consider the need for a protocol on biosafety. Arts. 20–21 – financial resources and financial mechanism. Arts. 23–25 – Conference of the Parties, Secretariat, scientific advisory body. Art. 27 – settlement of disputes. Art. 33 – signature at Rio "from 5 June 1992 until 14 June 1992" and at New York "from 15 June 1992 to 4 June 1993". Art. 36(1) – entry into force on the ninetieth day after the thirtieth instrument of ratification. Art. 37 – "No reservations may be made to this Convention." India: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (No. 18 of 2003), preamble: India is a party to the CBD signed at Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992; ss. 3, 7, 21 and the three-tier authorities. Constitution of India: Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g) and 253 (Parliament's power to make laws to implement treaties).
en.meaning: Earth Summit: the popular name of UNCED, the UN conference on environment and development held at Rio de Janeiro, 3–14 June 1992. Convention on Biological Diversity: the treaty opened for signature at the Earth Summit that sets the world's legal framework for conserving biodiversity , using it sustainably and sharing its benefits fairly. Key definitions in Art. 2: Biological diversity – "the variability among living organisms from all sources", including the ecological complexes of which they are part; it includes diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems . Biological resources – "includes genetic resources, organisms or parts thereof, populations, or any other biotic component of ecosystems" with actual or potential use or value for humanity. Genetic resources – "genetic material of actual or potential value." In-situ conservation – "the conservation of ecosystems and natural habitats and the maintenance and recovery of viable populations" of species in their natural surroundings. Ex-situ conservation – "the conservation of components of biological diversity outside their natural habitats." Sustainable use – use "in a way and at a rate that does not lead to the long-term decline of biological diversity". Country of origin of genetic resources – "the country which possesses those genetic resources in in-situ conditions." Biotechnology – "any technological application that uses biological systems, living organisms, or derivatives thereof," to make or modify products or processes for specific use. In simple words: the CBD says the variety of life is valuable, each country controls its own living resources, every country must protect them, use them without using them up, and share the profits fairly with the country and communities that provided them.
keyPoints: Earth Summit: UNCED, Rio, 3–14 June 1992; CBD opened for signature on 5 June 1992; in force 29 December 1993. Three objectives: conservation, sustainable use, fair and equitable benefit sharing (Art. 1). In-situ conservation is the "fundamental requirement"; ex-situ only complements it (Art. 9). Prior informed consent of the providing State is needed for access (Art. 15(5)). Mutually agreed terms govern access and benefit sharing (Art. 15(4), 15(7)). Access and benefit sharing: detailed in the Nagoya Protocol; in India, the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.

caseLaws.facts: 7 read with s. 23). The petition was dismissed. Why it matters: The Court read the Indian Act in the light of the CBD's third objective and the Nagoya Protocol, so that benefit sharing reaches local communities whoever the user is.

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Asiatic lion lives only in the Gir forest of Gujarat
caseLaws.facts: The question was whether some lions should be moved to Kuno in Madhya Pradesh as a second home; Gujarat objected. Principle: "our approach should be eco-centric and not anthropocentric"; the Court applied a "species best interest standard", referred to international instruments including the CBD, and directed the Ministry "to take urgent steps for re-introduction of Asiatic lion from Gir forests to Kuno". Why it matters: It is the kind of in-situ conservation the CBD treats as fundamental (Art. 8): protecting a threatened species by securing viable populations in natural habitats.
DCM Shriram Ltd v. National Biodiversity Authority, Appeal Nos. 61 to 63 of 2021 (SZ) (National Green Tribunal, Southern Zone; Pushpa Sathyanarayana JM and Dr. Satyagopal Korlapati EM; 30 May 2023)

caseLaws.name: Facts: A listed seed company applied for access to watermelon, cotton and bitter gourd for research;
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Tribunal noted that "the international legal arrangement under the Convention of Biological Diversity (CBD) gave the frame work at the global level", and held that a seed company doing "Conventional breeding" "would be slotted under the concept of 'Research' which also requires approval under Section 3(1)". Why it matters: It shows the CBD's access and benefit sharing system (Art. 15) being applied in India through NBA approvals.

te.inOneMinute: భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు (Earth Summit): పర్యావరణం, అభివృద్ధిపై ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి సదస్సు (UNCED) , 1972 స్టాక్‌హోమ్ సదస్సు 20వ వార్షికోత్సవం సందర్భంగా బ్రెజిల్‌లోని రియో డి జనీరోలో 3 నుండి 14 జూన్ 1992 వరకు జరిగింది. నాయకులు, దౌత్యవేత్తలు, శాస్త్రవేత్తలు, మీడియా, స్వచ్ఛంద సంస్థలు "from 179 countries" (అర్థం: 179 దేశాల నుండి) వచ్చారు. భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు ఫలితాలు: ఎజెండా 21 (Agenda 21) (స్వచ్ఛంద కార్యాచరణ కార్యక్రమం); 27 సూత్రాలతో రియో ప్రకటన ; అటవీ సూత్రాలు (Forest Principles) (అడవులపై చట్టబద్ధంగా కట్టుబడి ఉండని ప్రకటన); సంతకాలకు తెరిచిన రెండు ఒప్పందాలు: వాతావరణ మార్పుపై ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి చట్రపు ఒడంబడిక (UNFCCC) , జీవ వైవిధ్య ఒడంబడిక (CBD) ; ఇది సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి కమిషన్ ఏర్పాటుకు కూడా దారితీసింది. CBD కట్టుబడి ఉండే ఒప్పందం. ఇది 5 జూన్ 1992 న రియోలో సంతకాలకు తెరవబడింది, 29 డిసెంబర్ 1993 న అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది. దీనిలో 42 అనుచ్ఛేదాలు, 2 అనుబంధాలు ఉన్నాయి, రిజర్వేషన్లు అనుమతించబడవు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 37). మూడు లక్ష్యాలు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 1): జీవ వైవిధ్య సంరక్షణ; దాని భాగాల సుస్థిర వినియోగం; జన్యు వనరుల వినియోగం వల్ల వచ్చే ప్రయోజనాల న్యాయమైన, సమానమైన పంపిణీ . ముఖ్య భావనలు: జీవ వైవిధ్య సంరక్షణ "a common concern of humankind" (అర్థం: మానవాళి ఉమ్మడి ఆందోళన) (ఉపోద్ఘాతం); తమ జీవ వనరులపై దేశాలకు సార్వభౌమ హక్కులు ఉన్నాయి (ఉపోద్ఘాతం, అనుచ్ఛేదం 3, అనుచ్ఛేదం 15); జన్యు వనరుల అందుబాటుకు అందించే దేశం ముందస్తు సమాచార సమ్మతి , పరస్పరం అంగీకరించిన నిబంధనలు అవసరం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 15). ప్రోటోకాల్‌లు: జన్యుమార్పిడి జీవులపై కార్టజీనా జీవ భద్రత ప్రోటోకాల్ (2000), అందుబాటు, ప్రయోజన పంపిణీపై నగోయా ప్రోటోకాల్ (2010). భారతదేశం: CBD ను అమలు చేయడానికి జీవ వైవిధ్య చట్టం, 2002 చేయబడింది. Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India (2018) దానిని భారతీయ కంపెనీలకు కూడా వర్తింపజేసింది.
te.meaning: భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు: 3–14 జూన్ 1992 న రియో డి జనీరోలో జరిగిన పర్యావరణం , అభివృద్ధిపై ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి సదస్సు (UNCED) యొక్క ప్రసిద్ధ పేరు. జీవ వైవిధ్య ఒడంబడిక: భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సులో సంతకాలకు తెరిచిన ఒప్పందం; జీవ వైవిధ్యాన్ని కాపాడడానికి, సుస్థిరంగా వాడడానికి, దాని ప్రయోజనాలను న్యాయంగా పంచుకోవడానికి ఇది ప్రపంచ చట్టపరమైన చట్రాన్ని ఏర్పాటు చేస్తుంది. అనుచ్ఛేదం 2 లోని ముఖ్య నిర్వచనాలు: జీవ వైవిధ్యం – "the variability among living organisms from all sources" (అర్థం: అన్ని మూలాల నుండి వచ్చిన జీవుల మధ్య వైవిధ్యం), అవి భాగమైన పర్యావరణ సముదాయాలతో సహా; జాతుల లోపల, జాతుల మధ్య, పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థల వైవిధ్యాన్ని ఇది కలిగి ఉంటుంది. జీవ వనరులు – "includes genetic resources, organisms or parts thereof, populations, or any other biotic component of ecosystems" (అర్థం: జన్యు వనరులు, జీవులు లేదా వాటి భాగాలు, జనాభాలు, లేదా పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థల ఏదైనా ఇతర జీవ భాగం), మానవాళికి వాస్తవ లేదా సంభావ్య ఉపయోగం లేదా విలువ ఉన్నవి. జన్యు వనరులు – "genetic material of actual or potential value." (అర్థం: వాస్తవ లేదా సంభావ్య విలువ ఉన్న జన్యు పదార్థం.) సహజ స్థల సంరక్షణ (in-situ) – "the conservation of ecosystems and natural habitats and the maintenance and recovery of viable populations" (అర్థం: పర్యావరణ వ్యవస్థలు, సహజ ఆవాసాల సంరక్షణ , జీవించగల జనాభాల నిర్వహణ, పునరుద్ధరణ), జాతుల సహజ పరిసరాలలో. సహజ స్థలం వెలుపల సంరక్షణ (ex-situ) – "the conservation of components of biological diversity outside their natural habitats." (అర్థం: జీవ వైవిధ్య భాగాలను వాటి సహజ ఆవాసాల వెలుపల సంరక్షించడం.) సుస్థిర వినియోగం – "in a way and at a rate that does not lead to the long-term decline of biological diversity" (అర్థం: జీవ వైవిధ్యం దీర్ఘకాలంలో తగ్గిపోకుండా ఉండే విధంగా, వేగంతో) వాడడం. జన్యు వనరుల మూల దేశం – "the country which possesses those genetic resources in in-situ conditions." (అర్థం: ఆ జన్యు వనరులను సహజ స్థల పరిస్థితులలో కలిగి ఉన్న దేశం.) జీవ సాంకేతికత – "any technological application that uses biological systems, living organisms, or derivatives thereof," (అర్థం: జీవ వ్యవస్థలు, జీవులు లేదా వాటి ఉత్పన్నాలను ఉపయోగించే ఏదైనా సాంకేతిక అనువర్తనం) నిర్దిష్ట ఉపయోగం కోసం ఉత్పత్తులు లేదా ప్రక్రియలను తయారు చేయడానికి లేదా మార్చడానికి. సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే: జీవుల వైవిధ్యం విలువైనది, ప్రతి దేశం తన జీవ వనరులను నియంత్రిస్తుంది, ప్రతి దేశం వాటిని కాపాడాలి, అవి అయిపోకుండా వాడాలి, వాటిని అందించిన దేశం, సమాజాలతో లాభాలను న్యాయంగా పంచుకోవాలి అని CBD చెబుతుంది.
keyPoints: భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు: UNCED, రియో, 3–14 జూన్ 1992; CBD 5 జూన్ 1992 న సంతకాలకు తెరవబడింది; 29 డిసెంబర్ 1993 న అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది. మూడు లక్ష్యాలు: సంరక్షణ, సుస్థిర వినియోగం, న్యాయమైన, సమానమైన ప్రయోజన పంపిణీ (అనుచ్ఛేదం 1). సహజ స్థల సంరక్షణ "fundamental requirement" (అర్థం: మౌలిక అవసరం); సహజ స్థలం వెలుపల సంరక్షణ దానికి పూరకం మాత్రమే (అనుచ్ఛేదం 9). అందుబాటుకు అందించే దేశం ముందస్తు సమాచార సమ్మతి అవసరం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 15(5)). పరస్పరం అంగీకరించిన నిబంధనలు అందుబాటు, ప్రయోజన పంపిణీని నియంత్రిస్తాయి (అనుచ్ఛేదం 15(4), 15(7)). అందుబాటు, ప్రయోజన పంపిణీ: నగోయా ప్రోటోకాల్‌లో వివరంగా ఉంది; భారతదేశంలో, జీవ వైవిధ్య చట్టం, 2002.

selfTest.q: భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు అంటే ఏమిటి, అది ఏమి సాధించింది?
selfTest.a: CBD ఎప్పుడు సంతకాలకు తెరవబడింది, ఎప్పుడు అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది? CBD మూడు లక్ష్యాలను తెలపండి. జన్యు వనరుల అందుబాటు గురించి అనుచ్ఛేదం 15 ఏమి చెబుతుంది? సహజ స్థల, సహజ స్థలం వెలుపల సంరక్షణ మధ్య తేడా చెప్పండి. CBD కింద రెండు ప్రోటోకాల్‌లు, వాటి విషయాలు చెప్పండి. Divya Pharmacy CBD, నగోయా ప్రోటోకాల్‌ను ఎలా ఉపయోగించింది?

hi.inOneMinute: Earth Summit: the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) , held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, from 3 to 14 June 1992 , on the 20th anniversary of the Stockholm Conference of 1972. Leaders, diplomats, scientists, the media and NGOs came "from 179 countries". What the Earth Summit produced: Agenda 21 (a voluntary programme of action); the Rio Declaration with 27 principles; the Forest Principles (a non-legally binding statement on forests); two treaties opened for signature: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) ; it also led to the Commission on Sustainable Development . The CBD is a binding treaty. It was opened for signature at Rio on 5 June 1992 and came into force on 29 December 1993 . It has 42 Articles and 2 Annexes , and no reservations are allowed (Art. 37). Three objectives (Art. 1): conservation of biological diversity; sustainable use of its components; fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of the use of genetic resources. Big ideas: conservation of biodiversity is "a common concern of humankind" ( preamble ); States have sovereign rights over their biological resources (preamble, Art. 3, Art. 15); access to genetic resources needs the prior informed consent of the providing State and mutually agreed terms (Art. 15). Protocols: the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) on living modified organisms, and the Nagoya Protocol (2010) on access and benefit sharing. India: the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 was made to give effect to the CBD. Divya Pharmacy v. Union of India (2018) applied it to Indian companies too.
legalProvision: Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992: Preamble – "Conscious of the intrinsic value of biological diversity"; "Affirming that the conservation of biological diversity is a common concern of humankind"; "Reaffirming that States have sovereign rights over their own biological resources". Art. 1 (Objectives) – conservation, sustainable use of components, and "the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilization of genetic resources", including by appropriate access, transfer of technology and funding. Art. 2 (Use of Terms) – definitions of biological diversity, biological resources, in-situ and ex-situ conservation, sustainable use, genetic resources, country of origin, biotechnology. Art. 3 (Principle) – States have "the sovereign right to exploit their own resources pursuant to their own environmental policies", and a responsibility to ensure that activities within their jurisdiction or control do not cause damage to the environment of other States or of areas beyond national jurisdiction. Arts. 6–14 – national measures: strategies (Art. 6), identification and monitoring (Art. 7), in-situ conservation (Art. 8), ex-situ conservation (Art. 9), sustainable use (Art. 10), environmental impact assessment (Art. 14). Art. 15 – access to genetic resources. Art. 16 – access to and transfer of technology. Art. 19(3) – the Parties to consider the need for a protocol on biosafety. Arts. 20–21 – financial resources and financial mechanism. Arts. 23–25 – Conference of the Parties, Secretariat, scientific advisory body. Art. 27 – settlement of disputes. Art. 33 – signature at Rio "from 5 June 1992 until 14 June 1992" and at New York "from 15 June 1992 to 4 June 1993". Art. 36(1) – entry into force on the ninetieth day after the thirtieth instrument of ratification. Art. 37 – "No reservations may be made to this Convention." India: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (No. 18 of 2003), preamble: India is a party to the CBD signed at Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992; ss. 3, 7, 21 and the three-tier authorities. Constitution of India: Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g) and 253 (Parliament's power to make laws to implement treaties).
hi.meaning: Earth Summit: the popular name of UNCED, the UN conference on environment and development held at Rio de Janeiro, 3–14 June 1992. Convention on Biological Diversity: the treaty opened for signature at the Earth Summit that sets the world's legal framework for conserving biodiversity , using it sustainably and sharing its benefits fairly. Key definitions in Art. 2: Biological diversity – "the variability among living organisms from all sources", including the ecological complexes of which they are part; it includes diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems . Biological resources – "includes genetic resources, organisms or parts thereof, populations, or any other biotic component of ecosystems" with actual or potential use or value for humanity. Genetic resources – "genetic material of actual or potential value." In-situ conservation – "the conservation of ecosystems and natural habitats and the maintenance and recovery of viable populations" of species in their natural surroundings. Ex-situ conservation – "the conservation of components of biological diversity outside their natural habitats." Sustainable use – use "in a way and at a rate that does not lead to the long-term decline of biological diversity". Country of origin of genetic resources – "the country which possesses those genetic resources in in-situ conditions." Biotechnology – "any technological application that uses biological systems, living organisms, or derivatives thereof," to make or modify products or processes for specific use. In simple words: the CBD says the variety of life is valuable, each country controls its own living resources, every country must protect them, use them without using them up, and share the profits fairly with the country and communities that provided them.
keyPoints: Earth Summit: UNCED, Rio, 3–14 June 1992; CBD opened for signature on 5 June 1992; in force 29 December 1993. Three objectives: conservation, sustainable use, fair and equitable benefit sharing (Art. 1). In-situ conservation is the "fundamental requirement"; ex-situ only complements it (Art. 9). Prior informed consent of the providing State is needed for access (Art. 15(5)). Mutually agreed terms govern access and benefit sharing (Art. 15(4), 15(7)). Access and benefit sharing: detailed in the Nagoya Protocol; in India, the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.

caseLaws.facts: The question was whether some lions should be moved to Kuno in Madhya Pradesh as a second home; Gujarat objected. en.inOneMinute: What it is: the Johannesburg Declaration on Sustainable Development , adopted on 4 September 2002 at the 17th plenary meeting of the World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) in Johannesburg, South Africa. When: the Summit ran from 26 August to 4 September 2002; the leaders "assembled at the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg, South Africa, from 2 to 4 September 2002" (para 1). It came ten years after Rio (1992) and thirty years after Stockholm (1972) (para 8). Form: a political declaration of 37 paragraphs in six parts, adopted with the Plan of Implementation of the Summit (para 6). It is soft law , not a treaty. Core idea (para 5): to advance "the interdependent and mutually reinforcing pillars of sustainable development — economic development, social development and environmental protection" at all levels. Three overarching objectives (para 11): poverty eradication , changing consumption and production patterns, and protecting and managing the natural resource base. Main messages: "The deep fault line that divides human society between the rich and the poor" (para 12); "The global environment continues to suffer." (para 13); the private sector "has a duty to contribute to the evolution of equitable and sustainable communities and societies" (para 27); corporate accountability (para 29); "more effective, democratic and accountable international and multilateral institutions" (para 31). India: the Declaration's ideas match Indian law on sustainable development ( Vellore , 1996; Narmada Bachao Andolan , 2000) and the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, s. 20.
legalProvision: Johannesburg Declaration on Sustainable Development, 2002 – adopted at the 17th plenary meeting of the WSSD on 4 September 2002; 37 paragraphs in six parts: "From our origins to the future" (paras 1–7); "From Stockholm to Rio de Janeiro to Johannesburg" (paras 8–10); "The challenges we face" (paras 11–15); "Our commitment to sustainable development" (paras 16–30); "Multilateralism is the future" (paras 31–33); "Making it happen!" (paras 34–37). Plan of Implementation of the World Summit on Sustainable Development – adopted with the Declaration (paras 6, 36). Report of the Summit: A/CONF.199/20. Earlier instruments it builds on: Stockholm Declaration (1972), Rio Declaration and Agenda 21 (1992). India: Constitution Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, s. 20 (principles of sustainable development, precaution and polluter pays).
en.meaning: World Summit on Sustainable Development: the UN summit held at Johannesburg, South Africa, from 26 August to 4 September 2002, ten years after the Rio Earth Summit, to review progress and commit to action on sustainable development . Johannesburg Declaration: the political statement of the leaders at that Summit, in which they "reaffirm our commitment to sustainable development" (para 1). Sustainable development: development built on three interdependent and mutually reinforcing pillars: economic development, social development and environmental protection (para 5). Plan of Implementation: the action document adopted at the same Summit, which the Declaration commits States to carry out (para 36). In simple words: in Johannesburg, world leaders admitted that the promises of Rio had not been fully kept, said that poverty and the gap between rich and poor must be tackled along with the environment , and promised to act together.
keyPoints: Adopted 4 September 2002 at the WSSD, Johannesburg; 37 paragraphs; ten years after Rio. Pillars of sustainable development: economic development, social development, environmental protection (para 5). Plan of Implementation: the action document adopted with the Declaration (paras 6, 36). Corporate accountability: "within a transparent and stable regulatory environment" (para 29). Multilateralism: "more effective, democratic and accountable international and multilateral institutions" (para 31). Soft law; Indian law gives effect to the same ideas ( Vellore , NGT Act s. 20).

Why it matters: It shows sustainable development, the idea the Johannesburg Declaration reaffirmed, being applied by a specialised Indian tribunal created by statute.

te.inOneMinute: ఇది ఏమిటి: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిపై జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్ ప్రకటన , దక్షిణాఫ్రికాలోని జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్‌లో జరిగిన సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిపై ప్రపంచ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు (WSSD) 17వ ప్లీనరీ సమావేశంలో 4 సెప్టెంబర్ 2002 న ఆమోదించబడింది. ఎప్పుడు: సదస్సు 26 ఆగస్టు నుండి 4 సెప్టెంబర్ 2002 వరకు జరిగింది; నాయకులు "assembled at the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg, South Africa, from 2 to 4 September 2002" (అర్థం: 2 నుండి 4 సెప్టెంబర్ 2002 వరకు దక్షిణాఫ్రికాలోని జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్‌లో సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిపై ప్రపంచ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సులో సమావేశమయ్యారు) (పేరా 1). ఇది రియో (1992) తర్వాత పదేళ్లకు , స్టాక్‌హోమ్ (1972) తర్వాత ముప్పై ఏళ్లకు వచ్చింది (పేరా 8). రూపం: ఆరు భాగాలలో 37 పేరాల రాజకీయ ప్రకటన, సదస్సు అమలు ప్రణాళికతో పాటు ఆమోదించబడింది (పేరా 6). ఇది సాఫ్ట్ లా , ఒప్పందం కాదు. ముఖ్య భావన (పేరా 5): అన్ని స్థాయిలలో "the interdependent and mutually reinforcing pillars of sustainable development — economic development, social development and environmental protection" (అర్థం: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి యొక్క పరస్పరం ఆధారపడిన, పరస్పరం బలపరిచే స్తంభాలు — ఆర్థిక అభివృద్ధి, సామాజిక అభివృద్ధి, పర్యావరణ రక్షణ) ను ముందుకు తీసుకెళ్లడం. మూడు అత్యున్నత లక్ష్యాలు (పేరా 11): పేదరిక నిర్మూలన, వినియోగ, ఉత్పత్తి విధానాల మార్పు, సహజ వనరుల ఆధారాన్ని కాపాడడం, నిర్వహించడం. ప్రధాన సందేశాలు: "The deep fault line that divides human society between the rich and the poor" (అర్థం: మానవ సమాజాన్ని ధనికులు, పేదలుగా విభజించే లోతైన చీలిక) (పేరా 12); "The global environment continues to suffer." (అర్థం: ప్రపంచ పర్యావరణం బాధపడుతూనే ఉంది.) (పేరా 13); ప్రైవేట్ రంగం "has a duty to contribute to the evolution of equitable and sustainable communities and societies" (అర్థం: న్యాయమైన, సుస్థిరమైన సమాజాల వికాసానికి తోడ్పడే కర్తవ్యం కలిగి ఉంది) (పేరా 27); కార్పొరేట్ జవాబుదారీతనం (పేరా 29); "more effective, democratic and accountable international and multilateral institutions" (అర్థం: మరింత సమర్థవంతమైన, ప్రజాస్వామిక, జవాబుదారీ అంతర్జాతీయ, బహుపక్ష సంస్థలు) (పేరా 31). భారతదేశం: ప్రకటన భావనలు సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిపై భారతీయ చట్టంతో ( Vellore , 1996; Narmada Bachao Andolan , 2000), జాతీయ హరిత ట్రైబ్యునల్ చట్టం, 2010, సెక్షన్ 20 తో సరిపోతాయి.
te.meaning: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిపై ప్రపంచ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు: రియో భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు తర్వాత పదేళ్లకు, పురోగతిని సమీక్షించి సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధిపై చర్యకు కట్టుబడడానికి, దక్షిణాఫ్రికాలోని జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్‌లో 26 ఆగస్టు నుండి 4 సెప్టెంబర్ 2002 వరకు జరిగిన ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సు. జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్ ప్రకటన: ఆ సదస్సులో నాయకుల రాజకీయ ప్రకటన, దీనిలో వారు "reaffirm our commitment to sustainable development" (అర్థం: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధికి మా నిబద్ధతను పునరుద్ఘాటిస్తున్నాం) (పేరా 1). సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి: పరస్పరం ఆధారపడిన, పరస్పరం బలపరిచే మూడు స్తంభాలపై నిర్మించిన అభివృద్ధి: ఆర్థిక అభివృద్ధి, సామాజిక అభివృద్ధి, పర్యావరణ రక్షణ (పేరా 5). అమలు ప్రణాళిక: అదే సదస్సులో ఆమోదించిన కార్యాచరణ పత్రం, దానిని అమలు చేయడానికి ప్రకటన దేశాలను కట్టుబడేలా చేస్తుంది (పేరా 36). సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే: రియో వాగ్దానాలు పూర్తిగా నెరవేరలేదని జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్‌లో ప్రపంచ నాయకులు ఒప్పుకున్నారు, పర్యావరణంతో పాటు పేదరికం, ధనిక-పేదల మధ్య అంతరాన్ని పరిష్కరించాలని చెప్పారు, కలిసి పనిచేస్తామని వాగ్దానం చేశారు.
keyPoints: 4 సెప్టెంబర్ 2002 న జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్‌లోని WSSD లో ఆమోదం; 37 పేరాలు; రియో తర్వాత పదేళ్లు. సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి స్తంభాలు: ఆర్థిక అభివృద్ధి, సామాజిక అభివృద్ధి, పర్యావరణ రక్షణ (పేరా 5). అమలు ప్రణాళిక: ప్రకటనతో పాటు ఆమోదించిన కార్యాచరణ పత్రం (పేరాలు 6, 36). కార్పొరేట్ జవాబుదారీతనం: "within a transparent and stable regulatory environment" (అర్థం: పారదర్శకమైన, స్థిరమైన నియంత్రణ వాతావరణంలో) (పేరా 29). బహుపక్షవాదం: "more effective, democratic and accountable international and multilateral institutions" (అర్థం: మరింత సమర్థవంతమైన, ప్రజాస్వామిక, జవాబుదారీ అంతర్జాతీయ, బహుపక్ష సంస్థలు) (పేరా 31). సాఫ్ట్ లా; భారతీయ చట్టం అవే భావనలకు అమలు రూపం ఇస్తుంది ( Vellore , NGT చట్టం సెక్షన్ 20).

selfTest.q: జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్ ప్రకటన ఎప్పుడు, ఎక్కడ ఆమోదించబడింది?
selfTest.a: ప్రకటనలోని ఆరు భాగాలను పేర్కొనండి. పేరా 5 కింద సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి స్తంభాలు ఏవి? పేరా 11 లోని అత్యున్నత లక్ష్యాలు ఏవి? ప్రైవేట్ రంగం గురించి ప్రకటన ఏమి చెబుతుంది? జోహాన్నెస్‌బర్గ్ ప్రకటన రియో ప్రకటన నుండి ఎలా భిన్నమైనది? భారతీయ చట్టం సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి భావనను ఎలా వర్తింపజేసింది?

hi.inOneMinute: What it is: the Johannesburg Declaration on Sustainable Development , adopted on 4 September 2002 at the 17th plenary meeting of the World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD) in Johannesburg, South Africa. When: the Summit ran from 26 August to 4 September 2002; the leaders "assembled at the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg, South Africa, from 2 to 4 September 2002" (para 1). It came ten years after Rio (1992) and thirty years after Stockholm (1972) (para 8). Form: a political declaration of 37 paragraphs in six parts, adopted with the Plan of Implementation of the Summit (para 6). It is soft law , not a treaty. Core idea (para 5): to advance "the interdependent and mutually reinforcing pillars of sustainable development — economic development, social development and environmental protection" at all levels. Three overarching objectives (para 11): poverty eradication , changing consumption and production patterns, and protecting and managing the natural resource base. Main messages: "The deep fault line that divides human society between the rich and the poor" (para 12); "The global environment continues to suffer." (para 13); the private sector "has a duty to contribute to the evolution of equitable and sustainable communities and societies" (para 27); corporate accountability (para 29); "more effective, democratic and accountable international and multilateral institutions" (para 31). India: the Declaration's ideas match Indian law on sustainable development ( Vellore , 1996; Narmada Bachao Andolan , 2000) and the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, s. 20.
legalProvision: Johannesburg Declaration on Sustainable Development, 2002 – adopted at the 17th plenary meeting of the WSSD on 4 September 2002; 37 paragraphs in six parts: "From our origins to the future" (paras 1–7); "From Stockholm to Rio de Janeiro to Johannesburg" (paras 8–10); "The challenges we face" (paras 11–15); "Our commitment to sustainable development" (paras 16–30); "Multilateralism is the future" (paras 31–33); "Making it happen!" (paras 34–37). Plan of Implementation of the World Summit on Sustainable Development – adopted with the Declaration (paras 6, 36). Report of the Summit: A/CONF.199/20. Earlier instruments it builds on: Stockholm Declaration (1972), Rio Declaration and Agenda 21 (1992). India: Constitution Arts. 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, s. 20 (principles of sustainable development, precaution and polluter pays).
hi.meaning: World Summit on Sustainable Development: the UN summit held at Johannesburg, South Africa, from 26 August to 4 September 2002, ten years after the Rio Earth Summit, to review progress and commit to action on sustainable development . Johannesburg Declaration: the political statement of the leaders at that Summit, in which they "reaffirm our commitment to sustainable development" (para 1). Sustainable development: development built on three interdependent and mutually reinforcing pillars: economic development, social development and environmental protection (para 5). Plan of Implementation: the action document adopted at the same Summit, which the Declaration commits States to carry out (para 36). In simple words: in Johannesburg, world leaders admitted that the promises of Rio had not been fully kept, said that poverty and the gap between rich and poor must be tackled along with the environment , and promised to act together.
keyPoints: Adopted 4 September 2002 at the WSSD, Johannesburg; 37 paragraphs; ten years after Rio. Pillars of sustainable development: economic development, social development, environmental protection (para 5). Plan of Implementation: the action document adopted with the Declaration (paras 6, 36). Corporate accountability: "within a transparent and stable regulatory environment" (para 29). Multilateralism: "more effective, democratic and accountable international and multilateral institutions" (para 31). Soft law; Indian law gives effect to the same ideas ( Vellore , NGT Act s. 20).

caseLaws.name: Facts: Tanneries in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated effluent into the Palar river, making about 35,0
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "In the International sphere 'Sustainable Development' as a concept came to be known for the first time in the Stockholm Declaration of 1972"; it developed "during the two decades from Stockholm to Rio"; the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle are "part of the environmental law of the country". Why it matters: The Court followed the same path from Stockholm to Rio that para 8 of the Johannesburg Declaration recalls, and made sustainable development part of Indian law.
Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India , (2000) 10 SCC 664 (Supreme Court; judgment of B.N. Kirpal J; 18 October 2000)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: The challenges were belated; "Dams play a vital role in providing irrigation for food security"; displacement "would not per se result in the violation of their fundamental or other rights"; the Court's concern was relief and rehabilitation under Art. 21. Why it matters: It shows the balance between the economic pillar and the social pillar that para 5 of the Johannesburg Declaration describes.

Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai v. Ankita Sinha, Civil Appeal Nos. 12122–12123 of 2018 and connected appeals (Supreme Court; A.M. Khanwilkar, Hrishikesh Roy and C.T. Ravikumar JJ; judgment by Hrishikesh Roy J; 7 October 2021)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The National Green Tribunal took suo motu notice of a news report on the Deonar dumping groun
caseLaws.facts: Principle: The Court quoted s. 20 of the NGT Act ("The Tribunal shall ... apply the principles of sustainable development, the precautionary principle and the polluter pays principle") and held that the NGT, with its "sui generis" character, "even in the absence of an application, can self-ignite action". Why it matters: It shows sustainable development, the idea the Johannesburg Declaration reaffirmed, being applied by a specialised Indian tribunal created by statute.
