environmental-law-u5-t14.subtitle: The parent climate treaty: its objective, principles and the Annex I, Annex II and non-Annex I groups

en.inOneMinute: What it is: the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (usually written UNFCCC), the basic world treaty on climate change. It was adopted at UN Headquarters, New York, on 9 May 1992 , opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit (June 1992), and came into force on 21 March 1994 . It has 198 Parties . Objective (Art. 2): "stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system". Principles (Art. 3): equity; common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities ; developed countries "should take the lead"; precaution; sustainable development. Two groups of commitments (Art. 4): all Parties: inventories, national programmes, cooperation; developed countries ( Annex I ): policies to limit emissions, aiming to return to 1990 levels; richer developed countries ( Annex II ): money and technology for developing countries. Institutions: Conference of the Parties (COP), the "supreme body" (Art. 7); secretariat; two subsidiary bodies; financial mechanism. A framework: it sets goals and rules, and leaves detailed targets to protocols (Art. 17) and later agreements: the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015). India: signed on 10 June 1992 and ratified on 1 November 1993, as a non-Annex I (developing) Party. The Supreme Court has recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
legalProvision: UNFCCC, 1992 (26 Articles, Annexes I and II): Preamble – climate change is "a common concern of humankind"; "the largest share of historical and current global emissions of greenhouse gases has originated in developed countries"; "per capita emissions in developing countries are still relatively low"; "common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities". Art. 1 – definitions ("climate change", "greenhouse gases", "sink" and others). Art. 2 – objective. Art. 3 – principles. Art. 4 – commitments (4(1) all Parties; 4(2) Annex I; 4(3)–4(5) Annex II; 4(7)–4(9) developing countries). Arts. 5–6 – research and systematic observation; education, training and public awareness. Arts. 7–11 – Conference of the Parties, secretariat, subsidiary bodies, financial mechanism. Art. 12 – communication of information (national reports). Arts. 13–14 – questions of implementation; settlement of disputes. Arts. 15–17 – amendments, annexes, protocols. Art. 20 – signature at Rio during UNCED and in New York "from 20 June 1992 to 19 June 1993". Art. 23 – entry into force on the ninetieth day after the fiftieth instrument. Art. 24 – "No reservations may be made to the Convention." Art. 25 – withdrawal. Protocols and agreements under it: Kyoto Protocol (1997); Paris Agreement (2015). Constitution of India: Arts. 14, 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
en.meaning: Framework convention: a treaty that sets up the objective, principles, general duties and institutions, and leaves detailed rules to later protocols. Art. 17(1): "The Conference of the Parties may, at any ordinary session, adopt protocols to the Convention." Key definitions in Art. 1: Climate change (Art. 1(2)) – a change of climate "attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere", in addition to natural climate variability. Greenhouse gases (Art. 1(5)) – "those gaseous constituents of the atmosphere, both natural and anthropogenic, that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation". Sink (Art. 1(8)) – "any process, activity or mechanism which removes a greenhouse gas" (for example, forests). Annex I Parties: developed countries and economies in transition (countries of Central and Eastern Europe moving to a market economy). Annex II Parties: the developed (OECD) countries in Annex I, without the economies in transition; they have extra duties of money and technology. Non-Annex I Parties: developing countries, including India. In simple words: the UNFCCC is the "constitution" of world climate law. It says what the world wants (stable greenhouse gas levels), who should do more (developed countries), and creates the COP where later agreements are made.
keyPoints: Framework convention: adopted 9 May 1992, in force 21 March 1994; protocols under Art. 17. Objective: stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations to prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference (Art. 2). Common but differentiated responsibilities: developed countries "should take the lead" (Art. 3(1)). Annex I Parties: aim to return to 1990 levels (Art. 4(2)); Annex II gives money and technology. Conference of the Parties: "the supreme body of this Convention" (Art. 7). India: signed 10-6-1992, ratified 1-11-1993; non-Annex I.

caseLaws.facts: Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change, Advisory Opinion (International Court of Justice; 23 July 2025)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By resolution 77/276 of 29 March 2023, the UN General Assembly asked the Court what obligatio
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Duties under the climate treaties include obligations of conduct assessed against due diligence, and the "Standard of due diligence stringent"; "Capabilities of State key factor for determining applicable standard of due diligence"; the principle of "common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities" is relevant; "Protection of environment is precondition for enjoyment of human rights"; breach leads to cessation and reparation. Why it matters: It is the world court's statement that the UNFCCC and the treaties built on it create real legal duties, read with the UNFCCC's own principle of differentiated responsibilities.
State of the Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation, ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007 (Supreme Court of the Netherlands; 20 December 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An environmental group sued the Dutch State; the lower courts ordered a reduction of emission
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights oblige a State "to take suitable measures if a real and immediate risk to people's lives or welfare exists"; "Each country is thus responsible for its own share." The Court relied on the UNFCCC framework, noting that "The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was ratified in 1992" and on targets for "the Annex I countries". The State's appeal was rejected. Why it matters: It shows a national court using the UNFCCC's Annex I framework and the idea of each State's own share to enforce climate duties.
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280 (Supreme Court; 21 March 2024)

caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 14 and 21 "are important sources of the right to a clean environment and the right against the adverse effects of climate change"; "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change." Why it matters: It gives India's climate obligations, which begin with the UNFCCC, a base in the fundamental rights of the Constitution.

te.inOneMinute: ఇది ఏమిటి: వాతావరణ మార్పుపై ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి చట్రపు ఒడంబడిక (సాధారణంగా UNFCCC అని రాస్తారు), వాతావరణ మార్పుపై ప్రాథమిక ప్రపంచ ఒప్పందం. ఇది ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి ప్రధాన కార్యాలయం, న్యూయార్క్‌లో 9 మే 1992 న ఆమోదించబడి, రియో భూ శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సులో (జూన్ 1992) సంతకాలకు తెరవబడి, 21 మార్చి 1994 న అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది. దీనిలో 198 పక్షాలు ఉన్నాయి. లక్ష్యం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 2): "stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system" (అర్థం: వాతావరణ వ్యవస్థలో ప్రమాదకరమైన మానవ జోక్యాన్ని నివారించే స్థాయిలో వాతావరణంలో హరితగృహ వాయువుల సాంద్రతను స్థిరీకరించడం). సూత్రాలు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 3): న్యాయం; ఉమ్మడి కానీ విభిన్న బాధ్యతలు, సంబంధిత సామర్థ్యాలు ; అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు "should take the lead" (అర్థం: ముందుండాలి); ముందుజాగ్రత్త; సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి. రెండు రకాల బాధ్యతలు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 4): అన్ని పక్షాలు: ఉద్గారాల జాబితాలు, జాతీయ కార్యక్రమాలు, సహకారం; అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు ( అనుబంధం I ): 1990 స్థాయిలకు తిరిగి రావాలనే లక్ష్యంతో ఉద్గారాలను పరిమితం చేసే విధానాలు; సంపన్న అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు ( అనుబంధం II ): అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న దేశాలకు డబ్బు, సాంకేతికత. సంస్థలు: పార్టీల సమావేశం (COP), "supreme body" (అర్థం: అత్యున్నత సంస్థ) (అనుచ్ఛేదం 7); సచివాలయం; రెండు అనుబంధ సంస్థలు; ఆర్థిక యంత్రాంగం. ఒక చట్రం: ఇది లక్ష్యాలు, నియమాలను నిర్ణయించి, వివరమైన లక్ష్యాలను ప్రోటోకాల్‌లకు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 17), తర్వాతి ఒప్పందాలకు వదిలేస్తుంది: క్యోటో ప్రోటోకాల్ (1997), పారిస్ ఒప్పందం (2015). భారతదేశం: అనుబంధం I కాని (అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న) పక్షంగా 10 జూన్ 1992 న సంతకం చేసి, 1 నవంబర్ 1993 న ఆమోదించింది. వాతావరణ మార్పు దుష్ప్రభావాల నుండి విముక్తి హక్కును సుప్రీంకోర్టు గుర్తించింది ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
te.meaning: చట్రపు ఒడంబడిక: లక్ష్యం, సూత్రాలు, సాధారణ విధులు, సంస్థలను ఏర్పాటు చేసి, వివరమైన నియమాలను తర్వాతి ప్రోటోకాల్‌లకు వదిలే ఒప్పందం. అనుచ్ఛేదం 17(1): "The Conference of the Parties may, at any ordinary session, adopt protocols to the Convention." (అర్థం: పార్టీల సమావేశం ఏదైనా సాధారణ సమావేశంలో ఒడంబడికకు ప్రోటోకాల్‌లను ఆమోదించవచ్చు.) అనుచ్ఛేదం 1 లోని ముఖ్య నిర్వచనాలు: వాతావరణ మార్పు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 1(2)) – సహజ వాతావరణ మార్పులకు అదనంగా, "attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere" (అర్థం: ప్రపంచ వాతావరణ కూర్పును మార్చే మానవ కార్యకలాపాలకు ప్రత్యక్షంగా లేదా పరోక్షంగా ఆపాదించబడే) వాతావరణ మార్పు. హరితగృహ వాయువులు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 1(5)) – "those gaseous constituents of the atmosphere, both natural and anthropogenic, that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation" (అర్థం: పరారుణ వికిరణాన్ని గ్రహించి మళ్లీ విడుదల చేసే, సహజమైన, మానవ కారకమైన వాతావరణ వాయు భాగాలు). శోషకం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 1(8)) – "any process, activity or mechanism which removes a greenhouse gas" (అర్థం: హరితగృహ వాయువును తొలగించే ఏదైనా ప్రక్రియ, కార్యకలాపం లేదా యంత్రాంగం) (ఉదాహరణకు, అడవులు). అనుబంధం I పక్షాలు: అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు, పరివర్తన దశలోని ఆర్థిక వ్యవస్థలు (మార్కెట్ ఆర్థిక వ్యవస్థకు మారుతున్న మధ్య, తూర్పు ఐరోపా దేశాలు). అనుబంధం II పక్షాలు: పరివర్తన ఆర్థిక వ్యవస్థలు లేకుండా, అనుబంధం I లోని అభివృద్ధి చెందిన (OECD) దేశాలు; వీటికి డబ్బు, సాంకేతికతపై అదనపు బాధ్యతలు ఉన్నాయి. అనుబంధం I కాని పక్షాలు: భారతదేశంతో సహా అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న దేశాలు. సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే: UNFCCC ప్రపంచ వాతావరణ చట్టానికి "రాజ్యాంగం". ప్రపంచం ఏమి కోరుకుంటుందో (స్థిరమైన హరితగృహ వాయువు స్థాయిలు), ఎవరు ఎక్కువ చేయాలో (అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు) చెబుతుంది, తర్వాతి ఒప్పందాలు చేసే COP ను సృష్టిస్తుంది.
keyPoints: చట్రపు ఒడంబడిక: 9 మే 1992 న ఆమోదం, 21 మార్చి 1994 న అమలు; అనుచ్ఛేదం 17 కింద ప్రోటోకాల్‌లు. లక్ష్యం: ప్రమాదకరమైన మానవ జోక్యాన్ని నివారించడానికి హరితగృహ వాయువుల సాంద్రత స్థిరీకరణ (అనుచ్ఛేదం 2). ఉమ్మడి కానీ విభిన్న బాధ్యతలు: అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాలు "should take the lead" (అర్థం: ముందుండాలి) (అనుచ్ఛేదం 3(1)). అనుబంధం I పక్షాలు: 1990 స్థాయిలకు తిరిగి రావాలనే లక్ష్యం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 4(2)); అనుబంధం II డబ్బు, సాంకేతికత ఇస్తుంది. పార్టీల సమావేశం: "the supreme body of this Convention" (అర్థం: ఈ ఒడంబడిక యొక్క అత్యున్నత సంస్థ) (అనుచ్ఛేదం 7). భారతదేశం: 10-6-1992 సంతకం, 1-11-1993 ఆమోదం; అనుబంధం I కాని దేశం.

hi.inOneMinute: What it is: the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (usually written UNFCCC), the basic world treaty on climate change. It was adopted at UN Headquarters, New York, on 9 May 1992 , opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit (June 1992), and came into force on 21 March 1994 . It has 198 Parties . Objective (Art. 2): "stabilization of greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system". Principles (Art. 3): equity; common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities ; developed countries "should take the lead"; precaution; sustainable development. Two groups of commitments (Art. 4): all Parties: inventories, national programmes, cooperation; developed countries ( Annex I ): policies to limit emissions, aiming to return to 1990 levels; richer developed countries ( Annex II ): money and technology for developing countries. Institutions: Conference of the Parties (COP), the "supreme body" (Art. 7); secretariat; two subsidiary bodies; financial mechanism. A framework: it sets goals and rules, and leaves detailed targets to protocols (Art. 17) and later agreements: the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015). India: signed on 10 June 1992 and ratified on 1 November 1993, as a non-Annex I (developing) Party. The Supreme Court has recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
legalProvision: UNFCCC, 1992 (26 Articles, Annexes I and II): Preamble – climate change is "a common concern of humankind"; "the largest share of historical and current global emissions of greenhouse gases has originated in developed countries"; "per capita emissions in developing countries are still relatively low"; "common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities". Art. 1 – definitions ("climate change", "greenhouse gases", "sink" and others). Art. 2 – objective. Art. 3 – principles. Art. 4 – commitments (4(1) all Parties; 4(2) Annex I; 4(3)–4(5) Annex II; 4(7)–4(9) developing countries). Arts. 5–6 – research and systematic observation; education, training and public awareness. Arts. 7–11 – Conference of the Parties, secretariat, subsidiary bodies, financial mechanism. Art. 12 – communication of information (national reports). Arts. 13–14 – questions of implementation; settlement of disputes. Arts. 15–17 – amendments, annexes, protocols. Art. 20 – signature at Rio during UNCED and in New York "from 20 June 1992 to 19 June 1993". Art. 23 – entry into force on the ninetieth day after the fiftieth instrument. Art. 24 – "No reservations may be made to the Convention." Art. 25 – withdrawal. Protocols and agreements under it: Kyoto Protocol (1997); Paris Agreement (2015). Constitution of India: Arts. 14, 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
hi.meaning: Framework convention: a treaty that sets up the objective, principles, general duties and institutions, and leaves detailed rules to later protocols. Art. 17(1): "The Conference of the Parties may, at any ordinary session, adopt protocols to the Convention." Key definitions in Art. 1: Climate change (Art. 1(2)) – a change of climate "attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere", in addition to natural climate variability. Greenhouse gases (Art. 1(5)) – "those gaseous constituents of the atmosphere, both natural and anthropogenic, that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation". Sink (Art. 1(8)) – "any process, activity or mechanism which removes a greenhouse gas" (for example, forests). Annex I Parties: developed countries and economies in transition (countries of Central and Eastern Europe moving to a market economy). Annex II Parties: the developed (OECD) countries in Annex I, without the economies in transition; they have extra duties of money and technology. Non-Annex I Parties: developing countries, including India. In simple words: the UNFCCC is the "constitution" of world climate law. It says what the world wants (stable greenhouse gas levels), who should do more (developed countries), and creates the COP where later agreements are made.
keyPoints: Framework convention: adopted 9 May 1992, in force 21 March 1994; protocols under Art. 17. Objective: stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations to prevent dangerous anthropogenic interference (Art. 2). Common but differentiated responsibilities: developed countries "should take the lead" (Art. 3(1)). Annex I Parties: aim to return to 1990 levels (Art. 4(2)); Annex II gives money and technology. Conference of the Parties: "the supreme body of this Convention" (Art. 7). India: signed 10-6-1992, ratified 1-11-1993; non-Annex I.

caseLaws.name: Facts: By resolution 77/276 of 29 March 2023, the UN General Assembly asked the Court what obligatio
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Duties under the climate treaties include obligations of conduct assessed against due diligence, and the "Standard of due diligence stringent"; "Capabilities of State key factor for determining applicable standard of due diligence"; the principle of "common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities" is relevant; "Protection of environment is precondition for enjoyment of human rights"; breach leads to cessation and reparation. Why it matters: It is the world court's statement that the UNFCCC and the treaties built on it create real legal duties, read with the UNFCCC's own principle of differentiated responsibilities.
State of the Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation, ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007 (Supreme Court of the Netherlands; 20 December 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An environmental group sued the Dutch State; the lower courts ordered a reduction of emission
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights oblige a State "to take suitable measures if a real and immediate risk to people's lives or welfare exists"; "Each country is thus responsible for its own share." The Court relied on the UNFCCC framework, noting that "The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was ratified in 1992" and on targets for "the Annex I countries". The State's appeal was rejected. Why it matters: It shows a national court using the UNFCCC's Annex I framework and the idea of each State's own share to enforce climate duties.
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280 (Supreme Court; 21 March 2024)

environmental-law-u5-t16.subtitle: The 17 Sustainable Development Goals: what they are, their environmental goals and their legal weight

en.inOneMinute: What they are: the Sustainable Development Goals , 17 goals with 169 targets, set out in the UN General Assembly's resolution "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" (resolution 70/1). When: adopted in New York on 25 September 2015 , at a summit held at UN Headquarters from 25 to 27 September 2015. They came into effect on 1 January 2016 and run "over the next 15 years", to 2030 . Builds on the MDGs: "The new Agenda builds on the Millennium Development Goals and seeks to complete what they did not achieve" (para 16). Five areas (the "5 Ps"): People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership. Key features: "integrated and indivisible"; "universal goals and targets" for all countries; "no one will be left behind"; national realities and "national policy space" respected. Environment goals: water (Goal 6), energy (Goal 7), consumption and production (Goal 12), climate (Goal 13), oceans (Goal 14), land, forests and biodiversity (Goal 15). Nature: a political commitment, not a treaty. Targets are "aspirational and global" (para 55). Follow-up is "voluntary and country-led", through the high-level political forum .
legalProvision: UN General Assembly resolution 70/1, "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" (25 September 2015): Preamble – the five areas; "The 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets"; "no one will be left behind". Declaration (paras 1–53) – vision, principles, the new Agenda; para 12 reaffirms the Rio principles, including common but differentiated responsibilities; para 16 on the MDGs; para 18 the 17 Goals and 169 targets; para 21 effect from 1 January 2016; para 40 means of implementation; para 47 follow-up and review. Sustainable Development Goals and targets (paras 54–59) – the 17 Goals; para 55 "Targets are defined as aspirational and global". Means of implementation and the Global Partnership (paras 60–71) – para 70 Technology Facilitation Mechanism. Follow-up and review (paras 72–91) – principles (para 74), global indicators (para 75), high-level political forum (paras 82–89). Linked instruments: Addis Ababa Action Agenda (GA resolution 69/313, 27 July 2015); UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement (Goal 13); Rio Declaration, 1992. Constitution of India: Arts. 14, 21, 47, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
en.meaning: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): the 17 global goals of the 2030 Agenda, each with targets, covering the economic, social and environmental sides of sustainable development , to be achieved by 2030. Goal, target and indicator: a goal is the broad aim (for example, Goal 13, climate action); a target is a specific aim under a goal (for example, 13.2); an indicator measures progress on a target, using "a set of global indicators" (para 75). 2030 Agenda: the whole resolution: declaration, goals and targets, means of implementation, and follow-up and review. Millennium Development Goals (MDGs): the earlier set of goals, "agreed" "almost 15 years" before 2015 (para 16), whose "unfinished business" the SDGs take up (para 2). In simple words: the SDGs are the world's shared to-do list for 2015–2030. They cover poverty, health, education and equality, and also water, energy, climate, oceans and forests, and they treat all of these as one package.
keyPoints: 17 goals, 169 targets; adopted 25-9-2015; in effect 1-1-2016 to 2030. Integrated and indivisible: economic, social and environmental together. No one left behind: "no one will be left behind"; universal goals. Means of implementation: Goal 17; Addis Ababa Action Agenda; Technology Facilitation Mechanism. High-level political forum: voluntary, State-led reviews; every four years under the General Assembly. Soft law: targets "aspirational and global"; Goal 13 respects the UNFCCC.

te.inOneMinute: ఇవి ఏమిటి: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి లక్ష్యాలు (Sustainable Development Goals), 169 ఉప లక్ష్యాలతో కూడిన 17 లక్ష్యాలు; ఇవి ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి సాధారణ సభ తీర్మానం "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" (అర్థం: మన ప్రపంచాన్ని మార్చడం: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధికి 2030 అజెండా) (తీర్మానం 70/1) లో ఉన్నాయి. ఎప్పుడు: ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి ప్రధాన కార్యాలయంలో 25 నుండి 27 సెప్టెంబర్ 2015 వరకు జరిగిన శిఖరాగ్ర సదస్సులో, న్యూయార్క్‌లో 25 సెప్టెంబర్ 2015 న ఆమోదించబడ్డాయి. ఇవి 1 జనవరి 2016 న అమల్లోకి వచ్చి, "over the next 15 years" (అర్థం: రాబోయే 15 సంవత్సరాలు), 2030 వరకు కొనసాగుతాయి. MDGల మీద ఆధారం: "The new Agenda builds on the Millennium Development Goals and seeks to complete what they did not achieve" (అర్థం: కొత్త అజెండా సహస్రాబ్ది అభివృద్ధి లక్ష్యాల మీద నిర్మించబడి, అవి సాధించని వాటిని పూర్తి చేయడానికి ప్రయత్నిస్తుంది) (పేరా 16). ఐదు రంగాలు ("5 Ps"): ప్రజలు (People), భూగ్రహం (Planet), సమృద్ధి (Prosperity), శాంతి (Peace), భాగస్వామ్యం (Partnership). ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు: "integrated and indivisible" (అర్థం: సమగ్రమైనవి, విడదీయరానివి); అన్ని దేశాలకు "universal goals and targets" (అర్థం: సార్వత్రిక లక్ష్యాలు, ఉప లక్ష్యాలు); "no one will be left behind" (అర్థం: ఎవరూ వెనుకబడరు); జాతీయ వాస్తవాలు, "national policy space" (అర్థం: జాతీయ విధాన స్వేచ్ఛ) గౌరవించబడతాయి. పర్యావరణ లక్ష్యాలు: నీరు (లక్ష్యం 6), శక్తి (లక్ష్యం 7), వినియోగం, ఉత్పత్తి (లక్ష్యం 12), వాతావరణం (లక్ష్యం 13), సముద్రాలు (లక్ష్యం 14), భూమి, అడవులు, జీవ వైవిధ్యం (లక్ష్యం 15). స్వభావం: ఇది రాజకీయ నిబద్ధత, ఒప్పందం కాదు. ఉప లక్ష్యాలు "aspirational and global" (అర్థం: ఆకాంక్షాత్మకమైనవి, ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తమైనవి) (పేరా 55). తదుపరి పర్యవేక్షణ ఉన్నత స్థాయి రాజకీయ వేదిక ద్వారా "voluntary and country-led" (అర్థం: స్వచ్ఛందమైనది, దేశం నడిపించేది).
te.meaning: సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి లక్ష్యాలు (SDGలు): 2030 అజెండాలోని 17 ప్రపంచ లక్ష్యాలు; ప్రతిదానికీ ఉప లక్ష్యాలు ఉన్నాయి; ఇవి సుస్థిర అభివృద్ధి యొక్క ఆర్థిక, సామాజిక, పర్యావరణ అంశాలను కవర్ చేస్తాయి, 2030 నాటికి సాధించాలి. లక్ష్యం, ఉప లక్ష్యం, సూచిక: లక్ష్యం విస్తృత ఉద్దేశ్యం (ఉదాహరణకు, లక్ష్యం 13, వాతావరణ చర్య); ఉప లక్ష్యం ఒక లక్ష్యం కింద నిర్దిష్ట ఉద్దేశ్యం (ఉదాహరణకు, 13.2); సూచిక "a set of global indicators" (అర్థం: ప్రపంచ సూచికల సమితి) ఉపయోగించి ఉప లక్ష్యంపై పురోగతిని కొలుస్తుంది (పేరా 75). 2030 అజెండా: మొత్తం తీర్మానం: ప్రకటన, లక్ష్యాలు, ఉప లక్ష్యాలు, అమలు సాధనాలు, తదుపరి పర్యవేక్షణ, సమీక్ష. సహస్రాబ్ది అభివృద్ధి లక్ష్యాలు (MDGలు): 2015 కి "almost 15 years" (అర్థం: దాదాపు 15 సంవత్సరాల) ముందు "agreed" (అర్థం: అంగీకరించబడిన) (పేరా 16) మునుపటి లక్ష్యాల సమితి; వాటి "unfinished business" (అర్థం: అసంపూర్తి పని) ని SDGలు చేపడతాయి (పేరా 2). సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే: SDGలు 2015–2030 కోసం ప్రపంచపు ఉమ్మడి పనుల జాబితా. ఇవి పేదరికం, ఆరోగ్యం, విద్య, సమానత్వంతో పాటు నీరు, శక్తి, వాతావరణం, సముద్రాలు, అడవులను కూడా కవర్ చేసి, వీటన్నింటినీ ఒకే ప్యాకేజీగా చూస్తాయి.
keyPoints: 17 లక్ష్యాలు, 169 ఉప లక్ష్యాలు; 25-9-2015 న ఆమోదం; 1-1-2016 నుండి 2030 వరకు అమలు. సమగ్రమైనవి, విడదీయరానివి: ఆర్థిక, సామాజిక, పర్యావరణ అంశాలు కలిపి. ఎవరూ వెనుకబడకూడదు: "no one will be left behind" (అర్థం: ఎవరూ వెనుకబడరు); సార్వత్రిక లక్ష్యాలు. అమలు సాధనాలు: లక్ష్యం 17; అడిస్ అబాబా కార్యాచరణ అజెండా; సాంకేతిక సులభీకరణ యంత్రాంగం. ఉన్నత స్థాయి రాజకీయ వేదిక: స్వచ్ఛంద, దేశాలు నడిపించే సమీక్షలు; సాధారణ సభ కింద ప్రతి నాలుగు సంవత్సరాలకు. మృదు చట్టం: ఉప లక్ష్యాలు "aspirational and global" (అర్థం: ఆకాంక్షాత్మకమైనవి, ప్రపంచవ్యాప్తమైనవి); లక్ష్యం 13 UNFCCC ని గౌరవిస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: SDGలు ఎప్పుడు, ఏ పత్రం ద్వారా ఆమోదించబడ్డాయి?
selfTest.a: ఎన్ని లక్ష్యాలు, ఉప లక్ష్యాలు ఉన్నాయి, ఏ కాలానికి? 2030 అజెండాలోని ఐదు రంగాలను పేర్కొనండి. పర్యావరణానికి సంబంధించిన ఏవైనా ఐదు లక్ష్యాలను పేర్కొనండి. "integrated and indivisible" (అర్థం: సమగ్రమైనవి, విడదీయరానివి) అంటే ఏమిటి? SDGలు చట్టబద్ధంగా కట్టుబడి ఉండేవా? వివరించండి. ఉన్నత స్థాయి రాజకీయ వేదిక పాత్ర ఏమిటి?

hi.inOneMinute: What they are: the Sustainable Development Goals , 17 goals with 169 targets, set out in the UN General Assembly's resolution "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" (resolution 70/1). When: adopted in New York on 25 September 2015 , at a summit held at UN Headquarters from 25 to 27 September 2015. They came into effect on 1 January 2016 and run "over the next 15 years", to 2030 . Builds on the MDGs: "The new Agenda builds on the Millennium Development Goals and seeks to complete what they did not achieve" (para 16). Five areas (the "5 Ps"): People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership. Key features: "integrated and indivisible"; "universal goals and targets" for all countries; "no one will be left behind"; national realities and "national policy space" respected. Environment goals: water (Goal 6), energy (Goal 7), consumption and production (Goal 12), climate (Goal 13), oceans (Goal 14), land, forests and biodiversity (Goal 15). Nature: a political commitment, not a treaty. Targets are "aspirational and global" (para 55). Follow-up is "voluntary and country-led", through the high-level political forum .
legalProvision: UN General Assembly resolution 70/1, "Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development" (25 September 2015): Preamble – the five areas; "The 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets"; "no one will be left behind". Declaration (paras 1–53) – vision, principles, the new Agenda; para 12 reaffirms the Rio principles, including common but differentiated responsibilities; para 16 on the MDGs; para 18 the 17 Goals and 169 targets; para 21 effect from 1 January 2016; para 40 means of implementation; para 47 follow-up and review. Sustainable Development Goals and targets (paras 54–59) – the 17 Goals; para 55 "Targets are defined as aspirational and global". Means of implementation and the Global Partnership (paras 60–71) – para 70 Technology Facilitation Mechanism. Follow-up and review (paras 72–91) – principles (para 74), global indicators (para 75), high-level political forum (paras 82–89). Linked instruments: Addis Ababa Action Agenda (GA resolution 69/313, 27 July 2015); UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement (Goal 13); Rio Declaration, 1992. Constitution of India: Arts. 14, 21, 47, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
hi.meaning: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): the 17 global goals of the 2030 Agenda, each with targets, covering the economic, social and environmental sides of sustainable development , to be achieved by 2030. Goal, target and indicator: a goal is the broad aim (for example, Goal 13, climate action); a target is a specific aim under a goal (for example, 13.2); an indicator measures progress on a target, using "a set of global indicators" (para 75). 2030 Agenda: the whole resolution: declaration, goals and targets, means of implementation, and follow-up and review. Millennium Development Goals (MDGs): the earlier set of goals, "agreed" "almost 15 years" before 2015 (para 16), whose "unfinished business" the SDGs take up (para 2). In simple words: the SDGs are the world's shared to-do list for 2015–2030. They cover poverty, health, education and equality, and also water, energy, climate, oceans and forests, and they treat all of these as one package.
keyPoints: 17 goals, 169 targets; adopted 25-9-2015; in effect 1-1-2016 to 2030. Integrated and indivisible: economic, social and environmental together. No one left behind: "no one will be left behind"; universal goals. Means of implementation: Goal 17; Addis Ababa Action Agenda; Technology Facilitation Mechanism. High-level political forum: voluntary, State-led reviews; every four years under the General Assembly. Soft law: targets "aspirational and global"; Goal 13 respects the UNFCCC.

en.meaning:
Transboundary pollution is best defined as pollution that:

Explanation. Transboundary pollution originates in one State's territory or control and causes or threatens environmental harm in another State or in areas beyond any State's jurisdiction.

Which of these is an example of 'diffuse or global' transboundary harm rather than 'point-to-point' harm?

Explanation. Greenhouse gases mix into the shared global atmosphere before causing harm, so no single source can be traced to a specific injury in a specific country — this is diffuse/global transboundary harm.

The 'no-harm' principle in international environmental law was first authoritatively established by:

Explanation. The Trail Smelter Arbitration between the United States and Canada first held that a State must not allow its territory to be used to cause serious, provable injury to another State's territory.

Why do ordinary domestic court remedies usually fail for victims of transboundary pollution?

en.meaning:
The Kyoto Protocol was adopted at which Conference of the Parties, and when?

Explanation. The Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997 at the UNFCCC's Third Conference of the Parties (COP3) in Kyoto, Japan.

The Kyoto Protocol's defining structural feature is that it:

Explanation. Kyoto applies 'common but differentiated responsibilities' in strong form — binding targets for Annex I countries only.

Under Kyoto's first commitment period (2008-2012), Annex I countries collectively committed to reducing emissions by approximately:

Explanation. In the first commitment period, 2008 to 2012, Annex I countries together aimed at about 5 per cent below 1990 levels, each with its own figure. The Doha Amendment set 18 per cent below 1990 levels for 2013 to 2020.

Which Kyoto flexible mechanism allowed Annex I countries to invest in emission-reduction projects in developing countries like India and earn credits toward their own targets?

Under general international law, State responsibility requires which two elements?

Explanation. State responsibility arises when conduct is attributable to the State under international law and that conduct breaches an international obligation.

In Trail Smelter, why was Canada held responsible even though the smelter was privately owned?

Explanation. A State is responsible for permitting or failing to prevent a harmful activity within its territory, even where the operator is a private entity.

environmental-law-u5-t15.subtitle: The agreement in which every country sets its own climate plan: NDCs, the temperature goal and the stocktake

en.inOneMinute: COP21: the 21st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), held in Paris (at Le Bourget) from 30 November to 12 December 2015. Paris Agreement: adopted at COP21 on 12 December 2015 by 195 Parties; opened for signature in New York on 22 April 2016 ; entered into force on 4 November 2016 (that is why the syllabus says "2016"). It has 194 Parties (as of 27 January 2026). Goal (Art. 2): hold warming "well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels" and pursue efforts "to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C"; build adaptation; make finance flows consistent with low emissions. The core idea: every Party, developed and developing, must "prepare, communicate and maintain successive nationally determined contributions" (NDCs) (Art. 4(2)), renewed every five years, each one more ambitious than the last. Checking progress: an enhanced transparency framework (Art. 13) and a global stocktake in 2023 and every five years after (Art. 14). Other pillars: adaptation (Art. 7), loss and damage (Art. 8), finance from developed countries (Art. 9), technology (Art. 10), capacity-building (Art. 11), cooperation and markets (Art. 6). Compliance: a committee that is "facilitative" and "non-adversarial and non-punitive" (Art. 15). India: a Party; its INDC is dated 2 October 2015. The Supreme Court has linked climate action to Arts. 14 and 21 ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
legalProvision: Paris Agreement, 2015 (29 Articles): Preamble – climate change is "a common concern of humankind"; human rights; intergenerational equity; "the importance for some of the concept of 'climate justice'". Art. 2 – purpose: temperature goal, adaptation, finance flows; equity and CBDR-RC "in the light of different national circumstances". Art. 3 – all Parties to undertake "ambitious efforts" showing "progression over time". Art. 4 – mitigation and NDCs. Art. 5 – sinks and forests (REDD+). Art. 6 – voluntary cooperation; market and non-market approaches. Art. 7 – adaptation. Art. 8 – loss and damage. Arts. 9–11 – finance, technology, capacity-building. Art. 12 – education and public awareness. Art. 13 – enhanced transparency framework. Art. 14 – global stocktake. Art. 15 – implementation and compliance. Art. 16 – the COP serves as the meeting of the Parties (CMA). Arts. 20–28 – signature, entry into force (55/55), no reservations, withdrawal. Parent treaty: UNFCCC, 1992 (the Agreement works "under the Convention"). Constitution of India: Arts. 14, 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
en.meaning: Conference of the Parties (COP): the supreme body of the UNFCCC, which meets every year. "COP21" means its 21st meeting. Paris Agreement: a treaty adopted under the UNFCCC at COP21, which sets a long-term temperature goal and requires every Party to make and update its own national climate targets. Nationally determined contribution (NDC): a Party's own climate plan and target, which it decides for itself ("nationally determined") and must prepare, communicate and maintain under Art. 4(2). Intended NDC (INDC): the draft contribution that countries announced before and around COP21; on joining the Agreement it became the first NDC. Global stocktake: a review of the collective progress of all Parties towards the Agreement's purpose (Art. 14). Loss and damage : harm from climate change that adaptation cannot prevent, including "slow onset events" and "non-economic losses" (Art. 8). In simple words: Kyoto told rich countries what to cut; Paris lets every country set its own target, but makes all of them publish it, report on it, and raise it every five years.
keyPoints: Nationally determined contribution: every Party; every five years; each one a progression (Art. 4). Global stocktake: 2023 and every five years thereafter (Art. 14). Enhanced transparency framework: "with built-in flexibility"; reporting from 2024 (Art. 13). Loss and damage: "averting, minimizing and addressing" (Art. 8). Adopted 12-12-2015 at COP21; in force 4-11-2016; well below 2°C and 1.5°C. No reservations (Art. 27); compliance non-punitive (Art. 15).

caseLaws.name: Facts: By resolution 77/276 of 29 March 2023, the UN General Assembly asked the Court what obligatio
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "The 1.5°C threshold of Article 2 is the parties' agreed primary temperature goal"; the Paris Agreement contains an "Obligation of result to prepare, communicate and maintain nationally determined contributions (NDCs)"; the "Standard of due diligence stringent."; breach leads to the "Duty of cessation and guarantees of non-repetition" and the "Duty to make reparation through restitution, compensation or satisfaction". Why it matters: It is the world court's reading of the Paris Agreement: 1.5°C is the main goal, making an NDC is a duty of result, and its content is judged by stringent due diligence.
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280 (Supreme Court; 21 March 2024)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Union asked the Court to modify its 2021 order protecting the Great Indian Bustard from o
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 14 and 21 "are important sources of the right to a clean environment and the right against the adverse effects of climate change"; "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change." Why it matters: The Supreme Court treated India's Paris commitments as relevant to deciding a case and linked climate action to fundamental rights .
State of the Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation, ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007 (Supreme Court of the Netherlands; 20 December 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An environmental group sued the Dutch State; the lower courts ordered a reduction of emission
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights oblige a State "to take suitable measures if a real and immediate risk to people's lives or welfare exists"; "Each country is thus responsible for its own share." The State's appeal was rejected. Why it matters: It reflects the Paris idea that each country is responsible for its own share, and shows that a court can order a State to cut emissions.

te.inOneMinute: COP21: వాతావరణ మార్పుపై ఐక్యరాజ్యసమితి చట్రపు ఒడంబడిక (UNFCCC) పార్టీల సమావేశం యొక్క 21వ సమావేశం; ఇది పారిస్‌లో (లే బూర్జే వద్ద) 30 నవంబర్ నుండి 12 డిసెంబర్ 2015 వరకు జరిగింది. పారిస్ ఒప్పందం: COP21 లో 12 డిసెంబర్ 2015 న 195 పక్షాలు ఆమోదించాయి; 22 ఏప్రిల్ 2016 న న్యూయార్క్‌లో సంతకాలకు తెరవబడింది; 4 నవంబర్ 2016 న అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది (అందుకే సిలబస్‌లో "2016" అని ఉంది). దీనిలో 194 పక్షాలు ఉన్నాయి (27 జనవరి 2026 నాటికి). లక్ష్యం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 2): ఉష్ణోగ్రత పెరుగుదలను "well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels" (అర్థం: పారిశ్రామిక పూర్వ స్థాయిల కంటే 2°C కంటే బాగా తక్కువగా) ఉంచడం, "to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C" (అర్థం: ఉష్ణోగ్రత పెరుగుదలను 1.5°C కి పరిమితం చేయడానికి) ప్రయత్నించడం; అనుసరణ సామర్థ్యం పెంచడం; నిధుల ప్రవాహాలను తక్కువ ఉద్గారాలకు అనుగుణంగా మార్చడం. ప్రధాన ఆలోచన: అభివృద్ధి చెందిన, అభివృద్ధి చెందుతున్న ప్రతి పక్షం "prepare, communicate and maintain successive nationally determined contributions" (అర్థం: వరుస జాతీయంగా నిర్ణయించిన సహకారాలను సిద్ధం చేసి, తెలియజేసి, కొనసాగించాలి) (NDCలు) (అనుచ్ఛేదం 4(2)); వీటిని ప్రతి ఐదు సంవత్సరాలకు కొత్తగా ఇవ్వాలి, ప్రతిదీ మునుపటి దాని కంటే ఎక్కువ ఆశయంతో ఉండాలి. పురోగతి తనిఖీ: మెరుగైన పారదర్శకత చట్రం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 13), 2023 లో, తర్వాత ప్రతి ఐదు సంవత్సరాలకు ప్రపంచ సమీక్ష (అనుచ్ఛేదం 14). ఇతర స్తంభాలు: అనుసరణ (అనుచ్ఛేదం 7), నష్టం మరియు హాని (అనుచ్ఛేదం 8), అభివృద్ధి చెందిన దేశాల నుండి నిధులు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 9), సాంకేతికత (అనుచ్ఛేదం 10), సామర్థ్య నిర్మాణం (అనుచ్ఛేదం 11), సహకారం, మార్కెట్లు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 6). పాటింపు: "facilitative" (అర్థం: సులభతరం చేసే), "non-adversarial and non-punitive" (అర్థం: వివాదాత్మకం కాని, శిక్షాత్మకం కాని) కమిటీ (అనుచ్ఛేదం 15). భారతదేశం: ఒక పక్షం; దాని INDC తేదీ 2 అక్టోబర్ 2015. వాతావరణ చర్యను సుప్రీంకోర్టు అనుచ్ఛేదాలు 14, 21 తో ముడిపెట్టింది ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
te.meaning: పార్టీల సమావేశం (COP): UNFCCC యొక్క అత్యున్నత సంస్థ, ఇది ప్రతి సంవత్సరం సమావేశమవుతుంది. "COP21" అంటే దాని 21వ సమావేశం. పారిస్ ఒప్పందం: COP21 లో UNFCCC కింద ఆమోదించిన ఒప్పందం; ఇది దీర్ఘకాల ఉష్ణోగ్రత లక్ష్యాన్ని నిర్ణయించి, ప్రతి పక్షం తన స్వంత జాతీయ వాతావరణ లక్ష్యాలను రూపొందించి, నవీకరించాలని కోరుతుంది. జాతీయంగా నిర్ణయించిన సహకారం (NDC): ఒక పక్షం తనకు తానే నిర్ణయించుకునే ("జాతీయంగా నిర్ణయించిన") వాతావరణ ప్రణాళిక, లక్ష్యం; అనుచ్ఛేదం 4(2) కింద దీనిని సిద్ధం చేసి, తెలియజేసి, కొనసాగించాలి. ఉద్దేశిత NDC (INDC): COP21 కి ముందు, ఆ సమయంలో దేశాలు ప్రకటించిన ముసాయిదా సహకారం; ఒప్పందంలో చేరినప్పుడు ఇది మొదటి NDC అయింది. ప్రపంచ సమీక్ష: ఒప్పందం ఉద్దేశ్యం దిశగా అన్ని పక్షాల సమష్టి పురోగతి సమీక్ష (అనుచ్ఛేదం 14). నష్టం మరియు హాని : అనుసరణ ద్వారా నివారించలేని వాతావరణ మార్పు హాని; ఇందులో "slow onset events" (అర్థం: నెమ్మదిగా వచ్చే సంఘటనలు), "non-economic losses" (అర్థం: ఆర్థికేతర నష్టాలు) కూడా ఉన్నాయి (అనుచ్ఛేదం 8). సులభంగా చెప్పాలంటే: క్యోటో ధనిక దేశాలకు ఎంత తగ్గించాలో చెప్పింది; పారిస్ ప్రతి దేశం తన లక్ష్యాన్ని తానే నిర్ణయించుకోనిస్తుంది, కానీ ప్రతి దేశం దానిని ప్రకటించాలి, దానిపై నివేదించాలి, ప్రతి ఐదు సంవత్సరాలకు పెంచాలి.
keyPoints: జాతీయంగా నిర్ణయించిన సహకారం: ప్రతి పక్షం; ప్రతి ఐదు సంవత్సరాలకు; ప్రతిదీ పురోగతి (అనుచ్ఛేదం 4). ప్రపంచ సమీక్ష: 2023 లో, ఆ తర్వాత ప్రతి ఐదు సంవత్సరాలకు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 14). మెరుగైన పారదర్శకత చట్రం: "with built-in flexibility" (అర్థం: అంతర్గత సౌలభ్యంతో); 2024 నుండి నివేదన (అనుచ్ఛేదం 13). నష్టం మరియు హాని: "averting, minimizing and addressing" (అర్థం: నివారించడం, తగ్గించడం, పరిష్కరించడం) (అనుచ్ఛేదం 8). COP21 లో 12-12-2015 న ఆమోదం; 4-11-2016 న అమల్లోకి; 2°C కంటే బాగా తక్కువ, 1.5°C. రిజర్వేషన్లు లేవు (అనుచ్ఛేదం 27); పాటింపు శిక్షాత్మకం కానిది (అనుచ్ఛేదం 15).

selfTest.q: COP21 అంటే ఏమిటి, ఇది ఎప్పుడు, ఎక్కడ జరిగింది?
selfTest.a: పారిస్ ఒప్పందం ఎప్పుడు ఆమోదించబడింది, ఎప్పుడు అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది? అనుచ్ఛేదం 2 లోని ఉష్ణోగ్రత లక్ష్యాన్ని తెలపండి. NDC అంటే ఏమిటి, దాని గురించి అనుచ్ఛేదం 4 ఏమి కోరుతుంది? ప్రపంచ సమీక్ష అంటే ఏమిటి? పారిస్ ఒప్పందం క్యోటో ప్రోటోకాల్ నుండి ఎలా భిన్నమైనది? మూడు అంశాలు ఇవ్వండి. 1.5°C పరిమితి గురించి అంతర్జాతీయ న్యాయస్థానం ఏమి చెప్పింది?

hi.inOneMinute: COP21: the 21st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), held in Paris (at Le Bourget) from 30 November to 12 December 2015. Paris Agreement: adopted at COP21 on 12 December 2015 by 195 Parties; opened for signature in New York on 22 April 2016 ; entered into force on 4 November 2016 (that is why the syllabus says "2016"). It has 194 Parties (as of 27 January 2026). Goal (Art. 2): hold warming "well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels" and pursue efforts "to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C"; build adaptation; make finance flows consistent with low emissions. The core idea: every Party, developed and developing, must "prepare, communicate and maintain successive nationally determined contributions" (NDCs) (Art. 4(2)), renewed every five years, each one more ambitious than the last. Checking progress: an enhanced transparency framework (Art. 13) and a global stocktake in 2023 and every five years after (Art. 14). Other pillars: adaptation (Art. 7), loss and damage (Art. 8), finance from developed countries (Art. 9), technology (Art. 10), capacity-building (Art. 11), cooperation and markets (Art. 6). Compliance: a committee that is "facilitative" and "non-adversarial and non-punitive" (Art. 15). India: a Party; its INDC is dated 2 October 2015. The Supreme Court has linked climate action to Arts. 14 and 21 ( M.K. Ranjitsinh , 2024).
legalProvision: Paris Agreement, 2015 (29 Articles): Preamble – climate change is "a common concern of humankind"; human rights; intergenerational equity; "the importance for some of the concept of 'climate justice'". Art. 2 – purpose: temperature goal, adaptation, finance flows; equity and CBDR-RC "in the light of different national circumstances". Art. 3 – all Parties to undertake "ambitious efforts" showing "progression over time". Art. 4 – mitigation and NDCs. Art. 5 – sinks and forests (REDD+). Art. 6 – voluntary cooperation; market and non-market approaches. Art. 7 – adaptation. Art. 8 – loss and damage. Arts. 9–11 – finance, technology, capacity-building. Art. 12 – education and public awareness. Art. 13 – enhanced transparency framework. Art. 14 – global stocktake. Art. 15 – implementation and compliance. Art. 16 – the COP serves as the meeting of the Parties (CMA). Arts. 20–28 – signature, entry into force (55/55), no reservations, withdrawal. Parent treaty: UNFCCC, 1992 (the Agreement works "under the Convention"). Constitution of India: Arts. 14, 21, 48A, 51A(g), 253.
hi.meaning: Conference of the Parties (COP): the supreme body of the UNFCCC, which meets every year. "COP21" means its 21st meeting. Paris Agreement: a treaty adopted under the UNFCCC at COP21, which sets a long-term temperature goal and requires every Party to make and update its own national climate targets. Nationally determined contribution (NDC): a Party's own climate plan and target, which it decides for itself ("nationally determined") and must prepare, communicate and maintain under Art. 4(2). Intended NDC (INDC): the draft contribution that countries announced before and around COP21; on joining the Agreement it became the first NDC. Global stocktake: a review of the collective progress of all Parties towards the Agreement's purpose (Art. 14). Loss and damage : harm from climate change that adaptation cannot prevent, including "slow onset events" and "non-economic losses" (Art. 8). In simple words: Kyoto told rich countries what to cut; Paris lets every country set its own target, but makes all of them publish it, report on it, and raise it every five years.
keyPoints: Nationally determined contribution: every Party; every five years; each one a progression (Art. 4). Global stocktake: 2023 and every five years thereafter (Art. 14). Enhanced transparency framework: "with built-in flexibility"; reporting from 2024 (Art. 13). Loss and damage: "averting, minimizing and addressing" (Art. 8). Adopted 12-12-2015 at COP21; in force 4-11-2016; well below 2°C and 1.5°C. No reservations (Art. 27); compliance non-punitive (Art. 15).

caseLaws.facts: Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change, Advisory Opinion (International Court of Justice; 23 July 2025)

caseLaws.name: Facts: By resolution 77/276 of 29 March 2023, the UN General Assembly asked the Court what obligatio
caseLaws.facts: Principle: "The 1.5°C threshold of Article 2 is the parties' agreed primary temperature goal"; the Paris Agreement contains an "Obligation of result to prepare, communicate and maintain nationally determined contributions (NDCs)"; the "Standard of due diligence stringent."; breach leads to the "Duty of cessation and guarantees of non-repetition" and the "Duty to make reparation through restitution, compensation or satisfaction". Why it matters: It is the world court's reading of the Paris Agreement: 1.5°C is the main goal, making an NDC is a duty of result, and its content is judged by stringent due diligence.
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, 2024 INSC 280 (Supreme Court; 21 March 2024)

caseLaws.name: Facts: The Union asked the Court to modify its 2021 order protecting the Great Indian Bustard from o
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 14 and 21 "are important sources of the right to a clean environment and the right against the adverse effects of climate change"; "there is a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change." Why it matters: The Supreme Court treated India's Paris commitments as relevant to deciding a case and linked climate action to fundamental rights .
State of the Netherlands v. Urgenda Foundation, ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007 (Supreme Court of the Netherlands; 20 December 2019)

caseLaws.name: Facts: An environmental group sued the Dutch State; the lower courts ordered a reduction of emission
caseLaws.facts: Principle: Arts. 2 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights oblige a State "to take suitable measures if a real and immediate risk to people's lives or welfare exists"; "Each country is thus responsible for its own share." The State's appeal was rejected. Why it matters: It reflects the Paris idea that each country is responsible for its own share, and shows that a court can order a State to cut emissions.

en.meaning:
Why does classical international law create a structural gap for multinational corporation (MNC) liability?

Explanation. International law in its classical form binds States, not private companies, so a victim usually cannot sue an MNC before an international tribunal the way one State can arbitrate against another.

In the Bhopal Gas Tragedy litigation, why did the US court dismiss the case against Union Carbide Corporation?

Explanation. The US District Court held India was the appropriate forum since the plant, victims, and evidence were all located there, sending the case back to Indian courts.

Which Indian legislation authorised the Government of India to represent all Bhopal victims in a single consolidated claim?

Explanation. The Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, 1985 authorised the Government of India to represent all victims in a consolidated claim, leading to the 1989 settlement.

The doctrine of 'separate corporate personality' creates difficulty in MNC liability cases because:

Explanation. UNEP was established by UN General Assembly Resolution 2997 (XXVII) on 15 December 1972, following the Stockholm Conference's recommendation.

UNEP's headquarters are located in:

Explanation. UNEP is headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya.

UNEP's primary role in the international environmental regime is best described as:

Explanation. UNEP does not have direct enforcement power; its role is catalytic and coordinating, supporting the negotiation and administration of multilateral environmental agreements.

en.meaning:
Where and when was the UN Conference on the Human Environment held?

Explanation. The UN Conference on the Human Environment was held in Stockholm, Sweden, from 5 to 16 June 1972.

The Stockholm Declaration is best described as:

Explanation. The Stockholm Declaration is non-binding soft law consisting of a Preamble and 26 Principles, not a treaty.

Which institution was directly created as a result of the Stockholm Conference?

Explanation. UNEP was created by UN General Assembly Resolution 2997 (XXVII) of 15 December 1972, following the Stockholm Conference's recommendation.

The Action Plan for the Human Environment adopted at Stockholm had how many recommendations?

en.meaning:
The Convention on Biological Diversity was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit on:

Explanation. The text was adopted at Nairobi on 22 May 1992 and opened for signature at Rio de Janeiro on 5 June 1992. It came into force on 29 December 1993.

Which two binding treaties were opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit?

Explanation. The UNFCCC and the CBD were both opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992.

The Convention on Biological Diversity's three objectives are:

Explanation. Article 1 of the CBD sets out three equally-ranked objectives: conservation, sustainable use, and fair and equitable benefit-sharing.

The CBD's benefit-sharing objective was designed to directly address which problem?

en.meaning:
The Bonn Convention's correct, full title is:

Explanation. The Bonn Convention's correct title covers all migratory wild animals, not birds alone.

When was the Bonn Convention signed, and when did it enter into force?

Explanation. The Bonn Convention was signed on 23 June 1979 and entered into force on 1 November 1983 — well before 1992.

Under the Bonn Convention, species listed in Appendix I are subject to:

Explanation. Appendix I species are endangered migratory species requiring strict protection and a general prohibition on taking, subject to narrow exceptions.

How does the Bonn Convention address Appendix II species?

en.meaning:
The Paris Agreement was adopted at which Conference of the Parties, and when?

Explanation. The Paris Agreement was adopted by consensus on 12 December 2015 at COP21 in Paris.

The Paris Agreement's core structural departure from the Kyoto Protocol is its use of:

Explanation. Paris replaced Kyoto's top-down Annex I-only targets with universal, self-determined NDCs from every party.

The Paris Agreement's temperature goal is to hold the global average temperature increase to:

Explanation. The Agreement aims to hold warming well below 2°C, with efforts to pursue 1.5°C.

Under the Paris Agreement, which of these is legally binding?

The UNFCCC was opened for signature at which event, and when did it enter into force?

Explanation. The UNFCCC was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in June 1992 and entered into force on 21 March 1994.

The UNFCCC's Article 2 objective is best described as:

Explanation. Article 2 sets a qualitative objective without binding numerical targets — those came later through Kyoto and Paris.

Which principle, found in UNFCCC Article 3, states that developed countries should take the lead in combating climate change?

Explanation. CBDR-RC recognises developed countries' greater historical contribution to emissions and greater capacity to act.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t3.subtitle: Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person if he defaults. There are three persons: the surety , the principal debtor and the creditor . Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines all four terms. It also says a guarantee may be oral or written. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the three persons, and the oral or written rule.
en.meaning:
The meaning of the definition (section 126)

Rule. A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. Take the definition in parts.

It is a contract. The contract is to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person. This is to happen in case of that third person's default.

Example. Ravi borrows Rs 1 lakh from a bank in Guntur. His sister Sita tells the bank: "If Ravi does not repay, I will repay." Sita's contract with the bank is a contract to discharge the liability of a third person, Ravi, in case of his default. It is a contract of guarantee.

The three persons: surety, principal debtor and creditor

Rule. Section 126 names the three persons by their roles.

The surety is the person who gives the guarantee. The principal debtor is the person in respect of whose default the guarantee is given. The creditor is the person to whom the guarantee is given.

Example. In the example above, Sita is the surety. Ravi is the principal debtor. The bank is the creditor.

Form: oral or written

Rule. Section 126 says a guarantee may be either oral or written. The Act does not require writing.

Example. Sita could give the bank a signed letter of guarantee. She could also give the guarantee by word of mouth. Section 126 allows both.

The three persons in a guarantee How to read this: start at the top. The principal debtor owes the creditor. The surety promises the creditor to answer for the principal debtor's default. 1. The principal debtor owes a promise or liability to the creditor. 2. The surety gives the creditor a guarantee. The guarantee is to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of the principal debtor in case of his default. 3. The principal debtor defaults. The surety's guarantee comes into play (see "Rights and liabilities of Surety").
keyPoints: Section 126 defines a contract of guarantee. It is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The surety gives the guarantee. The principal debtor is the person whose default is guaranteed. The creditor is the person to whom the guarantee is given. A guarantee may be oral or written.

selfTest.q: 1. What is a contract of guarantee under section 126?
selfTest.a: A contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. 2. Who is the creditor in a guarantee? The person to whom the guarantee is given (section 126). 3. Must a guarantee be in writing? No. Section 126 says a guarantee may be either oral or written.

hi.inOneMinute: A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person if he defaults. There are three persons: the surety , the principal debtor and the creditor . Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines all four terms. It also says a guarantee may be oral or written. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the three persons, and the oral or written rule.
hi.meaning: The meaning of the definition (section 126) Rule. A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. Take the definition in parts. It is a contract. The contract is to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person. This is to happen in case of that third person's default. Example. Ravi borrows Rs 1 lakh from a bank in Guntur. His sister Sita tells the bank: "If Ravi does not repay, I will repay." Sita's contract with the bank is a contract to discharge the liability of a third person, Ravi, in case of his default. It is a contract of guarantee. The three persons: surety, principal debtor and creditor Rule. Section 126 names the three persons by their roles. The surety is the person who gives the guarantee. The principal debtor is the person in respect of whose default the guarantee is given. The creditor is the person to whom the guarantee is given. Example. In the example above, Sita is the surety. Ravi is the principal debtor. The bank is the creditor. Form: oral or written Rule. Section 126 says a guarantee may be either oral or written. The Act does not require writing. Example. Sita could give the bank a signed letter of guarantee. She could also give the guarantee by word of mouth. Section 126 allows both. The three persons in a guarantee How to read this: start at the top. The principal debtor owes the creditor. The surety promises the creditor to answer for the principal debtor's default. 1. The principal debtor owes a promise or liability to the creditor. 2. The surety gives the creditor a guarantee. The guarantee is to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of the principal debtor in case of his default. 3. The principal debtor defaults. The surety's guarantee comes into play (see "Rights and liabilities of Surety").
keyPoints: Section 126 defines a contract of guarantee. It is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The surety gives the guarantee. The principal debtor is the person whose default is guaranteed. The creditor is the person to whom the guarantee is given. A guarantee may be oral or written.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t1.subtitle: Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A contract of indemnity is a contract in which one person promises to make good the loss of another. The person who promises is the promisor . The person who is protected is the promisee . Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines it. The loss may be caused by the promisor's own conduct or by the conduct of any other person. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two sources of loss, and the Act's illustration.
en.meaning:
The meaning of the definition (section 124)

Rule. A contract of indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss. The party who promises is the promisor. The party who is promised protection is the promisee. Section 124 uses these two words.

Take the definition in parts, as you would in the exam.

It is a contract. Section 124 begins "A contract by which...". One party makes a promise. The promise is to save the other party from loss. The loss is caused to the other party by conduct. The section names whose conduct it may be (see below).

Example. Rao owns a shop in Guntur. Sita tells Rao: "If anyone takes proceedings against you over the cheque you accepted from my brother, I will make good your loss." Sita is the promisor and Rao is the promisee. The promise is to save Rao from loss, so it is a contract of indemnity.

First source of loss: the conduct of the promisor himself

Rule. The loss may be caused to the promisee by the conduct of the promisor himself. The promisor then promises to save the promisee from the results of the promisor's own acts.

Example. Kumar sells a cart-load of grain to Latha and promises: "If my earlier sale of this grain to anyone else causes you loss, I will make it good." The loss would come from Kumar's own conduct. The promise fits section 124.

Second source of loss: the conduct of any other person

Rule. The loss may be caused to the promisee by the conduct of any other person. The section says "any other person". In the Act's illustration, C is a third person.

The Act's own illustration is of this kind. A promises B protection against the consequences of proceedings that C may take against B for a sum of 200 rupees. C is a third person. The loss would come from C's conduct in taking proceedings. The Act says this is a contract of indemnity.

Example. Dev agrees to indemnify Esha against any proceedings that Farid may take against Esha for Rs 200. Farid sues Esha. The loss comes from Farid's conduct, not from Dev's. Dev's promise is still a contract of indemnity. This is the Act's own illustration with new names.

Is section 124 the whole law of indemnity?

Rule. No. Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive of the law of indemnity. The Contract Act is both an amending and a consolidating Act. It does not contain the whole law of contract applied by Indian courts ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 3).

What section 124 covers. One kind of indemnity only: a promise to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or of any other person. What it does not cover. Indemnity for loss caused by events or accidents that do not or may not depend on the conduct of the promisor or any other person. It also does not cover a liability the indemnified person incurred by doing something at the request of the indemnifier (para 3). What section 125 covers. Only the rights of the indemnity-holder when he is sued. The indemnity-holder has other rights besides those in section 125 (para 4). Application. In Gajanan Moreshwar the plaintiff became liable by doing something at the defendant's request. So the Court held that section 124 did not apply at all (para 4). Result. The Indian courts apply the same equitable principles that the courts in England apply (para 7).

When can the indemnity-holder sue?

Old common-law rule. Under English common law, the indemnity-holder could not sue until he had actually suffered loss. This was hard on him. If he was sued, he had to wait for the judgment and pay it first. If he could not pay, he could not use his indemnity at all ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 7).

The rule of equity. Equity softened this. Once the holder's liability has become absolute, he can make the indemnifier pay off the claim. He can also make the indemnifier pay enough money into Court to meet the claim when it is made (para 7).

The test used in India. The Court asks two questions. Has the indemnified person incurred a liability? Is that liability absolute? If yes to both, he can call on the indemnifier to save him from the liability and pay it off. He need not wait to suffer actual loss ( Gajanan Moreshwar , paras 5 and 7; approved in Khetarpal Amarnath , quoted in VPS Healthcare , para 19).

Absolute and contingent liability. A liability is absolute when the promisee has no answer to a claim on it, for example where he has personally promised to pay ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 8). The defendant in Gajanan Moreshwar argued that the liability was only contingent, because a sale of the mortgaged property might leave no deficit. The Court rejected this (para 8).

Absolute obligation and indemnity. A promise to take on an absolute obligation can be enforced without any actual loss. In a true indemnity, the risk of loss stays contingent. A contract of indemnity is one in which a party undertakes to save another party harmless from loss or damage arising from a particular transaction or claim ( VPS Healthcare , para 19). So the wording of the promise decides whether it is an indemnity or an absolute obligation (para 19).

Contrary decisions. Two earlier decisions had said that a suit on an indemnity before actual loss is premature: Shankar Nimbaji v. Laxman Supdu (1939) 42 Bom LR 175 and Chand Bibi v. Santoshkumar Pal (1933) ILR 60 Cal 761. Chagla J. confined the first to its own facts, where no loss could be known until the security was sold. He would not read it to mean that actual loss is always needed (para 5). He did not follow the second. He called it an unconsidered judgment, with no authorities cited, that may turn on the wording of the covenant. He preferred Osman Jamal & Sons v. Gopal Purshattam (1928) ILR 56 Cal 262, a considered decision that allowed the suit before payment (para 6). It was also conceded in Gajanan Moreshwar that such a suit would lie in England (para 7).

What the Court may order. The Court may direct the indemnifier to get the promisee released from the liability within a fixed time. If he fails, he may be directed to pay into Court the amount needed to meet it ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 10).

How to test a promise against section 124 How to read this: start at the top and answer each box. If you can answer yes to all three, the promise is a contract of indemnity under section 124. 1. Is there a contract? 2. Does one party promise to save the other from loss? That party is the promisor. The other is the promisee. 3. Is the loss caused by the promisor's own conduct, or by the conduct of any other person? If yes, it is a contract of indemnity (section 124).
keyPoints: Section 124 defines a contract of indemnity. One party promises to save the other from loss. The loss may be caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person. The party who promises is the promisor. The party protected is the promisee. The Act's illustration: A indemnifies B against proceedings C may take against B for 200 rupees. The rights of the promisee when he is sued are in section 125.

caseLaws.name: Gajanan Moreshwar Parelkar v
caseLaws.facts: Moreshwar Madan Mantri , AIR 1942 Bom 302. Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive. An indemnity-holder whose liability is absolute can sue without first suffering loss. Khetarpal Amarnath v. Madhukar Pictures (1955 SCC OnLine Bom 73). Agreed with Gajanan Moreshwar and stated the test (quoted in VPS Healthcare , para 19): has the indemnified person incurred a liability, and is it absolute? VPS Healthcare Private Limited v. Prabhat Kumar Srivastava , 2026 INSC 361. Supreme Court. Quoted that test (paras 19 and 24). Held that the promise to "ensure" that no liability is recovered points to an absolute obligation (para 19). It was a case of a liability that had already crystallised, not an indemnity that matures only on final confirmation (para 28). The promoters had to pay or deposit the amount within 30 days (para 29).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a contract of indemnity under section 124?
selfTest.a: It is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person. 2. Whose conduct may cause the loss? The conduct of the promisor himself, or the conduct of any other person (section 124). 3. In the Act's illustration, who takes the proceedings and for how much? C may take proceedings against B in respect of a certain sum of 200 rupees. A has contracted to indemnify B against the consequences. This is a contract of indemnity.

నియమం. నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందం అంటే ఒక పక్షం, మరొక పక్షాన్ని నష్టం నుండి కాపాడతానని వాగ్దానం చేసే ఒప్పందం. వాగ్దానం చేసే పక్షం వాగ్దానకర్త. రక్షణ వాగ్దానం పొందిన పక్షం వాగ్దాన గ్రహీత. సెక్షన్ 124 ఈ రెండు పదాలను వాడుతుంది.

పరీక్షలో రాసినట్లే నిర్వచనాన్ని భాగాలుగా చూడండి.

ఇది ఒక ఒప్పందం. సెక్షన్ 124 "A contract by which..." అని మొదలవుతుంది. ఒక పక్షం వాగ్దానం చేస్తుంది. ఆ వాగ్దానం, ఇతర పక్షాన్ని నష్టం నుండి కాపాడతానని. ఇతర పక్షానికి నష్టం ఒక చర్య వల్ల కలుగుతుంది. ఆ చర్య ఎవరిదై ఉండవచ్చో సెక్షన్ చెబుతుంది (కింద చూడండి).

ఉదాహరణ. రావు గుంటూరులో ఒక దుకాణం యజమాని. సీత రావుతో ఇలా అంది: "నా తమ్ముడి నుండి మీరు తీసుకున్న చెక్కు విషయంలో ఎవరైనా మీపై చర్యలు తీసుకుంటే, మీ నష్టాన్ని నేను భర్తీ చేస్తాను." సీత వాగ్దానకర్త, రావు వాగ్దాన గ్రహీత. వాగ్దానం రావును నష్టం నుండి కాపాడడానికే, కాబట్టి ఇది నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందం.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 124 ప్రకారం నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఒక పక్షం, మరొక పక్షాన్ని వాగ్దానకర్త సొంత చర్య వల్ల గానీ, మరే ఇతర వ్యక్తి చర్య వల్ల గానీ కలిగే నష్టం నుండి కాపాడతానని వాగ్దానం చేసే ఒప్పందం. 2. నష్టం ఎవరి చర్య వల్ల కలగవచ్చు? వాగ్దానకర్త సొంత చర్య వల్ల, లేదా మరే ఇతర వ్యక్తి చర్య వల్ల (సెక్షన్ 124). 3. చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణలో ఎవరు, ఎంత మొత్తం విషయంలో చర్యలు తీసుకుంటారు? C, B పై 200 రూపాయల నిర్దిష్ట మొత్తం విషయంలో చర్యలు తీసుకోవచ్చు. వాటి పర్యవసానాల నుండి B ని కాపాడతానని A ఒప్పందం చేశాడు. ఇది నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందం.

hi.inOneMinute: A contract of indemnity is a contract in which one person promises to make good the loss of another. The person who promises is the promisor . The person who is protected is the promisee . Section 124 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines it. The loss may be caused by the promisor's own conduct or by the conduct of any other person. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two sources of loss, and the Act's illustration.
hi.meaning: The meaning of the definition (section 124) Rule. A contract of indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss. The party who promises is the promisor. The party who is promised protection is the promisee. Section 124 uses these two words. Take the definition in parts, as you would in the exam. It is a contract. Section 124 begins "A contract by which...". One party makes a promise. The promise is to save the other party from loss. The loss is caused to the other party by conduct. The section names whose conduct it may be (see below). Example. Rao owns a shop in Guntur. Sita tells Rao: "If anyone takes proceedings against you over the cheque you accepted from my brother, I will make good your loss." Sita is the promisor and Rao is the promisee. The promise is to save Rao from loss, so it is a contract of indemnity. First source of loss: the conduct of the promisor himself Rule. The loss may be caused to the promisee by the conduct of the promisor himself. The promisor then promises to save the promisee from the results of the promisor's own acts. Example. Kumar sells a cart-load of grain to Latha and promises: "If my earlier sale of this grain to anyone else causes you loss, I will make it good." The loss would come from Kumar's own conduct. The promise fits section 124. Second source of loss: the conduct of any other person Rule. The loss may be caused to the promisee by the conduct of any other person. The section says "any other person". In the Act's illustration, C is a third person. The Act's own illustration is of this kind. A promises B protection against the consequences of proceedings that C may take against B for a sum of 200 rupees. C is a third person. The loss would come from C's conduct in taking proceedings. The Act says this is a contract of indemnity. Example. Dev agrees to indemnify Esha against any proceedings that Farid may take against Esha for Rs 200. Farid sues Esha. The loss comes from Farid's conduct, not from Dev's. Dev's promise is still a contract of indemnity. This is the Act's own illustration with new names. Is section 124 the whole law of indemnity? Rule. No. Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive of the law of indemnity. The Contract Act is both an amending and a consolidating Act. It does not contain the whole law of contract applied by Indian courts ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 3). What section 124 covers. One kind of indemnity only: a promise to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor or of any other person. What it does not cover. Indemnity for loss caused by events or accidents that do not or may not depend on the conduct of the promisor or any other person. It also does not cover a liability the indemnified person incurred by doing something at the request of the indemnifier (para 3). What section 125 covers. Only the rights of the indemnity-holder when he is sued. The indemnity-holder has other rights besides those in section 125 (para 4). Application. In Gajanan Moreshwar the plaintiff became liable by doing something at the defendant's request. So the Court held that section 124 did not apply at all (para 4). Result. The Indian courts apply the same equitable principles that the courts in England apply (para 7). When can the indemnity-holder sue? Old common-law rule. Under English common law, the indemnity-holder could not sue until he had actually suffered loss. This was hard on him. If he was sued, he had to wait for the judgment and pay it first. If he could not pay, he could not use his indemnity at all ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 7). The rule of equity. Equity softened this. Once the holder's liability has become absolute, he can make the indemnifier pay off the claim. He can also make the indemnifier pay enough money into Court to meet the claim when it is made (para 7). The test used in India. The Court asks two questions. Has the indemnified person incurred a liability? Is that liability absolute? If yes to both, he can call on the indemnifier to save him from the liability and pay it off. He need not wait to suffer actual loss ( Gajanan Moreshwar , paras 5 and 7; approved in Khetarpal Amarnath , quoted in VPS Healthcare , para 19). Absolute and contingent liability. A liability is absolute when the promisee has no answer to a claim on it, for example where he has personally promised to pay ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 8). The defendant in Gajanan Moreshwar argued that the liability was only contingent, because a sale of the mortgaged property might leave no deficit. The Court rejected this (para 8). Absolute obligation and indemnity. A promise to take on an absolute obligation can be enforced without any actual loss. In a true indemnity, the risk of loss stays contingent. A contract of indemnity is one in which a party undertakes to save another party harmless from loss or damage arising from a particular transaction or claim ( VPS Healthcare , para 19). So the wording of the promise decides whether it is an indemnity or an absolute obligation (para 19). Contrary decisions. Two earlier decisions had said that a suit on an indemnity before actual loss is premature: Shankar Nimbaji v. Laxman Supdu (1939) 42 Bom LR 175 and Chand Bibi v. Santoshkumar Pal (1933) ILR 60 Cal 761. Chagla J. confined the first to its own facts, where no loss could be known until the security was sold. He would not read it to mean that actual loss is always needed (para 5). He did not follow the second. He called it an unconsidered judgment, with no authorities cited, that may turn on the wording of the covenant. He preferred Osman Jamal & Sons v. Gopal Purshattam (1928) ILR 56 Cal 262, a considered decision that allowed the suit before payment (para 6). It was also conceded in Gajanan Moreshwar that such a suit would lie in England (para 7). What the Court may order. The Court may direct the indemnifier to get the promisee released from the liability within a fixed time. If he fails, he may be directed to pay into Court the amount needed to meet it ( Gajanan Moreshwar , para 10). How to test a promise against section 124 How to read this: start at the top and answer each box. If you can answer yes to all three, the promise is a contract of indemnity under section 124. 1. Is there a contract? 2. Does one party promise to save the other from loss? That party is the promisor. The other is the promisee. 3. Is the loss caused by the promisor's own conduct, or by the conduct of any other person? If yes, it is a contract of indemnity (section 124).
keyPoints: Section 124 defines a contract of indemnity. One party promises to save the other from loss. The loss may be caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person. The party who promises is the promisor. The party protected is the promisee. The Act's illustration: A indemnifies B against proceedings C may take against B for 200 rupees. The rights of the promisee when he is sued are in section 125.

caseLaws.name: Gajanan Moreshwar Parelkar v
caseLaws.facts: Moreshwar Madan Mantri , AIR 1942 Bom 302. Sections 124 and 125 are not exhaustive. An indemnity-holder whose liability is absolute can sue without first suffering loss. Khetarpal Amarnath v. Madhukar Pictures (1955 SCC OnLine Bom 73). Agreed with Gajanan Moreshwar and stated the test (quoted in VPS Healthcare , para 19): has the indemnified person incurred a liability, and is it absolute? VPS Healthcare Private Limited v. Prabhat Kumar Srivastava , 2026 INSC 361. Supreme Court. Quoted that test (paras 19 and 24). Held that the promise to "ensure" that no liability is recovered points to an absolute obligation (para 19). It was a case of a liability that had already crystallised, not an indemnity that matures only on final confirmation (para 28). The promoters had to pay or deposit the amount within 30 days (para 29).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a contract of indemnity under section 124?
selfTest.a: It is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person. 2. Whose conduct may cause the loss? The conduct of the promisor himself, or the conduct of any other person (section 124). 3. In the Act's illustration, who takes the proceedings and for how much? C may take proceedings against B in respect of a certain sum of 200 rupees. A has contracted to indemnify B against the consequences. This is a contract of indemnity.
