law-of-contract-ii-u1-t2.subtitle: Section 125 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: In a contract of indemnity, the person who is protected is the promisee. He is also called the indemnity-holder. Section 125 gives him three rights against the promisor when he is sued. He can recover the damages he is compelled to pay, the costs he is compelled to pay, and the sums he paid under a compromise. The first right has no extra condition. The second and third rights depend on conditions. Key points for the answer: the opening words "acting within the scope of his authority", the three clauses, and the conditions on costs and compromise.
en.meaning:
The opening words: "acting within the scope of his authority"

Rule. Section 125 gives the three rights to a promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". The rights are therefore for a promisee who acts within his authority.

The section does not define "scope of his authority" in other words.

Right 1: damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1)

Rule. The promisee can recover all damages which he may be compelled to pay in any suit. The damages must be in respect of a matter to which the promise to indemnify applies. Clause (1) has no condition about the promisor's orders or about prudence.

Example. Ravi promises Meena: "If anyone sues you over the stock you bought through my broker, I will indemnify you." A supplier sues Meena over that stock. The court orders Meena to pay Rs 50,000 as damages. The suit is about the matter the promise covers. Meena can recover the Rs 50,000 from Ravi under clause (1).

Right 2: costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2)

Rule. The promisee can recover all costs which he may be compelled to pay in the suit. Clause (2) lets him recover costs in two cases.

He did not contravene the orders of the promisor in bringing or defending the suit, and he acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to bring or defend the suit.

Example. The supplier sues Meena. Ravi had authorized her to defend the suit. She defends it, loses, and is ordered to pay Rs 5,000 as costs. She can recover the Rs 5,000 because the promisor authorized her to defend. Suppose instead that Ravi had told her not to defend, and she defended anyway. She would have contravened his orders, so the first case in clause (2) would not help her.

Right 3: sums paid under a compromise (clause 3)

Rule. The promisee can recover all sums which he may have paid under the terms of any compromise of the suit. Clause (3) lets him recover in two cases.

The compromise was not contrary to the orders of the promisor, and it was one which it would have been prudent for the promisee to make in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to compromise the suit.

Example. The supplier's claim against Meena is Rs 50,000. Ravi has not given any orders. Meena settles for Rs 30,000, a figure a careful person would have accepted even without an indemnity. The compromise was not contrary to Ravi's orders. She can recover the Rs 30,000 under clause (3).

What can the promisee recover under section 125? How to read this: start at the top. The promisee has been sued on a matter the promise covers. Then check each kind of sum. 1. The promisee, acting within the scope of his authority, is sued on a matter the promise to indemnify applies to. 2. Damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1). Recoverable. No extra condition in the clause. 3. Costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2). Recoverable if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. 4. Sums paid under a compromise (clause 3). Recoverable if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it.
keyPoints: Section 125 gives rights to the promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". Clause (1): all damages he is compelled to pay in the suit, on a matter the promise covers. Clause (2): costs, if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. Clause (3): compromise sums, if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it. The test of prudence is what he would do "in the absence of any contract of indemnity". The definition of a contract of indemnity is in section 124.

caseLaws.facts: The 15-mark question of May 2018 needs a judgment on whether sections 124 and 125 are exhaustive. That judgment has to be found in an official source and read before a case is added. Until then, the text of section 125 is the authority for the 6-mark answer.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section gives the rights of the promisee in a contract of indemnity when he is sued?
selfTest.a: Section 125 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. 2. When can the promisee recover costs under section 125? When he did not contravene the promisor's orders in bringing or defending the suit and acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity, or when the promisor authorized him to bring or defend the suit (clause 2). 3. Does clause (1) on damages have a test of prudence? No. Clause (1) covers all damages he is compelled to pay in the suit, in respect of any matter to which the promise to indemnify applies.

te.inOneMinute: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 లోని సెక్షన్ 125 — నష్టపూరణ హక్కుదారు హక్కులు
te.meaning:
నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందంలో రక్షణ పొందే వ్యక్తి వాగ్దాన గ్రహీత (promisee). అతడినే నష్టపూరణ హక్కుదారు (indemnity-holder) అని కూడా అంటారు. అతడిపై దావా వేసినప్పుడు, వాగ్దానకర్త (promisor) పై అతడికి సెక్షన్ 125 మూడు హక్కులు ఇస్తుంది.

అతడు చెల్లించాల్సి వచ్చిన నష్టపరిహారం, చెల్లించాల్సి వచ్చిన ఖర్చులు, రాజీ ప్రకారం చెల్లించిన మొత్తాలను రాబట్టుకోవచ్చు. మొదటి హక్కుకు అదనపు షరతు లేదు. రెండవ, మూడవ హక్కులు షరతులపై ఆధారపడతాయి. సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: "acting within the scope of his authority" అనే ప్రారంభ మాటలు, మూడు క్లాజులు, ఖర్చులు, రాజీపై షరతులు.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందం నిర్వచనం సెక్షన్ 124 లో ఉంది. అది "Indemnity and Guarantee-Contract of Indemnity, definition" అంశం.

నియమం. సెక్షన్ 125 మూడు హక్కులను "acting within the scope of his authority" వ్యవహరించే వాగ్దాన గ్రహీతకు ఇస్తుంది. అంటే తన అధికార పరిధిలో వ్యవహరించే వాగ్దాన గ్రహీతకే ఈ హక్కులు.

"scope of his authority" అనే మాటను సెక్షన్ మరో విధంగా నిర్వచించదు.

నియమం. దావాలో అతడు చెల్లించాల్సి వచ్చిన నష్టపరిహారం అంతా వాగ్దాన గ్రహీత రాబట్టుకోవచ్చు. ఆ నష్టపరిహారం నష్టపూరణ వాగ్దానం వర్తించే విషయానికి సంబంధించినదై ఉండాలి. క్లాజు (1) లో వాగ్దానకర్త ఆదేశాల గురించి గానీ, వివేకం గురించి గానీ షరతు లేదు.

selfTest.q: 1. నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందంలో వాగ్దాన గ్రహీతపై దావా వేసినప్పుడు అతడి హక్కులను ఏ సెక్షన్ ఇస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 సెక్షన్ 125. 2. సెక్షన్ 125 కింద వాగ్దాన గ్రహీత ఖర్చులను ఎప్పుడు రాబట్టుకోవచ్చు? దావా వేయడంలో లేదా ఎదుర్కోవడంలో అతడు వాగ్దానకర్త ఆదేశాలను ఉల్లంఘించకుండా, నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందం లేకపోయినా వివేకంతో ఎలా వ్యవహరించాలో అలా వ్యవహరించి ఉంటే, లేదా దావా వేయడానికి లేదా ఎదుర్కోవడానికి వాగ్దానకర్త అనుమతి ఇచ్చి ఉంటే (క్లాజు 2). 3. నష్టపరిహారంపై క్లాజు (1) కు వివేకం పరీక్ష ఉందా? లేదు. క్లాజు (1) నష్టపూరణ వాగ్దానం వర్తించే ఏ విషయంలోనైనా దావాలో అతడు చెల్లించాల్సి వచ్చిన నష్టపరిహారం అంతా కవర్ చేస్తుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: In a contract of indemnity, the person who is protected is the promisee. He is also called the indemnity-holder. Section 125 gives him three rights against the promisor when he is sued. He can recover the damages he is compelled to pay, the costs he is compelled to pay, and the sums he paid under a compromise. The first right has no extra condition. The second and third rights depend on conditions. Key points for the answer: the opening words "acting within the scope of his authority", the three clauses, and the conditions on costs and compromise.
hi.meaning: The opening words: "acting within the scope of his authority" Rule. Section 125 gives the three rights to a promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". The rights are therefore for a promisee who acts within his authority. The section does not define "scope of his authority" in other words. Right 1: damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1) Rule. The promisee can recover all damages which he may be compelled to pay in any suit. The damages must be in respect of a matter to which the promise to indemnify applies. Clause (1) has no condition about the promisor's orders or about prudence. Example. Ravi promises Meena: "If anyone sues you over the stock you bought through my broker, I will indemnify you." A supplier sues Meena over that stock. The court orders Meena to pay Rs 50,000 as damages. The suit is about the matter the promise covers. Meena can recover the Rs 50,000 from Ravi under clause (1). Right 2: costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2) Rule. The promisee can recover all costs which he may be compelled to pay in the suit. Clause (2) lets him recover costs in two cases. He did not contravene the orders of the promisor in bringing or defending the suit, and he acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to bring or defend the suit. Example. The supplier sues Meena. Ravi had authorized her to defend the suit. She defends it, loses, and is ordered to pay Rs 5,000 as costs. She can recover the Rs 5,000 because the promisor authorized her to defend. Suppose instead that Ravi had told her not to defend, and she defended anyway. She would have contravened his orders, so the first case in clause (2) would not help her. Right 3: sums paid under a compromise (clause 3) Rule. The promisee can recover all sums which he may have paid under the terms of any compromise of the suit. Clause (3) lets him recover in two cases. The compromise was not contrary to the orders of the promisor, and it was one which it would have been prudent for the promisee to make in the absence of any contract of indemnity. The promisor authorized him to compromise the suit. Example. The supplier's claim against Meena is Rs 50,000. Ravi has not given any orders. Meena settles for Rs 30,000, a figure a careful person would have accepted even without an indemnity. The compromise was not contrary to Ravi's orders. She can recover the Rs 30,000 under clause (3). What can the promisee recover under section 125? How to read this: start at the top. The promisee has been sued on a matter the promise covers. Then check each kind of sum. 1. The promisee, acting within the scope of his authority, is sued on a matter the promise to indemnify applies to. 2. Damages he is compelled to pay (clause 1). Recoverable. No extra condition in the clause. 3. Costs he is compelled to pay (clause 2). Recoverable if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. 4. Sums paid under a compromise (clause 3). Recoverable if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it.
keyPoints: Section 125 gives rights to the promisee "acting within the scope of his authority". Clause (1): all damages he is compelled to pay in the suit, on a matter the promise covers. Clause (2): costs, if he did not contravene the promisor's orders and acted prudently, or if the promisor authorized the suit. Clause (3): compromise sums, if the compromise was not contrary to the promisor's orders and was prudent, or if the promisor authorized it. The test of prudence is what he would do "in the absence of any contract of indemnity". The definition of a contract of indemnity is in section 124.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section gives the rights of the promisee in a contract of indemnity when he is sued?
selfTest.a: Section 125 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. 2. When can the promisee recover costs under section 125? When he did not contravene the promisor's orders in bringing or defending the suit and acted as it would have been prudent for him to act in the absence of any contract of indemnity, or when the promisor authorized him to bring or defend the suit (clause 2). 3. Does clause (1) on damages have a test of prudence? No. Clause (1) covers all damages he is compelled to pay in the suit, in respect of any matter to which the promise to indemnify applies.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t4.subtitle: Sections 126, 127, 142, 143 and 144 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 does not list the essentials of a guarantee in one place. They come from several sections. A guarantee is a contract to answer for a third person's default (section 126). It needs consideration (section 127). It is invalid if the creditor obtained it by misrepresentation or by keeping silent about material circumstances (sections 142 and 143). Key points for the answer: the third person's default, the three persons, consideration under section 127 with its illustrations, and the invalidity rules in sections 142 to 144.
en.meaning:
Characteristic 1: a contract about a third person's default (section 126)

Rule. A guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The third person is the principal debtor.

Example. Ravi borrows Rs 1 lakh from a bank. His sister Sita promises the bank to repay if Ravi does not. This is a contract about a third person's default.

Characteristic 2: three persons and any form (section 126)

Rule. A guarantee has a surety, a principal debtor and a creditor. It may be oral or written.

Example. In the example above, Sita is the surety, Ravi the principal debtor and the bank the creditor. Sita may give the guarantee in a signed letter or by word of mouth.

Characteristic 3: consideration (section 127)

Rule. Anything done, or any promise made, for the benefit of the principal debtor, may be a sufficient consideration to the surety for giving the guarantee. The section speaks of a benefit to the principal debtor.

The Act gives three illustrations.

Illustration (a): B asks A to sell and deliver goods to him on credit. A agrees, provided C will guarantee payment of the price. C promises in consideration of A's promise to deliver the goods. This is sufficient consideration for C's promise. Illustration (b): A sells and delivers goods to B. C afterwards asks A to forbear to sue B for the debt for a year, and promises to pay if B does not. A agrees to forbear. This is sufficient consideration for C's promise. Illustration (c): A sells and delivers goods to B. C afterwards, without consideration, agrees to pay for them if B defaults. The agreement is void.

Example. Hema delivers goods to Gopi on credit because Ibrahim promises to pay if Gopi does not. Hema's delivery is for the benefit of Gopi, the principal debtor. It is sufficient consideration for Ibrahim's guarantee.

Characteristic 4: no misrepresentation by the creditor (section 142)

Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by misrepresentation concerning a material part of the transaction. The misrepresentation must have been made by the creditor, or with his knowledge and assent.

Example. A creditor tells Chandu that the principal debtor's shop is free of debt, knowing it is not. Chandu gives a guarantee on that statement. The guarantee is invalid under section 142.

Characteristic 5: no concealment by the creditor (section 143)

Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by keeping silence as to material circumstances.

The Act gives two illustrations.

Illustration (a): A engages B as clerk to collect money. B fails to account for some of his receipts, so A asks him to furnish security. C guarantees B's duly accounting. A does not tell C about B's previous conduct. B makes default. The guarantee is invalid. Illustration (b): A guarantees to C payment for iron to be supplied to B, to the amount of 2,000 tons. B and C have privately agreed that B should pay five rupees per ton beyond the market price, the excess to pay off an old debt. This agreement is concealed from A. A is not liable as a surety.

Characteristic 6: a guarantee on a condition about a co-surety (section 144)

Rule. Where a person gives a guarantee on a contract that the creditor shall not act on it until another person has joined as co-surety, the guarantee is not valid if that other person does not join.

Example. Kiran agrees to guarantee a loan to Lata, on the condition that the bank does not act on it until Mohan also joins as co-surety. Mohan never joins. Kiran's guarantee is not valid.

Checking a guarantee How to read this: start at the top and go down. A "no" at any box may make the guarantee invalid or void. 1. Is it a contract to answer for a third person's default (section 126)? 2. Is there consideration for the benefit of the principal debtor (section 127)? Where goods are already delivered and the promise has no consideration, the agreement is void (illustration (c)). 3. Did the creditor obtain it without misrepresentation (section 142) and without concealment (section 143)? Otherwise it is invalid. 4. If it was given on a co-surety condition, did the co-surety join (section 144)? Otherwise it is not valid.
keyPoints: A guarantee is a contract about a third person's default (section 126). Three persons: surety, principal debtor, creditor. It may be oral or written. Consideration: anything done or promised for the principal debtor's benefit is enough (section 127). A guarantee after delivery, with no consideration, is void (illustration (c) to section 127). Misrepresentation by the creditor makes it invalid (section 142). So does keeping silence as to material circumstances (section 143). A co-surety condition that is not met makes it not valid (section 144).

selfTest.q: 1. Whose benefit counts as consideration for the surety's guarantee under section 127?
selfTest.a: The benefit of the principal debtor. Anything done, or any promise made, for his benefit may be sufficient consideration to the surety. 2. Which section makes a guarantee obtained by keeping silence as to material circumstances invalid? Section 143. 3. C, without consideration, agrees to pay for goods already delivered to B, if B defaults. What is the effect? The agreement is void (illustration (c) to section 127).

te.inOneMinute: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 లోని సెక్షన్లు 126, 127, 142, 143, 144 — హామీ ఒప్పందం ముఖ్య లక్షణాలు
te.meaning:
భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 హామీ ముఖ్య లక్షణాలను ఒకే చోట జాబితాగా ఇవ్వదు. అవి అనేక సెక్షన్ల నుండి వస్తాయి. హామీ అంటే మూడో వ్యక్తి విఫలమైతే బాధ్యత వహించే ఒప్పందం (సెక్షన్ 126). దానికి ప్రతిఫలం (consideration) కావాలి (సెక్షన్ 127). రుణదాత తప్పుడు ప్రకటన చేసి, లేదా ముఖ్యమైన పరిస్థితుల గురించి మౌనంగా ఉండి హామీ పొందితే అది చెల్లదు (సెక్షన్లు 142, 143).

సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: మూడో వ్యక్తి విఫలం కావడం, ముగ్గురు వ్యక్తులు, సెక్షన్ 127 లోని ప్రతిఫలం, దాని ఉదాహరణలు, సెక్షన్లు 142 నుండి 144 లోని చెల్లని హామీ నియమాలు.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

హామీదారు బాధ్యత పరిధి (సెక్షన్ 128), హామీదారు హక్కులు "Rights and liabilities of Surety" అంశంలో ఉన్నాయి.

నియమం. హామీ అంటే మూడో వ్యక్తి విఫలమైతే అతడి వాగ్దానాన్ని నెరవేర్చడానికి లేదా అతడి బాధ్యతను తీర్చడానికి చేసే ఒప్పందం. ఆ మూడో వ్యక్తి ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత.

ఉదాహరణ. రవి ఒక బ్యాంకు నుండి రూ. 1 లక్ష అప్పు తీసుకున్నాడు. రవి చెల్లించకపోతే తాను చెల్లిస్తానని అతడి సోదరి సీత బ్యాంకుకు వాగ్దానం చేసింది. ఇది మూడో వ్యక్తి విఫలం కావడం గురించిన ఒప్పందం.

నియమం. హామీలో హామీదారు, ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత, రుణదాత ఉంటారు. అది మౌఖికంగా లేదా వ్రాతపూర్వకంగా ఉండవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 127 ప్రకారం హామీదారు ఇచ్చే హామీకి ప్రతిఫలంగా ఎవరి ప్రయోజనం లెక్కలోకి వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత ప్రయోజనం. అతడి ప్రయోజనం కోసం చేసిన ఏ పనైనా, చేసిన ఏ వాగ్దానమైనా హామీదారుకు సరిపోయే ప్రతిఫలం కావచ్చు. 2. ముఖ్యమైన పరిస్థితుల గురించి మౌనంగా ఉండి పొందిన హామీని ఏ సెక్షన్ చెల్లనిదిగా చేస్తుంది? సెక్షన్ 143. 3. B కి ఇప్పటికే డెలివరీ అయిన సరుకులకు, B విఫలమైతే C ప్రతిఫలం లేకుండా చెల్లిస్తానని అంగీకరించాడు. దాని ప్రభావం ఏమిటి? ఆ ఒప్పందం శూన్యం (సెక్షన్ 127 కింద ఉదాహరణ (c)).

hi.inOneMinute: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 does not list the essentials of a guarantee in one place. They come from several sections. A guarantee is a contract to answer for a third person's default (section 126). It needs consideration (section 127). It is invalid if the creditor obtained it by misrepresentation or by keeping silent about material circumstances (sections 142 and 143). Key points for the answer: the third person's default, the three persons, consideration under section 127 with its illustrations, and the invalidity rules in sections 142 to 144.
hi.meaning: Characteristic 1: a contract about a third person's default (section 126) Rule. A guarantee is a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. The third person is the principal debtor. Example. Ravi borrows Rs 1 lakh from a bank. His sister Sita promises the bank to repay if Ravi does not. This is a contract about a third person's default. Characteristic 2: three persons and any form (section 126) Rule. A guarantee has a surety, a principal debtor and a creditor. It may be oral or written. Example. In the example above, Sita is the surety, Ravi the principal debtor and the bank the creditor. Sita may give the guarantee in a signed letter or by word of mouth. Characteristic 3: consideration (section 127) Rule. Anything done, or any promise made, for the benefit of the principal debtor, may be a sufficient consideration to the surety for giving the guarantee. The section speaks of a benefit to the principal debtor. The Act gives three illustrations. Illustration (a): B asks A to sell and deliver goods to him on credit. A agrees, provided C will guarantee payment of the price. C promises in consideration of A's promise to deliver the goods. This is sufficient consideration for C's promise. Illustration (b): A sells and delivers goods to B. C afterwards asks A to forbear to sue B for the debt for a year, and promises to pay if B does not. A agrees to forbear. This is sufficient consideration for C's promise. Illustration (c): A sells and delivers goods to B. C afterwards, without consideration, agrees to pay for them if B defaults. The agreement is void. Example. Hema delivers goods to Gopi on credit because Ibrahim promises to pay if Gopi does not. Hema's delivery is for the benefit of Gopi, the principal debtor. It is sufficient consideration for Ibrahim's guarantee. Characteristic 4: no misrepresentation by the creditor (section 142) Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by misrepresentation concerning a material part of the transaction. The misrepresentation must have been made by the creditor, or with his knowledge and assent. Example. A creditor tells Chandu that the principal debtor's shop is free of debt, knowing it is not. Chandu gives a guarantee on that statement. The guarantee is invalid under section 142. Characteristic 5: no concealment by the creditor (section 143) Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by keeping silence as to material circumstances. The Act gives two illustrations. Illustration (a): A engages B as clerk to collect money. B fails to account for some of his receipts, so A asks him to furnish security. C guarantees B's duly accounting. A does not tell C about B's previous conduct. B makes default. The guarantee is invalid. Illustration (b): A guarantees to C payment for iron to be supplied to B, to the amount of 2,000 tons. B and C have privately agreed that B should pay five rupees per ton beyond the market price, the excess to pay off an old debt. This agreement is concealed from A. A is not liable as a surety. Characteristic 6: a guarantee on a condition about a co-surety (section 144) Rule. Where a person gives a guarantee on a contract that the creditor shall not act on it until another person has joined as co-surety, the guarantee is not valid if that other person does not join. Example. Kiran agrees to guarantee a loan to Lata, on the condition that the bank does not act on it until Mohan also joins as co-surety. Mohan never joins. Kiran's guarantee is not valid. Checking a guarantee How to read this: start at the top and go down. A "no" at any box may make the guarantee invalid or void. 1. Is it a contract to answer for a third person's default (section 126)? 2. Is there consideration for the benefit of the principal debtor (section 127)? Where goods are already delivered and the promise has no consideration, the agreement is void (illustration (c)). 3. Did the creditor obtain it without misrepresentation (section 142) and without concealment (section 143)? Otherwise it is invalid. 4. If it was given on a co-surety condition, did the co-surety join (section 144)? Otherwise it is not valid.
keyPoints: A guarantee is a contract about a third person's default (section 126). Three persons: surety, principal debtor, creditor. It may be oral or written. Consideration: anything done or promised for the principal debtor's benefit is enough (section 127). A guarantee after delivery, with no consideration, is void (illustration (c) to section 127). Misrepresentation by the creditor makes it invalid (section 142). So does keeping silence as to material circumstances (section 143). A co-surety condition that is not met makes it not valid (section 144).

selfTest.q: 1. Whose benefit counts as consideration for the surety's guarantee under section 127?
selfTest.a: The benefit of the principal debtor. Anything done, or any promise made, for his benefit may be sufficient consideration to the surety. 2. Which section makes a guarantee obtained by keeping silence as to material circumstances invalid? Section 143. 3. C, without consideration, agrees to pay for goods already delivered to B, if B defaults. What is the effect? The agreement is void (illustration (c) to section 127).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t6.subtitle: Sections 129, 130 and 131 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 names one kind of guarantee: the continuing guarantee. A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is a continuing guarantee (section 129). The surety may revoke it by notice to the creditor, as to future transactions (section 130). The death of the surety also revokes it, as to future transactions, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Key points for the answer: the definition, the Act's illustrations, and the two ways of revocation with their effect.
en.meaning:
What is a continuing guarantee? (section 129)

Rule. A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is a continuing guarantee. The test is whether the guarantee extends to a series of transactions.

The Act's illustrations show the test at work.

In illustration (a), the guarantee covers the collection and payment of rents. This is a continuing guarantee. In illustration (b), the guarantee covers any tea supplied from time to time. It is a continuing guarantee, so A is liable up to £100 for the later supply of £200. In illustration (c), the guarantee covers the price of five sacks of flour to be delivered by B to C. It is not a continuing guarantee, so A is not liable for the later four sacks.

Example. Anil guarantees payment to Babu, a rice dealer in Guntur, of up to Rs 50,000 for any rice Babu supplies to Chandu from time to time. The guarantee covers a series of supplies. It is a continuing guarantee.

The other side: a guarantee that is not continuing

Rule. A guarantee which does not extend to a series of transactions is not a continuing guarantee. Illustration (c) to section 129 shows one. The 2017 paper calls such a guarantee a "simple guarantee". The Act does not use that label.

Example. Dev guarantees payment of the price of one consignment of cement that Esha will deliver to Farid. This covers one transaction. It is not a continuing guarantee.

Revocation by notice (section 130)

Rule. A continuing guarantee may at any time be revoked by the surety, as to future transactions, by notice to the creditor. The effect is limited to future transactions. Past transactions remain covered.

The Act's illustrations show this.

In illustration (a), A revokes after B has discounted bills for 2,000 rupees. A is discharged from liability for any later discount. A is still liable for the 2,000 rupees if C defaults. In illustration (b), B has already drawn on C and C has accepted the bill before A gives notice of revocation. C dishonours the bill at maturity. A is liable.

Example. In the rice example, Anil gives notice to Babu after Babu has supplied rice worth Rs 20,000. Rice supplied after the notice is no longer covered. Anil remains liable for the Rs 20,000 if Chandu defaults on it.

Revocation by the surety's death (section 131)

Rule. The death of the surety operates as a revocation of a continuing guarantee, as regards future transactions. This is so in the absence of any contract to the contrary. The guarantee may say otherwise.

Example. Anil dies. Babu then supplies rice to Chandu. The guarantee is revoked as to that future supply, unless the guarantee contract says otherwise.

Revoking a continuing guarantee How to read this: start at the top. Check whether the guarantee is continuing. Then check the way of revocation and its effect. 1. Does the guarantee extend to a series of transactions (section 129)? Yes: it is a continuing guarantee. No: it is not. 2. The surety gives notice to the creditor (section 130), or the surety dies (section 131). 3. Effect: the guarantee is revoked as to future transactions. Transactions already made stay covered (section 130, illustrations).
keyPoints: A continuing guarantee extends to a series of transactions (section 129). The surety may revoke it by notice to the creditor, as to future transactions (section 130). The surety's death revokes it as to future transactions, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Revocation does not affect transactions already made (illustrations to section 130). The Act names only the continuing guarantee. It does not use the label "simple guarantee".

selfTest.q: 1. What is a continuing guarantee?
selfTest.a: A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions (section 129). 2. How can the surety revoke a continuing guarantee? At any time, as to future transactions, by notice to the creditor (section 130). 3. What is the effect of the surety's death on a continuing guarantee? In the absence of any contract to the contrary, it revokes the guarantee as regards future transactions (section 131).

te.inOneMinute: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 లోని సెక్షన్లు 129, 130, 131 — హామీ రకాలు
te.meaning:
భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 ఒకే ఒక రకం హామీకి పేరు పెడుతుంది: కొనసాగే హామీ (continuing guarantee). వరుస లావాదేవీలకు విస్తరించే హామీయే కొనసాగే హామీ (సెక్షన్ 129).

హామీదారు రుణదాతకు నోటీసు ఇచ్చి, భవిష్యత్ లావాదేవీల విషయంలో దాన్ని ఉపసంహరించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 130). హామీదారు మరణం కూడా, ఒప్పందం వేరే చెప్పకపోతే, భవిష్యత్ లావాదేవీల విషయంలో దాన్ని ఉపసంహరిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 131). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: నిర్వచనం, చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణలు, రెండు ఉపసంహరణ మార్గాలు, వాటి ప్రభావం.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. వరుస లావాదేవీలకు విస్తరించే హామీ కొనసాగే హామీ. హామీ వరుస లావాదేవీలకు విస్తరిస్తుందా అనేదే పరీక్ష.

చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణలు ఈ పరీక్షను చూపిస్తాయి.

ఉదాహరణ. గుంటూరులో బియ్యం డీలర్ బాబు, చందుకు ఎప్పటికప్పుడు సరఫరా చేసే ఏ బియ్యానికైనా రూ. 50,000 వరకు చెల్లింపునకు అనిల్ హామీ ఇచ్చాడు. ఈ హామీ వరుస సరఫరాలను కవర్ చేస్తుంది. ఇది కొనసాగే హామీ.

నియమం. వరుస లావాదేవీలకు విస్తరించని హామీ కొనసాగే హామీ కాదు. సెక్షన్ 129 కింద ఉదాహరణ (c) ఒకదాన్ని చూపిస్తుంది. 2017 పేపర్ అటువంటి హామీని "simple guarantee" అని పిలుస్తుంది. చట్టం ఆ పేరును వాడదు.

selfTest.q: 1. కొనసాగే హామీ అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: వరుస లావాదేవీలకు విస్తరించే హామీ (సెక్షన్ 129). 2. హామీదారు కొనసాగే హామీని ఎలా ఉపసంహరించవచ్చు? ఎప్పుడైనా, భవిష్యత్ లావాదేవీల విషయంలో, రుణదాతకు నోటీసు ఇచ్చి (సెక్షన్ 130). 3. హామీదారు మరణం కొనసాగే హామీపై ఎలాంటి ప్రభావం చూపుతుంది? ఒప్పందం వేరుగా చెప్పకపోతే, అది భవిష్యత్ లావాదేవీల విషయంలో హామీని ఉపసంహరిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 131).

hi.inOneMinute: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 names one kind of guarantee: the continuing guarantee. A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is a continuing guarantee (section 129). The surety may revoke it by notice to the creditor, as to future transactions (section 130). The death of the surety also revokes it, as to future transactions, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Key points for the answer: the definition, the Act's illustrations, and the two ways of revocation with their effect.
hi.meaning: What is a continuing guarantee? (section 129) Rule. A guarantee which extends to a series of transactions is a continuing guarantee. The test is whether the guarantee extends to a series of transactions. The Act's illustrations show the test at work. In illustration (a), the guarantee covers the collection and payment of rents. This is a continuing guarantee. In illustration (b), the guarantee covers any tea supplied from time to time. It is a continuing guarantee, so A is liable up to £100 for the later supply of £200. In illustration (c), the guarantee covers the price of five sacks of flour to be delivered by B to C. It is not a continuing guarantee, so A is not liable for the later four sacks. Example. Anil guarantees payment to Babu, a rice dealer in Guntur, of up to Rs 50,000 for any rice Babu supplies to Chandu from time to time. The guarantee covers a series of supplies. It is a continuing guarantee. The other side: a guarantee that is not continuing Rule. A guarantee which does not extend to a series of transactions is not a continuing guarantee. Illustration (c) to section 129 shows one. The 2017 paper calls such a guarantee a "simple guarantee". The Act does not use that label. Example. Dev guarantees payment of the price of one consignment of cement that Esha will deliver to Farid. This covers one transaction. It is not a continuing guarantee. Revocation by notice (section 130) Rule. A continuing guarantee may at any time be revoked by the surety, as to future transactions, by notice to the creditor. The effect is limited to future transactions. Past transactions remain covered. The Act's illustrations show this. In illustration (a), A revokes after B has discounted bills for 2,000 rupees. A is discharged from liability for any later discount. A is still liable for the 2,000 rupees if C defaults. In illustration (b), B has already drawn on C and C has accepted the bill before A gives notice of revocation. C dishonours the bill at maturity. A is liable. Example. In the rice example, Anil gives notice to Babu after Babu has supplied rice worth Rs 20,000. Rice supplied after the notice is no longer covered. Anil remains liable for the Rs 20,000 if Chandu defaults on it. Revocation by the surety's death (section 131) Rule. The death of the surety operates as a revocation of a continuing guarantee, as regards future transactions. This is so in the absence of any contract to the contrary. The guarantee may say otherwise. Example. Anil dies. Babu then supplies rice to Chandu. The guarantee is revoked as to that future supply, unless the guarantee contract says otherwise. Revoking a continuing guarantee How to read this: start at the top. Check whether the guarantee is continuing. Then check the way of revocation and its effect. 1. Does the guarantee extend to a series of transactions (section 129)? Yes: it is a continuing guarantee. No: it is not. 2. The surety gives notice to the creditor (section 130), or the surety dies (section 131). 3. Effect: the guarantee is revoked as to future transactions. Transactions already made stay covered (section 130, illustrations).
keyPoints: A continuing guarantee extends to a series of transactions (section 129). The surety may revoke it by notice to the creditor, as to future transactions (section 130). The surety's death revokes it as to future transactions, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Revocation does not affect transactions already made (illustrations to section 130). The Act names only the continuing guarantee. It does not use the label "simple guarantee".

In the absence of any contract to the contrary, it revokes the guarantee as regards future transactions (section 131).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t5.subtitle: Sections 124, 125, 126, 140 and 145 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: In a contract of indemnity, one party promises to save the other from loss (section 124). In a contract of guarantee, a surety promises the creditor to answer for the principal debtor's default (section 126). The two are different contracts with different rules. The differences that follow from the Act are in the persons, in what is promised, in what sets the promise working, and in the rights after payment. Key points for the answer: a table of differences based on sections 124 and 126, with the sections on rights (125, 140 and 145).
en.meaning:
Difference 1: the definitions (sections 124 and 126)

Rule. Section 124 speaks of a promise to save the other party from loss. Section 126 speaks of a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default.

Example. Dev promises Esha: "If Farid takes proceedings against you over Rs 200, I will save you from the loss." That promise is a promise to save from loss. Now Sita promises a bank: "If my brother Ravi does not repay his loan, I will." That promise is to discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default.

Difference 2: the persons

Rule. Section 124 speaks of "one party" promising "the other". These are the promisor and the promisee. Section 126 names three persons: the surety, the principal debtor and the creditor.

Example. In Dev's promise to Esha there are two parties, Dev and Esha. In Sita's promise to the bank there are three persons: Sita (surety), Ravi (principal debtor) and the bank (creditor).

Difference 3: what sets the promise working

Rule. In indemnity the loss is caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person (section 124). In guarantee the promise operates "in case of his default", meaning the default of the third person (section 126).

Difference 4: rights after payment (sections 125, 140 and 145)

Rule. The indemnity-holder's rights against the promisor are in section 125: damages, costs and compromise sums, on the conditions stated. The surety's rights are in sections 140 and 145. Under section 140 he takes the creditor's rights against the principal debtor once he has paid all he is liable for. Under section 145 the principal debtor impliedly promises to indemnify him.

Example. Esha is sued by Farid and is ordered to pay Rs 200 as damages. She recovers it from Dev under section 125, if the conditions of that section are met. If Sita pays the bank Ravi's loan, she takes the bank's rights against Ravi (section 140) and can recover what she rightfully paid from Ravi (section 145).

Difference 5: form

Rule. Section 126 says a guarantee may be oral or written. Section 124 does not say anything about the form of a contract of indemnity.

Which contract is it? How to read this: start at the top and follow the answer for the promise you are testing. 1. Does one party promise to save the other from loss caused by the promisor's or any other person's conduct? Yes: contract of indemnity (section 124). 2. Does a person promise a creditor to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person if that third person defaults? Yes: contract of guarantee (section 126).
keyPoints: Indemnity: section 124. Guarantee: section 126. Indemnity has a promisor and a promisee. Guarantee has a surety, a principal debtor and a creditor. Indemnity: a promise to save from loss. Guarantee: a contract to discharge a third person's liability in case of his default. The indemnity-holder's rights are in section 125. The surety's rights are in sections 140 and 145. A guarantee may be oral or written. Section 124 is silent on form.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section defines a contract of indemnity and which defines a contract of guarantee?

te.inOneMinute: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 లోని సెక్షన్లు 124, 125, 126, 140, 145 — నష్టపూరణకు, హామీకి మధ్య తేడా
te.meaning:
నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందంలో ఒక పక్షం మరొక పక్షాన్ని నష్టం నుండి కాపాడతానని వాగ్దానం చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 124). హామీ ఒప్పందంలో హామీదారు, ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత విఫలమైతే బాధ్యత వహిస్తానని రుణదాతకు వాగ్దానం చేస్తాడు (సెక్షన్ 126). ఇవి వేర్వేరు ఒప్పందాలు, వేర్వేరు నియమాలు.

చట్టం నుండి వచ్చే తేడాలు వ్యక్తులలో, వాగ్దానం చేసిన దానిలో, వాగ్దానాన్ని అమలులోకి తెచ్చే దానిలో, చెల్లింపు తర్వాత హక్కులలో ఉన్నాయి. సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: సెక్షన్లు 124, 126 ఆధారంగా తేడాల పట్టిక, హక్కుల సెక్షన్లతో (125, 140, 145).

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. సెక్షన్ 124 ఇతర పక్షాన్ని నష్టం నుండి కాపాడతానని చేసే వాగ్దానం గురించి చెబుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 126 మూడో వ్యక్తి విఫలమైతే అతడి వాగ్దానాన్ని నెరవేర్చడానికి లేదా అతడి బాధ్యతను తీర్చడానికి చేసే ఒప్పందం గురించి చెబుతుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. దేవ్ ఈషాతో అన్నాడు: "ఫరీద్ రూ. 200 విషయంలో మీపై చర్యలు తీసుకుంటే, ఆ నష్టం నుండి నేను మిమ్మల్ని కాపాడతాను." ఇది నష్టం నుండి కాపాడే వాగ్దానం. ఇప్పుడు సీత బ్యాంకుతో అంది: "నా సోదరుడు రవి తన అప్పు తిరిగి చెల్లించకపోతే, నేను చెల్లిస్తాను." ఇది మూడో వ్యక్తి విఫలమైతే అతడి బాధ్యతను తీర్చే వాగ్దానం.

నియమం. సెక్షన్ 124 "ఒక పక్షం" "మరొకరికి" వాగ్దానం చేయడం గురించి చెబుతుంది. వీరు వాగ్దానకర్త, వాగ్దాన గ్రహీత. సెక్షన్ 126 ముగ్గురు వ్యక్తులను పేర్కొంటుంది: హామీదారు, ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత, రుణదాత.

ఉదాహరణ. దేవ్ ఈషాకు చేసిన వాగ్దానంలో ఇద్దరు పక్షాలు ఉన్నారు: దేవ్, ఈషా. సీత బ్యాంకుకు చేసిన వాగ్దానంలో ముగ్గురు వ్యక్తులు ఉన్నారు: సీత (హామీదారు), రవి (ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత), బ్యాంకు (రుణదాత).

selfTest.q: 1. నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందాన్ని ఏ సెక్షన్, హామీ ఒప్పందాన్ని ఏ సెక్షన్ నిర్వచిస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 124 నష్టపూరణ ఒప్పందాన్ని నిర్వచిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 126 హామీ ఒప్పందాన్ని నిర్వచిస్తుంది. 2. హామీ ఒప్పందంలో ఎంతమంది వ్యక్తుల పేర్లు ఉన్నాయి? ముగ్గురు: హామీదారు, ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత, రుణదాత (సెక్షన్ 126). 3. చెల్లించిన తర్వాత హామీదారు హక్కులను ఏ సెక్షన్లు ఇస్తాయి? సెక్షన్ 140 (ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై రుణదాత హక్కులు), సెక్షన్ 145 (అంతర్లీన నష్టపూరణ).

hi.inOneMinute: In a contract of indemnity, one party promises to save the other from loss (section 124). In a contract of guarantee, a surety promises the creditor to answer for the principal debtor's default (section 126). The two are different contracts with different rules. The differences that follow from the Act are in the persons, in what is promised, in what sets the promise working, and in the rights after payment. Key points for the answer: a table of differences based on sections 124 and 126, with the sections on rights (125, 140 and 145).
hi.meaning: Difference 1: the definitions (sections 124 and 126) Rule. Section 124 speaks of a promise to save the other party from loss. Section 126 speaks of a contract to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person in case of his default. Example. Dev promises Esha: "If Farid takes proceedings against you over Rs 200, I will save you from the loss." That promise is a promise to save from loss. Now Sita promises a bank: "If my brother Ravi does not repay his loan, I will." That promise is to discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. Difference 2: the persons Rule. Section 124 speaks of "one party" promising "the other". These are the promisor and the promisee. Section 126 names three persons: the surety, the principal debtor and the creditor. Example. In Dev's promise to Esha there are two parties, Dev and Esha. In Sita's promise to the bank there are three persons: Sita (surety), Ravi (principal debtor) and the bank (creditor). Difference 3: what sets the promise working Rule. In indemnity the loss is caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or of any other person (section 124). In guarantee the promise operates "in case of his default", meaning the default of the third person (section 126). Difference 4: rights after payment (sections 125, 140 and 145) Rule. The indemnity-holder's rights against the promisor are in section 125: damages, costs and compromise sums, on the conditions stated. The surety's rights are in sections 140 and 145. Under section 140 he takes the creditor's rights against the principal debtor once he has paid all he is liable for. Under section 145 the principal debtor impliedly promises to indemnify him. Example. Esha is sued by Farid and is ordered to pay Rs 200 as damages. She recovers it from Dev under section 125, if the conditions of that section are met. If Sita pays the bank Ravi's loan, she takes the bank's rights against Ravi (section 140) and can recover what she rightfully paid from Ravi (section 145). Difference 5: form Rule. Section 126 says a guarantee may be oral or written. Section 124 does not say anything about the form of a contract of indemnity. Which contract is it? How to read this: start at the top and follow the answer for the promise you are testing. 1. Does one party promise to save the other from loss caused by the promisor's or any other person's conduct? Yes: contract of indemnity (section 124). 2. Does a person promise a creditor to perform the promise, or discharge the liability, of a third person if that third person defaults? Yes: contract of guarantee (section 126).
keyPoints: Indemnity: section 124. Guarantee: section 126. Indemnity has a promisor and a promisee. Guarantee has a surety, a principal debtor and a creditor. Indemnity: a promise to save from loss. Guarantee: a contract to discharge a third person's liability in case of his default. The indemnity-holder's rights are in section 125. The surety's rights are in sections 140 and 145. A guarantee may be oral or written. Section 124 is silent on form.

selfTest.a: Section 124 defines a contract of indemnity. Section 126 defines a contract of guarantee. 2. How many persons are named in a contract of guarantee? Three: the surety, the principal debtor and the creditor (section 126). 3. Which sections give the surety's rights after he pays? Section 140 (the creditor's rights against the principal debtor) and section 145 (the implied indemnity).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t10.subtitle: Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act does not list the essentials of bailment in a separate section. They come from the words of section 148 and section 149. Every bailment needs a delivery of goods, between two persons, for some purpose, upon a contract, with a duty to return the goods or to dispose of them as the person delivering directs. Key points for the answer: the elements in the order of the definition, with section 149 on delivery and the explanation to section 148 for goods already in the bailee's possession.
en.meaning:
Requisite 1: delivery of goods

Rule. Bailment is the "delivery of goods". Section 149 says delivery may be made by doing anything which puts the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf. The explanation to section 148 adds the case where the bailee is already in possession of the goods.

Example. Anil's goods are placed in the possession of a clerk whom Babu has authorized to hold goods for him. Delivery to Babu is made. In a separate case, Chandu only promises Dev that he will look after Dev's goods one day, but the goods never reach Chandu or anyone authorized for him. There is no delivery.

Requisite 2: one person delivers to another

Rule. The goods are delivered "by one person to another". The deliverer is the bailor. The receiver is the bailee.

Example. Esha leaves her bicycle with Farid. Esha is the bailor. Farid is the bailee.

Requisite 3: for some purpose

Rule. The goods are delivered "for some purpose". Section 148 says "some purpose" and lists none.

Example. Gopi gives cloth to a tailor to be made into a coat. The purpose is stitching. Hema leaves her car with a friend while she travels. The purpose is safe keeping.

Requisite 4: upon a contract

Rule. The delivery is "upon a contract". Section 148 itself speaks of a contract that the goods will be returned or otherwise disposed of.

Example. Ibrahim delivers goods to Kiran on the agreed terms that Kiran will return them after a month. The delivery is upon a contract.

Requisite 5: return or disposal as directed

Rule. The contract must provide that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them.

Example. Lata gives wheat to a mill to be ground. The mill must return the flour, or deliver it to a person Lata names. This meets the requisite of return or disposal as directed.

The requisites How to read this: all of them must be present for a bailment under section 148. 1. Delivery of goods (section 149). 2. By one person to another. 3. For some purpose. 4. Upon a contract. 5. That the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs, when the purpose is accomplished. All present: bailment.
keyPoints: Elements in section 148: delivery of goods, by one person to another, for some purpose, upon a contract, with return or disposal as the person delivering directs. Delivery: anything putting the goods in the possession of the bailee or of a person authorized for him (section 149). A person already holding another's goods may become a bailee by contract (explanation to section 148). If one requisite is missing, the transaction does not fit the definition.

te.inOneMinute: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 లోని సెక్షన్లు 148, 149 — బెయిల్‌మెంట్‌కు అవసరమైన అంశాలు
te.meaning:
బెయిల్‌మెంట్‌కు అవసరమైన అంశాలను చట్టం ప్రత్యేక సెక్షన్‌లో జాబితాగా ఇవ్వదు. అవి సెక్షన్ 148, సెక్షన్ 149 లోని మాటల నుండి వస్తాయి. ప్రతి బెయిల్‌మెంట్‌లో ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరికి సరుకులను అప్పగించడం, ఒక ప్రయోజనం కోసం, ఒక ఒప్పందంపై ఉండాలి. సరుకులను తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలని, లేదా అప్పగించినవారి సూచనల ప్రకారం వ్యవహరించాలని ఆ ఒప్పందం చెప్పాలి.

సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: నిర్వచనంలోని వరుసలో అంశాలు, అప్పగింతపై సెక్షన్ 149, బెయిలీ స్వాధీనంలో అప్పటికే ఉన్న సరుకులపై సెక్షన్ 148 వివరణ.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. బెయిల్‌మెంట్ అంటే "సరుకుల అప్పగింత". ఉద్దేశించిన బెయిలీకి, లేదా అతడి తరఫున వాటిని ఉంచుకోవడానికి అధికారం పొందిన ఏ వ్యక్తికైనా సరుకుల స్వాధీనం ఇచ్చే ఏ పనితోనైనా అప్పగింత చేయవచ్చని సెక్షన్ 149 చెబుతుంది. బెయిలీ వద్ద అప్పటికే సరుకులు ఉన్న సందర్భాన్ని సెక్షన్ 148 వివరణ కలుపుతుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. బాబు తన తరఫున సరుకులను ఉంచుకోవడానికి అధికారం ఇచ్చిన గుమాస్తా స్వాధీనంలో అనిల్ సరుకులను ఉంచారు. బాబుకు అప్పగింత జరిగింది. వేరే సందర్భంలో, దేవ్ సరుకులను ఒక రోజు చూసుకుంటానని చందు వాగ్దానం మాత్రమే చేశాడు, కానీ సరుకులు చందుకు, లేదా అతడి తరఫున అధికారం పొందిన ఎవరికీ చేరలేదు. అప్పగింత లేదు.

నియమం. సరుకులను "ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరికి" అప్పగిస్తాడు. అప్పగించేవాడు బెయిలర్. అందుకునేవాడు బెయిలీ.

ఉదాహరణ. ఈషా తన సైకిల్‌ను ఫరీద్ వద్ద ఉంచింది. ఈషా బెయిలర్. ఫరీద్ బెయిలీ.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 148 ప్రకారం బెయిల్‌మెంట్‌కు అవసరమైన అంశాలు చెప్పండి. సరుకుల అప్పగింత, ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరికి, ఒక ప్రయోజనం కోసం, ప్రయోజనం పూర్తయినప్పుడు సరుకులను తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలని లేదా అప్పగించినవారి సూచనల ప్రకారం వ్యవహరించాలని ఒప్పందంపై. 2. బెయిలీకి అప్పగింత ఎలా జరుగుతుందో ఏ సెక్షన్ చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 149. 3. సరుకుల అమ్మకం బెయిల్‌మెంటా? కాదు. అమ్మకంలో సరుకులు తిరిగి ఇవ్వబడతాయని, లేదా అమ్మినవారి సూచనల ప్రకారం వ్యవహరించబడతాయని ఒప్పందం ఉండదు, కాబట్టి సెక్షన్ 148 నిర్వచనం సరిపోదు.

hi.inOneMinute: The Act does not list the essentials of bailment in a separate section. They come from the words of section 148 and section 149. Every bailment needs a delivery of goods, between two persons, for some purpose, upon a contract, with a duty to return the goods or to dispose of them as the person delivering directs. Key points for the answer: the elements in the order of the definition, with section 149 on delivery and the explanation to section 148 for goods already in the bailee's possession.
hi.meaning: Requisite 1: delivery of goods Rule. Bailment is the "delivery of goods". Section 149 says delivery may be made by doing anything which puts the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf. The explanation to section 148 adds the case where the bailee is already in possession of the goods. Example. Anil's goods are placed in the possession of a clerk whom Babu has authorized to hold goods for him. Delivery to Babu is made. In a separate case, Chandu only promises Dev that he will look after Dev's goods one day, but the goods never reach Chandu or anyone authorized for him. There is no delivery. Requisite 2: one person delivers to another Rule. The goods are delivered "by one person to another". The deliverer is the bailor. The receiver is the bailee. Example. Esha leaves her bicycle with Farid. Esha is the bailor. Farid is the bailee. Requisite 3: for some purpose Rule. The goods are delivered "for some purpose". Section 148 says "some purpose" and lists none. Example. Gopi gives cloth to a tailor to be made into a coat. The purpose is stitching. Hema leaves her car with a friend while she travels. The purpose is safe keeping. Requisite 4: upon a contract Rule. The delivery is "upon a contract". Section 148 itself speaks of a contract that the goods will be returned or otherwise disposed of. Example. Ibrahim delivers goods to Kiran on the agreed terms that Kiran will return them after a month. The delivery is upon a contract. Requisite 5: return or disposal as directed Rule. The contract must provide that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. Example. Lata gives wheat to a mill to be ground. The mill must return the flour, or deliver it to a person Lata names. This meets the requisite of return or disposal as directed. The requisites How to read this: all of them must be present for a bailment under section 148. 1. Delivery of goods (section 149). 2. By one person to another. 3. For some purpose. 4. Upon a contract. 5. That the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs, when the purpose is accomplished. All present: bailment.
keyPoints: Elements in section 148: delivery of goods, by one person to another, for some purpose, upon a contract, with return or disposal as the person delivering directs. Delivery: anything putting the goods in the possession of the bailee or of a person authorized for him (section 149). A person already holding another's goods may become a bailee by contract (explanation to section 148). If one requisite is missing, the transaction does not fit the definition.

selfTest.q: 1. Name the requisites of bailment under section 148. Delivery of goods, by one person to another, for some purpose, upon a contract that the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs when the purpose is accomplished. 2. Which section says how delivery to the bailee is made?
selfTest.a: Section 149. 3. Is a sale of goods a bailment? No. A sale has no contract that the goods will be returned or disposed of as the seller directs, so the definition in section 148 does not fit.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t9.subtitle: Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that the goods will be returned or otherwise disposed of as the person delivering directs. The person who delivers is the bailor . The person who receives is the bailee . Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 define bailment and say how delivery is made. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two names, the explanation to section 148 and the rule on delivery in section 149.
en.meaning:
The meaning of bailment (section 148)

Rule. Bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them.

Goods are delivered by one person to another. The delivery is for some purpose. It is upon a contract that the goods will be returned, or disposed of as the bailor directs, when the purpose is accomplished.

Example. Ravi gives his scooter to a garage in Guntur for repair. The garage will return it when the repair is done. Ravi delivers goods to the garage for a purpose, on a contract that they will be returned. Ravi is the bailor and the garage is the bailee.

Bailor and bailee

Rule. The person delivering the goods is the bailor. The person to whom they are delivered is the bailee.

Example. Sita leaves her sewing machine with Lata for a week. Sita is the bailor. Lata is the bailee.

The explanation: a person already in possession

Rule. If a person already in possession of the goods of another contracts to hold them as a bailee, he thereby becomes the bailee. The owner becomes the bailor, although the goods may not have been delivered by way of bailment.

Example. Kiran already holds Mohan's bicycle. Kiran and Mohan now make a contract that Kiran will hold it as a bailee. By that contract Kiran becomes the bailee and Mohan the bailor, although the bicycle was not delivered by way of bailment.

How delivery is made (section 149)

Rule. Delivery may be made by doing anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf.

Example. Dev sends his goods to Esha's warehouse. Esha's authorized warehouse manager takes them in. The goods are in the possession of a person authorized to hold them on Esha's behalf. Delivery to Esha is complete.

Is it a bailment? How to read this: start at the top and answer each box. If you can answer yes to all, the transaction is a bailment under section 148. 1. Are goods delivered by one person to another (section 149 says how)? 2. Is it for some purpose? 3. Is it upon a contract that the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs, when the purpose is accomplished? If yes to all three, it is a bailment. The deliverer is the bailor and the receiver is the bailee.
keyPoints: Section 148 defines bailment: delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that they will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs. The person delivering is the bailor. The person receiving is the bailee. If a person already holds another's goods and contracts to hold them as a bailee, he becomes the bailee (explanation to section 148). Delivery means doing anything that puts the goods in the possession of the bailee, or of a person authorized to hold them for him (section 149). Pledge is bailment as security for a debt or a promise (section 172).

selfTest.a: The delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. 2. Who is the bailor? The person delivering the goods (section 148). 3. How may delivery to the bailee be made under section 149? By doing anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf.

te.meaning:
నియమం. బెయిల్‌మెంట్ అంటే ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరికి ఒక ప్రయోజనం కోసం సరుకులను అప్పగించడం. ప్రయోజనం పూర్తయినప్పుడు వాటిని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలని, లేదా అప్పగించినవారి సూచనల ప్రకారం మరో విధంగా వ్యవహరించాలని ఒప్పందంపై అప్పగిస్తారు.

ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరికి సరుకులను అప్పగిస్తాడు. అప్పగింత ఒక ప్రయోజనం కోసం. ప్రయోజనం పూర్తయినప్పుడు సరుకులు తిరిగి ఇవ్వబడతాయని, లేదా బెయిలర్ సూచించినట్లు వ్యవహరించబడతాయని ఒప్పందంపై.

ఉదాహరణ. రవి తన స్కూటర్‌ను గుంటూరులోని గ్యారేజీకి మరమ్మతు కోసం ఇచ్చాడు. మరమ్మతు పూర్తయ్యాక గ్యారేజీ దాన్ని తిరిగి ఇస్తుంది. రవి ఒక ప్రయోజనం కోసం, సరుకులు తిరిగి ఇవ్వబడతాయని ఒప్పందంపై గ్యారేజీకి అప్పగించాడు. రవి బెయిలర్, గ్యారేజీ బెయిలీ.

selfTest.a: ఒక వ్యక్తి మరొకరికి ఒక ప్రయోజనం కోసం, ప్రయోజనం పూర్తయినప్పుడు వాటిని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలని లేదా అప్పగించినవారి సూచనల ప్రకారం మరో విధంగా వ్యవహరించాలని ఒప్పందంపై సరుకులను అప్పగించడం. 2. బెయిలర్ ఎవరు? సరుకులు అప్పగించే వ్యక్తి (సెక్షన్ 148). 3. సెక్షన్ 149 ప్రకారం బెయిలీకి అప్పగింత ఎలా జరగవచ్చు? ఉద్దేశించిన బెయిలీకి, లేదా అతడి తరఫున సరుకులను ఉంచుకోవడానికి అధికారం పొందిన ఏ వ్యక్తికైనా సరుకుల స్వాధీనం ఇచ్చే ఏ పనితోనైనా.

hi.inOneMinute: A bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that the goods will be returned or otherwise disposed of as the person delivering directs. The person who delivers is the bailor . The person who receives is the bailee . Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 define bailment and say how delivery is made. Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two names, the explanation to section 148 and the rule on delivery in section 149.
hi.meaning: The meaning of bailment (section 148) Rule. Bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that the goods shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. Goods are delivered by one person to another. The delivery is for some purpose. It is upon a contract that the goods will be returned, or disposed of as the bailor directs, when the purpose is accomplished. Example. Ravi gives his scooter to a garage in Guntur for repair. The garage will return it when the repair is done. Ravi delivers goods to the garage for a purpose, on a contract that they will be returned. Ravi is the bailor and the garage is the bailee. Bailor and bailee Rule. The person delivering the goods is the bailor. The person to whom they are delivered is the bailee. Example. Sita leaves her sewing machine with Lata for a week. Sita is the bailor. Lata is the bailee. The explanation: a person already in possession Rule. If a person already in possession of the goods of another contracts to hold them as a bailee, he thereby becomes the bailee. The owner becomes the bailor, although the goods may not have been delivered by way of bailment. Example. Kiran already holds Mohan's bicycle. Kiran and Mohan now make a contract that Kiran will hold it as a bailee. By that contract Kiran becomes the bailee and Mohan the bailor, although the bicycle was not delivered by way of bailment. How delivery is made (section 149) Rule. Delivery may be made by doing anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee, or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf. Example. Dev sends his goods to Esha's warehouse. Esha's authorized warehouse manager takes them in. The goods are in the possession of a person authorized to hold them on Esha's behalf. Delivery to Esha is complete. Is it a bailment? How to read this: start at the top and answer each box. If you can answer yes to all, the transaction is a bailment under section 148. 1. Are goods delivered by one person to another (section 149 says how)? 2. Is it for some purpose? 3. Is it upon a contract that the goods will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs, when the purpose is accomplished? If yes to all three, it is a bailment. The deliverer is the bailor and the receiver is the bailee.
keyPoints: Section 148 defines bailment: delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, on a contract that they will be returned or disposed of as the person delivering directs. The person delivering is the bailor. The person receiving is the bailee. If a person already holds another's goods and contracts to hold them as a bailee, he becomes the bailee (explanation to section 148). Delivery means doing anything that puts the goods in the possession of the bailee, or of a person authorized to hold them for him (section 149). Pledge is bailment as security for a debt or a promise (section 172).

selfTest.a: The delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. 2. Who is the bailor? The person delivering the goods (section 148). 3. How may delivery to the bailee be made under section 149? By doing anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the intended bailee or of any person authorized to hold them on his behalf.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t8.subtitle: Sections 130, 131, 133 to 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A surety is discharged when the Act says so. The Act gives several ways. A continuing guarantee may be revoked (sections 130 and 131). A change in the terms of the contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, made without the surety's consent, discharges him as to later transactions (section 133). The surety is also discharged in these cases. The principal debtor is released (section 134). The creditor makes a composition with the debtor, gives him time or promises not to sue (section 135). The creditor's act or omission impairs the surety's remedy (section 139). A security is lost (section 141). Key points for the answer: each section, its words and the Act's illustration.
en.meaning:
Discharge by revocation of a continuing guarantee (sections 130 and 131)

Rule. The surety may revoke a continuing guarantee by notice to the creditor (section 130). His death also revokes it, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Both operate as to future transactions only. The full treatment is in the topic "Kinds of Guarantee".

Example. Anil guarantees all rice supplied to Chandu by Babu for a year. After four months Anil gives notice to Babu. Supplies after the notice are no longer covered. Supplies before the notice remain covered.

Discharge by variance in the terms of the contract (section 133)

Rule. Any variance, made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.

The Act gives five illustrations. Three of them show the point clearly.

(a) A is surety for B's conduct as a manager in C's bank. B and C agree, without A's consent, to raise B's salary and to make him liable for one-fourth of overdraft losses. B allows an overdraft and the bank loses money. A is discharged and is not liable. (c) A is surety for B, a clerk paid a fixed salary. C and B agree, without A's knowledge or consent, to pay B a commission instead. A is not liable for B's later misconduct. (e) C contracts to lend B 5,000 rupees on 1 March and A guarantees repayment. C pays the money on 1 January. A is discharged, because C might sue B for the money before 1 March.

Illustration (b) covers a later Act that materially alters the office. Illustration (d) covers a continuing guarantee of 3,000 rupees for oil supplied on credit, which the debtor and creditor change, without A's knowledge, into supply for ready money. A is not liable for goods supplied after the new arrangement.

Example. Hema sells goods to Gopi on three months' credit, with Ibrahim as surety. Without telling Ibrahim, Hema and Gopi change the credit period to one month. Ibrahim is discharged as to later transactions under section 133.

Discharge by release of the principal debtor (section 134)

Rule. The surety is discharged by any contract between the creditor and the principal debtor by which the principal debtor is released. He is also discharged by any act or omission of the creditor, the legal consequence of which is the discharge of the principal debtor.

(a) B becomes embarrassed and contracts with his creditors, including C, to assign them his property in return for releasing him from their demands. B is released from his debt to C, and A, his surety, is discharged. (b) A contracts with B to grow indigo and C guarantees A's performance. B diverts the water that A needs and prevents the crop. C is no longer liable. (c) A contracts to build a house for B, who is to supply the timber. C guarantees A's performance. B omits to supply the timber. C is discharged.

Example. A co-operative society lends Rs 1 lakh to Ravi on Sita's guarantee. The society and Ravi agree that the society releases Ravi from the loan. Sita is discharged under section 134.

Discharge by composition, time or promise not to sue (section 135)

Rule. A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety, unless the surety assents to such contract.

Example. The bank agrees with Ravi, without asking Sita, to give him one more year to repay. Sita is discharged unless she assents to the agreement.

Not discharged: time given to the debtor by a contract with a third person (section 136)

Rule. Where a contract to give time to the principal debtor is made by the creditor with a third person, and not with the principal debtor, the surety is not discharged.

The Act's illustration: C, the holder of an overdue bill of exchange drawn by A as surety for B and accepted by B, contracts with M to give time to B. A is not discharged.

Example. The bank promises Ravi's neighbour Kiran, not Ravi, that it will give Ravi time to repay. The promise is made with a third person, not with the principal debtor. Sita is not discharged.

Not discharged: forbearance and release of a co-surety (sections 137 and 138)

Rule. Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor, or to enforce any other remedy against him, does not discharge the surety, in the absence of any provision in the guarantee to the contrary (section 137). The Act's illustration: B owes C a debt guaranteed by A. The debt becomes payable. C does not sue B for a year. A is not discharged.

Where there are co-sureties, a release by the creditor of one does not discharge the others. It also does not free the released surety from his responsibility to the other sureties (section 138).

Discharge by the creditor's act or omission impairing the surety's eventual remedy (section 139)

Rule. If the creditor does any act which is inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and the eventual remedy of the surety against the principal debtor is thereby impaired, the surety is discharged.

(a) B contracts to build a ship for C, payable by instalments as the work reaches certain stages. A is surety. C, without A's knowledge, prepays the last two instalments to B. A is discharged by the prepayment. (b) C lends money to B on a promissory note made by B and by A as surety, with a bill of sale of B's furniture. C sells the furniture, but through his misconduct and wilful negligence only a small price is realized. A is discharged from liability on the note. (c) A puts M as apprentice to B and guarantees M's fidelity. B promises to see M make up the cash at least once a month. B omits to do so and M embezzles. A is not liable to B on his guarantee.

Example. A builder is to be paid by instalments as work proceeds. The owner, without telling the builder's surety, pays the last two instalments in advance. The surety's remedy against the builder is impaired. The surety is discharged, as in illustration (a) to section 139.

Discharge by loss of securities (section 141)

Rule. The surety is entitled to the benefit of every security the creditor holds against the principal debtor when the guarantee is given. If the creditor loses it or parts with it without the surety's consent, the surety is discharged to the extent of its value.

(a) C lends B 2,000 rupees on A's guarantee and also holds a mortgage of B's furniture. C cancels the mortgage. A is discharged to the value of the furniture. (b) C holds a decree against B and a guarantee from A. C takes B's goods in execution and then, without A's knowledge, withdraws the execution. A is discharged. (c) A is surety for B, and C afterwards obtains from B a further security and later gives it up. A is not discharged.

Is the surety discharged? How to read this: find what happened and follow the line to the section and the result. 1. The surety revokes a continuing guarantee by notice, or the surety dies. Discharged as to future transactions (sections 130, 131). 2. The creditor and the principal debtor vary their contract without the surety's consent. Discharged as to later transactions (section 133). 3. The creditor releases the principal debtor by contract, or an act or omission of the creditor discharges him. Discharged (section 134). 4. The creditor compounds with, gives time to, or agrees not to sue the principal debtor, and the surety does not assent. Discharged (section 135). 5. The creditor's act or omission impairs the surety's eventual remedy. Discharged (section 139). 6. The creditor loses or parts with a security held when the guarantee was given. Discharged to the extent of its value (section 141).
keyPoints: Revocation of a continuing guarantee, by notice or by the surety's death, operates as to future transactions (sections 130, 131). A variance without the surety's consent discharges him as to later transactions (section 133). Release of the principal debtor discharges the surety (section 134). Composition, time or promise not to sue the principal debtor discharges the surety, unless he assents (section 135). Time given by a contract with a third person does not discharge the surety (section 136). Mere forbearance does not (section 137). Release of one co-surety does not discharge the others (section 138). Impairing the surety's eventual remedy discharges him (section 139). So does loss of a security, to the extent of its value (section 141).

selfTest.q: 1. Which section discharges the surety when the creditor gives time to the principal debtor by a contract with him?
selfTest.a: Section 135, unless the surety assents to the contract. 2. Is the surety discharged by mere forbearance of the creditor to sue the principal debtor? No, in the absence of any provision in the guarantee to the contrary (section 137). 3. To what extent does the creditor's loss of a security discharge the surety? To the extent of the value of the security (section 141).

చట్టం చెప్పినప్పుడు హామీదారు తన బాధ్యత నుండి విముక్తుడు అవుతాడు (discharged). చట్టం అనేక మార్గాలు ఇస్తుంది. కొనసాగే హామీని ఉపసంహరించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్లు 130, 131). హామీదారు సమ్మతి లేకుండా, రుణదాతకు ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతకు మధ్య ఒప్పంద నిబంధనలలో జరిగే మార్పు, ఆ మార్పు తర్వాతి లావాదేవీల విషయంలో అతడిని విముక్తుడిని చేస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 133).

ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత విడుదల (సెక్షన్ 134), ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతకు ఇచ్చిన రాజీ, గడువు లేదా దావా వేయనని వాగ్దానం (సెక్షన్ 135), హామీదారు పరిష్కారానికి భంగం కలిగించే రుణదాత చర్య లేదా విస్మరణ (సెక్షన్ 139), తాకట్టుల నష్టం (సెక్షన్ 141) కూడా అతడిని విముక్తుడిని చేస్తాయి. సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: ప్రతి సెక్షన్, దాని మాటలు, చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణ.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. హామీదారు కొనసాగే హామీని రుణదాతకు నోటీసు ఇచ్చి ఉపసంహరించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 130). ఒప్పందం వేరుగా చెప్పకపోతే అతడి మరణం కూడా దాన్ని ఉపసంహరిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 131). రెండూ భవిష్యత్ లావాదేవీలకు మాత్రమే వర్తిస్తాయి. పూర్తి వివరణ "Kinds of Guarantee" అంశంలో ఉంది.

ఉదాహరణ. చందుకు బాబు సరఫరా చేసే అన్ని బియ్యానికి ఒక సంవత్సరం పాటు అనిల్ హామీ ఇచ్చాడు. నాలుగు నెలల తర్వాత అనిల్ బాబుకు నోటీసు ఇచ్చాడు. నోటీసు తర్వాత సరఫరాలు ఇక కవర్ కావు. నోటీసుకు ముందు సరఫరాలు కవర్ అయి ఉంటాయి.

నియమం. ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతకు, రుణదాతకు మధ్య ఒప్పంద నిబంధనలలో హామీదారు సమ్మతి లేకుండా జరిగే ఏ మార్పైనా, ఆ మార్పు తర్వాతి లావాదేవీల విషయంలో హామీదారును విముక్తుడిని చేస్తుంది.

చట్టం ఐదు ఉదాహరణలు ఇస్తుంది. వాటిలో మూడు విషయాన్ని స్పష్టంగా చూపిస్తాయి.

selfTest.q: 1. ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతతో ఒప్పందం ద్వారా రుణదాత గడువు ఇస్తే హామీదారును ఏ సెక్షన్ విముక్తుడిని చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 135, ఆ ఒప్పందానికి హామీదారు అంగీకరిస్తే తప్ప. 2. ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై దావా వేయకుండా రుణదాత కేవలం ఆగడం హామీదారును విముక్తుడిని చేస్తుందా? చేయదు, హామీలో విరుద్ధమైన నిబంధన లేనప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 137). 3. రుణదాత తాకట్టును పోగొట్టుకుంటే హామీదారు ఏ మేరకు విముక్తుడవుతాడు? తాకట్టు విలువ మేరకు (సెక్షన్ 141).
