hi.inOneMinute: A surety is discharged when the Act says so. The Act gives several ways. A continuing guarantee may be revoked (sections 130 and 131). A change in the terms of the contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, made without the surety's consent, discharges him as to later transactions (section 133). The surety is also discharged in these cases. The principal debtor is released (section 134). The creditor makes a composition with the debtor, gives him time or promises not to sue (section 135). The creditor's act or omission impairs the surety's remedy (section 139). A security is lost (section 141). Key points for the answer: each section, its words and the Act's illustration.
hi.meaning: Discharge by revocation of a continuing guarantee (sections 130 and 131) Rule. The surety may revoke a continuing guarantee by notice to the creditor (section 130). His death also revokes it, unless the contract says otherwise (section 131). Both operate as to future transactions only. The full treatment is in the topic "Kinds of Guarantee". Example. Anil guarantees all rice supplied to Chandu by Babu for a year. After four months Anil gives notice to Babu. Supplies after the notice are no longer covered. Supplies before the notice remain covered. Discharge by variance in the terms of the contract (section 133) Rule. Any variance, made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance. The Act gives five illustrations. Three of them show the point clearly. (a) A is surety for B's conduct as a manager in C's bank. B and C agree, without A's consent, to raise B's salary and to make him liable for one-fourth of overdraft losses. B allows an overdraft and the bank loses money. A is discharged and is not liable. (c) A is surety for B, a clerk paid a fixed salary. C and B agree, without A's knowledge or consent, to pay B a commission instead. A is not liable for B's later misconduct. (e) C contracts to lend B 5,000 rupees on 1 March and A guarantees repayment. C pays the money on 1 January. A is discharged, because C might sue B for the money before 1 March. Illustration (b) covers a later Act that materially alters the office. Illustration (d) covers a continuing guarantee of 3,000 rupees for oil supplied on credit, which the debtor and creditor change, without A's knowledge, into supply for ready money. A is not liable for goods supplied after the new arrangement. Example. Hema sells goods to Gopi on three months' credit, with Ibrahim as surety. Without telling Ibrahim, Hema and Gopi change the credit period to one month. Ibrahim is discharged as to later transactions under section 133. Discharge by release of the principal debtor (section 134) Rule. The surety is discharged by any contract between the creditor and the principal debtor by which the principal debtor is released. He is also discharged by any act or omission of the creditor, the legal consequence of which is the discharge of the principal debtor. (a) B becomes embarrassed and contracts with his creditors, including C, to assign them his property in return for releasing him from their demands. B is released from his debt to C, and A, his surety, is discharged. (b) A contracts with B to grow indigo and C guarantees A's performance. B diverts the water that A needs and prevents the crop. C is no longer liable. (c) A contracts to build a house for B, who is to supply the timber. C guarantees A's performance. B omits to supply the timber. C is discharged. Example. A co-operative society lends Rs 1 lakh to Ravi on Sita's guarantee. The society and Ravi agree that the society releases Ravi from the loan. Sita is discharged under section 134. Discharge by composition, time or promise not to sue (section 135) Rule. A contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the creditor makes a composition with, or promises to give time to, or not to sue, the principal debtor, discharges the surety, unless the surety assents to such contract. Example. The bank agrees with Ravi, without asking Sita, to give him one more year to repay. Sita is discharged unless she assents to the agreement. Not discharged: time given to the debtor by a contract with a third person (section 136) Rule. Where a contract to give time to the principal debtor is made by the creditor with a third person, and not with the principal debtor, the surety is not discharged. The Act's illustration: C, the holder of an overdue bill of exchange drawn by A as surety for B and accepted by B, contracts with M to give time to B. A is not discharged. Example. The bank promises Ravi's neighbour Kiran, not Ravi, that it will give Ravi time to repay. The promise is made with a third person, not with the principal debtor. Sita is not discharged. Not discharged: forbearance and release of a co-surety (sections 137 and 138) Rule. Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor, or to enforce any other remedy against him, does not discharge the surety, in the absence of any provision in the guarantee to the contrary (section 137). The Act's illustration: B owes C a debt guaranteed by A. The debt becomes payable. C does not sue B for a year. A is not discharged. Where there are co-sureties, a release by the creditor of one does not discharge the others. It also does not free the released surety from his responsibility to the other sureties (section 138). Discharge by the creditor's act or omission impairing the surety's eventual remedy (section 139) Rule. If the creditor does any act which is inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and the eventual remedy of the surety against the principal debtor is thereby impaired, the surety is discharged. (a) B contracts to build a ship for C, payable by instalments as the work reaches certain stages. A is surety. C, without A's knowledge, prepays the last two instalments to B. A is discharged by the prepayment. (b) C lends money to B on a promissory note made by B and by A as surety, with a bill of sale of B's furniture. C sells the furniture, but through his misconduct and wilful negligence only a small price is realized. A is discharged from liability on the note. (c) A puts M as apprentice to B and guarantees M's fidelity. B promises to see M make up the cash at least once a month. B omits to do so and M embezzles. A is not liable to B on his guarantee. Example. A builder is to be paid by instalments as work proceeds. The owner, without telling the builder's surety, pays the last two instalments in advance. The surety's remedy against the builder is impaired. The surety is discharged, as in illustration (a) to section 139. Discharge by loss of securities (section 141) Rule. The surety is entitled to the benefit of every security the creditor holds against the principal debtor when the guarantee is given. If the creditor loses it or parts with it without the surety's consent, the surety is discharged to the extent of its value. (a) C lends B 2,000 rupees on A's guarantee and also holds a mortgage of B's furniture. C cancels the mortgage. A is discharged to the value of the furniture. (b) C holds a decree against B and a guarantee from A. C takes B's goods in execution and then, without A's knowledge, withdraws the execution. A is discharged. (c) A is surety for B, and C afterwards obtains from B a further security and later gives it up. A is not discharged. Is the surety discharged? How to read this: find what happened and follow the line to the section and the result. 1. The surety revokes a continuing guarantee by notice, or the surety dies. Discharged as to future transactions (sections 130, 131). 2. The creditor and the principal debtor vary their contract without the surety's consent. Discharged as to later transactions (section 133). 3. The creditor releases the principal debtor by contract, or an act or omission of the creditor discharges him. Discharged (section 134). 4. The creditor compounds with, gives time to, or agrees not to sue the principal debtor, and the surety does not assent. Discharged (section 135). 5. The creditor's act or omission impairs the surety's eventual remedy. Discharged (section 139). 6. The creditor loses or parts with a security held when the guarantee was given. Discharged to the extent of its value (section 141).
keyPoints: Revocation of a continuing guarantee, by notice or by the surety's death, operates as to future transactions (sections 130, 131). A variance without the surety's consent discharges him as to later transactions (section 133). Release of the principal debtor discharges the surety (section 134). Composition, time or promise not to sue the principal debtor discharges the surety, unless he assents (section 135). Time given by a contract with a third person does not discharge the surety (section 136). Mere forbearance does not (section 137). Release of one co-surety does not discharge the others (section 138). Impairing the surety's eventual remedy discharges him (section 139). So does loss of a security, to the extent of its value (section 141).

selfTest.q: 1. Which section discharges the surety when the creditor gives time to the principal debtor by a contract with him?
selfTest.a: Section 135, unless the surety assents to the contract. 2. Is the surety discharged by mere forbearance of the creditor to sue the principal debtor? No, in the absence of any provision in the guarantee to the contrary (section 137). 3. To what extent does the creditor's loss of a security discharge the surety? To the extent of the value of the security (section 141).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t11.subtitle: Sections 150, 158, 159, 162 and 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act has no section that lists the kinds of bailment. Its words refer to a bailment for hire (section 150) and a gratuitous bailment (sections 158, 159 and 162). A bailment of goods as security for a debt or a promise is a pledge (section 172). Key points for the answer: the two kinds, the rules the Act gives for each, and the link to pledge.
en.meaning:
Kind 1: bailment for hire

Rule. Section 150 speaks of goods "bailed for hire". There the bailor is responsible for damage arising directly from faults in the goods whether he was or was not aware of them.

Example. Anil hires a carriage from Babu. The carriage is unsafe, though Babu is not aware of it, and Anil is injured. Babu is responsible to Anil for the injury. This is the Act's own illustration (b) to section 150.

Kind 2: gratuitous bailment

Rule. The Act uses the word "gratuitous" in sections 159 and 162. Section 158 speaks of a bailee who is to receive no remuneration. The Act gives these rules.

The bailor must repay the bailee the necessary expenses incurred for the purpose of the bailment, where the goods are to be kept, carried or have work done on them and the bailee gets no remuneration (section 158). The lender may at any time require the return of the thing, even though he lent it for a specified time or purpose. If the borrower acted on the faith of the loan so that early return would cause him loss exceeding the benefit he derived, the lender who compels return must indemnify him for the excess (section 159). The bailment is terminated by the death of the bailor or of the bailee (section 162). The first part of section 150, the bailor's duty to disclose faults of which he is aware, applies to every bailment. The second part adds the rule for goods bailed for hire.

Example. Chandu lends his bicycle to Dev for a month without charge. After a week Chandu asks for it back. Under section 159 he may require its return at any time. If Dev had, on the faith of the month-long loan, made arrangements so that early return would cost him more than the benefit he got, Chandu would have to indemnify him for the excess. If Chandu dies during the month, the gratuitous bailment ends (section 162).

Pledge: bailment as security (section 172)

Rule. A bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called a pledge. The Act gives pledge its own sections (172 to 179).

Example. Esha borrows Rs 50,000 and hands her gold chain to the lender as security until she repays. This is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt. It is a pledge.

Which kind of bailment? How to read this: start at the top and follow the answer. 1. Are the goods bailed as security for a debt or a promise? Yes: pledge (section 172). 2. If not, are the goods bailed for hire? Yes: bailment for hire (section 150). 3. Otherwise, where the Act's words speak of a gratuitous loan or a bailee who is to receive no remuneration: Gratuitous bailment (sections 158, 159, 162).

బెయిల్‌మెంట్ రకాలను జాబితా చేసే సెక్షన్ చట్టంలో లేదు. దాని మాటలు వీటిని ప్రస్తావిస్తాయి: అద్దెకు బెయిల్‌మెంట్ (సెక్షన్ 150), ఉచిత బెయిల్‌మెంట్ (సెక్షన్లు 158, 159, 162). అప్పుకు లేదా వాగ్దానానికి భద్రతగా సరుకులను బెయిల్ చేయడం తాకట్టు (సెక్షన్ 172).

hi.inOneMinute: The Act has no section that lists the kinds of bailment. Its words refer to a bailment for hire (section 150) and a gratuitous bailment (sections 158, 159 and 162). A bailment of goods as security for a debt or a promise is a pledge (section 172). Key points for the answer: the two kinds, the rules the Act gives for each, and the link to pledge.
hi.meaning: Kind 1: bailment for hire Rule. Section 150 speaks of goods "bailed for hire". There the bailor is responsible for damage arising directly from faults in the goods whether he was or was not aware of them. Example. Anil hires a carriage from Babu. The carriage is unsafe, though Babu is not aware of it, and Anil is injured. Babu is responsible to Anil for the injury. This is the Act's own illustration (b) to section 150. Kind 2: gratuitous bailment Rule. The Act uses the word "gratuitous" in sections 159 and 162. Section 158 speaks of a bailee who is to receive no remuneration. The Act gives these rules. The bailor must repay the bailee the necessary expenses incurred for the purpose of the bailment, where the goods are to be kept, carried or have work done on them and the bailee gets no remuneration (section 158). The lender may at any time require the return of the thing, even though he lent it for a specified time or purpose. If the borrower acted on the faith of the loan so that early return would cause him loss exceeding the benefit he derived, the lender who compels return must indemnify him for the excess (section 159). The bailment is terminated by the death of the bailor or of the bailee (section 162). The first part of section 150, the bailor's duty to disclose faults of which he is aware, applies to every bailment. The second part adds the rule for goods bailed for hire. Example. Chandu lends his bicycle to Dev for a month without charge. After a week Chandu asks for it back. Under section 159 he may require its return at any time. If Dev had, on the faith of the month-long loan, made arrangements so that early return would cost him more than the benefit he got, Chandu would have to indemnify him for the excess. If Chandu dies during the month, the gratuitous bailment ends (section 162). Pledge: bailment as security (section 172) Rule. A bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called a pledge. The Act gives pledge its own sections (172 to 179). Example. Esha borrows Rs 50,000 and hands her gold chain to the lender as security until she repays. This is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt. It is a pledge. Which kind of bailment? How to read this: start at the top and follow the answer. 1. Are the goods bailed as security for a debt or a promise? Yes: pledge (section 172). 2. If not, are the goods bailed for hire? Yes: bailment for hire (section 150). 3. Otherwise, where the Act's words speak of a gratuitous loan or a bailee who is to receive no remuneration: Gratuitous bailment (sections 158, 159, 162).
keyPoints: The Act does not list kinds. Its words show bailment for hire and gratuitous bailment, and pledge is bailment as security. For hire: the bailor is responsible for damage from faults whether aware or not (section 150). Gratuitous: the bailor repays necessary expenses (section 158). The lender may require return at any time (section 159). Death of either party ends it (section 162). Pledge: bailment as security for a debt or promise (section 172).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t13.subtitle: Sections 153, 159, 160, 161 and 162 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act has no single section on how a bailment ends. Sections 153, 159, 160, 161 and 162 deal with these events. The bailor may avoid the contract when the bailee acts inconsistently with its conditions (section 153). A gratuitous lender may require the goods back at any time (section 159). A gratuitous bailment ends on the death of the bailor or of the bailee (section 162). On expiry of time, or accomplishment of the purpose, the bailee must return the goods (sections 160 and 161). Key points for the answer: each event with its section and the Act's illustration.
en.meaning:
Event 1: the bailee's act inconsistent with the conditions (section 153)

Rule. The bailment is avoidable at the bailor's option if the bailee does any act with regard to the goods that is inconsistent with the conditions of the bailment. The bailment is not ended automatically. It ends if the bailor chooses.

Example. Ravi hires out a horse to Sita for her own riding. Sita yokes it to her cart. This is inconsistent with the condition. At Ravi's option, the bailment is terminated. This follows the Act's illustration.

Event 2: return of a gratuitous loan on demand (section 159)

Rule. The lender of a thing for use may at any time require its return if the loan was gratuitous, even though he lent it for a specified time or purpose. If early return causes the borrower loss exceeding the benefit he derived, the lender must indemnify him for the excess.

Example. Dev lends his bicycle free of charge to Esha for a month. After a week he asks for it back. He may require its return (section 159).

Event 3: death in a gratuitous bailment (section 162)

Rule. A gratuitous bailment is terminated by the death either of the bailor or of the bailee. Section 162 speaks only of a gratuitous bailment.

Example. Farid lends his cart to Gopi free of charge for a fortnight. Farid dies in the first week. The bailment is terminated (section 162).

Event 4: expiry of time or accomplishment of purpose (sections 160 and 161)

Rule. When the time for which the goods were bailed has expired, or the purpose has been accomplished, the bailee must return them, or deliver them as the bailor directs, without demand (section 160). If, by his default, he does not return, deliver or tender them at the proper time, he is responsible for any loss, destruction or deterioration from that time (section 161).

Example. Hema gives her scooter to a garage for repair. When the repair is done, the garage must return it without waiting for Hema to ask. If the garage fails to return it at the proper time by its own default, it is responsible for any loss or damage to the scooter from that time.

How a bailment ends How to read this: find the event and follow it to the section. 1. The bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions. Bailor may avoid the contract (section 153). 2. The loan is gratuitous and the lender asks for the thing back. He may require return at any time (section 159). 3. The bailor or the bailee of a gratuitous bailment dies. Bailment is terminated (section 162). 4. The time expires, or the purpose is accomplished. Bailee returns the goods without demand (section 160). Default makes him responsible (section 161).
keyPoints: Bailee's inconsistent act: bailment avoidable at the bailor's option (section 153). Gratuitous loan: the lender may require return at any time (section 159). Gratuitous bailment: terminated by the death of the bailor or the bailee (section 162). Expiry or accomplishment: return without demand (section 160). Default: responsible for loss from that time (section 161).

selfTest.q: 1. Which section makes a bailment avoidable at the bailor's option?

బెయిల్‌మెంట్ ఎలా ముగుస్తుందో చెప్పే ఒకే సెక్షన్ చట్టంలో లేదు. సెక్షన్లు 153, 159, 160, 161, 162 ఈ సంఘటనల గురించి చెబుతాయి. బెయిలీ షరతులకు విరుద్ధంగా ప్రవర్తిస్తే, బెయిలర్ ఒప్పందాన్ని తన ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 153). ఉచితంగా అప్పు ఇచ్చినవాడు ఎప్పుడైనా సరుకులను తిరిగి కోరవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 159). బెయిలర్ లేదా బెయిలీ మరణంతో ఉచిత బెయిల్‌మెంట్ ముగుస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 162). గడువు ముగిసినప్పుడు, లేదా ప్రయోజనం నెరవేరినప్పుడు, బెయిలీ సరుకులను తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి (సెక్షన్లు 160, 161).

సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: ప్రతి సంఘటన, దాని సెక్షన్, చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణ.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. బెయిల్‌మెంట్ షరతులకు విరుద్ధంగా సరుకుల విషయంలో బెయిలీ ఏ చర్య చేసినా, బెయిల్‌మెంట్ బెయిలర్ ఇష్టం మేరకు రద్దు చేయదగినది. బెయిల్‌మెంట్ దానంతట అదే ముగియదు. బెయిలర్ ఎంచుకుంటే ముగుస్తుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. సీత సొంత స్వారీ కోసం రవి ఒక గుర్రాన్ని అద్దెకు ఇచ్చాడు. సీత దాన్ని తన బండికి కట్టింది. ఇది షరతుకు విరుద్ధం. రవి ఇష్టం మేరకు బెయిల్‌మెంట్ ముగుస్తుంది. ఇది చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణను అనుసరిస్తుంది.

నియమం. అప్పు ఉచితమైతే, నిర్ణీత కాలానికి లేదా ప్రయోజనానికి ఇచ్చినా, వినియోగం కోసం వస్తువును అప్పుగా ఇచ్చినవాడు దాన్ని ఎప్పుడైనా తిరిగి కోరవచ్చు. త్వరగా తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం వల్ల రుణగ్రహీతకు అతడు పొందిన ప్రయోజనం కంటే ఎక్కువ నష్టం కలిగితే, అప్పు ఇచ్చినవాడు ఆ అదనపు నష్టాన్ని భర్తీ చేయాలి.

ఉదాహరణ. దేవ్ తన సైకిల్‌ను ఒక నెల పాటు ఏ ఛార్జీ లేకుండా ఈషాకు అప్పుగా ఇచ్చాడు. ఒక వారం తర్వాత దాన్ని తిరిగి అడిగాడు. అతడు తిరిగి ఇవ్వమని కోరవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 159).

hi.inOneMinute: The Act has no single section on how a bailment ends. Sections 153, 159, 160, 161 and 162 deal with these events. The bailor may avoid the contract when the bailee acts inconsistently with its conditions (section 153). A gratuitous lender may require the goods back at any time (section 159). A gratuitous bailment ends on the death of the bailor or of the bailee (section 162). On expiry of time, or accomplishment of the purpose, the bailee must return the goods (sections 160 and 161). Key points for the answer: each event with its section and the Act's illustration.
hi.meaning: Event 1: the bailee's act inconsistent with the conditions (section 153) Rule. The bailment is avoidable at the bailor's option if the bailee does any act with regard to the goods that is inconsistent with the conditions of the bailment. The bailment is not ended automatically. It ends if the bailor chooses. Example. Ravi hires out a horse to Sita for her own riding. Sita yokes it to her cart. This is inconsistent with the condition. At Ravi's option, the bailment is terminated. This follows the Act's illustration. Event 2: return of a gratuitous loan on demand (section 159) Rule. The lender of a thing for use may at any time require its return if the loan was gratuitous, even though he lent it for a specified time or purpose. If early return causes the borrower loss exceeding the benefit he derived, the lender must indemnify him for the excess. Example. Dev lends his bicycle free of charge to Esha for a month. After a week he asks for it back. He may require its return (section 159). Event 3: death in a gratuitous bailment (section 162) Rule. A gratuitous bailment is terminated by the death either of the bailor or of the bailee. Section 162 speaks only of a gratuitous bailment. Example. Farid lends his cart to Gopi free of charge for a fortnight. Farid dies in the first week. The bailment is terminated (section 162). Event 4: expiry of time or accomplishment of purpose (sections 160 and 161) Rule. When the time for which the goods were bailed has expired, or the purpose has been accomplished, the bailee must return them, or deliver them as the bailor directs, without demand (section 160). If, by his default, he does not return, deliver or tender them at the proper time, he is responsible for any loss, destruction or deterioration from that time (section 161). Example. Hema gives her scooter to a garage for repair. When the repair is done, the garage must return it without waiting for Hema to ask. If the garage fails to return it at the proper time by its own default, it is responsible for any loss or damage to the scooter from that time. How a bailment ends How to read this: find the event and follow it to the section. 1. The bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions. Bailor may avoid the contract (section 153). 2. The loan is gratuitous and the lender asks for the thing back. He may require return at any time (section 159). 3. The bailor or the bailee of a gratuitous bailment dies. Bailment is terminated (section 162). 4. The time expires, or the purpose is accomplished. Bailee returns the goods without demand (section 160). Default makes him responsible (section 161).
keyPoints: Bailee's inconsistent act: bailment avoidable at the bailor's option (section 153). Gratuitous loan: the lender may require return at any time (section 159). Gratuitous bailment: terminated by the death of the bailor or the bailee (section 162). Expiry or accomplishment: return without demand (section 160). Default: responsible for loss from that time (section 161).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t12.subtitle: Sections 150 to 161, 163 to 167, 170, 171, 180 and 181 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Act gives the bailor and the bailee duties and rights. The bailor must disclose known faults (section 150), repay necessary expenses where the bailee is unpaid (section 158) and answer for his title (section 164). The bailee must take proper care (section 151), use the goods only as the bailment allows (sections 153 and 154), bear the consequences of mixing goods (sections 155 to 157), and return them with any increase (sections 160, 161 and 163). The bailee has a lien for his service (section 170). Bankers, factors and certain others have a general lien (section 171). Key points for the answer: the duties of each party, the liens and the Act's illustrations.
en.meaning:
Duties of the bailor

Rule. The bailor has these duties under the Act.

Disclose faults (section 150). He must disclose faults he is aware of that materially interfere with the use of the goods or expose the bailee to extraordinary risks. If goods are bailed for hire, he is responsible for damage from faults whether aware or not. Illustration (a): A lends B a horse he knows to be vicious without saying so. The horse runs away and B is injured. A is responsible. Illustration (b): A hires a carriage from B. It is unsafe, though B is not aware, and A is injured. B is responsible. Repay necessary expenses (section 158) where the bailee receives no remuneration. Indemnify for early return of a gratuitous loan (section 159) , to the extent the borrower's loss exceeds the benefit he derived. Answer for his title (section 164). He is responsible to the bailee for loss the bailee sustains because the bailor was not entitled to make the bailment, to receive back the goods or to give directions.

Example. Ravi lends his scooter to Sita knowing that its brakes are faulty and does not tell her. The brakes fail and Sita is hurt. Ravi is responsible for the damage arising directly from the fault (section 150).

Duties of the bailee: care, and no unauthorised use

Rule. The bailee must take the care of section 151. If he has taken that care, and there is no special contract, he is not responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration (section 152).

If the bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions, the bailor may avoid the bailment (section 153). If he uses the goods otherwise than as the bailment allows, he must compensate the bailor for damage arising from or during that use (section 154).

Section 153, illustration: A lets a horse to B for hire for his own riding. B drives it in his carriage. At A's option, this terminates the bailment. Section 154, illustration (a): A lends a horse to B for his own riding only. B allows C, a member of his family, to ride it. C rides with care, but the horse accidentally falls and is injured. B must compensate A. Section 154, illustration (b): A hires a horse in Calcutta from B expressly to march to Benares. A marches to Cuttack instead. The horse accidentally falls and is injured. A must compensate B.

Example. Kiran borrows Lata's sewing machine for his own use at home. He lets his neighbour use it, and it is damaged during that use. Kiran must compensate Lata for the damage arising during the use (section 154).

Mixing the goods: consequences for the bailee (sections 155 to 157)

Rule. The effect of mixing depends on consent and on whether the goods can be separated.

With the bailor's consent: both have an interest in the mixture in proportion to their shares (section 155). Without consent, goods can be separated: the property remains with the parties. The bailee bears the expense of separation and any damage from the mixture (section 156). Illustration: A bails 100 marked bales of cotton to B, who mixes them with his own differently marked bales. A may have his 100 bales back and B bears all the expense of separation. Without consent, goods cannot be separated: the bailee must compensate the bailor for the loss of the goods (section 157). Illustration: A bails a barrel of Cape flour worth Rs 45 to B, who mixes it with country flour worth Rs 25 a barrel. B must compensate A.

Duties of the bailee: return, and increase or profit

Rule. The bailee must return the goods, or deliver them as the bailor directs, without demand, as soon as the time has expired or the purpose is accomplished (section 160). If by his default they are not returned at the proper time, he is responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration from that time (section 161). In the absence of a contract to the contrary, he must deliver any increase or profit from the goods (section 163). Illustration: A leaves a cow with B to be taken care of. The cow has a calf. B must deliver the calf as well as the cow.

Example. Dev leaves his goat with Esha for a month. The goat has a kid. At the end of the month Esha must return the goat and the kid (section 163).

Joint owners, a bailor without title, and rival claimants (sections 165 to 167)

Rule. If joint owners bail goods, the bailee may deliver them back to one of them without the consent of all, unless they agreed otherwise (section 165). If the bailor has no title and the bailee in good faith delivers them back to the bailor, the bailee is not responsible to the owner (section 166). A person other than the bailor who claims the goods may apply to the Court to stop delivery to the bailor and to decide the title (section 167).

Rights of the bailee: liens (sections 170 and 171)

Rule. A bailee who has rendered service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment, may retain them until he receives due remuneration, unless the contract says otherwise (section 170). This is the particular lien.

Illustration (a): A delivers a rough diamond to B, a jeweller, to be cut and polished. B may retain the stone until he is paid. Illustration (b): A gives cloth to B, a tailor, to make a coat. B promises to deliver the coat as soon as it is finished and to give three months' credit for the price. B is not entitled to retain the coat until he is paid.

Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers may retain goods bailed to them as security for a general balance of account, in the absence of a contract to the contrary. No other persons may do so unless there is an express contract (section 171). This is the general lien.

Rights against third persons (sections 180 and 181)

Rule. If a third person wrongfully deprives the bailee of the use or possession of the goods, or injures them, the bailee may use the remedies the owner could have used. Either the bailor or the bailee may sue the third person (section 180). What is obtained is dealt with between them according to their respective interests (section 181).

Rights of the bailor

Rule. The bailor may avoid the bailment where the bailee does an act inconsistent with its conditions (section 153). He is entitled to compensation for damage from unauthorised use (section 154), for goods lost by mixing (section 157), and for loss after default in returning (section 161). He may require return of a gratuitous loan at any time (section 159). He is entitled to any increase or profit (section 163).

Can the bailee keep the goods until he is paid? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the bailee render a service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment? Yes: particular lien (section 170), unless the contract says otherwise. 2. Is he a banker, factor, wharfinger, attorney of a High Court or policy-broker? Yes: general lien for a general balance of account (section 171), unless the contract says otherwise. 3. Neither? No right to retain for a general balance, unless there is an express contract (section 171).
keyPoints: Bailor: disclose known faults (section 150), and for hire he is responsible whether aware or not. Repay necessary expenses where the bailee is unpaid (section 158). Bailee: ordinary prudence (section 151). Not responsible if he took that care and there is no special contract (section 152). Unauthorised use: bailor may avoid (section 153). Bailee compensates for damage from or during such use (section 154). Mixing: with consent, shared in proportion (section 155). Without consent, separable: bailee bears the cost (section 156). Not separable: compensation (section 157). Return without demand (section 160). Increase or profit goes to the bailor (section 163). Particular lien: service involving labour or skill (section 170). General lien: bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court, policy-brokers (section 171).

selfTest.q: 1. What standard of care must a bailee take under section 151?
selfTest.a: As much care as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value. 2. Who has a general lien under section 171? Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers, in the absence of a contract to the contrary. Others only by an express contract. 3. What must a bailee do with the calf of a cow left with him? Deliver the calf as well as the cow to the bailor (section 163, illustration).

te.meaning:
చట్టం బెయిలర్‌కు, బెయిలీకి విధులు, హక్కులు ఇస్తుంది. బెయిలర్ తనకు తెలిసిన లోపాలను తెలియజేయాలి (సెక్షన్ 150), బెయిలీకి పారితోషికం లేనప్పుడు అవసరమైన ఖర్చులను తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి (సెక్షన్ 158), తన యాజమాన్య హక్కుకు జవాబుదారీ ఉండాలి (సెక్షన్ 164). బెయిలీ తగిన జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాలి (సెక్షన్ 151), బెయిల్‌మెంట్ అనుమతించిన విధంగానే సరుకులను వాడాలి (సెక్షన్లు 153, 154), సరుకులను కలిపితే కలిగే పర్యవసానాలు భరించాలి (సెక్షన్లు 155 నుండి 157), పెరుగుదలతో సహా వాటిని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి (సెక్షన్లు 160, 161, 163).

బెయిలీ చేసిన సేవకు, చెల్లింపు వచ్చే వరకు సరుకులను ఉంచుకునే లియన్ (lien) అతడికి ఉంటుంది (సెక్షన్ 170). బ్యాంకర్లకు, ఫ్యాక్టర్లకు, మరికొందరికి సాధారణ లియన్ ఉంటుంది (సెక్షన్ 171). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: ప్రతి పక్షం విధులు, లియన్లు, చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణలు.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. చట్టం ప్రకారం బెయిలర్‌కు ఈ విధులు ఉన్నాయి.

ఉదాహరణ. రవి తన స్కూటర్ బ్రేకులు లోపభూయిష్టమని తెలిసి, ఆ సంగతి చెప్పకుండా సీతకు అప్పుగా ఇచ్చాడు. బ్రేకులు విఫలమై సీత గాయపడింది. ఆ లోపం వల్ల నేరుగా కలిగిన నష్టానికి రవి బాధ్యుడు (సెక్షన్ 150).

నియమం. బెయిలీ సెక్షన్ 151 లోని జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాలి. ఆ జాగ్రత్త తీసుకుని ఉంటే, ప్రత్యేక ఒప్పందం లేనప్పుడు, నష్టం, నాశనం లేదా క్షీణతకు అతడు బాధ్యుడు కాడు (సెక్షన్ 152).

షరతులకు విరుద్ధంగా బెయిలీ ఏదైనా చర్య చేస్తే, బెయిలర్ బెయిల్‌మెంట్‌ను రద్దు చేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 153). బెయిల్‌మెంట్ అనుమతించిన దానికి భిన్నంగా సరుకులను వాడితే, ఆ వినియోగం వల్ల లేదా ఆ వినియోగ సమయంలో కలిగిన నష్టానికి బెయిలర్‌కు పరిహారం ఇవ్వాలి (సెక్షన్ 154).

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 151 ప్రకారం బెయిలీ ఎలాంటి జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోవాలి?
selfTest.a: అదే పరిమాణం, నాణ్యత, విలువ ఉన్న తన సొంత సరుకులను ఒక సాధారణ వివేకం ఉన్న వ్యక్తి ఇలాంటి పరిస్థితుల్లో ఎంత జాగ్రత్తగా చూసుకుంటాడో అంత జాగ్రత్త. 2. సెక్షన్ 171 కింద సాధారణ లియన్ ఎవరికి ఉంది? బ్యాంకర్లు, ఫ్యాక్టర్లు, వార్ఫింజర్లు, హైకోర్టు అటార్నీలు, పాలసీ బ్రోకర్లు, విరుద్ధమైన ఒప్పందం లేనప్పుడు. ఇతరులకు స్పష్టమైన ఒప్పందం ద్వారా మాత్రమే. 3. తన వద్ద ఉంచిన ఆవుకు పుట్టిన దూడను బెయిలీ ఏం చేయాలి? ఆవుతో పాటు దూడను కూడా బెయిలర్‌కు అందజేయాలి (సెక్షన్ 163 ఉదాహరణ).

hi.inOneMinute: The Act gives the bailor and the bailee duties and rights. The bailor must disclose known faults (section 150), repay necessary expenses where the bailee is unpaid (section 158) and answer for his title (section 164). The bailee must take proper care (section 151), use the goods only as the bailment allows (sections 153 and 154), bear the consequences of mixing goods (sections 155 to 157), and return them with any increase (sections 160, 161 and 163). The bailee has a lien for his service (section 170). Bankers, factors and certain others have a general lien (section 171). Key points for the answer: the duties of each party, the liens and the Act's illustrations.
hi.meaning: Duties of the bailor Rule. The bailor has these duties under the Act. Disclose faults (section 150). He must disclose faults he is aware of that materially interfere with the use of the goods or expose the bailee to extraordinary risks. If goods are bailed for hire, he is responsible for damage from faults whether aware or not. Illustration (a): A lends B a horse he knows to be vicious without saying so. The horse runs away and B is injured. A is responsible. Illustration (b): A hires a carriage from B. It is unsafe, though B is not aware, and A is injured. B is responsible. Repay necessary expenses (section 158) where the bailee receives no remuneration. Indemnify for early return of a gratuitous loan (section 159) , to the extent the borrower's loss exceeds the benefit he derived. Answer for his title (section 164). He is responsible to the bailee for loss the bailee sustains because the bailor was not entitled to make the bailment, to receive back the goods or to give directions. Example. Ravi lends his scooter to Sita knowing that its brakes are faulty and does not tell her. The brakes fail and Sita is hurt. Ravi is responsible for the damage arising directly from the fault (section 150). Duties of the bailee: care, and no unauthorised use Rule. The bailee must take the care of section 151. If he has taken that care, and there is no special contract, he is not responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration (section 152). If the bailee does an act inconsistent with the conditions, the bailor may avoid the bailment (section 153). If he uses the goods otherwise than as the bailment allows, he must compensate the bailor for damage arising from or during that use (section 154). Section 153, illustration: A lets a horse to B for hire for his own riding. B drives it in his carriage. At A's option, this terminates the bailment. Section 154, illustration (a): A lends a horse to B for his own riding only. B allows C, a member of his family, to ride it. C rides with care, but the horse accidentally falls and is injured. B must compensate A. Section 154, illustration (b): A hires a horse in Calcutta from B expressly to march to Benares. A marches to Cuttack instead. The horse accidentally falls and is injured. A must compensate B. Example. Kiran borrows Lata's sewing machine for his own use at home. He lets his neighbour use it, and it is damaged during that use. Kiran must compensate Lata for the damage arising during the use (section 154). Mixing the goods: consequences for the bailee (sections 155 to 157) Rule. The effect of mixing depends on consent and on whether the goods can be separated. With the bailor's consent: both have an interest in the mixture in proportion to their shares (section 155). Without consent, goods can be separated: the property remains with the parties. The bailee bears the expense of separation and any damage from the mixture (section 156). Illustration: A bails 100 marked bales of cotton to B, who mixes them with his own differently marked bales. A may have his 100 bales back and B bears all the expense of separation. Without consent, goods cannot be separated: the bailee must compensate the bailor for the loss of the goods (section 157). Illustration: A bails a barrel of Cape flour worth Rs 45 to B, who mixes it with country flour worth Rs 25 a barrel. B must compensate A. Duties of the bailee: return, and increase or profit Rule. The bailee must return the goods, or deliver them as the bailor directs, without demand, as soon as the time has expired or the purpose is accomplished (section 160). If by his default they are not returned at the proper time, he is responsible for loss, destruction or deterioration from that time (section 161). In the absence of a contract to the contrary, he must deliver any increase or profit from the goods (section 163). Illustration: A leaves a cow with B to be taken care of. The cow has a calf. B must deliver the calf as well as the cow. Example. Dev leaves his goat with Esha for a month. The goat has a kid. At the end of the month Esha must return the goat and the kid (section 163). Joint owners, a bailor without title, and rival claimants (sections 165 to 167) Rule. If joint owners bail goods, the bailee may deliver them back to one of them without the consent of all, unless they agreed otherwise (section 165). If the bailor has no title and the bailee in good faith delivers them back to the bailor, the bailee is not responsible to the owner (section 166). A person other than the bailor who claims the goods may apply to the Court to stop delivery to the bailor and to decide the title (section 167). Rights of the bailee: liens (sections 170 and 171) Rule. A bailee who has rendered service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment, may retain them until he receives due remuneration, unless the contract says otherwise (section 170). This is the particular lien. Illustration (a): A delivers a rough diamond to B, a jeweller, to be cut and polished. B may retain the stone until he is paid. Illustration (b): A gives cloth to B, a tailor, to make a coat. B promises to deliver the coat as soon as it is finished and to give three months' credit for the price. B is not entitled to retain the coat until he is paid. Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers may retain goods bailed to them as security for a general balance of account, in the absence of a contract to the contrary. No other persons may do so unless there is an express contract (section 171). This is the general lien. Rights against third persons (sections 180 and 181) Rule. If a third person wrongfully deprives the bailee of the use or possession of the goods, or injures them, the bailee may use the remedies the owner could have used. Either the bailor or the bailee may sue the third person (section 180). What is obtained is dealt with between them according to their respective interests (section 181). Rights of the bailor Rule. The bailor may avoid the bailment where the bailee does an act inconsistent with its conditions (section 153). He is entitled to compensation for damage from unauthorised use (section 154), for goods lost by mixing (section 157), and for loss after default in returning (section 161). He may require return of a gratuitous loan at any time (section 159). He is entitled to any increase or profit (section 163). Can the bailee keep the goods until he is paid? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the bailee render a service involving labour or skill on the goods, in accordance with the purpose of the bailment? Yes: particular lien (section 170), unless the contract says otherwise. 2. Is he a banker, factor, wharfinger, attorney of a High Court or policy-broker? Yes: general lien for a general balance of account (section 171), unless the contract says otherwise. 3. Neither? No right to retain for a general balance, unless there is an express contract (section 171).
keyPoints: Bailor: disclose known faults (section 150), and for hire he is responsible whether aware or not. Repay necessary expenses where the bailee is unpaid (section 158). Bailee: ordinary prudence (section 151). Not responsible if he took that care and there is no special contract (section 152). Unauthorised use: bailor may avoid (section 153). Bailee compensates for damage from or during such use (section 154). Mixing: with consent, shared in proportion (section 155). Without consent, separable: bailee bears the cost (section 156). Not separable: compensation (section 157). Return without demand (section 160). Increase or profit goes to the bailor (section 163). Particular lien: service involving labour or skill (section 170). General lien: bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court, policy-brokers (section 171).

selfTest.q: 1. What standard of care must a bailee take under section 151?
selfTest.a: As much care as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods of the same bulk, quality and value. 2. Who has a general lien under section 171? Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers, in the absence of a contract to the contrary. Others only by an express contract. 3. What must a bailee do with the calf of a cow left with him? Deliver the calf as well as the cow to the bailor (section 163, illustration).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t7.subtitle: Sections 126, 128, 132, 137, 138 and 140 to 147 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A surety stands behind a borrower. The lender is the creditor . The borrower is the principal debtor . The surety's duty to pay is as wide as the borrower's. The lender may ask the surety to pay at once. After paying, the surety gets rights against the borrower, the lender's securities and other sureties. Key points for the answer: the section 128 rule, the case Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad and these three rights.
en.meaning:
Liability: as wide as the debtor's (section 128)

Rule. The surety is liable for as much as the principal debtor owes, including interest and charges that fall due. The only limit is what the contract provides. This is what coextensive means in section 128.

The bond may cap the amount, as in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad (Rs. 12,000 and interest). Section 145 separately limits what the surety can recover from the borrower: no more than the borrower really owed.

Example. Meena guarantees a bank loan of Rs 2 lakh taken by her brother Ravi in Vijayawada. Ravi defaults . Meena is liable for the whole Rs 2 lakh and the interest due. If her bond had capped her at Rs 1 lakh with interest, that cap would govern. The Act's own illustration holds a guarantor of a dishonoured bill of exchange liable for the amount, the interest and the charges.

Liability: immediate, with no need to sue the debtor first

Rule. The creditor does not have to sue the principal debtor first. In Bank of Bihar the bond made demand the only condition. Once the creditor demanded payment and it was not met, the surety was liable at once. A guarantee may set other conditions, so always read its terms. The Supreme Court said the liability was immediate. It was not deferred until the creditor had exhausted his remedies against the principal debtor.

The surety cannot tell the creditor to chase the debtor first. In the absence of some special equity, the surety also cannot restrain execution against him on the ground that the debtor is solvent.

Example. This is what happened in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad (see the case below). The Supreme Court set aside an order that made the bank exhaust its remedies against the borrower first.

Liability: delay by the creditor does not free the surety (section 137)

Rule. Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor does not discharge the surety. The guarantee may say otherwise, and then it governs.

Example. Kiran owes Mohan a debt guaranteed by Suresh. The debt becomes payable. Mohan does not sue Kiran for a year. Suresh is not discharged. This is the Act's own illustration to section 137.

Liability: two persons liable together, one acting as surety only between themselves (section 132)

Rule. Two persons may take a liability together and agree privately that one of them will pay only if the other fails. The creditor is not a party to that private agreement. Each of the two stays fully liable to the creditor, even if the creditor knows of the arrangement.

Example. Hari and Gita sign one joint loan document for Rs 1 lakh with a cooperative bank. Privately they agree that Gita will pay only if Hari fails. The bank knows this. The bank can still sue Gita directly. This follows the Act's illustration to section 132, where a joint and several promissory note signed by A as surety for B does not stop C from suing A.

Liability: none where the guarantee was obtained by misrepresentation or concealment (sections 142 to 144)

Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by a misrepresentation about a material part of the transaction, made by him or with his knowledge and assent. It is also invalid if he obtained it by keeping silent about material circumstances. An invalid guarantee binds no one, so the surety owes nothing.

Section 144 deals with a related case. A person may give a guarantee on the condition that the creditor will not act on it until another person joins as co-surety. If that other person does not join, the guarantee is not valid.

Example. Anand employs Bala as a cashier. Bala has already failed to account for some of the money he collected. Anand asks Chandu to guarantee Bala's accounts and does not tell him about this. Bala later defaults. Chandu's guarantee is invalid. This is the Act's illustration (a) to section 143.

Right against the principal debtor: subrogation and indemnity (sections 140 and 145)

Rule. The surety pays first and recovers afterwards. A surety who pays all he is liable for steps into the creditor's shoes under section 140. This is subrogation . The surety can then proceed against the principal debtor with the creditor's rights.

Section 145 adds a second route. The principal debtor impliedly promises to indemnify the surety. The surety recovers sums he has rightfully paid, and not sums he paid wrongfully.

Example. Suresh is surety for Kiran's debt to Mohan. Mohan sues Suresh. Suresh defends on reasonable grounds but loses and pays the debt with costs. He recovers both the debt and the costs from Kiran. Had he defended with no reasonable ground, he could recover the debt but not the costs. This follows the Act's illustrations to section 145.

Right against the creditor: benefit of securities (section 141)

Rule. The surety is entitled to every security the creditor holds against the principal debtor when the guarantee is given. This is so even if the surety does not know about it. If the creditor loses it, or gives it up without the surety's consent, the surety is discharged to the extent of its value.

Only the security that exists when the guarantee is given counts. A further security that the creditor obtains later is not covered.

Example. Lakshmi lends her tenant Venkat Rs 2,000 on Ramesh's guarantee. She also holds a mortgage of Venkat's furniture for the debt. She cancels the mortgage. Venkat becomes insolvent and Lakshmi sues Ramesh. Ramesh is discharged to the value of the furniture. This is the Act's illustration (a) to section 141.

Right against co-sureties: sharing the loss (sections 138, 146 and 147)

Rule. Where several sureties guarantee the same debt, each must bear an equal share unless they agreed otherwise. If they are bound in different sums, they pay equally within the limits of those sums. So a surety who pays more than his share can claim the excess from the others.

If the creditor releases one co-surety, the others are not discharged (section 138). The released surety is also not freed from his responsibility to the other sureties.

Example. A, B and C are sureties to D for Rs 3,000 lent to E. E defaults. As between themselves they pay Rs 1,000 each. In the Act's illustration to section 147, sureties are bound in sums of Rs 10,000, Rs 20,000 and Rs 40,000, and the debtor defaults by Rs 40,000. A pays Rs 10,000, and B and C pay Rs 15,000 each.

From default to recovery How to read this: start at the top and follow the boxes down. The last box shows who the surety can recover from. 1. The principal debtor defaults and the creditor demands payment. 2. The surety is liable at once (section 128). The creditor need not sue the principal debtor first. 3. The surety pays all he is liable for. 4. The surety takes over the creditor's rights (section 140) and has an implied indemnity (section 145). Sums rightfully paid can be recovered from the principal debtor. 5. Co-sureties share the loss (sections 146 and 147). A surety who paid more than his share recovers the excess from the others.
keyPoints: Section 128: the surety's liability is coextensive with the principal debtor's, unless the contract says otherwise. The liability is immediate. The creditor need not exhaust remedies against the principal debtor first (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). Mere forbearance to sue does not discharge the surety (section 137). The surety's rights against the principal debtor begin on payment: section 140 (creditor's rights) and section 145 (implied indemnity). Section 141: the surety has the benefit of the securities held when the guarantee is given. A later security is not covered. Sections 146 and 147: co-sureties contribute equally, within the limits of their sums. Release of one co-surety does not discharge the others (section 138). A private arrangement between two joint promisors does not bind the creditor (section 132). A guarantee obtained by misrepresentation or concealment is invalid (sections 142 and 143).

caseLaws.name: Bank of Bihar v
caseLaws.facts: Damodar Prasad (1968) Facts. A bank lent money to Damodar Prasad on the guarantee of Paras Nath Sinha. The trial court decreed the suit against both but barred execution against the guarantor until the bank had exhausted its remedies against the borrower. Principle. The surety's liability is immediate. Without some special equity, he cannot restrain execution against him until the creditor has exhausted his remedies against the principal. The surety must pay and then recover from the principal under section 140. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court authority for the point that a creditor may proceed against the surety without first proceeding against the debtor.

selfTest.q: 1. What does it mean to say that the surety's liability is coextensive?
selfTest.a: It means the surety is liable for as much as the principal debtor owes, unless the contract provides otherwise (section 128). 2. Can a surety insist that the creditor sue the principal debtor first? No. The liability is immediate. In the absence of some special equity, the surety cannot restrain execution until the creditor has exhausted his remedies against the principal (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). 3. What does a surety get on paying the creditor? All the rights the creditor had against the principal debtor (section 140), and an implied indemnity for sums rightfully paid (section 145).

te.meaning:
హామీదారు (surety) అంటే అప్పు తీసుకున్నవారి వెనుక నిలబడే వ్యక్తి. అప్పు ఇచ్చినవారు రుణదాత (creditor). అప్పు తీసుకున్నవారు ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత (principal debtor).

హామీదారు చెల్లించాల్సిన బాధ్యత, అప్పు తీసుకున్నవారి బాధ్యత అంత విస్తృతమైనది. రుణదాత వెంటనే హామీదారును చెల్లించమని అడగవచ్చు. చెల్లించిన తర్వాత, అప్పు తీసుకున్నవారిపై, రుణదాత వద్ద ఉన్న తాకట్టులపై, ఇతర హామీదారులపై హామీదారుకు హక్కులు వస్తాయి. సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: సెక్షన్ 128 నియమం, Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad కేసు, ఈ మూడు హక్కులు.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత ఎంత బాకీ ఉన్నాడో అంత వరకు హామీదారు బాధ్యుడు. గడువు వచ్చే వడ్డీ, ఖర్చులు కూడా అందులో ఉంటాయి. ఒప్పందంలో ఉన్న పరిమితి మాత్రమే హద్దు. సెక్షన్ 128 లో సమాన పరిధి అంటే ఇదే.

హామీ పత్రం మొత్తానికి పరిమితి పెట్టవచ్చు, Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad లో లాగా (రూ. 12,000 మరియు వడ్డీ). సెక్షన్ 145 వేరుగా, రుణగ్రహీత నుంచి హామీదారు రాబట్టుకునే మొత్తాన్ని పరిమితం చేస్తుంది: రుణగ్రహీత నిజంగా బాకీ ఉన్నదానికంటే ఎక్కువ కాదు.

ఉదాహరణ. విజయవాడలో తన సోదరుడు రవి తీసుకున్న రూ. 2 లక్షల బ్యాంకు అప్పుకు మీనా హామీ ఇచ్చింది. రవి చెల్లించడంలో విఫలమయ్యాడు . మీనా మొత్తం రూ. 2 లక్షలకు, దానిపై గడువు వచ్చిన వడ్డీకి బాధ్యురాలు . ఆమె హామీ పత్రం వడ్డీతో సహా రూ. 1 లక్ష వరకే పరిమితమై ఉంటే, ఆ పరిమితే వర్తిస్తుంది. చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణ కూడా ఇదే చెబుతుంది: తిరస్కరించబడిన హుండీకి (bill of exchange) హామీ ఇచ్చినవాడు అసలుకు, వడ్డీకి, ఖర్చులకు బాధ్యుడు.

నియమం. రుణదాత ముందు ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై దావా వేయాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు. Bank of Bihar లో హామీ పత్రం ప్రకారం చెల్లింపు డిమాండ్ ఒక్కటే షరతు. రుణదాత చెల్లింపు కోరి, అది అందకపోగానే హామీదారు వెంటనే బాధ్యుడయ్యాడు. హామీలో ఇతర షరతులు ఉండవచ్చు, కాబట్టి దాని నిబంధనలను ఎప్పుడూ చదవాలి. ఆ బాధ్యత వెంటనే తలెత్తిందని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. రుణదాత ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై అన్ని చట్టపరమైన మార్గాలన్నింటినీ ఉపయోగించే వరకు అది వాయిదా పడలేదు.

selfTest.q: 1. హామీదారు బాధ్యత ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత బాధ్యతతో సమాన పరిధిలో ఉంటుందంటే అర్థం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఒప్పందం వేరుగా చెప్పకపోతే, ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీత ఎంత బాకీ ఉన్నాడో అంత వరకు హామీదారు బాధ్యుడని అర్థం (సెక్షన్ 128). 2. ముందు ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై దావా వేయమని హామీదారు రుణదాతను కోరగలడా? కోరలేడు. బాధ్యత వెంటనే తలెత్తుతుంది. ప్రత్యేక న్యాయసమ్మతి లేనప్పుడు, ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై రుణదాత అన్ని చట్టపరమైన మార్గాలను ఉపయోగించే వరకు డిక్రీ అమలును హామీదారు అడ్డుకోలేడు (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). 3. రుణదాతకు చెల్లించిన తర్వాత హామీదారుకు ఏమి లభిస్తుంది? ప్రధాన రుణగ్రహీతపై రుణదాతకు ఉన్న హక్కులన్నీ (సెక్షన్ 140), న్యాయంగా చెల్లించిన మొత్తాలకు అంతర్లీన నష్టపూరణ హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 145).

hi.inOneMinute: A surety stands behind a borrower. The lender is the creditor . The borrower is the principal debtor . The surety's duty to pay is as wide as the borrower's. The lender may ask the surety to pay at once. After paying, the surety gets rights against the borrower, the lender's securities and other sureties. Key points for the answer: the section 128 rule, the case Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad and these three rights.
hi.meaning: Liability: as wide as the debtor's (section 128) Rule. The surety is liable for as much as the principal debtor owes, including interest and charges that fall due. The only limit is what the contract provides. This is what coextensive means in section 128. The bond may cap the amount, as in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad (Rs. 12,000 and interest). Section 145 separately limits what the surety can recover from the borrower: no more than the borrower really owed. Example. Meena guarantees a bank loan of Rs 2 lakh taken by her brother Ravi in Vijayawada. Ravi defaults . Meena is liable for the whole Rs 2 lakh and the interest due. If her bond had capped her at Rs 1 lakh with interest, that cap would govern. The Act's own illustration holds a guarantor of a dishonoured bill of exchange liable for the amount, the interest and the charges. Liability: immediate, with no need to sue the debtor first Rule. The creditor does not have to sue the principal debtor first. In Bank of Bihar the bond made demand the only condition. Once the creditor demanded payment and it was not met, the surety was liable at once. A guarantee may set other conditions, so always read its terms. The Supreme Court said the liability was immediate. It was not deferred until the creditor had exhausted his remedies against the principal debtor. The surety cannot tell the creditor to chase the debtor first. In the absence of some special equity, the surety also cannot restrain execution against him on the ground that the debtor is solvent. Example. This is what happened in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad (see the case below). The Supreme Court set aside an order that made the bank exhaust its remedies against the borrower first. Liability: delay by the creditor does not free the surety (section 137) Rule. Mere forbearance by the creditor to sue the principal debtor does not discharge the surety. The guarantee may say otherwise, and then it governs. Example. Kiran owes Mohan a debt guaranteed by Suresh. The debt becomes payable. Mohan does not sue Kiran for a year. Suresh is not discharged. This is the Act's own illustration to section 137. Liability: two persons liable together, one acting as surety only between themselves (section 132) Rule. Two persons may take a liability together and agree privately that one of them will pay only if the other fails. The creditor is not a party to that private agreement. Each of the two stays fully liable to the creditor, even if the creditor knows of the arrangement. Example. Hari and Gita sign one joint loan document for Rs 1 lakh with a cooperative bank. Privately they agree that Gita will pay only if Hari fails. The bank knows this. The bank can still sue Gita directly. This follows the Act's illustration to section 132, where a joint and several promissory note signed by A as surety for B does not stop C from suing A. Liability: none where the guarantee was obtained by misrepresentation or concealment (sections 142 to 144) Rule. A guarantee is invalid if the creditor obtained it by a misrepresentation about a material part of the transaction, made by him or with his knowledge and assent. It is also invalid if he obtained it by keeping silent about material circumstances. An invalid guarantee binds no one, so the surety owes nothing. Section 144 deals with a related case. A person may give a guarantee on the condition that the creditor will not act on it until another person joins as co-surety. If that other person does not join, the guarantee is not valid. Example. Anand employs Bala as a cashier. Bala has already failed to account for some of the money he collected. Anand asks Chandu to guarantee Bala's accounts and does not tell him about this. Bala later defaults. Chandu's guarantee is invalid. This is the Act's illustration (a) to section 143. Right against the principal debtor: subrogation and indemnity (sections 140 and 145) Rule. The surety pays first and recovers afterwards. A surety who pays all he is liable for steps into the creditor's shoes under section 140. This is subrogation . The surety can then proceed against the principal debtor with the creditor's rights. Section 145 adds a second route. The principal debtor impliedly promises to indemnify the surety. The surety recovers sums he has rightfully paid, and not sums he paid wrongfully. Example. Suresh is surety for Kiran's debt to Mohan. Mohan sues Suresh. Suresh defends on reasonable grounds but loses and pays the debt with costs. He recovers both the debt and the costs from Kiran. Had he defended with no reasonable ground, he could recover the debt but not the costs. This follows the Act's illustrations to section 145. Right against the creditor: benefit of securities (section 141) Rule. The surety is entitled to every security the creditor holds against the principal debtor when the guarantee is given. This is so even if the surety does not know about it. If the creditor loses it, or gives it up without the surety's consent, the surety is discharged to the extent of its value. Only the security that exists when the guarantee is given counts. A further security that the creditor obtains later is not covered. Example. Lakshmi lends her tenant Venkat Rs 2,000 on Ramesh's guarantee. She also holds a mortgage of Venkat's furniture for the debt. She cancels the mortgage. Venkat becomes insolvent and Lakshmi sues Ramesh. Ramesh is discharged to the value of the furniture. This is the Act's illustration (a) to section 141. Right against co-sureties: sharing the loss (sections 138, 146 and 147) Rule. Where several sureties guarantee the same debt, each must bear an equal share unless they agreed otherwise. If they are bound in different sums, they pay equally within the limits of those sums. So a surety who pays more than his share can claim the excess from the others. If the creditor releases one co-surety, the others are not discharged (section 138). The released surety is also not freed from his responsibility to the other sureties. Example. A, B and C are sureties to D for Rs 3,000 lent to E. E defaults. As between themselves they pay Rs 1,000 each. In the Act's illustration to section 147, sureties are bound in sums of Rs 10,000, Rs 20,000 and Rs 40,000, and the debtor defaults by Rs 40,000. A pays Rs 10,000, and B and C pay Rs 15,000 each. From default to recovery How to read this: start at the top and follow the boxes down. The last box shows who the surety can recover from. 1. The principal debtor defaults and the creditor demands payment. 2. The surety is liable at once (section 128). The creditor need not sue the principal debtor first. 3. The surety pays all he is liable for. 4. The surety takes over the creditor's rights (section 140) and has an implied indemnity (section 145). Sums rightfully paid can be recovered from the principal debtor. 5. Co-sureties share the loss (sections 146 and 147). A surety who paid more than his share recovers the excess from the others.
keyPoints: Section 128: the surety's liability is coextensive with the principal debtor's, unless the contract says otherwise. The liability is immediate. The creditor need not exhaust remedies against the principal debtor first (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). Mere forbearance to sue does not discharge the surety (section 137). The surety's rights against the principal debtor begin on payment: section 140 (creditor's rights) and section 145 (implied indemnity). Section 141: the surety has the benefit of the securities held when the guarantee is given. A later security is not covered. Sections 146 and 147: co-sureties contribute equally, within the limits of their sums. Release of one co-surety does not discharge the others (section 138). A private arrangement between two joint promisors does not bind the creditor (section 132). A guarantee obtained by misrepresentation or concealment is invalid (sections 142 and 143).

caseLaws.name: Bank of Bihar v
caseLaws.facts: Damodar Prasad (1968) Facts. A bank lent money to Damodar Prasad on the guarantee of Paras Nath Sinha. The trial court decreed the suit against both but barred execution against the guarantor until the bank had exhausted its remedies against the borrower. Principle. The surety's liability is immediate. Without some special equity, he cannot restrain execution against him until the creditor has exhausted his remedies against the principal. The surety must pay and then recover from the principal under section 140. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court authority for the point that a creditor may proceed against the surety without first proceeding against the debtor.

selfTest.q: 1. What does it mean to say that the surety's liability is coextensive?
selfTest.a: It means the surety is liable for as much as the principal debtor owes, unless the contract provides otherwise (section 128). 2. Can a surety insist that the creditor sue the principal debtor first? No. The liability is immediate. In the absence of some special equity, the surety cannot restrain execution until the creditor has exhausted his remedies against the principal (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad). 3. What does a surety get on paying the creditor? All the rights the creditor had against the principal debtor (section 140), and an implied indemnity for sums rightfully paid (section 145).

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t14.subtitle: Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A pledge is a special kind of bailment. Section 172 says the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called a pledge. The bailor is the pawnor . The bailee is the pawnee . Key points for the answer: the definition word for word, the two names, and the link to bailment.
en.meaning:
The meaning of pledge (section 172)

Rule. A pledge is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise. Take the definition in parts.

It is a bailment of goods. The goods are bailed as security. The security is for payment of a debt or performance of a promise.

Example. Anil borrows Rs 50,000 from Babu and hands his gold chain to Babu as security until he repays. This is a bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt. It is a pledge.

Pawnor and pawnee

Rule. The bailor in a pledge is the pawnor. The bailee is the pawnee.

Example. In the example above, Anil is the pawnor. Babu is the pawnee.

Pledge and bailment

Rule. Every pledge is a bailment, but not every bailment is a pledge. Section 172 calls a bailment a pledge only where the goods are bailed as security for a debt or a promise.

Example. Chandu gives his cycle to a repairer for repair. This is a bailment for repair, not a pledge, because the goods are not security for a debt or a promise.

Is it a pledge? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Are goods bailed (section 148)? 2. Are they bailed as security? 3. Is the security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise? If yes to all, it is a pledge (section 172). The bailor is the pawnor and the bailee is the pawnee.
keyPoints: Pledge is the bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise (section 172). The bailor is the pawnor. The bailee is the pawnee. Every pledge is a bailment. A bailment is a pledge only where the goods are security.

law-of-contract-ii-u1-t15.subtitle: Sections 173 to 177 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The pawnee may retain the pledged goods for the debt, the interest and his necessary expenses (section 173). He may not retain them for any other debt unless there is a contract to that effect (section 174). If the pawnor defaults, the pawnee may sue on the debt and keep the goods as collateral security , or sell the goods after giving reasonable notice (section 176). The defaulting pawnor may redeem the goods before they are actually sold (section 177). Key points for the answer: the pawnee's right of retainer, his right on default, the duty to give notice and pay over any surplus, and the pawnor's right to redeem.
en.meaning:
Rights of the pawnee

Rule. The pawnee has these rights.

Retainer (section 173). He may retain the goods for payment of the debt or performance of the promise, for the interest of the debt, and for all necessary expenses incurred in respect of the possession or preservation of the goods. Extraordinary expenses (section 175). He is entitled to receive from the pawnor extraordinary expenses incurred for the preservation of the goods. Remedies on default (section 176). He may sue on the debt and retain the goods as collateral security. Or he may sell the goods after reasonable notice.

Example. Anil pledges his gold chain to Babu for a loan of Rs 50,000. Babu may keep the chain until Anil pays the Rs 50,000, the interest, and the necessary expenses Babu incurred in keeping it safe (section 173).

Limits and conditions on the pawnee

Rule. The Act sets these limits.

He may not retain the goods for any debt or promise other than that for which they are pledged, in the absence of a contract to that effect (section 174). Such a contract is presumed for subsequent advances he makes, in the absence of anything to the contrary. He must give the pawnor reasonable notice of a sale (section 176). He must pay over to the pawnor any surplus if the sale proceeds exceed the amount due (section 176).

Example. Babu holds Anil's chain for the Rs 50,000 loan. Anil also owes Babu Rs 10,000 on a separate old debt. Without a contract to that effect, Babu may not retain the chain for the old debt (section 174). If Babu lends Anil a further Rs 20,000 later, a contract to retain the chain for that advance is presumed, unless there is anything to the contrary.

The pawnee's remedies on default (section 176)

Rule. If the pawnor makes default in payment, or in performance of the promise at the stipulated time, the pawnee has two remedies.

He may sue the pawnor on the debt or promise, and retain the goods as collateral security. He may sell the thing pledged, on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale.

After a sale, the accounts work as follows.

Proceeds less than the amount due: the pawnor is still liable to pay the balance. Proceeds more than the amount due: the pawnee must pay the surplus to the pawnor.

Example. Anil defaults on the Rs 50,000 loan. Babu gives Anil reasonable notice and sells the chain for Rs 45,000. The amount due is Rs 50,000. Anil still owes Babu the balance of Rs 5,000. Had the chain fetched Rs 55,000, Babu would have to pay Anil the surplus of Rs 5,000.

Rights and duties of the pawnor

Rule. The pawnor has the right to redeem the goods after default, at any subsequent time before the actual sale, if a time was stipulated for payment (section 177). He must then pay, in addition, any expenses that arose from his default. He must pay extraordinary expenses incurred by the pawnee for the preservation of the goods (section 175). He is liable for any balance after a sale (section 176), and entitled to any surplus.

Example. Anil defaults on the due date. Before Babu sells the chain, Anil pays the Rs 50,000 with the expenses that arose from his default. Anil may redeem the chain (section 177).

What happens when the pawnor defaults How to read this: start at the top. 1. The pawnor defaults at the stipulated time. 2. The pawnee may sue on the debt and keep the goods as collateral security, or sell the goods on reasonable notice (section 176). 3. Before the actual sale, the pawnor may redeem by paying the debt and the expenses from his default (section 177). 4. After a sale, a shortfall is still owed by the pawnor. A surplus is paid to him (section 176).
keyPoints: Retainer: for the debt or promise, the interest and necessary expenses (section 173). No retainer for another debt without a contract. Presumed for subsequent advances (section 174). Extraordinary expenses for preservation: from the pawnor (section 175). On default: sue and retain as collateral security, or sell on reasonable notice. Shortfall owed. Surplus paid over (section 176). The pawnor may redeem before the actual sale, paying the expenses of his default (section 177).

te.inOneMinute: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 లోని సెక్షన్లు 173 నుండి 177 — pawnor, pawnee హక్కులు, విధులు
te.meaning:
తాకట్టు పెట్టిన సరుకులను అప్పు, వడ్డీ, తన అవసరమైన ఖర్చుల కోసం pawnee ఉంచుకోవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 173). వేరే అప్పు కోసం, అందుకు ఒప్పందం లేకపోతే, వాటిని ఉంచుకోలేడు (సెక్షన్ 174). pawnor చెల్లింపులో విఫలమైతే, pawnee అప్పుపై దావా వేసి, సరుకులను అదనపు భద్రత (collateral security) గా ఉంచుకోవచ్చు, లేదా సహేతుకమైన నోటీసు ఇచ్చి సరుకులను అమ్మవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 176). చెల్లింపులో విఫలమైన pawnor, సరుకులు అసలు అమ్మకానికి ముందే వాటిని విడిపించుకోవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 177).

సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: pawnee ఉంచుకునే హక్కు, చెల్లింపులో విఫలమైనప్పుడు అతడి హక్కు, నోటీసు ఇవ్వడం, మిగులును చెల్లించడం అనే విధులు, pawnor విడిపించుకునే హక్కు.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. pawnee కు ఈ హక్కులు ఉన్నాయి.

ఉదాహరణ. రూ. 50,000 అప్పుకు అనిల్ తన బంగారు గొలుసును బాబుకు తాకట్టు పెట్టాడు. అనిల్ రూ. 50,000, వడ్డీ, గొలుసును భద్రంగా ఉంచడంలో బాబు చేసిన అవసరమైన ఖర్చులు చెల్లించే వరకు బాబు గొలుసును ఉంచుకోవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 173).

నియమం. చట్టం ఈ పరిమితులు పెడుతుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. రూ. 50,000 అప్పుకు అనిల్ గొలుసును బాబు ఉంచుకున్నాడు. వేరుగా ఒక పాత అప్పు రూ. 10,000 కూడా అనిల్ బాబుకు బాకీ. అందుకు ఒప్పందం లేకపోతే, ఆ పాత అప్పు కోసం బాబు గొలుసును ఉంచుకోకూడదు (సెక్షన్ 174). తర్వాత బాబు అనిల్‌కు మరో రూ. 20,000 అప్పు ఇస్తే, విరుద్ధమైనది ఏదీ లేనప్పుడు, ఆ అప్పు కోసం గొలుసును ఉంచుకునేలా ఒప్పందం ఉన్నట్లు భావిస్తారు.

selfTest.q: 1. తాకట్టు సరుకులను అమ్మే ముందు pawnee, pawnor కు ఏమి ఇవ్వాలి?
selfTest.a: అమ్మకంపై సహేతుకమైన నోటీసు (సెక్షన్ 176). 2. చెల్లింపులో విఫలమైన pawnor సరుకులను ఎప్పటి వరకు విడిపించుకోవచ్చు? ఆ తర్వాత అసలు అమ్మకానికి ముందు ఎప్పుడైనా, తన విఫలం వల్ల తలెత్తిన ఖర్చులను కూడా చెల్లించి (సెక్షన్ 177). 3. అమ్మకం ద్వారా వచ్చిన మొత్తం రావాల్సిన మొత్తం కంటే ఎక్కువైతే pawnee ఏమి చేయాలి? మిగులును pawnor కు చెల్లించాలి (సెక్షన్ 176).

en.meaning:
Which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines a contract of indemnity?

Explanation. Section 124 defines a contract of indemnity. Section 125 deals with the rights of the indemnity-holder when sued, and section 126 defines a contract of guarantee.

A contract of indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to:

Explanation. Section 124 says a contract of indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself, or by the conduct of any other person.

In a contract of indemnity, the party who promises to save the other from loss is called the:

Explanation. The party who makes the promise is the promisor. The party who is promised protection is the promisee.

Under section 124, the loss may be caused by the conduct of:

en.meaning:
Under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, the person to whom the guarantee is given is called the:

Explanation. Section 126 calls the person who gives the guarantee the surety, the person whose default is guaranteed the principal debtor, and the person to whom the guarantee is given the creditor.

Section 128 provides that, unless the contract provides otherwise, the liability of the surety is:

Explanation. Section 128 makes the surety's liability coextensive with the principal debtor's, unless the contract says otherwise. The Act's illustration holds a guarantor of a dishonoured bill liable for the amount, interest and charges.

In Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad (Supreme Court, 1968), the trial court had directed that the Bank could enforce its dues against the guarantor only after exhausting its remedies against the borrower. The Supreme Court:

Explanation. The Supreme Court held that the surety's liability was immediate and not deferred until the creditor exhausted his remedies against the principal debtor. It set the direction aside and ordered the surety to pay the Bank's costs.

In Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad, the Supreme Court held that the solvency of the principal debtor is:
