hi.inOneMinute: Contracts made through an agent have the same legal consequences as if the principal had made them himself (section 226). Where an agent does more than he is authorized to do, the principal is bound only by what is within the authority if it can be separated (section 227), and not at all if it cannot (section 228). Notice given to the agent in the course of the business is notice to the principal (section 229). The Act also deals with a contract made with an agent who is supposed to be the principal (sections 231 and 232), with inducing a belief that only one of them will be held liable (section 234), with a principal who induces belief in the agent's authority (section 237), and with an agent's misrepresentation or fraud (section 238). Key points for the answer: each section with the Act's illustration.
hi.meaning: Enforcement and consequences of the agent's contracts (section 226) Rule. Contracts entered into through an agent, and obligations from acts done by him, are enforced and have the same consequences as if the principal had done them. Example. Ravi's agent Sita, with authority to receive money, receives Rs 10,000 due to Ravi from Chandu. Chandu is discharged of his obligation to pay it to Ravi (illustration (b)). Agent exceeds authority (sections 227 and 228) Rule. If the part within authority can be separated, the principal is bound by that part only (section 227). If it cannot be separated, the principal is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). Example. Anil authorizes Babu to buy 500 sheep. Babu buys 500 sheep and 200 lambs for one sum. The excess cannot be separated. Anil may repudiate the whole transaction (the Act's illustration to section 228). Notice to the agent (section 229) Rule. Notice given to, or information obtained by, the agent in the course of the business he transacts for the principal has the same consequences as if given to or obtained by the principal. Contract with an agent supposed to be the principal (sections 231, 232 and 234) Rule. Where a person contracts with an agent without knowing or having reason to suspect that he is an agent, the principal may require performance (section 231). The other party has against the principal the rights he would have had against the agent. If the principal discloses himself before the contract is completed, the other party may refuse to fulfil it if he can show he would not have entered into it had he known who the principal was or that the agent was not a principal. The principal obtains performance only subject to the rights and obligations between the agent and the other party (section 232). A person who induces the agent to believe that the principal only will be held liable, or the principal to believe that the agent only will be held liable, cannot afterwards hold the other liable (section 234). Example. A, who owes B 500 rupees, sells B rice worth 1,000 rupees as agent for C, and B does not know this. C cannot compel B to take the rice without allowing B to set off A's debt (the Act's illustration to section 232). Principal who induces belief in authority (section 237) Rule. The principal is bound by the agent's unauthorized acts if by his words or conduct he induced third persons to believe they were within the agent's authority. Misrepresentation or fraud by the agent (section 238) Rule. Misrepresentation or fraud by agents acting in the course of their business has the same effect on agreements as if by the principals. In matters that do not fall within the agents' authority, it does not affect the principals. Illustration (a): A, B's agent for sale, induces C to buy by a misrepresentation he was not authorized to make. The contract is voidable, as between B and C, at the option of C. Is the principal bound? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Was the contract entered into through an agent? Yes: same consequences as if the principal made it (section 226). 2. Did the agent exceed his authority? Can the excess be separated? Yes: the principal is bound only by the part within authority (section 227). No: he is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). 3. Did the principal by words or conduct induce the third person to believe the act was authorized? Yes: he is bound (section 237).
keyPoints: An agent's contract has the same consequences as the principal's own (section 226). Excess of authority: separable, the principal is bound by the part within authority (section 227). Not separable, he is not bound (section 228). Notice to the agent in the course of the business is notice to the principal (section 229). Undisclosed principal: sections 231 and 232, with set-off. Inducing belief of exclusive liability bars a later claim against the other (section 234). The principal is bound where his words or conduct induced belief in the agent's authority (section 237). An agent's misrepresentation in the course of business binds the principal as his own (section 238).

selfTest.q: 1. What if the agent's excess of authority cannot be separated from what is within it?
selfTest.a: The principal is not bound to recognize the transaction (section 228). 2. Under section 232, on what footing may the principal obtain performance of a contract made with an agent supposed to be the principal? Subject to the rights and obligations subsisting between the agent and the other party. 3. If an agent induces a buyer by a misrepresentation he was not authorized to make, whose option is the contract? The buyer's. It is voidable at his option (section 238, illustration (a)).

en.meaning:
Under section 190 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agent cannot lawfully employ another to perform acts which he has undertaken to perform:

Explanation. Section 190 prohibits delegation of acts the agent has expressly or impliedly undertaken to perform personally, unless by custom of trade a sub-agent may, or from the nature of the agency must, be employed.

A sub-agent is a person employed by, and acting under the control of:

Explanation. Section 191 defines a sub-agent as a person employed by, and acting under the control of, the original agent in the business of the agency.

Where a sub-agent is properly appointed, the principal, as regards third persons, is:

Explanation. Section 192 says the principal is represented by the sub-agent and is bound by and responsible for his acts as if he were an agent originally appointed by the principal.

Under section 192, the sub-agent is responsible for his acts to the agent, and to the principal:

Under section 211 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, in the absence of directions from the principal, the agent must conduct the business according to:

Explanation. Section 211 says that in the absence of directions the agent must act according to the custom which prevails in business of the same kind at the place where he conducts it.

Under section 212, an agent must compensate his principal for:

Explanation. Section 212 requires compensation for direct consequences of the agent's neglect, want of skill or misconduct, but not for loss indirectly or remotely caused.

Under section 213, an agent must render proper accounts to his principal:

Explanation. Section 213 says an agent is bound to render proper accounts to his principal on demand.

law-of-contract-ii-u2-t7.subtitle: Sections 201 to 210 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An agency is terminated by the principal revoking his authority, by the agent renouncing the business, by completion of the business, by the death or unsoundness of mind of either, or by the principal being adjudicated an insolvent (section 201). Where the agent has an interest in the subject-matter, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest without an express contract (section 202). Reasonable notice is needed (section 206), and the termination takes effect only when it becomes known (section 208). Key points for the answer: the ways of termination, the limits on revocation, and the effect of notice.
en.meaning:
Ways an agency ends (section 201)

Rule. An agency is terminated in these ways.

The principal revokes the authority. The agent renounces the business of the agency. The business of the agency is completed. Either the principal or the agent dies or becomes of unsound mind. The principal is adjudicated an insolvent under any Act for the relief of insolvent debtors.

Example. Ravi appoints Sita as his agent to sell his scooter. Sita sells it and hands over the price. The business of the agency is completed, and the agency ends.

Agent with an interest in the subject-matter (section 202)

Rule. Where the agent has himself an interest in the property which is the subject-matter of the agency, then, without an express contract, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest.

Example. Anil authorizes Babu to sell Anil's land and to pay himself out of the proceeds the debts Anil owes him. Anil cannot revoke the authority, and Anil's death or insanity does not end it (the Act's illustration (a)).

Revocation (sections 203 and 204)

Rule. Subject to section 202, the principal may revoke at any time before the authority has been exercised so as to bind him (section 203). He cannot revoke after it has been partly exercised, as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done (section 204).

Example. Chandu authorizes Dev to buy 1,000 bales of cotton for him, to be paid for from Chandu's money in Dev's hands. Dev buys in his own name, making himself personally liable. Chandu cannot revoke Dev's authority as regards payment for that cotton (section 204, illustration (a)).

Compensation and notice (sections 205 and 206)

Rule. Where there is an express or implied contract that the agency will continue for a period, the party who revokes or renounces earlier without sufficient cause must compensate the other (section 205). Reasonable notice must be given of revocation or renunciation. Otherwise the damage must be made good by the one to the other (section 206).

Express or implied revocation (section 207)

Rule. Revocation and renunciation may be express or implied in conduct. If A empowers B to let A's house and then lets it himself, this implies revocation of B's authority.

When termination takes effect (section 208)

Rule. Termination does not take effect as regards the agent before it becomes known to him, or as regards third persons before it becomes known to them.

Example. A directs B to sell goods at five per cent commission and later revokes by letter. B sells for 100 rupees after the letter is sent but before he receives it. The sale binds A, and B is entitled to 5 rupees commission (the Act's illustration (a)).

Duty on the principal's death or insanity, and sub-agents (sections 209 and 210)

Rule. When the agency ends by the principal's death or unsoundness of mind, the agent must take all reasonable steps, on behalf of the principal's representatives, to protect and preserve the interests entrusted to him (section 209). Termination of the agent's authority terminates the authority of his sub-agents, subject to the rules in the Chapter (section 210).

Can the principal revoke? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Does the agent have an interest in the subject-matter, and is there no express contract to the contrary? Then the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest (section 202). 2. Has the authority been partly exercised? The principal cannot revoke as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done (section 204). 3. Otherwise he may revoke before the authority has been exercised so as to bind him (section 203), giving reasonable notice (section 206). The termination takes effect when it becomes known to the agent and to third persons (section 208).
keyPoints: Section 201: revocation, renunciation, completion, death or unsound mind of either, insolvency of the principal. An agent's interest in the subject-matter limits termination (section 202). No revocation after partial exercise, as regards acts already done (section 204). Reasonable notice (section 206). Compensation for earlier termination without sufficient cause (section 205). Termination takes effect when it becomes known (section 208). Termination ends sub-agents' authority (section 210).

selfTest.q: 1. Name the ways an agency ends under section 201. Revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, completion of the business, death or unsound mind of either, and adjudication of the principal as an insolvent. 2. When does termination take effect as regards the agent?
selfTest.a: When it becomes known to him (section 208). 3. Can the principal revoke after the authority has been partly exercised? Not as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done in the agency (section 204).

te.inOneMinute: భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 లోని సెక్షన్లు 201 నుండి 210 — ఏజెన్సీ ముగింపు
te.meaning:
ప్రిన్సిపల్ తన అధికారాన్ని ఉపసంహరించడం (revoking) ద్వారా, ఏజెంట్ ఏజెన్సీ వ్యాపారాన్ని త్యజించడం ద్వారా, ఏజెన్సీ వ్యాపారం పూర్తి కావడం ద్వారా, ప్రిన్సిపల్ లేదా ఏజెంట్ మరణించడం లేదా మతిస్థిమితం కోల్పోవడం ద్వారా, లేదా ప్రిన్సిపల్ దివాళా తీసినట్లు ప్రకటించడం ద్వారా ఏజెన్సీ ముగుస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 201).

ఏజెన్సీ అంశంలో ఏజెంట్‌కు ఆసక్తి ఉంటే, స్పష్టమైన ఒప్పందం లేనప్పుడు ఆ ఆసక్తికి హాని కలిగేలా ఏజెన్సీని ముగించలేరు (సెక్షన్ 202). సహేతుకమైన నోటీసు అవసరం (సెక్షన్ 206), ముగింపు తెలిసినప్పుడే అమలులోకి వస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 208). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: ముగింపు మార్గాలు, ఉపసంహరణపై పరిమితులు, నోటీసు ప్రభావం.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. ఏజెన్సీ ఈ మార్గాల్లో ముగుస్తుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. తన స్కూటర్ అమ్మడానికి రవి సీతను ఏజెంట్‌గా నియమించాడు. సీత దాన్ని అమ్మి ధరను అందజేసింది. ఏజెన్సీ వ్యాపారం పూర్తయింది, ఏజెన్సీ ముగుస్తుంది.

నియమం. ఏజెన్సీ అంశమైన ఆస్తిలో ఏజెంట్‌కు సొంత ఆసక్తి ఉంటే, స్పష్టమైన ఒప్పందం లేనప్పుడు, ఆ ఆసక్తికి హాని కలిగేలా ఏజెన్సీని ముగించలేరు.

ఉదాహరణ. అనిల్ భూమిని అమ్మడానికి, అమ్మకం సొమ్ము నుండి అనిల్ తనకు బాకీ ఉన్న అప్పులను తీర్చుకోవడానికి బాబుకు అధికారం ఇచ్చాడు. అనిల్ ఆ అధికారాన్ని ఉపసంహరించలేడు, అనిల్ మరణం లేదా మతిస్థిమితం కోల్పోవడంతో అది ముగియదు (చట్టంలోని ఉదాహరణ (a)).

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 201 ప్రకారం ఏజెన్సీ ముగిసే మార్గాలు చెప్పండి. ప్రిన్సిపల్ ఉపసంహరణ, ఏజెంట్ త్యజించడం, వ్యాపారం పూర్తి కావడం, ఇద్దరిలో ఎవరి మరణం లేదా మతిస్థిమితం, ప్రిన్సిపల్ దివాళా తీసినట్లు ప్రకటించడం. 2. ఏజెంట్ విషయంలో ముగింపు ఎప్పుడు అమలులోకి వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: అతడికి తెలిసినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 208). 3. అధికారాన్ని పాక్షికంగా వినియోగించిన తర్వాత ప్రిన్సిపల్ ఉపసంహరించగలడా? ఏజెన్సీలో అప్పటికే చేసిన పనుల నుండి తలెత్తే పనులు, బాధ్యతల విషయంలో కాదు (సెక్షన్ 204).

hi.inOneMinute: An agency is terminated by the principal revoking his authority, by the agent renouncing the business, by completion of the business, by the death or unsoundness of mind of either, or by the principal being adjudicated an insolvent (section 201). Where the agent has an interest in the subject-matter, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest without an express contract (section 202). Reasonable notice is needed (section 206), and the termination takes effect only when it becomes known (section 208). Key points for the answer: the ways of termination, the limits on revocation, and the effect of notice.
hi.meaning: Ways an agency ends (section 201) Rule. An agency is terminated in these ways. The principal revokes the authority. The agent renounces the business of the agency. The business of the agency is completed. Either the principal or the agent dies or becomes of unsound mind. The principal is adjudicated an insolvent under any Act for the relief of insolvent debtors. Example. Ravi appoints Sita as his agent to sell his scooter. Sita sells it and hands over the price. The business of the agency is completed, and the agency ends. Agent with an interest in the subject-matter (section 202) Rule. Where the agent has himself an interest in the property which is the subject-matter of the agency, then, without an express contract, the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest. Example. Anil authorizes Babu to sell Anil's land and to pay himself out of the proceeds the debts Anil owes him. Anil cannot revoke the authority, and Anil's death or insanity does not end it (the Act's illustration (a)). Revocation (sections 203 and 204) Rule. Subject to section 202, the principal may revoke at any time before the authority has been exercised so as to bind him (section 203). He cannot revoke after it has been partly exercised, as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done (section 204). Example. Chandu authorizes Dev to buy 1,000 bales of cotton for him, to be paid for from Chandu's money in Dev's hands. Dev buys in his own name, making himself personally liable. Chandu cannot revoke Dev's authority as regards payment for that cotton (section 204, illustration (a)). Compensation and notice (sections 205 and 206) Rule. Where there is an express or implied contract that the agency will continue for a period, the party who revokes or renounces earlier without sufficient cause must compensate the other (section 205). Reasonable notice must be given of revocation or renunciation. Otherwise the damage must be made good by the one to the other (section 206). Express or implied revocation (section 207) Rule. Revocation and renunciation may be express or implied in conduct. If A empowers B to let A's house and then lets it himself, this implies revocation of B's authority. When termination takes effect (section 208) Rule. Termination does not take effect as regards the agent before it becomes known to him, or as regards third persons before it becomes known to them. Example. A directs B to sell goods at five per cent commission and later revokes by letter. B sells for 100 rupees after the letter is sent but before he receives it. The sale binds A, and B is entitled to 5 rupees commission (the Act's illustration (a)). Duty on the principal's death or insanity, and sub-agents (sections 209 and 210) Rule. When the agency ends by the principal's death or unsoundness of mind, the agent must take all reasonable steps, on behalf of the principal's representatives, to protect and preserve the interests entrusted to him (section 209). Termination of the agent's authority terminates the authority of his sub-agents, subject to the rules in the Chapter (section 210). Can the principal revoke? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Does the agent have an interest in the subject-matter, and is there no express contract to the contrary? Then the agency cannot be terminated to the prejudice of that interest (section 202). 2. Has the authority been partly exercised? The principal cannot revoke as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done (section 204). 3. Otherwise he may revoke before the authority has been exercised so as to bind him (section 203), giving reasonable notice (section 206). The termination takes effect when it becomes known to the agent and to third persons (section 208).
keyPoints: Section 201: revocation, renunciation, completion, death or unsound mind of either, insolvency of the principal. An agent's interest in the subject-matter limits termination (section 202). No revocation after partial exercise, as regards acts already done (section 204). Reasonable notice (section 206). Compensation for earlier termination without sufficient cause (section 205). Termination takes effect when it becomes known (section 208). Termination ends sub-agents' authority (section 210).

selfTest.q: 1. Name the ways an agency ends under section 201. Revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, completion of the business, death or unsound mind of either, and adjudication of the principal as an insolvent. 2. When does termination take effect as regards the agent?
selfTest.a: When it becomes known to him (section 208). 3. Can the principal revoke after the authority has been partly exercised? Not as regards acts and obligations arising from acts already done in the agency (section 204).

A, B's agent with authority to receive money, receives from C a sum due to B. Under illustration (b) to section 226, C:

Explanation. The illustration says C is discharged of his obligation to pay the sum to B.

en.meaning:
Which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 lists the ways in which an agency is terminated?

Explanation. Section 201 lists revocation, renunciation, completion, death or unsound mind of either party, and insolvency of the principal.

Which of these does NOT terminate an agency under section 201?

Explanation. A change of the agent's residence is not among the ways listed in section 201.

Under section 202, where the agent has himself an interest in the subject-matter of the agency, the agency, in the absence of an express contract, cannot be terminated:

Explanation. Section 202 says the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest.

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t1.subtitle: Sections 1 to 5 and 64 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: A contract of sale of goods is a contract in which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). It is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and its acceptance (section 5(1)). If the property passes at once, the contract is a sale. If it passes at a future time or after a condition is met, it is an agreement to sell (section 4(3)). Key points for the answer: the definition, the two kinds, how the contract is made, and the rules of an auction sale (section 64).
en.meaning:
Contract of sale: the definition (section 4(1))

Rule. A contract of sale of goods is a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price.

Four things follow from the words of the section.

There are two parties, a seller and a buyer. The subject-matter is goods. Goods are moveable property other than actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). There is a transfer, or an agreement to transfer, of the property in the goods. "Property" means the general property in goods and not merely a special property (section 2(11)). The consideration is a price. "Price" means the money consideration for a sale of goods (section 2(10)).

There may be a contract of sale between one part-owner and another (section 4(1)). A contract of sale may be absolute or conditional (section 4(2)).

Example. Ravi agrees to sell his scooter to Sita for Rs 40,000. Ravi is the seller, Sita is the buyer, the scooter is the goods, and Rs 40,000 is the price. This is a contract of sale.

Sale and agreement to sell (section 4(3) and (4))

Rule. If the property in the goods is transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract, the contract is called a sale. If the transfer is to take place at a future time, or subject to some condition to be fulfilled later, it is called an agreement to sell. An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled.

Example. Anil sells a specific table to Babu and the property in it passes to Babu now. This is a sale. If Anil instead agrees that the property will pass to Babu on 1 January, this is an agreement to sell. On 1 January it becomes a sale.

How a contract of sale is made (section 5)

Rule. A contract of sale is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and the acceptance of the offer.

The contract may provide for immediate delivery, immediate payment, or both. It may provide for delivery or payment by instalments. It may provide that delivery or payment, or both, are postponed. Subject to any law in force, it may be in writing, by word of mouth, partly in writing and partly by word of mouth, or implied from the conduct of the parties (section 5(2)).

Example. A customer picks up a packet of rice from a shop shelf and pays at the counter. The contract is implied from the conduct of the parties. No writing is needed unless some other law requires it.

Application of the Indian Contract Act (section 3)

Rule. The unrepealed provisions of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 continue to apply to contracts for the sale of goods, except where they are inconsistent with the express provisions of the Sale of Goods Act. Section 2(15) also gives expressions defined in the Contract Act but not here the meaning assigned in the Contract Act.

Auction sale (section 64)

Rule. Section 64 sets six rules for a sale by auction.

Goods put up in lots: each lot is prima facie a separate contract of sale. The sale is complete when the auctioneer announces it by the fall of the hammer or in another customary manner. Until then any bidder may retract his bid. The seller may reserve a right to bid, expressly. Only where it is so reserved may the seller, or one person on his behalf, bid. If the sale is not notified to be subject to a right to bid on behalf of the seller, the seller may not bid or employ anyone to bid, and the auctioneer may not knowingly take such a bid. The buyer may treat a sale in breach of this rule as fraudulent. The sale may be notified to be subject to a reserved or upset price. If the seller uses pretended bidding to raise the price, the sale is voidable at the option of the buyer.

Example. At an auction, a bidder says Rs 5,000 for a lamp. Before the auctioneer brings down the hammer, the bidder changes his mind. He may retract his bid, because the sale is not yet complete (section 64(2)).

Sale or agreement to sell? How to read this: start at the top. The property means the general property in the goods. 1. Is there a contract by which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price? If yes, it is a contract of sale (section 4(1)). If not, it is not a contract of sale under this Act. 2. Is the property transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract now? If yes, it is a sale (section 4(3)). 3. Is the transfer to take place at a future time, or after a condition is fulfilled? Then it is an agreement to sell. It becomes a sale when the time elapses or the condition is fulfilled (section 4(3) and (4)).
keyPoints: A contract of sale: seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). Sale: property transferred now. Agreement to sell: property to pass later or on a condition (section 4(3)). An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled (section 4(4)). Made by offer and acceptance. It may be in writing, by words, or implied from conduct (section 5). The Contract Act applies unless inconsistent (section 3). Auction: the sale is complete at the fall of the hammer, and a bidder may retract before it (section 64(2)). Seller bidding without a reserved right: the buyer may treat the sale as fraudulent (section 64(4)).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a contract of sale of goods under section 4(1)?
selfTest.a: A contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. 2. What is the difference between a sale and an agreement to sell in section 4(3)? In a sale the property is transferred under the contract. In an agreement to sell the transfer is to take place at a future time or subject to a condition to be fulfilled. 3. When does an agreement to sell become a sale? When the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled subject to which the property in the goods is to be transferred (section 4(4)). 4. When is an auction sale complete? When the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer or in other customary manner (section 64(2)).

te.inOneMinute: సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 లోని సెక్షన్లు 1 నుండి 5, 64 — సరుకుల అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం ఏర్పడటం
te.meaning:
సరుకుల అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం అంటే, అమ్మేవాడు సరుకులపై ఆస్తి హక్కును కొనేవాడికి ధరకు బదిలీ చేయడం లేదా బదిలీ చేయడానికి అంగీకరించడం (సెక్షన్ 4(1)). ధరకు సరుకులను కొనడానికి లేదా అమ్మడానికి చేసిన ఆఫర్‌ను అంగీకరించడం ద్వారా ఈ ఒప్పందం ఏర్పడుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 5(1)).

ఆస్తి హక్కు వెంటనే బదిలీ అయితే అది అమ్మకం (sale). భవిష్యత్తులో లేదా ఒక షరతు నెరవేరాక బదిలీ కావాల్సి ఉంటే అది అమ్మడానికి ఒప్పందం (agreement to sell) (సెక్షన్ 4(3)). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: నిర్వచనం, రెండు రకాలు, ఒప్పందం ఏర్పడే విధానం, వేలం అమ్మకం నియమాలు (సెక్షన్ 64).

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. సరుకుల అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం అంటే, అమ్మేవాడు సరుకులపై ఆస్తి హక్కును కొనేవాడికి ధరకు బదిలీ చేసే లేదా బదిలీ చేయడానికి అంగీకరించే ఒప్పందం.

సెక్షన్ పదాల నుండి నాలుగు విషయాలు వస్తాయి.

ఒక భాగస్వామ్య యజమానికి, మరొకరికి మధ్య కూడా అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం ఉండవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 4(1)). అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం నిరపేక్షమైనది లేదా షరతులతో కూడినది కావచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 4(2)).

ఉదాహరణ. రవి తన స్కూటర్‌ను సీతకు రూ. 40,000 కు అమ్మడానికి అంగీకరించాడు. రవి అమ్మేవాడు, సీత కొనేది, స్కూటర్ సరుకులు, రూ. 40,000 ధర. ఇది అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 4(1) ప్రకారం సరుకుల అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: అమ్మేవాడు సరుకులపై ఆస్తి హక్కును కొనేవాడికి ధరకు బదిలీ చేసే లేదా బదిలీ చేయడానికి అంగీకరించే ఒప్పందం. 2. సెక్షన్ 4(3) లో అమ్మకానికి, అమ్మడానికి ఒప్పందానికి తేడా ఏమిటి? అమ్మకంలో ఒప్పందం కింద ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అవుతుంది. అమ్మడానికి ఒప్పందంలో బదిలీ భవిష్యత్తులో లేదా నెరవేరాల్సిన షరతుకు లోబడి జరుగుతుంది. 3. అమ్మడానికి ఒప్పందం ఎప్పుడు అమ్మకంగా మారుతుంది? సరుకులపై ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ ఏ కాలానికి లేదా షరతులకు లోబడి ఉందో, ఆ కాలం గడిచినప్పుడు లేదా షరతులు నెరవేరినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 4(4)). 4. వేలం అమ్మకం ఎప్పుడు పూర్తవుతుంది? వేలందారు సుత్తి దెబ్బతో లేదా ఇతర సంప్రదాయ పద్ధతిలో అమ్మకం పూర్తయిందని ప్రకటించినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 64(2)).

hi.inOneMinute: A contract of sale of goods is a contract in which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). It is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and its acceptance (section 5(1)). If the property passes at once, the contract is a sale. If it passes at a future time or after a condition is met, it is an agreement to sell (section 4(3)). Key points for the answer: the definition, the two kinds, how the contract is made, and the rules of an auction sale (section 64).
hi.meaning: Contract of sale: the definition (section 4(1)) Rule. A contract of sale of goods is a contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. Four things follow from the words of the section. There are two parties, a seller and a buyer. The subject-matter is goods. Goods are moveable property other than actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). There is a transfer, or an agreement to transfer, of the property in the goods. "Property" means the general property in goods and not merely a special property (section 2(11)). The consideration is a price. "Price" means the money consideration for a sale of goods (section 2(10)). There may be a contract of sale between one part-owner and another (section 4(1)). A contract of sale may be absolute or conditional (section 4(2)). Example. Ravi agrees to sell his scooter to Sita for Rs 40,000. Ravi is the seller, Sita is the buyer, the scooter is the goods, and Rs 40,000 is the price. This is a contract of sale. Sale and agreement to sell (section 4(3) and (4)) Rule. If the property in the goods is transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract, the contract is called a sale. If the transfer is to take place at a future time, or subject to some condition to be fulfilled later, it is called an agreement to sell. An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled. Example. Anil sells a specific table to Babu and the property in it passes to Babu now. This is a sale. If Anil instead agrees that the property will pass to Babu on 1 January, this is an agreement to sell. On 1 January it becomes a sale. How a contract of sale is made (section 5) Rule. A contract of sale is made by an offer to buy or sell goods for a price and the acceptance of the offer. The contract may provide for immediate delivery, immediate payment, or both. It may provide for delivery or payment by instalments. It may provide that delivery or payment, or both, are postponed. Subject to any law in force, it may be in writing, by word of mouth, partly in writing and partly by word of mouth, or implied from the conduct of the parties (section 5(2)). Example. A customer picks up a packet of rice from a shop shelf and pays at the counter. The contract is implied from the conduct of the parties. No writing is needed unless some other law requires it. Application of the Indian Contract Act (section 3) Rule. The unrepealed provisions of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 continue to apply to contracts for the sale of goods, except where they are inconsistent with the express provisions of the Sale of Goods Act. Section 2(15) also gives expressions defined in the Contract Act but not here the meaning assigned in the Contract Act. Auction sale (section 64) Rule. Section 64 sets six rules for a sale by auction. Goods put up in lots: each lot is prima facie a separate contract of sale. The sale is complete when the auctioneer announces it by the fall of the hammer or in another customary manner. Until then any bidder may retract his bid. The seller may reserve a right to bid, expressly. Only where it is so reserved may the seller, or one person on his behalf, bid. If the sale is not notified to be subject to a right to bid on behalf of the seller, the seller may not bid or employ anyone to bid, and the auctioneer may not knowingly take such a bid. The buyer may treat a sale in breach of this rule as fraudulent. The sale may be notified to be subject to a reserved or upset price. If the seller uses pretended bidding to raise the price, the sale is voidable at the option of the buyer. Example. At an auction, a bidder says Rs 5,000 for a lamp. Before the auctioneer brings down the hammer, the bidder changes his mind. He may retract his bid, because the sale is not yet complete (section 64(2)). Sale or agreement to sell? How to read this: start at the top. The property means the general property in the goods. 1. Is there a contract by which the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price? If yes, it is a contract of sale (section 4(1)). If not, it is not a contract of sale under this Act. 2. Is the property transferred from the seller to the buyer under the contract now? If yes, it is a sale (section 4(3)). 3. Is the transfer to take place at a future time, or after a condition is fulfilled? Then it is an agreement to sell. It becomes a sale when the time elapses or the condition is fulfilled (section 4(3) and (4)).
keyPoints: A contract of sale: seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price (section 4(1)). Sale: property transferred now. Agreement to sell: property to pass later or on a condition (section 4(3)). An agreement to sell becomes a sale when the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled (section 4(4)). Made by offer and acceptance. It may be in writing, by words, or implied from conduct (section 5). The Contract Act applies unless inconsistent (section 3). Auction: the sale is complete at the fall of the hammer, and a bidder may retract before it (section 64(2)). Seller bidding without a reserved right: the buyer may treat the sale as fraudulent (section 64(4)).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a contract of sale of goods under section 4(1)?
selfTest.a: A contract whereby the seller transfers or agrees to transfer the property in goods to the buyer for a price. 2. What is the difference between a sale and an agreement to sell in section 4(3)? In a sale the property is transferred under the contract. In an agreement to sell the transfer is to take place at a future time or subject to a condition to be fulfilled. 3. When does an agreement to sell become a sale? When the time elapses or the conditions are fulfilled subject to which the property in the goods is to be transferred (section 4(4)). 4. When is an auction sale complete? When the auctioneer announces its completion by the fall of the hammer or in other customary manner (section 64(2)).

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t2.subtitle: Sections 2(6), 2(7), 2(14), 6, 7 and 8 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: The subject-matter of a contract of sale is goods: every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). Goods may be existing goods, owned or possessed by the seller, or future goods (section 6(1)). A contract for specific goods is void if, without the seller's knowledge, the goods had already perished when the contract was made (section 7). An agreement to sell specific goods is avoided if they perish later, without fault of either party, before the risk passes to the buyer (section 8). Key points for the answer: the definition of goods, the kinds of goods, and sections 7 and 8.
en.meaning:
What counts as goods (section 2(7))

Rule. Goods are every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims and money.

Included: stock and shares, growing crops, grass. Included: things attached to or forming part of the land which are agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale. Excluded: actionable claims and money.

Example. A farmer sells the standing sugarcane in his field to a mill. The sugarcane is a growing crop and so falls within the definition of goods.

Existing goods and future goods (sections 2(6) and 6(1))

Rule. Goods that are the subject of a contract of sale may be existing goods, owned or possessed by the seller, or future goods. Future goods are goods to be manufactured or produced or acquired by the seller after the contract is made.

Example. A furniture maker agrees on 1 March to sell a cupboard to Rani. He will build it in April. The cupboard is future goods on 1 March.

Goods depending on a contingency (section 6(2))

Rule. There may be a contract for the sale of goods the acquisition of which by the seller depends upon a contingency which may or may not happen.

Example. A trader agrees to sell a consignment he hopes to buy at an auction next week. His acquiring it depends on whether he wins the bid. The contract is allowed by section 6(2).

Present sale of future goods (section 6(3))

Rule. Where the seller purports to effect a present sale of future goods, the contract operates as an agreement to sell the goods.

This links to the topic on sale and agreement to sell. A sale needs the property in the goods to pass under the contract (section 4(3)). Goods the seller does not yet have cannot be transferred now, so the contract is an agreement to sell.

Specific goods (section 2(14))

Rule. Specific goods are goods identified and agreed upon at the time a contract of sale is made.

Example. Karan agrees to buy "that black horse in the stable", which both have seen. The horse is identified and agreed upon when the contract is made. It is specific goods.

Goods perishing before the contract (section 7)

Rule. If a contract is for specific goods, and the goods, without the seller's knowledge, had perished or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the contract when the contract was made, the contract is void.

Example. Lata agrees on Monday to sell a specific car to Mohan. Unknown to Lata, the car was burnt in a fire on Sunday night. The contract is void under section 7.

Goods perishing after the agreement, before the risk passes (section 8)

Rule. If there is an agreement to sell specific goods, and afterwards the goods perish or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the agreement, without fault of the seller or the buyer, before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is avoided.

Example. Nisha agrees to sell a specific tractor to Om, delivery next month. Before the risk passes to Om, lightning destroys the tractor. Neither party is at fault. The agreement is avoided under section 8.

Did the goods perish? Which section applies? How to read this: start at the top. Both sections speak only of specific goods. 1. Are the goods specific, that is, identified and agreed upon when the contract was made (section 2(14))? If not, sections 7 and 8 do not apply on their words. 2. Had they perished, without the seller's knowledge, when the contract was made? The contract is void (section 7). 3. Did they perish later, without fault of seller or buyer, before the risk passed to the buyer, under an agreement to sell? The agreement is avoided (section 8).
keyPoints: Goods: all moveable property except actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). Includes stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things agreed to be severed. Existing goods or future goods (sections 2(6), 6(1)). Contingent goods are allowed (section 6(2)). A present sale of future goods is an agreement to sell (section 6(3)). Specific goods: identified and agreed upon at the time of the contract (section 2(14)). Section 7: specific goods already perished at the contract, without the seller's knowledge, so the contract is void. Section 8: specific goods perish later, without fault, before the risk passes, so the agreement is avoided.

selfTest.q: 1. What is excluded from goods under section 2(7)?
selfTest.a: Actionable claims and money. 2. What are future goods? Goods to be manufactured or produced or acquired by the seller after the making of the contract of sale (section 2(6)). 3. What is a present sale of future goods under section 6(3)? The contract operates as an agreement to sell the goods. 4. What is the difference between sections 7 and 8? Section 7 applies where the specific goods had already perished when the contract was made, without the seller's knowledge. Section 8 applies where they perish afterwards, without fault of either party, before the risk passes to the buyer.

te.meaning:
అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం అంశం సరుకులు: వ్యాజ్య హక్కులు, డబ్బు తప్ప అన్ని రకాల చర ఆస్తి (సెక్షన్ 2(7)). సరుకులు అమ్మేవాడి సొంతమైన లేదా అతని స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న సరుకులు కావచ్చు, లేదా భవిష్యత్ సరుకులు (future goods) కావచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 6(1)).

ఒప్పందం చేసే సమయానికే, అమ్మేవాడికి తెలియకుండా, నిర్దిష్ట సరుకులు నశించి ఉంటే ఆ ఒప్పందం చెల్లదు (సెక్షన్ 7). నిర్దిష్ట సరుకులను అమ్మడానికి ఒప్పందం చేశాక, రిస్క్ కొనేవాడికి బదిలీ కాక ముందే ఎవరి తప్పూ లేకుండా అవి నశిస్తే ఆ ఒప్పందం రద్దవుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 8). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: సరుకుల నిర్వచనం, సరుకుల రకాలు, సెక్షన్లు 7, 8.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. సరుకులు అంటే వ్యాజ్య హక్కులు, డబ్బు తప్ప అన్ని రకాల చర ఆస్తి.

ఉదాహరణ. ఒక రైతు తన పొలంలో నిలబడి ఉన్న చెరకును మిల్లుకు అమ్మాడు. చెరకు పండుతున్న పంట కాబట్టి సరుకుల నిర్వచనంలోకి వస్తుంది.

నియమం. అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం అంశమైన సరుకులు అమ్మేవాడి సొంతమైన లేదా స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న సరుకులు కావచ్చు, లేదా భవిష్యత్ సరుకులు కావచ్చు. భవిష్యత్ సరుకులు అంటే ఒప్పందం చేసిన తర్వాత అమ్మేవాడు తయారు చేసే, ఉత్పత్తి చేసే లేదా సంపాదించే సరుకులు.

ఉదాహరణ. ఒక ఫర్నిచర్ తయారీదారు మార్చి 1 న రాణికి ఒక అల్మారా అమ్మడానికి అంగీకరించాడు. దాన్ని ఏప్రిల్‌లో తయారు చేస్తాడు. మార్చి 1 నాటికి ఆ అల్మారా భవిష్యత్ సరుకులు.

selfTest.a: వ్యాజ్య హక్కులు, డబ్బు. 2. భవిష్యత్ సరుకులు (future goods) అంటే ఏమిటి? అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం చేసిన తర్వాత అమ్మేవాడు తయారు చేసే, ఉత్పత్తి చేసే లేదా సంపాదించే సరుకులు (సెక్షన్ 2(6)). 3. సెక్షన్ 6(3) ప్రకారం భవిష్యత్ సరుకుల ప్రస్తుత అమ్మకం అంటే ఏమిటి? ఆ ఒప్పందం సరుకులను అమ్మడానికి ఒప్పందంగా పనిచేస్తుంది. 4. సెక్షన్లు 7, 8 కు తేడా ఏమిటి? ఒప్పందం చేసే సమయానికే, అమ్మేవాడికి తెలియకుండా, నిర్దిష్ట సరుకులు నశించి ఉన్నప్పుడు సెక్షన్ 7 వర్తిస్తుంది. రిస్క్ కొనేవాడికి బదిలీ కాక ముందు, ఎవరి తప్పూ లేకుండా తర్వాత నశించినప్పుడు సెక్షన్ 8 వర్తిస్తుంది.

If there is an agreement to sell specific goods, and afterwards the goods perish or become so damaged as no longer to answer to their description in the agreement, without fault of the seller or the buyer, before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is avoided. Example. Nisha agrees to sell a specific tractor to Om, delivery next month. Before the risk passes to Om, lightning destroys the tractor. Neither party is at fault. The agreement is avoided under section 8. Did the goods perish? Which section applies? How to read this: start at the top. Both sections speak only of specific goods. 1. Are the goods specific, that is, identified and agreed upon when the contract was made (section 2(14))? If not, sections 7 and 8 do not apply on their words. 2. Had they perished, without the seller's knowledge, when the contract was made? The contract is void (section 7). 3. Did they perish later, without fault of seller or buyer, before the risk passed to the buyer, under an agreement to sell? The agreement is avoided (section 8).
keyPoints: Goods: all moveable property except actionable claims and money (section 2(7)). Includes stock and shares, growing crops, grass, and things agreed to be severed. Existing goods or future goods (sections 2(6), 6(1)). Contingent goods are allowed (section 6(2)). A present sale of future goods is an agreement to sell (section 6(3)). Specific goods: identified and agreed upon at the time of the contract (section 2(14)). Section 7: specific goods already perished at the contract, without the seller's knowledge, so the contract is void. Section 8: specific goods perish later, without fault, before the risk passes, so the agreement is avoided.

selfTest.q: 1. What is excluded from goods under section 2(7)?
selfTest.a: Actionable claims and money. 2. What are future goods? Goods to be manufactured or produced or acquired by the seller after the making of the contract of sale (section 2(6)). 3. What is a present sale of future goods under section 6(3)? The contract operates as an agreement to sell the goods. 4. What is the difference between sections 7 and 8? Section 7 applies where the specific goods had already perished when the contract was made, without the seller's knowledge. Section 8 applies where they perish afterwards, without fault of either party, before the risk passes to the buyer.

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t4.subtitle: Sections 14 to 17 and 62 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: Some terms of a contract of sale are written by the parties (express). Others are implied by the Sale of Goods Act unless the contract shows a different intention. The Act implies a condition that the seller has a right to sell, and warranties of quiet possession and freedom from encumbrance (section 14). It also implies a condition that goods sold by description correspond with it (section 15). It implies conditions of fitness and merchantable quality in the cases set out in section 16, and conditions in a sale by sample (section 17). Section 62 lets the parties negative or vary implied terms by express agreement, course of dealing or usage. Key points for the answer: each section and whether it implies a condition or a warranty.
en.meaning:
Express and implied terms

Rule. An express term is one the parties themselves state in the contract. An implied term is one the law reads in. Section 62 speaks of a right, duty or liability arising "by implication of law". Section 16(4) says an express warranty or condition does not negative an implied one unless it is inconsistent with it.

Example. A contract says "warranty: six months service". That is an express term. The law adds an implied condition that the seller has a right to sell (section 14(a)) even though the contract does not mention it.

Implied undertaking as to title (section 14)

Rule. Unless a different intention appears, three terms are implied.

Condition: in a sale, the seller has a right to sell the goods. In an agreement to sell, he will have a right to sell when the property is to pass (section 14(a)). Warranty: the buyer shall have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods (section 14(b)). Warranty: the goods shall be free from any charge or encumbrance in favour of a third party not declared or known to the buyer before or at the time of the contract (section 14(c)).

Example. Dev buys a motorcycle from Eshan. Later a bank proves that it holds an undisclosed charge on the motorcycle, which Dev did not know about. The implied warranty in section 14(c) is broken.

Sale by description (section 15)

Rule. In a sale of goods by description there is an implied condition that the goods shall correspond with the description. In a sale by sample as well as by description, it is not enough that the bulk corresponds with the sample. The goods must also correspond with the description.

Example. Farid orders "Grade A basmati rice" by description. The goods delivered are another grade. The implied condition in section 15 is broken.

Quality or fitness (section 16)

Rule. There is no implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose, except as follows.

Fitness for purpose (section 16(1)). The buyer makes known the particular purpose, expressly or by implication, so as to show he relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in the course of his business. There is then an implied condition that the goods are reasonably fit for that purpose. Exception: where a specified article is sold under its patent or other trade name, there is no implied condition as to fitness. Merchantable quality (section 16(2)). Goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description. There is an implied condition that they are of merchantable quality. Exception: if the buyer has examined the goods, there is no implied condition as regards defects which the examination ought to have revealed. Usage of trade (section 16(3)). An implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for a particular purpose may be annexed by the usage of trade. Express terms (section 16(4)). An express warranty or condition does not negative a warranty or condition implied by the Act unless inconsistent with it.

Example. Geeta tells a chemist she needs a cream for an infant's skin rash and relies on the chemist's advice. The chemist supplies a cream of a kind he sells in his business. There is an implied condition that it is reasonably fit for that purpose (section 16(1)).

Sale by sample (section 17)

Rule. A contract is by sample where it has a term, express or implied, to that effect. There is then an implied condition (a) that the bulk corresponds with the sample in quality, (b) that the buyer has a reasonable opportunity of comparing the bulk with the sample, and (c) that the goods are free from any defect, rendering them unmerchantable, which would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample.

Excluding implied terms (section 62)

Rule. A right, duty or liability arising by implication of law may be negatived or varied by express agreement, by the course of dealing between the parties, or by usage if the usage binds both parties.

Which implied term applies? How to read this: each step names the section and whether it creates a condition or a warranty. 1. Title and possession (section 14) Condition: right to sell. Warranties: quiet possession, freedom from encumbrance. 2. Description (section 15) Condition: goods correspond with the description. 3. Quality or fitness (section 16) Conditions in sub-sections (1) and (2), and by trade usage in (3). Otherwise none. 4. Sample (section 17) Three conditions: bulk like the sample, chance to compare, no hidden defect. 5. Can the parties change these (section 62)? Yes, by express agreement, course of dealing or usage binding both.
keyPoints: Section 14: condition of right to sell. Warranties of quiet possession and freedom from encumbrance. Section 15: sale by description. Goods must correspond with the description. Section 16(1): fitness for a known purpose when the buyer relies on the seller's skill. Not for patent or trade name articles. Section 16(2): merchantable quality in a purchase by description from a dealer. Not for defects the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Section 16(3): trade usage may annex terms. Section 16(4): express terms do not displace implied ones unless inconsistent. Section 17: sale by sample has three conditions. Section 62: implied terms may be negatived or varied.

caseLaws.facts: Until one is added, sections 14 to 17 and 62 of the Act are the authority. The August 2016 question about a stolen car would be settled by a decided case on the effect of use of the goods, which has to be found in an official source.

selfTest.q: 1. Which part of section 14 is a condition?
selfTest.a: Section 14(a): the seller has a right to sell the goods. 2. Name the two implied warranties in section 14. Quiet possession (section 14(b)) and freedom from any undeclared charge or encumbrance (section 14(c)). 3. Does section 16 imply fitness in every sale? No. It says there is no implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness except as it lists. 4. How can implied terms be excluded? By express agreement, by the course of dealing between the parties, or by usage binding both (section 62).

Implied termA term that arises under a contract of sale "by implication of law" (section 62). The Act does not define "implied"అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం కింద "చట్టం ద్వారా అంతర్లీనంగా" (by implication of law) వచ్చే నిబంధన (సెక్షన్ 62). చట్టం "implied" ను నిర్వచించలేదు
Sale by descriptionA contract for the sale of goods by description (section 15). The Act does not define itవర్ణన ద్వారా సరుకుల అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం (సెక్షన్ 15). చట్టం దీన్ని నిర్వచించలేదు
Merchantable qualityThe quality which section 16(2) implies as a condition where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description. The Act does not define itఆ వర్ణనగల సరుకులతో వ్యాపారం చేసే అమ్మేవాడి నుండి వర్ణన ప్రకారం సరుకులు కొన్నప్పుడు సెక్షన్ 16(2) condition గా అంతర్లీనంగా చేర్చే నాణ్యత. చట్టం దీన్ని నిర్వచించలేదు
Sale by sampleA contract of sale in which there is a term, express or implied, that it is by sample (section 17(1))నమూనా ప్రకారం అమ్మకమని ఒప్పందంలో స్పష్టమైన లేదా అంతర్లీన నిబంధన ఉన్న అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం (సెక్షన్ 17(1))
Quiet possessionThe buyer shall have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods (section 14(b))కొనేవాడు సరుకులను ఎవరి ఆటంకం లేకుండా స్వాధీనంలో ఉంచుకుని అనుభవించడం (సెక్షన్ 14(b))
EncumbranceSection 14(c) speaks of "any charge or encumbrance in favour of any third party". The Act does not define it. In plain terms, a third party's claim over the goodsసరుకులపై మూడో వ్యక్తికి అనుకూలంగా ఉన్న భారం (సెక్షన్ 14(c) "charge or encumbrance" అంటుంది)

te.inOneMinute: సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 లోని సెక్షన్లు 14 నుండి 17, 62 — స్పష్టమైన, అంతర్లీన షరతులు, వారంటీలు
te.meaning:
అమ్మకం ఒప్పందంలోని కొన్ని నిబంధనలను పక్షాలే రాస్తారు (express). మరికొన్ని, ఒప్పందం వేరే ఉద్దేశం చూపిస్తే తప్ప, సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం ద్వారా అంతర్లీనంగా (implied) చేరతాయి. అమ్మేవాడికి అమ్మే హక్కు ఉందనే condition, ప్రశాంత స్వాధీనం, భారం లేకపోవడం అనే warranties చట్టం అంతర్లీనంగా చేరుస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 14).

వర్ణన ప్రకారం అమ్మిన సరుకులు ఆ వర్ణనకు సరిపోవాలనే condition కూడా చేరుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 15). సెక్షన్ 16 లో చెప్పిన సందర్భాల్లో తగినతనం, వ్యాపార యోగ్యమైన నాణ్యత conditions, నమూనా ప్రకారం అమ్మకంలో conditions చేరతాయి (సెక్షన్ 17). అంతర్లీన నిబంధనలను స్పష్టమైన ఒప్పందం, పక్షాల వ్యవహార తీరు లేదా వాడుక ద్వారా పక్షాలు తొలగించవచ్చు లేదా మార్చవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 62). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: ప్రతి సెక్షన్, అది condition ని చేరుస్తుందా warranty ని చేరుస్తుందా.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. స్పష్టమైన నిబంధన అంటే పక్షాలే ఒప్పందంలో చెప్పినది. అంతర్లీన నిబంధన అంటే చట్టం చేర్చినది. సెక్షన్ 62 "చట్టం ద్వారా అంతర్లీనంగా" తలెత్తే హక్కు, విధి, బాధ్యత గురించి చెబుతుంది. స్పష్టమైన warranty లేదా condition, అంతర్లీనంగా ఉన్నదానికి విరుద్ధం కానంత వరకు దాన్ని నిరాకరించదని సెక్షన్ 16(4) చెబుతుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. ఒప్పందంలో "warranty: ఆరు నెలల సర్వీసు" అని ఉంది. అది స్పష్టమైన నిబంధన. ఒప్పందం ప్రస్తావించకపోయినా అమ్మేవాడికి అమ్మే హక్కు ఉండాలనే అంతర్లీన condition ను చట్టం చేరుస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 14(a)).

నియమం. వేరే ఉద్దేశం కనిపిస్తే తప్ప, మూడు నిబంధనలు అంతర్లీనంగా చేరతాయి.

ఉదాహరణ. దేవ్ ఈషాన్ నుండి ఒక మోటార్‌సైకిల్ కొన్నాడు. దేవ్‌కు తెలియని, ప్రకటించని భారం ఆ మోటార్‌సైకిల్‌పై బ్యాంకుకు ఉందని తర్వాత రుజువైంది. సెక్షన్ 14(c) లోని అంతర్లీన warranty ఉల్లంఘించారు.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 14 లో ఏ భాగం condition?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 14(a): అమ్మేవాడికి సరుకులను అమ్మే హక్కు ఉంది. 2. సెక్షన్ 14 లోని రెండు అంతర్లీన warranties పేర్లు చెప్పండి. ప్రశాంత స్వాధీనం (సెక్షన్ 14(b)), ప్రకటించని ఏ భారం లేకపోవడం (సెక్షన్ 14(c)). 3. ప్రతి అమ్మకంలో సెక్షన్ 16 తగినతనాన్ని చేర్చుతుందా? లేదు. అది జాబితా చేసినవి తప్ప నాణ్యత లేదా తగినతనం గురించి అంతర్లీన warranty లేదా condition లేదని చెబుతుంది. 4. అంతర్లీన నిబంధనలను ఎలా తొలగించవచ్చు? స్పష్టమైన ఒప్పందం ద్వారా, పక్షాల వ్యవహార తీరు ద్వారా, లేదా ఇద్దరినీ కట్టుబడే వాడుక ద్వారా (సెక్షన్ 62).

hi.inOneMinute: Some terms of a contract of sale are written by the parties (express). Others are implied by the Sale of Goods Act unless the contract shows a different intention. The Act implies a condition that the seller has a right to sell, and warranties of quiet possession and freedom from encumbrance (section 14). It also implies a condition that goods sold by description correspond with it (section 15). It implies conditions of fitness and merchantable quality in the cases set out in section 16, and conditions in a sale by sample (section 17). Section 62 lets the parties negative or vary implied terms by express agreement, course of dealing or usage. Key points for the answer: each section and whether it implies a condition or a warranty.
hi.meaning: Express and implied terms Rule. An express term is one the parties themselves state in the contract. An implied term is one the law reads in. Section 62 speaks of a right, duty or liability arising "by implication of law". Section 16(4) says an express warranty or condition does not negative an implied one unless it is inconsistent with it. Example. A contract says "warranty: six months service". That is an express term. The law adds an implied condition that the seller has a right to sell (section 14(a)) even though the contract does not mention it. Implied undertaking as to title (section 14) Rule. Unless a different intention appears, three terms are implied. Condition: in a sale, the seller has a right to sell the goods. In an agreement to sell, he will have a right to sell when the property is to pass (section 14(a)). Warranty: the buyer shall have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods (section 14(b)). Warranty: the goods shall be free from any charge or encumbrance in favour of a third party not declared or known to the buyer before or at the time of the contract (section 14(c)). Example. Dev buys a motorcycle from Eshan. Later a bank proves that it holds an undisclosed charge on the motorcycle, which Dev did not know about. The implied warranty in section 14(c) is broken. Sale by description (section 15) Rule. In a sale of goods by description there is an implied condition that the goods shall correspond with the description. In a sale by sample as well as by description, it is not enough that the bulk corresponds with the sample. The goods must also correspond with the description. Example. Farid orders "Grade A basmati rice" by description. The goods delivered are another grade. The implied condition in section 15 is broken. Quality or fitness (section 16) Rule. There is no implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose, except as follows. Fitness for purpose (section 16(1)). The buyer makes known the particular purpose, expressly or by implication, so as to show he relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in the course of his business. There is then an implied condition that the goods are reasonably fit for that purpose. Exception: where a specified article is sold under its patent or other trade name, there is no implied condition as to fitness. Merchantable quality (section 16(2)). Goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in goods of that description. There is an implied condition that they are of merchantable quality. Exception: if the buyer has examined the goods, there is no implied condition as regards defects which the examination ought to have revealed. Usage of trade (section 16(3)). An implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for a particular purpose may be annexed by the usage of trade. Express terms (section 16(4)). An express warranty or condition does not negative a warranty or condition implied by the Act unless inconsistent with it. Example. Geeta tells a chemist she needs a cream for an infant's skin rash and relies on the chemist's advice. The chemist supplies a cream of a kind he sells in his business. There is an implied condition that it is reasonably fit for that purpose (section 16(1)). Sale by sample (section 17) Rule. A contract is by sample where it has a term, express or implied, to that effect. There is then an implied condition (a) that the bulk corresponds with the sample in quality, (b) that the buyer has a reasonable opportunity of comparing the bulk with the sample, and (c) that the goods are free from any defect, rendering them unmerchantable, which would not be apparent on reasonable examination of the sample. Excluding implied terms (section 62) Rule. A right, duty or liability arising by implication of law may be negatived or varied by express agreement, by the course of dealing between the parties, or by usage if the usage binds both parties. Which implied term applies? How to read this: each step names the section and whether it creates a condition or a warranty. 1. Title and possession (section 14) Condition: right to sell. Warranties: quiet possession, freedom from encumbrance. 2. Description (section 15) Condition: goods correspond with the description. 3. Quality or fitness (section 16) Conditions in sub-sections (1) and (2), and by trade usage in (3). Otherwise none. 4. Sample (section 17) Three conditions: bulk like the sample, chance to compare, no hidden defect. 5. Can the parties change these (section 62)? Yes, by express agreement, course of dealing or usage binding both.
keyPoints: Section 14: condition of right to sell. Warranties of quiet possession and freedom from encumbrance. Section 15: sale by description. Goods must correspond with the description. Section 16(1): fitness for a known purpose when the buyer relies on the seller's skill. Not for patent or trade name articles. Section 16(2): merchantable quality in a purchase by description from a dealer. Not for defects the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Section 16(3): trade usage may annex terms. Section 16(4): express terms do not displace implied ones unless inconsistent. Section 17: sale by sample has three conditions. Section 62: implied terms may be negatived or varied.

selfTest.q: 1. Which part of section 14 is a condition?
selfTest.a: Section 14(a): the seller has a right to sell the goods. 2. Name the two implied warranties in section 14. Quiet possession (section 14(b)) and freedom from any undeclared charge or encumbrance (section 14(c)). 3. Does section 16 imply fitness in every sale? No. It says there is no implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness except as it lists. 4. How can implied terms be excluded? By express agreement, by the course of dealing between the parties, or by usage binding both (section 62).

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t5.subtitle: Sections 9, 10, 63 and 64A of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: The price in a contract of sale may be fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in the manner agreed, or determined by the course of dealing between the parties (section 9(1)). If it is not determined in any of these ways, the buyer must pay a reasonable price , which is a question of fact (section 9(2)). If the price is to be fixed by a third party's valuation and he does not make it, the agreement is avoided, except that the buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price (section 10). A change in customs, excise or sales tax after the contract can change the price, unless the contract shows a different intention (section 64A). Key points for the answer: the three ways in section 9(1), the reasonable-price fall-back in section 9(2), and the effect of failure of valuation.
en.meaning:
How the price is ascertained (section 9)

Rule. The price may be (1) fixed by the contract, (2) left to be fixed in the manner agreed, or (3) determined by the course of dealing between the parties. If none of these applies, the buyer pays a reasonable price. What is reasonable is a question of fact in each case.

Example. Rita regularly buys milk from a dairy, and the dairy has always charged the same rate. They agree to continue. The price is determined by the course of dealing (section 9(1)). If Rita and the dairy had agreed nothing about price at all, Rita would pay a reasonable price (section 9(2)).

Agreement to sell at valuation (section 10)

Rule. If the agreement is to sell at a price fixed by a third party's valuation and the third party cannot or does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided. But if the goods or any part have been delivered to and appropriated by the buyer, he must pay a reasonable price for them.

If the third party is prevented from making the valuation by the fault of the seller or the buyer, the party not at fault may sue the party at fault for damages (section 10(2)).

Example. Sunil agrees to sell his painting to Tara at the price a named valuer will fix. The valuer dies before valuing it. The agreement is avoided (section 10(1)). If Sunil had already delivered the painting and Tara had taken it as her own, she would have to pay a reasonable price (proviso).

Reasonable time (section 63)

Rule. Wherever the Act refers to a reasonable time, what is a reasonable time is a question of fact.

Changes in taxes after the contract (section 64A)

Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, the seller and the buyer share the effect of changes in customs duty, excise duty, or a tax on the sale or purchase of goods after the contract is made.

If a tax or an increase takes effect, the seller may add to the price the amount paid or payable, and may sue to recover it (section 64A(1)(a)). If a decrease or remission takes effect, the buyer may deduct the amount of the decrease or the remitted tax from the price (section 64A(1)(b)). The taxes covered are duties of customs or excise on goods and taxes on the sale or purchase of goods (section 64A(2)).

Example. Umesh agrees to sell goods at Rs 1,000 with no mention of tax, when no tax was chargeable. A sales tax of Rs 50 is imposed afterwards and Umesh has to pay it. Unless the contract shows a different intention, he may add Rs 50 to the price and sue for it (section 64A(1)(a)).

What price must the buyer pay? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the price fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in the agreed manner, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1))? That price is payable. 2. Is the price to be fixed by a third party's valuation (section 10)? If he does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price. 3. Is the price not determined in any of these ways? The buyer pays a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). 4. Did a customs, excise or sales tax change after the contract (section 64A)? Unless a different intention appears, the seller adds an increase and the buyer deducts a decrease.
keyPoints: Price: the money consideration (section 2(10)). Fixed by the contract, left to be fixed as agreed, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1)). Otherwise a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). Valuation by a third party fails: agreement avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price (section 10(1)). Party at fault for preventing valuation: suit for damages (section 10(2)). Reasonable time is a question of fact (section 63). Tax changes after the contract: seller may add, buyer may deduct (section 64A).

selfTest.q: 1. In what ways may the price be fixed under section 9(1)?
selfTest.a: By the contract, in a manner agreed in the contract, or by the course of dealing between the parties. 2. What if the price is not determined in those ways? The buyer pays a reasonable price, which is a question of fact (section 9(2)). 3. What if the third-party valuer does not make the valuation? The agreement is avoided. If the buyer has received and appropriated goods, he pays a reasonable price (section 10(1)). 4. What does section 64A do? It lets the seller add an increase in customs, excise or sales tax made after the contract, and the buyer deduct a decrease, unless a different intention appears.

te.meaning:
అమ్మకం ఒప్పందంలో ధరను ఒప్పందమే నిర్ణయించవచ్చు, అంగీకరించిన పద్ధతిలో నిర్ణయించడానికి వదిలేయవచ్చు, లేదా పక్షాల మధ్య వ్యవహార తీరు (course of dealing) ద్వారా నిర్ణయం కావచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 9(1)). వీటిలో ఏ విధంగానూ ధర నిర్ణయం కాకపోతే, కొనేవాడు సహేతుక ధర చెల్లించాలి. అది వాస్తవ ప్రశ్న (సెక్షన్ 9(2)).

ధరను మూడో వ్యక్తి విలువకట్టడం ద్వారా నిర్ణయించాలని ఉండి, అతను ఆ విలువ కట్టకపోతే ఒప్పందం రద్దవుతుంది. కానీ సరుకులను అందుకుని స్వీకరించిన కొనేవాడు సహేతుక ధర చెల్లిస్తాడు (సెక్షన్ 10). ఒప్పందం తర్వాత కస్టమ్స్, ఎక్సైజ్ లేదా అమ్మకపు పన్ను మారితే ధర మారవచ్చు, ఒప్పందం వేరే ఉద్దేశం చూపిస్తే తప్ప (సెక్షన్ 64A). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: సెక్షన్ 9(1) లోని మూడు పద్ధతులు, సెక్షన్ 9(2) లోని సహేతుక ధర, విలువకట్టడం విఫలమైతే ప్రభావం.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. ధరను (1) ఒప్పందం నిర్ణయించవచ్చు, (2) అంగీకరించిన పద్ధతిలో నిర్ణయించడానికి వదిలేయవచ్చు, లేదా (3) పక్షాల వ్యవహార తీరు నిర్ణయించవచ్చు. వీటిలో ఏదీ వర్తించకపోతే కొనేవాడు సహేతుక ధర చెల్లిస్తాడు. సహేతుకమైనది ఏది అనేది ప్రతి కేసులో వాస్తవ ప్రశ్న.

ఉదాహరణ. రీటా క్రమం తప్పకుండా ఒక డెయిరీ నుండి పాలు కొంటుంది, డెయిరీ ఎప్పుడూ ఒకే రేటు వసూలు చేస్తుంది. వారు కొనసాగించడానికి అంగీకరించారు. ధరను వ్యవహార తీరు నిర్ణయిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 9(1)). ధర గురించి రీటా, డెయిరీ ఏమీ అంగీకరించకపోతే, రీటా సహేతుక ధర చెల్లించాలి (సెక్షన్ 9(2)).

నియమం. మూడో వ్యక్తి విలువకట్టడం ద్వారా నిర్ణయించే ధరకు అమ్మడానికి ఒప్పందం ఉండి, ఆ మూడో వ్యక్తి విలువ కట్టలేకపోతే లేదా కట్టకపోతే ఒప్పందం రద్దవుతుంది. కానీ సరుకులు లేదా వాటిలో కొంత భాగం కొనేవాడికి అప్పగించి, అతను స్వీకరించి ఉంటే, వాటికి అతను సహేతుక ధర చెల్లించాలి.

అమ్మేవాడి లేదా కొనేవాడి తప్పు వల్ల మూడో వ్యక్తి విలువ కట్టకుండా ఆగిపోతే, తప్పు లేని పక్షం తప్పు చేసిన పక్షంపై నష్టపరిహారం దావా వేయవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 10(2)).

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 9(1) ప్రకారం ధరను ఏ విధాలుగా నిర్ణయించవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: ఒప్పందం ద్వారా, ఒప్పందంలో అంగీకరించిన పద్ధతిలో, లేదా పక్షాల మధ్య వ్యవహార తీరు ద్వారా. 2. ఈ విధాలుగా ధర నిర్ణయం కాకపోతే ఏమవుతుంది? కొనేవాడు సహేతుక ధర చెల్లిస్తాడు, అది వాస్తవ ప్రశ్న (సెక్షన్ 9(2)). 3. మూడో వ్యక్తి విలువకట్టేవాడు విలువ కట్టకపోతే ఏమవుతుంది? ఒప్పందం రద్దవుతుంది. కొనేవాడు సరుకులు అందుకుని స్వీకరించి ఉంటే సహేతుక ధర చెల్లిస్తాడు (సెక్షన్ 10(1)). 4. సెక్షన్ 64A ఏం చేస్తుంది? వేరే ఉద్దేశం కనిపిస్తే తప్ప, ఒప్పందం తర్వాత కస్టమ్స్, ఎక్సైజ్ లేదా అమ్మకపు పన్ను పెరిగితే అమ్మేవాడు ధరకు కలపడానికి, తగ్గితే కొనేవాడు తగ్గించుకోవడానికి అనుమతిస్తుంది.

hi.inOneMinute: The price in a contract of sale may be fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in the manner agreed, or determined by the course of dealing between the parties (section 9(1)). If it is not determined in any of these ways, the buyer must pay a reasonable price , which is a question of fact (section 9(2)). If the price is to be fixed by a third party's valuation and he does not make it, the agreement is avoided, except that the buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price (section 10). A change in customs, excise or sales tax after the contract can change the price, unless the contract shows a different intention (section 64A). Key points for the answer: the three ways in section 9(1), the reasonable-price fall-back in section 9(2), and the effect of failure of valuation.
hi.meaning: How the price is ascertained (section 9) Rule. The price may be (1) fixed by the contract, (2) left to be fixed in the manner agreed, or (3) determined by the course of dealing between the parties. If none of these applies, the buyer pays a reasonable price. What is reasonable is a question of fact in each case. Example. Rita regularly buys milk from a dairy, and the dairy has always charged the same rate. They agree to continue. The price is determined by the course of dealing (section 9(1)). If Rita and the dairy had agreed nothing about price at all, Rita would pay a reasonable price (section 9(2)). Agreement to sell at valuation (section 10) Rule. If the agreement is to sell at a price fixed by a third party's valuation and the third party cannot or does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided. But if the goods or any part have been delivered to and appropriated by the buyer, he must pay a reasonable price for them. If the third party is prevented from making the valuation by the fault of the seller or the buyer, the party not at fault may sue the party at fault for damages (section 10(2)). Example. Sunil agrees to sell his painting to Tara at the price a named valuer will fix. The valuer dies before valuing it. The agreement is avoided (section 10(1)). If Sunil had already delivered the painting and Tara had taken it as her own, she would have to pay a reasonable price (proviso). Reasonable time (section 63) Rule. Wherever the Act refers to a reasonable time, what is a reasonable time is a question of fact. Changes in taxes after the contract (section 64A) Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, the seller and the buyer share the effect of changes in customs duty, excise duty, or a tax on the sale or purchase of goods after the contract is made. If a tax or an increase takes effect, the seller may add to the price the amount paid or payable, and may sue to recover it (section 64A(1)(a)). If a decrease or remission takes effect, the buyer may deduct the amount of the decrease or the remitted tax from the price (section 64A(1)(b)). The taxes covered are duties of customs or excise on goods and taxes on the sale or purchase of goods (section 64A(2)). Example. Umesh agrees to sell goods at Rs 1,000 with no mention of tax, when no tax was chargeable. A sales tax of Rs 50 is imposed afterwards and Umesh has to pay it. Unless the contract shows a different intention, he may add Rs 50 to the price and sue for it (section 64A(1)(a)). What price must the buyer pay? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the price fixed by the contract, left to be fixed in the agreed manner, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1))? That price is payable. 2. Is the price to be fixed by a third party's valuation (section 10)? If he does not make the valuation, the agreement is avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price. 3. Is the price not determined in any of these ways? The buyer pays a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). 4. Did a customs, excise or sales tax change after the contract (section 64A)? Unless a different intention appears, the seller adds an increase and the buyer deducts a decrease.
keyPoints: Price: the money consideration (section 2(10)). Fixed by the contract, left to be fixed as agreed, or determined by course of dealing (section 9(1)). Otherwise a reasonable price, a question of fact (section 9(2)). Valuation by a third party fails: agreement avoided, but a buyer who has received and appropriated goods pays a reasonable price (section 10(1)). Party at fault for preventing valuation: suit for damages (section 10(2)). Reasonable time is a question of fact (section 63). Tax changes after the contract: seller may add, buyer may deduct (section 64A).

caseLaws.facts: Until one is added, sections 9, 10, 63 and 64A of the Act are the authority.

selfTest.q: 1. In what ways may the price be fixed under section 9(1)?
selfTest.a: By the contract, in a manner agreed in the contract, or by the course of dealing between the parties. 2. What if the price is not determined in those ways? The buyer pays a reasonable price, which is a question of fact (section 9(2)). 3. What if the third-party valuer does not make the valuation? The agreement is avoided. If the buyer has received and appropriated goods, he pays a reasonable price (section 10(1)). 4. What does section 64A do? It lets the seller add an increase in customs, excise or sales tax made after the contract, and the buyer deduct a decrease, unless a different intention appears.
