law-of-contract-ii-u3-t3.subtitle: Sections 11 to 13 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: A stipulation in a contract of sale may be a condition or a warranty (section 12(1)). A condition is essential to the main purpose of the contract, and its breach gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated (section 12(2)). A warranty is collateral to the main purpose, and its breach gives a claim for damages only (section 12(3)). Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends on the construction of the contract, not on the name used (section 12(4)). A buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty, and after accepting the goods in a contract that is not severable he can generally only claim for breach of warranty (section 13). Time of payment is not of the essence unless a different intention appears (section 11).
en.meaning:
Condition and warranty (section 12)

Rule. A stipulation about the goods may be a condition or a warranty.

A condition is essential to the main purpose of the contract. Its breach gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated. A warranty is collateral to the main purpose. Its breach gives a claim for damages, but no right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated.

Example. Asha orders a "new" refrigerator. The refrigerator delivered is old. Being new is essential to what she bought, so this is a breach of a condition, and she may treat the contract as repudiated (section 12(2)). If instead the seller had promised a free carry-bag with it and did not give it, that stipulation is collateral to the main purpose and the claim is for damages (section 12(3)).

Name does not decide (section 12(4))

Rule. Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition though called a warranty in the contract.

Stipulations as to time (section 11)

Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not of the essence of a contract of sale. For any other stipulation as to time, whether it is of the essence depends on the terms of the contract.

Example. A buyer agrees to pay on the 1st of the month and pays on the 5th. Unless the contract shows a different intention, the seller cannot treat the contract as repudiated only for the late payment (section 11).

When a condition is treated as a warranty (section 13)

Rule. Section 13 gives three rules.

Where the contract is subject to a condition to be fulfilled by the seller, the buyer may waive it, or elect to treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). Where the contract is not severable and the buyer has accepted the goods or part of them, the breach of any condition to be fulfilled by the seller can only be treated as a breach of warranty. He cannot reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated, unless there is a term of the contract, express or implied, to that effect (section 13(2)). The section does not affect a condition or warranty whose fulfilment is excused by law by reason of impossibility or otherwise (section 13(3)).

Example. Bala buys a whole lot of 100 chairs under one contract that is not severable. He accepts the lot. Later he finds that the chairs do not match the stipulated condition. Unless the contract says otherwise, he can only treat it as a breach of warranty and claim damages. He cannot reject the chairs (section 13(2)).

Breach by the seller: reject the goods or claim damages? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the broken stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract (section 12(2))? If yes, it is a condition. Go to step 2. If it is only collateral, it is a warranty: the buyer claims damages and cannot reject the goods (section 12(3)). 2. Has the buyer waived the condition or chosen to treat the breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1))? If yes, he claims damages only. 3. Is the contract non-severable and has the buyer accepted the goods or part of them (section 13(2))? If yes, and the contract has no term to the contrary, he can treat the breach only as a breach of warranty. Otherwise he may treat the contract as repudiated.
keyPoints: Condition: essential to the main purpose. Breach gives a right to repudiate (section 12(2)). Warranty: collateral to the main purpose. Breach gives damages only (section 12(3)). The construction of the contract decides, not the name (section 12(4)). Time of payment is not of the essence unless a different intention appears (section 11). The buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). After acceptance in a non-severable contract, breach of condition is treated as breach of warranty, unless the contract says otherwise (section 13(2)).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a condition under section 12(2)?
selfTest.a: A stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated. 2. What is the remedy for breach of a warranty under section 12(3)? A claim for damages. There is no right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. 3. Is a stipulation called a warranty always a warranty? No. It may be a condition, because the construction of the contract decides (section 12(4)). 4. Are stipulations as to time of payment of the essence? Not unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract (section 11).

te.inOneMinute: సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 లోని సెక్షన్లు 11 నుండి 13 — షరతులు, వారంటీలు
te.meaning:
అమ్మకం ఒప్పందంలోని నిబంధన condition కావచ్చు, warranty కావచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 12(1)). Condition ఒప్పందం ప్రధాన ఉద్దేశానికి అత్యవసరమైనది . దాన్ని ఉల్లంఘిస్తే ఒప్పందాన్ని తిరస్కరించినట్లుగా పరిగణించే హక్కు వస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 12(2)). Warranty ప్రధాన ఉద్దేశానికి అనుబంధమైనది. దాన్ని ఉల్లంఘిస్తే నష్టపరిహారం కోరవచ్చు, అంతే (సెక్షన్ 12(3)).

నిబంధన condition లేదా warranty అనేది ఒప్పందం అర్థాన్ని బట్టి తేలుతుంది, వాడిన పేరును బట్టి కాదు (సెక్షన్ 12(4)). కొనేవాడు condition ను వదులుకోవచ్చు, లేదా దాని ఉల్లంఘనను warranty ఉల్లంఘనగా పరిగణించవచ్చు. విభజించలేని ఒప్పందంలో సరుకులు అంగీకరించాక అతను సాధారణంగా warranty ఉల్లంఘన కోసం మాత్రమే కోరవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 13). చెల్లింపు సమయం, వేరే ఉద్దేశం కనిపిస్తే తప్ప, ఒప్పందానికి సారాంశం కాదు (సెక్షన్ 11).

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. సరుకుల గురించిన నిబంధన condition లేదా warranty కావచ్చు.

ఉదాహరణ. ఆశ "కొత్త" రిఫ్రిజిరేటర్ ఆర్డర్ చేసింది. వచ్చినది పాతది. కొత్తది కావడం ఆమె కొన్న దానికి అత్యవసరం కాబట్టి ఇది condition ఉల్లంఘన, ఆమె ఒప్పందాన్ని తిరస్కరించినట్లుగా పరిగణించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 12(2)). అమ్మేవాడు దానితో పాటు ఉచిత క్యారీ-బ్యాగ్ ఇస్తానని చెప్పి ఇవ్వకపోతే, ఆ నిబంధన ప్రధాన ఉద్దేశానికి అనుబంధం, కాబట్టి నష్టపరిహారం కోసం మాత్రమే దావా వేయగలదు (సెక్షన్ 12(3)).

నియమం. నిబంధన condition లేదా warranty అనేది ప్రతి సందర్భంలో ఒప్పందం అర్థంపై ఆధారపడుతుంది. ఒప్పందంలో warranty అని పిలిచినా, నిబంధన condition కావచ్చు.

నియమం. ఒప్పంద నిబంధనల నుండి వేరే ఉద్దేశం కనిపిస్తే తప్ప, చెల్లింపు సమయ నిబంధనలు అమ్మకం ఒప్పందానికి సారాంశం కావు. ఇతర సమయ నిబంధన సారాంశమా కాదా అనేది ఒప్పంద నిబంధనలపై ఆధారపడుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 12(2) ప్రకారం condition అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఒప్పందం ప్రధాన ఉద్దేశానికి అత్యవసరమైన నిబంధన, దాన్ని ఉల్లంఘిస్తే ఒప్పందాన్ని తిరస్కరించినట్లుగా పరిగణించే హక్కు వస్తుంది. 2. సెక్షన్ 12(3) ప్రకారం warranty ఉల్లంఘనకు పరిహారం ఏమిటి? నష్టపరిహారం కోసం దావా. సరుకులను తిరస్కరించి ఒప్పందాన్ని తిరస్కరించే హక్కు లేదు. 3. Warranty అని పిలిచిన నిబంధన ఎప్పుడూ warranty యేనా? కాదు. ఒప్పందం అర్థం నిర్ణయిస్తుంది కాబట్టి అది condition కావచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 12(4)). 4. చెల్లింపు సమయ నిబంధనలు ఒప్పందానికి సారాంశమా? ఒప్పంద నిబంధనల నుండి వేరే ఉద్దేశం కనిపిస్తే తప్ప కాదు (సెక్షన్ 11).

hi.inOneMinute: A stipulation in a contract of sale may be a condition or a warranty (section 12(1)). A condition is essential to the main purpose of the contract, and its breach gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated (section 12(2)). A warranty is collateral to the main purpose, and its breach gives a claim for damages only (section 12(3)). Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends on the construction of the contract, not on the name used (section 12(4)). A buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty, and after accepting the goods in a contract that is not severable he can generally only claim for breach of warranty (section 13). Time of payment is not of the essence unless a different intention appears (section 11).
hi.meaning: Condition and warranty (section 12) Rule. A stipulation about the goods may be a condition or a warranty. A condition is essential to the main purpose of the contract. Its breach gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated. A warranty is collateral to the main purpose. Its breach gives a claim for damages, but no right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. Example. Asha orders a "new" refrigerator. The refrigerator delivered is old. Being new is essential to what she bought, so this is a breach of a condition, and she may treat the contract as repudiated (section 12(2)). If instead the seller had promised a free carry-bag with it and did not give it, that stipulation is collateral to the main purpose and the claim is for damages (section 12(3)). Name does not decide (section 12(4)) Rule. Whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition though called a warranty in the contract. Stipulations as to time (section 11) Rule. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not of the essence of a contract of sale. For any other stipulation as to time, whether it is of the essence depends on the terms of the contract. Example. A buyer agrees to pay on the 1st of the month and pays on the 5th. Unless the contract shows a different intention, the seller cannot treat the contract as repudiated only for the late payment (section 11). When a condition is treated as a warranty (section 13) Rule. Section 13 gives three rules. Where the contract is subject to a condition to be fulfilled by the seller, the buyer may waive it, or elect to treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). Where the contract is not severable and the buyer has accepted the goods or part of them, the breach of any condition to be fulfilled by the seller can only be treated as a breach of warranty. He cannot reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated, unless there is a term of the contract, express or implied, to that effect (section 13(2)). The section does not affect a condition or warranty whose fulfilment is excused by law by reason of impossibility or otherwise (section 13(3)). Example. Bala buys a whole lot of 100 chairs under one contract that is not severable. He accepts the lot. Later he finds that the chairs do not match the stipulated condition. Unless the contract says otherwise, he can only treat it as a breach of warranty and claim damages. He cannot reject the chairs (section 13(2)). Breach by the seller: reject the goods or claim damages? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is the broken stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract (section 12(2))? If yes, it is a condition. Go to step 2. If it is only collateral, it is a warranty: the buyer claims damages and cannot reject the goods (section 12(3)). 2. Has the buyer waived the condition or chosen to treat the breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1))? If yes, he claims damages only. 3. Is the contract non-severable and has the buyer accepted the goods or part of them (section 13(2))? If yes, and the contract has no term to the contrary, he can treat the breach only as a breach of warranty. Otherwise he may treat the contract as repudiated.
keyPoints: Condition: essential to the main purpose. Breach gives a right to repudiate (section 12(2)). Warranty: collateral to the main purpose. Breach gives damages only (section 12(3)). The construction of the contract decides, not the name (section 12(4)). Time of payment is not of the essence unless a different intention appears (section 11). The buyer may waive a condition or treat its breach as a breach of warranty (section 13(1)). After acceptance in a non-severable contract, breach of condition is treated as breach of warranty, unless the contract says otherwise (section 13(2)).

selfTest.q: 1. What is a condition under section 12(2)?
selfTest.a: A stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated. 2. What is the remedy for breach of a warranty under section 12(3)? A claim for damages. There is no right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. 3. Is a stipulation called a warranty always a warranty? No. It may be a condition, because the construction of the contract decides (section 12(4)). 4. Are stipulations as to time of payment of the essence? Not unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract (section 11).

law-of-contract-ii-u3-t6.subtitle: Section 16 and sections 14, 15 and 17 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: Caveat emptor is a Latin phrase meaning "let the buyer beware ". The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 does not use the phrase. Its rule is in the opening words of section 16: there is no implied warranty or condition as to the quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale, except as the Act provides. The exceptions are the implied terms of the Act: the seller's right to sell and the other terms in section 14, correspondence with description (section 15), fitness for a known purpose and merchantable quality (section 16(1) and (2)), terms annexed by trade usage (section 16(3)), and the terms of a sale by sample (section 17). Key points for the answer: the rule, then each exception with its section.
en.meaning:
The rule (opening words of section 16)

Rule. The Act implies no warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale, except as the Act provides. The buyer must therefore satisfy himself about quality and fitness, or get an express term.

Example. Rohit buys a second-hand pump from a neighbour, who is not in the business of selling pumps. Rohit did not state any particular purpose. If the pump is weak, section 16 gives no implied condition of fitness or quality, and none of the exceptions below applies on these facts.

Exceptions: terms the Act implies

Rule. The Act gives these exceptions.

Title (section 14). Implied condition of right to sell. Implied warranties of quiet possession and freedom from undisclosed encumbrance. Description (section 15). Implied condition that goods correspond with the description. Fitness for a known purpose (section 16(1)). Where the buyer makes known the purpose, relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in his business. Not for a specified article sold under its patent or other trade name. Merchantable quality (section 16(2)). Where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods. Not for defects which the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Usage of trade (section 16(3)). A term as to quality or fitness annexed by trade usage. Sample (section 17). Three implied conditions in a sale by sample.

Example. Sheela tells a dealer in bicycles that she needs a bicycle for daily use on a rough village road, relying on the dealer's advice. He supplies one that breaks on the first day. The exception in section 16(1) applies: there is an implied condition of reasonable fitness for that purpose.

Express terms and exclusion (sections 16(4) and 62)

Rule. An express warranty or condition does not negative an implied one unless inconsistent with it (section 16(4)). Implied terms may also be negatived or varied by express agreement, course of dealing or usage binding both parties (section 62).

Is the buyer protected, or must he beware? How to read this: start at the top. Stop at the first step that fits. 1. Is it a question of the seller's title, possession or an undisclosed charge (section 14)? The Act implies terms. The buyer is protected. 2. Was the sale by description (section 15), or by sample (section 17)? The Act implies conditions. The buyer is protected. 3. Did the buyer make known the purpose and rely on the seller's skill, or buy by description from a dealer (section 16(1), (2)), or does trade usage supply a term (section 16(3))? The Act implies conditions, subject to the provisos. The buyer is protected. 4. None of the above? No implied warranty or condition of quality or fitness (section 16). The buyer must beware.
keyPoints: Caveat emptor: "let the buyer beware". The rule is in the opening words of section 16. No implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness, except as the Act provides. Exceptions: section 14 (title), 15 (description), 16(1) (fitness), 16(2) (merchantable quality), 16(3) (trade usage), 17 (sample). Fitness needs the purpose made known and reliance on the seller's skill or judgment. No fitness condition for patent or trade name articles. No quality condition for defects the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Implied terms can be negatived or varied (section 62).

selfTest.q: 1. What does caveat emptor mean?
selfTest.a: "Let the buyer beware". The Act states the rule in the opening words of section 16. 2. Name three exceptions to the rule. Any three of: title (section 14), description (section 15), fitness for a known purpose (section 16(1)), merchantable quality (section 16(2)), trade usage (section 16(3)), sample (section 17). 3. When is there no implied condition of fitness under section 16(1)? When a specified article is sold under its patent or other trade name. 4. What does the proviso to section 16(2) say? If the buyer has examined the goods, there is no implied condition as regards defects which the examination ought to have revealed.

te.meaning:
Caveat emptor అనేది లాటిన్ పదబంధం. దాని అర్థం "కొనేవాడు జాగ్రత్తగా ఉండాలి ". సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 ఈ పదబంధాన్ని వాడదు. ఈ నియమం సెక్షన్ 16 మొదటి మాటల్లో ఉంది: అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం కింద సరఫరా చేసిన సరుకుల నాణ్యత లేదా ఏదైనా ప్రత్యేక ప్రయోజనానికి తగినతనం గురించి అంతర్లీన warranty లేదా condition ఏదీ లేదు, చట్టం చెప్పినవి తప్ప.

మినహాయింపులు చట్టం అంతర్లీనంగా చేర్చే నిబంధనలే: అమ్మే హక్కు సహా సెక్షన్ 14 లోని నిబంధనలు, వర్ణనకు సరిపోవడం (సెక్షన్ 15), తెలిసిన ప్రయోజనానికి తగినతనం, వ్యాపార యోగ్యమైన నాణ్యత (సెక్షన్ 16(1), (2)), వ్యాపార వాడుక ద్వారా జోడించిన నిబంధనలు (సెక్షన్ 16(3)), నమూనా ప్రకారం అమ్మకం నిబంధనలు (సెక్షన్ 17). సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: నియమం, తర్వాత ప్రతి మినహాయింపును దాని సెక్షన్‌తో.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. అమ్మకం ఒప్పందం కింద సరఫరా చేసిన సరుకుల నాణ్యత లేదా ఏదైనా ప్రత్యేక ప్రయోజనానికి తగినతనం గురించి చట్టం ఏ warranty లేదా condition నూ అంతర్లీనంగా చేర్చదు, చట్టం చెప్పినవి తప్ప. కాబట్టి కొనేవాడు నాణ్యత, తగినతనం గురించి తానే నిర్ధారించుకోవాలి, లేదా స్పష్టమైన నిబంధన పొందాలి.

ఉదాహరణ. పంపులు అమ్మే వ్యాపారంలో లేని పొరుగువాడి నుండి రోహిత్ సెకండ్‌హ్యాండ్ పంపు కొన్నాడు. రోహిత్ ఏ ప్రత్యేక ప్రయోజనాన్నీ చెప్పలేదు. పంపు బలహీనంగా ఉంటే, సెక్షన్ 16 తగినతనం లేదా నాణ్యత గురించి అంతర్లీన condition ఇవ్వదు, ఈ వాస్తవాల ప్రకారం కింది మినహాయింపుల్లో ఏదీ వర్తించదు.

నియమం. చట్టం ఈ మినహాయింపులు ఇస్తుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. గ్రామీణ గతుకుల రోడ్డుపై రోజూ వాడటానికి సైకిల్ కావాలని షీలా సైకిళ్ల డీలర్‌కు చెప్పి, అతని సలహాపై ఆధారపడింది. అతను ఇచ్చిన సైకిల్ మొదటి రోజే విరిగిపోయింది. సెక్షన్ 16(1) మినహాయింపు వర్తిస్తుంది: ఆ ప్రయోజనానికి సహేతుకంగా తగి ఉండాలనే అంతర్లీన condition ఉంది.

selfTest.q: 1. Caveat emptor అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: "కొనేవాడు జాగ్రత్తగా ఉండాలి". చట్టం ఈ నియమాన్ని సెక్షన్ 16 మొదటి మాటల్లో చెబుతుంది. 2. నియమానికి మూడు మినహాయింపుల పేర్లు చెప్పండి. వీటిలో ఏ మూడైనా: హక్కు (సెక్షన్ 14), వర్ణన (సెక్షన్ 15), తెలిసిన ప్రయోజనానికి తగినతనం (సెక్షన్ 16(1)), వ్యాపార యోగ్యమైన నాణ్యత (సెక్షన్ 16(2)), వ్యాపార వాడుక (సెక్షన్ 16(3)), నమూనా (సెక్షన్ 17). 3. సెక్షన్ 16(1) కింద తగినతనం condition ఎప్పుడు ఉండదు? పేటెంట్ లేదా ఇతర వ్యాపార పేరుతో నిర్దేశించిన వస్తువును అమ్మినప్పుడు. 4. సెక్షన్ 16(2) షరతు ఏమి చెబుతుంది? కొనేవాడు సరుకులను పరిశీలించి ఉంటే, ఆ పరిశీలనలో బయటపడాల్సిన లోపాల విషయంలో అంతర్లీన condition ఉండదు.

hi.inOneMinute: Caveat emptor is a Latin phrase meaning "let the buyer beware ". The Sale of Goods Act, 1930 does not use the phrase. Its rule is in the opening words of section 16: there is no implied warranty or condition as to the quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale, except as the Act provides. The exceptions are the implied terms of the Act: the seller's right to sell and the other terms in section 14, correspondence with description (section 15), fitness for a known purpose and merchantable quality (section 16(1) and (2)), terms annexed by trade usage (section 16(3)), and the terms of a sale by sample (section 17). Key points for the answer: the rule, then each exception with its section.
hi.meaning: The rule (opening words of section 16) Rule. The Act implies no warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose of goods supplied under a contract of sale, except as the Act provides. The buyer must therefore satisfy himself about quality and fitness, or get an express term. Example. Rohit buys a second-hand pump from a neighbour, who is not in the business of selling pumps. Rohit did not state any particular purpose. If the pump is weak, section 16 gives no implied condition of fitness or quality, and none of the exceptions below applies on these facts. Exceptions: terms the Act implies Rule. The Act gives these exceptions. Title (section 14). Implied condition of right to sell. Implied warranties of quiet possession and freedom from undisclosed encumbrance. Description (section 15). Implied condition that goods correspond with the description. Fitness for a known purpose (section 16(1)). Where the buyer makes known the purpose, relies on the seller's skill or judgment, and the goods are of a description the seller supplies in his business. Not for a specified article sold under its patent or other trade name. Merchantable quality (section 16(2)). Where goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods. Not for defects which the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Usage of trade (section 16(3)). A term as to quality or fitness annexed by trade usage. Sample (section 17). Three implied conditions in a sale by sample. Example. Sheela tells a dealer in bicycles that she needs a bicycle for daily use on a rough village road, relying on the dealer's advice. He supplies one that breaks on the first day. The exception in section 16(1) applies: there is an implied condition of reasonable fitness for that purpose. Express terms and exclusion (sections 16(4) and 62) Rule. An express warranty or condition does not negative an implied one unless inconsistent with it (section 16(4)). Implied terms may also be negatived or varied by express agreement, course of dealing or usage binding both parties (section 62). Is the buyer protected, or must he beware? How to read this: start at the top. Stop at the first step that fits. 1. Is it a question of the seller's title, possession or an undisclosed charge (section 14)? The Act implies terms. The buyer is protected. 2. Was the sale by description (section 15), or by sample (section 17)? The Act implies conditions. The buyer is protected. 3. Did the buyer make known the purpose and rely on the seller's skill, or buy by description from a dealer (section 16(1), (2)), or does trade usage supply a term (section 16(3))? The Act implies conditions, subject to the provisos. The buyer is protected. 4. None of the above? No implied warranty or condition of quality or fitness (section 16). The buyer must beware.
keyPoints: Caveat emptor: "let the buyer beware". The rule is in the opening words of section 16. No implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness, except as the Act provides. Exceptions: section 14 (title), 15 (description), 16(1) (fitness), 16(2) (merchantable quality), 16(3) (trade usage), 17 (sample). Fitness needs the purpose made known and reliance on the seller's skill or judgment. No fitness condition for patent or trade name articles. No quality condition for defects the buyer's examination ought to have revealed. Implied terms can be negatived or varied (section 62).

selfTest.q: 1. What does caveat emptor mean?
selfTest.a: "Let the buyer beware". The Act states the rule in the opening words of section 16. 2. Name three exceptions to the rule. Any three of: title (section 14), description (section 15), fitness for a known purpose (section 16(1)), merchantable quality (section 16(2)), trade usage (section 16(3)), sample (section 17). 3. When is there no implied condition of fitness under section 16(1)? When a specified article is sold under its patent or other trade name. 4. What does the proviso to section 16(2) say? If the buyer has examined the goods, there is no implied condition as regards defects which the examination ought to have revealed.

Under section 12(2) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, a condition is a stipulation:

Explanation. Section 12(2) defines a condition as a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated.

Under section 12(3), the breach of a warranty gives rise to:

Explanation. Section 12(3) says a breach of warranty gives rise to a claim for damages but not to a right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated.

Under section 12(4), whether a stipulation is a condition or a warranty depends:

Explanation. Section 12(4) says it depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition though called a warranty.

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t2.subtitle: Sections 27 to 30 and 54(3) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: Nemo dat quod non habet is a Latin maxim meaning "no one gives what he does not have". Under section 27 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where goods are sold by a person who is not the owner and who does not sell with the owner's authority or consent, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had. The Act itself lists exceptions where a non-owner can pass a good title: the owner is precluded by his conduct, or a mercantile agent sells in the ordinary course (section 27); a joint owner in sole possession sells (section 28); a seller who obtained possession under a voidable contract, not yet rescinded, sells (section 29); a seller or buyer in possession after sale disposes of the goods (section 30); and an unpaid seller resells (section 54(3)).
en.meaning:
The rule (section 27)

Rule. If a person who is not the owner, and who does not sell under the owner's authority or with his consent, sells goods, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had. The exception in the same section is where the owner is by his conduct precluded from denying the seller's authority to sell.

Example. Tarun finds a camera lying in a park and sells it to Usha, who knows nothing of this. Tarun has no title, and the owner did not authorise the sale. Usha gets no better title than Tarun had, and the owner can claim the camera.

Exceptions in the Act

Rule. A buyer gets a good title in these cases.

Owner precluded by conduct (section 27). The owner by his conduct cannot deny the seller's authority to sell. Mercantile agent (proviso to section 27). A mercantile agent in possession of the goods or a document of title with the owner's consent sells in the ordinary course of business of a mercantile agent. The buyer acts in good faith and has no notice that the agent lacks authority. Joint owner (section 28). One of several joint owners has sole possession by permission of the co-owners, and sells to a buyer in good faith without notice. Voidable contract (section 29). The seller obtained possession under a contract voidable under section 19 or 19A of the Contract Act, which had not been rescinded when he sold. The buyer buys in good faith and without notice of the defect of title. Seller in possession after sale (section 30(1)). Having sold, he continues in possession of the goods or documents of title, and delivers or transfers them under a sale, pledge or other disposition to a person in good faith without notice of the previous sale. Buyer in possession after sale (section 30(2)). Having bought or agreed to buy, he obtains possession with the seller's consent and transfers under a sale, pledge or other disposition to a person in good faith without notice of any lien or other right of the original seller. Resale by an unpaid seller (section 54(3)). An unpaid seller who has exercised lien or stoppage in transit re-sells. The buyer gets a good title against the original buyer.

Example. Vimal gives his goods to a commission agent, who customarily sells goods for others, to sell. The agent sells in the ordinary course of business to Wasim, who acts in good faith and does not know of any limit on the agent's authority. Wasim gets a good title (proviso to section 27).

Does the buyer get a good title? How to read this: start at the top. Good faith and lack of notice are stated in sections 27 (proviso), 28, 29 and 30. Section 54(3) and the owner's-conduct exception do not state them. 1. Did the seller sell with the owner's authority or consent? If yes, the title passes in the ordinary way. 2. Is the owner precluded by his conduct from denying the seller's authority (section 27)? If yes, the buyer gets a good title. 3. Is the seller a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent (section 27 proviso), a joint owner in sole possession (section 28), a person with a voidable title not yet rescinded (section 29), or a seller or buyer in possession after sale (section 30)? If yes, and the buyer acted in good faith and without notice, he gets a good title. 4. Otherwise The buyer acquires no better title than the seller had (section 27).
keyPoints: Nemo dat: a buyer from a non-owner gets no better title than the seller had (section 27). Exceptions: owner's conduct, mercantile agent (section 27), joint owner (section 28), voidable title (section 29), seller or buyer in possession (section 30), unpaid seller's resale (section 54(3)). Good faith and no notice are stated for sections 27 (proviso), 28, 29 and 30. Section 54(3) does not state them. Mercantile agent: section 2(9). Section 27 is subject to the Act and to any other law.

selfTest.q: 1. What does section 27 say about a buyer from a non-owner?
selfTest.a: He acquires no better title than the seller had, unless the owner is by his conduct precluded from denying the seller's authority to sell. 2. Name the three kinds of seller or possessor in sections 28, 29 and 30. A joint owner in sole possession, a person who got possession under a voidable contract not yet rescinded, and a seller or buyer in possession after sale. 3. What does section 29 require of the buyer? That he buys in good faith and without notice of the seller's defect of title. 4. What is a mercantile agent? An agent having in the customary course of business authority to sell goods, consign them for sale, buy goods, or raise money on their security (section 2(9)).

te.inOneMinute: సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 లోని సెక్షన్లు 27 నుండి 30, 54(3) — యజమాని కానివారి అమ్మకం
te.meaning:
Nemo dat quod non habet అనేది "తన దగ్గర లేనిది ఎవరూ ఇవ్వలేరు" అనే అర్థం గల లాటిన్ సూత్రం. సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 సెక్షన్ 27 ప్రకారం, యజమాని కాని వ్యక్తి, యజమాని అధికారంతో లేదా అంగీకారంతో కాకుండా సరుకులు అమ్మితే, అమ్మేవాడికి ఉన్న హక్కు కంటే మెరుగైన హక్కు కొనేవాడికి రాదు.

యజమాని కాని వ్యక్తి మంచి హక్కును బదిలీ చేయగల మినహాయింపులను చట్టమే ఇస్తుంది: యజమాని ప్రవర్తన వల్ల అతను అడ్డుకోలేకపోవడం, లేదా మర్కంటైల్ ఏజెంట్ సాధారణ వ్యాపార పద్ధతిలో అమ్మడం (సెక్షన్ 27); ఉమ్మడి యజమాని ఒక్కడే స్వాధీనంలో ఉండి అమ్మడం (సెక్షన్ 28); రద్దు చేయదగిన హక్కు ఉన్న అమ్మేవాడు రద్దుకు ముందు అమ్మడం (సెక్షన్ 29); అమ్మిన తర్వాత కూడా అమ్మేవాడు, లేదా కొన్న కొనేవాడు స్వాధీనంలో ఉండి సరుకులను పారవేయడం (సెక్షన్ 30); చెల్లింపు అందని అమ్మేవాడు తిరిగి అమ్మడం (సెక్షన్ 54(3)).

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. యజమాని కాని వ్యక్తి, యజమాని అధికారంతో లేదా అంగీకారంతో కాకుండా సరుకులు అమ్మితే, అమ్మేవాడికి ఉన్న హక్కు కంటే మెరుగైన హక్కు కొనేవాడికి రాదు. అదే సెక్షన్‌లోని మినహాయింపు: యజమాని తన ప్రవర్తన వల్ల అమ్మేవాడి అమ్మే అధికారాన్ని కాదనలేనప్పుడు.

ఉదాహరణ. తరుణ్‌కు పార్కులో ఒక కెమెరా దొరికింది, అతను దాన్ని దీని గురించి తెలియని ఉషకు అమ్మాడు. తరుణ్‌కు హక్కు లేదు, యజమాని అమ్మకానికి అధికారం ఇవ్వలేదు. తరుణ్‌కు ఉన్న హక్కు కంటే మెరుగైన హక్కు ఉషకు రాదు, యజమాని కెమెరాను తిరిగి కోరవచ్చు.

నియమం. కింది సందర్భాల్లో కొనేవాడికి మంచి హక్కు వస్తుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. ఇతరుల కోసం సరుకులు అమ్మడం వ్యాపారంగా చేసే ఒక కమిషన్ ఏజెంట్‌కు అమ్మడానికి విమల్ తన సరుకులను ఇచ్చాడు. ఆ ఏజెంట్ సాధారణ వ్యాపార పద్ధతిలో, ఏజెంట్ అధికారంపై పరిమితి గురించి తెలియని, మంచి విశ్వాసంతో కొన్న వసీమ్‌కు అమ్మాడు. వసీమ్‌కు మంచి హక్కు వస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 27 షరతు).

selfTest.q: 1. యజమాని కాని వ్యక్తి నుండి కొన్నవాడి గురించి సెక్షన్ 27 ఏమి చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: అమ్మేవాడి అమ్మే అధికారాన్ని యజమాని తన ప్రవర్తన వల్ల కాదనలేకపోతే తప్ప, అమ్మేవాడికి ఉన్న హక్కు కంటే మెరుగైన హక్కు అతనికి రాదు. 2. సెక్షన్లు 28, 29, 30 లోని మూడు రకాల అమ్మేవారి లేదా స్వాధీనదారుల పేర్లు చెప్పండి. ఒక్కడే స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న ఉమ్మడి యజమాని, ఇంకా రద్దు కాని రద్దు చేయదగిన ఒప్పందం ద్వారా స్వాధీనం పొందిన వ్యక్తి, అమ్మిన తర్వాత స్వాధీనంలో ఉన్న అమ్మేవాడు లేదా కొనేవాడు. 3. సెక్షన్ 29 కొనేవాడి నుండి ఏమి కోరుతుంది? అతను మంచి విశ్వాసంతో, అమ్మేవాడి హక్కు లోపం గురించి నోటీసు లేకుండా కొనాలి. 4. మర్కంటైల్ ఏజెంట్ అంటే ఏమిటి? వ్యాపార సంప్రదాయ పద్ధతిలో సరుకులను అమ్మడానికి, అమ్మకం కోసం పంపడానికి, కొనడానికి లేదా సరుకుల భద్రతపై డబ్బు సమీకరించడానికి అధికారం ఉన్న ఏజెంట్ (సెక్షన్ 2(9)).

hi.inOneMinute: Nemo dat quod non habet is a Latin maxim meaning "no one gives what he does not have". Under section 27 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, where goods are sold by a person who is not the owner and who does not sell with the owner's authority or consent, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had. The Act itself lists exceptions where a non-owner can pass a good title: the owner is precluded by his conduct, or a mercantile agent sells in the ordinary course (section 27); a joint owner in sole possession sells (section 28); a seller who obtained possession under a voidable contract, not yet rescinded, sells (section 29); a seller or buyer in possession after sale disposes of the goods (section 30); and an unpaid seller resells (section 54(3)).
hi.meaning: The rule (section 27) Rule. If a person who is not the owner, and who does not sell under the owner's authority or with his consent, sells goods, the buyer acquires no better title than the seller had. The exception in the same section is where the owner is by his conduct precluded from denying the seller's authority to sell. Example. Tarun finds a camera lying in a park and sells it to Usha, who knows nothing of this. Tarun has no title, and the owner did not authorise the sale. Usha gets no better title than Tarun had, and the owner can claim the camera. Exceptions in the Act Rule. A buyer gets a good title in these cases. Owner precluded by conduct (section 27). The owner by his conduct cannot deny the seller's authority to sell. Mercantile agent (proviso to section 27). A mercantile agent in possession of the goods or a document of title with the owner's consent sells in the ordinary course of business of a mercantile agent. The buyer acts in good faith and has no notice that the agent lacks authority. Joint owner (section 28). One of several joint owners has sole possession by permission of the co-owners, and sells to a buyer in good faith without notice. Voidable contract (section 29). The seller obtained possession under a contract voidable under section 19 or 19A of the Contract Act, which had not been rescinded when he sold. The buyer buys in good faith and without notice of the defect of title. Seller in possession after sale (section 30(1)). Having sold, he continues in possession of the goods or documents of title, and delivers or transfers them under a sale, pledge or other disposition to a person in good faith without notice of the previous sale. Buyer in possession after sale (section 30(2)). Having bought or agreed to buy, he obtains possession with the seller's consent and transfers under a sale, pledge or other disposition to a person in good faith without notice of any lien or other right of the original seller. Resale by an unpaid seller (section 54(3)). An unpaid seller who has exercised lien or stoppage in transit re-sells. The buyer gets a good title against the original buyer. Example. Vimal gives his goods to a commission agent, who customarily sells goods for others, to sell. The agent sells in the ordinary course of business to Wasim, who acts in good faith and does not know of any limit on the agent's authority. Wasim gets a good title (proviso to section 27). Does the buyer get a good title? How to read this: start at the top. Good faith and lack of notice are stated in sections 27 (proviso), 28, 29 and 30. Section 54(3) and the owner's-conduct exception do not state them. 1. Did the seller sell with the owner's authority or consent? If yes, the title passes in the ordinary way. 2. Is the owner precluded by his conduct from denying the seller's authority (section 27)? If yes, the buyer gets a good title. 3. Is the seller a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent (section 27 proviso), a joint owner in sole possession (section 28), a person with a voidable title not yet rescinded (section 29), or a seller or buyer in possession after sale (section 30)? If yes, and the buyer acted in good faith and without notice, he gets a good title. 4. Otherwise The buyer acquires no better title than the seller had (section 27).
keyPoints: Nemo dat: a buyer from a non-owner gets no better title than the seller had (section 27). Exceptions: owner's conduct, mercantile agent (section 27), joint owner (section 28), voidable title (section 29), seller or buyer in possession (section 30), unpaid seller's resale (section 54(3)). Good faith and no notice are stated for sections 27 (proviso), 28, 29 and 30. Section 54(3) does not state them. Mercantile agent: section 2(9). Section 27 is subject to the Act and to any other law.

selfTest.q: 1. What does section 27 say about a buyer from a non-owner?
selfTest.a: He acquires no better title than the seller had, unless the owner is by his conduct precluded from denying the seller's authority to sell. 2. Name the three kinds of seller or possessor in sections 28, 29 and 30. A joint owner in sole possession, a person who got possession under a voidable contract not yet rescinded, and a seller or buyer in possession after sale. 3. What does section 29 require of the buyer? That he buys in good faith and without notice of the seller's defect of title. 4. What is a mercantile agent? An agent having in the customary course of business authority to sell goods, consign them for sale, buy goods, or raise money on their security (section 2(9)).

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t3.subtitle: Sections 2(2) and 33 to 40 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another (section 2(2)). Under section 33, delivery of goods sold may be made by doing anything which the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of any person authorised to hold them on his behalf. Sections 34 to 40 give the detailed rules: part delivery, the buyer's application, place and time, delivery of the wrong quantity, instalments, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger, and risk where goods go to a distant place. Key points for the answer: the meaning of delivery, then each rule with its section.
en.meaning:
What delivery is (sections 2(2) and 33)

Rule. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. It may be made by doing anything the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of a person authorised to hold them for him. The Act does not use the words "actual", "constructive" or "symbolic" delivery.

Example. A seller hands the goods over the counter to the buyer. The goods are in the buyer's possession, so delivery is made. If the parties agree that handing over the keys of the godown shall count as delivery, that too is delivery under section 33.

Part delivery (section 34)

Rule. Delivery of part, in progress of the delivery of the whole, has the same effect for passing the property as delivery of the whole. Delivery of part with an intention of severing it from the whole does not operate as delivery of the remainder.

When the seller must deliver (sections 35 and 36)

Rule. Unless the contract says otherwise, the seller need not deliver until the buyer applies for delivery (section 35). Section 36 then gives these defaults.

Whether the buyer takes possession or the seller sends the goods depends on the contract. Apart from it, the place of delivery is where the goods are at the time of the sale or agreement, or, if not then in existence, where they are manufactured or produced (section 36(1)). If the seller must send the goods but no time is fixed, he must send them within a reasonable time (section 36(2)). If a third person holds the goods, there is no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. This does not affect the issue or transfer of a document of title (section 36(3)). Demand or tender of delivery may be treated as ineffectual unless made at a reasonable hour, a question of fact (section 36(4)). Unless otherwise agreed, the seller bears the expenses of putting the goods into a deliverable state (section 36(5)).

Wrong quantity and instalments (sections 37 and 38)

Rule. If less than the contract quantity is delivered, the buyer may reject, or accept and pay at the contract rate. If more is delivered, he may accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, reject the whole, or accept the whole and pay at the contract rate. If contract goods are mixed with goods of a different description, he may accept the contract goods and reject the rest, or reject the whole (section 37). The buyer is not bound to accept delivery by instalments unless otherwise agreed. For separately paid instalments, whether a default is a repudiation of the whole or a severable breach depends on the terms of the contract and the circumstances (section 38).

Example. Kiran contracts to buy 100 kg of sugar. The seller delivers 120 kg. Kiran may take 100 kg and reject 20 kg, or reject all 120 kg, or accept all and pay at the contract rate (section 37(2)).

Delivery to a carrier, and distant places (sections 39 and 40)

Rule. Where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger is prima facie delivery to the buyer. Unless authorised otherwise, the seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier or wharfinger on the buyer's behalf. If he omits to do so and the goods are lost or damaged in transit or custody, the buyer may decline to treat it as delivery to himself or hold the seller responsible in damages. For sea transit where it is usual to insure, the seller must give the buyer notice enabling him to insure, failing which the goods are at the seller's risk during sea transit (section 39). If the seller agrees to deliver at his own risk at a distant place, the buyer takes, unless otherwise agreed, any risk of deterioration necessarily incident to transit (section 40).

Has delivery been made? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the parties agree something shall count as delivery, or are the goods in the buyer's possession or that of a person authorised to hold them for him (section 33)? Delivery is made. 2. Are the goods held by a third person (section 36(3))? No delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. 3. Were the goods sent to a carrier or wharfinger as the contract required (section 39)? Prima facie delivery to the buyer. 4. Does the quantity or description match the contract (section 37)? If not, the buyer may accept or reject as section 37 allows.
keyPoints: Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). It may be made by what the parties agree, or by putting the goods in the buyer's possession (section 33). The seller need not deliver until the buyer applies (section 35). Third person holds the goods: no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer (section 36(3)). Wrong quantity: the buyer's options are in section 37. Instalments: section 38. Delivery to a carrier is prima facie delivery to the buyer (section 39).

selfTest.q: 1. What is delivery under section 2(2)?
selfTest.a: Voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another. 2. If the seller delivers more than the contract quantity, what may the buyer do? Accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, or reject the whole, or accept the whole and pay at the contract rate (section 37(2)). 3. Is the buyer bound to accept delivery by instalments? Not unless otherwise agreed (section 38(1)). 4. What is the effect of delivery to a carrier? Where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods, it is prima facie deemed delivery to the buyer (section 39(1)).

te.inOneMinute: సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 లోని సెక్షన్లు 2(2), 33 నుండి 40 — సరుకుల అప్పగింత
te.meaning:
"Delivery" అంటే స్వాధీనాన్ని ఒకరి నుండి మరొకరికి స్వచ్ఛందంగా బదిలీ చేయడం (సెక్షన్ 2(2)). సెక్షన్ 33 ప్రకారం, అమ్మిన సరుకుల అప్పగింతను, పక్షాలు అప్పగింతగా పరిగణించాలని అంగీకరించిన ఏదైనా పని చేయడం ద్వారా, లేదా సరుకులను కొనేవాడి స్వాధీనంలో లేదా అతని తరఫున వాటిని ఉంచడానికి అధికారం పొందిన వ్యక్తి స్వాధీనంలో ఉంచే ప్రభావం ఉన్న ఏదైనా పని చేయడం ద్వారా చేయవచ్చు.

సెక్షన్లు 34 నుండి 40 వివరమైన నియమాలు ఇస్తాయి: పాక్షిక అప్పగింత, కొనేవాడి అభ్యర్థన, స్థలం, సమయం, తప్పు పరిమాణం, వాయిదాలు, క్యారియర్ లేదా వార్ఫింగర్‌కు అప్పగింత, దూర ప్రాంతానికి సరుకులు వెళ్లేటప్పుడు రిస్క్. సమాధానంలో ముఖ్యమైనవి: అప్పగింత అర్థం, తర్వాత ప్రతి నియమం దాని సెక్షన్‌తో.

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. అప్పగింత అంటే స్వాధీనాన్ని స్వచ్ఛందంగా బదిలీ చేయడం. పక్షాలు అప్పగింతగా పరిగణించాలని అంగీకరించిన ఏదైనా పని ద్వారా, లేదా సరుకులను కొనేవాడి స్వాధీనంలో లేదా అతని తరఫున వాటిని ఉంచడానికి అధికారం పొందిన వ్యక్తి స్వాధీనంలో ఉంచే ఏదైనా పని ద్వారా దీన్ని చేయవచ్చు. చట్టం "actual", "constructive", "symbolic" అప్పగింత పదాలను వాడదు.

ఉదాహరణ. అమ్మేవాడు కౌంటర్ మీదుగా సరుకులను కొనేవాడికి ఇస్తాడు. సరుకులు కొనేవాడి స్వాధీనంలోకి వచ్చాయి, కాబట్టి అప్పగింత పూర్తయింది. గోడౌన్ తాళాలు ఇవ్వడాన్ని అప్పగింతగా లెక్కించాలని పక్షాలు అంగీకరిస్తే, అది కూడా సెక్షన్ 33 కింద అప్పగింతే.

నియమం. మొత్తం అప్పగింత ప్రక్రియలో భాగంగా కొంత భాగాన్ని అప్పగిస్తే, ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ విషయంలో అది మొత్తం అప్పగింతతో సమాన ప్రభావం కలిగి ఉంటుంది. మిగిలిన దాన్ని వేరు చేసే ఉద్దేశంతో కొంత భాగాన్ని అప్పగిస్తే, అది మిగిలిన దాని అప్పగింతగా పని చేయదు.

నియమం. ఒప్పందం వేరే చెప్పకపోతే, కొనేవాడు అప్పగింత కోసం అభ్యర్థించే వరకు అమ్మేవాడు అప్పగించాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు (సెక్షన్ 35). సెక్షన్ 36 ఈ ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నియమాలు ఇస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 2(2) ప్రకారం అప్పగింత అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: స్వాధీనాన్ని ఒకరి నుండి మరొకరికి స్వచ్ఛందంగా బదిలీ చేయడం. 2. ఒప్పంద పరిమాణం కంటే ఎక్కువ అమ్మేవాడు అప్పగిస్తే కొనేవాడు ఏమి చేయవచ్చు? ఒప్పందం పరిమాణాన్ని అంగీకరించి మిగిలినవి తిరస్కరించవచ్చు, మొత్తం తిరస్కరించవచ్చు, లేదా మొత్తం అంగీకరించి ఒప్పంద రేటు చెల్లించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 37(2)). 3. వాయిదాల్లో అప్పగింతను అంగీకరించడానికి కొనేవాడు బద్ధుడా? వేరుగా అంగీకరించకపోతే కాదు (సెక్షన్ 38(1)). 4. క్యారియర్‌కు అప్పగింత ప్రభావం ఏమిటి? అమ్మేవాడు సరుకులను పంపడానికి అధికారం పొందినా లేదా పంపాల్సి ఉన్నా, అది ప్రథమ దృష్టిలో కొనేవాడికి అప్పగించినట్లు భావిస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 39(1)).

hi.inOneMinute: "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another (section 2(2)). Under section 33, delivery of goods sold may be made by doing anything which the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of any person authorised to hold them on his behalf. Sections 34 to 40 give the detailed rules: part delivery, the buyer's application, place and time, delivery of the wrong quantity, instalments, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger, and risk where goods go to a distant place. Key points for the answer: the meaning of delivery, then each rule with its section.
hi.meaning: What delivery is (sections 2(2) and 33) Rule. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. It may be made by doing anything the parties agree shall be treated as delivery, or anything which has the effect of putting the goods in the possession of the buyer or of a person authorised to hold them for him. The Act does not use the words "actual", "constructive" or "symbolic" delivery. Example. A seller hands the goods over the counter to the buyer. The goods are in the buyer's possession, so delivery is made. If the parties agree that handing over the keys of the godown shall count as delivery, that too is delivery under section 33. Part delivery (section 34) Rule. Delivery of part, in progress of the delivery of the whole, has the same effect for passing the property as delivery of the whole. Delivery of part with an intention of severing it from the whole does not operate as delivery of the remainder. When the seller must deliver (sections 35 and 36) Rule. Unless the contract says otherwise, the seller need not deliver until the buyer applies for delivery (section 35). Section 36 then gives these defaults. Whether the buyer takes possession or the seller sends the goods depends on the contract. Apart from it, the place of delivery is where the goods are at the time of the sale or agreement, or, if not then in existence, where they are manufactured or produced (section 36(1)). If the seller must send the goods but no time is fixed, he must send them within a reasonable time (section 36(2)). If a third person holds the goods, there is no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. This does not affect the issue or transfer of a document of title (section 36(3)). Demand or tender of delivery may be treated as ineffectual unless made at a reasonable hour, a question of fact (section 36(4)). Unless otherwise agreed, the seller bears the expenses of putting the goods into a deliverable state (section 36(5)). Wrong quantity and instalments (sections 37 and 38) Rule. If less than the contract quantity is delivered, the buyer may reject, or accept and pay at the contract rate. If more is delivered, he may accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, reject the whole, or accept the whole and pay at the contract rate. If contract goods are mixed with goods of a different description, he may accept the contract goods and reject the rest, or reject the whole (section 37). The buyer is not bound to accept delivery by instalments unless otherwise agreed. For separately paid instalments, whether a default is a repudiation of the whole or a severable breach depends on the terms of the contract and the circumstances (section 38). Example. Kiran contracts to buy 100 kg of sugar. The seller delivers 120 kg. Kiran may take 100 kg and reject 20 kg, or reject all 120 kg, or accept all and pay at the contract rate (section 37(2)). Delivery to a carrier, and distant places (sections 39 and 40) Rule. Where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods, delivery to a carrier or wharfinger is prima facie delivery to the buyer. Unless authorised otherwise, the seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier or wharfinger on the buyer's behalf. If he omits to do so and the goods are lost or damaged in transit or custody, the buyer may decline to treat it as delivery to himself or hold the seller responsible in damages. For sea transit where it is usual to insure, the seller must give the buyer notice enabling him to insure, failing which the goods are at the seller's risk during sea transit (section 39). If the seller agrees to deliver at his own risk at a distant place, the buyer takes, unless otherwise agreed, any risk of deterioration necessarily incident to transit (section 40). Has delivery been made? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Did the parties agree something shall count as delivery, or are the goods in the buyer's possession or that of a person authorised to hold them for him (section 33)? Delivery is made. 2. Are the goods held by a third person (section 36(3))? No delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer that he holds them on the buyer's behalf. 3. Were the goods sent to a carrier or wharfinger as the contract required (section 39)? Prima facie delivery to the buyer. 4. Does the quantity or description match the contract (section 37)? If not, the buyer may accept or reject as section 37 allows.
keyPoints: Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). It may be made by what the parties agree, or by putting the goods in the buyer's possession (section 33). The seller need not deliver until the buyer applies (section 35). Third person holds the goods: no delivery until he acknowledges to the buyer (section 36(3)). Wrong quantity: the buyer's options are in section 37. Instalments: section 38. Delivery to a carrier is prima facie delivery to the buyer (section 39).

selfTest.q: 1. What is delivery under section 2(2)?
selfTest.a: Voluntary transfer of possession from one person to another. 2. If the seller delivers more than the contract quantity, what may the buyer do? Accept the contract quantity and reject the rest, or reject the whole, or accept the whole and pay at the contract rate (section 37(2)). 3. Is the buyer bound to accept delivery by instalments? Not unless otherwise agreed (section 38(1)). 4. What is the effect of delivery to a carrier? Where the seller is authorised or required to send the goods, it is prima facie deemed delivery to the buyer (section 39(1)).

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t1.subtitle: Sections 2(2), 2(11) and 18 to 26 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: "Property" in goods means the general property in them, not merely a special property (section 2(11)). "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). A seller who gives possession does not necessarily pass the property, and the Act has separate rules for when the property passes to the buyer. No property passes in unascertained goods until they are ascertained (section 18). Otherwise the property passes when the parties intend it to pass, judged from the contract, conduct and circumstances (section 19). Sections 20 to 24 give the rules for specific goods, unascertained goods and goods on approval. Section 25 allows the seller to reserve the right of disposal. Risk prima facie passes with the property (section 26).
en.meaning:
Property and possession (sections 2(2) and 2(11))

Rule. Property is the general property in the goods. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. The Act treats them as different things: section 25(1) says that even after delivery to a buyer or carrier, the property does not pass until conditions imposed by the seller are fulfilled. Section 26 says the goods are at the buyer's risk once the property passes, whether delivery has been made or not.

Example. Kavya hands a laptop to Lalit to try for a week. Lalit has possession. Whether the property has passed depends on the rules in section 24 and on the intention of the parties.

Unascertained goods (sections 18 and 23)

Rule. No property passes in unascertained goods unless and until they are ascertained (section 18). Under section 23(1), in a contract for unascertained or future goods by description, the property passes when goods of that description and in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract, by the seller with the buyer's assent or by the buyer with the seller's assent. Under section 23(2), delivery to the buyer or to a carrier or other bailee for transmission, without reserving the right of disposal, is deemed unconditional appropriation.

Example. Manoj agrees to sell Nita 100 kg of rice out of a godown full of rice. Until the 100 kg is set apart for Nita with her assent, no property passes (section 18). When Manoj puts 100 kg in sacks marked for Nita, and she agrees, the property passes (section 23(1)).

Intention of the parties (section 19)

Rule. For specific or ascertained goods, the property passes when the parties intend. Regard is had to the contract's terms, the parties' conduct and the circumstances. Unless a different intention appears, sections 20 to 24 are the rules for finding that intention.

Specific goods (sections 20, 21 and 22)

Rule. Three rules apply to specific goods.

Unconditional contract, goods in a deliverable state: the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed (section 20). Seller bound to put the goods in a deliverable state: the property does not pass until he does so and the buyer has notice (section 21). Goods in a deliverable state, but the seller must weigh, measure, test or do some other act to ascertain the price: the property does not pass until it is done and the buyer has notice (section 22).

Example. Om buys a particular secondhand bike, in running order, under an unconditional contract. He will pay and collect it next week. The property passes to Om when the contract is made (section 20).

Goods on approval or on sale or return (section 24)

Rule. The property passes (a) when the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or does any other act adopting the transaction, or (b) if he does not, but keeps the goods without giving notice of rejection, when the fixed time for return expires, or, if no time was fixed, when a reasonable time expires.

Example. A jeweller sends a necklace to Pooja on approval with no time fixed. Pooja keeps it, gives no notice of rejection, and a reasonable time passes. The property passes to her (section 24(b)).

Reservation of the right of disposal (section 25)

Rule. The seller may reserve the right of disposal until certain conditions are fulfilled. The property then does not pass until they are fulfilled, even if the goods are delivered to the buyer or a carrier. Where goods are shipped or delivered to a railway for carriage and the bill of lading or railway receipt makes them deliverable to the order of the seller or his agent, the seller is prima facie deemed to reserve the right (section 25(2)). If the seller sends the bill of exchange with the bill of lading or railway receipt and the buyer does not honour the bill, he must return the document, and if he wrongfully retains it the property does not pass to him (section 25(3)).

Risk (section 26)

Rule. Unless otherwise agreed, the goods are at the seller's risk until the property passes, and at the buyer's risk afterwards, whether or not delivery has been made. If delivery is delayed by the fault of either party, that party bears any loss which would not have occurred but for the fault. The section does not affect the duties of either as a bailee of the other's goods.

When does the property pass? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Are the goods unascertained? No property passes until they are ascertained (section 18). Then it passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). 2. Are they specific or ascertained goods? The property passes when the parties intend (section 19). The rules in sections 20 to 22 help find that intention. 3. Sent on approval or sale or return? The property passes under section 24. 4. Has the seller reserved the right of disposal? The property does not pass until the conditions are fulfilled (section 25). 5. Who bears the risk? The owner of the property, unless otherwise agreed (section 26).
keyPoints: Unascertained goods: no property until ascertained (section 18). Passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). Specific goods: property passes when the parties intend (section 19). Section 20: unconditional contract, deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made. Sections 21 and 22: property passes after the seller's act and notice to the buyer. Section 24: approval or sale or return, property passes on adoption or on expiry of time. Section 25: the seller may reserve the right of disposal. Section 26: risk prima facie passes with the property.

selfTest.q: 1. When does property pass in unascertained goods?
selfTest.a: Not until they are ascertained (section 18). Then on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). 2. What is section 20? For an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed. 3. When does property pass in goods on approval? When the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or adopts the transaction, or when the fixed or a reasonable time expires without notice of rejection (section 24). 4. Who bears the risk unless otherwise agreed? The seller until the property passes, the buyer afterwards, whether delivery has been made or not (section 26).

te.inOneMinute: సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం, 1930 లోని సెక్షన్లు 2(2), 2(11), 18 నుండి 26 — ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ నియమాలు
te.meaning:
సరుకుల విషయంలో "property" అంటే వాటిపై సాధారణ ఆస్తి హక్కు, కేవలం ప్రత్యేక హక్కు కాదు (సెక్షన్ 2(11)). "Delivery" అంటే స్వాధీనాన్ని స్వచ్ఛందంగా బదిలీ చేయడం (సెక్షన్ 2(2)). స్వాధీనం ఇచ్చిన అమ్మేవాడు ఆస్తి హక్కును కూడా తప్పనిసరిగా బదిలీ చేసినట్లు కాదు. ఆస్తి హక్కు కొనేవాడికి ఎప్పుడు బదిలీ అవుతుందనే దానికి చట్టంలో ప్రత్యేక నియమాలు ఉన్నాయి.

గుర్తించని సరుకులు (unascertained goods) నిర్ధారణ అయ్యే వరకు వాటిపై ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ కాదు (సెక్షన్ 18). లేకపోతే, ఒప్పందం, ప్రవర్తన, పరిస్థితుల నుండి తేలే పక్షాల ఉద్దేశం ప్రకారం ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అవుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 19). నిర్దిష్ట సరుకులు, గుర్తించని సరుకులు, అంగీకారంపై పంపిన సరుకులకు సెక్షన్లు 20 నుండి 24 నియమాలు ఇస్తాయి. సెక్షన్ 25 అమ్మేవాడికి పారవేసే హక్కును రిజర్వ్ చేసుకునే అవకాశం ఇస్తుంది. రిస్క్ ప్రథమ దృష్టిలో ఆస్తి హక్కుతో పాటు మారుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 26).

ముందు ఈ పదాలు చదవండి. ఈ అంశంలో ప్రతి పదం పదే పదే వస్తుంది.

నియమం. ఆస్తి హక్కు అంటే సరుకులపై సాధారణ ఆస్తి హక్కు. అప్పగింత అంటే స్వాధీనాన్ని స్వచ్ఛందంగా బదిలీ చేయడం. చట్టం వాటిని వేర్వేరుగా చూస్తుంది: కొనేవాడికి లేదా క్యారియర్‌కు అప్పగించినా, అమ్మేవాడు విధించిన షరతులు నెరవేరే వరకు ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ కాదని సెక్షన్ 25(1) చెబుతుంది. ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అయ్యాక, అప్పగింత జరిగినా జరగకపోయినా సరుకులు కొనేవాడి రిస్క్ మీద ఉంటాయని సెక్షన్ 26 చెబుతుంది.

ఉదాహరణ. ఒక వారం ప్రయత్నించి చూడటానికి కావ్య ఒక ల్యాప్‌టాప్‌ను లలిత్‌కు ఇచ్చింది. లలిత్ దగ్గర స్వాధీనం ఉంది. ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అయిందా అనేది సెక్షన్ 24 నియమాలపై, పక్షాల ఉద్దేశంపై ఆధారపడుతుంది.

నియమం. గుర్తించని సరుకులు నిర్ధారణ అయ్యే వరకు వాటిపై ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ కాదు (సెక్షన్ 18). సెక్షన్ 23(1) ప్రకారం, గుర్తించని లేదా భవిష్యత్ సరుకులను వర్ణన ప్రకారం అమ్మే ఒప్పందంలో, ఆ వర్ణనగల, అప్పగించదగిన స్థితిలో ఉన్న సరుకులను అమ్మేవాడు కొనేవాడి అంగీకారంతో, లేదా కొనేవాడు అమ్మేవాడి అంగీకారంతో ఒప్పందానికి షరతు లేకుండా కేటాయించినప్పుడు ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అవుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 23(2) ప్రకారం, పారవేసే హక్కును రిజర్వ్ చేసుకోకుండా సరుకులను కొనేవాడికి లేదా అతనికి పంపడానికి క్యారియర్‌కు లేదా ఇతర బెయిలీకి అప్పగిస్తే, షరతు లేకుండా కేటాయించినట్లు భావిస్తారు.

ఉదాహరణ. బియ్యంతో నిండిన గోడౌన్ నుండి 100 కిలోల బియ్యాన్ని నీతకు అమ్మడానికి మనోజ్ అంగీకరించాడు. ఆ 100 కిలోలను ఆమె అంగీకారంతో ఆమె కోసం వేరు చేసే వరకు ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ కాదు (సెక్షన్ 18). మనోజ్ 100 కిలోలను నీత పేరు గుర్తు పెట్టిన బస్తాల్లో ఉంచి, ఆమె అంగీకరిస్తే, ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అవుతుంది (సెక్షన్ 23(1)).

selfTest.q: 1. గుర్తించని సరుకులపై ఆస్తి హక్కు ఎప్పుడు బదిలీ అవుతుంది?
selfTest.a: అవి నిర్ధారణ అయ్యే వరకు కాదు (సెక్షన్ 18). తర్వాత అంగీకారంతో షరతు లేని కేటాయింపుపై (సెక్షన్ 23). 2. సెక్షన్ 20 ఏమి చెబుతుంది? అప్పగించదగిన స్థితిలో ఉన్న నిర్దిష్ట సరుకుల షరతు లేని ఒప్పందంలో, చెల్లింపు లేదా అప్పగింత వాయిదా పడినా, ఒప్పందం చేసినప్పుడే ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అవుతుంది. 3. అంగీకారంపై పంపిన సరుకులపై ఆస్తి హక్కు ఎప్పుడు బదిలీ అవుతుంది? కొనేవాడు ఆమోదాన్ని తెలిపినప్పుడు లేదా లావాదేవీని స్వీకరించినప్పుడు, లేదా తిరస్కరణ నోటీసు ఇవ్వకుండా నిర్ణయించిన లేదా సహేతుక సమయం ముగిసినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 24). 4. వేరుగా అంగీకరించకపోతే రిస్క్ ఎవరిది? ఆస్తి హక్కు బదిలీ అయ్యే వరకు అమ్మేవాడిది, తర్వాత అప్పగింత జరిగినా జరగకపోయినా కొనేవాడిది (సెక్షన్ 26).

hi.inOneMinute: "Property" in goods means the general property in them, not merely a special property (section 2(11)). "Delivery" means voluntary transfer of possession (section 2(2)). A seller who gives possession does not necessarily pass the property, and the Act has separate rules for when the property passes to the buyer. No property passes in unascertained goods until they are ascertained (section 18). Otherwise the property passes when the parties intend it to pass, judged from the contract, conduct and circumstances (section 19). Sections 20 to 24 give the rules for specific goods, unascertained goods and goods on approval. Section 25 allows the seller to reserve the right of disposal. Risk prima facie passes with the property (section 26).
hi.meaning: Property and possession (sections 2(2) and 2(11)) Rule. Property is the general property in the goods. Delivery is the voluntary transfer of possession. The Act treats them as different things: section 25(1) says that even after delivery to a buyer or carrier, the property does not pass until conditions imposed by the seller are fulfilled. Section 26 says the goods are at the buyer's risk once the property passes, whether delivery has been made or not. Example. Kavya hands a laptop to Lalit to try for a week. Lalit has possession. Whether the property has passed depends on the rules in section 24 and on the intention of the parties. Unascertained goods (sections 18 and 23) Rule. No property passes in unascertained goods unless and until they are ascertained (section 18). Under section 23(1), in a contract for unascertained or future goods by description, the property passes when goods of that description and in a deliverable state are unconditionally appropriated to the contract, by the seller with the buyer's assent or by the buyer with the seller's assent. Under section 23(2), delivery to the buyer or to a carrier or other bailee for transmission, without reserving the right of disposal, is deemed unconditional appropriation. Example. Manoj agrees to sell Nita 100 kg of rice out of a godown full of rice. Until the 100 kg is set apart for Nita with her assent, no property passes (section 18). When Manoj puts 100 kg in sacks marked for Nita, and she agrees, the property passes (section 23(1)). Intention of the parties (section 19) Rule. For specific or ascertained goods, the property passes when the parties intend. Regard is had to the contract's terms, the parties' conduct and the circumstances. Unless a different intention appears, sections 20 to 24 are the rules for finding that intention. Specific goods (sections 20, 21 and 22) Rule. Three rules apply to specific goods. Unconditional contract, goods in a deliverable state: the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed (section 20). Seller bound to put the goods in a deliverable state: the property does not pass until he does so and the buyer has notice (section 21). Goods in a deliverable state, but the seller must weigh, measure, test or do some other act to ascertain the price: the property does not pass until it is done and the buyer has notice (section 22). Example. Om buys a particular secondhand bike, in running order, under an unconditional contract. He will pay and collect it next week. The property passes to Om when the contract is made (section 20). Goods on approval or on sale or return (section 24) Rule. The property passes (a) when the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or does any other act adopting the transaction, or (b) if he does not, but keeps the goods without giving notice of rejection, when the fixed time for return expires, or, if no time was fixed, when a reasonable time expires. Example. A jeweller sends a necklace to Pooja on approval with no time fixed. Pooja keeps it, gives no notice of rejection, and a reasonable time passes. The property passes to her (section 24(b)). Reservation of the right of disposal (section 25) Rule. The seller may reserve the right of disposal until certain conditions are fulfilled. The property then does not pass until they are fulfilled, even if the goods are delivered to the buyer or a carrier. Where goods are shipped or delivered to a railway for carriage and the bill of lading or railway receipt makes them deliverable to the order of the seller or his agent, the seller is prima facie deemed to reserve the right (section 25(2)). If the seller sends the bill of exchange with the bill of lading or railway receipt and the buyer does not honour the bill, he must return the document, and if he wrongfully retains it the property does not pass to him (section 25(3)). Risk (section 26) Rule. Unless otherwise agreed, the goods are at the seller's risk until the property passes, and at the buyer's risk afterwards, whether or not delivery has been made. If delivery is delayed by the fault of either party, that party bears any loss which would not have occurred but for the fault. The section does not affect the duties of either as a bailee of the other's goods. When does the property pass? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Are the goods unascertained? No property passes until they are ascertained (section 18). Then it passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). 2. Are they specific or ascertained goods? The property passes when the parties intend (section 19). The rules in sections 20 to 22 help find that intention. 3. Sent on approval or sale or return? The property passes under section 24. 4. Has the seller reserved the right of disposal? The property does not pass until the conditions are fulfilled (section 25). 5. Who bears the risk? The owner of the property, unless otherwise agreed (section 26).
keyPoints: Unascertained goods: no property until ascertained (section 18). Passes on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). Specific goods: property passes when the parties intend (section 19). Section 20: unconditional contract, deliverable state, property passes when the contract is made. Sections 21 and 22: property passes after the seller's act and notice to the buyer. Section 24: approval or sale or return, property passes on adoption or on expiry of time. Section 25: the seller may reserve the right of disposal. Section 26: risk prima facie passes with the property.

selfTest.q: 1. When does property pass in unascertained goods?
selfTest.a: Not until they are ascertained (section 18). Then on unconditional appropriation with assent (section 23). 2. What is section 20? For an unconditional contract for specific goods in a deliverable state, the property passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed. 3. When does property pass in goods on approval? When the buyer signifies approval or acceptance or adopts the transaction, or when the fixed or a reasonable time expires without notice of rejection (section 24). 4. Who bears the risk unless otherwise agreed? The seller until the property passes, the buyer afterwards, whether delivery has been made or not (section 26).

Right of disposalThe right the seller may reserve under section 25(1), by the terms of the contract or appropriation, until certain conditions are fulfilled. The Act does not define itకొన్ని షరతులు నెరవేరే వరకు, ఒప్పంద నిబంధనల ద్వారా లేదా కేటాయింపు ద్వారా, సెక్షన్ 25(1) కింద అమ్మేవాడు రిజర్వ్ చేసుకోగల హక్కు. చట్టం దీన్ని నిర్వచించలేదు

law-of-contract-ii-u4-t5.subtitle: Sections 45 to 54 of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930

en.inOneMinute: A seller is an "unpaid seller" when the whole of the price has not been paid or tendered, or when a bill of exchange or other negotiable instrument received as conditional payment has been dishonoured or its condition otherwise not fulfilled (section 45). Even if the property has passed to the buyer, the unpaid seller has by implication of law a lien on the goods while in possession, a right of stopping them in transit if the buyer becomes insolvent, and a right of re-sale as limited by the Act (section 46(1)). If the property has not passed, he has a right of withholding delivery similar to and co-extensive with lien and stoppage in transit (section 46(2)). Sections 47 to 49 deal with lien, sections 50 to 52 with stoppage in transit , and sections 53 and 54 with sub-sales and re-sale.
en.meaning:
Who is an unpaid seller (section 45)

Rule. A seller is an unpaid seller if the whole of the price has not been paid or tendered, or if he received a negotiable instrument as conditional payment and the condition failed by dishonour or otherwise. Within the Chapter, "seller" includes an agent of the seller to whom the bill of lading has been endorsed, or a consignor or agent who has himself paid, or is directly responsible for, the price.

Example. Rajan sells goods to Salim for Rs 20,000. Salim gives a cheque as payment on the condition that it is honoured. The cheque is dishonoured. Rajan is an unpaid seller (section 45(1)(b)).

The unpaid seller's three rights (section 46)

Rule. Even if the property has passed, the unpaid seller has by implication of law: (a) a lien while in possession; (b) a right of stopping the goods in transit if the buyer becomes insolvent; (c) a right of re-sale as limited by the Act. If the property has not passed, he has a right of withholding delivery similar to and co-extensive with his rights of lien and stoppage in transit.

Right of lien (sections 47 to 49)

Rule. The unpaid seller in possession may retain the goods until payment or tender of the price in three cases: sold without stipulation as to credit, sold on credit but the credit term has expired, or the buyer becomes insolvent. He may exercise the lien even if he holds the goods as agent or bailee for the buyer. After part delivery he may exercise it on the remainder unless the part delivery shows an agreement to waive it (section 48). He loses it when he delivers to a carrier or other bailee for transmission without reserving the right of disposal, when the buyer or his agent lawfully obtains possession, or by waiver. Obtaining a decree for the price does not by itself end it (section 49).

Example. Tara sells a machine to Umesh with no credit term and keeps it in her godown. Umesh has not paid. Tara may retain the machine until she is paid or tendered the price (section 47(1)(a)).

Stoppage in transit (sections 50 to 52)

Rule. When the buyer becomes insolvent, the unpaid seller who has parted with possession may resume possession of the goods while they are in the course of transit, and retain them until payment or tender of the price (section 50). Goods are in transit from delivery to the carrier until the buyer or his agent takes delivery. Transit ends if the buyer obtains delivery before arrival, or if the carrier acknowledges that he holds the goods for the buyer after arrival, or if the carrier wrongfully refuses to deliver to the buyer. Rejection by the buyer does not end transit if the carrier still holds the goods (section 51). The seller exercises the right by taking actual possession or by notice to the carrier or bailee. The carrier then re-delivers to the seller or as he directs, at the seller's expense (section 52).

Example. Vimla sends goods to Waqar by rail. Before they arrive, she learns Waqar is insolvent. She gives notice to the railway. Because the goods are in transit, she may stop them and retain them until she is paid (sections 50 and 52).

Effect of a sub-sale or pledge by the buyer (section 53)

Rule. The seller's right of lien or stoppage is not affected by the buyer's sale or other disposition unless the seller assented to it. But if a document of title has been issued or lawfully transferred to a person as buyer or owner, and that person transfers it to someone who takes in good faith and for consideration, then a transfer by sale defeats the seller's right, and a transfer by pledge or other disposition for value allows it to be exercised only subject to the transferee's rights. Where the transfer is a pledge, the seller may require the pledgee to satisfy the debt first, as far as possible, out of the buyer's other goods or securities in his hands (section 53(2)).

Re-sale (section 54)

Rule. Lien or stoppage does not by itself rescind the contract of sale (section 54(1)). The unpaid seller may re-sell in two cases, and the effect differs.

Perishable goods, or notice to the buyer of intention to re-sell followed by the buyer's failure to pay or tender within a reasonable time: the seller may re-sell within a reasonable time and recover damages for loss. The buyer is not entitled to any profit. Without that notice, the seller cannot recover damages and the buyer is entitled to any profit (section 54(2)). On re-sale after exercising lien or stoppage, the new buyer gets a good title against the original buyer, even without notice to the original buyer (section 54(3)). Where the seller expressly reserved a right of re-sale on default and re-sells on default, the original contract is rescinded without prejudice to a claim for damages (section 54(4)).

Which right does the unpaid seller use? How to read this: start at the top. 1. Is he an unpaid seller (section 45)? If not, none of these rights arises. 2. Is he still in possession of the goods? He has a lien (sections 46(1)(a), 47) if the goods were sold without credit stipulation, the credit has expired, or the buyer is insolvent. 3. Has he parted with possession, and is the buyer insolvent, with the goods in transit? He may stop them in transit (sections 50 to 52). 4. Has the buyer failed to pay after notice of re-sale, or are the goods perishable? He may re-sell and claim damages (section 54).
keyPoints: Unpaid seller: price not paid or tendered, or conditional payment instrument dishonoured (section 45). Rights even after the property passes: lien, stoppage in transit, re-sale (section 46(1)). If the property has not passed: right of withholding delivery (section 46(2)). Lien: seller in possession, no credit stipulated, credit expired, or buyer insolvent (section 47). Lien lost: delivery to a carrier without reserving disposal, buyer lawfully takes possession, waiver (section 49). Stoppage: buyer insolvent, seller out of possession, goods in transit (section 50). Good-faith transferee of a document of title for consideration defeats the seller's right on a sale (section 53 proviso). Re-sale: notice and reasonable time (section 54(2)). New buyer gets a good title (section 54(3)).
